Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī; once Jālandhara himself, the lord of Vṛndā, arrived together with the asuras for the purpose of worshipping Śukra.
On the full moon day of the month of Āṣāḍha, all the Daityas and Dānavas, as well as Rāhu, Ketu, and others, arrived there for the purpose of worship.
Śukrācārya was honored and saluted by those devoted ones.
Having bestowed his words of blessing upon them, he inquired after their welfare and other matters.
(3) Having been offered seats, they all sat down in the assembly where the sacrifice was being performed;
Jalandhara, exceedingly delighted, beheld Rāhu devoid of his head. (4)
There, the son of the Ocean (Lakṣmaṇa) asked Bhārgava with wonder:
"By whom was this head of Rāhu severed? Tell me, how and when?
Having heard this and remembered Śiva, Śukrācārya spoke to him.
Prahlāda was the son of Hiraṇyakaśipu, and his son was Virocana.
His son was King Bali, possessed of great strength,
who rules the kingdom of Rasātala as a sovereign lord of devotees.
All the gods, including Indra, know that the powerful armies of the Asuras remain under his control. Then,
on one occasion, Durvāsas descended from Vaikuṇṭha.
Holding in his hand a flower garland given by Nārāyaṇa,
Bhuvaṃ beheld Indra sporting with an elephant on the path of the sky.
Then, recognizing the lord of the gods, the sage gave the garland to Indra.
As if counting the garland, Vāsava held it in his hand;
the elephant then placed it upon its frontal globe with its trunk-staff.
Having grasped it and placed it in a leaf-cup, he crushed it at that very moment.
Durvāsas, overcome with anger, uttered a curse to humble his pride:
"O Indra, let there be the destruction of Lakṣmī; let this be the fruit for you of destroying the garland!
As soon as he had spoken thus, Indra fell from the back of his elephant to the surface of the earth.
All Lakṣmī was destroyed and entered into the ocean;
for a period of a thousand years, the deities and others were devoid of fortune.
All those gods, suffering in misery, went to the Lord of Ramā (Viṣṇu) for refuge.
"Without Lakṣmī we are miserable," thinking thus, those who were devoted to their own interests [acted].
Then, for the sake of accomplishing their own purpose, those heroes—who were devoted to the practice of deceit—made peace with the asuras by following the path shown by Viṣṇu. (15, 36)
The gods, with Viṣṇu as their ally, united indeed with the Asuras;
for the sake of Lakṣmī and for the sake of the nectar and other treasures, they performed the churning of the ocean.
All those jewels which belonged to your father, those the gods [seized].

The arrogant ones seized it with effort, and they even drank the nectar by means of a stratagem. Having consumed the nectar, the gods became exceedingly proud, being nourished by Viṣṇu and endowed with the power of immortality acquired from drinking the nectar.
From that time forth, the gods constantly caused suffering to the Daityas and others;
the defeat of the Asuras occurred perpetually and in every way.
Then Rāhu, assuming the form of a god, came for the sake of drinking that nectar.
Having entered between the sun and the moon, he was surrounded by ambrosia;
as soon as Viṣṇu began to drink it, [the two] informed him,
and Viṣṇu instantly slew him with the edge of his discus.
A mere mouthful of nectar became stuck in his throat;
because of that, this Rāhu did not die, even though he was severed in two at the neck.
Two [heads] were born, yet here Rāhu remains as a headless trunk (kabandha) that lives on.
"His head, including his topknot, shall remain as a banner even while he lives.
Thus were the Daityas and Dānavas defeated by Viṣṇu;
and your father was completely stripped of his jewels after they had been taken away.
Thus [Śukra] related the severing of Rāhu’s head, the churning,
the seizure of the jewels by the gods, and the defeat of the Daityas.
Having heard that, the mighty and powerful Jalandhara [spoke].
Hearing of the assault upon his father, his eyes reddened with rage and he became incensed.
Summoning the messenger named Ghasmara at that very moment, he informed him of the matter; then, after honoring him and granting him immunity, he dispatched him as an instructor.
"O Ghasmara, go and inform the Lord of the Gods of my message:
'Either take refuge, or remain firm for the sake of battle.
Furthermore, report the other matters as well, such as the previous assault upon my father."
"Jalandhara cannot endure this; he desires the cleansing of our enmity.
Having taken up these and other such words, the gluttonous one departed quickly.
From his own group, the gluttonous one reported all the speech of the Lord of the Gods.
Jalandhara is a great hero, the lord of the Daityas, and the son of the Ocean;
I am his messenger, a gluttonous servant acting under his command. Sent by that hero, I have come into your presence.
Listen to what King Śatrujit, whose commands are unimpeded, has said:
"Why did you churn my father, the ocean, with Mount Mandara, and why did you carry off all the jewels belonging to my father? (33–34)
"Accept me as your refuge and grant me the jewels;
otherwise, fear will come upon you and the destruction of your kingdom will occur.
Having heard these words of the messenger, the Lord of the Celestials spoke.
"The mountains that were shattered by me have been protected in your father's womb.
Tell me, how can others who are my enemies also be protected within it? Having become my foremost enemy, no one shall remain there as a traitor. (36–37)
The jewels previously stolen I shall now take away from his very life. How did your father protect my enemy, Śaṅkhāsura—that very Śaṅkha whom my younger brother, the imperishable Viṣṇu, slew? (38)
"Go, messenger, and speak to Jālandhara regarding the cause of the churning:
'Mahendra indeed does not punish anyone who is innocent;
since you are innocent, why do you harbor this new hatred toward me?'"

"I shall grant you the fruit [of your labor] quickly; be prepared, O Lord of Asuras! Having been addressed thus, that voracious one indeed went swiftly to where Jalandhara was in the ocean, and there he announced this.
Having heard the words spoken by Indra, his eyes copper-red with rage,
he surveyed the gods and made an effort to conquer them with the Asuras.
From all directions, the Asuras, Daityas, and Dānavas assembled.
Numbering in the millions, billions, and trillions, they ascended to heaven with a desire for victory.
Having appointed the two named Śumbha and Niśumbha as commanders of their army,
Jalandhara, the son of the Ocean, himself set forth as a hero.
Standing in the Nandana grove, he reached the celestial realm and blew his conch for battle.
The heroic Daityas roared as they surrounded the city of Amarāvatī;
and Indra, having learned of this, also prepared for war with the best of the gods clad in armor.
Accompanied by his city, he indeed set forth with crores upon crores of warriors;
a battle then took place between those two, the armies of the gods and the asuras, fought with arrows, missiles, mantras, illusions, and sorcery. || 47 ||
With stones, mountains, trees, and meteors, as well as with lotuses;
with thunderbolts, discuses, *śataghnīs*, iron arrows, javelins, and trunks of trees;
with clubs, iron bars, fragments, swords, spears, and *śaktis*. (48–49)
With maces, axes, elephants, chariots, hands, with grappling-hooks, fists, arms, elbows, and so forth,
those two armies struck one another; the carnage was beyond counting.
Rivers of blood arose upon the earth, bearing waves that reached the horizon;
with elephants, horses, and foot-soldiers fallen and falling,
the ground in battle shone like a mass of clouds at twilight.
Śukra indeed restored to life the Daityas, Dānavas, elephants, and horses that had repeatedly died in battle by means of the Saṃjīvinī mantra and consecrated waters; likewise,
Bṛhaspati restored even the gods there who had died.
Seeing the gods repeatedly raised from death by various divine herbs brought from Mount Droṇa, Jālandhara, filled with extreme rage,
said to Śukra: "How is it that these deities, once dead, come back to life?"
"I believe that the *sañjīvinī* lore has reached even the gods through you.
Having heard this, Śukra spoke with great certainty regarding Jalandhara:
"The *sañjīvinī* lore has not yet reached the gods even today."
However, Bṛhaspati brings medicinal herbs from Mount Droṇa and quickly restores the gods to life; therefore, bring Mount Droṇa here.
Either bring it under your control, or else cause it to enter within the ocean.
"If liquor is not obtained, they will perish and shall certainly not live again;
if this is done, your victory will be certain, otherwise it will not.
Having heard this, Jalandhara went and quickly uprooted a mountain.
Having brought Mount Droṇa, he cast it into the midst of the ocean.
Then Jalandhara, filled with joy, struck the gods with his weapons.
Bṛhaspati [went] for the sake of medicinal herbs in order to revive the slain gods.
He went to the land of Droṇa, but there he did not see the mountain. Despairing and realizing through his intellect that the mountain had been seized by the Daityas,
he approached the gods and said, "O gods, flee from here!"
"Either Mount Droṇa has been destroyed by Jalandhara or carried away elsewhere.
For this Daitya, born of Rudra, cannot be conquered at present.
Flee, flee! To that place where those who have died have gone! (63–64)
"I shall somehow restore those who have died by means of the remaining leaves," he said;
and having been told this, all the gods abandoned the battle and fled.
Seeing the gods in flight, the Daityas, accompanied by Jalandhara, [pursued them].
They entered Amarāvatī to the sounds of conchs, kettledrums, and cries of victory.
Out of fear, the gods and goddesses abandoned heaven and dwelt upon Mount Meru,
taking refuge in its caves to protect themselves from the enemy.
Then the extremely wicked Daitya Jalandhara, out of great envy,
consecrated the Daityas in the vacant positions of the gods.
Having brought the kingdom of heaven under his control, he went to the forests of Mount Meru.
Accompanied by the army of the Daityas for the purpose of destroying the gods,
all the deities became terrified; leaving even their mountain caves,
they went toward Brahmā in distress, though uninvited.
At that time, even there, the gods saw that place empty;
having seen the kingdom of the Daityas even in Satyaloka, they fled.
They went to Vaikuṇṭha, a region situated within the coverings of water and fire.
The gods and goddesses departed, and Brahmā was also seen there.
Those lords of creatures praised Hari, Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa:
"O protector of the gods, O peaceful-souled one, O destroyer of the Daityas, salutations to you!"
Salutations to you, O Viṣṇu, who took the form of a fish and brought forth the Vedas;
salutations to you in the form of a tortoise, who supported the mountain during the churning for nectar.
Salutations again and again to you in the form of a boar, who bore the earth upon your tusk.
Salutations to You who deceived Bali by assuming the form of a Brahmin dwarf; salutations to You.
(75) Salutations to Paraśurāma, the destroyer of the wicked kṣatriyas;
salutations to You, Rāmacandra, the swift bringer of Rāvaṇa’s end. (76)
Salutations to the Lord of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, Rādhā, and Ramā;
salutations to You who are the very embodiment of the Buddha and who cause delusion among the Daityas;
salutations to You in the form of Kapila, the bestower of the knowledge of reality.
Salutations to You, the Creator, who is the very embodiment of the swan and the bestower of knowledge.
Salutations to You, who are the embodiment of Vedavyāsa and the source from which all learning flows.
Salutations to You in the form of Kalki, the destroyer of the evils of the Kali age.
Salutations to the Lord of Pārvatī, Prabhā, and Māṇikī;
salutations to the noble son of Kaṃbharā, the Son of Gopāla.
Salutations to the one worthy of refuge, the protector of the gods, and the possessor of knowledge.
Salutations to Kṛṣṇa, who possesses a beautiful form and is dear to you;
salutations to you, the teacher of knowledge, the divine, and the protector of servants.
Salutations again and again to the protector of devotees and others who are afflicted by the Daityas.
Salutations to You, the All-Eyed One, who dwells in the heart, the Lord of Ramā;
salutations to the one whose emblems are the banner, the lotus, the goad, the thunderbolt, and the barley-corn.
Salutations to the one who bears the svastika, the jāmbavaṣṭa, the eight-pointed star, and the upward-pointing line.
Salutation to the one who bears the bow, the triangle, the jar, and the crescent moon.
Salutation to the one who bears the cow’s footprint, the sky, the fish, and so forth; salutation to the one on the footstool.
In the right hand are the banner, the wheel, the bow, the trident, and the svastika.
Salutations again and again to Him who has lines on His hands like those of a fish and a staff;
salutations to that Kṛṣṇa whose five parts— the arms, the eyes, the knees, the nose, and the space between the breasts— are long.
Salutations to the one who possesses beautiful hips, back, neck, and shanks.
Salutations to the bearer of fine hair, finger-joints, teeth, and bones.
[Salutations to] the armpits, the belly, the chest, the nose, the shoulders, and the forehead.
Salutations to that Śrī Hari, whose six parts are elevated:
the corners of the eyes, the nails, the palate, the tongue, the lips, and the soles of the feet.
And salutations to Him whose palms are red.
Salutations to You whose chest, head, and forehead are broad;
salutations to You whose voice, disposition, and navel are deep;
salutations again and again to You who bear the mark of Lakṣmī upon Your left thigh.
Salutations to You, Kṛṣṇa, whose chest possesses a clockwise curl;
salutations to You, endowed with a navel resplendent with three folds.
Salutations to You, whose form is cool and radiant, the bestower of nectar.
Salutations to You, the Imperishable, whose name is Unmanifest, the Goloka;
salutations to You, the Vaikuṇṭha, the Lord of Badarī, the Śvetadvīpa;
salutations to You, the Abode of Milk, the Life-force, and the Source of Life.
Salutations again and again to the Self, to that very Self, to the Self of all;
salutations to You who abide in fire, who abide in the sun, and who abide in gold. Salutations to the abode of gods and asuras, to the remover of the suffering of devotees.
Salutations to you who are without faction, who are beyond opposition, and who favor those devoted to you.
O Blessed One, salutations to you, the abode of sacred narratives and the abode of all news; salutations again and again to you, the Brahman who is the dwelling place of all knowledge.

O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, protect us who have come to you for refuge! Since Jalandhara has indeed driven the gods from heaven and brought it under his own control, O Lord, how can you endure this?
The sun, the moon, fire, Śeṣa, and Dharma have been cast down.
We have come to you for refuge; let his slaughter be considered.
O Lord, we wander through the forest regions like wretched creatures. (1.325.100)
Having praised him thus, Indra and the other gods then desisted;
Kṛṣṇa, the ocean of compassion, spoke these fearless words:
"O gods, cast away your fear; I shall go to that Jalandhara."
"Today I shall destroy that supreme enemy who causes such great suffering to the gods.
Having uttered this, he rose up and, while still mounted upon Garuḍa,
he urged his vehicle forward just as he spoke.
Distressed at the thought that her brother’s death was certain to occur, Lakṣmī,
with tears in her eyes and palms joined in reverence, spoke to Hari, her beloved:
"O treasure-house of compassion, how can my brother, who is your sister's husband, be put to death?"
"If I am dear to you, O Lord, do not bring about his destruction.
Viṣṇu replied: "Indeed, for the sake of protecting the lords of the gods, I must go there by all means; however, I shall not kill your younger brother."
"O beloved, because he is a portion of Rudra and by the word of Brahmā—and not by my own word—your brother must not be killed; do not despair, my dear.
Having spoken thus and consoled her, she went to where Jalandhara was.
Having led the gods and others along with him, the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa [acted].

(108) Thus, in the first section, the *Kṛtayugasantāna*, within the narrative of Jalandhara and Vṛndā in the *Śrīlakṣmīnārāyaṇīyasahitā*, titled "The Description of the Praise of Viṣṇu of Vaikuṇṭha and Other Matters Following the Battle between Gods and Asuras Waged by Jalandhara, After the Gods Were Defeated, Upon Seeing Rāhu Headless Among the Asura Hosts Worshipping Śukrācārya on the Full Moon Day of Āṣāḍha, and Having Discerned the Cause of That—His Partiality for the Drinking of Nectar from the Churning of the Ocean": [End of Chapter]
Chapter Three Hundred and Twenty-Five:
325. *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga).
Chapter 326.
[The Author: Chapter 327.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O Nārāyaṇa, O Hari, O Viṣṇu, my brother has given that reply.
"Having seen Viṣṇu, tell me what was done by Viṣṇu and what was done by me.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
"Listen, O Lakṣmī! Father, daughter, and likewise son—"
All things are indeed fickle and restless; what, then, cannot happen therein?
(2) Having seen Viṣṇu, he became exceedingly enraged, filled with pride in his own strength.
Beholding the divine army prepared for battle, he blazed with intense fury. (3)
Jalandhara commanded the Daityas for the sake of battle:
"O all you foremost Daityas, go forth with great weapons to wage an insurmountable war against the immortals! || 4 ||
Then the Great Destroyer acted so that the gods would not return;
at that time, there were Mauryas numbering in the hundreds of thousands, Dhaumras numbering in the hundreds, Asuras numbering in the tens of millions, and Kālakeyas numbering in the tens of millions.
Kaṅkālakṣas, as well as those protected by Śumbha and Niśumbha,
and the great Daityas Tālajaṅghas, went forth there by the tens of millions;
and Rākṣasas and Dānavas also marched out with foot-soldiers numbering in the crores and billions.
Having formed an alliance, they then arrived, resolved upon the destruction of the gods.
At that time, the battle-flags were seen in the sky like eyes;
and the kettledrums and war-trumpets indeed sounded, portending fear.
By the command of Jalandhara, the Daityas fought with the gods from afar using missiles, arrows, *bhūśuṇḍīs*, and *śataghnīs*; then, rushing forward,
they approached with maces, spears, and javelins.
With spears, axes, swords, and maces;
with trees, mountains, thunderbolts, and likewise with javelins; and with iron arrows, crescent-headed shafts, and barbed missiles, they struck one another.
Those hosts of Daityas struck back, and the deities also fought with their discuses;
those great heroes battled while uttering roars like lions.
Some were slain by arrows, and others were killed or wounded by javelins.
Some were slain with axes and spears within the forest of battle.
Seeing that great slaughter of the Daityas, Jalandhara, having made the peak of the battlefield resound, himself cried out with force. (14–15)
Having rendered the Dānavas powerful, he descended to the forefront of the battle;
consequently, the Daityas of great heroism then became highly emboldened.
And, becoming exceedingly fierce and blind, they rushed together in the fray.
"May the deities slay them, cut them, and divide them in two;
may they crush them, trample them, and grind them like sesame seeds!
May they not retreat from the battle, but perform the oblation for their own selves. (17–18)
"The sacrifice of battle for heroes indeed never returns nor can it be regained;
let the gods drink the blood, and let their beloveds enjoy it thereafter!"—
such was the great outcry at that time within the host of the Daityas.

The blows dealt by the Daityas were indeed powerful and capable of destroying the gods. At that time, no blow was seen that did not result in the destruction of a god; wherever such a blow was seen, there the deities were seen struck down.
At that moment, a great terror arose within the heart of Viṣṇu for an instant;
even Vāsava fled, and the remaining gods likewise fled.
Seeing them intent on flight, Viṣṇu entered among them.
Having rendered the remaining gods entirely powerless,
Hari, mounted upon Garuḍa, repeatedly challenged them for battle, saying:
"I shall restore all the gods to life, but I shall destroy the Dānavas."
"Let them not flee from the battle; I shall fight, standing at the forefront!
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu then, from his own Sudarśana discus, instantly created hundreds of thousands of Sudarśanas.
He urged those very [weapons] to slay the Dānava army.
And having created hundreds of thousands of fires, he urged them against the Asura host;
Hari, too, dispatched the Sudarśana [discus] to destroy the army.

The gods reduced the asuras to ashes with their fire-wheels, just as one might burn them to cinders; having witnessed this, the gods—extremely bold, fierce, and desiring victory—called out to those who were fleeing and struck them down. (28)
Viṣṇu, having sprinkled them with water, likewise raised the dead back to life.
Then those [revived ones] struck the Dānavas with swift weapons and missiles. Viṣṇu saw that everywhere the Dānavas had fallen into a state of terror.
Then, like a forest, they were seen cut down, destroyed, and mangled;
the survivors fled from heaven, abandoning the field of battle.
Thus, a great defeat befell the asuras there.
Unable to endure the fear that the ocean-born [god] inspired in the hosts of gods,
he advanced to fight Śukra, pointing him out as the life-giver of the Asuras.
And Śukra quickly revived the Daityas who had been consumed by his [Agni’s] fiery knowledge.
Jalandhara let out a great roar that pierced the ears;
by that terrifying sound, the entire world was then filled.
And by the roar of Viṣṇu as well, the whole world trembled.
Taking up their bows, which produced a twanging sound, the two fought—
one the husband of his sister and the other his enemy— both moving as adversaries. At that time, they made the sky appear to have no space at all with their arrows.
Viṣṇu cut down the asura’s banner, umbrella, bow, and arrows with his shafts,
and struck him firmly in the heart with an arrow.
At that moment, the lord of the Daityas, mace in hand, leaped up toward Hari.
Running with his feet, he struck Garuḍa on the head with force out of rage;
he then violently struck Viṣṇu in the heart with a spear.
Viṣṇu, for his part, cut the mace and the spear with his sharp sword.
Then the Daitya, having again taken up another bow equipped with arrows,
struck Viṣṇu in the heart and indeed cut off his sword as well.
Viṣṇu, having severed that approaching arrow with half of his sword—
Quickly taking up the Śārṅga bow, he discharged a formidable arrow.
The powerful Daitya, his lower lip bitten in rage, warded off that arrow with Sītā and severed the Vaiṣṇava bow, the Śārṅga, with another shaft.
Furthermore, he struck Viṣṇu in the chest with exceedingly sharp arrows.
His bow being severed, Hari indeed hurled the Kaumodakī mace;
it was as irresistible as lightning, and Sāmudra likewise possessed such strength.
Even while being struck by the mace, he did not waver in the least.
The Daitya hurled a trident emitting showers of fire at Hari;
Hari cut that trident apart with his sword Nandaka.
Then the Daitya, seizing the thunderbolt-born spear named Lambā, which was one yojana in length,
possessed eight edges, adorned with a thousand bells, and capable of destroying mountains and other things,
hurled it at Hari for his destruction.
A great and terrifying cry of "Alas! Alas! arose among the gods.
That final thunderbolt of the Daitya had taken the form of a spear.
[He thought: "If I do not destroy it, he will certainly not engage in battle."
"Therefore, having seized him with the beak of Garuḍa and brought him under my control,
I shall grant him victory so that there may be battle once again.
Having reflected thus, Hari indeed grasped her with the beak of the bird.
As she was coming, protected by a single feather from her own wing,
the asura beheld a great marvel; descending from the sky, he struck Viṣṇu, who had alighted on his chest, with a firm fist.
Just as [the Daitya] had struck Garuḍa’s neck with his foot-lash,
Viṣṇu then seized the Daitya firmly by the head,
while Garuḍa held the Daitya by the feet with his beak.
Having been lifted up, he was thrown and fell indeed a hundred yojanas away.
Rising once more, the ocean-born one returned by way of the sky;
at that moment, Viṣṇu, exceedingly enraged, struck him again in the heart.
And he struck Viṣṇu repeatedly in the chest with his fist;
right there upon Garuḍa, those two of great strength fought with their arms,
fists, and knees, as they were intent on death.
Having disregarded death, the powerful Daitya fought.
"Whether I must die or whether I shall conquer, in either case there is indeed gain for me.
For where is death at the hands of Viṣṇu, and where is the state of being a conqueror of Viṣṇu? (56–57)
"Great is the gain for both of us; let whatever is destined to be, surely come to pass.
Having reflected thus upon his intention and likewise upon the death ordained by Śambhu, the Blessed One laughed and said: "Blessed are you, O you who are fierce in battle!"
"Even before me, who am indestructible, you have come to your destruction like a moth [into a flame].
O son of Śaṅkara, you who have arrived at the forefront of battle having surrendered your life and your vital breaths, thus fulfilling the duty of a warrior."
"You are not at all afraid of my weapons, by which many heroes have been slain;
indeed, no hero like you has ever been seen who engages in combat by seizing the enemy by the throat.
Choose a boon, O Lord of Daityas; I am pleased with your prowess."

"Even that which is not to be given must be given by you on the field of battle to one such as yourself. O Lakṣmī! Having recognized the condition of the suitor, the intelligent Jalandhara replied to Hari, bringing the Lord under his own control: 62–63. "If you are pleased, O Blessed One! If you grant a boon, then dwell with my sister, together with me and your retinue, in my own home.
Having heard that, the Blessed One indeed said to him, "So be it."
Then the Lord, accompanied by Lakṣmī and her retinue,
went to Jalandhara’s residence; honored by Jalandhara,
he dwelt there at his word, bound and awaiting his future destruction.
Jalandhara established the city of Jālandhara upon the earth,
and he held extensive sovereignty over the world as far as the ocean's edge.
All the Dānavas were appointed as officials in heaven and other realms.
The Daityas themselves were appointed to positions of authority in Pātāla and other realms.
He dwelt in the middle island between the western ocean and the earth;
whatever jewel was gathered among the gods, Gandharvas, and Siddhas, [all that he possessed].
Having brought all that under his own control, he enjoyed the earth free from thorns;
having made the lords of the gods, gandharvas, siddhas, serpents, rākṣasas,
and men his own citizens within his own continent, he ruled over the three worlds.
Hari restored to life all those gods who had died in battle;
and Śukra restored to life all those Daityas who had been slain.
The gods returned once more to Meru and other forests, just as before.
Not even a small fruit was obtained; it was like the threshing of husks.
The news spread throughout all the worlds that Viṣṇu had been defeated.
One who is self-controlled becomes subject only to devotion, and not by any other means.
He was captivated by Lakṣmī and by his affection for his sister's husband;
abandoning the work of the gods, he took refuge in the house of his sister's husband.
The gods became destitute and sorrowful, being without a protector or a refuge.
The goddesses, too, having fallen into misery and being greatly oppressed by the asuras, thought:
"What should be done? Where should we go? Viṣṇu has resorted to the Vṛndā creeper.
Now, may the destruction of the Daityas indeed occur quickly."
From the Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, who resides within the inner self,
there arose the gods and goddesses who were the citizens of the island of Jālandhara;
they and others became such that no one could recognize them as demons.
Having deliberated thus, those excellent ones went into the presence of Śaṅkara and praised Śaṅkara for the cessation of their own suffering.
Then Mahādeva, having summoned Nārada, who was intent on performing what was beneficial—
Desiring to accomplish the work of the gods, he dispatched him to that city.
Nārada also then departed quickly for the city of Jālandhara;
having first met with the gods and learned of their distress, he returned once more.
Having accepted the worship performed by the gods and the hospitable reception of guests,
and having heard about the emergence of the Sun, Moon, Dharma, and Fire,
as well as Viṣṇu’s defeat and the wickedness of Jalandhara; ||| 82 ||
Having consoled the gods and informed them for the sake of accomplishing their task,
and having declared, "I shall indeed perform the work of the gods according to my wisdom," the sage himself bowed to the gods and went to the assembly hall of Jalandhara.
Having bowed to the arrived sage, Jalandhara offered him a seat;
and having worshipped him according to the prescribed rites, the Daitya smiled and said to Nārada:
"Is all well with you, O best of sages? From where have you come here?"
"Tell me the purpose for which you have come here; I shall accomplish it.
Having heard this, Nārada, with a gracious soul, spoke to the Asura:
"Blessed are you, O powerful king; you now abide as a lord of kings."
I heard in heaven that you were an enjoyer of the luster of all jewels,
and subsequently I heard of the most excellent enjoyments of Śaṅkara in the great forest of wish-fulfilling trees, extending for ten thousand yojanas.
It was filled with hundreds of wish-fulfilling cows (kāmadhenus), brilliantly illuminated by thought-gems (cintāmaṇis),
entirely made of gold, divine, and adorned with wonderful beauty on all sides;
it was attended by vehicles, mounts, male servants, and female servants.
There, upon the peak of Kailāsa, I beheld Śaṅkara—
fair-complexioned, beautiful in every limb, three-eyed, and moon-crested—
well-served by young women who were slightly less than sixteen years of age.
On that mountain, Śiva rejoices with many beautiful women who are like moon-balls or who have emerged from the golden sun. Then, without further reflection, he heard of the bliss of Jālandhara.
"What might such prosperity be like, or perhaps it is not even like this?"—
having reflected thus with wonder, I have come to your home.
Desiring to behold that [prosperity], I have arrived here in your presence.
"There is an island for you, O fortunate one, adorned with gardens and groves;
it is surrounded by a moat and is beautiful to behold.
When he had spoken thus, the Daitya showed it to him in every respect. (95–96)
Having observed that prosperity which was established within the house, outside the house, and in the depths [of the heart],
the king of sages, having reflected, spoke— acting for the sake of Devala’s gain—
in such a way that delusion might enter the Daitya through the instigation of Viṣṇu.
"O Jalandhara, there is no end to your prosperity!
It would not be surprising at all if such things were found in the house of the Lord of the Three Worlds: these wonderful palaces, vehicles, and mounts. (98–99)
Utensils, jeweled offerings, treasuries of gems,
pearls, diamonds, gold, and lands by the hundreds—
elephants, horses, and so forth— these do not exist elsewhere as they do here.
Here [are found] Airāvata, the elephant of Indra; Ucchaiḥśravas, the horse of the Sun;
the Kalpa-mandāra trees; the treasures (nidhis) of Kubera; the swan-vehicle of Brahmā; and also Garuḍa, the vehicle of Viṣṇu. (10.1–2)
The buffalo of Yama, as well as the Sudarśana of Viṣṇu;
the jewel of King Śeṣa, and likewise the nectar of the Moon;
the umbrellas of the Manvantaras, and likewise their golden staffs.
The yak-tail whisks of the world-protectors and the bracelets of the goddesses—
all such jewels shine within your home. Indeed,
you possess the preeminence over both noble women and handmaidens.

But not even a single jewel of a wife shone for them in such a way as this one who stands before Śaṅkara; indeed, you are deficient by that much. [106] Truly, with a most excellent jewel of a wife, resembling the sun and the moon—
The palaces of the king do not shine with such splendor through their riches [as they do now].
(107) The royal residence does not shine with hundreds of thousands of Kirāta women as it does when you, of celestial fame, are present; indeed, no wife of yours is like you. (108)
Or rather, what is the use of beautiful slave-girls if one’s fame has not been spread through marriage?
Without a white-complexioned wife, everything is like the palace of a jackal-king.
Indeed, without a wedded wife, a king can never possess true splendor anywhere.

The queen shall be the mother of the kingdom, divine and the increaser of the lineage. (1.326.110) For the prince is not considered [the son] of the king among hundreds of thousands of slave-girls; even those born of slave-girls by the hundreds are not deemed worthy of consecration. (111)
"Therefore, you ought certainly to bring that maiden, a jewel among women.
I shall go to those worlds where jewels are gathered.
Upon hearing this, the exceedingly arrogant Jalandhara spoke to the celestial sage:
O divine sage, just as I possess the preeminence among all jewels,
so too shall there be something most excellent and supreme throughout the fourteen worlds; if such a thing is known to exist, show it to me according to my wish.
By you have been seen everywhere women, queens, and maidens—the daughters of the Vedhas, the Śaṅkaras, and the Viṣṇus;
as well as the daughters of the Ṛṣis, the Pitṛs, and the gods. (115)
O Sage, you have seen everywhere all the maidens of humans, nāgas, daityas, dānavas, and rākṣasas,
who possess supreme beauty, form, youth, and excellent qualities. (116–117)
Show me that jewel where it dwells;
I shall take it to my assembly of queens from the fourteen worlds, so that its form may be revealed as a wife, blazing with great splendor like the sun. (118)
"O learned one, show me such a woman as that no other may be her equal, much less superior;
for before her, all other queens will appear in every respect like mere moths. (1.326.120)
"If there should exist such a jewel among maidens, I shall carry her away.
Upon hearing this, Nārada said: "Indeed, such a one exists;
there is but a single supreme jewel among maidens here in this entire universe. (121)
Since the day that beauty—the very fuel of all women—was reduced to ashes before my eyes, from that day forth I have striven again to attain it; having gone there, I find no restful sleep. (122–123)
In her heart, in the movement of her eyes, in sleep as well as in waking,
and even upon her head, that maiden delights, having come to his memory.
What is her beauty, what is her form, and what is her youth like?
That brilliance which exists even at the tips of her nails, by which the moon appears blackened;
that [brilliance] which is in the two regions of her face and likewise upon her cheeks—were four suns fashioned here for this purpose, or how else could they be so? (125–126)
How slender was her waist, and how much was that region of desire?
How large were her two breasts, so rich with burgeoning emotion, and how much space did they occupy?
Indeed, do lightning vines dwell here and there within them? || 127 ||
"O King, that which cannot be obtained by me—how can it be obtained by you?
Nevertheless, exert yourself; you shall obtain it, for victory is yours.
Whether it is to be attained or even to be died for, make the effort with this resolve. (128–129)
Otherwise, that task could not have been accomplished; for what is impossible for the brave?
Today it remains on Mount Kailāsa, held in the palm of Śambhu’s hand by that yogi, who has assumed the form of Śambhu’s consort.
But Śambhu remained a yogi; he stayed steadfastly in meditative absorption (samādhi).
Reflecting upon her as a maiden, he did not touch that woman; by means of his yogic powers, he protected her in every way from that most wonderful [temptation]. (131–132)
I truly believe that there is no one in the three worlds equal to Śambhu in the matter of the jewel of a wife, since I have seen this with my own eyes:
it was by the sight of her feet that Brahmā indeed discharged his seed. (133)
Even Kāma, upon merely beholding her, was infatuated and reduced to ashes.
Having obtained that jewel which remains unscarred, you shall indeed achieve your purpose here;
otherwise, abandon your life-breaths and resort to the next world.
Having spoken thus, Nārada, who is honored by the gods and acts for the welfare of the gods,
departed after informing the deities about the portion [of the sacrifice] that would destroy the Daityas.
The gods, being well-pleased, went to Viṣṇu along with that Nārada.
Having bowed, he related all of that and went to his own true abode.

(1.37) Thus, in the first book of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, within the lineage of the Kṛta-yuga, in the narrative of Jalandhara and Vṛndā, [described are] the battle between the armies of the asuras and the suras; the resuscitation of the asuras and suras who had died; the battle between Jalandhara and Viṣṇu; the granting of a boon consisting of residence in Jalandhara’s home by the gratified Viṣṇu; again, the distress of the gods; their report to Śaṅkara; Nārada’s departure for Jalandhara’s house; and [the account] of bringing Pārvatī, who was of beautiful form, as a wife.
The three hundred and twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Enchantment of Jalandhara," etc., [ends].

Chapter 327.
[Author: Chapter 328.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O Great King Nārāyaṇa, [I am afflicted] by my enemy Jalandhara.
Once Nārada had departed, what was indeed done thereafter?
O Lord, O Master Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, tell me in detail:
what did the great Daitya Jalandhara do for the sake of Pārvatī?
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī! Thereafter, the Daitya made a thorough effort according to the instructions spoken by Nārada; I shall relate it to you exactly as it happened. (3)
Thinking only of that slender woman, tormented by the arrows of the bodiless god of love,
his fortune diminished and subject to time, he— his intellect lost and utterly deluded—
summoned the wise Rāhu, the son of Siṃhikā, as a messenger.
To the great Rāhu who had arrived, he said: "O accomplisher of my task!
Go to Mount Kailāsa for the sake of achieving my purpose.
There resides the yogi Śaṅkara, who does not touch even the most excellent of women."
Nārada told me that he possesses a jewel among maidens in his hand, and that this very jewel must indeed be obtained by me. Indeed, she whose name is Pārvatī must certainly be won by me.
Having gone there, you must speak with a fearless heart:
"O great yogi dwelling in the forest, what use have you for this jewel of a wife?
Give her to me, named Jalandhara; O Hara, she is the jewel of my hand."
Whatever jewels exist throughout the three worlds, all of them have been brought by me, the king, to my palace by force.
[Among them are] Airāvata, Uccaiḥśravas, the Kalpa tree, and the Pārijātaka.
The celestial chariot yoked with swans, the thunderbolt, the spear,
and the fly-whisk; the pearls, the diamonds, and the renowned parasol—
all that is indeed for my enjoyment, for I have brought it all to my home.

The treasures, the great garland, the noose, the staff, and likewise the nectar—all these are in my house, O Hara, except for the jewel of a maiden. You are a yogi; those nine maidens must not be touched by you. Let them indeed be given to me.
Having thus received the command, Rāhu went to where Śaṅkara was;
because he had been appointed as a messenger by Nandin, he was ushered into the midst of the assembly.
There he beheld Śaṅkara, whose every limb was divine and who was adorned with celestial ornaments.
He prostrated before Hara there and likewise approached his presence;
he said to Śaṅkara, "I am indeed the messenger of Jalandhara.
Sent by the Lord of the Three Worlds, I have come here to your side."
Listen to what he said concerning you, the yogin:
"O Digambara, this jewel of a maiden, lovely as gold and like a mass of moonlight, would be of no use to a yogin; give her to me. (17–18)
"I am the enjoyer of jewels; that jewel among women shall not be yours.
How can there be a jewel for one who subsists on alms? A jewel of a wife belongs only to a sovereign.
Whatever jewels exist in the three worlds have been gathered by me from every quarter. (1.9)
"And I desire this auspicious maiden; let her be given to me.
O Hara, grant me this jewel of a sister-in-law, for subjects bring happiness to a king.
Since you are contained within the three worlds, you are my very subject, O Hara."
Behold, O Lakṣmī! With his intellect destroyed, he said to his father and mother, "Give me Pārvatī. What indeed is the nature of Hari’s illusion?
In this world, those whose minds are destroyed by it truly contemplate only their mothers.
All these Jalandharas, deluded by the illusory power (māyā) of Viṣṇu, must be awakened to enlightenment.
Even though he has female servants, he still lusts after another's wife;
that Jalandhara too must be awakened, for he is consigned to the mouth of destruction.
Listen now to what happened immediately as Rāhu spoke:
a great and most terrible host arose with the sound of fierce thunderbolts;
a great being with flaming eyes emerged from the middle of his brow out of the Lord’s wrath.

With a lion’s face, a flickering tongue, and hair standing erect, the terrifying Tālajaṅgha, afflicted by hunger, rushed toward Rāhu as if to devour him; but seeing him approaching, Rāhu fled in haste. (26–27)
Nevertheless, he forcibly seized Rāhu to devour him.
Having reviled Śaṅkara, Rāhu said: "Protect me, who have sought refuge!
Save me, save me, O Lord; protect, protect me, O ocean of compassion! (28)
"This servant of yours is devouring me, a messenger who has come for refuge.
O Śaṅkara, protect me so that he may not devour me!
Do not devour me, a Brāhmaṇa; salutations to you, have mercy! (1.327.30)
Having heard these words, "O Brāhmaṇa," Śaṅkara then said to his attendant:
"O messenger, do not devour this Brāhmaṇa named Rāhu.
Hearing the messenger's words, he released that excellent meal.
He said to Śambhu, "I am hungry; my food has been taken away.
O Śambhu, hunger afflicts me; O Maheśvara, give me food.
Śiva said, "If your hunger is indeed very intense..."
"Hunger afflicts you excessively; eat your own flesh here indeed!
Eat your own hands, feet, and so forth here," by this command, that Gaṇa devoured all his own flesh produced from his own trunk.
When his head was restored and Śaṅkara became gracious, he said:
"O great devotee, observer of my commands!
I am satisfied; tell me, O terrifying one, what shall I give to you? (35–36)
"O Great Hero! I grant you the status of being worshipped alongside me, under the name Kīrtimukha. Dwell at the door of my abode!
From that time forward, he remained at the entrance of Śambhu’s temple.
He should be worshipped especially for the sake of Śambhu’s satisfaction.
(38) Then Rāhu went to where Jalandhara was stationed; he reported his own death as well as his survival. (39)
But Jalandhara, enraged upon hearing of Śiva’s actions and considering the insult to his messenger to be a great personal humiliation,
spoke to the foremost of the Daityas: "Be ready, indeed, in an instant!"

Let all the Daityas, such as Kālanemi and others, as well as those led by Śumbha and Niśumbha— those born of crores of heroic lineages, the Kaṃbuvaṃśyas, the Daurhṛdas, the Kālakeyas, and the Kālakas— come forth. (41–42)
The Mauryas, the Dhaumras, and other Dānavas and Asuras all assembled, fully prepared; taking them with him,
Jalandhara quickly set forth, surrounded by tens of millions of Daityas.
At the front, Rāhu, with his head severed, became an inauspicious omen;
Śukra, though one-eyed, also became an inauspicious omen as he moved ahead. Furthermore, Śumbha’s sword fell from his hand, serving as another ill omen. (44–45)
The sneezing of Niśumbha and others, as well as their stumbling in their gait,
and even the falling of Jalandhara’s crown from his head—
all of that became an ill omen, causing distress at the time of departure.
Inauspicious omens indicative of a great sleep also occurred.
Then the terrified gods, seeking protection, went toward Śaṅkara;
they offered hymns of praise for the destruction of the wicked and for the attainment of happiness by the deities.
O Great God, immersed in meditation! O You who abide in *samādhi*! Salutations be unto You.
Your son Jalandhara has been surrendered for destruction.
Having caused the slaughter of the gods as well as the assault upon Pārvatī, [he now stands before You].
"Having insulted you, he was then destined for destruction.
Or rather, O Lord of Compassion, was the Daitya already destined for destruction previously?
Or has it been so determined by you, the Lord of Lakṣmī?"
It is better to destroy poison before consuming it;
it is better to punish a wrongdoer before they cause joy to the wicked.
Viṣṇu dwells in his house, attended by Vṛndā.
Śaṅkara sleeps in his own abode within Brahman through his own meditative absorption.
O Lord of the world, consider what will become of Pārvatī here;
and O Śaṅkara, behold the miserable plight of the gods as well.
Brahmā does not cease from his work in the construction of the cosmic egg;
the guardians of the quarters and the protectors of the worlds have fallen under the sway of Jalandhara.
There is no protector at all, and Lakṣmī is his only assistant.
"Be our protector, for we have been displaced from our station and are of undisciplined mind. O son, slay the son of the Ocean for our protection;
he approaches, arrogant in his strength, to wage war against you. (56–57)
"You ought to slay him without delay, for he pursues contrary ends.
Distressed as you are, protect all the gods and us who have come to you for refuge.
Having heard these words of the gods, Śaṅkara called Viṣṇu to mind.
Viṣṇu arrived swiftly so that the Asura might not know.
Śambhu said to Hari: "O Viṣṇu! How was Jalandhara slain by you? And why do you still dwell in his house even now?"
Viṣṇu said: "O Mahādeva, Śrī is your brother and this one is your son;
for this reason, he has not been killed. Do not slay him, O Śaṅkara!
I have waged war with him in every way, seeking to seize his very life."
Restrained by Lakṣmī, I did not kill him at all.
O Śambhu, he was indeed not killed out of respect for you;
moreover, by your boon, I am established in my own abode and no longer dwell upon the wings [of mountains].
His wife is the highly fortunate Vṛndā, a resident of Kṛṣṇa’s Goloka; she is rich in virtue, a chaste woman, and ever devoted to her husband.
It is by her power that this Daitya dies, and not otherwise—this is indeed my word.
And it was out of a desire to know the cause that I took up residence in his house.
O Śambhu, that powerful cause has now been fully understood by me;
therefore, O Mahādeva, engage in battle, for I shall provide you with assistance. 66.
In that Vṛndāvana, some deception will have to be practiced;
I shall act only with justice, never unjustly.
And that Daitya desires to seize your wife out of lust.
"In that regard, an opportunity for me to act presents itself at this opening:
(68) the destruction of one who pursues wealth obtained through his mother’s misconduct must certainly come to pass.
This is not a son, but an enemy created by you upon seeing Indra. (69)

"He alone is the one who goes against justice and must be destroyed; no deliberation is required here. In the meantime, the Daitya, accompanied by Mahāsena, arrived at the edge of Kailāsa and, having besieged the mountain, let out a roar.
Hearing the clamor of the army, Śaṅkara then became enraged. He commanded Nandin and the other leaders of the Gaṇas to engage in battle.
Nandin, the elephant-faced one (Gaṇeśa), the commander-in-chief, and others, all experts in warfare, [prepared for the fight].
All the hosts descended from Kailāsa, filled with wrath;
those hosts were indeed by the millions, as were the foremost of the Daityas,
making the sounds of battle throughout the valleys of Kailāsa.
Roaring fearsomely, the heroic Pramathas and the Dānavas shone forth with floods of spears,
javelins, and arrows, with maces, nooses, and sharp-edged spears,
and with tridents, missiles, thunderbolts, hammers, and various weapons.
Resounding with the booming sounds of kettledrums, clay drums, and conchs that gladden heroes,
and filled with the noise of elephants, horses, and chariots, the earth trembled. There, amidst both armies, terrifying sounds arose.

O Lakṣmī! Then there commenced a mutual slaughter, fierce and accompanied by thundering roars—a most terrible destruction. Elephants were slain, horses were slain, and heroes were slain by the thousands. (77–78)
The hosts of Daityas were struck down by the Pramathas, and likewise the Gaṇas were struck down by the Daityas;
having fallen into the great sleep, the earth, covered by them, shone forth.
Rich with the mire of fat, blood, and flesh, the earth then became impassable.

Śukra revived the Daityas by the power of the *mṛtasaṃjīvanī* [life-restoring] spell. "The Gaṇas who have died do not rise; this is a great and terrifying danger," the Gaṇas reported to Śaṅkara regarding their destruction.
Having learned all the deeds of Śukra, Hara became enraged;
from his mouth, with eyes copper-red from anger, there arose a terrifying Kṛtyā.
She had legs like palm trees, a cavernous mouth, fingers like clubs, and breasts like mountains.
She reached the battlefield and roamed among the asuras (83).
Devouring those daityas, she went to where Bhārgava was;
seizing Śukrācārya by the throat, she indeed cast him into the middle of her womb (84).
Having placed [him] within her own body, she vanished into the sky and departed.
Seeing this destruction of Śukra, the Daityas, their faces withered,
fled from the battlefield, intent on saving their lives.
Then the great army, struck down by the Gaṇas, broke apart.
Śumbha, Niśumbha, and Kālanemi—these three—engaging in battle, slaughtered the divine host of the Pramathas. (86–87)
Discharging showers of arrows, they caused the army of the Gaṇas to tremble;
and the Gaṇas, in turn, obstructed the Daityas with rains of shafts.
The Gaṇas and the Dānavas became as radiant as springtime *kiṃśuka* flowers.
Then that army of Dānavas took to the sky and obstructed the army of the Gaṇas with a most terrible rain from the heavens.
At that time, the army of the Pramathas, being shattered, fled into the mountain caves.
Seeing this reversal, Nandin, Bhānumukha, Ṣaṇmukha,
and other exceedingly powerful Gaṇas took up the sky and,
having seized the great boulders, carried the armies through the air.
Out of indignation, they rushed forward to slay the foremost of the Daityas;
leaping again and again, the lords struck down the preeminent Daityas protected by Jālandhara.
With their heads shattered by stone weapons,
others fell to the earth while still others fled;
thus was that demonic army broken and forced to abandon the sky.
"Having taken refuge in the Kailāsa forest, he remained hidden for a moment.

(94) Thus ends the three hundred and twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of how Jālandhara dispatched Rāhu as a messenger to Śaṅkara, how he was routed by Kīrtimukha, how Jālandhara’s army arrived, how Śukrācārya was cast into the womb by Kṛtyā, and how a terrible battle ensued," within the first section on the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. Śrī Lakṣmī said: "O Lord, tell me what happened then regarding Śukrācārya, who had been placed within the womb of Kṛtyā,
and what kind of battle took place there."
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Until the destruction of Jālandhara occurred, Śukra was crushed within his own womb by Kṛtyā; at that time, he was unable to emerge.
By the power of yoga and mantra, this man, though on the verge of death, somehow sustained his life through self-restraint; he remained there in a state of deep sleep, as if unconscious.
And when Jālandhara had perished, he was urinated upon from outside by Kṛtyā.
After a long time, he regained consciousness and woke up.
(4) Now, O Lakṣmī, hear of the incidental battle between them; thereafter, a great duel arose between those two great warriors. (5)
The great asura Kālanemi rushed toward the one named Nandin;
Śumbha rushed toward Lambodara, and Niśumbha toward the six-faced one (Kārttikeya).
Niśumbha pierced the peacock in the heart with five arrows.
Then Kārtikeya pierced his horses, his charioteer, and even his banner with five exceedingly sharp arrows;
with a single keen shaft, he struck Niśumbha.
Niśumbha also roared at the roaring Ṣaḍānana;
he struck him with many arrows and pierced his armored body.
Then Kārttikeya, enraged, seized a spear in his hand.
The powerful Niśumbha, acting with force and speed, hurled that life-destroying weapon.
But Niśumbha, who knew the proper timing, warded it off with his own power;
meanwhile, Skanda then launched a second weapon capable of ending life.
She, released with great speed, struck him in the heart and felled him.
Then Nandīśvara pierced the great asura Kālānemi there with five sharp arrows and likewise with seven.
With four arrows he struck the horses, with two the banner, and with one the charioteer. Then Kālanemi cut Nandin’s bow with arrows and likewise pierced Nandīśvara on the head with feathered shafts.
Nandīśa also struck Kālaka in the heart with his trident. With all his possessions destroyed and the interior of his heart pierced by the spear,
Kālaka uprooted a mountain peak and struck Nandin with it.
Nandī, seizing his spear, struck Kāla in the chest.
Kāla fell into a swoon, stretching out his hands and feet;
then Hastimukha, O auspicious one, pierced him in the heart with an arrow.

He pierced the horses with eight arrows and struck the charioteer with one. Then Śubha, with great speed, pierced the mouse on its head with a single arrow; the mouse, making the sound "cū-cū," fled away.
Leaving him behind, Gaṇeśa, the leader of the hosts, advanced on foot;
he then pierced Śubha with his spear and felled him to the earth. Thereupon, Kālanemi and Niśumbha, having shaken off their swoon— ||| 1.328.20 |||
Both of them, formidable, came together to slay Gaṇeśa;
seizing him, they threw him down and pierced him with arrows.
Seeing him thus afflicted, Vīrabhadra rushed forward.
He seized them by their two bellies and indeed crushed them repeatedly.
Those two great asuras were cast upon the earth, nearly dead;
from them arose the kūṣmāṇḍas, bhairavas, pretas, bhūtas, and piśācas.
The Vināyakas, Vetālas, Vīras, and Rākṣasa hosts,
as well as the Yoginīs, Kṛtyakās, and Ḍākinīs, marched forth as armies.
Then there arose a tumultuous sound of "kila-kila" and lion-like roars accompanied by gurgling cries.
The sounds of their hand-drums then made the earth tremble;
they devoured the Dānavas and slew them with tridents,
cutting off their throats and crushing those great Asuras.
Then they struck down the Daityas and Dānavas with mountain-like peaks,

as well as with elephants, horses, and chariots turned into weapons. The Daityas and Dānavas also, both those who were conscious and those who were unconscious, [attacked] with weapons turned against them.
Seizing them by their feet with their own feet, they struck them with those very feet.
Thus, a great slaughter was wrought by the armies of Bhūta and the others;
those who were the warriors, such as the Daityas and the rest, became weapons themselves. (28–29)
By those very weapons having attained their functional state, the preeminent warriors of one's own army were destroyed;
for where there are spirits, Rākṣasas, Vetālas, and Vināyakas, what battle— whether possible or impossible— is not conceivable there?
The army of Jalandhara was cut down, shattered, and destroyed;
it was crushed, annihilated, pulverized, and torn to pieces.
When not a single asura or dānava remained there to be seen, [the battle ended].
Then the great hero Jalandhara, overcome with extreme distress and filled with intense grief at the destruction of Śukra, shed tears again and again, thinking:
"With the death of Ujjīvaka, everything of mine has indeed perished today."
"I too must die here after displaying my prowess in battle"—
having thus resolved, he suddenly seized the Kṛtyā by her feet;
meanwhile, she discharged her own semen mixed with urine for the purpose of tearing him apart.
When he had placed [the chariot] there on the chariot and rested for a moment, Śukra then regained consciousness; thereafter,
by means of the Saṃjīvinī vidyā, he raised the Daityas back to life and roared.
Then Vīrabhadra, having brought Śukrācārya, Jalandhara,
and the entire chariot together, entered the cave;
he delivered Śukrācārya to the Kṛtyās and led Jalandhara away.
Vīrabhadra brought [him] before Hara and roared;
meanwhile, Jalandhara, having assumed numerous forms,
departed from that place in his original form out of fear of death.
By the *bhūtas*, *pretas*, *piśācas*, *kūṣmāṇḍas*, and the leaders of the *gaṇas*— those Daityas who had been cut, pierced, and slain, yet restored to life by Śukra—
the army was then seen to be utterly devastated; and Jalandhara, beholding that host thus destroyed, [acted accordingly].
Again, in a chariot adorned with a great banner, he advanced against the hosts;
like a cloud, he released a rain of arrows upon Śiva’s army.
Then the sky became shrouded by the clouds that were Jalandhara’s arrows.
Śailādi, the lord of the Gaṇas, was pierced by five arrows;
Vīrabhadra by twenty, and Kārttikeya by seven.
Having been thus pierced by that Daitya, Kārttikeya also quickly [acted].
With his spear, he pierced that hero and felled him to the ground.
Then Jalandhara, rising up in an instant and blazing with rage,
struck Kārttikeya with a mace and crushed him.
Then Vīrabhadra struck the son of the Ocean with his spear.
Jalandhara rose up and, armed with an iron club, leaped forward;
rushing swiftly, he struck Vīrabhadra.
Vīrabhadra fell to the earth, and Jalandhara roared;
a great clamor arose among the spirits in the presence of Rudra.
Hearing this, the fierce Mahārudra arrived at the battlefield, laughing aloud.
Indeed, upon seeing the terrifying Rudra, all the Daityas fled.
Then the Daitya Jalandhara, having resolved to meet his death,
rushed toward the Lord of Caṇḍī, discharging arrows by the thousands.
But those bull-like Daityas who had been restored to life by Śukra—
the survivors of the slaughter and others— rushed toward Śaṅkara.
These were Śumbha, Niśumbha, Ghasmara, Kālanemi, and Balāhaka.
With their fierce sword-hair bristling and their lips bitten in rage,
they pierced Rudra and the hosts of Rudra with arrows;
the sky on all sides became shrouded in the darkness of those shafts.
Hara, having torn apart that net with his arrows, covered the sky;
then Śaṅkara severed Khaḍgaroman’s head from his body. Having slain Balāhaka, he also killed Ghasmara.
He cut down Mahāvīra and Pracaṇḍa with his triple-pointed spear.
Thus, indeed, many were slain there and did not rise again.
Then Śaṅkara himself hurled the great spear Jaladhara.
Assuming another form, he vanished into the sky for a moment;
that spear, rendered fruitless against the earth, struck down other Daityas.
Then the remaining great Daityas fled from the battlefield out of fear.
But Jalandhara, seeing them, spoke again, uttering words of reproach: "Fie upon you!
What is gained by your fleeing—drinking only the milk of your mothers—and being struck from behind? Is heaven or liberation not attained thereby?"
For the brave, death in battle bestows heaven and even liberation;
let there be death by weapons that grant immortality while facing the foe. Let there not be death by turning away, which leads to the path of hell.
Having pierced the orb of the sun, the warrior shall go to the supreme state.
That great yogi is a true renunciant who is slain in battle facing the enemy.
Indeed, the wise should not entertain fear of death, which is truly unavoidable.
"Indeed, death is fixed and certain for the body from the very moment of its birth;
therefore, O Asuras, casting aside the fear of that death, fight in battle!
Having spoken thus, those Daityas were indeed terrified by Śaṅkara at that time.
In the battle at Aya-yuraṇa, Jalandhara did not become angry;
rather, he said to Śaṅkara, "Show me here whatever strength you possess.
Having spoken thus, Bāṇa struck his father Hara with seven arrows.
Before they could reach him, Mahādeva cut them down with sharpened arrows.
Then the bearer of the ocean (Varuṇa) rushed forward and hurled his mace at Śaṅkara.
Śiva, however, split that mace, which was coursing through the path of the sky, into two pieces with his spear.
Then the Daitya attempted to strike Hara with his fist;
he was then crushed for a league by Śaṅkara with his trident.
Thereupon Jalandhara, perceiving Rudra to be supported by great strength, [attacked].
The Gandharvas created an illusion that deluded Rudra, consisting of Apsarases;
then the Gandharvas appeared and sang in voices enchanting to the ear,
and the Apsarases danced with sweet-toned melodies.
Others played the cymbals, flutes, and drums.
There, Śambhu’s attendants became so absorbed in that [music] that they forgot the battle; those devotees of Śambhu listened, completely entranced.
Seeing Śumbha and the others hidden, the Daitya left them at that battlefield;
overcome by desire, he went quickly to where Gaurī was in her abode.
He had ten arms, five faces, three eyes, and wore matted locks.
Adorned with rudrākṣa beads, the serpent Vāsuki, a trident, a hide, garments, and other ornaments, Rudra assumed a demonic form through his illusory power (māyā) and went inside the house.
Seeing Rudra approaching, Pārvatī, the beloved of Bhava, [perceived him]. (73–74)
Knowing him to be desirous of sexual union, Satī, radiant like the sun, the moon, fire, gold, and lightning, lay upon her couch in the house;
as soon as he saw her, that dull-witted man discharged his semen.
Seeing him in such a state, Pārvatī reflected within herself:
"He has certainly neither touched me nor come upon my bed;
nor did he see me naked—how then did he discharge his seed? (76–77)
"Therefore, this is not Mahādeva, but must be another Dānava;
or perhaps he is a son of Śaṅkara born from a mere drop of breast-milk.
Having reflected thus, she suddenly vanished as if out of fear.
Not seeing her, his vigor lost, he went to fight with Śambhu.
Pārvatī also repeatedly remembered Mahāviṣṇu in her mind.
Kṛṣṇa arrived there, and Pārvatī spoke to Keśava.
"O Viṣṇu! Jalandhara has arrived here at my house, having become Rudra;
driven by lust, he comes to deceive [you]—is this not known to you?
Viṣṇu replied, "It is known to me; command what I should do in this matter."

Pārvatī said: "O Lord of Lakṣmī, to one who is such, you must act accordingly. Perform exactly that task which was shown by him toward him. By my command, destroy the virtuous conduct of Vṛndā. (82–83)
Otherwise, that great Daitya will die, not by his own power.
Chastity toward one's husband is a supreme dharma; it provides protection and likewise bestows liberation.
She remained exactly so in Goloka, and you shall incur no fault for enjoying her company.
"O Lord, all living beings are your wives; what need is there here for you?
Having heard this, O Lakṣmī, Viṣṇu himself informed Hara and, in order to bring about the destruction of Jalandhara, the Lord departed to employ a stratagem. 85–86.
In that city on the island of Jālandhara where Vṛndā resides,
she awaits her victorious husband in battle, longing for the sight of him.

Thus, in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, in the narrative of Jalandhara and Vṛndā: the death of the generals in battle; the restoration of life by Śukrācārya; the casting of Śukrācārya into the womb of a *kṛtyā*; the subsequent destruction of the Daityas; the duel between Jalandhara and Vīrabhadra; the battle between Jalandhara and Śaṅkara; Jalandhara’s departure to deceive Pārvatī in the form of Rudra by producing the *gāndharvī* illusion; and Viṣṇu [approaching] Vṛndā.
The three hundred and twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Departure to Deceive," etc., [ends].

Viṣṇu showed her a dream indicating widowhood.

Adorned with black flowers and attended by hosts of flesh-eaters,

it portends inconceivable results and brings about great misfortune for all.
Therefore, give gifts to the twice-born, for they destroy even the most unimaginable fear. (8–9)
Cows, garments, jewels, elephants, and ornaments— indeed,
gifts that grant the pacification of misfortune were given by her.
Nevertheless, at that time, there occurred throbbings in the right limbs.

perceiving that too as an ill omen, she was submerged in an ocean of grief and found no peace anywhere upon the terraces or floors of the palace.
Drawn away by Viṣṇu through his illusory power (māyā), she went to the garden in distress;
accompanied there by her two friends, she found no happiness anywhere.
Wandering from forest to forest, she beheld two terrifying beings.

intent on flight, she ran toward her protector. (14–15)

regarding him as her protector, she approached him for refuge and, clasping his neck with both arms, said to him, "Save me! Save me!"

By his own power and with the sound "huṃ," the Sage drove away both those Rākṣasas and protected the virtuous woman from their fear. Then Vṛndā, her mind composed, bowed and spoke these words: (17–18)
O holy man, dispeller of distress, protector from the fear of the wicked!
O Brahmin, if you know, tell me: is Jalandhara my husband?

"Tell me here whether my condition is one of stability, health, victory, or something else.
The sage replied: "I am the son of Bharadvāja; I shall tell you:
your condition is a state of great sleep from which there is no awakening."
"Victory has indeed been attained in the hereafter; my husband’s well-being has reached heaven"—hearing these most terrible words, she wept, utterly overwhelmed.
Just then, the two monkey-lords arrived and stood before Vṛndā.

Vṛndā, seeing this once more, wept most piteously with a loud voice;
beholding Jalandhara dead, she cried out like a female osprey.
"Alas! My destiny is shattered; all my wealth is lost.
I have fallen into widowhood, and indeed my auspicious fortune has vanished.
I requested that I not have to fight with Śambhu upon my departure."
"Nevertheless, O Lord, because of your heroic nature, you did not heed my words.
Even now, O Vīraka, I must die by means of your body. Having said this, when Vṛndā desired to burn that corpse, ||| 26–27 ||

Having spoken thus, the sage Viṣṇu restored her husband to life.
Having fashioned, caused to be made, and shown that very Jalandhara— who was his own self, a living being within a deceptive corpse—
he then held a great festival in that forest for the sake of Jīvaka.
Vṛndā too, having regained her husband—her very life—at that very moment, cast off her grief; embracing him, she then kissed his face.
She took delight right there upon the bed with Kāma again and again.
Viṣṇu, the holder of the Māyājāla, described the battlefield:
"O beloved, my head was severed by the fierce Rudra with his discus;
it has been quickly brought here into your presence by your messenger. (32–33)
"O Goddess, by this mantra spoken by me, accept your life through your chastity; take this betel-leaf and delight in the skill of amorous play.
Having said this, Mahāviṣṇu took pleasure with her again and again.
From the sweat of Vṛndā’s body, she emerged upon the earth as one exceedingly purifying;
she is called Vṛndā-Tulasī, and that place is Vṛndāvana. It is the sacred seat (pīṭha) of Jālandhara, and its kingdom is of the nature of Jālandhara. || 35-36 ||
Thus, O Ocean-born one, it became well-known there from of old that Viṣṇu took delight here with Vṛndā in the practice of intense amorous play; consequently,
through the violation of the duty of a faithful wife toward her husband, [she incurred his curse].
O beloved, as Jalandhara’s splendor and strength waned,
he became increasingly exhausted there at every moment, even as he continued to take his pleasure. || 38–39 ||
The battle continued for exactly five days and was even more terrifying than before.
Viṣṇu enjoyed Vṛndā’s company again and again in the garden palace,
while he dispatched Garuḍa in a hidden form day and night.
Keśava Hari was unable to ascertain whether Jalandhara was dead or not.
On the fifth day, when Vṛndā had fallen asleep after engaging in amorous play upon the bed, Garuḍa arrived at that moment.
Since Viṣṇu had gone inside the house, he became four-armed;
Garuḍa then reported the entire account to Viṣṇu:
"The Daitya has not died until this day; he merely wishes to die—do not delay! (43)
"He will die today, tomorrow, or the day after; of this there is no doubt.
Having spoken these and other such words, just as Garuḍa was departing from the house, Vṛndā saw him and quickly rose up in apprehension.
She saw within the inner chamber Viṣṇu with four arms. Crying out, "Who is this? Who is this other man who has entered the interior of my house?
she began to search for her husband throughout the house.
At that moment, Viṣṇu arrived, having assumed the form of Jālandhara.

"By this delusion, you shall become a servant here along with this serpent.

"My devotion to my husband has been lost, and my beloved has fallen into a state of doubt.
Having spoken thus, she bathed in the waters of the Pārśva lake;
then, having assumed the lotus posture on the bank and having made her mind free from sense-objects, she sat.
Then Vṛndā herself, having prepared a heap of dry wood and reflecting upon Viṣṇu’s deceit, entered the sacrificial fire.
Thereupon Vṛndā blazed up and in an instant became a mass of ashes.
And that ash became there a dark grove of *tulasī* plants;
the sweat of Vṛndā, moreover, became a green grove of *tulasī*.
Through the ritual of marriage with the *tulasī*, she obtained Hari once again as her husband.
Constantly meditating upon Viṣṇu, she indeed became merged in Viṣṇu;
by the will of Viṣṇu, Tulasī attained Viṣṇu once again.
Even in the form of a tree, that goddess was eternally accepted by Viṣṇu.
She who was his own daughter, a golden apsaras in Goloka,
was born as a daughter in the house of Kālanemi; though she was beloved by Viṣṇu,
due to the fault of being Rādhā’s co-wife, she became the beloved of Jalandhara.
Embracing Viṣṇu once again, she was indeed born as the beloved of Viṣṇu;
at that time, Vṛndā’s splendor merged into the power of Viṣṇu.
That Vṛndā became Tulasī, born upon the earth in the form of a tree.
"Indeed, as was one's conduct in the past, so shall be one's destiny.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have told you of the deceptive display of Vṛndā’s dharma,
which was enacted by Viṣṇu at that time for the destruction of Jalandhara.

Thus, in the first section of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, within the narrative of Jalandhara and Vṛndā during the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga, [is described] the inauspicious dream shown to Vṛndā by Viṣṇu; the ill omens at the rising of the sun and other times; the protection of Vṛndā, who was terrified by two artificial Rākṣasas in the garden, by Viṣṇu in the form of a holy man (sādhu); the restoration to life of the artificial Jalandhara who had died while in the form of a false sage; and [the events] by means of that which had become the artificial Jalandhara.

Chapter Three Hundred and Twenty-Nine: Description of Viṣṇu’s making love with Vṛndā in Vṛndāvana; the Vṛndā-tree arising from Vṛndā’s perspiration; thereafter, upon learning of this, Vṛndā’s entry into the funeral pyre and her transformation into the form of Tulasī from the ashes; and the description of Viṣṇu’s sorrow and the curse incurred on account of his wife being abducted by two Rākṣasas. Chapter Three Hundred and Thirty: The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga (Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā, Part 1). Chapter 330.
