Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī! Then the messenger, having gone quickly to Jalandhara, spoke.
Having heard Vṛndā’s words, the son of the Ocean wept and said:
"Whatever action is performed by whom, that very same [result] is experienced by him alone.
By me Gaurī was deceived, and by Hari my bride was deceived. (1–2)
A person should never, under any circumstances, allow their sister’s husband to stay in the house;
he gradually takes possession of everything, including wealth and wives.
A wise man should never place his trust in a son-in-law who resides in the home.
"Surely the wise one, having given him his daughter, will dismiss him.
My wife has certainly been deceived by Viṣṇu through the employment of illusion.
Shall I go to conquer Hari, or rather the formidable Hara?"
If I go to conquer Hari, Hara will strike me from behind.
One who abandons a present opportunity to follow another surely perishes.
Both my enemies are exceedingly powerful; victory has become uncertain for me.
"I have been defeated and half of my wife has been reduced to ashes.
Therefore, after conquering Paśupati, I shall indeed proceed against Viṣṇu;
having conquered Śambhu, I shall become the Lord of all lords in the world."
"Or else, having died by Śiva’s arrows, I shall go to his abode.
Having reflected thus, he went right there to fight with the wielder of the Pināka bow.
In the battle, Jālandhara beheld a scene terrifying with heaps of headless trunks.
In the battle, he beheld the Lord of Pārvatī mounted upon his bull, amidst a difficult terrain of heaps of flesh, marrow, fat, and bones that were pleasing to the Śavas;
as well as many sharp and exceedingly thick arrows and iron pillars. (1.330.10–11)
The invincible one released [them] in battle like a rain-cloud at the onset of the monsoon.
Then, struck with fury by Rudra with fierce showers of arrows,
his armor was cast down to the earth by Rudra’s shafts.
Pierced by arrows, his body took on the color of the *kiṃśuka* flower;
copious blood flowed from Jālandhara’s body.
The gods, together with their forces, were emboldened, while the Dānavas trembled with fear. (13–14)
Hara quickly pierced the son of the Ocean in the heart with a sharp arrow.
With his body mangled by the shaft, the son of the Ocean fell and became unconscious.
At that moment, Jālandharī’s army was struck down by Rudra with iron bolts.
Jalandhara, however, mentally remembered Śukra and sent him forth.
But he, being under the control of Kṛtyā, remained in a mountain cave;
he was unable to come to that place where the battle was taking place.
Jalandhara, slowly regaining consciousness from his faint, arose;
he quickly fashioned an auspicious illusory Gauri of similar appearance.
Śiva [beheld] Pārvatī upon the chariot, bound and crying out in distress.
He beheld her being struck by the Daityas Niśumbha and Śumbha.
Seeing Gaurī in such a state, Śiva became deeply distressed in mind;
his limbs grew limp, his soul was despondent, and he then cast his face downward.
Then Jaṃladhara swiftly pierced Rudra with three arrows— so that they sank up to their feathers—
into his head, his chest, and his belly. Thereupon, Rudra,
assuming a fierce form, became exceedingly enraged.
Then Śaṅkara became as terrible as the fire of universal dissolution.
At that moment, Śumbha took that illusory Pārvatī from his chariot into the sky and released her upon the tip of his trident; she fell down upon the trident.
Weeping before Śaṅkara, she died, pierced by his trident.
Seeing Māyā-Gaurī dead, Hara was overwhelmed by grief and delusion;
he cursed the demons headed by Śumbha, saying, "Gaurī shall slay you."
Having become fierce, she slaughtered them all on the field of battle.
Then Brahmā, having arrived there, spoke to Śrī Śaṅkara: "O Hara, this is an illusion created by Jālandhara; she is Pārvatī. (25–26)
Satī, however, has been protected by me and by Viṣṇu as well;
she dwells within the interior of a lotus bud, having attained a state of subtlety.
Fight and slay the multitude of your enemies, but do not slay Pārvatī.
Having reflected upon these words of Brahmā, the great lord Maheśvara, possessing supreme wisdom,
recognized that it was the illusion of the Dānava; he released a massive boulder,
shattered that deceptive form, and reduced it to dust in that very instant.
Then, beholding Śarva abandoned by his illusion, the son of the Ocean quickly manifested another great illusion of immense power.
Jālandhara became ten-thousand-armed, with stones and trees as his weapons.
Enraged and equipped with missiles and weapons, he repeatedly obstructed Śambhu in battle.
Then, insulting Hara, he spoke these forceful words:
"Behold, O Śaṅkara, what kind of power I possess; do you not recognize it at all? (31-32)
"Who in the three worlds is invulnerable to my arrows, O Maheśvara?
Viṣṇu was protected in his home by a child;
and Brahmā himself, the bestower of boons, was gratified by my asceticism."

Indra, Agni, Yama, Kubera, Vāyu, Varuṇa, Īśvara, and the others—all have been brought under my control; I have brought forth their vehicles. All the mountains have been subdued by me, and the rivers have been restrained with ease.
Indeed, the inhabitants of heaven were conquered; Vaḍavāmukha was firmly bound.
Airāvata and the others were cast down, as was Indra along with his chariot.
Even Garuḍa was bound by me, and the goddesses were led to my home.
"You do not know me, O Rudra, as the one who brings victory to the three worlds.
Having heard this, Mahādeva laughed again and again;
Jalandhara then swiftly struck the laughing Śiva with his arrows.
Then the Dānava was struck in the chest by Rudra with his trident;
from the mouth of the Dānava there issued forth a supreme fever.
Jambha, having the face of a lion and the body of a man, rushed toward the Lord.
The Lord uttered the syllable "Huṃ," and there Śarabha appeared.
Then the lion, struck by Śarabha,
seized the Dānava bull by the tail with force and whirled him around upon the ground.
Then the Lord of the Daughter of the Mountain released an exceedingly fierce trident;
seizing it with his hand, the Daitya rushed toward Hara.
Thereupon, the Daitya Ayutabhuja bound Śiva in the battle.
Śiva cut off the demon's hand with his own sword.
Although his hand was severed, the demon continued to fight; then Maheśvara, being pleased, spoke for the purpose of granting a boon, and the Daitya then chose a boon from Hara.
"Quickly grant me success; give me your own station!
"So be it," said Hara, and he took the Sudarśana discus, filled with fire and possessing prowess equal to ten million suns.
For the destruction of Jalandhara, Lord Hara hurled [the spear];
it swiftly severed his head, which possessed large and wide eyes.
His body fell in two parts like an immovable mountain of collyrium.
From his throat emerged hundreds of thousands of Daityas, equal to Jālandhara in battle; they were all slain by him with that discus.
That headless trunk of Jālandhara, crimson with blood, began to dance.
The entire earth was filled with the fat of the son of Sindhu;
the world became completely full of his fierce blood.
Wherever the blood dried, that indeed became the city of Śoṇitapura.
Then the Yoginīs— Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, Māhendrī, Kaumārī, and whomever else there were—
took the heaps of flesh to all directions and caused them to be destroyed.
Then the radiance that had issued from his body dissolved into Hari.
The hosts of Yoginīs were devouring the flesh of Jalandhara and drinking his blood;
for that reason, he who was slain in battle does not rise even now.
Seeing Jalandhara slain, the gods attained great joy;
the deities, Siddhas, and lords of sages uttered cries of "Well done! (54).
Showering flowers, they sang the auspicious praises of Śiva’s glory.
The gods danced all around, honored by the Apsarases;
all the quarters became serene, and the gods and others were freed from their bonds.
The Sun, the Moon, Varuṇa, and the rest were liberated from his imprisonment.
Furthermore, they were appointed by Viṣṇu, Hara, and Brahmā;
the lords of the gods bestowed jewels upon them.
Śukra, having been dismissed from his duties, returned once more to his own abode.
After the destruction of the Daityas, the sovereignty of the gods was established in every region.
Having attained lordship over the worlds, the gods enjoyed their sacrificial shares;
the goddesses and the other deities likewise remained happily in their respective abodes.
Then Bṛhaspati, the preceptor of the gods, having brought forth the Droṇa mountain and the oceans from outside, obtained the life-restoring herb (*jīvanī*) at that place where the Pramathas,
the attendants of Śambhu, had perished on the battlefield.
There, they employed [the power] upon bones, flesh, corpses, and so forth.
All those hosts of Rudra who had been slain in battle were restored to life;
entirely without exception, they all went happily to Kailāsa. (61–62)
Just as Parvata was previously established in that place for the sake of the world by the vehicle of Viṣṇu, so too does what is appropriate arise in due time.
O Lakṣmī, know this without doubt: everyone experiences their own karma.
As long as the body exists, actions and the experience of pleasure, pain, and so forth continue.
Having heard this history, one is not overcome by sufferings;
even though afflictions arise again and again, they remain far removed from such a person.
Whatever kind of union one has, such is one's bondage;
even Viṣṇu’s firm bondage in Vṛndāvana arose through the performance of yoga.
O Lakṣmī, listen further: everything occurred according to the ways of the world.

Deluded by Vṛndā, Viṣṇu, despite being advised by the gods and others, did not abandon the place of Vṛndā’s immortality (Vṛndāvana) even for the sake of regaining Vṛndā herself. And Vṛndā, constantly meditating upon him, indeed became a *satī* (a chaste woman who follows her husband in death). || 67-68 ||
He desires Viṣṇu right there once again in Vṛndāvana;
indeed, from the very body of Viṣṇu, he emerges outwardly in a subtle form.
He becomes manifest in a secluded place and then dissolves back into Viṣṇu.
Viṣṇu’s power is threefold— Gaurī, Lakṣmī, and Ramā— who always abide within Hari in both visible and invisible forms. Beheld by them there, Hari was utterly enchanted by Vṛndā.
Vṛndā, too, upon the death of her husband, desired another husband;
yet, having been accepted by Viṣṇu, she desires to take Viṣṇu as her own.
In solitude, she indeed becomes embodied and serves Viṣṇu.

She said to Viṣṇu: "O Lord, since I have been accepted by you in every respect, therefore take my hand according to the marriage rite. First I shall dwell in the abode of Goloka, and afterwards I shall be the beloved of Jalandhara. (73–74)
"Furthermore, you have made me your own; therefore, carry me as your own.
Viṣṇu said, "Become the daughter of Kedāra; I shall carry her.
That was indeed seen and observed by Gaurī, who is Lakṣmī, known by the name Ramā.

Then, at that time, seeds were indeed given there by those Śaktis; and they [the brothers] cast them for the deities upon that spot. From those seeds cast there, three auspicious trees came into being.
The three—dhātrī, mālatī, and tulasī—are as follows:
that dhātrī is remembered as a portion of Gaurī, and mālatī is remembered as a portion of Lakṣmī.
Ramā, however, became tulasī, appearing in the form of a tree.
And those women there also assumed divine forms.
Seeing the trees possessing the forms of beautiful women, Viṣṇu was filled with great joy;
and seeing Viṣṇu, Tulasī and Vṛndā were likewise exceedingly delighted.
In this way, she and he gazed at one another with passion alone; Tulasī gazed at Viṣṇu and Dhātrī gazed at him with passion alone.
At that time, the seed was offered by you, Lakṣmī, out of envy alone.
Therefore, the woman born from her became possessed of jealousy toward Viṣṇu;
hence she received the most contemptible name of Barbarī.
Because of her passion for them, Dhātrī and Tulasī always grant pleasure to Viṣṇu.
Having taken you both away, Viṣṇu reached Vaikuṇṭha;
there, having married you both, Viṣṇu became united with Vṛndā.
Having become the daughter of Kedāra, Vṛndā indeed attained Viṣṇu.

There in that forest, the beautiful Vṛndā had woven a captivating garland of Mandāra and Pārijāta flowers. O woman of excellent complexion, the goddesses and gods arrived at that auspicious place in Vṛndāvana. || 85-86 ||
Having caused a pavilion to be constructed and having prepared a sacrificial pit,
he kindled the fire right there and performed the fire-oblation according to the prescribed rules; then,
having performed the purification of Tulasī’s body and its adornment.

Having caused [her] to perform auspicious bathing with fragrant substances and to adorn herself with garments, ornaments, and the like, she devoutly fed Tulasī; and having adorned Viṣṇu, she [honored] the millions of gods beginning with Brahmā. (88–89)
Equipped with vehicles and mounts, followed by goddesses,
accompanied by groups of singers, and resounding with the music of instruments—
all of them, mounted upon divine conveyances, went to the home of Gaurī.
Gaurī, Lakṣmī, Ramā, and the others worshipped Viṣṇu with great devotion.
Having performed the customary rites, they brought the young maiden Vṛndā, who was now a youth, into the pavilion and settled her there. (91–92)
Having caused the fire-oblation to be performed and having directed the circumambulation to be done,
Bṛhaspati, after bowing to that fire,
placed the hands of those two together and caused the garland of choice to be laid down.
Then, with the permission of Gaurī and the others, he performed the taking of the *vṛnda* [of disciples].
There, shouts of "Victory! from the gods and goddesses, auspicious songs, showers of flowers, and words of increase arose for the sake of both.
Then, having been given wedding gifts and food,
all of them— the gods and the others— departed from Vṛndāvana for their respective lands.
[This account] leads to heaven, removes sin, is meritorious, and destroys grief and delusion.
Having heard this sinless narrative, which is dear to the hearts of the virtuous,
a Brāhmaṇa attains knowledge, a Kṣatriya becomes a possessor of a kingdom,
a Vaiśya becomes endowed with prosperity, and a Śūdra becomes happy. (97–98)

One should satisfy the reciter with gifts of gold, sesame seeds, clothing, and the like, as well as by the donation of cows and land; for when he is satisfied, the fruit [of the rite] will arise. When the reciter—the guru—is honored, the deities also become propitious.

Then, having bestowed the gift of food, one should honor the Brāhmaṇas and others. Thus, O Lakṣmī, by this pretext, you have heard the cause of Tulasī’s origin; [one who does so] becomes eternally victorious, endowed with an abundance of sons and grandsons. (1.330.10–101)
Having heard that which has been proclaimed, one obtains supreme merit.
Even the *tulasī* planted in one’s own home is a destroyer of sin;
by its mere sight, sins such as the killing of a Brahmin are destroyed—of this there is no doubt.
In the months of Vaiśākha, Kārtika, and Māgha, one should worship Tulasī extensively. (102) One should worship Viṣṇu with Tulasī and likewise with a thousand flower-clusters.
By offering these to Viṣṇu in the morning, the fruit of ten million sacrifices shall be attained. (104)
Where Vṛndā and the green Tulasī of dark luster were born in Vṛndāvana, there Viṣṇu became utterly infatuated;
Keśava took up residence there and never abandoned his enchantment.

Then, three powers of that Self were manifested (106), illuminating the sky with their most wonderful splendors. By means of those [powers], seeds were then deposited right there, from their own portions. (107)
At that time in Vṛndāvana, the Dhātrī, Mālatī, and Tulasī likewise took on the forms of trees; seeing them there, Keśava was enchanted,
and both Tulasī and Dhātrī fell in love with him.
Out of affection for him, the Dhātrī and Tulasī plants were always the objects of his love.
Then Viṣṇu took them both and returned to Vaikuṇṭha;
there, Lakṣmī, becoming jealous, was separated from him and turned into a Barbarī plant.

Whoever should constantly recite this, cause it to be recited, or likewise listen to it, for him there shall be a good destination, residence in heaven, and liberation. (111) Thus ends the account of Jālandhara and Vṛndā in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. It includes: the display by Jālandhara of the destruction of the illusory Gaurī through his own magic; the battle fought with that magic; the destruction of Jālandhara by means of Śaṅkara’s discus; Vṛndā’s request for a boon from Viṣṇu; Vṛndā’s becoming the daughter of King Kedāra; the marriage of Tulasī by Viṣṇu; and the portions of Gaurī, Lakṣmī, and Ramā residing in Vṛndāvana.

[The Author: Chapter 332.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī, to the majesty of Tulasī, which is equal to that of Viṣṇu.
Having heard which, liberation occurs—that [goddess] who bestows the presence of Viṣṇu.
She who is eternally devoted to one person certainly cannot belong to another;
such is Vṛndā, the tree-dweller, who was the wife of Viṣṇu and has now attained Viṣṇu once again.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
"Indeed, at that very spot where Vṛndā was reduced to ashes, she remained invisible for some time, meditating upon Viṣṇu. (3)
The female species is truly pure, and all of them are devoted to their husbands.
Indeed, at the beginning of creation, the Creator fashioned all castes as being of a single kind.
All of them are portions of Prakṛti—pure, wise, and embodiments of auspiciousness.
How indeed has Dharma, whose very essence is devotion to one’s husband, come to destruction?
For Viṣṇu is the husband of women, and he is the eternal Dharma;
men are always portions of Viṣṇu—how then has Dharma gone to ruin? (5–6)
"Indeed, in the beginning, at the time of creation, when men were devoted to the primordial natures (prakṛtis), dharma alone was supreme; how then did it come to destruction?
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī! To this divine narrative which destroys many doubts:
in the beginning, women were always pure and possessed of pure hearts;
for the sake of the increase of creation, a man must always serve a woman.
This was indeed the most ancient and eternal law in former times:
whenever women became pregnant by serving any man whatsoever, at that time, service to any man was the eternal duty for women. (1.331.10)
At that time, there was indeed no desire or passion-born craving there;
however, due to the curse of Kedārakanyā, that Dharma went to ruin. Then, out of anger, the Creator made women possessed of passion.
From that time forth, O Lotus-born One, another law for women was established:
a man who is approached by women with passion for the sake of satisfying desire—
therein lay unrighteousness (adharma) due to the change of the age.
If there is no passion in the woman, there is likewise no passion in the man;
if their union is solely for the sake of conception, then dharma consists in the bestowing of the seed.
If the union is out of a desire for sensual enjoyment, that is proclaimed to be unrighteousness (adharma).
Due to the division of the ages (yugas), passion and thirst arose among people.
Because of that, the pursuit of desire became a form of unrighteousness;
consequently, the dharma of devoted wives became a mere semblance of dharma.
The former dharma perished and a new, different dharma arose;
all of this occurred in the past due to the agency of Vṛndā.
I shall relate it to you in brief; understand from me how it came to be.
In ancient times, there was Manu Svāyambhuva, the son of Brahmā.
His wife was Śatarūpā, who was devoted to her husband. They had two sons, Priyavrata and Uttānapāda. (18–19)
Uttānapāda’s son was Dhruva, who was indeed a Vaiṣṇava.
His son was Nanda Sāvarṇi, and his son was Kedāra. This Kedāra, the lord of the seven islands, became a Vaiṣṇava.

For the sake of its protection, Viṣṇu’s Sudarśana was always present in his house. He constantly gave as gifts a hundred thousand cows with golden horns, various garments, and likewise a hundred thousand pieces of gold.
He constantly gave gifts of jewels, diamonds, and pearls;
he daily fed hundreds of thousands of brahmins;
and he bestowed vessels for water and food made of gold.

That king gives as gifts to the poor, the helpless, and the twice-born golden sacrificial threads, rings, and seats. There are one hundred thousand brahmins who act as cooks, and two hundred thousand who serve as waiters.
Indeed, at every lunar festival (parvan), there are for him enjoyments possessing a radiance of a hundred lakhs;
there are delightful streams of ghee, streams of honey, and streams of curd,
as well as streams of molasses and streams of milk, available for him day and night.
He constantly performs the worship of the virtuous and likewise the worship of virtuous women;
he offers perpetual honor and the like to the elders,
and he performs the daily worship of cows, gods, and Brahmins.
Subsisting on fruits and roots, O Lotus-born One, the king is solely intent on surrendering everything to me; having offered all to me, he constantly accepts [only what is given].
He eternally chants my name alone and remembers me, endowed with splendor.
Indeed, he always worships me as Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa.
Once, on the morning of the twelfth day (dvādaśī), for the purpose of breaking the fast and feeding the brahmins in the king’s palace, ten lakhs [of coins] were presented.
Indeed, having immediately caused a sacrificial offering to be performed by the king,
they were fed with sweet foods and various dishes, including rice-milk porridge (pāyasa),
diverse fried cakes (pūrikās), as well as milk and curd.
The six types of twice-born ones, having attained satisfaction and being filled with joy by the sacrificial fees, bestowed upon him auspicious blessings:
"May Lakṣmī indeed dwell in your home!
Then, during the midday oblation, he performed the fire-sacrifice in many ways with clarified butter.

Then, through the grace of Viṣṇu, Vṛndā, who was established in Vṛndāvana, remained there performing austerities for the sake of her husband and for the sake of Viṣṇu, being devoted to her husband with offerings of sesame seeds, fruits, milk-rice,
flowers, and leaves. (25)
Indeed, due to the destruction of the ocean, she remained in another form;
by the command of Nārāyaṇa, she attended the sacrifice of Kedāra.
Kamalā was born from a portion [of herself], emerging from the sacrificial pit.
Clad in garments as pure as fire, adorned with jewel ornaments,
full of divine splendor, and possessing lotus-like eyes,
that lotus-eyed maiden was a passionate youth even at birth, carrying out the commands of her Lord. (38)
"I am your maiden daughter, O Great King," she said to the monarch.
Having honored her as his daughter and having offered her as a wife, the king remained there.
Then that mother spoke to the queen about her father, Kedāra.
From that time forth, by the power of this king’s fortune,
five hundred thousand lords of kings would daily present at the assembly of Kedāra priceless gems,
rubies, pearl necklaces, and the Maṇīśvara jewel.
He gave the jewel of an elephant and the jewel of a horse as tribute to Kedāra.
Thus his kingdom became filled with prosperity and comprised the seven continents;
yet the princess, rich in her longing for Viṣṇu, set her mind upon asceticism alone.
Having paid obeisance to his mother and father, he went again to Vṛndāvana,
specifically to the vicinity of the Yamunā where she had previously been reduced to ashes.
There, through her ascetic penance, she requested me as a boon, the most excellent of boons.
Brahmā granted her a boon: "You shall obtain Viṣṇu-Kṛṣṇa.
Then one day, while the beautiful woman was sleeping on the bank of the Yamunā, Dharma went there to test that female ascetic, Vṛndā.
In a secluded place, she beheld a supreme young man, appearing sixteen years of age, radiant as gold with desire,
richly fragrant, adorned with ornaments, and captivating to women. 47.
Loving, possessing the beauty of ten million Cupids,
with a face like the full moon (48), eyes resembling lotus petals, smiling, and filled with emotion;
standing at his side, singing and playing a beautiful lute (49).
Yayāti, displaying his inner disposition here and there, sat down upon seeing her there, honoring the beautiful woman greatly.
Vṛndā also then rose and offered him hospitality.
He honored her with fruits, roots, flowers, leaves, water, and other offerings.
Having accepted the worship, he spoke affectionately and joyfully to her:
"Whose daughter are you, and why do you perform such severe penance? (51–52)
"What is the reason for this, maiden? Tell me your name here.
Why do you dwell alone in this desolate place, O auspicious one? What do you desire?
Choose a boon—blessings be upon you—whatever dwells in your heart. (53)
Vṛndā, the daughter of King Kedāra, said to that brāhmaṇa:
"I am performing penance here, Vṛndā; I meditate upon Hari as my husband.
If you are capable of granting it, bestow upon me this supreme boon. (54-55)
"If you are incapable, O Brahmin, I shall worship elsewhere.
Dharma said to Vṛndā: "Who, other than the virtuous Lakṣmī Śrī, has the power to make that Supreme Soul, the Lord, her husband? (56)
He is Rādhā, Ramā, Pārvatī, Śāradā, and likewise Prabhā;
he is Sarasvatī, Māṇikī, Śāradā, and Virajā.
He has four arms in Vaikuṇṭha, but in Goloka he has two arms.
In that supreme abode known as Akṣara, he indeed exists with two arms.
His consorts are innumerable, and they are exclusively liberated beings (muktāṅganās).
Rādhā, Lakṣmī, and others, however, worship those who are beginningless women (anādiyoṣitas).

He is as beautiful as a beloved, fully endowed with the prowess of ten million Cupids. (1.331.60) O Vṛndā! That which constitutes a single *nimeṣa* (twinkling of an eye) of Brahmā is indeed equal to seventy-one *satya-yugas* of Indra’s duration until his fall. (1.331.61)
A day of Brahmā consists of a period of time delimited by fourteen Indras;
his night is likewise of that same duration, and he possesses a lifespan of one hundred such years.
Sanaka and the others serve him until the end of his life.
Even for tens of billions of eons, there is nothing so great that it cannot be accomplished;
even Śeṣa, who possesses a thousand mouths,
serves and mutters [the mantra] with devotion day and night for hundreds upon hundreds of millions of eons.
Even so, the Supreme beyond the supreme is indeed difficult to propitiate;
even Brahmā, whose nature is Brahman, must worship Him birth after birth. Since He is unattainable even by him, how can He be attained by you?
Even Rudra, the destroyer of the worlds, does not reach his end;
he too does not attain it at that time—how then, O young girl, could you possibly attain it?
You are the Supreme Sovereign, the Root Nature (Mūlaprakṛti), whose essence is Brahman.
Nārāyaṇī, Viṣṇumāyā, Vaiṣṇavī, that eternal one,
and even Sarasvatī, the supreme goddess, are unable to praise him. O auspicious one, how can you desire as your husband one who has transcended primordial nature (prakṛti)?
"O illustrious lady, accept me as your husband, the lord of kings!
O woman of excellent complexion, enjoy all pleasures in my home!
Beyond the seven oceans lies my golden city."
"Come right here, may you be blessed; take delight with me, O Rāma!
Come, let us enjoy each other; set your mind on me, for I am a young woman.
Having been addressed thus, the princess spoke to him from her palace out of anger:
"Be steadfast, O Lord of the Earth! Your vow consists of austerity and truth.
However, this lack of association with your wife for your sake is unrighteous; through that, misfortune may arise, which would bring about your destruction along with your very roots. (72–73)
In this matter, my ascetic merit would be destroyed, and likewise yours would perish.
Having seen this secret and this calamity, you desire to assault me;
however, here are the world-protectors, Dharma, Yama, Hari, and the Moon.
The sun, the earth, water, fire, the intellect, the witness, and others likewise abide within all living beings; where is there anything hidden, where is there any secret?
Forgive me, go, may it be well with you, for a Brahmin is considered inviolable.
"I am capable of reducing you to ashes; go, O brahmin, as you please.
The Lord Viṣṇu, the inner self of all, protects me, O twice-born!
Viṣṇu is always the protector of the helpless, the children, and the elderly."
Even though she was thus addressed by Kama, as he was about to approach her for sexual union, she cursed Dharma out of anger: "O base Brahmin, go to ruin!
O man of evil conduct, O destroyer of Dharma, go to ruin, go to ruin!"
Then Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara arrived there;
seeing Dharma prostrate, fallen, motionless, soiled, consumed, and struck by the fire of Satī’s wrath, those lords of the thirty gods wept. (1.331.80)
"O Vṛndā, endure the Dharma, which removes birth, death, and old age.
O devoted wife, sustain the Dharma and protect your father, who is the Dharma!
Thus Viṣṇu spoke then, and Brahmā likewise spoke to her.
"O Vṛndikā! The world has become filled with darkness due to the absence of Dharma;
both the moon and the sun tremble, as do Śeṣa and the earth.
May it be well with you, may prosperity be yours; O auspicious one, restore this bull to life!"
"You practice dharma through asceticism, yet how is it that you destroy dharma?
Dharma, assuming the form of a twice-born, has come here to test you; though he was faultless, he was destroyed by you, having been sent by Brahmā. (84–85)
Dharma is acquired by men through austerity, and the fruit [of action] comes through dharma.
How could there be a fruit from austerity if dharma has gone to destruction?
For the practitioner of action, action is fruitless without dharma, O righteous one.
When dharma has perished, even your unprecedented ascetic power will perish.
O beautiful one, you have come here to perform the acquisition of your own dharma;
yet, through ignorance, you destroy that very dharma—revive dharma with all haste!
Having heard this, the ascetic Vṛndā then said to the gods:
"O gods, I did not recognize that dharma was in the form of a brahmin.
Out of anger, I brought about the destruction of one who desired to violate me. (89)
I shall surely restore the eternal Dharma, which has died, once again. However, it will not become that very same Dharma here once more;
due to differences in place, time, and other factors, this Dharma will be different.
If my austerity and truthfulness are real here, and if my worship of Viṣṇu is true,
then by that merit may this Brahmin be restored to life immediately.
If my vow of truth is true, and if my austerity is truly mine, [then let it be so].
"By that merit, let this Brahmin here be restored to life immediately.
Then Mūrti, his lawful wife, said to the Lord of Kamalā:
"If I am indeed devoted to righteousness, let Dharma be restored to life."
Having bowed at the feet of Nārāyaṇa, Mūrti and Vṛndā performed a salutation for the sake of the life of Dharma. Then Nārāyaṇa said:
"O Mūrti! O Vṛndā! May this Dharma live on for your sake."

"In the Tretā age he has four feet, in the Dvāpara three feet, and in the Kali age he shall have but one foot; thus, through the curse of the three [sages], his purpose is to undergo gradual decline. Having said this, Hari summoned Dharma by means of a sound.
Dharma, having attained life, was pleased by the multitude of forms;
Dhruva was honored, and Vṛndā was praised there.
Commanded to grant a boon, she prayed to Viṣṇu himself.
"I have performed penance for the sake of Viṣṇu, and may Viṣṇu become my husband;
having married me, may Viṣṇu himself lead me to Vaikuṇṭha.
"So be it," Hari replied, as Vṛndā attained a state of great joy. (1.331.100)
There, the maiden Vṛndā was married by Viṣṇu;
having attained Viṣṇu, that princess went to Vaikuṇṭha. Yet, Vṛndā did not wish to leave the beautiful Vṛndāvana. (101–102)
Then Viṣṇu said to Vṛndā: "Stay here, embodied as Tulasī;
I shall come and marry you with great honor. I cannot bring myself to abandon this beautiful Vṛndāvana."
"Having found another pretext, I shall remain here with you;
you will attain fame in the world as the bride of Viṣṇu’s Tulasī.
O Vṛndā, I shall act accordingly; dwell here in the form of Tulasī. || 104-105 ||
Then, after some time, you shall indeed become the shadow of Rādhā;
at that time, I shall again marry you, the daughter of Raivata.
I am Kṛṣṇa, the son of Vasudeva and the Lord of Rādhā himself.

"O beloved, I shall become Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, your husband here. Having spoken thus to Tulasī, Viṣṇu, the infallible Acyuta, took her along with Vṛndā and went to Vaikuṇṭha; the other gods likewise departed for their own abodes.

Thus ends the three hundred and thirty-first chapter, titled "The Description of Vṛndā Becoming the Daughter of Dhruva’s Grandson Kedāra, Her Ascetic Practice in Vṛndavana, the Test by Dharma, Her Death after Being Defeated by Dharma and His Subsequent Curse, the Arrival of the Three Deities, the Resurrection of Dharma, the Decline of Dharma and its Internalization as Śīla, Vṛndā’s Abiding in the Form of Tulasī, and Her Departure for Vaikuṇṭha in the Form of Vṛndā," in the narrative of Jālandhara and Vṛndā within the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga in the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. || 331 ||
← Chapter 331: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga) Chapter 332 [[Author: Chapter 333 →
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī! I shall relate the story of the yoginī Vṛndā.
Tulasī, the wife of the Lord, became a small tree in Vṛndāvana. (1)
Just as she was born, so in the course of time she was married by Viṣṇu.
I shall relate her story exactly as it happened; learn it from me.
Understand from me how this event took place in my own abode, Goloka.
By the mere hearing of which one is liberated from all sins.
(3) Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, and Gaṅgā—these three wives of Hari also remain constantly in the presence of Hari, equal in their love. (4)
Once, Gaṅgā, full of desire and casting sidelong glances, beheld Acyuta;
she looked at him again and again, causing Sarasvatī distress. Indeed, Kṛṣṇa laughed repeatedly and in many ways upon seeing Gaṅgā’s futile gaze.
Hari took his pleasure with Gaṅgā, but not with Sarasvatī (6).
He delighted Lakṣmī, who was filled with passion and full of desire; yet Kṣamāvatī did not perceive any internal distress (7).
Sarasvatī was fickle and could not endure her inner torment.
Lakṣmī sought to awaken her and consoled the grieving goddess;
yet even so, Vāṇī remained filled with anger and did not become calm.
Trembling with the force of her anger, she spoke to her husband regarding Gaṅgā:
"A virtuous husband maintains an attitude of equanimity toward all his wives;
however, the attitude of a wicked husband—one who is selfish—is partial and unrighteous."

Your affection for Gaṅgā is known, and your love for Lakṣmī is constant; yet toward me, your beloved and lifelong companion, it appears truly deficient. Vain indeed is the life of that woman who is deprived of her husband’s love.
Having heard this, the Blessed Kṛṣṇa went silently out from his house.
When Nārāyaṇa had departed, the goddess of sound said to Gaṅgā:
"O shameless and lustful woman, you are obstructing Hari in his home!"
"Abounding in pride for my beauty and youth, I shall strike you; receive the fruit [of your actions]!
What will your lover do for you, O beloved of my lover?
Having thus reviled her, he raised his hand to seize the hair of Gaṅgā, who was intent on grasping it.
Then, having gone into their midst, Padmā restrained her [the goddess] who was composed of speech.
Enraged, she cursed Padmā: "You shall become a tree. She, being furious, cursed Gaṅgā: "You shall become a river. (15–16)
Having heard the curse and understood Viṣṇu’s maneuvering, those two goddesses did not utter that speech; rather, Gaṅgā spoke to Padmā:
"O Padmā, by her very nature, this Goddess of Speech is fickle and playful."
"She does not know what should or should not be said; I swear that she shall never speak!
And you, O Vāṇī, become a river; be barren except during your season. Let her always be devoid of menses and grant no desires. (18–19)
O beloved! Having thus received that curse, Sarasvatī was then [stricken].
In the meantime, the Blessed One arrived there;
having pacified the quarrel, he spoke to those distressed women.
"O beloved ones, do not grieve; this has come about solely by my will.
O Lakṣmī, go with a portion of yourself to the house of Dharmadhvaja.
Having become a daughter born not from a womb, you shall later [be revealed] under a pretext. (21–22)
"O Tulasī, after being born, you shall subsequently become the beloved of Śaṅkhacūḍa;
through the rites of marriage, you will become my wife.
By a portion of yourself, you shall become the river named Padmāvatī."
Then, O Gaṅgā! become a river that destroys the sins of embodied beings.
For the sake of the liberation of the oceans, become the beloved of the ocean.
O Sarasvatī! become the consort of Brahmā in the abode of Brahmā.
Become Sarasvatī in the form of a river, free from menstruation;
become the bestower of liberation, eternally devoted to celibacy.
At the end, I shall provide for your welfare and security as is appropriate.
"O my dear ones! You must not think that grief and delusion will carry me away.
(27) Three wives, three houses, three servants, and kinsmen—these are certainly adverse to well-being; indeed, they do not bestow auspiciousness. (28)
The birth of those householders in whose home the man is under the control of the woman— just as a woman [is controlled by a man]— is indeed fruitless and inauspicious at every step.
(29) He whose wife is corrupt of mouth, corrupt of womb, and fond of quarreling...

He should dwell in the forest and never indeed with a woman. (1.332.30) Dwelling in a place teeming with tigers is better than living in the house of a wicked woman. The flames of disease and poison are preferable to the fire from the mouth of a wicked woman. (31)

In this world, the life of a man conquered by a woman becomes fruitless; moreover, for many co-wives, a stable existence together is not auspicious. A man with a single wife may find happiness somewhere, but never one who has many wives.
Indeed, the husband of many wives is as good as dead while living, impure, and miserable. (33) Go to the abode of Śiva, O Gaṅgā! Go to the abode of Brahmā, O Sarasvatī!
Let Kamalā, the all-enduring one, remain here for my sake. (34)
"He whose wife is easy to manage, virtuous, and devoted to her husband—his is the happiness of heaven in this world, and dharma and liberation in the next.
Having spoken thus, Kṛṣṇa ceased; then they wept.
And they spoke, trembling, with tearful eyes and pained by the sorrow of separation:
"O Lord! Grant us that expiation which is appropriate for the three [offenses]. Show us favor so that there may be an end to the curse. (3.6–3.7)
"Having taken the form of rivers, when shall we behold your feet? How long will our stay there be, and when shall we meet you again?
I am Lakṣmī, known by the name Tulasī, the virtuous daughter of Dharmadhvaja. (38)
Having thus become the form of a tree, when shall I attain your state?
When will Gaṅgā [be freed] from the curse of Sarasvatī, and Sarasvatī from the curse of Gaṅgā; and when will they both obtain you?
"Therefore, O Lord, forgive me; do not send me to another place.
Having spoken thus, Kamalā took hold of her beloved’s feet and wept.
Placing that Prabhā upon his chest, the Compassionate One spoke to her.

"Let all three of them go to the earth in other forms, according to my word; however, let them remain here always in their divine forms—this is my wish. Indeed, those tasks for which they were intended must certainly be performed. (42–43)
Having brought those to completion, I myself shall indeed depart from here.
Let Padmāvatī take the form of a river, Tulasī the form of a tree, and Sarasvatī the form of a river;
let them go to another world.
"When four thousand years of the Kali age have passed, O best of rivers, you shall come to my abode again and again in every age.
Misfortune is the cause of prosperity, and suffering is the cause of happiness. (45–46)
The greatness of prosperity does not arise without adversity;
therefore, adversity must first be experienced, for it is indeed the price of prosperity.
These rivers were created by me for the purpose of destroying the sins of sinners.
By bathing in the presence of my virtuous devotees, your sins shall be destroyed.
By the touch and sight of my devotees, one attains the purity of countless sacred fords (*tīrtha*).
My devotees sanctify the entire earth with their every step.
Wherever my devotees reside, they wash their lotus feet;
that place becomes a great sacred ford (tīrtha) that delivers even sinners from worldly existence.
[Even those who are] killers of women, killers of cows, ungrateful, killers of Brahmins, or violators of the guru’s bed [are purified there].

One who violates vows, an atheist, a betrayer of trust, a destroyer of dharma, one who falsely slanders others, as well as a betrayer of friends or a misappropriator of deposits—such a person becomes purified by serving my devotee. By the mere sight of my devotee, they become pure. (5.1–5.2)
One who is uninitiated, unconsecrated, impure, a reviler of others,
and one who eats what has not been offered— such a person becomes purified by serving my devotees.
[53] [He purifies] his mother, father, wife, brother, son, and daughter.
He who does not support his guru, his family, his sister, those dependent upon him, his kinsmen and others,
his mother-in-law, his father-in-law, the elderly, and his wife— he shall become a sinner; yet he is purified by the touch and sight of my devotee.
Those who have stolen the wealth of gods, brahmins, and others, those who have sold their daughters,
and those who have caused the mixing of liquids— such people become purified by serving my devotees.
By association with them, may rivers always remain pure.
The earth is purified by the dust of their feet and by the water used for washing them;
all sacred fords are sanctified by the bathing and immersion of the virtuous.
The gods desire, in every way, the sight and the touch of such persons.
The meeting with Vaiṣṇavas is the supreme gain among all gains;
neither are sacred waters, nor earthly gods, nor sacrifices involving fire and the like, nor even meditations on the vital breaths equal to it. (59)
Oh, those devotees of Viṣṇu purify themselves in a mere moment after a long period of time!
(60) He into whose ear the excellent mantra of Viṣṇu enters from the mouth of a guru becomes a knower of the Vedas, the Vedāṅgas, and the Śāstras—an exceedingly supreme devotee of Viṣṇu. (61)

He at whose birth the denizens of hell attained liberation is a great devotee of Viṣṇu, the most excellent among all the excellent. By the mere fact of being born even as animals and other such beings, living creatures [attain this state].
Through union with whom they become liberated, that devotee of Viṣṇu is most excellent:
(63) one who is endowed with devotion to me, intent upon my worship, possessed of my qualities, worthy of praise for my qualities, absorbed in me, and consisting of me. (64)
Merely by hearing of my qualities, he is filled with bliss,
his hair stands on end, his voice falters, his eyes fill with tears, and he even forgets his own self.
He no longer desires happiness, nor liberation, nor even the fourfold state of *sālokya* and the rest.
"Those who desire to serve my feet day and night—such are my devotees, the virtuous and the saintly women who act for my sake;
they shall purify the rivers. Do not grieve, my beloveds."
"Let all depart, or let them remain in the form of water, trees, and so forth;
then the divine Sarasvatī herself stood at the feet of Hari.
By means of her second form, Sarasvatī became Brāhmī.
That goddess who presides over speech is celebrated here as the beloved of Brahmā. Then, impelled by Brahmā in the form of water,
she became the river Sarasvatī, a sacred ford that is exceedingly purifying.
Then Gaṅgā, possessing a divine form and consisting of water, emerged from the hollow of his egg-like forehead;
she was situated within Brahmā’s water-pot, touching his dwarf-sized thumb.
Brought down by Bhagīratha, she clung to the top of Śarva’s matted locks.
A portion of the world-purifying Sarit arrived;
she, a young woman of divine form, herself took her place at the feet of Hari.
And Padmā, through a portion of herself, became the auspicious river Padmāvatī.
By her second form, Lakṣmī was born in the house of Dharmadhvaja as a daughter named Tulasī, in the form of a maiden.
Indeed, Lakṣmī herself dwells there eternally in her divine form.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, has been told your former birth and your deeds.
She who was Vṛndā is Ramā-Lakṣmī; she who is Lakṣmī is Ramā;
she who is Ramā is Vṛndā-Lakṣmī; and she who is Lakṣmī is Vṛndikā.
In Vṛndāvana, Lakṣmī herself took the form of a tree; she alone became that very [Tulasī].
Then, cursed by Gaṇeśa, she became the beloved of Śaṅkhacūḍa.

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-second chapter, titled "The Description of how Gaṅgā, Sarasvatī, and Lakṣmī became rivers, and how Lakṣmī took the form of Tulasī, following their mutual curse for the sake of Rati among the wives of Śrī Kṛṣṇa in Goloka," within the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, in the narrative of the marriage of Tulasī.

Chapter 334 →
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O Keśava, tell me how and when did that Tulasī become the beloved of Śaṅkhacūḍa? And for what reason was she cursed by Gaṇeśa, and when did that happen?
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī! Having received the command of Hari, Padmasaṃbhavā became the river Padmāvatī, Lakṣmī herself in the form of a sacred ford. 2.

Once that beautiful maiden, radiant with the brilliance of youth, possessing lovely limbs and resembling heaven itself, became overwhelmed by desire. Devoted to Nārāyaṇa through her ascetic penance, she wandered at a sacred pilgrimage site. (3)
On the bank of the Gaṅgā, she beheld Gaṇeśa, endowed with youth;
exceedingly handsome, captivating to the heart, fragrant with the scent of sandalwood,
illuminated by excellent ornaments, and possessing a facial splendor that was intensely heart-stealing.
Tulasī said: "O Brahmin, you who possess beautiful and well-nourished limbs yet are free from desire—whom do you, full of longing, meditate upon?
Why is your belly so pendulous, and why is your face like that of an elephant? (6)
"Why do you meditate on the face of Hari with its single tusk?
Abandon this meditation, O well-nourished one; evening has arrived.
One should not remain alone at evening, at the onset of night."
Having spoken thus, she joined her palms together upon his belly;
consumed by the arrows of Kāma, she laughed again and again upon his cheeks,
temples, chest, and the region of his belly.

Then, even in the region below that, she touched him with the *karamudrā*. At that moment, his meditation was broken; and she, who is dear to Rati, struck his *liṅga* and her own hips in vain with the tip of her forefinger.
When his meditation was destroyed, Gaṇeśa’s anger became uncontrollable;
opening his eyes, he beheld the beautiful woman who was full of desire. She was endowed with fresh youth and filled with the impulse of passion.
Seeing her distressed, devoted to jests, and scorched by the forest fire of passion,
the compassionate Lambodara reflected for a moment:
"For it is the goodness of the virtuous that they remove the suffering of those who are afflicted."
How can I reject her who is tormented by the forest fire of desire? In rejecting her, there would be great suffering, and I would incur an undesirable consequence;
yet in accepting her, too, there is a great fault, namely that she would become pregnant. (15)
Therefore, having reflected upon this with the utmost humility, I shall console her—who is tormented by the impulse of desire—with words of peace:
"Come, O maiden, O female ascetic, you who are devoted to Nārāyaṇa! (16–17)
"Stay, sit in this comfortable place, and dwell here indeed in happiness.
What do you require—food, water, or something else? Tell me that.
"I am the god Lambodara, and I am the deformed Vṛndala."
"O Goddess, bathe in the water; remember Viṣṇu and remain steadfast.
Maintain your composure—blessings upon you—and my touch shall bring you well-being.
Come, let us bathe in this lake and then enjoy ourselves."
"May your distress be pacified; therefore, perform your bath and other rites.

Who are you, my child? Whose daughter are you? You possess the form of Lakṣmī, O auspicious one. You appear to me as one worthy of worship and salutation, like a Mother of the World. Tell me, who are you and how did this come to be?"

O wife of Kṛṣṇa! May Kṛṣṇa grant auspiciousness to both of us and destroy our obstacles; for the interruption of meditation is the destruction of the ascetic’s penance. Let not the mind be fickle, for fickleness causes the breaking of vows.
For those who meditate and observe vows, passion and desire cause the destruction of their vows;
therefore, the agitation of the senses must be especially endured.
A practitioner of austerity must, in particular, destroy all mental constructs (saṃkalpa).
"You are an ascetic woman of beautiful brows, O lady! And I am a practitioner of vows, possessed of meditative concentration.
We two are capable of conquering the mind and restraining desire itself.
Therefore, O Lakṣmī, wife of Kṛṣṇa! Do not perform this black deed."
"Be steadfast, O young girl; I am Gaṇeśa, conquer the hosts!
Hearing these words of Gaṇeśa, she, afflicted by the god of love, said to him:
"I am the daughter of the son of Dharma, and I have performed austerities for the sake of a husband. (27)
"The fruit of your asceticism is the attainment of a husband; become my master, my lord.
Hearing Tulasī’s words, he spoke to her while remembering Hari:
"O Mother, I have no desire for taking a wife, as it brings only suffering."
Taking a wife is a great net, a bond, and a house of strife;
the pursuit of sensual pleasure is an obstacle to attaining Hari and does not grant liberation.
Asceticism without fasting is considered a bolt upon the door of liberation.
She is the one who casts the noose around the neck, she who provides residence in the prison of the womb;
she is the destroyer of the knowledge of reality, the instiller of doubt, and the giver of birth.
She is the supreme mother of all rash acts and the casket containing all illusions.
One should not take refuge in faults that destroy the flow of desire. Turn back, O Great Illusionist! Seek another lover instead.
For only through union with a lover does a woman of desire obtain her goal.

Upon hearing this, the maiden Tulasī was deeply distressed and afflicted by desire. She said to Gaṇeśa: "Since you do not accept me even though I am devoted to you, by my curse your wife shall become one who does not worship you."
Then Gaṇeśa said to her, "You shall be seized by an asura;
later, you shall become a tree by my curse as well.
Having heard that curse, Tulasī wept, and the Gaṇa spoke to her.
"Do not weep, O my worshipful one! You shall become Puṣpasārā (Essence of Flowers).
Always tender, you shall become Patrasārā (Essence of Leaves) for Viṣṇu Kṛṣṇa.
And through your worship, Viṣṇu shall always be the bestower of liberation."
"I shall not eat your leaf, nor your flower-cluster, nor even your wood!
O fair-browed one, become the object of Kṛṣṇa’s enjoyment; prosperity shall be yours!
Having spoken thus, Gaṇeśa departed for the Badarikā forest.
Tulasī also went to Puṣkara, feeling deep inner anguish.
Having performed penance there, she subsequently became the beloved of Śaṅkhacūḍa.
Then that lord of the asuras was slain by the trident of Śaṅkara.
That beloved of Nārāyaṇa attained the state of a tree by a fraction of her portion;
and as a maiden, she was duly married to Nārāyaṇa.
Then she again obtained Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the dweller in Goloka.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have told you again of the return of Tulasī.
She was taken up by Hari; she is indeed the one with limbs like Hari’s, the wife of Hari.
O Lotus-born One, Tulasī washes away all sins.
Leaves, flowers, fruits, roots, branches, bark, and what is known as the trunk—
all these originating from the *tulasī*, as well as earth and other such items, are purifying.
Even the cremation of a corpse that is performed with wood from the *tulasī* tree [is purifying].
For one who has attained liberation, there is never again a return to this world.
(46) Even if a man is burdened with great sins or heinous crimes, if he is cremated with *tulasī* wood, he is liberated from the force of death. (47)
Even one who merely touches *tulasī* is liberated from all sins. For him whose name of Hari is uttered at death, for whom *tulasī* fuel-sticks are used in the cremation,
and for whom gifts to the Lord are made during the *śrāddha* ceremony, there is no return to this world.

If, while burning a heap of wood, there should remain even a single piece of wood, his sins are destroyed and he becomes destined for liberation. Just as waters mixed with the water of the Gaṅgā attain sanctity, [so too does that piece of wood]. || 1.333.50 ||
Words mixed with the name of Hari attain sanctity;
pieces of wood mixed with *tulasī* wood attain sanctity.
As long as a funeral pyre is kindled while mixed with *tulasī* wood, [so too does it become sacred]. (51)
His sins, accumulated over ten million kalpas, are consumed by fire.
Upon seeing a corpse upon which tulasī wood has been placed, the servants of Yama flee,
abandoning the man, and the attendants of Viṣṇu lead him away.
One who is joined with *tulasī* wood goes to the abode of Hari when liberated;
in the excellent heaven, the gods and apsarases honor and celebrate him who approaches with a handful of flowers and whose corpse dwells upon *tulasī*. (54)
Viṣṇu becomes exceedingly pleased with one who enjoys the company of Tulasī.
Wherever a fire made from Tulasī wood is kindled,
that ground destroys sin and takes the form of a sacred pilgrimage site (tīrtha).
Wherever there may be a fire sacrifice on a festival day using *vṛndā* wood,
for him there shall be the fruit born of the *agniṣṭoma* for every single piece of wood.
By offering incense of *tulasī* in the temple of Kṛṣṇa, one shall obtain [that same fruit].

The merit arising from the gift of a hundred cows is equal to the fruit of a hundred sacrifices. For one who offers to Keśava as an oblation food cooked on a fire kindled with Tulasī wood, the fruit shall be equal to Mount Meru. (58–59)
Even by offering a lamp to Viṣṇu with a Tulasī wick,
one gains the merit of thousands of lamps made with clarified butter. This applies to the giver of sandalwood paste produced from the wood of the Tulasī plant.
The Lord grants the station of Viṣṇu; Viṣṇu bestows equality with Himself.
One should worship Hari with sandalwood paste ground upon a *tulasī* leaf.
The grace of Hari, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, should be understood by him.
Anointed with *tulasī* and sandalwood paste, he performs the worship of Hari;
honored by *tulasī* in the abode of Hari, he indeed rejoices there.
He who, even in the offering of funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) to the ancestors, uses only a *tulasī* leaf—
To him who offers [these], there accrues here merit that bestows the happiness of enjoyment.
Furthermore, for the ancestors, satisfaction lasting a hundred years arises from the leaf or petal;
indeed, bathing with the earth of the *tulasī* plant is remembered as being equivalent to bathing at a sacred pilgrimage site (*tīrtha*). (64–65)
Whoever performs the worship of Viṣṇu with the fresh leaves and blossoms of the mañjarī,
by him a worship is performed with all flowers that bestows liberation.
The tulasī plant should be preserved, protected, and especially nourished within the home.
By seeing or touching it, sins such as the killing of a Brahmin are dissolved.
In whatever village, house, enclosure, or garden the *tulasī* plant may be found,
there Hari, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, dwells everywhere.
Wherever Tulasī is found in a house, there is no sickness;
nor is there fear, sorrow, poverty, or separation for the members of the family.
This is especially so when the planting of Tulasī is performed in a sacred field of the gods.
One obtains the merit arising from the nourishment of all trees planted; (1.333.70).
The gift of *tulasī* in a temple is superior to the gift of *lakṣmī*. By planting *tulasī* here, one attains happiness and, in the end, the abode of Hari. (71)
Indeed, the *tulasī* plant drives away portents that cause fear, bring about the loss of fortune, or are ill-omened, even when they have suddenly appeared.
The wind, mingled with the fragrance of *tulasī* leaves and other elements, [carries them far]. (72)
Wherever it purifies embodied beings in the ten directions—
where there is the yoga of the root of Vṛndā, there are Brahmā, Śiva, and Viṣṇu;
where there is the yoga of the leaves of Vṛndā, there is the circle of the gods and others.
Where there is contact with its blossoms, there the ṛṣis and sages are said to be present;
where there is water and *tulasī*, there the host of ancestors is said to be present;
and where there is even a stalk of *tulasī*, there indeed is Vaikuṇṭha itself.
Wherever there is a *maṇi* and *tulasī*, there is Hari accompanied by Lakṣmī.
Wherever there is the shadow of *tulasī*, there is eternal satisfaction for the ancestors.
Wherever there is a heap of *tulasī*, whatever is given there becomes eternal.

At its root Brahmā always resides, and Viṣṇu dwells upon its branches; Śambhu is present in its blossoms and so forth—thus Tulasī embodies the three gods. People should always plant Tulasī in a temple of Śiva.
For as many seeds as are produced from it each year, for that many yugas they enjoy unbroken heaven— whether on the eleventh day, the full moon, the new moon, or the day of their vow. (1.333.80)
During the auspicious time of a solar transit (saṃkrānti), one should offer *tulasī* at the temple;
one should plant it with great devotion and nurture it by watering it.
By worshipping it with offerings such as lamps, even a poor person shall become wealthy.
Wherever there may be a Śālagrāma stone or wherever there may be a Tulasī plant,
bathing, recitation, and giving of gifts there are more than a hundred times superior to those performed at Vārāṇasī;
they are more than a hundred times superior to those performed at Kurukṣetra, Prayāga, and Naimiṣa.
O Mahālakṣmī! That person who meets their death having kept Tulasī [nearby], Tulasī leads them to the abode of Hari. ॥84॥

Thus ends the three hundred and thirty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Marriage of Tulasī, the Journey of Padmāvatī—who had assumed the form of a young woman through the force of her youth—to Gaṇeśa in the guise of Lakṣmī, her entreaty to Kāma for him as a husband, the curse pronounced by Gaṇeśa that she become a tree and the wife of a demon, and the majesty of Tulasī," in the first section concerning the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga within the *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*. || 333 ||

Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O Tulasī, where was the beloved of Nārāyaṇa born?
In whose lineage was she born, and to which demon was she the wife? (1)
"By what austerity did she regain Nārāyaṇa as her husband?
O Hari, tell me in detail my story that has been forgotten by me.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
I shall speak; listen, O Lakṣmī, to your story beginning from Manu.
Though forgotten, I shall relate to you that which was brought to mind by way of your question.
Dakṣasāvarṇi Manu was indeed born as a partial incarnation (aṃśa) of Viṣṇu.
His son was Dharmasāvarṇi, and his son was Vaiṣṇava;
he is called Viṣṇusāvarṇi, and his son was indeed Vaiṣṇava. The son of this one was Devasāvarṇi, and Rājasāvarṇi was his offspring.
His son was Vṛṣadhvaja, who was devoted to Śiva;
for Śiva’s affection for Vṛṣadhvaja was even greater than that for his own son.
King Nārāyaṇa regarded neither Lakṣmī nor Sarasvatī as superior to him.
When he did not regard the sacrifice, the Sun-god, or the gods, as if intoxicated,
Ravi then cursed him, saying, "O King, may you be deprived of your fortune!
Thereupon, the king went quickly to Śiva for refuge in order to be protected.
Śambhu, taking up his trident, came to strike the Sun;
out of fear, the Sun fled and went to Brahmā for refuge.
Placing the Sun before him, Brahmā proceeded quickly to Vaikuṇṭha.
They bowed down to Nārāyaṇa and made their full report;
Nārāyaṇa, out of compassion, then granted them freedom from fear,
while Śiva, trident in hand, followed behind them in a rage.
Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa, he sat down upon the offered seat.
Nārāyaṇa said to Śiva, "Tell me the reason for your arrival.
Thereupon Mahādeva spoke to Hari, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
Sūrya cursed my devotee Vṛṣadhvaja, who is very dear to me.
Out of grief born from affection for my devotee, I went to kill Sūrya;
he, however, placing Brahmā at his head, has come to you for refuge.
Those who have sought refuge in you, whether through meditation or even by word alone, are free from calamity and devoid of fear; indeed, they have conquered old age and death.
But, O Nārāyaṇa, for one whose splendor has been destroyed by the curse of the Sun—
"O Lord of the World, tell me what will become of me, your devotee.
Nārāyaṇa said to Hara: "The bull-bannered one has arrived here;
his son, Haṃsadhvaja, is now also a king who has reached old age. (16–17)
O Hara, their two sons, Dharmadhvaja and Kuśadhvaja, are indeed Vaiṣṇavas; today they remain bereft of fortune along with their two wives.
Lakṣmī shall become my wife in two forms, and there will be two daughters.
"O best of kings, they shall both become endowed with perfection and devoted to me.
Half a *ghaṭikā* in Vaikuṇṭha is indeed equal to twenty-one *yugas* on earth; since this much time has passed, O Śambhu, there is nothing strange in this."
Having been addressed thus, they all departed to their respective places;
Vṛṣadhvaja, having returned to his own kingdom, met his end,
and Haṃsadhvaja also eventually met his death in due course of time.
Then, by means of fierce asceticism, the two kings Dharmadhvaja and Kuśadhvaja propitiated Nārāyaṇa and obtained their desired boon:
"The Goddess Lakṣmī shall certainly become the daughter of you both in two forms."
"By her power, you two shall become endowed with the most excellent kingdoms.
Then the two of them performed the worship of Lakṣmī.
And as she became pleased by their vow, Lakṣmī spoke to them regarding a boon.

"May you two be wealthy, possessed of sons, lords of the earth, and endowed with prosperity; by the grace of Nārāyaṇa, may you be honored by kings. Flooded with this blessing, they replied, "So be it."
"O Lotus-born one, make the statement 'endowed with Śrī' come true. Having thought thus, Lakṣmī then assumed a twofold form.
In due time, she was born as a daughter in the house of Kuśadhvaja, bringing prosperity.
The beloved wife of Kuśadhvaja gave birth to a daughter born from a portion of Kamalā.
As soon as she was born, the maiden uttered the sound "Veda";
therefore, she attained fame by the name Vedavatī at that very moment.
Having paid homage to her parents, she went to a virtuous forest for penance.
While performing austerities at Puṣkara, that virtuous woman heard a voice from the sky:
"In another birth, Hari himself shall become your husband."
Having heard this, she became angry once more and performed penance again.
Taking refuge on Mount Gandhamādana, she remained there for a long time and practiced austerities.
There, she saw before her a brahmin named Rāvaṇa.

Having paid homage to her guest, she offered him water for his feet, fruit, water, and other refreshments; yet that wicked man became truly agitated in mind. Seizing her by the hand, he prepared to engage in sexual union with her.
Vedavatī, with a glance of anger, paralyzed him;
she then cursed him, saying, "For my sake, you shall perish along with your kinsmen.
Having spoken thus, that virtuous woman dissolved her body and vanished from sight.
She was Vedavatī, the daughter of the Earth and the joy of Janaka,
who became the goddess Sītā for whose sake Rāvaṇa was slain;
she is indeed Lakṣmī, and you yourself were she in all ways throughout other kalpas.
"You shall become Sītā in form, and I shall become Rāma.
Indeed, this has been ordained by me for the destruction of the Rākṣasas;
for there is no other cause for the destruction of those characterized by darkness (tamas) than you."
The great ascetic Lakṣmī obtained Hari as her husband Rāma;
remembering her former births, she endured only suffering.
By the command of his father Śataratha, Rāma [went] to the forest.
He indeed went together with Sītā and his younger brother Lakṣmaṇa.
There Rāma beheld the Fire-god in the form of a brahmin.
The Blessed Fire-god said: "For he is the one who shall bring about the end of Rāvaṇa."
The appointed time has arrived by way of Sītā’s abduction.
I am Agni, sent by the gods and assuming the form of a brahmin.
Having entrusted Sītā to me, you must indeed take her shadow-Sītā.
"I shall give Sītā back at the appointed time, once my son has been tested.
Upon hearing those words, Rāma immediately acted accordingly;
Lakṣmaṇa did not even realize it—what need is there to mention anyone else?
In the meantime, Rāma saw a golden deer;
out of Sītā’s insistence, he indeed went after it to destroy it.
Lakṣmaṇa also followed behind, while Rāvaṇa carried Sītā away.
That attendant named Vijaya, having died in battle,
went once again to the state of a preta; then Jaya, though he was of the same color (savarna), also died within the conflict and went to the state of a preta for the sake of the third birth.
By Rāma’s arrow, many rākṣasas were slain in Laṅkā;
Vibhīṣaṇa became his devotee, and Hari gave him the kingdom.
Then, for the sake of purification, Rāma performed an ordeal by fire.
There, Hutāśana gave him the real Jānakī.
The Blessed One said to Chāyā, "Go to Puṣkara, my dear;
having performed penance there, you shall become the Fortune of Heaven."
Having performed austerities for ten thousand years, she indeed became Lakṣmī in heaven;
that very Lakṣmī shall be born as Draupadī in the sacrificial pit.
In the Satya Yuga, she was Vedavatī, the daughter of Kuśadhvaja.
In the Tretā age, she was Sītā, the daughter of Janaka and the wife of Rāma;
at the end of the Dvāpara age, she will be the goddess Draupadī;
and in the Kali age, she will be the goddess Māṇikī, devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa.
Thus, in age after age, there arises an ascent of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
This which has been told to you is the first form; now hear the second.
The wife of Dharmadhvaja was renowned as Mādhavī.
On the peak of Gandhamādana, she became pregnant;
on the full moon day of the month of Kārtika, she gave birth to a daughter, Padminī,
whose pair of lotus-feet shone with rubies.
To Lakṣmī, the queen of the kings of kings, beautiful in every limb,
endowed with the marks of royal fortune, the presiding deity of royal splendor—
moon-faced, with eyes like lotus petals and auspicious lips red as the bimba fruit.
With palms and soles of the feet reddish, with a deep navel and three folds [on her belly],
possessing the hue of a white campaka flower— she whom they named Tulasī because the comparison (tulana) of other women fails when set against her; she was his daughter.
As soon as she was born, that exceedingly beautiful young woman smiled;
she was certain within herself: "Nārāyaṇa shall be my husband.
To attain Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, she went to the Badarī forest.
There she performed supreme penance for a long time;
that maiden practiced the "five-fire" austerity in the summer, remained standing in water during the winter,
and endured the downpour of rain while performing penance during the monsoon.
First eating fruits, then eating leaves, then subsisting on water, then subsisting on air,
and finally fasting entirely, she remained standing on one leg.
Seeing her long-standing and fierce austerity, Brahmā arrived.
When Brahmā arrived there at Badarikāśrama to grant a boon, she bowed down to him; Brahmā then spoke to her:
"Choose a boon, O Tulasī, whatever is desired in your heart! (64–65)

"Listen, dear one! Devotion to Kṛṣṇa, liberation, or even immortality—formerly, in the supreme abode of Goloka, I was situated there as the wife of Kṛṣṇa, His servant, His partial expansion, His companion, and His beloved. (66)
At that time, I myself became Ramā, Vṛndā, and Lakṣmī.
Then, out of anger, Rādhikā cursed me, her servant, who was in the form of Ramā—Vṛndā, whose mind was attached to Govinda and who was situated in the state of amorous delight. || 67-68 ||
In that very same way, he cursed both Vāṇī and me, Padmā, once again:
"Go to a human womb; I remember this from my former birth.
Then, in the past, Gaṇeśa cursed both Padmāvatī and me.
"Go to the state of a tree," he said, "and likewise become the wife of a Daitya.
But after the curse was over, Kṛṣṇa spoke joyfully with a smile in Goloka:
"O Lakṣmī, Sudāmā, who is a portion of myself, was indeed my own attendant!"
He too, by the curse of Rādhā, will become Śaṅkhacūḍa;
you shall be his wife according to the prediction spoken by Gaṇeśa.
Then, after performing penance for me, you will obtain him—of this there is no doubt.
"I desire to obtain now as my husband my ancient beloved Nārāyaṇa; grant me this boon. Since I am one who remembers her past lives, I know all that has been told to you. (73–74)
"Therefore, O Brahman, pronounce a curse such that it may be appropriate.
Brahmā then said, "O beautiful Lakṣmī, you know everything;
you yourself remember your past lives and are the daughter of Dharmadhvaja."
"That asura Śaṅkhacūḍa has now been born on earth as Sudāmā.
O beautiful lady, become his wife now;
afterwards, you shall obtain Nārāyaṇa, Kṛṣṇa himself, as your husband."
O Tulasī, you shall become a tree in Vṛndāvana;
you shall be the foremost of all flowers and shall become a purifier.
Indeed, without you, the worship of all [deities] would be as fruitless.
In this way, Kṛṣṇa will make you, his beloved, dearer even than his own life.
In Vṛndāvana, you shall indeed become the tree named Vṛndā or Vṛndāvanī;
with your leaves, people will worship Keśava.
In that manner, you shall dwell constantly with him;
you, O fortunate one, shall become equal to Rādhā for Govinda.
You shall become as dear to Kṛṣṇa as his own life, and equal to Rādhikā in being his very breath.
Having heard this, Tulasī said, "Let it be so; act quickly.
Then Brahmā spoke to Lakṣmī the supreme mantra for the purpose of recitation:
"Oṃ, I surrender myself to Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa; obeisances! (82–83)
Having thus bestowed [the boon] enriched by sixteen syllables, he vanished from sight;
she too recited that mantra at the holy Badarikāśrama.
In a short time, through that mantra, the perfection of her asceticism was attained.
With a serene mind, she beheld Kṛṣṇa before her.
Kṛṣṇa said to Tulasī: "O beloved, the perfection of your penance has been attained;
from this day forward, having become the wife of a personal attendant (pārṣada), you shall attain me."
Having spoken thus, he vanished from sight; she too abandoned that penance, and having eaten and drunk to her satisfaction, she slept upon a beautiful bed. (87)

Thus ends the three hundred and thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Sun’s Curse upon Vṛṣadhvaja of the Lunar Lineage during the Marriage of Tulasī," within the account of the marriage of Tulasī in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. It describes how, through prayer in Vaikuṇṭha, Lakṣmī became known as Sītā in the house of Kuśadhvaja of that lineage, while Lakṣmī became known as Tulasī in the house of Dharmadhvaja; and it further details Tulasī’s penance at Badarī and its successful fulfillment.
