Śrī Lakṣmī said:
"O Lord, what then happened to Tulasī in the forest named Badarī?
O Master, O Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, remover of distress, tell all of that to me."
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen; I shall tell you what happened afterwards—understand me.
Everything has been forgotten by you, so I shall remind you of it exactly as it occurred.
Sleeping upon her auspicious bed, she indeed beheld a vision for a moment. In that dream, Tulasī saw Sudāmā arrive;
he whom she perceived in the dream was none other than the one named Śaṅkhacūḍa.
Having taken him by the hand, she kissed his hand;
then, under the influence of delusion, he suddenly vanished from sight.
She quickly became wide awake and for a moment fell into a state of agitation.
For a moment she was consumed by fire; for a moment she fell into heedlessness;
for a moment she regained consciousness; for a moment she was overcome with despondency.
For a moment she rose from her bed; in the next moment she moved toward him.
For a moment she wandered about in agitation, and in another moment she entered her home.
For yet another moment, out of great distress, she fell asleep;
then, once more in her sleep, she saw that well-attired man.
He was handsome, youthful, and smiling, the Lord of Rasikas;
he was recounting the story of the Sun and kissing [her] again and again.
He lay well-reclined upon her couch, embracing her with great affection.
Then, as he was departing once more, the virtuous woman spoke to him:
"Where are you going, O one as dear as my own life? Stay! she said to him. Having regained her composure, she lamented, longing for him.
Thus she attained a destined state there in that penance grove.
At that time, however, the yogi Śaṅkhacūḍa,
having obtained from the sage Jaigīṣavya at Puṣkara the perfection born of mantra and austerity, [proceeded].
Having received the boon from Brahmā and by the command of the Creator,
he went to that Badarī where that Tulasī resided.
And [he saw] a youth approaching, whose splendor was equal to that of Kāmadeva.
Beholding Śaṅkhacūḍa— resembling the color of a white campaka flower, adorned with all ornaments, handsome, with very firm limbs,
wearing earrings, a tilaka mark, and a necklace, and appearing fresh— she [was struck with wonder]. (15)
Having determined it was Sudāmā, she considered him to be Śaṅkhacūḍa.
Looking at him, she became bashful with her face cast down;
covering her face with her garment, she was abashed by this first union.
With her eyes fixed upon his lotus-like face, she was filled with horripilation. Śaṅkhacūḍa also, seeing that large-eyed woman standing there veiled by her garment, recognized her as Tulasī.
With the palms and soles of her feet reddened and surrounded by her own radiance,
she was full-limbed, golden-hued, and in the bloom of fresh youth;
she bore a line of vermilion upon her braid, which was adorned with jasmine flowers.
Seeing her—graceful, with beautiful teeth, virtuous, and her forearms adorned with bracelets—he reflected and spoke to her with deep emotion:
"Who are you, O lovely woman? Whose daughter are you, this enchantress of sages?"
"If you consider it right, please engage in conversation with me, who have come to you having abandoned my vow of silence.
Hearing this, she, with a face of humble smile, spoke to him with desire:
"I am the daughter of Dharmadhvaja, and I am established in ascetic practice."
"Go wherever you wish to go; who are you to ask such an improper question?
One born of noble family does not question a woman who is alone and in private. One should never, even in one's heart, direct [such thoughts] toward a group of women upon merely seeing them. (24)
An offense would arise therein only if it were done against one's will.
[25] In the heart it is like the edge of a razor, yet on the tongue it consists of sweet syllables; sweet at first appearance, it is like Death’s grasp in the end. [26]

Resembling the fruit of the *indravallī*, she is pleasant on the outside but inauspicious within; for her own sake, she remains dependent on her master, yet always seeks refuge elsewhere afterwards. Outwardly, she appears detached through guile, while inwardly she is greedy for enjoyments and the like.
Externally, she is called "not so" (neti), yet internally she is full of desire, ever-new and ever-fresh.
Externally, she is proclaimed as the virtuous wife of one's own self with great effort;
she is of the nature of extreme daring and likewise the locus of all faults. (28–29)
It is the bolt on the path of austerity and the door-leaf of the gate to liberation;
it acts as an obstacle to devotion for Hari and takes the form of a shackle.
It is like a magical illusion, a proponent of false doctrines.
"Men should not place their trust in one who is not a ground for confidence.
Having spoken thus with deep emotion, she, being exceedingly tender-hearted, fell silent.
Then Śaṅkhacūḍa said to her: "First, [tell me of] that excellent ground of confidence."

Having recognized her as one full of desire and having observed that she was like one who has feasted in a dream, listen: the Creator fashioned the female form in two ways throughout the three worlds.
That which is of the nature of a *kṛtyā* is deceptive and always a source of suffering.
Indeed, the form of Satī is truly praiseworthy, and not the locus of the defects you have described.
Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Durgā, Sāvitrī, Māṇikī, Prabhā, Pārvatī, Rādhikā, Kṛṣṇā, Ramā, Padmā, Jayā, and others [are likewise]. (34–35)
These and others were their portions— honorable, virtuous, and devoted to their husbands:
Śatarūpā, Devahūtī, Svadhā, Svāhā, Kaṃbharā, Dakṣiṇā,
Rohiṇī, Chāyā, Saṃjñā, Śacī, and Vāruṇī.
Kuberāṇī, Pavanānī, Aditi, and Diti; Lopāmudrā, Anasūyā, Muktā, Tulasī, Kaiṭabhī;
Ahalyā, Arundhatī, Menā, Tārā, Mandodarī, and Dayā. (37–38)
Damayantī, Vedavatī, Vṛndā, Gaṅgā, Yamī, Manu;
Puṣṭi, Tuṣṭi, Smṛti, Medhā, Ṣaṣṭhī, Kālī, Vasundharā;
Caṇḍī, Mūrti, Svasti, Śraddhā, Śānti, Kānti, and Tuṣṭikā. (39)
These virtuous women have been born in every age as the refuge of the gods.
A man born of noble lineage does not inquire after another’s wife, who is like a ritual act performed for a malevolent purpose;
yet, knowing you to be Tulasī who remembers her past lives, I have come to you.
"I am Sudāmā, formerly a servant of Hari born in the lineage of Danu; I am Śaṅkhacūḍa, who remembers my past lives, and I have come here by the command of Brahmā.
O beautiful one, I shall take you as my wife through the Gāndharva rite."
Having heard those words, Tulasī began to speak:
"Indeed, you were tested by me for the sake of awakening [my] understanding of the power of knowledge (*vidyā*).
For a loving woman chooses a husband only after she has conducted an examination of him. (43–44)
A daughter should be given to one who is peaceful, virtuous, young, and learned, as well as to a Vaiṣṇava; this shall yield the fruit of ten horses.
[But] to a bridegroom who is devoid of virtue, old, and likewise ignorant...
To one who is poor, foolish, diseased, and contemptible;
to one who is excessively prone to anger and exceedingly foul-mouthed;
to one who is lame, deformed in limb, blind, and deaf. (46–47)
It must certainly not be given to one who is dull-witted, mute, like a eunuch, sinful, or addicted to vices; otherwise, one would fall into the Kubhīpāka hell.
In the meantime, O Lotus-born One, Brahmā arrived there.
Śaṅkhacūḍa bowed his head and prostrated before Tulasī.
Brahmā then said to the Gandharva, "Perform the marriage ceremony;
may there always be happiness free from conflict in your union."
The jewel of a woman and the jewel of a man, when united, become filled with bliss—
just as Lakṣmī is with Lakṣmīśa, and Rādhikā with Kṛṣṇa;
just as Sāvitrī is with me, and Bhavānī with Śiva.
As the Earth is to Varāha, as Menā is to Himālaya;
as Anasūyā is to Atri, as Damayantī is to Nala;
as Rohiṇī is to the Moon, and as Rati is to Kāma—so was Satī. (52–53)
Just as Diti was to Kaśyapa and Arundhatī to Vasiṣṭha;
as Ahalyā was to Gautama and Devahūtī to Kardama;
as Tārā was to Bṛhaspati and Śatarūpā was to Manu.
Just as Dakṣiṇā is to the sacrifice, as Svāhā is to the Fire-god;
as Śacī is to Mahendra, as Puṣṭi is to Gaṇeśvara;
as Devasenā is to Skanda, and as Mūrti is to Dharma; so [is she] to him. (55–56)
As Kaṃbharā was devoted to her husband Gopāla,
so may you, O Vṛndā Tulasī, be truly devoted to Śaṅkhacūḍa.
As Pārvatī was devoted to Prabhā-Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, so may you be likewise.
After enjoying happiness for a long time, you will undoubtedly become a *tulasī* tree for the sake of Śaṅkhacūḍa’s liberation;
then Kṛṣṇa will take you away from there according to the rites of marriage.
Having thus bestowed this blessing and united the couple through the Gāndharva form of marriage, Viśvasṛj indeed departed for Satyaloka. In heaven, kettledrums resounded and a rain of flowers fell.
In Rōma, upon the bed of Tulasī, Śaṅkhacūḍa, the beloved of Hari,
attained a swoon as he was united with Tulasī in a new union;
[she experienced] the sixty-four arts and the sixty-four kinds of pleasure.
The Lord of Connoisseurs performed all those erotic delights, which were enchanting to women and preceded by the joining of limbs and members;
she too served him for many years, saying, "I am your slave."
In forests, on mountains, by rivers, in oceans, in the sky, and on Mount Raivata, as well as on the golden Mount Meru, she performed service for him; Śaṅkha departed with her.
By the power of his asceticism, he established a kingdom on the banks of the Candrabhāgā.
Having brought the kings under his control, he enjoyed the earth together with her;
supported by the Daityas, Rākṣasas, and Dānavas,
he seized the kingdoms of the gods and installed those Asuras in them.
The gods, deprived of their authority, wandered about like beggars.
Śaṅkha, the Dānava, seized their station, their worship, and their nectar; the gods became devoid of effort, like painted dolls. (67–68)
But they all, dejected, went to the assembly of Brahmā;
they related the account and wept profusely and greatly.
Then Brahmā, together with the gods, went into the presence of Śaṅkara.
Then Brahmā related everything to that Śaṅkara.
All the deities, led by Brahmā and Īśa, went eagerly to Vaikuṇṭha;
they entered the assembly hall, which was beautifully adorned with the Lord’s attendants and others.
Having conciliated the four-armed attendants and gatekeepers—
who were dark-complexioned, marked with the signs of the conch and discus, clad in yellow garments,
and stationed at the sixteen doors— he passed them and stood before the city of Hari.

They went to Śrī Hari, who is served by hosts of gods and four-armed attendants in the form of Nārāyaṇas adorned with the kaustubha gem. That divine assembly hall, inhabited by Nārāyaṇa, shines with great splendor.
Shaped like the orb of the full moon, illuminated by the light of the finest lordly jewels, it was adorned with pearls, rubies, diamonds, and other gems set in gold.
Its sides featured mirrors rich with precious stones, and it was decorated with various and wonderful paintings. (75)
It was enchanting, with fully blossomed lotuses made of rubies;
it was adorned with hundreds of beautiful staircases made of the Syamantaka gem; and its pillars were fashioned from gold-threaded cloth and leaf-patterns. ||76-77||
It was resplendent with jars filled with the seven precious gems and adorned with networks of garlands;
it was sprinkled with musk, saffron, lotus-water, and sandalwood paste;
it was scented with fragrant perfumes and made resonant by the songs of Vidyādharīs.
Extending for a thousand yojanas and accompanied by perfected sages and their retinues, they beheld there in the center Śrī Hari shining resplendent;
and the divine throne of Hari, made of jewels and gold, shone brilliantly. (1.335.80)
There he beheld the auspicious Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa,
wearing earrings, a crown, and adorned with a forest garland, a discus, a lotus, and other ornaments; four-armed, dark as a rain cloud, and graced with every kind of jewel.
Beholding him whose forehead was adorned with sandalwood paste as he watched the dance and song;
the Lord of Vāṇī, Lakṣmī, Ramā, Prabhā, Māṇikī, and Pārvatī;
served by Gaṅgā, Jayā, Vijayā, Maṅgalā, Amṛtā, and others.
Having seen that distinguished, beautiful, and lovely [palanquin], resplendent with the glory of a king of kings and adorned with parasols and chowries, they prostrated themselves like a staff and,
their limbs bristling with joy, praised him with devotion and voices choked with emotion. (84)

Then Brahmā, the knower of all states of being, having heard that account, laughed and spoke to the gods: "The Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa [is the master] of the cowherd Śaṅkhacūḍa, my devotee who knows the ancient truths. (85–86)
"I know the entire account: my attendant Sudāmā [became] Śaṅkhacūḍa, who, due to Rādhā’s curse, attained the womb of a demon.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
Tell me, how did Rādhā bestow a curse upon that devotee of mine?
For by your will alone do birth, nourishment, dissolution, and so forth come to pass.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī: once I indeed went to the circle of the Rāsa dance,
leaving behind the proud Rādhā— who is dearer to me than life and dwells in my heart—
having taken with me my wife Virajā, who follows me with great affection.
When Rādhā learned from the mouth of her maidservant that I was united with Virajā,
she arrived there in a state of anger where I was joined with Virajā;
for it was at that very time that I was indeed enjoying myself in the rāsa dance with Virajā.
Seeing this, she became exceedingly enraged as if it were something most undesirable;
she then said to Virajā, "Become here indeed in the form of a river.
Thereupon, I merged into that Virajā.
But having realized that Virajā was in the form of a river and that I had vanished,
she then turned back from the circle of the *rāsa* dance and went to her own abode;
I, however, came there to my pavilion and to my palace.
Having arrived right there in the presence of Sudāmā, his beloved severely rebuked me; Sudāmā became enraged at her,
and he in turn rebuked her, while she also became angry with him.
Rādhā said to me: "O fool! O lustful one! O servant of Kṛṣṇa!
By acting exactly according to your name, you have indeed disgraced the Queen of the Rāsa dance.
O Kṛṣṇa! O gambler who has stolen the hearts of women, how are you not ashamed? (96–97)
Indeed, there is no other dog equal to a queen; how can you have such friendship with a dog? You are not ashamed, like a dog yourself.
Go from the kingdom of Goloka and dwell in the house of Virajā.
"I have no concern with you here; you are entirely one whose nature is deceitful.
Arise from this seat and go toward that Virajā.
Let her lick [you] constantly; do not come near me at any time. || 1.335.100 ||
When Rādhā had spoken thus and was filled with anger, Mādhava said nothing to her.
Sudāmā, however, said: "O Mother, why do you boast in this manner?
Such a disregard for the King and his Queen, who are worthy of worship, is truly improper. (101)
"Subdue your anger—blessings be upon you—and do not speak such things again.
Then Rādhā, becoming exceedingly enraged, rebuked her devoted devotee Sudāmā: "O fool! O lowest of men, who takes refuge at Kṛṣṇa's back! (102–103)
"You are base, you are a mere servant; how then can you restrain me?
You surely and constantly teach him all manner of crookedness.
O rogue! O practitioner of yoga with a woman who desires only you! O lecher!"
"Go quickly from this abode and become a Dānava on earth!
Your master delights with many women, deceiving them again and again;
and you, out of lust, gaze upon Lakṣmī with side-long glances from your eyes."

"There is no fitness for you to dwell here, O deceiver!"—having been addressed with these and other words, Sudāmā, taking refuge in the heart of Kṛṣṇa, then spoke to Rādhā: "O crafty woman! O lustful one! O lecher! || 107 ||
O jealous woman! O cat! O chachundarī! O dog! Are you not ashamed?
(1.08) O house-lizard! Out of pride you do not even acknowledge anyone; and yet, O slut, you revile even your husband, the Lord of All! (1.09)

"O barren one! O you whose fruit is barren! O you who are intent on your own ends! O you who are devoid of luster! O you who speak what should not be spoken! O image of metal! O puppet! O barking dog! O delusion! Who are you, O Govālī, unworthy and deserving of beating in the house of Hari? (1.335.11)
O fiercely blazing one! O calamitous one! O inauspicious one who is devoid of the sacred tradition!
Go, you who are spread out like a beast, outside the very boundaries of Goloka! O Queen! O you who are equal to a she-demon! O you whose conduct brings about the destruction of the home! 111–112.
"Fall down! Go to the earth, O you who dwell in the forest!
You are of the same nature as dung-mixtures, one who has gone to a family devoid of dharma. Act in such a way that you shall never again behave in this manner. (11.3)
"O you who deserve punishment! O you who insult your master! Be intent on insulting [us]!
When he had spoken thus, Lord Keśava consoled him and consoled Rādhā; nevertheless, she found no peace.
She gave orders to her circle of friends to cast Sudāmā out; then the friends expelled Sudāmā from Kṛṣṇa’s house. Rādhā, having received the curse, wept excessively, utterly overwhelmed.
But Sudāmā, having been cursed by her, departed from the borders of Goloka.
The gopīs and gopas wept and tried to restrain him;
they likewise restrained her, and he and she [restrained] each other.
Nevertheless, what was done out of a desire for Kṛṣṇa shall not come to pass; it will be false.
After that, O beloved, Rādhikā was informed by me there:
"She will arrive within half a moment after fulfilling the curse."
Half a moment of Goloka shall constitute one *manvantara*.
Then that Śaṅkhacūḍa will return once again to this very place.
And you, O Rādhā, who are the embodiment of Ramā, Padmā, Lakṣmī, and Sarasvatī— ||| 1.335.1 20 || ... ||| 121 ||
At the end of the Dvāpara age, you shall become my wife Rādhikā;
I too shall come from the heaven-dwellers, such as Brahmā and others,
for the sake of fulfilling their resolve, and I shall lead them to my own abode.
Thus has the history of the Daitya named Śaṅkha been told to you.
He certainly protects my armor, together with the mantra, upon his neck;
therefore, by that means, he becomes invincible and a conqueror of the world.
"Taking my trident, let this Śiva go toward him;
I, indeed, shall beg for that armor in the guise of a Brahmin.
When I cause the violation of his wife's chastity through a stratagem,"
Then his death will be certain; of this there is no doubt. (126) At that time, Śaṅkhacūḍa must be slain by him with this trident. When her husband is killed, Tulasī shall become my beloved. (127)

Having spoken thus and having given the trident to Hara, Mādhava entered his inner chamber, and the gods departed for their own abodes. Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have related to you the life-story of Sudāmā exactly as it occurred.
"And due to a quarrel with Rādhā, he previously became a Dānava.

(1.29) Thus, in the first book of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, within the section on the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga, in the narrative of Tulasī’s marriage: Tulasī’s vision of Sudāmā—who was Śaṅkhacūḍa in essence—in her dream; Śaṅkhacūḍa’s journey to Badarī; the Gāndharva marriage following the dialogue between Tulasī and Śaṅkhacūḍa; the gods oppressed by Śaṅkhacūḍa going to Vaikuṇṭha; and Nārāyaṇa [explaining] the mutual curse previously incurred by Sudāmā, Virajā, and Rādhā.

He caused it to be heard: "Sudāmā has become Śaṅkhacūḍa; the offering of the trident to Hara for the sake of destroying Śaṅkhacūḍa," and so forth. This is the three hundred and thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description [of these events]," from the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Book 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga), Chapter 335.
Chapter 336.
[Author: Chapter 337.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Taking up his trident, Śiva [stood] on the bank of the river Candrabhāgā.
Assuming another form, Hara made his own dwelling beneath the banyan tree;
having appointed the attendant Puṣpadanta, the best of the Gandharvas, as his messenger, he sent him with respect to the presence of the gods.
The attendant also went toward the city of Śaṅkhacūḍa,
which was five yojanas wide and ten yojanas long,
and was surrounded by walls made entirely of crystal stone.
It was well-protected by seven moats filled with water.
(4) In the center, easily accessible to the people, he beheld the excellent abode of Śaṅkhacūḍa, which was circular in shape and guarded by four ramparts. (5)
It was resplendent with twelve gates guarded by gatekeepers,
and beautified by palaces made of jewels, pearls, mirrors, gems, and gold.
It was constantly protected on all sides by Dānavas of heroic lineage.
Puṣpadanta entered through the nine gates and went inside.
There, he was recognized by the gatekeeper as a messenger;
Śaṅkhacūḍa summoned him to learn the news.
Puṣpadanta beheld the splendid abode of Śaṅkhacūḍa;
in its center was a golden throne, surrounded by courtyards adorned with gems and beautified by jeweled flowers and the like. (9)
Where millions of Dānavas roam about, bearing weapons,
[he] spoke to Śaṅkhacūḍa, his former friend, who was resplendent upon a golden throne beautifully adorned with a parasol, chowries, and other regalia.
O Indra among kings! I am a messenger of Śiva, named Puṣpadanta.
Listen as I speak that which has been spoken by Śaṅkara himself:
"Give up your kingdom and surrender your authority over the gods."
"Grant them a domain, or certainly provide them with battle.
Having gone there, what shall I say to Śambhu? You ought to tell him that.
Laughing, Śaṅkhacūḍa indeed spoke to him for the sake of combat.
"I shall come at dawn; go and tell Śaṅkara.
Puṣpadanta went to the banyan tree and spoke to Śambhu exactly as he had been instructed. Then, summoned by Śiva, the lords of the Gaṇas arrived there.
Skanda, Gaṇeśvara, Vīrabhadra, Nandin, Subhadraka;
Mahākāla, Viśālākṣa, Bāṇa, Piṅgākṣa, Kampana; Virūpa, Vikṛti, Maṇibhadra, Vikara, and Bāṣkala. (16–17)
Kapilākṣa, Dīrghadaṃṣṭra, Balībhadra, Kuṭīcara, Kālaṃṭaka, Kālajihva, Tāmrākṣa, Durjaya,
and Agama; [there were] the eight Bhairavas, the eleven Rudras, and the eight Vasus.
The twelve Ādityas, as well as Vahni, Candra, and the two Aśvins;
Viśvakarman, Kubera, Yama, and Nalakūbara; Vāyu, Jayanta, Varuṇa, Budha, Dharma, and Maṅgala. (1.336.20)
Śani, Īśa, and Kāma, as well as other preeminent leaders of the Gaṇas;
Ugradraṃṣṭrā, Ugracaṇḍā, Koṭarī, and Kaiṭabhī;
Bhadrakālī, Caṇḍī, Kālī, and likewise Kātyāyanī.
Then, remembering Śambhu, they arrived there dancing,
bearing tridents, spears, mallets, conchs, discs, clubs, arrows, thunderbolts,
swords, bows, shields, maces, iron bludgeons, and other such weapons.
And they, bearing [their weapons], carried staves, stones, and barburu trees;
the Vaiṣṇava weapon, the Vāruṇa weapon, the Āgneya weapon, and the Nāgapāśaka;
the Nārāyaṇa weapon, the Brahmāstra, as well as the Gāndharva and the Gāruḍa.
The Pārjanya, the Pāśupata, and the Pārvata for the purpose of paralyzing;
the Māheśvara weapon, the Vāyavya, the Daṇḍa, and likewise the Sammohana—these the Yoginīs, Ḍākinīs, and Vikaṭās were bearing. ||25-26||
Bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, kūṣmāṇḍas, brahmarākṣasas,
vetālas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and kinnaras—
all gathered at the abode of Hara for the purpose of destroying Śaṅkhacūḍa and the others.
Having bowed to Hara there, Skanda sat down beneath the banyan tree.
Śaṅkhacūḍa also told Tulasī the story related by the messenger during the night,
saying that he must go toward Śaṅkara for battle in the morning.
Upon hearing the news of the battle, Tulasī’s face became parched;
overcome with grief and her heart burning with anguish, she said:
"O Lord, my right limbs are throbbing here, which is not auspicious."
And last night, I saw a bad dream: a buffalo as a vehicle;
a palace destroyed from its very foundations, fallen and filled with water;
and then fire was born again, just as it remains in the remaining forest. (3.1–3.2)
"I was carried off by someone and brought to this dwelling among the branches of a tree. O Lord, has the end of my life or even the end of my prosperity arrived?
My vital breaths tremble within me, and my mind seems as if lost. (33)
Having thus heard the words of Tulasī, and having eaten and drunk,
Śaṅkhacūḍa spoke to her at the appropriate time:
"O beloved, everything joined with Time comes to pass."
Auspiciousness, joy, happiness, suffering, fear, grief, and inauspiciousness—
just as trees are produced at the proper time, bear fruit, and wither away;
so too are eggs and living beings, and even Brahmā and the other gods, likewise.
He alone is Kṛṣṇa, the soul of time, the creator, the protector, and the destroyer.
O Tulasī, worship Kṛṣṇa; let that which is destined surely come to pass.
O beloved, worship Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, who removes birth and death! || 37-38 ||
Seek refuge in that very Kālā, who is Time itself and is black; what other kinsman or protector is there? Devote yourself to Him, the kinsman and the protector.
As for us two, He alone has joined us with that karma and He alone will separate us from it.
The ignorant person is despondent in grief and calamity, but not the wise man.
O Tulasī, remember the beloved Nārāyaṇa at the time of death—
he for whose sake you performed penance long ago in the Badarikāśrama.
"I have obtained you through my austerity, and I have been obtained by you due to the curse upon the Gaṇas.
O lustful woman, for the sake of Lord Śiva, you shall perform penance and attain Hari;
indeed, you will find Govinda in Vṛndāvana and that very Kṛṣṇa in Goloka."
Just as you shall obtain [the Supreme Lord], so shall I obtain the Supreme Lord. Having cast off this demonic body, I shall attain eternal liberation;
there you shall see me, and I shall behold you forever.
"For you, having cast off this body and assumed a divine form, shall behold that beloved Hari; O beloved, do not be despondent!
Having thus deliberated with their spouses regarding the auspiciousness of their playful curiosity, [they proceeded].
Considering everything indeed to be perishable, they were immersed in an ocean of bliss;
with all their limbs covered in horripilation, exceedingly joyful and eager for amorous play,
they slept happily while conversing in that manner about stories overflowing with aesthetic flavor.
Laughing and chewing betel nut with one another,
they spent the night entirely enveloped in sleep.
Rising in the morning, that demon meditated upon Kṛṣṇa in his mind.
Having bathed, put on [clean] garments, and applied the *tilaka* and *candraka* marks,

and having performed the worship of the gods, the satiation of the ancestors, and the salutation of the guru, as well as the worship of the cows and the viewing of parched grain, curd, honey, and clarified butter. (1.336.49–50)
He gave garments of jewels, gems, gold, and so forth to the twice-born;
he gave pearls, rubies, and diamonds to the Brahmin Śakuni.
For the sake of the auspiciousness of the journey, he bestowed elephants, horses, and cows.
He joyfully gave treasuries, lands, and towns to the Brahmins.
Having made his son Sucandra the king among the Dānavas, he entrusted his wife, his own kingdom, and all its wealth to that son. (52–53)
Having himself eaten and likewise drunk, and having bid farewell to his sons and others, he donned his armor and took up his weapons; with bow in hand, he stood ready.
Having summoned his armies there, he then became prepared for battle.
One hundred thousand horses, two hundred thousand elephants,
five hundred thousand chariots, thirty million archers, and likewise thirty million shield-bearers and trident-wielders for each [of those two groups]. (55–56)
There was no counting the foot-soldiers among the Daityas and Dānavas,
where the commander-in-chief was a master of all weapons, missiles, mantras, and illusions;
he was an expert in aerial vehicles, watercraft, and subterranean travel.
There, indeed, were three hundred thousand soldiers and full akṣauhiṇīs;
thirty times that number of the foremost and most excellent warriors,
the great asura went outside the camp, remembering Śrī Hari in his mind.
O Lotus-born one, the armies of Śaṅkara also numbered twenty-five crores; they were the foremost among all the warriors there.
As for the others, there was indeed no counting them; they numbered hundreds of crores.
The mighty Skanda became the commander-in-chief of Śaṅkara’s army.
At that time, Rāhu became the commander-in-chief of Śaṅkhacūḍa’s army.
There in the battle, they both repeatedly sounded their musical instruments.
On the bank of the Puṣpabhadrā river, Śaṅkhacūḍa, traveling in his celestial chariot,
beheld at the foot of a banyan tree that Śaṅkara, who had entered into yoga—
wielding a trident and a sharp-edged spear, clad in a tiger skin, and most excellent.
Having seen Hara, the Lord of Death, who possesses the luster of molten gold,
adorned with a mass of matted hair, three-eyed, five-faced, and wearing a serpent as a sacred thread—
peaceful and the remover of death for his devotees. (64–65)
Having descended from the celestial chariot, he bowed with devotion to Śaṅkara.
And Mahādeva, out of compassion, having indeed bestowed auspicious blessings upon him, spoke:
"The son of Brahmā is Marīci; his son is Kaśyapa."
To him, Dakṣa duly gave thirteen daughters:
Aditi, Diti, Danu, Kālā, Ariṣṭā, Surasā, as well as Surabhi, Vinatā, Tāmrā, Krodhavaśā, and Irā.
Kadru and Muni were among them; from them were born various offspring of mixed species.
From Aditi were born the twelve Ādityas as her first-born sons:
Dhātṛ, Aryaman, Mitra, Varuṇa, Aṃśa, and Bhaga.
Indra, Vivasvat, Pūṣan, and Parjanya is remembered as the tenth;
then Tvaṣṭṛ and Viṣṇu—these are the sons of Kaśyapa.
Of Diti, there were two sons: Hiraṇyakaśipu along with his elder brother [Hiraṇyākṣa].
Hiraṇyākṣa was another, and both had Saṃhikā as their daughter;
she was the mother of Rāhu and the wife of Vipracitti. Hiraṇyakaśipu had four sons who were possessed of great strength.
Prahlāda, Anuhrāda, Saṃhrāda, and Hlāda—
these were the six sons of Hiraṇyākṣa, all of whom were indeed possessed of great strength;
as well as Utkara, Śakuni, and another named Kālanābha.
Mahānābha, Vikrānta, and Bhūtasaṃtāpana—
these were the hundred sons of Danu, the Dānavas headed by Vipracitti;
as well as Dvimūrdhan, Śaṅkukarṇa, Śaṅku, and Nirāmaya.
Śaṅkunāsa, Mahāviśva, Gaveṣṭhi, and Dundubhi;
likewise Ajāmukha, Bhagahṛt, Śila, and Vāmanasa; as well as Marīci, Akṣaka, Mahāgārgya, and Aṅgirāvṛta. (76–77)
Vikṣobhya, Suketu, Suvīrya, and likewise Suhṛda; Indrajit, Viśvajit, and also Suravimardana;
Ekacakra, Suvāha, and the mighty Tāraka.
Vaiśvānara, Puloman, Pravīṇa, and Mahāśiras;
Svarbhānu, Vṛṣaparvan, and the great Asura Muṇḍaka;
Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Sūrya, Candra, Indra, and Tāpana.
Sūkṣma, Nicandra, Ūrṇanābha, Mahāgiri, Asiloman, Sukeśa, Sada, and likewise Balaka;
Vyomamūrdhan, Kumbhanābha, Mahodara, and Mahāhanu.
Pramodāha, the powerful Kupatha, Hayagrīva, the Asura Virūpākṣa, Supatha, the great Asura,
Aja, Hiraṇmaya, Śatamāyu, and Śambara. ||82–83||
Śarabha and Śalabha were also prominent sons of Danu;
these and other Dānavas indeed stood ready for battle.
Kṣaṇa and others became his sons, who were dark-complexioned and possessed forms like Time itself.

To Ariṣṭā were born thousands of invincible sons who were obstacles [to others]. To Surasā were born the nāgas and serpents, such as Vāsuki, Takṣaka, and others. Surabhi bore to Kaśyapa eleven sons who were the Rudras. (85–86)
Aṅgāraka, as well as Sarpa, Nirṛti, Sadasaspati; here [are] Ekapāda, Ahirbudhnya, Ūrdhvaketu, and likewise Jvara;
Bhuvana, Īśvara, Mṛtyu, and the renowned Kapāla.
Vinatā had two sons, Aruṇa and Garuḍa;
she is also remembered as having thirty-six younger sisters.
Of Tāmrā, there were Śukī, Krauñcī, Dhṛtarāṣṭrī, and Pakṣiṇī.
Śyenī, Bhāsī, and other female birds likewise became their offspring. Now, twelve daughters are recorded as belonging to Krodhavaśā:
Mṛgī, Mṛgamandā, Haribhadrā, and Irāvatī.
Bhūtā, Kapiśā, Daṃṣṭrā, Niśā, and another, Tiryā;
Śvetā, Svarā, and the renowned Surasā—these were born. Then Irā indeed gave birth to three daughters of beautiful eyes. (91–92)
From her were born numerous offspring: creepers (*latā*), climbing vines (*vallī*), and shrubs (*virudh*);
Kadrū gave birth to a thousand *nāgas*, who are known as the Kādraveyas.
Then from Muni came the Mauneyas, the Gandharvas, and the Apsarases.
The expansion of their lineages became more than ten million in number.
Aditi is known for her virtuous character; Diti is remembered as being characterized by strength.
Surabhi is devoted to austerity, while Danu is known for her illusory power.
Munī is indeed characterized by fragrance, while Ariṣṭikā is characterized by movement;
Kālāsyā is characterized by hunger, and Kadrū possesses a cruel nature.
Irā is characterized by favor, and Ariṣṭā is full of anger.
Vinatā was indeed of a nature to carry [burdens], while Tāmrā was possessed of nooses.
By virtue of their righteousness, character, intellect, forbearance, strength, and beauty,
the offspring born of Kaśyapa were equal to their mother in noble birth.
O Śaṅkhacūḍa, know those who have gathered on your side: the gods, asuras, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and pannagas; the piśācas, beasts, wild animals, birds, and plants. 99.

And these Daityas and Dānavas belonging to the faction of the Asuras are the adversaries of the gods; they are guests for my weapons. O Asura, those who belong to the faction of the gods and are equal to the deities are [the guests] for me.
"O Dānava, you must be prepared here; all must be protected by me! Vipracit, the son of Danu, had a son named Dambha who was a devotee of Viṣṇu and my friend; you are his great son."
For the sake of obtaining a son, your father chanted the mantra of Kṛṣṇa at Puṣkara (103).
Your father performed severe penance for a thousand years;
by the power of that, you were born as his son, Sudāmā Śaṅkhacūḍa (104).
What is the use of this quarrel with you today, if you know me to be Hara? If you know Sudāmā to be your own devotee,

even though he is a Dānava, [then grant him] the states of being in the same world as Hari (sālokya), sharing his power (sārṣṭi), having the same form (sārūpya), being in his proximity (sāmīpya), and even oneness (aikya) with him.
Vaiṣṇavas do not accept what is being given without service. What use have you, a devotee of Kṛṣṇa, for a kingdom or for strife?
O Dānava, give the kingdom to the gods and show me your affection.

Dwell happily in your own kingdom, and let the gods remain in their respective places. Enough with this enmity toward your brother, for we are all indeed sons of Kaśyapa. There are no sins whatsoever that are equal to the betrayal of one's kinsmen. (108)
In due time, destruction will surely come even to Brahmā; what then of you? (10.9) In no state whatsoever is there ever equanimity for anyone.
O Lord of Devotees, abandon [this] through knowledge; O Dānava, do not [strive] through opposition! (1.336.110)
The sun, the moon, and all others wax and wane;
by time the earth becomes rich with crops, and by time it is bereft of fortune. By time you were immensely prosperous; that very time is now passing away for you.
I am Kāla, the conqueror of death, who withdraws embodied beings;
yet I constantly perform the chanting of the true qualities and names of Kṛṣṇa.
You, however, having renounced everything, should likewise perform the chanting of Kṛṣṇa.
Having spoken thus, Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world, ceased;
nevertheless, the mind of Śaṅkhacūḍa did not change even in the slightest.

Thus ends the three hundred and thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of Śaṅkara, armed with a trident, sending the messenger Puṣpavant to Śaṅkhacūḍa; the knowledge of Śaṅkhacūḍa and Tulasī; Śaṅkhacūḍa’s departure for battle in the morning; and the reminder by Śaṅkara that Śaṅkhacūḍa is a Dānava born in the lineage of Kaśyapa’s thirteen wives, named Sudāmā," in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, within the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, in the narrative of the marriage of Tulasī. 336.
