Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: O Lakṣmī, thereupon Śaṅkhacūḍa spoke these ethical words to Śaṅkara:
"A war rooted in pride is indeed destructive and characterized by darkness (tāmasa). || 1 ||
O Lord! Everything you have said is true and not false.
O Śaṅkara, if there is great sin in betraying one's own kin, then how was Bali, having seized all his possessions, sent down to the netherworld?
How was Hiraṇyākṣa, along with his brothers, slain by the gods?
How was the nectar consumed by the deities during the churning of the ocean?
And why do you slay the Dānavas, yet neither the gods nor your own Gaṇas?
How was her father harmed at that time while Satī was still present?
How did Viṣṇu’s Sudarśana become truly effective even against the asuras? And why did there arise such hostility between the two female descendants of Kaśyapa?
Great shame arises [in me], O Hara: how can I compete with them?
(6) A human being who elevates his own paternal lineage goes to heaven; however, one who follows the lineage of another falls into a low state of existence. (7)
Whatever may happen by the power of time, let that indeed come to pass here in my abode; whether it be defeat or victory, that which is wrought by time is surely respected by me.
Now, O Lord of Pārvatī, you are Mahākāla to me.
Whatever may happen there in due time, I am content; engage in battle!
If I die, I shall go to Goloka; if I conquer, I shall enjoy the rewards ordained by Brahmā.
In this battle, there is no loss for me, nor even the slightest gain for you.
Having reflected thus: "O Blessed One! O Śaṅkara! desist!
For the great, association with the small results only in loss, not in growth.
"I pay homage to you, O Śambhu! And yet, I rise for battle."

Having resolved thus, he mounted his own vehicle and departed for his army. Therein were those who belonged to the faction of the asuras—the daityas, dānavas, and others—who were the adversaries of the gods; they followed the asuras in battle.
Those who were like gods and belonged to the faction of the gods became followers of Hara;

they all arrived in the armies of Śaṅkhacūḍa and the wielder of the Pināka bow. At that time, the two armies, consisting of ten million, one hundred billion, and one hundred trillion warriors, were like the ocean.
"O Lakṣmī! You are truly beautiful when you have swiftly conquered the enemy's war-drums! (15) Then the kettledrums resounded in heaven and a rain of flowers fell.
Skanda became the commander-in-chief there, and Rāhu became the king. (16)
A battle took place in the sky between the two [armies] with *śataghnīs*, arrows, and spears;
with axes, iron clubs, *bhūśuṇḍīs*, javelins, and discuses;
and also with arrows, *śilīmukhas*, hissing darts, and *golakas*. (17)
And with thousands of slaying weapons and mountain peaks, there was a wondrous and fierce battle between the two armies, resembling the great dissolution of the world;
it was a crushing, tearing, cutting, and a splitting in two. (18–19)
Cutting, pulverizing, the mangling of living beings, and crushing indeed took place;
there was a rain of arrows along with crescent-headed shafts, spears, *bhallas*, and triple-edged missiles.
A slaughter pervading all sides occurred between the two armies.
There was a terrifying destruction of elephants, horses, and mules;
there was the ruin of chariot-warriors and foot-soldiers beyond counting.
Chariots were shattered and vehicles were crushed by the thousands.
Horses were cut down by the hundreds of thousands, and lords of warriors by the millions;
they perished, were mangled, and lay lifeless, forever prostrate upon the earth.
Day and night, it was most terrible and constant, like the very nature of universal dissolution.
The battle raged there, such that even hunger and thirst were not taken into account.
Then, the arrows of the archers, the weapons of those bearing arms, and the armor of those clad in mail were entirely consumed by destruction. (24–25)
When the natural dissolution of the hosts of Dānavas occurred,
they became terrified and fled from the field of battle;
indeed, Kārttikeya wrought a great slaughter with a rain of arrows.
Rāhu also performed a supreme lopping off with a rain of arrows.
Both of them continuously rained down mountains, serpents, rocks, and trees—a torrent difficult to withstand and terrifying. (27–28)
Shrouded by a shower of arrows from Rāhu,
the son of Śiva cut off Skanda’s bow, shattered his chariot, and struck down his two horses;
with a divine weapon, he rendered the peacock mangled.

Rāhu hurled a spear, radiant as the sun, which was capable of piercing the chest; Skanda, having crushed it with his mace, took up a divine bow and rained down weapons in every way for the destruction of Rāhu.
The son of Śaṅkara, in his wrath, cut down the serpents, the mountains, the trees, and the boulders as well, using all his divine weapons.
Guha indeed neutralized the fire-weapon with the water-weapon.
He effortlessly severed the chariot and the bow of the son of Siṃhika (Rāhu).
Having slain both the horses and the charioteer, he hurled a spear;
struck in the chest, the Dānava then fell into a swoon.
Śaṅkhacūḍa, the best among illusionists, arrived swiftly mounted upon his chariot;
that foremost of magicians created nets of arrows through his illusory power.
Concealing Gūha in the battle with a web of shafts, he [discharged] a spear.
Then he seized the arrow named Śatasūrya, which was infused with the splendor of Viṣṇu.
He hurled it at Kārttikeya; it struck him, and he fell down unconscious.
Kālī took him in her lap and carried him into the presence of Śiva.
Śiva quickly urged on his own army and the gods; then a terrifying battle once again took place there with the lords of the Dānavas and their hosts.
There, Mahendra fought with Vṛṣaparvan.
Bhāskara fought with Vipracitti like the fire of universal destruction;
Candra fought with Dambha, Kāla with Kāleśvara, Kṛśānu with Gokarṇa, and the king of the Yakṣas with Kālakeya. (1.337.39–40)
Maya was [mounted] by Viśvakarman, and Mṛtyu by Bhayaṃkara;
Yama by Saṃhāra, and Varuṇa likewise by Kalaviṅka;
Pavana by Cañcala, and Budha indeed by Ghṛtapṛṣṭha.
Śani was accompanied by Raktākṣa, and the Vasus by their hosts of splendors;
Jayanta with Ratnasāra, and the Aśvins with Dīptimān;
Nalakūbara with Dhūmra, and Dharma with Dhanurdhara.
Īśāna fought with Śobhākara, Maṅgala with Maṇḍūkākṣa,
and Manmatha with Piṭhara, all using missiles and weapons;
[and he fought] with Ulkāmukha, Dhūmra, Khaḍga, and Dhvaja as well.
The Ādityas fought fiercely with Kāñcīmukha, Piṇḍa, Ghana, Nandin,
Viśva, and Palāśa;
the eleven Mahārudras fought with those named Bhaya.
Then Mahāmārī fought with Progradandyā and the others; likewise, Nandīśvara and all the others fought together with Daṇḍi and the other Dānavas.
Thus those lords of the armies fought their respective forces on all sides.
Śaṅkhacūḍa rested for a moment, and likewise did Kārtika.
The Dānavas, Asuras, and Daityas fought on all sides;
the gods trembled in fear and fled in the ten directions.
Skanda became enraged and granted fearlessness to the gods; then, out of intense fury,
he fought together with the hosts of Dānavas and slew a hundred akṣauhiṇīs in battle.
Enraged, Kālī drank the blood and then danced in the battle.
Taking ten lakhs of lordly elephants and a hundred lakhs of horses, she repeatedly seized them and cast them into her mouth with ease. (51–52)
By Skanda’s showers of arrows, the Dānavas and others fled;
Kālī, having entered the battle, let out loud, boisterous laughter.
Ugradaṃṣṭrā, Ugradaṇḍā, Koṭarā, and the hosts of Yoginīs [also joined].
The ḍākinīs devoured the asuras and drank the honey-wine.
Then, seeing Kālī, Śaṅkhacūḍa rushed toward her for battle.
Thereupon, Kālī hurled an āgneya weapon, equal to the fire of universal dissolution.
Śaṅkhacūḍa indeed effortlessly countered that with the Vāruṇa weapon;
Kālī hurled the Vāruṇa weapon, but the Dānava [neutralized] it with the Gāndharva weapon.
Then Kālī cut [his attack] and hurled the Māheśvara weapon.
Then the Dānava struck [her] effortlessly with the Vaiṣṇava weapon.
Thereupon the Dānava hurled the Nārāyaṇa weapon at Kālī;
she prostrated herself on the ground like a staff, and by that weapon of devotion, the [other] weapon was extinguished.
She discharged the Brahmāstra, and he swallowed it with the Brahmāstra;
she discharged the Pāśupata, and he destroyed it with the Pāśupata;
the Goddess hurled a Śakti, and he likewise neutralized it with a Śakti.
Then Mahākālī, filled with rage, discharged the Mahākāla weapon preceded by mantras; at that moment, a voice from the sky spoke:
"There is no death for the Dānava, for he bears the armor of Hari upon his throat."
"As long as the chastity of Tulasī remains intact,
he shall have neither old age nor death, except through the destruction of that chastity.
Upon hearing this, Kālī turned back, and he let out a roar of victory.
At that moment, Viṣṇu, assuming the form of a brāhmaṇa, arrived at the banyan tree.
"O Śambhu! Take the spear offered by me and go to the battlefield for the destruction of the Daityas; I am Viṣṇu, the teacher of the world. (63–64)
"I shall go as a mendicant and entreat the Dānava for armor, O Lord of Beings! Afterward, I shall go to Tulasī.
O Īśvara, I shall do so in the form of Śaṅkhacūḍa for the sake of depositing my seed."
"Then the death of the Dānava will surely come; of this there is no doubt.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Viṣṇu, assuming the form of an old Brāhmaṇa, approached the lord of the Dānavas and said, "Give me alms."
"Take it! What do you desire? the Dānava then asked.
The Brāhmaṇa replied, "O Dānava, give me the armor; become my brother.
Having heard that, the best of the Dānavas gave him the supreme armor.
Having taken his armor, Kṛṣṇa went toward Tulasī.
In the form of Śaṅkhacūḍa, he went to Tulasī’s house;
he sounded the dundubhi drum and raised a cry of victory.
Having heard that, filled with supreme joy and rising up in excitement,
she beheld her husband Tulasī from the window of the royal highway.
She bestowed wealth upon the Brahmins, the reciters, and the mendicants.
He had the bards recite auspicious verses and also gave wealth to them.
Having descended from his chariot, Kṛṣṇa went to the abode of Tulasī;
having reached her beloved, Tulasī washed his feet.
With great joy, Nanāmā embraced him as he sat upon a golden throne, bringing him victory;
she massaged his limbs for his peace.
She also gave him betel leaf, exquisitely fragrant with camphor and other spices.
"Today my birth has become fruitful; I behold your victory.
How did victory come to you in battle against the Destroyer of the Universe?
Tell me that, O Lord of my life! Thus spoke the virtuous Tulasī.
Viṣṇu said: During that great destruction of the gods and the Dānavas, Brahmā arrived there and brought about a reconciliation.
"Let the gods be fearless within their respective domains."
"Śaṅkhacūḍa! May you remain happy in your kingdom along with your wife.
Thus was peace established between us by Brahmā. Thereafter, I returned to my own abode, and Śiva departed for the world of Śiva.
Having spoken thus, Kṛṣṇa made Tulasī his bed;
there, the Lord of Ramā took delight in amorous pleasure upon Tulasī’s bed.
She too, due to the excess of her bliss, experienced a state characterized by intense attraction and the like.
And because her state was unshakable, she reflected upon the other [possibility]:
"Tell me, who are you? You have the form of a great king here through your power of illusion (*māyā*).
My virtue has been cast aside; I have been enjoyed by you through your *māyā*. (8.1–8.2)

"Speak quickly to me; having heard this, I shall curse you out of fear of a curse. Hearing this, he effortlessly assumed his own form as Nārāyaṇa—dark as a fresh rain-cloud, with eyes like autumn lotuses.

Having seen Nārāyaṇa, who possessed the loveliness of ten million Cupids, adorned with jewel ornaments, his face brightened by a slight smile, and graced with yellow garments, as well as the passionate woman who was fainting with desire, [he was struck with wonder]. (84–85)
And again, having fallen into a state of delusion, she embraced Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
then Śrī Kṛṣṇa indeed deposited his seed within Tulasī.
At that time, Śambhu struck Śaṅkhacūḍa with his trident.
The soul of the deceased, four-armed Sudāmā, departed for his divine abode.
Having fallen into a swoon once more and then regaining consciousness, she said to Kṛṣṇa: "O Lord! Your heart is as hard as stone!"
"You have no compassion nor even a trace of it! You have killed my master by deceit under the guise of dharma, while he lived his life through the power of truth.
Therefore, you shall now become a stone-like deity upon the earth. (89)
"Therefore, you shall be devoid of knowledge for one birth.
Having said this, Tulasī fell at the feet of Hari and wept and lamented; then the Blessed Lord spoke to her.
In order to lead my devotee Śaṅkhacūḍa, as well as Sudāmā,
back to Vaikuṇṭha, I indeed employed a stratagem against you.
To bring about his destruction, I gave the trident to Śaṅkara.
Blazing with the brilliance of a hundred midday suns in summer,
its tip is presided over by Nārāyaṇa, its middle by Brahmā,
its base by Śiva, and its supporting root by Kāla.
It was difficult to ward off, likewise unfailing, and a destroyer of all weapons;
it was unbearable for Śiva, Keśava, and others, and capable of destroying the cosmic egg.
It was a thousand *dhanus* in length and a hundred *hasta*s in width.
Śambhu cast that living form of Brahmā upon the Dānava.
O Daitya, because my infusion of virility within you caused Śaṅkhacūḍa, along with his chariot, to be reduced to ashes at that moment. (96–97)
And once again he became divine, two-armed, and holding a flute;
surrounded by millions of cowherds richly adorned with various jewels,
he ascended a vehicle that had arrived from Goloka and went to that city.
Then the trident went swiftly into the hand of the wielder of the trident.
With that trident, Śaṅkara quickly cast the network of bones of the Dānava into the salt ocean out of affection.
That which is born from a conch is the most excellent and pure for the worship of the gods;
the water from a conch is highly praised and brings delight to the deities.
Wherever there is a conch, there is Lakṣmī, and there is Tulasī and a sacred bathing place (tīrtha).
The water of a conch is the water of a sacred ford; where there is a conch, there is Hari.
O Padmā! Abandon your grief; become one who remembers her past lives, my beloved!
O virtuous lady, you performed penance for my sake in the forest of Badarī.
For your sake, Śaṅkhacūḍa performed austerities at Puṣkara;
having made you his beloved, that lustful man enjoyed her as the fruit of those deeds.
He then sought refuge with Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa in the circle of the *rāsa* dance.
"My devotee resides in Goloka; go there, O beautiful one!
Having cast off this body here and assumed a divine form, you shall sport with me in the Rāsa dance, becoming equal to Lakṣmī. || 105-106 ||
"By your curse, I shall indeed become a stone, the Śālagrāma;
unable to endure separation from you, I curse you: 'Become a river!
This body of mine, in the form of a river, shall be renowned as the Gaṇḍakī."
May this [bath] be purifying, bestowing liberation upon men, and granting merit through its immersion.
May the multitude of your hairs indeed become meritorious trees;
may the trees born from the hairs of Tulasī truly become Tulasī plants.
In the river Śālagrāma, I carry water and *tulasī*;
among all flowers and leaves used for the worship of the gods in the three worlds,
may *tulasī* always be my beloved in her preeminent form.
"O lotus, your separation from me, caused by Rādhā’s curse, has come to an end. Out of compassion for me, become Ramā here in my abode, O Tulasī!
By the rite of marriage in Vṛndāvana, I shall wed you, a virtuous maiden. (111–112)
"I shall take you as my companion and go," having said this,
Viṣṇu proceeded to where Śambhu stood in the fray.
Hara and Hari paid homage to one another and conversed with each other.

All the gods were raised up by Viṣṇu, and the army of Śiva was restored to life. Then, even those who had died were revived by both Viṣṇu and Śaṅkara; the army of the Dānavas was brought back to life by Śukra with the Sañjīvinī [mantra].
They celebrated a festival there, and then the offering of the materials was performed.
Everyone went to where the future Śālagrāma stone of Hari would be, and where the Gaṇḍakī river and the Tulasī plant were likewise destined to appear. (116)
Then, having attained that very form and having worshipped them, the gods and others went to the beautiful Vṛndāvana, where the future Tulasī was located;
having performed their ablutions in the Yamunā, they celebrated a great festival there. (11.7–11.8)
And by the will of Hari, she was born there in the form of the Tulasī tree;
likewise, she then became a divine maiden of excellent form.

Thus, in the first section of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, within the account of the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga and the narrative of Tulasī’s marriage, [is described] the speech of the Dānava to Śaṅkara; the battle between Skanda and his army; the battle fought with the weapon of Kālī; the begging for the Dānava’s armor by Viṣṇu in the form of a Brahmin; the infusion of Tulasī’s vital essence by Viṣṇu in the form of Śaṅkhacūḍa; the death of Śaṅkhacūḍa; the two curses—“May Tulasī become a stone Śālagrāma,” and “May Viṣṇu become the Tuṅgaṇḍakī river and Tulasī-tree”—[pronounced during] the battle.
Chapter Three Hundred and Thirty-Seven: The Description of the Resuscitation of the Dead, the Arrival at Vṛndāvana, and Other Matters.
[Chapter 337] Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga).
Chapter 338.
[The Author: Chapter 339.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
And having beheld the Tulasī plant adorned with clusters of excellent leaves...
Then the gods and others were overwhelmed with great wonder;
likewise, Lakṣmī and the other goddesses paid homage to Tulasī.
Nārāyaṇa, the Great Viṣṇu, spoke to them concerning her majesty.
Listen, Lakṣmī! At that time, the maiden Tulasī, possessed of a divine form, remained by my side and listened to her own greatness:
"She is indeed Tulasī, in whom the comparison of all things perishes. (3)
In heaven, on earth, in the netherworld, in Vaikuṇṭha, and in the imperishable abode—
may Tulasī trees always remain in my presence.
In Goloka, on the banks of the Virajā, in the Rāsa dance, in Vṛndāvana, and upon this earth— may they ever abide.
May there be *bhāṇḍīra* trees, *campaka* groves, *aśoka* trees, and sandalwood forests;
may there be groves of *mādhavī*, *ketakī*, *kunda*, *mallikā*, and *mālatī*;
and wherever I am, may there be *tulasī* trees along with me.
And there shall be residence at a sacred ford (tīrtha) upon the ground at the root of the Tulasī plant.
(7) Where a Tulasī leaf falls, there is the presence of the gods and others.
One who has bathed in Tulasī water and who eats Tulasī leaves— (8)
He who takes refuge in Tulasī has bathed in all sacred fords and been initiated into all sacrifices; he partakes in the merit of all pilgrimages and all acts of charity.
I do not derive such satisfaction from the sight of a jar filled with nectar as I do from that of Tulasī.
O gods, whatever satisfaction I derive from the offering of a *tulasī* leaf—[that same satisfaction arises for one who] swallows *tulasī* water at the time of death;
liberated from all sins, that king among devotees goes to Vaikuṇṭha. (1.338.10–11)
He who daily drinks water touched by *tulasī* with devotion should be known as one liberated while living; he obtains the fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā.
One who performs my worship with *tulasī* partakes in the merit of a hundred thousand horse-sacrifices.
He who should give up his life while holding a *tulasī* leaf in his mouth,
or he who should meet his death while wearing a *tulasī* garland around his neck—
he, having enjoyed [the fruits of] heaven for ten million *yugas*, goes to the world of Viṣṇu.

One who bears the name of Tulasī gains the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice at every step. Furthermore, that person who obtains even a single drop of Tulasī water during a meal, or who receives a leaf of Tulasī at the time of death or in times of distress, [attains the highest state]. (15)

Having ascended a jeweled vehicle, he goes to Vaikuṇṭha, my abode. O gods, pure Tulasī leaves that have been kept for three nights may be offered during a Śrāddha, a vow, a gift, a consecration, or the worship of the gods.
Having washed that which has fallen on the ground or fallen into water, one should offer it;
thus offered to Viṣṇu, it becomes divine and pure.
On festival days, at the two junctions of time (dawn and dusk), and at night, one must not cut that leaf.
In the abode of the tree-deity, Tulasī is very dear to me.
On earth, Gaṇḍakī, the river-deity of the ocean, is dear to me;
and Ramā, who is Padmā by her very nature, is dear to me even in Vaikuṇṭha. (1.338.20)
"By virtue of Tulasī’s curse, she shall eternally delight with me in the Rāsa dance at the root of the Gaṇḍakī riverbank;
as for me, today I become a mountain-form consisting of the Śālagrāma stone."
The insects there shall have adamantine bodies and adamantine fangs;
those insects will act as my wheels and shall become my attendants (pārṣadas). I am established here as a stone image, enriched by a wheel consisting of golden lines. (22–23)
That which has one door, four discs, and is adorned with a garland of forest flowers,
and is marked with golden lines, is indeed named Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa.
If it has one door and four discs, but lacks the garland of forest flowers—

Indeed, that which is marked with a golden line and bears the name Lakṣmī-Janārdana [is one type]. That which has four discs on two sides and is accompanied by a "cow's footprint" (goṣpada) is to be known as Raghunātha, provided it is devoid of a garland of forest flowers (vanamālā). //25-26//
The small [conch] with two circles and a golden line like a garland should be understood as named Prabhākṛṣṇa; it bestows happiness upon householders.
The large [conch] with two circles and devoid of a golden line [is likewise to be known].
That which is known as Pārvatīkṛṣṇa is remembered as bestowing happiness upon renunciants.
That which is called Dadhivāmana is very small and has two wheels;
it may also be marked with lines or a pair of garlands, and it grants happiness to householders. (28–29)
The form with two wheels, joined by a garland, is Śrīdhara, who always bestows prosperity;
it is large and circular in shape, yet devoid of a forest garland.
The form with two wheels, known as Dāmodara, should be understood as the giver of grain and wealth.
One should likewise understand that which produces fields, gardens, and groves, as well as that which bestows fine garments.
(3.1) The middle [type] is circular in shape, possesses two wheels, and is pierced by arrows; it is to be understood as named "Delight in Battle" (*raṇarāmā*), provided with a bow and a quiver. (3.2)
The middle [form] has seven wheels and is equipped with an umbrella and quivers;
it should be understood as the Lord of the Kings of Kings (Rājarājeśvara), bestowing royal prosperity upon men.
The [third form] has fourteen wheels, is massive, and has an upward-facing face adorned with hoods.
That which is known as Ananta should be understood as bestowing the fruits of the four aims of life (caturvarga).
That which is reddish in the center, marked with two wheels, and named Māṇikīkṛṣṇa,
indeed bestows wives, progeny, houses, jewels, and vehicles.
That which is wheel-shaped, possessing two wheels, endowed with splendor, and marked by a cow’s footprint is known as Madhusūdana; it bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Sudarśana, however, has a single wheel, its wheel is concealed, and it bears the mace.
Hayagrīva is proclaimed as having two wheels and the appearance of a horse's face.
He who consists of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa is proclaimed as five-faced.
Nṛsiṃha, by name, has an exceedingly wide mouth and two wheels.

That [image] which bestows dispassion and renunciation, and which is auspicious when situated in an assembly hall, is considered to be named Lakṣmī-Nṛsiṃha; it likewise destroys obstacles. At the doorway, that which has two wheels, is accompanied by Śrī, and is symmetrical—
That indeed is known as Vāsudeva, which fulfills all desires.
But the subtle wheel with many apertures and numerous holes is Pradyumna;
it bestows happiness upon householders and increases good fortune and other blessings.
Two wheels with a single axle and a thick, rounded back are to be known as Saṃkarṣaṇa;
this always brings happiness to householders.
Aniruddha is yellowish in luster, circular, and exceedingly beautiful.
Wherever there is a Śālagrāma stone, there Lakṣmī and Hari reside; it bestows happiness upon householders and increases their prosperity.
All sacred fords dwell therein, and its worship destroys all sins. (43–44)
If it is shaped like an umbrella, there is universal sovereignty; if circular, all prosperity;
if shaped like a cart, there is suffering; and if shaped like a trident, death occurs.
If the mouth is deformed, there is poverty; and if it is tawny, there is indeed loss.
If the ascendant wheel (lagnacakra) is pierced, there will be disease; if it is split, death is certain.
That man who bathes with the waters of the Śālagrāma stone has performed ablutions at all sacred fords and is well-initiated into all sacrifices. 46–47.
Vows, charity, the consecration of temples, ancestral rites, and the worship of deities—
when performed near a Śālagrāma, they yield ten million times the merit.
A circumambulation of the Śālagrāma is considered equivalent to a circumambulation of the entire earth.
The merit of the Vedas and the merit of ascetic penance arise from the worship of the Śālagrāma.
By drinking the water from the Śālagrāma, one becomes eternally liberated while living. Indeed, all sacred pilgrimage sites (tīrthas) desire the touch of its feet. (1.338.49–50)
The earth is purified by his feet; it is the liberation of the lineage of a hundred thousand of his kin.
At death, by the falling of that water [upon him], he shall go to the world of Viṣṇu.
He attains nirvāṇa and is absorbed into the feet of Viṣṇu.

He who causes a separation from the Śālagrāma stone or from the Tulasī plant will certainly suffer the dissolution of his marriage or the loss of his wife. Furthermore, he who indeed causes a separation from the Tulasī leaf within the conch shell [shall likewise suffer].
For him who places a Śālagrāma stone, Tulasī, and a conch together and preserves them, there shall be no separation from wealth or wife for seven births,
nor shall he suffer the loss of his spouse or affliction by disease.
A woman desiring [merit] should always offer *tulasī* to the *śālagrāma*.
Therefore, let the gods always worship me with *tulasī*.
O highly blessed *Tulasī*, become for me here in the form of a tree! (55–56)
"I shall become a celestial maiden in form and marry you here," having said this,
Śrī Hari ceased speaking; and then she,
casting off her former body, assumed a divine form.
Just as Śrī and Lakṣmī abide, so did she dwell in the heart of the Lord.
Viṣṇu, in the form of the Śālagrāma stone, situated within the water like a cloud, remained upon the ground as Piṅgala, established there through his fervent devotion.
Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Gaṅgā, Padmā, Tulasī, Ramā, Rādhā, Śrī, Prabhā, Vṛndā— all these are the wives of the Blessed Lord.
Jayā, Pārvatī, Māṇikyā, Pāñcālī, and likewise Lalitā.
The powers beginning with Joṣṭrā indeed belong to that Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
Now, when the maiden Tulasī, possessing a divine form,
became attached to the chest of Kṛṣṇa, Sarasvatī and the others could not endure it.
Sarasvatī could not endure it and looked at her with a sidelong glance;
out of fear of her, Tulasī then vanished from that place.
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa then enlightened Sarasvatī.
Having meditated upon her, he worshipped her and composed a hymn of praise for her.
Reciting the twelve-syllable mantra—"Oṃ Hrīṃ Klīṃ Aiṃ Vṛndāyai Tulasīyai Svāhā"—Viṣṇu performed that worship. (64–65)
The person who worships according to the prescribed rite shall obtain all perfections (siddhis),
by means of a ghee lamp, incense, vermilion,
sandalwood, food offerings, flowers, garments, ornaments, and collyrium.
The Supreme Lord worshipped her with offerings of lac-dye.
And she, the maiden, being pleased even by his hymn of praise, appeared from that tree;
having fallen at his feet, she sought refuge in Hari.
Viṣṇu granted her a boon, saying: "Become worthy of worship by the entire world;
I shall bear you upon my head and upon my chest.
"All the gods and others shall themselves bear you upon their heads. (69)
Then the goddess Tulasī was worshipped by the gods as well.
An invocation was performed for her, a seat was offered,
and then water for the feet, the arghya offering, and water for sipping were presented.
Then oil was also offered by the gods for the purpose of massage;
likewise, curds, milk, ghee, honey, and sugar were presented.
A bath with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and a bath with water from sacred fords (tīrtha) were also performed.
A silk garment, a water-pot, a bodice, and so forth were offered;
(73) musk, sandalwood paste, camphor, sandalwood, collyrium, and the like;
saffron, hair-oil, vermilion, and so forth were also offered. (74)
Lac-dye, ornaments, and other articles of decoration;
likewise, the sacrificial thread (*yajñasūtra*), the purificatory ring (*pavitraka*), the meditation-band (*yogapaṭṭa*), and so forth;
as well as the Kaustubha gem, the protective amulet, the auspicious thread (*maṅgalasūtra*), and the rosary (*sutantika*).
[The offering] consists of a turban, a fan, a mirror, a cord, and substances resembling drops;
it is presented by the gods with saffron, unbroken rice, perfumes, incense, lamps, and so forth, as well as sweet foods, milk-rice, *laḍḍu*s, fruits, betel, and water. (76–77)
In the pavilion, adorned with banana pillars and clothed in archways,
upon a *sarvatobhadra* diagram and a water-pot endowed with the five jewels,
they then performed the *ārārtika* rite with tulasī leaves and fruits.
A garment, conch-water, incense, and a lamp were whirled around her;
then prostration, the offering of water (arghya), a handful of flowers, circumambulation, and the pleasing of Tulasī with a hymn were performed. || 1.338.80 ||
A twelve-year-old girl was meditated upon by them as being equal to gold;
then Hari praised her— listen, Lakṣmī, I shall speak—
[praising] my beloved wife Padmā, Tulasī, and Ramā at all times.
I worship Vṛndā, Gaṇḍakī, Vanaspatī, and Kanyā.
In Goloka, my beloved is eternally dear; I worship her as my wife.
With whom I delight in Goloka, that Ramā I worship as my wife.
I worship Padmā, the wife of the Lord, who became the river Padmāvatī;
I worship that Tulasī whose equal does not exist in all the worlds;
and I worship Vṛndā, the mistress of Vṛndāvana, in Vṛndāvana itself.
I worship that Gaṇḍakī river which is united with the Śālagrāma;
I worship her who flows between my two cheeks (gaṇḍa) and my two temples (kapola).
I worship the Vanaspati, who has the form of a tree and whose essence is flowers. 85–86.
"I worship that dark-complexioned maiden of beautiful limbs,"—
having offered this praise, the Lord of Ramā stood there.
Then he beheld the maiden Tulasī, bowing at his own feet.
Viṣṇu granted her a boon, saying: "Become one worthy of worship by the entire universe;
you shall be borne upon the heads of all, and you shall be saluted and honored as mine.
By this boon of Viṣṇu, that goddess indeed became thoroughly satisfied.
Smiling, Lakṣmī, Gaṅgā, Sarasvatī, Virajā, Rādhikā, Padmā, Śrī, and the other wives of Kṛṣṇa paid him honor.
On the full moon day of Kārtika, the auspicious birth of Tulasī took place.
In that regard, worship should be performed; it was ordained by Hari himself.
That person who offers a *tulasī* leaf to Viṣṇu in the month of Kārttika obtains the fruit of giving ten thousand cows. (91–92)
Through the recollection of this hymn, one shall obtain sons, beloved ones, wealth, clothing, houses, food, vehicles, and carriages; as well as health, fearlessness, merit, and so forth.
(93) There is no comparison for it among flowers, nor likewise among goddesses.
“Tulasī, who purifies all things and sanctifies the universe, has been made her own by [Kṛṣṇa].
Thus honored by Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the maiden Tulasī, the small tree and mistress of Hari, became filled with joy. (94–95)
The maiden said to Śrī Hari: "O Lord, O Master!
If you have made me your own every day through your word, your heart, and your very self, then my hand must be taken by you according to the rites of marriage."
"So be it," Hari replied; and the gods and goddesses sang likewise.

Thus ends the three hundred and thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Nature and Greatness of Tulasī and Śālagrāma, and the Description of Worship, Hymns, and so forth," within the account of the marriage of Tulasī, in the first section on the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
← Chapter 338: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga) Chapter 339 [[Author:
Chapter 340 →
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O Keśava, I desire to hear in full about the marriage of Tulasī—the bride’s side, the groom’s side, and the wedding festival as well. (1)
"Where and how were the parents of the maiden and likewise the parents of the groom? How was she married, and who was her officiating priest?
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:

Listen, Lakṣmī! I shall tell you; through its mere remembrance and hearing, I relate to you this account which destroys sin and grants liberation. Vṛndāvana is exceedingly beautiful, adorned by the banks of the Yamunā.
The place where the marriage ceremony of Tulasī and Viṣṇu took place is most beautiful.
It extends from Govardhana as its starting point to the limit of Paścima Kosala,
and likewise from Kurukṣetra to the limit of the Khaṇḍakāraṇya forest.
Then that great field was made the site for the wedding.
Viṣṇu remembered the divine plowmen for the sake of purifying the ground;
they arrived instantly, and the site of the earth was consecrated by them.
Viṣṇu remembered Viśvakarmā, and he arrived.
(7) He constructed a preeminent pavilion in Vṛndāvana measuring eight yojanas;
he also built other pavilions extending for a hundred yojanas. (8)
Now, since King Vṛṣadhvaja was a devotee of Śiva,
his descendant was Dharmadhvaja, and Tulasī was his daughter.
Therefore, may Pārvatī and Hara become the parents of Tulasī.
Thus commanded by Viṣṇu regarding that marriage ceremony,
the parents of Satī and Hara became honored by all for the purpose of performing the rite of giving the daughter in marriage; Tulasī, too, was filled with joy.
Then, Viṣṇu’s parents, Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa— who were highly esteemed and residing in Goloka— were desired as witnesses here;
reminded by Viṣṇu, they arrived there together with their retinue.

Nārāyaṇa Viṣṇu, the Lord of Vaikuṇṭha, was indeed the most excellent officiant here. Bṛhaspati, the preceptor and priest of the gods, arrived as the family priest for the maiden’s household, having been summoned by Viṣṇu. 1–2, 14.
And Viṣṇu remembered Dhaumya, the family priest who resided in an excellent household;
accompanied by Garga, Kṛṣṇa’s priest arrived.
Auspicious rites were performed, and the customary social observances took place.
The marriage horoscope, inscribed with saffron, was written and sent [to him].
There, on the banks of the Yamunā in a grove of Tulasī trees, a new wedding pavilion four yojanas in extent was constructed by Tvaṣṭṛ. (16–17)
Likewise, the sacrificial pit, the altar, the installation of the water-pot (kalaśa), and so forth;
the worship of Gaṇeśa, the installation and worship of the Mothers (mātṛkā) and others;
the worship of the planets, and the planting of the pillar known as the Māṇika. || 18 ||

And the customary rite for the maiden—the application of turmeric paste—was all performed according to tradition by Sadāśiva. They also summoned their respective relatives from all directions. (1.339.20)
The camp for the bridegroom's party was established in the Khāṇḍava forest,
while the camp for the bride's party was established in the Tulasī grove. In the great pavilion at Vṛndāvana, the festivities of the marriage ceremony took place.
The parties on the side of the bride were in Nyūṣu, while those on the side of the groom were at Khāṇḍava.
There, the god who is devoted to his wife was summoned by Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa;
that brahmin, a master of the Vedas and all branches of knowledge, arrived there.
By him, saffron leaf-notes were likewise written and sent;
they were dispatched by those experts in various matters to indicate the auspicious time for the creation of Jīva, the creation of Īśa, and also for the creation of Brahmā. (24)
On the twelfth day, the pavilion [is erected]; on the thirteenth, the auspicious rite for the people;
on the fourteenth, the consecration of the ground; and on the full moon day, the wedding ceremony.
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, the raising of the pavilion and other rites are performed.

Thus, on the thirteenth day, the highly auspicious worldly custom was performed. On the fourteenth day, all the great devotees arrived at the house of Kṛṣṇa, which is the abode of the imperishable and is served by both liberated and unliberated beings.
The Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), departed from Goloka.
The hosts of cowherds and cowherdesses, as well as the wives of Kṛṣṇa and the attendants of Kṛṣṇa, also came to Kṛṣṇakhāṇḍava. || 28-29 ||
From Vaikuṇṭha, Nārāyaṇa arrived together with his consort;
his male attendants and female attendants arrived from all sides. Vāsudeva and the other members of the Vyūhas also arrived, accompanied by their consorts and their attendants.
Then they all arrived for the marriage of Tulasī and Viṣṇu.
From the unmanifest abode likewise came the circle of the Bhūma-puruṣas,
and the Vairāja Mahāviṣṇu arrived together with his retinue.
Likewise, all the Saṃkarṣaṇas, as well as the principles (tattvas) and primordial nature (prakṛti),
and the primary elements (pradhānas), entered into the garland attached to Tulasī and Viṣṇu.
So too did the incarnations and their consorts, such as Māṇikī, Pārvatī, and Prabhā.
Jayā, Āramā, Lalitā, and the other goddesses, the sovereign mistresses, arrived;
Śrī Rāma, Sītā, and all others also arrived there.
The sages, seers, gods, and ancestors likewise arrived. (34–35)
Brahmā’s wives— Sāvitrī, Gāyatrī, and the others— as well as the creators of the universe, the mental sons of Brahmā, and the seven ṛṣis, arrived.
So too did the guardians of the quarters, the Manus, the lineage of Dharma, and the hosts headed by Artha and Māna.
The months of Śrāvaṇa, the southern regions, the ancestors, and the fires arrived;
Indra, Candra, Sūrya, Maṅgala, and Budha—these planets, as well as the stars and constellations, came to the festival of Tulasī. (37–38)
The Siddhas, Vasus, Rudras, Maruts, as well as the Nidhis,
the Kṛttikās, the other Mothers, the gods, the quarters, the Kalās, and the lunar days— the thirty-three kinds of deities— indeed all arrived.
Yakṣas, classes of spirits, and the hosts of Śaṅkara;
here also the circles of Yoginīs, goddesses such as Caṇḍī,
Bhairavas, Piśācas, Vīrabhadra, Jvara, and others.
The other creation was of the nature of *tamas*; those belonging to the side of Śiva arrived, including the Brahmins such as Patnīvrata and others, as well as women such as Pativratā and others;
likewise, the various castes and stages of life (*varṇāśrama*) came, as did those dwelling in the water and those moving in the sky. (42)
The deities of the household and other such [divinities], rivers, mountains, and forests;
ditches, oceans, villages, islands, and trees arrived there, as did creepers, shrubs, grasses, beasts, and likewise birds. (43–44)
Living beings, as well as grains, elephants, and serpents, arrived there;
those dwelling in jujube trees, those dwelling in white [shrubs], and those dwelling in milk, all assembled.
All the women of creation and the men who were destined for existence also gathered there.
Summoned by Śiva and Viṣṇu, they arrived at the great festival of Tulasī.
Possessing the fame of sovereign kings, they were accompanied by umbrellas and chowries;
mounted upon excellent celestial chariots, they rode on swans, Garuḍas, and elephants.
Resembling campaka flowers, with unblinking eyes, and adorned with golden crowns, neck-ornaments, and earrings,
they arrived at the great festival of Tulasī accompanied by male and female servants,
bringing various foods— those to be chewed, swallowed, licked, and sucked. 48.
There were oceans of milk-based drinks, the essence of milk, and nectars;
[oceans] of sweet foods, side dishes, vegetables, soups, rice, sugar, tubers, and fruits. (1.339.49–50)
There, mountains were fashioned from fresh butter and ghee;
lakes were prepared, as were excellent rivers of cooling drinks.
There were streams of ghee, streams of curd, streams of juice, and rivers of honey.
There were also rivers from the Mādhavī and Vāruṇī [plants],
as well as lakes; and salt, bitter, pungent, sweet, and sour— just as they were, of whatever kind, and as much as desired, all gathered together like the ocean.
There were couches for reclining and millions of male and female servants;
there was dancing and dancers, as well as bards, panegyrists, and heralds;
and there were hired singers, wandering minstrels, scholars, astrologers, and innumerable mendicants.
Virtuous women, truthful women, women who are practitioners of Sāṃkhya and Yoga, female renunciants, and female ascetics;
celestial nymphs, courtesans, and female serpents at the great festival of Tulasī;
sacred fords, gods, Gandharvas, actors, and the sounds of songs. (55–56)
The Vedas and all branches of knowledge flocked to the festival of Tulasī.
Cold and warm drinks, cold and warm foods, and infinite objects of enjoyment for the senses—all these were present at that festival. (57)
Fuel-sticks of every kind, sesame seeds, grains,
and other materials for the sacrificial oblations were present in incalculable numbers.
Furthermore, millions of twice-born men learned in the fourfold Vedic rites assembled there.

Having established their dwellings on every side within their respective factions, the great dignitaries— having been offered a welcome, food, and other honors— were delighted and shone resplendently.
On the full moon day, the gods and others, having performed their ablutions, worship, and other rites, [shone forth].
By the command of Śiva, they performed oblations and sacrificial rites.
At that time, those who have Agni as their mouth were indeed exceedingly satisfied.
Then, the tumultuous sounds of musical instruments became exceedingly loud.
At that time, the songs and melodies of women will become exceedingly prevalent;
the performances of dramas and entertainments will become exceedingly common;
and the chanting of the Vedas by the Brahmins will become exceedingly frequent.
Then the dances of the apsarases become exceedingly frequent;
then the songs of the courtesans become exceedingly frequent; then the displays of magic illusions become exceedingly frequent. (64–65)
Then, objects fashioned by illusion appear most vividly;
then, excellent songs and poems arise most intensely; and then, floods of love and marriage ceremonies come into being most abundantly. (66)
At that time, the teachers' discourses on reality prevail exceedingly;
at that time, the efforts of artists in their arts are seen exceedingly.
Indeed, at that time, there are all tastes, all fragrances, and all forms.
At that time, all sounds and all touches were experienced to the utmost degree.
What was lacking where the Blessed One was marrying Tulasī?
In the morning, the excellent bridal procession arrived there from Khāṇḍava.
Viṣṇu appeared as a youth of nearly sixteen years with four arms;
he was resplendent with the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, adorned with a forest garland, and equipped with the Kaustubha gem, earrings, a head-ornament, and bracelets. (1.339.70–71)
At that time, his face was encircled by a fresh garland of lotuses;
he was mounted upon a divine white horse, radiant with a sword in hand,
and adorned with the splendor of excellent garments shimmering with golden stars.
Adorned with ornaments of jewels, diamonds, pearls, gems, gold, and the like;
the Lord wears yellow garments and is endowed with lotus-like feet shod with sandals.
He is as tawny as yellow-colored flour and is resplendent with the hue of filaments.
Adorned with armlets, garlands, crowns, necklaces, and crest-jewels; resplendent with saffron, unbroken grains of rice, moon-shaped marks, and forehead tilakas;
and graced by Śrī, Bhūti, Hrī, Prabhā, Kānti, Siddhi, and Lakṣmī. (75)
He traveled with that army, ten yojanas in length,
which was attended by kings, supreme monarchs, lords of kings, and great sovereigns who carried parasols, fly-whisks, and staffs, and served by male and female slaves. (76–77)
For the sake of establishing worldly conduct, Sadāśiva took his stand;
and having been invited to partake of food and drink by the emperors of the Koṭīśvaras,
they stood with jars upon their heads containing water and leaves from the auspicious *śrīphala* tree.
Fortunate divine maidens approached the bridegroom.
Satyā indeed offered to the bridegroom flowers, saffron, bilva fruits, unbroken grains of rice, garlands, parched grain, and svastika figures, all held in a golden vessel.
Then he was honored with sandalwood paste, flowers, parched grain, and unbroken rice by his female attendants;
saluted by the followers of Śiva and blessed with benedictions by the brahmins.
He was celebrated in every way by the women and gazed upon by those of great honor.

Delighted by the sounds of musical instruments, he was led to the pavilion of rest. (82) Those guests of honor from both sides were fed, honored, allowed to rest, and treated with hospitality; they attained a state of perpetual happiness. (83)
Tulasī wore all the garments, ornaments, and other items sent by her husband, as well as the jewels and such belonging to her father-in-law;
it was illuminated at moonrise by the light of ten million moons, suns, and lightning flashes. (84)
Having brought him home, Hara performed the hospitable reception for the bridegroom. Then, having observed the worldly custom by offering water for drinking and honoring him with various gifts,
Hara [prepared] the wedding pavilion.
Then they played musical instruments as they led that excellent king away;
at that time, there arose the sounds of the Vedas, the sounds of songs, and the sounds of trumpets.
Then the goddesses rained down a shower of flowers mixed with unbroken rice and other offerings.
Having broken the skull with his foot, Śrī Viṣṇu approached the sacrificial altar.
Then the excellent one sat upon the preeminent throne there,
and he was seated upon a plank near the sacrificial pit.
Joined with the thread of the forearm and the fruit of desire,
it was consecrated there for the sake of well-being by preceptors who had mastered the Vedas; then,
having been strengthened by the tilaka-mark, it was honored by Śaṅkara.
Having applied a *tilaka* with both hands, he was made auspicious by Pārvatī.
Then, having brought that Tulasī plant from the left side, he was joined with his bride;
both were then honored with a drop of *tilaka* by the two priests.
Then, having been consecrated and purified by being sprinkled with flowers, unbroken rice, water, and other ritual substances, and having sipped water for purification,
the two were impelled toward the fire sacrifice and offered oblations.
And the bridegroom’s garland was placed upon the neck of Viṣṇu by the maiden.
The priest joined the couple with the bridegroom’s garland;
thereafter, having had them perform worship to the deities of the limbs and other rites,
he caused them to place morsels of food into each other’s mouths.
Having caused [the bride] to drink water and having recited the Vedic mantras,
he placed his left hand upon Viṣṇu’s right hand;
then, making them hear the mantras beginning with "sahadharmaṃ caretām" (let the two of you perform dharma together).
At that moment, drops of perspiration appeared on their two bodies and their hair stood on end.
Then musical instruments were sounded and the chanting of the Vedas arose;
cries of "Victory! were raised by Viṣṇu upon his taking hold of Tulasī.
Having circumambulated the fire, the two of them sat down once more;
and having performed the remaining oblations, they engaged in the play of exchanging rings.
Cows, land, gold, rubies, garments, various jewels, and plots of ground—these were the stakes.
Hara gave to the Brahmins numbers in the hundreds of millions, billions, and trillions;
Kṛṣṇa gave to the Brahmins jewels, diamonds, queens, vehicles, mounts, excellent elephants, houses, fields, and abundant wealth.
Then they gave gifts to the bridegroom and the bride as wedding presents.
Then the pestle, winnowing basket, and other items were lowered from the head of the bridegroom.
Having led both the bride and the bridegroom to the house, they served them food.
Having provided a private bedchamber and performed the morning bath and other rites,
and having caused the meal and so forth to be prepared, he should bestow the dowry according to the prescribed rules,
as well as countless treasures such as gems, diamonds, gold, and the like. (103–104)
Tens of millions of horses, elephants, cattle, living beings, vehicles, and conveyances;

male and female slaves by the hundreds of millions, and household utensils and the like—these were bestowed by their ancestors and others, according to what was appropriate and according to their wealth. (10.5)
Having placed all that at the disposal of the groom, and having offered betel-leaf according to worldly custom,
as well as water for drinking and a request for forgiveness,
he then seated his daughter, joined with the groom, upon the vehicle.
Having bestowed auspicious blessings and received the prostrations of the maiden,
Śambhu sent them both to the pavilion of rest. The members of the groom's party, along with their attendants, went to the house of rest.
Having turned away from the Śiva sects, they set out for the hermitage of Śiva.
On the first day of the lunar fortnight, after feeding everyone with great devotion and having honored the carriages of the people, Hara sent forth his excellent followers.
Then Hara dismissed the lords of his own abode; having caused the dismantling of the pavilion and other structures by the Gaṇas and others,
the Lord went from that place to Kailāsa by means of a celestial chariot.
In the form of the Tulasī tree, she remained upon the site of the marriage;
then, having assumed the form of a bride, she went to the Khāṇḍava forest grove. There, she also performed the dismantling of the pavilion and other concluding rites.
Having bowed to Kṛṣṇa and the others, and having taken his new bride with him,
Viṣṇu departed for his own Vaikuṇṭha along with Garuḍa and his attendants. There, Viṣṇu took delight with his newly wedded wife in various amorous pastimes.

Thus, by him, his own wife was liberated from the curse and brought back to her own abode, which was filled with supreme bliss. And Tulasī, too, having obtained Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa as her husband, [was likewise restored].
Her desires fulfilled, she became established in the world as Tulasī.
Listen, Lakṣmī! Those people who shall worship me incessantly with the blossoms and leaves of Tulasī—my devotees who have taken refuge in me—[shall attain my state]. (1.17)
I shall lead men and women to my feet, just as the *tulasī* plant does.
On this earth, the *tulasī* tree and likewise the *śālagrāma* stone—I myself exist here, having assumed these two forms. (1.18–1.19)
"By means of water, stones, leaves, flowers, grains, or clay—in whatever manner possible—I grant liberation from living beings; that is my pretext.
Having heard this account of the marriage of Tulasī, [he then spoke].
One should worship the preceptor and the reciter, who are honored by all, according to the prescribed rite with wealth, garments, ornaments, vehicles, mounts, and articles;
with food, silver, gems, and the like, as well as gold, diamonds, and various finery. (121–122)
With leaves, flowers, fruits, and water; with milk, curd, clarified butter, and the like;
with sugar, grains, wheat, *khārīka*, dates, and so forth;
with *śrīphala* fruit, sandalwood, oil, umbrellas, chowries, and thrones. || 123 ||
With cattle, land, houses, mansions, and the like; with gardens, vehicles, and horses; with couches, beds, and swings; with beds, mirrors, and vessels;
with sesame, rice, fine grain, and food; and with fresh butter and well-formed cakes. (124–125)
One should worship the guru with many articles of household utility and should give abundant gifts according to one's capacity and wealth.
One should feed many Brahmins and cause virtuous men and women to be well-fed.

One should satisfy children, girls, the destitute, the blind, and the wretched with gifts of water; one should perform the ancestral rites (śrāddha) and cause the worship of the gods to be performed, as well as great offerings.
One should perform the worship of Śiva and Śivā, as well as the worship of Tulasī and Viṣṇu;
one should worship Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa and offer [oblations] to Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. Then, having distributed the *prasāda* to all the listeners...
Then, having performed the *nīrājana* rite and offered praise to the couple,
and having asked for forgiveness for any transgressions and given an auspicious sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*),
one should bid them farewell with prostrations and remember Tulasī and Mādhava.
In this manner, one should worship Tulasī and Mādhava with these sixteen supreme and most excellent articles; the worshipper shall obtain both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
[One shall also obtain] wealth, wife, progeny, sons, fields, kingdom, houses, and so forth.
By hearing of this worship of Tulasī and Kṛṣṇa, one obtains [all blessings]:
a barren woman indeed obtains a son, the poor man becomes wealthy, the diseased is freed from disease, and the debtor attains freedom from debt. (133–134)
One bound in shackles shall be liberated; the sinner shall attain sinlessness.
A maiden shall obtain a husband equal to Kṛṣṇa, who always bestows good fortune.
She shall obtain everything as she desires and become a worthy recipient of all prosperity.
"The suffering of those who suffer shall be destroyed; one should cause this to be heard and should hear it oneself.

(1.36) Thus, in the first book of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, within the section on the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga, in the narrative of Tulasī’s marriage: the construction of the pavilion for rest and other facilities on the bank of the Yamunā in Vṛndāvana on the twelfth lunar day; the camp of Viṣṇu’s ancestors in the Khāṇḍava forest; the camp of Tulasī’s ancestors in the Tulasī grove; the arrangement of the sacrificial pits, pavilions, and so forth; the arrival of the bridegroom's party and the wedding procession; and the arrival of the groom's escort and the multitude of people.

Chapter 341 → Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O Hari, Lord of Śrī, how was the name "Śālagrāma" ever given to Viṣṇu? What is that place? Please relate this story to me. (1)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī! to this narrative which elucidates the purpose of the Śālagrāma;
by hearing it, such devotion shall arise, and likewise liberation shall be attained. (2)
Listen to me as I relate everything exactly as it happened there, concerning that great river which was born with the name Gaṇḍakī. (3)
Having recognized the ground known as Śālagrāma to the east of the Tulasī plant,
Acyuta was then sworn by him, saying, "May you become the Śālagrāma stone."
And as Hari was performing penance, a wondrous stream of water emerged from the regions of his cheeks and fell upon that very spot. (5)
Having recognized that field as the Gaṇḍakī-field, which had indeed already come into existence, Viṣṇu then, in ancient times, cursed it, saying, "Become the Gaṇḍakī! (6)
In the Siddhakṣetra of Śālagrāma, Keśava became a stone;
in the spring of the Gaṇḍakī, that [stone] became the river Gaṇḍakī. || 7 ||
Listen to this field, adorned and fashioned, in detail.
In former times, during the Kṛta Yuga, there was a supreme Brahman-sage named Sālaṅkāyana. He [came] from the ten directions for my propitiation.
The great devotee wandered about, possessed by the desire for sons.
For the sake of obtaining a son, he performed penance with a concentrated mind on the peak of Mount Meru,
as well as at Piṇḍāraka, Lohārgala, and on Mount Raivata.
Since peace does not come to me in his absence even in my direct presence, he has arrived there for the sake of penance in the vicinity of Hrima. (11)
The sage named Sālāṅka constantly performed austerities for many years;
by him, a small leaf-hut was constructed there for the sake of his wife. (12)
Other forest deities as well, dwelling together with their wives, made a village of Śāla trees among those Śāla trees in that forest. (13)
The founder of the lineage was Sālaṅkāyana, so called because he lived by a *sāla* tree;
and due to his residence among the *śāla* trees, the place became known as Śālagrāma. (14)
Having learned of that previous account regarding Tulasī, the Lord in his stone form said to me, "Become a resident of Śālagrāma," and so I became. (15)
Having arrived there, I indeed abide in the form of a mountain by my own will;
for I was then pleased with Sālaka’s fierce asceticism. (16)
Having granted his own audience and being joined with blessings for his son, he said:
"O Lord, may there truly be a son equal to you for me. (17)
I replied, "So be it," and from that moment my son was born.
I took up residence on the Śālagrāma mountain;
there, O beloved, I remain forever like an insentient stone.
Then the sage Sālaṅka himself met his death right there. ||19||
And my mother, known as Śalākā, was virtuous and remained with him;
having indeed brought about their liberation, I, Viṣṇu, am present in that very place. (1.340.20)
Having become invisible, I dwell eternally within a heap of stones;
yet, when cursed, I indeed reside here with even greater intensity.
In that sacred field, Hara, united with the Goddess in my own form, dwells upon that Śālagrāma mountain in the form of a stone. (22)
Indeed, I remain right there eternally in the form of a mountain; all the rocks therein are my own self, of this there is no doubt. (23)
All of them are indeed worthy of worship, how much more so those marked with the discus;
on this mountain, the stones in the form of lingas should be understood as being the very form of Śambhu. (24)
Śambhu is the stones with Śiva as their navel, while I am the stones with the discus as their navel;
this is due to the power of the asceticism of the sage known as Sālaṅkāyana. (25)
O my beloved! Having consulted with Śambhu, we two remained here;
the Śālagrāma mountain is Viṣṇu, and that peak of Śiva is auspiciousness itself. (26)
On those two mountains, there is indeed a rock named Viṣṇuśivā;
formerly, Revā performed penance there which brought great satisfaction to Śiva.
With the intention, "May I have a son like you," he indeed granted a boon to Revā in the form of a *liṅga*. (28)
"O beloved of Śiva! I shall dwell within your womb, having become your son.
Having spoken thus, Śiva departed from the Śālagrāma mountain. ||29||
Indeed, the very self of the Liṅga went to the waters of the Narmadā in the form of stone;
on the bed of the Narmadā were stones that were the peaks of the Śiva-liṅga.
"All of them are indeed of the nature of Śiva, and likewise, I myself am Hari here.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, has that which explains the significance of the Śālagrāma been told to you. (31)
Moreover, listen to this account: I performed great penance, and from the sweat-water on my cheeks, a stream of water was produced. (32)
That lotus-eyed maiden also became conscious of her form,
and she performed severe penance there out of a desire for a son.
Having subsisted on withered leaves, she thereafter lived on air alone;
for a hundred divine years, she constantly practiced austerities, intent solely upon meditation on Viṣṇu.
There, manifesting myself as Hari Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, I, being pleased and affectionate toward those who bow before me, spoke sweetly to her. 35.
"Gaṇḍakī! O sinless one, I am pleased with you and amazed by your asceticism.
Because of your uninterrupted devotion, choose a boon, O female ascetic!
What should be given? Tell me quickly; I am gratified, O lady of excellent complexion! (36)
The Gaṇḍakī river also, having seen before her the one who holds the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, [became pure]. ||37||
Having prostrated herself like a staff, she then began to offer praise:
"O Lord! Having manifested from your rod as the essence of water... (38)
As long as I remain here, you have become invisible;
O Keśava, how shall I dwell alone here in this forest? (39)
Indeed, he who was difficult even for yogis to behold has been seen by me once again;
having entered his own yoga-māyā, you have assumed this form.
Standing in the midst of this deluded world, knowing nothing at all, I have been created and sustained by you, unable to distinguish between what is appropriate and what is inappropriate. (41)
O noble one! You have indeed seen me today having been raised to greatness by you;
out of ignorance, I have made this request, and it behoves you to grant it to me. (42)
"O Soul of All, you are compassionate, especially toward the distressed.
Having spoken thus, with palms joined in reverence, he requested his desired boon. (43)
"O Viṣṇu! Having entered my womb, become my son!
Then Viṣṇu said to her: "Listen, O Goddess, to my words. (44)
In the form of the Śālagrāma stone, I shall always abide within your womb as your son, for the sake of bestowing grace upon my devotees. (45)
Come with me to Vaikuṇṭha; O sinless girl, do not dwell here!
My wife Tulasī, who has become a river, will arrive here. (46)
"She shall be known as Gaṇḍakī, my future great nurse," having said this, the Blessed One led the girl away by means of a bird.
Having protected both Vaikuṇṭha and her right there, he returned once more to where that stream of water, the Gaṇḍakī, flows, and into its waters he [entered]. ||48||
He dwells in the form of stone for the sake of granting boons;
therefore, O Lakṣmī, I am that very Viṣṇu, eternally embodied in the form of stone. (49)
Because of my presence, that river indeed became most excellent;
[it is so] through seeing, touching, bathing, drinking, and immersing oneself in its waters. || 1.340.50 ||
He who bathes in the Gaṇḍakī while offering libations to the gods, sages, and ancestors shall remove great sin born of speech, mind, and body;
having delivered his ancestors, he shall go to the world of Brahmā.
If one should give up their life there, they too shall attain Vaikuṇṭha. ||52||
Then Lakṣmī said to Viṣṇu: "How indeed did the Blessed One formerly perform such severe penance that the Gaṇḍakī river arose from the water of his cheek? (53)
Then Nārāyaṇa said to Lakṣmī: "Listen always, O beloved!

For the sake of the welfare of the worlds, for their ultimate good, and for the protection of dharma, I shall perform various kinds of austerities for the sake of auspiciousness and satisfaction. (54)
This sacred ford existed in a previous creation in order to bring about such a result. ||55||
There, I undertook penance for the sake of much auspiciousness;
I know all that which was done in the past, but no one else knows it. (56)
O Lakṣmī! when even Nara and Nārāyaṇa, the two sons of Dharma, were not present in the Himālaya for the protection of the world,
I performed supreme austerity near the Himālaya.
At that time, my abode was at Śālagrāma in the great sacred field (mahākṣetra). ||58||
While I was performing penance there, after a great deal of time had passed, a fierce radiance appeared by which the worlds, both moving and unmoving, [were affected]. 59.
Greatly agitated and astonished by its heat, they looked in every direction;
and from that heat, a flood of sweat broke out upon their cheeks.
From him was born the divine river Dhunī, which removes the sins of the worlds;
those who desire to know its source are not able to do so in any way whatsoever. (61)
Then all the gods, filled with eagerness, went toward Brahmā;
Brahmā also, though ignorant, went together with the gods toward the illustrious Śaṅkara. (62)
"O Lord, tell me: what is this wonder, why has it occurred, and how?
Śiva, having meditated for a moment, replied to Viṣṇu, who was established in penance. (63)
"Let us go where he dwells," they said, and they went to that place.
Śambhu, smiling, said to him: "O Lord, how is it that you practice penance?
For one whose every desire is fulfilled, what is the purpose of your austerity? (64)

Thus addressed, Mahāviṣṇu, having paid homage to the lords of the gods, spoke for the sake of the welfare of the world, being intent on performing austerities: "Having obtained the sight of you all, I have indeed become one who has achieved his purpose today! (65–66)
May this field be a divine land and the most excellent of sacred sites;
likewise, may the gods show their grace in every way through their words of blessing. (67)
Having heard that, Brahmā, Śambhu, and the other deities then said: "O Viṣṇu! Because of your vision, this is indeed a sacred field (kṣetra) that grants liberation. (68)
Moreover, because of the vision of the gods, this shall become a field of liberation, where the Gaṇḍakī, the best of rivers, was born from the sweat upon [the god's] cheeks. (69)
There is no doubt that she will become so, in whose womb you shall dwell;
for while you, the Lord of the World, abide therein, it shall be by virtue of your presence.
O Lord of the worlds! We—the gods, the sages, the Vedas, the sacred fords, and indeed the sacrifices—shall dwell here forever upon the Gaṇḍakī. ||71||
He who bathes in its waters throughout the entire month of Kārttika will be liberated from all sins and shall attain liberation; of this there is no doubt.
It is the supreme sacred ford among all sacred fords and the most auspicious among all auspicious things;
by remembering it, seeing it, or touching it, one obtains a fruit greater than that of the Gaṅgā. (73)
This is that supreme and meritorious Gaṇḍakī, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
another, known by the name Devikā, has joined together with the Gaṇḍakī. (74)
In former times, Pulastya and Pulaha performed supreme austerity at that place, having separately established hermitages for the purpose of performing sacrifices for the sake of creation. (75)
Thereafter, they obtained the power to perform the act of creation;
from that, she became the daughter of Brahmā, who then merged with the Gaṇḍakī. ||76||
There, at the confluence of the three rivers, Hari liberated the elephant and the crocodile;
with his Sudarśana discus, he swiftly tore open the mouth of the crocodile. (77)
That wheel was thrown again and again, striking against the rocks;
from that impact of the wheel, the rocks were marked by the wheel.
Then, in that same manner, they were constantly nourished by the Vajrakīṭas and the gods;
indeed, it was for the very purpose of protecting the devotees in the sacred field of Śālagrāma.
I commanded Sudarśana to revolve everywhere;
there, all those stones were indeed marked by the discus.
Extending from Muktikṣetra as far as Hariharakṣetra,
that sacred field consisting of Śālagrāma stones measures twelve yojanas.
O beautiful one, wherever I have established my presence for the sake of protecting my devotees, there also exist Sāla trees, which are portions of myself.
This tree seen by the Gaṇḍakī is none other than I; of this there is no doubt.
That place on the high peak of the mountain is pleasing to me. ||83||
The place known as Śālagrāmasthala grants liberation from the cycle of existence to devotees;
indeed, in the region of Cakrasvāmī, there are stone discs scattered here and there. (84)
By my yoga, that entire place is seen to be purifying;
the Gaṇḍakī, Tulasī, Vṛndā, and Padmā have taken refuge in my body. (85)
O beloved! By the power of me, one who relies upon the Śālagrāma, the Gaṇḍakī river, and the Tulasī plant shall certainly attain my world. (86)
Just as you have related my own abiding in asceticism, so too was it for the purpose of establishing sacred fords and for the sake of the welfare of the world. (87)
In the form of stone, for the sake of the acquisition [of merit] by embodied beings;
in the form of metal, leaves, and so forth, for the sake of the acquisition [of merit] by living creatures. (88)
For the sake of providing for all—through water, drink, shelter, and so forth—I created my own forms at the moment of creation. (89)
Thus, O Lakṣmī, this is my compassion for one who is intent on the upliftment of living beings;
this chapter, O highly fortunate lady, brings about all auspiciousness. (1.340.90)
Those who follow my path and recite this indeed obtain splendor, glory, fortune, and the perfect fulfillment of all their desires. (91)
O wise lady, for as many syllables as there are in this chapter, for that many thousands of years one is honored in my world. (92)
One who desires the supreme goal should never, at the time of death, forget even a single verse or a single quarter-verse of this. (93)
This secret, the station of all that is auspicious, has been told to you, O blessed lady!
It is my own field, O highly fortunate one! What else do you wish to hear? 94.

Thus, in the first section of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, within the account of the Kṛta Yuga lineage and the narrative of the Śālagrāma region, is the ancient history explaining the meaning of the names Gaṇḍakī and Śālagrāma; the penance performed by the sage Sālaṅkāyana and his son Viṣṇu in the form of a stone remaining right there; the penance performed by Revā for the sake of a son; the presence of Śambhu in the river Revā in the form of a Liṅga that is his son; and the designation of the stream flowing from the cheek (*gaṇḍa-sthala*) of Viṣṇu while he was performing penance under a *śāla* tree as "Gaṇḍakī."

She is the very embodiment of Tulasī; this is the three hundred and fortieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Disc-Marks and Other Signs Resulting from the Impact of the Discus Thrown at the Crocodile for the Sake of Liberating Gajendra, as Well as the Transformation of the Stone-Beetle. 340.

Śrī Lakṣmī said: "Having heard of the Śālagrāma stone, the Śambhu stone, the Gaṇḍakī river, the Śāladruma tree, the Munisālaṅka, and the holy Tūlasī," (1)
My mind finds no satisfaction in its longing to hear;
O Keśava, tell me of the holy sites situated within the field of Śālagrāma,
by the mere hearing of which there shall be liberation even for the sinful.
And by performing this, one may also possess wealth, wives, and other such blessings here in this world.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Oh, what fortune! Oh, what merit! Is this the hearing of the discourse concerning Śālagrāma?
Oh, what divine fortune! Oh, what liberation! Is not the worship of the Śālagrāma stone [itself] such? (4) Oh, what heaven! Oh, what sovereignty! Is not dwelling at the site of the Śālagrāma such?
Oh, what prosperity! Oh, what contentment! Is not the service of the waters of the Gaṇḍakī such? (5)
O Lotus-born One! When the rise of great merit occurs for living beings, the conjunction with the site of Śālagrāma comes to pass, and not otherwise.
Having gone to the site of Śālagrāma, I shall perform [my rites] in the waters of the Gaṇḍakī.

For one who thus forms the resolve, "This is for bathing and libations," the satisfaction of the ancestors in this very life arises; what need is there to mention the result for one who actually performs them? [It serves] for the destruction of the sins of the sinful, and for the sake of heaven for those possessed of merit. (7–8)
For the fulfillment of the desires of those who possess devotion and for the sake of liberation,
I created the sacred field of Śālagrāma at the beginning of creation.
The image of my form, the Śālagrāma stone, was fashioned by me.
To the one who performs worship with the sixteen articles, I grant both worldly enjoyment and liberation. Whatever else is desired— wealth, wives, houses, and so forth—
I have created that out of mere compassion for the sake of uplifting living beings.

Listen, Lakṣmī! I shall describe in their entirety all the sacred fords (tīrthas) that exist there on land, and exactly how they came into being. Indeed, at the Sālaṅkāyana-tīrtha is the mountain known as Śālagrāma.
There, Hara was established by Soma as the Lord Someśvara;
Soṃeśvaragiri and the Gaṇḍakī have also been described to you.
To the south of Someśa, Bāṇa pierced the mountain.
Having performed austerities there, Rāvaṇa manifested the Bāṇagaṅgā, which bestows great merit; it is a supremely purifying sacred site (tīrtha).
To the east of Someśa is the penance grove of Rāvaṇa.
There, the mountain became famous as Nartanācala because of Rāvaṇa’s dance.
Pleased by his dancing, Śambhu then granted him a boon:
the auspicious Bāṇeśvara, located at the Bāṇagaṅgā tīrtha, which bestows heaven.
Staying there for three nights, one obtains the fruit of asceticism;
by bathing, one gains the fruit of a bath in the Gaṅgā, and by beholding it, one attains the fruit of worship. Now, the Triveṇī Tīrtha is indeed the most excellent among all sacred sites.

Where indeed the river named Devikā joins the Gaṇḍakī—(1.9)—that river arose for the sake of regulating the asceticism of the gods performing penance; she is truly the bestower of liberation upon the gods. (1.341.20)
Then, from the hermitage of Pulastya and Pulaha, another Devikā joined with the Gaṇḍakī; that confluence known as Triveṇī is called the Gaṇḍakī.
That great holy site is most efficacious and provides supreme satisfaction to the ancestors.
Listen now to that narrative here concerning what is known as Triveṇī.
Formerly, Viṣṇu performed austerities on the Himalayas out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds; at that time, a very long period passed.
Then, from the body of Hari, a fierce fire manifested;
by its heat, a flood of sweat arose upon his cheeks.
From that was born the divine river Gaṇḍakī, the best of streams.
Then the river named Devikā joined with her;
because she arose there through the ascetic power (*tapas*) of the gods, she is considered Devikā.
Another river was born from the ascetic powers of Pulastya and Pulaha. (25–26)
Thereupon, knowledge of creation was indeed obtained by those two through their ascetic penance.
That third river, the illustrious daughter of Brahmā named Yaśasvinī,
joined there with the Gaṇḍakī and is celebrated as Triveṇī.
By bathing there, a human being obtains the fruit of ascetic practice.
Now I shall tell you another thing regarding that site of Triveṇikā:
there Hari effected the liberation of the lordly elephant and the liberation of the crocodile.
In ancient times, the two sons of Vedanidhi, named Jaya and Vijaya,
propitiated Hari and were born as attendants in the abode of the Blessed Lord.
Due to the curse of Rādhikā, those very same two were born again on earth in another kalpa.
Both sons of Tṛṇabindu arrived upon the earth;
they were performers of sacrifice, masters of the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas,
and with their senses and minds fixed on Him, they worshipped Hari with devotion.
At the time of worship, Hari always attains their presence.
Once, they were invited by Marutta for the sacrificial rites.
When the sacrifice was completed, the king gratified them with sacrificial fees and other offerings.
The two began to divide their wealth and other possessions among themselves.
They vied with one another, [the elder] saying, "An equal share must be made," while Vijaya replied to him, "For that which is acquired by someone belongs to him. (34–35)
"I am indeed skilled; therefore, I have obtained this in particular.
You are not capable in that way, so I will not give you an equal share.
Jaya said, "Why do you speak thus, considering me to be incapable?"
"Since you took [the fruit] and did not give it to me, therefore become a crocodile!
(37) Vijaya also said, "Surely you have been blinded by wealth;
become an elephant, blind with rut! Thus they both pronounced their curses separately. (38)
Indeed, Jaya and Gaja were both born with the memory of their former lives;
Jaya was in the forest of the Triveṇī sacred field, while Vijaya was in the midst of the water.
There, in that forest, the crocodile seized the elephant who had come there to bathe.
A crocodile dwelling in the midst of the water seized him, remembering its enmity.
A battle took place between the two for many years through their mutual dragging.
Then Hari, moved by devotion, was entreated by Varuṇa.
By the gift of the elephant Kamala, he reached the Triveṇī;
with his Sudarśana discus, he split open the mouth of the crocodile.
Thus, liberation was granted to the elephant, and the crocodile was also set free.
By the act of striking with the Sudarśana [discus], wheel-marks appeared upon the stones and other materials;
thus has your greatness been proclaimed.
In this way, this sacred ford (tīrtha) is the supreme means of liberation for embodied beings.
O beloved! There Mahādeva Jaleśvara shines resplendent.
When the discus was hurled by me upon the earth, it became water;
that place indeed became the Cakramaya Tīrtha known as Jaleśvara.
A person who dwells there for five days shall obtain both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
In ancient times, Nandīśvara, the grandson of Sālakāyana, was a Gaṇa;
he resides eternally in Vṛndāvana, constantly tending the cattle.
Once, having taken the cows with him, he went to Harikṣetra;
Nandin was himself told by Hara, "Go to Harikṣetra," and so he went.
He made his residence for many nights on the bank of the Gaṇḍakī.
That field where cows graze upon the lush pastures day and night is known from that very day as the field whose essence is Hari and Hara;
and because the gods wander there, it is also remembered as Devāṭa.
Once, the Blessed Lord Śambhu was seated upon an excellent throne;
there, from the three matted locks of Śambhu, there issued forth three streams:
the Gaṅgā, the holy Yamunā, and the river Sarasvatī.
This is the Traidhātaka Tīrtha, where Śambhu is eternally present,
bestowing knowledge upon his devotees by which they are liberated from saṃsāra.
Having bathed there, offered libations to the ancestors, and worshipped the gods, one is completely released.
In the eastern direction of that very place, there is indeed Haṃsatīrtha.
Once, some hungry crows flew up from there;
then, as one crow was departing having taken food, another crow [attacked him].
Having seen this, they fought there and then both fell into the pool.
Having become two swans, they emerged and went indeed to Lake Mānasa.
Because of that wondrous event, it was indeed made known as Haṃsatīrtha.

Twelve yojanas from the Muktikṣetra lies the Haṃsatīrtha field; it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon those who visit its sacred sites, and it has been inhabited by me. Now, that is where the sage Sālaṅkāyana indeed practiced his austerities.
That cluster of *sāla* trees became famous as Śālagrāma.
Therein lie fifteen hidden holy sites (*tīrthas*).
There is a sacred field (*kṣetra*) named Bilvaprabha, possessing four groves. 58–59.
