There, by bathing in that river and residing day and night,
a person obtains the fruit of four horse-sacrifices (aśvamedhas).
Next is another sacred site, Cakrasvāmītīrtha, which consists of a stone discus.
A person should dwell for three nights at that place which is three yojanas in length and breadth.
Indeed, one who performs this at a great sacred ford (tīrtha) obtains the merit of a three-night sacrifice.
Moreover, if death occurs there, one shall obtain the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
Now, at that sacred field of Viṣṇupada, where three streams fall from the Himālaya,
one obtains the fruit of the holy ford simply by bathing there.
By giving up one's life there, one becomes a partaker of the merit of three Atirātra sacrifices.
Therein is the supremely purifying sacred ford named Kālīhrada.
Indeed, from the root of the Badarī tree, a stream flows into that lake.
By bathing there, one obtains the fruit of a human sacrifice and is liberated.
Now, at the Śaṅkhaprabha Tīrtha on the twelfth lunar day at midnight, conch sounds are heard; those who hear them become partakers of liberation.
Now, indeed, at the Gadākhya Kuṇḍa, the sacred site in the southern stream—
By bathing there, a human being attains the fruit of the knowledge of Vedānta and other sciences.
(67) Now, there is the auspicious Agnisuprabha Tīrtha, whose waters flow toward the northeast;
its water is warm during the winter and becomes cool during the summer. (68)
It falls in the form of a stream; having bathed there, one becomes a partaker of the five fires and the moon.
Now, that sacred ford consists of all weapons and is composed of seven currents.
Having bathed there, one becomes a great king; he should dwell there for seven days.
Then, having bathed there at the Devaprabha tīrtha, which is endowed with four streams, one obtains the awakening of the four Vedas. Next is the Vidyādhara tīrtha, which is endowed with five streams.
Having bathed there, one goes to the world of the Vidyādharas; of this there is no doubt.
There is a sacred bathing place on a holy river there, surrounded by rocks, groves, and creepers.
One who performs a bath there shall become the sovereign of the seven continents.
Having bathed at the Gāndharva-tīrtha at Ekadhāra, one shall become happy;
he rejoices among the world-protectors and goes to my own world.
Next is the Devahrada-tīrtha, where there are fish along with cakravāka birds.
Golden lotuses are seen there at the rising of the sun;
those who bathe there, purified of the impurities of speech and body, go to heaven.
A human being obtains the fruit of ten horse-sacrifices.

O beloved! Wherever the confluence of divine rivers occurs, there the gods and goddesses abide in the form of sacred fords (tīrtha). Gandharvas and Apsarases dwell there, along with Naga maidens and their serpents.
Indeed, the celestial rishis, all the sages, the lords of the gods,
the perfected ones (siddhas), the virtuous, and the kinnaras descend from heaven to this very earth of Paśupati here in Himālaya and Nepal.
From those various places, rivers flow across the earth.
Joining with the Śvetagaṅgā, the many rivers that follow the forests reach their confluence with the Gaṇḍakī and the Kṛṣṇā; they all originate from Śiva.
That Triśūlagangā became the assembly of all sacred fords (tīrthas),
as well as the Siddhāśrama tīrtha, which is purifying and increases merit;
it is also the penance grove of Śambhu at the confluence of the two holy rivers.
By bathing there, one will certainly obtain the fruit of a hundred horse-sacrifices.
By bathing there on the full moon day of Vaiśākha, one obtains the fruit of a thousand cows.
Furthermore, by bathing again in the month of Māgha, one obtains the fruit born of bathing at Prayāga.
In the month of Kārtika, by bathing at Satulārava, one attains liberation; of this there is no doubt.
By bathing there for three nights, one obtains the fruit of a Rājasūya sacrifice.
Indeed, sacrifice, charity, austerity, fire-offerings, ancestral rites, and worship performed there yield infinite merit.

O Lakṣmī! In the great sacred field of Śālagrāma, at the confluence of the two divine rivers, I always dwell facing eastward as the bestower of liberation. Śiva is always on my right side, and Brahmā is always situated on my left.
That place consists of both Hari and Hara, and indeed Viṣṇu and Brahmā;
those who die there certainly attain liberation, as well as eternal and certain heaven.
First is the field of liberation (Muktikṣetra), and after that is Rurukhaṇḍa.
Then follows the confluence of the two divine rivers and the Triveṇī;
this very field of Gaṇḍakī is where the Gaṇḍakī has merged with the Gaṅgā, the Bhāgīrathī. (88–89)
That sacred field is named Hari-hara; its greatness is difficult even for the gods to attain.
By reading or even by hearing [this account], the fruit of bathing at a holy ford (*tīrtha*) shall be obtained.

Thus ends the section on the Śālagrāma field, including Sālaṅkāyana, Someśvara, Gaṇḍakī, Bāṇa, the confluence of the Gaṅgā, Devikā, Brahmaputrī, Gajagrāha-tīrtha, Jaleśvara, Traidhārika-tīrtha, Haṃsa-tīrtha, Śālagrāma-tīrtha, Cakrasvāmi-tīrtha, Viṣṇupada, Śaṅkhaprabha, Gadākuṇḍa, Agniprabha, Sarvāyudha, Devaprabha, and Vidyā—within the first book, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter Three Hundred and Forty-One: The Display of Sacred Fords such as Dhara, Ekadhāra, Devahrada, Triśūla, Gaṅgā, Hariharakṣetra, and others.
*Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Book 1: The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga.
Chapter 342.
[The Author: Chapter 343.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
How did Ruru-kṣetra come into being, and what is the nature of Ruru-tīrtha?
"Tell me that, O ocean of mercy; I desire to hear it in its entirety.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: "In ancient times, there was a brāhmaṇa named Devadatta, born of the lineage of Bhṛgu."
In that hermitage, crowded with deer, he formerly performed divine austerities.
Ten thousand years passed while the sage remained engaged in penance;
then Indra thought of creating an obstacle for him as he practiced his asceticism.
At his command, Kāma went forth again accompanied by Vasanta, along with the Gandharvas and their friends; he also dispatched Pramlocā and the Malaya breeze.
Having received Indra’s order, they set out toward his hermitage.
In a delightful grove nearby, resounding with the warbling of cuckoos (5),
cooled by breezes carrying the fragrance of mango blossoms,
echoing with the humming of bees and the thunderous strains of Gandharva songs (6).
Having entered that place, exceedingly beautiful with water and land, which was graced by the splendor of the lotus-eyed one, Pramlocā sang a most sweet song.
As she sang, the sage ceased his meditation, and the Gandharvas began their singing.
Then Kāma, having found his opportunity, drew his bow;
perceiving that the sage was agitated, he discharged his arrows.
Thereafter, the sage wandered through the hermitage, listening to beautiful songs.
From afar he beheld the slender-limbed maiden engaged in playing with a ball;
he approached her, and she likewise drew near to him.
Bewildered, the sage asked her, "Who are you, and how are you in the forest?"
She said, "I have come for the sake of serving the sages; take me.
Then, as she laughed, he took his pleasure with her according to his desire.
Thus, he enjoyed himself at will for many series of days.
Having immediately attained world-weariness, he spoke again and again:
"Aha! Behold the power of Māyā, by which I have been utterly deluded;
though I knew it would lead to the ruin of my asceticism, I fell into it, compelled by divine force. (13)
"A man melts at the mere sight of a woman, being utterly deluded by her;
therefore, the fault does not lie with the woman, but with the man whose senses are unsubdued.
Having reflected thus, the sage then dismissed her. (14–15)
Having abandoned that place filled with obstacles and gone toward the hermitage of Bhṛgu,
he performed a fierce penance upon the peak of Bhṛgu above Śiva, in a secluded spot in the eastern direction after bathing in the Gaṇḍakī.
Śiva himself, having arrived in person, said to that best of sages:
"By perceiving Viṣṇu and Śiva without distinction, you shall attain perfection.
This Liṅga at this site of Śiva was established by him as 'Samāṅga' (the unified form)."
That holy site of Samaṅgeśvara arose on the bank of the Gaṇḍakī;
having realized this, Devadatta attained supreme union with the Divine (sāyujya).
Pramlocā also [delivered] the sage’s matured womb in the form of a girl.
O beloved, having previously abandoned her hermitage, she then went to heaven.
That virtuous maiden, having been reared by the excellent ruru deer,
did not find anyone in her heart even though she was sought after by young men.
Meditating upon Hari Kṛṣṇa, the young woman remained steadfast in her ascetic penance;
in the first month, she subsisted solely on fruit,
taking food every other day, and in the second month, every three days.
In the third [period], on the fifth day; in the fourth, within seven days;
in the fifth, after nine nights; in the sixth, after fifteen days;
in the seventh, after one month; and in the eighth, subsisting on withered leaves. (23–24)

Having abandoned even those [practices], that young woman subsisted on air alone. When a hundred years had passed in this manner, I, Viṣṇu, appeared before her in person and said, "Ask for a boon that is difficult to obtain."
Seeing me, she bowed and replied with palms joined in reverence:
"It is fitting that you remain in my place in this very form;
let this sacred field (kṣetra) be known by my name in every respect."
O Lord of the World, grant these boons: let this body here in the sacred ground become the purifying Ruru-tīrtha;
may every person who has performed their ablutions in my tīrtha be cleansed of sin;
and likewise, may they attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Having thus granted her boons, he vanished on the spot and remained there.
She too, in the course of time, became a sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*);
for it was by restraining her senses that [the Lord] became manifest to her.
It is renowned as Ṛṣīkeśa, and its location is likewise such.
The field of Ruru is called the field of Ṛṣīkeśa; that is said to be a sacred ford (tīrtha).
Now, I shall describe the field known as Goniṣkramaṇa; listen to that.
O beloved, in a former kalpa there was a Prajāpati named Aurva.
Having arrived here for this creation, he performed severe penance;
yet he desired no fruit whatsoever, and in this manner a great length of time passed.
He too arrived at Gaṅgādvāra from the peak of the Himalayas for the sake of obtaining lotus flowers and other offerings; then Śaṅkara himself,
perceiving that the Ṛṣi had departed, reduced his hermitage to ashes.
Then, seeing that hermitage consumed by fire,
Aurva, his eyes copper-red with rage, spoke as if burning the burner himself:
"May he by whom this hermitage was burnt be tormented in every way."
At that very moment, O Goddess of gods, even Śambhu, the burner of Kama, became tormented by a great burning sensation and spoke to the Goddess:
"Having seen the ascetic power of Aurva, the gods have uttered [this curse] out of fear. (37)
"The entire world is being consumed here, yet he desires nothing at all.
What remedy could there be for this so that it might happen for everyone?
When I had spoken thus, his hermitage was scorched by my wrath. (38–39)
He was consumed in an instant, and we emerged from him.
Tormented by this sorrow and overwhelmed with grief, Aurva cursed us out of rage; O Śivā, we were thereby scorched.
Tormented by that burning heat, I am unable to move.
Therefore, let us go to Nārāyaṇa for the sake of pacifying the curse.
Then, having recognized Nārāyaṇa and informed him, we shall proceed together from there.
Having gone to Aurva, they said to him, "Avert the torment of the curse.
Aurva replied, "O Mādhava, bring the herd of Surabhis;
let them bathe Śaṅkara and the others with their milk, and the curse will be pacified."

In the meantime, O Lakṣmī! seventy-seven auspicious, milk-yielding cows of the Surabhi lineage were brought down by me. Their bodies having been bathed with that [milk], they attained supreme peace. || 44-45 ||

Śaṅkara and the others declared this supreme, most meritorious holy field and sacred ford (tīrtha), named Goniṣkramaṇa, to be the excellent Aurvakṣetra. One should perform a ritual bath there; by that, the world of Gaṇeśa (Gāloka) is attained.
Endowed with the conch, discus, and mace, he is honored in my world.
Here, at the root of the Mūlavaṭa tree, the five streams fall;
bathing here in those five streams bestows the fruit of the five great sacrifices. 47–48.
The sacred field that bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation is proclaimed to have five streams.
Now, the field has five divisions where there are five great stones;
since they remain very firm, taking recourse to the direction to my east.
There, in the center of the pool, is a stone slab marked by two *brahma-padas*.
Above that, with the circumference of its stalk, is my *viṣṇu-pada*.
Those who bathe there go to the pure worlds beloved by the *bhāgavatas*.
This is the sacred field of Brahmapada; here the stream falls toward the west.
Having bathed there, one rejoices in the world of Brahmā together with Brahmā.
Next, in the direction of the wind (the northwest), is the certain holy site named Koṭivaṭa.
One should perform a bath there within a distance of five *krośas*;
having enjoyed the fruit of ten million sacrifices, one attains my world.
Now, to the northeast is the beautiful Viṣṇusaras, a most excellent sacred ford.
O beautiful one, even if a mountain were five *krośas* wide and likewise long, for as many steps as one takes while circumambulating it,
that many thousands of years will pass for the one who wanders there.
That meritorious soul is honored in the world of Brahmā on every step.
In that sacred field, a great wonder occurs during the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha;
on the twelfth day, the sounds of cattle are heard from the path of the sky.
O sinless one, this Gosthalaka Tirtha is the destroyer of both physical suffering and sin.
For the speaker and likewise for the listener of this chapter,
there shall be a stay of a thousand years in my abode for every single syllable.
And there shall be a dwelling where twenty-one families are uplifted.
O highly fortunate one! My domain of cows extends over a circle of five yojanas;
I indeed always abide here on the eastern side of the Gaṅgā.
Furthermore, O beautiful one, having reached the Dvāpara Yuga, I abide there in that supreme sacred field named Stutasvāmin;
there dwell Śāṇḍilya, Jājali, Bhṛgu, Kapila, Sāyaṇa, and others.
They shall establish me, who have gone to the earth as the embodiment of Dharma.
Saṃkarṣaṇa, Vāsudeva, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha—
they too will remain there for the welfare of the world.
By my grace, men shall attain the perfection that is supreme to me; however,
for those who harbor envy toward my dharma and my form,
this higher world shall not belong to them, as their souls are struck down by envy.
Avarice leads to total ruin; avarice is the destroyer of Dharma.
(65) Even those engaged in many rituals, devoted to giving and study, or endowed with austerity and knowledge, remain constantly intent upon virtuous deeds. (66)
Furthermore, those consumed by envy do not see me anywhere.
Therefore, no one at all should practice envy, for it destroys peace.
Many have met their end through the fault known as envy.

Listen, Lakṣmī! On Mount Bhūta, there is my image made of iron in the form of a boar; it is indeed impenetrable, yet it is visible. Some see it as made of bell-metal, while others even see it as made of iron.
Others see her as a stone, and still others as a diamond-pig;
some behold that image situated on Mount Maṇipūra.
Freed from all sins, they indeed go to the supreme goal.
This is indeed the Vārāha-kṣetra, which assumes the form of the earth's upliftment. (71) Now I shall describe another sacred site called Pañcārūma;
for one who bathes there, there shall be residence in heaven frequented by Apsarases. (72)
Now, on my southern ground, there is the Bhagukuṇḍa holy site;
one who has bathed there becomes liberated and rejoices in the region of Dhruva.
Now, there is the Maṇikuṇḍa holy site, an unfathomable ocean and an abode of the gods.
Where jewels are seen and Mount Malaya stands firm,
having bathed there, one becomes a king who possesses gems and is liberated.
Formerly, three *krośas* from me, there is a place named Dhūtapāpa.
In Kuṇḍa is the sacred field; its water has the luster of gold and is radiant with emeralds.
Having bathed there, one whose sins are washed away attains the sovereignty of Indra.
Furthermore, a miracle occurs on my mountain at Maṇipūra.
The stream does not fall until the sin has been shaken off.
It is said that there is an Aśvattha tree; one who is pure goes there.
And in the west is the Āmalaka tree, which yields all fruits.
He washes away even the sins of the most wicked through mere touch;
praised by the gods, he dwells daily in the great field of Maṇipūra.
"Stutasvāmī" (Lord Praised) is the name assigned to me by the gods themselves.
Through both recitation and hearing, it bestows enjoyment and liberation upon men.
Now, there is the sacred field of Lohārgala, situated on the Himalayas;
it is preeminent, fifteen *yojanas* in length and five *yojanas* in circumference on all sides.
There, in the northern direction, I dwell within a golden image.
At that time, the Dānavas there were indeed givers of suffering to the gods;
and the Daityas constantly oppressed the humans there as well. (82)
Having personally created a Vaiṣṇava illusion as an inner barrier,
and having established a boundary and a bolt, I hurled my wheel of great splendor and brought about the destruction of thousands of millions of Dānavas.
Then the gods and humans indeed attained happiness at that spot.
Thus, that sacred field named Lohārgala was established by me;
likewise, the auspicious Lohārgala Kuṇḍa, a holy bathing place, was created by me.
There, indeed, a white-colored horse should be given as a gift; it bestows the heavenly realm.
Now, there is the Pañcasaras Kuṇḍa, a sacred ford that grants the world of the Gandharvas.
Here, four streams fall down, conch-white in color and bestowing liberation.
Then there is the Nārada-kuṇḍa, a sacred site possessing five streams;
then the Vasiṣṭha-kuṇḍa, a sacred site possessing three streams.
Then there is the Pañcakuṇḍa, a sacred site endowed with five channels that bestows great merit.
The Saptarṣikuṇḍa Tīrtha, where the seven streams descend;
the Śarabhaṅga-kuṇḍa Tīrtha, joined by the river Śarabhaṅgā;
and the pool named Agnisaras, a Tīrtha that bestows the abode of Fire.
The Bṛhaspatikuṇḍa Tīrtha has one stream issuing from the snow;
the Vaiśvānarakuṇḍa Tīrtha has one stream issuing from the snow;
the Kārtikeyakuṇḍa Tīrtha has fifteen excellent streams.
Meritorious beings descend from the snowy mountains for the sake of bathing.
(92) There is the sacred site known as Umākuṇḍa, where Gaurī went to take birth.
Having bathed there, one should indeed behold Gaurī; such a person rejoices in the world of Gaurī. (93)
Indeed, there is the pool of Maheśvara where Umā was married;
having bathed there, one who is devoted to Rudra goes to the world of Rudra.
And there is the famous Brahmakuṇḍa, where the Vedas emerged.
And four streams of the Vedas fall from the Himalayas:
the auspicious white one in the east, the golden one in the north, the blue-colored one in the west,
and that which has the luster of an indragopa insect in the south— these are the four streams of the Vedas.
Having bathed there, one attains the world of Brahmā; of this there is no doubt.
Thus the sacred field of Lohārgala extends for twenty-five yojanas.
By me, the divine Himālaya has been made the source of all holy fords.
Because the purifying rivers flow [from you], granting liberation to men;
because the gods dwell there and the sages dwell there;
O Daughter of the Ocean, I myself dwell there for the sake of the welfare of the worlds! (8–9)

"Those people who have performed bathing, giving, and religious duties at each of those sacred fords (tīrthas) certainly attain heaven and liberation by my grace forever. Thus ends the [section on] Rūrukṣetra, Ṛṣīkeśa, Niṣkramaṇa, Pañcapada, Brahmāpada, Koṭivaṭa, and Viṣṇusaras in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.

Chapter Three Hundred and Forty-Two: Description of the Holy Tirthas beginning with Stuta-Svāmī, Varāha, Kṣetra, Pañcāsa, Bhṛgu-kuṇḍa, Maṇi-kuṇḍala, Loha-argala, the Five Lakes, Nārada, Vasiṣṭha, the Seven Sages, Śarabhaṅga, Agni, Bṛhaspati, Vaiśvānara, Kārttikeya, Umā, Maheśvara, and Brahma-kuṇḍa. *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā*, Section 1: The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga.
Chapter 343 [Author: Chapter 344 → Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O Sun of primordial knowledge! Eternal witness of all! O Everlasting One!
You alone are the creator of all worlds and the eternal Tīrthaṃkara.
Through your yoga, even insentient earth and water become sentient.

You alone are the supreme ford that carries embodied beings across; thus you are the highest sanctuary. (2) It is held that for living beings, the attainment of liberation here is greater than the attainment of a body.
Without liberation, all those who have attained a body and then met their end have achieved nothing at all. (3)
Vṛndāvana, Māthura, the eternal Śālagrāma, Tulasī, Kṣetrapati, and others—these ancient [places] have been described by you.
O Lord, tell me: how many manifestations did you obtain there?
"And how many will they be, and on what earth? Tell me, O Lord!
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
"O Lakṣmī, indeed my manifestations are innumerable."
Among humans and gods, among animals, beasts, and birds;
among aquatic creatures, forest-dwellers, and among sages and virtuous people;
among seers, holy men, and chaste, virtuous women—they exist in great numbers. (6–7)
O Lotus-born One, at the end of every four yugas I manifest on earth in the regions of Vṛndāvana, Mathurā, and on the banks of the Yamunā;
there I wander and sport, acting as the destroyer of the Daityas.

There are one hundred and five Nārāyaṇas, and five hundred who recline upon the waters. There are thirty forms of the Tortoise, twenty forms of the Fish, one hundred and eight Gopālas, and Buddhas exist by the thousands. (1.343.10)
There were thirty Paraśurāmas and one hundred and one Rāmas;
O my beloved! there have been other incarnations as well, occurring according to necessity, either appearing suddenly with you or alone.
Indeed, there are many cosmic eggs, and many Daityas and Dānavas;
likewise, there are countless gods and ascetics filled with desires.
[I have come] for the destruction of the suffering of the afflicted, and for the attainment of the objects sought by those who seek them.
For the sake of fulfilling the desires of those who possess longing, I manifest in various places:
in some instances as a partial manifestation, in some as complete, and in others through the form of divine possession;
sometimes by a single digit of my power, and at other times in the form of my full majesty.
I manifest indeed as a virtuous being, as a king, and in the form of a true guru;
I appear as Vyāsa and in the very form of the enlightened ones. I alone am Viṣṇu, dwelling in the midst of the realm of liberation.
I have taken birth many times in Vṛndāvana and Mathurā.
That field of Mathurā exists as the foremost of all sacred fords (tīrthas).
Age after age, I am born again and again on the banks of the Yamunā.
In the form of Kṛṣṇa, fulfilling the desires of millions of male and female servants,
and drawn by the devotion and amorous longing of infinite women in creation, I manifest in the form of a king who destroys the pride of millions of desires. (18–19)
Vasu is my father, the Goddess is my mother, and Saṃkarṣaṇa is my brother;
whether others exist or not, I dwell together with these.
Indeed, in the first Dvāpara age, I was joined with Saṃkarṣaṇa.
O beloved, a pair of sons was born to Vasudeva and Devakī.
At that time, there were indeed asuras there born from the lineage of Kālanemi;
I, Kṛṣṇa, the husband of the daughter of the Earth, slew them all.
At that time, you were the daughter of the Wind-god named Kamalā, my beloved;
and in the first Dvāpara age, I was Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Kamalā. I was the destroyer of those born of the lineage of Kālanaimeya in the city of Mathurā.
From that time onwards, O beloved, the sacred field of Mathurā has remained eternally purified by the soles of my feet. After that,
there have been thousands of my manifestations.
O Kamalā! I cannot count their end, whether here or elsewhere;
there will be future incarnations, and men shall sing of them.
And the Vyāsas shall describe them as appropriate for the sake of liberation.
Listen, my beloved! That sacred field of Mathurā is supreme.
Neither in heaven nor in the netherworld is there a holy site equal to Mathurā.
It is delightful, entirely divine, and forever my birthplace. (27–28)

O beloved, by dwelling there, human beings as well as other living creatures attain heaven and liberation, for that place of mine is like Goloka. At Prayāga, on the full moon of Māgha, one obtains the fruit [of bathing] daily in the waters of Yamī.
The fruit that is obtained at Kāśī in a thousand years is indeed attained here in a single day;
the fruit of the full moon of Kārtika at Puṣkara is indeed attained here in a mere moment.
Bewildered by illusion, those who abandon Mathurā wander elsewhere in delusion.
Even from merely hearing the name of Mathurā, multitudes of sins dissolve away.
Whatever holy fords (tīrthas), sacred fields (kṣetras), lakes, rivers, streams, cities, forests, and groves exist upon the earth— [32] — all of these are present here.
When Janārdana is asleep in the month of Āṣāḍha, as [the people] arrive in Mathurā,
the ancestors remain satisfied for an entire Yuga due to the Śrāddha performed in the district of Mathurā.
The people residing in Mathurā go to my own abode at the time of their death.
For those residing specifically at Kubjāmraka and Saukarava, the birthplace [of the Lord], liberation is certain even without Sāṃkhya or Yoga.
Those men who bestow food and clothing are liberated; of this there is no doubt. (35)
O lady of excellent hips, when the Dvāpara age has arrived,
I shall become Kṛṣṇa, the destroyer of the Daityas,
in the lineage of Yayāti, where the Yamunā— the beloved daughter of Vaivasvata— flows beautifully.
Having reached the Gaṅgā at Prayāga, she flows forth as the Triveṇī;
and having received the Sarasvatī, she becomes renowned as the remover of sins.
Yamunā, in the Mathurā region, is superior and possesses a hundredfold the merit of the Gaṅgā.
In that place, O my beloved, there will be other sacred fords (tīrthas) as well;
by bathing in them or drinking their water, liberation is attained without a doubt.
One who dies in the sacred field of Mathurā becomes four-armed [Viṣṇu].
The holy ford named Viśrānti bestows the attainment of rest;
it is the most excellent and greatly meritorious, granting Goloka to men through bathing there.
Whatever bathing, charity, meditation, fire-offerings, or austerity is performed at all other holy fords—
O Lakṣmī! One obtains all that from the sight of the Viśrānti tīrtha (42).
But one does not obtain that fruit through sacrifices, nor through austerity, nor through meditation, nor through restraints, as one who has bathed at the Viśrāntighaṭṭaka does. (43)
By beholding [the deity] at the three times of day, by performing two circumambulations,
and by offering five prostrations, one is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
I have established my place of rest there, at the landing-place on the Yamunā.
Eternal peace exists here, just as it does in the abode of Goloka.
Now, there is another supreme holy site belonging to me located there: Prayāga, which is difficult for even the gods to attain, secret, and the liberator from all worldly existence.
One who bathes there attains my world and shares in the merit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice;
if he has desires, he becomes like Mahendra, and thereafter he goes to the supreme goal. Furthermore, there is another holy site, Kanakhala, which bestows heaven through bathing.
Now, there is another holy ford named Tinduka, which bestows my abode of Goloka.
In the land of Pañcāla, there is the city of Kāmpilya, whose inhabitants are righteous.
There, indeed, a barber named Tinduka always resides. (48–49)
In time, the family of that barber indeed fell into ruin.
Thereupon, he went to Mathurā and lived constantly on the bank of the Yamunā.
For the sake of restoring his family, he performed śrāddha ceremonies and other rites.
Constantly bathing in the Yamunā, he met his death in due course. Thereafter, having obtained birth as the son of a brāhmaṇa in Mathurā,
he became a supreme Vaiṣṇava and departed for the abode of Goloka.
Thus, that twice-born man known as Tinduka, possessing the memory of his former births,
informed everyone and made that sacred site famous, then passed away. (53) Now, there is another supreme solar tirtha that destroys all sins.
Having propitiated [the Lord] with the desire for wealth and sovereignty, Bali,
with arms raised and abstaining from food, performed supreme austerity here. The Blessed One, Sūryanārāyaṇa himself, became pleased with him.
Having approached, Bali asked, "What is the purpose of your penance?
Bali replied, "The Sun is the lord of the three worlds and the eye of the universe;
I am destitute and possess no kingdom, and I perform this penance for the sake of wealth."
Then Sūrya gave him a *cintāmaṇi* jewel from his own crown.
Having obtained that *cintāmaṇi*, he went indeed to Pātāla.
After bathing in the waters of Yamī, Sūrya went to the golden orb.
Thus this excellent holy ford (tīrtha) was born, which destroys sin and suffering.
By bathing there, one attains heaven and thereafter liberation; one shall become four-armed.
On Sundays, at the transit of the sun (saṃkrānti), during lunar and solar eclipses, and on auspicious lunar days—

One who performs a ritual bath at Sūryatīrtha shall obtain the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice. (1.343.60) Now, here is Dhruvatīrtha, where in ancient times Dhruva performed austerities; by bathing there one gains sovereignty, and by dying there one attains the station of Dhruva. (69)
Through faith, the ancestors cross over here and attain liberation.
To the south of Dhruva is that sacred ford, indeed the king of all tīrthas (tīrtharājaka).
By bathing there, O Lakṣmī, one shall surely attain my Goloka.
Now, O Lakṣmī, to the south of that is considered the supreme Ṛṣitīrtha.
By bathing there, one goes to the world of the sages (Ṛṣiloka) upon the departure of life, and reaching Goloka.
Further to the south of that is my supreme Mokṣatīrtha.
Whereby bathing brings liberation and one attains my Goloka,
right there is Koṭitīrtha, which is difficult even for the gods to obtain.
By bathing there, as well as by giving gifts, reciting prayers, performing fire-sacrifices, and feeding [the hungry], [one attains the same].
Through offering libations and fasting, one is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
By him who has visited Koṭitīrtha, his ancestors are delivered;
likewise, seven generations before him and seven generations after him—seven lineages in total—are delivered.
Now, indeed, there is Vāyutīrtha, the supreme savior of the ancestors;
those who offer funeral cakes (piṇḍas) certainly deliver the ancestors in every way.
For here, the fruit of offering funeral cakes at Gayā is truly obtained.
In the month of Jyeṣṭha especially, ancestors cross over [to liberation] by means of the Śrāddha rite.
These sacred fords (tīrthas) have indeed been described as bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
for bathing, giving, recitation, and burnt offerings performed there yield a thousandfold merit.
Through the remembrance, salutation, and likewise the sight of sacred fords (tīrthas),
as well as by drinking even a single drop of their water, eternal liberation is attained. Now, here [is] the preeminent among sacred fords, a collection of descent-places (avatāras).
All the incarnations of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, having gathered together at the very moment of his birth, remained for a moment on that auspicious bank of the Yamunā near his birthplace;
that sacred site remains hidden. (72–73)
By bathing there, by drinking the water, and even by sprinkling it upon oneself, [this place] completely destroys all sins and bestows the realms of Goloka, Vaikuṇṭha, and others.
Indeed, by dying there, liberation will surely be attained; of this there is no doubt.
Even by fasting for a single day, one shall obtain the fruit of ten million sacrifices.
Even those embodied beings whom the particles of dust from Mathurā touch—
even if they be animals, insects, and the like— they too shall attain liberation.

Indeed, even in another land, one who utters His name becomes a partaker of enjoyment; so what need be said of where the Supreme Brahman Himself resides? Wealth, dwellings, land, wives, sons, daughters, and all such prosperities—[are not found there]? 77.
Authority over fields and gardens, sovereignty, political power, and lordship over people;
gold, silver, great fortune, prosperity, wealth, palaces, and so forth—these indeed come to a devotee here through the yoga of Hari, by a mere drop of his grace. (78–79)
Just as it is a savior, a sustainer, a protector, and a guardian, so too is the supreme Mathurā-tīrtha the bestower of heaven and the giver of liberation. 1.343.80.

Thus ends the three hundred and forty-third chapter, titled "The Manifestation of the Infinite Incarnations of the Lord, the First Dvāpara Age Incarnation of Kṛṣṇa, and the Display of Viśrānti-tīrtha, Prayāga, Kanakhala, Tinduka, Sūrya, Dhruva-tīrtha-rāja, Ṛṣimokṣa-koṭi, Vāyu-avatāra-tīrtha, and Others," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, within the *Mathurā-kṣetra-māhātmya* of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. Chapter 344 *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā* — Section 1 (*Kṛtayuga-santāna*) — Chapter 344.
[The Author: Chapter 345.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, Lakṣmī! In Mathurā there is the supreme and great Śivakuṇḍa.
At that place, Hara himself performed austerities for a long time at the holy site established by Śiva.
Then Kṛṣṇa, Mādhava, having arrived there, spoke to Śiva:
"O Śambhu, why indeed do you perform such extremely severe penance?"
Śambhu said, "O Great King! The gods are being excessively tormented by the Daityas;
you ought to descend here for the destruction of the Asuras.
Hari replied, "So be it. Then, having bathed in the Yamunā, Hara—
Having completed his ascetic penance there, he departed for Kailāsa itself.
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa also went indeed to Goloka;
he was born as that very Kṛṣṇa at the junction of the first Dvāpara age.
This Śivakuṇḍa is a sacred ford that caused Kṛṣṇa’s arrival;
it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, for by bathing there, one attains Vaikuṇṭha.
To the north of Śivakuṇḍa is the Saṃyamana Tīrtha, which grants great merit.
Through bathing, fortune, good luck, and beauty are produced.
Heaven as well as supreme liberation are attained; there is no doubt in this matter.
Whatever ancient events occurred at the great holy site of Saṃyamana— || 7–8 ||
Listen, Lakṣmī! This is most wonderful and destructive of sins.
A Niṣāda dwelling in the Naimiṣa forest, whose mind was once contented, arrived one day at Mathurā while following a sinful course of conduct. (9)
He bathes daily in the Yamunā by swimming with his arms;
he comes to one bank and likewise goes back again.
Thus he bathes and swims on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight.
Desiring to cross, that Niṣāda fell into the waters of the Yamunā;
he then crossed the Yamunā toward the Saṃyamana tīrtha. O auspicious lady, as soon as he reached the bank and arrived at Saṃyamana—
Exhausted by fatigue, he indeed sank down and drank the water.
That great sinner, being powerless, was instantly deprived of his life. By the power of that sacred ford (tīrtha), the basket of his sins was destroyed.
Great merit was produced by him, and by that he was born as the lord of the earth.
In the region of the Saurāṣṭra country, he became the king, the sovereign of Saurāṣṭra. That archer ruled over the empire of Bhadrāpattana.
By name he was a Kṣatriya king known as Yakṣmadhanu;
relying upon the duty of a warrior (kṣatradharma), he protected the earth.
Indeed, he was a devotee of the Siddhas who dwell on Mount Raivata.
He used to go daily with joy by carriage to the mountain for the purpose of seeing [the sage],
to the auspicious shore of the lake of Aśvapaṭṭa in the east.
Having gone to the hermitage of Patnīvrata, he beheld that great sage.
He beheld the goddess Kambharālakṣmī and the Lord Gopālakṛṣṇa;
he also beheld Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa constantly. By His power, this king was indeed a devotee of Kṛṣṇa and a Vaiṣṇava. (1.344.20)
He was born great and powerful, for whose protection a protective necklace was bestowed—
one that consists of armor and protects the king in every way.
By means of it, the king was always protected and victorious even in battle.
For this reason, he obtained the kingdom of the Gaurjaras and the Marus.
By means of an aerial vehicle, he went specifically for the purpose of a pilgrimage to Kāśī;
for the King of Kāśī, having recognized him as a supreme Vaiṣṇava, [granted him passage].

Having honored the victorious and illustrious [prince], his own daughter named Pīvarī was bestowed upon him; taking her, he departed for his city. Having arrived at Bhadrāpattana, the auspicious Pīvarī was wed by him.
She was made the beloved chief among hundreds of principal wives.
And he delighted her in beautiful gardens and forests,
in lovely palaces, and on the sandy banks of rivers.
As he protected his subjects and likewise bestowed gifts,
time passed for that king, who came to be joined by sons and grandsons;
and as he remained attached to worldly enjoyments, ten thousand years indeed went by.
He had five hundred very beautiful sons and daughters;
all the girls were married by him according to the prescribed rites in every way.
He bestowed the great kingdom upon the eldest son, and indeed, the cities upon the middle ones.
Then, having assigned the land suitable for livelihood to his younger brothers,
he himself attained happiness and withdrew from the affairs of state.
He subsequently established a means of subsistence for the queens by providing them with certain dwellings.
While sleeping with Pīvarī, he converses in his dream as if awake:
"Alas! Alas! Oh, let us go! What indeed is the use of life here?
Having remembered that land of Mathurā, and having remembered the holy site of Saṃyama. (3.1–3.2)
Then Pīvarī said, "O King, why do you speak thus?
Having heard the words of his beloved, the king replied to her:
"One who is intoxicated, asleep, or heedless speaks incoherently."
"O beloved, you must not disregard the words of one who is under the influence of sleep!
Pīvarī said: "O Lord, I have heard this again and again;
since it has been repeated many times, it must indeed be born of a firm latent impression (*saṃskāra*)."
O Great King, you appear to me to be one who remembers his past births; therefore, speak! O sinless King, tell me that which pertains to your previous existence.
If I am dear to you, tell it to me today.
"O King, I shall give up my life if you will protect me.
Having heard the words of his beloved, the lord of men replied:
"If it must certainly be said, we shall go to the city of Mathurā."
"In the light, however, our death will surely occur; of this there is no doubt.
Having gone there, I shall indeed relate the account of my previous birth.
O fair-eyed one, bestow abundant gifts upon the Brahmins."
Having established his sons and grandsons, and having observed each in their respective positions;
and having bestowed villages, treasuries, jewels, and his sons upon them,
the king honored the people residing in the city.
Having entrusted his sons to protect the kingdom inherited from his father and grandfather in due order, and having likewise informed his dear kinsmen and householders,
he instructed them for their own welfare and appointed his wives to the task of protection.
Then he spoke to his friends, allies, servants, maidservants, and female slaves:
"This kingdom that has been acquired is in every way a bondage.
Indeed, for the sake of my own liberation, I shall go to the city of Mathurā."
From contentment and likewise from renunciation, there is no other supreme happiness.
There is no eye equal to knowledge, and there is no strength equal to the eye.
There is no suffering equal to passion, and there is no happiness greater than renunciation.
He who pursues all desires, and he who abandons them entirely— of these two,
the renunciation of all desires is generally superior.
Therefore, I must depart for the sacred site, the city of Mathurā.
Having thus informed all the people and appointed his sons to guard them,
he arrived at the city of Mathurā endowed with an appropriate force.
By him the beautiful city was seen, and it was beheld by Pīvarī as well.
Endowed with sacred fords that bestow liberation, it is meritorious, sin-destroying, and auspicious.
O Lakṣmī! The delightful place named Vṛndāvana is the unsurpassed abode of Viṣṇu;
by seeing it, a person indeed becomes one who has fulfilled his purpose. (1.344.50)
On the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa, one who has bathed at Yamī is liberated.
Likewise, there is my unsurpassed abode, Madhuvana, which is auspicious;
by beholding that second forest, one truly becomes one who has accomplished all that was to be done.
The third is the excellent Kunda Forest, known as Caitra;
one who bathes there on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada is liberated.
The fourth is the auspicious Kāmyaka Forest, which bestows my own abode.
One who bathes in the pool of Vimala is indeed liberated from sin;
he who gives up his life there goes to my world.
The fifth is Bakulavana, the site of my monastic grove.
Having gone there and bathed accordingly, one proceeds to the world of Fire (Vahniloka).
On the further bank of the Yamunā is my sixth sacred grove, Bhadravana;
having gone there and bathed accordingly, one proceeds to the world of the Nāgas (Nāgaloka).
My seventh forest there is made of khadira wood, resembling a sacrifice;
by seeing this purifying place, a man shall go to my world.
And my eighth is the Great Forest (Mahāvana), endowed with all kinds of trees.
Having gone there, a person is glorified in the world of Indra.
The ninth forest is the Lohajaṅgha forest, the best of forests;
for a person who goes there, it destroys even the greatest of sins.
The tenth is the forest named Bilvavana, which is worshipped by the gods;
having gone there, a person is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
The eleventh is Bhāṇḍīra, for it bestows yoga upon yogins.
Where indeed stands the tree known as Bhāṇḍīravaṭa, where my marriage with Rādhā took place;
by the mere sight of it, a person does not conceive. (61–62)
Having seen Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa there, one is not subject to rebirth.
O beloved, the grove of Tulasī trees alone is my twelvefold forest;
it consists of trees made of Kṛṣṇa’s own skin, and it is the site of my wedding, which bestows liberation.
Vṛndāvana is indeed a forest of green trees for me.
Having gone there, having plucked leaves and likewise petals from you, and having seen the multitude of Tulasī plants, I shall remember you in the waters of the Yamunā. ||64-65||
Having bathed and attained liberation, he is honored by me in Goloka.
O beloved, those people who behold Vṛndā, Tulasī, and Govinda do not go to the city of Yama;
they go only to my Goloka.
"Those with desire go to heaven; from there, indeed, they reach my supreme abode.
Having approached such a great sacred site, Mathurā, the two of them attained joy and performed the rites of the pilgrimage with devotion.
Having eaten and fed her husband, Pīvarī then asked him about the account of his dream, that secret which he had previously mentioned:
"I shall tell you what was said by the king regarding Mathurā."
"Tell me that, O Great King, which was previously spoken as something to be kept secret! (1.344.70) The king also spoke to his own wife regarding the story of their previous birth:
"Listen, my wife! I was a Niṣāda who dwelt in the Naimiṣa forest. (1.344.71)
Having come here and died at the Saṃyamana Tīrtha within the waters,
by that merit he was born as a powerful king in Saurāṣṭra,
[born] from the seed of Kṛṣṇa, known as Pāṇḍu-vrata, through his prowess.
"Even though sovereignty has already been obtained by you, you have [further] gained [merit] from the King of Kāśī.
Always remembering my former births, I recall this sacred ford while on your bed; sometimes, when overcome by sleep, I indeed speak of it."
"Alas, alas! Oho! Let us go; what indeed is the use of life here?
Thus did she relate her past-life history to me, O lady!
Having heard this, the queen, who remembered her former births, spoke of her own history as well.
I am indeed named Pīvarī, a resident on the banks of the Gaṅgā.
Having come to see this city on the twelfth lunar day of the month of Kārttika, I boarded a boat and, while traveling here, fell into the waters of the Yamunā. ||76-77||
I was instantly deprived of my life-breaths and became the daughter of the King of Kāśī;
yet, O King, though married by you, that memory did not abandon me.
By the power of this sacred ford, I have become your queen.
My death occurred at the sacred ford of Dhārāpatanaka.
Again, O King, as we were performing meritorious acts, the Mokṣatīrtha was seen in Mathurā; the end of our lives has now arrived.
"Today itself, many gifts must be given by my own hand," she said;
having spoken thus, she bathed at the bank of the Yamunā and gave those gifts.
The king also performed meritorious acts, giving gifts and feeding the Brahmins and others.
The gift of cows, the gift of gold, the gift of sesame seeds, and the bestowal of wealth;
the gift of land, and indeed the joyful giving away of Brahmin maidens;
the gifts of sacred threads, as well as the giving of garments and food. (8.2–8.3)
Then, having performed everything, both the king and the queen remained together; at that very moment,
the attendants of Goloka arrived on the bank of the Yamunā,
accompanied by a celestial chariot, along with Pīvarī and Yakṣmarāja.
Having assumed divine bodies with four arms, they were led to the abode of Hari.
Thus, having reached Mathurā and bathed in a holy ford of the Yamunā, the two beheld me there according to their discipline and met their death in that very place.
Having abandoned all worldly existence, they attained my very same world.
This which was a great marvel has been told to you, O Lakṣmī!
A person, having cast off their body at the sacred ford known as Dhārāpātana, [attains this state].
One attains the world of the gods and Goloka without a doubt.
Having reached Yamuneśvara and surrendered one's own life,
one attains the world of Viṣṇu, possessing a divine form with four arms.

Thus ends the three hundred and forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of Śivakuṇḍa Tīrtha, Saṃyamana Tīrtha, the Attainment of the Kingdom of Saurāṣṭra by the deceased Niṣāda, the Marriage of the Daughter of the King of Kāśī, their Death in Mathurā as those who remembered their past lives, and the Majesty of Yamuneśvara," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 345: [Continuation of the Kṛta Yuga Section] — *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Book 1.
[The Author: Chapter 346.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, Lakṣmī! I shall likewise describe another sacred ford (tīrtha) to you.
Nāgatīrtha is the supreme sacred ford, for it was from here that the Nāga was banished. Having bathed here, those who die go to heaven and are not born again.
Now, Ghaṇṭābharaṇaka is indeed another supreme purifying sacred ford.
Having bathed there, one goes to the world of the Sun; of this there is no doubt.
Furthermore, there exists another sacred ford (tīrtha) called Brahmatīrtha in the waters of the Yamunā.
Having bathed there and drunk its water, one is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
Now, there is another sacred ford called Somatīrtha in the purifying waters of the Yamunā.
There, the Moon-god, having seen me, then worshipped me with devotion.
One should perform an ablution there; such a person is glorified in the world of Soma.
Now, there is another supreme holy site, the Sarasvatī-prapātana.
O Lakṣmī! A man who bathes there becomes a renunciant (yati), even if he is of low caste.
In the district of Mathurā, on the Yamunā, a person who fasts for three nights [attains the same].

By merely bathing there, one who has performed the vow is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin. (7) Now, there is the purifying holy site named Daśāśvamedha on the Yamunā; that place is situated in the western part of Mathurā and is exceedingly sacred. (8)
Those who bathe there with self-restraint will find heaven not difficult to attain.
Indeed, it was in ancient times that Brahmā created the Mānasa-tīrtha on the Yamunā;
having bathed there, which is honored by the ṛṣis, they surely go to heaven.
Now, the Vighnarāja Tīrtha is meritorious, sin-destroying, and auspicious. On the eighth, the fourteenth, and especially on the fourth lunar day,
the Lord of Obstacles (Vighnarāja) does not afflict one who has bathed in that best of tīrthas.
In all undertakings of learning and in all acts of sacrifice and charity,
the son of Pārvatī constantly ensures that there be no obstacles for him. Furthermore, there is another holy site called Koṭitīrtha, where bathing yields the merit of giving ten million cows.
Upon the loss of life, he goes to the world of Soma and to my own world.
Beyond this lies the sacred field of Śiva, measuring half a krośa;
there the god Hara dwells and constantly protects Mathurā.

Having bathed there and drunk the water, one obtains the fruit of Mathurā. Furthermore, if one gives up their life-breaths here, they go to my world. Now, there is another holy ford (*tīrtha*), always the most excellent among all holy fords, known as Sudhana.

I dwell there eternally out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds. Upon seeing me and bathing there, human beings become partakers of liberation, especially during the solstices, the equinoxes, the full-moon days of Viṣṇupadī, and during solar eclipses.
Having bathed there, one obtains infinite fruit and is liberated from all sins;
a person attains the merit arising from the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices.
One who has bathed at the Sudhana Tīrtha partakes in the religious merit of bathing at Prayāga.
Listen, O beloved, to what occurred here in the first Dvāpara age!
There was one named Sudhana who was indeed always my devotee, and he was prosperous with wealth, grain, sons, wives, cattle, houses, and so forth. (1.345.20)
Characterized by moral conduct, contentment, honoring the virtuous, compassion, and charity,
that devotee of mine lived indeed together with his wife and children.
Days passed for him, as did months and years.

Through devotion to me alone and by constant service to virtuous and chaste women, he performs his household duties with whatever wealth he has obtained. He never practices deception with measures or weights. (22–23)
He constantly performs my supreme worship three times a day,
with the invocation, the five nectars such as milk,
and water; with bathing, ornaments, various garments, and excellent unguents.
With flower-lamps, incense, sandalwood, nectar, and excellent fruits; with food offerings of most delicious foods, water, betel-leaf, and lime-powder;
and thus with nightly waving of lights, hymns of praise, and songs of glorification—(25–26).

He always worshipped me with circumambulations and prostrations like a staff; he observed the fast on the eleventh lunar day and likewise kept a vigil. He constantly performed his ablutions three times a day at the Yamunā with devotion.
Having reached the bank of the Kālindī, near my own form,
he dances during the first watch of the night and then goes to his own home.
He does this every day, but especially on the eleventh lunar day (Ekādaśī).
On the night of the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, having bathed, he went to the temple on the bank of the Yamunā for the sake of keeping a vigil; at that moment,
he was seized by some arriving Brahma-rākṣasa.
Black-complexioned, with a massive body and hair standing erect, he was exceedingly terrifying.
He said: "I am a Rākṣasa here; I wander about for the sake of food.
I dwell in the distant forest; I shall devour you, so do not grieve. (31-32)
"I have been hungry for a long time; indeed, I shall find satisfaction for a long duration.
Having seen, heard, and understood this, the merchant then spoke with fortitude:
"I am Sudhana; I shall give you a great feast. Be gracious to me."
"Wait for a moment of mine today; I shall give you an abundance.
You shall eat my body, mixed with much delicious food.
Having performed the rites for the gods, I will give all of that to you."
"I perform the vigil for the God of gods on the day of Hari;
indeed, my vow is for all time that I keep watch before Hari. Having performed that vigil there, in the morning, I shall be in your presence. (36)

"Wherever you tell me to go, there I shall come under your control. You may devour me at your pleasure once I have performed the vigil, provided that you grant me permission to perform this vow for the satisfaction of Viṣṇu. (37–38)
"There is a meritorious vow that grants all desires and bestows liberation;
do not break my vow, have mercy, and may it be auspicious.
Having heard Sudhana’s words, the hungry Brahmarākṣasa—
He said to Sudhana: "O merchant, you speak falsely;
for once one is released from the jaws of death, one does not indeed return to death again.
Having been liberated from my noose, how could you come back to me once more?"
Having heard the words of the Rākṣasa, the merchant Bhaktottama said:
"The entire world has truth as its root; everything is established in truth. All living beings have goodness (sat) as their foundation. If you have hunger, it must exist within that which is real."
"In that case, I am one whose food is truth; how can there be food for you when hunger is absent? Hunger and thirst were indeed created by Brahmā as the very work of Brahman.
If I have been created for that purpose, then your success shall be achieved, and not otherwise."
If I, as a merchant, have not been corrupted by past actions,
and if the inner self dwells within my heart just as it does in yours;
if I am devoted, if I am established in truth and righteousness, and if I speak with sincerity— then [grant me your grace].
Listen to my promise, O Rākṣasa! By means of which I have returned.
Having kept a vigil at night and performed a dance before Hari, I shall come back again, O Rākṣasa! There is no falsehood in me.
Brahman is acquired through truth; dharma is protected by truth.
A daughter is given in marriage through truth, for the gods of the earth (brāhmaṇas) are speakers of truth.
Kings have crossed over [perils] by means of truth, and the earth is sustained by truth.
O Rākṣasa, heaven and liberation are obtained through the vow of truth.
By truth the sun shines; by truth the moon waxes;
by truth Time brings [the seasons]; and by truth rain is produced. (1.345.50)
"I live by truth; I have never committed an untruth.
May that truth of mine perish indeed if I do not return again. (5.1) But as for that person who forcibly enjoys a woman through the impulse of lust—
I shall be stained by that sin if I do not come before you.
(52) I shall be stained by the sin of one who, having performed the gift of land, a cow, or other such acts, takes them back again, if I should not return once more. (53)
Having enjoyed a woman or a man solely for one's own sake, one should then abandon them;
yet one should not act for the sake of another, for that sin shall not exist in my scripture.
He who abandons a virtuous, devoted wife who is indeed innocent—
May I be tainted by that sin if you do not come before me again.
May I be tainted by the sin of one who creates a breach in the row of those eating together in a single line, if you do not come before me.
May that sin which belongs to one who breaks their vow not come upon me;
may the sin of one who harms others not come before me, if you stand in my presence.
May the sin of one who abandons the twice-born, or reviles virtuous women, holy men, and the gods [not come upon me].
May that sin be mine, O Rākṣasa, if I do not return again!
Whatever sin belongs to one who commits treachery against a guru, a friend, or a well-wisher—that very sin shall be mine if I do not come before you; I speak the truth, O Rākṣasa! (58–59)
May the sins I have committed at sacred fords not follow me again;
[may they fall instead] upon the slayer of a Brahmin, the drinker of liquor, the thief, the breaker of vows,
the rogue, the betrayer of trust, the assassin, and the killer of a child.
May I attain that very destiny if there is no return for me;
may whatever sin exists here from the confinement or the killing of innocent beings be mine if there is no return for me. (61–62)
"If I were to abandon the truth and fail to return, I would incur the sin of this life and undergo birth as a Rākṣasa. Having heard these words of the merchant, that Rākṣasa was pleased.
He inspired confidence in him when he was in distress, saying to him, "Go," and "Come here.
The merchant quickly came to my house and honored me;
having performed a dance before me, he joyfully kept a vigil. (64–65)

At dawn, repeatedly uttering "Obeisance to Nārāyaṇa," he went to the bank of the Yamunā, prostrating himself like a staff again and again. Having performed his bath in the Kālindī, the devotee set out upon the path of the Rākṣasa.
Having become intent on compassion, I stood blocking his path. 67.
Beholding the Supreme Person, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, who possessed a divine form and four arms, the devoted Sudhana spoke to me. 68.

Oṃ, obeisances to you, O Blessed One, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the bestower of liberation upon devotees here and the giver of divine vision! (69) And he was asked by me, O Lakṣmī: "Where has the merchant departed in such haste?"
Sudhana replied: "I am going into the presence of the Rākṣasa. Having heard this, he was restrained [by his father], who said: "You must not go, truly, you must not go!
While living, dharma is abandoned; when dead, what means for liberation can there be?"
Nevertheless, having heard this and bowed to me, he went to the presence of the Rākṣasa and said: "O Rākṣasa, eat me as you wish, without delay!
Whether according to the prescribed rule or in whatever manner pleases you. (72)
"Truth must always be protected by me; eat, O Rākṣasa! Do not delay!
(7.3) And the Rākṣasa, perceiving this marvel, became pleased toward him and said: "O merchant, you have won. (7.4)
By you, the dharma of truthful vows has been protected; through that, I have attained satisfaction. My hunger has vanished and eternal contentment has arisen.
Oh, how could I commit an act of treachery here against one who is so devoted to truth?
"But grant me the merit of my vigilance;
by the power of that true merit, may I attain liberation.
Having heard those words, Sudhana then spoke to the rākṣasa: || 77 ||
Do you know, O Rākṣasa, what kind of merit indeed belongs to keeping vigil? The merit of staying awake for even one *ghaṭikā* bestows the station of Indra;
for those who stay awake for two *ghaṭikās*, it grants the supreme station of Brahmā. (78)
For one who remains awake at midnight, there is indeed the supreme station of Vairāja; for one who remains awake during the *ūnarātra* (the waning night), there is surely the station of Vaikuṇṭha;
and for one who remains awake until dawn, liberation that bestows the world of Brahmā shall come to pass.
Indeed, by remaining awake for even half a *ghaṭikā*, a universal empire is surely attained;
for one who dances while awake, Goloka is certainly attained.
Therefore, I shall not grant the fruit of complete wakefulness.
"Give half, or else give half of that, or give me half of that half.
O lord of devotees, do not be greedy; grant me liberation as well!
Though thus entreated, Sudhana, being covetous of liberation, did not give anything at all.
And again the Brahmarākṣasa entreated Sudhana:
"O best of merchants, give me the merit of a single dance!
Sudhana asked him: "Tell me, what was your former birth?"
"Afterwards, I shall tell you the entire account and the fruit of my single falsehood.
"Do you not know me? the Rākṣasa said to the merchant;
"I am the Brahmin Agnidatta, living near your house. (85–86)
I am that very same friend of yours, who by my own past actions became a Brāhmaṇa learned in the Vedas, yet has fallen into the state of a Rākṣasa.
Like your earthly palace, I have begun to construct a magnificent two-storied mansion for you.
For that purpose, I was always stealing bricks belonging to others at night.
I committed the sin of theft, yet my house did not become full.
Afflicted by fever and possessed by a longing for home, I dwelt in the middle of the palace.
Due to the sin of theft, even though I am a Brahmin, I have become a Brahma-rākṣasa. Recognizing that I am indeed your friend, O excellent merchant,
show compassion toward me who has come to you as a friend and grant me your assistance.

“O devotee! Grant me the merit of a single dance so that my destination may become one characterized by liberation; I entreat you repeatedly. Hearing this, the merchant, his heart moistened with compassion, spoke to the Rākṣasa.
"Excellent, Rākṣasa! I have granted you the fruit of one dance.
Having spoken thus, just as he was placing water into the hand of the Rākṣasa, the body of the Rākṣasa fell to the ground at that moment.
Having become four-armed like an attendant of Śrī Hari,
he shone before the merchant, appearing as a youth of sixteen years.
Viṣṇu himself had come to lead him away, adorned by his divine attendants.

Seeing Hari, Sudhana fell to the ground at his feet and said there to his Lord: "O Blessed One, we have been delivered by you from even a mere fragment of the Rākṣasa's dance; you are indeed the granter of liberation."
"And may you also become the bestower of liberation for me, O Mādhava.
Then Janārdana, the God of gods, spoke sweetly to him:
"Come, you too, O lord of devotees! And let the lord of brahmins also come to me."
"O Sudhanā, let your family quickly assemble at my vehicle;
having ascended this excellent celestial chariot, let them indeed go to my world.
Having spoken thus, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa [placed] everyone upon the celestial chariot.
Having caused him to ascend that well-constructed [vehicle], he went to the eternal abode of Vaikuṇṭha.
At that place where this miracle occurred, there is the holy site known as Sudhana;
for those who perform their ritual bath there on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika—
Through giving gifts here, one obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice, and heaven shall be the fruit;
the one who performs the ritual release of a bull on the full moon day shall deliver his lineages.
Furthermore, the performer of a Śrāddha at this sacred ford shall deliver his ancestors.

"Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have related to you the liberation of Sudhana. (103) Thus, in the first book of the Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā, within the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga and the majesty of the Mathurā-kṣetra, this is the forty-fifth [chapter], titled 'The Description of the Liberation of the Brahmarākṣasa through the Merit of the Dance Offered by Sudhana at the Nāga-tīrtha, Ghaṇṭābharaṇaka-tīrtha, Soma-tīrtha, Sarasvatī-daśāśvamedha-tīrtha, Rāja-vighnarāja-koṭiśiva-kṣetra, and Sudhana-tīrtha.'"
Chapter Three Hundred and Forty-Five:
345. *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 1 (*Kṛtayuga-Santāna*: The Lineage of the Kṛta Age).
Chapter 346.
[The Author: Chapter 347.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī! In the region of Mathurā, there is another sacred ford (tīrtha).
The Vatsakrīḍanaka Tīrtha is fashioned from red stone.
By bathing there, a human being shall indeed go to the world of Vāyu;
and upon the relinquishing of life there, supreme liberation shall occur—of this there is no doubt.
Then there is the supreme Bhāṇḍīraka Tīrtha, which bestows the status of husband and wife;
it is there in the forest region that Rādhā was indeed married by Kṛṣṇa,
amidst *sāla*, *tāla*, and *arjuna* trees, as well as *tamāla*, *iṅguda*, and *pīluka*.
At the site of Bhāṇḍīraka, which is filled with Karīra and red flowers,
he who bathes is liberated from sin and goes to the world of the Moon;
if he gives up his life there, he attains Goloka— of this there is no doubt.
Vṛndāvana is my sacred pilgrimage site, where the cows, cowherds,
and gopīs shall always sport with me in various wonderful pastimes.
It is a place difficult for all to attain, located at the holy pool within the region of Vṛndāvana.
Having bathed in a forest of many shrubs and creepers,
he rejoices for many years in heaven, served by hosts of *apsarases* and *gandharvas*.
If he gives up his life there, he will certainly rejoice in Vaikuṇṭha.
Furthermore, one who bathes at the place in Vṛndāvana where the demon Keśī was struck down undoubtedly obtains a hundredfold merit;
and the Hariviśrāma-tīrtha there yields a hundredfold merit even more than that.
There, by the offering of alms-food, one obtains a fruit equal to that of Gayā.
Bathing, giving gifts, and performing fire-sacrifices there yield the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
Now, the sacred site of the twelve suns is considered the most excellent and supreme.
On the banks of the Kālindī, Kṛṣṇa danced upon the head of the serpent Kālīya for the purpose of subduing him; there, O Lakṣmī, ten blazing suns were stationed by me alone at that time,
having been informed [of the task] for the sake of granting a boon.
Then the Ādityas said:
"If there is a boon to be granted to us, let there be liberation for people through bathing here at our tīrtha—north of Lord Hari and south of Kālīya. (13–14)
"Those who have died in the middle [of the river] shall attain liberation in the abode of Goloka"—
this was requested by them, and "so be it," I granted.
Now, on the further shore of the Yamunā, there is the sacred site of Malayārjuna.
There, a cart has overturned, and a water-pot is found there.
By bathing and fasting there, one shall partake of infinite fruit;
by bathing, giving gifts, and beholding [it] on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha.
Through the perfect worship of Acyuta, one attains the supreme goal;
Kṛṣṇa himself comes to lead away the person who has observed the fast.
Moreover, one born in our lineage who has bathed in the waters of the Yamunā—

Having fasted, he will worship Govinda in Mathurā. Blessed is he who shall offer the funeral cakes (piṇḍa) in the Yamunā on the twelfth day of the month of Jyeṣṭha; for him, there shall be no further need for [ordinary] satiation.
Thus do the ancestors, having gone to the other world, always sing:
"Now here is a blessed sacred ford, the forest known as Bahula.
Having bathed there on the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī), one proceeds to the abode of Rudra."
Having bathed on the tenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, one shall attain my state.
Now, the Bhāṇḍahrada tīrtha is found on the opposite bank;
there, every single day, the suns known as Supataṅgaka are seen.
The person who performs a bath at that sacred site in the Arkakuṇḍa,
being liberated from all sins, goes to the world of the Sun.
Now, here is a pure well named Saptasāmudra.
Having bathed there, one may attain whatever is desired; he goes to his own cherished world.
But at the departure of life there, he attains my abode.
Now, there is a supreme and auspicious sacred field called Vīrasthala.
And there is the site near the water, adorned with lotuses and lilies;
having bathed there, one reaches the world of heroes and, at the end, goes to my abode.
Likewise, there is the sacred field of Kuśasthala, which is most meritorious and supremely purifying.
Having bathed there, one goes to the world of Brahmā; upon death, one attains Goloka. There, at the Puṣpasthalatīrtha, is the unsurpassed sacred field of Śiva;
by bathing there, a person proceeds to the world of Śiva.

Then, at Gopīśa-tīrtha, there is the form of Gopīśvara, which destroys great sins; established by Mātali, it bestows liberation. Indeed, thousands of gopīs were there for the sake of sporting with Kṛṣṇa.

Then Kṛṣṇa appeared, assuming a thousand forms; the Lord, the bestower of happiness, dallied with each and every gopī as He desired. Then Mātali arrived there and, having installed the Lord of the gopīs [on his chariot], 3–2. Then Kṛṣṇa appeared, assuming a thousand forms; the Lord, the bestower of happiness, dallied with each and every gopī as He desired.
Then Mātali arrived there and, having installed the Lord of the gopīs [on his chariot],
Having brought seven jars overflowing with gems and medicinal herbs, she performed the consecration ceremony for the Lord who was wearing the dress of a cowherd.
The cowherd girls sang and danced, crying out, "Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa!"
There he established a well with seven jars;
it is a sacred ford named Sāmudrika, which bestows the abode of Goloka.
There, by one who offers water and offers funeral cakes (piṇḍa) during a śrāddha ceremony, [the result] is attained in every respect.

By him, seventy-seven generations of his lineage are delivered. On a Monday coinciding with the new moon, the ancestors of one who performs a *śrāddha* are indeed satisfied for hundreds of millions of years.
A person who dies between the god Govinda and Gopīśvara goes to the same world as Mahendra;
likewise, one who dies between Bahularudra and Govinda [attains the same].
Likewise, one who performs the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) and ritual bathing at the confluence of the Vedhas and the Gopīśa shall uplift a hundred generations of their lineage.
Vasutīrtha is to the south of Mathurā, as is Phālgunaka.
Having bathed and drunk there, one is glorified in my world.
There, at the Phālgunaka tīrtha, is the site of Vṛṣabhāñjana;
having performed an ablution there, one rejoices together with the gods.
Now, there is the sacred grove named Tālavana, situated to the west of Mathurā.
One who bathes in the pool there, or makes a gift, shall obtain their heart's desire.
There is also the Saṃpīṭhaka tīrtha; one who bathes there partakes in the merit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
O Lakṣmī! On the seventh lunar day falling on a Monday at Kṛṣṇajanmasthala, she who performs the vow and worships me shall become possessed of sons.
My domain, Mathurā, extends for twenty yojanas. || 43-44 ||
Having bathed anywhere there, one is liberated from terrible sins.
During the rainy season, one should remain in such a place as may be conducive to happiness.
In the seven continents, there are sacred fords and holy shrines.
They shall go to Mathurā while I am always asleep;
and seeing me awakened from sleep, they become vessels for liberation.
Having performed their ablutions in the Yamunā and having beheld Keśava... [587]
Being freed from all sins, he attains my own world;
at every step he obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices.
By him who has performed a circumambulation of Keśava in Mathurā, [that merit is attained].
By him the earth with its seven islands has been circumambulated clockwise.
Likewise, one should offer a lamp of ghee and a garment to Kṛṣṇa in his temple;
[the garment] five yojanas in width and five and a half yojanas in length.
A person obtains a celestial mansion (vimāna) strewn with rows of lamps,
enriched with all objects of desire, frequented by hosts of apsarases,
delightful, granting every wish, and resplendent with all splendor. //5.1//
If the Siddhas, Cāraṇas, and Gandharvas who have gone to heaven desire it,
and if merit has indeed been performed, then such a house may be obtained;
in the end, liberation is surely attained through the power of Mathurā.
Indra protects the eastern Mathurā, while Yama protects the southern;
the Lord of Waters protects the western, and Kubera likewise the northern.
Śaṅkara, the husband of Pārvatī, who is my devotee, protects the center.
Whatever person builds a house or a palace in Mathurā should be known as four-armed; he is liberated while living, without a doubt. In Mathurā, there is a great pool named Vimalodaka.
In the winter it becomes warm, and in the summer it becomes cool;
it does not increase during the rains, nor does it diminish even in the summer.
This is a great wonder of mine regarding that pool.
In my field of Mathurā, one should bathe in pits and rivers;
likewise in wells, lakes, natural pools, streams, and confluences—or wherever one may bathe—by that act, the supreme goal shall be attained. (58–59)
On the ninth day of the month of Kārttika, the king of my devotees,
having performed a circumambulation, proceeds with the bull-like stride that traverses the earth.
Such a fruit is not obtained through gifts, nor through austerities, nor through sacrifices.
The merit from properly circumambulating the earth would be equal to that obtained by visiting sacred fords (tīrthas).
In measuring the distance of the circumambulation of the earth,
the extent is sixty thousand and sixty hundred crores of yojanas.
There, the holy fords (tīrthas) and the gods were indeed enumerated by Pavana,
as well as by Brahmā, Lomaśa, Nārada, Dhruva,
the brāhmaṇa Patnīvra, Garuḍa, and Hanumān.
By these many gods, all of whom were powerful, the earth— with its oceans and its enclosures—
was traversed in various ways along the outer boundary line of the mandala;
likewise, it was traversed by certain others perfected in yoga, such as Mārkaṇḍeya and his peers.
Whatever fruit may arise from wandering through the sacred fords of the seven islands,
even more than that is obtained by circumambulating Mathurā.
When the circumambulation of Mathurā is performed according to the prescribed sequence of rites, [the merit is unsurpassed].
I shall now correctly describe the fruit of circumambulation and the sequential procedure [for it].

Whatever merit is found among all the gods, whatever fruit is found in all the sacred fords (tīrthas), whatever merit is found in all acts of giving, and whatever fruit is found in sacrifices and works of public utility (iṣṭāpūrta)—[all that is obtained through circumambulation]. 67–68.
O Lakṣmī! That fruit is obtained by performing the circumambulation of Mathurā.
On the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Kārtika, Brahmā and ten million other deities, together with divine sages and seers, undertook the journey to Mathurā.
On the eighth day, having reached Mathurā and bathed at Viśrāntitīrtha,
he performed worship of the ancestors, the gods, and the sages, as well as the adoration of Yamunā;
then, having visited Viśrānti, Dīrghaviṣṇu, and Keśava.
Having undertaken a fast, or else eating only a very small amount of pure food,
one should be devoted to celibacy and diligently maintain silence.
Having brought sesame seeds, unbroken grains of rice, and *kuśa* grass, one should offer a lamp at the time of rest.
On the ninth day, one should commence the pilgrimage from this very spot at dawn.
At the hour of Brahmā, before the sun rises, one should bathe at Dakṣiṇakoṭika;
having washed one’s feet and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should propitiate Hanumān.
"O bestower of all auspiciousness, performer of success, witness of the fruit;
grant the fulfillment of this pilgrimage through my circumambulation.
Having thus addressed Hanumān, the lord of the Gaṇas, according to the prescribed rites.
Then, having worshipped [him] with lamps, flowers, offerings, and so forth,
one should worship Padmanābha and Dīrghaviṣṇu, the bestower of happiness; likewise, having beheld the goddess Vasumatī and the other, Aparājitā.
Having bowed to the one stationed in the armory, he should then proceed further ahead;
likewise, having bowed there to Kaṃsavāsanikā, Auprasenā, Carcikā,
and the young bride who brings about the destruction of the Dānavas.
Then, having bowed to Jayadā and the Mothers worshipped by the gods,
and having looked upon the household deities and the deities of the site (Vāstu-devīs) and obtained their permission, he should depart.
Reaching the southern extremity, he should bathe and offer libations to his ancestors.
Having bowed down to the god Kṛṣṇa, one should go to the virtuous Ikṣuvāsā,
where the holy site was indeed established by Kṛṣṇa with children's toys.
From there, O son of Vatsa, one should go to Arkasthala.
Vīrasthala, Kuśasthala, Puṇyasthala, and Mahāsthala—
by beholding these five sacred sites, one rejoices together with Brahmā.
Having seen Śiva at Siddhamukha, one should then behold Hayamukti.
Since the horse has attained liberation here along with its companion,
the prince should remain there and not undertake a journey by carriage.
Having beheld Mallikā, he should proceed to the grove of Kadamba trees.
Having seen the Yoginī Carcikā, one should then go to the Mother (Mātṛ).
Both she who is untouchable and she who is untouched—these two are indeed the protectors of children.
Then, having gone to the pit dug during the rains, one should offer libations to the ancestors at the sacrificial pool (kuṇḍa).
One should go to and worship Kṣetrapāla Śiva, the Lord of Beings;
then one should go to Kṛṣṇakrīḍā-setubandha and then to Bali-hrada.
Thereafter, one should go to the place called Kukkuta-krīḍā, which bestows a favorable state of existence.
One should worship that collection of pillars with its beautiful pinnacle and circumambulate it;
he is liberated from all sins and shall go to the world of Viṣṇu.
[There is] the place where Vasudeva and Devakī lay together in solitude. 88–89.
Having gone to the abode of Nārāyaṇa, one should enter and circumambulate it;
having bowed to Vighnavināyaka, as well as to Kubjikā and Vāmanā,
and having bowed to the two Brahmin women who are servants of Kṛṣṇa, one should proceed to Garteshvara.
Upon seeing Mahāvidyeśvarī, the fruit of success in one’s journey shall be attained.
One should go to Prabhāmallī Mahāvidyeśvarī and worship her;
likewise, one should worship Siddheśvarī and Saṅketeśvarī.
In front of which Hari made his appointment for the destruction of the Daityas;
having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) at the pool, one should go to Gokarṇeśvara.
Having seen the river Sarasvatī, one should approach Vighnarāja.

Having seen and likewise touched the Gaṅgā, one should go to Rudramahālaya. Having honored that guardian of the field (Kṣetrapa), the lord of the Northern Koṭi hosts, one should worship him where the game of dice was played by Kṛṣṇa. ||94–95||

Thence one should go to the great and pure holy site in the waters of the Yamunā known as Rudramahālaya; there one should bathe and offer libations to the ancestors. Then one should go to Gārgyatīrtha, Bhadreśvara, and Somaka.
Only by worshipping Someśvara does a person obtain the fruit of the pilgrimage.
And at the confluence of the Sarasvatī, having duly gratified the gods, sages, ancestors, and humans, and having made offerings, one attains union with Kṛṣṇa.
Having gone to Ghaṇṭābharaṇaka, as well as Garuḍakeśava;
having gone to Dhārālopanaka, Vaikuṇṭha, and Khaṇḍavelaka;
[and] Mandākinīsaṃyamana, Āsikuṇḍa, and Gopaka.
Then, having gone to the sacred sites of Muktikeśvara and Vailakṣagaruḍa,
