one should offer libations to the ancestors and the gods everywhere,
and pray: "May my pilgrimage to Mathurā be fruitful."
Having thus addressed Śiva, the Lord of the gods and protector of the field,
he bathed at the place named Viśrānti and performed the libations for the ancestors.
Then, having circumambulated Viśrānti and bowed to his Guru as well as to Hari, [he departed].
Then one should go to Sumaṅgalā to propitiate the success of one's journey, [praying]:
"By your grace, may this journey of mine be fruitful.
Having gone to Pippalādeśvara, one should circumambulate it while reciting the Upāli hymn.
Then the pilgrim should establish a single *śiva-liṅga* in his own name;
he shall obtain the fruit of the pilgrimage by worshipping and likewise prostrating before it. He should then go to the serpent Karkoṭaka and to the goddess Caṇḍikā.
Then, having meditated upon Vajrānana and then upon Sūrya, the Lord of the Family (kuleśvara),
and having seen [him] right there and offered a gift, one should conclude the journey. Indeed, by performing this for each of the families, one’s abiding will be in the world of the Sun.
One who performs circumambulation is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu;
one who performs circumambulation of me is glorified in Goloka.
Even those who are killers of Brahmins, drinkers of liquor, thieves, and those who have broken their vows [are purified].
Those who act with violence, those who seize wealth and fields,
those who are harmful, givers of suffering, revilers, rogues, and scoundrels—
by performing the pilgrimage to Mathurā, they indeed become free from sin.
Even those who have come from another land and perform a circumambulation from afar—
by the mere sight of such a person, other men become purified.
Having drunk even a drop of water from the Yamunā, those living far away [attain purity].
Freed from all sins, they go to the supreme goal.
Those who make their dwelling in Mathurā, those who frequent the holy sites (tīrtha) of Mathurā,
and those who behold the forests of Mathurā become partakers of liberation.
Madhuvana, Tālavana, and Kunda-vana as the third;
Kāmyaka-vana, Bahuvana, and likewise Bhadravana;
Khādira, the great forest, and likewise Lohārgala-vana.
Bilvavana, Bhāṇḍīra, and Vṛndāvana as the twelfth—
those who behold these places do not go to the realm of Yama; indeed,
those who undertake pilgrimages to these forests go to the world of Indra.
"And those of my devotees, whether men or women, who perform a pilgrimage for my sake, go to me alone, the eternal, in Goloka.
(1.17) Thus ends the first section, the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga, in the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.

In the *Mathurākṣetramāhātmya*, there is a description of the Vatsakrīḍanaka, Bhāṇḍīraka, Vṛndāvana, Hari-viśrāma, Sūryatīrtha, Malaya, Arjuna, Bahula, Bhāṇḍahrada, Arkakuṇḍa, Vimalakūpa, Vīrasthala, Kuśasthala, Puṣpasthala, Gopīśvara, the seven Sāmudrikas, Vasu-phālgunaka, Vṛṣabha, Añjanaka, Tālavana, Saṃpīṭhaka, Vimalodaka, and Kuṇḍas; the procedure for the circumambulation (*pradakṣiṇa*) of Mathurā; the sequential enumeration of the holy sites (*tīrthas*) therein, including their commencement and conclusion at the Viśrāntighaṭṭa; and the forests.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Now I shall tell you something else, O Mahālakṣmī; listen to that.

At Cakratīrtha, situated to the north of Mathurā, there was a Brāhmaṇa who resided in the city of Mahāgṛhodaya on Jambūdvīpa; he was a knower of the Vedas who had brought with him his daughter and his son. || 1-2 ||
He went to Śālagrāma, that great sacred field, specifically for the purpose of pilgrimage.
There he made his dwelling, bathing regularly and worshipping the deities of the holy sites.
While he was visiting the gods, a certain Siddha appeared on the path of his vision.
A perfected being (siddha) in human form, a resident of the village named Kalāpa, arrived there. He constantly comes and goes for the purpose of seeing [the sage],
and he also finds rest in the leaf-hut of the brahmin.
He described the extreme opulence of Kalāpa village;
having heard this, the Brahmin then conceived the thought of going there.
The twice-born man said: "Indeed, you have today become my perfected friend."
"O friend! Lead me to Kalāpa; there I shall behold those manifestations of power.
The Siddha replied: "But, O best of Brahmins! You will have no access there.
Your body, O twice-born one, will perish from the cold winds!"
Nevertheless, the Brahmin said, "Lead me by means of your yoga. Thus entreated, the Siddha took the maiden, the son, and Mitruka by the hand and flew up into the sky by the power of his yoga.
The three Brahmins had been placed by a perfected being (siddha) in the hermitage of Kalāpa.
There, as time passed, one of the Brahmins then became ill;
and his son carried his father, who was at the point of death, to the bank of the Gaṅgā.
The daughter also attended to her father with wholesome provisions.
Once, she prepared a meal in the leaf-hut for the sake of her father.
At that time, a certain brahmin also arrived at the house for the purpose of begging alms.
Questioned by that Bhadrā, "Where have you come from here?
he replied: "I am a brahmin from Kānyakubja who has attained perfection;
I wander happily at all times in this great sacred site, Kalāpa."
Informed by his daughter, he, possessing a perfected body, was approached;
after due deliberation, the father gave that maiden to the perfected Brahmin.
For this perfected one, as a son-in-law, dwells in the house of his father-in-law.
At the appropriate time, she questioned her father-in-law who had fallen into a state of distress:
"What is this illness? When will its destruction come about?
I shall perform service in such a way that the destruction of the disease may occur."
Having heard the words of his son-in-law, the father-in-law attained peace.
He said to his son-in-law, "If you know it through your spiritual perfection (*siddhi*), then speak.
The son-in-law, possessing *siddhi*, meditated and said to his father-in-law, "O twice-born one!"
"While residing here in Kalāpa, Śūdra food was eaten by you.
It was offered by him unknowingly and consumed by you also unknowingly.
Because of that fault, O twice-born one, this disease remains in your body."
"Food is found at his feet, but above the knees it is not found.
O Brahmin, for one deprived of the food of a Śūdra, death will surely come!
Having heard these words of his son-in-law, the Brahmin reproached himself severely.
Afflicted by suffering and emaciated, that best of brahmins desired to die.
(22) Then, at dawn, those three—the son-in-law, the daughter, and the son—went out from the house for some business; it was but a moment later. (23)
Having found an opportunity when no one was present and having reflected upon death,
he rose from the bank of the Gaṅgā and looked in all directions;
seeing a stone nearby, he took it and went to the house made of leaves.
The twice-born man, distressed by the pain, crushed those two feet with his foot.
Then, having cast off his life-breaths, he went to the highest heaven.
The son-in-law, the daughter’s son, and the [other] son, having accomplished their task, returned home.
Seeing that old man dead, they wept excessively;
for those killed by a snake, those killed by a horned animal, those killed by a fanged beast, and even those who have committed suicide, there is no fitness for the funeral rites. (27)
"Considering how his cremation might be performed," they deliberated further;
"one should prescribe an expiation, but one must not perform the water-libation rites.
Relying upon this injunction, they then carried out the cremation and other funeral rites.
They performed the expiatory rites and went to the village of Kalāpaka.
There, having bowed to a perfected being (siddha) who was a friend of the deceased brahmin,
they informed him of the death and other details, and mourned for a moment.
Established in the *kalāpa* [scripture], this perfected one (*siddha*) spoke to his son-in-law, the twice-born:
"The sin of killing a Brahmin has occurred for you; therefore, perform an expiation.
Having heard the words of the aged *siddha*, the son-in-law spoke these words: [31–32]
"O venerable one, I have never at any time committed the killing of a Brahmin.
By what fault does this fruit of Brahman-slaughter come to me? Tell me.
Having heard the words of his son-in-law, the aged Siddha said to him:
By you, it was shown that there was food belonging to a Śūdra at his feet;
likewise, it was shown that death occurs upon the exhaustion of that food.
And by that Brahmin, his own two feet were similarly crushed.
"Since death was brought about there by you, you likewise became the one who bears the fault;
thus, O best of the twice-born, the means for his slaughter was indicated by you.
Because of that fault, O brahmin-sage, you shall incur the fruit of killing a brahmin."
Sin is transferred to a manifest being through sharing a bed, food, or conversation,
as well as by walking together;
therefore, purification must be performed, lest he dwell in my house.
"O brāhmaṇa, abandon Kalpagrāma and go to Mathurā;
know that your purification will not occur elsewhere, so depart!
Having heard those words of the elder, the three of them went to Mathurā.
His wife and his brother-in-law were carried off by that son-in-law, who had mastered the sciences,
as he flew through the path of the sky toward Mathurā.
They respectfully took up residence in a place outside the city for the Brahmins.
Then, at the sacrificial session of King Kuśika in Mathurā,
two thousand Brahmins ate pure food every day;
thereafter, those three ate the remnants of the Brahman-sacrifice.
Having reached Cakratīrtha, they always perform their ablutions.
Having fed her husband—who had arrived for alms at night with the remnants of a sacrifice—his wife then ate; and thus half a year passed by.
Then the brahmins, performers of sacrifices, respectfully questioned the perfected one who had arrived for alms: "O twice-born one, where do you reside?
Tell us truthfully, staying where do you take your meals? (45)
And the Siddha related his own beneficial account:
"Having taken alms here together with my wife and brother-in-law, I bathed at this Cakratīrtha and distributed [the food]."
"I shall indeed take food here for the sake of removing the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Hearing that, all the Brahmins said, "O twice-born one, you are indeed pure!
By the power of Cakratīrtha, you are entirely liberated from sin."
"And by the words of the Brahmins, O twice-born one, you are indeed purified once again!

(49) Thus was the purification performed for those treated with hostility, as well as for those who had visited Cakratīrtha, those who had performed expiation, and likewise through the eating of the grace-food (prasāda). (1.347.50)
Having attained perfection, the Siddha rejoiced along with his wife and brother-in-law;
having arrived at Cakratīrtha, he settled down to eat the alms-food.
With a joyful heart, his wife spoke these words to her husband:
"Take your meal, O best of Brahmins! I perceive that your sin of killing has departed.
By the power of Cakratīrtha, O most excellent of the twice-born, your slaughter has been destroyed.
Therefore, you must certainly remain here in Mathurā forever. (52–53)
Having resolved upon this, those three remained constantly there in Mathurā, completely abandoning Kalāpa; for Mathurā bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Furthermore, that sacred site is Bhadreśvara, which is frequented by the Siddhas.
Indeed, Cakratīrtha bestows merit a hundred times more than Kalāpa.
By fasting for a day and night there, even the sin of killing a Brahmin is destroyed.
What need has one then for Kalāpa, or even for Vārāṇasī?‍55–56.
If Mathurā is attained and Cakratīrtha is visited,
even a worm or an insect is born four-armed.
O beloved, those three Brahmins met their end there.
Indeed, they attained my eternal divine Goloka, becoming four-armed.
Listen further as I shall describe another power born of the Vaikuṇṭha-tīrtha:
the people dwelling in Mithilā went to Mathurā for the sake of visiting the holy site.
Having reached the Vaikuṇṭha-tīrtha, they remained there; among them was a certain brāhmaṇa who was greatly tormented by the sin of killing a brāhmaṇa. Indeed, a stream of blood flowed from his hand.
Although she was seen visibly present even after bathing at many holy fords, she did not depart;
however, she vanished through bathing at the Vaikuṇṭha-tīrtha.
One should not feel wonder here, for that is indeed the fruit of Vaikuṇṭha.
Having bathed here, one becomes free from sin and goes to Vaikuṇṭha.
O Lakṣmī, I shall further describe another [holy site] born of Gandharvakuṇḍa;
the performer of a bath here rejoices together with the Gandharvas.
The district of Mathurā is a lotus twenty yojanas in extent.
In its pericarp I dwell as Kṛṣṇa, eternally bestowing liberation upon those who have died there.
To the west, I reside as Hari, the upholder of Govardhana.
Govinda is in the north and Devaviśrama is resting in the east;
I am Varāha in the south, possessing a massive body and exceeding Keśava in size.
In the Kṛta Yuga, I was gratified by King Māndhātṛ.
Indeed, being pleased with him, I bestowed upon him my own image:
a beautiful and auspicious Vārāhī icon made of radiant material, possessing a divine form, fashioned by the blessed Kapila through his mind alone. (67–68)
Even Indra constantly meditated upon her after receiving the Saukarī form from Kapilā;
he worshipped that image with great reverence in his own abode.
Rāvaṇa also went to heaven in order to conquer Śakra.
Having conquered Śakra, he entered that palace there and assumed his divine boar-form. He bound Rāvaṇa with many rays of light, and Rāvaṇa offered praise: "O Mādhava, you ought to protect me!"
"Grant your grace in every way to me, who am filled with devotion.
Then the Blessed Lord Hari, being pleased, released Rāvaṇa.
At that time, Rāvaṇa also desired to take the image back to Laṅkā.
He was unable to lift her up, and at that he was filled with great astonishment.
He did not say this to her feet: "It is my intention to take you to Laṅkā.
The Boar replied: "O Rākṣasa, you are indeed not a Vaiṣṇava; therefore [you have failed]. || 73-74 ||
"I will not come from there; if you are a Vaiṣṇava, then take me.
Rāvaṇa, having become a Vaiṣṇava, indeed took that image to his city.
That image was then destroyed by Rāma.
She was brought to his own city and honored there for many years.
By him, his brother, who is the very embodiment of Śeṣa, was appointed to the destruction of the Rākṣasas;
having arrived at Mathurā, he [then] dealt with the Rākṣasas.
And there he destroyed that image of Vārāhī;
for the sake of protection, he brought it and established it as the presiding deity (vidhi).
Blessed is this earth of Mathurā, and blessed are the people who dwell therein.
By those who have always bathed [this image], seen it, touched it, meditated upon it, contemplated it,
and worshipped this Varāha, liberation will be granted in every way.
By the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) in the presence of Varāha, one's ancestors are indeed liberated.
The fruit of the *śrāddha* performed at Gayā indeed arises, as does the fruit born of Puṣkara;
likewise, one should behold the white Boar and seek repose there.
Then, having beheld Govinda, the upholder of Govardhana.
"Behold," O Lakṣmī! Thus has your greatness been described.
Whoever should hear this, or read it, or likewise cause it to be read—there shall be for them the attainment of the merits described, and there shall be liberation. 83.

Thus ends the three hundred and forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Destruction of the Sin of Brahmin-Slaughter and the Liberation of a Brāhmaṇa Residing in Kalāpa Village at Cakratīrtha in Mathurā-kṣetra, as well as the Destruction of the Sin of Brahmin-Slaughter of a Brāhmaṇa from Mithilā at Vaikuṇṭha-tīrtha, and the Successive Establishment of the Boar Incarnation Created by the Blessed Lord Kapila from His Mind in Mathurā," in the first section concerning the lineage of the Kṛta-yuga within the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī! There is a most meritorious place known as Govardhana;
it is situated two yojanas to the west of Mathurā.
This sacred field bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon embodied beings through circumambulation;
here, O beloved, it destroys the sins of men through bathing. The Aindra-tīrtha is in the east, and the Yama-tīrtha is situated in the south.
In the west is the Vāruṇa Tīrtha, and in the north indeed is the Kaubera Tīrtha.
(3) One who performs a ritual bath at each respective Tīrtha is glorified in the world corresponding to that [deity].
One who remembers me at the time of casting off their life-breaths goes to my own world. (4)
Having reached the site of Annakūṭa, one should perform a circumambulation of it;
he goes to the supreme world, which is enriched with wealth, grain, and other such prosperity.
Having bathed in the Mānasa-gaṅgā and beheld Hari at Govardhana, [one attains the same].

By circumambulating Annakūṭa, one is not born again in this world. (6) Having gone to the site of Govardhana on a new-moon day falling on a Monday, one should satiate the ancestors; then there shall be satisfaction through the offering of the *piṇḍa* at Gayā. (7)
Having circumambulated Govardhana and beheld Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa,
one undoubtedly attains the merit of the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices.
One should observe a fast on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada.
Having bathed in the Mānasa-Gaṅgā and performed the vision of the Sun at the hour of Brahmā,
and having bowed to Govardhana and to Hari stationed upon its peak,
she should descend and, while fasting, perform the circumambulation of the mountain.
One should go to the Puṇḍarīka site and perform a bath in the pool;
one should worship the ancestors and the gods and offer full adoration to Puṇḍarīka. He who performs this rite thus goes to the abode of Hari.
Then one should bathe in the Apsaras Kuṇḍa and offer libations to the ancestors;
by that, one indeed obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices.
Thereafter, one should bathe in the Saṃkarṣaṇa Tīrtha and perform the ritual of libation.
There, sins such as the killing of a cow or the killing of a Brahmin shall be dissolved.
One should then proceed to Śakratīrtha, near the mound of grain (annakūṭa),
where indeed the destruction of Mahendra’s sacrifice was performed by Kṛṣṇa.
Then Indra rained down out of wrath, desiring the destruction of all;
but Kṛṣṇa held up the mountain to protect the cows and the others.
There, the gods, goddesses, cows, and great sages were fed. (15–16)
The cowherds, the cowherd women, insects such as moths, worms, beasts, and birds—[all were gathered there].
Thus, that mountain became renowned by the name Annakūṭa (the Hill of Food).
There, indeed, through the distribution of food and the offering of water, [they were satisfied].
By offering libations there, a traveler shall obtain the fruit of a hundred sacrifices.
(18) Thereafter, one should indeed bathe in the Kadamba-kuṇḍa, which bestows the world of Brahmā.
Then one should go to Devagiri, bathe, and behold it with devotion. (19)
One should behold Mahādeva and offer libations to the ancestors in the sacred pool;
having obtained the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice and being liberated in heaven, one shall go to Hari.
[This extends] as far as the north of the Gaṅgā, up to the Lord of Gods who bears the discus.
On land, a battle took place between Kṛṣṇa and the demon Ariṣṭa.
Having slain the demon Vṛṣa, Hari bathed there again and again;
then, having come together with Rādhā, Kṛṣṇa was bathed by her.
Renowned by the name Rādhākuṇḍa, it is auspicious and a destroyer of sins.
By bathing there, one obtains the fruit of the Aśvamedha and Rājasūya sacrifices.
Through that bath, even the sin of killing a cow, a human, or a Brahmin is destroyed.
Having bowed to the holy site known as Mokṣarāja, one should proceed to Indradhvaja.
Having bathed at the Indradhvajocchraya tīrtha and bowed there, one should return;
then one should go to the pool named Pañcatīrtha and thus complete the pilgrimage.
Having offered the fruit of the pilgrimage to Śrī Hari,

one should perform a night vigil at Govardhana on the twelfth day (dvādaśī); then, at dawn, having bathed, offered the funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa), and bowed down, one should depart while meditating upon Hari.
He who undertakes such a pilgrimage delivers even his ancestors;
having completely shaken off his sins, he attains the Supreme Brahman.
Even during the month of Āṣāḍha, one should perform the circumambulation of the heap of food (annakūṭa).
Whoever hears this, reads it, or likewise causes it to be read, shall obtain the fruit of a pilgrimage, the merit of a ritual bath, and the grace of Kṛṣṇa.
Listen, Lakṣmī! There was indeed a Vaiśya named Suśīla in the southern region.
A resident of the city of Pratiṣṭhāna, he was wealthy and had many sons. He was merely concerned with filling his own belly, intent on maintaining his family;
he performed neither ritual bathing, nor charity, nor recitation, nor fire-offerings, nor worship of the gods.
He never once associated with the virtuous;
he neither listened to sacred discourses nor performed any religious duties.
He possessed no devotion toward the gods or the Brahmins.
But for him who was immersed in evil, no inclination toward the gift of Dharma arose.
Having reviled and utterly insulted the giver of counsel, he behaved in this manner until death indeed came upon him. (33–34)
Having attained the state of a preta on a parched, waterless land,
he remains miserable, wandering through the desert afflicted by hunger.
In the desert, that fierce and terrifying preta dwelt within a thicket of shrubs.

Long-tusked, with a protruding jaw, a cat-like face, and a massive belly—along that very path, a certain merchant engaged in buying and selling came out; as he was dancing, he then spoke to him. (36–37)
"I have obtained my food; where do you wish to go now?
I shall devour your flesh and drink your blood.
Hearing the words of the preta, the merchant summoned his courage and said to him:
"I am going for the sake of supporting my family, out of a desire for wealth.
My father is old at home, and my mother is a devoted wife;
O Rākṣasa, when I have been devoured, my family will perish. (1.348.40)
"Furthermore, being joined with sin, you shall not be released from the state of a preta.
Having heard this, that preta asked him, "From where have you come?
The merchant replied, "I have come from Mathurā to your forest."
There is Govardhana, the best of mountains, and the great river Yamunā.
(42) Between them, in Mathurā, I have lived for many generations.
Being poor, I go to foreign lands in search of wealth. (43)
The preta said: "Listen, O wretched one! If you have any business, do it for me.
On this condition I shall release you: go toward Mathurā.
Having performed your bath according to the rules at the confluence of the four oceans," ||| 44 || ||| 45 ||
"Perform the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍadāna) with diligence in my name;
grant me the fruit of your bath, and my liberation will come to pass.
Wealth exists in your house! There is no poverty for you, O merchant! || 45-46 ||
"A load of gold, accumulated and kept in a pit, remains in your house.
Return with full contentment and grant me my release, O merchant!
The merchant replied, "How can you have the knowledge that this well is my liberator?"

The Rākṣasa said: "In the city of Pratiṣṭhāna, the great sage Agastya recited the narrative of the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*. At evening time, I went to the temple of Viṣṇu to hear that story. (48–49)
"I have heard from there that there is a well which grants liberation to the departed spirits (pretas),
where indeed the four oceans are said to be gathered together.
Such was the story heard there by the people regarding the reciter.
Out of deceit, I gave a gift; indeed, I offered a copper vessel.
Then, when my time had come, my death occurred by the command of King Yama and through the power of my past actions.
Having attained the state of a preta, I was deprived of both giving and fire-offerings;
at that time, no sacred ford was visited, nor were my ancestors propitiated.
No religious duty was performed, and consequently, I have reached this state of a preta.
"By the power of the ḍhabbuka and by hearing this story, knowledge still remains within me; go, and grant me liberation. The merchant named Vibhu said, "Tell me, how do you live? || 54-55 ||
The Rākṣasa said: "I planted a Pippala tree in the courtyard of my own house for the sake of its shade; it was then nourished with water.
Indeed, its fruits appear only twice a year. (56)
By that [gift], living beings live, and by its merit, I too am sustained.
My satisfaction is constant, just as it is produced by water and food.
Having heard this and having consoled the preta, the merchant went to Mathurā.
Having indeed removed the funeral materials from the ground, he performed the rites for the deceased;
he offered the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) into a well containing the waters of the four oceans.
That deceased person, having arrived there and eaten the cakes, departed for heaven.
In the same way, having acquired wealth, the merchant rejoiced in his own home.
O Lakṣmī! Whether at a sacred ford, in a house, in a forest, in a temple, or at a crossroads—wherever they may die, those who offer funeral cakes (piṇḍas) attain liberation.
For one who has committed sin elsewhere, liberation at a sacred ford (tīrtha) is indeed certain;
even for one who has committed sin in Mathurā, there is destruction [of that sin] at Kūpārṇava.
A sin committed in Mathurā perishes right there.
This city is of great merit, wherein no sin is found. Even an ungrateful person, a drinker of liquor, a thief, or one who has broken his vows—
upon reaching Mathurā and the Yamunā, he is liberated from all transgressions.
If someone were to stand on one foot for a thousand yugas anywhere,
the merit of a resident of Mathurā would be even greater than that.
All those who dwell in Mathurā are indeed divine gods in human form.

Even those gods who take human form are devoted to bathing at sacred fords (tīrtha). However, the fruit that is obtained elsewhere by worshipping a thousand Brahmins is attained here in Mathurā by worshipping just one.
Indeed, Māthura is like the Ṛgveda, while another is like the four Vedas;
yet nowhere shall one equal to Māthura be found even with all four Vedas.
All holy pilgrimage sites and sacred shrines exist [there].
Indeed, all auspicious things are present wherever that Māthura brāhmaṇa resides;
all liberations have occurred and will occur for embodied beings there,
wherever the Māthura holy site and likewise the waters of the Yamunā are found.
The residents of Mathurā should know that the attendants are indeed four-armed;
by reading or hearing this, one shall attain the state of having four arms.
Listen further, for I shall proclaim another majesty born of Asikuṇḍa.
In ancient times, there was a king named Vimati who resided in the city of Puṇyanagara. Once, Nārada arrived at Vimati’s house;
then Vimati offered him water for his feet as well as the guest-offering (arghya).
Having accepted it, Nārada, the upholder of dharma, then said:
"O lord of kings, you are capable of discharging your debt to your father;
for my friend was always your father, O giver of honor."

Immediately after his death, however, you named Sumati performed great acts of charity and accumulated exceedingly abundant merit; yet, since no pilgrimage to sacred fords was undertaken by you, you have not discharged your debt to your father. (75–76)
"Having discharged his debt to his father, this son shall become a partaker of dharma.
Having spoken thus, Nārada indeed departed for the Badarī forest.
The king, moreover, thereafter desired to go on a pilgrimage to sacred sites for the sake of his father.
The thought arose in him: "Let us go to the city of Mathurā.
Having thus resolved, that king came to the city of Mathurā;
indeed, I shall dwell in Mathurā for the four months of the rainy season.
"All sacred fords reside right here during the four-month period.
Having reflected thus, the king indeed made his residence there for a long time,
accompanied by a thousand attendants and served by male and female servants.
Everywhere at sacred fords (tīrtha), servants perform the removal of impurities;
likewise, male and female slaves of the Śūdra caste engage in sexual intercourse even on days of religious observance, and they bathe without restraint in the waters of the fords.
They forcibly seize the household utensils and other belongings of Brahmins and others;
they revile virtuous men and Brahmins, and indeed they utter threats.
Unrestrained, they even void urine and excrement upon the ground of the gods.
The king does not inflict punishment upon those wicked men who eat fish;
that sin of the king’s wickedness falls upon his own head as well.
When the month had passed, the sacred fords spoke to one another out of distress: (84–85)
The king, however, must be expelled from this place for the sake of our happiness;
we ourselves are unable to engage in battle with one who harbors such ill-will.
Having gone to Kalpagrāma, we shall [worship] Varāha, the Supreme Lord.
"We report this hardship; he will act appropriately and correctly.
Having gone to Kalpagrāma, they entreated him with reverence:
"Victory to you, O Viṣṇu! Victory to you, O Lord of the Earth! Victory to you, O Lord of Kings! (87–88)
"O Nārāyaṇa, salutations to you who destroy the suffering of the holy places (tīrthas)!
Having heard this, the Blessed Lord Varāha spoke respectfully to the holy places:
'Choose a boon—may it be well with you—whatever dwells in your hearts. (89)
The holy places said, "O Hari, O Kṛṣṇa, you ought to grant us fearlessness.
A most terrible terror has been wrought by a wicked-minded and great sinner;
subdue that most sinful meat-eater who is frequented by the wicked."
Then Śrī Varāha said, "I shall slay the great enemy.
Thus, by the command of the holy ford, he arrived at the city of Mathurā.
Varāha engaged in a fierce battle with King Svāsina.
Then the Boar slew the king with his sword.
Having placed the tip of his own sword’s edge upon the earth,
he sat down on the ground to obtain a moment's rest.
That ground is purifying where the pool was fashioned by the divine sages;
it is called Asikuṇḍa, a sacred ford (tīrtha) that is supremely purifying.
Indeed, bathing in the pool on the twelfth or fourteenth lunar day bestows liberation.
Then I shall reside at Varāhatīrtha, bestowing liberation.
At that holy site, my fourfold forms are to be installed:
one named Varāha and the second Nārāyaṇī. ||96-97||
The third day belongs to Vāmana and the fourth to Rāghava.
On those days, one should by all means perform their viewing, worship, installation, and likewise the giving of gifts; through that, one shall become a partaker of liberation.
Whoever, having bathed in the pool named Asī, should behold these four [deities],
by him the earth bounded by the four oceans has been traversed;
he shall certainly partake of the fruit of the sacred sites of Mathurā.

Even one who has risen from sleep on the twelfth day, a man who bathes in the Asikuṇḍa and beholds those images, is fit for union with Brahman. By the grace of Nārāyaṇa, there is no returning to this world again.
"By reading or hearing this, one shall indeed attain liberation after having enjoyed [worldly pleasures].

Thus ends the three hundred and forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Mathurā-kṣetra in the First Section on the Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga, including the Circumambulation of Govardhana, the Annakūṭa, and Other Holy Sites; the Liberation of the Vaiśya Suśīla who was in the Form of a Preta; and the Destruction of Vimati by Vārāha, as well as the Greatness of Vārāha-kṣetra," in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, Lakṣmī! To the explanation of the Viśrāntighaṭṭa on the Yamunā.
In Ujjayinī there was a brāhmaṇa who had fallen from right conduct and was an atheist.
Abandoning the conduct of the virtuous, he does not perform ritual bathing;
he does not worship the gods, nor does he pay homage to the holy sages. Disturbed by worldly desires, sleeping at the time of twilight, he is a reviler of his ancestors.

A reviler of the *śrāddha* rites, a companion of sin, and one of very wicked mind, he was constantly supporting his own family’s belly through theft and other such means during the night. Once, while committing theft at night along with other evildoers, [he was caught]. (3–4)
Being watched by the king’s soldiers, he fled with great speed, taking a wrong path;
as he was running away, he then fell into a deep blind well.
Having died upon falling there, he subsequently attained the state of a rākṣasa.

But he, dwelling constantly in a jīrṇa-tree situated on the path by the side of that [river], always drank the blood and ate the breaths and feathered creatures [of those passing]. Once, a great caravan arrived along that path. (6–7)
Protected by a Brahmin standing in their midst who recited mantras that destroy demons, the caravan, being utterly exhausted, fell asleep beneath a tree near a well.
Then a demon, having arrived there, said to the Brahmin: "O twice-born one!"
"I shall give you whatever wealth is in your mind.
"O Brahmin, this food, obtained after a long time and treated with great honor, give it to me to eat; go elsewhere and show me mercy!"
"By which means may I devour this caravan until my hunger is satisfied?
The Brahmin replied: "I am not ungrateful in any way whatsoever.
What friendship can there be with a wicked one? What profit is there in being with a Rākṣasa?"
The Rākṣasa and the attainment of friendship both offered invitations that would cost them their lives.
(1.2) "I have profit from the caravan, but none at all from you. Having set out on the same caravan, I will not abandon a fellow traveler. (1.3)
"Therefore, O Rākṣasa, go away, leaving my caravan!
You are truly unable to look upon me by the power of my mantra.
The Rākṣasa said: 'If my prey is killed, the fault will be yours.'"
"O best of Brahmins, have mercy! Let food be given to me.
(15) When the Rākṣasa was thus entreating him for his purpose, the twice-born one asked him:
"By what fault in action have you come to this state of being a Rākṣasa? (16)
The Rākṣasa spoke of the faults of theft and immoral conduct, saying,
"Even a Brahmin has attained the state of a Rākṣasa through his sinful deeds.
Then Kṣmādeva, who was traveling with a caravan, heard this and was moved to compassion.
The Rākṣasa said: "Tell me, O twice-born one, so that I may purify you;
tell me of whatever sins there are, and how liberation may be attained.
Since I have rendered you assistance, what pleasing service may I do for you? (18–19)
Having heard this, the Rākṣasa said to the Brahmin: "You have performed many pilgrimages;
however, as for that bath you took at Viśrāntitīrtha in Mathurā, grant me the fruit of that bath so that I may attain liberation."
Having heard that, the brahmin questioned the rākṣasa Prāgudantaka:
"O rākṣasa, how do you know this sacred ford named Viśrānti?
And why does it have such a name? Tell me everything, if you know."
The Rākṣasa said: "O best of Brahmins! Formerly, my residence was always in the city of Ujjayinī; indeed, I lived there in the temple of Viṣṇu.
[There,] the Brahmin [related] the narrative of the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā."
He always acts with great devotion for the sake of the people. (24) O twice-born one, at that time I heard of the greatness of Viśrāntitīrtha;
by the mere hearing of it, devotion took root in my heart. (25)
That name, having been heard there, brings about the understanding of the ultimate rest:
"Vāsudeva is the Supreme Brahman, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, Hari, who indeed eternally takes His rest upon the bank of the Yamunā. (26)
That place, situated near the water, became known as Viśrānti. Having bathed there, one enjoys heaven for ten million ages (koṭiyuga), and thereafter,
having enjoyed the worlds known as Vairāja, one goes to the supreme state.
Therefore, O chief of Brahmins, grant me the fruit of even a single bath,
by which I may be liberated from this state of being a Rākṣasa and attain heaven;
and at the end, may there be final liberation— show mercy toward me.
Having heard the words of the rākṣasa, the merchant-brahmin then said:
"O rākṣasa, the fruit of a single bath has indeed been given to you!
Having spoken thus, just as he was about to give water to the rākṣasa...
Having become pure and attained a divine body, he went to heaven;
there, O Lotus-born One, having enjoyed supreme pleasures, he attained liberation.
Then that Brahmin indeed departed with his caravan toward his own country.
Listen, Lakṣmī! In ancient times, Śambhu performed severe penance for the sake of pleasing Hari.
Being pleased by that, I then approached Śaṅkara and granted him my very sight. (33–34)
Being told, "Choose a boon," Hara chose a boon from me:
"O Blessed One! If you are pleased, O Kṛṣṇa, let a place for me always be granted anywhere within the sacred precinct of Mathurā. (35)
Then I said: "You shall become a guardian of the field (kṣetrapāla).
O Mahādeva! when you are seen, the fruit of my field shall accrue to me.
O Śambhu! always provide protection for my field on all sides. (36–37)
Upon entering my field, worldly existence indeed ceases;
for Mathurā, the city of Vaikuṇṭha, is dear to me.
Indeed, my Maṇḍala of Mathurā extends for twenty yojanas.
By my yoga, at every step one shall obtain the fruit of horse-sacrifices (aśvamedhas).
Indeed, here reside sixty thousand crores and sixty hundred crores of holy places (tīrthas) that bestow heaven and liberation.
Having heard this and obtained the boon, Śambhu remained right there;
he is my supreme Vaiṣṇava devotee, the king of devotees, in the form of Kṣetrapāla.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have told you this supreme majesty which bestows liberation.
Those who read and those who hear [this] go to the supreme state.
They deliver two hundred and twenty families as well.
And when death has arrived, that person who remembers the Mathurā pilgrimage site— || 42-43 ||
He shall attain the supreme perfection that destroys this cycle of existence.
Among all sacred fords (*tīrthas*), the one at Mathurā is the most excellent and great;
it is the sacred ford where Kṛṣṇa played, for it is indeed pure at every step.
The region of Mathurā, situated between the southern and northern hemispheres of the earth, is always [sacred].
Having departed from his home in silence, he should indeed perform his bath until the conclusion of the worship;
thereafter, he should speak and give milk-yielding cows as gifts.
One should give gold and wealth, feed virtuous brahmins,
reside in Mathurā during the Cāturmāsya period, and perform the prescribed rites; for such a person, there is no return to this world, and he is glorified in my realm.
O Lakṣmī! Those who die in Mathurā indeed go to my world.
Furthermore, for those who die elsewhere but are cremated within the district of Mathurā, there is residence in heaven and likewise in my abode, Goloka.
Whatever form belongs to the people of Mathurā, that is my four-armed form.
O son of Vinatā! I am always satisfied when the people of Mathurā are satisfied.
Listen, Lakṣmī, to what happened regarding the high-souled Garuḍa.
Having arrived in Mathurā with a longing for a vision of Kṛṣṇa, Garuḍa offered praise and bowed before Kṛṣṇa:
"Victory to you, O Lord of Lakṣmī, Kṛṣṇa! Be victorious, O Lord of Māṇikī! (5.1–52)
Victory to the Lord of Light! Victory to the Lord of Rādhā! Victory to the Lord of Śrī Pārvatī! Victory, O Viṣṇu! Victory, O Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, Lord of Ramā!
Victory, O Kṛṣṇa, Lord of the Gopīs! Victory, O Lord of Garuḍa! Victory!
"Victory to you, O Lord of all! Victory to Brahmā! Victory to Kṛṣṇa! Salutations be unto you!
(54) Thus praised by the high-souled Garuḍa, the god Kṛṣṇa stood before Garuḍa, possessing a beautiful body. (55)

The king of birds said, "Tell me quickly what you intend to do and why you have come; having heard it, I shall grant it. Garuḍa then replied, "I have come to Mathurā with a longing for a vision of you."
Your form was not seen by me, and thus delusion has entered me. (57) You were present in Mathurā together with the people, having assumed your own true form;
you were not recognized by me, and therefore delusion has entered me. (58)
"Now that I have seen your divine form, peace has come to me.
Having heard the words of Garuḍa, Mādhava smiled and said:
"O best of the twice-born, I abide in my own true form among the people of Mathurā."
"Those sinful people who do not see the inhabitants of Mathurā, who resemble my own form—
I dwell right there, though I sometimes wander elsewhere.
Having spoken thus, Kṛṣṇa then vanished on the spot.
Garuḍa also went to Vaikuṇṭha at the feet of Kṛṣṇa.
The residents of Mathurā, remaining in Mathurā, indeed attained divinity;
they all purify [the world] just like the personal associates of Kṛṣṇa.
Even a worm, a moth, or one situated in the womb of an animal,
becomes four-armed through the majesty of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Now, O Lakṣmī, listen to another marvel of Mathurā.
In a former age, a Brāhmaṇa named Patnīvrata, a resident of Mount Raivata in Saurāṣṭra,
went with his family to the region of Mathurā for the purpose of visiting the Yamunā.
Having bathed in the Yamunā for his rest,
he performed a circumambulation of Mathurā, as well as of Govardhana, another forest, Vṛndāvana, and even the Tulasī grove. (66–67)
Having fed many brahmins and taken waters from sacred fords,
Marudeśa returned to his own country;
he arrived there at a dry, thorny place in the forest consisting mostly of *śamī* trees.
He beheld a company of more than a hundred ḍākinīs and śākinīs, dancing and shouting haughtily, "Eat! Devour!
They were deformed, naked, black-complexioned, and terrifying.
Upon seeing the multitude of magical spells (*kṛtyā*), he who was devoted to his vow as a husband immediately remembered Kṛṣṇa; and lo, the blazing discus appeared at once.
That discus consumed those spells, which had taken the form of ghosts, from the outside.
They wept, they cried out, and they entreated him most intensely:
"Save us, O Brahmin! We shall not be devoured; protect us here, for we shall die!
We were indeed one hundred and more wives of the king of the Maruts. (72–73)
Consuming liquor and meat, sinful and devoid of dharma,
the king met his death during a great pestilence and a major epidemic;
his kingdom was seized by Tripura, and we were thereby cast down.
During the earthquake, when our dwelling was destroyed, we were all afflicted there and died. O Brahmin! We have entered the wombs of *ḍākinīs*, *śākinīs*, and *bhūtas*.
O Keśava! Grant us liberation through the water of a sacred ford! || 75-76 ||
Having heard this, that Brahmin Kṛṣṇāṃśa, who was devoted to his wife's vow,
took water in his hand from the Yamunā and then sprinkled them with it.
Abandoning their forms as spirits, they became divine and four-armed.
Then they were transformed into the form of Rāmās; having bowed down, they praised [him] with devotion:
"You yourself are indeed Kṛṣṇa; you have been lifted out from the ocean of suffering.
O Kṛṣṇa, lead us to your own abode. When this was said, a celestial chariot arrived.
That Brahmin, who was the very form of Kṛṣṇa, led her indeed to Goloka;
then, together with his family, he went to his own country, Raivata.
Thus [ends the account] of the holy site of Viśrānti and the waters of the Yamunā.
The divine majesty that effects the liberation of the departed has been proclaimed to you.
Wherever Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, I myself, am present in contact with the waters of the Yamunā,
there at that time reside heaven, Goloka, and even final liberation.
O Lakṣmī! For those who hear this, as well as those who recite it or cause others to hear it, there shall be heaven in Goloka and even liberation itself.

(83) Thus ends the [section on] the greatness of Mathurā-kṣetra within the first book, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*. It describes the liberation of a Brahmin residing in the city of Ujjayinī who had fallen from proper conduct and become a Rākṣasa, through the fruit of bathing for rest; the protection of the sacred field performed by Śambhu; and the divine vision granted to Garuḍa through his hymn of praise when he was unable to recognize Kṛṣṇa in his form at Mathurā.

Chapter 351 → Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
I shall relate the majesty of Gokarṇeśvara on the bank of the Yamunā in Mathurā; listen, O Lakṣmī! It bestows sons, heaven, and liberation.
There was a Brahmin named Subhadra, the son of Pāribhadra.
Engaged in the livelihood of a Vaiśya, he made his living through buying and selling.
(2) Dwelling in the region of Saurāṣṭra on the bank of the Śatrujita river, he practiced agriculture there and also tended cattle and other livestock. (3)
His wife, known by the name Jīvantī, was endowed with excellent virtues;
she was a virtuous woman who acted for the pleasure of her husband, yet she had not given birth and was advanced in years.
Seeing other women with children, she constantly felt grief.
She went to her father’s house at the festival in Kuṅkumavāpī.
Her father, the brahmin named Kratu, a great yogi,
upon seeing her so full of grief, asked her the cause of her sorrow.
She too spoke to her father, stating that childlessness was the cause.
Then the sage Kratu, having meditated for a moment, said to his daughter Jīvantikā:
"Come, daughter! Go before Kṛṣṇa and make this report."
Having resolved upon this, they went to the abode of Kṛṣṇa, who was observing his vow toward his wife. Having arrived and bowed to that Lord, they reported their situation:
"O Sage Kṛṣṇa! For this unfortunate woman, there is no happiness of offspring. (8–9)
Having heard her, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa spoke to her who was longing for a son:
"By the grace of Kambharā Mahālakṣmī, you will surely have a noble son;
therefore, perform the pilgrimage that grants a virtuous son."
In Mathurā, on the bank of the Yamunā, there is the Gokarṇavakeśvara—
a delightful sacred site (tīrtha) that yields the fruit of obtaining a son, O lady of excellent vows!
Approach it quickly and worship him together with your husband.
"O Jīvanti! Accomplish this by propitiating [the deity] with offerings of bathing, lamps, and various hymns of praise, together with your sons.
When she had been told this, she bowed to her husband and went home.
He reported everything that had been said by Hari.
Having heard those words, he spoke with great joy to his beloved wife:
"O wife, this is my own opinion as well, regarding what was then spoken by Hari."
On the tenth day of the month of Caitra, having traveled through the sky by means of a splendid vehicle to Mathurā,
they bathed in the Yamunā at evening and, after bowing to Śaṅkara,
fell asleep upon the ground at Gokarṇeśvara.
Having risen in the morning, they both performed their ablutions and worship with devotion.
Then the blessed Lord, the lord of Uma, being pleased, said to them:
"You two shall have a son endowed with virtue, beauty, and wealth."
Thus addressed by the Lord, the two of them bathed in the Sarasvatī,
bowed to Yamunā at their confluence, and after staying there for a moment,
they gave to the twice-born wealth, food, clothing, and other gifts along with abundant sacrificial fees.
Having performed a pilgrimage in the region of Mathurā on the eleventh lunar day,
the two of them returned to their own home by means of a beautiful aerial vehicle.
While his wife was still living, the brāhmaṇa performed the rite of conception.

In the tenth month, she gave birth to a son who possessed the splendor of the moon. Then, on the great festival of his son's birth, she bestowed upon all the social classes many thousands of cows, along with gold and fine garments. (22)
He performed the birth-rite (*jātakarma*), the ancestral offering (*śrāddha*), and the naming ceremony (*nāmakarma*).
"Let this one, given by Gokarṇeśvara, indeed be known by the name Gokarṇa.
Having been consecrated with the sixteen purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*), he became a youth.
He married those four wives, yet they were all childless; not even one among them had a son.
Therefore, that king indeed began the practice of *dharmapuṃsavana* with each of his wives in turn.
There were ponds, wells, and tanks, as well as temples of the deities;
there were water-stations, rows of trees, perpetual food-distributions, service to the gods, and service to the distressed.
On the bank of the Śatrujit river, he [saw] the auspicious Lord Gokarṇeśvara Śaṅkara.
To the east of Gokṣurapattana, he established the Yāmuna [temple];
he had a temple built for Hari consisting of five shrines (pañcāyatana).
There, a vast garden was laid out, as well as various species of flowering plants.
He likewise caused various kinds of fruits to grow, as well as varieties of vegetables, leaves, and tubers. He had a rampart constructed along with a circular moat,
and he installed water-lifting machines at the wells by which he could irrigate the gardens.
All those excellent wives of his gather flowers;
his wives always perform bathing, worship, and other rites, as well as the sweeping of the ground and the lighting of lamps in the temple of the deity.
The gardener himself constantly waters the branches.
Once grown, the trees become laden with beautiful flowers and abundant fruit;
from these fruits and other produce, everyone constantly partakes and enjoys them as if at a festival.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī! To the Kṛṣṇagaṅgā-tīrtha, which flows with the waters of the Yamunā.
There, in the first Kṛta Yuga, the Lord Vyāsa himself, the Blessed One who possesses knowledge of creation,
bathed and constantly taught the Vedas.
He shall remain for as long as he stays upon the land of the Yamunā.
Hari bathes daily in the waters of the Kṛṣṇagaṅgā at that place;
indeed, that Kṛṣṇagaṅgā is considered to lie between Soma and Vaikuṇṭha.
There, in that divine hermitage, dwell sages of celestial forms.
Those who come seeking the Cāturmāsya vow arrive invisible;
compassion arises for those merciful ones upon whom they look, and only for them do those sages come within the range of vision, and not otherwise.
At the Kṛṣṇagaṅgā-tīrtha during the Cāturmāsya, this was witnessed by a Brahmin named Vasu, a vessel of compassion and the sole thread of the Pāñcālya lineage.
Listen, Lakṣmī! I shall tell the story that effects the liberation from sin.
Then, a certain Brahmin from Pañcāla known by the name Vasu,
being extremely oppressed by famine, went with his wife to the excellent city of Varapattana on the banks of the Bhadrā and took up residence there, subsisting on alms.
While he was staying there, two children were born to him—a son and a daughter.
The daughter was given in marriage to a Brahmin for the sake of increasing his wealth and grain.
Subsequently, that Brahmin, the husband of the daughter, was afflicted by disease in his youth.
Thus, bereft of his kinsmen and deprived of his family, he died.
Having collected the bones of the maiden, he indeed returned to Mathurā.
This account of the casting down of the bones is as told in the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*.
In that region of Mathurā, on the site of the Half-Moon (Ardhacandra),
whatever embodied being performs [this rite] shall indeed attain liberation according to their desire.
Then, by the daughter [of the Sun], the bones were placed in the current of the Yamunā according to the prescribed ritual.
When they were cast away by the hand of the Brahmin, her husband then attained liberation.
That beautiful young widow, with dark, curly hair, well-formed and delicate-limbed, was left without support and exceedingly distressed. (13–14)
Her thighs were very fleshy, resembling the trunk of a plantain tree;
her feet had well-knit toes, and her auspicious nails were bright with a coppery glow.
Her navel was deep, spiraling to the right, and adorned with the three folds of skin.
She has a fragrant scent, symmetrical hips, and full, elevated breasts (16).
She has a neck like a conch shell, a well-proportioned face, beautiful teeth, and lovely lips and jaws.
She has beautiful nails, beautiful eyes, beautiful eyebrows, perfect proportions, and speaks with grace (17).
She had beautiful hips and a slender waist; her face was like the moon and her eyes were like lotuses.
In every respect, she possessed a perfect form.
She was named Tilottamā, a golden-hued young woman of great beauty.
Devoted to bathing at various sacred fords (tīrtha) here and there,
that woman of beautiful limbs— whomever she looked upon, and whoever looked upon her—
each became momentarily motionless, as if fixed in a painting.
He chose his own residence in such a Mathurā.
At that very time, the king who was the sovereign of the Kānyakubja region established a feast of food (annasatra) at the temple of Lord Mārtaṇḍeśvara in Mathurā.
There indeed were truthful Brahmins and virtuous Brahmin women;
(21) there, one hundred virtuous mendicants, the poor, and the helpless ate.
There, this excellent woman, the well-behaved Tilottamā, ate as well. (23)
At the time of his meal, music was performed beautifully,
with instrumental and vocal songs like those in the palace of Śakra.
And the dancers and singers belonging to that king—
She was enticed by female messengers and courtesans;
through singing, dancing, and other arts, she became affectionate toward them and adopted their way of life.
Thus, that virtuous woman, surrounded by unvirtuous women, was transformed in a mere few days.
Having come into the presence of the king, she became a vessel for his enjoyment;
as a young woman, she desired ever-new [pleasures] due to the burning of desire.
Thus, she became one who followed the path of sexual union amidst the objects of desire.
Now, her brother, a Pāñcāla born of a Brāhmaṇa father,
having become destitute in his home and having reflected upon his course of action,
arrived at Mathurā after some time had passed, finding himself without support.
At that time, he was a servant to a certain eminent merchant;
through his business acumen, at the end of the year, he too gained profit from his trade. By the power of fortune, he became wealthy, even though he was a widower.
He always goes to the Yamunā for the purpose of bathing, where she herself bathes. Having seen that woman of beautiful limbs, he fell under the power of infatuation.
Having bathed there at that excellent holy site, he was adorned with garments and ornaments.
Having beheld the gods and others, and having worshipped Garteśvara,
he followed the path of Tilottamā and proceeded slowly;
where her residence was, there he beheld her foster-sister.
And by her too, you were summoned to the house as a charming youth;
with a gracious mind, you went into the interior of the residence of that young woman, who showed him great honor through her foster-sister. || 34-35 ||
Deluded, he gave her garments of fine texture, golden bracelets, necklaces made of jewels, and wealth;
he also gave her the essence of agallochum, along with camphor and sandalwood.
She lived there day after day in that excellent house.
When half a watch of the day had passed, she would then go to her own quarters,
having always bathed at the holy site near the confluence of the Kṛṣṇā and the Gaṅgā.
Thus, constantly attached to that, he performed his own daily duties;
and as he was always going to the hermitage of Sumantu, he was observed by him. Then one day, while the Brahmin was indeed proceeding to bathe, he was seen by Sumantu.
While staying in his own hermitage, he beheld with divine vision that [body] covered in worms and insects.
(1.352.40) Numerous worms were seen falling from the pores of his skin;
indeed, they fell as long as he performed his ablutions. (1.352.41)
When the bath was performed, they were no longer seen, and he was born with a beautiful form.
Thus Sumantu witnessed this marvel for many days.
Then Sumantu called out to them, inquiring after their names and deeds.
Then the Pāñcāla said to him: "I am born in the land of Pañcāla.
A brahmin, I dwell here alone, having taken up the life of a merchant.
Having spent the night in this camp, which is well-guarded by Tilottamā..."
Having bathed in the morning and worshipped the Lord of Trigarta every day, I carry out my business during the day and reside in the camp at night.
Then Sumantu said: "Listen, O Brahmin, to the truth exactly as it is!"
It is a marvel that I constantly see something emerging from this body of yours:
when you have not bathed, it is filled with worms; when you have bathed, it possesses a stainless luster.
There must be some great sin in you, arising from a concealed source.
By bathing here through the power of this sacred ford (tīrtha), one goes far away;
indeed, a body purified by contact with the Lord of Trigarta is seen.
Having observed it, tell us truly what hidden sin you possess.
Having heard this from the sage Sumantu, who knows the three periods of time,
he announced, "I shall unite with my wife in my own quarters.
Having gone there, he then questioned her in private regarding the matter from its very beginning.
"Who are you? Whose daughter are you? And from what country have you come here?
For I shall surely give up my dear life if you do not speak the truth.
Perceiving his persistence, she spoke her own story with sorrow.

In the city of Varapattana in the country of Pañcāla, there lived a Brāhmaṇa named Vasu; I am his daughter, Tilottamā. Having married, my husband perished, and taking his bones, I went to Mathurā. ||52-53||

Having come at the request of the King of Kānyakubja through the power of passion, this woman, who follows the ways of desire, has entered into the practice of sexual union. My brother, however, the Pāñcāla, remains in his father’s palace.
"Formerly, I had a house there on the bank of the Bhadrā river.
Now, I live here alone and helpless, having resorted to the way of life of an unchaste woman.
Tell me your own story, if you consider me a worthy recipient. (55–56)
Having heard this, the Pāñcālya prince then became tearful-eyed; Tilottamā questioned him as he regained his composure,
and he then related his own history, including his lineage and name.
Indeed, he became extremely dejected due to having approached those who should not be approached.
Despondent, the twice-born man set his mind upon penance regarding [the transgression of approaching] his mother,
his teacher’s wife, his sister, his daughter, and his daughter-in-law.
Having gone there, she should enter the fire; no other means of purification is prescribed.
But Pāñcālī, recognizing that very brother of hers as being her husband, gave all her jewels, garments, wealth, and so forth to the twice-born.
Having given jewelry, wealth, and other gifts to the lord of Kāliñjara and Tri-garta,
she constructed a funeral pyre according to the prescribed rites at the holy ford of the Kṛṣṇagaṅgā and kindled the fire for her own purification.
The King of Pañcāla also, having given his own wealth as a gift with nothing remaining,
and having duly set aside a portion for the sake of the funeral rites,
bathed, bowed to the gods, and likewise to the Brahmins and Sumantu.
Having approached the sage, he said: "I have committed the sin of approaching one who should not be approached.
To purify myself of that sin, I shall indeed cast off my body.
Having spoken thus, he prepared a funeral pyre, drenched it with ghee, and set it ablaze.
Just as he was about to enter it, an incorporeal voice spoke:
"And do not do this rash act while she is intent on entering; for both of you are indeed free from sin."

Where Kṛṣṇa’s movements and sports took place at his pleasure; that ground, marked by the placement of his wheel-adorned feet, is truly divine. It is the very form of Brahman and the abode of light, where the destruction of sins occurs. (67–68)
For a sin committed elsewhere is destroyed upon reaching a sacred ford (*tīrtha*);
yet a sin committed at a sacred ford becomes as indelible as diamond-paste (*vajralepa*).
However, the destruction of both occurs at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean.
At the confluence of the Gomatī and the ocean, and at the five holy sites (pañcatīrtha) of the Yamunā—
whatever fruit is considered to arise from bathing in all the holy sites on earth is not equal even to the fruit of bathing in these five holy sites of the Yamunā.
For on the eleventh day at Viśrānti, on the twelfth at Saukara, on the thirteenth at Naimiṣa, on the fourteenth at Prayāga,
and on the full moon day at Puṣkara— by bathing and by performing each respective vow on these occasions during the month of Kārttika— [one attains great merit].
By bathing at every sacred ford (*tīrtha*), a person is liberated from all sins.
[This applies to] all the sacred fords in Mathurā, at Viśrānti, at the five sacred fords (*pañcatīrthaka*), at Asikuṇḍa, at the confluence of the Sarasvatī, and likewise at Garteśvara. 73–74.

The merit arising from bathing in the Kṛṣṇagaṅgā, even if done but once, is ten times greater than the fruit obtained from other baths; of this there is no doubt. Whatever evil deed has been accumulated, whether knowingly or unknowingly, [is destroyed by it].
Upon contact with the waters of the Kṛṣṇagaṅgā, even that which is called "adamantine" perishes.
(76) For Mathurā is the very form of Kṛṣṇa; likewise, the river consists of Kṛṣṇa.
There, both men and women are the form of Kṛṣṇa; no sin exists there. (77)
In one part of whose ear there is indeed only a mere trace of space;
in the corners of whose eyes light is also dissolved;
in whose breath the vital air is dissolved, and in whose sweat water is absorbed.
The earth, becoming as minute as an atom, remains forever within His belly;
all the oceans are always dissolved within His womb; and from the hairs of His body, the cosmic eggs constantly emerge. (1.352.80)
Since it is by His will that incarnations such as the Boar and others come into being,
while Kṛṣṇa remains present here, not even a trace of sin exists.
Wherever the Lord Varāha, the protector of the earth, is present, [there is no fear].

O best of Brahmins, by the mere sight of it here, the destruction of great sins occurs at that very moment; no doubt should be entertained in this matter. [This occurs] by bathing in the waters of the dark Ganges on the ninth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha. || 82-83 ||
By offering a lamp, a human being is indeed purified for three nights even from the sin of killing a pig;
O Tilottama, even Mahāvajrā is liberated from great sins.
Having bathed on the twelfth day at Kāliñjara and having worshipped the deity, [one attains the same].
Having become divine four-armed beings, they are glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
Thus, O Lakṣmī! Both Pāñcāla and Tilottamā, enlightened by the divine speech, then went to the hermitage of Sumantu.
Falling at his feet, they said to him, "You are our father and our preceptor;
O Brahmin, tell us with your divine vision what we should do here.
The sage replied, "The voice from the sky was true and never false."
I have seen with my own eyes the sin upon your bodies;
it exists before the bath, not after. Therefore, there is indeed no sin remaining.
Always perform your ablutions at Pañcatīrtha in Trigartaiśa.
"Stay constantly in my hermitage and perform your recitations;
remain free from evil for as long as you both live.
By my blessing, may both you, brother and sister, [prosper]."
"Free from sin, you two shall go to the world of Brahmā.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, in that hermitage, the great sages such as Suyajña and others dwell with divine bodies; therefore, it is remembered as the most excellent of sacred fords (tīrtha)."
Having attained divine bodies, both that brother and sister were born there in that hermitage as sages, granting liberation even by their mere sight.
Then, having ascended the celestial chariot of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, they—

Together with Śrī Kṛṣṇa, they went to the eternal abode of Goloka. (94) Such is the power of the holy site in Mathurā at the waters of the Yamunā, as well as of the place of the Kṛṣṇagaṅgā and of Kāliñjara. (95)
O Mahālakṣmī! What need is there to speak of even a place for pigs?
If that which is sinful in nature is offered to Kṛṣṇa, it ceases to be sin;
but if it is not offered to Kṛṣṇa, even that which is sinless would take on the form of sin. (96)

Therefore, whatever great gift of merit one may perform, it should be given to me, Kṛṣṇa—whether it be faultless or possessed of faults. Desire, anger, great greed, pride, and the taste for sensory enjoyment delude [the giver]. (97–98)
All these divine [narratives] dedicated to Kṛṣṇa indeed lead to liberation.
O Mahālakṣmī! whoever hears this with faith or certainly recites it, all the sin committed throughout seven lifetimes is entirely dispelled for that person.
If a person recites this even once in the morning during the Cāturmāsya period,
he will obtain the fruit arising from the gift of a hundred cows;
not even a trace of sin remains for him, and immortality is firmly established for him.

Thus ends the three hundred and fifty-second chapter, titled "The Demonstration of Sinlessness," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga in the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. It describes the majesty of the Mathurā Tīrtha, wherein the sinless nature of a Pāñcāla Brahmin residing in Varapattana in Saurāṣṭra—who had unknowingly committed an act of sexual intercourse with his sister named Tilottamā while in Mathurā—is revealed by a celestial voice and the sage Sumantu through the power of the five holy sites (Pañcatīrtha) and the Kṛṣṇagaṅgā Tīrtha.
