Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī! The conduct of women is indeed always fickle.
Upon seeing a handsome son, or a father, or another man, [their minds waver]. (1)
For a moment the passionate woman may come under the sway of her own resolve;
yet the mind is as fickle as that Rajasic experience of desire.
It surely makes one dependent on another, just as she will do to Samba.
Listen: Śrī Kṛṣṇa will have a son named Sāmba.
Due to the delusion of his mothers there, he will become the recipient of their curse; at that time, the disease of leprosy will manifest upon Sāmba’s body. (3–4)
Having arrived at Mathurā, he will perform the worship of the Sun, establish [the deity], and bathe in the waters of the Yamunā.
By that, his leprosy will be destroyed; of this there is no doubt.
Such is the holy site of Mathurā, which destroys disease.
Listen in detail, O Lakṣmī! I shall tell you what will happen as he dwells in Dvārakā together with his wife, sons, and daughters.
The sage Nārada arrived there at the abode of Kṛṣṇa;
Śrī Kṛṣṇa joyfully offered him a fitting welcome.
Then, in private, Nārada made a representation to Hari.
"O Kṛṣṇa! I wish to say something; listen, for I have heard it in heaven:
There is a son of Kṛṣṇa named Sāmba, a youth of exquisite beauty, desirable to women, and beloved—indeed, no other is his equal. (1.353.10)
Even the wives of Kṛṣṇa longed for him upon seeing him; and as for those who are of divine origin, numbering sixteen thousand,
their minds were indeed agitated upon beholding Sāmba.
"How is this being sung by the deities in the worlds of heaven and elsewhere?
Indeed, fame is the dwelling in heaven, while its opposite is hell.
O Great Lord, I have come here for the sake of what is dear to you, in order to speak. (12–13)
As long as one's merit is heard of, for so long is one called a "man";
when his lack of merit is heard, he is indeed proclaimed to be in hell.
Therefore, whether it be true or false, I shall certainly investigate that.
"Therefore, summon Samba as well as the host of goddesses to the assembly.
Having been addressed thus, Kṛṣṇa summoned the goddesses from all sides; having seated them and summoned Samba, he also had him sit down by his side.

Having beheld the exceedingly beautiful form of Sāmba here, all those excellent women were agitated, even as Kṛṣṇa himself looked on. Having paid homage to Nārada, they departed for their respective abodes.
Sāmba stood there, while Kṛṣṇa hung his head in shame.
(18) There is no moment of privacy, nor is there any opportunity for secrecy;
having seen a handsome man, women always lose their self-control. (19)
This is the very nature of women; what cause for lamentation is there in that?
Just as a chariot cannot move with only one wheel, so too women, being unable to exist without a man, flow away [from virtue] when deprived of him.
They considered themselves to have accomplished their purpose by merely casting a glance at the men;
yet upon seeing Pradyumna, they all experienced intense shame,
and upon seeing Samba, they were all tormented by the god of love.
This Sambhu, who infatuates even your wife, is the excitant (uddīpana-vibhāva).
I have heard from the world and repeatedly from the Brahman-sages the difficult-to-overcome rumor that has arisen concerning you in Satyaloka. (23)
"O Keśava, having abandoned Sāmba, you ought to wipe away that infamy!
Having spoken thus, Nārada then observed silence;
thereupon Hari cursed Sāmba: "O son, become deformed! (24-25)
At that moment, Sāmba became afflicted with leprosy and was indeed deformed.
Then, seeing Sāmba in such a state, Nārada spoke to him sorrowfully:
"Sāmba, Sāmba, son of Kṛṣṇa! Listen, O son of Jāmbavatī! (26)
"O sinless one, always pay homage to the rising sun!
O son, the Sun-god, being pleased, will destroy your leprosy.
And having gone to Mathurā, you shall obtain the fruit of worshipping the six suns."
O sinless one, worship the Sun at the Ṣaṭsūrya Tīrtha in the morning;
likewise at midday and in the evening—attain the fruit immediately.
Having bathed in the Kṛṣṇagaṅgodbhava and having worshipped the Sun with diligence, [you shall attain the fruit].
"Completely freed from all sins, he is liberated from leprosy and other ailments.
(1.353.30) Having been addressed thus, O Mahālakṣmī, Sāmba departed by the command of Kṛṣṇa;
he beheld Mathurā, which removes all defects and bestows liberation. (31)

Restraining himself through ritual bathing and libations, he worshipped the six suns: the one at the time of Brahmā’s birth, the rising one, the one ascending upward, the one at the meridian, the one setting, and the one already gone to its decline;
thus Sāmba worshipped them constantly.
Satisfied, the Sun appeared before Sāmba in a very short time.
"Choose a boon; may prosperity be yours! Your leprosy and other ailments have departed," he said.
Having spoken thus, he touched every limb of Sāmba, and at that very moment, Sāmba [was restored].
Devoid of leprosy, he shone with a luster equal to the sun;
the sun itself existed in a second form together with Sāmba.
In the Brahma-mantra, Sāmba established the sun known as Virāṭ.
The sun named Udaya is established on the Yamunā in the south;
Kālapriya-ravi is established upon the upper wheel (ūrdhvayānta). On the western wheel of Vaikuṇṭha is the Mādhyandinīyaka sun. (36–37)
Having descended and established Sāmbārka in Mathurā,
and having established Kṛṣṇagaṅgārka on the southern bank as he was setting,
Sāmba remained in Sāmbapura and performed the rites of worship and other ceremonies for them.
In Mathurā, however, that became Sāmbapura Kuleśvara.
On the seventh day of the month of Māgha, those people who shall perform the divine chariot procession toward Sāmbapura for Sāmbasūrya [shall attain their goal].
Having bathed in the Kṛṣṇagaṅgā and beheld the orb of the six suns, people shall go to that peaceful state which pierces the solar disc;
freed from sins, diseases, and other afflictions, they will proceed to the supreme abode.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have told you that which destroys mental sins and the like.
Even the sin of approaching those who should not be approached, as well as the sin of approaching those who are forbidden to be approached, this Tīrtha of the Six Suns quickly consumes away.
Whatever mental wickedness one shakes off through longing, that is quickly [removed];
even for all offenses, Hari himself in Mathurā— Kṛṣṇa,
who honors the people of the Gopīs— does not take them into account at all.
Sāmba became cleansed of his sin and vanished right there;
remaining forever upon the chariot of the Sun, he would inquire about the future,
and the son of Kṛṣṇa came to know all of that by making it new once again.
Having established Sāmbapura in Mathurā, he departed for his own home.
By reciting or hearing this, one obtains the fruit of worshipping the six Ādityas;
at the end of life, one attains the world of the Sun and the abode of Kṛṣṇa.
Listen, Lakṣmī! O beloved, even regarding the offenses committed by devotees:
a man who is entirely innocent and pure may, through the disparity of place and time, come to be regarded as guilty even without having committed an offense. (48–49)
Indeed, offenses occur through action, mind, or speech; namely,
the failure to bathe, as well as violence, sexual intercourse,
the voiding of excrement and urine, and likewise the birth of a child.
Indeed, touching a corpse and the like are offenses during the worship of the deity.
Likewise, stretching out one's feet in the presence of the temple or the image, turning one's back [to the deity], urinating, and eating whatever one pleases [are offenses]. (51–52)
Being impure, eating unclean food, worshipping with forbidden flowers,
failing to remove the remains of the offering (*nirmālya*) when the worship has ended,
and walking about in the temple of the deity while wearing shoes— these are [faults]. (53)
Consuming liquor and meat, awakening the Lord in darkness,
likewise failing to offer salutation, vulgar chatter, caviling, smoking, spitting, and so forth— these are transgressions of ritual action (karmāparādha). (54–55)
Lack of meditation upon Śrī Hari, lack of remembrance, lack of constant retention [of Him],
forming thoughts of others, contemplating sense objects and the like,
attachment, aversion, thirst, latent impressions, and censuring others. (56)
Fallacious reasoning, doubt regarding causes, delusion, and likewise error; laziness, lack of inquiry, pride, and self-conceit;
desire, anger, greed, intoxication, and envy as well—[these are the obstacles]. (57–58)
Envy, ill-will, improper reflection, and the like are indeed mental offenses.
[The objects of these offenses include] mother, father, friend, companion, teacher, twice-born, deities, and so forth;
likewise, virtuous women, chaste wives, beloved consorts, children, the unborn, cattle, and so on. (59)
All things, from blades of grass and insects to sentient beings, have Nārāyaṇa within them.
One must never offend those who are masters, servants, or dependents.
Idle chatter, false rumors, and even useless speech [are to be avoided]. (1.353.60–61)
Non-participation, the giving of faults, the employment of abusive words,
quarreling, reviling, clamor, and shouting;
excessive noise, loud sounds, and even the uttering of insults.

Harsh speech, loud shouting, as well as cracking the thighs and so forth—these, along with unrestrained blows and the like, are words that cause offense. One should not utter them; rather, one should deliberate first, for they yield undesirable fruits. (63–64)
One should never commit offenses against deities, sacred fords, gurus, brahmins, holy men, virtuous women, or devoted wives— all of whom are saviors;
for a man who commits such offenses does not behold Viṣṇu at all.
One should never perform the rākṣasī or tāmasī worship. O Dear One, worship that offers meat and liquor is called rākṣasī;
that worship which is joined with acts such as violence is considered tāmasī.
Adultery, the theft of another's property, the harming of others,
and actions that cause the destruction of others are proclaimed to be Rākṣasa-karma (demoniac action).
For those who have committed offenses through their actions, purification occurs by means of ritual bathing and other such rites.
By bathing at sacred fords (tīrtha), by consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya),
by fasting, by performing sacrifices over a long period of time, and likewise by means of the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and the Brahmakūrca vow; 1.353.70.
Purification is sought through service to the gods and through service to the virtuous;
for those who have committed offenses with the mind, purification comes through meditation and the like.
Through the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind, as well as through the restraint of the senses, [purification is attained]. 71.
Through knowledge, through the abandonment of defects, through austerity, and through the cultivation of merit;
(72) through the hearing of the sacred narrative, through reflection, and through reaching a definitive conclusion;
through inquiry into the Self, and through the discrimination between consciousness and the unconscious; (73)
Purification of the mind is held to arise from the realization of the nature of the soul and primordial matter (*puṃprakṛti*);
however, purification for those who have committed offenses through speech shall be achieved by means of recitation (*japa*) and other such practices.
O Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa! O Viṣṇu! O Hare! O Mādhava! O Keśava!
O Lord of Lakṣmī, O Sovereign of Ramā! O Lord of Śrī, O Lord of Pārvatī!
||75|| O Lord of the Gopīs, O Master! O Lord of Māṇikī, and O Lord of Prabhā! O Lord of the virtuous, O Lord of the Imperishable, O Lord of the Liberated, O Supreme Person! ||76||

"O Lord of Goloka and other realms! O Supreme Brahman! O Śrī Puruṣottama!"—by thus chanting these names, as well as by the recitation of the *oṃkāra* and other mantras, by begging for forgiveness, and likewise by reading the sacred narratives.
Through the chanting of Kṛṣṇa’s glories, through the wearing of a garland of Kṛṣṇa, and through the firm establishment in the vow of truth, purification of speech is desired;
indeed, a person reciting the hymn of Viṣṇu is liberated from all transgressions. (78–79)
Indeed, one becomes pure by bathing at sacred fords (tīrtha) even after a year,
such as in Kāśī, Mathurā, Dvārakā, and Puṣkara; in Badarī, in the city of Jagannātha, and in the city of Sāketa.
At Haridvāra and at the Gaṇḍakī, at Godāvarī and Janārdana;
at the Kāverī and Setubandha, at Padmāvatī and Raivata; in the waters of the Svarṇarekhā, at Aśvapaṭṭasara, and at Mānasa.
At Nārāyaṇa, Indradyumna, Kāverī, Padmanābha, Kāñcī, and on the Narmadā, during the avabhṛtha bath and the paṭṭakotsava festival—
through bathing, drinking [the water], as well as through meditation, chanting, and wearing [the sacred ash or marks]— [one attains liberation].
Through hearing, reflecting, and also through seeing, there is the destruction of sin.
(84) Having wandered to all the sacred fords (*tīrtha*), one reaches the Mathurā region; however, ultimate rest occurs at Viśrāntighaṭṭaka. (85)
In Mathurā, the fruit [of one's actions] is produced multiplied by a hundred million;
for those seeking a destination, Mathurā is the supreme goal.
That same goal which belongs to one disciplined in yoga likewise belongs to one possessed of Sāṃkhya knowledge.
That is the destination for one who gives up their life in Mathurā; of this there is no doubt.
(87) There is no sacred site equal to Mathurā, no deity like Kṛṣṇa, no liberation possessing the splendor of the abode of Brahmā, and nothing superior to Puruṣottama. (88)
"When it is made the support, there shall be the dissolution of all sins;
when it is held within the self, one's own absolute liberation shall arrive.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, has been told to you this supreme knowledge among all knowledges.
"By hearing or even by reading this, a person shall partake in its fruit.

(1.353.90) Thus ends the three hundred and fifty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Mathurā Tīrtha in the First Section on the Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga within the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā," concerning the agitation of the minds of Kṛṣṇa’s wives upon seeing Sāmba in the form of a woman at Dvārakā, the resulting leprosy of Sāmba due to the curse given by Kṛṣṇa, the removal of that leprosy through the worship of Āditya in Mathurā, the installation of the six Ādityas, and the physical, verbal, and mental offenses as well as their remedies. 353.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī! In Mathurā there is the Dhruva-tīrtha, which bestows excellent liberation;
through libations and the gift of food, it brings satisfaction to the ancestors.
In Mathurā there was a king named Candrasena, who performed deeds of righteousness.
His wife was Candraprabhā, a mother of heroes who gave birth to heroic sons. Among her hundred maidservants, there was one maidservant named Prabhāvatī.
O beautiful lady, Prabhāvatī’s ancestors, numbering one hundred,
had all fallen into hell due to their own faults;
yet Prabhāvatī neither performs nor causes to be performed the libation for them.
Whether it be a *śrāddha* ceremony or some other gift intended for the satisfaction of the ancestors,
they perform these for her and even for her family members, yet they do not offer libations (*tarpaṇa*) to her.
Consequently, her group of ancestors once fell [into distress] on the bank of the Yamunā.
A subtle multitude of living beings indeed gathered at Dhruvatīrtha;
black in color, moving about, and resembling the shape of mosquitoes,
these ancestors were seen by the Ṛṣi who is known as the knower of the three times.
Knowing the three periods of time, he always offers handfuls of water to the ancestors on that river;
thus the ancestors, being satisfied, go to the realm of light.
That sage indeed always observes the vow of milk, eating only at the sixth mealtime.
Subsisting on the drinking of the sun’s rays, he remained moving in accordance with the movement of the sun.
(9) Seeing the assembly of his ancestors who had arrived, and being utterly bewildered by that very sight, he looked upon them with compassion and did not perform his vows or recitations. (10)
The day drew to a close with only a fourth part remaining.
There, some ancestors descended from the sky to the earth;
others came from the east, the north, the south, and likewise from the west.
Hundreds of thousands of ancestors had gathered there at Dhruvatīrtha;
seeing those who were coming and going, he was filled with wonder.
There, he beheld a single group whose limbs were joyful and well-nourished, and who were full of contentment.
Having received the *svadhā* offering from his sons, he drank the water and went to heaven. Another group was seen as well—a practitioner of austerities with an emaciated body.
Rugged and devoted to bathing, he too drank the water and returned to the earth.

Then another group was seen, adorned with garments and ornaments; with their limbs joyful and well-nourished, they went to heaven after drinking the water. Then the other assembly was seen, their bodies naked. (15–16)
Well-nourished and endowed with happiness, he drank the water and went to the sky.
Then, at the end, many were seen seated upon excellent celestial chariots (vimānas). There were various kinds of vehicles, filled with abundant food.
Having taken [the offerings], they travel by way of the sky to Mahāra and other regions. Then others appeared, uttering auspicious blessings;
satisfied, they were mounted upon the backs of swans, Garuḍas, and the like, as well as upon elephants and horses.
Others were seen deformed, angry, and excessively tormented by hunger; with bellies clinging to their backs, devoid of dignity, and ready to utter curses.
Then others were likewise seen, honored with offerings of flowers.
Having eaten at the *śrāddha*, they were full of great enthusiasm and as radiant as the gods.

(21) Some, holding the funeral cakes (*piṇḍas*) in their hands, and others, having consumed the fruits, departed for the world of men and other realms, accompanied by the sixteen articles and the rest. (22)
Some were seen engaged in beds, provided with objects of enjoyment and pleasures, contented and serene-minded, yet intent upon ascetic penance;
others were adorned with crowns, fanned by chowries, and shaded by royal parasols.
I saw ten thousand who had departed for Satyaloka in celestial chariots.
Furthermore, I saw other ancestors wandering along the Yamunā, dressed in new garments and adorned with ornaments and the like. (24–25)
Indeed, at the Dhruvatīrtha on the Kālindī, after midday and until evening,
the ancestors were thus beheld by the ṛṣi who knows the three periods of time.
When the host of ancestors had departed, the sons, along with their wives and families, remained.
The performers of the *śrāddha* rites themselves departed for their respective homes in the evening.
At that time, Dhruvatīrtha became desolate and devoid of people.
Even the king of sages, though he knew the three periods of time, arose from there in astonishment. (27–28)
He saw one man with emaciated limbs, wasted by hunger and unsteady in his gait; trembling as he waited, his small belly pressed against his back, terrified by the pain in his thighs,
skin, and bones, yawning again and again.
With hollow eyes, a withered face, a feeble and faint voice, and emaciated—compassionate as he was, that sage asked him: "Who are you?
Why are you so distressed and disfigured, covered all over by swarms of gnats?"
"You do not go, nor is there a place for you; you are without support—what do you say?
Today I have indeed seen many fathers here by the millions.
The time for beholding them has now entirely passed for me."
"Today I have no daily ritual (*naiṣṭhika*) to be performed for the purpose of seeing you.
Now that you have been seen by me, my [current] rite is indeed destroyed.
I shall perform my daily duty later; tell me the truth. (33–34)
"I shall indeed do as much as I am able, provided it is possible and beneficial for you.
Having heard this, Jantu spoke to the sage exactly as it was:
"Today itself, there is a great occasion that will bring satisfaction to the ancestors."
A śrāddha performed at Dhruvatīrtha, as well as the offering of water with sesame seeds and so forth—
food, clothing, fruit, flowers, water, bedding and the like, sandals, a house, an umbrella, ornaments, milk, and likewise other things [are all meritorious]. (36–37)
O Brahmin, whatever is given today by sons, daughters, grandsons, wives,
and kinsmen at Dhruvatīrtha becomes a hundred-thousandfold gift that provides complete satisfaction to the ancestors;
indeed, everything given there becomes eternally certain.
Vehicles, mounts, cows, gardens, and even fields—
having taken these that were given, as well as gold, wealth, and other things, they depart together.
Today the ancestors, satisfied by sesame seeds and satisfied in every way, have been exceedingly gratified.
Today all the ancestors, possessing sons, go to heaven satisfied—
those whose bodies are nourished by their descendants through the śrāddha offerings and water libations given by their progeny.
Thus, for those whose lineage remains imperishable and who possess such offspring, [the ancestors are content].
They go to the supreme goal accompanied by their sons who have been honored with *svadhā* offerings.
Today, the ancestors of King Candrasena were seen by you being honored;
likewise, others have gone to heaven, visible through your divine vision.

The ancestors of all those who perform the *śrāddha* rites— whether they be Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, or those of Śūdra occupation, including both those born in the natural order (*anuloma*) and those born in the inverse order (*pratiloma*)—
have been seen by you, as have their imperishable progeny.
I, however, remain here waiting for the *śrāddha* ceremony;
bound by hundreds of snares of hope, hungry and seeking satisfaction,
I previously fell into hell due to the fault of mixing castes (*yonisaṃkara*).
"O Brahmin, neither by the atheists nor by those of my own lineage has a śrāddha been offered to me today.
Although I come here every year, I have no access to a śrāddha.
Having taken up the livelihood of a slave to another's father, I live on, O Brahmin. (47)

Today, during this performance of the ancestral rites, not even for a moment have I obtained a kinsman among hundreds of years; indeed, I have found no satisfaction today. I am utterly distressed by the three-fold torments, having become unable to proceed on my journey.
All of them went forth endowed with strength; for what recourse is there for one who is weak?
Indeed, some will surely arrive who offer libations to all the ancestors.
Then, having obtained something [of sustenance], I shall go to a nearby forest.
These tiny, emaciated gnats that exist upon my body have taken refuge in my frame because their progeny has been destroyed. Indeed,
I am their ancestor, for these people are born of my own lineage.

"At times of hunger, they devour me, distressed by the severing of my threads. In this lineage of mine, there exists a single daughter made of thread, who serves as an attendant to King Candrasena in Mathurā. (53)
A maidservant named Prabhāvatī was devoted to serving the queen.
Her son, a laborer known as Virūpanidhi, was the thread of our lineage; we [performed] his śrāddha rites. (54–55)

With hearts bound by our intentions and desiring the satisfaction of the ancestors through funeral offerings, we remain here for this long alone; beyond that, we shall go to the forest, even if it be to a bottomless hell or to old age with broken spirits. (56)

"If that thread [of our kinship] should provide water, funeral offerings (śrāddha), and handfuls of sesame seeds, then, having become nourished, we shall go to the lowest heaven. Listen: even an offering given by one from a low birth is indeed received. (57–58)
We shall be satisfied by what is given by her; we shall be truly possessed of a daughter.

By the ripening of past karma, whatever downward state our ancestors have reached, or whatever upward state they have attained—those fathers who possess sons find their support through their daughters.
The funeral rites, the offering of rice-balls and water, and the gift bestowed by a daughter are thus obtained.
There is no other path for the ancestors; fathers become truly possessed of sons through a daughter.
"May there be someone in our lineage who shall offer us a handful of water."
Especially in rivers with abundant, cool water,
standing in water reaching to the navel, one should offer a handful of water mixed with sesame seeds and fruit at the midst of sacred fords (tīrtha),
or even with water containing silver.
Holding *darbha* grass in his hand, he should offer [the water]; by that we are always satisfied.

(63) Holding *darbha* grass in his hand, the son, pronouncing the names of the three lineages (*gotra*) and the names of the ancestors, should say: "May [he] whose name is so-and-so be satisfied; *svadhā*! (64)
One should offer a single añjali to the gods, two añjalis to the sages,
and three añjalis to the ancestors, reciting, "May they be satisfied.
One should first offer to one's father, and thereafter to one's mother.
He should offer [water] to his maternal grandfather and to his paternal grandfather;
he should also offer three handfuls of water to the ancestors beyond them.
Likewise, he should offer to his maternal grandmother and to his paternal great-grandmother.
By this offering of a funeral ball (*piṇḍa*), I cause you to be freed from the state of being invisible to the sun (*asūrya*).
This water given by me—may it bring you inexhaustible satisfaction.
Even water, when given with faith, conduces to infinity.
Some ancestors, while receiving [the offerings], become agitated in appearance.
Listen to the cause of that, O Brahmin, so that the śrāddha may not be fruitless:
that which is given at an improper place and time, devoid of ritual procedure, and without sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā). || 70 ||
An impure substance given to an unworthy recipient does not lead to satisfaction at all.

That which is offered without faith, by one excluded from the company of diners, or while being looked upon with a wicked gaze, is devoid of sesame seeds, mantras, and kuśa grass; such an offering becomes demonic (āsura).
Impure houses, impure śrāddha offerings,
gifts given while possessed by anger, and śrāddhas performed without the prescribed ritual or worthy recipients and without dakṣiṇā— these indeed fall to the rākṣasas. (72–73)
Indeed, the Rākṣasa consumes the fruit of a sacrifice devoid of sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
O Lakṣmī! Those who make vain oaths in the presence of gods, Brahmins, or teachers—whatever they have done, the inhabitants of Pātāla consume it all.

Śrāddha rites performed by those who have not studied the Vedas, offerings and gifts made without mantras, the praising of a disciple who is not devoted to his guru despite his meritorious deeds, and the premature disclosure of a righteous act one intends to perform— [these are all fruitless]. (75–76)

All that was prepared for the satisfaction of those dwelling in the netherworld is in vain, for any vow performed with false ostentation indeed becomes an offering of charity, ancestral rites, austerity, and fire-oblation for the *rakṣasas*. (77)
Consequently, the groups of ancestors do not attend [the rites] while naked;
they are robbed by Rākṣasas and others who consume the fruits of the gifts and other offerings.
Just as they were summoned, so they depart fruitless and without food.
Maintaining silence, they all remain there, hungry and thirsty;
they come and go, yet they do not partake in merit.
All this has been told to you regarding the cause of the deformity of the ancestors.
He who gives what is new, highly valuable, excellent,
and substantial— his ancestors, becoming prosperous, indeed travel to heaven seated upon celestial vehicles.
But if he gives at the śrāddha what is worn out, inferior, lowly, and unsubstantial—
"Those ancestors who are indeed poor wander and travel on foot;
they are poor for those who are poor, and they share in the prosperity of those who are prosperous.
Having spoken thus, that elder assembly of ancestors then fell silent.
Knowing the three periods of time and moist with compassion, he spoke for his benefit:
"I shall not eat until you have reached full satisfaction;
remain steady and wait for my return, for I am going to bring that little girl."
Having said, "I shall then perform the *śrāddha*," he departed from the king.
Seeing that the sage had arrived, the king bowed at his feet:
"I am blessed, I am graced; my home has been purified."
"Today my birth has become fruitful; accept these water for the feet, the guest-offering, and the cow.
To the king who was speaking thus, [the sage], having received such hospitality, replied:
"O King, listen and do that by which I may be satisfied."
"Bring the queen together with Prabhāvatī.
Once she had been brought by the king, she bowed to the sage and took her seat; the muni then said:
"I shall tell you of the wonder that was seen by me at Dhruvatīrtha."
All the ancestors, by the tens of millions, went to heaven, honored by their sons.
Yet one old man remained—his body withered, emaciated by hunger, and his flesh dried up;
hopeless and desiring to go to hell, he stayed at Dhruva-tīrtha.

Out of great compassion, I asked him, "Who are you, and what do you desire? He replied to me: "In my lineage there was a maidservant named Prabhāvatī, and her son is indeed known by the name Tantuvirūpakānidhi."
"O Brahmin, if he were to perform a *śrāddha* for me, I would attain satisfaction.
Indeed, the libation (*tarpaṇa*) for the ancestors must be performed by Prabhāvatī through her son;
for whatever gift, water, fruit, or the like is given for the sake of the ancestors [is effective]. (93–94)
"Let the *svadhā* and the milk-rice (*pāyasa*) śrāddha be a source of satisfaction and liberation.
Having said this, for the sake of providing proof, the sage struck her, who was overwhelmed by intoxication:
"Did you offer water for the sake of satisfying the ancestors, or not? (95)
She replied, "It is not so; moreover, I do not know those ancestors.
I do not know the ritual action nor the rite, and I never perform them.
The sage said, "Let them come; you shall see a marvel today. (96–97)
Having thus resolved, all the citizens, the Brahmins, the king, and many other people then went to Dhruvatīrtha. There,
the sage showed them an old man who was unconscious and emaciated.
Surrounded by tiny mosquitoes and excessively tormented by hunger, the sage said to him:
"O creature! Your daughter, born of your lineage, has arrived here with her son for the sake of nourishment; tell me what you desire. (1.354.100)
Then Agati said: "Having bathed here according to the prescribed rite, let him perform the libation (tarpaṇa) by my name, and thereafter let him perform the ancestral rite (śrāddha).
Let him also offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa) along with silver, clothing, and sesame seeds."
Likewise, let each of you here indeed perform another gift according to your ability,
by which you shall behold me right here endowed with happiness.
Let them perform the *śrāddha* and the gift according to their capacity through this thread.
Having heard this, the king’s wife had a *śrāddha* ceremony performed with abundant sacrificial fees by her maidservant and by her son in every respect.
[She provided] fine silk cloth, fruit, incense, camphor, agallochum, and sandalwood.

He was satisfied by all that was offered— sesame seeds, milk-rice, sweet food with rice-balls, water, and water with sesame seeds. Being virtuous and full of splendor, he shone like a god, radiant with light.
Likewise, even the mosquitoes, resembling them, were born beautiful, well-formed, and exceedingly robust; they shone like gods and were fully satisfied.
Indeed, the sky there was covered with celestial chariots that had arrived from heaven.
Then all those ancestors, with minds as satisfied as gods, said:
"May the lineage of our family increase through those born of a noble descent who shall always deliver us by means of various *śrāddha* rites. (108–109)
"May all hear these words of ours, which bring satisfaction to the ancestors:
the sacred fords, rivers, wells, mountains, and lakes;
Kurukṣetra, Gayā, Gaṅgā, and all other holy places and shrines."
There has never been, nor will there ever be, anything else that grants liberation to the ancestors as this does.

Having bathed on the *proṣṭhapadī* day in the month of Bhādrapada, and then reaching the sacred ford with haste at the beginning of the first lunar day, they should remain there until the end of the bright fortnight’s first day.
The ancestors, who receive the funeral cakes at the *śrāddha* rites, have certainly taken their place in Āśvina;

having rendered the city of the departed empty, they now reside in heaven and the netherworld (pātāla), seeking after their own sons, the continuers of their lineage, as well as their younger brothers. (113)
"We shall remain here together with our ancestors born of our respective lineages.

When the sun has entered the sign of Virgo, whoever shall offer a *śrāddha* and libations (*tarpaṇa*) to our ancestors at Dhruvatīrtha during the sixteen-day period, [they shall attain the highest state]. (1.14–15)
"We are forever fully satisfied; we shall go to the supreme goal.
You have indeed seen the means for the liberation of the ancestors, just as it is.
By the grace of the Knower of the Three Times, our insurmountable sin has been crossed over."
Having thus addressed the king, the people, and the ṛṣi,
and having spoken to the queen, the maidservant, and their son, saying,
"May it be well with you all," they mounted excellent vehicles and, surrounded by the gods, went to heaven.
Then the king, the queen, their son, the maidservant, the subjects, the women, and the men—
filled with great wonder— returned to their respective homes. And they performed the ancestral rites and libations at all appropriate times.
By the power of Dhruva-tīrtha, their ancestors were uplifted by them.
This greatness arising from Mathurā has been told to you, O Lakṣmī;
by the mere remembrance of which the sins of previous births are destroyed.
Whoever recites or even hears this shall possess the merit of the Dhruva-tīrtha;
he shall possess the merit of bathing in the waters of the Yamunā at Mathurā.
Indeed, wherever one may stand near water, if they offer a funeral cake (piṇḍa), [they obtain that same merit].
Having remembered the eternal holy site (tīrtha) of the Yamunā and having invoked the ancestors there,
the satisfaction of the ancestors arises just as it does from the waters of the Yamunā. Furthermore, the increase of his lineage, health, and prosperity are well produced for him.

Thus ends the three hundred and fifty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Śrāddha Rite and its Greatness, Including the Liberation of the Ancestors by Performing a Śrāddha through a Daughter in the Form of a Maidservant of King Candrasena, after the Satisfaction of Ten Million Ancestors at Dhruvatīrtha by the Sage named Trikālajña upon Seeing One Hungry Father," in the section on the Greatness of Mathurā-tīrtha within the first book, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
