Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, Lord of the universe! I have heard this glorious majesty of Mathurā-kṣetra, which is fruitful and bestows both heaven and liberation. (1)
O Hari! Out of compassion, you have heard from me about the *śrāddha* and the fruit of the *śrāddha*.
But by whom was the *śrāddha* first originated? Tell me this in detail.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O beloved! I shall relate the definitive account of the origin of the *śrāddha*.
At the beginning of creation, Brahmā was born from the lotus of my navel.
He then brought forth the gods and others as his own sons.
The Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, the two Aśvins, and the hosts of Maruts;
for the sake of the deliverance of all, [he created] Brāhmaṇas everywhere on earth,
as well as Kṣatriyas, those of the Vaiśya caste, those of the Śūdra caste, and likewise animals.
[He created] birds, stationary beings, and animals such as insects as required;
likewise, through Diti he created the Daityas, and through Danu the Dānavas.
In this manner, [he created] the Ṛṣis who possess Vedic knowledge and whose wealth is austerity.
Their sons and likewise their grandsons were born, by whom the world was filled. From the eye of the Creator (Brahmā) was born Nimi, a mental son, O King;
from him also was born a glorious mental son named Śrīmat.
A mere youth by birth, yet possessing the memory of his former lives and likewise the memory of the Vedas,
he performed supreme austerity, having fixed his mind on Hari.
He practiced the penance of the five fires, subsisted on air alone, stood on one leg, and kept his arms raised upward.
Subsisting on withered leaves and water during the winter, he lay in the water;
performing the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for more than ten thousand years,
he reached the time of death and attained the state of the five elements.
Nimi, having fallen into extreme grief, reflected upon that matter;
on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, having created a mental realm, he conceived with faith: "What indeed shall I do for the sake of a son?"
Then his son, possessing a divine body, arrived from the path of the celestial chariots in the sky and said:
"Give gifts for my sake;
give water, give fruit, and give sweet food and garments."
Give me ornaments, vehicles, vessels, and milk-rice;
give me whatever foods I may eat, as well as roots and juices.
Give me those vegetables and side dishes that are most dear to me. (15)
Having thus dwelt there for some time on the banks of the Devadhūni in the snowy region,
Nimi, having become pure and composed, took leave of the Seven Sages;
and those best of sages performed everything according to the clockwise ritual sequence.
Seven times they sat down together there simultaneously; they gave you various kinds of vegetables, roots, and fruits.
O beautiful one, Nimi honored the brahmins seven times over.
Then, with a disciplined mind, having arranged the *kuśa* grass with their tips pointing southward,
he offered the funeral cakes (*piṇḍas*) to the illustrious one, pronouncing his name and lineage; he also gave water, fruit, leaves, food, milk-rice, garments, and other such things.
He gave [the food] to his divine son, and he accepted it in every way;
he brought everything before his very eyes, and he ate and drank it all visibly. Likewise, having entered again among the seven seers (saptarṣis), he ate repeatedly.
Having uttered, "I am satisfied, I am thoroughly satisfied," and having partaken of the sacrificial food (*vastuka*),
he ascended a celestial chariot and departed, gratified by the *śrāddha* rite.
When the sun had set, the king performed the evening twilight devotions (*bhāvasandhyā*).
At night he began to reflect upon what he had done for the sake of a son;
having performed the offering of funeral cakes and other rites, he felt remorse, thinking:
"What have I done that was never done before by the sages?"
"The act of providing food for the dead is impure, yet it was employed by me for the sake of my son.
Alas! By the power of affection, I have performed what is beyond death. This is not the ritual for the corpse; rather, a censurable act has been committed by me. (25–26)
"What will all those who stand in my father's place say to me—
the gods, asuras, gandharvas, piśācas, uragas, and rākṣasas?
While he was reflecting thus, the morning dawned, O Brāhmaṇa.
Having performed the twilight rites and offered oblations into the fires, she again fell into reflection:
"Alas! My life is in vain since my son is not seen;
indeed, the hell named Pūtika is described as being right here in my heart."
When there is a son, there is indeed no sorrow, and heaven is attained in every way.
Through a son one obtains heaven, and through a grandson the grandfathers do so;
furthermore, through the grandson of a son, the great-grandfathers rejoice.
"Deprived of my illustrious son, I have no desire to live.
In the meantime, O Lakṣmī, Nārada arrived;
seeing him radiant with splendor, the king indeed worshipped him.
Having been honored, Nārada sat upon a seat and said to him:
"O Nimi! Listen, O one of great wisdom! Do not grieve, O destroyer of grief!
Why do you, being wise, mourn for this body which is impermanent and subject to decay? (33)
The wise do not grieve for what is dead, lost, gone, or passing away.
(34) What has departed never returns; people laugh at one who grieves.
I see no immortality in the world of mortals, among the moving or the unmoving. (35)
All people, from the highest heaven down to the netherworld, are subject to time.
For every living being that is born, death is indeed certain.
You, I, and even the Creator must inevitably go [to our end].
Your son was a high-souled one named Śrīman, a treasure-house of glory.
Having performed great and complete penance, he attained the supreme goal.
Thus, for the sake of one who is liberated, you ought not to grieve at all.
Thus addressed, Nimi, bowing his head at the feet of the sage, spoke to Nārada with shame, sighing and terrified like one in distress:
"O Brahmin, I have been consoled by you; however, listen as I speak. (39)

Once gone, he has indeed departed and does not return once gone. (40) That which I have done after fashioning a corpse behind me was never heard of before by me, nor was it ever done by the gods or my ancestors. (41)
Under the very influence of grief, he performed for the sake of the corpse:
having gratified seven twice-born men with food, rice, and even fruits;
and afterwards, having spread darbha grass upon the ground, he offered the funeral ball (piṇḍa) and dismissed them.
"Indeed, the fetching of water was performed with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (aprasavya).
All this has been done anew; for that reason, I am truly afraid.
Having heard that, Nārada said: "O King, you must not fear!"
"I see no unrighteousness here; go to your father for refuge.
Thus addressed, Nimi reflected and went to his father for refuge.
At that moment, the illustrious son Tapodhana arrived.
He said: "O Nimi, this ancestral sacrifice (pitṛyajña) has been devised and performed by you.
Indeed, the dharma consisting of the ancestral sacrifice was ordained by Brahmā;
and that very dharma, which is essentially ritual action, has been revealed by you under my name."
The dharma of the śrāddha, the sacrifice to the ancestors, has been established by you.
This ancient dharma of the śrāddha is the dharma of the successive creations;
it was previously created by the Self-born One as the very rite whose essence is the śrāddha.
The funeral rites and the dharma of *śrāddha* must be performed by people in every way. (49) For one who has been born, after death there is inevitably an abiding somewhere;
for the sake of attaining that state, an offering here must be made with faith. (50)
For one who has not attained liberation, there may be satisfaction, but in liberation, satisfaction is eternal.
Liberation is certainly achieved through specific ritual actions and through expiation;
for even those of long life attain it, how much more so those of short life?
In the future, at the end of the age, people will become short-lived;
they will be predominantly characterized by the qualities of darkness (tamas) and passion (rajas).
For them, however, the ancestral rite (śrāddha) shall become the means of securing a favorable rebirth in an evil state.
One should know that hell and the demonic animal realm are born of *tamas*.
Cruelty, fear, despondency, violence, shamelessness, ignorance,
and the state of a *piśāca*— these are the qualities inherent to the nature of those characterized by *tamas*.

One should know him to be *tāmasa* who, even when being spoken to, does not understand. The *rājasa* person is arrogant, lacks faith, is intent on harming others, is forceful in speech, and always holds himself and his own people in high regard.
The hero, the one manifest in all things, and the one whose desire for sense objects is not fulfilled—for the sake of the satisfaction of these in the next world, the *śrāddha* is requested.
The *sāttvika* person shall partake of liberation; he is patient, self-controlled, and pure of heart.
One who is full of faith, endowed with austerity, and possessed of self-study and other virtues— (58)—
if even such a person possesses the desire for sons, the desire for worldly objects,
as well as the desire for wealth, the desire for a wife, or the desire for sensual pleasures; (59)
By that very current, he may go to the state of a preta in another life;
for his satisfaction, the Creator previously devised and you have now expanded the ritual acts of śrāddha, giving, and fire-offerings.
Reflecting thus, you ought not to grieve.
Abandon your grief, O man of great wisdom! Grief is the destroyer of all.
Grief burns the limbs; through grief, the intellect perishes.
Modesty, fortitude, righteousness, prosperity, fame, memory, and statesmanship— all these virtues,
as well as all religious duties, abandon a man who is overwhelmed by grief.
Therefore, O King, casting off this sorrow, become free from grief!
The deluded person, through the power of attachment, enters the bondage of saṃsāra.
Therefore, having thoroughly restrained attachment, one should apply the intellect to dharma;
dharma is for the sake of the welfare of the world, consisting of faith, charity, and worship.

Hospitality (*satkāra*) and sacrifice (*havana*)—these five are generally considered [the forms of] *śrāddha*, which grants satisfaction to the deceased; while giving (*dāna*) brings happiness to the living. Worship of an image is auspicious, and hospitality brings happiness to sentient beings.
Even one who merely offers a sacrifice for those departed to heaven shall partake in the fruit.
If there should be a wish at the time of death, it must especially be fulfilled;
for the satisfaction of one who is dying bestows a favorable rebirth in the next world.
When the life-force has reached the throat, one should quickly have the person removed from the house.
Having placed him upon a bed spread with *kuśa* grass, one should address him with affection.
One should place gold in his mouth, offer water, and administer the vows and other rites.
One should bestow merit and one should give a cow that brings benefit to the next world.
By the gift of milch cows, one is quickly liberated from sin.
One should whisper the name of Hari—the means to liberation—into its ear.
One should offer the *madhuparka*—honey, clarified butter, and curd—to his lips.
When the vital breath (*prāṇa*) has thus departed, he does not enter into further worldly existence (*saṃsāra*).
Then, having performed the purification of the body with fragrant substances such as ghee and the like, [one should proceed].
Having placed the head toward the south, one should perform the ritual bath at the sacred ford (tīrtha).
Having constructed a funeral pyre according to the rules using the wood of the most excellent trees,
and having positioned [the body] with the head to the south, one should place the fire in the hand.
Then, having said, "Burn his limbs," and having performed a circumambulation,
one should cause the ashes to be offered at the location of the head after the reduction to ash has occurred.
Then, having washed the limbs and the two garments, one should depart.
Then, intending it for the deceased, one should offer a funeral ball (*piṇḍa*) upon the ground.
On the third day after the life has departed, one should perform a bath in river water;
one should offer a funeral ball with *cūrṇa* and should offer three handfuls of water.
On the fourth, fifth, and sixth days, one should offer a single morsel of food and a handful of water;
likewise on the seventh, eighth, ninth, and tenth.
On the tenth day, there is the complete purification of the clothing and the purification of the body in every respect.
Then, the kinsmen born of the same lineage (gotrajas) should perform the offering of rice-balls (piṇḍadāna) using sesame and myrobalan oil.
Having completed the offering of the rice-balls, one should have the rite of shaving (kṣaurakarma) performed.
Then, on the eleventh day, having bathed together with the kinsmen, [the rites should be concluded].
Having bathed, one should join the deceased with the Brahmins, or cause it to be done so; one should feed a single Brahmin with excellent food for the sake of the Ekoddiṣṭa rite.
Having bathed again, one should then join that deceased person with the ancestors.
The *ekoddiṣṭa* rite for the three [higher] castes should be performed with cooked food;
however, for the fourth caste, uncooked substances should be collected.
On the thirteenth day, one should feed virtuous Brahmins with cooked foods.
Becoming like the wind in spirit, take refuge with virtuous Brahmins; service rendered to Brahmins and the virtuous shall bring happiness to the deceased.
Indeed, the body for the enjoyment of the departed is fashioned from the presence of Brahmins.
When the night has turned to dawn and the sun has risen, the barbering of the Brahmin must be performed according to the prescribed rule;
likewise, the bathing and anointing that grant satisfaction to the deceased should be carried out. (85–86)
One should prepare a sacrificial mound on the ground and perform the rites for the deceased.
One should choose a place that neither a cock, a dog, nor a pig can see;
a dog drives [the spirits] away with its barking, while a pig does so with its snorting.
A cock [is defiling] by the wind of its wings, and a Cāṇḍāla by sight.
Whatever śrāddha one performs there brings bondage to the ancestors.
One should offer the portion for the deceased on a bare ground; that is the rite of the forenoon.
And one should perform the formal dedication of the rice-balls (piṇḍa-saṃkalpa), pronouncing the name and the lineage (gotra).
Thereafter, those born of the family and belonging to the lineage eat together as a single meal.
Thus, by what has been given, the people who have gone to the world of the departed (pretaloka) are gratified.
One should give an umbrella that wards off fire, ashes, showers of stones, and the like;
and one should give sandals that prevent thorns and other obstacles on the path.
One should also offer incense, a lamp, garments, and ornaments.
One should indeed offer fruits that are well-ripened for the enjoyment of the preta;
having thus completed everything, one should feed a twice-born with cooked food.
First, the brahmin there should designate a portion for the preta.
Then, having performed the purification of the hands, the Brahmin should indeed eat the sweet food.
Together with kinsmen, relatives, and friends, the portion for the deceased (pretabhāga) should be given to the Brahmin again and again; it must not be withheld by anyone.
When an obstruction is made there, the ancestors certainly do not receive [the offerings];
thus the Dharma is subverted, and the deceased finds no satisfaction therein.
When the Brahmin is satisfied, cool and auspicious water should be offered.
Indeed, the remains of the food should be given to the fish in the river and other such places.
One should also give a bed, a seat, as well as collyrium and a bracelet.
Then, having arrived at the place of the funeral offering (nivāpa), one should offer water with sesame seeds.
Having lifted up the tail of a cow, one should place it in the hand of a Brāhmaṇa;
having prepared water with black sesame seeds in a vessel made of udumbara wood,
one should then offer that water consecrated by mantras, after sprinkling [the recipient] with water.
One should dismiss the deceased from the Brahmin and give gifts to the twice-born.
One should set aside a portion for the deceased for beings such as ants;
by giving to the poor, the helpless, and those devoted to him, the deceased becomes satisfied.

"O Nimi, this purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*), which consists of the *śrāddha* ceremony and which cleanses one of all states of existence as a *preta*, must indeed be performed; yet it has been performed by you.
This ritual procedure for the *śrāddha* act is proclaimed to be a singular sacrifice."
"From this point forward, the ancestral sacrifice (pitṛyajña) shall take place in the worlds.
O Nimi, you shall become the performer of the sacrifice and go to the world of Brahmā.
Thus, the portion for the deceased must be offered by all on the third day. (103–104)
In the seventh, ninth, and likewise the eleventh month,
one should then perform the annual rite for the liberation of the deceased.
When the full year has passed and the funeral rites have been completed, [one should perform the Śrāddha].
Some living beings attain liberation, while others wander in the sky.
The grandfather, daughters-in-law, wives, kinsmen, relatives, and friends—all these many things that exist here are like a dream. (106–107)
Having wept for a moment, they all indeed turn their faces away;
bound by the snare of affection, they are released in another instant.
Whose mother? Whose father? Whose wife or children?
Day after day, those bound by the snares of delusion continue to revolve.
(1.09) Thousands of mothers and fathers, and hundreds of sons and wives, are experienced throughout the cycles of existence; to whom do they belong, or to whom do we belong? (1.355.110)
The procedure for the sacramental rites of the deceased was proclaimed by Svayambhū.
This sacrament for the dead must indeed be performed out of affection.
Once the rites for the deceased have been concluded, the status of being an ancestor (pitṛtva) arises.
Indeed, the libation to the ancestors must be performed every month on the new moon day.
The father, the grandfather, and likewise the great-grandfather,
are satisfied by the oblation offered into the mouth of a Brahmin and by the offering of excellent food.
Having spoken thus, Nārada, the best of sages, departed for heaven.
In this manner, in a former age, King Nimi performed the Śrāddha.
From that time onwards, the Brahmins have performed the Śrāddha and offered the Piṇḍas.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have related to you the account beginning with the origin of the *śrāddha* and the *piṇḍa*.

Thus ends the three hundred and fifty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Performance of the Śrāddha Rite," in the first section on the Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga within the *Māthura-kṣetra-māhātmya* of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. In this chapter, it is described how King Nimi performed a *śrāddha* for his deceased son named Śrīmān; subsequently, when Nimi realized that his fabricated ritual was not established as a valid tradition and fell into grief, Nārada instructed him that the *śrāddha* is an ancient dharma and explained the sequence of the *śrāddha* performance.
← Chapter 355: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga) Chapter 356 [Author: Chapter 357 →
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O Keśava, by your grace I have heard about the *śrāddha* intended for the feeding of the deceased.
But surely, it is the Brahmins who receive the gift of food as the portion of the deceased? (1)

O Supreme Person, by what action is a Brahmin released after having eaten food that is undesirable, censurable, and [eaten] through the possession of a *preta*? How might he, who is himself blameworthy, deliver his donor?
"Thus, O Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, sever my doubt!
(3) Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: "O Lakṣmī, you have asked well; I shall destroy your doubt."
But that brahmin who is an ascetic and a great devotee of the Lord (mahābhāgavata),
who is a great yogi and a man of great knowledge, adorned with perfections and sovereign powers;
and he who is rich in great austerity and proficient in the Vedas and the scriptures— (5)
He who possesses meditation, mental retention, and concentration;
who knows the three periods of time and is adorned with the excellent garland of restraints, observances, and other virtues;
who is constantly devoted to the six duties and intent upon the worship of Hari.
By the touch of the dust from whose feet a deity is born as a god in heaven;
he who is of virtuous character and ever pure shall be a purifier like fire. Having indeed eaten the food of the *preta*s and having accepted gifts as well, [he attains this]. (7–8)

Having performed the rites for the deceased, one who knows the distinction between the individual soul (*puruṣa*) and primordial nature (*prakṛti*), and who is devoted to the identity of Brahman and the Self, is not tainted by that fault;
being capable of washing away sin, he is not stained by its defect.
The darkness created by night never obscures the sun anywhere.
Darkness attains the state of light in the presence of the sun’s rays.
In the same way, through such a means, the state of a ghost may become that of a deity.
Through the yoga of Brahman, the state of a preta is transformed into divinity;
even sin becomes most meritorious, and for one who is capable, there is no fault.
But he who is neither rich in self-strength nor devoted to Brahman—

Neither nourished by the vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), nor engaged in the six duties and other yogic practices, neither a knower of the Self nor a knower of discrimination— that Brahmin is indeed defiled by sins. By eating for the dead, he becomes a ghost himself, born impure from his consumption.
For the sake of purifying his own body, he should observe one fast;
having performed the morning twilight ritual and having offered libations to the sacred fire,
the twice-born man should perform an oblation of sesame seeds while reciting the peace-mantras.

Having gone to a river flowing eastward and bathed, one should drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) mixed with honey and curd-offering (madhuparka). Then, having swept the house, one should sprinkle it with water;
having offered libations to the gods beginning with Agni, one should present the bali-offering to the spirits.
One should give food to the Brahmins and perform the gift of a cow;
the Brahmin who acts in this way certainly becomes purified.
When death occurs after such an act has been performed, he attains the supreme goal.
Otherwise, when he has passed away according to the law of time, if [the food] goes into the belly of a *preta*,
he himself would become a *preta* or would obtain residence in hell;
he would attain the state of a *rākṣasa* and only then be released from that sin.
The expiation (prāyaścitta) should be performed mentally, bringing happiness to both the giver and the receiver;
it consists of cows, elephants, horses, wealth, jewels, fields, female slaves, and ornaments.
He who accepts [these] with the appropriate mantra should perform the expiation.
He shall also purify and deliver the donor; of this there is no doubt.
At rites for the gods, at one's birth-star, at the time of a śrāddha, on the major lunar festivals, and in all funeral rites, [one should employ] a Brahmin who is devoted to the six duties.
One who has completed the ritual bath after studying the Vedas and their branches, who is most righteous and ascetic,
endowed with virtues such as good conduct, contentment, and truthfulness, possessed of forgiveness,
committed to the restraints of non-violence and the like, and whose supreme refuge is the Blessed Lord.
Having obtained such a worthy recipient, one should indeed perform the śrāddha, give gifts, and offer worship.
He, being purified, shall deliver all [ancestors] and deliver himself as well;
for a stone can never deliver another stone anywhere without a savior.
For one who is impure and burdened by sin cannot save others anywhere; indeed, only one who is pure can save others. Therefore, one should employ [one's wealth] upon a worthy recipient.
Listen, Lakṣmī! Formerly there was a great king named Medhātithi.
In Avanti, however, there was Candraśarman, his family priest.
The king, having given a gift of a hundred cows, ate every day.
Then the day for the ancestral rites (śrāddha) of the king’s father arrived during the month of Vaiśākha.
Having bowed to the invited brahmins and performed the śrāddha according to the prescribed rules,
and having offered the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) at the śrāddha, he gave abundant prepared food.
Likewise, he bestowed gifts of garments and ornaments upon the brahmins.

In their midst was a certain Brāhmaṇa who was weak and exceedingly sinful; born of adultery and mixed with the seed of a Śūdra, he took the food of the Śrāddha there. Because of that fault, [the king] of the earth—
The ancestors, fallen from heaven and cast down into a thorny forest,
are constantly tormented by hunger and thirst, and they indeed cry out again and again.
By a stroke of fate, Medhātithi went into the forest for the purpose of wandering.
He asked those who were wandering about, "Who are you, so deeply distressed?
Then his fathers said to him, "In our lineage there was indeed a king named Medhātithi; we are his ancestors, dwelling here in the forest."

"O King, we have fallen from heaven, cast down by the fault of performing a *śrāddha* ceremony. That *śrāddha* food was requested by that most sinful wretch of a Brahmin—a mere nominal twice-born whose conduct had lapsed and who was born of illicit union. (36)
Due to that very fault of their actions, they desire to go to hell;
having experienced great suffering there, we shall return again to heaven. But by giving cows to Brahmins, through that merit, we shall once more go to heaven.
"We shall go, but there is no food there that will provide satisfaction.
Having heard this, the king said: "I am indeed Medhātithi.
Tell me, what further task must be done for the sake of your liberation?"
The ancestors said to him, "In such a way that we may indeed be satisfied,
the śrāddha must be performed again, and the best of the twice-born should be fed.
Having heard those words of theirs, Medhātithi went home.
He summoned virtuous brahmins who had exerted themselves in the study of the Vedas—
men of merit devoted to dharma, patient, of good character, and great ascetics;
men endowed with self-restraint and observances, truly devoted to the Blessed Lord.
Then the king performed the ancestral rites (śrāddha), offering funeral cakes (piṇḍas) in every way;
he fed the Brahmins after honoring them with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās). Having bowed and dismissed them, the king then partook of his meal.
Then, having gone to the forest himself, he saw his own ancestors—
joyful, nourished, endowed with strength, and prepared to ascend to heaven.
Upon seeing them, the king rejoiced greatly, and the ancestors spoke to the monarch:
"May it be well with you; O King, we shall depart for the heavenly realm.
Never, under any circumstances, should this be given to an unworthy recipient or to a great sinner, for whatever is offered there—whether to the gods or the ancestors—is entirely fruitless."
If a worthy recipient for offerings to the gods or ancestors cannot be found among Brāhmaṇas,
that prepared food should be given to cows according to the prescribed rule.
In the absence of cows, one should diligently cast the food into a river.
"It must not be given to one who is unworthy, nor to an atheist, nor to one who betrays his guru;
it must not be given to a golaka, nor to a kuṇḍa, nor to one born of mixed castes.
Having spoken thus, all the ancestors departed for heaven in celestial chariots.
Having understood the strength and weakness of the recipient, Medhātithi returned home;
therefore, O Lakṣmī, devoted to Dharma, even a single most excellent Brāhmaṇa saves one from the difficult states of the sense-objects—of this there is no doubt. (5.1)
Therefore, at a śrāddha ceremony, virtuous brāhmaṇas who are devotees of the Lord should be fed—
those whose wealth consists of their sacrificial vessels and penance— either month by month or during the fortnight of the ancestors (pitṛpakṣa).
[They are the recipients for] the gods, asuras, humans, gandharvas, serpents, and rākṣasas.
Those people who are intent on the awakening of Brahman should indeed be fed with *tāraka* [the saving mantra];
likewise, virtuous and truthful women devoted to celibacy (*brahmacarya*) should be fed.
Thus it has been told to you, O Lakṣmī! Such a worthy recipient (*satpātra*) delivers one's ancestors.
One should indeed cause such an unworthy recipient to fall [from his status], and thereafter perform an expiation (*prāyaścitta*).
Having heard that, Śrī Lakṣmī said to Hari Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa:
"Embodied beings go to another womb due to their own actions. || 55-56 ||
"How is it that beasts, birds, humans, and others have come here to eat?
O Kṛṣṇa, who are these ancestors who have arrived to partake of the śrāddha?
Some who are dead have fallen under the power of Yama’s noose in hell."
Some among the host of gods have indeed fallen under the control of their householders;
others, by the power of karma, are in this world subject to the eighty-four thousand classes of birth,
embodied beings who have fallen there into perpetual bondage.
"O Lord, they are capable of performing the śrāddha, yet they do not come; how then can they partake of the śrāddha? Please dispel this contradictory doubt of mine.
How is the ancestral lineage protected by the performance of the śrāddha?"
"Whatever must be done in each age and in the interval between ages by which [the world] is protected"—
having heard these words of Mahālakṣmī, the Supreme Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa spoke to Lakṣmī, wiping away her doubt.
Listen, Lakṣmī! In the ancestral sacrifices (pitṛyajña), there are always three who partake as lords:
the father, the grandfather, and likewise the great-grandfather.
These three indeed become the divine recipients of the śrāddha offerings.
The father, whose deity is Brahmā, was fashioned from the limb of Vedha;
the grandfather, whose deity is Viṣṇu, was fashioned from the limb of Viṣṇu;
and the great-grandfather, whose lord is Rudra, was fashioned from the limb of Rudra. (64–65)
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara have been appointed here for the śrāddha ceremony.
First, one should offer the śrāddha with the piṇḍas to the portion of Brahmā;
second, one should offer the śrāddha with the piṇḍas to the portion of Viṣṇu.
One should offer the third śrāddha, together with the piṇḍas, to the portion of Rudra;
[the first] to the father, then to the grandfather, and to the great-grandfather—
for the all-pervading Lord Nārāyaṇa himself has assumed the form of these three deities.
Wherever they have died and attained birth,
Kṛṣṇa, existing as the all-pervading Inner Controller (antaryāmī), remains there and brings them satisfaction as well. Thus, that Kṛṣṇa exists as the Inner Controller within the virtuous brāhmaṇas.

At the time of the *śrāddha*, the Lord assumes the form of that for whom the offering is intended. Having received the *śrāddha* and the funeral rice-ball (*piṇḍa*), Hari, Kṛṣṇārāyaṇa, causes it to reach the deceased wherever he may have gone.
"Know this, O Mahālakṣmī! In this *śrāddha*, I myself appear in the form of the ancestors and others, bestowing the intended fruit upon those who have entered other wombs.
Now hear another thing, O Lakṣmī; I shall explain it to you in detail."
Some indeed perform the *brahmayajña* (sacrifice to Brahman) in the form [of the deity] or in the mouths of the virtuous;
some indeed perform the *devayajña* (sacrifice to the gods) in the sacrificial pit or in the fire; some indeed perform the *bhūtayajña* (sacrifice to beings) in the animal or in the mouths of cows.
Some perform sacrifices to men in the human form, O twice-born one;
some indeed sacrifice to the ancestors in water, fire, or on earth, O twice-born one.
All of them abide in me; I tell you this as the truth.
Furthermore, in every kind of sacrifice, fire is the primary mouth;
through the mouth of fire, the spirits of the deceased, the ancestors, the seers, and the deities eat.
And I, the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa, indeed eat through the mouth of fire.
I am the fire situated in the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), and likewise I am the southern fire (dakṣiṇāgni).
I am the āhavanīya fire, the purifier and the purifying one.
Indeed, I am the Vaiśvadeva fire, and I am also the gārhapatya fire.
I am Bārhaspatya, and I alone am Āvasathya;
with them as my mouth, I, whose self consists of the three gods, eat in all sacrifices.
In the sacrifice to the ancestors, I, whose self consists of those three, eat through the mouth of Brahmā.

At a śrāddha ceremony, one should feed a twice-born brāhmaṇa who is learned in the Vedas, virtuous in conduct, a great devotee of the Lord, self-controlled, and contented. First, having offered [the oblation] to the sacrificial fire, which is the very embodiment of the deity of the sacred ford.
Afterwards, one should offer [the food] into the mouth of the Brahmin for the father and the grandfather;
indeed, one should also offer it for the great-grandfather, recollecting them again and again.
One should feed the Brahmin in secret and there invoke the ancestors.
Three balls of rice, accompanied by condiments, should be offered.
With the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya), water mixed with sesame seeds should be offered month after month.
I, the Supreme Self residing within the body, carry forth the offerings for the deities.
Thus, by what is given, the ancestors are gratified; of this there is no doubt.
The three gods and likewise the three ancestors have issued from Hari;
they shall become the ancestral deities and the enjoyers in age after age.

When a Brahmin has been fed and is satisfied, his ancestors bestow upon that giver of the funeral cake (piṇḍa) long life, fame, strength, splendor, wealth, sons, cattle, women, and health; [and] those in the animal, hellish, and human realms [are likewise satisfied]. 87.
Wherever they may be situated, others who are gratified by the *śrāddha* offerings find satisfaction;
being satisfied, they go to the supreme heaven by the pure path of *sattva*.
I shall speak further; listen to the truth of it, O beautiful one. (88–89)
Enveloped by the darkness of ignorance, sinful, fallen, and deceased people,
bound by hundreds of cords of affection, are cooked in the impure hell. Their sons, grandsons, and even those born in their lineage— [are likewise affected].
Upon reaching a reservoir of water in the afterlife, they release drops of water;
by that alone is there satisfaction for those going to hell. Likewise, libations, funeral rites, rice-balls, and water with sesame seeds [are offered]. (91–92)
A twice-born man, through a spirit of devotion, should deliver his ancestors by offering [a bull];
indeed, a dark-blue bull should be given, for it destroys the agony of hell.
Even if one merely raises water at the tail of a dark-blue bull, [the ancestors are liberated].
By him, the ancestors were gratified for sixty thousand years.
If a lump of mud were indeed lifted from the mire by his horn,
then by that act the ancestors were uplifted and led to the world of Soma.
For sixty thousand years and sixty hundred years, they rejoice in the worlds of Soma, entirely free from hunger and thirst.
Thus is this dharma of the householder performed by sons, grandsons, and their descendants.

Consisting of the *śrāddha* rite, it was created for the sake of uplifting those possessed by craving. (97) Insects and other creatures, moving beings and birds, as well as stationary things—all these depend upon householders; of this there is no doubt. (98)
Those who perform the ancestral rite (śrāddha) month after month while in the householder stage of life, on the proper lunar day,
during a festival, and under an auspicious constellation, deliver their ancestors. Indeed,
those ancestors have departed and entered the bodies of Brahmā and Viṣṇu.
The father, the grandfather, and likewise the great-grandfather—
in this sequence they subsequently became the Kāśyapa deities;
thus they were indeed appointed for the Śrāddha rites.
At that time, what was given solely into the mouth of the Brahmin during the ancestral sacrifice (pitṛyajña) resulted in indigestion for the ancestors; afflicted by indigestion,
they went together with Soma and bowed down to the Grandfather (Brahmā).

"Afflicted by indigestion, we beg you, O elephant, to act in such a way that our indigestion may be destroyed and the ancestors may find happiness. Then Brahmā said: "There is a noble son of Śāṇḍilya."
Dhūmraketu is the radiant Vibhāvasu who brings about decay;
at a *śrāddha*, his portion should first be offered among human beings.
Together with him, one should consume that which has been released as the *piṇḍa* for the ancestors.
At that time, the fire-god Agni— the carrier of oblations, the consumer of all, and the devourer of offerings—
was remembered by Brahmā and appointed to the five sacrifices and all ritual acts.
"O Fire, you must first consume that which is offered as a funeral pinda for the ancestors."
The deities and these ancestors shall eat through you;
the second *śrāddha* meal is to be eaten together with the fire-gods and the ancestors,
while the third, the offering of the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*), is for Soma, the ancestors, and the fire-god.
"Indeed, one should eat only after gathering together, so that there will be no indigestion.
Having been told this, they always eat together at the ancestral sacrifice (pitṛyajña).
Agni is the father, the grandfather, and the great-grandfather.
The ancestors, the gods, and the sacrificial fires indeed consume [the offerings] along with Soma.
At that time, those Brahmins who are unworthy of the row (apāṅkteya) must never be fed.
I shall now declare those who are unworthy of the row, who have fallen to a state of degradation through their actions.
Eunuchs, painters, cattle-herders, and revilers;
likewise, those who steal gold, the one-eyed, those afflicted with leprosy, and atheists;
as well as dancers, singers, and those who live by acting. (112–113)
Also those who sell the Vedas, those who perform sacrifices for all sorts of people, those who live by the labor of servants, royal functionaries, as well as those who deal in leather;
those devoid of sacramental rites, the fallen, and those who subsist on the work of Śūdras.
Astrologers, village priests, scribes, and likewise hypocrites;

those who perform all manner of menial tasks, the fallen, and those who indulge in liquor, meat, and sexual misconduct—whatever others are defiled, they are indeed Rākṣasas in the form of twice-born Brahmins. (115–116)
Seeing them eating, the ancestors would suffer;
therefore, one should quickly perform an expiation and perform the śrāddha rite again.
One should offer clarified butter into the fire and gaze upon the sun.

Having performed the *punarāvapana* (re-sowing) for his father and grandfathers, he should offer perfume, incense, a lamp, the water-offering (*arghya*), and sesame-water. He should also feed a Brahmin; by this, the ancestors are satisfied. (118–119)
To that Brahmin who always remains pure and does not eat the food of the deceased,
a gift should be given during the Vaiśvadeva rites: rice, wheat,
ghee, and so forth, as well as sugar and vegetables.
One should not employ milk, curd, or clothing in Śrāddha rites. (121) A penance is prescribed for those who eat the food of the deceased (preta).
On the twelfth day of the month of Māgha, however, [one should offer] excellent milk-porridge mixed with ghee. (122)
Then, for the sake of purifying the body, one should smear [the image] with honey;
likewise, for one's own purification, one should donate a tawny cow along with its calf.
One should bathe at a sacred ford and likewise recite the Gāyatrī mantra a thousand times.
Alternatively, one who desires the purification of the body and the self should perform the *śrāddha*.
Having bathed and smeared the ground, he should address the most excellent Brāhmaṇa:
"O Mahālakṣmī! On the new moon day (*amā*), one should not chew a tooth-stick."

If Soma, the deities, or the ancestors should be offended by that brahmin at dawn, he must perform the cutting of his beard and nails, as well as bathing, anointing with oil, and [partaking of] cooked food. 126.
When midday has arrived, one should offer water for the feet (pādya) to the Brahmin.
One should lead him into the interior of the house, provide a seat, and offer the excellent water of honor (arghya).
Having worshipped with perfumes, garlands, incense, and lamps, [one should offer] water and sesame seeds.
Having given the vessel, one should place it auspiciously before the Brahmin for the purpose of eating.
One should draw a mandala with ashes to ward off the defects of the row.
Having offered oblations into the fire, one should serve sweet food to the Brahmin.
One should say to the twice-born, "Eat as much as you please.
Having satisfied the Brāhmaṇa, one should then offer the scattered food (vikira).
After providing an upper garment and a seat, one should cause the inquiry regarding the rice-balls (piṇḍa) to be made.
Facing the south, having spread darbha grass upon the ground,
one should perform the offering of rice balls (piṇḍas) for the triad beginning with the father; likewise,
one should perform the worship of the rice balls according to the prescribed rule for the increase of the lineage.

The self-possessed man should place [the offerings] into the hand of the Brāhmaṇa so that they become inexhaustible. Having satisfied them with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), he should cause them to pronounce a blessing and then dismiss them. As for the three funeral cakes (piṇḍas), they should remain right there upon the ground.
The ancestors remain in the house for that long while being nourished.
Having sipped water and become pure, one should then offer the waters of peace (śāntyudaka).
Then, having bowed to the Vaiṣṇavī earth, the inexhaustible Kāśyapī.
One should eat the first ball; the middle one should be given to the wife.
One should cast the third into the water and dismiss the ancestral deities. One should bow down according to this rite; thus the ancestral deities are satisfied. (136–137)
They bestow long life, as well as sons, grandsons, and wealth.
Listen, Lakṣmī! One should offer the *madhuparka* at the time of the departure of the vital breaths.
Indeed, the *madhuparka* is a person who has emerged from my right limb. 138.
By me he has been joined to all duties for the sake of liberation from worldly existence. (139) Where there is the *madhuparka* offering, or for whomever it exists, there is liberation;
where the *madhuparka* does not exist, there liberation is not found. (1.356.140)

One should likewise prepare honey, curd, and ghee; thus, one should give this triad in equal measure to a Brahmin for the sake of merit and for the liberation of the deceased. At the conclusion of the rites such as the Śrāddha, one should cause the recitation of peace-mantras (śāntipāṭha) to be performed.
Salutations to You, the Lord of Rādhā, the Lord of Ramā, and the Lord of Lakṣmī.
Salutations to the Lord of Māṇikī, the Sovereign of Pārvatī, the All-pervading One.
Salutations to You, the Lord of Prabhā, the beginningless Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
Look toward the quarters, look below, and protect yourself constantly from diseases.
Be gracious toward your own kingdom, the king, and all his forces;
likewise, [be gracious] toward pregnant women, the elderly, the rice crops, and the cattle.
Bring peace to the Brahmins and the virtuous; bring about auspiciousness. (141) Provide food, grant good rain, and bestow abundance and fearlessness.
O All-pervading Lord! May the kingdom flourish, and may there be peace forever. (146)
May there be perpetual peace for the gods, for human beings, for devotees, for maidens, for animals, and for all living beings.
(147) Having thus recited this prayer for peace, one should offer the *madhuparka*.
One should place ghee, honey, and curd into an udumbara vessel of equal capacity.
O Mahālakṣmī! In the absence of honey, one should mix it with jaggery;
in the absence of ghee, one should mix it with parched rice. 148–149.
If curd is unavailable, one should mix it with milk;
or one may prepare equal parts of curd, honey, and ghee.
"O Lord of Gods, Kṛṣṇa! I offer unto You clarified butter, ghee, and honey."
But if none of these are available, one should offer water into the mouth.
Indeed, for one who is about to give up his life-breaths, one should offer the honey-mixture (madhuparka) into the mouth;
this is pure, stainless, and the fulfiller of all desires.
He who hears this supreme narrative concerning the madhuparka offering and other rites attains the highest divine liberation by virtue of my grace.
Whether at a royal court, in a cremation ground, or likewise in times of fear or calamity, [he shall be protected].
Those who recite this peace-mantra (śānti) will quickly attain their own desired goal.
A sonless man obtains a son, and one without a wife obtains a beloved. A woman without a husband obtains a husband, and one who is bound becomes free from bondage. (154–155)
"By merely remembering this, one shall also partake in the fruits of śrāddha and other rites.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have told you the supreme inner meaning of śrāddha and the like. (156)

Thus, in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā, concerning the majesty of the Mathurā Tīrtha: the purification of one who has eaten at a Śrāddha through expiation; the downfall of the ancestors of King Medhātithi of the city of Avantī due to feeding unworthy Brahmins at a Śrāddha, and their return to heaven by performing the Śrāddha for worthy recipients; and how the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather were born from the bodies of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa, as well as Soma, the Pitṛs, and Hutāśana, in the form of a virtuous Brahmin.

Chapter Three Hundred and Fifty-Six: The Description of Feasting Together, the Gift of a Blue Bull, the Offering of Madhuparka, the Recitation of Peace Hymns, and so forth. [The Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā – Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga)] Chapter 357.
[The Author: Chapter 358.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī! On the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika, Yamarāja—
On the second day, the elder brother was fed and honored by the daughter of the Sun;
and Yama, being pleased, spoke to Yamī regarding the granting of a boon:
"Whether in the water of your holy site, or on its banks, or upon the ground, for all embodied beings..."
"O sister! Whether they be sinful or meritorious, even those belonging to the four modes of birth who have attained yoga do not deserve to be punished by me.
Then Yamunā said to her elder brother: "If you have compassion for them..."
Today, deliver them entirely from dwelling in the city of Yama.
Likewise, [I shall give] the great fruit of bathing, the fruit of drinking water, and also the merit of giving a multitude of *tulasī* leaves. (4–5)

"I shall indeed give [freedom] to those in hell; release them from their bonds. Having accepted his sister's words and saying, "So be it," Yama granted all the inhabitants of hell the merit bestowed by Yamī.
He sent her indeed to heaven, having emptied the realm of Yama.
Then, as time passed again, she was filled with sinners;
she was established on the far shore beyond the Lokāloka mountain, in dense darkness.
Indeed, that court of justice was established by Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa for the purpose of bestowing the fruits of auspicious and inauspicious actions upon living beings;
there, the Lord of Yama administers justice according to the law for both the sinful and the meritorious. (9)
The King of Dharma himself, whether cruel or gentle, bestows the fruit [of one's actions].
(1.357.10) All living beings who have died—whether they be sinful or meritorious, performers of deeds—having gone there, proceed either to that world or to another. (11)

Those with much evil and those with little evil go to the abode of Yama according to their karma; having experienced the fruit of their actions in the hells, they indeed proceed to further existence. The hellish regions are indeed innumerable and are based on mental states.
Indeed, they were created by the King of Dharma (Yama) in that place;
according to one's karma, he bestows that punishment upon him.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
Blessed One, I wish to hear about the ground where the fruits of the ripening of karma occur.
What is it like? What is its extent? What is its form? By whom is it seen?
What kind of fruit from the ripening of karma is experienced by human beings? (14–15)
"Tell me all of this, which is for the benefit of people: how may a person never go to the abode of the King of the Dead?
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī! To this most beautiful story of ancient times, which is purifying of all sins and brings about auspiciousness when undertaken.
During the churning of the ocean, Alakṣmī was produced by the gods and others.

In accordance with dharma, she was given as a beloved wife to the sage Uddālaka. From her was born a son named Naciketas, who was born of his father's mind (mānasa), a knower of the truth of the Vedāṅgas,
and one who always abided by his father’s command.
In the forest, he possessed a wealth of cattle numbering ten thousand;
therefore, every morning at dawn, the great sage Naciketa,
having performed his ritual, would indeed give away a hundred as a gift.
In that regard, at one time he gave cows to a brahmin.

They were ones whose enjoyment was finished, who had reached their final state, whose teeth were broken, and who were subject to old age; they had consumed their grass, their milk was dried up, and the signs of pregnancy had vanished. (21–22)
To his father, who was about to give away such cows,
the son Naciketas, moved by compassion, said: "Father,
cows are in every way fit for giving only when they are capable of yielding milk."
"Such [cows] as these—worn out and possessed of diminished fertility—do not exist [in our house].
Having heard this, the father said: "Only old cows remain;
there are no young ones now in our house that have been given away in charity. (24–25)
Having heard this, his son indeed ceased speaking;
then, on another day, a certain brahmin mendicant arrived seeking the sake of a cow.
He begged for the gift of a cow, and Naciketas likewise offered him his wealth of cattle.
He gave to the twice-born the remainder that was very old.
Then the son Nāciketa said repeatedly to his father:
"O Father, cows that have never been milked must not be given away. (27–28)
Those cows were merely a burden, with nothing remaining but death.
Then his father, becoming somewhat distracted in mind, said to his son:
"What then shall I give you here? I give you this place where the cows stand."
Having heard this, the son spoke again, "Give me [your hand]," O father.
Then the father, out of anger, spoke these terrifying words to his son:
"O son, since you repeatedly and so quickly obstruct me!"
"You say, 'Give me [yourself],' and you have been given to Death by me.
As soon as the father had spoken these words, Death arrived there.
"So be it," the son replied with "Oṃ," and in an instant he vanished.
"Let not my father's word prove false; I shall go to the abode of Yama.
Having heard his son’s words, the father, with a distressed mind, said:
"You are my only child, dear one; indeed, no other kinsman exists."
"O son, you have been entreated by me; indeed, you ought not to go there.
That which I spoke out of anger was not my considered view regarding the true essence of dharma.
However, the word of a father must be honored when it does not involve unrighteousness."

If King Vaivasvata were not to release you back [to life], behold, I would perish as the destroyer of the bridge of my lineage. "Pu" is the name for hell; indeed, they know that hell is suffering. (36–37)
The protection of one who has sons shall exist through his sons in every way, both in this world and the next;
for the oblations offered, gifts given, austerities performed, and even the parents nourished—all these certainly become fruitless for one who is sonless. (38)
"Whether one has performed extensive austerities, given gifts according to dharma,
offered oblations into the fire, or recited strings of mantras—
if one is childless, one shall not attain heaven; this I have heard from the three gods."
A father is counted by his son, and a grandfather by his grandson;
indeed, the great-grandfather rejoices through his son’s great-grandson.
"I shall not abandon you, my child—you who increase my lineage! [he said].
"Even though you are being entreated with such effort, you ought not to go there.
Hearing this from his father, the humble Naciketas said:
"O father, you should not despair; you shall see me returned here."
"Having seen King Yama and having made your word come true, I shall return here again; therefore, I have no fear.
Truth is the staircase to heaven; may you indeed abide in truth."
Everything is obtained through truth; everything is established therein.
A thousand horse-sacrifices and truth were once held on a scale;
indeed, truth alone outweighed the thousand horse-sacrifices. (45–46)
The great Vindhya mountain, though growing, does not increase beyond its bounds because it stands firm in truth;
Bali, the son of Virocana, remained bound while observing his own vow of truth.
Truth and righteousness, when protected, protect their own protector.
"Therefore, fulfill the truth this day; protect yourself by means of your own self.
Having spoken thus, Nāciketa, with a tranquil mind, departed for Death;
he reached the abode of Yama, where at that time Yama was not present in the house.
While he had gone to the great festival of the sacrifice performed for the sake of the world-protectors,
the Brāhmaṇa guest Nāciketa stood in the courtyard of the house,
afflicted by hunger and thirst, and without even a welcome.
One day and a second passed without his welcome;
on the third day, there was the falling of a crown upon the earth before Yama.
Then it was known that some great sin had been committed somewhere.
This cause has been understood; it was investigated by the messengers.
Having recognized that the guest’s lack of welcome indeed destroys merit, Yama said to the messengers there: "I arrived here yesterday."
Not a single excellent messenger informed the guest:
"Let them offer a welcome to that truth-abiding brahmin, whose wife remains as a guest, deprived of water, food, and a seat. (54-55)
The merit of that householder is entirely reduced to ashes;
[therefore], having washed his feet, one should place water upon his head as an offering of food,
for by doing so, the householder’s merit increases.

Whether it be very little or much, one should give according to one's ability with great faith. For if a guest turns away from a house with his hopes frustrated, he departs taking away the merit of the householder and leaving behind his own sin. (57–58)
A learned brahmin, a virtuous man, a chaste woman, a holy wife, and an ascetic in his first stage of life—these indeed are guests of righteousness; what is given to them yields infinite fruit.
So too are the departed spirits, the elderly, and ancestors, whether they have their own dependents or are without support.
These—those who are distressed, children, the dull-witted, the blind, and guests on account of some sign—are [to be honored].
(1.357.60) One should perform the washing of the guest's feet, the massaging of his limbs, bathing, feeding, providing water for drinking, and the offering of auspicious gifts. (61)
Having thus instructed his servants, Yama himself returned toward the gate to meet Naciketas; he did not ask him about that bliss.
When his life span was restored, the brahmin arrived, saying, "This is my supreme good fortune."
"O virtuous one, accept this sweet food, the meal, and the drinking water.
Enter here into my house and accept from me water for the feet and the respectful offering.
Accept from me various seats, garments, and ornaments. (63–64)
"How and for what purpose have you come? Speak, O Brahmin! I shall grant it;
indeed, by your grace, I have obtained [all things] from Yama. Tell me, however, the knowledge of the Self alone.
|| 65 || "I have received garments, ornaments, and so forth; tell me that which is the knowledge of the Self."
Yama, the Yogī, and Hari—these are the ones who have directly perceived the Self.
Therefore, I pray for that vision of the Self; grant it to me if you have great compassion.
Yama replied: "Take this gold and this collection of jewels."
Furthermore, he gave him a wish-fulfilling tree, the moon-creeper, a wish-granting gem, and a body;
a beautiful golden mansion, hundreds of male and female servants,
vehicles, mounts such as elephants and horses, and exquisite gardens.
"O sir, accept these gardens of gold and this treasure-trove;
but I shall never give you the knowledge of my own self, which is directly perceived.
"So be it; by your grace alone, O Lord, everything has been obtained by me."

Having spoken thus, Naciketas requested him for the sake of self-knowledge. Yama said: "Accept from me the sovereignty over the earth as a universal monarch, or else heaven, or the netherworld (pātāla), or even the true kingdom of the Creator."

"O, accept all sovereign powers, the supernatural attainments beginning with atomization (aṇimā), and the capacity for entering the bodies of others! But do not, for the sake of these, seek self-knowledge, which is difficult even for yogins to obtain. (72–73)
"So be it; by your grace alone, O Lord, everything has been obtained by me.
Having said this, Naciketas requested that knowledge of the Self from him.
Yama said: "Choose something else that dwells in your mind."
Yet, for those of poor discipline, that thorough knowledge of the self is difficult to attain.
Nevertheless, Naciketas likewise requested this knowledge of the self.
Yama said: "Listen; the self is perceived through divine vision. (75–76)
"I grant you divine vision; behold the Self abiding in the heart.
Having spoken thus, Dharmarāja gave him water of great merit.
With that collyrium for the eyes, Nāciketa indeed beheld the Consciousness.
Having seen that which is radiant, being-consciousness-bliss, subtle yet embodied, a mine of virtues,
the locus of all perfections, shining as the innermost Self dwelling within,
Nāciketa, possessing divine vision, rejoiced exceedingly. (78–79)
Seeing his firm resolve regarding the knowledge of the Self, Yama was pleased and said to the Brahmin: "Choose another boon as you desire. Naciketas then replied: "Let my corpse remain uncorrupted."
"Where my life may be eternal and divine, without decay;
and so that no offense against my father may occur, I behold this as a bestower of peace—I shall become Fire, known by the name Nāciketa. (81–82)
"May my fame endure forever everywhere, reaching up to the abode of Brahmā.
I request these boons, as well as those previously mentioned, which have been granted by you.
"So be it," Yama said, and he bestowed everything upon his guest.
Then he showed them his own palace, the auspicious dwellings of the officials,
and the prisons for the wicked; furthermore,
the penal settlements for those in hell and the celestial realms for the meritorious.
The King of Death himself showed everything to his venerable guest;
having seen all that wealth, prosperity, and excellent sovereignty,
Naciketas went to his own home where his father was.
The corpse, endowed with consciousness, indeed rose up, most divine.
Then, O Lakṣmī, having seen his son, that treasury of asceticism was delighted in mind;
embracing him with both arms and smelling his head, he said to him: ||| 87-88 ||
I hope you have not been slain, my child! I hope you have not been bound in the abode of Yama.
I hope your path has been auspicious as you traveled, my son!
I hope no diseases have afflicted you in the residence of Yama, my son!
What did you do upon arriving there, and what house did you see?
(1.357.90) Was Yama seen by you as harsh or very gentle;
was he pleased or filled with anger, and how were you quickly dismissed? (91)
I trust you were not detained by the gatekeepers there, nor ushered inside;
I trust that the fruits of your merits and demerits did not cause you any hindrance.
I trust the path you have traveled has been free from obstacles and well-honored.
Having spoken thus to his son Naciketas, Naciketas,
with a joyful heart, embraced him and said to his ascetic wives:
"Behold the power of my son, which bestows victory."
Having seen the abode of Yama, he returned once more to his body through the power of service to his father and also through service to his guru;
by means of truth witnessed by the gods, he beheld his son still alive.
"Oh, how supreme is my fortune! Having crossed over death, my son has returned.
Truly, the gods, the sages, the virtuous ones, and the lords have been gracious to me, since Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa is pleased that my child has come back. (96–97)
While he was speaking thus, the forest-dwellers heard it from ear to ear; having abandoned their vows, recitations, and worship,
and having relinquished their austerities and fire-offerings, they all assembled to see him.
Some had their arms raised upward, while others stood on one foot;
some had their eyes fixed upon the sun, and others had their heads touching the ground;
some were naked, and others likewise used their teeth as mortars.
The Aśmakūṭas, the Maunas, those who eat withered leaves and grass, those who inhale smoke, those who drink vapors, and others who subsist on water—
all of them surrounded Naciketas and questioned him.
"O you who observe the vow of truth! O lover of service to your guru!
Naciketas, speak the truth: what has been seen and what has been heard by you?
Whatever conduct of Yama there may be—whether secret or manifest—tell it all."
Everything must be told by you, including whatever was done for your sake—
the suffering, the rebukes, the insults, and even what was kept secret as well as what was made public.
Speak everything that is destined to serve as an instruction for the world.
Whatever is done right here is what will be utilized in the next world. Living beings who look only to the further shore do not see the end of their own actions.
Have you seen Citragupta? Or does he perhaps do nothing at all?
What is the form of the King of Dharma, and what is his form as Time?
Likewise, what is the form of Death, and what is the nature of diseases?
And of what kind is the ripening of the fruits of karma that is experienced?
How do those who have conquered their own selves and are of such virtuous conduct depart?
And how do the sinners depart, and how indeed do the indifferent ones depart?
[They depart] according to what has been seen, according to what has been born, and also according to what has been experienced.
"Tell us everything in detail and according to the truth— how and what was enjoyed by you, and likewise whatever else remains in your memory.
Having spoken thus, they were exceedingly eager to hear that which is indeed extraordinary.
Their hearts were captivated; Nāciketa spoke to them.

(111) Thus, in the first book of the *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, within the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga, in the majesty of Mathurā-kṣetra: the emptiness of Yama’s city due to the power of the Yamunā; how it was again filled by ritualists (*karmi*); Nāciketa’s journey to the abode of Yama due to his father’s curse; his return to his own body after receiving Yama’s blessing, attaining self-realization, and beholding the city of Yama; and the sages’ inquiry as to what he had seen and heard there.
Thus ends the three hundred and fifty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description [of the Lineage]," from the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Book 1: The Continuation of the Kṛta Yuga.

O Brahmins, listen with curiosity as I relate this account of Yama.

Those who speak untruths, the cruel, those who kill living beings, women, and children;
(4) those who slay virtuous Brahmins, those who cause suffering, those who betray trust, the deceitful, the ungrateful, the greedy, and those who seize the wives of others; (5)
Those who kill virgins, those who destroy the path of Dharma,

Those devoid of faith, atheists, merciless, and lacking in purity; those bereft of wives and sons, and those who cause the breaking of vows;

Those who cause suffering to women and those who indeed steal away wealth; those who practice deceitful pride and those who cast false blame and stains [upon others];

Those who strike with fire or weapons, those who operate oil-presses for sesame and other seeds; those who destroy temples, food-distributions, and charitable feasts, and those who ruin trees;

and covered with divine, auspicious mansions made of Jāmbūnada gold.

(25) Slave-girls, messengers, wives, attendants, maidens, and sons—all those who are the subjects of King Yama dwell there as members of that household. (26)

Flocks of birds, such as parrots, cranes, and pigeons, indeed dwell there. (27)
The noble city of King Yama is crowded with all living beings.
There flows the river Puṣpodakā, beautifully adorned with trees, creepers, and groves; its banks are graced by flourishing gardens, and it possesses golden steps and sandy shores.
In that place, where lotus ponds served as water-channels for every palace,
there were Gandharvas, Kinnaras, messengers, and most beautiful Kinnarīs, all possessing divine forms, amidst lakes of sweet, cool water.
With broad hips, their limbs shimmering with ornaments,
these women who grant delight sport at the time of bathing, assuming forms according to their desire;
there, men delight them as they wish and according to their pleasure.
Agitating that river as they sing together with their beloveds,

Always full of divine water, adorned with swans white as kunda flowers,

Women, their natural beauty enhanced by intoxication, plunge into that place filled with groves of fruit and flowering trees and provided with bulbs, roots, and other provisions, and sport there. Likewise, they sing together in harmony with vocalists, instrumentalists, and beat-keepers.
In the groves, gardens, and parks along the banks of the Tīrthas,
as well as at the bathing-ghats, charming men and women sport and sing with the melodies of lutes and mṛdaṅga drums. (37–38)
The wind, fragrant with the scent of aguru and sandalwood, blows pleasantly and gently through the mansions, creating a delightful aroma.
And there are celestial palaces and vehicles that travel through the sky.
They move through the water and the sky together with their beloved women;
the royal roads and dwellings are overflowing with bliss, endowed with every kind of prosperity, and resplendent with marketplaces and other such features.
There are divine assembly halls and divine spectacles,
as well as houses for divine dramas, dances, and songs.
Thus was seen the vast city of Yama, filled with such pleasures.
To the meritorious, however, it appeared as a second Vaikuṇṭha.
(43) Then there was that beautiful gateway, resplendent with golden ground, ten yojanas in width and twice that in length. (44)
With its walls on both sides adorned by hundreds of palaces,
it seemed as if it were painting the sky itself with various lattices of mechanical devices;
rich in splendor like heaven, it was an entrance through which those who perceive the Dharma might pass.
It is easily entered by gods, sages, and those who perform meritorious and virtuous deeds.
Therein a gate has been fashioned, possessing the luster of a mass of autumnal clouds;
therein an entrance has been constructed for men of righteous conduct.
Then, there was an iron gate to the south, smoke-colored and endowed with many defects; it was fearsome to behold,
fierce, heated, and like a forest fire, where the entrance for sinners lay.
For the cruel, the slayers, the flesh-eaters, the evil-minded,
for all those who are sinful and who inflict suffering upon living beings—
there, the western gate was constructed with many weapons and other materials. (1.358.50)
Smeared with a net of fire from *audumbara* wood and causing intense burning,
it was personally constructed by Yama for the purpose of admitting evildoers.
In that city stands a vast, divine assembly hall made entirely of jewels.
And that assembly was appointed by Yama with men who were practitioners of dharma and asceticism;
it was graced by those who speak the truth, who have conquered anger, and who are free from greed and passion.
That assembly is for those endowed with dharma; that assembly is for evildoers as well.
That assembly is the dispenser of justice for all the world, both for the auspicious and the inauspicious; it is the embodiment of dharma for everyone.
Therein dwell impartial and disinterested reciters of the law.
They indeed contemplate only the fruits for the benefit of the entire world, reporting according to the rule, according to the record, and according to the time.
[These are] Manu, Vyāsa, Atri, Āpastamba, Śukra, and Bṛhaspati. (55–56)
Nāciketa, Gautama, Śaṅkha, and Likhita;
Pulastya, Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, Vahni, Vāyu, and the Yugas;
Patnīvrata, Pulaha, and others who recite the Dharma.
Together with Yama, they all contemplate a remedy.
All of them are preoccupied with their duties, adorned with earrings and armlets;
they are difficult to behold due to the splendor of the crowns and other ornaments bestowed by Brahmā.
Then, on both sides of him, there were divine sages who discoursed upon Brahman,
who were masters of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, who held truth and righteousness as their foremost principles;

Time hears their resolutions and likewise joins embodied beings [to their destinies].
(64) Furthermore, there are other servants resembling Time who are intent on calculation; here, there are tens of millions of executors of the command who indeed declare the fruits [of actions]. (65)
Properly honored by Yama with divine perfumes and ointments,
she is the destroyer of all worlds, consisting indeed of terrible torments;
for even the asuras and the sages whose wealth is penance fear her.

Asuras, gods, and even yogins of great luster—these diseases produced by Time emerged from her body; they were most terrible, causing great affliction, and were intensely intent on inflicting punishment. (67–68)
Just as I was seen by him, so too was I seen by that most terrible Great Wrath (Mahākrodha).
He is by nature ill-behaved and free from old age and death.
He is a great being, hideous, and likewise a person named Death (Mṛtyu).

He was seen composed of divine splendor, accompanied by all his bonds. Singers and jesters as well, who awaken all living beings and know the proper time, were seen by me, adorned with garments and ornaments of light.
Many kinds of fevers have been seen, as well as diseases and pains;

They are observed in various forms, bestowing the forest fire of wrath.
Fierce in their wrath, assuming various forms, these women are destroyers;

The Kūṣmāṇḍas, Yātudhānas, and flesh-eating Rākṣasas—
those with one foot, two feet, three feet,

Some had ears like spikes, some ears like winnowing baskets, and others ears like reeds;

Some carried axes, spades, and wheels, with spears in their hands; others held pikes, javelins, *bhūśuṇḍīs*, bows, and mallets;

Then other men were seen, adorned with every kind of beauty;
they were equipped with armlets, chains, variegated crowns, and bracelets;

Others, however, were traveling in vehicles drawn by horses, elephants, swans, and the like;

Thus have I seen the gentle ones, while others have been seen who are terrifying.
Others there were radiant, while others were entirely soiled;

Others, such as the Śatamārakas, were sweet in their polished speech;
Kali, Kṛṣṇā, Mahākṛtyā, and Kālī were also beheld.
Others had Dharma in their hands, Yaśas in their hands, and Kīrti in their hands.
These exist in the presence of the End-maker (Death), devoted to his word:
some are eaters of livestock, some are eaters of men, and others are eaters of women;
indeed, there are many who are eaters of corpses, eaters of children, and eaters of birds. (85–86)
Those who eat raw food, those who eat birds, those with lotuses in their hands, and the followers of Yama;
those with great fangs, those who are terrifying, and those who cannot be overcome by fire or water;
those with bodies of fire, bodies of water, and bodies of earth—such are these.
I have seen those who cannot be struck by weapons, as well as others who are untouchable like the wind.
Indeed, these soldiers of King Yama were observed to possess supernatural powers;
they had beaks and wings, and could travel everywhere, including through the sky.
They were seen by the servants of Yama, who have no power over the restraint of breath;
they were seen as being graspable by all, touchable by all, and visible to all.
And however many people there are here in the cosmic egg and in the worlds—
Indeed, such are the natures of embodied beings and their conscious qualities;
such are the qualities of the insentient, whether they be material or immaterial;
and in whatever manner stationary or moving things come to be, such they remain. (91–92)
To mete out punishment for all those kinds of offenses, those soldiers are endowed with every power,

Some indeed possess subtle bodies, while others take the form of mountains;

Some take the form of rivers and streams, while others have the nature of flames.
Some were as hot as the sun, and some were as cold as the Himalayas;

I saw them in many forms, and I was struck with wonder. (97–98)

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, Lakṣmī! Nāciketa beheld the torments of Yama.

He spoke to all the brahmins: "I shall tell you what I have seen. Naciketas said to the twice-born ones: "The king, the lord of the city of the dead, was seen by me in the midst of the assembly, skilled in many affairs."
Yama likewise gave me this one bull for the sake of honoring me;
he offered me a seat, water for the feet, and the guest-offering, performing my worship according to the prescribed rite.
He seated me upon a golden throne adorned with flowers.
Previously his face was fierce, but then it became gentle.
His two eyes also turned red, yet became like lotuses.
Having seen this, I felt confident there, filled with devotion.
Then, with a truly peaceful heart, he offered praise to him:
"O Dharmarāja, you are indeed the supreme and great bestower of the fruits of actions for the ancestors; you are the creator and the ordainer in the śrāddha rite. Salutations be unto you!"
O Death of Death! O Knower of Karma! O Lord of Pretas! Homage be to you!
(7) O Staff-in-Hand! O Noose-in-Hand! O Embodiment of Dharma!
Homage be to you! O You of Solar Hue! O You of Black Hue! O Consumer of Oblations to Gods and Ancestors! Homage to you! (8)
"O Surūpa! O Nyāyamūrti! Salutations to you, even though you possess a cruel form.
Neither ascetics nor even sages are able to move you from your path.
Having heard this auspicious hymn of praise, King Yama spoke to me.
"I am well-pleased; may it be well with you. Tell me, what shall I do for you?
(1.359.10) I then said to him, "O Lord, show me that place!
I wish to see the torments of both the wicked and the virtuous. (11)
"I wish to see Citragupta, your chief; show him to me.
Yamarāja summoned his messenger and dispatched me [to him].
Having seen me with affection, Citragupta [spoke] toward Citragupta.
Rising up with palms joined in reverence, he gave him a most warm welcome.
He said to him: "Let the servants show you the abode of the departed;

Urged by my message, messengers quickly led me to the abode of the fruits.
Listen to this terrifying sight seen by me near the gate:
the messengers of Yama were binding and burning embodied beings. (15)
They tear them apart and strike them again and again with blows;

Broken, shattered, their limbs mangled and their backs and necks fractured— 16–17.
They weep piteously and terribly, yet they find no protector;
some are cooked in hell and burned in fierce fire.
They are boiled in oil and likewise dissolved in alkaline lye.
Some are crushed in machines, from which blood flows;

They are impaled upon great spikes and likewise bound by their feet.
They are cast into the Vaitaraṇī river, where fanged beasts bite them;
whirled about by whirlpools above and below, they suffer from the waves.
Thousands are seen there, while others wither away in the wind.

Many embodied beings are seen there fainting, vomiting, and losing consciousness; they find no protector. Then others, having been hoisted upon the Kūṭaśālmalī tree by many messengers, [suffer likewise].
They are struck with blows from swords and spears and by iron thorns;

Some, having sucked others, likewise release them onto the earth.
Then, though they have been sucked, they become joined with life once more;
they are born again just as before, and they suck those [others] again. (25–26)
"O sinners! Save us! Release us!"—even as they cry out thus, the followers of Yama strike them again and again for the sake of the fruit of their sins.
Some are struck by showers of stones, while others are struck by showers of dust.
They are crushed, they flee, they enter holes, and they burn;
struck by messengers, they are cooked in a great fire while being beaten with bamboo canes.
"Give us water! they cry, "Be gracious to us! (28–29)
Then hot water is given, and they drink it;
at that moment, they are burned by internal torments and cry out most terrifyingly.
Then, the ground of the meritorious was seen by me repeatedly.
Indeed, living beings who were happy were seen to be overflowing with joy,
before whom there were heaps of desired foods and edibles—
curds, milk, juices, as well as rice mixed with sesame (kṛsara) and milk-rice (pāyasa).
There were also heaps of fruits, jars and pools of drinks,
and many foods— eatables, chewables, and lickables— were present nearby;
and substances for oiling and betel-nut preparations shone forth.
The divine objects acquired through austerity remain for those of virtuous soul:
