likewise, captivating, lovely, and radiant women provide them with delight. (34–35)
Adorned with every ornament, young women were seen serving food to their beloveds while seated upon golden thrones;
others likewise held water-jars and pitchers, with vessels in their hands. (36)
With flowers in their hands and water for the feet, they feed him by the thousands.
Adorned with the beauty of anklets and chains, and making sweet sounds with their clusters of small bells, those enchanting women stand nearby, offering excellent objects of enjoyment.

And at times, women attend upon youths who are deeply rested and mines of beauty and virtue; they speak with sweet and melodious voices. Furthermore, there are those who offer instruction, as well as messengers and spies.

Striking and laughing, cruel and speaking harshly—O you ungrateful, greedy ones, forever devoid of compassion! You people who delight in slandering others and inflict suffering upon the bodies and souls of others. (1.359.40–41)
Though worldly wealth was available, you did not give away water, wood, or sweet food that came to you easily;

Having brought about the exhaustion of their karmas, let those who are liberated indeed go to the earth.
Those born into impoverished families must not commit sin again;

Therefore, becoming devoted to truth, compassionate, and highly righteous,

"Or else, you shall attain a prosperous heaven filled with beautiful women"—
this excellent instruction I clearly heard there from him.
Nevertheless, the servants led me further to another part of the grounds.
There, I beheld the tormenting of living beings—those who were sinful—which was terrifying; it involved piercing, beating, crushing, cutting, grinding, splitting, and burning them like refuse. (48)
I am unable to provide a full description, for my heart is softened by compassion;
nevertheless, O sages, because of your persistence, I shall speak.
There, the entire surface of the earth is covered with iron thorns.
Uneven, smeared with poison, pervaded by fire, and filled with darkness—
here, those of sinful conduct, though possessing bodies, are cast down by the servants of Yama with their feet, hands, and necks severed. (51)
Women, who are in essence like malevolent spirits (*kṛtyā*), await those who seek sexual union.
When they have arrived, they cast them onto a stone slab heated by fire.
Many such wicked men suffer; they find no protector. (52–53)
Then I saw others being devoured from the soles of their feet to the tops of their heads by fierce dogs, crying out again and again;

Hungry and thirsty, those with needle-like mouths are indeed tormented.

"Why do you cry out, O evildoer? Embrace me and take your pleasure!"
"Wherever you may run, I will not abandon you, you adulterer!

Some had their limbs crushed by mallets, while others were impaled on spikes;
I saw others cast by me into ponds, lakes, and rivers,
as well as into pools of blood, wells, and lotus-pools.
Smelling the stench of putrid flesh, worms, insects, and impurities in the lakes, those sinners were seen sinking down;
likewise, they were crushed by rains of bones, stones, and blood. (69)
I heard them running and leaping, crying out, "Alas, we are destroyed! Wailing piteously there, they were obstructed and pierced;

Tapta, Mahātapta, Raurava, and Mahāraurava;
Saptatāla, Kālasūtra, Tāmisra, and Andhatāmisra.

Desiring to drink water, he is led by messengers to a lake of hot water;

Having seized them and torn them apart, they devour them and laugh.
(82) Then they are indeed thrown by them into a great lake of alkaline water;

In the terrifying Kumbhīpāka hell, which is filled with glowing cow-dung pits,

Thus I saw those wicked ones crying out nearby.
Then, at the place called Śṛṅgāṭaka, I saw those who were being scorched on ground with intensely heated sand,
and who were being burned, cut, and pierced by thorns.
The sinners are split apart, cast down, and tormented by the messengers of Yama; they are dragged along, disemboweled, and torn asunder.
Dark, brindled dogs devour them, as do serpents and scorpions.
Then I saw another hell, Kūṭaśālmalī.
There the sinners are dragged until they are reduced to mere skeletons;
there the living beings are beaten and pulverized by fierce messengers.
With their limbs severed in every part of their bodies, they experience intense suffering.
Then another river was seen by me, consisting of mud and sand,
with a current of flaming fire, filled with serpents, scorpions, and crocodiles.
Indeed, those mortals are rescued from that river which is filled with fire and crocodiles.
Likewise, they see the Vaitaraṇī river, consisting of salty mud, with its mire of skin,
flesh, and bone, and its marrow, saliva, and blood.
There are creatures with adamantine fangs and claws, and those with adamantine tongues;
there are crocodiles of great venom, as well as fish that pierce through bones.
There, they devour, swallow, and vomit up the wicked.
Furthermore, they become fleshy as before, and indeed remain sinful.
(94) Then, ahead on the ground, an empty house with a deep pit was seen;
there, mice with diamond-like teeth and venomous ones were devouring them. (95)
Their limbs were devoured by mice until only their bones remained;
yet, when touched again by the wind, they became fleshy once more.
Then, ahead, a forest of rough trees was seen, inhabited by fierce birds.
Where even one who has climbed a tree is devoured by flesh-eating birds;
there the sinner is made fleshless, skinless, boneless, and likewise devoid of the network of veins, as well as eyeless and earless, by those with sharp beaks. (97–98)
Then, ahead of me, I beheld a great, blood-red banyan tree, with wood as hard as a diamond, incapable of being burned, and joined by thousands of swings.
Beneath it was indeed the hearth of Yama, extending ten yojanas in width.
It is indeed three yojanas deep and perpetually ablaze.
Thousands, millions, and hundreds of millions of *preta*s are constantly being cast into it by the *rākṣasa*s who are the servants of Yama.
Having bound the sinner upside down in the intermediate space with a cord like a hanging branch of a banyan tree, they roast him and eat him;
some throw him into a furnace and even eat those who have been roasted.
Likewise, the servants of Yama and the pretas, filled with joy, feast upon them.
From the interior of the furnace, a swift river named Śakunī flows, carrying fat and marrow; there they cast the sinners.
Then, having seen those seven extremely fierce hells there,
each one of which is difficult to cross and terrible, the sinner experiences them in succession.
Therein are ten great spikes and thirteen *kumbhīpākas*.
Impaled upon spears heated by fire, they are indeed roasted.
With their heads hanging downward, they dangle over a dry, smoky well;
likewise, they are set ablaze and cooked in cauldrons of boiling oil.
Cast into a pit of dried cow-dung, they are cooked by the fire of their own fat.
Thus have I seen living beings being cooked and severely burned. Then I saw the River of Yama, with its flowing currents of molten lead.
Having plunged into it, living beings who have committed evil deeds are indeed cooked there.
(1.359.109) Then a long pond with cool waters and a cool grove was seen, where, having drunk the cool water, a moment’s rest is obtained. (1.359.110)
There, indeed, Yami, the sister of Yama, provides food and drink;
there I saw a mountain named Śūlabhraha, a hundred yojanas in extent, upon which the cloud Jīmūta rains.
Living beings sink there, and then they indeed move forward from that place.
(1.12) Then the Śṛṅgāraka forest is seen, filled with gadflies and mosquitoes;
if a sinner is seen or even touched there, he is indeed born in the form of a worm. (1.13)
Then another stage is seen, wherein he beholds his kinsmen—
his mother, father, sons, wives, and likewise beloved people.
Being slaughtered before them, he then cries out in a manner that inspires terror.
With clubs, mallets, staffs, knees, and likewise with bamboos;
with fists, sticks, whips, chains, and so forth—
then another stage was seen, which bestows the state of a stationary preta.
Having gone there, the deceased spirit proceeds to whatever immobile state it may be;
for sixty thousand years, however, it experiences the condition of a beast.
Thereafter, it is born as a sweat-born creature, and from that, it is born as a bird.
Then, having gone to the womb of a cow, that human being is born again.
Indeed, in whatever manner the wheel of worldly existence is traced out by his state of being,
having experienced those torments accordingly, he is born among the Brahmins and other castes.
Thus far indeed was it seen by me, as shown by the messengers of Yama;
exhausted, the messengers went with me to Citragupta.

Thus ends the three hundred and fifty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of Nāciketa’s Praise of King Yama in the Southern Wheel, the Command of King Yama to Behold the Various Hells, the Observation of the Torments of Painful Nirayas, the Description of Those Torments, and the Return of the Messengers Accompanied by Nāciketa to Citragupta," in the first section on the Continuation of the Kṛta Age of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 360. *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā*, Section 1 (Continuation of the Kṛta Age).
Chapter 360.
[The Author: Chapter 361.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī! [I shall tell you] what was done by Nāciketa in the house of Citragupta.
"What was seen, that I shall relate," so Nāciketa spoke to them.
"Let all the Brāhmaṇas listen as I describe everything that was seen by me in the courtyard of Citragupta."
Commanded by Citragupta, the Rākṣasas named Mandehas and other messengers were instructed by the officer to inflict torments upon the doers of deeds;
they assumed various forms, were terrible, armed, and devourers of flesh.
O you heroic Mandehakas, and likewise you messengers endowed with prowess!
Bind the living beings and seize the sinners for the sake of torment;
kill them, devour them, and crush them according to their deeds.
Thus commanded, those Rākṣasas and messengers, capable of assuming any form at will,
quickly equipped themselves; they were fearsome, appearing as elephants and lions,
as well as tigers, jackals, buffaloes, serpents, and scorpions.
Taking the forms of vultures, hawks, serpents, bears, donkeys, and so forth;
with tridents, spears, and clubs in their hands, and equipped with sharp-edged spears, swords, and scimitars—those messengers possess terrible prowess. (7–8)
"Split! Cut! Seize! so cry those with blood-red eyes.
Impelled by Citragupta, the Mandehas devour and strike down.
There are thousands of diseases and tens of thousands of messengers.
Thousands of Jvaras, Kālamuṇḍas,
and Keṅkārākṣas set out to carry out the crushing of sinners who perform evil deeds,
acting by the command of Citragupta as instructed by Dharmarāja.
Some, deserving of punishment according to their deserts, were bound by the Rākṣasas with various fetters;
some were scorched by fire, and others were gnawed by fangs.
These were men of evil conduct, devoted to sin, pitiless, and wicked-minded.
Dogs, beasts of prey, and cattle devour those of wicked soul.
Citragupta stands there and makes the fever-demons hear the verdict of justice;
he also [summons] the messengers and the Rākṣasas—this indeed I have heard with my own ears.
Having impaled this slayer of his father and slayer of his mother upon a śālmali tree,
let the messengers tear him apart with their exceedingly sharp thorns without delay;
let them cook this lowest of men in the Pācaka fire.
But for animals and other creatures, having cast them into a cauldron of boiling oil or onto a heated copper floor,
let them roast this roaster of living beings in a blazing fire according to his own deeds.
Let them cast into the Vaitaraṇī river the one who steals beds and seats, as well as the one who sets fire [to property]; let them subsequently throw him into fire.
Let them indeed cause the destroyer of holy fords, sacred fields, and centers of dharma to fall [into hell].
Let his vital organs be pierced with stakes heated by fire!
Let fire-stakes be applied to the ears of this slanderer who provides false testimony, and to the tongue of this reviler.
Indeed, let this deceitful priest— a rogue, a scoundrel, and a hypocrite—
be bound to a stake in prison, and let nothing at all be given to him.
Let the tongue of this speaker, who is wicked in speech and a liar, be cut out.
Having forcibly severed the organ of that sinner with the edge of a sword by means of lustful delusion,
let both caustic alkali and fire be applied.
By him, having employed this sixfold stratagem, many people have been made his heirs.

"Let them destroy him for the sake of their own interests; let them indeed pierce him with arrows. Having crushed this thief of gold, this ungrateful betrayer of his father, and this slayer of cows with mallets, let them roast him in caustic fire."
"Let the *kṛtyakās* swiftly devour this Brahmin who abducts maidens!
Let tigers with sharp fangs devour this treacherous Brahmin; let them cook him in various ways in their ovens, for he pierces the vital organs. (25–26)

May they release from the Karkaṭa hells those who neglect the worship of gods and fire, those who slay heroes, those who revile the gods, and those who destroy the property of the deities. May they cast into a boiling lake this man who officiates as a priest for all types of sacrifices.

Let them strike with most cruel punishments— using bamboo staves, whips, iron rods, and clubs— the twice-born who refuses to give, the seller of the Dharma, the wicked man, and the one who steals water and food. (28–29)
Water and food must never be given to him;
having killed one who has gained his trust, let them cook that slayer in a great fire.
Let them likewise cook him by whom the property of the gods was stolen.
"Against the slayer of the king, the slayer of the guru, and the slayer of children,
let them apply the disease of royal consumption (rājayakṣman) and cast them into mountain caves.
As for the killer of a woman, let them surely cause him to be executed at the Kūṭaśālmalī tree."
May the followers of Yama devour that meat-eater for a hundred years;
thereafter, may that lowest of men be cooked in terrible hells.
Then, having attained human status, may he die repeatedly while still in the womb.
Having died within a ten-month womb, let him be born as a partaker of afflictions;
let him be constantly tormented there by the transformations of hunger and disease, and let this betrayer of friends be crushed by a mechanical press. (34–35)
Then let him burn in a terrible fire for two hundred years;
thereafter, having entered the womb of a dog, let him be afflicted by disease forever.
Then, with a body tormented by illness, let this man be born as a human being.
May he who steals juices and he who steals salt and other such things be born as a worm for five hundred years; thereafter, may he become a dung-worm, and after that, a bird;
and finally, in a waterless place, may he become a wolf.
Let them heat this giver of fire in the fire again and again;
thereafter, let him become a deer for a hundred years, and after that, a worm for a hundred years.
Then, filled with extreme suffering, let him be born as a human being who is full of compassion.
And may they cast those who steal the property of others into the Raurava hell;
having cooked them in the Kumbhīpāka hells, let them throw them into a family of donkeys,
then into a family of pigs due to their filth, and thereafter into a family of thieves.
Wherever those who are overwhelmed by suffering indeed experience the results of their deeds—
having bound this person who was a harmer of others with his head downward to a tree,
they should cook him with fire and cast him into births as hunters.
Then, when a hundred years have passed, the followers of Yama shall release him;
having cast Piśuna onto the banks of the Vajra river,
they shall thereafter hurl him into the womb of a pig, and from there into births as mongooses.
Cast this liar, this stealer of fields, and this false witness into the Andhatāmisra hell; thereafter, among animals, beasts, and trees,
they shall obtain birth according to their karma, becoming deaf and blind in the human state.
May he be born again and again as mute, one-eyed, and afflicted by disease!
Having bound this usurper of land and fields, let them cook him;
thereafter, may that sinner be born as a hungry cat, tormented by hunger.
May these wicked fowlers be struck down by dogs and fierce vultures;
thereafter, may they be cast into the lineage of cocks.
May they cast this evildoer into the womb of stinging insects among mosquitoes.
"May the buffaloes surely slaughter this sinful butcher of pigs!
Then, having passed successively through the wombs of a pig, a buffalo, a cock, a hare, and a jackal, let him become food there."
"Therefore, let this evil-souled woman become a forest-dwelling hunter.
Furthermore, let them repeatedly roast the one who gives her leftover food with burning coals—she who has violated her conduct, is ill-behaved, and has acted treacherously toward her husband. (51)
"Let her embrace seven iron men on all sides;
let her become a mangy bitch, and thereafter a miserable sow.
Afterward, having obtained birth as a female slave, let her become one who provides enjoyment for many. (52–53)
By him many servants have been deceived and made miserable;
therefore, let them cast him into the Raurava hell, which is difficult to endure.
Afterwards, may he be born in the species of cruel beings, such as serpents and the like.
Having repeatedly been born as a pig, a jackal, a crane, a sheep,
a horse, a donkey, and so forth, and having been born into the species of a dog or a bull,
he shall indeed then be born among the class of slaves, for this [existence] is most miserable.
"O Brahmins, all of this has been heard and seen by me directly;
furthermore, Citragupta assigned other sins as well to those who were devoid of religious vows and the like, and who followed the side of evil. (57)

Let the messengers of Yama indeed cause those who delight in violence, as well as informers, those who corrupt affairs, and those who betray their gurus, to dwell for a thousand years in the grasp of Yama. (58–59)
Let the soldiers of the Fire-god bring about the ripening of those who set forest fires within the fire itself;
then, let them cast [the seeds] into the womb and into human beings. By their own sins, they shall become short-lived and afflicted by disease.
Some children will die in the womb, or they will perish as infants;
some, not yet having reached youth, will die as destroyers [of others],
by means of wooden nooses, the noose of weapons, or through wind, fire, or water.
They shall meet their destruction through falling, or by poison;

likewise, they shall suffer the agony of killing their mother and father, as well as the loss of life. Furthermore, those who are injurious and murderous shall experience suffering from their own kinsmen.
Blacksmiths, artisans, ditch-diggers, and those who harm living beings;
those who destroy urine and eggs, those who administer poison, and those who set cities on fire;
those who construct cages and those who slaughter with spears and other weapons—[these go to the Raurava hell]. (64–65)
May those who are slanderers, quarrelsome, and those who falsely bring accusations;
those who cause the destruction of animals, who terrify living beings, and who are murderers—
may they repeatedly behold the agonies in the terrible hells.
Upon the exhaustion of their karma, may they be born with deficient limbs;
through their actions, may they become impoverished there, and likewise suffer the cutting off of their ears,
the severing of their noses, and the amputation of their hands and feet.
May they always experience mental and physical suffering;
may they have throbbing pain in their heads and ailments in their bellies.
May they be dull-witted, blind, deaf, mute, lame, and crawling on their hands.
Those with one eye destroyed, the one-eyed, those with deformed nails, and those afflicted by disease; the hunchbacked, the lame, the crippled, those with cracked feet, and those with pot-bellies;
those suffering from trickling leprosy, white leprosy, wind-swollen testicles, and those devoid of testicles.
May those afflicted by urinary disorders and diabetes, those suffering from pain in the womb and eyes,
those with asthma and pain in the heart and private parts, and those with diseases such as splenic enlargement and abdominal tumors,
experience the fruits of their own karma while in human form.

"O messengers of Yama! May you cause those who speak falsehoods, the cruel, the harsh, the slanderers, the malicious, the bitter, those who deplete the essence of others, the dry, those who strike at the vital organs, and those who corrupt speech to undergo their punishment. (73–74)
Let them bind those lowest of men— those who give insults, who are cruel, shameless, deceitful, merciless, envious, jealous, and violent—
and then indeed cast them among the animals, insects, birds, and beasts.
Therefore, let them exist in human form as destroyers of the world—contemptible, ignorant, ruined in mind, and devoid of reputation;
unworthy of honor, undeserving of respect, and held in utter disdain by their own kin. (76–77)

May these people— who cause hatred in the world, who are loathsome, who are rejected by friends and kinsmen, and who consume false accusations— meet their destruction through thunderbolts, weapons, poisons, and the like,
for they are defiled by the stain of falsehood.
Then, another thing was heard there, much that had been spoken by Citragupta:
"He who commits theft, inflicts blows, or practices deceitful conduct; he who performs acts of stealing and carries out forcible seizures. (1.360.80)
Those who eat from the king’s hand, those who subsist on the king’s shadow, and those lowest of men and sinners who oppress all subjects;
as well as those who practice fraudulent buying and selling of gold, gems, pearls, and the like—[these should be punished]. 81.
And those who are ungrateful at the proper time, devoted solely to their own self-interest;

those who destroy spirits, ghosts, and malevolent spells, as well as those who cause disturbances in the bodily elements; those who steal the purpose of sacred deposits (nyāsa), and those who perform the deluding of mantras and so forth. (82–83)
May those who inflict suffering upon the wretched—the poor, the destitute, the miserable, and those dependent on others—be boiled for a long time in the hell of Prapāpin.
May they be cast into a great pit of darkness infested with scorpions. (84)
But when their karma is exhausted, let them be joined there among the people by those people—
where there is fear of thieves, fear of water and hunger, fear of the king,
great fear of calamities, fear of epidemics, and likewise fear of disease. (85–86)
Where the people possess the wit of rogues and the city is inhabited by the crafty,
there calamities never leave for even a moment.
Now, O twice-born ones, listen again to another thing that was heard by me in this regard.
May these evildoers be born where there is torment;
afflicted by manifold sufferings even while dwelling in the womb, may they be one-handed or two-handed, maimed, and deformed in their bellies. (88–89)
Suffering from the pain of diseased channels, those with deficient limbs, and those afflicted by wind-disorders; constantly wailing, devoid of wives, and sexually unrestrained;
childless, miserable, and having infants with terrifying cries.
May those who eat the leftovers [of others] be completely overwhelmed by intense sufferings;
may they be inferior in beauty, in virtue, in strength, and likewise in conduct;
and may they become like blades of grass even to their own servants. (91–92)
Where the king’s punishment is constant— whether execution or even severe hardship—
and where there is agitation caused by rain and cold, and the ruin of all undertakings;
where people share in infamy and partake of misfortune even in auspicious matters.
Even when there is good rain, the rain indeed avoids their field;
or where lightning may fall, that field perishes.
For those who possess such a field, there is neither happiness nor death, but only suffering. (94–95)

Let those wicked ones, such as thieves and others who cause suffering to the world, remain there. Now, O soldiers, hear of the torments for those who have forcibly attached themselves to the wives of others and other such sins, wherein indeed these sinners must be cast.
Those who, being lustful, forcibly sport with the bodies of animals or humans, or who, as women seeking pleasure, corrupt the practice of dharma;
or those who, having given threats of fear, violate women of noble family—[these are the ones reborn as such]. (97–98)
May those who cause the intermixture of castes be repeatedly cast into fire;
may they be cooked there for many thousands of years, and thereafter,
may they be cast into human existence where they are born from mixed wombs.
They will be like courtesans, deceptive, and fraudulent; they will not be born from the wombs of a single husband.
They will be captors of women, destroyers of women, wearing the dress of women, and sporting with women.
They will be slaves to women, objects of women's enjoyment, possessing the nature of women, and performing the acts of women.
"Let people cast those individuals who are loathsome to behold here and there;
let even women become of that same nature and likewise fall into misery.
Thus I have heard everything that Naciketas said to them.

Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have related to you the command of Citragupta. (102) Thus ends the three hundred and sixtieth chapter, titled "The Demonstration of the Torments of Hellish Beings Inflicted by Rākṣasas such as Mandeha and Others, in Accordance with the Order Given by Citragupta for the Infliction of Punishment upon Sinners in the Wheel of Yama," within the first section on the Continuation of the Kṛta Yuga in the *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*. Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī! To the instruction of Citragupta, and furthermore, that which was spoken by Nāciketa to them.
"O messengers! Seize him quickly so that time does not pass by.
Why is such compassion shown toward him? Seize him and kill him without delay!
Let there be no hesitation here; do not stand with your faces turned away!"
"Why do you not go with speed? Do not be dilatory!
Go quickly to that very place and bring [him] back at once.
One's inability should not be displayed, nor should one calculate the hospitality [to be received]. (3–4)

Neither marriage, nor asceticism, nor lifelong celibacy; neither dalliance with new women, nor devotion to a husband, nor the state of being a virtuous wife; neither the status of a chaste woman, nor childhood, nor the state of being established in charity, nor stability in pleasure. (5)
"State affairs, the assembly hall, the celestial vehicle, and worship—
none of these should be considered at the expense of ensuring that time does not pass by.
Quickly bring them here, according to the administration of duties."
"Quickly become a serpent, and you also become a tiger; become a reptile, a crocodile, or a tiny worm. Become the form of a disease, and you also become dysentery."
May you become vomiting, rebirth, ear-disease, and cholera;
may you become fever, wind-disease, and dropsy;
may you become epilepsy, insanity, constipation, and delusion.
"Run quickly, run with speed! All of you, go without delay!
Let the embodied beings be subdued, dragged away, and brought here according to their due, according to their deeds, and according to the time—do not tarry!"
Let them kill [him] at the end of his lifespan so that death does not overtake him prematurely.
Whether he is awake, asleep, unconscious, or in deep sleep,
act according to what must be done so that the appointed time does not pass.
"As Rudra commands, as the Lord Saṃkarṣaṇa commands,
as Brahmā and Dharmarāja command, so does the Lord Citragupta command.
Thus Citragupta issues his order, and they depart accordingly.
The messengers of Yama bring embodied beings into his presence.
Having examined their deeds, Yama and Citragupta indeed dispense punishment there; this is what I shall tell you as it was heard by me. (15–16)
"Let this meritorious donor go to the heaven of the lords of the earth;
let him indeed become a tree and be born as a beast;
let him be a serpent, yet let him attain the supreme goal."
"May this scorner of his own ancestors go to a terrible hell;
may they indeed consume him, who abandons his wife, in the Raurava hell.
May these others be released, and may they be freed from their sins. (18–19)
Let those most righteous ones, having dwelt for many kalpas in heaven,
go to birth as humans on this earth abounding in all prosperity—
those who have met their death for the sake of Brahmins, for the sake of cows, or for the sake of the kingdom.
Let them send him to Śakra’s Amarāvatī without delay;
let his residence there for one kalpa be conducive to his happiness.
He is devoted to giving much and compassionate toward all living beings.
Let them honor him with perfumes and garlands, and present him with gifts;
let him be fanned with yak-tail whisks, and let a vehicle be provided for him.
Let him travel by means of a celestial vehicle to the city of Indra.
Honored by the sounding of conchs and trumpets, may he obtain happiness.
May this man go to the world of the virtuous, the auspicious abode of the famous;
through his virtues, such as service and the like, may he indeed possess the lifespan of Indra in the third heaven.
May this giver of jewels and gold indeed go to the world of the Aśvins;
may this performer of the gift of abundant food indeed proceed to the world of Śiva;
and may this milker of sweet milk and giver of cows [attain the same].

The donor of golden cloth shall dwell for thirty million years in the third heaven. Let alone one who has fallen from there; even such a person, if he remains here on earth as an excellent sage and gratifies the ancestors, shall indeed go to Satyaloka.
Granting all desires and devoted to the welfare of all beings,
may this giver of land indeed go to heaven for a long time.
In this way, may those who perform meritorious deeds go to the heavens that bestow desired enjoyments.
"Indeed, let evildoers go down to the hells of accumulated afflictions.
Thus have I heard, O Brahmins! And I have also heard of the arising of its fruit.
I shall relate all of that; listen with concentrated minds."
May this man, who honors guests, shows compassion toward all beings,
provides food equally, and eats only what remains,
go to the realm of Vairāja, endowed with all fortune and happiness.
The Gandharvas shall sing of him, and likewise the Apsarases shall dance at his departure.
Let a divine seat be given; let a celestial vehicle be given.
Whatever desires he may wish for, let them be granted at my command.
Let them indeed bestow upon him those desiring heaven, those desiring ancestors, those desiring truth, and those singing the Virāj hymns—
along with male and female slaves and household furnishings.
Let there be gifts bestowed by him, such as jewels, gold, cows, and so forth.
Cows, elephants, horses, fields, and garden groves;
the many gifts of daughters and also the gifts of food that were given here—let that illustrious one be beheld as he enjoys them in heaven along with his followers. (36–37)
As celestial chariots arrived from heaven in their entirety, he, along with his followers and retinue, went by means of those excellent vehicles to the abode of the gods,
highly honored by the deities.
Let that meritorious man take delight right there as long as he remains in heaven.
Now, let them honor this performer of sacrifice, the giver of many daughters, with all their desires; may he indeed attain the station of Viṣṇu.
"Let this meritorious man, who is compassionate toward all beings, take his delight there for a thousand times ten thousand years. Let worship be offered to him;
let him remain in heaven like a god for ten thousand divine years."
Therefore, offer him worship by presenting the umbrella, the bowl, as well as the garment, the sandals, and food that have been given by him;
let this man become a Vidyādhara, marvelous with his lotus-like hands and feet.

"Let these four great lotuses remain forever in heaven. Because of this milk, curd, and ghee given by him to the helpless and the poor, let it be taken to the flavorful heavens; and you must offer him worship."
And provide vessels filled with cow's milk.
Having given these to his own kinsmen, and having drunk [the milk] together with his own people and relatives,
let him go to the Anasūyaka heaven and rejoice there for ten million years.
Constantly served by many beautiful women, may this immortal one always dwell in the Golokas, provided with all objects of enjoyment;
for he is the giver of the essence of sugarcane and the bestower of the essence of milk.
The giver of the essence of food, as well as the giver of garments and ornaments;
the giver of houses and fields, and the giver of all household utensils—
let him be led to the worlds of Goloka, accompanied by the bull-vehicle.
There dwell goddesses who are the embodiments of all deities, acting as attendants;
these auspicious ones hold nectar and serve [it] day and night.
Curds, milk, ghee, nourishment, the purifier, the sacred ford, and nectar—[these are present there].
The gods and others are satisfied by curd, while Maheśvara is satisfied by milk.
Pāvaka is always satisfied by ghee, and Pitāmaha by milk-rice (pāyasa). By offering these even once, they are gratified for thirteen years.
By drinking the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice (vājimedha).
The products of the cow are supremely pure; indeed, cows are sacred deities.
Among the tamed [limbs] dwell the Maruts and the gods; Sarasvatī dwells upon the tongue.
In the middle of his hooves dwell the Gandharvas, and in the tips of his hooves the Pannagas;
in all his joints reside the Sādhyas, and the moon and sun are in his eyes;
the constellations are upon his hump, and Dharma is established in his tail.
All sacred fords reside in the *apāna*; Lakṣmī dwells in the excrement;
the goddess Jāhnavī is in the urine; and the oceans are in her breasts.
The sages are in the pores of her skin, while the *vidyādharas* are upon her body hairs.
In the skin is Vaikuṇṭha itself, and on the two sides are the two pathways.
Forgiveness, fortitude, peace, nourishment, growth, memory, intelligence, wisdom, modesty, physical splendor, fame, learning, tranquility, and progeny [reside there]. (57–58)
The wives of Dharma, such as Kriyā, Utkarṣiṇī, and others, are established among cows.
Wherever there are cows, there are the gods, Lakṣmī, and Dharma as protectors. The giver of a cow obtains everything—palatial mansions and dwellings.
Young women, male and female servants, beds, seats, and drinks;
objects of enjoyment, stores of beverages, houses, edibles, and meals;
horses, elephants, vehicles, mounts, and gardens.
"O followers, by the command of Citragupta, deliver this donor of cows;
likewise, deliver this donor of mangoes and the one who has offered a garden.
Grant him a beautiful mango grove and an excellent, divine maiden."

Thus, in many ways, he both heard and saw such things there as he traveled from house to house and from place to place— experiences ranging from hardship to even greater hardship, and likewise from gentleness to even greater gentleness, and from pleasure to even greater pleasure. (63–64)
I have witnessed both the destruction of karma and the great rise of karma;
therefore, I am here in the assembly of the Lord Dharmarāja.
Just then, Nārada, radiant with splendor, arrived there.
Having honored him, Yamarāja seated him upon a throne.
He said: "We have all been purified, and this region has been sanctified by your arrival.
O Blessed One, tell us what task must be done, or for whose sake it must be done."
Having heard this, Nārada said: "Sever my great doubt:
by what means do they attain immortality—by gift-giving or by observance, by a vow or by austerity, or by recitation or by worship? (68)
By what means do people attain incomparable prosperity, fame, and eternal status?
By what do they go to the most sinful hell, which is censured by the world?
Tell me all this in accordance with truth; it will be for my supreme benefit.
King Yama said to him in the hearing of those present there:
"By righteousness people go to heaven, which is acquired through merit;
but by unrighteousness they go to hells and to various kinds of bonds. (71)
O Nārada, one who maintains the sacred fire never goes to hell at any time.
[Such a person is] possessed of sons, a donor of land, heroic, and proficient in the Vedas and Śāstras;
he is endowed with knowledge, walks the path of truth, is devoted to his wife, and she is devoted to her husband.
Embodied beings who are free from deceit and hypocrisy, devoted to their masters, non-violent, ungratefulness-free, and established in celibacy and other virtues;
who are charitable, devoted to the twice-born, and devoted to their parents—such are the virtuous ones. (74)
The virtuous— those who are free from stealing, free from adultery, compassionate,
and knowers of the Self within all beings— never go to the hells.
[Those others go] to the hells filled with torment, full of suffering, inhabited by the most wicked, and shrouded in darkness.
Those people here who possess knowledge, those who have attained supreme learning,

those who remain indifferent and do not act for the sake of their master, and those people who have been slain— all these were devoted to the welfare of all, intent on service, and truly generous. (77)
Likewise, those who have performed the gifts of sesame, cows, land, gold, and maidens;
those who have given food and water, as well as those who have established sacrificial sessions (*satra*);
those who are performers of sacrifices, the skillful, and those who have undertaken the vows of the four-month period (*cāturmāsya*). || 78–79 ||
Those who observe vows such as the Kārtika-vrata, who abide by the commands of their guru,
who possess virtues such as silence, and who constantly engage in the study of sacred texts;
those who are self-controlled, gentle, established in their own true nature, and likewise have conquered their senses on the full-moon days.
Having turned away from all desires, free from hope, and having conquered their senses,
they do not go to the hells and they attain immortality.
Indeed, through devotion to Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, they truly attain immortality.
Through the gift of knowledge and fearlessness, through the rule of lifelong commitment (*naiṣṭhika-niyama*),

through the vow of Brahman, through the austerity of the self that is knowledge, and by the chanting of *oṃ hariḥ*, as well as by the worship of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, one indeed attains eternal immortality.
Indeed, service to Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa bestows prosperity and Lakṣmī.
Service to the virtuous and service to cows indeed bestows fame and a high station. But by performing an action censured by the world, one goes to a censured state. (84–85)
Through austerity, heaven is attained; through austerity, fame is attained.
Indeed, longevity, enjoyments, and knowledge, as well as wisdom, health, beauty, good fortune, and prosperity, all come about through austerity alone. (86)
Wealth, a wife, sons, and servants—all this is obtained through austerity (tapas).

Likewise, perfection of speech is attained through silence (mauna), supreme happiness through contentment (santoṣa), enjoyments through giving (dāna), and long life through celibacy (brahmacarya). 87–88.
Through non-violence one attains freedom from agitation, and through initiation, birth into a noble family.
For those who subsist on fruits and roots, the reward is sovereignty; for those who subsist on leaves, it is heaven.
Those who subsist on milk go to the celestial realm, and those who give wealth attain prosperity.
Through service to the guru and the giving of funeral offerings (śrāddha), one obtains an auspicious lineage.
By the gift of juices, those who sleep on grass obtain cows and other cattle.
By performing the three daily ablutions oneself, one attains Brahman; by the falling of water [as a gift], one shares in the world of the gods.
The performer of sacrifice goes to heaven and rejoices in good fortune;
by the gift of food, one obtains food, intelligence, memory, and the celestial realm.
By the gift of an umbrella, one attains sovereignty; by the gift of a house, houses and the like.
By the gift of a chariot, one shall possess vehicles and mounts;
by the giver of clothing, one shall obtain fine ornaments, wealth, and sons;
and the giver of water indeed attains eternal satisfaction in heaven. (93–94)
One is well-satisfied by the enjoyment of sensual pleasures through the gift of food, drink, and so forth.
The giver of trees bearing flowers, fragrance, and fruit possesses a home like a jewel among women.
[He gives] beds, ointments, perfumes, collyrium, and incense.
He who gives a garland, a bed, a grove, or a fruit-bearing tree,
attains a house abounding in women and filled with elephants and horses.
Furthermore, the giver of incense and lamps attains equality with the Vasu gods.
By the gift of an elephant, a cow, or a bull, eternal heaven is attained.
By the gift of clarified butter, one indeed becomes radiant and delicate.
By the gift of oil, one becomes smooth and possesses a wondrous charm.
One who gives honey, sweet sugar, and so forth, shall have a satisfied household.
From the gift of lamps one becomes radiant; from milk-rice (*pāyasa*), the body becomes firm.
From *kṛsarā* rice, one attains an oily and gentle disposition as well as beauty of form. (1.361.99–100)

Through fruits one obtains a son, and through flowers, good fortune as well; furthermore, through chariots one obtains a divine celestial vehicle (*vimāna*), or a carriage, or even a mount. Moreover, by the gift of fearlessness and the gift of life, [one attains these rewards].
"By granting all desires, one shall obtain all desires.
(102) Thus, O Lakṣmī, has been told to you that fruit which was spoken by Yama to Nārada, and all of that was [further] told by Nāciketas to the Brahmins. (103)

Having heard this, Nārada bowed repeatedly to Yamarāja and departed through the air for Satyaloka, taking with him the honors [he had received]. Thus ends the three hundred and sixty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Activity of the Messengers to Bring the Sinners to the Wheel of Yama by the Command of Citragupta, the Arising of the Fruits of Given Gifts, the Arising of the Fruits as Told to Nārada by Dharmarāja, and His Arrival," in the first section on the Continuation of the Kali Age of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
← Chapter 361: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga) Chapter 362 [[Author: → Chapter 363
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, Lakṣmī! I shall tell you what happened there after that—how Nāciketa spoke to the twice-born ones exactly as he had seen it in truth.
Let the Brahmins there listen: the wise Dharmarāja saw ascetics endowed with spiritual perfection, traveling toward heaven in celestial chariots as bright as the sun,
accompanied by their wives and kinsmen.
They were full of affection, their faces radiant with a mass of merit.
(3) Then, instantly, Dharmarāja became deeply distressed;
his face turned pale from rage, and he was deprived of his splendor and luster. (4)
Seeing him in such a state, I asked him directly:
"How is it that you, who are so radiant, have come to such a loss of color?
O King, why do you suffer thus? I wish to know this."
Then King Yama spoke, causing [the messengers] to turn pale with grief:
"The Yāyāvaras, who subsist by gleaning grains, who are devoted to the study of the Vedas, who perform hospitable rites for guests, who are yogis, and whose senses are conquered; || 6-7 ||"
But those virtuous men who are devoted to the celibate life (*brahmacarya*), as well as faithful wives—
they all disregard me and go above me, O twice-born one!
They do not wait upon Yama, for they are certainly not under my control.
They go to my head, accompanied by their wives and followers;
their limbs are anointed with divine perfumes and adorned with garlands and ornaments,
as they speak so that I may become withered.
We do not take Yama into account; we go to that supreme state.
O Death! For whose sake do you stand? Who is death, and who is Yama?
For our sake, this Yama and even the Lord of Yama are rendered purposeless.
"You always strike down those possessed of faults, the most wicked who are devoid of dharma.
"Even though you are capable of obstructing us, we shall go to the supreme state"—speaking thus, they depart as celestial beings in their chariots; this I have heard.
"O best of the twice-born, I am unable to perform the acts of restraint or favor that are possible for yogis; though I am capable, I hear this [from them], and because of it, I suffer.
O twice-born one, perceiving my own lack of power in relation to them, I am deeply distressed."
Thus spoke Dharmarāja to me there in that moment.
Then, a certain virtuous woman devoted to her husband arrived before us in a celestial chariot;
she was of great splendor, accompanied by her followers, her husband, and her attendants.
Full of joy, she spoke words that were pleasant and beneficial to the King of Dharma:
"O King of Dharma! O most venerable one! O Lord, do not fall into dejection!
The Brahmins, ascetics, peaceful ones, the virtuous, the noble women, and the forest-dwellers—"
They are beautiful to behold, worthy of homage, and by their own power they have reached the further shore.
O Dharma! The majesty and power of these ascetic practices bestow the attainment of liberation, grant the world of Īśa, and are higher than the highest. (18–19)
Virtuous Brahmins are inconceivable to all beings;
Brahmins who are virtuous are always worthy of worship, for they are all the gods themselves.
One should not harbor ill-will toward them, and one must utterly avoid envy.
"Passion, anger, and likewise delusion must never be indulged in by the virtuous.
Having spoken thus and paid her respects, she departed for the supreme heaven.
Thereupon, I indeed questioned Dharmarāja as to what had occurred.
Then Dharmarāja told me the entire story from the beginning:
"O Brahmin, in former times, during the Kṛta Yuga, there was a highly illustrious king named Nimi, endowed with righteousness, splendor, heroism, and a vow of truth. (23)
His son was named Mithi, by whom Mithilā was built.
Because he was the progenitor (janaka) of Mithilā, his secondary name was Janaka.
His wife was named Rūpavatī, who did what was dear and pleasing to her husband.
Devoted with great affection and obedient to the words of her husband,
old age, disease, and death did not prevail in their kingdom;
the rain fell constantly, and no person anywhere was afflicted by illness.
The queen, upholder of dharma, spoke these words with humility to the king:
"O King, you have performed sacrifices and fed the brahmins therein;
you have given various kinds of gifts, and no small amount of wealth has been distinguished."
Whatever wealth you possessed on this earth, as well as in your home— belonging to your servants, the twice-born, and your attendants—
all of that was entirely employed for the purpose of giving.
"O King, you do not understand from where one should request food.
There is not even a single cowrie shell in the house, nor anywhere else;
indeed, only leaves, flowers, fruits, and roots have been given to the sages."
The fields, the gardens, and the entire kingdom were placed at the disposal of the Brāhmaṇas;
there was not even a cow or anything else, nor ever any garments.
Furthermore, there was no annual income whatsoever for their food.
"Tell me, O Lord, how indeed should one conduct oneself for the sake of pacifying hunger!
(33) Having heard these words of his beloved, Janaka said to the beautiful woman:
"Listen, I shall speak what is beneficial; if you consider it credible. (34)
"O beloved, for those of us who subsist on sacrificial offerings, these hundred years have passed;
we have indeed cleared the field with spades and wooden tools.
From this, the acquisition of food, drink, clothing, and so forth will result, and our religious duty shall be fulfilled."
"Having obtained food to chew, food to eat, and other things besides, you shall attain happiness.
Thus addressed, the queen, greatly delighted, said to the king:
"In your residence, there are thousands of male servants and female slaves."
In your house there are tens of millions of horses, elephants, and cows;
tens of millions of camels, buffaloes, and donkeys;
and tens of millions of bulls and servants.
"O King, employ all of them in your desired agricultural work.
The king said: "O Queen, those indeed have already been given away by me in charity—the oxen, donkeys, horses, elephants, camels, and men. (1.362.40)

All have been appointed to the acts of giving; indeed, I have no ownership over them. Whatever wealth there is here—whether of iron, tin, copper, silver, or gold—all that has been employed for the purpose of giving in this sacrifice.

"O knower of dharma! Indeed, I do not see any gold or even iron in the house, O Queen, with which I might fashion a spade for the work of cultivation. Thus addressed, the beautiful Rūpavatī spoke to the king, greatly delighted:
"Let us go, O King! May it be well; exertion bestows prosperity.
Thus addressed, the son of Nimi went to the sacred field accompanied by his wife.
"This auspicious field of mine is always filled with forest trees."
"Stay here; that which is unprepared, unplowed, or given away in vain shall not be [harvested].
I will cut down those few shrubs and thorns, and you, my dear, clear away these very few blades of grass and the like. (45–46)
Thus addressed, the great queen, devoted solely to her husband,
took refuge in the shade of a tree and began cutting grass and shrubs.
Meanwhile, by virtue of the power of her merit, she who protected her husband’s word—
A great golden thicket, bestowing gold, was seen at her side.
That gracious queen spoke these sweet words:
"A tree is seen here at our side; it is a supreme, golden thicket. (48–49)

Just then, she saw another tree adorned with fruits and the like; then a third tree was seen there, provided with things for eating. Yet, no water was seen there in the vicinity of that forest ground.
Delighted, she said to the king, "Food has been obtained, but indeed no water.
Seeing this, the king also spoke to her: "How is this possible?
Previously, the water and food were given; everything runs ahead [of me]."
"Everything that is done is indeed attained, but never that which is not done;
even the water that has been offered will certainly be reunited [with its source].
Having spoken thus, the king, together with his wife, purified the sacred field.
In the midst of the sky, that fierce sun blazed intensely;
the heat grew great and terrible, and the queen became parched with thirst.
Her smooth, copper-palmed feet were overcome by the feverish heat.
Her hands were as red as coral and her body was likewise delicate;
distressed by the heat of the sun and severely tormented by its intense warmth,
the beautiful woman fell to the ground in a swoon due to the force of her thirst.
As she was falling, she beheld the sun with a distraught gaze.
As she fell by chance, the sun was gazed upon with anger;
because of that, the exceedingly radiant sun became terrified in the sky.
Deprived of his celestial station, he fell from heaven onto the surface of the earth;
he became lusterless, his complexion faded, and he grew cold.
In the presence of that devoted wife, the splendor of the sun vanished.
King Janaka said: "Protect [me], you who are empty of intrinsic nature!
For what purpose have you come here to the earth, abandoning your splendor?
What shall I do for the sake of your worship? I pay homage to you, O Bhāskara!"
To the king who was speaking thus, Sūrya replied with humility:
"This wife of yours is devoted to her husband; she has become slightly angry with me.
By the power of her wrath, I have fallen down unconscious."
A woman equal to her does not exist anywhere in the three worlds.
Oh, what supreme service! Oh, what supreme austerity!
Oh, what fortitude and power! Her auspicious qualities are just like yours.
She is worthy of you, pure, and follows your mind;
through her devotion to her husband and her asceticism, this virtuous woman is intent on your welfare.
Like a wish-fulfilling tree, she is a fitting match for you in the worship of the gods.
The worthy recipient has obtained a vessel containing the great fruit of his meritorious deeds.
Whether the desire you formed was appropriate or inappropriate,
it shall surely not be frustrated by the power of her devotion to her husband.
Make of this field whatever you desire, just as you have conceived in your mind.
I shall indeed provide water like divine nectar;
I shall also provide this food and these two most excellent, celestial sandals.
An umbrella, a celestial bed, the wish-fulfilling cow, and an auspicious gem;
even an inexhaustible vessel that constantly fills itself with food and other provisions—
having spoken thus, the Sun himself created a water-vessel.
Savitar, overflowing with affection, gave sandals, a jewel, an umbrella, a bed, a vessel, and likewise a cow to that king of Mithilā.
He spoke again to the monarch: "Give [these] to the queen and bring her comfort."

The field will be glorious, yielding fruit, and even granting all desires. Then, having been revived by the king with water, that queen regained consciousness, her fear vanished, and she spoke thus to the king.
"By whom were the cool water, the divine parasol, the sandals, the bed, the cow, the jewel, the vessel, and the food given? Tell me this.
The King replied, "O Queen, it was Sūrya himself, out of compassion for you."
"Having abandoned all these gifts, I have come here [to you] like the open sky.
Having spoken thus, Sūrya was honored by the two of them; and being treated with hospitality by Sūrya, they requested of him: "O Blessed One, what shall we do for you?"
Thus addressed, Vivasvān spoke for the sake of his own protection:
"Let there always be safety for me from those women who are devoted to their husbands;
let no affliction ever come to me from such faithful wives."
Having heard the words of Sūrya, the queen said, "So be it.
"Fear not, O Sarvanetra! It shall be as you have requested.
Thus addressed, the Sun-god departed for his own orb in the sky.
This very Janaka’s lady, devoted to her husband and endowed with beauty,
has obtained everything in the forest through the power of her devotion to her husband.
Even I, the son of the Sun, worship her who is firm in her vow to her lord.
O Brahmin, she has no restrictive rule; for her ascetic practice is indeed independent.
She observes neither fast nor performs any act of giving, nor does she worship a deity apart from her husband.
When he sleeps, she sleeps; when he is awake, she remains vigilant. (8.1–8.2)
If she eats only after her husband has been fed, she certainly conquers death;
if he remains silent and she remains silent, and he stands and she stands, she likewise conquers death.
With a single gaze and a single-minded focus, she acts according to her husband's word.
We all—gods, daityas, and dānavas—stand in awe of her.
She is a virtuous woman worthy of worship even by the gods, devoted to contentment and noble vows;
she who, once addressed by her husband, would never refuse him. (84–85)
Though she remained devoted in her service, she was rejected by her beloved;
yet she never turned to any deity other than her husband.
Thus, that woman who is devoted to her husband does not enter the mouth of death.
Thus, she who is always devoted to the pleasure and welfare of her husband follows after him constantly like a shadow;
she shall never indeed enter the gateway to the mouth of death. (86, 88)
"He is my mother, he is my father, he is my kinsman, and he is my supreme deity.
Thinking thus, she always triumphs over me by serving her husband;
meditating upon her husband, she follows after her husband. (89)

Lamenting for her husband, she does not perceive the door of death. (1.362.90) She who neither hears nor sees songs, instrumental music, dances, nor various spectacles, does not perceive the door of death. (91)
Whether she is bathing, standing, or even performing her adornment,
if she returns when summoned, she does not behold the gateway of death.
Or, she who attends to her husband while he is worshipping the deities or eating—
She who does not abandon food out of mental attachment sees no door of death;
she who does not look upon another with her mind sees no door of death; and she who daily sweeps the house before the sun has risen sees no door of death. (93–94)
She who gazes upon her husband’s face, who conforms to her husband’s mind,
and who conducts herself for her husband’s welfare, does not behold the door of death.
She whose eyes, body, and inner disposition are always well-restrained—
Endowed with purity and proper conduct, she indeed does not behold death.
These women of renowned merit are seen in this world as goddesses in heaven;
even the wives of men are seen in heaven as goddesses.
Those devoted wives were honored by my father, Āditya;
therefore, I too always honor those devoted wives.
Thus, indeed, devoted wives always proceed by this very path.
Having constantly rescued many [beings], they are always worshipped by me;
yet they are not restrained by me, for I am not capable of restraining them.
But that wife of Janaka, out of a desire for water, [remained] for half a moment. (1.362.100)
Just as she arrived there, the Sun appeared and gave her water;
having accepted the worship performed by me, he quickly departed for his own Lord.

(101) Thus ends the three hundred and sixty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Attainment of All Prosperity—Fruits, Food, Water, Gold, and so forth—through the Power of Chastity by Rūpavatī, the Wife of Janaka named Mithilā, in the Forest, and the Narration of the Dharma of Chaste Women," within the section on the Greatness of Chaste Women in the Southern Circle, in the first book, the *Kṛtayugasantāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. (362)
