Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Having heard the dharma of devotion to one’s husband from the mouth of Yama, Nāciketa asked Yama about that which is auspicious and brings benefit to all the worlds. (1)
Listen, O Lakṣmī! I shall speak according to what was asked by Nāciketa:
"O Dharmarāja! O mighty-armed one! O you of great asceticism, please tell me.
All people desire happiness through penances, vows, and other such means. (2)
Thus, for those who have taken refuge in such hardships, how can the mind give rise to evil?
(3) Indeed, human beings possess hundreds of various vows and means as virtuous dharmas leading to the highest good;
whose is this sinful deed, and who is the doer or the instigator? (4)
"How does the mind arise toward hatred, or how is it born toward passion?
Who alone draws forth the fourfold collection of beings in this world?
Having heard this, the god Yama said: "O Brahmarṣi, let that be heard."
Human beings were created by Brahmā solely for the sake of their ultimate welfare (śreya).
Those born of other wombs are indeed subject to suffering, whereas humans are truly happy.
Having become devoted to dharma and knowledge, they are intent upon the supreme good through bhakti.
"By means of austerity, vows, and gifts, may they go to heaven and liberation"—
for those possessed of passion, sensory pleasure is provided therein for the sake of attaining happiness,
such as wealth, wives, and the like, as well as constant tactile pleasures. (8)

They are always content and satisfied, practicing the remembrance of the Self (ātma-smaraṇa). They are not dragged away by excessive force, because they turn back from it and find happiness therein. Through indulgence, craving arises; its strength is thereby produced. (1.363.10)
Abandoning the path of right reasoning, one proceeds toward evil through craving, through a mind intent on self-interest, and through that which is mixed with desire, anger, and the like—
craving which takes the form of a mirage and is like the loss of objects experienced in a dream. (11)

For the most part, one who is helpless is enveloped by actions that are fruitless or result in bondage. (12) The activity of another is not sinful; rather, it is the activity of one possessed by craving alone.
There is no other agent or instigator except for one's own craving. (13)
When one's desires are not attained, one becomes an object of hatred; when they are attained, one becomes filled with passion.
Drawn there by craving, the undiscerning person proceeds further.
He performs both right action and wrong action, and that which is thus performed becomes accumulated karma.
The self causes itself to fall; it experiences the fruit of the action performed by itself.
O Brahmin, the self becomes both its own enemy and its own friend, according as it encounters previously committed good or evil deeds. (15–16)
Having entered hundreds of wombs, the individual soul (jīva) indeed experiences in this world the suffering ordained by its own past actions as its own object of experience.
The inner self (antarātman), residing within the heart, perceives the entire universe.
Through volition as well as through power, in accordance with the karma of living beings,
that which is auspicious or inauspicious manifests at the proper time. Indeed,
knowledge and action belong to living beings, and by means of these two, they perform karma.
Knowledge and action, however, reside in the soul; for these two are dependent upon the soul like the wings of a bird.
With its two wings, it indeed flies forward toward objects and places out of thirst.
One who acts rightly becomes truly good, partaking in the merit of heaven and other realms.
One who performs evil becomes an evildoer and partakes in the sin of hell.

(21) Through *māyā* and the body, however, Brahman may possess the status of being the material cause (*upādānatva*); through time, which is the Great Power (*mahāśakti*), its status as an auxiliary cause (*sahakāritva*) is declared. (22)
In that regard, Hari is indeed merely the instrumental cause by virtue of His volition;
just as the Lord is the cause in creation, so too is the individual soul the cause in action.
For in the procreation of a son, the embodied soul is the material cause.
Even by taking [the seed] at the time of the season, there is likewise the state of being a co-operator;
and for the soul endowed with desire, there is also the status of being merely an instrumental cause.
Thus, in all cases, souls possess both causality and a share in the fruit. (24–25)
Therefore, having understood through the scriptures and other means, one should perform that action which leads to the highest good;
one should abandon by all means that which leads to what is not the highest good, through both knowledge and effort.
Indeed, in whatever measure the inauspiciousness of a person comes to an end—
In that very way, pure intelligence increases and proceeds;
he performs auspicious deeds that destroy the afflictions and remove evil.
Indeed, when stainless merit has been acquired, he is honored among the immortals.
Indeed, the attainment of the manifestation of fruits is brought about by the Inner Controller (Antaryāmin).
Heaven is the attainment of auspicious fruits, while hell arises from sin. O Nāciketas, listen in that regard to the path of virtue created by yourself.
By means of mind, action, speech, austerity, or conduct,
he who relies solely on what is auspicious is liberated from sins—
he who is equal toward all beings, self-conquered, and tranquil in mind. (1.363.30–31)
One who performs service for others turns away from the suffering of others;
one who constantly bestows happiness upon others is liberated from sins.
He who correctly understands the true nature of reality—the insentient, the sentient, and their qualities—[is liberated].
Free from delusion and without dependence, he attains the eternal state.

(33) Having fully understood the qualities and the absence of qualities, possessing discernment regarding the perishable and the imperishable, and being intent on meditation upon the Self, that knower is liberated from all evils. (34)
One who regards his own body and the bodies of others as equal to himself and to another,
who is observant of the vow of non-violence and possessed of wisdom, shall certainly be liberated from sin.
He who causes no agitation and is free from thirst, anger, and the like— || 35 ||
He who follows the path of justice is liberated from sins.
He who is constantly devoted to breath control (prāṇāyāma), who possesses concentration (dhāraṇā) and meditation (dhyāna),
and whose mind is completely withdrawn [from worldly objects], is liberated from sins.
He who has no desire for anything whatsoever, who is not covetous of desired objects,
and who is eternally contented, leaves the body and attains the supreme state.
One who possesses faith in the worship of the gods and is devoted to the service of the ancestors [attains this].
One who does not covet the property of others is liberated from sins.
One devoted to the service of the guru, free from malice, free from envy, and devoid of cruelty—one whose conduct is noble and whose character is not mean—is released from bondage. (1.363.40)
He who performs praiseworthy deeds, who is free from cruelty and malice,
and who performs auspicious festivals, is liberated from sins.
He who constantly goes to sacred fords (tīrthas), always remembering the pure Brahman, [is likewise liberated].
By following a blameless mode of livelihood, he is liberated from sins.
(42) Having risen, one should pay homage to the father as a deity, to the mother, to the teacher, to the twice-born, to the virtuous, and to the chaste woman; thus, he is liberated from sins. (43)
The giver indeed does not encounter suffering, nor does the striker lack happiness;
the devotee does not enter the cycle of worldly existence, nor does the seeker of sense-objects lack liberation.
This has been declared as the highest good and the benefit for all.
Nevertheless, I shall now describe a swift means for the destruction of sins—
one that is simple, achievable in an instant, and free from any exertion. Furthermore,
I shall speak of those holy teachers who are the sages that ferry one across the ocean of worldly existence.
The devotees of Hari, the gods, the sages, the great seers,
those who are truthful, virtuous women, those whose character is celibacy, and those who are bhāgavatas—
placing their heads at the feet of these, one should fix the mind upon their hearts.
One should abide by their command and remain intent on serving them.
(48) In whatever way and by whatever action the virtuous may repeatedly become pleased, one should conduct oneself accordingly; thus, one is liberated from sins. (49)
By chanting the Gāyatrī mantra, the meditator beholds both Soma and Sūrya;
through this vision with the realization of Brahman, the sin of the practitioner is destroyed.
One should circumambulate the Guru, meditate upon him, and worship him fully.
One should serve the Guru, who is Hari; he is liberated from sins.
By performing a hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), one is liberated from all sins.
Then, one should meditate upon the Sun and the Moon situated in the eyes, and [the Supreme] residing in the heart.
One who beholds [the Lord] complete, stainless, and perfectly radiant—
whether his sin be very small or as vast as the ocean— it is utterly destroyed.
By seeing the dwarf Brahmin and the Boar arisen from the waters...
And for one who bows to the lion mounted upon Siṃhikā, there is the destruction of all sins. (54) Cows are purifying, auspicious, and the deities even of the gods;
he who serves them with devotion is liberated from all evils. (55)
He who drinks the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) during an auspicious moment is liberated from the sins committed throughout his entire life at that very instant.
That person who receives upon their head the water drawn up by the tail [of a cow]—
Having obtained the fruit of all sacred fords (tīrthas), he is liberated from sins.
He who bathes with cow urine during the Rohiṇī asterism by means of a stream of urine—whatever faults have been committed through all sins are instantly burnt away; of this there is no doubt.

He who holds and drinks the stream of milk emerging from the udder of a cow at its very crest is liberated from all sins. In the morning, one should pay homage to the cow, the sun, a virtuous Brahmin, and a chaste woman.

He who offers curd, unbroken grains, and water is liberated from sins. (1.363.60) On the full moon day, having bowed to Arundhatī and the planets, he who offers curd, unbroken grains, and water to Soma is liberated from all sins. (61)
A Śūdra who serves a twice-born man has his sin destroyed.
This applies always during the equinoxes, at the yogas, at the transits of the sun and other such occasions,
on all days of religious vows, and in houses where festivals are held.

A Śūdra, by giving milk and curd, is liberated from all sins. (6.3) Having spread out Kuśa grass with its tips pointing eastward and likewise having established a bull, and having paid homage along with the twice-born, he is liberated from all sins. (6.4)

Having bathed on the southern bank of the river that flows toward the east, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and offer salutations; thus he is liberated from all sins. Taking water with a right-spiraling conch, he should place it upon his head.
A person surely pacifies the sins committed since birth.
Having gone to the Prāksrotas river and standing in water reaching up to the navel,
a man, after bathing, should offer seven handfuls of black sesame seeds mixed together.
Having performed three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), one should meditate upon Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa;
the sin committed throughout one's entire life perishes at that very moment.
[This is done] with a flawless lotus leaf and water containing all kinds of jewels.
The man who bathes three times [at this place] is liberated from all sins.
(69) He who performs the vow of the Ekādaśīs, who observes the Dvādaśīs, and who is a devotee of Nārāyaṇa—sin does not touch him at all. (70)
Those who seize the property of Brahmins, likewise those who kill Brahmins;
those intent on betraying their gurus, as well as those intent on betraying gods and friends;
those intent on betraying their masters, and those who violate the wives of others.
Those who steal the property of others, those who consume what is unfit to be eaten,
the hypocritical, those who violate the bounds of propriety, those who revile the Vedas and Brahmins,
those addicted to accepting gifts from the unworthy, and those who delight in approaching women who should not be approached; ||| 72–73 ||
Even those who are harmful, ensnarers, killers, or plunderers; those who are rogues, deceitful, fraudulent, and devoid of merit—
if they observe the eleventh and twelfth lunar days with faith, [they attain the highest state].
Having fasted upon it and becoming empty [of worldly attachments] today, they go to the supreme state.
(75) Therefore, no other means exists for the destruction of sin;
the white [fortnight] should be understood as bestowing devotion, while the black [fortnight] grants liberation. (76)
The Ekādaśī observed by men burns away the sin accumulated through mind, speech, and action over the course of a month.
One must not eat, one must not eat when the day of Hari has arrived.

But for one who is unable to fast on the full Ekādaśī, he should instead perform the *nakta* (eating at night) or the *ayācita* (eating only what is unasked for). Alternatively, the vow of Dvādaśī may be observed by means of a single meal or through the giving of gifts. (78–79)
But for those unable to observe fasts, the twelfth day, known as Prabodhinī, should be observed with a single fast;
it burns away all sin committed throughout one's life.
By worshipping Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord, on that day—
One obtains all this—the fruit of twelve Dvādaśīs.

That which is performed on the twelfth lunar day conjoined with Pūrvābhādrapadā is inexhaustible; the fruit when it is conjoined with Uttarābhādrapadā is ten million times greater than that. (8.1–8.2)

Everything performed during the *prabodhinī* [Ekādaśī] shall yield infinite fruit. By fasting according to the prescribed rule on the days of Hari’s lying down, waking, and turning over, the observer of the vow shall attain purity. (83)

The eleventh day (Ekādaśī) in the bright fortnight of the month of Kārtika, when joined with the moon and conjoined with the Uttarābhādrapada nakṣatra, is considered to bestow infinite fruit. When that Ekādaśī is joined with Mars, it yields the fruit of twelve Dvādaśīs. (84–85)
Therefore, one should observe the fast on the twelfth day with every effort.
They are blessed, they have achieved their life's purpose, and by them alone has merit been performed— those who,
after propitiating the Supreme Lord throughout thousands of previous births, [attain this].
O Brahmin, when all sins have been destroyed, one attains the state of a Vaiṣṇava.
Indeed, the highly fortunate Vaiṣṇavas purify the entire world;
likewise, by worshipping me, one goes to that supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
O twice-born one, whether remembered, praised, seen, or even touched,
a devotee of the Lord purifies— even if he be a cāṇḍāla— by the will of Hari.
Those high-souled Vaiṣṇavas who are intent upon the worship of Viṣṇu...
They cross over [the ocean of existence] and cause others to cross—women, Śūdras, and sinful people. (1.363.90) O Nāciketa! Listen to this supreme, purifying secret that must be guarded;
it is the great destroyer, swift and immediate, of even the most heinous sins. (1.363.91)
This is the purification for those who are utterly impure, as well as for those who have fallen from their status, for those engaged in ritual acts [of transgression],
for outcasts (cāṇḍālas), for those who commit violence, for those who consume liquor or commit theft, for those who engage in sexual misconduct,
and for those who cause the intermixture of castes.
I shall describe to you the cleansing of sins that are as indelible as adamantine cement:
the water washed from the feet of virtuous Vaiṣṇavas, the water in which they have bathed, and the water that has been drunk by them. (93–94)
Indeed, even water that has merely been touched must be drunk by the sinner;
for when even a single drop is drunk, his sins truly burst into flames.
[This applies] during drinking, bathing, sprinkling, casting water over the head, or smearing it on the limbs.
Upon the touch of the eyes, that water destroys the sins of lifetimes;
whatever evils there may be, even those of a sinful nature,
are indeed consumed by drinking the water from the vessel of the virtuous.
In the sight of the virtuous, even women, Śūdras, and even dog-cookers (śvapacas) are purified;
through the touch of the virtuous, even sinners become purifiers by their destruction.
A body devoted to the service of the virtuous becomes divine and non-material.
For those devoted to the service of the virtuous, divine fortune becomes the bestower of liberation.
Those who have bathed in the dust of the feet of the virtuous are partakers of emancipation.
That which is a vessel for the affection of the virtuous is declared to be a vessel of Śrī Hari.
O Nāciketa! The yoga of the virtuous is the yoga of Hari; of this there is no doubt.
My messengers do not go where the messengers of Viṣṇu—namely, the saintly—are present. Those women, men, and eunuchs who are oppressed by the messengers of Yama [are saved].
Then, by embracing the virtuous, they are swiftly liberated from Yama.
(1.02) Union with the saintly through all the senses bestows liberation and the state of Brahman;
this divine association with the virtuous is unsurpassed, and nothing else is superior to it. (1.03)
Through union with Hari, the saintly indeed become free from the modes of nature and embodiments of Brahman; through union with the saintly, even sinful souls become embodiments of Brahman.
Whatever object is touched by the virtuous becomes divine, transcendental, and free from the modes of nature.
Whether secret or manifest, all that conduces to becoming Brahman.
Thus, O Brahmin, I have told you the means for liberation;
go forth, endowed with self-knowledge, having obtained whatever else has been given.
Having spoken thus, O protector of the earth, that Lord Yamarāja rose from his own seat,
performed the appropriate worship for me, and after speaking pleasant words,
dismissed me with a deeply pleased heart.

"O Brahmins, this has been told to you concerning that king in his excellent city, exactly as it was seen and heard, and how I have come here. Thus, O Lakṣmī! Having heard these words of Naciketas, the gods on earth (the Brahmins) [were amazed].
Having recognized that water— which is the most supreme among all things, pleasing to the virtuous, and like nectar— the holy men, who are compassionate toward the distressed, were filled with joy.
Some among them there were forest-dwellers (vaikhānasas), and some were those who remained without seats (nirāsanās).

Some were Yāyāvaras, others were Vānaprasthas; some were Śālīnas, while others adopted the pigeon-like (Kāpotī) mode of subsistence. Still others lived by gleaning ears of grain (Śila-uncha), some were cooks, and others were those who did not cook for themselves.
Some were performers of various sacrifices, while others were self-conquered;
some observed silence and remained stationary, while others lived in water.
Likewise, some slept on their heads upon trees, and others lived like deer.
Likewise, there were others who maintained the five fires, some who subsisted on leaves and fruits,
those who lived on water, those who lived on air, and others who subsisted on vegetables;
these various ascetics were all established in eternal wisdom.
Having heard this account, the sages of divine luster were filled with wonder upon hearing of the majesty of the waters and their reliance on the virtuous;
they then went to the hermitage of the holy Badarī, where Nara and Nārāyaṇa dwell.

Intent on devotion, they desired to drink the water from his feet. (1.17) Then the righteous-souled Naciketas, seeing his son honored by Yama and seeing that the one whose wealth is austerity had returned, reflected once more upon Dharma alone. (1.18)
Nāciketa also taught his disciples the knowledge of the Self and strictly observed the purifying dharma of the virtuous.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have told you of the one of great power in the southern wheel.
That water which effects their deliverance is great and pleasing to the virtuous;
it belongs in every respect to the Yamunā, the Gaṅgā, and the Gomatī,
as well as to the Godāvarī, the Sarayū, and the Revā.

From all the waters of the Gaṇḍakī, the Svarṇarekhā, and the Tapatī, as well as from those of the Kāverī and the Tāmraparṇī, and from all the waters of the oceans and of every sacred bathing place (tīrtha)— from all these indeed [he drew].
The water from the feet of the virtuous is always divine, supreme, and purifying;
it grants all desires, bestows liberation, and is a great source of prosperity.
By hearing or reciting this, one shall obtain a fruit that bestows everything.

Thus ends the three hundred and sixty-third chapter, titled "The Description of Nāciketa’s Departure after Hearing the Words of Yamarāja," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. In this chapter, Nāciketa concluded his discourse by declaring that he had heard how King Yama described the causes for the occurrence of auspicious and inauspicious deeds, the means for liberation from sin, and how supreme well-being is attained through the service of cows, the Ekādaśī vow, the drinking of the nectar of the conduct of the virtuous, and other such practices; thereafter, the sages departed for Badrī-Nārāyaṇa.
Chapter 363. *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā* — Section 1 (*Kṛtayuga-santāna*).
Chapter 364 [Author:
Chapter 365 → Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O Kṛṣṇa! Previously, I heard from the lotus of your face that at the beginning of creation, you yourself manifested the *pativratā* (the devoted wife).
She exists on earth, in the netherworld (*pātāla*), in heaven, in the realm of truth (*satya*), and likewise in the two envelopments (*āvṛti*).
In Vairāja, in Vaikuṇṭha, and within the manifestations of the lords— indeed,
she is present everywhere in both the creation of individual souls and the creation of the Lord.
That all-pervading Great Power is the very embodiment of your sovereign capability.
In the beginning, she was born as Mahālakṣmī, named Kaṃbharā;
you yourself were born as Gopāla, the manifest Supreme Brahman.
The brāhmaṇa named Patnīvratā was Hari, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
The great king was self-born, the promoter of all dharmas.
His wife was Kambharālakṣmī, in whose house the mental son Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa was born as Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa himself. (5–6)
She is Lakṣmī and you are Kṛṣṇa; through your grace, I remember that.
For the dharma consisting of devotion to one’s husband is indeed the dharma of a virtuous wife, which bestows liberation, grants happiness, bestows heaven, and fulfills all desires. (7)
How could that which is identical with you and identical with me not deliver people?
(8) The dharma consisting of service to the virtuous prevails above all;
truthful, devoted wives, and saintly women cross over by means of service to the righteous. (9)
"You are one of virtuous form; indeed, you are one of chaste form.
The dharma of a chaste woman and the dharma of a virtuous man are as difficult to traverse as the edge of a sword.
Having heard that Janaka’s daughter was a beautiful and chaste woman, [he spoke thus].
I am particularly desirous of hearing about the power of virtuous women (*satī*).

By hearing of the efficacy of the power of virtuous wives, women who are objects of enjoyment and subject to the laws of desire will cross the ocean of worldly existence upon hearing of the strength of those devoted to their husbands.
Therefore, O Viṣṇu! O Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa! Please cause me to hear the wonders of the sovereignty of chaste wives that bestow happiness.
O Keśava! I wish to hear of those that have occurred, those that are occurring, and those yet to come.
Indeed, [I shall tell] the deeds of the virtuous women whose very nature is the power of existence.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to this supreme and auspicious matter which you desire to know.

"You appear to me to be compassionate for the sake of doing what is beneficial for women. I shall relate many wonderful accounts of virtuous women—of maidens, of married wives, and of lifelong celibates. (15–16)
Of virtuous wives, of widows, of self-sacrificing noble women, of yoginīs, and of those established in the state of the Bhāgavatas; of the splendor of the gods, of the wives of the ṛṣis,
of the consorts of the deities, of the wives of Brahmā, and of the women of Kṛṣṇa.
I shall relate these wonders; listen and be attentive to my words.
She who is Rādhikā in Goloka is Sāvitrī, who was created by Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa for the sake of Brahmā. 19.
At the very beginning of creation, she remained situated in the primordial Śvetadvīpa.
At that same time, O King, King Priyavrata was performing austerities at Badarikāśrama, and Nārada arrived there.
Seeing the sage in the sky, the king stood up with great joy.
Having offered him a seat and water for his feet, he asked respectfully:
"O Blessed One, is there some wonder occurring in this place known as Kṛta?"
"O Nārada, tell me of anything seen or even heard by you in this age!
Then Nārada spoke to him of a single marvel exactly as it had been witnessed:
"O Indra among kings, yesterday I went to Śvetadvīpa."
There he beheld a divine lake adorned with lotuses.
On the bank of that lake, seeing a large-eyed maiden, I was struck with wonder at that girl of long, beautiful eyes. (24–25)
I questioned her, O Indra among kings, that sweet-spoken lady: "Who are you, blessed one? How have you come to be here, and what is your purpose?
Tell me, O beautiful one, whose every limb is lovely, O auspicious lady, what must be done by you."
When she had been addressed thus by me, she gazed at me with unblinking eyes;
as soon as she stood silent after remembering [her past], my supreme knowledge,
all the Vedas, the Saṃhitās, and the fruits of ritual action were forgotten.

"O King, as soon as I saw everything, it was snatched away from me by the maiden in an instant. Thereupon, overcome with wonder and paralyzed by anxiety and grief, I went to her for refuge; and as soon as I looked at her again—"
At that moment, a divine man was seen within her body;
within the heart of that man was another,
and upon his chest yet another, glorious one with blood-red eyes, resembling twelve suns.
Thus I saw three men here who had entered the body of the maiden;
in an instant those three dissolved, and I beheld the maiden alone.
Then I asked that goddess, "How is it with my daughter?"

"The Vedas have perished; tell me, O blessed lady, the cause of their destruction. The maiden replied: "Because you do not recognize me as Sāvitrī, the mother of the Vedas, therefore your Vedas have been destroyed."
Having heard this, Nārada asked, "Who are these men?
The maiden replied, "This is the Ṛgveda within my heart, who is Nārāyaṇa;
he is Viṣṇu in the form of fire, the burner of sins through the mere utterance of his name."
In his heart is the second, the Yajurveda, who is Pitāmaha;
in his heart is the third, the Sāmaveda, who is indeed Śaṅkara.
When remembered, these two quickly burn away sins like the sun.
"O Sage! These three great Vedas are indeed the three gods. O Brahmin, accept the Vedic Gāyatrī and chant it as Vaiṣṇavī.
Then, O Nārada, accept the Vedas and omniscience."
"O son, perform your bath in this lake of the Vedas!
By bathing here, O son, you shall remember [the events] of another birth;
having bathed, I obtained that knowledge which was produced over a thousand years."
Formerly, there was a twice-born man named Sārasvata in the city of Puṣkara; I am indeed that very person, the mind-born son of Brahmā, standing here before you.
Sāvitrī was my mother, and she has since passed away.
With my divine vision, I beheld her in the world of truth (Satyaloka).
She is the lawful wife of the Creator, rich in majesty and devoted to her husband.
Having brought forth all beings, Brahmā repeatedly cast off his own body. (42–43)
Then, by the power of her devotion to her husband, Sāvitrī repeatedly created Brahmā from his corpse through the touch of her own hand;
she brought forth the Unborn One many times as he had died many times.
When creation had proceeded as desired, it then ceased from further death.
Having obtained that eternal Lord Brahmā as her husband, she, being devoted to her husband,
shall continue to live and does indeed live by the power of her wifely devotion.
Having addressed Death and repeatedly offered Brahmā to Death,
she restored her husband to life through the power of her devotion to her husband.
Furthermore, having offered the three Vedas as oblations, she gave back the three generations of her ancestors.
"By the power of her devotion to her husband, Sāvitrī is my mother.
O King, having performed my ablutions, I have come here desiring to see you.
Having paid homage to the Lord Nara-Nārāyaṇa, I shall now depart. (48–49)
Having spoken thus and bowed to Hari, Nārada departed for Satyaloka.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, has been described to you the great power of devotion to one's husband (pativratā).

Thus ends the three hundred and sixty-fourth chapter, titled "The Vision by Nārada of Sāvitrī as the Embodiment of the Three Vedas and the Three Deities, and the Description of how Brahmā’s Body was Restored Again and Again by the Power of Sāvitrī’s Devotion to Her Husband," in the first section on the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga within the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā, concerning the majesty of devoted wives.
← Chapter 364: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga) Chapter 365 [Author: Chapter 366 →
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, Lakṣmī! In heaven there are the gods, Gandharvas, and Maruts, as well as the planets, comets, constellations, and those who are the guardians of the directions.
The Vasus, the Nidhis, the Rudras, the Rishis, and likewise the Ravas;
the goddesses, the Apsarases, the Munis, the female servants, and the male servants;
Airāvata and the other elephants, the elephants of the quarters, and the horses.
Uccaiḥśravas and others, the swans, the Garuḍas, and the parrots;
the wish-fulfilling cows, the cattle, and the species of dogs beginning with Saramā;
as well as the rams, the buffaloes, and the lions that serve as the vehicles of the gods. (3–4)
They were all divine, capable of going wherever they desired, and likewise able to assume any form at will.
They were all endowed with the eight supernatural powers (aṣṭasiddhi) and possessed unobstructed vision. Their movements were unhindered, and they were proficient in all languages.

All those who know the divine language, who rely upon the merit of the Dharma, and who abide by their observances, enjoy the happiness of heaven for a long life. Even the peacocks, mice, and snakes that dwell in the houses of the gods [enjoy such bliss]. (6–7)
They were all capable of assuming any form at will and were devoted to their respective duties;
however, there was one female dog there who was Indra’s servant.
Saramā remained constantly under the authority of her husband, being a devoted wife.
The husband of Saramā was named Dyumeya, a servant of Indra.

Devoted to him, Saramā was faithful to her own lord and did what was pleasing to her husband; she remained obedient to her husband’s command and enjoyed the pleasures bestowed by her husband. (1.365.10)
This radiant one does not take food or anything else anywhere in between [meals],
having offered back to his master whatever has been received from whichever deities.
Thereafter, he indeed constantly takes [only what is necessary] and carries out the commands of his master.
Once, in the Kṛta Yuga, two Rākṣasas named Vidyut and Suvidyut suddenly went to heaven to fight with Indra. Having been defeated by those two most powerful beings, Mahendra fled.
The male and female servants, the mounts and others, including Saramā and the rest, having fled,
established a secret dwelling in the forest regions of Mount Meru.
The two Rākṣasas also, having seized the realm of Mahendra, became arrogant.
Rejoicing with delight, they went toward Mount Meru for the sake of recreation.
There, in that forest, having seen a beautiful, auspicious cave that was pleasant, fulfilling all desires, and enchanting, they entered it and took up their residence. (15–16)
Having gone to Indra’s city and returned to that cave,
both Asuras took their pleasure, embraced by many handmaidens.
But the gods fell into distress, being without King Indra.
Desiring the station of Indra, they deliberated calmly;
all of them, well-armored, united their armies against those two.
Then Bṛhaspati, the preceptor of the gods, spoke to them there.
"Perform first the Gomedha sacrifice to Viṣṇu, the Lord;
[offer] the pure milk and clarified butter of cows to the form of Agni.
Having fed [the priests] and regained strength, you should then perform sacrifices with further rites."
"When this is done, victory will be yours, but not otherwise.
This instruction has been given by me; let it be carried out quickly.
Having been addressed thus, the gods then [set out] for the sake of the milk-rice and other offerings.
Having brought the wish-fulfilling cows (*kāmadhenūḥ*) to the sacrificial ground in the Merv forest,
they, constrained by their preceptor, undertook the performance of the sacrifice.
In the morning, they [offered] milk, curds, ghee, and abundant clarified butter from the cows.
They constantly offer [the milk] to Kratu, Agni, Viṣṇu, and also to the gods.
During the day, all those cows go to the grassy lands and to the fearless open spaces for food, for the sake of grazing on grass and the like. (24–25)
Then Indra was urged and instructed there by the gods:
"For the sake of protecting the cows, dispatch messengers constantly.
At that time, Saramā, a devoted wife, was given as a dog by Indra.
By the power of her devotion to her husband, she was a protector against all dangers.
She released the cows for grazing and gave Saramā to guard them.
Free from anxiety, the gods performed sacrifices to obtain strength. (27–28)
Those cows, devoid of their divine protector, while being guarded in a grassy meadow,
then went to where those asuras were grazing.
Seeing the herd of cows, Śukra and Mūka [informed] the family priest.
"Behold, O divine messenger, how we two, Brahmā and I, are being obstructed by Saramā as she guards [the horse].
Tell us how Indra may be deprived of it by Saramā, so that an obstacle may arise;
instruct us quickly regarding the sacrifice performed for the gods, and we shall act accordingly. (1.365.30–31)
Thus addressed, Śukra then replied to the Asuras:
"Let the cows be taken away quickly, O Asuras; do not delay for even a moment.
For cows are the root of sacrifice and the providers of nourishment for the gods."
If that [river] were blocked, there would be a cessation of sacrifice, and the gods would suffer distress.
Having been addressed thus, the Daityas then abandoned those cows at will.
When they had been taken away, Saramā became intent on searching for their tracks.
She saw the cows, the supporters of the sacrifice, being led away by the sons of Diti;
she also saw the dog Saramā, who had seen the path and was well-guarded by the Daityas.
Having seen Saramā, they spoke these words to her with conciliatory intent:
O Saramā, by no means report this to the gods;
do not say that the cows have been carried off by the Daityas, for it would bring you misfortune.
O auspicious Saramā, the milk of these cows is exceedingly dear to them. || 36–37 ||
Having said, "Drink at your leisure," they then gave her milk.
Having given her that incomparable milk, those leaders of the Daityas said:
"O blessed lady, do not [give this] to the king of the gods; rather, present these [other things] to him."
They spoke thus repeatedly to her; having heard them, she said to the Dānavas:

"I am not a dog of the gods, O Lord; indeed, I shall not become the opposite of a god."

"If I accept the food of my master as a token of his favor,
may the Daityas indeed be consumed here by fire through that merit."
"If I am always established in truthfulness in my speech,

By that merit, may the Daityas indeed be consumed by fire here,
if I am pleased with my own husband and am not pleased with any other.
By that merit, may the Daityas indeed be consumed by fire here.

May I share in their happiness when they are happy, and may I transcend suffering when they suffer.

When she had spoken thus, the Daityas, assuming the forms of dogs, surrounded her on all sides with a circle and were just about to touch that bitch,
when a fire arose— an exceedingly terrible forest conflagration.
He completely reduced everything to ashes, extending as far as the end of the Daityas.
Then a dog, having approached Indra and the other deities along with its own master,
related the entire account of what had occurred at the sacrifice.
Having heard this, the gods went there; taking the cows, they returned to the sacrifice.
Śukra, having raised the Asuras by means of mantras from the leaves of the *sañjīvanī* plant, led them away and, filled with pride, went to the sacrificial ground for the sake of battle.
Saramā, having taken leave of her husband, seized Śukra by the head. Meanwhile, Mahendra and the other gods, having attained strength and nourishment through the power of the sacrifice,
zealously arrayed their armies for the destruction of the Daityas.
Through the sacrifice being performed, the power of the deities increased.
When their strength had thus increased, Indra spoke to the divine armies:

Thus addressed, the gods then immediately donned their armor;

Chapter 367 → Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:

Listen, Lakṣmī! Hear of the supreme and most excellent power of Sāvitrī’s devotion to her husband, by which her lord was restored to life. She who was declared the mother of the Vedas and was worshipped by Brahmā in ancient times— || 1 ||

likewise, in the first age, the Satya Yuga, she was worshipped by King Aśvapati,
and subsequently, that devoted wife was honored by all human beings.
In the land of Madra, there was a virtuous great king named Aśvapati. He had a queen, Mālatī by name.
That chaste woman, following her husband's instructions, performed his worship.
Through supreme devotion to Sāvitrī and by the instruction of Vasiṣṭha,
she propitiated the Brahmanic Sāvitrī for many years;
yet she did not behold Sāvitrī, nor did she obtain even the slightest fruit.

The king, employing skillful policy, consoled her with words of comfort and, demonstrating fortitude, entrusted the burden of the kingdom to her while appointing her to the household.
For the sake of accomplishing the *sāvitrī*, he went to Puṣkara to perform austerities.

"A single recitation of the Gāyatrī removes the sin committed during the day."
Recitation ten times removes the sin committed during a day and night;
recitation a hundred times destroys the sin committed in a month;
and recitation a thousand times shall completely destroy the sin of a year. (13)
A recitation of one hundred thousand times destroys the dry and the moist sins of this birth.
(14) A recitation of ten million times destroys the sins of three births.
A recitation of one billion times will certainly destroy the sins of all previous births. (15)
A recitation of ten crores certainly grants liberation; of this there is no doubt.

Having made the hand into the shape of a serpent’s hood and raised it with the fingers joined at the tips, the twice-born man, standing motionless with his head bowed forward, should perform the recitation while facing the east. (16)
One should perform recitation in a temple or at a sacred ford (tīrtha) with a rosary made of *tulasī* wood,
or with a rosary of seeds or crystal beads numbering one hundred and eight,
strung upon seven leaves of the *aśvattha* tree and fashioned from beautiful gems.
Then, having placed it there, one should bathe it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
One should bathe it with water from sacred fords (tīrtha) or with meritorious water from the Gaṅgā.
Having recited the Gāyatrī mantra one hundred times, one should indeed cause it to become fit for recitation.

He should be known as liberated while living (jīvanmukta), and he effects the destruction of the sins of others.

One who performs sacrifices for Śūdras, one who has sexual intercourse with a woman in her menses, a sword-seller, an ink-maker, one who lives by agriculture, one who eats fish, one who lives off his wife’s earnings,

"O royal sage, become a Vaiṣṇava and perform your recitation at midday! On the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, having become pure and observing the vow, one should perform the vow on the fourteenth day, repeatedly taking refuge in Sāvitrī. (28)

She possessed the excellent color of molten gold, blazing with the splendor of Brahman;

Clad in golden raiment, that virtuous lady bestows compassion, peace, happiness, and liberation.
I worship the beloved consort of Śrī Parameṣṭhin, who bestows all prosperity;
the Goddess who presides over the Vedas, the Mother in the form of the seed-syllable (bīja), the giver of all intentions, and the bestower of knowledge. (35–36)
Having meditated thus, and having held the meditation while placing a flower upon one's own head,

One should offer a bath with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), fragrant unguents and the like for anointing, as well as an ablution, garments for wiping, fresh clothing, ornaments, flowers, and articles of adornment. (38–39)
Incense, the sacred thread and so forth, liquids for the sake of prosperity,
a lamp, food offerings, water, betel leaf, sandalwood paste and the like,
the waving of lights (ārātrika), fruit, leaves, a comfortable bed, prostration, and so on.
He should perform a divine massage of the feet and seek forgiveness with a pure mind. (41) Then, having offered a handful of flowers, he should dismiss that Mother.
The observer of the vow should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Brahmin who has arrived. (42)
One should recite "Śrīṃ Hrīṃ Klīṃ Sāvitryai Svāhā" one hundred and eight times. Indeed,

In ancient times, Sāvitrī was given by Kṛṣṇa to Brahmā in Goloka.

O you whose nature is Nārāyaṇa! O Nārāyaṇī! O Maheśvarī! O you who consist of splendor! O you who consist of supreme bliss! O increaser of the twice-born!
O eternal one! O ancient one! O Lakṣmī! O you whose form is all-auspiciousness!

O annihilator of the accumulated evils born of body, mind, and speech! 47–48.
"You who were praised by Brahmā and went to Satyaloka together with him—

Prabhā, Pārvatī, Lakṣmī, Māṇikyā, Kamalā, and Satī— [are her forms].

By action one goes to heaven and proceeds to Satyaloka;

The state of Indra, the state of Vaidhasa, the state of a sage, and the status of the brahmin caste;

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī! Having disregarded what was spoken by Yama out of excessive devotion, [she acted].

What is auspicious action and what is inauspicious action? What is the seed, and who is the bestower of the fruit?
By what means does an action become of such a nature, and what is the cause therein in every respect? (1–2)
Who indeed experiences the fruit of action, and who remains untainted? Furthermore, how do virtuous people truly uproot action?
Who is said to be the agent of action, and what is the body, and who is the embodied one?

What is consciousness, what is the mind, and what is the intellect? What indeed is the vital breath? (4) What is the sense organ, and who are the deities? Who is the enjoyer and who is the one who causes enjoyment? What is enjoyment, and what is its cessation? Who is the self, and who is the supreme Lord? (5)
"O Yamadeva! If you know all this, tell it to me here.
Having heard this, Yama was exceedingly delighted and spoke to Sāvitrī according to the truth:
"It is that which bestows prosperity, bestows peace, and is revealed in the Vedas and other scriptures. (6)
Auspicious action brings about welfare, while the opposite is certainly not auspicious.
(7) Whether it be latent impression (*vāsanā*) or mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*), it is declared to be the seed of action.
Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, who dwells within all, is the one who bestows the fruit. (8)
Through the desire for the auspicious (*śubhecchā*), one performs auspicious action; through the desire for the inauspicious (*aśubhā*), one performs only inauspicious action.

Effort is considered the cause of action, and the will (*vāñcchanā*) is the cause of that effort. The cause of the will, however, is consciousness (*vijñāna*) residing in the individual soul (*jīva*) upon its objective substratum.
The will of the Supreme Lord, however, is established as the cause of knowledge.
Therein, the all-pervading power (Śakti) conjoined [with that will] indeed bestows action and birth.
Through the will and power of Hari, knowledge and action are held to reside in the individual soul (jīva).
From those two, all action produced through their succession arises;
ultimately, in every respect, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa is considered the cause.
The individual soul (jīva) experiences the fruit of its actions, but its true Self is not tainted.
The Inner Controller, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, is indeed entirely unattached.
(13) The saintly ones are in every way free from any desire for the fruits of their actions; day and night they perform auspicious deeds consisting solely of service to Viṣṇu. (14)
Whatever is performed for the pleasure of Hari—whether it be causeless or free from conceptual construction—all that is indeed of the nature of devotion and is capable of uprooting karma.
A devotee of Hari is always liberated; his liberation is considered to be twofold.
Liberation while living (jīvanmukti) and liberation into Brahman (brahmamukti) bestow the state of nirvāṇa.
Vaiṣṇavas always desire liberation while living in the form of devotion;
virtuous ones desire the supreme liberation into Brahman and service in the divine abode.
That power which impels action is established in Kṛṣṇa;
abiding in the form of the Inner Controller (antaryāmin), it unfailingly generates activity.
The body, composed of the five elements, is designated as the gross (sthūla).

(1.9) Knowledge is said to be the comprehension of the twenty-four principles, as well as of the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman), through their essential natures, qualities, and effects. (1.367.20)
Consciousness, which is the seed of all worldly transactions, resides within the Self;

The Supreme Soul, the Supreme Brahman, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, Hari;

Worship, praise, service, friendship, and total surrender—thus, this ninefold yoga in the form of devotion is the bestower of supreme liberation. Dharma is like a decoction of medicinal herbs, while detachment is the purgative. (37–38)
Awakening is a delightful linctus, and devotion there is the elixir;
dharma is the healing medicine that joins [the broken], while discernment is the remover of wounds.
Devotion is the extractor of arrows, and renunciation is the life-sustaining tonic.

That bond of affection which is preceded by abundant honor is to be understood as devotion that bestows liberation; it should always be practiced by people. One whose heart is free from黏腻 (cikkaṇatva—slime/stickiness) and who is immersed in intense bliss [attains it]. (1.367.40–41)

Devotion (*bhāva*) is to be understood as affection (*sneha*); indeed, it should always be directed toward Hari. An uninterrupted internal state of mind, bound by affection for Hari, is devotion (*bhakti*), love (*prema*), and delight (*rati*); service (*sevā*) toward Hari indeed bestows liberation.
The *vaidhī* [type of devotion] is produced by injunctive words and consists of nine forms, beginning with hearing (*śravaṇa*).
Love for Hari—characterized by knowledge of His majesty, firm, and superior to everything—is considered in every respect to be *bhakti*, which bestows liberation. (43–44)
Affection for devotees, abandoning hypocrisy toward the image, and approval [of their practice];
worship of Him with a pure mind, respect for hearing His stories; performing bodily acts for His sake, mindfulness of Him, and chanting His name. (45)
All these eight types of devotion are always non-different and grant their fruits.
They consist of taking refuge at the feet of the Guru, accepting initiation, serving the Guru,
abiding on the true path through faith, and likewise inquiring about the true Dharma.
Renouncing enjoyments for the sake of Hari, dwelling in sacred places and other such lands,
conducting one's affairs according to necessity, and likewise observing a vow on the day of Hari;
honoring trees and other objects as divine— these ten increase devotion.
Detachment from attachment to sons, disciples, and the like; avoidance of association with the wicked;
lack of engagement in great undertakings and the like; avoidance of futile disputes and the like; giving wealth for the sake of Hari; and avoidance of grief, delusion, and so forth. (1.367.49–50)
Not causing distress to others, not censuring gods, gurus, and the like, not committing offenses against the gods, and not tolerating the censure of the gods—
these ten should be practiced by devotees for the increase of their devotion. (51)
Then, there is the wearing of the black insignia and the constant remembrance of Kṛṣṇa’s names within the heart;
the wearing of flower garlands and the like, dancing, prostrating like a staff before Him, rising up in His presence, and following after Him when He departs. (52–53)
Circumambulation, as well as hymn-singing, service, chanting, and recitation;
spiritual realization, the reading of hymns, tasting the water used for washing the offerings,
receiving the fragrance of the remnants, and touching and beholding Lord Hari.
The waving of lights (nīrājana), witnessing the festivals of Hari;
waiting expectantly for compassion, meditating, remembering, and supreme servitude;
friendship, self-surrender, and likewise all activity performed for the sake of Hari. (55–56)
Constantly offering one's dearest possessions, serving with devotion, and taking refuge;

worshipping Tulasī, the scriptures, sacred fords, Vaiṣṇavas, and others; performing service according to one’s wealth; and engaging in righteous discourse with the saintly—[these are the duties]. (57)

Service to the distressed, the festival of Hari’s birth, service at the feet of Hari, abundant love with faith, the supreme tasting of the meaning of the scriptures, association with the virtuous, chanting of my names, dwelling always among the virtuous with the virtuous— [these are the means]. 58–59.

These forty-four qualities, beginning with "abiding in the Self," consist of devotion; they nourish devotion and increase affection. (1.367.60) One should serve the virtuous, and one should always seek the compassion of the virtuous.
Supreme faith in the true dharmas, as well as hearing of the qualities of Hari;
the emergence of the sprout of love, and the supreme taking of refuge in Śrī Hari;
the increase of passion for Hari, and the constant manifestation of the vision of Hari’s worship.
Devotion to Kṛṣṇa, the abode of all virtues; constant abiding in dharma dedicated to Hari—these ten qualities, when perfected, cause love to increase exceedingly.
[This occurs] through the distinctions of *sāttvika* and so forth, and by the gradations of weak, moderate, and intense.

Indeed, there are many subtle varieties of devotion that bestow liberation. (64) Now, that which is the ultimate limit of love, wherein no prescribed rule exists—that is the eternal devotion, supreme above all else. (65)
To the extent that the reality of love is nourished by its own nature according to the branches [of its manifestations],
so too is the natural state of embodied beings infinite according to those branches.
Indeed, the reality of love is divided in such a way that its number cannot be reached.
Therefore, devotion possesses innumerable varieties and is thus "in full bloom.
For that Great Goddess of Devotion, the supernatural powers of worldly enjoyment, liberation, and so forth, always follow her like maidservants devoted to their queen. (67–68)
The bliss of Brahmā, multiplied by a hundred million, is like a mere atom compared to the bliss of devotion; indeed,
even the pleasures of Brahmā appear as mere puddles in the ocean of the nectar of the bliss of love for one who is immersed and flooded with the joy of divine affection.

Those whose firm devotion to Hari is always of the nature of love do not see the abode of Yama, the consumer of the dead, even in their dreams. Practicing such devotion, which is attained through the merits accumulated over ten million births, they remain steadfast. (1.367.70–71)
Just as Hari purifies even great and excessive sins,
so too enemies, malevolent planets,
Yama’s messengers, and Rākṣasas do not afflict a devotee of Hari, nor do Bhūtas, Pretas, Piśācas, and the like.
"Devote yourself to that foremost of gods, the eternal Blessed One.
Everything you asked has been told; go, my child, as you please!
Having spoken thus and bowed, O Lotus-born One, Yama indeed ceased speaking. (73–74)

Thus ends the three hundred and sixty-seventh chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Answers Given by King Yama to Sāvitrī’s Questions Regarding Auspicious and Inauspicious Karma and Related Matters, as well as the Modes and Greatness of Devotion to the Lord," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga Lineage, within the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, concerning the majesty of the devoted wife (*pativratā*). Chapter 368 *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā* — Section 1 (Kṛtayuga Lineage) — Chapter 368
[The Author: Chapter 369.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
O Lotus-born One! Even though she was addressed in this manner, Sāvitrī did not turn back.
Again she spoke these words, which were appropriate for one bearing the burden of devotion to her husband:
"O Yama, having abandoned my beloved husband and you, my guru who is an ocean of knowledge, where shall I go? A desire to know has arisen in me; O Lord, grant me the means to resolve it! (1–2)
O Yama, by what karma does the living being go to this or that womb?
By what karma does one go to heaven or even to hell, or by what karma is there liberation? By what karma is one diseased or free from disease, long-lived or short-lived?
How is one born happy, miserable, with impaired limbs, one-eyed, blind, or deaf?
(4) How is one born negligent, wretched, deranged, greedy, or a killer?
And by what specific actions does one attain the supernatural powers (*siddhis*)? (5)
By what means is the enjoyment of heaven and so forth attained, as well as Vaikuṇṭha and immortality?
By what means is Goloka and the imperishable realm (Akṣara) attained, as well as the fourfold states beginning with Sālokya?
Or how many kinds of hell are there, and who remains there for how long?

"By what action does such a disease arise in a human being? Tell me everything exactly as you know it, for it will be of benefit. Having heard this, Yama spoke this reply to Sāvitrī: 7–8. "By what action does such a disease arise in a human being? Tell me everything exactly as you know it, for it will be of benefit. Having heard this, Yama spoke this reply to Sāvitrī.
Filled with wonder, Yama said: "O girl, you are sixteen years of age; from where have you obtained such knowledge, my daughter?
I believe you are Sāvitrī, the consort of Brahmā, who has arrived here."
But that knowledge which was attained long ago by King Aśvapati through austerity—
knowledge such as belongs to the ancient sages, the yogis, and the wise— is now yours,
just as Śrī is on the lap of the Lord of Śrī, or Lakṣmī upon the chest of Nārāyaṇa.
Just as Rādhā is to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Bhavānī to Bhava, Mūrti to the Chest of Dharma, and Sāvitrī to the Chest of Brahmā;
and just as Devahūti was to Kardama and Śatarūpā to Manu.
Just as Aditi was to Kaśyapa, as Arundhatī was to Vasiṣṭha; as Śacī was to Mahendra, as Ahalyā was to Gautama;
as Rohiṇī was to Candra, and as Rati was to Kāmadeva. (13–14)
As Svāhā is to the sacrificial fire, as Svadhā is to the ancestors,
as Saṃjñā is to the sun, and as Dakṣiṇā is to the sacrifice;
so is Lakṣmī, Māṇikī, Pārvatī, and Prabhā to Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
And Varuṇānī was with Varuṇa, as Dharā was with Varāha;
in the month of Kārttika she was Devasenā, as Alakṣmī was with Uddālaka;
and as Pativratālakṣmī was with the Brahmin Patnīvra. || 16–17 ||
Just as the fortune of Kambharā resides upon the chest of the cowherd Kṛṣṇa,
and as Jayā and Lalitā reside in Hari, the Lord of Akṣara, so too,
O beloved Satyavatī, may you become Saubhāgyā, the most dearly loved one.
"Thus has this boon been granted to you by me with a gracious mind.
Choose another desired thing as well, O Goddess; I shall grant it to you.
Having seen Yama thus pleased, that virtuous Lakṣmī spoke to him in this manner.
"By means of Satyavān alone as my son, may I have a hundred sons;
for this purpose, I choose the eyes of my father-in-law here.
May there also be the recovery of the kingdom for me, and may I have a hundred brothers. (21)

"Then, after a hundred thousand years have passed, I shall go to the abode of Hari along with Satyavān, O Lord; grant me this excellent boon! Furthermore, I wish to hear all that I desire to know; please speak of that."
Having heard that, Yama spoke, honoring Sāvitrī greatly:
"O Goddess! Everything you desire shall come to pass; let it be so. He continued:
"I shall tell you of something else you wish to know; listen to the ripening of karma."
Just as I know all of that, I shall relate it in brief:
on this earth, human beings here experience the fruits of their auspicious and inauspicious karma, as do the gods, daityas, dānavas, gandharvas, rākṣasas, and others. (25–26)
And not all men who perform actions live equally;
all those with distinguished lives experience the fruits of their actions within various wombs.
Human beings, in particular, wander through all these wombs.
By auspicious action one indeed goes to heaven, but by inauspicious action to hell. By merit characterized by passion (rājasa), however, a human being is born on earth;
by the increase of merit characterized by goodness (sāttvika), one is surely born as a deity.
And through [the influence of] tamasic evil, there arise rākṣasas and others,
piśācas, bhūtas, pretas, beasts, birds, trees,
and creepers; as well as insects, moths, serpents, reptiles, and other living creatures.

They are born with an abundance of suffering within the eighty-four thousand classes of birth. Those characterized by *sattva* are born in the higher realms; those characterized by *rajas* exist in the middle; and all those characterized by *tamas*, being born from inferior wombs, are indeed born below.
Through merit one is born in heaven; through mere sin, in hell.
Liberation comes through devotion to Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa by means of serving Him with affection.
A living being becomes diseased through evil action and healthy through auspicious action.
Through auspicious or inauspicious [karma], one becomes long-lived or short-lived, happy or miserable (34).
Through contemptible action, those with missing limbs, such as the blind and others, are produced;
a man who has caused another's eye to be pierced becomes blind or one-eyed (35).
One who is greedy for hearing the censure of others will certainly be born deaf;
one who causes distress to others here will always be born as a fool;
and one who steals the property of another will become poor and destitute. (36)
Excessively cruel and a scorner of others, he becomes utterly cast out.
Failing to obtain the wealth of enjoyments, he plunders other property and the like;
he is born as a murderer and a hunter, a man of extreme sin.
One who does not repay a debt certainly takes rebirth; of this there is no doubt.
Through most excellent action, one attains perfection and other such states.
By means of giving, a person obtains all things, including the enjoyments of heaven. (39)
Through devotion to Viṣṇu, one attains Vaikuṇṭha; through knowledge, the immortal state. Through devotion to Kṛṣṇa, one attains Goloka; through supreme knowledge, the imperishable realm.
By the grace of Hari, the fourfold states beginning with *sālokya* may be attained.
Hell has been described in many ways due to the vast variety of karmic actions.
Indeed, because sinful deeds are innumerable, the hells are likewise innumerable.
A sinner remains there for as long as his sin persists; upon its exhaustion, he is no longer there. 42.

Because they cause suffering to others by burning them from within, diseases overcome that person who inflicts pain upon others. All this has been stated in general; now hear the specific details, O beautiful one! (43–44)
Among all classes of beings on this earth, human birth is difficult to obtain.
Among them, the Brahmin, the virtuous man, and the virtuous women are the most excellent; they are people possessed of devotion.
Furthermore, one who possesses devotion while still having worldly desires becomes a practitioner of *karmayoga*.
One who is free from desire and possesses devotion attains liberation in Brahman within the Supreme.
For those performers of selfless action, there is no returning again;
however, the devotees of Kṛṣṇa go to Goloka, traveling on divine two-tusked elephants.

Those who worship Nārāyaṇa go to Vaikuṇṭha; indeed, those with four arms and devoted to the earth go to the realm called Amṛta, possessing a thousand arms. People established at holy fords and ascetics go to Satyaloka.
Those devoted to the Sun go to the Sun; those who cherish Śiva go to Kailāsa.
Those dedicated to sacrifice go to the heavenly world; those whose contemplation is fixed on Indra attain the state of Indra.
Indeed, they go to those respective worlds and return again by virtue of their karma.
Devotees of Hari who are free from desire indeed go to the realm of Hari;
because that supreme, imperishable station is from which there is no return.
Those who are devoid of their own duty and have fallen from right conduct go to an inferior state.
They experience the torments of hell even among the animal species.
All those devoted to their own duty partake of the excellent fruits upon this earth;
all those devoid of their own duty go to dreadful hells.
The giver of a maiden goes to the world of the Moon for as long as the reigns of fourteen Indras;
it is said that the fruit of giving her adorned is twice as great.
[One should give] cow-products, silver, a wife, clothing, grain, fruit, and water.
Those who give these things go to that very heaven of eternal prosperity.
After remaining there for a very long time, they indeed return again to the earth.
As for those people here who give gold, cows, copper, and so forth— 55–56.
O virtuous lady, those who give land and grain dwell in the world of the Sun for ten thousand years;
they dwell in Śvetadvīpa.
Furthermore, the giver of a house attains the world of the gods.
It is held that one must dwell there for as many years as there are particles of dust in the house;
and whichever deity a person offers a house to, that person goes to that deity’s world for a supreme number of years equal to the measure of those particles of dust. (58–59)
In a mansion, the merit is fourfold; in works of public utility (*pūrta*), the fruit is a hundredfold;
in an excellent structure, the merit is eightfold; and in a divine one, it is held that the fruit is divine.
The builder of a tank goes to Janaloka for ten thousand years.
The fruit [of a gift] at a step-well is a hundredfold, and at a dam it is a thousandfold.
A step-well measuring four thousand *dhanus* in length yields a fruit equal to ten step-wells when given to a worthy recipient.
A daughter [given in marriage] yields a fruit equal to ten such step-wells.
If one gives [a daughter] adorned with ornaments there, the fruit is twofold.
The fruit of clearing away the mud from ponds, wells, tanks,
and the like is also attained by one who tends to the holy fig tree (aśvattha) and by one who plants it.
In this world, one who bestows [the gift of] asceticism goes to the highest state for ten thousand years.
O virtuous lady, a giver of flower gardens shall dwell in the eternal realm (dhruva) for ten thousand years;
a giver of celestial chariots (vimāna) shall dwell in the world of Viṣṇu for the duration of a supreme manvantara.
One who gives vehicles, carriages, palanquins, or chariots to a worthy recipient (pātra) who is a devotee of Viṣṇu obtains fourfold the fruit, which indeed bestows supreme happiness.
One who offers swings and other such items shall go to the world of Viṣṇu for the duration of a Manvantara.
He who constructs a royal highway lined with palatial mansions attains the realm of Indra.
Having enjoyed sovereignty over the earth for ten thousand years, he goes to an auspicious abode.
What is given returns to the giver; what is not given does not remain [with him].
Having enjoyed happiness such as that of heaven, they indeed return again to earth;
they obtain birth in an excellent dwelling among superior people here. And they become Brahmins, or protectors, or earners of wealth, or servants.
Just as they become on earth according to their karma, so it is always elsewhere;
everything performed here must certainly be experienced there.
Thus I have told you everything; go, Sāvitrī! Do not delay.
Having spoken thus, Yama assumed a vow of silence and proceeded slowly ahead;
Sāvitrī also followed slowly behind him toward the abode of Yama.

Thus ends the three hundred and sixty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Journey to Places of Auspicious and Inauspicious Results According to One's Karma, the Attainment of Boons—namely, her own hundred sons, the eyesight of her father-in-law, her own hundred brothers, and a lifespan of a hundred thousand years for Satyavat"—in the first section, the Kṛta-yuga Cycle, concerning the Greatness of Devotion to One’s Husband, within the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
