Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Seeing Sāvitrī approaching his back, Yama was struck with wonder;
bowing again to the virtuous lady, he said, "Tell me here, what do you desire?"
Having heard these words of Yama, Sāvitrī questioned him once again: "Listen, Lakṣmī! I shall tell you; understand me.
[Tell me] by what means people especially go to heaven and other worlds. (2)
In brief, those who possess merit likewise proceed by means of their actions.
(3) Having asked his question regarding the Sāvitrī, Yama spoke this answer:
"The giver of food is honored in the realm of Indra for showers of years of food. (4)
In this matter, there is no examination of the recipient's worthiness, nor is there any restriction regarding time;
even a person who merely provides a seat for a deity, a Brahmin, or others,
rejoices happily in the world of Agni for ten thousand years.

For as many years as there are verses in that Sūtra, for ten thousand such years he dwells in heaven. Furthermore, he who gives a milch cow to a deity or to a Brahmin is honored in Vaikuṇṭha for as many Yugas as there are hairs on the cow’s tail.
A gift given on a meritorious day yields fourfold merit; at a sacred ford (tīrtha), the fruit is a hundredfold;
and a gift in the field of Nārāyaṇa becomes ten millionfold in fruit.
Likewise, one who gives a cow to a Brahmin who is Hari himself and seeks it for the purpose of a sacrificial rite [attains great reward].
He rejoices in the heavenly world of the Moon for ten thousand years.
(9) One who gives a cow with a calf and two faces rejoices happily in Vaikuṇṭha for as many years as there are hairs on its body. (1.369.10)
One should indeed give a Śālagrāma stone, along with ornaments and other gifts, to its worshiper;
the donor rejoices in Vaikuṇṭha for as long as the moon and sun endure.
A giver of an umbrella rejoices in the abode of Varuṇa for ten thousand years.
One who gives sandals is honored in the world of Vāyu for ten thousand years;
one who gives a bed rejoices in the world of Candra, possessing a lifespan equal to that of the Moon.
One who gives a lamp to a Brahmin who is a devotee of Hari, providing oil or ghee, [attains the same]. (12–13)
For as long as a manvantara, he too is glorified in the world of Brahmā;
he possesses divine vision, and blindness never arises for him.
A giver of elephants shall dwell perpetually upon half of Indra’s throne.
A giver of horses shall remain for a kalpa in the world of Varuṇa;
one who gives a palanquin is honored in the world of Viṣṇu for a manvantara;
and a giver of chowries and fans is honored in the world of Vāyu.
One who gives grain dwells for ten thousand years in the world of Viṣṇu as equal to a single grain of rice; this reciter of the name of Śrī Hari dwells there,
and great death flees from him— he becomes long-lived.
That man on earth who swings Hari upon a swing,
or who causes a fine swing to be made during a vow, a festival, or a great celebration— he,
being liberated while living, shall enjoy happiness and at the end go to the abode of Viṣṇu.
He shall dwell there in Vaikuṇṭha for the duration of a hundred manvantaras;
the fruit of [giving at] Uttaraphalgunī shall be twice that even more.
He shall live until the end of the kalpa, becoming an abode of all prosperity and virtues.
The giver of sesame seeds rejoices in the abode of Viṣṇu for as many years as there are sesame seeds. By giving sesame seeds in a copper vessel, one indeed obtains double the fruit.
The giver of a daughter in marriage shall certainly dwell in the world of the Moon for one kalpa.
The giver of a maidservant rejoices for ten thousand years in the Gāndharva realm;
he obtains a virtuous wife endowed with good fortune for a thousand births.
The giver of fruit-bearing trees is honored in the world of Śakra for as many years as there are fruits.
On earth, the donor shall become an eminent householder possessed of sons together with a beautiful wife. (24) The giver of fruit dwells for a long time in heaven, which brings him happiness;
the giver of wealth, grain, and houses shall dwell in the abode of Kubera. (25)
Thereafter, O virtuous one, for the duration of a *manvantara*, he is born as a wealthy person on earth in a holy land,
possessing a field of grain and being a worthy recipient of merit.
Then, for a hundred *manvantaras*, he rejoices in Vaikuṇṭha, and after that, for another hundred.

On this earth, he indeed becomes very prosperous, possessing fortune, sons, and wealth; likewise, he shall be a possessor of women and cattle and happy for a further hundred births. He who gives excellent land and a village to the wielder of the Śārṅga bow (Viṣṇu) shall be blessed with progeny. (27–28)
For a hundred thousand manvantaras, the donor is glorified in Vaikuṇṭha; on earth, he is born for a hundred thousand lifetimes as a king of a hundred thousand villages,
[ruling over land] abounding in progeny, excellent in nature, and endowed with crops such as sugarcane.

He who gives a field or a city provided with ponds and wells is honored in Vaikuṇṭha for ten lakhs of lifespans as Indra; on earth, he is born as a lord of a hundred thousand cities and a king of kings.
He who gives a hundred cities as a gift to Viṣṇu is honored in Vaikuṇṭha for the duration of ten million manvantaras;
thereafter, he undoubtedly becomes the lord of Jambūdvīpa.
The Earth indeed does not abandon him for ten million births;
he shall become a great lord of kings, living until the end of the kalpa,
and as the bestower of his own authority, he shall obtain fourfold fruit.
And the giver of Jambūdvīpa shall obtain tenfold the fruit [of other gifts],
compared to one who gives the earth with its seven continents, who frequents all sacred fords,
who performs all forms of austerity, and who observes every fast. (35)
And for one who gives all other gifts, as well as for one who possesses all perfections, there is indeed rebirth;
but alas, for the devotee of Hari, there is no return.
O Satī, the Vaiṣṇavas behold the passing away of countless Brahmās! || 36–37 ||
Those residing in Goloka, those dwelling in Vaikuṇṭha, those who have gone to the imperishable abode (Akṣaradhāma),
and even those situated in the supreme realm (Paradhāma)— they all behold this return [to birth].
However, one who worships the mantra of Hari, having cast off the human body, [does not do so].
Having become divine in form like Hari, he goes to the abode of Hari.
The devotees of Kṛṣṇa residing in Goloka and the Vaiṣṇavas residing in Vaikuṇṭha, having attained the same form as Kṛṣṇa and also as Nārāyaṇa... [39-40]
Those who perform service to these two indeed attain non-friendship, the state of the common folk, and dissolution;
even gods, lords, perfected beings, and all that exists perish.
But the devotees of Hari do not perish, for they remove birth, death, and old age.

He who offers *vṛndā-tulasī* leaves to Hari in the month of Kārtika rejoices in the abode of Hari for as many yugas as there are leaves. And he who indeed offers a lamp of ghee to Hari in Kārtika [enjoys the same reward]. (42–43)
He rejoices in the abode of Hari for a year equal in measure to a *pala*;
if, by the will of Hari, he returns to the created world,
he becomes a devotee of the Lord, immensely wealthy, endowed with keen vision, radiant, and a performer of devotion.

Whether it be the preceptor, the place of descent [of the Lord], or a portion thereof, it shall be the bestower of liberation. One who bathes in the Gaṅgā or other holy fords at dawn during the month of Māgha rejoices in the abode of Hari by the will of Hari for sixty thousand yugas.
In all the cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas), that disciple of the Lord, who is a devotee with conquered senses and who bathes in the Gaṅgā at Prayāga every morning during the month of Māgha,
rejoices in Vaikuṇṭha for the duration of a hundred thousand manvantaras.
In the creation by Nārāyaṇa, he indeed becomes a supreme teacher;
having cast off his human body, he returns once more to the abode.
For one who has gone to the abode of Hari, there is certainly no returning again.
Having attained the state of having the same form as Hari (sārūpya), he then performs service to Him;
constantly bathing in the Gaṅgā, O virtuous lady, he attains at every step the fruit born of a horse-sacrifice,
and being purified, he becomes like the sun.
By the mere dust of his feet, the earth is instantly purified.
He rejoices in Vaikuṇṭha for as long as the moon and sun endure.
Through the grace of Nārāyaṇa, he becomes an ascetic teacher upon this earth.
He who gives water at the beginning of summer goes to Vaikuṇṭha for the duration of a kalpa;
and he who indeed offers sandalwood paste and other gifts to Hari in the month of Vaiśākha rejoices in the abode of Viṣṇu for sixty thousand yugas.
In the month of Vaiśākha, the giver of roasted barley flour (saktu) rejoices in the abode of Viṣṇu for as many years as there are particles of dust in that flour. Then, by the will of Viṣṇu,
he becomes a preceptor in this world, an ascetic and the most excellent of deliverers.
He who observes the Kṛṣṇajanmāṣṭamī on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Bhādra becomes purified at that very moment of all sins committed throughout a hundred lifetimes.
By the will of Kṛṣṇa, he rejoices in Goloka and likewise becomes a devotee of Kṛṣṇa.
He who observes the Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa-Janmāṣṭamī with devotion during the dark fortnight of the month of Kārttika on a leaf attains the abode of Hari;
as a servant of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, he remains there for infinite time. (57–58)
He who performs the Śivarātri vow and offers a bilva leaf measuring the size of a yuga-leaf shall enjoy all desires offered to Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa and rejoice in the abode of Śiva.

By the will of Śiva, one indeed becomes possessed of knowledge, sons, prosperity, progeny, and land for the duration of seven manvantaras; having become happy during the great creation, one shall go to the abode of Śiva.
One should worship Śambhu during the months of Caitra and Māgha, performing dance before Him for a month,
or half a month, or for ten, seven, or even five days;
such a person is glorified in the world of Śiva for as long as a Yuga.
The devotee who, observing the vows, performs the vow of Śrī Rāmanavamī,
rejoices in the abode of Rāma for the duration of seven manvantaras.
Furthermore, having become a devotee of Rāma and established in the position of a teacher (ācārya), he [attains liberation].
Through devotion to Rāma, he indeed goes to the second Vaikuṇṭha.
On the full moon day of the autumn season, that king of great devotees who performs the worship of Hari and Hara with many ritual offerings, [attains that state].
With food offerings, presents, as well as incense, lamps, and the like; with dance, song, musical instruments, and various auspicious festivities—
he shall dwell in the world of Hari or Śambhu for the duration of seven manvantaras.
Furthermore, having become pure and devoted, he shall attain prosperity;
endowed with great power and accompanied by elephants and horses,
he will undoubtedly become a lord of kings, possessed of sons, grandsons, and so forth.

Having reached the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada, one should worship Mahālakṣmī with devotion using the sixteen articles; such a person goes to Vaikuṇṭha for the duration of a kalpa,
and is thereafter born on earth as a Sāttvata king of kings.
On the full moon day of Kārtika, he who performs the Rāsa-maṇḍala ceremony should fashion two hundred golden figures— representing a hundred gopīs and a hundred gopas—
and having fashioned Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa, he should worship them with ritual offerings.
With whatever various offerings he has obtained, the worshiper goes to Goloka.
Having remained there for the duration of Brahmā’s lifespan, he returns at the time of creation.
Then, having again cultivated devotion to Kṛṣṇa and received a mantra of Hari from him, [he proceeds].
Having attained a form similar to Kṛṣṇa, he becomes an attendant;
he dwells eternally in Goloka, free from rebirth.
One who observes the Ekādaśī vow travels [to that realm] for as long as the lifespan of Brahmā.
Then, having returned from Vaikuṇṭha to the earth once more,
that devotee of Hari goes again to Vaikuṇṭha and shall not fall back.
That person who worships Śakra on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada [attains this].

For sixty thousand years he is honored in the world of Śakra. By giving sacrificial food (haviṣya) on a Sunday coinciding with the sun's transit (saṃkrānti), or on the seventh day of the bright fortnight, one goes to the world of the Sun for a kalpa.
Returning again to the earth, he shall become free from disease and endowed with prosperity.
On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, one should worship you as Sāvitrī;
such a person rejoices in the world of Brahmā for the duration of seven manvantaras.

Furthermore, he shall become endowed with prosperity on earth and possessed of the perfection of knowledge. He who worships Sarasvatī on the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha is honored in Vaikuṇṭha for one kalpa and becomes a poet once again.
The giver of cows and gold attains twice the merit of the hair on a cow's body;
thereafter, he rejoices in Vaikuṇṭha and subsequently becomes a devotee of Viṣṇu on earth—
a lord of kings, a possessor of cattle, and endowed with learning, wisdom, sons, and other blessings.
He who feeds the virtuous, the holy, noble women, Brahmins, and likewise guests,
rejoices in the abode of Viṣṇu for as many years as there are hairs on the body of the eater.
Having returned here, he becomes happy, prosperous, long-lived, and valorous.
He who gives the name of Hari is honored in the world of Viṣṇu.
Chanting ten million names, he is to be known as liberated while living; of this there is no doubt.
Indeed, he attains eternal union with Viṣṇu in Vaikuṇṭha.
A worshipper of Śiva goes to Śiva, [measuring] the size of a grain of Bāṇa-dust;
having remained on Kailāsa for ten thousand Yugas, he becomes a sovereign emperor upon the earth.
A devotee who worships the Śālagrāma and partakes of its grace [attains the same].
He is glorified in Vaikuṇṭha for a hundred lifetimes of Brahmā;
having been born again on earth as a king, he goes to Vaikuṇṭha and does not fall.
One who performs austerities, vows, and other observances goes to Vaikuṇṭha for the duration of a kalpa.
Having been born on earth as that lord of kings, he shall indeed be liberated thereafter;
performing the Aśvamedha sacrifice, he shall dwell upon half of Śakra’s throne for as many years as there are hairs on a horse,
and four times that duration for the Rājasūya.
In the human sacrifice (naramedha), the fruit is half that of the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha); in the cow sacrifice (gomedha), it is likewise [half].
In the Putreṣṭi sacrifice, it would be half of that; in the Lāṅguleṣṭi, the fruit is that born of the cow sacrifice.
In the Vipreṣṭi and the Vṛddhi-yāga, the fruit shall be that born of the cow sacrifice.
In the Padmeṣṭi, however, it is half of that; in the Viśokeṣṭi, it is born of freedom from sorrow (viśoka);
in the Vijayeṣṭi, it is equal to the lotus; and in the Prājāpatya as well, it is the same.
In the Ṛddhi-yāga, there is great sovereignty; in the Viṣṇu-yāga, however, it is Vaiṣṇava.
A devotee shall obtain merit and the eternal realm of Viṣṇu.
O beautiful one, the sacrifice to Viṣṇu is the foremost among all sacrifices;
there is no sacrifice superior to the sacrifice to Viṣṇu that bestows such excellent fruit.
The author of that [work] shall live for many kalpas and become liberated in this world;
through both knowledge and splendor, he may even become equal to Viṣṇu.
By means of a hundred horse-sacrifices, one attains the status of Śakra in heaven.
King Pṛthu attained the station of Viṣṇu by means of a thousand [meritorious acts],
which is superior in its fruit to pilgrimages, sacrifices, austerities, the Vedas, and vows.
Service to the lotus feet of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa is the bestower of liberation.
The description, meditation, worship, chanting, devotion, hymn of praise, remembrance, salutation, and recitation of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa alone,
as well as the eating of the nectar-like food offerings from His feet, bestow all that is desired. (98)
"O child, worship your Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme beyond the supreme! Accept a husband and go happily to your own home.
Having spoken thus, O Lotus-born One, Yama remained silent and stood still. (1.369.100)

Thus ends the three hundred and sixty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Various Kinds of Fruitful Answers Given by Yama to Sāvitrī’s Questions Regarding the Results of Her Deeds," within the section on the Greatness of Devoted Wives (*pativratāmāhātmya*) in the first book, the *Kṛtayugasantāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 370 *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā* — Part 1 (*Kṛtayugasantāna*) — Chapter 370.
[The Author: Chapter 371.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Having heard the greatness of devotion to Hari, Satī spoke again to Yama.
She asked: "By what method is Hari himself to be worshipped?
(1) Yama, having heard Sāvitrī, spoke of the practice that grants excellent liberation:
"Listen, Lakṣmī! I shall tell you how Yama spoke to the virtuous woman. (2)
Having risen in the morning, one should remember Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa in the heart;
one should meditate upon his form and contemplate it again and again, whether during bathing, purification, external rites, or internal practices. (3)
One should remember Hari while eating, dwelling, sleeping, and performing household duties.
(4) There, with supreme faith, one should indeed joyfully engage all the senses as well as the internal organs in Śrī Hari. (5)
While drinking, sitting, sleeping, dreaming, waking, or moving about; whether in auspicious or inauspicious matters, Hari should always be remembered.
Let the tongue perform his glorification, and let the ears attend to his hearing.
The eye should behold Him; the nose should perceive His fragrance.
The skin should experience His touch; the hand should perform service to His feet.
The foot should go to His temple; the speech should practice His worship.
The male organ of sense, for the purpose of destroying obstacles, shall attain the state of a virtue;
having obtained bliss from Śrī Hari, one should practice meditation upon Śrī Hari.
Furthermore, there should be determination, honor, and reflection upon Śrī Hari.
Thus, one should perform everything for Hari alone and not for anyone else. One should act neither for one's own sake nor for the sake of others, but indeed solely for the sake of Hari.
By acting in this manner, one will before long attain the abode of Hari.
Thus addressed, Sāvitrī, recognizing Yama as the supreme among devotees, spoke the *Yamāṣṭaka* (Eight Verses on Yama): "Listen, Lakṣmī! I shall tell you;
formerly, at the Puṣkara tīrtha, Nārāyaṇa [worshipped] the Sun through austerity."
I bow to that Dharmarāja, the son whom Dharma obtained. Salutations to you, O God Śamana, who, having ordained the end of the experience of karma for all living beings, brings about peace.
I bow to that Kṛtānta, who brings about the end of all embodied beings through the proper administration of their committed deeds;
he who is the dispenser of punishment for sinners and who wields the rod that bestows purification. (15)
Salutations again and again to you, the wielder of the rod of punishment, who are joined with political wisdom according to the treatises.
(16) I bow to the God in the form of Time (*kāla*), who effects the determination of all things and actions, and who measures the entirety of life. (17)
I bow indeed to that Yama, who in every way restrains living beings by the infliction of punishments, bestowing fruits according to their actions;
he gives according to the deed, neither out of passion nor out of anger. (18)
Therefore, I bow to the friend who brings about purification, the friend of all.
And I bow to that Brāhma, who was born in ancient times from the form of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, and who subsequently arose as a portion of Brahmā.
Having spoken thus, he bowed to him, and Yama became truly pleased.
For one who recites the *Yamāṣṭaka*, there shall be no fear of Yama;
moreover, through the manifestation of his body, his purification from karmic deeds comes about.
The King of Dharma said, "She is released from the noose of Yama," as he spoke to Satī. And Yama, having bestowed upon her the mantra of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa,
[had her recite] "Oṃ, I bow to Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa" three times.
Yama himself spoke to her regarding the ripening of unwholesome karma:
"By means of evil deeds, a person goes to hells that are exceedingly terrible.
Furthermore, there are various kinds of pits for those hells."
Indeed, they are vast, deep, and cause fear and affliction.
There are eighty-six terrible and loathsome pits located in Saṃyamanī; learn their names. (25–26)
The fire-pit, the heated pit, the terrifying pit of decay,
the pit of feces, the pit of urine, and the unbearable pit of phlegm;
the pit of poison, the burning pit, and likewise the great pit of fat.
The pit of semen, the pit of blood, and the loathsome pit of tears;
the pit of filth, the pit of virility, and the pit of menses which produces foul odors;
the fierce pit of earwax, and the painful pit of nails. (28–203)
The pit of marrow, the pit of flesh, and the pit of bones, which bestow suffering;
the pit of hair, the pit of affliction, and the great pit of copper and iron;
the pit of sharp thorns, and the burning pit of poison.
The Pit of Heat, the Pit of Boiling Liquor,
the Pit of Scorpions, the Pit of Boiling Oil, the Pit of Teeth which causes obstacles,
the Pit of Worms, the Pit of Pus, and the terrifying Pit of Serpents. (3.1–3.2)
The pit of gadflies and mosquitoes, the pit of sharp-pointed vajras,
the pit of arrows, the pit of tridents, the pit of swords which is truly destructive,
the pit of iguanas, the pit of crocodiles, and the terrifying pit of crows.
The pit of friction (ghṛṣṭikuṇḍa), the pit of powder (cūrṇakuṇḍa), the pit of bondage (bandhakuṇḍa), and the supportless pit (nirāśraya);
the pit of heated stones (taptapāṣāṇakuṇḍa) and the pit of sharp-edged rocks (tīkṣṇagrāvāgrakuṇḍaka);
the pit of saliva (lālākuṇḍa), the sword-pit (asikuṇḍa), the pit of powder (cūrṇakuṇḍa), and the pit of crushing (mardana).
The Cakra-pit (Wheel-pit), the Vajra-pit (Thunderbolt-pit), the Kūrma-pit (Tortoise-pit) which is most formidable,

the Jvālā-pit (Flame-pit), the Bhasma-pit (Ash-pit), and the terrifying Pūti-pit (Putrid-pit); [and] the Taptasūrmī (Heated Iron Statue), the Asipatra (Sword-leaf Pit), the Kṣuradhāra (Razor-edge Pit), and the Sucīmukha (Needle-mouth Pit).
Kṛkalāsaprakuṇḍa, Jagadaṃśa, Cipīṭaka;
Kumbhīpāka, Kālasūtra, Adhaḥkandhara, Ugraka;
Pāṃśubhojya, Pāśakaṇṭha, Śūlaprota, and Sukīlaka. (37–38)
The fire-mouthed pit, the blind well, the piercing, the flogging with rods, the binding with nets, the pulverizing of the body, the crushing, the drying up,
the serpent-flame, the poison-smoke-blinding, and the serpent-noose. (39)
The Dvaidhībhāva-kuṇḍa, and also the Lāvaṇa-kuṇḍa;
the Bhaguprapātana, and also the Vaitaraṇīprapātana;
the Carmotkartana-kuṇḍa, and also the Bhrāṣṭrakaṭāha.
"O Sāvitrī, these are indeed the pits that purify sinners;
they cause only suffering to the wicked and are guarded by the followers of Yama, who carry staffs in their hands and hold tridents, nooses, spears, and lances. (42)
[They were] intoxicated with pride, characterized by darkness (tamas), merciless, copper-brown and tawny, assuming various forms, unassailable by all, visible to sinners,
yet invisible to those who perform meritorious deeds, to the righteous, and to yogis. 43–44.

Listen: for whom and where does the punishment take the form of residence in a pit? One who burns his kinsmen with harsh speech and wickedness goes to the fire-pit for as many years as there are hairs on his body. (45)
Having burned away his sins in the fire, he shall obtain the state of a beast for three births.
He who does not feed a guest who has come to his house, nor likewise one dependent upon him,
shall indeed remain in the Taptaloma-māna hell.
In a desert region of a hot land, one may become a bird for seven births if,
on a Sunday, during the sun’s transit (saṃkrānti), on the new moon day, or on the day of a Śrāddha rite,
one destroys insects found in clothes using an alkaline substance while observing a vow.
He indeed goes to the Kṣārakuṇḍa hell for as many years as there are hairs on the body of the animal;
O beautiful one, he shall enter the womb of a royal beast for seven births!
For he who seizes the livelihood, whether given by himself or given by another— || 1.370.50 ||
For sixty thousand years he goes to Viṭkuṇḍa;
for sixty thousand years he is a dung-eating worm born from dung. He who destroys a pond goes to Mūtrakuṇḍa.
Then, drinking urine on the earth, he rains down particles of that dust;
for seven births he shall be a monitor lizard dwelling in the wall of a house.
Eating sweets all alone, he goes to the pit of phlegm for a hundred years.
One who eats phlegm becomes a preta that drinks urine, pus, and the like.
He who does not support his father, mother, wife, teacher, daughter,
son, friends, or the helpless, goes to the Kṣveḍakuṇḍa hell.
He who eats that [food] becomes a *preta* for a thousand years, and thereafter remains a *preta* for a hundred years.
The ancestors and the gods do not accept the water or the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) of one who looks upon a guest with a cruel disposition; consequently, the destruction of the lineage occurs.
Furthermore, those slayers are cast into the Pit of Filth (malakuṇḍa);
there they subsist on filth for a hundred years. Subsequently, for seven births, he is born poor, miserable, and stumbling at every step.
If, after giving a gift to one person, it is then given to another,
the giver of that fat goes to the Vasākuṇḍa hell for a hundred years.
Furthermore, he becomes a Cāṇḍāla for three births and a lizard for seven.
Consequently, that man or woman becomes poor, short-lived, and a doer of evil; for if out of lust they cause one another to drink their own semen or menstrual blood, he goes to Śukrakuṇḍa.
And for one hundred years he shall be a worm in a womb, and for another hundred years a worm in excrement.
(6.1) Now, he who strikes one worthy of worship, or his guru, or likewise his parents, and causes blood to flow, goes to the terrifying Pit of Blood. (6.2)
For a hundred years he becomes a consumer of blood, and thereafter he is born as a hunter;
having committed sins for seven lifetimes, he shall again go [to such a state].
He who [sees] even a devotee weeping, singing, or dancing...
But one who makes jokes while laughing in the presence of Kṛṣṇa goes to the Aśru-kuṇḍa;
there he eats tears for a hundred years and becomes a Cāṇḍāla for three births.
A wicked person goes to the Gātra-mala-kuṇḍa for ten years thereafter.

He who laughs at or even mocks a deaf person, or makes sport of them, becomes a donkey for three births and a monkey for three births, suffering hardship. He goes to the pit of ear-wax, where he eats that [wax] for a hundred years.
Then, for seven births he will be deaf, and for seven [births] he will be deficient in his limbs.
He who kills one that provides a livelihood goes to the Majjākuṇḍa hell;
eating that [flesh], he remains there for a hundred thousand years, and for seven births he is reborn as a hare.

Seven fish and seven deer [are required]; thereafter, one is born purified. Those who sell their daughters go to a most dreadful pit of flesh for as many years as there are hairs on the girl's body; they are tormented by the agents of Yama.

Afflicted by hunger, they devour your own flesh and blood from your head for sixty thousand years. Thereafter, he becomes a worm among those who violate virgins; then, for seven births, he is a hunter, then a boar, and then a dog.
For seven births, that person who does not have the ritual shaving performed according to the prescribed rule becomes a frog, a leech, and even a crow. Furthermore,
one who eats from their fingernails goes to Nakhakuṇḍa for as many years as there are nails.
Likewise, the one who feeds upon hair, having been struck down, goes to the Romakuṇḍa.
That person who worships an earthen linga with hair attached goes indeed to the Keśakuṇḍa for a period of a hundred years of human measure, consisting of particles of dust.
Consequently, that Yavana is born on earth for a hundred years;
failing to offer funeral cakes (piṇḍas) to his ancestors, he falls into the fierce Khaṇḍa of bones.
Thereafter, for seven births, he is lame and utterly destitute.
He who has sexual intercourse with a woman in her courses, with one who is pregnant, or with one about to give birth,
remains for a hundred years in a cauldron of molten copper.
He who eats the food of a menstruating woman remains for a hundred years in an iron cauldron.

Having fallen into a royal womb seven times and then into that of a leather-worker, he is born thereafter as one with great sores and impoverished; only after that does he become pure. And he who applies his hand, dripping with sweat from the heat, to the property of the gods [is likewise reborn].
He remains in the pit of heat for a duration of one hundred years;
and the drinker of spirituous liquor goes to the pit of spirits for a hundred hot years.
Thereafter, that Śūdra shall be utterly destitute for seven births.

She who speaks harsh words to her husband falls into a pit of sharp thorns and is beaten by messengers; she remains there for four yugas. Subsequently, she is born as an Aśvinī on earth for seven lifetimes.
The giver of poison remains indeed in a pit of poison for a thousand years.
The consumer of poison, as well as the slayer of a human, shall become a lizard for seven births;
for seven births he shall be afflicted with leprosy, and thereafter he is born purified.
He who, as the controller of that bull, strikes the servant with a staff,
shall remain for four yugas in a cauldron of boiling oil.
Thereafter, he becomes a bull on earth for a number of years equal to the hairs on its body.
With a hook, a spear, an ivory tusk, or a wooden peg—
whosoever kills a bull, or any other embodied living being with an iron weapon,
shall indeed dwell in the Kuntakuṇḍa hell for ten thousand years.
Then, one who eats forbidden food is born as a sufferer of dropsy for one lifetime; indeed, such a man goes to the pit of worms for three lifetimes,
becoming a barbarian on earth at the end of a period equal to the number of hairs on his own body.
One who eats food from a sinful person goes to the pit of pus for a hundred years.
Thereafter, that Śūdra shall become a bearer of intense colic for seven lifetimes.
A killer of snakes, however, goes to the pit of snakes and is devoured by a snake.
After consuming snakes and excrement, he is indeed born as a snake upon the earth;
thereafter, having a very short lifespan, he likewise becomes afflicted with the disease of ringworm (dadru).
His death is caused by a snake, and it is held that he is devoured by a snake.
The evildoer kills living beings and falls into the hell called Daṃśa.
Having remained there for a lifespan of one thousand years, he is born repeatedly among thousands of minute creatures;
thereafter, he will certainly become deformed in his limbs.
One who kills bees or strikes at flies shall fall into the *kuṇḍaka* hell;
after remaining there for a duration equal to his own lifespan in days, he will enter the womb of a fly.
One who punishes those who do not deserve punishment will certainly fall into the *vajrakīṭa* hell.
Having remained on earth for as many years as there are hairs on his body, he becomes a worm;
a king who covets wealth through unjust means shall fall into a pit in Scorpio (Vṛścika) for as many years as there are hairs on his body,
experiencing suffering for seven lifetimes as a scorpion.
Then that person shall become maimed in limb and afflicted by disease upon the earth;
indeed, a Brahmin devoid of dharma falls into the Śara-kuṇḍa.
Pierced by arrows, he remains there for as many years as there are hairs on his body, and thereafter he becomes purified.
A person imprisons innocent living beings in a prison;
[for that], he falls into a pit of boiling water filled with hair for as many years as there are hairs on his body.
Thereafter, he is indeed born on earth as a low-born servant, pierced by insects. (97–98)
The slayer of crocodiles and fish then falls into a pit of crocodiles;
having remained there for as many years as there are scales on a crocodile, he then becomes a crocodile in the water.
Then, seeking another opening, he falls into a pit of crows.
His eyes will be crushed like those of a crow, and there he shall dwell for a hundred years of his life. He is born poor for seven lifetimes and blind for three lifetimes.
Indeed, a thief of gold, copper, or iron goes to the Vajrakuṇḍa hell.
Even one who misappropriates the property of the gods shall remain in a pit of vajras for as many years as there are hairs on his body;
struck there by vajras, he becomes a consumer of vajras, his body aflame.
A thief of cows, parrots, or idols shall go to the place called Taptopala.
Then, for as many years as there are hairs on his body, he falls into a pit; thereafter, for three births, he becomes a crane.

Then he becomes a swan, then a conch-bird (*śaṅkhacilla*), and thereafter he suffers from diseases such as blood disorders for seven births, being short-lived; one who steals from a water-vessel is likewise [punished].

A thief of brass, bronze, and the like, as well as one who steals sharp stones or the tips of sacrificial vessels, shall dwell for a year in his own hair within a pit of sharp stones. Thereafter, he becomes a horse for seven births.
Following that, he is born with redundant limbs, as a hunchback, and with a diseased foot.

One who eats the food of an unchaste woman and lives off it will certainly fall into the Lālā-kuṇḍa (the Pit of Saliva). For as many years as there are hairs on that woman’s body, he shall subsist on saliva, suffering from eye disease and colic.
One who serves Mlecchas or one who uses ink as a livelihood falls into the intensely heated Maṣī-kuṇḍa (the Pit of Ink).
Thereafter, for as many years as there are hairs on his body, he shall dwell as a black beast for three births;
then for three births each, he shall be a goat, a serpent, and a palm tree.
One who steals grain, betel, bedding, offerings, seats, crops, and so forth—
For a hundred years he shall indeed dwell in a pit of dust, and thereafter as a ram and a cock.
Then, throughout three births, that man shall be afflicted by the disease of cough;
he shall be deprived of lineage, impoverished, short-lived, and full of suffering.
One who manufactures wheels, weapons, and the like falls into Cakrakuṇḍa for a hundred years;
thereafter, for three births, he becomes an oil-presser, diseased, and deprived of his lineage.
One who is competitive and envious falls into Vajrakuṇḍa for the duration of a Yuga.
For seven lifetimes he shall have crooked limbs and be deprived of a wife and lineage;
by eating the flesh of tortoises and other such creatures, he shall fall into the Kūrma-kunda for a hundred years.
For three births he shall be a tortoise, then a pig, and then a peacock.

And a thief of ghee, oil, and such things is born as a cat for three successive births; he falls into a pit of flames or into ashes. A stealer of oil falls into a pit for a hundred years, [and this occurs] for seven births.
Then he becomes a fish and a mouse for seven births; thereafter he is purified.
However, one who steals substances such as fragrant oil or a nurse's fee is born in a *kuṇḍaka* hell;
for as many years as there are hairs on his body, he remains there, and after that he is born with a foul odor.

For seven births he shall have a foul odor, for three births he shall be musk-deer, and for seven births he shall be fragrant; thereafter, indeed, the human being becomes pure. A stealer of land shall fall into the Taptashula hell and then into boiling oil.
Afterwards, for seven manvantaras, he becomes a worm in excrement for sixty thousand years;
then, deprived of land and impoverished, he indeed becomes purified.
A killer of a human being shall dwell in the Sword-Leaf Hell (Asipatra) for a kalpa, and after that, once again...
A slayer of a Brahmin shall dwell in a forest of swords for a hundred *manvantaras*,
with his limbs severed by sword-blades; thereafter, he becomes a *cāṇḍāla* for a hundred births,
and then a pig, a dog, a jackal, a tiger, and a wolf.
A gong-beater is born as a buffalo for seven successive lifetimes.

One who sets fire to villages and the like shall fall upon the razor-edged hell for three eons; thereafter, he becomes a preta with a mouth of fire, feeding on impurities, and after that, once more [into further births]. (121–122)
For that duration, he becomes a firefly for seven births and suffers from a great piercing pain; then, as one with leprosy for seven births, he is purified by giving firewood.
One who causes a blemish and one who reviles [others] remain in the Sūcimukha hell for three yugas.
Then, for seven births, he shall become a scorpion and a snake;
for seven births, a diamond-insect (vajrakīṭa); then a man who is a bhasmakīṭa, a destroyer of houses, and a thief of cows, lizards, rams, and goats. (124–125)
For seven births each, the man shall be diseased and incapable of bearing burdens;
then he becomes a thief of wealth with the face of a crocodile for a *yuga*, and thereafter he is afflicted by disease.
For three *yugas* he is a killer of cows, elephants, horses, and men, [suffering] from the bite of an elephant.
Then, after three births in various such barbarian (mleccha) species, he becomes a bull;
he certainly goes to the Gomukha hell, which inflicts the suffering of the bovine species.
Having remained there for a manvantara in the Kṛmitaptodaka hell, he becomes a bull.

For seven births thereafter, he shall be diseased, impoverished, and of the lowest caste; likewise, one who has committed the murder of a cow, a Brahmin, or a saint, or who has killed his wife, a friend, or an embryo,
shall fall into the Kumbhīpāka hell for a kalpa and be ground to powder by the messengers of Yama.

In fire, for a moment; in a heated pit, in hot oil, and likewise in water, on stone, and in heated iron—he certainly experiences these miseries. For ten million births he becomes a vulture, and for a hundred births he is a pig.
For seven births he shall be a crow, and for seven births a serpent;
then he becomes a worm in excrement, a low-born man, and one afflicted with trickling leprosy.
Thereafter, seized by consumption and deprived of his lineage and wife, he finally becomes pure.
One who perceives a sense of difference between Śrī Hari, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa, the Infinite (Bhūman), Vāsudeva, Śiva, Viṣṇu,
and Brahmā should be known as a committer of the sin of killing a Brahmin; such a distinction is considered equal to the murder of a Brahmin.
One who makes distinctions between Akṣarā, Rādhikā, Lakṣmī, Śrī, the body of Ramā, Pārvatī, Prabhā,
and Māṇikyā incurs a sin equal to that of killing a Brahmin; this applies even regarding Lalitā and Jayā.
One who creates a sense of duality toward one’s own guru, one’s chosen deity, father, or mother;

one who harbors a notion of difference during the worship of Hari; and likewise one who avoids even the water used for washing the food offerings (naivedya) of Viṣṇu—these are considered equal to the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Likewise, one who reviles the ancestors, the gods, or the guru is considered [an equal sinner].
Those who slay Brahmins revile Śiva, Viṣṇu, Śivā, and Lakṣmī. They likewise revile the birth-anniversary days of Hari, the lunar day sacred to Śiva, and Ekādaśī. (138)
They indeed censure those who observe vows [but neglect their duties], for they are as guilty as killers of Brahmins.
(139) He who does not support his teacher, mother, father, virtuous wife, son, daughter, or dependents, is indeed a killer of Brahmins. (140)
One who fails to worship the gods, one who strikes cows or bulls,
and one who destroys their grazing grounds and so forth, is indeed a perpetrator of the sin of killing a Brahmin (brahmahatyā).
Likewise, one who causes suffering to cows incurs the same sin as that born from the slaughter of a cow.

He who deprives cows of their livelihood, or he who strikes them with his foot; he who lives by [prostituting] women, who neglects the three daily junctures (saṃdhyā) and other duties, and who destroys righteousness;
he who fails to serve the gods, the ancestors, and guests—he is considered a killer of cows.
She who creates a sense of division between her own husband and Kṛṣṇa, and strikes her beloved with harsh words, is considered a committer of cow-slaughter.
[She also commits it] regarding the cows' livelihood, their means of subsistence, water, the home, and likewise their shelter. (144)
He who [treads upon them] would certainly become an outcaste guilty of the sin of killing a cow.
Whatever water, food, or flowers have been offered for the sake of worshipping the gods—he who should step over those with his feet is indeed a perpetrator of the sin of killing a cow. (145–146)
A speaker of falsehood, one who hates his guru, one who hates the gods, and one who hates his father—even he should be known as a sinner guilty of cow-slaughter; there is no doubt in this matter.
(147) A mother is a hundred times more venerable than a father, and a guru is a hundred times more venerable than a mother.
The teacher who imparts knowledge and mantras is always considered worthy of worship.
(148) The wife of the teacher is even more venerable than the teacher himself.
The wife of one’s chosen deity and the chosen deity itself are also to be worshipped. (149)
O virtuous lady! A Brāhmaṇa who drinks liquor, eats excrement, is the husband of a low-caste woman (vṛṣalī), or eats on the day of Hari (Ekādaśī), shall go to the Kubhīpāka hell.
[Likewise, one who violates] the wife of a guru, the wife of a king, a co-wife, a mother, or [one’s own] daughter...
A daughter, a daughter-in-law, a mother-in-law, a pregnant woman,
a beloved sister, the wife of a uterine brother, a maternal aunt, one’s own mother,
the mother of one’s mother, her sister, a sister, and the daughter of a brother. (151–152)

The Lotus-born One has declared that a disciple, a disciple’s wife, the beloved of one’s nephew, and even the wife of one’s brother’s son are women who must not be approached. A lustful man who has sexual intercourse with these incurs the guilt of a hundred murders of Brahmins.
That great sinner goes to the Kumbhīpāka hell, which is very difficult to cross.
O virtuous lady! Without service to Hari, one cannot attain the destruction of karma;
he who eats all kinds of food goes to the Kālasūtra hell for a hundred years.
Consequently, the Śūdra shall become exceedingly afflicted, poor, and destitute.
She who looks upon her husband with a face full of wrath out of anger,
speaks harsh words to him, and indeed goes to the Ulkāmukha hell.
And Yama’s servant constantly places a flaming torch in her mouth;
he shall strike her on the head with a staff [the number of blows] equal to the number of hairs on her body for as many years as there are hairs.
Consequently, she shall become a human widow for seven lifetimes. (157–158)
That Brāhmaṇī who was enjoyed by all [men] indeed goes to a blind well;
having suffered there for a full kalpa in water heated by purification-fire, she thereafter becomes a female crow, a sow, a hen, a jackal, and a pigeon. (159)
She shall become a female monkey for seven births, and thereafter a Cāṇḍālī woman. O virtuous lady, she is purified after becoming a washerwoman and an oil-presser.
A prostitute shall dwell in the Vedhakuṇḍa hell, and a harlot in Daṇḍatāḍana.

A prostitute shall dwell for the duration of a *manvantara* in the *jālabandha* hell; an unchaste woman, in *dehacūrṇaka*; a wanton woman, in *dalana*; and one who has borne a child out of wedlock, in *kuṇḍa*.
Furthermore, he who takes the *tulasī* plant in his hand and does not fulfill his vow [shall likewise suffer].
He who makes a false oath shall fall into Jvālāmukha.
He who, having extended his right hand, does not fulfill his promise—having touched a cow, a Brahmin, a deity, fire, a virtuous man, a chaste woman, or water. (163–164)
He who does not fulfill his promise shall indeed fall into Jvālāmukha;
likewise, the betrayer of a friend, the ungrateful person, the violator of trust,
and he who gives false testimony— these too shall go to Jvālāmukha.
Then he shall dwell [in hell] for an eon; thereafter, for three births, he shall be mute and deaf.
A betrayer of friends becomes a mongoose, and an ungrateful person becomes a eunuch.
A betrayer of trust becomes a tiger, while a false witness becomes a bear.
One who is devoid of vows and fasts, who reviles the words of the virtuous,
and who is crooked-minded, shall dwell indeed in the Haime hell for a hundred years.
Through a succession of a hundred births as an aquatic creature, he becomes a small fish.
One who steals the property of gods and others shall fall into the Dhūmrāndha hell.
There he shall dwell for the duration of four yugas; then, for seven births, he is born as a mouse.
He is subsequently born among animals, birds, worms, and various species of trees.
Then, being devoid of a wife and lineage, the Śabara shall become afflicted by disease;
likewise the goldsmith, the merchant, the physician, the trader, and the seller of mercury (171).
One who uses false measures goes indeed to the terrible Nāgaveṣṭa hell.
Then he becomes a cowherd, and from that, O virtuous woman, he indeed attains purification.
(172) O devoted wife, the well-known sacrificial pits have been described;
there are also others, unknown, which exist according to the specific ritual action. (173)
There are evildoers who enjoy the fruits in the hells;
consequently, they wander through saṃsāra. This much has been reported to you. However, the service of Kṛṣṇa is the most desired, essential, and auspicious of all things.
O auspicious one! It is the deliverer from birth, death, old age, disease, grief, and suffering;
it causes the sprouting of the tree of devotion and cuts down the tree of karma;
and it bestows the states of living in the same world, sharing the same powers, possessing the same form, and dwelling in close proximity [to the Divine]. (175–176)
O Satī! The servants of Śrī Kṛṣṇa do not see the pits, the messengers of Yama, Yama himself, or the minions of Yama, even in their dreams.
This applies to householders who observe the vows of Hari, as well as renunciants and women. (177)
Those who bathe in the Haritīrtha, do not eat on the day of Hari (Ekādaśī),
remember Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, and worship him— they do not go to my terrible city of Saṃyamanī, which is full of suffering. (178–179)
Those who abide by the path of the traditional scriptures and logic— whether they be renunciants or householders— who are pure and devoted to dharma, go to the imperishable abode of Kṛṣṇa.
I shall now describe those messengers of his who approach them with nooses in their hands.
"Except for the hermitage of the devotees of Hari, you shall go everywhere"—thus [it is said].
Indeed, Citragupta offers a handful of flowers to the devotees of Hari, while Brahmā always provides them with the honey-mixture (madhuparka) and other honors. (181–182)
As the virtuous pass beyond my world, Satyaloka,
the sins of those embodied beings belonging to Yama perish by their mere touch.
Those Bhāgavatas are purifiers, even without a body composed of the five elements.
With their very subtle bodies, they proceed with an upward momentum.
Having bathed in the Brahma-lake near the abode of Brahmā,
they cast off their subtle body within Māyā and [enter] the abode with a body of Brahmā.
Those embodied beings who have gone to the realm of Yama for the sake of the fruits of their karma, possessing many powers and lordly senses, rejoice through their identification with the self;
they bear a subtle body whose destruction never occurs.
That body would not turn to ashes in the blazing fire of the abode of Yama;
it would not be destroyed in water, nor does it perish even under a blow. Likewise, it remains unharmed by weapons, by blades, by thorns, by the trident, or by molten metal. (187–188)
Just as the fruit of one's actions does not perish even when fashioned into an image of heated iron or stone, so too does one experience its results; yet,
in the abode of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, there is not even a trace of suffering.
"O Sāvitrī, worship Him alone! Go to your husband’s home!"—
having been addressed thus even by Yama, she did not go to her own abode,
for she had brought Satyavān, in his subtle body, under her own control within her heart.
Desiring to know, she then asked about the pits (*kuṇḍa*) and so forth.
"Listen, Lakṣmī! I shall tell you that which was spoken by Yama.

(192) Thus ends the three hundred and seventieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Eightfold Hymn to Yama performed by Sāvitrī, the Sixty-four Pits of Hell, Falling Therein According to One's Karma, Sins such as the Killing of a Brahmin or a Cow, and the Defeat of Yama by Devotees," within the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, concerning the majesty of the devoted wife (*pativratā-māhātmya*), in the *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
