Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, my dear wife! To that which was spoken by Yama for the benefit of the worlds—the measurements of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and so forth—for Sāvitrī. || 1 ||
Each sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) indeed has the shape of the full moon’s orb;
it is deep and low-lying, bestowing most formidable merit, yet not perishable.
Therein, the length of the fire-pit is measured at one hundred cubits.
Indeed, there are crores of circular fire-pits (agni-kuṇḍas).
One should understand that the multitude of individual pits is due to the great number of sinners.
Furthermore, the pit of boiling water measures exactly half a krośa.
The pool of boiling caustic water is proclaimed to be one *krośa* in extent;
the pool of boiling liquid urine is indeed one *gavyūti* in measure.
The pool of phlegm is one *krośa*, and the pool of poison is half a *krośa*.
The pit of eye-secretions is half a *krośa* in extent and filled with insects;
the pit of fat is a quarter *krośa*, and the pit of semen is likewise considered [to be the same size].
The pit of foul-smelling blood is like a pond, measuring one hundred *dhanus*.
The pit for eye-tears is half a *vāpī*, and the pit for filth is likewise;
the pit for ear-wax is exactly the size of a fourth *vāpī*.
The pit for marrow is a quarter *vāpī*, and the pit for flesh is a hundred *dhanus* long.
The Nakhakuṇḍa (Nail-pit), Lomakuṇḍa (Hair-pit), Asthikuṇḍa (Bone-pit), and Dantaka (Tooth-pit)—
each measuring four times the size of a small pond and exceedingly terrifying—
[followed by] the Tāmrakuṇḍa (Copper-pit), which shone with ten million images of molten copper.
A pit of molten iron measuring one *gavyūti* in extent,
as well as a pit of boiling water, a pit of liquor, and half a pit of iron;
below the *śālmali* tree is a pit of sharp thorns.
It was one hundred thousand paces deep, one *krośa* in circumference, and circular.
Around its walls stood thorny spikes measuring one *dhanus* in length.
There was a pit of poison one *krośa* in measure, and likewise a pit of weapons that was elongated.
The pit of boiling oil measures two *gavyūtis* in extent;
the pit of the bed of weapons measures a quarter of a *krośa*;
the pit of pus measures half a *krośa*, and the pit of teeth is likewise long.
The pool of icy water is two *gavyūtis* in measure;
the pool of gnats and stinging insects is likewise considered to be half a *krośa*;
and the pool of diamond scorpions extends for half a *vāpī*.
The Śarakuṇḍa is for the purpose of a pond, and the Nakrakuṇḍa is likewise elongated;
the Kākakuṇḍa measures one hundred thousand bow-lengths, and the Gṛdhrakuṇḍa is similarly elongated.
The Vājakuṇḍa is likewise long, while the Vajrakuṇḍa measures one hundred bows.
The Taptapāṣāṇakuṇḍa is twice the length of a vāpī; the Lālākuṇḍa measures one krośa, the Taptatoya one hundred dhanus,
the Cūrṇakuṇḍa one krośa, and the Cakraka one-quarter of a krośa.
Whirling like a potter’s wheel, it contains sixteen pits:
the Pit of Flames, the Pit of Tortoises and other creatures, and the Pit of Wailing;
the Pit of Wailing, the Pit of Hot Ashes, and the Pit of Darkness, each extending for one *krośa*.
The Dagdhakuṇḍa is one krośa in extent and likewise extended with heated alkaline liquid;
the Taptatoyaprakuṇḍa measures exactly two gavyūtis,
as do the Utaptasūrmikuṇḍa and the Asipatravana.
The Raktakuṇḍa is likewise half a krośa in length;
the terrifying Kṣurāstrakuṇḍa measures one hundred dhanus;
and the piercing Sūcikuṇḍa measures fifty dhanus.
The Godhā-kuṇḍa is of a distorted shape and measures twenty dhanus.
The Naramukha-shaped kuṇḍa measures sixteen dhanus. The Gaja-kuṇḍa, which is shaped like an elephant's tusk, measures one hundred dhanus. || 24–25 ||
The Gomukha pit is recorded as being thirty *dhanus* in measure;
the Kālacakra and Bhrami pits are each two *gavyūtis* in measure.
The Mānava pit measures one hundred thousand [parts] and is provided with oil, iron, and stone.
And that [hell] is heated by fire and measures four *gavyūtis* in extent.
O beautiful one, whatever sinners exist in all the other pits, those in *Kumbhīpāka* are four times greater than them. (27–28)
Kumbhīpāka is proclaimed as the foremost of all pits;
Kālasūtra and Taptatoya are each twenty bows long, while Avaṭoda is a hundred bows long and filled with diseases and ailments. (29)
The Tapta-pāṃsu-prakuṇḍa, which causes burning, measures one hundred bows;
the Krośārtanāda-kuṇḍa measures twenty bows;
the Śūla-kuṇḍa is of the same measure; and the Himatoyaka measures half a krośa.
The Ulkā-kuṇḍa is proclaimed to measure twenty dhanus;
the Andhakāra-prakuṇḍa is even greater, measuring one hundred dhanus.
The Śastra-kuṇḍa has a depth of twenty dhanus.
The *daṇḍatāḍana* pit is sixteen *dhanus* in measure;
the *jālakuṇḍa* is proclaimed to be thirty *dhanus* in size;
and the *lohavedicūrṇa* pit is one *koṭi* in measure.
The Mūrchā-kunda, filled with darkness, measures twenty *dhanus*;
the Dalana-kunda is said to measure sixteen *dhanus*.
The Taptavālukikā-kunda measures thirty *dhanus* in extent.
And the pit for leather-tanning is foul-smelling, measuring one hundred bows (dhanus).
The pit with a winnow-shaped opening measures twelve bows.
Likewise, the Agniśikha pit measures twenty bows.
The Jvālāmukha is proclaimed as being curved or semi-circular;
the Dhūmrakuṇḍa is one hundred *dhanus* in length and filled with poisonous smoke and the like.
The Nāgaveṣṭana-kuṇḍa is one hundred *dhanus* and filled with serpents.
"And eighty-six sacrificial pits have been described by me, O virtuous Sāvitrī!
Speak further, if you wish to hear more.
Then Sāvitrī, being well-pleased, spoke that which is difficult for even the gods to obtain.
The female species has been created by the Creator as devoid of knowledge of reality, even though they possess devotion to Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa characterized by the essence of the Bhāgavata.
What is that essential knowledge which I should receive? Tell me that here.
Indeed, all forms of giving, fasting, bathing at sacred fords, religious observances,
and austerities do not equal even a sixteenth part of the gift of knowledge when one is ignorant.
A mother is a hundred times more venerable than a father, and a teacher is a hundred times more venerable than a mother.

Having heard this, Yama said: "May you have devotion to Keśava—that which even Śeṣa with his thousand mouths is not able to describe, nor Śambhu with his five faces, nor likewise Brahmā with his four faces. (44)
Even Kārtikeya, with his six faces, is not able to describe her;
nor are Sarasvatī, Gaṇeśa, Sanatkumāra, Dharma, Sanaka, Sananda, Kapila, and Sanātana. (45–46)
Sūrya, Patnīvrata, and Nārada, the sons of Brahmā— even the Siddhas,
the lords of sages, and the yogis are not capable of describing her.
What then of others, or who are we, in the description of the devotion to the Blessed One?
Someone knows something of the glorification of the Lord’s qualities.
(48) From that, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, knows something.
From that, Gaṇeśa, the teacher of the wise, knows something. (49)
Śambhu alone is omniscient; he knows everything beyond all else.
Lakṣmī alone knows even more than that—of this there is no doubt.
Rādhā, Prabhā, Māṇikī, Pārvatī, Jayā, and the others [know much as well].
The liberated ones know supreme devotion; they know it boundlessly.
By Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa himself, who is the form of Puruṣottama, all knowledge regarding Śrī Kṛṣṇa and his own true nature is perfectly preserved.
The supreme Self, Kṛṣṇa, imparted this knowledge to Śambhu in the exceedingly secluded and beautiful Rāsa-maṇḍala in Goloka. Śiva himself then recounted it to Dharmarāja in the world of Śiva.
Dharma recounted it to Bhāskara at Puṣkara;
Sūrya recounted to me the glorification of devotion to Kṛṣṇa and other matters.
Even he does not know it in its entirety—what then can be said of anyone else? || 54–55 ||
The Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, Hari, is the inner self of all, the witness of all, the possessor of all forms, and the cause of all causes.
For the sake of bestowing grace upon his devotees, he assumes a dual form.
Desirable and beautiful, a youth of solid form;
possessing the loveliness of ten million Cupids, filled with the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra-rasa);
with eyes having the luster of lotus petals and a face like the full moon. ||57-58||
Wearing ornaments and jewels, clad in yellow garments, served by Rādhā and others,
seated upon a jeweled throne in the midst of the *rāsa* dance,
holding a flute, adorned with a forest garland, the Kaustubha gem, and other ornaments, smiling, and most excellent.
It was honored with saffron, agallochum, musk, sandalwood, and other fragrances;
it was adorned with beautiful garlands of campaka flowers, lotuses, and jasmine blossoms;
and it shone with a crown of shimmering, exceedingly brilliant, and artificial jewels.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva— Aniruddha, Pradyumna, and Karṣaṇa—
perform creation, nourishment, and dissolution by His command.
By His grace, the wind blows and the sun and moon shine.
Indra rains, and Mahākāla likewise makes his morsel;
fire is hot and water is cold—all that has been made by Him alone.
Out of fear of Him, the guardians of the quarters protect the directions, and the planets revolve.
Trees bear fruit and blossom, and the seasons arrive in their proper order;
likewise, living beings thrive on land, in water, and in the sky.
By his command, Yama is the dispenser of justice, and the Bull (Dharma) is the bestower of righteousness.
Whether falling into a blazing fire or into the deep ocean,
upon the tip of a tree or the edge of a sharp sword, into the mouths of serpents and other creatures,
or amidst various weapons and missiles in battles and treacherous conflicts— (66–67)
Through whose grace there is protection, and likewise through whose anger there is destruction;
he who sustains the wind, and the fire sustains the submarine fire, and the fire sustains the oceans of water;
water sustains the tortoise, the Great Tortoise sustains the serpent Ananta, and he [Ananta] sustains the earth.
May he, by whose grace [the world], including the oceans and mountains, is sung [of]—may he be praised!
(69) The lifespan of Indra is seventy-one divine yugas;
when twenty-eight Indras have fallen, it constitutes one day and night of Brahmā. (70)
Thus, thirty nights and days constitute a month, and two such months an *ṛtu* (season).
Six *ṛtus* make a year, and one hundred years is the lifespan of Brahmā.
Indeed, the passing of Brahmā Vairāja constitutes a single day [of the next higher deity].
A hundred years of the Vairāja [Brahmā] constitute a single day of Mahāviṣṇu.
A hundred years of Mahāviṣṇu constitute a day of Pradhānapuruṣa.
A hundred years of that [Pradhānapuruṣa] shall indeed be a day of Prākṛtapuruṣa.
Every hundred years, the blinking of the eyelids of Hari occurs;
this very Hari is the Lord Śrīśa, the Master Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Hara, and all others are essentially Kṛṣṇa—of this there is no doubt.
Upon the closing of his eyes, his dissolution becomes natural (prākṛtika).
Those of natural form dissolve into Kṛṣṇa’s navel-lotus;
likewise Viṣṇu, who reclines upon the Ocean of Milk and possesses four arms in Vaikuṇṭha.
They dissolve into the left side of Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul.
Śiva, who is established in knowledge, dissolves into Hari; Durgā shall go to dissolution in His intellect.
Skanda dissolves in the chest, and Gaṇeśvara in the arm of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Padmā, Rādhā, and the gopīs have attained dissolution into the life-breath of Kṛṣṇa. Sāvitrī has merged into Sarasvatī, who resides upon the tongue of the Supreme Self.
The cowherds have entered the body hairs of Kṛṣṇa, and the winds and other elements have entered his vital breaths.
The fire is in his stomach-fire, the water is at the tip of his tongue;
the Vaiṣṇavas are in the lotus of his feet, and devotion and righteousness are within his heart.
Indeed, the powers of sovereignty belong to that form which is the Lord himself.
In whose very pores all things without exception [dwell];
by whose closing of the eyes there occurs the dissolution of the world of beings,
and by the opening of whose eyes there is the creation— of that very Supreme Self.
Thus, O lady of noble vows, there is indeed no limit to the number of creations and dissolutions;
who, then, is capable of enumerating those multitudes within the cosmic eggs?
Yet, devotion to Hari is the most preeminent, even superior to liberation itself.
O daughter, if you wish to go to the further shore of dissolution (*laya*), that [devotion] must be practiced.
One [form of devotion] grants residence in the same world as Hari (*sālokya*); another grants a form similar to Hari’s (*sārūpya*);
then another grants proximity to him (*sāmīpya*); and yet another grants equal power (*sārṣṭi*). (84–85)
But other devotees do not desire that [attainment] which brings about oneness;
indeed, having abandoned service, there is nothing whatsoever to be desired.
Liberation is devotion devoid of service, while devotion is that which increases service.
This is the distinction between devotion (bhakti) and yoga: therefore, one should always practice devotion.
Indeed, the offering of all actions performed with the body, all the senses, and the internal organs in every way unto Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa brings about liberation.
A woman should always perform service to Hari by surrendering herself to her husband; O Goddess, she should do so with love in every way. This knowledge, however, is the most essential of all.
Go, Sāvitrī! Be happy together with your husband.
Having spoken thus and having restored her husband to her, the son of the Sun gave her auspicious blessings and prepared to depart. Seeing Yama departing, Sāvitrī bowed down before him.
Having clouded her eyes and placing her head at his excellent feet, she was overcome with the grief of separation; for the loss of a virtuous person indeed causes suffering.
Then the compassionate Yama said, "O noble lady, do not grieve!"
Having enjoyed happiness for a hundred thousand years in every way within that field of merit,
you will certainly go to Goloka in the Nara-Nārāyaṇa-khaṇḍa.
Having returned home, O auspicious lady, perform the vow of Sāvitrī accordingly.
Indeed, that [vow] bestows liberation upon women for up to fourteen years. Perform the vow of Sāvitrī on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha;
perform the vow of Mahālakṣmī on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada.
This vow lasts for sixteen years, indeed for one fortnight every year.
On the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kārttika, perform with supreme devotion the vow of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa; at its conclusion, you shall go to the abode of Hari.
And on every Tuesday, one should worship the goddess Maṅgalacaṇḍikā;
every month on the sixth day of the bright fortnight, one should worship the bestower of auspiciousness, Ṣaṣṭhī;
Rādhā at the summer solstice (Āṣāḍha-saṃkrānti); and her [Rādhā] again on the full moon day of Kārtika.
Whichever woman worships with devotion on the eighth day of the bright fortnight every month Durgā, the destroyer of difficult distress, as well as Kambharā, the virtuous bestower of happiness—
with such affection on the white eighth day, she attains the supreme goal.
For the sake of obtaining wealth and progeny, she who honors a virtuous woman endowed with a husband and sons,
as well as chaste women, pure idols, and sacred images,
shall become happy and, in the end, attain the Imperishable.
Having spoken thus and bowed to that virtuous woman, Yamarāja went to his own abode.
Taking her husband, who was subtle in nature, Sāvitrī returned to her own home.
Satyavān, having been as if in deep sleep, immediately arose and became restored to life.
Ānanda was present there in every way, both in the city and in the house.
Sāvitrī related the account concerning Satyavān in due order, and having heard it, they all were filled with wonder. (1.04)
Sāvitrī’s father obtained a hundred sons in due order;
her father-in-law, the son of Akṣuṣā, obtained a kingdom that destroyed poverty;
and she herself obtained a hundred sons from Satyavat in succession.
Thus, O Lakṣmī! by the power of her devotion to her husband, Satī, the most excellent of women, conquered death and instead attained prosperity.
If devotion to one's husband is maintained, it is indeed equal to the wish-fulfilling cow, Kāmadhenu.
It is equal to the wish-fulfilling tree and even superior to the thought-gem.
For yogis who have attained perfection in yoga, devotion to the husband (pātivratya) is distinguished as being superior;
it cannot be stolen by thieves, it is not subject to affliction, and it is not of a nature that can be separated.
That [virtue] remained hidden indeed, firmly established in the eternal Self and in Dharma.
Having enjoyed happiness on earth for a hundred thousand years, that great chaste lady,
possessing a divine form, went to Goloka together with her husband.
Highly honored by the gods, she traveled through the air in a celestial chariot.
In her second form, she was the divine presiding deity of the sun;
she was also Sāvitrī, the deity who presides over the mantras of the Vedas.
She herself was born in manifold forms through devotion to Puruṣottama.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have narrated to you this excellent account of Sāvitrī.
Any woman who hears this shall certainly attain the status of a chaste wife.
Indeed, apart from devotion to her husband, she should not practice any other primary duty.
(1.14) Everything—liberation and devotion—is found in the image of the husband; all supernatural powers wait like handmaidens upon devotion to the husband. (1.15)
All forms of sovereignty, wealth, grain, and garments; gold, silver, gems, jewels, and ornaments in every respect—
all these prosperities exist within the water at the feet of the Lord, specifically in His big toe.

The Great Brahman resides in the husband’s face; indeed, all pleasures reside in the husband’s limbs. (1.17) Great satisfaction arises from the husband’s contentment; bliss is found in the husband’s dalliance.
Great fortune resides in the husband’s hand; the immortal state resides in the husband’s belly. (1.18)
The sacred fords (tīrthas) reside in the husband’s nāḍī, and liberation is indeed found in the husband’s vital breath (prāṇa).
Dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa are established within the body of the husband.
Therefore, O Lakṣmī, for the sake of a virtuous wife, the husband alone is the Supreme Brahman.
Kṛṣṇa is the Lord; Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa is the Supreme Lord.
Viṣṇu is the Lord; Vāsudeva is the Lord; Śrī Puruṣottama is the Lord.
So too are all the gods, as well as the Vedas, sacrifices, prayers, and rosaries.
The methods of giving sacrificial fees, various forms of knowledge, yogic practices, acts of service to others, as well as auspicious virtues such as non-violence,
all meritorious deeds that ought to be performed, worship, and vows in every respect— [all these are taught]. (122)
Baths, eclipses, and all transits of the sun;
all auspicious days as well as festivals and other auspicious occasions; marriage rites and ceremonies for the gods, as well as others—[all these should be performed]. (123–124)
O Lakṣmī! When the husband is the sovereign power, there exist both worldly journeys and divine paths.
Recognizing the husband alone as the Supreme Brahman, the devoted wife should worship him.
Furthermore, by reading, hearing, or reciting this [text], [one attains the same result].
Through remembrance and through honor, both enjoyment and liberation are held in the palm of one's hand.
For a wife, there is no duty other than that of her husband; here, the duty of a *satī* is distinguished as supreme.
Indeed, that supreme duty consists of service to Lord Hari. (126–127)

Thus ends the three hundred and seventy-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Dimensions of the Eighty-six Hells, the Knowledge and Devotion Spoken by Yama to Sāvitrī, the Restoration of Satyavān’s Life, and the Preeminence of the Duties of a Wife," in the section on the Greatness of Chaste Wives within the lineage of the Kṛta Age, in the first book of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. [Chapter 372] *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā* — Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Age) — Chapter 372.
[The Author: Chapter 373.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī! To the sin-destroying life-story of Padmā.
In ancient times,

while Padmā— the daughter of Anaraṇya— was observing her auspicious vow of devotion to her husband and abiding by her father’s command, she caused a decline in dharma due to the differences between the ages (yugas). (1–2)
O Lakṣmī! By her alone was youth rendered fruitless as soon as it was born;
childhood, then boyhood, then youth, and thereafter old age—such things have been brought about by her in the world in their natural succession.
That king Anaraṇya, born of the lineage of Manu, was of great fame;
he was long-lived, virtuous in character, a devotee of Viṣṇu, and had conquered his senses.
He was the son of Maṅgalāraṇya and was descended from the lineage of Indrasāvarṇi.
Maṅgalāraṇya was indeed the son of Dharāraṇya.
Being childless, Dharāraṇya went to Puṣkara to perform austerities.
Having performed penance for a very long time, he obtained a boon from the Supreme Lord.
Having obtained his son Anaraṇya, who was a devotee of Viṣṇu and had conquered his senses,
he gave him his own kingdom and departed for the forest to practice asceticism.
Thereafter, Anaraṇya, with Bhṛgu as his domestic priest, [ruled].
Having performed a hundred excellent sacrifices, he remained established in the discipline of detachment;
considering even the status of Śakra to be trivial, he did not seek that perishable state.
He had a hundred sons, all of whom were equal to their father in virtue.
There was a certain maiden, beautiful, charming, and like Padmā herself, who dwells in a lotus.
He made an effort to search for a suitable husband for her;
meanwhile, in that secluded penance grove, the sage Pippalāda was there.
Having seen a Gandharva sporting with women, he became filled with desire.
Then, as this lord of sages was going to bathe in the Puṣpabhadrā river,
he beheld the young woman Padmā, who was an incarnation of Lakṣmī.

Upon seeing the beautiful woman, he conceived the desire to take her as his wife and asked the ascetics standing nearby, "Who is she, and to whom does she belong? They then informed him, "She is Padmā, born of the forest. (1.3–1.4)
Having bathed and worshipped his chosen deity, Puruṣottama, the sage,
filled with desire, went to the courtyard of Anaraṇya’s assembly hall for alms.
Upon seeing the sage, the king quickly prostrated before him with great devotion.
Having offered the madhuparka and other honors, he worshipped him with great respect.
When the sage was requested by the king to choose a boon as he desired,
Pippalāda then asked for the auspicious maiden Padmā.
Having heard this, the king became silent, unable to say anything in reply.
Then the sage said to him: "O best of kings, give me the girl;
otherwise, I shall surely reduce everything to ashes in an instant."
All the servants were overwhelmed by the ascetic’s splendor.
Seeing the old man afflicted with fever, the king and the queen grieved; all the queens also lamented, not knowing what ought to be done.
Reflecting upon the suffering of her daughter, the girl's mother lamented.
Seeing that, Pippalāda enlightened the king,
the queen, the princes, the servants, and likewise the maiden.
Whether today or on another day, the maiden must be given away.
To whomever she is to be given, O King, give her to a Brahmin! I see no worthy recipient other than a Brahmin in the three worlds. (22–23)
"You ought not to give her to anyone other than a brahmin.
O King, having given me your daughter, protect all your prosperity;
let not your entire wealth be reduced to ashes on account of this maiden. (24)
Having heard these most formidable words, the beautiful maiden,
reflecting upon her father’s welfare and the venerable power of the sage’s asceticism,
as well as the absence of obstacles to all his prosperity, said to him: "Give me to the king."
Then, with joy, the king gave his beloved queen Padmā, adorned with ornaments, to Pippalāda; and Pippalāda, blazing with ascetic power, being delighted at having obtained his beloved,
revealed his own form through the strength of yoga, manifesting youth.
It was suitable for an eighteen-year-old and fit for a maiden, indeed granting all desires.
(28) The king and others were exceedingly delighted, and the maiden rejoiced within her heart. Having taken the dowry and his beloved, the king of sages departed. (29)
With a fulfilled mind, Anaraṇya then departed for ascetic practice;
there he fixed his mind on liberation, meditating upon the Lord of Rādhikā.
Having attained Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, he went to Goloka.
Kīrtyaraṇya, his eldest son, indeed ruled the kingdom for him.
Then Anaraṇya’s daughter served the sage with devotion through her actions, mind, and speech, just as Lakṣmī serves Nārāyaṇa.
Constantly devoted to her husband, she served Śrī Hari just as she did;
she repeatedly massaged the sage’s limbs and attended to his feet. Following him with devoted service, she perpetually fulfilled his every desire.
Having bathed herself, she bathes [her husband]; having fed the twice-born, she feeds her husband;
having put him to sleep, she sleeps herself, and she attends to his duties.
Just so does the aged ascetic, the passionate one, and the youthful sage.
The virtuous woman served him day and night with a serene mind,
always considering her own fortune to be superior to the most excellent;
for she had obtained a Brahmin, and even more so, a sage and ascetic.
He is pure, of the nature of merit, and the very embodiment of Nārāyaṇa;
he is a yogī and a knower of the Self. What other woman is as blessed as I?
Indeed, I have always become pure, having been personally requested by the sage himself.
There is no limit to my good fortune, nor is there any end to my merit;
for it is through the merits of many lifetimes that the Lord as husband is attained. This very Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa himself has been obtained by me as my husband.
Through service to Him alone is liberation; through His satisfaction is the imperishable state.
Within His very heart dwells Brahman, and from that, Brahman was attained by me.
For my deliverance, no other means remains here.
My father gave me this auspicious gift; may there be well-being for my father Janaka.
May there be well-being for my mother, by whom I was born endowed with happiness.
O Pippalāda, lord of sages, everything has been obtained by me here.
Satisfaction in knowledge, satisfaction in pleasure, and satisfaction in enjoyment are obtained;
satisfaction in fame, satisfaction in renown, and satisfaction in honor are obtained.
The burden of sovereignty brings great suffering, and the status of a queen is even greater than that.
There is indeed no peace for these queens, like that of birds in a cage.
Here, dharma, artha, and kāma are enjoyed by me with ease;
they are not enjoyed in such a manner by the queens whose minds are tormented.
Whatever auspiciousness has arisen, all that has been acquired by me through destiny.
I have not fallen into the hands of kings who consume liquor and meat;
that very merit of mine is now rejoicing here as my protector.
Young women do not know that kings cause suffering to their subjects;
later, having fallen [into misfortune], they lament, "Where have we gone to hell?
A husband who is virtuous in character and possesses divine qualities is difficult to find everywhere.
A husband who is a consumer and a destroyer is found everywhere, like a dog;
he exhausts the body with enjoyments and destroys merit with sins, leading one to the realm of Yama—such a husband is easily obtained. (1.372.50)
He who is intent solely on his own interests and provides no assistance for the next world is not a husband in the true sense; through union with him, hell is certain.
Therefore, he protects her both in this world and in the next, as if she were his own half-body.
In creation, liberation, happiness, and suffering, the husband is one who goes along with her; he is the husband.
Having obtained such a husband, she who does not serve him in deed, thought, or speech is always a person who has deceived herself.

A woman of noble family must by no means preserve her pride before her husband— whether regarding her lineage, her web of virtues, her beauty, her intellect, or her righteousness. Her body belongs to her husband, her mind is his master, and her very self-concept is her husband's.
The aggregate of cause and effect, pleasure, and pain—my Lord is mine.
That which is to be enjoyed, enjoyment, the state of the enjoyer, and all that is to be experienced—my Lord is mine.
Trust, the granting of boons, and even the act of entrustment—my Lord is mine.
My husband is my humility, my excellence, my steadfastness, and my compliance;
my husband is my vow, my righteousness, as well as my merit, my sacred ford, and my charity.
My husband is my study of the Vedas, my recitation, my worship, and the duty of the twilight prayers.
Festivals and social gatherings, the exhibition, my husband;
carriages and delightful dramas, dancing and singing, my husband; palaces, the prosperity of a kingdom, elephants and horses, my husband. (58–59)
The Guru is Brahmā, Hara, Viṣṇu, and all the gods; he is my lord.
The Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, the honoring of guests, and the arrival of visitors are my lord. The embryo, the son, pleasure, affection, and the highest good are my lord.
"My home, my field, the earth, my kingdom, and whatever is my entire possession—all this belongs to my husband.
"Both prohibition and injunction, even my own will—all this belongs to my husband.
Thinking thus that she has attained supreme satisfaction, O Sage, I indeed perform service for the Rishi.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, that princess, satisfied by eternal bliss,
served that best of sages as if he were Nārāyaṇa himself.
Then, for the purpose of testing her righteousness, the God of Dharma reflected.
"How indeed does this woman, devoted to her husband, conduct herself?
(64) Once, Dharma, assuming the form of a king through his illusory power, saw the virtuous lady on the road as she was smiling while proceeding to bathe in the celestial river (Ganges). (65)
Mounted upon a chariot made of gold and jewels, adorned with gold, gems, and other ornaments,
and rich in the beauty of fresh youth, he was like a second God of Love.
Seeing the beautiful and lovely Padmā, he spoke to her through his illusory power.
"Aha! How beautiful is this beloved, and where is the decrepit sage?
O lovely one! Like Lakṣmī herself, you are worthy of a king, exceedingly radiant, established in the prime of youth, and auspiciously capable of removing the pride of desire. (67–68)
Why do you shine so brilliantly in the presence of this old man consumed by decrepitude, who is like wood or stone and remains as nothing but skin and bone?
O Queen Indrāṇī, you are worthy of a king; you shine upon the chest of a monarch.

O beautiful one, with your limbs anointed with sandalwood and aloe-wood, adorned with gold, jewels, and other ornaments, and accompanied by hundreds of male and female servants, be happy! [Do not look upon] the Brahmin, emaciated by asceticism, withered, intent on the Supreme Brahman, and whose life is exhausted.
"Abandoning [this], O King, behold the lord of the earth, a hero in love;
behold one like me, enriched with the pleasures of heaven and established in equanimity. Is there any happiness at all in a leaf-hut? || 72 || What pleasure is there in a hut of leaves?
What happiness is there in the neck of a bird?
Why do you cling to this bag of bones?
Come here; the wish-fulfilling gem is found in Acyuta.
"O Acyuta, obtain the jewel of consciousness within me; I choose that you become for me a wish-fulfilling creeper.
A gem set in gold shines with great splendor."
Indeed, upon the neck of a beast, which is not worthy of a conch-shell [ornament], one does not obtain beautiful beauty born of merit from a previous birth;
yet that [beauty] becomes entirely fruitful through the embrace of a connoisseur. || 74–75 ||
O beloved! Just as you are lovely, so too is my lover, who is skilled in the arts of love. O blameless one, make me your servant; I shall give you everything.
Whether in a watery place, a secluded spot, a delightful forest, a wilderness, or on a mountain—
In rivers, in streams, in blossoming gardens fragrant with scent;
in vehicles, in celestial chariots, in sovereign empires; on Mount Malaya and Mount Raivata, or elsewhere rich with sandalwood trees—I shall indeed sport there with you. (77–78)
"I am capable of bringing peace to one consumed by the fever of passion;
sport with me and make this birth fruitful.
To the king who had spoken thus and was eager to take her hand—
As Dharma approached nearby, the devoted wife said to him:
"Go far away, go far away! For you are intent on sinful thoughts.
If you touch me with lustful desire, you shall instantly turn to ashes."
"I am a married woman, the beloved wife of the sage Pippalāda.
Devoted to my husband, I do not look upon another man even in my heart.
How could I, a sinner, touch a king who is a slave to women and a lecher? (82)
By the mere touch of one who practices unrighteousness, all merit is destroyed.
(83) You have now exerted yourself to forcibly violate another’s wife; O King, there is no sinner like you upon this earth. (84)
"I am the wife of a brahmin there, belonging to an aged ascetic.
It was he who, having assumed the form of a woman, spoke to me as your mother.
Your destruction shall come here through my curse for having violated me."
"O King, you shall surely go to destruction through your sinful heart and actions.
(86) Having heard this curse from Satī, Dharma abandoned his royal form;
becoming the god Dharma himself, he appeared and spoke to her. (87)
O Mother, know me to be Dharma, the teacher of those who know dharma,
the protector of the world who regards the wives of others as his own mothers.
O Padmika, I have come here to understand what is within you!
"O righteous one, I assumed the form of a king in order to test you.
Nevertheless, people must experience the consequences of their own actions;
thus, I have caused you humiliation through my harsh words. (1.372.90)
I must enjoy the fruit of that; of this there is no doubt.
My subduing here has been done appropriately and is not improper.
O Satī, I always pray that death may never come to me by any means.
"The Lord has ordained instruction for those who have gone astray.
Let your teaching prevail, O Satī, provided it is bearable to me!
Padmā then said: "You alone are the witness of the dharma for all embodied beings. (92–93)
How was this tested by you while assuming the form of a king? What was the reason for which I was cursed, and what indeed was my offense?
A curse upon a virtuous woman can never possibly become false. (94)
Upon your destruction, the destruction of creation would surely follow; of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, O Indra of Dharma, listen as I speak according to the distinctions of human beings, so that both your life and your curse may become meaningful. (95–96)

O Dharma, O Bull, be present in every way with all four feet among people who abide in the Truth (Satya Yuga); be present in every way with three feet among people pervaded by the Age of Three (Tretā Yuga);
and, O Dharma, arise with two feet among men pervaded by the Age of Two (Dvāpara Yuga).
When people are pervaded by the Kali age, may your dissolution remain as a single foot;
O Dharma, when beings are like cattle and dull-witted, you shall be hidden.
May you possess fullness in those of a sattvic nature, and incompleteness in those who are rajasic and the like.
O Bull! Listen as I tell you what place serves as your support:
among all devotees of Hari, especially among the Vaiṣṇavas;
among virtuous women, holy men, ascetics, sages, and celibate students. (1.372.10)
Among women devoted to their husbands, among the wise, among forest-dwellers and mendicants;
among all those of virtuous character belonging to the Vaiśya and Kṣatriya castes;
among Śūdras who serve the twice-born and who abide in the company of the righteous. (101–102)
In horses, banyan trees, bilva trees, and in *tulasī* and sandalwood; in initiations, examinations, oaths, assemblies, cow-pens, and the ground marked by a cow’s hoof;
in marriages, and everywhere among flowers and species of trees.
Always in temples, at sacred fords (tīrthas), and in the homes of the virtuous;
in the deliberations on the Vedic scriptures, among those who chant the glories of Kṛṣṇa;
and likewise in places of vows, worship, and as witnesses to righteous sacrifices.
Furthermore, among cattle, living beings, swans, and garuḍas, as well as among those who abide in truth, there will be emaciation in every respect.
But listen: there will be emaciation in other places besides those.
In the case of all unchaste women, in the houses of those who have killed a man, and among those who are base, foolish, wicked, intent on reviling others, and deceitful;
and among those who seize the wealth of deities, gurus, brahmins, and those worthy of protection. (107–108)
Toward rogues, the wicked, thieves, and those who are promiscuous;

toward those addicted to gambling, wine, meat, quarrels, and transgressions; and toward those who obstruct the service of *śālagrāma* stones, holy men, sacred fords, and pilgrimage sites— [one should avoid them]. (109)
In those most arrogant in the acts of bandits; in ink-sellers, swordsmen, and those who live by harming living beings;
in women censured by their husbands; in those who subsist on violence toward life;
and in those stained by being devoid of initiation, the twilight rituals, and devotion to dharma. (1.372.110–111)
In men who sell maidens, women, gods, sacred texts, or knowledge;
in those who betray friends or commit ingratitude; in those who destroy truth and trust;
in those who harm those who have sought refuge, the miserable, the blind, or their dependents; and in those who speak falsehoods. (112)
You cannot remain among those who are constantly habituated to speaking falsehoods, nor among those who seize boundaries,
nor among false witnesses, nor among kings who practice unjust legal proceedings,
nor among any who obstruct merit. (113–114)
Dwell always as four-footed in those who are pure, characterized by *sattva*, and tranquil; dwell as three-footed, consisting of three parts, when *rajas* increases mixed with *sattva*.
Dwell as two-footed, as the *dvāpara* age, when *tamas* increases mixed with *rajas*.
But in those whose hearts consist solely of darkness, you dwell as Kali with but a single foot.
In former times, truth, sacrifice, austerity, and charity were your four feet;
today, non-violence, self-restraint, faith, and generosity are your feet.
"In the future time, there will be virtue, purity, service, and recitation; these shall be your feet in due order during the age of decline.
Having spoken thus, Dharma ceased speaking and bestowed his blessings upon her."
Blessed are you, devoted to your husband; may well-being be yours forever.
May your husband be youthful, handsome, and possessed of enduring youth.
May he indeed live longer than even Mārkaṇḍeya.
"May you possess wealth and sovereignty, and may you be born with enduring youth. May you become the mother of ten sons who live for a very long time.
Having heard this, Padmā circumambulated the bull, bowed down, and [departed].
The virtuous woman went to her own home, and Dharma also returned to his own place.
In every assembly, he praised that devoted wife;
indeed, by the power of her devotion to her husband, that Padmā remained truly faithful to her spouse.
She became possessed of a hundred sons and endowed with every form of prosperity.
Thus, a woman devoted to her husband is herself capable both of destroying and protecting dharma;
what other person could ever overcome her?
Thus, O Lakṣmī, this narrative of Padmā has been told to you;
it constantly nourishes righteousness, bestows the power of wifely devotion,
grants both heaven and liberation, and likewise bestows all forms of dharma.
This supreme teaching, which bestows service to one’s husband and pacifies the cycle of worldly existence,
shall cause a woman who listens with devotion to become firm in her wifely fidelity (pātivratya).
Furthermore, Dharma will surely provide protection for both the listener and the speaker.
Devotion to one's husband and surrender (*prapatti*) are always two equal bulls.
By means of either one alone, one attains everything; there is no need for the second. O Lakṣmī! Where both are present, what more need be said? (1.28–29)

"Devotion to the husband (*pātivratya*), the duty of a servant (*dāsadharma*), and surrender (*prapatti*) characterized by affection—having attained supreme servitude and affection, one shall obtain both worldly enjoyment (*bhukti*) and liberation (*mukti*).

Thus ends the three hundred and seventy-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Marriage of Padmā, the Daughter of Anaraṇya and a Devoted Wife, with Pippalāda; the Curse of Dharma during the Test of Virtue; and the Gradual Decline of the Four Quarters of Dharma over Time," within the section on the Greatness of Devoted Wives in the first book, *Kṛtayugasantāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
← Chapter 372: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga) Chapter 373 [[Author: → Chapter 374
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī! I shall tell you a story concerning another woman devoted to her husband, which took place in Vaikuṇṭha for the complete destruction of pride.
Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, Hari himself, the sovereign of Vaikuṇṭha,
shone in the midst of the assembly, surrounded by many attendants;
the Supreme Lord was served by male and female servants as well as Vaiṣṇavas.

The Great Holy One (Mahāsatī), the bestower of prosperity, who possesses great desire and takes the form of Lord Hari’s resolve, was born from the chest of Akṣarādhipati. Seeing herself as distinct from those who possess liberated forms, Lakṣmī— [remained] within. (3–4)
Then, out of modesty, she prayed to Śrī Hari, the Lord of All: "O Master,
please construct a dwelling worthy for my residence,
so that I may serve you, the Supreme Lord, through my devotion as a faithful wife."
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa is the manifest Supreme Self, the Supreme Lord.
(6) Having heard her worthy prayer and knowing that the woman was his own servant, he created a new and auspicious Vaikuṇṭha for the sake of the couple. (7)
Out of a desire for Mahālakṣmī, he himself became four-armed—
the Supreme Brahman in the form of a husband, possessing the conch, discus, mace, and other emblems;
eighteen years of age, lovely, and exceedingly radiant.
Complete in the strength of all her limbs, she was Lakṣmī herself, sixteen years of age.
She was lovely, fit for the service of a husband, liberated, and exceedingly beautiful.
With fine breasts, a beautiful face, a charming waist, and a golden complexion, she was most delightful. (1.373.10)
She is complete in the beauty of all her limbs, the refuge of all supernatural powers (siddhis),
possessed of the great bliss of all sovereignty, and the bearer of a form created by mere thought.
She is the beloved woman, skilled in the art of love, and solely devoted to Nārāyaṇa.
Richly adorned with the splendor of all ornaments and decorated with divine garments and the like,
she was embellished with all the finest substances of erotic grace, including powders and collyrium.
And Anaṅga (the Bodiless One) remained within her as if inseparable from her body.
To fulfill her resolve, Hari, the four-armed Nārāyaṇa,
took his own four-armed wife Lakṣmī and went to his self-created abode,
Vaikuṇṭha, where there is no duality except for the two of them.
The third form is manifest; there the Couple does not rejoice.
There, indeed, thousands of accomplishments through mere will have arisen;
they are all fifteen-year-old handmaidens of Mahālakṣmī. (15–16)
For their sake, delightful palaces as bright as the moon were constructed there;
for his own sake, a divine new mansion and a palace were built.
There was also an exceedingly vast rampart and a city of great length and breadth.
There Śrī Hari created a multitude of lotus ponds, rivers, streams, reservoirs, garden groves, and parklands;
as well as diverse monasteries, pleasure halls, and long oblong ponds. (18–19)
There were dining halls, as well as halls of refreshment and pleasure grounds;
in the assembly area was a great, divine throne, most supreme. There were also rows of palaces richly furnished with all necessary articles.
Having manifested it there himself, he always rejoices with his consort. When Nārāyaṇa dwells in the home together with Lakṣmī,
then the maidservants, immersed in love, approach him with devotion.
Endowed with love for the Blessed One and summoned by their passion for the dust [of His feet],
they come for the sake of amorous play and embrace the Supreme Lord. Hari, moreover, assuming many forms, takes delight even among them.

And Mahālakṣmī also delights there in her own abode. At the same time, Hari himself, the Lord who assumes millions of forms, delights in thousands and tens of thousands of ways through his manifold nature.
Thus, in the abode of Vaikuṇṭha, in the perfect realm of Vaikuṇṭha,
no other man exists besides Nārāyaṇa;
yet there are always millions upon millions of female servants who constantly attend upon him.

On one occasion there, the Lord Hari, assuming all forms, engaged in dalliance with all [the women], bringing satisfaction to ten million maidservants. Mahālakṣmī, exulting in Nārāyaṇa, was in her own abode.
She was deeply immersed in great bliss and at that moment became as if absorbed in it.
At that very time, the eternal and liberated Sanatkumāras, having perceived through the power of yoga that Vaikuṇṭha had been made new, [arrived]. (29)

They also beheld the true form of Nārāyaṇa and the true form of Lakṣmī; they saw ten million female attendants and new palaces. Having set their hearts on seeing these directly, they were liberated and assumed the forms of children.
Having failed to achieve union during their time of passion, they were as if unaware of the woman;
and being likewise unaware of their union with the woman, they did not even perceive the obstacle.
Then, making an effort to see [her], they descended from the path of the sky.
Having gone to the courtyard within the enclosure wall, they entered the chamber of pleasure.
Then, seeing Lakṣmī embracing Nārāyaṇa,
they approached the two of them and respectfully massaged their bodies.
All those five-year-old boys, free from fear, massaged their feet and served the two lords. Lakṣmī, having attained bliss, served Nārāyaṇa.
Having become pure, the virtuous woman gave food and other offerings to those boys.
Once fed, honored, seen, touched, and bowed to, they departed.
Then Mahālakṣmī spoke to the Lord Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa.
O Blessed One, such a vision as this is never appropriate for you;
for children are free from faults and likewise devoid of passion.
However, there are other great souls, sages, gods, and so forth.

From this time forward, having learned of us from the ignorant, they will always come here out of a longing to see us, desiring a vision again and again. Indeed, an untimely sight of us would constantly result in obstacles for them.
"Maidservants should be appointed there as gatekeepers at the city gates and other locations;
or rather, O Blessed One, do as you wish, according to your desire.
Having heard this, Nārāyaṇa appointed suitable female gatekeepers.
Even though they are assigned to specific duties, out of an excess of love for Hari, they sometimes abandon their posts and go elsewhere; thus, even the door to the temple becomes empty.
Yet, when the seers and sages, perceiving this, arrive with hearts full of devotion, [the door is once again filled].
Then, for the sake of beholding Vaikuṇṭha— that is, for the purpose of seeing Hari— Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa was again entreated by Lakṣmī:
"O Blessed One, let the office of gatekeeper be firmly bestowed upon this devotee."
"But those friends of mine, submerged in affection, do not stand at the door at all;
let those who have exerted effort for the office of gatekeepers remain there.
Having heard this, Hari then recollected his divine powers and excellent qualities.
Possessing lordly powers and virtues, the attendants, beautiful in form,
assumed human shapes with four arms and approached his presence.
Having praised Nārāyaṇa and bowed to Lakṣmī, they spoke these words of instruction:
"O Great King, show us here! We have been born by your will.
To them, Keśava spoke of the sovereignty known as Jaya and Vijaya;
he said that their duty there was to serve as his gatekeepers according to his instruction.
In this manner, he appointed Nanda and Sunanda, Puṣpadanta and Sāttvata, as well as Kumuda and Kumudākṣa,
to the city gates; these attendants, who embody the eightfold sovereign powers, protect the gateways.
Accompanied by ten million handmaidens, Lakṣmī serves her husband without hesitation.
Through the dharma of devotion to her husband, she recognizes no other man as equal to or superior to Nārāyaṇa, just as a shadow follows its own body. || 51-52 ||
She never beholds any other group of men, not even the gatekeepers;
Lakṣmī does not converse with others, nor does she ever touch anyone else.
She knows no pleasure other than that of Hari, the dweller in Vaikuṇṭha.
He perceives no other being than the four-armed Nārāyaṇa;
he speaks of no other qualities except the qualities of Nārāyaṇa;
he meditates on nothing else, remembers nothing else, thinks of nothing else, nor resolves upon anything else.
"Nārāyaṇa is the Supreme Brahman; Nārāyaṇa is the Supreme Lord;
Nārāyaṇa is the Seer of all; there is no other Lord higher than him.
Thus, with her whole being, she becomes absorbed in Him and exists [in that state].
She who gives a responsive reply, who bestows happiness upon her husband, and who follows her husband’s will;
she who attends to him during sleep, lovemaking, bathing, reclining, eating, and honoring;
she who accompanies him in his wanderings and in all that is to be done—such a woman is Lakṣmī herself, devoted solely to her husband.
There, Nārāyaṇī indeed served Śrī Hari upon his bed;
at that moment, the boys—the sons of Brahmā, Sanaka and the others, who were eternally perfected youths—arrived there once more for a vision of him. (59)
In this very manner, they too, having come for the sake of beholding Hari,
left the ramparts and gates from the great sky; assuming the form of Brahman, they descended and went into the presence of Nārāyaṇa.
Having performed service as before and having repeatedly offered their vision,
those five-year-old girls departed with delighted hearts and minds fully satisfied.
When this occasion had thus arisen, [the discourse] concerning Mahālakṣmī then proceeded.
The gatekeepers and others were commanded to block the passage of those who come from elsewhere.
They should not come without an order, nor indeed should they enter;
whoever they may be, the duty of the gatekeepers must certainly be performed. (63–64)
Thus commanded by Mahālakṣmī, they protect all directions.
Without the command of Mahālakṣmī, as well as that of Hari,
they do not grant entrance anywhere, even if they were Śiva or others.
Thus, Lakṣmī, ever devoted to service, constantly serves Kṛṣṇa;
free from fear, exceedingly innocent, and honored by millions of maidservants, she,
eternally dedicated to her husband’s devotion, serves Śrī Nārāyaṇa.
After her yogic sleep, the lotus-born goddess enters into yogic slumber;
while sleeping on her bed, she constantly performs a massage of his limbs.
Having first abandoned the water-nectar [of the ocean], she enters the yogic sleep of Hari.
He gives tooth-powder for the purpose of cleansing the mouth and teeth;
he also provides warm water scented with fragrant sandalwood for bathing and other needs, as well as garments, ornaments, and the like, and he offers flowers and other such items. (1.373.69–70)
For the sake of nourishing the sentiment of love (śṛṅgārarasa), she adorns Hari;
she always causes him to partake of delicious food and the drinking of milk.
She provides cool water, fruit, and mouth-cleansing [betel].
He indeed offers betel and other items, as well as the washing of garments.
He personally washes the vessels used for Kṛṣṇa’s food and the like,
provides seats and other furnishings, and attends to the dressing of Keśava’s hair and so forth.
She offers musk, collyrium, saffron, unbroken rice, and other articles; she provides a breeze with a fan and spreads out the bedding for his bed.
In this manner, this devoted wife attends to all the needs of his body.
Vows, worship, recitation, fire-offerings, reading, and even hymns—all this she performs by the command of Kṛṣṇa; indeed, as a devoted wife, Nārāyaṇī is engaged in the service of Nārāyaṇa. (75–76)
Then once, Mahālakṣmī, accompanied by a thousand female attendants,
went to a beautiful garden with the desire for diversion.
There, it was resplendent with rows of trees rich in various spreading branches.
On a soft and auspicious spot covered with lush grass and rich with the fragrance of flowers,
he took his pleasure together with his companions and praised his own happiness;
the beautiful woman, highly honored him, and attained a sense of pride.
O friends, although the divine Nārāyaṇa is the Lord of all,
he always carries out his actions only after taking into account my intention.
Indeed, by my service, the Lord Mādhava has been brought under my influence.
Indeed, she cannot remain in the palace for even a moment without me;
overcome by hiccups, she must surely be looking at me, for Keśava remembers her.
He will arrive here in an instant, or else let us go to him at once.
He does not disregard my words, whether they are spoken in jest or as the truth;
whatever Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa says, he does exactly that.
Through me alone he possesses a home, and through me alone he always shines.
"By me alone have you also been given to that Supreme Self.
O friends, there is no other woman here equal to me—neither respectable nor fortunate.
Having thus fallen into such pride, she was recognized by Nārāyaṇa. (84–85)
And this Mahālakṣmī, devoted to her husband, having attained excessive pride through arrogance, returned from that place along with her companions; filled with haughtiness,
she came back toward her home and reached the city gate.
Hari, who humbles all pride, entered both Jaya and Vijaya.
As she, surrounded by her female companions, was about to enter the Lord’s spacious gate, she was stopped at the entrance by Jaya and Vijaya. (87–88)
Then, having been defeated by those two, that great goddess Mahālakṣmī—
being highly virtuous and possessed of self-respect—
bowed down and, mindful of the lotus feet of Hari, prepared to cast off her body in response to her own humiliation.
Then, all the deities came there for the purpose of seeing [him]:
the Grandfather (Brahmā), Maheśa, Viṣṇu, Dharma, Bhāskara (the Sun),
Candra (the Moon), Kāmadeva, Vaiśvānara (Fire), and the Lord of Wealth (Kubera).
The sages, the seers, the Manus, and the leaders of obstacles; Mahendra, Varuṇa, Vāyu (the life-breath of the world), and Agni— all of them,
stationed at the city gate, offered praise to Mahālakṣmī.
Forgive me, O Blessed Mother! O you whose nature is forgiveness! O Supreme Beyond the Supreme! (93) O you whose essence is pure being, worshipped by virtuous goddesses!
Without you, the entire world is like a corpse and devoid of fruit. (94)
You are the embodiment of all prosperity, and all women are but your portions.
Those people who worship you, who are worshipped by the entire creation,
obtain a well-behaved wife even if they were previously without one, as well as a virtuous daughter.
A sonless man obtains a son who is well-behaved, beautiful, charming, exceedingly dear, and eloquent;
indeed, he also obtains a long-lived grandson who is endowed with virtues, learned, and illustrious. (96–97)
One whose kingdom has fallen may regain his kingdom; one whose fortune has perished may recover his fortune;
one devoid of fame may attain fame; and one who has lost his wealth may obtain wealth.
Indeed, you yourself exist as such a person, possessing the sovereign power of a great yoginī.
"O Goddess! Do not set your heart on destruction; be merciful!
Having heard this from the gods, Mahālakṣmī said to them:
"I shall not abandon my body now out of anger, nor out of world-weariness."
Having reflected upon this in your hearts, O gods, listen to this auspicious truth: when one regards both a blade of grass and a mountain with equanimity toward the Lord, the Master;
and maintains equality toward servant and wife—what indeed is the use of such a life?
"I am the chief wife of Kṛṣṇa, yet I have been turned away by this doorkeeper.
A woman who lacks fortune for her husband is unfortunate in every respect; she finds no happiness in bed or at the meal, and her life is in vain. (102–103)
The birth of that woman who has no affection for her beloved is meaningless;
what then of [affection] for a son, wealth, beauty, prosperity, or even youth? She who has no devotion for her husband is indeed unfortunate toward her lord.
She is impure, devoid of dharma, and excluded from all religious rites.
He alone is her husband, kinsman, refuge, supporter, deity, and preceptor;
there is no master superior to him, nor is there any preceptor superior to the master.
A father, mother, son, or brother indeed gives only a small amount of wealth;
but the husband is the giver of all possessions to his wives, for he is the lord of women.
Only a rare few truly understand the supreme greatness of the husband.
Born of an excellent lineage, she was a great, virtuous ascetic. (1.08) But she who is born of an ignoble lineage is ill-behaved and devoid of dharma;
intent solely on her own self-interest and wicked, she reviles her husband out of anger. (1.09)
That woman who hates her own husband— the master who is equal to Viṣṇu and her guru—
shall fall into the Kumbhīpāka hell for a duration measured by a day of Brahmā.
[Even if she has performed] vows, fasting, charity, truthfulness, merit, and long-term austerity.
For one devoid of devotion, [all] is reduced to ashes and rendered meaningless.
(111) Therefore, I shall say nothing harsh toward my husband;
yet, by insulting the servants of Hari, I shall certainly give up my life. (112)
Even when her husband is at fault, a great virtuous woman should not speak harshly to him;
if she is unable to endure it, she may lawfully renounce her life.
Service to the husband is the vow of women; service to the husband is the supreme austerity.
Service to her husband is the highest dharma; service to her husband is the worship of the gods.
Service to her husband is the supreme truth; it is the proclamation of gifts and sacred pilgrimage sites.
Her husband embodies all the gods; he is pure and the very embodiment of merit. (114–115)
The deities always desire the sight and the touch of that virtuous woman who eats the remnants of her husband’s meal and always drinks the water used for washing his feet; indeed,
all sacred fords purify even sinners of their evil through her.
Having heard this, Brahmā himself, full of devotion, said to Satī:
"Neither Jaya nor Vijaya shall fare well;
for you, fearing an offense against your master, did not curse those two servants."

If a righteous person does not curse an offender out of forgiveness, O virtuous lady, his total destruction will surely come; do not delay! If he is unable to curse and is not empowered to inflict punishment, [he must remain silent].
For when a man has committed an offense, Dharma indeed inflicts punishment upon him.
(1.373.120) "O Mother, forgive everything! Go, go to the presence of your beloved.
By this sight of Hari here, there shall be gain for us as well. (121)
Then Lakṣmī said: "O gods! If I am devoted to my husband;
if I am eager for the duty of a wife and have given my life for the sake of my husband;
and if I am eternally steadfast and unwavering toward my lord through my devotion to my husband. (122)
"If you always abide by the duties I have prescribed,
then by the power of your devotion to your husband, may Narayana come here;
may my husband come to the city gate to grant me his vision."
"If I am truly the wife of Hari, always the object of His affection,
having renounced all possessions for the sake of Hari, then let Hari come here.
If I am a living wife, devoted to Him alone and faithful to my husband,"
"Then Nārāyaṇa must come here; otherwise, I shall die.
Having spoken thus, Mahālakṣmī produced fire from her foot, and just as she was about to burn him, Kṛṣṇa arrived.
Holding that Lakṣmī to his chest, he kissed her and embraced her;
saying, "Forgive my cruelty, O Goddess! he became drenched in tears.
With eyes full of tears, he said to her, "You are truly a devoted wife."

"Indeed, by the power of your devotion to your husband, I have come here to the city gate. Come, O virtuous lady! Do not be angry with me. This was done by me through a servant for the sake of testing you and to quell your pride. (1.373.130)
My equanimity is the same toward my devotee, my wife, and my kinsman in all circumstances;
yet, especially, my devotee is even more dear to me than my wife.
Your two sons, who are my devotees, shall be the gatekeepers who expound the meaning of my stories.
"Forgive my offense and that of those two who are full of devotion.
Having spoken thus, the Lord of the worlds, having delighted in and placed Lakṣmī within his heart, granted his vision to the gods and departed for the interior of his own abode.
Then Hari, having summoned the gatekeeper, spoke to him pleasantly:
"Do not fear, my child; remain at ease. What cause for fear have you while I am present? Who indeed is the punisher of my devotees? Go, my child, to your own seat. (134)
Indeed, I have conceived this seed for its dissemination throughout the worlds. For that purpose, this has been composed; indeed, human beings shall sing it.
And through my life-story, my devotees shall surely attain liberation by means of it.
There Hari spoke to the gods: "Let them all hear this stainless truth:
her supreme dharma is devotion to her husband (*pātivratya*); by that she has brought me under her control.
Abandoning the throne, he has come even to the city gate."
By the power of devotion to her husband alone, even the deities who are the support of all [are won over].
Therefore, there is indeed no dharma equal to this which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Whether a man or a woman, a devotee who serves through devotion to her husband [attains these fruits]. (138–139)
"He attains my own state; O gods, I go toward him.
I dwell in their home and am entirely dependent upon them. Having been addressed thus, the gods bowed, offered worship, and returned to their own abodes.
Satī became devoted to service; such is the fruit for both the listener and the speaker.
Jaya and Vijaya were formerly the embodiments of Hari’s sovereignty;
in the previous creation, they were the sons of the treasure-house of the Vedas, who became attendants through their vow.
Due to the curse of Rādhikā, both of them were born as the two sons of Tṛṇabindu;
due to a mutual curse, they became performers of Marutta’s sacrifice for the sake of wealth.
Then, having been sent forth from Vaikuṇṭha, they were born as an elephant and a crocodile.
Hari, by his own will, expelled those two attendants once again;
they should be understood to have been born here repeatedly as Daityas due to a curse,
and finally, at the end, they will become the two attendants known as Aiśvarya.

Thus ends the three hundred and seventy-third chapter, titled "The Description of Nārāyaṇa’s Attraction of the Gateway by Means of His Wife’s Devotion, after She Was Blocked at the Gateway by Mahālakṣmī of Vaikuṇṭha for the Purpose of Destroying Her Pride," in the section on the Greatness of Chaste Wives within the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga, in the first part of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 374 *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā* — Part 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga) — Chapter 374.
[The Author: Chapter 375.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, Lakṣmī! To how the devotion to her husband (pātivratya) of Śacī was so firm.
Indeed, as fourteen Indras came and went,
Indrāṇī’s devotion to her husband remained steadfast in every respect.
Once, however, Bṛhaspati arrived at the assembly.
And while Mahendra was intent on bestowing blessings upon the gods, Indra,
out of pride, did not rise from his jeweled lion-throne in the assembly hall even upon seeing his own preceptor, Bṛhaspati, who was most devoted to Brahman.
All the other members of the assembly rose and paid their respects.
Having offered them blessings and disregarding Mahendra, the Guru, filled with indignation and resentment over his own slight, departed in great wrath. (4–5)
The great sage, being righteous, did not utter a curse, maintaining his composure;
for without a curse, Indra’s pride would have been shattered to pieces.
Indeed, a great person should not curse one who is sinful or guilty of an offense.
The offense bears its fruit; dharma destroys the offender.
(7) For if a righteous man, out of anger, should curse a violent person who has committed an offense, the offender might perish, but the righteous man would become possessed by anger. (8)
All the merit of one who is angry is destroyed from its very root.
Therefore, one who desires their own welfare should never give way to anger toward anyone.
Even when a living being has committed an offense, forgiveness—which bestows great merit—must be maintained.
For one whose nature is forgiveness, the True Dharma itself provides protection.
(1.374.10) From insulting even a venerable Brahmin ascetic, a sin equal to the murder of a Brahmin arises for the offender. (11)
The killing of one who is established [in his position] is proclaimed as an insult;
by that unrighteous act, Indra incurred the sin of Brahman-murder.
That sinful entity then coiled itself around Indra’s head.
Becoming as if intoxicated and appearing like one deranged,
he abandoned his status as Indra out of fear and departed for Lake Puṣkara. There, indeed, he took up residence in secret within the thread of desire.
Then, perceiving the kingdom to be vacant, all the gods and sages made the royal sage named Nahuṣa the presiding Indra.
King Nahuṣa sat by the side of Indra’s throne.
Having attained an existence corresponding to the very being of Indra,
he then indeed governs the kingdom of the fourteen worlds like Indra himself;
at times, in some places, he even occupies half of Indra’s throne.
In the palace of Indra, in his chariot, on his palanquin, and in his vehicle,
Nahuṣa would go to the garden and sport there out of pride.
Having seen Śacī, who was of beautiful form, childless, and lovely—
Abounding in the beauty of fresh youth and endowed with many forms,
she was exceedingly delicate and possessed beautiful teeth; though Indra was absent, she was permeated by grief—
a great chaste lady, a queenly figure, yet bereft of her husband, and captivating to the mind.
Nahuṣa fell into a swoon from desire and youth;
standing before her, he spoke with humility as if she were his own wife: "Alas!
The course of destiny is wondrous and cannot be understood even by the wise."
He perceives the state of Brahmā as a mere moment and the state of Indra as a mere moment in every respect.
O Queen, enjoy my youth for a moment, for you are like Indra’s equal;
how could the great lord Indra abandon a woman such as you? (22–23)
He who approaches women among men, even as he did with Ahalyā and a maidservant—such is his mind that it finds beauty only in the wives of others.
This is not surprising; for desire ever seeks the new.
In her presence, what indeed are Rambhā, Urvaśī, or Tilottamā?
What is Menā, or Ghṛtācī, or Ratnamālā, or Kalāvatī?
These and other Apsarases are certainly not her equals. (25–26)
Having praised me thus, Nahuṣa said with devotion, "Accept me;
I have attained the station of Indra, and the former Indra has vanished from sight.
Therefore, by my good fortune, become the abode of my happiness upon my breast."
O Goddess, by my mere playfulness I am the Lord capable of conquering thousands of Indras.
Having accepted me—who am free from old age and death due to the boons of Brahmā—enjoy your pleasure with me, adorned with flowers and sandalwood paste. (28–29)
"O blessed lady, make me your husband, one whose youth is eternally stable.
I have no desire for the wives of others; yet, having seen you, my mind has become covetous.
Even there, I shall become Indra today, and you shall be my wife by nature."
"O Bhavīnī, become my wife today, but not by force, for you have been requested.
Having spoken thus, Nahuṣa sought her reply;
then the virtuous Śacī spoke to that human king, who was like a servant.
Listen, O King! My devotion to my husband has always been consistent with righteousness.
I was created by Brahmā for as long as fourteen Indras endure;
