Therefore, you are by no means worthy of being my husband. O Great King, you are a human, and I am a goddess. || 34-35 ||

"I am not worthy to be your wife; a goddess would not consort with a mortal. Listen further, O Great King! Even that very station of Mahendra was not bestowed upon you by the gods; only the task itself was entrusted to you."
But the status of Indra was not bestowed upon you; rather, servitude was offered to you. (37) In the absence of Indra, perform that which is Indra’s duty;
for the entire range of tasks has been entrusted to you by virtue of your preeminent existence. (38)
Neither Indrāṇī, nor a throne, nor even a palace, nor the status of Indra was bestowed upon you by the sages; do not, therefore, harbor vain pride.
Listen further, O Great King, you who are devoted to the duty of protecting your subjects!

Indeed, you are counted as equal to my father, having attained the status of a father. The role of father among the gods shines through Indra by virtue of his sovereignty; likewise, the role of father has been transferred to you in relation to one such as me.
"I am not married to you, nor was I intended for you;
therefore, I am not yours to enjoy. Do not persist with me in vain.
Furthermore, O King, listen to the truth: when the former Indra had passed away..."
Having first burned my body in the form of Satī, I assume a new one.
In this manner, thirteen times over, I take on a new body;
I have taken up another Indra as well, and by that means, I am a woman of devoted virtue.
O King, if you are capable, then indeed cast off this human body;
take up a new divine one, and thereafter once again attain the station of Indra.
Obtain a place among the fourteen [worlds] in the assembly of the celestial sages.
"Afterwards, granted by Brahmā and the others, I shall become your beloved.
O passionate one, I am not yours otherwise; I am not to be enjoyed by you in any way as long as Indra, along with the Asuras, remains away at Puṣkarābjaka."
And you are indeed the king of the land of action (karmabhūmi), but not of heaven.
A king should be a protector from fear, the guardian and father of all.
Even Mahendra, having fallen from his glory today due to the wrath of his preceptor, has gone to the earth.
But you have been appointed to this task, for you are like a father to the subjects.
You have been assigned the burden of duty; Indrāṇī has not been appointed to you. Indeed, whatever other king is consecrated on earth after a former king, [he must follow this path].
He is renowned throughout the earth as his son and his disciple;
for the wife of the former king is reckoned as the queen mother,
while the wife of the new king is reckoned as the queen.
"In this manner, O Great King, I am your royal mother;
I am certainly not your queen. Knowing this, do not harbor desire for me.
I am the wife of your guru, the wife of the king, likewise the wife of a god, and your daughter-in-law. (52–53)
The mother’s sister, the wife of a disciple, the wife of a servant, the maternal aunt, the father’s wife,
the brother’s wife, the mother-in-law, the sister, the daughter,
the wet-nurse, and the chosen deity— these are the sixteen mothers of a man. (54)
"You are a man, and I am a goddess’s wife; indeed, I am your mother in every way.
Go, my child, to Aditi to sport with her if you so desire.
There is no atonement for anyone, my child, who approaches his own mother."
They are cooked in the Kumbhīpāka hell for as long as the lifespan of Brahmā;
thereafter they become worms for seven kalpas, and after that,
they are born as lepers and barbarians for seven lifetimes, whereupon their sin is destroyed.
O King, tell me this: where does your mind go? Does it go toward the womb of a mother?
(58) There are many celestial nymphs here; if you desire goddesses, [know that they differ from those] in places full of secretions, rich in filth, and abodes of foul odors. (59)
"Even though you have experienced many such things, tell me this: how can you still harbor a latent desire (*vāsanā*) in your heart for female organs, which are so similar [to what you have known]?
"O virtuous one, since you, the lord of heaven, have been born as a lamp for your lineage..."
O Indra among kings, how can you desire the secret urine of another's wife?
Even though heaven has been attained, why does thirst not cease here?
O virtuous one, tell me: what happiness is there for the righteous in the wombs of women?
The vow of devoted wives is the austerity consisting of service to their husband;
for women, this husband is like a son and is their very dharma.
Just as kings protect their subjects like their own biological sons, [so too do they protect their husbands]. (63)
And kings look upon their subjects as mothers look upon their children.
Kings, who are the protectors of gods and brahmins, perform sacrifices;
they provide restraint for the wicked and protection for the virtuous.
"Indeed, kings protect virtuous women;
O King, why do you here adopt such a contrary course?
Having spoken thus, the devoted wife Mahendrāṇī fell silent.
King Nahuṣa, speaking with arrogant words, said to Śacī:
"Listen, Śacī! If it pleases you, you should accept these words as being consistent with justice.
Having performed auspicious or inauspicious deeds on earth, one takes the fruit thereof. (67–68)
Elsewhere, a human being enjoys what is ordained by the Vedas in heaven and other realms;
having performed great merit on earth, the virtuous person goes to heaven.
Having taken all the maidens, he rejoices in heaven for a long time.
A human being goes to heaven after casting off the human body.
O beautiful one, behold my merit: I have arrived here in my own physical form!
By virtue of the merit accumulated over many births, I have reached this desired heaven. (1.374.70–71)
By merit even greater than that, he attained the station of Mahendra.
This meeting of mine with you is a great merit;
for this place is not merely a field of action, but indeed a realm of celestial enjoyment.
In a place of enjoyment, it is not possible to abandon the object of enjoyment.
(73) But you are the object of enjoyment for Mahendra, while I am seated upon his throne;
now, being without a master, you become my object of enjoyment. (74)
You were created for my enjoyment, by which I have attained the station of Indra;
since I am inscribed upon your fortune, I remain established in the rank of Indra.
And you, O beloved, are worthy of me as long as I remain Indra.
"But once the position of Indra has been relinquished, I shall certainly not behold you again.
Come, my beloved! I shall take delight with you within the inner chamber of my home.
Cast away this mental duality and rejoice, O divine among men! || 76-77 ||
Having spoken thus, Śacī ceased; and having heard this, she grieved:
"Today I shall hear all manner of talk from this insentient fool, who knows not what ought and ought not to be done, and who is tormented by lust. (78)
Intoxicated by wine, intoxicated by liquor, and intoxicated by passion, one loses their senses;
a lustful man whose mind is carried away by desire does not take death into account.
Thereupon, he indeed spoke this fitting reply to Nahuṣa.
Heaven is indeed a place of enjoyment, for the fruit of one's actions is experienced there.
Yet you have not performed such deeds by which I might become an object of your enjoyment.
Ask the King of Dharma, and likewise ask your other preceptor.
Even if flies and other small creatures were to occupy the vacant throne of Indra, they would not truly become Indras;
nor do I become their object of enjoyment. Indra alone is my husband, not flies or other small creatures.

But you, O King, being as you are, should not indeed persist in falsehood. Listen, O King, to this secret which I must now tell: today is the first day of my menstrual period, O monarch! (84) Today is the first day of my fertile season, O King!
On the first day, a woman is as impure as a Cāṇḍālī;
on the second day, she is equal to a Mleccha; and on the third or fourth day, she becomes pure for the sake of her husband. (85–86)
Thereafter, she becomes fit for rites dedicated to the gods, ancestors, and so forth;
however, he who approaches her while she is menstruating incurs the sin of a portion of the murder of a Brahmin.
On the second day, he who eats [with her] becomes guilty of the sin of killing a cow.
On the third day, he who would eat [with her] becomes possessed of the sin of killing an embryo.
On the fourth day, having bathed, she becomes a virtuous woman fit for her husband.
The husband should give the *ṛtudāna* (gift at the time of the season); this is the rule established by the Vedas.
If a gift is given on nights that are not paired [i.e., odd-numbered], a daughter is born;
but if a gift is given on paired nights [i.e., even-numbered], a son is born.
Up until the end of the sixteenth night, there remains the capacity for conception.
Beyond that, there is tranquility; indeed, conception shall not occur.
In that state, one must not approach one's wife, for it would be a defilement resulting in the destruction of the seed.
Such is the established dharma, yet you have indeed abandoned that dharma.
"I am overcome by passion today; go to your own queen on earth.
Obtain peace, O Great King! I shall observe a long vow.
Having heard those words of Śacī, Nahuṣa then laughed.
She spoke words contrary to dharma, devised out of a desire for enjoyment:
"The wife of a god is always pure; menstruation does not exist [for her]. The sin caused by menstruation exists in the world of mortals, but certainly not here in heaven. (94–95)
"In this world, I am of the Lunar dynasty, Mahendra, who dwells among the ranks of the gods.
I have no affliction from my royal menstruation; come to me, O beautiful one!
If there were any sin of [missing] the fertile season upon me, what would it matter to you? Delight me, O lovely one! (96)
"Prepare a bed for the sake of pleasure; let there be a union today.
Having spoken thus, the king ceased speaking, waiting [for her response].
Śacī said: "Listen, O King! Your intellect has gone to ruin. (98)
"Knowing that devotion to one's husband is invincible, yet brings destruction to the audacious who would violate it—
having reflected thus, you indeed proceeded to speak in my presence.
If there is no protector for you here, I shall curse you."
Devotion to one's husband is a great dharma, possessing the very nature of Nārāyaṇa.
Nārāyaṇa, Hara, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Vairāja, and the other lords—
even they tremble and are shaken by this supreme dharma of devotion to one's husband.
The sun, the moon, Varuṇa, Yama, Death, old age, and the like; Time, Saṃkarṣaṇa, and Rudra—even these fear a woman devoted to her husband.
So too do the clouds, Saturn, Rāhu, the Dānavas, and even the Rākṣasas.

The Daityas, the Devas, the fires, the oceans, and likewise the mountains—these all tremble because of devotion to a husband; reflect upon this in your mind. Indeed, a devoted wife, a virtuous spouse, can restore her deceased husband to life.
That very virtuous woman alone pacifies the dissolution of waters;
that devoted wife alone makes the heat of fires cool.
Turning back even Mahākāla, the devoted wife indeed lives on.
A devoted wife truly causes the movement of the sun and moon to cease;
a devoted wife truly brings about the abundance of flowers and fruits on trees;
[she can even neutralize] Viṣṇu’s Sudarśana weapon and Brahmā’s world-destroying missile.
A devoted wife pacifies [even great sins] instantly through her resolve alone. A virtuous woman brings about the destruction of the merits of one who has committed an offense;
indeed, a devoted wife is capable of even bringing about the dissolution of the universe.

A devoted wife is capable of turning land into water in the water, water into land on dry ground, earth into sky in the sky, and sky into earth upon the earth; she can turn a woman into a man and a man into a woman.
Do you not know this, O King of Kings? What thought has arisen in your mind? 109.
"A devoted wife is capable of completely severing the nooses of Yama;
therefore, O King, go to the earth and do not let your mind become clouded.
While this debate was taking place, Bṛhaspati arrived there.
Because the king was of the very nature of Indra, he performed a most excellent reception;
yet Śacī, filled with shame, went back into her own abode.
Having received hospitality from Nahuṣa and having bestowed her blessing, she then departed. (112)

He went to the house of Śacī, and there, upon a beautiful seat offered by Śacī, the Guru sat down; he was informed of the purpose of his visit by Śacī, even though he had been earnestly entreated by the distressed Śacī at that time. (113–114)
Protect, protect me, O illustrious one! I am submerged in an ocean of grief;
my husband, your disciple, has been driven away from his own kingdom by you.
Nahuṣa, assuming the status of Indra, has rendered my hermitage destitute of prosperity.
"He is making a vehement effort to establish me as his wife.
O Guru, I am a woman devoted to my husband; I do not desire another husband.
O Guru, I cannot bring myself to abandon the supreme dharma of devotion to one's husband."
Both the king and the preceptor are always considered worthy of honor and worship;
however, one should employ conciliation only so long as it brings about the pacification of conflict. A virtuous woman, even if she is capable, must never under any circumstances utter a curse.
Having reflected thus, I cursed King Nahuṣa;
yet you were not cursed by me because of my respect for your husband.
O Preceptor, if what was spoken by me should not come to pass correctly, [then let it be so]. (1.374.120)
"I curse you and Nahuṣa; total destruction shall come to pass.
Nevertheless, let there be no haste in my mind regarding the destruction of great beings.
Having said this, I report it to you: O Guru, grant peace and happiness! (121)
"Act in such a way that my husband Mahendra may return to his own home, while Nahuṣa shall be cast down. Having offered him the dust of your feet, bestow blessings upon that Mahendra. (122–123)
Among all gurus, however, the one who gives birth is the supreme guru.
A mother is a hundred times more worthy than a father; she is to be honored, saluted, and is most venerable.
Furthermore, the giver of knowledge, the giver of mantra, the giver of wisdom, and the giver of devotion to Hari [are also gurus].
The Guru is a hundred times more worthy of honor, reverence, and service than one's mother.
Salutations to that illustrious Guru, by whom the eye of one blinded by the darkness of ignorance has been opened with the ointment-stick of knowledge.
The progenitor and the provider of food are considered gurus, as are others;
those upon whom one has placed the burden of authority are gurus, as are those who have been forcibly made gurus.
Likewise, there are those who are near-gurus, instructors, and even those who are gurus by virtue of their teaching.
They are unable to reach the further shore in the terrible ocean of saṃsāra.
(128) The knower of knowledge and mantras, skilled in the act of crossing over, is capable of uplifting his disciple—especially if he is a lord among lords. (129)
The Guru is Viṣṇu, the Guru is Brahmā, the Guru is the Lord Maheśvara;
the Guru is Dharma, the Guru is Śeṣa, and Keśava, the soul of all, is the Guru.
He dwells in all sacred fords and is the abode of all the gods.
Hari himself, the divine one who embodies all the gods, exists in the form of the Guru.
(131) Indeed, when the chosen deity is angry, the Guru is able to protect;
but when the Guru is angry, the chosen deity is truly unable to protect. (132)
When the Guru is angry, the planets are angry, and the gods are entirely angry; even one's fortunes are angry when the Guru is angry. One should never cause the Guru to be angry.
Neither the self nor even a beloved son is dearer than the Guru.
Wealth, a wife, austerity, dharma, merit, and truth are indeed not dear [to one who lacks them].
There is no teacher higher than the guru; the king is no kinsman other than he;
the mantra, sacred knowledge, the deity, and likewise the husband obtained previously, are supreme. (134–135)
He is to be known as higher than the highest, standing above all;
the mother is to be revered, the father is to be revered, and a teacher such as you is to be revered. You are the most excellent among Brahmins and the most venerable among ascetics.
"You are the most devoted to Brahman among those who know Brahman, and the most righteous among all who follow dharma. I have always known you to be worthy of worship by the gods in every way;
therefore, I beg your forgiveness, for I do not curse my own guru. (137–138)
"Be satisfied, O best of sages! Bring Śakra without delay;
quickly cast Nahuṣa down to the earth from Indra’s abode.
Having spoken thus, Śacī was inwardly satiated, yet outwardly gentle at that time.
Resorting to silence with fortitude, he quickly sought the fruit [of his actions].
Then Bṛhaspati said: "O devoted wife, you are blessed!
You were indeed capable of cursing me, yet even I, the king, have been protected."
"May women become such as Śacī, the protectress.
Having said this, he spoke to Indrāṇī: "Everything will turn out well;
by my blessing, you shall immediately regain your husband, Mahendra."
"O beautiful one, you are to me just as Kaca’s wife was;
a pupil is like a son—there is no difference between a son and a pupil in matters of offering libations, presenting funeral cakes, protection, and gratification. (143–144)
Just as the giver of fire and a son are certain [to be supported], so too is a disciple.
Father, mother, teacher, wife, child, and the protectorless kinsman—these are the perpetual dependents of men; this is the eternal dharma.
He who, intoxicated by prosperity, treats his own guru with contempt adopts a human mindset toward his mother, father, and teacher;
his ill-repute spreads everywhere, and he encounters obstacles at every step. (146–147)
"Before long, his own total destruction will surely come to pass.
Look now, O virtuous lady: having seen me in the midst of the assembly, Indra did not rise;
yet it is Indra who is currently reaping the fruit of that [action]."
"I shall bring about your liberation, for I am capable of it, O devoted wife!
By the power of your devotion to your husband, even Nahuṣa will perish;
Indra will come to you quickly, and everything will be restored."
O virtuous lady, your power shall be equal to that of Durgā;
your established status shall be equal to Lakṣmī’s, and your fame shall be equal to her fame.
Your good fortune shall be equal to Rādhikā’s, and your love for your husband shall be equal to hers.
Respect for her equal to that [of your own mother], honoring her, and placing affection as the primary concern—this is what is prescribed.
(15.2) You shall be as dear to Rohiṇī as she is herself; you shall be as worthy of worship as Sarasvatī; you shall always remain pure, forever like Sāvitrī. (15.3)
Having spoken thus, the preceptor there instructed her in protection:
"O virtuous lady, tell that Nahuṣa: 'If you wish to enjoy Śacī, you shall come at night having mounted an unprecedented vehicle. (154)
"If you place your auspicious palanquin upon the shoulders of the Seven Sages and,
having ascended it, come here, then you shall be worthy to enjoy Śacī.
Those very words of Śacī were then reported to the king.
Laughing, Nahuṣa also spoke quickly to his servant:
"Go, go, go with haste; bring the Seven Sages here at once!
Thus addressed, the messenger departed and swiftly brought the Seven Sages.
Having seen them all, the king bowed and spoke with reverence:
"You are indeed the sons of Brahmā, devoted to the service of others;
you are free from delusion and envy, and devoid of pride and egoism. (158–159)
"All of you are equal to Nārāyaṇa, blazing with the splendor of Brahman;
may you indeed be gracious for the sake of accomplishing my purpose.
Having heard him, the sages said to him, "Choose what resides in your heart."
"We are all capable of giving for your sake; do not delay.
Nahuṣa said to them there, "You are indeed compassionate toward your devotees;
now quickly grant me the gift of Śacī that I desire."
"The great chaste lady Śacī desires the beloved vehicle of the Seven Sages;
make this very boon of mine accomplished today without delay.
Hearing this, the sages laughed at the deluded king.
They placed a palanquin upon his shoulder, and the king proceeded toward Śacī.
But the aged sages walked slowly;
then the king repeatedly said to the sages, "O sages, walk with equal pace; proceed more quickly! || 164-165 ||
Hearing this, Durvāsas became filled with anger and spoke these foremost words:
"Since you said 'let them crawl,' become a serpent, a python!
Thus addressed, the king immediately became a massive python.
Having fallen from the palanquin, he offered praise to the ascetics.
The sages, however, said to the king: "From the sight of the Son of Dharma, liberation from the serpent will come, and you shall go to Vaikuṇṭha. (167–168)
Having spoken thus, the compassionate sages departed for the truth.
Upon hearing this, Śacī went and bowed with reverence to her preceptor.
Bṛhaspati then went quickly to Puṣkara, [to sit] upon the fibers of a lotus stalk.
Where indeed Indra was shining, he invoked the Lord of the Gods:
"O child, come here; I am your preceptor, Bṛhaspati.
Hearing the subtle voice of his preceptor, Indra abandoned his subtlety and arrived.
He fell prostrate like a staff and placed his head upon Indra’s chest.
Having led him away and caused him to perform a sacrifice, Indra restored him to Amarāvatī and bestowed upon him supreme sovereignty four times greater than before.
Śacī regained her husband through the power of her devotion to her husband (pātivratya).
Thus, O Lakṣmī, the story of Śacī’s virtuous conduct has been told to you here;
it pacifies the sin of killing a Brahmin and bestows the fruit of the Soma sacrifice.
The sacrificer performed the drinking of *soma* juice for one year;
he subsisted on fruits for one year, and drank only water for another year.
Indra performed this three-year vow and then regained his lordly power.
"This sacrifice, which provides abundant food and great sacrificial fees, is not for everyone to accomplish.

(176) Thus ends the three hundred and seventy-fourth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Power of Chastity, Beginning with Śacī’s Attainment [of Her Husband] While Traveling on the Vehicle of the Seven Sages—Having Become a Serpent—After Being Sought by Nahuṣa as Indra’s Proxy, Following the Fall of Indra Due to His Disrespect of Bṛhaspati," within the section on the Greatness of the Devoted Wife, in the first book, the Continuation of the Kṛta Yuga, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Chapter 376 →
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī! Hear the wonderful power of the devoted wife Ahalyā.
Ahalyā was the wife of the sage Gautama, and she was a devoted wife. (1)
In that youth, a mass of splendor existed on all sides of his body,
just like the halo surrounding the moon at all times.
On the banks of the Gaṅgā in Kāśī lived the wise sage Gautama.
In the city of Brahmā, within a leaf-hut on a high ground, [he remained] always.
(3) Once, upon the snowy mountain, there occurred a downpour of rain like the fall of clubs;
the floods of water caused the rivers to abandon their boundaries on both banks. (4)
In the wrong paths, terrifying currents surged;
having swept away villages, hamlets, and market towns, they carried the cities along.
The waters swirled around Kāśī with great height.

The sages, other ascetics, and the subjects dwelling in the lowlands were all submerged in the water and died; a cry of "Alas! Alas! arose. Hundreds of thousands and tens of millions of those residing in the countryside were drowned there.
Having witnessed the destruction and dissolution of humans, beasts, winged creatures, and forest-dwellers, as well as Gautama himself absorbed in meditation,
he emerged from his trance and spoke to his wife Ahalyā.
"Alas! Behold this destruction caused by the water, which brings about the loss of all possessions.
These waters of the Gaṅgā are rushing even toward your house;
indeed, they are approaching with great speed even on elevated ground. (1.375.10)
"The leaf-hut, as well as you, I, the horses, and the cows—all have perished in many ways, and even now that dissolution has not ceased.
Tell me, O auspicious lady, what is to be done? Water has reached the very stairs!"
"Behold, dear ones, the female calves are crying out at the sight of the clouds!
Make such an effort quickly that we may yet live;
for there is no place of refuge higher than our home here, other than the house itself."
"How will human beings survive by clinging to trees? Or what will be the fate of the cows, O virtuous lady? A great calamity has arrived!
Having spoken thus, the god Gautama, his eyes filled with tears, lamented.
Ahalyā said to him: "O Lord, whatever is destined to happen will happen.
However, having touched my husband, I shall indeed strive to move.
Having spoken thus, the virtuous woman quickly went into the interior of the leaf-hut.
She kindled the fire and performed an oblation with clarified butter.
By the power of her devotion to her husband, Ahalyā indeed called upon Gaṅgā:
"Come, sister Gaṅgā! Why do you cause my destruction? (17)
"If you do not come, O auspicious one, I shall surely reduce you to ashes!
(18) Terrified, Gaṅgā arrived in the form of a beautiful maiden;
becoming a servant, she paid homage to Ahalyā, the wife of Gautama. (19)
Ahalyā said to her quickly: "O Gaṅgā, what calamity has been wrought?
Today your waters are bringing about the dissolution of living beings.
O Gaṅgā, withdraw your waters immediately; otherwise, in an instant—"
"I shall perform the funeral oblation for you; having died, you will surely go to dissolution.
Hearing that, she trembled and, distressed, spoke to Satī:
"What shall I do, O great virtuous lady? No fault of mine is found in this matter."
"The Himalaya, the vast mountain, does not indeed obstruct the waters;
rather, it protects them within itself, and for that reason, this calamity has occurred.
Having heard this, she laughed and said to Gaṅgā, "Stay, O beautiful one, in my home."
"I shall summon Himādri and even devise a means for that.
Having spoken thus, Gautama’s wife, in the presence of the Fire-god, called to mind:
"O Himālaya! Come here; otherwise, your oblation shall be consumed!"

"I shall do so; do not delay—behold the great slaughter of living beings! At that moment, the King of Mountains trembled and, appearing in personified form, approached and bowed to Ahalyā, who was there in Kāśī, and spoke to that virtuous lady.
Speak, O Goddess! How was I remembered here? Tell me quickly.
Behold this dissolution by water; why do you not protect the waters?
Restrain the waters in the forests and upon the mountains.
Then the Himalaya said: "O Mother, I am not capable there;
it is not my fault that the water must always be guarded by me.
My water is upon the peaks, in the valleys, and in the caves. (29)
In the belly and in the heights, on the plateaus and in the valleys;
in the wildernesses, in the forests, above and even in the rivers and on the dry lands—I hold back the waters on all sides as much as is possible. (1.375.30–31)
But for seven days, there was incessant rain and excessive downpour;
day and night it fell like a continuous stream of pestles.
I am submerged in water; what can I do? I have no power. (32)
Today the waters, measured by me, increase and overflow.
Indeed, the clouds do not withdraw the rain that causes the dissolution.
For if the clouds were to withdraw their waters, they would go to destruction. (33–34)

Having heard him, Ahalyā said to him, "Wait; I shall summon a cloud. Summoning a cloud there with a swift mind, she called out, and clouds, agitated by the fear of death, arrived there immediately. (35)
Trembling, they set forth, and the beloved of Gautama said to them:
"O clouds! You are destroyers; why have you not reflected? Withdraw the waters immediately, or else you shall be dead!"
Hearing that terrifying sound, those virtuous women trembled and said:
"O Mother, it is not our fault; the fault lies with Indra.
We are indeed his servants; we rain down only by his command. (38)

Terrified, exhausted, weary, and deprived of water, we have been struck by the thunderbolt as if out of anger; indeed, we all rain down here—forgive us! We are always powerless, living only by the command of Indra. (1.375.39–40)

"O virtuous lady, we were not able to do anything without his command. Having heard these words of the clouds, the great satī [Ahalyā] remembered Indra by means of a mantra and offered him as an oblation into the midst of the fire.
At that moment, Indra, drawn away by the mantra, fell from his throne;
he swiftly descended through the path of the sky and alighted upon the leaf-hut, crying out:
"I am dead! I am destroyed! May the hosts of deities protect me! (42–43)
Speaking thus, he stood within the leaf-hut due to the power of the virtuous woman's majesty.
Then the great virtuous woman, having bowed, spoke to Mahendra, the mountain of the gods:
"O Indra! There is indeed a great slaughter of living beings upon the earth."
"Why do you not bring about the destruction of that which has been produced by this rain?
Indeed, perform the withdrawal of the water right now and quickly create a blockade.
Otherwise, O God, I shall perform a fire sacrifice within your own midst! || 45-46 ||
Thus addressed, he became greatly enraged; however, seeing her to be a devoted wife and perceiving that his own destruction was imminent within a moment,
Purandara recognized that to be the time for humility.
She then spoke to the clouds: "Quickly create an obstruction!
Even though the clouds gathered there on the Himalayas, there was still no lowering of the waters; then the devoted wife spoke.
"O Indra! O clouds! O Gire! O Gaṅgā! Why indeed do you not descend?
The waters of the rivers are not seen; tell me this! Indra replied: "O great virtuous lady! Varuṇa resides within the waters."
The waters then became constricted and the rivers indeed became low-lying;
at that moment, the virtuous woman called to mind Varuṇa,
the lord of aquatic creatures and the presiding deity of the waters, and he arrived there immediately.
Ahalyā said to that Lord of Waters: "You do not even see your crusher!
What kind of dissolution has occurred? Withdraw the waters indeed!
Otherwise, death shall come to you by fire; there is no doubt about this. (5.3)
In that moment, he too quickly bowed and performed *prāṇāyāmas*. At that time, indeed, the waters became agitated and the rivers everywhere became constricted.
Then, seeing her kinsmen and relatives indeed distressed and dead,
the compassionate Ahalyā then asked the Fire-god for the means of restoring them to life:
"Let a remedy be told by which these who have died may indeed come back to life here."
Agni, Indra, Varuṇa, Gaṅgā, the clouds, and the mountains—
all declared that King Yama is considered the bestower of life and non-life.
Ahalyā then remembered him, and Yama arrived there at once.

With palms joined in reverence, he said to her, "O virtuous lady, what task must I perform here? To him, Satī replied: "When this dissolution has passed and the waters have receded, quickly [bring back] the deceased humans—forest-dwellers, householders, and those living in the wilderness."
By my power, restore to life all animals, living beings, other species of birds, and reptiles who have met untimely deaths. If you do not restore them to life today, your own death has arrived.
"I shall consume you like a mere blade of grass; quickly restore the dead to life!
At this, Yama, the lord of death, trembled and spoke with a distressed mind:
"My very existence is dependent on Rudra, and I am ever a follower of Saṃkarṣaṇa."
Indeed, the death of embodied beings is dependent upon that [Kāla] and according to their karma.
At that very moment, Satī remembered Rudra and Saṃkarṣaṇa;
the two destroyers of Time arrived, and having bowed to Satī, they stood before her.
Satī said: "Let both of you, the lords, restore all these dead to life;
otherwise, by virtue of my devotion to my husband, I shall take away your very lives.
Rudra and Saṃkarṣaṇa replied: "Creation, nourishment, and destruction—"
Indeed, in this matter, that which was fashioned by Nārāyaṇa proceeds according to its own sequence.
We are not capable here of doing it, nor of not doing it, nor even of doing it otherwise; Śrī Hari alone is the supreme capable agent.
Then Satī remembered Hari, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa; by the power of her devotion as a faithful wife, Hari arrived there in an instant.
Bowing to Hari with a mind full of great humility, Satī spoke to him:
"O Nārāyaṇa! O Master! O Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa! O Lord!
During this great deluge of rain, millions of living beings have perished here—human beings, animals, species of birds, and likewise other creatures. (1.375.70)
"O Hare Kṛṣṇa, bring these back to life, for they have met with untimely death! The Blessed Lord then said to her, "Make a firm resolve:
if the dharma consisting of devotion to my husband has been maintained by me..."
"Then, let all living beings who have died by the force of the rain come back to life!"—
by this command of Hari, a resolve was made there by her named Ahalyā; and at that very moment, all these embodied beings were restored to life.
Wherever their corpses were placed, there they arose; as many as were living at that time, extending as far as the edge of the ocean.
By the command of Hari, Gaṅgā, the clouds, Indra, and the other gods [restored them].
Himādri, Salileśa, Rudra, and Saṃkarṣaṇa;
Nārāyaṇa, Yama, Kāla, and Mṛtyu—these are the attendants of Hari. Having led them all back to their former positions and their respective abodes, [he restored them]. (75–76)
By the power of her devotion to her husband (*pātivratya*),
the lords restored her to a beautiful form, endowed with great capability and the splendor of fresh youth.
Then, having bowed down, all the gods departed for their own abodes.
Those who are born alive by virtue of their birth are indeed fortunate.
Indra was bewildered upon seeing Gautama’s wife;
though she was devoted to her husband, the lord of the gods went far away and then returned. (78–79)
Then, although he had seen her before, the King of the Gods did not see her after;
thus, becoming despondent, he indeed went to heaven, yet at another time he returned.
Even then, he did not see her at all, for she remained within the leaf-hut.
Because his heart was defiled, he did not see the devoted wife. (81) Having returned from there to heaven, he came back again after some time;
even then, he did not see her standing in the leaf-hut, though she was indeed there. (82)
"Women devoted to their husbands never come within the range of sight of those who are sinful, impure, defiled, and devoid of virtue.
Thus Indra came and went many times.
In order to violate Ahalyā, though trembling and fainting with fear,
he— blinded by lust— did not perceive his own or another’s death.
Then, after some time, he arrived at the surface of the earth during the night.
Where that virtuous and devoted wife Ahalyā, who was composed of righteousness, resided,
there in the darkness of night, a great light spread all around;
this light was seen by Mahendra throughout the hermitage of Gautama.
He descended to the earth and beheld only pure radiance,
as if it were the orb of the full moon amidst the circle of the autumnal moonlight;
yet he did not see Ahalyā there, and then he returned to heaven.
She told Candra of her mental agitation:
"I am a divine form composed of splendor, long desired as an object of enjoyment.
This was reported by Candra to him [the sage]: "You have assumed the form of Gautama."

"I am indeed a Brahman-indicating cock. Let us go to where she resides; by employing a stratagem, the fruit may be attained. If it does not happen, there will be death; no hesitation should be made in this matter. (1.375.90–91)
Having thus deliberated, the cat and the cock then departed after midnight and approached the vicinity of Gautama’s house. There,
the cock, like the moon, crowed at the hour of Brahmā.
Having heard all that, Gautama then went to the celestial river (Svarṇadī) to bathe.
Meanwhile, Mahendra, assuming the form of a cat, entered the house through a crack and,
taking on the form of Gautama, went to his beloved wife’s bedchamber.
But Ahalyā, seeing her husband arrived with amorous intent,
being attentive to the desire for sexual enjoyment, offered him a kiss. At that moment, however, the celestial river suddenly spoke to Gautama.
"O Sage! This is no time for Brahmanical conduct; there might be deceit in your home.
Go quickly and see Satī. Upon hearing this, Gautama returned swiftly to his own house, and by the time he arrived, Hari was already seated to eat. (96–97)
Gautama beheld Indra, who had assumed his own form while remaining full of guile; perceiving that Turāṣāṭ was greedy for fortune,
the sage indeed cursed Śakra, saying, "May you have a vulva upon your body."

Ahalyā also recognized him as someone other than her husband; nevertheless, that devoted wife did not curse him while he was in the form of her husband’s likeness. She did not offer him an embrace so long as she knew him to be someone other than Gautama. (1.375.99–100)
Although she was capable of inflicting a great punishment upon Gautama—who had appeared in his own form and deserved such a penalty—she did not do so because he was in the form of her husband.
"The husband himself is returning; Gautama knows this for himself. (101)
"Until I embrace him, he shall pay the penalty"—
thinking thus, Ahalyā, who was exceedingly proud of her husband's form,
did not utter a curse against Indra, but instead herself inflicted a counter-penalty upon him. (102–103)
Indra, though endowed with a thousand wombs, went to heaven while still possessed of impurity;
the Moon, overwhelmed by fear, fled from him in secret.
Then Gautama said to his wife: "O gentle one, what do you desire?"
Excessive beauty brings happiness, yet womanhood itself is a source of suffering.
O beloved! You uphold the foremost of duties in every way; as for me, my mind is constantly consumed by heat, and assistance between the two of us brings no comfort. (105–106)
"If I abandon you out of detachment, you will become sorrowful;
if I keep you by my side, such anxiety as this arises.
Therefore, tell me, my dear! What indeed shall I do so that [this may be avoided]?"
“Let there be no anxiety for me, and let there never again be an obstacle to your dharma.
Having heard this from her husband, the chaste and devoted wife spoke to her husband:
“O Lord! I always reside here within this vessel as your own Pārvatī.”
Likewise, O Lord, I dwell here as a stone in the form of your seat;
I am eternally dependent upon you, occupying the ground presided over by you. Therefore, you shall have no anxiety, nor shall there be any obstacle to your dharma.
"My devotion to my husband shall always be preserved,
O Lord, and your own liberation shall indeed come about through yoga.
Having spoken thus and bowed to her husband, she was quickly consecrated by him.
For there, a stone always served as a support for her feet;
then the Lord Rāma himself spoke to his beloved wife:
"He will come right here and shall find rest within you."
Then, O wife, you will certainly go with me to Vaikuṇṭha.
Until then, I shall always perform here such penance as my heart desires;
I am free from desire and profoundly peaceful, and so indeed are you and they always here.

Those possessed of worldly desires are always submerged in the great ocean of suffering; they never reach the further shore of the latent tendencies of saṃsāra. O Beloved! Liberation is like a stone—devoid of obstacles and the like.
"By you, service to your husband has been obtained, which shall be as enduring as a stone seat forever.
(117) I shall remain upon the surface of the stone and perform penance here for a long time;
in the Tretā age, through union with Rāma, we two shall go to the supreme state. (118)
"O virtuous lady! By means of this second divine form, remain forever steadfast in my service; this is my desire.
Thus addressed, the chaste Ahalyā became a stone right there.
Her husband Gautama, however, performed austerities upon that stone.
During the Tretā age, through the union with Rāma, those two attained the supreme state.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have told you of the wonderful sovereignty of Ahalyā.
"By reading and hearing this, one's devotion to the husband shall become firm.

(121) Thus, in the first section, the *Kṛtayugasantāna*, within the *Pativratāmāhātmya* of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, [it is told] how, through the power of Ahalyā’s devotion to her husband, during a great deluge when Kāśī was submerged, there arrived Gaṅgā, Himādri, Meghendra, Varuṇa, Rudra, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Yama, Nārāyaṇa, and others; how the excessive rain was pacified and the dead were restored to life; and how, by the mere touch of Ahalyā, Indra’s body became possessed of female organs (*bhaga*).
Chapter Three Hundred and Seventy-Five, titled "The Description of the State of Being a Stone and Liberation," etc., [ends].
Chapter 375. *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga).
Chapter 376.
[The Author: Chapter 377.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī! What was the nature of Sītā’s devotion to her husband as well?
Having given her life for the sake of her husband,
she indeed experienced great suffering from birth throughout the vast forest and in the dwellings of Rākṣasas and others;
in the end, though she was the very embodiment of Lakṣmī, that virtuous woman sank into the earth.
She was the daughter of Kuśadhvaja, born from the womb of Dharaṇī,
and Rāma indeed married her after breaking the bow.
In the city named Sāketa, there was a king who was like Indra.
His son was Śātamakhī Rāmāditya.
His brother was Narāditya, who was born from Dyutivarṇa.
At the request of Brahmā, Viṣṇu himself became Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
Vāsudeva became Rāmāditya, a most righteous being on earth;
the Blessed One appeared in the first part of the Tretā Yuga through a woman of mixed caste.
Sent by Viśvāmitra for the sake of slaying the Rākṣasas, he... [6]
Accompanied by Narāditya, he set out together with the sage.
Having seen Ahalyā, devoted to her husband, in the form of a stone and presided over by Gautama on his own path, he, possessing divine vision, [beheld her]. (7–8)
Then Rāma, the lord of the world and purifier of the universe, having heard that account of former events, questioned Viśvāmitra regarding the cause;
and having recognized her through his divine form as one solely devoted to the service of her husband.

She touched [the earth] with her toes and became a lotus pond. Having offered blessings to Rāma, she departed with her husband in a celestial chariot to the supreme world, the realm of truth, relying upon her own lord.
Gautama also bestowed auspicious blessings upon Rāmāditya.
Then, ahead of him, Rāma beheld the ground purified by the feet of Vāmana; there he knelt, desiring to grasp the dust.

The dust on his body was indeed purifying; having thoroughly rubbed it off there with devotion, he went to Viśvāmitra’s hermitage and slew the Rākṣasa Mārīca. Then, having gone to Mithilā, he broke the bow of Śambhu.
And there, O Lakṣmī, the Blessed One took Sītā’s hand in marriage;
having performed the wedding, he joyfully departed for Ayodhyā.
The King, having shown him great respect, desired to appoint his son as the monarch.
Having quickly brought the heated water from the sacred ford, O best of sages, and having seen Rāmārka— who had been consecrated with perfumes (adhivāsa) and endowed with all auspiciousness—
the wife of the sage named Kalahā, by the power of her previous words, [acted].
He restrained the king from the previously accepted boon—
the exile of Rāma to the forest and the kingship for his own son—
even though that son was entirely unworthy and destined for destruction by time.
The great king, abiding by the path of justice, did not wish to grant the boon.
Then the wise Rāmārka spoke to that king, who was endowed with righteousness and truth:
"Whatever merit is gained from the gift of a hundred tanks, even more than that [is gained by this]. (1.376.20)
O Father! By the gift of a single step-well (*vāpī*), men in this world obtain merit;
and by the gift of ten step-wells, they obtain even greater merit than that, which can be acquired in every way on earth by men through a single sacrifice.

The happiness obtained here in these lands of action by beholding the face of a son is greater than that which is gained through the merit of a hundred sacrifices. And the merit found in seeing a hundred sons is even greater than that. (22–23)
O King, by the preservation of truth, a meritorious person attains [great rewards];
for there is no dharma higher than truth, nor is there any sin greater than falsehood.
There is no kinsman superior to dharma, and there is no wealth greater than dharma.
Who is superior to one whose nature is truth? Protect your own duty with effort.
O King, when one's own duty is protected, there is constant auspiciousness everywhere, as well as fame, firm establishment, majesty, and supreme honor.
Having lived according to dharma for fourteen years, I shall abandon the pleasures of home and wander; I will dwell in the forest to fulfill your word of truth.
For one who has made a vow of truth, whether intentionally or unintentionally, [the consequence follows].
He who does not provide protection [to his dependents] finds atonement only in ashes;
he is cooked in the Kumbhīpāka hell for as long as a day of Brahmā.
Thereafter, that man shall become mute and afflicted with leprosy for seven births.
Having spoken thus and bowed to his parents, Rāmāditya— accompanied by the sun-like man (Narārka)— bound his matted hair with bark garments and departed for the forest;
and Sītā, devoted to her husband, also set out together with her lord.
Rāma said this to her: "O beloved, stay here or return;
O Jānakī, there are indeed many sorrows in the forest at every step, and you are unable to endure them all."
Sītā replied: "O Prince, my body belongs to you; I am devoted to my husband and dear to him.
I am a virtuous woman, dedicated to the duty toward my husband and a protector of the vow of fidelity. I was indeed bestowed upon you by Janaka, and not given to anyone else. (33)
My husband’s command must be obeyed by me; such is indeed my duty.
Nevertheless, O Ocean of Compassion, I pray to you: without you, death is certain.
Without my husband, there would be no refuge for me here. (34–35)
Death in the forest is better for me than being in the presence of my husband;
for wives, there is no path to the world beyond without their husband,
nor is there any worldly path without him.
She is happy when he is happy, sorrowful when he is sorrowful, and serene when he is serene.
A virtuous wife should be hungry when he is hungry and satisfied when he is satisfied. One who is intent on the joy of her own self-interest and partial [to others] shall go to hell. (37–38)

By good fortune, she becomes a virtuous woman endowed with auspiciousness; yet, though she lives, she who is bereft of her husband is as if dead, while she who has her husband is truly alive. A woman is the side of her lord, and she is his half; indeed, I am yours.
"I am not fit to be separated from him, for my husband alone is my heaven. A wanton woman who desires happiness after abandoning her suffering husband is a sinner;
a devoted wife, though sharing in his misery, attains great merit. (1.376.40–41)
If a husband can be made happy by the giving away of all one's possessions,
or even by one's life or body, then a wife must always seek her husband's happiness.
A husband must be protected by a wife, even by selling her own body in times of distress.
Having surrendered her wealth and even her very self, a virtuous wife must protect her husband.
To her, the husband is the Supreme Brahman, the husband is her duty, the husband is her happiness, and the husband is her sacred ordinance.
The husband is everything; indeed, there is no other means whatsoever for her to attain happiness.

Therefore, O Lord, as one who is like a shadow to you and is devoted to you, I must always remain with you; I must never remain apart from you. Wherever the husband is, there is heaven, Vaikuṇṭha, and likewise liberation.
Sovereignty, supreme prosperity, abundant wealth, dharma, and even the aesthetic delight of love—
without a husband, a home is like a royal palace or the den of a jackal;
and all objects of enjoyment are in every way equivalent to poison.
Heaven is not what is called heaven; for a woman, her husband is always her heaven.
Vow is not what is called a vow here; for a woman, her husband alone is her vow.
Dharma is not what is called dharma; for a woman, her husband is always her dharma.

Charity, recitation, worship, good fortune, and even peace—all these are accomplished for a wife who remains by her husband's side, and not otherwise. A woman whose husband is absent or deceased does not obtain the fruit [of such acts]. (1.376.50)

Behold, my beloved! When a husband has gone to another land, a woman’s fortune becomes devoid of luster and stripped of all energy and vigor. A kingdom, though once universal, when bereft of its lord, is indeed equal to that of a shaven-headed beggar. (51)
The leaf-hut occupied by her husband was superior even to the abode of Mahendra. For a woman, the forest is not truly a forest, nor is a palace truly a palace;
a forest with her husband is heaven, while a palace without her master is merely a forest.
A body with a husband is divine; a body bereft of a husband is of the nature of a corpse.
Ornament is not said to be an ornament; indeed, the husband alone is the ornament. A woman without a husband, even if adorned with ornaments, is known as a prostitute.
Water, food, garments, auspicious substances, and collyrium—when accompanied by the husband, these possess splendor; otherwise, they bring about defilement.
Therefore, O Lord, one must always dwell together with one's husband.
"Indeed, a wife without her husband at her side is destined for destruction.
O beloved! May my own destruction not come to pass while separated from you here in this house.
Therefore, O Keśava, it is right that you alone should show me supreme compassion."

Having spoken thus, her eyes filled with tears, she donned garments of bark and, perceiving Rāma’s inner resolve, prepared indeed for the journey. Rāma said: "O virtuous lady, hunger will become unbearable in the forest."
Sītā said: "O Lord, at home my hunger will not be appeased.
Rāma said: "O virtuous lady, in the forest thirst will lead to death.
Sītā said: "O Lord, at home thirst for you will kill me."
Rāma said: "O lovely one! You will die in the forest at the hands of lions and other beasts. Sītā replied: "In the home, O beloved, separation from you will consume me.
Rāma said: "O wife! In the forest, the heat of the sun will take away my life."
Sītā said: "In the home, the fire of separation from Rāma will blaze;
the forest fire of cold is superior, for it is measured against the cold fire of the home.
Rāma said: "In the forest, some demon might perhaps carry you away."
Then Sītā said, "Rāma will become one whose duty is to be meditated upon.
Rāma then said, "He will not accept her while she is stained by blemish.
Then Sītā said, "The dharma of the virtuous shall be made manifest."
Rāma then said, "Satī will undergo separation.
Sītā then said, "Sītā will attain union in Vaikuṇṭha.
Rāma said, "True happiness is certainly not to be seen with this body."
Sītā said: "Surely you have never experienced suffering together with me.
Rāma said: "O Sītā! In the forest, you will become a giver of sorrow.
Sītā said: "By abandoning [me] at home, you will become one who suffers exceedingly."
Afflicted in the forest and tormented again and again, Sītā,
whose sole support is her husband, will not utter even a sound of distress, not even in her sighing.
[She maintains] the resolve for his favor and the avoidance of anything contrary to him.
Sītā, devoted to her husband, will conduct herself in every way in the forest. Protected by the fire and approved by Rāma,
she will cast away the Rākṣasa with her shadow and manifest her wifely devotion.
Having caused the Rākṣasas along with their letters to vanish by means of her shadow,
Sītā, endowed with purity, will once again be united with Rāma.
By the will of her husband, that shadow shall indeed be dissolved into the fire.
Considering her husband’s words to be for the protection of the Dharma,
Sītā, the virtuous wife who does what is pleasing to her husband, will instruct him further:
"Whether it be the teacher’s hermitage, the forest, or heaven— whatever my husband desires shall be honored."

The word of the husband is the supreme dharma; the husband is the glorious Supreme Lord. Through Sītā, Lord Rāma, having slain tens of millions of rākṣasas, will command his wife, desiring that she protect her heart.
"In Vaikuṇṭha you possess a divine form, and in Sāketa you reside within the heart;
O Sītā, invisible to people, always perform service unto me.
Having accepted this command, she will indeed enter into the earth.
"You ought to take this young Jānakī with you," she said,
and thus, filled with enthusiasm to go into forest exile,
Sītā— she who was Māyā manifesting as a guide on the path— assumed a divine form.
She went ahead there, and Rāma saw her then;
though possessing a human form, that virtuous woman followed behind Rāma.
Thus, even that Sun among men proceeded in the guise of a servant.
Rāma, that sun among men, departed for the forest accompanied by Sītā, the daughter of the sun;
and Indra, O beloved, abandoned his own body due to grief for his son.
To fulfill his father’s truth, Rāma wandered through the forest.

In the course of time, in the great forest, Rāvaṇa’s sister Śūrpaṇakhā—she being a Rākṣasī in the form of a Brahmin woman—beheld Rāma while afflicted by desire. She said to him: "O Rāma! O abode of beauty! take me as your wife! (82–83)
Rāma said, "I am accompanied by my wife; go instead to my younger brother, who is without a wife.
I am devoted to the vow of having only one wife, and taking another would cause me distress.
Having heard this, she indeed said to that sun among men, "Devote yourself to me."
Narāditya, observing the vow of celibacy, spoke thus to that Rākṣasī:
"It is not the time for me to take a wife; go, O gentle one, to another person!
Enraged, Śūrpaṇakhā said: "If you reject me in vain..."
"Indeed, a calamity shall befall both of you; of this there is no doubt.
By my curse, this Rāma shall have his wife stolen away.
To her who had spoken thus as a Rākṣasī, [Rāvaṇa replied] under the pretext of slaying the demons:
With a weapon, Narārka cut off the nose of the woman.
On account of that, indeed, Narāditya dispatched fourteen thousand rākṣasas along the path of Yama in battle. ||88-89||
Having performed austerities, the ascetic Śūrpaṇakhā became humpbacked; for she obtained Kṛṣṇa as her husband after securing a boon from Brahmā. Then Śūrpaṇakhā went to the island named Siṃhala.
She indeed spoke of the deeds of Hari to that king Rāvaṇa.
And Rāvaṇa, his mind incensed by the words of Śūrpaṇakhā,
and having recognized Sītā as a virtuous woman, made a firm resolve in his heart to abduct her.
Rāvaṇa was strongly dissuaded by his wife Mandodarī from the violation of another's wife,
who was devoted to her husband there:
"O Lord of Siṃhala, do not go at all toward that which results in total destruction!"
Even though he was thus entreated, Rāma abducted Sītā through his illusory power (māyā).
With the assistance of Sugrīva, having granted a boon to Hanumān and having given the monkey-lord a ring as a token of trust, [he departed].
Hanumān traveled through the sky directly to Siṃhaladvīpa;
there, in the Aśoka grove, he beheld Sītā, who was filled with grief.
She was fasting, exceedingly emaciated, and remained intent on the chanting of Rāma’s name.
Having prostrated before her mother— who was meditating upon her lord and husband and was adorned with a mass of coarse matted hair— she gave her a jeweled ring and spoke the message from Rāma;
she then reduced Siṃhala to ashes.
And that devoted wife, her eyes filled with tears, spoke to Rāma’s messenger:
"O, does my Rāma live? Is my lord safe from this terrible ocean of my grief?
Is my master not destroyed by sorrow? (99)
"Even while born in the forest,
how much suffering has my lord, that master of mine, endured for my sake?
What food does he eat— he who is dearer to me than my own life?"
"Will I see that Rāma again when he has reached the shore of the ocean?
Will I once more serve the lotus feet of my lord?
For the life of a foolish woman who is deprived of service to her husband is in vain."
"Ah! My son of Dharma, that sun among men, still lives!
My brother, who is like a god, is submerged in an ocean of grief for me.
Having thus informed her from the sky that he was entirely free from ailment, Hanumān—
He departed and recounted Rāmāditya’s vow of chastity;
then that monkey, having built a bridge with his armies, went forth.
Having slain the lord of Siṃhala, he effected the liberation of Sītā.
He went to Sāketa with Sītā by means of the Puṣpaka chariot.
Having celebrated the festival of victory and having placed Sītā upon his chest,
both Sītā and Rāma— the sun— extinguished the flames of their separation.
The two sons of Rāma, the righteous Kuśa and Lava,
auspicious and founders of the solar dynasty, were born in the hermitage of Vālmīki.
Sītā, however, then sank into the earth at the city of Sāketa.
Rāma indeed ruled the kingdom for twelve thousand years.
Then, having established righteousness upon the earth, he departed for Vaikuṇṭha.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have related to you this supreme account of Sītā’s life.
This life-story of Śrī Rāma, devoted to his wife and afflicted by the cruel demons of the forest, always bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
No one has ever been born equal to Rāma in compassion, righteousness, and purity.
And hereafter no one shall be born except Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa;
nor shall there be a wife equal to Sītā— a devoted wife who lived in sorrow,
who survived her husband, and whose like has never been born nor even heard of before.

Thus ends the three hundred and seventy-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of Sītā— the Daughter of Janaka and Wife of Rāmāditya— Experiencing the Hardships of Forest Dwelling with Her Husband Solely for His Sake, and Her Devotion to the Dharma of Chastity," within the first section on the Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga, concerning the Greatness of the Devoted Wife, in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. [Chapter 377] *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā*, Part 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga), Chapter 377.
[Author: Chapter 378.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, Lakṣmī! Rādhā herself, the beloved of Hari, resides in Goloka.
He spoke of the duties devoted to devotion toward one’s husband to his daughters Lakṣmī, Gaṅgā, Sarasvatī, Padminī, Prabhā, and Śivā:
“Listen, all you daughters; I shall declare the eternal duties.”
For women, the dharma of devotion to their husband (*pātivratya*) is supreme; there is nothing higher than this.
In it lies enjoyment, great liberation, and eternal bliss of the Self.
[This applies] to those of the various castes (*varṇa*) and stages of life (*āśrama*), as well as to renunciants and householders alike.

O sons! For widows, for Vaiṣṇavas, for virtuous women, and in every way for sons, daughters, disciples, and those endowed with servants, devotion to one's husband is the supreme duty for all people in every respect. (4–5)
A woman who is always purified by meditation performs service to her husband;
she constantly enjoys his favor, having offered everything to Kṛṣṇa.
She, an eater of the remnants of Viṣṇu’s grace, becomes a virtuous woman liberated while living.
Constantly devoted to austerity, pure, peaceful, and endowed with wisdom;
(7) such a woman is always a devoted wife who takes refuge in vows and sacred fords.
Having received the mantra of Viṣṇu and having performed service to a true guru, (8) she remains steadfast.
Having received the blessings of her teacher, the disciple becomes a devoted wife;
the teacher’s command must always be obeyed, and everything should be reported to him.
Of all those worthy of reverence, the father is the greatest teacher.
The mother is a hundred times more venerable than the father; the deity is a hundred times more venerable than the mother.
Among them, the true Guru who imparts the mantra is four times more venerable than the deities.
And the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa is the manifest Guru, the Supreme Lord himself.
The husband alone is the teacher and the deity, whose essence is Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa;
he is one's own Guru, the manifest enjoyer, the embodied Janārdana himself.
The Guru is Brahmā, the Guru is Viṣṇu, and the Guru indeed is Śiva himself.
All the gods always reside with joy in the guru and the husband. When the guru is pleased, Hari is pleased; when he is pleased, the deities are pleased.
By drinking the water from the guru’s feet, a virtuous woman becomes as one who has bathed in all sacred pilgrimage sites (tīrthas).
She is liberated from all sins and becomes fit for the world of Viṣṇu;
she has effectively bathed in all sacred fords and been initiated into all sacrifices—
that woman who herself performs an ablution with the water from her husband’s feet.
The auspicious water of the Śālagrāma is ten times more meritorious than the water of the Gaṅgā.
Even superior to that, by a factor of ten, is considered the water from the feet of one's husband.
The wife who constantly partakes of this is liberated while living and is equal to the gods.
The daily duty of virtuous women is to eat only by the grace of their husband;
they should worship him with effort and partake of the water from his feet.
O beloved! Whatever holy places exist on earth are present within the water from a husband’s feet.
Indeed, they always remain for the sake of attaining the fruit of serving their husbands.
As long as the earth remains moistened by the water from her husband’s feet,
so long is that wife worshipped by the gods as the very embodiment of Mahālakṣmī.
Indeed, she who enjoys the favor of her husband makes the earth pure;
for she is liberated while living, sanctifying both the sacred fords and all creatures.
She who walks before her husband becomes a partaker of the fruits of religious vows.
At every step, that virtuous woman obtains the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice.
Purified like fire and wind, and radiant like the sun,
she rejoices thereafter in Vaikuntha together with her husband, Hari.
Indeed, for that Vaiṣṇavī woman who worships the mantra of Viṣṇu and serves her husband,
there exists no goddess on earth more supreme or purifying than she.
She is a devotee of Hari, a great saintly woman, and entirely devoted to the service of her lord.
From the mouth of one who is a Vaiṣṇava,
the name of Hari, "Nārāyaṇa," indeed issues forth in the form of a mantra;
whoever that name enters the ear of, even he becomes greatly purified.
Even he might pierce the entire cosmic egg and go to the abode of Hari;
yet a devotee rescues seven ancestors, seven descendants, seven beginning with his maternal grandfather,
his siblings, his mother, and his mother’s mother.
Indeed, a woman who is exclusively devoted to Viṣṇu can uplift a hundred thousand men.
Even if she is entirely devoid of youth, devoid of knowledge, devoid of learning, devoid of noble birth, or devoid of ritual action—provided she is solely intent on devotion to her husband. (28–29)
She is indeed the most excellent, equal to Lakṣmī, and endowed with ten million virtues;
by the power of her devotion to her husband, that virtuous woman uplifts the worlds.
Likewise, even one who is devoid of youth, short-lived, lacking knowledge, or unlearned—
One devoid of knowledge, one devoid of caste, a fool among fools, and a great sinner;
one who does not belong to any stage of life, one bereft of fame, one who is diseased, one afflicted by chronic illness;
one without a lineage, one whose lineage has perished, and one who is destitute and without a wife. (31–32)
Even a man who is devoid of devotion to Viṣṇu, who has abandoned righteous deeds and duties, who is indifferent, ill-behaved, and destitute of wealth—
[he too is blessed] by the blessings of a truthful, devoted, and virtuous wife, through her age and strength. (33)

One attains heaven, one’s own desired prosperity, worldly enjoyment, and liberation. (34) Merely by acquiring renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*), a man becomes Nārāyaṇa; through the attainment of service to her husband, a woman becomes Nārāyaṇī. (35)
Having burnt away her own past karmas and severed the karmas of others,
that virtuous and chaste woman goes to the abode of Hari;
just as the earth is instantly purified by the touch of the feet of renunciants.
By the touch of the feet of virtuous women, the earth is likewise purified. Holy fords purify immediately; indeed, a Vaiṣṇava woman devoted to her husband purifies instantly.
By the word of women devoted to their husbands, offspring become free from sin.
By feeding a devoted wife, one obtains the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice;
by bowing to her with devotion and beholding her, one obtains the fruit of a Rajasuya sacrifice.
The fruit is equal to that of renunciants, ascetics, and celibate students.
The sons of virtuous, chaste Vaiṣṇava women are always [righteous].
Even a Brāhmaṇa woman who is bereft of her husband should remain forever free from desire;
eating but one meal at the end of the day, she should be devoted to food fit for an oblation (haviṣya).
She does not wear divine garments, nor perfumed substances, nor fine oil; nor does she wear garlands, sandalwood paste, or ornaments such as conch-shell bangles and vermilion.
She shall always wear non-royal clothing and constantly worship Nārāyaṇa.
She should perform service to Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa constantly;
O daughters, she should always utter His name with devotion.
Furthermore, according to the dharma of widowhood, she should regard any man as equal to a son.
She should not eat delicious food that increases desire as she would otherwise;
nor should she enjoy such opulence except for her husband, who is Nārāyaṇa.
She too is equal to a devoted wife if she is solely intent upon her husband, Kṛṣṇa.
One should listen to the duties of the virtuous and perform service to one's guru.
A chaste woman devoted to her husband shall be liberated from the bonds of worldly existence.
O daughters, listen; I shall indeed declare what must be done by virtuous women.
A woman should always remain in her heart full of longing for her husband;
she should devotedly drink the water that has washed his feet with his permission.
She should perform vows, ascetic practices, and the worship of the gods only by the command of her husband.
She should perform service at his feet, offer praise, and bring him satisfaction.
A devoted wife must never perform any action without her husband’s permission;
indeed, that virtuous woman should meditate upon her beloved as being even greater than Nārāyaṇa.
A virtuous woman should never engage in contact with the passion of other men.
A chaste wife should perform processions, festivals, dancing, singing, and likewise playing,
solely for the sake of her husband, and never for the sake of anyone else.
Whatever is the constant food of her husband, that indeed is for virtuous women. That virtuous woman, devoted to service, should never abandon the company of her husband.
A wife devoted to her husband should never give a retort to her husband.
She should not become angry even when struck in anger; she should remain pure.
She should feed her beloved husband when he is hungry and give him drink and food.
When he is asleep, she should wake him, but she should never urge him toward worldly labors.
A virtuous wife should feel a hundredfold more affection for her beloved husband than she does for her son.
For a woman of noble family, her husband is her kinsman, her refuge, her sustainer, and her deity;
while the virtuous wife, her face bright as nectar and her countenance smiling, beholds her beloved.
One who beholds her with a spirit of devotion shall indeed become the bringer of all prosperity;
such a virtuous woman may even deliver a thousand men.
And the husband of those women devoted to their husbands is liberated from all sin.
Indeed, by the power of her devotion to her husband, they have no experience of [the fruits of] their own karma;
for together with her, being freed from karma, they rejoice in the abode of Hari.
Whatever holy places exist upon the earth, they are all contained within the feet of a virtuous wife (satī). || 58–59 ||
The splendor of the gods and the sages resides in virtuous women;
the entire austerity of ascetics and the vow of those who observe vows reside in them. The fruit of givers lies in their giving, and that same fruit resides in them.
Nārāyaṇa himself, Śambhu, the Creator, and the gods and others—
even the sages and ascetics— certainly stand in awe of the virtuous wife.
By bowing down to a devoted wife, one is liberated from the bondage of sin.
A devoted wife, possessing great merit, is indeed capable by her own splendor of reducing the three worlds to ashes in an instant; likewise,
the husband of virtuous women is righteous, and their son is ever pure.
He has no fear whatsoever, neither from the gods nor even from Yama.
Born in the home of those possessing the merit of a hundred lifetimes, she is a devoted wife;
her father, the progenitor of that devoted wife, is likewise purified and liberated while living.
A virtuous wife, having risen in the morning and discarded her night-garment,
bows to her husband and joyfully offers him praise.
Then, having performed her household duties, she bathes and puts on two clean garments.
Having taken white flowers, she should worship her husband with devotion.
Having bathed him with pure water rich with fragrance,
she should joyfully give him clean garments and wash his feet.
Having seated him on a seat, having applied sandalwood paste to his forehead,
having smeared fragrant unguents upon all his limbs, and having placed a garland around his neck, the virtuous woman,
having praised and fully worshipped her husband with ritual offerings, should bow down before him.
Having offered incense, a lamp, water, food, and betel leaf,
she should then joyfully perform the *nīrājana* ceremony for her husband, who is the very essence of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
Having performed circumambulation and prostration, she should then offer hymns of praise.
Salutations to the beloved, the true husband, who is the very form of the parasol for the head;
salutations to the bestower of all happiness and the embodiment of all the gods.
Salutations to the one whose nature is Brahman, who is as if born from the truth of the virtuous woman.
Salutations to You, who are worthy of homage and worship, the support of the heart; salutations to You!
(73) Salutations to You, whose very nature is the life-breath of Satī, the bestower of the glory of good fortune, and the embodiment of supreme bliss for Your consorts! (74)
The Lord is Brahmā, the Lord is Viṣṇu, and the Lord alone is Maheśvara;
the Lord is the deity who sustains the lineage—to You, whose self is Brahman, I offer salutations.
Forgive, O Blessed One, the faults committed through both knowledge and ignorance.
"O Lord who binds His wives, O ocean of mercy, please forgive the faults of Your maidservants.
Then Rādhā spoke to Her daughters regarding their respective husbands:
"If you perform such a hymn of praise, it will surely grant you all your desires."
Then, at the beginning of creation, this meritorious hymn was composed by Padmā;
it was also composed by Sarasvatī, Dhara, Gaṅgā, and Ramā;
and likewise by Sāvitrī, Pārvatī, and the wives of the sages.
Then, having obtained their own respective husbands who grant all powers,
this auspicious hymn of praise by all the devoted wives was revealed as a form of grace by Kaṃbhārā in the Kṛta Yuga.
Thus it was sung by Mahālakṣmī, as well as by Prabhā, Jayā, Māṇikya, Lalitā, and Mohinī in the past.
If a man or a woman should hear this, they shall obtain all their desires.
A childless woman obtains a son, and a penniless woman obtains wealth.
A sick woman shall be freed from illness, and one bereft of a husband shall obtain a husband.
By praising her husband, a devoted wife obtains the fruit of bathing at sacred pilgrimage sites.
A virtuous woman obtains the fruit of all austerities and the fruit of all vows;
by pleasing her husband, she attains both heaven and liberation.
For that man who has no mother in his home and no devoted wife, there is nothing.
She must go to the forest; that indeed is her liberation from hell.
The wicked woman always hates her husband and looks upon him as if he were poison;
she does not give him food and constantly reviles him. (85–86)
Yet that most wicked and arrogant woman, though her husband is worthy of worship and equal to a sage,
constantly treats him with contempt as if he were a blade of grass;
scorched by the fire of his harsh words, she lives on, though she is as good as dead.

Having obtained an unchaste woman as his wife for the duration of his life, such a man is not called a householder; indeed, she is said to lead him to hell. A true housewife, however, is devoted to her husband and is worshipped like a deity by the gods. (88–89)
Having risen early in the morning, that pure woman, having paid homage to her husband and the gods,
should perform auspicious rites in the courtyard with cow dung and water.
Having completed her household duties and bathed, the virtuous woman returns to the house.
Having bowed to her husband, the guru, and the Lord, she should worship the household deity.
After having fed her husband and having honored the guest with sincere devotion,
the virtuous woman herself eats happily together with her sons, grandsons, and others.
A devoted wife should never regard her teacher, father, husband, mother, father-in-law, or mother-in-law as merely human beings.
A father, mother, teacher, wife, disciple, son, and one who is always dependent [upon her]— [these are the ones she must serve].
The sister, the daughter, the mother-in-law, and even the father-in-law— when they are without a protector— these,
as well as the husband and his brothers, must always be served by the wife at the husband’s command.
Indeed, the female species is inherently pure, and all such women are devoted to their husbands.
Indeed, every birth was of a single form, created in the beginning by the Self-Existent One;

all of them are portions of primordial nature (prakṛti), pure and always bestowing happiness. Among them, she who is devoted to her husband and endowed with the duty toward her husband is the most excellent.

The middling wife is devoted to her husband and is also intent on accomplishing her own interests. The lowest wife, though devoted to her husband, is a wife who has resorted to a lover; she is intent solely on sensual pleasure and is attached even to another man. (97–98)
"Among those, three lead to dharma, while the fourth leads to the loss of dharma.
This must always be understood by embodied beings; having known this, one should marry a suitable wife.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, that which was spoken by Rādhā to her daughters has been told to you.

And having heard those teachings on the duties of devotion to one's husband, they were filled with joy. Thus ends the three hundred and seventy-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Observing the Duties and Conduct of Devotion to One’s Husband as Told by Rādhikā to Her Daughters in Goloka," within the section on the Greatness of Devotion to One’s Husband (*pativratāmāhātmya*) in the first book, the *Kṛtayugasantāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā*, Book 1 (*Kṛtayugasantāna*).
