Chapter 378 [Author:
Chapter 379 → Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī! To another tale concerning a house-lizard, which was narrated in the past to nourish the dharma of wifely devotion.
King Rukmāṅgada, who took his pleasure on Mount Raivata, became [the protagonist].
Mounted upon his horse, he beheld the unsurpassed beauty of the mountain.
As the horse moved from one stretch of ground to another, digging into the earth with its own hoof,
it indeed tore the ground apart with its exceedingly sharp hoof.
A certain earth-lizard, which had been buried underground, was being torn apart;
the king, who was devoted to compassion, saw it as it was being split open.
He sprinkled that unconscious creature with cool water.
O Lakṣmī! He regained consciousness from being sprinkled with cool water.
(5) Seeing the king before him, the iguana spoke these words: "O Rukmāṅgada, O mighty-armed one, listen to my actions. (6)
Formerly, in the city of Śākala, I was the wife of a brahmin;
though endowed with beauty and youth, I was not dear to him.
He was always filled with hatred toward me and spoke harsh words.
Then, filled with anger, I went to a certain female ascetic in order to obtain a subjugation mantra that brings all under control. There,
having bowed down and placed my ring at her feet, I spoke.
Having reported this insult to my husband, I remained steadfast.
Then, O King, she said to me for the purpose of the ritual:
"This powder, accompanied by a protective mantra, brings all beings under one's control."
"You must apply this to your husband when he drinks milk and upon his head.
(11) Your husband will become submissive and will never harbor hatred toward you.
Having taken this protective powder, I have come alone to my husband. (12)
At dusk, the protective powder was applied to the head of her husband;
furthermore, at dusk, it was administered to him for drinking along with milk. When that husband had indeed drunk the powder, from that very night on—
Suddenly, as if afflicted by consumption, my husband became emaciated day by day.
With his luster destroyed and utterly weakened, he spoke to me while grieving day and night: "O beautiful one, I am your slave. (14–15)
"Save me, who have come to you for refuge; death is near for me.
Having heard this, I went to the female ascetic and informed her again:
"My husband has fallen under [her] control; how might he live and be happy? (16)
That medicine was given to him once more, and by it my husband became healthy.
Indeed, the burning pain arising from the previous powder was pacified by that medicine.
From that time forward, my husband became submissive and remained obedient to my word.
O King, having died in due course, I went to the torments of hell;
I was indeed burned in a copper cauldron after being repeatedly cut into pieces. After the duration of a Yuga, I was born on earth as one of a sinful caste.
And here there dwell land-lizards of the species of house-lizards.
Therefore, for a thousand years, that woman who seeks to bring her husband under her control—
her dharma being in vain and her conduct in vain— is burned in a copper frying pan.
The husband is her lord, her refuge, her master, her deity, and her guru.
How can she who acts under his control attain happiness?
She enters a hundred animal births, afflicted by worms and leprosy.
Therefore, O protector of the earth, women must always obey the words of their husbands.
Devotion to the husband (*pātivratya*) is the supreme dharma, the auspicious means of salvation for women.
Furthermore, she should never instill rivalry toward her husband in her co-wife.
O King! That wife who behaves wickedly toward her husband’s beloved wife goes to hell for as long as the day of Brahmā.
She who harbors a spirit of rivalry toward the husband’s love and his beloved likewise [goes to hell]. (25)
The fruit of that [misconduct] is obtained in the realm of Yama as the torment of being roasted in a copper frying pan.
A wife should indeed act in such a way that her husband may have happiness;
she should perform what is favorable and beneficial for her beloved husband.
Just as she regards her husband, so indeed should the devoted wife regard him;
even by serving one who is inferior, she goes to the third heaven.
She who performs what is pleasing to her husband attains all enjoyments.

By abandoning the state of envy, one attains the station of the Lord of All. (29) She who, though having a co-wife, always performs service for her husband upon seeing what is pleasing to him, shall attain an imperishable world. (1.378.30)

Listen, O King, to the story of a courtesan named Padminī, devoted solely to the service of her husband, whom I have seen; I shall relate it to you. Formerly, by the side of my house, there lived a Śūdra together with his wife.
The wife of this man named Bhāluka was named Māṭulī;
she was endowed with beauty and youth and devoted to her husband.
Bhāluka, however, had a beloved Śūdra woman, Piṅgalī, who was a courtesan.
The virtuous and devoted wife served a man of Śūdra birth who was extremely wicked and had abandoned all sacred rites; she attended upon him together with a prostitute.
She washed the feet of both and ate the remnants of their food.
She lies beneath both of them, indeed devoted to the welfare of both.
Though restrained by the courtesan, she remains on the path of virtuous conduct.
Thus, while serving her husband along with the courtesan, [she acts].
A very long time passed while she remained devoted to the service of her husband.
Then one day, that foolish husband ate buffalo meat along with radishes, flat beans, and oil.
Because he consumed unwholesome food and disregarded his devoted wife, a terrible disease called *bhagaṃdara* (fistula-in-ano) arose in his anus.
He was excessively tormented by it many times, both day and night. (38–39)
Then the courtesan, having taken his wealth, indeed departed;
devoted to passion, she affectionately gave it to another young man.
Thereupon, the Śūdra, dejected in mind and greatly overcome with shame, [remained].
Weeping, he said to his wife: "Protect me, my beloved!
O beautiful one, O devoted wife, for many years this sinful, wicked man, addicted to courtesans, has not performed even the slightest service for you."
That wicked man who, out of pride, does not consent to his wife’s prostration shall undergo fifteen inauspicious births.
Therefore, I shall obtain a contemptible birth in the house of a *divākīrti*.
"O wife devoted to the service of your husband! This [misfortune] has come upon you because of your own disrespect.
Having heard these words of her husband, the wife said to him:
"Indeed, it is the sins committed in former lives that bring about such sufferings."
The wise man condones them; through patience, there will be an end [to suffering].
Having spoken thus, having comforted him, and having instructed her husband, she brought wealth from Janaka and performed service.
The virtuous wife regarded her husband as the very embodiment of Nārāyaṇa.
Day after day, she diligently performed the cleansing of his hemorrhoids three times daily,
and she also provided him with medicinal oil.
That devoted wife did not sleep either by night or by day;
tormented by her husband’s suffering, she saw the entire world as ablaze.
"If there exists the goddess Earth, and likewise the ancestors and the gods... (49)
"May they make my husband free from disease and cleansed of all sin. I shall offer a bilva fruit and a buffalo to Caṇḍikā, and likewise observe the Navarātra vow for the sake of my husband's health."
I shall indeed perform ten fasts with great devotion;
I will sustain my body upon a bed of fine thorns. I shall not consume sweets, nor shall I consume clarified butter.
"I shall remain for many days without even external ointments;
indeed, while my husband lives, may he be free from disease for a hundred autumns.
Having thus formed this resolve, she served him with the thought that he was Kṛṣṇa.
By the power of her devotion to her husband (*pātivratya*),
her husband also became entirely free from disease and a source of daily happiness for his wife.
After a long time had passed, he was subsequently afflicted by a fever arising from the three humors (*tridoṣa*).
Once, however, by the course of time, Antaka (Death) was born from Antikā.
With great effort, she gave Trikaṭu to her husband;
afflicted by the cold and trembling, he bit off his wife’s finger.
The union of their two teeth became very firm;
even though a fragment of her finger remained in his mouth,
the beautiful woman served him with supreme affection, and he indeed gave up his life.
Then, having sold her bangles and purchased a great quantity of wood, she prepared a funeral pyre smeared with clarified butter; placing her husband in its midst, she then descended and,
drawing him toward the fire with her arms and feet, [entered it].
Placing her face against his face, her heart against his heart,
and her hips against his hips,
the auspicious and devoted wife placed herself close to her husband’s body and caused it to be cremated.

Together with her husband, the lady of beautiful limbs suddenly cast off her body in the blazing fire and went to the world of the gods, having purified herself of the accumulation of great sins and other defilements. (62–63)
"Thus, O King, have I personally witnessed the Śūdrāṇikā vow, which bestows heaven and happiness; therefore, one should not hate a wife who is dear to her husband.
A virtuous woman should feed her beloved husband with her own hand."
O King, whatever food a co-wife gives to another co-wife becomes infinite,
and its fruit shall be endless.
She should be known as a devoted wife who always guards her source of birth.
For women, service to their husbands; for sons, service to their fathers;
for Śūdras, service to the world; and for kings, the protection of the world—this is declared to be their devotion to their respective lords, and they should practice such protection.
If the husband of a woman who has many wives becomes miserable,
it is said that for that prosperous yet sinful woman there is a downward path;
that sinful woman goes to the hell named Pūya for the duration of a Yuga.
Then she shall become a muskrat for seven births on the mountain; thereafter a female crow, then a sister-in-law, and then a monitor lizard; through these births as a cow, she becomes purified.
But she who, for the sake of her husband, does not give away the wealth that is in her possession—
Whether her life or her own body, she shall become a worm in excrement.
Released from that worm-birth, she is then born as a *kāṣṭhīlā*.
What was previously told by *Kāṣṭhīlā*—which I have heard—I shall now tell you.
In my youth, however, there was a woodcutter in my village who used to split wood suitable for the hearth in his house. There,
I saw a shaven-headed woman emerging from the wood, having come out from a log.
With a body as soft as fresh butter, she shone like the little finger;
in her face she resembled collyrium, and in girth she was like a finger-measure (aṅgulimānikā).
Seeing her fallen upon the ground, a crow approached to devour her. (74–75)
As soon as he tried to seize it with his beak, I immediately drove the crow away with pebbles and clods of earth. Wounded and struck by the blow from my beak, she was unable to flee.
O King, she was indeed unable [to speak], trembling and deeply fainting.
Then, sprinkled with water by me, she regained her composure and consciousness; thereafter, she recounted her previous birth to me in human speech. (77–78)
For I was the daughter of the omniscient sage named Sumantu;
moreover, I was a highly virtuous wife to the very proud Kauṇḍinya.
Indeed, because of my great affection for my mother, my kinsmen, and my father—
That which was given to me as a dowry by my father, and that which was bestowed by my father-in-law—
ten thousand pieces of gold and many excellent garments—
I then became exceedingly prosperous through the wealth of both my father and my father-in-law.
I was endowed with cows, buffaloes, and other livestock, as well as wealth and grain;
I was beloved by my parents-in-law and esteemed by the people for my virtuous character.
In due course, my most righteous father-in-law met his death.
Taking her deceased husband with her, his mother-in-law entered the fire.
Then, when two months had passed, my husband went to the royal palace for the purpose of completing the sacrificial rites; there he saw courtesans.
From among those women, who were rich in beauty and endowed with youth, he took two— the jewels among courtesans— and kept them in his house.
Through their service, his entire wealth was brought to exhaustion.
When three years had passed, my husband became destitute;
he then entreated me, saying, "Give me wealth for the adornment of my body.
But I did not give that to my afflicted husband at that time. (86–87)
But taking everything with me, I went to my father’s house;
my husband sold and squandered the household goods and other property.
Whatever wealth belonged to my father-in-law was also located here and there [and lost].
All that— his fields, vessels, and belongings— was lost by him. Then, having boarded a ship with his mind intent on wealth,
he traveled far out upon the ocean path by means of the winds.
Driven by the winds, the ship was brought under their control and went to ruin;
others died, but by fate my husband took refuge upon a piece of wood.
By means of auspicious merit, he reached a small island through the wind.
Where indeed there were millions of oceanic gems, he rested for a moment on that shore, overcome by hunger;
having eaten the fruits of ripe trees and drunk water, he became comforted. (92–93)

Exhausted, he slept at night at the foot of a *sāla* tree. Then a terrible *rākṣasa* approached, carrying with him a beautiful maiden—the virtuous Ratnāvalī, the auspicious daughter of the Lord of Kāśī. (94)
The Rākṣasa carried her from the royal palace for his wife to eat. He said to his wife: "A man in human form is indeed staying at the mouth of the cave; bring him here without delay."
Having been addressed thus, she went to the entrance of the cave toward my husband.
She said to my husband: "I have come to make you my husband;
indeed, I shall place a spear in your hand to slay my husband."

If you do not slay the Rākṣasa with this power, that evil-minded one will undoubtedly devour both you and me. That wretched fate which is attained by people through the murder of a Brahmin—[that shall be yours]. (98–99)
"If I speak an untruth, may I indeed go to that same destination," she said.
Having spoken thus, she led the Brahmin toward the Rākṣasa in the cave and said to him,
"Throw this woman, who possesses great power, into [the fire]."
Upon hearing this, she immediately released that spear toward the Rākṣasa.
Having reduced the Rākṣasa to nothing but ashes, it returned to the sky.
Then, delighted, she said to the twice-born man: "O beloved, enjoy pleasures here with me!"
"My beloved was not killed by me at all, but rather liberated from sin;
my husband has been made a Brāhmaṇa, and I have indeed become a Brāhmaṇī.
May he who destroyed my maidenhood not be ruined, nor may my husband be destroyed."
"I shall come with my daughter to where your home is," she said;
having spoken thus, the Rākṣasī took all the wealth from the cave,
assumed the form of a female elephant, and placed my husband upon her back.
He traveled through the path of the sky toward the palace of the King of Kāśī.
From behind the female elephant, the twice-born man descended along with the maiden;
the female elephant became the maiden, a human wife of the twice-born man.
Then Ratnāvalī went to her father’s house and related what had happened:
"Though I was staying on my bed at night in my own city, I was abducted by a Rākṣasa;
yet I have returned alive and unhurt—console yourself for my sake. (107–108)
"And I have remained chaste, O father, protected by this Rākṣasī.
Furthermore, this Brāhmaṇa has been protected; therefore, give me to this Brāhmaṇa.
Since I have shared a single seat with him, he shall be my husband from now on."

Then Sudyumna gave that maiden to the brahmin according to the prescribed rites. Taking his two wives, including the Rākṣasī, the brāhmaṇa departed for the city of Mahodaya, mounted upon an elephant, in an instant.
That husband who was previously abandoned has now returned accompanied by two wives;
he is very prosperous and well-known, and by him I too have been summoned. Having reached my husband’s house again, I am honored by him as his principal wife.
"All my wealth as well as my two wives were surrendered to me.
Indeed, in a very short time, I, unfortunate as I was, died;
and due to my betrayal of my husband, I have fallen into the Yāmya-kuṇḍa and am now upon this tree."

And she who, afflicted by extreme suffering, becomes a wooden post, shall go to the womb of a beast; and she who does not offer her wealth and even her life to her husband, O fair-faced one, shall undergo birth as a bird a thousand times over.
She too will surely reach such a state; of this there is no doubt.
Knowing this, she should constantly protect her husband’s wealth and his life.
The husband is the mother, the father, the wealth, the life, the guru, and the refuge.
When the husband is pleased, Padmeśa certainly becomes pleased.
But she who deceives her husband even with her life or her wealth,
having passed through a hundred births as a worm, is born as a Pulkasī.

That wicked woman who, though asked for sexual union, does not grant it even when wealth is offered as a gift by a proud man, shall certainly be born as a *kāṣṭhīlā* (a wooden post). [She who withholds] wealth, her body, a son, or whatever other property she may possess— (1.378.120).
All would be a humiliation for women without a single husband;
for his sake, one should abandon wealth and even life in every respect.
One might give up wealth, one might give up servants, wives, life, and home. (121)
One should abandon a country, as well as a king; one should abandon heaven, a friend, and a teacher.
(1.22) One should abandon a sacred ford, one should abandon dharma, and one should abandon that which is most dear.
One should abandon yoga, one should abandon charity, one should abandon a vehicle, and one should abandon meritorious deeds. (1.23)
A virtuous woman may abandon austerity, she may abandon knowledge, and likewise she may abandon supernatural powers and even liberation;
yet she must never abandon service to her own husband, for that is superior to all those things. Service to her husband is proclaimed by the Vedas to be the duty of women.
Whatever the husband says, that should be done without hesitation. One should say "white" when it is white; indeed, the service of the husband is truly white.
In his presence, everything—even that which is black—is for the sake of one devoted to her husband.
Then Kāṣṭhīlā told me her entire life story; having fallen into such misery that her life was at its end, she said for the sake of liberation:
"O sister! Take my hand and give me merit right here in this very water!"
"Grant me here the merit that arises from serving my husband for even a single day,
by which I may die from this body and obtain another birth, so that I may again perform service to my husband."
"I shall go to heaven, and after that, I will surely attain liberation through service.
Having been told this, she granted me one day for the service of her husband.
By the very merit previously acquired by me, she died [at that time].

Having obtained a human birth according to her karma at the proper time, she became devoted to the service of her husband and attained the highest good. O King, I am that earth-lizard; I wish to cast off this body.
"O King, listen to what was done by your wife Sandhyāvalī:
the merit arising from serving her husband for even a single day, which bestows happiness.
Indeed, even when the merit is earned by the wife, the husband certainly enjoys its fruit in every respect. (133)
"What you have given shall be as if given by your wife.
Thus addressed, he who was named Rukmāṅgada then gave his merit;
having abandoned his body as a lizard, he then went to a radiant state.

Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have told you how a woman attains merit through the act of serving her husband, as well as liberation and deliverance. By reading or hearing this, the fruit of serving one's husband shall be obtained.

The sin committed through treachery toward one's husband is surely destroyed; of this there is no doubt. A sinful woman who serves her husband for even a single day rescues herself; how much more so if she does so for her entire life—what will she not bestow?
Whether her husband is devoted to courtesans, addicted to vice, or has gone astray, the husband alone is the wife’s husband; no other may serve as his substitute.
A substitute may be found for other matters, but there can be no substitute in sexual union.
Men look upon the various limbs of other women;
however, that part of the womb which is unfit to be seen must not be looked upon by anyone other than her husband.
Whether he be intoxicated, aged, a beast, or even a demon— [he alone may see it]. (1.378.140–141)
Whether he be a Daitya, untouchable, a Cāṇḍāla, filthy,
filled with pus, foul-smelling, smeared with excrement, diseased, or swarming with worms— whatever his state may be, he who witnesses the womb is himself exactly like that.
O Emperor, there is indeed no other deity who is suitable for the womb according to the law of dharma.
According to dharma, he enters the form of the womb as a latent essence; having become latent in the form of the elements, he is born as the self of a son. (143–144)
He protects in the form of a husband, he will protect in the form of a son,
and he is indeed considered the protector in the next world;
whatever a woman has performed for his sake, all of that brings about her liberation.
Knowing this always, O Lakṣmī, one should practice devotion to one’s husband.
Just as Hari, when worshipped by his devotees, himself delivers those devotees,
so too the husband, when worshipped by his wife, himself delivers that wife.
Whether they are filthy, insane, diseased, or filled with pus;
whether they are foul-smelling, misshapen, like wolves, dull-witted, or infested with insects;
or whether they are addicted to liquor and meat, foul-spoken, wicked, and full of impurities— (148)
Whether she be a Rākṣasī or a Piśācikā,
a Bhūtī, a Pretī, a Vetālī, a Ḍākinī, or even a Kālikā—
in her very wife, the husband indeed desires to take his pleasure within the home.
Where there is fearlessness and delight, that indeed is the eternal Dharma;
where there is fear and delight, that is proclaimed as Adharma. Fearless and delightful, it delivers both the enjoyer and the enjoyed from fear.
"Then there is the vow of the wife (*patnīvrata*), which is the ever-exalting devotion to the husband (*pātivratya*).

(152) Thus, in the first book of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, within the section on the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga and the majesty of devoted wives (*pativratā-māhātmya*), [is contained] the subjugation of her husband by Queen Rukmāṅgada through a domestic cow; the account of Bhālukī, Māṭulī, and Piṅgalī; the account of Kauṇḍinya’s wife Kāṣṭhīlā, daughter of Sumantu; and the account of the daughter of the King of Kāśī. [It describes] how these women attained liberation by the gift of the merit earned from a single day of serving their husbands, as well as the special qualities of devoted wives toward their husbands, and so forth.
The three hundred and seventy-eighth chapter,
titled "Description," [from] the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Book 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Age),
Chapter 379.
[The Author: Chapter 380.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī! I shall relate what Menā said to Pārvatī.

Having performed the marriage with Pārvatī according to the auspicious duties devoted to devotion to one’s husband— which bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation— Menā, the beloved wife of Himavat,
instructed her daughter in the supreme dharmas and had her rest.
O Girijā! Listen with great affection to these words that increase righteousness, which bring joy both here and hereafter, and bestow happiness upon those who hear them.
Blessed is the devoted wife, like you, who is dear to Śaṅkara.
She is the purifier of all beloved women and the destroyer of all sins.
(4) That virtuous woman who serves her husband Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa with love enjoys all pleasures here in this world and, at the end of her husband’s life, attains the supreme goal. (9)
Through the dharma of devotion to her husband, a wife attains great honor;
she becomes worthy of reverence by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara, and is even honored by sages.
You must always serve your husband, Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world.
A woman devoted to her husband should eat only after her beloved husband has eaten;
she should remain where he remains when he is at ease;
she should sleep only when he sleeps; and she should always be the first to wake.
A virtuous woman, whose conduct is free from deceit, should always act for his benefit and speak kindly.
She should never appear before him without ornaments.
When he has gone abroad on business, she should remain devoid of all adornment.
A devoted wife should never utter her husband's name here [in this world].
Even when reviled, she should not revile him; even when struck, she should remain gracious.
When called, she should set aside her household duties and go to his side.
Then, being beloved, she should perform her duties both mentally and physically as directed.
She should not remain for long at the door of another's house, nor should she wander about.
She should not disclose the secrets of the household to others, nor should she entrust them to them.
She should provide all articles for worship even if they have not been specifically mentioned.
She should never go anywhere on a pilgrimage or other journey without her husband’s permission.
Desiring to visit sacred sites, a virtuous wife should drink the water used for washing her husband’s feet.
In the water used for her husband’s feet, she sees all sacred pilgrimage sites and holy fields;
she should enjoy the favor of her husband, as well as sweet food, water, and the like.
She must never eat without first sharing with the gods, guests, and ancestors.
Among the circle of attendants, the cattle, and the community of mendicants,
she should be well-prepared with her utensils, joyful, and averse to excessive expenditure;
by her husband’s command, she should observe vows and be devoted solely to her husband.
She should never rouse her husband from his seat when he is sitting comfortably and at ease.
She should not revile him even if he is miserable, impotent, diseased, or old.
During the three nights of her menstrual period, she must not show her own face to him.
Having bathed well, she should look upon the face of her husband and never that of another man. When her husband is not present, she should look at the sun while remembering him.
[She should apply] turmeric, saffron, a dot [of sandalwood paste], vermilion, collyrium, and so forth.
Betel, the auspicious thread, ornaments for adornment, hair-dressing materials, the braided coiffure, bracelets, ear-ornaments,
a nose-ornament, a string, and the substances for conjugal prosperity. (21)
A virtuous woman who desires long life for her husband should never distance herself from him.
A devoted wife must never even converse with those who are hostile toward her husband. Wherever her husband finds pleasure, there she should find love and delight.
When her husband is joyful, she is joyful; when his face is dejected, her face is dejected; when he is dear to her, she is dear to him.
In both adversity and prosperity, a virtuous wife remains of one mind with her husband.
Even in times of hardship, such as the depletion of ghee, salt, oil, and other provisions, she should not cause distress.

In every way—whether from Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Hara, or even Nārāyaṇa—the husband alone is the supreme lord for Satī, being the very embodiment of the Supreme Brahman. Without her husband’s permission, she should not perform fasts, vows, or other such observances. (25–26)
If she gives a reply in anger when spoken to, she becomes a *saramā* (a female dog);
if she is contemptuous, she becomes a *śṛgālī* (a female jackal); and if she is insolent, she becomes a *vānarī* (a female monkey). She should not occupy a high seat, nor should she be full of pride.
She should not cause slander, quarrel, or reproach toward her beloved. In the presence of elders, a virtuous woman should neither speak loudly nor laugh.
Seeing that her husband is returning from outside, the virtuous woman should hasten [to meet him].
She should fully please her husband with water, food, fruit, betel, massaging his feet, and other such services, as well as with pleasant words that dispel his fatigue.
A father gives but a limited amount; a mother, a brother, and a son give only a limited amount.
She should always please her husband, who is the giver of the immeasurable.
(3.1) The husband is a god, the husband is dharma, the husband is the sacred ford, and the husband is the guru;
he bestows happiness both in this world and the next—she should serve that husband at all times. (3.2)
Without her husband, the *tūlūkī* becomes a secret wanderer among the trees;
she who strikes her husband becomes a tigress and a female gadfly.
She who gives poison to the eyes of men becomes a squint-eyed *miñjarī*.
But she who abandons her husband for sweets and such things becomes a sow or a bitch.
She who speaks ill of her husband is mute or has a small tongue; she will be filled with hatred for her co-wife, unfortunate, and secretly afflicted by disease. (34–35)
She who shows her own face to another man with lustful intent shall become one-eyed,
humpbacked, deformed, and foul-faced.
Even a woman of beautiful complexion who is without a husband is considered equal to a corpse.
Blessed is the mother, blessed is the father, and blessed are the relatives and kinsmen;
blessed is the village, the district, and the country where a devoted wife dwells.
Three generations on the father’s side, three on the mother’s side, and three on the husband’s side [are purified].
By the abundant merits of devoted wives, they indeed become gods in heaven;
the earth where the footsteps of a devoted wife have been set is called Vaikuṇṭha.
Through her purity, the footprint of a virtuous wife becomes the moon, the sun, fire, and wind.
In the same way, one who merely touches water becomes pure; likewise, a sacred ford (tīrtha) becomes purifying.
A wife is the root of the householder’s life, the root of bliss, the bestower of progeny, the root of merit in all the worlds, the giver of victory, and she is indeed the home itself.
O virtuous lady, you are like the Gaṅgā, purifying and ever pleasing to your husband;
you are the goddess who destroys the sins of those who remember you and bestows the supreme goal upon them.
O Satī, such wifely devotion is difficult to attain, arising from one's very nature and bringing forth glory.
Having attained the state of a virtuous wife, she should not destroy that true dharma through negligence.
A faithful woman should always protect her chastity even when facing calamities. She who has attained the status of a faithful wife through merit does not disregard it out of atheism.
But that woman who has fallen from righteousness falls into the state of a wanton woman;
whereas she who is devoted to her own duty, truthful, and has conquered her senses,
attains the vast heaven that is difficult even for the gods to reach.

Therefore, with every effort, a virtuous woman devoted to her own duty should protect her chastity (*pātivratya*), for it is indeed the cause of all human goals. She who acts for the sake of cows, for the sake of a Brahmin, or for the sake of her master [is truly virtuous]. (46–47)
She attains her own liberation, earned through service to her husband.
Listen, O virtuous daughter! Hear that which was spoken by Pañcacūḍā.
In ancient times, Nārada questioned the Apsaras named Pañcacūḍā.
"I wish to hear from you about the nature of women; speak of this to me.
Thereupon Pañcacūḍā spoke to Nārada, the best of sages:
"The description of the nature of women turns into a matter of censure. (1.379.50)
"O Sage! Tell me, how can one woman criticize another?
You know women as they truly are and what their nature is by its very essence.
O divine sage, you ought not to direct me with such a question."
"Nevertheless, at your command, I shall speak the truth exactly as it is.
O Nārada, let the fault committed by my speech be attributed to you.
"So be it," the sage agreed; then the best of apsarases spoke.
Women of noble birth, who possess protectors and are endowed with beauty, do not abide by the bounds of propriety; indeed, fickleness is the blemish among women.
Through this fickleness, they lose their own dharma—chastity—which bestows a [higher] destination.
They do not strive to protect themselves, and therefore they go to a low rebirth.
O Lord, this is the unrighteous nature of us women:
that we abandon shame and consort with even the most wicked of men. (55–56)
Women desire that very man who seeks them out, approaches them closely, and even performs a slight service for them.
This is because men do not seek them out and because they fear their husbands.
Women, who are themselves beyond restraint, abide by the restraints of their husbands. There is no one they do not despise, nor is there any certainty regarding their age;
whether he be handsome or ugly, they enjoy the company of a man.
"Neither out of fear, nor from reproach, nor for the sake of wealth in any way,
nor because of their connection to a family of wise men, do women remain faithful to their husbands," thus spoke Pañcacūḍā, the foremost of the Apsarases, regarding the inherent nature of women.

Having thoroughly crushed those inherent tendencies and having restrained the mind with effort, one should recognize the Lord as the supreme Master and apply one's mental restlessness toward Him. One should know the Lord alone as the Supreme Brahman and the Lord alone as the vessel [of all]. (61–62)
Having understood that [the recipient] is the supreme vessel for service, as well as a vessel for merit, a vessel for dharma, and likewise a vessel for liberation;
a vessel for the entire other world, and likewise a vessel for heaven. (63)
He is a vessel for virtuous qualities and a vessel for supreme bliss;
he is a vessel for the glory of his lineage and likewise a vessel for moral restraint;
he is a vessel for the pacification of fickleness and, furthermore, a supreme vessel for righteousness.
It is the vessel for the pacification of desires, as well as the receptacle of modesty;
it is the cleansing of mental peace and the means for the non-arising of misfortune.
It is the seed-vessel for the lineage’s origin and the vessel for heaven, liberation, and so forth.
A devoted wife should indeed worship her husband as the divine one in the form of Hari.
On one side are the Ender, the Pacifier, Death, the netherworld, the submarine fire, the razor’s edge, poison, the serpent, and fire; on the other side is woman.
Therefore, having completely dissolved these innate qualities whose nature is beginningless and so forth,
a virtuous wife must conduct herself in every way toward her husband;
for that woman who, knowing her husband to be eternally Hari, constantly worships him, is truly devoted to her husband.
"The worship of Śrī Hari does not exceed the worship of one's husband.
Knowing this always, my daughter, serve your husband according to dharma;
through your husband's grace, you will attain worldly enjoyment, liberation, and whatever you desire.

"Thus, O Lakṣmī! These duties of wifely devotion (*pātivratya-dharma*) were indeed spoken by Menakā to Pārvatī, and they have been recounted by me to you here in this context. (72) Thus ends the three hundred and seventy-ninth chapter, titled "The Conclusion of the Duties of Wifely Devotion," etc., within the first section, *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, concerning the greatness of devoted wives (*pativratā-māhātmya*), wherein the duties of wifely devotion as spoken by Menakā to Pārvatī and the natural dispositions of women as spoken by Pañcacūḍā to Nārada are demonstrated. (379)

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, Lakṣmī! There was a wild doe devoted to her husband who became the wife of a beast-like Ṛṣi at Puṣkara. (1)
Just as that devoted wife behaved while in a human body,
even so did she conduct herself with devotion to her husband while in the body of a deer. From the day the doe, driven by the law of desire, embraced the deer, [she remained faithful].

From that very day, having accepted a certain beautiful and auspicious deer as her husband and relying upon him, she lived as a devoted wife. She did not think of any other deer, nor did she look at any other with affection.
She never touches another nor delights in another;
having been born again as a doe within a herd of deer, she is now in her season.
Then, the powerful deer pounce after that female deer.
But she, having abandoned her husband, did not desire union with any other.
Then, having been driven out from the herd by other enraged deer, she nevertheless took her husband-deer and left the deer-herd behind. (6–7)
For the sake of protecting the Dharma alone, she came to a forest region devoid of wild animals,
to a place on the middle Puṣkara tīrtha that was grassy and free from fear.
There, she constantly served her husband with devoted attentions.
With the tips of her horns, she truly dispels her master’s itching out of affection;
likewise, licking her beloved with her tongue and full of love, she delights that deer by touching him with her mouth and other parts. (1.380.10)
At places where there are thickets of trees, clusters of blossoms, and grassy grounds,
and where there is coolness— neither rain nor the heat of the sun—
is found; there, having reached the base of a tree, its middle, or the interior of a thicket, [one should remain].
Having spent the night together with her beloved,
that doe, while her lover was still awake, first abandoned sleep and, gazing steadily at her beloved’s face, began to lick it gently with her tongue. (1.2–1.3)
But the deer, having attained wakefulness and seeing his devoted wife,
would then scratch his beloved with his horn and his tongue.
In this way, they were both possessed of mutual vows toward their wife and their husband.
Having abandoned her bed on the ground, she came outside to the open space.
(15) As long as her beloved does not take even a blade of grass or a tender leaf, so long does the doe not consume a leaf, grass, or even a sprout. (16)
If a leaf is given by her beloved in the morning, then even the female deer accepts only that leaf,
and not any other grass or sprout.
If her beloved takes up a blade of grass, then that female deer follows suit.
There, he eats only the grass produced from the husband's favor (18).
He does not take what is unfit for his master to eat, even if it is succulent or excellent. And while he is eating grass and such, if he obtains something fresh (19), [he still eats only the former].
Whether it be sweet, excellent, or soft food, or leaves, flowers, fruits, grass,
sprouts, bulbs, roots, crops, branches, or the like— if she finds such things,
she calls her beloved husband and gives them to him.
Even when drinking water, the deer surely drinks first;
immediately after that, the doe indeed performs the act of drinking. When he moves, she always follows; when he stands still, she remains standing.
But when he flees, she follows after him in flight;
whether threatened or struck, she takes no account of her own pain.
If it were a deer, it would surely remain with joy in the heat of the sun's rays.

As long as she perceives her husband as the Dharma, she remains steadfast in her devotion; thus, when her husband has gone into the shade, she follows after that shade. Always intent on serving her beloved, the virtuous woman considers this to be her own welfare. (24–25)
While they were living thus in the forest, a drought occurred there as well; because of that, the crops did not sprout for lack of water.
The land became parched, and the food supply was exhausted.
Searching here and there for a dry twig, a stalk, or a leaf, they might find something in one place, yet in another they find nothing at all; thus, when night falls,
those two who follow their own dharma pass the time, hungry, from forest to forest.
Then, that herd of deer, which had previously been abandoned and was now wandering through the forest filled with nectar, arrived at the place where that devoted wife resided.
Seeing that family group indeed suffering and hungry, she—

Rejoicing there at the memory of her husband, and repeatedly bowing to the elders, she said: "If I am indeed a devoted wife (*pativratā*), then let this forest of mine serve for the sake of honoring these guests with food."
Even without rain, let this grassy meadow for a moment be lush, adorned with fresh sprouts,
fruitful, and graced by the beauty of excellent crops;
let it be covered in greenery and filled with water.
When this had been said, that forest indeed became entirely green;
it was filled with an abundance of edible foods and was refreshing.
Then all the members of the family, having eaten and drunk water, departed.
Singing of the greatness of the devoted wife, which brings about prosperity,
they related that wonderful news everywhere.
Then, deer afflicted by hunger arrived from within the forests.

This devoted wife, having bowed repeatedly to her husband, constantly made a formal resolve for the sake of feeding guests; and for a mere moment every day, even what was dry would become moist. (36–37)
Then the deer ate the green grass as their food;
having satisfied themselves, they departed for other regions, and the forest became dry once again.
Then, on one occasion, a forest fire broke out there in that forest.
Resembling a fire of frost and causing the destruction of beasts and birds,
she was then remembered by everyone for the sake of extinguishing that fire.
Having touched her husband’s razor and bowed to him, the doe spoke to her lord.
"O Lord, if service has always been rendered to you by me with devotion,
then by that merit, let this destructive forest fire be pacified.
When he had thus resolved, the fire became a black antelope.
He arrived at the place where that deer was, she who was devoted to her husband;
he bowed to that virtuous woman and said: "O Goddess, I am pacified by your fear;
henceforth I shall not set the forest ablaze, so let the deer roam in happiness."
"I am afraid of Satī’s curse; forgive me, O devoted wife!
Having spoken thus and bowed to Satī, the forest fire was extinguished.
Then the lions, tigers, bears, and whatever other predatory beasts there were—
They too, having learned that the animals had gone there, arrived at that forest.
The predators began to slaughter the animals, and a cry of distress arose in the forest.
Then the animals, gathering together in fear, also came to that place.
When the devoted deer-maiden was present there at Puṣkara on earth,
she then prayed for Śiva for the sake of destroying their great suffering.
Thereupon, Mahādeva, the Lord of the Deer, appeared there in person.
She said to him, "O Lord Hara! Always protect us in the forest.
Cruel beasts devour our devotees; you ought to save us.
Then Mahādeva assumed the form of a fierce śarabha.
He roamed through the forest in every direction to put the predators to flight;
the cruel and violent beasts fled far from that forest.
Then, Parśurāma beheld that divine Śarabha.
While the son of Jamadagni remained at Puṣkara to perform austerities,
as he was about to strike with an arrow after taking up his bow,
Śaṅkara himself appeared as a Śarabha and spoke these words to the god.
"O Rāma, O highly fortunate one! I am the protector of my devotees;
I have indeed arrived here through the resolve of the devoted Mṛgī.
I am Śaṅkara in the form of a hymn; do not exert yourself in vain."
Having spoken thus, Hara revealed to him his own form.
The two gods, Rāma and Hara, embraced one another.
[Hara] showed Śambhu the bliss-bestowing bank of the celestial river, a place for ascetics.
Then Rāma vanished; he went there to obtain the fruit [of his penance].
He composed a hymn to Kṛṣṇa, and by it Hari became pleased.
Keśava appeared before the sight of that son of Jamadagni.
He indeed gave him weapons and missiles for the destruction of the host of Kṣatriyas. Then Kṛṣṇa vanished, and Rāma also returned toward Puṣkara.
Having arrived there for the purpose of bathing and other rites, he saw a virtuous doe.
By whose power that forest repeatedly becomes green;
by whose majesty the forest fire there was extinguished;
and by whose power Hara indeed assumed the form of a Śarabha.

Seeing that divine and virtuous doe, he was struck with wonder. Recognizing Rāma as an expansion of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa through her divine and noble intellect, the doe bowed to him, offered praise, and performed the rites of hospitality for a guest.
The deer also bowed to that Paraśurāma with affection; at that moment,
a hunter devoted to the chase arrived there,
parched by the heat, thirsty, and eager to drink water.

While Rāma was looking on, a deer and a doe arrived at the shore of that lake. As they were drinking the water, filled with fear, a hunter saw the deer and the doe and took up his bow for the sake of hunting. (63–64)
But upon seeing Paraśurāma, he stood with his arrow cast aside;
apprehensive and terrified of Rāma, he then reflected:
"Having drunk water, the deer and the doe have taken refuge in the shade of a tree."
Seeing Rāma, the doe spoke with a fearless mind:
"O beloved! Let us remain right here as long as that Rāma stays;
in the presence of this hero, the hunter will not strike us."
At that time, when he is seen by the sage, he shall be reduced to ashes. The deer said, "So be it; I know this Rāma to be Bhārgava, [the descendant] of Śiva, Nārada, Śuka, and Māruti."
And the supreme [form] of Ambarīṣa, Bali, and Vibhīṣaṇa;
the supreme [form] of Prahlāda, Rantideva, and Uddhava;
and as the supreme [form] of the gopīs, of Prabhā, and of Pārvatī.
Just as Māṇikyā and Lakṣmī possess devotion toward Kṛṣṇa,
so too does this Rāma practice such devotion while remaining steadfast in austerity.
Indeed, through the sight of this Rāma, knowledge of his true birth has arisen today.
Listen, my beloved! I shall tell you how we two came to the state of being deer.
Long ago, in the Draviḍa country, in an auspicious family of Brāhmaṇas, my father—born of the Kauśika lineage—was named Satrāyaṇa. (72–73)
I was his son, Vedasūri, possessed of great devotion,
intent upon serving my guru, and dedicated to the study of the Vedas.
Once, having bathed at dawn in Kṛtamālā, I went to the mountain.
And having mounted it, a thirsty doe came there. Seeing her intent on drinking water, I quickly approached her out of compassion;
she too was full of trust.
Having come there, she indeed bowed down at my feet;
just then, a most terrifying tiger arrived at that place.
The doe fled in terror, but the tiger seized her.

I exerted great effort for the sake of destroying the tiger and for the sake of saving the life of the doe; nevertheless, she was wounded at that time. Indeed, having assumed the form of a girl approximately fifteen years of age, [she departed]. (78–79)
Having approached me, she fell at my feet;
filled with wonder, I questioned that young maiden:
"O Goddess! Who are you, a girl in the form of a doe, who are like a goddess yourself?"
"Whose daughter are you, and how have you come to this mountain all alone?
The maiden then said to me: "I am the daughter of Parameṣṭhin;
among the goddesses of the Brahma-lakes, I am known by the name Hariṇī."
"I have indeed become worthy of being chosen as a bride; sent here by Brahmā, I have come to marry Sātrāyaṇi, the sage of the Vedas.
I arrived in the form of a doe so that no one else might violate me. (83)
"I am a doe, yet I am intact, free from menses, and a maiden;
I have reached the age suitable for conception—may you take me as your wife.
Having been addressed thus by me there, she was wedded by me through the Gāndharva rite.
Having kindled a fire right there in the forest and offered fruits and other oblations,
the couple performed a circumambulation and donned garlands of flowers; having thus entered into the duties of householders, they were indeed yogins capable of assuming any form at will.
Sometimes they took the form of sages, sometimes the form of deer;
sometimes they were gods, and sometimes birds;
sometimes they were fish in the water, as well as swans and Garuḍas.
Having lived as we pleased again and again in the forest of the mountain, you remained devoted to your husband’s vow and I likewise remained devoted to my wife’s vow; thus,
we two, intent on dharma, remained with deep mutual affection for one another.
Remembering their past births and knowing the three periods of time, they were always devoted to dharma and righteous deeds.
On that mountain there were hundreds of thousands of other deer, male and female;
they acted in such a way that they would not perceive us as being of the nature of deer.
Having become such, we always dwelt together, having joined with them.
Once, due to rain,
we took refuge at the base of a tree trunk and remained in a place free from fear amidst a heap of fallen leaves and branches.

Having separated from that herd of deer out of a desire for the pleasure of sensual indulgence, the night was spent; yet in the morning, the rain did not cease at all. Just then, a certain hungry lion arrived there.
Then, suddenly seized by him, the two deer were wounded; yet,
protected by the doe through the merit of her vow of fasting,
they met their end while still in the form of deer, possessing the memory of their deer-existence.
"Whatever one's mindfulness was before, such shall be one's destiny.
With this contemplation, after the tiger had been killed there, she died and was born as a doe, and I became a deer together with her. (97)
Likewise, you are devoted to your husband and are dear to me as a faithful wife.
Because of us both, Bhārgava Rāma— who is Viṣṇu himself in person—
will depart for the auspicious worlds, having gone to which one does not grieve.
Having said, "Both of them have indeed found refuge in Rāma," they both spoke to Paraśurāma, who had lived for a thousand years:
"O Rāma, Rāma! O Hari, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, Teacher of the World! (1.380.100).
"Remembering their past births, the deer and the doe were devoted to their respective duties;
they have come to you for refuge for the sake of liberation—release them from bondage.
Having spoken thus to Paraśurāma, the deer and the doe offered him praise.
As soon as his feet were touched, a celestial vehicle arrived.
Then, followed by four wonderful, perfected beings who could assume any form at will and move with the speed of thought,
the man and woman leaped up like deer.
Having bowed at the feet of Rāma, they joyfully ascended [his chariot],
assuming divine bodies marked with the conch, discus, and other signs;
they then departed for the realm of Viṣṇu, which is saluted by all the gods.

"O Lakṣmī! For those who hear or read this, there shall be the attainment of liberation. (1.05) Thus ends the first section, the *Kṛtayugasantāna*, in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, concerning the greatness of the devoted wife (*pativratā*): the marriage of Brahmā’s daughter Hariṇī with Vedasūri; her maintenance of the vow of devotion to her husband while in the bodies of a doe and a deer; the greening of the forest even without rain; the quelling of the forest fire; the arrival of Śiva in the form of a *śarabha* to destroy predatory beasts; the appearance of Paraśurāma; and the recounting of the previous events at Puṣkara.
The three hundred and eightieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Liberation of the Two Deer," etc., [Chapter 380].
*Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga).
Chapter 381.
[Author: Chapter 382.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī, to another story devoted to the virtue of devotion to one's husband.
Reṇukā was the wife of Jamadagni, devoted to her husband;
she, taking her deceased husband with her, entered the fire of the funeral pyre.
Her son was Paraśurāma, who remained established in ascetic penance in the forest.
On the bank of the Narmadā, not far from Māhiṣmatī,
there was an excellent hermitage belonging to Jamadagni, filled with trees. There resided Jamadagni, the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu), Paraśurāma, and Reṇukā.
These were the principal ones, as well as other disciples and sons by the thousands. Reṇukā, however, served her husband with devotion;
being a virtuous woman honored by the gods, she followed the dharma of fidelity to her husband.
Listen, Lakṣmī, to her story in detail, which bestows liberation!
For the sake of obtaining a son, Reṇukā performed severe penance;
during the cold season, that virtuous woman served her husband day and night.
In the morning, she indeed performs the worship of Kṛṣṇa with a wet garment;
she observes the vow of eating only once a day and performs the worship of the Sun.
She also performs the worship of Fire, of guests, and of cows.
For one year she subsisted on fruits; for a year she lived on leaves;
for a year she lived on water; for a year the virtuous lady subsisted on air.
For a year she subsisted on vapors; for a year the virtuous lady remained without food.
She chanted the name Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa incessantly,
and indeed, she served her husband with a second form.
Thus, the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa became pleased with her.
He went directly into her presence and said, "Choose a boon.
Satī replied, "May you yourself become my son here in this house as my protector.
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa said, "So be it," and vanished.
Then, in the course of time, Rāma appeared bearing an axe made of wood;
he became renowned in the forests by the name Paraśurāma.
Once, having bowed to his parents, he went to the house of his grandfather.
Having bowed to his grandfather Ṛcīka, he took a seat;
devoted to his service, he dwelt there for several months.
Then he went to the renowned Bhṛgu and, full of humility, paid him homage.
Bhṛgu spoke for the benefit of the worlds to the infallible Rāma:
"Go, my son, at my command to the Himavat to perform penance;
Śaṅkara, being entirely pleased, will bring about your welfare. (16–17)
Having bowed to those two, Rāma then went to the Himalayan mountain;
having constructed a leaf-hut on the shore of a lake, he performed austerities.
When many years had passed, Śiva, assuming the form of a hunter, [appeared].
Pleased by his asceticism, he went to him and said to the ascetic:
"Bathe in all the sacred fords and perform severe penance.
By that merit, O Rāma, you shall obtain all the divine weapons."
Having spoken thus, Śambhu vanished; Rāma proceeded to various sacred fords (tīrthas) and went to Kailāsa, where Hara gave him the Śaiva weapon.
Having given him the axe (paraśu), he said: "Always slay the enemies of the gods."
Having slain many demons, Rāma returned to his own hermitage.
Śambhu arrived there and bestowed upon him all the divine weapons in their entirety—
the fourfold collection of missiles, complete with the methods for both their employment and withdrawal.
Śaṅkara gave to Rāma an excellent chariot that was free from agitation, drawn by white horses, and adorned with a beautiful banner; he also gave him two quivers containing inexhaustible arrows,
as well as a divine bow that was impenetrable, undecaying, possessed of a firm string, and victorious.
He gave to Bhārgava a wonderful and highly valuable armor capable of withstanding all weapons, as well as the fierce power of his asceticism;
and then, in the forest, [he saw] the son of a brahmin who had been killed by a tiger.
This Rāma restored him to life; having made the son of the sage Śānta his disciple—though he had not yet performed the ritual prostration—Rāma departed for home.
He prostrated himself like a staff upon the ground before Jamadagni and Reṇukā.

Then, after some time, the Haihaya king arrived there at the hermitage on the bank of the Narmadā, accompanied by his fourfold army. Upon seeing Jamadagni, the king approached and bowed his head in salutation.
Jamadagni then caused that hospitality to be performed by means of the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu);
she produced cities, groves, gardens, palaces,
female attendants, male servants, cattle, all necessary provisions, and foods and drinks.
Reṇukā also spoke again to the milch-cow Kāmadhenu:
"This King Kārtavīrya is my guest and your guest as well;
therefore, O sister, manifest all your divine power for me."
Thus addressed, the wish-fulfilling cow said, "O Sovereign Lady, form a resolve!
By the power of your devotion to your husband, I shall bring you the riches of Vairāja.
Then, by the power of those two, a city of gold appeared in that forest.
At that time, the residence of Bhaguvaṃśin was equal to the palace of the king of the gods;
it possessed inconceivable forms through various divine manifestations, with paths radiant with gold and jewels, and was like a quadrangle of gardens. (34–35)
It was adorned with clusters of sand on the waves of its royal highways and other thoroughfares;
it was graced by palaces whose peaks shone like the full moon;
and it was resplendent with mansions made of gold, silver, brass, copper, and mercury.
[The city] was adorned with rows of jewels interspersed with crystals and precious stones;
it was endowed with the unimpaired radiance of great jewel-lamps, and possessed excellent houses with staircases and altars made of gold resplendent with gems. (37–38)
With walls and other structures richly adorned with garlands of jewels, with doors, bolts, and gate-towers; with thresholds and courtyards covered by golden carpets;
provided with night-quarters and beautified by quadrangles and archways.
With divine pillars, variegated walls, golden lion-thrones and the like,
with seats, foods and edibles, with endless vessels and drinks, with an abundance of food fit for the gods, and with charming young women— [the palace was] enchanting. (1.381.40–41)
It was adorned with fortresses of gold and jewels, seven-storied storehouses,
and divine moats beautified by water-channels;
it was equipped with lightning-lamps, long-range machines, and mirrors visible from afar.
It was equipped with vehicles capable of traveling through the air and hearing from afar;
it was adorned with oblong ponds, square pools, and bathing tanks; and it was graced by various spectacles and theatrical performances that dispelled all fatigue.
It was graced by wrestlers with great exertion, by entertainers and dancers,
by singers and music halls, and by royal assemblies;
it was provided with armories, implements, and halls for liberation.
It was endowed with bathing halls, service quarters, and celestial palaces that grant all desires;
it was auspiciously filled with swans, garuḍas, peacocks, cranes, cātaka birds, parrots, and indeed with divine voices speaking.
That city was made fragrant with the divine scents of trees, creepers, fruits, and flowers; it was adorned with lakes of milk and sugarcane juice,
and nectar was prepared there in every house and in the ponds.
Reṇukā gave birth to a daughter who was adorned with water-vehicles and fire-vehicles;
she was a maiden worthy of a bridegroom, distinguished by various costumes, ornaments, flowers, perfumes, garments, and the like. (49–50)

Endowed with the qualities of beauty and the like, through gestures such as the grace of amorous passion (*śṛṅgāra*), splendor, majesty, loveliness, and the various emotional states (*bhāva*); and by means of fickleness, brilliance, purity, slight smiles, and attractiveness; they possess gentle smiles and beautiful countenances. (51)
Adorned with rows of teeth resembling jasmine buds (kundakalikā), they were radiant;
endowed with the fullness of fresh youth, they were auspicious and possessed charming, sweet voices.
Their eyes were languid with love, adorned by the casting of side-long glances. 52–53.
With hearts serene with joy, possessing the true splendor of the erotic sentiment and passion,
their chests were adorned with rows of pearl necklaces made from the blossoms of the wish-fulfilling tree;
endowed with supreme divinity and great good fortune, they surpassed even the celestial nymphs.
They were graced by forms that were sweet, endowed with delicacy and beauty;
their slender waists were bent by the weight of their full breasts,
and they were bowed by the burden of their hips, possessing red feet and beautiful palms.
Adorned with necklaces, armlets, bracelets, throat-strings, and the like;
resplendent with ornaments for the ears, cheeks, forehead, and so forth;
and graced by decorations for the forearms, fingers, and waist. (57)

Exceedingly beautiful with flower ornaments and adorned with lovely braided hair, they were graced by the tinkling of their waist-bands, small bells, and anklets; they were experts in playful jesting, consoling words, laughter, offering of honorific water, amorous play, and song. 58–59.
Possessing beautiful voices, speaking with sweet honey-like tones, and uttering words that are both pleasant and profound;
they are bold in passion, rich in emotion, and experts in the arts of love. With eyes like lotus petals, they are endowed with abundance and generosity.
And such female attendants were skilled in domestic duties;
furthermore, there were hundreds and thousands of household servants and slaves—
cooks, massagers, foot-massagers, and carriers.
They constructed temples, chariots, horses, elephants, donkeys, camels, and many domestic animals such as cattle,
goats, and sheep; as well as vassals, lords of men, kṣatriyas, and mounted warriors.
[He saw] horsemen and foot soldiers, generals and leaders;
Brahmins and others, chariot-warriors, charioteers, bards and panegyrists;
as well as Magadhas, wandering minstrels, dancers, and actors. (64–65)
Kinnaras of many forms, courtesans, and eunuchs;
ruddy geese, swans, ospreys, cranes, and cuckoos;
and clusters of white water-lilies, lotuses, night-blooming lilies, blue lotuses, jasmine, and kadamba flowers.
Mangoes, priyālas, and jackfruit trees; madhūkas and plantains; nāgas, ketakīs, punnāgas, mandāras, kunda, and campakas;
karavīras and yūthikās—[he gathered] all kinds of fruits and flowers. (67–68)
The wish-fulfilling cow, Reṇukā, was employed to create winds that spread very gently, bearing the fragrances of all seasons.
As for the King, he performed the hospitable reception of the gods and others, which is indeed difficult to obtain.
He entered the holy city, which had been built for his own sake;
a city that was the abode of every enjoyment, adorned with millions of silken garments and brilliant, variegated, woolen cloths, and shining with splendor. (1.381.70–71)
Having entered the city, which possessed such splendor as to delude the inhabitants of heaven, he and his army were struck with amazement; then he understood the cause to be the Earth.
And when the king had been ushered in, women [sprinkled him] with sandalwood waters.
And those situated at the windows showered her with heaps of flowers and parched grain.
Having beheld the splendor of Brāhmī’s asceticism, the king was utterly infatuated;
he praised her with his mind and his speech, and considered her to be a new kind of woman in whom the Kṣatriya power predominated.
Thinking that his own royal splendor was not capable of approaching even a hundredth part of this [river's] beauty,
the king became filled with pride and arrogance;
yet he received honors such as garlands of jewels and diamonds.
Having been ushered in by servants who had created an army with the wish-fulfilling cow (kāmadhenu),
Arjuna slowly passed through three inner courtyards and entered the palace, which was brilliantly radiant with the light of golden lamps.
Honored by maidens with curd, mirrors, perfumes, flowers, durvā grass, unbroken rice, and other offerings,
the king ascended a golden throne. Meanwhile, the matrons purified him with honors and services befitting a monarch.
And together with them, the king spent the day as if in heaven.
In the evening, he entered the assembly hall with his ministers, feudatory chiefs, and leaders;
there, entertainment consisting of music, dance, laughter, and storytelling commenced.
The amorous sports of the courtesans, such as laughter and play, took place;
then, after midnight, he went to the upper palace for the sake of rest.
Indeed, the royal army was present amidst the equal splendors of the king’s form and majesty.
Having attained peace as if in palatial mansions, they became exceedingly joyful.
Like that of a king, there was food, drink, and every object of enjoyment for the royal armies;
all these were provided equally by him, and they said, "We shall dwell right here."
Approaching the king as he slept, the bards, panegyrists,
and eulogists sang aloud with honeyed voices in the morning to awaken him— songs blended with the sounds of lutes and flutes, and perfectly attuned to rhythmic measures and modulations. (84)
Rising with eyes free from sleep, the king performed his daily rites.
Approaching the treasure-house of asceticism who was attended by courtesans, he bowed;
then the sage said, "Has the night passed happily?"
"We are like wild animals, sustained by the forest;
yet kings consider the suffering in the forest to be utterly unbearable.
Thus addressed, the king, free from pride, laughed and spoke to the sage.
My soldiers, their hearts struck by the power and majesty born of your influence, do not wish to depart from here, for they have become abodes of happiness.
O Lord, this is not at all surprising for you, a yogin perfected through asceticism.
"Even for the wish-fulfilling cow, for a devoted wife, and for a woman, heaven is attained right here; what prosperity, then, could there be for a petty king?
O Brahmin, I shall go home; may you grant me leave."
Having been told "So be it" by the sage, he set out for his own city.
He then reflected upon that cow, the most excellent of all wish-fulfilling cows:
"Of what use to me is an entire kingdom, which is like a mere cowrie shell?"
The prosperous realm of Indra is not worth even a sixteenth part of the cow’s power.
By the cow, heaven was established in the forest; by the cow, it was destroyed in an instant.
Such is the power of that cow; she is fit for a kingdom, not for an ascetic.
"Having paid the price for the cows, horses, and so forth, they must be brought by me to the city.
Having thus resolved, King Candragupta dispatched his minister. He said to the sage: "A king indeed is the possessor of jewels on this earth. (94–95)
"Taking these jewels, you ought to give the cow as a jewel to the king.
However, O Sage, this sacrificial cow must not be given to anyone at all.
I am neither a seller nor a buyer; furthermore, I am not under the king's authority."

"But by seizing [the earth] by force, the life of you and that king shall perish. Thus addressed, the minister became enraged; however, having realized the situation, Jamadagni then drew back the earth as much as he could and restrained him.
Commanded by the minister, the servants struck the Sage excessively with whips;
they drove the Rishi far away, yet he endured it, while they forcibly seized the cow.
But she, having ascended into the sky, went on after holding her calf; indeed, they followed her.
The sage died, and at that moment Parśurāma arrived.
Having just returned from the forest, the son heard his mother weeping and the cry of "Rāma! Rāma! coming from ahead; he rushed forward quickly.
Having set down the load of sacrificial fuel and seeing that his father was dead,
he, with tearful eyes, consoled his weeping mother.
At that time, Reṇukā was overcome with grief, fearing she would soon become a widow.
He struck his belly with both hands twenty-one times.
Then Rāma, overcome by emotion, said to his mother:
"Since you have struck this chest of yours twenty-one times," ||| 1.04 ||
"I shall slay as many Kshatriyas as that number; do not grieve.
Then Renuka, devoted to her husband, spoke to her sons:
"O sons, I am a woman devoted to my husband; your father has indeed gone to heaven."
I wish to follow him here by kindling the fire with my own body,
so that I may proceed with him eternally in the next world as well;
I shall become the beloved guest of my husband in the realm of the ancestors.
At that moment, a profoundly deep, disembodied voice spoke there:
"O devoted wife, do not commit this rash act; maintain your fortitude.
O devoted wife, form a resolve for the awakening of your husband."
"Before long, your husband shall regain his senses.
Having been told this, she carried her husband's body into a small hut;
there, the virtuous woman formed a resolve for her husband’s rising and restoration to life.
Just then, the sage Bhṛgu, who is honored by the gods and is an ocean of the science of reviving the dead, arrived there and restored him to life. Jamadagni rose and bowed to that grandfather.

attain peace, may prosperity be yours. Having spoken thus, they vanished.

Thus ends the three hundred and eighty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Destruction of the Kṣatriyas by Paraśurāma through the Power of the Chaste Reṇukā and the Wish-Fulfilling Cow, the Resuscitation of the Deceased Jamadagni, and the Heavenly Abode of Reṇukā and Jamadagni," within the first section on the Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga, concerning the Greatness of Chastity, in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
