Swans, lions, bulls, and peacocks by the millions;
divine horses by the millions, as well as śarabhas, gavayas, and other such creatures;
crores upon crores of couches for Śeṣa and palanquins numbering in the billions.
The infinite attendants of the Lord,
moving about with their wings spread, were eager for the wedding festivities and joined the procession.
There were also the infinite, imperishable, and eternal ones who reside in Goloka.
Innumerable beings residing in Vaikuṇṭha went along with Śrī Kṛṣṇa—
those dwelling in Amṛta, those dwelling in Hiraṇya, those dwelling in Āvṛti, and those established in Virāṭ;
as well as those established in Satya, those beginning with Janaloka, the gods, reptiles, and human beings.
All beings, both stationary and moving, arrived joyfully at the army camp.
"A marriage ceremony for Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa with the daughter of Bhṛgu is taking place;
let us go to witness it, and let all our family members come along. (1.27–28)
Thus, all of them—beginning with the children and ending with the elderly—having been honored and fed, departed with joy; they then gathered together and mingled within the army.
The bridegroom was perfectly adorned, appearing like another Lord of Rādhā.
She was further honored with blessings and presented with unbroken grains of rice, saffron, flower garlands, garments, and ornaments;
with jeweled necklaces, pearls, golden chains, rings, and collyrium;
and with fragrant liquids, powders, and other offerings. (1.382.13–131)
At sixteen years of age, he went for the sake of the marriage with the daughter of Bhṛgu.
That river, flowing from the world of the Imperishable Brahman down toward the realm of Vaikuṇṭha,
became a long stream followed by the followers of the bridegroom’s party.
Delighted by the sounds of dancing, auspicious musical instruments, and vocal chants, she,
numbering in the hundreds of millions, arrived at Śuklatīrtha; and at that time,
auspicious events occurred throughout all the cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas).
In the divine and auspicious Vaikuṇṭha on the banks of the Revā,
spanning ten million leagues in extent and rising a hundred thousand leagues high—
unapproachable by the will of Nārāyaṇa and composed of vast dimensions and height— (135).
By the will of Hari, countless world-systems went there.

The supernatural powers (siddhis) are: atomization (aṇimā), magnification (mahimā), extension (prāpti), efficacy (prākāmya), levitation (laghimā), gravity (garimā), mastery (vaśitā), and the power of fulfilling desires (kāmāvasāyitā).
But where there are [innumerable] Hari-s, what indeed is surprising?
For even countless universes reside within the pores of a single hair;
what indeed is surprising that they exist even in a space the size of an atom?
Thus that excellent army, having assembled at Śuklatīrtha,
rested happily there with joy in its own Vaikuṇṭha-like camp.
Those who dwell in the abode of the Lord bathed, were fed, and slept.
Everywhere auspiciousness arose, and at that time the living beings, full of eagerness, came to Śuklatīrtha, thinking, "This is the wedding of the two lotuses.
Brahmā was accompanied by Sāvitrī, and Bhava himself was with Bhavānī.
Ananta, along with Bhoginī, and Dharma together with Mūrti and the others; Bhāskara with Prabhā, Hutāśana with Svāhā, Kubera with Śrī, and Varuṇa joined by Vāruṇī. (142–143)
Pavana also arrived with Āñjanī, and Yama came together with Dhūmryā;
the Moon was joined by Rohiṇī and others, and the Lord of the Gods (Indra) was accompanied by Śacī;
the Rudras were joined by Rudrāṇī and others, and the Ādityas came along with Saṃjñā.
The Vasus, Gandharvas, Kinnaras, Devas,
and Dānavas also arrived at Śuklatīrtha, thinking, "This is the wedding of the two lotuses.
Having seen that Vaikuṇṭha had indeed been made anew, the gods and others [were amazed].
Having reached the bank of the Narmadā by means of celestial chariots from the sky,
they arrived at a new city near Bhṛgukaccha,
which was resplendent with rows of jewels such as pearls, rubies, and diamonds.
It was square on all sides, measuring one hundred yojanas,
surrounded by seven deep moats,
sixteen lakhs of ramparts, and thirty-three lakes. (148–149)
It was made fragrant everywhere by thousands upon thousands of flower gardens, auspicious on all sides and adorned with lotuses, and by breezes filled with blossoming flowers;
it was also perfumed by cool, gentle sandalwood winds.
It was adorned with tens of millions of trees, including mango trees,
coconut palms, jackfruit trees, pomegranates of nine colors, grapes, betel vines, cardamom, and cloves. (151–152)
With jujube trees, bilva trees, rose-apple trees, and campakas;
with bakulas, tamarinds, citrons, and likewise sugarcane; with dates, oranges, and myrobalans—[it was filled] with such fruit-bearing trees. (153)
It was endowed with various excellent gardens and covered with lush meadows;
it was adorned with countless beautiful and exceedingly lofty mansions,
and it shone with the diverse splendors of those various abodes, each topped with a pinnacle.
It was likewise radiant with divine pillars and clusters of jeweled staircases;
it was adorned with mirrors, fine fabrics, and white chowries;
its courtyards were embellished with rubies and other gems, as well as sapphires. (156)

Upon seeing Vaikuṇṭha-nagara, adorned with crossroads, royal highways, and divine gods and goddesses, they were all filled with wonder. Viṣṇu, Padma, Śrī, Padmā, and her father-in-law Bhṛgu himself [were there]. (157–158)
Where the Blessed One, the son-in-law, is present, what indeed could be lacking?
There are Gandharvas, Kinnaras, Vidyādharīs, Kinnarīs, and Īśikās;
likewise, there are dancers, singers, instrumentalists, and vocalists. (159)
Beggars, astrologers, courtiers, kings, physicians, and servants; actors, wrestlers, men of many forms, and likewise men in disguise—
all full of enthusiasm, they arrived there for the wedding of the two lotuses.
In Bhṛgukaccha as well, renunciants, ascetics,
and lifelong yogis, summoned by Bhṛgu, arrived for the wedding of the two Padmās;
namely, Sanaka, Sananda, Sanat, and Sanātana.
The marriage of the two lotuses took place with three crores of disciples;

Durvāsas came with a hundred thousand disciples, Kaśyapa with a hundred thousand attendants, and Patnīvat with a hundred thousand disciples—the marriage of the two lotuses was thus celebrated. (163–164)
Gautama had ten thousand disciples, Vālmīki had ten thousand disciples, and Śukra had ten million disciples; thus there was no marriage between the two lotuses (the Sun and Moon).
Bhāradvāja had ten thousand disciples, while Bṛhaspati himself had ten million.
Aṅgiras had ten thousand disciples, and his marriage was with two lotuses (166).
Vasiṣṭha had a hundred thousand disciples, as did Pracetas;
Pulastya also had a hundred thousand disciples, and their marriages were likewise with two lotuses (167).
Agastya arrived with a hundred thousand disciples, as did Pulaha accompanied by a hundred thousand disciples; Kratu came with a hundred thousand, and Atri with ten million disciples;
Marīci came with a hundred thousand disciples, and Śatānanda with thousands.
They arrived at the house of Bhṛgu for the wedding of the two lotuses.
Ṛṣyaśṛṅga and Vibhāṇḍaka came with a thousand disciples;
likewise Pāṇini with ten million disciples, and Kātyāyana with ten thousand.

Yājñavalkya [performed] with thousands, Vyāsa with ten million disciples, and Garga, together with his disciples, performed the marriage of two lotuses. Gālava also [performed it] with a thousand, and Saubhari with another thousand.
Koṭi, Lomaśa, and Padmapa also performed their wedding ceremonies.
Sāndīpani, Devala, Mārkaṇḍeya, Pañcaśikha, Gopāla, and Voḍhu were accompanied by hundreds of thousands of disciples. (172–173)
Likewise, I am the self-luminous Lord Nara-Nārāyaṇa;
Viśvāmitra [performed] a marriage with ten million [brides], as did Padmaja.
Jaratkāru [performed it] with a hundred thousand, and Astīka with ten thousand disciples.
Parśurāma’s marriage with a thousand [maidens] at the two lotuses;
Vatsa’s with a hundred, Dakṣa’s with three hundred, and Kapila’s with ten thousand; and Savarta’s marriage with the ten thousand disciples and others at the two lotuses. (175–176)

Utathya with a hundred disciples, and Bhāguri with another hundred, as well as countless others, arrived for the wedding of the two lotuses. [The daughter] Lakṣmī, the beloved of Nārāyaṇa, had been born to Bhrigu by Khyāti.
"We are going to wed Kṛṣṇa; this is the marriage of the two lotus-feet.
Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ, the two gods who are both the sons-in-law of Meru and the brothers of Lakṣmī, indeed paid them great honor. (178–179)
Āyati and Niyati were also the two daughters of Meru, devoted to their husband;
from Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ, Prāṇa was born as their son, and Mṛkaṇḍu was his legitimate offspring.
From Mṛkaṇḍu, Prāṇa begot Mārkaṇḍeya, and Vedaśiras was the son of Mārkaṇḍeya.
From Marīci, Pūrṇamāsa was likewise born as a son;
his four daughters were Tuṣṭi, Vṛṣṭi, Kṛṣṭi, and Apaciti.
Virajas and Parvata were both the sons of Pūrṇamāsa.
Kṣamā was the wife of Pulaha; their sons were Kardama, Varīyān, Sahiṣṇu, and Kanīyān.
Anasūyā was the wife of Atri; their sons were Soma and Dattaka.
Then there was Durvāsas, and the daughter of Aṅgiras named Smṛti;
the Vāsiṣṭhas headed by Śakti; the Vāhneyas, the sons of Kratu;
and likewise the Agniṣvātta, Bārhiṣada, Ājyapa, and Somapa ancestors.
The Vālakhilya sages, the Earth, Meru’s beloved,
the mountains, the rivers, the lakes, and the groves—
thus were the lineages and expansions of the sages present at that great festival.
They arrived at the house of Bhṛgu for the marriage of the two lotuses. [The incarnations are:
Matsya, Kūrma, Varāha, Nṛsiṃha, and likewise Ṛṣabha; Kapila, Vāsudeva, Pṛthu, Datta, and the lord of sages (Nārada). (187–188)
Haṃsa, Hari, Vāmana, Paraśurāma, the Kumāras, Yajña, Rāma, Agravīra, Nārada, the king of kings,
Vyāsa, Kṛṣṇa, Buddha, Kalki, and Nārāyaṇa himself.
Likewise, other disciples who were practitioners of yoga and observers of the *palī* vow arrived;
those from Saurāṣṭra, perfected in yoga, came from Mount Raivata accompanied by their wives,
having come for the marriage of the two lotuses.
Indeed, the Māṇḍavyas on the bride's side numbered more than a hundred million (*koṭy-abjaka*),

while those on the groom's side, belonging to the Vāhinī clan, were even more numerous, beyond counting. On the twelfth day, the honored guests were treated with hospitality through food, drink, and other offerings.
And they rested during the night, delighted by songs, dances, and other such entertainments. (1.93) Various auspicious rites and supreme worldly customs were performed;
for all were joyful at heart and satisfied with great delight. (1.94)

Thus ends the three hundred and eighty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Arrival of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa at the White Tīrtha near Bhṛgukaccha to Have Vaikuṇṭha Constructed for the Purpose of Marriage, Being Satisfied by the Austerities Performed by Lakṣmī, the Daughter of Bhṛgu and Granddaughter of Bhṛgu, within the Section on the Greatness of Chaste Wives in the First Book, the Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga," of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 382. [End of] Book 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga).
Chapter 383.
[The Author: Chapter 384.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, Lakṣmī! Mahālakṣmī was indeed the golden daughter of Bhṛgu.
She possesses the radiant luster of the color of the *campaka* flower, with a divine form.
(1) She is exceedingly beautiful and charming, the most honored among lovely women;
she is endowed with fresh youth and adorned with jewel ornaments. (2)
Rich with the luster of molten gold and adorned by a halo of radiance,
she was the embodiment of pure truth, devoted to her husband, and possessed of the character of truth.
She was peaceful, self-controlled, exceedingly tranquil, and endowed with infinite virtues.
Indrāṇī, Varuṇānī, Candranārī, and Rohiṇī;
the wife of Kubera, the wife of Sūrya, Svāhā, Śāntā, and Kalāvatī;
as well as others such as Ahalyā and the like, and Pārvatī and others, all exceedingly radiant. (4–5)
They do not equal even a sixteenth part of Bhārgavī, the daughter of Bhaga.

Upon seeing her— who was richly adorned with the splendor of the full autumnal moon and possessed eyes like autumnal lotuses— even the celestial women and the wives of the gods were struck with wonder.
Seeing that virtuous young woman, fit for marriage, her face bowed with modesty, all those ladies were bewildered; beholding her form which was a perfect match for her beauty,
they stood transfixed, as if dissolved and made as inert as wood.
"Aha! She by whom Nārāyaṇa himself has been determined as her husband—what indeed could be secondary in her case regarding her virtues, her beauty, or her stature?
No such woman has ever been created by the Lord in his creation."
There is no celestial woman, nor shall there ever be one destined to be such;
this Padmā here is indeed Nārāyaṇī in person, the daughter of Bhṛgu.
She is worthy of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, and he, too, is worthy of her.
Thus they spoke of this supreme wonder, rejoiced, and gazed upon her again and again; for,
having meditated upon that maiden as Lakṣmī herself, the daughter of Bhṛgu, they were satisfied within their own souls and considered him a worthy bridegroom,
endowed with fresh youth.
One who is virtuous in character, true to his word, the sovereign Nārāyaṇa;
a scholar learned in the Vedas and Vedāṅgas, beautiful, auspicious, peaceful, self-controlled, patient by nature, endowed with good qualities, and long-lived. (13–14)
Born from the family of Brahmā and established everywhere,
he is Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the perfect Brahman, the glorious Puruṣottama—
untainted, desireless, and the witness of all actions.
That which the four Vedas do not know, nor the virtuous deities;

which the lords of the Siddhas and the lords of the Munis, as well as the gods beginning with Brahmā, do not know; and which the yogins, purified by meditation, do not perceive while they meditate—[that is this]. (16–17)
Sarasvatī has become dull-witted, as have the Vedas and whatever scriptures exist;
so too Śeṣa with his thousand mouths, Sadāśiva with his five faces, the four-faced Creator of the world, Kumāra, and likewise Kārttikeya. (18)
The sages and seers, as well as the supreme Vaiṣṇava devotees—
even others do not know him as he truly is, nor to what extent, nor his qualities.
Having attained this most excellent one, the fruit of human birth is fulfilled for the descendant of Bhṛgu.
Thousands of streams of clarified butter, tens of thousands of streams of honey,
thousands of streams of curd, and tens of thousands of streams of milk;
likewise, lakes of oil, mountains of molasses, and heaps of sugar.
There were mountains of sweet foods and likewise heaps of flour;
there were mountains of barley and wheat flour, of *pṛthuka* grains, and heaps of side dishes,
all appearing as inexhaustible sources.
"Oh, how great is our good fortune that we behold with such enthusiasm this marriage of the two lotuses, which is worthy of being beheld!
Palaces equal to heaven exist here, and rivers of nectar flow. (24)
There were vehicles and celestial chariots of every kind moving through the sky,
as well as millions of mounts such as swans, eagles, and elephants;
and there were cities on Mount Bhṛgukaccha on all sides of the mountain.
Indeed, Bhṛgu caused new mental temples to be built,
just as Nārāyaṇa has caused a new one to be built in Vaikuṇṭha;
likewise, Bhṛgu constructed a vast and radiant temple on the shore of the ocean.
There, he caused a divine palace of Bhṛgu to be built, one hundred yojanas in width and one hundred thousand yojanas in height;
and there the Ocean himself appeared, bestowing hospitality upon the Goddess Śrī.
Meru and others, as well as various Siddhas and other sages—
those perfected since the beginning of the Kalpa and those from the Kṛta Yuga who bestow honor—
were indeed ascetics equal to Kṛṣṇa on the side of the maiden’s maternal kin.
And the ascetics were equal in splendor to Śrī herself; there was not even the slightest deficiency [in them].
On the thirteenth day, auspicious rites were performed according to the conduct of the learned;
the worldly customs were likewise observed, and [the guests] were honored and fed.
During the night, auspicious songs and dances were performed;
and on the morning of the fourteenth day,
the women conducted worship of the goddesses and deities according to worldly custom.
Those auspicious women, accompanied by their daughters-in-law, performed the worship ceremonies.
On the fourteenth day, having fed Nara and Nārāyaṇa on the ground at night,
they indeed had Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa adorned with beautiful garments.
Having fully worshipped that which is exceedingly beautiful, incomparable, and difficult to find within the three worlds, he caused a most excellent and superior pilgrimage to be performed.
Likewise, Kṛṣṇa and others, as well as Nārāyaṇa and other incarnations [were honored].
Likewise, Vairāja and others who were liberated, as well as those engaged in the creation of Brahmā—Rādhā, Ramā, Prabhā, and the rest; and Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara;
their wives, the lords of the Gaṇas, the sages, and the inhabitants of heaven. (37–38)
All the gods and goddesses went to the pavilion at Bhṛgupati.
There, indeed, were tens of millions and billions of golden lion-thrones.
By him, the Sudharmā assembly hall was constructed on the ocean shore amidst golden sands.
There were hundreds of thousands of female dancers and likewise hundreds of thousands of celestial musicians (gandharvīs).
Kinnarī singers, numbering in the tens of millions, were present there;
all this was created by Bhṛgu for the pleasure of the Blessed Ones.
Neither existing nor yet to be, it was fashioned anew by the power of *siddhi*.
There were a hundred thousand *vidyādharīs* and likewise a hundred thousand *apsarases*.
That divine city of Bhṛgu, Bhrigupattana, was filled with great splendor.
It was even more radiant than the palace of Vairāja;
in its wall-cupola the sun was installed,
and in the very center of its interior the full moon was fixed.
Thus, radiant and eternal pillars were erected along every street;
there, in Bhṛgupattana, light exists without any external cause.
Indeed, the principles (tattvas) themselves, having taken form, were established there for the sake of service.
Cakra entered Bhṛgupattana with a magnificent procession.
On the morning of the full moon, while the sun was visible, he was honored by the people of Bhṛgu. In the meantime, Bṛhaspati arrived before him.
Accompanied by tens of millions of billions of ṛṣis, he came before Hari;
having offered auspicious fruit along with a moon-shaped mark and unbroken grains of rice,
and having placed a garland of flowers around his neck, he showered Hari with blossoms.

At the vicinity of the village gate, the maidens and virtuous women performed the worldly custom of auspiciousness by gazing upon the water-pitcher. And the sages caused the sounds of the Vedas, which bring about prosperity, to be heard. (1.383.50)
Bṛhaspati, reciting Vedic hymns, led him into the city.
Daughters of gods, daughters of nāgas, daughters of kings, and daughters of sages, as well as daughters of seers, arrived with smiles to behold the bridegroom. (51)
All the women gazed with eyes that did not blink at him who was serene,
dark as a rain-cloud, adorned with yellow garments,
his entire body anointed with sandalwood paste, and decorated with forest garlands and other ornaments. (52–53)
Resplendent with jewel-encrusted armlets, bracelets, and necklaces;
adorned with a pair of jeweled earrings that illuminate her cheeks;
and made radiant by the tinkling anklets fashioned from the finest essence of precious gems.
Smiling, He gazes at a jeweled mirror while holding a flute in His hand;
He is served by hundreds of thousands of attendants with white whisks,
endowed with fresh youth, and possessing eyes like autumn lotuses.
His face is like the full moon of autumn; it fills the hearts of Lakṣmī, Nārāyaṇa, and others.
His beauty equals that of ten million Cupids, and he is worshipped by Brahmā, Śeṣa, and Īśvara.
His form is supremely gladdening, with a radiance equal to ten million moons.
To the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, who bears the full weight of desire and vigor,
who holds a blade of dūrvā grass, a silk thread, a mirror made of the essence of the finest gems,
a small knife, and a shimmering cluster of plantain blossoms— [I bow]. (58–59)

Seeing the Supreme Lord, whose crest was shaped like the three strides and adorned with a garland of *mālatī* flowers, and seeing the flower offered by the young woman as a crown shining upon his head, the young maidens fell into a state of delusion.
"Living as a descendant of Bhṛgu is blessed and praiseworthy," they said, expressing their desire.
Khyāti, the beloved wife of Bhṛgu’s son, beheld her son-in-law with eyes and face bright with joy, gazing at him without blinking. (61–62)
Bhṛgu, with a serene countenance, accompanied by the sages and the family priest,
approached Hari-Kṛṣṇa and bowed down to the gods and the brāhmaṇas.
He then offered a resting place extending for a hundred yojanas.

Filled with various foods and drinks, and graced by playful female attendants, he performed the auspicious consecration (*adhivāsana*) of Hari upon the ground with mantras. Having worshipped all the *Mātṛkās* and all the deities in person, [he proceeded]. (64–65)
Having bestowed a stream of wealth as well as the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* and other rites,
he fed everyone and caused them to drink excellent flavors;
he had musical instruments played and had auspicious ceremonies performed.
He caused the wedding preparations to be made for the peerless bridegroom;
he had a beautiful human carriage well-adorned and ready.
Thus did the sage Bhṛgu also prepare for the highly auspicious marriage ceremony.
With his preceptor, the family priest, he had the ritual performed with sacred mantras;
he gave gems and wealth such as pearls, rubies, and diamonds,
as well as foods and garments, bestowing gifts upon those who sought them.
He had musical instruments played and caused auspicious rites to be performed.
He had the daughter of Bhṛgu dressed in beautiful and most enchanting attire,
while the goddesses and the wives of the sages carried out the appropriate ceremonies according to tradition.
Then, when an auspicious moment had arrived, during the supreme exaltation of Indra,
at a wedding-appropriate *lagna* joined with its presiding lord,
purified by the aspect of benefic planets and devoid of the aspect of malefics— (72) —
On an auspicious moment and under an auspicious lunar mansion, when the moon and stars are pure,

free from defects such as planetary piercing (vedha), devoid of [inauspicious] lines on the divination sticks (śalākā) and so forth, and at a time suitable for the welfare of the couple and bestowing the happiness of marriage; ||| 73–74 ||
When this time had arrived, Hari came to the courtyard of the sage Bhṛgu, accompanied by the lords of the gods and others, as well as by sages, brahmins, family priests,
powerful lords, blessed ones, and those devoted to dharma and piety.
With abundance of splendor, along with his attendants, liberated souls, and sages; with divine beings,
both stationary and moving, scholars of the scriptures, dancers, actors, singers, garland-makers, and also Vidyādharīs.
The gods, goddesses, and the consorts of the lords beheld that place, [frequented] by apsarases, kinnarīs, and female practitioners of Sāṃkhya and Yoga.
It was adorned with hundreds of thousands of golden plantain pillars embellished with fine silk cords.
With sprouts of *campaka*, sandalwood, and mango trees;
with various kinds of garlands consisting of yellow, red, and white flowers;
and with auspicious jars placed all around, filled with fruits and sprouts.

It was occupied by lords, sages, brahmins, gods, and ancestors, who were adorned with leaves smeared with musk and sandalwood, shining with saffron, and graced with parched grain, fruits, flowers, and dūrvā grass.
It was enchanting, furnished with an altar fashioned from the finest essence of precious gems;
it was worshipped with offerings of smooth sandalwood, blended with musk and saffron,
and rendered fragrant by breezes that were cool, gentle, and sweet-scented.
It was radiant with millions of jewels and brilliant lamps,
well-perfumed with various kinds of incense and fragrant substances;
it was made beautiful on all sides by the charming and diverse works of artisans.
It was graced by the exquisite songs of the Gandharvas, the beautiful dances of the dancers,
the amorous gestures of the Vidyādharīs, and the melodious singing of the Apsarases;
it was watched with great delight from the windows by the young brides.
With an auspicious water-pot, accompanied by a learned and excellent priest,
Bhrigu, with kusha grass in hand, performed a gift-offering of precious objects;
having seen the gods, headed by Brahma and Ishvara, in the beautiful courtyard of Bhrigu.
Having suddenly beheld Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa, Vairāja, and likewise the Fish-incarnation and all the others, Bhṛgu, accompanied by his family,
bowed his head to the gods, the lords, and the sages, offering them due honor.
Having honored them with great respect, he seated them individually upon most delightful jewel-thrones one after another.
He said, "Today my birth has truly become fruitful; today my life has attained its purpose."
He became the severer of the roots of karma for tens of millions of births.
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa himself, the Lord of the Imperishable,
is the giver who always bestows prosperity, liberation, worldly enjoyment, and heaven.
I was truly unable even to behold his lotus feet in a dream;
yet today, that Creator, the bestower of the fruits of penance, has appeared in my very courtyard.
To those who are self-contented and fulfilled, what desired auspicious inquiry could there be?
That Blessed Lord Śrī Hari—who is unseen even by the lords of yogis, the lords of perfected beings (siddhas), the lords of gods, and the sovereign sages—now stands in my courtyard.
He is the Lord of Time, the Master of the Imperishable, and the Sovereign Lord of all incarnations. || 94-95 ||
Having assumed a human form, you have come within the range of vision of men;
you have arrived at my courtyard to make my daughter’s life fruitful.
You are the Lord who dwells within all beings and the bestower of all desires.
He whose end is not found even in the Vedas— that Hari is today in my courtyard.
He who is the Lord of lords and whose worship is foremost among all—
he Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Goloka, has indeed come into my courtyard today by my good fortune.
He whose beloved wives are indeed the infinite Ramā and others—
Nārāyaṇa, for the sake of taking my daughter, stands today in my courtyard.
So too do the Vairāja gods and others, the Pitṛs, and those who are human beings.
The Bhāgavatas dwelling in Pātāla say, "I am blessed today in my courtyard!
There are millions of the consorts of Kṛṣṇa, as well as those liberated ones who do not return and dwell in the Imperishable, along with all things moving and stationary."

"O Lord, today in my courtyard all the divine hosts of beings are present; I am blessed! Those sons of Brahmā, my great-grandsons, and those born of my lineage who have never been seen before—all of them are here in my house this very day, as is my blessed daughter!"
Oh! Until the end of the eon, my hermitage has become a sacred ford for them.
My home is a purified sacred ford by the water from their feet.
Whatever sacred fords exist on earth, they are all contained within the ocean.
Whatever sacred fords exist in the ocean truly reside within the footsteps of the virtuous.
As long as the earth remains moistened by the water from the feet of the virtuous,
so long do the gods and the ancestors remain satisfied on this earth.
It is the cutter away of calamities and the bestower of prosperity;
it is the destroyer of diseases and the medicine that removes the sickness of illusion.
It is the giver of happiness, the bestower of auspiciousness, the essence, and the nectar from the feet of the divine sages.
"Today I shall obtain the nectar of the feet of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.

That very Lord Kṛṣṇa himself is today manifest in my home."
Having spoken thus and prostrating like a staff, Bhṛgu praised the Imperishable One:

"You alone are the cause of everything for me; grant me the supreme state, purify my life!

Satī, Menā, Jayā, Khyāti, Māṇakī, Pārvatī, Prabhā;

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
"O devoted wife, what meanings do you truly understand from my names?
Tell me so that, having recognized your supreme knowledge, I may be pleased."
Thus addressed, you, O daughter of Bhṛgu, indeed set forth this etymological derivation:
the word *kṛṣi* denotes the earth, and the syllable *ṇa* denotes fulfillment (*nirvṛtti*).
The supreme Brahman, which is the unity of these two, is designated as *Kṛṣṇa*.
He is called Kṛṣṇa because he draws away sufferings and leads [beings] to his abode.
(3) The syllable *rā* is always said to be the name for prosperities (*saṃpad*), and *ma* is said to signify measure (*māna*).
Kṛṣṇa, who bestows the measure of prosperity, is thus rightly called by the name Rāma. (4)
He delights with Ramā; therefore he is called Rāma.
He who is the place of delight for Ramā is Kṛṣṇa, and he is called Rāma. He who is the abode and the dwelling place within the assembly of human beings—[he is Rāma].
This Lord Nārāyaṇa performs [all actions]; He is called Kṛṣṇa. (6) "Nārā" refers indeed to sins; since their destruction occurs through Him, He is Nārāyaṇa.
That very Lord is Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. (7)
"Nārāḥ" means waters; he who dwells therein is indeed Nārāyaṇa.
Or, "nārāḥ" refers to Lakṣmī, the daughter of Bhṛgu; he who makes her his abode (ayana) is [Nārāyaṇa]. The root "kṛṣ" signifies love; he who leads that [love] is truly Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.

You are my husband, the illustrious Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, Hari. (9) You take away the sorrows of your devotees; you are Hari, the Lord himself. Endowed with the sixfold opulences, you are always called the Bhagavān. (1.385.10)
Because you possess that fortune which belongs to a devotee, you are therefore considered "Bhagavān. The sprout of the tree of devotion grows through association with devotees (11),
as well as by being watered with the nectar of discourse concerning the stories of Hari.
But even by a fraction of the flame of the lamp of conversation with the non-devotee, the sprout withers;
yet, watered by the devotee, it flourishes.
Therefore, being vigilant, I indeed avoid the company of the non-devotee.

The syllable *kṛṣ* denotes the most excellent, while *ṇa* signifies true devotion; *a* also denotes the giver, and thus you are called *Kṛṣṇa*. Furthermore, *kṛṣ* refers to supreme bliss, and *ṇa* to the act of serving that bliss.

You, Kṛṣṇa, are the giver of those two, as is the daughter of Bhṛgu, the servant of Kṛṣṇa. Because of the destruction of "kṛṣi"—which means suffering—the term "Kṛṣṇa" applies to you. Just as a lotus pierces through the water, so too does a devotee, by taking refuge in you.
By means of the name Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, You rescue [beings] from the ocean of worldly existence.
Through Śrī, You are indeed Śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, united with me.
O Supreme Lord, I consider my own fortune to be great because of Your union.
Blessed is that Lakṣmī Kambharā, and blessed is Gopāla Kṛṣṇa,
in whose home you, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, always abide,
and from whose speech the name of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa ever proceeds. (18–19)
Indeed, tens of millions of his great sins are reduced to ashes;
having become divine and being fully liberated, he is not born again.
Even hundreds of thousands of all sacrifices and vows [are surpassed by this].
All pilgrimages to sacred fords, all austerities, and all fasts;
thousands of recitations of the Vedas and a hundred circumambulations of the earth—
these do not equal even a sixteenth part of the name of Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
May there never be [attachment to] the eternal Śrī of Brahmā, Vaiṣṇavī, Nārāyaṇī, Mahālakṣmī, or Bhārgavī; Mādhava alone is their Lord.
May there always be devotion to You, the Lord of All, and may there be service unto You for me forever.
May the worship of Your names always remain within my heart.
O Lord! May the service of You alone—through body, mind, speech, action, and all deeds—be my constant desire. (24–25)
"I shall indeed perform penance for that purpose to serve my beloved husband,
and I shall enjoy the eternal bliss granted by you.
Having spoken thus, O Lakṣmī, the daughter of Bhṛgu ceased speaking before Hari.

Her face was radiant with a luster like ten million moons, her eyes were like autumn lotuses, and they were brightened by collyrium; she was adorned with ornaments of gold. (66–67)
Her body was adorned with colorful ornaments, her form perfectly beautiful and fulfilling all desires;
she was full of aesthetic relish and longing, her mind fixed upon the lap of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa;
she wore garments as pure as fire, and her inner being was filled with the intensity of the passion of Rati.
She was radiant at her ears and cheeks with a pair of beautiful earrings;
she possessed a fine nose and golden locks of hair, adorned with garlands of elephant tusks and flowers.
She was anointed with saffron, lac, musk, and smooth sandalwood paste.
She possessed a nose like the beak of the king of birds, was soft-limbed, and very amorous;
she had beautiful cheeks and was as lovely as a female elephant.
She was the abode of the desires of Love, slender, and her side-glances were the arrows of the bodiless god.
She was indeed holding *pārijāta* flowers for play;
she was richly endowed with the remembrance of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa’s affection through action, mind, speech, sleep, and likewise while awake, and was filled with love. (72–73)
Attached to the contemplation of the divine essence, pure in devotion, and faithful to her husband;
fair-complexioned, filled with red [radiance], and eternally situated upon the chest;
she who is dear among beloveds, devoted among devotees, and sweet-spoken among the faithful.
Upon seeing Bhārgavī, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa was indeed overcome with passion.
Seeing her husband upon the bed—his life’s beloved, filled with desire, wearing auspicious attire, the handsome lord, and smiling—Bhārgavī [was likewise moved]. (75–76)
Dark as a fresh rain-cloud, clad in yellow silk garments,
with all his limbs anointed with sandalwood paste and adorned with jewel ornaments;
wearing a crown with a beautiful golden crest and beautified by a garland of *mālatī* flowers.

With a face brightened by a slight smile, his very form being the embodiment of grace toward his devotees, she quickly placed upon her chest her beloved husband—the Lord of the Supreme—who was desirous of sporting, charming to the mind, and the beloved of Kāma; and she spoke to the Supreme Lord. (78–79)
My birth has become fruitful, for I have such a husband;
my life is well-lived, for my beloved is Nārāyaṇa.
Having beheld the moon of your face, my eyes and mind have become deeply affectionate.
My five vital breaths have melted away, and joy no longer finds room within my body.
(81) Sprinkled well by the rain of nectar from your glance, I am now facing toward bliss;
yet, O Lord, the separation from my Master is a most terrible forest fire. (82)
Having spoken thus, Lakṣmī, the daughter of Bhṛgu, laid her husband Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa upon her own seat and performed a massage of his feet and other limbs.
She offered fragrant water, the essence of oils, and a mirror.
She gave to Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa betel nut, drinking water, flower garlands, excellent sandalwood,
honey, edible sweet fruit, the Anaṅgabala pill, and nectar; thereafter,
she gave him her own self.
The Lord made his enchanting bed of flowers fruitful;
he made the daughter of Bhṛgu, his newly wedded bride, fruitful in the chamber of love.
Smiling, the lovely woman gazed at her smiling and tranquil beloved.
On the bed, Lakṣmī, overcome with bliss, served him with her whole being.
Satisfied, the daughter of Bhṛgu spoke to her satisfied beloved in accordance with dharma:
"She alone is a wife who is devoted in spirit; he alone is a husband who protects his wife. (87–88)
The happiness of love between husband and wife is indeed difficult to attain through mere religious duty;
only a devoted wife, a connoisseur of beauty, truly knows a virtuous husband.
A bee runs from afar for the sake of the lotus, driven by its greed for honey.
For a frog does not know that; one should place one's foot upon its head.
A musician knows the essence of music, but the instrument certainly does not.
One who is hungry knows the taste of milk, neither the ladle nor the vessel.
Those who enjoy pleasures know the taste of the ripened fruit,
yet they do not remain forever in one place, just as those who bear fruit [do not stay] anywhere.
Farmers, however, experience the taste of very cool water.
Just as a pond and a water-jar do not abide together in one place, so it is with the enjoyer;
for the enjoyer perceives the supreme, delicious taste of the rice, yet neither the field nor the vessel abides in that same place. || 93-94 ||
A donkey seeking sandalwood does not perceive the scent of sandalwood;
yet a devoted wife understands that good fortune, dignity, and love—which are difficult to attain and ever-new—become easily accessible through service to her husband. (95)
Indeed, both the husband who observes the vow of fidelity to his wife and the wife obtain that which is easily attained.
O Lord, let my devotion to you be the practice of *pativratā* (faithfulness) toward you!
I choose as my lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, who is devoted to his wife.
"So be it," Hari said to the daughter of Bhṛgu, who was devoted to her husband.
He then revealed those very forms which belong to Lakṣmī.
"Behold them, O daughter of Bhṛgu! See where and how each of these has been assumed."
"But you remain with me through your devotion as my wife (pātivratya) amidst all forms.
And I, the Supreme Person, abide in the imperishable Brahman;
therein you exist in the form of the imperishable consciousness and bliss."
In Goloka, Gokula, and Vṛndāvana, you are Rādhikā to me;
I am Kṛṣṇa, two-armed, dressed as a cowherd, the husband of Rādhikā.
In Vaikuṇṭha, I am four-armed; thus I am eternally Nārāyaṇa in two forms.
Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, and you yourself dwell with me as your beloved.
You are indeed Lakṣmī, the daughter of the ocean, and at that time the mortal was the Lord of Lakṣmī;
and in Śvetadvīpa and the Ocean of Milk, the four-armed one was the Lord of Lakṣmī.
I am the sage Nārāyaṇa and Nara, the eternal Dharma;
you are Śānti, whose very nature is Lakṣmī, and you are the devoted wife within me.
I am Kapila and you are Siddhi; thus do you manifest everywhere.
I am devoted to my wife, and you conduct yourself as a devoted wife.
In Vaikuṇṭha, you are indeed Mahālakṣmī and Sarasvatī;
you are also Mṛtyulakṣmī, the beloved of the one who reclines upon the ocean of milk.
You are the daughter-in-law of the Son of Dharma (Yudhiṣṭhira), and you are Peace (Śānti) whose very nature is Fortune (Lakṣmī).
You are the beloved wife of Kapila; on earth, you are the virtuous Bhāratī.
You manifest as Sītā, my wife who possesses the form of Rāma.
Then you will become Rukmiṇī, my beloved, in the form of Kṛṣṇa. You are Kaṃbharā, the Great Lakṣmī, the consort of Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa. Thus you have been born as Bhārgavī, and I am Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
You are Padmā, you are Ramā, you are Prabhā, and likewise Pārvatī;
you are Māṇikī, you are Jayā, you are Śrī, and you are Kṛṣṇā, my beloved.
You are Haṃsā, Mañjulā, Campā, Haimī, the Goddess, Ramā, and Dayā.
Mauktikā, Jayā, and Śānti— you are their presiding deity.
Whenever and wherever you take birth as my beloved, I shall marry you,
take you as my wife, and lead you away with me.
O my beloved, auspicious one! I am always present everywhere in manifold forms, either through my own portions or through a fraction of myself, together with you; I shine forth in all places.
I am the most perfect Supreme Being, and you indeed are the most perfect one.
"Wherever and whatever task may arise, there I shall go with you.
Indeed, there is no other equal to you among devoted wives, nor is anyone else like you.
O Queen of the Gods! I am exceedingly pleased that you remain constant in your singular nature."
"Those women who shall hear of this service to their husband with devotion, and those who shall read it, will indeed attain Me as their husband.

Thus ends the three hundred and eighty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of Bhārgavī’s Adornment, Her Service to Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, and the Demonstration of Her Devotion to Her Husband," within the section on the Greatness of Chaste Wives (*pativratāmāhātmya*) in the First Book, the Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī! I shall tell you another auspicious story that bestows liberation, which brings about the salvation of a devoted wife for her own husband. 1.
That man from whom gods, sages, ancestors, and spirits depart from his house unhonored as soon as they have breathed upon it— no sinner is more wretched than he;
for his body and his home are destroyed by the sighs of the gods and others.
All his fortune is destroyed, for he is destined for ruin.
(3) By a virtuous wife, the holy men, virtuous women, the elders, the ancestors, the deities, and guests must be honored day after day. (4)
By means of her own meritorious deeds, a devoted wife should always increase the lifespan of her husband; auspicious sacrifices should be performed.
Without having first honored the sages, the gods, the ancestors, the spirits, and guests, [one should not eat].
He who eats certainly destroys his own merit.
It is heard that in ancient times there was a famous king on earth named Śatadhanu,
and his wife was Śaibyā, who was entirely devoted to the duty toward her husband.
Devoted to her husband, highly fortunate, endowed with truthfulness, purity, and compassion,
intent on serving the elders, peaceful, and possessed of prudence and humility—
she, that king, together with her, [worshipped] me, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
He propitiated the All-pervading Lord with supreme concentration,
through burnt offerings, recitations, gifts, and fasts performed with devotion,
and by means of daily worship, with his mind fixed on Me alone and no other.

Once, on the full moon day of Kārttika, that husband and wife, having fasted and bathed together in the waters of the Bhāgīrathī, emerged from the river. Having observed the vow on the eleventh day, they indeed rose at dawn on the twelfth.
They both bathed in the Bhāgīrathī and then returned home.
For the sake of breaking their fast, they had cooked rice along with side dishes, curd, and milk;
yet, having first offered these to the gods, sages, ancestors, and spirits, the food remained kept in the cooking pots.
Śaibyā was waiting at the gate for a brahmin guest, her own guru;
then the brahmin guru himself arrived, known by the name Āpāryaka.
Having personally performed the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice and the offerings to the sages, ancestors, and cows, [he entered].
"He will grant us that favor which we shall consume as our breaking-fast meal.
(15) Just then, guests arrived at the king's house; the time for honoring them by the king and the queen had already passed. (16)
The teacher also arrived and, seeing many guests,
observed for a moment that the husband and wife were intent on their worldly affairs;
he then offered food and water to the gods, sages, ancestors, and spirits.
Time passed and the midday hour departed; he went to his own home.
The cooked food remained just as it was, and the gods, sages, and ancestors who had assembled, being hungry, received neither worship nor water or food. (18–19)
Hopeless and exceedingly enraged, they departed for their own abodes.
But that devoted wife, knowing her husband had resorted to the gods,
provided him with food, water, and other necessities until he was satisfied.
Then, by virtue of that divine grace, the food remaining from her husband became intended for his wife.
However, that food produced by divine grace had not previously been eaten by the husband;
because of that fault, the husband was tainted, but the wife was not tainted according to dharma.
The food obtained without favor was for the husband's sake, while that born of favor was for the wife's sake;
what arose from the husband’s portion became a source of fault for him, yet it became a bestower of merit for the wife.
Having fed the honored guests, the husband and wife then ate themselves.
Then they both remembered their guru, who honors the celestial sages and the ancestors. They realized that the food they had eaten had not been offered to the gods and others.
In the afternoon, they performed all the rites, beginning with the worship of Viṣṇu.
Furthermore, as long as the destruction of one who has incurred faults does not occur,
he must experience [the results] either in this life or in another existence.
As time passed, the king died, afflicted by fever.
His wife ascended the funeral pyre after her husband, the lord of the earth.
At that very moment, they both traveled along the path to heaven by means of their vehicle;
meanwhile, the ancestors of the celestial path became enraged.
Suddenly arriving and causing the celestial chariot to descend,
they glared at the king with cruel eyes from the sky;
at that moment, the husband and wife fell from that chariot to the earth.
Due to his former transgression, the king was born as a dog in the city of Vaidiśa.
The queen, her memory restored, was born as the daughter of the King of Kāśī,
perfected in all branches of knowledge and endowed with every auspicious mark.
Inevitable events come to pass and cannot be averted;
even for a devoted wife, her father’s anger became an obstacle.
Yet, when that beautiful woman had become a worthy and devoted wife, [he released her].
Her father desired to give her away to a suitor, but he was forbidden by her;
thus obstructed by his daughter, the king desisted from the commencement of the marriage.
Through divine yogic vision, she perceived her husband as a dog.
Taking her father’s command, the daughter set out for her journey;
having reached the city named Vaidiśa, she beheld a dog as her husband.
Upon seeing his wife, the dog then remembered his former birth.
He wept for a mere moment and felt ashamed for a moment;
she too, seeing him in that state and deeply distressed, wept.
She bestowed upon him the grace of the gods, along with words of honor and water.
He touched the dog’s back, ears, and head with his hand;
eating the very delicious and desired food given by her,
he performed the playful antics characteristic of his canine species and offered many flattering words.

By him, practicing such flattery, the young woman was made exceedingly bashful. (3.9) "O Great King! Remember that affectionate body of yours, born from the womb of a beast; remember that food which was not offered to the gods and others. (1.386.40)

O Lord of Men! Do you not remember that, having fallen from the celestial chariot in the sky along with me due to your father’s wrath, you entered the womb of a dog and have now reached this contemptible birth? (41) O Master, do you not recall that?
When he had been thus reminded by her of the lack of rain caused by his actions in a previous birth,
he then reflected for a long time; having attained an extremely rare state of dispassion,
his mind became despondent, and he departed from the city.
Protected by the maiden at the boundary and repeatedly sprinkled with water,
his sins indeed emerged from his body:
one in the form of a jackal and the second in the form of a wolf.
The third was in the form of a vulture, and the fourth had the form of a crow;
the fifth was seen in the form of a peacock, each appearing individually.
The maiden spoke to them all: "Who are you, and how have you become such as this? (45–46)
Then they said to the maiden: "We are indeed the sins of the dog;
I am that very sin by which the king previously committed theft in another kingdom, and I am that sin by which the subjects' wealth was devoured like a wolf."
When his divine wealth fell into his treasury, I was the vulture there;
when his food acquired through injustice was digested in his stomach, I was the crow;
and when the property of rivers, forests, mountains, and so forth was released [into his possession], I was the peacock.
After that, you will have five more births as the wife of your husband;
then, by the power of your merit, this King Janaka will indeed become your husband.
Having obtained him as your husband at a *svayaṃvara*, you shall go to heaven.
"When your ancestors attained liberation through the *śrāddha* rites of Janaka, then shall his heaven be secured by you.
Go, O virtuous lady, to your own home; do not destroy us with your sprinklings! (51–52)
Thus addressed, that virtuous woman said: "If I am indeed chaste, if I am truly a devoted wife, then let there be the deliverance of my husband here.
If I am a servant of my husband, may I be the one who effects the liberation of my ancestors."
"By this merit, may Yama himself come here and stand before you.
Having said this, he then took water and sprinkled it all around;
at that moment, in the body of the dog and toward the southern direction, Yama himself appeared.
Having arrived, he said to Satī: "O daughter of Śibi! How have you remembered me?
Speak, O virtuous lady! Act quickly; what is it that dwells in your mind?
Śaibyā replied: "Whatever sins indeed exist within the body of a dog..."
"Only after bringing about their destruction shall my husband be attained by me along with you.
Speak quickly here, O King; otherwise, I shall reduce them to ashes.
Yama said: "Listen, O virtuous lady! The exhaustion of karmas occurs through experience."
"O virtuous lady, let it be resolved by you, and let justice also be administered!
Or rather, I shall demonstrate it here; do so quickly, if you will.
By the power of your dharma, the end [of this] will come swiftly."
For every single person, the constant experience of suffering for their sins would occur.
Therefore, having stayed here for five days, perform your penance.
For that which a virtuous woman maintains by the power of her devotion to her husband—
O devoted wife, you are capable of doing so here;
therefore, take water today and make a formal resolve (saṃkalpa) in my presence:
"By this application of water, may my husband be released from the dog. (62)
For one day he will exist as a jackal with the body of a preta.
Tomorrow morning, having indeed become that very jackal, he will come into your presence;
by this gift of water, let him be released from his state as a jackal.
For one day he will become a wolf with a corpse-like body; on the following day, he will come—give him water, so that he may be released from this wolf-birth.
For one day he will become a vulture with a corpse-like body; on the fourth [day]...
"He will arrive tomorrow; give him water and let the vulture go.
For one day that peacock shall have the body of a ghost; on the fifth day he will become a peacock again—give him water and let this peacock be released. (66–67)
But cast even this peacock body of yours into the waters at the concluding bath (*avabhṛtha*) of Janaka’s great horse-sacrifice (*vājimedha*).
Then the son of the sacrifice will become your husband, O daughter of Janaka.

"Born as soon as you were conceived, youthful, robust, divine, wise, and majestic— O virtuous lady, by the power of your devotion to your husband, accept [this] at your *svayaṃvara*! Thereafter, rule the kingdom for many thousands of years."
Having spoken thus, Dharma vanished after bowing to Śaibyā, the devoted wife;
and Śaibyā joyfully performed everything for her in that very manner every day.
Even the dog, having become a ghost, would daily cast off his body.
Thus, on the sixth day, that prince was born.
As soon as he was born, he became a youth, strong, and was named Ṛtudhvaja.
Then that virtuous woman, having returned to her own home, made a request once more.
Then Śaibyā, with her own mind, chose that very divine being as her husband; she then urged her father to arrange the marriage.
And Śibi likewise caused a *svayaṃvara* (self-choice ceremony) to be held for her.

When the *svayaṃvara* had been performed, that virtuous and beautiful woman recognized her own husband; with joy, the passionate lady chose him once again as her lord. And the king, in turn, enjoyed royal pleasures together with her.
He ruled the kingdom inherited through his paternal lineage over the lands of Videha;
he duly brought about his father’s liberation through sacrificial rites.
He performed many sacrifices and bestowed gifts upon those who sought them.
Having enjoyed the earth and its royal sovereignty, she gave birth to sons;
then, at the end of eighty thousand years, she abandoned her own body.
Thereafter, that devoted wife [placed] her husband, who was lying upon the funeral pyre, once again [within herself].
Filled with joy, she ascended according to the prescribed rites as before. Then that king, together with the princess,
attained worlds superior to those of Indra— worlds that yield all desires and are imperishable.
She attained incomparable and imperishable heaven, as well as a most rare conjugal union;
having reached the realm of Vairāja, which is even beyond Satyaloka,
she obtained there the fruit of her merit through the power of her devotion to her husband.
Vaikuṇṭha, situated within the waters and light, she reached together with her husband;
for Queen Śaibyā was a Vaiṣṇavī who, accompanied by King Ṛtadhvaja, [attained that state].
Thus, by such a devoted wife, her own husband was uplifted.
The ancestors have been delivered and established as residents of Vaikuṇṭha;
by his own power, their sins are destroyed day by day.
Through reading and hearing this, their certain liberation shall surely come to pass. (84–85)

Thus ends the three hundred and eighty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of how, through the Power of Chastity, the Husband of Śaibyā—after completing five births as a jackal, a wolf, a vulture, and a crow due to his failure to offer food to the gods and ancestors and other sins—attained the status of a prince named Ṛtudhvaja and final liberation in Vaikuṇṭha," in the section on the Greatness of Devoted Wives within the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga, in the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
