Chapter 388 → Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī! I shall tell you a delightful story concerning a brahmin woman who relied on the power of her devotion to her husband—a tale that increases righteousness through its hearing.
In the primordial age, there lived in the land of the Vindhyas a man who was highly proficient in yoga.
The great seer Vedaśravas was devoted to the sacrifice of silent recitation (japayajña).
Having constructed an auspicious leaf-hut in a delightful, grassy area near water, crowded with many trees, he lived there in the forest forever. (2–3)
Having performed the fire sacrifice (homa), the worship of the deities, the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā), the honoring of guests,
and the recitation of the Sūrya-mantra and other rites, subsisting on wild fruits, intent upon his own spiritual welfare, accompanied by his wife, he dwelt in the forest.
He lived according to virtuous conduct, devoted to his wife. (5) At times he would remain for six days in the meditative absorption of yoga.
His wife, too, being of excellent vows, was constantly intent upon serving him. (6)
The yoginī named Suśruti was most devoted to Brahman and faithful to her husband;
she was constantly engaged in virtuous activities such as bathing, meditation, worship, and study.
Having meditated upon Brahman and having bowed to and worshipped her husband, she [performed these rites] right at dawn.
She considers herself to have attained the highest good while still alive. (8) The Self exists as a ray of the Supreme Brahman, and He is my husband;
the husband alone is the Supreme Brahman, and indeed, O beloved, all dharma resides in him. (9)
That which is pleasing to her beloved should always be dear to her who does what is pleasing to him.
Just as a shadow follows the body, so should a wife follow her husband.
All the various forms of dharma for a wife are established solely in the husband.
When the husband is pleased, Hari is pleased; when the husband is angry, Hari is angry.
(11) She should satisfy her husband through the giving of enjoyments, the offering of food and other provisions, service, the offering of sweetness and the like, and through respectful worship. (12)
There shall always be the massaging of her limbs and the rubbing of her body;
she shall sleep with her husband both during lovemaking and in repose;
and there shall be bathing with water and other substances, as well as adornment with divine articles.
Fragranting [the heart] with the essence of flowers and the like, nourishing it with fruits;
protecting it through states of wakefulness, delighting it with playful sports;
satisfying it by dwelling within its heart, and proceeding with it in a single-minded state. (14–15)
Gladdening [the Lord] is through the gift of the body; satisfying Him is through the gift of the eyes;
offering oblations is through the gift of offspring; chanting is through the utterance of "Oṃ"; bathing is through the gift of pleasure; and meditation is through the surrender of the self. (16–17)

A devoted wife, being virtuous and faithful, should make her marriage meaningful for her husband through gifts at the proper seasons, through the practice of dharma together with him, through vehicles along with pleasure gardens, and through death by following him in self-surrender. (18)

Thus, having recognized in her own mind other duties that are devoted to the master as the highest of all duties, Suśruti, a yoginī, serves her husband in the forest; at times she remains in yoga and meditative absorption (samādhi).
Even among the wild animals of the forests,
that natural mutual enmity was indeed pacified while they lived together.
And the sage, too, always had his auspicious and righteous wife as his companion.

Having attained the supreme state through the vision of Brahman, he perceived his wife as the Self. He did not regard his wife merely as a wife; rather, he regarded her as the Supreme Goddess, born from the body of the Supreme Brahman and possessing the very nature of the Supreme Brahman.
Having renounced his wife, that brahmin did not consume roots, fruits, and the like;
nor did he ever engage in false exertion for the sake of his own service.
He regarded the body as perishable and transitory, like a drop of water.
He remains forever serene, considering the state of Brahman to be dear and true;
he has no attachment to the taste of the tongue, nor to the hearing of the ear, nor to the scent of the nose, nor likewise to the touch of the skin. (25–26)
He was not attached even to his eyes or to forms, and he possessed dispassion.
His wife, Brāhmī, who was devoted to her husband, became the very essence of the *rasas* and other aesthetic qualities;
for the duty toward one's wife is the supreme dharma, and liberation comes from serving one's wife.
By the satisfaction of a devoted wife, the gods and asuras are pleased.

Whether in eating, sleeping, traveling, drinking, wandering in the forest, in pleasure, in dreaming, in action, in knowledge, in recitation, or in the worship of the gods—(all these depend upon her). 28–29.
In the erotic sentiment, at festive occasions, in dispassion, in listening to the aesthetic flavor (rasa),
in singing, dancing, and instrumental music; when resting upon a grassy lawn,
in wearing ornaments, in household duties, in forest activities, and in diversions.
In laughing, hearing, debating, investigating, and meditating upon Brahman;
in the menstrual period, in physical transformation, in health, in pleasure, in pain, and in distress;
in doubt, in reasoning, in eating, in drinking, in purification, and in speaking; (3-4)
In matters of adornment, purification, protection, and passing the day;
in idleness, idle chatter, and recounting past events—in all such things, the Brahmin acts by prioritizing his duty toward his wife, and never otherwise. (33)

Thus, having attained the Dharma, they lived at that time as one with each other; possessing non-differentiated qualities, husband and wife fulfilled their respective duties. Both performed for one another service consisting of the Brahman.
Moving at will and assuming forms at will, they were devoted to the duty of service,
considering that through such service they would attain the satisfaction of Brahman which grants self-contentment—
that very sight of whom indeed causes all sins to dissolve away. (36)
Having attained such perfection, you two dwellers of the Vindhya forest became such that no man could ever perceive you as deer,
nor could any beast ever perceive you two as parrots. (37–38)
Just as a bird might not see those two, or as fish might never encounter you; just as one might not see you anywhere, or as a bull might never encounter you;
nor might anyone ever overcome you, for you have become tigers in every respect.
In that forest, you two sometimes became lions, swans, serpents, or monkeys; at other times, you were ascetics with matted hair;
and during the arrival of the rainy season, you took the forms of the wish-fulfilling creeper and the wish-fulfilling tree.
In some places they were of the nature of jewels, and in some places they were of the nature of wind;
in some places they were of the nature of gods, and in some places they were of the nature of children. In some places they became old men and youths, invisible and visible.
In some places, O Brahmin, through the union with guests, they were born in the form of teacher and disciple,
or in the form of father and son, according to the requirements of the situation;
just as a woman devoted to her husband does not incur a breach of her vow if she acts in accordance with his will.
In such and such ways, those two lived together in the forests and other places in their true forms.
Then, at the end of her monthly period, when the chaste wife had bathed after her menses,
he united with her according to the law of desire in order to provide the seasonal offering.
The sage, devoted to the pleasures of amorous play according to human custom, [was there].
In the vicinity of the hermitage of the two lovers who were intent on the dharma of desire,
a certain man spoke a human word amidst thick, spreading darkness.
Then, while speaking thus, he suddenly arrived there.
Not seeing the two brahmins, and considering it an obstacle to his desire, he recognized them as humans by their voice; though disguised in the form of deer, they remained hidden.
Then, remaining inseparable there, they were filled with desire.
Not having attained the satisfaction of their longing, they resorted to the behavior of beasts;
though appearing in human form, they were lovers following the nature of animals.
People do not feel shame for them, nor do they reproach them;
being addicted to lust, men regard them as mere beasts.
They are like beasts—naked, devoid of knowledge, and lacking in shame, virtue, and other such qualities.
Thinking thus, men do not obstruct animals during sexual union;
even animals engaged in mating do not take account of men.
Today, the offering of the fertile season and the satisfaction of desire may occur even in the form of an animal. (52–53)
If it should happen that the hospitality due from a human to a human falls upon one who is impure, how could that be accomplished? That must certainly be avoided.
Thinking the leaf-hut empty and not seeing the sage there, [he entered].
This man shall go to another forest; may it be auspicious for him.
Let not the night be fruitless, and let there be the seasonal offering at the proper time.
May the fire, which quenches desire, not cause distress to his wife.
The seed, having reached the state of being half-crushed and so forth, shall not undergo transformation;
and just as no fault arises from the non-giving of the season,
so too everything shall be easily attainable when the form of a deer is assumed.
Having done this, they both assumed the forms of deer, mounted by passion;
yet even so, at that moment, a reversal occurred:
that man, seeing the deer, pierced it with an arrow. (58–59)
The deer and the doe fled, having truly abandoned their desire for pleasure;
and as they ran away in terror, the man seized them from behind. Then, perceiving him to be a human hunter who harms animals, they [fled].
Having abandoned their animal forms, they became sages.
Even when this was done, that hunter did not desist from the two men;
seeing them as Brahmins, he was delighted and rushed forward with speed to seize them.

That Rākṣasa quickly seized the Brāhmaṇa for the purpose of devouring him. His beloved wife, Kāmadharman, who lived in the desolate forest, was without support; she lamented and spoke, leaning upon her husband as her only refuge. (6.3)
Falling at your feet here, [I say]: "O devourer, eat me!
Knowing me to be without refuge, give back my husband's wealth to me;
for a woman who has sought the protection of one worthy of providing refuge is indeed your servant.
Beholding me, who am devoted to the duty of a wife, release me from the power of desire.
[Do not look upon] one who is destitute of wealth, one who is intoxicated, one who is asleep, or one who has turned his back;
nor toward a person who has sought refuge, who is dependent, who is wretched, or who says, "I am yours."

One must never kill, nor cause to be killed, a guru, a father, a sick mother, a sister, a beloved wife, a virtuous man, a virtuous woman, a child, a cow, a woman attached to another man, a woman engaged in sexual intercourse, one who is asleep, or one who is sinless. (67–68)
"Nothing has been killed by him, nor has anything wicked been contemplated. He is devoted to the dharma of the forest-dwellers and has never been a harbinger of harm to you.
This man is a Brahmin; he must not be killed, for otherwise you would incur the sin of killing a Brahmin. (1.387.70)
The killing of a fetus is a great sin, for it is indeed equivalent to the killing of a child.
There are other living beings available for your food; do not harm my husband, this man.
He is the lord of my life and, in every way, my very existence.
Upon his death, I would become a widow, deprived of all auspiciousness.
Do not let my life be fruitless, burdened as it is by the sin of widowhood.
Be compassionate toward my words; I entreat you for everything I possess.
"With this husband, I shall indeed possess both heaven and liberation here;
upon his destruction, this world of Yama will surely become my body.
O Lord, show mercy and release him, and heaven shall truly be yours."
"Do not abandon my husband here; do not forsake my bull-like lord!
Be gracious, O ornament of the Ikṣvāku dynasty!
O King, abandon [this course] and protect righteousness; I entreat you again and again. (75–76)
"Be compassionate toward me, who have not yet fulfilled my desires for the objects of passion!
You do not realize that you are a great sinner, though you claim to know the pleasure of the seasonal rite.
When she had thus entreated him, he did not give heed to her words.
While she was thus lamenting, he devoured her husband.
That virtuous woman, distressed and exceedingly tormented, wept there;
filled with intense anger, she, in her grief, cursed that king.
"Since my husband was devoured by you while I was still unsatisfied,
you too shall certainly meet your end when engaged in the enjoyment of your beloved.
Having said this, that virtuous woman took a fragment of her husband's bone in her hand.
By the power of her devotion to her husband, she restored that husband to life.
Although she desired to burn the Rākṣasa, she was restrained by a voice from the sky;
for that Saudāsa, having become a Rākṣasa, had already been consumed by the curse of Vasiṣṭha.
Having become Kalmāṣapāda, he shall wander for twelve years;
thereafter, released from the curse, he will become King Madayantīpati, a protector of his subjects. Do not join him with this curse.
O virtuous lady, in the lineage of Manu, son of Vivasvat, there were born kings such as Ikṣvāku, Nṛga, Śaryāti, and Nābhāga, who were dear to Hari;
as well as Sudyumna, Ilā, Purūravas, Gaya, Śatamukha, and others. (84–85)
Karandhama, Avikṣit, Marutta, Tṛṇabindu, Viśālaka,
Śaryāti, Ānarta, Raivataka, Kukkudmi, Ambarīṣa, and others; Śaśāda, Kakutstha, Pṛthu, Yuvanāśva, and Māndhātṛ.
Rukmāṅgada, Mucukunda, Anaraṇya, and Triśaṅku;
Hariścandra, Sagara, Aṃśumat, Dilīpa, and Bhagīratha; Janaka, Badarāyaṇa, Ṛtuparṇa, Sudāsa, and Saudāsa. (87–88)
Divodāsa, Indradyumna, Toṇḍa, Madra, Amaka, and Yādhuja—
these kings became devotees of Hari, great bhāgavatas,
enriched by the wonder of being objects of Vasiṣṭha’s and others’ compassion.
This Saudāsa, while in the forest, beheld two tigers.
After the two tigers had devoured the entire forest, leaving it devoid of deer, the king, out of rage because he could no longer obtain game for his hunt, [acted]. (1.387.90–91)
Then he killed a single tiger, whereupon another tiger fled;
and as that tiger was dying, it became a rakshasa of terrifying form,
while the second rakshasa there rendered himself invisible.
Having said, "I shall perform a retaliatory act," he vanished from sight.
Then, in the course of time, Saudāsa performed a Vaiṣṇava sacrifice when his preceptor Vasiṣṭha had departed along with the sacrificial fees.
Assuming the form of Vasiṣṭha, that Rākṣasa arrived and said, "O sir, prepare quickly here the meat for my meal;
I shall return here in a moment. Having said this, he indeed departed.
Assuming once again the guise of a cook, that Rākṣasa entered the kitchen,
prepared human flesh, and presented it to the king.
Saudāsa, for his part, took that meat in a golden vessel and offered it to the Ṛṣi.
Having observed the enclosure, the devoted man became intent on waiting;
when Vasiṣṭha arrived, he offered him human flesh.
Vasiṣṭha did not know at all by whom this had been said or what this was that had been done.
Becoming absorbed in thought, he wondered, "What object is this?
Having realized through meditation that it was human flesh offered to him, he thought:
"Alas! What wickedness is this king's, that he offers me his own flesh! || 1.387.100 ||
"Even there, he offers this human [flesh], which is fit for Rākṣasas," he said, and becoming overcome with rage, he quickly cursed the king:
"Since you give me this, even though you know it is unfit to be eaten by us... (101)
"Therefore, O King, become a despised eater of human flesh.
(102) The king made his intention clear: "Whose deed was this that the sage perceived?
There was no fault on the part of the royal seer; for that was indeed done by the Rākṣasa. (103)
Thus, having realized the truth, the sage Vasiṣṭha, the mine of compassion,
brought about a state of rakshasa-hood for twelve years in Saudāsa;
yet he did not grant him ultimate liberation.
Saudāsa, having taken water in his hand,
was then prepared to utter a curse upon Vasiṣṭha; however, his virtuous beloved Madayantī suddenly restrained her husband from cursing the Guru and did not allow it.
"Indeed, gurus are not to be cursed; they are protectors and deliverers.
Their words bring auspiciousness and are in every way for the benefit of their disciples.
Thus entreated, the king sprinkled water upon [the sage's] feet.
His two feet, scorched by the curse of the mantra, became mottled. Thereupon, that Saudāsa, known as Kalmāṣapāda, a consumer of flesh,
having attained the state of a Rākṣasa at the sixth mealtime, wandered upon the earth.
He has devoured many humans in various forests;
this is that very King Saudāsa, who, due to the curse of Vasiṣṭha,
has been consumed by the state of a Rākṣasa and is now a devourer of your husband.
"The sin committed by him through the destruction of pleasure shall fall upon his union with a woman.
This king will surely die; do not cast another curse upon him. Be gracious, O virtuous lady! Your husband has been restored to life by you. || 111-112 ||
Thus it was said by Vasiṣṭha: "When the seer Vedaśravas, together with Suśrutā, shall perish in the forest, thereafter your deliverance from the state of being a rākṣasa will occur. (11.3)
"By the hand of the Creator, the end of Vedaśravas has already been inscribed;
his lifespan is exactly that much and no more.
Therefore, although he was restored to life by the power of his wife's devotion to her husband," ||| 1.14-1.15 |||
It is indeed not fit for him to remain on earth; he shall go to heaven with his wife.
And Saudāsa, by the great seer Vasiṣṭha, was appointed for the sake of seed upon Madayantī, [whereby] he obtained a hundred sons of the lineage of Vasiṣṭha.
Having obtained [her] later, he will indulge in sensual pleasures with Madayantī.
There, deluded by death and failing to find the fulfillment of his desires, he will meet his end very soon; that time has now arrived.
Aśmaka and others shall indeed be his sons, the Sātvatas;
then there will be Khadvaṅga, Dilīpa, Raghu, and Daśaratha.
Furthermore, Rāmacandra and others will arise as bestowers of liberation.
Therefore, having thus resolved, O Suśrutā,
you should prepare a pyre of wood here for your own husband according to the rites of *pātivratya*. Then, having kindled the fire, [he emerged] from his thumb in the form of a human woman.
Having united with the bones of your husband and restored your lord to life,
you shall dissolve right here after completing everything brought about by this union;
for you are divine, purified by fire, and destined for a celestial husband among the gods.
"Taking your husband here to this celestial chariot with his very body, depart indeed.
No other wife shall be equal to you in devotion to her husband;
having attained happiness in heaven until the end of Brahmā’s day," || 1.24 ||
"Then you shall go to Vaikuṇṭha together with that very husband.
Having spoken thus, that voice from the sky ceased, O noble listener.
Then the king bowed toward that direction, and Satī also bowed at that time.
Having made her request, she departed toward her own city on the earth.
There, Suśruti remembered Vasiṣṭha, and he appeared before her.
Having bowed and placed her husband upon the wooden pyre with her own fire, she [prepared for death].
Having reduced their bodies to ashes and restored them to divine forms,
the two of them bowed to Vasiṣṭha and departed for heaven by means of a celestial vehicle.
The drums of the gods resounded and a rain of flowers fell.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have told you this supreme and most wonderful account of the past,
which bestows divine perfections and other blessings through its recitation;
likewise, from hearing it, there arises firmness in dharma, as well as heaven and liberation.

Thus, in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, concerning the majesty of devoted wives (*pativratā*), [are described] the wonders of Suśruti, the devoted wife of Vedaśravas; the arrival at the hermitage of Vedaśravas and Suśruti by the Rākṣasa Kalmāṣapāda who was infatuated with desire; the devouring of Vedaśravas by the Rākṣasa; the curse bestowed by Suśruti; and the voice from the sky.

The three hundred and eighty-seventh chapter, titled "The Narration of the Causal Factors for Saudāsa’s Transformation into a Rākṣasa, and the Description of Suśruta and Vedaśravas Attaining Heaven through the Power of Satī in the Presence of Vasiṣṭha," from the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 1 (*Kṛtayuga-Santāna*).
Chapter 388 [Author:
Chapter 389 → Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī! I shall proclaim the conduct, filled with wonder, of Nanda, the wife of Dharaṇī and a devoted wife. There was a king of Jambūdvīpa named Nandasāvarṇi.
The ocean served as the moat surrounding that kingdom on all sides.
A devotee of the Lord Vārāha, delighting in the worship of Vārāha,
[resides] in the great sacred field of Vārāha, always following the true path of realized knowledge.
Having come together, he practices supreme devotion as desired by the God.
In order to bring back the earth seized by Hiraṇyākṣa,
the Blessed One himself assumed the form of a boar; having slain Hiraṇyākṣa,
he brought the earth back and established it upon the waters.
Then, while wandering in his celestial chariot through the sky,
King Nanda beheld the Great Boar-form, the Lord of the Cosmic Egg.
Descending from his chariot, he then offered a hymn of praise to Him.
Salutations to the one whose nature is infinite, who is named Puruṣottama. Salutations to the creator of his own world and the protector of the earth;
salutations to you, the abode of all principles and the sovereign of the imperishable.
May my salutations be again unto Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa;
by you, through your grace, the earth has been protected today, and we too have been protected.
O Lord! Kings are without support and the subjects are unprotected;
for the sake of protecting the subjects, You indeed assume a new form. (1.388.10)
You are the abode of all powers; salutations to you, whose nature is the form of all things.
Having praised him thus, that king bowed at the feet of Vārāha.
The Boar, being pleased, spoke indeed to the king who was worthy of a boon:
"Speak, O King, for I am gratified; what is it that dwells in your mind? (12)
"I shall grant whatever the mind desires; I am the one who always bestows the wishes of my devotees.
Having been addressed thus, he spoke to the gracious Supreme Lord: ||13||
"What shall I choose, O Ocean of Compassion? Give back to me the earth that was seized by Hiraṇyākṣa; I shall protect this garment granted by you. (14)
Let the earth remain in my house; make me the lord of the earth, for without the earth, the life of a king is indeed fruitless. (15)
Then Vārāha said to the king, "So be it," and Nandasāvarṇi then worshipped the Lord of the Self, Vārāha. ||16||
With leaves, flowers, fruits, water, food, and tubers, as well as unbroken grains (akṣata),
gems such as diamonds and jewels, necklaces, sandalwood, saffron,
golden bracelets, and other golden ornaments;
With crowns, signet rings, bracelets, chains, earrings, and so forth. ॥18॥
Having daily worshipped Vārāha at dawn with anklets, small bells, garments, fragrant water, incense, lamps, hymns of praise, and prostrations seeking forgiveness for his offenses, that king— ||19||
Then that great Vaiṣṇava of the Sātvata lineage performed another act;
being well-pleased, the Boar-god gave a crown to the king, saying:
"May your sovereignty over Jambūdvīpa extend everywhere, as far as its moats."
"And let Dharaṇī today become your wife, devoted to her husband.
Having said this, the Blessed One applied a tilaka upon Nanda-sāvarṇi. (22)
With the stroke of his royal authority, he gave the brought earth to her;
then the Blessed Lord spoke to Dharaṇī, who possessed a divine form. ||23||
O Goddess! Having become the queen Satī, always serve the king;
having bowed down and worshipped Nārāyaṇa with devotion, Dharaṇī [did so]. ||24||
Placing his command upon her head, that goddess Vārāhamānasī assumed the form of a maiden, sixteen years of age and exceedingly beautiful. (25)
As soon as she was born, she was like a beautiful young woman adorned with a garland of flowers; endowed with all auspicious marks, she was devoted to her husband and to dharma. ||26||
Then, wearing the garland offered by Vārāha upon her hands,
she placed it around the auspicious neck of Vārāha at his command.
With true devotion, she chose Nanda-Sāvarṇi alone as her husband.
Having circumambulated the Boar-form Lord and his consort, the couple bowed down before him.
They both worshipped the Boar-form, who was Janārdana himself in visible form.
Dharitrī constantly worshipped her husband Nārāyaṇa. ||29||
Likewise, by his command, Vasundharā, having bathed daily with joy using the sixteen articles, properly worshipped her supreme husband Nanda-Sāvarṇi,
and thereafter [worshipped] that former husband Vārāha.

Having fed him and paid homage, that most excellent daughter-in-law then honored Nanda with all her heart and fed him with all her heart; she constantly served the king as the earth serves the mountain with her second form.
In this way, the Earth always performs service to the Blessed One and service to Nanda with devotion, through the duty of a devoted wife. (33)
But for her whose Lord is the Blessed One—the protector and the regulator—all her duties of devotion to her husband are carried out according to his command. (34)
By the word of Varāha, as well as by the word of Nanda, she who was the earth became the wife of Varāha in accordance with his command. (35)
That beautiful woman, the daughter of Nanda Sāvarṇi, took the form of a maiden;
she constantly served Nanda, who was indeed the Lord in the form of a boar. (36)
Once, however, the Boar said: "O Earth, listen to my words!
I desire to withdraw this very form of mine as a boar. (37)
"Tell me what you desire; I shall grant it to you here without delay.
Upon hearing those words, Dharaṇī was overcome with supreme grief;
she prostrated at his feet and chose the highest honor for him.
The form of the Blessed One was there, present without interruption, for the purpose of being seen. ||39||
The Blessed One said to Dharaṇī: "I give you this tooth of mine;
guard it, worship it, look upon it, and serve it just as you would me. (1.388.40)
Having spoken thus, he indeed gave the tusk to Dharaṇī for worship;
understand that a most fierce power resides within that tusk. (41)
Whether in the forest, on a mountain, in heaven, or within the coverings of the earth and other realms;
in the subterranean worlds, in the oceans, even amidst fires, or in the furthest reaches of the quarters—wherever you may wish to go, take my tusk with you. (42)
Proceed, O Earth! wherever your unimpeded will may lead you. (43)
May your course indeed be unhindered; go happily, endowed with tusks.
Fire, water, poison, cold, stone, wind, and likewise space—[may these not obstruct you]. (44)
"They do not indeed afflict my teeth, nor those of people joined with teeth," having said this and having bestowed his own teeth along with an excellent blessing,
he gazed upon the earth and Nandasāvarṇi and then vanished from sight.
The celestial drums resounded and a rain of flowers fell. ||46||
All the gods and sages arrived there in celestial chariots and praised the Lord of the Earth, Vārāha, who possessed a divine form. ||47||
As Hari was departing for his own abode, they led him away with great festivity.
Now, at that time, Nanda’s wife Dharaṇī, a devoted wife, was constantly worshipping the tooth of the Supreme Soul in the form of the Boar. 48.
Having taken her along with Nanda and Sāvarṇi by means of a celestial chariot, ||49||

In some places he went upon the earth, in some places into creation, in some places into the expanse of the netherworld; in the waters of the ocean, in milk, and in the great sea, he went here and there.
As the queen and the king lived in this manner, the gods, sages, and ancestors, full of great respect, presented them with offerings. ||51||
Even those dwelling in the netherworld, the gods of heaven, and the serpents who lie in the waters [brought] gems, rubies, jewels, diamonds, and pearls. (52)
Gold, silver, copper, and other elixirs;
metallic ores, nectar and the like, and a circle of excellent weapons and missiles—whatever was presented to him as offerings by the inhabitants of that place. (53)
And Nanda, overcome by greed, led him to his own palace.
When his treasury and other stores were filled with wealth and the like, he then reflected: "Indeed, another treasury is required. (55)
"I must create such a treasury within the womb of the earth—one that is inexhaustible, inaccessible, invisible, and beyond the reach [of ordinary perception]. (56)
Having reflected thus, he questioned his wife Dharaṇī, who was of similar disposition. The wife said to the king: "O King, direct your anger toward the surface of the earth. (57)
The tusk of the Boar is there as your companion that provides you passage;
without the tusk, there is no passage for you, so how could there be one for anyone else? (58)
Having reflected thus, King Sarada went to the vicinity of the ocean;
at that moment, the Ocean arrived in personified form through the power of his tusk. (59)
Trembling, Nanda made way for King Nanda by contracting his waters,
having created a vast and wonderful treasury within the ocean.
Then, having fashioned a treasury within the depths of the ocean by means of ivory, he deposited all his wealth, such as jewels and other riches, therein. (61)
Once the treasury had been established and was free from obstacles, his greed increased;
having seized all the wealth of the earth, including gold, silver, and other treasures,
he would always bring them back and deposit them right there.
Indeed, for one whose conduct is driven by greed, there is no end to it here without tranquility.
For that long, his conduct was governed by greed and caused him extreme suffering;
consequently, the entire earth and all its subjects were rendered destitute of wealth. (64)
The wealth located in the mouth of corpses buried underground—whether it be a piece of mineral ore or a small vessel—is brought forth even when it has been buried there. (65)
In Jambūdvīpa, wherever a corpse is known to be buried in the ground, one should have that place excavated and recover the object taken from the mouth of the corpse. 66.
It was held by the assistant Danta in a sea-shell treasury on the palm;
then, at one time, it was indeed presented by Dharaṇī to the King. (67)
O King, perform the great Vaiṣṇava sacrifice and also the Raudra;
conduct the Aśvamedha, the Rājasūya, and various sacrificial sessions (satras) upon the earth. ||68||

Perform for the virtuous the great recitation (*pārāyaṇa*) of the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā* for a long time; it constitutes both the sacrifice of Brahman (*brahmayajña*) and the sacrifice of liberation (*mokṣayajña*). (69)
Material substance is perishable, we are perishable, and the world is perishable;
having performed our duty for the sake of the Lord, let us go to the supreme state. (1.388.70)
Although addressed in this way, the king, being possessed of great greed, did not give any grain at all.
That divine queen Dharaṇī, having bowed again and again to Nanda, [spoke]. (71)
Then, having remembered his boar-form, he vanished from that body.
The king wept profusely, though consoled by the people;
remembering his wife's words, he performed a sacrifice and grieved.
The king constantly worships the tusk of the boar.
Out of a greedy disposition, he gave away all his wealth just as before;
having taken it along with his companion, he likewise preserved it at the bottom of the ocean.
The sixteen-year-old Paṅkajā, daughter of the ocean, was made his second queen by King Nanda, who was seized by lust. The ocean felt a longing for an inexhaustible treasury of wealth.
And this king said to his daughter: "On account of the boar's tusk, he has placed a treasury at my feet; it constantly comes and goes.
I must perform service to him constantly, for there is agitation for me in the water. (76–77)
All of that must be avoided; such is what I must do.
Listen, daughter! You are Meruputrī, Upalā, the beloved wife of Nanda. (78)
"By that means, I must indeed create a blockade here so that he does not pass;
I shall go now to Kubera, Viṣṇu, and likewise to Brahmā. (79)
In order to report to Nanda the intense account of his greed, [the sage spoke];
for that which is destined to happen will indeed come to pass, ordained by Hari.
"Effort must certainly be exerted so that the fruit may come into the hands of Mādhava";
having said this, the king departed for that abode of Kubera. (81)
Having led him away, he went to the world of Hari and related that account to Viṣṇu;
and upon hearing it, Viṣṇu indeed made a firm resolve for his restraint.
He quickly remembered Nārada and related that very account to him.
Then Nārada, having formed a deliberation within his own mind, [proceeded]. 83.
Nanda went quickly to Nanda’s palace, but Nanda was not at home.
Nārada said to Upalā, "May there be auspiciousness for you, O virtuous lady!
Where is Nanda? And where are the other friends, O virtuous lady? The ground is muddy."
Upon seeing the sage, Upalā performed acts of hospitality such as bowing and offered him the guest-offering (*arghya*) and other honors; she then asked the reason for his arrival.
Nārada then said: "That which I have heard in heaven—" (85–86)
Whether it be truth or falsehood, I have come to test you;
for indeed, apart from direct perception, there exists nothing worthy of honor that can be sung by the voice alone. (87)
What has been established by direct perception becomes an accomplished fact that cannot be set aside;
for even the wise Emperor Nanda, the universal monarch, [could not avoid it],
because [the matter] was secondary, censurable to the subject, audible, and indeed appropriate.
"Having made [this] manifest before my very eyes, I shall afterwards go back to heaven once more.
In the midst of the assembly of the gods, the gods describe me as one full of compassion,
for indeed Nanda performs the worship of the bones of the deceased Dharaṇī."
Other new women are not such objects of our love as the earth was formerly, nor even as that bone was;
O stone! tell me, what kind of love does King Nanda have for you?
"What kind of affection does Nanda have for Paṅkila and the other women? [Nārada asked].
The stone replied to the celestial sage: "The king must spend a moment with me in order to stand, eat, breathe, enjoy himself, and likewise live. (92–93)
O celestial sage, he is not even able to eat once he has seen my face;
such affection as he displays toward me does not exist for him toward other women. (94)
The celestial sage said: "If what was spoken by the gods were false, then what was spoken by the gods would indeed be true, and what was spoken by you would be false. (95)
"O virtuous lady, just as the king does not eat without having seen your face, so too King Nanda does not eat without seeing the bone of the earth.
Test how much truth there is in this; where indeed is his greater affection? (96)
Even having seen it, I shall depart; behold the object of worship! 97.
Having been addressed thus, Upalā quickly went from there to the place of worship;
having observed the articles for worship, she saw the casket of offerings. (98)
At that moment, a bone in the form of a tooth was seen there;
instantly, she became bereft of joy, her face withered, and her splendor vanished for a moment. ||99||
Her face having become copper-red with anger, Nārada said to that virtuous lady:
"O Queen, do not grieve! This worldly existence is indeed devoid of substance. (1.388.100)
The gods speak the truth: the king honors the bones of his wife. Your affection for the bone of the earth is greater; you are neither she, nor even equal to her.
O virtuous lady, you are blessed that you endure the sorrow of co-wifehood with such composure!
Indeed, this impure bone has been preserved for worship as if it were a cremation ground.
O King, having abandoned you who are equal to heaven, he now frequents a cemetery.
Put that cemetery far away; cast it into the fire so that it may turn to ashes. (102–103)
Having said, "Perform your bath and purification with water," Nārada departed;
while Upalā was like a stone herself, she was consumed by the fire of anger toward her co-wife. (104)
Once it was burnt, she immediately threw the boar’s bone into the fire;
by the will of Nārada and the will of Hari, the fire consumed it at that very moment. (105)
In her rage, she even threw his bones and ashes into the river water; filled with grief and anger, the virtuous woman returned home and took no food. (106)
The king returned in the evening, but Satī did not speak to him;
meanwhile, the monarch remained there having bathed in the morning for the purpose of worship. ||107||
He saw no bone belonging to the treasury for the purpose of worship, nor the key;
he grieved for a moment and, with a mind fixed on death, questioned you. (108)
"O Goddess, tell me where that bone, the cause of all life, has gone? The stone replied, "That bone has gone into the fire of the hearth. (109)
"O King, you boast falsely for the sake of deceiving us, saying, 'Indeed, I never eat without beholding your face.'"
The bone of Dharaṇī, who has died, is being preserved by you for worship, even though she was by you treated as having no value at all, like a blade of grass. (111)
O Lord, having yourself become a liar, how can you deceive me?
That bone was burnt, and its ashes were carried away by me into the river. (112)
O King, show affection toward me while my beloveds are still alive;
do not show affection for one who is dead, for that creates the bonds of worldly existence.

Thus addressed, that king, greedy for wealth and identifying with that very wealth, [failed to see] within the composite aggregates—which are impermanent, impure, suffering, and non-self—[the true nature of things]. (114)
Crying out "Alas! Alas! while experiencing the misconception that his eternal consciousness, bliss, and self had vanished, King Nanda died due to the complete obstruction of his heart.
Then his wives, who were devoted to their virtuous husband, took him upon their laps;
having cremated their bodies, they went to heaven by means of the Vārāha-yoga.
By the power of Dharaṇī, the ocean became the surface of the earth;
from Dharaṇī, Dhanasāvarṇi was born, who then ruled the kingdom. (117)
His son was Dharmasāvarṇi, a devotee of Viṣṇu, who became the lord of the earth.
Through hearing and reciting this [account], one shall attain knowledge as well as heaven. (118)

Thus, in the first section of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, concerning the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga and the majesty of devoted wives (*pativratā*), it is told how, through the devotion of King Nanda, the Earth was given to him by Vārāha in the form of his wife Kumārikā; how, by virtue of Dharaṇī’s chastity, he obtained a tusk-bone as a boon; and how, by means of that bone, Nanda established a treasury of wealth in the ocean. Furthermore, after Dharaṇī’s passing, Nārada arrived and informed Upalā that the king was performing the worship of her co-wife’s bones.
Having spoken thus, [the body] was reduced to bone and ashes; by that blow, King Nanda died—this is the three hundred and eighty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description [of the Event]. ||388||

→ Chapter 390
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī! I shall relate the auspicious story of Merudevī, the devoted wife of Nābhi, whose son was Ṛṣabha. (1)
Formerly, there was a king named Āgnīdhra, the sovereign of Jambūdvīpa. His son was Nābhi, who, being childless, took refuge in Hari.
Nābhi’s wife was Merudevī, who was devoted to her husband.
She regards her Lord as the God, her Lord as Kṛṣṇa, her Lord as the supreme Nārāyaṇa;
(3) her Lord as Dharma, her Lord as Karma, and her Lord as the armor whose essence is Nārāyaṇa—the Supreme Brahman.
Having realized him thus, she serves him always as if he were her own self. (4)
And she was a knower of Brahman among the wives of the brahmin-sages, most excellent in her knowledge of Brahman;

she was possessed of the Vedic lore of the *brahmatantu*, devoted to the *veda-vidyā*, and intent upon the fire-oblation (*homa*). She was skilled in the performance of the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*) and dedicated to worship and recitation.
She, who was the very embodiment of the power of Brahman, remained devoted to Brahman like another Sarasvatī; even while in the kingdom, she was pure and dedicated to the Supreme.
Having bathed in the morning, having bowed to her husband, and having worshipped the gods with offerings, she remained thus.
Devoted to her husband, she began to perform worship for him;
having bathed her husband and adorned him with garments and other ornaments,
that virtuous woman then drank the water from his big toe and performed the great worship.
Having joyfully seated her husband upon an auspicious golden throne, she says:
"I offer this seat to Viṣṇu in the form of my husband;
I also offer water for the guest, water for the feet, and water for sipping to my own master."
I offer a tooth-cleansing twig as a limb of worship to the Protector;
I also offer fragrant water from sacred sites for rinsing the mouth,
and I provide other water for the sake of purification and so forth for him who seeks me.
Having brought about supreme purification with clay and other substances, and [offering] the nectars—
curds, milk, ghee, sweets, and honey— I offer them to the Master.
I present the water for the purpose of consecration to the Master.
I massage my husband with oil made fragrant;
O Mistress, I sprinkle upon him the appropriate water for his bath.
With a soft cloth, I wipe the water from his body.
I offer to the Lord a garment of golden hue, a washed sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), an upper cloth, and a sacrificial sash;
as well as the grooming of his hair through the application of flowers and fragrant oils. (15–16)
I prepare sandalwood paste for the pleasure of my Lord and offer it to Him;
I apply a beautiful tilaka and crescent moon mark upon His forehead. I adorn the eyes of the Lord of Satis with lovely kohl.
Upon his head I bestow a beautiful crown, auspicious earrings upon his ears,
and around his neck most excellent necklaces strung with gems; I also give him two bracelets for his hands and auspicious bangles for his arms.
On her two forearms she wore bracelets, on her waist a girdle, and on her feet lovely anklets; she wore flower garlands and crests,
necklaces around her neck, clusters of blossoms in her hand, and auspicious sandals upon her feet.
I offer these items fashioned from gold to the Lord:
an umbrella and two beautiful chowries, a lion-throne made of gold, incense, a lamp, unbroken grains of rice, saffron, and a golden staff. (21–22)
I offer this sweet meal as a food offering to the Lord—śaṣkulīs, laḍḍukas, and other delicacies presented in a golden vessel;
milk-rice, side dishes, curd, milk, and fruit. (23)
I offer to the Lord, whose self is Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, food to be chewed, eaten, licked, sucked, and drunk, as well as sweet water and the like;
I offer the waving of lights, betel leaf, and cool water from a conch shell. (24–25)
I offer circumambulation, the sacrificial fee, and a handful of flowers;
I also offer prostration, the request for forgiveness, and surrender my entire service.
I perform the massaging of the feet and all other forms of service as well. (26)
"I am the devoted wife of Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇasvāmin.
I eat the grace of my divine husband, which destroys all sins.
Thus, when that virtuous woman daily worships her husband in the morning, ||| 27-28 ||

Then, by virtue of her devotion and chastity, that great satī beheld her husband there as the divine, four-armed Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa. In this manner, she served him in the morning, at midday, in the evening, and at night.
Once, while that virtuous woman remained in meditation after having served her husband,
she beheld a great splendor extending as far as the world of Brahmā;
then the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa Hari revealed Himself.
Golden-hued, wearing yellow silken garments, endowed with splendor, he holds the conch, discus, mace, lotus, shield, sword,
and sacrificial ladle; he is adorned with a shining crown, earrings, bracelets, and a waist-belt.
Adorned with necklaces, armlets, anklets, and other bodily ornaments,
she, a devoted wife, worshipped Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa in that manner with offerings of tulasī leaves, dūrvā grass, water, flowers, and other gifts. (33–34)
O Blessed One, you are the most worthy of honor, endowed with divine qualities.
May the singing of your virtues and service to you be within the reach of me, your devotee.
My husband is a royal sage, eternally desirous of progeny, and a king among devotees.
"May his son be equal to you, so that I may obtain happiness. The Blessed One said: "O maidservant! O virtuous woman! Your mouth is my own mouth.
Let the truthful words requested by you become true; let it be exactly so."
"I shall descend into your home through a portion of the Āgnīdhrīya fire," having said this and received due honor, that supreme person vanished.
On that day, at the time of night, Narāyaṇa [entered] Merudevī.
Then he entered [the house], and in the morning he descended into that dwelling.
As soon as he was born, he became a youth, filled with the perfection of all knowledge,
and endowed with the abundance of equanimity, tranquility, dispassion, sovereignty, and majesty.
He spoke of that son Ṛṣabha as being endowed with such fame, strength, vigor, splendor, and virtues, as well as heroism, valor, righteousness, and devotion.
"This Ṛṣabha is indeed an incarnation of Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa."
Out of rivalry with whom Mahendra did not send rain for three years,
that Lord of Yoga, Ṛṣabha, smiling, became a cloud through his yogic power (yogamāyā) and sent down rain upon his own kingdom, Ajanābha.
Having himself consecrated his son Ṛṣabha upon the throne, Nābhi,
together with Merudevī, attained the great yoga of the supreme self within the individual self.
Having meditated upon Nara and Nārāyaṇa, the couple went to liberation.
Ṛṣabha established a splendid institution for the imparting of knowledge and training;
for the sake of obtaining instruction in dharma, he founded a great academy of learning.
Although he was himself the king and himself the teacher of instruction, he personally provided the education.
Indra himself came and gave his virtuous daughter, named Jayantī,
who was like Lakṣmī in form, to the Blessed One Ṛṣabha.
Through the domestic dharma, Ṛṣabha begot one hundred auspicious sons upon her.
He indeed produced a maṇḍala of yogins that was truly peerless.
There, King Bharata, the sovereign of the Bhāratas, shone resplendent, along with Kavi, Hari, Antarikṣa, Prabuddha, and Pippalāyana.
Āvirhotra, Drumila, Camasa, and Karabhājana—
these were all great devotees of the Lord (mahābhāgavatas), yogis who followed the path of Brahman.
Other sons were born as kings, such as Kuśāvartaka and others.
Others became Brāhmaṇas, devoted to sacrifice and learned in the Vedas.
The blessed Lord Ṛṣabha, compassionate and the bestower of peace upon men,
performed his penance when the materials, place, age, faith, and time were all perfected.
Once, the land of Brahmāvarta became crowded with hundreds of thousands of Brahmanical sages;
there the illustrious Ṛṣabha went and attained awakening.
He then renounced his kingdom, prosperity, happiness, and everything belonging to himself. (53)
And even though the body is nourished by the king, it belongs to another;
and since it is of the nature of moisture through food and other things that cause decay, it is of the fettered (pāśava) kind.
Having attained consciousness within that body, the acquisition of Brahman is praised. (54–55)
How could there be purity of being while the body exists and worldly enjoyments are accumulated?
Let the people exert themselves toward the eternal bliss of Brahman!
For the virtuous are indeed Brahman, the Self, the form of Brahman, and the bliss of Brahman.
Yogis and ascetics who are great devotees (mahābhāgavatas) should be served by people.
House, wife, children, gardens, cattle, fields, and whatever else there may be—these are indeed bonds, provided they exist apart from me, Nārāyaṇa. 57–58.
If those very [senses] are employed by others while placing me at their head,
they become gateways to liberation, just like virtuous friends;
yet, having abandoned me, this collection of senses remains greedy for sense-objects here in this world.
He who always delights while bound does not become a true sage.
But he whose body— rich with the self, the senses, the objects, and the internal organ—
is rendered favorable through the attainment of the reality of the Self, is indeed liberated from the bond.
If one who performs action should do so with devotion to me,
all that becomes free from the qualities (nirguṇa), grants attainment of my state, and is dear to the self.
Since everything performed for one's own sake causes bondage, whereas that performed for the sake of others bestows liberation.
Having contemplated the state of being male or female as residing within the heart in the form of a knot,
the wise man who abandons delusion will then loosen that bond;
his latent impressions of karma will dissolve, and he shall be liberated, [abiding] by the Self within the Self.
In the abode of desire, the cessation of effort arises for one who is free from thirst;
when the refuge of fulfilled desires is attained, all thirst ceases.
I am the ender of all suffering and defects, and likewise, I am devoid of worldly striving.
Having reflected thus, the man of learning should take refuge in a paramahaṃsa.
Having renounced all actions in Me, he should do so through listening to My stories and the like, through association with My saints, and through the chanting of My divine pastimes. (66–67)
By practicing with me through the state of being devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), they shall attain liberation;
perceiving Me as their own Guru within whatever is seen, heard, or touched,
let a person become virtuous in conduct and then desist from further yoga.

Through devotion, through service, through forgiveness, through freedom from thirst, through endurance, through perceiving faults in *māyā*, through the desire to know, through lack of personal effort,
through my stories, through service to me, through viewing all with an eye of equality toward me, and through the desire to abandon [worldly attachment].
Through inward awareness, through service to those who have attained tranquility, through celibacy, through faith, through mastery of the senses, through the practice of restraints and observances,
through meditation free from negligence and the like, and through knowledge— ||71||
With a yogic disposition, with a mind focused on the essence of being, and with my gracious compassion,
one who has attained my favor should uplift others by uplifting them—
living beings who have fallen into the snare of hope and are carried away by their innate greed. (72–73)

One should not cause those who dwell in ignorance, who crave their desires, who are restless, who are deluded by ritual action, who are dull-witted, and who are intoxicated by the pursuit of mere fragments of pleasure— those who travel on wrong paths and are pervaded by hatred— to fall into the blind well.
And one should apply oneself to that dispassion (*naiṣkarmya*) by which there is indeed eternal peace.
Son, wife, teacher, mother, father, kinsman, husband, sister, friend, companion, children, and caravan—only he who can liberate one is truly all these. (75–76)

Placing *dharma* upon his chest and casting *adharma* behind his back, he who is devoted to Kṛṣṇa with his whole soul is indeed a bull among men and a swan. By virtue of their righteousness, such men are worthy of worship; for they are the most excellent of deities.
The sages, beginning with Brahmā, who are the best among beings, [are so] by means of the powers of Brahman. Those who are endowed with the power of Brahman are declared to be Brāhmaṇas.
All those Brāhmaṇas who are devoted to me are dear to me as great Bhāgavatas.
I weigh the virtuous alone as equal to my own heart, and nothing else;
for wherever an offering is given with faith, I remain there to accept it. Indeed, those very people, who are my own form, are to be served by all creatures.
At every step where honor was shown to me, you were like purifying fires.
I am that very one in person, the embodiment of the virtuous, the conscious preceptor of kings;
I am that supreme one in the form of a swan, bestowing whiteness upon those of auspicious nature.
Having reached the dissolution of great delusion and severed the noose of Death,
the Swan (Haṃsaka) is easily attained here by those rich in villages bound together by knots.
Let those who fashion swans seize the Supreme Swan among their own swans.
Having received this instruction and having made his disciples like swans,
he— clothed in the directions, the enjoyer of Brahman, solitary and most excellent— departed.
He wandered in the forest like one who is dull-witted, blind, mute, deaf, and mad.
He whose mind is devoted to the dharma of both self and others, who is free from the sense of "I," who is blossomed with the smile of fulfillment and contentment in the bliss of Brahman,
who possesses infinite beauty of desire, and who blazes with his own splendor. (86)
The quality of the Blessed One draws away the minds of mature women.
(87) Indeed, whether in a field, a grove, or a forest, one who has adopted the lifestyle of a python—lying down, eats, drinks, chews, and even urinates. (88)
Thus he wandered about with the gait of a cow, a deer, a crow, and so forth;
he was the sovereign of absolute liberation, absorbed in the great bliss of the Self.
Possessing the power to move through water, land, and air, he was endowed with the accomplishment of all purposes.
He did not rejoice even in his heart at the supernatural powers and masteries obtained by chance.
A person should never form a friendship with one whose mind is unstable; for such a friend quickly destroys the long-practiced austerity of the trusting devotee.
Showing only what is sweet and sweet, he casts the yogi into a pit;
for he bestows desire, anger, strife, delusion, fear, and wretchedness.
Though he is the very form of the Blessed Lord, he displays his sovereign power.

Remaining in the state of an Avadhūta and desiring to abandon his own body, he made a morsel of stone and offered it into the fire born of the bamboo. At that moment, the incarnations of Hari arrived there to lead him away. (93–94)
They led the virtuous Ancient Person, whose deeds were perfected by auspiciousness,
with honors, musical instruments, and other offerings, in order to attain the purity of his station:
to Svarga, Janaloka, Tapoloka, Maharloka, Satyaloka, Vairājaka, and Sthāvara.
Having rendered the golden-embryonic (Hiraṇyagarbha) and earthly nectars purifying,
he went to the supreme world of Brahmā, which is the personification of existence, consciousness, and bliss;
there indeed dwell the eternal yogis, the knowers of Brahman, and the divine beings.
"Even though they are eternally satisfied, they drink the supreme Brahman.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have related to you the auspicious account of Merudevī,
as well as the life of Nābhi, whose son was Ṛṣabha Hari.
The small creatures that depend upon it shall become possessed of life;
having become swans, they shall go to the world of Brahmā, the state of absolute liberation.
By reading or hearing this, one shall partake in the state of absolute liberation.

"O Beloved! Whatever benefit is gained from taking refuge [in a teacher], from renouncing the home, from receiving initiation, and from dwelling in the forest—that shall be his through hearing with faith. (101) Thus ends the ninety-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Devotion to the Husband," within the first section on the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. It describes how, through the practice of wifely devotion (*pativratā-dharma*) and the performance of a great worship by Merudevī for Nābhi, the Lord took incarnation as his son Ṛṣabha; it further details his sons such as Yogeśvara and others, his instructions, his forest life, an analysis of the conduct of the ancient *paramahaṃsas*, and the knowledge born of discernment (*viveka-jñāna*).
Chapter Three Hundred and Ninety-Ninth [389] The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā — Section 1 Chapter 390
[The Author: Chapter 391.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to this narrative concerning the world of Vaikuṇṭha.

On the eighth lunar day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika, during the festival of my birth anniversary, I was born upon the earth in the house of Gopāla and Kambharā amidst a great celebration of dance. (1–2)
For that purpose, my attendants in Vaikuṇṭha prepared a great festival;
indeed, Vaikuṇṭha became filled with celebration by my male and female attendants and devotees.
Beautiful pavilions were constructed, adorned with golden finials.
Adorned with plantain trees and other pillars, featuring archways made of Aśoka leaves and the like;
richly beautified by lamps of lightning, resplendent with Vedic instruments and other ornaments; endowed with divine splendor, including beautiful painted banners and rows of necklaces. (4–5)
Richly adorned with the splendor of lion-thrones and the like, beautiful with various foods and drinks,
abounding in sections of dance pavilions and frequented by throngs of dancers;
featuring excellent musical instruments attended by Gandharvas, and surrounded by circles of divine sages.
The houses were also variegated, and mansions were constructed;
they were adorned with divine splendor, and the streets and roads were well-decorated.
All the dwellings were refined, and both men and women were beautifully adorned.
The cows were made to bloom with the great festival of food, drink, and other delights; the young women were adorned with ornaments and graced by garments, jewelry, and the like.
They wore *ajīra* powders upon their limbs and were encircled with decorative flourishes.
Musical instruments were played in every house for that festival;
and songs were heard from all the inhabitants of Vaikuṇṭha.
Then, in the morning, when the golden sky was illuminated by the sun, [the festival proceeded].

Having bathed her own Lord, the Supreme Sovereign Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa— who possesses the splendor of divine celestial damsels, Lakṣmī, Māṇikī, Pārvatī, and Śrī— with nectar-like waters and fragrant, choice sandalwood pastes; || 1-2 ||
Having perfumed [the image] with oils, essences, and the like, and having adorned it with garments and ornaments—
[specifically] with necklaces of gems, diamonds, jewels, and the like, with flowers and articles,
and with crowns, earrings, necklaces, bracelets, chains, and so forth. (13–14)
Adorned with finger-rings, anklets, staffs, earrings, forehead marks, and the like, the Blessed Lord was rendered magnificent by his maidservants;
accompanied by his wives and tens of millions of his own attendants, he shone forth. (15)
Accompanied by maidens, male and female servants, and liberated souls, he entered the assembly hall.
There were shouts of "Victory! as his beloved showered him with flowers, unbroken grains of rice, parched grain, blossoms, precious substances, gold coins, and other offerings. || 16-17 ||
The cane-bearers produced a sound of their rattles that was enchanting to the ears;
those seated in the assembly bowed down, and the subjects of Vaikuṇṭha gazed upon him.
All the attendants, who were devotees of the Lord, honored him in due order.
All the liberated women, the other wives of Kṛṣṇa, and the female servants;
all the maidens, the progeny, and the inhabitants of Vaikuṇṭha—[they were honored] with a tilaka on the forehead and the offering of *darbha* grass upon the ears. (1.390.20)
With a handful of flowers upon his head, with a cluster of blossoms upon his hands,
with strings of pearls around his neck, and with water at the feet of Kṛṣṇa;
by bowing before him in his heart, which is the very self of Nārāyaṇa, with love.
Having honored them with offerings at the feet in the assembly,
they all took their places according to rank, and a wondrous dance commenced.
The musicians sang, and the lords played instruments.
The female singers followed along, and the beaters of rhythm performed the rhythmic beats;
Nārada and others were there, as were women such as Vipracitti;
sages, ascetics, and gods all assembled for that great festival.
Then at that time,

a daughter of the Sāttvata attendant of Nārāyaṇa— eighteen years of age, exceedingly beautiful, and adorned with ornaments— arrived there accompanied by a hundred thousand maidens in order to perform worship. (25–26)
There, a follower of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa who stood by His side—
a preeminent Gandharva named Saliladyumna, born of the Gandharva race—
beheld that woman of excellent limbs and, his eyes flickering with desire, fell in love with her. (27)

Having worshipped Kṛṣṇa, the maiden took water from Kṛṣṇa’s feet, placed it in her mouth, and poured the remainder upon the ground. Recalling only Gāndharva, she cursed him: "Become a human being with diminished wealth and a fickle nature. (28–29)
The Gandharva also perceived Sukanyā’s intention and cursed her: "O human woman, you too shall follow after a man whose wealth is exhausted;
from this place, go forth as a fickle woman until you find a husband."
Having spoken thus and bowed to him, he went to the home of Nārāyaṇa.
At that moment, Cyavana fell upon the earth and was born not from a womb;
he wandered constantly in the forest and remained even within the water.
Remembering his former births, the sage Cyavana, whose body was worn with age, wandered about;
leaning against a bamboo pole on the earth, he performed severe penance.
An anthill grew upon his head, and the bamboo pole also took root there.
Sukanyā, the daughter of the Sātvata, went to the great abode. She reported all that to her father; the Sātvata, a companion of Hari, consoled his own daughter and spoke to the fair-eyed maiden.
"Do not grieve, my daughter! For your sake, I shall indeed become a universal monarch on earth in a second form.
Afterward, you must come to me; I shall destroy your sorrow."
Having spoken thus, the Sāttvata became King Śaryāti on earth.
He was a supreme king, a sovereign of devotees, most devoted to Brahman, and fond of brāhmaṇas;
he was a Vaiṣṇava who remembered his past lives and was the lord of the land from sunrise to sunset.
When a moment of Vaikuṇṭha had passed, Sukanyā came to the earth;
Śaryāti became one hundred thousand years old, while Cyavana was two hundred thousand.
In the house of Śaryāti, there was a daughter, a mind-born (mānasī) girl.

Divine, equal to the divine Rāmā who dwells in Vaikuṇṭha, she is eternally devoted to Nārāyaṇa; auspicious, she is a servant to her parents, supremely dedicated to her husband, and endowed with every extraordinary wonder. (1.390.40–41)

Remembering her former births, that divine woman who traveled through the sky followed the king everywhere— in forests, wildernesses, sacred fords, on the earth, on mountains, in the ocean, in the sky, in heaven, in the netherworld, and upon the battlefield where armies fought.
He remembered the Sun, who was scorching the expanse of his lineage.
Accompanied by her and joined by his army, the king went to the forest;
and she, together with her female companions, was indeed searching for flowers.
She went to where the ascetic sage resided, taking refuge in future service;
and looking toward the south with her flickering eyes,
she beheld him within a lovely and auspicious hole in an anthill, where his pupils were shimmering.
Impelled by fate, the girl pierced [the horse] with a thorn;
blood then flowed out, and there was an obstruction of urine and other excretions in the army.
Seeing that, Śaryāti spoke repeatedly to the distressed soldiers: (46–47)
This must surely be some divine realm, or perhaps gods, sages,
ascetics, or even rākṣasas dwell here in this excellent forest.
Surely some offense has been committed here by me and my army.
Otherwise, there would not be the obstruction of the army's urine and so forth;
for whatever thing, in whatever manner, by whomever,
or wherever it may have arisen, if it has come into being, it must necessarily be manifest.
"If we were protected from the Lord by means of remedies against that [evil], then the girl Sukanyā, remembering her past lives, spoke to her father:
'In this very trunk of the lineage, a pair consisting of light has been observed. (51)

"O King, I pierced the opening of an anthill with a thorn, and from that, blood flowed out; I believe that was my offense. Having understood this, the Sāttvata king himself remembered [the cause]. (52–53)
Having heard the words of his daughter regarding Saliladyu, Sukanyā, and the curse at Vaikuṇṭha,
the king went to the vicinity of the anthill and propitiated the sage who was hidden within it.
The embodied one said, "Give me Sukanyā; [then] my obstruction of urine and other ailments will perish.
The king said, "So be it," and Cyavana rose from the clay.
With a bamboo staff upon his head, he shone like a horned beast.
Right there, his daughter was given to him by Sūrya as witness;
his army became healthy, and the king went to his own home.
Cyavana was pervaded by ascetic power, his body being one whose channels were dried up.

There, in that hermitage, the aged and emaciated [Cyavana] dwelt in a leaf-hut. Having obtained Cyavana as her husband, who was exceedingly irascible, Sukanyā— knowing his mind and understanding the proper time— pleased him through devoted service.
The virtuous wife massaged the body of her aged husband with oil, the essence of flowers, fragrant sandalwood, and other such substances;
she then devotedly caused him to be bathed with warm water.
He offered garments and provided them daily;
he fed him excellent forest fruits, grains, and tubers,
and gave him sweet water brought from a spring to drink.
She had the virtuous lady lie down upon a bed made of plantain leaves;
having kindled the fire, she performed the *agnihotra* sacrifice with excellent juices.
She served the guests who had arrived for the purpose of seeing her.
The virtuous woman performed the service of the deity according to the prescribed rites with faith, using tulasī leaves, lotuses, fruits, and water;
she also brought sacrificial fuel-sticks produced from the pavitra trees standing nearby.
She recited from memory songs, hymns of praise, and sacred knowledge;

thus, by following the will of the sage, that virtuous woman brought him delight. Having attained the highest devotion to her husband, that chaste lady found fulfillment even without the pleasure of sensual desire.

Once, he thought of the two horse-headed sons of the Sun for the sake of restoring the body of the aged sage whose frame was withered; remembered by Sukanyā, the two sons of the Sun appeared in an instant. (67–68)
The two physicians, bowing low, said to her: "Speak, O Mother; salutations unto you.
Sukanyā replied: "So that the body of the sage may become suitable for me—beautiful, endowed with youth, strong, and most heroic—"
"Likewise, let our master be granted a lifespan capable of enjoying pleasures.
"So be it," said the two sons of Aśvin, and having bowed to Cyavana, they chose a share of the Soma at every sacrifice from him. (1.390.70–71)
The sage said to them, "Very well," and then he had them bathe that sage in a pool specially prepared right there, which was filled with elixirs (*rasāyana*).
The sage was indeed twenty years old, a youth who could enchant even goddesses.
Fleshy, handsome, and delightful, his virility was fully developed;
never before had such a being been seen or heard of as having been produced by elixirs.
Even in former times, that form had never been seen or heard of even by Sukanyā.
And in order to test the maiden's devotion to her husband,
those two physicians also assumed different forms through a chemical elixir;
joined with the young sage, they became identical in appearance to him.
As the maiden was looking on, three men were seen rising from the pit (kuṇḍa).
They were identical in appearance, wearing earrings and fine garments;
their bodies were permeated with fragrance, and they were oceans of the essence of beauty.
Wearing divine garlands and possessing splendors like other suns, that virtuous woman, not recognizing her husband, meditated upon him through contemplation:
"Which sage here should be awakened, for whom I am a devoted wife? (78)
"He alone is to be chosen today; the other two must be rejected.
Having reflected thus, Satī produced a great fire from her own body, and enveloped by that fire, she went forth to test those three.
She said to Agni, "Kindle those other two without my beloved.
Thereupon the fire blazed up, and indeed those two others [the wind and the water] also blazed with flames;
meanwhile, they both cried out, having abandoned the sage in order to reduce him to ashes.
With their limbs blazing intensely, they both paid homage to the two most excellent physicians.
For the sake of protection, they made a plea, and by that truth, Vahni was restrained.
Through the power of her devotion to her husband, Satyā offered a garland to Cyavana.
Recognizing her supreme devotion to her husband, the two sons of the Aśvins were satisfied;
having taken leave of the sage and bowed to Satī, they departed for heaven.
Then the sage Cyavana [set out] toward his father-in-law, the king.
He dispatched messengers to that forest to summon him;
Śaryāti, with a very serene soul, arrived at the hermitage of the excellent sage.
Seeing the youth standing by his side, transformed into another form, they both were filled with wonder.
The king became filled with wonder and was distressed in mind.
Seeing her father, the daughter rose and paid him homage.
Then the king said to his daughter: "Why have you left the aged sage?"
"You serve a paramour; you are destroying your husband's and your father's lineage.
(88) Rebuked by her father, the daughter, with a serene mind, said:
"Father! This sage Cyavana is your son-in-law. (89)
The sage then related the entire account and said to the king:
"Welcome to you; may your sovereignty be entirely free from obstacles.
O Great King, perform the sacrifice named Soma at my command."
"O Aśvins, drinkers of Soma, grant me a draught of Soma at this sacrifice.
(91) That King Cyavana performed a sacrifice by his own splendor;
he then caused the two physicians, the Aśvins, to drink the Soma. (92)
Indra, having raised his thunderbolt, came to slay the sage;
Cyavana paralyzed that arm of Hari along with the thunderbolt.
Then they all gave their consent, saying, "He shall always have the Soma draught."
Because he had previously thought that the two physicians were the younger ones and thus excluded them,
the king gave abundant sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) to those who had gone to heaven—
the gods, the brahmins, and the guests— and Cyavana went to his own hermitage.
Śaryāti’s son was Ānarta, who was devoted to Kṛṣṇa.
He brought from Goloka a fragment of a jewel given by Kṛṣṇa;
this is that very land of Ānarta, known as Saurāṣṭra, situated on the shore of the western ocean.
From Ānarta, Revata was born; he founded the city of Kuśasthalī.
His son was Kakudmin, whose daughter was Revatī.
She went with her father to the world of Satya to consult the Grandfather (Brahmā).
"But whom shall I obtain as a suitable husband? she asked; then the Grandfather (Brahmā) said:
"When this period of time has passed, twenty-seven cycles of four yugas will have elapsed on earth, and the original kings and others will have perished."
"Even among those belonging to his lineage and its successive branches, no such mark exists.
Therefore, give my consent to Baladeva, the brother of Kṛṣṇa.
Having been thus addressed, he approached Baladeva and gave her to him.

Kakudmin, however, went to the hermitage of Nara and Nārāyaṇa known as Badarī in order to perform penance; there he constantly worshipped Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have related to you this account devoted to the virtue of wifely fidelity.

From reading or even hearing this *Camatkāra* of Sukanyā, there is the destruction of sins as well as liberation; enjoyment increases further, and O Lakṣmī, when Kṛṣṇa is beloved, one obtains the fruit resulting from service rendered to Him. (103–104)

Thus, in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, it is told how, during the *Jayantī* festival on the bright eighth day of the month of *Urgā* in Vaikuṇṭha, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa was engaged in dancing and other festivities; at that time, due to a curse incurred by the glance of the flickering eyes of Sukanyā—a daughter of the Sāttvata clan—upon the water-dwelling Gandharva Yugāndhara, they both descended to the earth, he becoming Cyavana and she the daughter of Śaryāti. Subsequently, in the forest, when the eyes of Cyavana were pricked by the tip of a thorn, his army suffered from the obstruction of urine, feces, and so forth.

The three hundred and ninetieth chapter, titled "The Description of Kanyāyāñca, Cyavana’s Household Life, His Attainment of Fresh Youth through the Aśvinīkumāras, the Test of His Wifely Devotion, the Two Physicians’ Entitlement to a Share of the Soma at the Sacrifice, and the Marriage of Revatī to Kakudmin— the son of Śaryāti and grandson of Ānarta— by means of Baladeva. || 390 ||
