Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the wonder of service to one’s husband, hearing which the doubts of devoted wives indeed come to an end. (1)
The husband is the very form of Kṛṣṇa, and Śrī Kṛṣṇa exists in the form of the husband;
Hari himself exists in every way for the sake of the wife's welfare.
As the husband, he performs various activities like an ordinary person.
Nevertheless, she is considered meritorious by virtue of her devotion to her husband.
For the highest good indeed resides in that very state of a devoted wife;
for even Adharma becomes a bull when he is thus propitiated.
A devoted wife should always do what brings pleasure to her husband;
by acting thus, she attains great joy together with her husband.
Whatever [is offered] to the gods, whatever to the ancestors, whatever to guests, and whatever to herself—
A devoted wife should indeed perform all that for the sake of her husband.
By the very service she renders to her husband, that virtuous woman enjoys half of his merit;
she always partakes in her husband’s spiritual merit and shall dwell for a long time in the world of her husband.
As long as the sun and moon endure, so long shall she remain like a goddess in heaven;
there and there, the virtuous woman shall be immersed in great happiness and bliss.
I shall now describe the service to her husband performed by a devoted Brahmin wife.
In the city of Pratiṣṭhāna there lived a young Brahmin named Kauśika, who was an expert in Vedic rites, a treasury of beauty and virtue,
devoted to storytelling and narration, and surrounded by many disciples and grand-disciples. (9–10)
He constantly practices righteousness and performs meritorious acts of charity;
devoted to the six duties and likewise engaged in the affairs of the king,
he always moves about as a trusted confidant within the inner apartments and among the circle of women.

He was the awakener of the queens and likewise the instructor of the maidens; most excellent in his mastery of the arts and dexterity, he was proficient in the knowledge of reality. By virtue of his counsel, he attended the festivals of the kings and their queens.
On the day of the king’s birth, the brahmin went to the assemblies by invitation;
there were various dancers, instrumentalists, and singers, who were like goddesses, golden-hued, sixteen years of age, and well-honored. (14)

Commanded by the king, they sang, danced, and played instruments. (15) For association is powerful, O Lakṣmī! Whosoever’s association arises, the mind of that individual becomes colored by it, like a crystal or similar object. (16)
Whatever kind of perception arises, a corresponding desire proceeds;
and for one who is deluded, an inclination toward obtaining objects of enjoyment is produced. Previously well-refined, the intellect becomes defiled when possessed by delusion. (17)
For one who is insatiable and full of craving, the acquisition of wealth becomes a mere servant.
This brahmin Kauśika had a wife who was devoted to her husband; she was a young woman named Śaibyā, a servant who carried out her husband’s commands as if they were the supreme command of the Lord.
Considering the supreme scriptural injunctions concerning the highest good, he followed them;
nevertheless, he indeed became happy through his virtuous wife and servant.
Whenever he went to the royal assembly, which was filled with the delights of dance, song, and graceful sport, [he remained content].
Then, O twice-born one, seeing those sixteen-year-old courtesans with moon-like faces—
who were skilled in the display of gestures (*hāva*) and emotions (*bhāva*), radiant with the beauty of love,
and possessing the hue of golden *campaka* flowers— that man became filled with desire.
There, the Brahmin indeed appointed one woman, rich in physical beauty and fit for enjoyment.
Then, by chance, he arrived at his home, severely afflicted by the disease of fever.
Indeed, a state of blood and water arose within his body.
From that, leprosy of the skin arose, as well as oozing leprosy on his nails.
Thus afflicted by disease and excessively tormented by the malady of love,
he burned within his heart and did not obtain even a moment’s sleep.
That virtuous wife, being well-behaved, serves her husband with her whole being;
regarding him as the Supreme Self, she feels no aversion.
She constantly washes his nails and other limbs with warm water.
He caused her to bathe properly and likewise provided her with clothing and other necessities. (27) There was a brahmin who was a disciple of Atri; his wife was Suśīlā, a devoted wife.
Anasūyā became his excellent disciple, possessing the true wealth of knowledge, dharma, and other virtues. (28)
Therefore, that virtuous woman constantly gratified her husband with her body, mind, intellect, actions, speech, and service. One day, the Brahmin, releasing a sigh, spoke to that faithful wife.
Sleep does not come to me; my mind is constantly burning.
Since the day I saw that courtesan in the royal assembly, I have a desire to enjoy her. Tell me, O wife, what shall I do?
"The fire of desire, centered on the courtesan, burns within my heart.
My feet are afflicted with leprosy and my hands are severed; being thus diseased, how can I obtain her?
O wife, if you can bring her to me, I shall attain a happy state."
"Otherwise, if she possesses latent impressions (*vāsanā*), her descent into the lower realms at death is certain.

(3.3) Having been told this, that virtuous and chaste woman bowed at her husband's feet and said: "Oh, what great fortune! Oh, what great fortune! I shall indeed bring satisfaction to my husband. (3.4)
I shall indeed act in such a way that my master may obtain a courtesan;

likewise, she who is endowed with good fortune must be understood as a wife who performs meritorious deeds. She who, when commanded by her husband for his satisfaction, immediately bestows satisfaction upon him—[she is a true wife].
"That service alone by which the master is satisfied, and never any other"— having said this,
the virtuous woman took leave of her husband and went to that house.
Bowing at the feet of the courtesan, the virtuous woman said, "Do what is pleasing."
"O sister! You are worthy of honor by my husband; day and night he remembers you.
Meditating upon none other than you in his heart, the Brahmin finds no sleep.
Having become your servant, I shall perform service for you."
"O most excellent lady, please delight my husband; whatever you desire, I shall give it to you.
Having been addressed thus, she asked for the name and wealth of the brahmin.
Then that courtesan revealed everything to that virtuous woman.
The virtuous woman said: "How indeed can I give my consent to one who is so afflicted?
Nevertheless, out of greed for wealth, I shall please your husband.
Give me a hundred silver coins here every night."
"Bring you into my house and make you my husband upon my bed.
If you yourself will always wash my clothes smeared with leprosy, as well as my hands and other limbs, then I shall grant you the fulfillment of your desire. (42–43)
"Give him golden ornaments and let him enjoy his desires.
Having been thus commanded, she became exceedingly joyful within her heart.
Meanwhile, she placed her husband upon her own shoulders and gave him whatever wealth he required.
He united with the beautiful courtesan Sundarī.
After many days, the master, satiated by the god of love, said to his wife: "O virtuous lady! May you possess an eternal place here in the world of the chaste. (45–46)
"Tonight, on our final night, take me and provide me with enjoyment;
afterwards, having become eternally satisfied, I shall have no desire for the house of a courtesan.
Having been addressed thus, that virtuous wife placed her good husband upon her shoulder.
At night, he went along a path shrouded in blinding darkness toward the courtesan.
Just then, O beloved, a great obstacle arose; listen!
A great sage named Māṇḍavya was staying at the foot of a tree during that night.
Then, by that very same path, the thieves, having stolen much royal wealth,
departed; the king's officers, pursuing them from all sides,
bound them and led them to the royal palace, seizing Māṇḍavya as well.
Then, suspecting him to be a thief though he was no thief,
the servants impaled Māṇḍavya upon a stake on the road while he was in that state; having thus placed him on the stake,
they returned to their own homes, and Māṇḍavya became filled with suffering.
Then that devoted and virtuous wife, having placed her husband Kauśika upon her shoulders while he was afflicted with grief, proceeded along the path shrouded in darkness;
as she went, her husband remained upon her shoulder.
That twice-born man shook Māṇḍavya, who was afflicted by extreme suffering.
Enraged by the treading upon his feet, Māṇḍavya said to him:
"At sunrise, death shall come to him by whom I have been shaken with his foot. (54–55)
Hearing that, his wife said:
"If I am devoted to my husband and dedicated to my lord, then by the great merit of my service to my husband, let the path of the sun be blocked. (56)
By her, indeed, everything was set in motion exactly as it had been described.
(57) Thereupon, the horses of the Sun, though being urged on, became fixed; they attained a state of stillness and, becoming paralyzed, could not proceed further. (58)
Then, due to the absence of sunrise, it became perpetual night.
That virtuous woman, having led her husband away and provided him with the pleasures of a courtesan,
and having caused her husband to be satisfied, went back once more to her own home.
Having bathed her husband according to the prescribed rite and washed away his leprosy and bodily impurities,
she herself bathed and likewise massaged her husband with fragrant unguents and other ointments.
She presented him with garments, ornaments, flower garlands, incense, lamps, and other offerings.
The virtuous woman gave him milk to drink and performed every act of worship;
her husband was satisfied, and all the prosperity of the household fell under the control of the courtesan.
Then the chaste woman thought of Lakṣmī, and Lakṣmī arrived there.
Having been saluted and honored, the truthful Lakṣmī then gave him a *cintāmaṇi* jewel;
and having bestowed words of blessing, she departed for her own abode.
Satī, by means of the *cintāmaṇi*, provided an abundance of wealth and grain.
All household utensils, ornaments, and finger-rings;
divine juices as well as enjoyments, the abundance of sweet foods and water—then, at the non-rising of the Sun, the gods fell into fear. (65)
They went to Brahmā for refuge, and the Lotus-born One said to them:
"Because of the greatness of this devoted wife, the sun does not rise;
for the splendor of a devoted wife’s asceticism is greater than the splendor of the sun."
Due to the non-rising of the sun, there would likewise be the destruction of mortal living beings;
there would be the cessation of the twilight worship, offerings, and sacrifices.
Furthermore, there would be the end of the meals for the gods, the eminent sages, and the ancestors.
Without the rising of the sun, [the world] will surely perish; of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, for the sake of desiring the rising of the sun, you must indeed propitiate the chaste and virtuous wife of Kauśika, who serves him.
Having received this command from Brahmā, the gods, sages,
and seers went to that place where the leper resided with his wife in his home.
Having arrived with dejected faces, they were indeed hospitably received by the woman.
They were honored, saluted, and questioned regarding the reason for their arrival.
(72) All of them, having been worshipped with seats, water for the feet, and other offerings for the sake of their comfort, bowed repeatedly to Satī after announcing their purpose. (73)
"O Goddess! Since you have now cast the Māṇḍavya curse upon your own husband, and since you have caused the non-rising of the sun—both of these are indeed destructive to the worlds.
What should be done here by the Goddess so that there may be welfare for the world?"
"O virtuous lady, show mercy and act so that both objectives may be fulfilled:
that the husband’s life and the rising of the Sun-god may bring happiness, and that the word of Māṇḍavya may likewise become true. (75–76)
Then, at that place, Atri’s wife Anasūyā—venerated by the world, the preceptor’s wife of Kauśika, and a virtuous woman—spoke to Suśīlā:
"Listen, daughter! I shall tell you what must be done; it is a triad."
The gods have come here; their request, which is for our benefit, must be fulfilled in every way by you, O Mother, and by me as well. Speak, and holding water in your hand, let the Sun rise.
"Speak, daughter! Let the two divine physicians make your husband free from disease.
For in this case, the destruction of the husband's illness is considered equivalent to the destruction of the husband himself;
the very body of your lord is reckoned as his death. (1.391.80)
"Your husband shall indeed become a youth of divine form, like a god.
Having been thus propitiated, the wife caused the rising of the sun and restored her beloved, sick husband, to life. 81–82.
She caused her husband to become a new god through two sons of the Sun;
having thus brought about the rising of the Sun, she restored her husband to life.
In an instant, Kauśika became endowed with strength, valor, and power.
Refined by the elixir (*rasāyana*) of the Aśvinī-kumāras,
she worshipped all the gods and then dismissed them;
she attended upon that lover of splendor and attained the great bliss of Brahman.
Māṇḍavya said to King Yama, "Tell me the fruit of my past action.
Yama replied, "In your childhood, at the age of five, while you were playing,
a grass-woodpecker was pierced by you with a sharp thorn out of ignorance."
"You have obtained that fruit here—the state of being pierced by a stake; do not grieve.
Then Māṇḍavya spoke words of dharma, consisting of justice:
"For a five-year-old child who acts entirely according to his own will..."
Corruption, sin, and punishment—all these do not exist at all for one who possesses awakening;
however, for his parents, that sin remains until the age of ten.
After ten years, both the instruction and the sin shall come to pass. (89)
"I have no such sin; why then have you been impaled upon the stake?
Therefore, you must experience the fruit of that [sin]. Be a Dharma in the four ages:
pierced by the dharma of Tretā, and likewise pierced by Dvāpara."
"Pierced by Kali, you shall suffer misery upon reaching the earth;
let there be the state of a Śūdra for you day and night, pierced as you are by the stake of unrighteousness.
Thus cursed, Dharmarāja removed him from the stake.
He begged for forgiveness regarding the spear and was made free from pain by the Aśvin;
having joined it and filled it, he restored it to its former state.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, has been told to you this account, which is devoted to wonders.
In this practice of devotion to one’s husband (*pātivratya*), even sin gives rise to merit,
and unrighteousness attains the state of righteousness through its power, O beloved!
Devotion to one’s husband is a great dharma that purifies all embodied beings.
Formerly, this twice-born man committed an act that caused suffering to a wretched person.
By that very act of violence, he has become afflicted with leprosy in this birth.
Previously, however, he did give gifts of three Gaurī-kanyās.
By that merit, there shall be a devoted wife in the house of the brahmin; and through the recitation and hearing of this, there shall be enjoyment, liberation, and happiness. 98.

Thus, in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, within the *Pativratā-māhātmya* of the *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*: the leper Kauśika, a Brahmin who was infatuated with a prostitute, was made to unite with that prostitute by his chaste wife Suśīlā; furthermore, when Māṇḍavya was impaled on a stake, Kauśika met his death before sunrise due to the pressure of Māṇḍavya’s feet, whereupon Suśīlā caused the sun not to rise as a result of her curse; subsequently, at the request of the gods, Suśīlā brought about the cessation of the curse and other afflictions for Dharma.

And the definition of the form of retribution in the various ages as the state of being subject to the specific dharma of each respective age—this is the three hundred and ninety-first chapter [391] of the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Book 1: The Continuation of the Kṛta Age.
Chapter 392.
[The Author: Chapter 393.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Mahāpadmā Lakṣmī! [to this] narrative that destroys all sins.
Listen to this beautiful discourse, which brings peace and bestows liberation upon those who hear it.
In a former age, there was a king of great prowess named Śatrujit,
by whom sacrifices were performed and through whom the gods, including Indra, were gratified.
His son was of great heroism and possessed divine power;
known as Ṛtadhvaja, he was a king among yogis who could travel through the sky.
Constantly attended by supernatural powers, he was an ocean of the qualities of realized wisdom.
To him, for whom nothing remains unknown and whose scholarship is supreme in every respect—
having heard of his unsurpassed fame, the lords of the fourteen worlds,
the sages, the seers, and the nāgas indeed come to behold him. (4–5)
Then, after some time, two Naga youths, the sons of Aśvatara, came from the world of the Nagas to the surface of the earth;
disguised in the form of Brahmins, they were young and pleasing to behold.
Having paid their respects upon seeing him, they departed and then returned again.
In this way, they always came and went with great affection;
and that prince attained supreme bliss through them.
Without them, the son neither ate, nor bathed, nor drank wine;
he neither took delight nor grasped anything without those two.
Indeed, for a long time, they spent much of their time in the presence of the prince.
Once, in that netherworld (pātāla), their father asked those two young nāgas: "By whom is our friendship maintained in the mortal world,
where you two fine sons spend so much time?"
The two of them said: "The son of Śatrujit is named Ṛtadhvaja;
he is handsome, endowed with uprightness, learned, friendly, and a mine of virtues.
He is devoted to his master and hospitable to guests; our minds have been captivated by him."
"O dear one! Without him, no happiness indeed arises here for us.
The father said: "Blessed is he whose virtues are thus proclaimed even in his absence by those who possess virtue; such a life is truly blessed."
A father truly possesses sons through whom his friends describe his virtues, his enemies his prowess, and others proclaim them in the assembly hall;
by him alone is a son’s purpose fulfilled, providing even a slight satisfaction to the heart.
Whatever gold, gems, vehicles, or seats are in my house,
and whatever else may be for his pleasure— that should be given without hesitation.
The gods desire the constant prosperity of one who performs such service.

And the two sons said: "O Father! Whatever jewels, vehicles, seats, conveyances, ornaments, and garments are in that house—none such exist in the three worlds, nor is there knowledge equal to it elsewhere. (18)
"He has one task to perform that cannot be accomplished by anyone other than a lord.
The father said: "What is impossible or difficult for a resolute man?
For those who exert themselves, there is nothing unattainable or inaccessible, whether in heaven or here on earth."
"Therefore, my sons, tell me; I understand this to be incurable.
The two sons said to their father: "Once, the brahmin Gālava arrived at Śatrujit, bringing with him an excellent horse."
"A certain Daitya is devouring living beings in my hermitage," he said.
"He likewise creates obstacles for my meditation and even my silence. If I were to consume him with anger, then my ascetic merit would be destroyed."
"Therefore, O King, the destruction of the Daityas must indeed be carried out by you in accordance with dharma.
Once, O King, having observed a Daitya in distress, I let forth this sigh;
and from that [sigh], this horse emerged from the sky."
Sent by the Sun, he arrived, moving unhindered through the three worlds.
He will wander tirelessly and eternally throughout the entire circle of the earth—in the mountains, the oceans, the subterranean realms, and the fires. (25–26)
Therefore, he shall attain fame in the world by the name Kuvalaya;
and having mounted this [weapon], Ṛtadhvaja will slay the Daitya.
O King, command your son so that dharma is not violated.
At his word, the king placed that son Ṛtadhvaja upon the jewel among horses, for whom the auspicious marriage-thread had been fastened,
and dispatched him; he himself went to the sage’s hermitage along with the sage.
And Ṛtadhvaja destroyed the obstacles in the hermitage;
that Daitya, having assumed the form of a boar, had come to assault the sage.
Seeing him, [the sage] quickly mounted that horse.
Armed with his bow, he whose banner is Truth pursued that boar.
Struck by the arrow, the fleeing deer entered a vast forest;
terrified, it fell into a cave shrouded in a mass of darkness.
Following him, the prince also, mounted on his horse, rushed forward to slay; meanwhile,
the boar became invisible,
while the prince beheld a magnificent realm in Pātāla, crowded with golden palaces.
He saw that the city was empty, including its walls, and he entered it.
There, an excellent woman was seen; she led him into the interior of the house, to a couch made entirely of gold upon the palace floor.
He showed him a young maiden with full breasts,
with lips like the bimba fruit, slender-limbed, and with eyes like blue lotuses;
she had red, elevated nails, was delicate, gold-complexioned, and possessed beautiful hair.
Then, upon seeing the prince endowed with such splendor, that young woman was infatuated;
overcome by agitation, she desired the king as her husband.
When questioned by Ṛtadhvaja, she related her own story.

O King, there is a king of the Gandharvas in heaven known as Viśvāvasu; I am his daughter, renowned by the name Madālasā. Devoted to my husband, regarding him as my very life, I have always remained for the sake of my husband.
"I await my husband, a worthy man who is as dear to me as my own life. While I was in the garden gathering flowers,
the demon Pātālaketu seized me and brought me here."
O King, on the coming thirteenth day, he is prepared to take my hand in marriage; however,
he has assumed the form of a boar and has been pierced by someone with arrows for the sake of protecting the sages.
"O King, having killed him while he remains hidden, take me away.
Tell me quickly, who are you? Even if you are already known, you will become a vessel of my love by revealing your own conduct."
"Are you a god, a Daitya, a Gandharva, a Pannaga, or even a Kinnara? Tell me that truly, so that my mind may be free from doubt.
Then Kuvalayāśva, whose banner is Truth (Ṛtadhvaja), spoke with a gracious heart.
The son of King Śatrujit came to the hermitage of Gālava. Having run behind a Daitya in the form of a boar who was struck by my iron arrow, I fell here into a pit in Pātāla.
"By name I am Ṛtadhvaja, and also Kuvalayāśva.
This is the account I have related; I am neither a god nor a Dānava, nor a serpent, nor a Gandharva, nor a Kinnara, O lady of pure smiles!"
"I am a man; O beloved, I shall protect you from the Daitya!
Having heard this, the maiden was overjoyed, her hair standing on end with thrill;
she rejoiced, thinking, "He for whose sake I was created has finally arrived."
And she said to him: "My heart perceives stability in you;
though I am one who remembers my past births, O King, I belong only to you and I remember [you].
Beauty goes to the moon alone, and radiance goes to the sun.
Prosperity attends the fortunate, steadfastness the wise, and forbearance the virtuous man.
"O beloved, accept me as your wife; quickly destroy this Rākṣasa!
Then Ṛtadhvaja said, "I am indeed under the authority of another."
"What can I do without the permission of my parents? I am not one to act contrary to them.
Madalasa, the virtuous wife, replied, "I shall carry out my father's word.
Having said this, she took water in her hand and invoked Tumburu.
Tumburu arrived instantly; having bowed, he asked the virtuous lady, "From where [have you come]?
(55). "O Queen of the Gods! Tell me, for I have been remembered; I shall accomplish that in an instant.
Madālasā said to Tumburu, her family preceptor: "O Guru! (56).
"Go quickly and inform Śatrujit that Madālasā desires to make Ṛtadhvaja her husband; give your approval.
Then Tumburu, by means of the vidyā called antardhāna, traveled through the path of the sky.
Having gone to Śatrujit and reported the news, and having received his command, he took up sacrificial fuel and kuśa grass;
then, with Madālasā’s great affection, he returned there again in an instant. (58–59)
Having kindled the fire and offered oblations, that knower of mantras, having performed the auspicious rites,
gave his daughter according to the marriage rite to Ṛtudhvaja.
Then the sage Tumburu returned once more to his own hermitage to practice asceticism.
The maiden said to that peaceful woman, "O fair-faced one, I have achieved my purpose!
O mother, command me to go to my husband’s home.
Then Kuṇḍalā said, "O devoted wife, may you be successful in your aim!"
"Though her sins have been washed away by the waters of sacred fords, she would not have become such as she is now—
purified by union with him and become a savior from the cycle of existence. Now,
impelled by the weight of my affection, I shall tell you something."
Indeed, a wife must always be supported and protected by her husband.
A wife is a companion to her husband for the complete attainment of dharma, artha, and kāma.
Where both wife and husband follow one another in mutual harmony, [there the household prospers].

In that regard, there is a connection between virtue (*dharma*), wealth (*artha*), and pleasure (*kāma*), as well as with liberation (*mokṣa*); likewise, a wife is necessary for her husband in the pursuit of virtue and the other goals,
whether for the sake of liberation in heaven, in the realm of truth (*satya*), in the world of Virāj, or upon the surface of the earth.
For the fourfold duty based on both [parents] is not possible;
the worship of deities, ancestors, servants, and guests cannot be performed by one alone. In this matter, the couple is the cause [of its fulfillment]. (67–68)
Even wealth acquired by men and brought to their own home comes to ruin without a wife, or even when one relies upon a bad wife.
Thus have I spoken regarding your eternal state of matrimony.
May you increase together with this [husband] in wealth, sons, happiness, and long life. But you, O girl Madālasā, having abandoned the intoxication of pride toward your husband,
become through this beloved one even more exalted than heaven itself.
Having spoken thus, Madālasā ceased; Ṛtadhvaja embraced Kuṇḍalā, mounted his horse, and leapt into the path of the sky.
Seeing this, the Daityas cried out in distress.
"The jewel of a maiden has been brought here; seize it, seize it in the sky!"—shouting "Stay! Stay!", they rained down a net of arrows. But Ṛtadhvaja also effortlessly cut through that net of arrows.
Then, taking up the Tvaṣṭra-weapon, he hurled it at the Dānavas;
by that weapon, all those Dānavas were reduced to heaps of shattered bones.
He quickly returned to his own city together with the jewel among women.
Having prostrated, he reported all of that to his father.
Having heard it, the father embraced his excellent son with affection and said:
"O son, I have been delivered by you, my great-souled and virtuous son!"
The sages were saved from dangers, and the maiden was protected and brought back;
whatever fame, wealth, or other prowess had been acquired by his father, he who is capable should make it exceed that through his own valor and increase his power. (78)
They say that he brings forth this best of men as something new.
"Therefore, I am blessed," he said, "having obtained such a son among those endowed with merit.
Today I have become truly praiseworthy by virtue of you, who are endowed with the True Dharma."
Fie on the life of that man who is devoid of his own prowess, wisdom, generosity, and other such virtues, yet is known in the world only through his father.
One is eminent and excellent by one's own self; one is middling by virtue of one's father and grandfather.
That lowest of men attains fame through his mother’s side and through his mother herself.
Therefore, my son! May you prosper happily with wealth and valor;
let not this daughter of a Gandharva be separated from you. (82–83)
Thus his father and mother spoke pleasant words to him again and again,
and blessings were also bestowed by the sage Gālava.
Then the son, together with his wife, [accepted] the duties of kingship and the life of a householder.
Protecting [her] and increasing their affection, he lived happily in joy with his virtuous wife.
Madālasā, a devoted wife who remembered her past lives, bowed at the feet of her mother-in-law and father-in-law and took delight with her husband, her own protector. (85–86)
When a great deal of time had passed in this manner, the king spoke again to his son:
"Go quickly and wander the earth for the protection of the brahmins.
Mounting this horse, carry out your circuit throughout the realm. (87)

"O son, act in such a way that there shall be no harm to the sages and the virtuous from the wicked Dānavas; protect them accordingly! He, however, wandered repeatedly over the earth exactly according to the instructions given by his father.
On the bank of the Yamunā, he saw the Daitya Tālaketu,
the younger brother of the Daitya who had taken the form of a boar, appearing in the guise of a sage.
Remembering their former enmity, that Daitya spoke to him there.
"O Prince! I am a sage, and I shall perform a sacrifice there.
Give me that excellent golden ornament of yours for my neck;
meanwhile, protect this hermitage of mine even while I remain within the water."
"I shall go to my hermitage after praising Varuṇa with Vedic mantras.
To the sage who had spoken thus, he gave a neck-ornament and said,
"I will remain here until your return."
Thus addressed, that demon in the guise of a sage submerged into the water.
Then, rising up before Madālasā, he spoke while weeping:
"The hero Kuvalayāśva is near my hermitage. (94–95)
Pierced in the chest with a spear by some wicked Daitya, he died;
yet, being reduced to ashes, he gave me his neck-ornament.
That Daitya seized my horse, and all of this has been observed by me.
"O Queen, take these ornaments and let the subsequent rites be performed!
Having said this and cast them upon the ground, he departed as he had come.
Hearing this, Madālasā and the others broke into lamentation.
Having gone outside and bathed, they offered water even to their son;
but the devoted wife, reflecting that she was inauspicious without her husband,
established a meditative concentration within her heart and produced fire inside herself.
Having dissolved her body, Sundarī indeed went to heaven.
Searching for her own husband there, she did not find him;
she then went to King Yama and asked, "Where is my husband?"
Then the King of Dharma said: "He is alive on the bank of the Yamunā.
For the sake of restoring you to life, your husband’s dear friend, a serpent, is performing penance before Śaṅkara in Pātāla."
"Remain here in my abode of dharma for as long as you wish, remaining invisible.
Thus she dwelt there in that house of dharma on this earth;
meanwhile, that Daitya Tālaketu emerged from the waters of the Yamunā.
He said to the prince, "I have been made successful by you;
go now to your home. Having heard this from the sage, he prostrated himself before him, mounted his horse, and set out for his own city.
He saw people who were first agitated, and then again with joyful faces:
"Aha! His obstacle has passed; he truly lives.
The report of his death has proven false. Live long, O young prince! (1.06–1.07)
Having heard these words of the citizens, he entered his father’s house;
the father, mother, kinsmen, friends, and people all rejoiced.
Not seeing Madālasā, the son questioned his father.
Having learned the news that it was not Aghata, he grieved for a moment.
Then, steadying his mind, he reflected again:
"If she has died on my account, I too shall give up my life."
"What service for the next world have I rendered to my wife through my husband?
Therefore, I believe that in this matter, the wife must renounce enjoyment;
whatever recitation and other rites are necessary so that her liberation may indeed occur, those must be performed."
"No other wife shall be taken by me; I have observed the vow of celibacy.
O Ṛtadhvaja, if Madālasā is not here as my wife, then certainly I cannot be the husband of another woman, for I am devoted to the vow of a faithful wife."
"Without that fawn-eyed daughter of the Gandharvas, I shall not enjoy any other woman; I speak this truth.
Except for that wife of mine who practices the true dharma and is devoted to her husband, I shall not take another."
"I shall not accept any [other] woman; this I speak as the truth.
Having heard these words of his two sons, the King of Serpents himself performed supreme asceticism and obtained a boon from Śaṅkara.
"Queen Madālāsā must be given to Ṛtadhvaja;
she resides within that very creation, so she must be taken from there by all means.
Having made this vow, he then took leave of his two sons.

Having gone to a sacred ford in the Himalayas, he performed most severe penance. That lord of the Nāgas, Aśvatara, being devoted to it, praised Hara at dawn, at night, at midday, and during both twilights.
After a long time, he said, "Let a boon be chosen.
Having bowed down, Aśvatara replied, "Grant me this boon:
the virtuous Madalasa, the wife of Kuvalayāśva, has died."
"By that very age, let her immediately become my daughter;
let her be born in my house as a virtuous woman, remembering her former births, endowed with beauty as before, a yoginī and a mother of yoga. || 121-122 ||
Hara said, "Let it be so; all this shall indeed be yours.
By my grace, perform the śrāddha ceremony according to your desire, without doubt.
And you may eat the prasāda from that middle hood."

The auspicious Madālasā, devoted to her husband, will be reborn. That virtuous woman now shines resplendent in the abode of Dharmarāja, awaiting her rebirth with a husband who remembers his former lives.
"And that beautiful daughter of yours shall be the beloved of Ṛtadhvaja.
Having spoken thus, Śaṅkara then vanished there,
and the king of serpents went to his home in Rasātala and performed the offered *śrāddha*.
In that same manner, he duly consumed the middle portion of the *piṇḍa*.
At that moment, Dharmarāja also said to her: "Go to the netherworld (rasātala).
There, the lord of the Aśvatara Nāgas remembers his excellent daughter."

"Be born as a divine maiden, produced from the mind, possessing perfect youth as soon as you are born, with beautiful hips and being a virtuous daughter; obtain your desired husband, Ṛtadhvaja. Having been addressed thus, she later returned from the funeral rite and took birth.
She shone like the maiden Sundarī of old when she was sixteen years of age.
Madly languid, she awaited her beloved during the three states [of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep].
Then that king of nagas, Aśvatara, spoke to his two sons:
"That prince, who has been a benefactor to you both, why is he not brought into my presence, my children? He must also be seen by me.
When they were thus addressed, the two sons went and engaged in some other conversation.
They spoke with affection regarding his return to their own home.
Considering himself [their] own, Ṛtadhvaja rose from his excellent seat,
bowed at the feet of his father, and departed for Nāgapura along with him.
That auspicious city was shown to them by those two Naga princes,
adorned with young and old Nagas of divine stature,
and made exceedingly beautiful by enchanting Naga maidens playing there. (1.35)
Then Ṛtadhvaja entered their dwelling with them.
There he beheld his father-in-law, wearing jeweled earrings,
adorned with celestial garlands and garments, handsome like a divine god.
Adorned with necklaces as beautiful as strings of clear pearls,
wearing armlets, he sat upon a magnificent throne made entirely of gold,
[resting] upon a form veiled by a lattice of jewels, coral, and lapis lazuli.
As he sat there with his two sons, he was shown to Ṛtadhvaja.
The prince bowed repeatedly to the father of his two friends.
The lord of elephants then embraced the prince firmly and with great force.
Having smelled the crown of his head, he said, "Live long!
Having destroyed the host of your enemies, perform service to your parents.
O child, the virtues of you, who are blessed, are being recounted by my two sons."
The life of the virtuous is praiseworthy; one devoid of virtue is dead even while living.
(142) Deities, ancestors, Brahmins, friends, supplicants, kinsmen, and enemies—likewise, both those on one's own side and others—all desire that the virtuous live long. (143)

"O Prince, the birth of virtuous people like you— who refrain from censuring others, who are compassionate toward those in miserable states— is truly fruitful. Having spoken thus, he bathed him and adorned him with sincere devotion.
Having caused him to enjoy pleasures such as drinking honey-wine and likewise providing food,
and having gratified him with various foods and drinks, the King of the Nāgas gave him a bed for rest and sent Nāga maidens to serve him. (145–146)
Then the king’s son, being weary, fell into a pleasant sleep; the maidens served him most diligently with massages and other attentions. (147)

Thus, in the *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, in the first section concerning the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga, within the account of the majesty of devoted wives (*pativratā*), [is described] the friendship of Ṛtadhvaja—the son of Śatrujit—with the two sons of the horse-ear serpent (*aśvatara-nāga*); his obtaining a divine horse; his entry into the netherworld (*pātāla*) to slay the Daitya who was creating obstacles at the hermitage of Gālava; how he beheld Madālasā in that city, slew the Daitya Pātālaketu, married Madālasā, and [married] Tumburu’s daughter Kuṇḍalā.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Then, at dawn, King Ṛtadhvaja’s son, with auspicious rites, [proceeded].
Awakened by musical instruments, songs, and stories of the underworld (pātāla),
as well as by Naga maidens with exceedingly sweet voices;
bathed, clothed, adorned, honored, and decorated.
He was fed and given drink, repeatedly delighted with pleasant touches,
and entreated in many ways to accept jewels and other gifts—
whether silver, gold, clothing, vehicles, or seats. (3)
Or rather, having been informed for the purpose of taking what was highly desired;
then Ṛtadhvaja spoke to Aśvatara, the yogi of the Nāgas:

"O Father, while you have been ruling this earth for thousands of years, nothing has been lacking; indeed, heaven itself exists within my home.
Even there, however, the illusory splendor of the Sātvatas is truly as insignificant to me as a blade of grass."
In this matter, people are surely greedy and utterly deceived by the illusions of the Creator.
(7) By this exceedingly sweet speech of yours, characterized by a nature of hospitality, I have achieved my life’s purpose; indeed, my life has become fruitful through your disposition. (8)
Life is indeed meaningful through a father, and life is happy through a mother;
likewise, life is fruitful through health, sovereignty, service to the elderly,
and through the mercies of those like you.
Then Aśvatara said: "O gentle one, you possess the happiness of the householder's life with a wife, or do you not? Tell me, are you a knower of Brahman?
Thus questioned, he replied: "My wife is devoted to her husband."
The daughter of the Gandharva king, renowned by the name Madālasā,
was deceived by someone with whom she had a grudge and abandoned her body.
From that time forward, I made this vow in the world:
"No other woman shall become my wife, with the exception of Madālāsā.
Beginning from that point, I have always been devoted to the vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*).
Indeed, by means of celibacy, the Vairāja worlds were fashioned.
A world of liberation has been fashioned for one devoted to celibacy (*brahmacarya*).
It is proclaimed in the *Saṃhitā* that this is the attainment of human birth;
that attainment is for my sake, as well as for the vow of a devoted wife (*ekapatnīvrata*). (15)
Then the mule said: "Listen, O prince!
You prosper constantly through good fortune and by virtue of your vow of having only one wife. Through your devotion to your wife, your spouse flourishes with conjugal bliss. (16–17)
When Queen Madālasā heard of her husband’s destruction,
she attained dissolution through meditative absorption (samādhi) and departed for the celestial city of Yāmyaka.
Dharmarāja then spoke to her as she went to search for her own husband.
"O virtuous lady, your husband is alive on the banks of the Yamunā;
he is striving for yoga with Aśvatara. Stay here for a moment.

"For your sake, a virtuous maiden born of my mind resides in my house.

"You are worthy of favor; even though you are a child, a guest who has come to my home is a teacher.
Having said this, he brought his daughter Madālasā before him.
He then said, "My son, is this Madālasā not your wife?"
Upon seeing her face-to-face, his hair stood on end with joy.
His mind overflowing with love, he wept as he remembered their former life.
Then Aśvatara, having tied a fruit that grants all desires to his hand, [presented it] to him.

Having kindled the fire according to the prescribed rites, he gave him the jewel of a daughter once more. Having obtained a virtuous wife, as well as abundant dowry wealth, Naga maidens, and other female and male servants and attendants, [he was satisfied].
Having received jewels and golden ornaments, and having been refreshed and made youthful once more, she then bowed repeatedly to her father-in-law, the lord of the Nāgas;
she embraced her two brothers-in-law, paid homage to her mother-in-law, and likewise to the others. (28–29)
Having departed, he traveled by means of his own wind-vehicle to his city;
arriving at his own city, he bowed to his parents and related everything in its entirety,
exactly how the slender-limbed lady had been recovered.
The virtuous lady bowed at the feet of her mother-in-law and father-in-law;
she also honored the others according to propriety and age.
Thereupon, a great festival arose, which was entirely dear to the citizens.
And Ṛtadhvaja sported with that slender-waisted woman for a very long time.
Then, after a great length of time, Śatrujit passed away.
Ṛtadhvaja became king; he was devoted to his wife and exceedingly righteous.
The queen Madālasā, the king’s mother, was devoted to her husband.
(3.4) Although there were hundreds of thousands of maidservants, Madālasā constantly attended to her husband like Lakṣmī herself, performing services such as massaging his limbs. (3.5)
Regarding her husband as the Lord Hari in the form of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa—
who bestows liberation and is eternally connected— she served him.
Having always fed him and offered him all things, she would then eat herself and continue her service.
And she always applies herself to her own duties in a manner pleasing to her husband.
Having offered morning meditation upon Hari, worship, charity, self-reflection, and food to the guest, she is indeed properly engaged for the sake of her own soul. (37–38)
Offering to Brahman, service to Brahman, and meditation on Brahman—this is the path of the Sātvatas.
Having accomplished this, the virtuous Mahābhāgavatī exists in the Supreme;
indeed, day and night she performs the chanting of the glories of Hari’s divine play.
She repeatedly caused others to hear of the miraculous deeds of Hari.
While she was living in this manner, her first son was born;
his wise father gave that intelligent boy the name Vikrānta.
Everyone was indeed pleased by that, and Madālasā laughed;
for she, whose nature was that of Brahman, regarded joy and sorrow as equal.
The virtuous woman then [beheld] her son, the infant Vikrama, lying on his back.
To pacify him as he wept under the pretext of lulling him to sleep,
Madālasā remembered Hari and her own self— which is eternally pure and stainless— and spoke thus to her son, who was liberated and free from the attributes of the body. (43–44)
You are yourself pure and possessed of the beautiful form of Brahman;
today you have assumed a fabricated name and attained an unprecedented body and so forth.
Why do you weep, O Ashoka, when you yourself are sorrowful?
One who possesses the nature of the body always weeps at the time of loss;
but that [loss] does not exist for you, O Brahman, who are stainless.
You are always full, sustained by your own contentment; for one who is eternally satisfied, what indeed is the point of weeping?
As for those adventitious qualities such as pleasure and the like—
They indeed engage [beings] in the experience of what is desired;
then, through activity resulting in auspicious or inauspicious fruits, they repeatedly cast them into this insubstantial wheel. 47.
Peaceful, terrible, and likewise deluded bodies undergo various transformations;
one who is impelled by their momentum, yet devoid of the momentum of the *guṇas*, [remains as such].
One who possesses the sense of "mine-ness" will be consumed by suffering.
There is nothing whatsoever to be attained by this body, nor is there anything eternal.
He by whom that which is to be obtained is attained is eternally full; how then can there be weeping for you, who are already complete?
All that is acquired has passed away; this is all impermanent.
In this and that birth, I have seen the nature of existence to be transient, fragile,
and a source of sorrow; you, however, are not like that.
Water exists, it is born, it grows, it remains stable, it diminishes, and it meets its destruction;
for these indeed are the properties found in the elements.
How could you have grief for the loss of anything?
For you there is no increase and no decrease;
since your nature is such, you are not like a garment here.
You should succumb to grief and cultivate self-knowledge, which is the praiseworthy state consisting of innate bliss.
"O father!"—to some; "O son!"—to others. 52.
Do not regard as "thine" that which consists of the elements— some as "a friend," some as "a beloved," some as "mine," and some as "not mine. (53)
Experience always occurs as a mixture, for it is perceived as both pleasant and unpleasant; indeed,
even in what is pleasant, there is no true pleasantness for the wise man.

Even in suffering, there is no sense of suffering for the deluded one. [For the enlightened,] the notions of "I" and "mine" have ceased; though new things arise and old ones pass away, he does not speak of them as "I" or "mine. || 54 ||
Futile indeed is the thought that brings suffering from childhood;
for even when the corruption has decayed, it will not depart.
The eyes, the ears, and the fine nose—
Face, teeth, skin, ears, and mind;
tongue, hands, feet, the passages for feces and urine, and the navel—these names indeed do not belong to you. (56)
Just as fields are indeed made of earth, just as lakes are indeed filled with water and the like,
and just as heavens are indeed composed of light and so forth;
And the vital breaths are the winds; indeed, they are not yours.
Just as you, being conscious, proceed here on this vehicle that travels many paths with a good charioteer. //57//
In that very same way, there is a driver within the divine consciousness-ether which has you as its essence; remember that Acyuta.
This body of yours and mine is indeed transient.
And that [body] of your father likewise passed away; just as it was such for him, so too will it be for your future one. Therefore, my dear, obtain an eternal body! (59)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa! Lord of Rādhikā! Lord of Ramā! Mādhava! Lord of Pārvatī! Lord of Lakṣmī! Lord of devotees! Lord of Prabhā!
O Raṭāṅga! Grant that eternal body which you have attained! (1.393.60) You have no sleep, nor do you have lassitude;
you have no mother, nor do I have a son.
For you there is no childhood, nor for me is there any growth; neither succession nor non-succession belong to you or to me in Brahman.
Thus knowing "I am the Self," one is a servant of the Supreme Self.
To be gathered by the heart and known by the mind,
one immersed in bliss drinks the nectar of Kṛṣṇa within direct experience and attains satisfaction. (6.2)
Just as on the earth there are feet that swing well, and cloth-feet fixed upon the pillars of a swing,
so too do your two feet rest within the space between the cloths.
Worship Him who dwells within your own self;
for He is the Lord, the protector, the giver of liberation, and the Sovereign of all lords, who, though formless, abides as if possessing a form. (63)
He alone is the mother and he alone is the father; he is the wide-eyed one and his name is Vikrānta—worship him! You are the Self, you are liberated, and you are the true Lord.
You are Brahmā, you are divine, you are eternally blissful;
you are Nara, you are protected by Nārāyaṇa, you are my own true nature—worship the Lord of the Imperishable. 65.
Vid is said to be knowledge (jñāna), and from that, krānta is considered action (kriyā).
The Self, endowed with both knowledge and action, is Vikrānta; tell me your own [nature].
Vipakṣī indeed has two wings: these are volition (saṃkalpa) and power (śakti).
"You have transcended the two wings of the power of *saṃkalpa*; tell me your own true nature.
The letter *vi* is said to be the organ of knowledge (*jñānendriya*), and likewise the letter *kra* is the organ of action (*karmendriya*).
The Self (*ātman*) resides within those two; tell me your own nature as you have triumphed over them. (67–68)
"Know yourself to be distinct from the body and the house; know yourself as the Lord, who is indeed Being-Consciousness-Bliss. Then sorrow shall not touch you.
Thus did that virtuous woman first instruct her son by bestowing knowledge upon him.

In her childhood, she made him a liberated king of yogis who had accomplished his purpose. As her son grew, the mother constantly provided him with ever-new and fresh awakenings consisting of self-knowledge during his lullabies and other such activities.
Having attained freedom from egoism and complete absence of possessiveness,
he gained supreme self-power and acquired knowledge that is truly real.
She alone was his mother, the one by whom he, as a child, was so thoroughly awakened.
Having entered the path to liberation, he is released from both bondage and worldly existence.
Through his mother’s instruction, he attained self-realization; thus was the son awakened by his mother from the very moment of birth. (73–74)
He became one who transcended bodily comfort, free from passion and unassailed by sense objects;
even in youth, he was not of a lustful nature, nor did he harbor hatred toward anything.
Regarding this impure body, which is merely the state of male or female, impermanent, suffering, and subject to destruction—
The notion of enjoyment did not arise in him as he lived in the form of Brahmā.
Regarding form, taste, smell, touch, and sound as belonging neither to himself nor to another, he was indeed not bound by them. (76–77)
When the body is nourished and strength has arisen, that strength is considered to be like stone;
the spheres of the senses are regarded as being like storehouses.
Thus, free from passion, he is beyond dualities and established in his own true nature.
Free from possessiveness, the wise man set his mind not upon the life of a householder;
he was without egoism toward his own body and devoid of the sense of "I" regarding the kingdom,
as well as toward his field, elephant, vehicle, mount, and realm.
Indeed, being devoid of the state of affection, he did not experience bondage—neither among his male servants and attendants, nor among female slaves, nor even in the cities;
nor in the houses, nor in garments, ornaments, or objects of enjoyment. (8.1)
Indeed, his mind did not turn toward anything at all, as if he were one who had attained liberation;
whether in eating, sexual pleasure, drinking, chewing, or even in all matters of taste,
he appeared entirely devoid of the relish for flavors, like a supreme ascetic.

He is free from attachment toward ornaments such as necklaces of jewels, fragrant substances, liquid materials such as oils, and collyrium; likewise, he is dispassionate toward the exhibitions of wrestlers and the sports of courtesans. (84)
He was as if despondent amidst the songs and dances of the female performers;
he lacked enthusiasm in royal assemblies, public festivals, and diversions;
and he remained detached even during travels to forests and the like, or during hunting expeditions and similar pursuits. (85–86)
He was dispassionate toward the infliction of punishment, toward violent acts, as well as toward verbal abuse, and toward legal proceedings that were cruel and merciless;
likewise, he was steadfast in celibacy, purity, contentment, and austerity.
He was always enthusiastic in the study of sacred texts and in the worship of the gods.

He remained steadfast in every form of truth, in silence, in non-stealing—both internal and external—and likewise in non-possessiveness, fortitude, and the avoidance of desire and other passions. (88–89)

In serving the guru, serving one's parents, honoring the elderly, welcoming guests, and looking upon devotees with devotion, he is indeed liberated. He remains ever full of faith and is in every way a virtuous practitioner of theistic conviction.
Discerning and rich in liberation, he is always devoted to the practice of Brahman;
he is intent on serving the virtuous and ever dedicated to the service of Hari; he performs what is beneficial for living beings and is free from causing joy or agitation. (91–92)
Thus, from his very childhood, he became equal to Sanaka;
seeing her son as a great liberated soul, a supreme and equanimous Vaiṣṇava,
the mother rejoiced exceedingly, and the father too was filled with bliss.
The subjects, the servants, and others likewise regarded him as a god.

His [powers] were: minuteness (aṇimā), magnitude (mahimā), heaviness (garimā), lightness (laghimā), attainment (prāpti), fulfillment of desires at will (kāmāvasāyitā), and mastery over all things (vaśitā). || 94–95 ||
Śabda, ūha, adhyayana, duḥkhanāśa, traya, suhṛtprāpti, jñānadāna, tārā, and sutārikā—all these were at his feet; indeed, he became the supreme Siddha. (96)
With his desires unimpeded, he shone like one who was well-born and liberated.

Thus ends the three hundred and ninety-third chapter, titled "The Return of Kṛtadhvaja to the Kingdom of the Ancestors in Pātāla after being united with Madālasā, the Birth of His Son Named Vikrama, and the Instruction on Discernment Given to Him by Madālasā," within the section on the Greatness of Devoted Wives in the first book, the Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Protect your subjects, perform the most excellent sacrifices, and offer clarified butter and other oblations into the fire. (4) Offer oblations, and give to Brahmins, holy men, and the destitute whatever they request.

Like the wind, one should gather [wealth] through movements that remain hidden among all classes of people;
he who is not dragged away by greed or the group of sensual desires is always happy. (3.1–3.2)

He protects the dharma that leads to heaven and guards the virtuous stages of life; for him there is eternal happiness both here and in the world beyond, through his establishment of the entire essence of dharma among his subjects.
||33|| For the king, however, [this is achieved] by establishing the totality of dharma within his people.
By that very means, one indeed attains a share [of merit] and goes to heaven again and again.
(34) One should perform sacrifices of action, sacrifices of knowledge, and sacrifices of devotion;
through pleasing Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, one shall attain the eternal state. (35)
Truthfulness, purity, non-violence, lack of malice, as well as forgiveness, benevolence, and freedom from harmful action—these are to be protected by people on this earth.
O child! By adopting the householder’s life, a person indeed sustains the world.
And by that merit, he attains the worlds he desires.
Whether they be gods, Daityas, Dānavas, humans, ancestors, sages, insects, moths, birds, animals, or trees—[all are sustained by it]. (37–38)
Householders support [others], and through them they attain satisfaction;
indeed, people even watch their faces, thinking, "Will he give?
The state of householdership is the nourisher and the foundation of all; it is like a cow consisting of the three Vedas.
That in which the universe is established and which is considered the cause of the universe; sacrificial rites such as *iṣṭāpūrta* must be performed in every way by the householder alone;
the utterances *svāhā* and *svadhā* are considered to have the householder as their support. (1.395.40–41)
The utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, the utterance of *hanta*, and even the utterance of *āho* consist of that [the domestic life].
He who brings about the destruction of the householder’s stage of life is indeed a doer of evil.
A wise man should nurture the householder’s life; he is thus prepared for heaven.

O child! A king or a wealthy man should nourish daily the gods, sages, ancestors, and humans, as well as all living beings, just like his own body. With a concentrated mind, he should perform the libations and the *śrāddha* ceremony for the ancestors at the proper time.
Likewise, the householder should worship the deities with jasmine, fragrant flowers, and other offerings;
he should give food and other necessities to the wretched, the helpless, and the poor;
and he should scatter food on the ground for dogs, outcastes, and birds.
To one who is hungry, weary, seeking alms, and destitute,
one should offer food and drink, regarding that guest as the Lord Hari himself.
When he is satisfied, the householder is indeed released from the debt arising from the sacrifice to men (nṛyajña).
If a guest turns away from a householder with his hopes frustrated,
he departs having transferred his own misdeeds to that host and taking away the host’s merit.
A householder should honor a guest even by giving water and vegetables.
One should give alms to those who come begging according to one's capacity and at every opportunity.
Only after having fed those who depend on him should the master of the house eat.
O son, for one who maintains the household in this manner, the life of a householder becomes truly beneficial.
The gods, the ancestors, the sages, the destitute, guests, and beggars;
the seers, kinsmen, birds, animals, and even the minute insects—these beings are indeed constantly intent on bestowing blessings and are the givers of happiness. (51)
They become givers of happiness and free from obstacles even in the next world.
Atri himself sang this auspicious verse;
for having given what is called the Vaiśvadeva, one should employ it, and not otherwise.
Just as that which is to be done upon the birth of a son, and that which is to be done at a wedding and so forth,
even so should expenditure be made on the service of the virtuous and on the day of Hari.
As for the scattering of food that is performed by men upon the earth—
By that [offering], even if it be stale, the piśācas and other spirits attain satisfaction.
Whatever water falls upon the ground from the bathing garment, by that very [water],
those who have attained the state of trees find their satisfaction.
Indeed, those drops of water which fall attached to the limbs of the body reach the gods and others and attain satisfaction through those drops that have fallen upon the earth;
and by means of the particles of the funeral rice-ball and food, even animals attain contentment.
But those fools who are thus burnt, unfit for ritual action and unrefined—having perished, they subsist on the scattered food and the water used for sweeping;
having drunk the water from the rinsing of the vessel, those dead ones attain satisfaction. (58–59)
Therefore, one should give at a great festival, one should give at a *śrāddha*, and one should give at a gift-giving ceremony.
A householder who gives in this way ensures that no one in his lineage suffers.
A householder must always maintain right conduct in accordance with the rules.
For one who is devoid of proper conduct finds no happiness either in this world or the next.
Indeed, a man of evil conduct certainly does not attain long life in this world;
therefore, one who desires a household must practice dharma for the sake of warding off all evils.
One should wake during the *brāhma-muhūrta* and reflect upon virtue (*dharma*) and worldly prosperity (*artha*).
Having bathed, one should perform the twilight devotions (*sandhyā*), meditation (*dhyāna*), and the worship of the gods.
One should avoid idle chatter, falsehood, and harshness of speech.
One should never engage in false doctrine or atheism;
one should bow to the elders and perform the worship of those worthy of honor.
One should offer a seat to gurus and perform acts such as rising to meet them.
One should respectfully greet one's teacher, parents, and husband as the most excellent.
One should not speak of the teacher’s misdeeds; rather, if he is angry, one should appease him.
One should never listen to the censure of others, nor should one ever engage in it oneself.
The way must be yielded to Brahmins, to a king, and to one afflicted by suffering;
to the virtuous, to the learned, to a pregnant woman, to one burdened by a load, and to a younger person; as well as to the mute, the blind, the deaf, the intoxicated, and the insane. (67–68)
One should avoid joking, striking, reviling, and backbiting toward those who are truthful, as well as toward enemies, children, and the fallen.
One should never practice hypocrisy, arrogance, or deceit.
One who desires long life should not approach another's wife. A woman in her menses must always be avoided by all for four nights;
to avoid the birth of a female child, one should also avoid her on the fifth day.
Then, on the sixth night, one desiring a son should certainly go;
for sons are born from women on even nights, while daughters are born on odd nights.
Indeed, the capacity for conception is held to last until the sixteenth night.
Thereafter, however, the lotus becomes closed and fruitless.
One should not cultivate friendship with those who are ill-behaved, nor with those corrupted by theft and the like,
nor with those who are excessively spendthrift, nor with the greedy, nor even with enemies.
One should not cultivate friendship with those who are more powerful, nor with those who are inferior, nor with those who are censurable;
nor with those who are suspicious of everything, nor with those who are devoted solely to fate.
Rather, one should cultivate friendship with virtuous people who follow right conduct.

Even those who are wise, free from malice, capable, and possessed of diligence in action— such a woman should never set foot toward [those who treat] her husband, gods, or teachers with disrespect. My son, one should not dwell in a place where these four are not present.
Where there is a lender of loans, a physician, and a Vedic scholar; where there is a river with abundant water;
where the king has conquered his enemies and acts as a protector of dharma;
where the citizens are well-restrained; and where the earth is rich with crops. (78)
Where people are free from envy, there residence brings about happiness.
But, O son, one should not dwell where these three are always present: those who are ever-desirous of victory, those harboring ancient enmity, and people who lack diligence. (1.395.80)
Listen, my son, to the rules for purification and so forth, as they are accepted for each respective material:
for wood, stone, gold, silver, ropes, and garments;
for vegetables, roots, and fruits; and likewise for split bamboo and leather. (81)
The purification of gems, diamonds, corals, precious stones, and pearls,
as well as the limbs of humans, is prescribed with water. However, the purification of vessels that contain oily substances is by means of hot water.
The purification of winnowing baskets, grains, skins, pestles, mortars,
and heaps of gathered clothes is by sprinkling;
for bark garments and woolen cloths, purification by water is prescribed.
The purification of grass, wood, and medicinal herbs is held to be by sprinkling (85).
Wool, hair, and the like are purified by wind or by sunlight.
Alms-food is pure, as is the hand of an artisan; likewise, the mouth of a woman is pure (86).
Sacrificial halls, alchemy laboratories, nursing infants, women, pure water, and flowing streams free from odor and bubbles—
earth is purified by time, by sprinkling, by smearing, and by thorough sweeping.

Likewise, purification of clay is held to result from rain and scraping; the purification of bell-metal is by means of ash, water, and scrubbing, as well as by fire. Other vessels are purified with earth and water, while tin and lead are purified with alkaline substances. (88–89)
Dust, fire, a horse, a cow, shade, rays of light, wind, the earth, droplets of water, flies, and the like do not become defiled through contact with the wicked.
A goat and a horse are pure from the mouth; a cow is pure except for her mouth, as is the face of a calf.
The flow from a mother’s breast is pure, as is the dropping of fruit by a bird.
Indeed, a seat, a bed, a vehicle, boats, and grass on the road are always purified by the rays of the moon and sun and by the wind. (91–92)
One should remove and discard the top portion of food that has been defiled by a large amount [of impurity].
One should then sprinkle the remainder with water, or purification may be achieved simply by fanning it with air.
Having touched a corpse, one must indeed perform a bath; purification is considered to result from that.

Upon the abandonment of impurity, one should perform a bath and the purification of the hands and other limbs. (94) Indeed, upon the birth of a child, one should observe purity for one month; for death-impurity, one should observe it for twelve days, as in the case of a child less than a year old. (95)
"Thus, O Alarka, you must at all times observe this conduct;
the purity of the self must always be protected by destroying the delusions of *māyā*.
Having been thus instructed with devotion by his mother, Alarka—
Instructed by his father, he took a lawful wife.
And his father said to him, "O Alarka, accept this worldly kingdom bestowed by me. Then Madālāsā spoke these final words to her son: (97–98)
O son! whenever you experience unbearable suffering born from separation from beloved kinsmen,
or arising from the harassment of enemies, or resulting from the loss of wealth and the like,
then draw [the remedy] from this ring given by me.
"The message to be proclaimed has indeed been written by me here upon this plate.
Having said this, the mother gave him a golden ring;
thereafter, she bestowed whatever blessings were appropriate.
Having received blessings from his father, Alarka indeed ruled the kingdom;
meanwhile, Madālāsā and Ṛtadhvaja went to the forest for ascetic penance.
Having meditated upon Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, they renounced all material things.
Having attained a divine body, they both indeed went to the abode of Brahmā.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, the chaste Madālasā, a Vaiṣṇava and devoted wife,
having brought forth sons who were fully liberated, went to the imperishable realm.
By reading or even by hearing this, liberation is attained;
all bonds shall perish and there shall always be happiness, O beloved!
Just as Alarka [attained it], so that no further bondage may occur according to the right principle.

In this way he governed his own kingdom, and all the subjects were filled with joy. The righteous-souled king protected his virtuous subjects like his own sons; likewise, he begot sons and performed great sacrifices.
To him were born sons of great strength and prowess,
righteous-souled, high-minded, and adversaries of the path of unrighteousness. Yet, he did not entrust the burden of sovereignty to his sons, though they were capable of ruling the kingdom.
No dispassion arose in him as he enjoyed manifold sense objects.
Seeing his brother thus attached to enjoyments, deluded, and with senses unsubdued, the forest-dweller was intent on instructing him for the sake of destroying his passion.

An elder brother named Subāhu, a renunciant ascetic, quickly came to his house and instructed him in liberation. He [received] that knowledge of the Self, a manifold science, which had been taught by his brother as well. (111)
Remembering [the Lord] again and again, he spoke to him for the very purpose of destroying his bondage.
Nevertheless, Alarka did not consider the renunciation of his kingdom to be beneficial;
at that time, [the sage], wishing to enlighten him and to make him abandon his bondage, [spoke].
But Subāhu, having reflected for a long time, considered battle to be better; having resorted to that enemy and instigated a fierce war, he thought:
"I shall bring about the ultimate welfare [of my brother] through his supreme detachment."
"Having produced indifference [toward worldly affairs], I shall effect his liberation.
Having reflected thus, Subāhu approached the King of Kāśī; that monarch then made preparations for a military expedition against Alarka.
He dispatched a messenger with the command, "Let the kingdom be given to your brother.
To that messenger who had spoken thus, he, filled with intoxication, replied:
"Let my elder brother come to me himself and beg for the kingdom out of affection."
"I will not surrender [it] by force out of fear of the King of Kāśī.
Then a most terrible battle took place between him and the King of Kāśī;
having fallen into great anxiety, he remembered that ring.
There he saw a leaf given by his mother, with its letters clearly visible:
"Association must be abandoned with all one's soul; if it cannot be abandoned, then one should associate with the virtuous, for association with the virtuous is indeed the medicine. (1.395.120)

Thirst (tṛṣṇā) must be abandoned with one's whole being; yet if it cannot be relinquished, then that very thirst, through the desire for liberation (mumukṣā), shall be its own remedy. Having thus recited this and having grasped the desire for liberation, King Alarka— || 122 ||
Seeking the company of the virtuous and restricting his possessions at night,
he went to the illustrious and unattached teacher Dattātreya;
having prostrated and honored him, he related everything as it had happened.
"Show favor for the destruction of my suffering and other afflictions," she thus entreated him.

Thus ends the three hundred and ninety-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of Madālāsā Teaching Alarka the Duties of Conduct, Her Attainment of Divine State with Her Husband, and Subāhu’s Efforts for Alarka’s Self-Knowledge," in the section on the Greatness of the Devoted Wife (*pativratāmāhātmya*) within the first book, the Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Listen, O Mahālakṣmī, to the wisdom as it was acquired by Alarka from Dattātreya—wisdom that is difficult even for yogis to attain.
The Guru said: "Tell me truly, for what reason do you have this sorrow?"
"O King, I shall remove your suffering this very day.
The disciple said: "My brother Subāhu, for the sake of the kingdom alone, has joined with the King of Kāśī and is fighting against me."
"Destroy that supreme suffering very quickly, even before morning!
The Guru said: "But this [suffering] never exists within you at all.
For how can there be the departure of that which does not exist within one's own self? (4)
Reflect upon this, O Indra among kings, and let it shine within your heart.
(5) By my grace, know yourself to be forever free from both suffering and worldly pleasure.
O King, take this water and drink even a single mouthful. (6)

"Place [the mirror] likewise upon his eyes and on his head so that he may see Brahman. Being thus addressed, he did accordingly; with the interior of his heart opened, he reflected upon himself, smiled, and then spoke this:
All nature consists of the three qualities (guṇas), but I am eternally free from the three qualities.

From nature arises the sense of "mine," and from that arises egoism (ahaṃkāra). Through that [egoism], the subtle elements (mātrās) become objects of enjoyment, as well as the sense organs, which are even soft [in their perception].
From the subtle elements come the gross objects of enjoyment; from those, the body which is dependent on the qualities (*guṇas*).
Pleasure, pain, and delusion—these are *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.
Their effects are of the same nature, and they also enter into those [elements].
For those [qualities] do not indeed come to me, who am such and yet not that.
Therefore, neither pleasure nor pain nor delusion exist in me.
I am neither earth, nor water, nor fire, nor air. || 11–12 ||
Nor am I space; indeed, qualities such as fragrance do not exist in me.
I am not earth, nor is fragrance mine; I am not water, nor is taste mine.
I am not light, nor is form mine; I am not air, nor is touch mine.

I am not space, nor do I have sound; how then could its attributes exist in me? The five elements, when combined, undergo decrease and increase, and the decrease and increase of pleasure, pain, and delusion are likewise observed.
Just as the objects of sight are perceived, so too are the qualities of the objects of sight—such as a jar or its color and so forth;
and just as they are seen with the eye, so too are pleasure and the like perceived by the mind.
Since these are of the very nature of the object of sight, they are perishable and do not belong to the Self.
How can that which is imperishable and eternal possess adventitious properties? (17) Thus, indeed, a fruit such as a mango, being insentient, is to be grasped by the hand;
form is to be grasped by the eye, and likewise taste by the tongue. (18)

Odor is to be grasped by the nose, and likewise intoxication by the mind. The quality of intoxication (*unmāda*) exists in fermented liquors and the like, while actual intoxication (*mattatā*) is indeed found in the *dhūstūra* plant. In buttermilk and similar substances, there is only dullness (*māndya*); such instances are to be understood as having flavor as their predominant quality.
They are grasped by the mind, and the mind, moreover, is superior to those objects of taste.
Then, the liberated soul becomes even subtler than a portion [of matter], and is indeed the mind itself.
Residing within the mind are dharma, knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty.
Since pleasure, pain, and delusion reside in the mind,
I am not the mind, nor do pleasure, pain, and delusion belong to me in any way.
I am not "I," I am not "mine," I am not the intellect, and indeed I am not the mind.
How can that pleasure or pain residing therein belong to me?
I am not the body composed of earth and other elements, nor am I the internal mind or the sense organs.
Nor am I the latent impressions of past karma, nor egoism, nor delusion, nor sufferings; what do these have to do with me?
[24] Sovereignty, the earth, and all the people—
That teaching was created by the intellect; it is not mine.
The intellect is the daughter of the Three Qualities (triguṇa);
that teaching is the kingdom, but it is not mine. (25)
Let his command be carried out; let either the intellect of Subāhu or the intellect of Nālarka carry it out—
neither the intellect of Nālarka nor the intellect of Subāhu [shall act otherwise].
Therefore, the designation "body" does not apply to the living being (jīva).
For that [jīva] does not possess hands and so forth under its control, nor flesh, nor bones, nor the distribution of veins. (26)
What connection does that man have here, even the slightest, with elephants, horses, chariots, or treasuries? Therefore, for me there is no enemy, nor is there any suffering.
I have no pleasure in my city; it is delusion.
Neither treasury, nor elephants, nor horses, nor ministers, nor wealth, nor wives belong to me, nor to anyone else, nor do they belong to him. (28)
Whatever exists in him is mine,
and whatever exists in me is his;
that which belongs to both is the pure Self.
Tell me here, by whom were suffering and happiness created?
For a person who perceives correctly, there is neither suffering nor happiness; for one who has realized the Self, there is no kingdom anywhere except within Hari. (1.396.30)
