The kind of mental engagement that proceeds toward the protection of one's own body, children, and so forth—such as [the attachment] found in the cakravāka bird or the mouse—is not present in the same way toward the body of a louse and the like;
on the contrary, it exists there only for the purpose of killing them. (32–33)
Indeed, from the very elements of a single body, various kinds of beings arise:
nits, insects, bugs, legitimate sons, and sons born of illicit union.
Even regarding nails, hair, and filth, the intellect is not uniform in its regard for all parts.
Therefore, that which is produced by the intellect is one's own, not another's, nor is it created by the Self.
Thus, O Guru, when there is the awakening to truth, I am neither miserable nor happy;
nor do I know any person as deluded, indeed, through Your grace.
Having heard these words of his disciple, Dattātreya said to him: "It is even so, O tiger among men! You know it exactly as it is:
'This is mine' is the root of suffering, and 'This is not mine' is the source of liberation."
And through my grace, this supreme knowledge has arisen within you.
It was previously instructed to you by your mother, and today it has indeed been recalled to you by me—
that [knowledge] by which the dullness of "I" and "mine" is cast away through discernment.
For that very person who is bodiless (videhin), there is indeed satisfaction in every respect.
House, field, son, wife, wealth, grain, offspring, and so forth—all these are false; through a false perception, they are impermanent things treated as permanent.
How could there be an absolute [liberation] for those who fall into the pits of deluded cognition and the like?

Those people by whom attachment and other such bonds were severed through the words of the Guru—those who remained steady like swans in the company of the virtuous and the good—have gone to the supreme state. (41–42)
Having reached the pure forest of the Self— free from duality, devoid of anger,
bereft of delusion, and beyond all limiting adjuncts— abide forever in happiness.
You are neither gross nor subtle, nor are you of the nature of a cause.
You are not composed of those subtle elements (*tanmātra*), nor are you made of egoity (*ahaṃkāra*).

Therefore, you are the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*) beyond the aggregate known as the *guṇas*, just as [the sky is distinct from] the water-moss, mud, reeds, fish, mosquitoes, and water. || 44–45 ||

O King, just as there is distinctness even within unity, so it is between the field (kṣetra) and the Self (ātman). You are the Self, supreme to the body— a mockery consisting of bodily sovereignty— eternally pure, eternally awakened, eternally liberated, and stainless.
For you have indeed gone beyond attachment to the earth, beyond attachment to kingship, and beyond attachment to sovereignty.

One who seeks liberation should abandon attachment; for when that [earthly life] perishes, it is the abode of possessiveness. Through the contemplation of the defects inherent in suffering, the state of dispassion arises.
The yogi dwells in a state free from passion, having renounced all enjoyments;
that is his home where he resides, and that is his food by which he lives.
Indeed, being without possessions, he shines forth as one liberated while living.
Knowledge leads to liberation, while ignorance becomes the cause of bondage.
O Arka, listen to the supreme path that likewise bestows the highest state;
by that path, many sages have attained liberation.
Yoga, which always bestows liberation (nirvāṇa), is indeed the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind.
The fluctuations are indeed right knowledge, misconception, conceptualization, sleep, and memory.
Right knowledge arises from the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa); misconception is false knowledge.
Conceptual construction devoid of a real object is considered to be non-perceptual and dream-like.

Recollection is held to be produced by latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) such as those of previously experienced objects. However, when there is contact with a real object, recognition is indeed produced by latent impressions.
Even that [memory] is here declared to be nothing but memory arising from mental impressions (*saṃskāra*).
Thus, the mental modifications (*vṛtti*) are to be understood as both known and unknown.
O King, the complete cessation of these is called *yoga*.
The union of the self with Brahman is considered the most excellent yoga.
Yoga is always practiced for the sake of destroying the impurity of the intellect.
Ignorance, egoism, passion, hatred, and fear—these are the five [afflictions]. (56–57)
The afflictions (kleśas) abound in the state of impurity; when they are destroyed, the mind becomes stainless.
For the sake of destroying them, the restraints (yamas) and observances (niyamas) must be practiced again and again.
The wise person should protect non-violence (ahiṃsā) and speak truth that is beneficial.
One should protect non-stealing in every way and likewise remain a celibate student.
He who possesses no sense of possession is indeed liberated from bondage.
One should practice mental purity as well as physical purification that is appropriate.
One should constantly increase contentment by accepting whatever is obtained by chance;
one should perform austerity consisting of the restraint of the senses as is appropriate;
and one should practice self-study in the form of the chanting of the names of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
One should always apply oneself with vigilance to meditative concentration upon his form.
For one who constantly acts in this way, the mind becomes free from defects;
since hatred and attachment are the two primary defects, you must abandon them.
One should make the posture very firm, such as the excellent Svastika and others;
here, Gorakṣāsana itself is the protector of celibacy (brahmacarya).
One should always perform breath-control (prāṇāyāma) according to one's capacity and as required.
One should burn away defects by means of breath-control (prāṇāyāma) and latent impressions (vāsanā) by means of concentration (dhāraṇā).
One should withdraw the senses from objects by means of withdrawal (pratyāhāra), and the non-divine qualities by means of meditation (dhyāna).
Having attained Hari through absorption (samādhi), one rejoices in the imperishable abode.
Indeed, the defects of the senses are burned away by the restraint of the vital breath (prāṇa).
A duration of twelve [breaths] is considered light; that which is double that is medium;
and that which is triple is declared to be superior. One should always practice this without weariness.
By the first [stage] one should conquer perspiration; by the middle, trembling;
and by the third, dejection—one should thus conquer the defects in their proper order.
Once mastered, it destroys the defects, just as a trained hawk destroys birds.
The absence of turbidity in the mind arises through breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Desires, anger, and other defects are burned away by the restraint of the vital breath.
Through the destruction of these defects, knowledge of the past and future arises.
Consciousness that awakens the Self arises from the restraint of the vital breath (prāṇa).
Likewise, a state of mental clarity and serenity is born.
When stability has thus been established, one should commence withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra).
Having restrained the senses from their objects, as well as the vital breaths and the internal mind, one should cause them to abide within; that is the nature of pratyāhāra (withdrawal).
One should always observe the activity of the self through the activities of the senses.
By that means, the withdrawal of the self into the self is also a benefit.
O King, after withdrawal, one should undertake concentration (dhāraṇā).
Twelve breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) constitute the common duration for this state.
Dhyāna consists of two types of dhāraṇā, wherein the mental state is focused one-pointedly.
When this is practiced upon the form of Hari, the masses of defects are destroyed;
and one beholds the Supreme Brahman, distinguishing it from the qualities of Māyā.
Just as one who is healthy and free from limitation perceives everything within himself alone,
so too the meditator, always established in his own nature, beholds everything within the Self.
[This occurs] in the navel, the heart, the throat, the palate, the forehead, and the eyes.
One should indeed practice concentration upon Śrī Kṛṣṇa within one’s own head.
By performing such concentration, one attains equality with the Imperishable.
This occurs through the purification effected by the steadiness of the place, as well as through the wonder of divine sovereignty.

One's capacity goes to ruin; therefore, one should turn away from that. Women, fame, discernment, sovereignty, wealth, power, divinity, the performance of many sacrifices, and a body made of elixirs—[all these perish]. 1.396.80–81.

Moving unimpeded through space, water, fire, and so forth—these obstacles must be destroyed; one should not apply the mind to them. By making the mind attached to Brahman, one is not struck down by calamities.
Intuitive knowledge of all things, the power of hearing, divine hearing;

divine sight, the power of vision, and the comprehension of all languages; and the capacity to perceive distant objects—these and other such supernatural powers (*siddhis*) are but forms of obstacles. (83–84)
And by these attainments, my son, the deities remain bound;
they are repeatedly drawn back again and again by calamities and great obstacles.
Therefore, making yoga your dwelling and wrapping yourself in the *brahmakambala*, [proceed].

One should meditate upon the Supreme Brahman; such a person shall go to the highest goal. One should dissolve the earth into water, dissolve water into fire, dissolve fire into air, and then dissolve air into space.
One should dissolve those [elements] into sound, that [sound] into ego-consciousness, that into the Great Principle (mahat), and the Great Principle into the Primal Matter (pradhāna).
One should dissolve the Great Intellect (buddhi) into the Uneven (viṣama),
the Uneven into the Equilibrium of the Guṇas (guṇasāmyaka), the three Guṇas into the All-pervading (vibhu), and that into a single part within the Equal Imperishable (samakṣara).
One should unite one's own self, which is the imperishable form of Brahman, with the Supreme Self within the Supreme Brahman;
that indeed is his supreme state.
For him who has respect for all beings, there is a firm bond [to liberation]. (1.396.90)
Whenever a person feels passion for any being,
he repeatedly attains attachment to that very being and perishes.
O King, the union with beings, which causes such destruction, leads to rebirth once again.
That equanimity toward all beings which consists of universal knowledge is indeed liberation.
(9.2) Atomicity, lightness, and likewise greatness, as well as attainment; irresistible will, lordship, and furthermore, mastery. (9.3)
Thus, having attained these divine qualities, including the power of fulfilling desires, he is no longer afflicted by the three *guṇas*. With his defects burnt away, he attains oneness with Brahman.
For he attains all desires together with that wise one.
Likewise, the soul attains identity with the Supreme Self, the Lord of Yoga;
it attains sālokya, sārūpya, sāyujya, and indeed eternal union.
And by the power of compassion, he indeed attains equality with me and other such lordly powers;
uttering the single syllable "Om," the supreme Brahman, and constantly remembering me,
O King, he abandons his dilapidated home and proceeds to my abode.
"O Alarka, having always taken refuge in me, you have attained true knowledge. Know, moreover, that through my grace your defects have been destroyed;
henceforth there shall be no further bondage for you, and may you forever partake in Nirvana."

"By means of the Self, which is Brahman, eternal bliss, and the one who rests in happiness; merging into the Supreme Brahman, become possessed of eternal bliss. (1.396.100) Thus ends the three hundred and ninety-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of King Alarka’s Liberation through the Possession of Knowledge-Yoga Granted by Dattātreya," within the section on the Greatness of Devoted Wives in the first book, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. (396)
← Chapter 396: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga) Chapter 397 [Author: Chapter 398 →
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Having thus received auspicious blessings and realizing his own nature as Brahman, Alarka spoke to the Lord, his spiritual preceptor Hari.
"O Blessed One! I desire to hear in every way about the conduct of the yogi.
By what extraordinary signs is one recognized as following the path of Brahman?
The Guru replied: "Listen, O Lord of the Earth! [I shall describe those] which are distinct from worldly conduct."
His conduct indeed becomes boundless and unrestrained.
(3) These two—honor and dishonor—which cause joy and agitation in ordinary men, are the very opposites for a yogi; they are poison and nectar. (4)
One should generally resort to silence while repeatedly chanting the name of Hari.
One who desires solitude should not go to social gatherings, sacrificial rites, pilgrimages, and the like.
[When] the people have all finished eating, the fire has been extinguished, and the embers have subsided— 5.
He should wander for the sake of the journey toward the divine, content with whatever may be obtained by chance;
or indeed, he should live by adopting the lifestyle of a python (ajagarī-vṛtti),
taking whatever fruits, roots, leaves, bulbs, or grains he may happen to find in his bowl.
One should employ that [scripture] after offering it to the gods, without defiling the path of the virtuous;
one should take from it only what is essential and as much as required, never more than that.
These three—the restraint of speech, the restraint of action, and the restraint of mind—are the [true] three-fold staff.
He whose senses are indeed restrained shall be the supreme king of yogis, possessing the triple staff (tridaṇḍin).
Constantly engaged in yoga upon the form of Kṛṣṇa and muttering "Kṛṣṇa," he remains perpetually immersed [in Him], upholding the highest state.
One should practice the chanting of the Lord’s name with a resonant voice;
for the lord of yogis, intent upon that, shall attain absorption into the Blessed One.
Just as the moonstone yields water through contact with the rays of the moon...
One who is not disciplined does not emit [the fire]; this is remembered as the simile for the yogin.
Through contact with the sun's rays, the sun-crystal produces fire;
it does not do so alone—this is remembered as the simile for the yogin. (1.2–1.3)
Ants, mice, mongooses, house-lizards, and pigeons dwell in the master’s house; when it is destroyed, they depart elsewhere.
Yet, they certainly do not experience the same suffering as the master does upon the destruction of his home. (14)
Thus indeed should the yogi cultivate himself, remaining unobscured by suffering.
Just as an anthill-insect, with its extremely minute mouth,
builds up a mass of an anthill, so too should one accumulate yoga.
Just as leaves, flowers, fruits, and so forth, along with the trees themselves, are stripped away by beasts, birds, humans, and others, so too must everything be stripped away by the yogin.
And having observed the tip of a young ruru deer's horn growing, [he should likewise observe his own growth].
Then the yogi prospers in yoga and shall attain perfection.
That is his home where he dwells; that is his food by which he lives;
that is his wealth by which his purpose is accomplished—this is happiness; what attachment can there be here?
Whether food is sweet or not sweet, pungent, alkaline, or bitter—
whatever the yogi does not perceive, nor even speak of, despite knowing it;
he has indeed completely conquered the tongue, taste, and flavor.
Having recognized what is soft, hard, rough, gentle, smooth,
harsh, broad, sharp, and burning, he no longer experiences suffering when applying them;
thus, he has completely mastered the pleasant touch of the skin.
Whether it be sweet, auspicious, melodious, delightful, or gentle song;
whether it be jesting that brings laughter, or that which causes anger, or likewise bestows honor—having understood the sound therein, one indeed perceives neither pleasure nor pain. (23)
And he has completely mastered both speech and its meaning.
[24] It may be beautiful, well-constructed, like gold, radiant, auspicious, white, variegated, or otherwise smooth or even sharp. [25]

Having seen a form, he who does not conceive pleasure or pain in his mind has completely conquered form; he is a king among yogis whose eye is not affected by what is seen. Upon encountering a sweet fragrance, the nose does not undergo transformation.
Upon encountering a foul odor, neither the nose nor its cavity is obstructed.
That yogi has conquered both the smell and the nose by their very nature.
Even when a piercing sensation occurs or there is some agitation on the skin, [he remains unmoved]. (27–28)
He does not even touch his ears, yet he performs the conquest of the skin;
with his feet he goes to the abode of Hari and circumambulates Him.
With his feet he undertakes pilgrimages and journeys to holy men.
With both hands, one should respectfully perform service to the gods, the spiritual preceptor, and the virtuous;
with speech, one should perform the chanting (*saṃkīrtana*) of Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa;
one should dance before the gods and engage in sacred discourse among the saintly.
He performs song for his devotees, meditation upon the forms,
and indeed contemplation, salutation, and hymn of praise toward the Supreme Self.
He also performs prostration, laughter, and invocation in all directions.
Seeing Kṛṣṇa here and there, he manifests his joy;
at times he becomes invisible, and at times he stays among the trees; sometimes he is in a watery place, and sometimes he is even on the battlefield.
In some places, in deep pits or among thorns and the like; in some towns, cities, villages, and the like; in forests, wildernesses, and solitary places;
in a region imagined by the mind, or upon the surface of the earth, or even in the expanse of the sky. (35)
She dwells exactly as she pleases and according to her own resolve.
Sometimes, holding a piece of stone in her mouth, she eats it as if it were sugarcane;
she also smears soot, mud, or dust upon her body.
Thinking sandalwood to be cool, one desires to seize it again and again; yet an object that is inaccessible and situated in a distant land cannot be held in the hand.
[Likewise,] a report arising in another country [is discussed] in the assembly of people.
And he describes [himself] exactly as it is: in some places like a virtuous woman;
in some places he sleeps on the roads; in some places he leaps among people;
and even among animals, without anxiety, he sleeps like one intoxicated, overcome by fear. (1.397.40)
With his limbs greyed by dust, he rejoices in his mind at times;
sometimes he goes about naked, or sometimes clothed in leaves.
At times he has the bark of trees for clothing, and indeed, at times he is clothed in ashes.
In some places he stands amidst torrents of rain, in others amidst the fires of the sun;
in some places in cool water, and in others in mud;
in some places his limbs are smeared with filth, and in others his body is pure.
In some places there is the foul odor of urine and the like, along with spittle and other such things; he is merciless, his nose is covered in filth, and he is devoid of bathing his body.
[Yet] he is one who delights in the Self, whose nature is Brahman, and whose form is divine.
Moving without obstruction, he distinguishes between men and women;
(45) he is fearless among beasts, birds, grass, creepers, thorns, and the like.
Though endowed with the radiance of Hari, he is devoid of the perception of a physical body and so forth. (46)
That which must not be forgotten and that which must not be abandoned— such a person,
though attentive, neither abandons nor forgets it.
At times they may behave like a child, and at other times like an elder.
At times he behaves like a crow, a crane, a cat, or an owl;
at other times he conducts himself with love like a peacock, a parrot, or a swan; sometimes he adopts the lifestyle of a honey-gatherer, and sometimes the behavior of a monkey.
In some places he adopts the conduct of a lion, in some that of a wretched man, likewise in some that of a hawk, and in some he indeed subsists by adopting the behavior of a fish;
for while his mind is fixed on Śrī Hari, elsewhere it is devoid of any such focus.
The passing of the days for that Brahman-yogi occurs in this manner.
At times, during mental worship, Dhruva feeds Hari;
having offered water and performed obeisance, he dismisses Him by means of a gesture.
In some places, having fashioned a couch from dust, he establishes the Lord there; and in some places,
by offering leaves, flowers, petals, foliage, fruit, gravel, or grass,
as well as *tulasī* and lotuses, he delights Hari.
Thus, for the practitioner alone, every activity— even without constraint—
is divine in its nature, promotes divine progress,
consists of the divine reality, and bestows the supreme good. (54–55)
O Alarka, the yogi always exists; the yogi knows the yogi.
Sanaka and others, Ṛṣabha and others, as well as Śuka and others, became so.
They were the Siddhas, the Nāthas, the Tīrthaṅkaras, the Haṃsas, and those who abide in the Aghora state.
The virtuous, other yogins, the dull-witted, Bhairava and others;
Śaṅkara, the circle of Yoginīs, the Avadhūtas, and others as well; the truthful ones, virtuous women, female servants, and the Vaiṣṇavīs who have attained meditative absorption. (57–58)

They indeed attained the supreme Brahman, their actions transcending the world; what more need be said here? For the yogi, exalted by yoga, perceives nothing else within his heart that is distinct from Brahman.
He in whom the Self exists everywhere, and who is the abode of the Universal Self;
he who has attained such a state of existence that the thread is in the gem and the gem is in the thread—
filled with the intoxication of that realization, he has attained the bliss of the most perfect plenitude.
Who is able to discern the equanimity of that yogi?
For he may act with agitation through his physical movements, yet be wise in his intellect;
he may speak as a virtuous man, yet abide in peace through his inner disposition.
The contented one abides in the heart; the fearless one abides in the body.
The deluded one abides in the qualities (guṇas); the affectionate one abides in the mouth.
The passionate one abides in Brahman; the wrathful one abides in that which is illusory (māyika).
In solitude he behaves like a greedy hunter, yet among people he behaves with compassion;
in rites for the gods and ancestors, and in the yoga of Hari, he conducts himself with faith.
He is indeed distracted regarding the affairs of the body, but fully attentive regarding his own true purpose.
He exerts himself toward the supreme good endowed with all his powers;
in worldly affairs he is dispassionate, but toward the Supreme Lord he is full of devotion.
Endowed with such characteristics, the yogi should conduct himself at all times.
In some instances he displays many and manifold wonders within himself;
in other instances, like a forest animal, he displays his own foolishness.
Having recognized such a person as one whose actions are repeatedly strange—
One should recognize him as a great lord of yoga, whose very nature is Brahman.

(69) Now, when the yogi, having himself recognized the signs, abandons the body, listen as I describe his portents, by which [he knows] that he will not remain [in this world] upon departing. (1.397.70)

He who does not see with his own eyes the path of the gods, Dhruva, Śukra, the shadow of the moon, and Arundhatī, will face death within a year. [Likewise, he who sees] the orb of the sun devoid of rays, or fire possessed of rays, [will meet his end].
But for one who sees death within a year with his own eyes—
if he sees vomit, urine, and feces as if they were gold,
even in a dream— he shall live for ten months. (72–73)
Having seen pretas, piśācas, and the like, as well as cities of the gandharvas and trees with golden foliage, he lives for nine months.
One who repeatedly and suddenly becomes fat and then thin, or thin and then fat, [does not survive].

He who suffers from dizziness caused by wind in the head has a lifespan of eight months. If, when placing his foot on the ground, his heel or his toes are cut into the mud, dust, or filth, he lives for seven months. (75–76)
If a vulture, a pigeon, a raven, a crow,
or even a blue carnivorous bird alights upon one's head, it indicates a lifespan of only six months.
Furthermore, if in a dream one is struck by a flight of crows or by a shower of dust, [the same result follows].
If one perceives one's own reflection as something other than it truly is, that person lives for four or five [days].
(78) One who sees lightning in a cloudless sky will go abroad;
one who sees Indra’s bow at night has two months of life remaining. (79)

He who sees his own body without a head in clarified butter, oil, a mirror, or water, does not live beyond a month. He whose bodily odor is like that of a goat or even like that of a corpse [does not live long].
Indeed, his life span should be understood as lasting for half a month.
However, he whose heart, hands, and feet wither upon merely bathing,
and who experiences dryness in the throat while drinking, lives for ten days.
If, by the force of the wind, a splitting sensation occurs in the staff [of the body], then Death has arrived; indeed, he shall die within a moment.
[If one sees oneself] with bears, monkeys, boars, camels, donkeys, jackals, and the like...
He who, while standing in his vehicle, travels toward the southern direction, will die.
If a woman wearing red and black garments leads him toward the southern quarter in a dream, laughing and singing, he too shall not live.
Upon seeing a naked ascetic, or a Rākṣasa, or even Time (Death) itself laughing and leaping about, one should contemplate death.
If one sees oneself completely submerged in mud, one will die.

Having seen fire in one's hair, a serpent, ashes, or likewise a dried-up river in a dream, one will die within ten days; of this there is no doubt. [One who sees] terrifying men with weapons and the like, or stones and the like... [87–88]
Even if he has been killed or beaten, he will die; of this there is no doubt.
For one whose teeth have become numb, death will occur; of this there is no doubt.
If, at sunrise, a jackal approaches facing him while howling—
Whether his vision is distorted or limited, he meets death immediately.
He for whom hunger oppresses again as soon as he has eaten, and who does not perceive the scent of a lamp, has reached the end of his life; of this there is no doubt.
One does not see one's own reflection in the eyes of another;
at night one sees Indra’s weapon (the rainbow), and by day one beholds the planets.
He whose nose is crooked and whose ears are sunken and protruding [is likewise ill-fated].
If the left eye constantly weeps, his life-span does not exist in any way whatsoever.
(93) The face becomes red, the tongue dark, and the teeth black;
likewise, there is no sound heard in the ear and the light of the eyes fades away. (94)
For one who has gone into a pit and whose exit is blocked by stones, death occurs after a moment; and for one who is cast into fire in a dream, death likewise follows.
When entering water or being struck by spirits, death has arrived.
The reversal of one's own nature and the inversion of one's innate character,
as well as the reviling of those worthy of worship and the like, are considered forms of death.
Therefore, on that day, one should practice yoga for the destruction of death.
Or rather, one should yoke the self to Brahman and certainly remember nothing else;
united with that Kṛṣṇa, he goes to that supreme state.
This is absolute liberation, for it is indeed the final death.
And that worship of the feet of Hari within the Imperishable is the fruit of the practice of yoga.
His birth is meaningful, and likewise his death is meaningful;
his exercise of sovereignty is meaningful, for he has attained the feet of Kṛṣṇa.
Having heard the name "Alarka," he bowed at the feet of his guru.
In that very hour of midnight, he attained both knowledge and yoga.
The blessed Dattātreya was repeatedly honored and saluted by him.
Greatly delighted, his body covered in horripilation,
he said: "By good fortune, that for whose sake you have come here— having been threatened by the vast army of the Lord of Kāśī— is now my own through association with you."
Blessed is my brother Subāhu, by whom he has been well-established in knowledge. By good fortune, I have likewise read the letter sent by my mother;
and by good fortune, I have likewise served the pair of your feet.
By good fortune, all your words have become firmly established in my mind.
(1.05) By good fortune, knowledge has arisen in me through the company of you, a holy man. By good fortune, compassion has been shown by your lordship toward me. (1.06)
"Thus, by your grace, my 'I' and 'mine' and other such notions have been utterly consumed by fire;
I shall indeed strive to proceed toward the abode of Brahman, departing from the life of kingship.
Then Dattātreya said to his disciple, "Go, and be happy."
"Free from possessiveness and free from egoism, conduct yourself thus for the sake of liberation.
Having been addressed in this way, he bowed to him and went home at nightfall,
to where King Kāśīpati and his elder brother Subāhu were.
Having gone there, he said, "Enjoy this powerful kingdom;
or, as you please, bestow it upon Subāhu.
Then the King of Kāśī replied, "Why have you abandoned the battle midway?"
Alarka said: "The knots within me have been destroyed by my guru;
through the grace of Dattātreya, the sense of duality has been dispelled.
Having fixed the mind upon Brahman, there is supreme victory in its conquest. (111–112)
Subāhu said: "That purpose for which I have come to fight you has been entirely achieved by me; I have no need for a kingdom.
The King of Kāśī spoke likewise for the sake of knowledge and dispassion.
"O Alarka! For the sake of your liberation, I have proclaimed this battle with you.
Since that knowledge and dispassion have arisen within you, I shall depart;
for one who is failing must be disregarded by kinsmen, relatives, and friends."
He is not called one's own kin; rather, he should be regarded as such by people. Indeed, the company of the virtuous has been described to you by me as the giver of fruit.
O King, strive for your own welfare through the attainment of the wisdom born thereof!

Having spoken thus and held a festival, the King of Kāśī departed from there. Subāhu, his purpose accomplished, returned once more to his own forest. Alarka, however, having emerged [from the water], sang this verse: 1.17–1.18. Having spoken thus and held a festival, the King of Kāśī departed from there.
Subāhu, his purpose accomplished, returned once more to his own forest.
Alarka, however, having emerged [from the water], sang this verse:
"Alas, what a wretched kingdom I have governed out of pride!
Through the grace of my guru and through yoga, there is no happiness higher than realized knowledge.
Having spoken thus, he consecrated his own son as the lord of men.
Having abandoned all attachments, he went to the forest for the sake of liberation.
Then, after a long time, he attained the nirvāṇa of Brahman.
By hearing and reciting this, one shall attain union with Brahman.

Thus ends the three hundred and ninety-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Conduct of Liberation, the Signs of Death for Yogis, and the Forest Dwelling of Alarka," within the section on the Greatness of the Devoted Wife in the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga, in the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: O Lakṣmī, in ancient times, during the Age of the Gods (Devayuga), there was Nārada, the best of sages.
Having gone to the summit of Mount Sumeru, he beheld the abode of the Creator.
To the north of that was a divine pavilion beneath a *pippala* tree,
adorned with thousands of pillars made of rubies.
Having entered that place— which was adorned with auspicious svastika symbols, beautified by divine archways,
possessed great gates of topaz, and featured seven-storied gate-towers—
he beheld within a celestial pavilion made of pearls.
In the middle of that is an altar, and upon it is a lofty throne adorned with eight legs. In its center is a thousand-petaled lotus,
and seated there is a beautiful being in human form.
He beheld Puruṣottama, four-armed and white-complexioned, with the face of a boar, bearing the conch, the discus, the gesture of fearlessness, and the gesture of granting boons;
he saw the Lord wearing yellow garments and possessing large, lotus-like eyes.
With a face as gentle as the full moon, his splendor radiant with a crown;
he is the sound of the Sāman chants, the embodiment of sacrifice, with the *sruk* ladle for a snout and the *sruva* spoon for a nose;
he is resplendent with the *śrīvatsa* mark upon his chest and adorned with a shining sacred thread (*yajñasūtra*).
Having praised Hari— who was radiant with the splendor of the Kaustubha gem, adorned with golden ornaments,
and resplendent with bracelets, armlets, neck-ornaments, and earrings—
Nārada stood in the presence of the Lord.
In the meantime, O Lakṣmī, Dharaṇī arrived there (1.398.10),
accompanied by her two friends Ilā and Piṅgalā;
she was a young woman, richly adorned with all ornaments and joined by her companions (11).

She bowed at the soles of Śrī Hari’s feet, scattering many fragrant flowers upon his head, and stood with her palms joined in reverence. Then the divine Varāha embraced that goddess and placed her upon his lap.
She asked after her welfare as well as the reason for her arrival.
Pṛthvī replied: "O Blessed One, by your grace all is well with me;
indeed, I have heard this from the mouth of Nārāyaṇa reclining upon Śeṣa."
"O Mādhava, I desire to see that great *tīrtha*, that very place where, by the will of Lakṣmī, she who was formerly Vedavatī [resided] on earth and in the water.
Having heard that, Nārada said, "That is indeed true, O Vasundharā."
"I heard this very thing in the assembly of sages at Satya.
Having spoken thus and bowed to Hari, Nārada went to Badarī.
Dharaṇī said to the Blessed One: "Show me that place."
"If you have compassion for me, I wish to see Padminī.
Having said "So be it" to her, Varāha called to mind the bird.
Vainateya arrived before him with his divine body.

Having personally lifted up the earth along with it, the Lord himself in the form of a boar ascended Garuḍa and proceeded to Janisthala. There he beheld Padminī, the shadow-like daughter of Viyadrāja. (1.398.20)
Having beheld Nārāyaṇapura, he went to Nārāyaṇācala,
where stands the mountain Śeṣācala, which is supremely purifying;
as well as Aruṇādri, Hastiśaila, and the river Suvarṇamukharī.
And on its northern bank is a lake named Kamala.
On its shore dwells the Lord Hari, the granter of boons to Śuka.
And on the northern side of the lake, he is adorned by *haricandana* trees.
The mountain named Śrī Veṅkaṭācala is the abode of Vāsudeva;
it is two yojanas in extent and half a yojana in height.
There, hosts of deities beginning with Indra and lords of sages beginning with Vasiṣṭha [reside].
The Siddhas and Sādhyas, the Maruts, and the Vaiṣṇavas who are dear to the Lord;
the hosts of Apsarases, such as Rambhā and others, dwell there always with self-restraint;
and the Nāgas, Garuḍas, Kinnaras, and others perform austerities there.
O Lakṣmī! On Nārāyaṇagiri is the auspicious Svāmipuṣkariṇī.
On its western bank is Vārāha accompanied by Dharaṇī. Descending from Garuḍa, Hari indeed made his dwelling there. (27)
On its southern bank dwells Śrīnivāsa, the Lord of the Universe.
O Lotus-born one, I too reside there together with Śrī and Bhūmi.
In the Kṛta age he was called Añjanādri, and in the Tretā age they spoke of him as Nārāyaṇagiri.
In the Dvāpara age they call it Siṃhaśaila, and in the Kali age, the gods proclaim that mountain Śrī Veṅkaṭācala to be the abode of the Supreme Self.
On its western shore, on the bank of Svāmipuṣkariṇī, which is honored by the world...
He dwells on Śeṣādri and Vṛṣabhācala with the face of a boar.
Having found rest there on Nārāyaṇagiri, the Earth,
accompanied by her companions, [worships] the Lord in the form of a boar.
Beholding the shadow of Lakṣmī, she asked with supreme affection:
"When will the Lord Śrīnivāsa, the Master of the Universe, appear within the range of my vision upon the great mountain named Veṅkaṭa, accompanied by Śrī and Bhūmi? (23)
The illustrious Varāha said to the Earth: "Listen, O beloved, to an ancient account!
Formerly, in the Kṛta Yuga, having beheld the great austerity of Vāyu, the Lord Śrīnivāsa indeed arrived here accompanied by Śrī and Bhūmi. (24–35)
On this most meritorious southern bank of the Svāmipuṣkariṇī,
Hari, who brings joy to Vāyu, resides in the celestial chariot named Ānanda;
there Hari remains within that vimāna, invisible until the end of the kalpa.
The Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, whose abode is Vaikuṇṭha—
Dharaṇī asked when and how Kṛṣṇa might become visible;
and if she should entreat him with true devotion, the king of sages, Agastya, [will grant her wish].
"Then the Lord of Śrī would become an object of sight for everyone.
Having heard this, the Earth remembered Agastya, and he too arrived.
Having propitiated the Supreme Self and pleased him again and again, [he spoke].
"For the sake of the world's welfare, I entreated that you become visible.
Thus addressed, the Lord Hṛṣīkeśa, accompanied by Śrī and Bhūmi,
that abode of compassion, indeed became an object of sight for everyone.
Having beheld him, the sage departed for his own hermitage filled with joy;
yet the celestial chariot that was present there could never be seen again.
Thereafter, the four-armed Lord remained forever visible.
Having beheld him, Pṛthvī became fulfilled.
Then there was a great chariot-warrior named Mitravarmā, born of the Lunar dynasty, who was the king in Nārāyaṇapura within the Tuṇḍīra district. (43–44)
While Mitravarmā ruled the world of mortals with righteousness,
the earth yielded crops without being ploughed and was endowed with every kind of grain. Free from pestilence, all the people were filled with devotion.
His wife was the charming Manoramā, the daughter of the Pāṇḍya king.
To him was born an auspicious son named Viyat, the ornament of his lineage;
and his wife was Dharaṇī by name, born of a pure family.
Having entrusted the kingdom to Viyat, Mitravarmā, a devotee of Viṣṇu,
went to the holy penance grove near Veṅkaṭādri.
Viyat, a sovereign emperor, became devoted to the vow of having only one wife.
With his mind fixed upon the earth, he cleared the ground.
For the sake of the sacrifice, he ploughed a vast area with a golden plough while the mountain himself was being drawn across the surface of the earth by the sky.
As he was scattering handfuls of seed, he saw a maiden risen from the earth;
there was a hidden, cavernous opening there, which was like a dwelling,
refreshed by nourishing breezes and auspicious with the spreading of fragrances.
Above the gate was a stone slab, and beneath it rested a young maiden.
That place, filled with every prosperity and worshipped by the gods,
became the site where Sītā became attached to the plough as the ploughshare was being drawn through it.
Then, rising from the rock, he beheld within a most brilliant white radiance;
the king also saw the various articles for the lotus-bed.
Upon that bed lay his daughter, appearing like one fashioned of gold.
Beheld by King Ākāśa with eyes wide open in wonder, the king took his daughter and said to him again and again, "She is mine alone. Then, a voice from the sky spoke to him in the air: || 55-56 ||
"It is true; she is indeed your daughter; raise up your own child.
Then, with a joyful heart, the king helped her down from the chariot.
A rain of flowers fell, and there arose the sound of victory proclaimed by the gods.
Resounding with the thundering of kettledrums, the quarters of the sky echoed in response.
(58) Leaving the garden grounds, the king entered his own city;
having summoned his wife Dharaṇī, the lord of the earth spoke this to her. (59)
"Behold this Devadattā, who has risen from the ground before me;
since we two are childless, she will certainly become our daughter.
Having said this, King Viyat affectionately placed her in his wife's hands.
Upon merely beholding the girl, the virtuous queen indeed began to reflect:
"Is she the Mother of the Gods, or is she the Mother of the Vedas?
Is she Śrī, or Lakṣmī, or Śāradā, or Arundhatī, or Pārvatī? (61–62)
Is she Prabhā, Māṇikī, Gaṅgā, or Śacī; is she Sarasvatī, Rādhā, Lalitā, Sītā, Jayā, or Vijayā?
Is she Ekādaśī, Jayantī, Dyau, or the devoted Vahalyā? (63)
"Could it be the divine Mahālakṣmī who has come for my sake?"—
as she was thus forming these conjectures, she beheld a great splendor manifested from her body, resembling the Great Vaikuṇṭha itself.
There he saw a beautiful lion-throne where Nārāyaṇa,
Hari, shines— four-armed, youthful, dark-complexioned, and exceedingly handsome.
Beside him, on his left side, he beheld his daughter, that virtuous Satī.
Seeing the young Vaiṣṇavī goddess Mahālakṣmī, who was identical in form [to herself], four-armed,
and holding her own wife Viṣṇu upon her hand, the Earth herself rejoiced and placed her at the feet of Mādhava.
Having taken her who was composed of a young woman, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Blessed Lord himself, gave her back to Dharaṇī and said:
"Protect her; I shall come there from Śrī Veṅkaṭācala."
"I shall carry her according to the prescribed rites; let her indeed perform service for me.
Having been addressed thus, Dharaṇī took her by the hand and stood firm;
at that moment, the entire splendor of Vaikuṇṭha vanished from sight.
Then the Earth became pleased and spoke from the sky;
Viyadrāja also rejoiced, perceiving that divine splendor was Śrī.
Considering Śrī to be his daughter, the Mother constantly performed service for her.
The deities and the liberated ones also come day and night to behold her;
having bowed down again and again, they worship her and indeed depart.
The home of Dharaṇī shone forth, renowned as being superior even to heaven.
At that very time, through the merit of her vow for a sacrifice, Dharaṇī, the wife of King Ākāśa, conceived a child; and King Viyat,
being well-pleased, observed the signs of her pregnancy-longing.
He said, "O fair-browed one, that *santānikī* creeper has borne fruit for me.
Then, as time passed, his wife Dharaṇī gave birth to a son at an auspicious moment,
while the sun was situated in Aries.
Seeing the boy, who was radiant, golden-hued, and like a god,
both the Earth and the King rejoiced exceedingly.
They gave many gifts, such as jewels, elephants, cows, and so forth.
Divine drums resounded and a rain of flowers fell upon the house (79).
On that day of his son’s birth, a breeze blew with a pleasant touch;
by that [merit], the poverty of those who announce the birth of a son was destroyed. (1.398.80)
On the first and sixth days, he gave a gift of ten million tawny cows and more than a hundred bulls, as well as ten thousand pieces of gold;
likewise, when the eleventh day arrived, he performed the naming ceremony.
Vasudāna caused delightful structures to be constructed as well.
Vasudāna indeed grew like the lord of stars (the moon) during the bright fortnight;
having been initiated, he was disciplined and likewise instructed by his teachers.

He studied the science of archery (Dhanurveda) in its four divisions, along with all its auxiliary branches and sub-branches; he also learned all the weapons of his father, together with their respective mantras.
He was invincible, unconquerable, difficult to withstand, and hard even to look upon.
Seeing that highly fortunate son, the king bestowed upon him the Vaiṣṇava initiation,
which removes worldly existence, along with the mantras under the name of Kṛṣṇa.
Then [he gave] his daughter, who was like a lotus, auspicious as another Padmā.
Knowing her to be equal to Lakṣmī, he gave her the name Padminī.
When she had reached the fullness of youth and was surrounded by her companions,
wandering in a grove resounding with the songs of parrots and cuckoos—
Nārada, the best among all-knowers, arrived there by chance.
Beholding the shadow of Lakṣmī—which was like the very splendor of the forest and appeared perfectly certain—he bowed to the Goddess and asked: "Who are you? Whose daughter indeed are you? (88–89)
"I believe your fortune is highly accomplished; show me your hand.
Thus addressed, she of beautiful limbs gave her own introduction:
"I am the daughter of Viyadrāja, and I have been raised by Dharaṇīpa."
"O Sage! She was raised in the royal palace and born upon this earth.
O Omniscient One! What do you know? Tell me, what kind of fortune does she possess?
Thus addressed, Nārada [described] her bodily marks and characteristics. (91–92)
Having observed each one, he was indeed delighted and then said:
"The nails of the toes are reddish at their bases and possess a prominent elevation;
the two feet are well-placed, white, and marked with the auspicious sign of the red lotus. (93)
The soles of your feet are the color of the petals of a land-lotus, auspicious and endowed with softness.
Upon your palms, the lines and other marks are clearly defined.
Your ankles are hidden, symmetrical, radiant, rounded, and well-proportioned.
Her shanks were hairless, lovely, well-proportioned, and exceedingly beautiful;
her knees were even and very smooth, and her thighs were symmetrical and gradually broadening.
They were indeed like the trunks of elephants—soft and cool as the moon.
Their hips were richly endowed with every excellence, soft and smooth, broad and full, for they met together;
and the roots of their thighs were tender, possessing the very pinnacle of beauty. (97–98)
The hips were richly adorned with lines like the *liṅga*, and the waist was as radiant as gold.
The navel was circular and deep, marked by three folds of skin.
Both sides [of the body] were bright and fleshy, resembling the petals of a land-lotus.
Her belly is beautiful with its three folds and adorned by a line of fine hair.
Your breasts are full, firm, smooth, elevated, with nipples that are slightly sunken;
your hands have the luster of red lotuses and are marked with lotus-like lines.

O maidens, your arms are very slender, with fingers that are red, well-jointed, continuous, and even; they possess a beautiful, bright luster like the moon and are well-filled with a reddish hue at the wrists. Long and tender, your arms resemble the stalks of flowers.
Your back shines like a sacrificial altar, with a slender waist that is well-proportioned.
Your throat is red, sweet-toned, suitably long, and exceedingly beautiful;
likewise, your shoulders are sloped and resemble those of a lion.
His face is ever serene, round, and possessed of bright luster; it is beautiful, radiant with a halo of splendor, captivating to the sight, and auspicious.
His cheeks resemble golden mirrors, shining with earrings.
O Padminī! Your nose has the appearance of a sesame flower.
Your forehead is broad, white, beautiful, and brilliantly radiant;
it is auspicious, marked with lines, and resembles the stainless moon of the eighth day. 106–107.
Resplendent with a form manifested by the roots of your dark-blue locks, you are equally adorned with auspicious marks and graced by every fortune.
Your head is perfectly rounded and endowed with smooth, long hair.
Your face, which is adorned with teeth made beautiful by a smile and endowed with a bimba-fruit-like lower lip,
and which shines with a row of teeth as radiant as jasmine buds—
that very face of yours is truly worthy of Nārāyaṇa. (1.398.110)

Your navel is clockwise-rotating, and your heart is like the hand of Viṣṇu; adorned with beautiful lines, you indeed appear in the form of Lakṣmī. Between your breasts, there is indeed the mark of Nārāyaṇa upon your heart.
Above the feet, there is also a mark known as the *tilaka* or *puṇḍra*. Below the navel, on the region of the hips, there is a line golden-brown in color and shaped like an arrow;
and on the forehead, it is shaped like a crown.
Moreover, on your right cheek and in the middle of your forehead,
there is a beautiful red mole as auspicious as the Sudarśana discus.
On your chest, there is a subtle line of Viṣṇu extending four cubits.
On the left arm is the mark of a mace, and on the left thigh is a sandal.
On the chest there is an auspicious line made of gold from the Vaijayantī garland;
and holding a lotus in his hand, there is an auspicious hand-mark upon his beautiful hand.
On the sole beneath the root of the big toe of your right foot, O Excellent One,
there exists a mark of a conch that awakens the form of Lakṣmī.
Likewise, at the base of your toes, there is a mark of a beautiful celestial chariot.
Indeed, near the base of the little finger, there is the mark of a boat.
There is also the mark of a mace, the mark of a fish, and the mark of a mountain peak.
Furthermore, on the heel, there are lines of fish as well as a betel vine.
At the base of his left thumb, there is a charming mark of a barley grain;
likewise, there is an auspicious, well-formed palace upon that line.
There is also the mark of an umbrella, an upward-pointing line, a lotus, and a hood.
A banner, a goad, a white water-lily, a bilva fruit, and likewise a jar;
as well as a land-lotus and the mark of a second moon—these ten wheels of yours are upon the golden line of the hood. (121–122)
"O girl, these marks of Hari are seen upon you; therefore, I consider you destined to be his beloved. Make him, who dwells within your heart, your certain husband.
[He is the one] in whose birthplace—the opening of the womb, the middle, the interior of the belly, and the region of the secret cavity—"
The binding [organ] is a ring in the form of Kuṇḍalinī,
firm and gradually acting as a grinder for the *liṅga*, characterized by both contraction and expansion;
such a woman is a lotus-lady (*padminī*) who is always fit for Viṣṇu.
"However, this firm bangle remains inside the womb of a certain woman;
it will bring happiness to her and to her husband, but it will not belong to any of the others.
Having spoken thus, Nārada, honored by the virtuous woman, then vanished.
Having heard this, her friends then said to the virtuous Padminī:
"O Mistress, we are going to the forest for the sake of flowers, fruits, and leaves;
let us gather flowers, for spring has arrived."
From there, accompanied by the daughter of Ākāśa, they went to the forest and beheld a certain lordly elephant with four white tusks,
shedding white ichor from his temples and accompanied by female elephants.
Seeing him letting out a fierce cry, they took refuge in the trees;
they hid within the thickets of the forest and then beheld the horse—
white, adorned with golden ornaments, and towering like an autumn cloud.
Behind him is a man of black complexion, carrying the bow of desire; his eyes are as broad as lotus petals, and he is clothed in fine silken garments.
He is adorned with necklaces, armlets, and earrings set with excellent gems and jewels.
Holding the divine Śārṅga bow and indeed a golden arrow in his hand,
his waist region was wrapped in yellow garments;
he possessed a beautiful midriff and was resplendent with jeweled bracelets, anklets, and a girdle-string.
His broad chest was graced by a clockwise curl of hair, and his shoulders were radiant with a golden sacred thread; he was truly captivating.
Seeing him, they all stood in respectful wonder, smiling.
Then the man, mounted on his horse, went far away with the elephant.
Seeing this, the maiden who had been resting by a tree approached him and said: "O maiden! Have you seen any deer here? (136–137)
They all replied to him: "No one has been seen by us.
For what purpose have you come? Go from our forest to the outside.
All the deer here are not to be slain, for they are protected by the King of the Sky. (138)
Having heard their words, he descended from his horse.
He asked: "Who are you here, and who is this lotus-like maiden?
Tell me, for having heard [your account], I shall go to Nārāyaṇācala."
"I always dwell there eternally; I wander and I go through the forest.
Then, prompted by the daughter of the Earth, Śāradā spoke to her, the daughter of King Ākāśa, who was born from the womb of Vasudhā. (141)
"Know that our female student is a girl named Padminī.
"Give us your own name and so forth; what caste do you belong to here?
Being asked thus, he said to them: "I am a person of the Solar dynasty (Sūryavaṃśī)."
O maidens, there is no exhaustive enumeration of my purifying names!
By both description and name, I am Kṛṣṇa, I am Nārāyaṇa;
I am he whose discus brings terror to embodied beings who are enemies of Dharma.
The sound of whose conch shell rends the hosts of enemies;
whose bow, the Śārṅga, eternally deludes the Daityas at the time of creation;
and who holds in his hand the lotus that bestows prosperity and increases the fortune of Lakṣmī. (145–146)
Thus, while staying on Mount Veṅkaṭa, I arrived there for the purpose of hunting.
A white leader of a herd of deer, who was the incarnation of Gaja, was pursued by me. Running from here with the speed of the wind, he soon vanished from sight.
"Having arrived, I beheld this beautiful lotus-lake.
Having abandoned the deer, I have reached the doe; what indeed can be gained by me [now]?
Hearing these words of Kṛṣṇa, they became enraged and spoke to the Aśvin. (148–149)
"Go quickly from this forest; never speak thus again.
Upon hearing you, King Ākāśarāja will bind you in fetters.
You appear indeed as Kṛṣṇa both within and without, according to your name and qualities."
"Do you not feel shame that you ask for another's divine daughter?
We shall all join together right here and surely bind you, and we shall certainly beat you here so that you will never say such a thing again. (151–152)
Thus threatened by them, the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa mounted his horse, and looking back with a sidelong glance, departed for the mountain.

Thus, in the first section of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, within the account of the Kṛta Yuga, regarding the majesty of the devoted wife (pativratā), Bhū and Nārada beheld the Varāha incarnation on Mount Meru; Garuḍa arrived and saw Nārāyaṇapura, the birthplace of Lakṣmī’s shadow-form; Padminī was born from the womb of the Earth; she was raised by the queen named Viyat; a son, Vasudāna, was born; and Nārada declared that she was equal to Lakṣmī by her characteristic marks.
Chapter Three Hundred and Ninety-Eight: The Description of How Nārāyaṇa, Mounted on His Horse, Came to the Garden, Gave His Introduction, and Departed for Veṅkaṭādri.
