Chapter 399.
[The Author: Chapter 400.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī! To this divine, delightful, and auspicious narrative concerning a former birth.
Having mounted that horse, I went to the glorious Veṅkaṭācala mountain. (1) Having dismounted from the horse, he entered my pavilion;
and I, named Śrīnivāsa, having passed through five courtyards, (2) [entered].
Having reached the pearl palace, Śrīnivāsa entered the couch while repeatedly remembering her; becoming helpless again and again,
he recalled his former lotus-like wife who had been created for his sake.
Lord Śrīnivāsa did not obtain even a moment’s sleep there.
When midday arrived, his friend Bakulamālikā [brought] food to be eaten and chewed, milk-rice, sweet fragrant rice, and so forth.
Condiments, soups, buttermilk, *pūrikās*, *vaṭikās*, meat juices, cakes, *vaṭakas*, *pūrṇapolikās*, curd with clarified butter,
and *rasānakas* such as plantains mixed with sugar.
Having placed the desired deity within a large vessel, they arrived together.
The other friends were Citrarekhā, Navaraṅgā, Mālatī, Kamalā, Kiṃśukī, Kalpalatā, and others who brought water and other necessities. (7–8)
Taking betel, a fan, an excellent sandal-paste box, sandalwood, and fruit,
they went to where Śrīnivāsa shines resplendent.
Bakulamālikā paid homage to Kṛṣṇa with a spirit of devotion.
As Hari was meditating upon his unprecedented form, a female friend addressed him:
"Arise, O Lord of the gods of gods! Come, O Mādhava, to eat.
Why do you appear distressed, when you, O Hari, are the remover of distress?"
Did you see someone new in the forest under the pretext of hunting?
The state of one who reflects clearly reveals what is in the heart.
Who was seen—was she a daughter of the gods, a human woman, or a daughter of the serpents?
"Tell us, O Blessed One, of that state of mind which captivates the heart. Having heard this, Śrīnivāsa, the Supreme Person, exhaled a deep sigh and, smiling, spoke there to his companion.
In a former age, I slew the great evildoer Rāvaṇa;
at that time, Vedavatī became Sītā’s companion as her handmaid.
Lakṣmī herself appeared in the form of Sītā from the surface of the earth to Janaka.
I, Rāma, obtained her there in the forest of Pañcavaṭī.
When the Rākṣasa Rāvaṇa arrived to carry her off, the god Agni, having entered into Svāhā, [protected her]. || 16-17 ||
In her place, he substituted the maiden Vedavatī, who possessed her very form.
The Rākṣasa carried off Vedavatī, and Rāma slew him.
Having cast Vedavatī into the fire, he obtained the true Jānakī.
Having accomplished my purpose there, the Fire-god then spoke to me:
"This maiden Vedavatī is a benefactor to Sītā;
for the sake of Sītā, she has fallen into the great ocean of misery, having come into the hands of the Rākṣasa."
"Therefore, gratify him with a boon along with Sītā.
Having heard these words of the Fire-god, Sītā also said to me:
"This friend Vedavatī of mine has undergone suffering for my sake."
"Therefore, O Lord, choose this supreme goddess, the devotee of the Lord (Bhāgavatī).
Then I promised, "At your word, I shall indeed choose Padminī, the daughter of King Ākāśa, who is the very embodiment of Śrī."
Let her remain for now as this maidservant of Śrī, appearing in the form of a friend;
for when she becomes the daughter of the Earth, she shall become the daughter of the Sky. And she will attain fame in the world by the name Padminī. ||re4||
"O Mālikā,
since she was previously granted a boon by me and Lakṣmī, saying, 'In that case, my wife shall indeed be a Padminī,' she has today been born from the surface of the earth in Nārāyaṇapura. || 25-26 ||
In the forest, I saw her gathering flowers—lotus-eyed and as beautiful as Lakṣmī herself, her loveliness matching her form. My heart is fixed upon her; therefore, please arrange a union with her.
"Go there, and having observed her, bring one who is suitable for my sake.
Thus addressed, Bakulā said: "I shall go indeed to where she is.
Tell me the way, O Lord of Ramā! I will fulfill your desire."
Then Nārāyaṇa said: "Since the cave of Śrī Nṛsiṃha is located there, descend from this Nārāyaṇa mountain by that path;
having reached Agastya’s hermitage on the bank of the Suvarṇamukharī river..."
Having worshipped Agastyeśa, go then to Kīravana. There,
on the shore of the lake named Padmasaras, which is adorned with lotuses,
bow down to Śuka performing austerities, and worship Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma.
Then, O friend, having taken a golden lotus from this lake,
and having crossed the Suvarṇamukharī as well as the forests situated along its banks,
you should reach the Araṇi riverbank and rest there for a moment.

Upon seeing Nārāyaṇapurī, you will be filled with wonder. Having gone by way of the north-eastern path to Ākāśarājanagarī, which is situated on the bank of the Araṇī river, go there and do what is appropriate.
Having thus instructed her and sent her away, that illustrious teacher, accompanied by his disciples, [remained]. Then Vakulā, having bowed to Śrī Hari and mounted her red horse,
departed toward Nārāyaṇapurī by the path as previously described.

Having descended onto the riverbank in the Agastya grove along the way, he bathed, drank, and rested; there he saw the female companions of the lotuses who had arrived for the sake of love and for the worship of the deity Agastyeśa. (37–38)
And Bakulamālikā questioned those female companions of Padminī:
"Who are you, O women? Tell me, for what purpose have you come?
Having heard this, they replied to her: "We are from the mountain in the sky."
"We are indeed the friends of your daughter named Padminī.
Tell us, for what purpose have you come, and where are you going?
Thus addressed, Bakulā said: "How is Padminī faring? 1.399.40-41.

Having seen that Supreme Person in the Puṇyavana forest—the Aśvattha tree with a gentle smile, adorned and clothed in beautiful yellow garments—she, who resembled molten gold, said, "Look! Look! (42).
While we were looking on, he quickly vanished from sight.
That friend of hers remained bewildered, and having seen such a state of affairs, the king questioned a Brahmin who was skilled in the knowledge of destiny; he, in turn, spoke to him.
A certain supreme person has arrived for the sake of the maiden;
having seen him, she will indeed be infatuated and shall enter into union with him.
Sent by that very person, a certain maiden will come.
Whatever words she shall speak will come true exactly as they are.
"Perform the worship of Agastyeśa; everything will turn out well.
Having been addressed thus, the king sent us to our home.
"Let us indeed gather the materials for the great worship here, such as flowers and the like.
Tell me, what is this story? How have you come here, and what do you desire as a favor?
Bakulā said to them there: "We have come from the Veṅkaṭa mountain."
"I wish to see Dharaṇī; shall I be able to see her or not?
Her friends said, "Come with us and you shall behold her.
Then Bakulā went with them into the interior of the king's fortress.
She spoke slowly with a reproachful tone, as one who knows the stars might declare:
"I speak the truth; listen to what has been, what is, and what will be.
Having heard this from her, the Earth asked Śukī, who stood before her.
"Tell me the result of the zodiacal sign; shall I give you a heap of wealth?
(5.2) Bakulā spoke the truth: that her daughter’s body was withered, tormented by the fever of love born from the sight of a man. (5.3)
That very God of gods has indeed come in person from Vaikuṇṭha;
today he dwells on the glorious Veṅkaṭa mountain, attended by Śrī. The Lord, who can assume any form at will and bestows the desires of his devotees, sports there.
O Queen! While mounted on his horse in the forest, he beheld your daughter Vedavatī, who was like a shadow of Sītā—a lotus-like maiden.
Desiring to make her his wife, he will send her into your presence.
"She will clearly tell Lalitā everything about that;
having approached him, she will enjoy herself happily for a long time, just like Rame.
Having spoken thus, Bakulā then maintained silence on the ground.
Having gone inside the house, he saw his daughter, who was infatuated by the god of love.
He said, "Daughter, what is it that you desire? Tell me so that I may do it for you.
Thus addressed, she, who remembered her past lives, spoke to her mother.
That which is delightful to the eyes in this world, pleasing to the minds of the virtuous,
the brilliance of even all brilliances, and the deity of even the gods;
that which is attainable here by the righteous devotees, but never by those who are not devoted.
"In this regard, O Mother, my mind constantly turns toward Kṛṣṇa.
(6.1) The mother said: "Daughter, tell me the characteristics of a devotee, so that I may know them.
Padminī replied: "He who is marked with the conch, the discus, the lotus, and the mace... (6.2)
Likewise, on his two arms and on his forehead there is the crescent moon of the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra*;
on his neck a garland of *tulasī* beads, and in his hand a rosary for recitation;
on his tongue the name of Śrī Hari, and in his heart an image of Hari.
Those who are devoted to worship and recitation, who speak the truth and are free from envy;
who do not revile others, are dedicated to celibacy, and are always intent on purity;
who enjoy the grace of Hari and act for the welfare of all living beings. (64–65)
Those who are compassionate, who practice the modes of devotion such as hearing [the Lord's glories],
who are satisfied with whatever comes by chance, who are intent on meditation upon Hari,
who always associate with the virtuous, and who are ever-peaceful— they are proclaimed to be Vaiṣṇavas.
That Brahman alone is attainable through them; indeed, I have great affection for that.
O Mother, from birth itself my mind has longed for its attainment.
O Mother, without Kṛṣṇa, my mind never runs toward anything else.
"I remember that Śrī Kṛṣṇa alone; I speak of him and even meditate upon him.
By him alone, O Mother, I live; let fate be considered regarding union with him.
Having heard this, the mother reflected on how to achieve union with Viṣṇu.
Viṣṇu, being pleased, devised many plans as to how he might become her husband. While she was thus reflecting, all the maidservants gathered there and, full of curiosity, asked about her anxiety.
"How does she exist through that which consists of reflection? Tell us so that we may bring about her welfare and happiness.
Then the Earth related everything regarding the daughter’s anxiety and so forth.
They said, "That Bakula met us at the site of the garden."
She said, "A friend of Lord Hari has also arrived from Veṅkaṭādri;
her name is Bakulamālikā, and she acts for the welfare of Nārāyaṇa.
Our Lord Nārāyaṇa resides on the glorious Veṅkaṭācala. (73–74)
Once, having mounted a horse as white as a swan and swift as thought,
he went to the vicinity of the forest of Veṅkaṭādri for the sake of hunting.
Having seen an elephant in the forest, the elephant then charged at his back.
Like a leader of a herd of female elephants in the forest, he ran toward him; he followed after him.
There in the forest, he [saw] Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, together with Śrī and Bhūmi, performing austerities and worshiping Janārdana with devotion. (76–77)

Nārāyaṇa, in the form of a king, alighted from his horse and beheld King Śaṅkha on the shore of the lake of the Śaṅkha-nāga at Veṅkaṭādri. Having descended, he asked: "Tell me, what is being done here in the forest of Veṅkaṭādri?"
Then Śaṅkha said to Viṣṇu: "I am born in the Haihaya country;
I am the king of Śveta, and for the sake of pleasing Mahāviṣṇu, I have repeatedly performed all the sacrifices in order to behold Hari. (1.399.80)
But Lord Nārāyaṇa did not grant me a vision;
consequently, I became despondent. Then, O King, the celestial Sarasvatī, bestowing peace, spoke: "In this matter, there is no vision of Me for you."
Go to Nārāyaṇagiri; perform austerities and perform recitation.
By means of propitiating me there, you will obtain a vision of me. There, a certain king mounted on a horse will join with you.
"By acting according to that method, you will surely attain supreme liberation.
Having been told this, I abandoned my country and came to the Vaikuntha [Vaikūṭa] forest,
where I constantly worship Nārāyaṇa-Kṛṣṇa.
"I indeed worship Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa together with Śrībhūmi.
Having heard these words of the king, Nārāyaṇa said to the monarch:
"May it be well with you; go to the abode of Śrī Hari on Mount Nārāyaṇādri."
Standing there upon the western peak, perform your service;
and having bowed down to Viṣvaksena seated at the foot of the banyan tree,
go to Svāmipuṣkariṇī and bathe on its western bank.
There you will see an *aśvattha* tree, and you will also see an anthill.
Standing firm between those two, perform the propitiation of Hari.
There, in that place, Hari known as Śvetavarāha wanders.
"You shall see him somewhere in an anthill by the power of your merit," having thus instructed Śveta, Hari reached the Araṇī river;
having dismounted from his horse, he wandered along its bank.
A cool and fragrant breeze served him, dispelling his fatigue.
(91) The trees served him with flowers and delicious, excellent fruits;
and then that lord gazed upon his elephant and his companions. (92)
The elephant became invisible in the forest, and your lord Prati returned. Having seen you—
slender, like Lakṣmī, golden-hued, and standing in his midst—
the lion’s mind became fixed there, as if upon a lotus-pond.
Greedily, he said to her, "Is she to be seized by my hand, or not?
Having been thus insulted by you all, that Viyadrāja indeed departed by force;
hearing this, he immediately mounted his horse and went to the Venkata mountain.
"I have been sent by her very self, the maidservant Bakulamālikā.
I am going to the earth to obtain for Padminī beautiful maidens for Hari.
Having spoken thus, that servant of Kṛṣṇa approached you before him.
He indeed requested those maidens for Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa:
"O Mother, having reflected with Viyat and the others, act as is appropriate;
for there is a worthy gift to be given to this Supreme Soul who is himself worthy. (97-98)
The lotus-eyed Ramā, who is like a lotus-lake, should be given to Rāma;
a beautiful maiden should indeed be given to a handsome man, and a passionate woman to a lover.
A divine woman should certainly be given to a divine one, and a devotee to the Blessed Lord.
Having heard their words, she questioned the king himself.
Out of compassion, she questioned Padminī once again. The king said: "I have a daughter who is not born of a womb; she is a goddess."
"Through Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, my desire has been fulfilled; grace has been bestowed, and today my heart's wish is complete, as surely is that of others.
Having heard all this, they rejoiced and spoke of the fulfillment of their lineage's purpose.
"This incomparable daughter of yours shall sport together with Śrī.
Let her be given to the Supreme Lord who dwells on the Veṅkaṭa mountain.
This spring season is graced by Śrī; let an auspicious act be performed quickly. (103–104)
"Having summoned the preceptor of heaven, let the auspicious moment for the marriage be determined.
"So be it," the king replied, and he summoned Bṛhaspati.
For the maiden, the asterism was Mṛgaśīrṣa, while that of the god was Śravaṇa.
Having investigated that very matter regarding their birth, the Guru declared the ascendant;
he said, "Uttaraphālgunī is favorable for the increase of happiness for the two of them;
let their marriage be performed according to the rites on that day in the month of Vaiśākha."
Having spoken thus and received the worship performed by the king, his own guru departed.
The king, however, dispatched a female messenger to the Lord of the Gods,
accompanied by Śuka, for the purpose of the formal betrothal of the maiden.
Śuka was the messenger, and Śāradā, Bakulā, and likewise Dūtī were the female messengers.
On that very same delightful day, they went to the auspicious Veṅkaṭācala to see the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, Śrīnivāsa, the Lord of the universe.
Having bowed down, they spoke with joy: "O Lord, our task is accomplished;
we have come here filled with devotion for this auspicious news.
O Mādhava, the daughter of the Earth says to you: 'Accept me!'"
I chant your names; I remember your image.
O Janārdana, I meditate upon your auspicious marks on my heart and other limbs, and I perform all my duties without forgetting you.
"Requested by you, I am yours alone, with the permission of my parents. Show me favor, O Lord of Lakṣmī! Accept me, O Mādhava!
Thus both the sky and the earth replied to the Supreme Lord.
A gift-vessel obtained from oneself bestows eternal fruit.
(1.15) Joy does not fit within my heart; O Hari, accept the maiden.
She has been given by the offering of my word; Śuka will announce it. (1.16)
"Having received your command once more, we shall become full of enthusiasm.
Bakula said: "O Preceptor of the World, recite the message!
O Lord Keśava, show favor to me and to Padminī as well."
"So be it," Hari said, accepting the gift of words. "O Śuka, go and tell them that I shall come with the immortals to perform the auspicious wedding. Thus the Lord spoke.
"Accept this forest garland, adorned with gold, jewels, and other ornaments.
Having taken the garland, Śuka and Śāradā went home.
Having bowed down, they said to everyone: "The task requested for our son has been accomplished."
They placed a jasmine garland, imbued with deep emotion, around Padminī’s neck.
Once the auspicious moment had been determined, the king sent a marriage proposal letter;
he also had his son Anila write out letters on saffron paper.
In order to bring Indra and the others, he dispatched [messengers] throughout the three worlds;
having summoned Viśvakarman, the Lord arranged for the construction of cities,
and he too fashioned them in an instant.
Indra released a rain of flowers and the throngs of Apsarases danced;
musical instruments were played and there was a great festival of women.
Dhanada filled that residence with wealth, grain, and other riches.
Yama made the men on earth free from disease;
Varuṇa filled them with collections of jewels, such as pearls and the like;
and Sūrya presented them with ornaments and other items made of gold and gems.
The ocean and likewise the mountains offered precious gems;
the wish-fulfilling cows, the wish-granting trees, the wish-yielding creepers, and the thought-gems each fulfilled their respective desires at that time.

By the command of the Lord, the rivers, streams, oceans, the heavens, the netherworlds, and the earths on Mount Veṅkaṭācala prepared their respective jewels— drinks, foods, and delicacies to be licked. (1.29)
Then Earth, Water, Fire, Wind, and Space— the lords—
constructed an auspicious pavilion in the palace of Viyadrāja,
measuring ten yojanas in width and one yojana in height.
For the purpose of his own residence, he caused a city to be built upon an excellent island in the ocean, extending for a hundred yojanas—
a great and meritorious place made of illusion, truly a second heaven on earth.
Abounding in the splendor of vehicles and carriages, it possessed a hundred thousand golden peaks (1.33).
It was endowed with alchemy laboratories, bathing halls, and chambers for adornment;
it contained circles for dancing, singing, amorous dalliance, storytelling, and legendary narratives (1.34).
It could be heard from afar, seen, read, and contemplated;
likewise, that divine house, the essence of all beings, was illuminated by lightning.
Having summoned Candramāhūya, the king had it constructed as a place for food.
Food of many kinds, sweet, like nectar, and endowed with flavor;
fit for the sacrificial offering (naivedya) of Viṣṇu, such as milk-rice (paramānna) and boiled rice—these are esteemed by the gods, the sages, and even by men. (136–137)
It was likewise approved by the liberated, the virtuous, and the holy;
it consisted of four kinds of food, rich in fragrance and filled with portions of nectar.
There were various types of elixirs (rasāyana), both drinks and ever-new foods to be eaten.
Having made these arrangements, the king, together with Dharaṇī,
caused the auspicious sound of musical instruments to resound;
Padminī, longing for the arrival of the gods, adorned herself.
Having adorned them all, the king, together with Dharaṇī and his ministers, sat in the assembly hall with a joyful mind.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, this supreme fortune of the lotus-lake is but your own shadow.
"The Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa will take her hand in marriage; thus has it borne fruit.

Thus, in the first book of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, within the section on the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga and the majesty of devoted wives (*pativratā*), Bakulamālikā was sent by the Blessed Lord Śrīnivāsa to Padminī; and Sītā’s shadow was born as Vedavatī, who became Padminī.

Chapter Three Hundred and Ninety-Nine: Description of Bakulamālikā’s departure for Dharaṇīgṛha, the indication through signs that Padminī was destined to be the wife of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the decision that she was to be given to Nārāyaṇa, the sending of the marriage horoscope, and the commencement of preparations for the wedding.
Chapter Four Hundred: The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga (Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā, Book 1).
[The Author: Chapter 401.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, Lakṣmī! On the Veṅkaṭa mountain, Śrīnivāsa [brought] his own beloved.
Having summoned Śrī, Lakṣmī, as well as her other female companions, he said:
(1) "Tell me, Lakṣmī! O Śrī! And you, my female friends—what is to be done?
Give orders to all regarding whatever is required for the sake of the wedding. (2)
"Let all of you, gathered together, perform what is auspicious, such as the rite of encouragement.
Having heard Kṛṣṇa’s words, Lakṣmī summoned all her companions.
At Śrī’s command, the companion Prīti took up fragrant oil.
The friend Śruti arrived, bringing silken garments;
the friend Smṛti stood before him, bringing ornaments;
and the friend Dhṛti held up a brilliant, divine mirror.
Then Śānti, her most excellent companion, held a fragrant musk-paste; Hrī stood before her holding yakṣakardama unguent;
and Kīrti, her companion, held a golden fillet and a crown set with jewels.
Indrāṇī held the parasol, while Sarasvatī held the fly-whisk.
Gaurī held a fly-whisk, and both Vijayā and Jayā held fans.
Then the Lord was consecrated with an ablution by Śrī; thus [he became] Śrī-Parameśvara.
Taking fragrant oil, the maidens anointed the God;
having rubbed his limbs with scented powders, they cleansed the body of the Lord.
Then, a hundred golden water-jars brought by elephants [were presented].
Taking each of those [articles] individually, Ramā and the others consecrated him.
Having perfumed his hair with incense and having groomed it with a comb,
the beautifully adorned Śrī bound his locks, which were curved and had shimmering ends.
Having smeared her limbs with fragrant yellow-colored paste,
she rubbed them well and put on a yellow garment and a beautiful golden girdle around her waist. Then Indirā adorned herself with ornaments and garlands of flowers.
And Dhṛti showed him a mirror, the source of auspiciousness;
the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa himself applied the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra). Thus adorned with ornaments, the Blessed One shone forth in his own splendor.
Then the lords arrived as guests at Kṛṣṇa’s house:
Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Śrī Nārāyaṇa, Virāṭ, the Lord Sadāśiva, Bhūmā, Hiraṇyagarbha, Vāsudeva, and others. (12)
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa, as well as the world-protectors and others;
the ancestors, the sages, the gods, the seers, and the guardians of the quarters;
the sun and other planets, as well as the Vasus and the treasures. (16)
The quarters, the Rudras, as well as the Ādityas, the Manus, Vāsava and the others,
the constellations, the principles (tattvas), the qualities (guṇas), and likewise the Maruts;
the Vālakhilyas, the digits (kalās), the rivers, the streams, the sacred fords (tīrthas), and the mountains.
The oceans, as well as the lakes, the shrines, the earth and other elements,
the trees and so forth, the netherworlds, fire, wind, space, the clouds, nights, days, and so on—
both the insentient and the sentient— are pervaded by Nārāyaṇa’s seal.
On Mount Veṅkaṭādri, millions and billions of glories arrived:
Satī, the Daityas, the liberated ones, the other Īśānyas, the wives of the gods, and the human women born of Kaśyapa who are the mothers of the three worlds. (21)
They arrived at Śrīnivāsādri by means of celestial chariots,
elephants, swans, horses, lions, the best of birds, and yogic jars;
they were holy men, virtuous, steadfast, Vaiṣṇavas free from passion.
Sannyāsins, celibate students, and renunciants arrived;
likewise, twenty-four in number came to the celestial mansion (viyadgṛha).
These were persons whose nature was that of the principles (tattva), as well as deities beginning with Earth.
Valleys, rivers, great plains, lands, and the heavens with their beautiful forms—[all these were present]. 25. The gods and goddesses arrived, full of eagerness and longing for a vision [of Him].
For them, there was food, honor, lodging, drink, and comfortable seats. 26.
Both parties performed the giving of appropriate gifts;
auspicious ceremonies took place there on Mount Veṅkaṭa, in the celestial abode,
as the wedding of Śrī Padminī and Śrīnivāsa was approaching.
Having mounted Garuḍa, Kṛṣṇa, Hari accompanied by Śrī Lakṣmī,
was attended by Brahmā, Īśa, Vajrin, Varuṇa, Yama, and Yakṣeśa,
as well as by the lords of sages such as Vasiṣṭha and by yogins such as Sanaka and others.
Adorned by devotees, followers of the Lord, and holy beings such as Nārada, Sanaka, and others;
magnified by Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa, Brahmā, and Hiraṇyagarbha;
and graced by the lords, Viṣṇu went to the city of Nārāyaṇa.
The Gandharvas sang his glory and the hosts of Apsaras danced;
the celestial drums resounded and the divine women sang songs.
The women were filled with wonder, and the forest deities gazed upon him.
The birds scattered flowers over the forests and sang of his victory;
the sages followed him while chanting hymns of auspiciousness.
The Lord was accompanied by hosts of gods, his disciples, and his attendants, headed by Viṣvaksena.
Accompanied by his friends seated upon chariots, elephants, and palanquins,
and by all the great lords numbering in the tens of millions and more,
the bridegroom reached the well-adorned city of King Viyadrāja.
In the garden outside the city, which extended for many yojanas and was completely covered by the path of the sky, the illustrious Blessed One remained for a moment. During that time,
according to worldly custom, she [the city] performed a circumambulation of the town.
Padminī, mounted upon an elephant, went to and returned from the city gate;
she stood waiting in front of the Lord with full attention.
Then Śrīnivāsa proceeded from the Vāṭyodyāna garden to the city gate.
Lord Īśvara, mounted upon Garuḍa, took up a garland in his hand;
Padminī, seated upon an elephant, likewise held a garland in her hand and moved forward.
Joining face-to-face, they offered two highly precious garlands.
And the bride and groom placed [the garlands] around each other's necks.
Seeing this, Ākāśarāja also rejoiced along with his kinsmen.
Viṣṇu then removed the garland from his own neck and placed it around Padminī’s neck.
Padminī placed a garland of jasmine flowers around Viṣṇu’s neck;
having done this three times, the two of them went to the pavilion hall.
After staying on the throne for a moment, they subsequently entered the auspicious inner chamber.
Then, having caused [the bridegroom] to rest, drink water, and perform worldly customs—
including hospitality and worship adorned with unbroken rice grains and crescent-shaped ornaments—
near the altar in the pavilion for the sake of the boon; 43–44.
The king brought forth excellent [offerings] and performed worship;
Brahmā was the chief officiant there for the marriage rites.
[He performed] the tying of the auspicious thread (māṅgalyasūtra) and so forth, as well as the offering of the sprouts (sāṃkura).
And he made a binding of the fruit of desire upon his forearm.
Then the Lotus-born One kindled the Āhavanīya fire,
while verses of benediction and auspicious hymns were being sung.
Having adorned Padminī with garments, ornaments, and necklaces obtained through the boon,
he led her to the pavilion in the presence of the bridegroom.
Having bowed to the bridegroom and placed the garland around his neck, she sat down.
Standing on the left side together with her husband, she performed the worship and the fire-oblation (*homa*).
Then the preceptor placed the garland of choice upon the necks of both.
Having circumambulated the fire four times, they performed the *homa*.
Then they both took turns swallowing mouthfuls of one another,
as well as playing with golden rings in the water of the arena,
and even throwing flower-buds at each other.
Then the auspicious mantras, which signify the state of husband and wife, were recited.
Surrounded there by Brahmins well-versed in the Vedas and filled with devotion,
the king performed the gift of the maiden, placing his hand in the hand of Viṣṇu.
Having obtained his beloved, Viṣṇu’s body was covered with horripilation;
at that moment, the bridegroom’s forearm became instantly perspiring.
Then, the bride's family placed a dowry into the hand of the bride.
The groom’s party gave much gold and wealth into the hand of the bridegroom:
jewels, gems, necklaces, pearls, ornaments,
as well as other fine silken garments and even flavorful delicacies.
And others, such as gods, sages, and humans, gave according to their capacity their own regional jewels, vehicles, mounts, vessels, divine objects,
fragrant substances, and the like, as well as the *brahmavallī* and other offerings. (57)
Thus Brahmā, together with Bṛhaspati, bestowed blessings there (58).
Having caused the wedding rites to be performed up to the offering of parched grain oblations,
and having given the instruction for the observance of vows, the two, Padminī and Hari, lay down to rest (59).
On the fourth day, the Four-faced One completed everything. King Viyat, with true devotion, caused the Vaiṣṇavas— who are dearer to him than life itself— to enjoy ever-new, fresh cooked food.
Having given whatever natural food was appropriate for each particular body, he caused them to attain supreme satisfaction;
and he provided various drinks, both sweet and sour.
Likewise, he gave betel leaves and other means for cleansing the mouth;
and by such modes of service, Hari was served by King Viyad,
as well as by crores of monkeys, celestial sages, munis, and humans.
The gods and goddesses were delighted by the male and female servants and attendants.
Then Brahmā, having obtained the permission of King Viyat and likewise of the Earth,
placed Hari— accompanied by Śrī Lakṣmī and Padminī— upon Garuḍa.
Just as he was about to set out, accompanied by Mahīmān and the others,
Viyadrāja, Dharaṇī,
and Vasudāna were for a moment filled with tears born of separation from their daughter. (66)
Padminī, having touched her mother’s feet, wept a little; then,
saying "I shall return" and embracing her to her chest,
she departed again on Garuḍa, and at that moment there was a cry of victory.
There was a great sound of musical instruments, and the *sūtas*, *māgadhas*, and bards raised shouts of victory; kettledrums resounded in the sky.
Thus did the excellent female attendant of Viṣṇu proceed to Śrī Veṅkaṭācala.

Having been gratified with water and food, they all rested in the house. (1.400.70) Then, desiring to depart, Śuka and the other hosts of sages, as well as the groups of deities headed by Brahmā, offered praise to Puruṣottama. (71)
And a magnificent golden throne was sent by King Viyadra;
for the sake of pleasing the daughter of Viṣṇu, there were golden jars of rice,
numerous vessels of mung beans, and tens of thousands of pots of ghee.
Divine fruits of the mango, plantain, and coconut; 73.
fruits of the *dhātrī*, *kūṣmāṇḍa*, king-plantain (*rājarambhā*), and others;
boxes of sugar, jewels, pearls, and likewise cows by the millions. 74.
Horses white as swans and the moon, four-tusked elephants,
and many women from the inner apartments as well as female attendants—
all this that was in the pavilion after the giving away of the maiden, he [saw] with his heart. (75)
And at that very moment, he sent everything that had been intended.
With his heart, he always sought the favor of Hari—
service at His feet and devotion— and nothing else, such as worldly happiness or the like.
The guests belonging to the bride’s party were fed and honored;
then, with the permission of King Viyadrāja, they returned once more to their own worlds.
Then, Śrī Veṅkaṭanātha, having indeed worshipped the gods and others—
Having worshipped the Supreme Lords— the infinite Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa,
Virāṭ, and the other ṛṣis, ancestors, humans, and all things animate and inanimate—
they were then permitted by Him to go to their own respective worlds.
Having bowed to Hari, all the male and female servants departed;
for all created beings indeed sing the glory of the Blessed One and the good fortune of Padminī.
As for Vedavatī, she who had served Sītā, [departed].
Though she was once lotus-less, she became Padmā, the beloved of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
Those who practice devotion by surrendering their very lives become like her, O Padmā; for such eternal devotees of Kṛṣṇa are indeed reborn as such.
When they had all departed, the Blessed Lord, ever endowed with Padminī and Śrī, and joined by Lakṣmī and Ramā, took his delight;
and Kṛṣṇa remained forever on the bank of the Svāmipuṣkariṇī.
On Mount Veṅkaṭa, the Lord is sometimes present in person within a divine temple;
in one place the Master is accompanied by Padminī, in another by Śrī,
in another by Lakṣmī, and in another by Ramā.
In some places on Mount Veṅkaṭa, the Blessed Lord Hari, Svāminārāyaṇa, indeed sports together with Bakulamālikā and the others;
and all those women are devoted wives who have eternally surrendered themselves to the Blessed One.
The wives serve Kṛṣṇa with their hearts, their bodies, and their actions.
Having obtained him as her husband, Padminī serves the one who dwells in the lotus;
rising early every morning, she always serves Kṛṣṇa first.
She performs the massaging of the feet and the rubbing of the limbs,
and she indeed pleases Śrīnivāsa on the bed with her service. She offers embraces, kisses, and love that grant the husband his desires.
Then, rising from his bed and having washed his hands and face,
he takes warm water for the sake of purifying himself by bathing the Blessed One;
having bathed, he offers pure water for the purification of his own hands and face.
Having offered fresh, succulent wood for cleaning the teeth, as well as moist, flowing milk-rice (pāyasa),
and fragrant powder, he gives a water-pot. Hari,
having performed his purification and other rites, washes his hands with clay.
Having rinsed his mouth with mouthfuls of water, he bathes upon a golden slab.
Having ground fragrant powders—sesame paste, the essence of flowers, scented oils, and so forth—upon the limbs of Śrī Hari, [he applies them]. (94–95)
Having offered [water], the beloved bathes the Lord, her husband, with nectar-like waters;
she wipes away the water with cloths and gives him a beautiful washed garment.
She indeed offers an upper garment, a sacrificial thread, and a cord. (96)
He offers a seat and water for rinsing the mouth to the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
He applies collyrium to his eyes and a thick mark with a crescent moon upon his forehead;
he places earrings on his ears and likewise a dot on his staff-like nose.
Having groomed the hair and applied oil, and having prepared excellent sandalwood paste,
he indeed offers a crown and necklaces made of gold and jewels;
he places them upon the neck of Kṛṣṇa, as well as upon his arms and forearms.
He gives bracelets for the hands, necklaces, chains, and likewise bangles;
rings for the fingers,
a beautiful chain for the waist, and lovely anklets for the feet that resound with the tinkling of small bells.
The Padminī woman gives garments and sandals for her feet;
a handkerchief for her hand, a golden staff, and an auspicious garland;
as well as an umbrella, a chowrie, and articles of adornment.
He offers a fan, a mirror, and likewise a lion-throne;
incense, a lamp, *abīra*, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), flowers, leaves, petals, water, fruit, food, and abundant sweet offerings (*naivedya*). (103–104)

According to one's preference, [one may offer] sweet milk, curd, honey, and sugar; betel-leaf, drinks, and other such items, as well as auspicious foods such as flour-mixtures and the like. (105) Also, cakes, *pūrikās*, *saṃyāva*, and *ghṛtapūraka*s.
Parpika cakes, as well as other types of baked goods, both sweet and savory;
fried snacks, laddukas, and likewise pleasant barley-meal (saktu);
rice, chickpeas, mung beans, soup, ghee, and so forth. || 106–107 ||
She constantly offers *āranāla*, buttermilk, milk, curd, and fruit juices for the sake of Śrīnivāsa’s meal; likewise,
she provides water for drinking and other edibles such as roots and fruits.
He gives gifts such as clean clothing and performs acts such as washing;
he offers the *ārātrika* lamp, circumambulates, prostrates like a staff, and performs hymns of praise and salutations both at midday and likewise at night. (109–110)
Thus, through constant devotion, she serves him just as Śrī Ramā does,
and just as Lakṣmī serves Nārāyaṇa, Hari, Kṛṣṇa, the son of Kaṃbhara, the supreme among men, so too is she intent upon his service. 111.

Even though she had hundreds of maidservants, her beloved served Lord Śrīnivāsa Veṅkaṭeśa, the Lord of the Lotus-lake, herself. Thus, like the lotus-plant Padmā, she attained the fulfillment of her birth.
Then Kṛṣṇa indeed granted a boon to Bakulā:
"Just like Padminī, I shall choose you as my bride on Śrī Veṅkaṭācala.
Having caused a sacrificial altar to be constructed in the midst of her friends, Mādhava stood there.
Having himself performed an oblation in the fire,
he took up the Bakula-ākara [vow] which bestows the fruit of attaining Padminī as a worthy goal;
the Blessed One made his companion Bakulamālikā his wife.
She too, though formerly a devoted wife, a maidservant, and a slave,
now serves Śrī Hari and has become an enjoyer of eternal bliss.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have narrated to you the story of Vedavatī.
Indeed, Padminī, the daughter of the Earth, who was devoted solely to her husband,
having become so, obtained Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Gods, as a cowherd boy.
By hearing this narrative, one shall obtain Śrī Kṛṣṇa as a virtuous husband.

"By hearing this, one certainly attains the acquisition of a virtuous son and husband, the earning of wealth, grain, and clothing, as well as fame, existence, and established status. Thus ends the four hundredth chapter, titled "The Description of the Marriage of Śrīnivāsa Bhagavān with Padminī, the Ritual, the Dowry, and the Nature of Devotion to the Husband," within the section on the Greatness of the Chaste Wife in the first book, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
