Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O Blessed One, you have narrated to me this delightful account.
Indeed, who other than you is capable of fulfilling the desires of your devotees? 1.
By whom was this vision of yours previously brought about here through a state of devotion?
Or by whom is Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the abode of compassion, beheld?
And who, O lady of noble disposition, shall construct a celestial chariot for the sake of the gods?
"You ought to tell me all those wonders of the Lord of Śrī.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
"Listen, Lakṣmī! I shall relate the wonders of old."
And whoever, even if they be a mere pauper, develops devotion toward me upon hearing this;
whether they be a king, a wretched man, an animal, a bird, a man, a woman, a virtuous wife, or a daughter—
I establish them as a most exalted Mahābhāgavatī who is devoted to me.
"O beloved, that which belongs to me must certainly come to pass, for by means of it you shall desire from me eternal happiness.
Listen to me as I relate the future events."
On Mount Veṅkaṭa, there was a hunter named Vasu who was devoted to me.
He became the guardian of the fields of śyāmāka grain and lived by means of that śyāmāka.
Having cooked the grains of śyāmāka rice and mixed them with sugar, [he offered them]. (7–8)
Having offered [the food] to Śrīnivāsa, who is accompanied by Śrī and Bhūmi,
he then eats together with his wife and proceeds with his duties.
Thus, being purified by the sacred food of grace, he remains forever pure.
He became a supreme Vaiṣṇava, and his wife also indeed became a Vaiṣṇava.
Named Citravatī, she was a virtuous woman devoted to her husband;
like a deity, she always served her husband, remaining entirely under his control.
He bathes, performs worship, and recites the mantra of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow;
he meditates upon Kṛṣṇa, remembers His forms, and listens to the sacred narrations.
Having always regarded his husband as equal to the Lord and honoring him as such, [he remains devoted]. (12)
Having become a servant to both, she performs service in every way.
At midday, at night, in the evening, and in the morning, that virtuous woman accepts all the food, water, and flowers offered to the Lord.
Blessed indeed is this woman of the Niṣāda caste, for she exists as a divine Brāhmaṇī;
like a Brāhmaṇa woman, she is most virtuous and the savior of three lineages.
Then, when the time had come, that beautiful woman became pregnant with a son.
His father indeed gave him the name Vīrarudra.
Accompanied by his son and his devoted wife, Vasu rejoiced in his own food and other enjoyments, being fully satisfied by his service to the deity. || 16–17 ||
Then once, having sent his son Śyāmāka away with the command, "Guard the field," he went to the forest accompanied by his wife for the purpose of protecting the crops.
Both of them wandered about, intent on their work of seeking honey.
At midday, they both arrived at a place where there was abundant honey.
At midday, the boy, having taken some auspicious ripe ears of *śyāmāka* grain,
placed them upon a fire, ground them, and joyfully [ate them] beneath a tree.
He offered food and water to Hari upon a leaf,
and having partaken of that offering and its grace, he remained in peace.
At that moment, his parents arrived, bringing sweet honey.
Seeing that the śyāmāka grains had been eaten, Vasu rebuked his son and,
raising his staff, lifted up his hand to strike him.
However, the Blessed Lord himself was stationed within the heart of Vīrarudra.
Manifesting before Vasu, he took up a staff with his hand.
Seeing who had seized the staff, Vasu beheld Kṛṣṇa— the omnipresent Lord,
whose hands held the conch, discus, and mace, and who was composed of divine splendor.
Casting aside his staff, Vasu bowed to Hari and said to him:
"O Blessed One, why have you come here for the sake of protecting your son? Look, the ripe grains of śyāmāka have been destroyed by him. (25-26)
"A staff and a bowl are indeed [required], but one should not make them in that manner.
Having heard this, Hari said: "Your son is devoted to me;
he is dearer to me even than you, and for that reason he has come for the sake of protection."

Then, having offered me as an oblation the śyāmāka grains—roasted, powdered, and ground into flour—that king of devotees ate them. He consumed his own selves, which had attained the state of śyāmāka seeds, by means of me. (28–29)
Liberation has been granted to you, and eternal merit has indeed been bestowed;
for whatever small grains of rice and other offerings were made by you to me,
I abide everywhere in the presence of my devotee.
I provide protection for my devotee both while awake and during deep sleep.
Day and night, I am indeed the constant protector of my devotees;
I dwell forever on the beautiful bank of the Svāmipuṣkariṇī in every way.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One,
Śrīnivāsa Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa himself, accepted the very sweet honey offered by Vasudatta, as well as the multicolored seat provided by Citravatī, along with fruits, water, and other offerings.
Laughing, the three indeed vanished and took refuge beneath the tree.
Thus, O Lotus-born One, the Blessed Lord, who is subject to his devotees,
directly granted his own vision to the high-souled Niṣāda.
Listen now to another story that occurred there at that time:
a Śūdra by caste, a devotee of Viṣṇu born in the Pāṇḍya region, arrived there as a pilgrim and departed by way of the road. (36)
A twelve-year-old boy asked Vīrarudraka:
"Does this path lead to the holy site (tīrtha) of Śrīnivāsa or not?
I must go there for the purpose of performing the rites of the sacred ford. (37–38)
Having asked this, he, filled with devotion, proceeded by the path to the abode of Śrīnivāsa as shown by Vīra. Upon reaching Nārāyaṇapurī and bowing down to Śrī Varāha, [he remained there].
Having remembered Śrīnivāsa, who dwells on the Veṅkaṭa mountain, in his heart;
having reached the Suvarṇamukharī river, bathed there, and then crossed it;
and having bathed in the Kamala lake, [he beheld] Hari and Bala situated on its bank.
Having paid his respects and reached the forest, he proceeded indeed to Śeṣādri;
having seen the waterfalls and Śiva worshipped by Kapilā,
and having performed worship at Cakratīrtha and bathed there, he went to the glorious Veṅkaṭācala.
The boy went slowly and ascended the mountain.
Having bathed in the Svāmipuṣkariṇī, he [reached] beneath a tamarind tree on the bank, where [the deity] was worshipped by the Vaikhānasa sage Gopīnātha. ||43-44||
Situated in the sky, having a yellowish-blue form, and served by Śrī and Bhūmi;
adorned with weapons such as the conch, discus, mace, sword, and lotus;
together with Garuḍa, who supports the canopy with his two wings.
The boy, filled with joy, perceived his fulfillment of purpose;
he even felt that his birth had attained its true meaning by dwelling right there.
Having thus granted him this vision, Śrīnivāsa vanished from sight.
"O son! Build a temple for me here," he said in a divine voice.
Hearing this, the wise boy Raṅgadāsa lived at the foot of a tree.
Having received the food offering from a forest-dwelling ascetic (vaikhānasa), he offered it to Viṣṇu.
Having offered [the fruit] and then eating the fruit and so forth, he likewise offers it as *naivedya*.
Constantly cutting down trees slowly, leaving only the tamarind tree (*ciñcā-bhūruha*) in between,
and avoiding the campaka tree of Ramā, he cleared the ground from the surrounding area.
That Raṅgadāsa made that exceedingly beautiful place treeless;
having cleared it of its foundations and refined it, he fashioned a vast circular arena protected by a fortress consisting of stone walls. (51)
There, on all sides, he constructed a garden filled with trees bearing flowers and fruits:
karṇikāra, mallikā, lotus, mandāra, mālatī, kunda, campaka, tulasī, plantains, and fresh raṅgaka trees. (52–53)
He cultivated mangoes, jackfruit, grapes, and other fruits, as well as bilva trees and the like;
having dug a well filled with abundant water, he nourished the trees.
He worshipped Śrīnivāsa with flower garlands from his groves.
Performing service in this manner, he remained right there, worshipping him.
Once, a Gandharva arrived at that lake to bathe, accompanied by beautiful and youthful maidens. (55–56)
Leaving his celestial chariot in the sky, Śrī Raṅgadāsa engaged in water-sports;
even he became infatuated with the maidens as he gazed upon them.
Because he looked at them with the innocent gaze of a lover, he stood there transfixed.
At that time, he forgot how to weave garlands and wreaths like one who is dull-witted;
thus he remained until midday, not even remembering the garland or the flowers.
The Gandharva, too, having played outside with his beloved women, [forgot]. || 58-59 ||
Having departed by means of his celestial chariot, he went to the abode of the Giver of Wealth (Kubera).
Raṅgadāsa, too, having bathed and become composed, tied together the flower garlands; then, taking the flowers, he went to the temple of Śrīnivāsa.
There, the worshipper said: "Why are you occupied with such a long task today?
Friend, the garland is not yet finished, and the time for worship has already passed.
Even when addressed thus, Raṅgadāsa did not speak out of shame.
Then Śrīnivāsa himself spoke to that embarrassed man:
"O Raṅgadāsa! Those maidens are remembered within your heart.
O king of devotees, do not feel shame because of my delusive power (māyā)."
"You shall become a king on the surface of the earth like a king of the Gandharvas.
Then, enjoy highly esteemed and divine pleasures that grant satisfaction;
furthermore, you shall cause a rampart, a celestial chariot, and my temple to be constructed."
"Then I shall grant liberation to you, my devoted servant;
perform service right here until the release from the body.
Having spoken thus, Śrīnivāsa Viṣṇu took the garland.
Having worshipped the garden, Raṅgadāsa returned once more.
Having lived for over a hundred years and having served Śrīnivāsa,
he cast off that body and was born as a king in the lineage of Soma.
Named Toṇḍamān, he was a recollector of past births (jātismara) and possessed divine vision;
he was the son of the king of Sauvīra, born of the mother Nandinī.
At five years of age, he was already filled with devotion to the Blessed One.
Adorned with all the auspicious marks and excellent qualities that grant nourishment through every form of devotion,
he married the daughter of the Pāṇḍya king named Cārupadma, who was most enchanting,
as well as other maidens who were like the very embodiment of desire.
King Toṇḍamān, the lord of Nārāyaṇapattana, took his pleasure [there].
Then, on one occasion, he went out for a hunt upon the glorious Veṅkaṭādri mountain. He pursued and caught sight of the leader of a herd of elephants in order to capture him.
Having crossed the Suvarṇamukharī and having bowed to Śuka and Reṇukā,
and having also bowed to the goddess in the form of an anthill, he went toward the west.
Pursuing a certain five-colored parrot with the desire to seize it, he followed after it.
Crying out "Śrīnivāsa!", the parrot immediately flew toward the mountain;
the king also, pursuing the bird, ascended Veṅkaṭādri.
Moving forward, he reached a green field of śyāmāka grain.
Having recognized Toṇḍamāna, the Guardian of the Field (Kṣetrapāla) paid him due honor.
Toṇḍamāna also questioned the Guardian of the Field: "Who is this Śuka?
The Guardian of the Field replied: "O King of kings, he is always dear to Śrīnivāsa."
Always remaining by his side, nourished by Śrī and Bhūmi,
he dwells perpetually near Hari on the bank of the Svāmipuṣkariṇī.
Having wandered during the day through the mountain forests, he returns to the temple in the evening.
"O King, that parrot cannot be captured by anyone at all!
Having said this, the guardian of the sacred field went with the monarch to the temple.
After bathing in the Svāmipuṣkariṇī, [he beheld] the Lord seated at the foot of the Bilva tree.
He beheld the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), whose beautiful form was most auspicious and endowed with splendor, whose lotus-feet were hidden by an anthill up to the knees.
Both the guardian of the field and the king bowed down and prostrated before him.
The guardian of the field, having offered a portion of ripened *śyāmāka* grain as an *arghya* oblation to Hari,
gave the remaining half to the king and then returned to his field. Toṇḍamāna also, having stayed for one night in the forest of Reṇukā— 82–83.
On the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, the king went and worshipped Reṇukā; he offered her sacrificial food, fine rice with milk, and various accompaniments.
The goddess, being pleased, granted the king a boon: a kingdom free from all thorns.
"And a royal capital shall arise near me, named after you.
You shall long remain a recipient of the grace of Śrīnivāsa.
Then Toṇḍi went to Śuka, bowed, and [received] thus from his mouth.
I have heard the sin-destroying majesty of this lotus lake.
Formerly, Viṣṇu performed supreme penance here together with Padmā.
Praised by the gods, the Great Viṣṇu created the lotus lake named Padmāsara.
Having heard this, Toṇḍi went to his father’s city, the capital.
Then Vasu, having been consecrated in his own kingdom by his father Vasu,
joyfully set out for the pilgrimage to Vārāhavalmīka.
There, the Blessed Lord Vārāha, having gone out from that place at night, would eat the śyāmāka grain while remaining invisible; by day, he would enter that place again.
Seeing the anthill in that state, the guardian of the field dug up the anthill. (1.401.90)
From an anthill, the Blessed One arose in the form of a boar.
In the presence of Kṣetrapa, he said to the king:
"Have a temple for me built here through your son; I shall dwell here."
Having washed the anthill with the milk of black cows,
and having carved an image of Varāha upon the stone slab produced there,
O King, install my own form in that temple and worship it perpetually! 93.
Having spoken thus, the illustrious Varāha vanished; thereafter,
Vasu went home and said to his son named Toṇḍamān,
"Build a temple for Śrī Varāha and install an image of him there."
Toṇḍamāna also saw all of that in a dream during the night.
Rising in the morning, he took his cows and went to the vicinity of the anthill;
there, he washed the Boar image upon the stone with milk.
Having had that Supreme Lord fashioned and installed in the temple,
he performed worship and established a capital city.
He [discovered] the cave that he had seen in a dream in the vicinity of an anthill.
Having constructed a subterranean chamber within the inner apartments, he caused a rampart to be built;
following the words of blessing, he established a city there.
And he preserved both the *ciñcā* and the *campaka* trees within the center of the fortress.
Having come daily through the subterranean passage and bowed to the Lord,
that Toṇḍamān ruled the kingdom with righteousness and governed the earth. Born of the lineage of Toṇḍama, there was a king named Nārāyaṇa, who was auspicious.
There, she caused a divine and auspicious celestial palace (vimāna) to be built within the enclosure wall;
it was divine and invisible, yet visible only to those who were devoted.
There, she worshipped Lord Hari in His divine form as the Boar (Vārāha).
He constantly worshipped Kṛṣṇa, the cowherd boy, the son of Kaṃbhara, the Lord of Śrī;
as well as Śrī Raṅga and Śrī Veṅkaṭeśa.
Thus, O Mahālakṣmī, this unsurpassed ancient narrative has been told to you.
The great temple at Toṇḍamatu, which is like a second birthplace of Śrīraṅga, exists there; in it dwells the Lord Vārāha together with Śrīdhara,
and He grants His vision to the devotee of the Sāttvata lineage.
Now listen to another power as well; I shall tell it to you.
A twice-born man from the South arrived with his wife, desiring to visit sacred pilgrimage sites.
At that time, his wife was pregnant and unable to travel. (106–107)
Having observed this, Vīraśarman approached the king and related everything regarding how there was such great obstruction at the sacred ford (tīrtha).
"Listen, O King: my wife is pregnant and intent upon her devotional worship."
"Having established her in your home, I shall perform my pilgrimage;
meanwhile, you must protect your beloved wife named Lakṣmī, who is devoted to her husband,
until I return after having visited Kāśī and other sacred fords."
Having spoken thus and dismissed her, the brahmin departed from there.
After the king had provided her with food and other necessities, she was settled in a garden. Before the brahmin’s arrival, she died, afflicted by fever.
The Brāhmaṇa also undertook a long-term pilgrimage on foot.
Nine months passed as he traveled wherever he went,
reaching the Gaṅgā, Kāśī, Prayāga, Gayā, and the city of Sāketa.
Badarikāśrama, Śālagrāma, and likewise Puṣkara;
Sarasvatī, Kuśasthalī, Raivata, and Somanātha;
Aśvapaṭṭasara, as well as Tapatī and Narmadā.
Having visited the holy sites of Kukūmavāpikā, Siṃhāraṇya, Gokarṇatīrtha,
and the Gomatī during the month of Caitra,
he arrived before the king on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight.
The Brahmin woman then said to the king,
"I am skilled," and the king went to the place where the protected Brahmin woman had died.
Having seen that she was dead, he quickly entered the palace through a tunnel.
The king went to Śrī Veṅkaṭeśa and then spoke to Hari:
"O Blessed One! A Brahmin woman who was the form of a deposit with a brahmin has died;
that brahmin will curse me. Please show mercy toward me."
"Bathe her in the Bone-Lake on the twelfth lunar day with this water, granted as a divine favor by Śrīnivāsa;
then she will undoubtedly regain her life just as it was before."
Having carried the corpse there, the king arrived at the place where the pool of bones was located.
After the king had submerged the body in water, he remembered that virtuous woman;
at that moment, she appeared with a divine form, like another queen of kings.
Having become pregnant, she remained in that state with a serene mind;
quickly bringing [the child] forth, she gave it to the Brahmin, who was filled with wonder.
"The fetus has not miscarried; this is surely the majesty of Hari. || 123 ||
Then, on the following day, her delivery took place.
A son equal to a god was born; after a month had passed, the brahmin, having accepted the gifts and other offerings bestowed by the king, departed for his own home.
Thus was Camatkāra instructed by the one who inspires devotion to the Lord. Then Kṛṣṇa, the abode of Śrī, spoke again to the king:
"At the conclusion of the food offering, my daily worship should be performed with golden lotuses."
"O King, do whatever you desire; all that shall indeed be yours.
(1.27) King Toṇḍī thus performed the daily worship of the lotus.
Once, however, he saw a tulasī flower made of clay. (1.28)
Filled with wonder, the king asked Śrī Hari, "Who indeed follows you? Hari replied, "O Lord of the Earth, a potter who is my devotee worships me in such a manner;
he worships me in his own home, and therefore I accept him."
Having heard this, he went to see the potter named Bhīma in his city;
and seeing him in such a state, worshipping [the deity],
the king was filled with wonder, as was the potter along with his wife.
Possessing a divine form, he went to the abode of Viṣṇu in his celestial chariot along with his wife.
When the king’s worship became renowned, Śrīnivāsa had previously declared that his arrival in your world would result in liberation. (1.32)
Yet that which has arisen exactly in such a manner cannot be described.

O beloved Padmaja! By reading or hearing of the wonders of Śrīnivāsa, who fulfills the desires of his devotees, one who is bound becomes liberated. Thus ends the [section] on the greatness of the devoted wife within the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga in the first part of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, concerning the deeds of King Toṇḍamāna upon the sacred ground of Śrī Vārāha.

Chapter Four Hundred and One: The Description of the Walled City, the Restoration to Life of the Deceased Brāhmaṇa Woman, and the Acceptance of Clay Flowers made by the Potter Bhīma, followed by the Liberation of the Potter together with his wife. *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā*, Book 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga), Chapter 402.
[The Author: Chapter 403.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Now, O Lakṣmī, listen! King Toṇḍī [bestowed] the kingdom upon his son.
Having given [these], he went for the sake of penance and performed arduous asceticism. While he was performing penance, Hari Kṛṣṇa, the infallible Lord, became manifest before him,
having mounted his own vehicle Garuḍa and accompanied by Śrī, Bhūmi, and Padminī.
Approaching King Toṇḍa, he said: "I am pleased by your devotion; speak, O devotee! Tell me what I may do for your sake.
Having heard him, King Toṇḍa, with palms joined in reverence, spoke as follows.
"I desire to dwell in Your imperishable world, which is free from birth, death, old age, and disease. Grant me this boon:
until I cast off my body, may my gaze be fixed solely upon Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. (4–5)
Having attained a body equal to that of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, that king of devotees indeed ascended a divine,
radiant celestial chariot that grants access to the divine abode.
Being praised by the liberated souls, he attained the same form as the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
He went to my imperishable state, which is free from rebirth.
O lotus-born one, I dwell eternally at the holy site of Svāmipuṣkariṇī;
by performing a ritual bath in that pond, one obtains the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
Knowledge of the Self brings about liberation directly, as do the fourfold [liberations].
By serving the Lord, one obtains the fruit of the Tulāpuruṣa gift;
by bathing in Svāmitīrtha, one gains the merit of giving a thousand cows.

Through giving at Svāmitīrtha, one attains dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa. (1.402.10) By residing at Svāmitīrtha, wisdom, fortune, fame, prosperity, dharma, knowledge, detachment, and purity of mind shall arise. (11)

The killing of a Brahmin, the drinking of liquor, sexual intercourse with the wife of a guru, and so forth; likewise, the theft of gold, the consumption of meat, and the faults of violence—these are surely destroyed at Svāmitīrtha through vows and other observances; of this there is no doubt.
Oh, the folly! Oh, the folly of people, for such is their nature:
that while the sacred ford of the Lord (Svāmitīrtha) stands present, the wicked mind delights elsewhere.
Oh, the power of delusion, which destroys the very ford of the home!
Indeed, for one who has bathed at Svāmitīrtha, there is no fear of Death (Antaka).
Those who praise it, extol it, touch it, and bow to it;
those who drink [its water], bathe in it, and behold it—for them, there is no fear of Death.

This entire surface of the earth where the Veṅkaṭa mountain casts its gaze bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation; it is the abode where Śrīnivāsa has made his residence, inhabited by Kṛṣṇa who is served by Śrī and Bhū, and is equal to the celestial realm itself. (16–17)

Listen, O Lakṣmī, to another story concerning King Dharmagupta— a tale that is meritorious, purifying, bestows the state of Nirvāṇa, and is superior in every respect. In the Lunar dynasty, there was a son of King Nanda who was devoted to righteousness.
He was renowned as Dharmagupta and was devoted to statesmanship.
He performed various kinds of sacrifices and gave gifts many times over.
The subjects were devoted to righteousness, and the women were devoted to their husbands.
Then once, having mounted his horse, Dharmagupta went to the forest. While he was pursuing the hunt, night fell; thereupon, having climbed a tree, he rested, and a bear arrived there.
Pursued by the lion, that bear climbed up a tree.
Seeing the king, he spoke, trembling with the fear of death:
"O lord of men, do not be afraid! We two shall dwell here for the night. (22-23)
A terrifying lion has come here to the foot of this tree.
Rest for half the night in happiness, protected by me.
Then, O excellent guardian, protect me while I am fast asleep for the remaining half of the night.
Having heard this, while Dharmagupta was asleep, the monkey spoke to the bear:
"We are all forest-dwellers, four-footed beings, not humans. Why should we concern ourselves with a human? Let this king be abandoned by me. (25-26)
"Let this be offered so that it may become a full meal for me.
Then the bear spoke to the lion in words consistent with dharma and sound policy:
"In this world, a great downfall is ordained for those who betray trust."
Human beings, beasts, insects, birds, children, and women—whether wild, domestic, or forest-dwelling—indeed live with confidence.
They live trusting in their refuge; being four-footed is not the cause [of fear]. || 28–29 ||

Whether it be bipedness, or having allies, or even living by means of trust—trust is indeed the supreme dharma; how then could I abandon it? One who seeks their own self-interest, however, becomes a destroyer by abandoning the dharma of trust.
"I must not do that; go, abandon this waiting!
(3.1) For the sin of those who betray their friends cannot be destroyed even by ten thousand sacrifices.
While there might sometimes be atonement for sins such as the killing of a Brahmin, (3.2)"
The sin of those who betray trust can never be destroyed.
Mount Meru does not become heavy as long as the burden remains upon the betrayer.
Violence is the supreme form of unrighteousness and brings about destruction.
"Violating trust is a sin greater than even the most heinous crimes there.
Therefore, go from this forest to another forest; there you will find food.
Having been addressed thus, Vanarāja remained silent and stood still.
When half the night had passed, the prince awoke;
meanwhile, the bear, filled with confidence, slept soundly upon the branch.
Then the lion said to the king, "O King, what use have you for this tree?"
"You surely protect my food; you must indeed be a sinner!
Just as a king is to his subjects, so am I the forest-king. For it is ordained by law that subjects are in every way the food of kings. (37–38)
"This wild deer has today presented itself as my food;
for the bear indeed climbed the tree after taking refuge with you.
Today, you, O King, stand as the one who obstructs my meal."
"What use have you for this bear? Give him up as my food!
Otherwise, I shall devour him this very morning or during the day;
likewise, I shall summon others like him and devour you as well."
Thus addressed by the lion, the king then released from the tree that bear who was sleeping unsuspectingly with his head resting upon the king's lap; meanwhile,
he [the lion] performed a whirling motion right there on the branch of the tree.
By the power of his merit, he ascended to the upper part and wept.
Both the king and Siṃha asked him, "Why indeed do you weep?
Your fear has now departed; tell us, O monkey, what is in your heart! (43)
The bear said: "O Lord, I do not weep for my own sake; rather, I weep for both of us. For many wild monkeys dwell with confidence in the forest.
Having encountered such a king—a rogue who betrays trust—" (44–45)
"Thinking that they will be slain, O lion, I weep;
may my death come face-to-face with you, and may there be no sudden death for us.
"O King, I am not a monkey, but I am born of the lineage of Bhṛgu."

"O King, why have you abandoned me, who am innocent and asleep, in the forest? You are known as Dhyānakāṣṭha, yet you possess a body of desire. Because of my curse, become utterly insane and wander upon the earth. (47-48)
Having thus cursed him, you then struck the lion, O sinless one; for in former times you were a minister of Kubera, accompanied by a circle of friends.
While sporting on the Himālaya mountains, you happened by fate to go to the hermitage of Gautama.
Upon seeing you naked, Gautama uttered a curse:
"Since you, a naked beast-like creature, behave wickedly in the vicinity of my hermitage, become a wicked and most violent being! (1.402.50–51)
"Be a naked lion here, indeed devoid of hair and the like.
By this curse you became a lion, and you propitiated the sage again and again.
He said to you: "When [you see] the tree of King Dharmagupta..."
"Indeed, through the good fortune of this piece of wood used for meditation, you shall behold [the Lord];
at that time, your release from the curse will surely come to pass, so do not grieve.
You are named Bhadra, and I know this indeed through my meditation that you are my servant."
Thus addressed, he bowed to that best of sages and likewise to the king;
and immediately casting off his lion-form, he assumed the form of a yakṣa.
Then, through the power of the sage's compassion, he remembered his former births and understood everything.
Having arrived by means of a celestial chariot, he indeed ascended to heaven.
The sage went to his own forest, while the king became intoxicated in the woods;
wandering like a beast, the subjects went forth to search for him.

Wandering in the forest like one mad, they led him to the banks of the Narmadā; having reached the presence of Jaimini, they confessed their transgression. Having heard them, Jaimini said to them on the bank of the Suvarṇamukharī:

"Let them bathe the king at the exceedingly purifying Svāmipuṣkariṇī tīrtha on Veṅkaṭādri; by that, he will be released from the curse. Having gone there, the people residing in that kingdom did exactly as instructed. (1.402.59–60)
Dharmagupta became healthy and bestowed wealth, jewels, and other riches;
he gave grain-fields and gems to Veṅkaṭeśa.
Thus the king was liberated from the curse and indeed ruled his kingdom.
The Svāmipuṣkariṇī Tīrtha exists as a bestower of such wealth;
it grants dharma, grants desire, grants liberation, and destroys suffering.
Through its water, the madness caused by bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, and other spirits perishes.
O lotus-born one, through bathing, drinking, touching, seeing, or even bowing down—and indeed through mere remembrance—sins are destroyed.
"Svāmitīrtha, Svāmitīrtha, Svāmitīrtha," [one should say], O beloved! 64.
Men who, having bathed, recite this three times obtain the same fruit as the bath of the Lord;
they attain the supreme station of Brahman, of this there is no doubt.
By hearing and by reciting this, one obtains the fruit of bathing there.
Listen, Lakṣmī! To another story concerning the brāhmaṇa Sumati.
In Mahārāṣṭra, there was a son of Yajñadeva named Sumati who, due to association with the wicked, abandoned his home and went to the land of Oḍhra.
Seeing a certain Kirāta woman in her house, he was infatuated with her;
he stayed there, took his pleasure, ate, committed theft, and drank liquor.
Then, at midnight, he killed a certain Brahmin with a sword.
Taking the wealth of the Brahmin, he went to the house of the Kirātī;
the terrifying, dark-complexioned Brahmahatyā pursued him.
Maddened by her, Sumati set out toward his own home.
Crying out, "Protect my father! Protect him! she went to him for refuge.
Then the Brahmahatyā spoke the truth to her father:
"This man is a drinker of liquor, a thief, and a killer of a Brahmin—a perpetrator of a great sin. (71–72)
"He is a traitor to his mother, a traitor to his father, an abandoner of ethics, and one who has cast aside virtue;
he is corrupted by association with Kirātī women. Release this evil-souled man!
Otherwise, [I shall destroy] you, your wife, this son, and likewise all others."
"I shall devour the lineage; you ought not to destroy the family.
Having said, "Sacrifice one individual and save the family," he seized him by the throat.
Just then, Durvāsas arrived there by chance.

Praised by them, he said to his father, "Bathe him in the waters of Svāmipuṣkariṇī; he shall be liberated from the sin of slaughter, of this there is no doubt. Then, together with Durvāsas, he went to the waters of the Puṣkariṇī.
Having bathed there, the Brahmin, though ruined by the sin of killing, became purified.
Such is the power of that sacred ford (tīrtha), which acts as an axe to the tree of evil;
it bestows the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice upon those who hear of it or recite it.
Having bathed at Kṛṣṇatīrtha on Veṅkaṭa, one is liberated from sin.
Even those of wicked intent who have shown contempt for their fathers, mothers, and gurus—
they too are purified merely by bathing in this Kṛṣṇatīrtha.

A certain sage named Kṛṣṇa performed auspicious penance on the Veṅkaṭa mountain while meditating upon Hari, and he established an excellent sacred ford (tīrtha). Another sage, devoted to liberation, was named Rāmakṛṣṇa.
He performed rigorous asceticism for many hundreds of years;
even though his body was covered by an anthill, he did not move from his place.
Vāsava then sent down a rain of clouds for seven days.
A great thunderbolt indeed fell upon the anthill;
the peak of the anthill was destroyed, but the sage remained with only his bones left.
Then Mahendra saw that Mādhava had been preserved for his protection.
The great lord Kāṃbhareya himself appeared before him as the cowherd boy, equipped with the conch, the discus, and other [emblems].
He said to him: "Arise, O blessed devotee! May it be well with you; I have been thoroughly pleased by your austerity."
In this sacred ford, whatever person bathes when the sun is situated in Capricorn, or on the full moon day, or on the auspicious day of my manifestation—
my attendants, possessing the radiance of ten million suns, lead them to my abode.
"And by your name, this excellent holy place shall attain supreme renown.
Having spoken thus, Śrīnivāsa vanished on that very spot.
Rāma and Kṛṣṇa then went to the abode of Hari along with Śrīkṛṣṇa.
By reading or even by hearing this, this sacred ford indeed bestows liberation.
(89) The gift of water, the gift of food, the gift of clothing, and the offering of wealth should be performed at the Vaiṅkaṭa Tīrtha; for that shall indeed become eternal. (90)
There was a royal sage named Hemāṅga, born of the Ikṣvāku lineage.
He bestowed gifts of cows, gifts of land, gifts of gold, and so forth.
O beloved, however, he gave only a single gift of water, with the thought that it was easily obtained.
"Since that which is priceless can be obtained from everywhere, what fruit could there be for the giver?
He spoke this with reason: "Merit arises from giving what is difficult to obtain.
Thus, he honored the wretched, the maimed, the poor, and those distressed by lack of livelihood.
He did not honor the Vedic scholars, the virtuous Brahmins, or those who discourse on the Absolute;
for all people, full of zeal, honor only those who are famous.
I am the refuge of the poor; therefore, they are the objects of my compassion.
Thus, because he gave [alms] to those wicked recipients,
for him indeed there were three births as a *cātaka* bird, one birth as a vulture,
and seven births as a dog; thereafter, he was born in a household.
A female house-lizard, indeed a devourer of flies, was born;
meanwhile, Śrutadeva arrived at the palace of the lord of Mithilā and other cities.
For that sage beheld her who was eighty-eight years of age.

Having fully honored Śrutadeva, the king bore the nectar of his feet upon his head; even though she was sprinkled by the drops from that [nectar], she immediately became one who remembers her past lives and cried out, "Save me! Save me! (98–99).
I was born in the Ikṣvāku lineage and became a king named Hemāṅga.
I showed partiality toward giving gifts, yet I did not give water in that manner;
for, having set aside a worthy recipient, I bestowed it upon an unworthy one.
I have cast my oblation into ashes, having abandoned the blazing fire;
I have watered a poisonous creeper, having discarded the *tulasī*.
Indeed, those who are crippled or otherwise helpless are the sole objects of compassion. (101–102)
Those who take refuge in austerity, wisdom, and true knowledge, who are of the very nature of Viṣṇu, and who are wise—these are always dear to Viṣṇu and worthy of worship.
Therefore, the man of knowledge is always to be honored; one should give to him for the attainment of the fruit.
He too is more worthy of worship than the most worshipful; he shall become the bestower of heaven and liberation.
(104) "Indeed, no water was given by me, nor were holy men served.
Because of that, this miserable state has arisen for me, even though I have gone to heaven. (105)
Having heard this regarding the fruit of bathing in the holy waters of Veṅkaṭādri, the sage bestowed it upon the iguana; and she, by virtue of the merit of a single day,
assumed a divine form and ascended an excellent celestial chariot.
Having offered praise, he departed for the heavenly realm, endowed with the fruit of his gift of water.
Thereafter, he obtained water in heaven; therefore, the giving of water and other gifts should always be performed on earth by men with true devotion. (107–108)
Then, after some time, he became the lord of the earth known as Kakutstha;
having become the ruler of the seven continents, he attained union with Viṣṇu.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have told you this supreme majesty of the worthy recipient.
The fruit of that [merit] is obtained even from giving water and so forth, and also from hearing [this account].

Thus ends the four hundred and second chapter, titled "The Description of the Liberation of King Toṇḍamān on Mount Veṅkaṭādri, of King Dharmagupta, of the treacherous Ṛkṣa, of the Brahmin named Sumati, of the sage Rāmakṛṣṇa, and of Hemāṅga," within the section on the Greatness of Chaste Wives in the first book, the Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
*Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā* — Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga). Chapter 402.
Chapter 403 [Author:
Chapter 404 → Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
In that place where Śrī herself appeared in the form of Sītā as a shadow,
and Vedavatī herself appeared in the form of Lakṣmī—
who indeed could possibly describe the great majesty of that sacred field? (1)
Veṅkaṭādri is the very embodiment of the abode of Brahman, by taking refuge in which [one attains liberation].
Therein shines Nārāyaṇa Kṛṣṇa himself, the self-effulgent Lord;
there the Blessed Varāha truly manifests again and again.
Where devotees are born who are Vaiṣṇavas and saviors of the world;
where even a single grain of dust from its soil is a savior of this world;
and where the water and earth of its ground destroy even the greatest of sins.
It directly bestows the abode of Brahman and grants the lordship of Kṛṣṇa; it is auspicious.
(5) Therein dwell women who are devoted to their husbands and have attained liberation—Vaishnavī women, great saintly ladies, solely intent on the service of their lords. (6)
Devoted to their husbands, they are indeed considered the wives of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa;
all of them are equal to Rādhā and Lakṣmī, and equal to Pārvatī and Māṇikī. They are indeed equal to Prabhā and Ramā, and equal to Jayā, Vijayā, and the others.

O beloved! By those who have worshipped Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, who is accompanied by Ramā and the other goddesses, eternal heaven—the abode of liberation from which there is no return—has certainly been attained through my grace; of this there is no doubt. (8–9)
Whatever sacred fords exist upon the earth and within the cosmic egg,
they all reside on the Veṅkaṭa mountain at the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa.
For the sake of serving that Lord, sages and lords likewise dwell there.
Gods, sages, perfected beings, yogis, and ascetics; virtuous women, holy men, and the steadfast— including the lords of the gods and others—
come every day with their families for the purpose of service.
Then, in the month of Kārttika, Brahmā performed the great festival of the banner of Veṅkaṭeśa; at that time, the lords of Satyaloka arrive every year at Vaikuṇṭheśvara,
located to the south of Svāmī Sarovara.
Then, O beloved, the merit of a Tīrthaṅkara becomes incalculable.
Whatever merit is acquired by people during ten years in the Kṛta Yuga, that same merit is accomplished in a single year in the Tretā Yuga. (14–15)
In the Dvāpara age, that fruit is obtained in five months, but in the Kali age, it is obtained in a single day;
yet the sight of Śrīnivāsa yields a fruit ten million times greater than that— O Lakṣmī, it arises at every moment, of this there is no doubt.
Even by a particle of dust released in the presence of Kṛṣṇa, liberation arises.
Those who glorify Śrīnivāsa, Mahādeva, Veṅkaṭeśa, and Nārāyaṇa with their hearts are liberated from the cage of worldly existence.
What is the use of gifts, what use other vows, other sacred fords, asceticism, or sacrifices?
What fruit is there in Kāśī, in Gayā, or even in Prayāga?
What is the use of Śambhu, the Creator of the Universe, or of Indra and the other immortals?
By whom Nārāyaṇa Veṅkaṭeśa has been seen with supreme devotion;
one should practice the eightfold devotion toward the Lord Veṅkaṭeśvara,
including the honoring and pleasing of His devotees through hospitality, worship, and other services.
Contentment through the worship of the Lord, bodily activity for His sake, listening to stories of His majesty, as well as hearing of His life-narratives,
an attitude of love manifested through dance, and meditation upon Veṅkaṭa— [these constitute the means]. (22)
And subsisting upon residence at Veṅkaṭādri—these grant liberation.
Such devotion should be understood as existing even without hearing the Vedānta.
Both Veṅkaṭa and Veṅkaṭeśa are the very nature of Nārāyaṇa. (23–24)
One should pray to Veṅkaṭa, who bestows the meritorious state of Nārāyaṇa.
O best of mountains! May I tread upon you with my feet;
show me Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who has made his abode upon your summit.
Having bathed at the Svāmipuṣkariṇī Tīrtha, first at Pāpanāśana,
and having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) at that Tīrtha, one should bathe at Pāpavināśana.
Formerly, there was a Brāhmaṇa named Sumati who followed the conduct of a Śūdra.
Seized by a *brahmarākṣasa* due to the fault of wearing a garland, he wept, wandered about, stumbled, became bewildered, raved, and laughed;
constantly crying out "Alas! Alas!", he utterly abandoned his auspicious intelligence.
His father took him to Veṅkaṭādri and caused him to perform ablutions. For three days he drank water at the Pāpavināśana Tīrtha;
by that means, his son was there liberated from the Brahma-rākṣasa.
Having been happy for a long time, he attained liberation at the end of his body;
even a Brahmarākṣasa, by virtue of drinking water at that holy ford (tīrtha),
attained liberation, O Lakṣmī, through my yoga at that very spot.
In this way, there was another twice-born man named Bhadramati who was also possessed of poverty;
he was learned in the scriptures, righteous, and indeed attended by six wives.
His sons and descendants were truly tormented by hunger.
Beholding them, Bhadramati, his senses agitated, lamented:
"Fie upon this life, devoid of fortune, destitute of wealth and fame!
Fie upon this birth, lacking hospitality, and devoid of wisdom and right conduct! (34)
Fie upon that which is devoid of effort, happiness, fame, kinsmen, renown, and so forth!
Fie likewise upon a birth lacking sovereignty and burdened with many offspring!
Alas! [Yet] there are virtues, gentleness, learning, noble lineage, and the like. (35–36)
For one devoid of wealth, even all of this—though excellent—is not beautiful:
daughters, wives, sons’ sons, kinsmen, as well as brothers, disciples, servants, and mothers; they all abandon one who is destitute of wealth. (37)
On this earth, whether he be a Cāṇḍāla or an ascetic, one who possesses wealth is honored;
one who is empty-handed is counted as a corpse, while one who has accumulated riches is counted as wealthy.
One devoid of virtues is considered virtuous, and a fool is regarded as a scholar.
A man devoid of virtue is nevertheless counted by people as virtuous if he possesses wealth;
therefore, poverty and hope are considered more painful than pain itself.
Those who are slaves to hope are always afflicted, whereas happiness increases for one who hopes for servitude.
Seized by the great crocodile of nothingness, he stood at the very brink of the mouth of death.
"Alas, what suffering! How indeed must this be crossed by one such as I?"—while he was thus reflecting, his wife, named Kañcana, [spoke]. 41–42.
Devoted to her husband, highly fortunate, always regarding her husband as a deity,
and endowed with all the virtues of the virtuous, she replied to that husband:
"O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, treasure-trove of knowledge regarding all matters!"
"O my beloved, you who are always worthy of worship, listen; I shall speak, so do as I say.
On the banks of the Suvarṇamukharī is the purifying Veṅkaṭācala, and there is a supreme holy site (tīrtha) named Pāpavināśana. ||44-45||
Merely by bathing [there], it burns away sins and bestows wealth and merit;
it pacifies all miseries and grants all prosperity.
This bestows both righteousness and sovereignty, as Nārada declared in the past.
One should perform the gift of land there, for it bestows the fruit of all desires.
There has never been, nor will there ever be, a gift superior to the gift of land.
The giver of land attains supreme nirvāṇa; of this there is no doubt.

By giving even a very small amount of land to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, to a twice-born brāhmaṇa, or to a virtuous person for the purpose of maintaining the *agnihotra* sacrifice, one is glorified in the world of Brahmā. The giver of land is said to be the giver of everything; through that gift, liberation indeed comes to pass.
By giving land measuring ten cubits, one is liberated from all sins.
Indeed, a giver of land to a worthy recipient obtains the fruit of all possible gifts.
[The land] is adorned with fields of sugarcane, wheat, betel-nut groves, and dates.
He by whom land is given shall indeed become a Vaiṣṇava in the Imperishable;
the giver of land for the sake of the gods becomes eternally liberated.
The giver of a *droṇa* measure of land on the bank of the Gaṅgā partakes in the fruit of horse-sacrifices.

"The giver of Bhārabhū indeed shares in the fruit of thousands of horse-sacrifices and hundreds of Vājapeya sacrifices performed on the banks of the Gaṅgā. Having heard these words of his wife, Bhadramati then departed.
In that city of Suśālī, he requested five cubits of land from the eminent brahmin Sughoṣa; he too gave it with joy.
[Sughoṣa] said, "I am fulfilled; my birth has become fruitful."
My family has become endowed with merit, since you, a Brahmin, are its supplicant.
(56) The earth belongs to Viṣṇu and is meritorious; the earth is protected by Viṣṇu.
It is given to a worthy recipient; may Janārdana be pleased with me. (57)
That devotee of Hari, having indeed accepted that earth,
then went to the Veṅkaṭa mountain where the Svāmisaras lake is located.
Having bathed there, he [worshipped] Śvetavārāha, the upholder of the earth.
Having bowed, he went to Veṅkaṭeśa, the supreme lord Śrīnivāsa.
Then he went to the supreme holy place named Pāpanāśana;
having bathed there, he gave a gift of land to a Vaiṣṇava who was well-versed in the Vedas.
At that moment, the Blessed One manifested there in person.
Bhadramati offered this hymn of praise: "Salutations to you, O Nārāyaṇa!
Salutations to the Cause, the Protector, the Destroyer, and the Leader! (6.1)
Salutations to you, the purifier, the one who inspires faith, and the bestower of supernatural powers.
Salutations to you, the Lord of Śrī, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, and the upholder of the earth;
salutations to you, the Lord of Lakṣmī, the Lord of Prabhā, and the Lord of Māṇikī.
Salutations to you, the Lord of Pārvatī, and to you, the cowherd boy;
salutations to you, born from the lap of Kaṃbhārā, and to you, the omniscient one.
Salutations to you, the supreme person, whose body bears the marks of the discus, the lotus, and other signs.
Salutations to You who dwell in the Ocean of Milk and are served by the illustrious Lakṣmī;
salutations to You, the bestower of desired happiness, who took the form of the Sacrificial Boar.
Salutations to You, the beloved of Kamalā; salutations to You, the beloved of Padmā.
"O Lord of the Lotus-Lake, O destroyer of the poverty of your devotees, O Kṛṣṇa in the form of a saintly man! Salutations, salutations to you again and again!
Having heard this, Hari said, "I am pleased, O best of Brahmins!"
"Endowed with all enjoyments, may you attain liberation at the end of the body.
Having thus granted this boon, he vanished on the spot.
That twice-born man, having bathed in the Pāpanāśana Tīrtha, went home.
Thereafter, the merchant became possessed of an abundance of gold, wealth, and grain;
through the power of his gift of land, he was like another Mahendra.
Now, there exists another great holy site that grants liberation to men.
I shall describe to you that greatness which is renowned as the Ākāśagaṅgā.
A certain brahmin, the younger brother of Rāma, was devoted to the meditation on Viṣṇu;
standing in the midst of five fires, he performed penance while chanting the eight-syllabled mantra.
Even while standing in the water during the rain, free from the touch of the pairs of opposites,
subsisting for a long time on withered leaves, or on water, or even on air,
he remained steadfast in his asceticism with great faith; and he, who is affectionate toward his devotees, was pleased with him.
There, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa himself went to inquire after them.
Śrī Rameśvara, whose body was adorned with golden ornaments and who was served by Ramā, Rādhā, and others, arrived accompanied by Viṣvaksena, Sunanda, and his other attendants.
Accompanied by Nārada and others, the Lord, clad in yellow garments,
had his two sides attended by great yogis such as Sanaka;
that twice-born ascetic praised that compassionate Veṅkaṭeśa.
Salutations to Rāma, the Great One who bears the discus and other emblems; salutations to Him whose nature is eternally pure. Salutations to the Remover of the distress of His devotees;
salutations to You, who exist as the supreme, the manifest expansion (*vyūha*), the empowered manifestation (*vibhava*), and in forms such as the image for worship (*arcā*).
Salutations again and again to You, the inner controller, whose nature is the self-pervading soul;
salutations to You, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Great Being, Nārāyaṇa.
Salutations to Hiraṇyagarbha, to Vairāja, and to the Creator.
Salutations to Sadāśiva, the beloved of Kāntā, to Viṣṇu, and to Brahmā.
Salutations to the Lord of lords, the Sovereign, whose eyes are like flowers;
to Him who is beyond name, genus, and the like, yet who assumes the forms of name, genus, and so forth.
Salutations again and again to you, the son of Kambharā, who is dark-hued, who performs the *rāsa* dance with the circle of cowherd girls,
who is born of a cowherd, and who is affectionate toward the service of cows. Salutations to the one known through Vedānta and Nyāya, the commentary itself, and the author of the commentary.
Salutations to you, who bring the end of the scriptures for the sake of attaining the Sugata and for the protection of the world.
Salutations to the Lord of the earth at Aśvapaṭṭa, whose true form is manifest in Saurāṣṭra, who dwells on Mount Raivata, and who is adorned by the Puṣkara forest.
"Obeisance to you, the Lord of Kāśī, who is worshipped with saffron and other offerings.
Having thus praised Śrīnivāsa, Rāmānuja attained peace.
Then Veṅkaṭeśa, having embraced Rāmānuja, spoke to him.
"Pleased by this hymn and by my ascetic penance, let him quickly grant a boon.
Then Rāmānuja said: "O Śrīnivāsa, O Hari, O Lord!
I have achieved my life’s purpose through the sight of you; what more could I possibly need beyond this vision today? (86-87)
The gods, the ancestors, the sages, those committed to lifelong asceticism, the performers of ritual acts, the yogis, and those skilled in knowledge—neither see nor know him.
Yet today I know him and see him; what indeed could be greater than this for me? (88)
"By this seed of liberation, I have attained my goal in every respect.
May unwavering devotion toward the pair of your lotus feet be mine.
Having heard this, Hari said: "May your devotion toward me be firm. (1.403.90)
Those people who come here to this place of asceticism and bathe in the celestial Gaṅgā shall go to my supreme abode.
And you, at the end of this present body, shall attain my own nature.

But all those who have bathed in the celestial Gaṅgā are the most excellent of Bhāgavatas. O best of Bhāgavatas, listen to the characteristics of the Bhāgavatas—those whose conduct, through action, mind, and speech, is permeated by the Blessed One. (92–93)
Those who perform all actions for the sake of Kṛṣṇa, who contemplate Kṛṣṇa,
who possess knowledge, are free from desire, and are peaceful— they are indeed the best of Bhāgavatas.
They perceive Kṛṣṇa in all things and are devoted to the sacred stories of Kṛṣṇa.

Those who are devotees of Kṛṣṇa’s lotus feet are the best of Bhāgavatas. They are devoted to the service and other duties toward their parents, who are the very embodiments of Kṛṣṇa, and they are filled with the intense joy of worshipping and honoring the gods. || 95-96 ||
Those who are devoted to serving the virtuous, who bestow honor upon the virtuous,
and whose conduct is directed toward the Supreme Lord— they are the most excellent of great bhāgavatas.
Those for whom all beings are as themselves and who regard them as their own eyes— they are the most excellent of bhāgavatas.
Those who know the scriptures, who uphold dharma, whose speech is truthful, and who are the best among the virtuous;
those who delight in the stories of Kṛṣṇa and feel affection for the narrator of those stories;
those who love sacred pilgrimage sites and serve the wish-fulfilling cow—these indeed are the most excellent of the virtuous. (98–99)
Those who are serene upon the rising of any [auspicious occasion], who are devoted solely to the name of Kṛṣṇa,
and who dig wells for the sake of Kṛṣṇa— they are the best of Bhāgavatas.
Those who construct temples and those who perform the recitation of the Devagāyatrī mantra are likewise so.
Those who are immersed in Hari with devotion and joy are the best of Bhāgavatas.
(101) They worship Tulasī, bow to Vṛndā, and hold Tulasī in their hands;
they wear garlands of Tulasī and are adorned with Tulasī-sandalwood paste. (102)
Those whose bodies are made of Tulasī clay are indeed the best of Bhāgavatas;
they are the perceivers of Hari Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa in the Vedas and other scriptures, and they are the constant contemplators of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa alone during hospitality and other rites. (103)
Those who have realized the truth, who awaken others to Brahman, and whose conduct is virtuous;
who accept all good qualities and the like; they indeed are the best of Bhāgavatas.
They observe vows such as Ekādaśī and perform actions for the sake of Kṛṣṇa. (104–105)
Those Vaiṣṇavas who, upon seeing Rādhā, Lakṣmī, Ramā, Śrī, Pārvatī, Prabhā, and Māṇikī— women who are portions of me and presided over by me—
always bow down to them and behold them in their hearts as being of my own nature and inhabited by me. (106)

Those who perceive me, Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, even in boys and girls, are indeed the best of Bhāgavatas. O sinless one, those women who likewise behold me as Nārāyaṇa among men are declared by me to be truly great Bhāgavatīs.
All men are forms of Kṛṣṇa, and all women are of the nature of Rādhā and Ramā;
those who possess such knowledge of the Bhāgavata are the most excellent devotees.
In brief, I shall tell you that they exist entirely for my sake.
"Men, women, and even animals—all are the most excellent devotees of the Lord (bhāgavatottama).
O younger brother of Rāma! You alone are likewise the most excellent devotee.
I am pleased with you, O beloved one, because you are ever established in unwavering devotion."
"The holy ford known as Ākāśagaṅgā is the deliverer that brings one across the ocean of worldly existence;
for those who bathe there, it bestows liberation and grants the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and emancipation.
Having spoken thus, the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa then vanished.
"By reading and by hearing this, devotion and liberation are placed within one's grasp.

(113) Thus ends the four hundred and third chapter, titled "The Description of the Liberation of Sumati, Bhadramati, and Rāmānuja— who were protectors of their Lord’s vow of devotion to their wife— at the supreme sacred site," within the section on the Greatness of Devotion to the Husband in the first book, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
