Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:

Listen, Lakṣmī! I shall describe to you the worthy recipient of a gift, which is the supreme sacred ford (tīrtha). Nārāyaṇa is the supreme tīrtha; indeed, that which is to be given should be offered to this wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
What is given to one who is virtuous, of righteous character, possessed of knowledge, high-souled, generous, and a knower of Brahman, becomes inexhaustible.
[It is likewise inexhaustible] when given to a virtuous woman devoted to enjoyment, the wife of Harikṛṣṇa.
What is given to Nārāyaṇī Mahālakṣmī becomes eternal. (3) Likewise, what is given to Satī, the wife of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, who is devoted to virtuous deeds and is a servant of Hari, becomes eternal. (4)
What is given to a devoted Yoginī who is without a protector is inexhaustible; likewise,
what is given to a devotee who is of the nature of Brahman, to Brahmā the knower of the Vedas,
and to the Teacher who is the very form of the deity Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
That which is given to a Brahmin who is a disciple of the gods and a performer of righteous deeds,
as well as to one who is indifferent to worldly peace, becomes inexhaustible. That which is given to a cow, a child, a maiden, or to one's parents, is also inexhaustible.
What is given to a wife, a sister, a daughter,
a meritorious grandson, a sister’s son, or a disciple becomes inexhaustible;
as does what is given to a teacher, a teacher’s wife, or a learned teacher’s son.

And that which is given to one who propagates the Dharma becomes inexhaustible. Likewise, what is given to an expounder, a giver of knowledge, a teacher, a learned man, one qualified for learning, or a worthy recipient of knowledge is indeed inexhaustible. (1.404.10)
Gifts should indeed be given to one who is destitute of livelihood, to a poor householder,
to a worshiper of the deity, and to one who performs service for others;
they should be given to a teacher and they should be given for the sake of the country.
It should also be given to a protector for the sake of prosperity alone.
What is given in the vicinity of Nārāyaṇa becomes inexhaustible.
It must be given to a Vaiṣṇava, by whom I indeed become pleased.
That which is given to one who acts with hypocrisy, to a thief, to an enemy, to a slanderer,
or to one intent upon the wealth and wives of others, is indeed fruitless. So too is that given to an ungrateful person, to a fool, or to one whose heart is possessed by malice.
What is given to a killer, to a seller [of living beings],
to one who causes suffering to others, to an atheist, to a fool, to a villain, to one whose nature is deceitful, and to one who violates the bounds of social conduct, becomes fruitless. (15–16)
Even for one who is heretical, deceitful, dishonest, unrighteous, quarrelsome,
or of fierce disposition, [a gift] given at a sacred ford (tīrtha), especially on the bank of the Cakrapuṣkariṇī, is never fruitless. (17)
In matters of charity, Cakratīrtha is the most meritorious and unsurpassed holy site.
Long ago, O bull among the twice-born, Padmanābha of the Śrīvatsa lineage performed severe austerities on the bank of the Cakrapuṣkariṇī.
For several years he subsisted on withered leaves;
for some time he lived on water, and for many years he lived on air alone.
Thus, at the end of the twelfth year, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa was truly pleased.
The Lord of Śrī Rādhā and Kamalā became manifest before his very eyes.
Having beheld Kṛṣṇa, the Abode of Śrī, he began to offer praise to Viṣṇu,
who possesses the form of Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa and is the son of Kaṃbhareya.
Salutations to You, Veṅkaṭeśa, who dwells on Śeṣādri;
salutations to You, Śrīnivāsa, who dwells on Nārāyaṇādri.
Salutations to You, the Lord of Lakṣmī, the Lord of the lotus-lake, who is dear to His devotees.
Thus praised, Śrīnivāsa, who is dark as a rain-cloud, was indeed pleased.
He said to the twice-born Padmanābha at this Cakratīrtha:
"O beloved best of devotees, dwell here forever until the end of the kalpa, worshipping me."
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa vanished right there. Once, while Padmanābha was dwelling there, a Rākṣasa arrived intending to devour him and seized the Brāhmaṇa at that time.
He cried out repeatedly, "O wielder of the discus! Protect me, protect me!
(27) "O Lord of Veṅkaṭa, Hare, Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, O Lord!
O son of Kambharā, O compassionate Master, protect me, who am seized by a demon! (28)
While he was thus offering praise, the wielder of the discus dispatched his own discus to the bank of the Cakrapuṣkariṇī lake for the sake of that very person's protection.
Upon seeing the Sudarśana with its great radiance, the rākṣasa fled.
He cut off his head, and this brahmin praised the discus:
"O Discus of Viṣṇu! Salutations to you, who are consecrated to the protection of devotees!
Salutations to you, the ornament upon the lotus-hand of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa! (1.404.30–31)
"Always remain established here; be my protector for my sake.
Salutations again and again to you, who are the very form of Nārāyaṇa and the bestower of liberation.
Having been thus entreated, Sudarśana spoke to the devotee of Padmanābha.
"O devotee! You must understand that this Cakratīrtha was established by you in my name.
Out of a desire for your welfare, I shall dwell eternally at Cakratīrtha.
From now on, there shall be no further affliction for people caused by Rākṣasas and other such beings. (33–34)
"Those who bathe here shall have their sins washed away and go to the abode of Śrī Hari.
Having said this, he entered the radiant Cakrapuṣkariṇī.
Thus, [the place] bestows liberation through the power of the devotion and chastity of the faithful.
O Lakṣmī! A sacred ford (tīrtha) has arisen at Cakrāśrita, which destroys all sins.
Listen to how even that Rākṣasa who has now died came to be;
formerly, in the city of Śrīraṅga, there were indeed Vaiṣṇavas such as Vasiṣṭha and others. || 36–37 ||
They paid homage to Śrī Raṅganātha with a longing for liberation.
Once, a Gandharva named Sundara arrived there;
he was performing his bath in the water while naked young women were present. (38)
Vasiṣṭha indeed engaged in various sports for that long;
then, having gone to bathe, he saw him naked and cursed the shameless one:
"O handsome one, since you do not put on a garment even upon seeing me, therefore—" || 1.404.40 ||
By those [curses], he immediately attained the state of a *rākṣasa*, and thus became a *rākṣasa*.
Then the young women, having approached the venerable Vasiṣṭha, entreated him for forgiveness:
"O ocean of compassion, having seen us, you ought not to harbor anger."
For the husband alone is considered the supreme ornament of women.
A woman who is bereft of her husband, even if she has a hundred sons, is not auspicious;
as a widow, she is inauspicious, and therefore her birth is in vain.
"O Lord, our beloved, one offense must be forgiven; please be gracious.
Thus praised, Vasiṣṭha said to them: "My curse cannot be fruitless.
After a period of sixteen years, the Rākṣasa shall thereafter attain the state of a Gandharva."
At Cakratīrtha, during his separation from Padmanābha, he will be liberated.
By means of the Sudarśana discus, his deliverance shall come to pass.
Furthermore, that beautiful husband will delight him once more in the celestial realm.
Having spoken thus, Vasiṣṭha indeed departed for the temple of Śrīraṅga.
The Rākṣasa became handsome, yet possessed great fangs and was terrifying.
Seeing him, the women, agitated by fear, went to heaven.
Sixteen years passed as the Rākṣasa wandered upon the mountain.
Then, liberated by Sudarśana through the power of a Brāhmaṇa,
Sundara became truly beautiful and ascended to heaven in a celestial chariot.
The discus resided there eternally; therefore, it became known as Cakratīrtha.
Indeed, upon hearing this, the destruction of the entire web of sins occurs with certainty.
O Lakṣmī! Listen to the majesty of Jābālitīrtha; I shall describe it to you.

A Brahmin named Durācāra, who lived on the banks of the Kāverī, was constantly associated with sinners; having lost his Brahmanical rites and virtues, he was seized by a powerful and terrifying Vetāla. (51–52)
After wandering for a very long time on Mount Veṅkaṭa,
he plunged into the water, whereupon he was released by a vetāla.
At that very spot in the water where he was liberated, there was the sage Jābālika.
He dwelt at that great holy site, which is called Jābāli-tīrtha. Formerly, there was a great atheist who was a brahmin;
because he reviled the gods and the virtuous, he attained the state of a vetāla.
By the power of that sacred ford (tīrtha), he too shall attain human birth once again.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have described to you the supreme Jābāli-tīrtha.
Now listen, my dear, as I also describe the Tumburu-tīrtha here.
Indeed, all sinful men bathe repeatedly in us;
having cast off their nets of sin, those people become purified.
How shall our own nets of sin be destroyed in every way?
Having reflected thus, they went to the sacred fords (tīrthas) at Veṅkaṭācala;
there, at Tumburu, they bathed in the waters of Svāmipuṣkariṇī.
On the bright lunar day of the Uttarāphālgunī constellation, during the auspicious festival, they bathed in that holy ford.
Their sins were destroyed and they returned to their own abodes.
[6] A person who is devoted to great sins, cruel, devoid of charity, the destroyer of his lineage,
a slaughterer of animals, a perpetrator of treachery, a slanderer, and a liar— [61]
One who betrays a friend, one who is ungrateful, a killer of an embryo, one who goes to another’s wife,
a betrayer for the sake of others’ wealth, one who betrays his master, one who turns away from the gods,
a rogue, a deceiver, an obstacle to dharma, and one who causes division within a family.
One who destroys gardens filled with trees endowed with beautiful foliage and fruit;
one who sets fires, one who administers poison, a wicked betrayer of trust;
one who harbors hatred toward his guru, a corrupt person, and one who causes discord between husband and wife. (63–64)
O Lakṣmī! This supreme Tumburu-tīrtha indeed purifies all these [beings] through bathing, drinking, and other such acts, and it bestows both heaven and liberation.
Long ago, the Gandharva named Tumburu spoke thus to his wife.
During the three months of Māgha, perform with me a bath that removes all impurities.
When the sun has risen in the month of Māgha, smear the ground with cow dung,
and decorate it with colored lines, creepers, and auspicious white lotuses and svastikas made of mineral pigments.
"O beloved, make the place for the worship of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa pure!
Prepare a fragrant lamp illuminated by a ghee-soaked wick.
Having become pure, offer cooked food to Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa."
Serve [the Lord] along with me through circumambulations and prostrations.
Perform the service of the Deity constantly; practice listening to the sacred narratives.
O Vaiṣṇavī, always receive food and water as the grace of Kṛṣṇa!
O Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, O Viṣṇu, O son of Kambharā, O Janārdana!
O Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa, O Govinda, O Lord and Master of Ramā and Rādhā!
O Lord of Śrī, Lakṣmī, and Pārvatī, O Māṇikośa, O Lord of Light! 71.
Always proclaim that he is the Inner Controller and the Bestower of Liberation.
Having abandoned anger, envy, greed, and the like, observe your vows;
by that alone liberation arises, and indeed the world of Viṣṇu is attained.

Having heard these words of her husband, the passionate woman became enraged and replied to her beloved: "In this month of Māgha, which is indeed afflicted by the cold and truly life-threatening, why do you hold bathing so highly? (74)
"O husband! I will not bathe; if I die, let there be a protector here for me.
(75) Dharma should be practiced by people only as long as it is possible and gentle.
One should not practice a dharma that causes suffering or brings about destruction; I will not do that. (76)
"I am not able to perform the rites for Viṣṇu in the morning," she said.
To her, who had spoken thus, Tumburu cursed that speaker of unpleasant words, saying:
"In the Ghoṇatīrtha on the Veṅkaṭādri mountain, within the hollow of a Pippala tree—"
"There, O fool, being devoid of water, become a solitary female frog.
Having heard this, she entreated her beloved; her husband said, "I shall grant you freedom from the curse:
once, while Agastya was in your vicinity together with the sages... (78-79)
Having stayed there, he will indeed then proclaim the greatness of Ghoṇa.
Upon hearing this from afar, you shall truly be released from your frog's body.
Returning once more to my abode, you shall sport with me.
Having spoken thus, the devoted wife, faithful to her husband, ceased speaking;
by her husband’s curse, she had assumed the most terrible form of a frog.
After many years had passed, Agastya arrived there.
Having bathed in Svāmipuṣkariṇī and bowed to the Lord Varāha,
and having beheld Veṅkaṭeśa Śrīnivāsa in the vicinity of the Pippala tree,
he arrived at Ghoṇatīrtha and spoke of its greatness to the people.
Then that female frog, released, shone with her former form.
She said to me: "Out of compassion, protect me, who have acted in opposition to my husband's word.
By my husband's curse I became a frog; I have been liberated by you. (84-85)
Then Agastya said to her: "Listen to the power of wifely devotion (*pātivratya*).
Your husband, who is well-versed in righteousness, has indeed cursed you truthfully;
for a curse is entirely appropriate for one who opposes the words of her husband. (86)
But she who disregards her husband’s reply and acts according to her own will falls into a miserable hell for the duration of an entire kalpa. Indeed,
a wife must never transgress the word of her husband.
By virtue of devotion to their husbands, through merit, and by serving their husbands,
women go to the abode of Viṣṇu— not by any other excellent vows. The husband is the mother, the husband is Viṣṇu, the husband is Brahmā, and the husband is Śiva.
The husband is the guru; the husband is the sacred ford; the husband is considered the supreme liberation.
But she who, having set aside her husband’s word, performs meritorious deeds, does not obtain the fruit thereof, nor does she become pure in that way. (1.404.90–91)
Even if she abides by the command of her guru, if she does not carry out the command of her husband,
she shall never be pure nor meritorious.
She should perform vows, religious duties, and so forth, only by the command of her husband.
Upon awakening, one should always perform service and other duties for Hari.
She who has bathed with the water from the lotus-feet of her husband is beloved by Hari;
she has undoubtedly bathed in all the sacred fords, such as the Gaṅgā and others. (93–94)
"You have experienced the fruit of suffering; you have been born again just as before.
Go now to the abode of Tumburu and be happy in every way.
This very place is the Tumburu-tīrtha; it has attained its renown because of him."
Those who bathe here on the full moon day partake in the fruit of sacrifice.
Day by day, they obtain the fruit born from the gift of a thousand tawny cows;
day by day, they obtain the fruit born from the gift of ten million jewels.
O fair-browed one, by bathing at Ghoṇatīrtha, one indeed obtains the fruit arising from the gift of a thousand elephants and ten thousand horses in a single day; and by bathing at Ghoṇā,
one gains the fruit of giving away ten million maidens.
One obtains that same fruit from bathing at the Tumburu-tīrtha which arises from the gift of a thousand pieces of gold at Kurukṣetra.
And he who would sacrifice his body for the sake of a guru, for the sake of the virtuous, or for the sake of his master, [attains that same fruit].
Whoever would sacrifice their body for the sake of a devoted wife, for the sake of a virtuous woman, or for the sake of Hari,
obtains that same fruit by bathing in the Ghoṇa-tīrtha. This is true for those who alleviate the suffering of the distressed and whose souls are intent on the service of sacred pilgrimage sites.
Whatever merit belongs to those who observe the vow of truth, and whatever may arise from Ghoṇatīrtha;
whatever fruit is found at the Gaṅgā, the Narmadā, the Sarayū, the Candrabhāgā, the Svarṇavatī, and the Yamunā— that same fruit shall be obtained here.
Having heard this and drunk the water, she went to the house of Tumburu.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, has this supreme Tumburu-tīrtha been described to you;
by merely hearing of it, a person shall attain the great fruit of a Vājapeya sacrifice.

To the supreme realm of Viṣṇu, to heaven, and likewise to the eternal station. (1.05) Thus ends the four hundred and fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Worthy Recipient for Gifts, the Majesty of Chastity at Cakratīrtha and Jābālitīrtha, the Power of the Holy Fords," and so forth, within the first section on the Succession of the Kṛta Yuga in the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*. (404)
← Chapter 404: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga) Chapter 405 [Author: Chapter 406 →
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, Lakṣmī! There are six principal holy bathing places (tīrthas) on Veṅkaṭādri;
they are Svāmipuṣkariṇī and Viyadgaṅgā, which is superior even to that. || 1 ||
There is also Pāṇḍutīrtha, the destroyer of sins, which is most excellent;
as well as Kumāradhārikātīrtha and Tumburutīrtha.
When the full moon occurs in the zodiac sign of Aquarius (Kumbha) and there is a conjunction with the Maghā nakṣatra, [it is a time of great merit].
The sacred fords (tīrthas) from all directions come to the Kumāradhārikā. By bathing there, one obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice and liberation in the abode of Viṣṇu.
One should give gifts of food; thus, eternal fruit is attained.
On the full moon day conjoined with the asterism Uttarāphālgunī,
when the sun is in Pisces, all sacred fords (tīrthas) flow toward Tumburu.
By merely bathing there in the afternoon, one is not subject to rebirth.

He who causes [the rite] to be performed by giving the sacrificial thread (*yajñopavītaka*), the vow of Brahman (*brahmavrata*), and the auspicious time for marriage (*vivāhalagnaka*)—and having given the requisite materials—his merit is infinite. This is especially so when the sun is in Aries (*meṣasūrya*), under the asterism Citrā, and on the full moon day (*pūrṇimā*). Indeed, it is so in every respect. (6–7)
Indeed, all purifying holy places (tīrthas) come to the celestial Gaṅgā.
Having bathed there, a human being obtains the merit of a hundred sacrifices (śatakratu).
Furthermore, the gift of gold, the gift of food, and especially the gift of a maiden [yield great fruit].
It should be given by one desiring the highest heaven or desiring a home.
On the twelfth lunar day, when the sun is in Taurus, at the beginning of a vow, or on the day of Hari (Ekādaśī),
people come from all directions to Pāṇḍutīrtha on the Gaṅgā when it is joined with Mars.
Having bathed and given a milch cow as a gift, one is liberated from tens of millions of sins on the seventh lunar day of the bright fortnight when the sun is in Aśvinī, on a Sunday,
when the sun is conjoined with Uttarāṣāḍhā and endowed with Uttarābhādrapadā.
On the twelfth day as well, there is a sacred ford that destroys sins.
By bathing and making an offering of a Śālagrāma stone, one is liberated.
This occurs at dawn on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Dhanus.
At the Svāmipuṣkariṇī Tīrtha, all holy places from every direction come together;
only he who has accumulated merit over thousands of births may bathe there, and certainly no one else who lacks such virtue.
Having bathed, one should give a gift according to one's capacity and is thereby liberated.
(15) One should especially give a Śālagrāma stone and a wish-fulfilling cow there;
one should perform the gift of the *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇasaṃhitā*. (16)
By the gift of this [image] in Saurāṣṭra, one will certainly attain Goloka;
by the gift of it in the south, one will attain the station of Vairāja;
and by the gift of it in Prāgjyotiṣa, one will attain the world of the Sun.
By giving at Jālandhara, one shall attain the world of Varuṇa;
by giving at Uttarakuru, one shall attain the state of Brahmā;
and by giving throughout the seven continents, one shall become the lord of the seven continents. (18–19)

Those who always listen to the story of Viṣṇu, which purifies the world, are considered liberated while living; they are the devotees known as the great Bhāgavatas. Even for a Muhūrta, or half of that, or for a single Kṣaṇa on Veṅkaṭācala...

Any man who listens with devotion even to a single chapter of the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā* shall attain eternal liberation. Whatever fruit is found in all sacrifices and whatever fruit is found in all acts of charity— [that fruit he shall obtain]. (21–22)
By hearing the *Saṃhitā* even once, a person attains that fruit;
for hearing the *Saṃhitā* is the glorification of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
Indeed, both of these bestow the merit of the wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpavṛkṣa*) upon human beings. (23)

In this world, one who drinks the nectar of Kṛṣṇa’s stories would alone become free from old age and death. By drinking the nectar of Kṛṣṇa’s stories, one’s entire lineage shall become free from old age and death.
And I, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, always dwell within the speaker.
One should know that my own form is the reciter, whose body is the mind and who bestows awakening;
I am the Lord manifest as the speaker, and Lakṣmī is my beloved as the listener.
Thinking thus, one should constantly worship both the listener and the reciter.

"Without my entrance, O Lakṣmī, who would be capable of being either the listener or the speaker, or indeed of hearing or speaking the inner essence of this divine narrative? Wherever this Saṃhitā exists, O Lakṣmī, there dwells one whose form is divine. (27–28)
"I shall certainly appear, accompanied by Rādhā, Lakṣmī, and others, joined by my attendants, and endowed with those who are the vessels of the sacred narrative.
Those with divine vision behold me, but not people with mere physical eyes. (29)
While this discourse is taking place, those who give up their lives—
I lead them by means of a divine vehicle to Vaikuṇṭha, the imperishable realm,
to Goloka, or the immortal abode, according to whatever the devotee desires.
Whether he be a child, a youth, or an old man; whether he be poor or even unfortunate—a narrator of the sacred story is always worthy of honor, for he is the very embodiment of the Supreme Self.
One should never harbor a low opinion of one who knows the *Saṃhitā*.
The speech arising from whose mouth bestows liberation and heaven upon men;
the observer of the vow of this narrative grants the gift of fearlessness to living beings who have perished again and again throughout infinite fields of birth. (33–34)
Vyāsa is the bestower of knowledge; what teacher is superior to him who occupies the seat of Vyāsa?
Until the completion of the narrative, he shall not bow to any other teacher—not even to a king, an emperor, a universal monarch, a great preceptor, or a spiritual guide. (35)
Or rather, all these [deities] are proclaimed by Vyāsa to be situated in the lower [positions].
The seat of Vyāsa is always considered to be higher than their seats. Upon their arrival, Vyāsa should never rise from his own seat.
In a temple, at a crossroads, or on ground where five streams meet;
in a house, at a sacred ford (tīrtha), or in an auspicious field—one should recount the meritorious narrative at such a holy site.
Those who are faithful, devoted, restrained in speech, and steady-minded [should listen].
Those who listen with undistracted minds, possessing faith and self-control, are vessels of merit.
(39) One should honor both the narrator of the story and the assembly with all necessary offerings;
for them, the fruit of that merit shall eternally bestow fortune, prosperity, and wisdom. (1.405.40)
But those who, drawn by greed, listen to the *Saṃhitā* without having given [the gift], for them there shall be no meritorious fruit; rather, there shall be poverty in birth after birth.
Those who create obstacles during the discourse, the talkative ones, and the mockers—
Those who compose other verses with minds intent on childish play and the like,
who cause distractions through storytelling and meditation, and who destroy what they have heard—
their enjoyments perish, as do their wives, wealth, and prosperity. (42–43)
Those who sit upon high seats, or likewise remain in the *vīrāsana* posture,
or sit upon lion-thrones with one foot placed upon the other—
such listeners are born as crows or trees.
And listeners who do not show respect become poisonous trees;
even while lying down, listeners truly become pythons. Sitting too close to the speaker, they become critics who are difficult to answer. (45–46)
Those who create obstacles are born for a hundred lifetimes as dogs, donkeys, lizards, and even pigs. But those who praise this narrative attain the eternal state.
Through these discourses, the disciples go to the eternal abode of Brahmā.
One who gives blankets, skins, garments, and an excellent seat shall indeed go to the heavenly world;
such a giver of wealth goes to the abode of Brahmā.
One who gives a beautiful cloth for a book shall become a partaker of happiness;
even those who have committed great sins become purified through the attainment of knowledge.
Having thus heard the majesty of the act of listening to this narrative, [one should listen].
The gods, sages, perfected ones (siddhas), seers (ṛṣis), and ancestors;
the guardians of the directions, the guardians of the worlds, the rivers, streams, and forests;
and the earthly elements and the worlds—all reside on the auspicious abode of Veṅkaṭādri.
The women and men heard the most purifying narrative of the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā* from the mouth of Śvetavārāha.
For the purpose of providing them with food, the cooks of Veṅkaṭeśvara [prepared it].
In the kitchens, they guarded cauldrons filled with sweet foods;
they fed countless gods, goddesses, and embodied beings.
That sacred site became purifying, known as Kaṭāhatīrtha.
Mahādeva alone knows the majesty of that sacred ford (tīrtha).
Others who abide in the system of castes and stages of life, as well as even animals, birds, and the like, attain the supreme state by dwelling at Kaṭāha-tīrtha. (56)
The destruction of sins for which there is no other atonement occurs by resorting to Kaṭāha;
the removal of suffering for those who are distressed occurs by resorting to this water.
[One should perform] bathing in the Svāmipuṣkariṇī and behold Varāha and Śrīśa. (57–58)
At Varāha-tīrtha, one should always partake of food and drink that water, listen to the *Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam* (Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-saṃhitā), and constantly serve the saintly devotees;
this sixfold set is difficult to attain even in the three worlds. (59)
At the commencement of the narrative of the *Saṃhitā*, the Lord Varāha himself,
Hari, with four arms, emerged from the hollow of the earth (*bhūkaṭāha*).
O beloved, that sacred site known as Bhūkaṭāha exists right there.
Satiated by that nectar-like water which was the [sacred] hearing, those who performed the listening were immersed in the narrative of the *Saṃhitā*; they knew nothing else.
Having heard it for a month, all the deities departed to their own abodes.
Then a Brahmin named Keśava,
a slayer of Brahmins who was overwhelmed by the sin of killing a Brahmin, went to the Kaṭāha-tīrtha.
Having bathed and drunk the water, he became purified through the power of that sacred ford.
On the banks of the Tuṅgabhadrā, his residence was in Vedagrāma;
there were thousands of Vedic Brahmins there who were experts in the scriptures.
This Keśava was a land-grant recipient (agrahāra), yet he was deceived by the snares of unchaste women.
Having abandoned his mother and father, as well as his devoted wife,
he lived in her house while remaining constantly attached to unchaste women. After a long time had passed, Keśava was indeed abandoned by her when he fell ill.
And being hungry, he committed theft at the house of a brahmin;
having taken wealth and gold, he struck the brahmin with a sword.
Taking that wealth, he went to the house of an unchaste woman.
Beaten and cast out, he went to his father’s house.
A demoness, with the sin of killing a Brahmin clinging to her back, spoke:
"This man, having slain a Brahmin, gave wealth to an unchaste woman."
Driven out by her, that wicked-souled paramour, who mocks his father and mother and has abandoned his wife, has come to his father’s house;
O best of the twice-born, Padmanābha, you should indeed consider him as your son. (71)

"Abandon this slayer of a Brahmin; if you do not abandon your son, O twice-born one, I shall devour his wife, his wife's [family], you, and this son, as well as your entire lineage. Therefore, release this evil-minded one. (72–73)
"I am the personification of Brahman-slaughter; I shall not release him under any circumstances.
You ought not to destroy an entire lineage for the sake of one individual.
Having spoken thus, that Brahman-slaughter coiled herself around her son Keśava.
They became like female demons intent on devouring his life-breaths.
At that time, all the householders wept with distressed minds.
On that occasion, the sage Bharadvāja arrived there.
Having offered praise, the brahmin Padmanābha repeatedly begged for refuge:
"O portion of Kṛṣṇa, protect my son so that this slaughter may come to an end!
I have but one son; if he dies, it will mean the destruction of my lineage. (77)
"There will be a cessation of the ancestral *piṇḍa* offerings and the twice-born will fall into hell.
Therefore, O Brahmin, deliver them; great merit shall be yours!
Then Bharadvāja, who was a portion (*aṃśa*) of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, spoke.

"O Brahmin! This son of yours shall bathe in the waters of the Kaṭāha Tīrtha on the great mountain Veṅkaṭādri—the enchanting abode of Nārāyaṇa accompanied by Śrī, Bhū, and Līlā—and he shall go to the destroyer of the sin of killing a Brahmin. || 1.405.80 ||
Having accepted these words, the twice-born Padmanābha took his son and went to Veṅkaṭādri; he bathed in the waters of the Puṣkariṇī,
bowed before Lord Varāha, and beheld Śrīnivāsa.
Having bowed to that divine celestial chariot, he went to the Kaṭāha-tīrtha.
Just as he drank the water, bathed in the water, and was with his son,
the sin of slaughter met its dissolution and the Blessed One appeared.
"Those people who come to this holy ford (tīrtha) and drink its water,
for them there shall always be both enjoyment and liberation.
Having said this, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa spoke to him regarding its greatness.
I have brought this Veṅkaṭācala from the abode of Goloka.
There, Brahmā was thoroughly pleased with the sage Agastya as he performed penance.
He said, "O son, choose a boon; I shall grant you whatever is in your heart."

Agastya said to the Creator: "On the great mountain named Veṅkaṭa, I shall bring the Gaṅgā, who is the eternal purifier of the worlds. And as soon as Gaṅgā was remembered by Brahmā, she arrived there immediately. (87–88)
Agastya went forth from the peak, and the river followed him,
making that region golden and resounding with the cries of cattle;
then, stirred by the wind, she became known by the name Suvarṇamukharī.
Spreading from the lowlands to Veṅkaṭādri, she entered the ocean.
Agastya, having shown her the way as a second Gaṅgā in the form of a river, reached his place of penance and dwelt there in happiness.
There dwells the illustrious Veṅkaṭeśa, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, Hari;
he who is the Lord of Śrī Rādhā, Pārvatī, Lakṣmī, Padminī, and Māṇikī; and he who is the Lord of Prabhā, Ramākṣī, Tilā, Līlā, Padmā, and Vṛndā.
Accompanied by her friends, she always bathes and drinks from its waters.
On festival days, the gods, the holy fords, the liberated ones, and virtuous women bathe there.
Born from the Agastya mountain, it flows toward the southern ocean.
Indeed, by taking refuge in Nārāyaṇa, one purifies the lands;
even a single *niṣka* of water, when drunk, destroys mountains of sin.
One should constantly remember Him, bow to Him, glorify Him, and worship Him with the mind.
One who desires purity, security, and auspiciousness should remember the Suvarṇamukharī.
Summoned by Brahmā and brought down to earth by Agastya, she is the sovereign Suvarṇamukharī, the second form of Gaṅgā in embodied form. (96–97)
On its bank, by performing the gift of land, the gift of wealth,
or the offering of a daughter according to the prescribed rites, an embodied being attains the eternal Brahman.
Recitation, fire-offerings, austerity, charity, ancestral rites, and the worship of the gods [are likewise efficacious].
Whatever is performed on the bank of the Suvarṇamukharī becomes a hundredfold more meritorious.
Those fortunate ones who perform their ablutions in this river during the month of Agastyodaya shall dwell for an entire kalpa in the abode of the gods.
Those who give golden [images of] Agastya indeed go to the eternal Brahman.
Agastya was born from a jar; he is the leader of Govardhana, the stayer of the Vindhya mountains, and the one who achieved the power of drinking the ocean in a single mouthful.
"May the Lord, who possesses the power to purify the waters and who carries the Suvarṇamukharī river,
obtain great joy through this gift of mine.
Having said this, one should offer the image adorned with matted hair, an antelope skin, and other ornaments.
One should offer [this image], which is equipped with a staff and a water-pot, seated in the svastika posture,
wearing bark garments, holding a rosary in her hand, and exceedingly beautiful, together with Nārāyaṇa, for the purification of sins.
One should remember all the sacred fords (*tīrthas*) at the time of giving; listen, O beloved!
At its base is Agastyatīrtha and Śaṅkara as Agastyeśvara. Wherever that may be, one should enter the water during the northern transit of the sun (*uttarāyaṇa*).
The fruit of a thousand *agniṣṭoma* sacrifices, which bestows heaven, is obtained there.
Below [that], extending for one *krośa*, is the sacred ford (*tīrtha*) named after the gods, sages, and ancestors.
Having bathed there, a human being becomes liberated from the three debts.
Then, at a distance of two yojanas, there is the excellent confluence of the river Veṇā.
There, by bathing, one obtains the fruit of ten horse-sacrifices.
Then, four yojanas further to the east, is the auspicious Liṅga known as Astyeśvara.
Half a yojana from there, indeed, is the confluence of the Vyāghrapadā.
There, at Śaṅkha-tīrtha, shines Śiva as Śaṅkheśvara;
he was formerly established by the sage Śaṅkha as the destroyer of sins.
There, the sin-destroying Kalyānadī flows into the lower reaches;
there, indeed, the beautiful Brahmaśilā stands in the middle of the river.
Furthermore, half a yojana to the north, the Vaikuṇṭhādri mountain shines resplendently.
Surrounding that very mountain, which is one *krośa* in height, there are other mountains as well:
Añjana, Ananta, Vṛṣabha, Nīla, Varāha, and Kesari.
[The Lord] made his dwelling on the Nārāyaṇa mountain, the glorious Veṅkaṭādri.
Because he holds a boar (vārāha) in his hand, that mountain is called Vārāhakṣetra.
On the banks of the Suvarṇamukharī, on the Veṅkaṭa mountain,
the Blessed Lord Hari dwells together with Śrī, with Bhū, and with Padminī.
He was endowed with victory, grace, the *bakula* flower, splendor, Pārvatī, radiance, fortune, ruby, and playfulness;
he was served by Siddhas, Gandharvas, Munis, humans, and Dānavas. (116)
Indeed, the desires of those who remember it are surely fulfilled.
(1.17) Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have described to you this auspicious circle of holy places (tīrthas).
By hearing or reciting this, heaven and even liberation shall indeed be attained. (1.18)

Thus ends the four hundred and fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Six Holy Tirthas on Mount Veṅkaṭādri, the Worship of Vyāsa named Śveta— the Narrator of the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā— , the Liberation of the Brahmin Keśava from the Sin of Brāhmaṇa-Slaughter, the Bringing of the Suvarṇamukharī River known as Gaṅgā, and the Enumeration of Other Tirthas," in the first section concerning the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, specifically within the discourse on the majesty of devoted wives (*pativratā*).
*Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā* — Section 1 (The Continuity of the Kṛta Yuga), Chapter 405.
Chapter 406 [Author: Chapter 407 → Śrī Lakṣmī said:
"O Lord of Śrī, Ramā, and Kamalā! On the highly meritorious Veṅkaṭādri, how did you first manifest? Tell me all this wonder.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī! I shall describe my majesty in brief:
I am Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the ground of all beings indeed.
In Goloka I am named Kṛṣṇa; in Vaikuṇṭha I am Nārāyaṇa.
In the immortal abode, I am Vāsudeva, the Infinite (bhūmā) in the unmanifested abode;
but in the supreme, imperishable abode, I become Puruṣottama,
as well as Hiraṇyagarbha, Vairāja, and Sadāśiva.
I am the thousand-headed Lord Mahāviṣṇu, and I also become the one-headed Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa upon the earth.
By my radiance the entire universe shines; I am the Sun.
Indeed, my creation is pervaded by knowledge, and I am that very one.
Residing within the hearts of all, I dwell as the inner controller (antaryāmī).
I am Hari, Sadāśiva, Brahmā, Kāmbhareya, and Janārdana.
I alone am these various manifestations; thousands of forms arise from me.
Whenever I desire to perform a virtuous act, then I descend to the surface of the earth.
I create this world through the quality of passion (rajas), and I sustain it through truth (sattva).

"I remove [the world] by means of darkness itself, and I sleep, thinking 'I am sleeping. "In the past, in order to bring back the earth that had gone beneath the surface of the water, I assumed, as it were in sport, a form resembling that of a boar according to my own will. (1.406.9–10)
Having reduced them to a state of mud by the power of my fangs' tips, I gathered them together and brought them above the water so that they might find a place to rest.
I established the waters within their bounds so that they would not destroy the earth.
For the sake of providing a foundation, I established the elephants of the quarters and Śeṣa as the tortoise.
By my command, Brahmā fashioned the universe as it was before.
And in every kalpa, for the purpose of protection, I sport upon the surface of the earth.
Assuming the form of a boar, I then resorted to Veṅkaṭācala;
I dwelt at the holy site of Svāmipuṣkariṇī together with Brahmā.
Being entreated by him for the sake of his original form, O beloved, I then became invisible!
There was indeed a king named Śaṅkha, born of the Haihaya lineage.
He was a supreme Vaiṣṇava devotee who constantly engaged in the ninefold worship;
that monarch always listened to the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā.
Nevertheless, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa did not appear before him directly.
Because of this, his mind remained unsatisfied, and he reflected repeatedly:
"How indeed might the Blessed Lord come within the range of my eyes? (17)
As he was thinking thus, the Blessed Lord spoke within his heart:
"Go to Śrī Veṅkaṭādri and worship for a thousand years;
remaining invisible, I shall become visible to you and to Agastya."
"Having propitiated me through your devotion to austerity, you two shall obtain my vision.
Having entrusted the kingdom to his sons Śaṅkha and Vajra, [King] Śrīveṅkaṭa went to [Mount] Veṅkaṭa.
Agastya also arrived at that mountain, surrounded by hundreds of sages.
He performed a circumambulation of this place inhabited by Brahmā and the other gods.
(21) All the gods, Sanaka and the other sages whose wealth is their austerity, waited for the direct vision of Hari, just like the pot-born Agastya. (22)
Having gathered together, they arrived where Śaṅkha, the king of devotees, was;
on the banks of the Suvarṇamukharī, they beheld King Śaṅkha.
Seated there, they all greeted one another with great eagerness.
Devoted to the chanting of Govinda’s glories and having Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa as their very soul, they beheld a vision at the end of the third watch of the night:
the Lord, holding a conch, a discus, and a mace in His hands, accompanied by Padminī. (24–25)
They beheld Hari as he had arrived to grant a boon;
having bathed in the lotus pond at dawn, they praised the Imperishable One.
They chanted the eight-syllabled mantra: *Oṃ Śrī Kṛṣṇa Narāyaṇa*.
Before them appeared a single, most wonderful radiance.
Seeing Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa there, they praised him with reverence:
"Victory to Viṣṇu! Victory to Kṛṣṇa! Victory to Śrīkṛṣṇa Keśava!"
Victory to you, O Upholder of the Earth, Govinda, Lord of Veṅkaṭādri! Victory indeed!
All have truly been made successful by the granting of this divine vision.
O Blessed One, who shows mercy to devotees, please dwell here forever.
"And make this Suvarṇamukharī river a purifier of the three worlds.
Always remaining on this mountain, be the bestower of desired objects.
Having heard this, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa spoke these pleasing words: "So be it."
By that Kṛṣṇa, the Suvarṇamukharī was made his own abode,
and the mountain Vaikuṇṭhaśaila was made his eternal residence.
O beloved, Hari became the bestower of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
Hari Kṛṣṇa said to Śaṅkha: "I am pleased with your devotion.
Residing in the world of Indra for the duration of a kalpa, served by hosts of apsarases, and having enjoyed manifold pleasures, you shall thereafter come to my own realm."
Having thus granted the boon to the gods and bestowed upon them a permanent residence,
Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Kamalā, vanished right there. Thus, having assumed a gentle form, Kṛṣṇa dwells on Veṅkaṭa.
By remembering Nārāyaṇa, Veṅkaṭādri, Svāmipuṣkariṇī,
as well as Kaṭāha and other sacred fords (tīrthas), they indeed become purified;
they shall attain Puruṣottama, the Lord of Lakṣmī, Śrī, Bhū, and Padminī.
Listen, Lakṣmī! Long ago, a certain virtuous woman named Añjanā, who was deeply devoted to Viṣṇu and yet childless, began to perform austerities.
While she was established in her penance, a certain sage named Mataṅga spoke to her.
"What do you desire with this severe austerity? Speak, O beautiful one!
Añjanā said: "My father, Kesarī, a Rākṣasa by birth, performed a formidable penance, meditating upon Śiva for the sake of a son. (1.406.40)
Śiva and Śivā, seated upon their bull and acting out of compassion, arrived;
and Śiva said: "In this birth, no son shall be given to you;
however, I grant you a daughter who will be renowned throughout the worlds."
"You should consider yourself her son and thus attain the status of a daughter; be happy.
Having granted him this boon, Hara vanished on the spot.
Thereafter, my father, the Rākṣasa, departed for his home contented.

I was born from his wife, and I was married to him at the proper time; by my husband, named Kesari, in the great city called Kiṣkindhā. [I performed] the vows of the month of Māgha and the vows of the month of Kārttika.
She performed the Vaiśākha vows as well as the Cāturmāsya vows,
and she practiced the ninefold devotion to Nārāyaṇa;
she gave gifts of Śālagrāma stones, food, cows, and lamps.

Out of a desire for the fruit of having a virtuous son, she performed in every way the gift of sesame seeds, the gift of clothing, the gift of land, the gift of water, and the offering of fruits and flowers;
and whatever merit she had acquired during the month of Śrāvaṇa, she dedicated it all.
"Even so, not having obtained a son, I remained engaged in ascetic penance for that purpose.
(48) Then Mataṅga said to that virtuous female ascetic, "The giver of sons is indeed here to the south, on the mountain of clouds, the dwelling place of Nṛsiṃha. (49)
Ten yojanas to the east of that place, at a distance of ten yojanas, flows the river Suvarṇamukharī; to the north of it stands Mount Vṛṣabha.
At its summit lies the beautiful lake Svāmipuṣkariṇī.
Go and bathe according to the prescribed rite; behold Keśava as Varāha.
Having paid obeisance to Veṅkaṭeśa, proceed to the Viyadgaṅgā.
O Vaiṣṇavī! Perform penance there, directed toward Vāyu.
Having heard this, that ascetic woman indeed went to Veṅkaṭādri;
she visited the sacred fords according to the rules and performed most rigorous penance.
Then, on the bank of the Viyadgaṅgā, the Wind-god appeared before her.
She said, "Grant me a boon," and he replied, "I shall become your son. Having spoken thus, the Wind-god vanished.
Then the great sages, having indeed taken up the seed of Śaṅkara, [prepared for its reception].
Then Vāyu, assuming the form of a lion, approached him;
he seized him by the ear of Añjanī and gave him [to her], and from that he became a son.
As soon as he was born, he was a youth, possessed of the memory of his former births, and surpassed the strength of the wind.
He became the excellent son of that ascetic woman.
On the fourteenth day of the month when the Sun was in Aries, during the conjunction with the Citrā nakṣatra,
the Wind-god himself appeared on the banks of the Suvarṇamukharī river.
Then, bathing, giving gifts, and other such acts performed here become inexhaustible.
The gift of food, the gift of clothing, the gift of gold, the offering of a daughter, the gift of a Śālagrāma stone, the gift of a cow, and the gift of land—[all these yield eternal fruit]. (59)
The gift of a water-station, the gift of sesame seeds, the gift of grain, and the offering of a house;
(60) perfumes, campaka flowers and the like, umbrellas, fans, and chowries; betel, camphor, and so forth, as well as household utensils. (61)
The person who gives a thousand divine garments there,
having enjoyed manifold pleasures, becomes an enjoyer of delights even in the heavenly world;
thereafter, having become a Brahmin, he attains liberation as a sovereign ruler of the earth.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have narrated to you the wonders of Veṅkaṭādri.
By hearing or reciting this, enjoyment and liberation will certainly be attained.
Now listen to another divine narrative concerning Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
Out of affection for you, I shall tell of her who was devoted to her husband.
Once, Śrī Veṅkaṭādri thought of going to Meru.
As he was flying up from the earth on his two wings, [he suddenly fell]. 65.66ab.
At that moment, a great earthquake occurred, bringing destruction to many embodied beings.
All living creatures cried out and went to the Boar for refuge, saying:
"O Blessed One, we are as good as dead because of this upheaval, being without a protector!"
"O Lord of the Earth! Grant us protection; O Master, establish us as we were before!
Thus entreated, the Lord Varāha himself, who is Nārāyaṇa, consoled all living beings and reassured Indra along with his thunderbolt.
Just then Indra arrived, raising his thunderbolt, the destroyer of wings.
Seeing Indra, Mount Veṅkaṭādri became terrified and trembled;
he then went for refuge to Viṣṇu in the form of the Boar.
Terrified of death, he offered praise; then the Blessed One himself said to him:
"O mountain, if you should ever travel through the path of the sky on your two wings, I shall provide protection; remain steady here."
Thus addressed, he then became motionless and perfectly steady after bowing down;
the boar became invisible, and Mahendra went to his own abode. By taking refuge in this [boar], Indra did not have his wings cut off.
Then once, that mountain indeed reflected in his heart:
"I have indeed come from Goloka and have dwelt here for many years;
now I shall go into the presence of Kṛṣṇa for the purpose of beholding Goloka."
Having reflected thus, on the day of Kṛṣṇajanmāṣṭamī,
they all went to the sacred fords to bathe at Kuśasthalī on the Gomatī river in Yaśas-kṣiti; indeed, all the sages, rivers, and streams, as well as the deities, departed.
Agastya and the others went to the confluence of the Gomatī;
then, seeing that place to be desolate, they set their minds on departing.
At that moment, the earth trembled there, and living beings perished due to the shaking.

At that time, there lived there a certain poor female ascetic (tāpasī), a Brāhmaṇī who was constantly devoted to the service of Brāhmaṇas and eternally faithful to her vows. She was named Suvarṇarekhā, and Hiraṇyā was her sister. ||78–79||
Hiraṇyā was a great and virtuous maiden, an ascetic;
Suvarṇarekhā was accompanied by her husband, whose name was Nārāyaṇa.
Having drunk water from the feet of the brahmin Nārāyaṇa, she spoke to him.
"Veṅkaṭādri has wings, yet he was prevented from flying away in the past. If he flies up again, our death will surely follow.
Therefore, by my husband’s command, I shall certainly paralyze him in every way."
"Then Śrī Veṅkaṭeśa and the others will surely become angry and bring us suffering;
therefore, O Lord, tell me what must be done here.
Thus addressed, he said to his beloved: "O beautiful woman, do as you wish!"
"O people here, if your devotion to your husbands is indeed firm, then all of you shall meet with defeat in his presence.
Do not fear, O virtuous lady; rather, instruct the mountain."
Having received these words from her beloved,
the virtuous woman then said: "If I am indeed established in my duty as a devoted wife,
then let the king of mountains here have wings within the earth."
"May they remain forever rendered inert, deprived of the power of their wings,
and having attained oneness with the earth, so that there may be no further flight.
As soon as this was said, those two birds became motionless and paralyzed.
Deprived of their power, they were stationed within the earth;
Veṅkaṭādri, with humility, repeatedly begged for forgiveness.
Satī said: "He is always here, as is Nārāyaṇa and I."
Therefore, our residence is not yet determined; we shall go to Mount Raivata.
You, however, remain forever inactive; O restless mountain, do not be fickle!
Otherwise, the Lord will surely bring about your destruction once again.
"Remain always thus with your wings; let there be no flying.
Out of compassion, I grant life to your two wings; do not grieve further.
There shall be millions of locusts and parrots upon your wings."
They will become powerful and will fly into the sky.
There, in the grassy glades, forests, and wildernesses, those locusts and parrots,
having devoured the medicinal herbs, will undergo dissolution within their wings.
"In this way, I shall indeed grant life to both your wings.
Having spoken thus and having made Veṅkaṭa firm, the twice-born Nārāyaṇa departed,
and the devoted wife Svarṇarekhā went to Mount Raivata.
The eternally devoted Svarṇarekhā became the river, and the eternal Nārāyaṇa became the lake; thus did the couple, Nārāyaṇa and Svarṇarekhā, dwell upon the mountain. (96–97)
Indeed, those two divine ones, appearing in the form of holy fords (tīrtha), made their abode on Mount Raivata; there, even by Viṣṇu himself, who is Dāmodara and devoted to his wife,
a śrāddha was performed, and they both granted supreme satisfaction to the conscious beings.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, this wondrous account has been narrated to you.

(99) Thus ends the four hundred and sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Manifestation of Varāha through Agastya and Śaṅkha on Veṅkaṭādri, the Acquisition of a Son by Hanumān through Añjanā’s Austerities, the Paralysis of the Two Wings of Veṅkaṭādri, and the Arrival of Tvaṣṭṛrekhā and Nārāyaṇahṛdaya at Raivatācala," within the section on the Greatness of Devoted Wives in the first book, the *Kṛtayugasantāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Chapter 408 →
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, Lakṣmī! To the auspicious story of Jayantī, the daughter of Indra, who performed the service of penance for the sake of Śukra’s devotion to his wife. (1)
During the wars between the gods and the dānavas, when the gods together with their armies were unable to defeat the circle of dānavas by the daityas,
they then praised Śukrācārya so that victory over the daityas might be achieved.
Then Śukra, perceiving that the agreement was indeed for the benefit of the gods,
abandoned all the Daityas and joined the gods. Thereupon, the Daityas challenged Śukra, who had gone over to the side of the gods.
Why have you abandoned us while we were looking on and taken refuge with the gods?
We are unable to remain upon the earth; we shall enter the subterranean realm (rasātala).
For without you as our protector, O Guru, how shall we endure?
Thus addressed, he spoke to the despondent Daityas, consoling them with his voice:
"Do not fear; I shall protect you with the splendor residing within me.
Indeed, the power of mantras, herbs, wealth, supernatural attainments, and elixirs abide in me."
"Whether that fourth part exists in full among the gods or not, I shall bestow upon you what has come to me; by that, you shall be protected.
Having understood this choice well, the gods, desiring to seize everything, [accepted it].
They held a consultation to bring him under their control through the power of mantras.
The gods began their studies in the presence of Śukra;
he gave them a little here and a little there, yet even that was incomplete.
As long as Śukra did not teach this [knowledge] to the Daityas,
the gods continued to slay the Daityas and send them to the netherworld (pātāla).
Then, the Daityas, being in a state of wretchedness, fled toward Kāvya himself.
Even then, the gods attacked the Daityas without hesitation.
Śukra was unable to provide protection or recite mantras at that time;
however, he spoke thus to the Daityas: "It is my opinion that there should be no battle."
"O gods, you are currently powerless because you are weak, whereas they are now most powerful.
Therefore, wait for the right time; I too shall go for the sake of penance.
I will go to Mahādeva to obtain a boon that brings victory."

"Having obtained these unsurpassed and excellent mantras from the god Maheśvara, when we fight the gods, then indeed you shall attain victory. Then the Asuras, having abandoned the scriptures, spoke to the Suras: || 16 ||
"We shall practice austerities, peaceful and clad in bark garments in the forest.
Having heard this, even the gods desisted from their assault upon him.
Then Śukra said to the Daityas, "Go you to the netherworld (rasātala)."
"Endowed with ascetic power, you shall indeed worship for a short time for the sake of your purpose.
Having spoken thus, the preceptor of the Daityas went to Śambhu on the Himālaya;
there he performed severe penance for a full thousand years.
With his head hanging downward and his feet placed in the sky above the pit of the earth,
he remained a celibate student and performed severe penance.
Remaining motionless and abstaining from food, he mentally recited the name of Śiva.

Then, at a certain time, the Daityas arrived on earth to dwell there. When they were struck by the gods, they went to the mother of Kāvya for refuge; she said to them, "May you have perpetual fearlessness."
"Do not fear, do not fear! Cast away your fear, O Dānavas!
I declare that for you who dwell in my presence, there shall be no fear.
Then the gods went there once more to strike down the Daityas by force.

The enraged Khyāti said to the gods, "I shall destroy you and Mahendra! Having spoken thus, that yoginī, rich in asceticism, paralyzed Mahendra with her magic power and held him motionless through a malevolent spell.
Then the gods fled upon seeing Indra brought under control.
Thereupon, Viṣṇu, having instantly drawn Mahendra back into his own form,
was just as he was departing for heaven when Khyāti, filled with rage, [appeared].
Seeing that he was protected by Viṣṇu, Khyāti spoke these words there:
"O Maghavan, I shall burn you along with Viṣṇu by force.
At that moment, Viṣṇu seized his discus for the sake of his own protection in that calamity.
Then, realizing that Khyāti intended a cruel act that would end his life,
Sudarśana, out of fear of him, indeed severed Khyāti’s head.
Seeing that killing of a woman, Bhṛgu then became enraged.
Then, through his wife Khyāti, he cursed Viṣṇu:
"Since you, though knowing the dharma, have slain a woman who should not be killed, therefore you too shall suffer the death of your head at the beginning of a kalpa. (1.407.30)
Thus, having become Kṛṣṇa by means of a curse, he was indeed Gaṇeśa;
and by the hand of Śaṅkara, he obtained the severing of his head.
Then, Bhagurī quickly joined the head back onto the body.

"O Goddess, this one has been struck down by Viṣṇu; I shall restore her to life. If the entire dharma of a wife’s vow has been observed by me, by that truth, and if I speak the truth, let her live! (33–34)
Having sprinkled her with cold water, he said, "Live!
When he uttered the word, "Arise," Khyāti was restored to life. "Excellent! Excellent! the gods and others cried out in every direction.
However, Indra did not find peace because of his fear of Śukra’s fame;
therefore, having deliberated on how to create an obstacle to Śukra’s asceticism, Indra said to his daughter Jayantī:
"O daughter, you have been entrusted by me to Śukra."
Go; you have been given to him, so exert yourself for my sake.
Śukra is performing a severe penance for the purpose of propitiating Śambhu.
He strives intensely for the sake of a mantra in order to bring about the destruction of the gods.

"Go and attend to him with means such as removing his fatigue, and with various services like providing a bed that are agreeable to his mind. Having been addressed thus, Jayantī remained steadfast in her father's command. (1.407.40)
She went to that mountain where he was engaged in terrible asceticism;
there, a maiden approached that lovely youth who sat with his head downward for the sake of poetry.
Having told him, "I am your bride," she remained in attendance upon him.
With agreeable words, by massaging her limbs and other such services,
and by providing desired objects at the proper time, she served her with pleasant touches for many years, attending to her in a manner consistent with her practice of vows.
When a full thousand years had passed, that virtuous woman, devoted solely to her husband, remembered Śaṅkara, wondering, "How might he not be pleased?
If Śambhu is indeed not pleased, I shall surely burn him up right here."
Just as she was overcome with anger because of this curse, Hara arrived there.
He said to Jayantī: "Your husband is indeed performing severe penance for the destruction of the gods; therefore, I have not come into his sight."
"But drawn by your exceedingly powerful devotion to your husband, I have come to grant you a boon; tell me what I shall do for you.
Jayantī said, "I was entrusted to my father for the sake of his own purpose."
She should indeed perform that duty, as well as the duty toward her husband.
A maiden should practice the dharma of him to whom she has been given;
she should act for his welfare, his prosperity, and his advancement alone.
The husband is said to be the entire possession of women who have been won by their virtue;
surely, when there is opposition to him, no good can ever come to a woman.
Therefore, being devoted to your husband, perform every duty as is appropriate for me.
A daughter should act for the welfare of her father and should never cause suffering to her husband.
O Śambhu, do what is appropriate so that the welfare of both may be secured;
I have performed service to this poem, filled with its inner spirit.
But no obstacle was indeed created for his austerity and celibacy,
because I have been given to him as his lawful wife by Indra.
How can I create an obstacle through desire when his austerity is already exhausted?
Therefore, having restrained my desire, I did not indeed indulge in pleasure;
for through this, the perfection of my asceticism has been achieved, which serves for my ultimate welfare.
Indeed, I have maintained my devotion to my husband and have never done anything undesirable.
"By that very devotion to her husband, she shall fulfill the desire of her heart.
Having spoken thus to Kāvya, the object of his affection, he ceased;
and Mahādeva, being pleased yet startled, then spoke.
O Śukra!
For the sake of such a maiden, you have lived your life entirely devoted to her side for a full thousand years;
yet even so, you have not abandoned your vow of celibacy. ||57-58||
Even by that devoted wife, her unsteady mind was restrained;
for though she remains sixteen years of age even today, she still sports.
Untouched and dependent on you, this blessed woman is indeed a devoted wife.
"Let there be this proclamation of your blessedness; you have reached the further shore in every respect.
This vow was performed by you alone and by no one else.
Therefore, indeed, by virtue of your austerity, intelligence, sacred learning, and power," || 1.407.60–61 ||
By your splendor alone you shall surpass all the gods;
through the power of your wife’s devotion to her husband and her celibacy,
you shall obtain everything you desire, provided it remains untold to anyone else.
"May the husband and wife go happily to the lordship over subjects and the lordship over wealth;
accept invincibility, true knowledge, and the *sañjīvanī* [life-restoring] spell.
Thus addressed, the god Śukra, remaining with his head bowed down, offered praise.
Salutations to You who are the embodiment of Brahman, the fulfiller of the desires of Your devotees;
salutations to You who are instantly gratified and eternally content;
salutations to You who are perpetually satisfied and are clad in the directions as Your garment.
Salutations to Bhīma, to Rudra, to you, Mahādeva; salutations!
Salutations to Ugra, to the wielder of the Pināka bow, to Śambhu;
salutations to the hunter of deer, to the ascetic, and to you, Kirāta! 66–67.
Salutations to the three-eyed one, whose forehead is adorned by the moon, who exists in the form of the *liṅga*;
salutations again and again to Sadāśiva, to Śarva, and to the Lord of Bhava.
Salutations again and again to you, the gentle witness and the husband of Satī.
Salutations to you, the blue-throated one, the fierce one, the one born in an instant, the wielder of the trident;
salutations to you, the sovereign lord, the tawny-hued one, whose garment is the hide;
salutations to you, the Lord of creatures, the Lord of all beings.
Salutations to the one with eight bodies, the soul of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa;
salutations again and again to you, the husband of Pārvatī, the radiant Lord.
Salutations to you, O Lord, who are everywhere, in all directions, and in all souls.
"Salutations again and again to you, the bestower of fruits and the creator of bliss, everywhere!
Having spoken thus, he ceased; Śambhu then said: "Your penance has become complete; arise and choose the boon you desire."
Nevertheless, Śukra did not rise, and Śambhu vanished from sight.
Seeing this, Jayantī spoke to him as the occasion required:
"O Lord, why do you not rise? Why do you disregard your boon?"
"Why indeed do you not pay attention to the words of Śambhu?
(75) As soon as the ascetic heard the sound made by his wife and rose from the ground, he no longer saw Śambhu, for He had vanished. (76)
Having fallen into extreme distress, he gave way to intense grief;
for when that which has arrived must be abandoned, reunion is indeed difficult to obtain.
Thus addressed by the voice from the sky, Kāvya was directed back toward his home.
Having taken Jayantī along with the merit of his asceticism,
Śukra respectfully led her home; for ten years,
he remained entirely concealed within the palace, enjoying pleasures together with Jayantī.

From her was born a daughter, Devayānī, the beautiful wife of Yayāti. Then, perceiving that Śukra had achieved his purpose, all the sons of Diti went to the house of their preceptor, desiring to see him.
Not seeing them, they then returned each to their own home. Then Bṛhaspati,
desiring the welfare of Jayantī and wishing for her satisfaction,
assumed the form of Śukra and summoned the asuras.
He said to those who had arrived, "I shall give you the sciences spoken by Śaṅkara.
Delighted, they approached him for the sake of the sciences for ten years.
But one after another, they were taught [false knowledge] and deceived by the teacher.
Then Kāvya went after ten years had passed to see his own officiating priests.
Having been deceived by the Guru in his true form, they were now deceived by the form of Kāvya; and Kāvya then spoke to them.
"Know me to be Kāvya; this Bṛhaspati is not Kāvya.
Then Bṛhaspati said, "I am Kāvya; he is certainly not he.
This one is your preceptor for the purpose of deception, for ten years more."
"He has come from my country; let it be known that he is Kāvya.
Having heard these words of the two who were identical in appearance, the Dānavas gazed at them both there and were then filled with confusion.
The wood held by Hālāra was not released until the end of his life;
for destiny is indeed more powerful and cannot be altered otherwise. Even though they were warned by Śukra, they did not heed his words.
"He who has indeed ruled us continuously for ten years is our lord;
this Kāvya is truly our guru, for he is not a newcomer.
Having thus resolved, those Daityas were deluded by long-standing habituation. (1.407.90–91)
They said, "Go quickly, O mind; our teacher is the Preceptor (Bṛhaspati). Whether he be Bhārgava or Aṅgiras, this Blessed One is our Guru.
Then Śukra became enraged and cursed the Dānavas.
"Indeed, with your splendor utterly destroyed, you shall all experience great suffering.
Cursed thus by Śukra, the Asuras departed; Vṛhaspati had achieved his purpose.
Then those Asuras vanished from that place once again.
O Lakṣmī! They became bewildered and said, "We have been deceived. Placing Prahlāda at their head, they went to the house of Śukrācārya.
They said to him, "Forgive us; show us favor, O Bhārgava!"
"If you do not show favor, we shall enter the netherworld.
Kāvya reflected: "Even without a patron, I have spoken falsely;
therefore, they must be protected by me, for I am their glory and they have served me."
Then he said to them: "You must not fear, nor must you go to the netherworld (rasātala).
When your light has vanished today, you shall regain it once more.
Having conquered the gods but once, you shall return to Pātāla."
Thus addressed, the Asuras, filled with joy, set forth to conquer the Suras.
Then a terrible battle took place between the Suras and the Asuras;
the Asuras defeated the gods, and the gods, in turn, held a council.
"Having summoned Śaṇḍa and Marka, those two preceptors of the Daityas, at the sacrifice, let us take refuge with them, honor them, and worship them; thus victory will be ours.
Having been thus addressed by the gods, those two brahmins were told: "Abandon the Asuras."
"We shall serve you both after we have conquered the Dānavas together. Having made this agreement, the gods waged a truly fierce battle;
abandoned by Ṣaṇḍa and Marka, the Dānavas were defeated.
Overwhelmed by the curse of Kāvya, they entered the subterranean realm (rasātala). Thus were the Dānavas rendered effortless by the gods through hardship.
Jayantī, who causes delusion, constantly serves her husband.
Śukrācārya even forgot about the prosperity of the Daityas.

(105) Thus was the task of Indra accomplished by Jayantī, who is the very embodiment of victory; indeed, even she, for the sake of her devotion to her husband, brought about the weakening of the Daityas. (106)
Through her vows, the maiden established her husband’s invincibility against Mahendra and others, his victory over the Daityas, and the inferiority of those demons;
for Nārāyaṇa is the Supreme Brahman, even though he resides in the imperishable abode.
Assuming a body characterized by righteousness, he performs protection at the proper time.
In the first [age], Kṛṣṇa, the dweller in Goloka, was known as Pativratā;
thereafter, Nārāyaṇa was born on the Himālaya mountains accompanied by Nara.
Furthermore, that very same righteous one became Yajña, the son of Dharma;
he became Narasiṃha, and he also became Vāmana.
He became Dattātreya, Jāmadagnya Rāma, and Āditya.
Vāsudeva, Vedavyāsa, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, as well as Kalki,
the son of Kambharā— he is indeed the Blessed Lord himself who is born at the turn of the Yugas for the protection of the dharma of the gods.
I am indeed that very one, and my portions are born by the thousands day after day in hidden forms, bestowing happiness;
they are marked on their hands with the signs of the bow, the discus, the banner, the fish, and the svastika. (113)
Above the three arches [of his feet] are the half-moon, the wheel, and the lotus;
by serving his feet, embodied beings become virtuous saints and, like gods, bestowers of liberation—they are indeed liberated, there is no doubt. (114–115)

Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have told you the supernatural powers of the renowned Jayantī, which, when recited or heard, bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation through the power of devotion to one's husband. (116)

Thus ends the four hundred and seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Stupefaction of Indra and Others Caused by the Devotion to Her Husband of Khyāti; the Destruction of Khyāti by Viṣṇu; the Restoration of Khyāti by Bhṛgu; the Austerities of Śukra; the Giving of His Daughter Jayantī to Śukra for the Purpose of Obstructing Him; Her Daughter Devayānī; the Interruption of the Austerities; the Defeat of the Asuras; and the Greatness of Devotion to One’s Husband," in the first section concerning the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
