Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī! I shall proclaim the great power of devotion to one’s husband, as demonstrated by Mālāvatī, the wife of Upabarhaṇa. 1.

When Brahmā, having fashioned the creation, created Nārada, he spoke to him for the sake of continuing the flow of creation; however, Nārada forbade it. The father is said to be the giver of liberation, while the son is considered one who has already attained liberation.
A brother, a mother, a husband, and a wife are always auspicious when they bestow devotion;
those family members who provide the bonds of *māyā* should not be recognized as such.
And you yourself, O Brahmā, though possessed of knowledge, employ me in that which pertains to *māyā*.
"I shall not accept Māyā, nor shall I create anything;
I shall worship the Supreme Brahman and deliver you and others.
I shall make your status as my son meaningful; do not harbor grief, O Creator of the Universe."
Thus addressed, Brahmā, his eyes copper-red with rage, cursed Nārada:
"Having met with death, you shall thereafter become a slave possessed of a wife;
O Nārada, indeed, you shall repeatedly become burdened by ritual actions devoid of knowledge."
Then Nārada said to him: "O Lord, do not do this!
For you too shall never attain worship anywhere in this cycle of existence.
Thus addressed, Brahmā was then entreated by Sanaka and the others.
He said to his son again: "Indeed, you shall obtain me in the fourth [state];
there, O son, you shall always be devoted to the life of a student (brahmacarya). Until then, you will be occupied with a wife and a household; of this there is no doubt."
Having spoken thus, Nārada vanished and became the son of Mārīca;
he attained the status of being the son of Viśvāvasu, the king of the Gandharvas.
That Gandharva, named Upabarhaṇa, was indeed a Vaiṣṇava.

Listen, Lakṣmī! I shall tell you: it is said that in ancient times Viśvāvasu, being childless due to his past actions, performed penance for Śambhu. Vasiṣṭha then bestowed upon him the twelve-syllable mantra.
He recited this for a hundred years at Puṣkara, and for exactly that long he beheld Śiva before him, with a gracious countenance and mounted upon his bull. Then Śiva said to him, "Choose a boon."
He requested from Śrī Hari a son who would be a supreme Vaiṣṇava and devoted to Him.
Śiva said, "I am pleased; let it be so for you, may it be auspicious. You have achieved your purpose through this one boon; anything else would be like chewing what has already been chewed. (15–16)
O child, he whose devotion to Hari is very firm and auspicious in every way is capable of protecting and creating the entire universe by his mere play.
May such a son, a supreme devotee of Viṣṇu, belong to that man of meritorious deeds.
Indeed, they effortlessly uplift ten million of his lineages.
A man has achieved his purpose through one boon; oh, how wonderful! What need is there for a second boon? For a man is never satiated with auspiciousness.
[May he grant] devotion to Hari, service to Hari, and a son who is a supreme Vaiṣṇava,
long-lived, virtuous, and eternally possessed of stable youth;
one who is wise, beautiful, excellent, devoted to his guru, and has conquered his senses.
Having said, "Receive this boon," Śambhu vanished.
Viśvāvasu went home to Mount Gandhamādana;
there Nārada obtained an auspicious birth from his wife.
The preceptor Vasiṣṭha gave him the name Upabarhaṇa.
Here, the prefix *upa* signifies "superiority," while *barhaṇaḥ* (masculine) means "one who is worthy of honor.
Since the boy was superior even among those worthy of honor, he was thus named Upabarhaṇa.
Upabarhaṇa performed difficult austerities for a long time.
Then, having reached the bank of the Gaṇḍakī, the daughters of the Gandharvas beheld him, who possessed perpetual youth, and fifty of them chose him as their husband. (24–25)
Having taken them, that lustful youth took his pleasure for two hundred thousand years.
Once, he went to the assembly of Brahmā and sang a story.
Then, upon seeing Rambhā, he became repeatedly agitated.
He suddenly abandoned his music and fell into a swoon upon the floor of the assembly.
The gods laughed loudly, and Brahmā, out of anger, cursed him:
"Go to the womb of a Śūdra and cast off this body of a Gandharva! (27–28)
"In time, through association with Vaiṣṇavas, you shall become my son.
That Gandharva Upabarhaṇa then cast off that body.
[29] [He entered] the Mūlādhāra, Svādhiṣṭhāna, Maṇipūra, and Anāhata.
Having pierced the six pure wheels of consciousness (*ājñācakra*) with his body, he departed;
through yoga, while remembering Śrī Kṛṣṇa in his mind, he attained Brahman.
And all the wives and kinsmen, having lamented, wept most bitterly.
Then, in the midst of fifty women, the virtuous Mālāvatī wept aloud and intensely, placing her beloved upon her breast.
The daughters of Citraratha and his other wives also wept.
Mālāvatī lamented: "O Kṛṣṇa, you are the Lord of the worlds;
I am not outside the world—why do you not protect me, O Lord? Alas, these gods who consume the sacrificial offerings are capable of consuming only the clarified butter on this earth! (33–34)
In an instant, by virtue of my chastity, I shall deprive you of your share in the sacrifice.
O Nārāyaṇa, beloved of the world, I am not outside the universe.
If my devotion to my husband remains complete and unbroken, [then let this happen].
"Quickly bring my beloved back to life; otherwise, I shall curse you.
O Prajāpati! Because of this curse upon your son, you shall be unworthy of honor on the surface of the earth.
I shall deprive you yourself of the authority for creation here."
"O Śambhu, I shall indeed cause the loss of your knowledge through a curse;
and I shall certainly bring about the loss of Dharma's merit in an instant.
Furthermore, I shall cast Yama’s authority far away, without a doubt. (38)
By truth, I shall curse Time and the most cruel Daughter of Death.
I swear that from this moment on, no one here shall suffer old age or disease;
for my husband has never experienced death through illness or decrepitude.
Having spoken thus, she went to the bank of the Kauśikī river specifically to curse them.
Seeing her prepared to utter a curse, Brahmā, preceded by Śambhu,
and the other deities went to the shore of the Ocean of Milk to seek refuge with Hari.
Having bathed there, they praised the Supreme Self, the Lord Viṣṇu, the beloved of the world; and Brahmā spoke thus like one struck with fear.
That maiden, the wife of Upabarhaṇa and the daughter of Citraratha, [was also there]. || 42-43 ||
O Mādhava, protect me so that she does not curse the gods for the sake of her beloved!
The virtuous and saintly remember the Supreme Lord even in the midst of great calamities.
O You who are solely devoted to the protection of the distressed and the wretched who have come for refuge!
Protect, protect us, O Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, we have come to you for refuge!
(45) Mālāvatī indeed sustains me, who am devoid of any qualification;
all my great Brahminical prosperity shall surely depart from me now. (46)

He said to Śambhu: "O Nārāyaṇa, this great knowledge, so difficult to obtain, has been granted by you. Formerly, at Puṣkara, through the fruit of austerities performed for a hundred manvantaras, I attained sovereignty, wealth, and power."
"Indeed, this jewel of knowledge of mine departs from me due to the curse of a woman.
Alas! The splendor of a devoted wife is superior to all other splendors.
O Lord Hari, protect and save me, who have been consumed by the fire of that splendor!"

Dharma said: "O Lord, Dharma alone is the great jewel and the eternal one. Yet I, who am that very Dharma, shall meet my destruction through the curse of a woman, O Supreme Lord, despite the fruit of my penance performed throughout seven manvantaras."
"The Dharma you attained has now been destroyed by this curse.
The gods said: "In the sacrifice, we were made consumers of clarified butter by you;
yet everything is being led to ruin by the curse of a woman—please show us mercy! (52)
While they were thus praising him, an incorporeal voice spoke:
"Go there yourselves; indeed, I shall go for the sake of protection.
Hearing this, the gods were delighted and went to Mālavatī at that very moment.
Seeing the gods, the devoted Mālāvatī prostrated herself. O beloved! Having established her husband near the gods, she wept.
In the meantime, a certain young Brahmin boy was there. (54-55)
Clad in white garments and adorned with the five-fold leaf-designs, he arrived;
having applied the *tilaka*, he entered the midst of the assembly and sat down.
He spoke: "How is it that these gods, Brahmā and the others, are here?"
"O you who have arrived, homage be to you! How is it that the Creator himself remains here?
(57) Oh, how is it that Rudra himself, the Destroyer, remains here as Dharma, the Witness?
How is it that the Sun, how is it that the Moon, and how is it that the Fire-god remain here? (58)
"How is it that Time and the Daughter of Death are here, or how are Yama and the others?
O Mālāvatī, who is this exceedingly white corpse now upon your lap?
To him who was speaking thus, Mālāvatī bowed and said:
Salutations to you, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, who are in the form of a Brahmin. (1.408.6) Suddenly, due to the curse of Brahmā, my husband gave up his life-breaths;
yet, addressing the gods, I lament that my husband now lives again. (61)
"I entreat all the gods for the gift of a husband that I desire.
If the gods grant me the gift of a beloved as I wish, then it shall be well;
otherwise, I shall pronounce a terrible curse upon them. (62)
"The curse of a virtuous woman is difficult to ward off; by what asceticism could it be averted?
(63) The Brahmin said this to her: 'What is done will bear fruit in due time. When the time has arrived, it will come to pass; one should not insist upon it. (64)"
Whatever lies within the domain of the gods, that alone they grant, and nothing else—
not strength, nor beauty, nor sovereignty, nor wealth, nor a son;
neither a wife nor a beloved husband can be obtained without austerity.
He who serves Prakṛti shall obtain a beloved wife endowed with virtues.
Through the worship of Śiva, she obtains unshakable prosperity, sons, grandsons, land, wealth, progeny, a virtuous beloved wife, and a good husband.
Through the worship of Brahmā, one may obtain knowledge, wisdom, skill in poetry, sons, grandsons, supreme prosperity,
strength, wealth, valor, and even great sovereignty; indeed,
through the worship of Brahmā, one attains all perfections (siddhis), as well as learning, fortune, and progeny.
From the worship of the Sun, one obtains knowledge, health, wealth, and sons.
(69) From the worship of Gaṇeśa, one attains the destruction of obstacles, the status of being worshipped by all, supreme bliss, sovereignty, a son, knowledge, wealth, and progeny. (1.408.70)
Through service to Viṣṇu, one obtains liberation, austerity, righteousness, fame, and prosperity;
and through the practice of Dharma, one shall obtain peace, happiness, and wealth.
Whichever deity one worships with devotion, one attains that very deity according to one's [inner] nature, such as sattva and the rest.
In time, he shall attain with him the supreme state of Kṛṣṇa.
He who worships Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, who is beyond material nature,
the imperishable, supreme Brahman, the eternal Lord.
The Lord is both with form and formless, consisting of His own will,
all-pervading, the support of all, the Lord of all, the Supreme Bliss;
He is untainted, the witness, and the embodiment of grace toward His devotees.
He is truly liberated while living; he certainly does not desire even the boon of heaven.
He considers the fourfold states, beginning with *sālokya*, as trivial, and regards even the status of Brahman and immortality as worthless as a clod of earth, O Noble Lady! (75–76)
He considers sovereignty to be equal to a clod of earth and transitory;
he knows that everything is perishable, like a bubble on the water.
Without servitude (*dāsya*), one should not beg for the supreme state of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Whether in dream or in waking, he indeed constantly desires service [to the Lord].
He who remains steadfast and always serves the most perfect Brahman delivers ten million ancestors of his own lineage, as well as a hundred of his maternal grandfather’s lineage. (78–79)
Having effortlessly first delivered a hundred ancestors of his father-in-law,
a devotee of Kṛṣṇa indeed delivers a hundred descendants— including servants, maidservants, mother, wife, and even sons— and goes to the abode of Goloka.
If even the mantra of Viṣṇu enters the ear of one from the mouth of a guru,
Yama immediately casts away the record of that person out of fear;
and Brahmā, having prepared the madhuparka and other honors for his sake, [bestows them].
He travels everywhere in the realm of truth; by this path he shall go.
Fearless, having cast off his human body, he goes to Goloka.
Whatever ancient karma he has performed, whether auspicious or inauspicious—
Kṛṣṇa constantly cuts [the world] with his sharp-edged discus.
O virtuous lady, leaving him behind out of fear of the discus, old age and death depart;
otherwise, the Sudarśana would indeed reduce them to a hundred fragments. (84–85)
Having gone there and assumed a divine body, he then serves Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
for as long as Kṛṣṇa remains in Goloka, the devotee shall dwell there forever.
The servant considers even a single moment of Brahmā’s lifespan to be perishable.
"Speak! There is no one else capable [of this] except Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
By what disease has your beloved now died, O virtuous lady?
As a physician, I know the treatment for every disease. (87–88)

I am capable of bringing King Death, Yama, and Time, along with Disease, before you and binding them to hand them over, just as a hunter binds and delivers a beast. Or, whoever abandons the body through yoga or through exhaustion [of worldly life], [for him I shall provide a vehicle].

"I know that means of his livelihood through the practice of yoga. Having heard these words of the brahmin, Satī, who was devoted to her husband, said to him: "O best of brahmins, if you are indeed capable of perceiving everything!"
"Bring Kāla, Yama, and the Daughter of Death into my presence.
Having heard Mālikāvatī’s words, Viṣṇu then summoned them;
first, he beheld the Daughter of Death, and she [beheld] Mālikāvatī.
She was black in color, of terrible form, and clad in red garments;
she had six arms, was endowed with compassion, and was accompanied by sixty-four sons.
Then the virtuous woman beheld Kāla of terrible form standing before her.
He has six faces, sixteen arms, and twenty-four eyes;
he has six feet, is black in color, wears red garments, and is most excellent. His splendor is equal to the summer sun, and his form is that of the universal destroyer.
Sati saw before her hosts of diseases, exceedingly difficult to conquer—
killers who were extremely aged, as well as youths and children.
Sati likewise saw Yama, the most righteous one, who was dark-complexioned.
Then Mālāvatī, skilled in reasoning, questioned Yama— the teacher who knows how to discern dharma and adharma, and the preceptor of sinners:
"O Dharmarāja, most righteous one, even though my time has not yet arrived..."

"But tell me, O Lord, how do you carry away your beloved at an improper time? Yama replied: "O virtuous lady, no one ever dies before their time has come. Without the command of the Supreme Lord, I truly do not take away even the nectar of immortality."
I am Time, the Daughter of Death, and the diseases that are so difficult to conquer; we shall indeed seize at that very moment him by whom we were appointed at his conception.
The Daughter of Death, dwelling with me, makes this request at this instant.
"At that very moment, I shall perceive; ask her for the sake of your husband.
Mālāvatī then said: "O Daughter of Death, how was my beloved taken by you prematurely while I, his dear one, am still alive?"
And the Daughter of Death, created here by the Creator of the Universe, said to her:
"I shall indeed withdraw [life] according to one's merit, in the task of separating beings from their vital breaths.
Impelled by Time, I abide together with the seminal infusion."

"I am constantly taking away life; there is no fault in this on my part, my dear. If there were some virtuous woman among the virtuous who was so radiant that she were capable of reducing even me to ashes, then indeed the entire world [would be consumed]."
That which is devoid of the maiden of death is truly immortal, and not otherwise.
I abide even within the womb of the physical essence of embodied beings;
though I eternally and perpetually withdraw [them], people do not perceive that at all.
What is born today is called "grown" by tomorrow;
what is born anew later is called "aged" when it has decayed. Indeed, old age proceeds constantly and everywhere. (108–109)

Foolish people rejoice, thinking, "I am young," "I am a child," or "I am not old"; thus, through ignorance, they do not recognize their own state of aging. Indeed, growth is said to be the process of aging, and the seed (niṣeka) is constantly increasing.
It grows constantly in the womb and increases during infancy and the other stages;
it indeed grows perpetually and no one ever becomes diminished. Impelled by the arrival of time, my sons, as well as diseases, likewise [increase]. (111–112)
"We perform our duty at every moment; indeed, there is no fault on our part, O virtuous lady!
Ask Time, the Great Soul; he will do what is appropriate.
Then Satī said to Time, "O Lord, you are truly the witness of all actions!"

"How can you carry away my beloved while I am still alive, O Lord! 11.4 Having heard Mālavatī’s grief, Kāla then said to the virtuous woman: "Who am I? Who is Yama? And who is the Daughter of Death, as well as these mental agonies? 11.5
We wander about as the executors of the commands of Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
she in whose left side is primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti), in whose womb are Viṣṇu, Śambhu, and Brahmā,
under whose direction the deities abide, and even Dharma is indeed subject to her will.
He under whose control are the planets, the zodiac signs, the guardians of the directions, and so forth—
of him alone is this Time a portion; Death, the Son of Death, and mental afflictions are all impelled by him, and we perform the joining together and the separation [of beings].
"Ask Kṛṣṇa; you are the punisher, so how is it that your master has died?
Having said this, Kāla fell silent. Then the Brāhmaṇa spoke to her:

"Now there is doubt regarding his caste; ask him again, O maiden.

"Now, if you have compassion, give me back my beloved, the lord of my life!
Having bowed before you, I shall go with my husband to our own home.
O Kṛṣṇa, where else shall I search here? For the Brāhmaṇa is indeed Kṛṣṇa himself."
"Whatever a brahmin does, Kṛṣṇa follows that twice-born one.
Having heard these piteous words, the brahmin, standing in the midst of the gods and moved by compassion toward them, spoke this supreme truth to the deities.
"This wife of Upabarhaṇa and daughter of Citraratha has come for refuge and entreated the gift of her husband's life. Therefore,
O gods, tell me what must be done here that would be effective."
Desiring to curse all the gods, Satī was restrained by me. (126) What would be gained now by much idle talk or delay?
Viṣṇu, though requested by you, has not yet arrived at Śvetadvīpa. (127)
Then a voice from the sky spoke: "Keśava is coming after;
however, that has turned out otherwise, since Keśava does not come.
Brahmā then said to the brāhmaṇa: "This Nārada is my own son."
By my curse, the Gandharva Tūbarhaṇa gave up his life through yoga at an improper time,
even though his allotted span remained;
yet he still possesses a lifespan of one thousand years remaining right now.

Two hundred thousand [verses] have been traversed by him; I shall now proclaim what remains, so that this curse may not touch him and the gods may be free from fear. Hari is indeed everywhere; he has neither come nor is he absent.
He is Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, existing in both visible and invisible forms.
"Why does Kṛṣṇa not come?"—even such talk regarding the sky is indeed false.

"Whose disciple are you, O twice-born one? Who is that Lord of Sages? What is your name? Where is your residence? From where have you come? To which lineage do you belong?
You mock even the gods as well as Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa."

Furthermore, those words you spoke—"Viṣṇu has not yet come to the assembly"—should not be heard, for they are derogatory toward the Supreme Self. Viṣṇu is all-pervasive; "viṣi" means pervasion, and with the suffix "nu," He is *viṣṇu*, the one who pervades everywhere.
Thus, since all beings are indeed equal, from where could there be coming and going? Where there is great censure, a virtuous person should certainly not hear it.
The slanderer, together with those who listen, shall go to the Kumbhīpāka hell for a yuga.

Indeed, the reviling of Viṣṇu is threefold: consisting of the destruction of his image, consisting of the denial of his existence, and consisting of the assertion of his equality with the individual soul (jīva). For such [sins], there is no atonement here for as long as a hundred Brahmās endure.
That lowest of men who reviles his guru or reviles his father goes to the Kālasūtra hell for as long as the moon and sun endure.
Having heard that, the Brāhmaṇa then spoke to the gods.
"Alas, O gods who are pillars of righteousness, what insult to Viṣṇu has been committed?
'Hari has not come here'—this empty sound from the sky was uttered by me; it was for my own welfare, and certainly no disparagement was intended. (141–142)
"You are indeed destined for realization; speak! Viṣṇu is the all-pervading Lord.
If this is so, then how did you go to Śvetadvīpa and receive the boon?
If there is no difference between the part and the whole, then there is no difference between the Supreme Lord and His parts.
How could the virtuous abandon a mere fraction [of the Lord] to serve the Most Perfect One?
Kṛṣṇa is the master of all parts, his form being the grace bestowed upon his devotees.
Indeed, Vaikuṇṭha is truly above the entire cosmic egg and is eternal.
In Vaikuṇṭha, the eternal Beloved of Lakṣmī has four arms;
fifty crores of yojanas above that is Goloka.
In Goloka, the eternal Kṛṣṇa, the Beloved of Rādhā, has two arms.
Therefore, the world is excessively pervasive; it transcends the imperishable Brahman-ātman.
Therein shines the supreme Brahman, the most perfectly full.
Tell me, how could there not be an arrival of that [Brahman] here today? (147–148)
The virtuous Vaiṣṇavas meditate upon Him, and they serve His divine form—
He whom the saintly Bhāgavatas and chaste women serve incessantly;
He from whose lineage I have arisen, and whose disciple is this boy.
"Having become a brahmin, he speaks thus: 'O hosts of gods, listen!

Then Brahmā poured the water from his water-pot upon the corpse.
He gave a beautiful form to that mind, which was capable of movement.
Then Śambhu bestowed the gift of knowledge, Viṣṇu gave life,

Now, having bathed, remember Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa within your heart. (156–157)
Without him there is indeed no revival; he alone truly remains as the living reality.
At the word of Brahmā, the virtuous woman praised the Supreme Lord:
"I bow to that Supreme Self, the cause of all causes. (158)
Without which all living beings are as good as corpses and devoid of purpose;
for it is through its entry that they become endowed with life, activity, and consciousness.
Yet even that service and meditation are not possible without a physical form.
Such was the divine form of the omnipresent Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, situated in the midst of a circle of light, surrounded by millions of gopīs;
he was exceedingly beautiful, dark-complexioned, and lotus-eyed. (161)
The Lord, whose face bears a gentle smile, as beautiful as ten million Cupids;
two-armed, clad in yellow garments, a youth, the husband of Rādhikā;
the Lord of Lakṣmī, Śrī, Pārvatī, Padmā, Padminī, and Māṇikī. (162–163)
I bow to Hari, who assumes all forms and is served by his attendants;
I bow to the Lord, the life-force of the life-force, the very essence of existence.
O Blessed One, come here to this Gandharva, who is dull-witted and insentient.
Having spoken thus, that Gandharva woman, being filled with rage,
spoke again: "O Blessed One, if you do not come, I shall indeed create women such as Ramā and others who resemble me, yet are deprived of their lord, and you shall be like a Gandharva."
Just as she was saying, "If I possess devotion to my husband, by that truth let this [curse] pass away," Kṛṣṇa arrived there at that very moment.
Having said, "Do not fear, do not fear," he indeed restrained Satī from the threefold curse.
He entered [the house], and at that moment the Gandharva rose up.
Having risen quickly, taken up his lute, bathed, and put on two garments, he bowed to the gods, as well as to Viṣṇu, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.

And for a moment Kṛṣṇa danced, O Hari, O Govinda, while speaking; the gods sounded their drums and rained down a shower of flowers. All departed to their respective abodes, and Nārada also went with his wife.
Accompanied by her mother and father, she went to the city of the Gandharvas.
The virtuous Mālāvatī gave ten million jewels and wealth,
provided food for the Brahmins, and had them pronounce blessings.
The Gandharva Upabarhaṇa also held a great festival upon regaining his life, which had been restored by the devoted wife; thereafter,
Upabarhaṇa practiced devotion to Hari and service to Hari.
O Beloved! whoever shall read or listen to this with devotion, for that person there shall be the attainment of prosperity and good fortune, without a doubt;
and there shall be enjoyment, liberation, and the unimpeded accomplishment of the four aims of human life.
Thus, in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīya-saṃhitā*,
[is described] how Nārada met his death due to a curse from Brahmā, was born again as the Gandharva named Upabarhaṇa,
and met his death once more there through the power of the conjugal fidelity (*pātivratya*) of his wife Mālavatī, along with Viṣṇu.
The four hundred and eighth chapter, titled "The Summoning of the Gods and Kāla and Others, and the Determination that the Lord has been Resuscitated."
← Chapter 408: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā - Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga) Chapter 409 [Author: Chapter 410 →
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī! I shall relate a most wonderful story concerning one devoted to her husband, which took place in a former age.
The daughter of Viśāla-rāja was Vīrā, devoted to righteousness. At the svayaṃvara, resplendent with kings, which was held by Viśāla, Avīkṣita— the son of Karandhama— indeed won her.
Then, having been defeated in battle by many groups of kṣatriyas while he was alone,
that maiden was offered as a sacrifice by the royal families.
Upon hearing this, Karandhama set out accompanied by a hundred thousand troops.
Having slain the kings and taken his son and daughter-in-law, he returned home once more.
Avīkṣit said to his father: "What fame will remain for me?
O father, I shall not take this woman, nor any other woman."
"In these battles, I have been defeated by enemies while she looked on.
Since I was defeated by others like a coward or like a weak woman,
what is the point of my being human while remaining in such a state of dependence?"
"By means of this woman, my reputation has been ruined here by others;
therefore, you must not marry a woman who brings about a state of dependence.
To him who had spoken thus, that beautiful maiden said to Avikṣita:
But all those who have many flanks [or allies] fight with ease.
A battle of one against many is merely a manifestation of valor.
O King, your great prowess has been thoroughly tested by many.
If a battle were to arise between one person and another,
I maintain that these [beings] became the servants of Yama.
This invincible great hero was conquered by many who had joined together.
In this matter, the truth shines clearly: even all those kings were defeated by you in battle.
Having conquered all these rulers of the earth—who were endowed with heroism and prowess—by means of unrighteousness in a righteous war, what shame is there in this? (12–13)
Therefore, this one created by me shall be my husband, and no other shall be my lord.
O King! If you do not accept me as your devoted wife, know this:
having performed penance here, I shall indeed attain you in heaven.

"I choose this boon, O Lord: if you do not desire me, let there be no other husband for me than you in this birth. Even when she had spoken thus, he looked upon her without looking, his mind turned away.

The maiden, having attained supreme detachment, went forth for asceticism. She remained without food for three months, and when she had passed that time, she prepared herself to cast off her body. Then the gods, having learned of this, approached her presence.
They dispatched a messenger, and that body said to her:
"O auspicious lady, you shall become the mother of a universal monarch (cakravartin).
By your son, enemies, barbarians, and wicked bandits are to be slain. (18–19)
"The surface of the earth must be protected, and therefore the subjects must be established in righteousness;
sacrifices must be performed with various rites, numbering six thousand.
She said, "Without a husband who is Truth itself, how could I have a son?"
"Except for my husband, whom I have never seen, there is no other for me in this birth.
And that hero, though entreated, has no desire for me, being filled with dispassion.
The messenger said: "Stay in the forest, O beautiful lady, and nourish your body!"
"By the power of your asceticism, everything you desire shall come to pass.
Having said this, the divine messenger departed, and she nurtured her body.
Then, the mother of Avikṣita said: "Your father has reached old age."
"O Avikshit, you are the only son, having renounced the company of a wife.
When your father has gone to heaven and you remain without a son, your enemies here will enjoy this earth upon the extinction of your lineage. (24-25)

When the lineage perishes, the ancestors—deprived of the offerings of *śrāddha*, the funeral cakes, and water—will fall into hell; therefore, act for the benefit of your forefathers. Grant happiness to your grandson and abandon all obstinacy.
Abandon the state of lifelong celibacy and practice the duty of marriage.
When the ruin of a lineage has occurred, the life of a student leads only to sin;
in a house of calamity, the vow of householdership that uplifts the family is superior. (27–28)
He accepted these and other words of his mother, saying, "So be it.
Then, having gone to the forest, he practiced hunting there in the woods.
Suddenly, he heard the cry of a woman: "Save me! Save me!"
Saying, "Do not fear! Do not fear! the prince went toward her. Seized by the Dānava, she, overwhelmed with terror, said:
"I am the virtuous wife of the son of Karaṃdhama; indeed, I have not been seen [by him]."
"Look! A forest-dwelling ascetic woman is being carried off by a *rākṣasa*!
Hearing this, he then gazed upon him and overwhelmed him with showers of arrows, as well as with clubs, trees, stones, *bhalla*-shafts, and other weapons.
A terrible battle took place between those two; heroes took refuge in the hero.
By the power of her devotion to her husband and by the bull-like virtue of her firmness in truth, she indeed offered a portion of her ascetic merit with water for the sake of his victory. (33–34)
Then, unseen, the virtuous woman performed her duty in the battle;
the prince, having regained his strength, severed the head of the demon. She, the faithful wife, attended upon her husband whose body was wounded by weapons.
"In the forest, she said: 'All my ascetic penance has been seen even in a dream. Two days ago, while I was in deep sleep, I went to a pool in the Ganges to bathe;
there, I was dragged away by someone and sank beneath the water. (36-37)
Then she was led to Rasātala, where thousands of Nāgas and their wives praised me and begged for protection. "The serpents will surely commit an offense against your son."
"Forgive him; he must be restrained—let favor be shown.
When I replied, "So be it," she was honored and sent to the forest. There I beheld the prince Avīvikṣit, who is indeed my chosen husband. (1.409.40)
My sleep then passed away, and at dawn I beheld a most auspicious forest.
A peacock, accompanied by his mate, approached my side;
he performed a dance there at daybreak, and at that moment, my left limb throbbed.
Then, my hips, private parts, and other limbs began to throb.
At that time, a male parrot together with his mate took a ripe fruit of immortality from the sky with their beaks and, speaking, dropped it into my lap. (42–43)
Having gone there, I saw early in the morning a white elephant in this forest, accompanied by female elephants and young calves, holding a lotus in its trunk:
"Take my hand; I am yours alone, and not anyone else's."
Thus addressed, he said, "May it be so; let that which is ordained by fate come to pass.
(45) Then, by her who held her husband as her very life, the Guru was reminded;
Tumburu arrived there and performed the fire-oblation according to the prescribed rites. (46)
Cāvīka took her hand in marriage in the midst of the forest;
then the gods arrived there and showered flowers. Celestial instruments resounded and throngs of apsarases danced.
The gods and gandharvas sang, and the forest deities were delighted.
There, the sages, gandharvas, and kinnaras presented the two of them with excellent food, ointments, garments, garlands, drinks, and other such things.
He took delight together with that slender lady, and she likewise with him, though unseen by others.
She went to her own father’s palace in the kingdom, and there was a great festival for her parents.
Then the parents bestowed all kinds of gifts for the sake of their grandson.
Then, together with his wife, he traveled through the sky to Mount Meru.
O beautiful one, while that hero was sporting with that lovely woman in the world of the Gandharvas, that virtuous lady gave birth to a son.
When the son was born, there was a great festival among the Gandharvas;
some sang, while others likewise played mṛdaṅgas, paṭahas, and ānakas,
as well as other instruments such as flutes, lutes, and mayūrakas.
And many hosts of apsarases danced to that enthusiasm;
clouds, shedding showers of flowers, thundered with soft sounds.
Remembered there by the couple, Tumburu himself arrived.
Then, with a mind full of exceeding joy, he performed the birth-rites;
he offered a benediction for that child preceded by hymns of praise:
"He shall be a universal monarch, of great heroism, mighty-armed, and possessed of great strength. (56)
May the Teacher, the husband of the virtuous, be the bringer of well-being to the entire earth.
(57) May all these world-protectors, beginning with Śakra, as well as the ṛṣis, grant you well-being, O hero, and may they grant you the valor that destroys your enemies. (58)
May the eastern wind blow auspiciously for you, which does not stir up dust.
May the southern wind, pure and inexhaustible, be for your lack of imbalance.
May the western wind grant you supreme vigor.
"May the Maruts grant you supreme strength, and likewise Uttara.
Thus did the Guru speak for the sake of his well-being to that Marutta;
and so Marutta became renowned as the son of the great seers.
Taking Marutta with them, the couple went to their own home;
meanwhile, the Gandharvas, gods, and sages remained in the presence of the king.
Having placed the child before his father and bowed down, you related the entire account in its entirety.

And they both announced [the news]; the king too, upon seeing his grandson, repeatedly praised himself, saying, "I am fortunate. And the queen also, having seen her son’s son, rejoiced, filled with joy.
Then there was great joy in the city and in the houses of the citizens;
the king also gave away his wealth, gems, cows, and ornaments at that time.
Having consecrated his son in the kingdom, he entered the forest together with his wife.
There, for a thousand years, he indeed performed severe penance.
Having cast off his body, the king attained the same world as Śakra.
His wife, having remained [in her own state] for a hundred years, obtained that very husband in heaven.
Then Avikṣita performed many sacrifices with abundant sacrificial fees;
his unimpeded chariot-wheel traversed the seven continents.
His son, Marutta, likewise performed sacrifices numbering ten million.
Then the mountain named Muñjavat was brought from there,
made entirely of gold; and all the gold was given away with satisfaction by the Brahmins, as were all the palaces and other structures belonging to his sacrifice.
The gods were indeed the servers of the Brahmins; that was my greatness.
At that time, all the Viśvedevas were the members of the assembly on the sacrificial ground—the Sādhyas, Maruts, Vasus, Rudras, and likewise the Ādityas.
At that time, the Nidhis and the Rishis became his servants.
His officiating priest (Ṛtvij) was Saṃvarta, the son of Aṅgiras,
a Brahmin who was the elder brother of Bṛhaspati and the leader of the gods.
Then, at the excellent hermitage of the seer Aurva, the king of serpents caused a disturbance and seized his bow for the sake of his destruction;
likewise, out of anger, he took up the great weapon Saṃvartaka.
Marutta performed the subjugation of the Naga kings by means of that [rite].
He returned once more to his own kingdom and ruled upon the earth.
His mother, the virtuous Vīrā, and his father, Avīkṣita, had both gone to the forest. (75–76)
Having attained heaven, they were uplifted by their devotion to their husbands and their fidelity as wives:
Marutta’s wife, the daughter of Vidarbha, Prabhāvatī;
and the second was Sauvīrī, the daughter of Suvīra, a woman of noble spirit. (77)
Keśī, the daughter of Ketuvīrya, was the third, a woman of great splendor;
the daughter of the King of Madra was the fourth, Kekayī;
and the daughter of the King of Sindhu, Saurandhrī, was indeed the fifth wife.
And Sulocanā, the daughter of the King of Cedi, became the sixth wife.
To those devoted wives, eighteen sons were born.
Among them, the eldest and preeminent was Nariṣyanta, who became king.
All these queens became auspicious and truly devoted to Viṣṇu.
The lineage of great devotees, dedicated to their respective duties,
worshipped the Blessed Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, Hari.
She did not indeed enjoy wealth or her husband without first offering them to Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
she offered everything to the Supreme Soul, Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
The goddesses beheld Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa standing before them in the form of their husband.
Thinking thus, they performed service; their wives were like Lakṣmī herself.
In this way, those rulers of the earth on the face of the world were indeed equal to Viṣṇu, and the royal women, the consorts of the kings, were equal to Lakṣmī, being devoted to Viṣṇu.
Once, during the worship of Mahāviṣṇu, there was a great festival.
While the king was absorbed in meditation, Rudra arrived there.
Since this was so, Rudra did not receive the customary honors.

Enraged by his excessive force, she hurled a trident to kill him. Having pierced the heart and taken the life-force of the king, that virtuous daughter of Vidarbha, Prabhāvatī, then departed. || 87–88 ||
Taking water in her hand, she said: "If it is truly the case that throughout my life I have served my husband and remained devoted to him, by that truth may this Rudra die again and again. (89)

If the gods have been worshipped and guests have also been honored, and if the husband has always been propitiated, the trident will gradually move far away. If service has been rendered to the mother-in-law and father-in-law with great faith... [91]
If I am always devoted to the duties of the household and regard my husband as a deity, may the family of my lord be propitiated and his heart be won over.
If my husband is faithful to the vows of a wife, may my beloved live on.
If my co-wives have been constantly honored and satisfied like sisters,
revered like mothers, and well-protected like daughters—
by that merit, may no sin remain for me after the destruction of Rudra. ||93-94||
When she had spoken thus, everything unfolded exactly as she said.
There was a great cry of "Alas! Alas! for the unbearable destruction of Rudra.
Then the virtuous and highly passionate woman was consoled by Marutta.
Then Śāntā spoke to her husband for the sake of reviving Rudra:
"O Lord, revive the Lord of Gods, Rudra, who is indeed Vaiṣṇava;
for those Rudras who are not Vaiṣṇavas exist only during the period of a kalpa's formation. (96–97)

"Those born from the Brahmamālā will surely meet their destruction," such was the curse I uttered repeatedly against Rudra at the beginning of the kalpa. Upon the release of the fierce Rudra, he shall touch them again and again.
The Vaiṣṇava Mahārudra will certainly remain; of this there is no doubt.
Having consecrated the water and made the ashes moist from that very source, this Lord Marutteśvara shall become restored to life.
Thus addressed by his wife, Maruta took up water and said:
"If indeed throughout my life I have been devoted to the vow of fidelity to my wife;
if I have always been a Vaiṣṇava, unswerving from the duty toward progeny and the duty of a king."
If this unrighteousness, committed through many transgressions, has not touched me at all,
then by that merit may this Rudra truly live as a Vaiṣṇava,
provided that his wife Satī remains his spouse just as Prabhāvatī is mine.
Likewise, there were other wives who were indeed full of devotion to their husbands;
I treated them all with impartiality and never practiced partiality.
By that merit, may this Rudra, along with his trident, live on.
Having spoken thus, as soon as he poured water upon the ashes,
the gentle Mahārudra appeared alive before him.
He was then saluted, worshipped, and repeatedly asked for forgiveness.
Even Rudra propitiated that virtuous Satī, who was [then] Prabhāvatī;
and the king was also propitiated, being honored and well-saluted by the king.
Hara remained in that palace in the form of Marutteśvara.
Then Śaṅkara, assuming a divine form, went to Kailāsa;
he realized the greatness of her devotion to her husband and spoke to Pārvatī.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have described to you this vow which bestows great merit.

"From hearing and from reciting this, the fruit of all sacrifices shall accrue; even from the mere remembrance of this narrative, the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation shall be attained. (1.409.110) Thus ends the four hundred and ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Destruction of the Rākṣasa and the Resuscitation of Rudra, along with the Marvels of Conjugal Fidelity of Vīrā, the Wife of King Avīkṣita, and Prabhāvatī, the Wife of Marutta," within the section on the Greatness of Chaste Wives in the first book, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. (409)

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī! I shall proclaim the prowess of Śakti’s wife.
Vasiṣṭha is a portion of Brahmā, a seer made the seer of the Vedas. (1)
Arundhatī was his wife—virtuous, chaste, and devoted to her husband.
In her, the blessed Vasiṣṭha begot a hundred sons.
Among them, the eldest was indeed named Śakti, in whose wife—
From Parāśara the sage was born, of whom I am the son known as Vyāsa.
I became his son, Brahmā Śuka in form,
whose glory is sung in every way for the sake of attaining liberation.
A Rākṣasa named Rudhira devoured the son of Vasiṣṭha, Śakti;
hearing that, Vasiṣṭha was deeply distressed.
Furthermore, eighty-nine sons were devoured by Rudhira.
Having heard that, Vasiṣṭha then resolved to die.
At that time, his daughter-in-law, the wife of Śakti, spoke to the great sage:
"O Blessed One, O best of Brahmins! This auspicious body of yours—" || 7 ||
"O Lord, protect my son, your grandson, so that he may see you;
for he who is born of Śakti, while still in the womb, shall accomplish all my purposes.
Then the child within the womb indeed spoke a verse with his voice:
Hearing that, Vasiṣṭha was filled with wonder, wondering how and from where it could have happened.
Just then, Nārāyaṇa Kṛṣṇa appeared visibly in his courtyard and said,
"The Ṛgvedic verses have issued forth from the mouth of your grandson."
"This grandson of yours, born of Śakti, shall be powerful and equal to me.
By the gain of such a virtuous grandson, your lineage shall cross over [to salvation].
Having spoken thus, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa vanished.
Vasiṣṭha affectionately touched Adṛśyantī’s belly with his right hand;
he performed the protection of the fetus for Adṛśyantī, the wife of Śakti,
who was then a virtuous and chaste woman, devoted to her great husband.
She cursed the Rākṣasa Kāla, Rudra, Yama, and Viśvāmitra:
"O Śakti! O Śakti! O Lord! I am devoted to my husband.
If I am a virtuous wife whose life is dedicated to you, [then let this curse be nullified]. (14)
My mother-in-law Arundhatī is a devoted wife equal to Rāmā.
Let Kāla, Rudra, Viśvāmitra, Yama, and the Rākṣasa—all of them—become as inert as stones. (15–16)
"Wherever you may be, there you shall take the form of stones;
remain inert and unconscious until the dissolution of all beings.
Thus were they cursed, and wherever they went at that time, [they became so].
For they have indeed arisen in the form of stone and shall remain for the duration of Brahmā’s life.
Wherever time existed upon the earth and other elements, there stones of black hue were produced, consisting essentially of the surface of the earth. (18–19)
When the clay that serves as the foundation indeed arose from the form of Time (Kālamūrti),
then Rudra became the stone— the magnetite— in the west. That stone is called Raudrī, the image within the cave of Śiva.
It draws all the clods of earth toward its vicinity within the ocean.
That very land which the ocean will eventually submerge after a long time—there, indeed, Viśvāmitra became a desert land in the west. (21–22)
From that very spot where he was born in the form of a stone,
the river Viśvāmitrī indeed arose from his sweat in Gaurjara.
Over time, the stone will sink away, and his image will remain upon the earth.
At that time, Yama indeed became black-complexioned on Mount Raivata;
mounted upon his buffalo vehicle, he went there for refuge out of fear into the presence of Dāmodara, together with his buffalo. ||24-25||
The mountain Māhiṣa indeed became the form of a black stone;
that Rākṣasa then fled, running toward the southern direction out of fear.
Fallen into the ocean by the curse, that mountain then became the bridge.
The mountain that had indeed obstructed Hanumān’s path as he traveled through the sky—being dull-witted, it fought the great-bodied Hanumān.
Then the entire world, rendered motionless, broke out into cries of "Alas! Alas! (27–28).
Without Rudra, without Kāla, and without Yama Viśvaka,
all the gods became distressed and approached Brahmā;
together with Viṣṇu, they all went to where Satī was staying.
There, the gods— Śakti’s wife, Vasiṣṭha, and Arundhatī— were present.
Distressed, they reported the destruction of the world-protectors to those excellent guardians and consoled them exceedingly so that they might live.

"O Mother, revive the protectors of the worlds so that there may be well-being. Adṛśyantī then said: "If you will revive my husband and brothers-in-law, then, O gods, I shall revive them; but not otherwise."
Brahmā said: "O Satī! Śakti and the others have been devoured by the Rākṣasa;
nothing remains of them but ashes, bones, skin, and their dust.
By what consecration could they now be restored to their bodies?"
Wherever the corpse, bones, flesh, ashes, or even soil of someone can be obtained, there that person is restored with a body by means of water consecrated with mantras.
Even for Śakti and the rest, including the hundred sons, this is done even without a remainder of flesh or bone.
"O speaker, if they exist, they cannot be brought back to life; what then could be done?
Adṛśyantī then said: "If my husband’s brothers-in-law can neither be procreated nor brought back to life, then [what is the point]? (36–37)
"Even the gods, beginning with Rudra, cannot be persuaded by me;
however, if I obtain a husband and so forth, you, the guardians of the world, will also obtain what you seek.
Such a response as this is, in my view, the proper course of action."
Brahmā said: "O Satī! I shall grant you divine powers and the like—bodies that are bodiless, subtle in form, and devoid of gross existence. Then Satī replied: "O Creator, I too desire such [powers]."
I bestow and indeed awaken those such as Kālarudra, who are devoid of grossness, possessing subtle forms, and transcending the state of being like stone;
by means of my second form as the atomic [individual soul], they become Kāla, Rudra, and likewise Yama.
"Let Viśvāmitra and the Rākṣasa perform the work pertaining to creation;
let them never remain in their gross forms as stones.
Having heard this, Śakti and the others were then [commanded] by the gods beginning with Brahmā and Viṣṇu.
And those of divine, subtle form, having been brought from heaven, were presented [to her].
Whether residing in heaven or on earth, they exist in atomic bodies.
Even then, though she herself was invisible, Kālarudra and the others likewise [were present].
In that very same way, those authorized for the task were made to have the nature of atoms.
Taking water in her hand, she who considered herself powerful spoke:
"Just as is the form of my master, and as is the form of the gods," || 46 ||
"Let such consciousness be attained as the embodiment of Time and the other [principles].
Thus, by her, Time and the others were made into subtle presiding deities (adhikārin).
Thereupon the gods went to heaven; indeed, they did not offend the virtuous Satī.

Even those who are powerful tremble through the power of devotion to their husbands. (48) The sun, the moon, Mahendra, Viṣṇu, and other deities indeed tremble at the mere name of a virtuous wife; what then need be said of others? (49)

The dharma of a virtuous wife is the supreme dharma; it has never existed before, nor will it ever exist again. Such subordination to her husband as has been ordained for a woman by Brahmā is a supreme splendor, a great power, and a sovereign authority bestowed upon her.
Just as a weak servant woman, so too is that Supreme Goddess;
though she possesses power, she always conducts herself through the dharma of devotion to her husband.
Thus it is for her, the invisible Power in the form of a woman, who manifests in this way.
In due time, the embryo was born as a great sage, a child endowed with supreme knowledge;
he became renowned on earth by the name of the seer Parāśara.
O virtuous lady, I am his son, the Blessed Lord in the form of Vyāsa.
Then the ancestors sang and the grandfathers danced;
indeed, all the great-grandfathers did so when Parāśara had descended.
And the sky-dwellers, beginning with Puṣkāra, released a rain of flowers.
When Parāśara arrived, there was a magnificent and supreme splendor everywhere.
Seeing his divine ancestors and brothers assembled there, the boy—
who possessed great wisdom from the moment of his birth— spoke and bowed down to them.
Increasing day by day, he brought joy to all;
until he had reached his youth, he sang the narrative of Viṣṇu,
which contains all accounts of the past, future, and present, and bestows excellent liberation.
Whoever should cause this to be heard with devotion, or likewise listen to it with faith,
and should also remember Parāśara, shall indeed attain his own desired goal.

Thus ends the four hundred and tenth chapter, titled "The Description of how Kālarudra, Yama, Viśvāmitra, and the Rākṣasa became mountains in the form of stones after being cursed by Adṛśyantī—the wife of Śakti—when the sons of Vasiṣṭha, such as Śakti and others, were destroyed by the Rākṣasa; and how Śakti and the others were restored to life by Brahmā and the other gods, while Kāla and the others were revived by Adṛśyantī in a subtle form, and how Parāśara was born as the son of Śakti," in the first section concerning the continuity of the Kṛta-yuga within the *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, specifically within the glorification of the power of devoted wives (*pativratā-māhātmya*). || 410 ||
← Chapter 410: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga) Chapter 411 [[Author: → Chapter 412
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī! To this most excellent narrative, which destroys the sins of those who hear it, bestows liberation upon virtuous Vaiṣṇava women, and grants their heart’s desires. (1)
Wherever the Vaiṣṇavī woman resides, there Nārāyaṇī is established;
there is Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, and there is Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa as well.
(2) When Hari is being praised, she whose hair stands on end repeatedly—
Trembling, perspiration, and likewise drops of water [tears] are seen in her eyes.
(3) Having seen those who possess devotion to Viṣṇu, she becomes joyful in her heart; rising up, she should perform worship toward Vāsudeva just as a virtuous wife does. (4)
She is a devotee who nourishes righteousness; she alone is truly devoted to her husband, for, ever intent on her marital duty, she serves her own husband as Lord Hari.
She should indeed wear all fragrant substances, flowers, and other pleasing offerings.
Thinking thus, "Everything belongs to Hari," that virtuous Vaiṣṇavī woman,
filled with affection, performs only auspicious deeds in the sacred field of Hari;
and she constantly worships the image of Hari as she would her own husband.
Whether through action, mind, or speech, while awake or even in sleep,
she who possesses oneness with Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa is indeed a great devotee (mahābhāgavatī).
She performs all acts of worship, including the offering of food, according to her capacity.
That virtuous woman was an eightfold devotee of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
Seeing her splendor and power, the gods were indeed struck with fear;
bowing down to her, who had taken refuge in Vāsudeva and was devoted to her husband, they departed.
A Vaiṣṇava woman excels over thousands of other women;
a woman devoted to her husband excels over thousands of devotees of Viṣṇu.
A chaste wife who treats her husband as her deity excels over thousands of women devoted to their husbands.
Because she possesses devotion to the Lord Viṣṇu as her master, she is distinguished above all others.
(12) Her sons, daughters, grandsons, and [other kin] such as the husband's brothers; her two sons-in-law, her father-in-law, her parents, and her relatives—(13)
Compared to co-wives, female slaves, friends, those residing in her own home, or any other women who are devotees of Viṣṇu and followers of Viṣṇu— she is superior to them all.
She was the beloved wife of Triśaṅku, graced with every auspicious mark.
The mother of Ambarīṣa was a virtuous and highly devoted bhāgavata woman.
Constantly intent upon her master, she served her master as a servant of Hari; regarding her husband Kṛṣṇa as the Supreme Brahman, that virtuous woman indeed served him. (15–16)
Triśaṅku, having bathed daily in the Sarayū, worshipped Hari;
she too, devoted to his service, served her husband at dawn, midday, and night.
Likewise, she served Kṛṣṇa with excellent articles at the time of worship.
She indeed applies sandalwood paste, incense, and likewise the sprinkling of the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) with her two hands,
never at any time with her mouth or other means.
Thus constantly intent on service, she behaves as if she were truly liberated.
He constantly worshipped Nārāyaṇa, who has four arms and reclines upon the couch of Śeṣa, through the actions of speech, mind, and body.
He performed everything himself, including the taking up of garlands and other such rites.

She herself performed the grinding of perfumes and other substances, as well as the cooking of sacrificial offerings; she also applied ointments and other preparations to the ground. Known by the name Padmāvatī, she addressed the King with the words, "Nārāyaṇa."
Constantly uttering only the name "Śrī Kṛṣṇa," that devoted wife, with her inner self intent upon Him, worshipped Govinda for ten thousand years with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
She constantly gratified the devotees of Viṣṇu, both men who were Bhāgavatas and women who were Vaiṣṇavīs,
with gifts, honors, worship, and wealth and jewels.
Then, on one occasion, that goddess, having fasted for the Dvādaśī day, [proceeded].
The highly fortunate lady slept before Hari together with her husband;
meditating upon her husband as Nārāyaṇa, she served him according to the duties of domestic life.
There, the divine Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person, spoke to her.

"What boon do you desire from me, O blessed lady? Speak, O beautiful one! (27) She chose a boon from Kṛṣṇa: "May my son be a devotee of Viṣṇu, a sovereign emperor of great splendor, and one whose devotion consists of the total surrender of all his possessions. (28)
Saying "So be it," Janārdana gave her a single fruit.
Seeing the fruit before her eyes, she reported everything to her husband.
Having looked at it, she ate that fruit with her mind fixed upon it.
Then, in the course of time, that Padmāvatī gave birth to a son who was the upholder of his lineage, a devotee of Viṣṇu, one who had Vāsudeva as his supreme goal,
endowed with the characteristics of a devotee, and whose body hair was marked with the discus.
The father performed all the birth-rites for that supreme devotee of the Lord, who was endowed with divine marks and was an abode of virtues; and as he grew,
he became known by the name Ambarīṣa, liberated from qualities and the like.
Though consecrated by his father in the kingdom,
he performed severe penance for a thousand years, chanting the name of Nārāyaṇa Hari—
the Lord of Rādhā, Prabhā, Pārvatī, Śrī, Lakṣmī, and Māṇikī.
[He who has] the Śrīvatsa mark upon His chest, the Lord of Vṛndā, Rāmā, Śrī, Padminī, Padmā, Tulasī, Vijayā, Lalitā, and Mañjulā;
[and] the Lord of Devī, Haimī, Dayā, Śāntā, Śānti, Campā, and Supuṣpikā. 35.
The king always worshipped Śrī Kṛṣṇa Puruṣottama, who has swans for his ornaments, the sun as his canopy, and the Lord of Lakṣmī as his pearl necklace.
Thereupon, the Blessed One, whose palms are marked with the discus and the lotus, became pleased.
Having turned the elephant into Garuḍa and become Indra himself, Hari approached Ambarīṣa and said, "I am Mahendra; choose a boon.
Tell me what I may give you here as the exalted fruit of your austerities."
Then Ambarīṣa said: "I am certainly not performing penance for your sake.
And I will not accept what has been given by you; go, O Indra, as you please!
I do not desire your perishable enjoyments, even those pertaining to the supreme state."
Indeed, those who have accumulated desires will fall into the Vaiśvara hells of enmity,
unless they attain the state of servitude to the lotus feet of Nārāyaṇa-Kṛṣṇa.
Then the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa himself laughed.

He assumed his own form as the four-armed beloved of Lakṣmī. Seeing the Guru seated upon Garuḍa, Ambarīṣa prostrated before him and praised him, saying: "Be gracious here to me, O Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa! (42–43)

O Mahāviṣṇu, son of Kambharā, child of the cowherd clan! Śrī Vyāsa, the primordial deity and lord of Lakṣmī, remains established in you, the Supreme Self, having performed all ritual action within you. 44.
"I have taken refuge in you, O beloved of devotees, O bestower of shelter!
(45) The Blessed One, smiling, spoke playfully to Ambarīṣa:
"Speak, O devotee! I have come here for the purpose of granting your desired wish. (46)
Ambarīṣa said to Hari: "You alone have been chosen by me;
I shall indeed practice devotion to you constantly, according to my understanding.
Having made the world Vaiṣṇava, I shall protect the earth."
I shall gratify those who abide among the gods through sacrifices, oblations, and worship;
I shall protect the Vaiṣṇavas and slay my heart-enemies;
I shall perform devotion unto you and lead many to the Imperishable.
Having said, "So be it," and having given the Sudarśana discus,
he vanished to destroy the torment of curses, diseases, and other afflictions.
Having placed the discus upon the lion-throne and envisioned it as the form of Viṣṇu, [he departed].
Thus Ambarīṣa and his mother Padmāvatī both performed worship.
The Discus always accepts the honors offered by mother and son.
Once, on the slopes of the Himalayas, there occurred a terrifying rainstorm.
There, the region of Sāketa was submerged and its destruction occurred.
Having worshipped the Discus, the beautiful Padmāvatī said to Hari:
"O Blessed One, protect my subjects in every way; they are indeed Vaiṣṇavīs."

A deluge has arisen from the rain; protect me, save me, and show compassion! (54) If I am devoted to my husband’s vow and intent upon taking refuge in you, by that merit and through devotion to you, may the water and the cloud perish! (55)
Sudarśana, having laughed, became terrifying with garlands of flames;
reaching the sky, he destroyed all the clouds.
He withdrew all the water and protected the creatures as if in play.
Having done so, the Cakra arrived and sat down in its own place.
(57) Now, King Ambarīṣa had a daughter named Śrīmatī, who was auspicious and beautiful.
Seeing that it was the time for Śrīmatī’s giving away in marriage, the king [consulted] Nārada. (58)
Having prostrated before the guest, he requested a boon;
then, upon seeing her beautiful form, Nārada desired her.
Parvata also arrived and likewise desired her, longing for her repeatedly.
The king said to both of them: "How indeed can I give that single daughter to both of you who are requesting her? Nevertheless, if one of you two should choose her, then [I shall grant it]."
"I shall give my daughter to him; otherwise, I have no power [to do so].
Having said, "So be it," they then spoke again, "We shall go tomorrow.
They both went to Viṣṇu and bowed down in a secluded place.
Ambarīṣa desires to give his daughter, named Śrīmatī, to me;
you ought to act accordingly so that he may give her to Nārada.
May the face of the mountain shine like the face of a monkey.
"Act accordingly," Hari said, and he departed saying, "So be it.
Then Parvata also arrived and said to Hari, "Let him deliver [the message] to me,
so that Nārada may be seen there with the face of a golangūla."
"Act accordingly," Hari said; "So be it," he replied, and he departed.
The king, for his part, personally adorned the site of the svayaṃvara assembly, which was filled with princes and resembled the site of the assembly in heaven.
Having led the adorned maiden away, Ambarīṣa entered;
those two, the celestial sage and the Siddha, who were both of beautiful form, stood there first.
All became free from desire, having abandoned their longing for the maiden.
The king spoke to his daughter Supadminī, who had eyes like lotus petals:
"O blessed one, give this garland to whichever of these two you desire in your heart. And so, the maiden looked upon them both.
Seeing Nārada and Parvata with the faces of monkeys at that time,
she, terrified, said to her father, "Who are these two, a man and a monkey?
Having spoken thus, she went away slowly and slowly, following behind them in fear.
In the space between those two, there appeared one who was slightly less than sixteen years of age,
resplendent with all ornaments, surpassing a land-lotus in beauty,
with long, red-cornered eyes like lotuses, and more beautiful than ten million Cupids. (72–73)
She beheld Acyuta, who was exceedingly handsome and laughing with rows of teeth that closely resembled jasmine buds;
seeing him, the maiden was utterly enchanted. The King said, "Give me the garland."
Nārada and Parvata looked at each other’s faces; seeing this monkey-like form in the mirror, they became deeply ashamed. And all the other kings laughed at those two who had monkey-faces. (75–76)
Then, having forcibly approached both of them there, they indeed said to the king:
"Let her choose one of us two; do not delay.
Thereupon, that intelligent maiden bowed to her chosen deity.
She offered a garland to the beloved Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, who stood in the midst [of the assembly] assuming a deceptive form for the sake of protection. Immediately thereafter,
that maiden was no longer seen by men or gods.
Then a clamor arose in the assembly, "What is this?
Taking her with him, Viṣṇu, the Supreme Person, went to Vaikuṇṭha. The assembly was dismissed; Nārada and Parvata likewise departed.
Having gone to the primordial Vaikuṇṭha, they beheld Nārāyaṇa;
they also saw his glorious consort, Śrīmatī, seated comfortably upon his lap.
Struck with great wonder, they addressed the Supreme Lord.
O Blessed One, how is it that after granting us a boon and deceiving us by promising the acquisition of a daughter, you have led us away from our goal?
Therefore, even in another birth, that [promise] will cause great suffering through the delusion of women.
"Your destination shall be there; you will dwell among the monkeys.
The Blessed One said, "Om! So be it," and he who upholds the excellent Dharma accepted this.
Then the two sages he consoled; listen now to the reason for that.
"How was this illustrious lady brought away by you after entering into their midst?
There are many Rākṣasas who follow the way of deceit, like Rāhu;
just as there was [the obstacle] for the drinking of the nectar, so here was the Krauñca Rākṣasa."
Expecting [you], I remained between you two, deluded by the form of a maiden;
thus I have come as a mediator to that distant place.
However, you two have mutually agreed upon a monkey-faced [son]. (87–88)
For it has indeed come to pass exactly so through the request of you two alone.
O bulls among sages, there is not even an atom of fault on my part in that matter;
rather, I have delivered you both, though you were deluded by my illusory power.

But listen further, O Brahmins! In a previous birth, penance was performed by this maiden for my sake, lasting for many years. She was formerly a great saintly woman who had observed celibacy from her very childhood. (1.411.90–91)
That mental daughter of the great seer Mārkaṇḍeya was the companion of Mahālakṣmī, known as Kambharā, at her place of penance;
by the name Śrī, she performed austerities for a thousand divine years.
With the desire for the fulfillment of her aim, "May Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa be my husband," when Mādhava arrived through the path of the sky to grant the Sudarśana [discus] to Ambarīṣa,
she then beheld Nārāyaṇa.
Filled with joy, she abandoned her asceticism and desired to obtain Kṛṣṇa;
by means of yoga, she suddenly leapt up into the sky and followed Hari.
Meanwhile, Nārāyaṇa, having entrusted [the child] in the house of Ambarīṣa...
Then, while the Sudarśana discus was [active], he became invisible to the king.
Indeed, the mind-born daughter of Ambarīṣa had become a rememberer of her past lives;
born as a Vaiṣṇavī for my sake, she was waiting for my arrival. (96–97)
"Driven by me alone, who remained within you,
you two went into her presence and returned deluded by me. Taking advantage of your pretext, I have come to fulfill her desire."
The four-armed Lord himself came to the house of Ambarīṣa.
Standing between you two, I then accepted the bridegroom’s garland from the hand of the maiden; that glorious lady became my beloved.
"She is here on my lap, laughing with those two monkey-faced ones.
When addressed thus, the two excellent sages bowed and departed in anger.
Having reached Ambarīṣa, both sages spoke to him.
"After having summoned [the groom], you have subsequently given the maiden to another.
Because of this, through the application of illusion (māyā), darkness (tamas) shall indeed overcome you. When this curse had been thus pronounced, a mass of darkness then arose.
Then the Sudarśana discus struck the king;
having swiftly destroyed that mass of darkness, it reached the backs of the two sages.
Those two, afflicted by fear, fled toward the farthest limit of the Lokāloka mountain.
"Save us! Save us! they cried, having reached Govinda, the Lord of Vaikuṇṭha. "Save us both, O Lotus-eyed One; you are our protector, O Supreme Person!
How is it that the maiden was obtained by you, yet the discus has been placed upon our backs? (105–106)
Having heard this and having laughed, the Blessed One then turned his wheel back;
the Sudarśana was thus obstructed and remained there just as it had been before.
The two best of sages, having bowed and made their promise in the presence of Hari, departed.
"From this day forward until the end of our bodies, we two shall not take a daughter as a wife. Having thus become intent on meditation,
Ambarīṣa, after meditating upon Hari, went to the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa.
She constantly serves Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa in the world of Viṣṇu;
like Śrīmatī, she serves Him as Śrī, Lakṣmī, and Ramā.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have told you the former account of the birth of Śrīmatī.
Whosoever virtuous woman reads it, hears it, or causes others to hear it—111—all those Vaiṣṇavas go to my Vaikuṇṭha, indeed to me alone.
One who constantly reads this meritorious [work] shall attain union with Viṣṇu. 112.

Thus ends the four hundred and eleventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Birth of Ambarīṣa from King Padmāvatī of Triśaṅku, the Monkey-Faces of Nārada and Parvata during the Marriage of His Daughter Named Śrīmatī, the Attainment of Vaikuṇṭha by Śrīmatī through Nārāyaṇa, and the Power of the Chastity of Padmāvatī and Śrīmatī," in the first section, the Kṛta-yuga-khaṇḍa, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, concerning the greatness of devoted wives (*pativratā*).
