Chapter 413 →
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī! I shall relate the story of Duḥsaha’s wife, which is devoted to the virtue of devotion to her husband and concerns the son of Adharma. 1.
Adharma was born from behind Brahmā;
he had a son named Duḥsaha, who was his mental offspring. Wherever he dwells, there the state of being difficult to endure arises even for living beings.
He had four wives by name:
Daridratā (Poverty), Bubhukṣā (Hunger), Kalahā (Quarrel), and Malinatā (Impurity); they were devoted to their husband and dwelt wherever the unbearable god resided. (3–4)
Family members, friends, and even neighbors—
whoever comes within the range of sight of one established in their own country or standing in the city—
upon seeing his prosperity, cannot endure it and burn with envy. (5)
Brahmā, the Grandfather himself, granted a permanent residence in his own mind to those who were always possessed by envy, malice, and hatred, as well as to Duḥsaha. Then,
there was born from Adharma a mind-born son named Varṇasaṃkara.
To that Confusion (Sāṃkarya) were born four daughters— Poverty (Daridratā),
Hunger (Bubhukṣā), Strife (Kalahā), and Impurity (Mālinatā)— who were married by him.
Though they were devoted wives, they were given over to him by Confusion because he was difficult to endure.
Poverty itself appeared devoid of luster;
hunger was misshapen, quarrelsome, and cruel in form;
and filthiness was covered with flies and the like, smeared with impurities. (1.412.10)
Deprived of the merits of bathing, giving, recitation, fire-offerings, meditation, and so forth,
he took up residence in the forest, enduring unbearable hardships.
Failing to find a livelihood there, he entered the city of Udyama.
Having established a residence in a palace among industrious Brahmins and others, he lived there with his wife. He could not endure the prosperity of others;
wherever he could not bear someone's success, he would go to that person's house.
Entering among the household members, he incites mutual blame and contempt toward both elders— even those who are virtuous and righteous— in every way,
and he certainly causes them to create obstacles to the acquisition of wealth.
Having determined [the nature of] that which increases [prosperity] as well as that which causes the loss of gain,
Śakra once entered Mahendra while it was not being worshipped by its preceptor; he could not endure the garland offered by Durvāsas because of its power.
Then that garland was thrown by the elephant onto the elephant's forehead;
however, having pulled it up with its trunk, the elephant crushed it with its own foot.
At that very moment, Durvāsas, who was difficult to endure, entered [the elephant].
Durvāsas cursed him as well, saying, "May you indeed be deprived of prosperity.
Consequently, these riches met their destruction in the waters and other elements;
and suddenly, in Indra’s palace, he was joined by the wife of poverty.
Duḥsaha, being constantly delighted, indeed made his own residence [his home];

yet, due to the fault of poverty regarding Śacī, he then [performed] acts of giving, honor, and so forth toward gods, brahmins, sages, ancestors, those worthy of worship, guests, and travelers. (1.412.20)
And when it had ceased, he entered into her out of hunger.
From whatever place—whether from a god or from a human—he took what was to be taken, gathering it together; there was nothing at all that was not to be avoided.
Driven by hunger, she seized everything that was to be grasped;
the great emperor Nahuṣa came within her sight.
Being exceedingly prosperous, she desired Śacī, and therefore [seized] his prosperity as well as his gifts.
She summoned the king and requested an excellent jewel—
one belonging to the earth, one belonging to the underworld, and whatever was acquired in the other worlds.
Indeed, the king, beholding her who was worthy of divine worship and fallen into distress, [granted it].
And she gave her away even though she was about to perish due to the curse of Durvāsas;
for Śacī always desires a new gift out of hunger.
Having obtained the consent of the gods, she established her upon the command of Indra.

The king realized: "By providing material gifts, these women who were hungry have been constantly satisfied; they shall become my objects of enjoyment. As soon as they are requested by Nahuṣa for the act of pleasure... (27-28)
During that time, Kalahā lived with Śacī and the king;
Mahendrāṇī became distressed because Nahuṣa used a sage as his vehicle.
He fell and became a serpent, while Śacī went to Puṣkara.
Then, for many thousands of years, impurity resided in the serpent, in Mahendra, and in Śacī; likewise, it was unbearable everywhere. Four women dwelt among his offspring in all places.
Then everything became filled with cries of "Alas! and afflicted by great suffering;
Udyogapattana was ruined, and its enterprises fled to the forest.
Prosperity flowed into the ocean, and even riches met their destruction.
Wherever he was seen, O Duḥsaha, he was indeed accompanied by women.
Without their husband, those four women, observant of their vows, did not remain;
they rejoiced, laughed, and danced from house to house.
Duḥsaha, however, holds a mṛdaṅga drum to his neck and plays it;
Poverty performs a powerful, frantic dance (tāṇḍava).
Hunger wanders about his side and begs for ladles as well.
Kalahā forcibly seizes whatever has been thrown at her by anyone.
(36) Whether someone gives her food that is dry or fresh fruit, she immediately takes it and eats it; indeed, she does not give any of it to another. (37)

If another woman takes her own share of the division, she immediately begins a quarrel, uttering insults and slapping her forehead. But if she receives more than she desires, she gives it to another wife.
No one here rinses her mouth with a handful of water, nor washes her hands, nor cleans her face;
even when she is soiled by dancing, she does not do so.
The house, the door, the courtyard, the water source, and the drain—[all these are neglected]. (1.412.40)
The alchemical laboratory, the bathing area, and everything else were covered in filth;
what more need be said of the chests, the carpets, and so forth?
Likewise, the walls of the house, the garden, and even the crystal throne were defiled.
The face, the eyes, the skull, and the forehead— all were covered in filth.
Everywhere in the world, beauty became ugliness,
and radiance lost its luster, becoming shrouded in thick darkness.
Having thus witnessed that *tāṇḍava* dance, the gods, Nārāyaṇa and the others,
performed the churning of the ocean; then Hari spoke to the auspicious Primordial Person, the righteous one born of Dharma, known as Udāra.
Take as many jewels as you desire and depart now.
Wander everywhere throughout all the worlds together with Contentment and the woman named Serenity; do not delay.
Then that son of Dharma, truly possessed of a tranquil countenance,
noble and accompanied by his younger brother,
moved swiftly among the subjects, taking up residence in house after house with great contentment.
Seeing that, Duḥsaha became enraged and went toward the gods.
Accompanied by his wife, he was indeed driven out from all sides;
he begged them, "Let a place for my dwelling and for my livelihood be granted to me by the gods. (48–49)
If I do not attain detachment, I shall die; of this there is no doubt.
My wives, devoted to their husbands, will enter the blazing fire.
All of them shall follow behind me in truth, and thus this worldly existence shall reach its state of worthlessness.
For I alone am the essence in this cycle of birth and death that bestows both life and death.
Without me, the court of King Yama would not function; without me, the portions of Śrī Hari would never come to be in any way whatsoever. (51–52)
"As long as I exist, unrighteousness will always find nourishment everywhere;
and as long as I remain present, fierce asuras will indeed prevail.
Let them do as they please—what is the use of saying more?"
Having spoken thus, he ceased; meanwhile, his wives—
deprived of food, rebuked, and treated with contempt by their offspring—
went there before the gods, hungry and thirsty.
Where their husband resided, they then became enraged;
they wept, beat their own breasts, and their heads burst asunder.
They uttered loathsome words and raised a great clamor.
"O each and every one, where shall we go? We are thirsty and hungry.
There is no field that provides food, nor is there a dwelling house; there is no tree with fruit, nor is any place of refuge to be found. (57–58)
She was indeed bestowed by her father upon one who is devoid of qualities and without a home.
Alas, what great fortune! We shall die in the forest without food or water.
There is no hearth, no house, and likewise no clothing or other such things.
Whether ground, sweet, or even divinely ordained, what indeed remains to be done?
What shall we eat, what shall we drink, without a place of residence?
Having cut off our own feet, shall we now kindle a fire in the hearth without fuel?
O Lord, why should we tear the children to pieces and devour our own?
Why should one fill a lamp with blood? What need is there here for oil?
Why strike the earth with your feet and crush your hair with your hands?
Shedding tears from their eyes, those women, with dejected minds, wept;
and those women uttered cries of lamentation filled with great sorrow.
Then Dharma, Yama, Sūrya, Indra, Śambhu, and likewise Hari [arrived].
Seeing this, the world-protectors and the goddesses were overcome with compassion;
they consoled them and, after due reflection, granted them a place where husband and wife might live in mutual opposition. (65)
A teacher, a disciple, a guest, a master, twice-born brahmins, and cows—these are [to be honored even if] opposed.
O Duḥsaha, dwell especially in their house along with your wife!
[Dwell] where there is no censure of the gods, the teachers, the masters, or of Śrī.
Dwell there among those who revile women, the elderly, and their parents;
enter into those assemblies where recitation, fire-offerings, charity, and worship are not practiced,
and which are devoid of service to others, even if accompanied by your wife.
Enter those houses where there is no discourse on Hari, nor any honoring of the guru;
where night after night mutual quarreling occurs within the home;
and which are devoid of the libations offered to the ancestors—enter such places along with your wife.
While the children were looking on, you ate edible foods there without giving any away; enter that place with your wife, full of joy.
There, the sinful ones, devoid of compassion, delight in acts of violence toward one another.
Dwell in whatever house they reside, and live in that very place.
Whether it be the house of a crow, a neem tree, a garden, or even a home, always enter it together with your wife, even if it be the house of a shaven-headed woman. (72–73)
Enter that house where there is a single maidservant, three oxen, five buffaloes, six horses, and seven elephants; enter it with your wife.
There, the wife is a mantra-practitioner, the *ḍākinī*, and the husband is a *ḍāka*.
Enter that dwelling where Piśācas reside, together with your wife.
Enter that place where a maiden is pregnant, a young girl has reached her menses, or a widow is attached to another man—enter there, together with your wife. (75–76)
Enter those places where men are revilers of the virtuous and harborers of hatred, smelling of onions and accompanied by their wives;
and where women speak ill of ascetics, chaste wives, and the righteous.
Accompanied by your wife, enter there the aged husbands and the Brahmins.

(78) There, after sexual intercourse, no bath is required, nor is there even purification; nor is purity observed after the menstrual period, nor is the ritual impurity of birth or death maintained. (79)
And enter among those who are devoid of knowledge and auspiciousness, together with their wives;
who have soiled faces and stained teeth, who consume wine and meat;
who are devoid of twilight prayers, meditation, and other such duties, and who are likewise addicted to gambling and prostitutes.
Enter wherever women take pleasure in jewelry and such things.
Enter the house of those for whom mortals delight in bestiality and beasts delight in human intercourse, and who vainly seek to refine their bodily elements.
Dwell always upon the shoulders of those thorny trees where cattle and other animals, hungry and sighing in distress, are slaughtered;
and in that pure place fit for habitation, you shall produce filth and the like. (83)
Even those who possess power,

who constantly violate the scriptures, who deviate from the justice of the kingdom, and who have fallen away from the path of the world— dwell always upon their shoulders and within their houses. (84–85)
"Those who are opposed to acts of charity and hostile to the pursuit of happiness, who destroy the affection between husband and wife— dwell with your wife among them.
Thus addressed, Duḥsaha bowed to the gods, headed by Viṣṇu.
She went to dwell wherever such a place could be found.
On the thirteenth, the fourteenth, during the festival of lights, and on the first day of the lunar fortnight—all those four unbearable women wander the streets. (87–88)
By offering lamps in the courtyard, at the gate-tower, on the walls, at the threshold, in the square, and outside; by filling in the svastikas, by means of beautiful arches (sutoraṇa),
by means of colored streaks and the like, and likewise by sweeping away the dust.
By making them clear and by the offering of curds as well;
where noble women are devoted to their husbands and husbands are devoted to their wives;
where both are intent upon Kṛṣṇa, and where the people are indeed Vaiṣṇavas.

O beloved, those [demons] do not come to a place where there are virtuous disciples who grant perfect satisfaction, where there are saintly women who are dear to Hari, and where Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa resides;
likewise, wherever there is worship of Lakṣmī as well as worship of Śāradā.
Where there is worship of Gaṇeśa and various kinds of gifts are given,
all [the women] return after bowing and do not come back for a year.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have told you how to ward off poverty and other such misfortunes.

Thus ends the four hundred and twelfth chapter, titled "The Demonstration of the Dwellings of the Wives of Adharma’s Son Duḥsaha—along with their Husbands—Who Were Chaste and Known as Poverty, Hunger, Quarrel, and Impurity," within the section on the Greatness of Chaste Wives in the first book, the Kṛtayuga Lineage, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. [The Author: Chapter 414.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī! To an ancient account that took place in the assembly of Brahmā.
In this world created by Brahmā and protected by the celestial sages— wherein dwell the silent seers,
the rishis, the gods, the ancestors, humans, birds,
those who reside in the netherworld, trees, gandharvas, kinnaras, and kings. (1–2)
The Sādhyas, the Viśvedevas, the Maruts, and the Vasus, the leaders of the gods;
also the ascetics devoted to celibacy and the practitioners of meditative yoga;
the Vidyādharas, the Kimpuruṣas, and many other divine beings.
The virtuous Apsarases from the lake of Brahmā, truthful maidens, female servants, handmaidens,
and women who accomplish the purpose of service— women who move at will, assume forms at will, and bestow pleasure according to one's desire. (4–5)
Equal in honor, equal in form, beautiful, and sixteen years of age— Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds,
gave these women born of his mind, Śacī and the others, as wives to Indra and the other gods.
The duties of those wives who have been accepted by their husbands as devoted to their spouses— duties which,
when undertaken with the spirit of devotion to the husband, truly bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation—
were described by Brahmā to the wives of the gods and to his daughters-in-law. (7–8)
They were instructed in the duties devoted to their husbands, which lead to liberation;
they heard with great respect the teachings known as dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
Having fully grasped these matters that bring about every form of well-being, those women were deeply satisfied.
But the women in the form of slave-girls, having heard all the duties in their entirety, reflected:
"What indeed is the duty for us who are servant-maids?
We have been created as slaves, dependent on others, by the Grandfather."
We shall become the maidservants of the gods and likewise of the divine consorts,
and we shall be their concubines, devoid of devotion to a single husband.
In servitude, the state of having only one master can never be well-protected.
And service is dependent on others, having the satisfaction of the master as its sole support.
(13) There may be many masters, and no single duty remains very firm;
indeed, through service to many, one’s life becomes that of a slave-girl. (14)
In that regard, through many such occasions, misconduct arises;
consequently, due to the fault of that ill-deed, one's destination will indeed be hell.
Therefore, servitude to women certainly does not bestow what is beneficial.

One should not perform such service as servitude where there is no higher goal. Serving all kings and wealthy men out of lustful desire, dancing for the sake of a fee, and living as a courtesan—these are [not to be done]. (16–17)
If it were harmful, then that should certainly not be accepted under any circumstances.
Therefore, just as all the celestial women were married, and as we daughters of the Brahma-lake were likewise married; ||| 18 || [so too was this done].
The Apsarases and others have indeed been taken as handmaidens by the gods and the rest.
We, however, shall always remain auspicious, devoted solely to the dharma of fidelity to our husbands—
whether toward sages who possess the form of Brahmā, or toward gods, or even toward men.
Even among the *nāgas*, *siddhas*, *gandharvas*, *cāraṇas*, and forest-dwellers,
we shall remain devoted solely to our husbands through marriage;
for we shall live by fully upholding the duties toward our husbands.
The husband is the supreme dharma, bestowing dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa. (22) Entrusting oneself to the husband is the supreme entrustment, granting sons, wealth, and happiness.
Protection by the husband is the highest protection; the husband is the supreme deity and the supreme guru. (23)
Without the rite of marriage, the status of a slave-girl is considered like that of a mere gem;
it is unstable, perishable, not inspiring confidence, and fraught with deceit and the like.
It provides no satisfaction, causes constant agitation, and always bestows suffering.
"Therefore, O Brahmā, we all together request that you grant us these Apsarases in marriage.
Having deliberated thus, they all [spoke] in the assembly of the Apsarases. (286–287)
They entreated Brahmā again and again for the sake of marriage. Then, for the sake of dharma, Brahmā [bestowed] these [teachings],
which bring about liberation, upon his own daughters who had become his daughters-in-law.
They bestow happiness and even grant heaven, and they bring about the destruction of evil deeds.
Taught for the sake of happiness as well as for the highest good, listen, O Lakṣmī! I shall describe the meritorious dharmas that are the refuge of bliss. (28–29)

Whether she is a maidservant dependent on others, a maiden, a married woman, or one without a husband; whether she remains in a state of servitude or possesses the status of a queen; or whether she has many masters or has no master known to her— (1.413.30)
Or those who are greedy for sensual pleasures, for whom there is no other recourse—
by them, kings equal to their masters or even charioteers equal to them should be served; for such women, that very [service] constitutes their good fortune.
Whoever provides a livelihood or even pays wages, they are considered protectors, saviors, and lords for as long as one lives. Indeed,
by serving them with devotion of heart, female servants cross over [the ocean of existence].
O giver of the bride-price, having remembered me, Hari Nārāyaṇa—
those women who shall perform service equal to that of Nārāyaṇa will, by the power of Hari, cross over [saṃsāra] through such conduct free from hypocrisy. (34–35)
One should serve him with the thought that he is Hari, like a guest who has arrived;
not out of thirst, nor with a greedy disposition, nor through deceit.
And considering the husband to be transient, he should be served as if he were Hari.
When an auspicious day has arrived for the ancestors and the deities,
gifts of cows, land, and gold should be bestowed according to one’s capacity;
likewise, blessings should be received from gurus, virtuous men, and divine beings.
Those [women] should strive for spiritual excellence and preserve their words.
When the sun is in conjunction with the asterisms of Hasta, Puṣya, or Punarvasu,
a courtesan should perform a ritual bath with all medicinal herbs.
One should bathe with *dhātrī* fruit, ground sesame, *apāmārga*, and *tulasī* leaves,
along with auspicious rice grains and water mixed with the water from the lotus feet of Viṣṇu; and in that manner, one should worship Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, who can assume any form at will.
Having established Rati and Kāma, and Rādhā and the golden Kṛṣṇa,
she should worship them after installing Lakṣmī and the golden Nārāyaṇa.
She should worship the feet for Kāma and the shanks for Mohakārin.

Salutation to the penis as the treasury of passion (Kandarpa), and to the waist as the one possessed of delight (Prītimat). Salutation to the navel as the ocean of bliss, and likewise to the belly as Rāma.
Salutation to the heart as the lord of the heart, and to the breasts as the bringers of joy.
To Vaikuṇṭha, who causes joy, [he offered] the left side;
to the flower-bowed one, the right side;
to Mānasa, the crown; and to Vilola, the hair.
Salutations to the Self of all, to Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Self who is ever-expanding; salutations to the Supreme Self who possesses a beautiful form and bears the discus and other weapons;
salutations to Nārāyaṇa, and salutations to the Self who is the god of love.
Salutations to you, the father of desire and the abode of the god of love;
salutations to Hari, the bestower of both desire and liberation, the remover of suffering.
Salutations to the one who creates the bonds of desire and who severs those very bonds of desire.
"O Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, O Kṛṣṇa, who bestows both desire and liberation, salutations unto You!
O Kṛṣṇa, You are our husband; there is no other husband like You. Other husbands are seekers of their own self-interest, and we women are likewise seekers of our own self-interest. (1.413.49–50)
You are the supreme goal and the Supreme Brahman; take us into Your own hand.
Let our devotion be fixed upon You alone, and never for even a moment upon others, O Giver of Moments (the Moon)!
You abide within the Givers of Moments; You alone, O Lord, are the husband.
"O Lord, ferry us across the ocean of worldly existence; lead us, O Lord who rides upon Kṛṣṇa!
Women were created for the sake of desire, and you are indeed our embodiment of desire.
Hari Kṛṣṇa is considered the form of the seed, while you are the form of the child. (52-53)
For we consider you alone to be the embodiment of love and the embodiment of the *liṅga*.
O beloved of yours, may your touch—which removes all suffering—not fail to reach us, your female servants and devotees, even if it should ever be for the sake of a price. (54)
Whatever auspicious action we perform while standing on the left side brings us happiness;
let that which is devoid of merit be relinquished to you alone.
O Lakṣmī! Thus should the offering of every action be made to Kṛṣṇa by a woman on her husband's day.
Likewise, prostitutes and female servants should indeed perform that service as an offering to Kṛṣṇa.
Then, regarding Lakṣmī, Rādhikā, and Rati, one should worship them with the thought:
"Obeisances to Puṣṭi, obeisances to Tuṣṭi, obeisances to the fulfillment of all goals."
I bow to the mother of the bodiless one; salutations again and again to the wife of Kāma.
Salutations to you, whose nature is desire, who are beautiful, and who possess the luster of Kṛṣṇa.
Salutations again and again to you, whose form is the essence of bliss, the savior.

Thus, every morning, the courtesan should always worship Śrī Hari, her husband and Lord of Lakṣmī, with the sentiment of a master; thereby she shall attain liberation. She should worship him with perfumes, garlands, incense, food offerings, water, and lamps.
A woman desiring a husband and the celestial nymphs (apsarases) should worship Śrī Janārdana.
One should give gifts of food, gifts of clothing, and gifts of wealth to a twice-born man who is virtuous, possesses the character of a Brahmin, and is a celibate student (brahmacārin).
"I offer this to Kṛṣṇa; may Śrī Kṛṣṇa be pleased with me.
With these words, the virtuous woman should cause the worship to be performed or perform it herself, which bestows merit.
Indeed, Kṛṣṇa shall deliver such a beloved and devoted woman.
One should indeed hold that this Kṛṣṇa is the Puruṣa, the God of Love;
and with one's whole being, one should offer oneself, becoming absorbed in Kṛṣṇa.
Then, whether she be a courtesan or a servant, she will not be stained by faults.
One should cause the gift of a prastha of rice to be given on Sundays,
during the months of Kārttika, Mādhava, and Māgha, and during the Cāturmāsya vows.
By practicing the ninefold devotion, even a courtesan shall become pure.
One should give a very beautiful bed to a Brahmin, equipped with all necessary furnishings—
auspicious, provided with pillows for rest, along with a mattress and a coverlet, and accompanied by a lamp, sandals, an umbrella, wooden shoes, and a seat. (67–68)
One should indeed offer a purifying gift of a bed in the temple of Kṛṣṇa,
along with golden threads, ornaments, necklaces, beautiful garments,
rings, girdles, bracelets, and various articles.
One should give an image of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, as well as an image of Kāma and an image of Rati,
to a learned Brāhmaṇa;
likewise, a copper vessel, a golden thread, and a pearl for the eyes.
One should give a stalk of sugarcane, a jar of molasses, incense, garlands, and ointments,
as well as fragrant oil and food to a twice-born man.
Likewise, one should give a milch cow and speak these words in the presence of the cow:
O Kṛṣṇa, just as I never perceive any difference between Kāma and Keśava, so may I always attain all my desires. O Keśava, just as Kamalā never departs from Your body, [so may she remain with me].
"O Lord of gods, O Master, place me likewise within your own body.
Then, having circumambulated the brahmin, the virtuous woman should bid him farewell.
In this manner, indeed, one should worship the form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
Whether it be a brahmin or another man who has arrived, she should satisfy Kṛṣṇa thoroughly;
she should gratify him according to his desire, and while he is away on a journey, she should please another. Indeed, being devoted to her husband, she should delight any guest who arrives by chance.
Even when this has been done, if the embryo should desire [to remain], one should protect that which is auspicious;
but if there is no such desire, after sixteen days have passed since the onset of the menses,
she may touch a man for the sake of sexual pleasure, or she may live as one childless.

For if, through lack of desire and without will, one were to engage in such conduct out of dependence on another, then the state of being pregnant would follow; yet one should perform these acts only as a formal convention. Indeed, this was previously told by the Creator to the Apsarases.
Therefore, this [practice] would not be unrighteous in any way for courtesans;
for in former times, Puruhūta likewise declared it so regarding Dānava women,
and in the ancient age, he likewise declared it so regarding female animals, birds, and women.
Therefore, all of this is now appropriate for you:
the pacification of all sins and the bestowing of the attainment of Kṛṣṇa.
By my command, the action consisting of the offering to Kṛṣṇa shall be free from the guṇas.
"O excellent women, do that which has been told to you, O auspicious ones.
Thus addressed by Brahmā, all the Apsarases acted according to his word among the gods,
the sages, and human beings.
Then, for the sake of destroying their sins, the gods spoke repeatedly:
"Those who are female servants dependent on others, maidservants without support, laborers, those standing under orders, messengers, and women who are slaves— " || 85-86 ||
May those noble women who are pure and without husbands become purified goddesses;
and may the wives of the week, the dancers, the instructors,
the female attendants, and all those concubines always remain pure.

"Thinking always, 'Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa,' those men who have taken refuge [in Him], being honored and living, shall become worthy of worship by the gods and shall go to the city of Hari; they shall be knowers of their own good deeds. I am the witness of women. (88–89)
"Aja indeed declared that all women become pure through their menstrual cycle, for it is their vow that occurs month after month;
and the vow of the Ṛṣipañcamī, observed with fasting, is considered supreme."
By that, passionate women are purified and there occurs the dissolution of all defects.
Through the contemplation of Kṛṣṇa, all chaste wives serve men;
Kṛṣṇa is the husband who is the Supreme Brahman, and those devoted to Him are truly chaste wives.
Kṛṣṇa finds satisfaction when established in the self of man;
Hari finds satisfaction when established in the self of woman.
Thus, the devotee consists of this very sentiment (*bhāva*); such a devotee does not deserve censure.
Thus has the duty of devotion to the husband been illustrated for courtesans;
it was proclaimed in the beginning during the Kṛta Yuga, and the celestial women practiced it. However, at the end of the age, when the mind is corrupted and devoid of devotion to Kṛṣṇa— 94–95.
When the time has arrived, there is indeed a fault in excessively indulging in desire;
merit will not arise, and the austerity already performed will surely perish.
Therefore, it is not fitting for a woman to behave as a commodity for sale.
It is not fitting for a man to behave as a paramour. Purity arises from purity; this is considered the dharma. Impurity is sin, and it is regarded as a stain.
Therefore, the dharma of attachment is held to be superior to a dharma consisting of mere commercial profit.
In truth, listen to all this: excrement and urine are impure, possessing an unbearable stench, base, inauspicious, and always filthy.
Indeed, "mala" (impurity) should be understood as sin; that which is free from sin is "nirmala" (pure).
Impurity flows from the nine gates in various forms.
(1.413.10) The impurity of dwelling in the womb is said to be urine, which consists of liquid waste. That indeed should be understood as a place of sin; contact with it is called sin. (101)
Yoga, however, is in every respect an evil, for it is the means of attaining impurity;
whether that [impurity] is joined with [the self] or even unjoined, marriage is said to be a restriction (niyama), and that restriction is always endured. 102.

Non-marriage is not a restrictive rule, for it is not tolerated by people. (103) Sinful action is equal to impurity; it is both tolerated and not tolerated. Since it is tolerated in certain cases, it does not follow that it lacks the quality of being sinful. (104)
Sexual intercourse is sinful in every respect; no meritorious action exists therein.
Desire is a fault in every way, for it is indeed the lineage of unrighteousness.
However, if one is offered as divine through union with Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, then [it becomes pure].
For that [offering] consisting of total surrender indeed bestows grace upon Hari.
Grace for Hari should be sought even by means of another wife;
for desire is a source of evil, yet it has been regulated by the elders through the rite of marriage. (106–107)
The Gandharva marriage was ordained by Brahmā for Apsarases;
for female slaves and women who have been purchased, that same Gandharva rite is merely momentary.
In whatever case a man is fit to marry a woman through a bride-price, [that is the rule].
He is indeed designated as a *veśya*, and she is likewise a *veśyā* for that very reason.
If their association is tolerated by men just as that of married couples, it is not on that account considered a violation of dharma (*vṛṣa*).
However, O beloved, that which is merely tolerated as thought, intention, or action is figuratively designated as "dharma";
having offered that to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, one should practice dharma in its true sense.
Thus has the truth been told to you regarding even courtesans, my dear.
For wives, the performance of duties equally with their husbands is considered to be dharma by rule.
However, the pursuit of sensual pleasure is a hell; it leads only to rebirth in the infernal realms.
This applies whether the women are wives, courtesans, prostitutes, or the wives of others. (112–113)
In ancient times, the great sage named Dālbhya declared the truth to women:
"Whatever action is performed through the senses while devoid of remembrance of Kṛṣṇa is entirely of the nature of sin; for even chanting and vows [performed thus] are merely lust and anger. (1.14)
All realms, beginning with heaven, and all hells are within Kṛṣṇa.
The multitude of enjoyments, beginning with desire, are hells within Kṛṣṇa.
Therefore, having made Kṛṣṇa the supreme beloved and having propitiated that Lord, [one attains liberation].
Having served Nārāyaṇa, the true lord, one becomes a Nārāyaṇī;
yet the enjoyment of desire does not arise for the sake of the body's lusts.
Rather, the unborn [Nārāyaṇa] performs the enjoyment of desire solely for the happiness of the self.
Nor do objects of desire exist for the sake of the senses;
even the enjoyment of desires exists only for the sake of the bliss of the Self dwelling within.
Furthermore, the solitary Self does not engage in desire without Hari being present within.
Therefore, for the sake of attaining Him alone, these seekers of the Self truly become desirous of Him;
for if Kṛṣṇa were not present within the self, the self would be purposeless. Thus, through union with Kṛṣṇa, desires indeed become givers of bliss.

"Thus, by propitiating Kṛṣṇa, the fruit of one's desires is to be obtained. O Lotus-born One, that alone is declared to be the virtue of devotion to a husband (*pātivratya*) for courtesans. Having heard this supreme dharma and considering it their own, the hosts of *apsarases*— 121–122. Thus, by propitiating Kṛṣṇa, the fruit of one's desires is to be obtained. O Lotus-born One, that alone is declared to be the virtue of devotion to a husband (*pātivratya*) for courtesans. Having heard this supreme dharma and considering it their own, the hosts of *apsarases*—
Devoted to the duty of paying tribute, they remained under the command of Brahmā;
as long as the Lord, honored along with his tribute, attained a state of delight, so too by performing service to him, they shall attain the supreme station. (123)
"By reading and by hearing this, the true nature of reality (*dharmatattva*) is awakened.

Thus ends the four hundred and thirteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Lord’s Devotion to His Wives Among Female Slaves and Prostitutes Who Were Without Husbands," within the section on the Greatness of Devoted Wives (*pativratāmāhātmya*) in the first book, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī! How is devotion to the husband (pātivratya) to be practiced toward the Supreme Soul?
This was told by Hara to Nārada, and by Kṛṣṇa to Śaṅkara. (1)
I shall tell you that which was spoken by Brahmā to Sanatkumāra;
it was told by me and has been proclaimed by my devotees in successive tradition.
Having recalled it once more, I speak it to you, who have already spoken it to Kambharādevī.
One should apply the intellect to the surrender of oneself to Kṛṣṇa; He alone is to be served.
One should worship the Blessed Lord, who is the form of the Master, together with Śrī.
For women, Hari is the husband alone; one should conduct oneself in a state of servitude toward Him.
That woman who serves Nārāyaṇa even in the state of a maidservant delivers twenty-one generations of her own family.
That very day is blessed; blessed too are her mother and her kinsmen.

Blessed is the father, blessed is the husband, and blessed is the entire family [of her who serves Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Lord, with the conviction that He is her husband]. All the sins committed by her over many lifetimes are utterly destroyed. (6–7)
The Supreme Goddess, the very embodiment of Lakṣmī, becomes the purifier.
In ancient times, Śambhu spoke of devotion to her husband to Satī, the Supreme Sovereign;
and likewise, Gaṅgādevī spoke thus—listen, O beloved, to that which is worthy of being heard.

Devotion to one’s husband is supreme love, directed toward the master alone and not toward others. (9) O Satī! Just as you meditated upon me, Śaṅkara, as your husband—just so is your love for your husband centered on Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. (1.414.10)
O beautiful one, Hari was meditated upon by me in all circumstances;
he alone is the protector, the nourisher, and the husband of embodied beings. True lordship over embodied beings resides in Kṛṣṇa.
Just as one afflicted by thirst remembers water, so do I remember Kṛṣṇa.
Just as one overcome by cold remembers fire, so do I remember Kṛṣṇa.
And just as a devoted wife remembers her husband, so do I remember Mādhava.
Just as one standing afar remembers home, or as the cātaka bird remembers the rain-cloud, so do I remember Kṛṣṇa, the Knower of Brahman, through the knowledge of Brahman.
Swans desire Lake Mānasa, and sages desire Hari in Mānasa.
Just as devotees desire devotion, so do I remember Kṛṣṇa.
(15) Just as Vaiṣṇavas desire purity, and as animals desire grass, and as the virtuous desire forgiveness, so do I remember Kṛṣṇa. (16)
One who is addicted to vice is attached to vice; one who does not know the Self is attached to the body.
One who possesses craving is attached to life; in that same way, I remember Keśava.
Just as bees [cling to] a flower and cakravāka birds [cling to] the sun, so do I cling to Him.
Just as one who loves himself desires what is dear to him, so do I remember the All-pervading Lord.
Just as those dwelling in darkness long for a lamp, and those afflicted by fatigue long for rest,
and as those who are awake long for sleep, so do I remember Kṛṣṇa.
Just as elephants devoid of the fatigue of rutting remember the forest terrain, and lions remember deer and other wild animals, so do I remember Kṛṣṇa;
just as fire exists within sun-crystal through contact with the sun, and within cotton.
Just as water is produced from the moonstone through contact with the moon,
and just as the night-lotus blooms with flowers upon seeing the moon, so too does Kṛṣṇa manifest through association with Satī.
Just as a female bee trapped within a lotus stalk at night might remember its protector,
or else, being trapped within the stalk, might give up its life and attain liberation;
even so, a virtuous maidservant who has come under Kṛṣṇa’s care should remember him as her protector.

Indeed, Kṛṣṇa was remembered by the gopīs in every way solely with the thought of him being their lover; and they attained union (sāyujya) with Him. In that same manner, I remember Kṛṣṇa—some indeed with a wicked disposition, and some with a deceptive disposition.
Some [meditated] out of greed, others likewise through a state of dispassion;
another through affection, through devotion, through hatred, and yet another through the feeling of love for her husband.
Some, having contemplated Śrī Kṛṣṇa Janārdana through knowledge, [meditated].
Having enjoyed happiness in this world, that virtuous woman went to Goloka.
Even by chance, the remembrance of a devotee bestows liberation;
through a single act of devotion to her husband, she was seen in his presence in an instant. (27–28)
Without mutual affection there is no wife, and without affection for his wife there is no husband;
though standing in close proximity, they remain as far apart as collyrium is from the eyes.
When devotion consisting of fidelity to her husband was attained, Hari was then attained.
Indra and the other gods attained the nectar of immortality, yet they remained miserable because they lacked devotion.
Having attained the nectar of devotion to their husband, suffering never arises again.
Just as swans leave behind water and drink only milk, and nothing else.
Abandoning illusion and abiding in truth, they drink Kṛṣṇa with their eyes.
A cloth pouch is not capable of binding water;
likewise, the pouch of illusion is not capable of uniting one with Kṛṣṇa.
Without devotion to her husband, a woman cannot desire Kṛṣṇa as her beloved.
And how could Kṛṣṇa come [to her] without the offering of devotion to her husband? Devotion to the husband is devotion to Kṛṣṇa; it must always be practiced by a woman of her own accord. (33–34)
Just as a fool desires to cross the ocean with his two arms,
so does she desire the ocean of worldly existence without Kṛṣṇa as her husband. Just as a poor man has a longing for gold, so do I have a longing for Hari.
Just as a woman has desire for Kṛṣṇa when her passion is aroused, so too do I have such longing for Him.
Even a tiny spark of fire, if constantly nurtured, consumes entire forests;
yet even a mere atom of devotion to Kṛṣṇa, if it is the nature of one’s fidelity to Him, [destroys all worldly bonds].
One should worship the Lord, remembering: "Kṛṣṇa is my husband; my husband is Kṛṣṇa. This [remembrance] reduces to ashes the mountains of sins accumulated over thousands of previous births.
It is heard from the company of the virtuous that hundreds of women possess the virtue of devotion to their husbands.
She is awakened by thousands of women, yet she is never guarded;
in this world, various kinds of women will offer their intelligence to others, but that woman who practices it herself is seen but once in ten million. (1.414.39–40)
Just as a boat [is used] in the ocean, or a small bucket for drawing water from a well,
so too does the Dharma manifest according to the nature of the recipient.
Water poured at the root of a tree reaches its leaves and branches.
Just as flowers, fruits, and seeds arise in their proper sequence, so too service rendered to the husband increases one's sons, grandsons, and progeny;
it surely bestows both heaven and liberation—of this there is no doubt. (42–43)
Just as a girl carrying water places her mind on the jar, the well, her foot, her hand, and herself, so too does she place it on her husband and on Hari.
Having eaten the molasses, the young girl asks her mother for more.
Satī, having addressed her husband, likewise entreated Śrī Kṛṣṇa:
"Just as water is mixed with water, milk with milk, and ghee with ghee,
so too must Kṛṣṇa be seen by Satī as inseparably merged within her husband."
Just as the sun is omnipresent through its radiance and its rays,
and just as fire is omnipresent through its heat and the digestive fire within,
so too is the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, Hari, who exists as the very soul of the husband.
O Goddess of gods, he is omnipresent; therefore, one should practice devotion to one's husband.
Just as stones situated in the midst of water are not stained by the water in the slightest, so women devoted to their husbands are not tainted by other embodied beings. 48–49.
For the moonlight is pleasant, and likewise the husband is a source of happiness;
a ripe fruit is always sweet, and so too is a husband for a woman.
A frog dwells in the water, while a bee indeed resides within the forest.
The six-legged bee perceives the fragrance of the night-lily, but the frog does not.
Some dwell on the banks of the Gaṅgā, while others live a hundred yojanas away;
likewise, some perceive the fruit of the Gaṅgā, and so too does the devoted wife of Kṛṣṇa.
Just as a camel constantly carries a load of camphor and aguru,
yet does not perceive their fragrance nor experience the bliss inherent therein,
so too is a wife who merely bears the burden of her husband's weight, lacking in devotion to her husband (pātivratya).
Indeed, she perceives neither the fragrance nor the bliss of her husband Kṛṣṇa.
Just as deer, desiring the scent of musk, smell the *śāla* tree but do not know it resides in their own navels, so too women cannot perceive this without the virtue of devotion to their husbands.
For instruction given to fools results in the opposite effect;
likewise, the command of a husband becomes poison for an unfortunate woman.
Milk drunk by a serpent turns into venom through its association with poison.
To one who is devoid of devotion to her husband, even her husband becomes like poison;
likewise, even the most intense instruction on wifely fidelity becomes like poison.
It is just as a lamp is useless without eyes, or as a mirror is useless to one without sight, or as a jar is useless to one who cannot see it.
One does not see him as such an entity without [the practice of] Kṛṣṇa; one does not see him [without it].
Fire [is not seen] when it has the reddish hue of smoke, and a mirror [is not seen] when covered by breath. In the same way, the self devoid of love, struck down by impurities, does not perceive Him.
Just as the embryo is enveloped by the amnion, so Hari resides within the husband.
Just as ghee exists in milk and oil always exists in sesame seeds, Kṛṣṇa resides in all things moving and unmoving; he resides in the husband, and one should become him.
Just as many clusters of jewels are held within a single thread,
so too are men and women interwoven in Śrī Nārāyaṇa.
Just as fire residing within wood is obtained by one who knows it through effort, [so is He found].
Likewise, Viṣṇu resides within the Lord (pati); He is attained through worship by one who knows Him.
Hari is the primordial Great Lamp; from that lamp, the lamps of the lords of creation, such as the Sun and others, are produced. One should take refuge in that root-lamp. (63–64)
All lamps are subordinate to the master-lamp; therein one should kindle Kṛṣṇa.
Just as at the rising of the sun, light spontaneously pervades everywhere, so too upon the rising of her husband Kṛṣṇa, her own light shines forth.
The wind always carries fragrance by its very nature.
In the same way, Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, my husband, carries the fragrance of love.
And just as water may become mixed with sugar or poison, [so too does the heart change].
And when mixed with the essence of cultivation, the master becomes such;
just as the earth, joined with seed, is produced in the form of various trees,
so too is water made rich with its own essence by means of the seed.
In that same way, a husband endowed with the essence of being is born as Kṛṣṇa.
O Lakṣmī! Whosoever thus beholds me, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, as her husband—O Lakṣmī! I make that woman Kamalā, my own beloved wife.
She who knows me thus in her husband is my devotee and a faithful wife.
I am one, yet I exist in many ways, appearing as the husband-form for all women. Indeed, names and forms were bestowed by me while I remained in the form of a husband.
The eye is nourished by the sun, not merely by seeing the sky;
likewise, O beloved, wisdom and affection always increase through Kṛṣṇa,
for without Kṛṣṇa, affection does not grow, even with a husband.
"The Supreme Self and likewise I am present in every body, whether in a woman or a man;
I am in every jar. Let that devoted wife behold Me truly as such.
Just as all things, such as wood and the like, possess power through Nārāyaṇa,"
In the same way, everything beginning with the husband is empowered by me, Kṛṣṇa;
just as various forms of gold arise through the work of a goldsmith,
so too do forms such as husbands, sons, and others arise from dwelling within Kṛṣṇa.
When [the husband] is not present within one's own self, then bliss turns into sorrow.
Just as fools perceive the sun shrouded by clouds to be devoid of luster,
so too does a wife perceive her husband to be without me when he is separated from his state of being [as her husband].
That virtuous wife who was born from my *sattva* nature is a devoted spouse;
she, the beloved of Hari, recognizes me as her husband in the form of her lord.
But she who is deluded by karma, relying solely on desire, does not recognize me.
But how could one who is deluded by ignorance conceive of me through her intellect?
Like those dull-witted nihilists, she perceives me as her own husband;
yet a wife should not be like an elephant's tusk, but rather like its trunk. (1.414.80)
The master should not exist [alone] like the sky, nor should he exist [alone] like a royal umbrella.
(81) Both should exist in relation to one another, always like water and milk;
when being heated by the heat, they act as mutual aids to each other. (82)
O Lakṣmī! When the essence of service is known, then Hari himself becomes attainable in this very life through such service, for he is indeed easily won by it.
That which is to be known—the Supreme Brahman—is attained through the internal states of the heart toward one's own [master] and others.
For all beings indeed, the purity of intention is what distinguishes them.
Sisters, daughters, mothers, children, other women, female slaves, mistresses, attendants, and so forth—just as is the intention, so is the fruit. (84–85)
Relatives, sons, enemies, the sons of enemies, friends, and others are touched [in dreams] according to their true nature; likewise is the result.
The beloved is the form of Nārāyaṇa, and the beloved woman is the image of Ramā.
Indeed, through purity of devotion, Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa is attained therein.
Just as a stone image is worshipped with purity of devotion, so too is Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa served within a beautiful form. (87–88)
Just as a beloved is embraced, so is the fruit according to one's inner disposition.
For one whose feet are shod with sandals perceives the earth as the Carmaṇvatī river.
In whatever manner a person’s intellect is constituted, in that same manner their manifestation is revealed.

Indeed, they return to their original nature through the intellect, but they undergo transformation through their disposition. (1.414.90) A neem tree, even if sprinkled with milk, will certainly not abandon its bitter nature;
however, if it is sprinkled with salt, it will give up its life. (1.414.91)
Just as a fruit may attain a sweet state through cooking,
so too the Lord may present the world through the nature of *māyā*.
One should always distance oneself from the world by means of the caustic quality of dispassion (*vairāgya*).
Through ripening brought about by the heat of Kṛṣṇa, the Lord may bestow immortality.
(93) But having cut down the mango tree, how could one obtain fruit or leaves?
Having abandoned Kṛṣṇa, O mistress, while your own husband remains, how could you obtain the fruit? (94)
How indeed could one prepare a golden plough for the cultivation of the *arka* plant?
Having cut down the *karpūra*, bamboo, and other such [trees], how could one protect the *kodrava* weeds?
Having abandoned her husband Kṛṣṇa and forsaken a human being, how could she render herself purposeless?
How could a goat's hoof-knob possibly burn in a vessel made of lapis lazuli?
(96) Having abandoned the treasure-trove residing in the householder, how could one resort to the service of a mere oyster shell?
Having abandoned Śrī Hari who resides in the husband, how could one wander elsewhere in vain? (97)
Having abandoned the wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi) in one's own home, how could one resort to a mere cowrie shell?
When the husband is indeed the very form of Kṛṣṇa, how can meanness be conceived?
Having abandoned the worship of Narasiṃha, how could one perform service to a dog?
Having abandoned her beloved who is the consort of Ramā, how indeed could she take pleasure in the presence of Death?
For what need is there for a bracelet on one's own hand when it is already in the market?
Since Lakṣmī is the maidservant in his house, how even can his sovereignty be described?
That Śrī Kṛṣṇa always resides with His Lord; let him not go elsewhere.
How can one perform meditation there upon a bodiless Kṛṣṇa? Having meditated upon Him as possessing form and a beautiful appearance, one shall go to the supreme state.
Thus, the virtuous wife should always remember Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa as her husband.
(102) When, through the joy of remembering Kṛṣṇa, her body is covered in horripilation and tears of bliss flow from her eyes, then liberation becomes her servant. (103)
Sin of speech is indeed destroyed by [the act of] cutting [the tongue], and mental sin through remembrance [of the Lord];
the evil of action perishes through the service and worship of Kṛṣṇa.
One should never practice severe austerity while abandoning the duty toward one's husband.
The dharma consisting of service to one’s husband is superior; there is danger in another’s bull (another man).
Having abandoned the hermitage of Kṛṣṇa-Kānta, how could she practice the stage of life of a wandering ascetic?
Having purchased Kṛṣṇa-Kānta with her husband’s wealth, she should satisfy him.
One should give pure white substances of excellent quality when making a gift to a brahmin or to Lord Hari;
one should give materials full of affection and faith to a wedded husband.
By such giving, great merit is attained, the measure of which is indeed beyond calculation.
One must not take pleasure with any other substance; one should take pleasure only with the husband, who is the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
For a woman who possesses such conduct, suffering indeed does not arise.
If it should occur, she must not feel distress, for that is the result of past deeds.
For animals are bound by ropes, and likewise, living beings are bound by their actions; having become devoted to the Supreme Puruṣa, one should joyfully sever that bond.
Like a monkey in the forest who moves from tree to tree with thirst, [so do worldly beings move about].
If a female monkey wanders from house to house in the city out of thirst,
yet that very thirst is directed toward the glorious Nārāyaṇa, her own husband,
she, being virtuous, shall obtain happiness by drinking the nectar of eternal immortality.
Just as a ball exists for the sake of play, so too is the body a sport;
with it, a virtuous woman (satī) should please Kṛṣṇa in the form of her husband.
By their past karma, living beings are led into many wombs.
The gods are bound in heaven by the power of their karma, as are the sages in the realm of truth.
Even the serpent dwelling within the body of Śambhu is venomous because of his karma;
likewise, Aruṇa is lame in the chariot of the Sun. Karma is indeed a powerful source.
The entire world is dependent on karma, yet it was created by me through Viṣṇu.
By my name and by my service, all karma is destroyed.
Water given as an offering is one thing, while water placed in a jar is another.
O beloved, liberation arises from surrendering to the gods as it does from surrendering to Me.
Thinking, "I am the wife and this husband is the Lord; we both take refuge in Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa," one should perform all actions as an offering to Śrī Keśava.
One should cultivate the sense of "I" in Hari and perform the offering of one's actions; one must experience the fruits of past karma, yet by offering everything to Kṛṣṇa, one is not tainted.
People praise planets, spirits, ghosts, mantras, and medicinal herbs.
Some praise accomplishment, valor, intelligence, exertion, daring, and strength;
others praise policy, fortitude, and likewise fortune.
But [the wise] do not praise a husband, dharma, or Hari out of delusion.
They do not praise the vow of devotion to the wife, nor the bull, nor good character, nor devotion;
thus, deceived by the wicked at home, they do not take refuge [in these] due to their folly.
When a living being is absorbed in Kṛṣṇa, then no sin exists.
Whatever merit and happiness there may be, one should offer it unto Kṛṣṇa as one’s husband. Then, through that perfect union, one attains the state of bliss which transcends duality.
When one performs external actions while the mind has no longing [for them], [then one is truly established]. || 1.23–24 ||
O beloved, that renunciation which consists of a longing for offering to Kṛṣṇa is the highest;
some renounce everything out of anger, and others renounce out of distress.
Still others renounce because they have not obtained [their desires]; however, renunciation unto Kṛṣṇa is considered supreme.
If a woman, though moved by her past karma, is devoted to Kṛṣṇa and is constantly intent on the service of her husband, that virtuous wife attains a happy state;
she is born in the home of those who are pure, prosperous, wise, and even among yogis.
A virtuous woman who is devoted to the service of Kṛṣṇa is born as a daughter; by the power of her yoga of devotion, she attains the fruit of serving her husband even with very little effort,
and through my grace and devotion, she reaches the state of consciousness and bliss.
By the very act of total surrender, one attains liberation; of this there is no doubt.
(1.29) Just as mud is washed away by mud and blood by blood, how can an action of a violent nature ever be capable of cleansing another action? (1.414.130)
Without the Lord Kṛṣṇa, how can there be the destruction of karma through one's own actions?
Through the Lord joined with Kṛṣṇa, the destruction of all karma occurs.
Eternal bliss is to be attained in Hari; it is not found in heaven nor through ritual acts.
"O Lakṣmī! Without devotion to Hari, there is never any eternal happiness for them anywhere. Therefore, O woman, a devoted wife must always act thus toward her husband;
she bestows both happiness and liberation. I myself am the witness to this in every respect. (13.2–13.3)

Thus ends the four hundred and fourteenth chapter, [414], titled "The Description of Divine Conjugal Fidelity as Taught by Śaṅkara to Kṛṣṇa, Who is Essentially Her Husband," within the section on the Greatness of Chaste Wives, in the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga, in the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 415 *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā*, Part 1: The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga.
Chapter 415.
[The Author: Chapter 416.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, Lakṣmī! Having told you this again and again, I am not yet satiated.
I shall tell you the reason for this; listen, O beloved.
By observing the great dharma of devotion to their husbands, virtuous women—and others as well—attain certain liberation; of this there is no doubt. (1–2)
Even though worldly pleasures may be many, they are impermanent;
there is no eternal happiness for them anywhere without service to Hari.
Whether it be the happiness of a sovereign ruler of the earth or even the bliss of Vairāja, [it is likewise impermanent].
Furthermore, no other divine state, however peaceful, should even be desired.
(4) For while a stone is split by metals, a diamond is never split;
likewise, devotion to one’s husband and devotion to Hari are never split by anything whatsoever. (5)
Just as a crane eats aquatic creatures while avoiding frogs and the like,
so too Yama, the destroyer of all, avoids the servants of Kṛṣṇa.
Every morning, having bowed to the Lord, one should always speak in the presence of Kṛṣṇa.
"Take this maidservant, who is burdened with hundreds of offenses, back to her own place.
O Kṛṣṇa, show mercy to one whose devotion to her husband was unknown [to you].
Indeed, even though the gatekeeper is present, if the master desires it," ||| 7-8 ||
Having prepared it in any way whatsoever, she should give it to one authorized by her affection;
that virtuous woman obtains the fruit, provided she is not inwardly unfaithful to her husband.
Thus, O Lord, even a servant who stands at a distance within this body—
O Lord, protect even those who are outside, yet keep those who stand near you close at hand.
Kubjikā, who had not attained liberation through any other means, was delivered by you;
that which is difficult for Brahmā and the others to obtain even in a dream became easily accessible in the house of the cowherd woman.
The cowherds, having enjoyed your grace, have gone to the world of Brahmā;
likewise, grant me your grace, deliver me, and lead me to your own abode.
O Keśava, so that I may attain you, the Lord of Śrī and the master of my husband’s lineage.
"Make me take refuge in you in such a way that you may be pleased with me.
Just as both thorns of the *badarī* tree—one crooked and one straight—are alike, the crooked one obstructs the traveler by catching hold of his clothes and other belongings. (13–14)
The straight arrow, having pierced the skin, burns the embodied being;
the crooked one, Nārāyaṇa, [burns] within the body, while the Lord alone is straight.
Without Nārāyaṇa, the master is a burner through sense objects and the like.
O Dear One, that very same Kṛṣṇa, when conjoined [with the self], is both a restrainer and a bestower of liberation.
Just as a slight contact with fire causes gold and other metals to become heated, yet an intense union with fire purifies and melts them. || 16–17 ||
Likewise, the union with mere offspring and the like produces only the state of being an object [of worldly attachment];
that very same union with the great fire of Śrī Kṛṣṇa bestows liberation.
Just as without a machine, its driver would be rendered useless; ||| 18 || so too without Him, all else is in vain.
Likewise, a machine consisting of a husband is useless without Kṛṣṇa;
just as a girl without hair provides no peace to the beholder,
so too a husband without Kṛṣṇa does not bestow eternal truth.
Just as a deer dwelling in the forest never leaves its circle,
so too a doe, though staying with her mate, does not abandon Hari who dwells within her heart.
Just as a lion moving through the forest repeatedly looks back behind him.
Likewise, as Siṃhī always beheld Hari whenever she went to her husband’s house,
so too does she who is filled with the virtue of devotion to her husband proceed toward Kṛṣṇa, her husband, just as a full river flows down from higher to lower ground. || 22–23 ||
The cloud always moves through the sky and releases its water upon the ground below;
likewise, a virtuous wife should always remain devoted to her husband and love him as she would Lord Hari dwelling within.
Just as there are indeed only minute fibers within the trunk of a plantain tree, so too is the essence found within.
In Kṛṣṇa, who is the inner self of all husbands, there are infinitesimal joys.

Without a very firm door, a chain is useless;
likewise, without Kṛṣṇa, the virtue of devotion to one's husband is useless.
Even if a marriage is properly performed, a husband is in vain without the seed.
Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa is the seed; without Him, a husband is merely a falsehood.

Just as in the summer heat, coolness that provides satisfaction does not arise without water, so too in the forest fire of worldly existence, a husband is not a source of bliss by himself without Kṛṣṇa. (28–29)
The Earth, the wife of all, was lifted up by the Boar;

The cowherd women, who were under the control of the cowherds, were rescued by Kṛṣṇa through their devotion.
Kṛṣṇa will certainly uplift a virtuous wife through her devotion to her husband.

Just as a bird has confidence in its egg regarding the chick, so should a wife place her confidence in her husband regarding Mādhava.
As a lineage is hidden in a son, as a tree in a seed, and as desire is latent within embodied beings; ||| 33 ||
Likewise, Hari bestows all desires and grants bliss to both husband and wife.
Milk mixed with a small amount of buttermilk yields butter;
similarly, a master mixed with Kṛṣṇa undoubtedly bestows liberation. (34–35)
A bird perceives the forest region by its own radiance;
a devoted wife perceives her life through Kṛṣṇa, who dwells within her husband;
and the celestial chariot of a sky-dweller moves with speed by means of his divine vision.
Moving along with that, she goes in every way together with the black one situated within it.
Just as a large water-wheel, repeatedly causing the buckets to revolve,
moves them back to their respective places again and again, so too should the virtuous wife go to the place of her husband.

Just as strength increases in the horns of a young calf, so too does strength increase in a wife toward her husband. Just as a boat made of wood certainly carries the wooden planks across, [so does she carry her husband]. 3.9.
Likewise, a wife created by the elements shall deliver her husband through Kṛṣṇa.
Indeed, when the season arrives, hidden flowers surely blossom;
when the husband has arrived, Hari, though hidden, will be made manifest through devotion.
Just as joy arises when a long-absent family member returns, so too, O Kṛṣṇa, may joy arise [for you] regarding your husband.
And just as the meaning contained within a verse shines forth once it has entered the heart.
Likewise, Kṛṣṇa manifests in the heart of the wife through devotion toward her husband.
Radiance is eternally situated in the sun, and blackness is established in Rāhu;
Kṛṣṇa is eternally present in the husband, yet he does not shine in the state of atheism.
All those activities of the Lord are indeed the activities of Kṛṣṇa and nothing else,
for they are divine, bestowing liberation, and are projected within the Supreme Brahman.
The desire, activity, effort, sleep, play, and crushing [of the enemy] of the Lord [are all His own].
Considering everything divine as being of the nature of Kṛṣṇa, the devoted wife,
having become divine and most divine like the splendors of Ramā, Rādhā, and Prabhā,
leads her husband to heaven and goes herself to that which is called the state of no-return.

Thus ends the four hundred and fifteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Wife’s Knowledge of Worshipping Hari as Embodied in Her Husband," within the section on the Greatness of Chaste Wives in the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga, in the first book of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

the daughter of Cākṣuṣa Manu, born from the sacrificial fire-pit."
As soon as she was born, that mental daughter became possessed of the memory of her former births.
A knower of the Vedas, the auspicious sister of Sudyumna, she was the fruit of sacrifice;

"The Earth is my mother and Sadāśiva himself is my father;

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:

Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Sāvitrī, Śivā, and Rādhikā— these are her names.
She who is Kārṣṇī, Rādhā, the Mother of Śiva, Lakṣmī, and Nārāyaṇī,
is indeed the mother of joyful endeavor and is the very nature of the perfect Brahman.
She bestows fame, auspiciousness, dharma, glory, truth, and merit;
she grants liberation and joy, and destroys grief, suffering, and affliction.
She is solely devoted to the protection of the wretched, the distressed, and those who have come for refuge.
Siddheśvarī, Siddharūpā, Siddhidā, Siddhideśvarī;
Intellect, Sleep, Hunger, Thirst, Shadow, Drowsiness, Compassion, Memory;
Birth, Forbearance, Peace, Beauty, Delusion, and Consciousness.

Contentment, Nourishment, Fortune, Conduct, Mother-form, and Wisdom—let these, who are the very embodiment of Lakṣmī and are devoted to their husbands, remain here. Fortune, whose essence is all crops and whose form is the means of livelihood, [should remain]. (6–7)
In Vaikuṇṭha she is Mahālakṣmī, devoted to the service of her husband;
in heaven she is Svargalakṣmī, and among kings she is Rājalakṣmī.
In the home she is Gṛhalakṣmī, and among embodied beings she is Śobhālakṣmī.

The fortune of joy resides in the meritorious; that same fortune of splendor resides in kings. The fortune of trade exists in merchants; the fortune of strife exists among the wicked. The fortune of compassion resides in devotees, and the fortune of wealth resides in the fortunate.
In her substantial form, she consists of gold, gems, rubies, and pearls;
without her, O beloved, the entire world would be as if dead while living.
She is Sarasvatī, the consort of Brahmā, the very embodiment of all knowledge.
Śāradā is the virtuous presiding deity of speech, intellect, learning, and knowledge.

She is also known as Subuddhi (Good Intellect), Kavitā (Poetic Power), Medhā (Retentive Memory), Pratibhā (Inspiration), Smṛti (Recollection), Kalpanā (Imagination), Bodhinī (Awakening), Śakti (Power), Vaktṛtā (Eloquence), and Granthikā (The Knitter). || 12-13 ||
She is the harmony of song, the union of rhythmic clapping, and speech in the form of exposition;
without her, the entire world would be mute, like one dead.
She is Sāvitrī, the Mother of the Vedas, and Brāhmī, appearing in the forms of the twilight prayers and other rites.
She is the form of mantra, the form of tantra, and the form of recitation; she is the ascetic lady.
She is the embodiment of the splendor of Brahmanhood and the form of all purificatory rites.
She is the purifier, the form of sacred pilgrimage sites, and Gāyatrī, the beloved of Brahmā.
She is the progenitor of all splendor, whose form is the light of Brahman’s luster;
without her, the entire world would be blinded by ignorance, like one who is dead.
She is Śivā, Śaivī, Raudrī, Durgā, Kālī, and Caṇḍikā.
She is the embodiment of all powers and the destroyer of all asuras. Devoted to celibacy, she is the form of Brahman and endowed with the quality of goodness (sattva).
She consists of all spiritual perfections; she is Jaya, Vijayā, and Prahāriṇī.
She is the withdrawer and the destroyer, the protector, and the devoted wife;
without her, the entire world would be powerless, as if dead.
She is Rādhā, the daughter of Karṣṇa, the Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā), the supreme devotee of the Lord, and the virtuous one.
Premadevī is equal to his life-breath, dearer than life itself, and the primordial beauty;
she is the supreme power who bestows good fortune, full of self-respect and endowed with dignity.
In her virtues, splendors, and sovereign powers, she is in every way equal to Kṛṣṇa.
She is the supreme and the inferior, the mother of all, blessed, venerable, and worshiped;
she is the presiding deity of the Rāsa-dance of Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul.
Born from the circle of the Rāsa, she is the essence of aesthetic delight and the embodiment of bliss.
The resident gopī of Goloka is the embodiment of both contentment and indignation.
She bestows all service upon Kṛṣṇa, yet remains unattached, being the very nature of the Self.
She grants the singular state of servitude to Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s devotees and all forms of prosperity. (24–25)
She is endowed with the glory of the radiance of ten million moons, her form composed of devotion;
by the touch of whose lotus feet the earth was purified,
she who is the very essence of the jewel among women, abiding upon the chest of Kṛṣṇa.
In the past, Brahmā practiced intense heat-penance for sixty thousand years so that he might behold the lotus feet of Him who grants boons to the best of men and for the sake of his own purification;
yet even in his own independent state, he did not see them— what then need be said of seeing them directly before one's eyes?
In that very same way, she was seen again in the forest of Vṛndāvana through ascetic penance;
that Rādhā was rich with longing for Kṛṣṇa, her form being entirely absorbed in Kṛṣṇa.
Thus, these are the five natures of Brahman, the Supreme Self.
Indeed, those five classes of goddesses are considered to be the most perfect.
All other women are of the nature of partial portions, sub-portions, and further subdivisions of them.
O daughter of the ocean, listen as I describe the principal ones!
The Gaṅgā, born from the lotus feet of Viṣṇu, is liquid in form;
she bestows liberation through being seen, touched, bathed in, and drunk.
White in hue, she is the beloved ladder and staircase to emancipation.
Then another virtuous Tulasī was created, the bestower of liberation;
she is the ornament of Viṣṇu, a chaste woman beloved by Nārāyaṇa,
by the touch of whose lotus feet the earth was instantly purified.
Without whom every action in all the worlds is fruitless,
she who is the embodiment of the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa), the bestower of liberation, and the form of the celestial tree;
she who is the beloved disciple of Śaṅkara and, in her mind, the daughter of Kaśyapa.
Now, another daughter of the Naga king Anantabhogin was known as Jaratkārvī;
she was considered the sovereign of the Nagas, the mother of the Nagas, and a virtuous woman.
Devoted to Viṣṇu, she was the mother of Āstīka and the beloved wife of the sage Jaratkāru. (36–37)
She who performed penance for three hundred thousand divine years for the sake of Hari,
who is of the nature of Brahman, established in yoga, and devoted to Kṛṣṇa and Śambhu as her husband—
she is Devasenā, the sixth goddess, truly devoted to her husband. || 38 ||
She is Mātṛkā, the youthful wife of Kārttikeya;
she is the one who constantly protects children throughout every universe,
the bestower of sons and grandsons, and indeed the nurse of the worlds.
It is fitting that this Yoginī, who has the form of an aged woman, is the supreme [protector] of children;
indeed, her worship should take place sixty times throughout the twelve months.
And the worship of the child should be performed in the lying-in chamber on the sixth day after birth.
And on the twenty-first day, there is a propitiatory rite that brings about auspiciousness.
She takes the form of a mother, the embodiment of compassion, and constantly provides protection.
Whether in water, on land, or in the atmosphere, she watches over children even within their dreams.
Then there is another great goddess, Satī Maṅgalacaṇḍikā,
who was born from the mouth of Prakṛti; she always bestows auspiciousness during creation,
while in the time of dissolution she takes the form of wrath, and she is worshipped on the day of Maṅgala (Tuesday).
She who is worshipped with the five offerings by all women;
she who bestows sons, grandsons, wealth, sovereignty, fame, and auspiciousness;
and she who destroys grief, torment, sin, extreme suffering, and poverty.
When pleased, she fulfills all the desires of every woman;
when enraged, she is capable of destroying the entire circle of the universe in an instant.
Then there was another, Mahākālī, a devoted wife to Śambhu.
Born from the forehead of Durgā, she is the destroyer of both auspicious and inauspicious results in battle.
She is the foremost of all powers, excellent, mighty, and virtuous.
Devoted to Kṛṣṇa, she is equal to Kṛṣṇa in splendor, valor, and qualities. (48–49)
Through her constant contemplation of Kṛṣṇa, she is eternally dark-complexioned and ancient;
she is capable of destroying the entire universe by a mere breath.
Then there is another, the Primal Nature (Pradhāna), who is the virtuous Earth.
She is the foundation of all things, the producer of all crops;
she is the mine of jewels, containing jewels within her, and the locus of all sources of gems;
she is the form upon which all depend for their livelihood, and the bestower of all prosperity.
Without whom the entire world, including all moving and non-moving beings, would be without support—
that goddess Vasundharā, the wife of Varāha, is devoted to her husband. Goddess Svāhā, the wife of Agni, is likewise devoted to her husband and highly honored.
Without her, the gods are not able to accept the sacrificial offering;
she is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), the wife of the sacrifice, and the consecration (dīkṣā) honored at the rite.
Without her, all ritual action in all the worlds is fruitless.
Svadhā is the wife of the Pitṛs, devoted to her husband and well-honored;
without her, the ancestral offerings made at śrāddha and other rites become fruitless.
Svasti is the goddess who is the wife of Vāyu, worshipped in every world.
Without her, both taking and giving would be fruitless;
she is Puṣṭi, the wife of Gaṇapati, honored and devoted to her husband.
Without her, both men and women become utterly wasted away. (57–58)
Anantapatnī and Tuṣṭi are always worshipped and saluted;
without them, all people everywhere would find no contentment.
Sampatti, the consort of Īśāna, is likewise worshipped by gods and men.
All the worlds and all beings would be destitute without her;
Dhṛti, the wife of Kapila, is honored by everyone everywhere. All the worlds would be lacking in fortitude within the universes without her.
She who is the patient, virtuous, and well-behaved wife of Yama, honored by all;
she without whom all the worlds would be utterly distraught and filled with fear—
she is the presiding goddess of play, the chaste Rati, the wife of Kāma.
Without her, all the worlds would be devoid of play and curiosity;
she is the true wife, the virtuous one, liberation personified, honored by the world, and beloved by all.
Without her, the world would be bereft of the sentiment of friendship.
Compassion is the virtuous wife of Delusion; she is honored and beloved by the world.
Without her, all embodied beings in the world would become cruel.
She is the meritorious wife, the foundation, the purifier, and she is worshipped by all.
Without her, the entire world is seen as living dead.
(66) Fame is the wife of good deeds; she is blessed, honorable, and worshipped.
Without her, the entire world is devoid of glory, like one who is dead. (67)
For Action (Kriyā) is the wife of Udyoga; she is honored and associated with all things.
Without her, O Lotus-born One, the entire world would be as if annihilated.
Falsehood (Mithyā), however, is the wife of Adharma; she is honored by all living beings.
Without her, the conduct of rogues—which was ordained by Fate—has been cut off. In the Kṛta age, it does not appear; in the Tretā age, it appears only here and there;
in the Dvāpara age, it exists among those devoid of shame; but in the Kali age, deceit is found in every house. (1.417.70)
Accompanied by his brother Deceit, he wanders indeed from person to person;
Peace and Modesty are his two highly honored wives.
Without these two, the entire world becomes as if insane.
Jñāna has three wives, all of whom are devoted to their husband:
Buddhi, Medhā, and Smṛti; without these, the world is as if dead and deluded.
And Dharmapatnī is his consort, she who is radiant in form and captivating to the mind.
The universe is the progenitor of the Supreme Self, for without her it would be supportless;
she is Lakṣmī, the very embodiment of all splendor, existing as a personified being—Śrī by form and Mūrti by form, venerable, blessed, and worshipped. (74)
She is Nidrā, the wife of Kālāgnirudra, who is the sleep of perfected yogins;
by her, all people in the worlds become inactive during the nights.
She is the terrible, tamasic sleep of men that causes their dissolution.
Time has three auspicious wives—dawn, night, and day—without whom the Creator himself could not even calculate a number.
Hunger and thirst are the two wives of greed; they are blessed, worthy of honor, and highly revered.
By these two the entire world is pervaded, and it always strives for their satisfaction.
Radiance and burning heat are considered the two wives of fire;
without them, the entire world would not attain maturation. (78–79)

Kālaputrī, Mṛtyu, and Jarā are the beloved wives of Prajvara; by means of these two, the world indeed undergoes destruction progressively, one after another. Nidrā’s daughter is named Tandrā, and Prīti is the beloved wife of Sukha.
By these two, the entire world is pervaded and finds rest for a moment.
(81) But detachment has two honored wives, Faith and Service;
by means of these two, the entire world is constantly perceived as liberated while living. (82)
