Lāḍitī is the mother of the gods, Surabhi is the progenitor of cows,
Diti is the mother of the Daityas, Kadrū is the mother of the Nāgas,
Vinatā is the mother of Garuḍa, and Danu is the mother of the Dānavas.
All these devoted wives were employed in the act of creation:
Rohiṇī, the wife of the Moon; Saṃjñā, the beloved of the Sun; Mahālakṣmī, known as Kambharā, the consort of Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa. (84–85)
Śatarūpā was the wife of Manu; Śacī is the consort of Indra;
Tārā is the wife of Bṛhaspati; and Arundhatī belongs to Vasiṣṭha. Ahalyā was the beloved of Gautama, and Anasūyā was the beloved of the sage Atri.
Devahūti was the daughter of Kardama and the wife of Dakṣa.
Asiknī and Paliknī were likewise the two beloved wives of Dakṣa.
And Menā, the mental daughter of the Pitṛs, was the mother of Pārvatī. (87–88)
Lopāmudrā and Hūti were likewise devoted wives of Kubera;
Varuṇānī was the wife of Yama, as was Vindhyāvalī of Bali;
Kuntī was the wife of Pāṇḍu, and Damayantī was the beloved of Nala.
Yaśodā, the wife of Nanda; Draupadī, the beloved of the Pāṇḍavas;
Devakī, the virtuous wife of Vasudeva, who is dear to Hara;
Gāndhārī, the wife of Dhṛtarāṣṭra; and Sāvitrī, the beloved of Satyavān. (1.417.90–91)
The beloved of Vṛṣabhānu, the virtuous Kalāvatī, mother of Rādhā;
Māṇikī, Pārvatī, Lakṣmī, Prabhā, Jayā, and Lalītikā—these are the wives of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the bestowers of auspiciousness and nectar. (92)
Mandodarī was the wife of Rāvaṇa; Kauśalyā was the mother of Rāma.
Subhadrā, Satyabhāmā, Kālindī, Lakṣmaṇā, Mitravindā the daughter of Nagnajit, and the virtuous Jāmbavatī likewise [were wives]. 93–94.
Lakṣmaṇā, Rukmiṇī, Sītā, Lakṣmī, Ramā, Padmā, Padmāvatī, Padminī, Vṛndā, and Śrī are indeed the beloveds of Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa;
they are great saintly women, the dear consorts of the glorious Nārāyaṇa.
Satī, who possessed a fragrance that reached for a league (*yojanagandhā*), the devoted wife who was the mother of Vyāsa;
likewise Uṣā, the daughter of Bāṇa; Khyāti, the devoted wife of Bhṛgu;
and Reṇukā, the virtuous and devoted wife of Jamadagni. ||96-97||
Rohiṇī is the mother of Baladeva; Durgā is the beloved of Hara;
Ekānaṃśā is the beloved of Durvāsas, for she is indeed the sister of Kṛṣṇa. Whatever village goddesses there may be, they are all portions of Prakṛti.
In every universe, women arise as portions of a fraction of that [divine power].
They are devoted to their husbands, virtuous, truthful, and deliverers from the cycle of worldly existence.
By whichever devotee they are honored, Puruṣottama himself is honored.
All those with a preponderance of *sattva* are excellent, virtuous, and devoted to their husbands;
those with a preponderance of *rajas* are middling, longing for enjoyments, pleasures, and the like;
while those with a preponderance of *tamas* are inferior, such as the Dānavīs and others, though they remain dear to their husbands.
Then Lakṣmī was first worshipped with various offerings by Rāmāditya.
First, the goddess Sarasvatī was fully worshipped by Brahmā;
and Sāvitrī was first worshipped with devotion, and thereafter by the gods.
Formerly, Śivā was worshipped by King Suratha;
formerly, Rādhā was worshipped by Kṛṣṇa in the pavilion of the rāsa dance;
and indeed, in Goloka, she was worshipped by the wielder of the Śārṅga bow together with the cowherds and cowherd-maidens.
Therefore, they are worshiped by the worlds as the powers (śaktis) of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s left side.
They are indeed incarnations in the form of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa;
[they grant liberation] through being seen, touched, served, and likewise through being saluted.
O virtuous women, because you are of the nature of Kṛṣṇa, you grant liberation through salutation and worship;
you are not of inferior bodies, but possess divine forms.
You bring about the welfare of the world and protect the dharma of virtuous women.
They are virtuous women, established upon the bull [of dharma], ascetic, and devoted to their husbands;
they are female teachers, wives of Brahman, and truly of the nature of Brahman.
They are givers of mantra, givers of knowledge, givers of dharma and honor, and protectors of all.
All these were manifested by Kṛṣṇa for the purpose of His own descent;
all were sustained by Kṛṣṇa, and Kṛṣṇa is eternally withdrawn within them.
Kṛṣṇa is the right half, and those [energies] are the left powers (vāma-śaktis).
Sovereign powers, supernatural accomplishments, and even the female organs are considered to be her forms. By him who honors a virtuous Brāhmaṇī woman who possesses a husband and sons,
all of them are honored with garments, ornaments, and sandalwood paste.
By him who worships an eight-year-old maiden endowed with sattva,
all those [goddesses] are worshipped with garments, ornaments, and sandalwood paste.
She is virtuous, chaste, a yoginī, and truly observant of celibacy.
By him who has honored the consecrated ascetic woman as well as his own mother,
and by whom Surabhi has been honored, indeed have those [goddesses] been honored.
For on this earth, Rādhā was first honored by Suyajña.

Then, O beloved, as instructed by Śaṅkara, the gods and others [understood that] *śak* denotes sovereignty and *ti* denotes valor. That which is of their very nature, the bestower of penance, and true— that is considered *Śakti*.
*Bhaga* denotes prosperity, intelligence, excellence, and fame.
(1.17) By virtue of that, the Goddess is *Bhagavatī*, and Lord Hari is *Bhagavān*.
He is Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Master and the regulator of his mistresses. (1.18)
In the beginning, Lakṣmī was worshipped by King Maṅgala;
you alone, O Mahālakṣmī, abide here in my presence.
I am Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, and I am also Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa.
I am the glorious Nārāyaṇa, and I am Nara-Nārāyaṇa;
I am Prabhā-Nārāyaṇa, and I am Pārvatī-Nārāyaṇa;
I am Jayā-Nārāyaṇa, and I am Māṇikī-Nārāyaṇa.
I am Ramā-Nārāyaṇa; I am Lalitā-Nārāyaṇa;
I am Padmā-Nārāyaṇa; I am Padminī-Nārāyaṇa;
I am Virāj-Nārāyaṇa; and I am Padmāvatī-Nārāyaṇa.
O beloved, I am Rādhākṛṣṇa as well as Sītārāma at all times;
I am Balanārāyaṇa and I am Brahmanārāyaṇa;
I am Rukmiṇīnārāyaṇa and Vāsudevanārāyaṇa.
I am Nārāyaṇa in the form of swans; I am Nārāyaṇa in the form of beautiful peacocks;
I am Nārāyaṇa in the form of pearls; and I am Nārāyaṇa as the Witness.
This family of Brahmins, devoted to their wives, shall remember me. (125)
"He who hears this, or whoever shall read it, will become destined for liberation.

Thus ends the four hundred and seventeenth chapter, titled "The Manifestation of Lakṣmī and Many Other Chaste Women from Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*. (417)
← Chapter 417: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga) Chapter 418 [Author: Chapter 419 →
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī! I speak before you from my very heart. O beloved, there is nothing whatsoever that I must conceal from you in any way.
I am Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, possessed of unfailing potency.
There is no end to my wives; they are all devoted to their husband.
They bring about the welfare of others and have fixed their devotion upon me.
Those who have performed spiritual construction for my sake were previously manifested by me.
(3) There are countless beloved ones of mine residing in the abode of the imperishable Brahman;
twelve thousand of them are the most excellent beloved ones who have attained the supreme abode. (4)
Some were residents of Goloka, some were indeed gatekeepers;
some were collections of ornaments, and some were attendants at the bedchamber. Some were beloved female associates, and some were protectors of Śrī Vṛndāvana.
Some dwell on Govardhana and create forest groves;
others reside in my own groves by the hundreds and thousands.
Some belong to the herd of Yamunā, while others belong to the herd of Jāhnavī.
Others belonged to the troop of Ramā; others belonged to the troops of Madhu and Mādhavī;
likewise, there were those belonging to the troop of Virajā and those belonging to the troop of Lalitā;
there were also those belonging to the troop of Viśākhā and those belonging to the troop of Māyā.
And likewise the Śrutis, as well as the women of Ārṣya, Maithila, and Kauśala; the Sākettīs, Sītās, and Pulindīs— my beloveds—
are always divine through my yoga, being solely devoted to their husbands.
I cannot enumerate all those wives of mine from previous births;
remembering them, I tell you this so that, upon hearing of your sisters, you may rejoice.
And in the Śvetadvīpa, the Śrutis once praised me as their Lord.
I then became pleased by those longing words;
"Choose a boon that is indeed desired by my mind for you.
The Śrutis replied, "That which is your very nature is pure bliss alone. (12–13)
"If a boon is indeed to be granted to us, then show that divine [realm] to us.
Having heard this, he showed them his own world and the imperishable Brahman. There, the Lord of Beings showed all the wives of Brahmā.
In their midst was Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the Imperishable Abode.
Having revealed Himself, He said to them, "Tell me, what shall I do for you?
Then the Śrutis replied, "Our minds are fixed upon You once You have been seen."
O Lord, we have undoubtedly become filled with the thought of loving you, whose beauty is like ten million Kāmadevas and who have been cast by Smara [into our hearts]. Please accept us;
having obtained you as our lover, may we worship you and make our lives fruitful.
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa said: "This desire is difficult to accomplish;
nevertheless, on the banks of the Yamunā in the universe of Trivikrama, in my field of Vraja upon the earth, you shall become gopīs. (18–19)
"In Vṛndāvana, I shall indeed become your beloved husband in the rāsa dance;
by serving me with the fulfillment of all desires, you shall have accomplished your life's purpose.
Thus spoke all those Vedas, my wives devoted to their husband.

Now hear of others, O Lakṣmī! Long ago, in the age of Rāmāditya—when I, the powerful youth Rāma, carried off Sītā at her svayaṃvara following the breaking of the bow—the people of Mithilā [were there]. (21–22)
Millions of women arrived and were struck with wonder upon seeing me; then,
perceiving them through my role as the Inner Controller (Antaryāmin),
I assumed ten million forms and granted my vision to each individual woman at that very moment.
And those matrons said to me, "Become our husband, O granter of desires.
I said to them, "For my sake,
perform sacred ablutions, acts of charity, austerities, penances, recitations, and constant remembrance [of me]."
Therefore, through supreme faith and devotion after the age of Dvāpara, I, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, shall become your beloved husband and fulfill your heart's desires;
O gopīs of Vraja, you shall become my wives.
"Having served me with the objects of desire, you shall have fulfilled your purpose.
Then, having conquered Bhārgava and taken that virtuous Sītā, I set out for Kosala;
and on the way, the women of Kosala approached me.
Seeing a handsome youth, they chose him as their husband with their minds.
To them, assuming ten million forms and granting a divine touch, I gave this boon:
"I shall fulfill your heart's desires."
"By performing *japa* with devotion to me, you shall become *gopīs* in Vraja;
by serving me through the fulfillment of desires, you shall have accomplished your life's purpose.
Then, having seen him in the city of Sāketa, the women of Sāketa..."

At that moment, having fallen into a state of delusion, they performed austerities while maintaining their vows, certain that the attainment of Rāma would occur in his own beloved form. And Rāma spoke to them through a voice from the sky: "Your heart's desires shall be fulfilled."
They shall become true and perfect on the banks of the Yamunā at the end of the Dvāpara age.
Having served me through the fulfillment of desires, you shall achieve all your goals.
Then, O beloved, when I depart for the forest in the form of Rāma...
The cowherd women of the Daṇḍaka forest were infatuated with me out of desire;
the Kirāta women and the ladies of the forest were likewise infatuated with me and chose me as their husband.
I granted them this boon: "At the end of the Dvāpara age, you shall come to be [with me]."
"I shall surely fulfill the desires of you gopīs, for I am your husband.
Having spoken thus, he who was indeed in the form of Rāma then departed for Pañcavaṭī.
There, the Pulindī women, overwhelmed with love, suffered from the pain of longing caused by the memory of seeing him.
Having touched the dust of Rāma’s feet, they approached Rāma, who was embraced by them;
Rāma spoke to those women of broken hearts regarding his vow of fidelity to his wife,
and they became filled with longing once more for Vṛndāvana.
"At the end of the Dvāpara age, you shall be fully perfected in me, my beloved. Having served me through the fulfillment of your desires, you will have accomplished your purpose.
Then, having seen Rāma on the island of Rāvaṇa, the wives of the twice-born—
Filled with devotion, they were bewildered and chose him in their minds.
Then, he granted them a vision in a dream and spoke to them:
"On the banks of the Yamunā, I shall act in every way in a beautiful form."
Then your desire shall grant you the bliss of love;
by serving me through the dharma of passion, you will have fulfilled your purpose.
Then, having arrived at the city of Sāketa, he performed many sacrifices.
And there, women who had arrived from various regions and foreign lands made their appearance;
and having beheld Rāma, they chose him as their mental husband.
Then, O beloveds, Rāma granted them a boon regarding Gokula.
"You shall all become mine; I will fulfill your desires. By serving me with the pleasures of passion, you shall have accomplished your purpose.
Then, following the abandonment of Sītā, [he performed] golden [sacrifices] during the rituals.
A collection of those [gopīs], formed for each sacrifice, came to the abode of Hari;
and having become embodiments of pure consciousness, they arrived to sport with Rāma.
Rāma said, "I do not accept them, for I am bound by the vow of having only one wife."
Then they said: "O Lord, why do you not accept your wives?
At the times of sacrifice, they always assist in accomplishing the rites with half their bodies.
By taking their hand [in marriage] and then abandoning them, you will incur sin. (48-49)
Rāma then said: "Sītā, whose nature is truth, is my beloved; she is one and not another, while you all are indeed her very shadow.
Therefore, I shall fulfill your heart's desire in another birth."
"At the end of the Dvāpara age, you shall be born in Vṛndāvana on the Yamunā.
Thus those Yajñasīs became my beloved Gopīs.
Now, O Lakṣmī, hear of my other wives belonging to the next world.
The Ramās who dwell in Vaikuṇṭha, the female companions of Śvetadvīpa,
those who reside in Urdhva-Vaikuṇṭha, as well as those who have taken refuge at the feet of Ajita;
the inhabitants of Śrīloka-parvata, the female friends of Śrī, and those born from the ocean.
And those [goddesses] indeed became the gopīs in Vraja, who were truly dear to me.
Then all the other goddesses gathered in Vṛndāvana;
they became my wives, numbering in the hundreds of millions and billions.
All the creeping medicinal plants performed austerities on the bank of the Yamunā;
they then became women who had fallen into a state of delusion and arrived at the rāsa dance. Through the influence of desire, they all then attained their fulfillment.
Then the women of Jālandhara, beholding me as the lord of Vṛndā, chose me as their beloved. Viṣṇu then said to them:
"Becoming women in the forest of Vṛndā, you shall worship me, your dear ones."
The daughters of the ocean, having seen the glorious Fish-form of Hari, were utterly infatuated;
by virtue of the boon granted by the glorious Fish, they became my beloved gopīs.
Those women who were bewildered upon seeing both Pṛthu and me in the kingdom of Pṛthu—
Those gopīs, by the command of Nārāyaṇa for the purpose of enchanting the army of Kāma, became beloved of Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the earth;
they were divine hosts of apsarases manifested from the thighs of Nara. (1.418.60–61)
Having seen the excellent Nārāyaṇa, they were then bewildered.
Hari said: "O gopīs, you shall become [the gopīs] on the bank of the Yamunā;
by serving me through the practice of desire, you shall have fulfilled your purpose."
The women dwelling in the world of the sons of Suta were enchanted upon seeing Vāmana.
Having received a boon from him, those Gopīs became daughters of the lords of Nāgas on the bank of the Yamunā, having seen Kṛṣṇa with devotion and a desire for that boon. (63–64)
On the bank of the Yamunā, those gopīs intensely entreated me;
having served me according to the law of desire, my women felt their purpose was fulfilled.
Yet, when I appeared before others such as Kapila in the form of a celibate student, they [perceived me] only as such.
Having seen them, those women were enchanted and became my lawful wives (66).
All these virtuous wives of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa were devoted to their husbands;
through union with Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, they became divine like Rādhā and Ramā (67).
Constantly devoted to their husbands and ever-abiding by my dharma, there are always millions upon millions,
billions upon billions, trillions upon trillions,
and quintillions upon quintillions of wives who are faithful to their husbands, O beloved, who belong to me.
And there are innumerable eggs within the hair-pores of Vairāja;
in each of those eggs, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara—
manifesting in my own form— are indeed appointed throughout millions of cosmic eggs.
"In that place, there are millions of my beloveds, each possessing individual splendor.
Behold, O Lotus-born One! I grant you here a supreme, divine vision.
Thus did Viṣṇu bestow that great divine vision upon her.
She gazed upon her husband Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa—
within every atom— as the Lord of Śrī, the Lord of Lakṣmī, the beloved Lord of Ramā,
the Master of Pārvatī, the Lord of Prabhā, and the Lord of Śrīmāṇikī. (72–73)
To Hari, the Lord of Rādhā; to the Master of Padmā; to the Lord of Kambharā;
to the Lord of Padmāvatī; to the Lord of all virtuous women; to the Lord of Rukmiṇī;
to the Lord of Māyā; to the Sovereign; to the Lord of Nārāyaṇī; to the Lord of Vaiṣṇavī.

Having seen Kṛṣṇa— the Lord of ascetics, the Master of the Sāṃkhya and Yoga practitioners, the Lord of maidens, the Lord of the Vedas, and the Great King— she rejoiced. Quickly turning her gaze away, she fell at the feet of Kṛṣṇa.
Indeed, by merely beholding the majesty of the Lord, even a hundred million [beings] come to understand it;
and by hearing or reciting this, one shall attain the state of being a servant of Kṛṣṇa.

Thus ends the section on the majesty of the devoted wife within the first book, the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga, concerning the countless devoted wives of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
The four hundred and eighteenth chapter, titled "The Exposition," [Chapter 418].
*Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga).
Chapter 419.
[The Author: Chapter 420.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī! To the duties of virtuous women (*satī-dharmān*), which bestow both heaven and liberation.
Truthful and always devoted to the duties of her husband, she was honored on earth.
In the forest of Vyāghra in Saurāṣṭra, on the bank of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake,
at Kuṅkumavāpī, at the beginning of creation, there was a twice-born man named Gopālakṛṣṇa.
Then, having departed for the forest for the sake of asceticism,
his devoted wife Kambharālakṣmī joyfully prostrated herself before her husband.
Her husband said, "O beloved, I am going to the forest to perform penance."
"Stay here in this leaf-hut in the presence of the sage's family until I have returned from my ascetic penance.
Then that devoted wife, Kambharā, her eyes filled with tears— || 4–5 ||
Then that virtuous woman spoke beneficial words with humility to her husband:
"O son of Brahmā! Father, mother, brother, son, and likewise daughter-in-law—all these enjoy their own merits and experience their respective fortunes. (6)
Indeed, only the wedded wife attains the fortune of her husband.
Therefore, I shall by all means come with you to the forest;
for neither father, nor son, nor one's own self, nor mother, nor friends can [share] that.
In this world and after death, the husband alone is always the refuge for women.
If you are departing for the difficult forest inhabited by ascetics,
I shall go before you, enduring the kusha grass and thorns.
"Lead me, O Lord, with confidence; no evil exists within me.
Whether on the roof of a palace, in celestial chariots, or traveling through the air—in every circumstance, the shadow of a husband's feet is superior."
I shall dwell happily in the forest, adorned by my husband’s feet,
not thinking of the three worlds but contemplating my devotion to my husband;
ever serving you, self-restrained, and living as a celibate student.
"I shall enjoy myself with you, O Brahmin, in the forests fragrant with honey;
I shall always subsist on fruits and roots, of this there is no doubt. Dwelling always with you, I shall never cause you any distress. (13–14)
I shall go before you and eat only after you have eaten;
devoted to you, I shall perform my ablutions together with you.
I shall not know any transgression, for wherever you may be, that indeed is heaven for me.

Without you, I do not even find that great heaven to be pleasing. Wherever you may be, whether it be a house or a forest, I shall go there; for me, even a forest that is difficult to endure becomes easy to bear when I am with you.
Then the Brahmin, the abode of dharma, remembering the sufferings in the forest, did not set his mind on taking the virtuous Kambharā—who was thus resolved—along with him.
He said: "O wife, O ever-virtuous one, O beloved devoted to dharma!"
Practice righteousness here in this world according to what brings peace to my mind.
In the forest, suffering is indeed abundant; the forest is always full of hardship.
Encounters with predatory creatures and wicked beings in the forest are painful.
During the rainy season, waters filled with crocodiles and rivers covered in mud are painful for bathing and crossing, and they inspire fear.
Likewise, rutting elephants, wild beasts in heat, and demons and the like cause great suffering.
Indeed, that forest is full of hardship, with its creeping vines, thorns, and stones. (22) One sleeps on beds of leaves upon the ground at night in the forest;
one must subsist on leaves, fruits, petals, and roots, finding contentment therein. (23)
In some cases, one might even have to observe fasts without any food at all;
wear matted hair and don garments of bark.
The forest, with its baths and other rites involving cold and hot water, is a place of great hardship.
One should practice contentment with whatever is obtained, whether fresh or dried [meat].
Excessive wind, darkness, and hunger arise constantly; indeed, even great fears that cause suffering arise. (25–26)
There are many reptiles of various guises wandering in the forest, and rogues who dwell by the rivers; therefore, the forest is even more miserable than that.
In the forest, there are flies, scorpions, insects, gadflies, and mosquitoes.
"O weak one! In the forest, everything is constantly more painful:
there are thorny trees such as the *badarī* and *barbara*, and there are blades of *kuśa* grass and other sharp things that pierce the feet; therefore, the forest is even more painful. (28–29)
"There are many bodily afflictions and various fears;
lust and anger must be abandoned, and the mind should be set upon austerity.
Having heard these words of Gopālakṛṣṇa, the virtuous Kambharā—
With her face bathed in tears, she spoke these words softly:
"Those faults you have enumerated regarding dwelling in the forest—I, who am devoted to my husband, know them only as virtues. (3.1–32)
Deer, lions, elephants, tigers, leopards, śarabhas and the like, yaks, sṛmaras, and other wild animals, as well as predatory men—
whether they be cruel or obstacle-creating— shall depart by the power of Brahmanic luster.

O Kṛṣṇa! Because of separation from you, my life would surely have to be abandoned. For no one at all, O Lord, would be able to violate me while I am by your side, as I am so well protected by my devotion to my husband.
"A woman who is deprived of her husband will truly not be able to live.
Therefore, O Lord, an order must be received here from your own mouth.
Having received your command, I shall go along with you. (36)
"Living in the forest always shines most brightly to me; it would be a source of happiness.
For a female mendicant of tranquil conduct like myself, there would be even greater bliss. By following my husband, I shall find fulfillment, for the husband is indeed the supreme deity."
"Even in the life hereafter, may my union with you in the forest be auspicious;
especially so, O lady of the Brahmins, among the circle of Brahmin women.
Indeed, in this world, whatever woman belongs to whichever twice-born man through her ancestors,"

"O Brahmin, she who was given by the waters according to her own dharma remains his even in the afterlife. (1.419.40) Thus [he spoke]. Indeed, [protect] your own wife, who is well-conducted, devoted to her husband, faithful, virtuous, and equal in both pleasure and pain. (1.419.41)
O best of Brahmins, you ought to take me with you, for I share equally in joy and sorrow.
If you do not wish to take me, your own handmaid, to the forest,
I shall resort to poison, fire, water, or the noose for the sake of death.

Know me to be devoted to you, like Sāvitrī to Dyumatsena’s heroic son Satyavān; I am under your control in this forest. Therefore, it is not fitting for you to go to the forest for the sake of asceticism without taking me with you.
Whether it be austerity, or the forest, or even heaven itself, let it be with you; for in the forest,
let there be predatory creatures who are great devotees of the Lord,
and let thorns, pebbles, and muddy grounds be pleasant to me.

O Lord, even the great winds and all the dust are like sandalwood in the forest to me; with you, the grassy grounds are a source of happiness. Even a very small amount of leaves, roots, fruits, and water in the forest becomes abundant for me. (46–47)
If you grant me your grace, it shall become for me the essence of nectar;
serving my husband while enjoying the seasonal flowers, I shall never again cause him grief.
For my sake, you shall have no sorrow, nor shall I be a source of grief to you.
"That which is with you is heaven; that which is without you is hell.
I must either die without you or live with you—this is my resolve, O virtuous lady. Be gracious, O Mādhava! (1.419.50)
"O Lord, I cannot endure separation from you for even a moment.
O Lord, once abandoned by you, death would be better for me.
Having heard these words of his beloved, the husband spoke to her.
"Follow me, O Goddess! Be my partner in dharma. O virtuous one, you have undertaken a resolve that is in every way worthy of me and of your own lineage; O beloved, it is most excellent. (52–53)
"O Kambharā! Now heaven itself does not please me without you.
Make your departure for the sake of the forest, wherever it may be most auspicious.
For there is no fear whatsoever from either the forest or the mountain in the woods. (54)
"O Kambarā, since you were created by me together with myself for the sake of dharma and purpose, I cannot abandon my beloved who is devoted to her husband;
for dharma is the most excellent, and Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa himself is my very self. (55-56)
He declared the *patnīvrata* (the vow of devotion to a husband) to be supreme; he made me a portion of that.
O Goddess of gods! through your yoga, even women who dwell in the forest shall become devoted to dharma, performing asceticism and being exceedingly faithful to their husbands.

Neither truth, nor charity, nor honor, nor even a sacrifice accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees, produces such strength as the dharma consisting of devotion to one’s wife. Likewise, heaven, wealth, grain, knowledge, sons, and pleasures [are not as effective]. (58–59)

Nothing is difficult for you to attain by virtue of your devotion to your husband. Noble virtuous women who are solely devoted to the service of their husbands reach the worlds of the gods, the Gandharvas, Goloka, Brahma-loka, and even those beyond.
"Follow me, O beloved; be my partner in dharma.
Having spoken thus, that great virtuous lady Mahālakṣmī Kambharā went with her husband to the Siṃhāraṇya forest for the sake of asceticism.
The illustrious twice-born Gopālakṛṣṇaka, devoted to his wife,
went with his wife to Siṃhāraṇya to achieve perfection through austerity.
On the eastern bank of the Hiraṇyā, he performed most rigorous penance.
For a full thousand years, he remained without food together with his wife.
Then the divine Lord Puruṣottama himself appeared from his abode,
accompanied by Dharma and Bhakti, and joined by Lalitā, Śrī, and Jayā.
He granted them direct vision of Himself and said, "Choose a boon.
Then the husband and wife spoke to Kṛṣṇa: "O Blessed One, if You are pleased with us, then always remain in our home in this very form."
"O Lord, you must protect the Dharma for both of us in every way.
O Kṛṣṇa, remain ever before our eyes and be the bestower of happiness. O All-pervading One, do not abandon us according to the requirements of the age! (67–68)
"I am a brahmin devoted to my wife, and she is a virtuous woman devoted to her husband.
Having first observed the true time and thereafter perceiving through yoga and meditative absorption the impending loss of time," [69]

O ocean of compassion, through austerity, through celibacy, and likewise through your grace, I meditate so that my laughter may not become devoid of dharma; O ocean of compassion, grant me the fruit of my austerities so that this may come to pass.
"So be it," he then said; and likewise, he spoke of the discourse on Time.
Kambharā and Hari, that first couple, listened as Hari described the divisions of time, the phenomena of time, and the decline of Dharma.
"And at all times, for the sake of protection, I shall accept our status as good sons;
I shall always remain present in divine form near you both.
Having spoken thus, Kṛṣṇa became invisible, and the husband and wife went to their home.
[The Author: Chapter 421 → Śrī Lakṣmī said:
What are those duties, how were they proclaimed, and how indeed does the decline of the ages occur?
"When was Kṛṣṇa, and when did the divine Lord become invisible?
(1) Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: "Listen, Lakṣmī! I shall tell you what I spoke at that time."
Listen, Lakṣmī, to how protection was provided by me against the changes of time and the characteristics of the ages. In the Kṛta Yuga, people took refuge in virtues such as truth;
they indeed consumed as food that which was called "earth-essence."
Those creatures moved according to their will, established in mental perfection;
for them there existed neither merit nor demerit, and those creatures were without distinction.
In that Kṛta Yuga, their lifespan, happiness, and form were equal.
At the beginning of the Kalpa, during the Kṛta Yuga, merit (dharma) and demerit (adharma) did not yet exist.
In that Kṛta Yuga, they were born according to their respective capacities.
That [Yuga] lasted for four thousand years by divine reckoning.
They say the first age is the Kṛtayuga, consisting of one hundred and eight periods of twilight (sandhyā).
Then, even though those progeny had multiplied by the thousands,
there was no hostility among them, nor any duality, nor even any exhaustion.
Dwelling among mountains and oceans, they indeed have no fixed abodes;
free from sorrow, abundant in purity (*sattva*), their subjects are perpetually happy.
They move about without desire, their minds always joyful. (8–9)
The time was one of every sensual pleasure, for there was neither excessive heat nor cold;
their desires were fulfilled by the mind, and they were present everywhere and at all times.
Indeed, on this earth, those who were meditated upon by them arose, overflowing with essence.
Their perfection brings strength and complexion and destroys disease. With bodies requiring no refinement, those subjects possess enduring youth.
From their pure intention, offspring are born as pairs.
Their birth and form were equal, and they died together.
At that time, truth, freedom from greed, forbearance, contentment, happiness, and self-restraint [prevailed].
Indeed, they were all without distinction in terms of appearance, lifespan, conduct, and activities.
The conduct of living beings arises spontaneously, without being preceded by conscious intent.
In the Kṛta Yuga, there was no engagement in either auspicious or sinful actions;
there were no fixed regulations for castes and stages of life, nor was there any intermixture at that time.
Free from desire and aversion, they live in mutual harmony;
equal in form and lifespan, they are devoid of the distinctions of low or high. Indeed, in the Kṛta Yuga, beings are born for the most part in happiness and free from sorrow.

Those great beings of immense strength possess minds that are eternally joyful. (17) For them, gain and loss, friend and foe, and the pleasant and unpleasant do not exist; for those who are free from desire, sense objects proceed as mere mental phenomena. (18)
In that [Kṛta Yuga], they did not desire one another's possessions, nor indeed did they seek to favor them.
In the Kṛta Yuga, meditation was prevalent; in the Tretā, knowledge was predominant.
Sacrifices were undertaken in the Dvāpara, while charity is practiced in the Kali Yuga.
Sattva was established in the Kṛta age, Rajas in the Tretā, and Rajas-Tamas in the Dvāpara.
In the Kali age, Tamas alone is to be known, according to the influence of the ages' progression.
In that [Kali] age, all the perfections of the Kṛta age became diminished by one quarter.
When that accomplishment had perished after it was achieved, another accomplishment came into being:
when subtlety had entered the waters, they then existed upon the earth in the form of clouds.
From those thundering clouds, the release of rain proceeded.
When the surface of the earth was thus united with that single rain,
trees appeared then, serving as dwellings for them; from those trees,
everything required for their enjoyment was produced.
For at the beginning of the Tretā Yuga, those beings brought forth offspring from them;
then, after a long time, a reversal occurred among them,
and a state consisting of passion and greed arose quite suddenly.
That which occurs for women at the end of their life is the *ārtava* (menstrual flow).
Therefore, by that very same yoga, let them then engage in union as couples;
because it is produced at that time for them, let them approach [their husbands] month after month.
Indeed, at that time, the menses appeared out of season and pregnancy occurred;
yet, due to the reversal of those [natural processes] by that impending time, all those trees situated within their homes perished. (28)
Then, when those [trees] had vanished, they became bewildered and their senses were distressed.
At that time, being intent upon truth, they meditated upon that perfection;
and those trees appeared for them, established as their dwellings.
From them are produced garments, fruits, and ornaments;
within those very fruits of theirs is born honey, endowed with fragrance, color, and flavor, which is free from bees and possesses great potency. (3.1) In every single blossom-cup there is honey.
At that time, during the Tretā Yuga, they lived happily;
indeed, through that perfection, the subjects were joyful, contented, and free from affliction.
Yet, after a further interval of time, they were once again enveloped by greed.
They forcibly seized those trees, which were like honey-bees’ honey;
and because of that transgression against them, committed by the people of the world,
the *kalpavṛkṣas* perished here and there along with the honey.
When that [day] had almost ended due to the onset of twilight, their couples then arose;
and because of the intense cold, wind, and heat, they became exceedingly distressed. (35–36)
Afflicted by the pairs of opposites, they constructed shelters;
having provided remedies for those pairs, they indeed resorted to dwellings.
They lived in those dwellings according to what was appropriate and according to their pleasure.
In the Marudhanva regions, in lowlands, on mountains, and by rivers;
they take refuge in fortresses, in arid wastes, and in places with perennial water;
according to necessity and according to their desire, whether on level ground or uneven terrain. (38–39)
They indeed began to construct dwellings to ward off cold and heat;
thereafter, they established hamlets,
cities, villages according to their respective portions, and likewise inner apartments.

Measuring with their own fingers again and again according to their wisdom, they then established the lengths, widths, and internal arrangements of those cities; they likewise determined the dimensions for the various objects of the mind.
Having reflected again and again, they began to act so that those trees which were formerly situated as houses would remain as such;
indeed, they constructed beautiful halls upon the branches of the trees.
Having suffered those afflictions caused by the pairs of opposites, they reflected upon the means of livelihood.
When the *kalpavṛkṣa* trees had vanished along with the honey,
those subjects became overwhelmed with despair, characterized by thirst and hunger.

Then, in the Tretā Yuga, the power of bestowing food appeared for them; furthermore, another means of livelihood, the pursuit of wealth through agriculture, arose according to their desire. Rainwater collected in depressions became streams and rivers.
At that time, the low-lying lands took the form of lakes and ponds;
they became forever conducive to the growth of crops. Then, through the union of water and earth, medicinal herbs came to exist within them.
Then those medicinal herbs were born that yield flowers, roots, and fruits;
they grew without being ploughed or sown, and their flowers and fruits appeared according to the seasons.
At that time, during the Tretā Yuga, all living beings subsisted upon those herbs.

Then, once again, passion and greed arose in them in every respect. Thereupon, they seized the rivers, fields, and mountains, as well as the trees, shrubs, and medicinal herbs, by force according to their strength.
There, some take hold of others and cause them to suffer;
some are peaceful, while others are harsh and cruel. Some people are malicious in their actions, some are radiant, and others are weak.
Then the servants of the powerful became weak.
Thus, while they were thus at odds with one another and had fallen into mutual conflict,
those medicinal herbs were then lost and carried away.

Then, when those [plants] had perished and the Tretā age was drawing to a close, the subjects, desiring to obtain a means of subsistence, approached Prajāpati. And at that time, Brahmā indeed placed mental seeds upon the earth.
Having fashioned them out of what was cast [into the earth], medicinal herbs were produced;
and in every way, crops became ripened by cultivation. Then the powerful Brahmins sustained themselves by means of those [herbs and crops].
Those Brāhmaṇas, authorized by Brahmā, provided protection for other Kṣatriyas who had sought refuge,
as well as for the Vaiśya castes who served as their livelihood-providers during the dissolution of the Yuga. ||58|| They thus established these roles, having been approved by Brahmā.
Brahmā, however, ordained their duties and laws once again;
likewise, the subjects protected the laws with devotion. Living according to the duties of their respective castes, they lived together in mutual harmony. (1.420.60)

Having understood that matter, Brahmā established for the Brāhmaṇas their Vedic duties of officiating at sacrifices and teaching, as well as the third means of livelihood, the acceptance of gifts. He ordained for the Kṣatriyas strength, punishment, and warfare as their means of subsistence.
The Lord assigned cattle-rearing, trade, and agriculture to the Vaiśyas;
he established the livelihood of crafts and wages for the fourth [the Śūdras].
Having thus provided them with means of livelihood through their respective labors, he then assigned them specific dwellings.
Indeed, for those devoted to their respective duties in other worlds,
it is as follows: the realm of Prajāpati belongs to the Brāhmaṇas, that of Mahendra to the Kṣatriyas,
the station of Marut to the Vaiśyas, and that of Gandharva to the servant.
Then Brahmā himself established the stages of life (āśramas) according to dharma.
First, the stage of the householder was ordained as consisting of the four social classes (cāturvarṇya);
it is the foundation and the very source of the other three stages of life.
Wife, sacred fires, hospitality, sacrifices, ancestral rites, and progeny— this, indeed,
is the summary of the duties of a householder.
Furthermore, he should carry a staff, wear a girdle, sleep on the ground, and likewise have matted hair.
Service to the teacher, living on alms for the sake of knowledge, and the wearing of bark, leaves, and skins are the duties of the student.
For those dwelling in the forest, there shall be grain, roots, fruits, and herbs, as well as immersion in water at both twilights and the performance of fire oblations. (68–69)
Alms-seeking after midday, non-stealing, purity, vigilance, celibacy, compassion for all beings,
forbearance, freedom from anger, service to the teacher, and truthfulness— this is the tenfold dharma.
Indeed, for a person whose inner being is corrupted, all external actions fail to succeed,
even if they exert great efforts;
for one who gives away even their entire possessions with a defiled inner self, [their deeds bear no fruit].
One would not be a partaker of the Dharma by that alone; rather, the underlying state of being (*bhāva*) is the cause here.

Then, in the latter part of the Tretā age, everything such as the Age of Virtue (*vṛṣa*) and so forth was again destroyed during the twilight period due to the mutual oppression of living beings and their resulting afflictions.
Then the king, the ministers, the emperors, and likewise the rulers—[they established] the existence of beings among the things of the world, among humans, cattle, and birds;
in fields, in occupations, and everywhere in the means of livelihood. (74–75)
O Lakṣmī! Everywhere, the religious duties were practiced according to their specific injunctions:
truthfulness, charity, compassion, sacrifice, and recitation—these five, along with all others, existed then in three parts; thus the religious duties were maintained by one quarter. (76)

O Lakṣmī, in the Dvāpara age, unrighteous Asuras—especially those characterized by tamas—prevailed; yet the subjects were primarily devoted to sacrifice. There, the Ṛṣis composed easy-to-follow Smṛtis and rules.
Therein were established the livelihoods of the gods, the livelihoods of brahmins, and the livelihoods of servants;
the livelihoods of artisans, craftsmen, and the like were also fashioned there.
Furthermore, the existence of marriage and other [social rites] for women was determined therein.
The right of inheritance for sons born of the womb has indeed been firmly established.
The right of inheritance for disciples and daughters has been apportioned;
likewise, the inheritance of the earth by kings over their subjects has been defined both generally and specifically.
In this world, the means of livelihood and the various occupations have been determined;
the meanings of words such as "father" and "son" are applied to individual persons.
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to how these were set in motion in the world by you.

The father is declared to be the provider of the seed, and the mother is the bearer of the embryo. (83) The husband of a woman who has no offspring is proclaimed an "upapitā" (secondary father), and the wife of one who does not bear a child is proclaimed an "upamātā" (secondary mother). (84)
The grandfather is the father of one’s father; his father is the great-grandfather (*prapitāmaha*).
The maternal grandfather (*mātāmaha*) is the father of one’s mother; his father is the maternal great-grandfather (*pramātāmaha*).
The paternal grandmother is the mother of one’s father; her sister is the paternal great-grandmother (*prapitāmahī*).

And she who is to be fully known by hearing of her is the great-great-grandmother (vṛddhaprapitāmahī). The maternal grandfather (mātāmaha), the mother’s mother, and she who is honored as equal to one's own mother should be known as the paternal grandmother (pramātāmahī); she is the beloved of the paternal grandfather (pramātāmaha).
The mother of one’s maternal grandfather is to be known as such, as is the wife of that [grandfather].
The father’s brother is the paternal uncle (*pitṛvya*), while the mother’s brother is the maternal uncle (*mātula*).
The father’s sister, the mother’s paternal aunt, and the mother’s sister are likewise recorded [as kin].

*Sūnu*, *tanaya*, *putra*, *dāyāda*, and likewise *ātmaja*—these terms denote a male offspring who is an heir and born of virility; they are used for a son. For a female offspring, *janyā*, *duhitṛ*, *kanyā*, and *ātmajā* are prescribed.
The son’s wife is known as *vadhū*; the husband of a daughter is *jāmātṛ*.
The husband is called *priya*, *bhartṛ*, and *svāmī*, and he also behaves toward his beloved as such.
The husband’s brother is *devara*; the husband’s sister is *nanāndṛ*.
The father-in-law is the father of one’s husband; the mother-in-law is the mother of one’s husband.
The wife is proclaimed by the names jāyā, priyā, kāntā, strī, and patnī.
The brother of the wife is called śyālaka, and the sister of the wife is called śālikā.
The wife, the mother, and likewise the mother-in-law; the father and the father-in-law are recorded as such.
The uterine brother is known as *sagarbha*, and the uterine sister is known as *sagarbhā*.
The son of the sister is the *bhāgineya*, and the son of the brother is the *bhrātṛputraka*.

The husband of one’s sister’s daughter, the lover of one’s sister, and the husband of one’s sister [are all addressed as *bhaginīpati*]. The brother-in-law (*śyālīpati*) and the brother [are addressed as *bhrātṛ*] because of their identity with the father-in-law (*śvaśura*).
O Sage, the father-in-law should be known as equal to the father who gave birth. (95–96)
The giver of food, the protector from fear, the husband who protects his wife,
the giver of knowledge, and the giver of birth— these five are the fathers of men. The mother who gives birth, the one who nourishes with milk, and the giver of knowledge are the mothers of men.
The wife of one who gives food, a sister, the wife of a teacher, a mother, her co-wife, a daughter, and likewise the beloved of a son;
a mother’s mother, a father’s mother, and likewise a mother-in-law or a father’s sister. (98–99)

The paternal uncle’s wife, the maternal uncle’s wife, and the mother—these are the sixteen [kinds of women with whom intercourse is forbidden]. The grandson is [the son] of the son, and the great-grandson is [the son] of that [grandson's] son as well. Those who are his sons and so forth, belonging to the lineage and born of the family, are proclaimed [as his kin].
The daughter’s son is the *dauhitra*; his sons and so forth are considered *bāndhavas*.
Sons of sisters and other such men are remembered as *bāndhavas*.
The sons of a brother’s son and their descendants are, furthermore, remembered as *jñātayas*. (101–102)
The teacher’s son, as well as his brother, are to be supported as supreme kinsmen;
likewise, the teacher’s daughter is to be supported like a sister and is equal to one’s own mother.
And for a son, the teacher’s brother is to be supported as a very affectionate kinsman.
The father-in-law of a son is considered his brother-in-law and matrimonial kinsman (bandhu).
The relationship with the father-in-law of a daughter is likewise proclaimed;
he is both her preceptor and a most affectionate brother. (104–105)
The teacher, the father-in-law, and brothers are proclaimed to be equal to one's own preceptor.
He with whom one shares kinship is celebrated as a friend.
A friend should be known as one who bestows happiness, while one who causes suffering is called an enemy.

By fate, a kinsman may become a giver of suffering, while one who is unrelated may become a giver of happiness. (107) In this world, for all people on the surface of the earth, relationships are proclaimed to be of three kinds:
those born of learning, those born of birth, and those born of affection. (108)
A friend born of affection should be known as a relationship that is very difficult to find.
A friend’s mother and a friend’s wife are undoubtedly equal to one’s own mother.
A friend’s brother and a friend’s father are for men equal to a brother and a father, respectively.

The fourth [chapter] concerns the connection of names; it arises everywhere among men. (1.420.110) A *jāra* and an *upapati* are terms for one who commits sexual union with a relative or a corrupt woman. A *navajñā*, a *preyasī*, and a *cittahāriṇī* refer to a beloved wife. (111)
The paramour is equal to the husband, and the housewife is equal to the new wife;
such words have come into use in the Dvāpara age, arising from worldly conventions.
In every age, the practices of those who are powerful do not constitute a fault.
Then, at the transition of the Dvāpara age, I became Kṛṣṇa, the protector.
I became the guardian of dharma, the destroyer of the Daityas, and the benefactor of the ascetics.
Indeed, when many afflictions arose regarding the dharmas in the Kali age, [I acted].
When four thousand years of the Kali age have passed on earth, the Gaṅgā and other rivers, as well as the sacred fords (tīrthas) and the deities,
will indeed go to the divine world; at that time, the son of Kambharā [will also depart].
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa will establish the Dharma upon the earth.
He is the son of Gopālakṛṣṇa, the Teacher who is the Lord himself;
he is the beloved of Śrī Rādhā-padminī and the husband of Kamalā and Pārvatī.
Māṇikīśa, the Lord of Prabhā-lakṣmī and the Supreme Lord of Ramā,
having established the Bhāgavata dharma in the world, will indeed go to the forest. Then, when a hundred times a hundred cycles of time have passed, Dharma shall return to the abode of Brahmā.
The bridges of Dharma that have been established will once again meet with destruction.
(11.9) Within a thousand years, the Śālagrāma—the form of Hari, the Lord of the Universe—along with the sacred narratives, all shall go to the abode of Śrī Hari. (1.420.120)
The Vaiṣṇava Saṃhitā texts, the conch shells, the ancestral rites of Śrāddha and libations,
and the rituals prescribed in the Vedas— all these shall likewise go to their destruction.
So too shall the worship of Hari, the name of Hari, the praise of Him, and the chanting of His qualities.

The Vedas, the scriptures, and the codes of dharma will naturally go to their dissolution. Purity, truthfulness, goodness, divinity, village deities, vows, asceticism, and fasting will all depart for the abode of Śrī Hari.
From that time forward, all will be devoted to left-handed practices (vāmācāra), possessed of falsehood and deceit,
and devoid of the *tulasī* plant. They will be bereft of the Ekādaśī fast and abandoned by all righteous duties.
Thereafter, they will turn their faces away from association with Kṛṣṇa.
Thereafter, all will become deceitful, cruel, hypocritical, and possessed of great ego; indeed, they will all become thieves and violent oppressors.
From this time forward, there shall be no distinction between men and women, nor marriage, nor legal disputes, nor the distinction between property and its owner.
All people will be under the sway of women, and unchaste women will abound in every house. (1.27)
They constantly strike their master with threats and reproaches.
The mistress of the house and the wife are [treated as such], while the husband is the lowest, worse than a servant.
The female servant is equal to the servants, as are the daughters-in-law, the mother-in-law, and the father-in-law.
Adulteresses become rulers of kingdoms, and kings are those related by birth.
In this world, those related by birth are the powerful kinsmen.
There is no conversation with the learned, yet there is intimate friendship with fools.

All the ritual actions of men will become inexhaustible [in their results] without the command of women. The sacred thread will be lost in its true significance, and there will be no recognition of caste; at that time, all the social orders and stages of life will adopt the conduct of barbarians.
They will study the scriptures of the Mlecchas, devoted to the food and practices of the Mlecchas;
at that time, all the social classes (varṇas) will become servants of the Mlecchas.
The women will become cooks for the Mlecchas and workers in leather.
All people were bereft of truth, and the earth was bereft of crops;
the trees were bereft of fruit, and women were bereft of offspring;
likewise, the cows were bereft of milk, and the milk was devoid of clarified butter.

The husband and wife will be devoid of affection, householders will be bereft of happiness, kings will be lacking in majesty, and the subjects will be oppressed by taxes. Rivers, streams, and ponds will be devoid of water, becoming mere hollows.
At that time, the castes will be devoid of dharma and devoid of merit, and thus they will lose their social standing.
Beyond that, among hundreds of thousands, not a single person will remain who possesses merit.
Men, women, and children will all be contemptible and deformed in appearance.
Thereafter, false rumors and wicked paths will prevail; some villages and cities will be on the verge of destruction and difficult to traverse.
They will be devoid of men, lacking inhabitants, and consist of only a few small huts.
In the Kali age, the forests will become the haunts of jackals;
all people will become forest-dwellers, oppressed by taxes;
and the crops will grow only in ponds and rivers.
In the Kali age, fields will be devoid of crops; the wealthy will be destitute of possessions;
thieves will be the most affluent;
and those endowed with strength and pride will be born into low lineages.
The deceitful liars appear as rogues and the crafty appear as speakers of truth;
the sinful appear as meritorious, and the uncultured appear as truly cultured;
those who have conquered their senses appear as libertines, and unchaste women appear as devoted wives. (143–144)
Ascetics, sinners, devotees of Viṣṇu, non-devotees of Viṣṇu, the violent, the compassionate, thieves, and murderers—
these rogues wearing the garb of mendicants revile and mock them. (145)

Those people who are skilled in the service of the body and likewise cause delusion among others will be honored; they will be deceivers, weak in knowledge. Everywhere there will be men and women who are dwarfish, diseased, and emaciated. (146–147)
In the Kali age, people will have short lifespans and be afflicted by old age even in their youth;
dharma will consist of the conduct of cattle, and kinship based on birth will become the primary concern. Furthermore, even the maternal instinct will be lost at that time in the Kali age.
But when five thousand years have passed, I shall again and again become a Brahmin in Camatkārapura; then,
in the Kali age, I shall be a great yogi perfected from birth, known by the name Bṛhadvrata.
At that time, I shall indeed establish devotion to the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa through the *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇasaṃhitā*;
and by the words taught by me, men shall attain liberation.
By taking refuge in me, their minds shall become purely sattvic.
From then on, all men and women—even the outcastes—will turn grey at the age of sixteen and become truly aged at twenty. (152–153)

A young woman of eight years who has reached puberty and becomes pregnant gives birth at the end of a year; by sixteen, she is overcome with old age. Among thousands of such women in every household, some are even barren.
Also those who sell their own daughters, as well as those who act as husbands to their own daughters;
those intent on procuring paramours for their mothers, wives, and daughters-in-law;
and those who live by procuring paramours for their daughters and sisters. (155–156)
At that time, there will be sellers of the names of Hari and sellers of merit;
giving a gift for the sake of fame, they will take it back again after a moment.
They will forcibly seize the livelihoods of the gods, the preceptors, and the Brahmins.

In the Kali age, there will be those who approach their daughters, mothers-in-law, daughters-in-law, sisters, co-wives, and mothers; those who approach women who should not be approached, such as the wives of brothers and others; and those who approach goats, cows, female donkeys, female camels, and does. (158–159)

In the Kali age, those who have sexual relations with female gavayas, female garuḍas, female dogs, and female peacocks, as well as those who consort with female pigs, female monkeys, female horses, and so forth,
will abandon their own wives and roam about everywhere.
In the Kali age, there is no certainty regarding wives or husbands;
this is especially true for offspring, possessions, and villages.
Everyone speaks falsehoods, and everyone is greedy for wealth through theft. (161–162)

In that Kali age, all will be mutual destroyers and slayers of men; women will then be united with all kinds of animals, kinsmen, and men, and they will be protected by outcasts (*vṛṣala*), devoid even of clothing.
Deprived of the sacred thread and devoid of purity through meditation,
they— prostitutes, usurers, Abīras, procuresses, and women in their menses— all shall become cooks in the kitchens of everyone. (164–165)
There is no certainty regarding foods, nor is there any certainty regarding wombs;
there is no certainty at all regarding sons—all shall become Mlecchas in the Kali Yuga.
When the terrible Kali age has set in, at its final moment upon the earth...
In that [age], a girl of five years shall become a mother;
she will be old at ten years, standing on the very brink of death.
And men of twelve years will indeed be vessels for death at that time. (167–168)
When the entire Kali age has passed, everything will then become diminished:
trees will be only a cubit in height, and humans will be the size of a thumb;
all beings will have a lifespan of two years, and quadrupeds will live for only one year.

In the Kali age, rivers will have a lifespan of but a month; men will be like cats to elephants, and they will be satisfied with a handful of food as if it were a mouse. Women will give birth to children who are like the offspring of mice. (1.420.170–171)

At that time, there will be no dwellings such as houses, and people will live with the earth as their garment; moreover, during the rainy season, there will be only a single shower, reaching no more than the joint of a thumb.
Thus, when all but the final portion of the Kali age has passed, (172)
The son of the brahmin Viṣṇuyaśas will be Kalki.
O Lakṣmī, I am that Nārāyaṇa, holding a sword in my hand,
mounted upon the white horse given by Kṛṣṇa, and traveling through the sky.
Having circumambulated the earth three times in three nights,
I shall subsequently purify the entire circle of the atmospheric realm by the touch of my own limbs, and then make the Mlecchas well-disposed in mind.
Having slain other exceedingly wicked ones, I shall restore them to a refined state;
I shall establish the Kṛta age, with men worthy of the sacrifice of truth,
once the unassailable Kali age has passed and the Kṛta age has fully set in.
Dharma, conjoined with austerity and truth, will become complete.
At that time, the brahmins will be ascetics, purified and devoted to Viṣṇu;
they will be the disciples of Kalki, most righteous and illuminators of the knowledge of the Vedas.
Then the women shall be true to their husbands, and the men shall be devoted to their wives.
Furthermore, the duties of the social orders (varṇadharma) will once again attain manifestation in their proper place;
indeed, sacrifices, gifts, ritual acts, and a sense of shame will truly exist among human beings.
All will be devoted to Viṣṇu and become Vaiṣṇavas;
indeed, there will not be even a trace of unrighteousness in the Kṛta Yuga, which is filled with dharma.
Everywhere there will be celestial vehicles and powers of hearing from afar.
In the Kṛta Yuga, there will be vehicles for traveling to heaven;
there will be yogic powers of far-sight and the ability to traverse the surface of the waters; and there will be chariots of lightning, fire, and wind in the Kṛta Yuga. (182–183)

In the Kṛta Yuga, the supernatural powers such as atomization (aṇimā) and others, which consist of power and bring about dissolution, destruction, and manifestation, will exist among material beings. In the Kṛta Yuga, there will be no distinction between the world of mortals and the world of heaven.
In the Kṛta Yuga, women shone like goddesses and men were like gods.
In the Kṛta Yuga, mantras, tantras, and yantras were effective;
in every house there were channels of light, channels of water, and channels of sound.
In the Kṛtayuga, there shall arise the mastery of the sixty-eight arts, the fire-like grasping of reflections, and the detailed knowledge of the distinctions of the body;
as well as the rules for conception and non-conception, and the powers of transformation into male and female forms. (187)
In the Kṛta Yuga, there will be the restoration of the dead to life and other such wonders.
In the Kṛta Yuga, the divine procedure for the medicinal plants (vānaspatya-vidhi), which transforms through elixirs (rāsāyana) and swiftly fulfills every desire, will become effective. (188–189)
In the Kṛta Yuga, there will be the great vidyā called Sañjīvanī, as well as the means for becoming invisible, the movement of divine possession and so forth,
the cognitions of the principle of Śakti and others, and those arising from the elements and their derivatives.
In the Kṛta Yuga, even machines shall perform divine labor.
Having thus established Dharma as the new Kṛta Yuga and having made the earth like heaven, the Blessed One will disappear from sight.
In the Tretā age, Dharma is remembered as having three feet; in the Dvāpara, it is said to have two feet.
When the Kali age has begun, it consists of only one foot, and after that, there is the total disappearance of all [Dharma].
O Lakṣmī! Indeed, my devotees wander everywhere as purifiers.
By the touch of the dust of their feet, the earth is always of the nature of a sacred ford (tīrtha).
Rivers, trees, and mountains are likewise purified by my devotees;
assuming the form of sacred fords, they indeed wash away the sins of people.
The virtuous, those with meritorious bodies, and likewise virtuous women who have taken refuge in Hari, purify the conscious sacred sites day by day.
Whatever sacred sites exist upon the earth, as well as sinful men and others—[these are purified by them]. (196)
Gods, humans, animals, and living beings— both stationary and moving—
shall become purified by the touch and sight of my devotees.
Thus, O virtuous lady, have the extensive duties of the ages been described to you.
"In every age, wherever there shall be women devoted to their husbands,
there heaven, constant happiness, wealth, and so forth shall exist.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have told you my birth as it arose in the course of conversation.
"By reading and by hearing this, one shall become a partaker of residence in Vaikuṇṭha.

Thus ends the four hundred and twentieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Duties of the Four Yugas within the Greatness of Wifely Devotion," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
(Chapter 420; *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā* – Section 1: The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga).
Chapter 421 [Author:
Chapter 422 → Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī! To the wonder at Prayāga, the king of holy fords, concerning Bharadvāja as he dwelt with his wife Triveṇī.
She was the daughter of Brahmā, born from his mind, a great virtuous woman from the moment of her birth.
In appearance she was like a hundred moons, a young woman devoted to her husband. Born from a portion of the three rivers, she was foremost among the women at Brahmasaras.
At Prayāga, she [served] Bharadvāja, who had been performing austerities for a hundred thousand years. (2–3)

During the ritual bath with the water-pot, she, having arrived from the world of Brahmā, beheld him. Thinking, "Aha! A divine sage worthy of being chosen as a husband shines here," she remained in his shadow, intent on service.
After Brahmā had performed his bath at Kumbhakāla, he recognized Triveṇī as the embodiment of the mind (mānasa) and offered her to Bharadvāja;
for she was indeed composed of portions of the Gaṅgā, Yamunā, and Sarasvatī. || 5–6 ||
Having offered that maiden named Triveṇī to Triveṇī,
and having praised her after making the offering to the sage, Brahmā departed for Satyasthala.
Through her devotion to her husband, Triveṇī [honored] the ascetic Bharadvāja.
She always serves [her husband] with devotion, through the increase of her wifely fidelity (pātivratya),
by means of daily morning baths and the like, by massaging his feet, by offering articles for worship, and by constantly presenting him with food. (8–9)
Through the knowledge of Brahman, through the constant performance of the *saṃdhyā-vandana* rites,
and by means of service while on her bed, that devoted wife serves [her husband] there,
where the wish-fulfilling cow (*kāmadhenu*) and the celestial tree (*kalpavṛkṣa*) are ever present. (1.421.10)
The *somavallī* creeper is always there, and the *cintāmaṇi* jewel resides in her hand.
Wherever there is a virtuous woman devoted to her husband,
there the presence of all jewels manifests.
Once, Bharata, the lord of Sāketa and Kosala, who practiced austerities during the month of Māgha, arrived there with his army for the purpose of performing the rites at the sacred ford.
Having stationed his army at a distance, he went forth to behold [the Lord].
Then Bharata, with joy, prostrated himself like a staff at the feet of his preceptor Bharadvāja, the most eminent among sages;
he also bowed at the feet of Bharadvāja’s wife. (14–15)
Then, having offered Bharata water for his hands, water for his feet, and fruits,
the knower of dharma inquired in due order after the welfare of his family,
as well as regarding his army, treasury, allies, and ministers in Sāketa.
Bharata also inquired after the welfare and other matters concerning Bharadvāja—
his body, his sacred fires, his disciples, his trees, and his beasts and birds.
Having thus promised him, "So be it," the highly illustrious Bharadvāja [proceeded].

Being pleased, he said right there: "Dwell here in this hermitage during this festival. Welcome to you; I shall provide hospitality and service according to your merit, O bull among kings, for as long as you reside at this sacred ford."
"Devotion to the guru, self-restraint, and following in the footsteps of the virtuous—all these qualities are present in you. Dwell here in my hermitage.
Thus addressed, Bharata replied to him, "So be it."
Then that sage, perceiving that Bharata— who was equal to a seer— had made up his mind to dwell right there, invited him with hospitality.
But Bharata said to him, "Surely this has already been done by you."
"Water for the feet, the respectful offering, and hospitality—whatever is available here in the forest—" (23) Then Bharadvāja spoke to Bharata, as if smiling:
"I know you are filled with affection; I shall satisfy you according to my means. (24)
I wish to offer hospitality to your entire army,
in accordance with my own affection and as is fitting for you, O sovereign of sages.
For what reason have you come here, leaving your troops far behind?
"Why have you not come here with your army, O king of those devoted to their beloved?
Bharata replied to that ascetic with palms joined in reverence:
"O Blessed One, I have not come with my army out of fear of the Blessed One."
For a king, O Blessed One, or one who holds authority over a kingdom,
ascetics must always be diligently avoided within his domain;
likewise, excellent horses, men, and rutting, noble elephants [must be kept away].
"O Blessed One, they follow me, covering the vast earth.
Thinking that they might not harm the trees, the water, the ground, the hermitages, or the huts, I have therefore come here alone. (1.421.30)
"Let the army be brought here from this place," was the command given by the supreme ṛṣi;
Bharata acted accordingly and brought the army's arrival.
Meanwhile, the ṛṣi said to his virtuous wife Triveṇī, "O beautiful one!"

"O beloved, having constructed a magnificent city through the dharma of wifely devotion (*pātivratya*), provide him a welcome and hospitality equal to that of a kingdom. Having been thus addressed, that virtuous wife bowed to her husband, who had bestowed this favor upon her.
Then, having entered the fire-hall, drunk water, and wiped his mouth,
he invoked Viśvakarman for the purpose of performing the rites of hospitality:
"I invoke Viśvakarman here, indeed Tvaṣṭṛ."
"I wish to offer hospitality; let that be prepared for me there.
(35) "I invoke the three world-protectors, the gods headed by Indra.
I wish to offer hospitality; let that be prepared for me there. (36)
May the rivers that flow eastward and those that flow crosswise,
both upon the earth and in the atmosphere, come together from all sides today;
may other streams flow with sweet, drinkable substances such as milk and the like.
And others [offered] cool water, resembling the juice of sugarcane stalks.
I summoned the divine Gandharvas—Viśvāvasu, Hāhā, and Hūhū—as well as the Apsarases and all the divine Gandharvas from every quarter. (38–39)
Then [he saw] Ghṛtācī, Viśvācī, Miśrakeśī, Alambuṣā, Nāgadattā, Hemā, Somā, Adri, and Kṛtasthalī—
those beautiful women who wait upon Śakra and those who wait upon Brahmā.
I summon you all, together with Tumburu and your retinues.
That divine forest of the Kurus, which possesses garments and ornaments for its leaves and celestial women for its fruits—that realm of Kubera shall be right here. || 41-42 ||
"O Blessed One, may Soma here provide for me the most excellent food—various and abundant kinds of what is to be chewed, eaten, sucked, and licked;
and diverse garlands fallen from the trees. (43)
And juices and other drinks, as well as various kinds of foods—
thus endowed with meditative concentration, that radiant and devoted wife,
having meditated upon Agni, remembered all [the gods], and they arrived individually. (44–45)
Having touched the sandalwood mountains, the auspicious wind blew— driving away perspiration,
most dear to the soul, pleasant, and peaceful— filling all with fragrance.
Showers of celestial flowers, bestowing divine splendor, were rained down by the gods.
Dense clouds rained down drops of sandalwood water, though only slightly;
at that time, the sounds of celestial drums were heard, bringing auspicious tidings,
and throngs of apsarases danced upon the earth.
The gods and gandharvas sang, and the lutes emitted their notes;
for the sake of a welcome, musical instruments were sounded at that time.
Then Bharata arrived, leading his army with great curiosity.
He beheld that army and the architectural arrangement of Viśvakarman. A vast expanse of ground had been prepared there, extending five yojanas on all sides,
covered with many lawns resembling blue lapis lazuli.
There, *bilva*, *kapittha*, *panasa*, and *sahakāra* trees,
as well as *āmalaka* and *kharjūra* trees, flourished, adorned with fruit.
And from the northern *Kuru* region, a forest possessing celestial enjoyments [was brought].
The river arrived, accompanied by trees, creepers, and fruits.
There were bright four-winged houses, halls for elephants and horses,
and auspicious gateways joined with mansions and palaces.
The royal palace, resembling a white cloud and adorned with beautiful archways, was decorated with white garlands and infused with divine fragrances;
it was square-shaped, spacious, and furnished with beds, seats, and vehicles.

Endowed with all divine jewels, possessing divine food and clothing; (56) with all kinds of food prepared, with vessels washed until they were spotless, with all seats arranged, and with glorious, excellent beds well-spread. (57)
The great devotee Bharata entered that jeweled palace,
followed by the ministers of the army along with the family priests.
And Vasiṣṭha and the others were filled with joy upon seeing the palace.
There, the divine royal throne, as well as the fan and the parasol, were present.
Bharata, together with his ministers, approached like a king;
he graced that divine seat, which was indeed worthy of a god.
Then all the ministers and priests sat down in order;
after them, the commander-in-chief and the counselor sat down.
At that moment, in an instant, rivers with mud made of milk-rice appeared there.
They attended upon Bharata at the command of Triveṇī.
On both banks of this Triveṇī were delightful and divine dwellings, plastered with white clay and built through her grace. (62–63)
And at that very moment,
twenty thousand women, adorned with divine ornaments and beautifully decorated with gold, gems, pearls, and coral, arrived, sent by Brahmā.
Twenty thousand women sent by Kubera arrived, by whom men were graced with divine bodies;
twenty thousand hosts of Apsarases from the Nandana grove also arrived. (65–66)
Nārada and other Gandharvas, equal to the sun in splendor, arrived;
they sang before Bharata with their Gandharva arts.
Alambuṣā, Miśrakeśī, Puṇḍarīkā, and Vāmanā [also performed].
At the command of Bharadvāja, they danced before Bharata.
Whatever garlands exist among the gods and whatever are found in the Caitraratha forest were then seen at Prayāga by the power of the Triveṇī.
At that time, by the splendor of Triveṇī, the *bilva* trees became drummers, the *śamī* trees became holders of the ritual staffs, and the *aśvattha* trees became dancers.
Furthermore, the *sarala*, *tāla*, *tilaka*, and *tamāla* trees [were transformed].
Then, having become hunchbacks and dwarfs, they arrived there in great joy.
Trees such as the śiṃśapā, āmalakī, jambū, and navaraṅga became servants who offered fruit and dwelt in the hermitage of Bharadvāja. (71–72)
Grapes, cucumbers, betel vines, *soma* and other creepers,
sweet sugar-canes, and whatever other vines there were in the forest—
all assuming the forms of beautiful women— dwelt in the hermitage of Bharadvāja.
"O servants, drink sweet liquors as you desire!
Let those who are hungry eat milk-rice and the finest foods.
Give fruits to be chewed and let them be eaten by the leaders of the army."
Having performed the ritual anointing once, those women— seven or eight of them— would bathe each man individually on the lovely riverbanks.
As one woman massaged him, large-eyed women would rise up to attend to him.

Holding their hands, the beautiful women made them drink honey and other drinks. The attendants of the mounts fed the horses, elephants, donkeys, camels, bulls, and excellent mules their respective fodder.
They fed the mounts with sugarcane, honey, and parched grain;
then the army shone forth, intoxicated, exhilarated, and joyful.
Satiated with all their desires and honored with red sandalwood paste, they were radiant.
And the soldiers, cheered by the Apsarases, then raised a great shout:
"Oh, the palaces! Oh, the treasures! Oh, the handmaidens and female servants!
Oh, the Kalpa-creeper trees here! This is heaven! they exclaimed. (1.421.80–81)
Dancing, laughing, and singing, the soldiers,
as well as thousands of men and women, cried out in great joy.
Following Bharata, thousands of people adorned with garlands went along.
Satisfied and filled with wonder, they paid homage to Bharadvāja:
"Blessed is this king of sages, whose wife is Triveṇī;
she is a virtuous woman who bestows all perfections, and by her majesty this auspiciousness has come to pass. (83–84)
Even if one should dwell in the forest, if his wife is devoted to her husband, heaven rests in the palm of his hand; what need has he for the splendors of sovereignty?
That wife who, having drunk the water used for washing her husband’s feet, [offers it] near the sacred fire...
Remaining here, she desires those great divine powers, which arrive at that very moment;
indeed, heaven or anything higher than this never comes from elsewhere.
Therefore, let virtuous women who are devoted to their husbands prevail everywhere.
"Likewise, may their husbands be men comparable to Bharadvāja,
devoted to their wives, for whom heaven is always within reach.
Speaking thus, all the soldiers indeed numbered in the thousands.
There were hundreds of thousands of residents of the Sāketa region who possessed excessive pride;
and millions of other heretics also arrived for the Kumbha festival.
Then, having beheld that divine heaven created by Bharadvāja, they [were amazed]. (1.421.89–90)
And [he saw] Kambharā, Mahālakṣmī, and the Lord Gopālakṛṣṇa;
there he saw the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa seated upon a lotus-throne,
as well as the Triveṇī in the form of a river and crores of sacred fords (tīrthas).
Having beheld and gazed upon the youthful Triveṇī, the beloved wife of Bharadvāja, they were purified and attained divinity. Then,
for those who had eaten that food which was like nectar, [the following occurred].
Beholding those divine foods, his mind became intent upon eating them.
Servants, maidservants, daughters-in-law, soldiers, local inhabitants, travelers,
female attendants, male slaves, and female slaves by the hundreds [all gathered there].
They were all exceedingly delighted and likewise clothed in new garments.
The elephants, donkeys, camels, cows, horses, beasts, and birds became satiated; they did not seek anything else at that time, such as grass or other fodder.
At that time, no one there was dressed in white nor was anyone hungry.
The lakes were filled with fruits and other delicious juices, soups, broths, and milk-rice; likewise, there were mountains of cooked rice.
And by the side of the hermitage there were wells with mud made of milk-rice (pāyasa);
those cows that yield all desires (kāmadughā) were present, as were trees dripping with honey;
there were ponds filled with wine and crores of golden vessels.
Then there were silver vessels and ten million copper ones;
thousands of bowls and millions of cooking pots,
as well as hundreds of millions of vessels made of gold.
There were cooking pots, jars, and vessels for parched grain, all well-prepared and filled with curd;
heaps of fresh butter, jars of buttermilk, lakes full of *rasālā* drinks, and sweet powders of bitter and sour flavors. (101–102)
In that hermitage, there were heaps of *parpaṭas* and mountains of *polikās*,
as well as great peaks of sweetmeats;
there were also piles of side dishes and of sugar-candies.
People at the riverbanks saw powders suitable for ointments and various bathing preparations kept in vessels,
as well as heaps of white *aṃśumat* wood for cleaning the teeth. (104–105)
White sandalwood pastes were kept in covered caskets;
there were excellent mirrors and vast quantities of variegated garments.
