Then, having heard of this supreme marvel from Pātāla,
the Nāga king named Svastika came there from his subterranean lair in order to see him.
And that well, known as Svastika, then attained the fame of a sacred ford (tīrtha).
Furthermore, a Liṅga named Barkarīśa was installed by the Nāga,
and an auspicious Liṅga named Svastikeśvara was also installed.
Having had a magnificent temple constructed there by that maiden,
she herself installed the Lord Ajāviṣṇu as her own husband;
she remains engaged in the service of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa through that image.

Whoever bathes in that well on the fourteenth day of the month of Kārttika and offers libations to their ancestors shall deliver twenty generations. Thus, having established that divine holy place, the maiden returned home.
In Siṃhala, she reported everything to her father, Śataśṛṅga.
Having heard this, the king, accompanied by his subjects, went there for the sake of visiting the holy site.
He bestowed gifts and provided a livelihood at his daughter’s residence.
The king became famous because of his daughter; blessed is he whose daughter is virtuous.
Then, having returned to his own city, he held a great festival.
And though the princess was unwilling, O Lotus-born One, he chose a groom and wealth.
Having divided his own realm of Ajnābhakhaṇḍa into nine parts, the father gave eight to his sons and gave the ninth to Ajā.
Kanyākumārikākhaṇḍa is that very kingdom in the south.
The great virtuous maiden Aja, devoted to the vow of Hari, performed [these acts].
That illustrious maiden remains at Stambhatīrtha on the bank of the earth;
she exists there with a divine form and always dwells within the kingdom.
In Ājanābha, which consists of nine divisions,
there are indeed ninety-six crores and seventy-two lakhs of cities.
Having thus arranged this supreme field of Kumārī, [she departed].
Having commissioned Mahākāla as its protector,
Satī then departed for Badarikāśrama to perform penance in the abode of Hari;
there, in Badarikāśrama, Citralekhā became an ascetic woman (tāpasī).
O Rame! when I become Kṛṣṇa in Vṛndāvana,
then my son Aniruddha, the most excellent husband of Uṣā,
will become visible in dreams by means of her having him painted in a picture.
Then, after five thousand years have passed on earth,
she will be born in Saurāṣṭra as the wife of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa;
equal to Śrī, she will serve her husband Hari with an invisible form.
"She shall go indeed to the Goloka of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, has the divine Satī Citralikhā been described to you.
By reading or hearing this, one obtains the fruit of the Kanyātīrtha pilgrimage.
He shall possess wealth, daughters, sons, wives, and prosperity; of this there is no doubt.
Even the beautiful Citralekhā, who was invisible, has become visible;
she too, who grants liberation, is remembered as a beloved equal to Kṛṣṇa.

Thus ends the four hundred and twenty-third chapter, titled "The Manifestation of Citralekhā from Goloka into the Lineage of Ṛṣabha in the First Section on the Kṛta Yuga of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā," describing therein her transformation into a he-goat due to the delusion caused by the ocean in the form of a he-goat, the display of miracles at the holy site of the confluence of the Mahī and the Ocean, the renown of the Kumārikā-khaṇḍa and other regions, and the attainment of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa by her in the form of Mañjulā. || 423 ||

Chapter 425 →
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, Lakṣmī! Long ago, there lived a brāhmaṇa named Bhikṣu with his wife Kalahā in the shade of Mount Revatācala.
This story, which counters opposing views and awakens one to the greatness of the Lord,
is as follows: In the city of Karavīra, there was a Brahmin named Dharmadatta,
who was devoted to bathing, the twilight prayers, austerity, fire-sacrifices, Vedic study, and the chanting of mantras.
The great devotee constantly served virtuous people.
Having gathered all the inhabitants of the village onto the surface of the earth,
he would perpetually perform the chanting of the Lord's names preceded by songs.
He performs dances in the presence of Kṛṣṇa and narrates sacred stories;
with devotion, he joyfully organizes many festivals.
Especially on occasions such as vows and festivals, he causes them to be celebrated by the merchant leaders.
The twice-born man satisfied his guests with words of welcome day and night;
he performed his recitation (*japa*) with garlands of beads, constantly chanting: "Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, Oṃ. (6–7)
And he went to the temple for the purpose of performing the worship of Nārāyaṇa;
having bathed well in the river during the Brāhma-muhūrta and taking his belongings,
as he was walking on the path toward the temple, a Rākṣasī was indeed seen by him.

Terrifying, hungry, cruel, with fangs protruding from her mouth, naked, (9) as massive as a black mountain, with a lolling tongue and carrying a skull-bowl, she said with a gurgling voice, "I devour! I consume! (1.424.10)
Leaping up with great speed, she was difficult to catch as she hung down;
Dharmadatta, seeing her, fled in terror while crying out.
She too ran after him from behind, intent on seizing and devouring him.
When she drew near, Dharmadatta became distraught;
intent on saving her life, he cried out for the sake of driving her away:
"Hare! Nārāyaṇa! Kṛṣṇa! Protect me, Govinda! Mādhava! || 12-13 ||
O Lord of Śrī, O Master of Māṇikī, O Lord of Ramā, O Lord of Prabhā;
O Lord of Lakṣmī, O Lord of Rādhā, O Lord of Pārvatī, O Lord of Kamalā;
O Lord of Jayā, Dayā, Ramā, and Campā; O Lord of Muktā, protect me!
"O Mañjulālalitādevī, O Śāntihaṃseśa, protect me!
Om, O Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa and Sudarśana, protect me here!
Reciting this, he cast a pair of *tulasī* leaves and water [into the fire]. || 15–16 ||
In the presence of the Rākṣasī, he spoke the words for the worship of Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa:
"O Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, protect me, protect me!
[17] "If you touch this brāhmaṇa, may the curse of Rāma fall upon you."
If you touch me, O wretched woman, may the curse of Caṇḍikā fall upon you!
(18) If you touch me, O naked woman, may the curse of the Yoginīs fall upon you! If you touch me, O slut, may the curse of Durgā fall upon you! (19)
If you touch me for a wicked purpose, O Kṛtyā, may the curse of Rudra fall upon you!
If you touch me, O Kṛṣṇā, may the curse of Kṛṣṇa fall upon you! If you touch me, O Rātri, may the curse of Māyā fall upon you!
"If you touch me, O wicked woman, let there be a curse upon you from Time!
Speaking thus, he struck her with stones in his rage under the name of Kṛṣṇa;
yet with the waters and the *tulasī* leaves used for worship, he burned away all sins.
Having regained her auspicious composure and remembering her previously committed sin,
and recollecting the web of her misdeeds, she spoke to Dharmadatta:
"In a previous birth, in Saurāṣṭra, in the vicinity of Mount Raivata..."
On the banks of the Bhadrā lived a Vaiṣṇava brāhmaṇa named Bhikṣu.
His wife was Iṣṭurā, who was of contrary conduct; she was of such character, such speech, and such contentious disputatiousness that she caused extreme suffering. (24–25)
My *kalmaṣa* (taint) resides in my heart; my tongue dances with insults at its tip; cruelty dwells forever in my eyes, and a state of darkness (*tāmasatva*) in my mind;
a fierce disposition is on my forehead, and great anger on the slope of my nose.
Contempt resides in my two lips, while quarrel is established in my speech.
Dwelling in my breath is the abode of unpleasantness, and agitation is established in my action.
Shame is always placed at my back, for shamelessness is maintained in front.
Insult and beating are held in the palm of my hand;
thus dwelling constantly, I reside in the houses of the twice-born.
In the land of Saurāṣṭra, throughout every region, in whatever house or wherever it may be.
If a dispute arises between a husband and wife, then I am remembered by the householder [with the thought]: "Where has this quarrel come from?
I am famous by this very name as one who always causes distress to her husband. (1.424.30–31)
Just as one remembers breakfast in the morning when it is no longer obtained,
so too was I formerly a wife of a mendicant, full of sin;
I caused my own husband to perform the massaging of my feet.

I even had the monk perform the washing of clothes and the sweeping of the house, as well as the polishing of the vessels; at that time, I became one whose nature was a great heap of such sins. (33–34)
I do not give my husband food that provides comfort or water;
rather than what he requests, I indeed give him the opposite.
Even that which is joined with a donkey is given to him—spoiled and ruined.
"O woman, eat this fruit of passion"—thus I would speak.
My lover was constantly distressed by me, yet I did not say anything sweet; I performed no auspicious deed whatsoever, and even as a courtesan, I gave him no happiness. (36–37)
"O Brahmin, even an unchaste woman who bestows contentment and never quarrels—such a wicked one as I have become, though a *kṛtyā* created by me, has granted you happiness.
Even a concubine (*upapatnī*) gives pleasure; I, however, am not so when married. (38)
Thus, extremely distressed, the monk went to the Raivata forest.
(39) Enraged and intent on inflicting suffering, I arrived there at that woodland site;
seizing him firmly by his topknot, I brought him to my own home. (40)
Afflicted by lust, devoted to sensual pleasures, and resorting to the conduct of beasts,
even then that twice-born man never killed me nor ever struck me.
Yet, on some occasions, filled with compassion, I would weep after a quarrel.
Once, while lying idly on a couch during the day, I became very angry and asked a brahmin for a drink of water.
He gave me that water, which was kept in a pitcher and lukewarm. || 42-43 ||
The clay vessel was indeed empty; there was no cold water in it.
Then, having seized a pestle in anger and stood up, she struck him.
A great sound was heard by the neighbors.
Having arrived, they said to the brahmin: "O sage, abandon this wife and her household;
O mendicant, take another excellent wife and cast away this *kṛtyā*. We shall even give you wealth; O protector of the earth, live in happiness. (45–46)

The Brahmin, having made his decision, went elsewhere to marry a second maiden who had previously been requested by him in words for that purpose. Then I consumed poison and abandoned my life at that very moment.
Bound by nooses by the messengers of Yama, they were led toward the abode of Yama.
At that time, on the path, I experienced great suffering from beatings and the arrows of their words, as well as the distress arising from walking upon fire and hot sands. (48–49)
Enduring hunger and thirst, the breaking of the body, fainting, and so forth—
having thus reached the abode of Yama and being slain again and again,
Dharmarāja beheld me and questioned Citragupta.
"Behold what kind of sin she possesses; observe her good and evil deeds!
Upon seeing her, the fruit of her actions appears most wicked.
Then Citragupta, having quickly seen that exceedingly terrible deed— || 51-52 ||
Addressing that wicked and sinful harlot, he said:
"Nothing auspicious has ever been done by this evil and depraved woman;
she constantly gave insults and administered beatings to her husband. (53)
But she never once fed me anything sweet while eating herself.
Because of that sin, may she become a female crow that eats its own excrement;
furthermore, may she become a bat, always eating its own excrement with its face turned downward.
Struck by that wicked man, she became a female donkey;
then she became a sow who eats excrement while cooking food in pots.
Furthermore, she became a female cat who was always hostile toward her husband.
Therefore, because she has committed suicide, let her become a preta wandering in a desert land.
Then, having become a piśācī who lusts after many piśācas,
let her thereafter become a wicked and evil-doing rākṣasī.
Having heard this principle from another, Yamarāja, having assigned me to various deeds,
repeatedly granted me those various births.
Having completed all of that, I became a sorrowful ogress.
"There is for me no end to my karma; evil arises again and again. Constantly smeared with sin, I am a rākṣasī in the forest;
I devour beasts, excellent birds, and humans in the woods."
"What shall I do? Where shall I go? There is no end to my karmas.
Thus filled with grief and excessively tormented by hunger and thirst, I writhed about and indeed entered the body of that merchant.
Accompanied by him, they indeed went to the auspicious southern region.
That merchant drank the water at the confluence of the Kṛṣṇā and Veṇī;
having become exhausted, he stayed there while the gods remained on the bank.
They struck me repeatedly, and I fled far away.
Afflicted by hunger and thirst, I was searching again for a vessel like that of a merchant;
then you were seen—you who are well-nourished—and my hunger shall be appeased.

For this purpose, I have come here quickly and joyfully to seize you. At that moment, you indeed chanted the most purifying name of Hari, and sprinkled water mixed with *tulasī* leaves from a sacred bathing place. ||66-67||
The sight of an excellent devotee such as you is purifying for me;
indeed, I am especially sanctified by the dust of your lotus feet.
I truly consider all my karmas to have reached their end.
All my evil has gone to destruction; now my merit increases.
Peace has arisen in my heart, and satisfaction [comes] from the sprinkling of water.
All delusion and internal fire, born of negligence, have departed.
O dull-witted one, I believe that the sin which brings suffering upon my husband has been destroyed here at this sacred ford through your power; O twice-born one, grant me liberation!
Whether I am a servant, a Cāṇḍālī, or a Śvapacī, I am still the same person I was.
I am indeed a wicked, wretched, and lowly woman, yet I am truly an object of your compassion.
By means of compassion, a living being crosses over here even terrible sin;
the compassion of the virtuous is the supreme merit, and it is the root of all wholesome deeds.
Without the compassion of the virtuous, even another good deed becomes a misdeed.
Compassion is merit; compassion is liberation; compassion is heaven, happiness, and wealth.
(74) The compassion of the virtuous and service to one's husband are obtained through great merit.
She who has no service to her beloved should always serve the virtuous. She who does not serve the virtuous has destroyed everything.
A master is to be served; a husband is to be served; he is indeed the Supreme Lord himself.
In the end, he alone is to be entreated and repeatedly asked for forgiveness;
the husband alone is the Supreme Brahman, he is eternal and merit itself.
The husband is always the giver of life, the giver of sons, and the giver of the world.
Lord Hari is the bestower of heaven, the giver of happiness, and the provider of bliss; he is the husband [of the woman].
He removes the suffering of his wife and himself endures it in her stead.
He bears the hardships born of the body and gives half of his own merit to her. (78–79)
He bestows his own earned wealth, merit, strength, and seed;
who else in this world should be understood as superior to him, the supreme lord?
For the husband alone is the highest deity for women.
"The husband is to be served; the husband is to be honored; the husband is to be attained by those preeminent in austerity.
Otherwise, women would fall into the state of *rākṣasīs*—such is the established law.
Having said this, the *kṛtyā* spoke again: "Tell me how my deliverance may come about."
Likewise, let there be the destruction of the remaining water-stalls as well.
O Brahmin, act in such a way that liberation will come about; it will be for your own welfare.
By rescuing this helpless woman, your own salvation shall be achieved.
Thus addressed, the compassionate Dharmadatta, with a humble mind, reflected and spoke these words that bring happiness to Kalahā:
"Listen, O beautiful one; through vows, sacred fords, and gifts, one becomes a dweller of sinlessness. (84–85)
The destruction of both *prārabdha* (commenced) and *sañcita* (accumulated) karmas occurs through meritorious deeds (*sukṛta*).
Furthermore, you are a *rākṣasī* and a *preta*; you have no entitlement regarding the wretched or the like.
A *preta* has no authority over sacred fords (*tīrtha*), gifts (*dāna*), vows (*vrata*), and so forth.
This karma, which bestows the state of a *rakṣasa* or a *preta*, cannot be exhausted by any other means;
however, I have performed a vow centered on devotion to Hari (*pātivratya*).
Since it was undertaken during the month of Kārttika, I shall give you half of its merit from my very birth. (87–88)
"The merit of devotion to Hari destroys the sin of unchastity.
Having said this, the Vaiṣṇava Dharmadatta took water mixed with *tulasī* and sprinkled it over her.

Saying "Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, Oṃ," she immediately took hold of merit and was indeed freed from the state of a ghost. She became a divine maiden, twelve years of age, adorned with every beauty.

Clad in fire-like garments, equal to the moon in luster, and radiant with tranquility, she bowed to the brahmin and, filled with great joy, spoke: "By a mere fraction of your grace, O brahmin, I have been purified and graced. (92)
"Having been delivered by you from affliction, I am going to the state of the Blessed One.
When she had spoken thus, a divine celestial chariot arrived,
resplendent with two attendants and accompanied by a multitude of female attendants.
Summoned by the two attendants, the maiden ascended quickly.
Then Dharmadatta bowed to those two attendants of Kṛṣṇa. When asked, "Who are you? the preeminent one replied to him.
Puṇyaśīla, approved by Suśīla, [discussed] his previous births and so forth.

(96) Thus ends the four hundred and twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of how Kalahā, the wife of a mendicant in Saurāṣṭra, attained the state of a bat, a female donkey, a sow, a female cat, a ghost, and a demoness due to the sin of unchastity, and her subsequent liberation through the destruction of that sin by means of the chanting of names, Tulasī water, and other rites performed by the Brahmin Dharmadatta," in the first section on the Kṛta Yuga of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. (424)

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī! Puṇyaśīla recounted the auspicious account of two individuals, which is devoted to devotion to Viṣṇu and bestows the status of being an attendant [of the Lord]. (1)

"O Brahmin, I am Puṇyaśīla, residing in a celestial chariot and devoted to the service of Viṣṇu; this second one here is Suśīla. O Brahmin, you have done well; she has been delivered by you through great merit."
The sin arising from hundreds of her previous births has gone to destruction.
She shall be led to Vaikuṇṭha and will become a servant of Viṣṇu.
And you, O Brahmin, having observed the Kārttika vow together with your two wives, [shall attain the same].
In time, through great merit, you shall go to the abode of Hari.
The vow of Hari performed by a devotee is indeed like the vow of a devoted wife;
it bestows both merit and liberation—of this there is no doubt. (5)
Having enjoyed the merit here on this earth for many thousands of years,
you will become King Daśaratha, born of the Solar dynasty (Sūryavaṃśa),
together with your two wives who have been married to you.
This third Kali shall be your wife, sharing half of your merit; then Viṣṇu will come to your house.
Having performed the work of the gods, he will depart for his own abode.
This very Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa shall become known by the name Rāma.
And those people on earth who shall seek refuge in Rāma,
they too shall attain liberation through the majesty of Vāsudeva.

Cultivation (*bhāvanā*), love (*prema*), devotion (*bhakti*), affection (*sneha*), and even tenderness (*ārdratva*)—these are distinguished from the ritualistic section (*kriyā-kāṇḍa*) directed toward Hari; such is the established principle. Knowledge is superior to action, and likewise, meditation is superior to knowledge.
Meditation is superior to [ordinary] cultivation, and affection arising from true devotion is supreme.

(3.2) Since disinterested affection is indeed superior to affection accompanied by desire, humility is superior to affection; its very form is that [humility], consisting of the essence of its flavor. (1.3)
O Brahmin! There is nothing whatsoever superior to that [devotion] ever directed toward Hari.
Listen to a charming story regarding this: devotion excels material gifts.
Long ago, in the city of Kāñcī, there was a king named Cola who was observant of religious vows.
He was a devotee of Viṣṇu, a giver of gifts, a protector of his subjects, and honored by them. He constantly performed worship of the gods, and under his reign the subjects were happy.
By him, many sacrifices were performed on the banks of the Tāmraparṇī river.
And that king departed for another world by means of a celestial chariot;
thus, having ascended the vimāna, he went to the abode named Śveta.
Then, through yoga, he proceeded to the abode where the Lord reclines upon the Ocean of Milk.
While he was prostrating himself like a staff before Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, who was reclining on the infinite bed, Nārāyaṇa arose;
he then worshipped the Lord of Śrī with jewels, pearls, and other offerings.
With excellent leaves of gold, flowers such as diamonds and the like,
with incense, lamps, fine food offerings, garments, and ornaments,
as well as with divine tens of thousands of jewels, he worshipped the Supreme Lord.
Having thus worshipped and bowed down, he sat down in the presence of Hari.
At that very moment, a Brāhmaṇa named Viṣṇudāyaka,
having brought tulasī, water, and flowers for the purpose of worship, arrived from that same kingdom.
He, too, performed the worship of Śrī Hari with offerings such as leaves and other materials.
Indeed, the diamonds and other gems were covered by her with leaves, flowers, and the like.
Then, seeing his own act of worship thus concealed, the king—
He said to the brahmin: "O brahmin, how is it that my worship—so beautifully adorned with gold, rubies, and other gems—was covered by you with leaves?
You have no sense of respect; you do not know how to perform true worship."
"You do not even calculate a price, yet you grant me the highest excellence;
O twice-born one, you treat the inferior leaves and such as the most excellent.
Thus addressed, that pure-hearted twice-born man spoke there concerning the *caula* ceremony.

O King, O sinless one, the worship of Viṣṇu performed with constant devotion is dear [to him]; that which is filled with pride and rooted in egoism does not become dear. Indeed, you perform worship with flowers made of gems, gold, and other precious materials.
"I too shall perform that very same worship with water and *tulasī* leaves; my worship of you is superior by virtue of its underlying intention.
Tell me, O King, what vow have you performed for the sake of royal prosperity?"
"If you say that nothing at all was done by me, yet something great was accomplished, then let it be so. Then Cūla, full of pride, said to the brahmin:
"That which was done by me was the gift of gold, as well as the gift of jewels and diamonds."
Indeed, infinite gifts of cows have been made and many sacrifices performed;
yet, for the constant worship of Śrī Hari, I offer diamonds.
Because of your devotion, though you are destitute, my own devotion is rendered superior.
"By you, no sacrifice was performed, nor was a temple built.
O Brahmin, see that everything has been done by me; furthermore, I shall perform another sacrifice. I shall go to have a direct vision of Hari. (33–34)
"The Brahmins will recognize that supreme devotion only then, and not otherwise.
First, for the sake of direct realization, I shall perform a sacrifice to Viṣṇu.
Having said this and bowed to Śrī Hari, he went to the region of Caula.
Caula began the sacrifice, having appointed Mudgala as his preceptor.
Then, from Satyaloka and the worlds above it, the Vairājas, celibate students,
sages, seers, elders, ancestors, and likewise the gods [descended].
Sacrifices, gods, gandharvas, and humans who are the gods of the earth;
rivers, streams, sacred fords, trees, and likewise creepers;
cities, sacred fields, and shrines located both in the netherworld and upon the earth.
The preeminent stars, the Vaiṣṇava deities,
all the goddesses who dwell in every abode, and the leaders of the liberated were summoned by the king for his own Vaiṣṇava sacrifice. (39–40)
Gold, wealth, diamonds, and all such things were offered there;
garments, food, drinks, and objects of enjoyment were presented in their entirety.
Indeed, the resonant chanting of the Vedas by the sages filled that great sacrifice.
There, the embodied forms of the Brahmins were indeed satisfied at the sacrifice;
the sacrificial fires attained contentment, the gods were liberated and gratified,
and the virtuous goddesses who dwell within the cosmic egg became joyful.
A great sacrifice was performed, and it became renowned indeed throughout all the worlds;
however, it was not performed out of a desireless state of mind, but rather out of pride. Furthermore, that which was performed out of rivalry, or even out of malice or envy— 44.
All that would not bear fruit, just like the fruit born of desirelessness.
Viṣṇudāsa performed service in the temple of Hari with his body and with his inner being, as well as the ritual bathing of Hari. (45–46)
Awakening, worship, adornment, incense, and lamps; the offering of *tulasī* leaves, the sprinkling of water, and adoration;
the presentation of flowers, leaves, fruits, and the *arghya* offering, as well as the application of sandalwood paste.
The offering of unbroken grains and saffron, as well as the presentation of bilva fruits and other offerings;
the waving of lights (nīrājana), circumambulation, hymns of praise, prostrations like a staff, and so forth;
likewise, the request for forgiveness, chanting, and listening [to the sacred names]. 48–49.
Sweeping, smearing [the floor], singing of virtues, and offering [food];
likewise, offering betel-leaf, water, and fragrant substances;
fanning with a fan and holding a chowrie.
Holding the parasol, attending to seasonal requirements and the like,
having constructed flower gardens as well as auspicious flower garlands and so forth,
and having prepared a grove of *tulasī* for the sake of Hari, one should perform the watering of it. (51–52)
Thus, with affection and devotion, Viṣṇudāsaka practiced supreme devotion to Lord Hari day and night;
he observed the vows of Ekādaśī and other days, joined with the recitation of prayers.
Through self-restraint, great devotion, and constant remembrance of Kṛṣṇa;
through worship performed with the sixteen articles, and through dance, song, and service characterized by intense emotion— he indeed passes his time entirely in this manner.
Seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, tasting, and even speaking;
grasping, walking, lying down, praising, meditating, and determining;
thinking, honoring, experiencing, and likewise cultivating—*56*.
Remembering, recognizing, doubting, erring,
reasoning, perceiving, and desiring— he exists only as Viṣṇu.
Knowing that Viṣṇu is the abode fashioned by himself everywhere, he meditated upon Viṣṇu.
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa; Oṃ, obeisance again and again.
By thus chanting these sixteen syllables, he indeed became one with Viṣṇu.
The Blessed Lord Himself always accepts the service of such a brāhmaṇa.
The Blessed One himself accepted the sacrificial materials from the king’s sacrifice.
The Lord became visible to the Brahmin, yet remained invisible to the king;
for such was the cause of presence and absence, as well as of pride and humility, in that situation.
Once, Viṣṇudāsa prepared sweet foods in the kitchen as if it were his daily routine; however, you remained there for a day, unobserved by anyone.
[Thinking,] "There might be an obstacle to the worship if the cooking were done again at midday," [he acted].
Having reflected, he did not cook again, nor did he eat himself;
indeed, he offered fruit and water as an oblation to the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
On the second day as well, he took away the food that had been prepared in the same manner.
On the third day as well, Mādhava carried away the cooked food in that same manner.
Thus, for seven days, he took the cooked food without its being offered.
Distressed with anxiety, the twice-born remained by the side of the cooking fire for the sake of guarding it.
Having prepared the cooked food and holding wood and stones in his hands, he stayed in a corner of the house.
Having fasted for seven days, he beheld a certain outcaste (cāṇḍāla) who was carrying away the cooked food—one who was filthy, hungry, and emaciated in body. (66–67)
Seeing him, the twice-born man was filled with compassion; remembering Hari within himself, he said, "Stay! Do not eat anything harsh; eat clarified butter and take it [with you].
Seeing the brahmin speak thus, he fled in fear.
Having fallen there and fainted, Viṣṇudāsaka went to him,
gave him water, and fanned him with the edge of his garment.
Thereupon, he rose up and became Viṣṇu, bearing four arms.
Having directly beheld the glorious four-armed Hari, Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, resplendent with the conch, discus, mace, lotus, Kaustubha gem, and other ornaments—
having seen Lord Hari manifest before his eyes, Viṣṇudāsa was exceedingly choked with emotion.
He became filled with love, yet he was unable to offer praise or speak.
Then the gods, who were present at the sacrifice, abandoned the ritual and arrived; they were asked by King Caula: "O lords of the gods, where are you going? (72-73)
They said to Viṣṇudāsa: "The Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa has indeed granted us a direct vision and appearance in his very presence.
We shall depart for the sake of seeing him, and we will return quickly. (74)
Having spoken thus, they went to where the four-armed Hari was.
There the gods performed his worship; the Gandharvas and Apsaras sang, the divine Gandharvas danced, and the sages bestowed their blessings.
At that time, that place became rich with the joy of song and instrumental music.
All the sacrifices, the gods and others, and the people of the fourteen worlds;
all the sacred fords and even the fires arrived there.
Then, for a moment, the sacrificial ground became empty, devoid of the gods. Near the temple, Viṣṇu spoke to Īśvara and the others with devotion,
service, affectionate feeling, and overflowing love.
"O deities, I am pleased with Viṣṇudāsa, my humble servant who is free from pride;
my direct manifestation has quickly occurred for him.
I do not approach one who is full of pride, even if he presents various kinds of offerings."
"I shall manifest my own vision [to you] directly"— this was his firm resolve.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu embraced Viṣṇudāsa,
placed him upon his own celestial chariot, and led him to the eternal abode.
As he was proceeding toward the temple of Śrī Viṣṇu, Caularāja saw him;
he then quickly summoned his preceptor Mudgara and spoke to that sage regarding the purpose for which he had commenced the sacrifice.
In competition with whom all my wealth was offered in sacrifice—
he, having previously attained Hari, went indeed to Vaikuṇṭha.
Indeed, this sacrifice consisting of ritual action cannot be completed by you.
I have not previously earned here the fruit of what ought to be done;
therefore, neither wealth, nor sacrifice, nor charity will satisfy Hari.
Hari, however, is pleased only by devotion of heart, by worship, and by the chanting of His names.
It is certain that he becomes gracious through remembrance.
O Guru, consider yourself as having performed the sacrifice; accept the sacrificial fee!
Depart for your home, having sent away those who have arrived and been given their fees. (87–88)
And I shall follow behind for the sake of propitiating him;
for the Lord of Devotees is pleased by devotion, not by sacrifices or extensive gifts.
This Brahmin has been born as an illustration for the propitiation of Hari.
Having spoken thus and having entrusted the burden of the kingdom to his nephew,
the lord of men went to sacrifice in order to propitiate Hari.
Standing before the sacrificial fire-pit, he offered the materials for the oblation.
"O Viṣṇu, grant me devotion always through my mind, speech, body, and actions.
Having recited this three times aloud while remembering Hari,
the king then fell into the Vāhni-kuṇḍa while everyone was looking on.
A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose, and at that moment Viṣṇu appeared.
Having made the king four-armed and taking him up onto his celestial chariot, Hari led the monarch to Vaikuṇṭha and granted him the status of an attendant.
Hari himself was pleased by my devotion, which was supreme in its fidelity to my husband.
When he is pleased with me, O King, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa himself is pleased.
O Dharmadatta, I am that very person; I am Viṣṇudāsa, his personal attendant.
The king named Puṇyaśīla, also known as Suśīla,
has come here for the sake of Rāma to take Kalahā away.
Because of your merit, he shall take her to Vaikuṇṭha during his birth as a king.
And at that time, Kaikayī shall become your third wife, named Kalahā, who shares in a portion of Dharma;
she will depart after placing her hand within the hub of a chariot wheel.
But seeing her devoted solely to her husband, you will fall into delusion. And she, having been told to grant a boon, will cause that gift— which is appropriate for the future time—
to be made at her own will, as if it were a mere deposit.
When Rāma’s consecration has been attained and the destruction of the Rākṣasas is at hand,
Viṣṇu will incite him to request the state of being a forest-dweller;
and indeed, the destruction of Rāvaṇa and the others shall occur under the pretext of Sītā’s shadow.
"Thereafter you shall exist, and then you will go back to Vaikuṇṭha.
(102) Thus has been told to you everything concerning the unfolding of future events;
by reading or hearing this, one's departure for Vaikuṇṭha shall come to pass. (103)

Listen, Lakṣmī! Even though the king has been consecrated in the kingdom of Cūla, the coronation of the heir apparent to the throne of the chief queen has not yet occurred. Indeed, the coronation in that kingdom takes place for her nephew as if he were his own.
In the Kali age, the creator himself becomes the primary punisher of his own subjects.
Furthermore, listen, O auspicious one! When King Cūla, though a devotee, committed suicide, O Brahmins, he then [sought refuge] with Mudgala. (105–106)
Then they laughed, mocked, and uttered cries of "shame";
they spoke of his incapacity and proclaimed him a murderer of kings.
Hearing this again and again, Mudgara too became enraged, his inner self ablaze with fury.
Just as he was about to fall into the pit, he was firmly and properly restrained by the Brahmins according to justice;
he was blocked by the queen, her female attendants, and others through forceful efforts. (108–109)
Then, out of anger, he tore out his own matted hair with both hands;
having plucked out the lock of matted hair, he invoked it into the circle of fire.
Because of that, even today there are Brahmins in that lineage who are without topknots (viśikha).
Then they made amends for their offense and all returned to their own abodes.

(111) Thus ends the four hundred and twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Account of the Birth of Daśaratha and Other Events Concerning Dharmadatta," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, describing how Colarāja and Viṣṇudāsa attained the forms of the divine attendants Suśīla and Puṇyaśīla through devotion to Hari, how the woman of Saurāṣṭra became Kaikeyī, and the narration of the birth of Daśaratha. 425.

Chapter 427 →
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Mahālakṣmī! In Gokula, the daughters of the cowherds performed a vow centered on devotion to their husband in order to attain Kṛṣṇa.
The great divine maidens are goddesses whose forms are the very abodes [of divinity]. They appear on the surface of the earth as if possessing physical bodies, yet that is not their true reality.
All of them are divine, equal to Rādhā, equal to Śrī, and are embodiments of Brahman.

Indeed, not even an atom’s worth of difference from the form of Kṛṣṇa exists among them. (3) Their states as embryos, birth, childhood, and then Gaurī-hood, followed by Rohiṇī-hood and maidenhood—these belong to the daughters of Kṛṣṇa and are truly divine. (4)
All those with eyes of leather perceive like those with normal vision, yet it is not so;
for their very activity consists in attaining Kṛṣṇa as their husband.
All are devoted wives to Kṛṣṇa and beloved of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
Having surrendered all their possessions for the sake of Kṛṣṇa, how indeed can they be described?
For Kṛṣṇa was constantly entreated by them, who remembered their past lives;
and Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa appeared to them in their dreams and in the morning.
Smiling and perceiving her inner intent, he granted her the vow of devotion to her husband (*pātivratya*).
By the command of Kṛṣṇa, those women performed that rite of wifely fidelity.
"In the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, during the month of Vṛṣa, perform this vow which is dear to me."
"I shall arrive and fulfill your desires.
Just as everything is for my own sake, so too is everything for my sake;
let everyone quickly do what is pleasing [to me], for I shall become your lord. (1.426.9–10)
Thus, for those maidens who had been so addressed, there arose through the grace of Kṛṣṇa a realization of their lifelong devotion to their husbands;
all those thousands of gopīs then undertook that vow.
Their minds were indeed fixed upon me, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa. At dawn, during the Brāhma-yoga, they gathered together in a group, and I bestowed upon them the wisdom for bathing in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa.
Having performed their ablutions in the Yamunā, they sing the praises of Kṛṣṇa;
they offer water and likewise offer unbroken grains (akṣata) into the water.
Even while remaining within [the water], I accept the offering of wealth that is given in the water as well.
In the morning, they offered food into the water while remembering Kṛṣṇa.
"Sometimes as Kṛṣṇa and sometimes as a fish, I take that which is given into the water—whatever leaf, flower, or fruit is offered into the water as being my own self. (15–16)
I accepted all of that with a feeling of being those very women in the water;
they went from house to house and performed worship for my sake,
and they ate the sacrificial food (haviṣyānna) offered to me as an offering to me.
Therefore, this entire vow was performed by me correctly for the sake of my grace.
Being pleased, I, the Lord of Beings, granted them the boon of myself as their husband.
Listen, Lakṣmī! I shall describe the ritual for the devoted wife of Kṛṣṇa.
Having risen at dawn during the Brāhma-muhūrta, they bowed to their venerable gurus; I was remembered, meditated upon for a moment, and the name "Kṛṣṇa" was repeatedly chanted.
Then, having gone to the bank of the Yamunā and performed the purificatory rites and so forth, they proceeded.

Having bathed and performed the purification of the face and other rites, they smeared themselves with the clay from the Tulasī plant and sprinkled their bodies with water infused with Tulasī leaves. Then, while keeping me in their hearts, they bathed in the river. (21–22)
Remembering Him, they uttered, "Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa," and also recited: "Oṃ namo bhagavate śrīkṛṣ�ṇanārāyaṇāya pataye namaḥ.
Then [they offered] unbroken rice grains, flowers, leaves, saffron, and other [substances].
Clad in wet garments, they gave me lamps, fruits, and other offerings.
Having offered them with the words, "Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord;
this is offered," they departed from the shore along with their clothes.
Having thus put on [the garment] and sipped water (ācamana), they then offered libations to their ancestors;
having paid homage to the sages and the gods, they applied *kuṅkuma* and *candraka* marks on the forehead,
the middle of the neck, and the heart with sandalwood paste and other substances.
Devoted to Kṛṣṇa, they drew the *bindu* and the lines as was appropriate.
Keśava was meditated upon on the forehead, Nārāyaṇa likewise on the abdomen;
Mādhava was meditated upon on the chest, and Govinda on the hollow of the throat.
Viṣṇu is meditated upon in the right side of the belly, while Vāmana is in the left side of the belly;
Madhuhā is in the right arm, and Śriyodhara is in the left arm.
Trivikrama is at the root of the ear, and Hṛṣīkeśa is in both ears.
Padmanābha was meditated upon on her back, and Dāmodara indeed on the area below;
Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord, was well-contemplated on all her limbs.
And they fashioned a conch, a discus, a mace, and a lotus upon her arms.
"Oṃ, obeisances to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; obeisances!
Thus they meditated in their minds upon the sixteen forms of Kṛṣṇa and offered their salutations.
They likewise placed fine tulasī garlands around their necks and held them in their hands.
Some placed garlands made of *dhātrī* fruits around their necks or in their hands. Having performed this rite and bowed to their elders, they returned home;
then, having all sipped water for purification (*ācamana*), they entered the pavilion.
Seated upon auspicious seats in the lotus posture and facing the east, they performed the regulation of breath (prāṇāyāma) in the center of the pavilion; there,
within the pericarp [of the lotus], they visualized the sun, the moon, and fire.
Having established the general outline, they placed those [offerings] upon the rice grains.
Then, with devotion, they fashioned an eight-petaled lotus out of rice;
therein, they envisioned me as their own divine husband, the most excellent one suited to each of them.
They saw Acyuta seated and smiling, resembling ten million moons; some saw him with four arms bearing weapons, while others saw him with two arms;
he had large eyes like lotus petals and was endowed with great heroism and strength.
[Behold] me, whose chest bears the Śrīvatsa mark and the Kaustubha gem, clad in yellow garments, resplendent with divine ornaments, adorned with celestial decorations,
my limbs anointed with divine sandalwood paste, and wearing divine garlands of flowers. (39–40)
Adorned with a forest garland (*vanamālā*) encircled by *tulasī* garlands,
resembling ten million rising suns, lovely and most enchanting;
his body embraced by the youthful Śrī, as he kisses me.
Having meditated, those charming women chanted "Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa" to me.
Then they placed a conch filled with fragrant water,
as well as a vessel containing fragrant flowers and other offerings, to my right.
On the left, they placed a water-pot filtered through cloth and well-perfumed;
they set down a bell and lamps, and offered incense on all sides.
Then the maidens placed four vessels there.
The maidens placed in the *arghya* vessel materials for the *arghya*, *pādya*, *ācamanīya*, and *madhuparka* offerings—
namely, mustard seeds, unbroken grains (*akṣata*), flowers, the tips of *kuśa* grass,
sesame, sandalwood, fruit, and barley. (45–46)

They placed *dūrvā* grass, *gaṅgā*, *yamunā*, and a lotus in the vessel for water for the feet (*pādya-pātra*). They also placed *kaṅkola*, cloves (*lavaṅga*), and jasmine fruit in the vessel for water for sipping (*ācamanīya-pātra*), as well as water from sacred bathing places (*tīrtha-jala*).
They placed cow’s milk, curd, honey, clarified butter,
and sugar in a vessel for the *madhuparka* offering before Hari; then, out of a desire to please Kṛṣṇa, they performed the ritual placement of their hands upon their own limbs.
May the head of Kṛṣṇa rest upon my head in every way;
may the auspicious forehead of the divine Śrī Kṛṣṇa rest upon my forehead.
May the eyes of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa dwell within my two eyes.
May Kṛṣṇakarṇa be established upon my ears, Kṛṣṇanāsikā upon my nose;
may Kapola be upon my cheeks, and Kṛṣṇagaṇḍaka upon my temples;
and may the Kaṭākṣas of Kṛṣṇa preside over my side-glances.
May the beloved pair of Kṛṣṇa’s lips dwell upon my two lips;
may Kṛṣṇa’s chin be upon my chin, and may the throat of Hari be upon my throat.
May the shoulders of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa be established upon my two shoulders.
May the two beautiful arms of Śrī Hari be in my two arms; may his two hands be in my two hands.
May Kṛṣṇa’s heart be in my heart; may Hari’s navel be in my navel. May Kṛṣṇa’s hips be in my hips; may Hari’s waist be in my waist. (54–55)
May Kṛṣṇa’s secret be hidden within my secret parts; may the thighs of Hari be within my thighs.
May Kṛṣṇa’s knees be within my knees, and his shanks within my shanks.
May Kṛṣṇa’s feet be within my feet; may Kṛṣṇa abide in me in every way.
"May the senses of Kṛṣṇa be present in all ways within my own senses;
may the inner faculties of Hari indeed abide within my inner faculties.
Thus did they perform this heart-touching remembrance of Me. (57–58)
Then those devoted wives remembered themselves as being equal to me and said:

"O Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, our beloved husband, grant us auspiciousness! You are the husband of the cowherd girls; grant us auspiciousness! (59) They cried out: "You are the husband of the cowherd girls; grant us auspiciousness!"
Then they worshipped Śaṅkha with flowers, sandalwood, and water;
they performed an anointing for him with highly fragrant oil,
and likewise performed an anointing with musk and sandalwood.
Then, although I had already been bathed with waters scented with fragrant perfumes,
they offered me the water from a conch shell again and again for the sake of bathing;
they presented the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and bathed me with great reverence.
They performed an ablution for me with the waters of sacred fords, which were pleasant to the touch;
they respectfully rubbed my body with sandalwood, *gandhasāra*, and other unguents, and wiped my frame again and again with a cloth.

They offered me the guest-offering (arghya) along with fruit, as well as water for washing the feet (pādya), water for sipping (ācamanīya), and the honey-mixture (madhuparka); then they gave me divine garments.
They also presented me with divine ornaments and jewels, perfumes, and other such items.
They gave collyrium, hair oil, and the like; sandalwood and other substances for the purpose of making forehead marks (puṇḍra);
saffron and other items; and thereafter they gave liquid essences.
Those maidens also provided lac-dye, cosmetics, and other such articles.
They presented him with a lion-throne, as well as an umbrella, chowries, and fans;
they gave him a mirror, combs for his hair, and white powder.
They also offered garlands of *tulasī*, flower necklaces, and crests.
Then they offered clusters of flowers, golden ornaments, and leaves;
they gave me the flute of sweet sound, which I played.
Placing me upon a swing, they rocked it with great devotion.
They offered an oblation consisting of milk-rice mixed with cakes,
as well as water, fruit, betel leaf, vegetables, areca nuts, and so forth.
They also served them with fans and attended upon them.
They again offered incense and lamps, and with devotion they gave flowers.
Out of affection, they fed me repeatedly with mouthfuls of food;
being fully satiated, I drank water and took betel leaf.
Having bowed down to them, they performed the lustration ceremony again and again;
they offered hymns of praise, prostrated themselves, and likewise circumambulated them.
They made a request for forgiveness for their offenses and presented a handful of flowers.
And they requested a boon: "Be our husband forever.
Having laid her upon a couch, they stood around her with reverence;
they massaged her feet and served her as she desired.
At that time, O beloved, I fulfilled their desires through touch, embrace, and indescribable passion; consequently,
they attained a happiness truly unprecedented.
Then, immersed in joy, they offered me auspicious water (arghya).
Having bid me farewell, they then attended to their household duties;
they partook of the sacred food (prasāda) that had been offered during my worship.

Remembering again and again the great joy given by me, they were exceedingly delighted; they performed their household duties and did not perceive any fatigue. While engaged in the task of fetching water, they saw me within the water-pot.
During the threshing of grain, they indeed saw me among the chaff;
during the work of the grinding stone for the sake of flour, they saw me on the millstone;
and at the time of sweeping, they saw me upon the floor.
At the time of cooking, whether in the cooking vessel, the pot, or the food bowl;
and whatever was seen, heard, or touched—they saw only Me.
In the mirror, on their own faces, in their eyes, in the oil, in the garments, and in the ornaments—
In their hearts and in all their actions, they beheld me alone.
They became possessed of divine bodies, free from the obstruction of walls;
having abandoned the perception of a physical body, they assumed the form of Kṛṣṇa.
One became a woman and the second became a man, and they took their pleasure;
one became the wife and the second became the husband, and they rejoiced;
one became the female friend and the second became the male friend, and they kissed each other.
One was a bride and the second became the groom, and thus they shone forth.
In this way, I made their inner being consist of Kṛṣṇa;
for those who are dyed red by the colors of devotion to Kṛṣṇa’s wifehood, no distinction exists for me. (87–88)
Having assumed such a state, they went to bathe in the waters of the Yamunā near a *kadamba* tree; there, remaining unobserved, I too went along with them,
having indeed taken the form of a young maiden for the purpose of bathing.
They descended into the sacred bathing place, laying their garments on its bank.
Then those maidens remembered me in their hearts, desiring to bathe and sport together with me,
each one individually, so that no other might know.
There, the external girls sported in the water while the inner person remained within;
at that time, each one perceived her own enjoyment, and no other did so.
Thus, having fully satisfied their minds, they were thereafter satiated.
Although in the water I was in the form of a maiden, I, Kṛṣṇa, came from the forest;
taking their garments, I climbed the Kadamba tree. That which had been intended by them in the forest was fulfilled by me through my mind.
I acted in that manner so that Kṛṣṇa might see our bodies;
for I disregarded Varuṇa, who was presiding over the vow.
O beloved ones, go outside and offer salutation with joined palms to the Sun.
Thus, in accordance with their dispositions, they were observed by me.
Then, being satisfied, they felt that they had accomplished their purpose.
I gave garments to them and repeatedly bestowed excellent boons.
"I shall delight you, I shall give you pleasure as much as you desire, for you are indeed dear to me;
I shall offer you the entire fruit of my vow, ever renewed. By this constant state of devotion, those truthful women have been perpetually gratified by me."
Day and night, they remained eternally absorbed in me.
I made Kāma divine, Rati divine, and Bhāva divine;
indeed, through my own divine nature, that state of theirs became divine.
Action performed without desire is said to be that which is always offered unto Me;
it destroys bondage, bestows peace, and directly brings about liberation—namely, offering unto Me.
Just as it was performed by them, no one else shall ever do so again.
Thus I became their gracious and beloved sole lover. Those beloved women devoted themselves to me and attained me in the supreme state.
All of them were beloved by Kṛṣṇa, observers of vows to Kṛṣṇa, and dear to Hari.
The wives of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, women devoted to their husband Kṛṣṇa,
constantly worshiped me and delighted me in my presence.
They also daily fed the Infallible One with sweet foods.
May they always hold me in their hearts, I who bestow eternal bliss.
(105) Thus, she who shall serve her husband through the vow of wifely devotion will attain me, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, as her husband, and thereby be fully liberated. (106)

Thus ends the four hundred and twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Attainment of Lord Kṛṣṇa as Husband by the Maidens of Gokula through the Performance of Vows and Worship with One Hundred and Eight Offerings," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 427 *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā*, Section 1 (*Kṛtayuga-santāna*) — Chapter 427.
[The Author: Chapter 428.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī! to the account concerning the nature of their re-attainment.
When Kṛṣṇa returned and resided in Dvārakā,
all of them, overcome with grief, abandoned water and food.
Then, by Śrī Kṛṣṇa and by me, they were repeatedly brought back to his presence.
Having gone there in an invisible form, they were consoled and gratified;
they were nourished and delighted by sporting as they desired and other such activities.
(3) In my own invisible form, I sport with each individual gopī.
Those standing nearby do not know at all, for they possess only physical eyes (carmacakṣus).
But those divine ones on the bank of the Yamunā recognize [me] and speak;
my friends meet in solitude, praise me, and laugh. (4–5)
Unable to remain even for a moment without me,
they met on the shore and resolved to go to Dvārakā to be near their beloved.
Then all of them, possessing divine bodies, assumed two forms each.
In one form, they remained there in Gokula at all times;
but by their second divine form, they arrived in their thousands,
bringing offerings according to their strength, as wives of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
Invisible in form to those composed of the elements, they traveled by way of the sky;
within a single hour, they reached the auspicious, divine lotus-pool.
Knowing their arrival through my yoga, I returned with great haste.

He welcomed them and assumed a thousand forms; he quickly bestowed joy upon them and then gave them food and other provisions. Afterwards, he accepted their offerings and dispelled their long-standing distress.
Thus, on the island of Dvārakā, he protected them for a long time;
all of them, gratified by his command, served him according to their desire.
Once, they were requested by me to sport on Mount Raivata.
They arrived, they wandered about, they rejoiced, and they called out to me.
On the bank of the river Svarṇarekhā, fragrant with sweet-smelling flowers,
in that delightful forest of ten million trees, they attained the bliss of desire.
Having seen that most delightful place, Raivatapattalam,
they resolved to feed me and remembered various foods.
Then the forest goddesses residing there, who were yoginīs of Yoginīgiri, [acted].
The wives of the Siddhas and the servants of Ambā brought all kinds of foods from every direction.
They brought golden vessels, silver vessels, and those made of leaves;
they brought various vessels made from the leaves of the *brahmadruma* tree.
They too, considering their births to have been fruitful, were filled with great joy;
they fed him most abundantly and performed the rites of hospitality with deep respect.
The daughters of Raivata and likewise the maidens of the Gaukulyas [did so].
They fed the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who was present in ten million forms.
Whatever foods were worthy of offering in the food-pile during the month of Kārtika,
they brought those very items for the sake of Hari to be given in Mārgaśīrṣa as well.
They fed them all near the Nārāyaṇa lake. Listen, Lakṣmī! I shall tell you in full the names of those who ate then, as well as the food, drink, side dishes, and so forth. (21)
Thousands of golden vessels and silver ones;
many spacious and beautiful vessels made of palāśa wood;
and thousands of jars, shallow bowls, and small cups.
Then, upon that vast ground, auspicious jars filled with water and accompanied by their respective vessels were placed near me.
Thereafter, milk-rice from the wish-fulfilling cows was offered by the maidens.
Milk pudding with sugar was excellent, as was fragrant rice.
(25) At that time, there were bowls filled with fragrant mung beans, and various dishes of side-dishes mixed with lime juice and other ingredients. (26)
There were hundreds of varieties of side dishes, fragrant with camphor and other scents, containing fruits and roots that had been cooked to perfection, all placed in small serving bowls;
there were also grapes mixed together with mangoes and karamarda fruits.
Decoctions combined with black pepper, long pepper, ginger, camphor, cardamom, and fresh ginger;
various types of *kvathikās* (infusions), *caṭanīs*, and bitter *iṣṭikās*; those mixed with the juice of the rose-apple (*jambū*), as well as *bharjakas* made from leafy creepers. (28–29)

And various kinds of *pralehanas*, filled with the fragrance of flowers, were placed by them in vessels; they were excellent and warm. There were also auspicious, round *maṇḍakas* mixed with sugar and milk.
Fully blossomed flower-bouquets were served upon the plates;
and excellent *haiyaṅgavīna* butter, along with its filaments and sugar,
as well as the finest ghee from buffaloes, was presented at the stalls.
Powders made from fresh leaves, fruits, and other ingredients were placed in small baskets,
while *saubāhlikā* cakes and *pūrikās* were set out on platters.
There were also *polikās*, *apūpas*, and *pūpakas*, each with a hundred holes.
Sweet polikās, beloved pūrikās, and twin polikās;
also large polikās and likewise full prapolikās;
*roṭakas* filled with ghee, and *śāṭakas* filled with ghee.
Then, chickpeas of many kinds, fresh seasoned mung beans and lentils,
*sūtrapheṇya*, *parpaṭa*, and *vaṭa* cakes made from pumpkin and mung beans,
as well as nine types of *vaṭikā*, were joyfully offered.
And there was milk-rice (pāyasa) enriched with nutmeg,
black pepper, cardamom, and saffron; likewise, prepared cooked rice (siddhānna) cooked in milk, served in vessels, multicolored, possessing many flavors, and excellent, seasoned with black mustard.
They prepared many kinds of foods made from tamarind, curd, and mango; they were fashioned from the juices of grapes, sugarcane, plantain, bilva fruit, and other ingredients.
There were also bulbous roots cooked in ghee and those cooked in oil.
Likewise, there were cooked leaves mixed with the juice of uparasas;
and [preparations] made with ground acārālī seeds and the kernels of coconuts,
combined with khasa seeds and cloves, along with ghee and sugar.
In a cauldron, small quantities of milk, sesame seeds, and rice were cooked;
these glossy and delightful *pheṇikās* were joyfully offered to them again and again.
Furthermore, *tripūrikās* fried in ghee and scented with camphor were presented.
And there were various kinds of sweetmeats (*modaka*) mixed with *cārālī* seeds, smeared with *khasa* seeds, and infused within with *drākṣā* (grapes);
they were prepared with jaggery, sugar, and candied sugar, and kneaded with milk. 43–44.
There were those cooked in water and those cooked in ghee, as well as those baked in fire-pits;
there were also cakes made from flour slightly moistened with ghee and cooked in ghee,
containing coconut, sugar, cardamom, cloves, and camphor.
Auspicious sweetmeats (modaka) mixed with bamboo flowers, jasmine flowers, and the like;
those combined with tree resins and mixed with ripe *gundra* and other ingredients;
almond sweetmeats, sesame sweetmeats, pearl-shaped sweets, and so forth. 46–47.
There were other sweets, such as *laḍḍukas* and *golakas*, made from the flour of mung beans and chickpeas;
there were also rice-based *laḍḍukas* and *laḍḍukas* made from peas and other grains.
These round and fragrant treats were placed by them upon platters.
Likewise, four auspicious and beautiful pieces of *mahāśubha* were given;
as well as pieces of *mohana-sthālaka*, *parpika-cūrṇa-paṭas*,
*bindukī-ḍāḍukas*, and various kinds of *māṣa-modakas*.
The book-makers, the makers of *kalikās*, the female servants, and those from the four banyan trees; the *bāṣpāṭas*, the weavers of cloth, as well as the makers of *śaṣkulīs* and *piṇḍakas*;
the makers of *gaṇagranthas*, the *śarkapāras*, the bronze-workers, and the painters.
Milk, water, sandalwood, yellow resin, and buttermilk;
(52) saṃyāva and other fillings, rose-apple fruits, and strings of garlands; likewise, sweets, non-sweets, bitter things, and savory condiments. (53)
Likewise, there were prepared *kulatthikā* beans, *rājamāṣa* beans, and others;
these were filled into vessels and leaf-plates according to the available ingredients.
There was also ginger, cloves, mangoes, and fermented gruel (*āranālaka*).
The fermented juice of *āmalaka*, of lemons, and of pomegranates;
the fermented juice of black peppers, of tubers, and of ginger; the fermented juice of *kairaṭa* fruits, of *karmada* fruits, and of *śigru* seeds.
Likewise, the juices of radishes, leaves, and dates;
the fermented gruel of wild bamboos;
and the condiments of *kṣīrikā*, *amṛtā*, and *galakī* fruits.
The condiment of *paravala* gourds that have been soaked in ghee and milk;
the condiment of *kunara*, *mṛdālu*, and *raktālu* tubers;
and side dishes of *bṛhatī*, *suvāsā*, and *methikā*. (58–59)
Sugarcane juice, the water of *puṣpikā*, grapes, and the fruit of the *kṣīrikā*;
mangoes with their nine colors, plantains that are like nectar;
*āmalaka* fruits, *bilva* fruits, and various juices.
Joyfully and repeatedly, those auspicious women placed into the bowls a prastha of milk with sugar,
a half-measure of ghee, a little honey, a little ginger,
a little black pepper, and a little camphor. (61–62)
They gave me filtered and boiled water for my drink,
as well as excellent betel leaves accompanied by the finest ingredients;
they likewise offered me water there according to the prescribed rite.
I was given gifts and fed by all of them individually;
I was repeatedly satisfied with mouthfuls that touched my throat and with excellent drinks.
Taking them all by the hand, they indeed gave me morsels of food.
I take [the food] into my mouth with devotion and eat it quickly;
the deities, the ṛṣis, the sages, and likewise the ancestors have arrived.
I ate for the sake of their sight, and they accepted the consecrated offering (prasāda).
Thus, they prepared for me food that provided great satisfaction.
Having eaten, I in turn fed them all individually,
offering them morsels of food, kisses, and touches.

To all of them, I offered the grace of all things that bring satisfaction; they were fed, and water and betel were presented to them. At that time, having become fish in the Nārāyaṇa lake, they were indeed deities.
Even birds, having become his ancestors, attained grace. There, in the groves, he was served by maidens with great satisfaction and was likewise highly adorned with garlands and wreaths of flowers.
On Mount Raivata, that mountain which always bestows happiness, he was saluted, worshiped,
and repeatedly entreated by me for the sake of obtaining a dwelling;
yet he gave them my command, saying, "Go indeed toward Gokula."
They said: "O Kṛṣṇa! Always protect us here on this mountain. O Mādhava! Come here always for our happiness;
we have all surrendered ourselves to you in body, deed, and thought. (73–74)
Now that you have arrived, where else could we go, apart from the feet of our beloved?
We are always your servants; grant us happiness indeed through union with our lover.
The Lord, who assumes many forms, has fully gratified Rati with his desires.
Then, O Lakṣmī, Brahmā arrived there for a specific purpose.
Others do not know what is to be kept secret; I alone, Nārāyaṇa, know it.
Then Brahmā said to me: "This secret must certainly not be spoken."
For as long as the Kṛta, Tretā,
and Dvāpara ages shall exercise sovereignty over the earth,
Kali remains utterly hopeless; finding no place anywhere, he went to the Lokāloka mountain in anger.
He performs penance right there for the sake of attaining that very place;
indeed, you must go there to bestow the fruit of his penance.
O ocean of compassion, you who protect the world, a boon must be granted.
The age of Dvāpara has passed; the Kali age shall prevail upon the earth.
O Lord, the Gaṅgā and other sacred fords, as well as Dharma and the deities, shall no longer remain on this earth for five thousand years.
For that duration, Kali shall dwell upon the earth powerless; however,
in due course, when the strength of the Tiṣya age arises on the surface of the world,
he will dwell manifest within the forms of all human beings.
Then he will sow the seeds of unrighteousness everywhere;
he will strive by every means to make the world uniform,
and for his own nourishment, he will render the entire world devoid of dharma.

At that time, there were distinctions of caste and distinctions of religious duty, as well as the avoidance of the untouchable, the approach of those who should not be approached, the eating of what is forbidden to eat, and so forth; likewise,
there was the purification of gods and outcastes, and the laws of Manu and other such codes.

Then all shall become afflicted; therefore, for the protection of the Dharma, O Kṛṣṇa, you must again manifest yourself on the bank of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake in the Raivata region of Saurāṣṭra. (86–87)
O Lord, since you are the presiding authority over all branches of knowledge and all phenomena,
you must certainly be known by the name Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa;
and through your instruction, [this shall endure] everywhere on earth for a long time.
The bull, nourished by his superior devotion, will live among every person. Then,
recognizing the Blessed One by the signs of the fish, the banner, the bow, the trident, the svastika, and the thunderbolt, those people shall take refuge in him.
They will come and they will cross over [the ocean of existence] through the sight and service of you;
O Kṛṣṇa, then devotion on earth, by your divine splendor,
shall attain nourishment everywhere, and people shall go to liberation.
"Oṃ, salutations to Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Lord; salutations! (92).
Having received this mantra from their guru, they shall go to the divine abode through devotion.
Then, when the power of the Kali age arises, the subjects will become like outcasts. (93)
Then, both the sense of "mine" and "otherness," along with their roots, will perish;
there will be only the bond of the womb, the bond of wealth, and the pursuit of self-interest.
At that time, O Kṛṣṇa, you must appear again and again.
For the destruction of the Kali age and for the sake of truth and the true dharma,
it is your duty to manifest yourself again and again,
as long as there are deities upon the earth, in images, and indeed in the waters at sacred fords. ||95-96||
"May purity and strength prevail among men, and may Kali [remain] as he is," Hari said; Brahmā, having bowed, stood before him.
Hari then served all the delicious food to Brahmā.
Then Kṛṣṇa spoke this reply to the young girls in a playful manner:
"I am indeed Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord upon the earth; for the sake of overcoming the Kali age, I shall appear in Surāṣṭra. (98–99)
"Therefore, all you beloved ones, perform penance on Mount Raivata;
when I manifest myself there, a perfect union with me shall be yours.
Hearing this, they became deeply distressed, their eyes filled with tears.
Indeed, they were unable to endure separation for even that long, and it caused them great torment.
Then the Blessed One, having consoled them again slowly, spoke once more:
"For those who cannot endure separation, [the duration is] five thousand years. (101–102)
Indeed, only a moment’s time remains before you depart for the world of truth (Satyaloka). O maidens, go this very day along with Brahmā;
let those who are eager behold the world of Brahmā for even a single instant.
Furthermore, let my beloved ones, impelled by Brahmā, come here once more.
With these divine bodies, let them be full of devotion toward me.
And I myself shall be present here in Saurāṣṭra as the Lord.
Indeed, Kṛṣṇa alone is to be recognized by his signs when he is in the midst of the virtuous.
All of you, possessing divine bodies, shall then take birth in every house throughout Saurāṣṭra and other regions,
and you shall truly become devoted to me.
"Due to your excellent company, millions of men and women alike will become practitioners of devotion to me in every household. I shall wander about in the form of a hidden teacher, like an ascetic."
Having attained happiness from Me alone, people shall go to My abode.
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya pataye namaḥ"—
those who perform this recitation (jāpa) shall indeed go to My state.
Those people who indeed perform service to me, worship of me, the chanting of my names,
and the listening to my stories,
shall go to the supreme abode, the eternal realm frequented by Śrī.
Having been addressed thus, they became joyful and, together with Brahmā, went to the true world of Brahmā (Brahmaloka); Śrī Kṛṣṇa went to Dvārakā.
Thus I have told you this account of Mine, which destroys sin and suffering.
Indeed, having recollected what occurred previously, I have related it here.
All of them are my wives, devoted to me;
they have renounced all their possessions for my sake, and all are faithful to their husbands.
"Indeed, by merely seeing or touching them, people shall attain liberation;
how much more so through my yoga and direct service with divine devotion!
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have told you this auspicious account of what occurred in the past.
"In age after age, I shall indeed become Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa;
many times, in every yuga, I come into being and manifest myself.
I am the one whose splendor is that of the Kṣatriyas, whose splendor is that of the virtuous, whose splendor is that of austerity, and the lord of sages."

He is the splendor of the scriptures, the splendor of knowledge, and the splendor of Dharma; he is the teacher of teachers, the nourisher of Dharma, the nourisher of devotion, the protector of devotees, and the ruler.
He is the savior of virtuous women, the husband of his beloved, the bestower of delight, and the Lord of Ramā.
The giver of kingdoms, the protector of sacrifices, the destroyer of Daityas, and the mendicant;
the remover of suffering, the bestower of happiness, the refuge, and the four-armed one;
the powerful, the one who has reached the further shore, and the one whose body is the site of the Kaṇa grain.
"O beloved, those who are steadfast in devotion to Kṛṣṇa’s wife will always cross over [all difficulties].
Thus I have told you my heart's secret: Kṛṣṇa alone is the husband, and no other.
I shall protect, I am protecting, and I have protected [you] day after day."

[To those] Mañjuhaṃsas, who were endowed with devotion and devoted to their chastity. (1.22) Thus ends the four hundred and twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Gopīs of Gokula Giving One Hundred and Twelve Kinds of Food and Enjoyments to Śrī Kṛṣṇa on Mount Raivata after Their Arrival at Dvārakā, the Statement of His Manifestation Everywhere in Saurāṣṭra and Other Regions, and the Re-attainment of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa through Chastity," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. (427)
