Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the delightful story of Vīrabāhu and his virtuous wife. In the city of Kāmpilya, there was a highly intelligent man named Vīrabāhu. (1)
The king was a speaker of truth and a supreme devotee of mine;
he was devoted to the Bhāgavatas and took delight in my stories.
He was a donor who provided refuge to the helpless, faithful to his wife, and possessed of sons.
His beloved wife was Kāntimatī, a great and virtuous woman devoted to her husband.
Vīrabāhu knew no other deity than me alone.
Once, the great sage Bhāradvāja went to his house.
The king offered hospitality, a welcome, the respectful water-offering (arghya), and a seat;
he bowed to him with devotion and spoke, being greatly delighted:
"Today my birth has become fruitful; today my day has become fruitful. (5)
Today my kingdom has become fruitful; today my home has become fruitful.
My hermitage is fruitful, and my wealth and kinsmen are fruitful as well, since I, who am ignorant of Brahman, have had the sight and the touch of his feet in my house.
The virtuous go to the home of one with whom Hari is pleased.
In whosever house there is a devotee of Hari, there occurs the destruction of ten million sins.
That very house becomes a sacred pilgrimage site (tīrtha) by the dust of whose feet heaven itself is reached.
"O Sage! My kingdom, my fortune, my elephants, horses, and everything else are for your sake alone.
By the grace of beholding you, I have become liberated while living;
you are a great devotee of the Lord, and there is nothing that I cannot give to you. (1.428.9–10)

Even a very small offering dedicated to a Vaiṣṇava yields fruit equal to Mount Meru. Yet, that house in which the feet of the virtuous yogi Kṛṣṇa do not dwell is fit for the abode of a corpse; such a day is utterly fruitless.

O knower of all dharmas, tell me what that house and what that day are which, though devoid of the company of the virtuous, become for those living the life of a householder a supreme means of liberation— a bond that grants entry into the abode of Hari. (12–13)
Being pleased and remembering Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, Bhāradvāja said: "O King, may it be well with you; you are the one who is dear to your devotees.
O King, prosperity is indeed easily obtained, but the state of the heart is truly difficult to attain. (14)
Indeed, that devotion which has been earned through many births toward you, O Devotee, belongs to him for whom the compassionate Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Śrī, is a friend;
his devotion toward the virtuous is truly divine and bestows liberation. (15–16)
Śrī Hari is indeed always to be served, and saintly persons are always to be served; likewise, women should serve those virtuous wives who are devoted to Kṛṣṇa as their husband.
Wealth, grain, sons, fame, kingdom, good fortune, and honor—[all these are attained through such service].
Health, beauty, and sovereignty are obtained from the blessings of the virtuous.
By him who has satisfied the holy ones, Kṛṣṇa himself is fully pleased;
for when Kṛṣṇa is satisfied, the entire world—including its gods, sages, and humans—is satisfied. (18–19)
If Hari is not pleased, everything—even that which is pleasing—is useless.
You are blessed, O great king! You truly shine as a great devotee of Viṣṇu. You are even more blessed, for you shine because your wife is devoted to her husband.
She by whom both [duties] were accomplished— that is, devotion to her husband (*pātivratya*) and [the service of] the Lord—
she has attained this world of happiness while Śrī Hari Kṛṣṇa was her wedded husband, and she shall likewise attain the divine abode (*dhāma*). (21–22)
In this world, there is no means for the salvation of the householder’s life like this:
a wife devoted to her husband at home, eternal devotion to Kṛṣṇa, and subjects in the kingdom who are devotees of the Lord, followers of Viṣṇu, righteous, and virtuous. (23)
One should always reside there, but never in a kingdom where a non-Vaiṣṇava rules.
It is better to dwell in a forest hermitage than in a kingdom that is not Vaiṣṇava;
[it is best] where a king devoted to the Lord governs the earth.
That indeed should be considered Vaikuṇṭha, for its very fruit is Vaikuṇṭha itself.
The king is a true devotee and a worthy recipient of the blessings of the virtuous.
By virtue of the conjugal fidelity of the royal couple, that kingdom prospers eternally.
O King, my eyes have become fruitful, for I behold you who are indeed a devotee of Viṣṇu;
likewise, my ears have become fruitful, as I hear of the devoted wife.
A devoted wife was created by Brahmā as the very embodiment of Lakṣmī herself.
The Vaiṣṇava who is devoted to his wife was appointed by Brahmā as a savior;
indeed, the sight of Vaiṣṇavas bestows peace as well as liberation.
And here, you have obtained the sight of one who dwells in the auspicious company of Śrī.
"May it be well with you; I shall depart. Be happy, O lord of men! (30) May there always be auspiciousness and freedom from widowhood for your wife Kāntimatī.
May there be unwavering devotion to her husband and devotion to Keśava for both of you. (31)
O radiant one, may you always possess the realization of oneness with your husband Kṛṣṇa.
Previously, you maintained your wifely devotion with great effort;
yet in a former birth, this husband of yours was a man of violence.
An atheist, of wicked conduct, a Śūdra devoted to the pleasures of others,
ungrateful, ill-mannered, and devoid of good behavior—
you have indeed always [treated him] like a god in deed, thought, and speech. (33–34)
Served by you with the thought that he was Kṛṣṇa and through the bull-like virtue of devotion to your husband,
no other man was ever conceived of by you, even though you were a Śūdra woman—
you, a devoted wife, a great saintly lady, who avoided the touch of any other.
Free from wicked intent and such faults, you served your husband Hari.
At one time, this husband of yours, being destitute of wealth, came to the forest;
even though you yourself were wasting away, you did not abandon your husband Hari. (36–37)
Once, while the two forest-dwelling spouses were subsisting on rabbits and other such food,
they beheld in the forest a sage who had lost his way—
a Brāhmaṇa, a devotee of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa and a true Vaiṣṇava.
At midday,
you two attended upon that Brāhmaṇa named Devaśarman, who was thirsty, fallen, and likewise unconscious, as he remembered Kṛṣṇa within his heart, by means of water and fanning with air.
Massaging his feet and offering him fruits and other foods,
they respectfully led the Vaiṣṇava brahmin— who was a savior— into the charming hermitage, which was pervaded by shade, while regarding him as Viṣṇu, Kṛṣṇa, and Hari.
"You have served him perfectly; you bathed him and likewise fed him.
Having prostrated with all eight limbs, that Vaiṣṇava was addressed by you with heartfelt devotion:
'For the sake of our liberation, you, O Viṣṇu, have arrived as our guest. (42–43)
"O brahmin-sage, by the sight of you, the destruction of our sins has occurred.
O brahmin, tell us if any assistance is required in the forest.
Then the brahmin replied: "Indeed, through the power of merit in this forest..."
"An encounter with you has occurred for me while living in the depths of the forest.
What may I do for you both? Tell me whatever you desire.
The Śūdra said: "May there be no further sight of the world of Sauri (the Sun)."
"I am going with my wife to the eternal abode of Kṛṣṇa;
you ought to show me favor by granting me instruction.
Then Devaśarman said, "Listen to your former history."
In a previous birth, you were indeed a righteous brahmin in Avanti.
At that time, this [woman] was your wife, a virtuous woman devoted to her husband, who was constantly dedicated to dharma and hospitable toward guests. ||48-49||
By your command, this woman prepared your food well on the eleventh day and offered it to the Brahmins and guests for their meal.
While merit arose from the gift of the food, sin also arose from its consumption.
By the power of merit and demerit, indeed along the path ordained by Yama,
you two took birth in a Śūdra family mixed with merit; as long as that merit remained, so long did you possess wealth, grain, and other such riches.
His merit was lost, and consequently, this forest life has come upon him;
however, in the city of Vidarbha, there dwells the son of your daughter.
By him, the Ekādaśī vow of Hari was performed according to the prescribed rite.
That merit was bestowed by him, and by the power of which your constant and auspicious progress upon the path of Dharma proceeds;
at that time, Kāntimatī’s mind was always fixed upon her devotion to her husband.
By the power of that merit, your union shall be eternal;
no separation shall ever occur—it has never happened before, nor will it happen in the future.
In a very short time, you both shall go to heaven.
There, having experienced happiness for a very long time through the power of the dharma of a devoted wife,
you two shall indeed obtain birth as Śūdras in the world of mortals.
And both of you, born thus, shall be entirely devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu.
"Then, by the power of my service, you shall attain a future auspicious birth;
and by the power of your devotion to your husband, you both shall obtain a long-lasting kingdom.
Having spoken thus, that brahmin departed for the sake of visiting sacred pilgrimage sites, and so did you two.
The queen and the king, both devotees of Viṣṇu, have indeed met their end;
you two have been born here once again, and Satī is your wife.
You, moreover, are devoted to your wife and always serve those like me.
Out of devotion to your husband, you serve Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa, Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Śrī, the Lord of Kamalā, the Lord of Lakṣmī, and the protector of the virtuous.
This virtuous wife of yours always serves you, O Kṛṣṇa.

The fruit of that is a long-lasting kingdom, and you have a son who is a true Vaiṣṇava. Furthermore, your subjects are always devoted to Nārāyaṇa and are followers of Viṣṇu; therefore, you shall triumph here in the pursuit of liberation.
Always practice devotion to Hari and serve your gurus and ascetics.
O virtuous lady, always observe the vow of a devoted wife and protect your fidelity to your husband.
By conducting yourself in this manner, you shall indeed attain eternal heaven even in this world.
"Before long, you two shall surely go to the supreme, divine abode, Goloka,
by virtue of the merit of this Ekādaśī, from serving as guests to the brāhmaṇa, and through the devotion of your wife. Thus did you obtain your kingdom and all else.
"Always worship Viṣṇu, the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa;
O virtuous woman, worship your husband, the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
Having spoken thus, the great sage Bhāradvāja departed for Badarī.
Both of them offered their devotion and both went indeed to my abode.
Listen, Lakṣmī! To him who chants my name through devotion to Kṛṣṇa as his sole husband, I grant Vaikuṇṭha, Goloka, or the imperishable state.
My name must be uttered especially at every moment;
one should say "Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa," which bestows joy, or "Prabhā-Kṛṣṇa," which grants supreme liberation and removes all suffering. (71)
This is my vow, O Lakṣmī: one who has come for refuge in every way attains all desires—both Vaikuṇṭha and even Kamalā. To my devotee, I indeed give whatever belongs to me.
I shall indeed deliver that person who speaks "Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa," remembers Him, or worships Him in any way whatsoever. As for those who utter "Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa" even in the presence of death—
O beloved, even Death, Yama, and his messengers depart, leaving him behind.
At the time of death, he into whose ear the words "Rāma, Rāma" have entered is led to Vaikuṇṭha by the attendants of Rāma; of this there is no doubt.

"Oṃ, salutations to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; salutations!"—as I recite this mantra, may my syllable [lead me] to where the devoted wife who is supreme in her chastity and the *tulasī* leaf are present. (77)
Wherever there is a virtuous and great devotee of the Lord, there I am present.
I am Kṛṣṇa, he is Kṛṣṇa; I am the husband, he is the master, he is indeed the beloved.
He is the lord of Ramā, Prabhā, Māṇikī, and Pārvatī; he is the husband of the woman.
"He who is the beloved of Lalitā is indeed the beloved of women;
for all chaste wives, O virtuous lady, arise from but a millionth part of her!
Thus has the practice of service been described to you through the state of oneness.
By reading or hearing this, one shall obtain the fruit of devotion to one's husband.

Thus ends the four hundred and twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of how Liberation was Granted by Bhāradvāja to the Couple Vīrabāhu and Kāntimatī— after Three Births as a Brahmin, a Śūdra, and a King— within the Devotion to Husband" in the first section, the *Kṛtayugasantāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Chapter 430 →
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī! To the story of my wife, the daughter of the Sun, who was a preeminent and most cheerful companion residing within Goloka. (1)
Whenever her friends gathered for a grand play in the garden,
she would laugh there again and again.
Once, accompanied by Rādhikā and millions of other women, the gopīs—
They went to bathe in the divine lake created for my sake.
Then, having stepped upon the moss with her feet, Rādhikā fell into it;
Yamunā ran toward Rādhikā to catch her and laughed.
Rādhā said: "O Yamunā! Why do you laugh at this jest?
Laughter filled with mirth is not at all appropriate when it is misplaced.
I have fallen, covered in mud, and struck on my back by a stone."
"Do not joke while water has entered your nose, mouth, and eyes.
Thus admonished, she too took hold of Rādhā and,
seizing her garments and other items, gave them to her for wearing.
Her face, hair, and back were washed and well-adorned;
then, seeing Rādhā once again, she laughed repeatedly.
But Rādhā, becoming angry, [directed her words] toward Yamunā, who was generally her servant.
"May you have hair like moss and be covered in mud," she said.
Then Yamunā, being angry, spoke again and again to Rādhā:
"O beloved, sport with me in the mud and even amidst the moss."
"Having abandoned you, I shall never wander about at any time.
Knowing both [of them], Kṛṣṇa said: "Do not say this, do not say this, my dear!
O beautiful ones, how shall I remain deprived of you two? (11)
"I shall go there, O worshipful Yamunā, where you are.
Having become the river Yamunā, the daughter of the Sun,
that virtuous one first created the Himalaya mountain and then went to Vṛndāvana.
Rādhā too, having become a cowherd girl and the daughter of Rāpaṇa, constantly wandered upon the banks of the Yamunā amidst its moss and mud;
through the expansion of her secret assignations with Kṛṣṇa, she became the beloved of Kṛṣṇa.
Yamunā, in the form of a maiden, serves her husband Hari.
Once, while the young wives of Kṛṣṇa were playing with Kṛṣṇa in that forest, Yamunā saw those young girls.
Upon merely beholding Kṛṣṇa, she, longing for her beloved, desired him.
Kṛṣṇa said to her, "O Yamunā! From now on, become a maiden;
O daughter of King Kalinda, I shall perform your marriage."
"Quickly become my wife; of this there is no doubt.
She, however, was born as a maiden from the second body of Kalindarāja, and she too was married by Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Once, the wives of Kṛṣṇa, distressed by separation from Śrī Kṛṣṇa,
beheld the joyful Kālindī and, free from envy, questioned her:
"O daughter of the Sun, just as we are the wives of Kṛṣṇa, so too are you."
"We are consumed by separation; how can you exist without it?
Hearing this, Kālindī, the daughter of the Sun and servant of Kṛṣṇa, said:
"I indeed attain the divine Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa at all times."
The Blessed One never goes far away from me;
the Great Queen Rādhikā is the very soul of Kṛṣṇa and possesses the form of Kṛṣṇa.
Indeed, I am a portion of Rādhikā, and I am not distinct from the form of Kṛṣṇa.
Without Rādhā there is no Kṛṣṇa, nor am I without Rādhikā;
and Kṛṣṇa does not exist at all without me—know this to be our very oneness.
Even so, service to Rādhā is indeed preeminent.
Then, through that bliss, I rejoice and truly experience no separation;
for a virtuous woman devoted to her husband keeps her husband within her womb, her heart, her vow, her side,
and her very self-consciousness— of this there is no doubt.
In dreams and in waking, she delights with her husband even during sleep;
there is no difference between their two bodies, for their state is one of union with the Lord.
Whenever he desires, then her husband, whose essence is Nārāyaṇa, [appears]. (27–28)
Having arrived, He is the bestower of bliss; there is never any separation.
Whatever happiness a virtuous, devoted wife desires, Hari assumes the form of a husband for the sake of granting that very happiness. (29)
She fulfills the heart's desires of her devoted wife in every way.
Therefore, for a noble, devoted wife, there is truly no separation from her husband;
he alone is this very Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, our lord and master.
"I am the fulfiller of all desires; I have no separation from anyone anywhere.
Hearing this, those women said: "O Kālindī!
If Kṛṣṇa always stays with you, show him to us right now."
Having been addressed thus, she laughed and, with her hand,
indeed separated her own garment from her right side by a distance of one cubit.
At that moment, Yama, standing there at her side, smilingly embraced Yamī.
Beheld by them as he repeatedly delighted Kālindī, Kṛṣṇa was gazed upon; then all those charming women, having seen their husband Hari for a moment,
praised the conjugal fidelity of the daughter of the Sun.
That alone is true devotion to one’s husband (pātivratya) wherein the husband himself is Nārāyaṇa.
He exists as the very nature of Nārāyaṇa and is, in every way, the inner self (antarātman).
He is never separate from her, just as the self (ātman) is never dissociated [from its body].

Thus, there may indeed be a woman who is devoted, wise, and faithful to her husband; yet she may be a virtuous wife (*satī*) by her actions, but not by her mind. Or, there may be one who is a virtuous wife by her mind, but not by her actions. (38)
If a certain woman is virtuous through her intellect, yet not through her mind nor through her actions;
or if she is found to be virtuous through all three, yet not through her very self— then everything born from her arises only for separation [from the goal] and is devoid of the Self.
That which is called *pātivratya* (devotion to one's husband) by oneself—that is the highest form of *pātivratya*.
Such a state has been attained by me eternally, certainly through the grace of Rādhā.
Therefore, because of my servitude, my lordship, and my *pātivratya*, Kṛṣṇa resides within me.
We are the consorts of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, existing as partial manifestations (aṃśa) of Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa.
Through our connection with Him, eternal enjoyment is also found within us.
He alone is He, she alone is She; that very Rādhā is indeed the treasure-trove of divine love.
The love of those two, being perfectly embodied, assumed the form of the flute.
I have perceived that the presence of Rukmiṇī and the others resides within Rādhā.
And you all, together with Śrī Kṛṣṇa, abide within Rādhā.
You are united with and never separated from the great ocean of eternal bliss;
yet, because you do not know this, you have fallen into agitation. However, if the souls were devoted to their own true nature (*pātivratya*), such agitation would not occur. (45–46)
Even regarding their devotion to their husbands, the gopīs, like yourselves, were under an illusion;
that semblance of separation existed [only as such] and was destroyed by Uddhava.
If there were a true reunion of Uddhava with you, [that illusion would vanish].
The disappearance of the appearance of separation shall occur, and you will obtain the bliss of your beloved.
On the ground of Govardhana Hill, Uddhava, in the form of the Vallī creeper, eternally desires the sanctity brought by the dust from the feet of the gopīs. (48–49)
But he always dwells in bliss, devoted to his wife;
if he is to be attained in embodied form,
then a great festival shall take place at that spot, joined by his wives with recitations, songs, and musical performances.
"An effort must be made there; his vision will certainly come to pass.
Likewise, the fulfillment of one's own endeavors is inevitable.
Having been told this, the wives of Kṛṣṇa went quickly to the grove of creepers.
Not far from Govardhana, they began a festival of kīrtana;
their minds became focused on nothing else but the aesthetic flavor of songs to Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
Meanwhile, the devotee was so overwhelmed by the weight of love that he [did not distinguish] from the mass of grass, shrubs, and creepers... [53]
Uddhava arrived, wearing a garland, divine, and clad in yellow garments;
singing of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, dancing, bowing, and laughing.
Bearing the very form of Kṛṣṇa, the women were filled with great wonder upon seeing him. (54–55)
They honored Uddhava, who was the very embodiment of Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
seeing him in the form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the women were bewildered and wept.
Then Uddhava perceived the fire of separation within those women.
Having drawn Kṛṣṇa from his own heart, he offered him to them for a moment.
There, by means of his yogic power (yogamāyā), Kṛṣṇa was manifested in a thousand forms;
in every bower and before every beloved, the charming one became the fulfiller of their desires.
He gave his beloved wife embraces, kisses, and love-filled dalliance;
he bestowed upon her supreme bliss and extinguished the fierce fire of their separation.
Kṛṣṇa granted them self-pacification, just as he had done for Uddhava;
likewise, he bestowed upon them lifelong devotion to their husbands, like that of Kālindī.
And he, the bestower of eternal self-bliss, remained dissolved by their side.
Just as one who desires a woman remains devoted to her through three stages,
so too did they take Kṛṣṇa by the hem of his garment and go to their home; Uddhava also, having led Hari to the creepers, departed.
O Lotus-born One! This indeed is declared to be the nature of *pativratya* (devotion to one’s husband).
By hearing and reciting this, one shall obtain that very vow;
there is no doubt that one will find Kṛṣṇa constantly at one's side, on one's garment, and in one's heart.

Thus ends the four hundred and twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of how Kālindī’s Devotion to Her Husband and Uddhava’s Devotion to His Master caused the other wives of Kṛṣṇa to attain firmness in their own devotion to their husband," in the first section, the *Kṛtayugasantāna*, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: When I, Viṣṇu, am the speaker and you, Lakṣmī, are intent upon listening—
Then, the hearing of the *Saṃhitā* bestows liberation within two months.
When Lakṣmī is the speaker, Viṣṇu is the listener, and I am also present,
then the hearing of the *Saṃhitā* bestows liberation within four months.

By means of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā*, Dhruva attained eternal prosperity; and by hearing it from my own mouth, you have attained the virtue of devotion to your husband. Indeed, Rādhā attained this through hearing the *Saṃhitā* from the mouth of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Likewise, from the mouths of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, [the truth was heard] by other gopīs.
In Kāśī, at Kuṅkumavāpī, in Badarī, and in other divine abodes,
she certainly possesses a portion of Him according to her fitness throughout the entire creation.
Men and women who attained supreme devotion to Narayana reached eternal liberation in my eternal abode.
Listen, Lakshmi, to this delightful narrative which destroys the bonds of worldly existence!
In the land of Pañcāla there was a king, a Vaiṣṇava, righteous and pure. (7) King Nirbhayavarman was devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa; he constantly worshipped Śrī Nārāyaṇa with a garland of tulasī. (8)

And where the mad Savitrī, the maidservant of Kṛṣṇa, shines forth; there,
in the western Vyāghrāraṇya forest of the Rākṣasa Tala,

Having spoken thus, they all poured the hot water from the Talaśyāma tirtha onto the corpse in a continuous stream, saying, "Become alive! Thereupon,
the Ṛṣi rose up and bowed repeatedly to those elders.

The water from their feet destroys even the sin of killing a Brahmin, and the auspicious dust of their feet utterly annihilates the sins of the wicked.
The worship, food, and all other offerings made to them always provide protection;
and their well-formed blessings protect one throughout both time and place.
This should be done according to one's capacity, according to one's available materials, and according to one's disposition.
The virtuous are always to be served; they are divine manifestations of Hari.
Indeed, being devoid of material qualities and free from all bonds, they truly deliver their servants.
O Lakṣmī, by the service of Trita, even the sin of killing a Brahmin was dissolved.
Then Prince Dānaka, filled with wonder, repeatedly thought:
"The company of the virtuous is the cause of her destruction.
Just then, the followers of Yama arrived there to take him away.

By the merit of his service, he remembered the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa—
the Lord of the gopīs, Hari, Kṛṣṇa, the Master, and the Lord of the worlds.

"He will become a servant of the virtuous, a great Vaiṣṇava;

"O auspicious one, Rādhā and Lakṣmī shall dwell with your two sisters and me;

"I shall dwell in your fortress; may it be well with you, O servant!

The Blessed Dhārmika is present before her every day—at her meals, her sleep, in the courtyard, during recreation, and at festivals. (64–65)

and who live for My sake, are considered Mine;
for they perform My work and have renounced their lives for My sake.
And with a serene soul, I am always present as their companion.
O Yama, whatever one does, that very act becomes supreme if it brings about liberation;
for an agent exerts himself to the best of his ability in the service of his master.

To that extent he becomes one who has accomplished his purpose and shall certainly not go to hell. When his capacity for the task has been fully exerted, he should indeed report it to his master. To that extent the servant is free from debt and, as an official, enjoys happiness.
Therefore, for one who has declared the truth, there is neither debt nor sin.
When one has exerted effort in what was one’s duty, there is no fault on the part of the embodied being.
Consequently, you ought not to grieve over this impossible task.
I shall renounce even Lakṣmī, or my life-breaths, or even my body;
or likewise the Śrīvatsa mark, the Kaustubha gem, and the Vaijayantī garland;
or even Śvetadvīpa, Vaikuṇṭha, and the Ocean of Milk.

I cannot bring myself to abandon Śoṣa and Garuḍa, who do not eat [ordinary food]. How could I bear to abandon those illustrious ones, who have renounced all enjoyments for my sake, who have sacrificed their very lives for me, and whose souls are absorbed in me?

Therefore, O King, I am going by means of this vehicle to grant you the gift of a vision of Hari himself at the time of the excellent meal, and to lead you away. Go first to the realm of Yama; after that, O Yama, I shall come.
"Tell him this from me:
'He will then become overwhelmed by my love and, abandoning the chanting of my names, will engage in laughter and dancing.
As soon as he does so, give him a vision of me and take him up into my celestial chariot. || 11.2-11.3 ||
"I shall go from the realm of Yama after having accomplished your task.
Having been addressed thus, Yama departed from there exceedingly joyful. He then announced the arrival of Kṛṣṇa to that slayer of demons.

Filled with love for the Blessed One, he too performed dances and other such acts. At that moment, a divine celestial chariot indeed arrived; and upon seeing the four-armed Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, Dānaka beheld him.
By the command of Kṛṣṇa, he ascended the celestial chariot, crying out repeatedly:
"Oṃ, obeisances to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, obeisances to the Master!
Dancing, meditating, and bowing to Kṛṣṇa, he then became immersed in divine love.
Accepting the worship offered by Dharmarāja, the Blessed Lord Hari,
accompanied by Rādhā and Ramā, went to the house of the donor in Durgā.
Having set down his supreme devotee, the Lord himself remained there for the night.

Having granted permission for Rādhā to dwell within her as a portion of her own beauty, and likewise for Śrī to dwell as a portion of her own splendor— just as one might permit a shadow to reside within—
He then took those two maidens and purified his own abodes.
Having bathed in the water of the Unmattā and drunk its purifying waters there,
she departed for her own abode by means of a divine, celestial vehicle.
When the gopīs learned of that event, they likewise [departed] from the district of Mathurā.
From Dvārakā, Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma departed, their forms divine.
Because it was the abode of Rādhā and Lakṣmī, as well as of the gopīs and the wives of Kṛṣṇa,
this sacred field became a city characterized by fortitude and the nature of Durgā.
Due to the residence of Śrī Hari there, that place indeed became like Goloka;
it became divine, equal to the abode of Brahmā, supreme, and a bestower of liberation.
By the sight of it, by touching it, and by drinking from or bathing in the waters of its river—
By wearing the dust upon the body, there is the destruction of sins and liberation.
[This occurs] through the majesty of Rādhā and Lakṣmī, through the bull-like virtue of their devotion,
and through the vow of Sāṃkhya-yoga of their innumerable maidservants.
It bestows the fruit of ten million sacrifices upon those who take refuge in Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa;
it grants the supreme imperishable state to the listener, the speaker, and the pilgrim. (1.29)

Thus, in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, concerning the devotion of a husband to his wife (*pātivratya*): during the pilgrimage of King Dādaka (or Dānaka) of the Saurāṣṭra and Pañcāla regions to the Talaśyāma forest, he was struck by a sage in the form of a lion. Consequently, the sin of Brahmin-slaughter arose; however, through service to the sage Trita, that sin was destroyed. Thereafter, the messengers of Yama arrived, but they were repelled by the Lord’s attendants (*pārṣadas*). By means of devotion to Hari, those in Yama’s realm and in hell were liberated. [This concerns] Dādaka (Da), Rādhā-Lakṣmī—

Chapter Four Hundred and Thirty (430), titled "The Description of Nārāyaṇa’s Blessing, Durgā’s Abode as a Portion of Jīvantī and Lāvaṇyavatī, the Residence of Rādhā and Lakṣmī, and Hari’s Own Dwelling in the Sacred Field of Durgā. Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā — Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga) — Chapter 431.
[Author: Chapter 432.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī! I shall tell you of the most excellent bull among women devoted to their husbands.
The husband is Nārāyaṇa-Kṛṣṇa; devotion to him is the vow of a faithful wife (pativratā).
[1] To the extent that she employs the actions of her intellect as means for the sake of her husband, so is it ordained by the wife that the husband may be glorified. [2]

Whether devoid of virtues, possessed of virtues, or even possessed of evil qualities, a woman is praised in every way by the tongue and the mind, just like the Lord. O Lakṣmī, that vow is considered the foremost, the supreme devotion to her husband.
Praise is like sugar for all living beings in every respect;
it is experienced everywhere as exceedingly sweet and most delicious.
Just as a father and mother rejoice through the praise of their son, [so do others rejoice in praise]. (4–5)
Sons rejoice with great joy through the praise of their father;
a husband rejoices within himself through the praise of his wife.
A servant [rejoices] through the praise of the merchant, and the subjects through the praise of the king.
By praising the bull, even the bull-driver rejoices;
by praising the disciple, the teacher rejoices; by praising the teacher, the follower rejoices;
by praising the country, the native rejoices; and by praising the scripture, the believer rejoices. (7–8)

O Lakṣmī! That which exists for the sake of another always brings praise to that other person; it is the abode of joy and delight, bringing forth enthusiasm and celebration, and is ever filled with the glory of her husband. (9)
Upon hearing news of her beloved who is abroad,
the devoted wife instantly becomes filled with a joy even greater than that of a festival for a son.
That vow of devotion to her husband, which brings forth such delight, is accessible only through the mind.
Others indeed do not perceive the affection residing in the heart of the Supreme Self;
for the qualities of the Supreme Self are by no means directly manifest,
due to the absence there of the cause, which is the conjunction of one's own self with the mind.

Through the application of practices such as possession (*āveśa*) and by means of traditional lineage (*paramparā*), these appear to others as if they were perceptible, yet they are not real. For conjugal fidelity is always affectionate—both when it is causeless and when it has a cause. (13–14)
Whether for her own sake or for the sake of another, it is her own interest alone that is experienced;
a woman’s persistent concern is, "How might my husband become renowned?
Indeed, she must always be mindful of being devoted to her husband. (15)
Just as you possess joy and intense longing upon hearing news of your husband,
so too does he who possesses an intense longing for the understanding of Kṛṣṇa’s stories,
or even for hearing, chanting, and praising them. (16–17)

For a devoted man and a devoted woman who are always virtuous and truthful toward Hari, their eternal devotion to their husband shines forth. Devotion to the husband is the highest form of service; it is auspicious and bestows divine grace.
Listening to the narrative is considered superior to [ordinary] devotion to one's husband;
chanting the narrative is even more excellent than that. Indeed, the constant singing of the glory of one’s own husband, one’s master, is difficult to attain.
Constantly singing the virtues of her husband, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, with a sense of non-difference from Him, is the supreme devotion of a woman to her husband.
Devotion to the husband consisting of the narration of Hari’s stories bestows the world of the virtuous husband.
There is no doubt for either the listener or the speaker: I, Janārdana, am well-pleased.
I lead that [man] to the great heaven and likewise the world of virtuous women (*satī*) for the virtuous woman;
and indeed, I send those free from desire to my own abode, my supreme state.
For by means of my stories, devotion to me has been continuously instilled in the hearts of millions and tens of millions of beings;
and through these stories, service to me has sprouted within those embodied souls.
My vow, my service, my worship, my honoring;
my recitation, my devotion, my remembrance, my refuge;
my desire, my realization, my meditation, my effort. (25–26)
My yoga, my desire, my offering, my grasping;
my concentration, my placement [of the mind] in Me, my dwelling in Me, my petition;
my non-duality with Me, my affection for Me, my longing for Me, and my delight in Me. (27)
My gift of all possessions, my life and my death are for my sake;
my acquisition of wealth is for my sake, and my service is for my sake.
My charity, vows, and merit, as well as my assistance to others, are all for my sake. (28–29)
He who has caused my arrival at his feet at the end and his constant acceptance of my service through my discourses within the hearts of people—
such a person is a speaker of my stories and a bestower of knowledge of the scriptures upon me.

O Lakṣmī, the devotion to her husband of that woman who nourishes my greatness and fosters my bhaktas is considered by me to be ten million times greater than ordinary devotion. Indeed, the eternal devotion to her husband spoken of by the Supreme is the most excellent of all excellences. (3.1–3.2)
I do not reach the end of the merit of reciting this narrative; yet,
by means of the Vaiṣṇava consciousness toward countless species of living beings and their lineages,
the teacher who recites the narrative indeed becomes their savior.
O Lotus-born One, he who is in the form of a fish is undoubtedly superior to you;
he is ten times greater than his father, and the teacher is ten times greater than the mother.
This is because the father provides the seed, while the mother grants birth.
The Guru is declared to be superior to all because he bestows liberation.
The husband is superior, the Guru is superior; yet the Guru is more superior than both. Father, husband, and Guru are all excellent, but the Guru is the most excellent among them.
The self is supreme; Hari is supreme; of these two, Hari is most supreme.
(37) The self is Hari, the supreme teacher; among them, the teacher is most supreme.
Through taking refuge in him, one attains Hari; without him, Hari is difficult to reach. (38)
The givers of land, the givers of livelihood, and the givers of life are always excellent;
yet, compared to them, the giver of liberation through knowledge is most excellent.
Knowledge of Kṛṣṇa is the highest form of devotion to one's husband, and he who bestows that knowledge is remembered as the true good husband.
Devotion to Kṛṣṇa is the duty of one's own master; He who bestows that [devotion] is the true husband for all time.
Any other husband who merely bears the name is a husband in name only, whereas the husband who grants devotion is the husband in the true sense of the word.
Knowing this, O beloved, one should always maintain devotion to Hari as one's husband.
The singing of Hari’s qualities, the contemplation of Hari’s form,
the exposition of Hari’s narratives, and devotion to one's husband— these are supreme.
Wherever the narrative [of Hari] is found, there reside the devotees, the sacred fords, and Acyuta himself.
The goddesses, the seers, the ancestors, liberation, devotion, and the bull [Dharma], and so forth;
the perfected ones, ascetics, the truthful, the virtuous, and likewise the yogis;
the ages, the scriptures, the Vedas, the sacred fields, and the forests. (43–44)
Vyāsas, the principles of reality, and those who are liberated—all of whom are characters in the narrative—come there and constantly listen to that story, overflowing with emotion.
Some are embodied and some are unembodied; likewise, some are invisible and others are visible.
All those devoted to their husbands listen indeed to the stories of Hari.
Having heard again and again the fame of Hari’s own glory, the renown of his devotees,
and their sacred narratives, they rejoice and bestow blessings upon them.
Likewise, the listeners and the assembly of disciples indeed pay homage to that teacher who recites;
therefore, the one who causes [the teaching] to be heard is the most excellent of all, for he bestows devotion toward the Guru.
He is to be known as equal to Nārāyaṇa and the awakener of devotion to the husband.
Having bowed to Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa and having heard the auspicious narrative of Hari, one is liberated from all sins and goes to the supreme abode of Kṛṣṇa. (1.431.50)
Long ago, on the banks of the Godāvarī, a wonderful story unfolded: there was indeed a complete recitation of the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*.
It destroys sin, it is purifying, it bestows heaven, and it grants knowledge and liberation. (51)
The disciple of the sage Durvāsas was an ascetic named Satyavrata;
he was established in Brahman, indifferent to worldly concerns, subsisting solely on alms, dwelling in caves there, and devoted to the vow of non-possession. ||52-53||
Wearing a garland of *tulasī*, and chanting the name of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa,
she would daily perform the recitation of His stories every evening at dusk, O beloved! Having meditated upon, remembered, and caused her husband Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa to be remembered—
Having offered salutations and having caused [others] to offer them, he narrates the stories of Kṛṣṇa.
Even in the absence of listeners and the non-arrival of commentators,
Satyavrata constantly narrates the stories of Śrī Hari.
Having performed his own daily obligatory rites, he indeed engages in the narration of Hari’s stories.
If there is anyone who would listen, he explains them to him day and night.
Even if there is no listener in that place, he carries on the narration even in solitude.
At that time, someone else explains the meritorious story of Hari;
[another] abandons his own duties and listens to the story of Śrī Hari; [and another], devoted to devotion toward Hari, delights in hearing the story. (58–59)
Abandoning the holy sites of the deities as well as their temples,
and abandoning other activities that are obstacles to the narrative,
he always listens to the divine story whenever a speaker is present.
In the absence of a speaker, she herself expounds the sacred stories of Kṛṣṇa.
Without such stories, she does not know the supreme virtue of devotion to her husband;
thus, both in the public square and in her own home, she expounds them with heartfelt emotion.
Necessary duties are indeed no more than what arises from the discourse;
the supreme necessary duty is that which consists of the discourse itself as the primary focus.
Indeed, upon the cessation of the discourse, other duties alone become predominant.

O Lakṣmī! For one who listens to this discourse, there is no bondage of karma. The lamp of knowledge becomes fully kindled, and renunciation increases. Likewise, purity of being and peace arise in him as he listens. (64–65)
Joy for Hari arises always for one who hears the narrative, and firmness is attained;
through love and great passion for Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa is held within the heart.
Toward those in whom Kṛṣṇa resides, a sense of kinship toward them as virtuous beings is born.
Hari, appearing in the form of a holy man, will certainly become manifest before him.
Then, having recognized his supreme devotion to his wife, the divine Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Śrī, will personally grant him a divine vision.
Therefore, both men and women should listen to the stories of Kṛṣṇa according to their capacity.
Indeed, without these stories there is no knowledge, and without that, there is no peace at all.
In this worldly existence which is a whirlpool of suffering, the glorification of Kṛṣṇa is the bringer of peace.
The hearing of the narrative is the supreme means for remembering Kṛṣṇa.
It also effects the purification of the *sattva* quality, and through that purity, meditation (*dhyāna*) arises.
Hearing it in many ways, reflecting upon it, and meditating upon it are the highest [practices]. (1.431.70–71)

This is considered the means for attaining Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa as one’s husband. Even the banks of the Gaṅgā should be abandoned if they lack stories of Kṛṣṇa and are devoid of saintly persons; without such a husband, that place is not dear.
Where there is no tulasī, where there is no temple of Hari,
where there exists no devotee devoted to the vow of fidelity to Lord Hari,
and where there is no discourse on Viṣṇu— that village is like a cremation ground. (73–74)
"Upon death there, a person goes to the realm of darkness ruled by King Yama.
Reflecting thus, that king of sages, Satyavrata, was a true Vaiṣṇava,
devoted to the knowledge of Brahman and solely intent upon the remembrance of Viṣṇu.
Constantly devoted to the stories of Hari, he considers his own actions to be for that purpose alone.
He never considers anything superior to hearing [the stories] or even to narrating them; indeed, for him, there is no dharma higher than that.
Every evening at the appointed time, he would regularly come to the Vyāsa-paṭṭikā and deliver his discourse there.
Once, the king’s army arrived at its side.
All the people were blocked, and Vyāsa himself was indeed obstructed.
"No one at all should proceed here along this path through the midst of the army"—
thus the path was blocked by him, and the flow of conversation was likewise halted.
The gods and others who had come to that place for the sake of hearing [the teaching] waited there for the arrival of the speaker, gazing in his direction;
yet Satyavrata did not arrive, and thus the appointed time passed away.
Then Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, assuming the very form of Satyavrata,
sat down upon a seat himself to narrate the story;
Hari then delivered the discourse of the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*.
The gods heard with their spiritual intuition that the army had then been routed from the path.
Satyavrata, having seen Vyāsa in his true form,
was struck by great wonder upon realizing that [Vyāsa] was remembering Hari.
He was made by Viṣṇu so that he would not be visible to others under any other name.
Then, having come, he became absorbed into the form of Viṣṇu’s seat, so that the discourse might proceed there without interruption. (85–86)
There, Satyavrata, who was dear to Viṣṇu, was reconciled with him;
Kṛṣṇa attained invisibility, and the story proceeds in that manner.
Satyavrata spoke a verse composed by Viṣṇu.
At that moment, the sweetness of his voice underwent a transformation;
its allure and divinity became of a different kind than before.
Then it was perceived by the gods and others, as well as by those practitioners of yoga absorbed in meditation. (88–89)
In the absence of Satyavrata, Kṛṣṇa himself narrated the story.
"Oh, how blessed we are to have come to hear this narrative from the mouth of Kṛṣṇa!"—
thus all were filled with wonder and listened to the story once again.
Just then, another disciple of Durvāsas arrived there, named Tapovrata. He was a man devoted to ritual action who always showed disregard for the discourse;
considering the story to be false, he treated both the listeners and the speakers with mockery.
Having heard the discourse, he laughed aloud and engaged in caviling;
after somehow managing to speak, the obstinate man declared:
"The speaker is deceiving these people, who are like cattle. (93)
"Bound by the net of deception, they repeatedly speak with false discourse.
Having said this, he then departed, leaving behind the story that was being told;
for he never explains anything himself, nor does he ever listen to such things.
Considering austerity to be the supreme task, he always performs auspicious domestic duties and the like; yet he indeed speaks in disparagement of those very stories.
Thus, when the end of his life arrives in the forest, it is indeed due to the sin of that disparagement.
He became a Piśāca in a Śamī tree in a waterless place, with his ears severed (97).
Without food, suffering great misery, his throat, lips, and palate parched,
he wandered like one intoxicated or insane, reflecting upon his own deeds (98).

For this man of sinful deeds, water becomes like fire, and fruits, flowers, and the like become poison; his very wind becomes equal to fire. Even while performing rituals in the forest, he finds neither peace nor satisfaction.
In a forest devoid of people and devoid of conversation, he was seen by Satyavrata, who happened to be traveling along the path, as he wept, distressed by hunger.
"Who are you? Tell me, why have you fallen into such a state? he asked.
Thus addressed, Tapovrata, whose ears had been severed, replied to him:
"I am a good disciple of Durvāsas, bearing the excellent name Tapovrata.
Due to the sin arising from the disparagement of sacred stories, I have become a Piśāca and am deeply distressed."
"By the sight of you today, my liberation shall indeed come to pass here.
Forgive me for my offenses, such as my contentious disputations.
Having spoken thus, weeping and desiring liberation, he touched the earth. (103–104)
He fell at the feet of Satyavrata, crying out, "Save me!
Satyavrata, holding water in his hand and remembering Hari, [spoke]:
"Oṃ, obeisances to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa; obeisances to the Lord."
Thus he whispered the mantra into his ear and sprinkled water upon his head.
Having placed his foot upon his back and burned away his sin according to his power,
he bestowed the supreme merit of a single day’s narration.
Having bestowed the knowledge arising from the narrative of the chapter of the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā* and having liberated him from his piśāca body,
he endowed him with a divine body and remembered the Lord Śrī Hari.
At that moment, Kṛṣṇa arrived, endowed with the splendor of Rādhā and Lakṣmī;
the Lord of Pārvatī and Māṇikī, the husband of Padmā and Ramā, the Lord of Lalitā and Śrī, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, together with his attendants.
Seated upon a supreme celestial chariot (vimāna) that outshone ten million suns,
the Blessed One was repeatedly bowed to, worshipped, and praised by Satyavrata.
He was entreated again and again to take him along with his ascetic observances to his own celestial chariot.
There, the Lord Hari, who fulfills the desires of his devotees, laughed and said,
"He indeed possesses no merit worthy of residence in Goloka.
Then Satyavrata, having been initiated with the mantra of the Guru, spoke.
O Kṛṣṇa, this meritorious man has been made a Vaiṣṇava by me here;
I have bestowed upon him the merit of a single chapter from the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*,
and I now give him a garland of *tulasī*.
O Keśava, I give this water from your feet to him once again;
and in an instant, I give him the prasāda and the naivedya of your own grace.
By that merit, through your mere favor, may this devotee [attain his goal].
"May you go to your abode, Goloka; you are the fulfiller of the desires of your devotees.
Thus addressed, Hari said to Satyavrata, "So be it.
Then, having bowed to the sage, he who was devoted to his ascetic vows [ascended] the celestial chariot by the command of Acyuta.
He ascended and departed for Goloka along with Viṣṇu. At that time, Durvāsas, possessing divine vision, arrived there and praised his own disciple Satyavrata, the narrator of the tale.
Then Durvāsas, his mind filled with joy, spoke again and again to that peaceful Vaiṣṇava, who grants liberation to his fellow students and delivers others from worldly existence:
"Oh, how one disciple has indeed delivered another diligent practitioner!"
Oh, how by a single disciple the entire world has been delivered!
Oh, how by a single disciple I, the teacher, have likewise been delivered!
Oh, how by a single disciple I now truly possess a disciple!
Though I have ten thousand disciples, I am truly possessed of excellent disciples because of Satyavrata, who serves the stories of Kṛṣṇa;
for there, the flood-tide of the stream of Kṛṣṇa’s stories flows forever.
"In that regard, liberation, brought about by dwelling [in the Lord], enters the hand-vessel like a maidservant.
(124) Thus, O Lakṣmī, have you been made to hear this story of the bull among men who was devoted to his wife.
By hearing and reciting it, one shall attain the station of the abode of Kṛṣṇa. (125)

Thus ends the four hundred and thirty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Liberation from Piśāca-hood and Attainment of the Divine Abode of Satyavrata’s Penance through the Gift of the Merit of a Single Day’s Story by Satyavrata, the Disciple of Durvāsas Devoted to Chastity; and how, when Satyavrata was absent at the time of the story, the Blessed Lord assumed the form of Satyavrata and recited the narrative," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. 431.1.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī!
I shall describe to you a divine marvel concerning one devoted to her husband, which destroys the heat of sin.
In the land of Pāñcāla and Saurāṣṭra, there was a king named Hemanta;
longing for merit, he ruled his kingdom with righteousness in the western region.
Previously, he had bestowed gifts of jewels and gold.
Water has no monetary value, yet he did not practice the giving of water.
Due to that fault, as the king was gradually becoming defiled,
his prosperity began to decline, and his elephants and horses were afflicted by disease.
Indeed, that excellent wealth of livestock— cows, buffaloes, and the like— which had perished,
as well as all the goats, sheep, and wild animals such as deer,
were all gradually brought to destruction, afflicted by disease. (5)
A drought occurred that brought about the departure of people;
consequently, the land became parched, and the subjects went to other regions.
The royal treasury and so forth became empty, void, and devoid of strength.
But other five kings, having learned of this, assembled and set out on their expedition;
considering him easy to defeat, they arrived from all sides.
They conquered the King of Pañcāla in battle and carried off his wealth.
In the Hemanta season, joined by his devoted wife on Mount Raivata,
he entered a mountain cave together with his nurses, servants, and others.
Accompanied by his proud wife, the king wandered through the forest regions.
In the Badarī and Jambu forest, he reflected in many ways:
"What is this suffering that has come upon me, though my sustenance consists only of fruits and roots?
Indeed, I have given gifts in many ways on every sacred festival. (11)

As a servant, I have performed everything beneficial for my mother and father. I have constantly gratified my gurus and protected the Brahmins; I have always well-guarded the Dharma and worshipped the gods. (12–13)
I am not under the sway of my senses, nor am I addicted to vices;
nor have I ever associated with those who commit theft, adultery, and the like.
Nevertheless, how has this poverty come upon me?
A great defeat has occurred; my kinsmen and others have become hostile.
(15) But all those who were formerly favorable have now turned adverse.
O Lord, for what action is this fruit that I have obtained? (16)
As he was thus reflecting incessantly in the forest of Mount Raivata,
his preceptor named Yājaka arrived there for the purpose of a pilgrimage; having reached him,
he was honored with forest offerings, satisfied, and prostrated at his feet.
The lord of the Pañcālas then asked for the cause of his misfortune:
"How have poverty, the depletion of the treasury, defeat by enemies, the loss of the kingdom, dwelling in the forest, and the turning away of kinsmen come to pass? (18–19)
"O Guru, why is there even drought in my country? Tell me this!
Thus questioned, the Guru meditated, discerned that the cause was entirely the result of actions born of a previous birth, and told him everything; listen, O King!
Formerly, you were a forest-dwelling hunter who harmed living beings;
you were cruel, skilled in theft, devoid of righteous deeds, and even an obstacle to the practice of chanting the name of Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (21–22)
Devoid of remembrance of Kṛṣṇa and always lacking in prostration,
you are a rogue who lives by weapons, oppresses the subjects obtained through your path,
and commits the slaughter of children, offspring, deer, and birds.
Offspring are not born, and for one who is born, there is miscarriage of the fetus (24).
Due to being a betrayer of trust, one has no kinsmen or brothers;
due to causing distress on the path, one is abandoned by friends and well-wishers (25).
Through the disparagement of the virtuous, you were defeated by your enemies;
indeed, poverty has now befallen you due to the fault of never having given anything.
You cause suffering to those who travel abroad, and your own misery is truly distressing.
You were the perpetrator of every insult, and now you have undergone great humiliation.
Because you did not give water and other necessities, you are tormented by thirst in the forest; thus, through the ripening of your past karma, you remain without food. (27–28)
Then, O Queen, while you were performing meritorious deeds that bestow sovereignty in the forest, listen: a certain sage named Karṣaṇa arrived there;
he was a practitioner of the vow of celibacy and was devoted to devotion to Kṛṣṇa and to his wife.

Then, having taken up your bow and standing before him blocking the path, you asked: "O forest-dweller! If there is anything, let it be given to me! The sage replied: "O rogue! An inexhaustible treasure is present here before me."
"If you wish [to give], I shall bestow it; take the vessel if you are worthy.
Hearing him, he was struck with wonder there, thinking, "What kind of vessel is this, and what is this wealth?
Having reflected, he said to him, "If I am worthy, then give it."
At his words, Karṣaṇa was pleased and said, "O rogue!
Tell me truthfully: how many killings have you committed here in the past?
The hunter replied, "In the forest, on the far side, a thousand were slain by me."
"Beasts, other birds, and even small humans—you, a sinful cultivator, desire to wash away your sins!
If you so wish, I shall wash those sins of yours here. (35)
The hunter said, "I desire the washing away of my sins.
Karṣaṇa said, "First, having bathed, come into my presence.
The hunter, having bathed, came afterwards, [carrying water] mixed with *tulasī* leaves.
He was offered beautiful, dark water for his drink;
he drank that remaining water and then placed it upon his head.
Having washed the feet of his guru, he drank the water once again.
Then, while pulling him by his right ear again and again, the great mantra was made to be heard three times: "Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine namaḥ. (1.432.40)
And from the pores of his body, thousands of sins, such as the murder of a Brahmin and others, emerged in embodied form on all sides;
they all wept, wretched and deformed. (41)
Then they all spoke of that plowing as terrifying:
"What offense have we committed, and why have we been expelled from his body by you, O Sage? Have mercy! Show compassion! (42-43)
"Give me lodging with you, or with him, or in some other place;
for what has been done by him in the depths of the forest must certainly be experienced [as its fruit].
Then Karṣaṇa said, "Indeed, by the name of Kṛṣṇa, his sins are truly being drawn away."
"Since you have been born into this life burning with such [passion], I shall reduce you to such a state in a mere moment. Therefore, depart far away!
There is no place for you to remain in equality with me; go far away by all means!"
When these words were spoken, the sins indeed departed in embodied form and wandered about on the mountain at the Dāmodara Tīrtha.
Then the Guru was fed with wild game and forest fruits by the hunter.
Having brought water from the lake, his thirst was quenched.
Having diligently brought fragrant and beautiful kunda flowers, he fashioned garlands and other offerings, and thus worshipped him on the neck and the head. ||48-49||

He performed the washing of his feet as well as the massaging of his body; then a cool breeze from a fan was fanned upon him. In this manner, the worship of the holy Karṣaṇa Ṛṣi was performed with heartfelt devotion.
By him, offerings for the worship of Kṛṣṇa were brought;
the prasāda was eaten and likewise the pleasing water was drunk.
Thus was service performed at that time by the devoted hunter.
Great merit was produced there, and blessings were bestowed by the Guru:
"O King, may you possess a kingdom, may you possess wealth, and may you be filled with prosperity!
Having spoken thus and received honors, the Guru departed for another sacred site.
The hunter passed away that very night due to the power of the snow;
and you, having been born as a prince in the house of the king of Saurāṣṭra, Bhūriyaśas, have performed service to the virtuous.

By that merit you became a king, yet all that merit has been consumed. Seeing the destruction of his merit, he indeed caused those sins of yours to be driven away at Mount Raivata in the presence of Dāmodara.
Beholding all of them, they indeed cried out to you once again.
O King, such wandering, falling, and so forth occurred for you by the power of those sins which you committed in a previous birth. (17–58)
The Ṛṣi did not ignite them at all out of compassion;
they returned to life and cried out once more:
"Therefore, O Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, Lord! (59)
O Hare Kṛṣṇa, Supreme Brahman, Vāsudeva, Lord of Ramā;
O Lord of Śrī, Beloved of Rādhikā, Lord of Kamalā; O Lord of Prabhā, Lord of Māṇikī, Lord of Jayā-Lakṣmī, Lord of Śrī Pārvatī.
O Lord of the virtuous, ocean of compassion, Lord of devotees, bestower of excellent liberation;
O Lord of Sāvitrī, beloved of Tulasī, Lord of Gaṅgā and Sarasvatī;
O Lord of the lords of yogis, Lord of the perfected ones, and Lord of the chaste wives devoted to their husbands.
O Inner Self, inflame and destroy my sins!
I am your slave; I am your servant—purify me who am worthy of service.
Protect me, for I am your foot-servant in the service of devotion to my husband.
"O King, make this request; everything will become most excellent.
When Kṛṣṇa, the bestower of auspiciousness, is pleased, everything becomes free from affliction.
Indeed, I am your officiating priest (yājaka), acting as a guru by the title of 'officiant'."
"I am a doer of good for you; tell me, what may I do for you?
Whether you desire happiness, a kingdom, wealth, grain, and other riches;
or heaven and liberation, or even union with the state of Hari. (66–67)
"Tell me, O King, what do you desire? May you achieve your purpose here through me.
Having heard this, Hemanta, his mind overwhelmed with joy, replied:
"I desire a kingdom free from obstacles, one that shatters the pride of my enemies."

"And therefore, O twice-born one, I always desire supreme devotion to the feet of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, characterized by lifelong fidelity to my husband. Having heard this, the officiating priest said to her, "Understand from me the appropriate duties."
Through giving, one obtains a kingdom, heaven, prosperity, and wealth;
through service, however, one obtains long life, good fortune, enjoyments, sons, and so forth.
Through devotion, one attains the feet of Govinda and the eternal abode.
Through association with the virtuous, one attains great peace, happiness, and a treasure of bliss.
O King, practice these four things according to your ability:
indeed, give a cow, and give land—even if it be but a small portion—to a twice-born brahmin.
By that means, you will swiftly regain both prosperity and the earth.
Give away beds, umbrellas, and other such things, and you shall indeed regain your kingdom.
Give gold, silver, and wealth; by that, you will obtain all riches.
Having bathed in the Nārāyaṇa lake, worship Dāmodara.
Vāmana will undoubtedly cause you victory once again.
Make an auspicious gift of the forms of Kṛṣṇa and Nārāyaṇa to your preceptor.
"O Indra among kings, perform the gift of water and the provision of drinking stations here within this forest; you shall obtain sons whose prowess is equal to your own.
Whatever is lacking, give that by means of a formal resolve, with water as your witness."
When [the time] has arrived later, it should be given; one should never practice deceit.
(78) Practice service toward virtuous people, and you will obtain long life, all manner of enjoyable things, a wife, and sons. (79)
O sinless Kṛṣṇā, practice the virtue of devotion to your husband in every way, like a faithful wife. Perform service and worship for him, offering excellent food and the presentation of water,
as well as seasonal baths, ornaments, enthusiasm, and great festivals.
Perform whatever other vows, concluding rites, or duties are possible for you.
Practice service, attendance, meditation, worship, and recitation;
by becoming a source of happiness for all, you shall attain the imperishable abode.
Rādhākṛṣṇa, the beloved of Ramā, the Lord Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa;
Śivā-Śiva, the Lord of Pārvatī, the Lord of Śrī, the Lord of Kamalā;
Māṇikīśa, the beloved of Prabhā, the Lord of Jayā, and the Lord of Lalitā.
The Lord of Padminī, the Lord of Padmā, the Lord of Durgā, the Lord of Tulasī;
the Lord of the Goddess, Hari, Kṛṣṇa, the Master, Śrī Nārāyaṇa;
the Lord of Kambharā, the Lord of Rukmiṇī, the Lord of those whose self is the Supreme Brahman.
Worship the Lord of the virtuous, the protector of all, the inner controller, and the Guru.
Like Rādhā and others, always maintain devotion to your husband, Keśava.
Take this auspicious tulasī garland as a necklace around your neck.
"Oṃ, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, salutations be unto You!
(87) Having uttered this, and having bowed to and meditated upon Hari, the beloved and enchanting one, [he says]:
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa; obeisance to the Lord. (88)
O King, perform this recitation one hundred and eight times each day;
by that, you shall attain liberation, which is the very nature of supreme attainment. Associate with virtuous and divine persons, for it bestows great merit.
Indeed, seek the sight of virtuous and chaste women who are true to the righteous.
Perform service, worship, attendance at their feet, and humble labor like a servant.
Always bear even the dust of their feet upon your own head.
Drink the nectar of their feet and employ it for your ablutions;
for they, O King, are truthful and virtuous, from the tips of their nails up to the crown of their heads.
Divine, pure, and meritorious, they are entirely free from the abandonment of their allotted shares.
Serve them just as you serve Śrī, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, and Nārāyaṇa. Always serve the Lord of Śrī with a desireless disposition;
by that, all the worlds will come under your control.
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa will become manifest in your home;
Lakṣmī, the increaser of your prosperity, will become manifest.
O King, this queen of yours shall daily perform the worship of Śrī in the morning.
One should fashion [the image] upon a Bilva leaf, made radiant with saffron, clearly visible in form through its lines, four-armed, and beloved of Hari;
[worship it] with incense, lamps, excellent food offerings, water, flowers, fruits, and so forth. ॥96–97॥
Worship her with affection and devotion; she will become pleased.
Through her service characterized by devotion to her husband, she will surely grant you your heart's desire.
Everything you wish for will be swiftly attained.

Having spoken thus and bestowed auspicious blessings upon him, O Lakṣmī, the priest then departed for another forest. Hemanta performed his ablutions, gave gifts, conducted worship and other rites, and rendered service to the residents of Raivata.

He indeed cultivated the company of yogis and Vaiṣṇavas, and in the temple of Lord Kṛṣṇa-Dāmodara, he listened to auspicious discourses. He practiced meditation and profound contemplation upon Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
At the end of the night, auspicious dream-visions appeared to him:
riding upon an elephant and holding a parasol, he went forth with his kingdom greatly expanded;
honored by those dwelling in the world of the gods, yet surrounded by his subjects.
He was honored by the Apsarases with flower garlands and ornaments;
Lakṣmī approached and bathed him with water from a pitcher;
and he was made to hear songs sung by the celestial Gandharvas and singers.
Adorned on his forehead with a tilaka made by the circle of elders and his mothers, together with unbroken grains of rice,
and honored with parasols, chowries, and other regalia—
having seen such a dream, he rejoiced and spoke to his wife.
Through the vision of Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, his kingdom will be reunited. Having observed an auspicious omen at Vijaya and beholding the royal banner,
he set out on his expedition and indeed conquered his own city-kingdom.
He conquered other great enemies and indeed brought some under his control (1.08).
The heroic king himself seized the treasuries, elephants, and horses of the monarchs; and those rulers, their resolutions shattered, became his tributaries (1.09).
Indeed, the kingdom in the regions of Saurāṣṭra became one under a single umbrella.
His son was Dhṛṣṭadyumna, who was exceedingly majestic.
Hemanta performed service for the devotees and the virtuous day after day.
In the royal palace, they constantly listened with joy to the stories of Kṛṣṇa.
The subjects became devotees of Viṣṇu and were devoted to their husbands;
they always practiced devotion toward Kṛṣṇa just as they did toward themselves.
And Kṛṣṇa himself, the four-armed Nārāyaṇa, being satisfied,
became manifest on the Akṣaya Tṛtīyā day,
accompanied by Lakṣmī, seated upon Garuḍa, and adorned with divine ornaments and the like.
Beholding [him], he danced with joy, intoxicated and his hair standing on end.
Filled with love, he praised [him] with supreme devotion, palms joined in reverence;
having washed the feet, he held the water upon his head.
The king worshipped the True Reality with the sixteen articles of offering;
he paid homage to Hari, the Ancient Person, with every kind of gift.
"O Lord, I bow to Your feet, the abode of all sacred waters, having taken them within my heart."
O Hari! By association with that saintly person, I have been delivered by you.
(1.17) For one who delights in the service of the saintly, this worldly existence becomes like the footprint of a cow.
O Hari, Kṛṣṇa! Through the association of the virtuous, my mind has become fixed upon You. (1.18)
The loss of my kingdom was actually Your grace toward me; whatever fruit remains, grant me service, mindfulness, servitude, and devotion as a faithful wife.
May my mind dwell at Your feet, and may my speech be occupied in chanting Your virtues.
May your two eyes be for the act of seeing, and your two ears for hearing your stories.
May your tongue be for your grace, and your nose for the fragrance of your form. May your skin be for the sensation of you, and may your two hands be for the sweeping of the temple.
May my feet be for traveling to your sacred fields, and may my other limbs be employed for your sake.
May my head be for prostrating before you, and may my desire be directed toward you alone.
May my intellect be for discerning the truth, and may my mind always be occupied with contemplation of you.
O beloved, let there be selfhood for me; let my life be offered unto you. (1.23) May my days be spent in the service of the virtuous with a spirit of love;
may there be association with the good, and may liberation be your service at your feet. (1.24)
"I do not desire any other glory anywhere except for the Lord of Glory (Śrīpati). Thus praised, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the glorious Mañjuleśvara,
smiling, spoke to him, granting him a supreme boon of ten thousand years of life.
"By practicing devotion to me, performing service, and observing the vow of fidelity to your husband,
you shall attain union with me (sāyujya) along with your entire family.
On the third lunar day known as Akṣayā, perform my worship just as you have done."
Those people who perform bathing, giving of gifts, and my worship shall certainly go to my abode. Indeed,
I shall lead both men and women to my imperishable realm.

Having thus granted the boon, Kṛṣṇa vanished right there. The king, together with his family, took up residence among the virtuous, listened to sacred narratives, and practiced devotion to Kṛṣṇa characterized by supreme fidelity to his wife.
Having enjoyed the kingdom for ten thousand years, he went at the end to the abode of Hari.
By hearing and by reading this, they too shall go to the abode of Śrī Hari.

Thus ends the four hundred and thirty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the King of Hemanta from the Pañcāla Country in Saurāṣṭra—His Loss of Kingdom Due to Past Karma, His Regaining of the Kingdom through the Dharma of Devotion and Chastity to Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa as instructed by his Guru, and His Vision of and Liberation by Śrī Hari," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
