Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Mahālakṣmī! Urvaśī, who was born from the Lord Nara-Nārāyaṇa through the power of her devotion to her husband— [1]

Formerly she was a dog; even earlier than that, she was a wicked Brāhmaṇī from the land of Kaśmīra, who hated her husband and was deceitful. She was the daughter of Devavrata, well-known by the name Mālinī, and possessed of great beauty.
The wife of the Brahmin named Satyaśīla was not at all beloved by her husband.
Together with her, the husband went to some region in the land of the Yavanas.
She, however, filled with anger toward her husband and greedy for means of subjugation, [remained behind].
He questioned many Yavana women regarding a medicine for subjugation. They pointed out to him a certain rogue woman who prepared medicinal herbs, saying,
"She will give you a medicine by which your husband will become like a slave."
And the Brahmin woman, full of longing, went to the house of the courtesan.
She saw her hut, furnished with skull-bowls and other such items, as well as many medicinal herbs in excellent vessels, stoves, and other utensils. (6–7)
It was adorned with the accomplishments (*sādhana*) and seats (*āsana*) of mantra-sciences;
it was beautifully graced by mystical diagrams (*yantra*), mantras, ash-ornaments, and dark blue garments;
and it was filled with the practice of yoga through bone-altars (*vedikā*).
Having seen that hut, illuminated by the auspicious long matted locks of female disciples, equipped with incense burners and staffs for purification,
and attended by many distressed women seeking to achieve their goals; (1.433.10)
The Brahmin woman bowed with supreme devotion to the deceitful Yoginī, who was smeared with ashes on her body and adorned with sectarian marks like a true yogi.
Then that crafty rogue informed her of her suffering.
She performed her cleansing with a broom made of peacock feathers;
she consecrated her body by sprinkling ashes over it while blowing upon them;
she fashioned a crescent moon of ash on her forehead and placed water in her hand.
Placing a black armlet and a rudrākṣa rosary upon his shoulder, he caused the brahmin woman to hear the subjugation mantra three times:
"Obeisance to the goddess Kāmākṣikā; bring [him] under my control, svāhā! (14)
Thus he gave her the mantra and presented her with a substance and a ring—
red, set with rubies, made of gold, and capable of bringing others under one's control—
as well as a red woolen cord for binding around the arm.
He gave him an auspicious medicinal powder endowed with protective power and said:
"Indeed, this powder is a great means for bringing others under one's influence.
By its application, even those who are powerful like the wind [will be subdued]. (17)
They will always remain submissive to their master like monkeys.
(18) You should always consume a small amount of this powder with your food and other meals for your husband; furthermore, you must certainly wear it as a protective cord around your neck. (19)
"O beautiful woman, tie this red cord upon your own arm!
Your husband will become submissive; recite the mantra while lying on your bed.
Give him consecrated food and likewise consecrated water."
"Give me a bed consecrated with mantras; give me everything well-consecrated.
(21) Within a very short time, your master will come under your control.
If there should be any task to be done, come to me quickly. (22)
Having been told this, the Brahmin woman gave the sacrificial fee and went to her own home.
She prepared a medicinal herb in milk and offered it to her husband in his meal;
she also gave him consecrated water, clothing, and a bed.
In this manner, she gave him the powder day after day; as she did so,
her husband became increasingly afflicted by asthma, cough, phlegm, and consumption, and there was excessive heat in his urine and other secretions.
In his body, red eruptions like intensely thorny prickles broke out.
Within a few days, the master became as if dependent on others;
incapacitated and suffering from disease, he was filled with the fear of death.
Then the husband, his splendor destroyed, spoke to the Brahmin woman in distress:
"I am yours here like a slave; protect me, O beautiful one!
O beloved, I desire no other woman whatsoever except for you."
"I shall abide by your command and remain forever your servant from now on;
I will offer no opposition when you have a task to be performed.
Then that lustful woman, intent on her own self-interest, [spoke] regarding her husband's life.
"When there is a husband, ornaments and such things are undoubtedly to be worn and enjoyed.
Thinking thus, she then went quickly to the deceitful Yoginī as if in fear, [saying]:
"My husband has fallen under her control, but he will certainly die."
"O auspicious one, my own self-interest would be destroyed; therefore, let him live.
Having understood this, the rogue informed her of everything else as well, and she gave her that very medicine which destroys suffering, burning sensations, and other ailments.
When that medicine was administered, her husband became healthy at that very moment.
She became exceedingly pleased, and her husband remained under her control; moreover, he did not speak even the slightest word to her regarding his encounters with other women.
The husband-in-law remained in the house under the pretext of attending to household duties,
while the husband did not say anything at all to her in any way.
Then that wicked Brahmin woman, who harbored hatred for her husband, gradually—
Her body became pervaded by disease, and worms were born within it.
Because of that, she met her death and underwent the torments of hell;
she was cast into a scorching copper cauldron for many years.
Then, for a hundred times over, she was a bitch afflicted by ringworm,
with limbs oozing and limping, and she was beaten from house to house;
yet, in the final instance, she came to the home of the brahmin named Padmabandhu.
She was born in the land of Sauvīra as a diseased bitch belonging to a maidservant.
When she, her limbs filled with worms, stood upon the stone used for washing the feet in the courtyard of a brahmin’s house, [she attained liberation]. (39–40)
Then, by the power of destiny, the son of a brahmin, remembering Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa,
chanting the Gāyatrī mantra, and having performed the worship of Kṛṣṇa,
[placed] in his water-pot (kamaṇḍalu) the grace-born water used for bathing Viṣṇu, mixed with tulasī.
Having led her home, he arrived by way of the stairs;
indeed, as soon as he ascended the last step of the five steps that formed the elevated courtyard of the house, [he beheld her]. || 42–43 ||
He stumbled, and the water-filled water-pot fell from his hand;
by the turn of fate, it landed on a low-lying rocky surface where she was standing.
Consequently, all the water in the water-pot fell into the void.
Then, by the power of her fortune, the dog bathed and drank;
by her good luck, she then ate the sweet consecrated food that had fallen.
O Lakṣmī! By that merit, she became one whose sins were utterly destroyed. ||45-46||
Remembering her past lives, she spoke to the twice-born man at that moment:
"O Brahmin! Save me, save me, O twice-born one, from this great sin!
Formerly, O sage, I was always a hater of my husband."
She who gave poison to her husband, as well as she who practiced spells for subjugation,
the giver of suffering, the exceedingly wicked woman who committed adultery with another—
on account of that sin, she was cast by the agents of Yama into the copper vats.
O twice-born one, I have been born a hundred times as a dog afflicted with scabies;
this is my final body, consecrated by you with water. By fate, I have become one who remembers past lives, and I recall what occurred throughout a hundred births.
I have experienced extreme suffering that truly cannot be exhausted by description.
(51) A woman who harbors hatred for her husband is cooked in molten copper;
then, being of evil conduct, she is forced to embrace glowing iron cylinders by those driven by lust. (52)
The husband is the protector, the husband is the guru, the husband is the supreme deity.
Having committed an offense against him, how could she be happy?
She enters a hundred animal births, filled with worms and terrifying.
Therefore, a noble woman should always perform service to her husband with compliant speech.
Devotion to her husband is the supreme duty; indeed, serving the husband is merit itself.
For the sake of delivering women, Hari himself resides within the husband.
Lame, one-eyed, maimed, squint-eyed, and eight-faced;
beautiful with collyrium on his body, deaf, dwarf-like, and emaciated;
diseased, leprous, insane, cruel, and possessed by excessive lust.
Whether he is a sensualist, a debauchee, a talkative man, or even one devoted to falsehood—
such a portion of Kṛṣṇa himself was created by Brahmā for the sake of a wife.
Only by him, who possesses the splendor of the sun, can a wife be rescued, and not by anyone else.
Whether he be such or such— blue, black, or having the appearance of collyrium—
the husband who is the master should be served once his purpose has been attained through desire.
If the husband is satisfied by desire through the granting of pleasure, [then he is to be served].
"Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa himself was satisfied by her," said Vṛṣa.
Thus, a husband should always be served by a woman;
he should be served when she is ill, be peaceful when she is happy, and likewise provide courage in times of calamity.
To the hungry she gives food; to the thirsty, she gives satisfaction; on the bed, she is beloved; in business, she is a helper; while traveling, she goes along; at home, she is a virtuous wife;
in social dealings, she is a friend; and in protection, she acts like a mother.

Whatever woman there may be, she enjoys heaven for ten thousand years; of this there is no doubt. (63) Even if in this life one does not have a handsome husband, then by devotion to her husband, a virtuous wife is able to make him equal to a god. (64)
Kālī was the daughter of Himagiri, yet she became Gaurī through her ascetic penance.
In the past, Kubjā became equal to Rādhā through association with Kṛṣṇa;
likewise, Śabarī became four-armed through union with Rāma.
In ancient times, Yavanī became divine through union with her Lord.
Through union with Rāma, Jaṭāyū became auspicious and four-armed.
Gaja and Grāha were liberated through union with Viṣṇu and became divine.
Arundhatī became a dog-eater’s wife because she took refuge with cows;
Saramā became a divine bitch because she served Surabhi.
Vṛndā became Tulasī plants, which, through union with Kṛṣṇa, have become identical with His own self.
The dull-witted become as if conscious through association with Śrī Kṛṣṇa. (6.9) The divine Sūta Paurāṇika became worthy of worship by Brahmā;
for even a flower rejected by Indra indeed causes the destruction of Lakṣmī. (1.433.70)
Furthermore, that which was offered by him [Viṣṇu] in the Ocean of Milk bestows prosperity.
Thus, if a man or a woman possesses an unattractive object, it becomes beautiful through penance; there is no doubt in this matter.
Through austerity, one always becomes endowed with good qualities and is freed from bad qualities.
Whether she be a hunchback or he a hunchback, whether she be a servant or he a servant,
they should both be served through one’s own austerity, devotion to the Master, and the thought that they are virtuous wives (or devoted partners).
Having acted thus, regarding Hari as their husband and Sati as their wife, the couple served one another, attaining patience and forgiveness through the attainment of happiness.
"O Brahmin! I have been served by you, not insulted, and have been brought under your control."
Afflicted and tormented by that [suffering], I am distressed within the ocean of existence.
O Brahmin, rescue me now by offering the fruits of the worship of Kṛṣṇa;
otherwise, my rebirth in wicked wombs is foreseen.
Thus addressed, the brahmin then felt compassion and bestowed upon her all the merit of the Ekādaśī and the worship and other rites of the Dvādaśī,
which is considered to yield inexhaustible fruit.
The twice-born man bestowed upon her all that had been performed—penances, gifts, oblations, and the worship of the gods—all in the form of devotion to Kṛṣṇa. He said to her:
"O most wicked woman, you are not worthy of compassion."
Though she was hostile toward her husband, a hater of the virtuous, and a reviler of the gods,
she was not said to be unworthy of compassion because she was dependent on him;
for, having recognized her as a wretched servant, I have shown mercy to her.
For those who are to be supported by a high-souled householder must be uplifted;
thinking thus,
even the Caṇḍālas, crows, and dogs were raised up as his servants.
Male and female slaves, servants, mongooses, parrots, and mainas;
rabbits, deer, swans, and whatever other creatures feed upon offerings;
as well as helpless boys and girls—these are indeed objects of compassion for householders. (83)
Or likewise, women who are afflicted and always without support must be supported by you;
all such persons are to be uplifted with effort.
If a householder does not support those dependent upon him, he will undoubtedly fall into ruin.
Devotion to the husband is supreme; the husband is the Supreme Lord.

Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa is the Master, and his command is the nourishment and protection [of those dependent on him]. (86) Having abandoned the protection of those dependent on her, she proceeds according to the designs of others.
One who commits treachery here goes to the abode of Kīnāśa (Yama).
Helping others is dharma; it is the bull [of dharma] and the liberation of servants.
The gift of liberation is a great gift, which is solely devoted to the attainment of Kṛṣṇa.
The Lord Hari is always pleased with that person;
for him, supreme liberation arises through the perfect practice of devotion to the husband.
In this world, service to others is liberation; therefore, it must certainly be bestowed by the man of knowledge.
Likewise, one who possesses devotion should give [these] to another by the command of her husband.
(1.433.90) The moon, the sun, the wind, day, night, water, the earth, sandalwood, trees, and virtuous men—all remain intent upon benefiting others. (91)
It was Dadhīci who gave his bones to the gods;
Śibi offered the flesh from his own body to the pigeon;
and likewise, in former times, the compassionate King Jīmūtavāhana did the same.
Garuḍa offered his own life for the sake of long-lived existence;
Dharmāṅgada offered his head to Mohinī for the sake of a vow; and by Brahmā, bodies were offered again and again for the sake of creation. (93–94)
For the sake of liberating the worlds, Gaṅgā and other rivers came into being;
Viṣṇu became the Śālagrāma stone, and Śaṅkara took the form of the Liṅga;
and Lakṣmī, for the purpose of liberating the world, took the form of Tulasī.
Kṛṣṇa assumed the state of a cowherd and likewise took on forms such as the fish;
all this was done for the sake of benefiting others by those of former and even more ancient times.
Like the rain-cloud, the moon, and the sun, he is equal toward all living beings.
Thus, O compassionate Guru, by you— acting as my servant,
free from desire, endowed with equanimity, and bestowing merit— I have been cleansed of all impurities.
Now that I am born, may there be on earth gurus like you who grant liberation.
"For the virtuous and devoted wives are indeed by nature inclined to help others.
Grant me permission to go to the abode of Hari, the dwelling place of bliss.
Having been addressed thus, the brāhmaṇa repeatedly gave her the mantra of Hari.
Oṃ, salutations to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa! Lift up Kukkurī!
Go to Kṛṣṇa’s Goloka, O dog! May you become meritorious!
(101) Having heard this, she became complete, divine, and beautiful in form.
Having abandoned her own body, she became auspicious and equal to the sun.
At that moment, a divine celestial chariot belonging to the world of the sun arrived there;
ascending it, she illuminated the expanse of the sky above.
She became a divine goddess with a moon-like face, adorned with ornaments;
having dwelt for a kalpa in heaven and enjoyed pleasures upon the earth,
she was born from the gods Nara and Nārāyaṇa by the name of Urvaśī.
An excellent woman was born, a Vaiṣṇavī beloved by the gods.

(109) Though endowed with the nature of an Apsaras, she was always devoted to Kṛṣṇa as her husband; intent on wifely fidelity, she became the bestower of liberation upon those who take refuge in her. (106)
Having gathered mango blossoms while Nara was pressing them upon his thigh,
she manifested as a great divine being who deluded the army of Mahendra;
for she had come to create an obstacle to the austerities of Nara and Nārāyaṇa.
From the region of Nārāyaṇa, Indrāṇī went to the abode of Indra.
That highly fortunate Vaiṣṇavī dwells there;
she constantly serves Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa as her husband.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have told you all this, which destroys sin and suffering,
is supremely devoted to the virtue of wifely fidelity, bestows liberation, and is auspicious and salvific.

Thus ends the four hundred and thirty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Kāśmīrī Brāhmaṇī’s State as a Dog for a Hundred Births due to Hatred for Her Husband, Her Liberation from Doghood and Attainment of Divinity by means of a Sauvīra Brāhmaṇa Devoted to Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa’s Wifely Devotion, and Subsequently Urvaśī’s Emergence from the Thigh of Nara-Nārāyaṇa," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 434 *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā* — Section 1 (*Kṛtayuga-santāna*) — Chapter 434.
[The Author: Chapter 435.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
O Lakṣmī, listen once more as I relate another wonder; pay heed.
Vasu, whose name was Vidhūma, and the excellent lake Alambuṣā,
both attained human birth on earth in former times due to a Brahmin’s curse;
through their devotion to Śrī Kṛṣṇa as their husband, they were liberated from that Brahmin’s curse.

Formerly, having gone to Satyaloka, Brahmā convened a great assembly of exalted beings in the hall known as Sudharmā on the festival day of Viṣṇu. There, the four-armed Lord sat upon a beautiful central throne.
He was resplendent on both sides by Sāvitrī and Sarasvatī;
he was further adorned by Gāyatrī, the four Vedas, and Mohinī,
as well as by Sanat, Sanandana, Sanātana, Sanaka, and Nārada.
The Great-Grandfather was accompanied by Dakṣa and others, the Vālakhilyas, Dharma and the other Pitṛs, as well as the clouds, sages, and goddesses;
he was joined by Indra and the other world-protectors, the guardians of the quarters, and the planets and stars.
He was likewise served by the *siddhis*, the *vasus*, the *nidhis*, and the *ṛṣis*;
by the *diśās*, the Rudra-deities, the Ādityas, and the circles of Kāma; as well as by the *manus*, the lunar days (*tithis*), and the *kalās*.
The unborn Lord is indeed worshipped by the principles (*tattvas*), the excellent constellations (*nakṣatras*), the hosts of gods and demons,
the qualities (*guṇas*), the winds (*maruts*), the castes (*varṇas*), enjoyments, and sacred fords (*tīrthas*);
he is also honored by the desires, the channels (*nāḍikās*), and the mines (*khanis*).
The Grandfather was indeed saluted by embodied beings of the wind, the earth, and the netherworld; by those dwelling in the sky and those born in the water;
and by the Kinnaras, the Kiṃpuruṣas, the Sādhyas, and the Gandharvas adorned with ornaments.
Honored by the Urvashis and those skilled in the great art of dance,
Brahmā himself shone in that assembly, beholding the heart-stealing dance of the Apsarases accompanied by musical instruments.
Gradually, the celestial women danced, delighting the assembly;
the sound of lutes, flutes, and drums became sweet,
and various melodious notes issued forth from the heavenly damsels.
Alambuṣā and Madayantī danced most beautifully;
they repeatedly cast their principal limbs, which captivated the mind.
They smiled there very softly and looked about again and again. (15)
With eyes filled with love, she cast side-long glances;
she caused only her breasts to tremble slightly, as did only her hips, her cheeks, and her thighs. (16–17)
Thus, having repeatedly observed her dancing,
the Vasu named Vidhūma became filled with desire for her and was infatuated.
Displaying his longing to her, he laughed again and again.
While the attendants looked on, Vasu repeatedly showed his intense longing with his unblinking eyes;
and Brahmā, perceiving the agitation of Vidhūma there, [spoke].
He said: "O Vasa, such fickleness on the stage of dance is not fitting for you;
you have acted in a manner entirely unsuitable for the assembly, since it causes an interruption of the dance, a disruption of the performance, and a distraction. (21)
Because of that fault, go and become a human on the surface of the earth.
Humans on this earth are fickle and free from the binding rope;
let your dwelling be among them in the mortal world—go from there.
"Alambuṣā shall indeed become your wife; go, do not delay.
Thus commanded by Brahmā, Vidhūma fell at his feet, repeatedly entreating for the removal of the curse and for his own protection.
Then Brahmā said: "All this shall come to pass for you truly, there is no doubt.
You shall indeed become a young prince in the city of Kauśāmbī, born of King Śatānīka’s chaste wife, Viṣṇumatī."
Having become a king and then having begotten a noble son upon Alambuṣā,
and having consecrated him in the kingdom,
you shall bathe at Cakratīrtha on the southern ocean together with your wife at that very time.
"Endowed with a wife and possessing a divine form, you shall attain your own world.
Having been addressed thus, this very Vasu fell truly upon the earth;
born in the house of Śatānīka, he became a prince of great discernment.
Śāṇḍilya gave him the name Sahasrānīka. Meanwhile, in the city of Ayodhyā, a daughter named Mṛgāvatī was born in the house of King Kṛtavarman, endowed with the virtues of a goddess.
By birth she was indeed a Vaiṣṇavī, devoted solely to the worship of Kṛṣṇa.
Though young, she was possessed of wisdom and dedicated to her husband;
she repeatedly performed the chanting of the name of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
Then Śatānīka was invited by Indra to fight with the Daityas;
having gone to heaven and died in battle, his corpse was handed over to his son.
Sahasrānīka alone performed the funeral rites for that corpse.
Having found the corpse, Viṣṇumatī lamented and spoke:
"O Lord! O Master of my life! Come, you who are dearer to me than life itself!
O God presiding over my vital breaths, my life-breaths depart without you. (34–35)
A woman’s pride increases day by day through her husband’s good fortune; therefore, if he is wealthy and happy, she should honor him in accordance with dharma.
For a noble woman, the husband is her kinsman, her presiding deity, and her eternal refuge.
He is the supreme embodiment of prosperity and the personification of bliss.
He is the eternal bestower of dharma, the giver of happiness, the constant giver of affection, and the perpetual giver of peace.
He is the conferrer of honor, the giver of respect, the one worthy of veneration, and indeed the crusher of pride.
The husband is the most essential of all essentials, the increaser of kinsmen among one's kin.
Indeed, among all types of relatives, no relative equal to a husband is seen.
He is called "bhartṛ" (sustainer) because he supports, and "pati" (lord) because he protects.
He is the Lord of the body; He alone is the Master who grants all desires and is truly beloved.
Because He binds one to happiness, He is the Kinsman; because He bestows affection, He is the Supreme Beloved.
Because He grants sovereignty, He is the Lord; and because He is the Master of the vital breaths, He is the Leader of Life.
Because he bestows pleasure, he is the "Delighter" (ramaṇa); there is no one dearer than the beloved.
Furthermore, a son is born from the master’s semen; therefore, he is dear.
To those of noble birth, the master is always dearer than even a hundred sons.
Indeed, one born of an ignoble family is incapable of discerning her beloved.
(43) [Yet this knowledge is superior to] bathing in all sacred fords, the sacrificial fees of all sacrifices, circumambulating the entire earth, and indeed all ascetic penances. (44)
All vows and the like, whatever great gifts there are, meritorious fasts, and all other such things in every respect;
as well as service to the guru, service to Brahmins, service to the gods, and so forth— 45.
They do not equal even a sixteenth part of service to the feet of one's master.
Among gurus, Brahmins, and beloved deities, the husband is the greatest guru for all;
as is the giver of sacred knowledge, so too is he dear to men of noble birth. (46–47)
"All my fortune has vanished; my parasol-like head is gone," she said to her husband, and with great devotion, she meditated there upon his body.
Viṣṇumatī was a virtuous wife devoted to her husband, and by virtue of her chastity, she remained steadfast.
Having produced fire from her big toe and paid homage to the great people,
she was consumed by that very fire and died along with him.
Her son, Sahasrānīka, performed the funeral rites for the deceased.
Vasu, whose chariot had a thousand horses, ruled his kingdom according to the law.
Once, having been invited by Indra to the great festival of the Nandana grove in heaven,
Prince Sahasrānīka went to the celestial realm.
There, in the abode of Indra, he likewise heard of his own status as a Vasu;
and then Vasu heard that Alambuṣā was to be his wife.
Having returned to the earth, he [married] Alambuṣā, the daughter of the king of Ayodhyā.
Having married Mṛgāvatī, he rejoiced with her;
she conceived a child from him and shone as if washed in nectar.
During the festival of the flower-swing, both the queen and the king were smeared with saffron.
In a lake filled with red water, richly colored and abounding in lotus filaments and the like,
the two of them, exhausted from bathing, stood on either side—
handsome, reddish-gold in hue, and exceedingly radiant. (55–56)
Then the king, overcome by fatigue, fell into a momentary sleep;
meanwhile, the virtuous queen, for the sake of satisfying her desire to bathe and for her own comfort, descended into the water in a small pool beside the arena. (57)
She of red hue respectfully performed her bath in the colored water.
Then, perceiving her—drenched in the colored water and moving within the depths of the water—to be a very large fish, [the hunter] from his garment [cast a net], thinking it to be meat. 58–59.
A certain bird born of the lineage of Suparṇa, formidable with a great roar, swooped down with speed; seizing her with his beak, he flew into the sky.
Recognizing her as some human woman on the Udaya mountain, [he carried her away].
Having abandoned the cave, he departed elsewhere through the sky.
She, however, wept in terror and shed tears again and again, crying:
"Alas, my lord! I am ill-fated; I have performed my bath without my husband."
"Afflicted by that very sin and by separation from you, what is my fate?
Where indeed shall I go? When shall I behold your face?
Having spoken thus before the elephants and lions, she stood there longing for death.
Abandoned by all the cruel ones, she did not meet her death there.
Indeed, in times of calamity, death does not desire friendship with men.
[Thus spoke] the excellent son of Jamadagni as she wept among the forest trees.
The compassionate king took her and presented her to the sage. Consoled by the sage, the queen was nourished and protected in the hermitage.
In due time, she gave birth to a boy named Udayana.
He grew up as a disciple of Jamadagni and became a knower of the Vedas. Once, a certain forest-dwelling hunter arrived at the hermitage of Jamadagni and [found] a serpent inside a basket.
Carrying it for the sake of alms, he entertained the serpent;
having given him alms, she gave the bracelet and released the snake.
Knowing of that bracelet, the hunter went to the king in order to sell it.
Then King Sahasrānīka, seeing the bracelet bearing his own name, asked for the account; the hunter reported everything to him.
Having given wealth to the hunter, the king then departed for that hermitage.
Seeing the sage performing austerities, he bowed his head in salutation;
the sage received the king with a blessing.
He honored him according to the prescribed rites with water for the feet, the respectful offering, and water for sipping.
He spoke words consistent with dharma and artha to the protector of the earth:
"O Lord of Men! This son born to you by Mṛgāvatī shall be the conqueror of the quarters; he has indeed been named Udayana. (73–74)
This wife Mṛgāvatī is devoted to her husband;
she is a faithful devotee of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, a virtuous woman of the Bhāgavata tradition. Like the pure Reṇukā, she has endured sufferings for your sake.
"O Great King, accept her along with her son without delay!
(76) Having heard this, the king bowed to the sage, took her, and bestowed wealth upon him.
Accompanied by his beloved wife, the king returned toward his own city. (77)
Remembering the words of Śakra and disparaging his human birth,
he gave the earth to his wise son Udayana.
Then the king went to Cakratīrtha together with Mṛgāvatī.
Standing on the shore of the ocean, he performed his ablutions according to the prescribed rites.
Having become a sage, King Vidhūma Sahasrānīka took up residence among the forest trees and sustained himself solely on wild produce. (1.434.79–80)
And Mṛgāvatī, devoted solely to the service of her husband in the forest,
ate only once a day, subsisting on fruits, and never partook of anything else.
She drank only the water used for washing her husband’s feet, and never any other drink.
She made her dwelling by her husband’s side and never elsewhere;
she bathed in the water used for washing her husband’s feet and never with any other;
she meditated on her husband as the abode of Hari and indeed had no other object of meditation—such a woman is truly a *satī*.
That virtuous woman who massages her husband’s limbs, the devoted wife who does not touch another even by mistake;
she whose joy is produced solely by her husband and not by any other even through delusion;
she who is constantly intent on worshipping her husband and devoted to serving her lord.

Having herself attained dispassion for the sake of her husband—she who was fond of auspiciousness—she regarded the Vedic words as the supreme command of the Lord. Thus that virtuous woman conducted herself according to his word; she was indeed like an Apsaras, yet unlike an Apsaras.
The restlessness directed toward liberation became something else, having turned into a state of absorption;
likewise, the state of possessing desire was transformed into desirelessness, bringing about liberation.
Even the embodied state of the Queen was transformed into the disembodied state.
The physical eye became the divine eye, and she indeed attained the form of Brahman.
Furthermore, the objects of the senses became free from craving, providing mere sustenance without causing any agitation;
they brought happiness to Mṛgāvatī’s husband, Kṛṣṇa.
She constantly worships Kṛṣṇa as she would her husband, and likewise Hari; having made everything consist of Kṛṣṇa, she offers all virtuous deeds to her husband.
Indeed, she offers the section on ritual action, the section on recitation, and the section on meditation unto Hari.
She perpetually offers the section on the body and the section on the functions of the senses into Janārdana,
into Nārāyaṇa, into Hari, and indeed into her Lord alone.
Having thus meditated upon Hari-Nārāyaṇa as her husband and having served him, [she attains liberation].
Having bathed at Cakratīrtha, the sacred ford of Hari, and at Patitīrthaka,
she herself likewise rendered her husband divine merely by that bath;
and having become divine, she was enchanting in form, equal to a hundred moons.

Indeed, joined with her husband, she departed for heaven by the path of the gods (devayāna). Having remained there for ten thousand years, she constantly worshipped Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Person, her lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
To all those men and women who have gathered at Cakratīrtha for the purpose of pilgrimage, and who are engaged in the practice of devotion to the Blessed One—
to them all, this most excellent Mahābhāgavatī Satī [is offered].
With a resonant voice and the rhythmic clapping of her hands, she, filled with intense joy, repeatedly caused this hymn of praise to be heard: "Obeisance to the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa! (97–98)
Having thus made countless embodied beings devotees of the Lord,
she went together with her husband to the true city of Brahmā.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, this divine narrative, which bestows great merit, has been told to you.
"From reading and hearing this, the fruit of the world of Brahmā shall accrue.

(1.434.100) Thus ends the four hundred and thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of how Vidūmavasu [became] King Sahasrānīka on earth by the word of Brahmā through the Apsaras Alambuṣā, and how Mṛgāvatī became the Queen; and how, following his discipleship under Jamadagni, he attained heaven and other realms again through the dharma of conjugal fidelity," in the first section, the Kṛta-yuga-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-nārāyaṇīya-saṃhitā*.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen together with your mind as I relate this most wonderful tale, O beloved lotus-born one; even the ignorant rejoice upon hearing it.
In ancient times, on a mountain in a desert region,
the sage Gālava constantly remembered the Supreme Brahman, Hari Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa,
and performed austerities upon that mountain in his own hermitage, which was provided with trees and water.

She had a daughter, a most fortunate and virtuous woman named Kāntimatī (4). She was a devoted wife to Kṛṣṇa, a faithful, chaste, pure, and great Vaiṣṇava lady; she constantly wore a dark garland of *tulasī* around her neck (5).
Holding a rosary in her hand, that virtuous woman, endowed with beauty and youth, constantly performs the recitation of "Kṛṣṇa,
Kṛṣṇa. Indeed, having abandoned Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, she desires no other husband.
Knowing her husband Kṛṣṇa to be the supreme truth, she was devoted to Kṛṣṇa as her only husband.
(6) Whether at rest, while eating, traveling, wandering, in the hermitage, by a tree, drinking, or even in the performance of bodily functions, she never forgot that husband. (7)

Śrī Kṛṣṇa indeed became manifest to her in private on certain occasions. Then, one day, the Blessed Lord Himself personally conducted a test to see how that young girl would perform her daily duties, such as sweeping the altar and other rites.
And likewise, that virtuous woman would every day perform the fetching of flowers and sacrificial fuel for the sage’s offerings. Then,
on the day she was prepared to gather flowers for the worship and the offering to Kṛṣṇa— ||| 1.435.10 ||
Having gone near the hermitage to a cluster of flowering trees, that maiden gathered beautiful flowers and placed them in a basket; just as she was returning, she saw her,
who was in the full bloom of youth.
While departing by means of a celestial chariot, a young Vidyādhara named Sudarśana,
having seen her and fallen under the power of the delusion of desire,
descended from the top of the aerial vehicle, longing to sport with her.
Showing his affection with tender words, he said to the maiden:
"O maiden! If you do not belong to another, I desire you;
if you deem it appropriate, let us unite here by the Gāndharva rite. (14)
"I am the son of the Vidyādhara named Sukaṇṭha.
And you are Sudarśanā by name; tell me what is in your heart.
O blessed lady, accept me, who have approached you as your devotee. (15–16)
Then Kāntimatī said: "I am indeed the maiden of Gālava;
I am unmarried, a pure Vaiṣṇavī devoted to the service of my father, and intent upon serving my beloved Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa. (17)
"I do not wish for another husband; my father will be angry.
"O Vidyādhara, go quickly with the flowers; do not delay.
A daughter is always dependent on her father and never independent."
"I am a devoted ascetic and a devotee of Viṣṇu; I do not desire even a husband," she said.
Thus addressed, that Vidyādhara went to her side with intent and seized her by the hair, whereupon the young woman cried out loudly.
"O King of the Vidyādharas, O Janaka, save me! he cried out suddenly.
At that very moment, Gālava and the others who were standing nearby heard this and quickly arrived; they beheld Sudarśana there.
As he was fleeing swiftly through the sky after abandoning his daughter out of fear, Gālava cursed him thus: "Become a wicked human!
Fall here from the path of the heavens; undergo the fruit of your assault."
"Go to infamy for a long time, and thereafter become a vetāla!
Become a consumer of flesh and blood, suffering in the great forest.
When he was thus addressed, that celestial chariot then fell to the earth.
The Vidyādhara fell from that celestial chariot, which then ascended to heaven;
by the power of his karma, he became a long-resident on the bank of the Yamunā. There, as the son of the wife of Govinda-svāmin, the Vidyādhara was born as a boy.
And his father, the brahmin, gave him the name Vijayadatta.
For he too was a rememberer of former births; he remembered even his past actions.
When his son had become a youth, [the father] went to the city of Kāśī for the sake of a pilgrimage.
Accompanied by his son and wife, Govindasvāmī proceeded slowly;
having performed his ablutions at Prayāga, which he encountered on the road,
he then heard of a certain yogin dwelling there who wore a garland of skulls.
"Having seen and heard what was said by him— that the destruction of your son would soon come to pass—
Govinda Svāmī, having heard this, went quickly toward Kāśī;
and on the way, a fierce, icy wind suddenly arose."
A cold wind blew, and the fire could not be kindled.
Meanwhile, the village folk who lived there on the banks of the Gaṅgā arrived at that spot to cremate another corpse.
His son went forth to dispel the cold with the funeral pyre’s fire.
Standing by his side, Vijayadatta took up the heat-dispelling fan.
At that moment, the cremator seized the bamboo pole for the corpse.
And he cast the head portion into the fire with a bamboo pole for the purpose of burning it;
at that moment, by means of the bamboo, the head was split in two.
Then, through contact with the fire and with great force, blood [flowed] from Vijayadattika.
As soon as he entered his mouth and became attached there, Vijayadatta instantly fell into a state of extreme transformation;
he became that very Vetāla—huge-bodied, with sharp fangs, and exceedingly terrifying. (36–37)
Licking the marrow of corpses, he drank it there again and again;
by the sound of his boisterous laughter and the dancing of the *vetālas*,
the cardinal directions, the intermediate directions, and the sub-directions seemed as if they were bursting asunder.
Then he rushed through the sky to slay his own father and others;
terrified, everyone fled from the cremation ground in all directions.
Having devoured the corpse, that Vetāla then became powerful.

Having joined with the *vetālas* who dwell in cremation grounds, he made his dwelling there. Once, a terrible battle took place between the *vetālas* and the *gandharvas* on the Vindhya mountain, and in that conflict, he achieved victory.

He became a Vetāla king, possessing a kingdom on the Vindhya mountain. (42) Then, having abandoned that form of a Vetāla, the brahmin, together with his wife, set out for his son and went to the city of Kāśī. (43)
There, he had a second son whose body was like a thunderbolt.
Devoted to Kṛṣṇa, he made his residence in Kāśī along with his son.
In the meantime, [he heard of] a king named Pratāpamukuṭa.
A powerful wrestler named from the land of Kāśī approached him. Then,
by the instruction of the King of Kāśī, the twice-born Vajradeha struck that great wrestler in a wrestling match until he breathed his last.
Five villages were bestowed by the King of Kāśī upon a brahmin.
Once, the King of Kāśī, accompanied by the son of a twice-born,
was wandering in a secluded place at the time of twilight.
From afar, he heard a piteous and miserable voice:
"Alas, what misery! Alas, what misery! Under the rule of the King of Kāśī, for even a slight offense, this most cruel execution upon the stake has been ordered. (48–49)
"Alas! My life-breaths do not depart; rather, thirst afflicts me excessively.
Hearing this, the Lord of Kāśī quickly went forth along with the Brahmins.
Just as Vajrāṅga was going there to fetch water for him to drink—
There, his housewife was seen standing by the twice-born man.
She too, being devoted to her husband, stood ready then to follow him in death.
He said to her, "I am short; I cannot wade across to give you water."
Then Vajrāṅga, endowed with compassion, said to that bride:
"O mother, climb upon my shoulder and give him cool water.
Thus addressed, that Vetālī ascended the shoulder of Vajrāṅga.

Taking water, his wife caused him—who was a *vetāla* on the stake with a magically assumed form, though falsely situated upon the stake—to drink that water. Then the son of the twice-born asked: "Who are you, and who indeed is this person belonging to you? || 54-55 ||
"How did you come to be under this punishment? Tell the truth, O fair-faced one.
Vaitālī replied: "Formerly, this master of mine was a twice-born man named Govindasvāmin’s son, Vijayadatta by name. (56)
Previously, this one was indeed the Vidyādhara Sudarśana;
he violated Gālava’s virtuous daughter for a moment in the forest.
Thereupon, he was cursed by the sage Gālava to such a state as this.
"I am his wife; rescue us two, O Vaitāla!
This trident and other items were made by me as a deceptive means for the sake of deliverance.
Purifying water has been obtained from your hand under the pretext of the trident. (59)
"By this, he has been purified, and likewise I have been purified by him.
O Brahmin, grant us both liberation; let it yield the fruit of all gifts:
the Rājasūya, the Vājapeya, the Gomedha, and the Naramedha. (1.435.60–61)

In the horse sacrifice, the plough sacrifice, the Viṣṇu sacrifice, the sacrifice for fame, the sacrifice to the Giver of Wealth, the sacrifice for land, the Phalgusacrifice, the sacrifice for sons, and the elephant sacrifice;
in the iron sacrifice, the gold sacrifice, and the removal of eye-disease and ailments— 62.
In the Śanaiścara sacrifice, the Rudra sacrifice, and the Śakra sacrifice;
in the Bondage [sacrifice], the Varuṇa sacrifice, the Ball [sacrifice], and the Subduer of Enemies;
in the Pure Sacrifice, the Dharma Sacrifice, the Purging, and the Liberation from Sin. (63–64)
Whatever fruit is obtained in the Bandhana sacrifice, the Karmayoga, the auspicious Maṇiyāga,
the Śyenayāga, the Vājapeya, the Sāvitra, the Kamalakrautu, the Japayajña, the Jñānayajña, and the Kathāyajña— [that fruit is attained here]. (69)
"The fruit of that [act] will surely come to you through the liberation of these *vaitālas*.
Having heard this, the twice-born man said to his own king:
'O King, these beings in the form of spirits dwell in your kingdom, in the kingdom of Kāśī, suffering.'"
"His liberation must be accomplished by the offering of water from the Gaṅgā.
The king said, "In the past, this Vetāla was your brother;
you gave him water to drink, and thus his destruction of sin has occurred."
"Whatever else might truly bring about his liberation must be performed.
Having said this, the king asked the man impaled on the stake:
"Tell me, by what action will your release from here come to pass?"
The preta said: "Liberation from the sage's curse cannot come from anyone else;
my liberation will occur only through the grace of the sage himself.
Likewise, Kāśirāja and my younger brother Govindasvāmī [must be saved]. (71)
"O sirs, you must go to the sage Gālava;
by the method he prescribes, there shall be a deliverance from my sorrow.
Then, having heard this, they all went to where that Gālava was.
Having bowed to the sage who was accompanied by ten thousand maidens, they paid homage again and again.
Then, having been honored by Gāvalgaṇa, they related that very account.
The sage said: "That virtuous and chaste maiden is mine, belonging to the Supreme Lord."
She consists of all perfections, the great devotee of the Lord, and the chaste Vaiṣṇavī;
she is the compassionate protectress of living beings who have come for refuge, devoted to Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, and endowed with sovereign majesty. (75–76)
Divine, attached to Nārāyaṇa, and devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa;
endowed with the vow of celibacy, she was a chaste wife whose very soul was Kṛṣṇa.
In an instant, she was capable of burning away even sins as vast as Mount Meru.
Likewise, the Sovereign Goddess grants liberation to the *koṭis* of *vetālas* and *bhūtas*;
the Sovereign Nature (*prakṛti*) creates the emanations of infinite Brahmās;
she is Vaiṣṇavī and a portion of Kamalā—may they propitiate that Satī. (78–79)
"Indeed, that Mahālakṣmī, the beloved of Kṛṣṇa and possessor of beautiful luster, being well-pleased,
will deliver the Vetālas by bestowing the mantra of Kṛṣṇa.
Having been addressed thus, all those [kings], including the King of Kāśī and others, [spoke to] the young maiden.

They bowed to, praised, sought refuge in, and prostrated before the Mother of the worlds, Lakṣmī, the radiant beloved of Hari. Having learned from them the account regarding the liberation of the Vetāla, [they acted] for that purpose.
The maiden spoke of the duties of Kṛṣṇa’s vow, which bestow all happiness:
"Happiness, suffering, fear, sorrow, joy, and even auspiciousness—as well as prosperity and adversity—everything comes about through one's actions. (83)
By action one becomes a son of Brahmā, and by action one is born into a low lineage;
by action one is handsome, and by one's own constant action one is diseased;
by action one becomes the son of a charioteer, and by action one becomes long-lived.
By action one becomes possessed of virtues, and by action one suffers physical deformity.
By action beings become *vetālas*, and by action they become deities; by action they become human beings.
When a virtuous deed is performed, auspicious worlds are attained; when an evil deed is performed, people are humiliated.
By that merit, he attained the status of a Vidyādhara;
yet by that very same [deed], through his wicked disposition, he also incurred impurity—despite having a virtuous wife and a pure daughter who was devoted to her husband. (87–88)
Those who employ evil glances indeed become blind from birth;
they likewise become afflicted with leprosy, one-eyed, lame, maimed, or dull-witted.
Through their corrupt disposition they become wicked, and through the fruits of their actions they suffer.
Through the cultivation of truthfulness, virtuous beings partake in happiness.
(1.435.90) Indeed, the breaking of restraints is certainly the breaking of dharma.
Those who proceed without restraint truly become liable to punishment by the king. (1.435.91)
They alone are subject to the rod of Yama and subject to the rod of Kṛṣṇa;
they are subject to every rod in this world, for there is no other path than that.
Devotion to one's wife is the supreme dharma, always bestowing happiness and peace.
In ancient times, Śrī Kṛṣṇa produced a twice-born man who was devoted to his wife.
All the brāhmaṇas born in his lineage— whether they were ṛṣis or munis—
are likewise entirely devoted to their wives and endowed with the vow of householdership dedicated to the Brahman.

The bodily constituents (dhātus), produced from food and situated within the bodies of embodied beings, cross over [suffering] and cause others to cross over when their course is dedicated to discipline (niyama).
When restrained, they take the form of celibacy (brahmacarya), which is the nature of Dharma and brings about happiness. ॥95॥
In the absence of restraint, there is a loss of dharma, which brings about the sufferings of dwelling in the womb and so forth.
Having abandoned the bliss of the Self and resorted to the bliss of sexual union, he who is deprived of the bliss of Brahman experiences the suffering of that sexual union. (96–97)
In the case of Dadru-candra, there was indeed scratching, followed always by burning;
and in the case of unjust sexual indulgence, burning in the southern direction is certain.
Therefore, desire is restrained and examined through marriage.
Touch is regulated, and the object of sight is likewise regulated.
Whose is what to be enjoyed? Everything has been regulated by the ancestors. This very regulation is indeed dharma; it is the vow of a wife observed in youth. (1.435.99–100)
Likewise, he who is devoted to his wife is surely a bestower of happiness at all times;
yet by him that [happiness] was destroyed because he committed the violation of a maiden.
Even the touch of one who is unwilling turns into the nature of fire.
But that [suffering] shall become pacified for him through the offering to Kṛṣṇa.
(102) If you desire the swift liberation of that being, [recite]: "Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, obeisance to the Lord. (103)
Having thus taken this mantra and wearing a garland of *tulasī*, let them take from me the remnants of Kṛṣṇa’s worship— water, food, leaves, and so forth—
and go there, wherever the preeminent *vetāla* may be.
And lead him, accompanied by a thousand *vetālas*, to the ocean,
to the shore of the southern sea in the vicinity of Cakratīrtha,
to the supreme Vetāloddhāraka Tīrtha, the sacred site where *vetālas* are liberated from their skins.
"Bathe thousands of vetālas there in that water. Then,
having offered them water, food, and leaves produced from my grace, recite the mantra I have given you three times again and again during their meal."
"Bring about their liberation; there is no other path that bestows happiness.
Having heard this from Kāntimatī at that very moment, they all [chanted]:
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, obeisance to the Lord! (1.08–1.09)
Having taken this mantra, and having received food, water, and so forth,
as well as the leaf offered by her, they praised him and departed for that Vetāla.
Having gone toward the Vetāla, these [beings] approached thousands of other Vetālas.
Having led them away from Cakratīrtha, they went to the shore of the ocean to the south,
to the Vetāloddhāraka Tīrtha. Having bathed them there at that time, they offered water, food, the remnants of Kṛṣṇa’s meal, and tulasī.
Having abandoned their terrible state as *vetālas* and attained divine forms,
and having obtained the four-armed form through the merit of his grace,
those thousands of Vaiṣṇavas ascended into celestial chariots.

Having indeed become attendants of Viṣṇu, they departed for Vaikuṇṭha. Thus, having brought about the liberation of the various classes of Vetālas, the king and the others went to Kāśī and Yamunā, and they themselves returned again to their respective places.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, has been narrated the supreme and great sovereignty of devotion to Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa belonging to the daughter of Gālava.
By hearing, remembering, or even reciting this, one obtains the fruit of wifely devotion.
"Having obtained the fruit of devotion to his wife, a man shall attain liberation.

(1.17) Thus ends the four hundred and thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of How the Vidyādhara Sudarśana, having treated with contempt the daughter of Gālava during the Kṛta age, took birth as a human and subsequently became a Vetāla, and how he was liberated through the power of the daughter of Gālava’s devotion to her husband Kṛṣṇa by means of the King of Kāśī," in the first section on the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga within the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
← Chapter 435: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga) Chapter 436 [[Author:
Chapter 437 →
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: O Lakṣmī! All that is auspicious among the auspicious resides in you.
Just as you are devoted to me, your lord, there is no other such as you.
O my beloved, you who dwell eternally upon the surface of my chest—without you, my form is devoid of splendor, like a withered log;
this is certain, there is no doubt. With you, it becomes beautiful and shines forth.
In my imperishable abode, O best of men,
you exist there as my beloved, known by the names Jayā and Lalitā.
In my Goloka, where I am named Kṛṣṇa, you are Rādhā, Durgā, and Sarasvatī.
You exist as Gaṅgā, Padmā, and Pañcarūpā, and thereafter as Koṭisvarūpiṇī; you abide as my wife, devoted to the vow of fidelity. In Vaikuṇṭha, you abide as the beloved of Nārāyaṇa.
My virtuous wife is Lakṣmī herself, who assumes millions of forms.
In the abode called Amṛta, which is fullness, you are my beloved of Nārāyaṇa;
and in the fourfold Vaikuṇṭha, you are the sovereign Mahālakṣmī.
You are Sītā, Prabhā, Māṇikī, Pārvatī, Maṅgalā, and Satī;
you abide as my great chaste wife, devoted to the vow of fidelity to your husband.
O Svāhā, wife of Agni, you reside within me, whose nature is that of fire.
Without you, I never accept an offering of food at any time.
Even for the gods, the oblation is received daily from your hand;
for the ancestors and my own forms, you, being virtuous, exist as the *svadhā* offering.
In offerings to the gods (*havya*), offerings to the ancestors (*kavya*), and in libations (*tarpaṇa*), that which is presented cannot be attained without you.
You are the eternal *dakṣiṇā* (sacrificial fee) for my sacrifice, embodying the dharma of devotion to one’s husband.
Indeed, without the *dakṣiṇā*, I as a ritual sacrifice am never complete.
In a sacrifice performed without a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), no fruit is produced, nor is a son born.
Everything done without fruit is mere labor, consisting only of expenditure.
I am Kārtika by name, and Devasenā is my designation.
O Mahālakṣmī, you alone are she; indeed, there is no victory without you.
You are that compassionate Goddess Ṣaṣṭhī, whose very nature is that of a mother.
You are the nurse of children and the ever-protecting Ṣaṣṭhikā.

You are the giver of offspring, the one who provides protection for offspring, and the giver of nourishment to offspring; you are devoted to the warding off of obstacles. You are indeed that mental goddess, Jaratkārvī by nature.
The mother of the Nāgas and the mother of Āstīka, she is the eternal protector from poison;
she is my devoted wife in the form of Jaratkāru.
In her mind, she is a female serpent, the supreme sovereign of the serpent species.
O maiden, you are indeed that venerable goddess, the mind-born daughter of Kaśyapa.
Having performed penance for three ages for the sake of Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul,
Hari beheld the body of Jaratkāru at the illustrious Puṣkara.
I am named Jaratkāru, the Lord of the Gopīs;
you are Jaradgaurī, a devotee of Viṣṇu, devoted to the vow of wifely fidelity.
Jaratkāru and Jaradgaurī are perfected yogis in mind.
You are Vaiṣṇavī, the sister of the Nāgas, and likewise Śaivī, the sovereign of the Nāgas (Nāgeśvarī). You are the beloved of Jaratkāru, the mother of Āstīka, and the remover of poison.
O Goddess, you are endowed with supreme knowledge and are worshipped by all.
For one who recites your names, no fear of serpents exists.
In ancient times, Kaśyapa gave you to Jaratkāru, the lord of sages;
that best of munis accepted you unasked, by the command of Brahmā.
Having performed the marriage, the great yogi rested for a long time through asceticism;
he then slept upon the lap of the goddess at the foot of a banyan tree in Puṣkara,
while the sun set and the time of twilight approached.
"Without the twilight prayer (sandhyā), my husband will be defiled by the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Therefore, that most virtuous woman exhorted her husband;
however, having understood this, he became enraged and spoke with words full of anger.
"O virtuous lady! Tell me, how was my sleep interrupted by you? For her whose actions are injurious to her husband, vows and the like are in vain;
likewise, her asceticism, fasting, charity, and religious observances are all fruitless. (27–28)

By her, the husband was honored, and Śrī Kṛṣṇa was likewise honored; for the sake of the vow of devotion to one's husband, Hari himself appeared in the form of the husband. All gifts, sacrifices, sacred pilgrimage sites, and ritual fees [are surpassed by this].

Austerities, fasts, vows, and the worship of the gods do not equal even a fraction of the merit of service to one's husband. A wife devoted to serving her husband dwells in Vaikuṇṭha together with her lord.
She who rejoices while being solely devoted to the worship of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa,
yet performs what is disagreeable to her husband and speaks unpleasantly even when it is pleasant,
shall go to the Kumbhīpāka hell and thereafter be born as a Cāṇḍālī.
Having heard this, Satī fell at her husband’s feet and said:
"Out of fear of neglecting the twilight prayers alone, you abandoned sleep.
O you of noble vows, grant forgiveness for my wickedness in disregarding your beloved command. (33-34)
"She who causes the interruption of passion, food, or sleep—
even a mere servant— shall go to the hell named Kālasūtra.
Having said this, she immediately fell at her husband's feet.
Seeing Jaratkāru about to curse him, the divine Sun indeed approached together with Sandhyā.
Upon seeing the Sun, Jaratkāru reproached him, saying: "O Ravi, why [have you come]?"
"O God, you wish to set without my *saṃdhyā*;
you perceive that my sleep has been interrupted without my *saṃdhyā*.
The Sun said: "Listen, O Brahmin! I did not set at that time."
"And how can I go to my setting without performing your twilight rites?
Forgive me, O Blessed One, O Brahmin; it is not fitting for you, O Sage, to curse me.
Upon the anger of a Brahmin the world perishes, but when a Brahmin is pleased, the world remains stable."
"That brāhmaṇa, a devotee of Kṛṣṇa, shall bring about the welfare of the world.
Having heard this, the twice-born sage became peaceful and bestowed his blessing.
Then Sūrya departed to his own abode, and Jaratkāru followed thereafter.
Considering his young wife to be a bond for him as an old man, and indeed a poison,
he reflected in his mind and abandoned his sorrow-stricken wife.
She, in turn, remembered her teacher Śambhu, her chosen deity Hari, and Brahmā.
They quickly approached Kaśyapa, their progenitor;
indeed, they came together through the power of their devotion to the dharma of wifely fidelity.
Then Jaratkāru, filled with wonder, bowed down to them.
"How did you come to be here? he asked this question.
Brahmā replied, "O great serpent! This beloved wife of mine is no ordinary woman;
by virtue of her devotion to her husband, she is capable of protecting the creation."
And this Mahālakṣmī-kalā exists here, devoted to righteousness;
she would speak in vain, so you must not act otherwise.
This righteous wife, who is faithful to her husband, must not be abandoned.
If you abandon her, there will be a constant loss of dharma for you;
because of that, you shall go to hell—consider the world beyond!
For the sake of preserving dharma, procreate offspring with her.
Whether he be an ascetic, a celibate student, a mendicant, or even a forest-dweller,
one should become a sage only after producing excellent sons through his wife.
However, he who, being devoid of passion, abandons his beloved wife without having produced offspring—
His austerity and merit would flow away, just as water from a ladle;
even a tree does not remove a creeper clinging to its trunk,
and the Self certainly never casts off its own wife, the intellect.
"Sound does not leave day and night, nor does it exhaust its power;
the sun does not leave the sky. How then could Jaratkāru [leave] his beloved?
Having been addressed thus, that Jaratkāru accepted the word of Brahmā.
He did not abandon his beloved; afterwards, those gods departed for heaven.
Then Jaratkārvī spoke to her husband, who was endowed with wisdom:
"The renunciation of sense objects is always better, even for a husband and wife."
The mutual abandonment of husband and wife is certainly not praiseworthy;
if one does not desire sense-objects, they should dwell together and live happily.
Any insult from a husband toward his wife leads to her death.
But she who is abandoned by her husband is devoid of honor on this earth;
she becomes a vessel for universal contempt and is stripped of all good fortune.
Consequently, even though her hair is fit for being adorned with drops of collyrium, it cannot be so.
The life of a woman who has been treated with contempt is indeed in vain;
therefore, O Lord Jaratkāru, if you desire supreme ascetic merit,
then grant me, by mere thought, a son born of my mind.

"By your command, I shall always perform penance in your presence; I shall serve my beloved, having abandoned all sense-objects. Or else, wherever my residence is deemed appropriate by the beloved's command, there I shall remain."
There I dwell, by my beloved’s command, either in the forest or nearby;
wherever I abide, O Lord, it is solely through your presence.
Deprived of my beloved’s presence, O Giver of Life, I have no desire to live.
I am yours and not anyone else's; where else could I dwell without you? (63) Keeping you at a distance within my heart, I shall dwell on mountains and in forests;
keeping you close in my heart and upon my breast, I shall remain—please show me mercy! (64)
Thus addressed, Jaratkāru, having reflected upon his pure wife,
brought about the touch of her navel through yoga for the sake of obtaining a son.
By the mere touch of the sage’s hand, a fetus was immediately conceived.

The husband said: "O Manasā! You shall have an excellent son—one who is the foremost among those who have conquered their senses, most righteous, a leader among the Vaiṣṇavas, radiant, ascetic, illustrious, and endowed with all virtues. (66–67)
He is the best among those who know the Vedas, the foremost among yogis and the wise;
he is a devotee of Viṣṇu, righteous, and the supreme upholder of his lineage.
You are a devoted wife of excellent character, very dear to him, and sweet-spoken.
"You are a virtuous mother of a son, born of noble lineage and a protector of your family.
Be such a mother of a son like him, honored by the world.
Who is a true mother? O virtuous lady, she is one who brings about the realization of the connection with Kṛṣṇa; no other."
Who is a son? He who is an assistant in attaining Hari, and no other, O beloved!
Who is a kinsman? He who bestows devotion to Hari, and no other, O auspicious one!
He alone would be a father who releases one from bondage and shows the path of Hari.
She who indeed bears the embryo is she who liberates one from dwelling in the womb. He who bestows the abode of Kṛṣṇa is the Guru who grants devotion to Viṣṇu.
He who protects liberation is the husband—whether he be Kṛṣṇa himself or a Vaiṣṇava.
O virtuous one, He alone is the Guru; He is Kṛṣṇa Himself, the giver of knowledge.
Kṛṣṇa—the giver of knowledge, the giver of liberation, and the giver of His mantra—is the Lord and the Guru.
Knowledge has been imparted by me to you, and the Vṛṣa (the bull/virtue) has been offered by you to me.
Knowledge and dharma do not excel the service of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
The Lord is the giver of knowledge and the giver of truth; through knowledge, bondage is shattered.
For the destruction of bondage, the Guru is the giver of devotion to Kṛṣṇa and the giver of knowledge. (75–76)
He is the husband, he is the righteous one, the master, the lord, the beloved Nārāyaṇa;
but he who does not liberate one from bondage is an enemy and a slayer of disciples.
[He is the protector] from the suffering born of the mother’s womb and from the pain of Yama’s punishment.
How can he who does not liberate you be considered a guru, a husband, or a kinsman?
O virtuous lady, by my command, observe your vows and worship Śrī Kṛṣṇa—the Supreme Brahman, the infallible Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the bestower of true liberation. (78–79)
"I abandoned you through a deception; O beloved, forgive this fault of mine.
You excel even me in righteousness, in virtuous conduct, in devotion, and in the chanting of prayers.
O devoted wife, you abide in knowledge, in worship, and in dispassion."
"Through you, my birth has attained its fulfillment, and liberation is now within my grasp.
Since you have granted me victory over the three worlds, I shall perform most rigorous penance at Puṣkara. (81–82)
Those who follow the path of worldly activity fix their intellect, senses, and other faculties upon the lotus feet of Śrī Kṛṣṇa,
yet maintain attachment to wealth, women, and home. In contrast, those seekers who desire freedom from longing find their refuge solely in the feet of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
"Speak, O Goddess! My mind may become wavering at some point while living together.
Therefore, for a husband and wife on this single earth, constant cohabitation would be a bondage; separation would instead lead to virtue. (84-85)
Therefore, separation is indeed appropriate; do that which is truly best.
Whether you dwell with me or far away, I am always pleased with you.
O noble lady, act so that there may be the severing of our bonds and our liberation.
Having heard the words of Jaratkāru, the mental daughter Kamalākalā considered separation to be appropriate and union to be like being bound by poison;
for even a wife who is always by one's side may yet be subject to the laws of her menstrual cycle.
A husband should unite with his wife in desire, or sometimes the wife may do so with impetuosity.
Therefore, when a husband and wife both possess knowledge and desire liberation,
it is proper for them to separate once they have understood this, provided there is no fear present.
Devotion to the husband consists in obeying his command, whether he be far away or near at hand.
A wife’s vow is for the sake of her husband; thus, a husband who desires his own welfare should always [uphold it].
Desire is not a fault; indeed, it bestows prosperity and does not lead to hell.
Therefore, it is better that this husband and wife who desire liberation be separated.
Today I must certainly go into the presence of Satī-Pārvatī;
indeed, on Kailāsa, liberation itself shall be attained through the words of my beloved.
Having reflected thus, Satī, the daughter of the Naga king born of his mind, her eyes filled with tears of grief, spoke with humility to her beloved, as dear to her as life:
"O Lord, for the sake of my welfare, you consider this separation to be a source of happiness. (93–94)
"As the Blessed One is pleased, so shall I act, and not otherwise.
I shall go to Kailāsa to worship the feet of Pārvatī incessantly;
there indeed I shall perform the devotion of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa."
"When I remember you, O kinsman, then you shall come to me.
(96) The separation from a kinsman causes distress, and the separation from a son is even greater than that;

As eyes are to the one-eyed, as water is to the thirsty,

Thus addressed, Jaratkāru replied, "So be it," and for a moment he held her in his lap; out of love, he gazed upon her face.
That ocean of compassion touched his beloved with his hand, even as she was about to depart.
She bathed that virtuous woman with the water of her eyes and with her mind. Trembling with fear of separation, she drenched the sage’s lap with her tears.
Then, through his wisdom, both of them became free from sorrow.
The two of them went to Kailāsa and paid homage to Pārvatī and Śiva.
Jaratkāru related his own story to Śambhu;
Śambhu became pleased, as did Pārvatī even more so.
For such yogis, there is no suffering of separation; this is their way.

Seeing his daughter together with her son, Kaśyapa attained great joy. That virtuous woman, devoted to the worship of Kṛṣṇa and intent upon the path to liberation, remained for a very long time in her father’s abode with her son.

O Lakṣmī! You are Mānasī; indeed, you were born from the mind as a female serpent (nāginī).

You were Mādhavī, not just one, but many protectors of my devoted husband.

Hemnī, Mauktikā, Svarṇā, Sītā, Padmāvatī, Prathā,
Rādhā, Gaurī, Kasturikā, Nalinī, Vijayā, Mudā, Hariṇī, Lalitā,

Thus ends the four hundred and thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of Lakṣmī’s Many Incarnations in the First Section on the Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga, including Jaratkārvī’s Devotion to Her Husband, the Departure of her Husband Jaratkāru for Asceticism, Her Residence on Kailāsa, and the Attainment of a Son named Āstīka," in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, Chapter 436, Book 1 (*Kṛta-yuga-santāna*). Chapter 437.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: O Lakṣmī! In ancient times, there was a king named Manojava in the Lunar dynasty.
He worshipped the gods with sacrifices, the brahmins with heaps of food, and he gratified the ancestors with *kavya* offerings; yet he served Hari with devotion.
However, pride arose within him, which brought about the destruction of his wealth, sons, and other possessions. (1–2)
Egoism, intoxication, greed, violence, lust, anger, and passion— these,
together with their companions, are all causes for the destruction of prosperity.
That king possessed greed for the acquisition of wealth belonging to Brahmins.
Out of greed, he indeed seized the wealth and grain of the Brahmins;
out of greed, the king also took the riches of the gods;
and out of passion, he seized their fields and their means of livelihood.
Then, due to the destruction of his merit and as a result of the ripening of his cruel karma,
his enemy Golaba besieged his city with a great army.
They fought for six months, and victory went to Golaba.

Mind-swift, accompanied by his wife and son, he went into the depths of the forest. (7) There, where no food was to be found and fruits were scarce in every direction, the hungry boy begged for food from his mother. (8)
"Mother, give me some food; hunger afflicts me greatly.
Father, give me some food to eat; otherwise, my death is certain.
(9) Having heard this, the father then spoke softly to his wife named Sumitrā:
"Sumitrā! What shall I do now, and where shall I go to seek food?
He will die before long, and that will surely be our fate as well.
How is it that Brahmā created me, so unfortunate and purposeless?"
Indeed, in my previous birth, I did not bestow gifts of food,
nor was Śambhu— Hari, Kṛṣṇa, and Nārāyaṇa— worshipped by me. Nor were the gods, such as Sūrya, Vahni, Varuṇa, and others, worshipped.
"O beautiful one, in my previous birth, I did not provide for the livelihoods [of others].
(13) I suspect that when people had departed, I seized what was given by another;
by that sin, indeed, I have become so arrogant in this present birth. (14)

Indeed, out of egoism, I seized the lands of gods and brahmins; I also seized wealth belonging to gods, brahmins, and even the righteous. Thus, all this evil deed of mine has resulted in the destruction of my kingdom.
Defeat, dwelling in the forest where food and such are not obtained;
and there, hungry and thirsty wives and sons look about in the forest as if overwhelmed by hunger and thirst, crying out, "Alas, what is our fate? (16–17).
Since previously neither water nor food was given in charity, neither oblations were offered, nor was a pilgrimage performed, nor was a *śrāddha* ceremony conducted;
neither was a guest honored, nor was even a meal provided for one's kinsmen. (18)
