"Even a garment, an ornament, a carriage, a mount, or anything at all—ultimately, it would not have been given by me in that manner. Because of that sin, this mountain of all-encompassing suffering has come upon me. (22-23)
Neither the *aśvattha*, the mango tree, nor the *kapittha* or *tintiḍī* were planted; likewise, trees bearing fruits such as the *amṛta* were not watered.
Nor were trees of the coconut or *āmalakī* planted.

O beloved, in the past, neither resting houses for travelers nor dharma-shālās for those seeking the sacred ford were ever built by me. Nor was service—such as sweeping and plastering—rendered in a temple by me. || 25–26 ||
Neither tanks and such were constructed nor dug,
neither flower gardens were planted nor groves of *tulasī* were established.
Because of that sin, this mountain of all my miseries has come upon me.
No sacrifices were performed, nor were sacrificial fees offered.
No fasting was observed as part of vows, nor was it caused to be done by another.
And during the month of Śreṣṭha and in the rainy season, no worship of the gods was performed.

I have not offered food oblations, water for drinking, or the waving of lights; I have not performed temple festivals, congregational chanting, or the concluding rites of worship. Nor have I ever worn around my neck the most purifying garland of *tulasī*.
"Neither was any recitation performed by me, nor was it ever caused to be performed.
Because of that sin, this mountain of all my sufferings has come upon me.
Lamenting thus, the king fell into a swoon of grief.
Then Sumitrā, whose very deity was her husband, embraced him and lamented:
"Alas, my lord! Have you not departed from this sorrow, perhaps seeking death in the forest?
Having abandoned me, helpless and with our son, in the desolate wilderness—"
"O Indra among kings, if you are dead, I shall follow you even into the depths.
And the son Candrakānta, having embraced his father, wept; meanwhile, the great sage Parāśara, the lord of yogis, [remained there].
Having arrived there by chance, the devoted wife Sumitrā and her son, upon seeing him, rose up and paid their respects.
Comforted by the sage, they then spoke to him.

"The kingdom was seized by Golabha; [he experienced] the arrival in the forest, hunger, and so forth. All this, as well as the king's fainting, was exactly as it happened. Having heard that from the devoted wife, Parāśara, the son of Śakti, [spoke]. (37–38)
He said to Sumitrā: "Let there be no fear in you upon my arrival here;
indeed, whatever inauspiciousness there was has been destroyed by the sight of me, a virtuous man.
I shall now inform the king; behold the power of Kṛṣṇa! ||39||
Having spoken thus, the king of sages took water in his hand and recited this mantra:
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; obeisance.
And with his hand, he touched that lord of men who was like a corpse.
King Manojava, having risen, bowed down to him and said,
"O Blessed One, protect me from this terrible and painful distress!
Parāśara then spoke the mantra again and again to his virtuous son.
He caused the evil to blaze away and made the devotees into true Bhāgavatas.
That lord of sages gave excellent food consisting of wild fruits and sublime water;
he bestowed upon the queen an inexhaustible fruit.
In the morning, having indeed bathed the form of the glorious Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa with water, worship should be performed; the fruit [of this] is obtained together with the image itself.
Therefore, it should be worshipped with flowers and other offerings, as well as sixteen fruits.
"Sixteen nectars shall be produced morning and evening;
those very same ones are to be consumed until the destruction of [her] calamities.
Having spoken thus to Sumitrā, he proclaimed her devotion to her husband.
Listen, Sumitrā! Always, in the forest, as soon as morning dawns, you should properly groom your body according to the requirements of place and time;
having worshipped your husband according to the prescribed rites, you should worship the fruit with devotion.
Having kindled the fire and offered fuel-sticks, flowers, and fruits—
for the sake of her husband’s victory and for the destruction of his enemies—
she plucked a single lock of hair from your head, and no other.
O virtuous lady, offer oblations to the purifier (Agni) separately at evening and at dawn!
Recite: "Svāhā to Rudra-Agni, the destroyer of enemies!
Perform the fire-sacrifice for forty days, observing the vow of Brahman.
"O virtuous lady, observer of celibacy! Victory shall be yours.
O noble one, you should perform this ritual at the Setubandha on Mount Gandhamādana, at the sacred ford named Maṅgala on the shore of the ocean."
Having been addressed thus by the king, that virtuous and devoted wife departed together with her son.
Having paid homage to Parāśara and subsisting on a diet of fruits, that faithful woman,
after bathing at the sacred ford, then fed her son and her husband.
As it has been said, she recited the mantra of Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
(55) Having offered the oblations and other rites into the fire, she sacrificed her hair with the mantra;
at the forty-second hour of the evening, she sacrificed that lock of hair. (56)
From that smoke there immediately arose a bow that struck fear into the world,
two inexhaustible quivers, and a sword with a golden hilt;
also a single shield, a mace, a spear, and a great club.
A conch shell, a chariot equipped with horses, banners, and a charioteer;
impenetrable armor, a commander-in-chief accompanied by his troops;
as well as many missiles and weapons, vehicles, and mounts. (58–59)
O Lotus-born One! All food and other necessities, divine garments, ornaments, and excellent royal regalia, as well as medicinal herbs and vehicles—everything has arisen from that fruit. (1.437.60)
A voice from the sky said to her, "O blessed one! O virtuous lady! May victory be yours!
(61) And thus was the worshipful great sage Parāśara reminded; that best of brahmins immediately arrived with a smile and stood before her. (62)
Then Parāśara instructed the king in the Brahmā weapon along with its mantras,
including its constituent parts, its secret lore, its method of discharge, and its method of withdrawal.
Having received it, the king then became a sovereign lord.
Urged by the sage, he bowed and then ascended the chariot.
There, he commanded the queen: "Remain steady in the middle of the chariot;
do not descend from the chariot until the battle is won."
The army of the hair upon your head is indeed a chowrie;
and as long as you remain seated in the chariot, your husband shall be free from all obstacles.
Indeed, while you are stationed in the chariot, there shall be life for one who is dead.
By the power of her devotion to her husband, this king shall be free from obstacles.
O virtuous lady, always remain in the chariot with your son by your side until you reach the courtyard of your own royal palace.
"You must remain in the courtyard of the palace until the chariot arrives;
before you yourself descend, you should first cause your son and husband Suvastuka to alight,
and only after that should you step onto the ground."
At that very moment, the chariot, the army, and Keśaja shall go to their destruction.
"Go, O virtuous one! Depart, O King! Prince, obtain the kingdom!
Having spoken thus, she made a mark like a drop of sandalwood paste upon her forehead and vanished.
Accompanied by his wife, his son, and his army,
that king went to his own city for victory and blew his conch shell again and again.
Golabha quickly came forth with his forces to do battle.
The battle lasted for three days, and King Gaulabha’s army was destroyed.
On the fourth day, King Gaulabha himself was slain;
thereafter, the lord of the earth, Manojava, together with his sons and wife, [returned] to his own [city]. || 73-74 ||
He entered the palace, and they descended from the chariot;
at that moment, the army, the chariot, the weapons, and the fruits vanished.
He ruled the kingdom with its enemies destroyed, yet he harbored no egoism.
He performed the sacrifice of Dharma, recitation, and giving, as well as meritorious deeds, without interruption (76).
He always rendered service to the gods, Brahmins, virtuous women, and the righteous;
he honored guests and practiced many acts of charity and virtue (77).

He practiced the duties of digging wells, the duties of providing charitable food, and likewise the duties of performing sacrifices; he performed the duties of watering trees and the duties of ancestral rites (śrāddha).
He also engaged in the duties of maintaining a livelihood, such as protecting the hands [from manual labor] and so forth.
He practiced the religious duties beginning with the protection of cattle (*gorakṣā*) and the observances of vows (*vratadharma*).
He himself performed the duties that protect the subjects, such as the worship of the gods,
and he caused the religious acts consisting of storytelling, knowledge, and so forth to be carried out.
Having abandoned malice, slander, and the like, he became devoted to non-violence;
and the beautiful queen also observed the duties of a virtuous wife,
especially as that auspicious ascetic woman had done before.
She was constantly devoted to meditation upon Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, her own Lord;
likewise, she was eternally intent on serving her beloved, devoted to celibacy, dedicated to the worship of the gods, a performer of vows for Kṛṣṇa, and free from worldly taints. || 82–83 ||
Bathing three times a day, devoted solely to her husband, eating but one meal a day, intent on the sacrifice of recitation (*japa-yajña*), serving the virtuous,
she always drank from sacred fords (*tīrtha*) and ate the food of sages and arhats. (84)
In this way, like a female servant to her master, she served her own lord.
The king, too, remained ever devoted to non-violence and was dedicated to righteousness;
by him, all his subjects were caused to be initiated into the Vaiṣṇava faith.
In particular, he would constantly summon virtuous men and have them form circles for the chanting of Hari’s names;
having settled sages in his home, he engaged in auspicious discourses on the Vedas and the Shastras.
Together with his family, he heard [the teachings] and served the Sātvatas.
Thus, for a thousand years, that Manojava protected [the kingdom];
then, having consecrated his son in the sovereignty, he departed for asceticism.
Meditating upon Kṛṣṇa, the king departed for Goloka without delay;
Sumitrā also remained as the shadow of her husband to perform penance,
embracing her husband’s body and generating fire from her own person.
Having ascended his funeral pyre, he attained the imperishable abode of Hari.
O Lakṣmī, this account devoted to the virtue of wifely fidelity has been told to you;
whoever hears it or reads it shall obtain the fruit of all religious duties.

Thus ends the four hundred and thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of King Manojava’s Loss of Kingdom and so forth due to Atheism, and the Recovery of his Kingdom and Attainment of Liberation through the Homa-offerings of Mantras taught by Parāśara and the Devotion of his Wife Sumitrā’s Chastity," in the first section, the Kṛta-yuga lineage, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:

who ruled over the kingdom of Mathurā-maṇḍala and was devoted to Hari.

having heard from the scriptures that the Setu-tīrtha, centered upon Mount Gandhamādana, was the most preeminent of all, he took his retinue, who were devoted to Hari, and departed.

Having arrived at Dhanuṣkoṭi, that Kamalālayā remained there.
After bathing and performing acts of charity, the king beheld that virtuous maiden,
who was exceedingly endowed with beauty and possessed lovely eyes.
The treasury of merit questioned her, who was composed of the splendor of all gems and adorned with a halo of moonstones: "Who are you? Whose daughter are you?
O maiden, tell me everything exactly as it is—how have you come here? (9)
Hearing this, the maiden became distressed and spoke to that best of kings:
"O King, my mother and father are not here; out of a desire for sacred pilgrimage sites, I wander about as one without a protector, O Lord of Men, and I earn my own food."
The king then said, "O maiden! Come together with me. The maiden replied, "O King! If you protect me while being my father, then, O King, I shall remain constantly with you as your daughter."
"I shall dwell in your house, O King, so that your father may always see you.
Let no one take my hand without my own consent;
then, O King, I will live in your palace as a servant to my father."
The king said: "O daughter!

O auspicious lady, I shall give you to whomever pleases you."

he then fell at His feet and offered praise to Lakṣmī, the consort of Viṣṇu.

Salutations to her whose very nature is compassion; salutations again and again to her who has been attained by herself. Salutations to her whose nature is that of a daughter; salutations again and again to the divine Goddess. Salutations to you, the subtle and hidden one, the consort of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
Salutations again and again to Kamalā, who dwells upon the chest of Viṣṇu;
salutations again and again to you, Rādhā, Sarasvatī, and Padminī.
Salutations to you, Durgā, Mahālakṣmī, and Śāradā.
Salutations again and again to you, Gaṅgā, Tulasī, and Vṛndā;
salutations to you, Padmāvatī, Bhārgavī, and Kambharā. Constant salutations to Siddhi, Puṣṭi, Svadhā, and Svāhā.
Salutations to Dakṣiṇā, Maṅgalā, Pārvatī, and Śrī.
(61) Salutations to you, Māṇikyā, Prabhā, and Lalitā;
salutations again and again to you, Jayā, the goddess Jānakī, and Draupadī. (62)
Salutations again and again to Nārāyaṇī, to Sandhyā, and to Goddess Ṣaṣṭhī; salutations again and again to Mātṛkā, to Kṛṣṇā, and to Mañjulā.
Salutations to you who are known as Śraddhā, Medhā, Bhūti, Dhātrī, and Haṃsā.

Salutations again and again to Dharaṇī, to Sarvavidyā, to Buddhi, and to Gopī. (64) Salutations again and again to you, O Mother of the World, as Prakṛti; salutations again and again to you as my daughter.
Whether it was in the capacity of a daughter that I insulted you or issued a command against you, [I beg your forgiveness]. (65)
O Lakṣmī, please forgive me in every way for my addressing you as "thou.
All worlds are your children, and you two are the parents of the universes.
Parents should forgive the transgressions of their children; therefore, be gracious.
Thus entreated by the two gods, Viṣṇu spoke to King Puṇyanidhi:
"O King, you must never feel fear;
for when you performed the sacrifice at Setubandha, I was indeed Hari."
Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person,
became well-pleased, and Kamalā was sent by me.
For the sake of completing your sacrifice, she was seen by you at the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha).
She remains here with you at that time by my command.
Out of devotion, I am subject to your will, restrained by the noose of your devotion;
I always forgive the offenses of a devotee, of this there is no doubt.
To always know your devotion, that Lakṣmī resides in your home;
she is my beloved Ramā, constantly protected and nourished by you.
Because of this, I am exceedingly pleased, for she is a virtuous woman who is my very own form.
He who possesses devotion to Lakṣmī in this world is called my devotee.
O King, he who is averse to her is my hater, without a doubt.
You have always worshipped Ramā with perfect devotion.
Since I am non-different from Lakṣmī, my worship has been performed;
therefore, no offense such as that arising from fetters has been committed by you. For protection was afforded to Lakṣmī by fulfilling her word.

"Since you have placed the committer of offenses against Ramā in fetters, I am exceedingly pleased with you as well; for by protecting my wife, O King, you have fulfilled the agreement that was made previously. (76–77)
That agreement was honored; that service was rendered by you to me.
That beloved one, O Indra among kings, is mine; that service also is dear to me.
This Lakṣmī is your daughter, and you have always acted with truth.
Thus addressed, that Puṇyanidhi became tearful-eyed.
Then Lakṣmī said to him: "O father, I am pleased by your service;
though I am always independent, I have always been protected by you."
"I, Viṣṇu, have come here for the sake of nourishing your devotion.
We two are satisfied by your devotion and service; be happy.
O King, by our grace, may prosperity likewise be yours."
May you always possess the sovereignty over a great realm of land, eternally and firmly.
May your devotion to our pair of feet be constant,
and at the end of this body, may you attain our eternal abode forever.
"May your devotion always be intent upon the chastity of Kṛṣṇa," having spoken thus to her beloved Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, Mahālakṣmī suddenly vanished,
and Garuḍa also became invisible.
And the attendants were seen intent upon offering blessings.
Vindhyāvalī, the king’s wife, rejoiced, overwhelmed with love, at the sight of Śrī Kṛṣṇa and the sight of the attendants. (85–86)
When the divine Lakṣmī realized that she had become my son,
she was constantly served by me, always cherished and protected;
that virtuous woman was repeatedly delighted, made to laugh, instructed, and fed.
She was bathed and stayed with me in the garden;
she was given drink, massaged, adorned upon her head, and filled with great joy.
She was summoned and seated by me upon a lion-throne of jewels. (88–89)
O daughter, O son, O maiden, O young girl!
O beautiful one, O dear one, O mother! You who are repeatedly consoled in times of sorrow;
you who are constantly touched and adorned by your friends, and sent forth with them.
She was delighted in the great gardens and gladdened by pleasing things;
she was gratified when favorable objects of desire were bestowed upon her.
Thus obtained through good fortune, she was not separated from him even in a dream. (91–92)
And my daughter was never once removed from my side.
Oh, what excellent fortune and supreme success for my wife!
For it is through her service that I have obtained this gain.
My house, my palace, my beds, coverings, and furnishings;
my bowls, seats, and so forth, as well as vehicles and mounts;
and the divine palaces that bestow worship and indeed liberation. ||94-95||
My house has undoubtedly become the divine Vaikuṇṭha;
whatever was touched by my daughter and beheld by Lakṣmī has all attained divinity. What fortune of mine shall I describe?

O Lakṣmī! O my mother! O daughter! O daughter! O you of virtuous deeds! (97) If I possess eternal devotion toward you, the illustrious one, and if I possess devotion to my husband Kṛṣṇa, who is Nārāyaṇa, (98) [then let this be so].
"O virtuous one! Grant me your sight, O mistress of my life, O daughter!
How have you become invisible? Why do you not appear before me?
Having spoken thus, she shed tears from her eyes with joy.
Then Lakṣmī, her face radiant with a gentle smile and as brilliant as the moon,
emerged from the chest of Śrī Hari and came to stand upon his lap;
for a moment, she was absorbed in affection for her mother’s breast like a little daughter.

The king’s beloved smelled the head of her daughter as she sat upon her lap and said: "O daughter, O beloved of Kṛṣṇa, since you reside in the abode of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, may you lead me, together with my husband, to that place at the end of my life."
Having said "Om," and having drunk the sweet water and looked upon her face,
Lakṣmī quickly vanished; Nārāyaṇa disappeared,
and O beloved, his attendants and Garuḍa also vanished in an instant.
Taking you with him upon Garuḍa, I reached Vaikuṇṭha;
meanwhile, the king, having attained detachment and entrusted the burden of sovereignty to his son,
went once more to the meritorious holy site known as Setumādhava.
Accompanied by his wife, he spent the remainder of his time meditating upon Hari;
having meditated upon Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, he attained liberation at the end of his body. And his wife, Vindhyāvalī, followed him in death.
The devoted wife, whose life was her husband, who was Lakṣmī devoted to Kṛṣṇa,
produced fire from her big toe upon the funeral pyre;
just as she began to burn herself, Lakṣmī and Narāyaṇa appeared.
The two arrived to lead the couple to the supreme Vaikuṇṭha.
Having caused those two devotees, who were devoted to Hari and faithful to their husband, to ascend a celestial chariot, they led them— possessing divine bodies— to the abode of Viṣṇu.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have related to you your own auspicious life story.
By reading or hearing this, one attains the state of Vaikuṇṭha. (111)

Thus ends the four hundred and thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of King Puṇyanidhi’s Attainment of Lakṣmī in the Form of a Daughter through the Performance of Sacrifice at Setubandha-Rāmeśvara during the Kṛta Yuga, as well as the Grace of Nārāyaṇa upon the King and his wife—who were supreme devotees—during Lakṣmī’s Test, including the Arrival in the Form of a Brāhmaṇa, the Divine Vision, and the Leading to Vaikuṇṭha," in the *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, within the first section concerning the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga. 438.
← Chapter 438: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga) Chapter 439 [Author: Chapter 440 →
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī! In ancient times, my father Dharmadeva gave instruction to the Apsaras Vardhinī at a place of austerity.
In ancient times, Dharma himself performed a truly severe and great penance for the welfare of all creatures in Dharmāraṇya for a thousand years. Upon that Dharma,
there were bamboo-tree pillars rooted in anthills.
Mahendra and the other gods became non-existent; having realized this, they were seized by intense fear:
"If Dharmadeva indeed performs fierce penance, then this world will be reduced to ashes by the fire arising from it. (3-4)
Then, having gathered together with the gods and others to obstruct his asceticism,
an Apsarā endowed with beauty and virtue was sent to Dharmāraṇya.
Having gone there, she paid homage to her aged father, who was covered in dust.
Having extracted him from the bamboo-thicket, she spoke the well-articulated Dharma.
He asked, "What is the cause of your asceticism? Dharma replied, "I perform this severe penance for the sake of protecting those who dwell on earth and those who dwell in heaven. (6–7)

"How have you come to this forest, being such a beautiful and virtuous young woman? She replied: "O father, Mahendra and the other gods, fearing [the success of] your penance, sent me here to ascertain the cause of your asceticism."
"O Worshipful One, the cause has indeed been understood; there is no fear because of this auspiciousness.
I shall speak [of the matter] so that Indra and the other gods will become free from affliction. However, if any offense has been committed by me, please grant me your grace. (1.439.10)
I am a virtuous woman sent under the authority of another;
I have come to behold my aged father, and thus I have become purified. Indeed, it does not please me to create an obstacle to anyone’s meritorious deed.
"But since I am impelled there by the power of destiny, I shall indeed go.
O Grandfather, if you will instruct me so that it may result in my welfare,
I shall inform Mahendra of the reason for my asceticism and then return."
O father, the state of being an Apsarā does not please me, for it involves dancing and such [worldly distractions].
To be a servant brings only suffering and destroys all one's merits, where indeed there is no self-restraint in becoming a handmaid to masters. (14)
O Father, for women who have committed many sins, servitude arises;
being placed in the hands of another and being enjoyed by another—these, O Father, obstruct one's merits and do not please me. (15–16)

Having heard these words of hers, Dharma, who is praised for his righteousness, was pleased with her, the upholder of dharma. He said to her: "O virtuous daughter, having informed Mahendra of the cause of your asceticism, return quickly; I shall do what is beneficial for you."
"O Vardhinī! Cast aside your fear and come here without delay!
(18) Thus addressed, she bowed to the bull and, being delighted, departed in haste, having informed Mahendra and the others of her purpose for penance and her protection of the subjects. (19)
Having quickly reached the Forest of Dharma, which is the counter-dharma to worldly existence,
the virtuous lady bowed with supreme reverence to Dharma, who was situated within an anthill,
and served him day and night, subsisting on fruits and roots.
She gradually uprooted the bamboo stalks situated within the anthill;
she slowly removed the earth from the body of Dharma until only his bones remained, which she then washed with the water of the sacred ford.
The virtuous one bathed him; his body attained the state of a sprout.
There, by the power of his resolve, he became Dharma himself, possessing a divine form and a radiance equal to a hundred suns. He beheld the chaste female attendant.
Vardhinī fell at the feet of Dharma and offered water;
she presented leaves, flowers, fruits, and other offerings to Vṛṣa.
She inquired after his welfare and performed the ritual washing of his feet.
The gracious Śrī Dharmadeva said to her:
"The glorious Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the soul of all, created eternal virtues, as well as insentient matter and sentient beings—both men and women—for the purpose of protecting dharma. (26)
In ancient times, the Blessed One himself created a Brahmin named Patnīvratā and his wife, who was devoted to her husband. He then spoke to them regarding their duties:
"Listen, O virtuous lady; I shall tell you those virtues which belong to one of a sattvic nature."
O virtuous one! By protecting [these vows], women shall attain the highest welfare.
As long as she remains a maiden, she should observe the *kumārikā-vrata*.
She should indeed serve her mother and father, and perform service to her guru.
Devoted to the celibate life (*brahmacarya*), she should worship Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa. If she is married, that woman should maintain her devotion to her husband (*pātivratya*);
if she is not married, she should remain a celibate practitioner (*brahmacāriṇī*).
Whether she has experienced worldly enjoyment or not, whether she is previously married or a widow, or even if she is unmarried—
if she certainly desires the supreme good which is centered on celibacy,
she should become a celibate woman devoted to devotion to Kṛṣṇa.

She always abides in dharma, devoted to her husband, who is as dear to her as Kṛṣṇa. O daughter, just as she remains intent on her devotion to her beloved husband, so too should she abide by those virtues; I shall tell you of them, for they bring about one's welfare. (33–34)
She should be pure in speech, mind, and body, devoted to the worship of those worthy of worship; she should be free from greed, possess faith, and be intent on devotion to Kṛṣṇa as her master.
Kṛṣṇa is her master and husband; for the sake of Kṛṣṇa, she has undertaken her vows.
One who is perfected in her vows for the sake of her husband is called a *pativratā*.
That woman is a *pativratā* who delights in service to her husband; likewise, she should remain observant of her vows toward her beloved husband, even when he has taken the form of Kṛṣṇa. (36–37)
O Lotus-born One! Having heard this, Vardhinī said to Dharmadeva:
"Tell me, what are the characteristics of all those women who are devoted to their husbands?
Then Dharmadeva spoke at length for the enlightenment of the people.
The life of that man in whose home there is a devoted wife is fruitful.
She is like his own body, like his very shadow, and ever intent on service;
her very mention constantly bestows merit and is itself a source of virtue. (1.439.40)
She eats when her husband has eaten, she remains still when he is still, and she attends to him when he is attending to his duties.
She sleeps only after he has fallen asleep and wakes up before him.
When her beloved has gone to another land, she does not adorn herself.
While her husband is away on business, she should remain devoid of ornaments;
desiring the increase of his life-span, she should not utter his name.
Even when reviled, she should not revile in return; even when struck, she should remain composed.
When commanded with a task, she says, "It is done, O Master," and she indeed performs it.
Summoned by her master, she immediately sets aside all other duties and goes to him. "Speak, my beloved; what shall I do today? I am here, standing before you as your servant. (44)
Thus, one should speak everything sweetly and do everything that he commands.
One should not say "no," but should say, "May your favor be granted to me.
One should act in such a way that the master becomes satisfied and pleased.
Standing at the door of the house, she should not look long at other men;
she should certainly not give away anything that ought not to be given while her husband is absent.
Without being told, she should herself prepare the requisites for bathing and worship.
She should arrange all things, such as leaves and flowers, at the proper time.
She should never be anxious, but remain joyful and serve her husband.
Anticipating his true affection, she should fully satisfy her husband.
She should always eat the food-grace (prasāda) consumed by her husband and avoid all else.
O Vardhinī! A woman who is devoted to her husband should never go to social gatherings, festivals, processions, weddings, theatrical performances, or similar events without her beloved.
Devoted solely to the duty toward her husband, she should indeed proceed only by his command.
Whether he is sleeping, sitting, standing, playing, or intent on business, the virtuous wife should attend to him for the sake of his own welfare, removing any obstacles in his way. (51–52)
When the onset of menstruation has occurred, being impure for three nights,
she should observe her state of ritual impurity and must not go outside the house under any circumstances.
Being present, she should not show her face, which is devoid of luster, to those outside.
A devoted wife should not let others hear her voice outside the house.
On the fourth day, having bathed, the beautiful woman becomes pure;
when the fourth night has passed, she is fit for the worship of the gods and other such rites.
Purified and fit for service, she should behold her own master;
or else, having remembered her own master, she should behold the sun.
Indeed, by obtaining seed during the odd-numbered nights, she shall give birth to a daughter.
If conception occurs during the even nights, one will indeed give birth to a son.
The opening of the lotus of the womb always remains until the sixteenth night;
beyond that, it becomes closed, and the bodily constituents (dhātus) become fruitless.
If a woman is menstruating or ill, another beautiful woman should touch her twelve times each time and bathe again and again;
she should then have the clothes previously worn by that woman moved far away.
At the end, she should sprinkle herself with water; thus the menstruating woman becomes pure.
(1.439.60) In marriage, at festivals, while traveling, in assemblies, on vehicles, on the road, during exile, on pilgrimages, at sacrifices, in acts of charity, and in times of calamity—(61)
In battle, in the narration of sacred stories, in knowledge, in the rite of initiation, in the forest, in the state of renunciation, in the state of yoga, in wonder, in the practice of austerity,
in being without refuge, in dependence on others, in prison, and in solitude. (62)
When one is without companions, when there is no servant or employee, when the mind is distracted,

(63) when there is an extremely urgent task, during the conjunction with a corpse, during a period of birth-impurity, when traveling abroad, in another's house and the like, while observing celibacy, during a vow, or at a sacrifice; (64)
For the acquisition of knowledge, for the observance of fasting such as the *cāndrāyaṇa* and others,
or when there is a necessary duty involving brothers, sons, parents, and so forth,
a woman in her menses becomes pure simply by bathing and observing a single fast. (65)
The embodiment of Dharma himself is the beloved; Kṛṣṇa himself is the husband.
Dharma is the husband, action is the husband, for purity indeed exists in no other way.
Through union with the husband, she remains pure only so long as she is in her menses.
Just as rivers are always in their menstrual flow during the four-month period [of the rainy season],
yet become pure upon union with the ocean and remain in their flow when not united with it;
so too, purity depends on the husband's control, for it is union with the husband that effects purification.
A virtuous woman should never speak ill of her husband.
Turmeric, saffron, forehead marks, vermilion, collyrium, head-cloth, betel, and auspicious ornaments— [these she should wear]. (1.439.70)
Desiring long life for her husband, a wife dear to her husband should avoid grooming her hair and fine ornaments such as bracelets.
She should not go outside alone, nor should she bathe naked.
She should be skilled in the arts of love and free from pride and laziness. In whatever matter her husband finds pleasure, she should act as his companion accordingly.
Dharma, vows, recitation, service, worship, and pleasing the husband [are her duties]. 72–73.
Thinking thus, one should act for the pleasure of the husband; in that way, everything becomes well-done.
[One should not strive] for the sake of the churning-stick, nor the grinding-stone, nor the hearth, nor the pestle;
nor for the ladle, nor the large cooking-pot, nor the threshold, nor the water-wheel.
One should not sit upon a stone, nor on ground smeared with clay, nor during the performance of ritual practices and the like.
[One should avoid] one who is destitute, devoid of beauty, impotent, aged, diseased, lacking passion, lacking desire, lacking vigor, or in a state of distress. (75–76)
Knowing her husband to be equal to Kṛṣṇa, she should not overstep his authority even if she were capable of doing so.
Just as one obtains ghee, salt, oil, and other provisions with ease even when they are depleted, so too should she speak; she must never cause him distress.
One should eat from an earthen vessel and should not allow her own leavings to be eaten by others.
She should always bathe in, drink from, and dwell within the sacred water of her husband’s feet.
To a woman, her own husband is superior to Śiva, Viṣṇu, and the five deities.
A virtuous woman should never perform vows or fasts in defiance of her husband;
nor should she ever give a harsh reply when spoken to. One who reviles her husband, becomes angry, or causes him distress is not a virtuous wife.
A bitch is born in a village, and a female jackal in a lonely forest. (8.1) Only after worshipping the feet of her husband should she partake of food by his grace;
she must never sit upon a seat higher than her husband's, nor go outside [without him]. (8.2)
She should never set foot in another's house,
nor should she ever utter words that are harsh or offensive.
In the presence of elders, she should not speak loudly, nor should she engage in jesting.
A virtuous woman should not call out her husband’s name in a loud voice in a place where people are present.
That woman of evil mind who does not find pleasure in her husband when he is upon her own bed is reborn as an owl, a female ruddy goose, or a dweller in trees.
A woman who strikes her husband becomes a tigress or a female cat;
she who casts amorous glances at another man will certainly become one-eyed.
She who eats sweets while separated from her husband becomes a sow or a flying fox.
She who addresses her husband as "thou" shall become mute and a servant-woman;
she who is envious of a co-wife shall have a perpetually diseased womb; and she who shows her face to another man shall become ugly and foul-faced. (87–88)
She might delight one with her charms, show her body to another, and touch yet another; such a woman becomes a lizard, a widow, or a prostitute.
Having exerted herself in her work, she sees him returning.
By means of water, seats, betel leaves, massaging the feet and so forth,
by fans, gifts of fruit, and pleasant speech,
she who thus pleases her husband enjoys eternal happiness. (1.439.90–91)
A father, mother, son, and brother are considered givers of very little and limited gifts;
but the beloved husband is always the giver of everything immeasurable.
He is regarded as the cherished god, the supreme teacher, the sacred ford, and the worthy recipient.
Dharma, merit, vows, and all forms of ascetic penance—all these reside in the husband; she should worship him.
(93) Without her husband, a wife is like a corpse and her [religious] efforts are in vain;
likewise, even if she is well-bathed, perfumed, and adorned with ornaments, she remains impure in his absence. (94)
The husband is the locus of all auspiciousness; without him, there is no auspiciousness.
Even a most wicked mother is auspicious for her son when she has a husband.
A woman who is a great devotee of the Lord, virtuous, and devoted to everyone, is auspicious to all.
A widow, one with shorn hair, one who has renounced worldly life, one clad in fire-like [red] garments, and Maṅgalā;
Vaiṣṇavī, a widow, and she whose husband is Kṛṣṇa—she is eternally Maṅgalā.
Whosoever has been made a beloved wife even by her paramour, she too is indeed Maṅgalā. (96–97)
Wearing a garment of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, she is eternally auspicious;
she is a devoted wife to Kṛṣṇa, supported by Kṛṣṇa, some indescribable auspicious woman.
A garland of tulasī is upon her neck, and a sectarian mark (puṇḍra) is on her forehead and hand.
She who possesses the *lakṣmī-bindu* is Maṅgalā, the beloved of Kṛṣṇa.
Maṅgalā is the giver of the guru’s mantra and the giver of knowledge.
Raṇḍā, Muṇḍā, Vyaṅgā, and Ṣaṇḍhā—she is always Vaiṣṇavī Maṅgalā. (1.439.100)
Seated upon the lap of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, beloved of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa,
and the consorts of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa— all these divine women are indeed auspicious.
During the giving away of a daughter, the Brahmins recite [the praises] of those sages who are devoted to their vows.

She should become the companion of her husband, whether he be living or even deceased. She who follows the corpse of her husband from the house to the cremation ground is virtuous; following him to the pyre, she earns the merit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice at every step.
Having dragged her husband from the hand of Yama, that virtuous woman would go to heaven;
seeing the virtuous woman, the followers of Yama flee, abandoning their master.
The sun, fire, the submarine fire, lightning, stars, planets, and so forth—
Before the splendor of a wife’s devotion to her husband, tens of millions of gods tremble.
(105) A virtuous woman possesses a lifespan in heaven equal to as many tens of millions of years as there are hairs on the body produced by the touch of her husband’s hand. (106)
She enjoys divine happiness with her husband and thereafter attains liberation;
blessed are her parents, blessed is her husband, and blessed is her family.
Three ancestors on each side—of the father’s lineage, the mother’s lineage, and the husband’s lineage—are likewise blessed.
By virtue of her devotion to her husband, she goes to heaven together with him.
(1.08) Indeed, the feet of a devoted wife sanctify the earth;
the sun, the moon, and the gandharvas truly fear to touch such a virtuous woman. (1.09)
Even the waters themselves long for union with the feet of a devoted wife;
yet there is no destruction here in this world for that sin which cannot be destroyed by the Gāyatrī mantra—
it is the devoted wife alone who brings about its destruction through her fidelity to her husband.
Is this cycle of existence not composed entirely of women who pride themselves on their beauty and charm?
Yet, a true *satī*, a devoted wife of the Vaiṣṇava tradition, is found only rarely.
A house is called a home only because of a devoted wife; by her, one is called a householder.
In the duties of the household, in the fruits of dharma, in happiness, in children,

in the worship of ancestors, guests, and gods— both in this world and the next— the home is rooted in the wife. Or rather, the home becomes sanctified by a wife who is devoted to her husband, just as it is by the Gaṅgā.
A family becomes sanctified by a woman who is devoted or by one who is faithful to her husband.
By serving her husband— who is her wedded lord—
she may attain heaven, liberation, and likewise the feet of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
She whose husband has gone to heaven while she is pregnant, yet remains devoted to him with piety,
shall become a *kṛṣṇa-pativratā* (one whose husband is Kṛṣṇa), empowered by the bull-like strength of widowhood. She should worship Kṛṣṇa constantly, feed Him, and cherish Hari.
A woman should serve Kṛṣṇa in every way, having made him her own husband.
Recalling Kṛṣṇa upon her own bed, the devoted wife may find sleep;
she should rub fragrant substances on Kṛṣṇa and offer them to Him.
Having remembered her husband as Śrī Hari, she should offer water with *kuśa* grass and sesame seeds.
She should meditate upon and worship her husband as the glorious Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
Whatever was dear to her husband, that she should always offer to Kṛṣṇa.
One should perform bathing, giving gifts, pilgrimage to sacred fords, listening to sacred narratives, and worship.
In the month of Vaiśākha, one should offer water-pots; in Kārtika, ghee lamps; and in Māgha, grains, sesame seeds, and other offerings, dedicating them to Lord Kṛṣṇa.
In the month of Vaiśākha, one should provide a water-stall; to Śiva,
one should offer a water-dripper, uśīra-root, a fan, an umbrella, fine garments,
sandalwood paste with camphor, betel-leaf, flowers, and excellent food.
A water vessel, the gift of flour, grapes, plantains, and other such excellent fruits—these should indeed be offered to Śrī Kṛṣṇa with the thought, "May my husband be pleased.
In the month of Kārttika, all kinds of grains, vegetables, and pulses should likewise be offered. (123–124)
One should offer clarified butter and the like, as well as blankets and other items, for the pleasure of Kṛṣṇa;
one should also give a bell, a bed, a vessel of clarified butter, wealth, and a milch cow. One should likewise offer the gift of a lamp for the complete satisfaction of the Lord, Kṛṣṇa.
Whether she be a maiden, a widow, or one who has lost her husband,
the duties toward Kṛṣṇa must indeed be observed in every way.
Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa is to be worshipped and served within the heart as the Sovereign.
Thus addressed by Dharmadeva, Vardhinī remained a lifelong celibate;
dwelling forever in Dharmāraṇya, she was devoted solely to the worship of Kṛṣṇa.
A virtuous woman, she was dedicated to her husband, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, as her beloved.
She constantly sent the Supreme Person, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, in his embodied form.
She, who served her father, attended upon Dharmadeva as he performed austerities.
Then Hari, Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, being pleased, arrived there.
Having transformed her into a divine body, he led her to his own abode;
likewise, having granted Dharmadeva the boon he desired, [he said:
"I shall also constantly protect my subjects through my ascetic power."
"Your penance must be ceased," he said; and Vṛṣa himself desisted from his asceticism and went to Satyājasthala. Nārāyaṇa, having taken Satī Vardhinī with him, departed for his own abode.
Thus has been narrated, O Lakṣmī, the account of Vardhinī’s devotion to her husband.
By reading or hearing this, a person shall attain heaven and liberation.

Thus ends the four hundred and thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of how Apsarā Vardhinī, who had arrived in Dharmāraṇya sent by Indra to disrupt Dharma’s asceticism, attained liberation through the realization of her own wifely devotion as awakened by Dharma and through her devotion to Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Chapter 441 →
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Now, O Lakṣmī! In the forest of Vṛṣa, there were chaste and highly virtuous women who protected the Brāhmaṇas and others, and who had been established as Mothers by Viṣṇu. (1)

Listen with respect as I describe those goddesses who were devotees of Nārāyaṇa, ever protectors of the world, and supremely devoted to their husbands; I shall tell the story of what occurred there among the Brahmins in former times, along with its narrative accounts. (2)
I shall also fully proclaim that auspicious account born of Dharma; listen!
(3) Long ago, in the abode of Goloka, the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa brought forth from himself a son, a brahmin devoted to his wife. (4)
By the command of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, that brāhmaṇa arrived here at Goloka accompanied by his own wife, who was devoted to her husband.
In Dharmāraṇya, he became the thousand-eyed, thousand-faced, and thousand-footed Indra.
Firm in his vow toward his wife, he manifested thousands of his own forms.
All these Brāhmaṇas were of virtuous conduct and auspicious vows; they were skilled in every duty and proficient in all the scriptures.
Renowned for their austerity and knowledge, devoted to the sacrifice to Brahman,
all those sages dwelt there— powerful ones who knew the three periods of time.
There were eighteen thousand sons of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
In ancient times, twenty-four lineages (gotras) indeed flourished here:
Bhāradvāja, Vatsa, Kauśika, and Kuśa;
as well as Śāṇḍilya, Kaśyapa, Gautama, and Śāṇdhana.
Jātūkarṇya, Vātsya, Vasiṣṭha, Dhāraṇa, Ātreya, Bhāṇḍila, Kṛṣṇāyana the worldly,
Upamanyu, Gārgya, Mauṣaka, and likewise Mudgala.
Gāṅgāsana, Kauṇḍinya, Puṇyāsana, and Parāśara—these twenty-four [sages] flourished in ancient times. Also Āṅgīrasa, Śaunaka, Kāśyapa, and Jāmadagnyaka. (12–13)

From him were born the Laugākṣas and the Māṇḍavyas as members of the same lineage; now hear from me their respective *pravara* lineages. Those belonging to the Bhāradvāja *gotra* are endowed with five *pravara*s.

Āṅgīrasa, Bārhaspatya, Bhāradvāja, Sainya, and Gārgya—these are the five pravaras of those Vaiṣṇava twice-born ones. O Lakṣmī! As for the twice-born in the Vatsa lineage, their five pravaras are as follows: [15–16]
Bhārgava, Cyavana, Āpnuvāna, Aurva, and Jamadagni;
those born in the Kauśika lineage are endowed with three *pravara*s:
Viśvāmitra, Aghamarṣaṇa, and Kauśika—these are the three.
Those born in the Kuśika lineage are endowed with three *pravara*s:
Viśvāmitra, Devarāta, and Audala—these are the three. Those born in the Śāṇḍilya lineage are joined with three *pravara*s. (18–19)
Asita, Devala, and Śāṇḍilya—
these three, O Lakṣmī, are Brāhmaṇas of the Kaśyapa lineage, endowed with three *pravara*s.
Kāśyapa, Apavatsāra, and Naidhruva— these three [are likewise].
Those who belong to the Gautama lineage have exactly five *pravara* ancestors:
Kautsa, Gārgya, Pravāhaṇa, Asita, and Devala.
However, O Sati, for Śāṇḍilya there was no independent *pravara*.
Likewise, for Jātūkarṇya as well, there is no independent *pravara*.
O Brahmins born in the Vātsya lineage, you are endowed with five *pravaras*:
Bhārgava, Cyavana, Āpnuvāna, Aurva, and Jamadagni.
Now, those born of the Vasiṣṭha lineage are endowed with three *pravara*s:
Vasiṣṭha, Bhāradvāja, and Indrapramada; these are they.
Furthermore, in the Dhārīṇasa lineage, there are likewise three *pravara*s.
Agasti, Darvi, Śveta, Dadhyavāhana—
these are the ones born in the Ātreya gotra who are endowed with five pravaras:
Ātreya, Arcanānasa, Śyāvāśva, Āṅgirasa, and Atri.
At that time, Bhāṇḍīla had no independent *pravara*;
likewise, Kṛṣṇāyana also had no independent *pravara*, and similarly, Laukika also had no independent *pravara*. (27–28)
Those belonging to the Upamanyu lineage are endowed with three *pravara*s:
Vasiṣṭha, Bharadvāja, and Indrapramada. As for those born of the Gārgya lineage, however, there are exactly three *pravara*s.
Aṅgiras, Ambarīṣa, and Yauvanāśva as the third— these were the lineages.
At that time, however, there was no independent *pravara* for Mauṣaka,
nor indeed was there an independent *pravara* for Mudgala.
In the lineage of Gāṅgāsana, there are indeed five pravaras:
Bhārgava, Āvanāpnuvāna, Aurva, Jāmadagnyaka, and Ātreya; Arcanānasa and Śyāvāsya—these three as well.
In the Gāṅga lineage, these three are sometimes found as the *pravara*s:
Kauṇḍinya, Puṇyāsana, and Parāśara.
O Lakṣmī! In former times, these *pravara*s were not independent within their respective lineages. (33–34)
Now I shall tell you of another five [gotras] belonging to Jamadagni:
Bhārgava, Cyavana, Āpnuvāna, Aurva, and Jamadagnika.
These are the five pravaras for those who share the same gotra as Māṇḍavya, as follows.
Bhārgava, Cyāvana, Āpnuvāna, Aurva, and Jamadagni— these indeed are the Bhārgavas of the Vātsyāyana gotra, endowed with five pravaras:
Bhārgava, Cyāvana, Āpnuvāna, Aurva, and Jamadagni.
Others belonging to the Kaśyapa gotra are endowed with three pravaras:
the renowned three—Kāśyapa, Āpavatsāra, and Raibhya. Those born among the Śaunakas are also endowed with three pravaras.
Bhārgava, Śaunahotra, and Gārtsyamada—these three were born in the Āṅgirasagotra, endowed with a triad of *pravara*s:
Āṅgirasa, Ambarīṣa, and Yauvanāśva. (1.440.40)
Now, in the Patnīvratagotra, there are Devānīka, Dasāyaka, and Santaka as their *pravara* ancestors; they were devoted to great acts of charity.
Their branches and sub-branches consist of twice-born men, including sons, grandsons, and others.
Many were born in the world who took up new branches. Indeed, there were three eminent ancestors belonging to the lineage of Dharmasāvarṇi:
Vaitahavya, Sāvetasa, and Bhāradvāja—these indeed they were.
Having sent these Brahmins forth, they will follow new and excellent paths;
when time has passed, everything will be a mere mockery of the times.
Listen, Lakṣmī! These twice-born ones [will dwell] in Dharmāraṇya and on other lands.
Then indeed, yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, and others caused great agitation.
There was a yakṣa named Jṛmbhaka near Dharmāraṇya; he constantly terrified those dwelling in Dharmāraṇya. (45–46)
That suffering was reported by those foremost of the twice-born to the gods.
Having placed their vow of devotion to their wives at the forefront, the gods went to the assembly of Brahmā.
Brahmā, however, went to Goloka and spoke to Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Then Śrī Kṛṣṇa sent hundreds of thousands of gopīs there.
They were divine wives of Kṛṣṇa, acting according to his command and dear to him; they were immersed in the dharma of devotion to Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa as their sole husband.
Truthful, serene, and possessing divine limbs, those daughters of the Vedic seers arrived at the house;
and by the command of Brahmā, all those maidens ascended to heaven. There, in an instant, they became the daughters of Viśvāvasu and Mānas.
The daughters were all beautiful in every limb, young women who remembered their past lives;
devoted to the dharma of celibacy, these maidens became the wives of Kṛṣṇa for the sake of protecting the Brahmins and out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds. (51–52)
The Yoginīs were established by the gods and Gandharvas upon the grounds of Dharma;
likewise, each individual Yoginī was established according to her respective lineage (gotra).
Whichever Śakti of a particular lineage is capable of protection and preservation [is assigned to it].
She appeared there visibly as his family deity (kuladevī).
O Lakṣmī, listen now to those twelve Śrīmātās, all of whom are twelve years of age:
Śrīmātā, Tāraṇī, Āśāpurī, and Icchārtināśinī.
Pippalī, Vikarāvaśā, and Jaganmātā as the seventh;
Mahāmātā, Siddhā, Bhaṭṭārikā, and Kadambikā; Vikarā, Miṣṭā, Suparṇā, Mātaṅgī, and likewise Vasujā.
Mahādevī, Tathāvāṇī, Bhadrī, and Mukureśvarī; Saṃhārī, Mahāśakti, and again Mahābalā;
and the great goddess Cāmuṇḍā—these are the Mothers of the Lineage (gotramātaraḥ). ||57–58||
Established by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and others for the protection of the Brahmins,
those Vaiṣṇavī goddesses, the chaste wives of the Lord, are worshipped by the best of Brahmins.
Then, at sacrifices, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, [sought] the products of the cow.
He remembered Kāmadhenu, and Kāmadhenu arrived. Brahmā spoke to her regarding the cows for each of the twice-born: "O Mother, be gracious to me; grant me one Kāmadhenu for every single brahmin."
Having said "So be it," Kāmadhenu manifested young female calves;
a hundred thousand white Nandinyas appeared, in the full bloom of youth,
auspicious, yielding milk, granting cows, and providing offspring by mere thought.
Auspicious sacrifices proceeded, and the gods were satisfied with excellent milk-offerings.
Then, ten thousand merchants of the Brāhmaṇa caste, who were servants of the twice-born Brāhmaṇas,
were produced there by the Brāhmaṇas from their minds.
Wearing sacred threads and topknots, proficient in all principles,
devoted to the twice-born, of virtuous conduct, young, and endowed with austerity—
two attendants were indeed assigned to each individual twice-born man.
Whatever be the lineage of Vāḍava, that shall be the lineage of his follower as well.
Indeed, for their benefit, Brahmā instructed them in discipleship.
"Follow their word and grant whatever they desire."
"Bring fuel, flowers, *kuśa* grass, and so forth day after day; abide by their permission and never show them disrespect.
Living in this manner, they were devoted solely to the life of celibate studentship (*brahmacarya*).
All the Vaiṣṇavas, distinguished by their observance of vows, serve the Brāhmaṇas.
For the sake of their support, the Creator has provided them with beautiful Gandharva maidens as wives, along with bulls.
Those daughters of Viśvāvasu, the wives of the Brahmins, were devoted to their husbands;
at that time, sixty thousand maidens became the forms of daughters-in-law.
Likewise, the other Brahmin women, who were their mothers, became the forms of mothers-in-law.
O beloved, there were forty thousand maidens;
then there were excellent goddesses, yoginīs, and protectors in the form of mothers.
In Dharmāraṇya, there were hundreds of thousands of women who were devoted wives to Kṛṣṇa.

Thus the householders became extensive with sons, grandsons, and so forth; all the women were devoted to their husbands, and the men were devoted to their wives. While the brahmins were thus living as householders in Araṇyaka, ||74||
The rakshasa Lolajihvaka caused a supreme calamity;
he was terrifying, with great tusks, a massive body, and a tongue like lightning.
But the goddesses, intent on protecting the brahmin, sought to destroy him.
Some held tridents and excellent weapons, others were endowed with conchs, discs, and maces; some were equipped with whips and swords, and likewise others with nooses and goads;
some held axes in their hands, and they all bore divine armaments.
They fought against the Rākṣasa there and remembered Nārāyaṇa.
Viṣṇu, having arrived, slew the Rākṣasa with his discus.
The Brahmins, moreover, lived together in a single city.
Formerly, that city of Dharmāraṇya was indeed the town of Satyamandira;
it was a most divine city where Brahmins resided, truly equal to heaven.
Furthermore, other Yoginīs were established there for the purpose of protecting the city.
In Madārikā is Śrīmātā, and likewise Śāntā in Nandāpura;
[there are] Sāvitrī and Jñānajā, as well as Gātrāyī and Pakṣiṇī;
Chatrajā, Cūṭikā, Dvāravāsinī, and Pippalā. (81–82)
Śīhorī, Śāpurī, Cetā, Raktavastrā, and Bhayaṃkarā; Ānandā, likewise Oṃkārā, and Dharmaputrikā—these, along with Śyāmalā, provide protection as they teach the Dharma. (83)
Then there was a Rākṣasa named Karṇāṭa who oppressed the Brahmins.
Yogamālinī drove him away to the south,
and after his name, that region became renowned as Karṇāṭaka.
By her, however, these cruel ones were produced while she was still a celibate student (brahmacāriṇī):
Śākinī, Ḍākinī, Kākinī, Hākinī, Ekinī, and Lākinī;
these are the powers (śaktayaḥ) who destroy the Daityas.
These women, devoted to their husbands, were settled by Dharmadeva for the sake of guarding the forest of Dharma. All of them are servants of the beloved of Rudra;
they are the constant protectors of the Brahmins and the guardians of the lineage of virtuous wives.
By her were produced Lakṣmī, other devoted wives,
the great goddesses observing the vow of Rudra, and those who have taken refuge in Dharmāraṇya.
These maidens are celibate and are the family deities.
By these [goddesses], the lineages of Brahmins on the surface of the earth are protected at all times:
Bhaṭṭārikī, Chatrā, Auvikā, Jñānajā, Bhadrakālī, Māheśī, Siṃhorī, and Dhanamardinī.
Gātrā, Śāntā, Śeṣadevī, Vārāhī, Bhadrayoginī, Yogeśvarī, Mohalajjā, Kuleśī,
Śakulācitā, Tāraṇī, Kanakānandā, Cāmuṇḍā, and Sureśvarī. ||92||
Each of these, beginning with Dārabhaṭṭārikā and the others, further multiplied a hundredfold;
all these Śaktis arose, having their abodes in Dharmāraṇya and other such places.
Then the Father of Dharma performed a great sacrifice in Dharmāraṇya.
There, the gods, the ancestors, the seers, the sages, and men—
the fourteen lords of the worlds beginning with Manu— arrived. There, he appointed you, the descendant of Aṅgiras, as the preceptor, along with Mārkaṇḍeya.
He appointed Atri and Kaśyapa as the Hotṛ priests;
he appointed Jamadagni and Gautama as the Adhvaryu priests;
and he appointed Bharadvāja and Vasiṣṭha as the Pratiprasthātṛ (Pratyadhvaryu) priests.
The King of Dharma (Yama) also envisioned Nārada and Vālmīki as the instigators;
he then established Brahmā upon the Brahma-throne. Thereafter, having constructed a magnificent altar measuring four *krośas* in extent, together with the gods—
All the twice-born were summoned—both those who recite prayers and those who read the scriptures.
Gaṇeśa, Skanda, Indra, and Jayanta were appointed as gatekeepers.
Then, with a mantra that destroys demons, oblations were poured into the sacrificial fire.
Then, O Lotus-born One, those gods offered oblations with Vedic mantras,
using sesame seeds mixed with barley and well-blended with honey and clarified butter;
and after that, having performed the *āghāra* and *ājyabhāga* offerings.
Grapes, sugarcane, betel nut, orange, citron, and pomegranate;
to the north, coconut and pomegranate in due order;
honey, clarified butter, milk, rice-and-pulse porridge mixed with sugar. (10.2–10.3)
Having performed a sacrifice with rice and lotuses accompanied by ritual fees,
they then sang the supreme and auspicious Vaiṣṇava hymn.
They gave food without restriction even to the poor, the blind, and the wretched.
Milk-rice mixed with sugar, accompanied by ghee and vegetables;
(105) *maṇḍakas*, *vaṭakas*, cakes, as well as auspicious *veṣṭikās*; a thousand *modakas*, and also *pheṇikās*, *ghurghuras*, and so forth. (106)
Rice, as well as dal made from *āḍhakī* and other grains into a liquid;
likewise, green gram dal, *parpaṭa*, and *vaṭikā*;
along with long pepper, cloves, black pepper, and *lohyaka* fruits.
There were also kulmāṣa beans, vellaka roots, and tender, auspicious vālaka shoots;
karkariṭas and fresh ginger combined with black pepper; various excellent vegetables, and likewise diverse kinds of cooked dishes. 108–109.
Having fed thousands of twice-born brahmins with milk-rice, sugarcane preparations, wheat-based foods, sweetmeats, and chickpeas,
as well as eighteen lakhs and tens of millions of other people, the bull [of dharma]... || 1.440.110 ||
Having performed the avabhṛtha bath, he obtained the fruit of the sacrifice.
Having completed the sacrifice, all those embodied beings returned to their respective abodes.
By hearing or reciting this, one shall obtain the fruit of a sacrifice to Viṣṇu.

Thus ends the four hundred and fortieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Circle of Family Deities of the Chaste Maidens of Śrī Kṛṣṇa who became Gandharvas in Dharmāraṇya, as well as the Gotras and Pravaras of the Brahmins and others, the Destruction of the Rākṣasa Lolajihva by the Goddess, the Establishment of the Yoginīs, and the Sacrifice performed by Dharmadeva," in the first section on the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 441 *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā* — Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga) — Chapter 441.
[The Author: Chapter 442.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, Lakṣmī! Just as women perform the worship of Kṛṣṇa...
I shall proclaim that Dharma by which liberation may also be attained.
(1) A wife who is wedded according to Dharma should be free from the ten defects;
she should not be impotent, nor should she be physically deformed, and she should be praised as being untainted by major diseases and other such ailments. (2)

Blameless, possessing auspicious qualities, free from eye diseases, devoid of deafness, not fickle, and sweet-spoken— such a maiden, free from the ten defects, [should be given] by men according to the prescribed rule. (3)
Once married, that wife is known as a virtuous householder.
She stands foremost in all meritorious deeds;
when dharma is well-performed by her, it becomes fruitful in its entirety.
O Kṛṣṇa, women should always perform the five sacrifices (pañcayajña) while constantly remembering You:
bathing, libations (tarpaṇa), fire-offerings (agnihoma), worship of Acyuta, and the hospitable reception of guests;
one should never neglect these five sacrifices.
The ancestors and the deities become satisfied by the five great sacrifices (pañcayajña). Furthermore, through the joyful service rendered to her husband by a devoted wife,
the ancestors and the deities become satisfied in Hari, who is the very self of the husband.

Indeed, all the gods dwell within the body of a devoted wife; therefore, through her union with her husband, there is the arrival of Dharma. When the minds of both are in harmony, the ancestors and the deities are satisfied.

And the auspicious fruit, the accomplishment of all undertakings, is attained. A wife born of an equal caste should be married; her husband shall share half of her portion in all religious duties in every respect.
Because she possesses authority over half of his body, she is the bearer of half of his dharma;
likewise, her husband is the bearer of half of her dharma, whether in good or even in evil. O beloved, she who follows her deceased husband through excellent austerity—
She should be known as a virtuous and great chaste woman by whom the family is uplifted.
Whether she has been married or is already a widow, she who remains steadfast when her husband dies uplifts that husband by means of the path of Vaiśvānara (the funeral fire).
Just as a savior rescues one who is drowning from the water,
so does the virtuous wife who follows her husband rescue him.
That maiden who, having exerted herself, is given by her father to a bridegroom—
A woman wedded according to the marriage rites, who fulfills the purposes of the ancestors and the gods—
she who has obtained a husband by resorting to any one of the ten types of marriage proclaimed— redeems her family. (16–17)
Even she who has been remarried is a virtuous woman (*satī*) if she is a benefactor to her family;
however, if she is purchased for a price, she is a slave—even if she has been married. A woman declared to be a *satī* is one who possesses righteousness (*dharmavatī*), and she uplifts her lineage.
Even if she is born of a lowly family and is poor, if she is a virtuous woman wedded according to dharma,
she purifies her entire lineage through the power of her devotion to her husband.
Furthermore, the Prājāpatya, Brāhma, Daiva, and Ārṣa forms of marriage are the most excellent among the righteous.
The Gāndharva, the Āsura, the Rākṣasa, the Piśācaka, the Prātibha, and the Ghātaka— these are said to be the ten forms of marriage.
Furthermore, there are the Aurasa, the Kṣetraja, the Datta, and the Kṛtrima.
The son born in secret, the abandoned son, the son of an unmarried girl,
the son received with a bride, the bought son, and the son of a remarried woman— these are considered the ten kinds of sons.
Thus [are described] the son, the one who receives a son, the wife, the husband, the father, and the head of the household.
By devotion to their husbands, virtuous women cross over [the ocean of worldly existence] through service to Kṛṣṇa;
truthful women devoted to their husbands sport in heaven like gods.
O Lakṣmī, for all women, devotion to Kṛṣṇa is always auspicious.

Service to the true guru is always declared to be the worship of the guru for the sake of purification. Service to the husband is always declared to be the worship of the husband for the sake of heaven.
But for women, the offering of everything to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa is for the sake of liberation.
Thus, in former times, by relying upon this dharma, the Śūdra Paijavana went to the world of Kṛṣṇa together with his virtuous wife.
He was devoted to righteousness and a worshiper of Viṣṇu and the brāhmaṇas.
Content with wealth acquired through righteous means, accompanied by his wife, he was a servant of the virtuous.
He was a speaker of truth and a devotee of Viṣṇu; and his wife was Sundarī, a noble woman born of an equal lineage, wedded according to the prescribed dharma. (28–29)
Devoted to her husband, highly fortunate, and intent on the welfare of the gods and the twice-born,
she was a maiden betrothed in Kāśī and married in Vaijayantī.
She was skilled in the practice of dharma and observed the vows of the Vaiṣṇavas.
Knowing her husband to be Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, she serves him.
Through the merits of her virtuous deeds, the attainment of wealth always increases in the home of this chaste wife of the Lord,
by means of successful trade and business.
In this manner, many sons were born to that seer of Dharma;
and indeed, O Vaiṣṇavas, two sons and daughters were also born, who were devotees of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa and dedicated to the service of their father. (33)
They were devoted to the service of their parents, and their wives were ever faithful to their husbands. All of them performed worship and service, honoring those worthy of honor;
and having remembered Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, they likewise honored their guests.
Their residence shall be endowed with supernatural power and filled with wealth and grain;
never shall one who has entered their home ever depart disappointed.
In the cold season they bestow wealth, and in the hot season they give water and food.

During the rainy season they were givers of clothing, and they were always givers of food. Established in the vow of devotion to Kṛṣṇa, they caused step-wells, wells, tanks, water-stations, and temples to be constructed at the appropriate times. (37–38)
In their home, there was no distinction of seating rows, for they were satisfied with equal shares.
While they were living in this manner, the sage Śrī Gālava arrived at their house,
surrounded by many devoted disciples.
Accompanied by his beautiful wife, the son of Pijavana, together with his sons and others,
offered him a welcome with rising from his seat, a gift of a seat, and other honors.
Overcome with great joy, he there drank the water from [the sage’s] feet.
Honoring his own family as having achieved their purpose, he said to them:
"Today my birth has become fruitful; today my life has become most excellent.
Today my dharma has been made successful, and my entire lineage has been uplifted by you. (42)
O Sage, my thousands of sins have been burnt away by your very sight!
Hari, Nārāyaṇa, Kṛṣṇa, and Gālava have come to my home;
my house, though belonging to a householder, has been purified by you, O Kṛṣṇa.
Having heard this, Gālava, his fatigue from the journey dispelled by great devotion and being well-pleased, asked the Śūdra many questions regarding his welfare:
"O gentle one, is all well with you? Does your mind incline toward dharma?"
I hope that your wives and children have surrendered all their possessions for the sake of Kṛṣṇa.
I hope your devotion to Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa is preceded by generosity.
And I hope your mind is indeed full of affection for virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation.
Is she indeed constantly bearing upon her head the water from Viṣṇu’s feet? Is she entirely devoted to the service of Kṛṣṇa, her beloved?
Truly, everything is maintained by Satī; likewise, everything is protected by Satī.
Truth crosses over suffering; truth is the means for attaining happiness and other goals.
Thus addressed, the son of Paijavana replied: "Your compassion toward me is such that everything remains as it was; this distinction is your favor. (1.441.50)
"Considering me your servant, instruct me; and you, O virtuous woman, instruct this female servant.
And you, my sons, instruct these servants regarding the cause for which we have come.
Gālava spoke to them: "He whose devotion is always fixed upon Acyuta..."
He whose wife is virtuous, saintly, and devoted to her husband as to Kṛṣṇa;
he whose sons are servants of Hari, and whose daughters are chaste servants of Hari;
and whose family members, kinsmen, and others are purifying Vaiṣṇavas—[he is truly blessed]. || 52-53 ||
At the holy confluence of these rivers, liberation is nowhere difficult to attain. Indeed,
that Vaiṣṇava family is auspiciously like a body of Brahman itself,
by the mere sight of which even a sinner becomes purified.
Through union with the attribute-less Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa,
everything of yours has attained a state of attribute-lessness through the practice of devotion and the duty of service.
Even for virtuous women, there is the practice of devotion and the duty of service.
The dharma of love for Hari arose in the cowherd women and in Śabarī;
the dharma of love in Piṅgalā became purifying and bestowing liberation.
The dharma of love for Śiva arose in the daughter of the White Mountain of Kṛṣṇa.
At the end of those thousand years, O beloved, she attained Maheśvara;
for her love for Pārvatī, Prabhā, Lalitā, Lakṣmī, Jayā,
and Māṇikyā had reached its highest peak.
They obtained Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa as their husband; the marriage of Vṛndā and Tulasī was rooted in love. By worshipping Kṛṣṇa with Tulasī leaves, liberation is certainly attained.
Liberation through Hari is considered to have its root in affection, as is the case with a husband for his faithful wife.
Even Vṛndā and others became saviors of the worlds on earth.
Listen, O sole devotee: in a former age, all the ancestors indeed [did so]. (61–62)
Then they went to Brahmā for refuge in order to satisfy their hunger;
for whatever auspicious water presided over by Varuṇa exists for the sake of satisfaction,
it must not be taken by us without libations (tarpaṇas), since it belongs to the ancestors (pitṛs).
Whatever is given by anyone is to be accepted, for it brings satisfaction.
Therefore, O elder brother, provide something for our own satisfaction.
Thus entreated, Brahmā then went for refuge to Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
He prayed for the sake of satisfying the ancestors and obtaining water.
Then, after reflecting for a moment, the Blessed Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Lord who is the soul of all, spoke: ||| 66 || "I am the Blessed Lord, the Self of all. ||| 67 ||
I am the one who brings satisfaction to all, and no other is like me.
Therefore, I must act in such a way that they may find fulfillment.
And where will all people find me, who possess this divine form? (67–68)
"Therefore, for the purpose of offering libations of water, I shall assume an auspicious form that brings welfare to all living beings in the world.
Having reflected thus, Kṛṣṇa himself became the form of the Aśvattha tree.
Janārdana, having assumed a physical form as Pippala with a divine body,
[performed] on the Revatādri mountain, at the site of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa-Dāmodara,
a Śrāddha ceremony previously performed by two [ancestors] there in the Nārāyaṇa lake.
Then, by means of the two Kṛṣṇas and through the power of mantra, he stood at the foot of the Plakṣa tree;
water from the sacred ford was offered, and consequently, his ancestors were satisfied.
Thus did the glorious Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa himself [act].
In a former age, he took his descent at Plakṣāvatāra on Mount Raivata.
(73) Furthermore, the Ṛṣis always perform the ritual water-offering to the Pippala tree;
the water offered to the Pippala is obtained by those who have gone to the three worlds. (74)
Then the gods, headed by Mahendra, as well as those headed by Śiva and the Vaiṣṇavas,
went there to the Nārāyaṇa lake to look for Kṛṣṇa.
Kṛṣṇa was searched for in the forest on the bank of the Svarṇarekhā river.
For although Hari was being sought there by some, the Blessed Lord, having assumed the form of a tree through his illusory power (māyā), was not recognized at all, not even slightly.
Thereupon the gods said to Bṛhaspati: "The Blessed Lord Hari [is here]. || 76–77 ||
"How indeed can he, who is united with the trees, be seen?
Then Bṛhaspati said: "If you wish to see him as a tree, Hari, appearing in the form of a tree, will become visible through the eyes of the trees. (78)
Thus addressed, all those gods assumed the form of trees near the Nārāyaṇa lake in order to behold Kṛṣṇa;
there, Śrī took the form of Tulasī, and Pārvatī was born from the sectarian mark on his forehead.
The great tree known as the *bilva* appeared there, and Pārvatī was born in the form of a *bilva*. At that time, Brahmā became a banyan tree (*vaṭa*).
Sāvitrī, known as the sesame bush (*tilagulma*), was born together with the sesame seeds.
Mahendra became a barley tree, and the lords of subjects became mango trees.
The Gandharvas became Malaya trees, and Aguru became the lord of the Gaṇas.
The oceans became reed trees, and the Yakṣas became Punnāga trees.

Then the Nāgas were the *nāga* trees, the Siddhas the *kaṅkolaka* trees, the Guhyakas the *panasa* (jackfruit) trees, and the Kinnaras the *marica* (black pepper) trees. Kandarpa was the liquorice tree (*yaṣṭimadhu*), and Vahni was the *raktāñjana* tree. (84)
Yama is the *bibhītaka* tree, Nirṛti the *bakula* tree;
(85) Varuṇa is the date palm (*kharjūrī*), while Māruta is the betel-nut tree (*pūga*).
Dhanada is the walnut tree (*akṣoṭaka*), and the Rudras are the jujube trees (*badarī*). (86)
The Seven Sages became great *tāla* trees; the other gods became *elā* trees.
Then the clouds became *jambū* trees, and the lightning flashes became *aśoka* trees.
The Vasus became *priyāla* trees, while the Ādityas became *japā* trees.
At that time, the two Aśvinī-kumāras became Madana trees;
the Viśvedevas became Madhuka trees, and the Rākṣasas became Guggulu trees.
The Sun became the Arka tree, and the Moon became the Palāśa tree. (88–89)
Maṅgala was born as the Khadira tree, and Budha became the Apāmārga; Bṛhaspati was then the Aśvattha, and Śukra became the Udumbara. Śanaiścara was the Śamī tree, and Rāhu became the Durvā grass.
The banner became the *darbha* grass, and likewise that tree of fruit became the *phaladruma*.
Those wives of the gods then became creepers.
Viṣṇu took the form of a *śāla* tree, and his vehicle was the *apāmārga*.
Śrīvatsa became the Kalpavṛkṣa tree; Kārtika became the Campaka; Nārada became the Pārijāta; and Gaurī then became Vṛndā.
Lakṣmī was born as Mālatī, and Sarasvatī became Dhātrī.
Then, in another place in the forest,
the Lord Viṣṇu himself, assuming many forms, was born there in the form of a *aśvattha* tree, possessing a beautiful appearance.
Rudra became a *vaṭa* tree, and Brahmā assumed the form of a *palāśa* tree.
At that time, Nandin was white in appearance, while Śambhu assumed the form of a *bilva* tree;
Indra became a *śirīṣa* tree, and the Sun-god became a *nimba* tree.
Śiva and Śivā were *bilva* trees, and Śivā took the form of the goddess Vṛndā.
Brahmā and Rudra became the *vaṭa* and *palāśa* trees; Brahmā took the form of the *palāśa*.
The Moon became a *palāśa*, while Nimbārka were both in the form of the Sun.
Viṣṇu and Bṛhaspati likewise became two types of *aśvattha* trees. || 97–98 ||
At that time, those two were considered to belong to sub-species of their respective trees.
These trees, having the form of black wood, gazed at him with eyes made of wood.
The Aśvattha tree, endowed with large leaves, was seen in the Nārāyaṇa lake.
In that very form, Kṛṣṇa,
the abode of mercy, remained there for the purpose of taking water so that the ancestors might obtain satisfaction.
At its base, [the rite was performed] by the brāhmaṇas and by the two Nārāyaṇas.
The water of the celestial river offered by the divine Lord who is devoted to His consorts—all that becomes offered to the ancestors when dedicated to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa;
it reaches them and becomes a source of satisfaction. Therefore, one should worship the Pippala tree. (102)
And by their power, those trees shall remain as givers of food and liberation;
as long as the *pippala* tree of Kṛṣṇa endures until the dissolution of the earth,
all these divine trees, when well-honored, shall be givers of liberation to everyone.
"Indeed, they grant liberation to women as well as those of other castes through their service.
Having spoken thus, Kṛṣṇa took water, offered it to the ancestors, and departed for his own realm, Gosthala, in his original form.
The gods, devoted to the worship of Kṛṣṇa, each went to their own world.
(106) This account was heard by Sundarī, the wife of Paijavana, from the mouth of Gālava; she then repeatedly resolved to be a faithful wife to her husband. (107)
"Just as this Gālava describes the deities—
if those gods and others, who are of the nature of trees, were indeed real in form—
then may I have a vision of them according to their respective true natures."
"O Lakṣmī! When she made this resolve, 'If I am devoted to my husband and dedicated to the duty of a faithful wife,' all the gods arrived;
they appeared in the form of trees and creepers, and she saw them as being of that very nature."
Furthermore, Sundarī made a resolve there: "May I be a devoted wife;
at that time, may meals for the disciples of Gālava come forth.
Immediately, O beloved, mountains of most delicious food appeared there.
O beloved, having eaten, Gālava departed for his own hermitage along with his disciples;
and the deities, honored and restored to their own forms, returned to their respective abodes.
From that time forward, virtuous noble women have repeatedly worshipped trees.
In sacrifice, those divine trees, which are of the nature of purifiers, bestow great merit;
they grant heaven, liberation, and prosperity when offered as oblations.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, the worship of trees and other such items by women has been described to you.
Through both reading and hearing [this], one obtains heaven, liberation, and great merit.

(115) Thus ends the four hundred and forty-first chapter, titled "The Description of Various Trees such as Tulasī as Incarnations of Deities and Others, and Liberation through Their Worship," within the section on the Straightforward Means for Granting Liberation to Women shown by Gālava, in the first part, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
*Note:*

1.441.93. In the *Sītopaniṣad* (Chapter 35), it is stated that Śrīvatsa became the *kalpavṛkṣa*. There are three forms of the power of will (*icchā-śakti*): the power of yoga (*yoga-śakti*) is Śrīvatsa; the power of enjoyment (*bhoga-śakti*) is the *kalpavṛkṣa* and so forth; and likewise, the power of heroism (*vīra-śakti*) is Goddess Lakṣmī, four-armed, who stands at the root of the *kalpavṛkṣa*.
— Chapter 441, *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Part 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga).
Chapter 442 [Author:
Chapter 443 → Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī! To the vow of the husband Kṛṣṇa, which bestows liberation, which is purifying, devoted to Kṛṣṇa, a great sacrifice, and the supreme Vaiṣṇava rite.
Indeed, there was a son of Brahmā named Svāyambhuva Manu.
Uttānapāda was his son, and his son was named Dhruva. Dhruva’s son was Utkala, who was devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa;
he performed a thousand Rājasūya sacrifices at Puṣkara.
