Brahmā himself gave him the name Suyajña.
He was a giver of food and a giver of jewels and all forms of prosperity.
He also gave ten lakhs of cows adorned with jeweled horns.
Filled with joy, he constantly gave away cows possessing the twelve auspicious marks. And every day, he fed sixty million Brahmins,
satisfying them day after day with foods to be sucked, chewed, licked, and drunk.
Thereafter, he fed thirty-six million billion cooks; on that day, at the conclusion of Suyajña’s sacrifice,
O beautiful one, the brahmins partook of excellent food and were completely satiated.
Being unable to carry the jewels they had taken back to their own homes,
they gave them away to various people many times along the way and even abandoned them;
furthermore, they provided meals for all those brahmins.
Nevertheless, a thousand heaps of men remained there.
Having thus performed that auspicious sacrifice,
Suyajña sat upon a beautiful throne fashioned with great jewels in the assembly of kings.
Adorned with fine silk cloths and perfumed with excellent sandalwood and other fragrances;
beautified by auspicious trees bearing full water-pots upon their branches; and consecrated with sandalwood, agallochum, musk, camphor, and vermilion. (11–12)
In this interval, while [the assembly] was attended by Vasu, Vāsava, Candra, Indra, Rudra, and the Ādityas,
and joined by the sages Nārada, Manu, and others, as well as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara,
a certain Brahmin arrived there.
Rough and clad in soiled garments, he offered auspicious blessings to the king.
Although the king bowed to him, he did not rise from his excellent throne; nor did the members of the assembly rise, but rather laughed at him slightly. (14–15)
Enraged by that, the twice-born man there cursed the king:
"May you now be deprived of your kingdom, afflicted with oozing leprosy, and devoid of intellect! At that, the members of the assembly bowed down, and the Brahmin rose up.
Then the king also, having fallen at his feet, abandoned his anger.
There, the sages Pulaha, Pulastya, Pracetas, Bhṛgu, and Aṅgiras gave that excellent brahmin a splendid seat.
Marīci, Kaśyapa, Vasiṣṭha, and Kratu; Śukra, Bṛhaspati, Durvāsas, and likewise Lomaśa;
Gautama, Kaṇāda, Kaṇva, Kātyāyana, and Kaṭha.
Pāṇini, Jājali, Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, Vibhāṇḍaka,
Taittiri, Āpiśali, Mārkaṇḍeya of great asceticism, Sanaka, Sananda, Voḍhu, Paila, and Sanātana.
Sanatkumāra, Nara, Nārāyaṇa, Parāśara, Jaratkāru who was devoted to his wife, Saṃvarta, Karabha,
Bharadvāja, Vālmīki, Aurva, and Cyavana.
Agastya, Atri, Utathya, Saṃkarta, Āstīka, Āsuri, Śilālin, Lāṅgalin, Śākalya, Śākaṭāyana,
Garga, Vatsa, Pañcaśikha, Jamadagni, and Devala.
Jaigīṣavya, Vāmadeva, and the Vālakhilyas by the hundreds of thousands;
Śakti, Dakṣa, Kardama, Praskanna, and likewise Kapila;
Viśvāmitra, Kautsa, Ṛcīka, and Aghamarṣaṇa.
Svayamprakāśa, Brahmiṣṭha, Śatānanda, and Suvrata—
these and other sages, as well as the ancestors who delight in the oblations of fire,
and all the guardians of the quarters and deities, spoke in turn to the brāhmaṇa. (26–27)
"O best of Brahmins, by your curse may the king's fortune come to an end;
for the heart of a Brahmin is always tender due to his asceticism.
Forgive me, grant me your blessing, and make his house pure."
If a guest turns away from someone’s house with his hopes frustrated,
his ancestors, the gods, and the sacred fire depart dissatisfied.
Those who look upon a guest who has arrived at their home with a crooked glance [are likewise punished].
Having given his own sin to him, he departs taking that man's merit.
O King, do not fail to rise for him due to the fault of your pride; grant him forgiveness. (3.1) He who, out of royal splendor or learning, treats a Brahmin with contempt—

One who is deprived of the ritual food offering (*naivedya*) for the vow shall immediately lose his prosperity. His initiation (*dīkṣā*) becomes futile, and he suffers the loss of wealth, sons, and other blessings;
he may even become bereft of a wife. Forgive this man’s transgression. (32–33)
He who shows contempt for a guest, for his parents, for a god, for a learned man, for a Brāhmaṇa, or for a guru, will certainly fall away from devotion in this world.
He who, upon seeing a Brāhmaṇa guest, does not rise to greet him—
One enters the womb of an elephant for seven births in the forest.
Therefore, quickly showing compassion, bestow auspicious blessings upon the king—
whether upon a preceptor, a Brahmin, or even an image of a deity.
Having seen him, one should not fail to bow quickly; such a person shall become like a common animal on earth.
"Forgive us all and accept our hospitality.
[This applies even to] those who have killed a woman, a cow, or a benefactor, as well as those who have violated the bed of their teacher.
"One who insults a guest shall share in the sin of those who slay Brahmins.
Having heard these words of the sages, the king questioned them:
"O best of yogis, tell me, what is the sin of those who kill women and the like?"

Vasiṣṭha said: "O Indra among kings, listen; for that [penance] arises from the killing of a cow. O King, in the case of intentional cow-slaughter, a man should wander to sacred pilgrimage sites for a year, subsisting on barley and barley-gruel, and drinking water from his hand."
Then, having given a hundred divine cows along with sacrificial fees to the Brahmins,
and having fed a hundred twice-born men, one is indeed released from sin. However,
even when the penance has been performed, one is not released from all sins.
Due to the remnants of his evil deeds, he becomes miserable and is indeed a *caṇḍāla*.
The sin incurred by killing a woman is certainly twice that of killing a cow.
He shall dwell in the *Kālasūtra* hell for sixty thousand years.
Then, for seven births, he shall become a pig and a serpent.
The sin of one who commits the murder of a Brahmin is twice that of the murder of a woman;
indeed, he shall dwell for a hundred thousand years in the most terrible Kubhīpāka hell.
O Indra among kings, the ungrateful person becomes a worm in excrement for a hundred years and a serpent for seven lifetimes.
The fault of ingratitude is four times that of killing a Brahmin;
O Indra among kings, no atonement has been ordained for those who are ungrateful.

O King of kings, there are sixteen kinds of ungrateful people, as is certain: those who fail in what has been done for them, in truth, in merit, in their own duty, in austerity, in their promise, in giving, and in protecting their own assembly. (47–48)
In matters concerning the guru, matters concerning the gods, rites for desired goals, worship of the twice-born,
daily obligatory duties, trust, and the bestowal of supreme dharma— he who destroys these,
that most sinful man is known as ungrateful (*kṛtaghna*).
For various kinds of ungrateful people, there are likewise various hells. Having made a truth in the form of an oath, he who kills it and does not uphold it—
that ungrateful person dwells indeed in the Kālasūtra hell for the duration of four yugas.
For seven births he was a crow, and for seven births a peacock;
thereafter he was a Śūdra afflicted by a great disease, and after that, for seven births, he became pure.
Having performed meritorious deeds, he speaks only for the sake of increasing his fame.
That ungrateful person dwells indeed in a cauldron of boiling oil for three *yugas*.
For five births he is a frog, for three births a crab;
thereafter he is mute and severely afflicted with disease, and then he becomes poor, and after that, pure.
He who, having performed his own duty, destroys it by obstructing the practice of the *saṃdhyā*;
he who reviles the worship of Viṣṇu, the recitation of mantras, the offering of food (*naivedya*), and religious observances;
and he who is devoid of vows dedicated to the gods and neglects the ancestral rites (*pitṛkṛtya*) and other such duties.
That ungrateful person dwells in the Kumbhīpāka hell for the duration of an entire kalpa.
For seven births he becomes a Cāṇḍāla, and for a hundred births he is a vulture;
for a hundred births he is a pig, and thereafter he becomes a Cāṇḍāla.
Furthermore, having gone to the Raurava hell, he becomes a donkey for five births;
then, after five more births as a cat and a frog,
he becomes a Brahmin who carries oxen and experiences great sufferings.

Whether by means of a servant or even personally, that Brahmin who acts as a bullock-driver should be known as ungrateful; for he is considered a destroyer of merit. The sin in constantly beating a bull is equal to the murder of a Brahmin. (1.442.60)
If one causes a bull to carry loads on its back, that sin becomes twofold.
He who drives a hungry and thirsty bull in the heat of the sun incurs the sin of killing a hundred Brahmins; of this there is no doubt.
He shall dwell in a pit of saliva as long as the moon and sun endure.
There, his food shall always be excrement and his drink urine.
At the three junctions of the day, the servant of Yama shall strike him with a trident.
He who places a firebrand in his mouth and constantly cuts with a needle [the flesh of others] is born as a worm in excrement for sixty thousand years.
Thereafter, he becomes a crow for five births, and likewise a crane.
For five births he was a vulture and for seven births a jackal;
thereafter he was a poor Śūdra and then one afflicted by great disease.
He who violates the dharma of a faithful and noble woman is proclaimed to be an ungrateful person (kṛtaghna).
That twice-born man who is the master of a *vṛṣalī* (a low-caste woman), the master of an unchaste woman, or is ungrateful,
is considered to dwell in the mouth of a worm for as long as fourteen Indras [reign].
He constantly embraces that image made of heated iron.
Then that Śūdra shall remain miserable for a thousand years.
One who destroys meritorious deeds by performing austerities is called ungrateful;
one who destroys the austerities performed by others is called ungrateful.
For one who violates a vow and for one who is ungrateful, there is the Kumbhīpāka hell for ten thousand years.
He who, having made a promise regarding a task and having inspired the highest confidence,
then breaks his own promise, is indeed an ungrateful person.
But in that heated iron pit, he causes him to burn for an eon—(71)—he who, out of deceit, destroys various kinds of gifts:
the gift of a word, the gift of a material object, and the gift of a daughter or knowledge. (72)

He who violates his word after having made it or after having given a promise, or he who destroys a social gathering, shall certainly dwell for ten thousand yugas in Kālasūtra. One who ruins a task or destroys a gathering shall dwell for ten thousand years in Pāśakuṇḍa.
He who indeed obstructs the teacher’s work, he who strikes the teacher, and the slayer of the teacher is truly ungrateful;
such a person remains in a fire-pit for ten thousand years.
One who seizes the livelihood of a deity during a rite for the gods is called ungrateful.
One who seizes the means of subsistence belonging to gods or others— whether given by himself or given by another—
shall remain impaled upon a stake for as many thousands of years as there are hairs on his body.
His food shall be glowing coals, and his drink indeed hot urine.
He lies upon glowing coals and is beaten by the servants of Yama;
thereafter, having become a worm in excrement for sixty thousand years,
he is then born poor, wretched, and destitute of both land and offspring.
A Śūdra who performs such acts becomes diseased and censurable, though he may become pure again after some time.
He is unfit for rites performed for specific desires and is a destroyer of his own and others' wealth.
That lowest of men who destroys the fame of others as well as his own [is likewise fallen].
That ungrateful person, who destroys the merit of sacrifices, charitable works, and other pious deeds performed in the Kāmyaka forest,
shall indeed dwell in a most terrible blind well until the end of the kalpa;
there he will be devoured by mongooses, vultures, worms, and the like, while drinking heated alkaline water.
From this point on, he shall be a serpent for seven births, and thereafter a crow for five;

he who destroys the worship of the twice-born is considered a great ungrateful person. Or, he who would seize the property of a Brahmin, the property of a guru, or even the property of a deity [shall suffer the same].
Even that ungrateful person might dwell in Avatoda for an entire kalpa;
after that he becomes a drinker of liquor, then a Śūdra, and finally pure.
But he who destroys his daily obligatory duty is a greater ungrateful person than those.
One who lacks devotion would neither protect nor bow down to one's father, mother, or guru; rather, one might even repeatedly strike them with words every morning.
Likewise, a woman of loose character would strike her own husband with her speech.
Those who obstruct the worship of those worthy of worship are proclaimed to be ungrateful.
They dwell in a pit of fire as long as the moon and sun exist;
thereafter, they become water-creatures for seven births, after which they become pure.
He who would commit the destruction of the entire world is the greatest of ungrateful persons;
he who gives false testimony out of desire, anger, or likewise fear,
and speaks with partiality in an assembly, is a destroyer of merit and an ungrateful person.

In all cases, for everyone, the destruction of the enjoyment resulting from a good deed performed is proclaimed as ingratitude (*kṛtaghnatā*). Those who destroy merit are called destroyers of what was done; merit, indeed, is always perishable. (1.442.89–90)
Therefore, there is no ingratitude toward the eternal one known as the grace of Kṛṣṇa;
for that which is eternal is indeed worthy of merit, whereas that which is perishable is not worthy at all.
False witnesses, partisans, those who betray trust, and those who destroy merit [are likewise unworthy]. (91)
He shall certainly dwell in a pit of serpents for as long as a thousand Indras;
devoured by the snakes and beaten, he indeed consumes their excrement and urine,
and is born as a frog and a chameleon for seven lifetimes.
Then he becomes a *śālmalī* tree in the forest, then a mute *śūdra*, and thereafter pure.
Engaging with the wives of others and the like, as well as the non-observance of one's own duty (*svadharma*),
indeed the practice of another's duty, is reckoned among the acts of ingratitude.

The obstruction of one's own appropriate duties, the undertaking of duties belonging to others, and ingratitude—these indeed constitute [the state of] being a *cāṇḍāla*. One who possesses such qualities dwells in the Kumbhīpāka hell for as long as a kalpa. (95–96)

Afterwards, one who has approached those who should not be approached shall become a eunuch; then, for seven births, he shall be afflicted with wasting leprosy, and thereafter he shall become a Śūdra, and finally pure.
He may even fall upon a red-hot iron spike, and after that, he shall become a eunuch.

Having first become a Cāṇḍāla and then a Śūdra, he subsequently becomes pure. He who, having performed a preeminent gift— such as the giving of a daughter in marriage or the offering of gold and other valuables—
subsequently destroys that gift, is proclaimed to be ungrateful (kṛtaghna).
One who destroys what has been done for them and does not recognize what was performed for them is ungrateful; O King, such a person is said to be ungrateful in sixteen ways in every respect.
Furthermore, ingratitude arises from the dishonor of a guest.
To eliminate that fault, you must honor the guest;
having brought him into the house, he should be worshipped, and his lotus-feet should be served. His favor should be accepted, and the *pāñjalam* should be drunk. 101–102.
Let the blessing of the guest be accepted and likewise let his offense be wiped away;
then depart for the forest, and thereafter, auspicious prosperity shall be regained.
Remember Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa Svāmī, the Lord and Master of Śrī.
"The infallible Lord will grant you again auspicious prosperity and liberation," having said this,
all the sages departed for their own abodes.
Suyajña first bowed down to him and then escorted the twice-born man to his home.
Having honored him repeatedly with worship, he asked about his name, lineage, and other details.
The sage replied that his own name was renowned as Sutapas;
his father was named Virūpa, and his grandfather was Viśvarūpa.
Tvaṣṭṛ was his father, and Kaśyapa was his grandfather;
Marīci was his great-grandfather, and his great-great-grandfather was Viśvasṛj himself.
O Lord of the Earth, I am the seventh Puruṣa from Brahmā.
Mahādeva is my guru, the giver of knowledge and the bestower of excellent counsel;
Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Lord and Master, is my chosen deity.
I meditate upon His lotus feet; I have no desire for worldly prosperity.
"I do not accept the attainment of the same world, the same power, the same form, or proximity to the Lord of Rādhikā that He has granted me, without the service of His feet. O King,
having heard this at Suyajña’s sacrifice regarding the arrival of the sages, [the king spoke].
I have come to lead you toward a longing for devotion to Viṣṇu;
you have been solely favored by me and have not been cursed now.
You have been lifted up from having fallen into the terrible, deep ocean of worldly existence.
For holy fords are not made of water, nor are gods made of clay or stone.
They purify only after a long time; but those devoted to Kṛṣṇa purify by their mere sight.
O King, depart from this house and give the kingdom to your son.
Worship Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Rādhā, and abandon everything else as perishable. O sinless one, by my curse, forever renounce your great kingdom.
With your body wasting away through austerity, take up residence upon the earth in the land of Kuru.
"Renounce the mind that is rich in the illusion of royal pomp.
(116) By the command of the Brahmin, the king accepted peace and likewise renunciation;
with intense spiritual urgency, he asked about the means of attaining Goloka. (117)

Thus ends the four hundred and forty-second chapter, titled "The Description of King Suyajña’s Curse due to His Disrespectful Treatment of an Ascetic Brāhmaṇa at the Conclusion of his Rājasūya Sacrifice; Furthermore, the Greatness of the Guest, the Sixteen Types of Ingratitude, and the Instruction Given by the Sages," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga Lineage, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Chapter 442. [Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā – Part 1 (Kṛtayuga Lineage), Chapter 443]
[The Author: Chapter 444.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī! Hear what Suyajña then said to Sutapas.
"O Sage! Tell me here, when and how is everything perishable?
And likewise, tell me of that supreme means for liberation which is intense.
Having heard these words of the king, Sutapas, the knower of reality, spoke.
Listen, O King, to how everything born of nature is indeed perishable.
A vessel made from six palas [of gold], deep and four finger-breadths wide,
with a hole made by a single māṣaka of gold, and measuring four finger-breadths in length with its handles— (3) — [such is the measure].
As long as a vessel remains submerged in water, that duration is one *daṇḍa*.
Two *daṇḍas* make one *muhūrta*, and four of those make one *yāma*.
A day consists of eight *yāmas*, and fifteen of those make a *pakṣa*. (4–5)
A month consists of two fortnights, and a year consists of twelve months.
Indeed, for humans, one month is a day and night for the ancestors (pitṛs).
The dark fortnight is declared to be their day, and the bright fortnight is proclaimed to be their night.
A year for humans is indeed a single day and night for the gods.
The northern course (of the sun) is their day, and the southern course is their night.
And the lifespan of humans and others, O King, corresponds to the sequence of the Yugas.
The Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali constitute the four ages (caturyuga).
These consist of four, three, two, and one thousand years respectively, beginning with the Kṛta.
Their transitional periods (sandhyāṃśaka) consist of eight hundred, six hundred, four hundred, and two hundred years respectively.
Two thousand years constitute one cycle of twelve thousand years; that is a *caturyuga*. Seventy-one such cycles form a *manvantara*. During one day of Brahmā, there are fourteen *manus*.
As by day, so by night, the time of the Creator passes;
for twenty-eight Manus constitute a single day and night of Brahmā.
O King, the first Manu was Svāyambhuva, the son of Brahmā.

Having received from Śaṅkara the knowledge of the Kṛṣṇa-mantra, which is very difficult to obtain, and having attained the state of service to Kṛṣṇa, he indeed went to Goloka. Svārociṣa Manu, the second son of Vahni, was also there.
The sons of Priyavrata were those two Manus, the third and the fourth.
Raivata was born as the fifth, and Cākṣuṣa is declared the sixth.
Śrāddhadeva, the son of Sūrya and a devotee of Viṣṇu, is the seventh Manu.
The eighth Manu is Sāvarṇi, the son of the Sun, a devotee of Viṣṇu.
The ninth is Dakṣasāvarṇi, who is devoted to the vows of Viṣṇu.
The tenth is Brahmasāvarṇi, who is proficient in the knowledge of Brahman.
And after that, Dharmasāvarṇi is remembered as the eleventh Manu;
the wise Rudrasāvarṇi is remembered as the twelfth Manu;
and this righteous-souled Devasāvarṇi is the thirteenth Manu.

The fourteenth, the great wise one Candrasāvarṇi, is the last. (1.9) The lifespan of the Manus is exactly equal to that of the Indras; a single day of Brahmā is delimited by fourteen Indras. (1.443.20)
O King, that is the night of Brahmā, and it is called the Brāhmī night. During that night of Brahmā, the minor dissolution (kṣudra-pralaya) is said to occur;
at that time, the ten worlds, including the gods and the Manus, truly perish.
Thus, thirty days and nights constitute a month for Brahmā.
A year for Brahmā, O King, consists of a thousand kalpas.
In this manner, the supreme lifespan of the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati) extends to one hundred such years.
Upon the dissolution of Brahmā, there occurs a single Vairāja Kalpa;
the lifespan of a Vairāja is one hundred years, after which his destruction follows.
That period is but a single day of Mahāviṣṇu, whose own duration is likewise one hundred years.
Then this day of the Pradhāna-Puruṣa passes away.
When a hundred years of that Prakṛti-Puruṣa have elapsed, it indeed becomes his day; furthermore, after another hundred years, there is dissolution.
Dissolved into the imperishable Brahman along with Māyā, one undergoes this natural dissolution (prākṛtika-laya); Rādhā is said to be Prakṛti.
Absolute dissolution (ātyantika-laya) is liberation (mokṣa), and that, O King, is exceedingly difficult to attain.
Having heard this, Suyajña quickly asked for the means:
"What is the bestower of liberation by which I may go to Goloka, the eternal abode?
Sutapas replied: "O Suyajña! Worship Rādhā, the beloved of Hari. (28–29)
Even Kṛṣṇa himself values her words, which consist of love for Kṛṣṇa;
by serving her with his grace, you will go quickly to Goloka.
But by propitiating Śrī Kṛṣṇa, people go to the divine realm of the cows only after a long time.
Indeed, by serving Kṛpārādhā, devotees go [to her] in no time at all.
She who is a portion of Rādhā and your wife, known by the name Rāseśvarī—
she is your Rādhā here, a devoted wife, highly fortunate, and hidden.
Having performed the supreme vow of a devoted wife and having protected those virtues,
you shall conquer great death through the power of her who is a portion of Rādhā.
O King, it is for this very reason that I have come specifically to tell you this.
"Worship according to dharma Rādhā, your wife, who is the Mistress of the Rasa-dance and a portion of [the Supreme] Rādhā.
For she is present here as a virtuous woman; behold her with your divine eye.
Having spoken thus, he immediately touched the eyes of the king.
He beheld his virtuous wife, Rādhikā, devoted to her husband;
becoming struck with wonder, he received the mantra of Rādhā:
*oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ rāseśvaryai rādhikāyai svāhā*.
Then she heard from Sutapas the duties of a wife’s vow:
"As is Kṛṣṇa, so is Rādhā; the portions of Rādhā are the very forms of Kṛṣṇa.
Just as devotion to her husband is the highest ideal for a woman’s body in Kṛṣṇa..."
Likewise, regarding the duty of a devoted wife toward one born from portions of Kṛṣṇa and Rādhā:
having risen in the morning, a true devotee should repeatedly remember Rādhikā;
he should bathe her, worship her, adorn her, and feed her well.
One should serve her, please her with gifts of desired objects, and delight her again and again.
One should perform the lustration ceremony for her, praise her, put her to sleep, and escort her;
thus, always observing the vow of a devoted wife, one should worship Rādhā, whose very self is Kṛṣṇa.
A house is not called a "home"; it is said that the wife is the home.
A house enriched by her, who is an expansion of Rādhā’s own essence, shines with splendor.
Indeed, the wife is the household Lakṣmī; without her, a house is merely a cave.
But with a wife, even a house pervaded by darkness becomes bright.
Even a dog, when joined with a mate, becomes a "village lion.
Even a pauper, when possessed of a wife, is counted among the members of a household.
Even a king, deprived of his beloved, is banished from his home by a woman;
yet even a servant, when accompanied by his wife, is protected within the house.
For him who has no virtuous wife in his home who speaks kindly, [there is no security].
One should go to the forest; for as is the forest, so is the home.
Alas, that house where there is no virtuous and beautiful wife—by him it should be regarded as a forest; for as is the forest, so is that home.

For one who has no devoted wife, well-disciplined and capable of accomplishing what must be done for her husband, the home is parched and devoid of affection, even if it is full of kinsmen and wealth.
A house empty of a wife is like a forest; a house with a wife is a true home.
But the housewife is the bestower of merit in the home during rites for the gods and the ancestors.
O King, all religious acts have their root in the wife; likewise, the home has its root in the wife.
All happiness of householders in the home has its root in the wife.
Joy is always rooted in the wife; auspiciousness is rooted in the wife;
worldly existence is rooted in the wife; and fragrance is rooted in the wife.
Indeed, for householders, the jewel of a woman is the foremost of all jewels.
As there is no lotus without water, so there is no home without a wife.
O King, that wife of yours in the palace is a portion of Rādhā;
she is devoted to her husband, virtuous, chaste, and a beloved who possesses all enjoyments.
Rādhā has been honored by Kṛṣṇa through the dharma of devotion to his wife;
likewise, may you also offer worship with reverence to her who has been praised.
For when she is satisfied, she will soon bestow heaven, liberation, and her own abode.
Suyajña, who had heard much and was a bull among those devoted to their wives, spoke in many ways:
"O King of kings, tell me what kind of person is one devoted to his wife—a bull among those devoted to their wives? I wish to hear this.
Sutapas then replied, having meditated upon the sovereign power of the wife.
Every morning one should constantly remember and meditate upon the wife, who is dear to Hari.
In the morning, one should look at the face of the wife first, and only afterwards look at others.
One should cause the wife to bathe with desired waters and dress her beautifully.
She should have her hair adorned by female servants and others,
or else the husband himself should arrange her hair and so forth;
he should embellish her with perfumes and the like, bestowing upon her beauty and the signs of good fortune.
She should wear ornaments and apply a drop of collyrium to her eyes;
she should provide food, water for drinking, and the like, and offer betel leaf. Whatever is pleasing to him, all that she should give and always seek to delight him.
One should perform a massage of her body to remove her fatigue;
likewise, one should wash away her impurities and rub her limbs.
By making her listen to sweet narratives and stories, one should illuminate knowledge for her.
One should practice ninefold devotion toward Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul.
One should provide a comfortable bed and delight the virtuous woman with pleasure.
One should not speak with another woman, nor should one ever touch another.
One should certainly not look at the face of another woman, nor engage in conversation with another;
one should never think of another woman anywhere, nor have a mind attached to another.
One should not take the scent of another, nor hear the voice of another. (64–65)

One who observes the vow of a wife (*patnīvrata*) should not watch the dancing and other performances performed by others; nor should he ever look upon the bodies, breasts, and such parts of other women.
He should never accept water, food, or anything else given by another woman.
One should never wear one's own clothes, oil, or other such items that have been touched by another;
nor should one consume well-prepared flowers, milk, or similar substances offered by another.
One should never sit in a vehicle or any other conveyance together with another woman.
One should not walk along a path or similar place with another woman, even for the sake of some purpose;
nor should one lie down with another woman in a field, garden, marketplace, or the like.
A person who observes the vow of fidelity to his wife should not perform any activity together with another woman.
One should never perform the *parāyoga* in places such as festive gatherings or assembly halls (1.443.70).
One should never consume anything given by another,
nor should one ever stand within the circles belonging to others (71).
One should not go to another's bathing ground or similar places for the purpose of bathing and so forth.
One should not look upon the beauty of another's form, nor contemplate it.
One should never consume food cooked by another.
One should not go outside at night, nor should one enter another's house.
O King, one should not stand on paths frequented by women, nor at crossroads and the like.
One should not listen to the music played by a woman during another's festival.
One should never cast a sidelong glance at another woman, nor should one indicate a secret rendezvous with her;
one should not praise another woman, nor should one sing of her virtues.
In this way, one should entirely abandon improper conduct toward another woman.
That vow of the wife, when fulfilled, becomes a bestower of nourishment and liberation.
One should never mistreat one's own wife, nor should one ever strike her; one should not cause her to hear harsh words, nor should one act with anger or contempt toward her. (76–77)
Having produced wealth through ethical means— by means of hard work, effort, occupation, other labor, agriculture, or service—
he should support his own wife and not make any distinction regarding food.
One should fully satisfy her with amorous play, delighting her, serving her, and sporting with her.
One should eat with affection the water, food, and other offerings given by one's wife, praising them;
one should never take account of defects such as an excess of saltiness or other flaws. (1.443.79–80)
Thinking of her as nectar, one should accept her and never treat her with contempt.
One should never use force against a woman who is unwilling, nor should one abandon a woman during her menses.
One should never awaken a sleeping woman, nor should one behave deceitfully toward a woman who is in love.
One should never cause her distress, even if compelled by thirst [for worldly ties].
One should act in such a way that she remains well-disposed.
The practitioner should entrust all household property without exception to his wife.
One should offer oneself to her and always practice respect toward her.
One should well protect the honor of one's wife and must never address her by name.
One should never oppress her with one's own nature nor insult her unjustly.
One should never revile her nor ever transgress the word of one's wife.
Always regarding the wife as a great goddess, one should offer salutations to her.
One should provide her with all desired objects and should certainly not say, "It does not exist."
In the dharma of service, one should not fall into a state of mental indifference regarding the sequence of rituals and so forth;
just as Nārāyaṇa never enjoys anything at all without Lakṣmī,
and just as Kṛṣṇa never enjoys anything at all without the virtuous Rādhā.
Likewise, one observing the vow should never eat anything anywhere without his wife;

[he should not even look at] his own penis and so forth without his wife being present. Nor should anything be looked upon by another woman, nor should his own cheeks, face, or other parts be kissed by another.
Her heart should not be drawn elsewhere, nor should she behave otherwise; even in a dream she should not touch another woman, nor should she look upon another.
She should perform all religious duties, rites for the gods, and ancestral rites together with her husband.
One who is devoted to his wife should never conceal household affairs from her;
indeed, having informed his wife, he should perform whatever task is to be done, and never act alone.
Without the consent of his wife, he should not perform religious duties, vows, or other such observances. (91–92)
One should always be under the authority of one's wife for the sake of spiritual welfare, not for the sake of hell;
one should be dependent on her for the sake of liberation, but never for the sake of hell.
One should always honor her for the sake of happiness, never for the sake of suffering. (93)
One should not place trust in unchaste women or the like based on a letter of confidence.
A husband may entrust his life, wealth, jewels, and so forth into her hands;
for the wife is always half of the husband, and likewise, the husband is half of the wife. (94–95)
The husband is born in the form of a son within the cavity of her womb.
Therefore, the wife is the one who has eaten [the seed], the progenitor, the mother, and the nourisher;
she must always be protected, always supported, and always guarded with excellent provisions. (96)
The satisfaction of desire is found in the wife; indeed, purity lies in urinating upon her. Service to the wife is the highest austerity; conversation with her is nectar.
For the beloved husband, there is true devotion even toward the mere form of his sovereign lady.
Non-violence is the absence of malice; truthfulness is not concealing that [truth].
Singleness of heart toward one’s wife is non-stealing, which is indeed the absence of deception.
Sexual enjoyment with one’s wife as desired constitutes the practice of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) for one established in the householder stage.
Taking all things for the sake of his wife is non-possessiveness.

When she is asleep, he should sleep; when she is awake, he should be alert. When she has bathed, he should bathe; when she is satisfied, he should be pleased; and when she has eaten, he should be fond of eating.
When she is yellowed, he becomes addicted to drink; when she is sporting, he becomes a playful companion;
when she is adorned, he is rich in splendor; when she is distressed, he is deeply sorrowful;
when she is unclean, he is not very bright; and when she is happy, he is filled with happiness. (102)
When she was sick, the husband’s mind became dejected; when she was in full bloom, he was filled with joy.
When she smiled, he smiled back; when she was satisfied, the husband was satisfied.
When she was merely thought of, his heart was broken; when she was engaged in a vow, he was likewise bound by that vow. (103–104)

If she remains steadfast in austerity, he, joined with her in austerity, becomes one who has performed good deeds; if she dies, he should follow her in death by burning upon the funeral pyre. Thus, a husband devoted to his wife's vow shall deliver his lineage.
In that same way, one uplifts oneself as well as one hundred and one wives.
O King, always worship Rādhikā, the Queen of the Rāsa dance and a portion of [the Supreme], saying:
"Oṃ, obeisances to Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇī; obeisances to You, my wife. (106–107)
Thus bowing and practicing the vow of a wife devoted to her husband,
he uplifts the entire world and in the end attains the imperishable Brahman.
Having drunk the water from his wife’s hand, he is glorified in the heavenly world.
Having obtained a son who has entered the vessel of his wife, one is honored by the ancestors.
Having attained the supreme vehicle of the wife, the highest state is reached.
Indeed, as many water-tirthas as there are, born of the earth, forests, and mountains—
All these rest indeed upon a wife who is devoted to her husband:
dharma, vows, austerity, sacrifice, silent recitation, study of the Vedas, humility, giving, merit, assistance, service, and even blessings. (111)
If she is served with devotion, everything resides within the body of the wife.
She is said to be the savior of her husband, and he is the savior of her;
both of them become the saviors of their entire lineage from the bonds of worldly existence.

Therefore, the vow of a wife must be observed; that indeed is celibacy (brahmacarya), because it eternally brings about the attainment of Brahman and bestows the abode of bliss. All the gods, along with the sages, and the goddesses who are virtuous wives devoted to their husbands [attained this].
Brahman dwells indeed within the body of the wife, and He dwells there as well.
A man who observes the vow toward his wife is the form of Viṣṇu; of this there is no doubt.
Just as Kṛṣṇa is beyond all qualities (nirguṇa) and the presiding deity of all living beings.
He is the savior of all and remains untainted by his very actions;
likewise, the Supreme Lord is another who rescues through his vow of devotion to his wife.
Upon merely beholding him, the sacred fires rise up to meet him with heartfelt devotion.
Successes, the power of yoga, and all sovereign lordships without exception—
these always become fruitful through her resolve, just as they do for Kṛṣṇa.
Kṛṣṇa himself, devoted to his wife, dwells within the vow of a faithful wife.
O King, worship the virtuous Rāseśvarī, the beloved born from a portion of Rādhā,
just as Dharmadeva, devoted to his vow of love, worshipped his wife Mūrti; and just as Manu, devoted to his vow of devotion toward his wife, worshipped Śatarūpā, so too should you worship her.
Having spoken thus, that Suyajña, rich in asceticism, fell silent, O beloved Kamalā!

Thus ends the four hundred and forty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Instruction on the Duties of the Wife's Vow by the Rishi Sutapas to King Suyajña," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
[Chapter 443] Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā – Section 1 (Kṛtayuga-santāna)
Chapter 444 [Author:
Chapter 445 → Śrī Lakṣmī said:
How did that King Suyajña, who was devoted to his wife, attain liberation after chanting hymns and performing what kind of austerity? Tell me that. Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Devoted to his wife and fond of performing sacrifices, that king obtained the mantra of Rādhikā;
having gone to Puṣkara accompanied by his wife, he who was devoted to austerity chanted it.
The monarch constantly chanted the mantra: "Oṃ rādhāyai svāhā."
He performed meditation and offered worship to Rādhā with great reverence.
(3) She possesses the luster of the color of a white campaka flower, a radiance equal to ten million moons, a face like the full moon of autumn, and eyes like autumn lotuses. (4)
Her lower lip is like a ripe bimba fruit, and she is adorned with a row of teeth as bright as pearls;
her face is radiant with a gentle smile, and she is decorated with necklaces of jewels and other ornaments.
She wears garments as white as fire and is graced by her grace toward her devotees.
Adorned with jeweled armlets and bracelets, and graced by jeweled anklets;
her ears beautifully decorated with the splendor of jeweled earrings;
her cheeks possessing the luster of the sun’s radiance; and resplendent with a halo of light.
Adorned with jeweled necklaces, radiant with a crown and diadem,
beautiful with jeweled rings and graced by jeweled loops;
beautified by the mass of her braided hair interwoven with garlands of jasmine.
Her limbs were proportioned to her form, and she was adorned with the most excellent ornaments;
her forehead bore a tilaka-mark made of sandalwood paste and other substances, and she was worshipped with such offerings.
She was radiant with the beauty of Kṛṣṇa’s fortune and was the very embodiment of Kṛṣṇa’s life-breath.
"I worship the Queen of the Rāsa dance, who bestows devotion to Kṛṣṇa, who is peaceful, who belongs to Viṣṇu, who is affectionate toward Kṛṣṇa,
and who is seated upon a jeweled throne in the Rāsa.
Having thus meditated, he offered her the sixteen articles of worship.
A seat, clothing, water for the feet, the arghya offering, scents and ointments;
incense, a lamp, beautiful flowers, bathing materials, jeweled ornaments, fifty-six varieties of excellent food offerings, betel leaf, and scented water. (12–13)

The king of devotees, with sincere devotion, offered the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*)— which is equal to jewels— and the sixteen types of service, as well as one hundred and eight [other offerings]. "O you who are worshipped by Kṛṣṇa, grant me devotion to Kṛṣṇa and service as Kṛṣṇa’s servant!"
Thus he offered this circumambulation and bowed to the Supreme Goddess. By worshipping that Supreme Sovereign on the full moon day of Kārttika,
one attains immovable prosperity and obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice.
A woman who meditates upon her with devotion shall attain the good fortune of her husband;
she goes to Goloka and is liberated from the bonds of worldly existence.
Thus, Suyajña indeed constantly chanted and worshipped.
He offered praise and meditated, repeatedly reflecting upon the names and their meanings:
"Rāṃ indeed bestows prosperity; Dhāṃ leads one to steadfastness at the feet [of the Lord].
I bow to Kṛṣṇa, the bestower of both worldly enjoyment and liberation"—thus he contemplated. (18–19)
Having subsisted on leaves, flowers, and fruits, the king performed most difficult austerities for a hundred years; he made everything consist of Rādhā.
Then Rādhā, being pleased with the king, appeared before his very eyes.
Then the Queen of the Rāsa dance spoke to that Suyajñaka, who was joined with her:
"O King, you have always observed the vow of devotion to your wife like Kṛṣṇa;
you have served me constantly, and I have been exceedingly gratified by your devotion."

The Queen of the Rāsa dance was always worshipped, saluted, and meditated upon by you; you maintained your vow of devotion to your husband unbroken, treating Kṛṣṇa as your very self. Indeed, regarding her as ever like a flower in her delicacy, you protected her.
She was thoroughly gratified with garments, ornaments, cosmetics, and other articles;
she was constantly nourished with gifts of food, drink, and fine enjoyments;
and perceiving her state of pregnancy, she was protected by the granting of her heart's desires. (24–25)
She was beheld without obstacle during states such as childbirth and the like;
yet she was delighted by all her moods even amidst conditions such as royal power.
When enveloped by darkness, she maintained her forbearance and was propitiated while held upon his lap.
Even in the presence of states such as fever, you were not separated from me for even a moment. O King, even in times of calamity, you did not distance yourself from my side;
having endured everything most terrible, you were never joined with misfortune.
Never were you caused to fall from righteousness by me during periods of impurity or similar occasions;
nor was a pregnant woman ever joined with you by me out of vain desire.
Nor was a woman with children ever made to do so by me without a valid reason.
When her beloved was hungry or thirsty, she was never made to undergo fatigue; in his amorous dalliances or when he was deeply anxious, she was never at any time distressed.
She was honored with every aspect of her being, according to the proper time and according to the available resources.

O King, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa has been pleased by my service in this way— he was worshipped, gratified, and propitiated everywhere with gifts of happiness. Sent by him alone, I, Rādhā, have come to take you [with me].
I am Rādhā, the Queen of the *rāsa*, who bestows the fruit of the *pannīvrat* vow.

Whatever has been performed for my sake, whether intentionally or unintentionally, I grant its fruit. Whatever is offered to me through the qualities of goodness (*sattva*), passion (*rajas*), or even darkness (*tamas*)—[I grant its fruit]. (33–34)
Through the yoga of Kṛṣṇa, I render all that devoid of qualities (nirguṇa).
Desire, anger, as well as relish, affection, greed, pride, and so forth—
even when offered for my sake or performed for me— become devoid of qualities.
Since I am indeed the quality-less wife of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa,
therefore the entire world— though devoid of qualities through my union with Him— is rendered active by the divine play of Kṛṣṇa, who is devoted to His wives. || 36-37 ||
If Kṛṣṇa did not act, the world would become devoid of ritual activity;
for all the rites of husband and wife originate from Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa.
Even those who appear similar [to them] remain devoid of true qualities, though they may be destroyers of bondage.
Brahmā, accompanied by Brahmī, indeed creates the world in this manner at the beginning of the aeon.
There is no day without night, nor is there a self without the intellect;
there is no Brahmā without Brahmī, and Kṛṣṇa is certainly not without Kṛṣṇā.
Sound does not exist without power, nor indeed do attributes without devotion;
Kṛṣṇa does not exist without Rādhā, and being and consciousness do not exist without bliss.
O King of kings, since you have been purified in every way by my vow, [you shall attain it].
"Come with your wife to the dark Goloka by means of a celestial chariot.
O best of kings, I have been propitiated by you through all your vows;
for when this Rāseśvarī was overcome by fever, [you offered me water]."
Previously, she did not take water or food for a month;
nor did you consume water or food for that same single month.
Even while remaining healthy, you protected your vow of devotion to your wife.

O King, whatever excellent food or other fine enjoyments your wife has discarded at the time of childbirth and so forth, all of that has likewise been discarded by you. Whether in a state of prosperity or adversity, in no situation whatsoever have you ever [enjoyed them]. (45–46)
Having left his wife and not entrusted anything [to her], he did not enjoy anything for himself.
O King, you conduct yourself like a virtuous man, having placed everything upon your wife.
Through your wife as the instrument, your merit from giving and other virtues has become inexhaustible.
Indeed, I have performed that eternal fruit solely for your sake.
Whenever the Cāturmāsya vow was observed by your wife, the Queen of the Rāsa-dance, you never ate anything at all without first informing her.
Whatever difficult vows were indeed performed by your wife during the months of Kārtika, Śrāvaṇa, Māgha, and Vaiśākha—
whatever was renounced there by the Queen of the Rāsa dance, that was renounced by you as well.
Indeed, nothing was ever taken by you at all while your wife was observing her vows. Whatever restraints (yamas) and observances (niyamas) were practiced by your wife,
those same ones were practiced by you as well for that same duration of time.
Bathing, giving gifts, recitation, and burnt offerings were performed by her, yet they were performed by you;
whatever was intended by her was all likewise determined by you.
No other woman has been touched by you out of desire, nor has she ever been looked upon.
The female slaves and laborers were protected by you like daughters;
the subjects—both maidens and young women—were regarded by you like disciples;
and the daughters-in-law, wives, and mothers were honored by you like goddesses. (54–55)
You have paid homage to the virtuous, truthful, and disciplined women who are as auspicious as Śivā;
you have protected the helpless widows and mendicants like a father.
Dancers and leading actresses, who assume many forms, are considered by tradition to be [the embodiments of] Dharma.
The wives of the Vaiṣṇavas and the female practitioners of Sāṃkhya-yoga were honored like the wives of one's own gurus.
Those seeking knowledge were always regarded as equal to Sarasvatī;
and those practicing celibacy were seen as being purified by sacred fords like the Gaṅgā.
Thus, O Suyajña, all those women were perceived by you, O King, as embodiments of Brahman, through your devotion to your wife and your steadfastness as a ruler.
You have liberated them from their debts and delivered them safely across all calamities.
Other women have been removed from suffering and made into Vaiṣṇavas.
O King, you are always blessed; blessed is your beloved Rāseśvarī;
and blessed is my own partial incarnation (aṃśasvarūpa), by attaining whom one reaches liberation.
He has placed his trust, his choice, his surrender, his humility, and his steadfastness of mind in me; he has shown favor toward me while avoiding all hostility.
No one else will ever protect my vow in such a manner.
O King, that vow of mine, the *patnīvrata*, which bestows liberation, has been fulfilled by you. My ancestors have been delivered, and my subjects have been delivered by you;
indeed, everything—whether animate or inanimate—in both the kingdom and the forest, has been delivered.
Having spoken thus, the goddess Rādhikā, the Queen of the *rāsa*, took Suyajñaka and her husband—
both possessing divine bodies— to Goloka upon a celestial chariot. Thus, O Lakṣmī, the vow of the devoted wife has been clearly explained to you.
"By reading and hearing this, the observer of the vow shall attain Goloka.

Thus ends the four hundred and forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Greatness of the Patnīvratam Vow," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. [In this chapter], having taken King Suyajña—the protector of the duties of the Patnīvratam vow—and his wife Rāseśvarī into a celestial chariot, Rādhā departed for Goloka.
*Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā*, Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛtayuga), Chapter 444.
Chapter 445 [Author:
Chapter 446 → Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:

Listen, Lakṣmī! Even though Tārā, the wife of her guru, was devoted to her husband, she was enjoyed by the Moon despite being without desire; yet, due to her devotion to her husband, she did not fall [from her virtue].
Atri was the son of Brahmā, and his son was Niśākara (the Moon).

Having performed the Rājasūya sacrifice, he indeed became the Moon. Once, the Moon, intoxicated by his success, went to the bank of the Jāhnavī and beheld his preceptor’s wife, Tārā, who was devoted to her husband and dharma.
Well-bathed, beautiful, and charming, with full and elevated breasts,
slender-waisted, handsome, with beautiful teeth and a delicate form;
a young woman dressed in fine garments and adorned with golden ornaments.
With a drop of musk together with a drop of sandalwood below, she is radiant in the center of her beautiful forehead with a dot of vermilion;
white as the moon, golden-hued, with red eyes, and filled with passion. (5–6)

Beholding her alone in a secluded place— she whose face was like the full moon of autumn, whose lips were like ripe bimba fruit, who was virtuous, who had bathed, and who walked with the gait of an elephant in rut as she was returning to her own home—
the King, afflicted by the god of love, became pale.
Casting aside her modesty and blocking her path, he spoke to her:
"Salutations to you, O beautiful one, O Brahmin lady of lovely form and divine nature!
Stay for a moment, O most excellent one; I bow at your feet."
Indeed, through association with virtuous women like you, there is the destruction of sin;
know that good fortune will also arise, for the mind is what dwells within.
I desire to make you my companion as we lie upon our bed at night.

"O virtuous lady! If my mind has become overwhelmed by passion, you are indeed capable of pacifying it once with the gift of sexual union. If so, I shall depart after leaving you; therefore, act accordingly. (11–12)
"If you do not grant me the gift of love, I shall take you away;
having indeed carried you off by force, I will depart—this is my firm resolve.
"Alas! You have been assigned to me by the ascetic preceptor of the gods."
What pleasure is there in sexual union that it should bring you peace?
I am the Moon; my kingdom is clearly visible in heaven. Come, or else remain there for twenty-two years as one who has been cursed.
Your youth is passing fruitlessly with an aged master;
Bṛhaspati remains lost in thought, both in sleep and in waking.
Your heart's desire is one thing, while your preceptor’s intended action is another.
For what joy can there be in the union of two whose objects of desire are different?
O fortunate young woman, you should rejoice right here upon a bed of vāsantī flowers, anointed with fragrant sandalwood paste.
Having spoken thus, he, intoxicated by passion, fell again at her feet.
With her path blocked by Candra, that devoted wife said to him:
"You are my disciple; Tārā is your preceptor’s wife, and I am like a mother to you."
"O lustful one, are you not ashamed to speak thus? How can you be born blind?
"I am not a lustful woman, O Moon! I am a virtuous and ascetic woman.
I am your pure and sanctifying mother, O wicked son."
"You have twenty-seven wives; what more do you need from me? Give me your heart and go in peace—what use have you for a virtuous wife?
You were born through the misfortune of Atri; your birth and life are in vain."
"Fie on you, who thirst for the pleasure of another! All your well-performed merit is in vain.
O wicked one, I am a wretched woman who has taken refuge with ascetics;
that king of yogis, Bṛhaspati, is my worthy bestower of liberation."
If one such as you, a paramour by trade and conquered by base desires,
destroys my chastity, you shall be seized by consumption. Kṛṣṇa, the destroyer of the pride of the wicked, will humble your arrogance.
"Abandon this resolve toward me; truth shall bring you well-being.
Having spoken thus, as soon as Tārā moved aside, the Moon seized her by force with his hand, took her onto his chariot, and departed for heaven.
Tārā wept and cried out, making the sun her witness,
as well as Dharma, Vāyu, Earth, Fire, Space, Brahmā, Water, and Acyuta.
Holding water from the ritual jar in her hand, the devoted wife Tārā [spoke].
Just as Satī was striving in her wrath to reduce the Moon to ashes, she was restrained by a voice from the sky: "Do not seek to turn him to ash;
everyone experiences the fruit of their own actions, and thus has this fruit come to you."
Listen, O virtuous and chaste girl; you have performed this unknowingly.
When you were ten years old and staying at your father’s house, a pair of dogs remained in your hermitage, embracing one another.
Then you saw them struck with a staff and even with a stone;
though they failed to attain the fulfillment of their desire, they were separated and driven away.
Because of that lack of satisfaction in your desire, you were then cursed by them in their own language as one who was empty.
"O wicked woman! Just as you cause my separation from my husband, so shall your separation from your husband come to pass.
And just as another dog will bite me, so shall it bite you."
Moreover, another misfortune shall surely fall upon you:
two small insects, or two birds, or two men of different castes who are attached to sensual desires—none of these should ever be separated from one another. (35–36)
The failure to obtain sexual satisfaction—whether one is righteous or unrighteous—should never be allowed by the wise;
it brings about either the destruction of the wife who creates obstacles to pleasure or the destruction of the husband. (37)
Separation or a great disease arises; of this there is no doubt.
The fire arising from the lack of satisfaction in desire reduces everything to ashes and brings obstacles.
Thus, O Tārā, you have performed such an action; indeed, experience its fruit. 38–39.
Otherwise, that action of theirs will not be well-done;
for he who gives nothing but suffering to another in every respect—
to him the Teacher Nārāyaṇa himself gives suffering in return.
Listen further, O Tārā! This was done for you by your husband in the past.
Bṛhaspati, Utathya, and Saṃvarta—these three were all sons of Aṅgiras, masters of the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas. (41–42)
Bṛhaspati gave not even the slightest portion of his inheritance to his youngest son, Saṃvarta, because Saṃvarta was a mendicant. O Bṛhaspati,
this household fortune of yours has been consumed by his very breath.
"Even by another, she shall be led away as your very own form; do not grieve in this matter.
Bṛhaspati, out of lust, carried off the virtuous and pregnant wife of Madhyama Utathya—that is, his brother's wife."
He who, driven by lust, would take his brother’s wife— whether she was willing or unwilling—
obtains the sin of a thousand Brahman-murders following his death.
He surely goes to the Kumbhīpāka hell for as long as a kalpa, and after that, he is born again.
For thousands of millions of years he is born as a worm in excrement;
thereafter, he becomes a worm in a womb, then a vulture for a hundred births, and then a dog.
After that, having become a pig, he is born as a man who is destitute of women.
Karma that has been encountered must indeed be endured; it is not exhausted until it has been experienced.
Bṛhaspati committed the sin of abducting Utathya’s wife.
You have a reason for this abduction, so do not reduce the moon to ashes.
"If you do this, O Tārā, you will incur a second sin of Brahman-murder;
therefore, act for your own peace according to your destiny.
Having been addressed thus by the celestial voice, she ceased speaking and did not utter a curse.
The virtuous Satī, devoted to her husband, forcibly took refuge with the Moon;
though she was unwilling, the Lord of Night repeatedly enjoyed her by force.
In the delightful Puṣkara, within the Puṣpaka grove in heaven filled with bliss—
As the two of them indulged in amorous play upon the earth, on Mount Meru, by a river, and in a stream,
a hundred human years passed like a single moment in heaven out of their joy.
Tārā then conceived an excellent and infallible embryo from Candra.
Then Candra, being exceedingly terrified, sought refuge among the Daityas;
he stayed in the house of Śukrācārya together with Tārā, having been received with hospitality.
The highly arrogant Śukrācārya granted her freedom from fear.
They laughed at Bṛhaspati, the preceptor of the gods and a great adversary;
in the assembly, the Daityas laughed and granted fearlessness to her who was afraid, while the sinful lunar orb defiled the chastity of Satī. (56–57)
And a stain in the form of a hare appeared as an impurity upon the stainless [moon].
Śukra said to Candramas: "Truly, you have not done what is fitting;
alas, though you are the grandson of Brahmā and the son of the venerable Atri! (58)

"O son, this ill-conducted deed of yours is disgraceful, like that of a base man. In the heavens, amidst the pure ocean of nectar which is the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice, you have produced a drop of wine in the form of a blemish. (1.445.60)
Abandon the wife of the preceptor of the gods, who is as great a virtuous woman as a mother;
for truth must be spoken toward both enemy and friend, and truth always triumphs.
Even the virtues of an enemy should be spoken of, and the faults of even a guru should be spoken of.
That preceptor of the gods is my enemy; indeed, he must be censured in the assembly.
For where there is Dharma, there is Kṛṣṇa; and where there is Kṛṣṇa, there is victory.
A cow gives birth to one calf, while a tigress or a lioness brings forth five or seven.
Violent people go to their destruction; Dharma protects the righteous.
Although the gods, teachers, and Brahmins are capable of protecting [others], nevertheless, they do not protect a sinful person who destroys Dharma.
Practice righteousness, O illustrious one; abandon the Brahmin woman at once.
By this means, your sin will quickly be removed.
One who is afraid, miserable, seeking refuge, and highly virtuous must be protected.
"In protecting one who is unrighteous, there is downfall on all sides.
Come, O Candra, and perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) in the Gaṅgā.
Having said this, the preceptor of the Daityas led him to the Mandākinī.
He bathed Hari and had his worship performed. He then fed Candraka with that most purifying food offering (naivedya) associated with Kṛṣṇa’s lotus feet, mixed with tulasī leaves.
Remembering Hari with *kuśa* grass in hand, he washed away his sin;
Śukrācārya, showing compassion, spoke again and again:
"If my austerity is true, and if the fruit of the worship of Hari is indeed true," [1.445.70].

Truth is indeed the fruit of vows, and truth is the fruit of truthful speech. (71) If truth is the fruit of bathing at sacred fords, if truth is the fruit of giving gifts, and if truth is the fruit of fasting—then I am a devotee of my disciple. (72)

A Vaiṣṇava and a devotee of Kṛṣṇa shall become free from sin and attain the state of the Moon. [One who reviles] a Brahmin devoid of Brahmanical duties, a husband who deceives his own wife, a woman habitually unfaithful to her husband, and one who has been deprived of divine grace—[these are the ones who must be purified]. (73)
One who praises himself, likewise one who reviles another;

one who fails to support those dependent on him, and likewise one who associates with unchaste women; a sinner who does not observe his vows, and one who destroys the character of virtuous women. (74–75)
One who cuts down the *aśvattha*, *tulasī*, or *bilva* trees; one who reviles Viṣṇu; one who harms holy men (*sādhu*s); likewise, one who hates virtuous women (*sādhvī*s);
one who causes suffering to mother and father; and one who destroys the livelihood of the gods and others—[these are those who must be avoided]. (76)
May those who strike cows, Brahmins, and others go to the *candrapātaka* hell.
By that lunar sin, may they undergo terrible and horrific torments;
together with their own sins, may they indeed endure the punishments of Yama.
Having thus purified Candra, Tārā spoke to him again:
"O Candra, by your union with me, Tārā has become pregnant.
You have now been made pure here; do not touch Tārā again. (79)
"Do not touch your mother at any time, whether unwillingly or willingly.
Having thus purified Candra, she spoke to Tārakā:
"O great virtuous lady, leave Candra and go to Bṛhaspati, your husband."
Without any penance, you alone are purified, for your mind is pure.
A woman who is enjoyed by force, even against her will, is not defiled.
When a monthly menstrual period occurs, a woman becomes completely pure.
Having spoken thus to Candra and the virtuous Tārakā,
Śukra bestowed blessings upon them properly, showing them honor and respect.
Then, at that moment, Bṛhaspati, a treasure-house of asceticism—
He asked his disciple, "How is it that your mother delays in her bath?
Look, go! Why has she not returned at the proper time after bathing?
The disciple, having searched for her and failed to find her, heard that she had been carried away by parrots.
Weeping, Tārā approached Bṛhaspati and spoke of her abduction.
Having heard that his beloved Tārā had been carried off by Candra, Bṛhaspati,
along with his disciples, wept aloud and lamented with a grieving heart.
He said: "Karma performed in the past afflicts one when its time has ripened.
Because I abducted Utathya’s wife, my own wife was indeed taken away by the Moon.
And because I did not give wealth to Saṃvarta, my entire property and home were seized."

He who acts in opposition to dharma undoubtedly meets with suffering. Alas, from whose house has she departed—she who was devoted in heart, virtuous, well-disciplined, faithful to her husband, and the presiding goddess of the home? (1.445.90)
"All happiness has its root in a wife; heaven and liberation have emerged from her.
Therefore, one should go to the forest as if the home were the forest.
Having lamented thus in many ways, he went to the abode of Indra.
That preceptor, having been honored with hospitality by that son of Marut,
spoke to him of his own situation, which was like a second thorn in his heart;
for upon hearing Bṛhaspati’s words, his inner self was ablaze with rage.
Mahendra dispatched the deities on a mission of espionage.
He said to his preceptor, "Abandon your anxiety; for whose prosperity is ever without calamity? The messengers found Candra, free from harm, having arrived at the palace of Śakra.
Seeing him terrified along with the stars, they spoke to Indra.
Having heard this, Indra was overcome with grief and, with a burning heart, said:
"Candra remains invincible when he has taken refuge with Bali. (95–96)
We must indeed fashion that most supreme wheel;
therefore, go quickly to the world of Brahmā along with us.
We shall go to Kailāsa together with Brahmā to see Śaṅkara.
Thus they departed; having bowed to the Truth and likewise to Brahmā, they related the entire account. Having heard it, Brahmā spoke to them:
"He who inflicts suffering upon another in vain indeed suffers in every way."
Suffering indeed came upon him from the court of his punisher;
those three were Saṃvarta, Atithi, and Guru, all of them Ātreyas.
The preceptor did not grant an inheritance to the youngest, Saṃvarta.
The wife of Madhyotathya, who was pregnant, was taken by his teacher.
The teacher has now reaped the fruit of that act; yet, though it is done, it perishes through its experience.
Nevertheless, we shall go to the auspicious Śiva, Śaṅkara, and strive for a remedy.

Śaṅkara is the son of Kṛṣṇa and the preceptor born of Kṛṣṇavara; because he was born from the wife of the sage Aṅgiras, he is indeed counted as his brother. At Dakṣa’s sacrifice, Satī was consumed by fire, and Śambhu fell into a state of unconsciousness.
Āṅgiras gave him that knowledge, and Śiva became the disciple of Āṅgiras.
In this manner, too, that brother Śiva became the disciple of Bṛhaspati.
Śukra fears only Mṛtyuñjaya; he does not fear anyone else anywhere.
"Śiva, having spoken of policy to him, will cause Tārā to be restored.
Having said this, all those excellent ones went to Kailāsa, the abode of Śaṅkara.
Upon seeing Bṛhaspati, Śambhu rose from his seat of kusha grass.
He gave lion-thrones to Brahmā and the others, and spoke to Bṛhaspati:
"O brother, tell me, why do you appear thus, with such a withered face?
Has your asceticism perished, or have you neglected the twilight prayers?"
Is it because he is devoid of service to the glorious Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa?
Or is it because he lacks devotion to his parents, to his chosen deity, and to his guru?
Or is it that one who has sought refuge truly cannot be protected? || 1.09 ||

Are your guests turned away? Are those whom you must support hungry? Or are your wife and son no longer under your control? And do your disciples, servants, and others indeed offer you no reply? (1.445.11)
Is it that Lakṣmī is displeased with your smile, or is your guru angry?
Are the Vaiṣṇavas, the Brāhmaṇas, or others enraged, or is your enemy powerful?
Or are you grieving because you are separated from your family or are destitute?
Or have you been tormented by wicked men, or perhaps abandoned by your kinsmen?
(1.13) Or has some sacred ford, vow, gift, or merit been seized by Rākṣasas?
Or have you heard direct insults—indeed, insults against one’s guru are worse than death? (1.14)
"What evil deed have you committed that has caused such dejection?
Speak! Even the sun, when fallen into calamity, abandons its splendor.
Thus questioned, the Guru related to Śambhu the distressing account.
Upon hearing of the abduction of Tārā, Śiva’s face became downcast for a moment.
Having reflected for a moment, he said: "O Guru, this is indeed the fruit of one's own actions; when the fruit of one's own action is obtained, [then it must be faced]."
That which has been cast out or beaten away becomes distant indeed from one's purpose, valor, prosperity, fame, lineage,
family, water, son, majesty, land, wealth, offspring, and Hari. (1.18)
In one's nature, speech, intellect, stage of life, and support;
likewise in worldly dealings, conduct, character, and the act of giving—the heart of men truly arises in accordance with what was done in the past. (1.445.120)
The heart of Candra was such as it was impelled by your own past actions; for whatever one's prior deeds may be, such indeed is the mind of those beings.
One is oneself the generator of karma, and karma is the cause of destiny.
Fate and the cause of one's own nature produce happiness, suffering, fear, grief, and mental agitation within oneself in every birth.
Alas! This undesirable act of approaching his mother was committed by the Moon.
May there always be auspiciousness for the virtuous, the Vaiṣṇavas, and the good; may there be misfortune at every step for the wicked who are devoted to sin.
For others, he who causes suffering shall encounter obstacles at every step.
[The remembrance of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa] is the cause of mental purity. (1.25) Oh, how pure is the heart of a devotee of Śrī Kṛṣṇa!
Even though his wife had been stolen, Bṛhaspati did not curse the moon. (1.26)
Even his preceptor Vasiṣṭha, who was always righteous and sattvic,
did not curse Viśvāmitra, the slayer of his hundred sons. Indeed,
by the mere breath of Bṛhaspati, the Moon would have been reduced to ashes.
Even by the curse of Tārā, the Moon became black as iron;
nevertheless, they did not hurl it away so that his ascetic merit might not be destroyed,
for among the social orders, the Brāhmaṇas have indeed attained preeminence through their forbearance.
Better than twice-born men devoid of devotion to Viṣṇu is even a dog-eater (outcaste). Whether they are spiritually mature or immature,
Vaiṣṇavas and saintly persons are always protected by the fierce Sudarśana, the discus of Viṣṇu.
Vāyu, Pavana, Vahni, Sūrya, Brahmā, I myself, and Hara;
Śeṣa, Dharma, and the witness of all—these we indeed seek refuge in Vaiṣṇava.
Even Candra is weak and afraid, protected by the Sudarśana [discus].
He went for refuge to Śukra, the preceptor of the Daityas and a devotee of the Lord;
yet, since no one is capable of conquering him, I shall nevertheless strive accordingly.
"Worship the Supreme Brahman, the Truth, and you will obtain a wife effortlessly."

In this world, men may have a desire for enjoyments and a longing for the pleasure of women only so long as they do not obtain the mantra of Hari from the lotus-like mouth of the Guru. Having obtained that mantra which is difficult to attain, a man indeed becomes free from thirst [for worldly objects].
Therefore, he desires neither sense objects nor liberation, but something between the two;
for if he should desire sense objects, he eats poison—of this there is no doubt.
"I am Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Dharma, Ananta, and Kaśyapa."
Kapila and Kumāra, the sages Nara and Nārāyaṇa;
Svāyambhuva Manu, Prahlāda, and Parāśara;
Bhṛgu, Śukra, Durvāsas, Vasiṣṭha, Kratu, and Aṅgiras. (1.37–1.38)
Bali, the Vālakhilyas, Varuṇa, the Fire-god, Vāyu, Sūrya, Garuḍa, Dakṣa, Gaṇapati, and the Earth—
all of us are the servants of Kṛṣṇa, his partial incarnations, free from pride.
Worship: Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord.
(1.445.140) Recite: Oṃ Śrīṃ Hrīṃ Klīṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Śrī.
We shall go to where Śukra, Candra, and the stars indeed dwell. (141)

Thus ends the four hundred and forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Abduction of Tārā, the Chaste Wife of Bṛhaspati, by Candra; Candra’s Flight to Śukrācārya for Refuge out of Fear; the Demonstration of the Purity of Both; and the Consequence of Bṛhaspati’s Abduction of the Wife of his Younger Brother named Utathya, as well as the Consultation among Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, Indra, and Bṛhaspati for the Recovery of Tārā," in the first section concerning the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
