Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, Lakṣmī! Having heard the words of Hara, Bṛhaspati himself, a great devotee of the Bhagavān, spoke out of a spirit of detachment. (1)
Having attained such knowledge, he became despondent and spoke to Hara:
"O Ocean of Mercy, give me your command; I shall go to perform penance for Hari.
Let Tārā remain right there; I have no need for her."
Ignorance afflicts the deluded one who is submerged in it; by your grace, may I overcome it.
Having become a man, I shall attain Hari; what need have I for womanhood?
That which is outside Hari appears as nectar, yet everything else is poison.
"I take refuge in Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the supreme beyond the supreme.
To him who had spoken thus, Śambhu smiled and said to Bṛhaspati:
"O Sage, having abandoned a woman seized by another, this austerity is not praiseworthy."
For one who has been highly esteemed, misconduct is worse than death.
(6) O Sage, having encountered your own wife seized by the hand of an enemy, you must now decide what is to be done: should you fulfill your domestic duties or practice asceticism? (7)
Let us all go, the upholders of the burden, to where Śukra is; for there are Sūrya, Dharma, Ananta-Śeṣa, Nara, Nārāyaṇa,
the Unborn, Kratu, Sanatkumāra, Vasiṣṭha, and Marīci.
Sanātana, Sananda, Voḍhā, Pañcaśikha, Patnīvrata, Kapila, and Aṅgiras—
having spoken thus, they all departed for the hermitage of Śukra, accompanied by Śiva.
Śukra bowed down to them all and honored them with respect;
at that time, the sons of Diti, filled with fear, also bowed to the gods.
Śukra, his hair standing on end and his eyes brimming with tears, then spoke.
Today my birth has become fruitful and my life well-lived.
(1.2) I have personally seen the Lord, the Creator himself, in his own abode;
and I have personally seen his sons, the eternal Lords. (1.3)
Today the glorious Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa is entirely pleased with me;
Nārāyaṇa himself, the Lord of Lakṣmī, has come to my home.
Śambhu himself, in the form of Brahmā, and the bestowers of liberation have also arrived.
"Out of compassion, you have indeed come to me to make me one who has accomplished his purpose.
To those who delight in their own Self, this inquiry in the form of a question is a mere pretense;
you have surely come here to purify my son."
"Tell me further, O Teacher, what else may I do for you?
Having heard this, the Creator of the Universe said, "May it ever be well with you;
I have come to see you, my grandson, being distressed by our long separation."
"O grandson, is it well with you and your family? Are you free from ailment?
(18) Is your daily worship of Śrī Kṛṣṇa proceeding auspiciously? And is your service to your own guru also proceeding auspiciously for you? (19)
The worship of the guru, Kṛṣṇa, one’s parents, and the elderly is meritorious;
it removes all suffering and protects against future calamities.
When the guru is satisfied, the beloved deity becomes pleased in this world.
When one's chosen deity is satisfied, all the gods are satisfied.
(21) But for those sinners here whose guru, brahmin, or god is enraged, there is no well-being; for them, obstacles arise moment by moment. (22)
I, your preceptor, am pleased with you, and Hari himself is likewise pleased. When Hari is pleased, all the gods are pleased; may there be well-being for you.
Now, O wise one, hear from me the reason for my coming here.

Having abducted Tārā, the virtuous wife of Bṛhaspati, the son of Kṛṣṇavara, the Lord of Night has come to you for refuge. Give back Tārā according to the path of justice; then all will be well with you. (24-25)
Previously, you learned that Candra has been purified according to dharma;
Tārā is a virtuous woman and remains eternally pure, for women are by nature ever-pure.
We shall not inflict punishment upon Candra; therefore, abandon all fear of him entirely.

If there should be war during Adāna, there will be destruction for both sides. Or, if the Moon or Jupiter occupies Tārā, there is destruction for the two factions—the gods and the demons—numbering in the tens of millions. (27–28)
But now, having censured injustice, you must practice justice;
for war between the gods and the Daityas is the cause of destruction for both.
O grandson, acting with great conciliation is the cause of all auspiciousness.
"O Tārā, grant alms to me, a mendicant and a wise man!
O illustrious one, give up Tārā, who is dearer to you than life itself; likewise, give up Candra.
Preserve your own fame for a very long time—we entreat you again and again."
Having heard that, Śukra spoke to the three gods, the great-grandfathers:
"The virtuous Tārā remains pregnant due to her union with Candra;
O great-grandfathers, you are the authority as to whether she should be given back now or not."
Brahmā said: "She must indeed be given; no hesitation should be made in this matter.
By our power, we shall certainly cause her to undergo pregnancy and childbirth.
O son, bring the Lord of the Night (the Moon) here, along with Tārā, who is pregnant."
Thus addressed, Śukra quickly summoned Tārā and the Moon,
and with great shame, he gave her to those two great beings.
Having given Tārā to the Moon, Śukra prostrated at the feet of Brahmā.
Brahmā beheld Tārā, who was devoted to his own station and bowing before him;
she had her face cast down with shame, was weeping bitterly, and was auspiciously pregnant.
Taking the moon, who was prostrate before him, onto his lap, the Creator granted him freedom from fear.
The Great-Grandfather spoke to the pregnant Tārā, who was filled with fear:
"You shall be endowed with good fortune toward your husband; cast away your fear.
A weak woman seized by a powerful one does not suffer a fall if she is free from desire."

She who is purified by mental distress or again by menstruation—thereafter, through union with her own husband, a woman is not defiled by a paramour. She who, being desirous, approaches a paramour out of desire for her own pleasure [is not at fault]. (1.446.40)
Even after performing penance, she was not purified so long as she was deprived of her husband;
you, however, are eternally virtuous and pure, as purifying as fire.
Indeed, it was only through the ritual act of Bṛhaspati that his wife was taken away.
Indeed, your abduction here occurred due to your own karma and yoga;
however, what the true reality is in this matter even the deities do not know.
Except for the three gods, behold that secret hidden by my power.
When the Moon indeed abducted you, he was not able to touch you;
for no one is able to touch a goddess who is devoted to her husband.
However, the radiance of the Sun, having arrived there in embodied form—
He created a second [form], Tārāchāyā, a likeness of Tārā.
Having caused the real Tārā to vanish, he led her into the orb of the sun.
From that time until today, she remains resplendent, great, divine, virtuous, and pure.
"Behold your own original form, brought here by my power exactly as it is;
likewise, behold this shadow-form, pregnant and attended by the Moon.
Having spoken thus, the Creator of the Universe showed Tārakā in two forms.
Then they gave another *mūla-tārā* to the preceptor of the gods.
They said to Tārā, "Release the fetus; by our power, it shall be fully developed.
Having been addressed thus, she quickly went inside her house and gave birth to him.
As soon as he was born, he became a youth with a golden complexion, equal to the moon.
There, the Moon himself performed the birth rites and other ceremonies.
Then, by the command of Brahmā, Tārā’s shadow became invisible.
Sūryaprabhā took that invisible maiden as her own daughter.
She, however, always worshipped Kṛṣṇa in the sun;
as Prabhā’s servant, she constantly performed service unto Kṛṣṇa alone.
During the month of Puruṣottama, that virtuous woman, together with Prabhā,
went to the imperishable abode of the glorious Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. Having become a divine, eternally liberated great-muktā, the virtuous Satī became beloved by Kṛṣṇa.
Having obtained her husband, Mūlatārā became fearless once again.
Brahmā joyfully explained to her the duties of a virtuous wife (*satīdharma*), which are performed in times of distress and were established during the Kṛta Yuga. ||54-55||
Listen, Lakṣmī! I shall declare those by which even women remain unstained:
when a woman is devoted to her husband’s vow of fidelity by the command of her lord, she is not defiled by speaking with another; therefore, the word of the master is dharma.

If a husband bestows a gift—whether momentary or permanent—upon someone, that woman, even though she has enjoyed it, is never at all defiled. Because ownership passes to the recipient through the act of giving, the woman is not tainted. (17–58)
A woman who, being helpless, is forcibly enjoyed by someone in a deserted place or similar setting—

even if she is unwilling and dependent on another— is never at fault in any way. Likewise, one who is enjoyed by perfected beings (siddhas) through yoga and other means after they have entered her husband, [is not at fault].
Even she who has been enjoyed by one in a fabricated form is not at all defiled.
O Lotus-born One, she who has fallen into sleep or a swoon while unconscious from eating intoxicants— even if she has been enjoyed by another in that state, she is not at all defiled.
If, during an extremely dire time, she is enjoyed by another for the sake of preserving the lives of her husband, father, son, or brother, she is not at fault.
She who is honored by another for the sake of offspring, for the sake of cows, or for the sake of the family [is likewise blameless].

Nor is there any fault in [accepting] a girl who has not been deflowered for the sake of a sonless man or for the sake of a maiden. (63) In times of calamity, when life is at stake, or during the upheaval of a country, village, or the like, a woman who has been enjoyed by another or is dependent on another is not at all defiled then. (64)

In the practice of yoga according to the Gāndharva rite, a woman who has been enjoyed by another does not incur fault. When her menstrual period has ceased and she is united with her husband during her fertile season, a woman who has gone to another man is indeed never at fault.
One who has been enjoyed by another does not incur fault if it is for the sake of accomplishing the master’s purpose.
(66) However, a host of Apsarases sent by their master Indra to create obstacles for an ascetic’s penance—even if she has been enjoyed by another—does not incur fault. (67)
Female servants who have performed service for kings and have been surrendered [to others],
even if enjoyed by another, are not at all blameworthy as attendants.
Those who have entered the state of being courtesans have done so solely for the sake of their livelihood when they were in distress.
If she has been enjoyed by another, there is no fault in her merely being without a protector.

A woman who has no husband, who is skilled in dance and song, and who, being under the control of another, has been deluded by a Gandharva [rite], is not at fault even if she is enjoyed by another. (1.446.70)
One who has been enjoyed by another for the sake of preserving her life does not incur sin;

nor does one who, terrified by the fear of curses and the like, has been enjoyed by another upon encountering separation from a powerful man, provided it is for the purpose of avoiding suffering. (71)

A virtuous woman who has been enjoyed by those who are portions of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa and others does not incur sin. However, union with Viṣṇu through Tulasī indicates the excellence of her husband; otherwise, such union with another may cause a woman to become a slayer of her husband.
Indeed, for the sake of obtaining a son who will continue the thread of her own lineage,
a woman who has been enjoyed by another is never at all defiled;
even if she has been enjoyed by divine beings or gods, she is not defiled at all.
Ahalyā’s transformation into stone through union with Indra was the fruit of her husband’s curse.
However, a virtuous woman who is enjoyed by another in a dream is not defiled;
nor is she defiled if she is enjoyed by spirits, ghosts, and the like, for they are merely portions of air.
She who is bestowed by her parents upon someone does not incur blame through that act;
nor is there blame in taking as a wife a young woman who has arrived without a protector. Devotion to one's husband is the supreme duty; to violate it out of one's own will is a transgression.

The fact that [the husband’s] purpose is for the sake of another is an ornament when it accords with the duty toward a husband; however, if it were by force, it would be a defect on the part of the stronger man, but not on the part of the woman. Furthermore, if dharma, characterized by injunction, were not to result in harm, [then this would be acceptable]. (78–79)
"In the case of failure, the fruit is certainly suffering that must be endured;
thus has Dharma always been determined by us gods.
Therefore, Tārā, who was ever pure, became a remarried woman yet remained devoted to her husband.
Even while experiencing the fruit [of his actions], Candra shall remain fixed as a deity.
Indeed, during the monthly period of menstruation, a woman’s purity is destroyed;
yet by bathing, that virtuous and faithful wife becomes pure, purifying, and equal to the earth.
The field is said to be the seed-vessel, fashioned for the sowing of seeds;
having provided ripening during the cool season, it is heated by the sun's heat in summer.
In the rainy season, through the bestowal of water, it becomes pure and yields grains.
The woman is a field, a vessel for seed, fashioned for the sowing of seed.
Always cool after ripening, she becomes heated during her menses;
purified by the giving of the seed through impregnation, she yields children. (84–85)
"Therefore, just as a field becomes pure every year,
so too does the field consisting of a noble soul become purified month by month.
Having thus bestowed her status as a devoted wife (*pātivratya*), all the gods and others [departed].
Having given the virtuous Tārā to her preceptor and having granted him complete protection,
the gods went to their own abode and Bṛhaspati to his own home;
that chaste woman continued to uphold the supreme dharma of devotion to her husband.
The Lord of Speech (Bṛhaspati) also observed the vow of fidelity toward his wife.
Then Budha, the son of Tārā and the planet born from the Moon,
reached his beloved and virtuous wife Citrā in the Nandana grove.
Born from the womb of Ghṛtācī through the seed of Kubera,
the son of Candra took her as his wife by the Gāndharva rite of marriage. Their son was Caitra, the sovereign of the earth with its seven continents.
His son was named Adhiratha, and his son was called Suratha.
Born through ascetic penance, he is the eighth Manu;
known by the name Sāvarṇi, he is indeed a supreme Vaiṣṇava.
"From reading and from hearing this, the fruit of wifely devotion (*pātivratya*) shall arise.

(93) Thus ends the four hundred and forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of Tārā’s Offering to Bṛhaspati in the Kṛta Yuga Lineage, the Birth of Budha, the Duties of Women in Times of Adversity and Purity, and the Faultlessness of Wifely Devotion," in the First Book, the *Kṛtayugasantāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Chapter 448 → Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
The gurus are stainless, peaceful, virtuous, and benefactors;
the name-mantra bestowed by them out of compassion becomes efficacious.
Devotion to the husband is the supreme dharma, made firm by the name of Kṛṣṇa.

It shall bestow spiritual accomplishments (*siddhi*), sovereignty, all desired objects, and wonders. Listen, Lakṣmī! To the story of Rājavatī, a Vaiṣṇava woman, and how she attained divine perfection through her devotion and service. (2–3)
In Mathurā there was a king named Dāśārha, who was steadfast,
generous, invincible, statesmanlike, and skilled in the scriptures.
He indeed [married] Kalāvatī, the devoted wife who was the daughter of the King of Kāśī.
He married Satī, the virtuous daughter of Viṣṇu, who was endowed with righteousness. From her childhood, Kalāvatī always worshipped the eternal Kṛṣṇa, saying:
"O Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, deliver me from the ocean of worldly existence."
"O Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa-Viṣṇu! O Lord of Śrī! O Lord of Kamalā!"—thus she, devoted to bhakti, offered her prayers daily.
"Kṛṣṇa is my husband; Nārāyaṇa is my husband; Śrī Rādhikā is my husband."
"I am indeed Rādhā, I am Lakṣmī, I am Śrī the inseparable"—
having thus attained identity with Hari within herself, she who perceives through yoga beholds her husband Kṛṣṇa day and night with divine vision.
When the young woman, that yoginī, had thus attained this state,
the descendant of Daśārha, having performed the marriage ceremony, brought her to his own palace and summoned his wife to the bed of love for union.
Having arrived, she quickly prostrated herself out of fear;
she sat comfortably in the midst of the young and old female disciples.
The king reflected: "What could be the cause of this?"
"Though she is young, that maiden does not desire me, though I am a youth.
Let it be as it may; the truth will gradually be known.
Having thus shown forbearance, the descendant of Daśārha, being composed, passed that night.
Thus that descendant of Daśārha, filled with lust, constantly challenges her.
But she, having arrived and offered her salutations, departs in haste, repeatedly saying:
"O Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa, Viṣṇu! O Lord, let there be salutation unto you again and again."
Having uttered this, she departs and takes her stand among women;
that devoted wife does not remain there alone anywhere. Solitude is not pleasing to her, yet the king desires solitude.
The young woman was repeatedly offered by the king for the sake of pleasure.
Thereupon, she firmly set her mind upon a life free from desire.
Though summoned by her husband and entreated many times, she remained steadfast. (17–18)
He did not fix his mind upon her, nor did he go near her;
for when she was summoned to the marriage, she did not come.
Desiring to take her by force, the lord of the earth rose up.
Then she said to the king: "O Lord of the Earth, do not touch me!
Do not commit an act of rashness toward me; I am engaged in a vow that contains a specific purpose.
I shall indeed show you that purpose for which I have undertaken this vow."
And you, O King, understand the Dharma that is more profound than the profound.
If the digestion of what has been eaten results in something unpleasant, it increases one's suffering;
yet, through the union of love between husband and wife, their coming together increases happiness.
"When affection arises within me, then let there be union with you.
[23] What pleasure or what happiness can men derive from women through forceful enjoyment—whether they are displeased, diseased, virgins, pregnant, or observing vows? [24]
A man should not forcibly desire a woman who is menstruating or one who is unwilling.
[He should instead cultivate] pleasing her, fondling her, nourishing her, delighting her, gentleness, compassion,
attracting her, unifying the mind, and the cultivation of a sense of her well-being.
Having performed the marriage rites, the loving husband should approach his young bride.
Even then, a righteous master should not engage in sexual enjoyment in vain;
for there is the sin of killing an embryo (bhrūṇahatyā) in the emission of seed in vain.
"O King, one should not deposit seed through sexual enjoyment upon a woman before her menses have been observed; do not, O bull among men, indulge in lust here with such a vain obsession for desire.
Though addressed thus by that virtuous woman, the descendant of Daśārha was driven by the force of passion.
Drawing the young woman toward him by force, he embraced her with a desire for dalliance.
She, having said, "Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord," bowed to her husband and cried out, "Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa! (1.447.30).
For that long, a fire indeed remained hidden within her body;
it was visible to the eye, yet it did not burn at all.
As soon as she was touched, she suddenly became like a heated ball of iron.
Overwhelmed by fear, he abandoned her as she seemed to consume him with fire.
The king recognized that queen, the virtuous one who was filled with wonder, and said:
"Oh, a great marvel has been seen here in you, my beloved! (32-33)
"How has this body, so delicate as a flower, become composed of fire?
Forgive my rashness in this matter; I shall not do such a thing again.
Thus he spoke in fear, and the devoted wife replied to him:

"O King, I am a virtuous woman, devoted to dharma and truth; I desire union [with you], not out of any other lustful impulse like a base woman seeking sensual pleasure. In my previous life as well, I observed celibacy in exactly the same way. (35–36)
In this life as well, I likewise desire the highest vow:
"May Agni himself provide protection for me, a wife devoted to dharma.
If you touch me at an improper time, he shall reduce you to ashes. (37)
By the power of my previously cultivated virtuous conduct, in this life,
the king of sages Durvāsas— a devotee of Kṛṣṇa and a supreme Vaiṣṇava—
bestowed upon me the purifying Śrī Kṛṣṇa mantra, which is my excellent protector. (38–39)
From my childhood, I have always chanted "Obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa" alone;
and furthermore, I constantly recite this second great mantra:
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya pataye namaḥ. (1.447.40)
And by that sixteen-syllable mantra, I am protected by him who is resplendent like fire.
(41) By the power of that mantra, my body is freed from impurity;
it cannot be touched by men who are possessed of sin and abandoned by fortune. (42)
O King, you have always served female slaves,
handmaidens, unchaste women, courtesans, and others who consume wine and meat.
Because of that sin, you remain devoid of luster, even though you are a Kṣatriya.
Even when she has been obtained, he is not fit for her; what could be more wicked than this?
(44) Even though she is his wedded wife, he is unable to enjoy her;
the life of that man who experiences the mountain of his former sins is indeed in vain. (45)
"You do not bathe daily, nor do you recite mantras;
you do not worship your husband Kṛṣṇa—how, then, can he be worthy of touching me?
O King, you have never observed the vows of a devoted wife."
O King, by that sin, your power has gone to ruin.
O King, what is the use of sensual enjoyment which does not accompany one?
One should acquire that happiness which is eternal and accompanies the self.
One who is greedy for wombs obtains birth from a womb; there is no doubt about this.
One who is greedy for Kṛṣṇa attains the abode of Hari; there is no doubt about this.
I am married, and I am entirely devoted to the dharma of Kṛṣṇa.

And being unattached to the nature of desire, therefore always abandon desire. Desire here takes the form of hell; it resides in the womb and in the sexual organ. How indeed could one who possesses true knowledge be lured by that which is hell?
The womb-cavity is ever-falling apart and filled with the foul stench of urine;
how could a pure being attach itself to such a place consisting of mere excrement?
There, those who have been cooked go again for the sake of being cooked.
There, the ignorant go by force indeed toward the cause of their downfall.
How then should the wise go again and again into the pit of death?
Abandon greed for the pit of rebirth; plunge rather into the pit of Brahman.
Offer your own body into the fire of another’s blackness for the sake of liberation.
You have enjoyed many female slaves and have looked upon all as equals;
yet does thirst still afflict you? What sin could be greater than this?
Food swallowed by the tongue is then roasted by the fire of the intestines.

Having become liquid, it moves downward; becoming hot, oily, and watery in nature, it undergoes a process of straining (*kharjana*), and by that means the pit of urine (*mūtrakuṇḍaka*) is remembered [as its destination]. (56–57)
Fie upon this food which does not indeed remind one of Kṛṣṇa!
Fie upon this state of desire which does not grant service to Kṛṣṇa! Fie upon that husband and that wife who have not dedicated themselves to Kṛṣṇa!
"O King, worship Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa after due reflection," he said.
Indeed, that is declared to be the vow of a wife (*patnīvrata*) by which Kṛṣṇa is attained;
and that is the duty of devotion to one's husband (*pātivratya*) by which Kṛṣṇa is indeed attained.
Thus addressed, the king then attained knowledge regarding his own wife; becoming dispassionate, he said to the virtuous woman: "Tell me that mantra as well.
Having my sins destroyed by its recitation, I desire a perfect union with you."
"But the door of my ignorance has been flung open by you, O beloved.
The Queen, having honored her husband, said: "I am not worthy of that;
I shall certainly not act upon your instruction, for you are my guru."
"O King, attend upon the preceptor Garga, the best among those who know the mantras.
While conversing thus, the couple reached the presence of Garga and,
with palms joined in reverence, bowed their heads at his feet.
Then the king, having honored his preceptor who was well-pleased again and again, spoke with a humble soul regarding the secret desire of his heart:
"O Preceptor, make me successful; I have come to you as one who has sought refuge."

You ought to instruct me in that supreme knowledge which bestows liberation. Whatever has been done by the king’s action—whether unknown or known, whether dry or moist, great or small—that sin born of the power of *māyā*. (67)
O Guru, grant me that mantra by which all of that may be purified!
Indeed, without the association of the virtuous, there can never be the destruction of the sins of sinners, nor even the purification of the self. (68–69)
In every age, men and women always serve virtuous persons for the sake of purifying their sins; for from them comes liberation, and from them comes Hari.
They are fed, saluted, seen, touched, and their feet are massaged.
When properly served within one's own body, they fulfill the desires of those who serve them. Whatever may be dear to oneself should always be given to the virtuous;
for the virtuous are beyond material qualities, they are the fourfold goals of life personified, and they are the very forms of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
The fruit of service to Kṛṣṇa is obtained even more abundantly through service to the saintly;
these sinless saints bestow the attainment of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
Just as love for a beloved arises in a woman of desire through her longing, [so does devotion arise through the saints].
Just as a thirsty person [longs] for water, and a hungry person for food;
just as affection arises for fire in one overcome by cold;
and just as there is longing for a son who possesses good qualities in a father who himself is full of desire. (74–75)
Just as medicine [is for one] suffering from a severe illness, or as a mother's [affection is for her] child, so too,
affection shown toward virtuous people certainly saves one.
Just as images made of stone and other materials, though insentient, become possessed of consciousness [when consecrated].
Likewise, the divine images of Hari possess auspicious forms and celestial consciousness.
Whatever is given, offered in sacrifice, cast, or dedicated there— whether auspicious or inauspicious—
all that bestows liberation, prosperity, and one's desired goals upon human beings.
For those men and women who have no other support,
the virtuous, the stars, and the devotees of the Lord are their supports and their protectors.
Therefore, O Garga, grant me purification through the bestowal of mantras.
Thus entreated by the king, Garga, the preeminent among the Vaiṣṇavas,
led the two of them to the auspicious and highly meritorious bank of the Yamunā.
There, the Guru himself sat down beside a *vṛndā* tree.
Having bathed in the waters of the Yamunā-tīrtha, having fasted, and having seated the descendant of Daśārha facing the east, he bowed to the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa,
placed his hand upon the other’s head, and imparted the mantra whose essence is Kṛṣṇa.
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; obeisance! (83).
He held this mantra, "Obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa," at his ear;
by the mere retention of that mantra and through the touch of his guru's hand, [he attained realization]. (84)
Hundreds of millions of crows emerged from his body;
with their wings scorched, they cried out as they fell upon the surface of the earth,
and then they were all seen by the thousands, reduced to ashes.
Having seen that, the king and queen questioned their preceptor Garga:
"O Blessed One, tell me clearly: what is this marvel? Why has this flock of crows emerged from my body and been consumed by fire?"
Garga said: "Indeed, while wandering through thousands of births, you have accumulated many sins that are difficult to overcome;
yet, by the power of merit, you have indeed been born here as a king of men. (88)
And those most wicked deeds you have now committed—
by the mere utterance of the mantra, they have emerged from your body;
these are all the crows, whose very nature is the darkness of sin.
The millions of your sins were seen being consumed by fire;
thus you are purified, O Indra among kings—worship the eternal Kṛṣṇa.
Then indeed you shall become endowed with the splendors of Kṛṣṇa.
Therefore, you shall always be fit to sport with this radiant woman during her fertile period,
at the proper, measured, and auspicious time.
Otherwise, the fire of that virtuous wife will consume you like a crow.
Having spoken thus, the sage Garga, having received hospitality and worship, departed for his own hermitage; the king went to his palace with the queen.
Those two Vaiṣṇava couple, possessing great splendor, shone forth.
Then, by the power of the mantra, after more than a hundred thousand recitations,
the king became a worthy recipient for his wife's touch, possessing a divine body. At that time, he firmly embraced his wife, who was cool as sandalwood.
Thus, at the time of her menses, Satyā attained supreme contentment;
indeed, she had observed for a full year Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s merit-bestowing vow, maintaining perfect celibacy throughout. (97)
At the end of a year, the king also became purified like fire.
Then he sowed the seed whose fruit was the attainment of a son.
When nine months had passed, he obtained a son who was a true devotee of Viṣṇu.

Thus, O Lakṣmī! This wonder arising from Kṛṣṇa’s devotion to his wife has been told to you; by hearing or reciting it, one obtains such a fruit. Thus ends the four hundred and forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of Wonders," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. It describes how, while King Dāśārha was in a state of sinfulness, the fire that was burning him was extinguished upon contact with the wife who was solely devoted to her vow of devotion to Kṛṣṇa; and how, thereafter, through the taking of Kṛṣṇa’s mantra, his sins were burnt away, resulting in purification and fitness for touch once again.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: O Lakṣmī! In the past, I assumed the form of Sadāśiva, which consists of renunciation and dispassion, and is the cause of the dissolution of all things.

In former times, in Āryāvarta, there was a most righteous king named Citravarmā, who was a worshipper of my form as Śiva on Mondays. He was a diligent protector of the bridges of dharma and a performer of sacrifices and other sacred rites.
He was a donor, a refuge for merits, and a devotee of Śiva and Mukunda.
(3) After many sons, a daughter was born to his wife; as soon as she was born, she spoke of the deeds of her previous births. (4)
She was a virtuous and chaste woman who remembered her past lives, devoted to the dharma of Kṛṣṇa,
always delighted in meditating upon the glorious Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, and pure. Devoted to her husband, she never at any time thought of anyone other than Kṛṣṇa.
Once, in his home, the king fed Kṛṣṇa’s saintly devotees,
thousands of brāhmaṇas, celibate youths, and young girls, as well as astrologers, fortune-tellers, palmists, and yogīs. (6–7)
For the purpose of giving them betel, the maiden became intent on their service;
upon seeing her, the astrologers each proclaimed a different result.
One said, "O King, your daughter shall be named Sīmantinī."
Like Pārvatī, she was most auspicious; like Rādhā, she was beautiful in form. Like Śaradā, she was skilled in the arts; like Lakṣmī, she possessed great virtues.
Like Devamātā, she was a mother of noble offspring; like Satī, O Kṛṣṇa, she was firm in her vows.
Like a ruby attached to gold, or like radiance resting upon Krishna,
she shall rejoice for ten thousand years together with her husband. Endowed with eight sons, she will be filled with happiness.
Then another twice-born man, fearless, spoke at that time by means of lines:
"In her fourteenth year, she will attain widowhood;
thereafter, she will again obtain a husband whose form is like that of a corpse."
Having heard the king’s words, which were like a thunderbolt, she too grieved;
yet, considering everything to be the work of fate, she abandoned her sorrow.
The young girl, named Sīmantinī, was apprehensive regarding her future widowhood.
He questioned Maitreyī, the wife of the sage Yājñavalkya:
"O Mother, you are a knower of Brahman, a Vaiṣṇavī who has offered yourself to Kṛṣṇa,
a preeminent treasury of knowledge, and indeed the destroyer of all calamities."
"O Mother, I have sought refuge at your lotus feet, afflicted as I am by fear.
The Brahmins say that widowhood awaits me here; tell me, what will happen?
Furthermore, they have also declared that I shall obtain that very same husband once again. (17)
"Therefore, O sinless one, tell me a meritorious deed for the sake of increasing my good fortune!
Having been addressed thus, Maitreyī spoke to her of the Śrīpārvatī-vrata:
"On Monday, worship Śiva, Gaurī, and the Lord of Śrī."
Having fasted, well-bathed, and wearing stainless garments, devoted to your chastity toward Kṛṣṇa, perform the worship in the morning.
Through the ritual ablution, there shall be the destruction of sins; through the worship of His feet, there shall be imperial sovereignty.
Through the offering of perfumes, garlands, and unbroken grains (akṣata), one attains all good fortune and happiness;

through the gift of incense, fragrance; through the offering of lamps, splendor; through food offerings (naivedya), great enjoyments; and through the gift of betel leaves, prosperity (lakṣmī). (21–22)
Through the offering of a handful of flowers with the salutation "Namo," there arise dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa;

and through the self-surrender to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the eightfold sovereign powers (aṣṭaiśvarya) beginning with siddhi are attained. Indeed, by means of the fire-oblation (homa), all desires come to fruition.
All the gods are pleased by the feeding of virtuous Brahmins. (24) In this manner, O daughter, propitiate Śiva and Śivā together with Kṛṣṇa;
O child, you will cross over a terror more terrible than the terrible, without a doubt. (25)
Having been addressed thus, the maiden honored Maitreyī with various gifts;
returning home, she performed this vow which increases good fortune.
By means of that, the virtuous woman became endowed with spiritual perfection, equal in splendor to Pārvatī.
Then the girl’s father, Citravarman, gave her to Candrāṅgada,
the son of Nala and the offspring of Indrasena. At that wedding, there was a great assembly of kings.
When the great festival had concluded, the son-in-law resided in his father-in-law's house for several months out of affection for his daughter.
Once, some boys boarded a boat to cross the Yamunā.
By the turn of fate, their boat was struck by a whirlpool as they traveled through the middle;
they sank into the water, and those delicate youths perished.
For once submerged in the great waters, those princes could no longer be seen.
A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose from the king, the queen, and the subjects;
likewise from the women, their friends, the leaders, and the priests.
The ministers wailed, and Indrasena also lamented.
In the great flood of the Yamunā, even corpses were submerged.
Citravarmā performed the funeral rites;
but that virtuous woman, a yoginī, was then like a yogi.
Remaining in her palace, she practiced self-restraint solely for the sake of her husband;
the virtuous woman quickly entered into meditative absorption within the depths of the water. Possessing many forms, that chaste lady was endowed with manifold powers.
Then that virtuous woman drank up the Yamunā with her cupped hands;
at once the Yamunā became as dry as the sacrificial ground.
Corpses were seen there, and she carried them to the bank.
She repeatedly summoned those who had gone to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*) as well as those who had gone to the realm of Yama; being devoted to truth, they arrived there.
All of them were seen alive, having fallen upon the earth.
As soon as Candrāṅgada was seen by the well-born daughters of the serpents,
who were filled with desire, he was led to Pātāla;
he was taken to the city of Takṣaka, which was more auspicious than Indra’s heaven.
Surrounded on all sides by a thousand Naga maidens who were radiant with beauty, youth, sweetness, charm, and graceful gait,
Takṣaka beheld that prince accompanied by the maidens.
He asked about the entire account, and the maidens told him exactly as it had happened.
Then Candrāṅgada, while muttering the mantra "Śiva-Kṛṣṇa," was heard,
seen, and addressed with great respect by Takṣaka.
I am well-pleased; may it be well with you who are endowed with devotion, for even though you are but a child, you chant the names of Śiva and Kṛṣṇa incessantly.
This world is composed of jewels, and these women possess beautiful eyes.
"All these are wish-fulfilling trees, and these ponds contain waters of ambrosial flavor. Sport among them as you please and enjoy the pleasures appropriate to you.
Having heard this, the prince replied, "I am already married."
My beloved wife is devoted to her husband, chaste, virtuous, and observant of auspicious vows;
she is dedicated to devotion toward Kṛṣṇa, yet thinking me dead, she will thereafter assume the signs of widowhood.
Or else, she will [assume them] with all the outward marks of widowhood.
Since that virtuous woman will enter the fire,
I must by no means remain here for much longer.
Therefore, out of compassion, you ought to lead me to that very same world.
To Candrāṅga, who had spoken thus,
Takṣaka gave for the sake of pleasing his daughters, for their enjoyment, and for their pleasure: habitations fit for enjoyment, vehicles, and all kinds of ambrosial foods.
Then, not seeing her beloved husband there,
that virtuous wife called out to the ocean, indeed by means of truth and her religious vow:
"If I am in every way a devotee of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa..."
If I am a devoted wife whose life is entirely dedicated to my husband,
and if I am endowed with vows for the sake of pleasing Śiva who is united with Śivā,
then let the ocean come here into my very presence.
Having spoken thus, she released the water held in her hand onto the ground.
At that moment, the Ocean, appearing in personified form, arrived in great fear;
he bowed before the virtuous lady and gratified her with gifts of jewels.
She said to her: "Your husband has certainly not been abducted by me.
The beautiful bridegroom has been led away to Pātāla by the daughters of the *suparṇas*. Having gratified those excellent serpent-maidens, he will return quickly. (56)
Having spoken thus, the ocean departed, and Sīmantinī was exceedingly joyful.
However, by the ignorant chief ministers, the royal priests, and others,
she was forcibly made to display the very signs of widowhood there.
Then, having gratified the maidens with a chariot and abundant jewels,
he took all those auspicious Naga daughters— adorned with ornaments, garments, and the like—
and having been presented by Takṣaka, he returned to the Yamunā.

The virtuous woman Satī, having seen you arrive in her dream at the waters of the Yamunā, rose up and went there with her companions, taking the materials for worship. On the riverbank, she beheld her beloved husband sporting there. (1.448.60–61)
Beholding her— studded with divine jewels, adorned with celestial garlands and ornaments,
possessing a body of divine fragrance, of unprecedented form, and brilliantly radiant—
the queen stood like one deprived of consciousness, her eyes fixed intently upon her.
And beholding her, Candrāṅgada fainted for a moment—she who was divested of neck-ornaments and bereft of her neck-thread; her hair-knot unbound and her body devoid of unguents. (63–64)
Having summoned her, who was somewhat stained by the duties of widowhood, he said this:
"O virtuous lady, what is this that is seen, which betokens your grief?
Thus questioned with affection, she, with eyes full of tears, did not speak.
A friend said: "She was forcibly made a widow by people;
for one who is without a husband and protectorless, that indeed is her lot.
Yet she has not abandoned her vow of Monday, nor has she forsaken her devotion to her husband."
Service to Kṛṣṇa has not been abandoned; everything remains exactly as it was.
O King, you have obtained the very fruit of the vow demonstrated by the wife of the sage through your beloved. Accept this blameless woman.
Thus addressed, he took his own wife onto his chest and pressed her close.
Then, seeing the prince arrived there, the citizens went quickly to the king and informed him; the king, the queen, and the townspeople [all gathered].
Having gone out to meet him and embraced him, they led him to their own home;
the prince, shedding tears, paid homage to his parents-in-law.
The subjects honored him and greeted him with blessings.
Seated in their midst, he reported his entire adventure in full to the king;
he informed the king of Takṣaka’s great friendship and presented all the divine jewels and other gifts that had been given.
Then, auspicious news concerning his wife spread throughout the kingdom;
likewise, the story was told by people in the kingdom of his father.
Both parents and all the subjects of Niṣadha were exceedingly joyful.
A great festival took place throughout the kingdoms, villages, cities, and other regions.
Having obtained a husband, the woman— having cast off the marks of widowhood and possessing the auspicious signs of conjugal bliss— circumambulated the fire and became blessed with good fortune.
Candrāṅgada personally presented the vermilion and other auspicious items;
they both applied a beautiful mark with unbroken grains of rice upon one another.
They also exchanged divine garlands with one another.
They both gave him betel-leaf and various other gifts.
Then, having bowed to his parents-in-law, he went with his wife to his own home in Niṣadha; there, he fell at the feet of his parents.
For ten thousand years, King Candrāṅgada enjoyed many worldly pleasures together with his wife Sīmantinī;
she bore him eight sons and one daughter of beautiful countenance.
The woman rejoiced with her husband while meditating upon Hari and Hara.
Day by day, moreover, she attained good fortune from the lunar day of the moon;
thus, O Lakṣmī, devotion to one’s husband always triumphs on earth.

If devotion to one’s husband is preserved in heaven, in the true world of Brahmā, in the nether regions, or among women, it shall grant all perfections. Always regarding her husband as the very form of Kṛṣṇa and meditating upon him, the virtuous woman [attains this].
One should practice the dharma of devotion to one's husband, which is equal to the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa).
For women who are dependent on others and whose desires are directed toward their husbands, their bodies—which are otherwise a refuge for sin—become instead givers of even greater merit. (84–85)
Sin is indeed an excess of desire, while merit is service performed at every step.
Service to one’s husband is service to Kṛṣṇa; it is the practice of vows, charity, and so forth.
It is service to guests, service to the virtuous, and service to cows at every step. (86)
Service to children who are free from sin and whose nature is that of Brahman;

service consisting of the protection of the home, the cooking of food and other items over the fire, the performance of the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, and the feeding of the helpless, dogs, and others. (87–88)
Service consisting of a feast of food is the sweet speech of a child;
service consisting of the gift of knowledge is the endurance that is the ornament of the virtuous.
Being dependent on her husband and free from selfish desire is the true adornment of one who is well-esteemed among the virtuous.
Thus, through such service alone, a woman always gains infinite merit;
therefore, she should practice devotion to her husband, for that bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
By reading and hearing this, heaven and liberation are held within one's grasp.

Thus ends the four hundred and forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of How Candrāṅgada’s Husband, though submerged in the Yamunā due to the miraculous power of his wife Sīmantinī— a devoted wife of Kṛṣṇa— and led away to the netherworld by Nāga maidens, was recovered again," in the first section on the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Now I shall relate to you the marvel of Sīmantinī Satī.

Listen, Lakṣmī! To a wife who is devoted to devotion to Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa is always well-pleased by her dharma of wifely fidelity (*pātivratya*). The wife is the very embodiment of Lakṣmī, and the husband is the essence of Nārāyaṇa. (1–2)
With such an understanding, one should serve [the other]; thus they are liberated from each other.
The firm resolves made by a husband and wife are never in vain; they are always fulfilled. (3) In the land of Vidarbha, there lived a wise Brahmin named Vedamitra.
His son was Sumedhas, who was devoted to righteous conduct. (4) There was also another brahmin named Sārasvata in his city;
his son was Somavān, who was likewise devoted to dharma. (5)
Sumedhas and Somavān were both excellent friends, equal in appearance; they became proficient in all branches of knowledge and possessed identical learning.
Once, those two spoke beneficial words to their two sons, who were twice-born brahmins.
"My two sons, you have both mastered the sciences in your youth and possess great luster.
This time for marriage has arrived equally for both of you.
Having propitiated this King of Vidarbha and having obtained wealth," (7–8)
"You two shall be married to daughters born of noble families.
Having been addressed thus, the two sons went and satisfied the king.
When they requested wealth for their purpose, the king, impelled by destiny, spoke to them:
My daughter, the virtuous Sīmantinī, the consort of the Lord of Niṣadha,
having worshipped the Lord of Śrī and the Lord of Pārvatī on Mondays,
gives abundant wealth to Veda-knowing Brahmins accompanied by their wives.
Therefore, in this matter, one of you two shall assume the attire and grace of a woman, and the other shall be her husband; thus you two shall become a Brahmin couple.
Having gone there and obtained wealth, return once more to my presence.
"If there should be a deficiency, I shall give you even more wealth.
When this was said, they both replied: "O King, fear arises in acting toward deities, gurus, parents, perfected beings (siddhas), yogins, and sovereigns."
One who practices deceit becomes an object of punishment and perishes instantly; however, a secret deception, when concealed, may sometimes attain renown.
O King, all the virtues acquired at that time will perish in a moment.
"Sin, censure, fear, and enmity certainly abide within the mask [of virtue].
Therefore, we shall never resort to the conduct of deceitful people.
Having heard this, the king said: "Of the gods, the ancestors, and the yogis..."
"The teaching of the true gurus and the Siddha-kings must not be transgressed, but must be observed;
whatever they command, whether auspicious or inauspicious, should be carried out for the sake of one's welfare.
When this was said, he who was both self-controlled and handsome replied, "So be it."
Like a young woman, she put on a female dress, ornaments, collyrium, hair-dressing, and desirable body-paste; having thus become a husband and wife, the two of them approached that lady.
That queen, together with her wife, honored them according to the vow;
for she had seen those two sons of a brahmin who had arrived there as a fictitious couple,
[endowed] with the virtue of wifely devotion and likewise through service to Kṛṣṇa.
Through his devotion to Hara, he recognized that the youth had been turned into a maiden.
Then, having understood that they had been sent by their father and smiling slightly,
he considered Gaurī and Maheśa to be Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa.
Having invoked the Brahmins, who were embodiments of Śiva and Kṛṣṇa, and their wives, who were the forms of Gaurī and Śrī,
he worshipped them with perfumes, garlands, incense, lamps, and other offerings.
He also offered milk-rice, sweet modakas, sweet polikās, and śaṣkulis.
The virtuous woman fed the brahmins with vegetables, various kinds of foods, and delicacies;
having given betel, sacrificial fees, cows, gold, a hundred thousand jewels, and a great abundance of garments to each one, she bowed and dismissed them. (25–26)
Having invoked auspicious fortune upon Sīmantinī, the twice-born Sāmavān was honored;
and though she had been prepared as a girl, she truly gave birth to a daughter.
All the female characteristics were transformed within her body.
Having obtained wealth according to their desire, the two of them indeed went to their own home.
She, however, having forgotten her male state, developed a longing for her friend;
binding the brahmin with both her hands, she, overcome by passion, said:
"O beloved, stay for a moment in this beautiful, well-flowered forest!
I desire to sport with you; I am your dear one, so take me!
Embrace me, your beloved, and let me drink from your fresh lower lip."
"I am not able to go, being tormented by the impulse of love.
Seeing her thus, never before heard of, and hearing her words, he was filled with doubt and asked that breast-endowed woman: "O friend, why do you speak in this manner?"
"O weak one, you must not speak such false and artificial words in jest.
Cast off this maiden’s attire and assume the dress of a youth.
Thus commanded, she became joyful and cast her garments far away.

Meanwhile, that beloved Satyadhammillā— graceful with the beauty of her hips and breasts, possessed of a vulva yet lacking a penis— was seen by Sumedhas. Then, as a new lover, she took hold of that brahmin for the sake of sexual union.
Sumedhā said to that maiden: "Wear garments and such;
indeed, wise men do not approve of practicing the conduct of a paramour.
Having deceived her own parents by the command of the king of rogues..."
"This misfortune has been brought about by ourselves through our own actions.
For you, a young son of a brahmin, have attained this contemptible womanhood; indeed, sensual pleasure leads to ruin for youths, like the fruit of poison. (37–38)
Thus, resorting to solitude, go home yourself in silence;
by the grace of the gods and the twice-born, your womanhood shall come to an end.
Or else, through the turn of fate, you may remain a woman.
"O woman of excellent complexion, given by your father, you shall sport with me," he said;
yet even though addressed thus, the bride, consumed by the forest fire of passion,
then forcibly embraced him and kissed his sprout-like lower lip.
Though assailed by her, the steadfast Sumedhas brought about her peace merely through touch,
having provided an external contact.
The maiden remained unviolated, she was satisfied, and the burning of desire subsided.
Having performed their purification with water and other rites, they went to the king’s palace.
Then, having learned of that event, the king was filled with wonder;
he summoned his two brahmin parents and told them of his own actions.
Having heard this, Sārasvata said to the king regarding the rogue’s deed:
"O King, by your command, my son assumed the guise of a maiden and became a girl, experiencing the loathsome state of womanhood."
"Today my lineage, as well as my own single son, has perished.
All my ancestors have become hopeless, deprived of the offerings of rice-balls and water.
Tell me, what must I do now? Truly, you deserve to be punished by me today. (46–47)
The king, having summoned all the great sages, spoke like one in distress:
"Please show me your favor so that she may possess masculinity.
They replied: "Favor from the Lord of Śrī, the husband of Satī, is difficult to obtain."
And by his grace, the devotees of that [deity] shall obtain their desired object.
Then the king, having summoned the great sage Bharadvāja,
caused the worship of the Lord of Śrī, the Lord of Pārvatī, to be performed.
The brahmins, the king, and the maidens—
all of them having fasted for three nights— performed worship with sixteen and other excellent articles.
They performed uninterrupted devotion and held a great festival.
"Victory, O Lakṣmī! Victory, O Cāmbī! O Consort of Śrī! O Consort of Pārvatī!
(52) Thus they performed that uninterrupted worship accompanied by musical instruments;
by this, the Lord of Śrī and the Lord of Pārvatī were thoroughly pleased. (53)
Seated upon their vehicles and accompanied by their wives, those two abodes of compassion arrived.
They said to the king, "Tell us, what is your desire?
He replied, "Out of compassion, let manhood be granted to him for my sake."
Then those two said, O King:
"What has been done by our devotees cannot be undone even in hundreds of millions of years.
Sīmantinī was a woman of great devotion, a virtuous wife, and devoted to Kṛṣṇa as her husband. (55–56)
The goddess, endowed with manifold perfections, who drinks the waters of the Yamunā,

Just as the human being is to embodied beings, as the heart is to the senses;
just as weak digestion is to diseases, as power is to the powerful;

Just as Viṣṇu is among the Ādityas, and Indra among the gods;

It must be performed, observed, and maintained, for it bestows excellent sons.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, Lakṣmī! I shall proclaim the devotion to her husband (pativratam) of Śabarī.
Does not everything that is filled with wonder arise for the sake of a husband?
She who is a *satī*, entirely devoted to the satisfaction of her lord and the like, is ever victorious in the world; for dharma, when protected, protects.

There was a Śabara named Caṇḍaka who was a servant of Siṃhaketu, the king of the Pañcālas; in his house lived a devoted wife. That Śabara woman was devoted to her husband, regarding him as her supreme lord.

She always served her husband with devotion so that he might attain satisfaction. Whether at meals or during recreation, in activities such as business or in service and household chores, she never experienced weariness. (4–5)
The servant girl always remains exceedingly serene with a smiling face.
Whether it be dry, parched, stale, oily, sweet, or coarse;
bitter, burnt, uncooked, or roasted or boiled—[she accepts it all]. (6)
Whether it be refined Sanskrit or whatever else it may be, even if it be of such a kind;
the Śabara feels no anger, and the Śabarī is not distressed.
The Śabara is always the object of her love and the giver of perfect peace.
Śabarī, remaining under the control of her husband, gives [food] to her beloved and eats;
always regarding her beloved as Viṣṇu, that virtuous woman performs service. 9. Always adhering to the dharma of a Śūdra, the couple live together.
They were sincere and free from deceit, devoted to the path of truth;
they served the virtuous and lived a righteous life acquired through just means.
They found contentment in whatever food and other necessities were obtained through such service.
When a task arises, the Śabara asks his wife and performs it;
the Śabarī also asks her husband and performs what is appropriate.
Even if it should result in the loss of life, she does not disregard her husband’s word.
Śabara also does not do that which is forbidden by Śabarī;
and Śabarī also does not do that which is forbidden by her husband.
Where there is indeed this unity of two minds, that is Vaikuṇṭha itself, that is heaven itself.
Where there is truth, sincerity, and mutual respect, there dwell Nārāyaṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Viṣṇu, Śiva, Śivā, and Lakṣmī; there reside prosperity,
auspicious gain, perfection, protection, and freedom from disease.
Once, Siṃhaketu, adhering to the duty of a warrior,
went to a forest inhabited by deer for the purpose of hunting, accompanied by his attendants.
In that forest, the Śabara saw an ancient temple of a deity.
There, seeing a linga that was slightly detached from its broken pedestal, he took it and said to the king: "Behold this beautiful Shiva;
I shall worship him with devotion according to my means. (18)
"Tell me the method of worship so that Śaṅkara may be pleased.
Thus questioned, the king laughed and spoke to him truthfully:
"The worship of this [deity] is arduous; it cannot be accomplished by you."
One should always perform the consecration with fresh water through mental resolve.
Having seated [the deity] on a pure seat, one should worship with auspicious, fresh fragrances, unbroken grains of rice, wild leaves,
flowers, incense, and lamps.
One should first offer an oblation of funeral pyre ashes (22).
One should always prepare the food offering with food that one intends to consume oneself;
furthermore, one should arrange the services such as incense, lamps, and so forth (23).
One should appropriately imagine dancing, instrumental music, singing, and so forth; one should perform prostrations and thereafter maintain a state of grace.
This common procedure for the worship of Śiva has been declared to you.
Śaṅkara is immediately pleased by an offering of funeral pyre ashes.
One should say, "Salutation to Śiva, salutation to the Lord of Pārvatī.
Reciting this, one should worship the God together with his family.
Thus addressed, the terrified Caṇḍaka accepted those words with his head bowed.
Then, having reached his own abode, he installed Sadāśiva in the form of a *liṅga* upon a pedestal at the foot of a *pippala* tree in a quadrangle.
Every day he performed worship, offering funeral ashes as his oblation.
Whatever object was dear to himself and whatever was dear to his wife—
be it perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains of rice, and so forth, or sweet food, or even a mere grain— he offered it all.
Having offered it daily to Śambhu, he then consumed it himself.
In this way, together with his wife, he worshipped Sadāśiva with devotion. The quickly-pleased Lord was gratified by him and granted him happiness, wealth, and other blessings.

Food, clothing, a house, wealth, a milch cow, and likewise fame—all this is obtained from the kingdom; a salary is obtained through the duty of service. Thus, happiness based on truth and centered on Śiva was attained by the householder.
In whatever way he became fearless, happy, and possessed of the necessary means,
he performed worship constantly and repeatedly offered honors according to the rule.
Having gone himself to the cremation grounds and other such places, he took the ashes of corpses.
He performed the worship of Śiva constantly, even during times of rain and other such conditions.
Once, when the best of the Śabaras had set out for the worship of Śiva,
he did not see the funeral ashes that were kept in his vessel.
During the night, a stream of water from the rain fell into the vessel through a hole;
all the ashes were washed away and carried off by the current.
Seeing that the vessel was empty, not even a single atom remaining, [he realized: 36.
Then, having obtained some ash, he went far away to the cremation ground.
However, because the ground of the funeral pyre had been washed away by the rain,
he did not find any ash there at all, even though he searched everywhere with great agitation.
Then, exhausted, empty-handed, and hopeless, he returned home.
"What shall I do? Where shall I go? For today on this earth, there has been a heavy rain everywhere, and it continues to fall in great abundance. (39)
Even throughout the entire village, the ground has been washed by the king of jackals;
today no ashes will be found, and no worship can take place.
Consequently, indeed, there shall be no food or anything else for me today.
When the rain has ceased, after the death of someone,
or at the end of a month, I shall collect that ash and take it to the Lord Hara. Then, having worshipped Him, I shall partake of food together with my family.
Having reflected thus, the Bhila summoned his wife and said, "O beloved!
I have not obtained the ashes from the funeral pyre; tell me, what shall I do?
A great and insurmountable obstacle has arisen for me today regarding my worship of Hara."
I have not obtained any funeral ashes to wash away the dust of the cremation ground;
nor do I see any means here for procuring the requisites for worship.
Without worship, I cannot endure to live for even half a moment.
"May my fasts be fruitful even without the offering of ashes.
Seeing her thus distressed, that virtuous Śabara woman reflected:
"We have always been happy through Śiva."
Śiva is the bestower of happiness, the bestower of prosperity, and likewise the bestower of liberation.
Indeed, nothing inauspicious can ever befall the devotees of Śiva.
Whatever is performed for the sake of Śiva, all that becomes a giver of auspiciousness.

Wealth, home, fame, clothing, food, and even water—everything intended for the sake of Śiva becomes divine and brings about auspiciousness. By Śiva, this beautiful body was bestowed and by him it is nourished. (1.451.50)
"For the sake of my husband and for the sake of Śiva, may this auspicious female body be mine.
What further gain is there beyond that, by which my liberation might be achieved?
Having reflected thus, Śabarī said to her beloved, "Do not fear."

Having burned down this very house, which is reinforced with old timber, I shall enter the fire; let it then become the ashes of a funeral pyre. With that, O beloved, perform the worship; no other woman should be honored by you.
"I shall reach Kailāsa upon the separation from your body;
I will come to lead you there along with Śambhu, so do not grieve.
Having heard these beloved words, the Śabara spoke to her.
The body is the supreme means for attaining dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
Why do you abandon this body, which bestows happiness and is in the prime of youth?
At present, you are childless and repeatedly worthy of enjoyment.
"How can you wish to burn one who is firm, well-nourished, and so powerful?
Śabarī replied, "O beloved, this is the fulfillment of my life:
to sacrifice my life for the sake of my husband, and even more so for the sake of Śiva. (57)
What terrible austerity was performed, or what was given by me in the past?
Or what worship of Śambhu was performed during hundreds of previous births?
What merit belongs to my father, or what fulfillment of purpose belongs to my mother? (58–59)
Since I am casting off this body into the kindled fire for the sake of Śiva,
the time for my liberation has arrived; it is now unfolding for me, a woman of the Śabara tribe,
that which cannot be attained by a timid woman even through many lifetimes.
How could I, a low-caste woman, fall into delusion and render that [act] fruitless?
I consider all my sacrifices, gifts, pilgrimages, and austerities to have been fulfilled once my ashes were offered to Śaṅkara. (61–62)
Seeing her mind thus steadfast and her devotion to Śaṅkara, the Śabara also set his heart upon giving his own sacred ash to her.
He said to his wife, the Śabarī: "Live, my beloved, for a hundred years!"
"Only after reducing my body to ashes shall I attain liberation, which is exceedingly difficult to reach.
Due to the sins of many births, I am a Śabara, most base;
yet having found this excellent gateway to liberation, how could I bear to abandon it? (64-65)
"O beloved, Śambhu should always be worshipped by you with my ashes; for Satī once restored her dear husband to life through ashes. Indeed, in ancient times, Sāvitrī brought Satyavān back to life."
"Or rather, O beloved, you, my dear wife, should act in such a way that, having yourself produced fire, you may go to heaven together with your husband.
Thus addressed, she said to her husband: "O Lord, after your death..."
My death is certain in every respect according to the way of virtuous women;
between the two deaths [that may come], my own death here is better.
A virtuous woman who dies by the hand of her husband at his sight—
For the sake of her husband and for the sake of Śiva, she attains the fruitfulness of her birth. May she be the one who uplifts a hundred and one generations of her lineage;
may that gain be attained by me here—may such grace be shown toward me.
Seeing her resolve thus firm, the Śabara, his determination strengthened, honored her righteous and beneficial words by saying, "So be it.
Having obtained her husband's permission, she bathed, became pure, and adorned herself.
Having set fire to the house, she circumambulated that flame with devotion.
(73) Having prostrated before her own guru, meditated upon her husband as Śiva, and turned toward the entry into the fire with palms joined in reverence, she spoke this: (74)
May my senses be the flowers, my body agallochum incense,
my heart a splendid lamp, and my vital breaths the sacrificial oblations;
O Śambhu, may my organs be the unbroken grains— thus do I worship you.
I do not desire great sovereignty, nor heaven, nor even the supreme state.
O Śaṅkara, I always desire your service together with my husband;
may my mind always abide in you. O Lord of my heart, salutations be unto you!
Having thus propitiated the Lord of Gods, Śabarī, with a joyful countenance,
entered the blazing fire and was reduced to ashes in an instant.
Śabara, for his part, carefully gathered those ashes.
With a concentrated mind, he performed worship to Hara near the site of the burnt house.
Then, at the conclusion of the worship, he remembered his beloved wife— who always came to him with palms joined in reverence and full of humility— to receive his favor.
As soon as she was remembered, he then saw her arrived and standing behind him—
possessing her former form, appearing as was fitting, beautiful in appearance, and bowed with devotion. Beholding his wife, who was smiling and had joined her palms in reverence, the Śabara [spoke].
When his body, though reduced to ashes, remained as it was before, he was struck with wonder for a moment and reflected within his heart:
"Fire burns with its splendors; the sun burns with its rays. (82–83)
A king burns with his rod of punishment; a Brahmin may burn with his mind.
An enemy burns with losses and the like; an unchaste woman burns with the blows of her words.
Poison burns because of its heat; the wicked burn by their very sight.
Anxiety burns because of its triviality; ice burns because of its coldness;
thirst burns because of lack of satisfaction; and a virtuous woman burns because of a curse.
A holy man burns away sins by mere touch—of this there is no doubt. (85–86)
"How is it that she is not burnt here, appearing exactly as she was before?
Is this a dream, or is it a magical illusion?
Thus, bewildered by wonder, he questioned his wife.
"But how is it that you remain, even though you have been reduced to ashes?
How is it that the burnt house has once again returned to its former state?
Having heard this, the devoted wife, her face bright with joy, spoke to her beloved husband. (88–89)
When I entered the blazing fire after setting the house on fire,
I was neither conscious of myself nor did I see the fire. Then I beheld Śambhu, anointed with nectar, standing by my side.
As he was making me drink nectar and touching me with his own hand,
not even a trace of heat remained within me, as if I had entered into water.
Like one who has been in deep sleep, I was awakened again in an instant.
At that moment, we saw the house standing firm as if it had not been burnt.
Now, having come at the conclusion of the worship of the deity to receive a gift, [she said:
"O beloved, grant me a favor; what fine object shall I bring for you? 93.
Having been told this, she took water and likewise gave him fruit and unbroken grains (akṣata).
In this manner, the two of them worshipped him with devotion every day.
Having heard of such a marvelous and wondrous miracle, hundreds of thousands of people [came there].
They gathered together for the sake of beholding both of them and Śaṅkara as well.
While the couple remained thus in mutual love,
a hundred thousand years passed in happiness through a mere fraction of Śaṅkara’s grace.
Sons, grandsons, wealth, houses, fields, cattle, servants, and wives—having received the mantra from Śaṅkara, these Vaiṣṇavas became heads of households.
At the end of their bodies, for those two devoted husband and wife, there arose a divine and wonderful [state]. (97–98)
A celestial chariot appeared there, and standing within it, the couple—
having attained divine bodies and visible forms through the touch of the hand of Śiva’s messenger—
went to the supreme abode, the dwelling place of Śiva.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have described to you the supreme vow of devotion to one’s husband (pātivratya).
Likewise, the vow of a wife, the vow of surrendering to Śambhu, and the vow of self-surrender—these indeed excel all other vows. (1.451.100–101)
Even a Śūdra who might read or hear this narrative shall go with devotion to the world of Śiva or the world of Viṣṇu; of this there is no doubt.
Having understood the vow of a devoted wife and her fidelity to her husband, one should likewise practice it.
"From that as well, O beloved, she shall obtain enjoyment in every way and liberation at the end.

Thus ends the four hundred and fifty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Marvels of Chastity, including the Revival of the Śabarī Woman through the Offering of Ashes from the Funeral Pyre by her Devoted Consort," within the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
