Chapter 453 → Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:

Listen, Lakṣmī! Hear once more the wonder of devotion to one’s husband. By her who has Kṛṣṇa as her beloved, the husband was worshipped, served constantly, and honored as God; the teacher was worshipped, served constantly, and honored as God; and Śiva was worshipped, served constantly, and honored as God—these three by that woman. (1)
For her, even falsehood may become truth, and the fruit of truth may be its opposite. (2) Suffering may also become happiness; barrenness may become the possession of children;
widowhood may become the state of being a married woman; and misfortune may become supreme fortune. (3)
Even misfortune may become good fortune,
and adversity may take the form of prosperity, when the husband, the preceptor, and Śivā are pleased.
In the region of Ānarta, there was a certain twice-born man named Vedaratha.
In Camatkārapura, however, there lived a man with sons, a wife, and a family.
He had a daughter named Śāradā, who was ever as virtuous as Kamalā.
From birth, [she offered] obeisance to her Lord, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
Thus, due to the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of her previous lives, she always spoke clearly.
Having heard this, the people were struck with great wonder and paid homage to the virtuous lady (*satī*).
Satī [also honored] Kṛṣṇa, Śiva, Hāṭakeśa, her guru, and her parents.
Having always offered salutations every morning, she thereafter constantly performed other [devotions].
Thus, at the age of twelve, she became filled with the bliss of worship.
Then Padmanābha, a brahmin honored by the king, made a request of her.

The father gave that maiden to the wealthy and tranquil Brahmin. Having performed the marriage, the twice-born man went to the river in the evening to perform the twilight rites (saṃdhyā). On the way, he was bitten by a serpent and consequently died.
The kinsmen wailed, and his wife [wailed] for her father-in-law.
Then Śāradā, the Brāhmaṇa woman who had attained widowhood, performed the funeral rites for the kinsmen and remained in her father’s very abode.
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Master; obeisance!
Thus the young girl always spoke, and she constantly chanted "Obeisance to Kṛṣṇa.
Knowing that Kṛṣṇa alone is her husband and no other, she worshipped Mādhava.
She constantly serves her parents, who are the very embodiments of Śiva and Śivā.
The Yoginī perceives Lakṣmī in the woman and Nārāyaṇa in the man.
Śiva is the master, the husband, Kṛṣṇa is the guru, the god, and Hari is the father. (14–15)
Lakṣmī is my mother; the Goddess is my friend; the circle of the virtuous is my family;

devotion to Kṛṣṇa is my bed; delight in His form is my meditation; auspiciousness is my happiness; merit is my fortune; righteousness is my action; service is my rest; and remembrance of the Blessed Lord is my repose. 16.
All her divine activities were entirely devoted to the Lord and composed of goodness;
even in widowhood, she remained auspicious through the power of merit acquired in the past.
Kṛṣṇa was her beloved husband, and her service was the very mother of the virtuous.
In that state, her good fortune alone remained while widowhood persisted;
as she lived thus in her father’s house,
once an aged and virtuous man named Naidhruva arrived.
Blind and grasping the hand of his disciple, he said, "Give alms.
Upon seeing the saint, who was like Viṣṇu himself, she offered him an excellent seat, saying, "Welcome to you, O most worshipful one; please sit upon this seat."
Having spoken thus, he established devotion, washed his feet,
fanned him, gave him water, and worshipped him with flowers and sandalwood.
He respectfully fed him with excellent and desired foods.
The blind sage, being satisfied and well-pleased with her, bestowed a supreme blessing:
"Having lived happily with your husband, having obtained a son of superior virtues,
and having attained great fame, may you be favored by the gods."
Having heard those well-spoken words, she was struck with wonder and replied to him:
"O virtuous one, your speech is true; how could it be otherwise for one as dull-witted as I?
It is like a heavy rain falling upon a mountain peak, or a noble service rendered to a bitch. (25)
Indeed, even the auspicious blessings of a virtuous donor become fruitless upon a widow.
[The king said: "I have become a widow; how can I be a recipient of your blessing?
The virtuous man replied to that goddess: "What has been spoken by me shall bear fruit."
Kṛṣṇa himself shines forth in the words of the virtuous;
Śambhu and the gods become his helpers when the words of the saints are spoken.
Impelled by the power of Lakṣmī and Śivā, I have come here.
"O virtuous daughter! By your devotion, you shall possess good fortune.
Indeed, no devoted young woman may suffer in misery;
thus spoke the Lord Viṣṇu, who has come here in a virtuous form for your sake. (1.452.30)
Worship Kṛṣṇa and Śiva, as well as Lakṣmī and Śivā, and always honor your parents. O daughter, observe the single vow known as Umā-Māheśvara;
by doing everything exactly as I have instructed, you will attain all auspicious fortune.
"How can I endure the widowhood of my devoted daughter, O fair one?
Come, I shall tell your parents the truth as it is.
Having spoken thus, Sādhu Viṣṇu led her into the presence of her parents.
Hari spoke of the account of the granting of blessings, his own auspiciousness, and the vow, as well as everything that was destined to happen; thereafter, he vanished.
Listen, Lakṣmī! This is the Umā-Māheśvara vow, which bestows great fortune.
I then spoke it to Śāradā, and she performed it.
In the month of Caitra or Mārgaśīrṣa, on an auspicious day during the bright fortnight,
or on the eighth or fourteenth lunar days, or even on both festival days (parvan).
By the command of her guru, the virtuous and auspicious woman should undertake the vow;
having performed the formal resolve (saṃkalpa) according to the rules, she should perform her morning bath.
Having offered libations to the ancestors, gods, and others, she should construct an auspicious pavilion.
In the center of that, one should draw a lotus with powders of five colors:
with fourteen petals on the outside, twenty-two in between, sixteen within that, and eight within that. (38–39)
Then one should make it square, with a circle within;
in the center, a *kūrca* [bundle of grass], and around that, heaps of rice and grain.
Having done so, one should then place a water-filled jar upon the *kūrca*.
Having placed a variegated cloth and a water-pot there, one should indeed install Śiva and Śivā,
and worship them with the sixteen articles.
One should bathe them with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and then bathe them with water.
Having recited the Rudra-mantra one hundred and eight times, eleven times each,
and having uttered "Salutation to Śiva," one should worship the form upon the pedestal.
Then, having performed breath-control (prāṇāyāma) according to one's ability, one should make the formal resolve (saṃkalpa).
I propitiate you for the destruction of the sins committed in previous births;
I worship you for the increase of good fortune, victory, health, dharma, and sovereignty, and for the attainment of sons, wealth, heaven, and liberation.
Then, having performed the ritual placement on the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*), one should meditate upon the Lord and Pārvatī.
One should meditate upon Śaṅkara as a yogi, and meditate upon Satī as a devoted wife;
likewise, one should meditate upon the three-eyed Lord with matted hair and the three-eyed Goddess with her hair.
I meditate upon the white [Lord] adorned with serpents, who is beautiful and endowed with golden ornaments;
the blue-throated one with a sweet voice, having two arms while she has eight arms;
him absorbed in meditation and her seated upon his lap; him white and her red. (47–48)
Having meditated thus, one should begin the invocation and other rites upon the image.
One should offer the invocation, as well as the water for honor (*arghya*), fragrance, flowers,
unbroken grains (*akṣata*), incense, a lamp, food offerings (*naivedya*), water, and betel leaf.
One should offer one hundred and eight oblations with the mantra "Śivāya namaḥ.
Then, one should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), prostrations, and the rite of seeking forgiveness.
Thereafter, having worshipped them with ritual offerings, one should feed the devoted couple.
In this manner, one should perform the evening worship and consume milk-rice (pāyasa).
One should continue doing so for a year, after which one should perform the concluding rite (udyāpana).
Having caused the recitation of the Śatarudrīya to be performed, one should offer worship.
One should offer clothing, gold, a water-pot, and an image to the preceptor.
One should feed virtuous Brahmins and give gold as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Then one should receive the sacred remnants (prasāda) and perform the gift of a cow and other such rites.
Thus, the performer or female practitioner of this vow shall obtain the happiness desired by themselves;
they shall attain lineage, good fortune, wealth, prosperity, and liberation.
In the end, they reach the state of liberation, the station of Śiva or the station of Kṛṣṇa.
This great vow was proclaimed by that holy man and performed by her;
at the end of the year, that virtuous woman completed its concluding rite.
Having fasted, that young girl chanted the mantra every day.
Śivā and Śiva arrived together, auspicious and assuming divine forms. Everything that was spoken by Viṣṇu is indeed for the sake of good fortune:
"May you obtain the happiness of a husband right here in this very body."
Thus both of them delighted the girl with words of blessing.
Then Śambhu said: "O dear child, summon your parents, kinsmen, and others here; I wish to tell you of your former birth."
Thus addressed, Śāradā summoned them all into the presence of Śiva.
While everyone was listening, Śambhu said to Śāradā, "O daughter,
in a previous birth in Draviḍa, you and another woman were both the wives of Brahmins."
Let it be; your husband was constantly infatuated with you there.
You never once bestowed upon your elder co-wife the happiness that your lover provided; because of that, the elder wife indeed died of grief. (62–63)
On account of that sin, you have now become a widow.
Whatever women in this world cause discord between husband and wife, they certainly suffer widowhood from their youth; of this there is no doubt.
But you have propitiated Kṛṣṇa and performed an auspicious vow.
By that, great merit has arisen; through that merit, this Brahmin from your previous birth shall grant you pleasure in a dream.
"Therefore, a son equal to Viṣṇu shall be born right here. While Śambhu, that best of brahmins, was speaking thus to her,
that youthful Lord of the Past appeared there before her very eyes.
Seen by everyone because of Śiva’s word, she offered the garland;
her beloved applied vermilion powder to her forehead, Sindūra-powder to her hair, bracelets to her forearms, and collyrium to her eyes. (68–69)
Having offered all the substances of good fortune, as soon as the Brahmin husband touched her head there with his hand,
black-colored hair immediately sprouted and became beautifully adorned.
He fashioned a braid for her and a golden sash for her garment;
right there, by the touch of his hand, he bestowed a blessing. Having thus given auspicious benedictions, Śambhu stood for a moment laughing.
He too became invisible, and her husband likewise vanished from sight.
By virtue of the merit of that maiden’s vow, a great festival arose for her.
Listen, Lakṣmī! Viṣṇu himself became the bestower of the vow.
Śambhu summoned Viṣṇu himself there, and he became the suitor for the maiden;
likewise, for the sake of convincing the family members, Mādhava assumed the form of her beloved from a previous birth. (74–75)

That very Lord Kṛṣṇa, becoming her husband, always at night grants eternal satisfaction of desire within the mind of his devotee. At times he appears in the form of Kṛṣṇa, and at times in the form of a brāhmaṇa.
In some places he assumes the form of Śiva, and in others the form of a holy sage;
the Blessed One always takes up residence in her home and delights there.
She, too, became radiant with the splendor of her beauty and majesty, like the goddess Śrī herself.
Thinking herself liberated, the virtuous woman did not reveal her state.
As the days passed in this manner,
that young woman obtained the union with her husband every night, which increased her happiness.
By the boon granted by Śiva and Śivā, Śāradā, whose vows were pure,
conceived a child through the power of her union with Kṛṣṇa even in a dream.
Unaware of the truth, people declared the maiden to be pregnant and unchaste.
Unbeknownst to them, a gathering of the village dwellers was held there;
the learned men who had assembled there were questioned for the purpose of paying a fine.
Among them, Kṛṣṇa himself arrived, having assumed the guise of a Brahmin.
Śiva, having become a great scholar there, arrived in Kāśī.
Listen, Lakṣmī! What happened then regarding Śāradā?
Having summoned the pregnant Śāradā, the elderly men— || 83-84 ||
Then they asked Śāradā and her father, "From where does this pregnancy come?
They replied: "Due to the union with a lover from a previous birth, earned through the merit of vows;
by the acquisition of the seed in a dream, this pregnancy is not at all defective. (85)
Then they all abandoned their families and departed;
some, being highly incensed, reviled them, while others turned their faces away.
They all consulted together, saying, "What shall we do? (86–87)
Some said: "This woman is a sinner who has brought ruin to both families.
Having shaved her head and cut off her ears and nose, let them banish her from the village and exclude her from her own lineage. (88)
Then the wise Viṣṇu said there to all the humans:
"Formerly, this woman heard of and performed the Umā-Māheśvara vow;
by that merit, she has forever obtained her husband in a dream."
There is no doubt that there was no embryo in her womb during her pregnancy;
no punishment should be inflicted upon her, for this woman has been virtuous.
However, the tongues of those who speak of misconduct shall split in two.
Upon hearing this, her mother, father, and the others rejoiced.
Then, for a moment, the village elders maintained silence out of fear;
among them, some who were untrustworthy spoke falsely of a dream.
Their tongues split in two and they vomited blood;
terrified, they all spoke nothing contrary to what was said.
Then Śambhu Paṇḍita spoke to Viṣṇu Paṇḍita.
Even a fetus can be conceived in a dream; such is the course of destiny.
This entire universe, which is composed of illusion (māyā), is both seen and heard. What is possible and what is impossible in this world created by Kṛṣṇa? || 95–96 ||
That which is unascertainable and unreal sometimes becomes reality;
everything is under the control of Śrī Kṛṣṇa—who knows his secret activity?
The semen of the royal sage Yūpaketu fell into the water.
Having drunk that water together with the semen, the maidservant indeed conceived a child.
And having drunk the semen of the sage Vibhāṇḍaka along with the water,
a doe became pregnant and gave birth to Ṛṣyaśṛṅga.
Likewise, the doe of King Saurāṣṭra, having been touched by his hand,
became pregnant at that very moment and gave birth to an ascetic sage.
Similarly, the woman Satyavatī was born from the womb of a Śapharī fish.
In that very same way, Mahiṣāsura was born from the womb of a buffalo.
Furthermore, in ancient times, even by eating the fruit, women who were pregnant became mothers of sons through women merely conceived in their minds. || 101–102 ||
The club was born from the womb of Sāmba due to the curse of the sages;
yet, through the power of the sages' mantras, it became the embryo within Yuvanāśva.
O people, the seed exists in both woman and man in every respect.
But the transformation of yogis occurs through their word alone.
Ahalyā became a stone by the very word of Gautama, and it is seen that she became a young woman again through the touch of Rāma. (104–105)
Likewise, many Maruts were born, created by Indra as their weapon.
At the word of Rādhā, Gaṅgā was born in the form of water. From the churning of the ocean, Lakṣmī arose, and Sītā was indeed born from the earth.
In this way, indeed, manifold creation arises for yogis.
By the grace of Vasudeva, [the Lord] was established as a fetus in Rohiṇī;
and from the matted locks of Śaṅkara, Vīrabhadra was also born.
Surely this blameless woman also, by the power of her vow,
by the majesty of serving the virtuous one, and by taking refuge in Kṛṣṇa,
bears within her womb the seed consisting of his blessing.
Thus addressed, the best of the assembly—the kinsmen and relatives—praised her, crying out, "Excellent!
Excellent! They shed tears from their eyes;
the women of the family, filled with joy, offered words of consolation directed toward her.
Nevertheless, for the sake of dispelling the doubts of human beings,
Śiva and Hari became two brahmins there for a mere moment. Viṣṇu assumed the form of a brahmin, holding Śāradā upon his lap.
He showed them all his own beloved form and his dear Śāradā; seeing the two of them in the form of a divine couple, they attained the highest wonder. Then Kṛṣṇa vanished, and Śiva also disappeared.
Then the people residing in Camatkārapura worshipped Satī, who was embodied as Śrī, and each went to his own home.
Then, in an auspicious time, Satī gave birth to a son.

That learned man named Śāradeya also became equal to Kṛṣṇa. Having performed service to Kṛṣṇa for many years and having established her lineage in the world, the virtuous Śāradā [attained union] with Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
By means of a divine vehicle, he went to Goloka, the eternal abode.
This meritorious narrative of Śāradā has been described;
it bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon those who read or hear it correctly.

[This bestows] upon women auspiciousness, good fortune, progeny, prosperity, and long life. (11.9) Thus ends the four hundred and fifty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Miracles of Chastity," in the first section on the Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. It describes how, in the city of Camatkāra in the land of Ānarta, Śāradā was freed from widowhood through the blessing of a saintly man; how she regained her good fortune and obtained a son; and how, for the sake of inspiring faith in the people, Kṛṣṇa appeared in the form of a Brahmin, and [how she] attained Goloka.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī! I shall relate the wondrous story of a courtesan who was devoted to me and whose mind was fixed on Nārāyaṇa.
O Hari, in ancient times there lived in Nandigrāma a devoted woman named Mahānandā, whose form was graced with beauty and charm.
Free from family ties, independent in her will, she was a servant of Śiva.
Although she was a courtesan, she was permeated by Kṛṣṇa;
she constantly bathed and worshipped Hari Viṣṇu with supreme devotion,
and she also performed dancing and singing in the presence of the Lord.
To those spectators who come for the dance, song, cymbals, and so forth, she—
who is the source of everything for the sake of Kṛṣṇa— gives water mixed with *tulasī* leaves as a pleasing offering for the sake of their purification. (5)
She constantly worships Govinda as a human being with the thought that he is Kṛṣṇa. Having dedicated all bodily activity to Kṛṣṇa, she performs her duties.
[She attains] a parasol resembling the full moon and a vehicle resplendent with gold.
Chowries with fine handles, golden sandals,
variegated garments, and a golden couch;
he guards a bed resembling moonbeams for the sake of Kṛṣṇa.
Cows, female buffaloes, milch-cows, lamps, ornaments, male servants, and female servants—
trusting her words, they worship Hara and Hari with priceless ornaments resplendent with the nine gems.
Anointing with fragrant saffron, musk, camphor, and agallochum; various garlands and ear-ornaments; delicious food according to one's desire;
and a house filled with various grains and adorned with diverse, variegated canopies. (11)

She always dedicated all her wealth— abounding in thousands of various jewels and consisting of gold, silver, and so forth— to the service of Hara and Hari. Thus, that courtesan was possessed of great prosperity and was devoted to the dharma of truth.
Devoted to the service of her husband and dedicated to the worship of Kṛṣṇa and Śiva,
she constantly listened to discourses on the scriptures and was intent on the chanting of the Lord’s names.
For the sake of diversion, she performed dances in the middle of the pavilion before the Deity.

Having adorned a single monkey and a single cock with rudrākṣa beads, he himself would always make them dance to the rhythm of hand-claps and songs. Adorned with armlets, earrings, and other ornaments fashioned from rudrākṣas, [he remained thus]. (15–16)
Through her instruction, the monkey always dances like a child;
with a rudrākṣa bead tied to its crest, the cock dances for a long time along with the monkey, an expert dancer bringing wonder to those who watch. (17)

Once, a certain merchant accompanied by his servants, being a true devotee of dance, came to her house for the purpose of witnessing a performance; wearing his bracelets, he saw the jeweled bracelet situated upon her forearm and said to him [the king]: ||| 18–19 ||
"This bracelet, studded with great jewels, rests upon your hand;
it captivates my heart, O devotee, for it is worthy of the ornaments of a celestial woman.
Seeing her looking at him with longing, the merchant then said to her:
"If this bracelet, my own ornament, pleases you, accept my auspicious decoration; what price will you give for it?
Then that courtesan laughed and spoke clearly to him.
"For one who is merely a guest, my duty is always to serve with my body;
yet, regarding you as the very form of Nārāyaṇa, I indeed perform this service.
If you give me this arm-ornament studded with jewels," [he said].
"For three days and nights, I shall be your wife.
For women who are the wives of others, there can never be the status of a devoted wife,
nor can there be the status of a single, exclusive wife, just as it is not so for the apsarases in heaven."
"So be it," the merchant said, "the moon and the sun shall be my witness.
Having made this truth three times and touched each other's chests,
they both became husband and wife for three days and nights.
"Let us practice the Dharma together," they both said, words that touched the heart.
(27) Then the merchant-chief gave her a jeweled bracelet.
The husband and wife spent the night happily in the fulfillment of their desires. (28)
Then, on the second night, within the dance pavilion,
a fire suddenly broke out from the contact of a lamp wick;
both the monkey and the cock were released from their bonds and set free.

Other male and female slaves, as well as cows, buffaloes, and so forth, were released from their bonds; those two also departed from there. At that time, the Śiva-liṅga and the image of Hari were reduced to ashes in the fire.
Remembering that, the couple fell into boundless sorrow.
The merchant said, "O beloved, through my union with you, everything has been consumed by fire;
Śiva and Viṣṇu have appeared in bodily form and burned me according to my own coming."
"O virtuous one! Having come here, I have incurred a great and terrible sin.
O beloved! I find no peace at all; I shall die from this unbearable sorrow.
Having spoken thus, the merchant drew in his life-breath and fell upon the earth.

Since that young woman had been his lawful wife for three days, she became exceedingly distressed; remembering her duty with its excellent witnesses, she summoned everyone there and spoke these piteous words: (25)
Taking a jeweled bracelet as witness before the sun and the moon,
I have become his wife according to dharma for three days; indeed, it is by dharma that I must enter his funeral pyre.
Having heard these words of hers, the merchant’s servant said to her:
"Do not say so, do not say so, O gentle lady; this man is not your husband by marriage. She who has been wedded by a husband in the presence of fire as witness—"
One who has been taken by the hand-grasping ceremony is proclaimed a wife.
But you are not such a wife, being devoted to infidelity; out of great greed for the sake of the bracelet, you merely boast under the name of "wife."
Just as there is hell for one who lives with a paramour, so too is the burning of this [house] while he is alive;

for the burning of a house together with a paramour and by means of the paramour’s hand brings no benefit to those seeking spiritual welfare. (41) The cremation of a woman with a paramour does not bestow any merit.
"Go far away, you ever-wicked, unchaste, and deceitful woman!
(42) I shall perform the cremation of my master’s corpse;
I will enter the funeral pyre of my master and die according to the duty of a servant. (43)
I am a servant of long standing who serves you without interruption;
indeed, without my master, my life-breaths are truly unable to remain here.
You are the giver of food, the giver of livelihood, the protector, and the bestower of knowledge.
The ancestors are remembered as those who provide the seed, the mantras, and the food.
In this world, one without a father is considered like a dead servant.
Having destroyed my master, how could I show my face?
"I am your servant, I am like a son to you, and I am always to be nourished by you according to dharma.
Afterward, I shall give you my body and enter the fire;
thus, eternal worlds will be mine along with you, O Master."
Having spoken thus, he gathered wood in every way and prepared a funeral pyre.
Then, having placed the corpse upon the fire of the pyre, the merchant gave some wealth as well as other items, such as chains, in charity to worthy recipients.
Just as he was about to enter, that beautiful woman ran forward, seized his hand, and cried out to him, "No, no, do not!
"O servant, do not act thus; my son, live forever upon this earth!"
Though addressed thus by all the people and though forbidden by them, he entered [the fire] indeed.
(51) When the servant had fallen into the funeral pyre, his lawful wife, a virtuous woman, then spoke to the assembly as they listened: "I am the wife of this man. (52)
"His devoted wife, highly esteemed, has been in my house for three days; by my power, this husband of hers has indeed been made dead.
Therefore, I shall enter the fire along with him."
By truth, the gods, the lords of the three worlds, attain delight.
Truth itself is indeed the supreme dharma; everything is established upon truth.
Through truth one attains both heaven and liberation, but through untruth there is no higher goal.
Therefore, relying upon the truth, I shall enter the fire;
purified by the yoga of devotion, I shall become a sanctifier.
O Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa, Viṣṇu, Śiva! Be the bestower of auspiciousness.
Oṃ, salutations to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Master;
salutations! (57) Salutations to Śiva-Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Śrī Rādhā; salutations!
Thus he performed the worship of Śrī Kṛṣṇa and gave many gifts. (58)
Having given away all her possessions to virtuous devotees, and having meditated upon Hara and Hari;
having bowed to all and meditated upon her husband, Satī,
a devotee of him, circumambulated him three times and stood facing the entrance of her husband’s funeral pyre.
As she was falling into the kindled fire with her mind fixed upon their own feet,
the two gods Śiva and Acyuta appeared and restrained her;
beholding those two gods of gods, whose splendor exceeded ten million suns, she [stood there].
As she was being born, she remained as if paralyzed, as if terrified, and as if inert.
The two Blessed Ones, treasuries of compassion, consoled her and said:
"Truly, you possess truth, righteousness, fortitude, and devotion toward the Lord who is the soul of men. (62)

In order to see both Śiva and Acyuta within the images of Śiva and Kṛṣṇa, [the two gods] produced fire through their illusory power (māyā) and burnt the beautiful pavilion. Having burnt both images, the servant Śiva himself joyfully [repaired them]. (63–64)
To demonstrate my devotion as a servant, I entered the fire here;
though appearing in the form of a merchant, O Nārāyaṇa-Kṛṣṇa, I am your husband. Having come to test you, I have arrived for my final service to you.
"Prostitutes are deceitful, self-willed, and deceivers of people.
Yet you, such as you are, having remembered the truth, have entered the fire together with your followers.
Therefore, I shall grant you your desire; speak, O most excellent one, what is the highest of the high."
Having heard this, she said: "I have no desire for enjoyments apart from your feet.
These servants and maidservants, as well as my other kinsmen—all are intent upon worshipping you, having surrendered their livelihoods to you. (68)
"Taking all these along with me, lead them to your imperishable abode;
always protect them in the service that is filled with eternal bliss.
Having thus welcomed her words with "So be it," Nārāyaṇa—
He led them all, together with her, to the state of the Unconditioned.
As for the cock and the monkey, they met their death in due time;
the dog became the prince of the kingdom of Kaśmīra through his merit.
At that time, the monkey became the chief minister and the prince became his subordinate.
Having been great devotees of Śiva and Viṣṇu, the two of them ruled the kingdom for a long time,
and at the end of their bodies, they went to the imperishable abode where that virtuous woman (Satī) resides.
Thus has been told to you, O Lakṣmī, this liberation from great sins;
by reading or hearing this, the destruction of sin shall occur.
Even a sinful woman, through hearing and likewise through performing [this rite], [is liberated].
"By serving the virtuous, another who was already liberated is likewise immediately released.

Thus ends the four hundred and fifty-third chapter, titled "The Description of How Śiva and Acyuta, having become a merchant and a servant respectively, underwent a test of conjugal fidelity through the devotion of a courtesan who offered her all to them, and how they granted her liberation," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
*Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā* — Section 1 (*Kṛtayuga-santāna*) — Chapter 453.

Chapter 455 → Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, my dear Mahālakṣmī! A woman’s devotion to her husband transcends all people;
dharma and adharma are certain to consist primarily of her husband’s word, and nothing else.
If a virtuous wife should show even slight disregard for her husband’s word, it would become like nectar [to her].
A virtuous wife should indeed render her husband’s words, even if they are harmful, as if they were meritorious.

(2) If it should be spoken by her beloved, a virtuous wife should practice theft, considering it to be just. And when commanded by her husband, a virtuous wife should practice sexual intercourse, considering it to be her duty. (3)
The husband alone is the Supreme Brahman, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa himself.
Whatever he may ordain, whether auspicious or inauspicious, the virtuous wife should carry it out.
Subject to his word, the virtuous wife shall obtain the fruit of her devotion to her husband.
If the husband should command an inauspicious act, he alone shall be the partaker of its fruit.
(5) In this matter, the virtuous wife does not share in the consequence of that inauspicious speech;
rather, by her own power, she should perform that inauspicious task so as to make it auspicious. (6)
She indeed transforms that which is undesirable and painful into that which bestows happiness;
by the mere power of her will, death, time, Yama, fear,
unrighteousness, and all causes of affliction truly become givers of happiness.
Devotion to one’s husband is the supreme dharma; devotion to one’s husband is the supreme strength.
(8) Before the bull-like husband, even sin becomes a source of merit;
through pleasing the husband, who is Kṛṣṇa himself, suffering takes on the nature of happiness. (9)
In this regard, O beloved, listen as I relate an ancient account: how,
by honoring the words of her husband, a woman engaged in sexual union attained everything meritorious and became one who pleases the gods.
In a village named Bāṣkala, indeed in the middle of the southern region (Dakṣiṇāpatha),
the subjects were unrefined, devoid of knowledge and dispassion;
both men and women lived by agriculture and the forest-dwelling way of life.
There lived a certain twice-born man named Vidura, who was devoid of righteous conduct; he was a cultivator who had formed friendships with Śūdras and others.
He was constantly engaged in agricultural work with female laborers.
He did not at all recognize the fault of consorting with another's wife and the like.
Having once united with a Śūdra woman out of desire during some work, that wretched woman began to beg Vidura for food and wealth. (14–15)
Overcome by compassion as well as by the influence of desire, Vidura would indeed occasionally give [food] to the Śūdra woman for the sake of sustenance;
even though he had a wife, he did not disregard his virtuous spouse, Bandulā.
He gave the wealth and food remaining in the house to the Śūdra woman.
Bandulā, though in the bloom of her youth, endured everything for the sake of her husband;
the wealth and food had been exhausted and were now surrendered by her master to the Śūdra woman.
Vidura, however, begged his virtuous wife, saying: "Give me wealth; give me food; give me clothing; O beloved, give for the sake of the Śūdra woman.
Thus addressed, that virtuous woman said: "Whatever indeed is found in the house,"
"O Lord, let all that be brought; my home is always under your control.
When you, my protector, are pleased, everything shall bring me happiness.
I have no wealth before me, yet I shall do exactly as you have said."
Vidura said to that virtuous woman: "Go, serve others;
by serving wealthy men, bring back wealth and give it to me. But Satī was obedient to her husband and as trusting toward him as she would be toward a lord.

Having performed service for someone—whether as a slave or as a wife—she brings wealth at her husband’s command and gives it to him. The husband alone is the supreme dharma; the husband’s word brings happiness. (23–24)
Thinking thus, she became intent on serving the desires of other men.
While that couple was thus engaged in such wicked conduct,
by the turn of fate, a certain storyteller Brahmin arrived at their village.
He arrived and spoke the discourse of the *Saṃhitā* according to righteousness. All the villagers heard that ancient compendium of dharma;
having completely abandoned the wrong path, they took refuge in the path of dharma.
The people indeed took up the Vaiṣṇava mantra and worshipped Acyuta; abandoning improper conduct, they honored the brāhmaṇas.
They felt remorse for their past deeds and remembered Hari.

After that, having been abandoned by Vidura, he became exceedingly righteous; he abstained from the company of Śūdras and took but one meal a day. He performed ritual bathing, the twilight prayers (sandhyā), recitation (japa), worship, the offering of food (naivedya), and the viewing of the deity.
Having prepared it, he would always eat in this manner, and his wife did likewise.
As Vidura’s life was thus coming to its end,
the messengers of Yama arrived then to lead him to the city of Yama.
Seeing those messengers, he cried out, "Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa!
Hearing him, his wife said to him, "My dear, why this lamentation?
He replied to her, "The messengers of Yama have indeed arrived to take me away."
Then the virtuous wife, taking water in her hand, spoke:
"If I am a beloved wife to my husband, always acting for the pleasure of my husband,
abiding by my husband’s command, and devoted solely to my husband, Kṛṣṇa..."
"By that truth, let those messengers go far away to the abode of Yama!
Having said this, she threw that water toward her husband;
at that moment, the messengers fled from afar, leaping down from that dry land.
Then the husband, having recovered his health, related the matter exactly as it had happened.
His wife spoke again to her beloved:
"O my dear, I give this to you; by this, may there be a good state for you through your service to your master. (37)
Just then, the attendants of Viṣṇu arrived joyfully;
seen by his wife at that very moment through the fruit of her devotion as a faithful consort,
they were honored and saluted, and they led her husband to the supreme abode.
Bandulā, having placed her husband upon her lap, wept for a moment;
then she reflected: "If I am truly devoted to my beloved, then let my life-breaths depart this very instant along with him."
Having fainted for that long, the virtuous woman instantly gave up her life-breaths;
endowed with a beautiful form, she departed together with her husband who possessed a divine body.
Possessing a celestial body and seated upon a celestial chariot, she was honored by the attendants of Viṣṇu.
The listeners beheld that radiant splendor and the celestial chariot.
Then that brāhmaṇa, together with his true devotees,
performed the funeral rites for those two according to the prescribed rules and fed the Vaiṣṇavas.
He gave the instruction of Kṛṣṇa and bestowed the dharma of devotion to one's wife;
likewise, the twice-born himself bestowed the dharma of wifely fidelity upon his subjects.
Indeed, all the men and women everywhere became Vaiṣṇavas.
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Master; obeisance!
Having received this mantra, they worshiped the infallible Kṛṣṇa, listened to the stories of the Lord of Lakṣmī, and performed His devotional service constantly.
In a dream, the Brahmin reciter of the story granted his own vision to both men and women: [he saw] Nārāyaṇa with four arms,
adorned with necklaces, armlets, a crown, yellow garments, and the Sudarśana discus.
Accompanied by Lakṣmī, the enchanting Lord appeared;
at the conclusion of the discourse, he was worshipped by all, and having accepted that worship,
he whose form consists of grace toward his devotees then instructed them all.
Having observed the supreme virtue of Bandulā’s devotion to her husband,
I, Nārāyaṇa, for the sake of her welfare, arrived in the form of a brahmin as the author of this story; thus you have all been delivered.
Having heard this discourse, they became Vaiṣṇavas and devoted themselves to my service.
"Worship me constantly and listen to the stories of Hari.
Men must observe the vow of devotion to their wives, and women must observe the vow of devotion to their husbands. (52)
From both [of these], the vow of Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa is the means of liberation (tāraka). (53) One must constantly listen to the sacred stories, which bestow supreme liberation.
Through the narration of Kṛṣṇa’s deeds, the mind attains the highest purity. (54)
Through discourse, meditation is perfected; from meditation comes supreme liberation.
The hearing of noble discourse is considered the seed of all that is auspicious.
Desire, anger, greed, as well as pride, arrogance, and other such passions—
The sons of Adharma depart far away upon hearing the narrative of Hari.
Likewise, violating the teacher’s bed, drinking liquor, and improper sexual union—these sons of Kāma depart far away upon hearing the narrative. (56–57)
The killing of a father, the killing of a mother, and the murder of a Brahmin—
these sons of anger perish from merely hearing this story.
The seizing of a deity’s property, the seizing of a Brahmin’s property, and the theft of gold [are likewise destroyed].
These sons of greed depart far away from hearing the stories [of the Lord].
Both lack of faith and dull intellect are indeed the two daughters of ignorance;
they go far away from hearing the stories of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. (1.454.60)
The auspicious narration of Hari bestows immediate liberation upon those bound to the cycle of worldly existence;
for women with feet stained by dust, for servants, and for the wives of servants,
the story of Hari is like a lamp for those blinded by the darkness of ignorance.
It is the supreme medicine easily accessible to those overcome by the disease of worldly existence.
The discourse [on this] is considered like a thunderbolt against the mountains of great sins;
it is the parching of the seeds of karma and the means for attaining all prosperity.
O sages, the dust from the feet of those virtuous ones who hear and likewise glorify the stories of Śrī Hari is itself said to be the most sacred pilgrimage sites.
Even one who is incapable should listen to them day after day for at least a single moment.
Whether for an hour, half an hour, or even a moment, discourse that purifies is [the means].

For those of dull intellect who are preoccupied with gross worldly affairs, there is no other path equal to the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa) than this discourse; no other way is so conducive to happiness. (65–66)
By drinking nectar alone with effort, one person may become free from old age and death;
but the drinking of the nectar of this narrative shall render the entire lineage free from old age and death.
The speaker of this narrative is Hari himself, the teacher of all teachers.
The supreme Guru is the bestower of liberation, the giver of merit, and the lamp of knowledge.
Even those people who praise his discourse and its speaker, though they themselves do not listen, go to the eternal, supreme state. (68–69)
Those people on earth who provide assistance in hearing the sacred narratives remain in the abode of Brahmā for more than a hundred times ten million kalpas.
Through the attainment of understanding from these excellent narratives, may there be remembrance of Hari.
Through the yoga of constant remembrance, the destruction of latent impressions (vāsanās) occurs.
When that is so, dispassion (virāga) arises; in the absence of passion, there is supreme bliss.
Indeed, the bliss born from the destruction of craving acts as an aid in the emergence of the bliss of the Self (ātman).

When passion is destroyed, its opposite, hatred, is also certainly destroyed. For one in whom the two defects of passion and hatred have perished, the engagement with action—whether auspicious or inauspicious—no longer results in birth or death. (73)
Due to the absence of even worldly activity, there would always be an absence of enjoyment.
[But] immersed in the essence of devotion through the state of being one with Śrī Kṛṣṇa, he enjoys his own self, which is eternal bliss, the bliss of consciousness, and perpetual bliss. (74–75)
"Ever-satisfied in my form, perpetually immersed in my own Self,
and consisting of the bliss of Brahman within my abode, he enjoys the uncreated happiness.
(76) Thus, from hearing this narrative, there arises merit that bestows liberation.

I am indeed pleased wherever there is the nectar of my discourse. By the application of my discourse, even sins such as those as hard as adamant are entirely reduced to ashes through the knowledge of how to propitiate me.
The true qualities of a husband are to be heard; this is the eternal dharma.
I am the husband who is the Supreme Brahman; one should listen to my auspicious discourse.
[One should perform] charity, sacrifice, pilgrimage, and festivals with the expenditure of wealth.
My devotee who is unable to perform [these acts] must certainly listen to my stories. My praise and that of my Lord must be performed daily, both at dawn and at night.
Worship must be performed for my sake, and the food offering (nivedita) must be consumed.
One should consume all that is offered—leaves, flowers, water, and food—provided it is pleasing;
through this, there shall be purification of the inner being and constant remembrance of the Lord.
By the remembrance of Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, even eternal liberation is attained.
In the case of mindfulness, however, the hearing of the glories of Śrī Kṛṣṇa is the cause in every respect.
(83) The attainment of heaven through one's own merit from the earth is certainly not certain;
but by devotion to hearing the narrations, one goes to the eternal abode. (84)
The narrative of Śrī Hari is superior even to the gift of thousands of millions of gold pieces;
the narrative of Śrī Hari is more excellent than a thousand Rājasūya sacrifices.
The narrative is more auspicious than vows, observances, and the chanting of mantras.
In this [work], the wonders of the virtuous, my devotees, and those women devoted to yoga have been described;
and their most divine and radiant deeds have been recounted. (86–87)

All those [deeds] are givers of prosperity and liberation; for the sake of your liberation, through my service to the true nature of reality, I have indeed assumed the form of a Brahmin for the purpose of delivering you. (88)

Arjuna saw in a dream that his beloved wife Manoramā was requesting him to go alone into the forest,
and that an angry brahmin, a renunciant, and his guru were cursing him. (11.2)
He saw painted dolls dancing upon the wall.
He saw himself being tormented by vultures, crows, and buffaloes;
he saw himself crushed by an oil-press and spun around by an oil-maker.
He saw himself held by naked men with nooses in their hands;
all the singers were dancing and singing songs in his house,
[describing] the supreme bliss of marriage and the sporting world-leaders.
And at night, Arjuna indeed saw those engaged in a hair-to-hair struggle;
he saw a battle between crows and dogs,
as well as cakes and funeral offerings, and a cremation ground filled with corpses.
At night, Arjuna saw a woman wearing red garments and white garments;
she was dark-complexioned, dressed in black cloth, naked, and with her hair disheveled.
In that dream, Arjuna indeed saw a widow embracing herself.
Arjuna saw in his dream a barber shaving a bald head and a thick growth of beard and chest hair; he saw his own chest torn open by his own nails,
and in his dream he saw a heap of sandals and leather thongs.
He saw a potter’s wheel spinning upon the ground,
and a withered tree rising up, whirled about by a whirlwind;
and in his dream, Arjuna beheld a headless trunk (kabandha) being tossed about.
In his dream, Arjuna beheld a garland of severed heads being pulverized by a whirlwind,
as well as terrifying spirits and ghosts with most dreadful teeth who were vomiting fire.
Arjuna beheld in his dream a burnt soul, a burnt tree, another man seized by disease, one who was maimed in limb, and a low-born man; likewise,
he saw the sudden falling of trees upon a mountain peak.
Again and again, Arjuna saw the falling of thunderbolts in his dreams;
he repeatedly heard the howling of dogs and jackals.
[He also saw] one with head downward and feet upward, with disheveled hair and naked as the sky.
At night, Arjuna saw him wandering and moving upon the ground,
making distorted sounds and cries like the wailing of a god at the edge of the village.
Having heard this, King Kārtavīrya Arjuna awoke in the morning.
As he was leaving his bed, sneezing and stumbling, he saw at night his beloved wife Manoramā, who was deeply distressed by a wicked dream she had seen;
seeing her, that virtuous and devoted wife, faithful to her husband, [beheld] her lord and husband. (128–129)
She performed her final service by placing her husband upon her lap;
for to virtuous women, a husband is indeed dearer than a hundred sons.
However, having perceived their impending destruction through evil omens, she [prepared].

"Knowing that my husband was going to fight with a twice-born man who was an expansion of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, she restrained all her vital breaths (prāṇas). Having pierced the six cakras, she departed through the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra). (131–132)
Quickly, she of divine form departed first for the world of the virtuous (Satī-loka).
Then Arjuna went forth to fight; he beheld inauspicious omens.
Satī, with her divine body, [prepared for] the battle with her husband.
Having mounted the chariot, his companion, standing by his side, departed invisibly.
At the gate, Arjuna saw a widow who was ugly, with a severed nose, dressed in black garments, weeping, shaven-headed, and wicked. (1.34–35)
He saw another unchaste woman who was foul-mouthed, foul-vaginal, afflicted by disease, a procuress, and bereft of husband and sons;
as well as a potter, an oil-presser, a hunter, and one who subsisted on snakes. (136)
One who wears tattered clothing, whose limbs are extremely coarse, one who is naked, or one dressed in saffron robes;
a corpse burnt on a funeral pyre, ashes, or extinguished embers;
likewise, one who sells fat and one who sells a maiden. (1.37–1.38)
A man bitten by a snake, a snake, a monitor lizard, a hare, poison,
the food prepared for a *śrāddha*, a funeral rice-ball (*piṇḍa*), a *moṭaka* offering, and likewise sesame seeds;
a Brahmin who eats the food of a Śūdra, a temple-priest (*devala*), and a village priest— [these are not to be touched].
A doll made of *kuśa* grass, one who performs the cremation of a corpse, an empty jar, a broken jar, oil, salt, and a bone;
cotton, a tortoise, powder, and a dog that makes a sound. (1.457.140–141)
On the right, however, [one should avoid seeing] a jackal making a terrifying sound, a cowrie shell, a razor, a person with shorn hair, a fingernail, or filth;
as well as quarreling, lamentation, and people who cause distress. (142)
One should avoid an inauspicious person, one who weeps, a sorrowful person,
a witness who gives false testimony, a thief, a murderer of men, the husband of an unchaste woman, the son of an unchaste woman, and one who eats the food of an unchaste woman. (143–144)
One who steals the property or wealth of deities, gurus, or Brahmins;
a thief who misappropriates what has been given; a robber; a violent person; a slanderer; a wicked man;
one who is disaffected toward his father and mother; and one who harms twice-born men or the Aśvattha tree—[these are those who must be avoided]. (145)
One who destroys the truth, one who is ungrateful, one who is wounded, and a betrayer of trust;

a reviler of teachers, gods, and the twice-born; one who is devoid of self-restraint, a eunuch, one afflicted with leprosy, one who is blind in one eye, and likewise one who is deaf—(these are not to be accepted). 146–147.
He saw a Pulkasa with a severed linga, a bald man devoid of facial hair,
one intoxicated by liquor, a woman who had been a widow, a fist, a buffalo, and a donkey;
he also saw a crow vomiting blood that had been thrown at it.
Urine, feces, phlegm, and a parched human skull;
a fierce wind, a rain of blood, bad music, and the felling of trees;
a wolf, a boar, a vulture, a hawk, a heron, and a bear. (149–150)
An iron chain, dry wood, a crow, and likewise sulphur;
one who lives by black magic, a quack physician, chaff, and likewise medicinal herbs;
a red flower, news of death, a Brahmin’s curse, and likewise sneezing. (151)
Kārtavīrya beheld the falling of his sacrificial staff and crown;
there occurred a throbbing in his left limb, a stiffness of the body, and the collapsing of his chariot, horses, and cattle.
A harsh rattling of the chariot wheels arose, and terror was born within his heart. (152–153)
Nevertheless, the king entered the field of battle without hesitation;
having bowed to Paraśurāma, he bestowed wealth upon the brahmins.
War-drums were sounded and both armies prepared for combat.
Parśurāma spoke to Arjuna that which is right for all to hear.

(155) Thus ends the four hundred and fifty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Seizure of the Kāmadhenu Cow by Jamadagni under the pretext of [Arjuna's] conduct, the Chastity of Reṇukā, Parśurāma’s Acquisition of the Śrī-Kṛṣṇa Mantra, Kavaca, and Stotra from Śakra, the Omens for Parśurāma in Dream and Wakefulness, the Ill Omens for Sahasrārjuna, the Chastity and Devotion to Her Husband of the Virtuous Manoramā, and the Arrival at the Battlefield," in the first section on the Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga in the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 457:
[The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga] Chapter 458 of the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā, Part 1.
[The Author: Chapter 459.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī! Paraśurāma, who is a portion of Mādhava, spoke to him.
O Kārtavīrya, in the midst of battle, listen to the words of the upholder of dharma as they were spoken:
"Listen, O Indra among kings, most righteous one born of the Lunar dynasty!
You are the disciple of the wise Dattātreya, who is a portion of Viṣṇu. || 1-2 ||
O evil-minded one, why have you killed the aged Brahmin? His virtuous wife, tormented by grief, has gone away with her husband.
O King, what will become of you in the next world from the murder of these two?

Where has that Kapilā of yours gone? What will the bank look like? (4) O King, what you have done, a plowman would not do; thus, both good fame and ill fame remain as nothing more than a mere story. (5)
"You have committed a most terrible injustice; receive its fruit!
O Indra among kings, give an answer in this assembly at the head of the battlefield.
Having heard this, Kārtavīrya Arjuna began to speak.
Listen, Rāma: you too are a portion of Hari; of this there is no doubt.
(7) He who, through right understanding and action, cultivates the realization of Brahman, being pure and devoted to his own duty—he is proclaimed a Brāhmaṇa. (8)
Because he reflects both internally and externally, he performs actions that yield fruit;
the silent sage who always speaks at the proper time for the sake of others' welfare is called a *muni*.
Whether toward gold or a clod of earth, in a house or a forest, or toward mud or very fragrant sandalwood—
One whose conduct is like Rāma’s, who possesses equanimity, and who is a yogi, is called one who speaks according to reality (yathārtha).
He who meditates upon Viṣṇu with a mind of equality toward all living beings,
and who practices devotion toward Hari, is called a devotee of Hari.

For Brahmins, sages, and likewise for yogis, wealth acquired through austerity is like a wish-fulfilling cow; so too is it for a Brahmin devoted to Hari. For Kṣatriyas, there is always a longing for sovereignty and a constant desire for jewels.
For Kṣatriyas, a longing for asceticism is highly disapproved;
for Brāhmaṇas, a longing for dispute is likewise severely censured.
One who is passionate performs rajasic action out of attachment to worldly activity. (13–14)

One who is blinded by passion and characterized by the quality of rajas is proclaimed a "king" (rājan). O sage, it was out of such passion that the wish-fulfilling cow was indeed requested by me from your father; however, he raised armies against me, and this was a transgression.
"O Brahmin, tell me, what fault is there for me here, who am full of passion?
For one who has prepared an army of thirty akṣauhiṇīs to destroy me, there is no fault in killing an assailant. (16-17)

And you too, having become an ascetic, have made a vow that is devoid of the dharma of a brahmin; tell me, is this not an injustice? For the sake of both your parents, you have set out to rid the earth of the kṣatriyas.
"O Brahmin, tell me, what is right in this matter of [the earth] being taken twenty-one times?
Having heard these arrogant words, Paraśurāma, filled with intense rage,
instantly twanged his bow and released his arrows.
With floods of arrows, he covered Arjuna, his chariot, and likewise the sky.
The divine and beautiful Satī, devoted to her husband, remained upon the chariot;
then the Goddess, accompanied by Mahālakṣmī, protected her own husband.
Meanwhile, the king also cut down the volleys of arrows with his own shafts.
Then all four other brothers of Rāma, who were like advanced disciples, with sharp weapons and swords in hand, struck down Arjuna’s army. (22–23)
The lord of kings warded them off with a net of arrows,
but then the sons of Jamadagni cut through that net of arrows as well.
The king discharged a divine weapon, but the sages cut that too.
With a divine weapon, O sages, she severed the bow along with the arrow,
as well as the king’s chariot, his charioteer, and even his armor.
Then the virtuous Manoramā, possessing a celestial form, protected her husband.
Seeing the king with his weapons laid aside, the sages were overwhelmed with joy;
desiring to slay the King of Matsya, they seized the tridents of Śūlin.
At the moment the tridents were cast down, an incorporeal voice arose.
"O best of Brahmins, cast aside your spear; that [spear] belongs to Śiva and is indeed not in vain.
This divine armor of Śiva, which protects every limb, is on the neck of the King of Fish; ask the king for this armor. (28–29)
Having heard this, Rāma became an ascetic and begged the king for his armor;
the king then gave him the armor for the sake of victory over the universe.
Rāma struck with his trident, and Arjuna fell unconscious.
Then the beautiful and virtuous lady, through her vows of truth and her perfections in yoga,
protected the life-breaths in her head with the hand of her husband.
At that time, that chaste woman, as pure as the sky, spoke to the kings.
Let Bṛhadbala, Somadatta, Vidarbha, the lord of Mithilā, the king of Niṣadha, and likewise the king of Magadha—
hear this: these are as dear to me as my own life, yet I am the protector of Prāṇa.
I shall do so; go, sirs, and wage a fierce battle!
For Kṣatriyas, battle is their dharma, and death in battle is not censurable.
In this world and in the Veda, "Svāhā" belongs to the Brāhmaṇas in battle; [for others] it would be a mockery.
The strength of Kṣatriyas is their weapons; the strength of Vaiśyas is their occupation;
the strength of mendicants is begging; and the strength of Śūdras is service.
Devotion and servitude to Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa are the strength of devotees; Hari is the strength of the devotees.
Austerity is the strength of ascetics; indeed, the harming of the wicked is their strength.
Dress is the strength of women, and youth is the strength of housewives.
An army is truly the strength of kings, while weeping is the strength of children.
Truth is the strength of the virtuous, while forgiveness is the strength of the holy;
falsehood is the strength of the wicked, and courage is the strength of the reckless.
Knowledge is the strength of the learned, and wealth is the strength of the wealthy.
Discrimination is the strength of the eminent; unity is the strength of subjects.
Virtue is the strength of the virtuous, while service to their husbands is the strength of chaste women.
Worship is declared to be the strength of the gods, and service to the guru is the strength of disciples.
Strength is the wife for householders, and for servants, it is pleasing their master;
for renunciants, however, strength is desirelessness, while the great vow of Brahman is their strength.
Merit is the strength of the virtuous, and water is the strength of aquatic creatures.

"Peace is the strength of Brahmins, but for Kṣatriyas, strength is their strength. Having said this, that virtuous Manoramā [spoke] to the unconscious Arjuna while all the Kṣatriyas with their armies were preparing for battle against the Brahmins.
"If I am in every way a devoted wife to my lord of life,
may my husband regain consciousness," the devoted wife said as she attended to him with various restorative treatments.
Then, having regained consciousness, he rose up for battle.
Thereupon Rāma struck Somadatta with a trident,
Bṛhadbala with a mace, and Vidarbha with a lance.
Having slain the King of Mithilā with a mallet, the King of Niṣadha with a spear, the King of Magadha with sharp iron arrows, and all the soldiers with a multitude of weapons,
he rushed toward Arjuna.
Meanwhile, the beautiful Satī remained standing nearby.
"O lowest of Brahmins, you shall be reduced to ashes if, resorting to injustice, you kill my lord Rāma! (1.458.50)
Having heard [the news] and seeing Sītā before him, Rāma turned back out of fear.
There were hundreds from Kānyakubja, as well as hundreds from Saurāṣṭra;
likewise, there were hundreds from the various kingdoms, from Mahārāṣṭra, and those born in Vaṅga.
The Gaurjaras and the Kaliṅgas were rendered lifeless by Rāma.
For twelve nights, Rāma slaughtered twelve akṣauhiṇīs;
meanwhile, King Kārtavīrya held the Śrīlakṣmīkavaca in his hand.
Having girded his loins and equipped himself with weapons and missiles, he mounted his chariot and advanced.
He fought with various missiles and slew many Brahmins.
Then Paraśurāma, bearing his axe and assuming the form of Death itself, rushed forward.

Just as Viṣṇu, assuming the form of a brahmin, was about to cut off [his] head, he seized him by the hand, saying "Do not go! and restrained him; for at that very moment, the armor of Śrī Mahālakṣmī had been held by him upon his arm.
"The king will not die; remain firm," [said the sage].
Then Viṣṇu, having assumed the form of a brahmin, came to that king to make a request. Having become a brahmin, the Lord himself requested the armor.
Then her rival, Manoramā, was seized with terror.
Arjuna, wishing to give [the armor] away, was restrained by Manoramā:
"O King, as long as the armor of Lakṣmī remains upon your arm," ||| 59 ||
"I am Lakṣmī herself; I am able to protect you.
Though he was told repeatedly, "Do not give her," the king nevertheless gave her away.
For a moment, Lakṣmī Manoramā bowed to her husband and wept.
Then, unable to go along with the armor and intent upon it,
Satī performed a test of Viṣṇu.
Viṣṇu, taking the armor, went toward Rāma.
He gave it along with the mantra to Paraśurāma; hear that, O beloved:
"Oṃ śrīkamalavāsinyai svāhā. He then gave the mantra, the seer (ṛṣi) of which is Prajāpati and the meter (chandas) is Bṛhatī.
The goddess Padmālayā is the one who bestows the fourfold aims of life.
Oṃ, may [the mantra] "Oṃ Śrī Kamalavāsinyai Svāhā" protect my head.
Oṃ, may it protect my skull; Śrīṃ, obeisance to Śrī, may it protect my eyes. (64–65)
"Oṃ Śrīṃ Śriyai Svāhā"—may this always protect the pair of ears.
"Oṃ Śrīṃ Klīṃ Mahālakṣmyai Svāhā"—may this protect my nose.
"Oṃ Śrīṃ Padmālayāyai Svāhā"—may this always protect the teeth. (66)
Oṃ Śrīṃ! May she who is dear to Kṛṣṇa always protect the cavities of my teeth. Oṃ Śrī Nārāyaṇeśāyai! May she always protect my throat.
Oṃ Śrīṃ Keśavakāntāyai! May she always protect my shoulders. (67–68)
Oṃ Śrīṃ, svāhā to the one dwelling in the lotus; may she always protect my navel.
Oṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, svāhā to the Mother of the World; may she always protect my chest.
Oṃ Śrīṃ Mo, svāhā to the beloved of Kṛṣṇa; may she always protect my back.
Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ, svāhā to Śrī; may she always protect my hands. Oṃ, may she who is the beloved of Śrīnivāsa always protect my feet.
Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ, svāhā to Śrī; may she always protect all my limbs.
May Mahālakṣmī protect me in the east; may Kamalālayā protect me in the southeast.
May Padmā protect me in the south; may Śrīharipriyā protect me in the southwest.
May Padmālayā protect me in the west; may she herself protect me in the northwest.
May Kamalā protect me in the north, and Sindhu-kanyakā in the northeast;
may Nārāyaṇī protect me above, and may Viṣṇu-priyā protect me below; may she who is dearer to Viṣṇu than his own life protect me constantly and from every direction.
"Wear this armor, which bestows all sovereignty, well upon your arm;
you shall certainly become invulnerable to both the lords of the gods and the lords of the asuras.
Having spoken thus and given the armor, Acyuta departed for Vaikuṇṭha.

Indeed, that most enchanting digit of Lakṣmī’s beauty departed from Arjuna and went with Viṣṇu to Vaikuṇṭha, having been taken away by Viṣṇu. Arjuna said: "O wife, O beloved, do not go, leaving me behind!"
But Manoramā said to him: "The connection has reached its end.
You have been slain by the weapon of Paraśurāma; you shall follow after me.
Slain swiftly by the hand of a Brahmin, you shall attain liberation."
"O King, for your sake Vaikuṇṭha is certainly where my abode lies.
Having spoken thus, the goddess departed; the king fought fiercely.
O daughter of Padma, he fought his two hundred thousand army together with the brāhmaṇas.
The king hurled his weapons, and the disciples of Rāma fled;
but Rāma then discharged the Āgneya weapon, and the battlefield became filled with fire. The king extinguished it with the highly powerful Vāruṇa weapon.
Rāma discharged the Gāndharva weapon, which consisted of ten million mountains, serpents, and other creatures;
Arjuna indeed warded off that terrible weapon with the Vāyavya weapon. Rāma then discharged the Nāga weapon, and the king (Arjuna) discharged the Gāruḍa weapon.
Rāma discharged the Māheśa weapon; the king discharged the Vaiṣṇava.
Rāma discharged the Brahmāstra; the king repelled the Brahmāstra.
At that moment, Dattātreya, the preceptor of Arjuna, being meditated upon, arrived.
Indeed, he gave a trident to Rāma for the sake of his destruction, and a black-pathed fire (Kṛṣṇavarmāgni) as well.
The king seized that trident and hurled it at Rāma’s neck;
Rāma fell into a swoon and collapsed while remembering Śrī Hari.
By the command of Nārāyaṇa, Śambhu restored the Brāhmaṇa to life;
and when Rāma regained consciousness,
Arjuna [confronted] him with the Pāśupata weapon bestowed by Dattātreya.
Right there, Rāma was indeed rendered motionless and paralyzed.
He saw King Kṛṣṇavarmā protected by Śrī Kṛṣṇa,
and he also beheld the Sudarśana discus, the protector of his enemy, whirling about.
In the meantime, an incorporeal voice arose there:
"O King, that supreme armor of Kṛṣṇa is upon your arm;
Śambhu protects that king—beg it from him as alms."
"Then this Bhārgava will be capable of slaying the king.
Thereupon Śambhu, having restored consciousness by means of perfected mantras and having removed the paralysis, Rāma took up his own axe.
Holding a *pāśupata* weapon in one hand and an axe in the other, he meditated upon Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa; at that moment, He arrived.
Śambhu, having himself become a brahmin, entreated Arjuna for that very thing.
Śambhu presented the armor bestowed by the king to Rāma. Then Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa, and Traya, having approached Rāma’s side, said: "Now you shall be victorious. (94–95)
The *pāśupata* is the most excellent weapon of Śambhu, and the *sudarśana* belongs to Hari alone. These two are the foremost among all weapons in the three worlds.
Having donned this supreme protective armor, the twice-born one spoke to him.
"O King, fight quickly; for when the time has passed, victory and defeat are uncertain.
You have studied [the Vedas], given much in charity, and ruled the earth.
Yet in battle, you have been rendered motionless by me and have fainted right here."
"All kings have been conquered, and Rāvaṇa was defeated with ease.
I was defeated by Śambhu when he gave me the trident, yet I was restored to life by him.
Quickly act; this moment is yours. Upon hearing this, he replied:
"O Rāma, what has been studied? What has been given? And who has been governed?
How many kinds of kings, superior even to me, have passed away, devoured by Time? [Tell me of] their intellect, their splendor, their prowess, their victory, and likewise their triumph."
Prosperity, sovereignty, intelligence, generosity, renown, supreme austerity, learning, pride, honor, and even universal dominion—
all these vanished from me in an instant upon union with Manoramā.
That Lakṣmī was a virtuous woman, devoted to her husband;
as soon as my protector died, she departed along with him.
O Brahmin, why do you merely watch the first battle?
The first cause for grief was that my previous battles had not been witnessed;
then the second was the death of a Brahmin at my hands.
Furthermore, the grief over the destruction of the elderly couple was exceedingly cruel.

In due time, a lion kills a jackal, and a jackal likewise kills a lion; in due time, a deer kills a tiger, and a small antelope kills a lordly elephant. In due time, a fly kills a buffalo, and likewise a serpent kills Garuḍa.
The king praises his servant, and likewise Mahendra praises a mere mortal;
O Brahmin, all this is wrought by Time, for Time is indeed insurmountable. And the killing of a Brahmin is the destruction of everything for me.
The death of a devoted wife results in the destruction of the Brahmin’s merit.
(1.09) O twice-born one, when the devoted wife died, I too died in every respect; for she was the very form of Lakṣmī, and that agreement had indeed been made with Acyuta long ago. (1.458.110)
"I entreat you, as well as the gods and all my gurus, with devotion:
forgive whatever offenses I have committed against you, so that there may be no hell for me hereafter.
Having spoken thus, he twanged his bow and repeatedly discharged his arrows.
Becoming like Death himself, he rained down many hundreds of thousands [of weapons].
Addressing Kṛṣṇa as "O Kṛṣṇa," and calling out "O King Manorama," he [discharged] crescent-headed arrows, spears, broad-headed shafts, and swords by the thousands.
When his life-force was exhausted, Rāma discharged [his weapons] there at the Brāhmaṇas with his bow;
having assumed two forms, he fought with that king.
With his artificial form, however, holding an axe in his hand—
Having gone before him, he ran and severed his circle of arms.
With his second form, he seized a most formidable weapon,
the Pāśupata, along with its mantra, and discharged it at the king as if in play.
A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose, for Kārtavīryārjuna had been slain;
likewise, those others who were the capturers of living beings were also killed by the brahmins in battle. Others fled, and still others established their own respective kingdoms.
Then Rāma gave Māhiṣmatī as a sacrificial fee to a brahmin;
he also gave other kingdoms as sacrificial fees to brahmins.
The gods, the sages, the goddesses, the Siddhas, Gandharvas, and Kinnaras [were present].
And all the lotus-born ones showered a rain of flowers upon the head of Rāma;
in heaven the kettledrums resounded and a cry of joy arose.
In this manner, twenty-one times over, he rendered the earth devoid of Kṣatriyas.
The world was filled with the fame of Paraśurāma as well.
Rāma gave the kingdoms to the Brāhmaṇas and desisted;
all the Kṣatriyas were slain, including those in the womb and the young children.
O beloved, some Kṣatriya women, devoted to their husbands— whether young, middle-aged, old,
or even infants— departed for the Himalayas, protected by divine powers and possessing celestial movement. (123)
Dwelling in mountain caves, they nurtured their own sons;
from them were born the Kṣatriyas of that lineage, who once again established kingdoms.
Having fulfilled his vow on the field of the Kurus, Paraśurāma—
Having prepared five sacrificial pits at Syamantapañcaka filled with the blood of Kṣatriyas,
he offered handfuls of water to his father, mother, and the Brāhmaṇas; then,
performing the Śrāddha ceremony, he brought satisfaction to the ancestral deities.
Then he himself partook of water and food with composure.
As for those among the Kṣatriyas who were weak and fond of life,
they protected living beings by speaking falsely.
Various other types of births have arisen, and the castes have become distinct.
Those who are not of the Kṣatriya lineage and are devoid of Kṣatriya duties are indeed robbers (dasyus).
Others are performers of various occupations, such as those engaged in servitude, agriculture, and so forth.

O Lakṣmī! Hidden Kṣatriya lineages existed upon the earth. (1.458.13) Then, having fulfilled his vow, Rāma went to his preceptor at the divine gateway of Kailāsa there, in order to worship Śiva. (131)
