Even she is truly devoted to her husband who, at the end, causes her husband Hari to be remembered.
They do not call a kingdom a true kingdom merely because it possesses royal splendor; for one devoid of a devoted wife, even an empire with its seven limbs is regarded as a mere blade of grass.
If a wife, having become [a demoness] herself, causes her husband to fall from his virtue, she is certainly not a wife, but a *kṛtyā*, an illusion, a female *rākṣasa*.
She goes to hell herself and leads her husband and sons there as well. (1.460.60–61)
Furthermore, she who does not cause one to remember devotion to Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa surely causes even entire families to fall from heaven due to their sins and other faults.
Yet, such a woman is called a virtuous wife when there is wealth and prosperity.
She causes one to remember Dharma, sacred fords, vows, merit, charity, and Hari;
she indeed causes one to perform pilgrimages, festivals, worship of the Guru, of the parents, and of the Wielder of the Śārṅga bow, as well as service to the virtuous and devotion to Hari. (63–64)
"The self is dearer than the dearest, and for that [self], Acyuta is most dear;
liberation is even more dear. Thus should the devoted wife remind him.
"O virtuous lady, by your power I have enjoyed the kingdom free from all thorns."
The objects of the senses have been enjoyed, our purpose has been fulfilled, and incomparable merit has been performed.
Children have also been born; what remains for me to do here?
We two must certainly go to the city of Vārāṇasī.
Having thus resolved and having entrusted the kingdom to his son,
the king gave many gifts and set out toward Kāśī.
Having beheld Viśveśvara and the Jñānavāpī, which is the very ground of his own city, [he attained liberation].
And those two, who were seekers of the feet of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, rejoiced.
Having bathed, he gave various gifts and gold;
with joy, he gave golden and silver jars and milch cows.
Wearing various fine silken garments and carrying articles for worship,
he went, accompanied by his wife, to the Muktimaṇḍapa pavilion where the funeral pyre was prepared;
there he listened to the sacred narrative of the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*.
Having given a sacrificial fee of excellent wealth, he performed the evening worship of Śiva according to the prescribed rites; thereafter,
the king went to Jñānavāpī and bathed there joyfully along with Kalāvatī.
There, having offered funeral cakes and gratified the ancestors with faith,
and having given gifts to the poor, the helpless, virtuous women,
and the righteous, the couple then ate their meal after sharing it out.

Then Kalāvatī, with joy and supreme devotion, repeatedly chanted the name of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa; the ascetic woman performed austerities, sometimes by fasting on alternate days and at other times by observing the three-day vow. ||75-76||
Furthermore, by eating only every sixth mealtime, by the observances of half-months,
by fasting for the latter half of the month, by monthly fasts and the like,
by the Cāndrāyaṇa vows, by Kṛcchra penances, and even by serving her husband; || 77 ||
That virtuous woman passed the remainder of her life as if it were a mere moment.
Once, after the two of them had bathed at dawn in the Jñānavāpī and were seated there,
a certain matted-haired ascetic arrived, greeted them with blessings, and— 78–79.
"Oṃ, salutations to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; salutations!
Having bestowed this mantra, with a gracious countenance and wearing a garland of tulasī, he said:
"Arise! For the sake of liberation, direct your supreme mind toward that end."
At that moment, he entered a celestial chariot (vimāna) adorned with clusters of tinkling golden bells;
it was joined by divine four-armed devotees of Hari along with their attendants (pārṣadas),
and it was exceedingly beautiful, pervaded by the splendor of the forms of Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa.
Lakṣmī herself descended, bestowed the supreme and transcendent knowledge that grants liberation, and led those two, who possessed divine forms,
away by means of a celestial chariot together with Nārāyaṇa and Mahālakṣmī.
"O beloved, having attained the divine body with four arms, they have gone to the abode of Kṛṣṇa.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have told you this auspicious vow of Kalāvatī. It bestows liberation, O virtuous lady, whether through its recitation or its hearing in every way."

Thus ends the four hundred and sixtieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Attainment of Sovereignty in a Future Birth by the Couple Following their Gāndharva Marriage, and their Liberation through the Power of Chastity, Concerning the Greatness of Jñānoda in the Field of Ānandavana," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. Chapter 461 *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā*, Part 1 (Kṛtayuga-santāna) [Chapter 461]
[The Author: Chapter 462.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
"I have heard from your mouth and understood that devotion to one's husband is the supreme dharma."
Is the purity of a woman’s body eternal or artificial?
Or is it attained through sacramental rites, or is it considered to be acquired through marriage?
O beloved, tell me the truth regarding that which nourishes the performance of dharma and other such duties.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Women are eternally pure; they are never defiled by anyone.
Month after month, their menstrual flow carries away their misdeeds.
In former times, women were enjoyed by the gods—by Soma, Gandharva, and Agni;
men enjoy them afterwards, yet they are not defiled by anyone.
Soma bestowed purity upon women, and Agni bestowed total sanctity.

Because they possess auspicious speech, Gandharvas always regard women as pure. Agni consumes the maiden at the time of her menses, the Moon at the appearance of body hair, and the Gandharvas at the budding of her breasts; therefore, she must be given away even before that.
One who gives away a maiden who has not yet been enjoyed by the Moon (Soma) and other [deities] obtains great fruit from that gift;
therefore, one desiring the fruit of giving a maiden in marriage should give her while she is still in her youth.
The appearance of menses, body hair, and the budding of breasts are the indicators of youth.
A girl of eight years is Gaurī, while one of nine years is Rohiṇī.
A ten-year-old is called a Kanyā; beyond that age, she is possessed of menses (rajas).
The giving away of a daughter in marriage is declared auspicious when she has reached fourteen years.
Beds, seats, vehicles, a corpse, the face of a woman, kusha grass, and all sacrificial vessels are indeed never defiled in any circumstance.
A calf is pure when it causes milk to flow; a bird is pure when it causes fruit to fall.
Women are pure during sexual intercourse; a dog is pure when seizing game.
(11) The mouth of a goat and a horse is pure; cows are pure on their backs;
those who know the Veda are pure at their feet; and women are pure in every respect. (12)

A beloved wife, even if enjoyed by force or fallen into the hands of thieves, must not be abandoned; she is as pure as a goat made of sacrificial wool. Holy men are purified by red ochre, and women are purified by their menses.
The entire world is purified by Kṛṣṇa; the husband and wife are purified by their marriage ceremony (udvāha). Semen is always purified by conception; the child is purified by birth.
Disciples are always purified by mantras; embodied beings are purified by initiation (dīkṣā). (1.4, 1.9)
The virtuous are always purified by their vows; the women of the household are purified by their husbands;
milk is always purified by the life [of the cow]; the teeth and other [parts of the body] are purified by the place [where they reside].
A maiden—whether young, adolescent, or old—is always purified by her inner disposition.
Water is pure by its very nature; fire is pure by its very nature.
(17) Fire, water, wind, and women born of noble lineage are always pure.
Therefore, such women should be honored with ornaments, clothing, and food. (18)
Those who desire prosperity should always perform rites of hospitality during ceremonies and festivals;
for there the deities rejoice, and there all actions become fruitful.
Where the husband is pleased with his wife, and the wife is pleased with her husband—
In that household, prosperity shall be attained at every step.
(1.461.20) If the wife is antagonistic, what then is the difference from hell?
But she who is skillful, fertile, virtuous, sweet-spoken, and submissive—(21)
That divine Śrī, who assumes a female form, follows after every breath;

if a woman possesses the auspicious marks, the householder always enjoys happiness. [Her] body, whorls, fragrance, luster, vitality, voice, and gait— 22. That divine Śrī, who assumes a female form, follows after every breath; if a woman possesses the auspicious marks, the householder always enjoys happiness. [Her] body, whorls, fragrance, luster, vitality, voice, and gait—
The grounds for the characteristics of women should be understood as eightfold, including complexion;
thus, there are sixty-six mines of excellent characteristics for a woman's body.
First is the sole of the foot and its lines, then the big toe, the toes, and the nails. (23–24)
The back, the two groins, the heels, the calves, the body hairs, the knees, the thighs, the waist, the buttocks, the hips, the private parts, the pubic region, and the bladder;
the navel, the two sides of the belly, the flanks, the abdomen, and the three folds of skin in the middle of the belly. (25)
The line of body hair, the heart, the chest, the two nipples of the breasts;
the collarbones, the shoulders, the upper arms, the armpits, the forearms, the wrists, and the two hands;
the back of the hand, the palm of the hand, the lines [on the palm], the thumb, the fingers, and the nails. (26–27)
The back, the nape of the neck, the throat, the chin, and the two jaws;
the cheeks, the mouth, the lower lip, the upper lip, the teeth, and the tongue;
the uvula, the palate, the smile, the nose, the sneeze, and the eyes. (28)
The eyelashes, eyebrows, ears, forehead, crown of the head, parting of the hair, and the hair itself—listen, my dear, women are indeed examined in these limbs!
The soles of women's feet should be glossy, fleshy, soft, and even. (1.461.30)
A palm that is sweatless, warm, reddish, and fit for great enjoyment is considered auspicious;
whereas one that is dry, discolored, rough, with broken reflections, shaped like a winnowing basket, and parched, indicates suffering and misfortune. (31)
She on whose soles there are lines resembling a wheel, a svastika, a conch, a lotus, a banner, a fish, or an umbrella shall indeed be the wife of a king. Furthermore,
a vertical line extending from the middle finger [of the foot] bestows great enjoyment and abundant prosperity.
Lines resembling snakes or rats bring poverty and suffering;
a thumb that is well-nourished, elevated, auspicious, and rounded bestows great enjoyment.
A thumb that is short, crooked, and flattened destroys good fortune.
A widow has a broad thumb, while one with a long thumb is unfortunate.
Fingers that are soft, elevated, thick, and rounded bestow prosperity; those that are long belong to an unchaste woman, and those that are thin indicate poverty. (35–36)
Women with short fingers and short life-spans, those with crooked fingers, are considered deceitful;
those with flattened fingers become slaves, while those with widely spaced fingers are poor.
Furthermore, women whose toes overlap one another [are likewise ill-fated].

They are considered widows and the wives of others many times over. (38) She from whose back dust rises as she walks along the road brings about the destruction of the families of her parents as well as her husband. (39)
That woman whose little toe does not touch the ground as she walks will slay her husband and take a second husband.
That woman whose ring toe does not touch the ground as she walks [will likewise do so]. (1.461.40)

She whose middle toes do not touch the ground as she walks destroys two husbands and makes a third her husband. She [whose middle toes] do not touch the ground as she walks destroys three husbands and makes a fourth her husband. (40–41)
If the ring finger and middle finger are excessively short, she will be separated from her husband;
if the forefinger is always joined with the thumb, she makes one unchaste.
The toenails that are glossy, elevated, copper-colored, and rounded are auspicious.
If the instep of the foot is elevated, smooth, soft, and fleshy,
free from perspiration and devoid of prominent veins, she will undoubtedly become a queen.
A foot instep that is depressed in the middle always indicates poverty.
A woman's feet that are veiny, prone to aching, covered with excessive hair, and like those of a servant, as well as being fleshless, should be understood to bestow great misfortune.
However, ankles that are hidden, round, and free of visible veins are givers of happiness.
The heels that are low-lying and flaccid bring misfortune to women.
A heel that is even brings great good fortune; a broad heel, however, makes one unfortunate.
A raised heel belongs to an unchaste woman, and a long heel brings much suffering.
The shanks of a queen should be hairless, smooth, tapering gradually, rounded, charming, and beautifully red; such feet are considered auspicious for a royal consort.
A woman with a single hair on each leg becomes a queen, while one with two hairs is a partaker of happiness.

If there are three hairs in each hair-pore, she will undoubtedly become a widow. The knees of a woman devoted to dharma are round, well-fleshed, and firm; those of a wanton woman are fleshless, while those of a poor woman are loose and flaccid.
The thighs should be shaped like plantain stems or the trunks of young elephants— smooth, white, firm, rounded, soft, hairless, without veins, and auspicious.
A woman with such thighs will be a queen, a woman of great wealth, learned, and devoted to her husband.
A woman with joined thighs will indeed be a widow, while one whose thighs extend toward another will likewise be so;
one with flattened thighs will be unfortunate and always filled with suffering.
One whose thighs have a gap between them will be a partaker of misery, as will one who suffers from headaches.
A waist that is firm, heavy, and always pervaded by poverty, measuring twenty-four finger-breadths and circular in circumference;
and a waist that has elevated hips and is square—such a waist is auspicious. (55)
A waist that is sunken, bent, flattened, withered, or long brings suffering.
A short waist covered in hair portends widowhood.
The hips, however, should be elevated, well-nourished, broad, firm, and fleshy. (56–57)
Like the fruit of the *kapittha* tree, the labia increase pleasure and enjoyment.
A vulva as broad as a tortoise and elevated like an elephant’s frontal globe is auspicious.
If it is elevated on the left, it bestows daughters; if elevated on the right, it bestows sons.
One whose pubic hair resembles that of a rat, whose middle is concealed yet broad,
whose joints are firm, whose banks are solid and elevated, who is shaped like a *plakṣa* leaf and elongated,
who has the color of a lotus, and who is slightly slender— such a woman is excellent and increases good fortune. (1.461.60)
That which has the shape of a deer's hoof or is circular like a hearth,
which is hairy and has a wide-open mouth with a long tongue, is considered the lowest.
One that resembles a conch-shell spiral is not fit for the maintenance of an embryo.
Flat and shaped like a shallow bowl, it always acts as a servant [to disease];
resembling the leaf of a bamboo or reed, and covered with long, coarse hair;
moreover, a vulva that is excessively elevated and filled with fleshy protuberances does not bestow auspiciousness. (62–63)
A vulva that has firm, elevated rims, a clear reddish luster, a narrow middle,
and is encircled by internal folds always bestows happiness.
It is covered with flesh above, protected by hidden bones, and guarded by submerged, stable tissues.
A vulva that is fleshy all around and within always bestows happiness.
One that is deformed, crooked, pendulous, wide, flaccid, cavernous, hollowed out, or raw and devoid of flesh never grants pleasure. (65–66)
The vulva should be broad, elevated, and fleshy;
it is excellent when soft, rich with fine hair, and spiraling to the right.
Conversely, one that spirals to the left, is fleshless, or crooked indicates widowhood.
A pelvis resembling that of a pregnant woman, or one with a protruding belly, does not grant peace.
A pelvis that is dry, contracted, depressed, and bony brings suffering.
The bladder located at the side of the pelvis should be soft, expansive, and tender. (68–69)

A navel that is slightly elevated and excellent bestows vehicles and conveyances; however, one that is hairy, veiny, marked with lines, or deep and turning to the right is not at all praised as a giver of happiness. (1.461.70)
A navel that spirals to the left, is turned upward, or has a clearly visible knot is not praised. (71) A woman with an expansive belly indeed gives birth to many sons;
a virtuous woman whose belly is shaped like a frog’s gives birth to a king. (72)
A woman with a protruding belly will be barren; one with a wrinkled belly will be virtuous;
one with a whorled belly will be a slave, a servant from birth.
She who has even, fleshy, and soft sides with hidden bones— ||| 73 ||

She shall possess good fortune, joy, excellent virtues, sovereignty, and happiness. (74) One whose navel is elevated with hair, whose channels are visible, and whose sides are emaciated, will be ill-behaved, childless, and a sea of suffering. (75)
A belly that is very small, headless (flat), and soft-skinned indicates the enjoyment of pleasures;
however, a belly like a water-jar, a drum, or a pumpkin gourd is indeed difficult to fill.
A woman with a pendulous belly kills her father-in-law, while one with a broad belly is childless.

A woman with a slender waist, fortunate, possessing the three folds [of skin on her belly], and granting sexual pleasure is a giver of delight. She whose line of body hair is straight and thin brings happiness and sport.
A line of body hair that is tawny, crooked, thick, or broken indicates she will be abandoned by her husband.
A woman whose heart is hairless and elevated, who always bestows affection upon her husband, and whose heart is broad, will be unchaste and merciless;
whereas one whose heart is covered with hair will certainly be a slayer of her husband.
That woman whose chest is eighteen finger-breadths in width and plump is said to be elevated, bestowing happiness; it is fleshy, beautiful, and excellent.
However, that which is hairy, uneven, or broad indeed brings suffering.
Breasts that are thick, rounded, firm, plump, and symmetrical are praised.
Those with thick tips, sparse nipples, or that are shriveled and soft do not grant happiness.
A woman whose right breast is elevated, prominent, and firm shall have sons.
A girl whose breasts are tilted toward the left gives birth to a daughter beautiful in her good fortune.
Breasts resembling the buckets of a water-wheel indicate a lack of virtuous character;
those that are thick at the base, separated by a wide gap, and broad at the edges are not auspicious. (83–84)
Those breasts which are thick at the base, gradually tapering, and sharp-tipped,
first bestow happiness but later cause grief and bring about suffering.
The nipples should be beautiful, firm, dark, round, and auspicious.
If the collarbones are sunken, long, or thin, they indicate affliction.
However, with stout collarbones, a woman possesses wealth and grain;
with loose, depressed, or uneven collarbones, she is poor. (86–87)
Shoulders that are unbound, well-sloped, neither too long nor too thin, and auspicious;
yet those that are crooked, thick, and covered with excessive hair indicate servitude and widowhood.
Shoulders with hidden joints, tapering at the tips, auspicious, and well-knit [are favorable].

When the two upper parts [of the armpits] are joined together, they bring widowhood; when they are fleshless, they cause extreme suffering. (89) The armpits are auspicious when they have fine hair, are elevated, smooth, and well-fleshed.
They are not auspicious when they are sweaty, deep, or veiny. (90)
The hands of virtuous women are red, fleshy, headless (without prominent veins), with hidden bones and tender skin; they are hairless, bright copper-colored, and straight.
If the hairs on the hands are thick, widowhood results; if they are short, they cause misfortune.
Likewise, hands that are rough and black at the tips of the fingers are considered to bring suffering.
However, for virtuous women, both hands joined together with the thumbs and fingers facing each other in the shape of a lotus bud indicate the attainment of great enjoyments. (92–93)

The palms of the hands are auspicious when they are soft, moderately elevated, red, and without cracks; they are most excellent when endowed with auspicious lines, while having very few lines indicates good fortune and prosperity.
One with many lines becomes a widow, whereas one without lines is poor.
The palms of the hands should have visible veins that awaken dispassion;
the backs of the hands should be hairless, smooth, auspicious, elevated, and possessed of veins yet devoid of flesh. Women who possess such hands with veins are destined to be widows. (95–96)

Red, distinct, deep, glossy, full, and circular—the lines on the hand are considered auspicious for women as lines of fortune (bhāgyarekhā). With a fish-shaped mark she is fortunate and virtuous; with a svastika she is a bestower of wealth. (97)
By means of a lotus, the wife of a king shall become the mother of a monarch.
(98) On the hands of a woman destined for a universal emperor (*cakravartin*), there are clockwise *svastikas*;
on the left [hands], there are a conch, an umbrella, a tortoise, a banner, and a parasol. (99)
The line of a balance, the wife of a merchant, one whose womb is bound, and the beloved of a merchant;
likewise, elephants, horses, and bulls on the left, as well as a palace and a cart—
if there is the sign of a yoke on the left, she will indeed be the wife of a Vaiśya.
A line that emerges from the base of the thumb and reaches the little finger, as if drawn by a yak-tail whisk, a goad, or a bow,
indicates a woman who will be the slayer of her husband, a murderer, and a bringer of suffering. (101–102)
A woman who has lines shaped like a trident, a sword, a mace, a spear, or a drum will be a donor, renowned, and devoted to her husband.
[She whose lines have the forms of] a heron, a jackal, a frog, a wolf, a scorpion, or a serpent...
Donkeys, camels, and cats held in the hand bring suffering to a woman.
(104) She whose teeth are black, who is tall, whose face is like that of a *miñjarī* bird, whose face cries out repeatedly, and who walks with a limp or moves sideways; (105)
One whose feet are blackish-yellow, whose face hangs down from the jaw,
and whose belly-joint is bent backward destroys one's station of fame.
A thumb that is auspicious is straight, rounded, with rounded nails and soft.
The fingers are auspicious when they have well-jointed, long, rounded, and slender digits.
Those that are flattened, rough, withered, and covered with hair on the back are inauspicious.
Fingers that are excessively short, thin, crooked, or widely spaced are causes of distress.
Fingers endowed with many joints always bring about suffering.
Nails that are reddish, possessed of crests, elevated, and rounded are auspicious;
those that are depressed, discolored, resembling mother-of-pearl, or yellow indicate poverty.
White spots on the nails indicate a woman's promiscuity. A back with the vertebrae deeply set and well-fleshed is auspicious;
however, if the back is covered in hair, it portends widowhood.
A back that is bent, depressed, or possesses prominent veins brings suffering;
one that is straight, with a raised nape, even-fleshed, and symmetrical is always auspicious.
One that is withered, veiny, hairy, broad, or crooked is inauspicious.
A neck that is fleshy, rounded, and four finger-breadths in circumference is praised.
A neck marked with three lines, with bones not protruding, well-knit, and not overly fleshy is auspicious; one that is flattened, long, and withered does not bestow good fortune. (113–114)
A woman with a thick neck is a widow, while one with a crooked neck is a servant.
One with a flattened neck is barren, and one with a short neck is childless.
A chin measuring two finger-breadths in width is auspicious when it is circular, full, and very soft.
The thick [chin] is of two kinds; that which is hairy and long is not auspicious.
A chin that is joined to the jaw, hairless, and very dense is auspicious.
One that is crooked, thick, thin, short, or hairy does not bestow good fortune. (116–117)
Full, rounded, elevated, and well-filled cheeks are auspicious;

those that are sunken, rough, hairy, and fleshless do not bestow happiness. A face that resembles the countenance of one's progenitor, possessing its own fragrance, circular, and symmetrical, [is likewise auspicious].
The face of a virtuous woman is glossy, beautiful, well-fleshed, and full.
(119) The lower lip, which bestows sovereignty, is deeply red, round, glossy, adorned with a line in the middle, and gradually thins from the center toward the edges. (1.461.120)
An underlip that is thin, pendulous, cracked, or rough indicates misfortune;
one that is thick and brownish brings the distress of widowhood.
An underlip that is slightly elevated in the middle, hairless, and smooth bestows wealth.
The line of the teeth is shaped like a bow, and the upper lip is marked by the *lakṣmī* (the sign of fortune).
The teeth of virtuous wives are white, resembling pomegranate seeds, glossy, even on both sides, and slightly elevated. (122–123)
Teeth that are yellowish, dark, thick and long, resembling mother-of-pearl,

sparse, rough at the base, uneven, or arranged in two rows belong to women devoid of fortune. A woman whose lower row of teeth exceeds the upper is considered to bring about the destruction of her mother.
One with protruding teeth is a widow, and one with crooked teeth is unchaste. A tongue that is red, soft, and white indicates a person who enjoys sweet and desired foods;
however, if it is constricted in the middle and broad at the tip, it brings suffering.
A white tongue brings death by water; a black one causes quarrels;
a fleshy one bestows poverty; a long one leads to eating what is unfit for consumption;
and a broad tongue is considered to constantly awaken one to negligence.
A palate that is very glossy, lotus-colored, and soft is praised.
(128) If the palate is white, there will be widowhood; if yellow, it belongs to renunciants.
If it is black, one is childless; if rough, one has a large family. (129)
A bell situated within the throat that is sharp, red, and circular is auspicious; it should not be hanging down, nor should it be thick. However, one that is thick and black brings suffering.
Furthermore, [the face] should have a smiling expression with teeth invisible and a slightly blossoming skull.
A woman’s smile with eyes half-closed is praised.
A nose with even nostrils and small openings brings good fortune;
one that is thick at the tip, depressed in the middle, or overly prominent is not praised. (131–132)
A nose with the curved tip resembling the beak of a parrot is excellent;
however, a nose that is short at the tip and reddish at the end brings about widowhood.
A flat nose makes one a servant, while a short or long nose makes one fond of strife.
The eyes with reddish corners and black pupils are praised as beautiful.
White, long like petals, very glossy, and with black lashes are auspicious;
one with upturned eyes does not live long, while one with round eyes is considered unchaste.
A woman with eyes like those of a ram, a buffalo, or a flat-faced bird is not praised.
One with eyes like a cow or a tawny monkey possesses the impetus of desire and becomes the resort of many enjoyments.
One with eyes like a pigeon is of bad character, and one with red eyes is a slayer of her husband.
A woman with eyes like a deep abyss or eyes like an elephant's is not praised.
A wanton woman has a left eye that is blind; a barren woman has a right ear that is blind.
A woman whose eyes are tawny like honey possesses an abundance of wealth and grain.
One who possesses eyelashes that are thick, fine, glossy, and black is a possessor of good fortune;
one with lashes that are tawny, sparse, and coarse is considered a performer of blameworthy deeds.
The eyebrows should be well-rounded, glossy, black at the edges, and situated separately [from each other].
The eyebrows of an excellent woman are praised when they are smooth-haired, very sharp, and shaped like a bow. However, eyebrows that are coarse-haired, wide-spreading, long-haired, tawny,
joined together, or scattered are not auspicious for a noble woman.
A woman’s ears that are long, with auspicious whorls, soft, and pleasant are auspicious;
those lacking the earlobes (*śaṣkulī*), or which are veiny, crooked, and thin, are censurable.
(142) The forehead that is free of veins, hairless, and resembles the half-moon is auspicious.
A forehead that is not depressed and measures three finger-breadths in width bestows good fortune, health, and happiness upon a woman.
A forehead marked with clearly defined svastika lines brings sovereignty.
A woman whose head is excessively long will become a slayer of her husband.
A woman with a prominent forehead and a high head is considered to be afflicted by disease.
A straight parting of the hair is excellent, as is a well-elevated crown of the head.
[The head] shaped like an elephant's frontal globe is circular and indicates good fortune and sovereignty.
A woman with a pot-shaped head becomes a widow, while one with a protruding head becomes unchaste.
One with a broad head or two heads indeed becomes unfortunate in this world.
Hair that is black, soft, fine, glossy, and curled at the tips [is auspicious]. (146–147)
Long, straight, and lustrous [nails] are indicators of devotion to one's husband;
whereas those that are rough, split at the tips, tawny, light, and dry—
sparse, thick, and hard— bring about suffering and poverty.
A mole between the eyebrows or on the forehead is considered to bestow sovereignty.
A red mole on the left cheek grants sweet food and drink.
A clockwise tilaka, or even a garland-like mark or a bee-shaped one, [bestows similar fortune]. (1.461.150)

A mole, a freckle, or a mark on the right breast that bestows the fortune of royalty— whether it be a sesame seed or a drop of blood— if such exists, she shall give birth [to these]. Indeed, she is a virtuous woman who gives birth to four daughters and three sons.

If there is a red sesame mark on the left breast, she will give birth to only one son; thereafter, that virtuous woman will attain widowhood. If she has a sesame mark on the right side of the private parts, that virtuous woman will become the mother of a king.
That queenly lady on whose nose-tip there is a red mole—
if that [mole] were black, she would indeed be a killer of her husband and a wanton woman.
A mole or a freckle below the navel is a sign of a devoted wife.
A mole or a freckle at the region of the ankle causes poverty.
(155) A mole or a freckle appearing on the left side of the neck, the hand, the forearm, or the cheek will first bestow the gift of a son. (156)
If there is a trident-mark on the forehead, she becomes a queen who is a preceptor’s wife;
if she grinds her teeth while sleeping and frowns, she is an ill-omened woman.
However, a clockwise curl of hair on the hand always brings about righteousness.
A counter-clockwise curl of hair on the hand brings suffering even to a woman. A clockwise curl at the navel, the ear, or the heart is indeed auspicious;
likewise, a clockwise curl on the right side of the back bestows great happiness.
A clockwise whorl on the spinal column bestows long life and sons;
a clockwise whorl at the apex of the vulva indicates the status of a queen.
If that [whorl] should be shaped like a cart, it grants the happiness of many children and other blessings.
If the lines on the abdomen are not commenced and end at the waist, they cause the destruction of sons and husband.
A depression on the belly or the tail, or a whorl on the back, or if they are excessively long, do not grant peace;
one such mark makes the husband a killer, while the other makes the wife unchaste.
A clockwise curl situated on the neck is considered to bring the misery of widowhood;
if it occurs at the beginning of the hairline on the forehead or in the braid, it brings extreme distress.
Furthermore, for a woman who has a whorl of hair on the nape of the neck or in the hollow of the throat, [the same result follows].
If the whorls turn to the left or to the right, she will become a widow.
If there be one or two on the left side of the head, then she will be a killer of her husband until the end of ten days; however, if there be a whorl at the waist, she is unchaste.
A woman with hair-whorls on her back is a killer of her husband; one with hair-whorls at her navel is devoted to her husband.
Even if she possesses inauspicious marks, a virtuous woman who is devoted to her husband and devoted to the gods is considered excellent.
Those who are dedicated to sacred fords, vows, austerities, fire-offerings, recitation, and charity—
By the grace of the virtuous and of Hari, chaste women endowed with auspicious marks—
those noble and virtuous ladies— transform even a beloved husband of short life into one of long life, and they deliver their entire lineages. (167–168)
Chastity toward one's husband is the supreme virtue and the foremost of all auspicious marks;
if that exists, then indeed all other marks will grant happiness.
O beloved, these marks have been described by me for the welfare of householders.
"From reading and hearing this, one's own knowledge shall become a giver of happiness.

(1.461.170) Thus ends the four hundred and sixty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Results of the Lines on the Limbs, Major and Minor Parts, and Other Signs Indicating the Purity of Women and the Auspicious or Inauspicious Nature of the Female Body," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
← Chapter 461: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga) Chapter 462 [Author: Chapter 463 →
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, Lakṣmī! I shall tell you a story of the future, as spoken by the Blessed One; she, being present with him, recounts a tale pertaining to all three periods of time.
O beautiful one, everything within the range of the Blessed One’s perception is true and uncontradicted;
yet, in every kalpa,
a certain story of Viṣṇu arises for me and for you that is distinct, though similar in its essential nature.
Listen, dear Lakṣmī! Hara himself is five-faced.
Having become fivefold upon the earth, Śiva performed the destruction at the sacrifice.
And Umā, the sustainer of the world, [became the daughter] of King Drupada.
From the sacrificial fire-pit, that beautiful maiden appeared;
and the five sons of Pāṇḍu, who were the very embodiments of Indra himself, descended here from heaven to earth for the removal of its burden. (5)
Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa also became his helper.
(6) In the world of living beings, prosperity and adversity, the whirlpools of delusion, and indeed the rise and fall of worldly creatures, arise as natural occurrences upon the earth. (7)
Once, those great heroes resorted to the forest-dwelling custom established by their kinsmen— a practice shared with those in times of calamity.
That queen, the daughter of the Pañcālas, went to the forest region along with them.
Devoted, faithful to her husband, and virtuous, she always worships them.
Devoted to her husband, chaste, and virtuous, a devotee of Kṛṣṇa and a friend of Hari,
that ascetic wife of Indra propitiated the Sun.
Devoted to the life of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) and subsisting on forest fare, she served her husbands;
for during the remaining times, without ceasing, she became intent on meditating upon the Sun.
Having meditated [upon him] from his nails to the tips of his hair, she invoked him into the *arka* tree.
She indeed honors him with devotion by offering many articles:
water, flowers, wild leaves, fruit, fragrant food, the waving of lights (nīrājana), and lamps; that virtuous woman offers these with faith. (12–13)
Bowing, remembering, praising, circumambulating, and seeking forgiveness— the devoted wife performed these acts along with offering handfuls of flowers and prostrations.
Then, the Sun, having been propitiated, granted her his own vision.
He said to that great goddess: "Tell me, what is it that you desire?
I am the Sun, and Kṛṣṇa is my body; you are Kṛṣṇā, born of sacrifice.
I recognize the identity of our two bodies: whatever is mine is yours as well."
Draupadī said: "O Lord of Gods, in the forest, without means of livelihood, even the food and other provisions for many people cannot possibly suffice;
for at times, there may be the arrival of thousands of guests. (17)
O Lord, having heard of the forest-dwelling of the Pāṇḍavas in the woods,
please grant them that faultless wealth so that for their sake there may arise a fitting and complete hospitality as before. (18–19)
"O river, grant me assistance for my dwelling in the forest so that my devotion to my husband and my reputation may not suffer;
provide me with a seat, water, wild fruits and food, and sweet speech. (1.462.20)
The affection in the eyes of guests is the cause of favor;
from it arise blessings born of a gracious heart.
But those arising from a grieving heart are considered curses that reduce everything to ashes. (21–22)
"Service to my husband is my supreme gain here in the forest;
service to guests equal to my husband through food and other offerings is my constant concern, O Lord.
Having heard this from the princess of Pañcāla, the Lord Bhāskara was pleased.
He gave her an inexhaustible cooking vessel together with a ladle and a lid.
With a gracious mind, he said to that virtuous lady, his own self-manifested body:
"O highly meritorious one, by means of this vessel, for as many people as there may be who seek food," || 24-25 ||
They shall obtain satisfaction as long as you do not eat;
once you have eaten, this vessel, though now empty, will become full of food—
a treasure-house of flavorful side dishes that provides whatever food one desires.
"As long as you dwell in the forest, so long shall it remain under your control.
Constantly serve your husbands by the hundreds of thousands, those who dwell in the forest;
acquire merit, O Queen of the Gods, and may all be well with you forever. (27–28)
You are Lakṣmī, you are Satī, you are Śrī; you are Prabhā and you are Māṇikī.
You are Pārvatī, Jayā, Rādhā, Ramā, Padmā, and Mohinī.
You are Padmāvatī, Rudrāṇī, Campā, Śāradā, and Śivā.
O Tulasī, you are Mahālakṣmī, Vṛndā, Sītā, and Rukmiṇī.
O Queen of the Gods, you do not know this, being engaged in human-like play;
but I know you truly, O virtuous one: you are in every way the beloved of Kṛṣṇa.
Arjuna is you in human form; your husband Kṛṣṇa is but half of you.
O Kṛṣṇā, you possess devotion to your husband; you are Kṛṣṇā, the beloved of Kṛṣṇa.
It was for your sake alone that the five heroes [protected] the earth.
O Daughter of Sacrifice, Kṛṣṇa indeed desires to remove the burden of the Daityas.
Both your own form and my vessel grant inexhaustible fulfillment;
from you come all true arts, and from my vessel come the excellent sacrifices.
Those who have taken refuge in Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa will indeed exist and will continue to exist;
for there shall never be another woman as tender and virtuous as you, who carries out the word of Kṛṣṇa.
Such a woman of sattva, pervaded by forgiveness, will not exist even without Lakṣmī.
That very word of Kṛṣṇa is your vow, your devotion to your husband.
Both dharma and adharma, as well as bondage and liberation, are subject to Kṛṣṇa’s word.
Pleasure and pain reside in the form of Kṛṣṇa; the Pāṇḍavas are embodiments of Kṛṣṇa.
May you always have well-being; may there be no suffering caused by dwelling in the forest.
Consider yourself to be in a state of happiness; remember Hari and me during times of distress.
I shall attend upon you at the proper time and provide whatever assistance is required.
Great women may suffer great hardship; what then could befall those who are lowly? (3.9) On this earth, Kṣatriyas rule kingdoms with the edge of a sword;
for those who are like jackals, their own domain would not be even a small plot of land. (1.462.40)
She who endures the heat of fire is adorned with the luster of fire;
indeed, she becomes the wife of Agni, possessing the brilliance of ten million suns.
For a female frog is not the mate of a lion, nor is a female crow a swan.
A maidservant is not the wife of a king, nor is a pauper the lord of Kubera. By you the entire world is made prosperous; without you, it appears lusterless.
O Draupadī, remember Govinda, who dwells within the heart and resides as the Master.
Having spoken thus, the Sun departed after bowing to her, and she too bowed to him.
Draupadī, in the midst of the forest, serves Śrī Hari and her husbands.
Durvāsas, who was served by ten thousand disciples, was [honored] by the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
He was sent for the purpose of bringing about the destruction of the Pāṇḍavas.
Then the Ṛṣi will not accept the food offered as hospitality for tens of thousands;
he will curse the Pāṇḍavas, and they shall consequently meet their end.
Intending this, Durvāsas, having been invited, went to that forest. Honored by the Pāṇḍavas, he was offered a meal;
meanwhile, he went to bathe, taking with him that vessel of the Sun.
"Having washed [the vessel] and set it aside, Satyā will certainly not give us food.
Furthermore, one must not increase the food after the time for the ritual observance has passed, because the King of Sages, becoming angry at the lack of food, will surely pronounce a curse. (48–49)
Then, being remembered by Satyā, that woman dear to Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa himself—the abode of mercy—arrived in his divine form.
"Tell me, O Goddess, why was Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa remembered? he asked.
Satī said: "What food shall I give to the son of Atri?
Everything has become empty; even the alms-bowl was eaten by me.
Having washed it, I have kept it in its place. There is no food, O Kṛṣṇa, O Mādhava. (51–52)
Kṛṣṇa said, "Bring the vessel; I shall examine it.
When it was brought, a betel leaf was found stuck to its side.
Kṛṣṇa looked at that leaf and placed it in his own mouth.
"May the illustrious Lord of the Universe be pleased, and likewise may the universe be pleased.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Kṛṣṇa ate that auspicious leaf;
he then drank water and belched again and again.
"Aha! Satisfaction has arisen for me, and indeed the three worlds are satisfied;
Durvāsas and his ten thousand disciples are likewise satisfied.
The bellies have been completely filled by the grace of Hari."
In whosever home Hari eats, He eats in all the three worlds.
In whosever home Hari is satisfied, the three worlds are satisfied for him.
Durvāsas, along with his disciples, attained great satisfaction and was filled with fear.
"What could happen? We shall eat [the food], even if we are cursed by the woman;
we will perish there, so we must certainly go from here.
Having reflected thus, they suddenly departed quickly from the bathing place.
All the disciples were intent on flight, while the sage was filled with wrath. The Pāṇḍavas remained composed, as did Draupadī in her reflection;
and Kṛṣṇa, Hari, the protector, was served by all in the forest.
"Whenever calamity should arise, you must remember me," having said this, the Lord departed.
O virtuous lady, this is the dharma of a devoted wife, which consists of having Kṛṣṇa as one's husband.
All women desire a husband who is fortunate, handsome, and endowed with youth.

Having obtained such a Kṛṣṇa— a husband who is wealthy, prosperous, endowed with sovereignty, and a bringer of fame— what woman would not serve as His handmaid? What devoted wife (*pativratā*) would not indeed make her own birth fruitful?
The goddesses, the Gandharva women, those of the Asuras, the wives of the Nāgas, and the beloveds of the sages;
the creepers, the rivers, the Earth and others, and the Kinnara women;
the daughters of Manu, the wives of the Kiṃpuruṣas, and likewise the Vidyādharīs—[all these came].
All those who became infatuated with Kṛṣṇa attained the supreme state.
Kṛṣṇa is born in this world for the sake of bringing happiness to them;
his birth and his deeds are divine, perceived as such, and are not brought about by ritual injunctions.
The births of Śrī Hari, Harikṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, and indeed those of Rādhā and others, as well as Ramā and others, are not born from a womb.
Whenever Kṛṣṇa Himself desires to descend [to earth], [He does so by His own will].

He gave the command to the god Vāyu: "Dwell firm within the cavity of the womb, so that the mother’s belly may appear auspiciously endowed with a fetus. Remaining steady for nine months, when the tenth month has arrived..."
At the time of birth, you must emerge from the womb like a child;
then, having fashioned me into the form of an infant son,
I shall fall upon a spot of the earth, so that people may indeed know me as one who has been born.
In every respect, my birth is likewise not born from a womb;
for all my incarnations, my birth is not produced by a womb.
Rādhā, Lakṣmī, Ramā, Padmā, Śrī, Prabhā, Kānti, and Śāradā— [these are my consorts]. 72–73.
Māṇikī, Pārvatī, Durgā, Sarasvatī, Satī, Jayā,
Padmāvatī, Lalitā, Kambharā, and others— these were not born from a womb.
Indeed, whenever they are born, the Wind enters the womb.
When the tenth month has arrived and the time has come, the Wind himself,
assuming for a moment the form of a child, emerges from the womb;
at that time, O Goddesses, they become embodied as girls.
They become like children so that others may not know [their true nature];
then ignorant people say of them, "These girls are born from a womb. But those who are intent upon divine vision see that these girls are not born from a womb.

This divine birth of that Kṛṣṇa and of his wives is indeed the creation of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, like a creation produced by mere volition. Desire is the seed, Rati is the womb; everything is manifest simply through his glance.
But the world perceives His play as being like the world, and His liberation also as being like the world; the gods, possessing divine vision, perceive it as the gods do;
the lords perceive it as the lords do, and the liberated perceive it as the liberated do. (1.462.80)
Śrī Puruṣottama beholds His own [devotees] as He Himself does.
Therefore, all activities performed for Kṛṣṇa are divine and bestow divinity.
Thus are the duties—the duties toward Kṛṣṇa—those who are solely devoted to Kṛṣṇa as their Lord.
Having obtained worthy husbands who are devotees of Kṛṣṇa, those devoted wives acquire heaven, liberation, virtue, desire,
and wealth; they acquire sons, daughters, happiness, and divine bliss.
Having performed everything for the sake of Kṛṣṇa, they worship Mādhava.
Always observing the vow of Kṛṣṇa and serving their husband Mādhava,
and having surrendered their own bodies to their husband, they attain the abode of Hari.
What need is there to say, O beloved Lakṣmī? You surely know such a vow:
my vow and your vow are entirely auspicious, consisting of the duties of a married couple;
they are devoid of [worldly] qualities, bestow supreme liberation, and have me as their presiding deity.
Since you are my beloved, I have told you that which is the most excellent among the excellent.

Whatever woman there may be—whether born of a lowly lineage or a high-born family—who has her affection fixed on me, who regards her life as being for me, and who has surrendered her existence for my sake; ||| 87-88 ||
The devoted wife, who has practiced my teaching without deviation,
and she who is devoted to Hari— both these faithful wives shall indeed attain me at the end.
She who listens to this chapter and performs the rites shown therein [shall likewise attain me].
"And she who constantly worships me shall indeed attain me, for she is truly virtuous.

Thus ends the four hundred and sixty-second chapter, titled "The Description of Draupadī’s Protection of Durvāsas and His Disciples Arriving at Mealtime in the Forest by Her Virtue as a Faithful Wife and Her Power of Chastity, and the Eating of Tāṇḍula Leaves Performed by Kṛṣṇa," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
