Chapter 464 → Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Mahālakṣmī! O Prabhā! O Pārvatī! O Padmajā! O Sarasvatī! O Ramā! O Kṛṣṇā! O Māṇikī! O Kambharā!
O Satī! O Durgā! O Rādhā! O Śāradā! O Vṛndā! O Tulasī! O Abdhijā! (1)
O Padmāvati! O Queen of the Pāṇḍavas! O Sāvitrī! O beloved Rukmiṇī!
[2] Likewise, tell the story of Vinatā and Kadrū from their previous birth, concerning the wager given by Dakṣa to Kaśyapa; and how both Kadrū and Vinatā [acted]. [3]
"O faithful wives, O great virtuous ones, devoted to the service of your husband, auspicious devotees of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa who can assume any form at will,
you two were performing penance for the sake of Kṛṣṇa, desiring offspring. (4)
From Kadrū were born auspicious serpents capable of assuming forms at will.
Those offspring of Kadrū indeed formed various groups, being black, red, green, tawny,
yellowish-red, brown, and variegated.
White, blue, as well as subtle, medium-sized, long, and very long;
these serpents and reptiles, the sons of Kadrū, came into being with forms like Kadrū herself.
They were dark-green, variegated, pale-white, and smoke-colored.
There were crores of species of nāgas with variegated colors, resembling scales and water-lilies.
Then Vinatā gave birth to her sons, Ulūka, Tārkṣya, Aruṇa, and others.
Although Ulūka obtained the sovereignty of the birds due to his seniority, [he was surpassed] by them thereafter.
Furthermore, because he was devoid of all virtuous qualities, he was deposed from the kingdom by them all.
He had cruel eyes, was blind by day, always possessed crooked claws, and was inauspicious;
his speech was terrifying, and thus he was not worthy of the kingdom.
Then, as they lived in a kingdom without a king and moved about according to their own will,
Vinatā, longing for the sight of her son, broke open the middle egg for the sake of the king. (11–12)
Indeed, when a thousand years had been completed and it was ripe, that egg split apart due to her longing at the eight-hundredth year.
At that time, all its limbs were certainly not yet fully formed. (13–14)
That embryo became enraged at the destruction of its success while still half-formed;
because the mother had thoughtlessly cursed her own child with anger,
she herself split the egg that was within her body.

"Since all my limbs have been produced by my own power, I curse you, who acted for the harm of my son! For when you saw the sons of Kadrū being caressed on their mother's lap, you shattered this egg of mine out of impatience under that very pretext."

"O bird, if you desire that 'having obtained a son, I shall quickly fondle him on my lap,' then you shall indeed become a slave to your co-wife. Having heard this curse uttered by her son, the mother was overcome with grief.
The Sun said: "O Anūru, speak! O son, bring about an auspicious end to this curse.
Anūru replied: "Do not break the third egg;
he who is to be born from the third egg will ward off this curse."
Having spoken thus and bowed to his mother, Anūru flew up and went to the forest.
Having propitiated the Sun with austerity and obtained a boon, he protects the Prabhākaras in the machine;
this one drives the horses of the Sun.
First the rising of Aruṇa was made, and afterwards the rising of the Sun.
Then, when a thousand years were completed, the third egg split open by itself; from it was born Garuḍa, resembling the Sun.
Even the young grasshopper, having emerged directly from its egg,
cried out to his mother while seeking food, saying, "Give me something to eat!
Delighted, the mother spoke to the hungry and mighty Garuḍa.
"O son, I am ultimately unable to satisfy my hunger.
Your father Kaśyapa is on Mount Meru; go to him.
He will give you food, and your hunger will be appeased. (25–26)
Having heard his mother’s words, the bird went to where Kaśyapa was;
bowing with his head, he spoke these words to his father:
"I am your son Garuḍa, sent here by my mother Vinatā."
"O Father, O Lord, I am afflicted by hunger; let food be given to me!
(28) Knowing him to be his son, Kaśyapa, bowing down out of affection, said to him: "There are many hundreds of thousands of Niṣādas from the ocean of milk... (29)
"Fish-eaters dwell on the shore; eat them and be happy.
Without a Brahmin, maintain your livelihood among the Niṣādas.
Thus addressed, he went there and then began to devour them.
Even though the Brahmin was invisible, he was swallowed by that bird.
Then a fire arose in his throat and blazed up to the middle of his neck;
the king of birds was unable either to vomit him up or to swallow him down.

Having gone, he then said to his father: "O father, a fire within my throat is constantly burning me; some person has clung to me who brings about my end. Kaśyapa said: "O son, it must be a Brahmin; otherwise, that could not be so."
Having spoken thus, Kaśyapa summoned the Brahmin from outside.
The Brahmin said, "O father, I will not go out, leaving these behind;
some friends and likewise beloved kinsmen have been swallowed. (34–35)
"I shall go with these [companions] to hell or to the blissful Hari.
Having heard this, Kaśyapa was astonished and said to the fallen twice-born man:
"Therefore, you have severed your connection with the Niṣādas."
Indeed, because of your evil association, you, being a sinner, shall go to hell.
(37) But if, having committed a most terrible sin through ignorance or delusion, one thereafter practices righteousness, he shall indeed attain the supreme goal. (38)
A doer of evil should not perform the *vṛṣotsarga* rite; if he should perform it, he will then commit sin.
His destination is such that he sinks into a most terrible hell.
O Brahmin, depart or go to your death; do not remain here at my throat.
Having heard Kaśyapa’s words, that twice-born man, who was observing a vow regarding his kinsman, spoke clearly to Kaśyapa: "Listen, dear father, to what is for my benefit.
Although I am a twice-born by birth, my beloved wife is a Niṣāda woman."
My Niṣādas, my brothers-in-law, and likewise my father-in-law and others were swallowed by Garuḍa;
they died within his stomach.
Yet, through the yoga of Pāvana, even that which is impure becomes purified.
Through separation from you they were all impure, but through union with you they became purified;
especially have they been sanctified by the power of the womb of Garuḍa.
And I am one who observes the vows of kinship, devoted solely to my wife.
O my father, if they all were released and restored to life, then I would depart from your throat; otherwise, death is certain. My vow is as firm as the *bandhujīva* flower or my own very life.
Having heard that, Kaśyapa spoke to the bird for the sake of his welfare:
"Vomit out these Niṣādas along with the Brahmins, all of them.
Thus addressed, Garuḍa vomited out those Niṣādas.
Indeed, those birds that dwell in the cardinal and intermediate directions as predators—
consumers of *garuḍas*, cocks, swans, pigeons, and so forth—
all shall assemble in the Kali age for a single meal among the people.

When no distinction of species remained between the fire and the serpent, nevertheless, overcome by hunger, he begged for excellent food. Then, commanded by Kaśyapa, he went to the vicinity of the ocean. (1.463.50)
There, seeing the two great beings— the tortoise and the elephant— whose bodies were many yojanas in length, the victorious one pierced them with his claws and leapt up into the sky;
having seen the massive branch of the Jambu tree on Mount Meru, he sat down upon it.
Having seized the broken branch, the elephant and the tortoise flew up into the sky and went to Satyaloka,
the abode of Brahmā, where Mādhava—
Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa Viṣṇu— had arrived after being praised there.
Hari said, "O Lord of Birds, how is it that you wander in the sky holding this massive branch and these two great beings, an elephant and a tortoise?
Garuḍa, the son of Vinatā and descendant of Kaśyapa, then replied to Hari.
"I am Garuḍa; having seized the Jambu tree along with its elephant and tortoise, I went there, but even that Meru tree was shattered. Where indeed shall I stay?
I am hungry and wish to eat; tell me, O Lord, where shall I go? (55-56)
“Neither trees and such, nor even mountains, can endure my weight or my speed;
the mountains tremble and the planets are agitated in the sky.
Thus addressed, the Blessed One said, “Stay indeed here upon my arm.”
"Quench your hunger; eat these two, the elephant and the tortoise.
Thus addressed, Garuḍa then alighted upon the arm of Śrī Hari, and leaving the branch behind, he devoured the elephant and the tortoise in the great ocean.
Nevertheless, his hunger was not yet appeased; therefore Hari said to him:
"Eat my own flesh; by consuming it, you shall become happy.
Thus addressed, he ate the flesh from his arm and attained satisfaction.
Nevertheless, seeing that no wound had been produced on his arm, he said to Hari:
"O Lord, tell me what dear service I shall do for you.
Hari replied: "Become my vehicle for all time."
May you be invulnerable among all beings, and may you be free from old age and death.
May you have access everywhere, and may your power of action be equal to mine.
You shall obtain full sustenance from the destruction of your mother’s rival.
Having been addressed thus, that bird went toward his father Kaśyapa. Desiring to ask for and receive permission, he spoke to his father;
and Kaśyapa, with a joyful heart, spoke these virtuous words to his son.
I am blessed; my mother is blessed; my family is blessed to possess such a virtuous son.
For he is a devotee of Viṣṇu who brings liberation to ten million generations of his lineage.
Through the destruction of all his sins, he shall attain the status of a servant of Viṣṇu.
He with whom Viṣṇu is pleased shall also be the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama).
Blessed is that embodied being here whose family is purified, and he for whom a son, a wife, a daughter, and a cow exist for the sake of Kṛṣṇa. (67–68)
"Viṣṇu is not attained by the gods even through many austerities, religious duties, or various kinds of sacrifices; yet that very Hari has been attained by you.
Having served your mother, go to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu."
Having thus received the command, he went quickly to his mother.
Having bowed to his mother, that boy— assuming a form at will despite his small body— delighted and rejoiced in her presence.
Seeing his mother standing there having become a servant to Kadrū, Garuḍa asked, "Tell me the reason for this, O Mother.
His mother replied, "Listen, my son; I shall tell you what happened previously."
"Understand from me that which was born together with Kadrū as her wager.

(73) Thus ends the four hundred and sixty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Serpents as the Progeny of Kadrū from Kaśyapa in the First Section on the Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga; the Birth of the Owl, Aruṇa, and Garuḍa from Vinatā; the Eating and Vomiting by Garuḍa of the Brāhmaṇas and Śabaras; the Consumption of the Flesh of Viṣṇu’s Arm; and the Granting of Boons and the Making of Viṣṇu’s Vehicle," in the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*. (463)
← Chapter 463: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga) Chapter 464 [Author: Chapter 465 →
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Formerly, Kadrū and Vinatā, the two daughters of Dakṣa and lawful wives of Kaśyapa, were sporting together once upon a time, O auspicious ones.
"Are the horses of the Sun, Uccaiḥśravas, dappled or white?
What will their forms be?"—thus they conversed in the house of Kaśyapa.
Kadrū said: "O Vinatā, your movement in the sky is unimpeded."
"Therefore, you shall know everything; tell me, what indeed is its form?
O auspicious one, O sinless one, make a wager that pleases you.
Vinatā said: "O auspicious one, O daughter of Dakṣa, what is the use of a wager here?"
"In a wager, there is happiness for neither of us; the wager causes suffering for one or the other.
Knowing this, one should never engage in a wager that causes the loss of affection.
What is my loss in your victory, and what injury to you is there in my victory? (5)
"It is certain that upon the victory of one, there must be the defeat of the other.
I shall speak thus even without a wager, O sister.
Kadrū replied, "In the practice of gambling, there is always a wager without which it cannot be played."
No mental relish arises, nor does any flavor whatsoever;
therefore, it is only by setting a wager before them that players take delight.
Even children make false wagers and laugh.

"They sport for the sake of passing the time; therefore, make a wager and speak. (9) Vinatā said, "As you desire in this matter. Then Kadrū, deceitful and cunning, spoke the terms of the wager. (1.464.10)
"Whichever of us is defeated by the other, she shall become the slave of the victor;
and in this wager, all these friends of ours shall serve as witnesses.
Having thus made the bet, Kadrū spoke of the piebald horse.
Vinatā spoke to Dhavala, and then they both went to their own abode.
Kadrū, having summoned her sons, the black serpents, made that her wager;
she said, "O virtuous sons, go quickly at my command."
"O sons, gallop that white horse, leaping according to every hair;
a black spot might appear anywhere and defile it on all sides.
Having heard these words of their mother, some said to their own mother:
"We shall certainly not go, being filled with the fear of the fault of falsehood.
Others also have said that such a fault destroys trust;
falsehood is the gateway to hell, and we will not commit that fault. (15–16)
Others as well, honoring their affection for their own kinsmen and likewise for their maternal aunt,
acted in accordance with that purpose while remaining guided by prudence.
To all of them, Kadrū, the serpent who was a treasure-house of wrath, uttered a curse.
"May those who oppose my words always become food for Tārkṣya!
Thus consumed by his curse, they went to Pātāla as their refuge.
Then there were other boys who were overwhelmed with affection for their mother.
Understanding their mother’s words, they went into the sky after the horse of the Sun;
they followed the horse on all sides and made it dark blue and variegated.
Then, scorched by the heat of the Sun, they returned home.
Then Kadrū spoke all that to her mother;
having summoned Rāhu, she honored him and commanded Suyojana to cover [the sun] with Rāhu during the lunar eclipse (parvan) in order to destroy the heat of the sun.
Having gone to the sun, the serpents cried out from all sides;
when Kadrū had mounted the back of Vinatā and they were traveling toward heaven,
the horse was seen by them to be dappled and dark-colored.
Vinatā said: "A white horse was indeed seen by me repeatedly.
Today, due to the rise of your good fortune, a piebald horse is seen.
Let it be as it shall be; who can ward off destiny? (24–25)
In all matters, destiny is more powerful; even that which is white appears as blue.
Whatever kind of unseen force (adṛṣṭa) presents itself for enjoyment in a particular place, it quickly arises as favorable even if it were previously adverse.
Having seen the dark-horsed one (Viṣṇu), the bird was indeed defeated;
Kadrū, who resided constantly in his house, always performed service for him.
Garuḍa, seeing his own mother in such a state as a servant— ||| 27-28 ||
She said, "O mother, how is it that this servitude is being imposed upon you?
Fie on those sons who are so powerful that their mother becomes the servant of another!
Indeed, the birth of a son is for the sake of supporting one's parents. (29)

A mother who is not supported by her sons is equated with a she-ass. When there are seven sons who are truly virtuous, the she-ass is the one that carries the burden; fie on those sons by whose living they cause their mother to suffer!
It would be better for her to remain barren than to have sons who perform the deeds of the barren,
by whom the mother’s womb was tormented and yet the mother does not rejoice.
Lakṣmī is the mother who gives birth and bestows one’s own self-ownership.
The birth of those by whom she was delivered from suffering is not in vain.
If my mother were in extreme pain while I am strong, what strength would that be for me? That strength is indeed remembered as the strength of hell.
Even if sons have committed evil deeds, if they protect their mother,
they cross over by means of the "mother-tirtha" through service that has satisfied her.
Neither sacrifice, nor vow, nor recitation, nor gift, nor even sacrificial fee [can achieve this].
They may at times attain even a hundredth part of the merit of serving one's mother.
Indeed, by the service of a mother and her very blessings, thousands of obstacles and tens of thousands of messengers of Yama vanish far away.
Having heard these words of her son, Vinatā spoke to her devoted child:
"In the past, I indeed entered into servitude to Kadrū on account of a wager.
Then, she [challenged me] regarding the horse of the Sun, saying it was white."
Then his sons indeed called him "Karbura" (the Spotted One). Having gone there, the horse was painted black, and I entered into a state of servitude.
For at whatever time I might give her the object she desired, [she would be satisfied].
"Then I shall attain freedom from servitude; ask the female serpent.
Having bowed to Vinatā and having bowed again and again to Kadrū, Garuḍa indeed questioned Kadrū regarding the liberation from his mother's state of servitude.
Kadrū said, "Give me the nectar; let there be my release from slavery.
Having heard that, Garuḍa took leave of his mother, remembered Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, and went to Kaśyapa.
Kaśyapa spoke to him regarding his journey for the sake of the nectar:
"Indeed, above the world of heaven, there exists the nectar—the food of the gods—which is guarded by the attendants of the gods with a discus. (44)
"Go quickly; by remembering Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, victory shall be yours.
(45) At his father's word, Garuḍa entered the sky and departed.
Having seen that treasury of nectar, the king of devotees rejoiced. (46)
Remembering Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, he beheld the treasury officials;
shaking them all away on every side with the wind from his wings,
the powerful one saw a scissor-like machine situated above the nectar.
Whirling with great speed like the Sudarśana discus,
that massive weapon would indeed shatter into pieces anything it touched;
yet Garuḍa, having reflected for a moment, attained the state of a subtle atom.
If I am devoted to my mother and a follower of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa,
then may the Blessed Lord himself grant me protection here.
For one whose parents are aged, who has young children, and who is destitute—
A virtuous wife is for his nourishment; thus, there is no fault in him even for an improper act [performed for her sake].
(51) For the sake of saving the life of a mother, a Brahmin, a child, a cow, a wife, or even a teacher, there is no blame for an improper act. (52)
Having done this, he beholds the nectar situated at the lower part of the wheel; having filled a jar with it and drunk that death-destroying elixir,
he then, by the power of yoga, uproots the wheel from its peg with a brush.
Having made it steady, free from wandering, and slow in its movement,
he rose up together with the jar of nectar for as long as it took;
upon merely seeing him, the guards with nooses in their hands fled.
Having violently rendered them all unconscious with the wind from his wings,
he emerged from that treasure-vault; meanwhile, Indra and the other lords of the gods,
being alerted by their messengers, quickly arrived there in a rage for the sake of battle.
Mahendra, accompanied by his weapon, said to him: "Who are you, this stealer of the nectar?
Stay! Stay, O mighty-armed one! I shall surely destroy you with my thunderbolt.
Upon hearing these words of Indra, Garuḍa then became enraged.
"Show your prowess! I shall carry you to the nectar," said Garuḍa.
Having been addressed thus, Indra struck him with his thunderbolt.
Despite the violent impact of the thunderbolt, the one of great strength was not at all shaken.
Seeing his own thunderbolt rendered futile, Indra became afraid and said to him:
"O bird, if you now give the nectar to the mother of the serpent,
then all the serpents will be made into immortals by you."
"Your vow would be ruined and you would surely have no food;
therefore, do not give that nectar to her, and do not make Kadrū immortal.
Having heard this, Garuḍa said, "O King of the Gods, I shall take the nectar myself."
"I shall give Kadrū as my slave; thereafter, she shall no longer be a slave.
You must strike her quickly so that she does not drink the nectar.
"So be it," Hari said, and the king of birds went to Kadrū.
Having given [the nectar] and cast off his servitude, he became free from debt toward his mother.
Then the King of Birds himself spoke to the serpents and Kadrū:
"The nectar must not be drunk while one is impure; otherwise, it would become impure itself."
"Since it has lost its potency through being tasted, let them drink it after bathing.
Having been told this, they went to bathe; meanwhile, Śakra seized that nectar.
When the serpents returned, they did not see the vessel of ambrosia at all.

At that place where the vessel had been placed upon a clump of *kuśa* grass, their tongues licked it; consequently, their tongues were split in two by the *kuśa* blades. Then those fierce serpents cried out for the sake of the nectar.
But at that time, Indra fashioned another artificial jar (6.9),
into which poison had been secretly placed in place of the nectar.
Taking that [jar], they all drank from it, each receiving a single drop according to their share (1.464.70).
The Mother said to those sons: "O sons, may drops always remain at your mouths;
let there never be a loss [of speech] for you.
Having received this blessing, those serpents went to their own home.
Then those nāgas, delighted by the delusion that it was nectar, were filled with joy;
but thereafter, the powerful and hungry Garuḍa devoured them one after another.
Those nāgas who fled took refuge in mountains and other such places.
Thus, that Garuḍa, having liberated his mother from the state of being a servant and having received the blessings of his parents,
departed for the realm of Vaikuṇṭha and became the vehicle of Hari.
He attained eternal service to Hari and reached a state of worshipfulness like that of Viṣṇu himself.
Because his mother Vinatā was the mother of a son devoted to Him,
she became eternally honored by Kaśyapa, remaining firmly established in truth.

The sons of the virtuous woman Vinatā were the givers of nectar (amṛtadaḥ), while the sons of the deceitful Kadrū, whose mouth was poison, were themselves deceitful. Therefore, O Lakṣmī, you must always protect my devotion to my husband, Hara.
By my own power, I shall indeed drive away their terrible end.
Devotion to one's father, devotion to one's mother, and devotion to one's teacher are deliverers;
devotion to one's husband, devotion to one's son, and devotion to a chaste wife are excellent deliverers.
Devotion to servants, devotion to the gods, and devotion to one's wife are deliverers;
devotion to the virtuous and devotion to Kṛṣṇa grant liberation in my abode.
Indeed, I am eternally present within all embodied beings along with you, O Śakti.
Thinking thus, embodied beings should practice devotion toward other embodied beings.
One should offer all that has been done unto Me alone, who dwells within;
considering it to consist of My grace, the devotee should enjoy it, and not otherwise.
Whether in a woman, a man, an animal, a tree, a creeper, or in that which is insentient or sentient,
Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa alone is both the enjoyer and everything that is enjoyed.
Realizing this, whatever the embodied soul eats is indeed devoid of the qualities (nirguṇa).
This devotion to the husband has been proclaimed by me with my whole soul.
By performing this vow in this manner, one is liberated; there is no doubt in this matter.
By reading or hearing this, one shall obtain the fruit of devotion to the husband.

Thus ends the four hundred and sixty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of how Garuḍa Effected the Removal of Vinatā’s Servitude through the Deceit of Kadrū Regarding a Bet on whether the Sun’s Horse was Spotted or White," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 465: *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā* — Section 1 (*Kṛtayuga-santāna*) — Chapter 465.
[The Author: Chapter 466.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī! [I shall tell you of] Līlāvatī, the great virtuous wife who was beloved by her husband.
[He was born as] the wife of Divodāsa, the King of Kāśī, who was firm in her vows. Divodāsa became an attendant of Kṛṣṇa and a dweller in [His] abode,
having come here to this earth by the command of Kṛṣṇa for the purpose of promoting devotion.
O beloved, he became a human king, a great devotee of the Lord;
his devotion to Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa was always pure, free from desire, and indeed granted him the grace of Kṛṣṇa. (2)
Līlāvatī was the wife of Hari, a maidservant residing in Goloka,
a friend of Lakṣmī who always remained by her side, and a lover of Kṛṣṇa.
By the command of Kṛṣṇa, that virtuous and chaste woman became the daughter of the King of Surāṣṭra.
At her birth, the lords of the gods, sages, ascetics, women, goddesses, Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, the Īśas,
and likewise the Manus came to her house and bestowed auspicious blessings.
Then the gods showered a rain of flowers and the women sang;
the Apsarases danced, and a magnificent, auspicious festival took place.
Then, as soon as she was born, that auspicious girl appeared for a moment with four arms.
The beautiful woman of excellent limbs appeared like Kamalā;
in another moment, she became a maiden, born lying upon her confinement bed. (9) Then, when she had reached a suitable age, the king performed her marriage.
Then indeed Pṛthivījinmahārāja and the attendants of Viṣṇu,
as well as all the millions of Gaṇas and others residing in Kāśī belonging to Śaṅkara, arrived from all sides for the marriage of this Līlāvatī.
And those gods and goddesses, exceedingly joyful, bestowed their blessings.
Then the virtuous lady, together with Divodāsa, went to Kāśī by means of a celestial chariot.
At that time, the gods showered flowers upon the top of the chariot.
Śaṅkara and the other Vaiṣṇavas caused the couple to prosper.
To the couple was born a son named Samarañjaya;
thereafter, there were five hundred sons who followed the path of righteousness.
The highly intelligent Divodāsa, the lord of kings, having consecrated his son Samarañjaya, set out for the conquest of the quarters,
taking with him upon his chariot the great chaste Līlāvatī, who was devoted to her husband. (15)
By the power of Līlāvatī, he conquered the kings of the South;
he conquered the kings of Prāgjyotiṣa and the mountain rulers of the Himālayas.
Having defeated those situated in the North and those in the West, he indeed went to Kāśī. (16–17)

On the western bank of the celestial river (the Ganges), he caused a palace to be built. Having crushed his enemies in battle, the king constructed temples with all the wealth that he had acquired. (18)
All the royal fortune of the king was bestowed there;
in its center, an auspicious image of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa was installed,
with Śambhu established on one side and Brahmā on the other side as well.
Other deities were also installed by the king for the gratification of Satī;
he likewise caused a temple for Mahālakṣmī to be built for Līlāvatī.
(21) O beloved, listen as I describe the wonder of Līlāvatī.

Having bathed at dawn, Līlāvatī performed the worship of the gods (22). She always performed the worship of her husband according to the prescribed rites. Once, she reflected: "Whose worship should come first? (23)
"What must be done by a devoted wife in the early morning?"—fallen into this doubt, she remembered the Lord of Kamalā.
The Lord of Lakṣmī, together with Lakṣmī, arrived, resplendent with light. (24)
Honored, saluted, worshipped, and questioned by the goddess in this manner:
"O treasure-house of compassion, whom indeed should I first worship?
The Blessed One, impelled by Śrī, quickly spoke to that devoted wife.
Devotion to one’s husband is the supreme duty; the worship of the husband is preeminent.
O beautiful one, the husband is twofold: of the body and of the self. O virtuous lady, the husband of both is the most excellent; he must first be honored by you.
Līlāvatī became pleased and then conducted an examination:
"Who is the master of the body? And who indeed is the master of the self?
Who truly is the master of both? Listen to this, O lotus-born one! (28–29)
The husband is the sustainer of the wife’s body; he protects and guards her body.
When his own elements (dhātus) decline, hers also decline; thus, protecting him is the vow of devotion to the husband (pativratam).
For a man, this is the vow of celibacy (brahmacarya); for a woman, it is the vow of devotion to the husband.
O Lotus-born One, by this Brahman-conduct and by devotion to their husbands,
those subjects who observe virtuous vows go from the world of Brahmā to a higher world;
as do renunciants, ascetics, those who have renounced worldly ties, and celibate students.
And for maidens, children, the elderly, men, and women;
likewise for youths, for couples, and for the protection of the elements—there is this vow. By means of this discipline, there shall be protection as well as the birth of offspring.

That which results in futile expenditure is never true devotion to one's husband (pātivratya). Devotion to one's husband is to be known as a vow that grants liberation, progeny, and heaven, and even bestows nourishment upon the body. Now hear also of that second [vow]. || 34-35 ||
That food which always protects the body through nourishment should be regarded as its lord.
From food all beings are born; they live by it and enter into it.
One should know that food is Brahman, to be worshipped through the five sacrifices. Bha...
Having divided it, one should first offer a portion to the deity, and thereafter eat;
furthermore, whatever food is considered contemptible here, one should first present that to the gods, then to the sages, the ancestors, the cows, and the servants. (37–38)
One should offer food that grants satisfaction to the husband and also to the Lord,

for the husband is the vow of the wife, and her devotion to her husband is her eternal vow. Indeed, through that devotion to her husband, she performs a perpetual sacrifice of food, and thereby attains both heaven and liberation.

O Lakṣmī, even if food is eaten, if the vital breath does not remain, then the body becomes a corpse; therefore, the vital breath is said to be the third [essential], the eternal form of the husband. One should practice the vow of the vital breath.
When elders and those worthy of honor arrive at one's own home, one must rise, go toward them, and likewise bow to them.
Indeed, if one does not rise, their vital breaths will forcibly depart.
Likewise, there may be a depletion of life-force; therefore, one should well protect one's vital breaths.
That which is always honored by the elders is known as the vow of the vital breaths (prāṇavrata).
Indeed, for the sake of her husband, a wife should practice that very vow of the vital breaths, which is fidelity to her husband (pātivratya).

One must not show disrespect toward one's mother-in-law or father-in-law, one's parents, one's master, ascetics, the learned, the most excellent of men who have renounced the world, the wife of a teacher,
kings, the Lord, virtuous women, or those endowed with good qualities. (45)
For that is declared to be the vow of breath-control (prāṇavrata), the supreme devotion to one's husband (pātivratya).
A virtuous woman should always protect it; heaven and liberation are in her hand.
Now hear, O Lakṣmī, the fourth: the mental [vow], which is always centered in the heart.
Scattered by millions of latent impressions (vāsanās), filled with desire, anger, and the like,
constantly burdened by attachment and aversion, and presided over by greed, delusion, and so forth—
if that mind is indeed characterized by sattva, it protects and guards the embodied being.
If his mind is established in its proper place, his fame arises everywhere.
(49) If the mind of that heedless person is distracted, there will be ruin.
The horse of the mind, when situated on the excellent path, bestows both heaven and liberation. (50)
In this cave, he alone who acts as the protector is declared to be the husband;
therefore, the mind, when restrained, is thoroughly protected by that which takes the form of the husband.
That very vow is indeed *pātivratya* (devotion to the husband), consisting of the avoidance of passion, hatred, and the like. (51)
The abandonment of illusion, latent impressions, and false desire;
fourthly, devotion to one's husband—that is the worship of the mind as Brahman.
One should know that the mind is Brahman and practice the vow of the mind.
Now hear, O Lakṣmī, about the fifth: knowledge protects the embodied soul. Knowledge is the protection of the body; specialized knowledge (*vijñāna*) is the protector of dharma.
Knowledge bestows wealth and desire, while specialized knowledge awakens the self.
Consciousness protects as its guardian; it indeed guards one even on the ground of sorrow. As long as there are embodied beings, consciousness alone is their protector.
O beloved, living creatures do not protect themselves at all when consciousness is absent.

Therefore, even in the case of a young infant, the husband’s well-understood vow of knowledge and devotion to his wife must be protected, even through the course of conversation. That devotion to one's husband consists in receiving the taste of the nectar of Kṛṣṇa’s stories.
The husband is the god; the husband is Kṛṣṇa; indeed, the husband of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow is knowledge itself.
(58) One should always perform his propitiation, accompanied by the worship of the deity.
For that vow of devotion to one's husband is supreme, bestowing both heaven and liberation. (59)
Listen, Lakṣmī, to the sixth vow, known as Ānanda. All beings— whether those of great wisdom or those of little knowledge, even down to grass and the like—
always desire bliss, happiness, affection, and joy.
Through that festival and through that enthusiasm, living beings exist; indeed,
by means of that joy, beings are born,
and they live as well, yet they even go to their death for the sake of joy alone.
Therefore, Ānanda is the protector; the Lord indeed protects all living beings.
One should know that this Ānanda is the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Lord.
Moreover, even yogis always abide in liberation within Ānanda.
That Supreme Brahman is bliss, and He is the husband of her who is devoted to her husband.

O Mahālakṣmī! Having understood this nature of devotion to the husband, one should practice it. Indeed, these [husbands] are merely the lords of the body, whereas [the Supreme] is the lord within the self, even slightly. 64–65.
In the body composed of the five elements and ever consisting of [the essence of] the beloved, these qualities always abide; likewise,
the specific virtue of fidelity to her husband abides in the woman,
and these same qualities also abide in the husband within his own wife.
Having understood this true nature of dharma, one should indeed observe the vow.
Now listen, O Lakṣmī, regarding the self; I shall tell you of devotion to the husband (pātivratya):
hearing [of Kṛṣṇa], chanting [His names], remembering Kṛṣṇa, and serving Kṛṣṇa. (68)

Worship, salutation, service, friendship, and self-surrender; trust, choosing [Him as one's own], entrusting oneself, humility, unwavering intellect, and constant conformity toward Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul, Mādhava. (69)
Hari alone is the protector, the sustainer, the one who gladdens, and the savior.
That vow consists entirely of the surrender of oneself, which is the essence of surrendering everything.
There is no other such vow that bestows either heaven or liberation.
It bestows heaven and accomplishes everything, wherein no remainder exists;
wherein there is no injury whatsoever, and wherein no bondage is found;
wherein there is no expenditure at all, and indeed, O beloved, there is no lack of gain.
Having performed this vow of devotion to the husband, countless souls have gone to heaven;
indeed, other men, women, and others likewise go and will go there.
This very Self is Brahman, the Lord; it is endowed with the vow of the Supreme Brahman.
"He is one who observes eternal vows and is devoted solely to his wife's fidelity.
Thus, O Sati, all forms of wifely devotion have been described to you in every way.
Having heard these words spoken by me to Līlāvatī, she was filled with both wonder and pride.
Having reflected for a moment and understood that her own beloved had been married,
the virtuous woman always maintained her devotion to her husband in two ways toward Divodāsa:
first, she observed celibacy toward Divodāsa, while maintaining her wifely devotion [toward her actual husband].
The offering of food to Divodāsa was her second act of devotion to her husband;
the offering of her life-breaths to Divodāsa was her third act of devotion to her husband;
the offering of her mind to Divodāsa was her fourth act of devotion to her husband.
In Divodāsa, she was the fifth devoted wife, consisting of knowledge alone;
and in [the next] Divodāsa, she was the sixth devoted wife, consisting of bliss.
Having protected her husband, the virtuous Līlāvatī honored him.

While Divodāsa was present within her own body, that virtuous woman maintained the chastity of her physical form; and while Śrī Hari resided in her soul, she likewise maintained the chastity of her very self. She protected that husband and worshipped him.
She indeed offered all sixteen types of ritual services to her Lord;
she offered her very self to Him through a state of complete absorption. She offered everything to the Inner Controller who abides within the self.
With devotion she offered herself and beheld there that Hari;
in Divodāsa she saw Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Lord, in a divine form. Seeing her supreme husband as her lord, the virtuous woman then rejoiced.
She directly and immediately beheld her own mistress in the form of Kṛṣṇa;
yet with her physical eyes she saw Divodāsa, while with her divine inner eye she beheld that Śrī Kṛṣṇa. (85–86)
Having thus attained that supreme divine vision, Līlāvatī,
through her devotion to the duty of fidelity to her husband, obtained eternal yoga and perfection—
which is unattainable even for yogis— by the grace of Kṛṣṇa.
She attained the imperishable state by means of that very same divine body,
together with her husband, her lineage, and likewise her virtuous offspring.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, has this auspicious and divine account of a devoted wife been told to you.
"Having thus dedicated their very selves, all of them attain the imperishable state, Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, as their husband; of this there is no doubt.

Thus ends the four hundred and sixty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of Queen Līlāvatī, Consort of King Divodāsa of Kāśī, Attaining the Servitude of the Feet of Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa through the Miracles of Her Various Divine Wifely Devotion," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
← Chapter 465: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga) Chapter 466 [[Author: → Chapter 467
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī! To this most purifying story of the wife of Dharma, who was devoted to her husband, which describes how she made the five Gaṅgās manifest at the holy site of Kāśī. 1.
The Blessed One himself occupies the Pañcanada tīrtha in Kāśī;
among the regions of Bhūr, Bhuvar, and Svar, the supreme tīrtha is Pañcanada.
Lord Kṛṣṇa himself is stationed there at that supreme Pañcanada tīrtha.

In former times, there was a sage of the Bhṛgu lineage named Vedaśiras, a great ascetic of self-restraint who was ever devoted to penance. Beholding him in his youth, an excellent Apsaras named Śuci [was struck with desire].
She, being pure, drank that which had been spilled by the rishi.
Vedaśiras declared her to be pure, righteous, and free from fault:
"Listen, O virtuous lady! This transformation of youth occurs in all embodied beings."

That [emission] does not constitute a fault for an embodied being who is free from desire. (6) The natural absence of mind during the discharge of the bodily elements, even when such a lapse occurs, does not lead to the destruction of one’s ascetic merit; rather, purification is held to be achieved through bathing. (7)
But in your mind there was the desire to obtain seed;
therefore, O beloved, this semen of mine has flowed even without sexual intercourse.
Therefore, O dear one, carry in your womb that which you have drunk.

O Queen of the Gods, you are indeed able to accomplish anything as you desire in every way. O my beloved, from my seed shall arise a jewel of a daughter, a foremost Vaiṣṇava and devoted wife, whose seed shall never be in vain, even for the sages.
Thus addressed, she remained in his hermitage with the desire for progeny;
then, in due course of time, she gave birth to a jewel of a daughter, a divine woman, who was exceedingly radiant, a treasure-house of beauty that brought delight to the eyes. (11)
Having given away her daughter, the excellent Apsaras named Śuci went to heaven.
The sage Vedaśiras, however, nurtured that girl with affection,
nourishing her with the milk from the udders of Hariṇī who resided in his own hermitage.
The sage gave her the meaningful name Dhūtapāpā (She Who Has Washed Away Sin).
Seeing that the girl was now more than ten years old, the sage questioned her:
"O auspicious one, tell me yourself: to which bridegroom shall I give you?"
Having heard her father’s auspicious words, she spoke with a devoted mind:
(15) “He who is the most pure among all, he who is saluted by all, whom all desire, and from whom the arising of all happiness comes. (16)
May that which never perishes at any time, which always persists, which protects one from great calamities both here and hereafter, and which possesses its own essential nature;
from which all my heart's desires arise fulfilled—[may that protect me]. (17)

By serving him, one's great good fortune increases day by day. By remaining constantly in his presence, I have no fear whatsoever from anyone; and even by uttering his name, intense afflictions dissolve away. (18–19)
"Obeisance to Him in whom such qualities as these reside— the support by which even the cosmic eggs endure throughout the creations— grant me peace.
Having heard this, the sage was exceedingly pleased and attained great joy.

I am blessed that in my home there is a daughter who is righteous and a deliverer of her lineage. Blessed is this one, whose name is true to its meaning, for she has shaken off all sins and is a treasure-house of knowledge.
Indeed, what manifestation of virtuous qualities could possibly be described by her?
I consider that one named Dharmadeva to be the best; I shall give her to him.
However, he is not easily obtained through mere pleasure, for he is adorned with every excellent quality.
He can only be purchased by the price of asceticism or perhaps by some great store of merit.
Having reflected thus, he said to his daughter: "O girl, there is such a bridegroom;
O maiden, he cannot be obtained through heaps of wealth, nor through noble lineage, nor even by the power of sovereignty, nor by intellect, nor by valor. (24–25)
"Through purity of mind, purity of the senses, austerity, and self-restraint, that highly wise and worthy husband is obtained; not otherwise.
Having heard these words of her father and having prostrated before him, [she departed].
Having obtained her father’s permission, she performed most rigorous asceticism.
Having made her body calloused, she stood amidst the downpours of rain;
even upon rocks in the icy winds, she did not tremble in the least.
Having surrounded herself with the five fires, she performed austerities in the penance grove;
though desiring water, the young woman did not drink any water at that time.
Having cast off all contact with worldly enjoyments, the virtuous lady subsisted on air alone.
Her body, emaciated and wasted by extreme asceticism, shone all the more brilliantly.
Brahmā, having approached her, said, "I am pleased; choose a boon.
Dhūtapāpā, having offered salutations to the illustrious Parameṣṭhin, spoke.
"O Grandfather, make me more purifying than even the purifiers.
And Brahmā, being pleased, said to her:
"Whatever things are indeed purifiers, may you possess a supreme purity even greater than those through the granting of this boon."
"O maiden, there are three and a half crores of sacred fords (tīrthas).
Among them, sixty-eight are preeminent and most excellent.
Indeed, all those sacred fords exist in reverse order within your body. (33–34)
"By my word, remain here and become the most purifying of all beings.
In another kalpa, you will undoubtedly become the embodiment [of Dharma];
you shall be the beloved wife of Dharmadeva and the mother of Hari, born of Dakṣa. (356)
Having spoken thus, Brahmā vanished, and she too went to her father’s house.
Having learned of everything, Vedaśiras was repeatedly pleased by her asceticism;
she, for her part, constantly envisioned the four-armed form of Dharma.

Every morning, she constantly worshipped the divine [image] with sixteen types of offerings. Through her virtue of devotion to her husband, she offered everything to Lord Viṣṇu. That woman, whose sins were cleansed, beheld Dharma in a dream every single day.

Once, that Dharmadeva himself came in person and requested the sage for a suitable daughter; the sage then gave her to him. The girl, radiant like the moon and full of luster, devoted herself to Dharma.
Then, in that great field, the great virtuous woman Dhūtapāpā shone within the temple of Dharma in an invisible form;
in her second form, she was herself the moonstone (candrakāntamaṇi).
Having become the Gaṅgā in the water, that ascetic woman shines;
and Dharmadeva, having become the Dharmanada within the waters,
joined with the moonstone (candrakānta-śilā), indeed shines day and night.
In the temple of Dharma, he shone even with a divine form.
Thus, in Kāśī, by the Gaṅgā, Dharma became the river Dharmatnadī;
and the river Dhūtapāpā, though small, was joined by other streams.
Then Sūrya, having arrived, performed fierce austerity.
From his rays issued forth a great stream of perspiration;
from that, the river named Kiraṇā was born, exceedingly purifying.
Then the great and virtuous Sarasvatī arrived there;
the purifying Yamunā stood there joined by the Gaṅgā.
Kiraṇā, Dhūtapāpā, Yamī, Gaṅgā, and Sarasvatī were all present.
The five rivers are great truths, and the river named Dharmānadā— when all these have merged together, they constitute the holy ford known as Pañcanada,
which became universally renowned by the name Pañcagaṅgā.
Having bathed there and drunk the water, one is released from all bonds;
having given gifts at Pañcanada and performed the libations for the ancestors,
and having worshipped Bindumādhava, one shall not undergo birth again.
That purification which is proclaimed as resulting from drinking the five-fold *kūrca* [mixture] is attained by drinking with faith a single drop of the water of the Pañcanada,
formerly known as the Dharmanada and later as the Dhūtapāpaka.
Beyond that is Bindutīrtha, and beyond that the one called Pañcanada.
Whatever— be it cows, land, sesame seeds, gold, horses, garments, food, garlands, or ornaments—
one gives here at Bindutīrtha, one shall obtain as inexhaustible merit.
Having arrived there, Agnibindu performed most rigorous penance.
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa himself came and said, "Choose a boon.
Agnibindu said to Hari, "Dwell here in my presence."
"So be it," Hari replied, and he joyfully established his residence there.
O lotus-born one, I dwell there under the name Bindumādhava. In the temple of Dharmadeva, my son, known as Bindumādhava, resides.
I, the divine one, dwell here eternally, O son, having shaken off all sins.
Dhūtapāpā is my mother, and Dharma is my father, my beloved;
and I, in the form of Mādhava, dwell at Bindutīrtha.

Lakṣmī, whose nature is that of the Vasus, is known as Nirvāṇa; she dwells at the side of Dharma, and I dwell in my heart even at Pañcanada. When the body has been thoroughly purified by vows, Dharma dwells therein eternally.
Kṛṣṇa, Dhūtapāpā, and Śrī dwell there in every way;
likewise, Artha and Kāma, along with Nirvāṇa, always reside there.
I am named Ādimādhava, and thereafter [I am] Anantamādhava.
Known as Śrī Damādhava, and then indeed as Bindumādhava—
in these names I, the Lord of All, shall abide in Ānandakānana.
My mother, my lawful wife Dhūtapāpā, is devoted to her husband.
Devoted to her husband,
she constantly served Śrī Dharma at the highly meritorious and divine Śrī Dharmamandira in Pañcanada.
Having bathed in that sacred field and performed the worship of the Bull (Vṛṣa), both men and women— 63–64.
Having performed the worship of Dhūtapāpa and my own worship as Mādhava,
and having made a vow of righteousness (dharma-pratijñā) along with the Cāturmāsya observances and so forth,
the practitioner who performs the Kārttika gifts and other rites shall attain liberation.
Likewise, there dwell his lawful wives in the practice of dharma.
In their second form, they are all the mothers of the universe:
Śraddhā, Lakṣmī, Dhṛti, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, Medhā, and Kriyā.
Intellect, modesty, physical form, tranquility, accomplishment, and fame— these thirteen, all remaining together,
indeed practice righteousness. Devoted to their duty toward their husbands, they all abide wherever righteousness resides.
Having shaken off her sins, she especially serves her husband, Śrī-Vṛṣa. Having bathed in the morning, that goddess bathes Vṛṣa in the morning with garments,
ornaments, musk, sandalwood paste, unbroken grains, and saffron.
Then, having worshipped him, the virtuous goddess performed the lustration ceremony for her husband;
having offered circumambulation and praise, and having bowed at his feet,
she washed both his feet with the water of the Gaṅgā.
Having drunk the pure nectar of the ritual rinsing (ācamana) and offered a beautiful handful of water (añjali),
that beloved wife then served Dharma five or six delicious dishes for his meal— dishes accompanied by side-dishes, savory foods, and various drinks.
He offers betel-leaf, performs body-massage,
dances before the Dharma, and proclaims the glory of the Wielder of the Śārṅga bow;
he recites the hymn of Nara and Nārāyaṇa while teaching the Dharma.
Then she performed service toward her co-wives, such as Faith and the others;
furthermore, by the command of Dharma, she also practiced devotion to Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
Once, the illustrious god Dharma was established in the Cāturmāsya vow.
He constantly recited the auspicious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā* at the holy site of Pañcanada and in his home.
Sages, seers, gods, ancestors, humans, and women [assembled there].
The inhabitants of the fourteen worlds arrived there for that festival.
Dhuṭapāpā provided excellent dwellings and other comforts for all—the rivers, streams, sacred fords, and various holy regions as well. (78–79)

Having shaken off her sins, Satī said: "If I am a practitioner of dharma, a lawful wife, a sustainer of dharma, and one who seeks devotion to my husband through dharma, then let there appear a divine and beautiful city fifty krośas in extent. (1.466.80)
Whatever riches belong to the foremost among Brahmā, Indra, and Śambhu,
even greater than those are the foods and drinks in my palace;
likewise, there are vehicles, mounts, objects of enjoyment, beds, and articles of adornment.
May there be vessels, savory foods, and various beautiful objects;
may garments purified by fire and other such things exist in the noble home of my husband.
May there be streams of curd, streams of ghee, streams of honey, and mountains of sugar.
"May there be rivers of milk, and may there be hundreds of thousands of male and female servants!"—
recalling this resolve, divine and manifold prosperities instantly came into being at the lotus-feet of Dharma.
Ornaments of gold and jewels, and collections of gems such as diamonds,
arose near that river from the intention of Dhūtapāpa;
and in an instant, O beloved, a divine assembly hall like Sudharmā was produced.
Durgā, Sarasvatī, Lakṣmī, Sāvitrī, Rādhikā, Dayā, Jayā,
Lalitā, Māṇikyā, Ramā, Padmā, Pārvatī, Prabhā, Haṃsā, Manasā, Mañjulā, Śrī, and Padminī. (87–88)
Śānti, Śāntā, Hemalatā, Devī, Muktā,
and Mauktikā were indeed the female attendants there at the festival of the discourse in the Dharma-hall for those listening to the narration of the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*. (89)

In great ceremonies such as the *svāgata*, they served food and drink. And in the month of Kārtika, on the day of *prabodhinī*, at the conclusion of the narrative, a supreme and grand worship was performed for Dharmadeva by all of them and by all of them together.
Filled with joy, he bestowed upon them all the various gifts of dharma, including jewels, gold, and diamonds— objects that bestow infinite merit.
To the gods, the assembly of listeners, and the brahmins, he gave exceedingly great wealth.
At that sacrifice, Hari Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa arrived;
Kaṃbharā, who is Mahālakṣmī, and Gopālakṛṣṇa also came by celestial chariot,
while Puruṣottama was visibly present before them all.
A divine rain of flowers fell and cries of "Victory! resounded repeatedly.
At the great sacrifice, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, together with his parents, performed the ten-fold oblation (daśāṃśahavana) by the command of Dharma with supreme devotion.

Having completed the sacrifice according to the rules and performed the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha), Dharmadeva bestowed divine sacrificial fees upon the twice-born. The King of Kāśī, the Lord of Mithilā, the Lord of Sāketa, and the King of Kaliṅga [likewise gave their gifts]. (96–97)
The lord of Saurāṣṭra, the lord of Maru, the king of Sindhu, the king of Nipāla,
the lord of Kurukṣetra, the king of Śveta,
and the king of Prāgjyotiṣa worshipped Dharmadeva, as well as thousands of brahmins, holy men, and virtuous women.
They gave gold, diamonds, silver, garments, and sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
Then Dharmadeva, having fed and honored them all, dismissed them; and Satī, by her own spiritual power, granted them exemption from taxes.
Having shaken off her sins, she joyfully took water in her hand and, without forming a formal resolve, said:
"May I know [the truth] for the pleasure of my lord, the god Dharma;
may she then grant everything by the power of my devotion to my husband. (101)
"Let my opulent palace and other such things become invisible to me.
As soon as he had thus resolved, everything instantly vanished in an instant.
Countless beings, including the gods and others, were filled with wonder.
Recognizing the power of her devotion to her husband,
the goddesses respectfully praised that virtuous lady, the sovereign who was cleansed of all sin.
Thus is the sacred site of Pañcanada, consisting of the hermitage of Dharmadeva.
It is purifying for all the gods by virtue of its power to wash away sins.
O beloved, I have thus described to you the power of the *dhūtapāpā* vow;
from reciting or hearing this, there shall be both liberation and worldly enjoyment.
The dharma consisting of devotion to one’s husband is indeed firm, bestowing liberation;
it grants all prosperity and likewise bestows devotion to righteousness.

Thus ends the four hundred and sixty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of how the Ṛṣi Vedaśiras’s daughter named Dhūtapāpā—born of the Apsaras Śuci—attained the status of a Mūrtidevī through her union with the god Dharma; how, during the discourse on the *Saṃhitā* at Pañcanada, she constructed a city over fifty *krośas* by the power of her devotion to her husband; how gods, kings, humans, and others arrived there; how the sacrifice and its concluding bath (*avabhṛtha*) were performed; and the marvel of the subsequent disappearance of that newly built city’s prosperity. (Chapter 466)

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, Lakṣmī! I shall proclaim the most excellent power of Kalāvatī, the wife of Vṛṣabhānu, who was devoted to her husband. 1.
The mind-born daughter of the ancestors, a portion of Kamalā, was Kalāvatī;
she became the beautiful Sundarī, devoted to her husband, the wife of Vṛṣabhānu.
Her daughter was Rādhā, who was dearer to Kṛṣṇa than his own life.
Born from half a portion of Śrī Kṛṣṇa and equal to him in splendor, three daughters were born to the Pitṛs from their mental power in ancient times:
Kalāvatī, Ratnadhanyā, and Menakā, on successive days. (3–4)
Ratnadhanyā chose the mountain king Himācala as her father; Menakā chose him, who was a portion of Hari.
Ratnadhanyā’s daughter Sītā, devoted to her husband, became the wife of Rāma.

Menā’s daughter was Satī, the wife of Śambhu, as well as Pārvatī; both were born without a womb, devoted to their husbands, delightful, and auspicious. Kalāvatī chose Sucandra as her virtuous husband.
Having obtained a king of the lineage of Manu, he enjoyed the kingdom for a thousand years; thereafter,
the king became truly detached and went to the Vindhya mountain with his wife to practice asceticism.
Having reached the hermitage of Pulaha,
he performed most rigorous penance for a thousand divine years without food, desiring liberation;
the king attained meditative absorption after contemplating the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa.
Seeing her husband motionless,
his body devoid of the movement of breath,
empty of flesh and blood, and with his frame reduced to a mere collection of bones, she cast the anthill that had enveloped his limbs far away. (11)
That queen, devoted to her husband, lamented and wept, O Kalāvatī. Crying out, "O Lord, O Lord!"—hearing her weeping, that abode of compassion was moved by pity. (12–13)
The unborn Grandfather of the worlds appeared in person;
and upon seeing her and the king, Brahmā was indeed filled with grief.
Then, having sprinkled the king’s body with water from his water-pot, he said:
The Creator of the universe, by means of his power as Brahmā, transferred the life-force [into the body].
But the king, seeing that very Sustainer of the world before him,
bowed down and praised him whose face and eyes were gracious.
Brahmā said to the king, "Choose a boon as you desire.
The king, however, chose nirvāṇa, the supreme state of eternal liberation.
When Brahmā heard this, he became intent on granting the boon.
The great and virtuous Kalāvatī spoke respectfully to Brahmā:
"O Lotus-born One, if you grant liberation to the king of men, then, O Brahman, what will be my fate as a helpless woman without my husband? (18–19)
Without a beloved husband, what beauty can there be for women in their widowed state?
According to the Vedas, for a devoted wife, her husband alone is considered her vow;
indeed, the husband is the guru, the chosen deity, and the very embodiment of austerity and dharma.
Indeed, for women, all other kinsmen are not as excellent as a husband.
Among all relatives, none is more beloved than one's own master; O Brahmin, service to the husband is superior to all dharma and is exceedingly difficult to attain. (21–22)
Whatever vows, charity, austerity, worship, recitation, fire-offerings, and so forth she may perform—
all that becomes fruitless for one who is devoid of service to her husband.
(23) Likewise, bathing in all the sacred fords and circumambulating the entire earth [is likewise in vain].
Initiation into all sacrifices, indeed the vows of great gifts, the recitation of the Vedas, and whatever austerities there may be;
feeding those who are virtuous, the honoring of Brahmins, and the service of the gods. || 24–25 ||
Likewise, the Cāturmāsya, Tapas, Kṛcchra, Cāndrāyaṇa,
and other such penances do not equal even a sixteenth part of service to one’s master.
Those who are devoid of service to their master speak harshly to that master.
They fall into the Kālasūtra hell for as long as the moon and sun endure;
there, serpents and worms bite them day and night, and they are made to consume urine, phlegm, and excrement. (27–28)
The servants of Yama thus place flaming torches into their mouths;
having experienced such torment, they enter the womb of worms.
There they devour filth, and from that state they eventually attain human birth.

Thus have I heard from the virtuous and from the words of the Vedas; therefore, O Sustainer of the World, what shall I say? For I am powerless and do not know [the truth], since you are the father of the worlds, the creator, the yogi, and the eternal teacher of the righteous.
"O All-Knowing One, what more can I say? Do not separate me from my father!
O Brahmin, if this husband of mine, who is dearer to me than life itself, has indeed been released, who will protect my virtue and my youth? (32)
If she is protected by her father while she is still a maiden, he is liberated by giving her to a worthy recipient.
Protected by her husband through their union, she remains so for as long as the husband lives.
In his absence, a son shall protect her; these three are remembered as her protectors.
If she is without a protector, a virtuous woman may seek refuge with another;
if she becomes dependent upon him, her devotion to her husband (pātivratya) will perish. At that time, the merit accumulated by the woman over many lifetimes is destroyed.
In childhood, youth, or even in old age,
the desire of a virtuous wife devoted to her husband remains equal toward her beloved at all times.
Indeed, the affection of mothers for their sons is the greatest of all.

The affection of self-interested people ends with the attainment of their own purpose; it is not constant. It does not equal even a sixteenth part of the devotion felt by virtuous wives toward their sons—affection that lasts until the child receives breast milk and extends as long as they enjoy sweet food. (38)
For virtuous women, affection for their beloved persists constantly, both in dreams and while awake.
The separation from kinsmen ends with memory, but that of sons is even greater;
there is no suffering more terrible for a woman than that of her husband. (1.467.40)
Just as an unskilled person is consumed by a blazing fire when eating poison,
so too is an unskilled woman consumed by the fire of separation from her lord.
She has no thirst for food, no thirst for water, no desire for clothing, nor any craving for objects of enjoyment.
In the home, in fame, and in beauty, for virtuous women there is nothing apart from their husband.
Their hearts are consumed by the fire of separation, and likewise their passionate faces are scorched;
their enjoyment is wasted and their wealth is burnt, just as straw is consumed in a fire.
There is no kinsman greater than the beloved; there is no one dearer than the beloved.
There is no deity greater than the beloved; there is no teacher greater than the beloved.
There is no life-breath greater than the beloved; for a woman, there is nothing greater than the beloved.
There is no duty higher than the beloved; there is no wealth higher than the beloved.
(45) Just as the minds of the virtuous are immersed in Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, as is a mother’s [love] for an only son, and as miserly people [cling] to their wealth; (46)
Just as the minds of the wise are directed toward the scriptures when they are terrified by dangers,
just as that of infants is toward sucking at the breast, just as that of artisans is toward their crafts,
and just as that of amorous women is toward their beloveds— so too is my mind fixed upon the Beloved.
O Brahmin, it is truly not possible for them to live even for a single moment without him;
death would be better for those virtuous women whose hearts are consumed by grief, for whom life has become like death since they are deprived of their husbands.
Grief for others may be kept at a distance by means of drinking, eating, and diversion;
yet grief for a beloved one indeed increases through drinking, eating, and diversion.
A virtuous woman is the very shadow of her husband; she ought never to be separated from him.
A form fashioned by the husband’s own merit adheres to the husband alone.
(51) For a woman devoted to her husband, the fruit belongs to that husband who performed the meritorious deed;
since the enjoyment of the fruit belongs to the husband, how could a virtuous wife be separated from him? (52)
In separation, she did not fail to enjoy the fruits of her husband’s deeds;
therefore, a virtuous and auspicious woman was ever united with her lord.
Others, however, by their very nature perish when the body perishes.
A woman’s form bears fruit through her actions; thus she becomes meaningful in birth after birth.
Therefore, O Brahmin, if you release your husband while excluding me, I shall curse you and forcibly hand you over to him, for the sin of killing a woman is indeed grievous.
Having heard Kalāvatī’s words, the Prajāpati was struck with wonder;
filled with apprehension, he spoke that which would be for Satī’s benefit:
"O child, I shall not grant you liberation, for I cannot bear my lord to be without you."
Your merit remains thus, and it is being exhausted by the enjoyment of heavenly pleasures.
(57) I am not currently able to grant you liberation along with me;
for a daughter, liberation is difficult for anyone to attain without the exhaustion of merit. (58)
Through the destruction of his merit by means of enjoyment, the possessor of dharma attains the state of nirvāṇa.
For a long time, enjoy the pleasures of heaven together with your husband.
Thereafter, the birth of you two shall take place on the banks of the Yamunā.
"When your daughter Rādhikā herself becomes a *satī*, you two shall go to Goloka together with her, both being liberated while yet alive.
She is indeed a virtuous woman endowed with the quality of goodness (*sattva*); you ought not to curse me."
"Being liberated while living, they are equanimous and devoted to Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
Having said this, Brahmā departed for his own abode, and those two went as well.

"Oh, how most blessed we are, as are you who are devoted to your husbands!
You whose wives are devotees of Kṛṣṇa, equal to Lakṣmī and Rādhā in their love for Hari."

Austerity, chanting, vows, knowledge, study of the Vedas, worship, bathing at sacred fords, and fasting—all these become fruitful through service to Kṛṣṇa. For those by whom Śrī Kṛṣṇa has been served, what need have they for mountains of merit? (55–56)
"For those by whom the wish-fulfilling tree has been attained, what need have they for ten million other trees?
For those in whose hearts Śrī Kṛṣṇa resides, what need have they for ten million ritual acts?
Thus [is described] the majesty of Kṛṣṇa and also that of his wives in every respect.
Knowing [the truth], they went to the sacrifice, and from there they indeed returned to their homes.
Then, their love for all activities and sports became even greater;
their courtesy and service were such that they remained entirely beyond the comprehension of the brahmins.
Since the Blessed One is attained through the supreme merits of previous births,
those women were formerly the wives of the seven sages, devoted to their husbands. They were virtuous, beautiful, and peerless in their supreme form.
All of them were in the bloom of youth, with full hips and breasts;
they were clothed in divine garments and adorned with jewel ornaments; they possessed the luster of molten gold, and their lotus-like faces were smiling. (61–62)
Standing at the site of the sacrifice together with their master, they performed the offering of substances and other materials into the fire. Upon beholding them, the Fire-god desired them;
then the Fire-god repeatedly touched them with the rays of his own flames.
Beholding their limbs again and again, Agni was overcome by infatuation;
and being exceedingly lustful, he would touch them while consuming the sacrificial oblation,
embracing them repeatedly with his invisible forms.
He performed a subtle act of love, embracing them with his flames; yet those devoted wives were not at all aware of the fire's movement.
But Aṅgiras, possessing divine vision, perceived the secret conduct of the fire.
Bearing Śeṣa, he cursed the Fire-god who was possessed by lust:
"From this day forward, O Fire, let there be no lust in your crest, nor in your hands, nor in your flames, nor in your embers and the like. (67–68)
"May you always be neuter, consisting of flames, yet bestowing great merit;
may you possess a form and be subject to desire, and Svāhā likewise shall be so.
Having been cursed thus, Vahni thereafter became devoid of desire for his flame.
"Since sacrificial rites and other such acts are meritorious by virtue of that power," [it was said].
Then Aṅgiras, because they had touched the fire out of lust and were thus impure, cursed them for the sake of attaining purification: "Go indeed to a human womb! (1.469.70–71).
"Your hands shall be taken by brahmins of noble birth.
Having been told this, they were overcome with grief for a moment and bowed before him;
all those devoted wives then requested that which was beneficial and true.
O best of sages, do not abandon us; we are indeed sinless and devoted to our husband.
Unaware [of his transgression], we have been touched by another; you ought not to forsake us.
You ought not to inflict punishment upon us, who are your devotees and your servants.

When shall we behold your lotus feet? For virtuous women, the cruel separation from their beloved is always unbearable, even more so than being cut by a sword, struck by a thunderbolt, or by any other weapon. (75)

"O Lord of Brahmins, how shall we depart for the surface of the earth after abandoning these great sages—who are most devoted to the Veda, virtuous, supremely beloved, and faithful to their wives? If we must go, tell us when we shall return here. (76–77)
Out of fear of others, women go for refuge to their husbands;
but when they themselves are agitated by the fear of their own husbands, to whom do they go for refuge?
O most righteous one, grant freedom from fear to those who are already possessed by fear. (78)
Who is unable to inflict punishment upon a son, a disciple, or a wife?
And who is not capable of restraining them even by inflicting such punishment?
Having heard the words of the amorous women, Aṅgiras indeed wept out of love.
Having regained consciousness and questioned her brothers, she then spoke to them words that were beneficial,
truthful, pleasant, appropriate, and supremely enlightening for others:
"Without the purification of that [sin], a husband cannot accept his own beloved who has been enjoyed by another."
One should never eat [with her] anywhere, O beloved, for sin is transmitted.
She who is joined with sin is unfit for offerings to the gods or to the ancestors.
By embracing her, a husband is deprived of his fortune and struck down by his own vital energy.
The deities and the ancestors do not truly become happy with his offerings and libations; they consume them only while they are lukewarm.
Therefore, one must diligently protect one's wife every day.
At every step, beloved women must be protected by highly wise men who are vigilant.
A woman should not be dependent on others, for she is indeed a casket of faults;
one ought always to guard both one's wife and one's cooking vessel.
Because of mutual contact, you two are impure; yet she is pure, being in her own hand.
The purification of those who are impure is achieved through the fourfold vow and through birth.
Therefore, a woman has been prepared by previous ancestors with great effort so that she remains unseen by others.
Those wives who do not look upon the sun [even after death] are pure and devoted to their husbands.
But that beloved woman who remains faithful out of fear for the traditions of her family, even though she must be supported by her husband,
certainly goes to Vaikuṇṭha together with her beloved.
In the blink of an eye for the world of the sages, twenty years will pass swiftly upon the earth; indeed, purity through birth is desired.
Go now to the human world, to the womb you have chosen.
Indeed, by giving food to Kṛṣṇa, you shall be liberated from the curse.
Through the power of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, you will assume three forms;
in the form of divine maidens, you will certainly go to Goloka.
In the form of celestial maidens, you shall go to the world of the sages;
in the form of shadow-maidens, you shall go to the houses of the brahmins.
Through portions of yourselves, you will certainly attain us as the wives of those brahmins when they die.
"Today this curse of mine upon you has become even more excellent;
enjoyment, liberation, and the attainment of a home—these three shall be obtained.
Having been addressed thus, they departed from the sacrificial ground and went to the earth on the banks of the Yamunā.
Having been born in the homes of worthy men, those wives of brahmins became devoted to Hari;
by offering food to Him with devotion, they went indeed to Goloka.
Likewise, through other forms, they then went to the world of their beloved.
Those women went to the houses of the brahmins in the form of shadows.
It became certain that for them, a curse was indeed superior to prosperity.
Oh! The immediate anger of the virtuous leads to great benefit.
"Indeed, from whom could greatness arise without adversity?
For it was through the abandonment by their beloveds that the wives of the brahmins were liberated.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, has this vow of the chaste wife and the vow of Hari been narrated.
"From reading and hearing this, there shall be enjoyment, liberation, and likewise exaltation.

(1.469.100) Thus ends the four hundred and sixty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Liberation of the Wives of the Seven Sages through their Devotion to Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa after being cursed to become the wives of Brahmins due to their enjoyment of fire, and the Deliverance of Śrī Kṛṣṇa and the other children tending calves on the banks of the Yamunā by providing them food," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
