Chapter 471 →

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī! Regarding a virtuous serpent born of the snake species who was devoted to his master: on the beautiful bank of the Yamunā, Kṛṣṇa went accompanied by Balarāma. || 1 ||
He sported near the water with cowherds, bulls, and cows;
the cows, bulls, and children, afflicted by thirst, drank that water.
(2) But that water was infused with poison due to the presence of the serpent Kālīya.
Some there fell into a swoon, while others gave up their lives.
Then Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, having perceived this, restored them to life;
Kṛṣṇa, having ascended a Kadamba tree, assumed a most massive body.
Mādhava fell into the midst of the water upon the serpent;
at that time, the emergence of the water was only the height of one hand.
Seeing the human being, that serpent fled with the force of its rage.
He assumed that human form in order to seize Hari;
indeed, by the power of Kṛṣṇa’s splendor, the serpent’s dark body became like heated iron.
With his throat and belly scorched by Kṛṣṇa’s radiance, the serpent became greatly distressed.
Having spoken thus, he indeed performed the act of vomiting again;
his teeth were broken and his mouth was smeared with blood from chewing the black diamond-like substance.
The Blessed One rose above the head of that blood-faced one.
O beloved, the serpent, crushed by the earth, fell down unconscious. Regaining his senses once more, he repeatedly struck Śrī Narāyaṇa with his hoods and Śrī Kṛṣṇa with his tail in a skillful manner.
The Blessed Lord Śrī Hari, the moon of arts, raised his hood and, with a playful maneuver, struck it again and danced;
the hood became slackened, and the serpent became exceedingly soft. (11)
Seeing him then unconscious, the female nāgas wept bitterly—
those whose life-breath is their husband, who are devoted to the duty of a master, and who live solely for the sake of their husband.
Among them was his excellent wife, the auspicious and virtuous one named Surasā.
Together with the nāginīs, the virtuous woman wept out of love before Hari; quickly bowing down to Śrī Hari with palms joined in reverence,
she clung to His lotus feet and, overwhelmed by fear, spoke to Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
"O giver of great honor, grant me that which is dear to me, O beloved of the world!
For women, the husband is dearer than life; there is no other kinsman so devoted.
I am a devoted wife to the Naga, yet I am one who acts according to her own will. (15–16)
"O Lord, if [the snake] or the deer were to die, I would be afflicted by the sorrow of widowhood;
therefore, O Master, let my death come first, and then that of my husband.
For upon his destruction, my own destruction follows, and you would incur the sin of killing a woman."
Having heard the words of the Naga’s wife, Śrī Kṛṣṇa said to her:
"Arise, arise, O Queen of Nagas! Choose a boon and cast away your fear.
Take back your beloved, O Queen of Nagas; may you live long, free from old age and death."
Abandoning this Yamī-hrada, go elsewhere with your family;
go to the region of Ramaṇaka and be happy there.
O auspicious lady, by the mark of whose lotus feet your husband Garuḍa [is distinguished].
Having offered praise with devotion, she will bow down at my feet.
(21) Having heard this, she, humble with devotion, spoke to Mādhava:
"O Hari, grant me firm and unwavering devotion to your lotus feet. (22)
"O Lord, may my mind wander like a bee around Your lotus feet;
grant me always that good fortune which is Your own beloved.
Having thus prayed, Surasā beheld the face of Śrī Hari.
With her eyes, she drank in his face without blinking;
with her every limb bristling with horripilation and drenched in tears of joy, she, overwhelmed by the surging tide of devotion, spoke before Kṛṣṇa. (24–25)
"I shall not go to Ramaṇaka; I have no need for it there.
Let the serpent do as he will in this world; make me your servant.
Having heard the words of the Naga’s wife, the Lord of Śrī said, "So be it."
In the meantime, a divine chariot quickly arrived,
accompanied by the foremost of the attendants (pārṣadas) and furnished with celestial equipment.
Then the attendants of Śrī Kṛṣṇa descended from the chariot of a hundred wheels.
Having bowed to Kṛṣṇa and led her away, they went to the supreme Goloka.
Kṛṣṇa, having created a shadow-form, gave that female serpent to the male serpent.
The serpent did not perceive even the slightest wonder regarding the Lord of the Kadamba tree.
Having descended from Hari’s head, he placed his hand upon the serpent.
The snake, having regained consciousness, beheld Hari before him,
as well as the female serpent Surasā, who was devoted to her husband and whose eyes were filled with tears.
Having bowed down to Bālakṛṣṇa, he wept, overwhelmed with love.
Śrīkṛṣṇa said to that supreme devotee, "Choose a boon.
"Since you are my devotee, O serpent, remain at ease and abandon your fear."

I bestow my grace upon him who is devoted to me and has surrendered everything to me. Having first subdued that [snake], I grant him my favor. As for any man who anywhere kills serpents born of your lineage, [he shall suffer].
The sin of that person who strikes with a staff upon the marks of my lotus feet will certainly be equal to the murder of a Brahmin. Indeed,
the murder of a Brahmin committed by him will certainly be doubled.
Having uttered a most terrible curse, Lakṣmī will depart from his house;
the decline of his lineage, lifespan, and fame will certainly come to pass,
and at the end of his body, his death will occur from the bite of a serpent.
There will be fear of your lineage for those born of his lineage. However, those who, upon seeing my footprint marked with a beautiful lotus,
bow down with devotion to those born of your lineage, shall be liberated from the fear of serpents.
"Go quickly to Ramaṇaka and abandon your fear of the lord of birds.
Seeing the mark of my foot upon your head, the bird will bow down;
neither you nor those born of your lineage shall ever have any fear of Garuḍa. (1.470.40)
"O serpent, choose now another boon as well that you desire.
Thus addressed, Kālīya said: "Grant me devotion and remembrance of You;
grant me eternal service at Your lotus feet in birth after birth."
That alone would be fruitful wherein there is remembrance of Your lotus feet.
Residence in heaven is fruitless if there is no remembrance of Your feet;
however, for one engaged in meditation upon Your feet, that very place is supreme.
Whether it be for a moment, or ten million eons, or even the full span of a human life—let it be but a single instant—if it passes in the service of you, it is fruitful; otherwise, it is fruitless.
For those who are servants at your lotus feet, there is no such thing as the exhaustion of their lifespan.

There are no longer births, deaths, diseases, sorrows, afflictions, or fears. (45) O Brahmin, as long as this Manu of yours remains attained from Ananta, for that long, by virtue of meditating upon you and through your grace, I shall remain of your own complexion. (46)
But Garuḍa, being himself possessed of firm devotion, having recognized me as either a devotee or one still immature, took me far from that place and humbled [my pride].
By you, however, I have been accepted as your own by bestowing upon me firm devotion.
And Garuḍa was addressed: "Do not devour my devotee, the serpent!
"I have been favored and always protected by you;
O Lord, ocean of compassion, friend of the wretched, forgive this lowly one."
To the Lord of Nagas who was speaking thus, Hari then said, "Let it be so.
Having granted the boon to the Lord of Nagas, Hari spoke again, saying, "Go.
The serpent asked, "O Viṣṇu, when shall I behold your lotus feet?"
Having prostrated himself a hundred times, he departed for the region of Ramanaka.
The water became like nectar, and all living beings were filled with joy.
Listen, Lakṣmī, to the reason for his abandonment of his former abode.
By the command of Śeṣa, the hosts of nāgas, out of fear,
perform the worship of Garuḍa every year on the full moon day of Kārttika,
with flowers, incense, excellent lamps, as well as food offerings and ritual oblations.
At that time, having bathed well at the great holy site of Puṣkara, they performed his worship;
yet the haughty Kālīya did not do so,
and he prepared to forcibly devour the materials for the serpent-worship.
Just then, Garuḍa arrived there and fought with those serpents of the Kālīya species; the snakes fled from him and sought refuge with Ananta. Having gone there, the king of birds [confronted] Ananta.
He waged a tumultuous and endless battle, but the bird (Garuḍa) was victorious.
Kālīya fled and went to the pool of the Yamunā;
yet, due to the curse of Saubhari, the lord of birds was not able to go there.
Once in the past, Garuḍa, desiring to eat fish, seized a fish with his beak near Saubhari as he was performing austerities on the bank of the Yamunā;
and by the turn of fate, the fish [was caught].
Then, separated from its beak, it fell near the son of Subhara.
The King of Fishes said, "Provide protection for one who has come for refuge.
To Garuḍa, who was preparing to seize it again, the Sage spoke.
"Go far away, go far away from my presence, O Lord of Birds!
If you come near my lake, I shall quickly reduce you to ashes.
By my curse, you will indeed be turned to ashes instantly."
Having heard the words of Saubhari, the lord of birds (Garuḍa) set forth;
repeatedly remembering the feet of Kṛṣṇa and bowing down to him, he departed.
For this reason, that Garuḍa does not come to the pool of the Yamunā.
Having thus attained fearlessness, Kālīya remained there;
by the power of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, he then became divine among the devotees.
Accompanied by the shadow of the serpent-maidens, he went to the region of Ramaṇaka.
In her original form, she, being Surasā, attained liberation;
yet in her serpent form, devoted to her husband,
she protected her husband after having become twofold at the request of Acyuta.
Having attained the state of a maidservant to Kṛṣṇa in His abode, even Chāyā followed her husband;
thus indeed was protection granted by Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
O Lakṣmī, what indeed is difficult to attain here for one who meditates upon the Blessed Lord?
Even in the hereafter, that which is difficult to obtain becomes easy to attain.
Therefore, one who desires happiness should always meditate upon Kṛṣṇa, who fulfills all longings;
by reading or hearing of Him, no fear of serpents arises.

Thus ends the four hundred and seventieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Attainment of the Lord by the serpent Kālīya dwelling in the Yamunā lake, the perpetual husbandly fortune of the chaste Nāginī Surasā, the fearlessness of the snake-eater Garuḍa in the Yamunā lake due to the curse of Saubhari, and his subsequent residence in Ramaṇaka," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 471: *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā* — Section 1 (*Kṛtayuga-santāna*) — Chapter 471.
[Author: Chapter 472.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī, to the story of Maṇḍūkī, which brings about liberation.
In the forest of Ānanda, there was a beautiful temple of Śambhu.
A certain female frog always resided there in the presence of Śiva;
she performed circumambulations, subsisting on the remains of offerings and unbroken grains of rice.
Once, while she had gone outside to gather grass and other materials for her monastery,
a certain crow spotted that female frog as it was leaping here and there;
seizing it with its beak, the bird departed from the field.
By that crow, the female frog was thrown outside the field.
She died from the blow of the beak, but due to the merit of her circumambulations and other virtuous acts,
she was reborn as a Gandharva maiden in the house of Puṣpabaṭu.
By consuming the moss and other growth upon the *liṅga* of Śaṃkara,
she became pure and endowed with a sweet voice through the power of that merit.
From her very childhood, she became highly proficient in songs.
By name she was Mādhavī; that virtuous woman became a devoted wife to Śambhu.

(7) With her beautiful limbs well-proportioned and marked by the most excellent characteristics, she became a great devotee of the Lord, one who remembered her past lives, and the foremost among his bhaktas. (8)
Knowing the secrets of correct singing and possessing an exceedingly sweet voice,
she sings at the proper time the *ṣaḍja* or *ṛṣabha* note,
or likewise the *gāndhāra*, *madhyama*, *pañcama*, or even the *dhaivata*.
In some places that young woman sings the Niṣāda scale with its excellent exaltation;
she sings with the Ṣaḍja-grāmas, the Madhyama-grāmas, and the Gāndhāra-grāmas.
Then, within that Ṣaḍja-grāma, she skillfully joins the *mūrcchanās*.
And on the third night, during the northern *mandā* and the northern *āyatā*,
there is the pure *ṣaḍja* [scale], characterized by envy, when the *aśvakrāntā* has risen.
Thus, among the *madhyama*-grāmas, there is likewise the *sauvīrī* and the *hāriṇā*.
And [he gave] Aśvā, Kālā, Upatatā, Śuddhā, Madhyamā,
Gīrmayī, Pauravī, and then in the Gāndhāra scales Nandikā,
Viśālā, Sumukhī, Citrā, Citravatī, and Sukhā. (13–14)
With her virtuous intellect, she properly joins the recitations exactly as they are prescribed;
she also joins those forty-nine [verses] in sequence according to their specific divisions.
Likewise, she performs the Agniṣṭoma, the Atirātra-Agniṣṭoma, and the Vājapeya sacrifices.
Having displayed the Ṣoḍaśī, the Puṇḍarīka, the Aśvamedha, and the Rājasūya (sacrifices),
he performs auspicious songs;
[he sings] one hundred and one tālas, as well as the *dhruva*, the *sāmya*, and others.

He takes up and likewise sings the *sannipāta* and other such [melodic structures], as well as the six *rāgas*: Śrī, Vasantam, Pañcama, Bhairava, Megha, and Jaṭularāyaṇa; he expels them with effort. (18)
And for each [of these], she—who is herself the virtuous one (satī)—manifests from her throat thirty-six passionate women and their lovers;
likewise, through the distinctions of place and time, there are another sixty-five. (1.471.19–20)
As many as there are musical notes (tāla), so many are the passions (rāga);
the virtuous Mādhavī, who is skilled in song, always sings all of them with sweet speech, [invoking] Oṃkāra and Śaṅkara forever.
He gratified [the Lord] with dances, worship, and hymns that aroused passion and other emotions.
(22) Even after attaining priceless youth, he held the syllable *Oṃ* in high esteem.
His mind, though naturally fickle, attained steadfastness in Śambhu. (23)
Hunger, thirst, sleep, fatigue, and the like did not indeed afflict her;
with an unwearied mind, she was a constant servant of Śaṅkara.
She regarded even a moment—the form of an obstacle—as useless time.

"Whatever time has passed for me in vain, even for the duration of a single blink of an eye, she performs penance for that because she did not look upon Śiva. Thinking thus, she did not abandon her service at all. (25–26)
Desiring only water, she drinks even the nectar named Śambhu;
her two eyes, though reaching to her ears, desire nothing else. Indeed, her two ears do not grasp any sound other than the word "Śiva."
Her hands, exceedingly beautiful, were always engaged in making garlands for Śiva.
Her feet never wandered elsewhere out of a desire for pleasure, nor did she ever utter the name of any other person whatsoever. (28–29)
She repeatedly chants the names Śiva, Śambhu, Hara, Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa, the husband of Satī, the Supreme Lord, and her own Master, whose name is Praṇava;
her tongue knows no other flavor than that.
Mādhavī always joyfully performs the sweeping and the decoration of the courtyard around the temple, as well as the worship of the image,
the daily cleaning of the vessels, and the service of the shrine. (3.1–3.2)
She was a devoted worshiper of all those who possess devotion to Hari;
with great devotion and the mindset of a daughter toward her father, she constantly served them.
On the fourteenth day of the month of Vaiśākha, however, Mādhavī [worshipped] him once.
Having kept a vigil at night and observed the vow of fasting during the day,
when the devotees who had gathered together had departed in the morning, she then performed the sweeping and other rites, and worshipped Śambhu with devotion. (34–35)
Singing a sweet song, dancing with her own playful grace,
and meditating upon Śrī Hari Kṛṣṇa within the image of Oṃkāreśvara,
she appeared before the ascetics who were watching her with an exceedingly melting heart. (36)
With this very earthly body, the high-minded one—
she who is of the nature of *rasa*— attained dissolution right there into the form of the syllable *Oṃ*.
There, that young woman became one with light, and being truly composed of light, she merged into that light.
On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, that devoted wife attained a divine state; there Śambhu, for her liberation,
bestowed upon her the mantra of Kṛṣṇa and placed a garland of tulasī around her neck.
"Oṃ, obeisances to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Master; obeisances! (1.471.40).
Hara gave him the mantra three times and the Vaiṣṇava tilaka.
Having become a four-armed Satī, the sovereign lady went to Goloka. (41)
On the banks of the Matsyodarī at the sacred site of Goghaṭṭa, devoted wives bathe in the divine pool and behold the temple of Lord Kṛṣṇa;
those who do so indeed go to the imperishable realm of the Dark-Cloud-Hued One.
Having first bathed at Pañcanada, then in the vicinity of Oṃkāra,
then having bathed at Matsyodarī, and after that at Goghaṭṭa,
[one should go] to the temple of Śrīghanaśyāma on the right side of the Matsyodarī garden.
By worshipping Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa and Viśveśvara of Kāśī,
and by bowing to Gaṇeśa and Hanumān, one indeed becomes liberated.
From the very moment that Viśveśa arrived from Mount Mandara...
In the Ānandavana grove of Kāśī, I am Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa;
and on the banks of the Matsyodarī, in a most beautiful palace adorned with seven peaks and shaped like a lotus, I am known by the name Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. 46–47.
I, who reside in the abode of Goloka as the son of Kambharī here on this earth, am that very same person dwelling there within the image along with you.
O Brahmins, they always chant my name there eternally.
O beloved, the learned worship Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa,
as well as Viśveśvara and Oṃkāra,
as long as there is no impairment of the senses and as long as there is no exhaustion of life.
As long as there is a favorable disposition toward merit and intense contemplation of the mind,
for that long should the Lord Hari, the bestower of liberation, be served with effort.
Those who have taken refuge in the abode of Śrī within the Forest of Bliss of Śambhu—
May unshakable prosperity, which bestows great happiness, never forsake them.
Having heard this chapter, people whose minds are fixed on the Lord of Śrī shall be liberated from all sins and attain the imperishable state. (52–53)

Thus ends the four hundred and seventy-first chapter, titled "The Description of Mādhavī’s Liberation after her Death as a Maṇḍūkī through the Grace of Śiva, and Her Attainment of the State of a Gandharvī by Singing in the Abode of Śiva due to Her Devotion to Śiva," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 472 *Section 1: The Kṛtayuga-santāna* of the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā* (Volume Vṛddham).
Chapter 472.
[The Author: Chapter 473.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī! Likewise, hear another story concerning Pārāvatī.
For the female pigeon dwelling in the temple, through her devotion to her husband,
through the dharma of wifely fidelity, through service, and through pleasing [him],
enjoyment and liberation were attained by the grace of the God of gods.
In the city named Rathantara, in the temple of Trilocana,
upon the Vīrajaka seat in the field of Ratnasāti,
which was most beautifully adorned with brilliantly shining golden jars. (3)
On the peak, a pair of pigeons lived, having made their home there.
Morning, evening, and at midday, they constantly performed circumambulations,
flying about here and there with the wind from their wings.

The name "Trilocana" was constantly uttered by the devotees; its particles were always received as guests by those two, Kṛṣṇa and Narāyaṇa, whenever it stuck to their palaces and was brushed away. (6)
The auspicious *rātrika* ceremony certainly increases their devotion.
Day after day, they wander around the temple, crowded with devotees during the day, eating rice and other foods while performing circumambulations. (7–8)
And those two drank the pleasing water that had come from Nala. As those two brahmins of virtuous conduct were thus wandering in the vicinity of Mahādeva, a great length of time passed.
Then, seeing them from within a window on the upper story of the temple,
a hawk descended with speed, desiring to seize them;
but they flew up and entered the interior of the temple out of a desire for protection.
The hawk watched for their departure from that place;
he reflected, "How might these two be captured by me simultaneously?
In the evening, the hawk went to another location, since they had not been found there.
Then Pārāvatī, who was skillful and devoted to her husband’s service,
observed the bird Kāla and spoke to her husband,
the pigeon: "O dear, wise pigeon, that hawk is a powerful enemy."
"O Lord, O Master, he will devour us both before we can reach another place—whether it be widowhood for one, loss of husband for the other, or the destruction of both.
If this were indeed done by a hawk, it would surely bring about a great calamity. (15)
"O Lord, your vow as a husband and likewise my vow as a wife would be violated;
by that, the higher world would indeed be obstructed.
Having heard this from the virtuous woman of sweet voice, her husband said to her:
O virtuous one! In this temple of Durgā, which is the refuge of Hara, there is no anxiety. From this day forward, my dear, you must dwell here with perfect purity.
One who dwells in Durgā shall never be overcome by anyone anywhere, even if they are weak.
"The temple there is indeed in the form of a fortress; what fear can there be?
Indeed, one shall not find another such secure place as one's own refuge.
Having heard these words of Pārāvata, Pārāvatī then [replied].
Adopting silence right there, with her eyes fixed upon the feet of her husband, a virtuous woman—
even though she has been instructed in the path of what is beneficial— should remain quiet out of a desire to do what is pleasing to her beloved; she must always carry out the word of her husband.
Then, on another day, the hawk returned and beheld the couple.
Wandering around the palace with an unobstructed gaze, he perceived them as invincible, situated like two peaks in the midst [of the building], and so he departed. (22–23)
Then, when the hawk had departed into the sky, the beloved female dove spoke again to her husband: "O Lord, that wicked destroyer has been seen;
he will certainly cause us some obstacle at some point. (24)
"Therefore, O Lord, we should go to another place that will grant us happiness.
Having heard her words, Kalara spoke again:
"What will she do, O innocent one? This fortress is indeed like heaven for the two of us."
Where he has no entrance and does not know the one who might enter,
O beloved, dwelling within the celestial palace brings him security and well-being.
Even if, by chance, there were a sudden visitor from the sky, [he would remain unperceived].
Nevertheless, I know those movements which my adversary does not know.
The eight movements—praḍīna, uḍḍīna, saṇḍīna, kāṇḍa, vyāḍa, kapāṭikā, sraṃsanī, and maṇḍalavatī—are thus described. (28–29)
Whirling, emptying, flowing, upward movement, curvature,
falling, fainting, and being bound— these are the eight movements, as well as others; O beloved, I know them all, and my skill therein is complete in every respect.
"Just as there is no other bird in the sky equal to me, so too [there is none equal to you].
"Stay at ease; what anxiety is there for you while I, your beloved, am alive?
Having heard these words of her husband, that virtuous woman remained silent as if mute.
On the following day as well, the hawk, his heart exceedingly joyful, remained perched for some time upon that lotus-stone;
having wandered about and thoroughly inspected the path leading inside.
Seeing that those two were still inside, she once again ascended the path of the sky.
Then, being terrified, Pārāvatī spoke again to her husband:
"O beloved! This place must be abandoned, for it is defiled by the gaze of our enemies."
"That cruel one is indeed approaching excessively with the desire to seize us.
Hearing his beloved's words, he said: "What will he do, my dear?
For this, O timid one, is generally the nature of women—a disposition toward cowardice. (36)
Then on the following day as well, that hawk arrived with the desire to seize them;
standing there facing the two of them for the duration of two watches, and having observed them again, he departed quickly from that place, whereupon she said to him: (37–38)
"O Lord, let us go elsewhere, since death is near to us here.
You have described many kinds of destinies; why this insistence?
We shall dwell wherever we may, for success awaits those who face their efforts with diligence."
The man who does not abandon his own country, even when it is beset by calamities, meets with destruction like a cripple, though he may be strong, if he is forsaken by fate.
Afflicted by his impending condition, the bird did not heed what was spoken by his beloved.
He said, "Do not fear, O virtuous lady; there is no place superior to this.
Then, on another day, that hawk arrived at the location on her path early in the morning and remained there until evening.
When the sun had set and the bird had departed, Pārāvatī said to her husband:
"O Lord, this is the time for your departure; leave this house.
Depart even after abandoning me, and later it will be appropriate."
While you live, nothing on the surface of the earth is difficult to obtain:
again a wife, again a friend, again wealth, and again a home.
If a man protects his own self, he can do so even at the cost of his wives and his riches.
This self is a beloved kinsman and a great treasure that must be protected.
This self is the supreme means for attaining virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation.
As long as there is well-being for the self, so long is there well-being in the three worlds.
"Therefore, O Lord, having heard my words which are conducive to your welfare and consistent with sound policy, go elsewhere from here; otherwise, you will remember me [with regret].
Though addressed thus by his wife, whose intellect was well-disposed toward her husband's service, he—
He did not depart from that place, being restrained by destiny.
Then, at dawn, a hawk arrived and spoke to him forcefully:
"Come outside this place; today you shall become my prey."
"Or rather, being hungry and intent on my own interest, I do not see the hardship [of others]. O beloved, I shall either enter your house or kill you," he said,
and having spoken thus, he entered within with his talons like a hawk.
Then the bird was seized by a hawk, and that female bird was seized by a powerful falcon.
They both cried out in distress, for neither was protected by anyone.
The hawk, repeatedly considering a place free from obstacles where he might devour him, remained there.
Then the bird Sumedhā, moving through the sky, cried out in agitation:
"O Lord, follow my final word!
For the sake of your own liberation, bite the enemy's foot firmly with your beak. (54)
Having been thus instructed, the hawk acted accordingly and was indeed overcome by pain.
Bitten excessively, the hawk then let out cries of distress;
from his mouth, a female dove escaped with great force.
She too, being questioned, repeatedly struck the killer with her beak and feet;
by that, the pigeon was indeed released by him as he became agitated. Both having fainted, the hawk fell from his flight in the sky.
"Even for one who is weak, fortune indeed bestows fruit upon the energetic;
therefore, those possessed of passion praise effort in all circumstances.
Then, although the two had sustained wounds, it was truly by the power of fortune—" || 58-59 ||
Having lived for a long time in the enchanting city of Sāketa on the delightful bank of the river Sarayū, the two of them, possessing life, met their death.
There, a bird became a Vidyādhara born from a garland of Mandāra flowers.
A repository of many sciences, known by the name Parimalālaya,
he reached the age of youth and became devoted to the worship of Śiva;
intent on the life of celibacy, he undertook rigorous religious observances.

"I shall observe the supreme vow of a devoted wife, remaining faithful during my fertile seasons; as long as I live, having worshipped Mahādeva, I shall not consume even the slightest morsel [without him].
Thus did that bird-woman constantly maintain her observance.
There was a Naga maiden named Ratnāvalī, devoted to the practice of virtue;
she could assume any form at will and lived eternally in the forest of Sāketa.
She had two female companions, Prabhāvatī and Kalāvatī.
When she had attained youth, beautiful, auspicious, and capable of assuming any form at will, the virtuous Ratnāvalī, though still a young woman, undertook a vow:
"Having seen Śambhu with his matted locks in the morning, I shall break my silence; not otherwise."
Day after day, having worshipped Hara with various flowers of diverse colors and fragrances, as well as garlands, sandalwood paste, lamps, and other offerings,
all three of them then sang a song beautiful with the radiant *gāndhāra* note.
Skilled in rhythm and tempo, the three Naga maidens joyfully play the lute,
flute, and drum,
performing the *lāsya* dance through various circular formations (*rāsamaṇḍala*).

They constantly serve Hara with various fragrant garlands, sweeping, and anointing; [they serve him] with dance, song, and excellent food. Once, in the month of Vaiśākha, on the third lunar day, they fasted. || 1.472.70–71 ||
They kept a vigil at night and performed worship in the morning;
they fed the virtuous, and then, at the hour of midday, they indeed offered delicious food and water to Śaṅkara. 72.
And when they performed the nightly lamp-offering and presented handfuls of flowers,
Śrī Śaṅkara, being pleased, appeared before them in person.
His body was as white as pure camphor, and he was adorned with a crown of matted locks.
With his left thigh resting upon truth, wearing a serpent as a sacred thread,
the God with a serene countenance— the enemy of Kāma and bestower of liberation—
was beheld by those maidens, who were then moved to horripilation.
With throats choked with emotion and voices exceedingly faltering, they bowed down and praised him:

"Victory to you, O Śambhu! Victory to you, O lover of your devotees! Victory, O Lord! Victory to you, O husband of the virtuous Sāvitrī! Victory to you, O Lord of Creatures (Paśupati)! Victory to you, O Lord of the Universe! (76–77)
"Victory to you, O Lord of Liberation, Lord of Devotees, Purifier, Śaṅkara!
May victory be yours; salutations to you; obeisance to you, salutations again and again.
Having spoken thus, the young maidens prostrated themselves on the ground like a staff.
Embracing them, the Blessed One, the treasury of compassion, said:
"He who is the son of Mandāra, named Parimalālaya,
shall become the husband of you all, a preeminent Vidyādhara."
"Having enjoyed pleasures in every way for a long time in the world of the Vidyādharas,
you shall thereafter attain detachment and achieve the perfection of liberation.
All three of you are my devotees, and that Vidyādhara is mine as well."
"All four of you shall attain liberation here at this very borderland.
In a previous birth, service was rendered by you to me;
because of that, servitude as well as the vow of celibacy (*brahmavrata*) was likewise performed."
By that merit, the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa himself shall become your guru and the bestower of liberation.
And may you all become highly fortunate women, devoted wives to Kṛṣṇa.
"I chant the name of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of all, as my husband. You too should worship Him; receive His supreme mantra, and accept this prasāda and water served by Acyuta. (85-86)
Thinking thus, Hara gave them the mantra that bestows easy liberation:
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇa svāmine namaḥ.
Having imparted it three times, he gave them a leaf of *tulasī*.
He also placed a garland of *tulasī* upon his neck and in his hand;
then Hara himself applied a drop of sandalwood paste to his forehead.
Having thus bestowed the image fashioned from jewels according to the prescribed rite, [he departed].
He said: "May there always be well-being for you, O Acyutā, and may unbroken good fortune remain with you.
May you always possess devotion to Viṣṇu, service to Kṛṣṇa, and likewise the vow of a devoted wife.
And may there always be worship of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa."
"May your service to the Lord and your service to Kṛṣṇa always be one and the same, without distinction.
Having spoken thus and placed his hand upon their heads, he vanished from sight.
With hearts full of joy, they returned home and spoke with delight.
Having attained a divine state, they are unobstructed by barriers such as walls and move through the paths of the sky like lotuses;
remembering their former births, these truthful women are devoted to the practice of celibacy.
Devoted to the worship of Kṛṣṇa by the command of Śambhu, these followers of the Sāttvata tradition have become liberated while living (jīvanmukta) and possess independent movement here on earth.
O Lakṣmī! Formerly, there was a brahmin named Nārāyaṇa who was a pigeon. 94–95.
The son of Āmuṣyāyaṇa was devoted to the vow of serving his father;
bitten by a serpent, he died and subsequently became this very pigeon.
Cārāyaṇa had two daughters, Bhavānī and Gautamī.
The two wives of Nārāyaṇa, the son of Āmuṣyāyaṇa,
having fallen into the misery of widowhood and overcome by wretchedness,
came by chance to the most wonderful hermitage of a certain ṛṣi. (97–98)
Then, as the sage was eating plantain fruits he had gathered,
those two maidens, having been lost due to his curse, became female monkeys. Thereafter, they fell into the water at that most excellent sacred ford and gave up their lives.
Once those two Naga maidens were born,
Prabhāvatī and Kalāvatī— both virtuous women devoted to the dharma of Kṛṣṇa—
became the two companions of Parimalālayā, the wife of the Vidyādhara king, by taking refuge in the hermitage of Devālaya.
Knowing that those two auspicious Vidyādharīs were full of love for him, his parents subsequently gave them to him in marriage— Parimalālayā and [the other].
Thus, Ratnāvalī, Prabhā, and Kalāvatī became his three wives.
Devoted to Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa and dedicated to her husband,

she remained filled with happiness as she constantly worshipped Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa through ritual worship, mantra-recitation, food offerings, hymns of praise, the waving of lights, and acts of atonement. (103–104)
They constantly perform offerings of handfuls of flowers and periodic festivals;
on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Kārtika, they worship Kṛṣṇa. Intending to observe the Jayantī, they undertook the vow of Kṛṣṇa.
Then Kṛṣṇa himself, the Lord of Rādhā and Ramā’s splendor,
arrived from Goloka in a celestial chariot to lead them away along with their husbands;
having granted his own divine vision, he took them in that most excellent of vehicles.

He went indeed to Goloka and granted liberation in the form of service; O Lakṣmī, tell me, there is no difference in the devotion of devotees before Kṛṣṇa. Wherever a devotee may be born, he shall attain the state of Hari.
Indeed, all the children of that Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa,
having worshipped him, go indeed to the supreme, eternal abode.
Having heard this narrative of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, one is liberated from sin.

Thus ends the four hundred and seventy-second chapter, titled "The Description of how the Pigeon Couple, by taking refuge in a temple of Śiva, obtained birth as Vidyādharas; how Parimalālaya the Vidyādhara had three wives—Ratnāvalī, Prabhāvatī, and Kalāvatī; and how all four attained liberation through the vow of the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Kārtika and through devotion to Kṛṣṇa," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
(Chapter 472, Book 1: *Kṛtayuga-santāna*).

Chapter 474 → Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī! In the sacred field of Ānandakānana, at the Dharmapīṭha, a marvel occurred regarding the practice of dharma; I shall describe it.
That which is called the Dharmapīṭha is indeed located in the sacred field of Ānandakānana.
Merely by beholding that sacred seat (pīṭha), a person is liberated from sins.
(2) In ancient times, Vivasvat’s son, Yama—the best among the upholders of dharma—performed austerities in that field for the sake of showing grace to the world. (3)
In the cold season he remained standing in the midst of water; during the rains, he stayed under the open sky;
in the heat, he stood amidst five fires, and at times he exposed himself to a violent wind.
For a long time he remained with his big toe touching the ground at its very tip.
Standing on one foot for a long time thereafter,
he then subsisted on air; subsequently, he drank water sparingly,
only as much as could be held on the tip of a blade of kusha grass, and finally, he abstained from all food.
Thus he spent a divine cycle of four yugas performing penance,
desiring through meditative absorption to behold Śrī Śaṅkara with his fourfold form.
Śaṅkara was gratified by the penance of that man of steady mind.
He went to that witness who had assumed the form of Dharma to grant him boons.
Dharma replied to him, "Choose a boon according to your desire.
Having seen me, he prostrated before me and likewise offered praise.
Then that sinless one chose to see my form as the agent of dissolution;
I revealed to him that very form of mine which is terrifying,
the nature of Mahārudra, which is the nature of Saṃkarṣaṇa.
Then [Brahmā said]: "May you indeed become Dharmarāja, possessing my own form;
exercise your authority over the dharma of all embodied beings.
Furthermore, be the witness of the actions of living creatures and omniscient as well."
May this field of Dharma, which fulfills all desires in that manner,
become a bestower of liberation and capable of incinerating the sins of living beings.
May my form as Dharmeśvara also exist through your name.
"Accept the mantra of Kṛṣṇa and become a supreme Vaiṣṇava.
Having spoken thus to Dharmarāja, Maheśvara gave him the mantra:
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya brahmaṇe namaḥ. (14–15)
He placed a garland around Vṛndā’s neck and gave her a rosary for the purpose of recitation;
he drew a tilaka on her forehead and bestowed many blessings.
Śrī Śaṅkara himself then gave manifold instructions on the path of right conduct.
Happiness is declared to be the fruit of dharma, and that consists precisely in the fulfillment of one's own desires.
Suffering, however, is indeed the frustration of one's desires, and that is the fruit of evil deeds. Heaven is happiness for the gods, and it arises through their propitiation. (17–18)
Complete happiness in all spiritual practices arises through giving alone;
for one who seeks bliss, life should consist solely in the satisfaction of others.
Everything that causes pain to another will result in suffering for oneself as well.
One should perform service to others, and one must practice self-realization.
Devotion to the worship of Kṛṣṇa and other such acts should be performed for the sake of liberation.
Indeed, in this world, the prosperity of men arises from previous acts of giving.
What has not been given cannot be obtained; therefore, one should practice righteousness (*dharma*).

Indeed, a universal rule has been established that there is the yielding of fruit for what has been done, whether it be auspicious or inauspicious; you must reach a definitive conclusion regarding this.
In each such case, Janārdana will surely grant the fruit thereof to them.
(23) Enjoyment according to the nature of the senses is not considered a sin;
enjoyment performed unjustly gives rise to sin by force. (24)
Action born of serene devotion produces contentment;
it is free from malice and does not lead to sin, for it bestows merit and contentment.
All such action, when offered to Kṛṣṇa without desire, indeed grants liberation.
Therefore, one should always practice Dharma; the vow that bestows liberation is what must be performed.
However, harming others, as well as malice toward others, censuring others, seizing the property of others, and likewise causing distress to other beings—[these must be avoided]. (26–27)
"This is declared to bestow sin, while the other is supreme for performing merit.
O best among the upholders of dharma, grant them their respective fruits.
Having said, "Go," Mṛḍa touched that bull with both his hands.
The son of the Sun spoke again: "O Lord, I make this request:
O Śambhu, for these young parrots whose births occurred in my presence and who are now fatherless, their mother, the female parrot, has passed away. (1.473.30)
Then the parrot was suddenly devoured by a hawk; whereupon I,
having said, "O Lord of Gods, be a granter of boons to those who are protectorless and conversant with the stories of ancient history," became intent upon observing silence.
Then Śambhu said to the parrots, "What boon shall be granted by me for your sake?
Having heard this, the young parrots sang to him:
"O Lord of Gods, even for birds, the sight of you is a great treasure."

O Lord, through our separation from this ascetic, we have come to know this story born of thousands of other births; we remember it among tens of millions of gods, among the Daityas, the serpents, the night-stalkers, and the Kinnaras. (34)
Among the Vidyādharas, Gandharvas, humans, and aquatic beings;
on land as well as in forests, in mountain clefts, and within the earth;
among supplicants and givers, and among protectors and slayers. (35–36)

Through his power, we remember his births among those who were happy and those who were suffering, among the foolish and the wise, among masters and servants, and among trees whose very nature was that of other beings. (37)
From this womb to that womb, from that womb to another—O wielder of the Pināka bow!
not even the slightest trace of happiness was obtained anywhere.
Now, merely by beholding you, we have become fulfilled.
Furthermore, if there is a boon to be granted out of your compassion,

grant us that knowledge by which we may be liberated from the bondage of worldly existence— knowledge by which the entire cosmic egg, and all else, becomes as clear to us as a myrobalan fruit in the palm of the hand. (1.473.40)

"Because we have resorted to the presence of Dharma within the range of our speech, we have become vessels of knowledge through the ascetic power of Dharmarāja. Having heard this from the young parrots, the Lord of Śivā spoke to them: 42.
In the Ānandavana grove at Kāśī, upon my Dharma-throne, is my residence called Mokṣalakṣmīvilāsa, constructed of jewels, gems, and other precious materials;
even birds are liberated by performing circumambulation there. (43)
In the form of Bindumādhava, I dwell upon the Dharmanadī river.
Lead those who have bathed in the Pañcanada to that supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
O Bālakīras, you are indeed worthy vessels of knowledge at the seat of Dharma.
Since you have been born [into this state], accept this supreme Vaiṣṇava mantra:
*Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya pataye namaḥ*.
Accept the garland of tulasī and chant [this name] for Acyuta every day.
"At the end of the body, you shall go by means of a divine vehicle to the abode of Acyuta.
Having spoken thus and having made the parrots Vaiṣṇavas, the Blessed Lord Hara then vanished; and those parrots remained there at Dharmakṣetra.
They worship the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the husband of Rādhā;
they recite the narrative of the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā,
and parrots daily cause people to hear the stories of other kalpas.
Those excellent twice-born ones were wise, learned, and capable of assuming any form at will.
Thus, they were always devoted to their devotion to Kṛṣṇa;
those birds constantly performed the worship of Kṛṣṇa and engaged in discourses about Kṛṣṇa.
Once, Paulomī, desiring the fruits of her vows, arrived there;
she performed the Manoratha-vrata and practiced supreme austerity.
These [sages] constantly recite to her this story that destroys all sin.
Having heard the story contained in the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, which bestows liberation,
Śacī worshiped Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa with devotion using the sixteen types of offerings on the bank of the river at Dharmakṣetra.
Having worshipped the omnipresent Lord Śiva, the Sovereign of the Universe, at Pañcanada,
Śacī worships him constantly and likewise performs a dance with song that is full of esoteric meaning and possesses the sweet warbling of a cuckoo. (55)
Highly pleased by that song, Hara appeared before her in person.
He said, "Choose a boon, O daughter of Puloman; I am gratified.
Śacī replied, "If you are pleased, then fulfill my heart's desire."
May he who is honored among all the gods, who is the most beautiful among all the gods, and who is the best among all those who perform sacrifices, be my husband;
may he possess the form as desired and the happiness as desired. (58)
"O Bhava, being pleased, grant me a lifespan according to my desire.
Whenever I might have union with my husband out of a longing for pleasure, at that very moment may I cast off this body and obtain another. (1.473.60)
"Even upon my husband’s death, may widowhood not befall me for even a single moment;
rather, may my devotion to my husband remain eternal even in his passing.
Thus, O Blessed One, I choose unbroken good fortune. (61)
Having heard this, Mahādeva laughed and said to her:
"O auspicious and pure one, perform the vow of Manorathatṛtīyā;
for by the performance of that vow, which bestows great good fortune," (62–63)
Your cherished desire shall certainly be fulfilled in this way:
Gaurī, who possesses twenty arms, shall be worshipped by Viśvabhuj;
and [your hand] shall become a hand granting boons, holding a rosary along with water.
Before the Goddess, Āśāvināyaka is to be worshipped by one observing the vow.

On the second day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, one should undertake the auspicious observance, remaining pure, rising early in the morning, practicing celibacy, and sleeping upon the ground. (65–66)
One should indeed use a twig from an *aśoka* tree for cleaning the teeth;
having performed all other daily rites (*nityakarman*), one should then perform the ritual bath.
And having fully worshipped Gaṇeśa, who is a portion of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
Having offered *ghṛtapūra* sweets, one should perform the worship of Gaurī.
With excellent *aśoka* flowers, *aśoka* wick-incense, lamps, and various kinds of food offerings, one should satisfy the virtuous goddess. 68–69.
Thus, adorned with the beauty of saffron, one should observe the vow of eating only once a day.
Beginning thus on the third day of the month of Caitra and continuing until the end of Phālguna,
this vow observed on twelve third days indeed grants all desires.
One should observe the vow with whatever pure articles for ritual service are available.

For the completion of the vow, one should perform the worship of the fire upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) and carry out one hundred and eight oblations (homa) with sesame seeds, clarified butter, and other such materials.
Worship is always prescribed for the night, and eating is always at night;
indeed, this fire-offering is at night alone, and the rite of expiation is at night alone.
Homage be to You, O All-pervading One! Quickly fulfill my heart’s desires.
Salutations to Āśāgaṇeśa; grant me my heart’s desire.

the children of that sage lamented because of the destruction of their mother.
Then the Jīva, moving through the intermediate space, spoke of her true nature:
"O Lord, you are all-seeing, possessed of knowledge, and the best among yogis.
O Omniscient One, you know everything; what can I possibly inform you? (82)
Whether it be pleasant speech or harsh speech, anger or even distress;

greed, delusion, and desire, as well as hunger, thirst, and the like; obesity, emaciation, and destruction; and the states of being peaceful, terrible, or utterly bewildered—[all these arise from the mind]. (83–84)
All bodily attributes—sound, speech, and abuse—are composed of the elements; likewise, *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* constitute the body as being of the nature of the three *guṇas*.
There may be a deficiency or excess among these, and by that, transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) arises.
Weeping, laughter, affliction, agitation, and even fear;
anger, tranquility, and cursing—these belong to the body and are not dear to the Self.
However, the desire for liberation arises from the emergence of *sattva*, while the desire for action arises from the quality of *rajas*.
From the quality of *tamas* arises the desire for quarrel; the darkness in both of us is equal.
Just as *tamas* is the progenitor of anger in you, so it is in me.
From anger comes harsh speech and insults, and through harsh speech, enmity is born.
But by that [transience], unpleasantness arises immediately; for who is the enemy of whom, and who is the friend?
Who indeed is dear or who is hateful? What is a friend and what is an enemy?
Passion and aversion are truly the primary factors in all cases regarding enemies and friends.
To women, their husband is dearer than life; to the husband, his wife is dearer than life.
Yet, enmity arose instantly through harsh words and in a moment through anger.
Whatever has passed away, all that is material, has perished due to the defects of the elements.

That which has gone is to be lamented; what has not been born will never come to be otherwise. (92) "I am burnt, your wife; you too have burnt that wealth of asceticism. Now that both bodies and both virtues are burnt, there is no returning again. (93)
"Once it has gone, all that is truly gone; once it is lost, it is indeed lost forever.
Therefore, we must now act in such a way that our welfare may be secured.
Forgive all offenses; tell me now what ought to be done."
"What shall I do? Where shall I go? Where will my birth be? [I thought.
"I am always your wife, and never anyone else's anywhere, at any time.
I have not existed before, nor shall I exist [independently]; I shall attain you again and again. (95–96)
Having heard her words, his mind was robbed by grief;
yet after a moment he regained his composure and prepared to give up his life,
for the separation from a woman indeed causes sorrow even to the wise.
Then, having assumed a yogic posture, the man about to die said nothing to her.
But she, seeing the sage about to die in the sky, overwhelmed with grief,
remembered Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the protector from distress.
Just then, Janārdana arrived there in the guise of a young Brahmin; smiling and dark-complexioned, he spoke to Durvāsas.

Thus ends the section in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, in the first part concerning the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga, which includes: the marriage of Durvāsas with Kadalī, the daughter of Aurva, following his vow to endure a hundred verbal insults; the description of her duties as a devoted wife (*pātivratya*); the birth of twenty sons and daughters; the reduction of Kadalī to ashes by the sage’s curse when she transgressed out of anger; the hymn of praise offered by Kadalī; and the arrival of Janārdana, among other events.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to how the young brahmin spoke to Durvāsas.
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa Viṣṇu acted exactly as was appropriate for the occasion:

Having bestowed his blessings upon him, the young brahmin said:
"O Durvāsas, by the grace of your preceptor’s mantra, you know everything;
nevertheless, O young brahmin, I shall speak—listen to me."
For Brahmins, austerity is dharma; the three worlds are to be accomplished through austerity.
(4) For Vaiṣṇavas, devotion to Hari and service to Him are the supreme austerity;
[likewise] listening to the stories of Hari and worshipping Him at all times. (5)
Indeed, all service and worship should be performed for a Vaiṣṇava;
especially for a sage, one should always perform what is auspicious and conducive to spiritual welfare.
Having abandoned all this, as well as grief and the causes of grief—
Why do you rely upon that which bestows suffering and destroys the intellect?
(7) In this wheel of worldly existence, who is whose wife, and who is whose beloved?
Hari employs his illusory power (*māyā*) merely to deceive fools. (8)
"This wife of yours was indeed illusory, yet she has now vanished in a mere moment.
For that which is eternal never becomes illusory, nor does it ever pass into invisibility.
This wife of yours, Kandali, was always created as a real being."
"O Sage, that shadow which was fashioned by you for the sake of your own support has been made into a teacher for you by Nārāyaṇa. Do not grieve over this matter; she shall be your wife once again."
There is no doubt that she will appear; having divided herself into two, she will choose [one].
Speak to your beloved, the devoted wife stationed in the sky, who is full of longing.
Tell her what she, who is awaiting your command, will do.
Then Durvāsas saw her and said, "Become a plantain tree (kadalī).
Granting auspiciousness, yielding fruit, lovely, giving birth but once and very rare,
possessing many children, be forever devoted to your husband from your very root."
Thus addressed, she replied: "And you too become Kardama.
Just as my name is, so too is my nature that of Kardama;
always be full of moisture at your root and endowed with the state of coolness."
Thus addressed, the sage Kardama indeed assumed another form;
Durvāsas and Kardama constantly resorted to the root of a plantain tree. That plantain, which bestows plantains, became a species of plantain known as Kandalī.
Though she had once borne fruit and provided both roots and offspring,
having become barren in the midst of the forest,
that plantain tree nevertheless remained a constant source of food for elephants in the woods.
Then that young brahmin spoke again for the benefit of the sage:
"Listen, O Brahmin, in kalpa after kalpa, your wife shall repeatedly become a plantain tree of tranquil form, bestowing happiness."
Known as Ekānaṃśā, the sister of Kṛṣṇa, the daughter of Śrī Devakī,
born from a portion of Pārvatī, the virtuous Suśīlā shall be your beautiful wife in every kalpa and live for a long time.
"Give your mind with joy to ascetic practice now that the time has arrived.
That girl, whose nature is peaceful, will meet Kṛṣṇa.
Having spoken thus, the four-armed Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa— 23.
Having granted him his own vision, he indeed vanished;
the sage, having abandoned all delusion, fixed his mind upon ascetic practice.
(24) Sometimes, the subduing of one who has risen too high is indicated to occur.
Indeed, for one who has been subdued, a twofold prosperity arises.
The kandalī, a species of banana tree, appeared upon the surface of the earth;
as fierce as it had been, it became just as cool.
On the auspicious bank of the river Sarasvatī, there was a beautiful hermitage belonging to Kandalī’s father;
it existed there due to Kandalī’s devotion to her husband,
as well as her vow of Brahmanical conduct and her devotion to the illustrious Mādhava.
All of his father’s garments, both dry and wet, O Lakṣmī, remain suspended in the sky by the wind at all times;
this is a wonderful marvel, occurring even without a peg! (28–29)
When that *kandalī* plant was consumed by fire due to the curse of Durvāsas,
at that very moment, washed garments fell from above onto the surface of the earth.
As the garment fell upon the ground, Aurva himself abandoned his ascetic penance.
Through meditation, he perceived the entire calamity involving the girl, the ashes, and the rest.
Overcome with grief, he went at once in an instant to his son-in-law’s hermitage;
weeping, he sprinkled the dust of the earth with drops from his eyes.
"O child! O Kadalī!"—thus he cried out repeatedly.
Recognizing the voice of his father-in-law, Durvāsas became overwhelmed with fear;
he emerged from the cottage and fell at his feet.
Having consoled his preceptor, the sage, he lamented bitterly;
then he related the entire account to that sage, beginning from the very start.
Upon hearing the news, Aurva again grieved in many ways.
He spoke to his son-in-law, who was terrified with his neck bowed:
"O Brahmin, O son of Atri, you are the auspicious grandson of Brahmā.
Why have you inflicted such a heavy punishment for a very minor offense?"
Your birth was from a portion of Śaṅkara; likewise, you are a disciple of Brahmā.
You are a knower of the Vedas, virtuous, possessed of wisdom, and established in your vows.
Anasūyā, a great and chaste woman who is a portion of Kamalā, is your mother.

He whose father is virtuous and whose mother is a virtuous woman—yet their son is devoid of compassion! Oh, how subtle is the course of creation! I know not by what fault such a disposition as this has arisen in you.
Devoted primarily to violence, it constantly destroys the prosperity of one's lineage.
However, I have a daughter, dearer to me than my own life, who has been entrusted to you;
she is a great devoted wife, possessed of no fault other than a mere flaw in her speech.
Indeed, the prescribed punishment for a woman who is corrupt in speech is abandonment; this is the established rule.
A father certainly protects his daughter once she has been abandoned.
Since my own child was reduced to ashes by you for such a minor offense, [you must now face the consequences].
"Even for you, there will be a great downfall; of this there is no doubt.
The Treasure of Compassion swiftly bestows the fruit of the actions of one who acts with malice.
Having said this, and lamenting excessively while repeatedly crying out, "Alas, my daughter! [he fell]. 43–44.
Having recognized her on the riverbank to be in the form of a plantain tree,
he dug her up from the roots, took her away, and went home.
She was indeed a daughter— a young maiden who lacked an owner and was devoid of fruit.
He nurtured a *kandalī* plant—which had the form of a banana tree—with the pouring of water.
Consequently, mud began to moisten at its base;
that foul-smelling mud then became Durvāsas due to a curse.
But from the union of those two, the offspring once again became fruitless;
indeed, they turned into forests that provided sustenance for elephants.
As for the forty offspring of Durvāsas, they likewise [became so].
Born from the interior of plantains, they went to the hermitage of Aurva;
protected by Aurva himself, their lineage flourished.
Then, remembering his beloved, Durvāsas became intent on ascetic penance.
Then, after some time, O Lakṣmī! listen as I tell you how that king suffered defeat at the hands of Ambarīṣa due to his father-in-law’s curse.
Ambarīṣa was a most righteous king of the Solar dynasty.
Indeed, his mind was constantly fixed upon the lotus feet of Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
for not even for a moment did his heart dwell upon kingdoms, nor upon wives, nor upon sons, nor upon subjects, nor even upon the riches acquired through meritorious deeds. (52–53)
The devotee meditates upon Hari day and night, both in waking and in dreams;
he is a great bhāgavata, peaceful, and solely devoted to the vows of Viṣṇu.
He is intent on the vow of Ekādaśī and dedicated to the worship of Kṛṣṇa. (54)
And the agent, though smeared by all actions, [is purified] when they are offered to Kṛṣṇa.
The Lord’s extremely sharp Sudarśana discus, with its sixteen spokes, was constantly kept by the Master for protection in the presence of the king. (55–56)
Having observed the Ekādaśī vow, when the twelfth day arrived,
he bathed, worshipped Hari, and gave gifts of gold and silver;
then, having fed virtuous Brahmins, he remained there for his own meal.
Just then, the sage Durvāsas arrived there, hungry.
Seeing him, the king rose, bowed, and having offered him water for his feet and a seat, he asked with affection: "What is your command? Tell me what you desire."
Durvāsas said, "Give food according to the prescribed rites to me who am hungry;
however, having chanted the Aghamarṣaṇa mantra, I shall indeed return before long.
Having said, "O King, wait for a moment," he then departed from there.
"Durvāsas does not arrive quickly, for the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) is passing away.
Seeing this, the king questioned Vasiṣṭha regarding his dilemma of dharma:
"The tiger among sages does not come, yet the time of the twelfth lunar day is slipping away."
"In this crisis, what ought to be done? he asked him.
Vasiṣṭha, the benefactor, replied to him with words that were truthful, merit-bestowing, and approved by all:
"When the twelfth day has passed, the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) should be performed on the thirteenth day."
Having destroyed the fruit of his fast, he certainly kills the one who observes the vow.
If a fool does not feed a guest who has arrived, that guest, terrified and hungry, eats him; such a person will surely go to the Kumbhīpāka hell. (64–65)
A man staying there for a hundred years falls into the state of a Cāṇḍāla;
moreover, he shall be afflicted by disease and poverty in birth after birth.
Therefore, we shall now tell you something extremely subtle regarding this supreme peril.
"Observe the dharma of both [parties] and I shall tell you:
protect the fruit of your fast by consuming the water from Kṛṣṇa’s feet.
O King, having quickly drunk that water, its consumption becomes non-consumption. (67–68)
Thus addressed, the king drank a little water while remembering Hari.
In the meantime, the wrathful sage arrived there;
the omniscient one, out of anger, cut off his own matted hair before the king.
Then, seeing that man— who had arisen with a sword in hand and was blazing like fire—
advancing to slay the lord of kings, the infallible discus cut down the *kṛtyā*-man in order to strike Durvāsas.
Upon seeing the discus depart, the Brahmin fled like one terrified;
as the Sudarśana pursued it across the universe,
he saw it and, crying out "Save me!", went to Brahmā for refuge.
Brahmā said: "O sage, how could you go to curse the servant of Hari?
Who can kill him whom the Blessed Lord protects in the three worlds?
Indeed, he exists for the protection of devotees, both the lowly and the great. (73–74)
Śrī Hari, who is affectionate toward his devotees, constantly protects the *cakra* [the Vaiṣṇava community];
yet, for that fool who hates a Vaiṣṇava person who is as dear to Viṣṇu as his own life,
Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa himself brings about the end.
"Go quickly to another place, my child; there is no protection for you now.
Otherwise, the Sudarśana will slay you along with me—it is capable of burning the world of Brahmā and the entire cosmic egg in an instant. (76–77)
"By what other power can that which is equal to Viṣṇu in its brilliance be warded off?
Having heard this, he fled and went for refuge to Śiva.
Out of fear, he said to Śaṅkara, "O treasure-house of compassion, protect me! (78)
Even Śaṅkara, though residing on Kailāsa, did not ask him about his welfare;
rather, Śambhu, the destroyer of the worlds, spoke quickly out of fear:
"O Sage, you are the grandson of the Creator and the son of Atri!"
"You are a knower of the Vedas who is a portion of me, yet your action is equal to that of a fool.
Since we have all arisen from him, how indeed can you strike one who is devoted to him?
I am Brahmā, Kamalā, Durgā, Vāṇī, and Rādhikā."
Prabhā, Lakṣmī, Pārvatī, Māṇikī, Śrī, Ramā, and Jayā—none of us are superior to the devotee, for the devotee is superior to us all;
he who constantly protects with effort both small and great devotees. (82–83)
The Blessed One indeed protects his devotee with his unbearable discus;
yet when that discus is difficult to restrain and does not succeed in providing protection,
then the glorious four-armed Lord himself goes to protect him.
For the sake of his devotee, Hari wanders constantly like a shadow;
indeed, there is no one in this world dearer than a beloved who is more precious than life, yet if she herself hates her devotees, the Lord quickly abandons her. (85–86)
To Hari, Brahmins are dearer even than his own body;

O Brāhmaṇa, take refuge in Govinda; remember his lotus feet.
"Go quickly to Vaikuṇṭha; Śrī Kṛṣṇa is your refuge.

If splendor, truth, and austerity have been long accumulated [by you], then let all those dwelling on Kailāsa likewise be free from distress. By my blessing and through devotion to Hari, may this Brahmin who has come for refuge [be so as well]. (91–92)
"May Durvāsā, the devotee of Viṣṇu, quickly be freed from his fever.

Having spoken thus, he drenched his lotus-feet with tears from his eyes.
Nārāyaṇa, however, said to him: "Arise and be firm;

Others acquire knowledge by hearing the scriptures from the mouths of the virtuous;
but the scriptures are my very forms, and the virtuous are the embodiments of the scriptures.

"That which is spoken in the scriptures is indeed my own word, for I abide within their hearts. To me, the virtuous are always superior to the Brāhmaṇas and the Vedas;

I am indeed the life-breath of the Vaiṣṇavas, and the Vaiṣṇavas are my very life-breaths.
He who hates them hates me; he is a destroyer of my life-breath.
Having abandoned sons, grandsons, wives, kingdom, and prosperity—
To those who constantly meditate upon me, who is dearer to me than they?
My life-breaths are not dearer to me than my devotees; nor are Lakṣmī, nor Śaṅkara, nor Bhāratī, nor Brahmā, nor Durgā, nor Gaṇeśvara.
There were no Brahmins, nor the Vedas, nor the supreme mother of the Vedas;

Whether in Goloka or Vaikuṇṭha, I appear with two or four arms.

"O Ambarīṣa, best of kings, how can you destroy one who is free from desire, non-violent, compassionate by nature, virtuous, and devoted to the welfare of all living beings— even if the food given by another were inedible, it would be like nectar? || 11 ||
Those virtuous ones who always show compassion toward all living beings;
and those who worship me with devotion, who possess my fortune and are established in me—

"I am unable to protect you from this enemy who harms my devotees.
Go to the abode of Ambarīṣa; he is capable of protecting you.
There, for the sake of pleasing the king, you should break your fast."
For a full year, you wandered here and there, filled with fear.
That king, O Indra among kings, remained fasting along with his wife and was overcome by grief;
therefore, I too fasted for the sake of my devotee’s fasting.
"By my blessing, Durvāsas, you shall be free from distress;
moreover, my discus shall never cause you harm on the road.
Today, I too shall certainly enjoy happiness, free from anxiety."
Having made the food offered by a devotee at the time of breaking the fast like nectar out of affection,

"Go quickly, O sage, and prepare a meal for Ambarīṣa!

O Lakṣmī! By hearing this, one’s devotion to the husband becomes firm; and having understood that service to the devotee is the supreme duty, a virtuous woman becomes a true devotee.
Having become a devotee of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, she becomes a wife devoted to Kṛṣṇa.
A virtuous wife should never commit an offense against her devoted husband;
she should endure everything from him as the patient earth endures all things. Like a plantain tree, she should remain cool and thus bring happiness to her husband.
Indeed, the story of Kandalī was narrated for my awakening:
"May the women toward me become like Kandalī when she was given abuse;
and may the men likewise become like the angry Durvāsas. (1.29)
"O beloved! By reading or hearing this, there shall be both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

(1.476.130) Thus ends [the section] in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, within the first book, the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga: the vision of Nārāyaṇa in the form of the young brahmin Durvāsas; the transformation of Kandalī into a plantain tree; the state of Durvāsas as "Durvāsa" (the one made of durvā grass) from his very essence; the arrival of great fear for Ambarīṣa caused by the offense and the curse of Aurva; the firmness of her devotion to her husband; and the marriage of Durvāsas with Ekānaṃśā, the daughter of Vasudeva.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī! I shall relate a story that destroys all sins.
Viśvakarman performed devotion to his guru, and the auspicious fruit of that was as follows:

"Service to the guru is the eternal duty of those living as religious students (brahmacārins).

Having reflected thus, he went to the forest and beheld it there.

All the arts shall reach full bloom within your intellect.
Receive from my mouth this mantra for the sake of purification and for the sake of becoming a worthy vessel:

O son of Tvaṣṭṛ, always recite this auspicious mantra which bestows prosperity.
(25) Take upon your neck and your hand this sacred garland of *tulasī*, which grants merit;
and take this mark (*bindu*) on your forehead, which consists of the digits of the moon and is the abode of auspiciousness. (26)

Having said this, Hara spoke: "And let the wisdom you desire be granted to you through the grace of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, augmented by ninefold skill. You [shall possess] knowledge of gold and other minerals, as well as of woods and even stones. (27)
Of gems and jewels, of flowers and even of garments;
of substances fragrant with camphor and the like, and even of waters;
of bulbs, roots, and fruits, and of the piths of trees as well as of their barks. (28–29)
You will master the craftsmanship of all types of objects;
you will learn how to create desired works according to the tastes of your masters.
You will master all forms of costume design and all methods of preparing soups and other delicacies.
You shall also know in its true essence everything beginning with the triple arts (tauryatrika),
as well as the mechanics of machines, weapons, water-works, dwellings, fortresses, and the art of weaving; the magic of illusion, the knowledge of the mind, and the arts pertaining to other worlds.
And you shall know everything that is even beyond the world from its very root.
Always worship Kṛṣṇa; he will quickly bestow knowledge upon you.
The Blessed One will address you by the name Viśvakarman.
But when King Divodāsa comes to be [ruler] by the boon of Fate,
then you shall construct my palace in Ānandavana;
the king, having incurred the expenditure of wealth, will cause the temple to be built.
"O Viśvakarman, go; abide by the command of your preceptor and do that.
Having spoken thus, Śambhu vanished, and the son of Tvaṣṭṛ went to the house of his preceptor.
And those who were told "Om" regarding whatever craft they were engaged in were satisfied by him.
Having bestowed those desired gifts and received their blessings,
he delighted them all with his artistic skills and deeds;
then, in the presence of Kṛṣṇa, he remembered his beloved helpers.

Śrī Kṛṣṇa then became manifest, and by the will of Kṛṣṇa, divine powers emerged from his own form; at that time, maidens were born from his left side—divine, beautiful, in the bloom of youth, and masters of the sixty-four arts. (39)
Devoted to their husbands, by the command of Kṛṣṇa they chose the son of Tvaṣṭṛ as their husband;
they served that son of Tvaṣṭṛ, who was the very form of Kṛṣṇa, and they performed the silent recitation: "Obeisance to Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Lord."
They performed meditation, worship, and service to Kṛṣṇa in the month of Bhādrapada.
Within a year, Kṛṣṇa appeared in their presence;
pleased by their devotion to their beloved, he granted them boons.
"Having enjoyed every pleasure here, you shall come to me at the end of the creation. For you, there is no other duty than the service of your beloved;
I am the beloved in the beloved, and by me the beloved is proclaimed."
Where there is neither I, nor that beloved husband, nor that beloved wife without me— in him,
through my devotion as a faithful wife, you shall all attain liberation.
O Indra and the other guardians of the world, the Viśvedevas, and the hosts of Maruts!
The Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Sādhyas, Vidyādharas,
and Uragas; the Ṛṣis, Apsarases, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, Siddhas, and Cāraṇas—
all these consist of my own self, and I alone am Viśvakarman.
"May his auspicious wives, having always propitiated me in the form of their husband, attain liberation at the end of every kalpa by taking refuge in me.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa then vanished from sight.
Those divine arts, consisting of the [sixty-four] kalās, served you, the son of Tvaṣṭṛ, as their lord.
By reading or hearing this, one shall attain skill in the arts.
O Lakṣmī, the auspicious fruit for one devoted to the husband who is the Guru has thus been told to you.

Thus ends the four hundred and seventy-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Artistic Skill of Tvaṣṭṛ’s Son through Devotion to His Guru by Means of Śambhu’s Boon, the Attainment of a Wife Possessing the Sixty-Four Arts through Devotion to Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, and Their Wifely Fidelity," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. [This concludes] Chapter 477 of the *Skanda Purāṇa* [Section 4.2.86]. *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Book 1 (*Kṛtayuga-santāna*).
