Chapter 479 → Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī! I shall relate the auspicious life of Vyāsa, who dwells eternally in Ānandakānana as a treasure-house of the scriptures.
Once, he spoke to his disciples: "Recite this verse indeed."
Kāśī is the refuge of all sciences, and Kāśī is the supreme abode of Lakṣmī.
This Kāśī is a field of liberation; Kāśī consists entirely of the three Vedas.
Indeed, Ka (Brahmā), Śa (Śiva), and A (Viṣṇu)—these three are truly present here.
Indeed, Brāhmī, Brahmā, and Parabrahmā—the three—dwell in Kāśī;
for here all three are attained: worldly enjoyment, liberation, and service.
Truly, in this place, a human being obtains action, knowledge, and devotion.
Having heard of the purity of that forest there,
Vyāsa wandered in every direction toward Kāśī for the sake of alms.
When he did not obtain alms, he cursed Kāśī out of anger.
"Since the people here are indeed most arrogant and do not give alms,
let there be no learning for three generations, let there be no wealth for three generations,
and let there be no liberation for three generations among the people who dwell in Kāśī. (7)
Having pronounced a curse and cast down his alms-bowl, he departed.
(8) Then, as he was walking along, the guest was requested for alms by the Great Goddess, who was seated at the door of her house in the form of an ordinary woman. (9)
"O monks, the Blessed One has not been seen anywhere today.
Without having honored a guest, my Lord will never eat.
Having performed the Vaiśvadeva and other rites, he always awaits a guest. (1.478.10)
Therefore, O twice-born one, may you become my guest today;
[for] that householder who consumes food alone without a guest, the master of the home partakes in sin along with his ancestors. (11–12)
"Therefore come, O best of Brahmins, and fulfill the desire of my husband.
Make the householder's life of both myself and my husband fruitful through your acceptance of alms.
Hearing this, Vyāsa, filled with wonder, questioned her who was full of compassion.
"O auspicious lady, who are you? You are indeed an embodiment of Dharma here, bestowing peace.
Upon seeing you, my inner self is gratified; are you Śivā?
Or perhaps you are Lakṣmī seated upon the lotus, or Rohiṇī residing in the moon?"
Or is it that Vārāṇasī herself is present, or that the Goddess who bestows liberation resides here? Or is it Compassion herself, or perhaps my own fortune which has taken the form of a woman?
Or is it Devotion, the consort of Śiva, or you yourself, the giver of food and beloved of Hari? (16)

"In every way you are not a woman; you are my chosen deity. Or rather, what need is there for this reflection on my part? O beautiful one, simply be [my guest]. If you would speak of yourself, I shall accept alms from you with devotion. (17–18)
Thus addressed, she said: "I am the wife of a householder residing right here.
I see you constantly moving about, surrounded by a multitude of disciples.
You alone do not know me, whereas I certainly know you."
"O ascetic, fulfill the hospitality due to my master through you.
Vyāsa said: "I have a certain vow; let it be fulfilled.
Only then will I accept a single alms-offering, and not more than that."
Satī spoke without hesitation: "Speak what is lacking here.
Vyāsa replied: "I choose a row [of seats] together with ten thousand disciples.
Satī said: "Without delay, be seated in rows along with your disciples."
"Everything is accomplished through the majesty of my husband; food is always ready.
I am not such a woman as to obstruct my husband's reputation. As soon as a guest arrives at the house, the meal is prepared. (23-24)
"All the halls were filled, all desires were fulfilled;
everything in the house was complete through the grace of the husband's feet.
Having been addressed thus, he, together with his disciples, became joyful and stood in rows.
At that moment, food, water vessels,
and sandalwood paste were placed by the sky according to the prescribed rite into the bowls simultaneously;
and all began to eat what had been served to them in accordance with the ritual.

Having eaten those divine preparations of cooked food, they easily attained satisfaction. Once they had sipped water for purification and were honored, just as they were about to depart, Satī asked him: "What is the bull here for one who stands at a sacred ford?"
"So that we may conduct ourselves accordingly at the sacred ford.
Having heard this, Vyāsa said to Satī: "I shall declare the duties of those who dwell at sacred fords.
This very dharma is the one you practice; there is no other. (1.478.30)
"You alone know the dharma, being devoted to the service of your husband;
[you know] that by which this long-standing husband of yours attains satisfaction.
Sati said: "That indeed is the dharma which is observed by me day and night."
"I ask about the common dharmas; tell them to me.
Vyāsa said: "Listen, O virtuous lady! One should never cause agitation to any living being, whether by thought, word, or deed. (32–33)
Upon seeing the excellence of others, one should cultivate gladness in one’s heart;
having reflected upon everything, one should act in such a way that auspicious success may arise.
Śambhu then said to Vyāsa: "Tell me, who among these is in you?"
The curse which was bestowed by you out of anger upon the residents of Kāśī causes great distress;
for the excellence of others cannot be endured.
Indeed, that act was not performed after due reflection, whereby auspicious results might have arisen.
The restraint you yourself declared has been broken by you alone through the giving of this curse.
For one behaving in such a manner, Kāśī is certainly not suitable for you.
Go outside forever, O Vyāsa; there is no dwelling here for you.
Thus addressed, he went to the eastern bank near the river.
Having established an auspicious hermitage, Vyāsa indeed remained there permanently.
Wherever Vyāsa went, the goddess Sarasvatī followed him.
In Kāśī, all people— men from children to the elderly— were liberated;
all forms of Viṣṇu and sages who had mastered the Vedas departed for Vyāsa’s hermitage, the auspicious refuge, along with all the scriptures.
Then Śaṅkara and all the others indeed became mute for a moment.
Having understood the cause there, which consisted of the expulsion of Vyāsa,
Śaṅkara, accompanied by Pārvatī, then went to Vyāsa’s hermitage.
Having bowed to Vyāsa and honored him, Hara offered this praise:
"Forgive my fault, O Vyāsa, Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa!
O God of gods, destroyer of pride, for this reason my city has become silent."
Without Sarasvatī and Vyāsa, and without the scriptures in every respect;
where the Vedas do not exist, where the Śāstras are not found, and where the mantras are not present—there the Brahmins are indeed mute. (44–45)
Where the Sarasvatī is not present, and where there are no learned men, that place is said to be a void; today Kāśī has become such a void.
O Acyuta, I spoke thus out of a state of ignorance, or perhaps due to pride in my intellect.
Forgive me, O Lord of Compassion; by you, Kṛṣṇa, I have been restored to life. Through you, the all-pervading God, I dwell in the eternal city.
Come, O Ocean of Mercy, and drive this muteness far away.
Thus requested at that time, the lord Vyāsa Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana said to Śaṅkara and Pārvatī:
"Let her dwell near you as the abode of Sarasvatī, and then she shall indeed attain the state of silence. ||49||
O Śambhu, if you, together with your retinue, come here every month on the full-moon day at dawn and perform a great worship for me,
then Sarasvatī will come there at my command.
"Build a temple for Sarasvatī to the east, in your presence;
she shall dwell there eternally.
Thus addressed, Śiva, accompanied by Śivā, said, "So be it."
Then Vyāsa, the well-composed scriptures, the Vedas, and Sarasvatī likewise departed;
the sages and brahmins went to their respective places and dwelt in Kāśī.
Everything became silent, and even Viśveśvara rejoiced.
In the palace offered by Śaṅkara, the mother Sarasvatī resided;
Vyāsa, having bestowed silence [upon her], returned once more to his own hermitage.
Śambhu, Śivā, and the gods likewise [celebrated] the monthly [Puṣpa] Pūrṇimā.
They perform their pilgrimage right there, where the hermitage of Vyāsa indeed is.
All the gods, along with Śaṅkara, the sacred fords, and the spirits,
go there for the sake of worshipping Vyāsa and for the attainment of the power of silence.
Thus has the power of Śaṅkara been described, O Lakṣmī,
as well as the devotion of Pārvatī to her husband and the supreme sovereignty of Vyāsa;
likewise, O Kṛṣṇe, the supreme devotion of Śaṅkara to his wife is ever-present.

O Lakṣmī! Among all the gods and even among Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana, his devotion to his husband is supreme; by hearing or reciting it, one attains enjoyment and liberation, and shall obtain whatever happiness one desires.

Thus ends the four hundred and seventy-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of Vyāsa’s Curse Due to Not Receiving Alms in Kāśī during the Kṛta-yuga Lineage of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā; the Hospitality Offered by Pārvatī; Śambhu’s Ordering of Vyāsa’s Residence Outside [the City]; the Bringing of Sarasvatī and Others by Vyāsa; the Deafness of the People of Kāśī; Śambhu’s Departure and the Bringing Back of Vyāsa and the Others; the Cessation of the Deafness; and the Instruction that Vyāsa-tīrtha Must Be Established on the Full Moon Day. || 478 ||

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī! I shall relate the auspicious story of Vālmīki.
There was a brāhmaṇa named Sumati, born of the lineage of Bhṛgu.
His beloved wife was Kauśukī, endowed with beauty and youth;
from her a son was born named Agniśarman. Although urged by his father, he did not engage in the study of the Vedas.
Then once, when the worlds were greatly oppressed by a drought,
Sumati, together with his family, established a hermitage in the forest and resided there.
Agniśarman, however, entered into association with Ābhīras and bandits.
Whatever people pass through that forest path here,
the cruel-acting Agniśarman kills them and seizes their wealth. Once, the Seven Sages, firm in their vows, arrived upon that path.
And Agniśarman, desiring to seize them, beheld those seven and said:
"Release all these garments, umbrellas, fans, and so forth; otherwise, I shall kill you."
Having heard these words of his, Atri spoke to the one named Agni:
"How indeed has this sinful act, which causes us distress, arisen in you, a Brāhmaṇa?
We are ascetics traveling on a pilgrimage."
Then Agniśarman said: "My mother, father, sister, wife, and sons are indeed hungry; I must support them. Without theft, how indeed could there be sustenance here in this forest? (9–10)
"Therefore, disregarding both good and evil, I am committing this sin.
To him, Atri said: "Listen to what is true, beneficial, and auspicious.
You must consult your father and others regarding the consequences of your own actions."
"Tell me, to whom does that sin belong which is committed for your sake?
(1.2) If they do not speak of it, or if they do not accept it as their own, and if they should say, 'The sin is yours alone,' then do not kill these living beings falsely. (1.3)
Then Agniśarman said: "I have never questioned you before;
at your word, I shall go and inquire into the disposition of my kinsmen.
However, I know how long you all will remain here."
Having said, "I shall come back to you again," he quickly went to his father.
He asked: "By the destruction of dharma through such acts as the harming of living beings, very great sin is produced; tell me, whose is this?"
He questioned his mother, and his parents said to him:
"O son, this sin shall belong to you alone, not to us. "What was done by you must be experienced by you; provide for our maintenance."
Then he spoke thus to his wife; she said, "That sin belongs to you alone.
(18) Then he spoke to his sons and daughter, and they spoke to him;
they said, "The sin is yours alone; not even a fraction of it belongs to us. (19)
Thus, recognizing his own self-interest and endowed with detachment,
the twice-born man bowed at the feet of the sages and, lamenting, said to them:
"I have no mother, nor father, nor wife, nor son."

"A daughter or a sister is not mine, since you are concerned only with your own interests. Therefore, you ought to protect him who has come for refuge from that sin. At this, Atri said to him while standing beneath a tree, "Practice meditation. (21-22)
O form of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, destroy the heap of my sins!
Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, obeisance to the Lord!
(23) Recite this constantly with faith, holding a garland of tulasī in your hand.
"Indeed, Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself will effect your deliverance here.
Having spoken thus, they all departed, and he too became intent on meditation. Established in that meditation, the yogi remained for thirteen years.
Remaining constantly in meditative absorption, he indeed recited the mantra with its proper intonation;
meanwhile, an anthill grew high above him, constructed by female termites.
Remaining motionless there, he continued to meditate and recite the mantra in that same manner.
He neither drank water nor anything else, nor did he eat at any time.
(27) Then those sages emerged from his presence by that same path;
they heard the sound of his mantra-recitation and were filled with wonder. (28)
Seeing them as mere anthills, like something inert within,
those lords consecrated them with the waters of the Gaṅgā and raised them up.
Having slowly risen from that state, he paid homage to the lords of sages.
"I declare that I have been delivered from sin and from this world of terrible karma. Having been uplifted by you compassionate ones, I chant that mantra of Kṛṣṇa;
through your grace, I have likewise acquired true knowledge."
"May I attain the path to liberation; grant me your favor.
Having said this, he drank the water used for washing the sage's feet.
And the sages addressed him by the name Vālmīki.
Those sages departed to the truth, while Vālmīki, worshipping Hari,
attained knowledge of the three periods of time and composed the poem on Rāma,
by which countless embodied beings will attain liberation.

Protecting the vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) for as long as he lived, that king of devotees indeed maintained his eternal devotion (*pātivratya*) to Kṛṣṇa. In the morning he performed his bath, and he observed the twilight devotions (*sandhyā*) with heartfelt devotion.
Every day the sage worshipped Viṣṇu, Śiva, Gaṇapati, Pārvatī, Anala, Ravi, and Rāmāditya— these seven deities—
with sixteen excellent articles accompanied by auspicious internal dispositions. (36–37)
He constantly offered oblations of wild fruits, as well as tubers, leaves, seeds, and so forth; likewise, he presented water from a well as the offering of libation.
With wood from wild sandalwood trees, he prepared incense and lamps.
She offered garments made of bark and other materials for the worship of Rāma.
With devotion, she presented flowers gathered on vines and threads;
she gave sweet honey, beeswax, and seasonal fruits and such.
With joy he gave rice that ripens without being plowed and is cooked by the sun;
likewise, he offered seeds such as *śigru* and others cooked by fire.
Deer, birds, and other animals were also free from fear.
Those seeking liberation come there to hear the name of Rāma;
they remain with steadfastness for as long as the worship continues, and at night they dwell right there, eager to hear the name of Rāma. (42–43)
Having given them leaves, flowers, fruit, water, roots, grains, and so forth— [all] from Rāma’s grace— he then eats with great joy.
Occasionally, by chance, forest-dwelling guests arrive somewhere.
Regarding them as having the form of Kṛṣṇa, he serves them with supreme devotion.
He does not forget to cry out "Rāma, Rāma" for even a moment.
By the power of his recitation, the perfection of speech—difficult for others to attain—has arisen within him. (45–46)
Indeed, the jewels desired by Vālmīki appeared before him.
Once, during the summer season, in a forest that was parched and intensely heated,
devoid of fruits, leaves, and petals, he did not obtain any fruit or the like.
He grieved, "What shall I offer as eternal *naivedya* for Śrī Hari?
There is no leaf or other edible food; what can I give as an offering to Kṛṣṇa?
Having reflected thus in his mind, he remained standing near the hut.
"O Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa-Rāma-Hara, O All-pervading Lord!
Having swallowed my mental impressions today, be satisfied, O Keśava!
While he was speaking thus, a certain cowherd arrived right there.
Accompanied by a milch cow and joined by her calf, he approached him [the sage] and said:
"O Sage, I wish to stay here for a moment;
having rested for a while in your hermitage, I shall go to another forest."
Having spoken thus, he stood for a moment in the shade of an *aśvattha* tree together with the cow;
he milked her into a leaf-cup and joyfully gave the milk to him.
Vālmīki, exceedingly delighted, accepted it for the purpose of worship.
Having offered that to the gods and distributed it with a gracious mind,
he drank what was purified by the *naivedya* of Kṛṣṇa and likewise gave some to him;
at that moment, the light of the imperishable Brahman arose within his heart.
His divine eye, possessing unobstructed and true radiance, arose; with it,
he beheld that Gopāla, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the husband of Rādhikā,
accompanied by Kāmadhenu and arrived for the sake of the devotee’s food offering.
Again, by the illusory power (māyā) of Hari, he saw him as a cowherd boy.
Filled with the weight of great wonder, he praised the Supreme Lord;
indeed, his eternal satisfaction was produced by that milk.
In an instant, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa became invisible;
Vālmīki, repeatedly remembering that divine form, danced indeed.
He constantly remembered that divine Kṛṣṇa, who is compassionate toward His devotees.
He indeed beheld everything through Valmīka in the form of Rāma,
as if it were all his own handiwork;
he constantly meditated upon Rāmāditya.
He departed before him to the abode of Hari, the eternal realm of Vaikuṇṭha.
Indeed, there is no evil destiny for those who commit sins if they are devotees of Kṛṣṇa;
for the people of the Lord are capable of effecting the deliverance of others as well.
Desire, anger, the life-force of the mind, the senses, and latent impressions—
these very things exist as such; however, through union with Kṛṣṇa,
they all arise in divine form and become bestowers of liberation for everyone.

Thus ends the four hundred and seventy-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of Agniśarman’s Attainment of the State of a Vālmīki, Omniscience, and Liberation through the Penance of Chastity; His Becoming a Sage through Association with the Seven Sages, and His Vision of Kṛṣṇa in the Form of a Cowherd Boy and a Cow," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 480 *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā* — Section 1 (*Kṛtayuga-santāna*) — Chapter 480.
[The Author: Chapter 481.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen to the auspicious and delightful holy place on earth, the city of Avantī.
Once, Rāma went to that place where the river Śiprā flows;
there, together with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa, he offered libations to his ancestors.
Then, he commanded Lakṣmaṇa to fetch water from the Śiprā.
Disregarding those words, Lakṣmaṇa said to Sītā: "Speak now!
If I were to bring Sītā here by force, what would she do for you?
O Rāma, I shall never at any time enter into a state of servitude to you."
"She is well-nourished, very firm, and indeed even plumper than I;
therefore, O Rāghava, tell me, what will you do with this Sītā?
Having heard those unprecedented words spoken by Lakṣmaṇa, Rāma [spoke] to Jānakī.
The two remained despondent; Sītā indeed took up water.
Having drunk and eaten there, they then went to Mahākāleśvara. Having spent the night there, Rāma spoke to his younger brother at dawn:
"Arise, dear son Saumitri; let us go to another forest region.
(7) Saumitri replied in anger, "I will not go by any means.
You yourself go with this beloved wife of yours. (8)
"I shall not go to the forest, nor indeed to Ayodhyā at any time.
To the son of Sumitrā who was speaking thus, the Blessed One himself said:
"Come slowly, O son of Sumitrā, my younger brother, together with Sītā."
"How indeed do you behave in anger, or how did you depart together [with me]? "Since you must go forth as an ascetic, you should proceed very slowly.
Lakṣmaṇa replied: "If this is so, I shall not follow your word."
"I will not perform service for you; then I shall go to the forest with you.
Rāma said, "So be it," and Lakṣmaṇa departed slowly.
Then he spoke again: "Indeed, I will not go to the forest with you."
Having spoken thus, Rāvaṇa sat down; meanwhile, Rāma went further and further ahead.
Then, rising up and having strung his bow, he fixed an arrow upon it and considered slaying Rāma and taking Jānakī.
I bring them under my control; as an ascetic in the forest, I am always happy.
Rāma departs swiftly, and Sītā also goes with great speed.
Even Lakṣmaṇa, though holding an arrow, was unable to release it.
"Alas! How can my brother be slain? And here is Janaki, my mother;
how can she, who is worthy of worship, be brought under subjection? Oh, what a delusion is this of mine!
Having reflected thus once more, his mind was again intent upon his arrows. (16–17)
Then, his heart full of compassion, Rāma saw a Plakṣa tree before him; having gone there, he sat down upon its ground.
Sītā also arrived and rested, and Lakṣmaṇa likewise proceeded slowly.
Rāma said, "How is it, brother, that you have indeed made the bow ready with an arrow?
Laksmaṇa, bowed down with shame, remained so for a mere moment;
then Rāma, knowing his inner state, spoke regarding the condition of the earth.
"O Lakṣmaṇa, this is not your fault; rather, it is the behavior of this very field.
In this field, there is no brotherly affection, for everyone is intent upon their own self-interest.
Driven solely by the pursuit of their own ends, they do not respect one another. (21)
Sons do not listen to their father, nor likewise does a father to his sons;
a disciple does not heed the word of his teacher, nor does a teacher attend to the service of his disciple.
Affection is bound up with one's own self-interest; no one is dear to anyone for their own sake.
"O younger brother, such power as this belongs to this earth;
there is no fault on your part in this, so do not feel ashamed, O sinless one.
Having heard this and bowed down, the son of Sumitrā asked: "How is it that such a place as this..."
"That which has arisen, though insentient, afflicts our consciousness.
Rāma said: "Formerly, there was here a very robust Rākṣasa named Ghorakhana, who was as tall as seven palm trees. (25–26)
Assuming any form at will, he would fly through the sky into cities and houses,
forcibly descending upon people and other beings to devour them as food.
Out of cruelty, he would carry off children, women, cows, and bulls.
Having established a hermitage in a forest on a stretch of land measuring one *gavyūti*,
that wicked man moves about in an invisible form and devours birds and other creatures;
at times he becomes a tiger, and at times a deer or a *gavaya*.
In one place he is a king, in another a brahmin, and in another a woman of beautiful form;
in one place a serpent, in another a monkey, and in another he even becomes harsh.
Whatever form is appropriate for him, he possesses that very form.
Having gathered together, lived together, and established a common vehicle,
he indeed inflicts violence upon them and devours those who have placed their trust in him.
At times, however, [he creates] a beautiful, artificial city or a splendid town.
He showed him that city adorned with offspring, which was like a magician’s display;
for in its marketplaces were seen the new enterprises of merchants, as well as the auspicious halls of the princes, gardens, and groves. (33)
He creates beautiful temples and a vast royal army;
thus, in some places, he indeed brings about a city of Gandharvas.
Then, on one occasion, Śrī Gopāla, together with his wife Kambharā, [again... 34–35.
On that path, Śrīgopāla, an expansion of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, and the virtuous Kambharā, an expansion of Lakṣmī, emerged as divine beings for the purpose of a pilgrimage to sacred sites.
They were seen on the road in the forest by the demon Ghorakhāna.
They were exceedingly radiant, tranquil, glorious, and possessed the splendor of the sun.
Then, having gained their trust through appropriate actions, that Rākṣasa formed this thought: "Since these two possess the fortune of gods, they have been secured by me. (37–38)
Having prepared a magnificent city favored by destiny and filled with festivities, he honored those two excellent beings according to the rites of hospitality;
having thus reflected, he made the city inhabited by divine men.
The city lord himself,
having become the host and having brought the guest-offering (arghya) before them,
went a great distance with great hospitality and led them both to his home. (1.480.40–41)
Then that couple experienced supreme wonder;
honored, fed, their feet massaged, and thoroughly gratified,
they became as if rested, refreshed, and even asleep.

Just then, that Rākṣasa went forth to seize his formidable weapon for the purpose of slaughtering the couple; at that moment, Gopālakṛṣṇa said to the virtuous Kambharā, "Behold this deceitful servant! (43–44).
"O Kambharā-lakṣmī! He has gone to fetch his sword;
this most wicked Rākṣasa devours many by means of deception in the forest.
His destruction must be accomplished by me, and for that purpose I have come."
"Be at ease for a moment, O virtuous lady! Behold my task for a moment.
While the Blessed One was thus addressing his wife, someone arrived, grasping a very sharp sword.
Then, having risen quickly, Gopālakṛṣṇa himself,
in an invisible form, departed from that spot along with his wife;
and they moved away from the bed so that they were no longer seen as they had been before.
Thinking it was [his enemy] on the bed, he struck with his sword;
at that moment, the sword, having struck the bed, broke in two—
one half remained in his hand, while the other half fell at the feet of the Rākṣasa.
He cut off the tips of his feet;
that sharp-pointed fragment which was the forepart flew up and became firmly lodged in [the king's] throat.
His throat was pierced and he leapt up, the Rākṣasa fainting for a moment.
The goddess Lakṣmī, compassionate and burdened with pity, went there to drink water.
Just then, out of a sense of enmity, the dying man seized her with his two arms; as she desired to devour him, he sought to swallow her whole. (52–53)
Then she cursed him: "O Rākṣasa, go to your death!
You act with such deceit everywhere in this city;
since you deceive others through your fraudulent nature, your own ground shall always be [the place of your downfall]."
May she who is deceitful by nature, a deceiver, and possessed of fraud and cruelty,
always dwell within you whose character is cruel. Furthermore, may other beings on this earth who possess the qualities of guile, ferocity, and the like, also reside there.
There is no doubt that they will become friends and enemies,
both their own and those of others, due to the fault of association with Rākṣasas;
and because of that sin, they shall again be denizens of hell, experiencing suffering.
"All the people on your land shall become the lowest of men.
As soon as the Rākṣasa was thus cursed by the Goddess,
that cruel one gave up his life, and the city went to ruin.
That ground became a solitary wilderness, a mere stretch of bare earth;
then Kambharā-lakṣmī, overwhelmed by extraordinary wonder,
asked the God of gods, "What indeed is this web?"
Gopālakṛṣṇa said to the Rākṣasa’s sorcerer:
“O beautiful one, everything was indeed already known by me beforehand;
for this Rākṣasa has been killed by his own hand once again.”
He will indeed enter the womb of a *rākṣasa* once again by the hand of Rāma;
he shall die through the fruit of our sight and service.
Then he will attain liberation on the island in the south.
"When Rāma shall abide, he will go; he will slay [the demon].
Having spoken thus, those two departed, and that land became as it was before.
O Lakṣmaṇa, by that power of yoga, your mind has been fixed here.
There is not even the slightest fault in you for having engaged in improper reflection.
For place, time, ritual action, association, mantra, meditation, and the preceptor—whatever these may be—they bear fruit in the disciple accordingly. (66)
Indeed, that ground was cursed by the dwelling of the Rākṣasa.
O son of Sumitrā, it was through contact with that ground that your mind became cruel.
That ground has departed, brother; be at ease and filled with happiness.
By the power of Sītā’s devotion to her husband, my mind indeed did not undergo any transformation;
nor indeed did my own mind undergo any change.
For those whose vow toward their wife is constant and whose devotion to their husband is likewise firm—
In their minds, the attachment to the earth and other such things does not take root at all.
And you too, brother, remain a celibate student and a great ascetic;
therefore, even now, your fortitude remains well-established despite the agitation of the heart.
But others might surely provoke a quarrel in such a place;
they would obtain the fruit of destruction—of this there is no doubt.
By the dharma of devotion to one's husband, people become happy.
My husband is Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Brahman, Nārāyaṇa, Hari, the Lord. Because Sītā is devoted to her husband, I find joy even in the forest;
and such is my brother, who observes vows and is the speaker of truth here.
"There is no suffering for three who travel together in the great forest;
heaven, liberation, home, and sovereignty all exist together for me in the woods.
Thus has this been told here, wherein the power of the earth was previously well-consecrated.
Since our touch of the feet has occurred here, therefore, very gradually,
the power of the earth, its cruelty, and its form will, in the course of time, come to an end.
The great region of Avantī shall become a sacred pilgrimage site (tīrtha) of auspiciousness.
Having spoken thus, those forest-dwellers departed ahead into the woods.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, has been told to you the curse upon the devoted wife,
as well as the power of devotion to a husband, which cannot be overcome even by a country or other such factors.
From reciting and hearing this, the intellect shall become pure.
Defeat encountered due to place, time, and other circumstances shall not cause distress.
The mind shall become nourished in dharma and pure in the performance of vows and other observances. (1.480.80)
"Indeed, the remembrance of this [deity] shall grant one's desired fruits and bestow peace;
it shall also grant heaven, liberation, and eternal bliss.

Thus ends the four hundred and eightieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Ground Consecrated by the Destruction of the Rākṣasa Ghorakhana through Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa Following Lakṣmaṇa’s Change of Heart During the Avantī Pilgrimage, as well as Lakṣmaṇa’s Mental Impurity and Sītā’s Devotion to Her Husband," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga Cycle, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
I shall further describe the vow performed by the wives of the sages;
listen to that which has been narrated by me, which is purifying and destructive of sin.
The wives of the seven ṛṣis— those seven devoted wives— went to the Gaṅgā to bathe; having seen the fire at Kuśasthala,
they were trembling from the cold and went into the presence of the fire to warm themselves.
That was not a real fire at all, but one cast forth by Gaṅgā.
It was the radiant seed of Śaṅkara, like fire, resembling a flame;
it was like fire within a clump of reeds, yet it was delivered into the waters by the Fire-god.
That very element, mixed with fire, having seen those wives devoted to their husbands who had bathed,
was then impelled by the fire and entered into them in an instant.
They became pregnant and were recognized as such by the sages.
Thus, fallen from their divine status and defiled by fire,
they were abandoned by the sages and wandered from forest to forest.
When a long time had passed in this manner, Nārada, the supreme devotee of Viṣṇu, [arrived].
Desiring their welfare, he indeed arrived within the forest.
There, that great sage of firm vows was honored by them;
while seated, he spoke words appropriate to the place and the time.
"What is this being done? A defeat has come upon you!
Why indeed have you, the mothers of the world and devoted wives, been abandoned by the sages?
They replied, "We have been abandoned on account of Kārttikeya."
The great power of Śaṅkara resided within the fire upon the kuśa grass.
When we, having recognized the fire and bathed, went there to perform our austerities,
Agni, assuming a hidden form, touched us and indeed entered our bodies.
And a mineral element (dhātu) adhered to the region of our womb within the circle of the birth canal.
Because of that, we became pregnant and were considered wicked; this was the established state of affairs.
By those performers of sacrificial rites, we were abandoned, left in great misery.
Whatever sin has arisen by the power of fate through public censure—
what can we do, where can we go, what austerity, or what deity,
by the merit of whose propitiation we may once again attain purity? (14)
"Having ascertained this, O Brahmin, tell us here according to the truth.
Thus questioned, Nārada reflected and spoke what was beneficial:
"Listen, O you of excellent austerity; there is a supreme penance which is the true cause of your welfare."
Gayātīrtha is most excellent and is situated in Mahākālavana;
having gone there to Akṣayavaṭa, you shall be cleansed of sin.
On the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada, remain devoted to fasting.
"Perform this most purifying vow accompanied by a night vigil.
Having heard Nārada’s words, the wives of the sages were greatly delighted and went to Mahākālavana, where the sacred site named Gayā is located.
Then, having beheld the banyan tree there, they performed meritorious rites such as bathing and giving gifts during the bright fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada.
Having fasted on the fifth day, they kept a vigil throughout the single night.
Having performed those [rites], they were then freed from the fault of contact with another man;
their anger toward their husbands having ceased, they immediately went to their own homes.
Welcome was offered by the sages with the same vision as before, just as it had been previously.
From that time forward, that lunar day became known in this world as Ṛṣipañcamī;
it was indeed established by Nārāyaṇa for women to obtain the merit of their vows,
as well as by Lakṣmī, Rādhā, Gaurī, Prabhā, and Jayā.
Having heard from the mouth of Nārada that Pārvatī, Padmā, Mañjulā, Māṇikyā, Sāvitrī, Saṃjñā, Śacī,
and Menā had likewise performed that very vow consisting of the Ṛṣipañcamī, [they too undertook it]. || 24–25 ||
Whatever sin a woman incurs through contact with another man during all twelve months— whether arising from intentional desire or unintentional association,
and whether it be slight or great, produced by sexual enjoyment or non-enjoyment— [is destroyed].
Or [impurity] arising from contact with a woman in her menses; or impurity such as that resulting from birth (sūtaka) and so forth.
Whatever impurity arises from contact—in household utensils and the like, in water, in food vessels, on the ground, or in all objects—[is removed by sprinkling]. 27–28.
Whatever fault may arise from contact with a woman in her menses, or that which is born of physical touch;
whatever fault exists among children, the elderly, or those who are dependent on others;
as well as faults born of bodily contact and likewise those born of sexual union.

All [the sins] of women perish through the Ṛṣipañcamī vow. (1.481.30) By means of the Ṛṣipañcamī vow, women become pure in every respect; they indeed become purified from the impurity of menstruation in every way. (1.481.31)
Having become pure, a woman or a man should partake of wild rice as food;
for them, no misfortune or suffering shall ever arise.
There will be no ill fortune for women, nor separation from their husbands.
There shall be no separation from one's children or from wealth.
(33) In Avantī, there exists such a sacred ford that destroys sin;
by performing acts such as giving charity here, one obtains imperishable merit. (34)
Whoever, relying upon the prescribed observances, listens to this discourse on the sacred festival days or constantly, shall obtain the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
A wife shall obtain the fruit of devotion to her husband by observing the fifth lunar day.
Thereafter, she shall obtain the imperishable abode of Hari together with her husband.
Whether she be a married woman or one whose husband is deceased, she may perform this supreme vow with the desire for purity in order to please Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa as her lord.
The glorious and compassionate Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, having purified those who are virtuous, will protect them if they serve at his feet;
this applies to whoever has properly offered their vow to Nārāyaṇa.

"Kṛṣṇa will certainly become the husband, lord, and protector of those two. Thus ends the four hundred and eighty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Ṛṣipañcamī Vow and the Demonstration of the Greatness of Chastity," in the first section on the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. In this chapter, the Ṛṣipañcamī vow is prescribed for the wives of the Seven Sages to ward off the defect caused by contact with fire during the context of the birth of Kārttikeya, and the greatness of wifely devotion is revealed. *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā*, Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga), Chapter 481.

Chapter 483 → Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:

Listen, Lakṣmī! to the deeds of Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana Vyāsa, and also to the prayer for desired objects on the bank of the Narmadā, which bestows excellent liberation. Formerly, there was a most eminent sage named Parāśara.
He performed severe penance for ten years in the waters of the Gaṅgā.
Having practiced breath control through the kumbhaka technique, he entered the waters of the Jahnavī;
then, when twelve years were complete, he emerged.
He went to the village for the sake of alms; there, he saw a beautiful girl standing on a boat—unblemished and in the full bloom of youth.
Upon seeing her, overcome by the god of love, he spoke these sweet words:
"Do not take pleasure today, O fair-browed one, for you are the agitator of my mind.
(5) Having been addressed thus, she bowed to the sage and said: "Where am I, a fisherwoman, and where are you, a great and virtuous sage? A union between us is not fitting. (6)
The sage, having meditated, said to the maiden: "You are not the daughter of a fisherman;
you are a princess. Listen, I shall tell you of your birth.
There was once a powerful king named Vasu in the Lunar dynasty."
The lord of Jambūdvīpa, O maiden, is indeed a husband of many wives;
he is a Vaiṣṇava, devoted to his guru, and rules his kingdom according to dharma.
The Mlecchas dwelling in Śākadvīpa are in opposition to him.
He indeed set out with his servants and sons for their victory;
a great battle took place with the mountain-dweller Vasu.
The Mlecchas were conquered and made to pay tribute, along with the lords of the various regions.
His chief queen became menstruating in her own palace.
A messenger was sent by her to the presence of the king;
that messenger, in the form of a parrot, recited [the message] just as a human being would.
Having taken the written letter with her beak, she flew through the air.
It was written thus in auspicious characters upon a birch leaf: "This queen-consort lives even during her fertile season without you."

The bird, dispatched by Satyabhāmā, went to where Vasu was; Śuka delivered the letter, and the king read it at that very moment. Having displayed his own prowess, he fashioned a sturdy casket. (14–15)
And he entrusted it to the parrot, saying, "Go, give that to the queen.
Having bowed to the king and grasped the seed-pod with its beak,
it flew up above the ocean and approached with great speed.
Perceiving the parrot to have meat, the hawk rushed toward him;
struck by a blow from the parrot's beak, that vessel of valor fell down.
Swallowed by a fish in the water, he was born there as two offspring.
The fish was caught by the fishermen and immediately pulled out;
within its belly, they saw twins, possessing a radiance equal to the moon and the sun.
Seeing both the boy and the girl, those fishermen were filled with joy.
Having given their son to the king, they raised your daughter.
O beautiful maiden, you are not the daughter of a fisherman.
Having been addressed thus, she indeed gave herself to Parāśara.
"If I am indeed a princess, let this fishy odor be removed!
Thereupon, Parāśara made her fragrant by means of his ascetic power right then and there;
and when the sage touched her on the boat while traveling upon the water during the day, [the odor vanished].
She said, "I am ashamed; the people are looking on, so provide a covering.
Then Parāśara meditated upon the night of darkness (Tāmasī Satī), which took the form of gloom and was filled with the waters of mist.
She was born there where no boat at all could be seen;
though she was but a girl, she became exceedingly radiant and took delight with the Brahman-sage.
Immediately after the offering of the seed, she gave birth to a child there in an instant.
There he saw a boy with matted hair, handsome, holding a staff,
carrying a water-pot, peaceful, adorned with a girdle around his waist,
wearing a sacred thread over his shoulder, and free from the qualities of illusion.
She gave that divine son there to Parāśara;
by Parāśara, that young girl was endowed with auspicious blessings:
"Even through my yoga, you remain a maiden; you are Satyavatī by name. (28)
"You shall become the wife of King Śāntanu, of this there is no doubt;
you will be his chief queen, an ornament to the Lunar dynasty.
Having spoken thus and taken his son with him, the sage Parāśara departed. (1.482.30)
Having prostrated with supreme devotion and affection by touching the ground with eight limbs,
Satyavatī, beholding her son as he was departing, spoke to him:
"If you have any affection for your mother, a desired boon must be granted by you."
"Teach me something by which I may attain perfection.
The son said: "O mother, you should always worship Hari;
let the essence of all actions be their dedication to Śrī Kṛṣṇa."
"Oṃ, salutations to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; salutations!
Perform this recitation, O mother, and liberation will be yours.
Then Matsyagandhā said, "I shall do so, my son."

But for a mother, the fire of separation from her son is always a source of suffering; therefore, my dear child, do not go. O son, because of your departure I shall surely meet my death, and not otherwise.
There is no affection equal to that for a son; there is no strength equal to that of a brother.
There is no place for rest like a son when old age arrives.
Vyāsa said: "Do not despair, do not despair! Remember me as your lord."
"Behold my divine, sovereign form which bestows liberation.
Having said this, he revealed a splendor possessing the radiance of ten million moons;
therein was his four-armed form, adorned with a crown and beautiful earrings.
Dark as a fresh rain-cloud, with eyes like autumn lotuses,
his lovely face bears a gentle smile and is adorned by a halo of splendor; marked with a tilaka, with rosy cheeks and bimba-fruit lips, he appears sixteen years of age.
Abundantly adorned with the splendor of the Śrīvatsa mark, resplendent with a forest garland (vanamālā),
endowed with very tender palms of hands and feet that are red,
graced by rows of nails resembling the moon, and equipped with a girdle. 41–42.
Resplendent in divine garments adorned with tinkling bells,
accompanied by Lakṣmī, Prabhājā, Padmā, Pārvatī, and Māṇikī,
his lotus feet were served by the hosts of attendants Nanda and Sunanda.

Greatly magnified by the shouts of "Victory! from infinite male and female servants, Satyavatī, beholding such a divine form in the likeness of Nārāyaṇa, considered her son to be the giver of liberation who had arrived out of compassion. (44–45)
Just then, a divine celestial chariot arrived there, attended by ten million associates and graced by the presence of Śrī, Ramā, Rādhā, Lakṣmī, and their handmaidens.
It spoke to his mother, saying: "I shall grant you liberation from the bonds of worldly existence."
"O Mother, by my power, make your form twofold as you desire.
With one form, go to my abode together with my attendants;
with your second form, remain here as a human maiden. || 47-48 ||
"You shall indeed become the destined wife of Śantanu and enjoy the pleasures of his kingdom;
however, in Vaikuṇṭha, you shall never experience separation from me.
Having said this, he took water from the Gaṅgā and sprinkled it upon her body.
Instantly, at that very moment, she became two-fold in form.
By the command of Vyāsa, she ascended that celestial chariot in one form;
in her second form, she remained upon the boat. (1.482.50–51)
Then Vyāsa concealed his own divine form and,
taking his mother Satyavatī with him, departed for Vaikuṇṭha in a celestial chariot.
The virtuous woman, remaining on the boat, was deluded by his illusory power and began to entreat him.
"O son, you must protect me; you must always grant me your vision.
Vyāsa said: "O mother, you should not feel any despondency.
In times of distress, you must indeed remember me for the accomplishment of your purpose."
"I shall deliver you from calamities; forgive me, O mother, for your son.
Whenever I am to be remembered, I shall appear before you in person.
Having spoken thus, Vyāsa departed together with Parāśara.
Parāśara, devoted to austerity, returned once more to his own hut.
There, seated in the midst of the forest, the son of Parāśara was told by Nārada about the birth of Vyāsa from the gods.
Then the deities, headed by Brahmā, gathered on the bank of the Gaṅgā:
the Sun, the Grandfather (Brahmā), Śakra, the great sages beginning with Sanaka,
Dakṣa and others, and the singers beginning with Nārada.
The Manus, the Pitṛs, the Vedas, and even the Śāstras arrived.
Sarasvatī, Lakṣmī, Śāradā, and other goddesses arrived;
then Nārāyaṇa and Śiva came together with Satī.
The ancestors—human and divine—arrived with their celestial bodies;
the sacred fords, lakes, forests, and groves also came.
Vyāsa, the lord Kṛṣṇa-Dvaipāyana, was honored by flowers.
Having bestowed various blessings and spoken words of "Excellent!
Excellent!", the Grandfather [Brahmā] consecrated that boy with the purificatory rites beginning with *garbhādhāna*.
He was Dvaipāyana because he was born on an island (*dvīpa*), and Pārāśarya because he was born from Parāśara. (62–63)
The Lord Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana, who is black in form and known by the name Kṛṣṇa,
was consecrated again and again by Viriñci and by hosts of sages;
likewise, he was strengthened by the blessings of Sarasvatī and the others.
Praised by the Vedas for the sake of supreme protection and for the purpose of the Vyāsa incarnation, O Vyāsa,
the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa was beheld by all through his own splendor.
Having bowed to everyone, he chose from them all that which is auspicious as well as [the role of] the mental son.
"It is conducive to the knowledge of the Self, free from bondage, and bestows liberation.
Then everyone said, "So be it," and they held a great festival.
A rain of flowers fell upon his head, and women danced.
Then the Vedas and the mantras, appearing in dark forms, sang with joy.
Sarasvatī, Ramā, Lakṣmī, and the others arrived there, were fed with sweet foods,
and honored with betel leaves and other offerings.
By the command of the Creator, they performed a grand assembly of festivities;
everyone returned to their respective places, while Vyāsa proceeded to various sacred fords.
He bathed in the Gaṅgā, and went to Kedāra and the site of Badarī.
Haradvāra, Puṣkara, and Nārāyaṇa-sarovara; the bathing at Dvārikā and the Gomatī, as well as Camatkārapura;
the Kuṅkumavāpikā Tīrtha and likewise the Aśvapaṭṭa-saras. (71–72)
Having bathed in the Bhadrāvatī river, he went to the sacred site of Vāmana;
there he beheld before him Mount Raivata, where one may immerse oneself in the Svarṇarekhā,
and also the immersion in the Nārāyaṇa-hrada of Dāmodara.
Having gone to the land of Balikhāta, he beheld Somanātha;
likewise, having bowed to Gopīnātha and plunged into the Sābhramatī, and having also bathed in the Narmadā and the Tapatī, he visited Tryambakeśvara. ||74-75||
Having likewise paid homage to Ujjayinī and Oṃkāreśvara,
he then proceeded to the Tāmraparṇī, the Candrabhāgā, and Setubandha;
thereafter, he visited with devotion the sacred fords beginning with Śrīśaila once again.
Having performed [these rites], he went to Jagannāthapura and also to Kāmākṣī;
thereafter, he went to the Brahmaputrā, to Kālī, to Kapilatīrtha,
to Gayā, Kāśī, Ayodhyā, the Gaṇḍakī, and Prayāga.
Then he went to Naimiṣa, Kurukṣetra, and the Sarasvatī;
having plunged into the Yamunā, he went to the bank of the Narmadā.
Seeing the Narmadā with joy, his heart, which grants peace, found rest.
He performed extensive austerities, having taken refuge on the bank of the Narmadā.
In the summer, he stood in the midst of five fires; during the rainy season, he slept upon the bare ground;
and in the winter, he wore wet clothes, meditating upon Lord Hari.
In an instant, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa became manifest before him;
he bestowed words of blessing, and at that time Śukī became his wife.
Śuka also became their son, and the best of sages arrived there.

Staying at Vyāsa’s hermitage, they were honored by Vyāsa with hospitable rites. [He said: "I shall give excellent wild vegetables and forest fruits to all of you, having been welcomed by Vyāsa himself. (83–84)
Having spoken thus and become purified, he took his stand upon the bank of the Narmadā.
He praised the Narmadā, and she, appearing visibly before him in an instant, spoke these words: "Choose a boon according to your desire."
Vyāsa said: "If you are pleased, and if a boon is to be granted to me, then you ought to grant me hospitality on your northern bank.
Narmadā replied: "My path is directed toward the south."
"Consider for yourself how you might cross the bank.
Then Vyāsa himself proceeded ahead, pointing out the path;
the Narmadā flowed along that route, and the gods offered handfuls of flowers.
The hermitage of Vyāsa was established there, and from that it became known as Vyāsatīrtha.
Right there, the Narmadā herself remained present in embodied form;
devoted to her husband, she serves Vyāsa, who is Nārāyaṇa-Kṛṣṇa.
Following the path taught by Vyāsa, that virtuous woman first went there and constantly bathed Vyāsa with her own pure water,
offering him food, water, flowers, betel, incense, and lamps.

The virtuous Narmadā constantly serves Vyāsa and Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa. Thus, ever devoted to her husband, Narmadā remains there; people, having bathed there and having worshipped Hari and Satī, [attain their goals]. || 92-93 ||

"O Rame, those who read or even hear this shall certainly attain the supreme fruit of devotion to their husband (*pātivratya*). Furthermore, they shall obtain the merit born of visiting sacred pilgrimage sites (*tīrtha*).

Thus ends the four hundred and eighty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Birth of Vyāsa from Parāśara, the Account of the Birth of Matsyagandhā, Vyāsa’s Pilgrimage, His Residence on the Banks of the Narmadā, and the Devotion of Narmadā," in the first section, *Kṛtayugasantāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Chapter 484 →
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, Lakṣmī! I shall describe to you the devoted wife Anasūyā.
Her husband was Atri by name, the son of Brahmā. (1)

Constantly devoted to the *agnihotra* sacrifice, she honored the deities and guests; free from malice, she was as dear to him as his own life and was intent on the welfare of her husband’s affairs. Devoted to her husband, she served him just as [one serves] Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
Thus, as time passed, no offspring was born to the couple at that time.
As they sat comfortably conversing about the joys and sorrows resulting from their past actions,
Atri said, "O dear beloved, in the three worlds including all things mobile and immobile— " (3–4).
There is no woman in the world equal to you, who is ever devoted to my welfare.
A wife who loves her husband and son conquers the worlds that are difficult to cross.
Through a son one conquers the worlds; through a son one attains the supreme goal.

No kinsman equal to a son is seen upon this earth. (6) A virtuous son protects one who is falling into the southern forest of sword-leaves; likewise, even in times of famine, in states of wretchedness, and in old age, he provides refuge. (7)
"But without a son, O blessed lady, what is the point? Or even if he be an ascetic, my dear, such a son will cross over [to liberation] his parents, being impelled by the shame of the world.
For one devoid of a son, how can there be happiness in this world or in the next? (8–9)
"Thinking of this day and night, I wither away and find no peace.
Anasūyā, having heard that, said: 'O Lord, I too grieve over that which causes you distress and which causes me distress as well.'"

"By which means I might have sons, and by which Prajāpati would be pleased. Atri replied, "O blessed one, O beloved, I have performed most rigorous penance through vows, fasts, observances, and subsisting on a diet of vegetables and the like."
"My body is worn out; since birth I have been an ascetic, yet I am now powerless.
Old age is visible in my body, and the departure for the next world is at hand. It is not far off; thus I have told you the truth. (1.3)
Anasūyā said to him: "O husband, I am a devoted wife to you;
I am the means for attaining the three goals of life and the one who increases my husband and son.
By your command, having performed severe penance, I shall become the mother of a son. (14–15)
"Recitation of mantras, austerity, pilgrimage, honoring sons, and the mastery of spells— these the teachers, protectors of the world, declare to be the duties of a devoted wife.
And having been granted permission, I shall perform severe austerities in this state of sorrow."
"Desiring a son, I have been approaching Viṣṇu for many days.
Atri said, "This is excellent; it brings me great satisfaction.
O blessed lady, permitted by me, perform penance for the sake of a son."
Having discharged the three debts, one should apply the mind to liberation.
Become free from debt to the gods, to human beings, and to the ancestors.
No other vessel is considered equal to a wife for crossing over [to the further shore].
The gods do not praise a home devoid of a virtuous wife.
Indeed, every other pleasure becomes parched when separated from a wife;
she comes forward to meet one face-to-face, but turns her back when one acts contrary to her.

Therefore, O devoted wife, O highly fortunate one, O you who always act for my welfare, perform fruitful asceticism that grants me a son at my command; for you are the object of praise for householders. (22)
"O beloved, may the command of my husband and the word of Viṣṇu bear fruit in you. May the Lord also swiftly fulfill that desire of yours.
Having thus received the favor of her husband, the devoted wife [spoke].
Having become empowered for her own purpose, she prostrated with the eight limbs and said:
"O best of Brahmins, by your grace, may I attain all of this.
And Anasūyā, devoted to her husband, was indeed joined with blessings.
Moving with the intense grace of a swan’s gait, she reached the bank of the Narmadā.
On the northern shore of the Narmadā, she lived subsisting on leaves;
remaining constantly established in her vows, she occasionally took only vegetables as food.
Devoted to hymns, she remained self-restrained, praising the gods in her heart with auspicious chants.
During the summer months, she stood in the midst of the five fires under the scorching heat by day.
During the rainy season, she performed the Cāndrāyaṇa vow while standing outdoors.
In the winter season, that virtuous woman practiced dwelling in the water during the three periods of the day (triṣavaṇa).
She performed the libations for the gods, their worship, and likewise the fire sacrifice;
she offered food oblations with festive rites, handfuls of flowers, hymns of praise, and prayers for forgiveness.
She lived thus in the forest, constantly accompanied by deer and other creatures.
When a hundred years had passed in this manner, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Pitāmaha,
perceiving her to be an ascetic emaciated by hunger and desiring a son, arrived there.
In the form of twice-born brahmins, those gods arrived at the confluence of the Eraṇḍī at that place of austerity and recited Vedic mantras. Hearing the Vedic mantras, Anasūyā was filled with love.
Looking repeatedly toward that direction from which she had risen from the ground, she saw the brahmins who had come to the hermitage as guests; she offered them the *arghya* water.
Having washed their feet, she drank [the water] and placed it upon her head.
Today my birth has indeed become fruitful through the sight of the brahmins;
today my purpose and my ascetic toil have become fruitful by the appearance of the brahmins;
today this ground of mine has become fruitful through the arrival of the brahmins.
Having spoken thus, she bowed at his feet and circumambulated him repeatedly;
then, performing another prostration with eight limbs touching the ground, she spoke these words of honor:
"Today I shall satisfy you with divine roots, tubers, and fruits."
"Take rest in the leaf-hut upon seats of darbha grass and the like.
Having heard this, those brahmins said to that virtuous female ascetic:
"O lady of excellent vows, by your intense austerity and by your truthfulness—"
We are satisfied by the sight of you through your dharma of devotion to your husband.
A curiosity has arisen in us: for what reason do you perform penance?
Is it for heaven, or worldly prosperity, or liberation, or something else entirely?
"What do you desire, O virtuous lady, through this indeed difficult austerity?
By austerity heaven is attained; by austerity the supreme goal is reached;
by austerity the abundant fulfillment of all desires comes to pass. (41–42)
"In youth, one should always enjoy those pleasures desired by the mind;
having abandoned all of them here, for what reason do you wither away?
Having heard this, Anasūyā spoke to the foremost of the gods:
"In youth, austerity should be practiced; in youth lies the supreme goal.
In youth one may procreate sons, but in old age everything is unpleasant.
When they had spoken thus, those best of gods said, "Excellent! Excellent! (44–45).
Having manifested in the forms of Brahmins, the triad of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara appeared before him in person and said, "Choose a boon!
Whatever you desire, we shall grant it all; speak now."
Vāsudeva appeared with four arms, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace;
he was accompanied by Garuḍa and by Śrī.
Brahmā, adorned with four faces, had a serene countenance.
Accompanied by Haṃsā and Sāvitrī, he held a rosary in his hand;
while Śiva was mounted upon a bull together with Pārvatī,
possessing five faces, three eyes, and endowed with ten arms.
Having seen these gods worthy of worship, the female ascetic was immediately filled with joy; having seen them and bowed to them, she spoke to them:
"What are your activities, and who are you—Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Pitāmaha?"
"Therefore, O compassionate one, I wish to hear this from you.
Brahmā said: "O Satī! I am the rainy season, and likewise, I am the water;
I am the cloud that pours down rain, and I am the eastern twilight."
Viṣṇu said: "I am Hemanta (the winter season), and I nourish [all beings] in every way.
It is my supreme duty that the entire world must be protected.
Rudra said: "O Satī, I am the Grīṣma (summer) season, the bringer of decay."
"O ascetic woman, in the form of Rudra I dry up the entire world!
Thus we three gods, the three times, the three fires,
and the three twilights, have eternally attained oneness."
"And we grant you a boon, O blessed lady, whatever dwells in your heart.
Anasūyā replied: "I am barren; what could I choose, O gods?
Let Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara here become my sons. (56–57)
Viṣṇu said: "O blessed lady, sons do not become givers of boons;
rather, they become like their [father] by virtue of the granting of boons.
O blessed lady, I shall grant you those sons whose prowess is equal to that of the gods."

To those who were endowed with qualities equal to their father’s and were performers of Soma sacrifices and deeply learned, Anasūyā said: "If there is one among you worthy of receiving a boon, come and become my sons; I wish to give you what I desire. (1.483.60)
"That must not be done otherwise while you dwell within my womb.
Viṣṇu said to that goddess: "We shall certainly not remain in the dwelling of the womb;
however, your wind (vital breath) shall remain in the womb like an embryo."
The wind shall make your womb manifest with its embryo.
After nine months have passed, we shall come to your auspicious home, accompanied by prosperity, for the sake of your delivery.
At the time of the wind's emergence, we three shall become sons in the form of children, born not from a womb;
for the gods, who have auspicious refuge, do not enter a womb at all.
Having spoken thus, they were seen for a moment in the form of children;
then, mounted upon divine vehicles, they departed for their own abode.
Having obtained the boon, that goddess, her body now withered, went to her home.
She saw her beloved, who observed the great vow, seated upon a stone slab.
Bowing down, she prostrated at his feet; having washed them, she drank [the water].
When asked about his welfare, she spoke with compassion, filled with fruitfulness.
"Having obtained this boon, I have indeed come to serve you without obstacle.
Through the merit of my husband, the wish-fulfilling trees bear fruit; thus, three sons named Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa have been acquired by me. (68–69)
"Indeed, after a long time, the fruit of service to the feet of the Blessed One has been attained;
and this husband, difficult for other women to win and very hard to obtain, has been secured. Therefore, I shall grant you sons who are sages rich in ascetic merit."
Thus addressed, she was filled with joy and became entirely devoted to the service of her beloved.
She gazed upon her lovely husband, and he gazed back at her;
by that very sight, a radiant circle appeared upon her forehead.
Rootless and yet having long roots, consisting of three parts, auspicious like a sphere, composed of light, and enveloped by a network of thousands of rays—
within its center, indeed, three deities shone forth in an instant.
Commanded by the gods, Vāyu dwelt constantly in the place of the womb.
Anasūyā, pregnant with him, became radiant with splendor.
Then, when nine months had passed, it was as if the tenth month had arrived.
At the auspicious moment, the virtuous woman entered the lying-in chamber;
the wind issued forth from the womb, and the gods became the boys.
The first son was golden-hued; he became Brahmā, the Grandfather.
The moon, consisting of sixteen digits, is Soma, the bestower of nourishment.
He is the first son, the delighter of Anasūyā;
the second, however, is the highly fortunate Maheśvara himself in person. (77–78)
That portion which effects creation and destruction became known by the name Durvāsas;
the third son was Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa, Hari,
the great yogi Dattātreya, the Lord, the Master of Śrī.
Janārdana himself, the Lord of the universe, is the pervader of the world.
Having thus obtained this boon of three sons, Satī, the devoted wife,
became fulfilled in her purpose, as did the sage Atri.
O beloved, as soon as they were born, those three became youths; Satī, Lakṣmī, and Sāvitrī arrived there from the divine realm.
Having bowed to Anasūyā for the sake of serving the lords of the worlds, they [remained].
The daughters-in-law served the gods with water, food, and sandalwood paste.
Those three, possessing divine forms, granted an audience to their parents;
indeed, the house of Atri was always made by them to consist of every kind of prosperity.
Gods, sages, perfected beings, and seers whose wealth is austerity,
as well as goddesses, attendants, and hosts, come constantly to behold [him].
Atri’s hermitage remains crowded with tens of millions of deities.
Sacrifices were performed constantly, and likewise festivals took place day after day.
Then these three gods spoke with respect to their two parents:
"We wish to perform austerities; therefore, we shall go to another forest."

Hearing this, the mother, longing for her sons, was indeed plunged into grief. She said: "Since I have performed penance for the sake of my sons' happiness—for their upbringing, protection, and well-being—these three alone [are the purpose]. (88)
"The gods have been well-treated by me for the sake of their vision and for the sake of service.
O infallible ones, how can you depart for asceticism, leaving us behind?
He will not endure our separation; therefore, we must certainly go."
Having heard this, the three gods then assumed two forms each;
with their divine forms, they went to another place for the purpose of performing penance.
Durvāsas went to his own Kailāsa in the presence of Śiva.
Candramas went to Satyaloka, and Datta departed for another continent. Then those three, having assumed the forms of children, remained in their own home,
playing on their mother’s lap like ordinary mortals.
Playing on their father’s lap, they roam about the hermitage;
with the young fawns of the deer, as well as with the birds and even with the ascetics, they behave like ordinary children. (94)
Spending their days in childhood play, in the worship of the gods, and in pleasing their ancestors,
they brought happiness to their mother and father.
Thus, O sage, the three sons of the rishi attained the status of gods through their ascetic penance.
Wearing the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) and engaged in the study of the Vedas,
those three sons of Atri constantly performed sacrificial rites in the presence of Atri;
indeed, they had received from Atri himself the essence of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
Those preeminent Vaiṣṇavas— the mantra, the Tulasī garland, and they themselves—
are long-lived and have secured passage for all the worlds;
they exist as divine saviors, the Vaiṣṇavas who deliver their lineages.
O Lakṣmī! This supreme and auspicious divine narrative has been told to you;
it is considered to bestow both heaven and liberation through its reading and hearing as well.

Thus ends the four hundred and eighty-third chapter, titled "The Description of How the Sons Somadatta and Durvāsas were Obtained by Anasūyā, the Wife of Atri, through Penance from Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa, as well as the Power of Her Chastity," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-Santāna, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā. Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī! Hear also of the supreme austerity performed by Rohiṇī in the past, by which that virtuous woman forever attained the preeminence among the wives of the Moon. (1)
Beloved by all women and especially by her husband,
that devoted wife once resolved to perform austerities.
Having gone to the bank of the Narmadā, she performed extensive penance.
For one night, two nights, six, and likewise twelve nights with others;
having emaciated her body through fasts lasting for a fortnight and a month,
she was constantly devoted to the propitiation of Hari, whose guru is Nārāyaṇa.
Constantly bathing again and again in the waters of the Narmadā,
she who was devoted to Hari worshipped the Lord Govinda, the husband of Nārāyaṇī.
The blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa, the husband of Nārāyaṇī, became pleased with her.
He said: "I am pleased with your vows and your observances.
O great virtuous lady, I grant you today whatever boon you desire; choose it!
Having heard these words of his, she bowed and worshipped him with devotion.
Having drunk the water from his feet and become purified by the sight of him, Rohiṇī chose this boon: "I desire service at your lotus-feet.
First, grant me that boon: let my devotion toward you be exceptional."
Then, as for the second boon, [grant that] she may always be in the moon's palace in this world;
and by your grace, O Bhavānī, act so that she may very soon become more beloved to the Moon than all her co-wives.
Hari said: "By my grace, maintain two forms;
go to Vaikuṇṭha with one, and dwell here with the second.
With that second form, become the beloved of the Moon. (11)
"Your wife is devoted to her husband and is the foremost among all co-wives.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa took that virtuous woman and departed for his own Vaikuṇṭha by means of a celestial chariot through the sky.
She, assuming a second form, went to the abode of the Moon;
from that time forth, she became the most preeminent of all women.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, has this supreme fruit of penance been described to you.
This beautiful form of my worship bestows both heaven and liberation.
(15) Now I shall tell you another account of mine that grants liberation:
there was a daughter of Dakṣa, renowned by the name Kumudā. (16)
Having given those [cows] to Soma, Dakṣa attained supreme joy.
Upon her, he begot a son named Amṛta. Then, having learned of this, the gods, seeking the fruit of the sacrifice, went to him.
Having drunk the nectar, those Daityas then departed;
they spoke to the Moon, saying: "Give us the supreme nectar for the purpose of drinking, otherwise we shall surely devour you. (18–19)
Because Candra was unable to give them the nectar, they seized him from heaven and cast him down from the sky.
A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose; Kumudā was his beloved wife.
Then, having taken water in her hand according to the dharma of devotion to her husband, she said:
"I am devoted to my husband, faithful to my husband, and established in my husband;
by the power of this devotion to my husband, let these Dānavas go to their destruction."
Having spoken thus, he cast water upon the Dānavas;
thereupon they were reduced to ashes. Those who remained went toward Śukra, their preceptor, and reported to him the state of the Daityas having been turned to ash.
Śukra arrived there and restored the Asuras to life.
Śukra bowed to Kumudā; the Daityas prostrated and went home.
Candra was raised from the earth by Kumudā through her own power.
Then, having been brought to rest by Brahmā, Maheśa, and the other gods,
he was established once more in heaven, and the deities became free from their feverish distress.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have related to you the great power of devotion to one’s husband.
It bestows all prosperity, removes obstacles, and increases good fortune.
(27) Now, O beloved, I shall describe another marvel; listen!
On the Narmadā, at the confluence of the four [rivers], there exists Yajñaparvata. (28)
In ancient times, the self-existent Svayambhū performed the Sautrāmaṇi sacrifice there;
likewise, O lotus-born one, Maghavan performed the horse-sacrifice at that very spot.
From that mountain issued forth the great river of the four directions.
She fell into the Narmadā at the confluence on Yajñaparvata,
where the sage Suparṇa Jābāli— born from the seed of Brahmā— resided;
his wife was Puruhūtā, a lawful spouse devoted to her husband.
Having become negligent, she spoke these words to her own husband, Puruhūta:
"O great sage, unite with me during my fertile period on the auspicious lunar day, so that a son may be born to me who shall purify our entire lineage. (32)
"Through a son one conquers the worlds; the ancestors and the gods are satisfied.
There is no destination for one who is childless; therefore, you have given birth to a son.
Having heard this, Suparṇa said to her: "Today is the new moon day (amāvāsyā)."
O wife! Kāmadeva must always be avoided on festival days;
indeed, it is forbidden during a meritorious vow, on auspicious days, and even on the lunar day dedicated to the ancestors (pitṛtithi).
O beautiful lady, sexual union by a husband and wife is likewise forbidden even during the fertile period (ṛtukāla).
His ancestors, who approach him during their fertile seasons, shall consume that flesh.
For a thousand divine years I have performed difficult austerities;
all of that would be utterly destroyed by your union with me on this sacred day.
"Behold, my dear, how after bathing here at this confluence for a mere moment,
a Cāṇḍāla is now departing by way of a celestial chariot to heaven, having surpassed me!
If even he is thus honored, why indeed should my constant penance be held in contempt?"
"O beloved, I am lost in thought, wondering how this could have happened.
Tell me the reason for it, O virtuous lady! How indeed was he censured by him?
O faithful one, if you agree, I shall afterwards bestow the sacred law (dharma) upon you. || 1.484.40 ||
"O beloved, if dharma were truly found in the ritual gift given at the time of a festival, then at that very moment a certain Niṣāda woman arrived on the bank of the Narmadā.
She heard the cry of 'Fie! and spoke to that Ṛṣi for that reason."
"With a self deluded by egoism, there is no ascetic equal to you.
For you, neither bathing, nor chanting, nor fire-offerings, nor Vedic study, nor worship of Acyuta, nor the practice of the prescribed mantra has been ordained. (42–43)
"Having become supportless and subsisting on air, you have incurred fruitless hardship;
your penance, meditation, and yoga are indeed fruitless and do not grant heaven.
He then spoke repeatedly to that Niṣāda woman with humble words.
"Who are you that have come to this sacred ford, having assumed the form of a Niṣāda woman?
Are you Umā, Sarasvatī, or Gaṅgā? You have come desiring to test me.
I consider this a favor; tell me the eternal Dharma."
The Niṣāda woman then spoke to him with joy regarding eternal dharma:
"O Brahmin lady, I too was a Brahmin; my husband lived in the Naimiṣa forest, constantly established in austerity. He did not touch me even during the monthly period."
For he was indeed entreated by me, afflicted by desire, after I had bathed for my menses;
on the day of the new moon, my husband was requested by me for the sake of obtaining a son.
Since I made this request at an improper time, I was cursed by that high-souled one.
"Since you are begging for unrighteousness, become a Śūdra born of a Niṣāda!
Cursed by me, become a Caṇḍāla wherever I am.
Thus, overcome by the curse, the couple went to the source of the Narmadā.
Having heard this narrative from the *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇasaṃhitā*,
which contains the supreme and divine majesty [of the Lord] that grants liberation through mere bathing—
my husband, that very outcaste, has arrived and attained heaven.
"I am a Niṣādī woman; having bathed, O Brahmin, I shall go to my liberation.
Therefore, you too should always worship Govinda with austerity.
Then all of this will become meaningful for you; otherwise, it will be fruitless. (53)
"Perform indeed rites such as fire-offerings and recitations for the sake of Hari;
you shall go to Vaikuṇṭha, which is presided over by Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
Having spoken thus, she bathed at the banks of the Narmadā and departed for heaven.
She followed by the same path that her husband had taken.
Having heard this, the virtuous Puruhūtā, bowing down to her own husband Suparṇa and to Jābāli,
then indeed begged for forgiveness.

Having understood the eternal dharma, sexual union for married couples is by no means appropriate on festival days or even during the fertile period. Having thus known this supreme dharma, those two Vaiṣṇava couples— ||| 57–58 ||
Having offered worship to the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa and performed daily recitation, the husband and wife,
devoted to their vows and dedicated to the dharma of chanting, went to Vaikuṇṭha in the course of time.
"Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have related to you the knowledge of dharma concerning the wife of the sage.

Thus ends the four hundred and eighty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of Rohiṇī Kumudā’s Austerity, the Liberation of Puruhūtā through Bathing in the Narmadā, and the Dharma of Giving and Not Giving Sexual Union on Sacred Occasions," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.

Chapter 486 → Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
I shall relate an ancient narrative concerning otherness; listen, O Lakṣmī.
The great sage Dīrghatamas, together with his family, attained liberation in the city of Citrasena, who was the king of Kāśī. (1) In his capital—
In that city of Kāśī, the sage Dīrghatamas always resided. (2) To the northern region of Kāśī is a place named Mandārārāma, thick with trees and creepers; there dwells the seer Dīrghatamas. (3)
He performs intense austerities and lives together with his wife and sons; all five of his sons as well as the others likewise serve him.
His youngest son, Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, is also an ascetic.
He was both a yogi and a celibate student, devoted to the study of the Vedas.
Sustaining himself on bulbs, roots, and fruits, he lived assuming the form of a deer;
dwelling constantly among the deer, he performed acts of homage for his parents.
Morning and evening he would come among the deer and then depart again. Then King Citrasena, the lord of Kāśī,
mounted upon his horse, went out with his people for the sake of hunting toward the Mandāra trees.
There, the king beheld a very great herd of deer;
the deer fled in the ten directions out of fear, and the king also,
being alone, pursued the deer into the dense forest.
Midday had arrived, and the king was disoriented by the confusion of the directions;
afflicted by hunger and thirst, he took refuge in the shade on the bank of the lake.
Having stayed there for a moment, he bathed in the water and gathered lilies.
Having taken [the water] and performed the libation, he drank as much water as he desired.
The yogi Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, of great asceticism, remained in the midst of the deer;
and the king, desiring to hunt the deer, took refuge at the foot of a tree.

By reading and hearing this, a person becomes possessed of knowledge.

Chapter 487. [Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā – Section 1 (Kṛtayuga-santāna), Chapter 488]
