Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O Blessed One, I desire to hear about the autumnal *rāsa*-maṇḍala.
Listen to the pastimes of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa with the gopīs.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, I shall describe to you that supreme delight of the rāsa dance.
With nine hundred thousand gopīs and nine hundred thousand Mādhavas,
that youth became a young man on the full moon of the autumnal month of Śarad.
O beloved, the young men and young women took delight with Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Having reflected thus, the illustrious Hari went to the forest of Vṛndāvana at night;
auspiciously, at the rising of the moon, he went there to fulfill the desires of all the gopīs.
Out of curiosity, he produced the playful sound of his flute.
Upon hearing that, Rādhikā quickly emerged from her house. Thirty-three companions, headed by Suśīlā, also went forth with joy;
they were equal to one another in dress, age, beauty, and virtue.
Other nine hundred thousand gopīs departed, abandoning their homes and possessions;
they all gathered together in one place, some with garlands in their hands,
some with beautiful sandalwood paste in their hands, and others with white fly-whisks in their hands.
Some carrying musk, some bearing saffron,
some with betel-leaf boxes, and some dressed in golden garments—
speaking of Kṛṣṇa, O Kṛṣṇa— they beheld the circle of the Rāsa dance.
They heard the sweet humming of bees and the song of cuckoos in that secluded place, which was in full bloom and perfumed by flower-laden breezes;
then Rādhā and the gopīs entered the beautiful circle of the rāsa dance.
Beholding Rādhā and the gopīs, Kṛṣṇa also appeared, smiling;
endowed with fresh youth, adorned with jewel ornaments, radiant with a beauty surpassing ten million Cupids, and captivating to the mind. (11–12)
With the corner of her sidelong glance, she beheld the cowherd girls again and again;
indeed, there were nine hundred thousand gopīs and an equal number of Kṛṣṇas,
as well as eighteen lakhs of couples within the circle of the Rāsa dance.
He took delight in the rāsa dance with songs, rhythmic beats, and frequent leaps;
with the clashing of hands, the keeping of time, playful facial expressions, the joining of staffs, the touching of shoulders, kisses, and the pressing of palms. (14–15)
Having thus sported in the Rāsa dance, they sat down, weary and with faces upturned;
they honored their beloved, their own dear one, and offered him excellent betel.
Filled with love, they took the betel from one another’s mouths.
Knowing their inner thoughts, Kṛṣṇa himself, who can assume any form at will,
took them all with amorous intent and kissed them; likewise,
he engaged in the eightfold erotic union with their bodies.
The Lord of Rasikas appropriately delivered blows with his nails, teeth, and hands,
and performed the eightfold kissing;
he joined limb with limb and minor member with minor member.
He gave an embrace to those amorous women that brought them great pleasure.
In the place of nine hundred thousand, Kṛṣṇa shone, devoted to his beloveds;
having granted them satisfaction through love, the self-effulgent Lord remained himself with his vital energy restrained (a celibate).
Having thus engaged in sports on land, they came for water-sports;
nine hundred thousand couples took delight in the waters of the Yamunā. Clad in garments and even without them, they sported for the sake of satisfying their desires.
The gopīs attained a state of swoon within the ocean of bliss regarding their Lord;
they firmly embraced their beloved, holding him to their chests and bodies.
Thus the Lord Kṛṣṇa gave them satisfaction even in the water for a very long time.
Then, having come out, they eagerly put on their garments;
thereafter, each one separately engaged in playful dalliance with her beloved. Full of pride, they performed various acts of amorous adornment for Kṛṣṇa.
Kṛṣṇa, however, created a new adornment for their braided hair and the like.
One woman, placing her lover in front of her, performed the dressing of her hair;
another placed an excellent peacock feather upon her crest.
One woman gave collyrium for her eyes and forehead-saffron;
another wound a garland of *guñjā* berries around his crest.
One gave fine cloth and an upper garment to her husband.
One woman placed a beautiful garland of flowers around his neck;
another applied a *tilaka* mark, while yet another wore a crescent-shaped ornament (*candraka*).
Another applied red lac-dye to the soles of his feet and to his nails. (1.488.30)
One girl placed a flute in His hand; another gave Him betel nut;
yet another showed Him her beautiful face in a lovely mirror.
Another joyfully performed the massaging of Kṛṣṇa’s feet.
One gave him water, while another gently provided a fine breeze;
one applied sandalwood paste to Kṛṣṇa’s body,
and another, taking his hand, untied the knot of his garment.
Another indeed performed a massage of the calves and thighs;
some danced and sang, while others, full of longing, kissed him.
One woman, taking Kṛṣṇa with her, went into a bower.
Another, having placed him upon her bed, joyfully took his pleasure;
yet another made him dance by force,
while he himself fashioned the beautiful braid of hair for someone else.
She applied vermilion upon her forehead along with dots of musk;

She then fashioned a beautiful leaf-design on her lovely cheeks.
Having placed anklets on her feet, she gave her beautiful red lac;

Having assumed many forms, the supreme teacher of yogis—

Overwhelmed by the joy of passion, they constantly fell into a state of swoon.
Having thus delighted the women and made the night last for six months, [he departed]. 42.
Having brought about a long sleep upon the earth and having made the course of the sun steady,

he sported everywhere as he pleased, even in secluded places,

in the thirty-three forests desired by women,

in the grove of coconut trees, in the grove of betel-nut trees, and in the grove of plantain trees.

in the grove of *aśvattha* trees, in the grove of *vaṃśa* trees, in the grove of *dāḍima* trees;
in the grove of *mandāra* trees, in the grove of *tāla* trees, and likewise in the grove of mango trees.
In groves of *ketakī*, in groves of *aśoka*, in groves of date palms;
in groves of *āmrātaka*, in groves of rose-apple trees, in groves of *śāla* and *suka*;
in groves of *kaṭādikā*, in groves of lotuses, and likewise in groves of *jāti* jasmine.
In the delightful thickets of *nyagrodha* trees, as well as in the groves of sandalwood and the forests of excellent *kesara* blossoms,
he took pleasure for six months’ nights.
Just as the desire of amorous women increases through the sentiment of love (*śṛṅgāra*), so did his delight grow.
In such and such a way Hari, the bestower of bliss upon them, took his delight;
nevertheless, the hearts of those amorous women were not yet fully satisfied.
Thus, throughout the morning, Hari bestowed the pleasure of desire during the rāsa dances.
When all of them had become satiated with desire, he released them;
thereafter, they went to the Yamunā to play in the waters.
Then Kṛṣṇa vanished from sight, and the gopīs returned to their own homes.
All these cowherd women did not consider the Lord to be their husband;
for lustful women, through the power of desire, regard him as a hero in love. Nevertheless, with their minds fixed on Him, those beloved ones attained the divine state.
Even that which is inert attains a divine state through divine union;
indeed, a clod of earth becomes fire through contact with fire.
Then [he beheld] the most excellent, auspicious, and artificial pavilions for the *rāsa* dance.
Viśvakarman made nine hundred thousand beautiful celestial couches, each a yojana wide, fashioned by Viśvakarman; in a mere moment, he caused them to vanish from sight. (6.2–6.3)
Then, as this young Śrī Kṛṣṇa was traveling alone toward his own home,
the best of sages, Aṣṭāvakra— dark-complexioned, naked, and with matted hair— beheld him on the path. (64)
With his nails and beard grown long, peaceful, and with his neck bowed,
that bull among sages indeed prostrated before Govinda and offered praise;
then, falling at His lotus feet, he abandoned his life-breaths through yoga.
That splendor rose up to the height of seven palm trees;
having become a most divine person, it stood near Kṛṣṇa.
Seeing the sage dead, Kṛṣṇa prepared to perform the funeral rites.
For sixty thousand years the sage remained without food.
His body became devoid of blood, flesh, and bone, and was indeed covered in ashes.
Taking that [body], Kṛṣṇa placed it upon the funeral pyre mixed with ashes.
In the meantime, a chariot arrived from the sky,
accompanied by excellent attendants who were like Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself.
Having bowed to Śrī Hari, the attendants took that divine person away.
When Aṣṭāvakra had cast off his body, they went to the supreme Goloka.
Listen, Lakṣmī! The son of Brahmā was Pracetas, and his son was Asita;
being destitute of offspring, he performed penance for a thousand years.
When, despite having a wife, he did not obtain a son even after many years,
he then indeed became intent on giving up his life. Then, an incorporeal voice arose to awaken him.
"Why do you abandon your life? Go to the presence of Śaṅkara!
Having received a mantra from the mouth of Śaṅkara, accomplish your goal;
by the boon of your chosen deity, a son shall certainly be yours. (74-75)
Having heard this, he went to Kailāsa with his wife and said to him:
"O Mahādeva, ocean of compassion, grant me a son; I bow before you.
Hara replied: "A son shall be born to you, who will be a portion of me and equal to me."
He chanted the mantra: "Obeisance to you, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, for the sake of Rādhikā.
After one hundred years, Rādhā indeed became manifest through the power of the mantra.
Having said, "Be blessed with a son," Rādhikā vanished from sight.
Then Asita had a son named Devala. After one hundred years, he took Suyajña’s daughter, named Ratnamālāvatī, in marriage.
Free from passion, he abandoned her on the bed and went to the forest himself.
For a thousand years, he practiced austerities on Mount Gandhamādana;
through that penance, the twice-born one became divine in body, like the sun.
Once, having seen Devala, Rambhā was deluded by passion;
as he approached for the purpose of breaking his asceticism, Devala did not accept her.
Enraged and filled with inner sorrow, she angrily uttered a curse.
Since you do not accept me because I am afflicted by the suffering of desire,
may you become hunchbacked, eight-faced, decrepit, blue and deformed,
devoid of ascetic power, ugly, and despised by women. (83–84)
Having cursed Rambhā, the sage named Aṣṭavakra went to heaven;
he became renowned as Devala and departed for the Malaya mountain.
There, he once again performed austerities for sixty thousand years.
Having learned of this Rāsa-sport, he arrived to witness it;
yet, lost in meditation and being slow-acting, he did not obtain the sight of the Rāsa.
Through union with Kṛṣṇa, that devoted sage departed for his own abode, Goloka.
Then Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, Viṣṇu, went to the house of Nanda;
in the morning, all those women remembered Him, transformed and absorbed in Kṛṣṇa.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have described to you the supreme Rāsa-maṇḍala.
"From reading or hearing this, the attainment of Kṛṣṇa will certainly come to pass.

Thus ends the four hundred and eighty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of Kṛṣṇa’s Deeds with the Gopīs in the Rāsa-maṇḍala through the Emotion of Desire; Aṣṭāvakra’s State as Such Due to the Curse of Devala and Rambhā; and His Liberation," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī, to another story that bestows the wealth of true fortune.
There was a king named Vṛka, born of the Lunar dynasty (Somavaṃśa). || 1 ||
He had a virtuous wife who was devoted to her husband. In their later years, they then had a single daughter.
Having examined the birth-lagna, the astrologers said to the king and queen:
When the sun is situated in Citrā on the fourteenth lunar day (caturdaśī) and the moon is also there,
whatever girl is born at that time shall be a poison-girl (viṣakanyā). The one who takes her hand in marriage will meet his death within six months.
The house in which she was born shall be devoid of prosperity;
O King, this daughter of yours is such a poison-maiden (viṣakanyā) that she will destroy both her father’s and her husband’s households.
Therefore, O King, having abandoned her, may you always remain happy in your kingdom.
Or rather, if she remains a virtuous woman, an ascetic, and a practitioner of Sāṅkhya and Yoga,
then she will undoubtedly effect the salvation of both families.
Even for the unfortunate, fortune turns toward generosity;
for even an ascetic covered in ashes becomes fine powder, and medicine is for the sake of well-being.
Wherever they may arise—an ascetic or a pearl—both are jewels.
"Gold, maidens, and all medicinal herbs attain divinity through initiation.
Therefore, O King, do as you wish, whatever pleases you.
Though addressed thus, that royal sage, reflecting upon his own past karma, [remained silent].
Though it was impossible to cleanse her, he, being full of affection, did not indeed abandon her;
for whatever action a person performs with whatever body,
in whatever state, and with whatever impulse— (11) — [he experiences the result thereof].
Therefore, one enjoys that [result] in that [place]; nowhere is anything obtained that has not been performed.
These five are created here for the embodied being while still in the womb:
lifespan, action, wealth, knowledge, and death itself.
Just as fruits and flowers on trees and creepers do not bypass their own appointed time, so too does karma performed in the past;
just as among thousands of cows, a calf finds its mother.
In the same way, the doer encounters the fruit of his action situated within the range of possibility;
no embodied being on earth, by means of either strength or wisdom, is able to alter an action previously performed by himself. (15–16)
The happiness and suffering of embodied beings attend upon what they themselves have done.
He who becomes attached through egoism and the sense of "mine" is bound.
His own karma runs after him as he runs very swiftly away.

By whatever means and wherever a man is to experience pleasure or even pain, he is led there by force, as if bound by a rope. (18–19)
Whether they are awake or sleeping, speaking or walking,
desiring to accomplish their tasks or even bestowing them upon others—
for those who offer their very self, [the Lord] inevitably stands present.

Just as a lamp reaches extinction when its oil is exhausted, so too one attains nirvāṇa upon the exhaustion of karma and the exhaustion of latent dispositions (*āśaya*). The fruit produced by that [karma] is experienced in the present or future birth;
neither mantra, nor austerity, nor charity, nor a sacred ford, nor even a refuge is capable of protecting a living being from the flow of past karma. (23)
Food and drinks, as well as all meals, are digested day and night within that very same belly;

"In my previous life as a Caṇḍāla woman, I quenched the thirst of a single cow.

Though I was censured, tormented by poverty, afflicted by hunger,

By that merit, I have indeed been born as the daughter of a king.

by serving the virtuous, ascetics, holy men, cows, righteous women, children, and those devoted to the gods, liberation shall come to pass. (54–55)

"O Śacī, I do not think of your favor;
I desire no boon from you, nor from any other celestial women. (66–67)
I choose as my boon that goddess who is the beloved of Śiva,
by whom penance was indeed performed for the sake of Śiva for thousands of years;
she who is the auspicious Prakṛti born from the left side of Kṛṣṇa.
"I choose as my boon her by whom all this is pervaded.

Having spoken thus and meditated upon Śivā, he descended into the expanse of his heart.

"Otherwise, I shall serve the fire, which is worthy of being kindled. At that moment, Airāvata became a lion in form, Śacī became a female jackal, and the Apsarases became her attendants. (77)

seeing that he was weary upon reaching his home, his virtuous wife— (8)

for that which is the true home of a virtuous woman always possesses a beautiful form.
For the sake of attaining happiness for my self, mind, body, and senses, I have purchased this house—known as "belonging to the masters"—by surrendering the wealth of my very life-force.
I go there constantly; indeed, nothing remains that must yet be gone to.
"O Lord, how can I, deprived of you, go to another house as a wifeless woman?
Therefore, O Master, I shall perform my pilgrimage to sacred fords together with you;
I shall sustain my body with whatever is obtained while remaining in your service."
"Bound by the bonds of dharma, I swear this of myself by truth: my wife, who shares in the practice of dharma, shall go along with me.
Having thus understood her firm resolve, that brahmin—
"I am exceedingly pleased and blessed, for such a virtuous woman is my beloved.
Thus did that couple conduct themselves, devoted to Hari,
during the great festival on the bank of the Nāgā river in the month of Śrāvaṇa.
In an assembly of more than a hundred thousand people, the two went to behold the sun and performed auspicious worship with special offerings.
At that time, the Brahmin became distressed by the great crush of the crowd.
Though fallen in the crush of the crowd, she was unable to rise again.
The helpless woman, exhausted by the pressure of the throng, was unable to lift herself up.
[She cried out: "Om, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa; obeisance to the Lord! (48–49).
Having thus performed her recitation, that virtuous and devoted wife [chanted]:
"Oṃ, salutation to Savitṛ, the witness-form, the Supreme Self.
Having thus performed his recitation, that detached brahmin devotee [chanted].
Then, for the sake of protecting the two of them, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa Ravi arrived at that very moment; taking both of them by the hand,
he placed them in the sky with his divine hand and wiped them clean.

"Having freed the twice-born man from leprosy and having restored the virtuous woman to a divine form, may there be auspiciousness for both and for all those dwelling at this sacred site who behold them.
Having thus increased their merit with these blessings, they bestowed the granting of boons.
"Having always been happy and having remained long upon the surface of the earth,
you two, as a husband and wife, shall in the end go to the abode of Vaikuṇṭha.
Having spoken thus, she then accepted the auspicious worship offered by them.
Then both Nārāyaṇas, taking him with them on two divine vehicles,
departed for their own world, as did the Brāhmaṇa accompanied by his beloved; at that time,
he became endowed with the beauty of fresh youth, like a god.
The city-dwellers were filled with extreme wonder.
Hundreds of thousands of men there performed acts of worship for the couple;
they became purified, having obtained the fruit of visiting a sacred ford.
Through separation from Sūrya and Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa,
they obtained a divine vision in the auspicious city of Camatkārapura;
having fulfilled their purpose and become free from sin, they remained in the solar field within the abode of the Sun.
The devotees of Hari were born and they always took refuge in Śrī Hari.
Thus, that virtuous woman devoted to her husband, having served her leper husband,
went at the end to the abode of Hari in Camatkārapura in ancient times.
From the recitation, hearing, or even the chanting of this, enjoyment, purification, and liberation certainly come to pass; of this there is no doubt. (62)

Thus ends the four hundred and ninety-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Liberation of the Brāhmaṇa named Kuṣṭhiśara from Saurāṣṭra, a thief of divine property residing in Viṭaṅkapura, through the construction of a Sun-temple at the Nāgamatī river in Camatkārapura and the vision of the Sun and Nārāyaṇa, together with his chaste wife Sudhāmnī," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Chapter 493 → Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:

Listen, Lakṣmī: in the city of Camatkārapura, the two wings of Garuḍa fell due to the blameless devotion of a faithful wife; I shall tell you that. Furthermore, I shall tell you how they were restored by her grace.
In former times, there was a Brāhmaṇa named Mitrabhṛgu, a descendant of Bhṛgu, who was a friend of Garuḍa. He had a daughter named Mādhavī, adorned with all virtues.
Then, for the sake of finding a husband for her, the twice-born sage spoke to Garuḍa.
"Search for a suitable, auspicious, and worthy Vaiṣṇava bridegroom of the Sāttvata lineage who is my equal, so that I may give my daughter to him.
Then Garuḍa spoke thus throughout the entire circle of the earth.
"Placing my daughter upon my back and you as well, I shall cause myself to whirl about.
Then, having personally seen a bridegroom who is worthy of that maiden and endowed with good qualities, give him to her; I shall be the means for this."
Thus addressed by the maiden, that brahmin immediately mounted the back of Garuḍa together with her and went to behold the auspicious bridegroom.
Whichever brahmin or youth that maiden beheld, she indeed regarded him with her heart.
At that time, he did not enter her mind in any way whatsoever.
(8) One who is well-born may be ugly, while one rich in beauty is not of noble lineage; someone endowed with both beauty and noble birth was seen to be devoid of virtues. (9)
One may be endowed with virtues but not possess wealth; one may possess wealth but lack virtues and such.

Even someone described as possessing every excellence has been seen to be physically deformed or mentally deranged. Conversely, one who is physically unimpaired and possesses the aforementioned virtues has been seen following the path of sexual union.
Thus, as a long period of time passed while they wandered daily upon the earth,
a desire arose in their minds to behold the Lord Nārāyaṇa.
They went to the abode of Śvetadvīpa and they went to the Badarī forest.
Afterwards, they joyfully went to the Ocean of Milk and then to Vaikuṇṭha;
they went to the abode of Bali and also to Kuṅkumavāpikā. They went to Bhṛgukṣetra, Vṛndāvana, and Śrī Raṅgaparvata.
They went to Mahendra, Gandhamādana, Meru, and likewise to Svarga.
By them, Satyaloka was reached, and there the sage Nārada was indeed seen. He was questioned with conciliatory words regarding Viṣṇu, the eternal Brahman.
"O Sage, where does the lotus-eyed Lord reside at present? All the abodes of Viṣṇu have been searched by us everywhere;
yet, though we were full of joy, Keśava was not seen there."
Nārada said: "The Blessed One is always present everywhere.
Yet, because you are impure, Keśava was not seen by you there.
He whose mind is free from latent impressions (vāsanā), devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), and has attained divinity [is able to see Him]."
Viṣṇu is seen by those very people who possess desire; He is not seen by others.
Therefore, for the sake of purifying the mind, take up residence on earth in the divine city of Camatkārapura, at the holy site of Hāṭakeśvara.
Right there, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa will join you. To attain Him, go to the city of Camatkāra without delay.
There, at the Mahāsarovara lake during the Cāturmāsya, Janārdana resides.
Nārāyaṇa was reclining upon the waters in the Nāga River.
Then, three [beings] arrived there at the Jalaśāyi lake;
having caused the Brahmin and his daughter to descend into the auspicious field.
Garuḍa said: "The Blessed One himself will be attained through austerity.
Let him achieve purification through austerity, recitation, worship, and vows:
'Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, obeisance to the Master.'"
"Thus, through constant recitation, purification occurs upon the destruction of latent impressions.
Having said this, Garuḍa went there to the presence of Nārāyaṇa.
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, obeisance to the Lord."
Thus, both remained in the midst of the water, fasting and chanting prayers.
The father and his daughter performed supreme austerity without food.
After many years had passed, Garuḍa beheld the female servant.
[He saw] you, Lakṣmī, intent on massaging [Viṣṇu’s] feet and gazing at his face;
and another aged woman likewise seated beside Lakṣmī;
and Śāṇḍilī, emaciated of limb, established in meditation, and observing celibacy.
The king of birds saw another woman of exquisite youth by her side—
Narmadā, the virtuous one who removes the sins of many lifetimes—
and also an old man, a tranquil and emaciated ascetic.
There Garuḍa beheld the great sage Mārkaṇḍeya;
having bowed down to them and to him, Garuḍa was honored by them and slowly [approached].
He beheld Viṣṇu, wide awake, with a smiling face, compassionate toward his devotees.
To him who asked, "From where have you come? the king of birds replied, "I have a dear friend, a Brāhmaṇa born of the lineage of Bhṛgu;
he has a daughter named Mādhavī who is indeed a celibate student."
No husband worthy of her has been found within the three worlds;
indeed, the lotus-eyed one, endowed with all virtues, is her husband.
That lotus-eyed one, who is my equal, dwells within my heart.
"Therefore, O Nārāyaṇa, accept her hand in marriage.
Having heard this, Nārāyaṇa said: "That maiden is an incarnation of Lakṣmī.
Listen, O sinless one, I shall tell you the ancient narrative concerning Vaikuṇṭha."
Once, that Mahālakṣmī became conceited, thinking:
"There is no other woman equal to me, nor even Nārāyaṇa himself;
it is through me and my prosperity that the entire creation shines so beautifully. (37)
"Without me, it would become harsh; therefore, I am in every way the best.
Today I must not go into the presence of Nārāyaṇa;
if his presence here in my house is necessary, let Nārāyaṇa come himself."
Thinking, "He will come; I shall see him and observe what kind of affection he shows," Lakṣmī did not go to the house of Nārāyaṇa.
And Nārāyaṇa, knowing that Jaya was his attendant, spoke thus.
"Today Lakṣmī exists here filled with pride, as if she were a haughty woman.
If she should come to my door, no entrance at all must be granted.
Furthermore, having recognized through divine vision that it is Nārāyaṇa, [she stands] with her face turned away. (41–42)
After a long time had passed, Lakṣmī returned, having abandoned her pride.
But Jaya, the attendant, said: "O Mother, there is indeed no command from Hari;
I am always the servant of Hari, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, and your servant as well. (43)
"Standing here at his door, I must obey his command.
Since I am stationed at his gate, his command is considered paramount. Do as you wish, Mother; the obstruction was ordered by my master. (44–45)
Having spoken thus, he fell at her feet with affection;
she was indeed prevented from entering by that doorkeeper.
Then, considering it an insult to herself, the proud Satī—
Having remembered the lotus feet of Hari, she prepared to cast off her body.
Then, Gṛhalakṣmī became enraged throughout the three worlds, in place after place.
Brahmā, Maheśa, Viṣṇu, Dharma, and Bhāskara learned of this.
Then Candra, Kāma, Kubera, Vahni, Vighneśvara, Anila, the Ṛṣis, the Munis, the Manus,
and Maheśvara arrived there, weeping before Padmā.
And they praised Mahālakṣmī, the virtuous, the compassionate, the sovereign of Hari: "Forgive us, O Blessed Mother, O you whose nature is forgiveness, O Supreme One beyond the supreme,
whose essence is pure being, and who is entirely free from anger and other such passions."
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, you are the peerless model of all virtuous goddesses;
without you, the entire world is like the dead and utterly fruitless.
You are the embodiment of all prosperity, possessing every form for the sake of all beings.
You are the presiding deity of the Rāsa dance; all women are but portions of you.
On Kailāsa you are Pārvatī, while in the Ocean of Milk you are the Daughter of the Sea.
In heaven you are the Lakṣmī of heaven, and on earth you are the Lakṣmī of mortals.
In Vaikuṇṭha you are Mahālakṣmī; in every mouth you are Sarasvatī.
You are Gaṅgā and you are Tulasī; you are Prabhā and you are Pārvatī.
You are Sāvitrī and you are Māṇikī; you are Padmā, Padminī, and Satī.
You are Mañjulā, Bhārgavī, Kambharā, and Satī in mind;
you are Vṛndā, Haṃsā, and Rādhā, the primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti) and the sovereign lady (īśvarī).
You are the beloved of Kṛṣṇa at Bhāṇḍīra, and Candrā in the sandalwood forest.
Virajā was in the Campaka grove on Mount Śataśṛṅga, while Sundarī was in the lotus grove;
Padmāvatī was in the Mālatī grove, and Mālatī was in the Kunda grove;
Kundadantī was in the Ketakī grove, and Suśīlā was in the Kunda grove. (58)
You are Durgā in the Kadamba grove;
you are the Royal Fortune in the royal palace, and the Household Fortune in every home.
Be gracious, O Mother of the worlds; do not go to death, O Lotus-born One!
Having heard this hymn of praise to the gods, Satī ceased her weeping and spoke with great composure;
they too listened with reverence:
"I do not cast off my body now out of anger, nor out of world-weariness."

But consider this: that which exists after death—in that Great Lord, who is all-pervading, equal to all, devoid of qualities, the soul of all, and eternal bliss—therein, grass and a mountain are equal. (62–63)
He who is capable of creating a hundred thousand Lakṣmīs by the mere play of a frown—
what need has he for service if he shows such equality toward his female servant?
I am the chief among his wives, yet now I have been turned away by the doorkeeper.
"O Mistress, even with your servants' servants' servants fully satisfied, my desires will not be fulfilled. Wretched as I am, I shall give up my life;
having made this resolve regarding the fire, may all go well."
A woman who lacks good fortune toward her husband is indeed unfortunate in every respect;
for her there is no happiness in bed or at the meal, and her life is in vain.
The birth of one who has no love for her beloved is purposeless.
Is it then in one's son, wealth, beauty, prosperity, or youth?
Or is it that she has no devotion to the Supreme, who is more beloved than even the most cherished husband?
Such a woman is impure, devoid of dharma, and excluded from all sacred rites. (68–69)
He is the kinsman, the refuge, the sustainer, the deity, and indeed the preceptor;
he is the master superior to all, for there is no preceptor higher than the master.
Father, mother, son, or brother—though they may be distressed—they can grant this wealth.
O gods, the husband is indeed the master of all things for foolish women.
However, only a certain woman—a great virtuous wife, born of an excellent lineage, well-behaved, and a protector of her family—truly knows her husband as her lord. (71–72)
Vows, propitiation, charity, truth, merit, and long-standing austerity—
all these are reduced to ashes and rendered useless for a woman devoid of devotion to her husband.
Therefore, I shall not say anything harsh to my husband, who is my lord.
I shall certainly give up my life due to the offenses of my master.
A great virtuous wife may speak to her husband without harshness when he is at fault; however, if she is unable to endure it, she may lawfully abandon her life. (74–75)
Service to her husband is the vow of women; service to her husband is the supreme austerity.
Service to her husband is the highest dharma; service to her husband is the worship of the gods.
Service to her husband is the highest truth, and it is the praise of all gifts and sacred pilgrimage sites.
The Lord consists of all the gods; he is pure and consists of all the gods.
Janārdana, in the form of the husband, is the embodiment of all merit.
She who is a faithful wife eats the remnants of her husband's meal and always drinks the water from his feet.
"The deities always desire the sight and the touch of her;
therefore, all holy fords purify even sinners from their evil.
Having said this, that great virtuous woman wept indeed again and again.
Brahmā, frightened and with his neck bowed low in devotion, said:
"No good will come to Jaya, the guardian of the gate;
Vijaya as well was a participant in your act of transgression."
Out of fear of offending your beloved, you did not curse those two fools;
yet they will become Rākṣasas because of their reviling of Sanaka and the others.
For if one who is most righteous does not curse an offender out of forgiveness, [he incurs no sin].
His total destruction will certainly come to pass; do not delay, O virtuous one!
(83) Even if you are unable to curse him and have no power to inflict punishment, Dharma indeed inflicts punishment upon a man who has committed an offense. (84)
"Forgive everything, O Mother; go, go to the beloved end-maker!
And appoint me, your devotee, to the task of creation.
Having spoken thus and placing her at the forefront, together with the gods and the lords of sages, [he departed].
He went quickly from there to the presence of Nārāyaṇa to offer praise:
"O Blessed One, bringer of happiness to the gods of gods as well as others, you who bestow the wealth of enjoyments, accept the virtuous Kamalā. || 86-87 ||
"By whom we all have become prosperous, and without whom we are like mere stones—what more is there to be praised? Accept this for the sake of the world.
Having heard the praise of Brahmā and seeing Lakṣmī standing before him, [he accepted her].
To her, who was weeping with a downcast face, he spoke:
"O lotus-born one, I am the omniscient one; I am the soul of all, the protector of all, the teacher of all, and the giver of the fruits of all actions. (1.492.90)
My equanimity is the same toward my devotee, my wife, and my kinsman in all circumstances. Yet, he who is exceedingly devoted to me is far superior even to my wife.
Your two sons, who are my devotees, are gatekeepers as formidable as Death himself. (91)
Forgive my offense and that of those two who are full of devotion. 92.
Filled with devotion to me, the powerful one does not fear the Daityas;
intoxicated by the wine of devotion, he is protected by my discus. 93.
However, I must come to your Creator because of your praise;
I shall come along with my two powerful sons, Jayanta and Vijaya, for the purpose of singing the praises of the virtues of all living beings. 94.
Therefore, my rebirth is inevitable, for I have indeed created the cause for it.
Furthermore, in the course of time, it will come to pass due to the wrath of Sanaka and the others. Listen now to another matter: on this earth, in the region of Ānarta near the ocean... (95–96)
In the city of Camatkārapura, there was a Brahmin named Śāṇḍilya;
desirous of a son, he performed austerities together with his wife. At the end of a thousand years, I appeared and stood before him.
With a serene countenance, he spoke to him for the sake of granting a boon:
"He chose for his wife a daughter equal to Lakṣmī and endowed with all virtues. I replied, "So be it," and thereafter I returned to my state of dissolution.

Śāṇḍilya, joined by his beloved, awaits the arrival of his daughter; however, it was for this very purpose that I brought about this occasion through Lakṣmī. Let her, endowed with Lakṣmī and appearing in the form of a shadow, go unto him.
I never wish for even the slightest fault in Lakṣmī’s devotion to her husband.
Indeed, Lakṣmī’s body is inherently flawed and is merely the nature of a shadow;
let it go to the wife of Śāṇḍilya as a boon for the sake of obtaining a daughter.
When all the gods were addressed thus, they were filled with wonder at Lakṣmī;
for indeed, no one truly knows the heart of Nārāyaṇa.
Then, having heard that, they became peaceful, and Lakṣmī herself was gratified.
By her husband’s command, Mādhavī departed quickly in the form of a shadow.
This very daughter of Śāṇḍilya is known as Mādhavī;
there, Śrī Hari took Lakṣmī in a divine form.
And Mādhavī, devoted to celibacy, desires only me as her husband— me, the Lord of Lakṣmī— and desires no other husband like herself.
O Garuḍa, you do not know this story at all because of your illusory power (māyā).
"Bring that Mādhavī, my devoted wife, into my presence—
she who is a portion of Lakṣmī, the very embodiment of honor, and the daughter of the sage, my beloved; for having seen her myself, I shall afterwards do what is appropriate."
Thus addressed, Garuḍa brought her into his presence.
The Brahmin, having bowed to that eternal Lord, spoke:
"O Blessed One, accept this maiden; she has always desired only you."

"O Blessed One, please come here," he said to her as they all listened intently. With a serene mind, the maiden, who was like Lakṣmī herself, sat down at the side of the Enemy of Mura on a bed to his right.
Then Lakṣmī, her limbs overcome with anger and adopting the behavior of a queen,
spoke to that maiden, considering her a rival wife:
"O sinful woman, since you stand before me, rejoicing in my husband— "
"Having cast shame far away, you have now mounted the bed;
therefore, you will surely become an old woman with a distorted face.
Upon hearing this, the maiden and her father were both overcome with grief. (11.3–11.4)
Viṣṇu himself, Hari, said: "Do not think thus; you shall become Lakṣmī.
To me, she who increases knowledge is considered an elder among the elderly, for she is the enhancer of wisdom.
She is devoted to the knowledge of Brahman; she is Madhuvidyā as well as Mādhavī."
"She shall become the presiding deity of the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā and one advanced in knowledge. Having been told this, that beloved of Hari became Mādhavī and,
in the form of Lakṣmī, the fortunate one dwells eternally in the Ocean of Milk.
Devoted to the celibate life and dedicated to the service of Nārāyaṇa,
Śāṇḍilya, having given away his daughter, felt his purpose was fulfilled.
Then Garuḍa, filled with doubt, questioned Śrī Hari there.
Indeed, celibacy for women is a matter of doubt;
I do not believe in it, especially when they have reached the stage of youth.
It is certain that one who is in the prime of youth and has fallen into the state of an animal [is incapable of it].
"Youth, indeed, must undergo transformation; it is not for the sake of remaining untransformed.
Having heard these words of his, the virtuous Śāṇḍilī, a celibate student and a devotee of Viṣṇu, observing a vow of silence, said nothing at all.
Due to the censure of that virtuous woman, both wings of the lord of birds were instantly destroyed,
and he thereafter became a mere torso,
unable to move even a single step anywhere.
Hari said: "O Garuḍa! Indeed, your two wings have been destroyed by censure because your celibacy was defiled through doubt regarding Śāṇḍilī.
Therefore, having bowed to Śāṇḍilī, propitiate her and become happy."
Garuḍa praised her and bowed down to her again and again.
Being pleased, Śāṇḍilī touched the twice-born man with her hand;
thereupon, wings were produced for him, joined at that very moment.

Having prostrated before Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, Lakṣmī Śāṇḍilī, and the local inhabitants there, as well as the Brāhmaṇa Śāṇḍilya, Garuḍa placed them upon his back and departed for the auspicious holy site of Camatkārapura.

Having installed that Brāhmaṇa, Garuḍa departed for heaven. Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have related to you this account of Lakṣmī’s former life, which is devoted to the virtue of wifely fidelity and which destroys both sin and suffering.
Whoever should hear this, or cause it to be read, or likewise cause it to be heard,
shall obtain enjoyment and liberation, as well as the very rare devotion of servitude in the Abode.

Thus ends the four hundred and ninety-second chapter, titled "The Description of [Events] Beginning with Mādhavī, the Daughter of a Brahmin from Camatkārapurī, Becoming the Wife of the Lord; Śāṇḍilī as an Incarnation of Lakṣmī; the Falling of Garuḍa’s Wings Due to Doubts Regarding Women’s Vow of Celibacy; the Restoration of His Wings through the Grace of Śāṇḍilī; and the Humiliation of the Lord by Lakṣmī for the Purpose of Her Descent," in the first section on the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. 492.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, Lakṣmī! Both Śāṇḍilī and Kamalā performed service for me, Nārāyaṇa, by massaging my feet in the ocean of milk. (1)
Dakṣa was supported by Lakṣmī at my right foot, while Vāmaka was supported by Śāṇḍilī at my left. Then Lakṣmī said to Śāṇḍilī:
"Give me your left foot; it is the supreme wealth for a servant. (2)
The left side is beautiful, with a beautiful woman and a beautiful luster, the part that enjoys pleasures.
(3) Take my right foot, for the left side belongs to me;
the nature of a woman is the left form, while that of a man is the form of half the body. (4)
"In the same way, the good fortune of one who conducts herself thus increases incessantly.
Śāṇḍilī said, "I will not give you [my daughter], for Dakṣa was previously chosen by me. [Dakṣa replied:
"How can you abandon me, who have been chosen by yourself, O daughter of Dakṣa?"
"I must perform service to the left [Vāmā]; I will not give you [to him] under any circumstances.
Lakṣmī became enraged and cursed her: "Become horse-faced!
Śāṇḍilya also cursed Lakṣmī: "You shall indeed become elephant-faced!"
Indeed, those two such [daughters] were born together in the Ocean of Milk in the presence of Viṣṇu.
The Blessed One fell into grief, saying: "O beloved, how has this been done?
Two curses, unfit and most difficult to overcome, have been directed at one another."
Then, being distressed, the two of them spoke to Viṣṇu, who was reclining upon Śeṣa:
"O Blessed One, act in such a way that our release from the curse may occur.
Nārāyaṇa then said: "Indeed, he has been born solely by my will."
By my will, there shall also be the release from that curse.
For the sake of destroying the burden of the earth, I shall go to the surface of the world;
there, this Śāṇḍilī shall indeed become my sister.
"You, Lakṣmī, shall become horse-faced, and you shall become elephant-faced.
There, I shall be the Lord Hari as the son of Devakī.
Now, she who is the other beloved wife of Vasudeva, named Suprabhā—" (12–13).
From her was born Mādhavī, who had the form of a horse-faced Śāṇḍilī.
Seeing that daughter born with such a deformed appearance, Jaṣuprabhā,
together with Vasudeva, fell into the deepest despondency.
She was born endowed with youth, her daughter possessing such a countenance;
yet no one chose her as a bride upon seeing that horse-faced girl.
Then the Blessed Kṛṣṇa [set out] toward Camatkārapura. || 15–16 ||
She was sent away to perform austerities, and she then practiced that penance.
Thereupon, Brahmā, being pleased, spoke to her for the sake of a boon:
"She chose for herself the auspicious, gentle, and beautiful face of a woman."
"Brahmā said, 'So be it,' and she indeed became fair-faced;
renowned by the name Subhadrā, a mother of heroes and beloved of her husband, whom the son of Pāṇḍu, the Pārtha who stays at Kṛṣṇa's side, married. (18–19)
In her was born a heroic son who is known as Abhimanyu;
at the end of time, that devoted wife indeed departed for the abode of Hari. Then Lakṣmī, in the form of an elephant-faced one, went to the land of Ānarta.
She performed penance at that excellent sacred field known as Hāṭakeśvara.
Indeed, she gratified Brahmā with her formidable austerity.
Then, at the end of a year, Brahmā, having attained satisfaction, spoke to her.
"Choose a boon, O Goddess of gods! Whatever dwells in your mind," [Brahmā said].
Lakṣmī replied: "O Lord! I choose that my face be turned toward the east.
Brahmā said: "So be it; you shall become Mahālakṣmī."
Having thus received the boon, that lady of auspicious countenance,
Mahālakṣmī, who is beautiful of form, went toward the one who reclines upon the Ocean of Milk.
In this way, both Mādhavī and the sovereign Mahālakṣmī departed.
Once the deity has been installed in the city precincts, Candrabhāryā will worship Mahālakṣmī and Mādhavī with devotion and true piety;
she shall become endowed with good fortune, possessed of sons, and virtuous.
For as long as a year, she who eats but one meal a day, observes the vow,
and avoids pungent food and salt while worshipping me— such a woman shall experience neither sorrow arising from her husband nor misfortune. (27–28)
However, all incomparable good fortune will come to pass perfectly;
wealth, grain, gold, palaces, and cattle will be obtained.
Having become pure, one should recite this with devotion, or cause it to be read, or cause it to be heard.
Whether a man or a woman, one who hears this shall attain great good fortune.

Thus ends the four hundred and ninety-third chapter, titled "The Description of How Aśvamukhī Mādhavī and Gajamukhī Lakṣmī Later Attained the State of Subhadrā and Mahālakṣmī," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Chapter 493. Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā—Section 1 (Kṛtayuga-santāna).

Now, O Lakṣmī, listen to another divine narrative concerning the land of Hāṭakeśvara— a tale full of wonders and endowed with the power of Brahmanical vows. There was a king named Camatkāra, by whose name that land was graced.
He founded the city of Camatkārapura on the bank of the river Nāgavatī.
For the protection of that city, he established deities;
installed according to the prescribed rites, those auspicious beings protect its inhabitants.
Then that monarch had two daughters:
one named Ambā and another daughter named Vṛddhā; both of them were adorned with virtues.
O Brahmins, he married both of them in the presence of the sacred fire.
Then, after some time, a great war broke out with the Yavanas dwelling in the north; the King of Kāśī met his death,
and the aged mother, too, fell into the sorrowful state of widowhood.
They went to their father’s house located in the land of Hāṭakeśvara,
where for a hundred years they performed supreme and rigorous penance. They performed the daily worship of Durgā, preceded by fire oblations (homa).
Durgā was not pleased; it was not for the sake of destroying her husband’s enemies, but rather [for their own destruction].
Then, having attained a state of world-weariness and desiring the dissolution of their own bodies, they [were addressed] by Brahmins with Atharvan mantras derived from the *Kṣurikāsūkta*.
Having repeatedly cut their own flesh, purified by mantras and offered with devotion,

Then, from that fire-pit, there emerged a woman of four cubits, with a beautiful countenance.

(11) Likewise, another [goddess] with eight eyes and faces, resembling molten gold, emerged from that pit, holding a sword and inspiring fear. (12)
There was yet another such power, most terrible;

some had mouths on their shanks, some on their hips, some on their chests, and some were faceless;

Some had one hand, some two hands, some ten hands, and some were handless;
others had twenty hands, some had many feet, and some were footless.
Some had only one foot, some had their feet turned upward, some had only one eye, and some had two eyes.

Mounted upon birds and other creatures, they dance, adorned with laughter;
many have their hair standing erect, or are disheveled, or have hair covering their limbs.
Others have long hanging hair, hair like that of horses, or short teeth.
There were those with prominent teeth, long teeth, and terrifying elephantine tusks;
those with iron teeth, long ears, deformed ears, and ears like winnowing baskets;
those with spike-like ears, misshapen ears, many ears, and beautiful ears. (23–24)
Some were clad in skins, some were naked, and others were clothed in hair;
they held swords in their hands, spears, arrows, nooses, and bows,
and were adorned with tridents, mallets, bhūśuṇḍis, prāsas, and tomara-javelins.
They set out indeed for the destruction of the Yavana clans;
the kingdom of those evil-minded ones, including their children and the elderly,
was devoured along with its women by those goddesses.

Having thus driven them out from that kingdom, those [goddesses] returned once more to Camatkārapura, which brings about the destruction of the Yavanas. They were honored and installed there by those two widows.
Then they said, "Give us food and clothing as well.

[She also gave it] to those women in this mortal world who are pregnant and sleeping.

Those who, at the time of twilight and at dawn, become addicted to sensual desires and do not perform their ritual ablutions—may your food be the womb of such women! Those who go weeping to the crossroads and to the forests—may your food be the womb of such women! (3.1)
"Their embryos have been bestowed upon you; let them be consumed.
Those who crawl about while impure, and who take delight and sleep—let the embryos of all those women indeed be for your food. (32–33)
That boy for whom the sixth-night vigil shall not be performed will become your food; of this there is no doubt.
Or, he shall not go where the fire is in the birth-chamber.
"He shall become your food, assuming the form of a child. That child who stays in the lying-in chamber—which is devoid of all auspicious rites—is ordained for you. (35-36)
Those children who sleep during the twilight hours in the open air—
all of them are offered to you for the sake of food.
Furthermore, for that person whose birthday falls at the end of the year, if [the rite] is not performed...

Then she gave him a gem-studded staff, two chowries, and a radiant parasol.

"Let Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara construct a dam for it.
Upon hearing these words of King Yama, Brahmā remembered Śaṅkara;
both Viṣṇu and Śambhu arrived, and the Creator of the Universe spoke to them.
"What should be done in this matter? Speak, O Śambhu; speak, O Lord!

For one who is engaged in the true dharma and seeks auspicious goals, how is he to be restrained there, and what is the punishment? Śambhu replied: ||| 33 || "How is he to be prevented there, and what is the restraint?"
"O Yama, tell me, how long does his life last,
so that when that time has arrived, I may lead him to my own abode?
Yama then replied that his lifespan was sixty thousand years.
Five thousand years have already passed for him;
fifty-five thousand remain for the future.
Beholding that lifespan to be so long, Śaṅkara departed.
Assuming the form of a tiger, he roared repeatedly with a sound like the thundering of clouds in the presence of that king. Then,
upon seeing him, the goats fled in every direction.
Then, when they had all been devoured by the tiger,
that lord of the earth discharged weapons charged with mantras in order to slay the tiger.
Śaṅkara seized those weapons, the mantras, and the missiles.

All [the weapons] did not reach the king by way of his own mouth due to the absence of missiles; therefore, he quickly engaged in a duel. At that moment, Śambhu became a tiger, three-eyed and bearing a trident.
The king, immersed in bliss, praised Śaṅkara with joy:
"O Śambhu, you have been insulted by me out of ignorance; please grant me forgiveness.
Śambhu replied: "I have forgiven everything, being entirely well-pleased."
A great deed has been performed by you, such as has never been done by others before. Indeed, the protection of the subjects was accomplished by you in a superhuman manner.
Therefore, O best of kings, come with me to Kailāsa.
Be happy together with this lawful wife of yours.
You must not remain in this world in opposition to Yama,
nor should you remain on the surface of the earth in opposition to the gods.
Thus addressed, that king said, "I shall do as you have told me.
However, the Goddess previously told me: 'When you rise up from the surface of the earth, then [you shall receive] all the missiles, weapons, and mantras.'"
"O Śaṅkara, having given these to me and performed that [rite], I shall depart.
Then Śambhu gave him those weapons, missiles, and mantras.
Thereafter, the king went toward the holy field of Camatkāra to visit Śrī Pārvatī.
Having bathed in the Pārvatī-kuṇḍa on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, the king placed all those items in the water, worshipped them,
and then departed for Sāketa, where Śambhu was waiting for him.
Having entrusted the kingdom to his son, the king departed for Kailāsa with his wife to be with Śambhu; then Śambhu [spoke] to the monarch:
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, obeisance to the Lord."
This mantra was bestowed upon him and a garland of *tulasī* was offered.
Having become a supreme devotee of Viṣṇu, O Lakṣmī, he worshipped Śrī Hari along with his wife;
he departed for Goloka and became eternally liberated.
His son was King Daśaratha, who was exceedingly righteous;
by means of a celestial chariot he would travel to heaven and descend to the netherworlds.
His son was indeed Rāmacandra himself, who is Viṣṇu.
Then, after some time, the astrologers told that king:
"The planet Saturn will cause a breach in Rohiṇī;
because of that, a famine will occur for twelve years."
"In this way, the entire surface of the earth will become devoid of men.
Having heard this, the king set out upon that path where Śani was located;
he pursued Śanaiścara in the celestial chariot given by Śakra.
Having prepared his bow there, he spoke slowly to Śanaiścara:
"Leave this path of Rohiṇī; otherwise, I shall slay you with a smooth-jointed arrow charged with the mantras of divine weapons. (58–59)
Having heard this, Śani said: "Who are you that obstructs me in the sky?
The king replied: "I am a king, the son of Aja, the lord of the earth;
by name Daśaratha, I have come here for the sake of protecting my subjects. (1.496.60)
Śani said: "I have no enmity with you anywhere.
O King, why indeed do you wish to obstruct my path with your bow?
The king replied: "O Śani, you travel by way of Rohiṇī."
"For you shall indeed shatter the cart born of Rohiṇī.
When that occurs, there will be no rain and no production of food.
Because of that, there will be the destruction of the people, the cessation of sacrifices, and the distress of the gods."
Having heard that the path was blocked by Rudra’s hymn, Śani spoke to him:
"I am pleased with your valor, O King, for that which has never been accomplished by anyone has indeed been achieved by you; choose a boon and I shall grant it to you."

"Therefore, for the sake of the welfare of the subjects, I shall not cause separation from Rohiṇī. The King said: "On your day, whoever performs an oil massage, you must by no means cause him any pain for seven days."
"O [Goddess], for one who performs the gift of sesame or the gift of iron on those days,
you must certainly never cause him any suffering for the duration of a year. Indeed,
when there is suffering within your range of movement, you must bring peace to the person who performs the rite of pacification."
"You must not cause affliction for seven and a half years," [he said].
"So be it," Śani replied, and the Lord of the Earth ceased speaking.
Having heard this, Mahendra went quickly to that place.
"O protector of the earth, I am pleased with your wonderful deed.
Choose a boon from me today. Hearing this, the king said to him:
"O Mahendra, may there always be auspicious friendship between you and me."
Indra said, "So be it; let there always be friendship between you and me.
O King, you must come to my abode every evening.
Having spoken thus, Indra departed, and the king went daily to heaven.
Having heard the beautiful songs of the Gandharva women in Indra’s assembly,
as well as the dances accompanied by rhythmic beats and the stories from the mouths of divine sages,
he returns to Ayodhyā every single day after seeing and hearing these things.
Whenever he emerged from the assembly hall of Śakra,
he would immediately have the chariot of Daśaratha sprinkled with water.
Then, on one occasion, Nārada joyfully spoke to that king.
"O King, Indra indeed sprinkles you with water from his own mouth.
Then Daśaratha departed; having returned and settled upon his own throne, he rose and looked toward his seat, which stood at a distance.
Then, by Indra’s command, the servant sprinkled the seat with water.
Seeing Mahendra there, the king asked him the reason for it.
Indra replied, "Until this day, you have remained bound by your debts to the ancestors."
"For one without a son there is no goal, nor is there heaven beyond that.
O King, when a man beholds the face of his son, he attains freedom from debt toward his ancestors, and thereafter [heaven]. (1.496.80)
Thus addressed by Vasiṣṭha, the king, who was then deeply distressed on account of his son, returned home and performed a sacrifice for the sake of obtaining a son.
Kauśalyā, the eldest, gave birth to a son, Rāma, who was like Nārāyaṇa.
Kaikeyī gave birth to her son, the prince Bharata;
Sumitrā gave birth to two sons, Śatrughna and Lakṣmaṇa;
and she also gave birth to one daughter, who became the adopted daughter of Lomapāda.
Indeed, Tāriṇī was granted as a daughter to one who was childless;
he attained freedom from his debt and went to Vaikuṇṭha itself.
Then, after his residence in the forest, Rāma became king.
For ten thousand years and ten hundred years, he ruled the kingdom after the time of Sītā’s death. At the end of eleven thousand [years], a divine messenger arrived. (85–86)
The king of the gods said: "I have come here sent by him;
therefore, listen to his message and make your home uninhabited.
After hearing this, Rāma spoke.
"O Lakṣmaṇa, make it desolate; I hear a messenger of the gods," [he said].
While the conversation was still being carried out, others arrived.
Therefore, having established a vow of silence regarding the matter, the messenger of the gods spoke.
Just as a snake that has fallen from its fangs, or an elephant deprived of its rut,
so too a king who lacks authority is treated with contempt by men.
Who are these who have arrived here, even at this secret discourse?
"Even that which you do not wish to hear in private, though it be but a whisper—having heard it and become deeply incensed, he then said to Lakṣmaṇa:
'Drive the others outside; let no one enter.'"
If any man should come within my range out of delusion, I shall slay him quickly with my own hand; of this there is no doubt.
If I do not kill one who comes before my eyes, then I shall have no standing in the path of Dharma.
"I declare that it shall be so; therefore, remain composed in this course of action. Having said "Om," Lakṣmaṇa stood firm at the door of the palace.
The divine messenger also held counsel together with Rāma.
The destruction of Rāvaṇa has been accomplished, dharma has been established upon the earth, and my full lifespan has been spent here; now, go to Vaikuṇṭha, for it pleases me.
In the meantime, Durvāsas arrived, overcome by hunger.
Agitated, he said: "Where is Rāma? Tell me quickly!
Go, Lakṣmaṇa, go swiftly; otherwise, I shall cast a curse upon you.
By that curse, I will surely consume the entire lineage; of this there is no doubt. (97–98)
Lakṣmaṇa, having shown humility, offered consolation to the great ṛṣi;
yet he, not being pacified, raised his hand to bestow a curse.
Hearing that, Lakṣmaṇa quickly spoke to Rāma regarding the arrival of the ṛṣi.
Rāma said, "Quickly bring in the sage Durvāsas.
Then Lakṣmaṇa immediately ushered the sage inside.
Taking the *madhuparka* offering, Rāma went to his side.
Having offered various kinds of *arghya* water, he welcomed him, saying:
"I am blessed and I am graced that you have come to my home.
This kingdom, these subjects, and all this wealth are yours through your favor."

Thus addressed, the king of sages said: "I am indeed fasting as part of my vow during the Cāturmāsya; I desire to break my fast here at its conclusion. Therefore, O best of the Raghus, quickly grant me food. Then [Rāma spoke to] the sage.
Standing before him himself, the Lord fed [the sage] with sweet foods.
Having eaten and bestowed his blessings, the sage departed as he had come.
Then, taking up a sword himself, Lakṣmaṇa spoke to Rāma.
"Strike me down with your sword and fulfill your vow.
Rāma reflected and said to him, "Exile is worse than death.
Go, Lakṣmaṇa; having been released by me, depart quickly for another land."
"Either the abandonment or the killing of the virtuous is equal to me;
Lakṣmaṇa, you must not see my face again.
Having been addressed thus, he went quickly indeed to the very bank of the Sarayū.
Having bathed and assumed the lotus posture, he emerged through the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*).
Radiant with light, he ascended into the sky and was seen by Rāma and all embodied beings.
They all departed, and they beheld the lifeless body of Lakṣmaṇa fallen upon the ground.
The kinsmen and others wailed piteously;
having prepared a funeral pyre of sandalwood and other materials, they then placed the body upon it.
Then a voice from the sky spoke: "O best of the Raghus, do not offer the fire."
"O Rāma, this kinsman of yours has gone to the abode of Brahmā.
You must go to that very realm only after taking with you Sugrīva—who is devoted to you—and Vibhīṣaṇa, who is likewise devoted, as well as Lakṣmaṇa. (11.2–3)
Then Rāma, having taken Sugrīva and Vibhīṣaṇa with him, departed toward the southern direction by means of the Puṣpaka chariot;
he returned to his own city, leaving Lakṣmaṇa behind in that vehicle.
Having installed Kuśa and Lava upon the throne, he departed for his own abode.
And the best of the Raghus, assuming a second form,
protected Vibhīṣaṇa— who was long-lived— in Laṅkā for the sake of the affairs of state.
"Because the bridge has been destroyed so that the Rākṣasas may not cross it,
O beloved, through hearing and reciting this, there shall be both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

Thus ends the four hundred and ninety-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Suppression of King Ajāpāla’s Diseases in the Form of a Flock of Goats, the Obstruction of Daśaratha’s Cart of Rohiṇī by Śani, and the Departure for Vaikuṇṭha according to Rāma’s Vow," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: There are sixty-eight sacred pilgrimage sites on the surface of the earth;
listen, O Lakṣmī, for I shall proclaim them, which indeed purify embodied beings. (1)
Somanātha, the great holy site; Revatācala in Saurāṣṭra;
the holy site of Kuṅkumavāpikā, as well as the holy site of Dvārikā;
Camatkārapura, the holy site; and the Nārāyaṇa-sarovara lake.
Arbudādri is a great sacred site (tīrtha), and Puṣkara is the most excellent sacred site.
Hiṅgalājī is a great sacred site, and likewise Haridvāra is most excellent.
The region of Kāśmīra is a sacred site, as is Badrikāśrama.
The sacred site of Kedāranātha, the purifying Kurukṣetra, the holy field named Śālagrāma, Kāmākṣī in Kāmarūpa,
the Pāśupata shrine in Nepāla, and Kapilāśrama by the ocean.
Likewise, the sacred field of Muktinātha, the abode of Mahālakṣmī;
the holy ford of Hariharakṣetra, as well as the city of Jagannātha;
the sacred field of Gayā, and the supreme holy ford of the city of Sāketa.
The sacrificial pits of Paraśurāma, the region of Mathurā,
the great holy site of Siddhapura, and also Prayāgarāja;
the sacred field of Kāśī, the Daṇḍaka forest, and likewise Śrī Tryambaka.
The Oṃkāreśvara Tīrtha and likewise the excellent Śuklatīrtha;
Bhṛgukṣetra, the Tīrtha of Śrī, and the confluence of the Narmadā and the ocean;
the birthplace of Kalki, Saṃbhala Tīrtha, and the Tulasī situated on the Candrabhāgā.
Aruṇādri is a great sacred site (tīrtha), and Śrīśaila is a most excellent sacred site;
the two Kāñcīs are auspicious sacred sites, and Cidambaram is purifying.
Janārdanakṛta is a holy field (kṣetra), and Bhūtapurī is a most beautiful region.
The field of Kumārikāsatī and the purifying Dharmāraṇya;
the great field of Rāmeśvara and the Mallikārjuna Tīrtha; the Tīrtha of Malaya Mountain and the purifying Tāmraparṇī. || 12-13 ||
Ujjayinī, Mahākālavana, and Naimiṣa forest; Mount Mahendra, the great holy site, and likewise Viśālākṣīvana;
Kālañjara, the great field, and likewise Gokarṇaka field.
The holy site of Amarakaṇṭaka, likewise Sāptagodāvara;
the holy site called Trikūṭa on the Vindhya mountain, and Pakṣitīrthaka;
the holy site of Mahākailāsa, and the confluence of the Tāpī and the ocean. (15–16)
The field of Paraśurāma, the hermitage of Jamadagni, Sutīrtha,
the holy ford of Pulaha’s hermitage, and also Kāverītīrtha;
the field of Vārāhatīrtha, and also the field of Ṛṣabha.
Nṛsiṃhācalatīrtha and Mīnākṣītīrtha as well—
these sixty-eight, O Lakṣmī, are indeed the great sacred fields (mahākṣetra) and beginningless holy sites (anāditīrtha) that exist upon this earth.
There are also thirty-three other crores of sacred fords (tīrthas).
There are likewise stars, virtuous ones, gods, sages, and ascetics;
as well as truthful women, chaste wives, and maidens devoted to their husbands.
There were female ascetics and male ascetics devoted to the vow of celibacy; likewise, there were most virtuous and wondrously gifted eminent renunciants,
as well as other cows who remembered their past lives, and Vaiṣṇava devotees.
The Śaivas, Sauras, Gāṇapatyas, devotees of the Goddess, and the Śāṅkaras;
the Brāhmās, Cāndramasas, devotees of Īśa, and those devoted to Vahni;
as well as the Sādhakas, Māntrikas, and those who enter the bodies of others. 23.

O Lotus-born One, wherever those who possess spiritual accomplishments dwell, as well as those free from passion, the virtuous, the supreme *paramahaṃsas*, and the practitioners of *sāṃkhya* and *yoga*— those places are sacred pilgrimage sites (*tīrtha*).

Even insentient objects are capable of destroying sins; indeed, sentient beings are holy places (*tīrtha*) that act as the makers of holy places for the insentient. For all abodes of deities are indeed holy places.
The dwellings of the guru and the gurus themselves are always sacred fords (*tīrtha*), O beloved.
Having delivered one from *saṃsāra*, they establish them in the state of Īśvara;
or rather, those sacred fords are indeed the washers away of sins in liberation.

The husband is a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), the father is a sacred ford, and the devoted wife is a sacred ford; the chaste woman is a sacred ford, the cow is a sacred ford, and the virtuous are the most excellent sacred fords.
The teacher is a sacred ford, Hari is a sacred ford, and the gods are always sacred fords.
Knowledge is the supreme, pure sacred ford; devotion is the sacred ford beyond that. Service is the best of sacred fords; worship is the sacred ford, the highest of all.
Through worship, every human goal, even those most difficult to attain, is obtained.
Service to Hari and service to the virtuous are the holy place, the most excellent of all holy places;
indeed, whatever other holy places there may be, they have their root in them.
"Oṃ namas śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine namaḥ."
Thus, japa is the supreme sacred ford that makes one a great Vaiṣṇava.
"Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa is my Lord; no other is considered my Lord"—this is proclaimed as the sacred ford of self-surrender. (33–34)
Indeed, the offering of one's gross, subtle, and internal [faculties] as service is itself a sacred ford (*tīrtha*);
whatever action causes Kṛṣṇa to be pleased is truly a sacred ford. Dancing is a sacred ford for the celestial nymphs; that by which Janārdana may be satisfied is indeed a sacred ford.
By that through which Mādhava is pleased, singing is the sacred ford for women;
by that through which Nārāyaṇa is pleased, instrumental music is the sacred ford for musicians;
and by that through which the Lord of Vraja is pleased, desire is the sacred ford for the gopīs. (36–37)
Meditation is the sacred ford for those possessed of yoga, by which Keśava is pleased. Thus,
regarding this as the supreme ford and knowing Śrī Kṛṣṇa to be the bestower of desired fruits,
the wise man, having surrendered everything to Him, should accumulate liberation.
"From reciting and hearing this, the fruit of all holy places (tīrthas) shall be attained.

Thus ends the four hundred and ninety-seventh chapter, titled "The Description and Enumeration of the Sixty-Eight Holy Places, Other Spiritual Holy Places, and So Forth," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
