Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to this wonderful tale of the Brāhmaṇas.
The king, the lord of Ānarta, being well-disposed, [bestowed] boons upon the Brāhmaṇas. 1.
Having summoned him, he prostrated himself again and again and said:
"Whether it be gold or elephants and horses at the transit of the sun into Capricorn—
whatever anyone desires to give, I am willing to grant even the entire earth."
"Grant your favor to me, who am wretched and prostrate before you.
(3) The Brahmins replied: "We are always followers of the duty of non-possession;
we are ascetics who subsist on alms. What need have we for elephants, horses, or gold? (4)
King Camatkāra said: "O purifiers of the world, you who are holy ones, please accept this gift for the sake of purifying the royal fortune.
There are seventy-two Brahmins present here on the riverbank."
Having constructed leaf-huts, those who travel through the path of the sky always go with devotion to various sacred fords by the power of their asceticism;
and having performed recitation, ritual bathing, and libations, they indeed return once again.
In Vārāṇasī, or at Prayāga, likewise at Puṣkara and Naimiṣa;
at Aśvapaṭṭasara, Prabhāsa, and Kedāraka—
somewhere they go during the transit of the sun (saṃkrānti), and they also go during the Cāturmāsya period.
"O twice-born ones, on this day and at this solar transit, on the bank of the Nāgavatī,
accept my gift and perform purifications for us!
Though addressed thus, those brahmins, being detached, departed for Puṣkara.
When the sun entered Capricorn at the time of the transit, for the purpose of staying for five nights,
the king, having learned all of that, then spoke to his beloved Damayantī:
"Take gold ornaments, garments, and excellent wealth."
"Go to the bank of the Nāgā river, where the wives of Brāhmaṇas dwell.
Give them their ornaments and other belongings as they desire; their husbands do not accept gifts from us. (1.2–1.3)
"Women will certainly accept gifts such as ornaments;
whatever kind of ornament a woman wears, she will do so. Having thus promised, she took many ornaments. (14)
Jewels, pearls, and corals, as well as beautiful earrings;
likewise, necklaces radiant as the moon, large anklets, and those inlaid with sapphires, great lapis lazuli, and cat's-eye gems. (15–16)
Taking with him rubies, diamonds, and enchanting māṇikya gems,
as well as divine armlets, bracelets, chains, and golden threads,
he went indeed to Nāgavatī to bathe on the occasion of the Saṃkrānti festival.
Having arrived, they brought large quantities of sesame seeds and sweet foods;
having bathed and set down this mountain of great ornaments on the bank,
they waited for the recipients of the gifts at the river's edge.
In the meantime, the female ascetics arrived, filled with curiosity;
having learned that Damayantī, the beloved of the king, had come for the purpose of giving alms, they wondered:
"What is that queen like? What is her form, and what are her ornaments?"
Filled with curiosity, the wives of the brahmins gathered together. Having arrived, they paid their respects, and the queen spoke these charming words:
"I have dedicated this collection of ornaments to the one whose banner is Garuḍa."
"Today, on this day, a gift bestowed upon Brahmin women yields fruit;
therefore, let the female ascetics accept these ornaments given by me according to my desire. Let them be many ornaments; please grant me this favor. (23)
Then one among them said, "Give this pearl necklace of mine to her.
Having heard this, the king’s wife herself washed her feet and gave the pearl necklace to her,
along with divine garments.
Likewise, perceiving that another desired a necklace, she gave her a necklace;
and knowing the mind of a third, she gave her two earrings.
Then the remaining female ascetics took the ornaments for themselves.
Whatever ornaments she gave to them, she gave each with joy.
As those female ascetics took up the ornaments,
so too did delight arise within Damayantī.
She then cast forth other [missiles] by the hundreds and thousands, saying, "Let them be seized! The beloved of the king remained silent;
however, all of them were indeed seized by the female ascetics.
"No satisfaction arises for them," the queen then said to them again:
"Let contentment be made; having gone, I shall bring [them] back again and again.
Having spoken thus, she departed quickly and returned swiftly, taking [them] with her.
He repeatedly bestowed infinite ornaments, garments, and wealth upon the Brahmin women for a period of five days.
Indeed, the female ascetics also wore those various clothes.
And with longing and great satisfaction, they adorned their limbs with ornaments;
they constructed huts filled with wealth, garments, and jewelry.
Then, four Brahmin women, adorned with bark garments and deerskins, [appeared]. (33–34)
Not wishing to accept the gift, they did not come near her;
however, on the fifth day, the queen,
taking costly ornaments for the sake of obtaining their consent, went quickly toward them.
The queen said to them all, "Let favor be shown;
let these ornaments indeed be accepted for the sake of decoration. But the female ascetics were dispassionate, always following the will of their husband.
Those devoted to their husbands said: "The minds of husbands do not belong to them [the wives].
If a wife adorns her body without her husband's permission, she incurs sin;
therefore, we shall not accept yours."
"We have no need for ornaments; we are adorned by our bark garments.
While they were thus conversing with her at that moment, their four husbands arrived at the hermitages by way of the sky.
Then Śunaḥśepa, Śākreya, Boddha, and Dānta as the fourth—these alone remained;
all the others, having suffered a loss of their celestial status, resorted to the path of the earth due to their craving for their wives and the fault of accepting gifts of ornaments. (41)

Seeing those four wives of the sages and the adorned maidens, they were overcome with agitation and cried out, "What is this? What is this? By whom have these ornaments been given that the female ascetics have been thus mocked? (42–43)
"Having given us wealth and garments, this hermitage of ours has been transformed.
Then the ascetics spoke indeed to King Camatkāra:
"This queen Damayantī is currently present here; by her—"
Ornaments and garments were bestowed upon all of them.
This very [woman] stands ready to give these to us as well; however, we did not accept them, and she was forbidden and turned back. (45–46)
Having heard this and seen her, the brahmins, due to the exhaustion of their ascetic merit, cursed her; listen, Lakṣmī, to the power of penance!
"O Queen, seventy-two of us went to Puṣkara for the purpose of bathing."
By means of their ascetic power, they traveled through the path of the sky with a speed like that of the mind-wind.
These four arrived, accompanied by their wives;
the others did not, for they fell from the celestial path at Puṣkara.
For virtuous women, the power of their chastity is great;
yet that celestial power has been lost through the acceptance of gifts.
By means of wealth, you have deceived this hermitage of ours from its ascetic merit.
"By means of gifts such as ornaments and the like, you shall indeed become a stone here.
Then that queen praised them for the sake of liberation;
and there they spoke of her as Mādhavī, Śāṇḍilī, and born from a portion of Kamalā.
A maiden of the Vipra caste will arrive and effect your deliverance;
in no long time at all, that Mādhavī will come.
She, in the form of Lakṣmī, shall indeed remain upon a stone on the riverbank.
She will become like Ramā in the very form of a stone maiden.
Listen, Lakṣmī! Having learned of that entire account regarding the stone maiden who had appeared at that very moment in the presence of the Brāhmaṇa, [he spoke]. 54–55.
The king arrived there quickly and grieved swiftly for his wife; meanwhile,
the four Brahmins, having taken their family,
traveled by way of the sky to the Himalayas, a place free from obstacles for ascetics.
Touching the stone and repeatedly recollecting the virtues of his beloved,
the king lamented for a moment and performed a *śrāddha* ceremony for that devoted wife;
the monarch then had a mansion constructed upon it.

He himself performed worship daily with camphor incense and other offerings, as well as with garments, saffron, and sandalwood; he also caused the brahmins to perform it. Then, sixty-eight auspicious twice-born ones traversed the earth on foot.
Having arrived at the bank of the Nāganadī, exhausted from having traveled a very great distance,
they saw those adorned with ornaments; and upon learning the circumstances,
they understood that the cause of their descent from the sky was the receiving of gifts.
Having realized that Damayantī had turned into stone,
they then took up water for the purpose of destroying King Camatkāra’s kingdom;
for our movement through the sky had been thwarted by their greed for the gift.
The minds of the Brahmin women became passionate and filled with desire. Thinking, "Let the king and the kingdom suffer the fruit of that," the wives of the Brahmins began to utter a curse. (63–64)
They restrained him excessively, saying, "A curse must not be given under any circumstances;
for we have been adorned by the wife of the king with divine garments and ornaments, with a mind purified by faith. (65)
"Afflicted by the fault of poverty, we have resided in your house;
yet we have not obtained in this mortal world the happiness arising from clothing, ornaments, and the like.
For ascetics alone is the next world a source of happiness. (66–67)
For those of low birth who remain attached to sense objects, there is only pleasure in this very world;
but for householders established in austerity and dharma, there is constant happiness in both worlds.
Therefore, we, abiding in dharma, must enjoy happiness here.
Thus, having always enjoyed the comfort of garments and ornaments,
and having practiced the duties of a householder, the service of our husband, and the worship of the gods,
we shall attain the two unsurpassed worlds.
Therefore, O Brahmins, you should take land from this king,
as well as a means of livelihood and beautiful houses;
having accepted these, you should then look toward the birth of sons and grandsons.
"And there will be happiness for the young maidens, especially for their kinsmen.
If you do not carry out these words spoken by us, we shall all give up our lives; of this there is no doubt. (72–73)

"Endowed with the sin of killing a woman, you shall go to the Raurava hell. Hearing this curse, the water held upon the surface of the earth was released at their word; that earth then became infested with saline soil.
Then, having heard that news, the king rejoiced and arrived;
at the word of the brahmins, the king had a city constructed for the purpose of bestowing land, wealth, and treasures upon them.
Adorned with walls, moats, gate-towers, and rows of palaces,
that city named Camatkārapura was truly marvelous.
There, sixty-eight Brahmin families resided.
The king had them appointed [to office] and even provided them with a livelihood.
Thereafter, that Lakṣmī, Mādhavī, and Śāṇḍilī indeed arrived before long at the city on the Nāganadī river to see the town.
Having bathed, that virtuous woman then sat for a moment upon a stone; Damayantī was restored to her former female form as she had been before.
Bowing to the Brahmin women, she was joyful, as if having just awakened from a dream.
He went to Rājagṛha, and the king held a great festival;
he gave as a gift sixty-eight villages that bestow happiness. Furthermore, O beloved, he gave four lineages of Brahmins and others as well. (81–82)
Sixty-four remained there and went to the Himalayas;
by them, sacrifices were duly performed with abundant oblations and excellent sacrificial fees.
When the sacrifice was completed, the king became severely afflicted by disease.

In that matter, there was indeed a reason concerning a certain Brāhmaṇa of the three castes: his offering of touched substances yielded cruel results. For the sake of testing that man of the three castes, water was prepared as a divine ordeal by means of fire.
A pit was pointed out there, and it was said that whoever experiences a rash upon bathing therein should be recognized as a *trijāta*; thus it was done by him.
Having been tested in this manner, that Brahmin was expelled and went to the forest.
He performed austerities while remembering Hara, and Hara became pleased.
"Choose a boon," Hara said; the Brahmin replied to Śaṅkara:
"Having cast out the defect of being born three times, grant me the highest and most exalted status. (87–88)
And Śaṅkara gave him a mantra—not poison, not poison—which by its mere utterance causes serpents to become venomless;
indeed, they would even meet their death [if otherwise]. "Take it and go to that place."
Having received this mantra, that twice-born man went to the city.
At that time, the twice-born residents of the city were indeed afflicted by serpents;
however, those twice-born men were protected on all sides by the mantra of Trijāta.
All those eminent Nāgaras, beginning with the Trijātas, remained there;
they were all devoted to Kṛṣṇa and worshippers of Hāṭakeśvara.
At that time, they received the mantra from the god Hāṭakeśvara.
"Oṃ, obeisances to Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Lord; obeisances!
(9.3) Both men and women constantly performed worship and japa.
Others went to Goloka, O beloved, and others continue to go there through such worship. (9.4)
Thus has been narrated the marvel of the ascetic Brahmins.
By reading or hearing this, one’s desired fruit shall be attained.

(95) Thus ends the four hundred and ninety-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Fall of the Sky-traveling Brahmins due to the Acceptance of Gifts of Jewels, Gold, and Other Valuables by Damayantī, the Wife of King Camatkāra; the Transformation of Damayantī into Stone through the Curse of the Brahmins, and Her Restoration to Royalty and Return to the City through the Touch of Mādhavī," in the first section on the Continuation of the Kṛta Yuga of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. (498)

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī! I shall tell you the divine and enchanting story of Bhadrikā, and the divine story of Revatī; understand it from me.
In the city of Camatkārapura, the Nāgas, out of devotion to Hāṭakeśvara,
indeed come from Pātāla and dwell here and there.
Once, a certain twice-born man [approached] a young Nāga named Rudramāla.
One named Kratha struck him pointlessly with a club in the water today.
Then he cried out, "Alas! I am killed!
His mother was a serpent, and at that time serpents arrived there, assuming human forms.
That boy gave up his life; the serpents, enraged and terrifying, rushed toward the destruction of the brahmin, while the brahmin fled to his hermitage.
Having gone there, the fierce snakes devoured him along with his family.
The sister of that brāhmaṇa, afflicted by the sorrow of childhood widowhood,
was a virtuous woman devoted to celibacy and dedicated to devotion to Kṛṣṇa.
At that time, the female ascetic named Bhadrikā cursed the serpent-woman.
"O Revatī, mother of the Nāgas, may you and your entire lineage meet with destruction!
Having received this curse, Revatī propitiated Pārvatī.
Then, after a few days, the Great Goddess was pleased with her.
"Grant me a boon," she said; Revatī replied, "I am the giver of boons. She requested this boon: "May the curse upon Bhadrī be destroyed.
Pārvatī said, "The destruction of the curse shall never come to pass. (1.499.10)
However, that serpent Takṣaka shall indeed become King Raivata in Saurāṣṭra;
he will be born in the region of Ānarta, and Kṣemaṅkarī will be his beloved wife.
A daughter will be born to them, and you shall become human.

Then Śeṣa himself will become your husband there. For the sake of obtaining a bridegroom for you, my departure toward Brahmā will last but a moment; indeed, it is there that the expansion of your lineage shall take place.
Thinking thus, "He will meet his destruction," there will be the extinction of the lineage;
yet, your marriage with Balarāma will take place once more.
Furthermore, the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa will bring about the destruction of his own family.
"Indeed, by the curse of Kaṇva, the curse shall bear fruit there in that very manner.
Having been addressed thus, Revatī departed for Pātāla and reported the remainder of the events that had transpired on earth to Śeṣa.
Then that Brahmin woman named Bhadrikā, being a widow,
heard the discourses of the scriptures from the mouth of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa;
she undertook pilgrimages to sacred sites and festivals of the gods, and practiced devotion to Nārāyaṇa.
Then once, Takṣaka arrived upon the surface of the earth;
seeing the beautiful Bhadrikā on the bank of the Nāgavatī,
he led her to the netherworld (pātāla) in human form, and Bhadrikā likewise led him there.

He cursed him, saying: "Having become a human together with your wife, you shall then experience suffering that brings about the destruction of your lineage. Takṣaka, overcome with fear, praised that auspicious lady.
Bhadrikā said to me, "Lead me back again to that spot on the earth.
Then she was brought by Takṣaka toward Camatkārapura;
subsequently, due to public scandal, she entered the funeral pyre.
While the elders of the people were watching, when Bhadrī was not burned, the horse Romaśa was likewise unharmed; the people were struck with wonder,
for the fire had become cool since Bhadrī was pure.
Then a great rain of flowers fell from the sky.
The pure gods said: "O Subhadrā, you abide in supreme purity;
there shall be no other virtuous woman equal to you."

O virtuous lady, among the thirty-five million hairs upon a human body, not even a single hair of yours has ever been touched by sin. You are a chaste and faithful wife, devoted to Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa as your husband.
Having become a renunciant, that goddess took refuge in Sāṃkhya-yoga.
"Serve the virtuous, perform meritorious deeds, and worship Keśava.
Having heard this from the god Janārdana, Bhadrikā made her request.
Then Kṛṣṇa, having assumed the form of a brāhmaṇa, descended to the surface of the earth.
He bestowed upon her the auspicious initiation and placed a garland of tulasī around her neck.
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya pataye namaḥ. (Om, obeisances unto Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; obeisances.)
Having spoken thus, the twice-born vanished from sight after reciting the Karṇa-mantra three times according to the rules.
Bhadrikā then constantly worshipped Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa;
there she performed supreme austerity, subsisting only on food obtained through alms.

And on the Nāga River, there arose an excellent holy ford (tīrtha) named after her called Bhadrikātīrtha, which produces wonder; by bathing there, one becomes free from sin. Then that Bhadrikā, having reached the end of her time, attained a divine body.
Having become [liberated], she indeed went to the abode of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. (33) Thus, O Lakṣmī, the power of virtuous women grants liberation and destroys sin;
through devotion to Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, this certainly comes to pass—of this there is no doubt. (34)
O Lotus-born One, by reading, hearing, or even reciting this, one shall obtain enjoyment,
liberation, excellent prosperity, health, and lordship.

Thus ends the four hundred and ninety-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Mother of the Nagas becoming Revati through the Curse of the Brahmin woman named Bhadrika, Takshaka’s human birth, and the Liberation of Bhadrika through Devotion to Krishna," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī, to the story of Karṇotpalā, the wife of Brahmā. In ancient times, there was a lord of the earth renowned as Satyasandha.
He had a daughter named Karṇotpalā who protected righteousness;
she was a partial incarnation of Lakṣmī, equal to Kamalā in her marks and lines.
Seeing that young woman fit for marriage, the lord of the earth—
And he reflected repeatedly: "To whom shall I give her?
There is no suitor worthy of her here upon the earth, nor in heaven, nor in the netherworld; therefore, I shall go to the Grandfather."
"In this matter, I shall certainly give my daughter to whichever suitor Brahmā shows me; indeed, I will not give her to anyone else under any circumstances.
Then, taking his daughter with him, he went to the world of Brahmā.
And for a moment the world-lord Brahmā was intent upon the worship of Kṛṣṇa.
At the conclusion of the worship, that king, true to his promise, bowed respectfully along with his daughter and spoke to Brahmā with humility: (6–7)
"O father, I have come from the mortal world into your presence.
I am the king Satyasandha, renowned in the land of Ānarta.
This daughter of mine, named Karṇotpalā, is a portion of Kamalā."
"No suitable husband for her is to be seen anywhere else in the world.
Therefore, tell me of a husband for her, so that I may give her to him.
Having heard this, Brahmā said to him: "Listen, O King, regarding Vṛṣa."
A daughter should be given in every way to one born of her own lineage, who is senior in age, for the sake of dharma, fame, and the prosperity of the family.
This very daughter of yours has, in the mortal world, assumed the status of an elder sister.
Listen now to how the old age of all those kings occurred here:
three yugas have passed while you have remained in my presence.
O King, those mortals on earth whom you previously beheld have all gone by.
Another creation has now arisen upon the surface of the earth; however,
those great seers who dwell here in my world of Satya do not,
under any circumstances, take human women as their wives.
The physical form of phlegm, urine, and excrement is utterly contemptible.
(15) If this girl, through her ascetic penance, should effect a change of body, the god of love will take your daughter, who will possess a divine form. (16)
"O Indra among kings, go therefore from here to the world of mortals with your daughter, who brings you joy by name and has surpassed Rati in beauty as your second wife.
In due time, you must give your daughter to Kāmadeva."
Thus addressed, he descended to the surface of the earth together with the maiden.
As he looked about, he saw that where there should have been dry land there were bodies of water,
and in the places where there should have been water, there had appeared various wonderful stretches of dry land.
Even when questioning others about other worlds, as well as the various duties established in that region, he did not understand his connection with anyone—
not even regarding sons, grandsons, servants, elephants, horses, and so forth.
All those kinsmen met their end during that interval between the ages.
Then, at that very moment, that mortal lord of the earth was touched by the wind,
and both he and the maiden were seized by old age, with white hair upon their heads.
With broken teeth, covered in wrinkles, deformed, and withered in body;
unpleasant to behold, with sunken eyes, and ancient—such was that king, trembling at every step. (23)
He asked the men, "What country is this, and what city is this? (24) Then the people said to him, "This country is named Ānarta;
the king here is called Bṛhadbala, and the city is the port of Prāpti. (25)
"This river is Śubhramatī, and this bathing place is known by the name Gartātīrtha.
Having heard these other names, the king was struck with wonder.
Afterward, having bathed in the river, that king grieved for a moment.
Accompanied by his daughter, he went toward the present-day Bṛhadbala.
Satyasandha said to him, "O King, learn from me what has transpired:
'In former times, I was the lord of Ānarta, known as Satyasandha. (27–28)
"I had a daughter named Karṇotpalā, endowed with excellent virtues;
she remains here with me, equal to Lakṣmī and a portion of Ramā herself.
Therefore, I have come from here to Satyaloka for the purpose of giving her away."
I remained there for a moment to question the divine Grandfather (Brahmā).
O King, during that time many more yugas passed away;
by the time I returned from Satyaloka and beheld the surface of the earth, [it had changed completely].
All water has turned to land, and both forest and city are as if unknown to me; yet they are perceived by men.
Your name was given to me, and so I have come into your presence.
O Lakṣmī! King Bṛhadbala, having heard about his ancestors of the lineage, and seeing Satyavrata arrived there as he had been told, became extremely overwhelmed;
with tears of joy in his eyes, he fell at his feet.
He said, "Welcome, O King; a most hearty welcome, O Father!
This kingdom, which was once my own, has been protected by me as your servant.
O Father, give gifts at your pleasure and rule your own kingdom."
Then that king, having embraced his own kinsman, the king, smelled him on the head and sprinkled him with eyes full of tears. He said:
"The kingdom has been governed by me; much charity was given in the past."
"I have performed sacrifices, foremost among them the horse-sacrifice, with complete sacrificial fees;
therefore, I shall practice austerities together with this daughter of mine.
Bṛhadbala said to him, "O King, do as you wish."
"The great kingdom is yours alone; either accept it or perform ascetic penance.
O Indra among kings, I have heard all this through tradition:
that the king, true to his promise, departed taking the maiden with him. (1.500.40)
Furthermore, after he had not returned for a long time, his son named Suhaya was consecrated as king by his excellent ministers.
I am his descendant, born in the seventy-seventh generation in due order.
"I am a man who has been uplifted; I am blessed by the sight of you.
O Grandfather, perform penance at Gartatīrtha together with your daughter, so that I, along with my attendants, may eternally serve your feet."
"I shall undoubtedly attain the highest good; let favor be shown.
Then the subjects, the Brahmins, and the men and women born in the kingdom, filled with curiosity, came together to see the one true to his promise.
Bestowing blessings, they honored him with great joy. (45) Then the king and the maiden, having reached the riverbank, constructed a leaf-hut there and both performed supreme austerities. (46)
Having installed Gaurī there, Karṇotpalā constantly worshipped her with devotion; and then the king likewise worshipped Śaṅkara.
Mahādeva, being visibly pleased, arrived there with a serene countenance.
He said to the king, "Merit increases through austerity;
tell me, what shall I give you here? The king chose liberation.
Śambhu replied, "Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa himself is supreme liberation. (48–49)
"The Lord will give you [this]; take this garland of *tulasī*.
Having said, "Take the mantra: *Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine namaḥ*," he gave him both the mantra and the garland.
Śambhu vanished; the king worshipped and chanted the praises of Mādhava.
(51) Then King Vṛhadbala met his death.
By Satyasandha, means of livelihood and other necessities were bestowed upon the brahmins. (52)
When the day had passed in this manner, Gaurī became pleased with the maiden and spoke to her directly: "O daughter, I am pleased; tell me your desire.
Karṇotpalā said: "For my sake, my father has undergone great hardship."

Having been deprived of my kingdom and family while seeking my husband, I, a maiden who had grown old, performed austerities out of renunciation. Then, O Gaurī, by your grace, I have become a fresh young woman once more. (54–55)
"Act so that I may be beautiful, endowed with form and youth;
likewise, let my husband be the most excellent among the best of gods, possessed of perfection of form, youth, and the like, and long-lived. (56)
"O Mother, act in such a way that my father may be satisfied.
Gaurī replied: "On the third lunar day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, on a Saturday, under the constellation presided over by Vasu, [I shall grant] youth."

"O beautiful one, by forming a mental image [of me] and bathing in the river, you will then become possessed of a divine body, endowed with fresh youth; of this there is no doubt. Devote yourself to Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa."
"Oṃ, obeisances to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; obeisances.
Always chant this mantra and likewise perform meditation on Hari.
Through austerity and devotion, you shall obtain everything desired; perform it for even a moment.
Having spoken thus and given the mantra of Kṛṣṇa along with a garland of *tulasī*, Gaurī vanished; and the maiden acted exactly as she had been instructed.
On the third lunar day, conjoined with Saturday and the asterism of Vasudeva (Śravaṇā), [she performed the rite].
Having meditated upon her own beauty, good fortune, and fresh youth,
she entered the water at midnight; and at that very moment,
she emerged from the water, enriched with fresh youth and beauty.
Then, commanded by the illustrious Brahmā himself, Kāmadeva, filled with affection, approached for the sake of a wife and spoke to her:
"I have been sent by Brahmā, endowed with fresh youth and beauty."
"With the permission of Pārvatī, I have come here for your sake.
Indeed, I am Kāmadeva, the long-lived Lord of Rati;
my wife is named Prīti—become her forever, do not delay! (66–67)
Karṇotpalā said, "Go and request my father himself for my hand;
a maiden can never act according to her own will in the presence of her father.
Therefore, having gone there first, I shall remain there as a maiden, O handsome one."
"You shall come later and joyfully entreat me for her hand.
Having spoken thus and prostrated before him, the maiden departed from her father.
Then her father, beholding his daughter in the full bloom of youth, [gazed upon her].

Filled with wonder, he asked about the cause of her beauty and youth. The maiden said, "O father, by the grace of Gaurī, through merely bathing in the river, I have obtained beauty, fresh youth, and a new body. (71)
Having propitiated Hari, as well as the beloved Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Goddess obtained everything;
and for my sake, she secured a husband who was graced with beauty, charm, splendor, and youth. (72–73)
"Sundara, the bearer of flower-arrows, has been sent; he too shall come into your presence. Upon seeing him and having entrusted me to you, become happy.
Having spoken thus, the father gazed upon his daughter, who was equal to Kamalā.
"O daughter, today the fruit of my asceticism has been realized," he said to me. In the meantime, Kāma approached the king and, having bowed, said: "O King, give me your beautiful daughter."
"Instructed by Brahmā and likewise permitted by Pārvatī,
I, Kāmadeva, have come here in person for the purpose of choosing her as my bride.
Then, he offered that maiden in the presence of the Fire-god.
And she, born from the practice of Rati, became his beloved named Prīti.
Having taken her, Kāma went to the world of Kāma, which possesses excellent kings.
Satyasandha too, his soul delighted upon seeing his daughter filled with happiness, departed.
United with her beloved husband, she indeed became one who had accomplished all that was to be done.
Having firmly established the lotus posture at the aperture of Brahma,
the knower of yoga drew the self out from the body along with Brahman.
He went to where that daughter, the beautiful Suputri, resided in the world of Kāma. Then, having taken that second daughter who possessed such beauty and other virtues,
and having given her as a single form to Kāma, he bestowed another body upon him.
The king, having been liberated, took his daughter Muktā along with his attendants and,
together with the liberated associates of Hari, attained the eternal abode of Goloka.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, Karṇotpalā [attained this] through devotion as well as through austerity.
Prīti, the wife of Kāma, became liberated and attained liberation.
And the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa was propitiated by the queen of Bṛhadbala for the sake of a son; Mādhava appeared in the form of a brāhmaṇa.
Having approached, he bestowed his mental offspring in an instant;
the son born from Nārāyaṇa became a rememberer of his former births, possessing a lifespan of twenty years and equal to Nārāyaṇa in virtues. (86)

A treasury of wonders such as the science of archery and the science of the Vedas, there was a king named Aṭacandra, known as Camatkāranarādhipa. Whoever hears this, or even causes it to be heard with a spirit of devotion, [attains the aforementioned treasures]. (87–88)
One attains the complete accomplishment of the fourfold aims of life; of this there is no doubt.
A maiden or a woman always obtains good fortune with joy.
[She also gains] enjoyment, liberation, prosperity, a son, grain, wealth, and so forth.
She obtains good fortune and a mass of merit; of this there is no doubt.

(1.500.90) Thus ends the five-hundredth chapter, titled "The Description of King Satyasandha’s Daughter Karṇotpalā—Who is a Portion of Kamalā—Traveling to the World of Brahmā in Search of a Husband, Then Returning to Earth to Become the Wife of Kāmadeva under the name Prīti, and Her Liberation through a Second Form," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. (500)

Chapter 502 →
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the captivating story of the sage Yājñavalkya.
There was a tiger among Brāhmaṇas, renowned as Śākalya.

Born in the lineage of Bhārgava, a master of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences (vedāṅgas), he resided in the city of Vardhamāna at Dharmāraṇya, surrounded by disciples and grand-disciples. He was a constant bestower of knowledge, adorned with the attainments of yoga and other such perfections.
Yājñavalkya became his disciple, devoted to his service.
And Śākalya was the domestic priest of King Vardhamāna;
he performed the duties of the priesthood in all the king's affairs.
And at dawn, he urges Yājñavalkya,
his most excellent disciple, to bestow blessings; Yājñavalkya also, having bathed in the morning, always goes joyfully to give his blessings.
Once, however, at dawn, the teacher Yājñavalkya was found without having bathed and clad in soiled garments. He then said this to Yājñavalkya: "Go quickly to the king."
Thus he engaged him for the sake of peace within the royal palace.
Having performed the recitation of the *śānti* mantras followed by the silent chanting (*japa*), Yājñavalkya departed.
He then proceeded toward the king to offer the water of propitiation (*śāntyudaka*).
The king also, seeing that the sage had not bathed, became apprehensive;
on that day, he neither accepted the water nor the words of blessing.
And the king spoke an untruth: "O best of the twice-born, I have not bathed."
"Unable to speak the truth to the sage who has not bathed, [the king said]:
'Therefore, pour this water upon this piece of wood brought into the hall.
Yājñavalkya, too, having understood the reason for his own lack of bathing, [spoke].
Realizing it was his own humiliation, he threw water upon the wooden post.
At that very moment, by the power of the touch of the water, the wood became covered with sprouts and was instantly endowed with branches and fruit.
Seeing this wonder and feeling remorse, the king spoke these words again in truth: "O Sage, I have indeed bathed;
however, out of fear of you alone, seeing my own impurity, I did not take up that water."
"Therefore, O Brahmin, perform my consecration so that I may have a son.
Yājñavalkya then replied: "O King, you are full of doubt;
at present, you are unworthy of receiving my consecration."
O King, spiritual preceptors are always pure, as are virtuous brāhmaṇas, whether they have bathed or not; for they are the very body of Lord Hari.
Among them, those who are learned are even more so, and among them, those who possess divine opulence are the most exalted.
Whether they be accomplished *siddhas*, Brahmins, gods, or radiant celestial dwellers,
even those who have engaged in sexual union with women are purifying when they have not yet bathed—
provided they are devoted to the perfection of mantras, the perfection of *brahman*, or the perfection of austerity. (18–19)

In that regard, one should never perceive impurity in the guru, the virtuous, the gods, Lord Hari, the father, the mother, the husband, the truth, or the cow. Desire, anger, greed, harshness, latent tendencies, and attachment— these [are the stains].
All divine things there are fit for enlightenment; there is no fault in their being used. For even the dusty earth, when touched by his feet, becomes purifying.
Water from the streets, when mixed with the Ganges, destroys sin just like the water of the Ganges itself.

One who eats only what is granted by the grace of Viṣṇu is indeed considered a liberated soul while living; he is remembered as a Guru who is constantly devoted to austerity, pure, peaceful, and learned in the scriptures.
Indeed, such a Guru becomes the purifier of all sacred fords (tīrthas).
Among all those worthy of veneration, the father is considered most venerable;
the mother is a hundred times more venerable than the father, and the deity is a hundred times more venerable than the mother.
Furthermore, the giver of the mantra and the giver of the tantra are each four times more venerable than the gods.
The Guru is supreme, the destroyer of the mass of sins, and the bestower of liberation;
the Lord Nārāyaṇa himself should be regarded as the Guru.
Here, the Lord is the manifest Ishvara, the Master who grants deliverance.
It is heard in the Śruti that an offering is given to him with the words, "To the God.
One's own Guru is the direct enjoyer; he himself is the embodied Janārdana.
The Guru is Brahmā, the Guru is Viṣṇu, and the Guru indeed is Śiva himself.
All the gods and others always dwell joyfully in the guru.
When the guru is satisfied, Hari is satisfied; and when he is satisfied, the deities are satisfied.
Purified by his splendor like fire and wind, he is equal to the sun in brilliance.
A Vaiṣṇava twice-born man who is a devotee of the Viṣṇu-mantra is indeed a Guru.
Upon seeing such a radiant Guru, one should receive everything from him—
mantra, water, prasāda, and blessings— without any hesitation.
The exclusive Guru is the God who may uplift hundreds of thousands of men,
he whose auspicious and inauspicious actions are offered at the feet of Viṣṇu.
Merely by receiving his mantra, one becomes liberated while living.
Having pierced the entire cosmic egg, he causes one to reach the abode of Hari.
O King, you have been deceived today by my illusory power and are suspicious of me;
water shall never again be given by me to one who is full of suspicion.
Especially when one begs after seeing profit for one's own sake,
the sages must never give to such a self-interested person or to an atheist.
Therefore, O King, you are not a fit recipient for the gift of consecration.
"I shall go to that very place where my guru resides.
The king said to Yājñavalkya: "If you grant me the consecration, I will give you garments, vehicles, and riches."
The sage said: "That mantra indeed does not manifest for me at the conclusion of the fire-oblation;
therefore, water of such power will not arise again.
O King, I am going home; what you desire cannot happen today."
Having spoken thus, the best of sages quickly went to his own home. On the following day at dawn, Śākalya himself went to give his blessings to the king; then the monarch [received him].
Having prostrated before the sage, he said: "That disciple who was sent by you yesterday should be sent again to my house for the sake of peace.
Having replied, "Certainly," the Guru indeed took up the offerings of worship.
Having summoned Yājñavalkya, he spoke again with reverence:
"Even now, go to the palace for the sake of the king’s peace;
especially since you have been summoned by the lord of kings, my son."
Then Yājñavalkya said: "O twice-born one, there is a king who is an atheist and filled with pride; therefore, I shall certainly not go back to him.
When I was about to offer water for his consecration..."
"Throw water on that wood," was said by that man of evil intellect.
I too quickly threw water on the wood, and then the wood immediately sprouted new shoots; seeing this, the king fainted.
Śākalya said: "Having observed your capability, that king is calling for you again; go to him with honor.
Kings should be served and never disregarded at any time. (47)
Servants may even ascend upon a king who is shaking them off.

One who is equal in honor and dishonor, who understands the king's mind, who always knows the proper time, who endures all things, who is patient, and who is wise—such a person indeed becomes the king’s favorite. (48–49)
"Even my command must be obeyed by you; go, my son, toward the king.
Yājñavalkya then replied: "I will not go toward an atheist.
Listen, O true Guru, for the destruction of Dharma exists here in four ways."

"O Guru, for whichever disciple the turn to go occurs today, the first fault is the breaking of that [turn], and the second is the fault of violating the proper order. Furthermore, not going when it is my turn is the fault consisting of the violation of my word. (51–52)
"Thirdly, there arises here for me the fault of violating the King's wish;
fourthly, it consists of the defect of failing to yield fruit. Therefore, that must not be done by me.
If you thus compel me against my will to join with him—"
"Having abandoned you, I shall go elsewhere; I will not go toward him.
Thus addressed, Śākalya became filled with anger and said to him:
"After having understood even a single syllable from a teacher, [one must not disregard him]. ||55||
There is no fee on this earth which, having been given, would leave a disciple free from debt.
Therefore, either obey my command or abandon my knowledge.
Otherwise, I shall cast a curse upon you; go elsewhere as you please.
Thus addressed, Yājñavalkya then performed a vomiting of that knowledge;
having bowed to his teacher, he said: "Behold the knowledge vomited forth!
Not even a single syllable of yours remains within my belly. (57–58)
"Therefore, I am not your disciple, nor do you stand as my guru.
Now, by my own will, I shall depart elsewhere; salutations be unto you.
Having spoken thus, [he departed for] that which bestows perfection, named Hāṭakeśvara.
He went to that sacred field and there worshipped the Sun;
self-restrained, restricted in diet, and devoted to celibacy,
he performed difficult penance after having established the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the Gāyatrī.
Satisfied, the Sun, while still in human form, spoke to him at the end of the year:
"O Yājñavalkya, choose whatever you desire; I, the Sun, shall grant it all to you.
Having bowed down, Yājñavalkya chose the Vedic knowledge.
Likewise, Sūrya spoke of another supreme Brahma-vidyā pertaining to mantra and tantra: "I shall indeed grant you the siddhi of *laghimā*.
Having become light, enter into the vicinity of my horses' ears and remain there. (63–64)
"Quickly undertake the practice of the Vedic sciences from me.
Thus addressed by him, he then resorted to Vājikarṇa;
from the Sun he studied the Vedas and taught them to Janaka.
The sage indeed imparted the knowledge of Brahman to his two wives:
Maitreyī was the first and eldest, and Kātyāyanī was the second.
Yājñavalkya had these two wives, and his son was Kātyāyana.
In the end, she taught all the sciences to Kātyāyana.
Once, Śāṇḍilī bestowed auspicious wisdom upon Kātyāyanī;
by means of that, on the bank of the Nāga river, she attained detachment.
The virtuous woman neither bathed nor ate, nor did she engage in laughter;
with eyes filled with tears, she remained merely sighing.
Day after day, Śāṇḍilī indeed gave her instruction.
Listen, O virtuous lady: my father is Śāṇḍilya, the foremost of sages.
I am his only daughter, born as a girl named Mādhavī.
I perform the appropriate service for my father at the time of the fire-oblation.
"I constantly bring wild rice and other grains for him.
Once, after some time had passed, the sage Nārada arrived at my father’s hermitage; being weary, he was attended to by me. (72–73)
Having been bathed, fed, and massaged with great devotion, he sat upon a seat and was then questioned by his mother with humility:
"O Sage, this is our only daughter; she remains here in our old age. (74)

Therefore, quickly proclaim her husband, who brings about such great happiness. [Tell me] of whatever vow, restraint, austerity, oblation, or recitation, or whatever mantra has been practiced by which she may have a gentle husband endowed with excellent qualities. (75–76)
Affectionate, with a serene countenance, speaking kindly and indifferent to his own pleasure or displeasure,
the venerable Nārada, having heard this, spoke of the supreme worship of Gaurī:
"Let your daughter go to the sacred field of Hāṭakeśvara and perform it."
"By the blessing of Gaurī, your daughter shall obtain a husband.
Thereupon, Gaurī went first to that auspicious place out of jealousy toward Gaṅgā;
then she reflected: "Which goddess shall I worship? (78–79)
Thinking, "So that other women may always worship me for the sake of good fortune," she worshipped herself with devotion,
having fashioned her own image from clay and placed it upon a single seat in one spot. (1.501.80)

And with the *ātmaprāṇāgnihotra* mantras as well as those of the *Atharvaveda*, that female ascetic of firm vows, having joined herself to these— earth, water, fire, air, and space— within her physical form, [performed the rite]. (81–82)
He worshipped Gaurī with flowers, incense, and unguents;
Śaṅkara, his mind drawn by her mantra, went there with haste.
"O Goddess, I have come, drawn here by your power, Gaurī."
"How is it that you perform this worship of your own form?
Gaurī forcibly draws me toward you in your presence.
Therefore, come to Kailāsa; tell me if there is any fault in me. (84-85)
Pārvatī said: "You bear Gaṅgā upon your head along with your wife;
therefore, I will not go until you abandon your beloved.
Śambhu replied: "King Bhagīratha, having performed most rigorous austerities..."
Tapa indeed requested me for the purpose of sustaining the Gaṅgā.
Having perceived that the force of the Jāhnavī was falling from the sky toward the surface of the earth and would otherwise go down into the netherworld (pātāla), he appointed me to the task. (87–88)
It was for this very purpose— that she might remain here— that I held her thus. Having slowly reached the Himalaya, the auspicious abode, by means of my head,
she will surely go to Bhārata for the purification of embodied beings.
"Having transformed her into the very nature of water, I shall give her to you, my father.
Come to me, my dear, my beloved; may you always possess good fortune.
You need not fear any co-wife, for she is not married to me."
"Neither a wife, nor a female slave, nor any other woman in the capacity of a spouse has taken refuge here; therefore, come to my very home.
Having spoken thus, Mahādeva caused Śivā to mount the bull.
Having ascended it herself, she later went to Mount Kailāsa.
"Let her quickly propitiate this Gaurī, your daughter;
then she will obtain a virtuous husband who brings her joy and fulfills her every desire. (93–94)

Having spoken thus, Nārada departed for the world of Satyaloka thereafter. By me and by Kumārī, with devotion, Gaurī was worshipped during the vow on the third day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, with food offerings, perfumes, and ointments.
"By her power, this brāhmaṇa Jaimini has become a husband [of such status].
Therefore, O auspicious lady, you too should worship her with a concentrated mind;
O beautiful one, you will obtain excellent good fortune equal to that of Maitreyī."
Having heard everything that was proclaimed by Śāṇḍilī, Kātyāyanī performed the Mārga-tṛtīyā vow and the worship of Gaurī.
Then her husband arrived and took her by the right hand.
Having sent her home with great honor,
he thereafter always lived with her in joy,
even more so than with Maitreyī.
Kātyāyanī gave birth to the excellent son Kātyāyana;
the son of Kātyāyana was Vararuci, an abode of virtues.
O Lakṣmī, hear of the power of Kātyāyana; I shall tell it to you.
Long ago, something consisting of living beings emerged from the earth—unprecedented, fierce, with black teeth and terrifying;
with spike-like ears, a thin mouth, upright hair, and ravenous hunger. (102–103)
Drawn by the powerful king with mantras,
that great and mighty [being] then rushed again and again toward the gods to devour them.
Abandoned by the powerful king, it was repeatedly struck by the gods.
Nevertheless, he sustained no injury when cast down upon the surface of the earth.
Then the gods sat down all around him;
Brahmā entered his belly, while Śakra and the others stood at his sides.
At that time, the Daityas, commanded by Śukra, arrived with their wing [of followers] to slay the gods; then the Lord Viṣṇu himself spoke to Bhūta:
"Listen, Bhūta, for your sake, regarding the matter between the gods and the Daityas."
A battle would surely occur here; it is certainly not auspicious.
May the gods and the Daityas dwell within you as if they were friends.
I shall thus perform your worship; you are considered by name to be Vāstu.
"There, I shall offer you food; accept it with devotion.
Then he accepted it with a mind free from doubt, and said:
"Whoever does not perform worship for me in this new place..."
"Perhaps some human being might become my prey.
When this was said, Viśvakarman replied, "So be it," and performed the rites;
Kātyāyana then constructed the house and worshipped the site-deity (vāstu).
Kātyāyana performed the entire Vāstupūjā in the sacred field of Hāṭakeśvara; from that time,
the worship was established so that one would never incur any defect arising from the house.
Whether it be made of stone, produced from a bad site, or even born of a poor foundation—
on the third day of the month of Vaiśākha, the worship of Vāstu was performed in ancient times;
by performing that worship, one's house shall become equal to a kingdom.

Thus, O Lakṣmī, this most excellent narrative has been told to you, which bestows enjoyment, liberation, great good fortune, a husband, sons, and other blessings. (116) Thus ends the five hundred and first chapter, titled "The Description of Yājñavalkya, the Disciple of Śāṇḍilya, Making Dry Wood Put forth Sprouts; the Emission of Knowledge by Yājñavalkya and the Marvels of his Son Kātyāyana; and the Worship of the Vāstu-Puruṣa," in the first section on the Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga within the *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*. (501)

Chapter 503 →
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī! In ancient times there was a sage named Hārīta who lived in the stage of life of a forest-dweller (vānaprastha). His wife was named Pūrṇakalā.
Seeing that virtuous and devoted wife, adorned with beauty, generosity, and youth,
and resembling Lakṣmī herself, Kāmadeva was indeed infatuated.
Beholding her bathing naked, he abandoned his affection for both Prīti and Rati.
Thinking that place to be secluded, he fell asleep for a moment on the bank.
Sighing repeatedly, he feigned curiosity while remaining within her sight, like a person who is sick and wretched.
She too, perceiving a certain auspicious, helpless mendicant in such a state, approached his side to give him some fruit and food for his meal.
Meanwhile, Kama, established in youth and radiant like fire, [appeared].

With eyes full of desire, firm and beautiful in every limb, he became impassioned and amorous in a mere moment. But Pūrṇakalā, seeing him thus impassioned in that secluded place, [was moved]. || 6–7 ||
Her body trembling from the exertion caused by the act of chewing,
she was quickly pierced by his arrow and became filled with longing.
She sat down beside him, laughing repeatedly as she touched him.
Being especially tormented by the arrows of desire,
that devoted wife drew lines upon the ground with her finger while gazing at his lotus-like face. Evening had arrived, yet Hārīta had not come to her.
Having learned this, he came for a long time to search for her where that virtuous woman was staying; yet, even after so much time, he did not obtain union with her.
Then Hārīta, seeing that virtuous and devoted wife, became infatuated with her.
Seeing him causing her such delusion and speaking with a mind full of passion,
he perceived the state of desire within Kama's heart and spoke out in anger:
"O sinner, because you have thus afflicted my wife with arrows..."
"Unaware of this, that virtuous woman, devoted solely to the duty toward her husband, is being deceived;
for one of handsome form, desiring to enjoy my beloved, has become afflicted with the disease of leprosy and thus appears loathsome. (14)
"In this way, you will be released from your own wife; of this there is no doubt.
Thus addressed, he prostrated himself and spoke this reply to Hārīta:
"O Sage, I indeed saw your wife through mere delusion."

I have neither eaten [forbidden food] nor committed any misconduct at all now; therefore, I am not a fit object for a curse. Grant me forgiveness, O treasure-house of compassion. Sin is threefold: mental, verbal, and born of action.
Sin born of mental anguish—that which is mental—is removed by [meditating on] Him;
verbal sin, however, is destroyed simply by recitation or even by mere praise, through His very grace, wherever it was committed. (18–19)
Through the prescribed expiations, one may go beyond the sin born of action;
that which is born of action—whether performed physically, mentally, or verbally—is not truly committed [if undone].
By Your grace, it shall perish; therefore, be gracious in every way.
Hārīta said: "That desire arises due to the power of the body.
First, everything is conceived by the mind; immediately after that, it is spoken by speech, and then it is performed through action. (2.1–2.2)
"For the mind is indeed the first [cause] in all actions and is thus faulty;
therefore, its restraint here has also been accomplished by me.
Through the propitiation of the Sun alone, your leprosy shall vanish."

"Having become my wife, this Khaṇḍaśilā shall, by the merit of worshipping the Sun, become a virtuous wife in an instant. Having spoken thus, the sage Hārītaka departed for his own hermitage. ||24-25||
Pūrṇakalā became a stone, and Kāma consequently became afflicted with leprosy.
On the bank of the Nāganadī, he performed worship while meditating upon the Sun;
at the end of a month, the Sun arrived and indeed destroyed Kāma’s leprosy.
Having touched the stone and restored his virtuous wife Satī to her former state,
Sūrya bestowed the Nārāyaṇa mantra upon her and departed for heaven; Kāma went to the abode of Kāma, and Satī went to the house of Hārītaka.
Having then prostrated before her husband, she who was in truth purifying departed; that virtuous woman served him with devotion and took refuge in Hari, Nārāyaṇa:
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, obeisance to the Lord."
She constantly chanted the mantra and became a divine Vaiṣṇavī. Then, a maiden named Dīrghikā would indeed come daily from within the house to her presence for the purpose of service.
Thinking that the leaf-hut was in close proximity,
he would always remain by the side of the full-moon orb at the tree in the courtyard;
and on the altar within the hall, he would chant the mantra of Śrī Hari.
"Oṃ, obeisances to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; obeisances! (3.3).
By the power of chanting this mantra in this way, the maiden indeed attained a divine body; she became a traveler of the sky and possessed unobstructed spiritual perfections. (3.4)
That daughter of the sage Vīraśānta was indeed Dīrghikā;
she was exceedingly tall in stature, increasing the laughter of the people.
No one sought her hand in marriage upon seeing that she was so very tall.
He who marries a woman whose hair is excessively sparse, or one who is too tall, or a dwarf,
shall meet his death within six months;
for this reason, people do not take her as a wife.
Then, having attained detachment, she performed most severe penance;
she repeatedly practiced Cāndrāyaṇa and Kṛcchra austerities,
as well as Pārāka rites as prescribed and Sāntapana penances.
Thus, as she remained steadfast in her vow, her splendor increased greatly.
By the power of her asceticism, the capacity to travel through the sky arose within her;
consequently, she went to the assembly of Mahendra on occasions such as festivals.
When she departed from the assembly of the gods for her own home,
Indra’s servants sprinkled water upon her seat.
Seeing that sprinkling, she questioned Purandara.
"O Śakra, seeing what fault of mine is my seat being sprinkled?
Indra replied, "O daughter, you indeed have a physical defect;
though you are still a maiden, you have reached the censurable time of menstruation."
And even now you have not been married; that impurity still remains within you.
For union with a husband during the fertile period is what purifies women.
Therefore, choose a husband by whom you may attain purity.
Having heard that, she went throughout the earth— at crossroads and triple junctions—
and raising her right hand, she spoke for the sake of obtaining a boon:
"If there is any twice-born man of noble birth, let him take my hand."
"I shall now give half of my ascetic merit to him.
As she spoke thus, the people laughed at her and joked with one another.
A certain leper Brahmin then addressed the pond:
"I shall marry you after performing the ritual grasping of your hand.
Then he took the hand of that maiden, and she then said to her husband: "Tell me, my lord, what service may I perform for you?"
The husband said, "I intend to go to the sixty-eight holy pilgrimage sites;
if you are able, do so with me as your companion.
Thinking, "Oh, what great fortune! the devoted wife then quickly [prepared].
He had a beautiful, auspicious bamboo hut constructed, which was easy to access and furnished with soft cotton seats; then he said to his husband:
"O Lord, please ascend my charming palanquin upon your shoulders."
"I shall take you to all the sacred fords and auspicious fields.
Thereupon, the leper, greatly delighted, sat down in his small hut.
She, having placed him upon her head, [carried him] to all the sacred fords at her ease.
She wandered through all the sacred fields, bathing her own husband.
Through bathing at the holy sites and through the power of her devotion as a *satī*, her husband’s leprosy was cured.
A constant diminution of his leprosy was observed, and he became even more radiant with splendor.
Thus, at the onset of night, she reached the sacred field of Hāṭakeśa;
resting her basket in the shade of a tree on the bank of the Nāgavatī river,
she took rest, while her husband remained on the riverbank.
Having risen slowly in the morning, the one known as Māṇḍūka went to bathe, leaping over the mass of leaves with his staff;
meanwhile, the king of sages, Māṇḍavya, was sleeping upon those very leaves. (57–58)
Touched by the foot of Māṇḍūkeya with his staff while staying between the leaves, Māṇḍavya—who was unaware of the path of travel—became alert.
He said: "Who is this great fool who has struck me here with his foot and staff?"
"That sinful man strikes me and causes the breaking of my sleep!
May your death surely occur even before sunrise!
Having heard this, Māṇḍūkī bowed down to him again and again.
Nevertheless, this son of Māṇḍavī did not attain satisfaction.
Having bathed quickly and returned to the vicinity of the tree, the son of Māṇḍūkī spoke to his wife as it had happened: "Perform the final service."
"And due to the curse of Māṇḍavya, I shall die before the sun can be seen [again].
Then the Dīrghikā said: "If my devotion to my husband is true—if I have performed pilgrimages according to the rules and served my husband with sincere devotion—"
"If my vow of truthfulness remains unfulfilled, let there be no sunrise here!"—
when he had spoken thus, the Sun-god suddenly brought about a paralysis of the horses in the vault of the sky;
because of that, the Maker of Light did not rise.
A great night had set in, and all were deprived of the rising sun. All sacrificial rites and other ceremonies were obstructed, leaving everyone in a state of extreme distress;
likewise, the ancestral offerings, Vedic studies, acts of charity, and whatever other religious duties there were, were all suspended.
All the supports of the sun were especially obstructed;
all the gods, intent on heaven, were deprived of their sacrificial shares.
Having become miserable, they all went to where the Maker of Day was.
"O Lord, why indeed do you not bring about Udayana's rise?
O Master, without you, this entire world has fallen into turmoil.
The Sun replied: "Out of fear of a devoted wife, there shall be no rising for me."
Therefore, let all the gods go and speak to her on my behalf,
so that by following her words I may attain a happy prosperity.
Otherwise, being devoted to her husband, she will surely curse me in her anger.
That queen of the gods conducts herself with the ascetic power of devotion to her husband.
Who is capable of making her word otherwise?
For this reason, I am afraid and do not emerge at all.
A woman who has attained the state of devotion to her husband realizes that fruit;
indeed, whatever fruit is produced by a thousand horse-sacrifices, that she obtains.
Thus, due to the power of such supreme austerity, I am afraid of a truthful wife.

"Then let the gods go quickly to where that devoted wife resides. (75) Then the gods arrived at the pond and said to her: "O devoted wife! Since the sun, the maker of day, has been stopped by you... (76)
"O auspicious lady, that auspicious deed was not performed; the ritual activity centered on the sun has perished.
Therefore, O wise one, let the Sun rise at your word!
For it is from him, O fair one, that sacrificial rites, recitations, and fire-offerings proceed."
Then Dīrghikā spoke with anger to Māṇḍavya:
"My husband has indeed been cursed; he shall die at sunrise. Therefore, I have obstructed the sun from rising. (78–79)
"Without my beloved, I have no need for the rising of the sun;
I have no need for funeral rites, acts of charity, or any other duties.
Then those gods, having deliberated, spoke with humility:
O blessed lady, let this beloved husband of yours rise;
having regained his bodily form, may he live once more at that very moment,
appearing like another God of Love twenty-five years of age.
And you, having become a fifteen-year-old maiden, shall behold [him];
thus you will achieve the highest happiness in this world according to your own desire.
At sunrise, the body of your husband will have met its end.
"Once again we shall restore [our youth]; indeed, grant us the rising of the sun.
Having been addressed thus, Satī agreed, saying "So be it," and spoke further:
"Just as the gods declare that the couple possess ever-new youth... (84-85)
"By that truth, O Udaya Bhāskara, you shall cause our two [suns] to rise.
As soon as this was spoken, the eastern quarter instantly became bright with dawn,
and the entry of Aruṇa was seen upon the Mountain of Dawn (Aruṇādri).
Just then, sunrise occurred, and the keeper of the pond fainted.
Touched by the rays of the gods, he rose once more, twenty-five years of age, able to assume any form at will, and exceedingly handsome. (87–88)
Dīrghikā also became fifteen years of age,
exceedingly beautiful, divine like a goddess, possessing a touch like that of a god, and equal to Kamalā.
The gods spoke with respect to her, who was devoted to her husband along with her consort.

"Choose a boon, O virtuous and noble lady; there is nothing that cannot be granted to you. She replied: "From this day forward, let my name be known throughout the three worlds as 'Dīrghikā,' the river-tirtha."
"May I attain the abode of Hari, the imperishable place of liberation, together with my husband. To her they said, "So be it," and the gods departed.
Then, having enjoyed happiness for a long time, that devoted wife—
When she had reached an advanced age and beheld her beloved husband dead,
this chaste woman, devoted to her husband, went with him to the world of Brahmā.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, has this supreme Dīrghikā-vrata been described to you.
"By reading, hearing, reciting, or even practicing [this], both woman and man shall obtain worldly enjoyment and liberation; of this there is no doubt.

(95) Thus ends the five hundred and second chapter, titled "The Description of the Leprosy of Kāmadeva, who was infatuated by Pūrṇakalā, the wife of Hārīta; the transformation of Pūrṇakalā into stone and her subsequent restoration; and the paralyzing of the Sun by Dīrghikā through the merit of serving her husband, as well as her attainment of fresh youth and liberation along with her husband," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
