Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the story of the sage Jābāli, which brings about liberation.
Jābāli was the son of the ṛṣi’s servant woman named Jabālā. (1)
He was indeed born from the seed of a Brāhmaṇa;
by him, through lifelong celibacy from his youth, asceticism was constantly practiced—Kṛcchra, Cāndrāyaṇa, and Pārāka penances, performed gradually and steadily. (2)
By him acting thus, the gods were indeed brought within the sphere of fear.
Then the gods, having assembled, held a consultation regarding the obstacle;
they dispatched Rambhā, who was to be the destroyer of his celibacy.
Celibacy is rooted in austerity and is a great means for accomplishing perfection.
From childhood, Jābāli was a celibate student and was great in spiritual luster.
Devoid of union with women, he did not know the nature of desire.
And in order to disturb him, the lords dispatched the god Spring with his weapons,
as well as Kāma, Rati, and Prīti. By the command of Indra, they all went to the land of Hāṭakeśvara.
In the vicinity of Jābāli’s leaf-hut, Kusumākara suddenly brought about the exquisite beauty of an aśoka tree with its clusters of blossoms;
he likewise bestowed the splendor of *tilaka* and mango trees with their budding flower-stalks and the like.
The lotuses attained a supreme blossoming on all sides;
a fragrant southern breeze, which awakens the god of love, blew.
In that interval, Rambhā approached the presence of that sage.
The sage watched her as she, too, cast off her garment and entered the nearby water to bathe.
Beholding her naked, he fell under the sway of desire.
Then, with all his limbs covered in horripilation, he became agitated.
Rambhā emerged from the water, clothed herself in half a garment,
and, appearing wet, went to the sage’s side and bowed with a smile.
He spoke sweetly, "O Brahmin, is all well in the hermitage?
The sage replied, "I am always well, and my welfare is increased by your arrival.
Who are you, O goddess or human woman, who increases the passion within me?"
Rambhā said: "How is it that there is perspiration on your body and such a transformation?
The sage replied: "From the sight of you, this perspiration has arisen in me from the god of love (Manmatha), even though I am devoted to celibacy and abide in a great vow."
Rambhā said: "If this is so, then enjoy me as you please;
there would be no fault in this, since I am approaching you of my own accord.
I am an Apsaras, the wife of a celestial being; I am devoted to you, so enjoy me. (17)
"He who would reject a woman who has come to him of her own accord, tormented by desire— he,
scorched by the sighs of that woman, is utterly ruined.
Having spoken thus, she embraced that great sage.
Thus he took his pleasure with her until the end of the day;
then, having reached the point of departure, he dismissed her.
She went and said to the gods, "The great sage has indeed been agitated."
"O Indra, all his ascetic merit has been destroyed; you shall now partake in happiness.
Then she conceived a child from the sage and gave birth to a girl;
and she went back to that very place where the sage was once again performing his austerities.
Having led away the lotus-eyed maiden with a face as beautiful as the moon, he went before the sage in his hermitage and released her; she then spoke these words:
"I was conceived from your seed and brought forth in my womb."
Protect your divine daughter, the maiden; salutations to you!
(24) There is no dwelling in heaven for humans by any means whatsoever.
For this reason, having given her to you, I shall go back to heaven once more. (25)
Having spoken thus, Rambhā departed, and Jābāli, filled with affection,
nurtured that girl with the juices of sweet fruits.
She grew up playing with the deer and sporting with the birds.
She used to assist that sage in all his affairs.
She would constantly bring sacrificial fuel, *kuśa* grass, and other necessities from the forest.
Once, she went far from her own hermitage in search of fruit.
Then, from the sky, a Gandharva named Citrāṅgada, seated in a celestial chariot, emerged; having seen her, he descended and spoke to her:
"Who are you, O young maiden, that wanders alone in the forest?"
The maiden said to Jābāli, "I am indeed a maiden who bears fruit;
I have come here for the sake of flowers and fruit, and my father is near me.
Then Citrāṅgada said, "Your father is without his wife."
"How indeed did a youth who practices celibacy (kumārabrahmacārī) beget you?
The maiden replied: "My mother was Rambhā, the most excellent of the Apsarases.
Having served a sage, she obtained me as a daughter through him; he, therefore, became my father."
"Jābāli is my father; I have been nourished by him with the six flavors.
Then Citrāṅgada said: "O lady of beautiful hips, accept me!
I am a Gandharva named Citrāṅgada, a dweller of the third heaven."
The maiden said: "I am a virgin and likewise remain under the authority of my father;
therefore, entreat my father, and he will give me to you.
You also please my heart, being a youth of handsome form."
Citrāṅgada said, "I am truly unable to request it in such a manner;
for who knows what his mind intends or what form he will take?
The maiden replied, "If this is so, what can I do without your permission?"
"If my father should learn of you, he will surely consume both you and me with fire.
As she was speaking thus, the impetuous and powerful Citrāṅgada took her onto his lap and dallied with her beneath a forest tree.
She too, completely possessed by desire, delighted him again and again.
Having abandoned her divine nature and taken recourse to the state of passion,
she did not perceive that the day had passed and evening had come.
Then Jābāli, immersed in thought and overcome with grief,
realizing at the onset of night that his daughter had not returned and was in distress,
wandered everywhere through forest after forest to search for her.
"Alas! Has she been devoured by tigers, or has she fallen from the tree?
Or perhaps she is submerged in bottomless water, or has indeed been carried off by force by another?
Thus lamenting, he wandered about, overcome with grief.
Hearing a certain sound and thinking it was the girl, he went toward it;
then, at the foot of a tree, he heard a sound produced by a maiden.
Quickly arriving there, he saw his daughter together with the man.
Overcome with rage, he seized a piece of wood and rushed toward that man:
"Fie, fie upon you, O sinner! You have defiled my daughter's maidenhood in the forest. By this act, O son, you have brought a stain upon me in the eyes of the world. (45–46)
Saying, "Therefore, I shall destroy both him and you," just as he was about to hurl a blow,
Citrāṅgada became invisible in the sky;
and that maiden was left naked and deprived of her power.
And out of fear of her father, she sat down right there, trembling.
The sage, having struck her with a blow of a wooden staff so that she fell to the ground, thought she was dead; and as he released her and looked up into the sky— 49.
Just then, Citrāṅgada was seen traveling toward heaven in a celestial chariot;
he was instantly cursed by the sage: "Become a leper and fall down here!
Thereupon, the Gandharva fell to the earth and became a leper in that very moment.
"Grant me forgiveness; be compassionate toward my daughter.
"That which has occurred has indeed occurred; for anger toward the virtuous is indeed slight.
Then Jābāli, having considered him worthy of punishment, spoke to him.
"Just as [your] daughter, so too you shall always remain without clothes.
Both of you must indeed always stay naked here upon the forest tree.
If you two should go elsewhere, your heads will surely burst."
Thus did those two receive a curse in the sacred field of Śrīhāṭakeśvara.
Having thus restrained them right there, the sage departed for his own hermitage.
Then, in the month of Caitra, during the bright fortnight at midnight, the Blessed Lord Hara [appeared].
By chance, he arrived in that forest to sport with the yoginīs.
There, at that time, both of them, being naked,
joyfully performed singing and dancing repeatedly for the sake of propitiating Śambhu.
Then Śambhu, being pleased, made this Gandharva free from disease;
Hara granted him the power of traveling through the sky and the status of a Gaṇa.
He [the Gandharva] accepted that maiden, the state of a Yoginī, and the power of traveling through the sky.
"Oṃ, obeisances to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; obeisances.
Having given this mantra to them, he gave them a garland of tulasī.
Those two became Vaiṣṇava devotees at the holy site of Hāṭakeśvara.
Cursed by Citrāṅgada, Jābāli was stripped of his clothes;
"Become like me, a constant object of public ridicule," he said.
Consumed by this curse, he began to revile women.
"Alas! For sinful men, attachment to women indeed arises.
What kind of suffering would be mine from even a single instance of indulgence with a woman? From birth until death, I have incurred naked sin. (62)
Then he wondered, "What is the destiny of those who are attached to women?
While he was speaking thus, his daughter, a yoginī, said:
"This auspicious universe, consisting of the moving and the unmoving, is sustained by women. (64)
"How is it that you revile her, O father? A reviler of his mother shall incur suffering.
The father replied: "Women are a constant source of misery in all circumstances;
neither in this world nor in the next can happiness be obtained from them. (65)
The daughter said: "Father, you truly have neither wisdom nor self-restraint.
Even an outcaste would not perform such an act as you have done.
I have been struck by you repeatedly with blows of a wooden staff. (66–67)
No thought occurred to you in your heart regarding the sin arising from the killing of a woman, and especially that of your daughter; what will become of your fate?
I have been cursed to remain eternally naked, and so too shall be your own transgression.

"Constantly arising as ever-new, born from my breath, and exceedingly great—O Father, even at the end of a kalpa, no end to it shall come. Therefore, you must continue to consume it just so, due to the curse of the Gandharva. (1.503.70)
Henceforth you should generally neither revile them nor strike them; all women are beyond reproach, for they can never be corrupted.
Indeed, every month their menstrual flow carries away their misdeeds.
The father said: "Women are sinful; they are never purified.
The daughter said: "It is not so indeed. Listen to the teaching declared in the Vedas:
Brahmins are pure from their feet, and cows are pure from their tails."
"Goats are pure in their mouths, and women are pure in all respects.
Then the father spoke this scripture, having set aside what was merely fabricated:
"Brahmins are pure in all respects, and cows are pure in all respects."
"Even goats are pure in some places, and women are not pure in others.
The daughter said: "In the house of one who has a beloved woman, there is the wish-fulfilling gem, the wish-granting tree, and Kubera himself as a servant."

The father said: "For him who has a lustful woman in his house, all calamities and suffering reside in his home; indeed, hell is right here for him. The daughter said: "Whatever pleasures and objects of enjoyment exist here—"
For indeed, those things born of dharma, artha, and kāma arise from women.
The father said: "Whatever sufferings there are for embodied beings arising from sins, and whatever hardships are reckoned to exist, they indeed arise from women. (78–79)
The daughter said: "Through marriage, by means of circumambulations of the fire, a woman makes certain that the goals of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa are attained.
The father said: "Through marriage, [the continuity of] births and future lives is secured."
It is the wandering of saṃsāra itself that makes women known through their delusions.
(8.1) The daughter said: Having obtained a virtuous wife who accomplishes all goals, what embodied beings—indeed, even those possessing knowledge—do not become attached? (8.2)
The father said: "Those who are free from passion and established in the Self are not attached;
the deluded fall into them like moths into a flame.
The daughter said: "The breasts, the hips, the loins, and the circle of the face—"
Those others who are bereft of fortune are served by the meritorious.
The father said: "The lines on the forehead that indicate one's imminent destruction belong to him;
it is by him that those other fortunate ones are served."
The daughter said: "The touch, sight, and arrangement [of ornaments] of a woman, as well as her embrace, are in every way givers of pleasure and destroyers of fatigue.
The father said: "The touch and other such things of a woman consist of sweet poison."
"Attachment and the like bestow suffering upon creation and are the destroyers of the virtuous stages of life.
The daughter said: "Who indeed is not wicked by reason of a woman? Who is not happy and meritorious?
And who among women is not most desirable, she who has a husband as her beloved? (88)
The father said: "Is there no sinful man who suffers misery when seen by a woman?
Who would not be held in contempt by women, whose beloved he is not?
The daughter also said: "Even for a worm, union with a woman is pleasing."
This applies to humans, gods, and others—how much more so for the wise!
The father said: "Feces are pleasing to a worm of extreme sin;
the impure female body is pleasing to the lustful, but certainly not to any other virtuous being. (1.503.90–91)
The daughter said: "How indeed did Brahmā himself create that noose in the form of a woman, which Brahmā himself enjoys?
How was Rambhā enjoyed by you, and how was I, your daughter, protected?"
If her price were not taken into account, how could she have been cursed for being attached to another?
And how was it that you yourself were obtained by your mother through the service of Jabālī?
Behold, then, the price of a woman even in the hermitages of the sages! (93–94)
When you were questioned by Yājñavalkya during his recitation, "Whose son are you?", you asked about your mother; at that time, what was the price of a woman to you?
Where indeed has that knowledge shown by the woman gone now?
"You are truly the son of your mother; you are certainly not the son of your father.
O Father, those like you who revile a woman whose father is unknown always cook in the Kālasūtra hell—those revilers of women. (96–97)
"O father, thinking that parents are always to be honored, you were not cursed by me; nevertheless, you have been cursed here by means of a *gāndharva* [rite].
Both you and I have obtained the fruit of our own actions. (98)
"A maiden should indeed be given to anyone at the proper time.
By the turn of fate, I have arrived; what harm is there in the Gāndharva rite?
I am the daughter of an Apsaras, and I have resorted to the Gāndharva form."
"What loss is there in this connection, or what gain indeed in a curse?
Without reflection, you have acted out of anger, being weak in wisdom.
Forgive my excessive words, since I am indeed one who ought to be conciliated. (101)
Having spoken thus, with eyes filled with tears, she prostrated at his feet.
But the father, feeling ashamed upon witnessing his daughter’s realization, said:
"Indeed, today I consider myself most blessed."
"O daughter! Since you have been born as my daughter, so proficient in such scriptures, my anger toward you has now indeed subsided; be happy.
Having spoken thus, the brahmin quickly departed for his leaf-hut.
There, situated in the midst of yoginīs, the daughter performed austerities.
Then, after some time, Nārāyaṇa, being pleased, arrived;
having assumed a divine form, he led her to liberation.

That virtuous woman, devoted to her husband Nārāyaṇa, became four-armed; Citrāṅgada went to his own hermitage in the world of the Gandharvas. Then Jābāli, worshipping Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa through austerity, [proceeded].
He was liberated from the curse through the majesty of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. By the power of Kṛṣṇa’s grace, he went to the supreme abode of Goloka.
What exceedingly rare thing does one who has surrendered their self not achieve?
That which is unbreakable, indestructible, invincible, and eternal— he,
having turned it back and made it new, restores it to its original state;
even destiny as firm as a diamond he certainly brings to ruin.
Devotion to Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa creates new fortune.
O Lakṣmī, I have told you all this, which fulfills every desire for those who read it and listen to it, both in this world and in the next.

Thus ends the five hundred and third chapter, titled "The Description of how Phalavatī—the daughter produced by Jābāli through Rambhā—was made a naked Yoginī by her father’s curse despite the enjoyment provided by the Gandharva Citrāṅgada; how she remained near her father; her subsequent liberation through penances; and the dialogue and dwelling of the two on Padmaśilā," in the first section, the Kṛta-yuga lineage, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*. Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
The Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, and the two Aśvins are the lords of the gods.
O Lakṣmī! They are always to be honored, for they are indeed the providers of security and prosperity. Varuṇa, as well as Sūrya, Bhānu, Pūṣan, and Tāpana;
Indra, Aryaman, Dhātṛ, and likewise Bhaga—[these are the twelve Ādityas]. || 1-2 ||
Gabhasti and Dharmarāja— these are the ten Ādityas, two for each [group].
Dharo, Dhruva, Soma, Makha, Anila, Nala, Pratyūṣa,
and Prabhāsa are indeed the eight Vasus by name.
Mṛgavyādha and Śarva, and Mṛgīvyādha as the third;
Ajaikapād, Ahirbudhnya, and Pinākin as the sixth; furthermore, Dahana, Kapālī, and Raivata as the ninth.
Vṛṣākapi and Tryambaka—these are the eleven Rudras.
Nāsatya and Dasra—these two are the sons of Aśvinī.
These are declared to be the thirty-three leaders of the gods.

By him, the Dānavas, the gods, and embodied human beings are always to be honored; thus, untimely death does not occur. And on the eighth and fourteenth lunar days, O beloved, the Rudras are always to be worshipped.
On the tenth day, the Vasus are to be worshipped, especially during the bright fortnight;
likewise, one should worship the Ādityas on the seventh and the sixth days.
Similarly, the two sons of Aśvin should be worshipped on the twelfth day with sixteen [offerings] and so forth.
The Rudras, when gratified, grant protection and even the supreme state. The Vasus, when worshipped, surely bestow pleasures such as amorous delights and heaven.
The Ādityas, when worshipped and satisfied, indeed bestow sovereign power.
The two Aśvins, the physicians of the gods, when worshipped, destroy all ailments; and Vyāsa,
the chronicler of the praises and virtues of all beings, including the gods,
is always worthy of worship as the preceptor who bestows knowledge and liberation.
His son, named Śuka, was born from Śukī as a Brahmin.
Furthermore, Vedavyāsa once felt a desire for a wife;
consequently, he [beget] sons who were capable leaders upon the wives of Vicitravīrya.
At the command of Satyavatī, that lord begot the Kauravas— Pāṇḍu, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, and Vidura.
Even while remaining in the forest hermitage, he caused the expansion of his lineage.
Then he thought, "Today I shall take a wife.
Thereupon, he requested Jābāli, the bull among sages,
for his second daughter, the auspicious parrot named Ceṭikā.
Jābāli, however, gave him his own auspicious daughter as a maidservant;
she too became pregnant, yet the fetus would not emerge.
Twelve years passed, but it certainly did not come forth.
Whatever the son hears while situated within the womb, he hears it all.
That Śukī shone with the splendors of her pregnancy like a source of the Vedas;
even as an embryo, she held within her heart all knowledge and reflection.
By him the Vedas with their auxiliary limbs were heard, as they were studied even while in the womb;
likewise the Smṛtis, the Saṃhitās, the treatises on liberation,
the codes of ethics, the study of the Brahmanas, and the spiritually elevating narratives.

Whatever was heard and whatever was studied—all that remains within the womb. (22) Just as the son grows while residing in the belly, so too does the mother become increasingly heavy, and from that, the father suffers pain. (23)
Vyāsa asked: "Who indeed are you who have entered here assuming the form of an embryo?
Why do you not come outside? Tell me everything exactly as it is.
The embryo replied: "I am a Piśāca, I am a Rākṣasa, and I am a human being."
"I am a god, I am a horse, I am an elephant, and I am a cock;
I am a goat, I am a prince, I am a tree, and I am a young boy—thus wandering repeatedly through eighty-four hundred thousand wombs. (25-26)
"I have come; how should I know? Who am I? Whom do you speak of as 'me'?
Though I am stainless, I have entered here into a human womb.
Having attained the knowledge born of the Vedas, I shall accomplish yoga here."
I am weary and await the eternal path to liberation (28).
Indeed, wandering in this terrible cycle of existence does not please me;
I shall not go outside the womb, but shall contemplate Brahman right here (29).
"I shall act and then I shall go to liberation through the power of your grace.
Vyāsa said: "Listen, O son, you who are stainless!
Tell me, how can you have any pleasure in dwelling within the womb-cavity, which is exceedingly foul-smelling?"
"Come out from that loathsome pit of urine, O wise one!
Having come outside, acquire either yoga or auspicious knowledge.
The fetus said: 'Neither new knowledge nor new yoga is desired.'"
Knowledge, dispassion, and likewise the memory of previous births remain only so long as I am situated in the womb; indeed, the desire for liberation lasts only that long.
But once a living being has emerged from the womb, he is touched by the external air.
All knowledge residing within the womb, as well as yoga and radiance, perishes.
Therefore, I shall by no means emerge from the womb, lest my performed merit be lost;
it is my firm resolve that I shall attain liberation even from the womb itself.
Vyāsa said: "O Ātman, the noose of Vāyu shall not ensnare you;
all your knowledge and yoga will certainly remain true to reality.
Māyā shall not afflict you, whether in the womb or outside."
"Therefore, show me your face, and I shall discharge my debt.
By the mere hearing of your birth, may the ancestors be quickly and fully satisfied.
The fetus said: "If you will have Viṣṇu as your witness, protect me!"
"Then I shall go outside; act appropriately there quickly.
Vyāsa, remembering that upon hearing it, [called] the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
The divine Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa arrived there immediately.

The witness was present there and said: "Listen, O Garbha, to what is for your benefit. Today I shall become your guarantor; all your knowledge and other qualities shall indeed remain outside [of you]. Go forth, go for the sake of yoga. (1.504.40–41)
The illusion created by the touch of the wind would not have pervaded you;
then the embryo emerged by the will of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa,
measuring twelve years of age and approaching the prime of youth.
As soon as he was born, he possessed the memory of his past lives and was conscious like a king of yogis.
Having immediately prostrated before Kṛṣṇa, his mother, and his father, that boy set out for the forest; Vyāsa said to him, "Stay! (43–44).

"I shall perform for you the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), such as the birth ceremony (*jātakarman*) and others; be firm! The son of a maidservant replied: "Purificatory rites have been performed by me thousands and tens of millions of times in every birth within the ocean of existence. (45)
By these forms of bondage with which I am surrounded in various wombs;
(46) then the Blessed One himself bore the name Śuka.
Śuka began to take steps to depart, and Vyāsa said to him: (47)
"O son, he who abandons his father and goes to the forest for the sake of yoga goes to hell; do not go, but dwell at home.
Śuka said: "Since existence has come to such a state, I am your son in that sense."
"You were my son and I was your father; in that regard, this is the instruction:
O Vyāsa, if this established order of dharma is to be maintained by you, I must not be forbidden from departing for the forest of asceticism. (1.504.50)

Vyāsa said: "Having obtained birth in the house of a twice-born, he who receives the purificatory rites (saṃskāras) prescribed in the Vedas is preeminent. Śuka replied: "Liberation of the self is not certain through purificatory rites alone."
If liberation were to arise from ritual action (*saṃskāra*), it would belong to such a rogue as well.
Vyāsa said: "First one should be a student (*brahmacārī*), then a householder;
thereafter, having prioritized renunciation (*tyāga*), liberation shall come about, my son. (52–53)
Śuka said: "If liberation comes from celibacy, then a eunuch would attain it;
and if liberation comes from the householder's life, then the entire world would attain it.
If liberation comes from dwelling in the forest, then deer and other such creatures would surely attain it."
If liberation were superior due to renunciation, then it would belong to the poor as well.

Vyāsa has declared that by following the path of the virtuous through the sequence of stages beginning with the householder, one bestows bliss both in this world and the next; therefore, liberation is the ultimate fruit of that path.
Śuka said: "One who is attached to household life, fallen under the sway of delusion and passion, and bound by the fetters of latent impressions, will reap the fruit of the path of Yama.
Vyāsa said: "Without passion, one should accomplish the rites for the ancestors and the gods."
Śuka said: "Without devotion, one may deceive the ancestral rites (paitrya) and the divine rites (daiva).
Vyāsa said: "Always perform devotion at home toward the ancestral and divine rites.
Śuka said: "My own self is my home; therein I perform them."
Vyāsa said: "Without a son, the hell named Put is certain;
one crosses over it by means of a son; therefore, a son is highly praised.
Śuka said: "If that were so, then donkeys, monkeys, and pigs [would also be praised]."
"Those who have sons will cross over; what distinction is there for a human being?
Vyāsa said, "If they too possess knowledge, then they shall also attain liberation.
Śuka replied, "Father, I have indeed acquired that very [knowledge] even from within the womb."
I shall go with devotion to Keśava, who has arrived as liberation;
for having obtained the wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi), how could one take up a mere pebble?
Having cast aside nectar at the first bite, how indeed could a fly swallow a fly?
When the essence of gold has been obtained before one, how could one grind mere mud?
Having abandoned the sight of the sun, how could one look toward Rāhu?
Having cast aside the divine lamp, how could one seek out a smoky firebrand?
When one is liberated from the first prison, how indeed could one fall into a second?
Once the path of Brahman has been realized, how could one proceed by a lowly way?
Having abandoned the superior that is present, one should not take hold of the inferior.
How could one abandon the truth already attained and embrace something artificial?
(67) If one should find honey at home, why go to the mountain?
For the attainment of a desired goal, what wise person would exert effort [elsewhere]? (68)
Having spoken thus, and having respectfully bowed to his father Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana who dwells in the heart, and to his mother, the maidservant who is the power (śakti) of Kṛṣṇa,
he went to the forest that is the eternal refuge, where even the Self exists.

Vyāsa and the maidservant both experienced grief and sorrow for a moment. Then Śukī said to Vyāsa: "I shall once again practice austerities so that there may be a son for my lineage who will cause it to flourish."
Having received the command of Vyāsa, that devoted wife performed austerities;
Vyāsa gave her the mantra, "Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, obeisance to the Lord," and she chanted it day and night.
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa arrived there with a joyful heart.
He said to her, "I am the giver of boons; choose a boon, O lady of virtuous vows.
Śukī replied, "Give me a son who will increase my lineage."
"So be it," Hari said, and then he vanished from sight. The maidservant obtained a fine son who was known as Kapiñjala.
Kapiñjala, a great yogi, acted according to the command of his parents.
He took the maiden Bharadvājī as his wife and entered the householder’s life. From that union, a son was born to Bharadvāja;
he was Taittira, the son of Bharadvāja, who was able to assume any form at will.
He went to the mountainous region of Prāgjyotiṣa; then,
returning once more to the mountain named Navalakṣa,
he took up residence there and worshipped the virtuous Kāmākṣī.
The great yogi Kāmarūpa was Maheśvara of the mountains;
by the power of his asceticism, he became the king and the preceptor of the mountain-dwellers.
Consequently, the mountains thereafter came to be known by the name Kāmarūpa.
Men became few and women were many due to their desire for virtuous conduct;
indeed, hundreds of women would serve a single man.
Then, the Lord of Yogins, in the form of a child, dwelt on the banks of the Brahmaputra.
Free from delusion, he performed severe penance like a child.
Then they all requested him for the prosperity of men:
"By my boon, may you all be intent upon giving birth to sons. (82–83)
"Let the number of girls be equal to that of the men;
in the event of equality, you shall become mothers of daughters and sons respectively, according to what is fitting. And so it came to pass for them.
Thus has this ancient history been told to you, O Lakṣmī, occurring age after age.
Just as in the world of becoming, a creation arises ever anew, so too do the Kāmarūpa Tīrtha and Bālavākuṇḍaka arise. 85–86.
It bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, is most excellent even through recitation or hearing,
grants whatever is desired, and indeed bestows the perfection of mantra.
Thus ends the first section, the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga, in the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.

Śuka and Kapiñjala were the two sons of Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana Vyāsa by Śukī; Bharadvāja was the son of Kapiñjala, and Taittira was his son. Due to the granting of a boon by Bālava-yogin, there arose in the land of Kāmarūpa a birth of men equal in number to women, and so forth—this is the five hundred and fourth chapter, titled "The Description [of these events]," from the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Book 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga), Chapter 505.

Hanumān, Jāmbavān, Aśvatthāman, Prahlāda, Āsuri, Voḍhu,
Pañcaśikha, Divodāsa, as well as Ambarīṣa, Uddhava,
Śaśin, Sūrya, Anila, and Hutāśana.
"These are your eternal devotees, your sons who carry out your commands;

dancing, and instrumental music for the constant propitiation of Gaurī.

"I shall quickly grant you everything, even that which is difficult to obtain, O Golaka. Gādhi replied: "O twice-born one, give me seven hundred horses with black ears on one side, all of them white in every other respect."

"O daughter, choose for my sake a son endowed with Brahmanic qualities;

"O daughter, in comparison to me, you shall have the excellence of the sacrificial porridge.

"O younger brother, by listening with faith to the accounts of pilgrimages, this son of yours shall become equal to Brahmā through his Brahmanic splendor.

Ṛcīka said: "It cannot be so; that which has gone is gone, and remains exactly as it was.

The Great Goddess known as Gomayā should be fashioned from cow dung.
On the third day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada, one should clean one's teeth in the morning;
remembering Gaurī, one should undertake the vow of fasting.
At the arrival of night, four clay images of Gaurī must indeed be fashioned.
A single Gaurī should be fashioned with five lumps as previously described;
when each watch of the day has arrived, one should perform worship upon them:
"O Goddess, beloved of Śaṅkara, you were born in the home of Himācala."
Born from the womb of Menā, accept this worship; salutations to you!
(51) One should offer incense with camphor, a red wick, a lamp of ghee, jasmine flowers, sweetmeats as the food offering, and the respectful water-offering. (52)
"Accept this *arghya* rich with *mātuluṅga* flowers; salutations to you.
At the end of the second watch, one should worship Ardhanārīśvarī.
[The offerings are] incense of *aguru* and sandalwood, food offerings (*naivedya*), jaggery (*guḍa*), and the *arghya*.
Then, one should indeed offer the *argha* accompanied by coconut, with the mantra:
"O Gods, Pārvatī and Parameśvara, please accept my *argha*.
When the third watch has arrived, one should worship with a hundred-petaled lotus.

One should offer guggulu incense, food offerings (naivedya), and an arghya of water with jasmine flowers; then, when the fourth watch has arrived, one should again offer incense made from granthi powder along with its own arghya and the fruit of the madana tree. || 56 ||
One should worship that Gaurī, who consists of five lumps, with *bhṛṅgarāja*.
"May Gaurī, who is composed of the five elements, accept this *arghya* offered by me.
One should offer the food oblation (*naivedya*), incense, lamps, and so forth, as well as a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*).
One should perform the *nīrājana* rite, offer prayers for one's desired goals, and observe a vigil;
with great effort, one should engage in dancing, instrumental music, and chanting amidst the festivities.
At dawn, the observer of the vow, having bathed, should worship a pair of Brahmins.
One should cause her to mount either an elephant or a mare, accompanied by four Gaurīs.
Amidst the sounds of musical instruments and festive celebration, one should cast her into a river or similar body of water, saying:
"O Goddess, you have been summoned by me; you have been worshipped by me, O auspicious one!"
"Go as you please to bestow good fortune upon me.
Thus was the worship previously performed by Lakṣmī, and especially so by Gaurī,
on the third day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada, throughout the four watches of the night.
In the morning, she saw those Gaurīs adorned with the luster of jewels. They said to that Mahālakṣmī, "Do not carry us away into the water;
instead, have a temple constructed here in the holy field of Hāṭakeśvara."
"Establish us for the sake of a vow, as those who bring happiness to women.
Thus were they established there by Lakṣmī as bestowers of fortune and sons.
O King, this very goddess is your wife, as well as the four Gaurīs.
Having fashioned an image of Gaurī made of cow dung and likewise consisting of five lumps,
one should worship it; by that means, one shall obtain sons and good fortune,
and furthermore, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa himself shall become one’s husband.
Having spoken thus, Durvāsas departed quickly;
then that virtuous woman, named Amā, went to the sacred field known as Hāṭakeśvara.
Having performed everything according to the prescribed rites, she became the mother of a son.
In the Bahukālottara [Purāṇa], it is said that Amā took the form of Lakṣmī;
having attained a divine body, she went to Viṣṇu’s Vaikuṇṭha and became his maidservant.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, have I described to you the vow of Amā.
But she who recites this with devotion shall obtain the fruit of the worship of Gaurī;
she shall never be separated from Lakṣmī, nor shall she encounter misfortune.

(71) Thus ends the five hundred and eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Pañcapiṇḍikā-Gaurī Vow performed by Amayā, the wife of the King of Kāśī, in the first section on the Succession of the Kṛta Yuga in the Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā, and how through it she attained sons, good fortune, and the state of Lakṣmī. (508)
← Chapter 508: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga) Chapter 509 [Author: Chapter 510 →
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī; once in the Satyaloka, Nārada, having wandered through the three worlds, went to see Brahmā and bowed down before him.
Brahmā asked, "From where have you come, my son? Speak!
Nārada replied, "Having surveyed the circles of mortals, I have come to inform you of what is in my heart regarding the procedure for your worship."
"I have come here, O Father; having heard this, do what is appropriate.
For the strength of the Daityas prevails everywhere in the world, as do sacrifices, truth, dharma, and virtuous deeds in every respect. (4)
"The gods and the devotees are being forcibly destroyed by them and are suffering.
Therefore, O Blessed One, you ought to perform what is beneficial as you see fit.
Having thus made this petition, he bowed down, worshipped [the Lord], and departed.

Brahmā indeed reflected upon a pure ground for the sake of the sacrifice. (6) To discover where that place free from obstacles might be, he spoke to the lotus-flower held in his hand: "Fall upon a sacred spot! (7)
Then he cast that flower, which, having wandered through all the worlds on every side,
fell upon the most sacred field born of Hāṭakeśvara.
In the meantime, his grandfather arrived behind him.
Having seen the sacrificial ground, the Great-Grandfather became delighted;
he then commanded Vāyu, "Bring Purandara here, together with the Ādityas, the Vasus, the Rudras, and the hosts of Maruts. (1.509.10)
"Let the Gandharvas, the world-protectors, the Siddhas, and likewise the Vidyādharas—
whoever may be my assistants— be present for the entirety of the sacrificial rite.
And Vāyu brought Indra, accompanied by the hosts of gods.
Brahmā said to Mahendra: "On the full moon day of Vaiśākha, I intend to perform the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice here;
indeed, bring together the necessary materials, as well as worthy Brāhmaṇas and suitable implements."
Indra brought those materials and the best of the twice-born;
then the Great-Grandfather (Brahmā) commenced the sacrifice according to the prescribed rites.
Śambhu also arrived there at that sacrifice together with the hosts of gods.
Brahmā spoke to the gods: "Stay each in your own respective places.
O Viśvakarman, construct the sacrificial pavilion and the sacrificial altars, as well as the wives' quarters, the assembly halls, and the necessary fire-pits."
Have the sacrificial vessels, the cups, and the ladles brought;
have the sacrificial posts, the beds, the pits, and the altars prepared.
And have a golden image of the Supreme Person fashioned, O you of beautiful form.

"O Bṛhaspati, bring all the officiating priests worthy of the sacrifice, numbering sixteen; O King of the Gods, perform service for them. And let Kubera provide you with sacrificial fees appropriate for the occasion. || 18-19 ||
O Creator, you must perform an examination of what ought and ought not to be done;
likewise, let the world-protectors, Indra and the others, guard the directions.
May there be no entry for spirits, ghosts, and goblins, nor for Daityas and Rākṣasas.
"Let it not be so; therefore, let this supreme gift be bestowed through sacrifice.
May the Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Viśvedevas, and the hosts of Maruts be the servers for the people who desire to eat."
Let the Brahmins worthy of sacrifice stand in the sacrificial pavilion— Maitrāvaruṇa, Cyavana, Atharvāka, Gālava, Marīci, and Mārkava; these are all experts in every ritual act.
Let Pulastya, the performer of the *prasthāna*, stand there as the *adhvaryu* priest;
likewise, let the sage Raibhya stand in the sacrificial pavilion as the *unnetṛ*. Let Nārada be the *brahmán* priest, and Garga be the overseer of the session (*satra*).
The three Hotṛ priests were Agnīdhra, Bharadvāja, and Parāśara;
Bṛhaspati was the Ācārya and Udgātṛ, while the sage Gobhila was the Prastotṛ.
Śāṇḍilya was the Pratihartṛ, and Aṅgiras was the Subrahmaṇya.
For the successful completion of this sacrifice, there were sixteen officiating priests (ṛtvij).
The Creator of the Universe, having been initiated by them, honored them as the Brahmā priest;
he became the patron of the sacrifice, and thereafter the sacrificial rites were set in motion.
And Brahmā said to Nārada, "Bring Sāvitrī quickly," while musical instruments were being played by the Siddhas, Kinnaras, and Guhyakas,
and by Gandharvas accompanied by their instruments, and by Brahmins intent on chanting.
Taking up the fire-drill (araṇi), Pulastya spoke these words: "O lords of brahmins, 'Patnī! Patnī! he cried out loudly as he stood there. Then Brahmā quickly signaled to Nārada with his hand."
He sent her back home, saying, "Let your wife be brought here.
He too went and said to Sāvitrī, "I have been sent by my father;
come, O Goddess, to the pavilion, for the sacrificial rites are proceeding."
"O Supreme One, what kind of form do you appear in when you are alone in the assembly?
Therefore, let the goddesses be brought; surrounded by them, you shall depart.
Having spoken thus, Nārada went to the sacrifice and spoke to the Unborn (Brahmā).
"Sāvitrī will arrive at an auspicious moment together with the goddesses.
Then Brahmā sent him back, and Nārada departed.
"O Mother, come quickly, surrounded by the goddesses!"
Then Sāvitrī also said, "I shall go only after I have dressed my hair.
Nārada then said to Aja, "She will indeed come after she has dressed her hair;
therefore, act with haste while there is still a portion of the *muhūrta* for drinking the soma remaining. (36-37)
Pulastya also went there, for Sāvitrī was indeed alone. "O Goddess, why do you appear so languid? Go quickly to the site of the sacrifice.
Sāvitrī said: "Tell him that he should wait for a moment."
"Until Śakrāṇī, Gaurī, Lakṣmī,
and other celestial maidens arrive at this assembly, I shall come accompanied by them.
Having gone quickly, he spoke to Brahmā, who was oppressed by the weight of the moon.
She said to me, "I am indeed coming to the sacrifice accompanied by the goddesses;
I shall go together with them, but never alone.
Knowing this, O best of gods, do whatever pleases you.
And the time for the sacrificial drinking was passing away.
Having heard this, Brahmā spoke to Mahendra: "She is now weary;
the sacrifice must be performed with another wife. (42-43)

By the command of Brahmā, the Lord of the Gods questioned a certain maiden who was wandering about—a slender girl with a moon-like face born of a cowherd, her head intent upon a water-pot, youthful and delicate: "Who are you, O maiden? (44)
"I am a cowherd's daughter," she said, "come here to sell buttermilk. "If you will take the buttermilk, give me the price quickly.
Indra took that cowherd's daughter along with the buttermilk.
Having caused it to enter through the cow's mouth, he then drew it out with urine.
Having thus rendered it most pure and bathed it with auspicious waters,
he dressed it in two fine garments, led it, and placed it in the presence of the goat.
"O Brahmin, this woman, endowed with every virtue, has indeed been brought for your sake.
The lineages of cows and of Brahmins constitute a single entity that has been divided into two: in one part reside the sacred mantras, and in the other resides the sacrificial oblation."
"Having emerged from the cow-pen, she has been brought to the state of twice-born status;
take her hand in marriage and perform the drinking of the sacrificial soma.
Rudra then said, "Indeed, she has emerged from the cow-stall."
"Let Gāyatrī, by name, be your wife here at this sacrifice forever.
Then the Brahmins said, "Let her be the best of Brahmin women;
perform the taking of her hand in marriage, for she is free from the status of being born as a cowherd."
Brahmā took her hand and began the auspicious rite;
Gāyatrī too, joyfully placing that fire-drill upon her head,
arrived at the sacrificial pavilion as musical instruments were being played.
After that, Vidhi performed the rite of shaving his own hair;
Viśvakarman then performed the clipping of Gāyatrī’s nails.
Then Paulastya gave a staff made of udumbara wood to Brahmā.
He likewise gave him a hide equipped with a deer-horn along with the mantras;
and having taken his wife Śālā, who observed silence like Gāyatrī,
he placed another auspicious girdle made of muñja grass upon her waist.
Then Brahmā, together with the officiating priests, performed the sacrificial rite.
While the ritual was being carried out, a great marvel occurred there:
a certain person appeared, naked, with a deformed face, and assuming the form of a rogue.

"Come with a skull in hand; let food be given!"—though thus forbidden by the Brahmins, he entered the sacrificial pavilion. But the members of the assembly held him in contempt, saying, "Who are you, a sinner, who has arrived here?"
"Carrying a skull, naked in form, and equipped with an impure begging bowl, the sacrificial ground would become defiled; go quickly away from here!
The wretch replied, "How am I impure? For I am a mendicant observing a vow."
Having understood this *brahmayajña* and having arrived here pure after bathing, [I ask:
that cowherd girl who was always impure by birth as a *śūdrī* has indeed been established here as pure; am I, a Brahmin, not likewise purifying? (62)
Just then, a brahmin of advanced age arrived there.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said to him: "Listen to my reply, O dear one:
this woman is not a śūdra woman; she is indeed a brahmin by birth. (63–64)
Listen; I know that account, for others who do not know this do not.
Long ago, at the commencement of creation, Sāvitrī was manifested by Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Self, as a form of his own portion from his own body.
Then the second daughter was named Pativratā,
and the son was made a Brāhmaṇa named Patnīvratā;
he was created by Brahmā from the body of Vairāja and was then entrusted to him.
Sāvitrī shall remain in the very presence of Śrī Hari in Goloka; meanwhile,
for the sake of maintaining the flow of sacrifice, Brahmā will perform the sacrifice on earth in a mortal form,
there assuming a human body.
"A wife will be required for the purpose of the sacrifice.
For this reason, Kṛṣṇa then commanded Sāvitrī:
"Indeed, you must go there in a second form."
Long ago, on the surface of the earth, for the sake of Brahmā, Sāvitrī assumed the form of a maiden and said to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, "Where are my parents?
Then Śrī Kṛṣṇa showed her those two auspicious ones.
These two—a brahmin devoted to his wife and a brahmin woman devoted to her husband—are portions of Me, possessing My own form;
they are not born from a womb and possess divine bodies.
They shall indeed appear on earth at the Kuṅkumavāpī in the sacred field of Aśvapaṭṭasāra.
At the beginning of creation, two most purifying beings shall exist in the form of Brahmins,
accompanied by cows for the sake of the sacrificial offerings and oblations of the Vaiśvadeva and other rites.
And when Brahmā arrives in Saurāṣṭra for the purpose of sacrifice—
Prior to that, they were known as Gobhila and Gobhilā;
having become cowherds, they will go to the country of Ānarta,
where the Ābhīras dwell, assuming their dress and occupations.
"Because of that [destruction], it would not happen for the two of them while they remain concealed. For this reason, out of fear of the affliction caused by the Daityas,
those two were born in Ānarta in the form of cowherds (*ābhīra*) prior to the sacrifice, by the command of Śrī Hari.

Indeed, those two Brahmins who are the protectors of the cows must be made by you to appear as cowherds, for they are both Brahmins in reality. O Sāvitrī, since they are portions of myself, you must do this by means of your second form. (78–79)
One must indeed become a divine woman, a daughter not born from a womb;
then one should go to that place as a seller of curd, milk, and other such items.
When a sacrifice takes place there, then, through excellent yoga, one should remember [the goal].
But as a human bride, you shall perform a sacrifice with him;
having entered into union with Brahmā, you will become Gāyatrī.
You will be the secret daughter of two Brahmins living among cowherds.
Then, having become Brahmāṇī, you shall go to Satyaloka;
thereafter, the Brāhmaṇas who have returned to the mortal world will recite [the hymn] to you.
Thus was this Gāyatrī born as the daughter of a Brāhmaṇa.
"She is merely wearing the dress of a cowherd; for she is not impure by birth.
Thus was that rogue answered by Kṛṣṇa at that time, when Gobhila and Agobhila arrived there with joy.

Our daughter possesses great fortune, for she has been wedded by Brahmā; ours too is great fortune, as the affliction of the Daityas is being warded off through the gateway of sacrifice for the sake of the gods, the Brahmins, and the virtuous. (86)
Having spoken thus, those two, having abandoned their cowherd attire, assumed the forms of Brahmins.
Indeed, they were the two grandfathers of the great-souled Brahmins,
their ancestors born there as divine protectors of the earth.
Then Brahmā and the others bowed down and respectfully offered him honor;
all the gods and others, filled with joy, established him at the sacrifice.
They honored Brahmā with garlands, saffron, unbroken grains, flowers, and other offerings.
Having performed the rites there in the sacrificial pavilion, they gave away their daughter.
An aged brahmin there assumed the form of Kṛṣṇa;
saluted by all, the gods and others exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent! || 1.509.90-91 ||
Upon seeing Kṛṣṇa Hari as well as Gāyatrī and her father, that wretch bowed down with devotion and said, "O best of Brahmins, I am hungry; give me alms. May the twice-born not reproach me. (92)
When all the poor, the blind, and the wretched have been satisfied, it is called an *iṣṭi* sacrifice.
Otherwise, even this sacrifice performed by you would lead to destruction: "A sacrifice lacking food burns the kingdom; one lacking mantras burns the officiating priests. (93–94)
"A sacrifice devoid of a sacrificial fee is not a true sacrifice; there is no enemy equal to a sacrifice [when it fails].
Then Śrī Kṛṣṇa said, 'O fool, give him food! The brāhmaṇas replied, 'Your begging bowl is impure.'"
"Come outside; we shall give alms from the side-kitchen.
In this food-hall where the ascetics eat, as well as the wretched, the blind, the miserable, and the twice-born who are emaciated by hunger. (96–97)
"Your skull is indeed impure; take it outside the sacrificial ground!
Cast this bowl far away and take another pure vessel.
Thus addressed, that wretch threw the bowl in anger.
And he himself became invisible in the middle of the sacrificial pavilion.
All the brahmins were struck with wonder; they threw their water-pots with their staffs outside, and immediately a second one appeared.
When that too was completed, a third [enclosure] was established;
in this manner, hundreds of thousands were indeed established at that time.
The Brahmins became exhausted, and the sacrificial ground was filled with distress.
Then, a cry of "Alas! Alas! arose from all sides everywhere.
Brahmā, bowing repeatedly toward that direction, indeed made this request:
"O Lord, what is this? Is it fitting that there should be such an injury to the ritual action in this sacrifice?"
"Therefore, O Maheśvara, withdraw all these skull-bowls;
let there not be a disruption of the sacrificial rite now that you have arrived.
Then a voice arose from the sky: "My vessel is indeed pure."
"But these gods on earth (brāhmaṇas) censure my eating vessel;
O Creator, they did not offer oblations into the fire for my sake as they did for other deities, even though the sacrificial offering was purified by mantras. (1.085–1.086)
"Therefore, in this matter, an oblation must be offered specifically into the fire with me as its intended recipient;
only then will the sacrifice reach its completion.
Then Brahmā spoke this reply to him from the sky.
O Yogin, your forms are indeed truly innumerable.
As long as the skull remains within the pavilion,
there can be no ritual use of a *camasa* cup here, nor even a *khappara* vessel.
That is not declared to be a sacrificial vessel, for it is indeed always impure.
Whatever the form of the vessel and whatever its nature, and whatever the station of the ritual act, such a [vessel] should be employed therein; this is not the application of a [proper] vessel.
It is ordained in the ritual that the oblation is to be cooked in earthen potsherds.
Therefore, let the potsherd from which the sacrifice was performed be taken far away;
for you have indeed displayed here such a form as that of a skull-bearer (kapālin).
"Let that form have the right of participation in the *puroḍāśa* of this sacrifice;
moreover, accept alms and attain satisfaction.
From this day forward, let the twice-born partake of the *puroḍāśa* in sacrifices. (11.3)
"O Lord of Gods, the Śatarudriya must be offered as a sacrifice for your sake;
it should especially be recited in all sacrifices, and particularly so here. Whoever, having commenced the sacrifice here, shall first worship you," ||| 1.14–1.15 |||
"His sacrifice will proceed without obstacle and reach completion.
When this was said, O Padmaja, listen to the wonder that occurred at that moment:
all those skull-bowls vanished instantly.
And thousands of goddesses known as Rudrāṇīs were born as Annapūrṇās;
all those women were forms of Pārvatī, identical with Annapūrṇā herself, who give alms, for without them alms cannot be obtained at all. (1.17–1.18)
Meanwhile, the five-headed Śrī Śaṅkara, filled with joy,
arrived at the sacrificial pavilion and stood near the altar.
The Brahmins, sages, and gods likewise paid homage to Hara.
They worshipped the Rudrāṇīs and commenced the performance of the sacrifice.
By the thousands, the goddesses who were the wives of Śiva sat at the sacrifice;
and other celestial women, numbering in the tens of millions, sat together with Śiva.
Thus Śambhu always established his share in the sacrifice;
by reciting or hearing this, one shall obtain the fruit of the sacrifice. (122)

Thus ends the five hundred and ninth chapter, titled "The Description of Brahmā’s Commissioning of the Construction of the Assembly Hall and its Furnishings through the Devas and Others for the Purpose of Sacrifice at the Hāṭakeśvara Kṣetra on the Banks of the Nāgavatī in the Kṛta-yuga Lineage of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā," including the arrival of Śaṅkara in the guise of a Jālma, the account of Gāyatrī’s birth as a Brāhmaṇī, the nature of the skulls as being the Goddess Annapūrṇā, and the place of Śaṅkara in the sacrifice. || 509 ||
