Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, as the Brāhmaṇa was performing the sacrifice at that time, ten million sages residing in the southern region arrived. (1)
Then, tens of millions of residents of the Siṃhāraṇya forest, those dwelling in the Naimiṣāraṇya forest, and those residing in other regions assembled together,
filled with curiosity upon hearing of the sacrifice of the Grandfather (Brahmā).
"What kind of sacrifice will it be where the Lotus-born One is consecrated?
(3) Having bathed at Rūpatīrtha in the Nāganadī, those sages, possessing divine forms, went to the sacrificial ground and bowed to the Grandfather. (4)
Seated and weary, they were honored with a welcome;
they indeed engaged in divine conversations arising from the performance of sacrificial rites.
Regarding the drinking of the Soma, they held a discussion among one another.
Likewise, a discussion concerning the true nature of reality took place between the Udgātṛ and the Adhvaryu.
Then, having all eaten, they spent the night in comfort.
When the second day arrived—the twelfth day of the lunar fortnight for the sacrificial rites—(they proceeded).
O Lotus-born One, listen to what occurred when the officiating priests had begun the rite: a certain mischievous young brahmin student,
laughing, quickly threw a water-snake onto the sacrificial ground in the presence of the Creator.
Wandering about, that Dundubha serpent approached the side of the Hotṛ priest;
yet even as it coiled around the Hotṛ Bhrigu, Bhrigu did not move from his own place out of fear of the ritual expiation.
Then, indeed, there arose a slight agitation and distress among everyone.
The sage Cyavana saw his father encircled by a serpent;
he cursed the boy who had thrown the snake and caused the disturbance.
"O evil-minded one, because a snake was cast by you into the assembly, therefore become a snake immediately! Having heard this, the boy said to him:
"This was a water-snake released by me here in jest, for sport. (12–13)
"Why do you cast a curse upon me, targeting the Hotṛ priest?"—
speaking thus,
that young student, the son of the sage Sanātana, fell into the state of a serpent within a moment and lamented repeatedly.
Taking his own Dundubha with him, he went and spoke to Bhṛgu:
"I am the son of Sanātana and the grandson of Parameṣṭhin; I have been cursed by your high-souled son, Cyavana. (15–16)
"O Sage, protect me, a brahmin boy who has come to you for refuge from this curse!
Hearing this, Bhṛgu was overcome with compassion and said to Cyavana, "O son!
This which you have done—cursing this boy—is improper."
"Even a venomous serpent would not dare to harm you, let alone this water-snake, which is as harmless as a rope. Grant him release from his curse; let this young Brahmin be at peace."
Cyavana said, "O father, my curse shall not be in vain.
Brahmā, having heard that, then said, "Everything has come to pass by my will.
Formerly, I desired to create a ninth race of Nāgas."
"Indeed, from you there shall arise your lineage upon the surface of the earth.
The Naga Karkoṭaka will give his own daughter to you as a beloved wife;
your lineage shall expand and make its dwelling in the world of mortals."
"On the fifth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa, people will perform the worship of that lineage;
your residence shall be proclaimed as Nāgatīrtha. While the Unborn One was speaking thus, the Nāgas arrived at the sacrifice.
And having been invited— Vāsuki, Takṣaka, Kṛṣīhara, Puṇḍarīka, Kambala and Aśvatara, Kālapara, Bala, Śeṣa,
and the others— they bowed and spoke to the god Pitāmaha at the sacrifice.
"O Brahman, grant us our appropriate service in this sacrifice, which is always fitting for us.
Brahmā said: "O auspicious ones, you who can assume any form at will, dwell here at the Nāga-tīrtha; and those among you who possess wickedness, let them stay at the sacrifice."
"And there may arise a desire to create obstacles for you; therefore, my sacrifice must be protected from you.
O Nāgas, this protection of my sacrifice is your most important duty.
On the fifth day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada, you shall receive worship from the people. (27–28)
Having said "So be it," they all took refuge at the Nāga-tīrtha;
accompanied by the son of Sanātana,
he married the daughter of Karkoṭaka, who was of fresh youth and a perpetuator of Sanātana’s lineage.
From that time on, their lineage became widespread upon the earth in every way.
Those born of the eternal lineage bore a four-cornered tilaka-mark with dots upon their hoods, devoid of a staff above.
The Vaiṣṇavas were of many forms— white, tawny,
pale, red, black, and green— arising according to the distinctions of time. Then, from their intermixture, those variegated and venomless ones were born.
Water-snakes, land-snakes, and those capable of assuming forms at will [were present].
Then they prepared the food and other offerings; in the evening, there was a vigil at night.
And on the third day, the thirteenth lunar day, those very same officiating priests [performed the rites].
Having reached the morning libation (prātaḥsavana), they remained engaged in the sacrificial rites;
once the sacrifice had commenced, there was no pause in the sound there.
"Let it be given! Let it be given! "Let what is desired be eaten! Let much be eaten! [35]
"Let the gift be led forth, let it be led forth—four times more than what was desired!
Mountains of cooked foods, heaps of riches, rivers flowing with ghee and milk, and lakes of sweet drinks. (36-37)
At that time, there were [seats] multiplied a thousandfold, providing satisfaction to ten million [guests].
In the meantime, a certain man of knowledge arrived there.
Knowing the three periods of time, he paid homage to Brahmā and sat down.
Then he related his entire personal history to them all.
Out of curiosity, the officiating priests questioned him regarding his own past deeds;
he recounted those to them, and they were filled with wonder.
They asked: "Tell us, why indeed do you possess this supramundane knowledge?
Tell us, O wise one, who is your guru—is it Brahmā, Hara, or Hari?
The man of knowledge replied: "These six are my gurus, as is Piṅgalā."
The osprey, the serpent, the bee, the arrow-maker, and the young maiden—42.
From their modes of conduct, O twice-born ones, I obtained this most auspicious knowledge. The lord of Saurāṣṭra had a hundred women, O brahmins. 43.
In his inner apartments there was also a mistress named Piṅgalā;
though deprived of her husband, she would sleep peacefully at night, free from desire.
But his other hundreds of wives, out of longing for pleasure, [remained awake] during the night.
They brought auspicious incenses, ointments, and flowers;
excellent unguents and fine garments.
Possessed by the impulse of the god of love, they were covered in horripilation. || 45-46 ||
"One knows me on the bed and will surely call for me;
another knows me as well, while the third knows neither me nor her.
Thus they vied with one another, watched, and waited for the king.
Among them, she calls out to one, or the second, or the third;
or the fourth, or the fifth, or sometimes ten at night.
The remaining ones, overcome with grief, sigh and fall asleep.
Those who have fallen into the suffering of hope never find a moment of sleep;
for hope is indeed the supreme misery, while freedom from hope is the supreme happiness.
Having turned hope into hopelessness, Piṅgalā sleeps in peace.
She never engaged in amorous dalliance nor did she ever show any rivalry;
Piṅgalā fell into no state of agitation and slept peacefully, even though I was constantly appointed to serve in the inner apartments. (51–52)
Then, having observed this, I abandoned all hope and even fell asleep.
For those who sleep happily at night, the fire of their digestive tract is kindled;
it receives food in abundance and attains nourishment. (53)
This very cause has arisen, which increases nourishment and knowledge.
Listen as I relate how that knowledge was obtained from the osprey:
I possessed abundant wealth, a great inheritance from my father and grandfather. (54–55)
For the sake of wealth, my sons, grandsons, heirs, kinsmen, and relatives harass me day and night; likewise,
whoever to whom I do not give anything constantly torments me.
One strives constantly to take away my life-breaths;
another, wielding a staff, begs while instilling fear;
and a third begs with conciliation as well as praise. (57–58)
One [type of person] seeks wealth through separation, while another does so by bestowing victories;
and finally, having become wretched, he repeatedly begs for riches.
Thus, I never obtain any happiness from their company.
Day and night, I find neither pleasant sleep nor peace.
Then one day, I saw a kurara bird carrying meat,
being struck from all sides by other birds in the sky for the sake of that flesh.
The flesh fell from his beak, and those birds flew after it;
the osprey, abandoned by them, became happy.
By the renunciation of the bait, the osprey prospers in happiness.
Indeed, I have already divided and bestowed wealth upon my sons and others.
Since then, being released by them, I remain in comfort and prosperity.
The attainment of wealth leads to delusion, and delusion leads to hell.
Therefore, one who seeks liberation should abandon both gain and loss from afar.
Just as bait is devoured by fish in the water, by beasts of prey on the earth,
and by birds in the sky, so too is the man of wealth preyed upon everywhere.
Even one who is free from fault is repeatedly punished by kings if he possesses wealth;
whereas a poor man, even if he has committed an offense, is generally let go by people.
Those who are constantly surrounded by others stumble at every step.

The wealthy speak incoherently, like those intoxicated by liquor; they harbor hatred toward their own food while showing outward affection. To them, even that which is wholesome is perceived as heavy, yet what is always pungent to the mouth is regarded as light—just as it is for those suffering from fever.
For the sake of wealth, this world of living beings frequents even the cremation ground.
Even sons abandon their own father if he is destitute.
Indeed, friendship lasts only so long as there is no application for wealth.
When a connection with wealth arises, enmity follows of its own accord.
Therefore, having abandoned riches, I remain happy like a kurara bird.
I shall relate how I previously obtained knowledge from a serpent.
A snake, having entered a dwelling made by another, enjoys itself with ease;
having dwelt there happily, it leaves for another region.
It does not conceive a sense of "mine-ness" at all, nor does it create one of its own accord.
The undertaking of a house leads only to suffering and never to happiness;
through the building of a house, attachment persists until the time of death.
Once a house is built, a wife is acquired, and from her come sons and daughters.
For the sake of that [enjoyment], it remains for further experience, performing what ought to be done and what ought not to be done.
Like a silkworm, it does not perceive itself to be enveloped.
Bound by the notions of "I" and "mine," and being attached, living beings perish. (75–76)
Sunk in the ocean-mud of affection for sons, wives, and wealth,
ignorant men perish like rutting elephants.
Servants commit sins, while great men enjoy their wealth.

The enjoyer is liberated from that sin, while the doer is tainted by the fault. (78) Therefore, I have abandoned this mansion which acts as a bolt upon the path to liberation; a virtuous person should never be a giver of suffering to householders. (79)

One should always dwell anywhere at all, taking refuge under trees while avoiding inhabited places; one should practice the *mādhukarī* mode of begging for alms while avoiding obstacles and remaining free from the smoke of worldly passions. One should meditate upon Nārāyaṇa and constantly chant the name Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
One should certainly not harbor passion or hatred, nor should one cultivate enmity or friendship.
One should regard a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as equal, as well as honor and dishonor.
For such a person, there is never any distinction between "one's own" country and "another's. (8.1–8.2)
Whether it be the earth, a family, or even the family of Brahmā;
the twenty-four principles constitute the house and the unstable family.
It is carried along with one eternally, yet there is no attachment to any other house.
Just as the spinning of a potter’s wheel comes to rest through its own momentum, so too should one acquire the vessel of liberation during that time.
Such knowledge, which bestows liberation, was indeed obtained by me from a serpent. (84–85)
By its power, my great splendor and happiness always endure;
nevertheless, I shall now declare the essence-born knowledge obtained from a bee.
Long ago, indeed, a bee was seen by me upon a certain tree.
Having taken refuge at the tip of a branch and made it his former dwelling,
he remained there during spring among the fragrant blossoms and fruits of many wild trees, extracting the most excellent essence. (87–88)
Having taken it, he constantly employed it in his own dwelling;
free from agitation, he filled a vessel with the finest honey. Many other bees attained satisfaction through that. (89)
I have extracted the essence of the scriptures, which is as auspicious as honey.
(90) People take up those well-composed treatises;
others indeed subsist upon them, just as bees do. (91)
By that merit, I am always radiant with splendor and possessed of wisdom.
The sages, who delight in the Self and are free from the thirst for enjoyment,
become exceedingly brilliant when satisfied by the essence of the honeyed nectar.
Those who are possessed by greed and delusion are indeed born devoid of luster.
The Vedas and the Śāstras were created by me for the welfare of the worlds; having extracted the essence from all of them, I have given it [to you], and thus I am truly happy. (93–94)
I shall proclaim that knowledge which I obtained from the arrow-maker;
for the sake of beholding the Self, I questioned thousands [of teachers]. Having attained renown through the vision of the Self, I have acted according to what they taught.
Through knowledge and through yoga, through the study of the inner self,
through divine practice, and with the divine eye, I have scrutinized it;
yet the Self was not seen by me, and therefore I became dispassionate.
I wandered upon the surface of the earth seeking such a teacher who would demonstrate the goal of the Guru;
however, I did not find such a Guru anywhere.
Then, I stood in a secluded spot by the royal highway.
And there is a certain practitioner who,
with a one-pointed mind, repeatedly pierces the target with an arrow;
he indeed pierces even that which stands at his side, for he knows nothing else besides it.
Accompanied by that army on its path, the king proceeded;
then, in another moment, he was seen by me as someone approached him—this man who possessed arrows and was skilled at hitting the mark, his mind dedicated to practice. (101)
Questioned as to how much time had passed since the king departed, the arrow-maker did not hear [the answer] and questioned him again;
yet even by her [the sound of the voice], he did not hear at all, having become absorbed in his target. (102–103)
Having touched him again and shaken him, the young man indeed questioned him.
Then he said: "I have not seen anyone shooting arrows; who has gone this way?
No army has been seen going from here. Ask someone else if [anyone] might have gone."

With my mind intent on the practice of archery, I did not look around. (105) Having heard that, I then reflected there upon one-pointedness of mind as the means for the vision of the Self, which brings about the realization of one's own nature. (106)

Knowledge of the Self, which is the science of Brahman, does not arise anywhere at all without the cessation of the mind; nor is there realization without practice. (107) "Since this knowledge has been attained by me, I shall therefore effect that cessation."
I constantly meditate upon Hari, who dwells within the lotus of my heart.
I bear in mind and meditate again and again upon Hari Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, whose form is the universe, both externally and within my heart, and who possesses a most beautiful form.

Then, through practice, I behold Hari in all directions and their extremities, in the sky and on the surface of the earth; in man, in a child, in a cow, in a tree, in women, in creepers, and in mountains; in front, behind, and in every reality.
I see only that one [Lord] in this way, and nothing else whatsoever except Hari.
By His splendor alone, I am thus illumined today and always;
such knowledge has been obtained by me through the practice of meditation in every respect.
Now I shall declare the knowledge obtained from the presence of the maiden.
Formerly, on the road, my wife emerged behind me;
that woman, who had both sons and daughters, spoke to me, her husband.
"Practice yoga at home; liberation will come of this, there is no doubt.
Become a celibate ascetic even while living as a householder, with your self fully restrained.
If you were to abandon me and go elsewhere, [it would be a great loss]. (1.14–1.15)
Therefore, I shall die, and your child shall also die;
the young girl too shall die. Therefore, O Lord, have mercy!
Do not go to any other sacred place, forsaking the sacred place that is home.
"Since the holy site of Hāṭakeśvara grants liberation through mere remembrance,
I have constructed a leaf-hut at his bidding and indeed dwell not far from the sacred field of Hāṭakeśvara. (1.17–1.18)
"A maiden belonging to me, a forest-dweller, is playing in my hermitage. On her forearm she wears many bracelets that make a great deal of noise.
While she was engaged in the task of carrying wood, she struck a piece of wood with another."
In some places each single bracelet breaks into pieces;
in other places, when time has passed in this manner, only two bracelets remain.
Then there is even a sound, and as that time passes further still—
Now, however, there is only one bangle on each finger;
for one who is alone, neither friction nor sound arises.
Having reflected upon this, I attained knowledge and abandoned that hermitage.
There is constant quarreling with many, as well as rivalry with two;
therefore, I shall wander alone like a young maiden’s bracelet.
Thus, having abandoned my wife, daughters, and sons, I shall roam about.
Wherever I lay down at sunset, and whatever food I obtained and ate, I would always remember Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa while free from all bonds.
Thus was this knowledge attained by me through reflecting upon those various circumstances.
From whomever knowledge may arise, he shall be your guru; and so it is for you.
Through the grace of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, I have obtained from these [gurus] the knowledge of other worlds as well as self-knowledge in abundance. (126–127)
"By hearing this, one also attains such knowledge as this.
Having spoken thus, that wise man, the guest of the sacrifice, then ceased speaking;
he was indeed Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa himself, residing at Aśvapaṭṭasaraḥ.

"He is to be honored as a guest at the sacrifice"— it was for the purpose of this injunction that he had come. Recognizing Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa through meditation, the brahmin Śrī Hari was honored by the officiating priests and sat down among them.

Thus ends the five hundred and tenth chapter, titled "The Demonstration of the Arrival of the Son of Sanātana in the Form of a Boy at the Sacrifice for the Purpose of Throwing a Snake, and Subsequently the Arrival of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa in the Form of a Guest for the Purpose of Bestowing Knowledge upon His Teacher and Others, as well as the Exposition of Knowledge," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. Chapter 511: *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā* — Section 1 (*Kṛtayuga-santāna*) — Chapter 511.
[The Author: Chapter 512.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, Lakṣmī! Then [he saw] this guest, Śrī Nārāyaṇa.
Those brahmins seated in the pavilion questioned him in the form of a brahmin:
"Where have you gone after leaving home, and how much time has passed for you?
Tell us what is appropriate for the sacrificial rites of us ascetics who have assembled here."
Then the guest said: "I have wandered through the three worlds—Brahmaloka, Īśaloka, and Jīvaloka—again and again;
I have traversed hundreds of continents, earths, and Golokas."
Thousands, tens of thousands, hundreds of thousands, and millions—
wherever I lay down at sunset, having performed the maintenance of my body,
I dwell there as if in my own body, for I reside mostly within the fundamental principles (tattvas).
I dwell everywhere at the sacrifice, and I also dwell during the dissolution of the universe. My years have passed beyond all calculation;
there is no numbering of my ages, for my life is considered eternal.
"Wherever I go, that place becomes a sacred ford (tīrtha) simply by my arrival. Having visited those infinite [sites], I have now come to this sacrifice for the gods.
I have wandered through all the islands, the regions, and every single sacred ford."
Having visited Dakṣiṇa, Pūrvajyotiṣka, and Himālaya, as well as the Northern regions,
Śvetadvīpa, Kṛṣṇadeśa, Siṃhāraṇya, and Raivata;
and having visited Sārasvata, Gāṅga, Vārāṇasī, and Puṣkara—
Having heard that my grandfather was performing a universal sacrifice in the western region,
I have come here to receive hospitality, provided it is granted.
Brahmā and the other gods said to Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, "Choose a boon."
"Accept hospitality as you wish, whether it be material or spiritual;
we shall certainly bestow that upon the knower who is our inner self.
The guest replied, "I always require the offering of oneself."

He is the refuge for those who have surrendered to him, the one to whom all things are offered, and the object of their desire. (1.3) Even if Brahmā and the other gods were to perform a sacrifice without giving to me, they would not obtain the desired fruit, just as one does not obtain the desired fruit by failing to give to a guest. (1.4)
"I pray for my share of the sacrifice, the portion of the gods, and divine status;
likewise, grant me both inner and outer [powers].
Having been addressed thus, the deities replied: "A guest has arrived from afar."
O best of Brahmins, you are the essence of truth; everything shall be given to you at this sacrifice.
Hari is remembered as the Lord of this sacrifice that is being performed;
for this reason, that God is called Yajñapuruṣa (the Person of Sacrifice).
You reside at Kuṅkumavāpī in the holy field of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa;
you are the beloved Kamalā, the consort of Śrīmad Gopālakṛṣṇa.
Through her penance, she obtained from you, who abide within the self, a son born of her own mind.
You are that very Śrī Hari himself—Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Lakṣmī; the Lord of Śrī Pārvatī; the Lord of Prabhā, the Lord of Māṇikī, and the Lord of Jayā;
you exist as the soul of sacrificial rites, the bestower of the fruits of actions. (1.511.20)
The Lord of the mind, the Lord of Maṅgalā, the Lord of Rādhā,
the Sovereign of the Imperishable, the Lord of Ramā, and also the Lord of the Liberated— the Supreme Self dwelling within— by your name, the full fruit of sacrifice shall always be granted. (21)
Whoever shall worship you in a *śrāddha* rite for the ancestors (*paitrya*) or likewise in one for the gods (*daiva*),
that [offering] shall become inexhaustible when accompanied by the name of Viṣṇu.
When Kṛṣṇa is satisfied, all the gods indeed become satisfied.
Having spoken thus, Brahmā, Lakṣmī, Śakra, Dharma, Śeṣa, Śiva,
and the others indeed offered everything to the guest Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
From that time forward, the worship arising from guests was established.
Therefore, O Lakṣmī! Worship of the guest should always be performed at an auspicious moment.
For householders, there is no higher duty than the honoring of guests. There is no god greater than the guest; one should never bypass a god. (25–26)
When a guest turns away from someone’s house with his hopes frustrated,
he departs having given that person his own misdeeds and taking away their merit.
[Even if one has] truthfulness, vows, austerity, study, and charity performed for a hundred years—
Everything is lost for him who does not honor a guest.
Indeed, he in whose house guests are fully satisfied is a true householder; others, however, are merely guardians of the home. (28–29)
In this world, three things reach those people who have previously performed meritorious deeds: the ancestral rite (*śrāddha*), charity (*dāna*), and auspicious speech.
When the guest is satisfied, all the deities of the householder are satisfied.
When he turns his face away, all [other deities] likewise turn their faces away; of this there is no doubt.
Even by the offering of one's own self, he must be propitiated—Nārāyaṇa, the gods and goddesses, guests, and the preceptor. (3.1–32)
A virtuous woman, an orphaned maiden, a female mendicant, and a guest are considered [worthy of offerings].
So too is one who arrives at the time of the meal during a paternal *śrāddha* rite,
or one who arrives at midday exhausted from a long journey.

But those who approach on the day after a meal has been taken, whether by day or by night, are declared to be guests (*atithi*); one who arrives beforehand is not a guest. Whether he be dear or hateful, foolish or wise— (34–35)
A householder should indeed give food according to his capacity,
as well as a seat, water, a hospitable disposition, kind words, and a loving glance.
These things are never lacking in the home of the virtuous.

Indeed, the ancestors become satisfied by the welcome offered to a guest. Likewise, satisfaction arises for Brahmā from the seat provided to a guest. Through the offering of the *arghya* water, Śambhu is pleased, and through the *pādya* water, the gods are gratified. (37–38)
"Through the gift of food, Viṣṇu attains eternal satisfaction.
He should always be honored according to one's ability, and especially so by being fed. Having spoken thus and performed the ritual for the sacrifice, the gods then—
Having made due arrangements, they fed the lords;
they passed the night with festivities and discourses on the Supreme Lord.
On the fourth day, they commenced the sacrificial rites as prescribed.
The drinking of soma and all other rites, as well as the sacrificial materials and so forth,
proceeded there appropriately; at that time,
a certain young Brāhmaṇa arrived, hungry and afflicted by thirst.
Seeing the auspicious materials for the fire-oblation, he ate them with eager anticipation.
Seeing him devouring the offering, the one who was about to depart cursed him,
saying "Fie!"— “O wicked one, like a Rākṣasa, you eat the materials intended for the sacrifice right here!”
"This is the work of Rākṣasas; become a Rākṣasa without delay!
Thus addressed, he became there exceedingly terrifying, with hair standing erect, long lips, a gaping mouth, and a dark complexion—a true Rākṣasa.
With spike-like ears and red eyes, he was terrifying to behold at first sight.
Upon seeing that Rākṣasa, the lords were struck with fear and trembled;
they repeatedly recited the hymns that destroy demons.
The Rākṣasa, too, casting off his fear, approached the Grandfather;
bowing down with palms joined in reverence, he spoke concerning himself:
"O Brahmin, I am indeed your grandson, the twice-born son of Pulastya."
"O father, I have been turned into a Rākṣasa today by my father, the Prasthātṛ, through a curse.
I am Viśvāvasu by name, a descendant of Pulastya; please show me mercy.
Whatever was prepared here for the sake of the *homa* has been consumed by me. (1.511.50)
"Forgive his offense and rid him of this state of being a *rākṣasa*.
Then Brahmā, filled with compassion, said to the *pratiprasthātṛ*:
"This boy is my grandson; he does not know what ought and ought not to be done. (51)
"Indeed, his demonic nature must certainly be removed by you.
Having heard that, the sage said: "Those born of Pulastya's lineage shall indeed become Rākṣasas because of their opposition to the work of the gods."

Indeed, no one is able to remove his demonic nature, for even though he possesses a human disposition, he has already rendered himself impure by what he has done. This is the very nature of sacrificial materials; who can prevent it? || 54 ||
"O Great-Grandfather, if fire were ever to become cold, or if the moon were ever to become hot, then my word might prove otherwise. Therefore,
let this lord of the Rākṣasas remain forever a Rākṣasa."
Having heard these words of his, Brahmā then said to Viśvāvasu:
"O grandson, remain forever in this form,
occupying the western site of this city of Camatkārapura."
In the west there are Rākṣasas, Kūṣmāṇḍakas, and Piśācas;
Bhūtas, Pretas, and Piśācas—ward them off by all means.
Therefore go there, my son, and become the sovereign of them all. (58–59)
"I have now bestowed the kingdom upon you for the sake of the Rākṣasas.
The Rākṣasa replied: "Why should I alone enjoy the kingdom?
And why should I, as a king, provide food for my servants?"

And that king who does not provide for the nourishment of his servants and subjects also attains hell; therefore, O Lord, give food. Brahmā said: "Your Śrāddha rite is indeed devoid of sesame seeds and Darbha grass."
If it is seen by a menstruating woman, gazed upon by a boar, or looked at by a dog or a donkey; if it is offered according to improper rites,
or where one who suffers from leprosy, has deformed nails, or is a buffalo-eater consumes what was offered to you.
[Food] prepared by those who have not bathed, or by those who have anointed themselves with oil, or by those wearing soiled garments;
or that which is eaten by one with black teeth, or by the husband of a Śūdra woman;
or that which is prepared by one devoid of Vedic knowledge, or performed without celibacy (brahmacarya). 64–65.
All that [offering] of yours will be devoid of the ritual for the gods;
salt and buttermilk will appear visibly transformed to you.
Furthermore, the sacrificer or the twice-born [priest] will be bereft of celibacy.
Wherever there is such an enjoyer, all that shall belong to you.
But whatever food is given with an iron vessel, devoid of purity, and always lacking the purification of mantras—may that be yours. (67–68)
Thus addressed, the Rākṣasa bowed, ate what was given, and departed from there. When the sacrificial rites were completed, the matter was thus resolved.
Then, on the fifth day, they were enlightened by Pulastya.
Having bathed and wearing washed white garments, they performed the rites at that sacrifice.
The *udgātṛ* priest joined the rituals with the chanting of the *Sāmaveda*;
and whatever was performed with wooden stakes was executed with great composure.
The gods, having arrived, joyfully partook of the soma;
as the oblation was repeatedly offered into the blazing fire,
and when the drinking of soma had begun, the songs were composed by the Udgātṛ priests.
A single maiden arrived, eager for the chanting of the Sāmaveda;
she was wise and desired Śaṅkukarṇa in her heart. She was the excellent daughter of the preeminent Chāndoga named Devaśarman. (73–74)
Known by the name Udumbarīti, she was eager to hear the Sāman; and in the assembly, she addressed the Udgātṛ with these words:
"In whatever manner the stakes indicated by the Sāman are set up," ||| 75 ||
"When an oblation is offered in the Dakṣiṇāgni fire, the destruction of sin occurs. (76) Thus instructed by her, the oblation was performed by the twice-born.
Then they asked her: "From where have you come, O maiden? (77)
The daughter of the sage Parvata, Udumbarī, spoke:
"I am one who remembers my former births, born here from the Gandharva world due to a curse.
Indeed, a flaw in his voice occurred for Nārada while he was singing. (78)
And then, as I was singing there, Nārada laughed at me.
Thereupon, he became angry with me, saying, "I have been laughed at falsely by you. Because of that, the curse of Nārada occurred: "Become a human girl, O maiden! (1.511.80).
Then, propitiated by my hymns for the sake of ending the curse, he said to me:
"You shall be born in the house of an eminent Brahmin woman;
having been born in the house of Devaśarman, I am now a maiden."
"Satyabhāmā is my mother, and she is devoted to her husband.
Then Nārada said, "Brahmā will perform a sacrifice;
at that time, during the reversal of Śaṅkha's [power]."
Then, at that place, you should say: "A ritual stake (śaṅku) has been properly established;
when the oblation is offered in the southern fire, there shall be the destruction of sin.
At that moment, your liberation will occur, without a doubt.
"Behold this splendor of mine, and likewise this celestial chariot that has arrived.
Today I shall go to my own heaven, for it is now my station as a Gandharva.
Then the Udgātṛ priest spoke at the sacrifice regarding the prevention of injury: (85–86)
"I am pleased; choose a boon. Trees do not receive my vision.
Then Udumbarī said: "Grant me this, O God, in your presence:
that in every sacrifice and in every assembly, there be for me a share in the midst of the food."
Then, in my presence there, the rite of moving the ritual peg (śaṅku) should be performed;
by this act of my vital energy, those dwelling in heaven shall likewise attain satisfaction.
Having heard these words of his, the Udgātṛ then spoke to her.
Having placed you in the center of the sacrificial assembly and worshipped you with garments, ornaments, perfumes, flowers, and ointments,
thereafter they will all perform the ritual movement of the *śaṅku* in your presence.

May there always be well-being for you; may you attain supreme contentment. (91) Any woman who worships you with fruits in the midst of the assembly, her ritual action performed without you will be entirely fruitless. (92)
"She shall obtain the full fruit of the sacrifice as well as spiritual merit;
she who honors you with garments, ornaments, and other gifts shall partake in the religious merit of the sacrifice.
Thus spoke the foremost of gods, as well as the Udgātṛ priest and the brahmins.
Then the goddess was said to have become divine, traveling in a celestial chariot in the sky.
While she was in that aerial chariot in the heavens, thousands of women came to offer her worship; they honored her with many articles of offering.
Upon hearing this, Devaśarman also arrived to see his daughter; accompanied by his wife, he prostrated before his daughter who was seated in the celestial chariot of the virtuous.
The daughter said, "O father, do not offer me salutation."
"Indeed, the attainment of heaven that I have reached will perish through the depletion of my merit.
Stay here together with your wife; I shall surely lead you both to heaven.
Then her parents became joyful and well-composed. (97–98)
Beholding the worship of their daughter and considering themselves fortunate,
other members of the household also remained there, thinking themselves blessed.
At that moment, Bhṛgu arrived outside the assembly hall before Brahmā.
He spoke again to the maiden, saying: "O Lord, by constantly taking her into the sacrificial rites, this Udgātṛ has made this Vedic path non-Vedic;
he has offered the status of a goddess to that mortal woman in the presence of the gods."
"The drinking of Soma with her was commenced by us at the sacrifice;
this has certainly not proven appropriate, therefore consider what is appropriate.
Thus addressed, the Creator of the Universe said, "She is indeed not a mere mortal woman."
But that goddess, the daughter of the Gandharva, was indeed always Udumbarī;
for she has been liberated from the curse of Nārada by means of the sacrificial peg (śaṅku).
As this deity of sacrifice, she shall certainly remain forever.
Then, at that very moment, the sixty-eight Mothers arrived from Kailāsa for the sacrifice; delighted, they spoke to the Creator:
"Invited by Pavana, we have come together to your sacrifice."
Having heard that the Udumbara tree had received worship and a share within the midst of the sacrifice,
O Grandfather, they arrived and said, "Grant us a permanent share and a place within the sacrificial assembly. (106–107)
Indeed, sixty-six positions were assigned by Brahmā;
they were well-established in those places during the sacrifice, honored with offerings at that time.
Satisfied and remaining there in silence, Sāvitrī then arrived.
She was addressed by the twice-born at the sacrifice, "Do not go," and thus forbidden;
hearing that the beautiful woman Gāyatrī had already been wedded by Brahmā, she regarded it as a thunderbolt and indeed grieved in her wrath.
"The sun has set; thus there was an excuse for the sacrifice. And for the sacrificial Brahmins, there arose a discussion on the ultimate truth during the night.

(111) Thus ends the five hundred and eleventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Granting of Boons to Atithi, the Eating of the Sacrificial Materials by Viśvāvasu, the Son of Pulastya, the Curse 'Become a Rākṣasa,' the Arrival of Udumbarī, the Daughter of the Mountain Sage, and Her Position of Honor at the Sacrifice, as well as the Arrival of the Host of Sixty-eight Mātṛkās," in the first section, *Kṛtayugasantāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*. (511)

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to those sixty-eight goddesses who are established there;
they are worshipped by the residents of the city in that sacrificial field.
The family deities were driven out by the city-dwellers;
hearing that they had been established on the sacrificial ground, Sāvitrī cursed them:
"Since a place has been made for you at this sacrifice before my arrival... (2)
Having met with her rival wife, she will always abandon us from that time forth.
(3) The worship performed for you in the city shall bear no fruit;
deprived of palaces, you shall be tormented by cold, rain, and heat. (4)
"You shall become wretched, wandering through the sky in emptiness.
Thus cursed, they all approached the Udumbara tree and made him hear that curse,
which was the very futility of their worship.
And then they prayed for the warding off of even that curse.
Udumbarī said to them: "I am certainly not able to make the word of Sāvitrī false; however, I shall grant you this boon."
Appointed by those residing in the city over sixty-eight clans,
the worship performed there shall bear fruit through the grace of the Grandfather (Brahmā).
Then, food, drink, and worship will be offered by the members of those clans.
There, you shall find satisfaction and a comfortable seat for yourselves.
By giving gifts at the city gate to those who provide invisible laughter and likewise to those who grant strength, as well as to the female worshippers, you will attain fulfillment.

Thus those auspicious ones were established all around the Nāga river. Then Devaśarman, the father of Udumbarī, arrived accompanied by his virtuous wife; seeing his divine daughter, he was filled with joy.

He was formerly the Gandharva Parvata in heaven by name. When he was repeatedly entreated by Udumbarī for the sake of her father, and at that very time cursed by Nārada for the sake of his mother, he [descended] to the earth.
"O Mother, O Father, come to the earth with me;
become my father and mother, for I am human, and you shall both be my parents there. || 14 || And so, I shall be your daughter there, and then they—
Devasharman and his wife were indeed born as humans among them;
their daughter was born as Udumbarī, who now dwells here in this celestial chariot.
Upon seeing her, Devasharman too cast off his body, accompanied by his beloved.
He indeed assumed a divine body and ascended a celestial vehicle;
accompanied by his wife and his son, he spent the night in the sky.
Thus passed the day and the fifth night of the sacrifice.
Then, when dawn had broken, it was ordained that the ritual bath of purification (*avabhṛthasnāna*) should be performed;
this act, which embodies all sacred fords (*tīrtha*), must be carried out according to the prescribed rules.
"Thereafter, we shall indeed go to heaven together with the deities. (18–19)
Having reflected thus, those three, stationed upon their celestial chariots,
awaited the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), the ritual exemption (*parihāra*), and likewise the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*),
as well as Brahmā and the sages and Brahmins seated in the sacrificial assembly (*sadas*).
There he gave a sacrificial fee and established the Puṣkara lake in the west— a sacred site that is purifying—
in the bright fortnight of the month of Kārtika, beginning from the eleventh day.
And for five days ending with the full moon, other sacred sites as well shall remain here in this very lake throughout all ages, O Brahmins;
and whoever performs a bath here in the midst of the five nights [of the festival], [shall attain the highest goal].
"His acts of giving and his recitations as well shall become inexhaustible.
(24) Then all those brahmins, being pleased, granted their permission for the fulfillment of the fruit of the sacrifice, so that it might be perfected through meritorious gifts. (25)
The sacrifice was completed, and abundant sacrificial fees were offered.
The virtuous brahmins and others were satisfied upon receiving their wealth.
Then Pulastya declared there, "The sacrifice has been fully endowed with its sacrificial fees."
May he always be endowed with [virtue], free from the need for expiations.
Beyond this, I shall perform the remainder of the ritual—the Varuṇeṣṭi sacrifice as well as the recitation (japa).
Thereafter, all [of you] should perform that which yields the fruit [of the rite].
"An auspicious bath called the *avabhṛtha* shall indeed be performed by you and me in the waters.
Having spoken thus, he went together with everyone to the sacred site of Puṣkara;
and at the Nāga River, [the sacrifice was concluded] by the officiating priests—the *ācārya*, *agnīdh*, and *hotṛ*.
Then, together with Brahmā, the Brahmins, and many members of the sacrificial assembly,
auspicious oblations were offered there by everyone according to the prescribed ritual, using sacrificial vessels, just as they are offered into the fire, so too into the water.

Then, for the sake of propitiating Varuṇa and for the pacification of all misfortunes, they entered the water together with the officiating priests, Brahmā, and everyone else. Indeed, whoever shall perform a ritual bath at the site of the *avabhṛtha* [concluding bath], [shall attain purification].
A mortal who performs this shall become free from all sin, as it embodies all sacred fords (tīrtha).
Whatever sacred fords exist throughout the three worlds,
they all come into the presence of one who has undertaken the Vāruṇī sacrifice.

Therefore, with every effort, those who have been initiated and possess the necessary purpose should perform their bath there within the water. Then Brahmā spoke to Mahendra for the benefit of the world:
In the great throng of people, the people will not recognize me at all.
At that moment, you shall bathe in the water, and then, mounted upon an elephant,
holding a bamboo pole in your hand and a black antelope in the sky above.
Cast that into the water so that everyone may know the time for bathing,
whereby this entire world, having learned it, shall bathe at that very moment;
whoever performs the bath shall attain the welfare as described.
Even one who is far away, even the very aged, even a child, and even women obtain the merit born of bathing; having heard this, Indra acted accordingly.
At that moment, the deities, the Brahmins, the seers, and the sages likewise [did so].
The peaceful humans, divine beings, Gandharvas, Guhyakas, and others who dwell in the fourteen worlds, being composed in mind, bathed there.
Then Brahmā said to Śakra: "Choose a boon; I shall grant it to you."
Indra said: "O King, whatever monarch shall cast aside his deer-skin at this very sacred ford every year and perform the avabhṛtha bath,
he— standing upon an elephant at the conclusion of the sacrifice— shall be freed from all sin."
By my blessing, may all enemies be invincible [to them], may those who have bathed be freed from sin,
and likewise may my subjects be filled with happiness and free from disease.
Having performed sacrifices, vows, and other rites for five days in the month of Kārtika, [may they attain these fruits].
Those people who bathe at the Kutupa hour on the morning of the Pratipad day will become victorious and freed from the sins of the year;
they will undoubtedly be liberated from mental anguish and physical disease. (45–46)
In the meantime, a terrible disease called yakṣma arrived;
it was incurable even for the gods and likewise for Dhanvantari.
It had blue garments, a red tongue, parched sides, and a melodious voice.
Coughing with dry phlegm and unable to move his foot, he said:
"Having heard of your fame from afar, O Grandfather, I have come here. Indeed, I was created long ago by Dakṣa when he was enraged for the sake of Candra. (48–49)
And I am the very fruit of Rohiṇī’s partiality.
Thereafter, Lord Śaṅkara was propitiated by the Moon through his ascetic penance;
Śambhu then granted me one fortnight—the dark fortnight—and not the other.
"In that regard, O Grandfather, where might food for me be obtainable?
If, at the full-moon sacrifice-sattra, the twice-born should say after eating, 'We are satisfied,' then by that, O Lord, the fruit of the sacrifice would be complete. (51–52)
If the Brahmins have not been satisfied during this sacrificial session,
my residence must be granted to that person who has caused the destruction of the merit of the sacrifice.
Act in such a way that I may be satisfied by your sacrifice.

"I am a Brāhmaṇa, the son of Dakṣa; let my satisfaction be provided. Brahmā said: "O Vipra, if your words regarding satisfaction are not fulfilled in this Kṛta age, you must remain there at the sacrifice as one whose merit is exhausted."
Furthermore, at the conclusion of the Vaiśvadeva rite, an offering (bali) should be given by you to the Brahmins;
by that, your satisfaction in the second fortnight will become complete.
You must never reside in the lineage or the house of one who gives such offerings.
Thus addressed, that Yakṣman said: "I am satisfied; give me a portion of the earth.
O Grandfather, I shall dwell here for the sake of penance until the end of the kalpa.
Thereupon, Brahmā granted him that portion of the earth as a hermitage.
Yakṣmā, however, established his own hermitage upon the northern side near the Nāga River,
having reached its confluence with the ocean.
Indeed, he who offers an oblation to Yakṣmā at the conclusion of the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice [attains his favor].
Consumption (yakṣmā) does not arise among his family members, nor among his cattle and other animals. For him there shall be no medicines, no mantras, and no physicians.
Having been told this, that Consumption departed, taking the food with him to the vicinity of the ocean.
Now listen, Lakṣmī, to the rebuke administered by Sāvitrī; I shall tell you what occurred there at the sacrifice of Brahmā—pay close attention.
[She rebuked] Gaurī, Lakṣmī, Śacī, Medhā, Arundhatī, and Pārvatī.
Prabhā, Māṇikī, Svāhā, Kambharā, Kṣamā, Dhṛti,
Svadhā, Puṣṭi, Saguṇā, Buddhi, Haṃsā, Mañjulā, Padmā, Ramā, Satī, Kṛṣṇā, Nārāyaṇī, and Sarasvatī. (63–64)
Likewise, taking with her the female attendants Ghṛtācī, Menakā, Rambhā, Tilottamā,
Urvaśī, Mohinī, Svarṇā, Lalitā, Jayā, and Dayā,
she proceeded to the site of the sacrifice amidst the sounding of musical instruments.
At that time, Sāvitrī’s right eye throbbed,
and likewise the right limbs of all those women throbbed.
Then, all of them, intent on songs and festivities, arrived at the sacrificial pavilion.
Knowing that his own mother had arrived, Nārada went forward to meet her and told her the entire account of the cowherd girl:
"The Creator has joined a girdle around her waist; she is as if wedded. (68)
Upon hearing this, Sāvitrī’s face withered;
she was drained of her natural luster, overcome by profound despondency, and her radiance and physical form faded away.
With a vacant mind, she walked on, stumbling at every step. (1.512.70)
She beheld that pavilion, which was like a prison cell;
seeing her husband there together with his new wife,
she, her eyes bloodshot with anger, spoke these harsh words.
"O wise ones, O Brahmins, O seers who are the lords of this assembly!
Let the women, having become silent, listen with focused minds.
How can this be fitting for you to do, you whose appearance is that of the most venerable elders? (72–73)
For she was married by both parties as one indeed impure;
devoted to the customs of cattle, she was always a seller of buttermilk and ever defiled.
Born of a lineage full of sin, she was taken [as a wife] despite her censurable deeds.

"O Creator, if you truly have need of an excellent wife for the sacrifice, why was she not obtained by you anywhere in the three worlds? This girl is surely an Ābhīra maiden whom you have married; you have certainly fallen from the path of the Creator."
Therefore, by this act, you shall not receive worship;
indeed, those who perform your worship will be destitute of wealth.
[This shall apply] to your sons, your grandsons, and other inhabitants of heaven as well.
And yet, this which you have done is unworthy of Brahmins.
Or rather, this is not your fault; indeed, those who act for their own self-interest behave in such a way.
They feel no shame and they do not distinguish between what ought and ought not to be done, nor between the auspicious and the inauspicious.
Driven by the power of self-interest, a person considers what should not be done as what ought to be done; he regards a friend as an enemy, and he regards an enemy as a friend.
Indeed, there is no truth in a gambler, nor is there any friendship in a thief.
There is no kindness whatsoever in the king, nor is there any shame among those who seek only their own interests.
(81) Indeed, this misfortune of co-wives that has now arrived would not cause me any pain;
for one who is powerful may indeed have thousands of women. (82)
This is for women of noble birth from one's own caste, and not for women of low origin. Yet this is a great sorrow: that I, an Ābhīra woman, am censured.
A cowherd’s wife whose character is ruined—what shall I do? I shall surely die.
Therefore, O Creator, mocked by you, I shall go quickly to the forest;
indeed, the one who performs your worship shall become poor,
since this daughter of an Ābhīra has been placed by you in my stead.
O Creator, by my curse, your lineage shall cease to exist;
this woman who worships Gāyatrī shall become a barren woman and suffer distress.
Should she ever have sons born from her mind, they will indeed belong to him.
In another age, all the Mlecchas will be night-prowlers, uncivilized, and without banners;
they will all become destroyers of the world.
O Indra, you shall be defeated by your enemies in battle and fall into captivity.
"O Viṣṇu, having become a human, you shall long remain in a state of servitude.
O Rudra, you shall experience for a long time the sorrow of separation from a wife.
O Agni, you have become a consumer of all things; O Brahmins, go forth into poverty! (89)
"O Kubera, your wealth shall never be available for your enjoyment. Just as the gods, despite being assisted by the Ābhīrāṇīs, remained childless at their sacrifices,
so too have you been repeatedly defeated by the Daityas."
"And those other [goddesses] who are situated here by the side of Gāyatrī—
there shall never be any union between them.
Having spoken thus, she then departed alone, leaving behind the wives of the gods.
Sāvitrī went to Pūrvapuṣkara on Mount Arbuda.
One should worship Sāvitrī properly, especially on the full moon day;
by offering lamps and food oblations, one attains all desires. (93–94)
As many threads as are consumed by that lamp,
and for as many moments as the ghee lamp remains burning,
for that many lifetimes shall that woman be endowed with good fortune.
Endowed with sons and grandsons, wealthy, and adorned by her virtue,
she shall never be unfortunate, barren, one-eyed, or deformed— she who,
beautiful as she is, performs a dance in the presence of Sāvitrī. (96–97)
She who sings a song shall dwell as a deity in heaven;
she who offers sweet food or fruit shall dwell as a deity in heaven.
O Lakṣmī! In Camatkārapura, at the excellent site of Sāvitrītīrtha.
Whoever, having bathed and performed worship, should listen to or recite this chapter,
shall be liberated from all sins and become a partaker of the fruit of sacrifice.
When Sāvitrī had thus departed, Gāyatrī raised her voice.
"Those Brahmins and others who have taken a vow here on my account by means of Sāvitrī—
I shall effect their deliverance through the power of my husband.
Indeed, in all matters concerning the work of Brahmā, there can be no success without Aja."
Brahmā shall occupy the preeminent position in all sacrificial assemblies.
Viṣṇu, dividing himself into two— as Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, the latter being his shadow-self—
Kṛṣṇa, though a mortal, will perform the roles of charioteer and servant for Arjuna.
Through their association with Kṛṣṇa, the cowherds will attain fame among the gods.
O Indra, Brahmā shall destroy your bondage caused by the Asura.
O Fire, though you consume everything, remain a purifier through your sanctity.
"O Rudra, upon the destruction of Satī, you shall be united with Gaurī.
O Kubera, you shall indeed become the giver of wealth to the gods.
Furthermore, the childlessness of the gods shall come to pass by their own will."
"But as for the other women who were cursed, their shadows shall remain separate;
they shall not be united with their original forms.
Having spoken thus, she ceased; and the gods said, "Well said!"
"The twice-born shall always perform worship, morning recitation, and likewise adoration of the Gāyatrī;
they shall never, never [worship] Sāvitrī.
Having spoken thus, they all performed the worship of Gāyatrī. (108–109)
All the deities and others, numbering in the tens of millions, departed for their respective abodes.
Udumbarī ascended to heaven in a celestial chariot along with her two parents.
Brahmā, having reached Arbuda, also took Sāvitrī with him.
And Satya, O Lakṣmī, explained to them the procedure for the sacrifice.
From hearing or reciting this, enjoyment and liberation will certainly be attained;
and wealth, sons, flocks of cattle, riches, and so forth, shall increase day by day. (111–112)

Thus ends the five hundred and twelfth chapter, titled "The Description of the Eighty-Six Goddesses’ Status as Family Deities (*kuladevī*), the Final Concluding Bath (*avabhṛthasnāna*) at the End of the Sacrifice, the Arrival of the Disease of Consumption (*yakṣmaroga*), the Curses Pronounced by Sāvitrī Due to Gāyatrī’s Opposition, the Interventions Made by Gāyatrī to Avert Them, and the Departure of All to Their Respective Worlds," in the first section, the *Kṛtayugasantāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
