Chapter 514 → Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:

Listen, Lakṣmī! In Camatkāra, there lived two friends, a Kṣatriya woman and a Brāhmaṇa woman, both of whom were entirely devoted to the practice of austerity. Formerly, there was a twice-born man who was a student of the Sāmaveda, known by the name Chāndogya.
In his later years, he indeed had a daughter as his offspring.
On the very day she was born, on that same day,
the ruler of Ānarta also had a daughter as his offspring.
The king indeed gave her the beautiful name Ratnavatī;
for there arose between Ratnavatī and the brahmin’s daughter a pure and inexhaustible friendship.
They shared a single seat, as well as a single bed, and ate together from the same food.
When the appropriate time for his daughter had arrived, the Brahmin reflected [on her marriage].
However, that maiden was distressed by the prospect of separation from her friend;
having gone there, she, deeply sorrowful, spoke to the king's daughter. (5–6)
"Friend, my father will now arrange my marriage;
by that, our friendship will perish and we shall be separated.
Having heard this from the king's daughter, she embraced her and wept.
Having heard this, Queen Mṛgāvatī came there in haste.
And having learned the cause of her weeping, she said to the fair-eyed one:
"Daughter, I am certain that you and my daughter are friends."
"I shall give you to my daughter as her dear companion in the form of a friend.
Having summoned the Brahmin, the queen said, "O Brahmin,
your daughter is indeed a very affectionate and beloved friend to my own daughter."
Therefore, do as I say and give your daughter to me. Or else, let your daughter be given to that king to whom she is offered;
she must be given to whichever brahmin serves as that king’s domestic priest.
When two people reside in one place, there will always be the happiness of friendship.
Having indeed understood the intention of his daughter, who was devoted to the practice of celibacy, the King of Chāndogya gave that maiden to the Queen.
The princess lived together with Ratnavatī in the royal palace. Having grown up there as a young woman of exceeding beauty,
the king desired to give his daughter to a most worthy bridegroom.
The king had the Brahmins search the earth for him; King Bṛhadbala, the lord of Daśārṇa, was chosen by her as her husband,
and that monarch arrived for the sake of the wedding.
At that time, there was a young man named Parāvasu, the son of the brahmin Viśvāvasu and the royal priest.
He, along with the king and that priest, arrived there together. (17–18)
At the auspicious moment of the wedding, the king arrived there at the pavilion in the presence of the sacred fire; and the maiden,
accompanied by her Brahmin friends and joined by her parents and other women, stood near Hedinī.
She was brought there for the purpose of being given away, and there occurred a great marvel:
the maiden was a rememberer of her former births (*jātismarā*), devoted to celibacy (*brahmacarya*), born from a portion of Śiva;
having been born as a digit of Pārvatī, she was a yoginī by birth. (1.513.20–21)
That virtuous Brahmin girl was likewise capable of assuming any form at will; she was the embodiment of all supernatural powers and remained devoted to the practice of celibacy.
By means of Gaurī’s power, a manifold manifestation of bodies (*kāyavyūha*) was accomplished by those two.
All supernatural powers (siddhis) were accomplished, and likewise Kāmadeva was conquered.
Then Pārvatī bestowed upon the two of them a Vaiṣṇava mantra that grants secrets:
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya pataye namaḥ. (23–24)
"None other than Kṛṣṇa is her husband; the devotion to her husband (pātivratya) must always be maintained toward Hari alone, and never toward anyone else," so said Śrī Pārvatī to them.
She then bestowed upon the two of them yogic perfections (siddhis), through which they attained divine splendor.
When the pavilion had become filled with wonder, those two maidens appeared there;
the princess became Siṃhikā, assuming that form— terrifying,
with a lolling tongue, wide-open eyes, and a roaring voice.
Then, in an instant, the daughter of the Brahmin became a cruel tigress.
Seeing her, all the people were terrified and fled outside the pavilion;
indeed, everyone except the two maidens ran away from the pavilion. (28)
A great clamor arose in the village, the kingdom, and among the subjects.
Then Bṛhadbala departed for his own city, even though he was restrained by his parents; yet they both remained in the very form of Pārvatī.
Then peace was indeed established among the people as they held [the two goddesses];
the two Pārvatīs, possessing divine bodies, were honored by the world.
Those two maidens, resembling a hundred moons, were united with Śaṅkara.
"Oṃ, obeisances to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; obeisances!
As the two girls were thus chanting, they became Vaiṣṇavīs.
Seeing them endowed with their former forms, the onlookers were filled with satisfaction. (32-33)

News of that very pair of Pārvatīs has spread throughout all the worlds; indeed, a pair of goddesses exists in every single household. People constantly worship them, behold them, and bow down before them.
And they always perform the *ārārtrika* rite in Camatkārapura.
Thus, as time passed, a supreme purifying holy site consisting of two goddesses came into existence within the sacred field of Hāṭakeśvara. (35–36)

Ratnavatī repeatedly remembered Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa: "I have surrendered my very self to you; therefore, lead me from here to the state of Kṛṣṇa. The brāhmaṇa’s daughter also said this: "Wherever you are, there I shall be too."
A female friend never goes elsewhere after abandoning her friend.
Then, when they both remembered the Goddess, Durgā arrived swiftly;
she gave them permission for their penance, and the two set forth.
Then Queen Mṛgāvatī, overcome by delusion and infatuation,
her eyes filled with tears and appearing distressed, spoke thus to her daughter:
"O daughter, you must never, under any circumstances, commit such a rash act for the sake of asceticism."
"You are a young girl with delicate limbs, always accustomed to comfort.
O blameless one, how are you capable of performing ascetic penance, subsisting on roots, tubers, and fruits, and wearing rags and bark garments? || 41-42 ||
Therefore, I shall give you to some preeminent king;
this highly esteemed friend of yours, Brāhmaṇī by name,
shall indeed go with you, having assumed the state of maidenhood.
"To the palace of whichever king you shall go as a married woman," Ratnavatī said to her mother, "O Mother,
if you wish to protect my life, you must never again speak such words on my behalf."
If you will obstinately create an obstacle for me,
then I shall abandon my body through the application of poison after having bitten off my tongue;
or I shall enter the fire and attain Śrī Hari as my husband.
"I shall not take another husband; this is the resolve I have made.
(47) She said, "I shall practice asceticism, observing the vow of lifelong maidenhood.
I shall obtain the glorious Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa as my husband, the true lord. (48)
Kings speak but once, and the twice-born speak but once;
the truthful speak but once—these things should be purchased once and for all.
A task is first conceived by the mind, and thereafter it is expressed through speech.
"Just as that [illusion] was produced by past action, so do I create it.
Having spoken thus to her mother, the beloved of Hari ceased.
Then the queen spoke to her friend, the Brāhmaṇī.
"My daughter does not desire a husband or even marriage, O daughter.
You must be married; go to your father's palace.
Or else, I shall have your marriage performed according to your wish. (52)
"Forgive whatever harsh words I have ever spoken to you, or whatever you have ever said to me; all that has been forgiven by me, my daughter.
Then the Brahmin woman spoke these righteous words to the queen.
A girl of eight years is Gaurī, and one of nine years is Rohiṇī;
at ten years she becomes a Kanyā, and the gift of such a maiden is highly praised.
Beyond that age, however, until she is no longer visible [in her virginity], [the gift is not so recommended].
"For it is heard that the gift of a maiden bestows full merit.
But my maidenhood is now lost, as my youth is passing away;
once the sixteenth year has passed, I shall indeed become subject to the nature of women."
He who marries a girl who has reached puberty,
his offspring indeed becomes joined with sin and causes ten others to fall;
and he too, the father who gives away such a girl when she has reached puberty, [is likewise guilty].
"He would cause ten ancestors and ten descendants of his own lineage to fall.
Therefore, I shall perform supreme austerity together with my friend;
I have no need whatsoever for father, mother, or even you."

"The supreme Lord, the Master Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, has arrived. Having spoken thus, the two maidens, endowed with yogic knowledge, bowed down, received the command of their parents, and paid obeisance to the Lord of the Gaṇas.
They traveled by way of the sky to the sage Bhartṛyajña in the forest.
There they beheld the auspicious and pure hermitage;
through the power of the seer’s asceticism, even those things that are mutually opposed [coexisted].
A meeting always takes place where enmity is not seen.
Having approached and bowed to the Vaiṣṇava Bhartṛyajña, they both stood there;
full of humility and with palms joined in reverence, they both spoke.
"We two have come to you for the sake of asceticism; therefore, tell us the rule for that austerity.
Bhartṛyajña, the great yogi, explained the rule of austerity by which liberation is attained—how much more so the abode of the gods.
The Cāndrāyaṇa fasts, the Kṛcchra penances, as well as the Sāntapana rites—
all the gateways of austerity— and the vows dedicated to Kārttikeya;
freedom from passion and hatred, and universal non-violence.
Truthfulness, celibacy, non-stealing, and the acceptance of Kṛṣṇa;
contentment, self-purification, and likewise the restraint of the vital breaths; meditation upon Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, and the offering of all to Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. (68–69)
Likewise, one should cultivate loving-kindness toward those who are happy, compassion for those who are suffering,
sympathetic joy toward those who possess merit, and equanimity toward those who lack merit;
as well as service to the virtuous in every way, which is itself the worship of the gods.
One should perform the worship of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa every day. Within the three bodies according to the three states, one should offer the three qualities to Him;
attachment to the body should be merely for the sake of its maintenance, while love for Śrī Kṛṣṇa should be eternal.
Action, mental construction, meditation, dreaming, perception, and the offering thereof—
whether performed with *sattva*, *rajas*, or *tamas*—
whether pertaining to the body or the mind, whether with desire or without desire, that is the offering thereof. (73)
He taught the recitation, remembrance, chanting, and performance;
looking upon, speaking, touching, approaching, grasping, and dismissal—all actions should be understood as having Kṛṣṇa as their essence; this is considered the supreme austerity. (74–75)

Whatever action— whether of the path of worldly engagement (*pravṛtta*) or the path of renunciation (*nivṛtta*)— by which Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa may be attained, that action is the highest austerity (*tapas*).
Indeed, everything else may be obtained, but if Kṛṣṇa is not attained, nothing is gained at all.

Without Kṛṣṇa, that hell is attained; therefore, that is not considered true austerity. When oneness arises between the one who grasps "Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa" and the Self which is to be grasped and sustained, then one shall attain liberation.
Service to Kṛṣṇa and devotion to Kṛṣṇa are said to be the supreme austerity.
Having attained a human birth through the penance of many lifetimes, if there is devotion to Kṛṣṇa, that human birth becomes fruitful. (79)
The life of one who performs this rite is fruitful,
yielding its fruit for thousands of ancestors, for his own mother,
for hundreds of maternal grandfathers, and for his uterine brother. (1.513.80–81)
O two daughters, even for a kinsman, a wife, teachers, a disciple, or a servant, that action is auspicious which is offered unto Kṛṣṇa;
for that is the most excellent penance, since it is the action that pleases Kṛṣṇa.
That alone is true austerity, that is truth, that is devotion, and likewise that is worship;
that alone is fasting with a specific purpose which bestows servitude to Hari.
[Compared to this,] the gift of the entire earth and circumambulating the world [are of little account]. (83–84)
It is equivalent to bathing in all sacred fords, performing every vow and austerity,
conducting all sacrifices, and likewise obtaining the fruit of all gifts;
it is also equal to the study and teaching of all the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences.
Protecting those who are afraid, the supreme bestowing of knowledge, honoring guests, protecting those who have come for refuge,
the worship of all the gods, as well as salutation and the chanting of the mantra. || 86–87 ||
Feeding brāhmaṇas and deities preceded by purascarana rites,
service to the guru, devotion to one's parents, and the nurturing of dependents—
all these do not equal even a sixteenth part of the service of a servant of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. (88)
Therefore, with great effort, the two daughters worship Lord Kṛṣṇa—
the eternal, true Lord, the divine Supreme Soul, the ever-present,
truthful Supreme Brahman, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa— as their husband.

Worship Hari, the supreme bliss, the inner beloved Lord—He who is most perfectly full, pure, untainted, and the witness; He who bestows devotion, grants servitude, and confers His own state of self-perfection. (91)
Whether it be water or land, whether night or day;
whether it be a vow or austerity, what food or drink;
whether it be the body or the mind—having forgotten all these, worship Hari. (92–93)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa! Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, O beloved Kṛṣṇa!
O Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, my inner self, O Lord of my beloved, grant me service at Your feet through love, devotion, praise, and worship. 94.
O daughter, by means of this offering, worship Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, who dwells within your heart as your inner husband,
your protector, and the bestower of happiness. ॥95॥
O daughter, worship the foot of Kṛṣṇa, which is honored by Ramā and Padmā, served by Lakṣmī, and graced by his own splendor;
it is kissed by Māṇikī, constantly sung of by Śambhu, and meditated upon in the heart by Pārvatī. (96)
Worship that state of Hari, which was meditated upon by the virtuous Sanaka and others.
O son, he who chants the name of the lotus feet of Śrī Śrī Kṛṣṇa even in a dream is liberated from the sins committed in a hundred lifetimes; of this there is no doubt. (97–98)
That vow, that austerity, that truth, and that merit— indeed, that worship—
is fruitful only when connected with Kṛṣṇa, for it alone prevents the futility of one's birth.
O daughter, what would be the use of austerity if one were to abandon that Śrī Kṛṣṇa?

One indeed attains the fruit of austerities by remembering Śrī Kṛṣṇa. That teacher who does not instill devotion toward Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul, is a supreme enemy; he renders one's birth fruitless.
Saying "So be it," they received that supreme, auspicious knowledge consisting of devotion;
having bowed and gone to the shore of the lake, they performed the Cāndrāyaṇa and other penances.
For three autumns, they indeed subsisted on food taken only at every sixth mealtime.
In winter they dwelt in the water, and in summer they practiced the austerity of the five fires;
during the rainy season, they remained without shelter. These two beloveds of Hari meditated day and night, chanting the names of their husband, Śrī Hari. (103–104)
Then for a hundred and fifty years they remained without food;
for that same length of time, they also subsisted on withered leaves. After that, they lived on water for six hundred years.
For a thousand years, they both remained there subsisting on air alone while constantly engaged in austerity. Then,
the Lord of the Universe, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa himself, became pleased with them.
A youth, handsome and dark-complexioned, arrived together with Garuḍa.
With his splendor pervading all directions, he spoke to the two female ascetics:
"Open your eyes and look; I have come to grant you a boon."
Having heard this, they cast their gaze outward and beheld the Lord—
the true master Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the beloved and enchanting one,
whose limbs were proportionate to his form, and whose lotus feet were worthy of service.
Abandoning their asceticism, they fell at his feet and said, "O Lord, accept this pair of handmaidens; grant us service and become our master.
With tearful eyes and deeply distressed, they embraced Kṛṣṇa around his neck.
Kṛṣṇa kissed her and touched her with his hand, perceiving her inner intention.
Having covered and then uncovered those two women of divine form who resembled Lakṣmī,
he placed them upon his own lap, resting them above his thighs.
Having carried them on his two arms to the side, he went to the sacrificial ground of his master;
having placed that Vaiṣṇava guru upon the back of Garuḍa,
those four indeed traveled by Garuḍa to the abode of Goloka.
Having learned of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s arrival, the sages went to that place. As he was traveling through the sky, they bowed down and worshipped the Lord.
That lake of the Nāga river is also well-known by the name Ratnasaras.
At that time, it became truly renowned as a bestower of liberation through bathing;
moreover, those two were born as eternal servants of Kṛṣṇa, serving His perpetual bliss.
When the goddesses arrived from heaven and requested that they remain there, [they did not agree].
Then, for the welfare of the goddesses, it was ordained that they should dwell in heaven;
and by Śrī Kṛṣṇa, those two Tārakas were established as forms of shadow that grant liberation through both recitation and hearing.

Thus ends the five hundred and thirteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Princess of Camatkārapurī and the Brahmin’s Daughter Assuming the Forms of a Lion and a Tiger at the Time of Their Marriage, Their Residence in the Hermitage of Bhartṛyajña, Their Difficult Penance, and Their Attainment of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa along with Bhartṛyajña and Their Departure for Goloka," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 514. *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā* — Section 1 (*Kṛtayuga-santāna*) — Chapter 514.
[The Author: Chapter 515.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī! [I shall describe] that which destroys all sins in the mortal world.
Likewise, there are three fields, three forests, and three cities;
three groves, three villages, and three supreme sacred fords (tīrthas);
as well as three mountains and three rivers that bestow all fruits.
By visiting Kurukṣetra, Hāṭakeśakṣetra, and Prabhāsakṣetra according to the prescribed rites, a person is liberated from sin. First, there is Puṣkarāraṇya, and also Naimiṣāraṇya.

And the third is Dharmāraṇya, which bestows all desired fruits. (4) Vārāṇasī-purī is the first, Dvārakā-purī is the second, and Avantikā-purī is the third, granting fruits according to one's wishes. (5)
Vṛndāvana, Dvaitavana, and likewise Khāṇḍavavana grant heaven and liberation through bathing and residence, and they destroy all sins. Kālagrāma, Śālagrāma, and Nandigrāma as the third;
It is the destroyer of thirst for the collection of sense organs and likewise the bestower of liberation.
(7) Agnitīrtha, Śuklatīrtha, and Pitṛtīrtha as the third—by bathing there, a human being certainly attains both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (8)

Śrīparvata, Arbudādri, and Raivatācala as well— by performing a pilgrimage to these, one becomes an enjoyer of heaven and subsequently attains liberation. [9] The river Gaṅgā, the river named Narmadā, and the river Sarasvatī.

From bathing there, one obtains food, as well as liberation; likewise, it always grants one's desires. Jñānavāpī, Kuṅkumavāpī, and Rohaṇavāpikā—by drinking their water, liberation is attained; for these three ponds are indeed purifying.
The Nārāyaṇa lake, the Indra lake, and the Mānasaka lake—
this triad of lakes bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation through bathing.
Pārvatī, Prabhā, Lakṣmī, Māṇikī, Jayā, and Ramā.

The eight names of Rādhā and Padmā deliver one from the ocean of worldly existence. Vastrāpatha, Uttarāpatha, and Dakṣiṇāpatha—these three alone grant liberation here through pilgrimage; of this there is no doubt.
Sins such as the killing of a Brahmin, eating the food of those of other castes,
dwelling in the house of a Cāṇḍāla, or the consumption of liquor and meat—
all these are purified in every way by performing a ritual bath in the Nāga river.
Nāgalīlā was indeed a maidservant of Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
in the presence of Kṛṣṇa, she playfully untied and loosened the braid of Rādhikā with her own hand. || 16–17 ||
Again, Rādhikā wound her hair and fashioned a braid;
then, with playful intent, she again loosened the knot that had been tied.
In Goloka, there was thus a repeated tying and repeated untying of those two.
But because it had arisen from their mutual companionship in jest, Rādhikā became angry and said: "Go, O you who sport with the Nagas; go to the surface of the earth!
Go to the house of an Ābhīra and be held by an Ābhīra! (1.514.20)
Having spoken thus, that friend praised Rādhā for her release from the curse. Rādhā said: "When you are taken by the cowherd, then you shall move about as a purifying river in the form of water."
Without Kṛṣṇa, you will become ungraspable; of this there is no doubt.
(22) When Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, your Lord, comes there, you shall become a maiden and come to Goloka. (23)
To that extent, you shall indeed always be the bestower of liberation, the washer away of sins, the giver of purity,
and the purifier of men fallen from their caste, such as the *śvapaca* and others; merely by bathing [in you], you will grant them purification.
Having been addressed thus by Rādhā, she bowed and then departed for the earth.
Indeed, she was born as a maiden in the house of a preeminent Ābhīra from Ānarta;
her father was Śyāmasura, known by the name Nāgalīla. (25–26)
Her mother Rāṇikā, who remembered her past lives, likewise called out to her;
she rejoiced at having obtained a daughter of radiant splendor and divine form.
Day after day, she would always gather cow dung on the bank of the lake.
Seeing her wandering in the cow-pen, a young cowherd boy,
full of vigor, assailed that beautiful young woman.
Remembering the curse of Rādhikā, she turned into water.
That river became known as Nāganadī, the dear friend of Kṛṣṇa himself;
by bathing in it, even the wife of a Cāṇḍāla becomes a Brāhmaṇī.
Listen, Lakṣmī, in the city of Vardhamāna there was one born of the lowest caste.
He had a son named Kumbhaka, who was a Caṇḍāla.
Known as Ghūkakarṇa, he was handsome; having undertaken a pilgrimage to sacred fords, he reached Camatkārapura, assuming the guise of a twice-born brahmin.
Subsisting on food obtained through alms, he bathed in all sacred fords;
because of his constant residence with the twice-born, he always conducted himself like a member of the twice-born and performed the rites of the twice-born.
Indeed, in that city of Camatkārapura, [he lived] with the brahmin Subhadra.
In her lineage, there was an only daughter who possessed twice the number of teeth;
she had three breasts, a large belly, and was terrifying.
Any man who should become her husband would meet his death within six months.
No one accepted her for eighteen years;
meanwhile, that man of the lowest caste, Ghūkakarna, arrived at her house to beg for alms. Upon seeing him, she swooned.

Her father, beholding his handsome form and his guise as a twice-born, then inquired about his lineage, caste, family, name, and so forth. Ghūkakarṇa said to the brahmin: "My residence is in the land of Gauḍa."
In the village of Bhojakata, my father was the Brahmin Mādhava, belonging to the Vasiṣṭha lineage; I am his son, named Candraprabha.
In my eighth year, however, my father indeed passed away.
Having studied just a little of auspicious action in Vārāṇasī, I have come here while wandering among the sacred fords; from here I shall go to the Gomatī,
then to Prabhāsa, then to the Śukla-tīrtha, and after that, home again.
Having heard this and thus learned of his daughter's conduct, the father of the daughter said:
"If you take my daughter here, I shall give her to you.
Having said, "So be it," that Cāṇḍāla then accepted her according to the prescribed rites.
After his marriage, he indulged in many diversions with foods,
drinks, fine garments, and festivities suitable for the twice-born;
yet, for the most part, he would go along whichever path presented itself.
Dogs bark at him and follow behind him;
and if he should ever utter a Vedic passage during a state of separation,
blood falls from the mouth of that evil-minded man at that very moment.
And in his sleep, he uttered words regarding the act of expelling impurities.
(46) Thus, because of these signs, people became somewhat suspicious that he was a Cāṇḍāla;
for the destruction of such suspicion, divine purification is required. (47)

Just as the suspicion regarding purity is removed by holding heated iron in one’s hand, so too must you act this morning; for if you are not burnt, O twice-born one, it shall certainly be certain that you belong to another caste.
If you are burnt, then indeed it shall be certain that you are of a different birth.
Then, at night, he said to his own wife: "I am certainly not a twice-born;
I am of the lowest caste, and having been recognized, I am feared by people.
I shall go to another country; you come with me."
The wife said: "In my destiny, there is indeed an evil intended for the sake of fire;
my entire family and my very body are defiled by sin.
Go outside at night, otherwise you will meet with great calamity. (51)
Having been addressed thus, he indeed departed for another country at night out of fear.
At dawn, her daughter, with eyes full of tears, said to her mother:
"O Mother, because of my previous sin, I was given away to an outcaste."
He set out in the middle of the night, announcing his lineage:
"For me, there is only purification by fire; there is no other on the surface of the earth.
Upon learning this, his father grieved greatly, and the others as well were overcome with sorrow.
Then all the brahmins assembled and declared a purifying expiation for the maiden: that she should enter the fire;
whereas for the others who had entered into association with him, they prescribed various vows.
Then, having taken wood and applied fire, the maiden bowed to her ancestors, remembered the gods, and as she was about to ascend [the pyre],
she said: "Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, obeisance to the Lord."
While she was thus engaged in her recitation, she placed her foot upon the fire.
However, out of compassion, the fire became cool and did not burn her;
therefore, she is without fault and is purified by her menstrual flow.
Then the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa arrived;
he was dressed as a saintly Vaiṣṇava and was learned in the Dharmaśāstras and other scriptures. He was the knower of the three periods of time, the Lord of Lakṣmī himself, the glorious Puruṣottama.
He asked, "How is she born, and how does she burn in the fire?
Thereupon, the people reported the account of the event concerning the birth.
Then the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, who is devoted to compassion, spoke to them.

Formerly, I heard in heaven that in the city of Camatkārapura there is a river named Nāgalīlā, the wife of Kṛṣṇa, who has come from the abode of Goloka for the sake of purifying those who commit sins through association with outcastes and others. (6.3)
"By bathing in that water, even outcastes and the like become pure.
Therefore, go there by all means and perform your ablutions.
Having heard this, Vahni said, "So be it," and then they all went to the river.
A certain maiden, having seen Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, approached Him;
bowing down and joyfully taking His hand, she said to her Lord:
"Indeed, there is a holy lake not far from here that destroys the sins of even the outcaste."
"O lords of the twice-born, come and perform your bath there.
Thus addressed by her, they went with her and bathed while still wearing their clothes.
When the brahmin girl had finished bathing, from her body—
The dog-cooker woman, who was black in color, emerged [from her body] merely by means of bathing.
From the bodies of others as well, crows, owls, and ants emerged,
black in color, and went toward the western region.
Then, on the surface of the earth, they reached the far shore beyond a thousand yojanas.
These brahmins were purifiers, and the Brāhmaṇī attained purity. Thus, they all arrived at their respective cities and hermitages.
Thereafter, that virtuous and chaste Brahmin girl, devoted to celibacy and faithful to her husband Kṛṣṇasvāmin,
would always go to the Nāgavatī river to bathe.
Remaining constantly as a maiden in the house with the Brāhmaṇī,
she goes forth for the purpose of beholding the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
And when the end of the Brāhmaṇī’s daughter’s life arrives, Hari [appears].
Having transformed that river and the Brahmin woman into divine forms,
Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa led them both to Goloka;
they were adorned with celestial jewels and possessed a radiance equal to ten million suns.

Having reached their husband Kṛṣṇa by means of a celestial chariot, they both departed with joy for the eternal abode of Goloka, which is adorned by Rādhā, Ramā, and others. Then Brahmā also, due to the curse of the unchaste woman, remained here at this excellent holy place.
Indeed, in ancient times, he was liberated from the curse of a wanton woman;
thus, O Lakṣmī, has this most excellent and purifying holy site been described,
where through bathing all impurity is indeed completely dispelled.
By reading and by hearing this, a human being is always purified.
Having received the mantra and bowed to the guru, he who bathes at Nāgavatī with a concentrated mind shall become pure like Kṛṣṇa; there is no doubt in this matter. (1.514.80)

Thus ends the five hundred and fourteenth chapter, titled "The Description of how, in the first section on the Kṛta-yuga of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā, Nāgalīlā’s friend became the river Nāgavatī in Goloka due to a curse from Rādhikā; how through bathing in that river, purification was attained by a Brāhmaṇa girl who had been married to the outcaste Ghūkakarṇa and by the Brāhmaṇas themselves; and how thereafter the Brāhmaṇa girl and the river Nāgavatī both became divine maidens and went to Goloka along with Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. || 514 ||

Śrī Lakṣmī said: When was Brahmā cursed by the unchaste woman, and for what reason? How did the creator of the universe then become purified by bathing in the Nāganadī? (1)
"O Nārāyaṇa, O Hari, O Kṛṣṇa, tell me that story here.
Having heard this, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa related that story to Lakṣmī.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī! In ancient times, Brahmā begot a daughter from his mind;
he himself made that Mohinī an Apsaras.
She then became the common wife of all the gods.
Then, on one occasion, having seen Brahmā, she indeed became infatuated;
forgetting her father, she engaged in a mental resolve of desire.
During the Manvantara of Raivata, there was a king named Sucandra, a devotee of Viṣṇu.
He went to the valley of Malaya for austerities for a thousand years.
Seeing his body covered by an anthill, the Creator approached him.
"Choose a boon; I am well-pleased," said the Father of the World to him.
He chose devotion to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa and the state of servitude.
Brahmā then sprinkled water from his water-pot and consecrated him;
the king, with his body perfectly composed, bowed down again and again.
Saying "So be it," Brahmā then granted him that boon; the king ascended the divine and supreme chariot that had arrived from Goloka.
Having assumed a divine form as an attendant (pārṣada), he went to the abode of Kṛṣṇa.
Brahmā saw Mohinī on the path as she was going to Satyaloka. Then, seeing her in that secluded place, he was instantly deluded with the desire to sport with her;
the one with curved eyes looked at him and protected her smiling face.
With all her limbs covered in horripilation and oppressed by the force of desire,
she slowly sat down upon the ground at the feet of Brahmā before him.
Brahmā, beholding his daughter, did not undergo any transformation himself.
Having consoled her like a father, he went to the world of Brahmā.
At that time, she became fulfilled in her desire, yet she was also hopeless and despondent;
day and night she remained lost in thought, seeing the Four-faced One in both her dreams and her waking consciousness.
Whether sitting, standing, or even lying down for a moment,
she wanders along the path just like grain in a heated pan; indeed,
having obtained Kāma as her companion, that deluding woman moves together with him.
She went to the world of Brahmā and beheld that unborn one in a secluded place.
Standing before him, she began to delude him;
for a moment she danced for a very long time with beautiful limbs, and for a moment she sang.
Having heard that beautiful voice, the Creator was bewildered, his eyes filled with tears;
seeing him thus enchanted, he displayed all his artistic skills in dance. Even after bestowing a reward, he eventually ceased and departed.
Her effort thus frustrated, she said: "O God, as you desire, let there be salutation to you!
O Kāmadeva, then discharge your own arrows at Vidhi.
Standing in the intermediate space, Kāma joyfully launched his great weapon.
Brahmā became restless and looked around repeatedly;
having approached Mohinī and reflected upon her, he said to Mohinī:
"O Mohinī, you are fickle; I am not fit for this task."
"Go, my daughter; you are not to be grasped by me, so dwell elsewhere.
He who trusts a wanton woman will meet with calamity at every step. Alas, child, go far away, leaving behind me, your father. (22-23)

"O Mohinī, behold the supreme God, the youth, who is worthy of you. Mohinī said to the Creator: "Since my mind is not steady, and because it has been especially agitated by looking at you, [it cannot remain fixed]. (24)
"Alas! Though I am unable to go, even though I have been rebuked by you, show mercy, O ocean of compassion; you ought not to kill me.

"Arise, O Lord of the World! Bring me to the further shore of this ocean of passion.

"Obeisance to you, O Mother Mohinī, who removes the multitude of worldly entanglements;

Her breasts were budding, her hips broad, and her cheeks rounded;

Seeing in the sky a maiden who was full of vigor, overflowing with love, eager to bestow grace upon her devotees, devoid of lustful passion, free from menstruation, and capable of assuming any form at will, all [the gods] became as if eunuchs. (67–68)
At that moment, their eyes were momentarily blinded by her splendor.

During the monthly course of women, the fire of desire increases;

The pacifying rite for women is a dharma that bestows peace upon men.

In that place where her vulvar opening was only the size of a chickpea,

Thus ends the five hundred and fifteenth chapter, titled "The Description of how the Apsarā Mohinī, upon seeing Brahmā, became infatuated; how she was not accepted by Brahmā and consequently cursed him; how Brahmā was purified in the Nāgavatī river; the birth of eunuchs from those who abandoned their bodies and food; and the liberation of eunuchs through the initiation of Bahucara, Hiṅgulāja, and others," in the first section, the Kṛta-yuga lineage, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.

For many years, my back was constantly pressed by the mountain.
However, sacrifices were performed by him and promoted by Lomaśa;
consequently, my back was scorched, and I entreated the sage [for relief]. (53)
The very compassionate Lomaśa said to me, "Go to Lake Mānasa at the edge of the Himālaya mountains; from there, I have come here.
Indeed, five years of my life passed while I was here with Brahmā.
Listen now to those kalpas of mine that have passed here during the life of Brahmā:
eighteen thousand and twenty-five;
these kalpas that have occurred in the Mānasa [kalpa] I remember exactly as they were.
And by my second form, I always abide here.
My back has become perfectly free from pain due to its reliance on the Himalayas.
The sage Lomaśa is my guru; go to that auspicious hermitage.
O King, you should first go to the city of Puruṣottama,
where in former times the Lord of the World was installed by your own hand.
From there, proceed to Mahākālavana, where your own residence is located.
From there, go to Surāṣṭra, where the Aśvapaṭṭa lake is located;
where Kuṅkumavāpikā is, and where the sage Lomaśa resides;
where indeed Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Lakṣmī himself, is present.
Hari, the supreme person, shines resplendent in a divine seven-storied palace as Pārvatīmāṇikīrādhāprabhāsvāmī.
Go there, O King, and having performed service, proceed from there to the highest state.
Then, at the time of the kalpa, you shall behold me again in Satyaloka along with these sages; your unimpeded fame on earth shall endure until that kalpa,
for having heard this truth, you will certainly go there.
Then, having accepted the beneficial and sweet words of the tortoise,
they departed from that place and returned to their respective abodes.
Subsequently, Indradyumna arrived before Lomaśa in due course.
Indeed, on the ground extending four yojanas in every direction from his side, there was no illusion, nor was there attachment or aversion; how then could there be latent impressions?
Having reached that hermitage which is the very form of Brahman, the king then became fully satisfied.
Having heard everything from the mouth of Lomaśa regarding Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa,
he worshipped Kambharā-Lakṣmī and the illustrious Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa, as well as the thirty-three gods; then, by their command, he resided there for one year.
There he constantly heard ever-new and excellent discourses from the lotus-like mouth of Lomaśa concerning the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*.
And there, from the mouth of Lomaśa, he heard of the sacrifices he himself had performed.
Likewise, [he performed] the auspicious installation of the glorious Jagannātha, which he himself had commissioned;
as well as sacrificial sessions (satras) everywhere, and the feeding of those named after you,
and gifts of elephants, cows, horses, gold, jewels, and women.
Whatever objects exist upon the earth, for all of them he has performed acts of giving, as well as recitations, worship, and so forth; and having heard [the teachings] from the mouth of his guru,
he possesses that knowledge which bestows the self, bestows heaven, and likewise bestows liberation.
He obtained everything from the mouth of Lomaśa, including the vision of the Self.
O Lakṣmī, listen! I shall declare to you that which was heard by Lomaśa from the mouth of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa—the means appropriate for a devotee.

Thus ends the five hundred and twentieth chapter, titled "The Narration of Events such as the Dwelling, Life Span, and Sacrifices of Indradyumna at the Aśvapaṭṭasara Lake in the Hermitage of Lomaśa in the Field of Kuṅkumavāpī," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, wherein the tortoise residing on Mānasa-sarovara describes his own and Śeṣa’s status as attendants (*pārṣada*) of Viṣṇu. Chapter 521: *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā* — Section 1 (Kṛtayuga-santāna) Chapter 521: The Arrival of the Tortoise and the Description of the Glory of the Aśvapaṭṭasara Lake. Śrī Nārada said: O sage, please describe further the arrival of the tortoise and the glory of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake. Śrī Sūta said: O brāhmaṇas, having heard the words of the sage, the great sage Lomaśa, who was seated upon a lotus pedestal, spoke again to Nārada. Śrī Lomaśa said: O Nārada, listen; I shall tell you the wonderful account of the arrival of the tortoise. O best of sages, the tortoise, being commanded by Viṣṇu, went from Mānasa-sarovara to the holy field of Kuṅkumavāpī. Arriving there, he saw the hermitage of Lomaśa and the sacred Aśvapaṭṭasara lake. Seeing that lake, which was filled with the splendor of the presence of the Lord, the tortoise was greatly delighted. He then entered the water of the lake, which was like nectar, and performed his ablutions. Having bathed and offered libations to the ancestors and the gods, he sat down on the shore of the lake. There, he beheld the supreme form of the Lord, the Supreme Person, who is beyond all material nature (*prakṛti*). He saw the Lord seated upon Garuḍa, holding a conch, discus, mace, and lotus, adorned with a crown, earrings, and a necklace, and wearing a yellow garment. Seeing the Lord, the Supreme Soul, the tortoise bowed his head and prostrated himself before Him. Then, with palms joined in reverence, the tortoise spoke these words to the Lord of the universe. The Tortoise said: O Lord of Lakṣmī, O Infinite One, O Supreme Person, O Govinda, O Hṛṣīkeśa, O Keśava, O Acyuta, O Janārdana, O Lord of Vaikuṇṭha, O Infinite Splendor! I am the servant of Your servants, a mere fragment of dust at Your feet. I have come here by Your command to see You, O Lord of the world. O Lord, please grant me Your grace. I wish to dwell here in this holy place, O Lord of the universe, for I am weary of wandering through the cycle of births and deaths. O Lord, please tell me how long my life shall be and what my duties shall be. Also, please tell me about the sacrifices of Indradyumna, O Lord of the world. Śrī Bhagavān said: O tortoise, you shall remain in this holy field of Kuṅkumavāpī for one hundred thousand years. O best of sages, you shall dwell here in the hermitage of Lomaśa and in the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake. O tortoise, your lifespan shall be one hundred thousand years. You shall perform various sacrifices and serve the devotees of Viṣṇu. O tortoise, you shall be the protector of this holy place and the guardian of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake. You shall be known as the "Tortoise of the Lotus" (*Padmakūrma*). O best of sages, you shall be famous in the three worlds. Śrī Sūta said: O brāhmaṇas, having spoken thus to the tortoise, the Lord vanished from that very spot. The tortoise, having received the command of the Lord, remained in that holy place, performing his duties. O best of sages, this is the wonderful account of the arrival of the tortoise and the glory of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake. By hearing this, one is liberated from all sins and attains the supreme goal. Thus ends the five hundred and twenty-first chapter, titled "The Arrival of the Tortoise and the Description of the Glory of the Aśvapaṭṭasara Lake," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*. [Author: Chapter 522.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, Lakṣmī! Indradyumna questioned the sage Lomaśa.
O Sage! Tell me how that knowledge which brings peace may arise.
(1) Without the peace of the self, every [other] net is considered a source of agitation.
There is no gain whatsoever equal to the peace of the self; tell me that. (2)
Lomaśa, having remembered Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, spoke to him:
"Listen, O King, I shall speak; perform the remembrance of Śrī Hari.
[He is] the imperishable Brahman, the supreme abode, all-pervading and most excellent. (3)
Where the eternal Supreme beyond the supreme (parāt para) is served by liberated beings through their various states of being;
there shines the glorious Hari, the illustrious Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the divine youth, exceedingly powerful, and a treasure-house of every form. 4–5.
He whose atomic portions constantly manifest the splendor of millions upon millions of suns,
who is present within the vision of all seers, and who is served by the liberated;
he alone is the glorious Puruṣottama, the possessor of infinite forms.
He is Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of all things beginning with the Imperishable (akṣara).
He is indeed beyond the Imperishable, possessing two arms and a divine form.
The Lord, the Consort of Śrī, is to be heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon.
Her eyes, beautiful with collyrium, were as long as lotus petals and reddish; they were ever steady with love, filled with inner emotion, and intensely captivating.
They were exceedingly charming, adorned with rows of golden lashes.
"Offer with devotion the very essence of your heart to those who, with their knitting of brows, cause the piercing of the millions of arrows of desire;
who are filled with the bliss of the Self, affectionate, and imbued with aesthetic flavor for the connoisseurs. (1.521.10–11)
O you who bestow the nectar of the drinking of stars, O you as tremulous as a fish,
O you whose corners reach to the very edge of the ear and are filled with skillful artistry;
O you who possess a red line, O white one, shining all around like crystal!
Upon the delightful object of meditation, which is endowed with the reflections of all that is visible—
[he beholds] the nose resembling a sesame flower, lips like the ripe *bimba* fruit, and a face adorned with a beard that produces the wonder of delicate lines. (13–14)
Then one should clearly visualize the chin as slightly depressed and elevated;
the cheeks as radiant as the sun and moon; and the forehead adorned with a dot (bindu).
One should visualize it as possessing a tilaka, exceedingly brilliant, and marked by a single line.

One should remember his beautiful, glossy, curved, black, and tawny hairs, radiant with the light of his crown and emitting long rays. His ears are adorned with lobes and decorated with earrings of jewels and diamonds. (16–17)
One should meditate upon the face of the Lord, pervaded by a halo and the radiance of light, enchanting to the heart and resplendent with the beauty of ten million Cupids;
one should also meditate upon his conch-like neck and his two firm, well-developed, and captivating shoulders.
His two arms were like the coils of a serpent, radiant as golden campaka flowers.
His hands were shaped like the trunks of elephants, and the palms of his hands shone like lotuses;
his nails were white as the rays of the moon, slightly reddish, and well-proportioned.

One should meditate on [the Lord’s] hands, all of whose fingers are marked with lines, as well as the two thumbs and forearms; and on His chest, which is elevated, marked with the signs of Lakṣmī, broad, bearing the Śrīvatsa mark, and covered with hair curling to the right. (21)
One should likewise meditate upon the two breasts and the belly resting on three folds;
the deep navel, the hips, and the two sides shining brightly;
the waist equal to that of a lion, the male organ, and the buttocks. (22–23)
One should meditate on the thighs as being like the trunks of elephants, and the knees as perfectly rounded.
One should meditate on the shanks as beautiful, slender, and pale like the petals of a lotus.
One should meditate on the fingers as adorned with moon-like nails, and likewise upon the ornaments and garments.
One should meditate upon the rows of necklaces, the rows of teeth, the heart, and the mind;
one should meditate upon the visualization, the qualities, all the sovereign powers, and the activities.
Indeed, by thus contemplating the form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa— 25–26.
O King, eternal peace will surely arise; of this there is no doubt.
Then one should meditate upon that Lord Hari, namely Śrī Kṛṣṇa and likewise Rādhikā.
One should meditate upon Nārāyaṇa and Lakṣmī, as well as Brahmā and Sarasvatī.
One should meditate upon Sāvitrī, Gāyatrī, Śiva, Durgā, and Pārvatī;
one should meditate upon Gaṅgā, Viṣṇu, Lakṣmī, Vṛndā, and Tulasī.
There, one should meditate upon that which transcends the imperishable, as well as the Vyūhas and the Vibhavas.
One should remember the images, the portions, the manifestations, and the divine powers within Hari.
One should remember Him as residing in milk, as residing on white ground, as residing in snow, and as residing within oneself.
Indeed, one should meditate upon that Viṣṇu, Janārdana, who dwells within all bodies.
One should always behold that very Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa in man and woman;
in truth, heaven, earth, the sky, the netherworld, and the ether of the heart;
in son, wife, animal, beloved, the insentient, and the entire realm of sentient beings. (3.1–3.2)
Whether toward what is visible or invisible, pleasant or unpleasant, what is to be grasped or what is to be avoided—
one should indeed meditate upon Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the youthful cowherd boy,
who is cherished by Kambharā and is divine, dwelling near Aśvapaṭṭasara.
He who is constantly meditated upon by Lomaśa and worshipped by Brahmā, Rudra, and others;
the Lord of Rādhā, Lakṣmī, Ramā, Padmā, Prabhā, and Padmāvatī; the Master of Māṇikī and Pārvatī; the Victorious Lord, the Consort of Lalitā. (34–35)
To the Lord of liberation, the Lord of incarnations, whose form is existence, consciousness, and bliss;
to the beloved of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Protector, the cause of the birth and other states of the universe;
to Him who is served by the Siddhas and who is the treasure-house of the wealth of knowledge and bliss.
One should meditate upon that beloved Lord, whose form is enchanting, within the lotus of the heart.
With single-minded concentration, a man or a woman should meditate upon their husband as the Supreme Lord,
the Highest Sovereign who is served at the holy site of Kuṅkumavāpikā.
One should constantly meditate upon, remember, chant, bow down to, and serve [the Guru];
likewise, one should worship, honor, and drink the nectar held within his lotus feet.
One should consume his grace and bring forth fragrances and other such offerings.
One should perform circumambulation and praise, offer a lamp and food offerings (naivedya). One should perform the waving of lights (ārārtika) and practice the offering of all one's possessions.
In this way, the self is to be offered and should always be surrendered to Hari.
Desire, anger, pleasure, affection, greed, delusion, and the like,
as well as compassion, charity, courtesy, self-restraint, and the entire circle of faults—
one should offer all these to Him and cast them into Him incessantly.
By that, just as a mineral is purified in fire, so is a human being purified.
O Indradyumna! Abandoning the desire for fruits, one should always perform service (dāsya) to Hari.
Through service to the glorious Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, may I attain divinity.
I obtained long life, a body equal to that of Brahmā,
liberation while living (jīvanmukti), as well as sovereign powers, the perfections (siddhis), and the wealth of dispassion;
I obtained contentment, the destruction of craving, and freedom from illusion.
Free from deceit, attachment, and the like, and likewise devoid of all veils,
having burnt away the afflictions and the latencies of karma, I move about like Hari.
Just as a clod of earth [is carried] by means of wood, one indeed crosses the ocean of waters.
Through union with Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, Lomaśa, the destroyer of all taints,
remains here liberated from Brahmā, destroying the cycle of time for many kalpas.
Indeed, the entire universe, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, is infinite.
He who effortlessly creates all that is moving and unmoving, the support of the universe—
him whom Brahmā, Śiva, Viṣṇu, Dharma, the Sun, Gaṇeśa,
the assembly of great sages, and Indra the lord of gods meditate upon day and night.
The Vedas praise that Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Lord of the universe;
delighted Prakṛti praises him, and Sarasvatī praises him with fear.
Ṣaṇmukha, Caturāsya, and Pañcāsya also praise that Hari.

He whom those with a thousand mouths, those with the Vedas as their mouths, and those with fire as their mouths praise—he who consists of his own will, who is effortless, devoid of qualities, and stainless;
the Brahman higher than the highest, the Supreme Self, the Lord. (52–53)

Worship eternally the Guru, the Lord and Master Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa— the eternal light pervading all, whose very form is the grace bestowed upon devotees, who is eternal bliss, eternal, and whose form is the eternal Imperishable (Akṣara). (54)
Thus the Blessed Lord has descended here to remove the burden of the earth;
the Lord, through His illusory power (māyā), assumes the form of a cowherd boy and is the Beloved.
He alone is the protector, the nourisher, and the destroyer—worship Him always.

O Lord of the Earth, worship Him alone as your father, mother, the bestower of knowledge and mantras, your true guru, and your husband— Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. O Indradyumna, understand from me this wisdom which is higher than the highest.
Abandon everything that causes obstacles and attain supreme joy in Hari.
What is a kingdom? What is fame? What is a village? What is one's own country, and what is another?
Who is whose son? Who is whose father? Who is anyone’s mother, and from where does she come? (58–59)
Beings come and go through saṃsāra solely by means of their own performed actions;
according to their karma, a living being is born in various different states.
By virtue of karma, someone is born from a Brahmin woman or from the wife of a king.
Whether with a Vaiśya woman, a Śūdra woman, an animal, a bird, or a tree—
within these objects granted by Nārāyaṇa, they were full of joy;
yet they were despondent at the time of casting off the body, as if at the loss of a kinsman.
All that was done by her through illusion— the maiden, the bride, and the dispassionate woman—
are indeed the various states of one and the same woman.
The severance of offspring, land, wealth, and so forth, is even greater than death.
This state is constant for the fool, but never for the wise man.
(64) Be a devotee of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, a sacrificer to Him, one who has Him as your supreme goal;
be a worshipper of the mantra of Kṛṣṇa and one intent on the service of Kṛṣṇa. (65)
Out of fear of whom this wind blows and the sun shines eternally;
out of fear of whom the moon and Mahendra shine, and who rains at the change of seasons;
[out of fear of whom] fire burns and Death indeed moves among living beings. (66)
In due time, the tree bears both flowers and fruits.
The wind, though supported by space, supports water and the like, which are supported by the wind.
The tortoise is the support of the waters, and Ananta is indeed the support of that tortoise. (67–68)
Within the infinite coils of Śeṣa are the cosmic eggs, the mountains, and the motionless waters;
from that [support] arises this earth situated upon the water, along with the seven heavens, the support of the earth, the wheel of luminaries, and the abode of the planets. (69)
The Great Virāṭ is the support of the cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas) endowed with the eight coverings.
His support is indeed Bhūman, Mahāviṣṇu, and Sadāśiva. Vaikuṇṭha is his support, and Goloka is its substratum.
Goloka is the support of all, the infinite and imperishable abode, supremely auspicious;
it is the world of Brahman, higher than the highest, that supreme and ultimate realm.
It is divine, pervading everywhere, and indeed devoid of boundaries.
Wherein indeed all abodes reside, and where His three-quarters are the immortality in heaven;
one quarter of Him consists of all beings, and beyond that nothing exists.
Therein resides Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the cowherd boy.
O King, worship Hari, the Lord of the Imperishable, the delighter of Kambharā.
In the supreme abode, this very Hari is Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa;
that Supreme Person (Puruṣottama) dwells in the midst of infinite liberated souls.
And likewise, the Imperishable Person (Akṣarapuruṣa) abides in the imperishable abode (Akṣara-dhāman).
Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa reside in Goloka; the Lord Śrīpati resides in Vaikuṇṭha;
he takes the form of Śiva in the world of Śiva; and in Satyaloka, he is considered to be Brahmā and Hari.
Among the radiant, he is indeed the sun; among the purifiers, likewise, he is fire.
Among liquids, he is Hari (water); and among the senses, he is the mind.
Among those that move swiftly, he is the wind; and among those who mete out punishment, he is indeed Yama.
He is Time among those who calculate, yet he is the one beyond syllables;
he is the Sāman among Sāmans, Indra among the gods, and the majestic sovereign among kings;
he is Īśāna among the lords of the quarters, and indeed Kubera among the wealthy. (1.521.79–80)
He is indeed the witness of all pervasive things, and He alone is their witness as well.
Among luminous substances, He is gold; among riches, He is the jewel.
Among gems, He is the Kaustubha; and He Himself is the Lord, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
Likewise, among those worthy of worship he is Śālagrāma; among leaves, he is Tulasī;
among flowers, he is Pārijāta; among sacred fords, he is Puṣkara;
among Vaiṣṇavas, he is Kumāra; and among the lords of yogis, he is Gaṇādhipa. (82–83)
He is Skanda among generals, for he is indeed the foremost of archers;
he is the Moon among the stars, for this Rāma is indeed the foremost of weapon-bearers.
He is Mārgaśīrṣa among the months, and he is the Spring, the best of seasons.
Among the lords of kings, he is Rāma; among incarnations, he is Nārāyaṇa.
Among the Blessed Lords, he is Śrī Kṛṣṇa; among days of the week, he is Sunday.
Among lunar dates, he takes the form of Ekādaśī; and among those who possess forbearance, he is indeed the Earth.
He is indeed the mother of offspring; he is truly the nectar among things to be consumed.
He is declared to be the clarified butter among products of the cow, and he is the wish-fulfilling tree among trees.
He is Surabhi among the cows of plenty, and he is Hari among rivers, like the Gaṅgā.
He is the speech of the wise and the *praṇava* among mantras;
he is the supreme knowledge (*parā vidyā*) among all sciences and the grain among crops.
He is the *aśvattha* tree among fruit-bearing trees and Kṛṣṇa, the giver of mantras, among teachers.
He is Kaśyapa among the lords of creatures, and he is indeed Garuḍa among the birds;
he is Ananta among the serpents, and he is indeed the king among men. He is Bhṛgu among the Brahman-sages, and Nārada among the divine sages.
He was Janaka among royal sages, and Śuka among great seers;
Citraratha among Gandharvas, and Kapila among the Siddhas;
Lomaśa among those of long life, and he indeed was the preceptor of the wise. (91–92)
Among the best of poets he is Śukra, and among the planets he is indeed Śani;
among artisans he is Viśvakarman, and among wild beasts he is indeed the king of beasts (the lion).
Among steeds he is the mount of Śiva, and among elephants he is Airāvata.
Among meters he is the Gāyatrī; among scriptures he is the Veda itself.
Among aquatic creatures he is Varuṇa; Kṛṣṇa is indeed among the Apsarases, for he is Urvaśī.
Among reservoirs of water he is the ocean; among mountains he is Sumeru. (94–95)
Among those possessing jewels he is Himādri; among the primary natures (prakṛtis) he is Rādhikā;
among goddesses he is Kamalā; and among women he is Kṛṣṇa and Śatarūpā.
Among beloved ones he is Kṛṣṇa; and among those of virtuous character he is Sāvitrī.
He is Prahlāda among the most powerful Daityas, and he is Bali;
he is the venerable sage Nārāyaṇa among the wise and those who observe celibacy;
he is Hanumān among the monkeys, and he is Nara himself among heroes.
To the Naga maidens he is Manasa, and to the Vasus he is indeed Drona; for those filled with desire, he is the one who assumes any form at will, appearing as Rambha among the lustful women.
He is Goloka among all worlds, and he is the imperishable abode (Aksharadhama) among all abodes.
He is indeed the Lord Vaikuṇṭha, the glorious abode and the dwelling place of the Vasus.
He is peace within the group of Mothers; he is indeed delight among beautiful women.
He exists as righteousness among the assembly of witnesses; he is indeed the twilight within the days.
Among the gods he is Indra; among the Rākṣasas he is Vibhīṣaṇa; he himself is Hari.
Among the Rudras he is Kālāgnirudra; among the Bhairavas he is Saṃhāra.
Among conch shells he is Pāñcajanya; and in the body, he is the head.
In his own narratives, he is the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*.
Among the Manus, he is Svāyaṃbhuva; among the learned, he is Vyāsa Mādhava.
Among the wives of the ancestors (*pitṛs*), he is Svadhā; among the beloved wives of the fires (*vahnis*), he is Svāhā.
Among sacrifices, He is the Rājasūya; among the wives of sacrificers, He is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Among those possessing right conduct and beautiful voices, He is the bard (sūta); for He is indeed Hari among narrators.
Among those skilled in weapons and missiles, He is Paraśurāma; and among divine powers, He is the Supreme Deity.
