Those two, O good friend, take refuge in the same tree and provide encouragement to one another in their task.
The one who is undisciplined eats sweets with greed, while another who is disciplined gives them away, being well-satisfied;
just as rivers reach the state of the ocean.
Having cast off the semblance of false cognition,
and likewise being devoid of the semblance of the knower and the known,
he attains the divine Person who is beyond the imperishable. //49//
He who knows the Supreme Brahman becomes Brahman himself;
he does not return to transmigrate, dragged by the force of karma.
Just as one abandons heat, he indeed relinquishes all agitation.
And he who has attained constant awakening here shines within the cave of the heart in this body for the sake of immortality, being released from the knots of the heart. (1.523.50)
Abiding within that, the creator of the universe and the destroyer of all exists as the transcendent one in the divine world.
The virtuous know this, and we too know it.
If there were no perception of that [Self], a great fall would have occurred;
through the realization of that very [Self], the wise became immortal, while others indeed went toward suffering born of ignorance.
Thus one should know the majesty of the Supreme Self;
for it has neither increase through actions nor diminution.
One who knows its true path shall go to its abode.
By taking refuge in that, one is not tainted by sinful actions.
Everything belongs to Him in whom the entire Brahman resides; whatever exists in the universe is attached to His multitude of liberated souls.
All that indeed has entered into the Lords, and likewise into this one who has become a living soul and others;
that which is in the Imperishable remains in the Absolute alone.
Thus indeed, in Śabalā and Nirañjanā,
in the golden one called Mahāviṣṇu, and likewise in Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Virāj who abide therein. ||55||
He shines here upon the seven layers of the eightfold cosmic manifestations beginning with *prakṛti*;
here on this earth, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa reigns.
Knowing him to be the immortal, go to that Lord!
For from Him, who is qualified by the subtle cit and acit, the gross world qualified by cit and acit is indeed born.
Because the material cause and its effect are non-different,
every reality is nothing but the one Supreme Brahman. [57] Of that Supreme Self, who descends in His fullness—
A certain power assumes the designation of *vyūha*;
through successive reduction, that same power takes the forms of *vibhava*, *avatāra*, *pūrṇāṃśa*, *mukhya*, *āveśa*, *gauṇa*, and so forth. (58)
Through union with this or that, there is the attainment of its specific nature;
for it enters into a state of being both merged and unmerged within that.
And by means of the worship of the Supreme Self, one [attains] the Supreme Lord.
That by which they attain supreme liberation is the Truth (sat).
[59] The support of the liberated, the pervasive non-consciousness, the imperishable, the support of all, the body of the Supreme Brahman—that is the Abode (dhāma) wherein He resides. [1.523.60]
That very syllable (akṣara) is the abode of Brahman, consisting of the splendor of Hari;
for as much as Vedic study, austerity, and celibacy have been practiced, so is that supreme state attained.
It is both bodiless and embodied, both with form and without form.
Pure and eternal, it is the body of Hari that illumines Māyā and the rest;
it is the self abiding in existence, consciousness, and bliss, transcending birth, death, and old age. United with Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, it exists as the supreme reality. (62–63)
Worship Hari, the eternal presiding Lord, who is non-different from the radiant splendor of the Supreme Brahman, who dwells beyond the further shore of *rajas*,
and who is partless, situated even above the golden sheath.
Worship Hari, the pure light among lights, who is the presiding lord therein;
whose every limb is of the form of a cow’s hair-tuft, whose individual powers are non-different from his own self,
and who possesses neither division nor abandonment, being of one essence with the Supreme Lord.
Worship Śrī Hari, who resides there, whose omniscience depends on no other,
and who is composed of light, abiding in the Supreme Brahman.
Indeed, the eternally liberated ones dwell in that eternal state.

O King, worship Śrī Hari, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, who resides there. (6.8) Having thus worshipped Him who dwells in the abode of Akṣara and who is situated in the supreme abode—the Supreme—many have attained the state of equanimity; always worship Him. (6.9)
He who is the bridge of all dharmas, whose ground is the imperishable Brahman—
knowing Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa to be situated there, worship Him always. He who would be ignorant of this and devoid of devotion and service [is lost].
Impure and enveloped by the cycle of rebirth, he would not go there.
But he who possesses direct experience of that Nārāyaṇa attains His abode, and from there he is not born again. (71–72)
He who possesses devotion as his strength and likewise has knowledge that provides nourishment,
mounted upon the chariot of service to the guru, attains the abode of Śrī Hari.
Higher than individual souls are the lords, and higher than the lords is the imperishable Absolute.
Having known that which is beyond the syllable (akṣara), most beautiful, one shall attain its abode.
All instruction culminates in the severing of the knot of the heart;
having reached the knot of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, go to the supreme state.
"O others, whoever exists in you, in me, and in others—worship Him with reverence.
He who perceives Him through duality falls into the snares of death.
Having known Him within the heart and with the inner eye as devoid of diversity,"
Having slain death, which is caused by manifold states of existence, go to the supreme state.
(77) "Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa; obeisance to the Lord.
O King, always chant this mantra, and He will carry you across to the further shore. (78)
For one whose body is falling away, no further bondage remains.
For you, who are unbound and liberated, what remains here?
This great tree, the Aśvattha, has its roots above and its branches below.
Leaving that behind, go to Hari, the imperishable Brahman, the immortal;
by whose fear all splendors shine forth according to their laws, and from whom the lords have attained their lordship—worship that Śrī Hari. (1.523.80–81)
Abandoning the desires residing in your heart, find fulfillment here in Kṛṣṇa;
enjoy the nectar of supreme bliss from Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
In Him, truth, austerity, celibacy, and devotional service are firmly established.
And for those among them who possess neither crookedness nor falsehood, there exists the world of Brahmā.
O King, there are two kinds of knowledge in every respect: the higher (parā) and the lower (aparā).
By the higher, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa is attained in the imperishable state.
All other words besides those, by which Brahman is not attained,
are surpassed by those who indeed always utter speech that is most dear to the Supreme Self;
they go to the holy abode of Brahman and serve the glorious Supreme Self.
He who knows, serves, and worships the Supreme Brahman—
whether in the waking state, in the dream state, or in the supreme glory of the state beyond the three— he enjoys all desires mingled with Brahman. (86–87)
Know that food, life-breath, mind, knowledge, and bliss are He;
worship Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa as the Self and the Inner Self.
By what bliss is one not filled through service to the Son of Kaṃbhārī? (88)

O King, by the service of cowherd boys and by the cows, that Lord is being nourished. Go to that bliss of Hari, whom neither speech nor mind can make an object; from Him, you shall have no fear whatsoever.
From knowledge, sacrifices are born and ritual actions also arise;
when offered to the glorious Kṛṣṇa, they result in supreme satisfaction.
He who knows the Supreme Brahman and does not falter because of that [knowledge]— || 9.1 ||
Having cast off the sin of illusion, one enjoys the delights of Brahman. Indeed, he who serves the virtuous Kṛṣṇa— whether He is speaking as a saint or meditating as a saint—
draws that person toward the state of the virtuous.
For having created that very thing, he entered into it; he is higher than the high.
Just as the unreal appears as real, by him [the Real] is perceived as "real.
And the unmanifest state, which is well-fashioned, is perceived by him as such.
Through the Puruṣa who is beyond the Imperishable (akṣara), he brought forth many cosmic eggs.
By virtue of his connection with that Supreme Self, truth and merit reside within them;
having understood this, as it is in the Imperishable, one shall attain liberation.
O King, in ancient times the Blessed One was indeed all that exists; from Him the entire reality, whose nature is Being, was manifested.
He is the essence of aesthetic flavor (rasa), the bestower of all flavors.
Having obtained its essence, they become blissful.
Indeed, by his bliss the worlds attain fearlessness;
where neither mind nor speech reaches—that Keśava, worship him. (97–98)
From Him these beings are born, and by that Lord they live;
in Him alone they dissolve, so go to that eternal dissolution.
The Supreme Self, of divine form, was the object of meditation in the primordial abode.
Having fashioned a second [form], He dwelt there; worship Him.
Everything, both stationary and moving, shines with wisdom as its eye.
Worship Mādhava, who exists within that wisdom and is its very eye.
Worship Hari— the peaceful, the all-pervading, the supreme Brahman, *kaṃ* and *khaṃ*,
the infallible leader with his divine luster— through faith and austerity. Worship Hari, who dwells within the divine and is the inner self of the bright fortnight.
Worship him who abides in the months of the northern solstice, who dwells within the year;
who resides in the sun and whose inner self is the moon. Worship him who bestows the light of lightning, who is situated in Varuṇa and within the waters. (103–104)
Worship that which is the inner Indra of Prajāpati, situated within the intermediate space, attained by Virāṭ;
the heart of Rudra, abiding in Viṣṇu, established in Mahāviṣṇu;
residing in the Stainless (Nirañjana), endowed with the variegated (Śabala), and existing as the Absolute (Kevala).
Having become one who has reached the imperishable Brahman, always worship that Supreme Person— Lord Hari,
the bestower of the fruits of all gifts, who resides in the smoke-colored night,
who dwells within the dark fortnight, and who moves during the southern solstice.

O King, always worship Him who dwells within the year, who dwells in the ancestors, and who moves through the sky; worship Him who dwells in the moon and who resides in Prajāpati. Worship Him who dwells in the wind, who abides in the clouds, who dwells in the rain-clouds, and who exists within the water-drops.
Worship Śrī Hari, who pervades all things—both those existing as seeds and those manifesting as effects.
Worship Hari within the Brahmins and others, who are mines of beauty;
worship Hari within the cows and others, who are mines of compassion.
This deity has destroyed all evil; he is free from old age and exempt from death.
He is without sorrow, devoid of hunger and thirst, and the fulfiller of true desires.
Worship that Lord who is your own essential nature, equal to you, and like unto you.
They are manifested through His form; therefore, worship Him in that way.
Always playing, dancing, singing, and bringing joy, while He Himself acts with His own form—worship Him in such a manner.
Without his devotee he finds no delight; therefore, he fashioned him as a second self. Always worship him who is pervaded by you, residing within your heart.
O King, this very Self must be seen by you with the eye situated in the heart.
He is to be heard with the ear and the heart, and to be reflected upon with divine luster;
He is to be determined by his own intellect, and He must never be abandoned.
Thus, behold the eternal Kṛṣṇa with the state of being the Self of all.
In Him all beings are established; worship Him. Worship Him who is in earth, water, fire, air, and ether.
Worship Him whose these bodies are, and who dwells within the body.

Worship that Keśava, whose self, existence, and very image [are one]. (1.18) Worship Nārāyaṇa, from whom all joys arise, by whom all living beings are gladdened, who has attained all desires, who is supreme bliss, and who is perfect. (1.19)
Abandoning desires, establish Hari within your heart with devotion; O King, recognize Him as truly present, go to Him for refuge, and worship Him.
Then there will be nothing unattained remaining for you here, nor indeed anything left to be achieved.
This very supreme Brahma-knowledge, which bestows liberation, has been taught to you.
Then this king, being fully satisfied, beheld within his own self Janārdana, the Supreme Person, the divine Puruṣottama.
He bears the radiance of the conch, discus, mace, lotus, bow, trident, and other weapons;
He is the Lord of Rādhā, Lakṣmī, Prabhā, Padmā, Pārvatī, and Māṇikī;
and He is served by all His female attendants as well as His male associates. (123)
Having beheld that Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa within her heart,
she saw Him, the Lord of Śrī, outside as well— by His will,
through the grace of Lomaśa, and by the power of the supreme knowledge (parāvidyā).
A divine and exceedingly beautiful celestial chariot descended from the sky,
consecrated by a divine messenger at the command of Brahmā.
The divine messenger said, "Come, come to the celestial chariot!"
"O King, I shall lead you to the true realm of Śrī Parameṣṭhin.
Indradyumna said to him: "I have no need for that truth;
I shall certainly go to the feet of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa."
"By the grace of Lomaśa, [he attained] the supreme abode beyond the syllable.
Having been told this, that messenger of the gods went to the world of Brahmā.
Indradyumna, however, took his leave in the presence of Lomaśa.
Lomaśa gave him an auspicious seat of grass on the shore of that lake,
near a *kadamba* tree, in the abode of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
Having bathed there, the king meditated upon Hari and worshipped Nārāyaṇa.
Having honored Lomaśa and bowed to the sages in that hermitage,
and having offered fruits and other items to Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa,
he presented them to his guru there, ate, and drank water.
Remembering Hari during the night, he obtained a blissful yogic sleep.

Thus ends the five hundred and twenty-third chapter, titled "The Recollection of the Self through the Brahma-Vidya and Upanishadic Teachings as Instructed by Sage Lomaśa to Indradyumna," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*. (523)
← Chapter 523: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga) Chapter 524 [Author: Chapter 525 →
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Mahālakṣmī, to the auspicious story of Lomaśa.
Having risen in the morning and performed his daily rites, the king [set out] toward his guru.
Having seen Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, he went for the purpose of beholding Him;
consecrated with blessings by his guru, he questioned the sage Lomaśa:
"O Blessed One, you are the giver of liberation, beyond Māyā, and one who has conquered the senses."
And just as you abide in your own abode, so too is your vision here at the tips of my hands.
Tell me, O Lord: since there is no time in your divine abode, what then is the momentary nature that regulates the modes of service and the like? (3–4)
"How is daily ritual practice performed by the devotees?"—
when asked thus, O King, Lomaśa spoke to the monarch:
"By the rays of the form of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, which are endowed with beautiful splendor..."
Through their spreading rays of diverse forms, the moments and other divisions of time exist at all times. Those who know this perceive morning, midday, and evening by means of those rays;
and there, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa accepts their service.
Sleep is a state of dissolution within the form; waking is service to the servant.
Day is the manifestation of white light, and twilight is the manifestation of red light.
And when there is the sight of a cloud-dark [form], stability within that form is night.
Likewise, in Goloka, all activities are carried out by the rays of Kṛṣṇa;
in Vaikuṇṭha, they are carried out by the expansions of Nārāyaṇa’s splendor; and in the supreme abode of Akṣara, they are carried out by the radiance of the Supreme Brahman. (1.524.10)
"Thus, O Indradyumna, you have heard from those who attained liberation what was told to them; what else do you wish to ask?
Then, O Lakṣmī, Indradyumna questioned the sage Lomaśa.
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa desires to manifest here in this sacred field.
At that time, does He reside within a mother’s womb or not?
Is His body material, or is it of a different nature altogether? (12–13)
"Cut through the doubt that has arisen in me and show compassion for this worldly matter.
Lomaśa replied: "O royal sage, regarding the incarnations and other manifestations of Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul, of Nārāyaṇa, whenever they occur—"
At the time of creation, upon manifestation, [it occurs] then according to the womb. Hari always commands the wind situated within the womb:
"You must remain within the cavity of the womb together with water for that long. (15–16)
Just as a pregnant woman is indeed seen on the outside,
so you must make her reach the state of having a distended womb in the time that is required;
and at whatever place, in whatever manner, and for whatever duration a particular occasion is awaited.
Having first demonstrated there the growth of the embryo,
at the time of birth, one should also demonstrate there the ordinary worldly process of the expulsion of the wind and water from the womb to the outside. (18–19)
At that time, remaining there, I shall remain unobserved so that my form may indeed appear like that of a newborn infant born from a womb;
I must manifest as mere light, enveloped by the waters of the womb.
For those whose eyes are covered by illusion, there is no access to me here.
Those with divine vision behold my divine and subtle creation;
those with gross vision behold [only] the child born from the womb.
In this very way, those born of improper causes are indeed liberated;
for that [knowledge] does not belong to the mother and father, since they are lovers of pleasure.
According to the manner of Kāmadeva, their appearance occurs at my birth.
But for those who do not desire it, my divine appearance occurs to them in an instant.
Therefore, O Vāyu, there is no entry into a womb for me, nor any reliance upon the bodily elements;
there is no dwelling within a fetal chamber, nor indeed any emergence from a birth canal.
"I have no state of childhood, nor indeed do I have both birth and death;
for my body is not composed of the elements, yet show it to be so.
Thus did the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa command.
O King, in accordance with that [devotion], Hari displays his activity;
likewise, for Hari who is eternally satisfied, there is no worldly need for food and so forth—yet the devotees perform these acts with sincere devotion. (27–28)
Whatever is dear to oneself, whatever is enjoyable, and whatever is captivating—by offering all that to Him, one should enjoy it; this is the eternal dharma.
Thus, service performed by a devotee bestows satisfaction upon Him who is eternally satisfied.

The boon that was formerly granted to Lakṣmī by the wielder of the Śārṅga bow—how could it possibly be rendered deficient? Hari replied: "It has been consumed by me; it shall increase and never suffer depletion."
Just as I consume it, so does it increase;
the inert becomes conscious and attains a divine state.
Having attained clarity, it then reaches full blossoming.
It becomes ever new, imbued with flavor, and bestowing auspiciousness.
Those with divine vision perceive this; those with external vision do not.
Thus, O King, has been described the enhancement of the food offering (naivedya). || 33-34 ||
"O King, for those things given to Kṛṣṇa, there is never any diminution;
on the contrary, everything increases. What else do you wish to hear?
Thereupon Indradyumna questioned Lomaśa, the true guru of Hari.

"Why is it that even during the summer season, when the sun has reached its zenith, you do not build a beautiful house for the purpose of dwelling? Lomaśa said to that king: 'I am, in every respect, short-lived.'"
"For whose sake should a dwelling be built, since life is impermanent?
If life were eternal and long-lasting, one might resort to a house.
The king said, "And it is heard that you possess long life among all people."
Therefore, I too have arrived here out of a desire to see you.
Lomaśa then said: "Listen, O King, I shall tell you this:
with the arrival of every kalpa, a single hair of mine perishes. (1.524.40)
"In the absence of hair on my chest, my destruction will come to pass.
Three hundred and sixty-five thousand kalpas have passed for me;
indeed, during that time, the vision of the Creator has vanished before my eyes."
O King, from my navel up to my throat, there are body hairs;
specifically, they number three hundred sixty-five thousand and six hundred thirty-six. (42–43)
Having dwelt for that many kalpas within the cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas), thereafter I shall go to the supreme world; indeed, what use have I for a home?
Behold here upon my body, below the knee, a mark extending the length of a finger.
"For as long as an eon, a rival has arisen that is devoid of hair.
Life is certainly not permanent; it is known by the loss of one's hair.
For that reason, O Lord of the Earth, I do not build a house. (45–46)
The king said: "O Sage! What karma was performed by you in the past?
What kind of austerity or gift was given, by which such a long life as this has been obtained?
Then Lomaśa replied: "Listen, O King, for a long time to my [story]."
In a former creation, I was a Śūdra afflicted by poverty.
While performing menial service, I then came upon the Badarī forest;
emaciated by hunger and tormented by thirst, I beheld Nara-Nārāyaṇa. (48–49)
Having offered water and lotus flowers and performed the worship, he then completed the ritual and set out upon the mountain path. Thereupon,
overcome by cold and hunger, he met his death in the house of a Brahmin.
Because of that, I became a rememberer of my past births; therefore, I maintain silence in every way.
My father, filled with great joy, gave me the name Īśāna.
Even when urged by others, I do not speak anything at all.
Having attained supreme detachment upon seeing the nature of worldly existence,
my father employed words as medicine for the sake of illumination.
Because of that, laughter arises within me toward those people who have merely recited the mantras.
Dwelling in the sacred field of Aśvapaṭṭasaraḥ,
with a spirit of devotion and a concentrated mind, I worship the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa;
subsisting by the practice of gleaning ears of grain, I maintain my life.
With oranges, jujubes, vegetables, cucumbers, fruits, and leaves—then Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa became manifest before me.
He said, "I am well-pleased; choose a boon, O observer of noble vows."
Then I requested: "Make me free from old age and death.
Kṛṣṇa said: "Indeed, immortality cannot belong to anyone in the mortal world.
Therefore, set a limit for your life; I shall grant you that. (57–58)
Then Hari was addressed: "In every kalpa, let there be the falling out of my body hair starting from the navel down to the throat;
let my lifespan be exactly that long—ten times more than the number of years it takes for the hair to fall away. (59)
"Wherein a hundred [years] might dissolve, from there I shall go to your abode.
"So be it," Hari said, and then he vanished from sight.
From that time forward, right here near Kuṅkumavāpikā—
I dwell for such a duration in the sacred field of Aśvapaṭṭasara;
my long life is the fruit of my service to Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
Thousands of dissolutions of worlds have been witnessed by me during this lifetime.
At the time of dissolution, I go to Vaikuṇṭha, which is situated upon the waters.
At the end of the veil of fire, during the new creation, I return toward the earth and dwell in the hermitage of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
Likewise, the brahmin Patnīvrata and his beloved wife Pativratā both became long-lived, their hair never turning gray.
Similarly, Śrī Kambharā Lakṣmī and Gopāla Kṛṣṇa Bhūsura—
Those two shall live long for you, and their hair shall never turn gray.
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa himself, the Lord of Akṣara, is born in their home at every creation and in every kalpa. 66–67.
I worship that very Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa at all times;
having observed their lifespans, pride no longer dwells within me.
I worship Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa; you too, worship that Hari.
"For one in this world who is devoted to Hari, nothing desired is difficult to obtain.
(69) Thus, O Indradyumna, my history has been told to you. You have become renowned in the world; go now to the imperishable abode of Hari. (70)
Then Indradyumna spoke regarding the liberation from the curse for all—the release of the tortoise, the owl, the vulture, the ṛṣi, the crane, and Mārkaṇḍeya.
"O learned one, tell me when this shall come to pass; you are omniscient like Hari."
Lomaśa then said: "When they all worship Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa preceded by the reception of the mantra, then liberation will indeed occur here in this sacred field; of this there is no doubt. (72–73)
Indradyumna, who had been repeatedly assisted by them, remembered all of them; and they, possessing the memory of their former births and able to assume any form at will, arrived.
Having bowed to Lomaśa, they worshipped Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
They worshipped Kambharā-Lakṣmī and honored Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa. (75) Then, on the shore of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake, the sage Lomaśa offered a welcome and indeed bestowed the mantra of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. (76)
"Oṃ, obeisances to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; obeisances!
Thus they chanted as they remained there in the sinless hermitage of Lomaśa.
Having bathed in the Aśvapaṭṭa lake and at Kuṅkumavāpikā...
Having gone there, they drank water and chanted mantras day and night.
By the grace of Lomaśa, their latent impressions (vāsanā) were dissolved;
liberated, they became recipients of the favor of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
The sage Kacchapa was at Lake Nārāyaṇa in the region of Kaccha;
the sage Ghūka was in the sacred field of Śrī Hāṭakeśa on the bank of the Nāga river;
and the sage Gṛdhra was on the auspicious Raivata mountain, at the site of Dattātreya’s ascetic penance.
The sage Bakari resides in the sacred field of Śrī Somanātha near the ocean;
Mārkaṇḍeya dwells in the forest at Talaśyāma-sthala.
They are divine, long-lived, and always able to assume any form at will.
They shall exist in every kalpa for the sake of the world’s welfare. Every year, during the month of Kārtika on the Raivata mountain,
they all come for the purpose of circumambulating the gods and Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
"I am Lomaśa; I shall go there for five days.
Thus speaking, they proceeded toward the mountain while chanting the sublime name "Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa."
I, Lomaśa, shall indeed declare the merit that arises from their treading upon the earth.
Then, through the devotion of King Indradyumna, Hari himself—
He was gratified by supreme devotion and by Lomaśa’s grace.
He bestowed upon his heart a divine, supreme vision free from all obscuration;
he beheld within his heart the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
Having placed the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) upon Lomaśa and having merged his own self into the Supreme Self,
as soon as he desires to depart by way of the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra),
a celestial chariot arrives, attended by liberated divine syllables.
The king ascended that [palace], which resembled ten million times ten million suns;
having bowed to Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, he went to the imperishable state of Brahman. Lomaśa performed the ritual offerings of water and other rites for him according to the rules.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, has been narrated to you the account of the origin of the name Lomaśātana,

and the narrative of the long-lived Ṛṣi Lomaśa. Thus ends the [section] on the acquaintance with the knowledge of the times in the abode of the Blessed One within the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, concerning the divinity in the taking of birth, the fulfilling nature of the food offering (*naivedya*), and the prior history of Lomaśa.

Chapter Five Hundred and Twenty-Four, titled "The Description of Long-Lived Beings such as Mārkaṇḍeya and Their Long-Term Residence in Saurāṣṭra and Other Regions," from the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section One: The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Once, a king known by the name Aśvaśiras arrived.
At the hermitage of Lomaśa, in the sacred field by the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake,
the highly effulgent Kapila arrived for the sake of a vision.
There, Aśvaśiras questioned that ṛṣi, Kapila, regarding his doubt.
"Is liberation attained through action or through knowledge? Speak a definitive conclusion.
"Listen, Lakṣmī! Hear the auspicious conclusion which the sage Kapila declared.
Out of a desire for the welfare of householders who perform ritual actions, I shall proclaim it. (3)
Whatever action an embodied being performs, whether good or evil, by consigning it all to Nārāyaṇa, he is not tainted even while acting.
Listen, O Brahmin: Saṃyamana was born into the lineage of Atri.
Devoted to asceticism, Niṣṭhuraka, a hunter by name, went to the Dharmāraṇya forest in the morning to bathe in the Bhāgīrathī river; there he encountered a herd of deer standing nearby,
equipped with his bow.
Desirous of killing, he arrived at the bank with his bow strung and his arrow ready.
But seeing that hunter who was devoted to the chase, the brahmin stopped him, saying:
"O gentle sir, do not commit this slaughter of living beings!"
Having heard this, the hunter laughed and said to that best of sages:
"I do not indeed harm living beings, nor do I act in such a way at all.
This Supreme Self merely plays with these elements through His own māyā."

Illusion (māyā) is indeed their birth, nourishment, and destruction in succession. O Brahman, we are merely the occasional agents (naimittika) therein; therefore, those seeking liberation must never entertain the sense of ego (ahaṃbhāva).
If one performs [these acts] solely for the sake of sustaining life, one is not tainted;
however, he who possesses egoism therein does not attain the state of a true seeker.
O twice-born one, having abandoned egoism, I shall seize a single deer.
Having heard this, that best of brahmins forbade the hunter:
"Committing violence is a sin in every respect; do not ever act in this way again.
There are fruits, roots, leaves, and water. (13–14)

Use grains and vegetable leaves for your sustenance; conduct yourself with them in such a way that you practice non-violence. If a journey can be accomplished without harming others, do not harm them pointlessly.
"I must not harbor egoism"—this is what dwells in your speech.
It is not for your own sake that you have become a destroyer of deer;
rather, all offer instruction for the purpose of abandoning pride.
Yet they do not themselves abandon pride, which is distinct from both speech and mind. (16–17)
They say one thing, they do another; having deceived others, they dwell in yet another way. Proficient in their own interests, they achieve only their personal ends.
They indeed depart after having destroyed others.
(18) The hunter said: "O Sage, I am not a deceiver seeking my own self-interest.
Conduct an examination of me in this matter; it shall surely become evident to you. (19)
"Construct a net made of clods of earth and bring fire beneath it;
let a great heap of dry wood burn there intensely. When the brahmin had done so, the fire was indeed blown up fiercely.
Thousands of flames issued forth from the windows and through the lattice-work;
at that time, when the iron lattice glowed like fire,
the hunter, having relied upon his own yogic power, [assumed] his true form.
He transformed himself into the form of fire, possessing a mass of heat like the sun;
yet the fire before him became devoid of luster.
Rising up, that hunter sat down upon that web.
Just as fire is not burned by fire itself, so too was the hunter not burned by the fire produced from the wood. The Brahmin Saṃyamana and others were likewise filled with wonder. (24–25)
They asked, "Who are you? Tell us. He replied, "I am the Fire-god (Hutāśana).
I am myself; there is no violence on my part, for embodied beings are cooked within me.
Having abandoned all conscious thought, I act according to my own inherent nature."
My egoism has been destroyed by penance joined with knowledge.
When egoism is destroyed, one is no longer smeared by actions.
Egoism is the root; possessiveness is called its trunk. (27–28)
Attachment is its branch, as are aversion, pride, greed, and delusion;
its leaves are actions, and its sap is constant relishing. Its flower is called "instigation," and its fruit is sweet pleasure.
"Unpleasant suffering is what embodied beings always experience.
[1.525.30] "Pour water at the base of the fire; flames will then issue from that spot.
Having been told this, the Brahmin quickly took a jar filled with water there. [31]
When Vahni suddenly cast it down and it was extinguished upon the ground,
all the flames were destroyed on every side due to the destruction of their root.
Then the hunter said to that brahmin, "This is indeed a visible demonstration."
When the root is destroyed, the destruction of the entire tree occurs.
(33) If the root-pride of those who perform actions is destroyed, they are never stained by either sin or merit. (34)

O best of beings, in this [body] the fire blazes with many branches; when the root is destroyed, it is extinguished. Likewise, I, who am always possessed of karma, have resorted to the body and thus assumed the nature of a physical form.
Overcome by hunger and thirst, eating and drinking, one who is active—
performing all actions while avoiding pride, which is the cause of attachment,
and being united with the inner self— does not come to grief. (36–37)
Then the hunter said to the brahmin, "O best of the twice-born, touch a clod of earth.
The clod was hot and caused a burning sensation; it was recognized and let go by the brahmin.
Then that hunter touched it, yet no burning occurred.
Then the hunter said to him: "Formations (saṃskāras) arise from conceit;
just as the formations produced by fire in a clod of earth seem to burn, so long as these [conceits] exist in persons, they are burned in every way. (1.525.40)
Likewise, as long as the impressions of egoism persist within embodied beings, they are stained by merit and demerit; of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, both egoism and the impressions must be abandoned through ascetic practice.

"By devotion to Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, by yoga, by the states of meditation, and by the devotion of total self-surrender, one is not tainted by karmas. When this had been said to the brahmin, from the sky above the hunter, [a voice spoke]. 42–43.
A shower of flowers fell slightly upon the brahmin;
then the hunter struck down that deer, even at that moment.
The brahmin said, "O soul of the deer, where are you going? Show me!"
The hunter conceived the thought of a celestial chariot born of the heavenly world.
At that moment, the best of brahmins beheld great, preeminent celestial chariots, moving at will and adorned with many jewels.
Among them,

the Brahmin saw Niṣṭhuraka, who was established as the most excellent among all, capable of assuming any form at will; he had attained perfection through the realization of non-duality and possessed many bodies by means of yoga.
And beholding the deer, who possessed a divine form and was of the nature of a god,
the brahmin Saṃyamana became filled with joy;
others there also became free from the egoism of the body.
Thus it should be understood that even while performing action according to one's own nature,
there is a persistence that is free from the taint of merit and demerit;
such a state never binds the self anywhere.
Just as the god Nārāyaṇa is untainted and a mere substance, so too, while acting, grasping, causing action, and causing others to grasp— all free from taint—
he instead makes that [object] attain his own state, which is devoid of qualities. 51–52.
Likewise, the Self, being devoid of *māyā*, neither acts nor is it tainted.
That which is obtained and enjoyed—a dull material object—it renders divine indeed;
it renders that very thing untainted, free from bondage, and established in liberation. (53)
Having understood this, the self-restrained brāhmaṇa departed for his own hermitage.
And Kapila spoke thus again to King Aśvaśiras:
"Therefore, O Indra among kings, you too [should worship] the Lord, the divine Nārāyaṇa."
"Behold the Lord while worshipping Him within your very own self, within your own body;
you will quickly become untainted, just as the hunter did of old.
Having heard these words of Kapila, that auspicious King Aśvaśiras—
And he considered that liberation for those who perform actions comes through action dedicated to Kṛṣṇa.
Then, at that very moment, the great sage Jaigīṣavya arrived there in Lomaśa’s auspicious hermitage; his lifespan was fifty kalpas.

Then those sages offered mutual greetings to one another and engaged in auspicious conversation concerning the worlds of heaven and other realms. While they were thus seated, Aśvaśiras bowed down to Kapila.
Having bowed down in the midst of all the sages, he questioned him:
"O Lord, how may I propitiate Hari Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme?
Kapila replied, "O King, indeed there are infinite Nārāyaṇas."
"Indeed, through the worship of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, [these fruits] come to be here.
O King, who is this teacher Nārāyaṇa of whom you speak?
We two are both Nārāyaṇas, O King, and we have appeared before your very eyes."
Having heard that, Aśvaśiras spoke to those two twice-born ones:
"Jaigīṣavya and Kapila, you have been heard of by me before as auspicious ones; you are perfected Brahmins whose sins have been burnt away by austerity. (63–64)
"How is it that you both say these words to me, 'We are Nārāyaṇas'?
[Yet] he who is endowed with the conch, discus, mace, lotus, bow, and svastika-banner;
who wears yellow garments; who is the Lord of Lakṣmī; and whose vehicle is Garuḍa—" || 65 ||
"Nārāyaṇa is the Supreme Brahman; who on earth is his equal?
Hearing these words of the king, those two brahmins, perfected yogis, laughed and said, "Behold Nārāyaṇa!"
Having spoken thus, that Kapila himself became Viṣṇu; and Jaigīṣavya instantly became Garuḍa. But the king, having seen Hari together with Garuḍa, was struck with wonder.
Having bowed, he said: "O Brahmins, be appeased; I do not ask about this Nārāyaṇa. Rather, I speak of this Nārāyaṇa, the father of Brahmā, from whose navel-lotus Brahmā was born. (1.525.70)
And having heard this, Kapila became Padmanābha there;
Jaigīṣavya became Brahmā, stationed upon the navel-lotus.
From the forehead of Brahmā, indeed, Rudra was born, with blood-red eyes.
The king, having reflected upon this, spoke again to those two brahmins:
"Nārāyaṇa, the soul of all and the pervader of all, cannot be seen by you;
what has been shown by you both, who are yogis, is merely an illusion born of yogic power."
But the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa, the sovereign who is the self of all, cannot be seen.
Then, at that time, Kapila and Jaigīṣavya displayed there all the forms of their own selves.
Bedbugs, mosquitoes, lice, bees, serpents, and birds;
horses, cows, elephants, lions, tigers, jackals, and deer; as well as other animals—both domestic and wild, including insects—[all arise from the same source]. (75–76)
"Beasts, humans, trees, creepers, and so forth—in every respect—having seen that multitude of beings, the king was struck with wonder. He understood the greatness of Jaigīṣavya and of Kapila. (77)
The sages asked them with devotion, "O best of the twice-born, what is this?
The two brahmins replied, "O King, remember what was asked by you:
how one may worship the supreme Lord Hari Nārāyaṇa."
Hari has indeed been manifested before you for your propitiation;
and I, Kapila, am also manifest here as Nārāyaṇa. If you have faith, worship me, for I have truly appeared before your very eyes.
All the qualities of the Omniscient One exist within me in part.
Therefore, everything has been obtained by me and presented to you through devotion.
That very Lord Nārāyaṇa is omniscient and capable of assuming any form at will.
Even beyond Padmanābha, it exists in the supreme realm of Mahāviṣṇu;
and even beyond Goloka and Vaikuṇṭha, within the imperishable abode (Akṣaradhāman),
Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa shines forth among the liberated souls.
It is said that this gentle one may be found here by men anywhere at his own will.
This Lomaśa has obtained that supreme Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa,
who is beloved by Śrī Kṛṣṇa, within the sacred field of Aśvapaṭṭasara.
We two have come to this auspicious hermitage for the purpose of beholding that infallible one who is the source of all incarnations.
He is indeed the Supreme Self, the Lord of the universe, who dwells within the bodies of all.
It exists within one's own body and is perceived through one's own devotion.
For this reason, O King of kings, the form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa has been shown to you, so that you may have conviction in both of us.

Thus, O King, the omnipresent God dwells even within your own body; for He indeed abides in all subjects, in servants, and even among ministers. All beings, including animals and swarms of insects, consist of Viṣṇu.
One should indeed make one's meditation firm, for Hari is truly composed of everything;
there is no other being among all beings equal to him, as he dwells within all beings.
One should serve that God who resides within, with the realization that "He is I."
This path of propitiation, which bestows supreme liberation, has been shown to you.
Worship Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa with a heart full of devotion,
using offerings for worship such as incense and the like, as well as food offerings, waving of lights, and so forth.
That Supreme Lord is easily attained through meditation and devotion as a servant.
He who is the divine Nārāyaṇa, the eternal Supreme Self, exists in many ways in various forms, the Lord who accomplishes all tasks. (93–94)
The Fish, the Tortoise, the Boar, Narasiṃha, Vāmana,
Rāma, Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, Buddha, and likewise Kalki and others—
these forms of his, beginning with Kapila, have been thus described.
The virtuous, the perfected ones, the virtuous women, the truthful,
and the yogis indeed serve as stairways for those who desire to obtain a vision of him;
yet even the gods do not behold that which is his supreme form.
He indeed fulfills one's contemplation by assuming forms such as our own;
therefore, this entire world is pervaded by Nārāyaṇa.
Worship him, O beloved, as the infallible Lord abiding in whatever form you desire.
In ancient times, Bṛhaspati spoke to Raibhya, the son of Brahmā:
"O King Vasu, during the Cākṣuṣa Manvantara, listen, O Raibhya, O King Vasu; hear this with due respect. (1.525.100)
Whatever action a person performs, whether good or evil,
by surrendering it all to Nārāyaṇa, he is not tainted even while acting.
And that glorious Nārāyaṇa abides within all living beings.
Worship that Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, who dwells within.
(1.02) Thereafter, the two of them constantly worshipped Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa;
they attained eternal liberation in the form of service in the supreme abode. (1.03)
Thus all this, which bestows the goal of life, was spoken by Kapila.
Then King Aśvaśiras, having consecrated his eldest son named Sthūlaśiras upon his own kingdom and having bowed repeatedly to his gurus, [departed].
He went to the distant forest named Naimiṣa and there worshipped the Lord Hari with austerity. Hari himself became manifest before him and,
by means of a celestial chariot, led his devotee to his own abode, Akṣaradhāma.

Thus has been told all this regarding the liberation of Aśvaśiras, through action offered to the Lord of lords by one endowed with knowledge. Thus ends the five hundred and twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Demonstration of Liberation through Action Consisting of the Surrender of All, Illustrated by the Examples of the Brahmin Saṃyamana, Niṣṭhura, and Kavyādha, and the Description of the Many Manifestations of Kapila and Jaigīṣavya," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī! I shall relate the previous history of Vasu exactly as it occurred, and thereafter I shall tell the wonder concerning Raibhya as well. (1)
The King of Kaśmīra himself, Vasu, was a great devotee who had taken refuge in the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. [He recited:
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa; obeisance to the Lord. (2)
He received this mantra from Nārāyaṇa during his old age.
O King, every year that monarch would go to Bādarī for the sake of serving and beholding Nārāyaṇa with devotion.
He always wears a beautiful garland of *tulasī* around his neck,
and he also always keeps a rosary in his hand for the purpose of recitation.
Knowing that his own stay [in this world] is but a moment and that the nature of worldly existence is likewise, [he remains thus].
All aggregates created within saṃsāra bestow sorrow and fear.
Wind, earth, space, water, and fire—the body of all embodied beings is composed of these five elements. (6–7)
It is a false delusion, artificial, and accompanied by illusion like a dream.
Who is whose son there, who is a woman, and who is whose husband?
All this is fashioned by karma and born from the bondage of karma.
Pleasure, pain, fear, and sorrow accompany the union with a body.
Through one's own actions, one undergoes birth among humans, animals, gods, trees, insects, living beings, birds, and even as grass. (1.526.10)
One indeed wanders again and again as long as the dissolution of karma has not occurred.
Truth (Kṛta), Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali constitute the four ages (caturyuga).
A *truṭi* is one-fourth of a *nimeṣa*; two of those make a *lava*.
Two *lava*s are said to be one *yava*; fifteen of those [make] one *kāṣṭhā*.
Thirty *kāṣṭhā*s are said to be one *kalā*, and thirty *kalā*s are considered one *kṣaṇa*.
Sixty *kṣaṇa*s are said to be one *pala*, and sixty of those [make] one *nāḍikā*.
Two *nāḍīs* constitute a *muhūrta*; thirty *muhūrtas* make up a day and night.
Thirty days and nights are considered a month, while two months are regarded as a season (*ṛtu*).
Three seasons form an *ayana*, and two *ayanās* constitute a year.
By this very measure, for the sake of human beings here,
the Kṛta Yuga is indeed determined to consist of seventeen hundred thousand solar years, along with another twenty-eight thousand. (15–16)
Those [mantras] numbering four thousand one hundred and eight,
when multiplied by three hundred and sixty, are considered to be the total in the Kṛta age.
Therein, indeed, the Lord himself is born in a white complexion.
The people were liberated from evil; they were patient, self-controlled, and had conquered their senses. Long-lived and immersed in austerity, they were free from desire, anger, and the like.
Among those progenitors, death in the form of the birth of a son was never seen anywhere.

Then the Tretā Yuga shall consist of twelve hundred thousand solar years, along with ninety-six thousand; this is the certain calculation established by the gods. Indeed, its number is three thousand six hundred [thousand] years.
Multiplied by three hundred and sixty, they [the years] constitute the *yuga* of the Trika.
Then, through one quarter of sin, the fierce Dharma enters;
thereafter, the glorious Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa attains the state of redness.
At that time, people become mutually competitive due to their sinful portions;
indeed, for the sake of heaven, they perform various acts of charity and sacrifice to reach the celestial realm. Yet, because of that very rivalry, some are born there with short lifespans.
While the progenitor exists, there is indeed no death for his sons;
there, desire, anger, and the like may arise or not arise.
Then, that excellent field has been sown once by means of cultivation.
The Vaiśyas, devoted to Kṛṣṇa, will indeed accept [gifts] seven times over;
all cows will be praised as jars, and buffaloes will be fourfold [in value].
At that time, human beings will be capable of both cursing and bestowing grace.
There will be no thieves, and all people will be devoted to the Dharma.
Then, in due order, the third age, the Dvāpara, shall exist;
therein, two quarters of evil and two quarters of Dharma are established.
And that [period] is proclaimed to consist of eight hundred thousand solar years;
at that time, a *yuga* consists of sixty-four thousand plus another two thousand four hundred years.
(29) Indeed, they are numbered as two thousand four hundred.
In that Dvāpara Yuga, they are multiplied by three hundred and sixty.
Desire, anger, pride, greed, hypocrisy, and envy—
these six arise there, and jealousy is the seventh.
Then, accompanied by them all, they indeed became mutually antagonistic;
yet some truly became peaceful, self-controlled, and masters of their senses.
Consequently, that age was then declared to be the Kali Yuga, the refuge of all defects.
Where the bull has but one foot, evil stands upon three feet.
(33) In the Kṛta age the Lord is white; in the Tretā age he is red;
in the Dvāpara age he is blue; indeed, in the Kali age he is born black like a bee. (34)
The duration of the Kali age is declared to be four hundred and thirty-two thousand solar years;
indeed, its total count consists of one thousand two hundred [years].
In the Kali age, they are considered to be multiplied by three hundred and sixty.
Indeed, one, two, three, four, and ten thousand years are respectively the durations of the Kali, Dvāpara, Tretā, and Satya Yugas. (36–37)
The human [ages] are two, four, six, and eight hundred years respectively;
when these are added together, they amount to two thousand years.
Thus, twelve thousand years of humans constitute a *caturyuga*.
Furthermore, the period of a *caturyuga* consists of forty-three lakhs and twenty thousand solar years;
indeed,
it is held that at the beginning of creation, the exhaustion of lifespan occurs simultaneously with the end of the *yuga*.
In the Kali age, men form friendships with those who possess wealth in their homes as well as charming women.
Sons are intent solely on their own self-interest, and beloved wives are devoted only to their own adornment.
And if the daughter-in-law knows [the value] by means of wealth, the mother-in-law will go to ruin.
My house would possess sovereignty; everyone desires it to be so.
Then the clouds will have little water, and the earth will have little grain.
In the Kali age, those who are virtuous will become rogues and mockers, and teachers will likewise be so;
cows will yield little milk, and there will be no clarified butter in that milk.
At that time, Brahmins will eat all kinds of food, and kings will be devoid of compassion.
All will be intent on acts of theft, and the earth will have lost its youth.
Times of departed auspiciousness and approaching horrors have arrived;
within four years, a maiden shall become pregnant.
If one dies at fifteen years of age or less, death itself will surely occur;
and at the end of the Kali age, people will be only a span (vitasti) in height.
At the end, when the lifespan is ten years, their home will be a hole within the earth.
At that time, indeed, the upper garment shall consist merely of a secret covering.
All castes will become of a single color, mutually intermingled;
they will have become barbarians (mlecchas), of evil conduct, and devoid of righteous deeds and duties.
Likewise, a Manu enjoys sovereignty for seventy-one cycles of four yugas;
Mahendra, moreover, enjoys a long life again and again.
The supreme lifespan is proclaimed to be equal for both the Manu and Mahendra.
When fourteen Indras have passed away, it is said to be one day of Brahmā.
Thus measured, his night is equal to his day; this constitutes a single Kalpa.
One hundred such years of Brahmā constitute his supreme lifespan.
By these four kinds of measures— the solar, the civil, the lunar, and the sidereal—
time passes for all beings on the circle of the earth;
specifically, by three hundred and sixty-five days.
That becomes the year of men; by subtracting five from those [years], it becomes the civil (sāvana) year.
The lunar year is [calculated] by subtracting eleven, while the sidereal year is [calculated] by subtracting thirty.
Cold, heat, and likewise rain are produced according to the year of men.
Sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma, marriages, festivals, and so forth,
as well as transactions such as lending at interest and whatever other things have arisen, indeed take place among all the social classes on earth according to the Sāvana [lunar] reckoning. (56)
For indeed, by means of the lunar month inclusive of the intercalary month, [the years] come to be;
however, by the measurement of the lunar mansions (nakṣatra), the stars along with their surrounding constellations differ.
In this way, gods, humans, Daityas, and others always [dwell] upon the earth.
This world thus revolves, is born, and dies;
therein, one who is shrouded by the bondage of *māyā* does not indeed reach the further shore.
Therefore, I have always [sought] Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the supreme among persons.
He is to be revered, worshipped, and meditated upon without interruption.
(1.526.60) Time devours everyone—whether in a moment, a year, or an eon.
With his hand placed upon my crest, Time desires to swallow me. (61)
Thus, endowed with such awakening and devoted to piety, King Vasu protected his own kingdom with the approval of Dharma;
he performed many great sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees.
By dedicating his actions to Hari, the Lord of gods, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa,
he pleased Him while conducting himself with many forms of servitude.
Then, after a long time, through the yoga of detachment, Vasu—
Having reached the end of the duality of desire for royal power and enjoyment,
and having consecrated his own son Vivasvat— the best among his hundred brothers—
in his own kingdom, he departed for Puṣkara.
There, where the illustrious Puṇḍarīkākṣa Nārāyaṇa shines resplendent—
there the king of Kaśmīra, Vasu, through his devotion and by means of fierce austerities he had accomplished, beheld Hari as he remembered him and saw him in his divine form. (66–67)
He praised the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the sovereign inner controller of all: "Salutations to You; O Lotus-eyed One, salutations to You!
O Universal Form, abode of all splendor, O Kṛṣṇa, salutations to You! (68)

I bow to you, O Viṣṇu, the refuge, the protector, the victorious one who dwells in the sky, the youthful Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa, the wielder of the discus. O Acyuta, I perceive nothing else whatsoever apart from you.
While he was speaking thus, a personified being indeed emerged from his body— dark blue in hue, massive and fierce, terrifying,
with red eyes and a short stature— and said, "O King, what shall I do? (71)
Vasu questioned that one who had the form of sin: "Tell me here, who are you? (72) That one in the form of sin replied: "I am indeed your sin;
O sinless one, I am not merely sin, but I am the *pāpapreta* (sin-ghost) for you. (73)
Listen, O King, to what happened previously in the Kali age: once, while you were king in the southern region, you arrived at Janasthāna for the purpose of hunting.
There, by means of your staff, [you encountered] a sage wearing the guise of a deer.
Struck on Mount Prasravaṇa, he died instantly.
Thinking that deer had been killed, just as you desired to seize it, you beheld a man in the form of a deer who was actually a brahmin. (75–76)
And you, indeed, fell into great terror because of the killing of the Mānava;
for I am that most terrible slaughter born from the destruction of a Brahmin-preta.
O King, I am Brahmagraha, and I dwelt within your body.
"Until today, O King, I have sought to afflict and devour your body.
I have beheld and enjoyed the pleasures of your kingdom, and I have always drunk your blood and eaten your fresh flesh. (78–79)

And you, O best of kings, do not appear at all emaciated by the power of your sovereignty, owing to your abundance of food, drink, and other luxuries. Now, you have reflected upon an expiation for that sin.
"O King, you have observed the pure Dvādaśī of Śrī Hari;
you have performed other vows with the thought, 'May Nārāyaṇa be pleased with me,' and likewise you have repeatedly given gifts of cows. (81–82)
Then, in the southern region, you will become ill with a pain in the belly at your own home and die; your virtuous wife, named Nārāyaṇī,
will place the nectar from the feet of Śrī Viṣṇu into your mouth.
But at the moment of death, you remembered and meditated upon your wife;
because of that, you were born again in the city of Viṣṇu for one kalpa as a youth endowed with latent impressions (vāsanā), since you were indeed deprived of liberation.
I remained there with you, dwelling indeed within your very body until the end of the kalpa, enjoying excellent pleasures while you were alive.
In that kalpa, heaven was enjoyed by you in many ways.
And, O King, by my own power I abide within you for the sake of heaven;
furthermore, I have remained in the form of a king for many years.
Then, when the conception of day has ceased and the conception of night has also passed, ||87-88||
Now, O lord of men, during the first creation in the Satya Yuga, you were born, O great king, in the house of King Sumanas;
I was born from the hair-pores of that sovereign of the land of Kaśmīra. (89)
I have dwelt here until this very day, consuming ever-new and fresh [food].
Though I performed many various sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees,
I was not liberated by them, for they were devoid of the remembrance of Viṣṇu.
And now, in Viśālā, devotion has been shown by you to Hari;
here, with a humble disposition and with your whole being, a hymn of praise has been offered.
By the power of your devotion toward the lotus-eyed one who bears the Śārṅga bow—
Hari himself, being propitiated even by the offering of his entire being,
Viṣṇu, the Lord Nārāyaṇa, dispatched his servants.
Behold them now stationed in celestial chariots within the great firmament.
Thus, struck by these maces of Viṣṇu’s attendants, I have reached destruction;
I have fallen away even from your pores.
By the power of your devotion, I have left behind my bodily hairs.
Having become one with it and being born again in the form of a hunter in your presence,
O King, I— having heard the hymn of praise to the Blessed One and through my devotion to you—
was freed from great sin even by the touch of the staff of Viṣṇu’s attendant. (96–97)
"I am liberated from the state of a preta, and I possess a righteous mind.
Therefore, O King, grant me—your own friend who has taken refuge in you, yet is now without support—a boon that bestows happiness; have mercy upon me, your devotee. (98)
Having heard this, Vasu granted a blessed boon even to the hunter:
"Listen, hunter! You have reminded me of my previous birth.
Therefore, by my boon, you shall henceforth become a Dharma-hunter."
Having spoken thus, that king, seated upon an excellent celestial chariot, went indeed to the abode of Akṣara along with the supreme Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa; thereafter,
he became an attendant of Hari.
Then this Dharmakarmā indeed became the righteous hunter (Dharmavyādha).
Thus, O Lakṣmī, has this supreme life-story of Vasu been told;
whoever reads or hears it shall obtain the fruit of bathing in sacred pilgrimage sites (tīrtha).

Thus ends the five hundred and twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of King Vasu of Kashmir’s Previous Birth as a Deer, the Departure of the Brahmin-Slaughter through the Power of Devotion, and Vasu’s Subsequent Liberation," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. Chapter 527: *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā* – Section 1 (*Kṛtayuga-santāna*) — Chapter 527.
[The Author: Chapter 528.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the life-story of Raibhya, which grants liberation from the body.
Then Raibhya, whose wealth was his asceticism, went himself to the holy Gayā. There, gratifying his ancestors with offerings of funeral cakes through supreme devotion,
he performed very great and intense penance, which is exceedingly difficult to practice.
While that wise Raibhya was performing that intense austerity,
a great yogi, exceedingly radiant, arrived seated upon a celestial chariot.
That pure celestial chariot, resembling a mote of dust and brilliant like the sun, [approached him].
There, a radiant person appeared, the size of an atom.
He said, "O Raibhya! O you of noble vows, for what purpose do you practice austerity?
Having spoken thus, that person indeed vanished into the space between heaven and earth.
Indeed, a celestial chariot was produced that pervaded both heaven and earth;
therein the wise one beheld infinite sages by means of his Indra-like power.
He saw that the chariot completely filled the world of Viṣṇu.
Then Raibhya, filled with wonder, asked him with affection:
"O great yogi, who are you? Please tell me.
The boy, whose life was but five years long, spoke to Raibhya.
"I am the younger brother of Rudra, the mind-born son of Brahmā;
by name I am Sanatkumāra, and I dwell in Janaloka.
I am indeed satisfied by your performance of rites such as those for the gratification of the ancestors."
"I have come into your presence for the purpose of bestowing words of praise.
You are always blessed, my child, the enhancer of Brahmā’s lineage;
by relying upon the Vedas, O sinless one, you always gratify the ancestors."
Sons who provide satisfaction to the ancestors through mantras, vows, recitations, fire-oblations, and the offering of funeral cakes at Gayā are true sons; others are merely born of the womb.
Listen, Raibhya! In ancient times, there was indeed a king named Viśāla.

For the sake of obtaining a son, that wise man questioned the most excellent brahmins. The brahmins said: "Go to Gayā and satisfy the ancestors with devotion through gifts of food, water, funeral cakes (piṇḍas), gifts of cows, and other offerings."
"Certainly, a son shall be born to you who will be a giver of happiness and a lord of the earth.
Then that Viśāla departed for Viśālānagara.
Under the Maghā asterism, he performed the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍadāna) to his ancestors at Gayā.
At that moment, three men arrived there in the sky.
Seeing one who was white, one who was red, and a third who was black in complexion,
he bowed to them and said, "Please take these fine lumps."
"Why are you being ignored by you? Tell me, for my curiosity is great.
Then Śveta said among them, "O son, I am your father;
I am Śveta by name, by conduct, by deed, and by lineage. (18)
"But this father of mine was lustful, cruel, and a destroyer.
His father was Kṛṣṇavarṇa by name, and by his occupation and deeds;
for in former times, many sages were slain by Kṛṣṇavarṇa."
These two, having died, have entered for a long time the hell named Avīci;

I, however, through my merits, have attained the throne of Śakra, which is so difficult to obtain. By you, the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) were offered at Gayā according to the prescribed rites with the sacred mantras.
Therefore, having been drawn out from hell and brought here, these two have been well-united.
"I shall gratify my fathers, grandfathers, and likewise great-grandfathers"—with this thought, that water was offered by you, O good son. (22–23)
Therefore, our simultaneous union has occurred here in your presence;
we accept this offering of rice-balls and water, and we are entirely satisfied.
By the power of this sacred ford, I shall go to the world of the ancestors, of this there is no doubt.

"By the offering of this funeral cake (piṇḍa), indeed, these two grandfathers of yours, though they were in a miserable state, have become purified and possessed of merit. Such is the power of a sacred ford (tīrtha); even the son of a slayer of a Brahmin [was purified] by it."
"By offering the funeral cake (piṇḍa) to one's father, one may effect his deliverance once again.
For this reason, O King, I am your white father.
I shall tell you something more, by which our liberation may indeed be achieved."
Listen to the knowledge concerning worldly existence, by which you shall attain liberation:

always rising in the morning and discarding the garments worn at night, [one should meditate upon] one's chosen deity in the lotus of the heart and likewise the Guru in the aperture of Brahmā (the crown of the head). 28–29.
Having reflected with the mind upon all morning duties, perform them all;
while bathing, cleansing, and in every ritual act, remember Hari again and again.
Having placed the Lord Supreme upon a washed cloth, worship Him.
Worship [the Lord] in a Śālagrāma stone, a gem, a yantra, an image, or even in water; also in a cow, in a brāhmaṇa, and especially in one's gurus;
as well as in a jar, an eight-petalled lotus, or a vessel smeared with sandalwood paste.
O virtuous lady, worship the Lord of Śrī in the Śālagrāma stone and within your mind; offer the sixteen articles of worship and perform devotional service repeatedly.
[Worship] Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Durgā, Rādhā, Gaṅgā, and Tulasī.
Worship always with devotion Nārāyaṇa, the unborn Śambhu, Kṛṣṇa, Vināyaka, and the Guru; worship the guest, the Sun, and the sacrificial fire;
worship your parents, the Brāhmaṇa, the virtuous, and the Sun with sincere feeling.
I tell you that they are invisible; they are not to be looked upon anywhere.
A wise person should not look at feces, for it is the very nature of the seed of disease.
Urine is likewise the seed of disease and a cause of hell.
One should not look upon the female organ—the source of sin, suffering, disease, and poverty—nor upon the male organ, which is the cause of destruction;
furthermore, one should avoid excessive indulgence, as it is the cause of diseases. (37–38)
At the time of sunset, one should not look at the sun or the moon, for that is a cause of disease.
One should not gaze upon the moon when it is eclipsed or partially risen, for that is a cause of mental anguish.
Furthermore, having seen the sun or the moon reflected in water, a person shall fall into grief.

One should not share a bed, food, or movement with a sinner; all such things are causes of destruction. [This occurs] through conversation, physical contact, sharing a bed or seat, and eating together. (1.527.40–41)
Sins committed by others certainly transfer to a person when they become manifest;
therefore, one should not go near predatory animals, as that is a cause of suffering.
One should not associate with a wicked person, for that is a cause of grief. (42)

One should not commit violence or cause harm to Brāhmaṇas, cows, Vaiṣṇavas, or virtuous people, for such acts are the cause of total destruction. This applies likewise to the gods, the deities of the gods, the twice-born, chaste women, and the righteous.
One must not seize property, goods, or wealth that is the cause of destruction;
rather, one should quickly give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), for otherwise it becomes a cause of ruin.
By committing violence against living beings, the destruction of one's lineage will certainly occur.
He who does not bow to the Lord and the Guru shall become a partaker of sin and go to hell.
That foolish woman of wicked conduct who, having treated her own husband— who is the very form of Hari—
with contempt, does not look upon him, shall fall into the Kumbhīpāka hell.
Through verbal abuse one becomes a crow; through violence, a pig;
through anger, a serpent; and through arrogance, a donkey.
Through wicked speech one becomes a female dog, and through the sight of poison, one becomes blind.
A devoted wife shall certainly go to Vaikuṇṭha together with her husband.
[One should worship] Śiva, Durgā, Gaṇapati, Sūrya, a brāhmaṇa, and a Vaiṣṇava; likewise, one's father, mother, son, virtuous wife, teacher, and husband. (1.527.50)
Having reviled a helpless sister or a maiden, one shall go to hell;
but those virtuous ones who consume the water of the Śālagrāma and the remnants of Kṛṣṇa’s offerings purify a hundred men and the entire earth.
One who eats food granted by Viṣṇu obtains the fruit of the Aśvamedha sacrifice.
Likewise, [one obtains the same fruit for giving] a radiant Śiva-liṅga, a Śālagrāma stone, a gem, an image, a sacred thread, gold, or even a conch shell. (52–53)
Having cast upon the ground a diamond, a pearl, cow urine, cow dung, clarified butter,
or the water from a *śālagrāma* stone, one shall go to the lower realms. One becomes poor, miserly, afflicted with leprosy, bereft of lineage, and even without a wife.

One who abandons these on earth shall become, in due order, a sinner: deprived of land, deprived of progeny, deprived of kinsmen, and despised; or he shall be blind, lame, dwarfed, crippled, or even lacking limbs. (55–56)
Having fashioned a *liṅga* from clay, ashes, balls of cow dung, or likewise from sand and other materials,
and having worshipped it even once, one shall dwell in heaven for a hundred *kalpas*.
Listen now as I describe the merit that accrues from the sight of those [images].
Beholding excellent Brāhmaṇas, sacred fords, Vaiṣṇavas, and virtuous persons;
likewise, beholding deities, one's parents, and one's husband;
as well as the sun, chaste women, ascetics, and celibate students—[these bring great merit]. (58–59)
Of renunciants, cows, fire, the guru, elephants,
horses, lions, cuckoos, wagtails,
parrots, swans, peacocks, blue jays, and conch-birds; (1.527.60)
Of cows accompanied by their calves, of *aśvattha* trees, and likewise of jewels;
of women possessing husbands and sons, and of people traveling to sacred fords (*tīrtha*);
of lamps, gold, pearls, and diamonds.
The sight of rubies, tulasī, and white flowers is considered meritorious,
a destroyer of sins, and a bestower of auspiciousness.
Fruits, white grains, ghee, curd, and honey [are likewise beneficial].
Upon seeing a full water-pot, parched grain, sugar, a mirror, water,
a garland of white flowers, yellow pigment (gorocana), camphor, silver, and a lake, a person shall attain merit. (64–65)
A flower garden, a place in bloom, the new moon in its bright fortnight,
nectar, sandalwood, the rising of a deity, a temple, a banner, musk, saffron, a natural pool dug by the gods, a banyan tree, and a drum.
A banner, a divine water-pot, and likewise fragrant incense;
a conch shell, a pearl-oyster, coral, silver, crystal, and *kuśa* grass;
copper, Ganges clay, an image of Viṣṇu, a book, a gem, and unbroken grains of rice.
An ascetic, a learned man, the ocean, a black antelope;
a sacrifice, a great festival, milk, cow urine, and likewise cow dung;
the dust raised by cows, a cow’s footprint, a cow-pen, and land where grain has ripened.
Having seen a beautiful, dark-complexioned lotus-like maiden, well-attired and virtuous,
one obtains merit and victory upon seeing her hand, fragrant substances, and consecrated food. Furthermore, he who offers funeral cakes at the foot of Viṣṇu and worships Viṣṇu [obtains great merit].
It effects the liberation from birth for one's ancestors as well as for oneself.
This has been told to you, O King, joyfully and as a source of merit-increasing [virtue].
Thus, by the power of merit, the intellect becomes perfectly pure.
Likewise, his devotion toward the ancestors increased within his heart. Sita, having given him extensive instructions, said: "Always worship Kṛṣṇa;
give to him the merit of the Ekādaśī fasts and the vows of the month of Kārtika. (73–74)
"Grant the fruit of the worship of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa for my liberation;
grant the merit of the Akhaṇḍa-mātrikā for my liberation.
Having been addressed thus, that king named Viśāla likewise granted the merit.
Having taken water in his hand, he released it upon the surface of the earth.
At that moment, the attendants of Viṣṇu arrived, seated in their celestial chariots, [reciting] the mantra:
"Oṃ, obeisance to the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa."
The four Vaiṣṇavas spoke here from their celestial chariot:
"May they ascend to Vaikuṇṭha, and may the attendants (pārṣadas) come as well!
Having been addressed thus, they departed for that abode at that very moment along with the attendants.
For this reason, O Raibhya, you are called blessed by me:
once in a lifetime one visits Gayā and once one offers the funeral cakes (piṇḍa), both of which are difficult to attain; yet you remain here constantly.
"O Lord Raibhya, what more can be said? This merit of yours is such that you have seen Nārāyaṇa himself, mace in hand, in person.
Having spoken thus, the eternal sage vanished right there.
Raibhya offered praise to Hari with a voice faltering with love:
"I take refuge in Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, who was white in the Kṛta age, ruddy in the Tretā age, blue in the Dvāpara age, and resembles a bee in the Kali age. (82-83)
He who exists in the supreme imperishable abode, in Goloka, or in Vaikuṇṭha—
that Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa dwells within my heart as well. To You, that omnipresent Supreme Lord residing in Lomaśavāsa, [I offer my salutations].
I bow to You and take refuge in You today for the sake of crossing over saṃsāra.
Fish and other such beings, as well as sacrifices and the like, are Your virtuous limbs and manifestations of Your power;
therefore, adorn me this very day with the circle of the Siddhas.
Thus praised, Viṣṇu then appeared, beautiful, holding the conch, discus, and mace, mounted upon Garuḍa, and moving through the sky.
He said, "O Raibhya, I am pleased; come with me."
O Lakṣmī, having mounted Garuḍa, Raibhya went to where Sanaka and the others were;
having gone there and bowed to them, he proceeded with Hari to Vaikuṇṭha,
in his divine body, into the presence of your beloved.

Whoever reads or even hears this account of Raibhya as well as of Viṣṇu, the wielder of the mace, shall obtain both worldly enjoyment and liberation. Thus ends the five hundred and twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of King Viśāla’s Liberation through Devotion to Hari, Raibhya’s Liberation through Knowledge of Reality and Devotion, and Raibhya’s Vision of Sanatkumāra and His Instruction at Gayā," in the first section, *Kṛtayugasantāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
