Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, O best of sages! Once, in the month of Kārtika, the sage Āvaṭya performed a circumambulation of Mount Raivata.
Then he dwelt for three months in the hermitage of Lomaśa,
on the shore of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake at the abode of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa. On the night of Śivarātri, he worshipped Lomaśeśvara.
When he fell asleep for a moment during the Brahma-muhūrta at dawn,
that sage named Āvaṭya beheld a dream there;
he then traveled by means of a divine vehicle to Satyaloka.
He went to the world of Viṣṇu, the world of Mahāviṣṇu, and to Kailāsa;
from there, he traveled by means of a celestial vehicle to Vaikuṇṭha.
After that, he went to Goloka, and finally, he went to the imperishable abode (akṣaradhāma).

And he went to the supreme abode, the infinite, higher than the highest, beyond the highest (6). Having gone to the Brahma-world, the most excellent of all, he beheld the Divine, glorious Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the Liberated in the Imperishable (akṣara) (7).

To Śrī Harī, who stood there before him, he spoke to Yāvaṭya: "Tell me, what have you observed throughout all the worlds? (8) [He addressed] the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, who is saluted by the liberated souls.

Āvaṭya said: "O Blessed One, whatever is indeed seen here—such a sovereign empire of happiness has not been observed anywhere else, neither in Akṣara, nor in Goloka, nor in Vaikuṇṭha, nor even in Amṛta. || 1.528.10 ||
In that truth and on that plane, no mere portion of worldly pleasure exists for you;
rather, you possess a bliss of a different nature, which bestows eternal joy and perfect satisfaction.
In the imperishable Goloka, there is an abundance of liberated souls, such as Rādhikā and others.
In Vaikuṇṭha reside Śrī, Ramā, and the others; in Satyaloka dwell the gods and other beings.
What need is there to speak of other places? For all those realms are indeed lands of enjoyment—Goloka, Vaikuṇṭha, Kailāsa, and even the imperishable abode (Akṣara-pada).
O Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, these four stages of yours have indeed been made eternal by you for the sake of the delight of your devotees;
and those devotees, in whatever manner they desire for the purpose of service, [you provide for them] in that very way.
Out of love, affection, and desire, You grant satisfaction to those in the state of servitude.
(15) The bliss of the Self within Your manifest form is distinguished by its presence in the supreme abode;
the bliss of service in the imperishable abode is distinguished even beyond that. (16)
The bliss of service is distinguished in Goloka, the bliss of friendship in Vikuṇṭha,
and the bliss of worship in Satyaloka, each according to its fitness.
Elsewhere, the bliss of sense objects is distinguished as being mixed with suffering.
O Blessed One, I have seen him here in the abode of Akṣara. And I have beheld Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Akṣara;
in Goloka, you, O Lord of Rādhikā, were seen as Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. (18-19)
In Vaikuṇṭha, you were seen as Lakṣmīśa Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa;
on Kailāsa, you were beheld as Hari himself, the Lord of Śivā, filled with the bliss of dispassion, the yogi, the wise one, and the ascetic.
In the world of truth (Satyaloka), you alone are indeed Sāvitrīśvara.
This very same golden Person who was seen by me in the sun is you;
on earth, in Kuṅkumavāpī, you are the young cowherd Kṛṣṇa.
O Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, son of Kamalā-Lakṣmī,
you reside there in the hermitage of Lomaśa, dwelling within that very temple. At times you are with Rādhā, at times with Lakṣmī, and at times with the virtuous Pārvatī.
In some places he saw the goddess Māṇikī, in others Prabhā and Ramā;
in some places Padmā, Jayā, Lalitā, Haṃsā, and Mañjulā;
and in others Padmāvatī, Satī, Vṛndā, Tulasī, and Sarasvatī.
In one place I behold Śivā by my side, the primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti); in another, the liberated Devikā, Campā, Haimī, and Śāntikā;
and in yet another, the virtuous yogin, the eternal wise one.
O Kṛṣṇa, I behold your forms; having seen them, I do not reach the further shore.
Today my birth has become fruitful, since I have reached the further shore of liberation.
Your vision is not obtained even through the merit of many kalpas.
"By your grace, O Lord of Śrī, I have obtained your vision today.
As he was saying this, Āvaṭaya’s sleep vanished at that very moment;
he beheld Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa smiling before him.
Having prostrated, the sage said: "O Lord, a dream has been seen by me.
Tell me its fruit today; what shall be my eternal reward?
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa replied: "Listen, O Āvaṭya, to that fruit."
"Your liberation shall swiftly come to pass in the presence of Lomaśa,
by the power of this sacred field of Aśvapaṭṭasara,
through the merit of the Śivarātri vow, and likewise, O Sage, by virtue of your arrival here. (32)
"Accept the mantra for liberation; may you be ready for this. 'Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine namaḥ.
Accept the tulasī garland and wear this necklace around your neck."

"Tell me whatever else you desire, and I shall grant it to you here; of this there is no doubt. Then Āvaṭya said: "Grant me liberation beyond the supreme Imperishable (akṣara), and for the sake of the welfare of all the worlds, tell me the knowledge of dreams here."
"So be it," said the Lord Hari Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
Then he spoke this knowledge at Āvaṭyā; listen to it, O beloved:
"The sight of a good dream is meritorious, provided one does not speak of it to a low person. (36–37)

Having abandoned Kāśyapa, the unfortunate, the lowly, the enemy, the ignorant, and women, as well as the night and the day, he speaks of the Brahmin as truly wise. And [he speaks of] the deity in the temple, as well as the Aśvattha, Tulasī, and Vaṭa trees.
Having spoken thus, the wise man obtains twice that merit, which is not to be disclosed, and fourfold if it remains secret;
upon seeing a good dream, he shall obtain the fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā, and he shall acquire wealth, riches, a wife, land, and a son. (1.528.39–40)
One obtains liberation, supreme sovereignty, and everything desired.
A dream occurring in the first watch of the night yields its fruit within a year;
in the second, within eight months; and in the third, within three months.
In the fourth case, a dream occurring within half a month yields its own fruit.
A dream seen at dawn yields its fruit within ten days;
however, a dream seen in the morning yields its fruit immediately if one is awakened at that very moment.
A man afflicted by anxiety or disease sees a dream;
all that is seen is fruitless, as is a dream seen during the daytime.
One who is dull-witted, oppressed by urine or feces, or overwhelmed by fear [sees dreams that are likewise ineffective].
One who is naked or has disheveled hair does not obtain the fruit arising from a dream.
Furthermore, one who falls back asleep after a dream does not obtain its fruit.
And for him who tells his dream during the night, no fruit arises.
If a person utters the name "Kāśyapa-gotra," they incur misfortune;
they go from one wretched state to another, suffer illness when in a low station, encounter fear at night, and meet with strife among fools. (47)
In the *kāminī* [dream], there will be loss of wealth, and at night there will be fear of thieves.
In the *nidrā* [dream], one experiences grief; in the *paṇḍitā* [dream], one obtains the desired fruit. O Kāśyapa, that dream must never be disclosed by a wise man.
Climbing upon cows, horses, mountains, palaces, elephants,
and trees in a dream is proclaimed to bestow wealth.
If eating, weeping, or playing the lute is seen [in a dream], it is likewise auspicious.
Or if one receives [something] in a dream, or touches ground rich with crops;
likewise, if one is pierced by a weapon or missile, or even smeared with a wound, excrement, or blood in a dream, one shall become wealthy. (51–52)
Indeed, even in a dream, approaching a woman who should not be approached brings the acquisition of a wife;
yet, if one is sprinkled with urine and drinks semen, he enters even hell.
He may enter a city of blood or drink nectar from the ocean.
He obtains auspicious news and shall acquire abundant wealth;
[he sees] an elephant, a king, gold, a bull, and even a cow;
a lamp, food, fruit, flowers, a maiden, an umbrella, a chariot, and a banner.
Having seen a family, one obtains fame and abundant prosperity;
likewise, by seeing a full water-pot, a brahmin, fire, flowers, betel, a palace,
white grain, a dancer, or a courtesan, one shall attain fortune.
Having seen the milk and ghee of cows, one obtains wealth consisting of merit.
By eating milk-rice on a lotus leaf, as well as curd, milk, ghee, honey, sweet food, and the *svastika* dish, one will certainly become a king. (57–58)
If a man eats the flesh of birds or humans,
he obtains great wealth, auspicious news, and his desired fruit.
Having obtained an umbrella, a sword, sandals, and grain, he departs.
He who crosses over water in a dream will certainly become preeminent.
Having seen a fruit-bearing tree, one will surely obtain wealth.
A man bitten by a serpent shall become a recipient of riches.
By seeing the sun and the moon in a dream, one's disease is destroyed;
by seeing a mare, a hen, or a female crane, a person shall obtain a wife.
He who is bound with fetters in a dream shall obtain high status and a son.

If one eats from a lotus leaf on a riverbank, or likewise from a lotus cup, curd-rice, or milk-pudding in a dream, he shall become a king; of this there is no doubt. If one sees a leech, a scorpion, or a snake in a dream, [the same result follows].
One obtains wealth, a son, victory, and high status;
even if one is afflicted by horned animals, fanged beasts, boars, or monkeys,
if one wears a crown upon the head in a dream, one shall become a king.
One shall obtain either abundant wealth or even a preeminent position.
(66) Upon seeing fish, meat, pearls, conch shells, sandalwood, diamonds, crystal, or silver, one shall acquire great riches. (67)
By seeing blood, one obtains gold; by eating excrement, one obtains wealth.
By seeing an image or a Śiva-liṅga, one obtains wealth and victory.
By seeing a bilva or a mango tree laden with fruit and flowers, one obtains wealth.
By beholding a blazing fire, one obtains wealth, intelligence, and prosperity.
By seeing an *āmalaka* fruit and a lotus, one becomes wealthy.
Deities, the twice-born, cows, ancestors, the virtuous, and the preceptor— [one should honor them]. (1.528.70)
Whatever a wife, a husband, a king, a virtuous woman, or chaste maidens give of their own accord even in a dream, that object will certainly be obtained.
Women wearing white garments, adorned with white garlands and unguents, [shall appear].
For one whom they embrace in a dream, prosperity and happiness come from every side.
(72) For him who embraces in a dream a woman wearing yellow garments and adorned with yellow garlands and unguents, well-being arises. (73)
Everything white is praised, except for ash, bone, and cotton; everything black is inauspicious, except for elephants, horses, cows, Brahmins, and gods.
A divine woman who smiles, O Brahmins, adorned with jewel ornaments, [is auspicious].
Whoever comes to his house certainly obtains what is dear to him.
In a dream, the Brāhmaṇa is a god, and the Brāhmaṇī is a celestial maiden— chaste, contented, smiling, and devoted to her husband.
To whomever it grants a fruit, he shall become his son;
and whatever auspicious blessing virtuous Brahmins bestow in a dream,
that very thing they speak of shall become his sovereignty.
For him whose house a satisfied Brahmin visits, prosperity indeed comes, as well as extensive fame and happiness. At every step he finds joy; he shall obtain honor and dignity. (78–79)

If, even in a dream, one should suddenly receive a fragrant [garland], there shall be gain of land for him, and his wife shall be devoted to her husband. If an elephant, taking it with its trunk, should place it upon his head—

He shall obtain a kingdom, as well as the status of an *ācārya* and the position of a *guru*. O Brahmin, that person whom a pleased Brahmin embraces in a dream shall become a bather at sacred fords (*tīrtha*), endowed with prosperity, and perfectly successful.
If a twice-born man, laughing, gives a flower to someone in a dream,
that person shall become victorious, wealthy, famous, and happy.
Having seen sacred fords and houses made of gold and jewels in a dream, [one shall likewise attain prosperity].
He who bathes at sacred fords shall indeed become wealthy and victorious.
(84) If someone gives a full water-pot to another in a dream, the recipient shall obtain a son as well as inexhaustible riches. (85)
If a beautiful courtesan, holding a *kuḍava* or an *āḍhaka* [of wine] in her hand,
comes to a man's house, he shall obtain abundant prosperity.
If a divine woman, having gone to a man's house, should void excrement, [he shall likewise attain great fortune].
There shall be gain of wealth for him, and even poverty shall depart,
if a Brāhmaṇa comes to his house together with his wife—
whether he be Śambhu accompanied by Pārvatī, or Nārāyaṇa accompanied by Lakṣmī. (87–88)
To him to whom a virtuous man, a virtuous woman, a guru, or a great teacher gives grain, a handful of flowers, or gold in a dream, prosperity shall indeed come from every direction.
A brahmin offers a pearl necklace, a garland of flowers, and sandalwood paste.
In whose house Lakṣmī and Śrī are present in every way;
and who obtains gorocana, a banner, turmeric, a stalk of sugarcane, and prepared food in a dream—for him, Śrī is present in every way. (1.528.90–91)
Whether it be a Brahmin or a Brahmin woman who places an umbrella, flowers, or white grain upon someone's head, that person will certainly become a king.
In a dream, one may be seated upon a chariot, adorned with white garlands and unguents.

"He who eats curd or milk-porridge in a dream shall indeed become a king. (93) "Or, O Brahmins, that Brahmin to whom another Brahmin gives nectar, ghee, or curd in a dream, using a golden vessel or the like, he too will certainly become a king. (94)
And a young girl eight years of age, adorned with jewel ornaments—
if she appears in one's dream and is pleased, that person shall become a learned poet.
If she gives him a book, he shall indeed become a sovereign among scholars.
If she teaches like a mother, he shall become a scholar of universal renown;
if a Brahmin teaches him like a father, he too shall become Bṛhaspati.
He who obtains a book in a dream shall become a celebrated scholar.
In a dream, if a Brahmin gives him a mantra as well as an image, that person— whether a Brahmin, a poet, a king, or one possessing wealth— shall become accomplished in mantras, virtuous, and wealthy,
provided he receives the blessing of the Brahmin. (98)

If a Brahmin, being well-pleased, gives to a person land filled with crops and grain in a dream, he shall certainly become a lord of the earth. If, in a dream, a Brahmin places one upon a chariot and shows him heaven and other such realms...
May he be long-lived, a long-enduring master of wealth;
and may that Brahmin, being well-pleased, bestow his daughter upon him.
In dreams, he shall always become a lord of the earth, rich in riches.
Having clearly seen a lake, the ocean, a river, or a stream in a dream;
or having seen a white serpent or a white mountain, one shall obtain prosperity.
Whomever one sees dead in a dream, that person shall become long-lived.

A healthy person, upon seeing a sick man, or one who is suffering, upon seeing one who is happy, should likewise [behave]. And he whom a divine woman declares in a dream, saying, "You shall be my lord," and who awakens having seen this, will certainly become a king.
But having seen Kālikā in a dream and received a crystal rosary,
a rainbow, or Śakra’s thunderbolt, he shall certainly attain stable consecration.
Furthermore, whatever brahmin says in a dream, "Become my servant," [he shall likewise attain it].
Having attained service to Hari and devotion, he becomes a true Vaiṣṇava.
In his dreams, the Brahmin may see Hari, Śambhu, Brahmā, Brahmāṇī, Kamalā, or Śivā;
or a fair-complexioned woman who is either the Mother of the Gods, Jāhnavī, or Sarasvatī.
A cowherd woman, a virtuous lady, a maiden, or a devoted wife—
when she is seen to be very gracious and bestowing her blessings,
the one who beholds her becomes like a deity, or a king, or a most excellent teacher. (108–109)
"Thus, O Āvaṭya, the fruit arising from this auspicious dream has been told to you here.
Having seen me, Nārāyaṇa, in a dream, one shall attain liberation.
Āvaṭya said: "O Blessed One, ten kalpas have passed for me."
"By the power of Lomaśa, having attained the fruit of your yoga, I shall today depart for your eternal abode. Having spoken thus, he, with a divine body, took refuge in Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa. || 112 ||
Having ascended the divine vehicle, he went to the abode of the Imperishable. O Lakṣmī, by hearing or reciting [this], a person shall become liberated while living.

Thus ends the five hundred and twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of how the Sage named Āvaṭya attained liberation after hearing the fruits of auspicious dreams as declared by Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa following his vision of various abodes in a dream," within the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
← Chapter 528: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga) Chapter 529 [Author: Chapter 530 →
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī! I shall describe those whose sight brings sin—a bad dream, the seed of evil, and a cause of obstacles alone. (1)
One who kills a cow, one who kills a Brahmin, one who is ungrateful, as well as one who is crooked;
one who harms the gods, one who harms his father or mother, a sinner, and a betrayer of trust;
one who gives false testimony, and likewise one who deceives a guest— [these are those who must be avoided].
One who steals the property of gods or Brahmins, one who seizes a field, (3) one who destroys an *aśvattha* tree, one who destroys a grove, one who reviles the gods,
one who hates holy men, one who is full of envy, one who is ill-behaved, and a temple-priest (*devala*)— (4) [these are to be avoided].
One with a severed nose, one devoid of devotion to her husband, an unchaste woman, a widow, an angry person, a wicked man, one burdened by debt,
one born of adultery, a thief, a liar, and the moon or sun eclipsed by Rāhu.
Having seen [the moon], one should perform a bath and also recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times.
In the month of Bhādrapada, during both the bright and dark fortnights, the moon that has set is not to be seen;
the moon that has risen on the fourth lunar day is never to be looked upon.
If a person sees the moon stealing the stars, he incurs an exceedingly unbearable stain;
he must offer it to that observer if he looks intentionally.
If he sees it unintentionally, the man should drink water purified by mantras.

"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, who is stainless, the remover of the moon's spot, and the proclaimer of the purity of the stars. With this mantra, one should then drink the well-purified water. (1.529.10)
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
Why is the sun, when seized by Rāhu, not to be looked upon, and likewise the moon? O abode of the ocean of compassion, dispel this doubt of mine in this matter. (11)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Once, filled with great curiosity and accompanied by Reṇukā, the delighted Jamadagni went to the bank of the Narmadā.
In a secluded place during the day, he engaged in sexual enjoyment with his wife— not out of his own desire, but according to her wish and for her satisfaction.
Then Sūrya, the witness of dharma and knower of righteousness, spoke to the sage.
You are yourself a knower, a performer of dharma, and the great-grandson of Brahmā.
(14) You are a man of great austerity, radiant, a celibate student, and one of excellent vows;
how indeed can you abandon dharma by engaging with a woman during the day? (15)
"I am the witness of those who abide by dharma; therefore, I speak this to you.
Having taken hold of his anger, the copper-eyed one spoke to Sūrya:
"For those of great splendor, there is no fault, just as for fire which consumes all things."

How was it that you embraced Saṃjñā, the mare, during the day, from whose nostrils the two Aśvins were born as sons? For if a young woman, consumed by desire, seeks out a lover, she will surely wish for such a thing. (17–18)
"May the fire of her passion be extinguished"—this was the great bull-like desire of her husband.
"Who are you, a preacher of dharma to me? Go back to your own place!
Today, in this secluded spot, you have thwarted my desire."
"By my curse, you shall become evil-sighted and eclipsed by Rāhu.
Because you have become arrogant through your own splendor, your radiance shall be destroyed;
covered by clouds and diminished in luster, may you likewise become one who is evil-sighted."
Thus cursed, Ravi spoke to the brahmin, the bull among sages:
"Forgive me; you are a pure Vaiṣṇava, so practice your own dharma.
Just as I have been cursed by you, so too have you been cursed by me."
"O lord of the twice-born, you shall be defeated by a kṣatriya;
your death shall also come at the hand of a kṣatriya’s weapon.
Jamadagni said to Ravi: 'You shall be struck down by Śambhu.'"
There, the Creator of the Universe himself performed the removal of the curse:
"O Jamadagni! Even though you have committed a killing, you shall have a place among the sages in heaven;
may my life-span be yours, be peaceful, and be happy."
Then, on a certain day at dawn, Brahmā said to Sūrya:
"Even when covered by clouds, you shall immediately become visible and be released;
yet during years of deficient or excessive rainfall, you shall be seized by Rāhu. (27)
At the time of the *aṣṭakā* when the sky is covered by clouds, and also when the sun is at the meridian in the water, and at the moment it has half-risen—you shall be visible to sinners;
otherwise, you shall be visible to the virtuous at all times. (28–29)
"You were defeated by Śambhu in the battle with Mālin and Sumālin;
having returned again to heaven, O best one, you shall obtain victory—do not grieve.
Then he spoke again to Jamadagni: "O son, even at the time of your death..."
"Nārāyaṇa shall become your son through his own portion;
by his prowess as well, your fame shall be eternal.
Having spoken thus and dismissed the two of them, Brahmā returned to Satyaloka.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, the disappearance of the Sun was described at that time.
On the fourth day of the month of Bhādrapada, the Moon, driven by lust, abducted Tārā.
The chaste Tārā, being free from desire, cursed him in her anger.

"Today you have touched the wife of your guru; therefore, on that day, you shall indeed become visible to all as a source of defilement. Like one seized by Rāhu or obscured by a cloud, you shall become visible to the wicked."
Having said, "Become stained," she spoke thus to Kāma:
"You shall be reduced to ashes by some radiant being.
Therefore, from that time forward, the Moon has been visible as a stain on that lunar day.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, the cause of the manifestation of sin has been told.
I shall now describe to you the bad dream that indeed yields evil fruit:
he who laughs with joy in a dream, or if he sees a wedding; || 38 ||
For one whose teeth ache while walking about and who sees them moving, dancing, singing, and performing desired acts, ruin is certain;
he shall suffer loss of wealth as well as physical affliction.
If a maiden departs from someone's house taking a water-pot,
or if his own wife, filled with anger, leaves her own abode—
even in a dream— there will be the destruction of fortune and poverty for the one who sees this.
If one who has been anointed with oil should travel toward the southern direction, mounted upon a donkey, a camel, or a buffalo, his death is certain; of this there is no doubt.
In a dream, [seeing] the *japā* flower, the *aśoka*, or the *karavīraka* on the ear—
If he sees salt or oil, misfortune will surely befall him.
Having seen a naked woman, a black woman, one with a severed nose, a female servant, or a widow,
or having seen cowrie shells or palm fruits, he shall experience grief.
If one sees an angry Brāhmaṇa or a Brāhmaṇī woman full of wrath in a dream,
there will be misfortune as well as the departure of Lakṣmī.
Likewise, [seeing] wild flowers, red flowers, or a Palāśa tree in bloom [portends the same].
Upon seeing cotton or white cloth, one shall experience suffering.
(46) Having seen in a dream a woman dressed in black garments who is singing and laughing, or a black widow, one shall meet with death. (47)
Where deities dance, sing, and laugh; where they clap their hands and run—there indeed death shall occur.
[48] Vomit, urine, and feces; a physician, silver, and gold.
Whether in a dream or in direct perception, the observer shall live for ten days.
A woman dressed in black garments, wearing a black garland, and adorned with black ointments and the like— whoever she embraces, his death shall be certain.
He who acquires a necklace of bones belonging to one whose children have died, or to a shaven-headed man, or to a deer or a human, meets with certain misfortune.
He who, being alone, mounts a chariot yoked with donkeys and camels, [meets with certain misfortune].
Even while staying there, death remains watchful over him for ten days.
If he is anointed with clarified butter, milk, honey, buttermilk, or even jaggery, he will experience extreme suffering. (52–53)
If one embraces in a dream a woman adorned with red garments, red garlands, and red unguents, illness will certainly befall that person.
Likewise, [dreaming of] fallen nails and hair, or a funeral pyre covered in ashes, [bodes ill].
Having seen the embers of nirvāṇa, one certainly meets with death.
Having seen a cremation ground, dry wood, a clod of earth, dry grass, something slightly black, a horse, or a śamī tree, one becomes a partaker of extreme suffering. (55–56)
Upon seeing a sandal, a wooden board, a red flower-garland, or something terrifying;
or upon seeing a black gram, a lentil, or a mung bean, one immediately becomes wounded.
[Or] a bracelet, a lizard, a crow, a bear, a monkey, or a cow.
One who sees pus or bodily filth in a dream will become afflicted by disease.

[Likewise, one who sees] a broken vessel, a wounded person, a Śūdra, a leper with oozing sores, a sick man, one dressed in red garments, a matted-haired ascetic, a pig, a buffalo, or a donkey. (58–59)
Having seen a most terrible darkness, a corpse, a living being that inspires fear, a vulva, or a phallus in a dream, one shall meet with calamity; likewise,
seeing one of foul appearance, a barbarian, or the terrifying messengers of Yama.

Seeing those with nooses and weapons in their hands, one quickly meets death. If a Brahmin, a Brahmin woman, a son, a child, a daughter, or a young girl laments in anger during a dream, the observer shall encounter suffering. (61–62)
Upon seeing a black flower, a garland of such flowers, grain, one bearing weapons or missiles,
or a barbarian of deformed appearance, one shall meet death. Upon seeing a dead body, a corpse whose life has departed, one shall meet death.
Indeed, he who sees fish and the like will suffer the death of a brother;
likewise, upon seeing instrumental music, dancing, singing, a singer dressed in red garments, or a mṛdaṅga drum being played, one shall encounter sorrow. (64–65)
Having seen a severed head, or a headless trunk, deformed with disheveled hair,
quickly performing a dance, one shall meet death.
Or [seeing] a dead man or a dead woman, or fearsome dark-skinned barbarians.
If one embraces someone in a dream, or if that person embraces him,
or likewise if he sees his own corpse, he should know that death is imminent. Furthermore, for one whose teeth are shattered and whose hair falls out, [death is near].

For him, there shall be loss of wealth and bodily affliction at every step. Those with horns and those with fangs, as well as children, humans, and the members of his household, will cause him distress in dreams. (69)
Likewise, he may have other servants, and there may be fear for him from the royal family.
Seeing a tree being cut down and falling, a shower of stones, chaff, or razors,
or seeing red embers and a shower of ashes, one shall experience suffering.
Upon seeing a house collapsing, a falling mountain, a terrifying comet,
or even a man with a broken shoulder, people become distressed.
[One should likewise avoid] [falling] from a tree, a mountain, a chariot, a house, a cow, an elephant, a horse, or from the sky.
For one who falls to the ground in a dream, misfortune is certain.
Those who fall from a height into pits filled with ashes and charcoal,
or into alkaline pits and powders, will surely meet their death.
If a wicked person forcibly seizes a parasol or even a turban from a Kāt,
there will be the destruction of his father, or of his teacher, or of the king. If a cow, accompanied by her calf, leaves someone's house in fear, [misfortune follows].
Prosperity and the proud Earth herself depart from his home;
for him who is bound by the noose of Yama and led away by the messengers of Yama,
or by barbarians, thieves, or others, death has arrived at his very side.
Whether it be an astrologer, a Brahmin, a Brahmin woman, a virtuous preceptor, or a holy man, if such a person becomes angry and pronounces a curse, calamity will surely befall him.
Furthermore, cocks, crows, and bears are his enemies and adversaries.
If these fall upon his body after returning, death is indeed certain.
(79) Likewise, buffaloes, bears, camels, pigs, and donkeys—if they run in anger toward someone in a dream, that person will certainly become ill. (80)
Whoever offers oblations of red sandalwood wood smeared with clarified butter while reciting the Gāyatrī a thousand times, by that act peace is ordained.
Whatever may be inauspicious for oneself, if it should be seen in a dream—
That which causes undesirable results for him becomes desirable, and that which causes desirable results [becomes undesirable].
By chanting the names of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, one attains freedom from sin;
at that time, an evil dream will no longer be capable of yielding its fruit.
By chanting the names of Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Rāma, Śrī Hari, Śiva, Śrī,
Lakṣmī, Rādhikā, Jānakī, Prabhā,
and Pārvatī— these twelve— one’s bad dreams become productive of good results.
"Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ, salutations to you, Durgā, the destroyer of suffering, svāhā. (85) Having recited this mantra ten times, an evil dream becomes auspicious.
Through a hundred lakhs of recitations, it becomes perfected and bestows the desired success. (86)
One should recite "Oṃ, salutation to Mṛtyuñjaya, svāhā" one hundred thousand times.
Even upon seeing death in a dream, the reciter shall become a centenarian.
Facing east or north, one should relate the dream to a wise, pure Brahmin.

One should reveal the dream to the guru, the deity, divine persons, or one who will grant its fruit. One may also reveal it to an *aśvattha* tree, an astrologer, a Brahmin, at the seats of the ancestors and deities, to a noble woman, a Vaiṣṇava, a friend, or to one’s husband. (88–89)

"O Kāśyapa, one should not describe a dream to one who is in a miserable state, of low birth, a reviler of gods and Brahmins, a fool, dull-witted, ignorant, or cruel. Thus, O Lakṣmī, has this been told for the benefit of the world.
It brings merit, fame, and long life through both recitation and even hearing.

(91) Thus ends the five hundred and twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Curse Occurring When the Sun and Moon Were Occasionally Invisible, and the Description of Bad Dreams, Their Results, and Their Prevention," in the first section, the *Kṛtayugasantāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīyasaṃhitā*.
Chapter 529. *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇasaṃhitā*—Section 1 (*Kṛtayugasantāna*).

Chapter 531 → Śrī Lakṣmī said:
"Tell me for my benefit the vow regarding the various duties to be performed by human beings, so that the arising of liberation may occur. Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Non-violence is the highest virtue in every respect; it is the vow that bestows merit upon all.
It is considered the supreme giver of merit, providing satisfaction to the self.
In whatever way possible, one should grant happiness and contentment to living beings.
Through body, mind, speech, action, and likewise through material offerings,
(3) blessings are obtained, as well as spiritual welfare, liberation, and prosperity.
Likewise, bathing, meditation, my worship, the offering of food, and service (4).
People should always perform acts of service to others and practice contentment;
by eating what is offered as the grace of Viṣṇu, a person becomes liberated while living.
Having received the mantra of Viṣṇu and having performed service to the guru, [one attains this state].
Having meditated upon the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa, one shall attain the state of liberation.
(6) One must constantly perform the worship and nourishment of one's gurus;
indeed, among all those worthy of veneration, one’s own father is the greatest guru. (7)

A mother is a hundred times more venerable than a father; a deity is a hundred times more venerable than a mother; a teacher who imparts the mantra is four times more venerable than a deity; indeed, a teacher who bestows liberation is even more so.
A teacher who grants both knowledge and liberation is a hundred times more venerable than one who merely grants liberation.
The Guru is the manifest Lord of lords; the Guru is the Lord Nārāyaṇa.
To that divine Guru, who is heard of in the Śruti, offerings are given during the ritual invocation (uddeśa).
One’s own Guru is the manifest enjoyer, the embodied Janārdana himself.

The Guru is Brahmā, the Guru is Viṣṇu, and the Guru himself is Śiva. Indeed, all the gods always dwell joyfully within the venerable Guru. When the Guru is pleased, Hari is pleased; through him, the deities are satisfied.
The Vaiṣṇava teacher, Nārāyaṇa, brings about the attainment of Śrī Hari.
(12) A Brāhmaṇa who is a perpetual Vaiṣṇava and a liberated teacher is equal to the gods;
by drinking the water from his feet, living beings are indeed purified from sin. (13)
One who eats the food granted by Viṣṇu makes the earth sacred;
at the end, he rejoices in Vaikuṇṭha together with Hari as his attendant. Therefore, one should take refuge in Him and likewise receive the mantra from Him.
By the mere reception of the mantra, one becomes liberated while living (jīvanmukta).
That pure person may effortlessly uplift a thousand men—[he] whose actions are directed toward the station of Viṣṇu and whose intentions are offered unto Him. (15–16)
That very Śrī Hari alone is to be known; I have no one dearer than Him.
One should never receive a mantra from a person who is impoverished or devoid of devotion.
It should be understood that meat is entirely forbidden to me, as is anything offered without the *naivedya*.
Even if it were equal to nectar, that is proclaimed as unfit for consumption.
For in the past, the Dharma-vyādha, knowing his daughter to be pure, gave her indeed to that Mātaṅga, the son of a Mātaṅga, who was a twice-born (dvija). || 18–19 ||
"Great good fortune will come to my daughter in the house of Pavitra.
Having reflected thus, she was given [in marriage]; however, one day, her mother-in-law spoke this to her again: "O daughter of a hunter! O daughter of a killer!"
"Do you know what the duty of dharma is, you impure one! You quarrelsome woman!
(21) Having heard this, the girl went toward her father.
"O son of a hunter! she said to me; and thus my mother-in-law spoke again and again. (22)
The hunter went to his son-in-law’s house and spoke of the onset of happiness.
His mother-in-law provided him with food, though it was not offered to the gods.
There, neither the worship of the deities nor the purification of the food was observed. (23)
The Vaiśvadeva offering was not performed, nor was a guest honored.
Water was not even strained, nor was clarified butter offered into the fire.
The Vyāhṛtis were not recited there, and indeed, no ritual bathing was observed in the house.
He was indeed a consumer of cow-fodder and a consumer of spirits; for even though he had been made a son-in-law, he performed neither the glorification of the gods nor likewise the bowing to the sun.
In his mother-in-law’s house, he certainly did not perform the rites for the gods or the ancestors, even with her own provisions.
Having observed all that, the girl’s father, sitting at the place for the Lord’s meal,
said: "I must certainly not accept this,
because her food is said to be meat, which is not offered to the God."
And water is equal to the nectar of the Goddess Vāruṇī only when it is apart from the nectar of the Lord’s feet;
therefore, O Lord, I must not partake of your food.
For I gave away my daughter only after recognizing your auspicious household as a true abode of Dharma.
That [food] was indeed given for the sake of liberation, and certainly not for the purpose of sin.
In that [state], there is no twilight prayer, recitation, meditation, worship of the gods, or offering; that food is like meat, and water is like wine.
"Unknowingly, I have cast my daughter directly into hell.
My purity comes always from your house, born of the offerings made to the deity;
indeed, I never eat without first offering it to the deity."
"That you are called the 'Hunter's Daughter'—this speech of yours is certainly not true.
Indeed, a hunter who is devoid of offerings to Hari is truly called a 'hunter' [in the literal sense].
Therefore, you, Maṅgala, are considered a hunter, being one who has abandoned the duties of a Brahmin. (33–34)
Even though I am a hunter by birth, I am not a hunter at all in my actions.
You, however, are always like a great hunter by your deeds.
I will not send my daughter back to your home when you return.
Having spoken thus, the Vaiṣṇava hunter, the king of devotees, departed for his home.
Having offered everything to Kṛṣṇa, he partook of the food, water, and so forth.
Therefore, O Lakṣmī, whatever is offered to Me by people of all castes shall be auspicious.
Divine food that grants liberation— such as water, leaves, petals, and the like—
is always fit to be eaten by Brāhmaṇas, as is sacrificial food (haviṣya) free from meat.
By abandoning meat, one becomes possessed of splendor like that of the sun.
One who eats without first offering [to the deities] becomes a consumer of liquor and meat.
One should always offer the *śrāddha* and indeed offer water to the ancestors and the gods.
Mother, father, teacher, wife, disciple, son, sister, and daughter—[these are the ones to whom offerings should be made].
Those who are helpless, those belonging to the paternal lineage, those who must be constantly supported, and those dear to their gurus—for by supporting them, Kṛṣṇa, the inner self, is truly pleased.
Whatever exists belongs entirely to Kṛṣṇa; I am not the doer of these actions.
One should constantly contemplate in this manner through action, mind, and speech.
All actions should be offered up as an oblation that cuts away prior karma.
Having deliberated upon what is fit and unfit to be consumed, one should perform the action that severs the bonds of karma.
One should not drink milk from an iron vessel, nor consume cow products, cooked food,
items such as those from a frying pan, jaggery, honey, coconut water,
or any fruit or root whatsoever from an iron vessel.
Food that has been burnt, excessively heated, left over from another's meal, or stale;
intoxicants; food produced from the injury of living beings; and whatever belongs to another; coconut water kept in a bronze vessel; and honey kept in a copper vessel—[these are forbidden]. (45–46)
In the month of Māgha, [one should avoid] cow's products kept in a copper vessel, all types of liquor except for clarified butter,
milk mixed with salt, honey, oil, jaggery, and clarified butter;
as well as water remaining after drinking and radish in the month of Bhādrapada, along with curd.
One should never consume liquids that have been passed from hand to hand.

One should not eat camphor placed in a silver vessel if it has been touched by one who is impure. [One should avoid the meat] of predatory beasts, of female dogs, of female pigs, of female yaks, and of forest-dwelling animals. 48–49.

One should never consume the milk of does, female monkeys, and female bears, nor that of mares, female camels, female elephants, female donkeys, and female gavayas; likewise, one should not eat the milk and other products of female rhinoceroses and female leopards.
Unstrained milk, water, buttermilk, oil, ghee, and so forth;
whatever is not offered to Hari and whatever is unfit for consumption;
honey mixed with ants; and cow-derived products such as molasses and juice—[all these are forbidden]. (51–52)
Food fit for birds, food fit for insects, and pure ripe fruits and the like are edible;
however, that which is fit for crows is inedible, even if it is a substance suitable for all.
[This applies to] what is cooked in ghee, cooked in oil, or cooked solely by fire.
If food ripened by the sun or ripened by time should be pure, it may be eaten.
One should discard all impure water and food;
for eating what is unfit to be eaten, one should perform purification through the vow of reciting the name of Kṛṣṇa.

But as for action that is auspicious or inauspicious, there is no destruction of it without experience [of its fruit]. An evil deed is never destroyed by a good deed, nor is a good deed destroyed by an evil action. (56)
However, through merit, the power of sin is brought to exhaustion.
(57) Merit arises from [the exhaustion of] power, and in some cases, sin [arises] from merit;
yet, when there is the disposition of offering to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, no new object of experience is produced. (58)
Heaven is attained through virtuous deeds alone, and hell through wicked deeds;
liberation is not achieved by mere ritual action, but rather through service to Me.
That karma which is offered as an oblation into the fire of knowledge is reduced to ashes.
Or rather, whatever invocation is directed toward me, that shall grant the fruit of liberation.
Listen to how the birth of people arises from sin;
I shall describe that birth which occurs following the punishment of Yama.
The killer of a cow becomes a venomous serpent, and the cow itself becomes a *cāṇḍāla*.
Having become a worm in excrement as a killer of a Brahmin, one then becomes a barbarian and blind.
The killer of a woman is seized by consumption (*yakṣman*), and the dog becomes utterly impoverished.
One who kills an embryo shall subsequently become a dog and likewise a horse;
one who kills a man shall become a lordly elephant, and thereafter a Kirāta hunter.
One who kills a cock shall become a dog, and one who kills a cat shall become a cat.
One who kills a snake becomes a snake; one who kills an elephant becomes a horse;
and one who kills small creatures is born as a small creature.
One who destroys an *aśvattha* tree becomes a *śālmali* tree, and thereafter becomes a *śūdra*.
One who gives false testimony, an ungrateful person, or one excessively ungrateful;
a betrayer of trust and a slayer of friends, shall become a vulture again and again.
Having become a pig and then a beast of prey, he is thereafter born as a Śūdra.
One who steals clothing, one who steals cattle, and one who steals silver or pearls,
having become a crane, shall thereafter become a Śūdra and then a leper.
One who steals from the treasury, one who steals fruit, and one who steals wealth becomes a Yakṣa.
Having become a blue jay, one shall thereafter become a Śūdra.
One who steals cooked food will take birth as a musk deer;
a stealer of grain will become a miser; and a stealer of gold will suffer from leprosy.
One who dies in a state of anger becomes a donkey, a crab, a snake, or a crow;
a thief of iron is born without a lineage, while a thief of ink becomes a cuckoo.
A thief of collyrium becomes a parrot, and a thief of sweets becomes a worm.
One who hates Brahmins and one who hates their gurus shall become a worm in the head.
One who steals red substances shall be afflicted with blood disorders.
One devoid of proper conduct becomes a barbarian, and a violent person becomes lame.

One who is full of ego becomes earless; one who reviles the scriptures becomes deaf; one who steals words becomes mute; and a violent person becomes hairless. A speaker of falsehood becomes beardless; and one who utters wicked speech becomes toothless. (74)
One who steals truth becomes tongueless; a thief of books shall become dull-witted.
A stealer of horses, moreover, is born again as a horse; thereafter he becomes a base mule. A stealer of elephants shall become an elephant. (75–76)
A thief of a goat becomes a goat; a stealer of gifts becomes a barbarian (mleccha).
One who eats sweets alone becomes a fly or an ant.
A thief of oil becomes an oil-presser; a thief of liquids becomes a turmeric-seller.
A person who gives unwholesome medicine shall become a snake-catcher.
A woman who is unchaste shall become a lizard, a jackal, or a female bear;
one who destroys a pond shall become a species of crocodile, a tortoise, or a fish. (78–79)

One who steals variegated garments shall become a peacock in forests and such places; one who steals vessels of luster shall become a *kāraṇḍava* bird for a long time. A thief of the images of the gods shall indeed become blind again and again.
One who obstructs the worship of ancestors and deities becomes a jackal that feeds on corpses.
One who hates his guru shall be poor, and one who betrays the gods shall be a hypocrite.
Furthermore, one who extinguishes lamps shall become a firefly in forest after forest.
The stealer of a cow becomes a pigeon; the stealer of a garland becomes a bird;
the stealer of grain becomes a *caraka* (a type of small bird); and the stealer of meat becomes an elephant.
Furthermore, one who causes suffering to the learned repeatedly becomes a frog.
One who hates poetry shall become a mongoose; after that, a chameleon (84).
One who sells his daughter shall repeatedly become a hunter;
one devoid of dharma shall become a beast, and after that, an oil-presser (85).
One who speaks false slanders becomes a washerman or even a mute;
one who performs malevolent magic becomes a killer or even a hungry ghost (preta);
and a false-speaking astrologer becomes a monkey or even a jester (bhāṇḍa).
Thus has been described, O Lakṣmī, the primary fruit born of ripening (vipākaja).
For one who has attachment toward desired enjoyments and aversion toward the opposite, there shall be birth again and again, resulting from karma born of ripening. 87–88.
He whose passion and hatred have departed, whose intellect is not defiled,
and who has abandoned both merit and demerit, is not bound by action.
Having realized that the senses do not function toward their own objects [as independent agents], he is not fettered.
The one who performs offerings within the Self alone is not bound by actions.
(1.530.90) He who does not conceive the thought "I am a woman" or "I am a man," but is always immersed in the state of the Self—for him, action does not cling. (91)
For one for whom suffering and pleasure, pleasure and suffering— these two pairs— have attained equality,
and who has abandoned the perception of "other-nature," action does not cling to him.
Having himself become the very form of Brahman, if he acts solely for the sake of Brahman, [he is untainted].
"Engaged in this, one abides in me, the Imperishable, and shall attain liberation.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, has the bondage of karma been described by me;
from reading or hearing this, the cutting away of karma occurs.

Thus ends the five hundred and thirtieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Duties of Man in the Kṛta Yuga Lineage, the Becoming of Hunters by Those Who Eat the Non-Consecrated Food of Hari under the Disguise of a Hunter’s Daughter, the Specification of Forbidden Foods, and the Demonstration of Birth and Other Results Arising from the Ripening of Karma Consisting of Sinful Fruits," in the first section, the Kṛta Yuga Lineage, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
[Chapter 531] *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā* – Section 1 (Kṛta Yuga Lineage), Chapter 531.
[The Author: Chapter 532.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, once upon a time at the beautiful Aśvapaṭṭasara lake.
The sages joyfully arrived at the Kuṅkumavāpikā field on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kārttika, for the sake of celebrating the Jayantī festival of Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa;
others who dwell on Mount Raivata also came.
By way of the sky, blazing with the splendor of Brahman,
Pulaha, Pulastya, Kratu, Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, Pracetas,
Vasiṣṭha, Durvāsas, and Kaṇva, together with their disciples, arrived.
Kātyāyana and Pāṇini, Kaṇāda and likewise Gautama; Sanaka, Sananda, and the sage Sanātana;
as well as Kapila, Āsuri, Vāyu, and Pañcaśikha. (4–5)
Viśvāmitra, Vālmīki, Kaśyapa, Parāśara, Vibhāṇḍaka, Marīci, Śukra, Atri, Bṛhaspati,
Gārgya, Vātsya, Vātsyāyana, Vyāsa, and likewise Jaimini.
Mitavāk, Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, Yājñavalkya, and Maṅkaṇa;
Saubhari, Śuddhajaṭila, Bharadvāja, Subhadraka;
Mārvaṇḍeya, Bagadāda, Āsuri, and Viṭaṃkaṇa. (7–8)
Aṣṭāvakra, Śatānanda, Vāmadeva, and Bhāguri;
Saṃvarta, Utathya, Nara, and likewise Nārada;
Jābāli, Paraśurāma, Agastya, and Paila as well.
Śālāyana, Gauramukha, Upamanyu, Śrutaśravas,
Maitreya, Cyavana, Vararuci, Suparṇaka,
Svayamprakāśa, Viśvātman, Sāyaṇa, and Pippalāyana. (1.531.10–11)
These and other eminent leaders gathered for the great festival.
Seeing them, Lomaśa rose up at once, saluted them with palms joined in reverence,
and seated them upon beautiful seats of kusha grass.
He honored him according to the prescribed rites, beginning with inquiries after his welfare.
In the meantime, a mass of light illuminating all directions, the eternal one, descended from the sky.
Within that splendor appeared the lovely Kumāra, with a golden radiance, appearing as if five years of age; he entered into the midst of the assembly.
All the sages, including Lomaśa, Nārada, and the others, bowed down to him.
And they offered a welcome to their brother, the eldest of all, the yogi.
The Blessed Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa likewise extended a welcome.
Then the Blessed Lord Sanatkumāra spoke to those sages.
"May there be constant welfare for you, O sages; may your desired fruit of asceticism be attained.
An inquiry after one's well-being is fruitless when directed toward Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
At present, your welfare is established by the very sight of the Supreme Self."
Now, having manifested solely for the purpose of removing the burden [of the earth],
Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa spoke to that yogi, the sage,
offering the desired inquiry after his welfare regarding his embodied self and also concerning Śrī Hari.
The blessed Sanatkumāra said to Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa:
"O Lord, misfortune indeed arises within a material body;
therefore, it is always appropriate for embodied beings to inquire after one's welfare. (21)
In the case of the eternal body, which is the very embodiment of well-being, an inquiry after welfare is meaningless.
(22) The bodies of living beings who have performed conditioned actions arise from drops of blood;
however, this is certainly not the case for Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, whose actions are unconditioned. (23)

How can an inquiry after welfare be addressed to Hari, who is the Lord of Nature (Prakṛti), the Sovereign of the Imperishable (Akṣara), whose nature is eternal, and who is the cause of all incarnations—
[an inquiry] made in that forest of eternal bliss? || 24 ||
Indeed, your body never at any time depends upon blood or semen;
rather, you are seen in a divine form solely through your grace toward devotees. By taking refuge in you, living beings shall always possess well-being. (25–26)
O Blessed One, you are blessed and worthy of honor even by the worlds, for by the touch of whom devotees attain a divine state such as yours.
You are the Lord of all lords; there is nothing beyond you in the universe.
Having thought thus, he bowed again and worshipped with devotion Śrīpati,
Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the sustainer of the imperishable realm (Akṣara).
In the meantime, Brahmā arrived together with Sāvitrī.
Śambhu arrived together with Pārvatī, and Dharma came accompanied by his own form (Mūrti).
Ananta was joined by the female Nāgas, and Sūrya was accompanied by Saṃjñā.
The Moon was joined by Rohiṇī, and the Lord of the Gods (Indra) was joined by Śacī.
The Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, the guardians of the quarters (Dikpālas), and other deities,
as well as Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa himself, rose up suddenly with devotion and performed a grand reception, offering the madhuparka and other honors. (3.1–3.2)
Then all the sages bowed to the gods, and the gods in turn bowed to the sages; they worshipped Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the illustrious Puruṣottama.
Then Sanatkumāra, seated upon his throne, spoke in the assembly.
I have seen the supreme abode, yet Puruṣottama has not been seen.
(34) The imperishable realm has been beheld, yet the Lord of the Imperishable has not been seen.
Goloka has indeed been seen by me, yet the Lord of Rādhikā has not been seen. (35)
Then Vaikuṇṭha was seen, but the Lord of Śrī-Ramā was not seen;
then the Ocean of Milk was seen, yet Hari himself was not there.
Exhausted and despondent, he bathed on the shore of the Ocean of Milk.
There, upon that vast expanse, I beheld a tortoise many yojanas in size.
"You are blessed! I said to him; he replied to me, "I am not blessed.
Blessed is the Ocean of Milk, wherein dwell creatures such as I. (37–38)
Then I offered words of praise to Sāgara.
The Ocean said to me: "I am not the recipient of these words of praise;
rather, the Earth, the sustainer of the world, is the recipient of praise. (39)
Where the seven oceans always dwell within the span of a single finger-breadth (vitastika),
I then offered my praise to the Earth.
But the Earth said to me, "I am not the recipient of this praise."
The worthy recipient of my thanks was Śeṣa Ananta, who is my very seat;
upon his hood rest infinite cosmic eggs as if they were a mere atom.
Therefore, I have indeed offered my gratitude to Ananta.
Ananta said to me: "I am not the recipient of this praise.
The great tortoise, my own support, is the true recipient of this praise;
upon his back dwell countless beings like me. (43–44)
Then I offered words of praise to the tortoise.
The tortoise said to me: "I am not the proper ground for words of praise;
indeed, the water where I dwell is the true ground for such praise. (45)
“O sage, there are indeed crores of tortoises like me in the waters.
Therefore, I offered my thanks to the great waters.
But the waters said to me, ‘O sage, we are not worthy of thanks; [the one who is worthy] is he who... (46–47)
"The recipient of this praise is the one of great splendor who dwells in the waters;
therefore, I have offered my gratitude to that embodiment of great splendor.
And Mahātejas said to me: "The recipient of this praise is indeed the Great Wind."
And it was fitting that I should have joined Vāyu with words of praise;
for it is upon him that the infinite spheres of creation indeed float.
Vāyu said to me, "O Lord, I am not worthy of such praise."
Indeed, the recipient of praise is the empty sky;
I offered my words of thanks to the sky, and the sky said to me:
"I am not praiseworthy, for I am inert space, subject to birth and destruction."
The sky of consciousness is the object of my gratitude, for from it my birth and destruction arise in every creation;
I am but a single portion of that [consciousness], within which reside Brahmā, Hara, and Hari. (52–53)
Those who dwell upon the ground of the hairs of Vairāja live for a hundred years;
therefore, I repeatedly offered my sense of blessedness to the Consciousness-Space (cidākāśa).
And the Consciousness-Space said to me: "I am not a fit recipient for your blessedness."
The state of being a worthy recipient belongs to the fortunate one toward the glorious Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa—
toward the Imperishable Lord, the beginningless Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person,
the Sovereign Lord who ordains all incarnations. (55–56)
To the Lord of All, who is infinite and boundless, from whom everything proceeds;
from whose single pore of hair there issue infinite spaces of consciousness (cidākāśa);
wherein the abodes such as Goloka shine forth in every place.

O Sanatkumāra, you who are indeed a mass of such celestial consciousness, grant through your rays auspiciousness to the beginningless and glorious Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa; O you who are the refuge of all that is most blessed! || 58–59 ||
Where the liberated souls dwell, from whom millions of incarnations arise,
and from whom the manifestations beginning with Vāsudeva proceed; from whom dharma and the Vedas originate, and wherein the state of being the Inner Controller (antaryāmitā) is established.
He who is all-pervading and the underlying substratum, who is omniscient and omnipotent;
from whom the sacrifices and the ritual sections [of the Veda] arise, and from whom the activity of souls proceeds;
in whom there is ultimately cessation, and from whom the fruit of action comes to be. (61–62)

"The giver of the fruit, the cause of karma, the beginning of all, and the agent of all— O Sage, he alone should be addressed with words of praise as the locus of merit, and no other. Thus was I addressed in the other world, which stands beyond the imperishable worlds.

By the power of yoga, I went to behold and offer my salutations to Him, the cause of all causes, within His own abode. Enveloped by the divine splendors of the liberated souls residing there, I am He. (64–65)
I was not at all able to see his holy, divine form;
yet it is possible to go there through yoga, and it is possible to see him through his grace.
Without having seen him, I asked the assembly of liberated souls, "Where is the Blessed One?"
Having known this, he shines resplendently near the auspicious Aśvapaṭṭasara lake,
in the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpī adorned by the hermitage of Lomaśa,
in the home of the goddess Kambharā-Lakṣmī, and in the temple of Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa.
"Anādinārāyaṇa is visible to all eyes, both divine and non-divine.
Go, O sage, and behold Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa on earth.
Having received this command, I have come here for the purpose of seeing him.
And let us offer our thanks to Him who shines here—
the child Śrī Kambharā-lakṣmī’s son, Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa—
wherein the Vedas dwell and wherein the supreme knowledge (parā-vidyā) abides. (1.531.70–71)
Salutations indeed to that primordial Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, in whose corner of the eye all joys and liberations reside, and from whose mind all the gods, sages, and lords have arisen.
Salutations to you, the Lord, who takes the form of a child and is the Beloved;
salutations again and again to you, the Master of the liberated and the Master of all lights.
Salutations to you, the Lord of lords, who assumes a multitude of incarnations.
Salutations to you, the lord of Rādhā and Lakṣmī, and to the husband of Jayā;
salutations to you, the lord of Lalitā, Māṇikī, Padmā, and Pārvatī.
Salutations to you, O Lord of Prabhā, Vṛndā, Tulasī, Śrī, and Padmāvatī.
Obeisance to you, Mañjulākānta, Haṃseśa, and Yogīśeśa.
Obeisance again and again to you, Kamalākānta, Siddhīśa, who are directly manifest.
Obeisance to the one dwelling in the heart; obeisance to the inner controller of all.
Salutations to the one who wears a crown adorned with peacock feathers;
salutations to you whose chest is resplendent with the Kaustubha gem.
Salutations to the one with earrings on his ears; salutations to you who wear a golden necklace.
Salutations to You, whose essential nature is all-powerful, who grants every desire.
Salutations to You, the destroyer of many asuras and the protector of devotees.
Salutations again and again to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the bestower of the desires of His devotees.
Blessed is this Kuṅkumavāpī, blessed is this sage Lomaśa;
blessed is Aśvapaṭṭasara, and blessed is the auspicious Vyāghravana.
Blessed are these sages, and blessed are the grasses and trees that grow here.
Blessed are the creatures that move through the air, blessed are those who dwell upon the earth;
blessed likewise are men and women, and blessed indeed is this entire world of moving and unmoving beings,
wherein you, O Puruṣottama, abide in the form of a child.
You are seen as the object of all things; indeed, You are attained by the wise.
Today our birth has become fruitful, and our merit is unsurpassed, since You—who are not reached even by the creators and sustainers of the universe—are beheld here by us.
For those purified through many births, your vision here is appropriate.
And for us, the four goals of human endeavor have been attained here;
that refuge which is the state you have reached has been directly realized, worthy of our service.
Having thus offered praise, they all worshipped with supreme devotion that best of men in the guise of a boy, the Lord of the Universe who adorns the world;
they presented offerings and applied the auspicious *tilaka* mark.
They performed the *ārārtrika* rite and bowed with reverence, offering praise;
they circumambulated [the deity] and presented various kinds of food offerings (*naivedya*).
The gods and goddesses showered flowers upon the head of Kṛṣṇa.
During the great festival of Jayantī for Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, indeed millions of inhabitants of the worlds have arrived;
they come for the sight of Him, for His grace, and also for the nectar of His feet.
Having received auspicious blessings, they went joyfully to their own abodes.
This auspicious hymn of praise to the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa generates supreme sovereignty, bestows happiness, and grants all forms of prosperity.

O Lakṣmī! It bestows the liberation of Nirvāṇa; it is supreme, granting devotion to Hari; it grants the station of the Lord of the Imperishable; it is the excellent giver of all perfections (siddhis);
and it cuts away the very roots of greed, delusion, desire, anger, and karma. (93)
It bestows strength and intelligence, and destroys birth and death;
it grants men wealth, sons, beloved ones, land, and sovereign power; and it removes grief and suffering for whoever reads or hears it. (94–95)
The suffering person is released from bondage; the frightened one shall indeed be freed from fear.
The sick person is liberated from disease, and the poor person shall become wealthy.
One seized by robbers, one seized by enemies, or one surrounded by predatory beasts [shall likewise be freed].
O Lakṣmī! By means of this hymn, people indeed obtain auspiciousness.
That which the blessed Sanatkumāra gave to Śrī Lomaśa, and Lomaśa gave to other sages, is the cause of liberation. (97–98)
This should be given in every way to a devotee of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, to a servant-devotee, to the learned, and to one who seeks liberation;
[it is superior] even to a thousand horse-sacrifices and to circumambulating the entire earth. 99.
"And this hymn, which bestows merit, is superior even to bathing in all sacred fords (tīrthas).

Thus ends the five hundred and thirty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty and Other Qualities of Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, Spoken in Succession by Sanatkumāra— who had arrived to offer thanks and blessings— to the assembly of sages on the anniversary of the Jayantī of Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa at the Lomaśa Hermitage in the field of Kuṅkumavāpikā," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
