Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the wonder of the sage Gauramukha.
In the Kṛta-yuga, there was a king named Supratīka, who was preeminent in strength. (1)
He had two wives, Vidyutprabhā and Kāntimatī;
being childless, he propitiated Durvāsas at Citrakūṭa through his service. From him, he obtained the boon: "Become possessed of excellent sons."
The king obtained a son named Durjaya from Vidyutprabhā;
he obtained a second son named Sudyumna from Kāntimatī.
Thereafter, the king bestowed the kingdom of Vārāṇasī upon Durjaya.
He himself, however, went to Mount Citrakūṭa for the sake of penance;
the lord Durjaya, for his part, reflected upon the expansion of his kingdom.
Accompanied by an army of thirty akṣauhiṇīs, he set out toward the northern direction.
Having conquered Kiṃpuruṣa, Harivarṣa, Romāvrata, and Kuru,
as well as Bhadrāśva and the region in the middle of Meru, he set out to conquer heaven.
Just as he was ascending Mount Meru and proceeding toward his goal, [he encountered the following].
Nārada told Durjaya’s victory to the king of the gods;
Indra, taking his army, set out for battle.
He was defeated by Śaṅkara’s invincible trident.
Indra fell under his control, and all the gods likewise came under his sway.
Invincible, he bypassed the world-protectors and went to the earth.
There, two asuras named Vidyut and Suvidyut [resided]. (1.532.10)
Having arrived, both spoke to Durjaya: "Listen, O King!
Without conquering the world-protectors (lokapālas), there can never be happiness.
We two shall surely conquer them; grant us heaven as well, if you will. (11)
Having said "Om," he gave the sovereignty of heaven to those two excellent friends,
Hetu and Hetṛ, who were accompanied by a vast retinue of troops.
Then Svāyambhuva Manu gave his two daughters to them.
Hetukanyā was Sukeśī, while Miśrakeśī was born of Prahartṛ;
having obtained both of them who were difficult to conquer, he went to his own kingdom.
From Sukeśī was born Prabhava, and from Miśrakeśī was born Sudarśana.
Durjaya had two sons of great strength and prowess.
Thus, as the king was prospering, he once went to the Himālaya mountains with his army into the forests for the purpose of hunting. (15–16)
He who had his capital at Hastināpura spent the summer season in the forests with his vast army;
for while he resided in the forest, his military force consisted of five akṣauhiṇīs.
The twenty-fifth [chapter] was composed in the city of Hāstinapura.
At that time, Durjaya, while wandering in the forest of the snowy regions,
beheld in a wild district a sage named Gauramukha.
It was frequented by many sages and was the foremost abode of the great bhāgavatas;
there, the great ṛṣis indeed taught the Vedas to the young boys,
and the sections of the Vedas were taught to the girls by the munis.
Durjaya had indeed gone to the circle of hermitages for the purpose of seeing [the sages].
Then the sage Gauramukha offered a welcome to the king and spoke of providing food according to his ability for him and his followers.
"I shall do so; let the mounts be released properly throughout the forest.
Because of his devotion, the king was pleased and quickly caused five akṣauhiṇīs of troops to encamp right near the hermitage.
The sage, remembering the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa in his mind, reflected, "What food should be given to him? and having entered the waters of the Gaṅgā, he offered praise to Śrī Nārāyaṇa. (24–25)
Salutations to you, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the abode of the imperishable (Akṣara-dhāman).
Salutations to you, the primordial form, who holds a lute and possesses two arms.
Salutations to the Lord of Lakṣmī, who is endowed with the conch and the discus, and who bestows all objects of desire.
Salutations to you, the giver of all, the divine one, and the protector of devotees.
Salutations to you who abide here within the five elements and reside in the heart;
salutations to you, the fulfiller of all and the imperishable.
Salutations to you who uphold the vow of Brahman and who rest upon Śeṣa in the ocean;
salutations to you from whom all this world has arisen and who are the giver of everything.
From you come sacrifice, as well as the offerings to the gods (havya) and the ancestors (kavya), food, and water.
"Indeed, give him all your body as food.
O Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, King Durjaya has arrived here;
he is a guest who has come to you, so offer him hospitality, O Mādhava."
"And I am your servant; prepare a store of food and other provisions.
Whatever I touch with my hand or whatever I see with my eye—whether it be wood, grass, or a bulbous root—that shall become the fourfold food. (32)
Likewise, may all that is to be drunk— sweet water, milk, curd, ghee, and so forth—
all that which has been meditated upon by my mind, be accomplished for me through your very power alone; O Acyuta, let there be hospitality.
Thus praised, the gracious-souled Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, seated upon Garuḍa, appeared visibly in their presence,
bearing in his hands the conch, the discus, the bow, the thunderbolt, the banner, and the trident. ||35|| Hari.
Having seen him, that sage bowed with palms joined in reverence and then said:
"Now this king, together with his army and vehicles, has taken his meal in my hermitage and shall depart for his own home tomorrow. (36-37)
"Act accordingly, O Great King! O Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa! Om, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, obeisance to the Master!
Having been addressed thus, Śrī Hari formerly granted him purity of mind.
Then he gave him a divine cintāmaṇi of great luster. Having given it, Kṛṣṇa vanished; and that sage Gauramukha, having touched the jewel, meditated upon a lofty and magnificent palace.
There were indeed houses shaped like the peaks of the Himavat, possessing a hundred stories,
pervaded by the rays of the moon, and adorned with articles of gold and silver;
of such [houses], there were thousands and hundreds of thousands in every direction.
By the power of Viṣṇu’s jewel, the brahmin constructed houses;
likewise, he built walls along the perimeter with attached gardens,
filled with cuckoos, swans, cranes, saras birds, and peacocks.
Abounding with *campaka*, *aśoka*, *punnāga*, and *nāgakesara* trees, as well as various trees, creepers, shrubs, flowers, and birds;
and the elephant stables for the elephants and the horse pens for the horses.
By his mere resolve, he fashioned camels, gavayas, bulls, and partridges; he prepared heaps of food,
including items to be chewed, eaten, licked, sucked, and drunk with sugar.
He prepared various kinds of food, vegetables,
and condiments, as well as vessels of gold and silver and diverse fruits.
Having done this, that brahmin [addressed] the king of great splendor.
He spoke to all the troops: "Let them enter their respective houses marked with their own names;
let them dwell there happily and rejoice.
[The city] is ten yojanas in width and thirty yojanas in length."
The armies entered the divine city, which shone like the sun;
the king, however, entered his own palace, which was as lofty as a mountain.
Then Gauramukha, taking the jewel, said to the king:

Having touched the jewel, he spoke after commanding: "I shall send slaves and courtesans for the purpose of bathing and eating. "By its power," he said, "slaves and slave-girls shall attain nine states. (51–52)
While that king was looking on, women emerged—divine beings with youthful vigor, their limbs adorned with delicate unguents and the like;
they possessed beautiful cheeks, lovely bodies, fine hair, and beautiful eyes. (53)
Likewise, hundreds of thousands of handsome youths, possessing the luster of the color of the golden campaka flower,
who were like gods and had recently entered their youth,
set forth, some carrying golden vessels. (54–55)
In this manner, all the young women and young men, as well as the attendants,
prepared the cooked food for the sake of the king and his army;
some provided garments, while others bathed them.
Some massaged her feet, while others prepared the bedding;
some offered betel leaves and likewise gave sweet water;
others fanned her, while still others performed songs.
The servants indeed performed service for the people according to their needs;
various kinds of musical instruments were played there in abundance.
As that king was immersing himself, other women danced.

Having thus bathed with divine offerings, the mighty king partook of various foods according to the prescribed rites; and so too did his army. As was the honoring of the king, so too was the honoring of his servants.
The king of sages performed the most excellent honoring of his elephants, horses, and other animals through his own male and female servants.
Then, the night arrived, endowed with the splendor of the moon.
Delightful spectacles were displayed by the sage;
dances performed by women and great festivals were shown,
as well as the auspicious combats of wrestlers.
Divine songs and the finest musical instruments were performed;
women skilled in the melodies of the Gandharvas displayed their jeweled anklets.
Explanations, pleasing discourses, and even humorous jests were offered.
Gambling matches, illusions like those of Indra, performances by actors and dancers,
and other optical deceptions were displayed during the middle of the night.
Then, upon their couches made of jewels and gold—
On soft surfaces strewn with flowers, the women performed their service;
and the king was attended by celestial maidens upon an excellent couch.
Thus, through the power of that sage Maṇi, his mind remained well-disposed.
Then the king and his armies slept soundly and joyfully.
At dawn, for the purpose of the morning rites, various musical instruments were played everywhere along with the songs of young maidens.
Having bathed, drunk water, and partaken of food, the king,
together with his army, quickly went to the leaf-hut where the sage Maṇi resided, in order to worship Gauramukha.
Then the maidens, the servants, all the houses,
the household utensils and so forth, and all the food and drink—
everything vanished in an instant, and that place became a forest.
Filled with wonder upon seeing that, the king reflected again and again: "How is it that this jewel belongs to me?
Thinking, "I shall take this wish-fulfilling gem from him," he—
Having bowed and gone outside the hermitage, he spoke to the minister:
"Virocana! Go to the sage and indeed make a request for the jewel.
Having approached that ṛṣi, he was intent on asking for the jewel.
"The king is the vessel for jewels; let a gem be given to him.
When addressed thus by the minister, Gauramukha spoke in anger:
"The king should always be the giver, while the recipient of gifts is the brahmin."
And how is it that you, having yourself become a king, beg like one who is wretched? (78) You are unworthy; you are not a fit vessel for the jewel. Do not make this request!
For whom the three worlds—both heaven and even the underworld—are under his control. (79)
Even though there is Mount Meru and the oceans of jewels, alas, there is still poverty!
You harbor an unjust desire for the wealth of a Brāhmaṇa.
For the ignorant man who is never satisfied, all objects of the senses remain within his very home.
Nevertheless, the wicked man does not attain peace because of his craving.
Speak thus to King Durjaya himself, who is of evil conduct:
"Go quickly, before some obstacle arises for you. (81–82)
The messenger went to the king and spoke as was appropriate;
the king, in anger, said to the vassal named Nīla: "Go, do not delay!
Having brought the gem from the brahmin, return quickly to my presence. (83)
As Nīla was thus proceeding swiftly toward the wall of the jewel,
there emerged from that jewel millions of warriors with weapons in their hands— some on chariots, others with banners, swords, and shields. (84–85)
Equipped with bows, quivers, and arrows, and provided with spears and short clubs,
there were fifteen akṣauhiṇīs and fifteen leaders.
By name they were Suprabha, Dīptitejas, and Śubhadarśana.
Sukānti, Sundara, Sunda, Pradyumna, Sumanas,
Śubha, Suśīla, Sukhada, Śambhu, Sudānta, Soma, and Suraśmi— all these formidable warriors fought [on his side]. (87–88)
Spiked maces, lances, swords, and bows, as well as clubs,
thunderbolts, and spears, fell upon the great warriors.
Chariots stood surrounding chariots, and likewise elephants surrounding elephants.
Horse indeed rushed against horse, and foot-soldier against foot-soldier.
While that battle continued unceasingly, a river arose there from blood;
the king’s minister, unconscious, was slain in battle along with his army.
Durjaya himself fought there with those born of jewels;
indeed, a total slaughter of the remaining army took place.
Then, the great battle of Jāmi was heard by Hetu and Prahetu.
While those two were fighting, fifteen fierce divisions and fifteen commanders were dispatched by him as allies to the front of the battle;
hear now their names, for they did not rise again but perished. (93–94)
Praghasa, Vighasa, Saghasa, Aśaniprabha, Vidyutprabha, Sughoṣa, Pronmattākṣa, Pratardana,
Agnidanta, Agnitejas, Bāhu, Śakra, and Virodhaka.
Bhīmakarman and Vipracitti, along with the Daityas armed with supreme weapons,
fought with great illusion against those preeminent warriors adorned with jewels.
Those fifteen akṣauhiṇīs of the Daityas were then slain.
Meanwhile, Hetā and Prahetā arrived with millions of troops;
likewise, Vidyut and Suvidyut, both lords of the Asuras in heaven,
having heard that they were to provide assistance in battle, arrived accompanied by thirty akṣauhiṇīs.
They arrived in the region of the Himalayas, and the earth trembled.
There, the river Raktavāhā flowed swiftly toward the ocean.
Then Gauramukha beheld that infinite army of Rākṣasas.

He remembered the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the master and lord of jewels. Then Śrī Hari, clad in yellow garments and seated upon his bird-vehicle, arrived before him and said, "Tell me, what task must I perform here?"
The sage said, "O Blessed One, slay this invincible king and the Daityas as well.
Having heard this, the slayer of Daityas released his discus;
the discus, equal to ten million suns, reduced Durjaya to ashes.
"Neither the armies nor the rākṣasas shall remain here; not even a single one will be left behind.
In the blink of an eye, this Dānava clan has been slain.
Therefore, let this forest be known as Nimiṣāraṇya."
And the settlement of the sages shall be true to its name.
I, the Sacrificial Person (Yajñapuruṣa), shall dwell here in this forest retreat;
and these fifteen leaders shall always be my patrons (yājyas).
"In the Kṛta Yuga, these kings shall be born in succession from this jewel.
Having spoken thus and taken the jewel, the deity vanished.
The twice-born man also remained in his own hermitage, filled with supreme joy.
And all the armies also attained absorption into Śrī Viṣṇu. Durjaya, having merged into Śrī Hari there through yoga, became dissolved;
the armies, struck by the discus, went to heaven through yoga.
Thus, O beloved, the portions of Nārāyaṇa born from the jewel have been described.
From reading and hearing this, there shall be liberation as well as heaven.
Now, the brahmin Gauramukha, desiring to propitiate Hari—
He came to the sacred field of Prabhāsa for the purpose of destroying the evil resulting from the war.
In Saurāṣṭra, on the Raivata ground, he bathed in the pool named Dāmodara,
in the Nārāyaṇa-hrada, and in the ocean joined by the Gomatī river.
He went to the Sarasvatī in the east and to Aśvapaṭṭasara; then, in the auspicious hermitage of Lomaśa at the sacred site of Kuṅkumavāpikā,
the great sage Mārkaṇḍeya, the king of seers, arrived there.
Having first bowed to Lomaśa, he prostrated before Mārkaṇḍeya;
then [he bowed] to the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the bestower of the jewel,
who was present in person as the son of Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa.
The sage Gauramukha indeed considered himself to have accomplished his purpose. Reciting the mantra "Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine namaḥ," he questioned the divine Mārkaṇḍeya.

"For the sake of liberating the deceased and for the destruction of evil deeds, what should I perform here at this sacred site? Instruct me in this matter. Mārkaṇḍeya then said to him, "Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa is Hari."
The Lord who exists here as the primordial one of all the gods—worship that Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the husband of Śrī, directly before your eyes.
Through him comes liberation for all and the destruction of all obstacles. (1.19)
"It shall indeed come to pass in this field; perform the *śrāddha* rites here.
Thus addressed, that sage performed the *śrāddhas* out of a desire for liberation, and he himself brought about the deliverance of those who had died in battle.
They all departed in their celestial chariots for the imperishable abode of the Supreme Self.
This Gauramukha was himself Bhrigu in a previous birth;
this lord of sages, Mārkaṇḍeya, is born from his lineage.
Through the *śrāddha* ceremony, the son awakened his father once again.
Then Gauramukha, having performed the libations there and understood [the truth], remembered all his previous births; and having remembered them, he [focused] upon Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
Having offered himself with his whole being, he went to the abode named Akṣara; he attained dissolution in the Lord of All, which is designated as the state beyond rebirth.

Thus ends the five hundred and thirty-second chapter, titled "The Description of Durjaya’s Sovereignty over the Three Worlds, the Welcome by Gauramukha with the Jewel Offered to Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa at the Hermitage, the Battle for the Cintāmaṇi, the Destruction of Durjaya and Others, Gauramukha’s Arrival at Prabhāsa, and His Liberation," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
