Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī! In the past, during a dispute among the gods, the Blessed Lord Varāha imparted this knowledge known as the Adhyātma to the Earth.
There was a king named Suprabha, born from a wish-fulfilling gem;
his second name, Prajāpāla, was indeed meaningful.
Once, he went with joy to see the sages in the hermitages of the seers.

There dwells a sage named Mahātapas, who possesses a lifespan of an entire kalpa. (3) He performs austerities without food, chanting the eternal Brahman. There, the trees, creepers, shrubs, grasses, and birds [are likewise endowed with that same longevity]. (4)
There were even beasts, wild animals, and reptiles who were seekers of liberation;
free from passion and hatred, they remained established in austerity like sages.
Beholding them, that protector of subjects [saw] the hermitage of those great ascetics.
He entered with joy and rejoiced upon seeing the sage.
With supreme devotion, he bowed down and prostrated himself like a staff out of delight.
At that time, from the very sight of the sage seated upon a mat of *kuśa* grass, [he was filled with bliss].
The king quickly forgot his world-encompassing mind that was composed of illusion;
through the presence of the sage, he set his heart upon righteousness,
as well as upon the desire to know self-knowledge and the scriptures concerning the means to liberation.
Seeing that sage, the king performed the rites of hospitality:
offering a seat, a welcome, a drink, food, and words of inquiry regarding his welfare.
Then the humble king questioned that tranquil sage.
"O Blessed One, tell me, who am bowed before you, that which must be done by men desiring victory who are submerged in the suffering of saṃsāra, so that it may bring them happiness.
Having heard this, the one of great asceticism said: "O King, understand from me."
For those submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra, the glorious Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the illustrious Puruṣottama, must be made their steady, constant, and firm boat.
Likewise, worship, gifts, sacrifices, meditation, and total self-surrender [should be offered]. (12–13)
And these divine steps are indeed considered to be service;
by taking hold of that ladder of devotion, ascend.
You will undoubtedly reach the further shore even of the ocean.
The king asked: "How indeed should the worship of that Hari be performed?
The sage replied: "The worship of Hari should be performed as I tell you:
either in an image made of metal and other materials, or in a *śālagrāma*, or in a *śiva-liṅga*. (15–16)
One should meditate upon Janārdana within virtuous people, virtuous women, cows, the guru, one's master, one's father,
a devoted wife, the sun, fire, a brahmin, a maiden, a child, and one who is helpless or without refuge. (17)
One should meditate upon Puruṣottama at a sacred tree (caityavṛkṣa) and upon Tulasī.
One should contemplate the mental [self] in the heart, and the physical self in the senses and the body.
One should meditate on the Self within the deities and likewise worship the Lord of Śrī.
In this way, Kṛṣṇa is pleased with both men and women.
All these have arisen from Hari alone; he is the body of Hara.
Likewise, Agni, the two Aśvins, Gaurī, Gaṇeśa, and the serpent.
Kārttikeya, as well as the Ādityas, the Mothers, and the Durgās;
the quarters, Kubera, Viṣṇu, Yama, Rudra, Śaśin, and the Pitṛs—these were all produced from the form of Nārāyaṇa. (21–22)
"These indeed are worthy of worship, for they are endowed with Nārāyaṇa;
they truly become the very forms arising from Nārāyaṇa.
The King said: "Where am I to obtain those excellent forms?"
"By means of which I indeed worship the objects of my senses with excellent offerings.
The sage said: "Listen, O King! For their forms are twofold;
they are divine and of the nature of deities, and those [forms] do not become perceptible. || 24-25 ||
The Ādityas dwell here within his body as its very range of experience;
they are always indeed the embodiments of the constituent parts of reality (tattvāṃśa).
Once, they each separately became filled with pride on all sides.
"I am worthy; I am the best; I am always the one to be sacrificed upon in this body.
"No one else here in this body is equal to me.
Thus, indeed, a dispute arose among those elements. (27–28)
To provide a resolution for them as they were disputing, the Lord Hiraṇyagarbha, the Sovereign, spoke to them with logical reasoning:
"That without which this [universe] would not exist is indeed the Greatest. (29)
When this had been said, O King, Fire first rose up and spoke:
"I am great; worship me in my abode.
Indeed, the body would meet its destruction if it were deprived of me."
Having spoken thus, Vaiśvānara, the digestive fire, departed;
having abandoned the body, he dwelt elsewhere for about a year.
Even after he had gone, that body did not decay.
Then Vahni realized, "I am indeed not the most excellent.
Thereupon, the two Aśvins, manifest in bodily form and consisting of the nature of prāṇa and apāna, declared in the assembly of the gods, "We two are the foremost. (33-34)
Having spoken thus, they abandoned their bodies and remained somewhere;
for a full year, that body remained stable even without them,
indeed perfectly steady through the practice of *kumbhaka* and devoid of the movement of breath.
Then knowledge arose in them both: "Since we two are not the most excellent.
Thereupon Gaurī spoke these words: "Preeminence belongs to me.
Having spoken thus, that auspicious goddess emerged from the sacred field (kṣetra) to the outside.
Even without her, that field remained deficient in speech;
through that silence, she realized, "I am not the most excellent, since [the field remains silent].
Then Gaṇapati, known as Ākāśa, spoke these words.
"Nothing in this body can remain for even a year without me.
Having uttered 'I am great,' he too emerged from the body;
yet, though separated [from it], this body did not perish."
Even that which is called destruction does not disintegrate without it;
devoid of cavities, it remains established exactly as before.
Because of this, the realization arose in the ether: "I am not the most excellent."
Then indeed all the elements, including the gross elements and the rest, said:
"Without us, this body cannot maintain its existence.
Having declared, "We are the most excellent," those born of the body abandoned the body. (42–43)
Even a field abandoned by the Person (Puruṣa) is still protected;
it is not destroyed, but rather becomes withered—even though it was once endowed with consciousness.
From that arises the knowledge of the elements (dhātus); we are not superior.
Seeing him, Skanda, who possesses the nature of ego-consciousness (ahaṃkāra), said:
"Even the very production of the body is not possible without me;
therefore, I am the most excellent, and there is no other equal to me. (45-46)
Having spoken thus, he departed from the body and remained separate.
For a year, without him, the body remained as if liberated—
neither decayed nor dead, but peaceful, remaining as it was before.
Because of that, he gained this knowledge: "I am not the most excellent, since [without me] the field does not function for even a moment.
Then the Sun, whose form is the eye, being enraged, quickly said:
"Indeed, without me, the field does not proceed for even a single instant."
Having spoken thus, that [body] departed; yet his own body did not perish.
Returning, he beheld that frame remaining just as it was before.
Through this, knowledge arose within him: "Since I am not the most excellent, [therefore I have not perished]."
Then the defects such as desire and the rest, the subtle elements (tanmātras), and the mothers [the sense objects] such as sound and so forth, all declared: "We are the most excellent;
there is no existence of a body apart from us. (51–52)
Having spoken thus, the group of elements went outside for a year;
yet the body did not decay at all, remaining exactly as it was before.
Then the elements realized: "Surely, we are not the most excellent."
The primordial Māyā, Durgā, who consists of the three guṇas, spoke in anger:
"Without me, there is no prosperity for this [universe]; therefore, I am superior in every respect.
Having said this, she vanished, and after a year, she appeared once again.
Having seen that the body had attained the state of yoga through consciousness,
it was indeed not decayed, nor destroyed, nor even dead, just as it had been before;
by the power of consciousness, it remained exactly as it was.
Then knowledge arose within her: "I am not the foremost.
Thereupon the quarters of the sky rose up and spoke these great words, having reflected: "The task must not be accomplished without us. || 57-58 ||
Having gone for a year joined with their ears, their bodies did not indeed decay;
it remained just as it was before, yet devoid of the hearing of Kṛṣṇa.
Because of that, knowledge arose within them: "We are certainly not the most excellent."
Then Vāyu, the lord of wealth, spoke to Dhanañjaya in every way:
"Even when my life-force has departed, I shall remain for three days within the corpses;
without me, the body would not exist, nor would it become foul-smelling or undergo destruction."
Then, having said, "I am the most excellent," he went far away;
nevertheless, it remained exactly as it was, endowed with consciousness.
Through that, he gained the knowledge: "Indeed, I am not the most excellent."
Then Viṣṇu said to the mind: "This body cannot exist without me.
Having said, "Therefore, I am the most excellent," he vanished;
yet the body remained just as it was before, devoid of thought.
Having seen this, knowledge said to him: "Since I am not the most excellent, therefore Dharma is the greatest. Then Action spoke:
"I am the most eminent; I have protected the body, and therefore I am superior in every respect."
"Now that I have departed, how will this come to pass?
Having spoken thus, both Dharma and Adharma, whose nature is action, departed.
Nevertheless, the body joined with the self does not perish.
Having arrived, those two most exalted ones indeed reached a decision;
then Mahādeva spoke to the Great Principle (Mahattattva), who was himself most exalted:
"I alone am the Great One; nothing exists that is devoid of me. (68)
Having spoken thus, Śambhu departed from his body as the Mahat-tattva.
Even after a full year, this body did not decay at all.
Then, knowledge arose within him: "The Great One is merely a name for me. (1.533.70)
"In truth, I am not great; my status as supreme is indeed false.
Then the fathers spoke here: "The objects of the senses are the greatest.
We, consisting of sound and the rest, are gross; by us the body is sustained. (71)
"Therefore, we are the strongest and greatest among all;
without us, this body will surely perish quickly.
Having spoken thus, they abandoned that body and vanished from sight.
Nevertheless, that body did not crumble even in the slightest;
therefore, they realized, "We are certainly not the most excellent.
Then, the female serpent Vāsanā spoke.
"I am the most excellent; indeed, without me the body does not remain.
(75) She too had gone far away for a year and returned once more.
Having seen her body as it was before, even I, though supreme, did not recognize her. (76)
Then, having all come together and abandoned the body, they went outside:
fire, prāṇa, as well as apāna, space, and all the bodily constituents (dhātus);
ego (ahaṃkāra), mind (manas), the sun, and likewise the groups beginning with desire (kāma).
Kāṣṭhā, Vāyu, Viṣṇu, Dharma, Śambhu, and the objects of the senses—
by these [deities], even though this field is abandoned, it remains well-established as if liberated,
because it is protected by Soma himself through his sovereign power of yoga.
Because it was protected by him, their host did not fall apart; yet their pride was destroyed, for our assembly is indeed not the best. Then, a most great pride arose in Soma and Jīva.
"Indeed, my body is protected by me; therefore, I am in every way supreme.
When Soma had thus resolved upon the sixteen-fold imperishable Self, we understood that you are the Great One, yet that remains a ground for doubt.
"That without which the body indeed could not remain established is truly great;
you too should perform a test here of your own self.
Only then shall we recognize your divine preeminence, and not otherwise."
Thus addressed, the individual soul (jīvātman) then departed from the body.
It wandered outside for a year, carrying everything [the senses] within the ether;
and standing outside, it beheld the body that had been permanently abandoned.
But there stood Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama;
Kṛṣṇa-Narāyaṇa remained there to destroy the pride of the individual soul (jīvātman), and he mindfully sustained and protected his body. (86)
By means of his own sovereignty and his own qualities, even without the internal self,
the individual soul (jīvātman)— having beheld his former state of embodiment protected by the Omniscient One and by those deities and principles— returned once more. (87–88)
Thereupon he realized, "I am certainly not the foremost being here.
Then those deities said to him, "We shall indeed remain;
go alone, O Self, for we do not live [without you]."
Having been addressed thus, Jīvavarman abandoned them and went outside. There, he became like one who is inert; without Nārāyaṇa, he was as if unconscious and entirely like one in deep sleep.
Without Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, he became as if devoid of luster, as if lacking light, smoky, and like one dead;
for fire and the other elements residing within the body [lose their power] without the living soul. (92)
Indeed, through their lineage from the glorious Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa,
they have attained a divine state and the state of Brahman by means of divine yoga;
through union with the Supreme Brahman, they have reached the state of Brahman.

Though they were originally insentient, they became conscious and resembled liberated souls through the association with Śrī Hari, who is capable of transforming things otherwise. All those field-deities (kṣetradevatās) then fell into a state of embarrassment.
The three bodies—the gross, the subtle, and the causal—are also [attained].
Through union with Nārāyaṇa, that [state] then becomes identical with Nārāyaṇa;
for it has attained the divine form of Nārāyaṇa, which is essentially Brahman.
Then all pride vanished from the living soul;
he also attained the realization that "I am not the most excellent.
Śrī Hari is always the best, worthy of worship, the object of meditation, and the one to be remembered at all times. (98)
By whom all the deities, beginning with Fire, were born and by whom they live;
by whom even I, the individual soul (jīva), though dependent, live and not otherwise at any time;
through union with that, the self becomes divine in every respect. (1.533.99–100)

Through union with that [divine power], even these principles (tattvas), though previously insentient, have become entirely divine; indeed, they have become truly divine. And even without me, those liberated ones shall dwell in the abodes as truly divine beings.
"If he should desire that, even after abandoning me, the dull-witted ones become divine—[then] who could prevent the manifestation of one who is capable of doing everything?
Therefore, Nārāyaṇa-Kṛṣṇa is regarded as the most excellent of all. (102–103)
Then the gods praised that Supreme Lord who dwells in all;
remaining in their respective places, they repeatedly spoke to Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa:
"You are Agni, you are likewise Prāṇa, and you also become Apāna."
You are speech and you are the ether; you are the elements residing within the body.
You alone are the sense of "I," and you alone are the eye. You are the objects of the senses, such as sound and the rest; you are Māyā, consisting of the three qualities.

You are the sense of hearing, and you are Dhanañjaya as well; you are the mind, and likewise you are dharma, you are the principle of Mahat, and you alone are the objects of the senses. You are the nature of pure latent impressions, you are the individual soul (jīvātman), and you are Nārāyaṇa.
You are the soul of all; indeed, without you, these [beings] would never possess existence.
By being with you, who exist, we exist; you are the Lord of all, the Supreme Lord, the master, the husband, the nourisher, the life-force, and likewise the protector.
"If we were to depart, how would this come to pass?
Thus, our very bodies have been surrendered here; you alone have protected that divine form. Therefore, you must protect us who remain."
"Our place must not be destroyed; we are always dependent upon you.
Thus praised, the God then attained supreme satisfaction with them and said to them:
"And you have been created by me for the sake of sport."
"I sport through you; there is no other purpose.
Choose a boon, O gods, for I am pleased and shall grant it.
Then the gods chose two-fold protection for themselves forever.

"According to their respective states within their bodies, and another through divine power—O Śrī Hari, speak now! Let each of these two forms remain with me out of compassion, assuming those two forms individually, and I shall speak. (1.14–1.15)
"In all matters concerning the elements, remain in my service in your formless essential nature; however, in the world of the gods, remain in your embodied form.
And at the time of dissolution, O deities, quickly enter into me for absorption."
I shall provide the names for you gods:
Agni Vaiśvānara is the god; Prāṇa and Apāna are the two Aśvins;
Vāṇī is Gaurī, the daughter of Himavat; and Vyoma is the father of Padmāvatī.
These bodily constituents and various elements shall indeed become [the gods];
Ahaṃkāra himself will become Skanda Kārttikeya.
The two eyes, in the form of the sun and the moon, will become the two gods of heaven.
The objects of the senses, beginning with sound, shall become the elephant-faced one (Gaṇeśa).
Māyā, the body, shall become Durgā at the end of the causal state.
The sense of hearing, having attained the nature of the quarters (the directions), shall become the form of the gods.
Dhananjaya shall indeed become Kubera, the Lord of Wealth; this Manu shall undoubtedly become Viṣṇu by name. Dharma also shall become the god of the southern quarter, Yama, by name.
The Lord Mahādeva will become the principle of the Great (mahattattva);
there is no doubt that the objects of the senses will become the ancestors (pitṛs),
and the latent impression (vāsanā) in the form of passion will become the passionate woman.
"My individual soul shall exist in human form by my side,
and at times, becoming the moon, it shall become the repository of nectar.
By the granting of such boons, they became the deities of creation.
Indeed, those [elements] abide within the body as well, established in the principle of Hiraṇyagarbha.
But that Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa who is proclaimed as the Supreme Brahman— he alone exists in the form of the deity during creation, O Lord.
That very same essence of reality dwells here within the body as well.
Therefore, O King, worship the gods and likewise the principles within the physical form;
always worship these within the body without distinction from Hari.
That very Self has indeed been found by you within yourself; do not go elsewhere.
Thus has the Person of the Vedānta been described, whose essence is Nārāyaṇa. Such is the power of this Lord Janārdana, who is to be known through the Vedas.
"Śrīpati Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa is indeed without beginning or end; O King, protector of subjects, I have described him to you—worship him!
Having spoken thus, that sage of great austerity then became silent.
The Boar said to the Earth: "Those gods are present within you as well;
O Goddess of Gods, worship those deities so that liberation may surely be attained.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, has this divine narrative known as the "Manifest" been told to you.
By reciting and hearing this, and by worshipping those principles (tattvas) as they have been described, a person becomes one who possesses the realization of Brahman;
the supreme accomplishment of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa is thereby produced.
"Thus, having realized the oneness of the Self, the sages worship Hari.

Thus ends the five hundred and thirty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Knowledge and Worship of the Puruṣa of Vedānta, Consisting of the Reality of the Body, as Given by the Sage named Mahātapas to King Prajāpāla," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga Lineage, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Chapter 533. Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā—Section 1 (Kṛtayuga Lineage).
Chapter 534 [Author:
Chapter 535 → Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:

Listen, O Lakṣmī: once Śambhu was seated near Varā, absorbed in meditation on Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa upon Mount Kailāsa, while recollecting the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā and the supreme pilgrimage site of Prabhāsa. (1)
The most delightful Vyāghrāraṇya, the Siṃhāraṇya of Raivata;
the holy site of Aśvapaṭṭasara, the river Bhadrā, and the Śatruñjaya;
Lomaśa, the Vaiṣṇava devotee, Viṣṇu, and Gopālakṛṣṇaka.

Remembering the goddess Kambharālakṣmī, he indeed became steady in meditation. Then, the goddess Śrī Pārvatī— the bestower of the perfections of yoga and the giver of liberation— approached his lap, possessing the luster of molten gold.
She sat down, and beholding the face of Śambhu, she became smiling.
With eyes filled with love, the Goddess spoke sweetly:
"Whom do you meditate upon day and night? You never cease from this at any time."
Having spoken thus with great emotion, her eyes clouded with rising tears,
Śambhu abandoned his meditation and spoke to his devoted Maheśvarī:
"O beloved, why indeed are your eyes clouded with tears— out of love or out of grief?"
"Tell me everything you desire; I shall always do it for you, O beloved.
You are my heart, O Queen of Gods, and likewise I am your heart.
I am your everything, and you are indeed my everything."
Upon hearing this, the goddess Pārvatī became composed in mind;
she again questioned her beloved about the cause of his absorption in meditation:
"O Lord, what is this that you meditate upon? Tell me, if it be eternal."

"O Satī! Śambhu has said that if the eternal true nature of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, who bestows liberation upon the world, is thus [described], it is indeed not possible for me to reach the further shore of this Hari while he remains absorbed in meditation. (11-12)
He, the Lord of Ramā, is constantly beheld in meditation and contemplated;
the Beloved of Kamalā is worshipped, and the illustrious Lord of Māṇikī is adored. He, the Beloved of Prabhā, the Lord of Lakṣmī, Nārāyaṇa, is served.
O Satī, this very one whom I meditate upon is Pārvatīśvara himself.
I have arisen from him; I am not separate from him. O Satī, I meditate upon that beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
I remember that Lord of Śrī, O Sovereign of All, in whom thirty-five million sacred sites (tīrthas) always reside;
I remember you, who stand by the side of Hari in the form of Lakṣmī.
I remember myself as being of the nature of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
(17) Where the hermitage of Lomaśa is, where Mount Raivata stands upon the earth, and where my holy place Prabhāsa is located in the region of Surāṣṭra. (18)
Where Śatruñjaya is, where Bhadrā is, where Kuṅkumavāpikā is,
and where Aśvapaṭṭasara is— there dwells the son of Gopālana,
the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa; of him I am mindful.
Those possessed of non-existence do not know this eternal field at all. O Goddess, those permeated by the state of existence know this everlasting place,
the auspicious site for the manifestation of Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
In every Kalpa, the names of this sacred field arise individually according to the distinction of the Yugas; people do not know them at all.
Formerly, by name Maṇikṣetra, it was the region of Surāṣṭra.
Thereafter, that very place became renowned by the name Padmakṣetra;
after that, it subsequently became known by the name Vaiṣṇavakṣetra;
and then indeed, it became famous by the name Lomaśakṣetra.
Thereupon, that sacred field became renowned by the name Patnīvrata;
from that, the field named Indradyumna arose;
and after that, the field known as Nārasiṃha came into being.
From that, the sacred field named Vyāghrāraṇya indeed came into being.
Then the sacred field known by the name Rukmāṅgada was produced.
After that, the sacred field Kuṅkumavāpikā became renowned.
Then the holy ford (tīrtha) known by the name Aśvapaṭṭasara was born;
thereafter, the sacred field (kṣetra) shall be called Prābhāsika. After that comes the field of Someśvara, and then again the one named Kaṅka.
Thereupon, that sacred field shall become renowned by the name Somapada.
Then, in the course of time, that field shall become Girināra;
and in the middle Kalpa, it shall be Surāṣṭra, according to my yogic power.
O Satī, through the yoga of the Ṛṣi, through the yoga of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa,
and likewise through your own yoga at the proper time, there will certainly be various names in every respect; indeed,
I know them all through my yogic power.
Such is that field of merit, which bestows liberation upon all embodied beings;
it is eternally the abode of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
Indeed, where Viṣṇu is on the left, there is Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
Where Talasvāmī is, and where Gopīnātha is as well;
where Siddheśvara is, and where I am, and likewise Bhadreśvara; and where Someśvara is, O virtuous lady, there you, Bhadrikā, shall be.
Wherein, in the central region, resides the Lord Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa;
where, in the capital city, there are many virtuous wives of Kṛṣṇa;
where lies the kingdom born of Ānarta; and where dwells Gopāla, the son of Kṛṣṇa. (35–36)
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa himself dwells there;
such is that vast sacred field (kṣetra), extending for a hundred yojanas,
which is mostly surrounded by the ocean on three sides and joined with the eastern land.
Even the mere sight of it wards off the torment of sin for all people.
Therein reside the families of the virtuous, of saintly women, and of yoginīs, as well as those of the great Sāttvatas who act as protectors of the earth. (38–39)
The families of those who possess wisdom, who are devoted to austerity, who observe celibacy,
and who bring about the welfare of the world, flourish even while living abroad; as do the families of women who are devoted to the virtuous and whose bodies are dedicated to their noble lords.

O Goddess, that is my ancient seat and sacred field where the portions and parts of Viṣṇu are born as divine manifestations for those devotees who have surrendered their all and serve Svāminārāyaṇa. (41–42)
I remember that great field; I go to my ancient peace.
O Goddess, whenever I remember you, I indeed emerge outside in an instant.
Thus is this field dear to me, obtained from Kṛṣṇa at the end of the kalpa.
And through your yoga, it shall become renowned by the name Pārvata.
O Great Goddess, in that sacred field, always in a secluded spot on the shore of the ocean, I dwell; this place has been established by me for my own purpose and remains hidden.
In every age, sacred sites arise and pass away;
however, for those who do not proclaim the scriptures, it is better to keep the field concealed.
On this earth, the wicked, failing to understand the greatness of Hari, revile him.

They wander from one sacred site to another, lacking true knowledge, [failing to recognize] the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, who is beginningless and born in Surāṣṭra. They do not know the sacred site of the household, which is marked by the fish, trident, bow, and banner. 47–48.
Indeed, Nārāyaṇa is perceived through the *vajra*, the *svastika*, and the *cakra*;
he is the lord of Rādhikā, Pārvatī, Lakṣmī, Māṇikī, and Suprabhā.
He is truly the master, the beloved, and the husband of all principles (*tattvas*).
"O Queen, I worship this Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Person—
him who resides in the supreme abode, him who dwells on the shore of Lake Aśvapaṭṭasara,
the beloved Lord of ten million gopīs in the hermitage of Lomaśa."
O Goddess, he whose dwelling is always there, both in this kalpa and in other kalpas— that ancient one I remember eternally;
my mind finds no stability in other excellent holy places.
At the sacred site of Kuṅkumavāpikā-tīrtha, he remains steadfast with his whole being.
Therefore, that [Lord] is indeed constantly remembered by the innate mind.
As long as I remember that holy field, so long does Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa remain present.
Laughing toward me as if I were an old friend,
that enchanting one, O beloved, truly delights me with many divine states and playful gestures suited to other kalpas.
Just as my mind is bound to Him and does not separate from Him,
so too does Anādikṛṣṇanārāyaṇa draw me toward Himself;
He never releases me from fear, but rather restrains me within His own being.
"O beloved Maheśvarī, remember such a supreme field;
O my dear one, remember Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
Having been addressed thus, the goddess Pārvatī was overwhelmed with the bliss of Brahman.
Merely by hearing of the holy field, she became one with Brahman.
At that moment, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa appeared within her heart—
a youth bearing a divine form, as beautiful as ten million gods of love.
He said, "O Mother, why indeed do you never come to my field?
Having spoken thus and bowed to Pārvatī, he, situated in the midst of a circle of splendor and served by the beloved of ten million beauties,
granted his direct vision.
Beyond that, He resides in the world called Akṣara, which is enjoyed by the liberated;
there He is established in Goloka, two-armed, and worshipped by hosts of gopīs and gopas.
Established in Vaikuṇṭha, He is four-armed and worshipped by Ramā, Śrī, and Kamalā.
Residing on Kailāsa, he was like a serpent-thread, brilliant as snow, firm, and youthful;
he had matted locks upon his head and Satī remained at his side.
Having thus granted his own vision, he once again vanished from sight.
But the goddess Pārvatī, having experienced a great wonder, arose from her meditative absorption and spoke to her husband, the illustrious Śaṅkara:
"O beloved, the sacred field has been seen by me; Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa has been seen. (65–66)
Now I have become one who has accomplished her purpose, having seen my husband Acyuta, who,
as the Supreme Person, manifests within the supreme imperishable abode.
He is indeed Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa at Aśvapaṭṭatīrtha.
"In Goloka, in Vaikuṇṭha, and even on Kailāsa, you are that very same person;
you exist as my husband—thus have I perceived you in my heart.
Tell me of a vast sacred field (kṣetra) for me, for a joy arises in my ears."
"O Śambhu! Today I have come to know the field of Kuṅkumavāpikā, the most excellent among all sacred fords (tīrthas). Tell me its greatness:
whatever chanting, giving, fire-offerings, ritual acts, penance, and deeds have been performed [there]—"
In which part of the Kuṅkumavāpikā field would there be something imperishable?
Tell me the circular boundary of the field and the essence of the field;
it shall be visible to you in every way, like an *āmalaka* fruit in the palm of your hand. (71–72)
Śaṅkara said: "O Goddess of the gods, Saurāṣṭra is dear to me;
the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā is dear to both Kṛṣṇa and myself.
[It lies] between Prabhāsa, Raivataka mountain, and the river Śatruñjītā."
That sacred field is also very dear to me, even more so than Camatkārapura;
for there Acyuta, the Blessed One himself, is eternally present,
where indeed Lomaśa and Brahmā reside, and where I myself dwell.
The Saurāṣṭra region is a sacred field extending one hundred yojanas;
it is divine, born of jewels, and always bestows liberation upon living beings.
To the west is the Raivata seat, and to the east is the one called Śatruñjaya.
To the north is Camatkāra, and to the south is Somanātha.
Within the sacred seat (pīṭha) are the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake and the Kuṅkumavāpikā,
where the Bhadrā, Hiraṇyā, Svarṇarekhā, and Ujjasvatī rivers flow.
The Hariṇī, Unmattagaṅgā, Śatruñjitā, Sarasvatī, Nāganadī, Gomatī, Kṛṣṇā, and the divine Haripriyā— these rivers,
which always deliver one from worldly existence, are found in Saurāṣṭra.
Nyaṅkumatī, Vajriṇī, Māheśvarī, and Mahāsatī—
these are the sacred sites (tīrthas) situated in the Siṃha forest. Furthermore, those sacred sites which exist in Saurāṣṭra were established by the will of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
Reservoirs, wells, ponds, sprouts, lakes and the like,
as well as marshes, rivers, and the abodes of the gods—
these villages inhabited by the virtuous are indeed pure and destroyers of sin. (82)
In Saurāṣṭra and the Middle Country (Madhyadeśa) is Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa Hari.
In the north is the Lord Śrī Vāsudeva, the sovereign of Goloka;
in the west is the god Vāmana, and in the south is Somanātha.
To the east dwell the glorious Lords of the Gopīs, who deliver beings from worldly existence.
If even a man who is deceitful should reside in the central part [of this place],
whether he be sinful or treacherous, he is liberated from all transgressions.
O Goddess, I always dwell in the middle portion together with you.
There reside Brahmā and the other gods, headed by Nārāyaṇa; there the yogis and holy men worship the sage Lomaśa.
Whatever inauspicious karma has been committed by the human intellect,
may all of that go to dissolution by taking refuge in Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
I indeed abide there in the midst of them, bearing the name Gopāleśvara.
Because the kalpas are innumerable, people do not know me at all.
Out of affection for you and because of your devotion, I have revealed this to you here.
Indeed, having become Vaiṣṇava, I always dwell within [all beings].

O Goddess, the state that is attained through sacrifices, gifts, recitations, fire-offerings, Vedic studies, libations to the ancestors, Cāndrāyaṇa penances, fasts, and likewise by visiting sacred pilgrimage sites—
that state of Hari is superior to them all.
The great abode known as the Imperishable is attained by taking recourse to the middle [channel].
(92) And those who have entered the wombs of animals—beasts, birds, wild animals, and the like;
worms, insects, moths, and so forth; those dwelling in water and on land—(93)
Immobile beings and others that are mobile— children, the elderly, men, and women;
even Cāṇḍālas and Puṣkasas, as well as those who are despised and of low birth—
all embodied beings are liberated by dwelling within me.
Lomaśa, Nārasiṃha, Sanaka and the others who are long-lived;
Mārkaṇḍeya, Pañcaśikha, Voḍhu, Āsuri, as well as Dattātreya, Hanumān, Gaṇeśa, and Vyāsa. (95–96)
Jāmbavat, Kapila, and others who dwell in that sacred field—
by their power, living beings are liberated simply by residing there.
[It measures] ten thousand arbudas and three koṭis.
In Saurāṣṭra, sages always abide in invisible forms.
O Satī! It is possible to describe the qualities of Mount Meru and the drops of the oceans, but not those of this divine field of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa. (98–99)
"His virtues cannot be fully described even in hundreds of millions of years," Śaṅkara said to the Goddess, and then he became silent.
O Lakṣmī! Such are the qualities of my husband, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
Having heard of that supreme, meritorious field, Pārvatī remembered Hari.
Constantly established in meditation, she remembered with devotion the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa-field, which bestows excellent liberation.

"By hearing, reciting, remembering, or even bowing down to this, the sacred field bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, as well as prosperity upon living beings. Thus ends the five hundred and thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Kuṅkumavāpī Tīrtha Field in Saurāṣṭra, Spoken by Śaṅkara to Pārvatī," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga Cycle, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
← Chapter 534: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga) Chapter 535 [Author: Chapter 536 →
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī! Then the goddess Pārvatī, remembering the words of Hari from her dream, praised and made a request to her husband, Śaṅkara. (1)
"O Lord of my life! The Blessed Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa himself said [in a dream]: 'O Mother, why indeed do you never come to my sacred field?
O beloved, thus was I addressed by the Lord in a dream."
I desire to see that sacred field adorned by Gopāleśvara (3).
Where the glorious Lord Viṣṇu, the Master Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, resides together with ten million liberated souls and others— I desire to see that place (4).
That which is the mechanism of the wheel of the world, and that which is the mechanism of the wheel of dissolution—
wherever that Lord resides, I desire to see that place,
for it is under His authority that the protection of the worlds proceeds.
I wish to see that place where Kṛṣṇa resides.
(6) I wish to see that place where he who holds all the great elements within his own body is himself held by the land. (7)
Because [he appeared as] the Fish, the Tortoise, the Boar, and Narasiṃha;
as Kapila and Hari, as well as Vāsudeva and Pṛthu;
as Dattātreya, the Swan, Ṛṣabha, and the Lord Vāmana.
Parśurāma, as well as Yajñanārāyaṇa and the Kumāras;
Sanaka and the others, as well as Rāma, Hayagrīva, and Nārada;
Vyāsa, Buddha, and Kalki, as well as Haṃsa and Mohinī.
Indeed, Viṣṇu and these incarnations are born as protectors of the world;
I wish to see that place where he shines.
Rādhā, Ramā, Satī, Lakṣmī, Padmā, Padmāvatī, and Prabhā.
Pārvatī, Lalitā, Kṛṣṇā, Jayā, Māṇikī, Tulasī;
Vṛndā, Śrī, Kamalā, Sītā, Rukmiṇī, Draupadī, Śivā;
Gaṅgā, Sarasvatī, Haṃsā, Śāradā, Mañjulā, and Rati. (12–13)
Mūrti, Mānasā, Sandhyā, Gāyatrī, Mūlaprakṛti, Sāvitrī, Devikā, Mukti, Śānti, and Bhakti are his wives;
from them were born the Mothers who bestow happiness upon the worlds. (14)
I wish to see that place where he shines;
I wish to see that place which is the Lord, the refuge of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, and the witness of both dissolution and creation. (15–16)
I wish to see that place where the god who takes a thousand strides, who possesses a thousand rays of knowledge, and who has a thousand necks resides;
from whose navel, by mere thought, arose the house of Brahmā.
From the *dharmabindu* on his forehead was born the Lord Śivāpati;
from whose heart indeed Lakṣmīpati was born,
and he too was born from him who is his great-grandfather.
O Śambhu, I desire to see that place where he shines resplendent;
there, seated upon the couch of Śeṣa, he made his bed in the Ocean of Milk.
I wish to see him who was born from that [place], as well as his own incarnation.
I desire to behold the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa,

who indeed delights appropriately with those who eat sacrificial offerings, those who eat raw flesh, those who eat with emotion, those who eat nectar, and likewise those who do not eat at all. (21–22)
I desire to see that Lord in the form of a child as seen in my dream—
that Supreme Lord who is the refuge of three and four;
I desire to see that Lord who is the refuge of five and sixteen.

O Śambhu! I desire to see quickly that Supreme Lord, the most beloved of the beloved, whom all splendors, austerities, and offerings take refuge in; whom sacrifices, renunciations, and relinquishments resort to. (24–25)
Thus addressed, Lord Śaṅkara, beholding the devotion of the woman and remembering Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, spoke sweetly to the Goddess: "O blessed one!
O honorable one! O ever-worshipful one! O beloved of Kṛṣṇa! O devoted wife!"
I rejoice upon hearing your words, which are nourished by the water of devotion.
I am blessed that my wife in my home is firm in her vows toward Nārāyaṇa, devoted to her chosen deity who effects the salvation of the world. (27–28)
"O Queen, there is no one as fortunate as I, even throughout the worlds,
since my wife is delighted by service to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
O virtuous lady, I too have a desire to see that place."
Since a long time has passed, I shall indeed go with you once again.
O beloved, may your good fortune increase, for you have pleased my mind.
We two shall travel by way of the sky, accompanied by many offerings of worship.

We shall perform the ritual worship of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa according to the prescribed rites during the month of Kārtika; indeed, we shall reside there in that beautiful place. We shall observe Śivarātri on that very Raivataka mountain.

Then, on the third day of the waxing moon of Vaiśākha (Akṣayatṛtīyā), we shall bathe at Somanātha; and we shall perform the Śrāvaṇa rites at Kṛṣṇapaṭṭana on the Gomatī river. Having observed the Navarātra at Camatkārapura, we shall go indeed to Kailāsa.
"O Great Goddess, we shall come! Speak likewise of Nandīśvara;
speak of Gaṇeśa and Kārttikeya, and speak of the circle of Yoginīs.
Also [speak] of the circle of Durgās and the eleven Rudras as well. (35)
Gangā, Vīrabhadra, Caṇḍa, and Pracaṇḍa;
Śṛṅgin, Bhṛṅgin, Rīṭin, Kirīṭin, and Īśāna;
as well as Agni, Maṅgala, Candra, Kāla, and Bhairava. (36–37)
Tell me likewise of Durvāsas, as well as of Lābha, Toṣa, and the Siddhis; tell me of Ṛddhi, Hanumān, and my other servants.
Also, tell me of your female attendants, the goddesses who are eager for the journey.
"Let them all go, taking with them a complete array of vehicles.
Having thus received this command from Śaṅkara, the virtuous Pārvatī,
being exceedingly pleased, rose up and made a proclamation in every way.
Let them quickly prepare for a successful journey to the region of Saurāṣṭra,
where dwells Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama;
[and where dwell] Somanātha, Vāmana, Bhaveśa, and Gopikāpati.
In that regard, for the sake of pilgrimage, all those who travel through the sky must go to the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā, to the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake,
to the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, and to the sage Lomaśa. ||42-43||
"Having seen, honored, and served our mother Kambharālakṣmī and our father Gopālakṛṣṇa, we shall go having fulfilled our purpose.
Thus spoke those residents of Kailāsa, who were provided with many jewels and other riches.
On the seventh day of the dark fortnight of the month of Ūrja, we set out on our journey filled with joy. Drums were sounded and cries of victory were proclaimed;
all [the deities] appeared in the sky and arrived within the span of a single ghaṭikā.
Adorned in the sky by the mounts of millions of goddesses,
Mahādeva, followed by them, spoke at various spots:
"I am this Kedāranātha, and likewise I am Dakṣeśvara."
Arbuda and this Puṣkara are likewise sacred fields of the Siddhas;
Raṇeśvara is my field, as is this Saurāṣṭra.
This is Sāleśa, the Great Viṣṇu, and this is the Bhadrā, the great river.
This is the river Śatruñjitā and this is Dhūnikā of Gorakṣa; and here is Aśvapaṭṭasara, which is like a western bridge. In the central island is the temple where Kuṅkumavāpikā is located.
This supreme place is the abode of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
To the south, amidst the expanse of trees, lies this hermitage of Lomaśa;
furthermore, this vast and extensive Vyāghra forest is seen stretching far away.
"To the west of this Raivata mountain lies another [mountain] five *yojanas* away.
Having spoken thus, Śaṅkara and the others, together with Pārvatī and their attendants,
offered handfuls of flowers mixed with sandalwood paste and consecrated with *akṣata* grains.
Placed upon the sky-path above the seven-storied mansions, [the sound] "Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa is most victorious!
filled all directions with words and resonances on every side. (54–55)
Lomaśa, Kambharālakṣmī, Gopāla, Kṛṣṇa,
and the sages who ascend upwards— seeing them thus in the sky, they then approached, and shouts of "Victory!", "Salutations!", and "Blessed! arose at that time.
Having assembled, they descended into the western region of Setumāṇḍala.
That region of the western quarter became known by their name as Teru.
Having gone to the east, they indeed performed a circumambulation of the bridge (Setu).
That region then became radiant, and because they had previously departed,
it became a terrestrial realm through its connection with the path of the immortals.
And by virtue of the sound of the drum, the earth became Dundubharavā.
Having gone to the mouth of the Vyāghrāraṇya forest by way of the bridge,
those deities then arrived at the southern-western bridge;
full of eagerness, they proceeded to the seven-storied temple on Vāpīdvīpa.
Lomaśa and the other sages offered a welcome and auspicious reception to Śambhu, the God of gods; they performed a perfect worship of Satī and presented him with seats of kusha grass,
water for the arghya offering, and fruits.
Then they went to see Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, who was situated within the palace.
There he, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, shines resplendent,
attended by hundreds of long-lived beings and worshipped by millions of liberated souls.
The Lord is adorned with his incarnations and attended by the gods;
on the night of the seventh day of the dark fortnight of Kārttika,
he is worshipped by them and praised by his countless consorts, beginning with Rādhā and Ramā.

Then Kṛṣṇa was consecrated with the sixteenfold rites and other Vedic mantras beginning with those of Śaṅkara; he was then sprinkled with the lustration water (nīrājita) and adorned repeatedly. Pārvatī then applied a mark of musk mixed with saffron upon his forehead.
Then Śambhu applied an auspicious *tilaka*, beautiful with the splendor of unbroken grains of rice;
thereafter, Pārvatī likewise applied a lovely *tilaka* made of sandalwood paste.
Then [he beheld] Hari’s cheek, which possessed the loveliness of ten million Cupids.
Having seen the charming Kṛṣṇa, the Queen of the Gods repeatedly colored her [forehead] with moist saffron along with camphor;
she then presented various offerings, such as jewels and gold.
Having prostrated like a staff, they engaged in conversation with one another.
Then the young Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Lord and son of the cowherd,
himself rose quickly from his seat after the worship was concluded.
The Supreme Lord bowed at the feet of Śambhu and Pārvatī.
Having washed their feet according to the rites of hospitality, he drank the water.
Then Lomaśa, by means of a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), prepared for the army’s stay.
He constructed a great circular city extending as far as Āraivata,
within an area of twenty-five *yojanas* on the earth;
he settled all those people there, providing them with food, drink, hermitages, and other necessities.
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa himself served them all.
Then Śrīmad Gopālakṛṣṇa, his eyes filled with tears, said to Śambhu:
"I am blessed; I have fulfilled my purpose; my abode has been sanctified by you."
You have granted me the foremost place among all those worthy of veneration;
for these other lords and others have come to my hermitage.
Blessed is this bright earth as long as the cosmic egg shall endure.
And for that long, she shall remain renowned as a purifying sacred ford (tīrtha).
Then Mahālakṣmī, known as Kambharā, spoke auspiciously to Pārvatī:
"O Satī, what more need be said of the Mother of the World? I have been purified by you! || 78-79 ||
"My young child was raised by you, who dispel all suffering; O virtuous lady, she who could not be seen even through austerities has been seen by me today.
Indeed, the merit acquired in my previous births has been made manifest here."
"Welcome in every way! O daughter of Himavat, O consort of Śambhu, bestow peace upon us.
Together with my maidservants, I shall perform service; bring us well-being.
Having spoken thus, Kambharā Lakṣmī then began massaging her feet.
In accordance with Pārvatī’s manner of hospitality,
Śaṅkara and the other deities performed services such as attending to them; they attained a radiant splendor upon most divine couches that surpassed even Kailāsa.
All the devotees of Kṛṣṇa gave food, excellent drinks, and betel leaves with devotion; they all accepted them, and may you be happy. Then Śaṅkara and the others indeed slept, as did Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
He said to his mother Pārvatī, "O virtuous lady, my word has been fulfilled.
Ramā and my other wives offer you a warm welcome.
This is my daughter named Pārvatī, and this is her companion, Prabhā."
This Māṇikī is my beloved; this Lakṣmī is devoted to her husband.
This Rādhā is Lalitā; this Jayā is indeed Kamalā.
This Padminī is Bhārgavī; this Mukti is Devikā.
This one is from Campā, this one is of gold, this mare is of Śānti;
this one is from Muktikā, this one is from Mañjulā, and this one is from Haṃsā and possesses excellent qualities.
In this manner, thousands of others exist here indeed.
"Let them perform service for you, while I go to my own abode.
Having spoken thus, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa went to his palace and slept happily; and at dawn, various musical instruments were sounded.
Divine instruments were sounded and the people awoke;
for this was the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Kārtika, my Jayantī of Śrī Hari.
Then, by them [the sounds], there arose [awakening] for the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
Having performed their daily duties, Śaṅkara and the others—well-prepared and resplendent—came to the temple in the morning to perform worship and consecration.
So too did the deities led by Śaṅkara and Indra, as well as the sages and seers. (93–94)
The Pitṛs, Kaśyapas, and other Brāhmaṇas as well as humans;
liberated goddesses, celestial maidens, and Nāga maidens with their serpent-like coils;
Gandharvas, Kinnaras, Guhyakas, virtuous beings, Kiṃpuruṣas, and others.
Virtuous women devoted to their husbands, those observing the vow of Brahman, and women established in Yoga;
mothers, forest goddesses, rivers, cities, and cows; these Gopīs are streams of milk, streams of curds, and clarified butter. (96–97)
Having gathered honey-syrups, sugar, and waters from sacred fords, and having brought golden jars filled with fruits and unbroken grains,
they performed the rites of the water-procession while singing songs upon their heads.
They arrived at the divine, beautiful palace presided over by the Lord of All.
There were flower garlands, sandalwood, musk, unbroken grains of rice,
as well as the essence of flowers, fragrant oils, and perfumes.
Taking with them delightful substances fit for crushing and those that cause redness [to appear], they approached Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
Anādi-Śrī-Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa [donned] his auspicious golden garment.

Having dressed himself, he then sat down upon an excellent golden throne on the shore of the lake. Then, by means of the deities beginning with Bṛhaspati, the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) was performed, and the ceremonial sips of water (*ācamana*) were offered.
Having offered the *argha* and caused the ritual bath with water to be performed, thereafter,
a beautiful-looking milk-bath was administered in a vessel of milk.
Then, clouds released their waters from the path of the sky.
The cowherd women, headed by Devī, showered thick curds upon Kṛṣṇa.
(105) The gods released streams of clarified butter, and the forest deities poured forth honey.
The Earth and other elements bestowed upon him a brilliant bath of sugar-candy. (106)
The oceans, rivers, supreme sacred fords, and waters from other sources performed an auspicious consecration; then, having applied an ointment made from sandalwood oil,
they massaged him and bathed him, after which they dressed him in garments.
The gods gave divine [garments], and the Giver of Wealth (Kubera) gave ornaments;
others likewise gave everything most excellent,
such as collyrium for the eyes, crowns, earrings, necklaces, rings, chains, and so forth.
Having held up a parasol, beautiful whisks, and a black [antelope skin], the deities joyfully performed the *nīrājana* ceremony with principal Vedic hymns and the like.
Having offered forgiveness and a handful of flowers, they placed food before him.
The Blessed One ate, drank, and gave to those who had assembled;
for from the golden vessel, his grace was inexhaustible and multiplied ten millionfold.
Then the great sages, headed by Gālava, fed them.
In the evening, they performed dances, songs, and hymns of praise;
Hari bestowed various kinds of gifts in incalculable numbers.
At night, they performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) and offered oblations into the sacrificial fire.
Having brought the festival to a close, the lords of the city slept;
all ten million couples entered the peaceful yogic sleep.
By reading or hearing this, one shall partake in the fruit of that pilgrimage.

Thus ends the five hundred and thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of how, after learning [the truth] from Śaṅkara while he was absorbed in meditation, Śaṅkara—desiring to go to the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpī together with his attendants, Pārvatī, Śakti, Satī, Devadevī, Tīrtha, Divyeśvara, and all the embodied manifestations—performed the worship of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa on the Jayantī day of the eighth lunar tithi of the dark fortnight of the month of Kārttika," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
(Chapter 535, Book 1: *Kṛtayuga-santāna*)
Chapter 536 [Author:
Chapter 537 → Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Then, on the morning of the ninth day, the sounds of musical instruments arose;
the gods and others woke up, bathed,
and donned their garments for the purpose of beholding the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
They arrived and worshipped the son of Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa.
Śrīmad Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa, as well as the venerable sage Lomaśa and Patnīvrata and the others, performed for them a most Vedic worship.
The sages residing there performed the worship of the incarnations;
thus, millions of sacred sites (tīrthas) were produced here within this lake.
Lomaśa performed the worship of Viṣṇu, Śambhu, and Brahmā.
The illustrious Gopālakṛṣṇa performed the worship of Śambhu.
Śambhu said: "I always dwell in the presence of Kṛṣṇa;
indeed, I shall become famous here by the name Gopāleśvara."
Satī said: "I, Kambharā Kamaleśvarī, who am always worshipped by Kambharā and Kamalā, shall dwell by the side of Śaṅkara;
by my own will, I shall become renowned through a divine form."
Ganesha and Kartikeya shall be my two sons along with me;
they will be known by the names Śuka and Śuṇḍha respectively.
And I, being contented, virtuous, and devoted to the life of celibacy, [shall remain so]. (8–9)
"And I shall become known by the name Santoṣadurgā before the Lord.
In this way, the Gaṇas, headed by Nandi and Vīrabhadra,
will always dwell before the temple of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, each according to their respective names."

Then Śrīmad Gopālakṛṣṇa reverently performed the worship of Viṣṇu and Brahmā together with their consorts according to the prescribed rite. He also established a residence for them there in a divine form.
Indeed, those holy places (tīrthas) of the gods became tens of millions in number;
likewise, there were deities, hosts, others, trees, rivers, and creepers.
There were also Gandharvas, Kinnaras, and other sons of Kaśyapa endowed with divine vision.
Possessing divine bodies, they indeed made their dwellings in the presence of Kṛṣṇa.
By the command of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, they settled in every way within the sacred field of Saurāṣṭra;
wherever it was in their hearts, there they resided at that time.
Then, having partaken of food and drink, those gods—
the male and female deities— joyfully bowed and departed for their own city.
Thus indeed did the deities dwell there for four months.
What fortune of the earth shall I describe, which has never existed before nor will ever exist again?
At that time, the great king Dattātreya would daily recite the stories of the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā* in their proper sequence. (17–18)
The goddesses and the deities,
as well as all beings of the fourteen worlds— both insentient and sentient—
together with their senses, remained in their celestial cities with supreme devotion until the end of the month of Māgha.
On Śivarātri, they all went to the Raivataka mountain.
The blessed Dattātreya, however, took up a firm residence on the peak;
Ambā, Bhava, and Viṣṇu likewise occupied their respective abodes.
The Gaṇas, gods, and goddesses took up residence there as they pleased;
and having performed the Śivarātri vow on that Raivata mountain,
they then went from there to Somanātha, the supreme sacred field of Prabhāsa.
By them, the auspicious Akṣayya-tṛtīyā was established there at Prabhāsa.
Pārvatī said: "O Blessed One, why is this sacred field (kṣetra) called by the name 'Prabhāsa'? Tell me its meaning according to its true significance."
Śambhu said: "Listen, O beloved! That which shines forth through my yoga is indeed that supreme radiance, renowned by the name Vetra.
By my very boon, the splendors of the moon became mine."
Because its splendor shines forth when the waning has passed, it is celebrated as Prabhāsa.
Prabhā, the daughter of the Sun, who was formerly the beloved of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa on earth, dwelt there in the past in the form of a beautiful maiden. || 26-27 ||
It is called Prabhāsa because it is where Prabhā attained the seat of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa through her ascetic penance;
and because it is there that the gods obtained splendor through their fierce austerities.
That which first appeared exists in all sacred fords (tīrthas).
Where Śrī and Bhāratī cast the Vāḍava fire into the ocean,
that shining place indeed became known as Prabhāsa.

That ninth part of Saurāṣṭra which shines upon the earth is called Prabhāsa because of its fame; it bestows radiance (*prabhā*) and knowledge (*jñāna*). Furthermore, that preeminent splendor (*prakṛṣṭā bhā*) which resided in the mouths of the Brahmins is *Bhāratī*. (31)
That sacred field, Prabhāsa, is indeed composed of the Vedas and is dear to the Brāhmaṇas.
Because the Sun-god is visibly present there in the form of the Arka tree from which he was born, it is therefore called Prabhāsa, as declared by the gods.

In ancient times, the splendor of the sun was unbearable; Viśvakarman, having ground the sun on a whetstone, rendered its brilliance manageable. He then divided the splendors thus diminished by the whetstone for the purpose of making weapons.
Weapons were fashioned by Viśvakarman from these splendors;
nevertheless, a remnant of that splendor remained here near the ocean.
That which was gradually established there became the tranquil Prabhāsa.
A sixteenth part of the sun’s splendor became established within the solar orb; that energy of his which consisted of the *Ṛgveda* was made stable at Prabhāsa.
And the heaven was brought to full nourishment by the energy consisting of the *Yajurveda*.
Heaven was nourished by Sāman and by the splendor of Viśvakarman;
the discus was fashioned by another, as were the trident of Viṣṇu and Hara,
the palanquin of Dhanada, and likewise the staff of the Lord of the Dead.
Likewise, the spear of Kārttikeya, the mace of Hanumān, the sword of the Goddess, the noose of Mahākāla, the Pāśupata weapon,
and the Nārāyaṇa weapon were each fashioned from a portion [of that power]. (1.536.40)
Indeed, other weapons as well were fashioned there according to their respective requirements.
Thus, O Goddess, the great splendor of the Sun situated near the ocean— that Prabhāsa— is that great sacred field (kṣetra), my own dwelling place.
To the south of Māheśvarī and the Nyaṅkumatī,
extending for twelve yojanas toward Prabhāsa, there is a mountain that has removed all recollection [of worldly desires].
There, the Sun attained the state of the Arkavṛkṣa tree through his lineage and sub-lineage.
Whoever worships the *arka* tree, his leprosy shall perish.
To the southeast of Someśvara, I am established as Siddheśvara;
here Jaigīṣavya, the perfected one, performed austerities for a thousand years.
Having established it, O Daughter of the Mountain, I am known as Siddheśvara.
There, the Vālakhilyas attained supreme perfection through their ascetic penance.
O Holy One, this extends from Kṛtasmara up to Arkasthala.
The eight Siddhis dwell here, devoted to my service.
Brāhmī and Hiraṇyā are indeed the two rivers, the daughters of Brahmā;
likewise, there are Maṅkīśa-ṛṣi and the Mothers beginning with Sunandā. (47–48)

Having seen Mount Mahādri, which preserves all that was done, the twice-born sages, undertaking the journey together with us, took up their residence there. Atri, Vasiṣṭha, Pulaha, Kratu, Bhṛgu, and Pulastya— 49. And having seen Mount Mahādri, which preserves all that was done, the twice-born sages, undertaking the journey together with us, took up their residence there. Atri, Vasiṣṭha, Pulaha, Kratu, Bhṛgu, and Pulastya—
Marīci, Kaśyapa, Bhāradvāja, Yama, Aṅgiras, Manu; Āpastamba, Sāṃvarta, Kāvya, Kātyāyana;
Gautama, Śaṅkha and Likhita, Vācaspati, and Aruṇi. (1.536.50–51)
Jāmadagnya, Yājñavalkya, Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, Vibhāṇḍaka,
Gārgya, Śaunaka, Dālbhya, Vyāsa, the auspicious Uddālaka,
Nārada, Parvata, and Durvāsas, the fierce ascetic.
Śākalya, Gālava, Jābāli, Mudgala, and Ṛbhu;
Viśvāmitra, Kauśika, Jahnu, and likewise Viśvāvasu; Dhaumya, Śatānanda, Śākaṭāyana, and Ekata. (53–54)
Dvita, Trita, and others who had assembled there likewise constructed their own dwellings as they desired at that site of Prabhāsa.
All of them remained on Mount Kṛta, blazing with the power of their ascetic penance.
On Mondays, the lords worshipped Somanātha.
Having bathed and performed the twilight prayers and other rites, and having worshipped Nārāyaṇa,
they placed a most beautiful pitcher within a truly suitable and delightful pavilion.
Richly adorned with the beauty of mango sprouts and worshipped with sandalwood paste and unbroken rice grains,
one should prepare a half-vessel filled with saffron and sandalwood,
accompanied by an image [of Śiva] joined with half of Umā’s body and endowed with half of Śaṅkara’s form.
There, those twice-born ones worshipped Śambhu together with Umā, who was adorned with ornaments as he was and decorated with garments and other finery,
offering various kinds of foods to be chewed and eaten, fruits, drinks, and ointments.
With the finest incense, lamps, and lustrations (*nīrājana*), and with hymns of praise, the lords worshipped them,
begged for their forgiveness, offered handfuls of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*),
and performed singing, chanting, and dancing accompanied by keeping watch through the night.
Whoever should observe the nine Mondays with devotion,
he too shall become equal to Śiva, free from old age and death.
When the ninth Monday has arrived, one should perform the great concluding rite (udyāpana).
One should have the mandala, the pavilion, and the sacrificial pit constructed, well-adorned.
One should have a beautiful altar made, square and well-painted.
And one should have a lotus drawn in the center of the grain-mandala.
In the eight directions, he should place water-pots individually, each containing gold;
he should worship the nine Durgās, and in the center, the Lord Hara as Someśvara.
The observer of the vow should worship the golden image mounted upon a golden bed.
Having gratified Hara with perfumes, garlands, incense, food offerings, garments,
ornaments, mirrors, umbrellas, chowries, betel, lamps, bells, and canopies,
one should thereafter give a gift to the venerable Guru.
One should cause a fire sacrifice (homa) to be performed and offer an auspicious oblation (bali) of milk-rice (pāyasa).
At night, one should remain awake, drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and meditate upon Hara.
Then, having bathed at dawn, one should again meditate upon Soma for a moment.
Then, having worshipped Someśa with various kinds of foods made from milk, sugar-candy, and other ingredients, one should offer a food-oblation (naivedya) to Śambhu.
One should feed the Brahmins, the gods, the sages, and satisfy the ancestors.
One should honor guests and likewise feed the maidens;
one should cause the gift of clothing to be given and arrange for the gift of cows.
One should receive blessings and perform the ritual dismissal.
Thus, having properly observed the vow, she obtains imperishable merit, as well as abundance of grain, wealth, and so forth, along with sons, wives, and the like.
She shall not suffer from barrenness, and her poverty shall come to an end. (73)
The sages and the gods likewise observed the Monday vow (somavāravrata);
they gave gifts in that manner and performed the concluding rites (udyāpana).
Śaṅkara said: "O Queen of the Gods! having abandoned the defects born of one's own nature..."
A person should create a sacred ford (*tīrtha*); by that, one obtains eternal fruit.
Walking on foot to visit sacred fords is a supreme austerity that bestows fruit. A pilgrim who is without an umbrella and sandals shall destroy his sins.
One should not eat food belonging to another, for even alms are indeed "belonging to another.
A seeker of liberation should remember the deities, the gurus, the mother and father, as well as virtuous people and one's family at the sacred ford (tīrtha). (77–78)
One should not perceive faults in a sacred place (*tīrtha*), for they are as indestructible as adamantine cement (*vajralepa*).
There, one should plunder while dancing, singing, and laughing;
with all one's limbs greyed by dust, one should remember Lord Hari at the sacred place.
"Oṃ, salutations to Somanātha; salutations to the Lord of Pārvatī.
(1.536.80) One should recite this mantra at Somanātha, which destroys all sins.
O Maheśvarī, one should meditate upon me as Someśvara together with you. (81)
"Oṃ, obeisances to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; obeisances!"—thus one should cause people to hear and have them perform the worship of Hari.
One should bow to Vaiṣṇavas on the path and hold the Lord of Śrī within one's heart.
Indeed, there is no country on the surface of the earth equal to Saurāṣṭra.
O Pārvatī, I have no holy site on earth equal to Somanātha;
it pacifies the sins of sinners and grants the desires of those who observe vows.
The gift of the Tulāpuruṣa brings good fortune to the unfortunate and bestows the world of Brahmā; likewise are the gifts of the Brahmāṇḍa,
the Earth, a sacred field, and the Kalpavṛkṣa.
The giving of gold, the wish-fulfilling cow, and elephants and horses;
(86) the giving of chariots, houses, and jewels;
and the giving of water-pots, daughters, and branches of knowledge. (87)
The gifts of wish-fulfilling creepers, the gift of life, the offering of water,
likewise the gift of a livelihood, the gift of a garden, the gift of a forest,
the gift of a seashore, and the gift of mountains. (88)
One should perform the gift of cows and buffaloes, the gift of groves and gardens,
the gift of knowledge, the gift of liberation, the gift of heaven, the offering of fruits,
and the gift of one's entire possessions in order to attain [the goal] once again.
The gift of wells, tanks, and ponds, the giving of stones and wood,
the offering of vehicles, machines, palanquins, and the like, and the presentation of sweet honey—
these should be performed according to one's ability at my sacred site in Saurāṣṭra.

One should have a white palace or mansion built, and one should restore what is dilapidated. (92) One should revive a ruined sacred site and practice benevolence toward others; O virtuous lady, for those who perform acts of service for others, the highest spiritual welfare shall accrue. (93)
Some men [attain it] through the power of charity, some through ritual bathing;
some people through the power of meditation, and others through yoga;
some through knowledge, some through recitation, and others through service.
Some [attain it] even by hearing the narrative; others through chanting and dancing; others through worship; others through visiting sacred fords; others through prostrations and hymns of praise;
others through renunciation with devotion; and others through service and the recitation of mantras. (95–96)
In every way, those situated at a sacred ford attain a good rebirth through the spirit of surrender.
O beloved, even one devoid of sense faculties becomes purified by a sacred ford;
having met his end at Prabhāsa, he shall become my own possession.
"Having meditated upon Prabhāsa in this manner, my follower should take refuge [there].
Thus, O Lakṣmī, was it told by Śambhu at Somatīrtha;
and the deities made the essential forms of the Cakras for Pārvatī.

"By reading or hearing this [account], even those residing in another land shall obtain the fruit of a pilgrimage to sacred sites (tīrtha-yātrā), as well as worldly enjoyment and liberation. Thus ends the five hundred and thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of Śaṅkara and Others’ Pilgrimage to Raivataka (Giranāra) Mountain and Somanātha Tīrtha in the First Section on the Kṛta Yuga of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā; the Etymology of the Name Prabhāsa; the Nature of Arka as the Sun-Tree; the Worship of Somanātha; Charitable Gifts and Other Matters; and the Majesty [of the Tīrtha]. || 536 ||
