Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, Lakṣmī! Other sacred fords (tīrthas) have also been described;
I shall tell them to you as well, just as they were told by Śambhu to the daughter of Himavat.
The Vāḍavāgni-kṣepa-tīrtha is always situated in the ocean;
one should perform a bath there, and one will become as purifying as fire.
Then one should go to Padmaka and have the hair on one's body shaved there.
Meditating upon Somanātha in her heart, she should cast her hair there;
when this is done, the sins residing in the hair dissolve.
A woman whose husband is living should have only a finger’s breadth of hair cut from the back of her head.
Then, having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should bathe in the ocean waters:
"O Agni, you are the womb; you are Iḍā, the body, the placer of seed, and the navel of immortality.
To you, whose womb is jewels, salutation! O water, you are the obstruction. (5)
Having bathed thus, one should satisfy the ancestors with water mixed with sesame seeds.
(6) Long ago, at Prabhāsa, the gods commenced a long sacrificial session (*dīrghasattra*) and gave their entire possessions to the preeminent Brahmins residing in Prabhāsa. (7)
Then the twice-born, though dwelling at a great distance, honored that gift;
even the gods, including Indra, desired the offering of sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
Yet, out of fear of the rejection of their requests, the gods remained empty-handed despite the giving of all one's possessions.
Having seen the Brahmins, they vanished, and the Brahmins followed after them. The gods entered the ocean and remained there within its belly;
the Ocean, assuming a physical form, stood upon the shore to pay them honor.
He gave the Brahmins delicious, artificial food mixed with fish; all the Brahmins ate it from golden vessels,
and they did not realize at all that hidden meat had been consumed.
Formerly, those Brahmins were indeed able to travel through the sky.
Immediately after their meal, they suddenly fell to the ground.
Full of wonder, they said: "What could be the cause of this? (12–13)
There, one [brahmin], through the practice of yoga, understood the activity of the ocean;
having realized that they had indeed been deceived, the brahmins spoke to the ocean:
"Our flesh has been concealed by you, combined with food."
"Since food was indeed given [to you] by me, therefore become untouchable at all times.
Thereupon, for a thousand years, the ocean became untouchable;
then, out of grief, he caused his own waters to dry up.
As soon as the land had taken form and the gods went to the Grandfather,
grains were produced on the earth through the union of oceanic waters and rain;
by means of that, all creatures were born and nourished in every way.
"Protect the water of the ocean so that it does not go to dryness. Having heard this, Brahmā went to the shore;
to prevent [the sages] from touching [the water], he requested the Brahmins.
"Let the Brahmins accept these jewels from the ocean, and let them, endowed with forgiveness, release the ocean from its curse.
Thus the Brahmins petitioned Brahmā: "Please act accordingly."
Then Brahmā said to the ocean: "You shall become pure in three ways.
At the times of the lunar festivals, at the confluences of rivers, and always at the sacred sites on your banks, you shall be pure; be the provider of purification through touch and bathing."
"He shall always be worthy of worship there and elsewhere during the worship of the gods;
moreover, the water used for your consecration shall always be pure.
Thus did the Brahmins and others bring about the destruction of his untouchability.
They all took the jewels and departed for their own abodes.
Then, whoever bathes properly in the salt-water ocean shall obtain here the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices.
Those people who die within the ocean of Śrīsomeśa,
even if they are sinners, shall go to heaven with their impurities shaken off.
Thus indeed did the watery ocean attain its state of purity in ancient times.

The sacred field of Someśa, extending as far as the ocean, consists entirely of ten million holy sites (tīrthas); it is supreme and bestows both heaven and liberation. Having bathed there in this manner, the observer of vows should then proceed to behold Somanātha.
Having bathed [the image] according to the prescribed rite, one should recite the Śatarudriya.
One should bathe it with milk, curd, ghee, and honey;
then, with sugarcane juice, and thereafter smear it with saffron.
Having gratified him with fragrant sandalwood mixed with camphor, uśīra, and musk,
as well as with incense, lamps, garments,
and food offerings, one should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) and likewise offer salutations.

One should perform praise, the eight-limbed prostration and so forth, singing, instrumental music, and dancing; one should circumambulate [the deity], recount sacred stories, and listen to the teachings of the Supreme Lord.
One should give wealth to Brahmins, ascetics, the destitute, the blind, and the miserable.
The observer of the vow should cause food and fine garments to be given and should meditate [upon them].
He who performs this according to the prescribed rite at the Someśvara Tīrtha will be wealthy for seven births and thereafter go to Kailāsa.
One should perform the evening worship of Māra; for him, liberation will certainly occur.
Now, O Lakṣmī! There is the Pañcanada Tīrtha, which bestows liberation.
[The rivers there are] Hariṇī, Brahmiṇī, Nyaṅku, Kapilā, and Sarasvatī.
At Prabhāsa, the Sarasvatī indeed flows in five streams.
Listen, Lakṣmī! Hear how in ancient times that Sarasvatī arrived here.
Long ago, Indra and the others, having conquered the Daityas, returned to the earth.
Having seen the hermitage of Dadhīci, they beheld the sage Dadhīci;
setting down their weapons before him, they indeed entrusted them to him, saying, "Protect these,
for they may have to be returned to us if we should have battle with our enemies."
Having released the weapons, the sage went to heaven after a hundred years had passed.
Having drunk up the weapons along with the water, he went to the Himalayas;
there, in the midst of *pippala* trees, he performed supreme austerity.
Then the gods, having assembled together, requested weapons from him in every way.
Dadhīci said: "Indeed, the forms of bones dwell within my body.
Having brought the cows from Goloka by means of Karkaśajihvika and the others—"
"Nandā, Subhadrā, Surabhi, Suśīlā, and likewise Sumanā—let them command me to lick up these bones for the sake of obtaining them. By this means, the gods indeed obtained the bones. (42–43)
Touched by the gods, those cows became pure and worthy of worship as they remained;
only their single mouth was not touched, being smeared with blood.
Having fashioned weapons from bones, the gods went forth into the sky.
To Subhadrā, Dadhīci begot a young son named Suplakṣaka.
He asked his mother, "O mother, where is my father?
She replied, "He has met his death for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods."
Then Bāla indeed performed austerities on the Himalaya;
from his thigh was born the one called Vaḍavā, who was of great size. She too became full of splendor, and that splendor issued forth externally.
This Aurva, the submarine fire, fiercely consumed that forest.
The gods said to Sarasvatī, "O Goddess, please extinguish him!
Sarasvatī, however, took him in the form of a child to Prabhāsaka.
Having arrived, he cast the submarine fire (vaḍavānala) into the ocean;
the young maiden’s forearm drank the salt water.
Remaining there, it indeed nourishes [the sea], yet even today it does not release the ocean.
Wherever she experienced torment, for a moment she would become invisible;
then, becoming cool again, she would seize [him] and lead him away, meeting him upon the ground.
Hidden in some places, she was visible in others. 51–52.
Having done this, she went to the ocean, cast herself in, and indeed dwelt there for a long time.
That Prācī Sarasvatī, however, remains eternally at Prabhāsa.
There, indeed, were four sages who were like Viṣṇu.
Hiraṇya, Vajra, Nyaṅku, and Kapila—
these were also summoned individually by them for the sake of bathing in the Sarasvatī.
Then Sāgara also suddenly stood before her.
For the sake of serving the sages, she manifested in five forms:
Hariṇī, Vajriṇī, Nyaṅkvī, Kāpilī, and likewise Sāgarī. All five of them are destroyers of sin and are always purifiers of the sinful.
She is the destroyer of the faults of meat-eating, drinking liquor, theft, and addiction to women.
Kṛtasmara, the obstructer, was burnt by that fire; those stones became white, known as *rāsanya* and *saudhakārikā*. (57–58)
In the interval of Cākṣuṣa, the fire was the son of Dadhīca;
in the interval of Vaivasvata, it was Aurva Bhārgava, the submarine fire.
That which is the fire from the forehead of Śaṅkara is said to be this very same one.
And here at the ford of the Sarasvatī is Gūheśvara, a most excellent holy site;
at the confluence with the Āmardakī river is Saṃgameśvara-tīrtha;
likewise there is Govatsaka-tīrtha and the supremely auspicious Jhillī-tīrtha.
The abode of the sage Kūṣmāṇḍa, known as Kūṣmāṇḍeśvara, is located there;
having arrived at that place, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa was then welcomed by the sage Kūṣmāṇḍa with a greeting to Sarasvatī.

She dispelled the exhaustion born from the burden of the submarine fire (vāḍavānala) and quelled the heat merely by the touch of her own hand. O Lord, that maiden requested [this] while she was alone with me. (63–64)
"And how, O Hari, is a maiden to dwell here without a protector? There is no one here in this forest to protect me or be my guardian!
Therefore, O Puruṣottama, become my protector here."
"Or else, having come to your home at either Kuṅkumavāpī or the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake, I shall remain there at your feet. Having spoken thus to Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, her eyes became moist with tears.
For a moment, the young maiden felt as if she were destitute and without a protector;
then the glorious Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, taking her by the hand,
drove away her sorrow, and she likewise [embraced] Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
The virtuous lady clung to his neck and chose Nārāyaṇa as her husband.
Sarasvatī placed a garland of flowers around Kṛṣṇa’s neck;
Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa accepted it with deep affection.
Having thus provided her with a protector, he said, "O Goddess of gods! remain firm here in the form of a river for the sake of uplifting the world.
Then Sarasvatī said, "O Lord, I cannot exist without my master."
"Therefore, how can you remain here? Dwell here as the bestower of liberation.
Thus addressed, the Blessed Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa himself, the manifest Lord of Sarasvatī, became the Pippala tree.
There, where that beloved one resides, stands the imperishable Pippala tree;
at its root, Sarasvatī always remains, having attained union with him.
There, O Lakṣmī, I am eternally absorbed in dissolution in the form of Kṛṣṇa.
I indeed exist, yet people do not know me as one within the range of their vision.
There, I always effect the liberation of my ancestors through the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa).
And Lakṣmī always dwells at my root, free from any reproach.
Then, after some time, he said: "I shall become the husband of many thousands of married women and meet my dissolution in that very place.
Having spoken thus, he transformed his virtuous wife into the form of water.
Taking my beloved along with a second young woman,
I, accompanied by my newlywed bride, went to the Aśvapaṭṭa lake,
my own abode, and I dwelt there together with her.
There, the goddess Sarasvatī always dwells at my feet;
she shines forth, bestowing victory upon the speech of people.
Thus, she is the daughter of Brahmā, the resident of Truth.
The maiden residing on the Golden Mountain arrived at Kurukṣetra;
likewise at Bhadrāvarta, Puṣkara, Śrīsthala, Siddhabhūtala, Pāñcāla, Aśvapaṭṭasara, and Svarṇapura. (81–82)
On Mount Raivata, at Prabhāsa, and likewise again at Bahusthala—
due to the difference in time and by the power of the devotees' worship—
as well as at Prayāga and other such supreme holy sites (tīrtha) for the sake of divine rites.
In the course of my travels, this beloved Prabhā, who is the eastern Sarasvatī—the ladder to heaven—came to Prabhāsa;
she remains here, abiding by my word, bringing welfare to all living beings. (84–85)
Those who drink from these three rivers—
the Candrabhāgā, the Gaṅgā, and the divine Sarasvatī,
as well as the Yamunā, the Gaṇḍakī, or the river Svarṇarekhā— are gods, not men. (86)
Just as cows are wish-fulfilling, yielding fruit at all times;
those three rivers are like the *cintāmaṇi* gem, fulfilling all desires. [There dwell] eighty-eight thousand sages whose vital energy is drawn upward (*ūrdhvaretas*). 87–88.
What indeed could be superior to that holy site where Nara,
together with Nārāyaṇa, dwells in another age?
Likewise [superior is the merit] of those who follow him in his form as Kalki, the future incarnation.
The Destroyer (Śiva), for the sake of destroying his faults, shall bathe here again and again.
The Prācī Sarasvatī destroys defects and even washes away [sins] born of ignorance.
Having fasted for three nights, one should bathe for the pacification of defects.
Having cast off the body on the northern bank of the Sarasvatī,
he indeed proceeds to the eternal world of Brahmā, which is free from rebirth and death;
and for the performer of the śrāddha, there shall be the deliverance of twenty-one generations of his lineage.
Whatever object of desire one contemplates when the departure of the vital breath occurs, endowed with that very state, such a person becomes upon departing.
Formerly, there was a king known by the name Bṛhadratha. (93–94)
He had a virtuous wife, the chaste Indumatī by name. Once, a sage known as Kaṇva arrived at his house.
The king welcomed him and inquired after his welfare and other matters.
Then that sage delivered a discourse on the Dharma in the presence of the king.
Having bowed to the sage, Indumatī asked about her own previous birth: "How did I obtain this kingdom, happiness, and good fortune, as well as a husband who is like a god? (96–97)
"Whose fruit is this happiness, honor, and prosperity that I have obtained?
Kaṇva replied, "Listen, O Queen! Do not be angry with me.
In another body, you were indeed an Ābhīrī woman devoid of virtuous character."
At that time, she went to Prabhāsa in the region of Saurāṣṭra to bathe; there,
having learned of the greatness of the holy site from the mouths of Brahmins, you offered a beautiful golden bracelet from your hand.
"By that merit, you shall become the daughter of the King of Daśārṇa on earth; you shall be wedded by Bṛhadratha and born as his most excellent queen.
Having heard this greatness of Prabhāsa, she once again—
Having performed the ritual ablution at the sacred ford (tīrtha) in the ocean, she cast her bracelet back into the water once more.
Thereupon, the auspicious goddess became a resident of heaven with a lifespan lasting for a kalpa.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, is indeed the majesty of the waters of the Prabhāsa ocean.
Śaṅkara recounted again and again all the stories concerning Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, which bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation. There, Pārvatī cast her golden bracelet into the ocean.
Śaṅkara became pleased, and the goddesses also restored those [limbs].

Thus ends the five hundred and thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of Vahnitīrtha and the Purification of the Ocean, the Account of Dadhīca, Plakṣaka, Vaḍavānala, and Sarasvatī, Sarasvatī Consisting of Five Streams, Pippaladruma and Kūṣmāṇḍatīrtha, the Attainment of Queenhood by the Ābhīrī through the Gift of a Bracelet to the Ocean, and the Greatness of Charity," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛtayuga in the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīyasaṃhitā*.
