Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī! Then Śambhu spoke to Satī Pārvatī:
"The Great Viṣṇu, known as Varāha, is established at Somatīrtha."
Likewise, Brahmā and Gaṇeśa stands there under the name Heramba;
likewise, he who is named Kapardin also stands there as the protector of the sacred field (kṣetra).
Therefore, at that great pilgrimage site (tīrtha), [resides] Kapardi, the illustrious Lord of the Gaṇas.
Likewise, Viṣṇu as Varāha is always to be worshipped and honored by people.
(3) O Goddess, in ancient times there was a king known as Śaśabindu.
Once, together with his wife, he traveled along the path of the sky. (4)
He traveled by celestial chariot to the supreme sacred site of Prabhāsa on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Phālguna at the onset of night. Then,
in the field of Someśvara, he saw those observers of vows who had assembled there.
And seeing the excellent sages standing there awake,
he bowed to Somanātha and the sages, and proceeded toward Kedāraka;
there he worshipped the Linga situated there with supreme devotion.
Those sages asked:
"O King, tell us the reason why you abandoned Somaka and worship Kedāra instead.
The king said: "In former times, I was born of the Śūdra caste in Saurāṣṭra."
I was with my wife when we arrived here at this field.
There, by the Hariṇī river, lotuses were seen by me; those were then gathered by me for the purpose of selling them.
I stood near Somanātha during the day for the purpose of selling [the fruit],
but even after the sun had set, no one purchased them at all.
Then, overcome by hunger, I went into the vicinity of the Liṅga.

There, I saw a certain independent woman named Anaṅgā, who was observing the Śivarātri vow; she was devoted to the festival of singing and dancing during the night vigil. Thus questioned by me, "What is this that you are doing? [she replied: (12–13).
She then spoke to me regarding the Śivarātri vow:
"The performer of the vow becomes free from suffering and endowed with prosperity;
for him, the destruction of fear, disease, and misfortune occurs at every step. (14)
Then, having heard this, my mind became intent upon that vow.
A natural inclination toward fasting arose within me at the lotus-pool.
Having bathed there, I then worshipped the Lord Rudreśa with those lotuses.
I performed the vigil together with my wife, desiring auspiciousness;
by that merit, I am now a king and this beloved woman is my queen.
Remembering my past lives along with my wife, I have indeed come to Rudreśvara.
I worship here Kedāra, which is situated here and was worshipped in ancient times.
Therefore, Rudreśvara is a sacred ford that bestows a kingdom through its worship;
it grants dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, as well as peace and happiness.
The woman who was then an independent worshipper became the captivating celestial nymph named Rambhā. Thus,
the Kedāra Rudreśa Tīrtha is established there.
Then one should worship Hara there as Śvetaketvīśvara.
In ancient times, King Śvetaketu performed supreme penance here and attained liberation; thus Śambhu became known there as Śvetaketvīśvara.
Then one should go to Ādityeśvara, where Hara is situated in the east.
Then, for the sake of destroying Tripura, Śambhu shed a tear from his own eye out of anger; that became the earthly planet Maṅgala (Mars).
Worshipped by him there, Hara became Bhaumeśvara.
Thus, O beloved, the Navagraha-tīrtha exists there;
it consists of those three powers of Nārāyaṇa: knowledge, action, and will.
Maṅgalā and Viśālā—these four stand there eternally.
Among them, the supreme *tīrtha* here in Prabhāsa bestows peace.
Likewise, Viśālākṣī was formerly born from Viṣṇu for the sake of battle.
For the sake of destroying the Daityas, O Lakṣmī, I indeed went to that holy site of Prabhāsa in a former age together with you. Likewise,
[I visited] Lakṣmītīrtha and the holy site of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.

The auspicious Kāmatīrtha and Ratitīrtha exist at Prabhāsa, bestowing liberation through the mere sight of them upon one’s own excellent field of merit. Gaurītīrtha and Iṣātīrtha shine forth as destroyers of sin.
In ancient times, Nārada once performed the Puṇḍarīka sacrifice;
that site is known as Nāradakratutīrtha and is located in Prabhāsa.
Formerly, the sage Gautama also arrived there for the purpose of pilgrimage.
He performed penance for four months; therefore it is called the Gautama Tīrtha.
In the first Kṛta Yuga, there was indeed a great Daitya named Meghavāhana.
He possessed a massive body, extending a yojana in both length and breadth.
Having ascended his two sandals himself, Ādinārāyaṇa slew that great Daitya; thus it is called Pādukātīrtha. The Daitya was killed by the sandal when it was struck against his chest.
Seated upon my sandals, I myself, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa,
abide at the Somaka Tīrtha as the bestower of liberation and the destroyer of demons. Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have narrated to you this majesty whose presiding deity is Viṣṇu.
Now, there are indeed the holy bathing places (tīrthas) of the eleven Rudras located there:
Ajaikapād, Ahirbudhnya, Virūpākṣa, Raivata, Hara, Bahurūpa, Tryambaka, and Sureśvara. (36–37)
Prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna are the vital airs;
and nāga, kūrma, kṛkala, devadatta, and dhanañjaya;
together with the self (ātman), these eleven are born in succession as the Rudras.
Those who were formless attained a physical form at that sacred site in Prabhāsa.
Nandin also performed penance there before Hara, the Conqueror of Death;
thus, the Nandi-tīrtha exists there, bestowing great merit.
In former times, having become cows, the Earth arrived there for the sake of pilgrimage;
the virtuous one bathed Someśa with a stream of milk.
Then, having bathed, she dissolved into that very place where the Gotīrtha is located.
Born from the earth through yoga, he became the beloved remover of the torment of sin. (42) Now, previously there was a Rākṣasa named Virāva in the ocean;
that man-eater was slain there by Viṣṇu with the Sudarśana [discus]. (43)
This very place, Virāvalayana, has arisen in the western region;
it is a most beautiful sacred ford (tīrtha) purified by the discus of Viṣṇu.
There, at Virāvalīnaka, I, the wielder of the discus, am to be worshipped.
My worshiper shall surely go to the supreme abode; of this there is no doubt.
(45) Now, twelve suns first go to Prabhāsa for the sake of beholding Viṣṇu, and from there to Aśvapaṭṭasāra. (46)
They go to the sacred field to behold Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
Viṣṇu, Dhātṛ, Bhaga, Pūṣan, Maitra, Indra, Varuṇa, Aryaman, Vivasvat,
Aṃśumat, Tvaṣṭṛ, and Parjanya— these indeed are the twelve.
At the conclusion of their respective months, they bathe and proceed to Prabhāsa.
Viṣṇu indeed bathes in Caitra, and Aryaman likewise in Vaiśākha;
Vivasvat in the month of Jyeṣṭha, and Aṃśumat likewise in Āṣāḍha.
Parjanya bathes in the month of Śrāvaṇa, and likewise Varuṇa in Bhādrapada;
Indra in the month of Āśvayuja, and Dhātṛ bathes in Kārttika.
Similarly, Mitra in Mārgaśīrṣa, and Pūṣan proceeds [to bathe] in Pauṣa.
Bhaga bathes there in Māgha, and Tvaṣṭṛ in Phālguna;
having performed their austerities and bathed at the end of their respective months, these indeed depart.
Thus exists the auspicious Ādityasthala Tīrtha in Prabhāsa.
Then, during the festival of Somanātha, Brahmā arrived at the age of eight years for the consecration ceremony; his seat was located to the east.
That place is called Brahmatīrtha, which destroys all sins through bathing.
Having placed the eight-year-old Brahmā upon a beautiful chariot together with Sāvitrī on the full-moon day of the month of Kārttika,
one should certainly cause the procession to be conducted toward Somanātha.
One should worship with a spirit of devotion using the sixteen and other ritual offerings.
One should by all means draw the chariot of that Four-faced Lord,
and then re-establish him in his temple accompanied by musical instruments and dances.
Seeking the welfare of the kingdom, one should organize a chariot procession.
O Lakṣmī! I shall tell you where and where the Grandfather (Brahmā) resides upon the surface of the earth, throughout the creation, in every Kalpa and even in other Kalpas. || 57–58 ||
In due time, one should also remember that place which bestows happiness;
that best of gods at Puṣkara, the Great-grandfather at Gayā, Vedagarbha at Kānyakubja, and Caturmukha at Bhṛgukaccha. (59)

Bṛhaspati, the creator, was in Nandigrāma in the north; he was eight years old at Prabhāsa, and indeed he was beloved by the gods in Kāśī. He was the master of the four Vedas in Dvārikā and the lord of the world in Vaidiśa.
In Pauṇḍraka he is Puṇḍarīkākṣa; in Hastināpura he is Pītākṣa; in Jayantī he is named Vijaya; in Jagannātha he is Jayantaka;
in Vādyadeśa he is Padmahasta; and in Tamolva he is Tamopaha.
In Ahicchatra he is Janānanda; in Kāñcī, indeed, he is Aja, beloved by the people. In Karṇāṭaka he is Brahmā; at Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, he is Munīśvara.
At Śrīkaṇṭha he is known as Śrīnivāsa; in Kāmarūpa, he is Śubhākara.
In Uḍḍīśā he is Devakṛta, and likewise in Jālandhara;
in Mallikā he is Viṣṇu, while in Mahendra and other places he is Bhārgava.
In Gohasta he is Sthavira Brahmā, and in Ujjayinī he is Pitāmaha.
Mahādeva is in Kauśāmbī; Arkapitāmaha is in Sāketa; Virañci is in Citrakūṭa; Vārāha-Viśvasṛj is in Vandhyā;
Sureśa is in Haridvāra; and Haṃsavāhana is on the Himādri mountain. (66–67)
In Haihikā he is Vedahasta; on Mount Arbuda, Padmahastaka;
in Vṛndāvana, Padmanetra; and in Naimiṣa, Kuśahastaka.
In Gopakṣetra he is Gocara, and on the bank of the Yamunā, Sucandra.
On the banks of the Gaṅgā he is Padmabhū; in Janasthāna he is Jalodbhava.
In the south he is Setupāla, and in the north he is Haṃsavāhana.
Brahmā resides at Arbuda, while in Utkala he is Nāradādhipa.
On the shore of Aśvapaṭṭasara is Parameṣṭhin Pitāmaha; at Prayāga is Yajurnātha; Svayaṃbhū is on Raivatācala;
in Kaccha is Nārāyaṇamadhu; and Asupriya is in Brahmavāha.
Brahmagarbha was in Aṅkulaka; Dvijapriya was in Vidarbhā; Nārāyaṇarṣi was in Gomanta; Durāsada was in Indraprastha;
Sudarśana was in Pampā; and Rāṣṭravardhana was in Surūpa. (72–73)
At Virajā he is Mahārūpa, the presiding deity of the gods; at Samasthala he is Kelanādhyakṣa; at Supīṭha he is Jaladeśvara;
at Kailāsa he is Devagaṅgādhraka; and at Śrīśaila he is Trinetradhṛk.
Tryambaka is at Tripurāri, and likewise the Wielder of the Discus (Cakradhṛk) is at Naimiṣa;
Śūra is at Śṛṅgaverapura, and Virūpaka is at Nandipurī;
Gotameśa is at Svacchapāda, and Mālavān is in the city of Hāstinapura.
In Vācikṣetra he is Dvijeśa; likewise, in Svarge he is Diveśvara; in the city of Bhūtikā he is Pureśa; in Candrā he is Haṃsavāhana;
in Campā he is Gāruḍa-Brahmā; and in Mahodaya he is Mahāyakṣa.
Suyajña is in Pūjākāraṇya, and Vṛṣātmaka is in Dharmāraṇya.
Śuklavarṇa is in the eastern region, and Supadmaja is in Vibhāvarī.
Keśī is in Devadāruvana, and Vināyaka is in Mātṛbhūmi.
In Alakā he is the Lord of the Lord of Wealth; on Trikuṭa he is the Unborn One, the King of Yogins; in Pātāla he is Brahmā, the source of the Nāgas; at Kovidāra he is the Creator of the Yugas;
in Strīrājya he is the Overseer of Sexual Pleasure; and on Paurṇādri he is the Sustainer of Enjoyment.
On the Śālmalī tree he was Takṣakeśa; in Ambiṣṭhā he was Sudarśaka. On the Naravīthī road he was Mahāvīra; in the wilderness he was Durganāśaka.
In Padmāvatī he was Padmagraha; in the sky he was Mṛgarūpadhṛk.
In the ocean he is Meghavāha, and in battles he is always Kṣārabhū;
in the wheels he is Mūlabīja, and likewise Guru on the forehead.
In Satyaloka he is Prapitāmaha, and likewise Darbha among the blades of grass.
In sacrifices he is the chief brāhmaṇa, and in Vairāja he is the lotus-born Brahmā;
on Mount Meru he is the form of Agni, and in the world of the ancestors he is the Lord of the Pitṛs.
In Camatkārapura he is Chinnaśiras, and in Kuru he is Vājapa.
Among the gods of fortune he is Brahmā, and in the context of creation he is the Ordainer (Vidhātṛ).
In the scriptures he exists in the form of Vidhi, possessing one hundred and eight forms.
Indeed, Brahmā, the progenitor and Supreme Lord, abides within creation.
At Prabhāsa, one should worship that Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin) in the form of a child;
the fruit of this worship shall be equal to that of worshipping one hundred and eight creators of the universe.
Furthermore, if at any time on the full moon day of Kārttika, the moon should happen to be in the constellation of Kṛttikā...

Or if that lunar day (tithi) falls on a Prājāpatya [nakṣatra], it is merit-bestowing there. When the sun is in Viśākhā and the moon is in Kṛttikā, that conjunction is named Padmaka; at Prabhāsa, that must certainly be performed.
Now listen further, O Lakṣmī! In ancient times, Dakṣa gave ten daughters to Dharma; among them, one was named Viśvā. From Dharma, that Mahāviśvā bore eight sons.
Āya, Bhava, Sāma, Dhara, Nala, Anila, Pratyūṣa,
and Prabhāsa are the eight Vasus, the sons of Vṛṣa. Among them, the seventh, through the desire for a son, [begot] Prabhāsaka.
At the end of that hundred-year penance, dawn arrived;
Somanātha, being pleased, granted his son Devala [the boon].
There, Pratyūṣaka worshipped the liṅga which [he had established].
Mahādeva, the bestower of sons, is called Pratyūṣeśvara.
Then Anila also propitiated Śaṅkara at that very place,
and He granted him a son renowned as Manojava.
Thus Śaṅkara attained renown as Anileśvara;
likewise, by Prabhāsa, the Liṅga was established as Prabhāseśvara.
Bṛhaspati’s sister Bhuvanā was his beloved wife.
From him, through Prabhāsa, a powerful son named Viśvakarman was born.
He indeed became the Great God (Mahādeva) known as Prabhāseśvara,
who was established by Prabhāsa during the dark fortnight of the month of Phālguna.
On the thirteenth day, Śivarātri, that place indeed became a supreme holy site (tīrtha). Then, at that great holy site named Vāmanasvāmī,
having bound Bali and requested his entire kingdom, [the Lord] was worshipped by the one who dug for Bali (Balikhātaka).
Where that first foot was set down, there is that most excellent sacred ford (tīrtha).
Known as Viṣṇutīrtha, it is situated near the edge of the ocean;
for it was there on the shore that the demon Śaṅkha was formerly slain by Viṣṇu.
Through the yoga of Hari, Śaṅkhatīrtha exists as a maker of sound;
and there also exists the Śaiva holy site of Vīrabhadreśvara.
Then, once upon a time, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa himself—

Accompanied by many gopīs, he went from the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake to the supreme sacred field of Prabhāsa on Mount Raivataka to sport; there he [established] Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇeśa and Gopīśvara as the second deity.
That excellent holy site was established by him as Bāṇa-śubhra.
Then once, those sixteen digits of the moon arrived at Prabhāsa and,
having bathed, they established the supreme holy site known as Kaleśvara.
Lambinī, Candrikā, Kāntā, Kūṭā, Śāntā, Mahodayā,
Bhīṣaṇī, Nandinī, Suparṇā, Vimalā, Akṣayā,
Śubhadā, Śobhanā, Puṇyā, Haṃsā, and Sītā are the Kalās in their respective order. (106–107)
Kalāditya was installed, and Sūrya also performed his pilgrimage.
Then once, sixty-four Yoginīs arrived there from the mountain of Yoginī behind Raivatācala.
They established these very goddesses as the sovereign Yoginīs.
O Lakṣmī, listen now to the names of those who are dear to Śaṅkara:
first is the principal Mahālakṣmī, then Nandā and Kṣemakarī. (1.538.110)
Śivadūtī, Mahābhadrā, Bhrāmarī, Candramaṇḍalā, Revatī, Harasiddhi, Durgā,
Viṣamalocanā, Sahajā, Kulajā, Kubjā, Māyāvī, Śāmbhavī, and Kriyā.
The primordial, all-pervading, pure, to be honored through contemplation, transcending the mind;
she is Vidyā, Avidyā, Mahāmāyā, Suṣumṇā, and Sarvamaṅgalā; the Great Goddess whose essence is the syllable Om, the mother of the meaning of the Vedas, the Auspicious One (Śivā). 1.12–1.13.
The ancient science of inquiry, the initiation, Cāmuṇḍā, the beloved of Śaṅkara;
Brāhmī, the bestower of peace, Gaurī, the friend of Brahman, and the one dear to the Brāhmaṇas.
Bhadrā, the Goddess, Kṛṣṇā, garlanded with planets and constellations.
Tripurā, Tvaritā, Nityā, Sāṃkhyā, Kuṇḍalinī, Dhruvā;
Kalyāṇī, Śobhanā, Nityā, Niṣkalā, Paramā Kalā;
Yoginī, Yogasadbhāvā, Yogagamyā, Guhāśayā. (115–116)
Kātyāyanī, Umā, Śarvā, and Aparṇā—these are the wives of Hara;
likewise, in other ages, others become his beloveds through the power of their worship.
Even yoginīs are born by the millions as the beloveds of Śaṅkara.

In the presence of Somanātha, there exists an excellent sacred site (tīrtha) for the destruction of sins, which is purifying and always bestows happiness. These [goddesses] should always be worshipped by people on the Aṣṭakā days.
Those established in sattvic devotion attain the state of divinity;
this auspicious [account], which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, is attained through reading and hearing.
I have related before you the majesty of Somatīrtha and Prabhāsa.
That which was spoken by Śaṅkara to Pārvatī at Prabhāsa has been related.

Thus ends the five hundred and thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of Many Renowned Tīrthas," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*. In this chapter, Brahmā is described as being distinct in various locations; the eight Vasus, the Sūryas, the Rudras, and the sixty-four Yoginīs are also recounted. *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Book 1 (Kṛtayuga-santāna). Chapter 538.
Chapter 539 [Author:
Chapter 540 → Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī! I shall likewise describe other holy places (tīrthas) to you—those which were indeed spoken by Mahādeva to Mahādevī at that time:
[the sites] of Vāmadeva, Sāvarṇi, and Aghora, as well as the supreme one.
The auspicious tīrtha of Kapila is located at Prabhāsa;
likewise, the forest known as Śrīmukha shines with splendor,
where Vaiṣṇava yogins and siddhas dwell at all times.
In ancient times, the Sun-god Bhāsaka was established there by Sāgara;
thus, that sacred ford known as Sāgarāditya-tīrtha exists at Prabhāsaka.
Furthermore, in former times, there was a young daughter of an outcaste named Akṣamālā.

In a previous birth, while she was a Śūdra woman and in her menses, she touched Śaṅkara; by that fault, she became the daughter of an outcaste. Then, through the power of his asceticism, she was accepted by Vasiṣṭha when she was offered by Janaka.
In former times, when the god did not send rain for many years, those people living in the snowy land begged food from an outcaste. Then Vasiṣṭha gave them food along with his daughter.
Having reflected upon the duty in times of distress (*āpaddharma*), he spoke there regarding the outcaste (*antyaja*):
"One who seizes [another] for the sake of protecting his own life is not tainted by sin.
Ajīgarta, being famished, approached to kill his own son. (8–9)
"In former times, Bhāradvāja, afflicted by hunger, seized cows;
and in former times, Viśvāmitra also, indeed, approached a cow while tormented by hunger.
Having said this, that son of Vasiṣṭha took hold of that rosary.
Having eaten food, they went to Prabhāsa, in the vicinity of the ocean.
Akṣamālā performed penance, and she gave birth to Arundhatī.
By her, Śaṅkara was then installed there as Akṣamālikeśa.
Now, there exists there the auspicious Siddhalakṣmītīrtha;
likewise, the Tīrtha established by Mahākālī also shines forth.
Furthermore, there is the auspicious river named Puṣkarāvartakā, which bestows lotuses.
And it exists at the auspicious holy site of Prabhāsa, bestowing a good rebirth.
Now, there was a certain scribe named Mitra on the face of the earth;
he had a son named Citra, and likewise a daughter named Citrā. (14–156)
Upon the death of their parents, those two boys then went to Prabhāsa;
there they praised the Sun for many days with austerity.
Citra’s father, the Sun, became pleased and said, "Choose a boon."
He chose maturity and eloquence in all undertakings. "So be it," said the Sun, and Dharmarāja likewise agreed to him.
Having recognized his supreme skill, he made him his own scribe.
And even Sūrya became renowned there as Citrāditya;
and Citrā became the wife of Dharmarāja as the fruit of her asceticism.
Thus, that goddess shines there as Citreśvarī.
And a sacred bathing place (tīrtha) has also arisen there, auspicious and a warder-off of diseases and defects.
Now, the goddess Śītalā, the destroyer of suffering, resides here;
for the sake of pacifying eruptive boils (visphoṭaka), one should make peacocks dance there.
There shall be the pacification of boils and even scabies for children.
Camphor, saffron, sandalwood, and flowers—
on the ninth day of the bright fortnight, one should offer her an oblation of ghee and milk-rice.
One should offer a rosary made of *bilva* wood; diseases will perish far away.
This very place is called Śītalātīrtha, which bestows happiness upon children and others.
That Citrā, the wife of Yama, is the excellent river Citrapathā.
Born from her second form at the site of Prabhāsa,
that very sacred ford (tīrtha) is declared to be for the purpose of pacifying sins and afflictions.
Likewise, there exists at Prabhāsa the sacred ford established by Dharmarāja.
Indeed, there is a pool fashioned by Brahmā that provides bodily adornment.
There exists the sacred ford (tīrtha) created by Nārada, which illuminates the celestial realms;
and there is the great sacred ford of the Sacrificial Pool (Yajñakuṇḍa), fashioned by the gods beginning with Brahmā.
On the bank of the Hiraṇyā, the gift of gold and other such acts indeed bestow merit;
likewise, there is the Vainateya Tīrtha, which wards off the fear of serpents.
There exists the great Raivantaka Tīrtha of the Son of the Sun (Yama).
By honoring that horse, one's sin perishes.
There is also the Svargavaidya-tīrtha, known as Sāvitrī-tīrtha; produced through ascetic penance, it is indeed located at Prabhāsa. (1.539.30)
The holy ford known as Talasvāmī, likewise endowed with hot waters, exists in the Siṃhāraṇya forest; it is purifying, bestows heaven, and is auspicious.
Listen, Lakṣmī! In ancient times, there arose at that place in Siṃhāraṇya [the story of] Talodbhava.
There was a Dānava named Mahendra who, by the power of his asceticism, conquered the gods. He requested a battle from Śaṅkara;
that destroyer of the cosmic egg first fought with Śaṅkara. (32–33)
Then, from Śiva’s body, many flames burst forth in anger;
in their midst, Tala was burnt and fled into the depths of the forest.
Śiva went to Someśvara and remained there at ease, while Tala stayed behind.
He afflicted Mahendra and bound the lords of the quarters.
Then Tala, filled with wonder, performed a dance of joy;
by his dancing, all that is stationary and moving trembled.
All the mountains were shaken and the salt ocean surged;
the three worlds became utterly distressed. Then the sage Lomaśa, having arrived at Prabhāsa, said to Śaṅkara, "Protect us!"
"O Lord of Gods, destroy Tala; do not delay, act quickly!
Rudra said: "Tala is invulnerable to me, for he stands as dear to me as a son.
However, [he may be slain] in the beautiful Uṣṇavana forest, near the waters of Tapta."
Durvāsā is present; you, the gods and others, should pray to him.
Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa is at Guptaprayāgaka, on Mount Śatruñjaya, by the lake named Aśvapaṭṭa.
The Blessed One himself resides in the great field of Saurāṣṭra.
Being praised with devotion by Durvāsas, Lomaśa, and others,
and being entreated by the gods, he will destroy that land.
"In age after age, the Lord remains in the tiger forest on the previous ground;
again and again, he slays the demon Tala who has entered the lion forest.
Having been addressed thus, Lomaśa [stood] near the hot water.
Having gone to the gods and brought Durvāsas along with Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa,
he went to his own purifying abode and spoke to Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa:
"O Blessed One, a fierce Rākṣasa exists who is indeed incapable of being slain by Hara."
"You must destroy him who brings suffering to gods and men;
having gone there with the discus, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa beheld the surface of the earth in the tiger-forest and indeed released the Sudarśana."
Tala fled toward a forest of lions and a cave of scalding water.
There, the Daitya was split in two by the discus and died.
He was honored by Durvāsas and worshipped by Mārkaṇḍeya.
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa gave him the name Talasvāmī.
Talasvāmī is a great sacred site (tīrtha) that takes refuge in Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa;
there are also three eternal, inexhaustible pools of hot water.
It is the washer of evil, the bestower of heaven, and likewise the bestower of liberation.
Therein is found the sacred ford (tīrtha) of Sāvitrī, the place of her ascetic penance;
furthermore, there is another sacred ford known as Bhūtamātṛka.
And there are abodes for hosts of *bhūtas* and *pretas* there as well;
one should worship Mātṛ, the dispeller of fear, there among those *bhūtas*.
O Lakṣmī! Formerly, in the *Kṛta-yuga* within the interval of Cākṣuṣa Manu, [she was] a virtuous woman (*satī*).
Having married Śaṅkara, she took delight in the forest;
thereafter, Śaṅkara became gratified by his amorous passion for Pārvatī.
Meanwhile, Pārvatī performed her ablutions there in the Kailāsa forest.
Merely by Pārvatī’s bathing, the Mothers emerged from the mire of the water—countless, formidable, and devoid of beauty;
they were dark, with gaping mouths, tawny eyes, and disheveled hair. (55)
Adorned with garlands of skulls, their heads bound with half-stacks of severed heads;
bearing skull-topped staffs (*khaṭvāṅga*) and likewise wearing garlands of severed heads;
clad in garments of tiger-skin and possessing girdles of tinkling bells. (56–57)
Filling the sky with the sounds of ḍimas and ḍamarukas and with cries of *cit*, ten crores [of beings] were produced; indeed, four heroines arose here:
Raktakarṇī, Mahājihvā, Kṣayā, and Pāpakāriṇī.
Many Brahma-rākṣasas are born in their lineage;
they generally dwell in the Śleṣmāntaka tree.
Tall and fickle, they dance and laugh.
Even though they dwell in forest after forest among fierce, thorny trees,
Śaṅkara nevertheless performed his ablutions in that mud at that time.
Countless spirits were produced there, hideous and terrifying.
Two principal men, exactly like him and adorned with his very same ornaments, appeared—
bearing skull-topped staves and skull-bowls, draped in skins,
and followed by many most terrifying spirits. (62–63)
With faces like those of lions, tigers, and other beasts, and with terrifying voices and deeds, those two—afflicted by hunger—repeatedly called out "Śivā! Śiva! at that time.
Then Śambhu said to them, "Food! Food!"
"By the touch of your hands, let flesh, blood, and the like arise [in me].
May you both share in eating at night and wandering about, as well as sleeping during the day.
Protect the worlds like sons, and always uphold the Dharma. (65–66)

When they were thus addressed, those two hosts, served by the leaders of the *bhūtas* and *mātṛs*, became united in an instant as brothers-in-arms. "Indeed, through our purity, we have become perpetually defiled. (67)
"By these two, clothing must be given away, [the merit of which] reaches far to the western land.
May he be born in the forest of Siṃhāraṇya near Somanātha, in the realm of lions, tigers, and beasts, in Saurāṣṭra. (68–69)
Where there are thorny trees and harsh, warlike regions; where garlands are indeed painted upon walls and such;
where the wife is a remarried woman, and there are anthills as well as *śamī* trees.
In whatever house there are five men, or where there are three women,
or where there are three lineages— there, in that house,
you shall dwell, even in darkness, in a subterranean cavern, in a deep abyss filled with wealth.
"One goat, two donkeys, three cows, five buffaloes, six horses, or seven elephants—staying in that house is indeed for you.
And in that house where there is a spade as well as a casket for gifts. (73)
In various places, cooking pots and other vessels lie broken;
they are cast here and there on the ground, and there is no order, nor even cleanliness.
Furthermore, women sit upon the threshold of the pestle and mortar. (74–75)
Where there is excrement and urine, where there is filth and refuse,
where grains— both cooked and uncooked— are trodden upon in the house,
and where the sacred scriptures are trodden upon; indeed, your dwelling shall be in such a house.
In whose house there is human bone, as well as *sevatī* and *vallikā*;
where there is *rohita*, *jaṭī*, *āgastya*, and *bandhujīvaka*; and where *karṇikā* and *sthalapadma* may be found— || 77–78 ||
And where Mallikā’s palace stands, there indeed shall be your dwelling;
where there are palm trees, *tamāla*, *bhallāta*, and *ciñcā* trees;
and where there are *bakula*, groves of plantains, *kadamba*, or even *khadira* trees.
The nyagrodha, aśvattha, āmra, udumbara, and likewise the panasa;
the aśoka and the oḍru tree— therein was the dwelling of spirits,
where there was no worship of the gods and no recitation of mantras and the like.
Where there is no devotion to Kṛṣṇa, that is indeed the dwelling place of spirits.
Those mortals who have soiled faces,
who wear dirty clothes, whose teeth are stained, and who are householders— such places are always the abode of spirits.
In that house where there is no lamp and no person within its vicinity, there is the entry of spirits and the like;
it is certain that men and women who have not bathed shall dwell there, filled with impurity, in vessels such as hollow tubes. (83–84)
May people who consume liquor and meat always be worthy of your dwelling—
at the crossroads, in the pasture, at the front of the village gate, in the cremation ground,
on the site where a dead calf lies, at a shrine, under a tree, or upon a stone slab. (85)
In places such as latrines and reed-thickets, spirits always have their dwelling.

Likewise, in the body of a mantra-practitioner, in that which is consecrated by mantra, and in the ear when mantra is recited—within the domain of the mantra and within the body—the dwelling of spirits occurs. (86–87)
Sudden death occurs on the ground near the bank of a pond, in a windy place, on impure ground, or where spirits always dwell;
likewise, [death may occur] on the new moon day, the fourteenth day, or during the months of Vaiśākha and Kārttika. (88)
May they never dwell in the homes of those who offer animal sacrifices or of those who worship [such deities].
O Nārāyaṇa! O Hari! O Kṛṣṇa! O Śiva! O Consort of Rādhā! O Lord of Ramā! O Viṣṇu! O Śrīmat-Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa! O Lord of Śrī-Kamalā! (1.539.90)
"O Lord of Light, O Consort of Mahālakṣmī, O Lord of Śrīmāṇikī,
O Sovereign of Pārvatī, O Lord of Padyā, O Supreme Lord of the Abode of Liberation, O Lord of the Imperishable"—
such is the worship of the Lord Hari through names beginning with "Akṣareśa."
May they indeed dwell where there is worship of the gods;
may they indeed dwell where there is purity, as well as righteousness, and where there is no quarrel; may they indeed dwell where there is no impurity. (92–93)
Where there may be internal purity, let the Bhūta not remain there;
where the power of spiritual practice (*upāsanā*) exists, the Bhūtamātā truly does not dwell there.
This applies even on the fifteenth days of the bright fortnight in the month of Vaiśākha.
One should perform the worship of Bhūtamātṛ with sprinklings;
likewise, one should worship her neck with vermilion, with flowers, and with incense, and offer a sacrificial oblation as is appropriate. (95–96)
O Prajāpati, he who eats black food such as mung beans (māṣa) is indeed satisfied by that;
neither Śākinīs, nor Piśācas, nor Rākṣasas, nor Bhūtas and other spirits afflict his house, and his lineage prospers in happiness.
One should feed [the deity] with milk-based cakes, *kṛsara* rice, and *pūya-pāyasa*. By this, one shall obtain abundance of sons and cattle, as well as physical health.
Then, on the eleventh and ninth lunar days, having washed the wall-painting...
One should have the faces of the Mothers, the Caṇḍikās, and likewise the Rākṣasīs, as well as the Bhūtas, Pretas, Piśācas, and Śākinīs, painted with various colors and red collyrium.
One should have faces fashioned there, endowed with the *hāva* and *bhāva* gestures.
On the new moon day, one should worship them at night together with a lamp.
Holding them upon one's own head, accompanied by friends and well-wishers—102.
One should perform the wandering of the hero at the edge of a village and at the edge of a cremation ground;
that lamp becomes powerful for all beings and for the practitioner.
One should constantly wander with the lamp at night in the village and in the cremation ground.
On the fifteenth day, one should perform the great festival of Bhūtamātṛ.
One should worship her, feed her, bow down, and after asking for forgiveness, return home.
For one who performs the worship in this manner, no obstacle caused by spirits shall arise.
Then, from the body of that Bhūtamātṛ, fifty million Piśācas were born from drops of sweat;
they were all terrifying, covered in veins, emaciated, bearded, and clad in skins. (106)
Adorned with mortars as ornaments, using winnowing baskets as parasols, and possessing harsh voices;
using their hands as bowls, wearing garlands upon their heads, they are hungry and misshapen.
From their hair, which is set ablaze by their nails, they spit out glowing coals.
With mouths gaped open as wide as their ears, with drooping eyebrows and thick noses,
with hands and feet positioned on their backs, and crawling upon their backs or their heels;
crying out with dejected faces, they dwelt within the maternity chamber.
They requested food from Śambhu, and Śambhu then granted them a boon: invisibility among living beings, the ability to assume any form at will,
and the power to move about during both twilights as well as the right to dwell in ruined houses.
They saw houses of improper conduct, ruined sanctuaries, royal highways, side streets, crossroads,
and altars; likewise, stones, corners, and the exits of the roads.
Hara likewise gave the *caitya* trees and other such things, as well as elevated peaks,
and places for the residence of the *piśācas*;
he also [assigned] those people who were unrighteous, as well as those who consume liquor and meat.
Hara also gave them dwellings filled with excrement and urine;
a wise person should offer an oblation to destroy their obstacles,
consisting of cakes, green gram, rice mixed with sesame, honey, and powdered sesame seeds.
She should offer rice mixed with fermented liquor, cooked rice with sesame seeds, and rice with jaggery;
as well as black garments, incense, and flowers.
By doing this, they remain satisfied and always remove all obstacles.
Thus, by Hara, the Mothers of the spirits and the Piśācas were sent to Prabhāsa, accompanied by all their sons and hosts; indeed,
a forest of lions extending for a hundred yojanas was granted to them as a dwelling place.
Wherever they found food, they always remained there in the western ocean.
Having abandoned Kailāsa, they arrived at Siṃhāraṇya,
and returning once more to the subjects, they indeed caused them great distress.

Then Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, in order to slay them, discharged the Sudarśana [discus] here in this forest; the Bhūtas, Piśācas, and others, as well as the Mātṛs, fled into the sky toward the west. (121)
Those dark-complexioned Piśācas went across the ocean;
being ill-formed, they made their dwelling there in a desolate region.
From them were born ten million humans who could assume any form at will.
But those gods who were slain by the discus became defiled at that time;
dwelling in the forest of lions, they took on other bodies.
They were the disciples and noble sons of Śambhu, the Lord of Somanātha.
Daughters, sons, and disciples indeed dwell in the Siṃhāraṇya forest,
on the mountains and in the groves surrounding the pool of hot water (Uṣṇodaka-kuṇḍa),
O Lakṣmī; for the sake of those characterized by tamas, there are always deities of tamas.

They indeed become like sacred fords (tīrtha) through their inherent nature, virtues, and meditative cultivation; yet among them, there is that great ford which is dark (tāmasa), like a lion in a forest,
and which is the abode of the Mother of Beings, of the Piśācas, and of all spirits.
"Indeed, those lineages who are oppressed and utterly crushed by the discus shall be born in the western land as beings resembling Piśācas. Thus was it told to the Goddess by Śambhu at Prabhāsa.
O Lakṣmī! I have related to you this account concerning Kailāsa under the guise of a pilgrimage to Somaka; for I myself was formerly the one who destroyed Tala. Listen now to another purifying story.
"From reading and hearing this, the destruction of sins arises.

(131) Thus ends the five hundred and thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Arundhatī’s Previous Birth, the Narration of Citrā’s Previous Birth, the Tīrtha of Śītalā, the Narration of the Talasvāmin Tīrtha, the Narration of the Bhūtamātṛ Tīrtha, the Abodes of the Bhūtas, and the Dwelling of Those Perishing in Uninhabited Lands and Other Regions," in the first section on the Continuation of the Kṛta Yuga within the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, concerning the description of the multitude of holy places (*tīrtha*) in the sacred field of Prabhāsa.
← Chapter 539: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga) Chapter 540 [Author: Chapter 541 →
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī! I shall relate in due order that answer which Śambhu gave to the Goddess regarding the various holy places (tīrthas). (1)

The Puṣpadanteśvara Tīrtha as well as the Māṇḍavya Tīrtha are indeed the abodes of those two ascetics, Māṇḍavya and Puṣpadanta. One should behold the five Prabhāsas on the principal bank of the Prabhāsa [region].
In the south is Prabhāsa, and in the west is Prabhāsaka;
in the north is Prabhāsa, and in the east as well is Prabhāsa.
Yama, Varuṇa, Dhanada, and Mahendra are situated on all sides.
And from there, they illuminate that fourfold radiance;
for the Jāmadagnyeśvara Tīrtha is likewise situated there.
That great Tīrtha, Kṛtasmara, is indeed of the nature of a mountain.

Having burnt Smara and then created him anew, Hara united him with Pārvatī. That mountain where Kāma was formerly restored to life by Śaṅkara should be known as Kṛtasmara, for it is the refuge of Śaṅkara.
And there is the Kāmakuṇḍa there, where indeed Kāma resides;
by bathing there on the thirteenth lunar day, one becomes fortunate and handsome.
The Sārasvata Tīrtha is meritorious, by which the Somakas live.

O auspicious lady, at the confluence of the ocean, one obtains the merit of all other holy fords; when the new moon is joined with the moon on a Monday, what need is there then for ten million festivals? (1.540.10)
One should offer at the place of union a bilva leaf, a śamī leaf, a karṇikāra, a mālatī,
as well as dhattūraka, campaka, aśoka, a śrīphala fruit, unbroken grains (akṣata),
sugar, sandalwood paste, sweets, and a bracelet.
On the Sarasvatī, Hari and Hara should indeed be meditated upon by men.
To them should be offered excellent worship, which bestows both liberation and worldly enjoyment.
There, the bones of a deceased body should be cast for the sake of final release.
As long as a human's bone remains in the waters of the Sarasvatī,
for that many thousands of years he dwells in the heavenly world.
The Sarasvatī, established at Prabhāsa, has become a ladder to heaven.
By beholding it and by sipping its water, one obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice.
There, the ancestors, being well-satisfied by the performance of a Śrāddha, attain liberation.
Furthermore, fifteen renowned Muhūrtas of the day are present there. (15–16)
One should know that there are three muhūrtas at dawn, three muhūrtas for the saṃgava period,
three muhūrtas for midday, likewise three for the afternoon,
and three muhūrtas for the evening; it is during these times that the performer of the śrāddha should act.
The evening is a time belonging to the Rākṣasas; one should not perform a Śrāddha at that hour.
That which is the eighth Muhūrta of the day is known as the Kutupa period.
It bestows infinite fruit, for midday consists of the Kutupa.
Because it is evil and contemptible, from where does its protection (pālana) or preservation (rakṣaṇa) come?
That is designated as *kutupa*; the *kutupas* are of eight forms:
midday, a ball, a vessel, silver, and likewise cow-ghee.
Darbha grass, sesame seeds, a cow, a daughter’s son, and the Kutupa vessel— these are required.
From one Muhūrta after the Kutupa until the four [subsequent] Muhūrtas,
this five-Muhūrta period is desired as the abode of Svadhā.
Kuśa grass and black sesame seeds were produced from the body of Viṣṇu.
Those who dwell on dry land should offer a handful of water with sesame seeds along with *darbha* grass.
In a *śrāddha*, three things are purifying: a daughter’s son, a *kutupa* vessel, and sesame seeds.
The grandson is a ball, for he indeed possesses horns upon his forehead.
That which is the vessel for those horns is remembered as the "grandson-vessel" (dauhitra).
And from the ghee that may be produced from the milk of a milch cow together with her calf— || 25 ||
Therefore, he is called "daughter's son" (dauhitra) in rites for the gods and the ancestors;
indeed, the daughter’s son is the most excellent for partaking in the śrāddha feast.
The tip of the darbha grass is said to belong to the gods, while that with sesame and fire belongs to the ancestors.
Among them, those that hang down are known as *kuśa* and *kutupa*.
(27) By means of wealth acquired through righteous means, the ancestors and the gods are satisfied;
by means of wealth acquired through unrighteous means, those born of the *puṣkasa* and other low castes are satisfied. (28)
Those born as Piśācas are satisfied by food dropped on the ground;
those born of low wombs are satisfied even by the water used for washing clothes;
and those who have attained the state of deities are satisfied by drops of fragrant water.
Those born of misfortune are satisfied by even the grains of food gathered from the funeral cakes (piṇḍa).
Those born of animal wombs are satisfied merely by the sipping of water (ācamana) after eating.
At a śrāddha, Brahmins, learned Vedic scholars (śrotriya), yogis, and those versed in the Sāmaveda and the Vedas [attain satisfaction].

One who has performed the Triṇāciketa rite, one who maintains the five sacred fires, one who knows the Trisuparṇa hymn, one learned in the six Vedāṅgas, a daughter’s son, a son-in-law, a sister’s son, and likewise an excellent man;
one devoted to the ritual of the five fires, one devoted to austerity, and a maternal uncle—[these are worthy recipients]. (32)
The mother and the father, as well as disciples, relatives, and kinsmen;
one who knows the meaning of the Vedas, a teacher, a celibate student, and a giver of thousands;
and those who are long-lived—these should be known as virtuous men who purify.
O Lotus-born One, a man should especially not bypass his sister’s son, nor even his circle of kinsmen, even if they are fools;
he should offer water, fruit, funeral cakes (piṇḍas), and milk-rice (pāyasa).
One should give sweet food and sugar, and always give whatever is most desired.
For that which is given brings satisfaction through the excellence of the substance, the vessel, and so forth.
One should likewise give on auspicious days, as well as during regular and occasional rites.
On the determined day, one should certainly give [the gift] year after year;
on the new moon day (amāvāsyā), one should give by all means, so that the deceased may surely attain [their goal].
Likewise, one should bestow great gifts (mahādāna) in the abode of Nārāyaṇa.

As far as the moisture from the water reaches the bank, or for a distance of four cubits, Nārāyaṇa is the master there; it is said that no other temple may exist in that place. Cows, gold, silver, gems, and Sarasvatī [are also his].
Sesame, a maiden, an elephant, a horse, a bed, clothing, as well as land,
grain, milk, an umbrella, and a house— these are the sixteen gifts. Truth, self-restraint, purity, contentment, steadfastness, and straightforwardness.

Knowledge, tranquility, compassion, and charity— this is praised as the worthy recipient. To one who delights in the path, is peaceful, is in distress, and maintains the sacred fires— to such a Śrotriya, even a single cow should be given, for it indeed bestows liberation.
A cow, a house, a refuge, and women should not be given away to many people.
Where palaces exist— golden, radiant with silver and gems, and auspicious—
and where there are excellent *apsarases*, there the givers of cows go.
The giver of land dwells in heaven for sixty thousand years.
Having thus visited the Sārasvata Tīrtha and the Mārkaṇḍeya Tīrtha,
one should proceed to where the sage remained for a long time through the ages to perform ascetic penance.
Then one should go to that place where the destruction of the Kṛṣṇa clan is held to have occurred— the divine battlefield of the first age, which bestows the abode of Goloka.
When that battlefield was formed, there were indeed ill omens.
O Lakṣmī, hear now of their births and also of the causes of their destruction.
Time itself is seen wandering through their houses in the form of a terrifying, hideous, shaven-headed man, dark and tawny-brown in hue. 48–49.
With a broom for his great banner, wearing a hibiscus flower as an ear-ornament,
having made a chameleon his necklace, and adorned with crows as his jewelry—
he was seen no more after he had looked upon the houses of the devotees of Kṛṣṇa and departed.
At night, young women saw the hair of sleeping men;
their bracelets and armlets were shattered and scattered everywhere.
And in the houses, the female jackals (menā) were constantly crying out, "cī-cī" and "kū-cī. || 51-52 ||
Harsh and dry winds, carrying fragments of bone, blew forth;
at that time, goats indeed mimicked the howling of jackals.
And birds, pale with red feet, were driven by Time.
Indeed, pigeons and lice wandered about in the houses;
donkeys were born of cows, and stallions of mules;
cats were born of bitches, and mice of mongooses.
Wives deceive their husbands, and likewise men deceive their wives;
the blazing fire whirls its flames to the left, emitting its own rays separately in blue, red, and madder hues. 56.

At both sunrise and sunset, the sun was constantly seen by people as being overturned and surrounded by headless trunks (kabandhas). On magnificent seats, there was exquisitely prepared and exceedingly radiant food fit for the perfected ones (siddha-anna). || 57–58 ||
As the food was being served, worms were seen in the dining hall;
and the stars were seen striking one another.
Donkey-like brays were heard even before the offerings had been presented before the gods.
The thirteenth lunar day, when seized by Rāhu, is always destructive.
A dark woman with pale teeth enters the city at night;
she steals from the hearts of women and runs toward the city.
Cocks let out terrifying cries upon the field of battle;
moreover, misshapen, two-headed, fierce beings with four arms were born from the wombs of women— Rākṣasas as well as Guhyakas.
Ornaments, umbrellas, banners,
and armor were seen being carried away by terrifying rākṣasas.
Having recognized such ill omens as these had arisen, Mādhava—
Taking his kinsmen with him, Kṛṣṇa, accompanied by his inner apartments and the Airāvata elephant, then proceeded to Prabhāsa, which abounds in Soma.
His own clansmen had been destroyed by one another out of a mutual desire for slaughter.
That ground of Kṛṣṇa’s nirvāṇa is declared to be the supreme sacred ford (tīrtha).
Even the grasses growing from the stalks of the *airaka* plant became, during that reversal [of fortune], like pestles and indeed like swords. (66–67)
O beloved, one should undertake a pilgrimage to that ground where all is dissolved and where the funeral pyres occupy an area of two *gavyūtis*; it bestows great dispassion.
Thence one should go to the river Hiraṇyā and bathe, which grants great merit.
From there, one should go to Rurukṣetra, where the goddess Kumārikā resides.
She manifested through the splendor of the gods for the sake of destroying the Daitya Ruru;
indeed, Pārvatī remains there as Kumārikā.
One should worship, offer salutations, and present auspicious garments;
then one should go to Ṛṣitīrtha, where in ancient times the great sages made their residence during the Cāturmāsya for the sake of sacrificial sessions.
Wherein dwells the eternal lineage of the three-eyed fish;
[there reside] Aṅgiras, Gautama, Agastya, Viśvāmitra, Bṛhaspati, Saṃvarta, Cyavana, Raibhya, Durvāsas, Kaśyapa, and Manu. (72–73)
Mārkaṇḍeya, Jamadagni, Uśanas, Kaṇva and Gālava,
Nārada and Parvata, as well as Bharadvāja and Bhāguri,
Medhātithi, Yavakrīta, and other auspicious Vaiṣṇavas.
And when the Viṣṇu sacrifice had commenced, King Vṛṣādarbhi then said:
"O bulls among sages, accept from me gifts—
mudga beans, māṣa beans, rice, as well as jewels and gold."
Then the sages said: "We do not accept gifts;
we certainly do not accept royal wealth, which is fraught with great faults.
A cartwright is equal to ten slaughterhouses; a liquor-seller is equal to ten cartwrights."
A prostitute is equal to ten gamblers, and a king is equal to ten prostitutes.
The gift of a king is most terrible; it cannot be digested.
O King, let this be given to others; may you be well in every way.

Having heard this, the king went to his own palace and subsequently had *udumbara* fruits filled with gold made for the purpose of giving as gifts. His ministers scattered them where those sages were staying.
Aṅgiras said: "O sages, do not indeed take the fruits;
for King Vṛṣādarbhi possesses secret gifts.
The accumulation of wealth is the destroyer of the accumulation of ascetic merit."
Indeed, no one who possesses accumulated wealth is seen to be free from calamity;
for those whose nature is to refrain from accepting gifts, their vital energy increases constantly.
When possessionlessness and sovereignty were weighed together on a scale—
Possessionlessness is superior even to sovereignty and even to wealth.
For wealth has the form of misfortune; it causes one to fall from the highest goods and bestows sorrow and delusion. Therefore, one who is happy should abandon it from afar. (84–85)
Even thinking it is for the sake of Dharma, one should certainly not engage in attachment to material wealth;
for it is better not to touch mud at all than to wash it off.
As one ages, the hair decays; as one ages, the teeth decay.
The eyes and ears grow old, but craving alone does not grow old.
(87) That craving is shoreless and infinite; the hope for wealth always bestows suffering.
It is also full of unrighteousness; therefore, one should always distance oneself from it. (88)
Those who are discontented perish through the hardships of greed for wealth;
contentment of mind alone is a treasure-trove of happiness everywhere.
Just as for one whose feet are covered by shoes, the earth itself is as if covered with leather.
For those satisfied by the nectar of contentment, there is peace and infinite happiness.
For the greedy, there is destruction through craving; whence can there be peace, and whence can there be happiness?
The desire of one who longs for objects is never at all fulfilled.
Then another desire pierces him even more deeply, like an arrow.
Desire is never appeased by enjoyment;
on the contrary, it increases when nourished, like a fire fed with clarified butter.

A living being who longs for sensual pleasures and is greedy does not find happiness. (93) Even if a king enjoys the earth together with its four oceans, he is still not one who has accomplished his purpose; he never becomes free from thirst. (94)
For those who do not grasp [at objects], the worlds bestow eternal bliss;
even without asceticism, their asceticism becomes manifold (a hundred thousandfold).
The thread of the lineage is craving, which dwells in the body and dries up the blood.
The demoness of craving, though cast off, does not decay even as one decays;
craving is a disease that ends life—abandon it, and one is forever happy.
Craving for the world, craving for wealth, craving for children, and desire—[these are all forms of craving]. (96–97)
"These thorns devour living beings; O Great Lords, we are afraid of them.
Therefore, let there always be only udumbara fruits for the king.
Having spoken thus, they abandoned the golden-fruiting trees and left the udumbara trees behind.
The ascetics devoted to the Supreme Lord performed a sacrificial session (*sattra*) while remaining in perfect health.
O beloved Lakṣmī, their sacred site is a holy ford (*tīrtha*) located at Prabhāsa;
that Tāraka-tīrtha must be visited, for it bestows liberation.

Thus ends the five hundred and fortieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Four Prabhāsa Tīrthas, the Sārasvata Tīrtha among hundreds of holy sites, the Kutupa period and other times, the matters concerning daughters' sons and others, the Mārkaṇḍeya Tīrtha, the Kṛṣṇakulanāśa Tīrtha, omens of misfortune in battle and elsewhere, the Guptasuvarṇa, Garbha, and Udumbara [Tīrthas] established by Vṛṣādarbhi, Aṅgiras’s refusal of gifts, and various other holy sites," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. 540.
← Chapter 540: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga) Chapter 541 [[Author: → Chapter 542
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī! I shall relate to you how Nanda-tīrtha was described by Śaṅkara to Pārvatī; for Nanda was indeed a devotee of the Lord (bhāgavata). || 1 ||
"Oṃ, obeisances to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Master; obeisances!
This mantra was indeed received from Vasiṣṭha by that king.
He became a great devotee of the Lord, solely intent upon Nārāyaṇa. (2)
There was neither famine nor disease, nor untimely death among men;
there were no thieves, no deceit, and no fear of drought or similar calamities.
While that lord of kings ruled, the subjects were always happy.
A celestial chariot was indeed granted to him by Viṣṇu himself, being pleased;
mounted upon that excellent chariot, he traveled through all the worlds.
Once, while wandering on earth, he went to Lake Mānasa.
Served by gods and others, perfumed with the fragrance of lotuses,
endowed with divine waters, auspicious, and providing coolness and satisfaction—
there he saw a beautiful, white, blooming lotus. (6–7)
There he beheld that most excellent of persons, standing there the size of a thumb; and having seen him, he said to his charioteer, "Go indeed to the water,
where this lotus is seen, resplendent with the person."
Adorned with a necklace of jewels and wearing yellow garments and other finery,
it is a two-armed, most divine form stationed upon its central part.
Bring this lotus quickly into my presence.
"I shall bear [this] upon my head; I shall have accomplished my purpose.
Having been addressed thus, the charioteer descended from the celestial chariot and, supported by the wind, alighted through the sky into the lotus pond.
While he remained with his head downward, stretching out his hand so far that he reached for the lotus situated on its stalk as if grasping it through the very sky,
at the moment he touched it, Dhūmra was born from him.
In that sky filled with darkness, the charioteer died;
and Nanda, in the midst of the celestial chariot, became black in color.
Deprived of strength and heroism, he was also bereft of intelligence and power.
Having seen his body like a lump of soot, with a face that was withered and parched as if he had gone mad, the king grieved:
"What has happened to me? My charioteer is dead! (15–16)

"May Vasiṣṭha protect me from this anger that has arisen against someone. As soon as he had spoken these words, his preceptor Vasiṣṭha arrived there and, having approached him by means of his yogic power, spoke to the king.
"Do not fear, O Indra among kings; may it be well with you and may peace be yours.
Upon seeing Vasiṣṭha, the king became free from sorrow;
having offered his salutations, he spoke to him like one who was distressed.
"O Blessed One, this transformation of my body has occurred for me;
by the power of Kamala, my charioteer has been lost.
Tell me, O Brahmin, what is this? Indeed, bring about his deliverance."

Vasiṣṭha said: "O Indra among kings, here in this Mānasa lake is this lotus of the *padma* species, known as 'Born of Brahmā' (*brahmodbhava*). Indeed, it was from the navel of Nārāyaṇa that Brahmā was born. (21–22)
That very lotus with its stalk is called *padma*;
such a lotus exists here in this Mānasa lake.
In the form of a bamboo staff (*vaṃśa*), the Blessed One indeed protects the lineage.

Indeed, within his excellent lineage, the unborn Brahmā, resembling the size of a thumb, always shines resplendent upon a lotus. For as many lotuses as there are here, they are all born from his lineage. (24–25)
Indeed, that many [lotuses] are consecrated by Brahmā;
other embodied beings, being devoid of merit, do not see them.
Only those of great merit who are destined for liberation behold this lotus.
By the mere sight of this, all the deities would be seen.
Indeed, this is seen by blessed people who are devotees of Brahman;
for that which has been seen by you is indeed seen by those highly fortunate great devotees.
Upon merely seeing this and having touched the water,
one is liberated from all sorrow and attains the state of Nirvana.
O Indra among kings, your charioteer likewise beheld such a lotus.
He touched the water and the stalk, and by that much he attained liberation.
"I always come through the path of the sky for the purpose of seeing you;
I do not touch the water, but rather bow to that Father, the Unborn."
I am going back to my own place, Puṣkara and Arbuda mountain;
but you are indeed a great Vaiṣṇava,
and for that reason you have truly beheld the eternal and meritorious lotus together with Brahmā.
"O King, because you did not touch the water, you live and flourish.
However, O Lord of Men, the desire arose in you to take the lotus; by that fault, blackness has come upon you, and through that defect, you have become blue in color. (33–34)
The deities, sages, and seers always long for this:
"When shall we behold that lotus of Brahmā in the Mānasa lake?
And when shall we attain the Supreme Brahman, reaching which there is no returning?"
Thus, O King, because you desired to seize that lotus which was so distinguished by its splendor,
you incurred the fault of theft through ignorance.
Therefore, [you must seek] Nārāyaṇa, who resides within the lotus and is endowed with creative power.
O ascetic, go to the sacred field of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa in Somaka and worship Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa together with Brahmā at Prabhāsa;
having fashioned a golden lotus, perform your worship there.
"Then you shall be liberated from the fault of your dark complexion; there is no doubt in this.
Having heard the words of Vasiṣṭha, King Nanda went to the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā and to the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake.
Having bathed there and bowed to Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa and Lomaśa,
and having gone to Raivataka mountain and bowed to Vāmana, he proceeded to Prabhāsa.
There, indeed, he beheld the golden image seated upon a lotus, accompanied by Brahmā.
Having installed the form of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa,
she worshipped him day and night with various ritual offerings and performed penance preceded by the propitiation of the Blessed Lord.
He worshipped according to the prescribed rites the five deities— Viṣṇu, Śiva, Gaṇapati, Pārvatī, and Divākara— as well as Śrī Hari.
On the delightful bank of the Māheśvarī, he established a place for penance.
Beholding his asceticism and devotion in that manner, the deities—Brahmā, Kṛṣṇa, and Lakṣmī—then granted him their vision.
They said, "We are pleased; choose a boon as you desire."
The king said: "A devotee of Hari does not desire anything of this world.
Grant me liberation; grant me the company of the virtuous and the eternal abode.
Then Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa spoke while smiling.
O King, that was indeed already decided by me for your sake.
For my devotee, there shall be no obstruction to either worldly enjoyment or liberation.
And I am pleased with you, O King; your blackness is born from the fault of the lotus.

"O you who have been born, let your worldly existence come to an end; becoming one of divine body with the complexion of a fine *campaka* flower, worship me, Puruṣottama. Whoever comes here and [worships] me, the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa..."

He shall worship the Creator and the five deities beginning with Sūrya; he shall be free from disease in this world and, at the end, attain the supreme goal. Having thus granted the boon and having assumed a golden complexion, Hari— 51–52.
Having established that supreme holy site (*tīrtha*) there, he then vanished.
By bathing at Nandīghaṭṭa, a person shall attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Likewise, by establishing the Nanda-tīrtha, one shall not return to the state of a mortal again.

Beside Nandatīrtha, there exists an excellent and purifying holy site known as Tritakūpa (54). It should be visited for the sake of attaining merit. Formerly, in the region of Saurāṣṭra, there was a Brahmin named Ātreya (55).
He had three sons—Ekata, Dvita, and Trita.
Trita was endowed with all virtues, while the two elder brothers were fools.
When their father had gone to heaven, Trita indeed took up the burden of leadership.
The thought arose in him: "How shall I perform a sacrifice?
Having invited the best of the twice-born who were established in sacrificial rites, he departed on a journey for the sake of obtaining the materials required for the sacrifice.
Having taken his two elder brothers, Trita set out for the sake of the cows.
Accompanied by his brothers, wherever he went in the villages,
there he received the highest honor and very abundant cattle.
Thus, having taken abundant wealth and a vast quantity of cattle,
he returned home accompanied by his two brothers;
Trita went in front of the cattle, while those two brothers followed behind.
Then, seeing that wealth of cattle brought for the purpose of extensive giving,
the minds of the two eldest brothers became exceedingly sinful due to extreme greed.
Those two evil-minded brothers spoke to one another:
Trita is skilled in sacrifices and likewise skilled in the Vedas;
he is honored and worshiped by all of us, while we two are fools and useless.
Moreover, Trita will give away this entire wealth of cattle as a gift.
We shall have nothing at all; on the contrary, whatever wealth belongs to our father must then be given away during that sacrifice.
Furthermore, people will offer many riches as well at the ritual.
"All those [treasures] belong to Trita; indeed, we two have not even a single cowrie shell.
Therefore, we two shall be destitute of wealth while Trita alone shall be rich.
For that reason, the killing of Trita is justified. (66–67)
Having reflected thus, the two elder brothers called out to Trita as he went further and further ahead, like two seekers of water upon seeing a well:
"O Trita, come here! We shall drink water."
Trita, having heard this, arrived; indeed, he was cast into a well by the other two.
Then those two, driven by greed, took the cattle and a great deal of wealth and set out for their own home with joyful hearts.
Having fallen into the well, the brāhmaṇa reflected in his mind:
"The brāhmaṇas have been summoned for the sake of a sacrifice, yet no mental sacrifice has been performed by me.
Therefore, what was destined to happen has occurred; here in this well, my mind itself shall be the sacrifice."
"I shall do so with water, as well as with my mind, for as long as I live.
Having thus reflected and having repeatedly recited the sacred hymns,
Kardama indeed performed an oblation with water using his joined palms.
The deities were even more satisfied by his giving with faith.
Coming to the brahmin, they said: "O learned one, we have been fully gratified.
We are pleased with your mental dispositions; tell us what you desire, and we shall grant it."
Trita said: "I have indeed performed a sacrifice here—a *bhāvayajña* (sacrifice of intention).
Having gone home, I shall likewise perform a *dravyayajña* (sacrifice of material substances) for myself.
O lords of gods, grant me well-being and an exit from this well. (75–76)
Thus addressed, the gods led the brahmin out of the water;
having gone home and performed a sacrifice, he was honored by his two brothers.
After giving various sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), Trita went back to the well.
He performed extensive austerities while remembering Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
By means of a divine vehicle, he went to the eternal abode of Śrī Hari.
That well is Tritakūpa, a purifying sacred site (devatīrtha).
Liberation shall come from drinking its water, and even from merely remembering it;
by hearing or reciting this, a person attains Vaikuṇṭha.
Thus ends the [section] in the first book, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.

The liberation of King Nanda’s charioteer upon seeing a Brahma-lotus at Lake Mānasa while he had gone there to seize it; the fruit of King Nanda’s mental sin of attempting to seize it, which was his dark complexion; and his restoration to a fair complexion through bathing at the Nandī-tīrtha; and the story of the Brahmin Trita, who was cast into a well by his two brothers but was rescued there during a water-sacrifice by the deities, followed by his performance of penance and liberation—this is the description of the Trita-tīrtha and other such matters, constituting the five hundred and forty-first chapter. ॥541॥
