Chapter 543 →
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī! To this most meritorious and auspicious account of a former birth, which destroys sin upon hearing and bestows supreme liberation through its retention.
I am indeed pleased by devotion, by faith, and likewise by service;

by the attitude of servitude and by the disposition of love, I become the fulfiller of the desires of my devotees. O Goddess, I am to be attained through devotion, not by wealth nor by recitations of mantras.
For my devotees, however, there may occasionally be physical hardship for my sake.
(3) A person whose mind is fixed on me should practice non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, and celibacy through action, mind, and speech. (4)
One should practice eating once a day, eating only at night, fasting, and so forth;
one should perform the chanting of my names, the remembrance of the saintly, and the avoidance of censure.
O Rāma, one should indeed engage in worship for my complete satisfaction.
In ancient times, there was a son of Brahmā named Āruṇi by name.
That best of the twice-born went to the forest for the sake of performing some austerity;
he practiced severe penance, being entirely devoted to fasting.
On the delightful bank of the Nāga river, he built a dwelling for you.
Once, having gone to the river to bathe, he stood on the bank after his bath.
There, he saw a hunter approaching, equipped with a bow and arrows.
That hunter approached to kill the twice-born man, desiring his bark garment.
But the seer, through his divine vision, perceived the hunter’s intention;
he grieved in his heart that this hunter was indeed a doer of many evils.
"Alas, the sin committed by my own hand shall become even greater for him!
When indeed will the deliverance of this evildoer come?
Therefore, let him take up the bark garments instead of the killing of a twice-born. || 11 ||

Having thus offered all the bark garments he possessed, the Brahmin remained silent, meditating upon the divine Lord Nārāyaṇa. Seeing that sage of firm vows, a Brahmin who had internalized Hari within himself, [the king spoke]. (12–13)
Compassionate, peaceful in heart, and averter of the sins of others—
the hunter’s mind, having indeed abandoned its cruelty there,
turned in an instant toward that which is characterized by goodness and endowed with righteousness.
The hunter, having cast aside his bow and arrows, spoke these words:
"O Brahmin, I had come here desiring to kill you;
however, now that I have seen you, my intent to do violence has vanished."
"O best of the twice-born, many Brahmins and women have indeed been slain by me, a sinner. To what destination shall I go, for I am a slayer of Brahmins?
Now, I desire to perform penance in your presence."
"You ought to show favor by granting instruction and so forth.
(18) Even though addressed in this way, that brahmin did not offer a reply, because sin is transmitted through conversation with a sinner. (19)
Even though he had not been told, that hunter, desiring righteousness, remained right there;
just like the brahmin, the hunter performed austerities beneath the tree.
Then one day, a certain lion arrived at the riverbank.
And being hungry, seeing that brahmin, the lion was about to devour him.
Just as the lion was about to seize the brahmin on the bank,
he was swiftly destroyed by the hunter with volleys of arrows.
The sage said, "Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa,
the Master," and having spoken thus, he immersed himself in the water and sat beneath the surface.
Upon hearing the name Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the lion died.
Having thus become free from sin, he rose up as a divine being.
Upon merely hearing [the name], he abandoned his life-breaths and thereafter attained a divine body.
He said, "I am going to that place where Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa resides."
"O best of the twice-born! By your grace, may I be freed from sin and attain liberation.
Having heard this, the brahmin who had been within the water came outside and then asked that man in the form of a lion: "Tell me, who indeed are you?"

The lion-man said to the brahmin: "Formerly, I was a Vedic scholar known as Dīrghabāhu, devoted to the performance of ritual acts. I knew every detail of sacrificial rites, and therefore I had no need for anyone else. (27–28)
"I know the Vedas, and I discern what is auspicious and what is inauspicious;
I have no need for Brahmins—what use are Brahmins to me?
When I spoke thus, all the Brahmins were filled with wrath.
They pronounced an invincible curse: "You shall become a cruel lion!
Your knowledge shall be destroyed, and you shall not remember me at all.
Indeed, at the time of death, you will hear the name Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa."

"Then, O beast, liberation will indeed come to you in the presence of Āruṇi! For at the sixth mealtime, whatever food of the nature of beasts, men, or birds has arrived by chance shall remain in your presence. (32)
But when, having received this arrow-wound while your life-breaths have reached your throat,
you hear Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa from the mouth of a brāhmaṇa,
then indeed liberation will be yours; there is no doubt in this matter.
I have even heard the name of Viṣṇu uttered from the mouth of another;
though I am a Brahmin who has committed offenses, he has become my bestower of liberation. Merely by the sight of him, Acyuta became manifest before my very eyes.

Furthermore, whoever receives [the name] of Śrī Narāyaṇa from one's own mouth becomes liberated at the time of the departure of the vital breath; this is indeed certain. Truth, truth, and again truth—it is said while raising up the arm.
"The Brahmins are the moving gods, and Puruṣottama resides there.
Through the union with the Brahmin Āruṇi, I shall go to the eternal state.
Having spoken thus and having honored Āruṇi, he departed for the imperishable abode of Brahman.
Then Āruṇi, his heart filled with joy, spoke to the hunter:
"O son of noble vows! Since I have been protected by you from the lion who desired to seize me, I am pleased with you; choose a boon."
The hunter said: "This is indeed a boon that you speak to me;
for your satisfaction with me as your son—what other boon could there be beyond this?
Therefore, instruct me; what further boon shall I grant?"
The sage said: "O hunter, you who seek ascetic merit have made a request of me.
At that time, I said nothing because you were possessed by sin.
Now, through my protection and by means of my ascetic power, your sins shall be purified."
Thus, by my very sight and by hearing the name of Kṛṣṇa, your sins have been destroyed;
you are now pure of body, of this there is no doubt.
O virtuous one, perform penance, and in this way you shall attain liberation.
The hunter said: "O Guru, how can the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, of whom you have spoken, be attained by those like me who are devoted to sin?
The sage replied to him: "One should offer everything in surrender."
He attains that supreme state through devotion, through vows, and through ritual action.
Knowing this, perform every vow with devotion to Him.
One should not consume what has not been offered as *naivedya*, nor should one ever speak untruth.
One should always perform the recitation of his name and likewise practice meditation on Hari.
O hunter, this vow has been prescribed by me; act accordingly.
Remain right here, endowed with austerity, for as long as you desire.
Having spoken thus, the sage again entered within the water.
Remembering his teacher, the hunter performed austerities, abstaining from all food.
At times of hunger, he occasionally ate withered leaves.
Then, gradually abandoning the eating of leaves,
he practiced austerities without food, remembering his guru with unwearied devotion.
While he was thus performing penance, the sage Durvāsas approached him.
He beheld that very hunter, whose body was withered yet who possessed life,
endowed with the splendor of austerity and established in his heart upon Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
Having recognized him as a sage, the hunter bowed his head to the muni.
He said to him, "O Blessed One, I have achieved my purpose through the sight of you.
Now you have arrived as my guest; you are a divinity to me.
Having prepared withered leaves and such, I shall gratify this best of the twice-born."
Durvāsas, wishing to test the excellence of his asceticism, spoke these words loudly to him, who was purified by his pure disposition and had conquered his senses:
"There is food made of barley, wheat, and rice, sweet and well-prepared."
"Let it be given to me, who am afflicted by hunger and have come here for your sake.
Thus addressed, the hunter, thinking "this man is a devotee," fell into deep reflection:
"Whence could such a thing be brought? How might that be possible for me? (57–58)
As he was thinking thus and remembering Nārāyaṇa,
by the grace of his guru, an auspicious vessel fell from the sky;
it was golden and endowed with supernatural powers, and he took it in his hand.
Taking that, he said to the sage: "Wait a moment, O Rishi!
Stay right here while I go out for alms;
during that time, O Guru, you should show me your favor."
Having spoken thus, he set out with his alms-bowl to beg for food;
keeping a city adorned with trees, creepers, and the like not too far ahead as his destination,
he proceeded along the path, observing the trees and creepers by the way.
As he proceeded there, beautiful maidens emerged from the trees before him, holding golden vessels in their hands; and lovely forest goddesses appeared with auspicious, cooked foods. (63–64)
Condiments, drinks, things to be sucked, and foods to be eaten;
edibles, auspicious linctuses, and honeyed juices of delicious flavor;
milks mixed with ghee, and milk-rice with sugar.
Those forest deities offered various condiments— bitter, sweet, and sour— of fifty-six different kinds. Then,
considering himself to have achieved his purpose, he returned once more to the hermitage.
He approached the sage and said: "Alms have been obtained according to my desire.
O Brahmin, wash your feet, sit upon this auspicious seat, accept these alms, and make me a vessel of merit."
Thus addressed, the sage, desiring to test the power of his asceticism, spoke again to that devoted hunter: "I have no vessel for water;
I am unable to go to the river, and you likewise possess no vessel."
"How might there be a washing of my feet, O hunter?
Having been addressed thus, that devotee of the hunter again became lost in thought;
he then remembered the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa as well as his spiritual preceptor.
Remembering her, he then went for refuge to that Nāga-river.
Bowing down, he said: "O River, you are my refuge!
I am a hunter, a man of sinful deeds, and a slayer of a Brahmin, O best of rivers! (72–73)
Nevertheless, protect me here, your devotee who has come to you for refuge.
I know nothing of the deity, nor the mantra, nor likewise the mode of worship.
Having meditated upon the feet of my teacher Āruṇi, I indeed behold what is auspicious.
"Thus, O Goddess, best of rivers, show mercy to me, your devotee!
O River, come near to the sage for the purpose of washing his feet.
Having been addressed in this way, the serpent-river assumed the form of a flowing stream of water.
He arrived at the place where Durvāsas stood, having taken refuge beneath a tree.
Seeing that great wonder, Durvāsas was filled with amazement.
Having washed his hands and feet, the sage [partook] of the alms-food with faith.
Having eaten and sipped water, he was exceedingly pleased and laughed repeatedly.
To that hunter, whose body was withered and who had become weak from hunger, he granted this boon:
"The Vedas indeed shall be yours, along with their auxiliary limbs, their meanings, and their word-by-word analyses."
"May all the Brahma-vidyās indeed become manifest to you;
and you shall become a preeminent Rishi named Satyatapas.
The hunter said, "How can I, a Śūdra, be one who studies the Vedas?"
The sage said: "Your body consisting of sin has certainly departed.
Now a second body, composed of austerity, exists for you.
Former ignorance has gone to its destruction; now knowledge has arrived. (81–82)
Thus you are one whose body is purified; I tell you this as the truth.
Indeed, through initiation, austerity, and devotion, the body is transformed.
By that means, the study of the Vedas and other such pursuits will now become manifest to you.
Your former state, known as unrighteousness (adharma) and devoid of perfect knowledge, has departed;
it was your hunter’s body. Now, indeed, you have attained this second state, which is supreme, endowed with the vows of dharma and purified by devotion. 84–85.
That nature which previously belonged to you as you were slaying living beings— that body known as sin, designated by the name "evil," has indeed departed from you.
Now, [you possess] a virtuous and noble disposition, endowed with austerity, uprightness, and devotion.
"But your second body is established as the form of Dharma.
The hunter said to the sage: "How indeed is Nārāyaṇa to be propitiated by a yogi who possesses no means of accomplishment and has no possessions?"
Durvāsas said: One should perform worship with the mind in every way;
neither wealth, nor lineage, nor prosperity is required therein.
Lord Janārdana is eternally pleased by one's inner disposition alone.

Having bathed and meditated upon Hari daily with mental offerings, one should worship Him, contemplate Him, perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), and likewise ask for His forgiveness. One should offer handfuls of flowers, water as an arghya offering, and present mental gifts.
One should offer the self in surrender, for by that Janārdana is pleased.
The Supreme Lord is attained by both the wealthy and the destitute;
yet He is not pleased by even millions of excellent gifts if they are devoid of devotion.
The Lord is well-pleased even by the gift of a mere vessel to a devotee.
He is satisfied with water, sandalwood paste, or even a single flower. Indeed, when worshipped with devotion, he is honored even by mud. (93–94)
Indeed, all the gods were satisfied by water alone; this is the illustration.
The Lord Hari was satisfied by the mere chanting of Prahlāda, and Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa was satisfied by the offering of the hearts of the gopīs.
The Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa was satisfied by the service of Lakṣmī;
Śaṅkara himself was satisfied by Aparṇā, who is Pārvatī;
and the Blessed One was satisfied by the devotion and worship of Ambarīṣa. (96–97)
Thus, the glorious Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the sovereign of Akṣara, becomes pleased through bhāva-bhakti; Acyuta is not pleased without bhāva.
Deities, gurus, saintly persons, parents, dharma, and the Lord [are all attained through it].
Liberation is the fruit; that it is real is indeed established as something to be accepted through faith.
Devotion, service, worldly interaction, acquisition, union, wealth, accomplishment, and happiness—this octad is to be achieved through action. (1.542.100)
Mantras, spells, quarrels, singing, muttering prayers, summoning, instruction, and explanatory discourse—these eight are accomplished through speech.
Furthermore, houses, beautiful women, obedient sons, and land [are likewise attained]. (101)
Fame, honor, a husband, and the Pārśvas; that group of eight is to be accomplished through merit (puṇya).

as well as by lumps of clay and creepers.
Covered by an anthill, he remained as if established in ascetic penance.
Then, after some time had passed, a king named Śaryāti came to the forest where the auspicious hermitage of the sage was located.
The king’s daughter, named Sukanyā, surrounded by her companions,
while wandering about, approached the anthill of Cyavana.
While gathering beautiful flowers from the anthill, she [pierced] the two eyes of the ṛṣi.
Seeing this, she was filled with wonder, thinking, "What is this? and she pierced [the horse] with Kaṇṭhaka.
Blood issued from the two openings of his eyes;
she became terrified by the wrath of the seer Śaryāti and likewise of King Sainya.
When his excrement and urine were obstructed, the king was greatly distressed.
The maiden said, "O father, it was indeed because of me that the sage was offended.
The king said to the sage, "You ought to forgive the girl."
Cyavana said, "Give me your daughter; I shall indeed forgive the offense.
Then the king gave his daughter, and the sage was appeased.
The army became healthy once more, and the maiden attended upon the sage.
The two lords, the physicians of the gods, approached the aged sage. They said to Sukanyā, "This beautiful woman is not suitable for an old man.
Therefore, leaving Cyavana aside, choose one of us."
The maiden said: "Whether my husband be a god, old, or even emaciated, O divine physicians, make him young and powerful for me. Those two physicians made that great sage resemble themselves.
The maiden reflected: "These three forms are indeed identical; they have not arisen as separate entities at all. Who among these is truly my husband?
Through her devotion to her husband and her inner composure, she [perceived] her own husband.
Having recognized him, she took him by the hand and fell at his feet.
The two physicians were struck with wonder, thinking, "She is indeed a devoted wife.
Those two physicians then spoke to Cyavana there regarding sacrifices in every respect.
"O Bhārgava, act in such a way that we two may also have shares;
the sage has granted shares in the sacrifice to those two best of physicians.
Then once, Śaryāti [experienced] the supreme happiness of his daughter.
Having arrived at that hermitage to see [the sage], he beheld a maiden serving a young man. The king questioned that maiden:
"Who is this, O maiden? Who is being served? Or is there some other delusion on my part?"
The maiden said, "Father, my husband is the venerable sage Cyavana;
through his union with the twin sons of the Aśvins, youth has been regained by my lord.
Upon hearing this, the king became pleased and said to the ṛṣi, "I shall do for you—"
"Tell me, O sage, what service is required here. The sage replied, "Perform a sacrifice.
Thereupon, Śaryāti was exceedingly delighted and, for the sake of the rite, had the necessary materials prepared; and Bhārgava officiated as the priest.
At that time, Cyavana made the two excellent physicians partakers [of the sacrifice];
however, Indra restrained him, saying, "These two are not worthy of a share, for they are contemptible both by their profession and by their birth. (85)
Disregarding Indra, the seer gave two shares to the two physicians.
Indra seized his thunderbolt to strike the seer and raised his hand;
the seer paralyzed him, and Mahendra fell for refuge. (86–87)
Afterwards, he gave them their share, and the paralysis was pacified.
Thus, the powerful brahmin, having built a hut on the auspicious bank of the Hiraṇyā,
lived for one year together with his wife Sukanyā.
He performed severe penance at Prabhāsa in Saurāṣṭra.
Indeed, Vaikhānasa sages also dwell in that hermitage. One should perform ablutions at that sacred ford with devotion; it bestows the wealth of capability and sovereignty.
"The supreme bestower of wealth, sons, daughters, health, and prosperity—
from reciting or hearing this, one is liberated from all sins.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, Śaṅkara spoke to Pārvatī.
...and the supremely purifying story of Śaryāti and Cyavana.

Thus ends the five hundred and forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Sūryatīrtha and Cyavanatīrtha, together with their accounts and the One Hundred and Eight Names," in the first section, the *Kṛtayugasantāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, concerning the rivers Nyaṅkumatī and Devikā at the Devarāta-tīrtha. *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā* — Section 1 (*Kṛtayugasantāna*) — Chapter 544.

Chapter 546 → Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī! Śaṅkara spoke these purifying words to Pārvatī;
I shall now relate to you the description of the holy pilgrimage sites (tīrthas) beginning with Agastya. (1)
On the bank of the Nyaṅkumatī, there was a divine and supreme hermitage of Agastya.
In the former Kṛta age, he performed penance there for the duration of one year.
Once, the Ṛṣi Agastya indeed went forth with the desire to visit sacred fords (tīrthas).
In that southern direction, Vātāpi was subdued there.
His elder brother, named Ilvala, who was filled with deceit, resided in the city of Maṇimatī; he, however, was none other than Vātāpi himself.
Having heard of Agastya’s miraculous power, he went toward him and said,
"O Blessed One, grant me a son equal to Mahendra.
However, Agastya did not wish to give his son to that asura.
That asura became enraged at that Brahmin who maintained his ascetic power.
While Agastya was on a pilgrimage along the middle of the path, Vātāpi took the form of a fruit—a perfectly ripe *kāliṅga* fruit. (6–7)
The third, Kāmarūpa, became the auspicious Parṇagraha,
a beautiful hermitage of sages complete with an altar.

Ilvala, however, always provided hospitality for those who arrived at his enclosure, including the offering of fruit and food. A traveler on the road who subsisted on fruit, having eaten that fruit as a guest, [proceeded on].
Indeed, as long as he drank water, so long did the Asura Ilvala remain.
He summoned Vātāpi, who resided within his belly in the form of excellent fruit, saying, "O Vātāpi, come out! Hearing this, [Vātāpi] went into the belly. (11)
Indeed, at that very moment, the living being burst through the belly and emerged;
the three brothers, filled with joy, gathered together around that deceased person. (12)
They were constantly devouring them in this way, committing the slaughter of sages;
for it was along that very path that Agastya had previously departed. (13)
Ātāpin became a leaf-hut and Vātāpin indeed became a fruit;
then Ilvala joyfully spoke to Agastya, who was his guest. (14)
O Sage, my fortune is blessed; please accept this fruit-offering.
Indeed, service rendered to a guest brings about supreme liberation. (15)
Agastya said "So be it" to him and sat down within the house; Ilvala then divided that fruit into two parts and then into four.
He fed Agastya and then summoned his younger brother;
however, he received no reply from him, so the sage cooked for him instead.
Having whirled his hand about in his belly, he produced a belch;
then Ilvala, overcome with fear, departed from that place.
He quickly made his escape and fled, crying out "O Ātāpin! as well;
the sage, by the mere glance of his wrath, reduced them both to ashes at that very moment. (19)
Then Agastya, wandering through various holy fords (tīrthas) to perform purification of his body, arrived here and remained firm on the bank of the Nyaṅkumatī.
He performed penance for exactly one year; indeed, this is the Agastya-tīrtha.
It is prescribed for the purpose of purifying the body; it is supremely sanctifying and bestows heaven. ||21||
Now, in former times, there was a king, a lord of men named Nṛga.
Once, he indeed set out for Prabhāsa for the purpose of a pilgrimage to sacred fords. ||22||
Accompanied by only a few servants, he rested during the night in a forest of trees within a lion-infested wilderness on the road, and obtained auspicious and pleasant sleep.
Then, the mountain-born thieves, numbering in the hundreds and equipped with weapons, having discovered him—
They surrounded him on all sides in order to seize his wealth, such as gold and other treasures.
The king's guards are few, while the thieves exceed them by hundreds. What is to be done? To lose one's life for the sake of wealth is not preferable. (25)
Thinking thus, Nṛga said: "Let them take this abundant wealth;
a wise man should protect himself through his riches, his wife, and likewise through his integrity.
Even though I am a king, these wicked men must be punished by me."
Nevertheless, I do not possess a sufficient army even for this forest. ||27||
Since the king has no concern for the loss of his life or the forfeiture of his kingdom, my only regret is that this journey, which brings about liberation, will not be mine. (1.28)
"Having given wealth and performed the departure rites, I shall go forth once more;
having sought out all of them, I will destroy them on the field of battle.
While Nṛga was reflecting thus and issuing orders to his servants, [the following occurred].
For it is from his own body that a king must give wealth to the thieves. (1.545.30)
A single woman, armed and exceedingly wrathful, appeared;
she struck all those thieves with her weapons as if in play during the battle. (31)
Once the king had recovered his health, he paid homage to that Prarakṣaṇī;
she, however, quickly entered the body of the king once again. (32)
Then, at dawn, the king set out on the road toward Prabhāsa;
there he saw the sage Vāmadeva performing austerities on the bank of the Devikā. (33)
Having rested for a moment at midday, he questioned his most venerable preceptor, Vāmadeva: "Who was this maiden born from Śarīra? (34)
Vāmadeva, having attained meditative absorption and recognized his own ancestor, spoke to that meritorious king: "In the past, you were Śūdraka. (35)
The eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Śrāvaṇa was observed by you, as well as the twelfth; that merit now resides within you. (36)
That maiden was of the nature of merit, embodying two lunar days:
she was the maiden Kanyā and the eleventh day, Ekādaśī; and she was the twelfth day, Dvādaśī. ||37||
By those two, the thieves and enemies were slain for you because of your vow at the sacred ford;
for in this way, merit performed here or in the next world indeed reaches its fruition. (38)
Merit, residing within oneself, is always a companion that brings joy;
therefore, in this human existence, one should perform pilgrimages, observe vows, and practice charity. (39)
Having been told this, Nṛga understood everything and became filled with joy;
bowing to the sage Vāmadeva and honoring him, he presented him with gifts. (1.545.40)
That holy site of Vāmadeva is also celebrated as that of Mṛga;
it is located in Saurāṣṭra within the field of Somaka, and it bestows protection as well as liberation. 41.
Having worshipped Somanātha thoroughly, he then went to his own palace.
Now, there was a twice-born man named Devaśarman, born at the Prabhāsa-tīrtha;
he, being destitute, made his dwelling on the bank of the Nyaṅkumatī river. 42.1–2.
For the sake of wealth, he abandoned his village and committed theft.
He had a son named Duḥsaha, who was indeed a thief;
addicted to vices, he lived in a forest in a dilapidated temple. (44)
Having lit a lamp for the deity, he then committed theft;
severely beaten by the people, he died in the temple of Śiva. ||45||
In the realm of Gāndhāra, there was a king known by the name Durmukha;
he was a fool who oppressed his subjects and was excluded from righteous deeds. (46)
Through the consecration of the temple of Śiva, he indeed became a devotee of Śiva;
he always worshipped Śiva with flower garlands, incense, food offerings, perfumes, and other such items.
He also worshipped other deities by offering lamps.
In whichever stage of life he may be, that descendant of Pṛthu surely proceeds toward the divine. ||48||
He constantly offered lamps in the temples;
once, while wandering among the sacred fords on Mount Raivata, he [did so]. ||49||
Having set out for Somanātha while traveling on the road through the Siṃha forest,
he met his death on the bank of the Nyaṅkumatī due to the power of time.
And by the fruit of his gift of lamps and his worship, that Durmukha became the son of Viśravas, known as Kubera, the king of the Yakṣas. ||51||
Then Kubera, remembering his former birth, went to Prabhāsa, where he had previously died on the bank of the Yamunā. ||52||
Having installed Śambhu there, he indeed constructed a temple; at that sacred site, he established Kubera-Śaṅkara, which was named after himself. (53)
Having performed what was auspicious there, he praised [Śiva] with a pure mind;
and Śaṅkara granted three boons to Kubera.

Friendship, sovereignty over wealth, and the status of a guardian of the quarters among the celestial dwellers—whosoever goes there and worships the Lord of Kubera with devotion [shall attain these]. (55)
In his house, Lakṣmī shall dwell for seven generations.
Now, there was a fisherman, a slayer of fish, during the Svārociṣa interval.
Having brought a water-soaked net from the shore of the ocean to the temple of Śiva, that net, fashioned from cords, was fastened to the staff of the banner. ||57||
And he established it so that the banner of the net could be seen;
thus, for the drying up of the water, there came to be the day known as Jāladhvaja. ||58||
By that merit, in another birth, that fisherman became a king named Kratudhvaja in the field of Kunkumavāpī in Saurāṣṭra;
he was a powerful monarch and always resided in the hermitage of Lomaśa. ||59||
Constantly chanting "Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya," [he attains liberation]. (1.545.60)
By the grace of Śaṅkara, he became a supreme devotee of Viṣṇu;
remembering his former births, he offered [worship] at Somanātha in Prabhāsa. ||61||
Then, every year, he gave away a large, very long white banner;
for ten thousand years, that king ruled his kingdom. (62)
In the middle of Aśvapaṭṭasara, King Śṛṅgavat had a new temple for Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa constructed when the old one had fallen into ruin. (63)
Then, by means of a divine celestial chariot, he went to Vaikuṇṭha itself.
By reciting and hearing this, the state of liberation will certainly be attained. 64.
Likewise, there exists at Prabhāsa a beautiful sacred field containing a temple,
where the delightful river Ṛṣitoyā flows and the deities reside. There,
during a time of drought, they were entreated by the sages for the sake of a sacrificial session.
Thirsty from many sacrifices, a most beautiful rain was born. ||66||
From the confluence of the deities, the sages, and the kulas, this excellent river known as Ṛṣikula is indeed a purifying sacred ford (tīrtha). 67.
In a former age, the sages who dwelt in the tiger-infested forest once went to Satyaloka in order to see Brahmā. (68)
They praised Brahmā, who was born from the lotus, with various hymns.
Satisfied, Brahmā said to them all: "Choose whatever you desire in your hearts. (69)
Then those sages said: "Whatever rite, such as bathing and the twilight prayers, is performed with ocean water, it bestows infinite merit. (1.545.70)
In providing water for drinking and in honoring guests and the like, the earth and water [are the primary elements];
they truly exist in wells and other such sources where we dwell eternally. (71)
Therefore, O Brahmin, you must send rivers toward the earth;
for their waters are sweet and suitable for ritual acts at Prabhāsaka.
"O Grandfather, act in such a way that we may obtain it;
O Grandfather, grant us a sacred river for our consecration."
Then Brahmā, having reflected upon what ought to be done, cast his gaze and summoned the rivers Gaṅgā, Yamunā, and Sarasvatī. (74)
Likewise the Candrabhāgā, the Revā, the Sarayū, and the Gaṇḍakī; the Tāpī, the Godāvarī, the Śiprā, the Kāverī, and the Devikā. ||75||
The Carmaṇvatī, the Māhendrī, the Bhadrā, and likewise the Śatrujit—
these all stood before Brahmā in embodied form.
Then, Brahmā cast his gaze toward his water-pot (kamaṇḍalu).
And having fully understood his state of being, they entered that water-pot. ||77||

Then those excellent rivers, in the form of water contained within the water-pots (kamaṇḍalu), were given by those sages to be led toward the earth. At that time, that auspicious river consisted of the waters of all [other] rivers.
A river named Ṛṣitoyā arose in Saurāṣṭra. ||79||
In the Devadāru forest, where water had formerly been deposited from their water-pots by the sages, that river came into being;
indeed, she was led to the ocean, having increased through her own auspiciousness and other virtues.
Then, at the Mūlacaṇḍīśa Tīrtha, she [was established] facing the east. 81.
O Lakṣmī! This beautiful [narrative], which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, was indeed told by Śaṅkara to Pārvatī; it has been recounted by me to you in brief. ||82||

Thus ends the five hundred and forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description with Narratives of Agastya’s Hermitage, the Destruction of Ātāpī, Vātāpī, and Ilvala, the Tīrthas of Vāmadeva, Nṛga, and Kubera, the Liberation of Kratudhvaja, and the Tīrthas of Devakula, Ṛṣitoyā, and Others," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā. || 545 ||

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, Lakṣmī! I shall relate the divine account of King Viśāla as it occurred in the past, which Śaṅkara told to Pārvatī.
Formerly, there was a very powerful king named Viśāla in the city of Kāśī.
Having been deprived of his kingdom by his kinsmen, he went to Mount Gandhamādana.
Reaching the auspicious Badarī in its valley, that best of kings—
He performed austerities while worshipping Hari Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
Once, the two ancient and most excellent sages, the divine Nara and Nārāyaṇa, sons of Dharma who dwell upon the Himālayas, arrived there. (3–4)
Having seen that auspicious king dwelling at Badarī,
performing intense penance and meditating upon Janārdana in the form of Viṣṇu— the Supreme Brahman—
and having beheld him with his impurities exhausted as Nara-Nārāyaṇa, they were filled with joy.
The two givers of boons said, "O King, choose the boon you desire.
The king replied, "Who are you two? I do not know; how can I choose a boon from those who are unknown? And what boon could I possibly grant to those who are unknown?"
"O twice-born ones, [I declare]: 'I propitiate Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Teacher of the World; from Him alone I shall receive a boon, and not from any other.
When they had spoken thus, the two of them asked: "Which Lord do you propitiate?"
"Which boon do you choose? Speak out of curiosity.
Thus addressed, the king spoke to the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa:
"I constantly worship [you]. Then the two of them spoke again: [546.10]
O King, by the grace of that very god, we have obtained this boon for you.
Accept it; tell us what desire dwells in your heart.
[Just as one worships] the Lord of Sacrifice with various sacrifices and sacrificial fees... 11.
"Grant me this boon: may I have the capacity to perform sacrifice.
Then, having revealed his supreme brother Nārāyaṇa, Nara said to the king: "Listen, O King, to the eternal truth."
"This is my elder brother, the guide of the worlds;
performing austerities together with me, he dwells in the Badarikāśrama.
Formerly he was a fish, and thereafter he became a tortoise."
He became the Boar (Varāha), and from that he became the Man-Lion (Narasiṃha).
Then he was born as the Dwarf (Vāmana), and after that as Paraśurāma.
Then came Rāma, Buddha, Kṛṣṇa, and then indeed this Kalki.
This very Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, who is without beginning and higher than the highest,
shines forth at the holy site of Kuṅkumavāpī on the land of Saurāṣṭra.
He is this very Nārāyaṇa himself, the Lord of Lakṣmī, the Lord of Ramā.
The Lord of Śrī, the Beloved of Kamalā; the Lord of Pārvatī, the Sovereign;
Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Rādhā, the Lord of Prabhā, and the Lord of Māṇikī; the Lord of devotees, the Lord of the liberated, the Lord of Satī, the Supreme Person. (18–19)
O King, one should worship the Fish for the sake of attaining knowledge of the Vedas;
O King, one should worship the Tortoise for the nourishment of physical strength;
O King, one should worship the Boar for the attainment of sovereignty over the earth and other such goals.
One should worship Narasiṃha for the removal of the enemy that is sin;
one should worship Vāmana for the attainment of universal sovereignty;
and one should worship Paraśurāma for the removal of cruel enemies. (21–22)
One should always worship Rāmāditya for the increase of dharma;
one should worship the virtuous Buddha for the attainment of self-knowledge;
and one should worship the beloved Kṛṣṇa for the attainment of Goloka and other realms.
O King, one should worship Kalki for the removal of passion, hatred, and other such afflictions;
one should worship the eternal Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa for the sake of liberation;
and one should worship the Divine Couple together for the abundant attainment of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Having spoken thus to him, the man said: "O King, always observe the vow born of Hari’s day;
likewise, fast on the Ekādaśī and perform the fast on the Dvādaśī, and become capable in sacrifice."
Having spoken thus, the two of them departed for Badarī;
thereafter, the king performed his vow according to the prescribed rites and indeed regained his prowess.
And the Sudarśana discus was granted to him by Viṣṇu, who was pleased with him.
Having taken back that which was offered, he returned once more to his own kingdom;
and having conquered his enemies, that king became a universal monarch (cakravartin).
By him, moreover, a place for penance had been established long ago on the Himalayas.
There, indeed, was a city rich with leaf-huts established by sages;
it was built for the sake of ascetics by that king under his own name,
and it was called Viśālā, consisting of hermitages at Badarī.
Named after King Viśāla, that auspicious city became known as Viśālā;
it was the abode of Nara and Nārāyaṇa, providing a pleasant dwelling for the sages.
Having established a supreme holy site there, one attains the highest realm. (32)

In that birth, having remained in his kingdom again and again, that king performed various sacrifices and made Hari pleased. Then, on one occasion, he went to Arbuda and Puṣkara for the sake of visiting sacred pilgrimage sites.
Then, having reached the sacred field of Lomaśa and the mountain Raivata,
and having arrived at the sacred field of Prabhāsa and beheld Somanātha,
he went to Guptaprayāga and performed a Vaiṣṇava sacrifice.
Then, having bowed to Lomaśa at the sacred site of Śrī-Kuṅkumavāpī,
he departed from his kingdom and went to Badarī, leaving behind the cycle of worldly existence;
having attained Nārāyaṇa through devotion, he went to the supreme abode of Hari.
By this king, a sacrifice was performed at Guptaprayāgaka;
for there exists that most excellent and supreme sacred ford (tīrtha) which is liberating.
Listen also to another king, after whose name an excellent sacred ford [is known].
Bhadreśvara was manifested at Jayantī on the banks of the Bhadrikā.
In the Kṛta Yuga, there was a king named Bhadrāśva, the sovereign of devotees;
after his name, the region came to be known by the name Bhadrāśva.
Once, the most excellent Agastya came to his house and said,
"I shall dwell in your home for seven nights.
Bowing his head to him, the king replied, "Please stay."
He had a wife named Kāntimatī who was devoted to her husband.
Her splendor on earth became equal to the luster of the moon.
Furthermore, the king had five hundred other wives.
By the power of her asceticism, those co-wives perform tasks for her like slaves;
moreover, her husband is highly fortunate, radiant, and the most excellent of all.
Out of fear of her, his other wives constantly perform service as if they were slaves.
Then Agastya, seeing that auspicious woman endowed with beauty and splendor,
and seeing the king there to be greedy and devoid of devotion to Hari,
and observing Kāntimatī to be likewise lacking in devotion, the sage spoke.
On the first day, seeing him gazing upon the face of his beloved, Agastya, filled with great joy, exclaimed: "Excellent, excellent, O Lord of the World!
On the second day as well, having likewise beheld the queen and the king, [he spoke thus].
"Alas, it is lost! Alas, this entire world of moving and non-moving beings is lost!
Thus Agastya spoke, shaking his head while the king was listening.
And on the third day, seeing the king and the queen, he said out of grief: [48-49]
"Alas, the fools do not know the Supreme Lord as the giver,
who, being pleased with the king in a single day, bestowed [this gift]. On the fourth day, raising his hands, he spoke again:
"Excellent, excellent, O Lord of the World! 'Excellent, excellent! [cried] the women and the Śūdras.
'Excellent, O twice-born ones! Excellent, O kings! Excellent, O Vaiśyas! they said again and again. 'Excellent, O Bhadras! Excellent, you! Excellent, O Agastya! Excellent to you! || 51-52 ||
"Excellent, Prahlāda! Excellent, you! Dhruva, excellent, O observer of great vows!
Having spoken thus, Agastya danced loudly in the presence of the king.
Seeing him in such a state, the best of kings, accompanied by his wife, [was filled with wonder].
"O Brahmin, what is the cause of your joy that you dance here in this manner? And why, O learned one, do you converse with such a mind of supreme bliss?
Agastya then spoke thus to Bhadrāśva and the queen.
"Alas! You are a foolish king, and this beloved wife of yours is foolish;
all your ministers are fools, and alas, your priests are fools. O King, your entire realm appears to be permeated by folly. (56)
"Those who do not understand my thought, which is simple and its meaning well-known...
(57) When this was said, the king spoke again with palms joined in reverence:
"O Brahmin, we do not understand what you have said, for it is filled with profound significance. (58)
"O great learned one, if you are inclined to show favor, then investigate [this matter].
Thereupon Agastya related the account of his previous birth as follows:
"In the city of Nagara, there was a Vaiśya named Haradatta."
You were his servant, belonging to the Śūdra caste and possessed of great devotion.
This queen, your wife, was at that time the servant of a Vaiśya.
That Vaiśya, remaining self-restrained, stood on the twelfth day of the month of Aśvayuj.
Oṃ, salutations to Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Lord; salutations!
Having gone to the abode of Viṣṇu while chanting [His names], he constantly worships Hari with flowers, incense, and other offerings, and indeed meditates upon Him for a long time. (62)
Having appointed you two as guards in the temple and having stationed two lamps there for the purpose of lighting them,
that Vaiśya indeed goes to his own home, while you two remain in the house of Hari.
Having performed the sweeping, the offering of water, and the placing of flowers and *tulasī* before Hari every day, as well as honoring those who arrive,
you two should maintain the unbroken continuity of lamps before Him both by day and by night. (65)
"Let it be; having rekindled [the fire], they remained there indeed guarding it.
By that merit, your sins, along with [your] lifespan, were dissolved when the night had turned to dawn, and you two were then [reborn]."
By the grace of Śrī Hari, having cast off their Śūdra bodies, they passed away;

This Kāntimatī is that very same woman who has come here as your wife.
"Even though this lamp was lit by another, it was offered in the house of Hari;

robbed by their own actions, they will be utterly deceived.
And you, O King, are always devoted here solely to your beloved.
"You do not remember the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa here;

'Alas, the world of moving and non-moving beings has been robbed! Alas, it has been robbed!'"
The entire world of moving and non-moving beings has indeed been robbed and deceived by the wife of Śrī Hari.
They do not worship Hari, the Supreme Person and the bestower of prosperity;

Even upon my arrival, these two do not worship Puruṣottama.
Indeed, through the company of the virtuous, even those who are not devotees everywhere may indeed develop devotion to Kṛṣṇa for a moment; but fools never do so.
Even when there is a perfect opportunity, those devoid of devotion are certainly deluded—of this there is no doubt.
"The king is a fool, and his queen appears to me to be even more foolish.

when on the fourth day I indeed raised my hands. (87–88)
Having reflected upon this, it has been declared to you both: all devotees are indeed virtuous.

Those kings who worship Hari constantly are said to be virtuous.
Having resorted to a demonic disposition, Prahlāda [worshipped] Puruṣottama. 96–97.
Having abandoned all else, he knows nothing other than Him; therefore, he is called a saint.
Dhruva, the son of Uttānapāda, while still a child, worshipped Viṣṇu in the forest and attained the most exalted station.

he reached the Śāṅkara tīrtha situated in the city named Jayantī.

And that place named Bhadreśvara destroys sin merely by being heard of. Furthermore, the king gave there the hermitage of Agastya, which consists of austerity and is frequented by Brahmanical sages, situated on the bank of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake.

(43) Such is the entirety of sovereignty, as manifest as the palm of one's hand;

Everything is directly under his own authority, for that means of accomplishment is born of himself. That kingdom is indeed the consecration of the pure subjects;

Forests, oceans, mountains, and cultivated lands—

Gautama, Kauśika, and Kuśika of great penance.
Jātūkarṇya, Vasiṣṭha, Satyatapas, Parāśara, Śāṇḍilya, Pulastya, Vatsa, Sāvasti,
Śūkara, Bharadvāja, Bhārgava, and Dīrghatapas. (35–36)
These and many other sages, such as Agastya and others,
having performed austerities and meditated upon Hara, then became absorbed in Him.
At that time, Śambhu indeed appeared before them in person.
He spoke for the sake of granting a boon, and they chose their own desired wish:
"O Lord of Gods, if you are pleased, bring the Gaṅgā here first;
having performed our ablutions there and worshipped you thereafter..."
"Out of ignorance you have wronged us; from that we shall attain purity.
Because you did not recognize Śaṅkara as yourself with both eyes, an offense has been committed by you, but it shall not be so for us."

"O Śambhu, grant me a third divine eye, just like yours, so that it may be a witness to Hari, Hara, and others, and may possess the power of valid cognition. O Śaṅkara, likewise grant me an inner eye for such discernment. (41–42)
Śambhu said, "So be it; you shall indeed be the purifiers of purifiers, and may you always possess three eyes. And here is Gaṅgā, who has arrived.
Having spoken thus, Śaṅkara quickly departed from that place.
And the sages, freed from sin through the grace of Śaṅkara,
performed a Vaiṣṇava sacrifice in that sacred field for eight days.
The Brāhmaṇas, the deities, the other holy places, and the forest deities [were present].

They gathered at his sacrifice; having eaten the food produced by the grace of Nārāyaṇa, other living beings indeed attained supreme satisfaction. All those born of water and those born of land were satisfied there at that auspicious rite.
The fish said to all the sages,
"Just as fishermen do not kill us when they desire to do so, so let a blessing be granted to us.
Then the ṛṣis said, "May you indeed become three-eyed."
May this very form of Śaṅkara— the third divine eye that grants far-reaching vision— be ever present for you.
And those forms of Śaṅkara were revealed by the sages to the fishermen.
Indeed, auspicious three-eyed fish must never be killed.
Furthermore, the reason for their having three eyes has been explained in the Gaṅgā-āgama.
Having arrived at that pool and bathed there, one should observe the fish.
One should give chickpeas and other such items to them, and offer gold to a brahmin;
one should also give cows, clothing, and sesame seeds—then one will certainly become three-eyed.
Having bathed in the waters of the Ṛṣitoyā river as well as in the pool of hot water (Taptodaka), [one attains this].
One should worship Śaṅkara there; he shall become the lord of the world.
There dwells the four-faced Vināyaka of great strength;
by worshipping him on a Monday, a person obtains their desired wishes. (53–54)
Then one should go to the supreme holy site of Hari Gopālasvāmin,
which pacifies the flood of all sins and destroys the torrent of poverty.
One should worship Bakulasvāmin Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
From there, one should go to Uttarārka, which destroys all diseases.
On the shore of the ocean there, the Ṛṣitīrtha indeed exists;
there, sages are always seen in the form of stones.
Then one should go to Maruddevī, who was formerly worshipped by the Maruts;
from there, one should go to Kṣemāditya, situated in the midst of the Śabara settlement.
Then one should go to the great goddess Śubhrā, the purifier of thorns.
In ancient times, the great seers performed a sacrifice on the banks of the Ṛṣitoyā river.
The sky was completely shrouded by the smoke arising from the sacrificial fires and *agnihotra* oblations.
Having smelled it, the Daityas emerged from the midst of the ocean and arrived there.
Deceitful, with massive bodies, dark complexions, and large bellies;
with drooping eyebrows, whiskers, and the tips of their noses, and with red eyes and red hair—
these beings caused disturbances for the purpose of destroying the sacrifice.
Seeing these, the sages fled, overcome with fear;
some, filled with haste, quickly entered the wife’s chamber.
Having placed the sacrificial materials for the *agnihotra* and the oblation according to the mantras, they departed.
And they offered oblations into the well-kindled fire for the sake of destroying the Rākṣasas.
As soon as the offering was made, a spear appeared, terrifying to the world,
blazing with great splendor, and held in its hands a sword, a spear, a trident, a scimitar, and a shield.
By her, all those Daityas were then slain;
thereafter, all the sages, being delighted, praised her, and she spoke to them:
"Choose a boon, O Munis; I shall grant you here whatever you desire."
The sages chose her as the purifier of the thorns of the gods;
"Dwell here in this place by the name Kaṇṭakaśodhinī and protect us!
she replied, "So be it," and remained right there.
On the eighth or the ninth day, one should worship her who brings about welfare;
for him, no fear shall arise from Rākṣasas or Piśācas.
He shall obtain the perfection of sacrifice as well as the fruit arising from ritual offerings.
Then one should go to the sacred ford named Unnata, situated in the northern region.
There, one should worship Brahmeśvara as well as Kṛṣṇanarāyaṇa. Formerly, on the banks of the Ṛṣitoyā, Brahmins indeed performed penance.
Having become an exceedingly fierce mendicant, Nārāyaṇa departed.
Then Śambhu, having become a bull, wandered in the presence of the sages;

Upon merely being seen, Śaṅkara, who had assumed the form of a bull, ceased [his advance].
There, Śambhu became established in the form of a Liṅga as Caṇḍikeśvara.
O Lakṣmī! I, Nārāyaṇa, was then earnestly entreated by them.
Then, for the sake of protection against the Asuras, I announced:
"Build a city here of great splendor for our residence. Let the twice-born always offer the Agnihotra oblations to the deities. (74–75)
Let sacrifices be performed with various rites, and let worship also be offered.
Let hospitality be practiced constantly, and let your devotion to me be unwavering.
By my grace, at the end, liberation shall be yours.
Then those sages, weakened by the oppression of the city, said:
"What shall we do here with the city, O Great King, since we desire devotion to you? Grant us liberation, O Great King; always provide for our protection! (77–78)
Hari said, "I shall always provide protection for you.
He then called upon Viśvakarman,
and Viśvakarman arrived at that square-shaped ground where Śambhu, the Lord of Caṇḍī, resided.
He took possession of that city, which was eight yojanas in extent. To the east was the glorious Śaṅkarā; to the west, the Nyaṅkumatī;
to the north, the Svarṇanandā; and to the south, it reached as far as the ocean.
In the center, Hari caused a supreme, elevated city to be built as a field for the protection of the fire; having had it constructed, he gave it to those brahmins so that they might dwell there.
The brahmins lived there, devoted to the performance of *homa* and sacrificial rites.
And for the sake of protection there, the exalted Vighnarāja was installed by Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa in the vicinity of Śaṅkara;
he is worshipped as the Giver of Wealth (Dhanada), who always bestows sons and prosperity. (83–84)
He will bestow both desires and liberation, of this there is no doubt.
For the work of construction, they worshipped Gaṇeśa, Śaṅkara, the illustrious Narāyaṇa,
Viśvakarman, the hosts of Mothers, and the Brahmins.
They worshipped the water-pot (kalaśa), and then Śambhu arrived.
Indeed, Kalaśeśa became manifest before the water-pot;
and at the spot where they had worshipped, Sthaleśvara came into being.
In the month of Māgha, there was a festival of worship throughout the entire city;
thereafter, that city became known as Unnata, a sacred place for Brahmins.
Furthermore, the Viśvakarmeśvara Liṅga was worshipped in that very same location.
Then Brahmā, in the form of a child, resided in the place called Unnata;
Vāmana, as a child, was at Raivata; and Hara, as a young boy, was at Prabhāsa.
In Unnata, Aja exists in the form of a child; those three are equal.
In the form of the child, there is no illusion, nor deceit, nor latent impression.
Indeed, the form of the child bestows liberation; it is worthy of worship, delightful, and free from affliction.
Desire, anger, greed, delusion, and the like exist within the one whose form is that of the child.
They are indeed rootless; they have never arisen and do not exist at all from birth.
Furthermore, they arise either from the fault of attachment or from mental impressions (*saṃskāra*).
In that regard, truth, the vow, and non-violence toward even a child are always [to be maintained]. (92–93)
Non-stealing prevails there, as does conduct like that of a Brahmin;
likewise, non-possessiveness and trust in what is offered by one’s mother [are present]. There is also freedom from passion, contentment, and moderation in eating.
Purity, freedom from hatred within oneself, austerity, dependence on a nourisher, study of knowledge, devotion to the Lord—all these indeed exist in the child;
as does the very nature of worldly existence, which leads toward the pursuit of sense objects. (95–96)
That [nature] does not exist in that child; therefore, Viṣṇu is indeed the child.
Even a serpent, perceiving him as a child, creeps over the child and proceeds fearlessly, due to the child's state of having no enemy.

Whosoever’s child is always looked upon with compassion, that child is likewise looked upon with love by all living beings belonging to every species of birth. That very state of being the embodiment of Nārāyaṇa is recognized in the infant. (98–99)
In ancient times, having worshipped Dhruva, Prahlāda, Sanaka and the others, as well as Śuka and the youthful Kṛṣṇa in his true form, they attained liberation.
Whether in youth, old age, or even in manhood, womanhood, or neuter state—
It might be argued that if childhood were indeed free from faults, then it too would be worshipped like a deity, because that child is faultless;
for both old age is devoid of faults, and childhood is likewise devoid of faults. (101–102)
There is equality between the two in their stainless purity, for both are places of sanctity.
Indeed, people bow to the young moon; mothers look upon the infant;
they marry the young girl; and those without lineage adopt the child. (103)

And where there exists the pure Nārāyaṇīya power born of creation, one who possesses that is designated as Bāla; therefore, Bāla is Nārāyaṇa. [One should provide] the gift of knowledge to children, the gift of food, and assistance.
Therefore, people entrust [their children] to him; thus the child is praised.
Since celibacy is always the very form of Brahman for the child, therefore the child who practices celibacy is entitled to the world of Brahman.
And just as Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa bestows Brahman and liberation,
so too one obtains the fruit by worshipping Gaurī, Bālikā, and Saumyā;
indeed, [the fruit] of the worship of Pārvatī and also of the worship of Lakṣmī.
The youthful goddesses, free from passion, always dwell in heaven;
likewise the youthful Sāvitrī, Gāyatrī, Śrī, and Lakṣmī.
Their lords are always the youths Brahmā, Kṛṣṇa, and Hara.
People imagine a state of perfect youth through their own conditioned perceptions.
Like themselves, the Daityas perceive even those who are divine as being utterly non-divine, though they are free from faults, eternally pure, and yet they grasp them as being tainted by defects.
How can there be liberation in that which possesses defects, or how can there be latent impressions in that which is free from defects?
Therefore, the gods are free from defects; they are eternally children who bestow liberation.
These children are eternal and ever-liberated, shining in the abode of Brahman.
"Always youthful, divine, and highly praised are the boys [there].
Having spoken thus to Pārvatī regarding Unnatā and the others, Śambhu said:
"O Lakṣmī, I have also described this holy site (tīrtha) which grants liberation through its mere hearing."

Thus ends the five hundred and forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of Various Holy Places such as Guptaprayāga-tīrtha, Śṛgāleśvara-kṣetra, Aparanārāyaṇa-tīrtha, Trinetratīrtha, Unnatanagara, and Sthāneśvara, along with the Explanation of the Essential Meaning for the Youth," in the first section concerning the lineage of the Kṛta-yuga of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
