(1.549.10) "By protecting the calves of cows, by scratching them, and likewise by protecting those who are exhausted or distressed, a person is glorified in heaven. (101)
Cows are proclaimed to be present at the beginning, outside, in the middle, and at the end;
they always protect the gods' milk, clarified butter, and nectar.
Therefore, cows should be given as gifts and should be worshipped constantly.
"These [cows] were created like a staircase for the attainment of heaven.
Having heard these words of the sage, the Niṣādas, quickly recognizing the greatness of the cows, bowed to Āpastamba and said: [1.04]
Conversation, sight, touch, as well as praise and remembrance—
these are indeed always purifying for holy men and yogis.
For we have been purified by that Nābhāga through this auspicious pair of cows.
"Since we have accepted your root [the cow], we shall certainly honor the cow.
Thus you are liberated, as are the fish, and the two cows are liberated;
we too are liberated, and Nabhaga is liberated through this meeting with the virtuous. (106–107)
"You are worthy of honor, as are these fish, and this pair of cows is worthy of honor.
We too are worthy of honor, yet Nābhāga is most worthy of honor because of this auspicious meeting.
The sage said, "I have already set the price for my own pair of cows."
"Furthermore, I am pleased by the instruction of Lomaśa. Therefore, O one of auspicious resolve, I shall act so that these fish may live. By the gift of two cows, the fish shall attain life."
"Therefore, O gods, give a pair of cows to a high-souled Brāhmaṇa;
by that means you fishermen shall live, and you will be free from fault.
Having heard that, the fishermen then gave those two cows to the sage.

To Āpastamba, right there, [the merit] was offered, and faultlessness was thereby acquired. The pleased sage said to them: "Behold the school of fish; by the gift of two cows, their life shall indeed be restored. (1.12–1.13)
When this was said, the fish that were still alive went into the waters of the ocean;

as for those fish that had been mutilated and those that had been cut up, the sage Āpastamba spoke these words again for their sake of liberation: [1.14] For the sake of the liberation of those [fish], the seer Āpastamba spoke further words.
"I accept this cow from you for the sake of your spiritual merit.
O Niṣādas, go to heaven along with the fish and the sinless ones, having produced joy in living beings even through a censurable deed. (1.15–1.16)
Even if I should reach hell, I shall see it as heaven itself;
may all those who are afflicted by suffering attain a fortunate rebirth through whatever merit I have performed by means of the actions of my mind, speech, and body.
Then, by his grace, the Niṣādas, along with the fish, went to heaven; and seeing them there, Nābhāga spoke:
"The virtuous, who are like the waters of sacred fords, should be served by those seeking their own welfare."
Even a moment’s service rendered here shall not be fruitless for those who sit with the virtuous, who engage in virtuous conversation with the virtuous,
who conduct themselves according to the conduct of the virtuous, and who do nothing at all with the wicked. (1.549.120)
By the mere company of the virtuous, even those who live by catching fish became like fishers of men;
they attained heaven just as those who have performed the horse sacrifice do.
There were the sage Āpastamba and the great sage Lomaśa.

The sage gratified the king with various desired boons and respectfully caused him to make the formal resolve for the sacrifice. When the king had said "So be it" out of affection, Āpastamba praised him.
"O Indra among kings, you are truly blessed; your mind is fixed upon righteousness.
You accept the command of a Brahmin, and thus your family is also blessed.
For kings, being generally overcome by pride, do not accept such commands at all. (124-125)
Those whose intellects are struck by constant calamities do not heed the words of the Brahmins:
"For kings, birth is certain, delusion is certain, and hell is certain.
Yet they disregard their kingdom and depart for a demonic lineage.
But the wise perceive sovereignty and such things as being like hell;
they accomplish the next world for themselves, the eternal goal.
Having spoken thus, the two great-souled ones departed for their respective hermitages.
Nābhāga, having received the boon, departed for his own city;
he duly performed an auspicious sacrifice on the banks of the Śatruñjītā,
[worshipping] the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Śrī Kamalā.
Having performed his worship, Brahmā went to the supreme, imperishable state.
Viṣṇu and Śaṅkara were installed by the sage at Jālasthala;
thus, that sacred field became famous in ancient times as Jāleśvara.
There, on the bank of the Devikā, are Nābhāga, Matsyajīvin,
Āpastamba, Lomaśa, and likewise Nārāyaṇa;
they grant liberation at the mere thought of them, for they themselves have attained liberation.
Whatever account occurred on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra—
should people perform a *śrāddha*, a pilgrimage, or the gift of a cow there,
they shall obtain enjoyment and liberation here and in the hereafter, exactly as desired.
O Lakṣmī! Just as Śambhu spoke to Satī, so has this been told by me to you.
By reading or even by hearing it, it shall bestow both heaven and liberation.

Thus ends the five hundred and forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Stories of Durgāditya, Goṣpada, Vena, King Śuddhi, Mukti, Nārāyaṇa, Gṛhajāleśvara Tīrtha, Nābhāga, and the Sage Āpastamba," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
← Chapter 549: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga) Chapter 550 [[Author:
→ Chapter 551
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, Lakṣmī! Hear now what Śambhu then spoke to Pārvatī: "I shall describe to you also that foremost of holy places, which bestows heaven and other rewards."
Long ago, on the bank of the Devikā, there lived a sage named Tuṇḍin.
There was a certain well there which, through the power of the sage’s yoga, became a bestower of liberation.
Fierce lions fell into it while coming there for the purpose of drinking water.
All those who had died were restored to life by the sage through the power of his asceticism.
Then, by the mere utterance of the syllable "hūṃ," the water in the well was filled;
it flowed over the bank, which was truly marvelous.
There, he established the deity Tuṇḍīśvara at that sacred site (tīrtha).
Having performed auspicious rites at that tīrtha, one should go to Āśāpura-Gaṇeśvara,
bringing an offering and giving gold as a gift.

From there, one should go to the auspicious Kāpila Tīrtha, which removes all sins. (6) Kapila went to Raivata and dwelt there for a year; it was there that the river Kapilā manifested itself as a sacred bathing place. (7)
If Tuesday should fall on the sixth lunar day of the dark fortnight of the month of Prauṣṭhapada (Bhādrapada),
and that sixth day is joined with the Vyatīpāta yoga and the Rohiṇī nakṣatra, it is considered the Kapilā-ṣaṣṭhī.
On the sixth day at the confluence of the Kapilā river, one should remain composed.
Having bathed, one should worship Viṣṇu as Śrī Kapila situated upon the sun;
one should pray, "May Kapilā and Kapila Viṣṇu protect me," and should give a tawny cow as a gift, whereby the fruit of a horse sacrifice shall be attained.
Then one should visit the supreme purifying holy site of Hāṭakeśa;
from there, one should go to the hermitage of Agastya, which was frequented for a year [by the gods].
In ancient times, the Kālakeyas were Daityas who dwelt within the ocean.
At night, having gathered upon the earth, they repeatedly devoured the sleeping brahmins and others;
knowing them to be the murderous Kālakeyas,
Agastya went there toward the shore of the ocean.
Standing on the bank, he performed penance according to the prescribed rules for the duration of one year.
On the fourth day of the month of Phālguna, having taken food only at night,
he ate ground sesame seeds on the fifth day and performed a fire sacrifice.

Having thus taken only one meal every four months, he then remained without food; he performed this supreme vow free from obstacles. After more than a year, that king of sages contemplated the protection of the world.
"Behold this marvel, O gods:
with my joined palms I shall drink up this ocean, including its fish, crocodiles, and other creatures; I shall dry it up!
Having spoken thus, he called upon Hari and established Brahmā within himself.
He made a single mouthful of the entire ocean, the lord of rivers.
The Kālakeyas were destroyed, and the water was boiled away. Then, by means of clouds raining down, the oceans became full of water once again.
Thus, whoever comes here and worships me, together with Lopāmudrā, at this beautiful hermitage of Agastya— a sacred ford that destroys all sins—
should worship Hāṭakeśa, who has been brought by me, according to the prescribed rites.
During the northern solstice, a mortal may obtain the fruit of a cow;
there, King Bhadrāśva arrived with a desire to behold Agastya, and having paid him homage, he inquired after his welfare. (21–22)
"O knower of dharma, if you have known or even seen anything wonderful, tell it to me; then I shall go to Prabhāsa.
Agastya told that king the story concerning Śvetadvīpa.
The Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Master, is of wondrous form.
The Supreme Person (Puruṣottama) shines at the sacred site of Kuṅkumavāpikā;
many various wonders have been seen there.
This very Nārāyaṇa always rests even in Śvetadvīpa.
Having seen Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa in Surāṣṭra, Nārada then saw Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Śrī Rādhikā, in Māthura. (26)
Having seen Śrī Nara-Nārāyaṇa on the Himālaya mountain,
the sage departed for Śvetadvīpa; there he beheld persons of equal form, possessing fierce splendor, bearing conches, discs, maces, and lotuses.
They were similar, identical in form, equal in the majesty of their qualities, youthful, endowed with beauty, well-proportioned, and captivating.
"This is Viṣṇu, this is Viṣṇu, this is the eternal Viṣṇu. || 29 ||
Seeing them, a thought arose in him: "Who among these is the Lord Viṣṇu?
To whom, then, shall I bow with devotion after seeing the others? For when the first among those worthy of worship is neglected, there is a transgression of the worship due to the venerable.
"There would be a loss of life, fame, and knowledge, and a great transgression would ensue.
As he was thinking thus, his mind became filled with anxious thought regarding Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa:
"How shall I propitiate Him? This worry has arisen in vain. (32)
"By whom I know the Supreme Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa—what more can I do?
(33) Having reflected thus, he meditated upon that God, the Supreme Lord.
Being thus meditated upon by him, the son of Kaṃbhara attained complete satisfaction. (34)
Nārāyaṇa, having become manifest before him, spoke with a gracious mind:
"Choose a boon—blessings be upon you—for my form has been beheld by you.
Those who come here in this world attain the fourfold state beginning with sāyujya."
To them he said, "Tell me right here, what shall I give you?
Nārada replied, "Tell me how my attainment [of that] may come about.
Then Nārāyaṇa said, "The Puruṣasūkta itself is mine."
O Sage, those people who, taking refuge in that Puruṣa of a thousand heads whom I have described there, shall perceive me as Nārāyaṇa,
will attain me constantly through the study of the Saṃhitā.
Those devotees who worship me according to the path taught in the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā* will certainly attain [their goal];
they shall go to my sacred field and behold me.
Those who will perform service to the virtuous will certainly attain me;
indeed, my name has been established as a distinct means for everyone to proclaim.
Without formal worship, people will surely attain me through devotion to my name.
O Sage, all knowledge will certainly become manifest to you.
O Sage, all knowledge born of discernment— both that which is fit for my vision and that which is beyond the range of vision— shall belong to you.
Having spoken thus to those who were identical to Viṣṇu, the Blessed One departed;
and Nārada did not recognize that Lord at all.
Perceiving the disappearance of Viṣṇu among those who were equal to him, [he was bewildered].
Having prostrated toward that very direction, Nārada, as he was departing for heaven,
arrived at Surāṣṭra where I, Agastya, indeed dwell;
having stayed there for a moment, he went to the city of Vaihāyasa.
That indeed is the auspicious Nāradatīrtha, a place that bestows knowledge.
Bhadrāśva, too, having bowed to the sage, departed toward Prabhāsa.
Thus, having learned that Nārāyaṇa was situated on the White Land (Śvetabhūmi), he then [proceeded].
Having known Him who resides in Viśālā, who resides on the Yamunā, and who dwells at Kuṅkumavāpikā—
the form beyond the Imperishable— one indeed attains liberation; for by remembering Viṣṇu, reciting the Vedas, giving gifts, and sacrificing to Hari, [one attains this].
A devotee who pleases the virtuous and the saintly attains liberation; of this there is no doubt.
A holy place (tīrtha) consisting of saints and consisting of virtuous women is supreme and bestows final release.
From there, one should go to the Bhīmanātha-tīrtha, which wards off all fear.
Then one should visit Suparṇeśī and Suparṇa Narāyaṇa.
Next, one should go to Kaubereśī, and then to the excellent tīrtha of Bhalla.
At the Bhalla-tīrtha, Viṣṇu is always present together with the Gaṅgā.
For the Gaṅgā is indeed a purifying Vaiṣṇava field, being the personified [form of Viṣṇu];
thus, by the Niṣāda Vallaka, the eternal Viṣṇu Kṛṣṇa,
having fixed an arrow upon his bow, was taken [as his prey] and became a dweller of Goloka.

Vallaka, too, mistaking Viṣṇu—who was stationed upon the trunk of a *plakṣa* tree—for a deer, struck him with a crescent-headed arrow. Upon approaching and seeing Mādhava, he was filled with remorse and offered praise; he then obtained his grace.
The fisherman went right there to Goloka along with Viṣṇu;
for that place is called Bhallakṣetra, where Hari was pierced in the sole of His foot.
It is the bestower of liberation, the giver of heaven, most excellent, and the piercer of the cycle of birth and death.
From there, one should go toward Raivata, north of Hiraṇyā;
then to the supreme Kauśika Tīrtha, and then to Vastrāpatha, Dāmodara, Raivataka, Bhava, and likewise Indreśvara. 57–58.
Cakrodyāna, Revatītīrthaka, and the hermitage of Vasiṣṭha—
listen, O Lakṣmī, to the sin-destroying story of this land.
There was a king named Gaja who, together with his wife, [ruled] as a sovereign.
He went for the purpose of bathing in the waters of the Gaṅgā and dwelt there. At one point, a sage named Bhadra came before him.
The elephant said to him, "O sage, grant me the knowledge for the sake of liberation."
Bhadra said: "The Self itself is the sacred ford that purifies all;
therein resides Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the most excellent of all sacred fords. Knowledge of Him, which takes the form of remembrance, is called the supreme knowledge in this world. (62)
O King, all other knowledge is merely a burden to the intellect.
(63) Holy fords are full of water, and deities are made of stone and clay;
those by whom [the Self] residing within themselves is not seen do not see that Supreme. (64)
There are many sacred fords (*tīrtha*) and holy shrines (*āyatana*),
as well as oceans and rivers with pure waters that are meritorious and sanctifying. Yet, among all those sacred fords, knowledge is considered the most supreme of the supreme.
[He meditated upon] the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, Viṣṇu, Narāyaṇa; [and his incarnations:
Matsya, Varāha, Nṛsiṃha (the tiger among men), Vāmana, Kūrma, Hari;
Rāma, Rāma, and Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and Śrī Puruṣottama. (66–67)
Hari, Śrī Kapila, Dattātreya, Buddha, and Paraśurāma;
Vāsudeva, Pṛthu, Haṃsa, Ṛṣabha, and the Kumāras;
Nārada, Kratu, Aśvagrīva, Vyāsa, and Janārdana.
The deluder, the king of kings, the destroyer of the Kalkas, the supreme person;
Nara, the divine Nārāyaṇa, the Lord and Master of Śvetadvīpa;
Padmanābha resting upon Śeṣa, and the Lord of the World stationed for battle.
By remembering his names and dwellings, one shall attain liberation.
[These are] the Gaṅgā, the Yamunā, and the auspicious river Godāvarī;
likewise the Śatadru, the Vindhyā, the Payodhā, and the Varadā.
The Carmaṇvatī, the Sarayū, and the Gaṇḍakī, which destroys fierce sins;
the Candrabhāgā, the Vipāśā, the Śoṇā, and likewise the Brahmasutā—these and many other rivers, as well as the mountains such as Himāśraya and others. (72–73)
Indeed, by the mere utterance of their names, evil is destroyed— namely,
those of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake, the Mānasa lake, the Nārāyaṇasara lake, and likewise the Puṣkarasara lake.
By the mere remembrance of Indradyumna’s lake, one shall be liberated.
By staying in Kānyakubja during the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, one shall attain heaven.
[One attains it] at Arbuda on the full moon of Pauṣa, and at the holy ford of Gayā on the full moon of Māgha.

On the full moon of Phālguna he should dwell on the back of the Himalayas, and on the full moon of Caitra at Prabhāsa; on the full moon of Aśvinī at Kuṅkumavāpī, and on the full moon of Vaiśākha at Avantikā; on the full moon of Jyeṣṭha at Trikūpaka, and on the full moon of Śrāvaṇa at the eastern ocean.
On the full moon of Bhādrapada at Sārasvata, on the full moon of Kārttika at Raivatācala,
likewise on the island of Kāpila and at Śālagrāma on the earth—
one should perform śrāddha, bathing, and japa during the Dīpotsava festival at Cāndrabhāga.
In Goloka, the imperishable abode, Vaikuṇṭha, or Kailāsa, the residence of those who observe vows and frequent sacred fords occurs according to their devotion.
Among months, Kārtika is the most excellent; in Kārtika is the Bhīṣmapañcaka.
Even there, O King, the twelfth day (dvādaśī) is most excellent when Dāmodara is in the water. In the vicinity of Somanātha, there is a great mountain ending at sunrise;
on its western side, the great Raivata mountain is remembered.
And there flows the auspicious river Suvarṇarekhikā;
there the minerals are red, white, blue, and variegated.
The stones are shaped like elephants and resemble gold and red ochre.
There, trees, creepers, and shrubs arise made of gold.
In that place, there is a lake named Nārāyaṇa on the river called Svarṇalekhā,
as well as the Dāmodara lake and the lake of Rādhā and the others.
Having bathed there and drunk the water, embodied beings indeed attain liberation.
By the mighty Hariścandra, by Śibi, by Nahuṣa, and by Nala,
great gifts were indeed offered at Raivata.
"They have gone to the eternal and unblemished abode of Viṣṇu.
Having heard these auspicious words, King Gaja arrived at the holy sites of Raivata and Prabhāsa.
Having given many gifts and having offered oblations into the sacrificial fire,
he stood with his feet upward and, facing downward, drank smoke.
Others who had come with him likewise performed penance in that manner.
There on the mountain, everyone performed a vow; Dāmodara was to be meditated upon.
By whomsoever the two syllables "Ha-ri" have been uttered even once, by him the girdle has been fastened for the sake of approaching liberation.
While that king remained there together with the sages,
thousands of celestial chariots indeed arrived there,
in which were the goddesses who are the handmaidens of Ramā and the attendants of Nārāyaṇa.
Others were likewise liberated by the hundreds and by the thousands.
Then that king, together with all his attendants and his wife,
ascended a celestial chariot and went to the supreme, imperishable state.
The proclamation of this mantra—"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Lord; obeisance"—resounded within all the celestial chariots.
With the clapping of hands, it echoed through the sky, by which the inhabitants of heaven and other realms were awakened.
For the sake of beholding the celestial chariots, those liberated ones, stationed in the midst of the path,
gazed upon King Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord,
and paid homage to the Lords.
Thus, having pierced through the worlds of the Pitṛs and the Munis outside the cosmic egg,
they all went to the state of liberation after making Raivata a sacred ford (tīrtha).
Śaṅkara then told Pārvatī this account of the holy field.
O Lakṣmī! I have also told you this auspicious narrative that brings about liberation.
By reading or hearing this story, there is the destruction of sin;
one shall attain heaven, truth, Vaikuṇṭha, and the supreme, imperishable abode.
Having heard this, one should rejoice with such devotion and offer praise;
being freed from all sins, one shall attain the Supreme Brahman.
O Lakṣmī, what more can I say regarding the sanctity of Saurāṣṭra?

The land known as Saurāṣṭra belongs to the glorious Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa himself, who is the embodiment of the jewel; it bestows liberation at every step. Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa has always resided there from time immemorial.
In the west is the god Vāmana; in the south is Somanātha;
in the north is Camatkārapura and the auspicious Dvārikā.
[There are also] Śatruñjaya, Svarṇarekhā, Bhadrā, Uṣṇā, and Hiraṇyakā.
The celestial river Nyankumati and other auspicious rivers that grant liberation are found there.
There also exist Raivata, Śatruñjaya, Varāṭaka, Śālamāla, Navanīta, and other preeminent mountains. (105–106)
For there dwell great sages who are indeed the very embodiment of the Blessed Lord;
there reside truthful goddesses, equal to Lakṣmī, who remain forever imperishable.
Even the moon, upon beholding her face, becomes momentarily transfixed.
There dwell such divine goddesses and children as radiant as the sun,
who abide in virtuous conduct, as does Nārāyaṇa himself in person,
as well as the gopīs of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. (108–109)
"O Lakṣmī, wherever in Saurāṣṭra hundreds of thousands of devotees and servants dwell, that entire land is permeated by Brahman; to me, it is like Vaikuṇṭha.
Thus, everything has been told to you exactly as spoken by Śaṅkara.
The reciters, the disciples, and the listening people shall also become liberated.

Thus ends the five hundred and fiftieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Legends Concerning Tuṇḍīśvara, Kapilātīrtha, Agastya, Nārada, the Marvels of Bhīmanāthatīrtha, the Bhalla-kṣetra, Raivata-tīrtha, and the Liberation of King Gaja," in the first section on the Continuation of the Kṛta Yuga of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
*Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā*, Section 1 (The Continuation of the Kṛta Yuga), Chapter 550.
Chapter 551 [Author:
Chapter 552 → Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:

Śaṅkara said to Pārvatī: "O Lakṣmī! O my beloved! I shall tell you of whatever other holy sites exist in Saurāṣṭra; listen to me. Unnabilla is an auspicious tīrtha, and there is also the Śāmbhava tīrtha known as Gṛhātmaka."
To the west of Raivata shines the beautiful Gaṅgeśvara;
and from the stone (Upala) shines the great holy site of Yakṣeśvarī.
Formerly, in the city of Vāmana within the great field of Vastrāpatha, [these were established]. || 2-3 ||
Tormented by grief for his son, the venerable sage Vasiṣṭha came to the bank of the Svarṇarekhā river to perform austerities (4).
[He went] to the waters of the Svarṇarekhā river in the northeast corner of the city.
That great Vāsiṣṭha Tīrtha exists, bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (5) At Makhatīrtha, near the presence of Kṛtasmara, lies Balikhāta;
there also exists Nāthatīrtha, which grants liberation and bestows peace upon the world. (6)
To the northwest of Vastrāpatha, there is a divine lake surrounded by Apsarases,
where the gods sport and bathe.
There also dwell Śambhu in the Jālī forest and the trident-bearing Goddess.
And Gaṇeśa, known as Heramba, resides there as an inhabitant of the sacred ford (tīrtha).
To the west of that, on the ocean, lies the city of Makarālaya;
there also is the city named Kunda and Maṇibhadra, which is a source of auspiciousness.
Śrī Dāmapura is preeminent, and the sacred field of Dvārakā is supreme;
thus, numerous holy sites dwell upon the shore of the ocean.
Having spoken thus to Pārvatī, the supreme goddess, Mahādeva—
Having performed the Prābhāsika sacrifice when the month of Śrāvaṇa had arrived,
he departed toward the city of Dvārakā accompanied by ten million attendants.
The lords, such as Śrī Kṛṣṇa and the other deities of the sacred sites, offered him a respectful welcome.
Having spent a month in the black soil, they went to Camatkārapura.
There, the sixty-eight goddesses were worshipped by Hara.
During the Navarātra vow, they all obtained Śrī Śaṅkara as their husband.
Immersed in the vast expanse of bliss within the ocean whose self is the bliss of Brahman,
they all went during the month of Āśvina to Mount Arbuda,
where Puṣkara shines eternally situated in the sky.
The second is on a mountain peak, and the third is situated on the surface of the earth,
where the beautiful hermitages of the great sages such as Vasiṣṭha are located.
On that mountain, there are auspicious sands with the appearance of shimmering gems and the like.
The trees, creepers, and shrubs appear like ascetics.
The forests are indeed as delightful as divine gardens, containing the grounds for sacrifices and the altars of the ascetics. (17–18)
There are excellent dwellings for virtuous women, as well as hermitages for the holy;
there exist auspicious abodes for Brāhmaṇas and Vaiṣṇavas,
sacred Sarasvatī pilgrimage sites, and rivers that purify.
It is the dwelling place of the peaks of clouds and the realm of winds mingled with fragrances;
it is where the abodes of cows and tens of millions of deities exist,
and where the circles of yogis and those who have attained perfection dwell.
Śiva and the others made their dwelling there on the Puṣkara peak;
the great sages, Vasiṣṭha and the rest, [resided at] the holy sites such as Puṣkara;
and other deities, beginning with Brahmā, paid homage to Śaṅkara. (22)
The gods offered water, flowers, fruit, the arghya offering, food offerings, and articles of service to the illustrious Supreme Lord, the husband of Pārvatī. Furthermore,
an especially distinguished worship was performed by Vasiṣṭha in his own abode.
Then they took complete rest on Mount Arbuda, which is like a hundred million peaks;
this Arbuda, possessing a divine form, offered them great hospitality.
At night, while seated upon his own throne, Śaṅkara spoke these words to Pārvatī.
Listen to this divine narrative which destroys sin and suffering.
Gautama was indeed a great ṛṣi, honored and blessed among sages;
having made his dwelling on Śataśṛṅga, he performed penance.
His wife Ahalyā was also an ascetic who discoursed on the Veda;
residing in the Daṇḍaka forest, she was always a servant to Gautama. That beautiful woman constantly performed the worship of guests.
Once, when a drought occurred and there was no food on the earth, the Brahmins deliberated: "Where will our meal be found?
Gautama is capable; he always honors his guests. (1.551.30)
Thinking, "Let us go to that house," they arrived from all sides.
Upon seeing that, Gautama remembered Brahmā, the Great-Grandfather; and Brahmā appeared before his very eyes. (31)
Gautama spoke, saying, "Choose a boon," and he declared on this earth:
"May water, wheat, grains, barley, awns,
and the like be produced from morning until midday, and may their chaff follow immediately thereafter."

"May we always receive their cooked food—the auspicious *vaiśvadeva* offering, the *śrāddha*, the oblation to the deities, and hospitality for the *brāhmaṇas*—in whatever manner it may be; so let it be for me. (34)
Having heard this, Brahmā said, "So be it," and departed from there.
Fresh grain was produced every morning, and it ripened daily;
likewise, food was provided for the constant feeding of thousands of Brahmins.
In this manner, for a full year, Brāhmaṇas were indeed fed by her;
through the power of her devotion to her husband, Ahalyā performed service [to him].
Every morning, she would constantly resolve to serve at the feet of her beloved.
Having bowed down and prostrated, having washed [his] big toe, and having offered the *arghya* water, [she said]:
"If I am indeed the wife of my lord, devoted to my lord, and faithful to my husband, then let a hundred thousand vessels be produced here perpetually. (38–39)
"Let male and female slaves, servants, cows yielding flavorful milk, and all kinds of food and drink be prepared; let the fire itself be the consumer.
And let the gods be the servers at my feast in Daṇḍaka."
Having thus made firm resolve and established great kitchens,
having cooked fresh grains and offered them to the Viśvedevas,
and having scattered morsels for the cows, portions for all creatures, and funeral cakes for the ancestors; || 41-42 ||
He daily fed one hundred thousand brahmins, and even more.
Then, at the end of the year, there was a bountiful rain upon the earth;
food was produced everywhere in all lands.
The Brahmins said, "We shall indeed go to other countries.
Then Gautama said to them, "O gods on earth, dwell right here!
Then those Brahmins replied, "O sage, we are independent!"
"Food has been provided by you, and we have always been protected by you. For one whose food is eaten, that person's body indeed remains under their control;
therefore, his word must be honored in every way. However, my desire to depart is firm."
Having spoken thus, they devised a wonderful pretext for departing.
One brahmin named Rodhana, having performed breath control (prāṇāyāma),
entered through his self-restraint into the inner heart of Gautama.
Then, by means of his illusory power (*māyā*), another auspicious cow was created there.
She went to the stall where fodder was kept,
and Gautama himself remained right there, firmly established in *prāṇāyāma*.
Gau had gone into the leaf-hut; seeing her, Gautama—
by blocking her entrance and confining her within— cried out, "Bhavātra gauḥ" (Become a cow here), and thus, with her breath obstructed, Gau became a cow.
Then the Brahmins, having fallen and fainted, repeatedly said:
"Gautama is indeed a cow-killer; the gods on earth (Brahmins) must not remain in his hermitage.
Gautama, however, repeatedly praised those venerable Brahmins with hymns of praise.
"She is not dead; how might this fainting fit be dispelled?
I shall perform an expiation here so that the Brahmins do not depart from the house.
When she had spoken thus, the Brahmins replied, "There is no expiation for one who is alive. (53–54)
Or, if she has fainted, it must be done so that she may indeed be freed from her fainting;
bring the water of the Gaṅgā and sprinkle this earth.
She will quickly be restored from her fainting, and we shall go into the depths of the forest.
Having spoken thus, all the brahmins departed from the Daṇḍaka forest.
Gautama traveled by way of the sky toward Śrī Śaṅkara.
Long ago, Śaṅkara had offered him a welcome there on Kailāsa.
Gautama, having bowed to Hara, requested the water of the Gaṅgā;
then Śaṅkara, plucking out a portion of his own matted locks, gave it to him.
Having placed that [portion] containing the Gaṅgā upon the head of the body of the cow, he brought her here.
Gautama flooded her with the water produced from that;
she became fair-complexioned, her heart restored, and free from fainting as she remained in the hermitage.
Indeed, by virtue of the boon for the gift of cows, she became the Gaṅgā known as Gautamī and Godāvarī.
Known as Godāvarī, she dwelt in the Daṇḍaka forest;
then the sage Gautama spoke to those fleeing Brāhmaṇas:
"May you all become followers of the dharma of hypocrisy in another age. (61)
"Violent, prone to seizing skulls, and revilers of those who give food.
This being so, they [described] this glorification of Gautama, which is full of great wonder, at the site of Godāvara. 62.
At that sacred ford on the Godāvarī, Gautama had a virtuous disciple named Uttanka, who, having studied as many Vedas as there were,
made a request to his teacher to give him the preceptor’s fee.
Then the guru’s wife said:
"The queen Madayantī of Saudāsa wears a necklace of jewels upon her own breast;
she always wears it there—bring it and give it to me. (65–66)
Thus addressed by the preceptor’s wife, he then set out in haste and reached the house of Sudāsa; there he saw Sudāsa, who had assumed the form of a tiger, approaching him to devour him. 67.
That Brahmin beheld him coming toward him for the purpose of eating him.
The Brahmin said: "Eat me as you please immediately after that.
A guest has arrived for you; give the pearl necklace to me.
Having offered it to my teacher, I shall then bestow upon you the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) you desire."
The king said, "O Brahmin, let my queen be requested for a favor!
Thus addressed, the Brahmin went to the queen and made his request regarding Mālikā.
The queen said, "Bring me a token of recognition from the king."

Having gone there quickly, he requested a token of recognition from the king. Saudāsa then spoke these words: "Tell me what that token of recognition might be—that by which there is no good rebirth, without which one goes to a miserable state."
"Go and speak thus to that virtuous woman; upon hearing you, she will give the garland.
She gave this garland of divine and excellent luster to the Brahmin.
Then the asura spoke there, standing near the battlefield:
Having come from Atala, he desired a beautiful garland from me.
The demon named Ajāmṛta caused that subterranean realm to be dug up;
he settled his own followers, the Rākṣasas, within the womb of the earth.
"Indeed, he has made a very long opening in the earth;
therefore, proceed with caution so that he may not come and seize [the pearl necklace] as it was brought.
Thus addressed, Uttaṅka took up the string of pearls.
Upon his arrival, he gave a diamond necklace to the wife of his own guru.
He asked the guru for the auspicious meaning of the statement; he replied:
"The twice-born, being propitiated with gifts, will grant you the supreme state. (77-78)
"The twice-born are never satisfied with one who is always in a state of misfortune.
Having understood this meaning, the Brahmin then rejoiced;
and the great sage, having received the heavy blessings of his guru, [departed].
Uttaṅka went to the beautiful Puṣkara tīrtha as his own abode. Here there is the Uttaṅka-tīrtha, which destroys the heat of sin.
Furthermore, this long and extensive cave was created by the Asuras.
Once, on one occasion, Vaśiṣṭha’s wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu) fell [from heaven].
Then, by means of his own yogic power, Vaśiṣṭha brought forth his own sacrificial cow (Homadhenu) from within;
from that time forward, she remained there for all eternity.
He considered filling the cavity with a great mountain.
Vasiṣṭha then went quickly to Himālaya through the air and requested his son to fill the cavity.
Vasiṣṭha gave him his son Nandivardhana and led him away;
he established him, named Nandivardhana, in a cave,
where he was duly supported by the Naga Arbuda.
Consequently, this mountain became renowned by the name Arbuda.
Since the mountain arrived on the fifth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada, many sacred fords (*tīrtha*) were also brought there by Vasiṣṭha. (86–87)

On its peak is the Nāga-tīrtha and likewise the hermitage of Vasiṣṭha; there also is the abode of Śaṅkara. Having bathed there in the mountain spring, wealth, prosperity, happiness, heaven, sons, fortune, and other blessings are attained.
A barren woman, having bathed there, shall certainly become possessed of sons; of this there is no doubt.
(89) Those ancestors who perform a *śrāddha* ceremony there will in every way attain liberation and proceed to heaven, and the performer of the rite shall likewise go to the state of liberation. (90)
Vasiṣṭha also summoned Gautamī and Sarasvatī,
Gaṅgā and Mandākinī, as well as Śaṅkara, the Lord of the Mountain.
Gautamī was a certain Brāhmaṇa woman who was distressed by her childlessness.
The virtuous woman went to the Nāga-tīrtha on Mount Arbuda.
Then she thought, "Fie upon me, who am bereft of sons!
While lost in such thoughts, she entered the Nāga-tīrtha to bathe.
As soon as she emerged from that water after bathing,
even without union with her husband, she became pregnant immediately.
And being serene, she then heard an incorporeal voice.

"Whoever, whether a woman or even a man, remains here in the midst of this water and desires something in their heart, obtains that very thing they have thought of. By you, however, while staying here in the water, a desire for a son has been formed in your heart."
"Therefore, you shall give birth to a son endowed with a fetus.
Having heard this voice from the sky spoken by the messenger of the gods,
she saw the fetus despite being without her husband and spoke these words:
"Aha! This power of the sacred ford appears unprecedented to me.
For there, a conception occurs in women even without semen or menses;
having gone home from there, she gave birth to an excellent son. (98–99)
The desires of those who bathe here at this sacred ford (tīrtha) are surely fulfilled;
there is no doubt, for as is the Gautamī, so is it here.
And the Gomatī was brought to this pool by the high-souled Vasiṣṭha.
Having bathed there, one attains the highest heaven; of this there is no doubt.
Listen, O Goddess! In the vicinity of Acaleśvara, there was a parrot that had built its nest there; it would perform circumambulations [of the deity]. (102)
Flying up again and again, he would rest repeatedly in his nest;
in time, that King died and indeed became one named Veṇu.
Remembering his former birth, that king recalled his state as a parrot.
Having reached Acaleśvara, he then performed a circumambulation.
He did nothing else at all; he simply continued his circumambulation. Seeing the king in such a state, Nārada and the other sages—
They asked: "How is the circumambulation alone performed?
Tell us, why do you not offer the food oblation, fruits, flowers, and so forth?
Viṣṇu replied: "In former times, I was a bird, a parrot, residing right here."
Performing circumambulation day and night of the Lord stationed there,
by His grace and through His power, I have now become a rememberer of my past births;
remembering that circumambulation of the Lord, I perform that great merit once again.
"I perform this circumambulation for the sake of attaining infinite merit.
Having heard the king, the sages exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent!
Then, after a long time, through his devotion to Hara, the king—

"Oṃ, salutations to the glorious Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Master; salutations! (110). Having received this mantra from Hara, he went to Vaikuṇṭha with devotion. O Lakṣmī! This account told by Śambhu to Satī has now been related by me to you. (111). Thus ends [the section] in the first book, the *Kṛtayugasantāna*, of the *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, concerning the journey of Śaṅkara and others to Dvārakā, Camatkārapura, Arbuda Mountain, and other places; the story of Gautama; the story of Saudāsa and Uttaṅka; the greatness of Nāgatīrtha; the liberation of King Veṇu; the account of the bringing of Arbuda, and so forth.
The Five Hundred and Fifty-first Chapter, titled "Description," from the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Book 1: The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga. (Chapter 551)
Chapter 552 [Author:
Chapter 553 → Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:

Listen, Lakṣmī! Having heard that Śaṅkara had arrived at Arbuda Mountain, Agastya came from the south for the purpose of seeing him. After bowing to Śambhu and worshipping him, he sat comfortably upon an auspicious seat.
Honored by Śambhu, Agastya then questioned Śaṅkara:
"O Lord, tell me how long life may be attained by me here!
Śambhu replied: "Worship Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the supreme among men."
Indeed, while residing in Saurāṣṭra as the Lord of Ramā at Kāmbharī,
divine status never arises anywhere without devotion to Hari;
and without that divine state, one does not become a long-lived being.
The destruction of time and other such factors never touch the divine at all.
Without divine yoga, the divine state never arises;
the divine is Nārāyaṇa, Viṣṇu, the Lord who brings beings into existence.
When He has entered that body, it shall possess divine qualities especially;
for those perfections (siddhis) abide where Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa resides.
Indeed, I, Śaṅkara, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the other celestial dwellers [are there].
She is divine, born from a portion of Nārāyaṇa; therefore, worship Nārāyaṇa.
(8) Om, salutations to Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; salutations!
Recite the great mantra constantly and always perform meditation on Hari. (9)
"Offer oblations to Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Lord; svāhā!
Being pleased, He will surely grant you divine splendor according to your desire.
Having been addressed thus, the eminent sage Agastya performed meditation and worship.
He indeed performed constant salutation and remembrance of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
Then, having gone to the hermitage of Lomaśa, he resided at Aśvapaṭṭaka.
Afterwards, on one occasion, that king of sages went to Kāśī for the sake of visiting sacred pilgrimage sites.
Having traveled through the sky to the Himalayas, he proceeded to Lake Mānasa;
there, the bull among sages beheld a divine tortoise in Mānasa.
He also saw most divine lotuses made of gold.
The tortoise offered a divine and auspicious lotus as a welcome gift.
At that moment, the king of sages, possessing divine vision,
flew up from there after bowing to the tortoise and departed for the place surrounded by Avilā.
On a plateau situated at the side of Meru, he beheld a magnificent lake. On its shore, he saw a certain beautiful and great hut.
There, he indeed observed an ascetic who was emaciated by fasting.
Reduced to nothing but skin and bone, clad in rags and bark garments, he was asked by the high-souled one for the sake of hospitality, "Who are you?
To which he replied to Agastya: "Stay, stay, O twice-born one! (17–18)
"O Brahmin, please accept this hospitality; enter my dwelling.
Having heard this, Agastya entered that leaf-hut and beheld a radiant man, a Brahmin who was like the Lord himself.
Seated upon an auspicious seat on the ground, chanting the eternal Brahman, he wore a rosary on his hand and applied a tilaka mark upon his forehead, reciting:
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Master; svāhā! (1.552.20–21)
While he was thus performing the fire sacrifice, having obtained a jewel for each [offering],
and while reciting the supreme *Puruṣasūkta* at the end of the rosary,
that man spoke the *Lakṣmīsūkta*.
Immediately after the hymn of praise, five maidens indeed emerged from the wall of that chamber from the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
Then, one gave him a golden throne;
the second performed the washing of his feet with a water-vessel. (23–24)
The third, holding a fan, gave air to the sage;
the fourth and fifth, holding chowries, stood on either side.
Then, having repeatedly recited the Śrīsūkta, that ascetic [continued] at the wall.

He performed the fire sacrifice (homa), and indeed hundreds of auspicious maidens were born there, holding golden jars in their hands. By means of the Varuṇa-homa, a lake was swiftly created right there on the side.
Having brought water, they approached and bathed him;
they wiped him with a cloth and then gave him ornaments.
They gave him garments, performed worship, and offered excellent food oblations (naivedya).
Then they gave him water and vanished in an instant.
(29) Then Agastya, beholding this marvel, entered into meditation;
while his eyes were closed, [he saw] himself on Mount Meru. (30)
Standing upon the high peak, he beheld his own self by means of his own self;
likewise, he saw the seven oceans and the principal mountain ranges.
Established upon Meru, he beheld the earth consisting of seven continents.
Having seen all this, the sage Agastya again entered into meditation.
He beheld Bhuvarloka, as well as Svarga, Jana, and Satyaloka;
and remaining there, he indeed beheld the assembly hall of Brahmā and Vaikuṇṭha.
There he beheld the four-armed Janārdana. As soon as he opened his eyes and looked outside,
there was neither Mount Meru, nor the divine hut, nor even the lake.
Neither Lake Mānasa nor the Kāśikā exists there.
On the shore of Lake Aśvapaṭṭasara, in the auspicious hermitage of Lomaśa,
Agastya then beheld himself within his own leaf-hut.
From that time onwards, Agastya’s divinity in this world,
his extreme longevity, and his exceedingly great powers became manifest;
yet, when shall I again reach that auspicious region?
Thinking thus, he went repeatedly to the Himālaya to see Śambhu;
he went to Naranārāyaṇa, and to Nārāyaṇa, and also to Śvetabhūmi and Satyaloka again and again. (38–39)
"Even so, his vision shall not arise again.
Thus did Śaṅkara speak to Pārvatī at that time. Then Agasti arrived once more at Arbuda in order to see him.
Having bowed to Śambhu and prostrated himself, he then spoke of what he desired to know:
"O Blessed One, tell me the vow, the austerity, or the dharma for the sake of attaining that divine world which was previously seen by me."
Having heard that, Śaṅkara said: "O Lakṣmī, listen to what I tell you:
without worshipping Hari with devotion, the attainment of those worlds will certainly not occur.
When Hari is worshipped, all the worlds will indeed be in the palm of one's hand."
The god who is worshipped as the officiating priest in sacrifice, from whom this entire world has arisen,
and in whom all things together with the gods are always dissolved—
he is the beginningless Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, higher than the highest. (44–45)
The glorious Lord of syllables, the perfect Śrī Puruṣottama, he who is the most complete—
He alone is to be worshipped always by people,
whether they possess desires or are free from them; for He is indeed the Lord who bestows all goals.
In the beginning, that very Puruṣottama became fourfold in nature:
in Goloka he is Śrī Kṛṣṇa; in Vaikuṇṭha he is Nārāyaṇa;
in the unmanifest (Avyākṛta) he is Vāsudeva; and in the golden realm he is Nara-Nārāyaṇa.
Furthermore, this Śrī Puruṣottama became fourfold:
Viṣṇu in Satyaloka, Viṣṇu in the Ocean of Milk,
Viṣṇu in Śvetadvīpa, and Viṣṇu as Ādityaka in heaven.
Furthermore, that Blessed One manifested himself in three ways:
as Sadāśiva, Mahāviṣṇu, and the eternal Mahākāla.
Again, that Blessed One manifested himself in three ways.
Aniruddha, Pradyumna, and the eternal Saṃkarṣaṇa— again,
that Blessed Lord manifested himself in three ways:
as Brahmā, whose form is characterized by *rajas*, and as Viṣṇu, who is characterized by *sattva*.
He is of the nature of *tamas* and the form of Rudra, the cause of creation, nourishment, and destruction.
Indeed, the Lord alone is born in every *kalpa*;
in each and every creation within the spheres [of worlds], he assumes innumerable forms.
He who is Viṣṇu is himself Brahmā; he who is Brahmā is Maheśvara. These four, or these three, are indeed one eternal reality.
It bestows liberation through its supreme form and prosperity through its active form.
Through sattva, the self is purified by the power of the illustrious Nārāyaṇa. Indeed, through purity a living being is liberated; purity has its refuge in Nārāyaṇa.
And the blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa manifests himself in the form of sacrifice.
In the Kṛta age, the pure Nārāyaṇa is worshipped in his subtle form; in the Tretā age, in the form of sacrifice; in the Dvāpara age, through sacred narratives;
and in the Kali age, he is honored through manifold ritual acts, even those devised by imagination.

If one worships these [deities] who bear forms with a mind of hatred, or if they are perceived through a sense of duality, there is indeed no liberation for such a person anywhere. He who, having known them as one, should worship them, will be liberated; of this there is no doubt.
If one makes a distinction and worships the One alone, and does not harbor hatred toward another,
there is no doubt that liberation will come to this person who is devoted to the vow of fidelity (*pātivratya*).
However, the person who makes a distinction and worships the One while censuring another—
Everything of his would be lost, and he would fall into an evil state of existence.
Listen to this from me, O Agastya, as I relate it according to what occurred in the past: at the beginning of creation, the inhabitants of the world were indeed devotees of Hari. (62–63)
All of them, established in the Dharma and destined for liberation, became as if omniscient.
Having worshipped Śrī Puruṣottama while situated on the fourteenth level, they indeed attained liberation in due course; thereafter, Brahmā [approached] the Lord Hari.
And Śrī Hari, the omnipresent one, having indeed manifested, remembered [Brahmā].
He said, "Tell me, what is the task? Then Brahmā spoke to Hari:
"O God of gods! All people are established upon the path to liberation."
"How indeed will creation come to be? Who shall dwell in the heavens and other realms?
In these worlds of hell, whose mind would find pleasure in dwelling?
Thus addressed, the glorious Nārāyaṇa then spoke to him.
"Many will approach me in their own portion throughout three ages.
In the final age, those of great soul will become rare.
I shall quickly create this delusion which will delude everyone. (68–69)
And Rudra will repeatedly assume many forms characterized by tamas,
such as Bhairava and others, while Pārvatī likewise will assume other supreme and formidable forms for the sake of destroying the Daityas.
Embodied beings, deluded and greedy for liquor, meat, and the like, will indeed rely upon those [practices];
deprived of the path of goodness (sattva), they will follow wrong paths.
Likewise, through the delusion of darkness (tamas), they will abandon the Veda.
Indeed, they will compose tantras that are purely characterized by darkness (*tāmasa*) and abound in violence according to their own whims;
and those who, being devoted to hatred, take recourse in them, shall have no liberation at all, for they are destined for hell. (73)

Then he said: "O Agastya! Since that time, I have indeed performed those acts of delusion as instructed by Brahmā, relying upon which people in this world shall surely become subject to rebirth. (74–779)
For the tantras characterized by tamas are indeed dear to those possessed of desire; the world is generally established in delighting in them,
flowing indeed through the cycle of existence, repeatedly in death and birth.
In the Kali age, people will for the most part take refuge with mere mortals;
considering them to be the Supreme Self, they will revile Śiva and the other gods.
Because of that sin, they shall all go to certain hells.
For teachers themselves deluded, will deceive human beings through censures and praises, through hatreds and the corruptions of the egoism of "I" and "mine," and constantly through deceit,
theft, betrayal of trust, and self-interest. (79)
By that sin, the gurus shall go to many hells;
in the worlds, people will come to regard their gurus as dogs.
And by the power of that [sin], the paths of Yama and the realms of the Lord of Death will be made manifest.
Therefore, O Agastya! this world has been filled in many ways by me through desirable action, yet liberation exists here and there.
O brahmin-sage, he who thus knows the supreme Lord Nārāyaṇa—

Neither delusion regarding myself as the Supreme Brahman—the soul of all—nor regarding our many others, prevails over him either primarily or even secondarily. Behold, O Agastya! In me, you see the supreme, eternal form of Brahman.
When the sage Agastya was thus addressed, he beheld Śaṅkara;
there he saw Brahmā within Śaṅkara, and within Brahmā, Nārāyaṇa.
Within Nārāyaṇa, he beheld the Supreme Brahman, the beginningless Puruṣottama.
Having seen him thus—possessing a blazing, radiant complexion, as beautiful as ten million gods of love—the Brahmin Agastya praised the Supreme Lord:
"O Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, you are Viṣṇu, the Supreme Brahman. (86–87)
The verbal root *viś* means "to enter"; from it, with the suffix *snup*, the word *viṣṇu* is formed. He is the all-pervading Supreme Lord among all the gods;
sometimes he is Brahmā, sometimes he is Rudra—you alone are the one higher than the highest.
Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa, Śambhu, Brahmā, and Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa—
by these names the supreme, eternal Brahman is proclaimed.
There is no difference among the incarnations within that single Incarnate One.
Those who meditate upon this otherwise are to be known as followers of the nature of the Kali age;
those revilers, sinful men, go to a terrible hell.
Such will indeed be the schismatics in the Kali age.
Deluded deceivers in the world, mockers of assemblies of knowledge, will say:
"We are wise; we know the Supreme Lord. Others, who contemplate incarnations and the like, do not know that reality. (92–93)
Thus, for these revilers who were hostile toward the incarnations of Hari,
the fields of Dharmarāja were indeed caused to be established within the city.
Because of that, though their external vows appeared pure, they were black-hearted revilers.
Those who are treacherous and contemptuous shall certainly go to hell.
In ancient times, I was created by Brahmā and told, "Create indeed the progeny. At that time, being incapable of understanding [my purpose], I was submerged in the water. (95–96)
There I beheld a divine and noble being, the size of a thumb, a youth resembling a dark cloud with eyes like lotuses.
