There she performed penance for the sake of destroying her barrenness;
she beheld Śambhu there and indeed obtained a boon of a son.
Then, by the grace of Śaṅkara, she obtained a hundred sons.
Where there is pure water flowing from mountain caves,
by performing the rites at this sacred ford (tīrtha), one shall obtain a wife, sons, and other blessings.
One who desires liberation must perform the ritual at the Māmuñca lake-ford.
In ancient times, the sage Mudgala performed most rigorous penance there,
constantly chanting "Oṃ Namaḥ Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
At Arbuda, he bathed three times a day until his impurities were completely destroyed.
A divine messenger has arrived to lead him to the great heaven.
Seated in a celestial chariot, he said to the sage: "Ascend this; let us go to the celestial realm.
I have been sent by Indra; come quickly, do not delay."
Mudgala asked him about the virtues and defects of heaven:
"Having heard this, if I consider my auspicious heaven to be fit for me, I shall go there.
The messenger replied, "O Sage, heaven is attained by one's own merits!"
The Sage spoke the truth: "O follower, tell me the result of that.
It is my firm resolve in my heart that I shall not go without having heard those [teachings].
I shall perform abundant austerity and I shall worship Nārāyaṇa."
The messenger said: "All virtues and youthfulness are equal [in value];
as are the delightful celestial forests of the gods, such as Nandana and others, where there are enjoyments unlike any other, always providing satisfaction and happiness. (75)
There is neither hunger nor thirst, nor laziness, nor even sleepiness.
The beautiful goddesses, uniform in appearance, are repeatedly fit for enjoyment;
and the Gandharvas constantly cause the sounds of singing and musical instruments to be heard.
In their homes, beautiful women delight them with song, dance, and laughter;
no diseases afflict their bodies, and they possess nourishment born of nectar. Their vigor is the perfection of all principles, and in them no decline is found.
Food is indeed nectar itself, prepared in many ways according to one’s own will.
Among the deities, there is no mixture of wind, bile, phlegm, and the like;
there is no foul odor or such, and their form is of a single, uniform measure.
There is no aging or decay of the skin, nor is there any impurity;
they possess divine vision, divine enjoyments, and divine garments.
Indeed, the gods and others move through the path of the sky and sport therein.
There were also innumerable celestial chariots, as well as jewels, gems, and diamonds.
All the divine palaces were composed of radiant light, with lamps produced by their very nature.
Every residence was pervaded by a splendor equal to the light of the moon.
Thousands of male and female servants who provide delicious drinks and grant all desires;
moving at will, enjoying objects of desire, created from the mind and possessing forms at will;
and a supreme lifespan lasting for a thousand yugas or even longer than that. //84//
Having enjoyed heaven in accordance with one's merit, the embodied being experiences its pleasures;
as long as that merit lasts, so long does he remain, after which he must undergo a fall.
Thus do these qualities function; for servitude is not for the sake of the belly.
No new merit whatsoever is produced in heaven;
therefore, when that merit is exhausted, the fall of the celestial dwellers occurs.
This very thing is the great defect: the fall is indeed terrifying.
O Brahmin, this is the land of action (karmabhūmi), while heaven is considered the land of enjoyment (bhogabhūmi). Whatever excellent merit is performed here is experienced there.
When the power of the Dānavas arises, the Dānavas sometimes carry [the merit] away from here.

Indeed, by force they seized his house, his wife, and all his possessions; this was a great transgression, as were the women who had been enjoyed by others. Yet, having seen those [enemies] possessed of the power of merit multiplied ten millionfold, [he reflected].
One who possesses great prosperity and abundant merit may even experience remorse.
(9.1) Furthermore, those by whom many virtuous deeds have been performed are not few, yet they suffer greatly;
for that which is not given away in the mortal world can never be obtained in heaven. (9.2)
That suffering is said to be great for a human being, according to their past karma.
All this regarding heaven, consisting of its merits and defects, has been explained to you. Come quickly, O excellent sage! Tell me here what you desire.
Having heard and reflected upon all of that, Mudgala spoke like a mortal:
"Just as it is here, so it is there; wealth, wife, home, and the like are vessels of suffering and likewise hold the fear of downfall. (94–95)
"O messenger! There is always a loss of merit for me, and no increase whatsoever occurs. Therefore, I have no need at all for that heaven.
By my command, you must clearly speak these words to the King of the Gods."
"Forgive my transgression; I have no desire for heaven.
I shall perform such actions that there may indeed be no falling back, and I shall attain those worlds which are forever free from fear. (97–98)
Having heard this, that messenger, who was indifferent to heaven, went quickly to Mahendra and spoke to him at length.
Then Śakra, having heard it, said: "Bring that sage here by force."
"Merit intended for the enjoyment of heaven shall not reach exhaustion until it has been experienced. (1.554.1) Having heard this, the messenger went to where Mudgala was staying.
Beholding Mudgala's virtuous conduct, he entered the water through the power of yoga. (101)
That messenger became motionless like a block of wood at the sage's glance.
Then Indra, the lord of the gods, being remembered by the messenger, arrived;
standing in the sky with the thunderbolt in his hand, he desired to take the sage away.
And with a mere glance, Mudgala paralyzed that Indra.
Then Śakra, his enthusiasm broken, offered praise: "Release me!
O Sage, whether you remain in heaven or in the mortal world, release me!"
Mudgala said: "O Lord of Devas! Your sight is difficult to obtain.
Go to heaven with your messengers; O sinless one, I shall remain right here.
I shall worship Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa and go to the imperishable abode."
"Release me," you said; therefore, let this sacred ford (tīrtha) be known by the name Māmuñca.
O wielder of the thunderbolt, let it remain forever famous by your word.
Those people who bathe here in this lake on the full moon day of the month of Phālguna— ||| 106–107 ||
"They shall satisfy the ancestors and indeed attain liberation.
Having heard this, the wielder of the thunderbolt (Indra) took the messenger and departed for heaven.
Mudgala, too, remained there, contemplating the Supreme Brahman.
"Having meditated upon the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, he went to the imperishable realm (Akṣara).
O Lakṣmī! Thus did Śaṅkara speak to Pārvatī on Mount Arbuda.
I have indeed told you that which bestows liberation and purifies the world.

Thus ends the five hundred and fifty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of Siddhatīrtha, Śukratīrtha, Maṇikarṇatīrtha, Paṅgutīrtha, Yamatīrtha, Puṇḍrodatīrtha, Śrīmātṛtīrtha, Vindhyācalītīrtha, Maṅkitīrtha, Piṇḍārakatīrtha, Raktoddhāratīrtha, Pārthātīrtha, Mudgalatīrtha, and Māmuñcatīrtha, along with their respective narratives, as well as the Determination of the Virtues and Faults of Heaven," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīyasaṃhitā*.
(Chapter 554, *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇasaṃhitā*, Book 1: The Lineage of the Kṛtayuga).
Chapter 555 [Author:
Chapter 556 → Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī! Then Śambhu said to Pārvatī on Arbuda:
"I shall indeed tell you of other holy fords that destroy sin.
There stands the Caṇḍikā-tīrtha, where Caṇḍī is worshipped by Brahmins."
And she, the destroyer of the demon Mahiṣāsura, was established there by means of Vedic mantras.
At Arbuda, there exists an auspicious bathing-pool of the Jāhnavī on a peak,
where Gaṅgā receives [the waters] from Śaṅkara once every year.
Furthermore, O Arbuda, through the granting of a boon during his service, he attained companionship [with the Lord]. Moreover, there exists the Śaiva pilgrimage site known as Acaleśvara,
where formerly a man of sinful conduct, his body emaciated by leprosy, [attained purification].
Having come there for alms, he received a portion of barley meal (saktu).
Having placed it in a small measure (kuḍava), when he had fallen asleep there for a moment during the night,
a dog approached and devoured the barley meal.
Other dogs, having gathered together, engaged in a fight with the dog; hearing this, he became wide awake and saw that the barley meal had been consumed.
Then, having drunk only water and bathed near the tree, [he sat down].
Then he fell asleep, and in the morning he indeed awoke.
As soon as he beheld himself resembling a god or a gandharva,
he realized the power resulting from his bath in the water and his drinking [of it].
Then, after some time, by the power of destiny, he met his death;
thereupon, he was born in the house of the lord of Vidarbha as one who remembered his past lives.
He was the best of kings named Bhīma, for he was indeed the father of Damayantī.
He obtained a kingdom as the fruit of giving flour to a dog.
Having gone there, he indeed gave flour every single day.
Gālava and the others asked him, "How is it that you give flour? || 12 ||
"Why are gifts of elephants, horses, and chariots not being given by you?
He then related the wonderful fruit of his previous birth:
"Since it was through the power of the gift of barley-meal that this kingdom was obtained by me."
"Indeed, my barley-meal (saktavaḥ) was eaten by dogs at that very sacred ford (tīrtha).
Thereupon, I performed my ablutions and drank the merit-bestowing water; thus, O King, my sins were exhausted as I made this gift of barley-meal. (14–15)
"Knowing that through this gift of barley-meal my fruit may become eternal,
I indeed offer these meal-grains with devotion at this sacred ford (tīrtha) which is endowed with liberation.
Having heard this, all those sages were filled with the utmost wonder.
"Excellent, excellent, O King! they said again and again.
(17) By either reciting or even hearing this, a ruler of the earth shall obtain eternal happiness both in this world and the next. (18)
On Mount Arbuda exists a sacred ford (tīrtha) that delivers one's entire lineage;
yet in ancient times, there was a king named Aprastuta who was devoted to sinful deeds, devoid of hospitality, and bereft of knowledge and charity. (19)
Whether by just means or unjust means, he accumulates wealth.
Then, having reached old age and being exhorted by other elders:
"O King, perform righteous deeds; at the time of death and thereafter, it will be auspicious."
The king said: "Dharma is power, and it was by power that I performed [these deeds].
Wealth, kingdom, wife, home, and many other things have been acquired by me. There is no dharma superior to this, nor is there anything else that grants such satisfaction to the senses. (22)
Having been addressed thus, they observed silence and went each to his own abode.
Then, at the end of that [period], his ancestors, being distressed, spoke to him:
"In former times, we were of pure conduct and devoted to the duty of giving. (23-24)
Having gone to heaven through their merits, they have today been cast down by a wicked son.
You, however, have become a wicked son, devoid of righteous deeds.
Therefore, perform some virtuous act and deliver us all.
"O evil-souled one, by your actions we have been cast into hell.
Ten future generations shall also go to hell along with you.
Having heard this, the king fell into extreme distress and spoke to his wife.
Having heard this, his wife said, "Lift up your ancestors with auspicious deeds.
The king summoned the brahmins and performed the Pitṛmedha sacrifice;
likewise, he undertook a pilgrimage to holy sites and arrived at Mount Arbuda.
Having reached Kulasantāraṇa, he performed his ablutions there.
Recalling his fathers, grandfathers, and ancestors, he offered handfuls of water.
His ancestors, liberated from the terrible hells, were filled with great joy.
Then, seated in celestial chariots and adorned with divine garlands and garments, they all said to him: "O son, we have all now been delivered by you;
since, O son, your family has been delivered by you at this sacred ford."

"This shall become a sacred ford (tīrtha) known as Kulasantāraṇa. Having heard this— namely, that he was to go to heaven after entrusting the burden of the earth to his own son Vasu— he did not hand over his own responsibility to his son, though it was the proper occasion.
Having given [the gift] and ascended the celestial chariot of his ancestors, he went to heaven.
O beloved, this power of the sacred ford has been described by me to you.
Thence one should go to the supreme sacred ford consisting of the hermitage of Paraśurāma.
There, he performed austerities and obtained divine weapons from Śaṅkara.
That place is renowned as Rāmatīrtha, which destroys both sin and suffering.
Having bathed there in the lake of water, one shall attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Thence one should go to the most beautiful holy site, Brahmapada.
Formerly, Brahmā was entreated by the brahmins: "Grant us that object which bestows liberation.
Brahmā said: "I shall indeed grant it; [liberation comes] from the worship of my station (pada)."
The liberation of people shall come from serving my lotus feet.
May all the sages and even the gods touch my foot;
they shall worship it when the full-moon day of the month of Kārtika arrives.
With water, fruits, flowers, perfumes, food offerings, and ointments,
they will undoubtedly go to my world, which is very difficult to attain—
that station of the Grandfather (Brahmā), for it indeed bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
O beloved, it is there indeed that the primary Puṣkara exists in its threefold form;
it is eternally cherished by the Lotus-born Brahmā, who established it in ancient times.
Formerly, the sages headed by Vasiṣṭha performed a sacrificial session (sattra) there.
Brahmā indeed arrived there at that sacrifice from Satyaloka;
however, for the sake of the three daily junctions (saṃdhyā), he had to return to Satyaloka again and again.
After reflecting upon this inconvenience with the sages, Brahmā [acted accordingly].
The Puṣkara [lake] was brought from Satyaloka to Arbuda mountain.
While the sacrificial session (sattra) was indeed taking place at Arbuda, their twilight devotions occurred;
at that time, other Puṣkaras also arrived there on earth.
The supreme Puṣkara is in the sky, the middle one is upon the peak,
and the third is indeed a lake upon the earth.
Those who perform their ablutions with devotion on the full moon day of Kārtika—
For them, the worlds are eternal, including even the heavens that bestow enjoyments.
There, moreover, is the Sāvitrī-kuṇḍa, which destroys all sins;
there is also a beautiful image of Brahmā, which grants liberation upon being seen.
In former times, Dhundhumāra was indeed a devotee of Śrī Śaṅkara;
by him was established Umāmaheśvara, the destroyer of worldly existence.
Only after fully worshipping that deity should one perform the Nimitīrtha rite.
Where indeed, in his old age, King Nimi was on Mount Arbuda,
Lomaśa also arrived there at that time along with many sages;
a Brahmayajña was performed there and a sacrifice to Viṣṇu was conducted.
The Rudra-sacrifice was performed, and the narrative of the Saṃhitā was told;
during that great festival, all the sacred fords (tīrthas) located within Jambūdvīpa also arrived there at the reservoir for the sake of the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha).
That place became known as Jambūtīrtha, and likewise, for the sake of providing proof, a tree appeared there;
a divine jambū tree was born instantly.
Then Nimi performed his ablutions there, which embodies all sacred fords (tīrthas).
Having become divine and resembling a god, he went to heaven with his very body.
O Pārvatī, all this majesty of Arbuda has been recounted to you;
O beloved, this sacred place of mine bestows merit.
Arbuda itself is a sacred ford (tīrtha), and there dwell, and will continue to dwell, millions of other holy sites due to the virtues and activities of the virtuous.
O Pārvatī, it is indeed by their association and through my own faith that [this place has become so]. || 56–57 ||

O beloved, I have indeed visited many sacred fords because of you; I am truly blessed, he whose wife is devoted to the gods, full of devotion for the Supreme Lord, enthusiastic for righteous deeds, and faithful in meritorious actions. (58)
She was exceedingly gracious toward guests, possessed of auspicious devotion to the service of the virtuous;
she was intensely eager for her own spiritual duty and always full of love for knowledge.
She was intent upon her reputation as if it were her primary goal, and remained devoted to the practice of silent recitation (japa).
Endowed with austerity, purity, and other virtues, devoted to fire-offerings and sacrifices,
regarding their husbands as gods and their ancestors as gods, likewise protecting their dependents;
honoring cows, the earth, Brahmins, the virtuous, and faithful women.
I am a servant of Nārāyaṇa, who has become the self of all beings;
I am equal to the earth in forbearance, like a tree in dispassion, equal to Brahmā in virtuous conduct, and a vessel of affection in service. (62–63)
That man’s household life is blessed, whose wife is always like a pillar to him as a companion, who surrenders herself in giving, and who is a helper in the next world;
he alone is said here to be a virtuous man whose wife is devoted to her husband.
He who has no such wife is not a virtuous man; he is a sinner.
He whose wife speaks harshly, casts a cruel glance, makes her face full of wrath, and does not even grant him her heart—[is a sinner]. (65–66)
Fie upon his life in this world, for him there is indeed hell;
he in whose house there is no merit and no service to the wielder of the Śārṅga bow. He has no enthusiasm for eating, nor does he possess fine clothing and such.

There is no speech filled with love, nor is there a gaze of affection toward a man, a woman, or one's offspring; his birth is meaningless. Blessed am I, fulfilled am I, who possesses such a virtuous wife as this.
I am always blessed by you, who, though detached, remain devoted to me;
others, having encountered agitation caused by women, go to the depths of the forest.
Yet, such perfection as yours is not attained by them merely through dwelling in the forest.
Such [benefit] as might accrue even to a householder through the favor of a woman [is possible for others as well].
[Likewise for] the weak, the protectorless, children, the sick,
the poor, the hungry, the thirsty, and those who are destitute.
For those yogis who are virtuous, true, and without worldly support, their blessings bear fruit here quickly, for they are indeed bestowers of accomplishment.
Where the goddesses and beautiful women rejoice for the sake of householders; 73.
Therein lie fortune and prosperity, and for the righteous, heaven and liberation;
where every kind of peace and cessation exists eternally, there indeed is liberation. Blessed am I, such a householder! 74–75.
That householder who, day and night, surely acquires wealth,
yet like a porter does not know how to provide for the protection of his wife and family—
[for whom] food, seating, clothing, and even festivals and the like [are merely burdens]. (76)
That wealth is indeed useless, for it is consumed by his own sighs.
That wealth which is not enjoyed by the gods, by householders, by family members, by descendants, and by one's own kin—that is equal to mere clay. (77–78)
The husband who was not pleased is no longer seen with a smiling face;
the word "pleased," rich with love, is no longer heard, nor is he seen with eyes full of affection. There is no one with a sympathetic heart, nor is there anyone endowed with such devotion.
He does not bestow favor, nor does he act out of necessity;
he neither takes pleasure nor causes others to take pleasure, nor does he practice meditation.
He does not invite [others] with sweet words, nor does he summon them from his heart.
One should not feed him sweet food, nor should one give him sweet drinks;
one should never mix honey with him, for he does not even mingle in solitude.
Nor does he touch for the sake of pleasure, nor does he remember even in an auspicious place.
One should not inquire about the state of being a householder, nor should one allow the mind to be colored by passion.
Of what use is such a husband in this world? Vain indeed is his birth upon earth.
Therefore, O Goddess, you must protect me, even though I am established in detachment.
Through you alone, my status as a householder shall be fully manifested in every way.
Having previously performed penance, you have increased my value.
By burning the body of Satī, you have enhanced my divinity.
By slaying the Daityas in that manner, you have manifested your status as the supreme lord.
By granting me the two sons, Gaṇa and Skanda, you have established my honor.
O Goddess, through you alone have I attained the state of a householder in heaven and liberation even in the forest.
"O Goddess, it is by you alone that these sacred fords have been established on earth today.
We shall now return to our own Kailāsa; tell me, what else remains? O daughter of Himavat!
Tell us whatever pleases you, and we shall fulfill your desire."
Having spoken thus, Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world, became silent. O Lakṣmī,
thus has the Arbuda-tīrtha been described to you—
removing the heat of sin, granting liberation, and supremely bestowing peace.

Thus ends the five hundred and fifty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Origins and Legends of Caṇḍikā-tīrtha, Jāhnavī-kuṇḍa, Acaleśvara, Bhīma-tīrtha, Kulasantāraṇa-tīrtha, Paraśurāma-tīrtha, Brahma-pada-tīrtha, Tripuṣkara, Sāvitrī-kuṇḍa, and Nimita-tīrtha on Arbuda Mountain, along with Śiva’s Praise of Satī," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 555. *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Book 1 (Kṛtayuga-santāna).
Chapter 556 [Author:
Chapter 557 → Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī! Having performed their ablutions at the sacred sites on Arbuda, Śaṅkara and the others traveled through the sky in celestial chariots, beholding the earth and other realms below.
And Satī, Pārvatī, having seen the most beautiful Ṛkṣaparvata mountain—
Bowing down, she asked Śaṅkara, "What mountain shines here?
Śambhu replied, "This is indeed the great mountain named Ṛkṣa,
where sages dwell as ascetics living in the forest."
"O Ṛkṣaka, I indeed dwell here with you, known by the name Oṃkāra.
Upon hearing this, Pārvatī spoke again:
"O Śambhu, on this earth, from the Himālaya mountains up to the ocean, there are [many] mountains."
"Tell me, how many are those who take refuge in you, and how many rivers are mine?
(5) Śambhu replied: "Listen, O daughter of Himavat! Here there are seven principal mountain ranges:
Mahendra, Malaya, Sahya, Śuktimat, and Ṛkṣaparvata; (6)"
The Vindhya and the Pāriyātra— these indeed are the principal mountain ranges (kulaparvata).
Others, however, are Mandara, Śāra, Kailāsa, Dardura, Maināka,
Vaidyuta, Vārandhama, and Pāṇḍuraka.
Tuṅgaprastha, Kṛṣṇagiri, Jayanta, and Ṛṣyamūkaka;
Airāvata, Gomanta, Citrakūṭa, and Śrīparvata;
Cakorakūṭa, Śrīśaila, Śatruñjita, and Kṛtasmara. (8–9)
The Raivata mountain, Baradāda, Śālamālā,
and others also exist as purifying sacred sites (tīrthabhūmi), auspicious and liberating.
Your great father, Himācala, dwells there, possessing ten thousand peaks.
Therefore, hear from me about those rivers which have issued forth as your sisters:
the Gaṅgā, the Sindhu, the Śatadru, the Vitastā, and the Sarasvatī;
the Vipāśā, the Candrabhāgā, the Sarayū, and likewise the Yamunā. (11–12)
The Irāvatī, Devikā, Kuhū, Gomatī, Bāhudā, Dhūtapāpā, Dṛṣadvatī, Niścīrā, Kauśikī,
Cakṣuṣmatī, Gaṇḍakī, Lohitā, and Brahmaputraka.
Those purifying rivers which have filled the ocean like a natural hollow—listen also, O beautiful one, to those originating from the Pāriyātra mountains:
the Vedasmṛti, the Vedavatī, the Sindhuparṇā, and the Carmaṇvatī. || 14–15 ||
Candranābhā, Rohipārā, Nāśadā, Ācāranāmikā,
Vedatrayī, Vidiśā, and Vapantī— these are the rivers that flow into the ocean.
Now hear from me about the auspicious and purifying rivers born of the Ṛkṣas.
The Śoṇa, the Jyotīrathā, and also the Narmadā and Surasā; the Mandākinī, the Daśārṇā, the Tamasā, and likewise the Pippalā;
the Citrakūṭā, the Karatoyā, the Citrotpallā, and the Piśācikā.
Viśālā, Vaṃjukā, Vāluvāhinī, Virajā, as well as Śuktimatī, Paṅkinī, and Rātrī— these are the daughters of Ṛkṣa.
Now hear also of those born from the foothills of the Vindhya mountains, which destroy all sins.
The Śubhā, Tāpī, Payoṣṇī, Maṇijālā, Kumudvatī, Veṣṇā, Pāśā,
Vaitaraṇī, Śīghrādā, Antyā, Girā,
Durgā, Toyā, Vaidipālā, and those born from the Vindhya mountains. (1.256.20–21)
And now hear also of the rivers flowing to the ocean that arise from the foothills of the Sahya mountains:
the Godāvarī, Bhīmarathī, Kṛṣṇā, Veṇī, and Vañjulā;
as well as the Tuṅgabhadrā, Suprayogā, and the one known as the Bāhyakāverī. (22)
The rivers born of the Malaya mountains— Tāmraparṇī, Utpalāvatī, Puṣpāvatī, and Śatamālā— these also flow to the ocean. Likewise,
the Mahendra-born rivers are Triyāmā and Ikṣulā.
The Ṛṣikulyā, Trivindālā, Vaṃśavarā, and Mūlinī;
then the Śuktimatī, Palāśinī, and Lūtasī—these rivers also flow toward the ocean.
|| 25 || Ṛṣikā and Mandagāmā likewise flow to the sea.
These are the greatest rivers, as well as the Gomatī and Bhadrikā;
the Ojasvatī, Svarṇarekhā, Nāganadī, and Devikā;
the Sābhramatī, Hiraṇyā, Nyaṅkumatī, and Śatruñjitā. ||26–27||
Manoramā, Candrakalā, Nārāyaṇī, and Māheśvarī—
these and others indeed become destroyers of sin and bestowers of liberation.
Having heard this, Satī then spoke further to Śambhu.
"O Lord, tell me, among these [rivers], where do you exist in embodied form?
Śambhu replied: "I abide in the Revā in the form of a *liṅga*;
my established position is that all the particles of the Narmadā are Śaṅkaras. (1.256.30)
Pārvatī said: "A desire arises in me to see the banks of the Narmadā. Show me the Revā, from where she emerged as well as where she entered the ocean;
O Śiva, show it all to me."
"So be it," Hara said, and then he descended upon the peak of Ṛkṣa.
Accompanied by Pārvatī and tens of millions of his own attendants,
Śambhu likewise descended at that very spot from which the Revā had issued forth.
On Mount Ṛkṣa, they all stayed overnight, bathed, and rested;
they drank water and took their meals. Then Pārvatī asked Śaṅkara in the midst of the assembly of the Gaṇas.
"Tell me truly of my origin and likewise of the sacred fords (tīrthas).
Śaṅkara then declared the origin of the Narmadā:
"Listen, O daughter of Himavat! In ancient times, there was a great Daitya named Hiraṇyakaśipu."
He oppressed the gods and others; the gods went to Nārāyaṇa and informed Viṣṇu of the most terrible suffering caused by the Daityas.
Viṣṇu, in the form of Narasiṃha, slew the lord of the Dānavas.
Then, at the request of the gods for the sake of purification, this purifying form of Hari— the divine Revā— emerged from Vaikuṇṭha. She was a divine maidservant and a devoted attendant of Nārāyaṇa.
Having herself become the form of water, she arrived together with the gods;
she indeed remained in the celestial realm of the gods for many years.
Then, on earth, there was a king named Hiraṇyatejas.
Born of the lunar dynasty, he once went to the forest for the sake of asceticism;
at the command of the Brahmins,
he performed intense penance for the gratification of Mahādeva and for the welfare of embodied beings.
Then, for the purpose of bringing the Narmadā to the earth, that lord of men,
the king, beheld Mahādeva directly before his eyes;
he chose as a boon the auspicious descent of the Narmadā upon the earth.
"May there be a complete deliverance for all embodied beings by this means," [he said].
Śambhu replied, "Let it be so; you have reflected well.
He then called to mind the Narmadā, and she appeared before Śaṅkara.
Śambhu said: "Go to the earth, O Revā, for the sake of liberation.
There, become the bestower of welfare upon people and the destroyer of sins.
Revā said: "O Śaṅkara, being without support, where shall I remain?"
Śambhu said: "There stands a mountain named Udayācala;
it is capable of supporting you, so descend upon its peak, my dear.
Thereupon, Narmadā slowly descended from heaven.
Hiraṇyatejas then satisfied the ancestors, beginning with his father and grandfather, with those waters; he indeed offered them water libations with sesame seeds.
All the ancestors were uplifted and went to heaven and liberation.
This very place is purified at every step by the waters of the Narmadā;
this Narmadā is now being described as she who flows through seven kalpas.
Those regions, those mountains, those villages, and even those hermitages are all meritorious.
Wherever this Narmadā, the best of rivers, flows throughout the seven kalpas,
she purifies the merit of the Sarasvatī in three days and that of the Yamunā in seven;
however, the Ganges purifies instantly, even by her mere sight.
Those trees that have fallen on the banks of the Revā at the turn of time,
being touched by the waters of the Narmadā, attain the supreme goal.
This applies wherever they may be— whether at a confluence of the Revā or even upon its banks.
Bathing, giving gifts, chanting, burnt offerings, self-study of scripture, worship of the ancestors,
devotion to the deity, the great initiation, the ritual placement of mantras (nyāsa), and the renunciation of the body—
whatever [act] there may be among human beings, it shall yield infinite fruit.
At the Mūlatīrtha on the Narmadā, that bestows the fruit of a horse sacrifice (vājimedha).
By bathing in the Revā-tīrtha, one shall uplift a hundred future generations, a hundred past generations, and oneself as well. (56–57)
By giving a gift of land here, one will certainly obtain a kingdom;
and by drinking the water of the Narmadā, bathing in it, or even beholding it, there is indeed a fruit greater than that of a hundred Cāndrāyaṇa fasts. (58)

He who remembers the holy Narmadā at dawn shall obtain liberation. That river, situated on the Mountain of Sunrise, was brought back to the earth by the royal sage named Purūravas, who was born in the Lunar dynasty.
He made the great kingdom of Candrapurī sovereign over all;
his subjects were free from affliction and devoid of poverty. The people were long-lived, and the cows yielded all desires.
Men and women were adorned with garments of silk and fine cloth;
from every tree flowed streams of nectar, and the earth was rich with crops.
Thus, when the kingdom was governed by the king, everything indeed became filled with success.
During that solar eclipse, the king gave away elephants, horses, cattle, and dwellings,
as well as gold, silver, and jewels in great abundance;
he also gratified the ancestors with offerings of *havya* and *kavya*.
Hear now of that wonder which occurred when the king beheld his ancestors:
it was seen that his ancestors, their throats, palates, and lips parched by hunger and overcome by exhaustion, drank water with great difficulty using only clay and water. (65–66)
Seeing hundreds and thousands of those who were naked and clad in soiled garments,
King Purūravas bowed to his ancestors and said:
"Who are you, of such deformed appearance, appearing like hungry ghosts?"
"Tell us how liberation from this state as a *preta* may be attained.
The ancestors then said to the king, "We are indeed your forefathers.
This field is currently devoid of truth and abandoned by righteous deeds. (68–69)
"Indeed, there is no liberation without a sacred ford (tīrtha), and such a ford exists on these lands.
Having said this, they departed for the southern direction; and at that very moment, the king, having entrusted the burden of the kingdom to his son, went to the Mountain of Sunrise (Udayaparvata).
Subsisting on roots, tubers, and fruits, he was devoted to the worship of Śiva.
He practiced supreme devotion, and Maheśvara, pleased by it,
became manifest before him and said to the king, "O King, choose a boon."
The king chose the glorious Narmadā river, which flows through seven kalpas, saying:
"For the sake of delivering my ancestors, please cause her to descend upon the earth.
At that, the river Narmadā was summoned by Śambhu for the sake of pleasing his devotee.
Mounted upon a crocodile throne, adorned with divine ornaments,
a radiant young maiden born from the body of Nārāyaṇa,
endowed with every auspicious fortune and beautiful with her dark locks of hair. (74–75)
Having arrived and bowed to Śaṅkara, he asked, "How indeed was I remembered?
Śiva said, "For your sake, King Hiraṇyataijasa performed penance for fourteen thousand years."
"For the sake of liberating your father from his state of existence, you must indeed go to Mount Ṛkṣa. Deliver all your ancestors who exist as *preta*s and dwell in hell.
Having spoken thus, Revā departed for Mount Ṛkṣa by way of the sky.
Śambhu gave her the foremost and very firm Ṛkṣaparvata;
Revā, falling from the sky, descended upon that mountain.
Then that royal sage Purūravas spoke thus to Narmadā:
"O Goddess, you have bestowed a favor upon me for the sake of the liberation of my ancestors!
(1.256.80) Thereupon, having bathed there in the river, the king thoroughly gratified the gods;
he also satisfied his ancestors and likewise pleased them with funeral cakes and other offerings. (81)
All have been rescued from hell and established upon the path of the gods—
worms, insects, moths, and the like, as well as birds and those born from eggs.
And this incarnation occurred again in the first kalpa, during the Kṛta Yuga.
Thus, that virtuous maiden Śrī Narmadādevī, born from the left side of Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa,
was brought to heaven by the gods;
from heaven, she was led to Mount Udayaśikhara by Hiraṇyatejas.
And Purūravas led [the river] from the mountain of sunrise to the mountain of the stars;
then, having reached that region of the earth, she became a purifier flowing toward the ocean.
Through bathing, immersion, drinking, remembering, and even chanting her praises, [she grants liberation].
All the terrible demerit born of many births is utterly destroyed.
Then, when the first Kali age arrives— at the end of five thousand solar years— all the rivers once again go to heaven.
When the Kṛta age had arrived, the powerful King Purukutsa performed austerities once again for the purpose of bringing down the Narmadā.
Then, being pleased with him, I granted him a boon, and consequently, she [descended].
Reva, being mindful, arrived upon the earth at my command.
She descended upon the lovely Paryaṅka mountain into a thicket of bamboo.
Issuing swiftly from the Paryaṅka, she flowed toward the western quarter and entered the ocean.
Having made Purukutsa her husband, she descended from heaven due to a curse;
she exists in the world as a purifier, a staircase to heaven.
Even those in this world who are devoted to unrighteousness, if they die in the Narmadā, [attain liberation].
They too attain the state of Rudra through contact with the waters of the Revā.
There, at the root of the bamboo tree, stands the god Vaiṇyeśvara;
that is indeed the primordial and supreme tīrtha, which destroys sin and suffering. (92–93)
To the north of Revodgama lies the excellent city of Anantapura;
it consists of the hermitages of sages, is divine, and always bestows liberation.
Formerly, there stood the supreme and most purifying hermitage of Vyāsa.
There exists the supreme Śaiva field, an eternal and auspicious holy site (tīrtha).
There dwells the one named Mādhava, known as Utpalāvarta;
there, Viṣṇu, who possesses a thousand heads, resides in that purifying place.
The sacred field of Hari on the Narmadā is proclaimed to extend for the distance of one krośa.
On the northern bank of the Revā is the supreme Kapilātīrtha.
Tripurītīrtha is located here, where Śaṅkara dwells, assuming that very form.
That auspicious place, which bestows heaven, extends for two *krośas*.
Having utterly destroyed Tripura, Hara rested there for a moment.
That sacred ford (*tīrtha*) is purifying and grants both heaven and liberation through the mere act of bathing. 98–99.
Thus Śaṅkara spoke to Pārvatī, whose companion is Narmadā:
"O Lakṣmī, that which was previously related by me is indeed what you desired in your mind.

Thus ends the five hundred and fifty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of King Purūravas’s Liberation of His Ancestors through the Descent of Revā at Veṇutīrtha and Anantapuratīrtha," within the historical accounts of the descent to earth from Mount Ṛkṣa, following the arrival of Narmadā from the world of Brahmā to the Eastern Mountain (Udayācala), in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī! Then Śambhu spoke a purifying narrative to Pārvatī; I shall relate that which took place in the Kṛta Yuga of the Ādi Kalpa.
There was a king named Manu, of the Solar dynasty and possessed of great strength.
At that time, his capital city was Sāketa, which was preeminent on earth.
Because it could not be slain by the Dānavas, it became known by the name Avadhyā.
Richly protected by seven walls and surrounded by seven circular moats,
extending ten yojanas in width and situated along the Sarayū river,
he ruled over the earth divided into nine regions while remaining devoted to the vow of having only one wife.
Once, that great king addressed Vasiṣṭha:
"A sacrifice must be performed by me in a remote forest region.
Show me such a purifying place as you see fit. (5)

And Vasiṣṭha, having heard that and having obtained the consent of the brahmins, gave this command in the past: "O King, perform the sacrifice there on Mount Ṛkṣa in the forest from which the Revā flows. (6–7)
Having gone there, he performed the great horse sacrifice (hayamedha).
That king bestowed land, cattle, gold, and jewels at the sacrifice.
For the purpose of the sacrificial rites, he constructed a pavilion extending ten yojanas.
And devoted to sacrifice, the king caused [a sacrificial ground] to be constructed on the bank of the Revā.
Having summoned all the deities, including Indra, the subduer of Pāka,
he gratified them with water for the feet (arghya), water for washing the feet (pādya), honey-mixtures (madhuparka), and ritual seats (viṣṭara).
He gratified the gods of the earth and the virtuous with food and other offerings,
as well as with necklaces, armlets, bracelets, and ornaments for the neck.
Having gathered together in rows within the excellent dining halls, they partook of the meals.
Other birds, insects,
and forest-dwelling creatures that had been mired in the remnants of the sacrifice were all born as beings made of gold.
In this manner, the great sacrifice was brought to completion on the bank of the Narmadā.
Praised at the final ablution (avabhṛtha) by the King, the wealthy river attained satisfaction:
"You have become a staircase to heaven for the ancestors, bringing about their liberation;
you are the destroyer of the sins of all worlds and a most venerable mother. (14)
"Lead me to heaven, O great virtuous one! O destroyer of the heat of sin!
(15) Having heard this hymn of King Manu, that illustrious lady, seated upon her crocodile-throne, then replied to the king, being well-pleased. (16)
Richly adorned with all ornaments, her face possessing the luster of the moon, she appeared in the form of a maiden and, accompanied by a smile, said: "Choose a boon desired in your heart.
The king replied: "In this world, you are always the embodiment of a sacred ford (tīrtha), the one who carries us across."
O auspicious Tārā, you who are ever-present here at this sacred ford on the sacrificial ground,
may rivers that carry you across likewise dwell within my kingdom for eternal ages, for the sake of the welfare of the subjects. (18–19)
"Come with me in another form, O Narmadā;
dwell together with me by the Sarayū in the city of Sāketa. "So be it," Revā said to him, and she departed in that other form.
Thereafter, he dwelt at Revākuṇḍa in the city of Sāketa.
At the great sacred site (tīrtha) on the sacrificial ground, known as Yajñasthāna in Ṛkṣaka,
embodied beings endowed with merit go to heaven by bathing there.
Now, the blessed Lord Viṣṇu resides at the exceedingly purifying Brahmakuṇḍa;
having bathed here in the northward-flowing Revā, one attains liberation. Beyond that lies Haṃsatīrtha, where the swans departed for heaven.
Beyond that is Siddhatīrtha, where perfected ascetics dwell.
Then follows the auspicious confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā in the waters of the Revā;
in ancient times, the sage Mataṅga summoned both the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā there.
Then, at the very dawn, for the sake of the bathing of the illustrious sages,
the Gaṅgā and Yamunā arrived in personified form within the water.
The auspicious sacred ford (tīrtha), consisting of the triple confluence, became manifest in the form of water.
Then there is the beautiful Yogatīrtha, as well as the supreme Ṛkṣeśvara;
there exists the sacred ford named Āpsarasa, which wards off curses.
Formerly, in the assembly of Indra, the Apsarases performed a dance.
Kāma himself, assuming a supreme form, arrived there.
Upon seeing him, the dancers were then struck with wonder and became enchanted;
they forgot the rhythmic beats, the melodies, the scales, the modulations, and the sequences of their dance.
Then Indra became exceedingly enraged and cursed those dancers:
"O Campakā, Sīmāpanā, Keśinī, Bhāminī, Kaumudī, Suprabhā, as well as Utpalā, Mahodayā, and Asimā! (1.557.30–31)
The world-protectors and the lords here shine resplendently in this assembly; yet,
because they have displayed negligence regarding their dance and their prowess,
let them therefore enter the womb of a Niṣāda, for that shall serve as sufficient instruction for them.
Then, having bathed repeatedly in the Narmadā during the Kumbha conjunction on the third day of the month of Māgha, remaining without food and without water,
and having worshipped Gaurī and Śambhu, you shall regain heaven once more.
Thus addressed, those Niṣādas likewise acted;
having bathed in the waters of the Narmadā, they attained liberation, for that is indeed the Apsaras-tīrtha.
Then there is another holy site, the Dattātreya-tīrtha, where the river flows with the Revā.
Having bathed there at Saṅgatā and having worshipped Keśava,
one shakes off all sins and goes at last to the abode of Śrī Hari.
Thereafter, one should go to the holy ford named Gāñjālabheda, which bestows liberation from worldly existence.
In the lunar dynasty there was a king renowned as Devānīka;
his son was the universal monarch (cakravartin) named Harikeśa.
His capital, most excellent of all, was located in Kanyāpura.
On the banks of the Tuṅgabhadrā, he performed many sacrifices.
Harikeśa gave a gift of one hundred thousand milch cows,
and during a solar eclipse, he gave a thousand gold coins to each priest.
Then, for the sake of victory in the science of the Vedas,
he again convened a great assembly of Brahmins there.
To whoever should be victorious therein, a cow with a single calf was to be given.
Having resolved that she should be given away—she who was a milch cow, richly adorned with gold ornaments, and beautifully graced by a necklace of diamonds—the king posed a question:
"In this conjunction of Rāhu and the Sun, what is the fruit obtained from bathing at Prayāga? || 42-43 ||
Is this bathing born of *prārabdha* (past karma), or does it occur even without *prārabdha*?
What indeed is the primary cause, and what might be the instigating factor?
The land of Prayāga is not present here, nor is there contact with that soil.

"When the question was asked, 'How could there be a fruit born from that [action], since there is no production without a cause?'— O King, at that time some learned sages said that it was merely an *arthavāda*, intended to convey praise."
Others say that without the [proper] ground, one does not obtain the fruit of Prayāga;
others then said that the fruit is equal to that of Prayāga,
while still others declared that bathing is equal to bathing at Prayāga.
Others say that bathing arises from *prārabdha* (the karma already set in motion), while still others say it occurs even in the midst of *prārabdha*.
Through effort, bathing indeed takes place even without merit (*puṇya*).
However, the primary cause in this regard is either the desire for liberation (*mumukṣā*) or the desire for enjoyment (*bubhukṣatā*).
Desire is the primary cause, whatever it may be; the caravan leader also serves as its stimulator. Furthermore, the instigator is the inquiry produced by the scripture again and again.
In the application of the scriptures, compassion is always considered the cause of the Guru.
(51) Such causes may indeed be of diverse forms;
thus has this discussion proceeded, for it has not been fully determined by any single person alone. (52)
But the primary cause therein, which bestows merit and resides within the heart—
the Supreme Brahman Himself as the giver of the fruit— was forgotten.
Because of that, the golden cow was not won by some at that time.

Even though the dispute had proceeded for the sake of victory, no decision was reached. In that dispute among the Brāhmaṇas, there was one particular priest named Raudrāyaṇa, a knower of the Atharva-mantras, who acted as the challenger.
Even though a dispute had arisen, he did not obtain victory at all;
enraged, the king immediately caused him to perform a fire-offering (*homa*) into the fire with fierce and highly potent mantras, while [the priest] remained ignorant [of the consequences]. //56//

By the oblation performed by the king, fire— equal in brilliance to the fire at the end of an eon and terrifying with its garlands of flames— arose from that sacrificial pit. Indeed, the pavilion and the men standing within the pavilion were consumed by it.
"Furthermore, another [body] has been reduced to ashes;
thus, O Brahmins, let an expiation be granted for my slain and burnt elephants so that it may be accomplished, and I shall perform it. (59)
Then the Brahmins said, "Go indeed to Kalpagrāma;
there you must consult the sages, Bhṛgu and the others, regarding the means of atonement.
Having been addressed thus, the king went on foot to Sukalpa.
Having bowed down to the great sages, he indeed engaged them in conversation;
then he reported the terrible sin of killing committed during the sacrifice.
Having heard him, the sages said: "Recite the Gāyatrī one million times."
O King, perform recitations at every sacred ford (*tīrtha*) until you have visited the sixty-eight holy sites.
Bestow gifts of cows and gold, and likewise perform ten thousand fire-sacrifices (*homa*).
Grant hundreds of thousands of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) to virtuous Brahmins.
In this way, there shall be liberation from sin; perform pilgrimages to the sacred fords (tīrthas) with devotion.
O King, perform the procession of the bones of those who have died and been consumed by fire along the Narmadā; by that, liberation will come to pass.
Through contact with the waters of the Narmadā, the state of a deity is attained in heaven.
(66) By the offering of water with sesame seeds, their liberation will certainly occur.
On the delightful bank of the Narmadā, one should perform an auspicious Vaiṣṇava sacrifice. (67)
"Practice once more that by which liberation will be possible.
Thus addressed, that royal sage went again toward the auspicious Śrī Narmadā and performed sacrifices and libations on her beautiful bank.
The current emerged there and entered the Narmadā;
it became the confluence with the Narmadā known as Gāñjālī.
By Harikeśa, the ancestors who had died and been cremated were [honored].
Having all been delivered there, they were satisfied and then said to the king:
"O illustrious one! By your grace, we have attained godhood.
Mounted upon divine vehicles, we shall indeed go to the abode of Viṣṇu."
Having heard this, King Harikeśa was filled with supreme joy;
having bowed to the Revā, who remains steadfast for seven kalpas, he then offered this praise: "Salutations to you, O best of rivers, who dwell for seven kalpas! (72–73)
Having bathed in you, people attain liberation everywhere;
O Great Goddess, by your grace, liberation from the ocean of worldly existence has been achieved!
Victory to you, O compassionate Goddess, for the sake of the ancestors consumed by fire!
Having heard those words, Narmadā became an embodied maiden.
She said to the king, "Choose a boon," and the king then chose a boon:
"O virtuous one! O purifier! If you are a granter of boons to me, make me pure. (75–76)
"By bathing, by immersion, by drinking [the water], by remembering, and even by chanting [her name],
may the sin committed in seven lifetimes perish instantly!
Revā said, "So be it," and then she disappeared.
Having bowed again toward that direction, Harikeśa, the universal monarch, mounted a celestial vehicle and departed for the city of Sāketa.
That auspicious Narmadā tīrtha destroys the sin of killing and bestows liberation. (78–79)
Harikeśa and Gāñjāla destroy the sin of killing;
they are auspicious, bestowing wealth, fame, long life, enjoyment, and liberation.
Now, in the southern direction, there is a sacred ford (tīrtha) named Vālukaśāṅkara.
Where indeed the confluence of the Kanyā and Narmadā occurs, it is a bestower of liberation.
Beyond that, the holy site known as Pūrṇamanoratha is proclaimed.
Formerly, there was a king named Harivarman, the lord of the city of Virāṭa. (81–82)
He performed a sacrifice there and bestowed a hundred thousand cows;
the gods were well-satisfied there, and the brahmins and the virtuous were honored.
Then there is another excellent holy site, the confluence of the Revā and the Matsya.
Where the waters are pure, always bestowing liberation through drinking and bathing;
on the northern bank of the Revā, beyond the confluence with the Kapilā, lies Narmadāpura, where there are brahmins who are ascetics. (84–85)
Indeed, millions [of sages] shine forth near the hermitage of Jamadagni.
Jamadagni performed most fierce ascetic penance dedicated to Śaṅkara.
Śiva appeared before him in person and said to him, "Choose a boon."
The sage chose the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu), and she arrived from Goloka.

For the sake of righteous deeds and auspicious purposes, for the worship of Śiva and the proper offering of libations, for the rites for the ancestors and the rites for the gods, cows are always most meritorious. (87–88)
From the wish-fulfilling cow, Jamadagni obtained all his desires— desires that were the very form of dharma, bestowing prosperity and granting access to heaven.
That twice-born sage constantly fed thousands of seers.
The great fame of Jamadagni was then spread throughout the earth because of his cows. He built a city named Māhiṣmatī after the daughter of the Daitya named Vipracitti, who was called Māhiṣmatī.
In whose presence Jamadagni had indeed dwelt in the great forest,
she went through the sky with her companions to behold Mount Mandara.
There she saw an ascetic performing austerities, who was without the perception of taste.
Having seen the beautiful hermitage, the beautiful woman reflected:
"I shall terrify him and remain here in the hermitage myself, assuming at will the forms of those who dwell in the forest. (93–94)
Having gone into the presence of the sages while assuming the form of a buffalo, she was indeed cursed by the sages: "For a hundred years you shall remain a buffalo;
then, having obtained Mahiṣa as your son, you will become restored to your natural state. (95)
Thus cursed, she went to the excellent Narmadā-tīrtha,
where the great ascetic Sindhudvīpa was performing severe penance. Indeed,
Sindhudvīpa’s virility spilled onto the surface of a rock.
Then that queen drank that fragrant water mixed with water;
subsequently, she gave birth to a firm son born from the seed of the Brahmin,
the cruel asura named Mahiṣa, whom indeed the consort of Śiva (Śāṅkarī) slew.
The great power Nārāyaṇī then went to her own city of Māhiṣmatī;
having reached the city of Māhiṣmatī near the hermitage of Jamadagni, she died in due course and attained heaven through the ascetic power of the sage. (1.557.100)
That most beautiful Tīrtha of Jamadagni at Māhiṣmatī,
Viśoka, and Aṇḍikā are considered the third purifier;
the fourth is the Narmadā, and at the confluence of these rivers is the Kapilā stone.
There exists a most meritorious sacred site (tīrtha) where, by the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa),
the ancestors attain liberation, having been delivered by Paraśurāma. This has been told to you, O Lakṣmī, as it was formerly spoken by Satyaśiva.
By hearing and chanting this, one attains the status of a deity in heaven;
even liberation and worldly enjoyment are obtained in the auspicious hermitage of Jamadagnya.

Thus, in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, the five hundred and fifty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Sacred Sites with Their Origins," has been narrated. These include Manu’s sacrificial site on Mount Ṛkṣa, Viṣṇu-Brahma Kuṇḍa, Haṃsa Tīrtha, Trisaṅgama Yoga Tīrtha, Āpsarasa Tīrtha, the confluence of Dattātreya, Gāñjālabheda Tīrtha, Vāluka, Pūrṇamanoratha Tīrtha, the confluence of Kanyā and Narmadā, the confluence of Matsya, Narmadāpura, Jāmadagnya Tīrtha, and others. || 557 ||

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī! I shall relate to you that other sacred site on the Narmadā which was spoken of by Mahādeva to Pārvatī. (1)
The confluence of the Matsyā and the Tāpyā bestows liberation.
Formerly, a celestial sage named Kalahaṃsa, intent on meditation,
established a beautiful hermitage there and performed most rigorous penance.
Subsisting on vegetables, roots, and fruits, he remained standing on one foot.
As he was thus intent on meditation upon Śiva, the King of the Gods himself,
fearing his ascetic power, arrived in the guise of a brahmin to deceive him.
He said, "O Kalahaṃsa! For what purpose do you perform penance?
The sage replied, "And why, O Indra, do you mock me, a twice-born?
I know you to be Turāṣāṭ; I do not desire the kingdom of Indra. (5)
"I shall propitiate Śambhu; rule the kingdom as you desire.
(6) Indra said, "O Brahmin, choose a boon! You shall behold Śaṅkara.
Kalahaṃsa then replied, "I choose no other boon. (7)
"If you are capable, grant me this: may I always have devotion toward Śambhu.
"So be it," said the Lord of the Gods, and having spoken, he departed for heaven.
Then Śaṅkara himself quickly arrived there, laughing aloud.
Kalahamsa paid homage and began to offer praise:

"Salutations to you, O Mahadeva, endowed with compassion for your devotees; salutations be unto you! Salutations to Shiva, the bestower of desired boons upon his devotees; salutations to you! (1.558.10)
Salutations to You, the deliverer of those submerged in the ocean of worldly existence;
salutations to You, whose nature is the Supreme Brahman, the foremost among the Vaiṣṇavas.
(11) Oṃ, salutations to You, whose essence is Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa; salutations to You!
Salutations to you, the Lord of Pārvatī, the radiant Lord Prabhāsāmin.
Salutations to you, the sovereign of victory, who possesses the form of Nārāyaṇī.
Salutations again and again to the Cause, whose essential nature is the seed of all things. 12–13.
Having heard the auspicious hymn of praise, Śambhu said to him, "Choose a boon.
And that best of sages chose the Kalahaṃseśvara Tīrtha as his boon;
he chose the auspicious boon that those who depart their lives there shall attain liberation.
Śambhu said, "So be it; and at the end, may there be liberation for you.
Having spoken thus, Kalahaṃsa vanished entirely.
And having resorted to the Narmadā-tīrtha, he went to the abode of Brahmā at the end.
At the confluence of the Matsyā and the Tāpī lies that divine site, Kalahaṃsa, which possesses excellent bathing places;
it destroys sin, bestows heaven, and grants liberation.
Another sacred site is the confluence of the Bṛhatī and the Narmadā.
There exists a place rich in the beauty of the Vindhya mountains, inhabited by ascetics.
A certain Niṣāda named Raktadharman arrived there in order to provide for his own family with wild roots, fruits, and other provisions. (18–19)

In the morning, for the sake of his welfare, he indeed brought water from the Revā river; filled with ignorant devotion, having bathed [the deity], he offered the fruit. Then, when the northern solstice had arrived, he constantly worshipped with flowers.
He offered bilva fruits and other offerings to Śaṅkara with devotion.
One day, that Niṣāda saw Śaṅkara in his house;
however, he did not see a third eye upon the deity’s form.
Then he reflected, "Surely this has been carried off by someone.
Having considered this, he instantly drew his own left eye with a sharp arrow,
cut it from the forehead of the God of gods, and offered it [to him].
There was no trembling, nor any wretchedness, nor despondency, nor agitation. Pleased by this, Mahādeva spoke to the Niṣāda with a laugh:
"Choose a boon, O great devotee, whatever is desired and wished for by your mind. (24–25)
Having heard these words, the Niṣāda prostrated himself with all eight limbs and chose a boon: "May all the Niṣādas, together with the flocks of birds,
along with their sons, wives, and cattle, and whatever other beings possess bodies born of sin [be liberated]."
"By your grace and through the granting of this boon, may they go to the world of liberation.
(27) Thus I choose this worthy boon out of a desire for the liberation of all beings.
Having heard this, Śambhu, being well-pleased, said: "Let it be so; let the boon be granted. (28)
"By my grace, you shall attain the fulfillment of all your intentions and desires;
and all shall attain liberation just as you have intended.
Having spoken thus, Mahādeva vanished right there.
Then, at that time, the Niṣāda, seated in a celestial chariot with his attendants and others,
held under a golden parasol and fanned by hosts of Apsarases,
was enriched with divine ornaments and garments and honored with divine sandalwood paste.
Since it was there that he went to the state of liberation together with the hosts of beasts and birds,
O daughter of Himavat, this has been described as the Śivanetrahrada.
Indeed, this sacred ford (tīrtha) is purifying, bestows all prosperity, and likewise grants liberation.
Now, there is another supreme sacred site on the northern bank of the Narmadā.
There, sacrifices were performed by Janaka, who arrived on a pilgrimage, and the twice-born were gratified with sacrificial fees.
Likewise, Dharmarāja and the other guardians of the quarters arrived.
Dharmarāja approached King Janaka, offering him the arghya and other honors.
[He had attained this state] through austerity, the yoga of meditation, as well as by gifts and the worship of the gods.
"By the grace of Śiva and Revā, all the worlds have been conquered by you. Then Janaka indeed questioned Dharmarāja with humility:
"Which countries, mountains, rivers, and hermitages are meritorious? || 36-37 ||
"Which are the sacred fords (tīrthas) in this world where what is given, offered in sacrifice, or practiced as austerity does not perish for men? Tell me that in truth.
Dharma said: "Listen, O King, to what was heard from the mouth of Śaṅkara."
In ancient times, King Kalmāṣapāda reigned over the Maṇḍala of Mathurā;
and in ancient times, a king named Nābhāga reigned over the Maṇḍala of Sāketa.
The celestial chariot of Nābhāga, however, traveled high up in the sky.
"However, the vehicle of Kalmāṣapāda travels upon the earth and not through the sky.
For this reason, having bowed to Śiva, King Kalmāṣapāda asked his own doubt in the hearing of all the Gaṇas.
O Hara, ten sacrifices were performed by me at Puṣkara;
likewise, a hundred each were performed at the Gaṅgā, in the Naimiṣa forest, at Prabhāsa, O Moon-adorned One,
and at Prayāgarāja and Kāśī.
"O Maheśvara, I have performed more than a full measure of sacrifices there;
yet my celestial chariot descends below the sky above Nābhāga.
How is it that such a deficiency in my merit has occurred, by which I am cast down?"
Then Śambhu indeed spoke to that King Kalmāṣapāda:
"On the northern bank of the Revā is the holy ford named Lakṣamedha;
there Śaṅkara, the Lord of Lakṣamedha, shines eternally."
There, Nābhāga performed a single sacrifice dedicated to Viṣṇu. By that merit, indeed, Nābhāga’s vehicle remained stationed in the sky.
You, however, did not perform even a single sacrifice on the banks of the Revā that yields great fruit.
Because of that, their celestial chariot travels toward the low-lying region rather than through the sky.
There is indeed no sacred ford superior to that of the Narmadā.
Having heard this, King Kalmāṣapāda then [proceeded].
He went to the bank of the Narmadā and performed ten sacrifices:
the Vaiṣṇava, the Raudra, and the horse-sacrifice (vājimedha);
as well as the Kārīrī, the Vājapeya, and the great Viśvajit sacrifice.
He performed the Puṇḍarīka, Naramedha, Gomedha, and Vaiśvadaivata sacrifices; likewise,
he performed the sacrifice of knowledge (jñānayajña), and furthermore,
he conducted the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā sacrifice.
Then that vehicle, rising of its own accord into the sky and ascending upwards,
went from there to Satyaloka and Vaikuṇṭha according to its will; indeed,
it traveled higher and higher above the aerial chariot of Nābhāga.
Thus, having indeed performed the dedication to Brahman,
Kalmāṣapāda then became worthy of going to Vaikuṇṭha with his living body;
at whose sacrifice Viṣṇu himself appeared together with Lakṣmī.
And a divine garland was placed upon the neck of that king by Viṣṇu;
by means of that yoga, he went to Vaikuṇṭha and returned from there to various places.
Thus, by the grace of Śrī Viṣṇu, the king became empowered.

That Jānaka Tīrtha and likewise Kālmāṣapādika exist on the bank of the Narmadā; they are purifying and supremely bestow liberation. Furthermore, there exists another beautiful and auspicious place called Saptasārasvata.
A Gandharva named Saptasārasvata, a servant of Śiva,
having performed a song on Kailāsa, departed for Mount Raivata. Then,
without the permission of Śaṅkara, he returned after a very long time.
Nandī cursed him in anger: "Go to the state of a Caṇḍāla on earth!
Having bathed at the Vyatipāta [conjunction] in the Narmadā, you shall attain liberation.
Thus that Gandharva entered the womb of a Caṇḍāla.
He became a rememberer of his past lives and wandered upon the earth along the banks of the Narmadā.
Having bathed in the waters of the Revā and worshipped Śambhu according to the prescribed rites,
he was liberated from the womb of a Cāṇḍāla and attained the state of a Gandharva once again.

The Saptasārasvata Tīrtha is proclaimed to be the bestower of liberation. On the southern bank of the Narmadā, within the Aśoka groves, there is another excellent and supreme Tīrtha known as Aśokajanana. (63–64)
There, the hermitage of the sage Aghamarṣaṇa was adorned by Brahmins;
it was there that sages most devoted to Brahman sought liberation.
Dharma indeed came to the hermitage of Aghamarṣaṇa in the form of a Vaiśya.
"In order to investigate what kind of sages dwell here,
that Vaiśya performed austerities exceeding those of the Brāhmaṇas;
he then bestowed deer-skins upon the Brāhmaṇas in their entirety."
He wore only a loincloth and lived on alms; then he went to Nāśika.
One year passed while he lived with the ascetics of the Vaiśya.
There was neither indulgence nor meanness, neither pride nor envy.
"O Viśā, faults such as hatred and passion no longer exist; therefore, everything has been conquered by you.
Having arrived at the Saptasārasvata and Nārmada tirthas, he bathed and worshipped Lord Hari, Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
Likewise, Hari reverently worshipped Śambhu in the form of Bāṇa. Having appeared before him in person, Śambhu said: "You are indeed Vṛṣa;
nevertheless, you have attained perfection especially through your ascetic penance."
"Ascend this celestial chariot and enjoy the happiness of divine pleasures.
Accompanied by your sons, wife, and daughters-in-law, go from here to the world of Viṣṇu.
Then Dharma said: "O Viṣṇu! The sages are on the bank of the Narmadā. (72–73)
"Here there are ten thousand whose wealth is austerity;
may they all, through my ascetic merit, go indeed to the world of Viṣṇu.
I consider this boon to come from Śrī Hari alone, and from no other."
Upon hearing this, all the sages, filled with pride and ego, indeed held that Vaiśya in contempt and said to one another:
"This Vaiśya is showing disrespect toward the great Brahmins. (75–76)
"Even though that Vaiśya has gone to Vaikuṇṭha through his ascetic penance, O Brahmins, he is now choosing a boon out of deceit in order to demonstrate it to the world.
Indeed, he chooses [this] in order to make known the superiority of the Vaiśya in the world. (77)
"We do not go to heaven by means of his asceticism;
rather, this Vaiśya shall cross over [to heaven] by insulting the Brāhmaṇa.
Having said this, the sages spoke to that Vaiśya: "Go forth, sir! (79)
"Accept the dharma of a Vaiśya and practice agriculture while remaining at home.
You are not fit to perform asceticism, for you possess pride in your caste.
Go, go to your home; do not come near the twice-born."
Having been addressed thus, that farmer, seeing the twice-born ones filled with pride and anger, spoke to the brahmin named Vimukta:
"The supreme duty of brahmins is the absence of anger and tranquility. (81–82)
Freedom from the notions of "I" and "mine"—he who possesses this is a true Brahmin.
A Brāhmaṇa endowed with anger and the notions of "I" and "mine" does not exist at all.
All the penance or even the Śrāddha rite performed by such a person is fruitless.
The determination of caste is profound and difficult to discern even for the gods.
A Vaiśya who performs the duties of a Brahmin is called a Brahmin;
and a Brahmin who is devoid of Brahminical duties is called a Vaiśya. (84–85)
"One should avoid from afar a twice-born man who is harsh, merciless, cruel, ungrateful, long-simmering in anger, and a hero in disputation.
Having said this, that best of Vaiśyas then ceased speaking for a moment.
The Brahmins asked him: "Who are you, appearing in the form of a Vaiśya?
The Vaiśya replied: "I am Dharma, come here for the purpose of testing you.
What kind of Brahmins are you who dwell on the banks of the Narmadā?"
Abandoning the notions of "I" and "mine," perform supreme austerity;
having renounced anger in every way, worship the Supreme Lord.
Thus, by means of this vow of Brahman, you shall attain liberation here.
Then they pacified their own faults through righteousness;
thereafter, having honored righteousness, those sages became free from fault.
Then celestial chariots arrived in the presence of Vṛṣa.
Indeed, by the command of Vṛṣa, all those who had washed away their sins,
together with Dharma, Viṣṇu, and Ramā,
ascended [the chariot]; having bowed to Saptasārasvata, they went to Vaikuṇṭha itself.
"Indeed, through hearing and even through reciting it, that bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Having spoken thus to the Goddess, O Lotus-born One, Śaṅkara ceased;
[and I have told you] this supreme holy site consisting of the seven Sarasvatis.
This has been described as bestowing liberation and granting emancipation, especially for one who bathes there;
it yields the fruit of numerous sacrifices and grants sons, wives, and wealth.

Thus ends the five hundred and fifty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Confluence of the Matsyā and Tāpī, Kalahaṃseśa, the Confluence of the Bṛhatī and Narmadā, the Śivanetra Lake, the Lakṣamedha, the Saptasārasvata, and other Tīrthas, along with their historical wonders," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
