Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī! Then Śambhu spoke this excellent [teaching] to Pārvatī;
I shall tell you of the yoga pertaining to the Śāṇḍilyākalpa and another sacred site (tīrtha). || 1 ||
In that place where the birth of the king named Arjuna occurred for a thousand times, Śāṇḍilya, Kauṇḍinya, and Māṇḍavya dwelt with joy. (2)
The hermitage of Śāṇḍilya was situated at the confluence of the Śāṇḍilyā and Revikā;
that place became famous in ancient times as Śāṇḍilyapura.
At night, a certain mouse was wandering here and there.
Just as he was being devoured by the cat, a wolf arrived. (4)
Leaving that mouse with only a small portion remaining, the cat ran away;
then, as a cloud appeared, a stream of water issued forth there.
Then, as his bones were being carried away by the current in the water, that mouse became a Yakṣa through the power of this sacred ford (tīrtha). (6)
Renowned as Bṛhadvṛnda and surrounded by ten thousand yakṣas,
the lord of the yakṣas ascended to heaven in a celestial chariot yoked with swans.
He was born as a lord in the world of the Yakṣas solely through the power of that holy ford (tīrtha).
Thence one should go to the great holy ford, the confluence of the Kubjā and the Revā. || 8 ||
Indeed, it was there that the most magnificent sacrifice was performed by Rantideva;
in ancient times, there was a king named Rantideva who was devoted to non-violence.
With the consent of Vasiṣṭha, he commanded his servants, ministers, and priests to perform an auspicious sacrifice on the banks of the Revā:
"Let the collection of sacrificial implements and materials be prepared immediately."
And ten lakhs of cows, yielding abundant milk, accompanied by their calves. ||11||
Let them bring a hundred thousand cows that are well-adorned with loads of gold, grant all desires, and highly auspicious; ten thousand horses, and ten thousand elephants with beautiful tusks.
Let there be an infinity of jewels, rubies, and gems therein.
There would be many thousands of celestial palaces in the sky.
"Let many other vehicles from the earth be brought here to this sacred site.
Having thus commanded, he himself indeed sat upon a celestial vehicle. (14)
Having gone to the bank of the Narmadā together with his harem and retinue, he rested there, [erecting] sacrificial posts of gold, sacrificial pits, and pavilions. ||15||
He caused various kinds of foods and edibles to be prepared, as well as mountains of cooked rice;
he adorned the Brahmins with ornaments made of jewels. ||16||
The lord of men, together with his wife, undertook the initiation for the sacrifice;
once the sacrifice had commenced, the bearer of oblations became accessible to all. (17)
Manifest in bodily form together with Svāhā, he accepted the oblation;
so too did the gods beginning with Brahmā and Śakra, the world-protectors, and the hosts of Maruts. (18)
The Viśvedevas, the Sādhyas, the Vasus, the Moon and the Sun;
the rivers, the oceans, the mountains, all the sacred fords, and the streams. (19)
The Mothers, the Siddhas, and the Gandharvas, along with the Yakṣas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas;
Rudra accompanied by Umā, and Viṣṇu joined by Nārāyaṇī. || 1.559.20 ||
They arrived, and he assigned separate sacrificial portions for them;
and hearing the sound of the Vedas set in motion, the foremost of the Dānavas [were alarmed]. (21)
Mahābāhu, Subāhu, and the others, inhabitants of Krauñcapura, arrived at the bank of the Narmadā together with their servants, armies, and vehicles. ||22||
Standing in the southern direction, they created obstacles for the sacrifice;
then Brahmā, agitated by fear, spoke to Rantideva.
"O King of kings! Ward off the obstacle so that the sacrifice may proceed in due order.
Hearing this, Rantideva, who was most devoted to Brahman, spoke while remembering Hari. (24)
If my truthfulness exists—that my supreme mind is fixed on devotion to Brahmā—then let the wicked Daityas, Rākṣasas, and others go to their destruction without battle. (25)
Having spoken thus, that royal sage remembered Viṣṇu, the Lord;
He, bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, appeared in person. (26)
"May Viṣṇu’s discus, the destroyer of Rākṣasas, remain here at the tip of this kuśa grass.
Having spoken thus, he immersed that kuśa blade in the excellent waters of the Narmadā. ||27||
He dispatched Dhruva to the southern direction for the sake of protection;
likewise, he also dispatched Darbhaka to the north. (28)
Having performed protection on all sides with the formidable mantra of Deva,
he indeed dispatched two blades of kusha grass toward the east and the west.
Having become embodied, they constructed fortresses on all sides;
blazing with fire, they were the burners of the Rākṣasas.
Those sky-rangers, difficult to overcome, went wherever there were Rākṣasas and,
having arrived at each such place, they seized them by the thousands.
Then this king offered *bilva*, mango, and cane wood into the fire;
from that [offering] there arose a *liṅga* possessing the radiance of a blazing, dark-blue fire. ||32||
All those standing on the sacrificial ground, having witnessed the miracle of Rantideva, gazed upon the Lord seated within the fire-pit. ||33||
There, even the gods and others offered their heartfelt praises;
all the demons fled in fear from the fire arising from the darbha grass. (34)
The gods and others went to Krauñcadvīpa, and thus the sacrifice reached completion; having bowed to and worshipped the Bilvāmraka Liṅga. ||35||
Praising the king at the Camatkṛti-tīrtha, they went to heaven;
and the monarch, having ascended his vehicle, went to Sāketa.
Having performed their ablutions at that sacred ford, they go to the eternal Brahman;
even by the mere sight of it, it incinerates sins and grants liberation. (37)
Furthermore, there is another holy site at Kubjā known as Hārikeśa.
A twice-born man named Harikeśa once lived in Śālagrāma. (38)
He was a righteous soul who lived by the practice of gleaning ears of grain; his wife was a devoted partner named Suvratā, in whom a hundred sons were born. (39)
Residing in Kapilāpura, Harikeśa obtained a *prastha* of food every day and night solely by gathering stones;
even his young sons did so in whatever manner they could.
They subsist on alms and such, for they do not go about seeking full meals. ||41||
Seeing such a state, the mother grieved, overwhelmed;
afflicted by intense sorrow, she spoke to her husband while censuring her own condition. (42)
One's aged mother and father, a virtuous wife, and an infant son must be supported with diligence; this is the eternal dharma. (43)
Therefore, having accepted gifts, one should maintain one's own family;
through a son one conquers the world, and through a son one prospers in happiness. (44)
One attains happiness through a son, and the son is the refuge for his ancestors;
such was indeed the great king Ambarīṣa, the sovereign of Ayodhyā. 45.
"O best of the twice-born, go to Kurukṣetra where a sacrifice is being performed;
for the Brāhmaṇas have gone there with the desire to receive gifts. (46)
"O Gā, gold and wealth have been obtained by those residing at Śālagrāma. Having heard these words of the beautiful woman, he took his family with him. ||47||
The twice-born one went to Kurukṣetra for a sacrifice and entered the sacrificial arena;
seeing him, Ambarīṣa honored him with offerings of water for the feet and respectful reception. ||48||
He said, "Request whatever you desire in the guise of a guest.
The Brahmin replied, "May I possess wealth for a hundred years. (49)
"O best of kings, give enough for my family;
give cows adorned with loads of gold for each of my sons. (1.559.50)
"Give me alms in such a way that I may not suffer poverty regarding ornaments, garments, fields, gardens, and houses. (51)
Being exceedingly pleased, Ambarīṣa gave him everything he desired;
in the auspicious field of Śālagrāma, a brāhmaṇa rejoices like a king. (52)
Then, when another period of time had elapsed, the Brahmin fell under the power of death;
in the waterless desert region, he became a Brahmarākṣasa due to his acceptance of royal gifts as well as his violation of the Brahmanical way of life. (93)
Because of possessing the latent impressions of sense objects, such as the latent impressions of wealth and so forth. //54//
In this world, trees scorched by a forest fire sprout again with the arrival of the rainy season;
but those burnt by accepting gifts from a king never sprout at all. //55//
He shall surely fall into the terrible Raurava hell;
this brahmin, having become a rakshasa and a preta, [will consume] his sons as well as his beloved wife. (56)
Coming again and again to the house, weeping, he said repeatedly:
"Please effect my deliverance; I am a Rākṣasa because of accepting this gift. (97)
"O you who offer the Mahānārāyaṇa-bali, may I be born!";
then his sons performed the Nārāyaṇa-bali for him. And by a voice from the sky, it was told to the sons: "Go to the Narmadā!"
At the confluence of the Kubjā, at that place of Bilvāmra, which is a sublime holy site (sutīrtha),
by bathing there, one indeed attains liberation from the state of a Brahmarākṣasa;
and through the destruction of sins and afflictions, one obtains the world of Brahmā.
Having heard this, the virtuous woman, accompanied by her sons, went to Bilvāmraka-sthala;
and the Rākṣasa also then departed invisibly with his family. (61)
Having arrived at the confluence of the Kubjā and Revā with great devotion, he bathed there, worshipped Śambhu, and duly honored Nārāyaṇa. ||62||
Then, while they remained absorbed in meditation, a beautiful celestial chariot arrived through the sky;
having ascended that brilliantly radiant vehicle, which was yoked with the attendants of Viṣṇu, [they departed]. (63)
At that very moment, having attained divine bodies, they then went to the world of Brahmā.
Thus is the destruction of sins through union with Kubjā on the banks of the Revā. (64)
Then the liberation of the householder Harikeśa occurred;
indeed, they all attained liberation, and so shall human beings do.
Then, the beloved wife of the Gandharva named Suvarṇa was the very beautiful daughter Hemagarbhā, who was renowned for her beauty. (66)
She was named Sukāmā and was married by the Giver of Wealth (Kubera). From her was born a son, King Ketumālin, in the city of the Vidyādharas. ||67||
And he had a wife named Śaśirekhā, who gave birth to two charming daughters, Rati and Prīti. (68)
He gave [her] to Kāmadeva preceded by the taking of hands in marriage;
and at that time, he also gave many other maidens in the form of female slaves. ||69||
And those maidens undertook a vow for the worship of Śiva: "Water and other offerings must be accepted [only after being consecrated]; never otherwise. (1.559.70)
Then once, they all went to bathe in the celestial river;
and the Gandharva Citrāṅgada, seeing them there, approached.
Having assumed a form at will and adorned with beauty corresponding to that form, he bathed in those waters; then those maidens were infatuated. ||72||
Together with Remuṣṭā, they forgot their worship of Hara.
Thus, when the day had passed, they remembered Śaṅkara in the evening. ||73||
Having eaten food and drunk water, they arrived for the purpose of worship;
but seeing them, Pārvatī became angry and cursed them that very evening:
"Having abandoned the rules of dharma and having failed to worship Śaṅkara and me..."

"Since they have eaten food with water [without first offering it], let them all indeed become afflicted by defects through my curse; let them become hunchbacked, and moreover, in the world of mortals, let them be dwarfs, deficient in limbs, and forest-dwelling Bhils. (75-76)
Thus cursed, they all descended to the world of mortals;
afflicted by the pain of the curse, they wandered through forests and wildernesses as female jackals. (77)
And once, Kubera, traveling through the sky by means of a divine vehicle along that path, saw them and was thus moved by their suffering. ||78||
He went quickly toward Pārvatī on Mount Kailāsa itself;
having bowed down, he wept, and then Satī asked, "How is it that you are here? (79)
"Tell me the reason why you weep here, so that I may provide a remedy. At that time, Kubera requested the removal of the curse upon his daughter. (1.559.80)
Having heard this, Pārvatī said: "Let all of you indeed go to the Narmadā;
having gone to the sacrificial cooking-ground at the hermitage, [visit] Bilvāmraka, that excellent holy ford. (81)
Then, by means of that curse, they will quickly be liberated from their state as hunchbacks born from the womb of Bhillas into the lineage of Gandharvas at that very confluence. ||82||
Having bathed and drunk the water there, one is liberated; that place is called Kubjātīrtha.
And that river which flows into the Narmadā is declared to be the Kubjānadī. ||83||
There, having bathed and been released from the curse, all those Gandharva women, seated in their vehicles, departed for their own abode in heaven once more, according to the word of Kubera. ||84||
Many have attained supreme perfection there through drinking water and other such means;
by merely hearing of it or chanting its name, they too are liberated from the bonds of worldly existence. //85//
Now, there is another sacred site there, consisting of the city of Maheśvara;
having reached the Raudra-Vāruṇa [site], it measures exactly one krośa. ||86||
Those who bathe here in this field of Śiva—be they beasts or even birds, and even insects, moths, and the like—go to the supreme heaven when they die. (87)
In ancient times, a great sacrifice was performed by the sage Sālaṅkāyana;
there was a king named Sālaṅkāyana who was the sovereign of Ayodhyā. (88)
When a drought had arisen, he questioned the great sage Mārkaṇḍeya regarding its cause, and Mārkaṇḍeya explained it to him. (89)
O lord of men, at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean within your kingdom, there were indeed those devoid of authority who were full of desire and longing for its fruits. (1.559.90)
Now, seven outcastes, with their feet upward and their hair hanging down, are indeed performing penance by drinking the smoke of grain-chaff. (91)
Sin arises from the asceticism of those who lack the right to perform it;
O King, ten parts of that sin reside in you, and from that comes this drought.
Therefore, O King, punish them and cause their ascetic practices to be obstructed!
Perform a great sacrifice at the sacred site of the Narmadā;
by that, rain will surely fall everywhere, there is no doubt.
You shall be liberated from the stain of sin, and you will attain both your kingdom and heaven.
Having heard this, the king commanded his servants to prepare the necessary materials so that the sacrifice might proceed within seven nights.
The king, the subjects, the ministers, and the princes [all gathered].
The seers, the sages, the brahmins, the queens, the gods, and the lords of the gods. ||96||
Invited there to the bank of the Revā, they arrived in numbers by the arbudas; and the king bestowed golden coins by the arbudas,
as well as gifts of ten million cows, elephants, horses, and other riches.
There were great pillars made of gold, and even the sacrificial ladles and other implements were of gold.
Various kinds of food—both solid and soft—as well as juices and other delicacies, unprecedented and endowed with divine flavors, existed on that ground;
there, Viṣṇu himself arrived in person.
Rudra, Agni himself, Brahmā, and their respective goddesses arrived;
the sacrifice was completed in its entirety, and the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) took place in the waters of the Narmadā.
They all performed [the rites], and a great rain fell upon the circle of the earth;
the gods and others were honored by the king, and the brahmins were fully gratified. ||101||
Such a great, auspicious, and sacrificial site on the Narmadā came into being;
meanwhile, the ascetics were obstructed from their penance by the king. (102)
And because those who were outcasts (caṇḍāla) performed penance, rain fell;
having thus completed the sacrifice, they each went to their own abodes. (103)
From that time on, that sacred ford was indeed called Yajñatīrtha;
thus did Śaṅkara speak to Pārvatī concerning the circle of sacred fords.
And I have declared to you, O Lakṣmī, that the water of the Narmadā destroys sin and suffering;
it grants liberation through both recitation and hearing. 105.

Thus ends the five hundred and fifty-ninth chapter, titled "The Miraculous Description of Śāṇḍilyākalpa-tīrtha, Rantideva-tīrtha, Harikeśa-tīrtha, Ambarīṣa-tīrtha, Bilvāmraka-tīrtha, Sālaṅkāyana-tīrtha, and Others," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
← Chapter 559: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga) Chapter 560 [Author: Chapter 561 →
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, Lakṣmī! I shall describe in brief those other holy places (tīrthas) which Śambhu recounted to Pārvatī.
In ancient times, at Camatkārapura on the bank of the Nāga river, there lived a sage named Aruṇi. Then, a certain hunter arrived there;
through the power of the sage's yoga, his mind became purified, and the hunter indeed performed penance.
He attained the status of a twice-born through his actions and was known by the name Satyatapas.
That Satyatapas, having been joined with a blessing by Durvāsas,
went to the confluence of the Kubjā and the Narmadā for the purpose of bathing.
Having bathed and drunk the water, he, endowed with merit, went to the Himalaya.
On the northern foot of the Snowy Mountain, on the bank of the Puṣpabhadrā river,
he sat upon a wonderful stone near a noble banyan tree.
There too, he performed austerities while worshipping Śrī Narāyaṇa.
Once, while indeed cutting sacrificial fuel with an axe,
he accidentally cut off one of his fingers— specifically, his left index finger.
The ash and dust fell away, revealing neither flesh nor blood;
by that act, his fingers were joined together as they had been before.
This wonder was witnessed by a single kinnara.
Then that Kinnara, traveling through the sky, went to heaven and related an unprecedented marvel in the assembly of Indra:
"Such a marvel as was shown by the ascetic has been seen by me. (1.560.10)
On the bank of the Puṣpabhadrā river dwells the ascetic Satyatapas;
his body is withered by penance, and there remains only ashes upon his frame.
Having heard that, Śukra immediately spoke to his younger brother Viṣṇu.
"Come, Viṣṇu, let us go to the supreme side of the Himavat.
There, indeed, an unprecedented marvel was told to me by a Kinnara.
Having been addressed thus, Viṣṇu then assumed the form of a boar.
The hunter and Indra likewise went toward that sage;
Viṣṇu, in the form of a boar, stood within the range of the sage's vision.
Having become visible, he became invisible once more, and then was seen again.
Then Indra, bow in hand and bearing sharp arrows,
arrived in the forest and spoke to this sage of true austerity:
"O Blessed One, have you seen here that broad and great boar?"
"O great sage, I shall kill him for the sake of supporting my servants.
Hearing this, the sage was startled and immediately reflected:
"If I show him that boar, he will surely kill it."
If not, his family will undoubtedly perish from hunger.
In either case, sin will surely accrue to me; there is no doubt.
For the boar has indeed come to my hermitage for refuge in order to protect its young.
For the hunter, having approached me and seen that I am a speaker of truth, [will think]:
"In false speech there is the fault of betraying trust; furthermore, there is the injury of one or the other, and in every way, the danger of being defiled. (1.560.20)
When things had come to this pass, what more could be said? Then, meditating upon Hari, the witness, he quickly regained his composure and steadiness for a moment;
and in that instant, a protective and sound intelligence arose within him.
The eye sees but does not speak; the tongue speaks but does not see. One sees, while another speaks; there is no single common function for the two.
The seer is mute, and the speaker is blind—who, then, would provide the answer? Tell me!
Having heard this, Indra and Viṣṇu were greatly pleased in that moment;
revealing their true forms, they spoke these words:
"Tell us what pleases you, and choose one supreme boon from us here. (24–25)
Having heard that, Satyatapas, his heart filled with joy, said:
"There is no other boon on earth for me greater than the sight of Viṣṇu;
by that alone my purpose is fulfilled, for the sight of you is difficult to obtain."
Nevertheless, those who bathe here in the waters of the Puṣpabhadrā near the banyan tree, and having meditated upon and remembered Hari, should dwell there for one month—
may their sins be destroyed, and may you grant them liberation as well. (27–28)
Having said "So be it," those two gods granted him that boon;
and while they remained stationed in their celestial chariot upon the path of the sky,
his preceptor Āruṇi arrived and was seen by him.

Then Durvāsas arrived, for he had been summoned by Satya’s truthfulness. Having recognized that his disciple was one who had accomplished his purpose through truthful austerity, and seeing him standing before him, perfected by penance and with his sins burnt away, [Satya honored him].
Āruṇi said: "You have attained perfection; you have become Brahman in every respect.
Now, the time for your liberation is considered to have arrived along with the Self.
Arise, my son, and come with me upon the celestial chariot."
"Accompanied by Nārāyaṇa, Indra, and Durvāsas,
we shall go to the supreme and auspicious Nārmada tīrtha, Kubjāmraka. Having spoken thus, the three— Cāruṇi, Ātreya, and Satyatapas— [set out].
Having meditated upon the god Nārāyaṇa, they ascended a beautiful celestial chariot;
and by the desire of his devotees, Nārāyaṇa and Indra likewise [ascended]. Having reached the sacrificial holy ford (yājñīya-tīrtha) and bathed there, they then went to heaven.
Then Satyatapas attained liberation and reached the supreme state;
others who were long-lived departed for their respective abodes,
while Durvāsas and the rest went to Kailāsa and other eternal realms.
Now I shall proclaim another sacred ford (tīrtha) in the waters of the Narmadā;
for there shines the sacred ford known as Maṇḍapeśvara.
Having bathed there and cast off the body, one becomes a king in the city of the Vidyādharas.
It shall indeed last for ten thousand years; of this there is no doubt.
(39) The two mind-born sons of Brahmā, Bādarāyaṇa and Śākaṭa, were dwelling in the forest; and King Ajāpāla went to them at one time. (40)
Having bowed down, the lord of Avadha asked the sages sweetly:
"For the sake of the deliverance of my ancestors, I must indeed give gifts here.
Which sages will accept them? Let them come into my presence."
Then, with the exception of Bādarāyaṇa and Śākaṭa,
the others accepted the gifts bestowed by the king;
there were ten thousand elephants adorned with bells and ornaments.
The king gave wealth to the brahmins and likewise constructed monasteries made of gold;
he performed three circumambulations of Mount Kalañjara,
and having paid homage to all the sages, he departed toward his own city.
When that protector of the earth had departed, the sages were deluded by wealth;
having attained supreme happiness through the king’s riches,
those passionate ones fell from their asceticism and became attached to sensual enjoyment.
And having died through the exhaustion of their merit— except for Bādara and Śākaṭa—
the acceptance of gifts from a king is terrible, fierce, sinful, and shrouded in fear; indeed,
who would be capable of enduring it, except for one whose nature is that of Brahman?
Then those brahmins, having become devoted to lust and anger, died;
they entered the womb of dogs and were born as eaters of impure things.
Furthermore, because of their residence among brahmins who were intent on accepting gifts, [they suffered this fate].
Due to the fault of their association, Bādara and Śākaṭa were born with the faces of dogs;
seeing their dog-like countenances, the two of them reflected:
"Indeed, through the fault of that association, sin has attached itself to us from accepting gifts from the king."
Having reflected thus, the two of them went truthfully to the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin).
Having saluted him, they, with distorted faces, related the account;
and having heard it, Brahmā declared that expiation was indeed in the waters of the Narmadā.
"Through bathing, purification shall come; let them go to Maṇḍapeśvara.
Having heard the words of the Grandfather (Brahmā), Bādarāyaṇa and Śākaṭa then set out for the Narmadā together with the dogs and the sages.

Having bathed there and drunk the water, those sinless ones, freed from all evil, went to heaven by means of divine vehicles; such is that most excellent holy place (tīrtha). By merely hearing of it or reciting its name, one obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice (aśvamedha).
Thence one should go to the supreme holy site known as Śvetakiṃśuka;
there, at the confluence of the Narmadā and the Dantivanikā, one should perform an ablution.
Then, one should visit the auspicious holy site called Kapiśilā.
Thereafter, one should go to the Śaśabindu-Narmadā confluence, a sacred ford (tīrtha).
After that, one should go to Rājatīrtha, which was frequented by Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa.
In ancient times, having crossed the Narmadā, Rāma went into the interior of the forest.
From there, one should go to the most auspicious Daśāśvamedha Tīrtha;
from there, one should go to Pipīlikoddhāra Tīrtha, which bestows liberation;
and from there, one should go to Vandhyārevāsamāyoga, which grants prosperity.
One should then go to Śuklatīrtha, the excellent bestower of heaven and liberation.
By bathing at Rāsabhīnarmadābheda, liberation becomes certain.
In a former age, the royal sage Havirdhāna was capable [of great feats].

Ātreyi had a son named Harikeśa, and she also had a daughter named Sutejā, who was the daughter of Agni. Then, according to the rites of marriage, that girl named Sutejā was given in marriage to Havirdhāna.
The royal sage Havirdhāna, having learned of her [impending] season, went to her.
Then once, a youth named Harikeśaka arrived there;
he too, out of desire, took hold of her hand.
In the hall of the Agnihotra, Harikeśa took her by the power of his desire; he sported with her according to his wish.
And Havidhāna beheld the couple engaged in sexual union.
For the Brahmin was indeed inviolable, and his wife was likewise inviolable, since she belonged to the female sex. Having reflected thus, Havirdhāna spoke slowly to the Brahmin: (66–67)
Having approached his mother, the wife of his teacher, a sister, or likewise a daughter, a man should enter the fire; thereby he becomes pure.
Having approached his teacher or the son of his teacher, a woman should enter the funeral pyre.

"Since you two are not capable of doing this, O Brahmin, you shall become a donkey; and she, Sutejā, shall become a female donkey. Thus, for a hundred years, they were born as those two donkeys in the forest."
Once, those two, remembering their past births, went to the hermitage of Agastya and asked about a penance and a vow for the sake of ending the curse.
Agastya said, "Both of you must indeed go toward Havirdhāna."
Then they both went with reverence to the Havirdhāna hermitage;
they begged for forgiveness and bowed at his feet. And Havirdhāna said to them, "Go indeed to the bank of the Narmadā."
"Having bathed and drunk her water, with your sins destroyed by that asceticism,
you two shall attain supreme liberation, which is the fruit of human birth.
Thus addressed, they went to the Narmadā and performed penance.
Upon purification, having abandoned their birth as donkeys, those two became divine;
mounted upon a celestial vehicle and adorned with every ornament,
they went to heaven and dwelt there for seventy yugas.
Then, at the end, those two went to the glorious abode of Nārāyaṇa.
There is the sacred ford (tīrtha) of Harikeśa, which possesses great splendor and bestows liberation;
there also is the Liṅga of Havirdhāneśvara at the confluence of the Revā and the Gardabhī.
The supreme merit that destroys sin exists through its very sight.
From there, one should go to the Karamarda Tīrtha, which bestows the highest merit;
it was there that King Kuśadhvaja arrived at the hermitage of Maitreya.
On the beautiful bank of the Narmadā, the king performed a śrāddha ceremony with devotion;
there he gave ten lakhs of cows as gifts—
golden-hued, adorned with bells and ornaments, and accompanied by their calves.
Having fed those brahmins at the śrāddha, the best of kings, the monarch, departed for his own home; meanwhile, the brahmins remained there.
Once, in the forest, some rākṣasas arrived to devour those cows.
The cows entered the enclosure; some then went to heaven.
Thereupon, the Rākṣasas rushed there to devour the Brahmins.
The Brahmins then remembered Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person.
[He saw] Lakṣmīpati, Prabhānātha, Pārvatīśa, Narāyaṇa,
Māṇikīśa, Haṃseśa, and Mañjuleśa, abiding within his heart.
At that moment, Viṣṇu arrived, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace.
With his discus and the *karamarda* fruit, he destroyed the Rākṣasas;
he protected the Brāhmaṇas, and the cows that had come there returned once more.
Śambhu, as Karamardeśvara, emerged from the discus of Viṣṇu.

The Karamardaśvara Tīrtha is considered a supreme place that provides protection. (87) Then, after some time, Viṣṇu, having caused the Brahmins and the cows to ascend his celestial chariot, led them to Vaikuṇṭha, the abode of liberation. (88)
"Those who bathe there go to heaven after death and are not subject to rebirth;
by merely hearing or reciting [this], one obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows.
Thus did Śambhu speak to Pārvatī, O Lakṣmī, and he has spoken it before you as well.
"Thus has been proclaimed the holy pilgrimage site of the Discus of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.

(1.560.90) Thus ends the five hundred and sixtieth chapter, titled "The Narrative Account of History," including the liberation of Satyatapas—the disciple of Āruṇi—in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga in the *Śrī Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*; the Maṇḍapeśvara Tīrtha; the removal of the dog-like deformity from Bādarāyaṇa and Śākaṭāyana; the confluence of the Narmadā and Dantivanikā; the account of the she-donkey at the Narmadā Tīrtha; and the Karamarda Tīrtha. (Chapter 560)

Chapter 562 →
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī! Śaṅkara spoke of a sacred ford (tīrtha) to Pārvatī;
O sinless one, I shall now describe to you that highly renowned Jvāleśvara.
Then Śaṅkara struck Tripura—the son of Bali—and Bāṇa with his arrow.
Thereupon, the weapon, enveloped in garlands of flames, fell;
as it struck the earth, its blaze was then extinguished.
Indeed, that is declared to be Jvāleśvara, the destroyer of sinful demons.
(3) Now, the supreme holy site of Revācarusaṅga shines forth.
In ancient times, there was a beautiful city in the sacred field of Naimiṣāraṇya. (4)
Beyond this is the city named Hiraṇyavegā, which is filled with golden seven-storied mansions and possesses a river of the same name; and there,
a king named Hiraṇyabāhu indeed performed a sacrifice.
In Naimiṣa, he asked all the sages for a sacrificial ground.
They, however, said: "Puṣkara is a great field suitable for sacrifice;
whatever is offered or sacrificed there becomes ten million times more meritorious."
The king said, "Let my auspicious sacrifice be performed at Puṣkara.
Thereupon, the royal sage, having gathered all the necessary materials, went to Puṣkara.
He brought ten million cows and one million five hundred thousand horses.
Fifty-two thousand lordly elephants and ten thousand chariots;
gems, rubies, jewels, garments, and ornaments—
their number was indeed incalculable, like the wealth of Kubera.
Edibles, foods, and drinks were served day and night;
thus the sacrifice was commenced, wherein the Creator of the Universe was invited.
Śukra was also invited at that time, for no other gods were summoned by the brahmins.
What need is there for any other [deities]? By these two alone, everything is fully honored.
Neither Viṣṇu, nor the Ādityas, nor the Moon, nor Varuṇa;
neither Rudra, nor the Maruts, nor others belonging to the quarters, nor the world-protectors—[none of these are needed].
When the sacrifice had commenced, the asuras— thorns to the gods, intent on seeking out flaws in the rite— arrived to create obstacles.
All the dānavas, daityas, bhūtas, vetālas, and rākṣasas [gathered there].
They drank the Soma, the limb of sacrifice, and they devoured the Brahmins.
The sacrificial fire was extinguished, the sacrificial post destroyed, and the pavilion demolished.
Seeing that Brahmā, Śakra, and the deities had suddenly perished, [they acted]. (15–16)
Then, having vanished from that place which was filled with obstacles, Hiraṇyabāhu became enraged toward the Brāhmaṇas:
"The gods have not been invited to the sacrifice; indeed, these Brāhmaṇas are merely beggars! (17)
They fled from my sacrifice, for they were intent only on their own interests.
Then the Daityas, taking up the sacrificial materials, departed for their homes;
the king did not reflect, thinking, "This is no time for my manly prowess."
When the assembly of gods and others is enraged, there is neither anger nor battle; alone, having mounted my horse with my wife,
I go to that place where neither the Ādityas, nor Viṣṇu, nor Rudra, nor the Moon exists.
Likewise, how can the sacrifice be successfully accomplished by other guardians of the quarters?
(21) The Brahmins were greedy and desired everything; they were not protectors, but rather became destroyers, rooted in greed and lacking in capability. (22)
"If truth exists for me, let the Brahma-rākṣasas become senseless in a thorny, waterless place!
Having heard the curse, the king was indeed cursed from afar by the Brahmins.
"You are a protector of the sacrifice and the lowest of Kṣatriyas!
Become indeed a donkey, a bringer of curses upon the sinless Brāhmaṇas!
For twelve years in the forest, they became donkey-demons.
Then, after some time had passed in the forest, the divine sage, the seer Nārada, arrived; he saw them as well as Khara and the other Rākṣasas.
Khara bowed to the divine sage and asked him the means for liberation.
Then Nārada spoke regarding the excellent water of the Narmadā:
"By bathing at the confluence of the Revā and the Carukā, you shall attain liberation;
even Brāhmaṇas and Rākṣasas, having bathed there, shall go to salvation. (27–28)
Thus addressed, they went to the Revā at the confluence of the Revā and Caruka;
having bathed there due to the contact with the waters of the Narmadā, they all attained liberation.
Mounted upon the Brahma-vehicle and being praised by bards, they departed.
They went to the divine world of Brahmā through contact with the waters of the Narmadā.
Where Viṣṇu, Rudra, Sūrya, and likewise Nārāyaṇa reside,
there is prosperity, victory, as well as eternal enjoyment and liberation.
In whom devotion toward the guru exists— just as toward the Lord—
the desires of such a person are fulfilled by the power of Hari, who is one with the guru,
through hearing, chanting, remembering, and serving him.
By means of either salutation or retention [of the name], one is liberated from the bondage of worldly existence.
(33) Now, the most excellent sacred site is called Amarakaṇṭaka;
from that point onward, the entire best of mountains is remembered as supremely meritorious. (34)
Indeed, as far as the great river Revā flows under four names,
to the north lies the great, purifying Yajñaparvata.
In ancient times, the Sautrāmaṇi sacrifice was performed there by Svayambhū himself.
In that very place, Maghavan formerly performed the horse sacrifice;
then Dadhīci and the gods also performed great sacrifices in that same spot.
[It extends] as far as the confluence of the river and as far as the Sacrificial Mountain.
Indeed, the entire Rajah Sarva is pure and bestows liberation,
where in ancient times the sage Suparṇa, the son of Brahmā,
an expert in all the scriptures, resided at the confluence.
Puruhūtā was his wife, a lawful spouse devoted to her husband.
Once, having gratified her own husband, she spoke these words:
"O great sage, please approach me at the proper time when I am in my season."
"May he be born as a son to me, one who purifies my entire lineage.
Through a son, one conquers the worlds; the ancestors and the gods are satisfied.
There is no destination for one who is sonless; therefore, I have begotten a son. (41)
Then the Brāhmaṇa said: "O beloved, this is the Amāvāsyā day, which must be avoided!
No attachment should be formed here, for it causes distress even to the ancestors.
For a thousand divine years, I have performed difficult austerities."
"O beloved, I shall strive for you to obtain a child so that such a destruction does not occur on another day; do not grieve.
Having been addressed thus, his wife then spoke to the sage Suparṇaka.

Behold here at the Narmadā-tīrtha, how by the mere act of bathing, this Cāṇḍāla was liberated from sin and ascended to heaven in a celestial chariot. Indeed, he had performed no austerities, offered no oblations, recited no prayers, nor observed the restraints. (45–46)
He did not know the religious observances (*niyama*), yet he went to heaven;
he performed no vows (*vrata*) at all, nor did he observe the rules regarding menstruation (*rājasvalya*);
he did not perform the fasts of the vow days, yet he went to heaven.

O Sage, the majesty of this sacred ford (tīrtha) is indeed supreme and of such a nature that by merely bathing here, the destruction of all sins occurs in every respect. Therefore, O ocean of mercy, enjoy yourself here and accept me! 48–49.
In certain circumstances, the word of a wife must be honored so that dharma is not violated—
specifically when a wife has bathed after her menses and her desire for offspring is intense;
in such a case, the wife's word must certainly be obeyed.
Then, by means of the ritual offering during the fertile period (*ṛtudāna*), a son will certainly be born.
On that occasion, one must abandon religious observances (*vrata*), as well as fast days (*parvan*) and festivals (*utsava*).
For at a time ruined by a lack of enthusiasm, the embryo does not grant offspring.
When a thousand years had passed there without any attachment,
in such a place, dharma alone prevailed, and nothing else— not the words of a beloved,
nor censure, nor oppression, nor any fault was found there. (53)
In a great forest fire, how insignificant is the grass and such;
in oceans of nectar, how insignificant is a blade of poisonous grass;
at the hour of the midday sun, how insignificant is the darkness within a house. (54–55)
Indeed, how much [merit] is there in fasting for a day on the mountain of Puṇyaparvata?
Therefore, O Lord, worship me this very day with a state of intense love;
whatever sin might arise from non-observance, no merit equal to that exists.
Thus addressed, her husband there took his wife according to his desire.
He bestowed the embryo upon his son, and that son was born resembling the sun.
And as for those ancestors who, having eaten at the *amā-śrāddha*, have attained satisfaction—
Having arrived at night, they then said with a laugh:
"Today, quickly perform the expiation for the bestowal of the fetus.
Having bathed again in the Narmadā, perform the fire-oblation and the recitation once more. (59)

We are satisfied and delighted for the sake of the continuity of our lineage. Furthermore, you were requested by your wife and took that water from the Narmadā—which is purifying and destructive of sins—for the sake of a son. (1.561.60–61)
The sin arising from killing a Brahmin, killing a child, or murdering an elder or a woman;
the sin born of the failure of vows and the like, as well as that produced by sexual misconduct and other such acts—
by merely bathing in the Revā, it is destroyed without a doubt.
Having spoken thus, his ancestors departed with delighted minds;
they, who had been slain by the sighs of childlessness, were restored to life by the embryo.
Then, after some time, two *suparṇas* arrived there along with their wives.
Standing in a radiant celestial chariot, he went to the supreme city of Brahmā;
there, at the most excellent confluence, Suparṇa attained both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Then, indeed, to the west of the Nīlagangā and to the north of the Narmadā—
There is a most beautiful holy site named Vyatīpāteśvara;
there is also Sāvitrīkuṇḍa, where Sāvitrī performed her ascetic penance. King Indradyumna became desirous of performing a sacrifice.
Then he questioned the great sages dwelling in Dharmāraṇya;
Mārkaṇḍeya and the others told him of the supreme sacred field on the Narmadā.
The king then proclaimed to his subjects that they should go to the Revā.
And there were three hundred thousand cows with their calves, yielding milk;
and one hundred and twenty-five thousand horses with dark ears;
and also ten thousand elephants adorned with ornaments of bells.
Four thousand vehicles that travel at will,
a hundred thousand camels, and a hundred thousand gems and rubies;
garments purified by fire and vessels made of gold.
Having gathered various kinds of foods, edibles, and diverse drinks,
as well as a hundred thousand laborers, sesame seeds, *darbha* grass,
and other items, the king, together with the brahmins, ascended a celestial chariot.
Filled with supreme joy, accompanied by his inner apartments and retinue,
the king went to Dharmāraṇya, where that river Narmadā flows;
there stands a delightful mountain for pilgrimage, adorned with cat's-eye gems.
Likewise, Śambhu, possessing great luster, shines forth as Oṃkāreśa.
In the vicinity of Oṃkāra, the Revā-koṭi-tīrtha shines;
whatever is given, offered in sacrifice, performed, or austerity practiced here becomes indeed infinite.
At all times and in all undertakings, the Narmadā bestows ten million-fold merit.
Within a radius of thirty yojanas, that king caused sacrificial posts, pavilions,
and various types of ritual pits to be constructed.
Resounding with the roar of the Vedas, [the sounds] touched both heaven and earth.
The fire became smokeless and accepted the offerings of clarified butter;
it likewise summoned Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śaṅkara.
There are the eleven Rudras, as well as the twelve Ādityas;
likewise the Viśvedevas, the Sādhyas, the Maruts, and the Vasus.
There are the world-protectors, the oceans, the rivers, the mountains, and the excellent trees.
The guardians of the quarters, the protectors of beings, the sacred fords, and likewise the ancestors;
the Siddhas, Kinnaras, Gandharvas, Nāgas, Rākṣasas, Guhyakas, Vidyādharas, and Cāraṇas— all these refreshed themselves there at the festival of the sacrifice.
Rivers carrying clarified butter and milk arose, with curds and milk-rice for their mud;
there were drinking waters and flavorful drinks everywhere.
There were various kinds of foods and edibles, as well as desirable vehicles and the like.
The gods, the sages, and the fourfold assembly of living beings were satisfied.
Thus the sacrifice was completed with its concluding bath (*avabhṛtha*) in the waters of the Narmadā;
there was satisfaction from the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) for all who partook in the sacrifice.
King Oṃkāreśa himself worshipped [the deity] with gold and jewels,
with gems such as *maṇi*, *māṇikya*, and diamonds, and with camphor, agallochum, and sandalwood;
with various fragrant flowers, banners, umbrellas, and celestial chariots.
Having honored Hara and Hari with yak-tail whisks and fans, he praised them both, saying:
"Obeisance again and again to you, O *oṃkāra*, the bestower of liberation.
Then, Rudra himself appeared in personified form in his presence.
He said, "Choose a boon," and Indradyumna replied to him:
"Make your residence always in the valley on the mountain of sacrifice;
there, indeed, shall be the liberation of even the dead, even of sinners. (89)
Whoever should encircle a mountain with a single thread at its peak,
by him the entire earth, including its mountains, forests, and groves, has been encircled. By that merit, his liberation here shall lead to the state of Brahman.
"So be it," Hara said, and vanished right there.
Then Brahmā spoke to the king for the purpose of granting him a boon.
The king replied, "O Brahman, please assume the form of a Liṅga here."
Having said, "So be it," Brahmā vanished from that place.
The king, having prostrated himself with all eight limbs, praised Viṣṇu— Keśava, Mādhava, Viṣṇu, Govinda, and Madhusūdana.
Padmanābha, Hṛṣīkeśa, Śrīdhara, Trivikrama, Dāmodara, Vāsudeva, Śrīhari, the son of Kambharā,
Gopālabāla, Rādheśa, Śrīśa, and the Lord Ramēśvara.
I bow down to the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama;
to Mañjuleśa, Pārvatīśa, Prabheśa, and Māṇikīpati; to Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa and Haṃsājayanātha. (96–97)
I bow down to the Lord of the worlds, the Lord of the universe, the Lord of Śrī, who is adorned with the conch, discus, mace, Śārṅga bow, and forest garland.
O Lord of the Imperishable, Lord of the Liberated, Lord of Lalitā, homage be to You!
O Lord of incarnations, O Lord of gods, O Lord of manifestations, salutations be unto you!
O Lord of lords, O Lord of Māyā, O Lord of Durgā, O Master of the Ganges,
O Lord of the individual soul, O Lord of infinite sacrifices, O Sovereign of sacrifice, salutations be unto you!
Salutations to you, whose self is the Vedas, the beloved, and the son of Dharma;
salutations be to you who uphold the vow of Brahman and are beyond the three qualities (guṇas).
Salutations to you, the Lord of Prakṛti, the peaceful one, who dwells in Vaikuṇṭha.
Salutations to You who assume the forms of Nṛsiṃha, Matsya, Vārāha, and Kūrma;
salutations to You who wear the guise of a holy ascetic and are the primordial cause; salutations to You who possess a thousand heads and are the Puruṣa to be known.
Salutations to You who assumed a physical form for the sake of subduing the asuras;
salutations to You who are Hiraṇyagarbha and whose abode is immortality. Salutations to You, Kṛṣṇa, the inner self who is the womb of all.

Salutations to You, the creator, the protector, and the destroyer, who takes the form of all that is to be accomplished. Salutations to You, whose form is all the guardians of the directions, whose self is the protector of the worlds.
Salutations to You, the triple-deity, whose very nature is half-female.
Salutations to You, the treasury of infinite bliss, the abode of Brahman;
salutations again and again to You, the bestower of the fruits of karma, who dwells within all.
Salutations to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Self, who made His residence in Saurāṣṭra.
O beloved of the ten million gopīs, salutations again and again to You, the bestower of happiness.

(108) Salutations to You, the splendor of the Brahmins; salutations to You, who are the very form of the valor of the Kṣatriyas; salutations to You, who are the embodiment of the prosperity of the Vaiśyas, and the refuge for all. (109)
Salutations to you, whose nature is devotion to one’s husband, the bull among wives;
salutations to you, O Kṛṣṇa, who are eternally chaste and the bestower of liberation. Salutations to you, who always abide among the virtuous and appear in the form of a child.
Salutations, repeated salutations, to you who fulfill the desires of the minds of your devotees.
Salutations to you, the giver of knowledge, the giver of will, and the giver of effort; to the giver of action, the giver of fruit, the enjoyer, and that which is to be enjoyed. 111–112.
Salutations to You, the Supreme Lord, the illuminator, and the one who dwells within all living beings;
salutations to You, the abode of all embodied souls, who are worthy of [divine] power.
Salutations to You, the repository of inconceivable qualities, and to You whose body is divine.
Salutations to you, the creator of boundless sovereignty; salutations to you in your visible form.
Salutations to you whose form is invisible, and to you who are eternal knowledge.
Salutations to you who are the essential nature of all principles, and to you who are the pavilion.
Salutations to you who have assumed the form of the five fires and who abide in your vow;
salutations to you, the bestower of merit, the Great Lord, and the Sovereign of all.
Salutations to you, the destroyer of all suffering, who takes the form of fire.
Salutations be to You, the sacrificial vessel consisting of the *sruk*, *sruva*, and other implements; salutations to You.
(1.17) Salutations to You, the Lord of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), and salutations to You as the blessing (*āśīrvāda*).
Salutations to You, who are satisfaction, whose form is peace, and whose form is the essence of taste (*rasa*). (1.18)
Salutations to you who dwell within all the senses, whose desires are ever-true;
salutations to you who are the very nature of the sun and other luminaries, and who take the form of the bull.
Salutations to you, the worthy recipient of prostrations and the vessel for all offerings.
"By your grace, O ocean of compassion, the success of my sacrifice has been achieved.
O Viṣṇu, take my hand, as a bridegroom takes the hand of his bride.
Grant me residence at your feet; I choose nothing else, O Keśava! (1.561.120–121)
Having heard that supreme hymn of praise, Viṣṇu was pleased and said to the king:
"Choose a boon, O King, choose a boon—whatever dwells in your heart.
I shall grant it to you, without a doubt; the success of your sacrifice shall be achieved."
Then Indradyumna said:
"O Kṛṣṇa, always make your residence on the Vaidūrya mountain in the presence of Oṃkāranātha,
so that liberation may come to those who have come there through the worship of you."
Through seeing you, through saluting you, through serving you, and through immersing themselves in you—
even by the relinquishing of their lives— embodied beings shall attain your state.
By the offering of food to the ancestors, may they indeed go to your Vaiṣṇava abode.
"May even insects, moths, and the like attain the supreme goal here," [said the Lord].
"So be it," Hari replied, and He descended there.
All sacred fords (tīrthas) also reside within the lotus feet of Nārāyaṇa.
And they descended to the sacred fords on the Narmadā, the land of sacrifice;
indeed, at the confluence of the Nīlagaṅgā, there are those that grant liberation.
The king praised the Revā: "Become possessed of seven streams!"

Thus she prayed; and so the seven-streamed Revā became the bestower of liberation, containing within her all sacred fords (tīrthas). Whatever gift is given, oblation offered, recitation performed, or austerity practiced here shall become inexhaustible.
Having thus performed the sacrifice, Indradyumna indeed paid homage to Viṣṇu, the gods, and Oṃkāra, and went home. The gods and others,
as well as the humans and others, being satisfied by the sacrifice, departed for their homes.
By hearing and chanting this, one obtains the fruit of a thousand cows.
Śaṅkara said to Pārvatī: "O beloved! Liberation shall be attained here.
O Lakṣmī! This supreme holy place (tīrtha), which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, has been described by me to you."

Thus ends the five hundred and sixty-first chapter, titled "The Description of Jāleśvara Tīrtha, the Liberation of King Hiraṇyabāhu from the State of Being a Donkey, Revā-Caruka-Sambheda Tīrtha, Amarakaṇṭaka Tīrtha, Yajñaparvata, the Story of Suparṇa, Oṃkāra Tīrtha, and so forth," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 562 *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā* — Section 1 (Continuity of the Kṛta Yuga) — Chapter 562.
[The Author: Chapter 563.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī! To the sin-destroying narrative proclaimed by Śambhu.
I shall relate that purifying account to Pārvatī on Mount Ṛkṣaka.
There was a king named Vasudāna, a sovereign ruler of the entire earth;
he worshipped Mādhava with a thousand horse-sacrifices.
All those subjects lived for more than one hundred and twenty-five thousand years.
At that time, there were indeed deceitful Daityas on the southern bank of the Revā:
Ketumālin, Suketu, Sumukha, and Dundubhi.
They became creators of obstacles to dharma and disruptors of sacrifices.
No one at Amarakaṇṭaka desired to perform sacrifices.
Then the mighty king went to the Revā river to perform a sacrifice.
Accompanied by learned Brahmins and officiating priests who had mastered the Vedas,
he gave five hundred thousand cows with their calves that yielded milk,
as well as one hundred and fifty thousand horses and ten thousand elephants.
Taking with him gems, rubies, and jewels, as well as gold, silver, and wealth;
various kinds of food and edibles, clarified butter, rice, and sesame seeds; and having brought together pavilions and sacrificial posts, that lord of the earth [set out]. (7–8)
Having gone there, he purified the ground and constructed pavilions;
he established the altars, the sacrificial pits, and the sacred fire.
He offered clarified butter and oblations, and thus gratified Mādhava.
He gratified the gods, the ancestors, the seers, and the learned brahmins with food offerings;
he satisfied living beings with gifts such as sacrificial fees, and even provided for those who subsist on gleaned grains and grass.
At that time, a host of asuras arrived there for the purpose of creating obstacles.
Struck and put to flight by the king with the discharge of divine weapons, that [demon] was destroyed;
thus the Vasudānaka sacrifice proceeded without obstacle.
The earth, fashioned of gold, was moistened by the waters of the final purificatory bath (āvabhṛthya).
Those beasts and birds that had been mired in the mud became golden-colored there through the power of merit.
Simultaneously, with streams of water, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara [emerged].
Having been worshipped, that water merged together into the form of a spring;
likewise, the bathing water of all the gods was prepared by the sages.
At that time, its flow also joined with that spring there.
There, streams of cow urine from hundreds of thousands of cows converged;
there were cascades of the remnants of various foods and drinks, as well as torrents of milk and clarified butter produced as the fruit of sacrificial offerings. (16–17)
These currents, consisting of rivers, have merged into the sacrificial basin.
This is indeed the river named Kapilā, with its wondrous waters, which purifies all;
this very place where she joins the Narmadā is the region known as Rudrāvarta.

Having beheld those waters of variegated beauty, that river was given the name "Kapilā" by the celestial sages and seers, following the satisfaction of Dakṣa. And they indeed granted a boon to the king for those who bathe at the confluence of the Kapilā.
They shall bathe in the Narmadā and behold Maheśvara and Viṣṇu Nārāyaṇa; through divine means, they shall go to the supreme state.
Even insects and other such creatures who die here indeed shall attain that same goal.
Having thus granted this supreme boon, they all departed for their own abodes.
Vasudāna, having performed the sacrifice, returned to Avadhyā.
By hearing and chanting [the glory] of this, one is liberated from the bondage of worldly existence.
Then there was a very powerful king named Viśravas in Mathurā;
for he was the son of a daughter of Dakṣa born of Arundhatī.
On the occasion of a pilgrimage to holy places, he went to Amarakaṇṭaka.
When the king, having bathed, was established in meditation on the bank of the Narmadā,
he then beheld at midday two suns from the solar disc in the western direction, gone toward the eastern quarter and two toward the southern quarter. (25–26)
Two [suns] were below in Pātāla and likewise two fierce-formed suns were above;
then the Saṃvartaka fire blazed in the sky,
and terrible, harsh winds blew, causing great agitation.
Then, a conflagration of the quarters, an earthquake, and terrible falls of meteors occurred upon the earth;
the king awoke from his meditation,
and afflicted by thirst and tormented by the burning heat, he went to the Narmadā to drink water.
As he went along, however, not even a little water was to be found;
the current had vanished, and he could find no water anywhere.
He thought to himself, "Without water, my death today is certain."
At that time, he indeed remembered the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa;
he then remembered Oṃkāranātha and beheld the blossoming,
fruit-bearing, and well-branched Kalpa tree, rich with the beauty of its leaves.
Seeing that and obtaining the cool shade, the king became steady; his body became as if immortal, and his thirst and fever subsided. Then, with hope for life restored, the king looked around.
He saw a divine man lying in the shade, blazing with splendor. Four jars full of water stood at his side.
Having bowed down to him, the king stood there and beheld him in the form of Viṣṇu.
He saw a second man, the three-eyed Śiva, asleep;
at that moment, the king also saw other gods and sages.
Then he saw a woman, agitated and drenched in blood.
With her hair disheveled and having placed the child upon her hip, she said to the king:
"O King, drink my breast-milk and abandon your thirst.
I am the goddess Earth; this child is the unborn creator of the universe."
This maiden Narmadā remains here; these jars are the oceans.
This banyan tree is the Kalpa-tree, and we all shall remain steadfast for a long time.
Imperishable and abiding through every kalpa, drink this water with reverence.
Having spoken thus, she vanished; the king beheld the Narmadā.
He drank her water, which was full of liquid, and attained satisfaction.
Having established a sacred bathing place (tīrtha), Viśravas returned once more to his own city, Mathurā.
Such an eternal sacred site exists in the waters of the Narmadā;
by hearing of it and by chanting its praises, one is liberated from the bondage of worldly existence.
It is located on the southern bank of the Narmadā and to the west of the Kapilā.
There lies the beautiful city of Viṣṇu, a holy site that bestows liberation.
Previously, the Daityas were destroyed there by Viṣṇu;
thereafter, having arrived at that place, the auspicious and lovely city was constructed by Viṣṇu.
To the west, however, lies the Kapilā, where the Nīlagangā is found.
Between them are Cakratīrtha, Vāmana, and Yugandhara;
there is also the sacred ford named Sudarśana, known as Daityasūdana.
The Viṣṇvāvarta, the Śivāvarta, and likewise the Lakṣmyāvarta—
by bathing and giving gifts there, one indeed enjoys infinite fruit.
That sacred field of Viṣṇu is proclaimed to be one krośa in extent.
There, the ancestors are satisfied by the faithful and attain liberation;
whatever chanting or austerity is performed there all becomes inexhaustible.
The twelfth lunar day in the month of Śravaṇa is meritorious, and the eighth lunar day under the asterism Rohiṇī is auspicious.
Having fasted there, a devoted person is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
Furthermore, whatever person performs a fast during either the month of Kārtika or Vaiśākha,
that person shall obtain the fruit of ten crore fasts.
A woman who is devoted to her husband and indeed devoted to Nārāyaṇa should worship Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa there. To her,
the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa grants eternal good fortune in heaven.

In that abode, he bestows upon you, filled with bliss, a fortune equal to that of Lakṣmī herself. (52) At this sacred ford, Dharmarāja, assuming a body of righteous splendor, comes to offer respectful oblations out of reverence for those who frequent the holy sites. (53)
Standing before the devoted wives, he bows at their feet;
having beheld the realm of Viṣṇu, he then returns.
Then the ascetics saw Dharmarāja returning along with Satyavān.
The sages, the mind-born sons of Brahmā, indeed asked:
"For what reason has he himself departed while practicing the path of dharma?
And Dharmarāja, smiling, spoke this most wonderful thing to them.
"Indeed, because of that [merit], the splendor of women devoted to their husbands and the splendor of those who fast for a month exists as something distinct from that of the gods;
and I myself have come here for the purpose of seeing them, while my servants were unable [to do so]."
And because I could not remain in their presence, I departed from there.
Thus, O Queen of the Gods, the purifying Nārāyaṇasthala, which always bestows liberation, exists there; it grants liberation even by being heard of.
The river Carukā flows forth, extending from the hermitage of Śākalya on Mount Yajña all the way to the bank of the Narmadā.
There lies the Dāruvana forest, which is celebrated by all the deities.
In ancient times, Śakra performed a sacrifice there with Bṛhaspati as his domestic priest.
There stands the Vyāghreśvara Liṅga, which destroys all sins.
Formerly, there was a king named Babhru who was supremely righteous.
A Vaiṣṇava resident of Puṇḍravardhana reflected:
"When the anniversary of my father's passing has arrived, it is the time for the Śrāddha;
yet that king could not find a Vaiṣṇava brāhmaṇa to partake of the Śrāddha food."
Having reflected, he threw the cooked food intended for the Brahmins into the water.
Then the *Ṛgveda*, personified, spoke these words to the king:
"Go, O King, and beg the auspicious Brahmin Bharadvāja. (64–65)
Having heard that, the king went to the supreme hermitage of Bhāradvāja;
having saluted and paid homage to the sage, he spoke what was in his mind:
"O Great Seer, this is the time for the *śrāddha* ceremony for my ancestors."
"You ought to act in such a way that you may feed the brahmin just as I do.
Having heard those words of his, Bhāradvāja spoke these words:
"There are thousands of great sages, satisfied ones whose vital energy is drawn upward (ūrdhvaretas)."
If you are capable of feeding the foremost of those with hair like swans, then perform the *śrāddha* as you desire; we shall indeed feed them.
Give a golden seat, and likewise give grain and wealth.
Likewise, a divine cow of honey, and similarly a cow of milk; a cow of curd, a cow of ghee, and also a cow of sugar;
as well as a cow of jaggery, a cow of cloth, and indeed a cow of grain.
Give me a water-cow, a gold-cow, and likewise a cow made of two grains;
also a cotton-cow, a tawny cow with its calf,
and even a loincloth for one whose garment has been purified by fire.
Having heard the words of Bhāradvāja, the king accepted them.
Having gone home, he reported everything to his wife with sincere devotion:
"I shall prepare meat and perform the ancestral rites."
He gratified those ancestors with pure meat alone.
Seeing the meat, the sages were enraged and then said:
"Having consumed what is unfit for food, a twice-born man should enter a fire of dried cow-dung. (75)
"Through your attachment to worldly gain, you have brought about the destruction of your very roots.
Babhru said: "I have performed what is ordained by the Vedas, and not otherwise:
the Gomedha, the Hayamedha, and likewise the Naramedha."
"A sacrifice for Kṣatriyas has indeed been performed by me according to dharma.
Having heard those words of the king, Bhāradvāja spoke this:
"O King, Brahmins have been invited by you for the feeding of the ancestors."
The Brahmins and the Vaiṣṇavas are indeed not eager even to look upon meat.
Therefore, since you have certainly not prepared what is appropriate for this Śrāddha rite, by that sin become a meat-eater; you shall be a tiger and your beloved wife a tigress.
"You two shall wander the earth in the forest for a thousand years.
Having heard this, the king's wife named Sudharmā spoke these words:
"Since my husband, who follows the dharma of a kṣatriya, has been cursed by you..."
"I am likewise devoted to my husband, faultless, and most righteous.
Then, by me as well, a terrible curse was pronounced upon the Brahmins:
"You shall indeed become most horrific Brahma-rākṣasas!"
In a waterless desert region, they were exceedingly distressed by thirst and hunger;
then Bhāradvāja went quickly to Brahmā himself and reported everything there, including the cause of the curse.
And Brahmā said: "Whatever action is prescribed in the Vedas, or even that which is prescribed by one's caste, if it is not honored by the world, one should never perform it at all.
However, that which is prescribed in the Vedas, honored by the world, and also agreeable to the heart—" || 85-86 ||
That deed shall indeed grant happiness, for happiness does not follow from a single source alone.
O son, let that which has arisen be as it is; I speak of the deliverance that has come forth.
Though he was a royal sage in the form of a tiger, there were queens, brahmins, and even rākṣasas.
"Let them go to the bank of the Narmadā toward the sage Mārkaṇḍeya.
Having been addressed thus, Bhāradvāja, the king of sages, took the brahmins, the tiger, the tigress, and those rākṣasas, and went to the sage Mārkaṇḍeya. (88–89)
They praised him with supreme affection and spoke of the cause of the curse;
for the sake of liberation, they entreated that sage as if he were their father:
"You are our father and our preceptor, you are Hari, the Sustainer, and Śiva himself."
"Rescue me from sin and from this terrible birth in a fearsome womb.
Then Mārkaṇḍeya said: "There is indeed the hermitage of Śākalya to the west of Vaidūrya, where many sacrifices have been performed."
And those born there on that holy ground should go to Maheśvara;
remaining firm in their vows, they should also worship Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
Constantly devoted to recitation and meditation, let them also perform fierce austerity.
"Let them remain subsisting on roots, tubers, and fruits;
while so abiding, let them be devoted to bathing in the Narmadā and intent upon the worship of the gods, so that you may quickly become liberated from the curse. (94–95)
"Oṃ, salutations to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; salutations!
Recite this syllabic mantra so that you may quickly attain [your goal].
Having been addressed thus, they departed for that place and performed the recitation again and again.
They bathed in the waters of the Narmadā and performed supreme austerities.
And within a month, right there, Lord Hari,
seated upon a divine vehicle and accompanied by divine Lakṣmī, arrived for the purpose of destroying their curse.
At the confluence of the Vyāghra and Revā, the Lord himself liberated the Brahmins from their curse,
as well as the tiger and the tigress from the curse;
then he departed for his own supreme abode, along with the king, the queen, and the gods on earth (the Brahmins).
Afterwards, at another time, they went to their own homes;
and having been liberated by the power of the mantra, they went to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
By hearing or chanting this [account], one obtains the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.

Thus ends the five hundred and sixty-second chapter, titled "The Historical Narration of the Kapilā-Reva Confluence, Viśrava Tīrtha, Viṣṇupurī Cakratīrtha, and Dāruvana-Vyāghreśa Tīrtha," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*. [Chapter 563] *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Part 1 (Kṛtayuga-santāna), Chapter 563.
[The Author: Chapter 564.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
"O Blessed One, tell me how honey, cows, and other such things are to be given."
"What is the merit? What is the ritual procedure there? And how much should the gift of a cow (godāna) be? Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
"Listen, Lakṣmī! I shall tell you. In ancient times, there was a great king."
The lord, renowned as Vinītāśva, performed many sacrifices.
He commenced the Sarvamedha sacrifice; by means of it, cows, elephants, wealth, all gold, and palatial dwellings were bestowed upon the Brahmins. (2–3)
At that time, he did not give food or water, considering them to be too little.
Then, having died on the bank of the Gaṅgā, he went to heaven in due course.
His body was cast into a cave in the earth by the twice-born.
Having recognized that the meritorious clay of the Gaṅgā was indeed deposited upon the earth,
this king— though dwelling in a celestial chariot in heaven and yet hungry and thirsty— came to the earth for the sake of food. (5–6)
Having dug up his own corpse there, he began to devour it.
Then, the king’s priest, named Hotṛ, saw him;
and seeing him eating his own body, he asked, "What indeed are you doing? (7)
The king said: "No food appears before me in heaven. "Tell me the reason for this," he asked; and having heard him, the Hotṛ spoke to him.
The Hotṛ said: "In the past, you did not provide gifts of water and food."
Thinking it to be very little, one does not perform [meritorious acts], and thus immortality is not attained.

Listen, Lakṣmī! These were spoken by Śaṅkara on the bank of the Narmadā, between Kapilā and Amarā, in the midst of the Narmadā-oṃkāra. || 1 ||
"Wherever people may wander, there indeed exist ten million sacred fords (tīrthas).

He who would wander to Śivaparvata through physical hardship [attains success]. (8)
"Śaṅkara has declared that for him there shall be the fruit of a sacrifice at every step;
for the river Sarasvatī herself has assumed the form of a female elephant. (9)
He comes to Koṭitīrtha to bathe, and having bathed there, he proceeds as far as the confluence of the Kāverī with the ocean. || 1.564.10 ||
In this interval, indeed, ten million holy sites (tīrthas) dwell along the Narmadā;

The meritorious mountain Amarakaṇṭaka indeed bestows liberation;

That river which arose through the penance of Kubera became known by the name Kauberī.

In ancient times, there was a king of the Lunar dynasty named Candrasena who was a doer of evil.
He was devoted to the wives of others, a thief, and a drinker of intoxicants.
She said to me, "Become my wife and enjoy abundant pleasures.
Having heard this, Saudāminī replied, "O King, ask for me as your wife.
The king, utterly infatuated by her, then questioned Śāṇḍilya.
And if you give me your wife, who stands in the prime of youth, today, I shall give you wealth for her price by the hundreds of thousands. (27)
The sage said: "O King, women are rooted in deceit in every respect; no one is truly dear to them. Do as you wish. (28)
Then the king, blinded by lust, seized that virtuous woman by the hand;

"By my touch today, you shall become a Cāṇḍāla;

In an instant, he became black in color and devoid of his former complexion;

Having reached the state of a caṇḍāla, they were filled with mutual wonder. ||33||
Vasiṣṭha, however, said to the king: "Go back toward her indeed;
go and beg for forgiveness, and everything will become peaceful. (34)
Having bowed to that sage and again to the Earth, the king departed;
and at that time, he repeatedly begged for forgiveness, while the couple spoke thus. (35)
O King, proceed quickly to the confluence of the Caṇḍavegā;

in the end, he also attained liberation through the power of Caṇḍavega. ||38||

Then, on another day, there is another supreme holy site, the confluence of the Eraṇḍī and the Narmadā;

"I have heard here that the ancestors accept the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) with their hands;

on the *darśa*, the ancestors take into their hands the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) prepared for that occasion.

Then he offered the funeral cakes (piṇḍas), yet the ancestors did not appear in bodily form. At that time, Durvāsas spoke again to the sage named Eraṇḍa, who was performing penance there. ||48-49||
"There can be no accomplishment of your purpose here; come indeed with me.
