Only those humans who are free from sin and possess pure hearts will always come within the range of their parents' vision; it can never be otherwise. (58)
In this very way, the Araṇḍikā-tīrtha came to be at the confluence of the Revā;
by hearing of it or by reciting its name, there shall be the deliverance of those who visit the tīrtha for their ancestors. ||59||
Then there is another supreme sacred ford (tīrtha) of the Revā and the Viśalyā,
where Bharata performed a sacrifice in which the arrows became painless (viśalya).
The two rivers that had arisen entered the waters of the Narmadā;
indeed, the Asuras who were creators of obstacles fought with Bharata.
At that time, many asuras were destroyed by Bharata with his arrows, for the sake of relieving the pain from the arrows of both Bharata and his soldiers. ||62||
From the base of the sacrificial post (yūpa) there arose a river named Viśalyā, which draws out all thorns [of pain].
Having bathed there with the horse of Yajñanārāyaṇa, Bharata and the others were freed from their afflictions;
they became entirely free from thorns and sinless.
Therefore, the two rivers are celebrated as Śalyā and Viśalyā. ॥64॥
That [confluence], consisting of two streams, is joined at the Narmadā;
this supreme and meritorious holy site on the bank of the Narmadā is purifying. (65)
When the Svāyambhuva Manvantara had arrived and the Kṛta Yuga began,
the gods, defeated by the Dānavas, took refuge on the banks of the Narmadā.
Those gods, together with Brahmā, went for refuge to the Lord;
then Bṛhaspati spoke to Brahmā, the Supreme Creator. (67)
"Perform a most fierce sacrifice that will bring about the destruction of the Dānavas.
In the meantime, the gods went to the bank of the Narmadā. ||68||
Then, having pierced the earth, a most brilliantly radiant Liṅga rose up;
it uttered the syllable Oṃ there and proclaimed the worlds Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ. ||69||
That mountain which has arisen from the mountain is called Oṃkāragiri;
Śambhu, having appeared in person, spoke these words to Pitāmaha.
"Perform a most fierce sacrifice that will bring about the destruction of the Daityas.
Thereupon, Brahmā performed a sacrifice for the peace of the gods. ||71||
Fleeing out of fear of him, they went to the netherworld (rasātala);
by the power of the syllable Oṃ, the gods became fearless. (79)
Having worshipped Oṃkāra Śaṅkara, the gods and others departed for heaven;
the great Liṅga, which endures until the end of the Kalpa, shines upon the mountain peak. (73)
The fivefold Brahma has five faces and is endowed with the nine powers;
his western face, Sadyojāta, resembles a conch, a kunda flower, and the moon.
From whom the Ṛgveda emerged, Brahmā is the presiding deity there.
Know that the northern [face] is Vāmadeva, yellowish in luster and most beautiful;
it is the source of the Yajurveda, and Viṣṇu is the presiding deity there.
Aghora, resembling the color of a cloud, is situated in the southern direction. ||76||
Know that which originates from the Sāmaveda to have the Sun as its deity;
it should be understood as Tatpuruṣa, resembling the color of saffron. (77)
Then the Atharvaveda emerged as the fourth, and the waters were its presiding deities;
his face was that of Īśāna, five-colored and of great form.
The presiding deity there is Soma, whose music is established by the Vedas;
the sixth is named Sadāśiva, who is partless and free from all affliction. ||79||
Thus has this entire description of the syllable Oṃ been told to you.
One should worship Dakṣiṇāmūrti as Oṃkāra and shall attain liberation. 1.564.80
One should provide the materials for the temple and the implements for worship;
one should cause the restoration of what is dilapidated and so forth, as well as the flagstaff, the bell, and other such items. ॥81॥
One should give garments, ornaments, mṛdaṅgas, and so forth to the embodiment of Oṃkāra;
one should offer gardens, groves, fields, and the like to him. (82)
It is impossible to calculate the measure of the fruit of that gift in this world;
the donor obtains both worldly enjoyment and liberation—of this there is no doubt. (83)
King Dhundhumāra, who was a worshiper of the deities and guests, went to the Vindhya mountain and entered the forest of the Revā there. (84)
He beheld a white-colored boar roaring;
as soon as he strove to kill it, at that very moment, the boar too entered the midst of the water at Koṭitīrtha. ||85||
Having entered, that king also followed behind him. ||86||
In that moment, Kroḍa, having assumed a divine body, ascended a celestial chariot;
seeing him in such a state, the king asked for the reason.
The divine Lord Varāha, assuming a celestial form, said to the mountain:
"I am indeed a follower of Śambhu, known by the name Aṅgada, a skilled singer. (88)
Having seen Urvaśī and Rambhā as well, I became deluded by passion;
uttering the speech of a boar, I became entirely absorbed in amorous play. (89)
Seeing me, Nandin cursed me, saying, "Become a boar in the forest.
I propitiated Nandin, who then granted me a boon as the end of the curse:
"Upon seeing Dhundhumāra and by resorting to Koṭitīrtha [you shall be released]."
Having abandoned the womb of a sow, you shall go to Kailāsa.
Having spoken thus and uttered the blessing "May it be well with you," the attendant departed.
Then the king sat down for a moment upon that stone slab.
Thereupon, the king’s horse drank water from the Narmadā.
At that moment, he too became divine and stood in the sky seated upon a celestial chariot (vimāna).
Having become a twice-born, he said to the king: "I was formerly Gālava, a Brahmanical sage in the land of the Kauravas, [who attained this state] through the acceptance of the gift of horses."
Having been purified by attaining the body of a bird through the yoga of Revā, I have attained liberation;
indeed, I am going to the true world of Brahmā, my own abode. ||95||
O King, in the past I accepted a gift from King Dyumatsena; listen, for I shall tell you the reason why. ||96||

Taking elephants, horses, chariots, and the like, as well as gold, jewels, garments, ornaments, and so forth, the King of Madhyadeśa arrived at Kurukṣetra during a solar eclipse to offer gifts in every way. ||97||
But the Brahmins, having reflected upon the king's terrible acceptance [of the gift], [spoke]. 98.
Then the king did not accept it and censured the Brahmins, saying:
"This place is unfit for Brahmins; it is devoid of sacred knowledge and unsuitable for officiating at sacrifices. (99)
"All the power of Brahmā has been withdrawn; no worthy recipient for a gift is to be found.
Having heard these words of the king, I manifested my power. (1.564.100)
"I am Gālava; give a gift, for I have the strength to receive it.
Then the king gave me various articles suitable for a kingdom. (101)
"I was born equal to a king, endowed with royal enjoyments.
Then the king departed, and I, having abandoned the *agnihotra* and other rites, wandered among many pleasures; after dying, I became your horse."
Thus, I have been liberated today by the waters of the Revā; may prosperity be yours.
Having spoken thus, Gālava departed for his own true abode;
the king, however, reflected: "Where indeed shall I go without the horse? (104)
At that moment, a three-eyed young woman appeared in person and said to him:
"I am the river named Kapilā, whose waters flow within the Narmadā. (105)
And you too, O King, having bathed here in my pool, drink this water;
having ruled your kingdom, go to heaven along with your harem and retinue. 106.
"O observer of noble vows, whatever desire you contemplate, that very thing you shall obtain.
Having spoken thus, that river Kapilā vanished from sight. (107)
Having prostrated before her, the king departed for his own city.
By hearing of her and by chanting her praises, one is liberated from the bonds of worldly existence. (108)
Thus, indeed, was the majesty of the sacred ford (tīrtha) described by Śaṅkara to Śivā; that same [teaching], O Lakṣmī, which bestows supreme liberation, has been told to you by me. 109.

Thus ends the five hundred and sixty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Wrapping of the Thread at Koṭitīrtha, the Piṅgala-liṅga of Sūrya, the Abode of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, the Confluences of the Kāverī, Payoṣṇī, Somagaṅgā, and Caṇḍavegā, the Liberation of Candrasena from his Cāṇḍāla State, the Confluence of the Eraṇḍī, the Confluence of the Śalyā and Viśalyā, the Liberation of Dhundhumāra from his Boar Form, and the Liberation of Gālava from his Horse Form," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīya-saṃhitā*.

Śrī Lakṣmī said:
By what various methods should a person perform their actions,
so that even a householder may attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation, thereby achieving success?

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, I shall tell you everything: even a householder who is devoted to his duties may attain the meaningfulness of his birth, even if he is possessed by desire, greed, and other such passions.
Having established his mind in Me, free from the notions of "mine" and "I," and always perceiving Me both in the object of enjoyment and in the enjoyer, he should be devoted to forgiveness.
Subsisting on fruits, roots, vegetables, milk, and the like, he should observe vows such as the *payovrata*.

The sixth, the eighth, the new moon day, and the fourteenth day of both fortnights (4); these are the days for vows and the time of the sacred festivals. On the twelfth day, during śrāddha ceremonies, and on occasions of worship, one should not engage in sexual intercourse, even when there are specific causes [for doing so] (5).
One should perform everything while remembering me; indeed, if one acts for my sake, that person of firm vows should perform their work through the application of yoga toward me.
Purified in soul, endowed with righteousness, and devoted to love for me—
For him there is no fading, no old age, no delusion, passion, or envy;
he whose [senses] do not obstruct his vision of Me goes to My world.
Having performed worship of Me throughout his life, he is glorified in My abode.
Having heard this, Lakṣmī again questioned Puruṣottama:
"Tell me now, at what time is your worship to be performed and how should it be done?
And at each respective time, O Lord of Gods, what kind of rite must be performed for you?"
How do you perform the installation, the invocation, and the dismissal here?
O Hari, tell me, what kind of incense and lamp do you accept?
How do you accept the water for the feet, the installation, and the unguent as well?
"O Blessed One, how do you accept seats, beds, vehicles, and roots, tubers, and fruits? Of what nature is the auspicious offering presented to you?
What kind of ritual action is performed in autumn, and what kind of ritual action in the winter?"
What kind of work is there in spring? What work do you consider appropriate in summer?
What work is there in the rainy season, and what should one perform at the end of the rains? And what flowers and fruits are to be enjoyed there?
What is the prescribed measure for your image, and what kind of installation do you consider appropriate?
What is its size, and what kind of fasting is required?
What kind of garment—yellow, red, or pale pink—do you wear?
What kind of garment do you consider to be beneficial for them? With which substances is the *madhuparka* mixed according to your view?
What is the merit of giving the *madhuparka*, and what are its qualities like? (16–17)
To which worlds do those who consume the *madhuparka* go?
What was the measure of the *madhuparka* and other offerings to be given in the past?
And what vegetables, foods, and drinks are dear to you?
By what ritual procedure is this food-offering given to you?
Having honored you during the vow, how should one act so that there may be no transgression—both in the matter of worship and likewise in touching [you]? (1.565.20)
What rites should one perform when feeding Your devotee?
How should the offering be presented to You, and what kind of vessel is prescribed?
And who in this world partakes of Your supreme purifying grace?
And those who eat but one meal a day and worship Keśava,
who constantly remember you and dwell among your devotees— what, O Lord, is the destiny of those who practice devotion to you? (22–23)

Those who perform the *kṛcchra* and *sāntapana* penances, or those who subsist on air during their vow—what destination do they attain when they touch upon the color black? And those who avoid pungent and salty foods, being solely intent on your service—[what is their fate]? (24)
And what destination do those devotees who observe the milk-vow attain?
(25) What kind of destination do those devotees reach who subsist on cow’s milk and similar foods, who are devoted to the service of cows, and who live by the practice of gleaning? (26)
And those who subsist on alms, yet rely upon the duties of householders,
and are always devoted to Mādhava— what destination do they attain?
And those people who give up their lives in your fields and sacred fords (tīrthas)?
O Lord, what destination do those who practice the five-fire penance attain?
Likewise, those who die in the heat of five fires, those who die by leaping from a cliff, those who sleep upon beds of thorns, and those who remain lying in the open air—what is their fate? (28–29)
O Keśava, what destination do those who abide on the path of devotion reach— those who lie down in a cow-pen and behold you?
[They are those who subsist] on vegetables, on grains, on cow-products, or on barley.
They subsist on a diet of groats and worship you without interruption.
What destination do those followers reach who are devoted to drinking milk?
And those who approach your abode carrying a lamp upon their heads? (3.1–3.2)
Carrying a leaf, a flower, a fruit, water, or a piece of wood upon their heads, they perform service unto you; what destination do those followers attain?
Having undertaken the vow of subsisting on stones, they take refuge [in you] constantly.
Those people subsist on leaves and are devoted to performing circumambulations;
they practice their own dharma and are intent upon serving virtuous women and holy men.
Those who go to your sacred field crawling on their knees [attain liberation]. (34–35)
O Lord, what will be the destiny in your world for those who go to your abode while prostrating themselves like a staff?
And for those who, having performed the ritual of lying on their backs, maintain a lamp before you?
Or else, with their faces turned downward, they proceed to your abode.
O Nārāyaṇa, tell me, what is the perfected destiny of those who, having abandoned their sons, wives, and homes, have come to you for refuge? || 37-38 ||
When the life-force has departed, while you are being honored with the honey-mixture (madhuparka),
what destination does one who possesses the perfect knowledge of Sāṃkhya and Yoga attain— whether the body is consumed by fire, carried away by water, or remains resting upon the earth? (39)
Having offered their bodies to Your field and having resorted to the path of renunciation, they are constantly devoted to Your name, saying: "Obeisance to Nārāyaṇa!
Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Lord! Svāhā! (1.565.40–41)

"O Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, what kind of destiny is considered for those men and women who are entirely devoted to the recitation of mantras and dedicated to your dharma, and who, slain by weapons in battle, chant your names? || 42 ||
What indeed will be the destiny of those who proclaim Your names?
And those who, having met with sudden death or even died through possession, remain devoted to the remembrance of You—what destination do they go to, O Mādhava? (43–44)

I am established as your disciple and your servant through devotion. Indeed, I have spoken thus to you— this secret, endowed with righteousness, which brings happiness to all the world and is filled with devotion to you.
Having reflected upon this, Your Honor ought to speak for the sake of the world’s benefit.
Those men who are without women, and those women who are without men, have by no means attained satisfaction of desire; they are instead solely devoted to you. 43–47.
And what destination do those people attain who die in this world unsatisfied, still possessed by the desire for enjoyments— those who have renounced, widows, and others,
as well as those who died as children before attaining the enjoyment of their desires? (48)
To what state do women devoted to your service, and men as well, go?

Even those intent on your initiation, those who always subsist on your alms, and those who take delight in your devotees and devotees—those who have mastery over their desires—[to what state do they go]? 1.565.50.
Devoted solely to love for those who are the very objects of your affection,
these Vaiṣṇavas— both men and women— do not go elsewhere;
with the desire to attain you, they never long for anything else in their hearts.
"O Mādhava, tell me this: what destination do such great devotees attain—those who offer up their very selves?
Are they teachers, kings of the world, householders, or those enveloped in enjoyments? (52–53)
"And what destination do those followers reach who are immersed in sense objects?
Even though this is a supreme secret, please tell me that out of affection for me.
Thus addressed, the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Master, [replied].
Devoted to his own duty, he spoke those dharmas to Lakṣmī:
"O Lakṣmī, listen to that which you ask, which brings happiness;
my way of life is such that my devotees do not indeed go to suffering. (55–56)
I am not pleased by a thousand gifts, nor even by hundreds of sacrifices;
I am not satisfied by wealth, but I am satisfied by love alone.
O Mādhavī, he who worships me with his mind fixed upon me— 57.
I am eternally pleased with him; my devotee, though full of many faults, is dear to me.
Those women and men devoted to me who bow down to me with devotion—at midnight or in the darkness, at midday or in the afternoon—[are dear to me]. (58–59)

Their minds, fixed upon my form, attend to nothing else; their lives are centered on me, and they are devoted to me. They are intent on my hair, intent on my hunger, and intent on my thirst. They dwell with me and are solely devoted to my body.
They enjoy betel-leaf with me; they kiss me.
They sleep soundly by my side, intent on ascending onto me.
Through meditation upon contact with my body, they maintain the concentration that brings me bliss.
Devoted to their duties within me, they perceive only me;
having attained their goal and recognizing my qualities, they remain steadfast in devotion to me.
Dwellers in my world, these ones who have taken refuge in me abide by my side.
Those men and women who follow me take delight upon my bed.
O my beloved Lakṣmī, my blisses are not attained by means of very little; for the sake of a single moment’s devotion, I, Nārāyaṇa, am difficult to reach for a man.
"O Mādhavī! They perform my rites, they behold me, and they remain established in devotion to me—even those who are likewise intent upon their own self-interest.
To them, O beloved, I grant the worlds of heaven and so forth for the sake of enjoyment."
Having observed a fast on the twelfth lunar day and being devoted with supreme faith,
one should offer a handful of water from a sacred bathing place (tīrtha) to the Sun at dawn.
Reciting "Obeisance to Nārāyaṇa," one should gaze upon the Sun in the sky.
As many fine drops as fall from the water in one's cupped hands,
for so many thousands of years is one honored in the heavenly world.
Those people who worship me with white flowers on the twelfth lunar day [attain the same merit].
They perfume [the offering] with refined incenses and, holding it in their hearts, remember me:
"Salutation to Viṣṇu! Accept this; may the Blessed One be pleased with me.
Salutation! Accept the food; may he be pleased. And drink the water. (1.565.70–71)
Thus, one should worship me with love and listen to my scriptures;
he shall indeed go to my world and be born as four-armed.
[One should offer] śyāmāka, wheat, mung beans, rice, and likewise barley.
Nīvāra, kaṅguka, and munyanna—these are always sattvic foods.
Having offered them as my *naivedya*, one who is devoted to me should eat them. Whatever actions one performs, being solely intent on devotion to me, [they should be done in this manner]. (73–74)
Devoted to the six duties, free from the egoism of "I," having abandoned gain and loss, subsisting on alms, with senses conquered,
engaged in my ritual actions, and devoid of backbiting.
One who follows the scriptures and remains impartial, whose mind is neither like that of an elder nor a child—
even such a Brāhmaṇa goes to me, the supreme imperishable. Having attained my very form, he enjoys pleasures together with me.
A Kṣatriya who is heroic in generosity, established in righteousness, skilled in sacrifices, pure, and devoted to his duties;
who is free from egoism, appreciative of virtues, and impartial—[such a one is worthy]. (78)
Speaking little, possessing great knowledge, free from envy, and avoiding those who are censurable;
skillful in rising to greet others and other such duties, and always dear to the devotees of the Lord—he who, being devoid of malice and deceit, remembers me constantly. (1.565.80)
He who constantly worships me goes to my abode—
even a Vaiśya who is established in devotion to me, devoted to his daily duties,
equanimous in gain and loss, peaceful, and free from the delusion of "I" and "mine. (81)
He who approaches his wife only during her fertile period, who is always affectionate toward his devotees,
who constantly honors his guru, and who is intent upon my worship— for him I am never lost, and he is never lost to me. (82–83)
The Śūdra, having become my servant, performs his work as a devotee;
the husband and wife are devoted to me, dedicated to my service. Both are followers of the Bhāgavata path, devoted to me, and established in their duties.
They know the proper place and time, being free from passion and darkness;
they are devoid of the notions of "I" and "mine," adorned with faith and humility; their souls are purified, they are free from greed and delusion, and they honor guests. (85–86)
Constantly intent on offering salutations and devoted to my service,
worshipping me alone and beholding me as the God,
they are ever absorbed in meditation upon me and endowed with a spirit of servitude toward me.
In this way, whether it be a Śūdra or a Śūdrī, let them perform my service.
Abandoning thousands of sages, I worship the Śūdra devotee;
having abandoned both gain and loss, and having cast off delusion and desire.
He who constantly contemplates me as being eternally free from cold and heat, and who feels no desire for what is bitter, pungent, sweet, sour, salty, or astringent, nor for anything that is savory,
to be licked, sucked, chewed, or drunk— [at him I am pleased]. (1.565.90)
Supporting his wife, son, and family, he remains solely devoted to Me;
ever intent on fortitude and faith, he always loathes other activities and is forever free from the latent impressions of childhood, youth, and old age. (91–92)
Having only minimal enjoyments and maintaining a livelihood solely for the sustenance of the body,
he is compassionate toward all sentient beings and ever intent on rising to greet them. Having especially observed silence, he indeed worships me constantly.
After giving food and other offerings to others, the observer of the vow shall eat;
he should remain intent on his practice, keeping his mind directed toward me.
At the proper time, having discharged urine and feces, he should be devoted to bathing. (94–95)
Always devoted to my service with flowers, incense, and perfumes,
subsisting on bulbs, roots, and fruits, or eating heaps of barley and parched grain;
eating at the sixth meal-time, the ninth meal-time, or even once every ten fortnights.

In this way, one performs actions for my sake for seven births. (97) Those who have renounced all attachments for my sake, who are solely devoted to renunciation—virtuous women, pure, enamored of renunciation, whose lives are dedicated to my service. (98)
Those men and women who possess the great initiation (mahādīkṣā),
even practitioners of yoga behold them constantly at dawn.
He who performs his duties according to the method thus described—
"I shall indeed protect you by my side, just as I do my beloved.

Thus ends the five hundred and sixty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of Dwelling in the Abode of Śrī Hari and Other Matters, Consisting of Actions and Renunciation of Action, in Response to Lakṣmī’s Questions Regarding the Mahābhāgavata Practices of All," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Chapter 567 → Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī, to the procedure for all the questions you have asked—such as how and when worship should be performed. I shall explain the ritual method:
[it should be done] at dawn during the Brāhma-muhūrta, at midday, and also in the evening.
My worship should be performed with sixteen types of excellent articles:
(2) bathing, feeding, the waving of lights (ārātrika), adorning with ornaments and so forth;
one should also perform the offering of water for drinking, betel leaf, handfuls of flowers, and other such rites. (3)
In the cold season, one should offer blankets and the like, as well as warm water and so forth;
likewise, delicious foods and other things that provide strength and nourishment. In the rainy season, however, one should offer food that is not hot, as well as water and clothing.
O my beloved! At that time, food that provides moderate nourishment should be given to me.
Furthermore, during the period of heat, cool, fragrant water, fine garments and the like, cooked food, fruits, and so forth should be offered. 5–6.
And at that time, the installation should be recited: "Come, O Lord, O Beloved!
Having taken your seat upon the throne of gold and other materials, accept my worship.
Come, O Blessed One, O Master, O Nārāyaṇa, O Consort, O Lord!"
Having accepted the worship, you must go to your own abode and not otherwise.
(8) O Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, O Master, accept this incense prepared from the powder of wood and other materials, mixed with fragrant juices. (9)
O Supreme Lord, accept this ghee lamp of gentle qualities.
With devotion, I offer this ghee lamp and sandalwood incense,
as well as a lamp of sesame oil and the incense of guggulu.
Or rather, even at this time, I shall take fragrant *puṣpasāra* paste;
having collected waters from sacred fords (*tīrtha*), my feet must be washed according to the season, and I shall accept the cleansing of my feet. (11–12)
The ceremonial bathing with the waters of sacred fords, with curd, milk, clarified butter,
honey, sugar, and oil;
the rubbing with a cleansing powder that produces purity, is unctuous, white, and brings about peace.
"Anointing oil should be given to my body, especially that which is suitable for it.
O beloved, I always accept with devotion the sandalwood paste, the essence of flowers, and ointments such as Viṣṇutaila offered by my devotees. (14–15)

O Lakṣmī! With sincere devotion, I accept a golden lion-throne and other such items, as well as a woolen seat, a wooden plank, and the consecration following my occupation of them—all given by a man or a woman. (16)
On a couch that was beautiful, soft, and spacious, provided with a fine covering;
equipped with two side-pillows, endowed with two cheek-rests,
adorned with a mattress, and furnished with a screen to ward off gadflies.
I always sleep upon a lotus provided with a hidden cord;
my vehicle is joined by swans, horses, and adorned with elephants and the like—
vast, moving through the sky, and fashioned from gold.

I carry either Garuḍa, or Māṇikī, or a divine chariot. Out of devotion to my master, I gather bulbs, roots, fruits, and other things that possess fragrance and flavor— ripened and produced in their proper season.

Just as one offers to oneself in the autumn season, just as one offers to oneself in the winter, just as one offers to oneself in the spring, and just as one offers to oneself in the summer— so too is this auspicious, refined food offered with love in a golden vessel.
And even during the rainy season, at the end of the rains, whatever pleases one's own taste—
whether it be that which is to be enjoyed, worn, drunk, eaten, clothing, ornaments,
water, vehicles, mounts, and so forth, wind, swings, forests, and the like— [should be used]. (23–24)
Dwelling, clothing, water, bedding, attendants, and so forth—all these must be provided for me; they must be given in this manner and not otherwise.
O beloved, the offering should be made to the Deity just as it is done for the body.
An image (arcā) measuring more than six finger-breadths (aṅgula) is considered auspicious;
beyond sixty-four finger-breadths, it is not recommended to be longer.
Furthermore, the foundation in the temple and the visual perspective should be proportionally balanced.
The ground level for the eye-line should be at a height of four parts above the door;
it is my opinion that the installation of the image should be such that this is achieved.
Below the image, within the interior of the lion-throne, gold, gems, and other materials should be placed.
O beloved! An image of Śrī Hari should be installed there within the inner sanctum (garbha).
To the right, the Lord should be placed; to the left, the auspicious Śrī Rādhikā.
Also [to be placed] are Lakṣmī, Māṇikī, Haṃsā, Prabhā, Pārvatī, and Mañjulā.
Jayā, Lalitā, Śāntā, Sarasvatī with her mind, Durgā, Gaṅgā, Kamalā, Sāvitrī, and likewise Virajā;
or any other beloved of Śrī Hari who may be desired by the devotee. || 3.1 ||
It should be established so that it is sloping toward the ear and as beautiful as possible to behold. On the preceding day, there should be fasting (nakta), beginning from sunset;
on the second day, the ritual act should be performed, and no food should be consumed by day or night.
Fasting on leaves, flowers, fruits, food, and so forth is also prescribed as such.
Taking a single meal, subsisting on fruit, or subsisting on water does not constitute a violation.
In the spring one should wear white garments, and in Phālguna, saffron.
In Āṣāḍha, [garments] dyed with safflower are worn, and in Āśvina, those of golden hue;
during festivals and the like, they are of variegated colors, while at all other times they are of a single color.
O beloved, I wear [garments] enriched with the splendor of gold, stars, and so forth. (35–36)
It is held that all clothing, except for that dyed with mercury (lohātāra), is conducive to well-being.
Red clothing is considered to bring prosperity, yellow is considered to bestow fortune,
white constantly imparts knowledge, and variegated clothing is considered to provide enjoyment.
In this context, blue [garments] are strictly forbidden and must never be worn.
The *madhuparka* is considered to consist of jaggery and ghee, or sugar and ghee,
or else sugar mixed with milk, as well as candied sugar and curd.
That in which there is satisfaction from drinking honey-sweetened or other sweet drinks within the stomach is considered *madhuparka*.
Honey, mango juice and the like, clarified butter, and sugar—these three as well [constitute it]. (1.566.40)
Among sweet fruits, that which is most delicious and mixed with honey should be offered to me as a *madhuparka* according to what is appropriate; it should be cool and beneficial to my qualities.
Through the offering of *madhuparka*, there are prosperities both in heaven and here on earth.
For the donor who constantly gives the merit of food, drink, and so forth,
there appear in his house streams of ghee, streams of honey, and streams of curd;
there also arise streams of milk, streams of buttermilk, and streams of water.
Wherever those channels exist in the world, there they go, bestowing honey.
As much honey as is required to pacify the stomach should be given—
sweet and satisfying— by which the eternal worlds are attained.
Indeed, all these become givers of nectar and givers of essence to the donor.
Vegetables such as the kūṣmāṇḍa and others are entirely of the nature of *sattva*,
as are eggplants, milky plants, gillikās, and so forth.
Rice grains and such, leaves, and mustard petals;
cucumbers, bottle gourds, and cirbhaṭas—these gentle tubers and roots, O beloved, are dear to me! (47–48)
Śrīkhaṇḍa, milk-porridge (pāyasa), and other auspicious boiled substances;
likewise, decoctions (kvathikā), black mustard (rājikā),
fermented gruel (rāddha), sour gruel (māranāla), as well as garbharī, arka, tiktaka, karavīra, and mangoes.
Such delightful things as these are always dear to me.
Enjoy at will whatever is sweet and desired, slowly and in full measure, which bestows tranquility.
O Lord Keśava, eat cooked foods and other delicacies according to your pleasure.
In this manner he should feed me and fan me with a breeze;
then, out of love, the devotee should serve food into my vessel.
Indeed, he should always feed me in this way, having placed me upon a golden seat.
Having filled a golden vessel with water and using vessels such as a golden platter,
one should lovingly serve everything and cause [the guest] to drink the water.
One should offer auspicious betel-leaf and perform a massage of the feet.
May it be so that they do not commit any offense during my worship;
may no one with an impure body ever touch me without having bathed;
and may no one approach me while I am in the temple without being like one who is mute.
A mute person must certainly not awaken me without the sounding of bells and other instruments.
One must never awaken me at an improper time or without restraint.
For the sake of merchants, men, or kings, one must not cause me to keep vigil.
One should never worship for one's own sake, nor should one ever show one's back [in disrespect]. One should not sneeze, engage in debate, or abandon the bounds of decorum.
Nor should one go to my temple wearing unclean clothing.
Having touched an impure object, one must indeed wash both hands;
otherwise, one should not touch me nor touch my belongings.
Having scratched oneself, one should never touch me at any time.
One should certainly not harbor even evil intentions while in my temple;
during my worship, one should not eat oneself, nor drink even water and the like.
One should perform the worship like a mute, never making noise except for my own chanting.
Having set aside the materials remaining from one's own garlands, one should not again take up the hand [to eat] without first washing it;
nor should one touch new objects [with unwashed hands].
One should not discharge phlegm, flatus, or similar waste within the temple.
If one should discharge urine or other such waste, one must bathe and then touch me;
while engaged in my worship, one must not be intent on any other task.
One should not be distracted in mind, nor should one consume foul-smelling substances.
He should not drink impure things, nor should he be intent on violence.
When offered garments, ornaments, and the like, he should not wear them by force.
He should act in a way that is favorable to me, just as he would for himself regarding cold, heat, and other such conditions. (65–66)
One should perform the washing of the face, the rubbing with oil, and the application of sandalwood paste as is appropriate, and not excessively, so that it does not cause distress.
When the fire is cold, one should attend to me, but not in an overly excessive manner.
You should always exchange my garments, and you must likewise change my ornaments. You should not utter insults, nor speak in disparagement of others, nor engage in vulgar conversation. (68–69)
One should not sleep in the middle of the temple, nor should one be naked in the temple;
one should not sit with me on one's back while facing the public.
Without washing one's feet, one should not enter the interior of the temple.
Having touched the *ārātrika* lamp, one should not touch it again without first using water;
one must wash one's hands, and indeed, one should not touch me nor any other object.
One should not allow anyone else to enter, nor any woman, into the interior of the temple.
One whose mouth or hands are defiled by food remnants and the like must not enter the temple at all.
Furthermore, having removed one's garlands, flowers, and so forth—
even if one were a sovereign king— one should not give them away to other people except at the moment of their removal.
Having removed [the deity] from the previous day, one should protect it and then offer [it];
or, having placed it in the hand, one should give the immediate propitiation.
One must never again raise the curtain of concealment in the center.
Standing before the spectators, he should not cast [the vessel] into the midst of them.
Having filled the conch with water and lit a beautiful lamp,
and having put on a garment fit for sweeping, he should hold a vessel filled with fragrant substances.
Having struck the bell, one should then perform the circumambulation with lamps.
At the time of my naked form, one must never open the door;
when putting on clothes or ornaments, one should ensure the door is closed.
One should indeed remove dust, dirt, and swarms of insects every moment.
Furthermore, one should not open the house from after retiring at night until midday, except in times of distress. (78–79)
Even at midday, one should not open [the door] in such a way as to cause distress within;
at the time of eating, one should announce the meal accompanied by musical instruments. One should not provide clothing or other items that are unrefined, impure, or lacking in sattva.

One should neither wear nor offer ornaments such as necklaces, nor pure food, nor water, nor other weapons and the like. Nor should one practice meditation on objects related to mountains or on the forms of minerals. (81–82)
I am divine, existing in every way as the all-pervading inner self;
omniscient and abiding in all things, I behold [the world] while established in form.
Indeed, one-pointedness of mind during worship must be protected with great effort.
Especially in my image, the functions of all the sense organs [should be directed];
sweet and pleasing food should be given to my devotee at his meal. Just as great honor is shown to me, so should it be performed for my person.
"O beloved, I shall eat especially delicious food there;
there must be an excellent supply of wheat, *kaṅku* rice, barley, and so forth.
For my sake, one should prepare auspicious cooked food and indeed offer it. (86)
A new vessel made of gold or other precious metals must indeed be given to me.
My devotees, the followers of the Bhāgavata, who have attained the status of being objects of my grace, are worthy of partaking in my prasāda when they are adorned with garlands of tulasī. (87–88)
Men and women who are initiated and endowed with great mantras,
who are devoted self-surrenderers, are worthy of consuming the *naivedya* (food offered to the deity).
Among my exclusive devotees who dwell here, they are the practitioners of *bhakti-yoga*.
In my world, their destination is equal to mine, possessing the form of four arms.
Even those people who perform difficult vows such as the *kṛcchra* and yet desire worldly enjoyments,
they go to the great heaven and even to the world of Vairāja.
Those who abstain from pungent food and salt, who observe vows, and are devoted to my rites,
surely go to Satyaloka even if they always desire enjoyments;
provided they are devotees intent on the service of cows and are great Bhāgavatas.
Then those people go to my eternal abode, Goloka.
Those devotees who are intent on the practice of gleaning, who are free from attachment, and devoted solely to the journey, go indeed to supreme Vaikuṇṭha. || 93-94 ||
Those householders who subsist on alms, those who are devoted to me, and those who are virtuous—
they go to my eternal abode, which is imperishable, immortal, and immutable.
[Whether they die] in my house, nearby, in a sacred field, in a monastery, or even in a temple— ॥95॥
He who is separated from his life-breaths goes to my imperishable state (96).
My devotees who possess desire go to heaven through the heat of fire;
those ascetics likewise go to the world of the Sun and to the abode of Indra (97).
Those who subsist on food such as vegetables, being devoted to me, go to my world called Amṛta; of this there is no doubt.
And those who are intent on offering lamps, devoted to austerity, and have taken refuge in me— [they too go to that world].
Those who offer leaves, flowers, and other gifts go to my supreme abode;
those who are most righteous and devoted to the service of the virtuous indeed go to my home;
and my devotees who travel on foot go to the supreme, imperishable realm.
Even those who sleep on their backs and other such [unconventional] postures go to the supreme divine state.
By renouncing everything, my virtuous ones indeed become of my own nature. Wherever the body is held, they have fixed their minds upon me.
By themselves, they go to my world, the station resorted to by Rādhā and Lakṣmī.
Indeed, those who renounce, as well as followers of Sāṃkhya and Yoga, become four-armed Viṣṇus; there is no doubt that, being liberated, they assume my own form.

Accompanied by the recitation of "Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya," men and women go to my supreme abode beyond the Imperishable (Akṣara). Even those slain by weapons, provided they are devoted to my name and endowed with devotion, [attain that same state].

Indeed, those who dwell within my mind, even if they meet with sudden death, become my eternal attendants in the imperishable abode, provided they remember me for even a single moment; they attain the supreme goal. (105–106)
My followers—whether groups of men or women—never grow weary;
they proceed to the worlds of the lords, served by ten million maidens.
Those devoted to my initiation attain the state of great-souled beings in the supreme abode.
If householders, though rich in the enjoyment of desires, are devotees, they attain the state beyond transformation (vaikṛta).

Free from the fever of worldly existence, even those who have renounced—such as widows and others—who are devotees yet still desire objects of pleasure, [attain this same state] through the power of Māyā, the primary source of the worlds. (108–109)

They are born in the abode as forms of Viṣṇu and forms of Ramā; they enjoy happiness for millions of kalpas in Vaikuṇṭha. Those devotees, both men and women, who are intent on love for me, are exceedingly full of longing.
My wives indeed become those who have attained eternal liberation.
Even my gurus and householders become forms of Kṛṣṇa;
in Goloka, they enjoy all pleasures, rejoicing in eternal bliss. (111–112)
Thus has this been told to you, O sinless Lakṣmī, as you requested.
By reading or hearing this, one shall surely attain the state of Śaṅkara;
or else, one shall attain the station of Brahmā or Viṣṇu—of this there is no doubt.
I shall also relate another matter which Pārvatī spoke to Śaṅkara at the foot of the Narmadā mountain in Ṛkṣa; that which was asked brings auspiciousness,
for both suffering and happiness for devotees are merely the conceptual constructions of the mind.
Indeed, at the end of time, for the sake of the enjoyment of my devotees, I have created countless abodes such as Goloka and others within the imperishable realm (Akṣara), which are full of bliss;
and I have also created pairs of devotees and their consorts who are entirely devoted to me.
By my will they remain among these [worlds] as long as their enjoyment has not ceased. Indeed,
upon the cessation of the pleasure derived from the satisfaction of enjoyments,
those couples, intent on my own nature, go to the imperishable abode.

Thus ends the five hundred and sixty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Resolution regarding the Destiny of Devotees and Other Matters in Response to the Various Questions Put Forward by Śrī Lakṣmī," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 567 *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā*, Book 1 (Kṛtayuga-santāna) [Chapter 567]
[The Author: Chapter 568.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī! Indeed, there are sorrows for a person without devotion.
Likewise, I shall describe all forms of happiness through my yoga.
(1) For one who is distracted by manifold thoughts, enveloped by my egoism, with senses unsubdued and dwelling in hope—what indeed could be more miserable than that? (2)
Dissatisfied and excessively greedy, he causes agitation and affliction;
with his heart drawn by latent impressions (vāsanā), what indeed could be more miserable than that?
(3) One whose self is impure, devoid of dharma, and bereft of compassion and charity—
Deprived of fortune and enjoyment—what indeed could be more painful than that?
(4) Disease, delusion, old age, exhaustion, being armed with weapons, deceiving others, and being a giver of suffering to others—what indeed could be more painful than that? (5)
If one is devoid of the act of worshipping me and shuns the service of the virtuous,
becoming a source of affliction within the home— what indeed could be more painful than that?
There is no God, there is no Dharma, and the next world does not exist.
What indeed could be more painful than the thought that there will be no further rebirth?
(7) What indeed could be more painful than a man who, despite being present and receiving proper hospitality, does not take refuge in me? (8)
One who eats everything, sells all things, and is devoid of humility—who would not resort to me? What indeed could be more painful than that?
(9) He who eats even his own kin without first giving to a guest or a visitor.
If one brings about the destruction of what is ripened, what indeed could be more painful than that?
(1.567.10) What indeed could be more painful than this: being a tormentor of others, discontented, dull-witted, a defiler of the gods, devoid of merit, and rooted in decline? (11)
Indeed, having failed to attain one's own welfare and having failed to burn away one's sins,
what could be more painful than falling under the power of the time of death?
Even while possessing a kingdom, one goes helplessly into the hands of the messengers of Yama.
He undergoes the suffering of a messenger; what indeed could be more painful than that?
(13) Abandoning elephants, horses, chariots, vehicles, armies, and his circle of servants, he goes under the power of another; what indeed could be more painful than that? (14)
Some eat intoxicants, while others eat rice, ghee, and the like;
some eat dry food, and others even roots and fruits.
They enjoy beds covered with fine cloths and well-adorned.
Some lie upon blades of grass and do not strive for their own spiritual welfare.
Death is common to all; it does not abandon one person while leaving another behind.
Knowing this, they do not worship Me—what indeed could be more painful than that? (16–17)
One is seen handsome, another is ugly or hunchbacked; one is virtuous, another is devoid of virtue; there is equality only in the filling of the belly.
Likewise, one is learned while another is mute; indeed, no one here is eternal.
Knowing me thus, he does not honor me; what indeed could be more painful than that?
(19) Some miserly people, though possessing wealth, are deprived of enjoyment;
while others, despite being poor, are intent on great expenditure even when they have nothing to give. (20)
Even so, at the end of the year, the house of both is empty.
What is the fruit of that wealthy man, and what is the fruit of the poor man?
In the absence of charity, sacrifice, and other such meritorious acts, what indeed could be more miserable than that? (21)
At that time, people come to have two wives or many wives.
When he is dissatisfied with one woman, he praises another; meanwhile, the one who is unfortunate there remains constantly intent on uttering curses. (22–23)
Wealth is smeared with curses and brings about destruction in the next world;
knowing this, he does not resort to me—what indeed could be more painful than that?
Those born in noble families and provided with all means of accomplishment [desist].

They perform sinful deeds; what indeed could be more painful than that? (25) Having attained human consciousness, which is endowed with all knowledge, yet they do not take refuge in Me alone; what indeed could be more painful than that? (26)

Having performed extensive work while being solely intent upon his own self-interest, he falls into a perverted state of mind and is born for the sake of suffering. Suffering is that which opposes one's own desire; happiness is conformity to one's own desire.

For oneself, the supreme suffering is the state of being devoid of eternal bliss. (28) Indeed, that which is described as attainable by a human after death—eternal happiness through [the performance of] action—if that is not attained, then birth is in vain. (29)
While living, he is joined with suffering, and even when dead, he partakes of suffering once more.
His birth has passed away in vain; what indeed could be more miserable than that? Having worshipped me and having prepared an excellent offering of food (naivedya), [he attains liberation].
He eats the remaining food; what indeed could be more blissful than that?
(31) They approach me at the three times of day, behold my image, and perform devotion for me with love; what indeed could be more blissful than that? (32)
Having divided the food among the deities, guests, mortals, and cows,
the master of the house eats afterwards;
those who come as dependents do not depart disappointed, but leave satisfied with his gift.
For one who conducts himself in this manner, what indeed could be more blissful than that?
(34) The new moon day (*amāvāsī*) is said to occur once every month;
for those whose ancestors are satisfied on that day, what indeed could be more blissful than that? (35)
And for one who gives milk-rice (*pāyasa*) to virtuous people at the beginning of a meal and so forth,
with a face whose expression remains unchanged— what indeed could be more blissful than that?
Even though he has many wives, his mind does not waver.
It surely bestows equal happiness; what, then, could be more blissful than that?
One whose inner self is pure should observe the vow of non-violence, abandoning anger.
Upon seeing a beautiful form, an object of enjoyment, or the like, one does not fixate one's gaze upon it.

With a tranquil self, free from desire and free from delusion in every respect, he looks upon gold as if it were a clod of earth; what indeed could be more blissful than that? (39) And if his life-breath departs while he is engaged in worship, [he attains the highest state].
If death should occur for the sake of the gods, what indeed could be more blissful than that?
One should never do anything contemptible; rather, one should effect one's own liberation.
Being content whether gain or loss occurs, what indeed could be more blissful than that?
For women, the husband always exists as their vow personified;
she who conducts herself by following her husband is a *pativratā*.
Likewise, the wife’s vow is the husband himself, and the *pativratā* is his very embodiment.
When a husband lives contentedly with his wife, he becomes a bestower of happiness.
If a husband and wife are full of love for one another, what indeed could be more blissful than that?
If one were to have their senses restrained, what indeed could be more blissful than that?
Such a person endures insults and remains ever dejected in times of calamity;
yet, being intensely devoted to my worship, what indeed could be more blissful than that?
Water is obtained for free, and food is acquired through begging;
there is no anxiety regarding the protection of wealth—what indeed could be more blissful than that?
Furthermore, the body is free from disease and the digestive fire is brightly kindled. (46–47)
It digests both the ripe and the unripe; what, then, could be more blissful than that?
Cold does not afflict it, nor does excessive heat overcome it.
Dwelling among trees and in the wind—what, then, could be more blissful than that?
The worlds are one's family, and the Supreme Lord is the support everywhere.
What indeed could be more blissful than constant contemplation of Śrī Hari?
For him whose home belongs to another, it is like a cave—free from all affliction. (1.567.50)
Nourishment like that of a cuckoo, food like that of a parrot,
and service that is natural— what indeed could be more blissful than that?
Whether with desire or without desire, one who makes my abode their home [attains this].
What indeed could be more blissful than for one who is separated from [the cycle of] life?
What indeed could be more blissful than for one who looks upon his mother, father, wife, teacher, and deities as if they were a god? 52–53.
Peace, knowledge, discernment, freedom from agitation,
discrimination, fortitude, stability, and desirelessness— what indeed could be more blissful than that?
One should worship Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa Hari, the Lord of the gods of gods.
The wise devotee of the Lord, being pure, fell upon the ground like a staff;
with his head bowed and palms joined in *añjali*, he said to Hari, "Be gracious.
He should constantly ask forgiveness from Hari—what indeed could bring greater happiness than that? (55–56)
He should give me an ointment, or he should provide a massage with oil;
he should anoint my entire body and even my head with ghee.
Likewise, for as many drops of oil as are being applied, [he should do so]. (57)
For that many thousands of years he is honored in the heavenly world.
Thereafter, that man attains the blissful worlds of those who have performed meritorious deeds.
Beyond that, he finds me, the Supreme Person, known as the Imperishable.
And let him give me an ointment for rubbing the body, by which my limbs may be purified.
Pippalikā, madhuka, aśvaparṇa, and karkaṭa—
the auspicious powder of these shall bring comfort to my body.
Having thus performed the rubbing and massaging slowly and gently,
the devotee should by all means bring about my stainless purity with his hands.
Then, [he should apply] both the *āmalaka* fruit and the most excellent fragrant powder.
Therefore, having massaged all my limbs, that one of firm vows should perform for me a cleansing with alkaline substances, oils, perfumes, and medicinal pills,
and provide a bath with streams of water that brings me comfort. (63)
Afterwards, one should offer incense as well as the essence of flowers and the like;
one should also cause an offering of garlands suitable for ritual use and a handful of flowers to be presented.
Thereafter, one should give me incense mixed with fragrant substances.
Afterwards, one should give me a garment—either white or yellow linen;
then, having given me ornaments, one should prepare a seat for me.
After that, indeed, having given food, one should then consume the *prasāda*.
Afterwards, one should give me water, excellent betel-leaf, and my bedding and so forth. In this manner, one should practice devotion toward me, perform the massaging of my feet,
delight me with stories and conversation, and likewise cause me to laugh and laugh along with me.
It would bring me joy; what indeed could be more blissful than that?
Whether a male devotee or a female devotee of Kṛṣṇa should perform the offering of all one's possessions;
Kṛṣṇa truly grants him or her every fruit in Goloka.
Thus, when liberation has been attained as the supreme gain, what indeed could be more blissful than that?
[One should serve] Kṛṣṇa like Rādhā, Nārāyaṇa like Lakṣmī, Śaṅkara like Pārvatī, and the Lord Bhāskara like his radiant power.

Just as [the goddess] Māṇikyā serves her Lord, Anādikṛṣṇanarāyaṇa, in his abode by every means— what indeed could bring greater happiness than that? O beloved, those who shall truly worship me according to this procedure, ||| 72 || [shall attain that same bliss].
They shall attain supreme, eternal perfection, having reached my abode.
O lady of beautiful hips, I alone am the eternal one of all beings; I abide below, above, across, in the intermediate directions, and on high. (73–74)
I am in the man, the woman, the maiden, and the widow; I am in the body aged by decrepitude, and also in the embodied soul, whether in childhood, youth, or dwelling in the womb.
Thus, he who would know me and worship me with total devotion—
For him, there is victory in *saṃsāra*; what indeed could be more blissful than that?
Listen, O daughter of the Ocean, to that by which one does not enter a womb:
even after performing extensive deeds, he does not praise himself. (76–77)
One performs all actions with a truly pure inner self;
endowed with sovereignty, one becomes capable of bestowing grace and other such powers.
Established in the dharma of Kṛṣṇa, one discerns what ought to be done and what ought not to be done.
Likewise, he endures cold, heat, wind, rain, hunger, and thirst;
he possesses black wealth, is free from laziness, truthful in speech, and free from envy;
he is constantly devoted to celibacy and likewise intent upon his own wife.
One who acts truthfully, whose soul is pure, and who is always dear to the Blessed One;
one who shares [with others], who discerns distinctions, who is devoted to the virtuous, and deeply affectionate;
one who speaks kindly to devotees and is intent upon my service.
Thus, whoever may be devoted to me does not go to a base rebirth.
He does not desire heaven and the like; he goes to my world.
He is one who has desisted from violence toward living beings and who acts for the welfare of all creatures. (82–83)
He was endowed with equanimity toward all things, regarding a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as equal.
Even while remaining in his childhood years, he was patient, self-controlled, and devoted to what is auspicious;
when wronged by another, he did not take it to heart at all.
He should remember my service and speak my truth;
he who has turned away from falsehood and is resolved upon what is real, who always abides in the excellence of silence, and who does not cast blame even in one's absence. (85–86)
One who desires offspring should approach a woman during her fertile period, not out of lust;
such people are auspicious and devoted to me.
They do not undergo residence in a womb, but rather they dwell in my own refuge.
One should act with self-determination, having designated me as one's witness;
one should not engage in the criticism of others and should avoid deceit and dishonesty.
Abiding on my path of dharma, one should not revile religious duties.
If one endowed with these qualities performs service unto me, he attains me alone; what indeed could be more blissful than that?
O Kamalā, my beloved, listen as I speak further.
By this means, men cross the ocean of the cycle of existence within the womb—those who have conquered their senses, subdued their anger, and are free from greed and delusion;
those who constantly act for their own spiritual benefit and are devoted to the gods, guests, and teachers. (9.1–9.2)
Those who constantly worship Kapilā, as well as those who perform pilgrimages to sacred fords,
those who honor virtuous men and women, those who show respect to the elderly,
those who protect the helpless, and those who harbor no sense of duality; ||| 93 ||
He who makes no distinction among all his sons;
he who, upon seeing his own guru enraged, seeks to appease him there; he who worships a tawny cow with devotion; and he who protects a woman devoted to her husband. (94–95)
One should not step over fire with one's feet, nor should one urinate in water at any time.
One should always be devoted to the guru, possessed of knowledge, and not a chatterer.
He who, endowed with such dharma, approaches me—
He shall indeed not enter a womb; he goes to my world.
He who eats the food of another and does not disparage it, and he who is constantly devoted to me even during his childhood—[he too goes to my world]. (97–98)
Content with whatever comes his way, honoring his mother and father,
he should be a giver and an enjoyer according to justice, independent, and ever-restrained.
Established in the vow of lifelong celibacy (*kaumāravrata*), he must not engage in improper actions.
Endowed with compassion for all beings and possessed of goodness, being utterly free from desire through his intelligence and always without longing for the interests of others—
such a devotee, my disciple, goes to my world.
"O lady of noble hips, this secret is difficult even for the gods to attain.
You have been proclaimed by me as my disciple, my servant, my devotee, and my wife.
Thus did Śaṅkara speak there to Pārvatī on Mount Ṛkṣa.
"In former times, he spoke of my devotion on the banks of the Narmadā at the holy ford.

Thus ends the five hundred and sixty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the State of Happiness and the State of Suffering, the Worship of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Fruit of Offering All Actions and so forth, and the Absence of Rebirth," in the first section, the Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Chapter 569 → Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī! To the supreme resolve of those devoted to me:
even if I should become grey with dust at my sacred ford, nevertheless, I shall indeed bestow a great kingdom upon the deceased.
Formerly, at the sacred ford named Kokā, which is the site of the Varāha incarnation,
a certain hunter came to the Kokāmaṇḍala intent on violence.
There, seeing a fish in the water, he caught it with a hook.
From his hand, however, a powerful fish quickly escaped.
Then the hawk, seeing it, swiftly seized it with his talons.
Even though he flew up, he was indeed weak, unable to bear such a great burden.
Then, deprived of his feet, the fish fell into Kokāmukha.
Touched by the dust, he died and became a pure prince.
Then, in the course of time, the wife of that very same hunter—
Taking the pieces of flesh upon her head, she indeed went there on foot. A single lizard, agitated by the meat, came there to seize it.
Struck by the hunter’s wife with an arrow, it fell down dead.
Born in Candrapura as the daughter of a king, she took refuge in the dust of the Tīrthaṅkaras.
Although she was a young woman, she felt revulsion toward and had no desire for any man;
indeed, she felt revulsion even toward all men who were gentle and handsome. (8–9)
Then, as time passed, a union between the two was formed through marriage;
and thus the couple remained, constantly observing their religious duties.
At midday, however, a headache arose for the husband that was exceedingly painful.
Despite thousands of physicians and medicines, that affliction did not cease at all.
Once, his beloved wife spoke thus to her husband:
"O Lord, what is this pain that does not subside through medical treatments?"
Being asked again and again, the husband spoke to his beloved:
"Relinquish this human state; remember that former birth of yours.
If you desire to know it, then receive the permission of our parents. (13)
"My parents wish to go toward the holy site of Kokāmukha.
Having gone there, I shall speak with them; do not be distressed, O beautiful lady.
Then the daughter-in-law propitiated her mother-in-law and father-in-law.
He said, "I wish to go to Kokāmukha for the sake of visiting its sacred sites;
because of the gravity of my purpose, you two were not forbidden in any way.
"Until today, nothing at all has ever been requested from you by me anywhere."
"Previously, I requested this of you both; it behoves you to grant it.
For this son of yours is constantly afflicted by a headache; at midday, being exceedingly tormented, he indeed becomes like one who is dead. (17–18)
"Without Kokāmukha, our suffering will not cease;
we wish to go quickly to that supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
Having heard these words of his daughter-in-law, the king spoke these auspicious words:
"Take, my son, jewels, male and female servants, chariots and the like;
take gifts worthy of giving and abundant wealth.
Perform pilgrimage, my son, and protect your husband with ease, my daughter."
King Śakra granted permission to the merchant and others for the husband and wife;
having gone there, they likewise visited Kokāmukha and Hari.
Having seen the gods and bathed in the water, they then gave gifts.
When the night had passed and the couple had bathed in the morning,
the husband, having bowed his head to Viṣṇu,
showed the bones of his former birth as a fish within the mud to his wife.
"These are indeed my bones produced from a former body.
In the past, I was a fish wandering among the flocks [of creatures] in the water. As a dweller of the water, I was seized by a hunter with a hook. (25)
Having escaped from his hand, it fell there upon the ground by force;
then, pierced by the claws of a hawk greedy for meat,
it was carried off through the path of the sky and indeed fell here.
And by that excessive blow, a pain arose in my head;
I alone perceive it and remember this intense sensation.
Because of that, my suffering is not pacified; indeed, it arises intensely at midday.
Having heard this, his wife also spoke of her own previous birth:
"In my former life, I was a female lizard (cillī) sitting upon a tree, afflicted by hunger and thirst; at that time, I was searching for food within its hollow. (1.568.30)
Then a certain hunter, having killed deer at that tree with his beloved,
arrived and placed the meat on the ground.
Meanwhile, I pierced a lump of meat with my claws, which were like thunderbolts.
There a hunter saw me and struck me with an arrow;
he brought me down to the ground, and having fallen, I met my death.
By the power of this sacred field, I have been born as your beloved queen, O King.
I remember all of this— the bones of those people and my own remaining bones, which have crumbled away until only a small portion is left.
And yet, in this very state, one must perform the work of Dharma that grants liberation.
Having thus resolved, the two of them performed there in the world of Viṣṇu acts that bring happiness,
such as worship and the giving of wealth, gems, and other gifts;
being supremely delighted, they gave their own possessions in their entirety to worthy recipients.
Remaining there, O lady of excellent hips, they were established in my service;
then, leaving their bodies at that place, they went to Śvetadvīpa,
wearing white garments and adorned with divine ornaments.
They were always devoted to me, my two divine devotees, possessing celestial forms;
they were radiant and handsome, with auspicious appearances like gold, four-armed and graced by power like Lakṣmī and Viṣṇu. (38–39)
Seeing their amazement, the attendant who was there became intent on my service and remained established in my work;
having cast off his human state, he has come to my world.
There, full of splendor in every way, he approached my presence.
O Lakṣmī, my female devotees indeed become identical in form to you;
they are radiant with brilliance and adorned with pure sattva.
All of them are filled with fresh youth, possess the fragrance of blue lotuses,
have the beautiful hue of campaka flowers, are liberated, and are devoted to their vows.
O lady of beautiful hips, by my grace, they are eternally filled with youth.
All of them are filled with eternal bliss and endowed with all supernatural powers (siddhis).
This is both righteousness and fame, as well as power and great glory;
it is the supreme act among all deeds and the greatest austerity among all austerities.
Of all discourses it is the supreme, and of all compositions it is the highest work;
of all virtues it is the ultimate dharma—that which is my supreme refuge.
Having taken refuge in my dharma and having placed [my emblem] upon the head, one attains purity.
Having partaken of my grace, one is glorified in my world.
Having drunk the water from my feet and bathed in the waters of my sacred fords, and having repeatedly maintained the service of my saintly devotee; ||| 47-48 ||
By constantly serving the virtuous, performing the worship of the Bhāgavatas,
and hearing the Saṃhitā known as the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya,
people attain supreme liberation, just as Cillī and Matsya did in ancient times.
Even by remembering this at the time of death, one shall be liberated from bondage. Furthermore, O Lakṣmī, I shall tell you the auspicious times:
the month of Kumuda (Kārttika), Mārgaśīrṣa, Vaiśākha, and likewise Śrāvaṇa.
These months are vessels for my supreme joy, and these are for my worship:
on the twelfth day of the month of Kārtika, one should worship with fresh grains, fresh flowers, and nine pots of water; such a person is fit for my world.
When the time of the arrival of the clouds had passed, resting in the clear autumn;
when the sky had become stainless and the orb of the moon was spotless;
at a season that was neither too cold nor too hot, resounding with the cries of swans. || 53–54 ||
On that auspicious twelfth day of the month of Kumuda, which is filled with the fragrance of white water-lilies, blue lotuses, red lotuses, and pink lotuses,
whoever worships me and likewise observes a vow for my sake, [attains the fruit]. (55)
And he who observes the Prabodhinī [Ekādaśī] attains the supreme goal.
Even in the cool season, he who performs my worship on the twelfth day of Mārgaśīrṣa with fresh flowers attains the supreme goal. (56–57)
Just as the month of Mārgaśīrṣa and Vaiśākha are dear to me,
so too am I to be worshipped with flowers and other offerings during the day of the vow.
For nine thousand years and nine hundred years [I remain pleased].
"He who offers me worship remains in my world.
Even the gift of a single leaf of fragrant wood yields this great fruit, especially during the month of Kaumuda and likewise in Mārgaśīrṣa. (1.568.60)
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Vaiśākha,
having become intent on single-minded devotion, one who offers a garland adorned with flowers,
ornaments, and fragrant blossoms— ||6.1||
By this, worship shall have been performed here for twelve years.
One should offer fragrant *śāla* flowers and sandalwood during the month of *Kaumudī*;
one should also offer auspicious blue lotuses and sandalwood during the month of *Mārgaśira*.
On the full moon day of Vaiśākha, one should offer me land-lotuses, cool water with sugar, and sugarcane juice;
this bestows peace as well as nourishment.
Indeed, he who offers these while being devoted to me attains [these benefits].

Indeed, for a thousand divine years he dwells in Vaikuṇṭha, and beyond that, he attains my supreme abode; there is no end to his merit. For him there is neither birth nor death, nor exhaustion, nor hunger, nor thirst.
A worshiper of me shall attain such a supreme world as this.
On the twelfth lunar day of the bright fortnight of the month of Phālguna,
one should worship me with beautiful spring flowers with a pure heart.

White, pale, fragrant, beautiful, and abundant—[he who offers these] does not go to the cycle of rebirth; he goes to my world. On the full moon day of Vaiśākha, [one should offer] auspicious, fresh *śāla* flowers.
Having given [these] to me and to my devotees, a person is prepared for liberation.
Having worshipped the followers of the Śrīmad Bhāgavata and having placed me before them,
a man or woman should worship with supreme love and a pure disposition.
The ṛṣis praise him with mantras, and the devoted women with hymns from their hearts;
the gandharvas and apsarases also praise him with songs, dances, and instrumental music; and the inhabitants of the divine worlds praise the ancient Puruṣottama.
The Siddhas, Vidyādharas, Yakṣas, Piśācas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas—
all of them praise me, the god Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
The Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, the two Aśvins, and the hosts of Maruts [do the same].
Even at the dissolution of the ages, they praise the Lord of the gods of gods.
Earth, wind, the Viśvedevas, fire, the sun, and the other planets— all together praise this Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Person.
Brahmā himself, Soma, Śakra, Agni, and Cidākāśa praise Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Great Lord of the worlds.
So too do Nārada, Parvata, Asita, and the sage Devala.
Pulaha, Pulastya, Bhṛgu, and also Aṅgiras—
these and many others, including Mitrāvasu and Parāvasu,
indeed praise me, the Lord of Ramā, the supreme teacher of yogins.
O Mādhavī! The inhabitants of Satyaloka, who dwell in the support of the eight enclosures and are the Vairāja lords, indeed worship me.
Furthermore, the Pitṛs, beginning with Aryaman, those belonging to Yama, and those known as the Śravaṇas [worship me].
The years, known as Time itself, constantly praise me;
likewise do all the ṛṣis, the munis, the guardians of the quarters, the protectors of the worlds,
the treasures, the Kṛttikās, the points of the compass, the bodiless god of love, and the Manus.
All the *kalās* and all the lunar days (*tithis*), as well as the *tattvas*, praise me; the constellations, all the gods, the qualities (*guṇas*), and the castes (*varṇas*) worship me.
All the enjoyments, all the serpent-beings (*bhogins*), the *yoginīs*, and the hosts of celestial nymphs (*apsaras*) [worship me].
The sacred fords, the lakes, the rivers, the channels, and likewise the springs;
the Vālakhilyas, the Piśācas and other beings, the Pretas—all these praise me.
So too do all the Kūṣmāṇḍas, the Caṇḍikās, the Vetālas, and the Vināyakas.
The ḍākinīs and śākinīs, as well as the kṛtyās, worship me;
those born from the womb, those born from eggs, those born from sweat, and the sprouts of the earth;
humans, those born in water, and those born on land—all embodied beings worship me.
In times of distress, those dwelling in hermitages constantly offer praise to the household deities, the village deities, and the deities of forests, jungles, and other such places;
as well as to the forests, mountains and the like, the ponds, and the flowing streams. (86–87)
Both natural ponds and excavated lakes praise me;
even the dwellings situated in villages, being sentient, truly worship me.
Those performers of ritual actions who have made their abodes in the realm of Yama resort to me again and again.
Afflicted by suffering, they remember me, the Lord of Compassion, for their deliverance from misery. In some instances, those seeking knowledge constantly praise me;
and one who desires wealth obtains it to the extent that it is necessary. (1.568.89–90)
The *sūtas*, *māgadhas*, *bandins*, *cāraṇas*, and others— all panegyrists, storytellers, and those possessing the *pāṇḍava* [epithet]— constantly remember, praise,
and worship me through the marrow [of their being]. (91)
Those who bestow justice, as well as rulers, thieves, and plunderers—
whether they be of the nature of darkness (tāmasa), goodness (sāttvika), or passion (rājasa)— they all praise me.
So too do the followers of the Bhaṭṭa school, those skilled in the Gandharva arts, the Kinnaras, and those seeking the goals of human life (puruṣārtha).
Sādhya goddesses, as well as Sādhyīs, Satīs, and even Brahmācāriṇīs,
and even Ābhicāriṇīs, praise me and worship me.
Nāgas, sarpas, uragas, reptiles, deer, and so forth—
Indeed, all who abide in their own true nature worship Me alone.
To them, I grant fruits according to their disposition and in accordance with their past actions.
But those who are liberated worship Me constantly, having granted Me a dwelling place within their hearts.
I give my heart to those devotees just as they belong to me.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, all living beings are always firmly strung upon me;
they do not exist without me, nor do they tremble without me.
Without me, who am situated within the heart, they do not attain illumination at all.
I am the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord; I am the son of Ambharīṣa, the Great King, reigning over all embodied beings. (98–99)
Indeed, my speech illumines the hearts of all;
by my power, the senses perform their functions of perception.
Through my lineage, the world-process proceeds, dissolves, and persists.
All this is for the sake of my service; it is entirely based on bliss.
Therefore, O Lakṣmī, Nārāyaṇa, who is higher than the highest, should always be served with excellent offerings produced in all seasons, as well as with mental palaces. 101–102.

For the sake of uplifting them, I remain awake and do not even sleep; for I have no sleep on account of my devotees, nor any indifference toward those who have taken refuge in me. I have no laziness regarding their protection, nor do I manifest a form for one devoid of love.
Knowing this, those men and women, O beloved daughter of the ocean, who worship, praise, and remember me, shall indeed partake in liberation. So too shall those who recite,
those who cause others to hear, those who listen, and those who seek to contemplate [this].
"If all the burdens of worldly existence were to attain the supreme state,

that would be the fruit of all sacrifices for those who follow my word. (106) Thus ends the five hundred and sixty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Sacred Dust of Viṣṇu, the Liberation of Those in Śvetadvīpa, the Fruit of Performing Worship of the Lord on the Twelfth Days of Kārttika, Mārgaśīrṣa, Vaiśākha, and other months, and the Attainment of the Lord through the Praise and other acts performed by all beings and living creatures," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
