Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī! Śambhu, the supreme devotee of Viṣṇu, spoke to Pārvatī regarding my greatness arising from the sacred fords and other such places.
Candradvīpa, Prabhāsatu, and Tāmraparṇeya; Gabhastimān, Nāgadvīpa, Saumya, and Gandharva;
Vāruṇa and Kaumārikeya—these indeed are the regions of Narmadā.
Sprinkled with the waters of the Narmadā and drinking that water,
those embodied beings, through the power of merit, go to heaven and even to liberation.
Living beings experience the auspicious and inauspicious fruits of their own actions.
For the sake of the highest good, austerity, fire-offerings, charity, meditation,
worship, compassion, and bathing in the Narmadā should be performed to attain auspiciousness.
I shall relate an ancient narrative exactly as it occurred.
In ancient times, during the Kṛta Yuga, there was a royal sage named Kuvalayāśva.
That king indeed gave many thousands of various kinds of gifts at all the sacred fords with true devotion.
King Kuvalayāśva, devoted to the practice of charity and righteousness, performed sacrifices— excluding those on the Narmadā—
and it is said that he went to Kurukṣetra during the conjunction of Rāhu and the Sun.
One hundred thousand horses and ten thousand elephants,
along with gold, rubies, gems, and various garments,
he gave to the Brahmins with supreme faith during the planetary conjunction.
O King, having scattered all the remaining material in that field,
handful by handful at every spot like tiny pebbles, he performed his ablutions.
Then he went to the city of Avadhya and took refuge in Hari within his own kingdom.
Now, King Mucukunda, a devotee of Viṣṇu who had conquered his senses,
was the lord of the Daityas; and he went during a solar eclipse to the Lord of Oṃkāra on the Vaidūryasiddha mountain by the Narmadā.
He resided at Koṭitīrtha at the confluence of the Narmadā and Kapilā;
there he possessed one hundred thousand milch cows, ten thousand horses,
a thousand elephants, and a thousand chariots.

Then, having performed his bath as was appropriate, he gave to the Brahmins a thousand desire-yielding vehicles adorned with golden garlands, as well as wealth, grain, fine garments, and various kinds of jewels. (15–16)
He gave ten thousand [gold pieces] as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to Oṃkāranātha;
whatever desire anyone wished for, he granted that to them.
Having performed this at the supreme holy site, he returned once more to his own abode.
Then, after some time, by the power of their respective merits,
the two kings attained heaven, where they were served by Apsarases and resembled Indra.
However, the chariot of Mucukunda indeed continues to travel perpetually upward in the celestial realm.
The vehicle of Kuvalayāśva, however, always travels beneath it.
Both were reported by messengers to the wise Dharmarāja:
"The royal sage Kuvalayāśva and the exceedingly powerful Mucukunda."
Both of these, situated in their celestial chariots, arrived together in another world.
At that moment, Mucukunda’s vehicle rose up above them;
indeed, it remained high above, at a distance of a thousand yojanas.
The vehicle of the Lord of the Unslayable (Yama) proceeded toward the lower region.
Upon hearing this, Dharmarāja also questioned Citragupta:
"Tell me, which of the two kings should I honor with offerings of *argha* and other rites?"
Having observed the power of the merit of the two, Citragupta indeed spoke:
"First honor Mucukunda by virtue of the majesty of the Revā.
He then questioned the Seven Sages, and they spoke just as Citragupta had.
"Having approached Mucukunda, honor him with water for the feet and the guest-offering (arghya).
The lord of the Dānavas, being exceedingly meritorious, is to be worshipped with a gift of Kapila cow's milk.
Thus addressed, Dharmarāja approached the lord of the Dānavas.
Then, having joined his palms in reverence, he stood before the vehicle:
"O Lord of Daityas, may you be well today; you are endowed with all virtues.
By this gift, the three worlds have been conquered by you upon the earth. (27–28)
"At the end of the southern Oṃkāra, at the confluence of the Mūrti and Kāpila rivers,
on the bank of the Saptakalpa— there is no counting its merit.
Having spoken thus and having performed worship, he showed him the path.
Mucukunda went to the world of Viṣṇu, Vaikuṇṭha.
Then, having approached King Kuvalayāśva, Dharmarāja himself said: "I truly offer you a welcome."
The king said: "There is indeed constant enmity between the gods and the Dānavas.
You are a god; how is it that you previously worshipped a Daitya?
Having abandoned me, that lord of the Dānavas was honored by you with water for the feet and the *arghya* offering."
"But how is it, O Dharmarāja, that all this has been done perversely?
Yama replied: "O King of kings, abandon your despondency; the course of karmic actions is profound. What remains for me to do must be performed according to the law."

Indeed, the merit on the banks of the Narmadā shall be even greater than that of Kurukṣetra; no other holy sites, even including Kalpagayā, can equal it by even a sixteenth part. As the witness of the actions of all, I indeed act according to what is right.
Filled with wonder, that king quickly bowed to Yameśvara and,
desiring to bathe in the Narmadā, proceeded toward the confluence at Kapilā. He bathed at the confluence, for the king’s [vehicle] was indeed divine.
Then, when it was full, he ascended to the eternal world of Viṣṇu.
Indeed, such is the supreme, merit-bestowing Narmadā-tīrtha, O beloved of Kamalā! It bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and washes away all sins.
Even sinful people attain liberation through immersion in the waters of the Revā;
by the dharma of Viṣṇu, the ocean of saṃsāra, so difficult to cross, is traversed. Yet people who are attached and deluded indeed persist in extreme wickedness.
They did not know themselves, nor Kṛṣṇa, nor indeed the gods;
they did not hear of the supreme good, just as one with eyes does not see when standing on level ground yet walking slowly,
stumbling at every step.
Even when awakened, living beings do not understand that they have been released from Yama;
under the sway of various passions and greed, those men suffer in vain.
Having seen the painful pit of the womb, which is directly manifest and awakens one to terror, [they still do not realize their plight]. (42–43)
They do not understand the path to liberation; for them, the Revā does not grant release.
All subjects have become like ghosts, subject to the jurisdiction of the realm of Yama.
Śiva said: "Listen, O Mountain! I shall relate to you an ancient narrative."

Formerly, the Sun-god related this narrative concerning the Narmadā to his own son Yama, for the sake of delivering the world: "One should take refuge in the virtuous goddess Narmadā, who carries her seven-fold current. (45-46)
Indeed, through bathing, immersion, drinking, as well as acts of giving and other such deeds,
that Narmadā bestows a divine abode, liberation, heaven, and ultimate bliss;
when meditated upon, she is the destroyer of the sins of the wicked.
When remembered and praised by name, she who bestows heaven wards off the messengers of Yama.
By uttering "Narmade, Narmade," a sinner does not behold the realm of Yama;
even if situated in hell, if he should remember Revā, Hari, and Hara, [he is liberated].
He is liberated from the messengers of Yama at that very moment; there is no doubt about this.
Vaidūryaparvata, Ṛkṣa, as well as Amarakaṇṭaka, Oṃkāra, and the Narmadā—these bestow the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Siddheśvara, Yajñeśa situated in the center, the moon-adorned [Śaśibhūṣaṇa],
and Kapileśa as the fourth— this is the field of Śiva that bestows liberation.
They perform worship of these [deities] with flowers, incense, lamps, and libations.
Those who go to the eternal world of Śiva, the domain of the Lord,
[attain it] through the gift of cows, the gift of gold, and likewise the gift of sesame seeds;
as well as the gift of food, the gift of water, and even all kinds of household utensils.
Those who give gifts of palaces and gardens attain liberation;
indeed, those devotees of the Blessed One do not go to the realm of Yama.
This world is always to be examined as it exists in a state of constant mixture.
Honor is met with dishonor; union with the beloved occurs during separation;
youth is seized by old age; and happiness is beset by suffering.
Furthermore, the body is worn out by wrinkles and grey hair.

That very youth and beauty of man and woman which is mutually pleasing, once seized by old age, is no longer pleasing to either. Likewise, one regards oneself, now possessed of infirmity, as something entirely new.
Who else would be more senseless than he who, seeing this, does not become dispassionate?
Overcome by old age, a man is humiliated by his wife, sons, and other kinsmen, as well as by servants of ill conduct, because of his incapacity. (59)
One who is not overtaken by old age is capable of accomplishing virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation;
therefore, one should practice virtue quickly.
The imbalance of wind, bile, phlegm, and so forth constitutes the entire range of diseases.
It indeed dwells eternally within the body, constantly causing manifold sufferings.
These sufferings are to be known by one's own self; what is there to be known by others?
One hundred and one deaths, O friend, proceed perpetually.
Among these, one is of the nature of time (*kāla-rūpa*), while the rest are known as adventitious (*āgantuka*).
Time, being tranquil, wears away the body at every moment;
indeed, the adventitious factors wear away the principles (*tattva*) at every moment. (63–64)
Adventitious causes of death do not indeed kill one absolutely;
they are driven away by remedial means such as medicines and the like.
Kālamṛtyu, however, whose nature consists of moments and so forth, is of the essence of Mahākāla.

Untimely death of the body, arising from poison, alcohol, and the like, as well as for all [beings] arising from falling into water, falling into fire, and so forth, is not pacified by recitations, burnt offerings, gifts, and medicinal remedies. (66–67)
Through floods of water and the like, he brings about the destruction of insects;
this man is ever aware and fears untimely death. Various painful diseases, as well as creatures such as serpents and the like, [afflict him].
Horned beasts and malevolent spells are the gates of death for embodied beings.
Even Dhanvantari himself cannot restore to health an embodied being seized by Time, even if that being is surrounded by diseases, serpents, and other perils. (69–70)
Neither medicine, nor austerity, nor charity, nor friends, nor kinsmen are able to protect a traveler seized by time.
There is no suffering equal to death; there is no enemy equal to death.
There is no time equal to death for embodied beings who imagine themselves secure in happiness.
Death severs everything—virtuous wives, sons, friends, kingdoms, sovereign power, and pleasures—even when it is being resisted with great force. (72–73)
"O son, this meaningful teaching has been told to you by me, Dharmarāja.
In the end, everything will result entirely in eating at the appointed time.
Therefore, with every effort, one should follow the path of Nārāyaṇa."
Revā removes all suffering and destroys all grief.
Whatever desires one may long for, Revā grants them all.
Knowledge, meditation, and study—all these are simply the service of Revā. (75–76)
O Lakṣmī! Sacrifice, charity, austerity, truth, and the service of the waters of the Revā are such that thousands of *brahmakūrca* penances are not equal to the water of the Revā.
Indeed, a gift of a cow given there bestows the merit of ten thousand *gomeda* sacrifices.
In ancient times, there was a king named Śaśānka who resided on the banks of the Narmadā.
He performed acts of charity, sacrifice, and austerity at the Amarakaṇṭaka mountain;
he gave a cow that had recently calved to a high-souled Brāhmaṇa.
By the power of this gift, he became a traveler of the divine upper realms;
as long as both the calf’s feet and its face were visible within the womb,
so long was the earth to be known as a cow, complete with its mountains, forests, and groves.
A cow with golden horns and silver hooves, accompanied by her calf and a bronze milking vessel;
together with *kuśa* grass and sesame seeds, she is offered at Koṭitīrtha—situated between Oṃkāra and Amara—by one who has bathed in the Narmadā, O Moon. (8.1–8.2)
He indeed assigned these, numbering one thousand, to the Brāhmaṇas.
By the merit of that gift, the king then shone in heaven by means of a celestial vehicle;
and at that time, the drums of the gods resounded in the sky.
At that very moment, King Hariścandra also ascended the vehicle;
having given a thousand cows at Kurukṣetra, he arrived by means of the vehicle,
with a golden parasol held over him and being fanned with chowries.
Indeed, Hariścandra was situated a thousand *yojanas* below;
seeing him thus in such a low position, he quickly approached the Unborn One (*Aja*).
With a dejected countenance, he then asked the Grandfather (*Pitāmaha*) for the reason.
By me, however, an infinite gift was given at Kurukṣetra;
by Śaśāṅka, likewise, an infinite gift was given at the Revā.
How is it that the merit of the Narmadā excels even that of Kurukṣetra? (87–88)
"By this means, I, Hariścandra, who was situated in a low place, have become elevated.
Having heard this, Brahmā said to Hariścandra: "Do not give way to grief.
Formerly, during a solar eclipse, on Mount Amarakaṇṭaka, by the Moon—"
O King, thousands of sacrifices have been performed by me elsewhere;
yet, when all other holy fords were once weighed against Amarakaṇṭaka,
the Lord of the Immortals was found to be superior.
"If one desires the supreme state, let the goddess who flows through the Kalpa be served.
Then Hariścandra, having bowed down, went to Amarakaṇṭaka;
there, on the bank of the Narmadā, he then gave away goods, wealth, and cattle.
Then, by the arising of his merit, his celestial chariot ascended upwards.
Having ruled the kingdom for a long time, he then attained great satisfaction and,
through the power of the Narmadā, went indeed to Vaikuṇṭha.
Although many gifts were indeed given by him to the Kaurava, the fruit of those was not at all equal to that of Narmada. Thus,
the sacred ford of Narmada is supreme and brings about all forms of welfare.
Bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation, it is endowed with ten million sacred fords (tīrthas).
All of this was indeed recounted by Śaṅkara to Śivā;
and I have now declared to you, O Mahālakṣmī, that fruit which arises from the Narmadā.
Any person who hears this, O Lakṣmī, shall obtain the fruit of giving a thousand cows;
by reading, hearing, or remembering it, one indeed obtains such a fruit.

Thus ends the five hundred and sixty-ninth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Superiority of the Greatness of Narmadā and Marakaṇṭaka, and the Disparity between the Vimānas of Kuvalayāśva and Mucukunda, and the Disparity between the Vimānas of Hariścandra and Śaśāṅka," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Śrī Lakṣmī said: O Kṛṣṇa! I have indeed heard the meritorious greatness of Narmadā and of Amareśvara; [I have heard] that which arises from Koṭitīrtha, and that which is a thousandfold compared to Kurukṣetra.
"How was it that you, O Lord, previously fashioned this through illusion?
In some cases, when merit is equal, [the result] is equal; in others, it is deficient or even excessive.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Everything I have composed is obtainable through Narmadā, who flows for seven kalpas;
likewise, she belongs to the gods, the ṛṣis, and the virtuous ones of those seven kalpas.
Due to my yoga, Narmadā is superior to all my incarnations.
And during the eternal dissolution, Revā remains near me in the Ocean of Milk;
devoted to the service of my feet, that beautiful woman stays by my side.
Through my yoga, my divine Māyā becomes most excellent.
Listen to how this entire world, consisting of illusion, has been fashioned by me;
having created it, I enter into it through my yoga, and thus it remains as mine.
Listen: even Rudra, Indra, and the Grandfather (Brahmā) do not know me.
"Even though the lords of the gods were created by me, Nārāyaṇa himself,
O beautiful one, they all consist of sacred fords (tīrtha) because of my dwelling within them;
when the rain-god pours down rain upon a region, that region is filled with water."

The sky becomes devoid of water; Māyā, which takes the form of my creative power, again causes the sky to be covered with waters in an instant. Again there is rain, and again it is empty—this is the Māyā fashioned by me.
O beautiful lady, all water is indeed purifying by my presence;
yet that which is specifically intended for a purpose is especially purifying,
just as the water of mountain torrents, when resorted to by the virtuous, is purifying.
Then, it becomes even more purifying when served by the gods;
yet, when served by me, it becomes most purifying.
What need is there to say it is so when served repeatedly, even throughout every kalpa?
The Revā was served by me in the Ocean of Milk; consequently, she became equal to me.
She is the purifier of purifiers, the most auspicious among auspicious things, the supreme bestower of liberation among those who grant liberation, for she exists through my own *māyā*.
That the moon wanes in one fortnight and waxes again in the next,
and that it is not seen at all on the new-moon day— this is an illusion created by me.
O beautiful one, in the winter, the water in a well becomes warm.
It becomes cool in the summer; this is an illusion created by me. Furthermore, the sun always travels along a single path and not otherwise;
it always rises in the east and sets in the west.
O beautiful one, through the variety of its arrangements, this Māyā of mine proceeds from depth to softness and coolness, and then upward to intensity;
thus semen and blood, though distinct, are produced within the body.
From the union of those two, conception occurs; it never happens otherwise.
And it is born from one of the same species, for it is not produced from a different species.
Having entered the womb, the living being indeed experiences pleasure and pain.
Without a body, there is indeed never any suffering or happiness for the self anywhere.
Having been born, one forgets the womb; this is an illusion created by me.
According to one's karma, a living being continues to exist even with a different body.
According to one's karma, death occurs; even while remaining in the body, one departs.
Within the embryo, a mixture of semen and blood resembling a jujube fruit, there arise the fingers, the feet, the arms, the head, and likewise the waist. (22–23)
The back, as well as the belly, the teeth, the lips, and the nose;
the ears, the eyes, the two skull-hemispheres, the forehead, and likewise the tongue—these are produced by my *māyā*, and from them living beings are born. (24)
Only that which he has eaten and drunk is digested by his fire;
below, urine flows out. This is an illusion created by me.
Sound, touch, form, taste, smell, and likewise other [objects]— [are likewise illusions. 25–26.

The elements beginning with the gross elements (bhūta), those beginning with the mind (mānasa), those beginning with the vital breaths (prāṇa), and even the constituent tissues (dhātu)—all these indeed proceed from the principle of food (annatattva). This is an illusion (māyā) created by me.
Even after thousands of all seasons have passed, it remains for a long time.
She does not know even how to turn back, nor does she know what is conducive to her well-being.
She does not truly understand matters such as food and so forth. Why? What kind of gain could there be? O beautiful one, this is but a deception of mine. (28–29)
The divine waters created by me, which manifest visible forms from the invisible,
become earthly rivers that appear full of abundant water;
yet in summer they all dry up, and the cycle is exactly like that.
They arise and wither away; this is an illusion that recurs every year.
Indeed, the sky is of the nature of emptiness, and the wind is its mover;
yet, upon reaching the Himalayas, it even becomes composed of ice.
The snow, consisting of stone, melts very gradually from the mountain peak;
having reached the earth, it becomes the Gaṅgā, which brings happiness to the land.
The clouds carry forth water, having drawn it up from the salt ocean.
They rain down sweetness upon the world, for the flow has been made by me.
Yet in some places that water is considered bitter in form, and in others sweet;
it arises with diverse qualities—this is my *māyā*, O Lotus-born One. (34–35)
"O herb, I deposit my power within you, which destroys disease.
Or, while the herb is being administered, I become Time and take it away.
[I am] the embryo, the child, the youth, the old man, the decrepit, and one devoid of strength."
The seed, the sprout, the leaf, the stalk, the stem, and the flower;
the fruit, the sap and so forth, the satisfaction, and from one seed, thousands of seeds—yet sometimes a seed is fruitless; this is the illusion (māyā) created by me, O beloved. (37–38)
The men and women created by me possess hundreds of sons, yet I have no son; this is my *māyā*, O Lotus-born One. From a single body alone, millions of living beings are born.
On the head there are insects and lice; on the clothes, bedbugs and the like;
in the pores of the skin, insects arise from sweat, such as nits and so forth;
and even when the limbs are cut away, worms emerge from within the flesh.
Just as minute insects arise within urine and stalks such as those of the *nalā* plant,
so too are embryos produced from semen born in the form of offspring.
Indeed, from a single body alone, various distinct creations are born.
All sons are one's own children because they are born from oneself;
however, worms and the like, though produced from the same source, are dissimilar, and thus no affection exists for them.
Sentient beings feel affection for a son who is similar to themselves, even when that son is merely a lump of flesh.
This illusion has been placed by me among all living beings:
hostility toward one insect, and excessive attachment toward another as a son.
Indeed, sons drink only the blood of insects, yet they drink the blood of everyone.
In the womb, you were a drinker of the mother’s blood; likewise, in her lap, you were a drinker of milk.
In childhood, you were a drinker of toys; in youth, a drinker of riches.
In the state of madness and at death, you were a drinker of peace and a drinker of breath.
"In this way, O beautiful lady, affection for everyone is but a deception of mine!
Affection may exist between man and woman, and the affection of a woman for a man;
but between two women or two men, there is no such thing—such is my deception."

In water, on earth, in taste, in the body, in rain, and in the seed that is eaten—therein I discharge nectar; when hunger is present, that is perceived as such. When there is no hunger, it becomes poison; this, O beautiful one, is my Māyā.
The world understands it thus: "Garuda carries Acyuta.
But I, remaining within, go forth having taken Garuda with me.
All the worlds, as well as the gods who eternally partake of the sacrificial offerings, understand this.
"But I shall worship the dwellers of heaven in the form of a sacrifice.
(52) All the worlds know that the preceptor bestows initiation;
however, through my power of illusion (*māyā*), I abide in the preceptor in the form of initiation itself. (53)
All the worlds know that Varuṇa guards the ocean;
however, standing within Varuṇa, I always protect the oceans.
All the worlds know that Kubera is the guardian of wealth.
However, I preserve his status as Kubera in the form of wealth.
All the worlds know that Vṛtra was slain by Śakra;
yet, by means of my power of illusion (*māyā*), I remained within Śakra and caused Vṛtra’s destruction.
Thus do people know that the great Sun is Nārāyaṇa;
however, it is I who, having entered the Sun, illuminate according to my capacity.
Stability was granted by me to Dhruva, and likewise impartiality to Meru.
In the ocean I am in the form of the submarine fire (vāḍava), and in the clouds I possess the form of the wind.
Water remains in the sky, yet people do not see it at all;
even the gods do not know where the nectar (amṛta) resides.
"An elixir created by magic remains in the forest in every way;
I shall certainly bestow upon it the power that always destroys disease.
For the world knows thus: 'The king protects the subjects.'"
But I, having entered the king, protect my subjects.
At the time of creation I take the form of evening; at night I possess the form of dissolution; and in the morning, by means of my very power of illusion (māyā), I become the nature of the embryo.
By means of my *māyā*, I abide in the sun and cause everything to ripen;
by means of my *māyā*, I abide in fire and cause everything to ripen.
I possess the form of the sun’s rays and illuminate the celestial sphere.
Having brought about the dissolution at the time of pralaya and having indeed withdrawn the universe, I lie upon Śeṣa;
yet even then, Śeṣa lies down by my power of illusion (māyā).
Behold the power of my illusion: you always exist in the form of a woman.
"How is it that you, Lakṣmī, are not born in male form? Tell me this.
This very Māyā of mine, O Lakṣmī, manifests its activity in your female form;
it is that same Māyā of mine which manifests its activity in my male form."
From the midst of the waters, I create Prajāpati, Hara, and Viṣṇu;
yet even they do not know me, being deluded by my Māyā.
In a former kalpa, I was a sage and a brahmin named Somaśarman. (67–68)
Though he was a devotee, being concealed by *māyā*, he did not recognize his own supreme [nature].
O large-eyed one! My *māyā* is Rohiṇī, the hair-raising one;
sometimes, through the fickleness of the senses, she binds even a yogin.
Somaśarman, emaciated by my power of illusion, indeed attained womanhood.
He had committed no such deed nor any offense;
even though he was intent upon propitiating me, he obtained birth as a Niṣāda woman.
"O Lakṣmī! He constantly meditated upon my beautiful form.
Then, after a long time, I was pleased by his acts of devotion and his constant austerities; thus, I became manifest before him. (72)
"For the sake of a boon, he was addressed by me: 'I am pleased; I grant you your desire.
[Choose] jewels, gold, cows, and even an empire free of thorns;
or else, if you wish for heaven, where there is happiness and beautiful women. (73–74)
Wealth, vehicles, mounts, armies, and even riches;
golden vessels, palatial mansions, and radiant golden ornaments;
as well as inexhaustible bowls and various kinds of nectar. (75)
"O twice-born one, tell me, I shall bestow upon you divine enjoyments and lordly powers.
O Brahmin, I grant you a boon, whatever your heart desires.
Having heard my words, the Brahmin bowed and spoke to me softly: (76–77)
"If you are not angry, O Lord, I beg for a boon:
whatever has been spoken by you, O God, all that must be granted to me.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, even though he was a devoted devotee, he made his request with intense longing.
I said to him: "O sinless one, why do you ask for all this?
Bondage for my devotee causes me distress.
At that time, desiring to see a marvel and wishing to behold my *māyā*, [he spoke]. (1.570.80)
He spoke these sweet words to me, which were tinged with passion yet devoid of worldly attachment:
"I desire neither gold, nor cows, nor jewels, nor a kingdom, nor heaven, nor beautiful women;
nor inexhaustible sovereignty, nor a worthy recipient, nor nectar, nor vehicles and mounts. (81)
"I wish to enjoy [this], O Blessed One; I do not desire divinity, O Lord.
(82) Likewise, even a single one of thousands of heavens does not please me.
But what is it that I desire, such that you play with me in this way? (83)"
"O Lord of Gods, for the sake of illustration, I choose to see but a small portion.
This *māyā* is indeed seen as real, yet it is called false by the great seers.
Of what nature is it to be known? Please demonstrate it by way of an example."
Then, having heard his words, I spoke there to him:
"O Brahmin, why do you seek my illusory power? Practice devotion and obtain happiness.
Even the gods do not know it, being utterly deluded by my illusion."
But you do not understand at all, even though you have fallen into illusion;
for you desire that which is unattainable, even though your task is already accomplished.
How then can you wish to remain as one whose work is undone, and why do you grieve?
Though addressed thus, that deluded one, enchanted by my illusory power (māyā),
said to me: "O Kṛṣṇa, if you are pleased with me because of my devotion or my austerity,
show me a small portion of your māyā, so that I may understand it as such."
"I shall indeed not be bound again to the entire wheel of saṃsāra.
Then I said to him, "Go to the place of Kubjāmraka;
on the most divine bank of the Gaṅgā, you will obtain everything there."
Having heard my words and having circumambulated me,
he then departed for the holy site of Kubjāmraka at dawn, desiring to employ his illusory power.
Thereupon, he took up his patched garment, bamboo staff, water vessel, and tunic.
Having placed his provisions on the bank and bowed to the Gaṅgā again and again,
he then took water upon his head, performed the ritual sipping (ācamana),
drank some water, and, remembering me, entered the waters to bathe.
Then, by my power of illusion, the brahmin vanished from view in the water;
he entered the womb of a woman in a Niṣāda dwelling nearby.
There, afflicted by the pains of the womb, he reflected in his heart: (94–95)
"Alas, what a misery I have encountered, surely due to some past misdeed, that I dwell within the womb of a Niṣāda woman, which is like a hell!
Fie on my asceticism! Fie on my actions! Fie on their fruit! And fie on this life! (96)
I, who now dwell here within the womb of a Niṣāda, amidst a mass of urine—
foul-smelling, unbearable, and filled with wind, bile, phlegm, and dust— what is the use of speaking here? What indeed is the use of weeping for one who is already lost?
Desiring to test his illusory power (*māyā*), he was made to enter a field of urine.
"Where is Viṣṇu? Where am I? And where indeed is that water of the Gaṅgā?
Where is this womb of the Niṣāda woman, and likewise, where is this pool of urine? (99)
"Having emerged from the cycle of existence within the womb, I shall afterwards attain peace.
While he was reflecting thus, the nine months passed as if they were a single moment;
when the tenth month was complete, he emerged from the womb.
As he fell to the ground, the thought concerning the embryo was lost;
then that girl was born as the daughter of a Niṣāda. Deceived by illusion, she forgot her entire Brahminhood.

Then, having been married by her father, the young woman, beloved of the fisherman, gave birth to six sons and seven daughters within a period of two years. She ate both what is fit and unfit to eat, and she drank both what is fit and unfit to drink. (103–104)
Having caused the killing of hares and other animals, she even makes a meal of their flesh;
she knows not what should or should not be done, nor does she discern what should or should not be said.
Since she is shrouded by a web of illusion, she knows not who is approachable and who is not.
When I was fifty years of age, she was impelled by me within my heart.
Taking a water-pot for the purpose of washing clothes smeared with oil, she went to bathe right there where her garment had previously been placed. (106–107)
Having set aside her clothes on the bank and placed her water-jar there, she—
tormented by the heat of perspiration and desiring a bath for her head—
entered the Gaṅgā to bathe; at that moment, that Brahmin was born.
The Brahmin named Somaśarman remembered his former history:
how he had come outside to the bank in the morning and seen the clothes,
staffs, and water-pots that he had placed there, which he saw again at the hour of midday.
Right there at his side, a woman was holding a jar made of human excrement; at that time,
at midday, the brahmin beheld a great wonder and immediately cast away the fisherman’s clothes and other belongings.
He took up the discarded garment of Dhautra and, out of shame, wore it.
Then, sitting upon the sand, he grieved greatly as he remembered:
"What blameworthy deed, leading to such extreme suffering, have I committed through my sinful actions?"
Because I fell away from right conduct and reached such a state,
I indeed became a Niṣādī; for I did not distinguish between what was fit to be eaten and what was unfit,
and I killed all living beings dwelling in water, on land, and elsewhere.
I have consumed what should not be drunk and committed forbidden sexual acts;
I have seen neither what should be said nor what should not be said, and I have repeatedly committed theft and other such deeds.
Furthermore, sons and daughters were begotten by me upon Niṣāda women.
Children who ought to drink my breast milk dwell in my house;
they await my return, for I have indeed become a man here.
What is to be done? What is not to be done? I do not cross over the delusion of Māyā.
Overwhelmed by grief for his offspring, he fell into a state of recollecting his former birth as a Brahmin;
having become a Brahmin once more, he sat in silence, filled with great shame. In the meantime, the Niṣāda and the boys were there.
Because she had been gone for a long time, they came then to search for her;
there they sought their wife and mother as they wept.
And the Niṣāda, accompanied by his children, questioned that brahmin.
"O twice-born one, you have seen my wife here as she came to bathe.
Her young daughters are weeping piteously at home, deprived of breast milk and even their midday meal. (121–122)
"O Brahmins, do you see any other men or women who have come here to fetch water for my wife, or to wash her clothes, or likewise to bathe? If so, tell me of them. (123)
If she had returned carrying the jar in her hand, she would have been spared;
but since she did not receive an answer, she wept again.
People saw that brahmin accompanied by his staff and water-pot.
Not seeing that woman, how could they give an answer? Bhīla, tormented by grief upon seeing the water-jar, the cloth, and so forth,
lamented piteously, not seeing his own wife.
Could she have been seized by some crocodile while bathing?
(1.27) Never before have I spoken anything unpleasant to her regarding her duties; nor have I ever spoken such words even in a dream, so self-destruction would not be possible. (1.28)
But has she been devoured by a cruel *piśāca* or a *rākṣasa*,
or perhaps forcibly carried away to another land?
What evil deed did I commit in the past that brings such bitter fruit?
"By whom my wife, while still young in life, has met her end before my very eyes—
come here, O blessed one, my beloved, you who follow my heart!
Behold these children and girls, weeping and likewise hungry."
"O Fate, you will surely know that I am both hungry and thirsty;
if you hear me here, grant me my beloved in accordance with dharma.
While the Niṣāda was thus lamenting here and there—
The Brahmin spoke with shame: "Go to the Niṣāda; she does not exist.
She has gone according to her karma, and in every way there is no turning back for you.
Protect those children; go, why do you distress yourself in vain? (1.33–1.34)
"Out of compassion, I shall tell you how she became your beloved;
by the mere act of bathing, the sage was restored to his former state through Māyā.
The Niṣāda said to that Brahmin, "How indeed did you attain womanhood?"
"And how did you also attain manhood? Tell this to me who asks.
The brahmin said: "At that time, Hari was directly perceived by me through devotion;
he invited me to choose a boon, and I too chose what was desired then."
"O Lord, show me your illusory power (māyā); what would it be like?
Then I was told by him, "Go to the water at Kubjāmraka.
Having said, "There you shall see it," he vanished from sight.

Having come here and bathed in the Gaṅgā, I, the daughter of a Niṣāda born from the womb of a Niṣādī, then became your wife. Having bathed today, I have indeed been reborn as a Brāhmaṇa just as before.
Upon hearing this, that Niṣāda and the boys vanished;
but I, O Lakṣmī, remained there in that form, manifesting through my illusory power (māyā).
At midday, the Brahmins arrived to bathe at the place of Somaśarman.
"How was it that the forenoon was made to pass today on the bank?
And how is it that you have remained here from morning until midday?
O beloved, at the half-day's mark, you displayed the illusion of being fifty years old!"
Then, having revealed myself, I said to him regarding his past deeds:
"In another life, you did not offer salutations to virtuous devotees.
Because of that sin, this experience has come to you in the guise of an illusion."
"Go, O Brahmin, to the supreme abode, Śvetadvīpa; may you be happy!
(145) Thereupon the Brahmin went to that abode and Nārāyaṇa vanished.
O Lakṣmī! This Māyātīrtha exists on earth as a bestower of liberation. (146)
"Indeed, from hearing and chanting this, there shall surely be both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Śaṅkara spoke thus to Pārvatī long ago at the sacred site of Narmadā.

(147) Thus concludes the section in the first book, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, concerning: the manifestation of Māyā by the Blessed Lord; the transformation of the Brahmin Somaśarman into a Niṣāda woman upon seeing Māyā; his becoming the mother of twelve children; and finally, his restoration to Brahminhood and liberation through immersion in the waters, along with the majesty of Māyā-tīrtha.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, I shall describe the supreme moving pilgrimage site (jaṅgama-tīrtha).
Those who are pure devotees of the Lord are truly my own forms.
Those virtuous ones who bow down to them indeed bow down to me alone;
O Kamalā, I am known here by them—of this there is no doubt.
Those twice-born ones and others who desire to see me and are devoted to me—
these pure devotees of the Lord (bhāgavatas) are always worthy of worship and should be visited by men.
Especially on this earth, I am present in the form of holy men and the twice-born.
Therefore, those who serve the virtuous are my devotees; of this there is no doubt.
He who desires for me, once attained here, the supreme liberation, should, with a mind focused on no other, please my devotees.
One should always satisfy me, as well as virtuous men and women,
through service, through obedience, and by giving them whatever they desire.
Listen, Lakṣmī, I shall tell you a story from a former age.
There was a great sage named Raibhya, dwelling at the bottom in the midst of the water.
(7) He was intent upon my very worship, established in the practice leading to liberation;
he was a yogi who had conquered his senses, an ascetic with a divine form. (8)
For ten thousand years he remained with his arms raised upward;
for a thousand years he subsisted on water, and for that same length of time he subsisted on moss.
Then, abandoning residence upon the earth, he dwelt in the water for ten thousand years.
Indeed, I was propitiated by that sage through his supreme devotion.
Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; obeisance.
Chanting the mantra and meditating upon Me, he remained dwelling in the midst of the water.
Delighted by that, I went into the water in the presence of Raibhya;
I went directly into the Gaṅgā, and the water was seen by me to have become dry.
Then Raibhya, rising on the bank, approached a mango tree.
At that time, even the broad mango tree became humpbacked.
Just as the tree stood covering the sage like an umbrella,
I likewise became humpbacked and went beneath the mango tree.
Indeed, that holy place on the Ganges is called Kubjāmraka on earth.
Seeing me, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, arrived in person,
she knelt upon the ground and praised me, the Lord of Ramā.
To him, my ancient devotee, who stood there having offered salutations,
I, the compassionate one, invited him to choose a boon.
He replied, "O Lord, please always make this your dwelling place."
May devotion to you, the Lord, always abide in me at this sacred place; O All-pervading One, devotion to any other deity never pleases me.
I shall worship you eternally, and by my good fortune, I shall behold you here as well.
"I shall dwell together with you, established as I am in the imperishable.
"O Upendra, if you are pleased with me, let this boon be granted:
'By me the boon has indeed been granted; you shall obtain your dwelling there.'"
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I am subject to the power of devotion, and I am a devotee; yet there is no difference between us two, just as there is always none between Śrī and the Lord of Śrī.
Therefore, O auspicious one, my abode is pleasing to me in that place of Kubjāmraka.
"O beautiful one, I dwell there by the name Puṇḍarīkākṣa!
A great and most wonderful marvel occurred long ago in my abode:
a female serpent dwells fearlessly indeed upon my heap of discarded flower offerings."
While she was eating perfumes, garlands, and offerings at her pleasure,
a mongoose once arrived from another place.
He saw that female serpent, and then a battle broke out between the two.
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha, at midday in my temple, a mongoose was bitten by a serpent, and the female serpent was also bitten by that mongoose;
both then met their death through those severe wounds. (25–26)
Vyālī, born in Prāgjyotiṣa, was a wrathful princess;
Nakula, however, was the son of the lord of Kosala and was full of anger.
Both of them, endowed with their former impressions (saṃskāra), grew up together.
Upon seeing the mongoose, that girl immediately rushed to kill it;
and upon seeing the female serpent, the prince suddenly came to kill her.
By the power of destiny and according to their former bond, the marriage of those two took place.

And affection arose between the two of them like that of a bird and its wooden perch. In this manner, seventy-seven years passed for them as they sported together in a garden on a grassy plot of land.
Seeing the female serpent, the prince rushed toward her to slay her.
Although his wife tried to restrain him, he killed the serpent while it was still alive.
At that moment, the queen, overcome with rage, experienced great sorrow in her heart.
And at that very moment, by the turn of fate, a mongoose emerged from the hole and came forth right before the princess.
Seeing that handsome-looking mongoose, the princess—
Though forbidden by the king, she struck her with a staff out of anger.
Seeing that Nakula, the auspicious ornament of the king, had been killed, the enraged prince spoke to the princess: (34-35)
A husband is always to be honored by women; yet, O cruel one, disregarding me—
who am worthy of being seen, beloved by kings, auspicious, and a harbinger of good fortune—
why was the mongoose killed even as I tried to restrain you?
Having heard these words of her husband, the princess replied:
"Since the snake killed him even though he was repeatedly warned, I too have killed the mongoose, that slayer of snakes. (37-38)
And the prince, rebuking her with these well-reasoned words, said:
"O wife, this was a serpent of virulent venom, by whose bite people die;
therefore, I have slain this wicked one who acted for my harm and was arrogant with poison. (39)
The king is declared to be the protector of his subjects; I punish those who stand on the path of unrighteousness.
Indeed, those who harm the virtuous who are free from offense, and those who harm women as well, are to be punished according to the dharma of kings.
"It was indeed by me that the duty of a king had to be performed, and for that reason she was killed.
Tell me, what offense did Nakula commit here?
He is handsome, auspicious, and worthy even of the homes of kings. (42)
"Is this Nakula, who is even skilled at dice, being killed by you?
Since you have taken my life despite being restrained by me,
therefore you are no longer my wife, nor am I established as your husband."
Furthermore, having said, "I shall not kill you, for women are always inviolable," the king left her in that garden and went home.
Thus, harboring anger, the two of them became estranged from one another.
Then that news spread from ear to ear among the people.
Having heard it, the aged parents of the prince, the lords of Kosala,
summoned their daughter-in-law and son to their presence.
Then, seeing his daughter-in-law and son, the father spoke these words:
"Son! Where has your mutual affection gone, and what indeed is the cause? You who were always so deeply attached, how have you come to such contrary conduct? (48)
"O son! You are capable; you ought not to abandon this most virtuous woman.

She has never before spoken anything unpleasant to you, nor has she ever done what was undesirable to you. Always skillful in pleasing you, it is not right for her to be abandoned by you. (1.571.49–50)
"The duty of the household, the duty of kingship,
and indeed the duty of the lineage and the duty of sacrifice always proceed from women alone.
Having heard these words of his father, the prince replied:
"O dear one, there is no fault whatsoever in my daughter-in-law anywhere!
Even though she was being restrained by me, why did she kill my mongoose right before my eyes?
Thereupon, anger arose within me, and I rebuked her. (52-53)
"She is not my wife, nor am I indeed your husband.
Having heard these words of his son, the king listened to the daughter-in-law;
bowing his head in prostration, he spoke these words: [54]
O King, that female serpent was innocent and terrified;
yet, while I was trying to restrain him, she was killed by the prince.
Thereupon, consumed by anger, I remained there observing a vow of silence.
Just then I saw a mongoose, and in my anger I struck it;
though I was being restrained by the prince, I struck it again with a staff.
Because of our mutual rivalry, I have indeed killed the mongoose.
"In this matter, O King, apply justice; inflict punishment, and I shall do the same.
Having heard the words of the daughter-in-law and the son, the king spoke these skillful words:
"For what reason have you two, though being animals, come to such a separation?"
But since Nakula has been killed, my son, what is the cause of your anger?
O princess, now that the serpent has been slain, why do you give way to wrath?
Why do you pointlessly accept such great loss for the sake of a trivial cause?
Having heard his father’s auspicious words, the young boy, who remembered his former births, replied to his father: "One's former nature continues to manifest;
all beings return to their natural state, and there is no way to restrain this."
"Even for a very slight cause, enmity from a previous birth manifests.
Having heard these words of his son, the father then said to him:
'Tell me, my son, according to the facts, the cause of this rupture in our affection.'"
Let that which was done in a previous birth be told here by both of them.
If good sons do not conceal what has been asked by their father, even if it is secret;
and if these sons do not speak, whether it be true or even false— [64–65]
They indeed fall into the Raurava hell of heated sand—
those who, when questioned by their father, speak of his back as being either auspicious or inauspicious.
But they attain the divine goal, which is the goal of those who speak the truth.
Having heard these words, the son respectfully said to his father:
"O Lord of the Earth! Having gone to that holy place called Kubjāmraka, it must be kept strictly secret, for it is the cause of the severance of worldly attachment."
Then the king said, "Very well," and the queen said the same.
Thereupon, the king summoned his ministers and elders and spoke to them:
"Let us go to the auspicious holy site of Kubjāmraka to perform its ritual service."
Let it be prepared quickly, and let the elephants and horses be harnessed.
(70) Elephants, horses, cattle, vehicles, and so forth; kārṣāpaṇa coins, cows, gold, jewels, garments, and various kinds of food as well. (71)
Then the king spoke to his son, appropriate to the place and time:
"O son, how shall we depart, leaving the kingdom empty?
That eldest son said: 'Give it to the younger one.'"

The king said: "If it were so, there would be a violation of dharma, for how can [the kingdom] be given to the younger son while the elder son exists? The elder brother said: "Father, I give my consent; give the earth to him. (73–74)
"In this matter, there shall be no violation of dharma, nor indeed shall my existence be lost.
Having gone to Kubjāmraka, I shall not return home again.
Considering these words of truth, please grant me your younger brother.
Having heard this, the king consecrated his younger son in the kingdom.
The king then departed for a sacred pilgrimage site together with his harem and attendants;
having performed the rites of the pilgrimage, he bestowed abundant gifts.
Food, clothing, gold, cows, elephants, horses, and houses [were given]. Then, when the night had passed, the eldest son,
together with his daughter-in-law, bathed, performed the rites for the sacred ford, and bowed again and again to his elders.
Having circumambulated his father and saluted his mother,
he went to where the heap of withered flower offerings was certainly located near the temple;
having arrived there, he said to his father, "I was Nakula in my previous life."
My residence was here in a grove of plantain trees;
for here, indeed, I saw a venomous female serpent nearby.
On the morning of the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, at that time, [we were together].
As the two of us fought out of a natural enmity,
biting each other fiercely, our deaths occurred simultaneously at the excellent pilgrimage site of Kubjāmraka,
at the Devāśraya shrine; through that merit, I have become your son.
"This serpent, who was once your daughter-in-law, has now become the daughter of the King of Prāgjyotiṣa.
Thus, due to the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of our former existence, enmity arises between us two—the snake and the mongoose—and that is the cause for our separation. (84)

"O Great King, our full lifespan has now come to an end at this sacred ford; indeed, we shall both go to Vaikuṇṭha," they said with clear voices. Having spoken thus, the two of them bowed down to Hari, the lotus-eyed one.
And likewise, their parents and ministers, having cast off their bodies in an instant,
became divine and, assuming four arms, both traveled by celestial chariot—
riding in the vehicle of Viṣṇu’s attendants— to Śvetadvīpa.
The king and the others were struck with wonder, and the king, being devoted,
was then tormented by grief for his son; he performed vows and penance,
and in a very short time, he indeed attained supreme ascetic perfection.
Having abandoned his body, he went together with his wife to Vaikuṇṭha itself,
the divine and supreme abode where Lord Janārdana resides,
by my extreme grace and through the power of his asceticism.
Having performed my worship there, he went to my imperishable abode (akṣarapada).
And that attendant of his, having likewise performed meritorious deeds at Kubjāmraka,
attained supreme perfection and departed for my realm.
Thus was the holy site of Kubjāmraka caused to flourish by Raibhya;
it is rich with the dwellings of the lotus-eyed Lord and bestows liberation upon princes.
Oṃ, salutations to the illustrious Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Master; salutations!
Having performed an auspicious bath, as well as drinking [the water] and ritual purification,
and having beheld my form, whether a woman or a man,
one washes away all sins and attains the supreme goal. (94–95)
The supreme mantra has been declared; it should always be recited by those of all four social orders (cāturvarṇya).
It is the primary object for all ritual acts, and the deity here is Kāmbhareya.
He is the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Rādhā and Prabhā.
Pārvatīmāṇikīnātha, the Lord Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa;
Mañjuleśa, Haṃseśa, Saguṇeśa, and Svayaṃprabhu;
Dayānātha, Śāntinātha, and the Lord of Jayā of Campā and Haimī. 97–98.
Having worshipped Him who is the greatest splendor among all splendors and the greatest austerity among those who practice austerity,
one becomes liberated before the Lord of Goloka;
then, like Kṛṣṇa, one is filled with eternal bliss here.
"He shall become four-armed and established in the worlds of the gods;
even by hearing this, one shall be liberated. Thus Śambhu spoke to Satī then.

Thus ends the first section, titled "The Marvel of Raibhya and the Account of the Liberation of the Snake and the Mongoose after their Birth in a Royal Family, Following their Mutual Enmity, and their Return to the Site of Their Previous Birth," within the *Kubjāmraka-Haridvāra Bhakta-Māhātmya* of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, in the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga. 1.02.
Chapter Five Hundred and Seventy-One (571).
*Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Book 1: The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga.
Chapter 572.
[The Author: Chapter 573.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī! [I shall describe] the great holy place Kubjāmraka, which bestows liberation.
Having arrived at the confluence of the Kubjā and Revā on the Narmadā,
Śaṅkara, while stationed on the Ṛkṣaparvata during his pilgrimage, declared to Pārvatī that this place would certainly remain established for seven kalpas. || 1–2 ||
Now listen as I describe other holy sites as well:
to the west of Māhiṣmatī is the holy site that destroys sorrow, known as Aśokavanikā, adorned by the hermitage of Mātaṅga. (3)

There, a devoted wife who worships Gaurī on the third lunar day shall obtain a husband according to her desire, endowed with wealth, beauty, and strength. The celestial sage named Mātanga performed difficult penance here.
In a previous birth, he was indeed a Niṣāda who possessed the memory of his former lives;
through his meeting with great sages at that place which destroys all evil,
he became a supreme knower of dharma, free from passion, and enlightened.
Indeed, by serving the Narmadā, he became meritorious.
Though he was a dog-cooker (outcaste), he became disenchanted with the world; wearing matted hair and bark garments, he dwelt in the Aśoka grove, subsisting on roots, tubers, and fruits.
For a thousand years, he indeed performed most rigorous penance. As he was thus performing penance, there emerged from the tips of his matted locks yakṣiṇīs of dark complexion, radiant and adorned.
Eighty-one thousand women bathed in the waters of the Narmadā.
By the mere act of bathing, they attained the worlds of the Yakṣas with excellent vehicles.
Even one devoid of mantras and yantras, by simply reciting "Namas Śivāya," [attains the same].
He became a possessor of spiritual perfection (*siddhi*). Śaṅkara came before him and said to the devotee, "Choose a boon as you desire; I am Śaṅkara.
Mātaṅga said, "May this sacred ford (*tīrtha*) become famous by my name."
Even Cāṇḍālas, Śvapacas, leather-workers, and those of sinful birth,
having come here, shall become pure and indeed attain liberation.
By bowing to the Mātaṅgeśvara Liṅga, they likewise obtain emancipation.
"Grant me this boon here, if I am indeed devoted to you.
Having heard that, Śaṅkara then said once more, "So be it.
Om, salutations to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, salutations to the Lord.
"Recite this, O Mātanga! Your supreme Vaiṣṇava liberation will indeed come to pass;
of this there is no doubt, nor for those who abide by your own caste.
Through the application of this mantra, liberation in Vaikuṇṭha shall occur. (16–17)
"Give me the mantra spoken by you, and make all [of us] Vaiṣṇavas.
Having said this, Śaṅkara thereafter vanished.
Mataṅga then bestowed the mantra upon the embodied beings of his own caste.
In former times, he sent many Vaiṣṇava Cāṇḍālas; then,
having personally ascended a self-moving, desire-yielding vehicle, he went to Goloka, the abode of Śrī Hari, and attained supreme, auspicious liberation in the month of Caitra.

This Aśoka grove is called Mātaṅgatīrtha. By the gift of sesame paste and the like, by the gift of roasted flour (saktu), and by the libation of water, the ancestors attain liberation; of this there is no doubt.
In that very place, on the southern side, is the sacred ford named Mṛgavana.
Having bathed there, one should worship Viṣṇu, who bears the conch, the discus, and the mace.
On the eleventh lunar day, fasting, one should worship the Supreme Lord.
A devoted wife should worship her husband as Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa;
by the power of bathing and giving gifts, she attains the Vaiṣṇava world.
In ancient times, there was a certain hunter who was ill-behaved and merciless.
There, afflicted by thirst, he killed deer with his bow.
Having rested for a moment under the shade of a tree without water, he fell asleep; thereafter, a fire born from the friction of the forest broke out.
Having risen, he consumed the forest filled with hunters and deer;
then, within a month, the rains arrived, and the ashes and fragments of bones were all carried away by the flood of the Narmadā.
Those deer, through contact with the Narmadā, became Gandharvas and millions of gods;
that hunter indeed became a king upon the earth, and other living beings as well attained [divinity] through contact with the waters of the Narmadā. || 28-29 ||
The Yakṣas and other deities remained as gods for ten thousand years;
having enjoyed heaven, they too, along with the king and his singers,
reached the station of Viṣṇu by means of a Vaiṣṇava vehicle.

Whether against his will or by his own choice, one who gives up their life on the Narmadā rejoices in the world of Viṣṇu for a thousand divine years. The confluence of the Aṅgārāvarta bestows the merit of donating a thousand cows.
And the god Aṅgāreśvara resides there at the confluence;
by merely bathing there, a man shall attain the status of a Gaṇapati.
On the fourth lunar day or on a Tuesday, [one should offer] an auspicious golden image.
Having prepared it, one should wrap it with a red cloth and likewise smear it with ghee.

One should give it secretly to a Brāhmaṇa; by giving this auspicious "Puruṣa" [image], through the power of the gift and the sacred ford (tīrtha), one shall become a sharer of half the throne of Śakra.
In former times, there was a great king named Yuvanāśva, the sovereign of Kosala;
in the Kṛta age, he was a universal monarch devoted to all duties.
Having saluted his family priest Vasiṣṭha, he spoke to him.
"In what place should one perform sacrifice—at a sacred ford (tīrtha), in a holy land, or in a temple?
Vasiṣṭha replied to him: "The supreme sacred ford of Naimiṣa;
there, the horse sacrifice becomes fruitful, yielding millions upon millions of times more merit."
"This was spoken by Matsya and Viṣṇu, and likewise declared by Sūrya.
O Yuvanāśva, that which is worthy of sacrifice has been declared to you by the son of Manu.
Having heard these words of his preceptor, the king commanded his ministers.
"Taking the sacrificial implements, assemble quickly! (1.572.40).
Thus was the proclamation made in the world, and the gods were summoned to the sacrifice:
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, the Lord of the Gods, Skanda, and likewise Vaiśravaṇa. (41)
Śambhu, the Vasus, the Rudras,
as well as the Ādityas, the two Aśvins, the guardians of the quarters, and all the world-protectors [were present].
Indeed, there were ten lakhs of cows accompanied by gold and jewels.
One hundred thousand horses, thirty thousand excellent elephants,
jewels, rubies, pearls, and infinite gold, as well as various kinds of goods and all types of food and drink in every variety. ||43-44||
Accompanied by all the sacrificial materials and whatever else was required, the king,
with thousands of various vehicles and thousands of diverse musical instruments,
filled the heavens with the great resonance of the Vedas and the sounds of songs.
He entered the sacred site of Naimiṣa, where there is a vision of Śrī Hari.
Then, having beheld the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the king gave one hundred thousand gold pieces to ten thousand destitute people.
Having bathed, he gave away immeasurable silver ornaments;
having uttered "Oṃ namo viṣṇave" and indeed placed water and *darbha* grass [in the vessel],
and having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) in a golden vessel, he caused the sacrificial enclosure (*yajñavāṭa*) to be constructed.
The king caused sacrificial pavilions to be constructed, extending over ten *kośas* and consisting of sacrificial posts (*yajñayūpa*),
which were beautifully adorned with golden pillars;
he also had altars (*vedikā*) and sacrificial pits (*yajñakuṇḍa*) made, including the principal pit.
Then the sacrifice was concluded by the twice-born led by Vasiṣṭha;
all the deities were delighted and indeed uttered cries of "Victory!
Having completed the sacrifice, the king, together with his harem and retinue, [departed].
Just as he had mounted his vehicle and departed from the Naimiṣa forest, a certain monkey approached and spoke repeatedly to the king:
"Stop, stop! Listen, O King; you are possessed of false pride."
I do not consider there to be any great fruit for you in the performance of sacrifices.
Long ago, during the sacrifice of King Satyadharma, which was presided over by the Lord of the Immortals,
everything became golden in color from my neck downward, with the sole exception of my face.
All our children there became golden due to the power of the sacrificial waters at the confluence of the Kapilā and the Narmadā,
through bathing, immersion, drinking, and wallowing in the mud of the sacrifice. (55–56)
The fourfold assembly of beings has reached the world of the Gandharvas. Now,
while I was immersed in your sacrifice at Naimiṣa,
my body, smeared with mud, was washed by the sacrificial waters.
No fruit whatsoever accrued to me, nor did my body turn to gold.
Your entire sacrifice, being rooted in egoism, was useless.
Ten thousand cows were given by you, as well as infinite wealth and grain. (58–59)
Gold and silver were likewise given, yet it was all in vain. This has been told to you, O King; your sacrifice was not like that of King Satyadharma on the banks of the Narmadā.
"May it be well with you; I shall depart for the Narmadā, which bestows the form of gold.
Having heard of your sacrifice, I indeed came to the Naimiṣa forest;
now, having come away disappointed, I go forth, for there was no gold in my mouth."
Having heard the words of the monkey, Yuvanāśva then said:
"Who are you, appearing in the form of a monkey? Tell me, O treasure-house of blessings!
The monkey replied: "I am the son of Jābāli named Kadamba, a knower of the Self."
"O King, through the theft of fruit, I became a monkey while possessing the memory of my past lives.
By means of this very disguise, I visited all the sacred fords (tīrthas), yet not even the slightest benefit accrued to me from those holy sites. (64–65)
Only in the sacred field of the Narmadā, at the supreme sacrifice of Truth and Dharma,
did my entire body become golden, with the exception of my face.
Having heard the words of the monkey, the king [returned] once more to Naimiṣa.
He went to that glorious Supreme Lord, the primordial God, the all-pervading Hari.
With supreme devotion, he praised the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa:
"O Blessed One, a sacrifice has been successfully performed by me in the sacred field of Naimiṣa."
At the conclusion of this, one who had assumed the form of a monkey made himself heard:
"There is no gain for me in your sacrifice; therefore, your sacrifice is in vain.
He, however, desires his own golden face as the supreme offering."
"Act in such a way that his face shall become golden.
Having heard this, the Blessed Lord, residing within the image, said to King Yuvana:
"Satyadharma will perform a sacrifice again on the Narmadā."
In that regard, his face will undoubtedly become golden;
O King, tell this monkey and go to the city of Kosala.
Having heard this, the king bowed to Hari at Naimiṣa and departed for the city.
The monkey went again to the confluence of the Revā and the Kapilā.
Having gone there, he related the Naimiṣa narrative concerning Satyadharma.
And Satyadharma, having heard that, accepted the words of Hari as authoritative.
After the concluding bath (*avabhṛtha*), the monkey performed the sacrifice once more;
rolling his own face in the mud, he thrust it in again and again.
His body became turned to gold, and his entire face was made of gold.
Then, having cast off the body of the monkey,
he was honored by the sound of celestial drums and by hosts of apsarases;
he departed for Vaikuṇṭha itself upon a vehicle drawn by swans.
At that sacrifice, even beasts of prey and other creatures went to heaven after eating a mere morsel [of the offerings].
Thus indeed, the Narmadā Tīrtha prevails as the most supreme of all.
By hearing of it or by glorifying it, one obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows.
Śaṅkara said to Pārvatī: "O Lakṣmī! I have declared this to you:
he who performs a sacrifice with his own wealth on the bank of the Narmadā, having enjoyed abundant pleasures, is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu. (1.572.80)
Having fashioned a golden image of the Earth (Dhātrī), one should bestow it upon a Brāhmaṇa;
by resorting to the banks of the Narmadā, one is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
He who gives a living cow adorned with gold and jewels [attains the same].
By giving a cow made of ghee, a cow made of molasses, or even a cow made of sugar,
one is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu during the conjunction of the Revā and Kapilā rivers.
Listen also to another story that destroys both sin and suffering.

The son of Mitrāyu was the family priest of the royal seer Vīraṇa. By him, on the banks of the Narmadā, was caused to be built a temple of Viṣṇu Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, adorned with a pinnacle reaching toward heaven.

By the merit of that sacred site and through the power of the Narmadā, Maitreya indeed rejoices in the world of Viṣṇu as a four-armed being. Then King Vīraṇa heard this from a messenger of the gods. (85–86)
"O King, your preceptor has gone to Hari’s Vaikuṇṭha, having made even heaven seem lowly; how is it that you have not yet gone there to behold him?
Having heard those words of the divine messenger, he asked, "How is such a journey possible?"
Then the divine messenger said:
"Perform a sacrifice on the beautiful bank of the Narmadā; by pleasing Hari Kṛṣṇa, you shall attain liberation.
Vīraṇa, for his part, performed the most excellent Vaiṣṇava sacrifice.
The gods arrived there, as did Maitreya and Nārāyaṇa;
Lakṣmī and the other Mothers, as well as the king, he indeed gratified them all.
Then, having performed the avamṛthaka bath and having given the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās), [he departed].
Vīraṇa, having indeed become divine as a Vaiṣṇava, traveled by means of a celestial vehicle;
most beautiful, he was fanned by maidens with four arms, and bearing four arms himself, he repeatedly cried out the name of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. || 91-92 ||
Honored with a welcome by the gods and his attendants along the way,
he went to Viṣṇu’s supreme abode, Vaikuṇṭha, which bestows eternal peace.
The royal sage Rantideva, having performed sacrifices on the Narmadā river—
Having offered *bilva* and *āmra* trees to the Supreme Lord in that sacred field,
and having gratified Hari and the gods, he then established the holy site of Bilvāmraka and received the command of Nārāyaṇa, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow. (94–95)
Taking with him some of his Vaiṣṇava subjects who were devoted to him,
he went to the shore of Hari’s abode along with his family and kinsmen.
Formerly, there was a royal sage named Dadhīci, the king of Avanti.
Having gone to the bank of the Narmadā and offered the backbone to Indra, he then,
out of devotion, went to the abode of Nārāyaṇa;
for by the weapons born from his bones, the gods indeed conquered the great asuras.
O beloved, by bathing at Bilvāmra on the conjunction of the new moon and Monday,
people attain worldly enjoyment and liberation through the power of the Narmadā field.
At Bilvāmra, the Viśvedevas attained supreme perfection.
"Even the reciters and the disciples shall go to the supreme goal.

(1.572.10) Thus ends the five hundred and seventy-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Mātaṅga Hermitage in the Aśoka Grove, Aṅgāreśvara, Nakula’s Attainment of a Golden Form at the Sacrifice of Satyadharma, the Liberation of Vīraṇa, and Other Matters," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga Cycle, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*. (572)
