Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Mahālakṣmī! To the supreme account spoken by Śaṅkara concerning the Suvarṇadvīpa Tīrtha located in the midst of the waters of the Narmadā.

In ancient times, during the Kṛta Yuga, the great ṛṣi Hārīta performed austerities. There, a beautiful vision of the dark-complexioned Nārāyaṇa appeared to him as well as to those yogis who were performing penance. (2)
Now, on the northern bank of the Revā is a mountain named Paryaṅka.
(3) There Viṣṇu himself, Mādhava, dwells as the remover of sins.
That sacred field of Hari is proclaimed to be one *krośa* in extent. (4)
Those who bathe there, even if they have died, attain the supreme goal.
On the southern bank of the Narmadā is the excellent hermitage of Māṇḍavya,
where in ancient times Vibhāṇḍaka, Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, and others dwelt.
Viśoka, Narmadāsaṅga, and Aśokeśvara Śaṅkara;
there, at the confluence of the two beautiful rivers, the Narmadā and the Vindhya,
the goddesses who bestow liberation dwell at that meeting place.
And Harṣasiddhā, Sāvitrī, Aditi the mother of the gods, Devayānī, the body of Brahmā, Rohiṇī, Kambharāyaṇī,
Lopāmudrā, Indrāṇī, Dākṣāyaṇī, Prabhā, and Dhruvā.
Ratnāvalī, Saṃjñā, Tārā, Siddhi, and Pārvatī;
Lakṣmī, Rādhā, Maṇikī, Haṃsā, Mañjulā, Amṛtā, Maṅgalā, Saguṇā, and Aśokā—these [goddesses] are each united with their respective lords. (1.573.10)
Dayā, Jayā, Lalitā, Mauktikī, Hemacampikā, Kastūrikā,
and Savitā dwell at the confluence of the Vindhya and Narmadā rivers.
At the junction in the grove of Aśoka trees, a boon was granted to Gaurī.
On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina, she who observes this vow—
whether she be childless, barren, unfortunate, or abandoned by her husband—
should bathe with the five jewels and fruits and worship [the deity] with divine articles.
One should bathe her with waters and likewise feed young maidens;
thus she shall possess unbroken good fortune, have sons, and be honored.
When this was first performed, Ravi and Candra became kings, lords of Kāñcīpura.
Born of the lunar dynasty and residing on the banks of the Narmadā,
the king went together with his priest Śāṇḍilya to the Brāhmaṇa Agastya, a descendant of Mitrāvaruṇa.
The king grasped the feet of that Brahmin Agastika, who bore many names. Agastya inquired after his well-being and offered him a seat.
The king said: "By the sight of you, who are performing penance, my sin has departed."
Today my birth, my kingdom, and even my very life have become fruitful.
In what place shall I perform a sacrifice so that the rite may reach perfection,
such that the gods receive inexhaustible satisfaction and the ancestors attain liberation?
The sage said: "The Narmadā, which flows through seven kalpas, is suitable for the sacrifice.
Aśokavanikā is renowned as a sacrificial ground, honored by the gods.
Perform there the Vaiṣṇava sacrifice, and you shall attain the supreme state."
Taking Agastya with him, the king went to the Aśokikā plateau on the southern bank of the Revā; there the lord of the earth caused sacrificial posts and a pavilion to be constructed,
extending for ten krośas.
The seven sages, as well as the Vālakhilyas and other gods on earth,
Lomaśa— who is visible to Brahmā— and those residing at Kuṅkumavāpikā,
along with the deities and other Brāhmaṇas, departed once the sacrifice had been inaugurated.
"All the deities were satisfied, and the Brahmins received their sacrificial fees.
Then the king of sages, Durvāsas, arrived there in a rage and said:
'There is no place for me here, nor is there any for Vaivasvata.'"
"Nārada and Parvata do not exist; Time and Death are not found.
Likewise, Citragupta does not exist—how then has the sacrifice been set in motion?
Then Ravi and Candra, having bowed to Durvāsas, spoke these words. (25-26)
Who among even the hosts of gods and asuras would be capable of obstructing me, by virtue of the grace of the Lord Aśokeśvara on the Narmadā?
The sacrifice has been completed by me; those worthy of worship have assembled at the sacrifice.
"O sirs, you too should accept my worship as well as the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
I give them to you, there is no doubt; Durvāsas, Nārada, and the others—whatever desire each one may have, that I shall grant to him."
The great sages, Nārada and others, arrived there and were gratified by the king with the granting of whatever they desired. Now hear, O Daughter of the Lotus, what was further requested by Durvāsas.

Formerly, due to the curse of Pārvatī, certain Brāhmaṇas residing in Pāṭalīputra were indeed cursed; having become dogs, they wander upon the earth. O King, grant them liberation through meritorious gifts.
The king said, "Tell me, how indeed did they receive the curse?
Durvāsas replied, "In former times, those brahmins, wearing bark garments,
went to Nepal to worship Paśupati."
They worshipped Śaṅkara with devotion, yet he was devoid of Gaurī.
Having abandoned the female portion of Ardhanārīśvara, they worshipped the mere male form with sandalwood paste and other offerings, because Pārvatī was then angry.
She cursed those brahmins who had caused the division of the woman, saying:
"For a thousand years, you shall all indeed enter the womb of dogs.
Then, by that curse, they all entered the state of being dogs.
"Summon them from the forest and release them here.
Then, dispatched by the king toward that forest,
the dogs— who remembered their past lives— quickly arrived together with the servants.
The king joyfully spoke to them regarding the site of the Aśoka grove:
"By the power of the deity Aśokeśvara, by the efficacy of the Narmadā, through the influence of my own gifts, and by the grace of the great sages... (3.9)
"Having abandoned their birth as dogs, let the sages indeed proceed to the world of Brahmā!
May all your sin, in the form of a curse, enter into me.
At that very moment, they were freed from the curse and ascended a celestial vehicle that moves at will.
Having become divine great sages, they offered praise to the Sun and the Moon:
"You are our mother, you are our father, you are our guru and the bestower of liberation.
Having spoken thus, they went to the auspicious heaven consisting of Satyaloka.
Then the sages, beginning with Durvāsas, also praised the king:
"Excellent, excellent, O highly fortunate one! You are indeed a treasure-house of sacrifice and austerity.
There is no other king born of the Lunar dynasty who is your equal. (43–44)
For the sacrifice of life is easy, but the sacrifice of merit is exceedingly difficult.
O King, you shall bestow merit; its fruit is indeed eternal.
Choose a boon—may it be well with you—whatever dwells in your heart.
The king said: "By my merit, may even people of wicked intellect attain the supreme world; this is my dear boon. Durvāsas and the other sages, having replied, "So be it," [departed]. || 46-47 ||
Then they all vanished, and Dharma arrived;
being well-pleased, Dharmarāja said to him, "I grant you a boon:
O King, the world of Yama has been conquered by you, and the world of the gods has been won."
By the gift of the merit of sacrifice, the dogs have been liberated by you.
On this earth, the performance of sacrifice and the bestowing of its merit are difficult deeds to accomplish. O Indra among kings, you are worthy of a boon; choose whatever you desire.
Then Ravi and Candra spoke to those who had gone to the realm of Yama—the sinners who experience suffering, the denizens of hell tormented by agonies:
"By a hundred sacrifices of mine, as well as by my gifts and penances... (51)
"By your grace, let them go to heaven, which is true and brings happiness.
Yama replied, "So be it; your merit shall increase greatly.
Merit dedicated to the salvation of others becomes multiplied a thousandfold."
By that merit, O Indra among kings, go you to the city of Brahmā—
that eternal abode which is filled with perpetual bliss and is the supreme imperishable.
For by you, indeed, those of sinful birth have been liberated from their wretched state.
O King, hundreds of Kṣatriyas and thousands of others as well [were present].
Having spoken thus and having given the prayer to the king, Dharmarāja said:
"Om, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, obeisance to the Master. (55–56)
Having uttered the sixteen-syllable mantra, he joyfully departed for his own abode.

In time, the king became divine; through the practice of the syllables, he reached that supreme realm beyond the syllables, which is the abode of the Supreme Person, higher than the abode of Brahmā. (57)

From hearing and chanting this, the fruit of a thousand cows shall be obtained. (58) Next, there is the sacred ford known as Vāgurāsaṅgama; after that, Brahmadatta became the king who ruled over the Kośalas. (59)
The solar dynasty king Kratu performed a sacrifice with great wealth at Āguyoga.
At that time, the sacrificial ground extended for ten yojanas.
In his sacrifice, the *preta*s were fully satiated and attained supreme liberation.
Listen, O pretas, how you were born and who you were in the past.
Formerly, on the full moon day of Kārttika at the sacred site of Puṣkara, great sages arrived:
Ayogandha, Svayaṃbhū, and also Puṇḍarīkākṣa.
Brahmā Kāvya, Hotṛ Sadana, Vedagarbhaka, Kṛtadhvana, Svastika, Sāvitra,
Vāmadevaka, Aghamarṣaṇa, Brahmatejas, and other Brāhmaṇas likewise departed.
All those established in the duties of the householder stage were indeed Vaiṣṇavas, free from craving.
Their wives were devoted to the duty toward their husbands, intent on serving their lords;
they wore garments of rags and bark, and subsisted on vegetables and śyāmāka grain.
Once, tormented by the affliction of poverty and despondent, they censured the six traditional occupations:
officiating at sacrifices, performing sacrifices for others, teaching, studying, giving gifts, and accepting gifts. (66)
In these six occupations of the Brahmins, extreme hardship is observed. Not even the slightest trace of royal splendor is found in the house of a Brahmin.
Having heard this, the great sages censured those [women] in such a manner.
With dejected faces,
they went with their wives and sons to the Kuru field during a solar eclipse to fulfill their heart's desire—
where Hariścandra used to give gifts during an eclipse of the sun.
Seeing those who had arrived with the desire to receive gifts, that king, with a gracious countenance, praised the fruitfulness of his giving:
"Blessed is my journey today at Kurukṣetra; it has become truly successful."
"Afflicted by hunger, suffering, children, the elderly, the emaciated, and the sick—
those who were weak and clad in bark, deerskins, and rags have indeed come to me.
Having spoken thus, he paid homage to each one individually.
A hundred thousand pieces of gold, as well as thousands of cows;
a thousand horses and even a hundred elephants;
and delightful seven-storied mansions with golden walls and gateways.
He bestowed upon them vehicles, mounts, male servants, and likewise female servants;
having received these as gifts from the king, they became merely consumers of sin.
Abandoning the six duties, they became captivated by worldly pleasures.
Having died at another time, they were born in the form of terrifying *preta*s;
this was the power of accepting gifts, since it led to the downfall of the Brahmin.
And all of them, along with their kinsmen, remembered their former births, having been consumed by the fire of their own giving.
Suffering, they arrived at the sacred ford of Puṣkara where Nārada was;
as he was departing for Badarī, he emerged from that region and,
seeing the sages in the form of ghosts, fell into the deepest despondency.
And he asked, "How did you become ghosts?
Thereupon they said: "We received gifts from King Hariścandra at Kurukṣetra; through greed we obtained them, and now we have gone to the fruit of that."
"Having entered into the state of ghosts, let our liberation be ordained.
Having heard them, Nārada said: "Go to the purifying Narmadā, and there to the city of Vāgīśa situated on the bank of the Narmadā."
"During the sacrifice of Brahmadatta, your liberation shall take place.
Having spoken thus, Nārada then departed for the hermitage of Nārāyaṇa;
the spirits went to that region, the supreme city of Vāgīśa.
Having bathed and worshipped Sūrya, Hari, and Śambhu, they went to the sacrifice.
Having partaken of the sacrificial offerings, they became free from sin and possessed of beautiful forms.
Seeing them thus purified, radiant as the sun, [the people were amazed].
Brahmadatta and the others bowed and asked: "Who are you here?
How did you fall into the state of ghosts, and how was your liberation achieved?
Then, they related their own history to them there.
Having ascended to heaven, they showered a rain of flowers upon the king;
then, mounting the vehicle of Brahmā, they departed for the world of Brahmā,
praising the king, the sacrifice, and the waters of the Narmadā.
The gods and the sages, gratified by the sacrifice, departed for their own abodes.
From hearing or reciting this [account], one obtains the merit of giving a thousand cows.
Furthermore, there exists another sacred ford known as Sahasrāvartaka.
There, for one who has bathed according to the prescribed rite, there shall be the fruit of the ritual release of a bull (*vṛṣotsarga*).
Likewise, there is the Karāvana Tīrtha and the Saugandhika forest.
Therein dwells the auspicious Sarasvatī, who effects the liberation of the ancestors.
Likewise, there is another holy site called Triśūla, which bestows the status of Gaṇeśa.
There is also another holy site, Brahmoda, where the seven sages performed their ablutions;
Kapiñjala, the best of sages, was the presiding sage, and Havyavāha was the deity.
The Blessed One, Devayāna, Viśvāvasu,
and the great sage [all] attained the world of Brahmā through the majesty of this sacred ford (tīrtha).
Likewise, there is the Vasvāśrama, a delightful and supreme sacred ford.
At that place is the Saptasārasvata Tīrtha, where Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa Himself shines forth visibly; Brahmā offered praise to Him, saying:
"May the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa be my refuge. (94–95)
May the Lord of the syllables, the Lord of the liberated, the illustrious Puruṣottama,
the Lord of Rādhā, the Lord of Lakṣmī, and the Lord of Pārvatī be my refuge. May the Lord of Jayā, the Lord of Lalitā, and the Lord of Māṇikī be my refuge.
May Vāsudeva himself, the Lord Nārāyaṇa, be my refuge.
May Bhūmā, Viṣṇu, Mahākṛṣṇa, and the Lord of Vairāja be my refuge. May Upendra, Haṃsanātha, and the Lord of the Earth and Śrī be my refuge.
May Prabhāpati, Mañjuleśa, Haṃseśa, Saguṇāpati,
the Lord Kāṃbhareya, and Harikṛṣṇa be my refuge.
May Hṛṣīkeśa, Mādhava, and Devīnātha be my refuge.
May Janārdana— the Lord who possesses the conch, discus, mace, and lotus as his weapons, whose throne is the illustrious Garuḍa,
and who is the root of all manifestations— be my refuge; he who is the Supreme Self, the Supreme Brahman, the Lord, the Child Gopāla.
May the Soul of the Universe and the Inner Self, who dwells within the heart, be my refuge;
may the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa, the husband of Sāvitrī, be pleased with his devotee. May the Lord of Sītā, Rāmā, and Prapūṣpā, the Master of devotees, be gracious.
Whatever has been earned by me since birth has been offered to you.
There is no deity more meritorious than another; there is no austerity superior to Viṣṇu; there is no knowledge greater than that of the Master; the entire world consists of the Master.
By this excellent hymn of praise, people shall attain liberation;
by hearing it or chanting it, one obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
Having praised [the Lord] and bathed in the water on the full moon day of Kārttika, Brahmā ascended his vehicle.
Chanting the name of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, he went to heaven.
This sacred ford, which yields the waters of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, is known as the bestower of liberation.
O Lakṣmī! I have related this truth to you, just as it was spoken by Śambhu. 106–107.

Thus ends the five hundred and seventy-third chapter, titled "The Description of Suvarṇadvīpa Tīrtha, the Confluence of Viśokā and Narmadā, the Liberation of the Dead at the Aśokeśvara Ravi-Candra Sacrifice, the Confluence of Vāgurā and Evā, and Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa Tīrtha," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Chapter 575 → Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:

Listen, Lakṣmī! Then one should go to the auspicious holy site (tīrtha) consisting of the gods. While stationed at the source of the Narmadā, Śambhu spoke thus to Satī: "There is the Sahasrayajña tīrtha, which is inhabited by Janārdana."
Having visited the southern city, one should never look back. Then one should go to Śuklatīrtha, the supreme site containing all holy waters;
by it, the gods Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara were made pure white.
Indeed, millions of sacred fords (tīrthas) reside there at Śuklatīrtha.
Indra, having bathed Śambhu, worshipped him with bilva leaves.
There, Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa was likewise worshipped by the guardians of the quarters (dikpālas).
The hermitage of Kaśyapa is meritorious, where a circle of ten thousand sages resides;
even tens of millions of munis worship Śukleśvara there.
For that sacred site consists of all holy fords and indeed embodies all the gods.
Where in former times the Lord of Sacrifice was worshipped by the Grandfather (Brahmā) in sacrifice,
all sins are destroyed by resorting to that ground.
For those who have died there without having attained liberation, that Śuklatīrtha grants release.
There was a righteous king named Yayāti who became a universal monarch (cakravartin).
He performed great sacrifices at the confluence of the Revā and the Madhumatī, where the Liṅga known as Madhyeśvara is located; there I am present as Mādhava, Nārāyaṇa.

Having bathed there, they go to heaven and liberation; they are not subject to rebirth. Once, a sacrifice was performed by Yayāti and the Brahmins at a place where there is no abode for Hari, nor indeed any abode for Śambhu.
Then the Daitya Jaṭāsura, seeing an opening, approached;
the sacrifice was destroyed by the Asuras and the sacrificial posts were cast down.
They consumed the offered sacrificial cakes and drank the Soma juice.
One hundred and eight gods emerged in the form of deer;
then, remembering Hari and Hara, the king seized his weapon.
He slew the Dānavas in battle, and the gods were summoned once again.
The sacrifice was set in motion once again through the grace of Hari and Viṣṇu. There, by Hari and Śambhu appearing in person with their own splendor,
the entire world was made white, like the imperishable Goloka.
Although Hara and Hari were entreated by Yayāti with a boon, [they replied]:
"O Lords, remain right here forever in your divine forms.
From that time forward, Hara and Hari remained white and radiant.
Indeed, at the Śuklatīrtha, both fortnights are auspicious for those devoted to merit;
for there, all acts such as sacrifice and charity become inexhaustible.
Whatever embodied beings drink even a little water there, [they obtain imperishable results]. (17–18)
By the power of Śuklatīrtha, all those men shall go to the divine abode;
whatever desires they may long for, those very things they shall obtain.
Yayāti, however, having caused a magnificent palace to be built there as his residence, [remained].
Having installed the two deities there, he returned to his own kingdom.
(1.574.20) "Oṃ, obeisances to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; svāhā!
By chanting this at the end of his life, both the listener and the speaker go to the divine abode and attain liberation. (21)
Likewise, one should go to the holy site of Dvīpeśvara situated on the bank of the Narmadā;
from there, on the full moon day of Kārttika, one should proceed to the supreme Vaiṣṇava tīrtha,
where Viṣṇu, being praised by Nābhāga, became manifest before his eyes.
Then, O beloved, one should go to the illustrious Śaṅkara named Meghanāda.
Formerly, indeed, the Rākṣasa Rāvaṇa, while wandering this earth,
went to Devagiri, where there is a Dānava named Maya.
Paulastya said to Maya: "Who is this maiden, and to whom does she belong?
What is her name, that she performs such fierce penance in your hermitage?
Maya replied: "She is a noble daughter born to my wife Tejovatī."
She took birth for the sake of a husband and performed severe penance.
Know her by the name Mandodarī; accept my auspicious welcome.
Then Rāvaṇa said: "I am a king; give her to me here."
Then, according to the prescribed rites, Maya gave his daughter to him; Rāvaṇa then went to his own island of Siṃhala, where she gave birth to a son.
As soon as he was born, the infant let out a roar from his throat.
Because of that name, he was called Meghanāda, "the Cloud-crier.
Meghanāda became a devotee of Śaṅkara just like his father;
he meditated upon Śaṅkara, the Lord of Gods, together with Pārvatī.
That body was emaciated by austerities such as fasting and other penances.
Once, Meghanāda indeed went to Mount Kailāsa;
taking a stone linga, he proceeded to the bank of the Narmadā.
It was installed in the water and worshipped by Meghanāda.
Thereafter, the village was named Meghārava, another was named Garjana,
and that sacred field (kṣetra) became known as Meghanāda.
Śaṅkara appeared before him there through his ascetic penance;
subsequently, after some time, he attained liberation when slain by Viṣṇu.
Now, there exists the sacred site of Dāruvana, which bestows merit.
In ancient times, Mātali was known as Dāruka, the charioteer of Mahendra.
Having come there, he performed intense penance in the waters of the Revā and worshipped Śaṅkara as Dārukeśvara with supreme devotion.
Śambhu was pleased and granted him a boon and a Vaiṣṇava mantra:
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā.
"Upon the partial incarnation of Viṣṇu, you shall become his charioteer."
Having gratified the Lord of the World, you shall thereafter attain a happy state.
Then Śambhu vanished, and Mātali departed for heaven.
In the course of time, that son of Vāsudeva became Mātali.
Indeed, by means of Kṛṣṇa’s yoga, he attained liberation in the abode of Goloka.
Now, there exists another supreme holy site, Karañjeśvara.
In ancient times, Karañja was born as the son of Danu from Kaśyapa.
It was there that he performed penance,
and Mahādeva, being pleased, granted him an auspicious boon:
"O son, I, Karañjaśambhu, shall indeed dwell here in this excellent sacred site."
Then that Karañja also went to heaven by the grace of Śambhu.
Next, there is the auspicious Pippaleśa Tīrtha, which bestows liberation;
it was established by Pippalāda, and one must certainly go there from that place.
Then one should go to Guhyatīrtha, which destroys the sin of killing a child.
There was a brahmin named Govinda, whose wife was devoted to her husband;
in her he begot a single, very handsome son.
Once, that brahmin also, eager to fetch firewood, went to the forest;
having brought back a load of wood, he returned home.
While he was in the house, the boy was sleeping in the darkness on his side.
The brahmin set down the load of wood quite unknowingly.
The boy died from the weight, yet the twice-born man did not realize it at all;
even so, the brahmin woman understood it after a moment.
He too, having returned to the forest, did not speak out of fear of him.
Then, when Govinda had arrived once more, she lamented;
yet, observing silence, she provided him with food and gave him a place to rest.
At night, she saw her beloved husband sleeping, covered with worms. All those worms, born from the murder of a child, were wriggling over him;
the Brahmin woman saw her own husband at night enveloped by sinful worms.
Having perceived [the truth] within his mind, he grieved, yet he did not manifest it outwardly.
Then, at dawn, the brāhmaṇa also rose quickly and went toward the Narmadā river and the forest to fetch firewood; he became thirsty.
Having drunk water and gathered forest wood, he returned home at nightfall;
having eaten his meal, he fell asleep upon his bed. Again, O Brahmins, they saw their master’s body free from worms. ||53-54||
"I must inform my husband of my son's death tomorrow morning.
Having reflected thus, she fell asleep; then, in the morning, she spoke to her husband:
"O Lord, this son of yours has been killed by you with loads of wood."
"O Lord, this terrible sin has fallen upon you in the form of a worm within your body.
It was seen previously at the end of the night; where has it gone now during this night?
Tell me, has some merit been performed, or what auspicious thing has occurred?"
The Brahmin said: "I drank the water from the Narmadā here;
at that time, I too saw those worms emerging from my body.
'What is this? What is this?'—thinking thus, I fell into a swoon."
However, considering that it should not be taken too seriously, I did not explain it to you.
O beloved! The will of the Lord is the cause of the flow of pleasure and pain.
Come, let us go to the bank of the Narmadā, leaving our son behind.
"Having bathed [the child], we shall perform the water-consecration rite (*jalavāhana-saṃskāra*).
Having thus resolved, the two took their son’s corpse in silence and went to the bank of the Narmadā; there they bathed the corpse.
Then those two bathed, and at that moment their son regained consciousness;
he quickly became endowed with breath once more. O Brahmins, the Brahmahatyā also departed swiftly from him and vanished, while she herself was then consumed by fire.
Having witnessed this supreme marvel, the two brahmins were delighted with their son;
taking him with them, they joyfully departed from the banks of the Narmadā for their own home.
[They reached] the supreme holy site named Jīvana, which destroys the sin of killing a child.
Having bathed there, one shall attain supreme perfection; of this there is no doubt.
Now follows the holy site consisting of the confluence of the Viśvarūpā and the Narmadā.
There, in former times, due to the curse of Mahendra, the excellent Apsarases—
That female sarika bird, dwelling in the mango tree, became Viśvarūpā.
Having worshipped Śaṅkara, she brought him into her direct perception.
Wherever the Lord manifested himself, there she attained liberation.
Having cast off her form as a sārikā bird, she became a beautiful and auspicious apsaras;
and there, by the grace of Śaṅkara, she was born as the river named Viśvarūpā, becoming a limb of the Narmadā. (68–69)
One desiring prosperity should bathe at that sacred ford for the sake of destroying the curse.
The cause of the curse was the excellent Gandharva Citrāṅgada,
who, while dancing in the assembly of the gods, indeed desired her with his heart.
Then, cursed by that fault, she met with destruction while dancing;
having returned once more to heaven, she went to Kailāsa as well.
Then King Dharmasena arrived at the Sārikā-tīrtha.
The lord of Kailāsa, a devoted Vaiṣṇava adorned with a horse-ornament,
immersed his own horse in the waters of the Narmadā and drank the water.
At that moment, the horse there became a captivating four-armed being.
Mounted upon a divine vehicle, he went directly to Vaikuṇṭha.
A messenger of Viṣṇu said to the king: "O King, look! This bitch has come up behind you; she has drunk water and bathed, and now she is returning. (74–75)
When the king had spoken thus, as soon as he looked at the dog, she abandoned her canine body and became a supreme apsarā.
Ascending a celestial chariot there, she departed for Vaikuṇṭha itself.
Then a voice from the sky spoke to the king: "Maintain your fortitude!
Prosperities are to be achieved through austerity by means of physical hardship.
Indeed, you who have come on foot must now travel on foot along with the feet of others."
O King, for one who arrives here traveling on foot, liberation is certain.
If you undertake a journey on foot from your own city once more, then indeed liberation shall be yours; go, O King, taking your merit with you.
Having heard this, King Dharmasena then returned home;
on the thirteenth day, traveling on foot, he arrived at the Narmadā.
Having bathed early on the fourteenth day, he beheld Sārikeśa.
Having directly beheld Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa, Kṛṣṇa, and remembering Hari,
he ascended a celestial chariot and went to the supreme domain of Vaikuṇṭha.
Then [he reached] the holy ford where the Candrabhāgā meets the Narmadā.
Candreśvara, who is Sadāśiva, shines here forever. Now, there is the sacred site known as Hāriṇa; formerly, at midday on the bank of the Narmadā, an excellent deer was killed by a hunter. (83–84)
Having fallen down, his life departed, yet he assumed a divine body;
by means of a celestial chariot, he went to the world of Brahmā.
Having seen this, the hunter attained a state of detachment and prepared for death.
Having reached a decision there, he indeed submerged himself in the water.
At that very moment, possessing a divine body, he went to the city of the Gandharvas.
This is the Hariṇeśvara Liṅga, as well as the Lubdheśvara.
There is also the holy site of Bāṇeśvara, as well as Dhanurīśvara;
and Rameśvara is the fifth holy site, for it indeed bestows liberation. There, one should devoutly offer eight flowers to the Lord.
The water-born, the lunar, the fiery, the windy, the earthly, the arboreal, the progenitor-born, and the eighth is the Śiva-flower.
The water-born should be known as water; the lunar is milk mixed with honey. (1.574.90)
Incense, lamps, and the like belong to Agni; sandalwood and the like belong to Vāyu; bulbs, roots, and the like belong to the Earth; fruits and the like belong to the Vanaspati;
auspicious food and the like belong to Prajāpati; and the worship with Śiva-flowers belongs to Śiva.
Non-violence is the first flower; the restraint of the senses is the second.
Compassion is the third flower, and the remembrance of Hari is the fourth.
Service to the true guru is the fifth, and the worship of the ancestors is indeed the sixth. (92–93)
The seventh is service to the Lord, and the eighth is taking refuge in Nārāyaṇa;
by these indeed is the Lord Anādikṛṣṇanārāyaṇa attained.
Rādhā is truly the first flower, and Lakṣmī is the second flower.
The third flower is Pārvatī; the fourth flower is Prabhā.
The fifth flower is Māṇikī; the sixth flower is Jayā.
Lalitā is the seventh flower; Mañjulā is the eighth flower. (95–96)
"These are indeed my forms as flowers, residing within flowers;
without them, O Lotus-born One, I never take up flowers at any time.
The *haṃsa*, the flower with qualities, the *campā*, and the excellent flower."
Dayā is the flower, Devikā the well-formed flower, and Muktā the beautiful flower.
Among these sixteen offerings, even though there are sixteen thousand [petals], my digit has indeed entered them; I then accept them.
"I always accept worship through the object, which is my own essential nature.
Having thus become one with Viṣṇu, he who worships shall attain the supreme goal. Having indeed visited the Hari-tīrtha, one should then proceed to the Bhārgava-tīrtha.
The supreme and most excellent of holy places, where the inhabitants of Kailāsa—
when the gods, having slain the demon Andhaka, came together with Śaṅkara to the Narmadā to bathe for the sake of the sacred ford— [reside]. (101–102)
Having diligently plunged into the northern and southern banks,
he went to the mountain named Bhṛgu on the southern bank;
there Hara pierced it with his trident, and by that piercing, the subterranean realm (rasātala) was split open.
The Gaṅgā emerged from Pātāla, for she is indeed known by the name Bhogavatī. There, a sacred ford (tīrtha) arose called Śūlabheda;
there, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva themselves always reside.
Where the Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Narmadā, and Sarasvatī are united in divine form and established at Śūlabheda—
there indeed the supreme Cakratīrtha always exists.
This supreme holy ford consists of all holy fords and is superior to all holy fords;
it is the merit exceeding all merit, the highest destroyer of all suffering.
This is the supreme and most excellent Bhṛgutīrtha, where indeed resides Lakṣmī, the daughter of Bhṛgu.
In ancient times, she was given to Viṣṇu by Bhṛgu according to the rites of marriage;
that sacred site, resembling Vaikuṇṭha, is called Bhṛgutīrtha.
Indeed, at that place, the gift of a daughter and the worship of Śrī Hari should be performed.

From hearing and reciting this, one obtains the fruit of giving gifts and performing worship. (1.574.110) Thus ends the five hundred and seventy-fourth chapter, titled "Description of Tīrthas such as Sahasrayajña-tīrtha, Śukla-tīrtha, Dvīpeśvara-tīrtha, Meghanāda-tīrtha, Dāruvana-tīrtha, Karañjeśvara-tīrtha, Jīvana-tīrtha, Viśvarūpa-revā-saṅgama, Candrāvatī-narmadā-saṅgama, Hariṇeśvara, Śūlabheda, Bhṛgukṣetra, and others," in the first section on the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. (574)
