Śrī Lakṣmī said:
"O Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, please show me mercy and tell me: what kind of gift for a daughter should be given at my father’s place?"
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
One should perform the excellent marriage of a daughter according to one's own means;
however, he who possesses no wealth at all should have the daughter beautifully adorned [with whatever he has].
Having touched a *tulasī* leaf with garments and other offerings in the presence of the fire,
the girl should be given away in the presence of water and in the presence of Brahmins within the pavilion.
Then, having taken the bridegroom’s garland, the girl should choose that groom.
If one has the inclination, one should give auspicious food and other provisions according to one’s ability.
Having obtained what is suitable, pleasing, and excellent, one should give it away without selling it.
Selling [the gift] involves acquiring wealth through trade and giving it away; this constitutes a great sin.
Having approached her of one's own accord, she should be given; that indeed is the highest form of giving (tāraka).
Having summoned her, she should be given; that indeed is the middling form of giving. And having taken her by force, she should be given; that indeed is the lowest form of giving.
She should be given away like a servant-girl; [otherwise] it is fruitless, like giving a slave girl.

(7) When the giving of the daughter is taking place, the women of the household should perform the chanting of the glories of Śrī Hari there in the pavilion resounding with the noise of musical instruments. (8)
Once that gift has been bestowed, the husband and wife should perform the worship and viewing of Hari, and thereafter they may enter their own home.
Every morning, they should regularly perform the worship and other rites with excellent materials.
They should perform worship with the most excellent services and never commit an offense.
For those who commit offenses against the worship, only sin arises.
Listen, O Lakṣmī, as I describe the faults along with their corresponding expiations.
My devotee should always be intent upon my rites;
having set aside even a small portion of his house as a temple for me, he should worship me there.
Having installed an image according to his desire, he should honor it with baths, garments, and pure sandalwood paste.
Devoted to Me, one should daily worship with leaves, flowers, water, food offerings, incense, lamps, and presentations;
with circumambulations, waving of lights, hymns of praise, prostrations, and the ritual dismissal,
having first offered meditative concentration.
One should listen to the discourse, perform its recitation, and provide instruction; one should engage in dancing and instrumental music, and hold a most enchanting festival.
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to my eternal dharma according to its true essence.
Even the gods who possess knowledge of yoga and understand the Sāṃkhya do not know this.
Without initiation into the Bhāgavata path, my worship is fruitless;
among hundreds of thousands, only someone rare obtains initiation that brings me joy.
Having made his mind peaceful within himself, he should approach the Guru. Honoring the Guru’s command, he should pray: "O Guru, instruct me!
He should then procure the materials for initiation and other necessities as pointed out by the Guru.
Parched grain, honey, and kusha grass, as well as clarified butter and what is called nectar;
milk, curd, cow urine, dung, and fine sugar; the sacred thread, fragrance, saffron, and likewise unbroken grains. || 1.575.20 ||
Flowers, *tulasī*, incense, a lamp, food offerings, fruit, water,
a garland, a necklace, a black antelope skin, a sacred thread,
a staff, a water-pot, clothing, an upper garment, a jar, and sesame seeds. (21)
The two sandals, the vessel for the arghya offering, the sacrificial pot, rice grains, and a ladle;
barley, jaggery, parched grain, fruits, and various foods; as well as all kinds of eatables, drinks, and articles suitable for ritual use. (22–23)
Whatever seeds and various kinds of jewels there may be,
glass vessels, jars, mango bowls, and cords;
the beautiful leaves of the *aśoka* tree, and even a wooden bench.
The three mantras, water for rinsing the mouth, the vessel for the fire-oblation (homa), the small wooden ladle (sruva) and other implements;
all the sacrificial woods—namely those of the Pippala, Udumbara, Khadira, Bilva, Apāmārga, and Arka trees. (25–26)
One should procure the wood of the *āmalaka*, *tulasī*, sandalwood, and likewise the *vaṭa* tree, as well as *śāla* and *madhuka*.
Having bathed and being endowed with auspiciousness, one should construct a most beautiful altar.
The Brahmin should cause a square mandala, sixteen cubits on each side, to be prepared there with grains; it should be the Sarvatobhadra design.
In the center, he should place a new water-pot adorned with flowers and sprouts.
One should place vessels made of gold, silver, or copper within a container filled with jewels;
having placed upon them a bowl full of sesame seeds according to the prescribed rite,
one should worship me, the Supreme Brahman, as well as the Guru, with excellent offerings.
One should indeed place consecrated, excellent substances in the center of the altar (vedi).
O beautiful one, one should place four water-pots (kalaśas) on the four sides,
filled with water, provided with fresh leaves, and adorned with fruits.
Having touched those [trees] which are wrapped all over in white cloths and adorned with mango blossoms,
and having performed the ritual sipping of water (upaspṛśya) in the dwelling and in the pavilion in the presence of the Guru,
the disciple [should receive] the mantra from the Guru, who faces east, while facing north.
One should receive the supreme Bhāgavata mantra through the left ear:
"May the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa be my refuge," and "Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; svāhā. (34–35)
The Guru should cause all women and men to hear these two mantras;
for the mantra is indeed a limb of initiation, and it is Hari himself in the form of knowledge.
By the power of the mantra, this disciple becomes a true devotee of the Lord (bhāgavata).
Upon seeing these devotees of the Lord (bhāgavatas), one should rise from one's seat.
Just as I am to be honored, so indeed are the people who are devotees of the Lord.
For he who, being himself a pure devotee of the Lord, sees other devotees of the Lord— ||| 37-38 ||

He did not rise to greet me; for that reason, I was insulted by him. Furthermore, he who gives a daughter to a devotee and then sends her away has, without a doubt, harmed the eight classes of ancestors.
That pitiless man who harms his wife— who is a dear friend, virtuous, faithful, a Vaiṣṇavī, the very form of Lakṣmī, and the deity of the home—
shall never again obtain a wife because of that very sin.
Those who cause suffering to women always remain miserable themselves.
[The following trees are auspicious: the bilva tree, the udumbara, the tulasī, the plakṣa, and likewise the āmra;
the aśoka, the bakula, the āmalakī, and the karṇikā as well.
For trees belonging to the deities must not be cut down at their roots during ritual acts.
Likewise, O Lakṣmī, one who is initiated must avoid what is unfit to be eaten;
likewise, he must avoid what is unfit to be drunk, as well as slander and violence.
Slander, theft, and seduction must be avoided, while the honoring of guests must be performed.
Sexual intercourse should be abandoned in every way, and celibacy is its restraint.
Furthermore, service to the guru must be protected with diligent effort.
Having seen the good fortune, wealth, prosperity, and so forth of others,
and having seen one's own poverty, one should never feel agitation.
In this way, indeed, one should observe the prescribed rules and serve one’s mother and father.
One should always perform the worship of Śrī Hari according to the prescribed rule.
Then, one should place two leaves of the *udumbara* tree upon the altar, as well as a water vessel and a razor; thereafter, one should invoke me.
"Come, O Blessed One, and be present here in this image and upon this altar.

Accept this water for the guest-offering and the water for the feet; then, have the auspicious shaving performed at the side of the pavilion, so that the impurities of the hair may depart. (1.575.49–50)
Having had his hair shaved— leaving only the crown-lock (śikhā)— and being free of blood, he should bathe, put on clean washed garments,
and likewise don an upper cloth; then he should pay obeisance to the Guru and to Hari.
Having kindled the god of fire within the sacrificial fire-pot,
he performed the oblation seven times with ghee mixed with honey, along with parched grain, black sesame seeds, and other offerings; and twenty times with rice and sesame.
Then, one should bow to you, the fire whose nature is truth, as it speaks.
Having performed three circumambulations of the Lord, the devotee of the Blessed One, and the Guru,
and having touched the feet of the Guru, one should then pray to the true Guru.
"By the grace of the Guru-deity, initiation has been obtained by my own will.
And whatever offense I may have committed, may the Guru forgive me.
To the disciple who has spoken thus, he should give the sacred thread (yajñopavīta). ||55-56||
Likewise, one should give a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu) for the sake of purification;
sandalwood paste, fragrance, and Vaiṣṇava oil to Viṣṇu.
Furthermore, the disciple should offer the madhuparka according to the sequence of worship.
One should offer clothing, ornaments, and a garland of flowers to Nārāyaṇa.
Then the guru should place a tulasī necklace around the neck of the disciple,
and likewise apply a forehead mark (tilaka) together with a crescent moon upon his forehead.

One should give him a name associated with Nārāyaṇa, endowed with the title of Ācārya, or one associated with Dāsa; likewise, one should provide him with appropriate attire. Furthermore, one should bestow gifts according to the individual and according to one's own capacity.
Having bowed to the sacrificial fire, the deity, the guru, and the Vaiṣṇavas,
and having given them a sacrificial fee, food, and clothing, he should go home. There,
the brāhmaṇa should prepare a seat made of the skin of a black antelope.
This Brāhmaṇa should always carry a staff made of *pālāśa* wood;
however, the Kṣatriya, having laid down his weapons, should undergo initiation according to the prescribed rules and take up,
in particular, the skin of a goat and a staff made of *plakṣa* wood.

Having caused an altar twelve cubits in size to be constructed as before, one should receive all other auspicious matters from the Guru during the initiation. One should observe the rules, thinking: "I shall not touch a weapon that causes harm. (64–65)
Then, having received the Bhāgavata initiation according to the previously stated procedure,
one should feed all the pure Bhāgavatas and present them with gifts.
Then the Vaiśya, having brought all the materials, prepares an auspicious altar.
One should have it made ten cubits long and smear it with cow dung.
One should also hold a goat skin and a staff made of udumbara wood.
Everything else should be performed as before, and one shall become initiated.
Having performed salutations to the gods and to the foremost among the Bhāgavatas,
one should give food to the virtuous and ask for forgiveness for any offenses.
Even a Śūdra may receive the auspicious initiation of the Bhāgavatas.
Indeed, all the ritual substances have been previously described by me.
One should arrange them upon the altar; the altar should be provided with eight corners.
There, one should perform the rite according to the previous rule and worship Hari.
The hide of a blue goat and a staff belonging to Viṣṇu—
by thus receiving initiation, a Śūdra becomes a Bhāgavata.
He should feed Vaiṣṇava saints and saintly women according to his means.
The umbrella for all four castes indicates the teacher’s knowledge.
The preceptor should cause to be given a white umbrella for a Brāhmaṇa, a red one for a Kṣatriya, a yellow one for a Vaiśya, and likewise a blue one for a Śūdra. (73–74)
O Lakṣmī, I shall tell you here what must be performed by those who have been initiated:
in every way, O beloved, I am to be meditated upon within the *gomukhī* [cow-faced] rosary made of *tulasī*.
That *tulasī* rosary, which effects the counting, is situated at the end of the *gaṇa*s.
This is the initiation known as Gaṇāntikā, which takes the form of the seed-syllable of the limbs of initiation.
By means of it, my worship must be performed so that the initiation may yield great fruit.
Having made Guṇāntikā secret, the best of the wise should meditate upon me. (76–77)
If one undertakes initiation on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight in the months of Kārttika, Mārgaśīrṣa, or Vaiśākha,
remaining without food until the morning of the twelfth day,
one is indeed liberated from the bondage of worldly existence.
One should indeed give me a beautiful comb for the purpose of grooming my hair;
one should give collyrium and a mirror, and likewise give a garland.
One who is impure from eating should not touch the garland; rather, one should place it in the open air.
My devotee should perform the twilight worship (saṃdhyā), which consists essentially of meditation;
having fixed his meditation for a muhūrta, he should repeatedly recite my mantra.
He should place a lamp before me that increases the mass of splendor.
Likewise, one should apply a moon-shaped tilaka on the forehead of the wrestler;
then one should offer fragrant incense and recite this verse:
"O Keśava, your limbs are fragrant by their very nature. (82–83)
Accept these houses perfumed with this auspicious incense.
One should offer a lamp produced from ghee, which is auspicious and a deliverer of the ancestors.
A vessel made of gold, silver, or bronze is recommended for me.
"Having abandoned all those here, indeed copper pleases me.
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the truth from me as to why copper is dear to me.
Formerly, O lotus-petal-eyed one, there was a great Asura named Guḍākeśa. (85–86)
Taking up the form of copper, he remained devoted to my worship alone for fourteen thousand years with perfect steadfastness. Filled with great delight, I went to his Copper Hermitage (Tāmra-āśrama).
Seeing me with four arms, he indeed bowed down to me repeatedly.
I said to him, "I am pleased with you; choose a boon desired by your heart.
Then Guḍākeśa spoke with a purified inner self.
"May my devotion to you be firm throughout thousands of births.
O Mādhava, I desire that my death be brought about by the discus released by you.
And whatever fat, flesh, and so forth belongs to one struck down by my discus—"
"O Lord, let that which is called copper be auspicious and purifying.
O Master, let your pleasure be supreme in the offering of a copper vessel.
"So be it," he said to me, for as long as the world endures. (91–92)
"Until then, you shall be my vessel in the form of copper.
Whatever abundant gift is given to me in that copper vessel—auspicious and pure—that copper was created by me at that time. (93)
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, when the sun was at its zenith, he who desired his own death by the discus, performing auspicious acts for my sake, thought:
"When shall I become established in Viṣṇu? || 94-95 ||
Then, having performed my worship, he prayed to me:
"O Lord, release, release the discus which has a brilliance equal to fire!
Let my soul be taken away quickly by cutting off my limbs on all sides. (96)
Slain by me and by my discus, he has come before me, the Supreme Lord.
That copper-colored flesh of his, dripping with blood, has been prepared by me as prescribed.
One should offer the *prāpaṇaka* oblation in the copper vessel, beginning with the worship and the meal.
For every grain of boiled rice [offered], he shall obtain the fruit born of a hundred horse-sacrifices.
For that many thousands of divine years, he rejoices in my abode;
thereafter, he goes to the supreme abode, the highest state.
Having thus fed me with food from a copper vessel, a golden one, or even a silver one,
and having offered betel-leaf, he should perform the ritual dismissal (*visarjana*).
In this manner, my devotee who has been initiated should indeed perform the worship.
"O beloved Lakṣmī, this has been declared by Śambhu as eternally true.
By hearing it or even by reciting it, a man, a woman, or anyone else shall attain my abode, provided they have received initiation according to the prescribed rite. (102)
"By worshipping me, one shall attain liberation for oneself; for that is indeed the fruit of birth.

Thus ends the five hundred and seventy-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Gift of a Daughter, the Procedure for Initiation into the Bhāgavata Path, and the Transformation of the Blood and Other Fluids of the Asura named Guḍākeśa into Copper Ore Following His Destruction by the Discus," in the first section, the Kṛta-yuga lineage, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
*Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā*, Section 1 (Kṛta-yuga Lineage), Chapter 575.
Chapter 576 [Author:
Chapter 577 → Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O Lord, having heard from the mouth of Nārāyaṇa this auspicious initiation and having understood your majesty, I have become pure.
Oh, how great is the majesty of the God, which brings happiness to the four castes!
Indeed, this was known through the granting of initiation, as well as other matters due to the cause of devotion.
(2) And I ask: regarding transgressions, what is the fruit and what is the remedy?
O Janārdana, tell us the purification for those who are intent upon Your worship. (3)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, I shall describe the purification of offenses.
Having become pure and a devotee of the Lord, one should be intent upon my worship. (4)
O Lord of Creatures, even when fallen into distress, the king who eats food accumulated through sin dwells in hell because of that sin.
The king proceeds by performing actions characterized by darkness (tamas) and passion (rajas).
His food is cruel, censurable, and a great burden of sin. A righteous person must not eat the food of a king, for it leads to hell.
Or rather, the food of kings may be eaten by men who are devotees of the Lord (bhāgavatas).
O Lakṣmī! if, having set me aside and having offered everything to me in every way,
one offers [the food] abundant with auspicious grains and wealth and accepts it for oneself—
then the remnants of my grace (prasāda) are considered accomplished by the devotees of the Bhāgavata.
For one who eats [there], no stain of sin is produced. O Lotus-born One, if one eats the food of a king without his favor,
purification for my devotee shall likewise come through the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
If one who has not chewed a tooth-stick and has not cleansed his mouth touches me after bathing, he will have foul-smelling breath; therefore,
that devotee becomes devoid of merit due to my own offense against him.
O Lakṣmī, a human being is indeed a sinner, for he is filled with the impurities of phlegm and bile;
since his mouth is always foul-smelling with pus and blood, he must inhale pure air and exhale that stench. (12–13)
Because of that, an offense against him arises on my part due to the proximity to his image.
Purity may be restored by means of a tooth-stick and the application of fragrant substances.
When such an offense has thus occurred, one who dwells in the open air (vyomaśāyī) [should remain so] for two days.
He should perform intense devotion to me; being devoted to Kṛṣṇa, he should perform the recitation of a hundred garlands [of beads], and no offense exists.
However, having engaged in sexual intercourse and not having bathed, he is indeed like a corpse.
And as a ripening of that transgression, he shall fall into the hell named Lāla.
For a human being, the supreme duty consists of bathing, meditation, and worship.
One who does not bathe and is laden with feces and urine shall fall into the hell named Mala.
An expiation must be performed for him with a mind endowed with devotion.
He should eat either barley-gruel or oil-cake for three days, and on the fourth day he should fast; by this, the purification of the devotee is accomplished.
Now, he who touches a corpse and goes to the cremation ground but does not bathe—
his ancestors fall because of his impurity, and he himself shall surely fall as well.
Having become jackals in the cremation ground, they become eaters of corpses.
An expiation must be performed for him by my devotee directly:
eating a single meal for one day, and likewise fasting for one day;
then, having drunk the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), he is purified—of this there is no doubt.
That pitiless man who touches me after touching a woman in her menses—
by that sin, even though he be a devotee, he goes to the realm of Yama consisting of dust.
Thereafter, he is born blind, impoverished, and devoid of intelligence.
The purification for that offense is indeed fasting alone.
Having slept in the open air, bathed with one's clothes on, and consumed the products of the cow (*gavya*), he who is devoted to my rites shall be released from impurity. (24–25)
O Lakṣmī! He who, having touched a corpse while residing in my sacred fields, does not bathe and yet touches me, shall attain birth as a Cāṇḍāla;
thereafter he is born blind, and then becomes a frog and a fly.
Whether it be a *ṭiṭṭibha* bird, a mosquito, a lizard, or even a donkey;
or perhaps a cat or a monkey—a wrongdoer is born as such [an animal] for the sake of purification, provided he is my devotee and devoted to my ritual service. (27–28)
One should subsist on a single meal for fifteen days;
thereafter, one should consume the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), and thus one is purified from the offense.
When I am touched by one [who has committed this], the wind of the lower apertures (*apānavāyu*) is released.
By that fault, he may be born as a fly or likewise a mouse;
or he may be born as a dog or a tortoise, after which he becomes a human being.
Therefore, he should observe three nights of fasting at night, and by that he is purified.
One devoted to devotion should perform the recitation of the *śatamālā* and bathe;
even one who voids excrement along with wind and humors,
or who stands engaged in my worship, or is intent upon other rites dedicated to me.
Thereafter, O Lakṣmī, he shall fall into the Yāmya Purīṣa hell; from that, he is born as a human being devoted to my rites. Then, an expiation must be performed, namely lying down in water.
One should also lie upon the bare ground for one day;
by performing a hundred recitations of the *mālā-mantra*, one is released from the transgression.
Even if, after bathing, one walks upon dirty paths, [one is purified].

Indeed, whoever approaches me without having washed his feet and so forth is impure and sinful; he is one who acts against my pleasure. Therefore, I do not truly accept the perfumes and garlands offered by him out of devotion.
Having washed his feet and hands in that manner,

and having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) according to rule, being thus purified, he should touch me. Likewise, having discarded the impurity, he should apply clay to himself seven times.
Having applied [the paste] to the cleansing organ, one should likewise apply it to the two hands;
then five times to the feet, and thereafter one should wipe the vessel clean.
Having performed seven mouthfuls of rinsing water (gaṇḍūṣa), one should then perform the bath.
O beloved, my devotee indeed becomes pure as a worshiper, and not otherwise;
if one with portions of perfume in hand should touch me, he would become a partaker of fault.
Having performed breath control (prāṇāyāma) and sipping water (ācamana), he should wash his hands.
In this way, O Lakṣmī, there shall be purity, and then no offense will occur.
However, that man who, even if he is my devotee, touches my limbs while possessed by anger, he shall then become a partaker of the fault.
By that sin he shall become a *cillī* bird, and thereafter he shall become a hawk;
through anger he becomes a black-colored insect known as a *mṛtkaṭika*.
One should not act out of anger, nor out of greed, nor with haste.
My worship should be performed according to the prescribed rite, for that indeed bestows liberation.
Having bathed, one should fashion a hundred garlands; by this, the purification of anger is considered achieved.
He who worships me on earth with unworthy flowers—
Furthermore, one who gives me flowers becomes a fool, a devotee of the Lord, or else is born as a monkey;
or he may become a cat, a bull, a goat, or a village cock;
or he may even become a buffalo—such is what does not please me.
And for the sake of that purification, one should indeed eat but once a day for seven days;
thus one shall be liberated from all sins and attain a place in my world.
If, moreover, one approaches me clad in garments smeared with blood, [one attains the same].
One who approaches me while wearing garments stained with the menstrual blood of a woman in her courses will, by that fault, be born as a dog-eater (śvapaca); of this there is no doubt.
He should subsist on a single meal for one month and recite the mantra a thousand times.
On the final day, however, he should observe a fast; thus he becomes pure.
He who touches me in the darkness without a lamp incurs a fault;
he shall be born blind, and I shall now declare the expiation for that.
One should eat only once a day for five days while keeping the eyes covered;
one should also recite a hundred malas, and then one shall become purified.
Black clothing must never be worn during my worship under any circumstances.
Due to that fault, one may thereafter become a mongoose or a tortoise, or even a pigeon;
I shall now declare the expiation for you:
one should eat but a single meal for seven days and cause a hundred garlands to be fashioned.
Then his purification shall occur, and he shall attain my world.
He who performs my rites while wearing unwashed garments—whether he be an elephant, a camel, a horse, or even a jackal—[shall likewise attain it]. //56//
Therefore, it must be a *sāraṅga* (a spotted deer); purification should be performed with great effort.
One should observe a single fast and recite the rosary one hundred times.
Furthermore, if that which was left over by a dog has been given to me in my ritual act, [purification is required].
He would even become a dog, a jackal, or a crow;
therefore, purification must be performed by subsisting on vegetables, roots, and fruits for three days.
On the fourth day, one should drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and likewise observe a fast.
My offense shall indeed perish, and I shall attain the world [of Kṛṣṇa]. When lighting a lamp, the finger becomes blackened with soot;
it should be diligently washed away, being filled with the scent of the burnt wick.
If one touches [the deity] without having washed one's hands, it would be an offense against me;
by that, one would become a leper and afflicted with disease. Therefore, one should purify one's hand.
When an offense has occurred, one should perform the recitation of the *mālā-mantra* one hundred times.
By fasting, one becomes pure; thus one becomes fit for ritual action.
That person who, having gone to a cremation ground, touches me without having bathed, is reborn as a jackal, a vulture, or a piśāca spirit.
Then one should fast for one day and recite the thousand-fold mantra;
by that, purification occurs, and not otherwise merely through bathing.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
"But if the cremation ground is indeed impure, how is it that Śambhu, the supreme devotee of the Lord,
dwells in your cremation ground like one who shares in its defects?
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī, I shall relate to you an ancient account concerning Śambhu.
There is indeed no cremation ground that is pure; it is always considered impure.
Yet, for a certain reason, Śambhu took pleasure in dwelling there.
He always considers that very dwelling to be the nature of his penance.
Even though the great Śaṅkara is my supreme devotee,
I do not accept offerings such as worship from him while he dwells in the cremation ground.
"After the performance of penance, I shall accept everything, and never otherwise;
just as Śaṅkara destroyed the three cities and likewise the Asura.
Then [he spoke of] the children, the elderly, and the women residing in the three cities.
Tainted by that sin, Śaṅkara’s sovereignty was lost;
indeed, his power of yoga perished and his power of illusion vanished.
With a pale countenance, he became unable even to move.
He became as if dead by the curses delivered by the Asura women;
deprived of consciousness, his knowledge destroyed, and his joy vanished, he was like one who is powerless.
Then, having beheld Śaṅkara, I approached him.
I said, "Do not grieve; I shall indeed swiftly do what is for your welfare.
Then, with my divine eye, I beheld Śaṅkara, and at that moment, the power of Rudra was once again made manifest.
I said, "I have come for the sake of destroying your sin.
Hearing this, Hara, his eyes inflamed by the heat of his own sin, spoke to me:
"O Viṣṇu, by your grace, the Asura Tripuraka has been slain."
The Dānavas were slain there, and those who were pregnant were struck down;
the young and the old were killed, and the three cities were consumed by fire.
By the power of that sin, I am unable to move.
"O Viṣṇu, my sovereignty and power are lost, and my knowledge, self, and true strength have perished. What should be done by me now, who am in such a state of sin?
O Viṣṇu, tell me in truth the means for the purification of this sin."
To me who was thus entreating, Rudra spoke:
"Wearing a garland of skulls, wander upon the earth as one possessed of impurity.
Śambhu asked me: "In what sense is 'impurity' proclaimed?"
I have indeed said that a cremation ground is impure and called putrid;
dwelling here in a cremation ground is proclaimed to be the state of being defiled.
O Śaṅkara, take up skulls there and sport right there!
Dwell for a hundred years together with my attendants, such as the bhūtas, pretas, and others.
During that time, no external worship of me should ever be performed;
rather, mental worship must be practiced, and there shall be no offense.
When a full hundred years have passed, go to the hermitage of Gautama.
Through the grace of the sage Gautama, you shall become free from sin.
Then, through the destruction of that evil, practice the purification of your body.
"Accept for a year the vow of subsisting on milk alone to achieve purification;
or else, perform the excellent monthly vow known as the *brahmakūrca*.
By doing so, you will become pure and worthy of worship. (86–87)
"O Śava! Hereafter, you must never dwell in a cremation ground if you desire my state of being worthy of worship and the virtue of a Vaiṣṇava.
Having thus granted this boon to Rudra, I vanished on that very spot.
Even Rudra wandered for a hundred years in a cremation ground,
lacking the purificatory rites and devoted solely to my command.
When a hundred years had passed, Rudra went indeed to the hermitage of Gautama.
Then Gautama proclaimed this instruction to him:
"O Rudra, always maintain a dual form according to your activity.
All your sin has departed here; you are indeed pure and a great Vaiṣṇava. (91)
Always assume the sattvic form of a great devotee;
always remain on Kailāsa and be devoted to your followers with a sattvic nature. And assume a second form, that of Bhairava, which is of the nature of a shadow.
"It is to be venerated by *bhūtas*, *pretas*, and *piśācas*;
it is impure, fit for dwelling in cremation grounds, and a constant refuge for those characterized by *tamas*.
Having been addressed thus, Śaṅkara then again assumed two forms.
"One who dwells in a cremation ground is neither my devotee nor even a Vaiṣṇava.
"Indeed, one who dwells on Kailāsa is my devotee, worthy of worship, and the best of Vaiṣṇavas.
O Lakṣmī! Thus has been described that cremation ground which is always impure.
Those dwelling in the cremation ground are indeed impure and certainly not pure in that place of corpses;
later, Śaṅkara’s Kailāsa was likewise described as a cremation ground by such people as the Bhūtas and others who are characterized by darkness (tamas).
In reality, this cremation ground beloved of Śaṅkara does not exist at all.
O Lakṣmī, a cremation ground is not dear to anyone;
how then could it be dear to the gods, who are characterized by virtuous actions?
Thus I have told you the truth; now I shall tell you the expiation.
One should consume the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) while fasting for one day.
A bath with clothing should be taken, and one should eat *tulasī* leaves.
Released from that sin, he shall become worthy of performing my rites.
However, one who commits the act of drinking liquor falls away from his body;
for him, purification occurs in every respect through the Brahmakūrca vow.
Otherwise, he would become an owl, and indeed he becomes a worm once again.
O Lakṣmī, listen as I describe the Brahmakūrca vow, which brings about purification;
it should be performed by an embodied being for either a month or a fortnight.
One should boil together curd-whey (*payasyā*), *āmalaka*, ginger, and *palāśa* leaves, along with sugar and *tulasī* leaves, and drink this during the day;
in such a way that it may be digested properly and not undergo any morbid transformation. 1.04–1.05.
One should eat nothing else and drink no water for the sake of purification;
this is the Brahmakūrca vow, to be observed either for a fortnight or for a month.
Whatever purifying leaves there may be of trees—
One should certainly boil the leaves of the *pālāśa* tree and drink them daily;
or one may drink the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) every fortnight or every month.
That is equal to the *brahmakūrca* rite and purifies one from all sins.
This, however, makes the body free from impurities and bestows liberation when death occurs;
it is indeed a purgative and a decoction for the sake of purifying the bodily elements. When performed with devotion to Brahman, that very act is ordained for the purpose of liberation.
If that [medicine] is administered as an expiation, it will indeed serve to wash away sin.
If it is for the purpose of destroying disease, it will bring about the purification of the bodily constituents (*dhātus*).
But if it is administered inappropriately at some point, it leads to death.

Indeed, a man who commits an offense against me shall become a pig that eats onions, vegetables, leaves, and the like; or he shall become a dog, or even a jackal. Having performed the Brahmakūrca vow, one should perform a hundred recitations of the Mālā-mantra.
By that, his purification shall be achieved, and he shall become worthy of performing rites for me.
(11.3) But he who touches me while wearing another's garment, even if it has been washed, attains birth as a deer and becomes one with crippled feet. (11.4)
In the month of Māgha, one should remain in water for exactly two *praharas*;
by that, purification is attained, and by reciting the *Śatamālā* mantra, one becomes stainless.
He who, drawn by sensual cravings, eats himself while not offering fresh food to me [is likewise stained].
One who enjoys [the offerings] without having given them becomes a partaker of evil; therefore, one should observe the fast (*samupoṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, by reciting the *mālā-mantra* a hundred times, that person is purified.
He who offers incense to me without first offering perfume and garlands—
He would become a *yātudhāna*; therefore, he must perform a fast (*samupoṣaṇa*).
Even by reciting the *mālā-mantra* one hundred times, that Vaiṣṇava is indeed purified.
He who approaches me while wearing sandals on his feet [is likewise defiled].
He shall be born as a leather-worker, and thereafter he becomes a dog and then a pig. O Lotus-born One, by performing the Pākṣika, Ekabhakta, and Śatamālā vows, my devotee shall attain purification.
If anyone indeed awakens me without the sound of a bell or other instruments, he becomes deaf; therefore, he must observe a fast.
Furthermore, my devotee who performs one hundred recitations of the *mālā* mantra is purified.
Having eaten food in great quantity, one who is overwhelmed by indigestion and returns with belching,
yet approaches [the sacrificial ground] without having bathed,
is indeed reborn as a monkey, a jackal, a dog, or a goat. (122–123)
One should fast for three days and fashion a hundred garlands. He who performs this expiation according to this rule shall not be tainted by sin; he goes to my world.
But that devotee who, rising daily at dawn, causes [this] to be recited,
or reads it, or even hears it, goes to my world. O Padmaja, what was spoken by Śambhu has indeed been told by me to you as the truth.
It is the greatest health among all forms of health, the supreme liberation among all liberations,
the highest purification among all purifications, and the state of being a worthy vessel among those who are serene.
This devotion to me, which I have proclaimed, is the highest austerity among all austerities.
My devotee must act [thus], without hesitation regarding the rākṣasas.
This has been proclaimed by me here for the sake of those seeking liberation, for yogins, for virtuous women, for the righteous, and for those endowed with devotion to me.
"O Lakṣmī, this purification has not been spoken by me for the sake of atheists whose hearts are seized by latent impressions (*vāsanā*) attached to the poison of the womb.

Thus ends the five hundred and seventy-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Offenses in the Worship of the Blessed Lord within the Lineage of the Kṛta Age in the First Book of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*," concerning their purification or the attainment of another body or another womb, as well as the explanation of Śaṅkara’s fondness for cremation grounds and his dwelling in places other than cremation grounds. 576.1–30.
← Chapter 576: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga) Chapter 577 [[Author: → Chapter 578
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī! After the death of the jackal and the vulture, through the occasion of touching a sacred ford (tīrtha), there was the attainment of a kingdom and liberation.
A princess who died at a sacred ford against her will became a female jackal,
yet she possessed large eyes and was endowed with the sixty-four arts.
Likewise, the vulture that died there also became a king.
"Oh, how great indeed is the power of sacred fords! Two animals have attained divinity. (3) In the land of Himālaya, there was Brahmadatta, the king of Kāmpilya.
His son, Somadatta, having reflected upon the purpose of the Śrāddha rite, (4)
At that time, having gone into the forest for the sake of his ancestors, he was seeking deer;
yet he found nothing there, and instead a female jackal was spotted by him. Pierced by that arrow, she went to the waters of the Gaṅgā.
Having drunk water at the bank, he quickly gave up his life at that sacred bathing place (tīrtha).
At that moment, the prince saw a vulture perched upon a banyan tree;
the royal youth struck down the vulture with an arrow.
Having fallen by the water's edge, even he who was dead attained merit.
Then Somadatta, having taken the two of them, went home;
and from there, the vulture became the handsome son of the King of Kaliṅga.
Thus she was born as a female jackal, the daughter of the King of Kāñcī.
By the power of the two holy places (*tīrtha*), a union occurred spontaneously between them.
Married, the two of them, full of deep affection, spent their time in happiness.
Pervaded by love for one another, they never endured separation at any time.
Then once, the bride, filled with affection, said to her husband:
"O beloved, I must perform a certain vow; please grant me your permission."
Out of affection for me, if this is pleasing to you, you ought to grant me permission here.
Truth is the root of subjects, and Viṣṇu is established in truth;
the kingdom always has truth as its foundation, and the vow prospers through truth.
Thus addressed, the husband said: "Request it, my dear; do what you wish.
Perform all that you desire, and I shall provide you with the highest assistance.
Hearing her husband's words, she spoke to him with full confidence.
"Being in such a state, I wish to sleep alone at midday,
so that no one may see me for even a very short time— neither my father-in-law, nor my mother-in-law, nor my husband, nor any other person. (15–16)
"He shall not see me while I am asleep; this is my vow for a moment.
Having heard this, the prince said "Certainly" to his wife.
He gave her a private palace where indeed no other person was present.
"May no one at all see the one of great vows upon her bed.
Having made this agreement, that young prince lived accordingly;
he enjoyed and ruled over that kingdom granted by his father.
He had five sons, to whom he gave the kingdom in order of seniority. Then, having undertaken a vow just like his wife, he would sleep alone where no person could see him. (1.577.20)
Seventy-seven years had indeed passed for him;
then, in his seventy-eighth year, that lord of men,
while the sun was at its zenith, remained in solitude, contemplating that very same matter.
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Vaiśākha, his mind was set upon the longing to behold his beloved:
"Who is to be worshipped? What vow is for her? She sleeps in a secluded place. (23)
For one who is asleep, no vow whatsoever is fulfilled, even by one who performs great merit.
No dharma has been performed by anyone; that very state of sleep is itself the vow.
Having indeed enjoyed sensual pleasures, and having eaten meat with rice, [one must perform penance]. 24–25.
Betel, silk garments and the like, ornaments, garlands, all things for adornment such as cosmetics, and fragrant unguents—
why would there be any religious vow here, since she performs whatever vow she does while asleep? (26)
She must certainly be seen to discover what kind of vow she observes.
Even if she becomes angry upon being seen, let her be angry; nevertheless, let her go wherever she pleases, even if she departs in a rage.
Or if some loss should occur, let it be so;
nevertheless, as he reflects thus, the sun has reached the sky.
Then, having bathed according to the prescribed rite, he was clothed in two linen garments.
Having done so, he dismissed all his attendants from his presence:
"Today I must remain in my vow; no people are to come to the house, nor even a man or a woman to the gate of the royal palace."
"If anyone should come here, he shall become my victim.
Having thus issued his command,
the king went into the interior of his palace and hid beneath the couch of the queen, concealed by coverings.

At the time of midday, the queen arrived at that seat. Afflicted by illness and tormented by a headache, she wept there, thinking: "What did I do in the past, the fruit of which is this painful sensation? (33–34)
My husband does not even know that I am afflicted with pain upon his own head.
What should I do? Where should I go? Indeed, I must surely die.
My husband does not ask here at all: "What vow is this, and of what kind is it?"
I must tell him; otherwise there will be no end.
If I speak, my death will come; if I do not speak, it will cause destruction. If I do not speak, I must always endure suffering that does not cease.
"Therefore, I must go to that place along with my husband,
so that I may relate to my lord the suffering I have encountered.
Having heard these words of his beloved, the king then rose up.
Embracing his beautiful wife with both arms, he spoke to her with fortitude:
"O blessed lady, why do you speak thus concerning yourself, who are afflicted?
There are many physicians who will eliminate this suffering."
Previously, under the pretext of a vow, you well concealed this knowledge,
O blessed lady, by which you indeed suffer, tormented by pain in your head.
And as for what you say, O blessed lady, when you are afflicted by suffering—
"Having gone there first, I shall speak to my husband.
O blessed lady, tell me what that place is, if you find the journey pleasing;
you must certainly go there with me and obtain happiness."
"What is this that you conceal, O Goddess, in the presence of your husband, you who are devoted to your husband?
The husband is dharma, the husband is fame, and the husband alone is one's own beloved.
According to the dharma proclaimed for a devoted wife, even that which is secret must be told to the husband. (44)
Thus addressed, she said to her husband: "In this narration there would be destruction;
therefore, O Lord, you must not speak what causes you pain.
For you always abide in happiness; you are a great king and handsome. (45-46)
"Many wives resembling me reside in your inner apartments;
enjoy yourself at ease, O Great King, without abandoning me alone.
I shall go to my own place, for otherwise my death is certain."
O King, you shine like a god; it does not behove you to question me thus.
You are my god, my manifest preceptor, my husband, and the eternal sacrifice.
O giver of honor, you are virtue, wealth, desire, fame, and heaven itself.
When questioned by me, you must speak what is beneficial, true, factual, and pleasant to you;
for this is the eternal duty of all women devoted to their husbands.
A husband who is established in happiness should not be subjected to doubt by his wife.
Having ascertained this, you ought not to ask me about my suffering here.
The husband said: "Listen, O blessed lady, whether it be auspicious or inauspicious;
a wife, when questioned by her husband, must certainly speak."
Virtuous women do not conceal what is already hidden, nor do they guard what is not hidden;
she who guards what is hidden in the presence of her husband is indeed not a virtuous wife.
The wife spoke these meaningful words, consistent with dharma, to the king, her beloved.
It is recited that "The king is a god, the king is a guru, the king is Soma. (54) One must not speak untruth before a king. Let us go to the place where the boar [was sacrificed].
At that sacred site, I shall tell you; show me special favor. (55)
"So be it," the king replied, and then he commanded his ministers:
"Go to the Saukarava Tīrtha, which flows toward Badarikāśrama.
[Bring] hundreds of thousands of elephants, horses, and chariots, as well as tens of thousands of milch cows."
Having taken wealth, grain, jewels, ornaments,
and garments for the purpose of giving, he went to the sacred ford known as Gaṅgātīrtha accompanied by his subjects and his aged mother, and resided there for six months.
Then, having performed the rites for the sacred ford, they gave gifts of all kinds;
and having fasted for three nights, the couple, endowed with self-restraint,
bowed down to the adorned Viṣṇu, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, Hari.

While Hari stood before him there, his beloved Satī said to her husband: "Come, come, O Lord; let us go and see our secret desire. Previously, I was a female jackal, established in the womb of an animal. (1.577.60–61)
"Long ago, he was pierced here on the head by an arrow from Somadatta;
it is because of that fault that this pain has settled upon my head as well.
Your beloved was born in the royal house of Kāñcī and was given to you by her father."
"By the power of this sacred field, this perfection has been attained by me; salutations be unto you!
(63) Having heard this, the king also remembered his former birth:
"O illustrious lady, I was a vulture here at this banyan tree, wandering in the forest. (64)
Pierced by Somadatta and having died here through the merit of this sacred site (tīrtha),
I have been born as the king of the Kaliṅgas and your husband, O beloved.
Behold the excellent fruit of this holy field, even though my death was against my will.
And those foremost devotees of the Lord,
as well as the inhabitants of the city and the countryside who had gathered there by the thousands—
all of them were filled with wonder and performed worship of Hari.
Having abandoned their physical bodies, the king and queen assumed divine forms;
becoming four-armed, they ascended a celestial chariot and went to the world of Brahmā,
where they were honored by the gods, while drums resounded in the heavens.
Those subjects, having departed together with him and abandoned all attachment,
attained death right there by the grace of Nārāyaṇa.
With four arms, they all went joyfully to the world of Brahmā.
All the male attendants hold conchs, maces, lotuses, and jewels;
the female attendants are endowed with four arms and possessed of all enjoyments.
These female attendants rejoice in the abode of Hari within the world of Brahmā.
Thus, by the power of the sacred ford (tīrtha), they attained eternal liberation.
Whatever merit was performed in previous births— whether it be small or great—
it inevitably bears fruit at some point, by which one comes to visit a sacred ford.
Whatever small portion may be produced, it conduces to greatness.
O fair-browed one, whoever recites this, hears it, or causes it to be heard,
by him my worship shall have been performed for twelve years.
"O Lakṣmī, in ancient times Śambhu spoke this truth; it has now been told by me to you.

Thus ends the five hundred and seventy-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Birth of the Jackal and the Vulture in the Royal Palace Following Their Death due to the Greatness of the Vārāha Tīrtha, the Revelation of Their History and Subsequent Liberation, and the Explanation of the Causes of Head Diseases and Other Ailments," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
*Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā* — Section 1 (*Kṛtayuga-santāna*) — Chapter 577.
Chapter 578 [Author:
Chapter 579 → Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī, to another narrative that destroys the sins of holy places;

Those who have gone to the abode of Brahmā serve Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, who is worshipped by Campā, Dayārāmā, Mahimā, and Muktādevī. In connection with Somatīrtha, gifts should be given with devotion.
His ancestors are satisfied and his lineage attains liberation.
Even a killer of a Brahmin, a drinker of liquor, one who violates the teacher’s bed, or a destroyer of an embryo is purified there; of this there is no doubt. (23–24)
Thereafter, one should go to the holy ford known as Ṛṇamocana.
By bathing at that site, one is liberated from the debts incurred here by oneself— whether divine, ancestral, or human— and like a god, one rejoices in heaven.
Then, on the northern bank, there is the supreme Vaiṣṇava tīrtha.
Formerly, Viṣṇu indeed resided here by the name Jalaśāyin.
In ancient times, there was a Daitya named Nalamegha, who caused great distress to the gods.
The gods went to Hari and spoke to Mādhava for the destruction of the Daityas.
The Blessed One, mounted upon Garuḍa and taking up his discus, arrived.
Nala, the friend of Meghasakha, set out for battle as Dhundhumāra.
He was indeed slain by Viṣṇu in a valley of the Himalayas.
Then, the highly enraged Nalamegha approached Hari;
he fought there in many ways with Viṣṇu and was also slain.
Then, with his Sudarśana discus, he beheld that abode; within a great cave, divine maidens were being guarded by the Daitya—
human women, goddesses, Gandharva maidens, and even those of the mountains.
Having repeatedly slain fourteen thousand people,
Viṣṇu saw there that beloved wife of the Daitya;
she was named Maṅgalādevī, and she wept most intensely again and again.
Having heard of the slaying of the Daityas, the devoted women chose Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa as their husband;
and all the maidens chose the Lord of Śrīmāṇikī,
the sovereign of Akṣara, the lord of the virtuous, who is seated upon Garuḍa.
Then they were brought to the Narmadā and bathed by Viṣṇu.
Having created a sacred bathing place (tīrtha) on the Narmadā in his own form as the one who reclines upon the waters, the Blessed One himself took all of them for a moment upon his bed.
Then the Blessed One, seated upon Garuḍa, arrived at his own abode in Kuṅkumavāpī together with all his wives;
and Lomaśa had brought them all there and presented them to him.
They remain eternally by the side of Viṣṇu, both in his abode and on earth;
those beloved of Hari who listen to this Vaiṣṇava narrative shall become liberated at the holy site of Aśvapaṭṭasara and in the temples. (38–39)
They are indeed blessed in the world of men, meritorious and most virtuous,
for whom there occurs a direct union with Kṛṣṇa upon this earth. Those men and women truly become divine, whether they be stationary or moving beings.
Having bathed in that divine water which has Brahmā as its support, they become divine.
(41) Next, one should visit the supreme, purifying holy site known as Candrāditya.
Formerly, there were two Dānavas named Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa on the bank of the Narmadā. (42)
There, performing austerities and meditating upon the Sun, the two of them pleased Sūrya;
he then said, "Choose an excellent boon.
"Grant us this boon: that we may be invincible by all the gods."
"So be it," Ravi replied; thus established by those two, Ravi was installed.
Candra was also installed, and that sacred site is known as Candrāditya.
From there, one should go to Vyāsatīrtha and worship the image of Vyāsa.
One should worship Siddhaśambhu and honor Dvīpeśvara;
likewise, one should visit the Mārkaṇḍeyeśvara Tīrtha and Saṃkarṣaṇeśvara.
There, Śrī Kṛṣṇa shines resplendent together with Rādhā and Balarāma.
From there, one should go to the purifying holy site named Eraṇḍī.
There, the wife of Atri, the beautiful Anasūyā, who was childless,
performed penance on the bank of the Revā at the confluence of the Eraṇḍī.

When a hundred years had passed, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Pitāmaha came to her and granted a boon for the sake of sons equal to themselves. Her sons were Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara, who were equal to Atri.
Candradatta and Durvāsas—these three were born to them.
That sacred ford (tīrtha) is the pacifier of the torments of sin and the bestower of liberation for one's sons.
Then one should go to Dhūmapāta, and from there to Sāgarasaṅgama.

The Lord of Rivers constantly offers the *argha* oblation to Revā. There, Narmadā says: "When people bathe at my confluence and offer libations to their ancestors, I shall [redeem] their seven generations."
I shall deliver my devotees and liberate them from distress;
indeed, I repeatedly offer jests, laughter, and the like to the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
I delight Hari eternally, being absorbed in Him upon His lap.
"Among men, she grants liberation (mokṣa) and gives (dadāti); thus she is Narmadā.
In this way, that supreme goddess Narmadā exists as the bestower of liberation.
O Lakṣmī, such is the supreme majesty of your friend Narmadā.
O Satī, what was spoken by Śambhu on Mount Ṛkṣa has been recounted by me.
Having heard it with devotion, every person attains my abode.
Having heard this from Śaṅkara, Satī ascended an excellent celestial chariot.
Attended by those possessing millions of virtues and accompanied by Śaṅkara,
she went forth full of joy to visit the auspicious holy places.
Reaching as far as the ocean, the mountain-born goddess worshipped the deities of the sacred sites.
Afterwards, the virtuous lady herself gave gifts of ten million jewels and other riches;
then, having met Bhārgavī at Bhṛgukaccha,
the chaste beloved, with the permission of Śaṅkara, departed for Kailāsa by way of the sky.
He also offered waters from sacred fords (tīrtha) belonging to the inhabitants of Kailāsa.
Thus was this pilgrimage performed by the high-souled Śaṅkara,
since he himself is of the nature of Brahman, for the sake of purifying the worlds.
The illustrious devotee Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world and the bestower of welfare upon all, resides on Kailāsa, the golden mountain,
where I formerly performed my austerities.
Having taken refuge at the Badarī tree, as many years have passed,
I have sustained myself on the Badarī with only a single fruit each.
There, for ten crores, ten years, and ten arbudas [of years], I have remained.
While established in austerity, I behold ten other lotuses of the earth;
yet the gods do not see me at all, so how indeed could humans?
Established in austerity, I see them all as they have gathered together.
Then, by my very will, they behold me standing before them as they satisfy me with hymns of praise;
and at that very moment,
they see the holy Śrī Badarī-āśrama where the devotee resides, provided that he remembers it.
He indeed goes to the abode of Viṣṇu, served by Rādhā, Lakṣmī, and others.
My devotee who is intent on yoga shall partake in the fruit of liberation.
He who understands Me as the Lord present in sacred fords is also liberated.
Having heard those words of Nārāyaṇa, Lakṣmī then spoke:
"O Keśava, having shown affection toward me as your servant, hear what I have to request.
O Janārdana, I shall speak to you with gentle and virtuous disposition."
Women possess little vital strength; women are fields of enjoyment. They are always associated with impurity and are devoid of righteous conduct.
They are dependent on others, dependent on their husbands, and subject to the will of their offspring.
Women are always impure due to the washing away of menstrual blood and urine.
Tell me, how could your worship and other rites be performed while you are in such a state of impurity? Furthermore, tell me, how could your worship be performed during your menstrual period? (72–73)
Then Nārāyaṇa said: "O sinless one, you have asked well!
This [account] bestows happiness upon devoted women as well as liberation.
It concerns those who are intent on washing their children, and those who are devoted to washing clothes."
And for those women who are devoted to serving their husbands and who remain during their menstrual period,
as well as those engaged in rites such as the purification of household impurities and other consecrations,
no constant purity is indeed observed. (75–76)

Indeed, for the sake of those women who are my devotees, I have declared that I dwell within their minds as the embodiment of the mind; I reside in their consciousness. Women were created by Brahmā in ancient times as pure by their very nature.
The field is indeed pure in every respect; therefore, it must certainly not be violated.
Even when there are impure causes present despite its purity, and even when impure acts have been committed, women indeed become pure simply by bathing.
Alternatively, my vision from afar of my body, which is so wonderfully variegated, must always be performed for as long as the state of menstruation lasts— that is, for four days;
nothing else should be done, though one may perform other mental acts.
Therefore, I am well-pleased with you, O lady, who are devoted to my deliverance.
O beautiful one, whether in a state of purity or impurity, one should always perform one’s duty,
placing the mind in me and being intent on devotion to me.
She is not stained by fault because of my grace;
listen, Lakṣmī! Furthermore, I am always pure, the Lord.
No worldly impurity ever touches me here.
Through union with me, even all impurities indeed attain divinity.
However, for the sake of preserving conventional conduct, purification and such were prescribed by me.
Whether they be men or women, they are neither male nor female.
Having restrained the senses and having caused the mind to enter into Me, they become purified through the yoga of renunciation in Me; of this there is no doubt.
By whomsoever the mind is always fixed upon My form through discernment, [they are purified].
In whatever state one may be— whether a man, a eunuch, or a woman—
that person indeed becomes pure and should perform worship and other rites themselves.
One should perform worship independently, either in a forest or in a secluded place.
One should perform worship alone; I do not consider that a fault.
For embodied beings, the mind, the intellect, the consciousness, and the self are dependent upon the Soul.
When men unite these with me through true love, they are indeed no longer smeared by worldly taints.
If the mind, the intellect, and the consciousness are established in Me and are equanimous,
then whatever action one performs is like a lotus leaf in water; one is not smeared by contact, precisely because of that equanimity and not otherwise.
Even those devotees who here perform a mixture of ritual actions day and night attain supreme perfection,
provided their mind is fixed upon me—
whether they are awake or sleeping, listening or even seeing. 92.

What fear can there be for my mind when someone thinks of me in their heart? (93) Whether it be a person of evil conduct, an outcaste, or even a Brahmin of such character—if they praise my mind, I do so; but I never praise the mind of anyone else. (94)
Worshipping all dharmas and purified by knowledge of me,
with their minds surrendered to me and devoted solely to my bhakti—
those who perform service to me and who protect me in their hearts.
Whether they sleep, eat, enjoy themselves, or even indulge in desire;
whether they act or desist— all those, O Lakṣmī, are dear to me,
because their minds are tranquil and they have fixed their resolve upon me alone.
For the destruction of the mind is the liberation of the world from saṃsāra;
therefore, having fixed their minds upon me, let women always touch me.
He who, with his mind ever fixed on me, worships me filled with love—
Having approached the side of the king, she becomes fit for my state.
On the fifth day of her menses, she is purified by the offering of the *ṛtudāna*.
For the sake of purification and for the sake of obtaining a son, the *ṛtudāna* must be given.
"I have observed celibacy by approaching my wife only during her fertile period (*ṛtukāla*).
Even while this is the case, if one should go [to her] at that time, there would be no fruitlessness of the *ṛtu*.
However, for those who are dispassionate (*virakta*), this rule intended for sexual union does not apply. (10.1)
For those who possess desire, union during the fertile period is praised.
O beautiful lady, a devotee of great fortune, maintaining the purity as prescribed,
should perform service to Me with the spirit of servitude.
Those men and women who serve me with devotion even in the state of a maidservant, and who are affectionate toward me— they always abide within my heart.
Even if the fault of one's menstrual impurity is unknown, there may still be the possibility of my touch and so forth.
Then, having bathed and having caused me to bathe on the fifth day—
or if another should bathe me— one should recite my hundred-name mantra. There, O Blessed Lord, the menstruating woman should pray for forgiveness.
"Forgive this touch committed by one who was unaware, O Mine of Compassion.
Having spoken thus, one who bows to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa becomes completely purified. In this way, O Lakṣmī, neither woman nor man is defiled.
Then those dear to me perform their duties properly;
O blessed lady, those men and women who follow my mind should daily perform the ritual observances (*parvan*) and carry out actions in service to me.
I shall certainly lead them to my own supreme and highest world.
Thousands of mothers and fathers, and hundreds of sons and wives,
revolve like a wheel because of delusion, for they do not know me.
The world is shrouded by ignorance and brought under the sway of delusion;
bound by many attachments, it does not perceive Me.
Indeed, the mother goes elsewhere, and the father goes elsewhere. (111–112)
Sons go elsewhere, and the wife goes elsewhere;
one is born in one's own place, arising from the accumulation of one's own respective karma.
O Lakṣmī, people who are deluded by ignorance remain bewildered in this cycle of worldly existence.
Considering the supreme state to be of short duration, they remain bound even though it is perishable.
But those who possess this knowledge of Brahman, which is centered in Me, O Lakṣmī, will indeed exist; they do not abide together with My physical form. || 1.14-15 ||
Having entrusted one's own self to me, one is liberated; there is no doubt in this.
That person who, having risen at dawn, should hear this daily, attains abundant perfection that leads to my world.
All women shall have the form of Lakṣmī, and men shall become like me.

Thus ends the five hundred and eightieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Destruction of Kaṇṭha’s Brahmin-slaughter at Soma-tīrtha in the Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga in the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā; the Destruction of the Dānava Nalamegha at Jalaśāyi-tīrtha; the Fourteen Thousand Maidens becoming Wives of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa; the Candrāditya-tīrtha; the Tīrthas extending to the edge of the ocean; Śaṅkara’s Departure for Kailāsa; and the Explanation of the Means of Liberation for Impure Men and Women. || 580 ||

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:

even by the mere mention of it, the inner darkness is destroyed.
And I am the Lord of the World, dwelling in the cave of the heart of all beings.

It extends for ten yojanas and possesses the beauty of sands.
In ancient times, after creating the world of moving and non-moving beings, Brahmā, resplendent with the great mountain Nīlācala, reflected:

"But I shall worship the Supreme Person for the sake of my own liberation.

Salutations again and again to the Lord of the syllables, the sovereign of the liberated;
salutations to You, the Lord of Rādhā, Lakṣmī, Prabhā, Haṃsā, and Māṇikī. Salutations to You, the Lord of Pārvatī, the Lord of the beautiful Sagunā.
You are Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Brahman, and you alone are Nārāyaṇa.
You manifest as Bhūman, Viṣṇu, Mahāviṣṇu, and Vairāja. You are the Inner Controller (Antaryāmī), the Light, the perceptible, and likewise the imperceptible.
You alone are the essence of reality and the knower of both nature and its transformations;
you are the one who dwells within the sheaths, subtle as an atom yet greater than the greatest.
You are substance, quality, and action; you alone are existence and non-existence.
You alone are both illusion and its cause; salutations be to you!
In this cycle of existence, for those who are greedy for a self, you alone are the essential self;
and even that which is essence-less appears as the very form of essence through your vision.
Therefore, having abandoned passion, I shall regard you as the Supreme Lord.
For what is gained by threshing husks whose very nature is essence-less?
A wise person should not undertake that which results in emptiness at the end.
"O Keśava, I must not create a world that is empty;
be gracious today and grant liberation to me who desires it.
Thus indeed was I, the one whose banner is the glorious Garuḍa, praised by Brahmā.
Then Śrī Nārāyaṇa, four-armed and radiant as ten million suns,
having manifested with the intent to enter [the body], spoke to him with a smile:
"O Brahmin, how is it that you have attained such detachment immediately upon birth?"
"Carry out my command, sustain the creation, and perform meditation for me.
Ignorance, beginningless and very firm, is difficult to sever due to the bonds of karma.
By you, in the past, was performed the action that bestows the status of the Supreme Lord."
Without the experience of worldly enjoyment, that which incites attachment to new things would not perish.
When that exists, how could birth and death be removed from creation?
Nevertheless, if your mind is firmly established on the path of devotion, [then they may be transcended]. //25//
"Wherever my mind is, there you are as well; hold this in mind.
Realizing Me thus to be non-different [from yourself], accept everything I have said.
O Brahmin, I shall always abide within your heart. (26-27)

I shall describe my task; act accordingly as it has arisen in my heart. Go indeed to that region on the earth which lies on the northern shore of the ocean and the southern bank of the great river—a place that bestows the fruit of all sacred fords (tīrtha). ||28||
There, only those humans who have acquired a mass of merit over ten thousand lifetimes take up residence;
indeed, neither the undevoted nor those with little merit do so.
[This extends] from the Ekāmra forest as far as the shore of the southern ocean.
Beyond step after step lies my divine domain;
there, the jewel named Nīla, which rests upon my neck,
was removed by me and established as the mountain Nīla.

Brahmā said: "O Lord, having heard that, tell me the reason why the sapphire (nīlamaṇi) was established there by you at that time. Hari replied: "Listen, O Brahmā; formerly, indeed, Madhu and Kaiṭabha..."
The two Daityas, who were capable of destroying the universe, were slain by me with my discus.
Devoted to me, they engaged in a fierce battle with me.
With a terrible mace, they struck me in the chest.
I set aside that most excellent jewel from my heart and held it;
as long as the battle lasted, I placed it in that spot.
There, my fierce devotees remained, and the earth stood terrified. (35–36)
The maiden, overcome with terror, remains supported by the jewel;
protected by this gem, she awaits my arrival.
Then, having slain the two Daityas, I went there specifically to bring him back.
Then, I, the Supreme Lord, was praised by the maiden Earth:
"O Lord, you are my protector and my refuge; you are my sustainer.
You alone are the lord of the earth, and you are the giver of life to me. (38-39)
"O Lord, O Nārāyaṇa, O Hari, O Master, protect me always!
O Hari, O Master, destroy my burden and annihilate my sins.
Thus addressed, I said to her, "Choose a boon; I shall grant it to you."
She said: "You ought to always protect this sapphire here, by which liberation shall indeed be attained through the destruction of the sins of embodied beings;
and my own protection shall also come from wearing it as an ornament for Kṛṣṇa. (41-42)
Having heard this, the Blessed One said to her, "So be it.
"This blue gem, in the form of an ornament, has been offered by me;
indeed, when worn upon the neck of the Earth, it will certainly always remain there eternally. (43)
The supreme sacred field consists of the throat and is of the nature of Śrī Puruṣottama.
Furthermore, when I desired to depart from that place,
she again requested that I must come here once more.
"And the Lord, intent on my deliverance, must always remain here.
I replied, "So be it," and I departed for Vaikuṇṭha.
There, I then received the command from the Lord, the Master of the Imperishable (Akṣara).
"O best of men, I desire to dwell on the land of Nīlaparvata;
out of compassion for my devotees, I shall be known there as Puruṣottama.
Thus indeed did the Blessed One, the primordial Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, speak there.
The Supreme Soul himself dwells upon the earth as Puruṣottama;
that Blue Mountain shines upon the shore of the ocean, illuminating all directions.
O auspicious lady, this place is hidden on earth and remains unknown to you.
My [nature], concealed by *māyā*, is difficult to discern for both the gods and the asuras.
(1.581.50) Endowed with all sovereign powers, I abide there in embodied form;
having transcended both the perishable and the imperishable, I exist as the Supreme Person (*puruṣottama*). (51)
My field, the supreme among men, has not been overtaken by worldly attachment;
and just as I am present within my own abode as a man bearing all weapons,
so shall you behold me there, adorned with the emblems of the Supreme Lord.
There, at the foot of the Kalpa-banyan tree on the slopes of the Blue Mountain (Nīlācala), you shall see me dwelling on the bank of the pool named Rauhiṇa.
Go there; for as you meditate upon me, I will become manifest to you.
Having thus instructed Brahmā, Śrī Puruṣottama then vanished right there while Brahmā was looking on.
Brahmā then proceeded to the place where Puruṣottama was staying.
He beheld Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Person, in such a form.
Overjoyed by this recognition, Brahmā, that ocean of knowledge,
then bowed to and praised Śrī Puruṣottama.
Just then, a certain crow arrived there from the sky;
wishing to drink water, it fell right into the pool and was submerged by fate.
It was then pulled out of the pool by that Brahmā.
Even while rolling on the ground, he beheld the Supreme Lord of blue luster;
then, casting off his crow body, bearing the conch, discus, and mace,
he became possessed of a divine form and stood there by the side of Kṛṣṇa.
Having witnessed the divine movement of the crow, which is difficult even for the lords of yogis to attain, Brahmā was struck with wonder and reflected at that very moment:
"Oh, how great is the majesty of this sacred field! For he has reached [this state] even without spiritual practice."
Even one who is tamasic and even one who is lowly has attained the state of having four arms.
A human being is authorized for liberation, and even a bird has indeed attained liberation.
Nothing whatsoever is difficult to obtain there where Śrī Puruṣottama resides. (62–63)
There is no distinction between the worthy and the unworthy where Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa is present;
wherever the Ancient Person is chanted by name by people,
even those who merely hear it attain liberation— what then to say of those who behold Him?
For both the meditator and the one who serves there, liberation is within reach.
For the Blessed One, when directly perceived, grants liberation to the devotee;
such is the wondrous majesty of Him who is named Puruṣottama.
Where even a crow attained Hari himself in his four-armed form,
how much more so those who are constantly devoted to the yoga of meditation on Kṛṣṇa?
There, on that divine blue mountain, in the sacred field of Puruṣottama.
"Even insects, moths, and the like shall attain liberation in every way.
Having seen that, Yamarāja indeed arrived there quickly;
Brahmā beheld that son of Vivasvat, Dharma, whose fire had been extinguished.
Even Yamarāja, sighing and feeling dejected that his own office had become useless,
prostrated before Śrī Hari on the Blue Mountain (Nīlādri) and praised Śrī Jagannātha for the firm establishment of his own authority.
Salutations to you, the single principle, to the dual, and to the infinite;
salutations to you who manifest all forms by yourself, who bestow stability and nourishment, the presiding deity of all appearances, and the source of all.
Salutations again and again to you, the Guru who is the witness for the sake of faith;
salutations to you, the ocean of compassion, who transcend the Supreme (Parātīta).
Salutations be to you, the destroyer of birth and death, the kinsman of the distressed.
Salutations again and again to You, the self who presides over *māyā*, who are clothed in yellow silk;
salutations to You, the wielder of the discus (*cakrin*), the cutter of the wheel of *māyā*. Salutations indeed to You, the Supreme Lord, the punisher and the sovereign authority.
Salutations to you, whose beautiful body is like a dark cloud, who dwell upon the Blue Mountain, who are adorned by the lotus-eyed one, and who bear the mace;
salutations to you whose chest is covered and illuminated by the splendor of the Śrīvatsa mark and the Kaustubha gem.
I bow to the Supreme beyond the supreme, the abode of compassion, blue-hued and dwelling in a cave of blue mountains, who destroys the suffering of those who take refuge in him;
by taking shelter at whose feet, unfailing prosperity was obtained.
The eternal Fortune that bestows sovereignty upon devotees exists; she,
who is by nature dependent on another, O Supreme Lord,
attains expansion by enveloping you through your will, for the sake of liberation from bondage.
And by Your will, You bestow upon him who has experienced all enjoyments the state of Nirvāṇa.
You alone are the Supreme Brahman; You exist in the form of Brahman, and likewise You exist in the form of Bhūman and in the form of the Vyūhas.

O Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, Viṣṇu, O Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa!
