O Lord of the possessed of attributes, I bow to Your wife, the remover of suffering.
"I bow to her who wards off anxiety for sons and who sustains them.
Having spoken thus, Yama ceased; meanwhile, the Lotus-born [Brahmā] was instructed by Nārāyaṇa, who was well-pleased with Dharmas' hymn of praise.
Having herself become filled with compassion, Lakṣmī spoke to Dharma:
"O King Yama, that for which you praise this place is indeed difficult to attain;
for this is the sacred field (kṣetra) of Śrī Hari, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, known as Puruṣottama."
It bestows liberation upon all; they do not see Yama at all. Those who behold this sacred site shall not go to the abode of Yama.
Likewise, our supreme field (Puruṣottama) must never be abandoned.
The lordship over all guardians, beginning with Brahmā, is not praised here [in this place].
Indeed, the ripening of the karma of embodied beings does not occur here;
for by dwelling here, even the very wicked karma of insects [is destroyed]. (88–89)
Through the majesty of the feet of Puruṣottama, dissolution occurs;
for those bound by the fetters of karma, no further bondage exists here.
Since you, Yama, have been ordained as the dispenser of punishment to evildoers, [it is through his grace that this occurs].
"You are not the ruler of those embodied beings who dwell upon the earth as Supreme Persons (Puruṣottama).
Here, the glorious Supreme Brahman, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa himself, my Lord, shines manifest, having made Mount Nīla his abode. (91–92)

Since sinners are indeed liberated upon seeing that Nārāyaṇa, your punishment does not apply to them; O Yama, you are the lord over others. O Yama, do not desire the execution of those who have taken refuge in the Lord of the World.
Even Brahmā, beholding the liberation of the crow, was struck with wonder;
he indeed abandoned the pride born of the worldly existence of embodied beings arising from karma.
You too, having likewise cast off pride, should govern them.

Except for those at the Puruṣottama-tīrtha, all embodied beings residing here are not subject to me, for they are under the control of their own masters. Dwelling right here, these are indeed liberated while living (jīvanmukta) and possess four arms.
Therefore, it is by no means, by no means at all, that they have fallen into your hands.
Go; compose your mind and fulfill your duty.
O Yama, do not grieve over this fact that they have not come into your own possession.
Thus enlightened by Viṣṇu in the form of Lakṣmī, Yama, feeling remorseful,
bowed again to Lakṣmī and, remembering Hari,
spoke to her: "O Mother, wherever the glorious Anādi-Śrī-Nārāyaṇa may be..."
Formerly, I had not heard of the greatness of that sacred field. Struck down by misfortune, how could I have known the power of Hari?
Indeed, the will of the Supreme Lord proceeds unrestrained.
Elsewhere, that very same [practice] bestows bondage; here, it bestows liberation alone.
How vast is this field, wherein living beings are untouched by "mine-ness"?
Tell me also, what is the fruit of residing in this field?
"By whom I have been fully authorized, I wander with independent steps.

(1.03) Thus ends the five hundred and eighty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Narrative of the Blue Mountain in the form of Nīlamaṇi at the Holy Puruṣottama-kṣetra; the Liberation of the Crow Brahmā while he was watching on the bank of the Rauhiṇa-kuṇḍa; the arrival of Yamarāja there; and how the messengers of Yama cannot touch the living beings of the Nīla-sthalī established by Lakṣmī," in the first section concerning the lineage of the Kṛta-yuga of the *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*. (581)
← Chapter 581: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga) Chapter 582 [[Author:
Chapter 583 →
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O King Yama, listen to the truth that you have asked, which is beneficial for you.
I shall describe the sacred field, its fruit, and likewise other auspicious things that grant liberation.
Just as I was formerly at the side of Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa,
so too during the dissolution (pralaya) did I abide upon His chest;
and when this entire world had completely dissolved, He beheld me.
And I, and this excellent field known as Puruṣottama—
these two were then of divine form; at that time, the sage Mārkaṇḍeya,
whose life spanned seven kalpas, was submerged here in the ocean of dissolution.
Wandering in the ocean of waters within the sacred field of Puruṣottama,
he beheld a divine banyan tree on the beautiful shore of the sea at the foot of Mount Nīla, which possesses the form of Puruṣottama himself.
There he beheld the beginningless Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa,
resplendent, smiling, beautiful, sixteen years of age, and four-armed;
upon whose chest that sacred field was situated, and who was likewise merged within that field.
"What are you saying? Are you bathing in the water? Mārkaṇḍeya, remain steady!
Come here to my side, to this spot in the shade of the banyan tree.
Hearing that and seeing the sacred field, the banyan tree, and Hari, he was filled with wonder.
It is not moistened by waters, nor is it burned by fire;
it is neither dried up nor moved even by the winds of universal destruction (saṃvartaka) and the like.
Indeed, this field is seen to be like a boat in a single vast ocean.
And this divine, vast banyan tree, the body of the Lord, is seen;
even by the wind of the great dissolution, its leaf does not tremble.
Therein, the Blessed One dwells within that banyan tree, even during the dissolution.
"How is it that this region of the earth remains firm even during the dissolution?"—
thinking thus, the king of sages [directed his thought] toward Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa; seeing me situated upon His chest, he went to Me and then returned to himself.
"Salutations, salutations to you, O Supreme Person; salutations, salutations to you who have Lakṣmī as your companion.
Salutations, salutations to you who became visible to my eyes in the ocean of water; salutations, salutations to you who dwell in the banyan tree.
Salutations, salutations to you whose dwelling is divine; salutations, salutations to you who provide a home for the world and reside here. (14)
Everything upon which you have taken refuge on this earth—
even the divine dissolution— does not consume it;
for it is omnipresent, situated within the illustrious Puruṣottama, the vast form established in the shape of the banyan tree.
I bow to you, Viṣṇu, who are beyond illusion, who are the supreme Brahman, who arise from dissolution and abide in dissolution.
(17) In this world of a single ocean, what is this supreme ground of the Lord, wherein you shine as the manifest protector, the bestower of grace upon me? (18)
Save me, O Viṣṇu, Lord of the World, from this terrible ocean of saṃsāra!
You are not separate [from us], since you are beheld by Mārkaṇḍeya at the proper time.
As is Lakṣmī, so is this Mārkaṇḍeya your follower.
"How is it that you remain, having abandoned me in this ocean of worldly existence at the time of dissolution?
O Lord, take me here; grant me a dwelling under the banyan tree.
I shall perform your service here eternally and without ever departing."
Thus addressed, the Blessed One said: "Come here, O Sage;
stay here at this banyan tree together with Lakṣmī and likewise with me.
In the morning, you shall behold all my prior creations once again."
I have shown you this divine field, Śrī Puruṣottama.
Build a hut of leaves and dwell here in the circle of banyan trees;
for it is on your account that I remain permanently established here.
Having heard the command of the Supreme Lord, the sage Mārkaṇḍeya then constructed an auspicious leaf-hut within the mass of roots of the banyan tree;
and upon entering inside, he beheld Hari stationed within.
And having dissolved into that form, he beheld millions of cosmic eggs.
Within one of these eggs, the Brahmin saw the fourteen worlds,
as well as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and the other guardians of the quarters who protect the worlds.
[He saw] the Siddhas, Gandharvas, Daityas, Rākṣasas, gods, and humans;
the Nāgas, Pitṛs, mountains, and oceans, as well as the celestial couches;
and Śeṣa, the supporter of the worlds, adorned with a thousand hoods.
He beheld the tortoise, the support of the remainder, as well as water and fire;
he beheld wind and space, and everything beyond the great ether.
And in the ether of consciousness, he indeed beheld Goloka and Vaikuṇṭha.
Then he beheld the imperishable abode of divine radiance,
where Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa himself, the Lord of Lakṣmī, resides.
There he saw a banyan tree and a leaf-hut built by him.
There he beheld the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa;
the supreme king of sages also saw his own son Mṛkaṇḍu, the sacred field of Puruṣottama, the divine ocean, and the Blue Mountain (Nīlaśaila).
Then, by the will of the Blessed One, in the very next moment,
I suddenly withdrew him once again into my heart,
where the Lord Hari, accompanied by Lakṣmī, was seated within my leaf-hut.
Beholding Śrī Hari as before, he was filled with supreme wonder.
With the highest devotion, he praised Śrī Kṛṣṇa Puruṣottama:
"O Supreme Lord, you are my beloved; what a marvel has been displayed! (35–36)
"O Lord Śrī Hari, tell me why you remain in this place.
The Blessed One then said to him: "The land of Puruṣottama is indeed my own abode; it has been eternally established by me. (37)

That divine second form, the Supreme Person together with his consort, shines within this leaf-hut temple where the virtuous dwell. You are my imperishable abode; you are Mārkaṇḍeya, the other supreme being.
And the eternity of this abode of mine has been shown to you even upon the earth.
That sacred field known as Puruṣottama is indeed my own abode.
Therefore, perceive this delightful field as my eternal domain.
Neither creation nor dissolution exists here, nor is there any cycle of worldly existence (saṃsṛti).
Having known me here as the Supreme Person, the eternal and most excellent of beings,
that pure-souled one enters the Field (kṣetra) and indeed goes to my own abode.
"Since he has entered into dense bliss, his birth shall not occur again.
Having heard this, the son of Mṛkaṇḍu,
his heart thrilled and filled with faith and devotion, chose to dwell there and spoke.
O Blessed One, show favor in this field, O Puruṣottama!
O Puruṣottama, so that I may not fall under the power of death while remaining here,
I may become immersed in Your eternal abode and Your bliss.
Then King Yama and Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa spoke to that sage: "I dwell together with you and with Lakṣmī;
I shall dwell here without a doubt for the sake of the welfare of the world. (46)
Until the destruction of the world, and again even at the time of universal dissolution;
at the end of dissolution, during the new creation, and even at the end of that creation, I dwell here.
I shall always reside here; you, therefore, dwell in Parṇapattana.
In this place, indeed, that city shall become famous as Parṇanagarī;
likewise, it shall be known as Puruṣottamapurī and Jagannāthapurī.
In age after age, it shall attain renown by these names and shall endure.
"And you, having become the remover of death, shall remain here; of this there is no doubt. Having spoken thus, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the universe, vanished.
The great sage Mārkaṇḍeya then chose to take up residence there.
Having established a purifying pit in the north-western corner of the banyan tree,
the Imperishable One himself conquered death through his intense austerity;
for there stands the purifying hermitage of Mārkaṇḍeya.
This sacred field extends for five *krośas* and is situated within the ocean.
Including the two *krośas* on the shore of the sea, it measures seven *krośas* in total.
It is richly adorned with the beauty of blue mountains and strewn with golden sands. (53–54)

O Lord of Yama, the ocean— the king of all holy fords (tīrthas)— attained the status of the sovereign of sacred sites because it was the supreme abode where the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa resides;
on its shore, the Blessed One and Lakṣmī shine forth.
I am that Kambharādevī, overflowing with the bliss of Brahman;
she who shines in the Kuṅkumavāpī of Saurāṣṭra, as Gajānanā in Camatkāra, and as Kārṣṇavāllabhī in Kāśī. ||56-57||
When she is in the imperishable abode of Goloka, she is indeed Rādhikā;
in Vaikuṇṭha she is Ramā, and in the golden realm she is the radiant Vinodinī.
In the realm called Śveta she is Māṇikī, in Kailāsa she is Lakṣmī, and she is Pārvatī.
In Satyaloka dwell the beautiful swans; on Mount Meru reside the virtuous and beloved ones. (59) These wives of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa remain together with Him.
In the east is Śrī Jagannātha, and in the west is the Lord of Dvārakā. (1.582.60)
To the north is Nara-Nārāyaṇa, and to the south is Janārdana;
these are indeed the forms of my Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
In Jagannātha I am Lakṣmī, and in Dvārikeśa I am Prabhāveśvarī.
In Nārāyaṇa she was Māṇikī, and in Janārdana she was Pārvatī.
In this very first kalpa, I became a devoted wife (pativratā) to all of them;
likewise in other kalpas and in other manifestations, she is also I.
By the will of Kṛṣṇa, I become enriched with manifold names and forms;
my duty is that which is desired by me, and likewise, for me, it is devotion to my husband.
My names, forms, and manifestations are many.
Even women will become incarnations of Hari;
indeed, hundreds of thousands and tens of millions of women shall become the wives of my husband,
whose prowess is unshakable and who remains a perpetual celibate.
For Hari, who is endowed with immutable existence and is free from number, women are excluded;
for that Lord of immeasurable splendor, the field is Śrī Puruṣottama.
From east to west it is shaped like a conch shell, and in the west stands the one whose banner bears the bull.
To the east, at Śaṅkhamukha, the blue-throated god (Nīlakaṇṭha) shines resplendent.
The interior region of the conch, however, is flooded by the waters of the ocean, extending from the lineage of the ocean up to the divine Nyagrodha tree. (68–69)
The Blessed One is seen there, bestowing grace upon his devotees; whoever comes within the range of the Blessed One's vision becomes a partaker of liberation.
By dying here, one reaches my abode; likewise, by bathing here, one goes to heaven.
Indeed, by remembering this, a human being becomes free from sins.
At the region of the navel, Śaṅkha is situated, along with Kuṇḍa, Vaṭa, and Hari;
there resides the great power Vimalā, the bestower of liberation.
She is the devourer of dissolution and the obstructer of the great dissolution.
He who beholds her and bows down to her enjoys eternal enjoyments.
The sacred field situated in the middle of the Banyan-tree ocean grants liberation even to insects and the like.
The inner altar (antarvedī) is indeed the central portion of the Bhāgavata field;
those who abide within it become bearers of the conch, discus, and lotus.
Puruṣottama is the [embodiment] of thirty-five million sacred fords (tīrtha).

Since the king indeed bestows liberation, he is called this "King of Tīrthas. Those men and women who bathe in the divine pool named Rohiṇa, in the water known as Kāruṇya, will certainly become Nārāyaṇas.
"Therefore, O Lord of Yama, let this anxiety regarding this place be removed from you.
O King of the Departed, you are not the master here over those who are qualified for liberation.
Having thus instructed Dharmeśa, Lakṣmī spoke to Brahmā.
Here, by the command of Nārāyaṇa, the guardian of the field (kṣetrapāla) named Kāmākhya always dwells,
endowed with austerity, and worships Śrī Nārāyaṇa.
And this Lord Nṛsiṃha resides to the south of Hari.
By giving up one's life in the presence of Nṛhari, liberation becomes certain.
Even by the mere sight of Nṛhari, both worldly enjoyment and liberation are placed in one's hand;
furthermore, acts such as charity and recitation performed here yield merit millions upon millions of times greater.
Both Nṛsiṃha and Vaṭa are indeed Nārāyaṇas;
therefore, their shade bestows liberation, and within it, ignorance comes to an end.
In Vārāṇasī, at Avimukta, [this occurs] at the root of the ear of one who desires liberation.
Śambhu then grants the supreme mantra as a means for awakening.
If one practices it progressively and knowledge arises, there is liberation;
however, in this case, upon the cessation of the vital breath, liberation occurs at that very moment.
Even whoever attains similarity [to that state] without internal consciousness—
be it by bathing in the shadow of a banyan tree while looking at the ocean,
or by [bathing] in dust at a sacred field or in the waters of the ocean— his liberation occurs either here or at death. ||85||
For the purpose of guarding the inner altar (antarvedi), eight Śaktis were created by me:
Maṅgalā is at the foot of the banyan tree in the west, and Vimalā is there as well;
Sarvamaṅgalā is stationed on the back of Śaṅkha.
Lambikā is situated in the north, and Kālarātri is established in the south.
Behind Kālarātri, Caṇḍarūpā is stationed.
In the east resides Marīcikā; these are the Vaiṣṇavīs, the female servants of the Lord.
By the sight of these eight, there is the destruction of sins and the fruit born of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
Now, even Rudra is a devotee, a great Bhāgavata, and a lord;
[he recites]: "Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Master, Svāhā! (1.582.90).
Chanting the mantra, he worshipped the Supreme Person here in eight ways;
having propitiated Kṛṣṇa through austerity, he requested this supreme boon:
"O Lord, wherever you are, there may I dwell, always worshipping you."
O Beloved of Kamalā, apart from you, there is no other cause for liberation.
You are my inner controller and my Lord; without you, how could there be a body?
Resembling the stainless sky, I have gone to you for refuge.
When this was said, the Blessed Kṛṣṇa created the devotee Rudra there as the Lord of the Guardians of the Field (Kṣetrapāleśvara), the most excellent among the eight supreme devotees,
as well as Kapālamocaneśa, Kṣetrapeśa, and Yameśvara.
Mādhava likewise established those eight: Mārkaṇḍeśa, Īśāna, Bilveśa, Nīlakaṇṭhaka, and Vaṭeśa.
By seeing, touching, and worshipping these, one is liberated. (95–96)
For those who die in this sacred field, Yama is not the ruler because of that;
if you have come for that purpose, then accomplish it elsewhere.
Hari’s Sudarśana discus is the supreme cutter of illusion.
"Let there be no illusion here by which the embodied soul might fall into your hands.
Having been addressed thus, King Yama worshipped the Blessed One,
bowed to Lakṣmī, and departed for the abode of Yama, satisfied while worshipping Hari.
Śrī said: Then,

in the Satya Yuga, the great king Indradyumna— a performer of sacrifices and a true Vaiṣṇava who is a leader among devotees— will very soon become the unborn one (Aja) established in the station of Parameṣṭhin.
Having come here, he will practice great devotion day and night.
O Brahmin, for the pleasure of the Lord, he will likewise perform a thousand horse-sacrifices here, and also for the sake of your own gratification.
Then, for the sake of bestowing grace upon him, the compassionate Blessed One will manifest in four forms produced from a single block of wood. Viśvakarman shall fashion these wooden images.
"And you, O Brahmin, propitiated by Indradyumna, shall become the establisher here at Śrī Puruṣottama. Those images like us, O Lord, do not differ from you even in the slightest degree. (104–105)
"Those who are dissimilar [to you], you shall establish in them.
Now go to Satyaloka, O Brahman, that supreme field of the Puruṣa.
Return again whenever you are remembered by me, even by the Lord."

Having been addressed thus, the Creator of the Universe departed for the world of Truth after honoring them both. The Lord Nārāyaṇa, a treasury of compassion, also said to Lakṣmī: "Everything that you have spoken shall indeed come to pass exactly so."
To those with the eye of flesh, my form will appear as wood;
yet to those with divine vision, I shall appear as divine along with you.
Residing within the cave of the Blue Mountain, I am like a dark blue cloud.
Bearing a wooden body and possessing the conch, discus, mace, and other [emblems], Saṃkarṣaṇa shall dwell with me; you, Subhadrā, shall remain near me;
and likewise, the Sudarśana discus shall dwell together with me.
For many are my incarnations—divine, inert, and human;
those born as animals and those born from the water—and among them, the divine ones possess the most excellent activities.
Likewise, in this case, my incarnation made of wood is considered by me to be such [a divine one].
It tears asunder the sufferings of saṃsāra and bestows imperishable bliss.
Therefore, although I am made of wood, the Supreme Brahman dwells within me;
for a wooden image never bestows liberation anywhere. (113–114)
O Lakṣmī, the state of being uncreated is never found in that which has been created.
For liberation is indeed uncreated; how could it arise from something created, such as wood?
Without a substratum, the divine sovereignty of Brahman does not manifest.
That image is my own, Nārāyaṇa’s, serving as a substratum and a means of representation. Even though it is non-worldly, I manifest there in a worldly form.
Where has it ever been heard or seen that an image should speak? (1.16–1.17)
To Indradyumna, he who bore a wooden form granted this boon: Hari,
the sole refuge for the wretched and the helpless, the crossing over the ocean of worldly existence,
the deliverer from all sins, and the one who dwells upon the Blue Mountain (Nīlādri).
O Lakṣmī! Those men who shall come to me alone for refuge— I,
assuming a divine wooden body, shall forgive even hundreds of their offenses and overlook all their faults, even if they possess but little devotion.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord himself ceased speaking at the banyan tree;
together with Lakṣmī, he meditated upon his own form within the circle of the Blue Mountain.

Thus ends the five hundred and eighty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Eternity of the Śrī Puruṣottama Kṣetra to Mārkaṇḍeya, its Dimensions, the Role of Śambhu with His Eight Forms and Pārvatī with Her Eight Forms as Guardians of the Field, the Divinity of the Banyan Tree, and the Future Installation of the Image by Indradyumna," in the first section on the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 583: *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 1 (The Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga).
Chapter 583.
[The Author: Chapter 584.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Now, O beloved, I shall tell you of a marvel here; listen.
I am divine, embodied in form, the bestower of liberation, the giver of happiness, and auspicious.
(1) Just as the elements such as earth are indeed the forms of the individual soul, so too, for me who am formless, the embodied image is my abode. (2)

The nature of the Self consists of a single reality, yet it is not perceived by the physical eye; therefore, I have not become an object of sight in the form of a physical body. (3) I am one whose body is earth, and likewise one whose body is water.
I am also one whose body is fire, and likewise one whose body is air;
I am one whose form is space, and likewise one whose form consists of the subtle elements (tanmātras).
I am one whose body is mind, intellect, and so forth, and one whose body is the Self and the Lord.
I am the one whose body is Brahman, likewise the one whose body is liberation;
I am the one whose body is everything, for through my support, everything becomes divine.
Regarding this divinity, the Vedic mantras and the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa) are the instrumental cause.
In that process of my entry, the primary cause is my abiding presence.
Therefore, through that very body, I perform everything like an embodied being.
If one should know me in this way, he who relies upon me becomes liberated.
Though motionless and possessing a body of wood, he performs divine sports and playful pastimes.
Even with very little devotion, I can forgive ten million offenses committed by a devotee.
Long ago, in Kurukṣetra, there were two men, a Brāhmaṇa and a Kṣatriya.
The two friends were devoid of dharma, fallen from right conduct, and utterly deluded.
Living together with courtesans, they were bereft of the utterances of *svadhā* and *svāhā*;
even in their dreams, no thought of the world beyond ever occurred to them.
Once, however, a sacrifice to Viṣṇu was being performed at Kurukṣetra.
As they went to the sacrificial enclosure and observed the ritual procedure,
and as they listened to the Vedic mantras, their sin was dispelled.

The minds of Puṇḍarīka and Ambarīṣa became fixed upon the Dharma. Discernment also arose in them for the purpose of crossing the ocean of worldly existence and for the sake of purifying the masses of sins they had committed, O Brahmins.
Having saluted him and made known their own impurity—

namely, the consumption of liquor, meat, and sexual intercourse, as well as theft, adultery, and the harming of women and others— they questioned him. Having heard that, the best of Vaiṣṇavas, the illustrious twice-born devotee of the Lord, [spoke].
Intent upon divine rites, he spoke to the two of them with devotion:
"O twice-born one, O scion of the Kṣatriya race, if you both desire liberation from this most terrible heap of sins, go quickly to Puruṣottama."
The supreme field is that wooden image where Puruṣottama resides;
by propitiating him, the Lord of the World and husband of Lakṣmī and Rādhā, you shall attain the destruction of sins as well as liberation in the imperishable state. 18.

"Therefore, do not delay; proceed there with all haste to Utkala, at the Blue Hill (Nīlaśaila) on the shore in the vicinity of the ocean. Having been addressed thus, the two of them bowed to the sages and went to Puruṣottama.
Meditating upon Viṣṇu with their minds, both of them, pure in diet and observant of vows,
went to the ocean that is the refuge of all sacred fords, bathed there, and proceeded toward the temple.
Standing at the gate like a staff-bearer, they remained there, desiring a vision [of the Lord].
When the two of them, gazing at the Blessed One, could no longer see him,
they became hopeless and undertook the vow of fasting;
chanting the names of Hari, their minds became absorbed in Him.
Then, on the third night, the two saw a single light; when that light had again dissolved, they remained steadfast in their fast.
And in the middle of the seventh night, the two beheld Śrī Hari.
[He meditated upon] the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama,
four-armed and bearing weapons, seated upon sandals enriched with jewels,
lotus-eyed, with a smiling face, and holding Lakṣmī by his left arm.
And at His side, She was pulling [Him] toward Her and taking from the hand of Śrī what was auspicious—
a betel-roll filled with a flood of love for His mouth and eyes—
while He was Himself enveloped in a halo of splendor and surrounded by His female companions.
With women holding jeweled canes, and others with chowries in their hands;
adorned with ornaments and bearing fragrant lamps,
one woman held a jeweled parasol, thereby beautifying Puruṣottama.
He was holding an incense burner and had perfumed the Supreme Person;
He was looking at a certain smiling woman and laughing most charmingly.
Likewise, He was praising the gods, the Siddhas, and Sanaka and the others.

They saw the Gandharvas headed by Nārada, the Vaiṣṇavas headed by Prahlāda, and a host of Apsarases dancing before them for the sake of propitiating [the Lord]. Having seen all this, the two became possessed of divine knowledge.
Having circumambulated that Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa three times with palms joined in reverence, the two of them praised him repeatedly— he who dwells within their hearts and is the object of their vision:
"We two were greedy for objects of desire and engaged solely in sinful sorcery."
Out of compassion for the sages, we have indeed come here to seek refuge in you.
O Lord, have mercy on us, who are most wretched, having come to you for protection;
we are deluded, performers of evil deeds, fallen into the ocean of existence.
Who else is a kinsman like you, the dispeller of great fear,
the Lord and Master of the helpless, who is devoid of self-interest and whose sole object of meditation is the welfare of others?
Your name, "Nārāyaṇa," is the singular means for attaining the four goals of human life.
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Master; svāhā!
(37) This mantra of yours indeed grants liberation even to the most sinful and is purifying;
for when chanted, it certainly causes one to reach the supreme shore. (38)
Therefore, be gracious to us, O Lord of Gods; grant us firm devotion.
O Keśava, deliver us from this terrible and impassable pit!
May our senses, mind, and intellect abide within Your form.
My very self, together with my conditioned impressions, is offered at your feet.
Be gracious, O God, the Self of all, you who possess innumerable heads and arms, innumerable nostrils, eyes, hands, and feet; salutations be unto you!
O Inner Self, you are the twenty-sixth principle; you proceed as the one beyond all phenomenal manifestation (*niṣprapañca*).
O Lord of the World, you are the embodiment of the four aims of human life; salutations be to you!
O Kṛṣṇa, through the propitiation of you, all perfections (*siddhis*) come to be.
And to this Kṛṣṇa, who [is attained] without the practice of yoga—to him, salutations again and again.
(43) May we two grant you firm devotion; there is nothing else to be prayed for.
As long as we maintain our lives, may our devotion to you remain firm. (44)
Therefore, O Lord Nārāyaṇa, grant us devotion even for the sake of the beyond;
for us who are submerged here in the unfathomable mire of worldly existence, you are our supreme refuge.
O Protector, O All-pervading One, always grant us the service of servitude (dāsya) and have compassion for us both.
Thus praising, those two devotees fell upon the ground like a staff;
crying out "Be gracious! again and again, they sought his vision.
Having beheld him thus with divine sight, they bowed down repeatedly.
Just then, their husband Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa vanished from sight;
yet those two perceived with their physical eyes the divine vision of the two lotus-clad ones, as if it were seen in a dream. 48.
Then they beheld again the Lord of Śrī seated upon his throne;
he was in the form of wood, yet endowed with a crown resplendent with divine ornaments,
and on the surface of his forehead was an upward-pointing sectarian mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) like a golden spot.
Resembling a fresh rain-cloud, with eyes as long as full-blown lotuses,
radiant with golden earrings set with the finest precious gems,
with red lips, a nose like a sesame flower, and wearing a forest garland.
He whose chest is broad and bears the weapons of the conch, discus, mace, and lotus;
whose face is graced with a gentle smile; whose arms are adorned with divine golden bracelets;
and whose chest is enriched by the Śrīvatsa mark, the Kaustubha gem, and necklaces of pearls and other jewels.
His pair of legs reaches down to his knees; his forearms are adorned with golden bracelets; his hands have fingers beautified by rings inlaid with excellent gems;
and with one hand he displays the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya-mudrā*), while the other is joined with a rosary. 54.
Clad in a saffron-colored garment of fine linen and anointed with divine sandalwood paste,
his chest was graced by the Goddess Śrī, who shone amidst garlands of flowers;
his hand held a cluster of blossoms, and his cheeks were perfectly rounded.
His lower lip was enchanting, shaped like the curve of a bow;
it was adorned with a fine line of slightly visible mustache.
His lotus-eyes were an ocean of love, possessing a beauty that could shatter ten million Cupids.
Summoning him with a sidelong glance and making her heart's desire known,
she had a waist adorned with twenty-seven rows of golden girdles,
and her two feet resounded with a network of tinkling anklets and small bells.
[The feet] are rich with a reddish hue clinging like lac and other substances;
the nails are fine, crescent-shaped, elevated, rounded, and well-formed;
and they bear hand-marks such as the bow, banner, trident, svastika, and fish. 59–60.
They both beheld the Lord, the Sovereign, the Supreme Person, who was adorned with vertical lines, half-moons, and so forth, as well as vajras, hooks, and other ornaments;
who stood amidst the fullness of fresh youth, and who was the master and lord who steals away the mind.
(61) They, being filled with devotion, saw the illustrious Master, the Puruṣottama.
To the right side of Śrī Hari, they beheld Halāyudha,
the Lord Saṃkarṣaṇa, who is Śeṣa with the many excellent hoods of numerous universes; that Balarāma, adorned by a circle of thousands of hood-jewels.
White-complexioned, wearing a crown and adorned with golden earrings, bearing a divine garland, dressed in blue garments, and lotus-eyed;
his elevated and broad chest resplendent with rows of jewel necklaces. (64)
[They saw him] bearing the conch, discus, mace, lotus, trident, and plow.
(65) Then, between those two, they beheld a gentle and auspicious woman, radiant as a *campaka* flower, beautiful, and having just entered the bloom of youth. (66)
Resplendent with a forehead-slab richly adorned with saffron-red dots,
her hair-parting beautified by golden streaks and sandalwood paste;
she was enriched by the beauty of her heavy braid, which was held fast by the drawing of a *dhammilla* ornament.
Adorned with ornaments for the ears, nose, neck, arms, forearms, and waist;
wearing a shimmering garment and bodice as bright as lightning, and equipped with a girdle; endowed with all beauty, she is the eternal Lakṣmī, the beloved of Kṛṣṇa. (68–69)
They beheld her, adorned with betel, lotuses, and other ornaments, attended by fans,
and dwelling in the bliss of divine finery, beauty, and amorous delight;
she possessed a single face as beautiful to behold as a hundred suns.
The thousand-spoked [discus] is the protector of devotees and the bestower of liberation.
Having seen the discus made of wood, as well as Hari, Bhadra, and Bala—Kṛṣṇa established in four forms—the two, the Brahmin and the Kṣatriya, [beheld them]. (71–72)
In the morning, they were filled with wonder and believed in its divine nature:
"This is not a wooden image; it is Brahman itself manifesting. The Blessed One stands here on the bank of the king of holy fords (tīrtharāja) in a form composed of wood. (73)
At the foot of the banyan tree, one beholds Him of divine form, by seeing whom people are liberated.
When the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama, descends upon the earth, He manifests in four forms.
"We two shall indeed remain in the presence of Jagannātha.
Having thus resolved, those two devotees, entirely devoted to Kṛṣṇa,
remained there for a long time, constantly offering salutations with their minds fixed on Kṛṣṇa.

Having become divine, he went to the imperishable realm of the glorious Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa—the supreme abode of liberation characterized by non-return. Thus, those who worship that beginningless Śrī Narāyaṇa [attain this state]. || 77-78 ||
Men and women shall dwell in the city of Puruṣottama;
having become divine and four-armed, they shall go to my imperishable abode.
Even those such as insects and moths who are deprived of their lives [there] shall do the same.
They too, by the power of Kṛṣṇa, shall go to the supreme state.
Having their desires fulfilled, they will go to the heavenly worlds known as Vairāja; having enjoyed divine pleasures there belonging to the Lord, thereafter—
“They shall go to my world, which is even higher than the Imperishable (akṣara).
Thus the Blessed One spoke to Lakṣmī at Puruṣottama in Utkala. On the shore of the southern ocean dwell my Vaiṣṇavas.
Men and women there are endowed with righteousness and devoted to me.
Having reached the river Ṛṣikulyā, which flows toward the southern ocean,
that region between the great rivers Svarṇarekhā and Ṛṣikulyā is Utkala.
This very region, Śrī Puruṣottama, is heaven upon earth;
by taking refuge in Nārāyaṇa, it bestows dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
There, the women are devoted to their husbands, and the men abide by the vow of fidelity to their wives.
Wherever my devotees prevail, there the Kṛta Yuga exists forever.
O Lakṣmī, by the mere sight of them, eternal liberation is attained.
By reading or hearing this, a person shall obtain both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

Thus ends the five hundred and eighty-third chapter, titled "The Description of Liberation through the Direct Vision of the Lord by a Brāhmaṇa and a Kṣatriya in the City of Śrī Jagannātha within the Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga," in the first section, the *Kṛtayugasantāna*, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. Chapter 583. [End of] Section 1 (*Kṛtayugasantāna*), Chapter 584.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī, to my ancient narrative concerning its origin.
In a former age, there lived this great king Indradyumna.
Mārkaṇḍeya does not know that time in which he existed;
neither the sage Baka, nor the sage Gṛdhra, nor even Indra and the other gods knew him.
However, the tortoise dwelling in Lake Mānasa knows that ancient [Indradyumna],
and Lomaśa also recognizes Indradyumna as having existed in the past.
He was the fifth lineage of the Creator, and they were Vaiṣṇavas upon the earth.
He was a knower of the inner self, a devotee of the Lord, and one who perceived Brahman in all things.
(4) He was learned in all branches of knowledge, possessed of excellent character, a performer of sacrifices, and devoted to Brahmanas;
he performed the Rājasūya sacrifice and a thousand Aśvamedha sacrifices. (5)
He resided in Mahākālavana, the capital city of Avantī,
and performed devotion to Kṛṣṇasvāmī through his mind, speech, and actions.
The Blessed Lord himself was present at the holy site of Kuṅkumavāpikā.

The illustrious Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa himself, having arrived at the occasion of the king’s worship, goes there and accepts the adoration; and after partaking of the food offering, he personally instructs the king. (7–8)
"O King, go to my field known as Puruṣottama;
there, construct for me a palace and a temple like Mount Raivata.
Thus addressed, that king said "Om" to Nārāyaṇa.
Having received the worship offered by him, Hari became invisible.
Then the king informed his own priest in the assembly:
"I wish to see that sacred field where the Lord of the Universe is personally present."
"And we shall travel by celestial chariot together with learned poets,
astrologers, Vedic scholars, as well as male and female servants,"—
having received this instruction from the side of the domestic priest, [he departed].
There, a Brahmin ascetic addressed the king:
"O King, he who was known by the name Patnīvrata and whose domain was the entire universe, said: 'I know and I see exactly how it is held in the hand.'"
That sacred field, which is the refuge of the Lord of the World, is indeed in the region of Oḍhra;
it is in Utkala, surrounding the Nīla mountain, by the southern ocean.
That field, existing both in water and on land, is known by the name Śrīpuruṣottama.
Where the Kalpaka banyan tree stands and where Rauhiṇakuṇḍa is located,
there, in the eastern direction of Hari, resides the divine form of Kṛṣṇa, fashioned from sapphires, which bestows liberation through attaining His own form.
To the west lies the village of the Śabaras called Śabaradīpaka;
there exists the path by which one may go to the abode of Viṣṇu.
Therein resides Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa in the form of a sapphire.
O King, I dwelt there for a year at Śrī Puruṣottama with divine vision,
observing vows for the sake of pleasing the God of gods;
and every night, the gods and sages would assemble there.
O King, this majesty of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa for the sake of whose vision [I have come] was never seen by me anywhere before; there,
I heard the stories of the Saṃhitās which pertain to the matters of other kalpas.
That place is indeed worthy of being seen, O best of kings.
Just as the land of Raivatī is, so is the site of Nīlagiri;
these two sacred fields have never existed before, nor will they ever exist again.
"Since you are a devotee of Viṣṇu, go and worship Śrīdhara.
Having spoken thus, that brahmin indeed vanished from sight.
Having attained great wonder, the king said to his domestic priest:
Having now heard these superhuman words,
the family priest’s mind is hastening him to go to where the Lord of the World resides.
O priest, my virtue, wealth, and pleasure are all dependent upon you.
"Now you go before him; my desire will be accomplished.
Having heard this, the Brahmin said, "Certainly, O King, you shall see Keśava.
"I shall do exactly as you have said for your sake."
There, we shall all dwell together in that Puruṣottama.
What greater fulfillment is there in this world than the sight of Hari?
Therefore, it pleases me to reside in the presence of the Blessed One in that sacred field.

"First, let my younger brother Vidyāpati go to that region accompanied by spies; having thoroughly examined the terrain and measured the ground, he shall likewise visit Jagannātha, Nīlādri, and the banyan tree. (1.584.30)
"Let him come, discerning that field which is the refuge of Nārāyaṇa.
(3.1) Upon hearing this, King Indraka commanded him, saying, "So be it," and the domestic priest likewise informed his younger brother accordingly. (3.2)
Having had the rites for auspiciousness performed by the twice-born, he dispatched him;
then, standing upon the Puṣpaka chariot, he spoke to his companions:
"Oh, our birth has become fruitful, and this night is truly auspicious for us!"
We shall behold the lotus-face of the Blessed One, which bestows liberation.
And we shall indeed behold that Lord of Śrī, who dwells upon the Blue Mountain, whom the supreme yogis constantly perceive within their hearts. (34–35)
Having beheld Him who is invisible, we shall cross the ocean of worldly existence;
by the remembrance of whose foot-dust we shall behold that Source of Beings. We shall make that Lord—the bestower of liberation in His own form—the object of our vision.
"Ah! Today, by the power of a mass of past merit, the Blessed One has appeared before us.
We shall all behold Hari with our own physical eyes.
Speaking thus, he traveled through the sky at midday to Puruṣottama.
He beheld the country of Oḍhra, the ocean, the banyan tree, and the Nīla mountain;
he saw people bearing conchs, discs, maces, and lotuses—the most wonderful dwellings of Hari himself in embodied form. (39)
Then, on a divine and exceedingly beautiful spot near the Blue Mountain (Nīlādri),
he brought his celestial chariot down onto level ground.
Eager to behold Mukunda, he ascended the mountain slope.
There, on the mountain, he repeatedly heard conversations concerning devotion to the Blessed One;
and having arrived there, he indeed beheld the dwellings of the Śabaras,
as well as the lamp of the Śabaras and those marked as devotees of Viṣṇu.
Having seen him, he bowed his head and stood there together with Vidyaka;
at that moment, a Śabara named Viśvāvasu, having worshipped the Supreme Lord, arrived and questioned him along with Vidyaka. (43–44)
"Here dwells the Blessed Viṣṇu, the Lord of the World, the Great Master.
For His sake, I have come from afar; grant me the sight of Him here.
[Thus spoke] Indradyumna, the king who resided in the city of Avanti.
I am the younger brother of the family priest, named Vidyāpati. Sent here by that king— who was desirous of knowing, wishing to depart,
and longing to see Hari— I have come to observe the path leading toward Nīlamādhava.
"Having seen all this, I too shall carry news of the king;
O virtuous one, I am certainly fasting, so show me that Kṛṣṇa.
Upon hearing this, the Śabara [recalled] the narrative of the Saṃhitā as he had heard it before.
Thereupon the king remembered that Indradyumna was indeed a Vaiṣṇava;
having arrived here, he will establish the Lord of Gods in four forms and will perform a thousand horse-sacrifices on this earth.
When Mādhava has dissolved and merged within the earth— [he who is] Nīlamādhava—
the king will come again and install him in a wooden [image].
This very time has arrived, provided that this verse proves true.
The Lord, composed of sapphire, will become invisible.
The disappearance of the Blessed One is imminent;
therefore, I shall indeed show him to you—Acyuta, who is like a sapphire-blue Indra-stone.
Having reflected thus, the Śabara spoke the thought within his heart to the Brāhmaṇa:
"We have heard the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*;
therein we encountered the account of King Indradyumna. (54)
He will make his own dwelling in the great sacred field of Jagannātha.
O Brahmin, the vision of you in the form of the blue stone (Nīlapāṣāṇa) shall come to pass;
therefore, you are indeed more fortunate here than even Indradyumna.
But there shall be no sight of this king who possesses the luster of a sapphire;
behold with your own eyes that Nīla-Mādhava dwelling upon the Blue Mountain.
Come, let us go to that one whose body is like a sapphire to the mountain ridge.
Having spoken thus, he took him by the hand and, by way of a dense path,
ascended higher and higher to a desolate place that was difficult to traverse, crowded with rocky thorns, passable for only one person at a time, and utterly secluded.
Having led him to a place mostly shrouded in the shade of trees,
that Śabara showed him the most purifying holy site, the Rauhiṇa-kuṇḍa.
On its eastern side stands a great banyan tree with a canopy as vast as a world-age.
"O Brahmin, behold Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the World, Śrī Puruṣottama himself, situated within a bower between these two. Having spoken thus, he showed him Hari in the form of the Blue Stone.
Having bathed there in that pool, that brahmin bowed down with his whole being to Hari from afar; and with one-pointed mind, he praised Him within himself:
"O Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Blessed One who transcends the Imperishable!"
Obeisance be to You, the Supreme beyond the individual soul, the heart of the liberated Lord!
Obeisance be to You, who are to be propitiated through all ritual actions and attained through yoga!
Obeisance again and again to You, whose self is the object of the bond of love, and whose self is the sacred ford! 64–65.
Salutations to you whose nature is splendor; salutations again and again to the Purifier.
Salutations to you, the divine Consumer of Oblations, who dwells within the heart.
Salutations to you who abide in the sacred mantra, who are life itself, and who are liberation.
Salutations again and again to You, the Lord Brahmā, the bestower of all bliss.
Salutations to You, the wielder of *māyā*, the essence of reality (*tattva*), the one possessing form, the witness of the universe, the victorious one with many heads, the Lord of Kamalā. 67–68.
"O ocean of compassion, lift me up; protect me who am possessed by latent impressions (vāsanā).
Fulfill the resolve of King Indradyumna as well.
Having thus praised him, Vidyāpati chanted "Om" indeed.
Then that Śabara said: "You have now achieved your purpose.
Let us go home; you are hungry and ill-suited to dwell in the forest.
This region is frequented by predatory beasts and is full of danger."
Having spoken thus, the Śabara led the Brahmin to his own home;
even on the rugged path, he felt no fatigue because of the sight of Kṛṣṇa.
The Śabara honored him exceedingly with food, drink, and other offerings.
He said, "O twice-born one, are you satisfied with these articles from the Śabaras?
By your satisfaction, Indradyumna will be pleased.
The Brahmin replied, "This is wonderful! There are divine splendors in your house."
"Since these people bypass the kingdom, tell me, where do they come from?
The Śabara replied: "O King, these gods always come here to worship the Lord of the World, Hari, bringing with them divine offerings. (75)
Having praised, honored, offered [oblations], and performed dances, they depart.
Indeed, these are our divine implements; by means of them, we dwell with all diseases eliminated and with a lifespan of one hundred million years.

Having heard that the destruction of sins and divine status result from enjoying the grace of Viṣṇu, the Brahmin was filled with wonder and considered himself to have achieved his life's purpose. "Ah! One must always dwell right here in the refuge of the Blessed Lord."
"I must become exactly like this devotee of Viṣṇu.
Having reflected thus, she said to him: "If you have favor toward me, I shall serve as a maidservant to Kṛṣṇa; what would I gain by going to my own home? (1.584.80)
"What need is there for service to others in this world? I shall perform service only to my master.
If one has merit from previous lives, one obtains service to a master.
O good friend, it is because of my own merit that I have met with you."
"Through association with the virtuous, I shall cross this difficult and treacherous saṃsāra.
Sitting together with a Vaiṣṇava is a merit more essential than the most essential.
Then the Śabara said, "So be it," but listen further. (82–83)
"O twice-born one, take Indradyumna with you and make your dwelling here;
meanwhile, the image fashioned from the Blue Mountain (Nīlaśaila) will meet its dissolution.
Furthermore, the king shall no longer behold this ancient image."
Hari will soon disappear within the sands.
And that king, having arrived and not seeing Puruṣottama, the Lord of Śrī,
while remaining seated in the vow of fasting unto death, shall behold Mādhava in a dream.
By the command of Hari, he will install four wooden images of Hari through the opening of a tunnel and worship them with devotion;
he will also cause a temple for the Lord to be built, reaching up to the heavens.
"Our lineage shall endure as long as this wooden image remains.
After remembering the one made of sapphire stone and bathing in the ocean, go thereafter to Indradyumna and bring that king here. (88–89)
Thus addressed, the brāhmaṇa bathed, bowed, and ascended a celestial chariot;
in the evening he went to Avantī and described what he had seen to the king.
At that time, in the sacred field of Jagannātha, a wind blew with fierce velocity.
At the time of evening worship,
golden sands were blown about by the wind; covered by them, that Mādhava became a mountain of sand, and even Rauhiṇakuṇḍa, being covered, became a mountain of sand.
The gods and others saw only a heap of sand; they did not see Mādhava, nor Rauhiṇa, nor the pool (kuṇḍa) in that moment.
They all entreated for forgiveness regarding their own transgression.
How is it that you are not seen by us all at once, having abandoned your servants?
Having assumed this physical form and body for their sake,
how have you vanished from the earth, leaving them without a protector?
There is no palace, no place, no path, nor even you;
nor is a sacrificial pit seen here—how can you have such anger?
Furthermore, drag us along with you into this destruction.
While the gods were thus grieving, a voice from the sky arose: "O gods, do not grieve; my will is firm even in dissolution.
Therefore, my manifestation has vanished, and a transformation is desired."
"Brahmā will declare everything regarding my other incarnations.
Having heard this, the gods went to heaven, while the Śabaras fell into grief.
The Blue Mountain (Nīlādri) became covered with sand and was seen on all sides.
"Since Nīlamādhava himself has vanished, this is my desire.
Then the Śabaras thought that the brahmin Vidyāpati had gone by means of a celestial chariot to Indradyumna’s abode in Avantikā.
He gave the *nirmālya* garland of Mādhava, known as Nīla, to the king.
The king was delighted while wearing the *nirmālya* garland upon his head.
Indeed, I behold Nīlamādhava here in the form of that very garland.
"I bow to the divine Mālikā, who fulfills the minds of her devotees.
(103) Having spoken thus, he placed the garland upon his neck with the hand of the Brahmin.
Then the king praised Śrī, the consort of the Supreme Lord, who is the very essence of the garland. (104)
"O Mahālakṣmī, lead me to where my lord, the Blessed One, resides.
Having spoken thus, the king sat down in the assembly of the inhabitants of Avantī.
Then the brāhmaṇa was asked about the account concerning the field of Puruṣottama.
Indeed, he described in detail before the assembly the sight of Bhilla-dvīpa and the bathing in the ocean,
as well as the ascent of the Blue Mountain (Nīlādri) and the vision of Nīlamādhava. (106–107)
He described in full detail the excellent bathing in the Rauhiṇa pool, the sight of the divine banyan tree,
and the dwellings of the Śabaras;
he also gave an accurate description of the form of the sapphire-blue Lord.
This ancient image is composed of sapphire stone;
it is the Āraseyī, radiant with shimmering luster, worshipped by the gods.
This garland has been offered to her by the gods, and it never withers.
O King, this [garland] reaching your neck cannot be surpassed by any fragrance.
I shall describe to you its divine worship and other rites performed there.
O King, both worldly enjoyment and liberation reside there simultaneously.
"For indeed, there exists no suffering such as old age, disease, or grief.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī! Then Vidyāpati spoke in the assembly hall:
"I shall describe to you exactly the divine nature of that sacred field."
At midday, the Brahmin spoke, and a wind of divine fragrance blew; the gods arrived by way of the sky to offer the gift of *naivedya*.
Then there arose the instrumental music and singing of the celestial women.
A thousand offerings were presented to him by the gods.
Having worshipped him with cries of victory, the deities then departed for heaven.
Viśvāvasu, the Śabara, [describes] this propitiation of Mādhava.
"O King, let pure food and garlands be given, as well as the sugar-based prasāda which was taken away by me here; let these be offered to the assembly.
Furthermore, let the sacred field named Nīlādri, which is surrounded on all sides by dense forests, be granted."
On the shore of the king of holy fords (tīrtharāja), it is covered with golden sand.
It is a wondrous sight even for the gods; what need is there to mention humans?
And on the peak of the mountain stands a great, lofty banyan tree that lives for an eon (kalpa).

In the midst of the kings, gods, and sages, [they stood] before the Lord of Śacī.
First, he honored [the Lord] along with the family priest with various opulences.
Then he worshipped the perfected beings (siddhas), the celestial sages (devarṣis), the gods, the Vaiṣṇava kings, and the brāhmaṇas and others, saying, "May they be pleased."
O Mahendra, grant me your permission;
I shall worship the Lord of Sacrifice with a thousand horse-sacrifices until they reach completion.
Until then, remain seated in the midst of the assembly together with the gods.
"I sacrifice for the sake of attaining Nīlamādhava, not for the sake of attaining the status of Indra.
When Kṛṣṇa was revealed once again, he said, "Your welfare too shall be secured.
Having heard this, the gods then said, "We are in agreement with you."
"O Indra among kings, perform the sacrifice happily for Vaikuṇṭha, who is affectionate toward his devotees.
For our part, we shall worship Hari here in human form.
Then, at the commencement of the sacrifice, he worshipped the Blessed Lord.
Having chosen the ancestors and the Brahmins, he stood together with his wife.

Having caused the pure twice-born ones to pronounce auspicious blessings, and having performed the rites for a holy day and for prosperity, he chose them as his officiating priests; and they, too, chose him as their king.
Having initiated him along with his wife, he brought the blazing Āhavanīya fire onto the altar;
then, after sprinkling it, he released the horse.
Thereupon, the consecrated king, remaining silent, [donned] a skin from the Ruru deer.
Remaining in the assembly hall, he gave his blessing and issued a command for the sake of the feast:
"Let all kinds of foods be served—
whatever edible things exist throughout the fourteen worlds."
He indeed caused to be bestowed various wonderful items worthy of sacrifice, characterized by purity (sāttvika):
wish-fulfilling cows, wish-granting trees, and thought-gems in their entirety;
as well as wish-yielding creepers and supernatural powers (siddhis), which produce whatever is desired.
Lakṣmī herself was present there, bestowing all prosperity and excellent enjoyments. At that sacrifice, nothing desired was lacking;
the splendors were then equal to those of the fourteen abodes.
Just as it was for the Vairājas, so it was through the majesty of their lord:
the rituals, the mantras, the objects, the sequences, and the vowels were all exactly according to their true meaning; indeed, there was no impairment of the ritual action.
In this way the sacrifice proceeds; but when it ceases, the stories of Hari [take its place]. (76) The knowledges of Brahman, praised by the virtuous and the virtuous women, proceed;
the story of the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā is produced. (77)
The gods, led by Agni, being satisfied, did not even remember Amarāvatī;
all the inhabitants of Pātāla were likewise perpetually satiated by those foods;
and all [the beings] possessed bodies of consciousness through those various foods and drinks.
Just as those who were satisfied did not desire to return home again,
so too was the sacrifice of King Indradyumna conducted in that unprecedented manner at the sacred field of Puruṣottama, which grants satisfaction to the three worlds. (1.586.79–80)
By the command of his grandfather, that lord of the earth, for the sake of propitiating Jagadīśa,
gradually completed one thousand horse sacrifices minus one;
having performed a thousand *hayamedha* sacrifices, the king attained divinity.
On the seventh night prior to the Soma consecration,
during the fourth watch, the king beheld in a dream Śvetadvīpa manifest before his eyes, situated in the midst of the Ocean of Milk. (82–83)
There, in that divine pavilion, he beheld the glorious Supreme Lord seated upon an excellent lion-throne, bearing the conch, the discus,
and other emblems; cloud-colored, wearing a garland of forest flowers, and radiant with beauty.
And [he saw] Śeṣa Ananta, white in color, standing on the right side [of Viṣṇu], the abode of the glory of beauty and adorned with all divine ornaments,
by whom a canopy was formed like a parasol with his thousand hoods. (85–86)
He then beheld Lakṣmī, adorned with earrings, dressed in blue garments, possessing four arms equipped with a plow and other weapons,
and decorated with necklaces, armlets, bracelets, and rings;
she stood upon his right side.
She holds a lotus, the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), and a boon-granting gesture (*vara*) in her hands; she is the hue of saffron and possesses beautiful eyes.
Her wondrous form serves as the standard of comparison for the multitude of young women in the three worlds.
She sits in the lotus posture (*padmāsana*), is enriched with qualities such as loveliness, and is exquisitely adorned. (88–89)
And he saw his grandfather before him with palms joined in reverence;
and he beheld the discus standing at his left side, adorned with various jewels,
while it was being praised by Sanaka and other lords of sages.
Having emerged from the dream, he paid homage to him repeatedly.
He considered his own thousand sacrifices to have borne fruit and his purpose to be fulfilled; he then related before Nārada exactly how the dream had been experienced.
Nārada declared that as the fruit of this [observance] would be a vision of Hari within ten days;
it shall become manifest, so perform the sacrifice completely according to the prescribed rules.
Thereupon, the King’s horse-sacrifice (vājimedha) commenced.
All kinds of gifts were bestowed, for the sacrifice had become like a wish-fulfilling creeper (kalpavallikā).
In its midst, a great pool was constructed for the avabhṛtha bath;
it was situated on the southern bank, in the vicinity of Bilveśvara. (94–95)
The appointed servants, seeing the banyan tree there, reported to the king with great agitation: "A great tree has been seen on the bank;
its roots are in the ocean water, and its branches reach toward the bathing-houses. (96)
He is marked with the conch and the discus, present everywhere, and radiant like the sun.
The celestial tree, fragrant and divine, has arrived in the guise of Viṣṇu.
Laughing, Nārada said: "Let the final oblation be performed. (97–98)
"In a dream Viṣṇu was seen by you, and likewise the banyan tree was seen by your followers.
Having completed the purificatory bath at the conclusion of the sacrifice and performed the festival on the bank,
install the Lord of Sacrifice, who is in the form of a tree, here upon the great altar."
Having deliberated thus, King [Pṛthu] and Nārada went to the tree.
Seeing the four-armed one outside the water within the tree that had four branches,
they had him drawn out by men and both worshipped him.
Accompanied by the sounds of singing and instrumental music, as well as Vedic mantras and the like,
they led the tree, adorned with garlands and perfumes, to the great altar. There, the king worshipped [the deity] upon the altar with thousands of ritual offerings.
The king asked Nārada, "By whom, and how, should the image be fashioned?
At that moment, an auspicious voice from the sky spoke there:
"Let the great altar, adorned with trees, be covered with beautiful cloths."
For exactly fifteen days, he himself will become the sculptor;
Nārāyaṇa himself will appear there, assuming the form of an aged carpenter.
That venerable man, skilled in his craft, will indeed arrive with a tool in his hand.
Having entered within, let them diligently secure the door;
let them make noise outside until the event takes place.
For the sound of the event, once heard, brings about deafness and blindness.
One who destroys the lineage and one who destroys the kingdom should never be allowed to enter within,
nor should they ever be seen.
If anyone other than those appointed should see [the king] or the kingdom, [he must likewise be punished].
Furthermore, there will be great terror for the beholder and blindness in both eyes.
Therefore, one must not look [at it] until the consecration ceremony is completed;
once the Lord has been fully installed, He Himself will speak at the conclusion of the rites.
Having said, "I shall construct it," the carpenter then vanished.
Nārāyaṇa was not seen on the altar, nor within the wood, nor beneath the cloth.
The king guarded the altar on all sides with bonds.
She moved about in accordance with that which the Goddess of Speech had spoken.

Thus ends the five hundred and eighty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Story of Bilveśa and Kapoteśa in the Lineage of the Kṛta Age," including the king's ill omens, the vision of the divine Narasiṃha and others, the construction of the sacrificial pavilion and other structures at the site of Kapoteśa, and the covering of the altar with a banyan tree as declared by a voice from the sky at the conclusion of the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*), within the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
