Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Then, O Lakṣmī, listen to how the manifestation of the forms occurred exactly as it happened.
Thus, as day after day passed, a divine fragrance was perceived.
There was a rain of *pārijāta* flowers, difficult for mortals to obtain,
as well as the sounds of divine music and charming songs;
there were drops of white water and droplets of sandalwood paste.
The rut of the lordly elephants, such as Airāvata and others, was manifested.
He was worshipped from the path of the sky by hosts of invisible deities;
the gods paid him homage, and divine signs appeared.
When the fifteenth day arrived, he himself became fully manifest;
seated upon a divine throne on the altar, the Lord of the World appeared with four forms: Bala, Bhadrā, and Sudarśana.
Indeed, this quartet is complete with the splendor of all ornaments and the like.
And this Bhadrā is herself Lakṣmī, the embodiment of all consciousness.
O beloved, you were mine; no distinction between us is ever appropriate.
"You cannot bear to let me go for even a moment while I am thus descending in sport.
Thus were four forms indeed manifested by him.
O King, a voice from the sky then spoke there: "Display [the performance] on the stage!"
Paint Viṣṇu blue, Bala white, and the discus red.
(9) And likewise, paint Bhadrā reddish-brown and adorned with various ornaments;
indeed, no one other than the painter himself shall behold them. (1.587.10)
It should be carefully concealed with the bark-exudate of trees;
it must be restored every year by removing the previous restoration.
Thus, the divine and ancient image, together with its coating of bark-paste, remains preserved.
If the application of bark-paste should fail, there will be famine and likewise death; indeed, there will be the destruction of one's progeny. Those protective coverings must not be looked upon;
if they are seen by men through negligence, they become causes of fear.
Therefore, they should be viewed as variegated and adorned with many ornaments.
On the Blue Mountain (Nīlādri), one hundred cubits to the northwest of the Kalpa tree,
and to the north of Nṛsiṃha, [is the image] one thousand cubits in height.

Having caused to be built a divine, very firm, and extensive palace, rich with pinnacles, and having consecrated it, install these [images] therein. A Śabara, the best of Vaiṣṇavas, who performs service to Nīlamādhava— 15–16.
In former times, Viśvāvasu was the friend of your family priest;

likewise, let the lineage of Śabara, who is not a priest, be appointed to perform worship at all festivals and other occasions. (17) Let him be employed always in the rites of honor during all festivals and the like.
Having heard this voice from the sky,
the king momentarily removed his covering garment and beheld those beautiful, full forms, seated upon jeweled thrones, pervaded by splendor, and perfectly circular.
[He saw] Kṛṣṇa, dark-hued and seated upon a lotus, and by his side, Balarāma, white;
[he saw] the extensive circle of hoods in the middle, auspicious and beautiful between the two;
and Viṣṇu’s Sudarśana discus situated on his left hand.
Having been seen for a moment by everyone, they were then covered again with a cloth.
Then all [the people] bowed; Citraśilpin applied the colors and so forth, and thereafter he performed the worship according to the Vedic ritual with sacred hymns (sūktas).
The king indeed worshipped Kṛṣṇa with the Pauruṣa Sūkta,
Bhadrā with the Lakṣmīsūkta, and Balarāma with the twelve-syllable mantra.
Then, with the Saudarśanī mantra, he worshipped Sudarśana and caused various gifts to be bestowed.
He gave away tens of millions of cows as part of the horse-sacrifice (aśvamedha) and vast wealth.
Due to the contact with the earth raised by their hooves, a most purifying pit was formed;
and because it was also saturated with the water of his gifts, that very place became the sacred ford known as Indrasaras.
It became a *tāraka* (liberator) by saving its ancestors through the offering of water;
it grants heaven through bathing, and likewise grants the abode of Vaikuṇṭha through drinking [its water].
It bestows prosperity through giving gifts, liberation through residing [there], and even through death [therein].
There is a lake created by Indradyumna, renowned as the supreme among sacred fords (tīrtha).
Then the king began the construction of the palace;
and when the temple was completed, it was provided with a golden pinnacle.
At an auspicious time and moment, having worshipped the Brahmins and the deities,
and having caused the recitation of benedictions for the success of the rite,
the king then offered the *arghya* to the Lord of the World for the sake of long-term residence in his palace.

Having requested the artisans, honored them, and performed the Vāstuyāga sacrifice, the king held a great festival, offered worship, gave gifts, and provided food. Then, in the assembly hall, the king declared: "Whatever wealth has been acquired by me—"
I give all this for the sake of the temple of Jagannātha, for my own liberation.
This body is the field where the All-pervading Lord dwells with the sense of "I";
through service to Him, may the prosperity of my reign bear fruit at His feet.

"This Viṣṇu, whose body is wood, is the bestower of happiness and the kinsman of the divine abode. (33) Then, coming from behind the image, a brahmin named Acyuta, resplendent with a halo of light, spoke in private: (34)
If one desires to go to the supreme abode, the abode of the Imperishable (Akṣaradhāma), the immortal abode (Amṛtadhāma), the Unmanifest (Avyākṛta),
Goloka, Vaikuṇṭha, Kṣīroda, Śvetadvīpa, Badarī,
or any other sacred realms; ||| 35 ||
Therefore, one should reside here in this divine field of Śrī Puruṣottama.

For it is desired that one may behold the Supreme Brahman, the Imperishable Brahman, and the Liberated Brahman, as well as their divine incarnations, their manifestations (vyūhas), their expansions (vibhavas), and their partial incarnations (aṃśas). || 36-37 ||
They must behold the form of Puruṣottama,
if they desire to enjoy the worlds of Īśa, the Satyaloka, the Vairāja realms, those known as Svarga, the human worlds, and the divine netherworlds (pātāla). (38)
Therefore, one should perform acts of charity, ritual bathing, and worship for him here in this world.
(39) If one desires to obtain all sovereign powers, all branches of knowledge, all arts, as well as virtues, capability, existence, and so forth— (40)
Therefore, let this Śrī Jagannātha be served with offerings as long as possible;
this wooden Brahman bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation,
granting the state of absolute oneness characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss even through mere sight.
Not even an atom of distinction exists here in this abode of Śrī Puruṣottama.
Therefore, O King, make your residence here and achieve liberation.
You are the most learned and a devotee; worship Him with all His limbs and secondary parts.

Leaves, flowers, water, roots, grains, clothing, and excellent sandalwood—even a tiny amount of water offered to the Lord of the World, who possesses the qualities of a lotus, shall become [meritorious].
Lakṣmī is his mother; she, the bestower of prosperity, will grant enjoyments to the devotee.
"I shall give everything to the giver; there is no need for deliberation here on my part.
Having spoken thus, the Brahmin then vanished from the form of Hari.
For everyone, Hari became the object of a divine and wondrous experience.
Remaining within his physical form, he shed tears out of love;
Nārada attained stillness, adopting the *naimiṣī* meditation posture.
Becoming motionless through *samādhi*, he remained for a moment immersed in love.
At that moment, joy overflowed there as if in Goloka.
Having said, "Today our task is complete," Nārada spoke to him:
"O King, remain here after honoring this one; I shall go to the Grandfather (Brahmā). ||48-49||
"O protector of the earth, therefore build a palace with great wealth;
having installed Nṛsiṃha there, you shall be liberated—be happy!
I shall report what has been done to Brahmā, that [Nṛsiṃha] is in your service."
And Indradyumna said to him: "Dwell here with me;
after having a temple built, we two shall go to our Grandfather.
We shall make a request to him, and he will surely come here in person."
"He will perform a great festival for the Blessed One in this temple. Nārada and the king both agreed, saying "Om. Then, desiring to depart quickly, the king set about the work of the temple.
Then he employed thousands of the most excellent artisans there;
indeed, the expenditure of wealth reached tens of millions, which cannot be calculated.
Through the king’s faith, devotion, and virtuous disposition, even Śrī herself [was present].
Then Prasannā rendered assistance in building the temple.

Having performed the ritual consecration of the foundation according to the rules, she placed a copper [image] and fixed a fine molding on the side to ward off obstacles such as lightning strikes. ||55-56||
Having commanded his chief ministers to construct a sky-reaching pinnacle resembling a mountain peak for the purpose of striking [the sun],
the king listened to auspicious divine songs concerning the palace.
What could be difficult for a king to obtain when he has Nārada as his companion?
(58) Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and likewise Lak�ṣmī [are at his service]; what inferiority could there be here?
Such a palace is being built as has never existed before, nor will ever exist again. (59)
"Indeed, such an upward-moving being does not exist on this earth in any other place.
Hearing this, the nameless one spoke to Nārada, and Nārada said:
"By means of sacred fords, mantras, recitations, gifts, and sacrifices with abundant sacrificial fees..."
O King of kings, that which was earned through vows, Vedic studies, and austerities has now come into your hand through devotion; it could not have been achieved otherwise.
Therefore, do not grieve further, for your application to devotion is now supreme.
If you wish to see the Grandfather and go into the presence of the Lord,
he too will instruct you in those various journeys and great festivals;
and the Blessed One himself will grant a boon to you.
When that palace has been consecrated by the Self-Existent One at that time,
I too shall come then along with the Seven Sages;
then we two shall go there to the stainless world of Brahmā.
Having spoken thus, King Nārada bowed to Kṛṣṇa, Balarāma,
and Satī, and requested permission to depart for the world of Brahmā.
Both of them then proceeded toward Brahmā by means of a divine celestial chariot.
Through the yoga of devotion, both Nārada and Indradyumna became Vaiṣṇavas;
by the grace of Hari, they conquered the fourteen worlds.
Even as the king was traveling to the world of Brahmā, he reflected for a moment upon that which [he had experienced].
"A hundred yugas pass upon the earth; what then will become of this temple?
When I return, my own work will have gone to ruin.
How can I go away, having witnessed its consecration, with my purpose fulfilled?"
To the king who was thus absorbed in thought, Nārada said: "Do not grieve.
Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa is the maker of long duration for time;
He is also the bestower of brevity, and He will make even a moment subtle."
In the time of the worlds Satya and Bhū, the Lord, having by his own will established equality for your sake,
will perform his own task.
He whose works have the four-faced Brahmā as his assistant— ||| 72 ||
In that place, no obstacle caused by time or by material things arises.
Behold before you this mass of splendors, delightful like ten million moons;
know it to be the arrival of the abode of Brahman.
Behold this city of Brahmā; behold its most beautiful assembly hall.
Beyond that lies Vaikuṇṭha, situated indeed above the waters.
Beyond that is the abode of Vairāja, and beyond that is the Immortal (Amṛta).
There is also Paravaikuṇṭha, and beyond that is Goloka;
beyond that is the imperishable abode (akṣara-dhāma), and beyond that is the supreme station (parama-pada).
There exists the abode of Puruṣottama, beyond which there is indeed nothing else.
As Nārada was thus speaking of Indradyumna,
his celestial chariot reached the northern gate of Brahmā’s assembly hall and came to a halt.
Seeing the king and Nārada, the gatekeeper bowed down to them.
Having received the command of Brahmā, he ushered the two of them into the assembly hall.
Bowing from a distance to Brahmā, who was accompanied by Sāvitrī and Śāradā, the king stood there for a moment; then Brahmā called out to the monarch.
"Come, O King, welcome to you! You are personally dear to the Blessed One.
By the power of Nārada’s yoga, you have arrived at this inaccessible place.
Accept this ambrosial food; drink this sweet, nectarine juice."
"Tell me what is the heart-pleasing reason for your arrival.
Thus addressed, the king said: "By your grace, a palace has been built;
come there and install Mādhava. (82–83)
O Father, O Grandfather, if you come and install Śrī Jagannātha, your grace toward me would become fruitful.
Be gracious to me and grant this: that you yourself shall indeed be Jagannātha.
Then, at that time, Brahmā spoke respectfully to the king:
"O King, you have indeed built a temple for the abode of the Blessed One.
Yet, O King, neither your kingdom nor your lineage shall endure in this age. (85–86)
O King, since you arrived here, a vast period of time has passed upon the earth;
more than a Manvantara, and a hundred Yugas have elapsed.
Your lineage too has been broken, and millions of rulers have gone.
But, O King, in the divine field named Śrī Puruṣottama,
there exists a power of Time’s decay; yet that Time has been withdrawn by me,
by the command of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, until the temple is completed.
There, the moments, the regions, and their inhabitants are equal to those of Satyaloka;
indeed, by the command of Hari, they exist there exactly as they are.
By the Lord, the sun was made the jewel upon his crown in the sky.
He creates a day equal to the realm of truth (satyaloka), leading it to divine status.
Therefore, O Great King, go immediately after me!
I am indeed coming for the sake of the consecration; prepare the appropriate materials.
O King, in the first *parārdha*, Janārdana, having assumed a body of sapphire stone, did not leave the sacred field of Śrī Puruṣottama. Now, however, my second *parārdha* has arrived.
This deity in wooden form shall remain for the duration of my life.
The hair of Kṛṣṇa residing in Śvetadvīpa consists of wish-fulfilling trees;
from among them, the banyan tree was brought for the purpose of this wooden image. (94–95)
The truthful Puruṣa himself emerged from the waters of the ocean;
he was previously entreated by me for the sake of destroying the terrible cycle of worldly existence.
And through the devotion of many devotees, Janārdana assumed a wooden body.
Having heard these words of Brahmā and having prostrated before the Grandfather,
Indradyuti returned to the earth in a celestial chariot with Nārada.
Seeing his beautiful, divine, and full palace, he rejoiced.
He prostrated like a staff upon the ground and bowed to Śrī Nṛsiṃha;
then the King himself said to the artisans and others: "The Grandfather Brahmā will come along with the gods for the rite of this consecration. (99)
Just then, the Lotus-Treasure (Padmanidhi), impelled by Brahmā, arrived there.
The king performed a welcome, offering hospitality, honor, and other marks of respect.
Nārada, having recorded all the items on a ledger of inventory, [remained].
For the purpose of the consecration, he quickly gave [the wealth] to Padmanidhi; he, in turn, caused the preparation of excellent materials and likewise a beautiful golden hall,
as well as a city extending for many yojanas.
He quickly had a pavilion and a sacrificial pit constructed.
He also had three excellent golden chariots made:
one for Viṣṇu, which had sixteen wheels and bore the banner of Garuḍa.
For Padmadhvaja, the excellent banner of Subhadrā, there should be twelve discs;
for Bala, whose banner is a mirror, there should be fourteen discs.
Alternatively, for Sīrin, the most excellent plough-banner (sīradhvaja) should be fashioned.
A stainless mirror was always held in his palm;
because it rested in his palm (*tala*), he is called *Tāla*, and thus the mighty one is marked with the *tāla* tree.
Indeed, the chariot of the wielder of the discus is sixteen cubits (*hasta*) in width. (106–107)
There are fourteen [auspicious moments] for Balarāma and twelve for Subhadrā;
however, that god must not be installed because he resides in a chariot without fixed foundations. Whether in a palace, a pavilion, or a city, [an installation at such a time] would be fruitless.
The king quickly had the installation of the chariot performed.
Having constructed a most beautiful hall in the northeast quarter of the chariot’s area,
he erected a pavilion in its center and prepared a pure altar there.
One should have a square pit, measuring four cubits [on each side] and likewise one cubit in height,
prepared during the first part of the night at an auspicious moment in the north.
Then, having proclaimed "Svasti," one should proceed with the ritual sowing of sprouts.
And one should offer the bali-oblation to the thirty-two deities according to the prescribed rule.
In the morning, one should place a water-pot upon a mandala in the form of a svastika on the altar,
using a decoction of the five trees, auspicious waters, and sprouts.
One should fill [the vessel] with collections of jewels, perfumes, and medicinal herbs, as well as the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
One should worship it, encircle it with cloth, and invoke that Hari.
One should worship Him according to the prescribed rite, and likewise offer sacrificial fuel-sticks in the northwest (vāyavyā) direction.

Having consecrated the clarified butter and the sacrificial porridge with mantras, one should then offer eight thousand oblations. Thereafter, one should pour the remnants of the offerings into the pitcher and then cause the chariot to resound.
Having placed the wind-god upon the banner, one should perfume it and fumigate it with incense.
Having worshipped Garuḍa and offered prayers, one should place that pitcher upon the front of the chariot;
one should sprinkle it and drench the chariot atop Garuḍa.
Then, having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should give abundant sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
Then one should feed the people and worship Balarāma and Kṛṣṇa.
With the twelve-syllable mantra and the Lakṣmīsūkta, one should pray to the Śrī-ratha: "O lotus, you who are the very seat of the navel of Kṛṣṇa... (118–119).
"You have been born for the sake of awakening the gods; remain steadfast.
Having thus raised the lotus-bannered [flag] upward, he should then bow down.
When the chariot has been established in this manner, he should mount all the gods upon it.

Those chariots should be led by men, women, elephants, horses, bulls, and so forth, through the village and paraded around the temple of the gods. Standing upon the chariot, the best of Brahmins should offer the supreme *bali* oblation.
O gods—Ādityas, Vasus, and Grahas;
Maruts, Aśvins, Rudras, Suparṇas, Pannagas, and others;
as well as Asuras, Yātudhānas, Rathadevas, and Vināyakas—may you accept this offering! (1.23)
May the guardians of the directions, the protectors of the worlds, and the sages bestow well-being.
May they ensure that there be no obstacles; may there be no adversaries.
May the Daityas, the hosts of spirits, and others become gentle and satisfied.
Then, one should move those chariots slowly while reciting Vedic hymns.
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the portents that occur there which bring about loss:
if the pole breaks, there is fear for the twice-born; if the axle breaks, there is the destruction of the Kṣatriyas.
If the balance-beam breaks, there is the destruction of Vaiśyas; likewise, if the yoke-pin (śamyā) breaks, there is the ruin of Śūdras.
If the shaft (dhurā) breaks, there will be drought; if the pedestal (pīṭha) breaks, there is fear for the subjects.
If the wheel breaks, there is another kingdom [to be conquered]; if the banner falls, there is another sovereign.
If the image breaks, death occurs; if it falls over, there is a calamity in the country;
if the chariot becomes face-down, there is the destruction of all the local people.
When such things happen, one should perform the offering of oblations and the propitiatory fire-sacrifice (*śāntihoma*).
In the north-eastern direction of the chariot, one should prepare the sacred fire.
One should perform oblations with fuel-sticks, clarified butter, honey, and ghee, using roots and tips [of the wood].
One should offer the sacrifice when a limb is broken, reciting words of peace and words of well-being.
May there be well-being for the devotees, and may there be well-being for men and women as well;
may there be well-being for the cows and cattle, and may there indeed be well-being for the entire world.
May there be peace, may there be auspiciousness, and may there be well-being for us from every side.
"O Lord, Master of the World, may he grant us protection and peace!
(133). Thus, O Lakṣmī, one should cause the propitiation of the planets, worship, and other rites to be performed;
all of that was then caused to be performed by King Nārada, the seer. (134)

Thus ends the five hundred and eighty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Completion of the Four Images, Their Worship, the Construction of the Temple for the Icons, the Departure of Indradyumna and Nārada toward Brahmā, the Arrival of Padmanidhi for the Consecration, the Manufacture of the Chariots, the Worship, the Flagstaff and other details, the Results of Obstacles on the Chariot, and the Performance of Peace-Rites," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*. 587.

Chapter 589 →
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, when Indradyumna indeed went to Satyaloka, King Khaṇḍeśvara was appointed to oversee the matter. (1)
The protector of the earth named Gāla was the lord of Utkala and Ilā;
he is indeed called the King of Oḍhra. By him, an image of Mādhava was installed for a short duration so that it might be seen constantly.
Having removed that image and those excellent lion-thrones,
King Indradyuti then caused them to be beautifully adorned in the central area of the palace.
Then, in the sky, the auspicious celestial chariot of Brahmā came into view;
it was drawn by swans, adorned with Sāvitrī and others, and endowed with splendor.
And Brahmā descended from it, accompanied by the waters of the Gaṅgā.
Then there arose shouts of victory, shouts of joy, and cries of "Homage!
There was a great thronging of embodied beings from the fourteen worlds, desiring a vision [of him], as they vied with one another, each saying, "Me first!"
They honored Brahmā with parched grain, flowers, and unbroken rice.
Brahmā went to Kṛṣṇa’s chariot, bowed down, and beheld him.
Then he proceeded to Bala’s chariot and afterwards to Bhadra’s chariot.
He bowed down, offered praise, and worshipped him with divine objects.
"Obeisance to Kṛṣṇa, to Śeṣa, and to Lakṣmī; obeisance indeed to the Discus.
Obeisance again and again to the non-duality of Viṣṇu, Rāma, and Subhadrā. (1.588.10)
"Salutation to the destroyer of ignorance, whose self is the Sudarśana [discus].
Having thus prostrated and departed, he followed the path directed by Nārada and arrived to behold the temple situated on the Blue Mountain (Nīlācala).
Having seen the temple, the pavilion, the altar, and the hall, he was indeed delighted.
The Unborn One himself sat upon the Brahma-throne in the grove,
while the gods, sages, and brahmins took their seats there in the pavilion.
Then, by the command of Brahmā, the officiating priests and others took their places according to their stations;
Bharadvāja began to perform the rites for peace and prosperity,
and the king then conducted the worship of the inhabitants of the three worlds.
Having established the physical remains of the Blessed One and the enchanting temple,
with its great banner raised high, Bharadvāja requested the Grandfather for the consecration of the life-breaths.
Having performed rites for auspiciousness, Brahmā, accompanied by sages and Brahmin priests, went along with the chariots amidst the sounds of musical instruments and shouts of victory;
having offered praises, they caused him to descend from the chariot by way of a flight of stairs.
The devotees, the bhāgavatas, slowly led [the Lord] into the vicinity of the palace. (18) While these cotton beds were being prepared, a rain of flowers fell repeatedly:
"Victory to You, O Lord of the worlds! Victory, O Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa! (19)
"Victory to Saṃkarṣaṇa, O auspicious one! Victory! Grant us happiness!"—with such proclamations they brought him to the pavilion at the palace gate.
Having seated him before a circular mirror for the sake of his consecration, they waited.
With jars that had been consecrated and filled with water from sacred fords,
the Unborn One (Aja) performed the ceremonial sprinkling (*abhiṣecana*) of Śrī and Puruṣa with two Vedic hymns (*sūkta*).
Then he adorned the gods, who were embellished with perfumes and garlands.
The Brahmins consecrated those lords seated upon their thrones;
Brahmā, his gaze lowered, anointed their eyes with a brush,
and he performed the ritual depositions (nyāsa) according to rule upon them, which were resplendent with divine ornaments.
He meditated upon those divine [deities], established in their forms and fully conscious. Then, having performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) for them, he prayed with devotion:
"O you who are the foundation of the entire world, remain steadfast here within this form."
When you are established, we and the gods as well shall be established.
Having assumed a divine form, dwell here permanently in this temple.
By your command, may this installation be complete through your grace.
Having spoken thus and touched his heart, he muttered the infallible mantra (27).
He offered up enjoyments, fed all embodied beings,
caused gifts to be given, and he himself granted exemptions from taxes (28).
On the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, in conjunction with the Puṣya asterism,
the installation was performed by the preceptor Brahmā, the Supreme Lord. On that very day, meritorious acts such as ritual bathing, giving gifts, and the recitation of mantras were performed.
Austerity, vows, and worship— all these shall become inexhaustible. Having gone there on that day, those who behold Kṛṣṇa, Rāma, Bhadrīkā, and Sudarśana, are liberated and go to my abode.
Then, O Lakṣmī! on that day, in the form of Kṛṣṇa, the Lord Nṛsiṃha was seen in the evening by all, a sight of great wonder. Then, in another moment, a fish and likewise a tortoise were seen.
In one moment a boar was seen, and in another a swan was seen;
Hayagrīva was seen, and Kapila was also seen;
Hari was seen, and Vāsudeva was also seen.
Pṛthu was seen there, and Dattātreya was also seen;
Ṛṣabha was seen afterwards, and Vāmana was also seen.
Paraśurāma was seen, and then Yajñanārāyaṇa.
Then Rāmāditya became visible, as did the Kumāras, Sanaka and the others;
Nārada appeared, and the king of kings also appeared;
then Vyāsa, Buddha, and furthermore Svāmī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
Vairāja was seen there, as were Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa and Nara-Nārāyaṇa; these too appeared moment by moment.
Having perceived this, everyone then attained a state of great wonder.
All the incarnations of Hari originate from Puruṣottama;
from him alone they are born, appearing in forms that correspond to the devotion [of their devotees].
Indeed, the kings and others were filled with joy upon seeing Hari in such a manner.
Doubts regarding the relationship between the descent and the one who descends have been dispelled;
for the Root Cause is Puruṣottama himself, who consists of all forms.
He bestows fruit upon each person exactly according to the manner in which he is worshipped.
To whatever extent one’s faith is firm, to that same extent is one’s success.
(42) Then Brahmā, with a faltering voice, prayed to the Lord of the World:
"O Blessed One, throughout the thousands of births of Indradyumna... (43)
While you were performing devotion here in former times, many ages have passed;
yet today, by your will, you have obtained the fruit of that devotion in this birth.
Through the yoga of devotion, the king desires to worship you.
"Grant this instruction and ordain the vows and festivals.
Thus entreated by Brahmā, Hari, whose form was wood, laughed and said:
"O Indradyumna, I am pleased with your exceedingly profound devotion."
"I grant you a boon, O King: may your devotion to me remain steadfast.
Since you have constructed this temple for me, even at the cost of millions of wealth, I shall never abandon it, O Indra among kings, even if it should fall into ruin. (47)
"With this wooden body, I shall remain here for a *parārdha*,
until that second [creation] of the Lotus-born is fully completed.
Then, those who [bathe] me with the water of the well situated to the north of the banyan tree..."
Those who bathe Rāma Bhadra shall attain my world;
he who beholds me while I am situated for the bath shall go to the supreme station.
On the fourteenth day, the twice-born should draw up water with golden jars.
On the full moon day of Jyeṣṭha, having placed me on a bed in the morning, Rāma in the pavilion,
and Bhadrā in the northeast quarter, and having bathed them, he should lead them back;
he who beholds me as I proceed facing south shall be liberated.
Then, O King, having established me for fifteen days,
one should never look upon me as either deformed or beautiful.
Having performed this Jyeṣṭha-bath, one shall be released from bondage.

Then, on the fifth day of the month of Māgha and on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, one should perform the Guṇḍicā procession; for it indeed bestows liberation and happiness. Also, the second day of Āṣāḍha, when conjoined with the Puṣya asterism, bestows liberation.
O King, in the absence of the constellation [Rohiṇī], a festival procession should be held on that lunar day for me. On that day, having placed Rāma, myself, and Bhadrakā upon the chariot,
one should proceed to the place named Guṇḍicā-maṇḍapa, where I was born.

"Where you have constructed the altar for a thousand horse-sacrifices—at that place on earth, which is my own abode—a pilgrimage must be undertaken. I shall go to the Indradyumna lake for nine days. (57–58)
After that, I shall indeed go to my own abode once again;
for one who witnesses me at every step on that occasion, the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice shall accrue.
[My rising, my sleeping, and my turning upon my side—]

One should also perform the great festival of the Puṣya-bath for the covering of the path; on the full moon of Phālguna, one should celebrate the great festival of the swing-play. On the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, one should perform the rite of fulfilling all actions.
"On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, you must worship me with *damanaka* flowers;
on the third day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, you should smear me with sandalwood paste.
Thus, O Indradyumna, these festivals should always be performed by you."
"Since they are turned toward me with grace, bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation, O Brahmā, let truth prevail! Let the gods go to heaven, and let the king remain here;
I shall stay here until the fullness of a lifespan as long as Brahmā's. (63–64)
Thus addressed, they all departed; Kṛṣṇa became an image, Brahmā went toward Satyaloka, and afterwards the king held festivals.
Listen, O Lakṣmī, I shall describe the auspicious Jyeṣṭha-snāna.
Having resolved upon the vow on the tenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha while remaining silent,
one should go at dawn on the eleventh day to the Mārkaṇḍeya well; there,
having sipped water (ācamana), bowed to Śaṅkara, and bathed, one should [worship] the bull between its two testicles.
Having touched the *liṅga* with his thumb and the *śakti* with his fist,
and having worshipped them, he should then proceed to the flawless Nārāyaṇa.
He should bow to the *nyagrodha* tree, perform circumambulation, and then pay homage.
Then, having bowed to Garuḍa, one should enter the temple of Kṛṣṇa.
Having circumambulated Him three times, one should worship Him, behold Him,
present the offerings, and, having obtained the permission of Ugrasena, [enter].
One should go to the ocean to bathe by way of the path to the gate of heaven.
Having sipped water (ācamana) while facing east, one should draw a maṇḍala and perform the ritual placement (nyāsa).
Having performed three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), one should firmly bind the armor (kavaca).
"May Govinda protect me in the east; may the lotus-eyed one protect me in the south.
May Pradyumna protect me in the west, and likewise Hṛṣīkeśa in the north.
May Narasiṃha protect me in the southeast, and Madhusūdana in the southwest. (72–73)
May Śrīdhara protect me in the northwest, and Gadādhara in the northeast;
may Trivikrama protect me above, and he who bears the form of the Boar protect me below.
May the Lord Nārāyaṇa Kṛṣṇa protect me everywhere within my mind.
May he who stands upon Garuḍa protect my mind; I am Janārdana, awakened by the intellect.
May the glorious Lord, the Master of Light, always protect my senses.
Having thus donned the armor, [one should worship] with the sixteen primary offerings and so forth.
There, in the maṇḍala, one should worship the illustrious Lord Puruṣottama.
For the sake of internal purity, one should perform ācamana; externally, one should sprinkle water with darbha grass.
One should bathe three times in the ocean, whereby the destruction of all sins occurs.
One should apply a *tilaka* mark and a dot (*binduka*) on the cloth, and having worn it, worship Hari.
In the mandala, one should invoke Śrīdhara and offer a seat (*bṛsī*).
Likewise, one should offer water for the feet (*pādya*), the respectful offering (*arghya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*), and the ritual bath (*āplava*).
Garments, the sacred thread, ornaments, fragrant unguents,
flower garlands, incense, lamps, sweet foods and drinks,
betel, the waving of lights, circumambulation, hymns of praise, and so forth.
One should perform forgiveness, the removal of offenses, dismissal, and sequential worship.
Meditation, charity, austerity, recitation, ancestral rites, and the worship of the gods— all these,
when performed for the Lord of Elephants (Gajendra), become multiplied ten millionfold.
Having bowed to the ocean and the temple, one should proceed to the lake of Indradyumna;
having prayed to Narasiṃha there, one should bathe according to the prescribed rite.
Then, facing westward, one should go and worship Nṛsiṃha.
Having performed an ablution in the ocean, one should behold Puruṣottama.
By performing the Pañcatīrthī in this manner, one will certainly attain liberation.
On the full moon day of the bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha, when the moon is in the constellation Jyeṣṭhā and Jupiter is likewise there...
Then one should visit the holy fords and the sacred field of Śrī Puruṣottama;
one should perform the concluding rite (udyāpana) of the vow known as Jyeṣṭhapañcaka.
One should worship Kṛṣṇa, Bala, Nṛsiṃha, Bhadrā, and the Discus.
One should worship Nīlamādhava, Garuḍa, and Puruṣottama;
one should worship Mādhava on the tenth day in a golden pitcher,
Nārāyaṇa on the eleventh day, and Yajñasūkara on the twelfth day.
Having worshipped Pradyumna on the thirteenth day, Nṛhari on the fourteenth, and all the gods on the full moon day according to the prescribed rite,
one should daily, or specifically on the full moon day, offer milk-rice (pāyasa) as a food offering (naivedya).
One should offer sweet foods, excellent soups, fruits, and the like;
one should perform one hundred and eight *homa* offerings and feed virtuous people.
One should also make gifts of cows, and thus one shall become a partaker of desired fruits.
Thus, by performing the pilgrimage and other rites, one shall certainly attain liberation.
By reading or hearing this, O Lakṣmī, one shall partake in the fruit of that pilgrimage.

Thus ends the five hundred and eighty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of Brahmā’s Arrival, the Consecration of the Life-Force (Prāṇapratiṣṭhā) of Jagannātha and Others, the Vision of the Incarnations in His Own Form, the Festivals, the Chariot Procession (Rathayātrā), the Fruits of the Chariot Procession, the Five Holy Places (Pañcatīrthī), and the Ritual for Them," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga Cycle, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, Lakṣmī! I shall describe to you the great festival of Mahāvedī.
On the third lunar day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, one should choose a brāhmaṇa.
One should also select a carpenter for the forest sacrifice.
Having gone to the ground in the midst of the trees, one should offer clarified butter one hundred and eight times into the fire at the foot of the tree,
and also present an offering to the Lord of the Field (Kṣetrapa).
At the foot of a tree, a twice-born man should cut a small amount of wood;
then a carpenter, having taken the timber, should construct a chariot for Hari with a height of twenty-two cubits and four doors, and he should worship Gaṇeśa. (3–4)
Adorned with sixteen wheels and graced by the Garuda-banner,
the [mandala] of Śeṣa has fourteen spokes, while that of Bhadrā has twelve.
Having thus caused them to be made complete with their limbs, one should cause them to be consecrated with the *ākacakyā* rite.
One should cause them to be adorned with fine cloths and embellished with excellent jewels.
On the second day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, at the break of dawn, one should worship Hari;
thereafter, one should conduct the procession toward the Guṇḍikā pavilion.
One should celebrate a festival with royal honors and a hundred thousand men;
for there is no greater means of attaining Viṣṇu than this.
During the Cāturmāsya, one should install [the deity], and in the month of Kārtika, one should offer food.
One should enjoy the grace of Viṣṇu, for its purity is established by Śrī.
The food offered as *naivedya* to the Lord of the Universe and the water of the Gaṅgā—these two are equal;
even if touched by a dog or a *caṇḍāla*, such divine water and food are sacred.
Indeed, twelve processions of the Lord of the World should be performed as bestowers of liberation.

On the third day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, there is the procession for the construction of the chariot. In the month of Jyeṣṭha, one should perform the Pañcatīrthī pilgrimage after traveling on foot.
In the month of Jyeṣṭha, the procession to Guṇḍikā, which is the chariot festival, should indeed be performed.
In Jyeṣṭha, the fourth is the procession to the temple; this is the southern pilgrimage.
In Āṣāḍha, the festival of the couch (Śayanīyātrā) should be carried out; thus there are four months [for these rites].
In Bhādrapada, there is the Pārśvaparivṛtti-yātrā, which takes the form of worship;
in Kārttika, the Bodhinī-yātrā, which is the nature of a great festival.
In Mārgaśīrṣa, there is the Prāvaraṇa-yātrā, consisting of the wearing of woolen garments and the like.
In the month of Pauṣa, the auspicious Puṣya-bath procession, consisting of a ritual bath of austerity (tapaḥ-snāna), takes place.
In Pauṣa, the procession of the Sun’s northern course (uttarāyaṇa) is considered meritorious.
And in Māgha, the Vasantayātrā (Spring Procession) is considered to consist of worship and festivals.
In the month of Phālguna, during the Puṣpa-dolā festival, or in Śrāvaṇa during the Dolā-yātrā—
thus should these great festivals be performed, which bestow liberation upon the Lord of the World.
In the divine city of Jagannātha, no distinction of caste exists.
There, no distinction between male and female should be made at all.
All are seen as divine with four arms, yet appearing with two hands.
All my liberated ones dwell there, bestowing heaps of merit. (18–19)
Everything belonging to me is pleasing, divine, and free from defect.
Both Goloka and Vaikuṇṭha have been established by me upon this earth.
The women are Lakṣmīs and the men are Nārāyaṇas for me, the Lord of the Universe.
They are considered by me to be [endowed] with compassion, majesty, and grace.
No impure food, drink, clothing, or the like exists there; for they have been brought under control by consuming food that consists entirely of the Ekādaśī vow. (21–22)
By my grace, there is no fault in eating food from others; rather, it is an ornament.
Service to the virtuous, service to the guru, and service to me here grant liberation.
Indeed, through the pastimes with the gopīs, I constantly grant my vision.
Divine play, which assumes forms at will, destroys the self possessed by doubt;
it bestows a mass of the bliss of liberation upon those whose nature is divine.
Having realized this divinity within their own selves, embodied beings attain that state of divinity. (24–25)
I am the Lord of the Gopīs, renowned in Vṛndāvana at Kuṅkumavāpikā, as well as in Puruṣottama-kṣetra and Durgā-bhūmi.
To whomever I may be pleased, nothing else remains for them.
Indeed, I am the bestower of bliss, according to how and by whom I am desired from me.
O Lakṣmī! In this field that grants liberation, my installation as the Lord of the Universe—seeing me, touching me, and even remembering me from afar—bestows liberation.
This first and most excellent section of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā*, titled "The Division on the Lineage" (*Kṛta-santāna-khaṇḍa*), has been narrated by me to you.
Herein, at the beginning, is the account of Nārada’s journey to Vaikuṇṭha and his devotion toward Hari.
The liberation of those who have attained release consists of a liquid liberation within the supreme Imperishable (Akṣara), which possesses form.
The creation of Goloka was for the sake of Rādhā by means of Kṛṣṇa’s form,
and the creation of Vaikuṇṭha was for the sake of Lakṣmī by the Lord of the Imperishable.
The creation beginning from Vāsudeva up to Parameṣṭhin;
thereafter, the multiplicity of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa;
and the divine nature of the unmanifest Badarikāśrama.
The creation as perceived by Brahmā through his intellect within the body of Nārāyaṇa;
the dispute between Brahmā and Viṣṇu regarding their greatness and the [bestowal of] armor and other [protective gear];
and the glorification of the manifestation of the Liṅga of Śambhu, which consists of the splendor of Brahmā.
Upon examining the ends of the *liṅga*, Brahmā was found to be a speaker of falsehood and the *ketakī* flower to be unworthy of worship; likewise, Viṣṇu’s worthiness for worship was established.
Furthermore, the origin of the minute eggs and those who dwell within the coverings [were revealed].
Following that is the calculation of time, beginning with the *kṣaṇa* and extending up to the Great Time (*mahākāla*).
Furthermore, Brahmā created the mental qualities such as *guṇa*, *ajñāna*, and *adharma*.
Likewise, he performed the creation of Dharma, Rudra, and Kṛtānta (Yama), as well as the dissolution of Rudra.
The manifestation of the Sāttvika Rudra, Rudrāṇī, and their male and female servants; the peaceful creation of Sanaka and others; the revelation of the Vedas;
the greatness of the virtuous; and the creation of the Divine Gītā and other such works. || 38 ||
The creation of the Upaniṣadic maidens is the propagation of knowledge;

the creation of the beloved of Brahmā, Gāyatrī, and Sarasvatī, along with others, is the propagation [of sacred speech]; and the creation of the worship through devotion to Ekādaśī, Jayantī, and other festivals is the production of spiritual practice. (1.589.40)
The manifestation of Mahālakṣmī, Ramā, Arādhā, Satī, Gaṅgā, and others;
the divine marks and qualities of virtuous women and celestial damsels;
and the various characteristics of men and women who are the incarnations of Nārāyaṇa.
Following that, the origin and the power of the devoted wife (pativratā) are described.
Then, it is declared how saffron, unbroken rice grains, betel nut, coconut juice, and so forth, as well as red ochre and other minerals, came into being. 42–43.
The origin of the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu), the creation of Kāmadeva and others,
the birth of the twice-born Patnīvrata, the greatness of service to the ancestors,
the majesty of Patnīvrata, and the state of having a son who binds one to his debts. 44.
Likewise, there is the intensity [of the embryo] during conception (*niṣeka*), arising from time, place, and other factors.
On the first day, the rite for removing the defect of menstrual blood (*rajodoṣa*) is the vow; for Brahmins, however, it is the dismissal of the Brahmins. (45–46)
In Satyaloka, the mental creation of the Ṛṣis is revealed;
likewise, in Mahar, Jana, and Tapolokas, the creation of the Pitṛs occurs.
To the Pitṛs, food and other offerings, as well as sacrificial oblations (havya) such as trees and the like, are to be given.
The origin of the sun, gold, and other treasures, as well as the birth of the moon;
the waning and affliction of the moon due to its partiality toward Rohiṇī;
and the absence of such waning resulting from the establishment of Somanātha in Saurāṣṭra. 48–49.
Gods, humans, spirits, Daityas, Dānavas, and moving beings— just as they were created and arisen, so too did the perfections (siddhis) such as the ages and the years arise.
There was a decline in perfection, as well as cities, medicinal herbs, the castes, the stages of life (āśramas), and so forth.
Also, the fourfold distribution of the slaughter of Viśvarūpa;
the thunderbolt fashioned from Dadhyañc’s bones; the destruction of Vṛtra; the horse sacrifice;
the incarnation as the Boar; and likewise the descent of Pṛthu. (51–52)
The movement of the creation of pairs, as well as the dream that bestows death;
the signs of a universal monarch, the slaughter, and the swift falling of birds;
the inherent characteristics of the Dvāpara age, and the arrival of Nārada at Raivata.
The enumeration of the principles (tattva), the description of the subterranean cavities (vivara) of the earth, and the filling of those cavities;
the transformation of Raivata into the Moon, the fragment of the jewel, and Raivata himself;
and the penance of Khadvaṅga at the Aśvapaṭṭasaras lake are described. 54–55.
The holy site of Kuṅkumavāpikā, the manifestation of Gopālakṛṣṇaka,
and the appearance of Kambharā Mahālakṣmī have been described. [Then follow] the birth of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa and the origin of Barhiṣāṅgada.
The placing of a dead snake around the neck of the sage Panini;
likewise, the biting by a fraudulent snake due to the curse of the sage’s son; the fasting unto death (prāyopaveśana) of the king; and the suspension of the story. 57–58.
The meditation on his form, the journey to the shore of the giver of vows (the ocean), the protection during the snake-sacrifice, and even the marriage of the Sun;
the assuming of two forms by Saṃjñā, the wife of the Sun. || 5.9 ||
Then follows the birth of Śrāddhadeva, Yama, and Yamī;
after that, the origin of Chāyā, the Aśvins, and the physicians;
then the description of the paths of Yama, the Purāṇas, and the description of the hells.
The fruits of karma for those in hell, as well as birthmarks and other signs;
bodily and divine marks, and the marks of women’s fortune; funeral rites for the deceased, the affliction of ghosts (preta), and the means of warding them off. 62.
The state of being a preta, the food of pretas and so forth, birth-impurity (sūtaka),
the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa), the fruit of giving, the identity of the funeral cake with the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), conception and birth,
the destinies of the deceased through acts such as the giving of gifts, and the means to liberation. 63–64.
Also the Nārāyaṇabalihoma, the story of Dhanvantari, the birth of Soma, the abduction of the preceptor’s wife, the birth of Budha,
the triple birth of Dhanvantari, and the narrative of Divodāsa.
Śambhu’s abandonment of Vārāṇasī; the presence of obstacles for Divodāsa;
the appearance of Yoginīs, the Sun, Brahmā, Śrī Gaṇeśa, and Viṣṇu in dreams;
Viṣṇu’s instigation of atheism; and the destruction of the king’s majesty. (66–67)
The seven-day recitation of the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*,
the consecration of Viśveśvara, and the increase of the king’s devotion;
and also the insult to the Guru Durvāsas in the assembly of Indra.
The humiliation of Mālā, the decline of Śrī, and the churning of the ocean;
the emergence of jewels for the sake of the nectar, as well as the deception of the Daityas; thereafter, the war between the gods and the asuras, and the application of counsel to Pārvatī.
The vow for merit and the vision of Kṛṣṇa for the sake of a son; the birth of Kārttikeya and his becoming the commander-in-chief of the gods;
the destruction of the demon Tāraka and the narrative known as the Tārakākhyāna.
The journey of Śrī Kṛṣṇa for the sake of alms, the birth of Gaṇeśa,
the destruction and restoration of the elephant’s head,
his worship, and the results of Saturn’s aspect— these [are described] in the sections on Gaṇeśa and Kārttikeya. (72–73)
Also, the circumambulation of the earth, the marriage to Mallikārjuna,
the manifestation of Nara and Nārāyaṇa, the service rendered to his parents,
the reception of the Vaiṣṇava initiation from Śambhu, and likewise the reception [of the same] by Satī.

The merit of being branded with the heated discus, the meanings of the mantras, the sectarian marks (tilakas), and the names of the abodes; the description of the supreme abode of Brahman, the description of the syllables (of the mantra), and likewise the description of Goloka. (75–76)
The description of the locations, such as the gate-towers (gopuras) and the noble ladies;
the narration of Mahāvaikuṇṭha and the description of the sevenfold manifestations (saptavyūha) and so forth;
and the description of the male and female servants, the dwellings, and the attendants (pārṣadas). ||77||
And the description of the second Vaikuṇṭha situated upon the waters;
[78] the description of the third Śvetadvīpa along with its glories;
and likewise the description of the fourth Vaikuṇṭha located in the Ocean of Milk. [79]
Likewise, the prevention of Śambhu’s apprehension regarding his being smeared with ashes; the birth of the demon Hayagrīva; the incarnation as a Fish;
the preservation of the boat; and the destruction of Hiraṇyākṣa by the Boar.
The exile of Jaya and Vijaya from Vaikuṇṭha;
then the re-establishment of the earth in its proper place by the Boar [incarnation];
the penance of Hiraṇyakaśipu and the granting of boons by Rudra.
Then follows the enmity of Prahlāda, the manifestation of Nṛhari,
the destruction of Hiraṇyakaśipu, and the protection of Prahlāda;
[then] the majesty of Vāmana on Mount Raivata and his circumambulation.
The sacrifice of Maya-rāja and various sacred fords (tīrthas);
the performance of penance by Aditi and the birth of Vāmana;
the request made during Bali’s sacrifice and the granting of the three worlds to Indra.
The milk-vow, the story of Mṛgīkuṇḍa, and the omens;
the ritual for sacred fords, various vows, and the narrative of Indreśvara;
the greatness of Śivarātri and so forth, as well as the Mandarāgama.
Visiting many sacred fords (tīrthas), the worship of Mahālakṣmī, the origin of Alakṣmī, and those places which are her abodes;
the state of being the abode of Hari on the twelfth lunar day, and the thorough worship of the place of Lakṣmī. 87–88.
The birth of Revatī and her marriage with Durmada;
likewise, the birth of Revata in the house of Kṛtavākya;
and again, the birth of Revatī and her marriage with Bala.
Likewise, at the sacred ford of Dāmodarakuṇḍa, there is the fruit of performing śrāddha and other rites; here,
the twice-born Patnīvrata beheld all the divine abodes,
and the two Nārāyaṇas initiated him into the performance of the śrāddha ceremony.
The holy places of Vastrāpatha, the origin of Rādhā, Lakṣmī, and others;
Hari’s manifestation as Mohinī for the sake of destroying the demons Madhu and Kaiṭabha;
and the manifestation of Kātyāyanī for the sake of destroying the demon Mahiṣāsura. ||92||
The birth of the great sages from the seed of Brahmā has been previously described.
[Next are recounted] the birth of Satī, the birth of Dakṣa, and again the birth of Nārada;
the birth of Śumbha and Niśumbha, and the birth of Kālī and Cāmuṇḍikā.
The destruction of Raktabīja and the others, as well as the emergence of the army of the Goddess; the slaughter of Śumbha and his followers, and the festival of the manifestation of Satī;
the appearance of the hosts of cowherds and cowherdesses, and the manifold birth of the Goddess.
The practice of penance by Satī, born from the forehead of Śambhu during his state of world-weariness;
the marriage [of Śiva]; the birth of the Vālakhilyas and others; the construction of the city of Kailāsa; and the offering of himself by Śiva. (96–97)
At Dakṣa’s sacrifice, the curses of the twice-born brought about his destruction;
Vīrabhadra performed the destruction of Dakṣa’s sacrifice;
Śambhu’s wearing of ashes and bones [is described], as well as the birth of Pārvatī.
These three daughters of the father were Menā, Dhanyā, and Kalāvatī. Their daughters were Śivā, Sitā, and Rādhā, the beloved of Hari.
[This concludes] the festival of Kālī’s mantra and the description of Pārvatī’s virtues. (1.589.100)
Then [the accounts of] Pārvatī’s penance, the origin of Maṅgala,
and likewise the manifestation of Śambhu in the form of a bull within the cows of Goloka;
also [the account of] Brahma’s horse born from Brahma’s seed at the Brahma-lake.
And from the seed of Śambhu, Hanumān emerged through the medium of Vāyu.
Then followed Śanaiścara, Pannati, Kāmadāha, and Vara;
thereafter came Gaurī’s penance, the vision of Śaṅkara, and the journey to his home.
The dance of Śambhu, the censure of Śiva, the determination of the auspicious moment, the auspiciousness, the decoration of the pavilion, the letter, and the bridal procession;
the cessation of Menā’s grief, and the worship of the groom.

The worship of the family deity (kuladevī), the arrival at Śiva’s pavilion, the marriage of Kālikā, and thereafter the birth of Gaurī; the fall of the Liṅga and the manifestation of the twelve Jyotirliṅgas. (105–106)
The greatness of the worship of the guru and so forth; the origin of the *sandhyā* and the ancestors (*pitṛs*); the birth of Svarṇa and likewise Nārada’s status as the son of a Gandharva;
his death and the granting of life; his Vaiṣṇavism and likewise his passing.
Furthermore, the birth of Nārada, the sage’s journey to Kailāsa,
his attainment of the knowledge of Brahman from Śaṅkara, the sage’s arrival at Badarī,
and the sacred fords that are the cause of Mārkaṇḍeya’s long life.
The holy sites beginning with Pañcaśilā, as well as Somakuṇḍa and others;
the auspicious sacred places such as the origin of Urvaśī;
the marriage of Nārada; and likewise the description of the lineage of Agni.
The *Kāśyapīya-prajñoddeśa*, the description of the beginning of the eon (*kalpa*), and so forth;
[111] the characteristics of the Kali age, the bringing of the Saurāṣṭra country from Ānarta, the description of Dvārakā, and also the description of the Gomatī river and others; [112]
The narrative of King Nṛga, the stay of Durvāsas upon the chariot,
the greatness of Gopītaṭāka, the holy sites such as Brahmakuṇḍa,
the destruction of the Daitya Kuśa and others, and the locations of the principal queens. || 11.3 ||
The worship of Kṛṣṇa, the liberation of Somaśarman’s father,
likewise the Śaṅkhapiṇḍāraka Tīrtha and the arrival at the Godāvarī;
the indestructibility of the Vajralepa and the destruction of sins, and the narrative of Māyānanda.
The Trispṛśaikādaśī, the destruction of the Daitya Uraṇa and others,
as well as the Unmīlanī, the Pakṣavardhā, and the vows of others;
[the stories] of Svarṇāṅgada, Vaiśvānara, and Luṃbhaka.
Likewise, there are the accounts of Ketumān, Kapilā, and the two Gandharvas;
the victory of Paraśurāma, the account of Dhātrī, the account of Medhāvin,
the account of the two Lalitas, and the proclamation of the rescue of Varūtha and other events.
The liberation of Dhṛṣṭabuddhi, as well as the release of the locusts;
the narrative of Kratu, the narrative of Hemamālya, and the ordeal of Vāmana;
the great accomplishment for those who hear [this], and the fulfillment of Rati’s desire.
Then follows the legend of Purūravas and the story of Hariścandra;
the account of Māndhātṛ, the penance of a Śūdra, and the destruction of Dharma;
as well as the story of Candrasena and the narrative of Vedaśiras.
The story of Indrasena and Candrabhāgā, the liberation of the outcaste,
the difficult vows, the increase of Śākaṭāyana’s prosperity,
and the attainment of the state called Akṣara by Puṇḍarīka and Kumudvatī.
The concluding rite (udyāpana) and the various observances (vratas) of the first lunar day,
as well as the observances of the second, third, and fourth days,
and those observances which belong to the fifth, sixth, and seventh days. || 1.23–1.24 ||
The vows of the eighth, ninth, and tenth [lunar days],
as well as the vows of the eleventh, twelfth, and thirteenth;
the vows of the fourteenth, the full moon, and the new moon.
The vow of the swing, the chariot procession, the month of Dhanus, and the spring season;
the solar transit (saṃkrānti), Holi, flowers, the swing, and the autumn festival;
the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa vow and the narrative of Sumati.
The vow known as Haripañcaka, the various Vāra-vratas,
the narrative of Rukmāṅgada, and the account of the delusion caused by Māyāmohinī;
then the lamentation of Yama and the subsequent birth of Māyāmohinī.
[She recounted] her role as the wife of Rukmāṅgada, the speech that caused the breaking of his vow,
then the offering of the head of the son named Dharmāṅgada,
and subsequently the burning of Mohinī and even the attainment of the status of a Vidyādharī.
The greatness of the vow and the gift of charity during the month of Puruṣottama;
thereafter, the transcendence of the intercalary month (malamāsa) at Badarī;
and finally, the attainment of the imperishable abode by the immeasurable Puruṣottama.
The fruit of the third worship was brought about by Ramā through the Caturthikā-vrata.
By the Pañcamī-vrata, Śāradā indeed became the wife of Śrī Hari.
By the Ṣaṣṭhī-vrata, Menā became the fortunate mistress of all arts. (1.32–1.23)
Śambhu, Rāma, and Kṛṣṇa became her sons-in-law, the supreme lords;
they are the supreme masters who are the husbands of Pārvatī, Sītā, and Rādhā.
Through the vow of the seventh lunar day, Śrī Gaṇeśvara was attained by Siddhi and Buddhi.

And he has obtained as his husband Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself, the Lord of Goloka. By virtue of the Aṣṭamī vow, he shall always reside in the presence of the gods amidst a multitude of musical instruments, such as bells, conchs, and kettledrums.
From the vow of the ninth day (Navamī) comes the worship of Fire and Gold;
from the vow of the tenth day (Daśamī), the descent of Hari upon the earth occurs eternally;
and from the vow of the eleventh day (Ekādaśī), the manifestation of Nara and Nārāyaṇa through their forms arises.

Through the vow of the twelfth day (dvādaśī-vrata), Sāvitrī indeed obtained Brahmā as her husband. Through the vow of the thirteenth day (trayodaśī-vrata), Jayā, Lalitā, and Pārvatī joyfully obtained the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa as their husband.
From the Caturdaśī vow, Lakṣmī and Māṇikī obtained as their husband the Lord Ādi-Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa-Svāmin.
From the Pūrṇā vow, Narāyaṇa became the husband of Preyasī and Śreyasī.

On the first lunar day (*pratipad*) of the other fortnight, by means of his vow, the thousand-eyed King [Indra] attained the auspicious and sovereign state of Vairāja. And on the second lunar day, by means of his vow, King Sarvahuta became the bearer of truth (*ṛtambharā*).
At the birth of [the second son], Parameṣṭhin and Gāyatrī were the two deities;
from the third vow, Brahman and Savitṛ likewise became the king and his queen. Bhūriśṛṅgā was his wife, and they both became known as Sūrya.

By performing the vow of the fourth lunar day, King Samitpīyūṣa became the Moon, accompanied by twenty-seven wives. Likewise, by performing the vow of the fifth lunar day, King Vasudāna [became so]. (144–145)
Rādhyā and her wife became golden;
and through the Ṣaṣṭhī-vow, Devayāvan and Girikṣit formerly attained the station of Mahendra in heaven together with their two wives.
By performing the vow on the seventh lunar day, Sandhyā indeed became Arundhatī.
Sandhyā was born in two forms: she who is the course of Kāma in youth, and she who, by performing the vow on the eighth lunar day, [resided] in the noble home of Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa Puruṣottama was the son of Kambharā Lakṣmī;
by virtue of performing the Navamī vow, he was born in the palace of King Śatamakhana.
From Dyudharṇā, Rāmāditya and Narāditya were born.
From the performance of the Daśamī vow, four Vaikuṇṭhas arose from the very form of Vikuṇṭhā. Furthermore, by the vow of Ekādaśī, the ant became the mother of the ten Pracetas. || 1.589.150–151 ||
The daughter of the tree became his wife, resplendent with a body of Brahmā;
by performing the vow of the twelfth day (dvādaśī), Jyeṣṭhā became beloved of Hari in three ways.
By the vow of the thirteenth day (trayodaśī), Sudughā became beloved of five husbands.
Through the vow of the fourteenth day (Caturdaśī), Dṛḍhadhanvan indeed attained liberation.
By performing the vow on the new moon day (Amāvāsyā), there occurred the liberation of the miser and other such deeds;
likewise, his lawful wives and sons, as well as Brahmā and the others, became perceivers of Brahman.
Through the fulfillment of their vows, they became those who behold Hari, following the curse of Rādhikā upon Vṛndā during the account of Jālandhara:
"You shall be the daughter of Kālanemi, and likewise, he shall be born as Jālandhara. (155)
Hari, defeated by the gods, dwelt in the house of Jālandhara. Jālandhara went to Mount Kailāsa to carry off Pārvatī;
[the narrative includes] the breaking of Vṛndā’s devotion to her husband and the destruction of Jālandhara.
Vṛndā was cursed by Dharmadeva, yet Vṛndā became Tulasī. Lakṣmī assumed the form of Tulasī, as did the rivers beginning with Gaṅgā.
Padmāvatī became Tulasī, while Sītā was born from Kuśadhvaja.
Sudāmā became Śaṅkhacūḍa, and his battle with Śambhu [is told]. Also, the breaking of Tulasī and the stone, Viṣṇu in the form of a Śāla tree and a stone,
the greatness of worship, and likewise the marriage of Tulasī and Viṣṇu.
The accounts of Gaṇḍakī, Viṣṇu, and Sālaṅkāyana; the Cakraka [tīrtha]; then the holy sites at Śālagrāma and in the Hariharakṣetra;
as well as the Ruru-Ṛṣīkeśa tīrtha and Lohārgala, and so forth.
The majesty of the sacred field of Mathurā, the ancient descent of Kṛṣṇa;
the birth of the Niṣāda as a king and the liberation of the Rākṣasa; the holy fords beginning with Bhāṇḍīra, and the traversing of the forests. 162–163.
Then follows the destruction of the Brahmin’s sin of killing a Brahmin through the gift of a tawny cow (kapilā);
thereafter, the divinity of the Vārāha form, as well as its consecration and other rites;
and finally, the warding off of the state of being a Rākṣasa by bathing at Viśrāmaghāṭa.
The liberation of the ḍākinīs and others was performed by Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa (165).
Subhadra obtained a son, and there is also the Gaukarṇa tīrtha;
furthermore, in the Kuṅkumavāpikā garden, there is the divinity of the trees, creepers, and so forth (166).
The liberation of Śuka; the release of the deceased through Gokarṇa;
the deliverance of the Pāñcāla brāhmaṇa; the destruction of Rati’s passion for her sister; the washing away of the sins arising from agitation in Sāmba; and [the purification] of Kṛṣṇa’s wives.
At Dhruvatīrtha, ten million ancestors were formerly liberated and made into servants.
Nimi performed a śrāddha according to the prescribed rites for the sake of satisfying his deceased father.
At that śrāddha, the story of Medhātithi was told and the ancestors were made manifest.
The narrative of Nāciketa, the description of the ramparts of the city of Yama,
the vision of the denizens of hell which stirs up the consequences of one's actions,
and the greatness of the devoted wife, [told] long ago in the forest to Janaka’s wife.
Thus, the story of her devotion to her husband became endowed with prosperity.
Through Sāvitrī, there was service to cows, service to the virtuous, and the vision of the Vedas;
and Saramā, the protector of the cattle, consumed the Daityas by means of a curse.
Sāvitrī became the daughter in the house of Aśvapati through her ascetic penance;
the narration of the fruits of actions and the restoration of Satyavān to life;
the marriage of Padmā with Pippalāda and the pronouncement of a curse upon Dharma.
The divine narrative of Mahālakṣmī and the serpent-hood of Nahuṣa; likewise, the story of Ahalyā, Indra’s transformation into a monkey,
and Sītā’s dwelling in the forest with Rāma and the destruction of Rāvaṇa and his followers.
The praise of Rādhikā’s instruction on devotion to her husband;
the story of the house-lizard and the narrative of Kāṣṭhilā;
the description of the duties of women, and the protection of the forest by Hariṇī. (176)
The divine story of Reṇukā and likewise the story of Bhārgavī;
the marriage of Bhārgavī with Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa; the story of the sage Cyavana and his marriage with Sukanyā. (177–178)
The story of Māṇḍavya Kauśika, the rising of the sun and so forth,
the marriage of Madālasā, the instruction of his sons,
Alarka’s realization of the Self, and his discipleship under Dattātreya. (179)
The birth of Padminī and her marriage to Nārāyaṇa;
the temple of Varāha built by Toṇḍamāna on Mount Veṅkaṭa;
and [the account] of the slayer of Ṛkṣaviśvāsa, Dharmagupta, and others.
Liberation and the release of Sumati, Bhadra, and Rāmānuja; the Jābāli-tīrtha and Tumburu-tīrtha; the worship and other rites of Vyāsa;
the warding off of the sin of killing a Brahmin; and the arrival at Suvarṇamukharī. (182)
The origin of Vārāha; the freezing of Añjanī’s wings due to her ascetic penance (183);
the freezing of Mahendra and others; likewise, the restoration of Khyāti to life; and the story of Jayantī, Devayānī, and Śukra is thus narrated (184).
The resurrection of Nārada was brought about by Mālāvatī;
likewise, the wonders of Vīrā and Prabhāvatī were recounted.
Yamadeva and the others, having been cursed, became stones—the wives of Śakti. (185)
The origin of Ambarīṣa and the liberation of Śrīmatī;
the removal of poverty, hunger, strife, and other such evils;
and the exposition of the duty regarding the gift of female slaves, male servants, and courtesans.
Devotion to the husband Hari-Kṛṣṇa was maintained by the young Nāginī;
there was the birth of Satyabhāmā from Lakṣmī and others, as well as the birth of countless wives.
Previously, there was the vision of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.

The penance of Śrī Kambharā Lakṣmī and Gopāla Kṛṣṇa [is described], as well as the religious duties (dharmas) of the four yugas, which were indeed fully set forth thereafter. A new heaven was established at the Triveṇī in the house of Bharadvāja.
Likewise, there is the liberation of Śabarī and Pampā through union with Rāma;
the marvel of Citralekhā at the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean;
and then the transformation of Kalahā into a rākṣasī and her subsequent supreme liberation.
The story of Colarāja Viṣṇudāsa and the birth of Kaikayī; (1.92) the liberation of the maidens of Gokula and the meeting of the cowherd women with Kṛṣṇa;
and the liberation of Vīrabāhu and Kāntimatī after three births. (1.93)
The turning of Kālindī, Uddhava, and others back to their husbands;
the expedition of King Dānaka; the liberation of the denizens of hell;
and the release from the state of being a piśāca through listening to the narration of this compendium.
Through her devotion to her husband during the winter season, Hemantā obtained a kingdom and her liberation.
[1.95] For Patidveṣṭrī, the state of being a dog and thereafter the state of being Urvaśī are described; following that, the liberation of Alambuṣā from Vidhūma is proclaimed. [1.96]
The warding off of Vetāla-hood by Vidyādhara Sudarśana; the wonder of Jaratkāru; the manifestation of Sumitrā;
Lakṣmī, the daughter of Puṇyanidhi; and the grace of Nārāyaṇa, and so forth. (1.97)
She became an increasing servant to the sun-god Dharmadeva.
[1.98] Due to her status as the family deity of the Gandharvas and other such qualities, she belongs to the lineage of Brahmins.
For women, there is liberation; for trees such as the *tulasī*, there is divinity. [1.99]
The discrimination of the ungrateful during the Suyajña-Rājasūya sacrifice;
likewise, the departure of Suyajña and his wife to Goloka;
the abduction of Tārā, the protection of Candra, and the instruction on dharma.

The King of the Daśārhas possessed the fitness to receive the mantra from Kṛṣṇa. (201) A woman whose husband had drowned in the water was restored to life; and for a son who was dressed as a girl, the state of being a daughter actually came to pass. (202)
The attainment of a son through Gaṇeśa by means of a meritorious vow;
the restoration to life of a Śabara couple by means of sacred ash;
and the reunion with her husband by Śāradā through devotion to Kṛṣṇa. (203)

Śiva and Acyuta brought about the liberation of the courtesans; likewise, the rescue of Bandulā, the growth of the Vindhya mountain, the devotion of Lopāmudrā, and thereafter the pilgrimage to Kāśī and other deeds. (204–205)
The destruction of Jamadagni, the virtuous conduct of Reṇukā,
the chastity of Manoramā, and the slaying of Sahasrārjuna; the single-tusked nature of Gaṇeśa and the protection of Gṛhapati.
Suśīlā obtained the kingdom and her liberation through devotion to her husband.

(207) Even though women possess many excellent signs of purity, Draupadī’s [endurance of] being forced to wear a single garment, being brought into the assembly for a meal, and other such events [are examples]. (208)
The dialogue between Kadrū and Vinatā concerning the horse of the Sun;
likewise, the state of servitude of Vinatā was destroyed by Garuḍa. Furthermore, there is the liberation of Līlāvatī, and the story of Dhūtapāpā, the devoted wife.
Having obtained Dharmadeva as her husband, Kalāvatī was filled with wonder.
Through union with Kṛṣṇa, the Gandharva woman went to the abode of Goloka.
By union with Kṛṣṇa, the wives of the seven sages attained divinity.
Named Surasā, she attained good fortune through devotion to Kṛṣṇa;
and Maṇḍūkī, through devotion to Śiva, became a Gandharvī.
A pair of pigeons attained eternal liberation through their devotion.
The sovereignty of Yama as Dharmarāja; Paulomī’s becoming the wife of Indra;
[21.3] the king Abhijit’s attainment of a son and his liberation for Goloka; the marriage of Durvāsas and Kadalī, and the Kadalī tree. [21.4]
Fear from Ambarīṣa, its prevention, and service to a devotee;
the acquisition of a wife skilled in the sixty-four arts from the son of Tvaṣṭṛ;
the wonder of Vyāsa at Kāśī, and likewise the majesty of Pārvatī. (215)
Agniśarman and Vālmīki attained liberation from that;
likewise, even Lakṣmaṇa’s mental impurity in Avantī was [removed].
The wives of the sages, though touched by fire, were indeed purified by the vow of Pañcamī.

At Aśvapaṭṭasara, there is the penance of Khaṭvāṅgada; the vision of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa; and the holy site (tīrtha) known as Kuṃkumavāpī, so called because of the flow of saffron drops caused by the appearance of saffron moon-marks. There, Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa descended in the forms of Kambharā and Gopāla, and they dwell there eternally. 84.

57. The birth of Barhiṣad and Aṅgada; his journey to the hermitage of Patnīvratā; out of anger at not receiving due honor, the casting of a dead snake around the neck of the sage; the curse bestowed by the sage’s son; the curse of death within a month due to the bite of a deceptive serpent; learning of this, [Barhiṣad’s] fasting unto death; the arrival of the sages and Śvetavyāsa; and the inquiry regarding the highest good. 81 58. The instruction of Vyāsa; the instruction on the recitation (*pārāyaṇa*) of the *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*; meditation upon the form of the Lord; and the visualization of the limbs of the Lord's form within the sacred ashes (*vibhūtis*). 87

59. Meditation on the form of the Blessed One; the journey to the world of Brahmā; and the worship and praise of his various manifestations. 89 60. The testing of the deceptive serpent and the physician Dhanvantari at the foot of a banyan tree on the bank of a river during a vow and a gift-giving ceremony; the snakebite; the deceptive sacrifice to the serpents performed by Indra; and the protection [of Indra] following the words of Brahmā and others. 91 61. The birth of Śrāddhadeva (Yama), Manu, Yamarāja, and Yamunā from Sūrya and Saṃjñā. 93
62. Having given her own shadow-form (Chāyā) as a woman to Sūrya, Saṃjñā departed for her father’s house; Chāyā, however, treated him with contempt due to her lack of affection toward Yama.

94 63. Saṃjñā performed penance in the form of a mare (Vaḍavā); Sūrya, in the form of a horse, begot upon her the two Aśvinī-kumāras and Raivata. By Viśvakarman, divine weapons such as the discus and the trident were fashioned from the fragments of the sun-disk that had been licked by Śoṇa.
96 64. The circumference of Yamapura; the cities of Citragupta and others; the eighteen cities on the path to Yamapurī, and the state of the deceased (preta-daśā) therein. 98

68. Physical characteristics of men and women; divine marks. 105 69. Divine line-marks of Kamalā (Lakṣmī); marks of other women. 106 70. Post-mortem rites for the corpse; the performance of funeral offerings (*piṇḍadāna*), mourning, the ten-day period for the deceased (*pretaśoka*), and the torment of the departed spirit (*preta*). 108

71. The dwelling place of *pretas* in impure lands; the afflictions caused by *pretas*; the dream-signs produced by *pretas*; and the visions in dreams along with the methods for averting them. 109 72. For whom does the state of being a *preta* occur? The dwelling, food, and so forth of *pretas*; and the fact that *pretas* are of three kinds.

74. The fruit of giving; the time of conception; the formation of the body in the womb; the bodily sheaths; the unity of the individual soul (*piṇḍa*) with the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), and so forth. 114 75. Miscellaneous gifts; the gift of a bed; the funeral rites for one who has died during the *pañcaka* [period]; the destination of one who dies by fasting, and so forth. 116 76. Various means for liberation; objects given without desire that grant liberation; purification of the self. 117

Atri begot Soma; his [Soma’s] son was Budha, born of Tārā, the wife of Bṛhaspati; his [Budha’s] son was Purūravas, who had six sons by the Apsaras Urvaśī. 122

Even Brahmā, sent by Śambhu, offered a blessing to Divodāsa through a deceptive verse; subsequently, after the performance of ten horse-sacrifices, he took up residence in Kāśī. (131) 85. Śaṅkara dispatched forty-two Gaṇas and Gaṇeśa. Through Gaṇeśa’s description of various dreams, direct visions, and the occurrence of auspicious and inauspicious omens and portents, the subjects were driven out from Kāśī. (132)

[He described] the holy places (tīrthas) sent by Hara to Viṣṇu; how the people were led to atheism by Viṣṇu in the form of Sugata through the teaching of nihilism; the decline of Divodāsa’s power; the hearing of the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā* for seven days; the establishment of Viśveśvara in Kāśī; and the departure of Divodāsa along with his subjects to Vaikuṇṭha by means of a celestial chariot (vimāna). 135

At the celestial dance festival of Urvaśī produced by Nara and Nārāyaṇa, Bṛhaspati’s humiliation in the assembly of Indra, Durvāsas’s trampling of the flower garland, and the destruction of the Fortune of Heaven. 140.

90. By a magical rite produced by Bṛhaspati, heaven was rendered almost desolate through the curse of Durvāsas; the jewels were cast into the ocean, and for their recovery, an alliance was formed between the gods and the Daityas, followed by the bringing of Mount Mandara.

142 91. During the churning of the ocean, the various forms of Viṣṇu appeared; the submarine fire (Vaḍavānala) was swallowed by Saṃkarṣaṇa, Śiva drank the poison, Gaṇeśa was worshipped, and various jewels were produced. 144

Due to the anger arising from the breach of the row during the drinking of nectar, a war broke out between the gods and the Asuras; the consecration of Indra. 148 94.
Śambhu’s instruction to Pārvatī, who desired to know about her son, and the imparting of the mantra of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. 150
