Examples of women who performed vows for the sake of obtaining sons; the arrival of the gods and others; their blessings; and the manifestation of Kṛṣṇa’s own form to Pārvatī. 153. 97. The manifestation of Kṛṣṇa to Pārvatī in the form of Skanda and Gaṇeśa; and the birth of Kārttikeya through Śaṅkara, Pārvatī, Agni, Gaṅgā, the Śarastamba, and the Kṛttikās. 155.
98. The appointment of Kārttikeya as the commander-in-chief of the divine army.
157 99. The destruction of the demon Tāraka in battle by Kārttikeya, the husband of the army of Mṛtyu’s daughter, and other events.
159 100. The birth of the demon Tāraka and other matters resulting from the granting of a boon by Brahmā. 161

101. While Śaṅkara was dwelling together with Pārvatī, Śrī Kṛṣṇa arrived in the guise of a Brāhmaṇa; having become a mendicant and made his request, he engaged in a dialogue with Śambhu. 162 102. After the gift of alms, the Brāhmaṇa vanished from sight; the birth of Piṇḍagaṇeśa occurred, and Pārvatī was appointed for the protection of the gate until her bath at the Gopura. 164 103. In the battle between Gaṇeśa and Śaṅkara, the head of Gaṇeśa was severed, followed by the grief and other consequences arising therefrom. 166
104. When this Śrī Kṛṣṇa was identified as Gaṇeśa by the celestial voice (*vyomavāṇī*), Viṣṇu performed the joining of the elephant's head, and Brahmā and other deities presented him with offerings.

168. 105. The specific primacy of Gaṇeśa’s worship, along with his mantras, hymns, armor-verse (*kavaca*), and so forth. 170. 106. Regarding the severing of Gaṇeśa’s head: Saturn’s gaze, Śiva’s curse from the Sun, Indra’s elephant crushing the *pārijāta* flower garland given by Durvāsas; the sanctification of the head through contact with the garland, and the joining of Airāvata’s head to form Gaṇeśa’s head, resulting in its worshipability. 172.
107. Kārttikeya performed a circumambulation of the earth, while Gaṇeśa performed a circumambulation of his parents and the cow for the sake of his marriage.

174 108. The Prajāpati Viśvarūpa gave his two daughters, named Siddhi and Buddhi, to Gaṇeśa; from them were born two sons, Kṣema and Lābha. Due to the wrath of Kārttikeya, he went to Mount Krauñca and visited the Mallikārjuna Tīrtha. 175 109. For the protection of his subjects and for the preservation of moral conduct, Nārāyaṇa told Brahmā (Vedhas) of the necessity for the incarnations of Nara and Nārāyaṇa. 177
110. After their own birth, Nara and Nārāyaṇa praise the duty of serving one’s parents.
178 111. Praise of celibacy (brahmacarya) and the sinlessness of Kārttikeya. 180 112. At Badarikāśrama, Nara and Nārāyaṇa bestow the Vaiṣṇava initiation upon Śaṅkara; its constituent parts. 183
113. On Mount Kailāsa, Śambhu bestowed the Vaiṣṇava initiation upon Pārvatī; [this section contains] the ritual manual for its constituent parts.
185 114. The sixteenfold devotion (*ṣoḍaśavidhabhakti*); Vedic authorities regarding the branding with the *taptacakra*, the sectarian marks (*puṇḍra*), and so forth, along with their greatness.

116. An exposition of the meanings of the various mantras for those who have sought refuge, as bestowed by the Vaiṣṇava guru. 190 117. A description of the manifestations and pastimes of the Supreme Brahman, such as the imperishable abode (Akṣaradhāma) and Vaikuṇṭha; and of the Brahmī form, Nārāyaṇa, Nārāyaṇī, the Brahma-lake (Brahmahrada), Virajā, and others. 192 118. A divine description of the Supreme Brahman residing in the imperishable abode (Akṣaradhāma), and a description of His throne, pavilion, and other features. 194

119. Śrī Hari, His palace and its surroundings, His garments, His liberated attendants (*pārṣada*), His incarnations, and other abodes, etc. 196. 120. A description of the dwellings in Goloka, such as Virajā, the Hundred Peaks (*Śataśṛṅga*), the Rāsa-maṇḍapa, Vṛndāvana, the Akṣaya-vaṭa, the Bhāṇḍīra-vaṭa, the royal road (*rājamārga*), Vṛndāraka, and others. 198. 121. The primary walls of Goloka, the palaces, gardens, the inner apartments (*antaḥpura*) of the devotees within them, the walls, palaces, gardens, inner walls, and so forth, including the sixteen gate-towers (*gopura*) and their guardians. 201.

122. A description of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s jeweled throne, Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Rādhikā, their opulence, the divine chariot, the four-armed forms, vehicles, mounts, Sarasvatī, Mahāmāyā, Lakṣmī, the hundred thousand eight noble ladies and other women, their palaces, and so forth.
203 123. In Mahāvaikuṇṭha: the divine Sarayū river, the Kauśala forest, their dwellings, the surrounding walls, the circular land of Sāketa, the Ramārāma gardens, the Vaiṣṇava abodes, and so on. 206

124. Description of the royal road, the *brahmapanasala*, the Lakṣmī-panasa tree, the great ramparts, the palaces, the gate-towers (*gopura*), the sevenfold array (*saptavyūha*), and other features in Mahāvaikuṇṭha.

209 129. Within Mahāvaikuṇṭha: the inner rampart, its dwellings, the residence of Ayodhyā within that, the palaces of the eight maidservants beginning with Ramā, the garden within those, and the palace of Mahālakṣmī in the center of that.

211 126. The various services performed by the forms of Ramā residing in Mahālakṣmī’s great palace; the jeweled lion-throne and the services rendered there by Nārāyaṇa, Mahālakṣmī, their attendants, and the other queens. 210

127. In the description of the second Vaikuṇṭha above the covering of water (jalāvaraṇa), there are the celestial Gaṅgā, the Devajayodyāna garden, the royal road, its splendors, the city walls, the city of Devavatī, the Vaiṣṇava palaces, their opulence, the Vaiṣṇava male and female servants, the jewel throne, Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa, His consort, and so forth.

216 128. In the description of the third Vaikuṇṭha called Śvetadvīpa, there are the sages, munis, ascetics, men and women, jewels, gardens, the Airāvatī river, pavilions, opulences, the lion throne, Lakṣmī, male and female servants, and so forth. 218

129. In the Milk Ocean, there are the abodes of the fourth Vaikuṇṭha, pavilions, divine enjoyments, the couch of Śeṣa, Lakṣmī, rivers, mountains, long-lived beings, and Vaiṣṇava devotees; [this raises] the doubt regarding the wearing of ash marks (*bhasmapuṇḍra*) and so forth by Vaiṣṇavas and Śambhus. 220. When a question is asked regarding the reason for the Vaiṣṇava Śambhu’s wearing of ash, bones, skull-bowls, and so forth by Pārvatī, who is herself Vaiṣṇavī, the resolution is that he wears them outwardly at the command of Viṣṇu for the purpose of deluding the asuras. 222.

131. The birth of Kaśyapa’s son Hayagrīva and the Daityas, the theft by them of the knowledge of the Vedas, and for the sake of destroying that [theft], Nārāyaṇa’s assumption of the Fish incarnation; and its destruction. 224 132. At the time of the daily dissolution (nityapralaya) at the close of the day of Brahmā, the assumption of the Fish incarnation for the purpose of protecting the boat containing the seeds; and the assumption of the Boar incarnation for the purpose of reclaiming the earth seized by Hiraṇyākṣa. 226

133. Diti’s penance for the sake of a son; Brahmā’s granting of a boon; her departure to Vaikuṇṭha; Viṣṇu’s granting of a boon for the attainment of a son equal to Nārāyaṇa; and the birth of Hiraṇyakaśipu and Hiraṇyākṣa as Diti’s sons through the curse of Sanaka and others upon Jaya and Vijaya, who were like unto himself.
228 134. Śrī Hari, in the form of a boar, slew Hiraṇyākṣa—who had carried the earth down along with his own palace—and restored the earth to its proper place. 231

135. Hiraṇyakaśipu, filled with wrath, incited the Daityas to destroy the sacrifices and rites of the Brahmins; he went to Mount Mandara to perform penance and obtained from Rudra the boon of immortality through the creation of Brahmā. 232 136. Regarding the enmity toward the gods, asuras, sages, and others perpetrated by Hiraṇyakaśipu, and for the purpose of destroying his power and himself, there was the petition made to Viṣṇu by the gods and others.

235 137. While Prahlāda, the son of Hiraṇyakaśipu, was studying, the means for his execution were employed by [his father] out of hatred, due to the manifestation of the Lord’s knowledge [within him]. 236
138. The futility of Māra’s means of killing; the instruction given by Śaṇḍa and Marka; the instruction given to the Daitya children by Prahlāda.

139. Nārada’s instruction to Prahlāda while in the womb; the dispute with Hiraṇyakaśipu; the blow of the sword; and the incarnation of Nṛsiṃha. 140. The vision of Nṛsiṃha; the pervasiveness of His splendor; the tearing asunder of Hiraṇyakaśipu; the hymn of praise offered by the gods and Prahlāda; the manifestation of the gentle form; and the hymn of praise offered by Lakṣmī. 241–244. [Section headings corresponding to the above.]
141. The granting of boons by Nṛhari to Prahlāda, his consecration in the kingdom, and the disappearance of Nṛsiṃha.

247 142. On Mount Raivata: the residence of Vāmana known as Dāmodara, the miraculous splendor of Pratāpadeva and others, the circumambulation of Kārtika, the divine abode, and the sacrifices performed by King Gaya.
248 143. On Mount Raivata and at Vastrāpatha: various holy sites (tīrthas), including Bhaveśvara, Dāmodara, Svayaṃbhū, Trivikrama, Vāsiṣṭha, Svarṇarakṣa, and others. 252

144. Nārāyaṇa’s residence at Sattīrtha and the description of Bali’s virtues; deliberations on Mount Mandara for the purpose of Bali’s sacrifice; the performance of penance by Aditi and Kaśyapa in Saurāṣṭra; the vision of Nārāyaṇa and his praise; the attainment of boons; the birth of Vāmana; Bali’s journeying about; and the commencement of the sacrifice in Saurāṣṭra. 254 145. Vāmana’s pilgrimage to sacred sites; the arrival of the inhabitants of the fourteen worlds at Bali’s sacrifice; the sacrificial pavilion, the fire-pit, the oblations, the gifts, and so forth; Vāmana’s journey to Raivatācala; his stay in Vāmanapura; and his approach toward Bali. 257

146. Vāmana’s entrance into the sacrificial ground, his request for land, the granting of three steps of land despite Śukrācārya’s prohibition, Vāmana’s growth, and the emergence of the Gaṅgā from the cosmic eggshell with his second step.

261 147. Bali’s binding by the noose, the granting of the kingdom of Rasātala, Vāmana’s residence in Bali’s palace, the gift of the three worlds to Indra, the final purificatory bath (avabhṛthasnāna), and the transformation of the site into the city of Vāmanasthalī.
263 148. The milk-vow (payovrata) that secures the birth of a son, and the vow for non-widowhood, are clearly described. 266
149. An account of the events of seven births of the deer-faced woman belonging to the king named Bhoja in a former *kṛta*-yuga, and the majesty of the Svarṇarekhā river.

268 150. Auspicious and inauspicious planets, asterisms, days, yoginīs, and omens regarding departure, journeys, and the like. 270 151. Rituals for sacred pilgrimage sites (*tīrtha*) and various types of gifts (*dāna*). 272
152. At the sacred ford (*tīrtha*), the observances (*yama*) and restraints (*niyama*) to be maintained, as well as various acts of charity, penances (*kṛcchra*), and vows (*vrata*).

274 153. On Mount Raivata, following the vision of Hari-Hara by a hunter, the installation of Indreśvara and Viṣṇu; the sites of Gajapada, Dhanadeśvara, Triśūlinī, Yameśvara, Citragupteśvara, and Nṛsiṃha-tīrtha; and the greatness of the vows of Vāmana-dvādaśī and Śivarātri. 277 154. On the Radiant Raivata Mountain (*taijasa-raivatācala*), the mountains Kumuda, Mandara, Aruṇa, Nīla, and others; Badarikāśrama; and Nara-Nārāyaṇa, Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, Sītā-Rāma—
279. 155. The arrival of Mravaṇa, Jagannātha, Sarasvatī, Prabhu, and others;

the arrival of Mahālakṣmī on Mount Raivata, her worship, offerings, and so forth; the emergence of Alakṣmī during the churning of the ocean, her nature, and her places of residence; and then the manifestation of Lakṣmī and Tulasī, as well as the greatness of that twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī). 282. 156. The reason why the twelfth lunar day is the day of Hari (harivāsara); the ritual worship of Lakṣmī; and the places of residence of Lakṣmī and so forth. 285.

157. Regarding the cause of the earth’s descent during the portion of the Revatī asterism: the birth of Revatī on Mount Raivata, which consists of five peaks; her marriage to Durdama under the conjunction of the moon with the Revatī asterism; the subsequent birth of Revata in Revatī; the greatness of the Revatī-kuṇḍa; the greatness of the Āmardaka tree; Revata, the son of Ānarta; the birth of Revatī in the house of Kakudmin, named Kṛtavāk, who was the son of that [Revata]; the meeting of Kakudmin and Revatī with Brahmā; and the marriage of Revatī to Balabhadra. 289.

158. At Raivataka Hill (Giranāra Mountain), regarding the *śrāddha* at Dāmodarakuṇḍa: the fruit of the lunar day (*tithi*), the fruit of the asterism (*nakṣatra*), worthy recipients (*satpātra*), the various types of ancestors (*pitṛs*), and the items to be offered there.

293 159. During a pilgrimage to Raivataka Hill, the brahmin named Patnīvratā obtained a direct vision [of the Lord] through the worship of Dāmodara; he beheld all abodes and all worlds in meditative absorption (*samādhi*); [the Lord] revealed Himself as an incarnation of Nārāyaṇa; and [the brahmin] arrived at Nārāyaṇahrada for the purpose of performing a *śrāddha*. 296

160. The fruits of the *sarvabhauma* śrāddha, tarpaṇa, and praise offered at the two Nārāyaṇas, at the Nārāyaṇa-hrada, and at the abodes of Brahmā, Goloka, Vaikuṇṭha, Amṛta, Avyākṛta, Śvetadvīpa, the Ocean of Milk, Badarikāśrama, Dhāmeśvara-loka, Jīvaloka, and other locations within the celestial sphere (*khagola*) and terrestrial sphere (*bhūgola*).
299 161. The majesty (*māhātmya*) and other qualities of the Raivata mountain, Vastrāpatha, the holy fords (*tīrtha*), and the sacred fields (*kṣetra*). 306

162. The forms of Mahāmāyā residing in the half-body of the Supreme Brahman, appearing as Rādhā, Lakṣmī, Sāvitrī, Śivā, and others; and the form of Mohinī assumed for the sake of destroying Madhu and Kaiṭabha. 308 163. The birth of Mahiṣāsura, the son of the demon Raṃbha, and the birth of Kātyāyanī Mahākālī, who is the destroyer of him. 310 164.
The battle between the armies of the Asuras and the Suras, the destruction of the Asura army by the Goddess, the slaying of Mahiṣāsura, and the hymn of praise to the Goddess. 312

165. The creation of the eight great sages by the Creator through his own *vīryahoma*; the cause of the goddess Satī’s birth in the house of Dakṣa, son of Aṅgiras; the cause of the birth of Pracetas and Dakṣa; the cause of the origin of Brahmā, Nārada, Kaśyapa, and Nārada; the sons and daughters of Dakṣa; the birth of the Dānavas such as Śumbha and Niśumbha; the defeat of the gods; and the prayer of the Goddess. 3.14.

166. Pārvatī’s praise by the gods on Kailāsa; Kauśikī, produced from Pārvatī’s own body, goes to the Vindhya mountain; the arrival of the messenger Sugrīva sent by Śumbha; the destruction of Dhūmrākṣa; the manifestation of Kālī; and the title Cāmuṇḍā given due to the destruction of Caṇḍa, Muṇḍa, and others. 317.

167. During the battle with Raktabīja, the emergence of infinite Raktabīja goddesses and Raktabījas; the destruction of the original Raktabīja and the slaying of Niśumbha; the ill omens for Śumbha; the gathering of the Dānavas; the arrival of the divine army from the fourteen worlds; the appearance of life-restoring herbs such as Sañjīvanī; when the battle was intensified by the sounds of kettledrums, conchs, and other instruments, the application of the Nidrā weapon during the great slaughter at nightfall; the restoration of the army to life; and the acquisition by the goddesses of the Kālakavala mantra. 319

168. The battle between the armies of the various goddesses and the various asuras on earth and in the sky, involving weapons and missiles consecrated with mantras that swallow up time; the employment of the Brahmāstra; Śumbha’s false magic; the destruction of Śumbha; the hymn of praise to the Goddess; the presentation of rewards; the fruit of the hymn; and the prophecy concerning the future manifestations of the Goddess. 323 169. The birth of Satī from Vibhāvarī; the great festival; the vision of the divine Satī to Dakṣa; his hymn of praise; his meditation upon his daughter; and the realization of the identity of Śivā and Śiva within the Supreme Brahman. 327

170. In Goloka, during Rādhā’s dalliance with Kṛṣṇa, a curse was pronounced upon Kṛṣṇa’s eyes for falling asleep; from the limbs of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, there appeared the forms of Rādhā, the cowherds, the cowherdesses, the multitude of cows, the swan, the white horse, the five lions, the chariot, Śiva, Śivā, Mahālakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Rati, Sāvitrī, and others. Upon Satī’s offering herself to Śiva, Śiva attained dispassion (vairāgya). The Śivā residing in Kṛṣṇa’s eye became the daughter of Vairāja, then the daughter of Devendra born of Indriyajā as Kātyāyanī, then the daughter of Dakṣa as Satī, and finally the daughter of Himālaya as Pārvatī. 331.

171. The birth of Śambhu from the forehead of Vīraja; after the manifestation of Śivā in the house of Dakṣa, the arrival of Brahmā and Nārada; the ascertainment of Satī’s status as Śiva’s wife by means of the lines and signs described by Nārada; Satī’s performance of a year-long vow of austerity (*tapovrata*); at the festival celebrating Satī’s birth (*satījayantī*) in the twelfth year, the arrival of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the gods accompanied by their wives; upon seeing Satī’s penance, the departure of Brahmā and the others for Kailāsa; and the instruction given to Śaṅkara for the purpose of granting him the boon of marrying Satī. 335.

172. Satī’s vision of Śaṅkara; the granting of the boon, "Be my wife"; Śambhu’s departure for Kailāsa; Brahmā’s journey to Dakṣa’s house; his return to Kailāsa; Śaṅkara’s journey to Dakṣa’s house with Janavāhinī; the marriage of Satī; the emission of semen by Brahmā, who was infatuated by Satī’s beauty; from that, the birth of the clouds and the Vālakhilyas; Janavāhinī’s arrival at Kailāsa; the dismissal of the group of attendants; and the sporting of Satī and Śaṅkara in a cave on Kailāsa. 338.

173. The sporting of Satī and Śiva on the Himācala; Satī’s request for the construction of a residence; the names of mountains and other sites suitable for a home; the construction of the city of Kailāsa upon the Himālaya; Satī’s inquiry regarding the means of crossing the ocean of worldly existence; the ninefold devotion to Hari as taught by Śiva; Śiva’s vision of Hari through the penance performed in a previous kalpa; the wearing of dhattūra flowers, ashes, and so forth, based on the principle that what is fit for Hari’s enjoyment is not fit for Śiva’s; and the majesty of the food offerings (naivedya) to Hari as described by Pārvatī. 343.

174. Dakṣa’s three visits to Śambhu’s house and his repeated humiliations; the mutual cursing of Bhṛgu and others during a sacrificial session (*sattra*) in the Naimiṣa forest; Dakṣa’s censure of Śambhu; the arrival of the gods and others at Dakṣa’s sacrifice at Kanakhala; and, upon Śambhu’s non-arrival, Dadhīca’s pronouncement of a curse upon Dakṣa and so forth. 349.

175. Satī’s observation of her own celestial chariot and others from the sky; Śambhu’s command to go to Dakṣa’s sacrifice; Nārada’s arrival at Kailāsa; Dadhīci’s departure from the sacrifice; Satī’s arrival at the sacrifice; her salutation to the elders and so forth; the disappearance of Śaṅkara’s seat; Satī’s words to Dakṣa; and Satī’s abandonment of her body. 354 176. The battle waged by Satī’s attendants; the celestial voice to Dakṣa; Nārada’s return to Kailāsa; the birth of Vīrabhadra from Śambhu’s matted hair; the arrival of the remaining Gaṇas at Kailāsa; and the [arrival of] the Kālikā-gaṇa...

The creation of the army consisting of Fever, Bhūtas, lions, and others; the dismissal of the sacrifice; Nārada’s return to the sacrifice; the announcement; the enumeration of the Gaṇa army and so forth; the ill omens for Dakṣa and others. 358. 177. The supplication of the terrified Dakṣa; Viṣṇu’s words of justice; the battle between the Śaivas and their opponents; the destruction of the sacrifice and other rites; the maiming of the limbs of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*); the failure of even the Sudarśana discus to destroy Vīrabhadra who was possessed by Śiva; the arrival of Śaṅkara; the restoration of all to life; the completion of the sacrifice; and the performance of penance by Dakṣa. 363.

178. After the cremation of Satī, Śiva takes her ashes and bones to the bank of the Gaṅgā and grieves; [this section contains] the hymn to Satī, the vision of Satī, and the account of Pārvatī’s birth. 367.

179. Śambhu’s indication of Satī’s birth to Menā; Menā, Dhanyā, and Kalāvatī—the three daughters of the Pitṛs—went to Śvetadvīpa, where they received a curse from Sanatkumāra. In due course, they became the wives of Himagiri, Janaka Sīradhvaja, and the Vaiśya Vṛṣabhānu, respectively, and their daughters were born as Śivā, Sītā, and Rādhā. To Menā were born three daughters—Sandhyā, Rāgiṇī, and Kuṭilā (the Brahma-nadī Kālī)—and a son, Sunābha. (369)

180. The gods’ hymn of praise to Himagiri, whose true nature was invisible; the granting of boons for the birth of Satī; the penance of Menā and Himādri; the conception in Menā’s womb; the birth of Kālī; the divine vision; and the great festival. 371 181. Nārada’s arrival at the home of Himagiri in the guise of an aged Brahmin; Pārvatī’s being declared by lines on her body to be the wife of one devoid of qualities (aguṇa); Himālaya’s anxiety; the clarification of the meaning of words such as *aguṇa*; the determination that she will become the wife of Śiva; and Nārada’s departure for Mahendra’s city through the path of the sky, abandoning his form as an old Brahmin. 374
182. Satī’s asceticism; her appearance in a dream to Śambhu, who was disguised as an ascetic, along with Himālaya.
376 183. The birth of the planet Maṅgala from a drop of sweat on the forehead of Śaṅkara. 377

184. Satī’s remembrance of Śiva while separated from him; the celestial voice; her departure for Goloka and her sporting there in the form of a bull; Satī’s prayer to Kṛṣṇa for Śambhu to return to the Himālayas; Kṛṣṇa’s arrival with Satī in the form of Mohinī; Brahmā’s emission upon seeing Mohinī; from his seed, hundreds of thousands of lotuses were born in the Brahma-lake; Kāma also was emitted by him, from whom Śṛṅgāraka and Vasantaka were born; [and] Mohinī.

Having taken Śaṅkara to the Himālayas, she embraced him; the seed of the Creator (Brahmā) fell, was caught by the Seven Sages in leaf-cups, and was offered to the Wind-god. A celestial voice arose, and the Wind-god, assuming the form of a monkey, placed it into the ear of Añjanī. From that, Hanumān was born. Mistaking the sun for a fruit, he seized it to eat it; taking his mother with him, he went to Vaikuṇṭha. Having established his mother there, he became a Vaiṣṇava and wandered upon the earth. With his foot, he gently struck Śanaiścara, who then assumed the form of a woman and sought refuge at his feet. 378.

186. At Gaṅgāvatāraśṛṅga, there was the penance of Śambhu and the service of Pārvatī; the discharge of arrows by Kāma sent by Indra; the burning of Kāma by the fire arising from the third eye; the lamentation of Rati; the granting of a boon to Anaṅga—who would later possess a physical body as Pradyumna; the residence of Rati in the house of Śambara; and the residence of the submarine fire (vaḍavānala), which is the fire of his wrath, in the ocean. 384.

186. Pārvatī’s grief, Nārada’s instruction, and the prohibition against her asceticism; nevertheless, she performed penance for five thousand years on Gaurīśṛṅga. While Gaurī remained engaged in penance, she was tested by the Seven Sages and endowed with their blessings. 389.

187. The seven sages reported Pārvatī’s life-consuming penance to Śaṅkara; Śaṅkara appeared before them in the guise of an old, matted-haired brahmin; he described his own lack of virtues and faults; Pārvatī was made to perceive the true virtues of Śambhu; Śambhu revealed his true form; they conversed happily with one another; there was a definitive declaration regarding the marriage; and the completion of the penance. 393.

188. Welcome to Pārvatī; Śambhu’s dance in the form of a dancer in the pavilion; Pārvatī’s request, which was not accepted by Menā and Śaila; Śambhu’s return in the guise of a Vaiṣṇava; the censure that [the girl] should not be given to Śiva; the disappearance and reappearance of Menā and Śaila. 398. 189. The arrival of the Seven Sages sent by Śiva at the house of Himālaya; the invitation of Parvata and the others; the consultation for the betrothal of Pārvatī; the betrothal and the determination of the auspicious date. 400.

190. Himālaya caused heaps of cooked foods, jewels, and utensils to be prepared; he had auspicious rites performed; the mountains and others were invited and arrived; and the beautification of the city and the pavilion was carried out by Viśvakarman.

402 191. Śaṅkara received the marriage proposal letter; those residing in the fourteen worlds were invited and came; Śiva’s attire suitable for the bridegroom was arranged; the auspicious ceremonies such as the installation of the pavilion and the *nāndī* rite were performed; the protocol for the procession of the bridegroom was established; and previously, Nārada had been sent forth. 405

192. The splendor of the bridegroom’s procession (*varayātrā*), the carriers of the bride (*varavāhinī*), and the crowds of people; Menā’s observation of the bride and the groom; and Menā’s grief upon seeing Śaṅkara’s unattractive form. 401 193. Menā’s distressed lamentations; Viṣṇu’s instruction that Śaṅkara assumes many forms for a specific reason in order to dispel Menā’s sorrow; Hara’s manifestation in the form of Viṣṇu; the Gaṇas being made to assume Vaiṣṇava forms; and the welcoming ceremony (*dvārācāra*) consisting of Menā and the Mountain’s honoring and increasing [the groom] with parched grain (*lājā*). 41.

194. The worship of the family deity; Pārvatī’s investiture with the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*); the ornaments and other gifts sent by Śiva; Śiva’s arrival at the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*); the offering of *madhuparka* and other honors; Śiva’s name, lineage (*gotra*), and so forth; the taking of Pārvatī’s hand in marriage; the giving of gifts and the circumambulation of the fire; the birth of Brahmā and the other *Vālakhilyas*; the conduct of the sacrificial altar (*vedikā*) and worldly customs; the use of irony and the like; the restoration of Kāma to life through the prayer for sexual union (*ratiprārthanā*); the hospitable reception with food; the duties of a devoted wife (*pativratā*); and the journey to Kailāsa. 411.

195. By means of a joking remark that Kālī was spoken by Śaṅkara, Gaurī performed penance and became fair-complexioned (Gaurī), while Kauśikī became Kālī; and the tiger Somanandī became a Gaṇa. 422 196. While Śaṅkara, naked, went to the Dāruvana forest for alms, his *liṅga* was struck down with a blade of *darbha* grass; those twelve fragments became the Jyotirliṅgas, and he later regained his *liṅga*.
424 197. The greatness and other qualities of worshipping the Guru. 428
198. The birth of Sandhyā, the assembly of the four classes of ancestors (*pitṛs*), Kāma, Rati, Bāṇa, and Arundhatī.
430. 199. The origin of gold mines and other minerals from the falling of Śiva’s bodily constituents upon seeing Mohinī.

432. 200. Brahmā begot mind-born sons through Sāvitrī; the birth of Nārada; Nārada’s refusal when commissioned for the sake of creation; and how, due to Brahmā’s curse, he became the Gandharva named Upabṛṃhaṇa.
Furthermore, there is the curse and the abandonment of the body during the time of singing in the assembly of Brahmā (435). 201.
The death of Nārada, who was the Gandharva Upabarhaṇa, the lamentations of his wives, and the petition to Brahmā and the other gods for his restoration to life (438).

202. The means for destroying diseases according to the system of Āyurveda and other sciences; the granting of life to Upabarhaṇa by Brahmā at the request of Mālāvatī’s wife; the armor-like mantra consisting of sixteen syllables that bestows that [life]; furthermore, the birth of Nārada from the seed of Kaśyapa and Nārada through Kalāvatī, the wife of the Śūdra cowherd Drumila; his initiation into Vaiṣṇava rites by Sanatkumāra; and after performing penance for a thousand years following his mother's death, casting off his body and going to Goloka, his subsequent mental birth from the region of Brahmā’s throat. 440.

203. Brahmā instructed Nārada for the purpose of creation; Nārada accepted this through the gateway of knowledge; and [the account of] his journey to Kailāsa for the sake of the meaning of the Vaiṣṇava guru-mantra. 445 204. Śaṅkara explained to Nārada the daily observances (āhnika), the worship of Nārāyaṇa, the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna), what is fit and unfit to be eaten, the Supreme Brahman, and so forth. 447 205. Nārada’s journey to Badarikāśrama, his vision of Nara and Nārāyaṇa, his hymn of praise through song, the attainment of divinity, the instruction on devotion, and the command to perform marriage. 450

206. [The description of] the Agnitīrtha, which removes the defect of fire consuming everything; the Nārada-tapasthala; the Nāradaśilā-tīrtha; and the Mārkaṇḍeyaśilā-tīrtha, preceded by the narrative of Mārkaṇḍeya’s longevity.

452 207. [The descriptions of] the Vainateyaśilā-tīrtha; the Gāruḍīśilā-tīrtha; the Pañcamukhīgaṅgā-tīrtha; the Nārasiṃhīśilā-tīrtha; the Brahma-tīrtha; the Sarasvatī-tīrtha; the Indrapada-tīrtha consisting of a flowing stream; the Mānasodbheda-tīrtha; the Vasudhārā-tīrtha; and the Pañcadhārā-tīrtha. 456
208. Narratives concerning the Soma-kuṇḍa Tīrtha, the Āditya-kuṇḍa Tīrtha, the Catuḥpuruṣārtha Tīrtha, the Urvaśī-samutpatti-kuṇḍa Tīrtha, and others.

458 209. The Meru Tīrtha, Daṇḍapuṣkariṇī, Mānasodbheda, the birthplace of Nara and Nārāyaṇa, the reunion of Dharmarāja and Urvaśī, the lifting up of the Tortoise (Kūrmoddhāra), Brahmāvarta, and other Tīrthas; the majesty of those sacred fields, temples, and the nectar of their feet. 461

210. Nārada’s arrival at the assembly of Brahmā; his commissioning for the sake of marriage; the wedding procession with Mālavatī, the daughter of Sṛñjaya; the auspicious moment (lagna); [the birth of] one hundred thousand sons and one hundred thousand daughters; and thereafter, two hundred thousand years later, his departure to the bank of the Kṛtamālā river for asceticism. 463 211. A description of the lineage of Agni. 465 212. An account of the subjects of Kaśyapa belonging to the fourteen worlds. 466
213. An account of the lineages and origins of the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Ṛṣis.
468 214. A description of two hundred and sixty-five kalpas, as well as kalpas exceeding that number, and the fourteen Manvantaras.
470 215. The manifestation of the nature, qualities, and defects of the Kali Yuga. 472

216. A specific description of the characteristics of the Kali age. 474 217. In the *Dvārakāmāhātmya*: the construction of Dvārakā and its gardens within Saurāṣṭra—which consists of the portion of Goloka brought by Ānarta, the son of Śaryāti—along with auspicious and inauspicious trees, creepers, and other features.

476 218–219. A description of divine Dvārakā; the arrival of countless gods, sages, and others who have remembered Śrī Kṛṣṇa; their worship [of Him]; their residence there; the majesty of its sacred fords (*tīrtha*); and the power of the forest [of Aṅgāra]. 479
219. The majesty of Gomatītīrtha and Cakratīrtha, preceded by their historical accounts.
482 220. The ritual procedures, fruits, and other details regarding Gomatītīrtha and Cakratīrtha.
484 221. The ritual procedure for the confluence of the Gomatī and the ocean, and for the Lakṣmītīrtha and Saptahrada-tīrtha. 485
222. King Nṛga’s birth as a lizard due to the transposition of the gift of cows, his liberation effected by Śrī Kṛṣṇa, and the Nṛga-well *tīrtha*.

487 223. The *Rukmiṇī-tīrtha*—so named for the water of the Gaṅgā that issued forth from a blow of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s foot to quench the thirst of Rukmiṇī while she was occupied with pulling the chariot of Durvāsas—and the threefold nature of Rukmiṇī.
488 224. The majesty of that *tīrtha* through the reunion of the Gokula cowherd women with Uddhava and with Kṛṣṇa at the Gopī-taṭāka lake. 489
225. The greatness of *gopīcandana*, its qualitylessness (*nirguṇatva*), and so forth.
491 226. The celestial lakes (*sarovara*) of Brahmakuṇḍa, Sūrya, Varuṇa, Kubera, and others; the five rivers (*pañcanadī*) and so forth; and the thirty-six sacred sites (*tīrtha*) and so forth.

492 227. The names of the protectors of the Dvārakā region; the destruction of the Kuśāda demons for the purpose of Durvāsas’s bath; the *Kuśeśvara* and other sacred sites; the *Vāmana* and other sacred sites; and the *Paṭṭarājñī* sacred sites. 415

228. The greatness and fruits of worshipping Śrī Kṛṣṇa while residing in Dvārakā. 498 229. The liberation of the ancestors of Somaśarman, a devotee of Śiva, through the pilgrimage to Dvārakā and other rites.
499 230. The majesty of the tīrthas of Śaṅkhoddhāra, Piṇḍāraka, the River Rukmīṇī, Agastyataḍāga, and Yajñavāṭa, as well as the observances of Ekādaśī, Dvādaśī, and the ritual vigil (jāgaraṇa). 502

231. When Jupiter is situated in the zodiac sign of Leo, there occurs the arrival and residence at the Dvārakā-tīrtha of all the holy fords (tīrthas), all the gods, and all the attendants (pārṣadas) together with the Godāvarī river.

5.03 232. The greatness of Dvārakā, established through the narration of the power of the pilgrimage to Dvārakā—which destroys sins as effectively as adamantine cement—and by means of the joy [experienced] by Māyā residing in Kāśī.
5.06 233. The fruit of the Trispṛśā-ekādaśī vow, worship, and other rites. 5.07
234. The appearance of the Ekādaśī vow occasioned by the battle between Mura and the Dānavas, including its injunctions and so forth.
510 235. The ritual procedure, worship, and so forth for the Ekādaśī vow named Unmīlanī.
514 236. The greatness of the worship and the vow of Pakṣavardhinī Ekādaśī, and so forth. 516
237. The greatness of the vigil (jāgaraṇa) observed during the Ekādaśī vow.

217 238. The procedure, fruits, and so forth of the Utpatti-Ekādaśī vow belonging to the dark fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa; the story of King Svarṇāṅgada. 520 239. Regarding the performance of the Mokṣada-Ekādaśī vow belonging to the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa: the liberation of King Vaiśvānara’s ancestors and other matters. 523
240. By means of the Pauṣa-kṛṣṇa-saphala-ekādaśī vow, King Luṃbhaka obtained his kingdom and other blessings.
526. 241. By means of the Pauṣa-śukla-putrada-ekādaśī vow, King Ketumant obtained a son.
529. 242. By means of the Māgha-kṛṣṇa-ṣaṭtila-ekādaśī vow, the noble lady Kapilā obtained food, nectar, and other such things. 531.
243. Through the *Māgha-śukla-jaya-ekādaśī-vrata*, Mālyavatī and Mālyavat, who were *gandharvas*, were liberated from their state as *piśācas*.
534 244. Through the *Phālguna-kṛṣṇa-vijaya-ekādaśī-vrata* and the ascetic penance (*tapas*) performed for the sake of destroying Sahasrārjuna, Paraśurāma achieved victory.

537 245. Regarding the majesty of the *Phālguna-śukla-āmalakī-ekādaśī-vrata*: the manifestation of the *āmalakī* tree for the purpose of adorning the forehead of Lakṣmī; the majesty of its worship and so forth; and the majesty of the *dhātrī* fruit. 539

246. By the vow of the Ekādaśī known as *Pāpamocanī* in the dark fortnight of Caitra, Medhāvin attained the fruit of the sage’s austerity, and Mañjughoṣā, an Apsaras, was released from her state as a Piśācī.

(543) 247. By the vow of the *Kāmada-ekādaśī* in the bright fortnight of Caitra, Lalitā was released from the state of being a Piśācī that had arisen due to the curse of the Gandharva Lalitagandharva upon Pauṇḍra.

(17) 248. By the vow of the *Varūthinī-ekādaśī* in the dark fortnight of Vaiśākha, Kalā, the wife of Marīci, was delivered from the sin born of the fault of association, even though she was devoted to the words of her husband, who was a disciple named Varūtha. (510)
249. Through the Vaiśākha-Śukla-Mohinī-Ekādaśī vow, the sinful Vaiśya Dhṛṣṭabuddhi attained liberation by performing the vow as instructed by Kauṇḍinya.

(553) 250. Regarding the greatness of the Jyeṣṭha-Kṛṣṇa-Apara-Ekādaśī vow: there is the destruction of sins such as the "vajralepa" and "saṃkarīkaraṇa"; and through the performance of the vow, the pregnant woman Śalabhāyatī, who was joined with a monkey, became free from blemish and attained liberation.
(556) 251. Through the Jyeṣṭha-Śukla-Nirjala-Ekādaśī vow, the hungry sage Kratu obtained the fruit of the pacification of his hunger and other benefits, along with the narrative account. (559)

252. By the vow of the Ekādaśī of the dark fortnight of Āṣāḍha associated with the Yoginī, Hemamālin Yakṣa was cured of leprosy and other diseases. 562 253. Regarding the greatness of the Śayanī Ekādaśī vow of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha: there is the reclining performed by Vāmana during his incarnation; and during the Cāturmāsya period, there are the observances of restraint (yama), regulation (niyama), self-control (saṃyama), vows, subduing the senses, emaciation through austerity, renunciation, service, giving, assistance, virtuous vows, and so forth. 565 254. By the Kāmikā Ekādaśī vow of the dark fortnight of Śrāvaṇa, the ancestors of Śravaṇa attained perfection (siddhi), and Rati regained her husband, who is named Kāma. 569

255. In the account of the greatness of the Śrāvaṇa-śukla-putrada-ekādaśī vow, there is the narrative of King Purūravas’s previous birth and the majesty of the Pavitrāropaṇa rite; through this vow, Purūravas obtained a son by Urvaśī. 8171 256. Through the Bhādrapada-kṛṣṇa-aja-ekādaśī vow, during the test of truth performed by Viśvāmitra, Hariścandra’s cessation of all suffering occurred. 574 257. In the account of the greatness of the Bhādrapada-śukla-padma-ekādaśī vow, when rain was obstructed in the kingdom of Māndhātṛ due to the asceticism of a Śūdra, rain was brought forth by means of this vow. 576
258. By means of the Āśvina-kṛṣṇa Indirā-ekādaśī vow, King Indrasena and his ancestors, beginning with Candrasena, were liberated from the realm of Yama.
579 259. By means of the Āśvina-śukla Pāśāṅkuśa-ekādaśī vow, Vedaśiras—the disciple of the sage Vāmadeva—was liberated even though he had reached the city of Yama due to his improper conduct.

581 260. Regarding the majesty of the Kārtika-kṛṣṇa Rama-ekādaśī vow: because Indrasena, the husband of Kundaputrī Candrabhāgā, died on the day of the vow, he went to heaven; subsequently, after his wife also attained heaven, both were liberated through the merit of the vow. 584

261. The greatness of the Kārttika Śukla Prabodhinī Ekādaśī vow; the liberation of the Rākṣasa Karmacaṇḍāla through the fruit of the vow; and the Cāndrāyaṇa vow. 586 262. A description of the Kṛcchra vows to be performed in the month of Kārttika. 590 263. The greatness of the Kamala Ekādaśī vow in the dark fortnight of the month of Puruṣottama; the observances; its concluding rite (udyāpana); the acquisition of jewels and Lakṣmī by Śākaṭāyana through the vow; and the attainment of gold and other benefits by Pulastya, Kubera, Rāvaṇa, and others. 592

264. By means of the Ekādaśī vow observed on the day of the moon’s splendor during the bright fortnight of the month of Puruṣottama, Queen Kumudavatī—the wife of King Puṇḍarīka—attained the abode of the Imperishable (Akṣaradhāma), even though she was devoid of service to her husband.
595 265. For all Ekādaśīs, there are great concluding rites (udyāpana), great gifts (mahādāna), and so forth.

597 266. Among the annual vows observed on the first lunar day (pratipad), [there are]: the creation of the world, the birth of Sarasvatī, the birth of Kūrma, the arrival of Karavīra, the Lakṣmī-vrata, the Mauna-vrata, and the Aśoka-vrata.

The Navarātra, Annakūṭa, Dhanavrata, Dvādaśabhānuvrata, Vahnyutpatti, Satībhasmadhūlīvrata, Naranārāyaṇajanma, Viṣṇujanma, and Brahmajanmavrata. (999) Among the annual second-day (dvitīyā) vows: the Brahmasāvitrī, Lagnacandrotpatti, Aśvinīkumārotpatti, Brahma-tapas, Sūryotpatti, Saṃkarṣaṇa-rāmotpatti, Viśvakarmā, Aśokaśayana, Indrajanma, Durgāvrata, Yamunā-yama-bhojana, Āryamādi-pitrutpatti, Kāmadhenūtpatti, Sūryaśāṇollīḍhatā, and Śambhutapas. (601)

268. Among the monsoon-season *aṣṭamī* vows are: the Pārvatī-jayantī, the Aśoka-kalikā-vrata-mahā-aṣṭamī, Durgā-aṣṭamī, the vow of Durgā-Trilocana, the Śukla-Durgā-devī-vrata, the Sāntati-vardhana-vrata, the Daśāha-phala-vrata, Kṛṣṇā-aṣṭamī, Rādhā-aṣṭamī, Durvā-aṣṭamī, Jyeṣṭha-Mahālakṣmī-aṣṭamī, Kambharā-Lakṣmī-jayantī, the Durgā-vrata, the Karakā-vrata, the Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa-Svāmī-Bhagavat-jayantī-vrata, Kālā-aṣṭamī, Gopā-aṣṭamī-vrata, the Darbha-mithunaka-vrata, the Kāla-śrāddha-aṣṭamī, Bhairava-aṣṭamī, and Bhadra-...

The vows of Kālīvrata, Śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇakāśyavataraṇavrata, Vidyāvrata, and the vow of worship performed by the Paṭṭarājñī; the vows of Bhīmādevīvrata, Śītalāṣṭamī, and Ṛṣabhajayantī. (615) 274. Among the annual Navamī vows: Śrīrāmajayantī, Śrīharijayantī, Bhadrakālīyoginīvrata, Ramāvratā, Umāvratā, Indrīvratā, Duḥkhahālakṣmīvrata, Nakulavrata, Nandādurgāvratā, Aduḥkhanavamīvratā, Avidhavānavamī, Navarātranavamīvratā, Akṣayānavamī, and Kūṣmāṇḍa...
[The rites include] the Navamī of the Nandinī, the Mahālakṣmī of the Navamī, the Mahānandā, the Ānandā-pūjā, the Satpātra, and so forth.

(619) Regarding the annual Daśamī vows, there are the Dharmarāja-vrata, the Viṣṇu-vrata, the Gaṅgā-daśahara, the Manvādi-tithi, the Sarvāśāpūrti-vrata, the Daśāvatāra-pūjā-vrata, the Vijayā-daśamī, the Sārvabhauma-vrata, the Ārogya-vrata, the Viśvedeva-vrata, the Aṅgiras-vrata, the Yama-vrata, and others. (621)

276. Among the annual Ekādaśī vows: the observance of the Ekādaśī fast, the vow of the consecration of the sacred thread (*pavitrāropaṇa*), the vow of the gift of the *līlā* [of Kṛṣṇa], the *dharmajayantī*, and others.

277. Among the annual Dvādaśī vows: the Madana-vrata, the Bhartṛ-dvādaśī, the Mādhavakara, the *kāśā* [vegetable] vow, the saltless (*alavaṇa*) vow, the curd (*dadhi*) vow, the consecration of the sacred thread (*pavitrāropaṇa*), the Vāmana-jayantī, the Padmanābha-vrata, the Govatsa-dvādaśī, the Dāmodara-vrata, the Nīrājana-vrata, the Tulasī-vivāha, the Sādhya-vrata, the Āditya-vrata, the Rūpa-vrata, the Sujātma-vrata, and others.
The Dvādaśī-vrata, Śālagrāma-worship, Hari-pūjā, Trispṛśā, Unmīlanī, Pakṣavardhinī, Vajjulī, Jayā, Vijayā, Jayantī, Aparājitā, and other Dvādaśīs;

623. Among the annual Trayodaśī-vratas: the Madana-kāma-vrata, Daurbhāgya-śamana-vrata, Trivikramārcana, Sāvitrī-vrata, Jayā-pārvatī-vrata, Rati-kāma-vrata, Gotrirātra-vrata, the Bālādi-śrāddha, the Tithi of the beginning of the Kali Yuga, the Trirātra-aśoka-vrata, the Yamadīpa-dāna, the Dhanalakṣmī-pūjana, and Śrīkṛṣṇa—
The worship of Nārāyaṇasvāmī, the Anaṅga-vrata, the worship of Kamalā and Hari, the Jayantī of Viśvakarman on its specific lunar day, the Mahāśivarātri, the Dhanada-vrata, and so forth; 626.

279. Among the annual Caturdaśī-vratas: the Śrīkṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa-Lakṣmī-udvāha-vrata, the Mahālakṣmī-yātrā, the worship of Śivā, the worship of Damana, the Jayantī of Hāṭakeśvara, the Jayantī of Narasiṃha, the pilgrimage and ritual bath at Oṃkāreśvara, the Jadalāharaṇa, the Rudra-vrata, the Pavitrāropaṇa, and the Ananta-caturdaśī-vrata.

The Kālīvrata, Hatanimagna, and others; the Śrāddha, worship of Dharmarāja, the Narakacaturdaśī, the Yamatarpaṇa, the oil-bath, the worship of me (Viṣṇu), the worship of Bhūtas, the Mantrasādhana, the Pāśupatavrata, the Brahmakūrcavrata, the Pāṣāṇavrata, the Śivavrata, the worship [of deities], the Dattātreya-jayantī, the Virūpākṣavrata, the Yamatarpaṇa, the Śivarātri, the Durgāvrata, and so forth.
629. 280. Among the annual full-moon and new-moon vows, the Śrāddha on the new-moon day and others, the Hanumaj-jayantī, the Vaiśākha-snāna, the commencement [of the year], and the Kūrma-jayantī.

The observance of the vow of Dharmarāja; the vows of Amāvasyā, Sāvitrī, Bilva, and Trirātra; the rites on the lunar days beginning with Anvādi; the consecration and procession of Jyeṣṭhā; the worship of Guru and Vyāsa;

the Gopadmavrata, Kokilāvrata, and the rules for the Cāturmāsya; the festival of Śivaśayana and the worship of lamps; the Nārīkelapūrṇimā; the Śrāvaṇī of the Ṛgveda, Yajurveda, and Sāmaveda; the Śrāvaṇī of the third day of Bhādrapada; the binding of the protective thread (Rakṣābandhana); the Jayantī of Hayagrīva; the offering of the sacred thread (Pavitrāropaṇa) to Śiva; the completion of the Kokilāvrata; and the taking up of the Kuśa grass.

The *prauṣṭhapady-umāmāheśa-vrata*, the *śakra-vrata*, the *sarva-pitṛ-śrāddha*, the commencement of the *amārā-salīlā* and the *kārtika-snāna*, the *śarad-vrata*, the *kojāgara-vrata*, the worship of Lakṣmī (*lakṣmī-pūjā*), the festival of lamps (*dīpotsava*), the worship of Śāradā (*śāradā-pūjā*), the oil-bath (*abhyaṅga-snāna*), the festival of divine lamps (*deva-dīpotsava*), the full moon of the three cities (*tripurī-pūrṇimā*), the conclusion of the four-month retreat (*cāturmāsya-samāpti*), devotion to the lunar days beginning with the *manu*-epochs,

the *jayantī*, the vow of beholding Skanda (*skandadarśana-vrata*), the commencement of the *māgha-snāna*, the *ambā-jayantī*, the *holikā*, the raising of the staff (*daṇḍāropaṇa*), the lunar day marking the beginning of the Dvāpara Yuga (*dvāpara-yugādi-tithi*), and the milk-vow (*payovrata*).

The swing festival (*raṃbhadola*), the spring festival (*vasantotsava*), the festival of oil-baths (*abhyaṅgasnāna*), the consumption of mango blossoms (*āmra-kusumaprāśana*), the honoring of the lunar days with dust (*anvāditithidhūlivandana*), and so forth. 632. Among the miscellaneous annual vows (*vārṣikaprakīrṇakavrata*): the vow of the swing (*dolāvrata*), the chariot procession (*rathayātrā*), the swing festival (*dolotsava*), the months of Śrāvaṇa, Kārtika, and Dhanus, the sun’s transit into Capricorn (*makarasaṃkrānti*), the spring festival (*vasantotsava*), climbing onto a swing (*preṃkhārohaṇa*), the Holi festival (*holikā*), the flower-swing (*puṣpadolaka*), sandalwood garments, the ancestral rites (*śrāddha*), the Sarasvatī festival (*sarasvatyutsava*), the vow of the twelfth day (*dvādaśīvrata*), and the concluding rite of the fruit-vow (*phalodyāpana*). 636.

282. The Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa vow, its concluding rite (udyāpana), the hoisting of the flag, the smearing [of the image], and the protection; the narration of the account concerning King Sumati and Queen Sumati—who were Śūdras in a previous birth—regarding Vibhāṇḍaka.
638 283. The Haripañcaka vow, the month-long fast vow (māsopavāsa) and its concluding rite, and the greatness of giving gifts on Yugādi and Manvādi lunar days. 641

284. The vows dedicated to the Sun, Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn. 642 285. Regarding the non-performance of the vow on the eleventh day (*ekādaśī*) when pierced by the tenth day (*daśamī*): in the narrative of Rukmāṅgada, due to the power of the *ekādaśī* vow, Yama’s city became empty; consequently, Yama’s sorrowful report to Brahmā and so forth. 644 286. Under the pretext of abandoning his intense suffering, Yamarāja converses with the Grandfather (Brahmā); the creation of the enchanting woman (*mohinī-strī*); after instructing her, she is dispatched from Mount Raivata toward Rukmāṅgada. 647

287. Rukmāṅgada, having entrusted the kingdom to his son Dharmāṅgada, departed for the forest. There, he heard from a female ascetic (vratinī) dwelling on the banks of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake an account of his own previous births and so forth; subsequently, [he learned of] his attainment of Mohinī on Mount Raivata and their agreement and oath. 649 288. During Rukmāṅgada’s Kārtika vow, there was an obstruction caused by Mohinī; furthermore, when he made a proclamation with his own drum to request permission for the Prabodhinī vow, there was again an opposition created by Mohinī. 652

289. At the commencement of Dharmāṅgada’s circumambulation of Raivata, accompanied by the sounding of drums, there occurred a dialogue between the king and the sages regarding the obstinate refusal of Mohinī to break her vow of the Ekādaśī, even upon the arrival of his father. 654 290. Dharmāṅgada’s conciliation toward Mohinī; Rukmāṅgada’s firmness in his vow; and despite the exhortation offered by Sandhyāvalī, Dharmāṅgada’s mother, Mohinī’s entreaty for the life of her son. 657

291. While the gods looked on, Rukmāṅgada severed the head of his son with his sword as a counter-measure against the cruel desire [of Mohinī]; the sons, wives, and kings attained the path of liberation; cries of "Fie! were raised at Mohinī; and Mohinī, who had been reduced to ashes by the curse of the family priest, was restored to life. 660 292. Having failed to obtain a residence within the cosmic egg (Brahmāṇḍa), Mohinī requested Brahmā and Vasu, who granted her a dwelling at the conclusion of the specific lunar days (tithis) associated with her vows; she became the one who directs the flow of destinies such as the realm of Yama and the creator of the pierced lunar days, even while possessing a physical body. 662

293. On the greatness of the month of Śrī Puruṣottama: the duties to be performed on the first day, such as vows, austerities, charity, and ritual bathing. 665 294. When the embodied beings who had come to Badarikāśrama to behold Nara and Nārāyaṇa treated the intercalary month (malamāsa) with contempt due to its perceived impurity, the intercalary month departed for Vaikuṇṭha; from there, it proceeded to Goloka along with Nārāyaṇa. Having worshipped Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Rādhikā there and received auspicious blessings, it then departed for the Abode of the Imperishable (Akṣaradhāma). On the second day, worship is performed. 669

295. [The account of] Śrī Nārāyaṇa, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, and Brahmā; the arrival near Śrī Puruṣottama after bathing in the Brahmahrada and Brahmasarovara during the intercalary month (malamāsa); the offering of oblations; the attainment of the sovereignty and the name "Puruṣottama" by the intercalary month; the fruit of worship, charity, and other rites on the third lunar day; and the return of Śrī Nārāyaṇa, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Brahmā, and the intercalary month to their own abodes. 672.

296. Regarding the glorious Nārāyaṇa and the *adhimāsa* (intercalary month), there is residence in Vaikuṇṭha; within the cosmic eggs (*brahmāṇḍa*), for the sake of the vow during the intercalary month, the drum resounds fiercely. Having heard that, by performing the vow, worship, and other rites on the evening of the third lunar day and the morning of the fourth, one attains the status of being the wife of Nārāyaṇa in Vaikuṇṭha—such is the majesty [of this practice]. 675 297. By performing the vow, worship, and other rites of Śāradā, the daughter of Virāja, on the fifth day of the intercalary month, one attains the status of being the wife of Nārāyaṇa, as well as purity, freedom from menstruation, perpetual maidenhood, freedom from pregnancy, and the state of being Sarasvatī. 678

298. Through daughters endowed with intellect, auspiciousness, and artistic skills—born of the mind of his father—and by hearing the great drum on the sixth lunar day, by the performance of the *nakta* vow at the three junctions of the day, and by the successive attainment of daughters named Pārvatī, Sītā, and Rādhā, he obtained the fruit of kinship with Śaṅkara, Rāma, and Kṛṣṇa as their son-in-law. 681.

299. By means of serving his parents, the two daughters Siddhi and Buddhi of Viśvakarman, hearing the drum that awakens one to vows, observing the vow of eating only once on the seventh day of the intercalary month (*adhikamāsa*), and [other merits], Viśvakarman attained the vision of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, a twofold form, residence in Goloka, and the status of being the wife of Kṛṣṇa in the form of Gaṇapati. 683.

300. After hearing the resounding proclamation of the sons of Brahmā—namely Dundubhi, Ghaṇṭa, and Kambu—and their daughters named Ghaṇṭā, Nīrājanā, and Jhallarī, as well as their offspring known as Kāṃsya, Pañcapātra, and Dhūpadhra, on the eighth lunar day of the intercalary month (adhimāsa), one beholds Akṣareśa, Golokeśa, and Vaikuṇṭheśa through the performance of the vow (vrata). Furthermore, there is the installation [of these deities] in various forms in every temple throughout those respective abodes and creations, as well as liberation and blessings. 686.

301. When the people residing on the Kalpa-vṛkṣa tree showed disregard for Virāṭ’s son Vahni, his son Hiraṇya—who was successively possessed of defects such as combustibility and inertia—and who, upon hearing the sound of Dundubhi while on Mount Meru and facing death, performed the ninth-day vow and worship with great intensity, he attained universal honor at sacrifices and other rites, the state of being in the presence of the Lord, the nature of being an ornament of the Lord, the status of a divine attendant (pārṣada), and the attainment of the divine abode. 609.

302. In Vaikuṇṭha, the Earth’s petition to the Lord regarding those who have become a burden; her acquaintance with them; how, by means of the Daśamī vow of the intercalary month, she became the divine earth and was born as a resident of Vaikuṇṭha; and the Lord’s promise for the manifestation of his incarnations in age after age within her. 693.

303. When the worship of Nārāyaṇa and the observance of the vow were performed on the eleventh day of the intercalary month by Dharmadeva, assuming the form of a beautiful woman, with one hundred and eight offerings made with devotion, he was born in the house of Dakṣa; his marriage took place through Dharma, and subsequently, on Mount Himālaya, he obtained four sons named Nara, Nārāyaṇa, Hari, and Kṛṣṇa. 696.

304. While Brahmā was absorbed in meditation, observing the creation of the Lord of Life (Viṣṇu) and Brahmā by Sāvitrī, who was an emanation of Rādhikā’s form, he saw her seated upon his own lap. Desiring to obtain the Vedas in the form of a wife, he meditated; then, upon hearing the sound of a drum, it was revealed that through the vow of the twelfth day of the intercalary month, Brahmā obtained her as his wife, she being the daughter of Vairāja. 700.

305. Regarding the daughters of Brahmā—Jayā, Lalitā, Pārvatī, and Prabhā—who were created for the sake of Sanaka and the others: through the observance of the Puruṣottama-māsa-trayodaśī-vrata at the abode of Śrī Puruṣottama, they attained the status of liberation-consorts (muktipatnī) of the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. As for Sanaka and the others, their disposition was one of detachment (virāga). 703.

306. By means of the vow observed on the fourteenth day of the intercalary month, [the devotee] attains the status of being the wife of Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa Puruṣottama in the imperishable realm (akṣaradhāman), surpassing even Śrī—the daughter of the Kalpa-tree in Vaikuṇṭha who hears the sound of the drum; Māṇikī—the daughter of divine opulence; and Lakṣmī—the daughter of the divine ocean of milk. Furthermore, in Vaikuṇṭha, she exists through secondary forms that are like shadows. 706.

307. In Satyaloka, through hearing the sound of the celestial drum, Dharmabhakti’s two daughters, Mānasīputryau—namely Preyasī and Śreyasī—performed service to their father; and by means of a vow observed during the intercalary month (adhikamāsa), they attained the abode of the Imperishable (akṣaradhāman) as Śrī Puruṣottama, becoming renowned by the names Bhukti and Mukti.

709 308. In a previous creation, when a thousand sacrifices were performed by the universal monarch Sahasrākṣa-bhūpa, he subsequently attained the station of Vairāja through the vows, gifts, and other rites observed on the first day of the second fortnight of the intercalary month. 712

309. In a previous creation, by King Sarvahuta and Queen Gaurtambharā, through the observance of the vow on the second day of the second fortnight of the intercalary month (*adhimāsa*), and by means of the worship of the city and its temples, they attained incarnation as Brahmā in the station of *Pārameṣṭhya* and as an incarnation of Gāyatrī. (715) 310. By King Savitṛ, named after the Brahmā of a former aeon, together with his wife named Bhūriśṛṅgā, through the observance of the vow on the third day of the second fortnight of the intercalary month and by the offering of lamps and other gifts, they attained the state of being known as the Sun (*Sūrya*). (718)

311. Following the hearing of the *dundubhi* drum, King Samitpīyūṣa and his twenty-seven wives attained sovereignty over the moon and the attainment of lordship over the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) in heaven through the vow of the fourth day of the second fortnight of the intercalary month (*adhikamāsa*), as did a maidservant’s attainment of the status of *Abhijit*. 721 312. Through the vow of the fifth day of the second fortnight of the intercalary month, Rādhyā, queen of King Sārāja, and King Vasudāna—both devotees of Śiva in a previous creation—attained the state of Vaiṣṇavas bestowed by Śiva, followed by the attainment of the great office of Kubera, consisting of lordship over the Golden Treasury (*hiraṇyakośa*), which is even above the rank of *Vairāja*. 724

313. Regarding the two Brahmins, Devayava and Girikṣita, from the Maru country, and their wives, Devajuṣṭā and Ārdradyuti, who, after losing all their possessions through the theft of temple property, attained the status of Mahendra, Jayanta, Māhendrāṇī, and Jayantī by means of the Ṣaṣṭhī-vrata performed on the sixth lunar day of the intercalary month (adhikamāsa). 727.

314. At the beginning of creation, when Dakṣa and the others were defeated by Kāma and fell into a state of transformation, Brahmā, at the word of the god Dharma, declared that Sandhyā was the daughter of a *śvapaca*. She was then taken up by the seven sages, Vasiṣṭha and the rest, under the pretext of begging for alms; she was cast into the mouth of the wish-fulfilling cow (*kāmadhenu*) and expelled through its urinary passage. Subsequently, Sandhyā performed penance on the banks of the Candrabhāgā river. Through the observance of the *adhimāsa-saptamī* vow, Puruṣottama appeared according to the method described by Gaurī, as did Kāmadeva.

The regulation regarding her gradual birth during youth; her appearance at both the morning and evening twilights; her entry into the sacrificial pit prepared by Medhātithi for the sacrifice; the purification of her body; her departure to the abode of Brahmā in her divine form as a maiden; and the marriage of her—who was born from the fire-pit under the name Arundhatī—to Vasiṣṭha, followed by her ascent to heaven. 730

315. When Puruṣottama was born as the presiding deity of the intercalary month (malamāsa) in Goloka, a great festival was celebrated during the Rāsa dance. Following the separation of the moonlight from the crest-jewels of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s crown, those two descended to earth in the Ānarta country—which is like a particle of Goloka—in the forms of Nimbadeva and Iṣṭādevī. In their home, Śrī Kṛṣṇa descended in the form of Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa, and Rukmiṇī-Lakṣmī descended in the form of Kambharā in the house of that jewel of love. This occurred after the wedding of Kambharā-Lakṣmī and Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa.

By hearing the sound of the drum of the intercalary month (*adhimāsa*) and by performing the vow (*vrata*) of the eighth day, Śrī Puruṣottama descended into their home, and that *Saṃhitā* became the presiding deity within them.

(734) 316. During a pilgrimage to Badarikāśrama, King Śatamakhana of the city of Sāketa and Queen Dyuvārṇā beheld Nara and Nārāyaṇa. Subsequently, through the observance of the ninth-day vow (*navamī-vrata*) of the second fortnight of the intercalary month, two sons named Śrī Rāmāditya and Narāditya—incarnations of Puruṣottama—were born in the city of Sāketa. (738)

317. By means of the vow on the tenth day of the second fortnight of the intercalary month (*adhikamāsa*) performed by Vikuṇṭhā, the daughter of Rādhikā, through the grace of Puruṣottama, she attained six forms of Lakṣmī and four forms of Vaikuṇṭha, which are identical with their presiding deities.

(741) 318. By means of the vow on the eleventh day of the second fortnight of the intercalary month performed by the Yoginī Vaśyā, the daughter of Satī-Rudra, she obtained a Brāhmī body suitable for the abode of Akṣara as her desired goal, and through other forms, she attained the state of being the wife of the ten Pracetas and the daughter of the trees. (744)

319. Through the service of the twelve daughters beginning with Joṣṭrī, the daughters of Vairāja, and by means of the vow of the twelfth day of the second fortnight of the intercalary month, one attains Puruṣottama and assumes a threefold form. 747.

320. In Goloka, by the command of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the cow Sudughā began to flow with the essence of nectar for the sake of increasing Indra’s prosperity; her birth as one not born from a womb occurred in the house of a sacrificial and learned brāhmaṇa; the death of her parents, the arrival of Durvāsas, the instruction on the vow of the month of Puruṣottama, her penance upon Śaṅkara, her fivefold petition to her husband, her attainment of five Indras as husbands in Satyaloka, and [the fruit of] the vow of the thirteenth day of the second fortnight of the intercalary month.

The boon granted by Puruṣottama: "Having become Yājñasenī on earth with five husbands, you shall attain liberation upon beholding Puruṣottama. (790) 321. In the forest, having heard the verse spoken by Śuka, Dṛḍhadhanvan asked Vālmīki about its meaning. [Vālmīki explained: In a previous birth, he was a virtuous Brahmin who had sons. When his son died, through the merit of a fast dedicated to Puruṣottama and the giving of gifts, the son was restored to life. That son was Śuka, the speaker of the verse; that Brahmin has now been born here as Dṛḍhadhanvan, one who knows the ritual for the worship of the intercalary month (*adhikamāsa*).

By the offering of a lamp during the intercalary month (*adhikamāsa*), it was told by Agastya that the Śūdra Maṇigrīva attained the status of King Citrabāhu in another birth and acquired a kingdom. Furthermore, by performing the vow (*vrata*) on the fourteenth day of the second fortnight of the intercalary month, Dṛḍhadhanvan, together with his family, attained liberation. 754

322. The procedure for the concluding rite (*udyāpana*) of the vow of Puruṣottama, performed by the lords of all creation within the abode of the Imperishable; gifts to be given upon the completion of the observance; the fruit of offering lamps; the liberation of the miser; the release of the monkey; the duties of a devoted wife (*pativratā*); the duties of a wife devoted to her husband (*patnīvrata*); the gift of the Cosmic Egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) consisting of a pair of bell-metal vessels; the worship of the drum (*dundubhi*); and the fruit of hearing [this account]. 728.

323. In the *Śrīpuruṣottamamāsamāhātmya*, there is the account of Dharmadeva, his wives, and his sons; thereafter, Śrī Hari, being pleased by the month-long vow performed by Brahmā and others, granted a vision and bestowed boons upon them along with their entire families. (762)

324. In the account of Jālandhara and Vṛndā: the descent from Goloka of Kṛṣṇa’s wife Vṛndā—who was unable to assist in the amorous sports of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa—and her becoming the daughter of Kālanemi; Bṛhaspati and Mahendra arriving to behold Śaṅkara, and failing to receive an answer to their question "Where is Śaṅkara? while he was in another form; Indra, with thunderbolt raised in hand, being paralyzed by Śaṅkara; and the birth of Jālandhara from the casting into the ocean of the mass of water produced by the fire of wrath arising from the eye on Śaṅkara’s forehead; and the marriage of Vṛndā with him. (765)

325. On the full moon day of Āṣāḍha, Śukrācārya, while worshipping among the hosts of Asuras, saw Rāhu headless; having understood the cause of this—the drinking of nectar during the churning of the ocean—and the partiality [of the gods], he sought to destroy the gods, Viṣṇu, and others, resulting in the defeat of the gods in battle and the subsequent hymn of praise to Viṣṇu Vaikuṇṭha. 768.

326. The restoration to life of those killed in battle; the battle between Jalandhara and Viṣṇu; the granting of a boon by the gratified Viṣṇu consisting of residence in Jalandhara’s house; the distress of the gods; their report to Śaṅkara; Nārada’s journey to Jalandhara’s house; and the enchantment of Jalandhara for the sake of Pārvatī, who was in the form of Surūpa’s wife. 770.

327. Rāhu was dispatched as a messenger to Śaṅkara by Jalandhara, but he was driven away by the Gaṇa Kīrtimukha; a terrible battle took place on Kailāsa with Jalandhara’s army; and Śukrācārya was cast into the womb by means of a *kṛtyā*. 774 328. There was a duel between Jalandhara and Vīrabhadra, and a battle between Jalandhara and Śaṅkara; having produced the illusion of Gāndharvī, Jalandhara went to deceive Pārvatī in the form of Rudra. 777

329. Vṛndā’s inauspicious dream as revealed by Viṣṇu; ill omens at sunrise and other times; Viṣṇu assuming the form of Jālandhara and engaging in dalliance with Vṛndā; Vṛndā’s entry into the funeral pyre; her transformation into the Tulasī plant; and the curse of Viṣṇu’s state of grief. 779

330. Jālandhara’s display of the destruction of Gaurī through illusion; the battle through illusion; the destruction of Jālandhara by means of Śaṅkara’s discus; Vṛndā’s request for marriage and her becoming the daughter of Kedāranātha; the marriage of Tulasī with Viṣṇu; in Vṛndāvana, the portions of Gaurī, Lakṣmī, and Ramā becoming the Dhātrī, Mālatī, and Vṛnda trees; and Lakṣmī’s transformation into a barbarī plant. 781.

331. The performance of penance by Vṛndā, the daughter of Kedāra and granddaughter of Dhruva, in Vṛndāvana; her testing by Dharma; her being overcome by Dharma; his cursing her, "Die!"; the restoration of Dharma to life; and Vṛndā’s remaining in the form of Tulasī and her departure for Vaikuṇṭha in the form of Vṛndā. 784 332. In Goloka, due to a mutual curse between the wives of Śrī Kṛṣṇa regarding their sexual pleasure, they became divided into two groups; Gaṅgā, Sarasvatī, and Lakṣmī took the form of rivers, while Lakṣmī remained in the form of Tulasī. 787

333. The journey of Lakṣmī in the form of Padmāvatī—who had assumed the form of a young woman through the force of her youth—to Gaṇeśa; her request for him as a husband; the curse pronounced by Gaṇeśa, "Become a tree, become the wife of a Daitya"; and the majesty of Tulasī. 789. 334. The curse of Sūrya upon Vṛṣadhvaja of the lineage of Manu; through prayer in Vaikuṇṭha, Lakṣmī became known as Sītā, the daughter of Kuśadhvaja in that lineage, and Lakṣmī became known as Tulasī, the daughter of Dharmadhvaja. The penance of Tulasī at Badarī and its successful fulfillment.

335. Tulasī’s vision of Sudāmā, who was Śaṅkhacūḍa, in a dream; Śaṅkhacūḍa’s departure for Badarī; the conversation between Tulasī and Śaṅkhacūḍa and their Gāndharva marriage; the gods, oppressed by Śaṅkhacūḍa, went to Vaikuṇṭha; Nārāyaṇa’s narration to Virajā, Sudāmā, and Rādhā of their mutual curses; Sudāmā became Śaṅkhacūḍa; and the offering of the trident to Hara for the sake of destroying Śaṅkhacūḍa. 794.

336. Accompanied by his trident, Śaṅkara dispatched the flower-bearing messenger Puṣpavanta to Śaṅkhacūḍa; [he conveyed] the knowledge of Śaṅkhacūḍa and Tulasī, and Śaṅkhacūḍa’s departure toward Śaṅkara for the sake of battle in the morning. Sudāmā was reminded that he was the Dānava Śaṅkhacūḍa, born from the lineage of Kaśyapa’s thirteen wives. This is the instruction. 798.

337. The speech of the Dānavas to Śaṅkara; the battle between Skanda and his army; the battle waged by Mahākālī with weapons and other means; the mendicant’s request for the Dānava’s armor made by Viṣṇu in the form of a Brahmin; the depositing of Viṣṇu’s seed in Tulasī by Śaṅkhacūḍa in the form of Viṣṇu; the death of Śaṅkhacūḍa through the agency of Śambhu; the two curses—"Become a Śālagrāma stone" for Tulasī and "Become the Gaṇḍakī river" for Viṣṇu; the restoration to life of those killed in battle; and the arrival at Vṛndāvana. 801 338. The nature and majesty of Tulasī and the Śālagrāma, along with their worship, hymns, and so forth. 804

339. On the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī), the construction of the rest-house pavilion and other structures on the bank of the Yamunā in Vṛndāvana; the camp of Viṣṇu’s ancestors in Khāṇḍava forest; the camp of Tulasī’s ancestors in Tulasīvana; the arrangement of the ritual pools and pavilions; the arrival of the great manifestations (mahīmānas); the arrival of the multitude of people carrying the bridegroom’s procession; the giving away of the daughter Tulasī on the full moon of Kārttika; the marriage ceremony; and the fruits of hearing about the performance of Tulasī’s marriage and so forth. 807.

340. The ancient account explaining the meaning of the names Gaṇḍakī and Śālagrāma; the penance performed by the sage Sālaṃkāyana; Viṣṇu in the form of his son; his remaining right there in the form of stone; the presence of Śambhu in the form of a Liṅga in the river Revā; the name Gaṇḍakī given to the stream flowing from the cheek (gaṇḍa) of Viṣṇu while he was performing penance under a Śāla tree; that Tulasī in the form of a river; and the marks of the discus (cakras) produced by the impact of the discus thrown for the sake of liberating Gajendra and by the stone-insects. 811.

341. The sacred sites (tīrthas) located in the Śālagrāma region include: Sālaṃkāyana, Someśvara, Gaṇḍakī, Bāṇa, Gaṅgā, Triveṇī, Devikā, Brahmāputrī, Gajagrāha, Jaleśvara, Dhārika, Haṃsa, Śāla, Cakrasvāmin, Viṣṇupada, Śaṅkhaprabha, Gadākuṇḍa, Agniprabha, Sarvāyudha, Devaprabha, Vidyādhara, Ekadhāra, Dehrahada, Triśūla, Gaṅgā, Hariharakṣetra, and others. 813.

342. The sacred fords (tīrthas) beginning with Rurukṣetra, Ṛṣīkeśa, Goniṣkramaṇa, Pañcapada, Brahmasthāna, Koṭivaṭa, Viṣṇusaras, Stutasvāmī, Varāhakṣetra, Pañcāruṇa, Bhṛgukuṇḍa, Maṇikuṇḍa, Lohārgala, Pañcasaras, Nārada, Vasiṣṭha, Saptarṣi, Śarabhaṅga, Agni, Bṛhaspati, Vaiśvānara, Kārttikeya, Umā, Maheśvara, and Brahmakuṇḍa. 816.

343. On the majesty of the Mathurā-kṣetra: the infinity of the incarnations of the Blessed One; the incarnation of Kṛṣṇa in the first Dvāpara age; and the greatness of Viśrānti-tīrtha, Prayāga, Kanakhala, Tinduka, Sūrya-tīrtha, Dhruva-tīrtha, the liberation of the royal ṛṣis, Koṭi-vāyu-prāvatāra-tīrtha, and others. 819 344. Śivakuṇḍa-tīrtha; the attainment of the kingdom of Saurāṣṭra by a Niṣāda who died at Saṃyamana-tīrtha; his marriage to the daughter of the King of Kāśī; their death in Mathurā as those possessing the memory of former births (jātismara); and the majesty of Yamuneśvara. 821

345. Through the fruit of the dance performed in the temple of Nāgatīrtha, Ghaṇṭābharaṇaka, Brahma, Soma, Sarasvatī, Daśāśvamedha, Tīrtharāja, Vighnarāja, Koṭiśiva, Kṣetra, and Sudhanatīrtha—all of which were established by the merchant Sudhana—and through the merit of that performance, the Brahmarākṣasa attained liberation, and so forth.
823 346. [The temples of] Vatsakrīḍanaka, Bhāṇḍīraka, Vṛndāvana, Hariviśrāma, and Sūrya...

The enumeration of the Tīrthamalaya, Arjuna, Bahulabhāṇḍahrada, Arkakuṇḍa, Vimalakūpa, Vīrasthala, Kuśasthala, Gopīśvara, Saptasāmudra, Vasu, Phālgunaka, Vṛṣabha, Añjanaka, Tālavanasapīṭhaka, and Vimalodakakuṇḍa; the procedure for the circumambulation of Mathurā; the sequence of the holy sites therein; the commencement and conclusion of the resting stations (viśrāntighaṭṭa); and the forests. 826.

347. The account of the destruction of the sin of Brahman-slaughter and the liberation of a Brāhmaṇa residing in Kalāpagrāma at Cakratīrtha; the account of the destruction of the sin of Brahman-slaughter of a Brāhmaṇa from Mithilā at Vaikuṇṭhatīrtha; and the establishment, through lineage, of the Boar manifested by the Lord Kapila from his mind in Mathurā. 829 348. The circumambulation of Govardhana, Annakūṭa, and other holy sites; the deliverance of the deceased Vaiśya Suśīla; the Nārāyaṇāsi-kuṇḍa and the Vārāha-kṣetra of King Vimati by the Lord in the form of the Boar. 832 349. [Continued]...

The liberation of a Brahmin of lax conduct residing in the city of Ujjayinī who had become a Rākṣasa, through the gift of the singular fruit of resting and bathing; the protection of the sacred field performed by Śambhu; the divine vision of Garuḍa through his hymn of praise when he was unaware of Kṛṣṇa’s form as a cowherd boy of Mathurā; and the liberation of more than a hundred Ḍākinīs and Śākinīs through the sprinkling of the water of rest performed by Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa in the form of the Brahmin Pan-nivṛta. 834.

350. A Brahmin named Subhadra from the region of Saurāṣṭra obtained a son by beholding Gokarṇeśvara at Mathurā; that son was named Gokarṇa. He established the deity Gokarṇeśvara on the bank of the Śatruñjaya river. For the sake of wealth, Gokarṇa went to the city of Vāmanasthalī, where he obtained a parrot on Mount Raivata. Returning home and going again to Kaccha for the sake of wealth, he had a vision of forest deities at Lake Nārāyaṇa. [Then] by the Gūrjara king...
The restoration of the ruined garden and the saffron pond; the majesty of the trees and creepers at the holy sites, as well as the male and female attendants (*pārṣada*) of the shrines.

837. 351. By the words of Śuka, Gokarṇa’s journey to Mathurā, the liberation of Śuka, and the installation of Śukeśvara; the meeting of Gokarṇa with five ghosts on his way back; the discernment of the causes of ghosthood and non-ghosthood at Puṣkara; the worship of Vāmana on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada; and the liberation of the ghosts through the merit of bathing and giving gifts. 840.

352. The sinless nature of the sexual union that occurred unknowingly in Mathurā between a Brāhmaṇa from Varapattana in Saurāṣṭra and his sister named Tilottamā was demonstrated by a celestial voice and by the sage Sumantu through the power of the five holy sites at the Kṛṣṇagaṅgā tīrtha. — 843.

353. In Dvārakā, due to the agitation of the minds of Kṛṣṇa’s wives caused by the display of Sāmba’s form as a woman, Sāmba was afflicted with leprosy by a curse from Kṛṣṇa; however, through the worship of the Sun (Āditya) in Mathurā, his leprosy was cured, and he established the six Ādityas. [This section also covers] physical, verbal, and mental offenses, and their prevention. 845.

354. At Dhruvatīrtha, after the satisfaction of ten million ancestors had been accomplished, a single ancestor was seen who was hungry and possessed knowledge of the three periods of time. Recognizing him as his own father—who had taken the form of a maidservant in the lineage of King Candrasena—the king caused the Śrāddha rite to be performed through her and thereby granted liberation to his father; such is the greatness of the Śrāddha ritual. 848.

355. King Nimi performed a *śrāddha* rite for the sake of his deceased son named Śrīmat. Later, realizing that the ritual he had devised was not firmly established, Nimi fell into grief; thereupon, Nārada instructed him that the *śrāddha* is an ancient duty and explained the sequence of the *śrāddha* performance. (851)

356. Purification for one who eats at a *śrāddha* is achieved through penance. At Avantī, King Medhātithi fell from his status (*pātitya*) because he fed unworthy Brahmins at a *śrāddha*; however, by giving a *śrāddha* to a worthy recipient, he again attained heaven. [It was revealed that] the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather were born from the bodies of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa, respectively; and that the Moon, the Ancestors, and Fire eat together with a virtuous Brahmin. [The rites include] the gift of a dark-blue bull, the offering of *madhuparka*, the recitation of peace-mantras (*śāntipāṭha*), and so forth. 855.

357. The city of Yama was emptied by the power of Yamunā, yet it was filled again by those performing ritual actions (*karmibhiḥ*). Nāciketas went to the abode of Yama due to the curse of his own father. Following the granting of blessings by Yama, his self-realization, and his vision of the city of Yama, he returned once more to his own body. Regarding this, the sages asked: "What did he see there? 358. On the path within the circle of Yama, the sinners were seen; as well as the city of King Yama, his palace, its ramparts, and its gate-towers (*gopurāṇi*). Also described are the forms, appearances, and characteristics of Kṛtānta, Kāla, Mṛtyu, Kṛtyā, the *kiṃkaras*, and other attendants.

359. The praise of King Yama performed by Naciketas; the command of King Yama to observe the various hells; the observation of the agonizing torments of hell; the description of those torments; and the return of the messengers to Citragupta along with Naciketas, and so forth. 865 360. The infliction of suffering by Rākṣasas such as Mandeha and others, acting upon the command of Citragupta, for the purpose of meting out punishment to sinners.

868 361. The dispatch of messengers to bring sinners [to Yama] at the command of Citragupta; the arising of fruits for those who have given gifts; and the descriptions of the arising of fruits as told by Dharmarāja to Nārada, and so forth. 871

362. In the *Yāmyacakra*, concerning the majesty of devoted wives (*pativratā*), it is described how Rūpavatī, the wife of Janaka’s brother named Mithi, obtained all forms of prosperity—including fruits, food, water, gold, and more—even in the forest, through the power of her devotion to her husband; furthermore, there is an exposition on the dharma of devoted wives, and so forth. 874 363.

Having heard what was spoken by King Yama regarding the causes for engaging in auspicious and inauspicious actions, the means for liberation from sin, and the attainment of the supreme good through the service of cows, the observance of vows such as Ekādaśī, the practice of virtuous conduct, and the drinking of the nectar of holy company, Nāciketa desisted, and the sages departed for Badarikāśrama. 876

364. Regarding the majesty of a devoted wife (*pativratā*), [this section describes] Nārada’s vision of the three Vedas as the three gods within Sāvitrī; and how, through the power of Sāvitrī’s devotion to her husband, the Creator (*vedhas*) repeatedly regained his physical body. 880 365. When the kingdom of the gods was seized by the Rākṣasas led by Vidyutprabha, Saramā was appointed by the gods to guard the cows at the sacrifice on Mount Meru while they were away. Through the power of her devotion to her husband (*pātivratyadharma*), she set the Daityas ablaze and protected the cows; subsequently, the kingdom of the gods was recovered by the gods. 881

366. Aśvapati, the ruler of the Madra country, obtained a daughter, Sāvitrī, through the propitiation of the goddess Sāvitrī; she was given in marriage to one named Satyavān. Upon Satyavān’s death, Sāvitrī followed the deceased by the power of her devotion to her husband (pātivratya), and there occurred her dialogue with Yamarāja and other such events. 883 367. Yamarāja’s responses to the questions posed by Sāvitrī regarding auspicious and inauspicious karma and so forth; the modes of devotion to the Lord (bhagavad-bhakti) and their majesty, and so on. 886

368.
