The movement to auspicious or inauspicious states according to one's karma; her own hundred sons, the eyes of her father-in-law, her own hundred brothers, and the attainment of the boon that Satyavat would live for a hundred thousand years. 888. 369. Sāvitrī’s questions and answers regarding the diverse ripening of various good and evil karmas. 890. 370. Sāvitrī’s hymn of praise (*stotra*) to Yama; the eighty-six pits of hell; falling into them according to one's karma; sins such as the killing of a Brahmin or a cow; and the fact that devotees cannot be overcome by the messengers of Yama. 892.

371. The dimensions of the eighty-six pits of hell; that which was proclaimed by King Yama regarding Sāvitrī’s knowledge, devotion, and other virtues; the restoration of Satyavān to life; his offspring and so forth; and the preeminence of the duties toward a husband, etc. (898) 372.

The marriage of Padmā, the daughter of Anaraṇya and a devoted wife, with Pippalāda; the curse of Dharma during the test administered by Dharma; and the description of the gradual decline of the four-footed beings over time, etc. (901)

373. The account of how Mahālakṣmī, stationed at Vaikuṇṭha, was obstructed at the city gate by Śiva for the purpose of destroying her pride; and how, through the power of her wifely devotion (*pātivratya*), she drew Nārāyaṇa toward that very gate. (905) 374. The narration of the power of wifely devotion, beginning with how Śacī, when Indra had fallen from his position due to the insult by Bṛhaspati and was dwelling in the hollow of a lotus stalk, was solicited by Nahuṣa acting as Indra’s proxy; and how, while traveling on the vehicle of the celestial sage (*ṛṣi*) Aṅgiras, she attained the form of a serpent. (909)

375. Due to the power of Ahalyā’s devotion to her husband (*pātivratya*), when Kāśī was submerged by excessive rain, there occurred the arrival of Gaṅgā, Himādri, Meghendra, Rudra, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Yama, Nārāyaṇa, and others; the cessation of the heavy rains; the restoration to life of those who had died; Indra’s transformation into a eunuch (*bhaga-aṅgatā*) upon merely touching Ahalyā; and Ahalyā’s transformation into a stone and subsequent liberation, and so forth. 913 376. Sītā, the daughter-in-law of Śatamakha (Indra) and Dyumat, [declared that] even the hardships of dwelling in the forest with Rāmāditya were solely for the sake of her husband; thus follows the discourse on her devotion to her husband (*pātivratya-saṃvāda*) and the destruction of Rāvaṇa and his followers. 917

377. In Goloka, Rādhikā spoke to her daughters concerning the greatness and other qualities of observing the dharma and conduct of a devoted wife (pativratā). 920. 378. To King Rukmāṅgada, Gṛhagodhā recounted how she brought her husband under her control; the story of Bhālukamāṭulī Piṅgalī; the story of Kāṣṭhīlā, the daughter of Sumantu and wife of Kauṇḍinya; and the story of the daughter of the King of Kāśī. Through the gift of the merit gained from serving their husbands for even a single day, these women attained liberation, as did all devoted wives through their particular excellence toward their husbands. 923.

379. An account of how the feminine traits described by Menā to Pārvatī, as well as those described by Pañcacūḍā to Nārada, are integrated within the dharma of devotion to one’s husband (pātivratya-dharma). 927.

380. The marriage of Hariṇī, the daughter of Brahmā, with Vedasūri; the maintenance of the vow of wifely devotion (*pativratā*) even while in the bodies of a doe and a deer; the greening of the forest despite the absence of rain; the extinguishing of a forest fire; the arrival of Śiva in the form of a *śarabha* to destroy predatory beasts; the vision of Paraśurāma; the narration of previous events at Puṣkara; and the liberation of the two deer. 929.

381. By the power of the chaste Reṇukā and the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu), Paraśurāma brought about the destruction of the Kṣatriyas, the restoration to life of the deceased Jamadagni, and the residence in heaven of both Reṇukā and Jamadagni, and so forth.

932 382. Pleased by the penance performed by Lakṣmī, the daughter of Bhṛgu, Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa established Vaikuṇṭha at the White Tīrtha near Bhṛgukaccha and arrived for the sake of marriage; [this section contains] a description of His procession and a description of the glories of Bhṛgu’s land. 936

383. The departure of the groom with his bridegroom’s party from Śuklatīrtha toward Bhṛgupattana; the auspicious rites and honors; the joyful words of Bhṛgu; and the arrival of the groom at the pavilion. 941 384. The bringing of the pavilion by the daughter of Bhṛgu; the ritual for the giving away of the bride; the departure of the groom and the honored guests after the wedding; the dissolution of the artificial Vaikuṇṭha and other realms; and the groom’s residence in the house of Bhṛgu in a second form, and so forth. 945
385. Bhārgavī’s [virtue]: her amorous devotion, her service to the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, and her demonstration of supreme dedication to her husband.

947 386. Śaibyā’s [virtue]: through the power of her devotion to her husband, her births as a dog, a jackal, a wolf, a vulture, and a crow—due to eating food not offered to the gods and ancestors and other sins—were completed within five days, after which she attained the status of a prince named Kratudhvaja and final liberation in Vaikuṇṭha. 950

387. The marvels of Suśrutī, the devoted wife of Vedaśravas; the return of the Rākṣasa Kalmāṣapāda—who was infatuated with desire for Vedaśravas and Suśrutī—to their hermitage; the devouring of Vedaśravas by the Rākṣasa; the curse bestowed by Suśrutī; the celestial voice’s narration of the cause for Saudāsa’s transformation into a Rākṣasa; and the ascent of Suśrutī and Vedaśravas to heaven through the power of their virtue in the presence of Vasiṣṭha, and so forth. 952.

388. Out of devotion, King Nanda Sāvarṇi was given the Earth as his wife in the form of a young girl by Vārāha in another manifestation. Through the Earth’s devotion to her husband, she obtained a tooth-bone as a boon; by means of that bone, Nanda established a treasury of wealth in the ocean. After the death of Dharaṇī, Nārada arrived and, having told Upalā that the king was performing the worship of his co-wife’s bones, he reduced it to ashes. From the impact of that [ash], King Nanda died. 956.

389. From the navel [of the Lord], through the great worship performed by Marudevī by virtue of her devotion to her husband (*pātivratya-dharma*), the Blessed One took birth as the son Ṛṣabha; his sons were Yogeśvara and others; [the account includes] his instruction, his forest-dwelling, and his demonstration of the ancient way of the *paramahaṃsa*, and so forth. 959.

390. In Vaikuṇṭha, on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārtika during the Jayantī festival, while there was dancing before Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the daughter of Sāttvata, Sukanyā, was gazed upon with a flickering glance by the attendant-gandharva named Salilyudya. Due to their mutual curse, she was born on earth as Sukanyā, the daughter of Śaryāti; her marriage to the sage Cyavana is recounted, as well as how, when Cyavana’s eyes were pricked by the tip of a thorn in the forest, his urinary and other excretions became obstructed, and subsequently, he obtained the maiden.

The householder’s life; the restoration of youth through the Aśvinī-kumāras; the testing of her devotion as a wife (*pātivratya*); the two physicians’ receiving a portion of the *soma* at the *soma*-sacrifice; and the marriage of Ānarta, son of Śaryāti, with Revatī by means of Baladeva, [the latter] being Kakudmin. 962.

391. Suśīlā caused the leper Kauśika, who was greedy for courtesans, to be joined with a courtesan; she brought about the non-rising of the sun through a curse against Kauśika—who had been impaled on a stake—stating that he should die before sunrise due to his kicking her feet; subsequently, at the request of the gods, Suśīlā brought an end to the curse and other afflictions; and it was established that the administration of punishment by Dharma takes the form of the specific duties prescribed for each respective age (*yuga*). 966.

392. Śatrujit’s son Kṛtadhvaja formed a friendship with the sons of Aśvatara and Nāga; he obtained divine horses; he entered Pātāla to slay the Daitya who was creating obstacles at Gālava’s hermitage; there in the city, he beheld Madālasā; he slew the Daitya Pātālaketu, who had assumed the form of a boar, and married Madālasā; after taking leave of Tumburu and Kuṇḍalā, he returned to his own home; and on the bank of the Yamunā, he slew the deceitful Daitya Tālaketu, his brother.
The death of Madālasā; the ascetic penance of Kumāra; Madālasā’s descent into the house of Aśvatara; and the summoning of Ṛtadhvaja and the subsequent restoration of Madālasā to him, and so forth.

967. 393. In Pātāla, Ṛtadhvaja, reunited with Madālasā, returns to the kingdom of his ancestors; the birth of his son named Vikrama; and the instruction on discernment given to him by Madālasā. 971. 394.
The instructions and other matters given by Madālasā to her sons Subāhu, Arimardana, Alarka, and [the fourth], respectively. 975.

395. Madālasā instructed Alarka in the duties of active life (*pravṛttidharma*); together with her husband, she attained liberation; and there was the exertion of Subāhu for the sake of Alarka’s self-knowledge (*ātmajñāna*), and so forth. 978 396. The narration of King Alarka’s liberation through the possession of the yoga of knowledge bestowed by Dattātreya, and so forth.

981 397. Alarka’s practice of liberation (*muktacaryā*) following the instruction of Dattātreya; the signs of death; his residence in the forest; his state of non-attachment (*asaṅgitā*), and so forth. 984

398. On Mount Meru, Lord Hari was seen by Bhū and Nārada in the form of a boar; Garuḍa arrived and beheld Nārāyaṇapura, the birthplace of Lakṣmī’s shadow; Padminī was born from the womb of the Earth; she was raised by King Viyat; a son named Vasudāna was born; Nārada declared that she was equal to Lakṣmī by her physical marks; and Nārāyaṇa, mounted on his horse, came to the garden, introduced himself, and departed for Veṅkaṭādri. 987.

399. Śrīnivāsa Bhagavān sent Bakulamālikā to Padminī; Vedavatī became Padminī as the shadow of Sītā; Bakulamālikā went to the house of Dharaṇī; the status of Padminī as the wife of Lord Śrīkṛṣṇa was indicated by her characteristics; the decision that she was to be given to Nārāyaṇa; the sending of the marriage horoscope; and the commencement of the wedding preparations and so forth. 992 400. The marriage of Padminī performed by Śrīnivāsa Bhagavān; the ritual procedures; the dowry; her wifely devotion (*pātivratya*), and so on. 996

401. A walled city established by King Toṇḍamāna on the grounds of Śrī-Vārāha; the restoration to life of a deceased Brāhmaṇa woman; and the acceptance of clay flowers by Bhīma the potter, followed by the liberation of that potter together with his wife. 999 402. On Mount Veṅkaṭādri, the liberation of King Toṇḍamāna, of Dharmagupta who betrayed a bear, of the Brāhmaṇa named Sumati, of the sage Rāmakṛṣṇa, and of Hemāṅgada, through the destruction of their sins, and so forth. 1003
403. The liberation of Sumati, Bhadramati, and Rāmānuja—who were observers of devotion to the Blessed One—at the most excellent holy fords (tīrthas).
1006 404. The recipient of gifts; the greatness of the devoted wife and the power of the holy fords at Cakratīrtha, Jābālitīrtha, and Tumburutīrtha.

1009 405. The six holy fords on Veṅkaṭādri; the worship of the sage named Śveta, who is the author of the *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇasaṃhitā* and an incarnation of Vyāsa; the liberation of the Brahmin named Keśava from the sin of killing a Brāhmaṇa; the bringing of the river named Gaṅgā, the Suvarṇamukharī; and other holy fords. 1012

406. The manifestation of Varāha at Veṅkaṭādri through Agastya and Śaṅkhadvāra; the attainment of a son for Añjanī there through penance; the immobilization of the two wings of Veṅkaṭādri; and the arrival of Svarṇarekhā and Nārāyaṇa at Revatācala. 1015.

407. The stupor of Indra and the other gods caused by the fame of Bhṛgu’s devoted wife; the destruction of that fame by Viṣṇu; the restoration of the fame by Bhṛgu; the performance of penance by Śukra; the daughter Jayantī being given by Indra to Śukra for the purpose of interrupting his asceticism; her daughter Devayānī was born; the cessation of the penance; the defeat of the Asuras; and the greatness of devotion to one's husband. 1018.

408. Due to the curse of Brahmā, Nārada met his death; upon being born again as a Gandharva named Upabarhaṇa, he met death once more. Then, by the power of her conjugal fidelity (*pātivratya*), his wife Mālavatī summoned Viṣṇu along with the gods and Kāla and others, whereby her husband was restored to life, and so forth. 1021 409. Through the wonder of the conjugal fidelity of King Avīkṣit’s wife Vīrā and Marutta’s wife Prabhāvatī, there was the destruction of a Rākṣasa, as well as the destruction and subsequent restoration to life of Rudra. 1026

410. When Vasiṣṭha’s sons, Śakti and the others, were destroyed by means of a Rākṣasa, Kālarudra, Yama, Viśvāmitra, and the Rākṣasa were cursed by Adṛśyantī, the wife of Śakti, and became mountains in the form of rocks. Thereafter, Śakti and the others were restored to life by Brahmā and the other gods, while Kāla and the others were revived by Adṛśyantī in a subtle form; thus Parāśara was born as the son of Śakti. 1029.

411. The birth of Ambarīṣa from King Triśaṅku and Queen Padmāvatī; the humiliation of Nārada and Parvata by assuming the form of monkeys during his marriage to his daughter named Śrīmatī; the attainment of Vaikuṇṭha by Śrīmatī, who was the wife of Viṣṇu in a former life; and the power of the wifely devotion (*pātivratya*) of both Padmāvatī and Śrīmatī. 1030 412. The dwelling places and other details concerning Duḥsaha, the son of Adharma, and his wives—who were devoted to their husbands—known as Daridratā, Bubhukṣā, Kalahā, and Mālinatā, along with their respective husbands. 1033

413. For those who are masters of female slaves, male servants, or prostitutes, [the practice of] charity, religious duty, devotion to the Blessed One, and fidelity to one’s husband [is prescribed]. 1036 414. The divine fidelity taught through the lineage beginning with Śaṅkara is to be understood as devotion to the Supreme Lord, Śrī Kṛṣṇa. 1039 415. For a faithful wife, there is the knowledge of worshipping Hari, who is identical with her husband. 1043

416. An account of Nāgalakṣmī Jyotiṣmatī, who was devoted to her husband through her asceticism; although she was enticed by hosts of gods, she took the form of Revatī and was married only to Baladeva, including the narration of the power of her curse and other matters.
1044 417. The manifestation and other details concerning Lakṣmī and many other virtuous wives from Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
1047 418. A description of the countless wives devoted to their husbands belonging to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, and so forth. 1050

419. Regarding the journey of Śrī Kambharā Lakṣmī and Gopāla Kṛṣṇa for the purpose of performing austerities: by the power of Kambharā’s devotion to her husband (*pātivratya*), she traveled with him; during his asceticism, he beheld the Lord (*bhagavat*); and he granted her a boon, saying, "In age after age, I shall become your son. (1052) 420. An exposition of the duties (*dharma*) of the four ages (*caturyuga*). (1055) 421. By virtue of her devotion to her husband (*pātivratya*), Triveṇī, the wife of Bharadvāja, created a new heaven at Prayāga for the sake of Bharata. (1060)

422. From Goloka, due to the anger of Rādhikā, the descent to earth of the two friends Pampā and Brahmapriyā; through union with Rāmacandra, the re-attainment of Goloka by Śabarī and Pampā; and [her] devotion as a faithful wife (pātivratya). 1063 423. From Goloka, the manifestation of the maidservant Citralekhā in the lineage of Ṛṣabhadeva; therein, her delusion caused by the form of a goat; the state of having a goat’s face; the wonders at the holy site (tīrtha) of the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean; her renown in Kumārikākhaṇḍa and other places; and the attainment of Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa by her in the form of Mañjulā, as well as her supreme devotion to the Lord as a faithful wife. 1066

424. In Saurāṣṭra, due to the sin of her lack of devotion to her husband, Kalahā, the wife of a mendicant, attained the state of a bat, a donkey, a sow, a cat, a female ghost, and a demoness; however, through the mediation of the Brahmin Dharmadatta and by means of the chanting of his name, *japa*, and *tulasī* leaves, her sins were destroyed and she attained liberation, and so forth.

1068 425. Through devotion to Hari, both Colarāja and Viṣṇudāsa became attendants (*pārṣada*) of Viṣṇu named Suśīla and Puṇyaśīla; Kalahā of Saurāṣṭra took the form of Kaikeyī, and Dharmadatta was born as Daśaratha, and so on. 1071
426. The attainment of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa as their husband by the maidens of Gokula, who were devoted to the vow of fidelity toward Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, and so forth.

1074 427. After the arrival of the cowherd women of Gokula in Dvārakā, the offering of one hundred and twelve varieties of food and enjoyments to Śrī Kṛṣṇa on Mount Raivata; the statement regarding the manifestation of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa everywhere in Saurāṣṭra and other regions; and the re-attainment [of Him] through their fidelity. 1077

428. It is stated that after three births as a Brahmin, a Śūdra, and a king, liberation was attained by the couple Vīrabāhu and Kāntimatī through their wifely devotion (pātivratya) under the guidance of Bhāradvāja.
1080 429. Through the wifely devotion of Kālindī and Uddhava, the other wives of Kṛṣṇa attained firmness in their own wifely devotion. 1082

430. During the pilgrimage of King Dādaka of the Pañcāla country to Talaśyāma in Saurāṣṭra, the sage Siṃharūpa was killed; consequently, the king incurred the sin of brahmin-slaughter (*brahmahatyā*). Through his service to the three sages, the sin was destroyed, and the messengers of Yama who had arrived were repelled by the Lord’s attendants (*pārṣadas*). Thereafter, through devotion, the denizens of hell were liberated. King Dādaka (or Dānaka) received the blessings of Rādhā-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa. Furthermore, Rādhā and Lakṣmī resided in that fortress as portions of Jīvantī and Lāvaṇyavatī, and Hari himself also took up residence in the sacred field of the fortress, making it a holy place (*tīrtha*), and so forth. 1084.

431. By the gift of the merit of a single day’s recitation of the *Saṃhitā* from his disciple named Satyavrata—who was devoted to narrating the stories of Kṛṣṇa’s devotion to his wife—the ascetic Durvāsas was liberated from his state as a *piśāca* and attained his own abode; furthermore, when Satyavrata was absent at the time of the narration, the Blessed Lord assumed the form of Satyavrata and read the story himself. (1088)

432. In Saurāṣṭra, the king of Pañcāla, who had reigned during the winter season, suffered the destruction of his kingdom and other losses due to his past karmas; however, through the dharma of devotion and service as a devoted wife (*pātivratya*) to Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa as instructed by his guru, he regained his kingdom, beheld Śrī Hari, and attained liberation, among other blessings. (1091) 433. A Brahmin woman from Kaśmīra who harbored hatred toward her husband was reborn as a dog for a hundred lifetimes; subsequently, she was liberated from that canine state and attained divinity through a Brahmin from Sauvīra who was devoted to the *pātivratya* of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa; thereafter, she became Urvaśī from the chest of Nara-Nārāyaṇa. (1095)

434. By the word of Brahmā, the Apsaras Alambuṣā and Vidhūmavasu attained the status of king named Sahasrānīka on earth and the status of queen Mṛgāvatī; they became disciples of Jamadagni, and through Kṛṣṇa’s devotion to his wife, they again attained the heavenly world of Brahmā.

1098 435. By licking the daughter of Gālava, the Vidyādhara Sudarśana attained human birth and subsequently the state of a Vetāla; meanwhile, through the power of Kṛṣṇa’s devotion to his wife, the daughter of Gālava was liberated by means of the King of Kāśī, and so forth. 1101

436. Among the many incarnations of Mahālakṣmī, [the story of] Jaratkārvī, the devoted wife, who, upon her husband Jaratkāru’s departure for asceticism, resided on Kailāsa and obtained a son named Āstīka. 1104 437. King Manojava, due to his atheism, suffered the destruction of his kingdom and other possessions through Golabha; however, through the devotion of his wife Sumitrā—who maintained her wifely fidelity—and the performance of oblations with mantras taught by Parāśara, he regained his kingdom and attained liberation via a divine army arising from those very oblations. 1107

438. King Puṇyanidhi’s attainment of Lakṣmī in the form of a daughter through the performance of a sacrifice at Setubandha-Rāmeśvara; during Lakṣmī’s test, the grace of Lord Nārāyaṇa upon the king and his wife—who were supreme devotees of the Lord—His arrival in the guise of a brāhmaṇa, the divine vision [of the Lord], and their attainment of Vaikuṇṭha, and so forth.

1110 439. At Dharmāraṇya, the liberation of the Apsaras Vardhinī, sent by Indra to interrupt the penance of Dharma, through Dharma’s instruction on wifely devotion (pātivratya) and her own devotion to Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, and so forth. 1113

440. In Dharmāraṇya, the status of the family deity (*kuladevī*) for the wives of Śrī Kṛṣṇa who were devoted to their husbands and had become *gandharvīs*; likewise, the lineage clans (*gotra-pravara*) and so forth of the Brahmins and others; the destruction of the Rākṣasa Lolajihva by the Goddess; the establishment of the Yoginīs; and the sacrifice performed by Dharmadeva. 1116 441. Among the straightforward means for attaining liberation for women shown by Gālava, [it is taught that] various trees such as the *tulasī* are incarnations of deities and the like, and that liberation is attained through their worship and other such acts. 1119

442. At the conclusion of King Suyajña’s Rājasūya sacrifice, [the sage] was insulted and provoked by the curse of the ascetic Suta; furthermore, there is the greatness of the guest through the instruction on the duties of a devoted wife (pativratā) given by Kṛṣṇa at his request, the sixteen kinds of ingratitude, and the instruction provided by the Ṛṣis, and so forth.
1123 443. [The account of] King Suyajña, the instruction on the dharma of the duties of a devoted wife given by the ascetic Suta, and so forth. 1126

444. Having taken King Suyajña, who was a protector of his wife's vows, and his devoted wife Rāseśvarī, in a celestial chariot, Rādhā went to Goloka; this is the greatness of devotion to one’s wife (*patnīvrata-māhātmya*). 1129 445. The abduction of Tārā, the wife of Bṛhaspati, by Candra (the Moon) despite her devotion to her husband; Candra’s flight to Śukrācārya for refuge out of fear; the demonstration of the purity of both [Tārā and Śukra]; this is the fruit of Bṛhaspati’s abduction of the wife of his younger brother named Utathya; and the consultation among Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, Indra, and Bṛhaspati for the sake of recovering Tārā. 1301

446. The gods approached Śukra and handed over Tārā to Bṛhaspati; the birth of Budha; the duties of women during times of adversity and their purification; and the demonstration that there was no fault in her devotion to her husband. 1139 447. When King Dāśārha was in a state of sin, even the touch of his wife—who was solely devoted to Kṛṣṇa—caused him to be consumed by fire; thereafter, upon receiving the mantra of Kṛṣṇa, his sins were burnt away, and following his purification, he became fit for her touch. 1137

448. By the power and wonder of her devotion to her husband, King Candrāṅgada’s wife, a chaste woman named Sīmantinī, recovered her husband even though he had been submerged in the Yamunā and taken to the netherworld (pātāla) by nāga maidens; and so forth. 1140.

449. Regarding the story of Somavān, the son of the Brahmin Sārasvata, who went to the King of Vidarbha with the desire for wealth for the sake of his daughter’s marriage; how he was honored as a mendicant in the guise of a maiden by the chaste Sīmantinī, who mistook him for a girl; how he attained the form of Somavatī’s daughter; and how his father, Sārasvata, obtained another son, and so forth. 1143 450. Regarding Pārvatī’s meritorious vow, the power of her devotion to her husband (pātivratya) for the sake of Śambhu’s sacrificial fee, their conversation, and the attainment of Gaṇeśa as a son, and so forth. 1145

451. Regarding the Śabarī couple’s performance of Śiva-pūjā, the offering of funeral ashes by the devoted Śabarī wife, and the subsequent restoration of the Śabarī to life, and so forth. 1148. 452. In the city of Camatkāra in the Ānarta country, regarding the widowhood of the goddess Yaśodā: through the blessing of a holy man (sādhu), she regained her fortune as a married woman; she obtained a son in the form of a Brahmin named Kṛṣṇa; for the sake of inspiring faith in the people, Kṛṣṇa appeared in the form of a Brahmin; and [the couple] attained Goloka—these are the wonders of her devotion to her husband (pātivratya). 1151.

453. Through her devotion in offering her all to a courtesan, Śivā and Acyuta became a servant and a merchant and tested her through the fire of her conjugal fidelity; they then granted her liberation. 1154 454. Bandulā, who was devoted to her husband, followed the command of her husband, a brahmin named Vidura; although sexual intercourse was not a fault in this case, she attained the abode of the Lord by gaining access to the stories of the Lord. 1157
455. The gods’ journey to the sage Agastya due to the obstruction of the sun’s path by the expanding Vindhya mountain, and a description of Lopāmudrā’s dharma of wifely devotion.

1159 496. The blocking of the Vindhya range by Agastya; Agastya’s vision of Mahālakṣmī; his hymn of praise; the various distinctions of sacred fords (tīrthas); the glorification of sacred fords; the worlds of chaste Apsarases and the causes for attaining the state of an Apsaras; and the bringing of Lopāmudrā and Agastya back to Kāśī by the goddesses residing there. 1162

457. Under the pretext of stealing the *kāmadhenu*, the destruction of Jamadagni; the chastity of Reṇukā; Parśurāma’s acquisition of the *mantra*, *kavaca*, and *stotra* from Śaṅkara; the omens for Parśurāma during sleep and wakefulness; the ill omens for Sahasrārjuna; the maintenance of chastity by the devoted wife Manoramā through the power of her devotion to her husband according to the method of yoga; and his arrival at the battlefield. 1165.

458. In battle with Paraśurāma, Sahasrārjuna was protected by his charming and divine wife Manoramā, who was devoted to her husband; when Lakṣmī’s armor was lost, Arjuna died due to separation from Manoramā; and Gaṇeśa acquired his single tusk [from that same event]. 1169 459. Through the power of asceticism, the son of the Brahmin Viśvānara, named Gṛhapati, attained long life; and through the strength of his mother’s devotion to her husband, Indra’s thunderbolt was turned into a door, resulting in the destruction of obstacles and other such [miracles]. 1173

460. In the sacred field of Ānandavana, which is the abode of the majesty of knowledge, [it is told] how Suśīlā, who was established in the vow of a virtuous woman, attained a kingdom in a future birth as a husband and wife following their Gāndharva marriage, and how they were liberated through the power of her wifely devotion (pātivratya), and so forth. 1176 461. The purifying nature of women; the results of the lines, marks, whorls, major and minor limbs, and other features situated on the female body that indicate auspicious or inauspicious fortune. 1178

462. Regarding the power of Draupadī’s chastity and devotion to her husband: the protection of Draupadī by Kṛṣṇa when Durvāsas arrived with his disciples at a time when no food was available in the forest, and how he fed them with *tāṃbūla* leaves, and so forth.

1182 463. From Kaśyapa, the serpents were born as the offspring of Kadrū; the birth of Ulūka, Aruṇa, and Garuḍa from Vinatā; the consumption and subsequent vomiting of Brahmins and Śabaras by Garuḍa; the eating of the flesh from Viṣṇu’s arm; and the granting of boons to Viṣṇu for making him his vehicle, and so forth. 1185

464. Regarding the wager between Kadrū and Vinatā as to whether the horse of the Sun was variegated or white—wherein the loser was to become a slave—the serpent-like gamboling of the horse, Kadrū’s deceit, and the subsequent cleansing of Vinatā’s state of servitude by Garuḍa, and so forth.

1187. 465. Concerning the divine wonder of the celestial devotion (*pātivratya*) of Līlāvatī, the wife of King Divodāsa of Kāśī, including her attainment of the status of a servant at the feet of the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, and so on. 1190.

466. [The narrative concerns] the daughter named Dhūtapāpā, born to the sage Vedaśiras by the Apsaras named Śuci; her attainment of the status of a Mūrtidevī through her union with Dharma, the lord of the gods; the construction of a city over fifty *krośas* by the power of her wifely devotion (*pātivratya*) during the discourse on the *Saṃhitās* at Pañcanada; the arrival of gods, kings, humans, and others; the sacrifice and its concluding bath (*avabhṛtha*); and the wonders of the disappearance of the splendor of that new city. 1192.

467. Regarding Kalāvatī, the mother of Rādhikā and wife of Vṛṣabhānu: in a previous birth she was Kalāvatī, the wife of Sucandra. Due to her devotion to her husband and the penance of the couple, they were born on the banks of the Yamunā in the forms of Vṛṣabhānu and Kalāvatī. Their daughter, Rādhikā, bathed Kṛṣṇa with cow’s milk during the festival of His birth, and so forth. 1195.

468. Through Śaṅkara, Kalāvatī the dancer, by means of her devotion as a devoted wife (*pativratā*) to Kṛṣṇa, attained the state of a *gandharvī* in another birth along with three companions; and having married Kṛṣṇa, she attained Goloka. 1197 469. Due to a curse from the fire-god Vahni regarding their enjoyment [of him], the wives of the Seven Sages were born as the wives of Brahmins; however, through their devotion as devoted wives to Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, they were liberated by providing food to Śrī Kṛṣṇa and the other boys while they were tending calves on the banks of the Yamunā, and so forth. 1200

470. The attainment of the Lord by Kālīya, the serpent residing in the Yamunā lake, and by the chaste Nāginī Surasā; the perpetual enjoyment of her husband’s favor [by Surasā]; the fearlessness of the serpent in the Yamunā lake due to the curse of Saubhari, despite Garuḍa being a devourer of serpents; and his subsequent residence in Ramaṇaka, and so forth. 1203 471. The story of Mādhavī, the female frog, who upon death attained the state of a Gandharvī through the grace of Śiva; and her liberation while singing in the abode of Śiva due to her devotion to her husband Śiva, and so forth. 1205

472. A pair of pigeons, by taking refuge in a temple of Śiva, attained birth as Vidyādharas; Parimalālaya, a Vidyādhara, [attained] a triad of wives—Ratnāvalī, Prabhāvatī, and Kalāvatī; and through the vow of the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Kārttika and through devotion to their husband, all four of them attained liberation.

1206 473. Through the penance of the son of the Sun, [Yama] attained the status of Dharmarāja; the young parrots attained omniscience; Paulomī attained the status of Indra’s wife; they all attained the state of Vaiṣṇavas and subsequently liberation, as well as the fulfillment of their desires through vows and so forth. 1209

474. Through the grace of Nārada, King Amitrajit obtained a devoted wife; by means of that wife Malayagandhinī, he obtained through the desired third-day vow (*tṛtīyā-vrata*) at Kāśī a son named Vīravīra, a great Vaiṣṇava; and for the king together with his devoted wife, there was liberation in Goloka. 1212.

475. The marriage of Durvāsas with Kadalī, the daughter of Aurva, following a vow to endure a hundred verbal insults; thereafter, the description of her duties as a devoted wife (*pātivratya*); the possession of twenty sons and daughters; the reduction of Kadalī to ashes by the sage’s curse for transgressing out of anger; the praise of Kadalī; and the arrival of Janārdana. 1214.

476. Durvāsas’s vision of Nārāyaṇa in the form of a young brahmin student; the transformation of the plantain tree into a plantain tree [by the power of devotion]; Durvāsas becoming *durvāsa* (durva-grass) through his own essence; the arrival of great fear for Ambarīṣa due to his offense caused by the curse of Aurva; the steadfastness of her wifely devotion (*pātivratya*); and the marriage of Durvāsas with Ekānaṃśā, the daughter of Vasudeva. 1217 477. The son of Tvaṣṭṛ attaining skill in the sixty-four arts through devotion to his guru and by the boon of Śambhu; and, through devotion to Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, his attainment of wives possessing those sixty-four arts, as well as their wifely devotion (*pātivratya*). 1220

478. When Vyāsa failed to obtain alms in Kāśī, a curse was pronounced upon him by Pārvatī; consequently, Śambhu caused him to dwell outside the city. Vyāsa brought Sarasvatī and others [to the city], which resulted in the inhabitants of Kāśī becoming mute. Śambhu went there and brought back Vyāsa and the others, whereby their muteness ceased. It was also ordained that the Vyāsatīrtha should be established on the full moon day. 1222 479. Through the power of her devotion to her husband, Agniśarmā attained the state of Vālmīki, omniscience, and liberation. Through association with the Seven Sages, she attained the status of a Ṛṣi. Furthermore, she beheld Kṛṣṇa in the form of a cowherd and his cow. 1223

480. Following Lakṣmaṇa’s change of heart during his journey to Avantī, the text describes how the ground was purified by the destruction of the Rākṣasa Ghorakhana and the slaying of Gopālaka and Kṛṣṇa; it then addresses Lakṣmaṇa’s mental impurity and Sītā’s conjugal fidelity. 1225 481. In connection with Kārttikeya, there is the presentation of the Ṛṣipañcamī vow for the sake of pacifying the sin arising from the fault of contact with fire on the part of the wives of the Seven Sages, as well as the greatness of conjugal fidelity. 1227

482. The birth of Vyāsa from Parāśara; the account of the birth of Matsyagandhā; Vyāsa’s pilgrimage to sacred fords (tīrtha); his residence on the bank of the Narmadā; the devotion of the Narmadā to her husband, and so forth. 1229 483. Through the power of asceticism (tapas), the wife of Atri, Anasūyā, obtained as sons Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, Soma, and Durvāsas; the power of her devotion to her husband (pātivratya), and so forth. 1231 484. The penance of Rohiṇī and Kumudā; the liberation of Puruhūtā, the wife of Jābāli, through bathing in the Narmadā; and that it is a duty (dharma) to offer one's wife during the fertile period (ṛtu) on auspicious days (parvan), and so forth. 1234

485. Regarding Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, who had taken the form of a deer: after his death by the arrow of Citrasena, the King of Kāśī, his father Dīrghatapas and others attained liberation through the casting of their bones into the waters of the Narmadā.

1236 486. Concerning Menakā, when questioned by Viśvakarman regarding her devotion to her husband (*pātivratya*), it is told that because the *apsarases* were intent on other duties, they incurred old age through mutual curses; however, the curse was averted by bathing in the river Nāgamatī, and so forth.

Likewise, for the purpose of destroying Indra’s pride, there is the curse of Prakṛti, the curse of his preceptor, and the curse of Gautama; the destruction of his prosperity through the curse resulting from his insult of his preceptor; the slaying of Vṛtra; the sin of Brahmin-murder; the destruction of that Brahmin-murder through the grace of his preceptor; the construction of a new palace; the obstruction of Viśvakarman; the arrival of Nārāyaṇa in the guise of a young Brahmin boy; the sight of a swarm of ants; the arrival of Lomaśa; Indra’s renunciation upon determining that his life would end with the falling out of his hair; the persistence of Viśvakarman; and the destruction of Indra’s pride. 1237.

487. Among the Nāgas, the application of mantras by Dhanvantari; and how the pride of Dhanvantari was destroyed by the application of mantras by Manasādevī. 1242 488. The account of Kṛṣṇa’s conduct with the Gopīs in the circle of the Rāsa dance out of amorous passion; Devala’s transformation into Aṣṭāvakra due to the curse of Raṃbhā, and his subsequent liberation, and so forth. 1243 489. The transformation of King Kalasha of Camatkārapurī into a tiger due to the curse of Durvāsas; his liberation through contact with the cow Nandinī and the vision of Śiva; and the power of Satyavrata. 1275

490. The penance of Śarmavatī, the poison-maiden (viṣakanyā) of Vṛkarāja, the king of Saurāṣṭra, following the loss of her father’s kingdom; her recollection of previous births and so forth; her propitiation of Gaurī and Śambhu; the trial; the granting of boons; the vision of Śivā and Śiva; her journey to Kailāsa; and thereafter, through devotion to Nārāyaṇa, her liberation in Vaikuṇṭha. 1247.

491. Regarding the Saurāṣṭrian brahmin named Kuṣṭhiśara from Viṭaṅkapura, who was a thief of divine property: by performing a solar eclipse rite at the Nāgamatī river in Camatkārapura and by beholding the Sun and Nārāyaṇa, he attained liberation along with his wife Sudhāmnī, a devoted wife; such is the account. (1250)

492. Mādhavī, the daughter of a Brahmin from Camatkārapurī, becomes the wife of the Blessed One; she, who is an incarnation of Lakṣmī, becomes Śāṇḍilī; the fall of Garuḍa’s wings due to his doubt regarding the vow of celibacy among women; the restoration of his wings through the grace of Śāṇḍilī; and the humiliation inflicted upon the Blessed One by Lakṣmī for the sake of her descent, and so forth. 1252 493. Through their ascetic penances, Mādhavī, who had the face of a horse, and Lakṣmī, who had the face of an elephant, later became Subhadrā and Mahālakṣmī, respectively, and so forth. 1255

494. Regarding King Camatkāra, it is established through the penances of his mother Ambā and his elder sister Vṛddhā that [his lineage] was indeed maintained by the worship of the sandals of Ambā and Vṛddhā and by the succession of virgins.

1256 495. Regarding the absence of rain caused by the sin of consecrating a younger brother to the kingdom while bypassing the elder brother, and concerning the curse and grace of Agni upon the elephant, parrot, lotus, fish, tortoise, and frog sent as messengers by the gods who were searching for Agni—[Agni] having hidden himself out of fear of the contact with the meat offered by Viśvāmitra and being apprehensive of the fault—[these matters are explained]. 1258

496. The subjugation of the diseases of King Ajāpāla by means of a circle of goats; the obstruction of Daśaratha’s chariot by Śani piercing the constellation Rohiṇī; and the departure to Vaikuṇṭha by Rāma in accordance with his vow, and so forth. 1260 497. The sixty-eight sacred fords (tīrthas), as well as the demonstration of other spiritual and internal fords. 1203 498. The falling of Brahmins traveling through the path of the sky due to Damayantī—the wife of King Camatkāra—accepting gifts such as jeweled and golden ornaments; the transformation of Damayantī into stone through the curse of a Brahmin; and her subsequent [restoration].
Through contact with Dhavī, [the princess] attained the status of queen, as well as residence in the city and other honors.

(1265) 499. By the curse of the Brahmin woman named Bhadrikā, the mother of the Nāgas became Revatī, Takṣaka attained human form, and through her devotion and contact with Kṛṣṇa-Dhavī, Bhadrikā attained liberation. (1267) 500. Karṇotpalā, the daughter of King Satyasandha, who was a partial incarnation of Kamalā, went to the world of Brahmā to seek a husband; then, having returned to earth, through her ascetic penance, she [pleased] Kāmadeva—named Prīti—...
The state of being a wife, liberation in a second form, and so forth. 1268. 501.

The making of dry wood sprout with leaves by Yājñavalkya, the disciple of Śāṇḍilya, at the royal court; the vomiting forth of knowledge by Yājñavalkya and his son Kātyāyana; their miraculous feats; and the narrative concerning the worship of Vāstupuruṣa, and so on. 1271.

502. The leprosy of Kāmadeva, who was infatuated with Hārīta’s wife Pūrṇakalā; the transformation of Pūrṇakalā into stone; her subsequent restoration; the paralyzing of the sun by Dīrghikā through the merit of serving her husband; and her attainment of liberation along with her husband in the prime of youth, and so forth. 1274.

503. Regarding Phalavatī, the daughter produced by Jābāli through Rambhā: her enjoyment with the Gandharva Citrāṅgada; her becoming a naked yoginī due to a father’s curse; her remaining in the presence of her father; then her liberation through penance; the dialogue between the father and daughter; and her dwelling upon a lotus-stone on a mountain peak.

1276 504. Regarding Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana Vyāsa: his two sons, Śuka and Kapiñjala, born of Śukī; Bharadvāja as the son of Kapiñjala, and Taittira as his son; and how, through the granting of a boon by a young ascetic, men were born in the land of Kāmarūpa in numbers equal to those of women. 1279
505. Śaṅkara’s five-facedness caused by Tilottamā; Pārvatī’s curse upon Tilottamā; and the cessation of that curse through bathing in the Nāgamatī. 1282.

506. The birth of Viśvāmitra; the distress of Viśvāmitra and Vasiṣṭha caused by the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu); the marriage of Ṛcīka with the daughter of Gādhi in exchange for a horse with black ears; the consumption of the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) intended for a son by the mother and daughter through mutual substitution; the qualities resulting from the transposition of the two grandsons; Gādhi’s son being Viśvāmitra and Ṛcīka’s son being Jamadagni; Viśvāmitra’s asceticism and attainment of Brahminhood; his son Viśvaṃsaha; and the paralyzing of Śakti sent by Viśvāmitra, and so forth. 1283.

507. The origin of the Sābhramatī river; the birth of Pippalāda from Yājñavalkya’s sister; the wonders of Pippalāda and others; and the progeny of Śanaiścara. (1287) 508. The performance of the Pañcapiṇḍikā-Gaurī-vrata by Amayā, the wife of the King of Kāśī; through that, the attainment of a son and good fortune, as well as the attainment of the state of Lakṣmī. (1290) 509. For the sake of a sacrifice, Brahmā caused the construction of pavilions and other structures with all necessary materials on the bank of the Nāgamatī river in the holy field of Hāṭakeśvara, by means of the gods and others; the arrival of Śaṅkara in the guise of a rogue; and [the account] of Gāyatrī. (1291)
The account of the Brāhmaṇī’s lineage, the nature of the skull-bowls as being the goddess Annapūrṇā, and Śaṅkara’s place in the sacrifice.

1292. 510. The arrival of the son of Sanātana in the form of a young brahmin boy for the purpose of casting a serpent into the sacrifice; thereafter, the arrival of the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa in the guise of a guest for the purpose of bestowing knowledge upon his own guru and others; and the exposition of that knowledge. 1295.

511. The granting of boons by Atithi; the curse by Viśvāvasu, the son of Pulastya, that he shall become a *rākṣasa* for consuming the sacrificial materials; then the arrival of Udumbarī, the daughter of the mountain-seer, and her place of honor in the sacrifice; and thereafter the arrival of the host of sixty-eight *mātṛkā*s. 1299 512. The status of the sixty-eight goddesses as family deities (*kuladevī*); the concluding purificatory bath (*avabhṛthasnāna*) at the end of the sacrifice; the onset of the disease *yakṣman*; the curses bestowed by Sāvitrī due to the opposition of Gāyatrī; the interventions made by Gāyatrī to avert them; and the departure of all to their respective worlds. 1302

513. The account of how the princess of Camatkārapurī and the daughter of a brāhmaṇa assumed the forms of a lion and a tiger through their penance at the time of their wedding; thereafter, their residence in the hermitage of their husband Yajña; then, their difficult penance; and finally, through the yoga of their husband, their attainment of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa and their departure for Goloka, and so forth. 1305.

514. Due to the curse of Rādhikā in Goloka, Nāgalīlā’s friend became the river Nāgamatī; by bathing in which, the purification of a Brāhmaṇa girl who had been married to the Cāṇḍāla Ghūkakarṇa and of the Brāhmaṇas themselves occurred. Thereafter, the Brāhmaṇa girl and the river Nāgamatī both became divine maidens and went to Goloka along with Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, and so forth. 1308.

515. The celestial nymph Mohinī, having seen Brahmā, became infatuated with him, but she was not accepted by Brahmā; consequently, she cursed him. Brahmā was purified in the Nāganadī river. From his abandoned body, the birth of eunuchs occurred. Liberation is attained through the initiation of Bahucara, Ahiṅgulā, and Ājā, and so forth. 1310 516. The removal of Śaṅkara’s pride; the state of being filled with supreme devotion; possessing the dharma of offering everything to the Supreme Bhāgavata; assuming the form of a renunciant (saṃnyāsin); subsisting on the grace of the Lord, and so forth. 1333

517. [The account of] the evil dreams and other ill omens of the Asura Andhaka and his wife; the auspicious omens of Indra; the battle of Andhaka with Śaṅkara, and so forth. 1316. 118. The Asura Andhaka was impaled on Śaṅkara’s own trident in battle and made into the attendant Bhṛṅgiriṭi; his son Vṛka was also slain by Śaṅkara, and so forth. 1320.

519. King Indradyumna’s renown was renewed on earth by the sages Mārkaṇḍeya, Baka, Dhūmra, Gṛdhra, and Kamaṭha; [the account includes] his previous births as a crane and others in the eastern and western oceans, as well as his long life resulting from his meritorious deeds.

1322 520. While staying at Lake Mānasa, a tortoise described his own status as an attendant of Viṣṇu along with Śeṣa; thereafter, [the narrative covers] his residence at the Aśvapaṭṭa lake in the Kuṅkumavāpikā field within the hermitage of Lomaśa, his lifespan, and the sacrifices of Indradyumna. 1325

521. At the sacred site of Kuṅkumavāpī, [the account of] the majesty and other attributes of the Lord, consisting of the knowledge and realization imparted by Lomaśa to Indradyumna, as well as the liberation of Priyavrata.

1327 522. In Śvetadvīpa, Nārada’s decline in knowledge regarding Sāvitrī; thereafter, his acquisition of knowledge concerning the Vedas and other scriptures from Sāvitrī herself; the narration of this to Priyavrata at Badarī; and the liberation of Priyavrata. 1330 523. For Indradyumna, the recollection of the Supreme Self through the Upaniṣads and the supreme Brahma-knowledge, as instructed by the sage Lomaśa. 1333

524. Familiarity with the conventions regarding the abode of Bhaga; divinity upon taking birth; the quality of fulfilling desires in the offering of food (*naivedya*); the prior account of Lomaśa; and the long-term residence in Saurāṣṭra and other regions by long-lived sages such as Mārkaṇḍeya, and so forth. 1338 525. Liberation through action consisting of the total surrender of all things, illustrated by the examples of the Saṃyamana twice-born and Niṣṭhuraka the hunter, during the imparting of knowledge by Kapila to King Aśvaśiras; and the possession of manifold supernatural powers (*vibhūti*) by both Kapila and Jaigīṣavya, and so forth. 1340

526. The previous birth of Vasu, king of Kaśmīra; the liberation from the sin of killing a deer and a Brahmin through the power of devotion; and Vasu’s subsequent attainment of liberation, and so forth. 1343 527. The liberation of King Viśāla through the worship of Hari; the liberation of Raibhya through the knowledge of reality and devotion; and Raibhya’s vision of Sanatkumāra at Gayā, along with the latter’s instruction, and so forth. 1346

528. After the Ṛṣi named Āvaṭya saw many visions in a dream, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa Svāmī declared the fruits of those auspicious dreams; having heard this, Āvaṭya attained liberation, and so forth. (1348) 529. In some instances, there is a description of curses resulting from the non-appearance of the sun and moon, as well as evil dreams, their consequences, and the means for their removal. (1351) 530. [There is a discussion on] the duties of human beings; the state of being a hunter for those who eat the remnants of food not offered to Hari under the guise of the hunter’s daughter; a description of forbidden foods; and the manifestation of birth and other states resulting from the ripening of karma in the form of sinful fruits, and so forth. (1354)

531. At the field of Kuṅkumavāpikā, in the hermitage of Lomaśa, on the Jayantī lunar day, Sanatkumāra—who had arrived to bestow blessings and words of praise—gradually related to the assembly of sages the majesty and other qualities of the Lord Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, who represents the ultimate pinnacle of those worthy of praise. (1357)

532. Durjaya’s sovereignty over the three worlds; the warm welcome at Gauramukha’s hermitage by Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, who had offered him the Cintāmaṇi jewel; the battle for the sake of the Cintāmaṇi; the destruction of Durjaya and others; Gauramukha’s arrival at Prabhāsa; his liberation, and so forth. 1359 533. King Prajāpāla’s practice of the worship and knowledge of the Puruṣa of Vedānta—the essential reality of the body—as bestowed by the sage named Mahātapas. 1363 534. A description given by Śaṅkara to Pārvatī concerning the greatness of the sacred site and holy pool (tīrtha-kṣetra) of Kuṅkumavāpī in Saurāṣṭra. 1366

535. Having learned from Śaṅkara, who was established in meditation on Kailāsa, that the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpī was to be visited, he, accompanied by his attendants, Śaṅkara, Pārvatī, Śakti, Satī, Devadevī, Tīrtha, Divyeśvara, and all the embodied manifestations [of the Lord], arrived there on the Jayantī day of the eighth lunar tithi of the dark fortnight of the month of Ūrja. There, they performed the worship of the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, and so forth. 1369 536. [The account includes] the pilgrimage of Śaṅkara and others to the Raivata Tīrtha (Mount Giranāra) and the Somanātha Tīrtha; the etymological derivation of the name Prabhāsa; the nature of the Arka tree as the essence of the Sun (Arka); the worship of Somanātha; and the greatness of giving gifts and other meritorious acts, and so forth. 1372

537. Vahnitīrtha, the sanctity of the ocean, the accounts of Dadhīca, Plakṣaka, Vaḍavānala, and Sarasvatī, the Sarasvatī consisting of five streams, the Pippaladruma and Kūṣmāṇḍa tīrthas, the Vāḍava fire, the attainment of queenship by an Ābhīrī woman through the gift of a bracelet in the ocean, the greatness of charity and other virtues, and so forth.
1379 538. Numerous and various well-known tīrthas; Brahmā described as being distinct in different locations; the eight Vasus, the Suns, the Rudras, and the sixty-four Yoginīs are recounted. 1378

539. In the description of the multitude of holy sites (*tīrtha*) in the field of Prabhāsa: the Akṣamālā-tīrtha, the Siddhalakṣmī-tīrtha, the account of Arundhatī’s previous birth, the narrative of Citrā’s previous birth, the Śītalā-tīrtha, the narrative of the Talasvāmī-tīrtha, the narrative of the Bhūtamātṛ-tīrtha, the origins and dwelling places of the spirits (*bhūta*), and the residences for those perishing in regions such as Abrikta. 1381.

540. The four Prabhāsa holy fords; among the multitudes of holy fords, the Sārasvata ford; the Kṛtasmaratīrtha and the Sarasvatītīrtha; the Kutupa tree; the wealth of daughters' sons and others; the Mārkaṇḍa ford; the Kṛṣṇakulavilaya ford; ill omens; the Kārṣṇasthalī ford and the Satra ford; the Guptasuvarṇa, Garbha, and Udumbara fords established by Vṛṣādarbhi; Aṅgiras’s refusal of gifts; and other holy fords as well. 1385.

541. The liberation of King Nanda’s charioteer who had gone to Lake Mānasa to seize a Brahma-lotus; King Nanda’s black complexion as the fruit of the mental sin of attempting to seize [the lotus]; his restoration to a fair complexion through bathing at the Nandī-tīrtha; the casting of the two brothers into a well by the Brahmin Trita, their rescue there by the deities during a water-sacrifice, and their subsequent asceticism, liberation, and the establishment of the Trita-tīrtha, and so forth. 1388.

542. The liberation of Siṃha in the presence of Āruṇi; the protection of the Brahmin and his performance of penance by the hunter; the curse upon Vaidika Dīrghabāhu that he would become a lion due to his contempt for Brahmins; the river Nāgamatī coming to wash the feet of Āruṇi at the request of the ascetic hunter; the purification of the hunter and his becoming the sage named Satyatapas; and the instruction on gratitude given by Durvāsas, who was honored with fifty-six enjoyments. 1390.

543. An exposition of the origins and accounts of the respective deities associated with each of the fifteen lunar days (tithis). 1393 544. At the rivers Nyaṅkumatī and Devikā, the Sūryālaya Tīrthas along with the one hundred and eight names of Devarāta Tīrtha, as well as Cyavana Tīrtha, together with their respective narratives.

1395 545. Descriptions accompanied by their legends of Agastya’s hermitage, the destruction of Ātāpī, Vātāpī, and Ilvala; the hermitages of Vāmadeva and Nṛga; Kubera Tīrtha; the liberation of Ṛtudhvaja; and the Devakula, Ṛṣitoyā, and other Tīrthas. 1398
546. [The account of] the Viśālātīrtha established by King Viśāla, the Bhadreśatīrtha established by King Bhadrāśva, the instruction given by Agastya, and so forth.
1400. 547. The greatness of the Guru of Self-Knowledge bestowed upon the King of Bhadrāśva by Agastya, and so forth.

1403. 548. The various holy sites such as the Guptaprayāgatīrtha, the Śṛgāleśvara-kṣetra, the Aparanārāyaṇatīrtha, the Trinetratīrtha, and the Sthāneśvara located in the city of Unnata, as well as the intended meaning of the word "Bāla. 1406.
549. Descriptions of Unnatakṣetra, Durgāditya, Goṣpada-tīrtha, Vena, King Śuddhi, Muktinārāyaṇagṛha, the cluster of Tīrthas at Jāleśvara, Nābhāga, the sage Āpastamba, Caritra, and others.

1409. 550. Descriptions, along with their narratives, of Tuṇḍīśvara, Kapilātīrtha, the wonders of Agastya and Nārada, Bhīmanātha-tīrtha, the Bhalla-kṣetra, Raivata-tīrtha, the liberation of King Gaja, and so forth. 1413.

551. The journey of Śaṅkara and others to Dvārikā, Camatkārapura, Arbuda Mountain, and other places; the accounts of Gautama, Saudāsa, and Uttaṅka; the majesty of the Nāga-tīrtha; the liberation of King Veṇu; the account of the bringing of Arbuda, and so forth. 1416 552. Agastya’s attainment of divinity, longevity, and other qualities; the miraculous manifestation of Rudra on Arbuda Mountain; and the continued existence in the stream of saṃsāra for humans of the current age who harbor mutual malice toward the Three Deities, and so forth. 1419

553. On Mount Arbuda, the hymn of praise to Nārāyaṇa composed by Śaṅkara, the Bhadrakarṇahrada Tīrtha, Kedārakuṇḍa, Maṅkaṇaka Tīrtha, Koṭīśvara Tīrtha, Rūpa Tīrtha, Ambarīṣa Tīrtha, and Ṛṣīkeśa Tīrtha—these have been described along with their legends.
1422. 554. At Arbuda, Siddha Tīrtha, Śukra Tīrtha, Maṇikarṇa Tīrtha, Paṅgu Tīrtha, Yama Tīrtha, Puṇḍroda Tīrtha, Śrīmātṛ, Vindhyācalī, Maṃ... [text truncated]
The narratives of Kipinḍāraka-tīrtha, Raktoddhāra-tīrtha, Pārtha-tīrtha, Mudgala-māmuñcata-tīrtha, and others; and a description of the merits and defects of heaven.

1425. 555. The narratives of Arbuda-caṇḍikā-tīrtha, Jāhnavī-kuṇḍa, Acaleśvara-bhīma-tīrtha, Kulasantāraṇa-tīrtha, Paraśurāma-tīrtha, Brahma-pada-tīrtha, Tripuṣkara-sāvitrī-kuṇḍa, Nimita-tīrtha, and others. 1428.

556. At Pārvatī’s persistent request to see the Narmadā, Śaṅkara went there and spoke: [He described] the Narmadā’s emergence from the world of Brahmā onto the Udayācala mountain; thence her arrival at Ṛkṣādri; then her descent to the surface of the earth; and finally, in the Itihāsas, the description of King Purūravas’s liberation of his ancestors through the descent of the Revā at Veṇutīrtha, Anantapuratīrtha, and other sites. 1430.

557. On Mount Ṛkṣa are the following: Manukṛtayajñatīrtha, Viṣṇubrahmakuṇḍa, Haṃsatīrtha, Trisaṅgama, Yogatīrtha, Āpsarasatīrtha, Dattātreyāsaṅgama, Gāñjālabheda-tīrtha, Vāluka, Pūrṇamanoratha-tīrtha, Kanyānarmadāsaṅgama, Matsyāsaṅgama, Narmadāpura, Jāmadagnya-tīrtha, and others.

558. [The accounts of] the confluence of the Matsyā and Tāpī rivers; Kalahaṃseśa; the confluence of the Bṛhatī and Narmadā; the Śivanetra lake; Lakṣamedha; the Saptasārasvata and other tīrthas—[herein lie] the wonders of their histories.

559. A description, accompanied by marvelous historical accounts, of the Śāṇḍilya-tīrtha, Kalpagā-tīrtha, Rantideva-tīrtha, Harikeśa-tīrtha, Ambarīṣa-tīrtha, Bilvāmraka-tīrtha, Kubja-tīrtha, Sālaṅkāyana-tīrtha, and Kratu-tīrtha.

1439 560. The liberation of Satyatapas, the disciple of Āruṇi; Maṇḍapeśvara-tīrtha; the removal of the dog-faced condition from Bādarāyaṇa and Śākaṭāyana; the confluence of the Narmadā and Dantivanikā; the account of the donkey at the Narmadā-tīrtha; and Karamarda-tīrtha—these have been narrated along with their histories. 1441

561. Jāleśvara Tīrtha; King Hiraṇyabāhu’s liberation from the state of being a donkey; the confluence of the Revā and Caruka Tīrtha; Amarakaṇṭaka Tīrtha; Yajñaparvata; the narrative of Suparṇa; and Oṃkāra Tīrtha and others. 1444 562. A detailed account with its associated histories (itihāsa) of the Kapilā-Revā confluence, Viśrava Tīrtha, Viṣṇupurī, Cakra Tīrtha, Dāruvana, Vyāghreśa Tīrtha, and others. 1448 563. An account of how King Vinītāśva performed the ritual procedures for the gift of the twelve-flavored cow, the Kapilā cow, and other such offerings. 1450

564. Koṭitīrtha, Sūtraveṣṭana, the Sūryapiṅgala-liṅga and others, the abode of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, the confluences of the Kāverī, Payoṣṇī, Somagaṅgā, and Caṇḍāvegā, the liberation from the state of a Caṇḍāla for Candrasena, the confluence of the Eraṇḍī, the confluence of the Śalyā and Viśalyā, the liberation from the state of a boar for Dhundhumāra, the liberation from the state of a horse for Gālava, and so forth. 1454 565. Through the rites of all the great Bhāgavatas, in accordance with the questions posed by Lakṣmī, there is the narration of their subsequent actions—consisting of both *karma* and *naiṣkarmya*—and the description of their residence in the abode of Śrī Hari. 1457
566. The resolution of various questions posed by Śrī Lakṣmī, including the destination of devotees and their spiritual absorption (*samādhi*).

1459. 567. The nature of suffering, the nature of happiness, the worship of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the fruits of surrendering all actions (*sarvakarmasamarpaṇa*), the absence of rebirth (*janmābhāva*), and so forth.

1463. 568. The greatness of the dust from Viṣṇu’s sacred sites (*tīrtha*), the liberated souls of Śvetadvīpa, and the fruits of worshipping the Lord on the twelfth lunar days (*dvādaśī*) of the months of Kārttika, Mārgaśīrṣa, Vaiśākha, and others.
The attainment of the Blessed One and liberation [are achieved] through praise and other acts performed by all beings and living creatures alone.

1465. 569. A description of the disparity between the celestial vehicles (*vimāna*) of Kuvalayāśva and Mucukunda, the disparity between the celestial vehicles of Hariścandra and Śaśāṅka, and the superiority of the greatness of the Narmadā and Amarakaṇṭaka.

1468. 570. The construction of illusion (*māyā*) created by the Blessed One; the Brahmin Somaśarman’s experience of illusion, wherein he assumes the form of a Niṣāda woman and becomes the mother of twelve children, then returns to his status as a Brahmin upon immersion in water, his subsequent liberation, and the majesty of the Māyā-tīrtha. 1471.

571. At Kubjāmraka and Haridvāra, regarding the majesty of devotion, there is the miracle of Raibhya; and how Nakula and the serpent, after being born into a royal family, went to the place of their previous birth due to mutual enmity, whereupon their words were made manifest and they attained liberation.

1479 572. In the Narmadā region, within the Aśoka grove, is the hermitage of Mātaṅga and the deity Aṅgāreśvara; furthermore, during the sacrifice of Satyadharma, Nakula was transformed into gold, and Vīraṇa attained liberation. 1478
573. Suvarṇadvīpa-tīrtha, the confluence of the Viśokā and Narmadā, the Pretoddhāra at Aśokeśvara, the Ravi and Candrayajña [sites], the Vāgurā and Evā confluence, and the Śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇa-tīrtha.

1481 574. The Sahasrayajña-tīrtha, Śukla-tīrtha, Dvīpeśvara-tīrtha, Meghanāda-tīrtha, Dāruvana-tīrtha, Karañjeśvara-tīrtha, Jīvana-tīrtha, the confluences of the Viśvarūpā and Revā, the Candrāvatī and Revā confluences, Hariṇeśvara, Śūlabheda, Bhṛgukṣetra, and other such tīrthas. 1484

575. The giving away of the maiden, the procedure for initiation into the Bhāgavata path, the destruction of the Asura named Guḍhākeśa by means of the discus, and the subsequent transformation of his marrow, blood, and other bodily constituents into copper ore.

1487 576. Purification through expiation and other rites for offenses committed during the worship of the Lord; the penalty consisting of the acquisition of another body or another womb; and the description of Śambhu’s fondness for the cremation ground and his residence therein, and so forth. 1497

577. By the power of the Vārāha-tīrtha, the jackal and the vulture were born in Rājagṛha after death; following the disclosure of this account, their liberation was attained upon the narration of the causes for their head ailments and other afflictions.

1493 578. The liberation of the singing wagtail is described, along with the attainment of fruits by one who plays instruments, dances, remains awake [in devotion], gives food, gives water, cleanses, smears [the floor], offers perfumes and flowers, presents incense, lamps, and excellent offerings, and performs recitation and sacrifice. 1495
579. Ādityeśa-tīrtha, Līneśvara-tīrtha, Gopāleśvara-tīrtha, Parāśara-tīrtha, Hanumadīśvara-tīrtha, and others have been described along with their respective legends.

1498 580. At Soma-tīrtha, the destruction of the sin of Brahmin-slaughter incurred by Kaṇṭha; at Jalaśāyi-tīrtha, the destruction of the Dānavas Nala and Megha, and the fact that fourteen thousand maidens became the wives of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa; Candra-āditya-tīrtha; the holy places extending to the edge of the ocean; the departure of Śaṅkara to Kailāsa; and the exposition of the means of liberation for impure men and women, and so forth. 1500

581. The narrative of the Blue Mountain (Nīla-parvata) in the form of a sapphire within the sacred field of Śrī Puruṣottama; the image of Śrī Puruṣottama on the bank of the Rauhiṇa-kuṇḍa; the liberation of the crow Brahmā while he was looking on; the arrival of Yamarāja there; and how Lakṣmī ensured that the messengers of Yama do not touch the living beings dwelling in the Nīlasthalī, and so forth. 1503.

582. To Mārkaṇḍeya is shown the eternal nature of the sacred field of Śrī Puruṣottama; the dimensions of that field; the role of Śambhu as the protector of the field through his eight forms and Pārvatī through her eight forms; the divine nature of the banyan tree; and the future installation of the image by Indradyumna, and so forth. 1506.

583. In the city of Śrījagannātha, liberation is attained by Brahmins and Kṣatriyas following the direct vision (sākṣātkāra) of the Lord, and so forth. 1509 584. Indradyumna’s direct vision of Śrī Puruṣottama; his dispatching of his priest’s brother, Vidyāpati, to the field of Jagannātha; [Vidyāpati’s] return and description of what he had seen; and the appearance of a blue and white halo amidst the sands due to a whirlwind, and so forth. 1512

585. Following the hearing of the description of Vidyāpati as told by Indradyumna, the decision to proceed toward Jagannātha; the arrival of Nārada; the departure; the visit to the Lord of Utkala on the banks of the Citrotpalā; and the worship of Koṭiliṅgeśa in the Ekāmraka forest, and so forth. 1515 586. The narrative of Vilveśa and Kapoteśa; the ill omens experienced by the king; the vision of the divine Narasiṃha and others; the construction of the sacrificial pavilion and other structures at the site of Kapoteśa; and the covering of the altar with the banyan tree as described by a celestial voice at the conclusion of the ritual bath (avabhṛtha), and so forth. 1518

587. The completion of the four images, their worship, the construction of the temple for the icons, the departure of Indradyumna and Nārada toward Brahmā, the arrival of Padmanidhi for the purpose of consecration, the construction of the chariots, their worship, the banners and other ornaments, the results of obstacles encountered during the chariot procession, and rites for pacification (*śāntikarma*), etc. (1521).

588. The arrival of Brahmā, the consecration of the life-force (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) of Jagannātha and the other deities, the visions of the incarnations (*avatāra*) during his own festival (*mūrti-utsava*), the festivals, the chariot procession (*rathayātrā*), the fruits of the chariot procession, the five sacred bathing sites (*pañcatīrthī*), and the ritual procedure for them (1525).

589. [The contents of Chapter 1527: The great festival of the construction of the chariot (*mahāvedī*); the twelve processions (*dvādaśayātrāḥ*); a brief summary of the stories told in the *Kṛtasantāna*; and the greatness of the worship of the author and reciter of the text, etc.
590. [The contents of Chapter 1535: The introduction to the second section consisting of the *Tretā-santāna*; benedictions; the dedication to Śrī Hari, etc.
Thus ends the table of contents for the chapters of the first section, the *Kṛtasantāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
There are 55,527 verses of the *Kṛtasantāna*.
